Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by the degeneration of the RPE, a process driven by cumulative oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation leading to cellular senescence and eventual retinal atrophy (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Batinić-Haberle et al., 2016). Given that the RPE expresses high levels of mitochondrial enzymes, including MnSOD, and relies on efficient mitochondrial respiration for normal function, the preservation of mitochondrial integrity is paramount (Fernandes, 2010; Rouco et al., 2020a). EUK-8 is expected to enter RPE cells and preferentially localize to mitochondria where its catalytic dual SOD/catalase activity would reduce the burden of superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, thereby mitigating oxidative damage to mitochondrial proteins, lipids, and DNA (Rosenthal et al., 2011; Rosenthal et al., 2009). By maintaining lower levels of mtROS, EUK-8 would be anticipated to stave off the mitochondrial dysfunction that underlies RPE degeneration and to prevent the activation of pro-inflammatory signaling cascades such as those mediated by the NLRP3 inflammasome, thus potentially preserving cellular viability and function (Batinić-Haberle, 2013; Bigham & Wilson, 2023). The ability of EUK-8 to act at submicromolar doses further enhances its appeal, as such potency suggests that therapeutic effects may be achieved with minimal exposure, reducing the likelihood of off-target effects and toxicity (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Fernandes, 2010).

Overall Evaluation:  
From a drug development perspective, EUK-8 emerges as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration, primarily because its dual enzyme-mimetic properties address two central features of RPE pathology—oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). One of the major strengths of EUK-8 lies in its robust catalytic activity; being a regenerative, non-stoichiometric antioxidant means that even at submicromolar concentrations, it can exert sustained protective effects by continuously dismutating ROS, in contrast to traditional antioxidants that are consumed in the process (Rosenthal et al., 2011; Rouco et al., 2020a). Overall, while the preclinical evidence underscores the strong potential of EUK-8 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, its translational success will depend critically on several factors. Strengths of EUK-8 include its well-documented catalytic efficiency, proven efficacy in multiple oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction models, and the capability for extensive structure–activity relationship optimization that allows fine-tuning of its redox properties (Fernandes, 2010; Bani & Bencini, 2012). From a strategic standpoint, the repurposing of EUK-8 for dry AMD appears promising based on its robust mechanistic foundation and extensive preclinical history in related oxidative stress models; however, a focused research program involving detailed studies in ocular tissues, optimization of drug delivery to the retina, and comprehensive toxicity assessments is warranted to overcome the current limitations and uncertainties (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rouco et al., 2020b). If these challenges can be successfully addressed, EUK-8 has the potential to fulfill an unmet clinical need by protecting RPE mitochondria from oxidative damage, thereby slowing the progression of dry AMD and preserving visual function in affected patients (Fernandes, 2010; Rouco et al., 2020a).  

In conclusion, as a candidate drug for dry age-related macular degeneration, EUK-8 offers a compelling therapeutic strategy that leverages its dual SOD and catalase mimetic activities to target the central biochemical derangements in the RPE associated with oxidative stress and inflammation (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). The natural alignment of its mechanism with the pathophysiological features of dry AMD—namely, mitochondrial dysfunction, excessive ROS production, and inflammasome activation—supports the hypothesis that EUK-8 could restore redox balance and inhibit degenerative processes in the retina (Rouco et al., 2020a; Bani & Bencini, 2012). Nonetheless, the ultimate utility of EUK-8 will depend on its ability to overcome delivery and stability challenges in the ocular environment and on the generation of robust preclinical data demonstrating efficacy in relevant AMD models. Given these considerations, it is recommended that targeted in vitro and in vivo studies be prioritized to validate the therapeutic potential of EUK-8 in dry AMD, with particular attention to mitochondrial function, inflammasome activity, and retinal cell survival parameters (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rosenthal et al., 2009).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
L-Carnitine is a naturally occurring quaternary ammonium compound, chemically defined as β-hydroxy-γ-trimethylaminobutyrate, that is both derived from the diet (predominantly found in animal-based foods such as red meat) and biosynthesized endogenously from the essential amino acids lysine and methionine via a vitamin C–dependent pathway primarily in the liver and kidneys (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Mollica et al., 2017). Historically, L-carnitine was first identified as a constituent of muscle tissue in the early 20th century and was later linked to its high content in meat, leading to its designation as “vitamin T” in certain insect models (Mollica et al., 2017). As a member of the carnitine family, it belongs to the class of metabolic cofactors or nutraceutical agents whose primary function is to shuttle activated long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondrial matrix, where they undergo β-oxidation, thereby facilitating aerobic energy production and maintaining the intracellular acyl-CoA/CoA balance (Moos et al., 2017; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). This class of compounds has historically been used as dietary supplements to treat primary and secondary carnitine deficiency, as well as in various metabolic and mitochondrial disorders (Flanagan et al., 2010). L-Carnitine is widely formulated in pharmaceutical products both as a standalone supplement and as an ingredient in combination formulations, which underscores its acceptance as a metabolic supportive agent with a favorable safety profile (Flanagan et al., 2010; Surai, 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, the carnitine family has a long record of use in addressing conditions where fatty acid oxidation is impaired. L-Carnitine has been employed effectively as a life-saving therapy in primary carnitine deficiency—a condition in which mutations of the carnitine transporter (OCTN2) impair cellular uptake—and also in secondary deficiencies associated with conditions like renal failure, liver disease, and certain inborn errors of metabolism (Flanagan et al., 2010). Beyond classical deficiency syndromes, both L-carnitine and its acetylated derivative (acetyl-L-carnitine) have been investigated in a broad range of clinical contexts, including cardiovascular diseases, diabetic complications, and neurodegenerative disorders. For example, acetyl-L-carnitine has been shown to improve parameters of visual function in patients with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and to confer neuroprotective effects in Alzheimer’s disease and mild cognitive impairment (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Calabrese et al., 2009).  
In ophthalmology, while most clinical studies have focused on the use of carnitine derivatives for systemic metabolic or neuroprotective effects, there is preclinical evidence supporting an ocular role. Animal studies have identified high intraocular concentrations of carnitine in the lens and other ocular tissues, hinting at a physiological role in maintaining ocular metabolic balance and osmotic homeostasis (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). Investigations into the protective effects of L-carnitine against oxidative damage, including its potential to safeguard retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and other ocular tissues, provide a rationale for its application in dry AMD, particularly in the context of geographic atrophy where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central features (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c). Moreover, combination therapy regimens incorporating acetyl-L-carnitine with n-3 fatty acids and coenzyme Q10 have also been trialed in experimental settings to address energy metabolism in retinal tissues (Shamsi et al., 2007). Despite these promising findings, direct clinical use of L-carnitine as monotherapy for dry AMD has not been extensively reported, thus making its repurposing an area that merits focused research to bridge the gap between its established metabolic functions and its potential application in retinal degeneration (Flanagan et al., 2010; Mollica et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
The central biochemical role of L-carnitine is to facilitate the transport of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle—a process that is critical for β-oxidation and ATP production. This shuttle is mediated by mitochondrial enzymes such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT-1) on the outer mitochondrial membrane, which converts acyl-CoA to acyl-carnitine, and carnitine acyltransferase (also known as carnitine acetyltransferase or CAT) within the mitochondria that re-forms acyl-CoA for oxidation (Moos et al., 2017; Jones et al., 2010). This process not only fuels ATP generation via the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation but also helps regulate the cellular acyl-CoA/CoA ratio, indirectly influencing multiple metabolic pathways (Surai, 2015).

L-Carnitine stands out as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to several compelling properties. L-Carnitine is a naturally occurring quaternary ammonium compound, chemically defined as β-hydroxy-γ-trimethylaminobutyrate, that is both derived from the diet (predominantly found in animal-based foods such as red meat) and biosynthesized endogenously from the essential amino acids lysine and methionine via a vitamin C–dependent pathway primarily in the liver and kidneys (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Mollica et al., 2017). Historically, L-carnitine was first identified as a constituent of muscle tissue in the early 20th century and was later linked to its high content in meat, leading to its designation as “vitamin T” in certain insect models (Mollica et al., 2017). As a member of the carnitine family, it belongs to the class of metabolic cofactors or nutraceutical agents whose primary function is to shuttle activated long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondrial matrix, where they undergo β-oxidation, thereby facilitating aerobic energy production and maintaining the intracellular acyl-CoA/CoA balance (Moos et al., 2017; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). This class of compounds has historically been used as dietary supplements to treat primary and secondary carnitine deficiency, as well as in various metabolic and mitochondrial disorders (Flanagan et al., 2010). L-Carnitine is widely formulated in pharmaceutical products both as a standalone supplement and as an ingredient in combination formulations, which underscores its acceptance as a metabolic supportive agent with a favorable safety profile (Flanagan et al., 2010; Surai, 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, the carnitine family has a long record of use in addressing conditions where fatty acid oxidation is impaired. L-Carnitine has been employed effectively as a life-saving therapy in primary carnitine deficiency—a condition in which mutations of the carnitine transporter (OCTN2) impair cellular uptake—and also in secondary deficiencies associated with conditions like renal failure, liver disease, and certain inborn errors of metabolism (Flanagan et al., 2010). Beyond classical deficiency syndromes, both L-carnitine and its acetylated derivative (acetyl-L-carnitine) have been investigated in a broad range of clinical contexts, including cardiovascular diseases, diabetic complications, and neurodegenerative disorders. For example, acetyl-L-carnitine has been shown to improve parameters of visual function in patients with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and to confer neuroprotective effects in Alzheimer’s disease and mild cognitive impairment (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Calabrese et al., 2009).  
In ophthalmology, while most clinical studies have focused on the use of carnitine derivatives for systemic metabolic or neuroprotective effects, there is preclinical evidence supporting an ocular role. Animal studies have identified high intraocular concentrations of carnitine in the lens and other ocular tissues, hinting at a physiological role in maintaining ocular metabolic balance and osmotic homeostasis (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). Investigations into the protective effects of L-carnitine against oxidative damage, including its potential to safeguard retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and other ocular tissues, provide a rationale for its application in dry AMD, particularly in the context of geographic atrophy where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central features (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c). Moreover, combination therapy regimens incorporating acetyl-L-carnitine with n-3 fatty acids and coenzyme Q10 have also been trialed in experimental settings to address energy metabolism in retinal tissues (Shamsi et al., 2007). Despite these promising findings, direct clinical use of L-carnitine as monotherapy for dry AMD has not been extensively reported, thus making its repurposing an area that merits focused research to bridge the gap between its established metabolic functions and its potential application in retinal degeneration (Flanagan et al., 2010; Mollica et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
The central biochemical role of L-carnitine is to facilitate the transport of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle—a process that is critical for β-oxidation and ATP production. This shuttle is mediated by mitochondrial enzymes such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT-1) on the outer mitochondrial membrane, which converts acyl-CoA to acyl-carnitine, and carnitine acyltransferase (also known as carnitine acetyltransferase or CAT) within the mitochondria that re-forms acyl-CoA for oxidation (Moos et al., 2017; Jones et al., 2010). This process not only fuels ATP generation via the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation but also helps regulate the cellular acyl-CoA/CoA ratio, indirectly influencing multiple metabolic pathways (Surai, 2015).  
Furthermore, L-carnitine exhibits antioxidant properties either directly, through free radical scavenging, or indirectly by preserving mitochondrial integrity and function under oxidative stress conditions (Shamsi et al., 2007; Surai, 2015). It has been shown to reduce lipid peroxidation and prevent the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential—a key step in the cascade leading to cellular apoptosis (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c). L-Carnitine stands out as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to several compelling properties. Its established role in promoting mitochondrial β-oxidation and energy production, combined with demonstrated antioxidant and osmoprotective actions, provides a strong mechanistic rationale for addressing the metabolic and oxidative stress components of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Jones et al., 2010). The compound’s extensive history of use as a dietary supplement and its well-characterized safety profile—in which high oral doses have been administered with minimal toxicity—support its potential for repurposing in an ocular application (Flanagan et al., 2010; Mollica et al., 2017).

Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is a naturally occurring nucleotide derivative that functions as a key intermediate in the biosynthesis of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), an essential coenzyme in cellular energy metabolism and redox regulation (Chen et al., 2020). Originally identified as part of the salvage pathway of NAD+ synthesis, NMN is synthesized endogenously from nicotinamide and subsequently converted by NMN adenylyltransferase (NMNAT) into NAD+ (Gerdes, 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). Commercially produced by chemical synthesis and available from suppliers such as Sigma-Aldrich (catalog number N3501), NMN belongs to the class of NAD+ precursors that have attracted considerable attention due to their potential to counteract the age-related decline in NAD+ levels (Chen et al., 2020). Compounds of this class have historically been explored mainly in the context of metabolic and aging interventions, with the rationale that restoring NAD+ pools may reverse or delay cellular senescence and mitochondrial dysfunction (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022). NMN, as a small molecule with a molecular weight of approximately 334 g/mol, has been demonstrated to readily cross cell membranes and enhance cellular bioenergetics, making it a promising candidate for diseases in which energy metabolism is disrupted, such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Chen et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). The compound’s natural occurrence and favorable safety profile observed in preclinical aging models have contributed to its development as a therapeutic candidate across multiple indications, which now includes potential ophthalmological applications (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ebeling et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, NMN has been investigated in a variety of preclinical settings addressing metabolic dysfunction and age‐associated decline, with numerous studies across biochemical, cellular, and animal models demonstrating that NMN supplementation effectively elevates NAD+ levels and improves mitochondrial function (Chen et al., 2020). In models of retinal degeneration, particularly in contexts simulating photoreceptor loss and retinal detachment, NMN administration has shown neuroprotective effects by restoring NAD+ levels and activating key deacetylases such as SIRT1, which are central to oxidative stress mitigation and cell survival (Chen et al., 2020). Preclinical studies conducted in mouse models of retinal detachment have reported that NMN treatment not only boosts NAD+ concentrations beyond the physiological baseline but also attenuates the inflammatory response and reduces photoreceptor cell death, thereby preserving retinal structure and function (Chen et al., 2020). In addition to these acute models, experimental data from primary retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells derived from donors with age‐related macular degeneration have revealed that NMN can improve mitochondrial respiration and restore the NAD+/NADH balance critical to RPE cell health (Ebeling et al., 2020). Moreover, NMN’s ability to limit cellular senescence has been documented in RPE models challenged with oxidative stressors and pro‐senescent compounds, where supplementation led to a reduction in markers such as p16INK4a and p21Waf/Cip1, along with preservation of SIRT1 expression (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022). Clinical exploration of NMN in the context of aging and metabolic disorders—though not yet fully extended to ophthalmologic diseases—provides an encouraging translational backdrop, indicating that NMN has a robust therapeutic history in conditions characterized by NAD+ depletion and mitochondrial dysfunction (Jadeja et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2024). Collectively, the therapeutic history suggests that NMN has been thoroughly vetted in preclinical settings relevant to neurodegeneration and retinal health, thereby supporting its potential repurposing for dry AMD (Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
NMN exerts its biological effects primarily through its role as a biosynthetic precursor of NAD+, a critical coenzyme involved in numerous cellular processes including energy production, DNA repair, and redox balance (Chen et al., 2020). Once administered, NMN is rapidly taken up by cells and converted via NMNAT enzymes into NAD+, thereby replenishing intracellular NAD+ pools that typically decline with age and stress (Gerdes, 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). This increase in NAD+ levels has a twofold impact. First, elevated NAD+ directly energizes metabolic pathways, namely glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation, by serving as a cofactor for dehydrogenases, which is essential for mitochondrial ATP production (Will-Orrego, 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Second, NAD+ acts as a substrate for a family of NAD+-dependent deacetylases—the sirtuins—most notably SIRT1, SIRT3, and SIRT5, which are involved in regulating mitochondrial integrity and function (Chen et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). In the specific context of dry AMD, the hypothesis posits that NMN-mediated restoration of NAD+ in retinal pigment epithelial cells leads to reactivation of mitochondrial sirtuins SIRT3 and SIRT5. SIRT3, located in the mitochondrial matrix, deacetylates key metabolic enzymes including manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), whose activity is crucial for neutralizing mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) (Gerdes, 2018; Ren et al., 2022). The proper deacetylation of MnSOD enhances its antioxidant capacity, thereby reducing mtROS accumulation and protecting the mitochondria from oxidative damage (Chen et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022). SIRT5, another mitochondrial deacetylase, plays a complementary role by regulating the acylation status of proteins involved in mitochondrial dynamics and energy metabolism; its activation, in turn, contributes to improved mitochondrial respiration and bioenergetics (Ebeling et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). Furthermore, the elevation of NAD+ levels via NMN supplementation is known to indirectly influence other signaling pathways such as those modulated by AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and Akt/mTOR, which are critical for mitochondrial biogenesis and cellular homeostasis (Ren et al., 2022). In dry AMD, where metabolic dysfunction and increased oxidative stress are central to disease progression, the biochemical cascade triggered by NMN restores the balance between energy production and oxidative damage by ensuring that sirtuins are adequately fueled (Jadeja et al., 2018). This cascade not only preserves mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and oxygen consumption rate (OCR) but also limits the proton leak and bioenergetic inefficiency that characterize dysfunctional RPE cells (Ebeling et al., 2020). In summary, at the molecular level, NMN’s mechanism of action in RPE cells aligns with a strategy of metabolic reconditioning, whereby the reactivation of SIRT3 and SIRT5—via increased NAD+ availability—leads to improved deacetylation of mitochondrial enzymes, reduction in mtROS levels, and enhancement of overall mitochondrial function (Lin, 2020).

In the context of a dry AMD model, the anticipated effect of NMN supplementation is the restoration of NAD+ homeostasis within RPE cells and consequent reactivation of mitochondrial sirtuins such as SIRT3 and SIRT5, which will correct mitochondrial deacetylation deficits that are known to contribute to cellular dysfunction (Chen et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). As a direct consequence of restored sirtuin activity, particularly SIRT3’s deacetylation of MnSOD, there should be a significant reduction in mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), which in turn decreases the oxidative burden on the RPE cells—a critical factor in the development and progression of dry AMD (Gerdes, 2018; Ren et al., 2022). The evaluation is organized into five sections: an overview of the therapeutic candidate, its therapeutic history, a detailed discussion of its mechanism of action, an explanation of its expected effects in the proposed assays, and an overall evaluation of its strengths and weaknesses for this indication.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
────────────────────────────────────────────  
PMX53 is a cyclic peptidomimetic antagonist designed to block the complement component C5a receptor (C5aR), which is a critical mediator of pro-inflammatory signaling. The compound is defined by its unique cyclic hexapeptide sequence, AcF[OP(D-Cha)WR], and its design is rooted in systematic modifications of linear peptides derived from the C-terminal region of the endogenous ligand C5a. Early studies revealed that linear C5a fragments possess partial agonist activity; however, by substituting specific residues—most notably replacing phenylalanine with tryptophan at position 5—and then imposing a cyclic conformation through peptide cyclization, researchers were able to generate a molecule that not only negated the agonist properties but also provided potent receptor antagonism (Leonar, 2017).

The cyclic nature of PMX53 is of paramount importance; cyclization confers structural rigidity through a constrained conformation and an inverse γ-turn, which in turn enhances receptor binding selectivity and increases metabolic stability. This rigid structure minimizes entropic penalties upon receptor interaction and enables PMX53 to act in a “pseudo-irreversible” or insurmountable manner, meaning that even transient exposure to the compound can yield a sustained suppression of receptor activity. The cyclic peptide design also imparts resistance to proteolytic degradation—an attribute that is particularly significant for peptide drugs, which are typically prone to rapid enzymatic breakdown (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

Synthesis of PMX53 employs standard peptide synthesis methods. In practice, either solid-phase or solution-phase peptide synthesis techniques are used to assemble the linear precursor via iterative amino acid couplings using Fmoc protocols and appropriate protecting groups. Under dilute conditions, the linear peptide is cyclized using coupling reagents—often in the presence of a base such as DIPEA—to drive intramolecular bond formation, thereby “locking in” the bioactive conformation (Kumar et al., 2020). Although the detailed conditions such as choice of solvent and specific reagents are not provided in the summarized literature excerpts, the robust manufacturing and successful scale-up of PMX53 in preclinical and early clinical settings are evidence of a reliable and reproducible synthetic pathway (Allegretti et al., 2005; Ramsey, 2018).

Belonging to the broader class of cyclic peptide C5aR antagonists, PMX53 represents a well-validated therapeutic modality for modulating complement-mediated inflammatory responses. This class of compounds has been characterized extensively across various models of inflammatory diseases. In addition to systemic inflammatory disorders such as sepsis and arthritis, cyclic C5aR antagonists have been employed in studies assessing tissue injury models including ischemia–reperfusion and immune complex-mediated inflammation (Hutchison & Krause, 2004; Brandstetter et al., 2015). In summary, PMX53’s origins in rational drug design based on structure–activity relationships—its cyclic, constrained architecture, and its demonstrated ability to produce sustained receptor blockade—categorize it as a promising small peptide therapeutic candidate, particularly in indications where complement overactivation is known to play a deleterious role (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
2. Therapeutic History  
────────────────────────────────────────────  
The preclinical history of PMX53 has been marked by extensive evaluation in multiple models of inflammatory disease. Researchers have employed PMX53 in animal studies where its antagonism of the C5a receptor effectively reduced myeloperoxidase (MPO) release from polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs) and inhibited the production of inflammatory cytokines in roles that are essential for mediating tissue damage. For instance, in diverse rodent models of arthritis, sepsis, and inflammatory bowel disease, administration of PMX53—whether via oral, intravenous, or subcutaneous routes—produced significant improvements in disease outcomes. These studies consistently demonstrate that blockade of C5aR by PMX53 can attenuate aspects of the inflammatory cascade that are driven by complement activation (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

Clinical investigations have also been pursued with PMX53. Early-phase clinical trials that targeted diseases characterized by complement dysregulation, such as rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis, indicated that PMX53 exhibits an acceptable safety profile and some limited evidence of efficacy—particularly in psoriasis where a high proportion of patients evidenced lesion improvement (Proctor et al., 2006a; Ramsey, 2018). Although the clinical trajectory for PMX53 was eventually limited by concerns over pharmacokinetic properties and species-specific receptor affinity differences—for example, PMX53 binds human and rat C5aR with submicromolar affinities (approximately 90 nM and 40 nM, respectively) yet exhibits markedly lower affinity for mouse C5aR (~36 µM)—the overall body of evidence from systematic preclinical evaluation supports its robust anti-inflammatory activity (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

Of particular note is that while PMX53 has been primarily investigated in systemic inflammatory models and conditions such as sepsis, arthritis, and immune complex-mediated injuries, there is an emerging conceptual linkage between complement-mediated inflammation and retinal degenerative diseases like dry AMD. Several independent studies have demonstrated that the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) expresses C5a receptors constitutively and that exposure to complement-competent serum or recombinant C5a upregulates receptor expression. These studies further show that C5a primes RPE cells for inflammasome activation—a critical process in the pathogenesis of dry AMD—and that modulation of C5aR signaling can affect pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β) (Brandstetter et al., 2015). Although PMX53 has not been used directly in ocular models or clinical trials for retinal degenerative conditions, its demonstrated efficacy in systemic models and the established role of complement activation in RPE pathology provide a compelling rationale to explore its repurposing for dry AMD (Proctor et al., 2006a; Proctor et al., 2006b).

Additional analogues in this compound class, such as PMX205, have been developed with modifications aimed at improving oral potency and pharmacokinetic properties. PMX205, for example, incorporates a hydrocinnamate moiety that confers increased lipophilicity and enables improved oral bioavailability—a factor that might be advantageous for addressing the challenging delivery needs associated with ocular tissues. While PMX205 itself has been evaluated primarily in models of inflammatory bowel disease and neurodegenerative conditions, the overall historical narrative underscores that the PMX series provides a well-characterized platform with potential for repurposing in retinal diseases (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Proctor et al., 2006b; Proctor et al., 2006a).

Taken together, the therapeutic history of PMX53 confirms that it has undergone extensive biochemical, preclinical, and early clinical scrutiny for diseases driven by complement-mediated inflammation. Despite the lack of direct evidence in ocular or AMD-specific contexts, the extensive data from nonocular models and the mechanistic similarities between systemic complement dysregulation and retinal complement activation lay a strong foundation for further exploration of PMX53 in dry AMD (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
3. Mechanism of Action  
────────────────────────────────────────────  
At the molecular level, PMX53 functions by directly binding to and antagonizing the complement C5a receptor (C5aR), a G-protein–coupled receptor that mediates the downstream pro-inflammatory effects of the anaphylatoxin C5a. The binding of C5a to its receptor on cells, including immune cells and RPE cells, initiates a cascade of inflammatory signaling events characterized by calcium mobilization, activation of kinase pathways (such as PI3K and MAPK), and subsequent transcriptional upregulation of inflammatory mediators including IL-1β. In the context of RPE cells, these events are further linked with the generation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome—a process that underpins cellular stress and eventual degeneration in dry AMD (Brandstetter et al., 2015).

PMX53’s mechanism of action is rooted in its cyclic peptide structure, which endows it with the ability to engage the C5a receptor in a manner that is both highly specific and functionally distinct from simple competitive blockade. Extensive structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies, including receptor mutagenesis and docking experiments, have revealed that PMX53 binds primarily to critical extracellular regions of C5aR—most notably the extracellular loop 2 (ECL2) and portions of the transmembrane domain. For example, mutations in ECL2 residues (such as R175) have been shown to significantly reduce the efficacy of both C5a and PMX53, underscoring the importance of this region in ligand–receptor interactions (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006b).

The binding model for PMX53 suggests that its aromatic and hydrophobic components—such as the tryptophan side chain and the d-cyclohexylalanine residue—fit within a hydrophobic pocket formed by receptor residues including I116 and V286. These interactions, which involve hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, and possibly cation–π interactions, contribute to the stability of the ligand–receptor complex and account for the “pseudo-irreversible” nature of the antagonism. In practical terms, once PMX53 binds to C5aR it exhibits insurmountable antagonism, meaning that even in the presence of high concentrations of the endogenous ligand C5a, the receptor remains blocked and unable to signal. This mode of binding is particularly attractive in chronic inflammatory conditions where sustained receptor occupancy can yield lasting therapeutic benefits despite fluctuations in plasma drug concentrations (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006b; Hutchison & Krause, 2004; Proctor et al., 2006b).

Downstream of receptor blockade, the interruption of C5a signaling by PMX53 results in a reduction in calcium influx and the inhibition of kinase cascades that normally lead to the activation of transcription factors such as NF-κB. The inhibition of NF-κB activity, in turn, leads to decreased transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1β) and chemokines, thereby damping the overall inflammatory response. In RPE cells, it has been demonstrated that complement activation—via either exogenous C5a or complement-competent serum—upregulates C5aR and primes the cells for inflammasome activation, which is dependent on increased mtROS production. Thus, by preventing C5a from binding to its receptor, PMX53 is expected to blunt both the immediate signaling events (calcium mobilization, reactive oxygen species generation) and the subsequent transcriptional upregulation of inflammatory mediators that lead to inflammasome assembly (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020).

Notably, crystallographic and docking studies have reinforced the concept that PMX53 interacts with the receptor in a manner that stabilizes an inactive conformation. These studies show that PMX53’s cyclic structure enables it to engage its target in a stable fashion by “locking” C5aR into a state where conformational changes required for receptor activation are prevented. This effect directly translates into a reduction in downstream signaling events and is consistent with the observed insurmountable antagonism in various functional assays. The pseudo-irreversible binding characteristic ensures that once PMX53 occupies the receptor, it remains bound long enough to counteract episodic or continuous C5a fluctuations, a feature that is particularly beneficial in a disease like dry AMD where chronic complement dysregulation is a hallmark (Liu et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Ramsey, 2018).

In summary, at the molecular level PMX53 functions as a robust inhibitor of C5aR by engaging critical residues on the receptor extracellular region, thereby preventing the pro-inflammatory interactions initiated by C5a binding. This blockade not only halts immediate calcium and kinase signaling events but also disrupts the longer-term transcriptional activation of inflammatory mediators, including those responsible for mtROS overproduction and inflammasome activation in RPE cells (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006b; Brandstetter et al., 2015).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
4. Expected Effect  
────────────────────────────────────────────  
The hypothesis underlying the repurposing of PMX53 for dry AMD is that by antagonizing the C5a receptor on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, the compound can attenuate a critical amplification loop in which complement activation leads to mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) production and NLRP3 inflammasome activation. In typical dry AMD pathology, RPE cells are exposed to chronic complement activation resulting from factors such as drusen formation and genetic predisposition. This persistent activation drives an increase in C5a levels that in turn upregulates C5aR expression on RPE cells, thereby priming these cells for a heightened inflammatory response. Specifically, the engagement of C5aR provokes intracellular signaling cascades that lead to excessive production of mtROS and the subsequent activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, culminating in the maturation and release of interleukin-1β (IL-1β) (Brandstetter et al., 2015).

In an in vitro assay using cultured human RPE cells, treatment with PMX53 is expected to demonstrate a significant reduction in mitochondrial superoxide levels. When RPE cells are challenged with either recombinant C5a or complement-active serum, the normal response is an upregulation of inflammatory mediators and a spike in mtROS production; however, with pre-treatment or co-treatment with PMX53, the binding of C5a to its receptor is blocked and these downstream events are attenuated. One would anticipate the readouts from such an assay to include a decline in the fluorescence signal from mitochondrial superoxide indicators, a reduction in caspase-1 activation (reflecting suppressed inflammasome activity), and lower concentrations of IL-1β in the culture supernatant (Brandstetter et al., 2015).

In animal models that mimic the chronic complement dysregulation observed in dry AMD, the administration of PMX53 may confer protective effects on RPE morphology and retinal architecture. Although PMX53 has not yet been directly deployed in ocular models of AMD, its robust anti-inflammatory effects in systemic models—such as those for arthritis, sepsis, and ischemia–reperfusion injuries—suggest that similar benefits may be observed in the retina when the compound is delivered via an appropriate route (e.g., intravitreal injection, nanoparticle formulations, or sustained-release implants). These models could offer endpoints such as reduced sub-RPE deposit formation, preserved RPE cell integrity, and maintenance of retinal function as measured by electrophysiological assessments (Proctor et al., 2006a; Proctor et al., 2006b).

Furthermore, the pseudo-irreversible binding characteristic of PMX53 represents an important advantage in a chronic condition like dry AMD. Even if the compound is cleared rapidly from the systemic circulation or ocular compartment, its long receptor residence time may ensure continuous inhibition of C5a signaling over extended periods. This sustained blockade is especially important in countering the slow, progressive damage associated with dry AMD, where intermittent complement activation can cumulatively lead to RPE dysfunction and eventually photoreceptor loss (Ong et al., 2024; Proctor et al., 2006b; Behnke, 2022). In this context, a reduction in mtROS generation and inflammasome-driven cytokine release would be expected to limit oxidative injury and maintain the homeostatic balance in the delicate retinal environment.

In summary, the expected pharmacodynamic effects of PMX53 in the proposed assays include a measurable reduction in mitochondrial superoxide production, a decrease in caspase-1 activity and IL-1β release, and overall preservation of RPE cell morphology when challenged with complement-active stimuli. These effects, if achieved in vitro and then recapitulated in vivo in an appropriate animal model, would support the notion that PMX53 can effectively disrupt the complement-driven amplification of oxidative and inflammatory damage that contributes to dry AMD progression (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Proctor et al., 2006b).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
5. Overall Evaluation  
────────────────────────────────────────────  
In evaluating PMX53 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several positive factors and potential challenges emerge based on the available literature drawn from preclinical and early clinical studies in systemic inflammatory models.

Strengths:  
•  PMX53 has been extensively characterized as a potent cyclic peptide antagonist of the C5a receptor with a well-rationalized design that exploits the structural features of the endogenous ligand C5a. Its cyclic architecture confers not only high receptor selectivity and metabolic stability but also a mode of action that is classified as “pseudo-irreversible” or insurmountable antagonism. This means that once it binds to the receptor, PMX53 is able to provide sustained receptor blockade even in the presence of high levels of circulating C5a—a feature that is especially appealing for chronic conditions like dry AMD where persistent complement dysregulation is a central pathological driver (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

•  The preclinical body of evidence supporting the anti-inflammatory activity of PMX53 is considerable. In numerous animal models, including those for arthritis, sepsis, and ischemia–reperfusion injury, treatment with PMX53 has been shown to reduce inflammatory cytokine production, limit immune cell degranulation, and preserve tissue integrity (Ramsey, 2018; Hutchison & Krause, 2004; Allegretti et al., 2005). These findings have translated, at least in part, to early-phase clinical studies in which PMX53 was evaluated in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis—diseases that share underlying inflammatory components with dry AMD. The favorable safety profile observed in these studies provides an additional layer of support for considering PMX53 as a repurposed drug candidate (Proctor et al., 2006a; Kumar et al., 2020).

•  A critical advantage of PMX53 for the treatment of dry AMD lies in its mechanistic targeting of the complement system, which is increasingly recognized as a central player in the pathogenesis of retinal degenerations. Studies using human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells have demonstrated that complement activation, particularly via C5a, leads to upregulation of the C5a receptor and primes these cells for inflammasome activation in response to additional stressors such as lipofuscin-mediated photooxidative damage (Brandstetter et al., 2015). By effectively preventing C5a from binding to its receptor, PMX53 is hypothesized to block the initiation of a cascade that culminates in excessive mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) production and subsequent IL-1β release. This would theoretically protect RPE cells from the oxidative insult and inflammation that characterize dry AMD pathology (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Leonar, 2017).

•  Moreover, the pseudo-irreversible nature of PMX53’s receptor binding offers the important potential for prolonged therapeutic effects despite the inherent challenges associated with peptide pharmacokinetics. While it is acknowledged that the peptidic nature of the compound might pose hurdles with respect to systemic clearance and bioavailability—particularly within the ocular environment where drug delivery is complicated by barriers such as the blood–retina barrier—the ability of PMX53 to remain bound to C5aR could mitigate the need for continually high drug concentrations. This quality could be beneficial if innovative delivery strategies, such as intravitreal injections, nanoparticle-based formulations, or sustained-release implants, are employed to achieve localized drug concentrations in the retina (Proctor et al., 2006b; Kumar et al., 2020).

Weaknesses and Concerns:  
•  Despite its many promising aspects, several critical challenges must be considered before PMX53 can be realistically advanced as a treatment for dry AMD. One of the most significant gaps in the current literature is the absence of direct preclinical or clinical data specific to ocular models of AMD. Although the complement system, and in particular the C5a–C5aR axis, is well documented as playing a role in RPE dysfunction and retinal inflammation (Brandstetter et al., 2015), PMX53 itself has not yet been rigorously tested in models that recapitulate the complex microenvironment of the retina. Animal models that faithfully mimic the chronic complement activation and oxidative stress seen in human dry AMD are necessary to determine whether the robust systemic anti-inflammatory activity of PMX53 can be translated to a localized ocular context (Proctor et al., 2006a; Hutchison & Krause, 2004).

•  A second concern relates to species-specific differences in receptor binding affinity. It is well established that PMX53 exhibits high affinity for human and rat C5a receptors (in the range of tens of nanomolar), whereas its affinity for the mouse receptor is markedly lower (approximately 36 µM) (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a). This presents a practical obstacle, as many preclinical studies in ophthalmology rely on murine models to assess disease progression and drug efficacy. To circumvent this pitfall, it may be necessary to utilize alternative animal models with receptor pharmacology that more closely mirrors the human system—such as rat models or non-human primate studies—or to develop further analogues that demonstrate improved cross-species binding (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

•  Another issue is the challenge of delivering a peptide drug to ocular tissues in a sustained and therapeutically effective manner. The ocular barriers, including the corneal epithelium and the blood–retina barrier, limit the penetration and retention of systemically administered drugs. In the case of PMX53, whose peptidic nature predisposes it to rapid clearance and potential degradation, specialized formulation strategies will be essential. Approaches such as encapsulation in biodegradable nanoparticles, development of sustained-release intravitreal implants, or formulation with permeability-enhancing agents could be explored to ensure that therapeutically relevant concentrations of PMX53 reach the RPE and maintain a prolonged therapeutic effect (Kumar et al., 2020).

•  Safety considerations within the ocular environment also warrant close attention. While systemic administration of PMX53 has demonstrated an acceptable side-effect profile in non-ocular applications, the retina is an immunologically privileged and sensitive tissue. Chronic inhibition of complement-mediated signaling in the eye could potentially impair local immune surveillance or interfere with normal cellular homeostasis. Such risks necessitate detailed ocular toxicology studies to assess the potential for adverse effects resulting from long-term C5aR blockade in RPE cells and other retinal tissues (Proctor et al., 2006a; Hutchison & Krause, 2004).

•  Furthermore, the translational relevance of the anti-inflammatory effects observed with PMX53 in systemic diseases may not directly apply to the intricate pathophysiology of dry AMD. Dry AMD is a multifactorial disease influenced by genetic predispositions, environmental stresses (such as oxidative damage from chronic light exposure), and complex interactions between complement proteins, RPE cells, and the extracellular matrix. While the blockade of C5aR is theoretically poised to reduce mtROS production and inflammasome activation, it is possible that additional redundant inflammatory pathways might offset the therapeutic benefit of targeting a single receptor (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Proctor et al., 2006a).

•  Finally, the overall clinical development history of PMX53 indicates that while the compound has progressed to early clinical trials for systemic inflammatory conditions, challenges related to pharmacokinetics and delivery have hindered further clinical advancements. As such, repurposing PMX53 for dry AMD will require a dedicated research program that not only demonstrates efficacy in ocular models but also addresses the unique drug delivery and safety challenges associated with the eye (Proctor et al., 2006a; Proctor et al., 2006b).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
6. Overall Conclusion  
────────────────────────────────────────────  
In summary, PMX53 is a well-characterized cyclic peptidomimetic C5a receptor antagonist that has been evaluated extensively in systemic models of inflammation and has reached early-phase clinical testing for conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis. Its design, which exploits a cyclic structure to achieve pseudo-irreversible antagonism, provides a strong mechanistic rationale for targeting the complement cascade—which is increasingly recognized as a major contributor not only to systemic inflammatory diseases but also to ocular conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

The expected effect of PMX53 in the context of dry AMD is to prevent the binding of C5a to its receptor on retinal pigment epithelial cells, thereby disrupting a key amplification loop that leads to mitochondrial reactive oxygen species overproduction, inflammasome activation, and subsequent IL-1β release. Such a blockade should, in theory, mitigate the chronic inflammatory stress that drives RPE degeneration and, by extension, slow the progression of dry AMD (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Proctor et al., 2006a).

Nonetheless, despite its strong conceptual appeal and preclinical promise in systemic models, significant knowledge gaps remain with respect to its application in the ocular setting. No dedicated studies have yet confirmed the efficacy of PMX53 in reducing complement-driven oxidative stress specifically in the retina, and species-specific differences in receptor binding mean that murine models—a common platform for AMD research—may not accurately reflect the human situation. Additionally, the challenges inherent in delivering a peptide drug effectively to ocular tissues, combined with the potential risks of long-term complement inhibition in the sensitive retinal environment, require careful and systematic investigation through both advanced formulation approaches and dedicated ocular safety studies (Proctor et al., 2006a; Hutchison & Krause, 2004; Kumar et al., 2020).

Overall, while the scientific and mechanistic basis for repurposing PMX53 for dry AMD is compelling—given its ability to disrupt complement-mediated inflammatory cascades and its pseudo-irreversible receptor binding—the translation of these benefits to the ocular milieu remains to be established. A focused research program is needed to conduct in vitro studies in primary human RPE cells exposed to complement activation, followed by in vivo evaluations in non-murine models that more closely mirror human C5aR pharmacology. Further development of ocular delivery systems, including intravitreal implants or nanoparticle-based formulations, will also be essential to overcome the inherent pharmacokinetic challenges posed by a peptide therapeutic.

If these hurdles can be successfully addressed, PMX53 could represent an innovative approach to slow or prevent RPE degeneration by attenuating the complement-driven amplification of mtROS production and inflammasome activation—a cascade that is a key driver of dry AMD pathology. In light of the significant unmet need for effective treatments for dry AMD and the robust preclinical data supporting the anti-inflammatory efficacy of cyclic C5aR antagonists in other contexts, further investigation into PMX53 is both scientifically justified and therapeutically promising (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a; Brandstetter et al., 2015; Ong et al., 2024).

This comprehensive review indicates that while substantial promise exists for PMX53 as a candidate to mitigate the complement-mediated mechanisms underlying dry AMD, its successful repurposing will depend on dedicated ocular pharmacology studies, careful species selection for preclinical investigations, and the development of targeted drug-delivery strategies tailored to the unique anatomical and immunological environment of the eye (Proctor et al., 2006a; Ong et al., 2024; Proctor et al., 2006b).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) is a synthetic derivative of fumaric acid that belongs to the class of fumaric acid esters (FAEs) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Chemically, DMF is the dimethyl ester of fumaric acid, with a molecular weight of approximately 144.13 g/mol, and is produced by reacting fumaric acid with methanol in the presence of a strong acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Moreover, DMF is classified as an electrophilic molecule that, due to its α,β-unsaturated ester structure, can covalently modify protein thiols, particularly the cysteine residues within KEAP1, thereby initiating its downstream effects on cellular redox homeostasis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Fumaric acid esters as a class have a long-standing history in pharmacotherapy, originally finding application in dermatology, most notably in the treatment of psoriasis, and have since been repurposed for neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis (MS) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, fumaric acid esters were introduced into clinical practice as antipsoriatic agents in Europe, with formulations such as Fumaderm® entering the market in the 1990s (Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). DMF in particular emerged as a key component in these formulations, and its efficacy in modulating immune responses and suppressing inflammation in skin diseases laid the foundation for its later repurposing in other systemic inflammatory conditions (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Over time, DMF was repurposed and further developed as an oral agent for the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), culminating in its FDA approval in 2013 under the trade name Tecfidera® by Biogen (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163). Clinical trials, including large-scale phase 3 studies, have demonstrated its favorable safety profile and efficacy in reducing relapse rates and slowing disability progression in MS patients (Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 14–16). Although there is no extensive historical record of DMF being used directly for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other primary ocular diseases, recent preclinical findings have indicated that its potent activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway may confer significant protective effects on the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This has sparked considerable interest in repurposing DMF for ocular indications such as geographic atrophy, a late stage of dry AMD, by leveraging its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities observed in nonocular settings (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, DMF functions primarily as a prodrug; upon oral administration it is rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases within the gastrointestinal tract to yield its active metabolite, monomethyl fumarate (MMF) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). However, when DMF covalently modifies KEAP1, it disrupts this complex, allowing Nrf2 to dissociate and translocate into the nucleus (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). In the nucleus, Nrf2 binds to antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoters of numerous genes encoding cytoprotective enzymes, including glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), and various enzymes involved in glutathione (GSH) synthesis and regeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). These molecular interactions lead to enhanced antioxidant defenses, improved detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and overall better maintenance of cellular redox balance (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). In addition to its role in promoting antioxidant gene expression via Nrf2 activation, DMF has been shown to have immunomodulatory properties; it can shift cytokine profiles by increasing interleukin-4 (IL-4)–expressing CD4+ T cells and decreasing the production of proinflammatory cytokines such as interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and interleukin-17 (IL-17) (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Furthermore, DMF has been reported to inhibit nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation in certain cellular contexts, thus contributing to a reduction in inflammatory signaling independently of Nrf2 (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Together, these molecular actions result in lowered cellular oxidative stress and an improved inflammatory milieu, which are critical factors implicated in the pathogenesis of chronic degenerative diseases (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry AMD, particularly the geographic atrophy form, is characterized by the gradual degeneration of RPE cells, which leads to subsequent photoreceptor loss and irreversible vision impairment. Central to the pathophysiology of dry AMD are oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation that progressively compromise RPE viability and function (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). The hypothesis being explored is that DMF, through its robust activation of the Nrf2 pathway, can enhance the expression of ARE-driven genes that encode for antioxidant and cytoprotective proteins, thereby counteracting the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in the RPE (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 13–14). In particular, the upregulation of enzymes involved in glutathione synthesis is expected to increase intracellular levels of GSH, a critical thiol antioxidant that protects mitochondrial membranes and supports cellular bioenergetics (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Preclinical studies in retinal models have demonstrated that DMF can effectively preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and reduce the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β), both of which are hallmarks of RPE distress under oxidative challenge (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Given that the RPE is highly metabolically active and particularly vulnerable to cumulative oxidative damage, the sustained activation of Nrf2 by DMF following oral dosing is anticipated to provide continuous reinforcement of antioxidant defenses and maintain mitochondrial integrity in these cells (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 3–5; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). Moreover, by mitigating inflammatory signaling, DMF may not only protect the RPE but also contribute to a more favorable microenvironment that limits the propagation of cell death signals, thus potentially slowing the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Collectively, these expected cellular effects support the rationale for using DMF as an intervention to preserve retinal structure and function by lowering oxidative damage and supporting bioenergetics in the RPE.

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential of dimethyl fumarate as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD rests on a solid mechanistic rationale combined with an established clinical pedigree in other indications. One of the primary strengths of DMF is its well-characterized pharmacological profile; it is FDA-approved for multiple sclerosis and has been safely administered to thousands of patients over several years, which significantly mitigates the risk and regulatory hurdles typically associated with repurposed drugs (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). The dual actions of DMF—in particular, its ability to both activate the Nrf2 pathway and attenuate proinflammatory signals—directly target the underlying pathological processes in dry AMD, where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central drivers of RPE degeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In vitro studies have provided encouraging evidence that DMF increases intracellular glutathione levels and protects RPE cells from oxidative insults, findings that are directly translatable to the pathobiology of dry AMD (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Nonetheless, several challenges remain. Although DMF is known to be effective in MS and psoriasis, the ocular milieu presents unique pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic challenges that may not be fully addressed by the current oral formulations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18). The rapid hydrolysis of DMF to MMF means that, while the active metabolite does exert therapeutic effects, fine-tuning the dosing regimen to ensure adequate drug levels in the retina while minimizing systemic side effects is necessary (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). In addition, common adverse reactions associated with DMF, such as gastrointestinal discomfort and flushing, though generally mild to moderate, could be more problematic in the typically elderly dry AMD population, necessitating careful monitoring and potentially modified dosing strategies (Camelo, 2025, p. 17; Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13). There is also the question of whether systemic administration of DMF can generate sufficient concentrations in the retina to achieve a meaningful therapeutic effect. While emerging evidence suggests that DMF can cross the blood-retinal barrier and activate Nrf2 in retinal cells (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3), further pharmacokinetic and translational studies are warranted to confirm its retinal bioavailability and the optimal dosing regimen for ocular indications.

Another consideration is the complexity of dry AMD itself, which is a slowly progressive, multifactorial disease with contributions from genetic predispositions, environmental exposures, and systemic metabolic disturbances. It remains to be seen whether the monotherapeutic approach of DMF, targeting primarily oxidative stress via Nrf2 activation, will be sufficient to halt or reverse disease progression, or whether combination therapies will ultimately be required (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Furthermore, while the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms of DMF are well supported by in vitro data and animal studies, there is still limited clinical data on its efficacy in ocular disease settings. Early-phase clinical trials aimed at evaluating DMF in geographic atrophy have to rigorously assess both structural outcomes (e.g., changes in the area of atrophy) and functional endpoints (e.g., visual acuity, retinal sensitivity) to establish its therapeutic benefit in dry AMD (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Despite these limitations, the strengths of DMF are compelling. The drug’s ability to upregulate a broad spectrum of cytoprotective genes via the Nrf2 pathway makes it a versatile candidate for mitigating the oxidative and inflammatory stress that drives RPE degeneration. The fact that DMF has already cleared extensive regulatory and clinical safety evaluations in nonocular indications is a significant advantage, as it greatly accelerates the translational pathway compared to a novel chemical entity (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Additionally, the repurposing of an already approved drug leverages existing manufacturing, formulation, and distribution infrastructure, favorably impacting the cost and timeline associated with drug development (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

In summary, the comprehensive literature review supports the potential of DMF to serve as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its mechanism of action—centered on Nrf2 activation leading to enhanced antioxidant capacity along with anti-inflammatory effects—directly addresses the key pathophysiological mechanisms implicated in dry AMD. The extensive clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis provides a reliable safety and tolerability framework, which is crucial for rapid repositioning into a new clinical area such as geographic atrophy (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). However, it is essential to conduct targeted preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials specifically in ocular disease models to optimize dosing, confirm retinal delivery, and demonstrate clinical efficacy before advancing to larger randomized controlled trials (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Overall, while challenges remain regarding optimal application in the retinal context and potential side effects in an older patient population, DMF—by virtue of its dual antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms and robust clinical background—stands as a viable candidate that merits further investigation for the treatment of dry AMD.

Given the current evidence, the following recommendations are proposed for advancing DMF as a candidate for dry AMD:  

1. Conduct detailed pharmacokinetic studies in animal models to assess the retinal bioavailability of DMF and its active metabolite MMF following systemic administration. This should include studies comparing different dosing schedules and formulations to optimize retinal exposure without exacerbating systemic adverse effects (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2).  

2. Develop and validate preclinical models of dry AMD that recapitulate the key features of human geographic atrophy, with a focus on evaluating the efficacy of DMF in protecting RPE cells against oxidative stress and preserving mitochondrial function (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

3. Investigate the potential benefits of combining DMF with other therapeutic agents that target complementary pathways in dry AMD. For example, agents that modulate complement activation or improve choroidal blood flow may synergize with the Nrf2-mediated antioxidant mechanism of DMF (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).  

4. Initiate early-phase clinical trials in patients with geographic atrophy to establish proof of concept. These studies should include robust biomarker assessments (e.g., measurement of ARE gene expression, retinal imaging for atrophy progression, and functional visual outcomes) to correlate molecular effects with clinical benefit (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

5. Carefully monitor the safety profile of DMF in the elderly population, as the incidence of gastrointestinal side effects and lymphopenia may differ compared to the population with MS. Consider the feasibility of modified-release formulations or alternative routes of administration (e.g., topical ocular delivery) to minimize systemic side effects while maximizing retinal drug concentrations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18).

Overall, the repurposing of dimethyl fumarate for dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a robust mechanistic framework and a significant body of preclinical and clinical data generated in other indications. Its capacity to activate the Nrf2 pathway, enhance mitochondrial glutathione synthesis, and modulate inflammatory responses in RPE cells directly addresses several pivotal aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). While there are challenges regarding optimal retinal delivery and management of systemic adverse effects, the clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis lends considerable support to its translational potential. Consequently, dimethyl fumarate represents a well‐justified and attractive therapeutic candidate for further exploration in the treatment of dry AMD, warranting additional preclinical optimization and clinical investigation to fully define its role in preserving visual function in patients affected by this progressive degenerative disease (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12).
