Originally synthesized as a potential remedy for mitochondrial dysfunction, idebenone belongs to the class of quinone derivatives that have historically been applied to conditions driven by oxidative stress and defective energy metabolism. The compound was discovered through efforts to mimic and improve on the natural electron carrier function of coenzyme Q10, with modifications engineered to optimize cellular uptake and bioavailability, thereby augmenting its use in various neurodegenerative and ophthalmologic applications (Gueven et al., 2015, pp. 4–5; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 7–8).

Therapeutic History:  
Idebenone’s clinical journey commenced with its use in Leber’s Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON), a mitochondrial disorder resulting in acute or subacute vision loss. In LHON, idebenone has been shown to improve visual function, as evidenced by improvements in photopic electroretinography (ERG) and other visual assessments, and has received regulatory approval in certain regions for this indication (Lyseng-Williamson, 2016, pp. 1–2). Preclinical studies have also demonstrated that idebenone exerts cytoprotective effects on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and retinal ganglion cells by preserving mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and reducing apoptosis in the face of oxidative stress (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13). Although idebenone’s original target was LHON, its biochemical properties—particularly its dual role as an electron shuttle and antioxidant—have spurred interest in repurposing the compound for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), a condition likewise characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction and heightened oxidative injury. Several studies have provided evidence from both biochemical assays and animal models that idebenone can modulate pro‐ and anti‐apoptotic protein expression (notably lowering Bax while increasing Bcl-2 levels) and activate the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway in RPE cells, thereby suggesting a potential benefit in retinal diseases beyond LHON (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 7–8).

Mechanism of Action:  
Idebenone operates through a multifaceted mechanism that addresses the dual challenges of mitochondrial energy impairment and oxidative damage. Fundamentally, idebenone is proposed to bypass defects in mitochondrial complex I by serving as an electron carrier that transfers reducing equivalents directly to complex III. This electron shuttling function is critical for maintaining the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and sustaining ATP synthesis when the conventional electron transfer through complex I is compromised due to oxidative damage—a scenario that is hypothesized to occur in the RPE under conditions such as drusen-induced stress (Arend et al., 2015, p. 2; Wang et al., 2025, pp. 5–8). In parallel, idebenone exhibits potent antioxidant activity by scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitigating the lipid peroxidation processes that are thought to contribute to drusen formation in dry AMD (Arend et al., 2015, pp. 7–8).

At the molecular level, idebenone has been shown to influence key cell survival pathways. It modulates the intrinsic mitochondrial apoptotic cascade by upregulating the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2 and concurrently downregulating the pro-apoptotic protein Bax. This shift in the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio helps to curb the initiation of apoptosis and contributes to cell survival in oxidative environments (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 5–6). Furthermore, idebenone stimulates the nuclear translocation of the transcription factor Nrf2, which in turn induces the expression of a suite of antioxidant genes. This activation of the Nrf2 pathway reinforces the cell’s intrinsic defenses against oxidative insult, which is of particular relevance in RPE cells tasked with handling the chronic low-grade oxidative stress present in AMD (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13). However, it is important to note that in certain settings—such as in cells deficient in the enzyme NQO1—idebenone’s efficacy as an electron carrier may be diminished, and higher concentrations may even elicit pro-oxidant or cytotoxic effects (Varricchio et al., 2020, pp. 18–20). These findings underscore the importance of optimizing the dosing strategy and ensuring appropriate cellular context to fully exploit idebenone’s protective actions.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of the proposed application for dry AMD, the hypothesis is that idebenone will act to shuttle electrons to complex III in RPE cells, thereby bypassing complex I defects induced by drusen-associated oxidative stress. This mechanism is expected to preserve the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and sustain ATP production, even under conditions of compromised oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). Preclinical data in RPE cell models have shown that idebenone treatment can mitigate the dissipation of Δψm in the face of hydrogen peroxide-induced stress, suggesting that similar protective effects could be harnessed in AMD where RPE cellular damage is a hallmark (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13).

Beyond its electron shuttling capacity, idebenone’s potent antioxidant action is expected to lower intracellular ROS levels and reduce lipid peroxidation, thereby protecting RPE cell membranes from the oxidative effects linked to drusen formation. This reduction in oxidative stress, coupled with the preservation of mitochondrial function, is anticipated to result in decreased activation of apoptotic pathways. The compound is also predicted to trigger Nrf2-dependent transcription of antioxidant genes within RPE cells—a response that is critical for combating the chronic oxidative stress implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13). 

Functionally, these molecular effects should translate into measurable improvements in cellular assays of mitochondrial function and viability. In vitro, one would expect to observe maintained or restored Δψm and ATP production in idebenone-treated RPE cells versus controls exposed to oxidative stress. In a more integrated system, such as in animal models or clinical assessments, improvements in photopic ERG responses—previously demonstrated in LHON patients under idebenone therapy—may serve as a surrogate marker for the preservation of retinal neuronal function and integrity (Lyseng-Williamson, 2016, pp. 1–2). Nonetheless, although the mechanistic rationale is robust, these expected effects depend critically on fine-tuning dosage to avoid the potential cytotoxicity observed at supra-therapeutic concentrations and to account for inter-patient variability in enzymes such as NQO1 that activate idebenone (Varricchio et al., 2020, pp. 18–20).

Overall Evaluation:  
The evidence reviewed supports idebenone as a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Among its key strengths is its dual action: the capacity to serve as an alternative electron shuttle to bypass complex I defects and the potent antioxidant activity that collectively mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage. These properties are especially relevant to dry AMD, where RPE degeneration and mitochondrial impairment form the basis of disease progression (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 2, 7–8).

Idebenone’s previous clinical approval and widespread use in LHON provide valuable precedent regarding its safety and efficacy in a retinal context. Moreover, preclinical data from in vitro studies in RPE cells offer compelling evidence regarding its ability to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential, sustain ATP synthesis, and modulate apoptotic pathways under oxidative stress conditions—mechanisms that are directly applicable to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 5–6). The activation of Nrf2 and subsequent upregulation of antioxidant defenses further consolidate its therapeutic potential (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13).

Nevertheless, several challenges remain. The efficacy of idebenone in bypassing complex I defects may be restricted by factors such as NQO1 expression, and potential pro-oxidant effects at higher concentrations necessitate careful dose optimization. In addition, while data from LHON and certain RPE cell models are promising, direct evidence from robust preclinical models of dry AMD is still limited. Some studies addressing these mechanisms have appeared in journals with variable impact factors, which calls for cautious interpretation of the data and underscores the need for further high-quality, reproducible research (Varricchio et al., 2020, pp. 15–18; Varricchio et al., 2020, pp. 18–20).

In summary, idebenone’s multifaceted mechanism—comprising electron shuttling to complex III, robust ROS scavenging, modulation of apoptotic signaling, and activation of Nrf2-driven antioxidant responses—aligns well with the therapeutic requirements for mitigating the mitochondrial and oxidative stress pathology present in dry AMD. While the compound’s history in LHON provides a strong foundation, the repurposing of idebenone for dry AMD will require additional rigorous preclinical investigations focusing on AMD-relevant models, followed by carefully designed clinical trials to validate its efficacy, safety, and dosing in this context (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13; Lyseng-Williamson, 2016, pp. 1–2; Gueven & Faldu, 2013, pp. 1–2).

Overall, idebenone represents a compelling candidate for further exploration in the therapeutic landscape of dry AMD. Its dual action addresses key pathophysiological mechanisms in the disease, and its established clinical use in a related ocular disorder provides a promising translational bridge. However, careful attention must be paid to the nuances of its mitochondrial interactions, dose-dependent effects, and the heterogeneous responses in different cellular contexts. Future research focusing on these aspects will be critical to determining whether idebenone can be successfully repurposed to prevent retinal degeneration and preserve vision in patients with dry AMD (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 2, 7–8; Russo et al., 2024, pp. 7–9; Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Alda-1 is a synthetic small molecule discovered through target-directed screening for modulators of mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2), originally identified as “ALDH2 activator 1” with the chemical name N-(1,3-benzodioxol-5-ylmethyl)-2,6-dichlorobenzamide and first demonstrated to reduce myocardial ischemic injury in rodents by directly activating ALDH2 (i.e., increasing its catalytic activity and rescuing function of the common inactive ALDH2*2 variant) (Budas et al., 2009; Kimura et al., 2019). Structurally and mechanistically, Alda-1 binds at the substrate entrance tunnel of ALDH2 and extends toward the active site, where it enhances dehydrogenase activity by favorably altering local dynamics, improving NAD+ engagement, and acting as a chemical chaperone that preserves the functional conformation of critical active-site loops and α-helices, while shielding key catalytic cysteines from irreversible electrophilic adduction by reactive aldehydes such as 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE) (Gao et al., 2022; Wang & He, 2018). In vitro biophysical and enzymology work shows Alda-1 increases wild-type ALDH2 activity approximately twofold and markedly rescues activity of the common East Asian mutant ALDH2*2 (Glu504Lys), restoring heterotetramer activity to near wild-type levels; importantly, Alda-1 is selective against several other ALDHs in original profiling, although later biochemical work suggests some degree of cross-activation of ALDH1A1 under specific assay conditions (Budas et al., 2009; Kotraiah et al., 2013).

Alda-1 belongs to the pharmacologic class of enzyme activators/allosteric agonists targeting mitochondrial ALDH2; the class is characterized by its ability to catalytically enhance clearance of reactive aldehydes generated by oxidative and nitrosative stress (e.g., 4-HNE, malondialdehyde [MDA], acrolein, and catecholamine-derived DOPAL), thereby acting as indirect antioxidants that reduce downstream carbonyl stress, proteotoxicity, and mitochondria-dependent cell death without directly scavenging ROS (Kimura et al., 2019; Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Wang & He, 2018). This mechanism has been applied preclinically across multiple organ systems to mitigate ischemia–reperfusion injury, chronic heart failure, metabolic and neurodegenerative toxicities, and toxin-induced organ damage, providing a consistent translational thread: activation of ALDH2 accelerates detoxification of stable electrophilic products of lipid peroxidation, interrupting aldehyde-driven positive feedback loops that amplify mitochondrial dysfunction, ROS generation, and apoptosis (Budas et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2014; Münzel & Daiber, 2018).

Therapeutic History  
Across cardiovascular models, Alda-1 has repeatedly demonstrated robust cytoprotection in vivo. In rat and mouse myocardial ischemia–reperfusion and infarction models, Alda-1 administration prior to or during ischemia reduced infarct size by approximately 60% and improved long-term survival following myocardial infarction, associating efficacy with increased ALDH2 activity, reduced 4-HNE-protein adducts and protein carbonyls, preserved mitochondrial respiratory control ratio (RCR), reduced mitochondrial H₂O₂ release, protection against Ca²⁺-induced mitochondrial permeability transition (MPT), and decreased cytochrome c release (Budas et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2014). In a chronic post-MI heart-failure model with established aldehydic overload, sustained Alda-1 treatment increased cardiac ALDH2 activity by ~2.7-fold, lowered 4-HNE adducts and protein carbonyls, normalized uncoupler responsiveness, improved RCR by preserving State 3 respiration, lowered mitochondrial ROS emission, and corrected MPT sensitivity; organ-level outcomes included increased contractility, reduced LV dilation, diminished hypertrophy and fibrosis, and anti-remodeling benefits (Gomes et al., 2014). In vitro, Alda-1 shielded isolated cardiac mitochondria from 4-HNE–induced respiratory inhibition, demonstrating direct aldehyde-dependent protection at the mitochondrial level (Gomes et al., 2014).

Hepatic and other organ systems provide convergent evidence. In a mouse acetaminophen hepatotoxicity model, Alda-1 pretreatment substantially reduced liver injury biomarkers (ALT/AST), histologic necrosis, 4-HNE adduct burden, mitochondrial depolarization, and cell death without altering upstream NAPQI bioactivation or JNK phosphorylation, demonstrating that protection is downstream via aldehyde detoxification and preservation of mitochondrial polarization and MPT control (Wimborne et al., 2020). Additional preclinical reports document Alda-1 efficacy in models of lung ischemia/reperfusion, intestinal I/R, kidney injury, neurotoxic injuries, and alcohol-related hepatic injury, again with mechanistic ties to accelerated clearance of reactive aldehydes, restoration of mitochondrial function, and modulation of stress/apoptosis pathways (Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019).

Retina-focused data, while more limited and not in dry AMD models, are directionally supportive. In streptozotocin-induced aged diabetic rats (an early diabetic retinopathy model), systemic Alda-1 improved ERG parameters, preserved outer nuclear layer (ONL) and total retinal thickness on OCT at 7–30 days, increased retinal SOD activity, and decreased retinal TNF-α and IL-6 across multiple timepoints; concurrent upregulation of ALDH2, Nrf2, and Sirt1 was observed by immunofluorescence and Western blot, suggesting that ALDH2 activation engages antioxidant and anti-inflammatory pathways in the retina under hyperglycemic oxidative stress (He et al., 2018). In a separate in vivo retinal degeneration study (MNU-induced photoreceptor damage), systemic Alda-1 preserved ERG amplitudes, mitigated photoreceptor degeneration (OCT, histology), increased retinal ALDH2 and SIRT1 protein, and reduced markers of ER stress (GRP78) and apoptosis (PARP1), supporting the hypothesis that enhancing aldehyde detoxification ameliorates retinal cellular stress downstream of lipid peroxidation (Yan et al., 2020; Carullo et al., 2020). Although neither model recapitulates RPE-centric dry AMD (drusen, complement activation, geographic atrophy), they provide proof-of-principle that ALDH2 activation can protect neural retina under oxidative/aldehydic stress in vivo (Yan et al., 2020; He et al., 2018).

Clinical translation status remains nascent. No human proof-of-concept trials of Alda-1 have been reported, and authoritative reviews note the absence of clinical efficacy data for ALDH2 activators like Alda-1, despite extensive rodent evidence across organs; moreover, no ALDH2 activators are in clinical use at present (Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019). Safety experience is therefore limited to preclinical settings: chronic Alda-1 dosing in naïve rats (10 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks) demonstrated acceptable tolerability (no hemodynamic, biochemical, or organ-weight changes), whereas a separate report described crystalline nephropathy and renal function deterioration after I/R under specific Alda-1 dosing/formulation conditions, suggesting potential tissue-specific or formulation-dependent risks requiring evaluation (Gomes et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2023). With respect to ophthalmology, existing Alda-1 studies are limited to rodent retina in DR and MNU models; there is no published use in dry AMD patients or preclinical AMD-like RPE atrophy models, and there is no reported ocular delivery pharmacokinetics or long-term ocular safety data in the provided literature (Yan et al., 2020; He et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action  
ALDH2 is a mitochondrial, NAD⁺-dependent dehydrogenase that catalyzes the oxidation of reactive aldehydes—most notably acetaldehyde, 4-HNE, MDA, acrolein, and DOPAL—to their corresponding carboxylic acids, thereby detoxifying electrophiles that otherwise form covalent Michael adducts and Schiff bases with cysteine, histidine, and lysine residues on proteins and nucleic acids (Kimura et al., 2019; Budas et al., 2009). The enzyme’s catalytic mechanism involves NAD⁺ binding in the Rossmann fold and activation of the catalytic cysteine (Cys302 in ALDH2), nucleophilic attack on the aldehyde to form a thiohemiacetal, hydride transfer to produce a thioacyl-enzyme intermediate, and Glu268-mediated hydrolysis to release the acid product and NADH; this canonical chemistry underlies ALDH2’s role as an indirect antioxidant via aldehyde clearance rather than direct ROS scavenging (Parajuli, 2013; Wang & He, 2018). Importantly, ALDH2 is highly susceptible to oxidative and electrophilic inactivation—its active-site cysteine cluster (Cys301–Cys303) can be adducted by 4-HNE at micromolar concentrations (>10 µM), establishing a pathogenic feed-forward loop in which lipid peroxidation products both injure proteins and progressively compromise the aldehyde-detoxifying capacity of mitochondria (Karan et al., 2023; Budas et al., 2009).

Alda-1 engages this system at multiple mechanistic levels. Structurally, Alda-1 binds to the substrate entrance tunnel and active site of ALDH2, altering the local environment to increase effective substrate/catalytic-cysteine proximity and improve NAD⁺ binding (lower Kₘ), while simultaneously acting as a molecular chaperone to stabilize conformational elements disrupted in the ALDH2*2 variant (e.g., restoring α-helix and active-site loop structures toward wild-type) (Gao et al., 2022; Wang & He, 2018). Functionally, Alda-1 increases wild-type ALDH2 catalytic activity approximately two-fold, but the effect is more pronounced in ALDH2*2 (10-fold or more in homotetramers), which is clinically relevant in East Asian populations; Alda-1 does not affect ALDH1/ALDH5 in initial selectivity panels, though subsequent biochemical reports indicate potential ALDH1A1 activation under specific conditions (i.e., DOPAL-inactivation assays), a detail that warrants further isozyme-specific profiling in ocular tissues (Budas et al., 2009; Kotraiah et al., 2013). Crucially, Alda-1 also reduces aldehyde access to catalytic cysteines (Cys302/301/303), protecting ALDH2 from 4-HNE–induced inactivation, thereby sustaining endogenous detoxification under aldehyde stress; in direct assays Alda-1 prevents rapid 4-HNE-mediated ALDH2 inactivation and shifts the enzyme to a higher-efficiency state (Gao et al., 2022; Kotraiah et al., 2013). The net biochemical outcome is enhancement of mitochondrial clearance of 4-HNE to the less reactive 4-hydroxynonenoic acid (4-HNA), alongside accelerated metabolism of other toxic aldehydes, which interrupts aldehyde-driven proteotoxic cascades (e.g., proteasomal inhibition, protein carbonyl accumulation) and preserves mitochondrial respiratory function (Budas et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2014).

Systems-level consequences of ALDH2 activation by Alda-1 have been delineated extensively in heart and liver. In failing hearts with elevated aldehydic load, Alda-1 decreased 4-HNE-protein adducts and total carbonyls without altering ALDH2 protein abundance, demonstrating a purely catalytic detoxification effect (i.e., activity increase without expression change) (Gomes et al., 2014). Mitochondrial bioenergetic protection is robust: Alda-1 preserved State 3 respiration, increased RCR, normalized uncoupler responses (CCCP), reduced absolute and relative H₂O₂ release, decreased cytochrome c release, and corrected MPT sensitivity, indicating mitigation of mitochondria-centered death signaling under chronic oxidative/aldehydic stress (Gomes et al., 2014). In isolated mitochondria, pre-incubation with Alda-1 prevented 4-HNE–induced declines in respiratory control and State 3 oxygen consumption, further supporting a direct anti-aldehyde effect on mitochondrial electron transport chain function (Gomes et al., 2014). In the APAP hepatotoxicity model, Alda-1 reduced tissue 4-HNE adduct burden by an order of magnitude, preserved mitochondrial polarization, and reduced cell death, consistent with detoxification of lipid peroxidation products downstream of parent electrophile formation (Wimborne et al., 2020).

Retinal and neuronal contexts provide complementary mechanistic observations. In cultured endothelial cells exposed to amyloid-β₁–₄₀, Alda-1 restored mitochondrial function, reduced 4-HNE adducts and ROS, and rescued angiogenic responses, indicating that ALDH2 activation can directly blunt aldehyde-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction in non-cardiac cells (Chen & Joshi, 2016; Roy, 2022). Within the retina, ALDH2 localizes across layers with predominant co-localization to CRALBP-positive Müller glia, and its expression diminishes with age; transgenic upregulation protects against retinal aging by decreasing oxidative-stress–related apoptosis and enhancing the unfolded protein response (UPR) in the ER, indicating that increased ALDH2 activity has cytoprotective effects in vivo in the aging retina (Karan et al., 2023; Long et al., 2020). In diabetic retinopathy rodent studies, Alda-1 increased retinal ALDH2, SIRT1, and Nrf2 signaling, decreased proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6), and improved electrophysiologic and structural outcomes, suggesting that ALDH2 activation enlists antioxidant and proteostasis pathways beyond direct aldehyde detoxification to preserve retinal function (He et al., 2018). In photoreceptor degeneration, Alda-1 upregulated SIRT1 and decreased ER stress/apoptotic markers, again consistent with mitigation of downstream stress signaling when aldehyde load is reduced (Yan et al., 2020).

Finally, the disease biochemistry underpinning our hypothesis—aldehyde toxicity as a conserved driver downstream of oxidative lipid peroxidation—is well defined in neurodegeneration and retinal biology. 4-HNE forms adducts that impair proteasome activity, promote accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and inflammation, covalently modify and crosslink amyloid peptides, impair ion pumps and transporters, and directly kill neurons at low micromolar concentrations; ALDH2 loss-of-function (including ALDH2*2) exacerbates accumulation of 4-HNE adducts and age-dependent neurodegeneration in rodent models (Chen & Joshi, 2016). In retinal disease, the RPE and photoreceptors operate in a high-oxygen, PUFA-rich environment, with continuous photo-oxidation and phagocytosis of outer segments generating lipid peroxides and aldehydes, and oxidative stress is a central driver of AMD pathogenesis; therapeutic strategies that augment endogenous detoxification (e.g., via Nrf2) have been proposed as rational approaches to bolster RPE resilience (Chen et al., 2023). Collectively, Alda-1’s biochemical action—activation of a mitochondrial enzyme that eliminates 4-HNE/MDA—integrates tightly with the pathophysiology of aldehyde-mediated mitochondrial and proteostatic injury that characterizes oxidatively stressed retinal tissues (Kimura et al., 2019; Budas et al., 2009).

Expected Effect  
In RPE mitochondria subjected to chronic oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, the proposed mechanism predicts that Alda-1 will (i) increase ALDH2 catalytic activity and resilience to aldehyde-induced inactivation, (ii) accelerate metabolic clearance of 4-HNE and related long-lived electrophiles to non-reactive acids, (iii) reduce covalent adduction/carbonylation of mitochondrial and cytosolic proteins, (iv) preserve oxidative phosphorylation (increased State 3 respiration and RCR), (v) lower mitochondrial H₂O₂ production, (vi) increase resistance to Ca²⁺-induced MPT and decrease cytochrome c release, and (vii) therefore reduce apoptotic signaling and downstream inflammation in RPE, which in aggregate should attenuate RPE dysfunction and slow progression of dry AMD (Gomes et al., 2014). While direct ALDH2 expression in RPE has not been demonstrated in the provided texts, ALDH2 is present across retinal layers (notably Müller glia) and declines with age, and increasing ALDH2 conferred protection in the aged mouse retina in vivo, supporting the rationale that ALDH2 activation in retinal tissue can be beneficial under oxidative stress; confirming ALDH2 expression and activity in human and murine RPE will be a critical enabling experiment (Karan et al., 2023; Long et al., 2020). The retina’s documented vulnerability to lipid peroxidation (PUFA-rich outer segments, high O₂ consumption, chronic light exposure) and the centrality of oxidative stress to AMD pathogenesis further support that increased mitochondrial aldehyde detoxification should reduce toxic aldehyde burden in RPE and adjacent cells (Chen et al., 2023).

Assay expectations and readouts for validation align closely with prior Alda-1 literature. In isolated RPE mitochondria or permeabilized cells, Alda-1 should preserve ADP-stimulated State 3 oxygen consumption and increase RCR versus vehicle under aldehydic load (e.g., exogenous 4-HNE) or oxidative stress conditions; decreased H₂O₂ release and normalization of uncoupler (CCCP) responses would be predicted based on cardiac mitochondria data (Gomes et al., 2014). Under Ca²⁺ challenge, Alda-1 should increase the threshold for MPT and reduce cytochrome c release; in intact RPE, Alda-1 should maintain Δψm under oxidative stress (e.g., blue light, NaIO₃, HOHA lactone), paralleling hepatocyte in vivo imaging under APAP (Gomes et al., 2014; Wimborne et al., 2020). At the biochemical level, 4-HNE-protein adduct quantification (IHC/ELISA/LC-MS) and protein carbonylation assays should show significant reductions with Alda-1 pretreatment; mitochondrial respiratory chain complex activities may be preserved relative to vehicle under electrophile exposure (Gomes et al., 2014; Cheng, 2019). Downstream stress responses (e.g., ER stress markers such as GRP78, UPR activation; SIRT1 and Nrf2 activity; inflammatory cytokines TNF-α/IL-6) should reflect improved homeostasis, consistent with diabetic retina and MNU data (He et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020). Methodologically, the respiratory chain enzymology and aldehyde reactivity analytics described for RPE systems (e.g., complex I–IV assays in 96-well format, reverse-phase HPLC quantitation of aldehyde scavenging, LC-MS/MS quantitation of aldehyde uptake) are directly applicable to evaluating Alda-1’s effects on mitochondrial function and aldehyde handling in RPE models (Cheng, 2019).

A critical caveat is that ALDH2 distribution within the retina emphasizes Müller cells rather than RPE in available reports, and ALDH2 can be inactivated by high aldehyde levels (>10 µM 4-HNE), implying that the therapeutic window may be constrained under extreme aldehydic stress; Alda-1 is explicitly reported to reduce 4-HNE accessibility to catalytic cysteines and reverse 4-HNE–mediated inhibition, which should mitigate this concern but does not obviate the need to quantify ALDH2 activity and 4-HNE load in RPE during oxidative stress (Karan et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2022). Given that dry AMD pathobiology includes chronic oxidative stress, complement-driven inflammation, lysosomal/lipofuscin pathology, and lipid/protein debris accumulation (drusen), the expected benefit of Alda-1 would likely be most pronounced on the oxidative–aldehydic damage axis (mitochondrial and proteostatic integrity) rather than directly addressing complement or lipid trafficking, suggesting it would be a mechanistically complementary therapy potentially combined with agents targeting other AMD pathways (Chen et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic coherence with AMD pathophysiology: Dry AMD is driven in part by oxidative stress in RPE with accumulation of lipid peroxidation products; ALDH2 is a mitochondrial enzyme that detoxifies 4-HNE/MDA and is susceptible to inactivation by aldehydes, establishing a feed-forward injury loop that Alda-1 is designed to interrupt (Chen et al., 2023; Budas et al., 2009; Karan et al., 2023).  
- Direct mitochondrial mechanism with robust preclinical performance: Alda-1 increases ALDH2 activity, reduces 4-HNE adducts and protein carbonyls, preserves State 3 respiration and RCR, reduces mitochondrial H₂O₂ emission, raises MPT thresholds, and decreases cytochrome c release under chronic aldehydic stress; these endpoints directly match the mitochondrial failure features observed in stressed RPE (Gomes et al., 2014).  
- Retinal in vivo signals: In diabetic and photoreceptor degeneration models, Alda-1 improved ERG, preserved retinal structure, increased SIRT1/Nrf2 signaling, reduced inflammatory cytokines, and diminished ER stress/apoptotic markers, collectively supporting retinal tissue benefit under oxidative stress (He et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020).  
- Protective breadth across organs and insults via aldehyde clearance: Repeated demonstration that Alda-1 reduces 4-HNE accumulation and preserves mitochondrial function in heart, liver, lung, intestine, and neuronal contexts increases confidence that the aldehyde-clearance mechanism is conserved and translatable (Wimborne et al., 2020; Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019).  
- Pharmacogenetic upside: Alda-1 rescues ALDH2*2 activity, suggesting potential efficacy in East Asian ALDH2*2 carriers, a large at-risk population for aldehyde-mediated diseases; this also provides a biomarker-based stratification opportunity in trials (Budas et al., 2009; Kimura et al., 2019).  
- Safety signs in chronic rodent dosing: Six-week daily Alda-1 in naïve rats showed no hemodynamic, biochemical, or organ-weight toxicity, supporting tolerability for longer-term therapy (Gomes et al., 2014).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Lack of dry AMD/RPE-specific data: No direct evidence in RPE-focused dry AMD models (e.g., NaIO₃-induced RPE atrophy, complement dysregulation models, aging-driven GA models) is presented in the context, and ALDH2 expression has not been explicitly demonstrated in RPE here; expression across retina with Müller co-localization and protection in aged retina is encouraging but not definitive for RPE (Karan et al., 2023; Long et al., 2020).  
- Clinical translation gap: No human proof-of-concept for Alda-1 or class; no ALDH2 activator currently in clinical use; ocular PK, distribution, and chronic safety are uncharacterized (Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019).  
- Potential safety concerns: A preclinical report of Alda-1–associated crystalline nephropathy after I/R cautions that formulation, dosing, or off-target deposition may cause tissue-specific toxicity; comprehensive toxicology and formulation work are essential, especially for chronic ocular indications (Jin et al., 2023).  
- Biological complexity and compensatory pathways: Chronic acceleration of aldehyde clearance could theoretically blunt electrophile-mediated adaptive antioxidant signaling (Keap1/Nrf2, PPAR), potentially reducing hormetic protection; the balance of detoxification versus adaptation requires careful evaluation in chronic degenerative settings (Münzel & Daiber, 2018).  
- Enzyme inactivation at high aldehyde loads: ALDH2 is inactivated by >10 µM 4-HNE; although Alda-1 protects ALDH2 from 4-HNE and enhances activity, in extreme aldehydic states therapeutic efficacy might be limited, necessitating combination with upstream ROS control or lipid peroxidation inhibitors (Karan et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2022).

Decision-oriented recommendations  
- Mechanistic validation in human/murine RPE: Quantify ALDH2 mRNA/protein/activity and subcellular localization in primary human RPE and iPSC-RPE; test whether Alda-1 increases ALDH2 activity and protects against 4-HNE–induced ALDH2 inactivation in RPE mitochondria; measure 4-HNE/ACR/MDA adduct load ±Alda-1 under blue-light/NaIO₃/HOHA lactone stress (Karan et al., 2023; Cheng, 2019).  
- Mitochondrial function endpoints in RPE: Using established microplate assays and Seahorse OCR, test Alda-1’s effects on State 3 respiration, RCR, Δψm, H₂O₂ release, CCCP response, MPT susceptibility, and cytochrome c release under aldehydic stress (Gomes et al., 2014; Cheng, 2019).  
- Retinal disease models aligned to dry AMD: Progress to NaIO₃-induced RPE injury, photo-oxidative stress, and aging/complement models relevant to geographic atrophy; evaluate RPE survival, autofluorescent lipofuscin, drusen-like deposits, inflammatory markers, and photoreceptor secondary degeneration with functional readouts (ERG/OCT) under Alda-1 (Chen et al., 2023).  
- Formulation and delivery: Develop ocular formulations (e.g., intravitreal, sustained-release) and conduct ocular PK/PD to quantify RPE mitochondrial exposure; evaluate chronic ocular and systemic safety with renal monitoring given crystalline nephropathy risk (Jin et al., 2023).  
- Biomarkers and patient stratification: Consider ALDH2 genotype (ALDH2*2 carriers), circulating/ocular 4-HNE-adduct biomarkers, and retinal imaging endpoints as stratification and PD markers; Alda-1’s rescue of ALDH2*2 suggests a precision-medicine angle (Budas et al., 2009; Münzel & Daiber, 2018).  
- Combinations: Given AMD’s multifactorial pathobiology, test Alda-1 alongside Nrf2 activators or lipid peroxidation suppressors to determine additive/synergistic effects on RPE resilience while monitoring for suppression of adaptive electrophile signaling (Chen et al., 2023; Münzel & Daiber, 2018).

Overall, Alda-1 presents a mechanistically compelling, enzyme-directed strategy to alleviate aldehyde-driven mitochondrial and proteostatic injury in oxidatively stressed retinal tissues, with in vivo retinal efficacy already demonstrated in DR and photoreceptor degeneration contexts, albeit without RPE-centric dry AMD models to date (He et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020). The totality of evidence across organ systems (cardiac, hepatic) underscores that Alda-1 reliably reduces 4-HNE load and preserves mitochondrial function in vivo—precisely the biology we seek to modulate in RPE for dry AMD—making this candidate worthy of structured, stepwise validation in RPE-specific systems and AMD-relevant models (Gomes et al., 2014; Wimborne et al., 2020). Key risks reside in translational gaps (RPE expression, ocular PK/safety), potential toxicity signals (renal crystalline nephropathy under certain conditions), and the possibility that aldehyde detoxification alone will be insufficient to arrest complex AMD progression without adjunctive modulation of complement, lipid trafficking, or lysosomal pathways (Jin et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). With these caveats, Alda-1 merits advancement to focused preclinical validation for dry AMD, with an emphasis on RPE mitochondrial protection endpoints, aldehyde-adduct burden, and rigorous ocular safety assessment before considering first-in-human studies.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Deferoxamine (also known as desferrioxamine B; DFO) is a natural microbial siderophore originally isolated from Streptomyces pilosus and developed as an iron‐chelating drug in the 1960s, with clinical deployment beginning in 1968 under the trade name Desferal for treatment of iron overload disorders (notably transfusional iron loading in β-thalassemia) (Faa & Crisponi, 1999; Sharpe et al., 2011; Birch et al., 2006). Chemically, DFO is a hexadentate, tris-hydroxamate ligand that coordinates ferric iron (FeIII) at six oxygen donors derived from three bidentate hydroxamate groups to form a very stable 1:1 FeIII–DFO complex with distorted octahedral FeIIIO6 geometry (Sharpe et al., 2011; Richardson & Poňka, 1998). The FeIII affinity is exceptionally high and selective: reported formation constants for FeIII–DFO include log β110 ≈ 30.5 and conditional pM/pFe values around 26–31, while affinity for FeII is ∼20 orders of magnitude lower, consistent with the observation that DFO selectively chelates FeIII in vivo (Sharpe et al., 2011; Kontoghiorghes & Kontoghiorghe, 2020; Birch et al., 2006). The compound is highly hydrophilic, carries a positive charge near physiological pH, and exhibits poor membrane permeability and oral absorption; as a result, DFO is administered parenterally and tends to localize extracellularly or within endosomal/lysosomal compartments after endocytosis (Birch et al., 2006; Kontoghiorghes & Kontoghiorghe, 2020; Zhao et al., 2021). Pharmacokinetically, native DFO has a very short plasma half-life on the order of minutes, with multiple studies reporting ∼10–30 minutes after intravenous dosing, rapid renal clearance, and elimination of chelated iron via urine and bile; the short exposure necessitates prolonged subcutaneous or intravenous infusions for clinical efficacy (Sharpe et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2020; Entezari et al., 2022). DFO is not blood–neural barrier penetrant, limiting access to the central nervous system and retina when given systemically (Li et al., 2023).

As a class, siderophores are low-molecular microbial metabolites evolved for FeIII acquisition and storage; medicinally, DFO is the prototypical siderophore drug and, for decades, has served as the clinical standard for chelation in iron-overload conditions (Hatcher et al., 2009). Within therapeutic iron chelators, DFO’s hexadentate hydroxamate architecture confers high thermodynamic and kinetic stability of FeIII complexes, limiting redox cycling and hydroxyl radical generation relative to weaker or redox-active iron ligands (Hider & Kong, 2013).

Therapeutic History  
DFO has an extensive clinical history as the benchmark iron chelator for transfusional iron overload, especially in β-thalassemia major and other transfusion-dependent anemias; it was approved in the United States in 1968 and used for decades as life-saving therapy, albeit limited by the need for prolonged parenteral infusions and high cost (Sharpe et al., 2011; Birch et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2012). Beyond chronic iron overload, labeled and established uses include acute iron poisoning and treatment of aluminum toxicity, reflecting DFO’s strong FeIII selectivity and capacity to form inert complexes with polyvalent cations in vivo (Jones et al., 2020). The standard practice has involved subcutaneous or intravenous infusions at 20–60 mg/kg daily for 8–24 hours over 5–7 days per week, with urinary and fecal excretion of iron–DFO complexes as pharmacodynamic endpoints; however, adherence and patient acceptance have been major barriers due to the burdensome administration (Tam et al., 2003; Entezari et al., 2022).

The clinical pharmacology and chemistry of DFO have motivated multiple improved-delivery strategies: liposomal encapsulation and multivesicular liposome systems to extend half-life, and macromolecular conjugates (e.g., starch or HES carriers) to prolong exposure and shift biodistribution to iron-storage organs; these approaches have demonstrated prolonged circulation, increased urinary iron excretion, and organ accumulation (Jones et al., 2020; Sharpe et al., 2011; Tam et al., 2003). Nevertheless, DFO remains orally inactive and requires parenteral dosing, in contrast to later oral chelators (deferiprone, deferasirox), which have supplanted it in many indications due to ease of administration while sometimes being deployed in combination regimens with DFO to enhance iron removal and cardiac protection via complementary pharmacokinetics and chelation kinetics (Hider & Kong, 2013; Ma et al., 2012).

In ophthalmology and retinal biology, DFO’s evaluation is mixed. On one hand, iron chelation with DFO has shown protective effects in experimental retinal contexts: it reduced retinal ganglion cell death induced by hydrogen peroxide and paraquat in oxidative-stress paradigms, consistent with inhibition of iron-dependent hydroxyl radical production (Rohowetz et al., 2018). In hemorrhagic retinal injury, DFO protected photoreceptor tissues after subretinal blood in animal models, suggesting iron chelation can blunt heme/Fe-driven toxicity in the subretinal space (Song & Dunaief, 2013). In RPE-relevant cell models, DFO mitigated lipid peroxidation, prevented glutathione depletion, decreased Fe2+ accumulation, and preserved viability of ARPE-19 cells under tert-butyl hydroperoxide and blue-light stress, and it enhanced cell survival by modulating antioxidant defense systems (GSH–GPX4 and FSP1–CoQ10–NADH axes) (Zhao et al., 2025). A zinc–DFO complex (Zn/DFO) designed to improve cellular delivery reduced retinal iron content, lipid peroxidation, and oxidative DNA damage, preserved photoreceptor structure, and improved ERG responses in rd10 mice, demonstrating in vivo neuroprotection when systemic penetration is enhanced (Zhao et al., 2025). Ex vivo, DFO decreased histochemically detectable chelatable iron (Perls–DAB) in macular sections from AMD eyes, supporting the feasibility of removing pathologic labile iron in human AMD tissue (He et al., 2007).

On the other hand, DFO has a documented profile of retinal/ocular toxicity in patients receiving systemic therapy: reports include macular and peripheral pigmentary degeneration, impaired night vision, optic neuritis/neuropathy, cataract, ERG amplitude reductions, and EOG light-peak abnormalities, prompting recommendations for ophthalmic surveillance, and leading some experts to conclude that DFO is a dubious candidate for AMD treatment (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021). In RPE culture, repeated DFO exposure was cytotoxic relative to a prochelator control, and clinical series describe deferoxamine retinopathy across pediatric and adult populations, indicating that while iron chelation can be protective in vitro under specific stress conditions, DFO itself can injure RPE and photoreceptors under sustained or high-exposure regimens (Charkoudian et al., 2008; Błasiak et al., 2011). Importantly, DFO’s poor cell permeability and lack of blood–retinal barrier penetration raise practical concerns about achieving therapeutic intra-retinal exposure without systemic toxicity when administered conventionally (Li et al., 2023; Birch et al., 2006). Finally, although iron chelation is mechanistically compelling for retinal degenerations in which iron accumulation and ferroptotic stress participate, application of systemic chelators like DFO to retinal vascular disease and AMD remains at the basic research stage, with unresolved issues including perturbation of systemic/local iron homeostasis and stability of intracellular chelate complexes (Li et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, DFO is a high-affinity FeIII-selective chelator that forms kinetically inert hexacoordinate FeIIIO6 complexes via three hydroxamate ligands, each providing bidentate O,Oʹ coordination; this renders FeIII chemically sequestered, suppresses redox cycling, and prevents iron from entering the Haber–Weiss/Fenton chemistry that generates hydroxyl radicals from superoxide/hydrogen peroxide (Sharpe et al., 2011; Richardson & Poňka, 1998; Hider & Kong, 2013). The FeIII/FeII couple of ferrioxamine is electrochemically very negative (reported around −468 mV vs. NHE), and the complex is redox-inert under physiological conditions, consistent with its ability to quench iron-mediated ROS production rather than participate in it (Hider & Kong, 2013). In biological systems, DFO preferentially binds non-transferrin-bound iron (NTBI), labile iron pools in hepatocytes/macrophages, and low-molecular-weight iron transiting endosomes/lysosomes after transferrin delivery or ferritin degradation; it can mobilize hepatic stores and iron released by reticuloendothelial cells but cannot effectively strip iron from metalloproteins such as hemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochromes, oxidases, catalase, or peroxidases (Hatcher et al., 2009; Richardson & Poňka, 1998; Faa & Crisponi, 1999). The drug is hydrophilic and generally membrane-impermeant; cellular uptake occurs via fluid-phase endocytosis and pinocytosis, leading to enrichment in endosomal/lysosomal compartments, where it chelates lysosomal labile iron, an activity proposed to block lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis—mechanistically relevant to RPE pathobiology (Zhao et al., 2021; Dayani et al., 2004).

In retina and neural tissues, oxidative damage pathways include iron-dependent conversion of H2O2 to •OH via Fenton chemistry; DFO reduces H2O2-induced damage in retinal ganglion cells and protects against paraquat-generated superoxide by depriving upstream Fenton catalysts of accessible iron (Rohowetz et al., 2018). In RPE and photoreceptors, ferroptosis—a regulated cell death driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation—is closely linked to antioxidant systems centered on glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and, independently, on FSP1-mediated ubiquinol regeneration; DFO’s chelation of FeII/FeIII within lysosomes and cytosolic labile pools acts upstream of these pathways to limit lipid hydroperoxide propagation, preserving GSH–GPX4 and FSP1–CoQ10–NADH defense capacity in ARPE-19 under oxidative stimuli (Zhao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023). In systemic contexts, DFO detoxifies NTBI, reduces heme-derived ferryl species, removes high-oxidation-state heme iron, and directly scavenges some radical species, converging on inhibition of membrane lipid oxidation; these activities potentially translate to retinal cells where heme/iron-driven oxidative stress is implicated (Hatcher et al., 2009).

Notably, DFO’s hexadentate size and hydrophilicity restrict direct ferritin iron extraction and limit chelation in tightly protein-bound pools; smaller chelators can penetrate cells more readily and directly efflux ferritin iron, whereas DFO works primarily by intercepting low-molecular-weight iron pools and forming kinetically inert FeIII complexes that are then cleared, often via hepatobiliary or renal routes (Sharpe et al., 2011; Richardson & Poňka, 1998). In inflamed or ischemic tissues, the depletion of accessible iron by DFO can blunt downstream ROS and inflammatory cascades; however, prolonged systemic chelation perturbs metal homeostasis and can deplete essential iron pools in sensitive tissues, underlying some adverse effects including RPE toxicity, auditory neuropathy, and bone dysplasia (Zhao et al., 2021; He et al., 2007).

Expected Effect  
For dry AMD models centered on RPE iron-dependent oxidative stress, the expected pharmacologic effect of DFO is to reduce the labile Fe pool in lysosomes and cytosol, thereby attenuating hydroxyl-radical production from H2O2 and limiting iron-driven lipid peroxidation; operationally, this should decrease oxidative damage readouts and preserve mitochondrial and cellular function in RPE assays (Rohowetz et al., 2018; Li et al., 2023). Specifically:

- Lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis markers: In ARPE-19 cells, DFO has been shown to mitigate lipid peroxidation under oxidant (tBH) and blue-light stress and to preserve viability, consistent with suppression of ferroptotic death; thus, in RPE assays one should observe reductions in lipid peroxidation assays (e.g., BODIPY-C11) and maintenance of GPX4 activity/content, with complementary preservation of the FSP1–CoQ10–NADH axis (Zhao et al., 2025). The same studies indicate decreased Fe2+ accumulation after DFO, reflecting lower catalytic Fe at sites of peroxidation; similar decreases in labile Fe can be measured via calcein quenching or analogous probes (Zhao et al., 2025).

- Oxidative DNA damage: Systemic Zn/DFO reduced retinal oxidative DNA damage in vivo in rd10 mice; although these are not AMD models, the result predicts that in RPE oxidative stress assays DFO will reduce accumulation of oxidative DNA lesions, including those arising in mitochondrial DNA, where iron-dependent ROS can be particularly damaging (Zhao et al., 2025). Ex vivo human AMD maculas showed decreased Perls–DAB staining after DFO chelation, supporting the feasibility of reducing chelatable iron burden and downstream oxidative chemistry in diseased human retina (He et al., 2007).

- Mitochondrial bioenergetics: Preservation of RPE oxygen consumption rate (OCR) is plausible under DFO exposure insofar as DFO limits lipid peroxidation and maintains the reductive antioxidant systems (GSH–GPX4, FSP1–CoQ10) that protect inner-mitochondrial membranes and electron-transport components from iron-dependent oxidative injury; in ARPE-19, DFO improved survival and redox balance under stress, suggesting OCR preservation would accompany reduced peroxidation (Zhao et al., 2025). In retinal ganglion cells, DFO lessened H2O2-induced cell death, indirectly supporting improved mitochondrial tolerance to oxidant stress; similar protection can be anticipated in RPE where iron-dependent ROS compromise mitochondrial DNA and respiratory complexes (Rohowetz et al., 2018).

- Tissue iron fingerprints: In tissue sections or organoids, DFO exposure is expected to decrease Perls–DAB positive iron signal in regions with elevated chelatable iron, as observed in AMD macular tissue; in vivo, systemic DFO does not cross the BRB well, so demonstration of retinal iron removal may require enhanced uptake strategies (e.g., Zn/DFO) or local delivery (Li et al., 2023; He et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2025).

Caveats critical to experimental design include DFO’s lack of blood–retinal barrier penetration and poor cell permeability, which could limit intracellular RPE exposure and lysosomal targeting in vivo after systemic dosing; thus, in vitro or ex vivo assays will show clearer pharmacodynamic effects than systemic models unless delivery is optimized (e.g., Zn-complexation or nanocarriers) (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025; Jones et al., 2020). Additionally, repeated or high-concentration exposure can be cytotoxic to RPE in vitro and has been associated with clinical retinopathy, so dose–exposure optimization and careful toxicity monitoring are required, especially in chronic paradigms (Charkoudian et al., 2008; He et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Rationale strength and translational plausibility. The mechanistic rationale for iron chelation in dry AMD is strong: AMD retinas accumulate chelatable iron, iron catalyzes hydroxyl-radical generation and lipid peroxidation, and iron-dependent ferroptotic stress has been implicated in RPE dysfunction and photoreceptor degeneration (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023). DFO is a high-affinity FeIII chelator with extensive human experience, and it is proven to suppress iron-mediated ROS by forming kinetically inert FeIII complexes, preventing Fenton chemistry (Sharpe et al., 2011; Hider & Kong, 2013). In retinal and RPE models, DFO reduces oxidative injury, limits lipid peroxidation, and preserves cell viability; improved-delivery variants such as Zn/DFO demonstrate in vivo protection of retinal structure and function with concomitant decreases in retinal iron and oxidative DNA damage (Rohowetz et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2025). Ex vivo AMD maculae show DFO-responsive chelatable iron pools, reinforcing target engagement in human disease tissue (He et al., 2007). Mechanistically, enrichment of DFO in lysosomes—an organelle central to RPE iron handling, ferritinophagy, and lipid peroxidation—supports a proximal mode of action relevant to ferroptosis biology in AMD (Zhao et al., 2021).

Key liabilities and translational risks. Despite its compelling mechanism, DFO’s drug properties and ocular safety profile are unfavorable for repurposing in dry AMD without substantial reformulation or targeting:

- Ocular toxicity. DFO has a recognized spectrum of retinal adverse effects in patients, including pigmentary retinopathy, optic neuropathy, ERG/EOG abnormalities, and visual loss; authoritative reviews judge DFO a dubious candidate for AMD because of these safety concerns, and clinical surveillance is recommended when patients receive systemic DFO (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023). RPE toxicity is documented in vitro and clinically across age groups, indicating a narrow retinal therapeutic window under repeated exposure (Błasiak et al., 2011; Charkoudian et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2021).

- Delivery limitations. DFO is hydrophilic, membrane-impermeant, and not blood–neural/retinal barrier penetrant, which undermines retinal exposure after systemic dosing; achieving therapeutic intra-RPE concentrations without systemic toxicity is unlikely with conventional infusion regimens (Li et al., 2023; Birch et al., 2006). The molecule’s very short plasma half-life further complicates exposure in avascular tissues like the outer retina (Sharpe et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2020).

- Systemic chelation risks. Long-term DFO perturbs systemic iron balance, interacts with microbiological iron acquisition in certain pathogens (e.g., Vibrio, S. aureus) that can exploit ferrioxamine, and carries recognized risks of growth retardation, bone changes, and infection, which are unacceptable for a chronic ocular disease with slow progression (Sharpe et al., 2011; Faa & Crisponi, 1999).

- Clinical maturity in ophthalmology. While iron chelators show promise in preclinical retinal models, clinical translation to retinal vascular disease/AMD remains at the basic research stage; challenges include maintaining retinal iron homeostasis, avoiding off-target metal depletion (e.g., Zn2+), and ensuring intracellular chelate stability and localization (Li et al., 2023).

Risk-mitigation strategies and development path. If DFO were to be advanced, development should avoid systemic DFO infusions for dry AMD. Instead:

- Leverage targeted delivery. The Zn/DFO complex that facilitates cellular uptake has shown robust neuroprotection, retinal iron lowering, and oxidative DNA damage reduction in vivo; such conjugate-based or carrier-based strategies could provide intracellular RPE delivery at lower systemic exposure, meriting further evaluation in AMD-relevant models (e.g., light damage, iron-loading, aged mice) with retinal safety readouts (Zhao et al., 2025). Nanocarriers or depot formulations that increase local ocular exposure while minimizing systemic levels could be explored, given DFO’s history of half-life extension in liposomal and multivesicular formulations systemically (Jones et al., 2020; Sharpe et al., 2011).

- Consider chemical alternatives within class. Other chelators with better cell permeability and ocular safety have shown retinal protection without the retinotoxicity seen with DFO; for example, deferiprone protected against iron-induced and light-induced retinal degeneration in multiple mouse models and was not found to be toxic to mouse retina in the contexts studied, suggesting that a more lipophilic, lower-molecular-weight chelator could be a safer starting point than DFO for dry AMD (Song & Dunaief, 2013; Picard et al., 2020).

- Exploit prochelation. Pro-chelators like BSIH that become active only under oxidative conditions were non-toxic with repeated exposure relative to DFO and may offer a way to achieve context-dependent iron chelation within oxidatively stressed RPE while sparing normal iron pools, lowering the risk of retinopathy (Charkoudian et al., 2008).

Decision framework for go/no-go. On balance, while DFO validates the iron-chelation mechanism in retinal tissues and provides useful tool-compound effects in vitro and in ex vivo AMD maculae, its physicochemical properties, delivery constraints, and retinal toxicity profile argue strongly against repurposing native DFO for chronic treatment of dry AMD (Li et al., 2023; He et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2021). The most credible development path for DFO derivatives would require:

- Demonstrating safe, effective RPE delivery with a DFO-based construct (e.g., Zn/DFO or nanocarrier) that reduces labile iron, lipid peroxidation, and oxidative DNA damage in AMD-relevant in vivo models without ERG/EOG or structural toxicity (Zhao et al., 2025).

- Establishing a therapeutic index in the retina with chronic dosing and appropriate safety pharmacology (ERG, OCT, histopathology), given reported human retinopathies on DFO (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023).

- Benchmarking against alternative chelators (e.g., deferiprone) that already demonstrate retinal protection and better permeability/safety in vivo, to justify a DFO-based approach scientifically and clinically (Song & Dunaief, 2013; Picard et al., 2020).

Strengths  
- Mechanistic fit: chelates FeIII with high selectivity and prevents Fenton chemistry; acts in lysosomes where RPE iron and lipid peroxidation intersect with ferroptosis (Sharpe et al., 2011; Hider & Kong, 2013; Zhao et al., 2021).  
- Demonstrated retinal pharmacology: reduces oxidative injury in retinal neurons and RPE, lowers retinal iron and oxidative DNA damage with improved delivery, and removes chelatable iron from AMD macula ex vivo (Rohowetz et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2025; He et al., 2007).  
- Extensive human experience: well-characterized PK/PD, safety liabilities, and clinical management of chelation therapy (Jones et al., 2020; Tam et al., 2003).

Weaknesses  
- Ocular toxicity liability with systemic DFO, including pigmentary retinopathy and electrophysiologic dysfunction, making native DFO a poor risk–benefit prospect for a chronic retinal indication (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021).  
- Poor retinal exposure after systemic dosing due to hydrophilicity and lack of BRB penetration; very short half-life complicates sustained intraocular levels (Li et al., 2023; Birch et al., 2006; Jones et al., 2020).  
- Systemic risks (growth, bone, infection) incompatible with large, elderly dry-AMD populations unless exposure is tightly localized to the eye (Faa & Crisponi, 1999; Sharpe et al., 2011).  
- Field immaturity: iron chelators for retinal disease remain in basic research with unresolved questions about homeostasis and intracellular stability (Li et al., 2023).

Conclusion  
DFO is a mechanistically validated iron chelator with documented ability to reduce iron-driven oxidative injury in retinal systems; however, as a repurposed systemic drug for dry AMD, its delivery barriers and retinal toxicity outweigh potential benefits (Li et al., 2023; He et al., 2007). If iron chelation is pursued for dry AMD within this program, prioritizing better-penetrant, safer chelators (e.g., deferiprone) or context-activated prochelators over native DFO is the higher-probability path; alternately, DFO-based constructs that demonstrably deliver into RPE (e.g., Zn/DFO) with acceptable chronic retinal safety merit targeted preclinical exploration before considering clinical translation (Song & Dunaief, 2013; Charkoudian et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin (also known as sirolimus and available as Abcam #ab120224) is a naturally occurring macrolide compound originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus. It belongs to the class of macrocyclic lactones and is known for its potent inhibitory effects on the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). This compound has been extensively used in various contexts such as immunosuppression, cancer therapy, and more recently, as a tool to modulate autophagy in age-related degenerative diseases. In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction and dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), rapamycin is being explored as a repurposed therapeutic candidate with the hypothesis that mTORC1 inhibition will enhance both general autophagy and selective mitophagy. This clearance of reactive oxygen species (ROS)–generating, damaged mitochondria may alleviate oxidative stress, reduce the accumulation of toxic lipofuscin compounds (including A2E), and ultimately slow the progression of dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, rapamycin was first discovered for its potent immunosuppressive properties and later developed for use in preventing transplant rejection and certain cancers. Its ability to inhibit mTORC1 has made it a valuable tool in research related to aging and neurodegeneration. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its effectiveness in modulating autophagy and protecting cellular integrity under stress conditions, particularly in the retinal environment. In animal models of retinal degeneration and even some early clinical trials, rapamycin was shown to reduce the accumulation of autofluorescent granules and inflammatory cytokines in the RPE, which are both hallmarks of dry AMD pathology (Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022). Notably, rapamycin has been administered via diverse routes, including intravitreal and subconjunctival injections, in attempts to treat geographic atrophy or other dry AMD phenotypes, although the clinical outcomes have been mixed. For example, clinical trials such as those referenced in studies with identifiers NCT00766649 and NCT01445548 demonstrated that while rapamycin was generally safe and well-tolerated in ocular applications, its efficacy in slowing down the progression of geographic atrophy and improving visual acuity remained limited (National Eye Institute, 2008; National Eye Institute, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These historical findings highlight both the promise and the challenges associated with translating rapamycin’s mechanistic benefits into robust clinical outcomes for dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary mechanism of rapamycin involves the formation of a complex with the immunophilin FKBP12. This complex binds to mTORC1 and inhibits its kinase activity, leading to a decrease in the phosphorylation of downstream targets such as ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K) and the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 (4EBP1). Under normal circumstances, active mTORC1 suppresses autophagy by phosphorylating these targets, which in turn prevents the formation of autophagosomes. By inhibiting mTORC1, rapamycin effectively removes this blockade, thereby promoting the induction of autophagy as evidenced by increased conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II and clearance of the autophagic substrate p62 (Zhang et al., 2015).

Within retinal pigment epithelial cells, this induction of autophagy is particularly important. RPE cells are responsible for the phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments; a process that generates large amounts of cellular debris and metabolic byproducts such as lipofuscin. In dry AMD, impaired autophagic flux leads to the accumulation of these compounds, which, in turn, contributes to oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Rapamycin’s inhibition of mTORC1 not only enhances general autophagy but also promotes selective mitochondrial clearance (mitophagy). Key players in the mitophagy pathway include the serine/threonine kinase PINK1 and the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin, both of which accumulate on depolarized mitochondria and signal their removal via autophagic mechanisms. By stimulating this PINK1/Parkin pathway, rapamycin enhances the clearance of damaged, ROS-generating mitochondria, thus preserving overall mitochondrial health (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).

Additionally, rapamycin’s downstream effects include activation of transcription factors such as TFEB, which regulates lysosomal biogenesis and further enhances the autophagic process. This dual action—promoting both autophagy and lysosomal function—helps to mitigate the accumulation of toxic aggregates such as lipofuscin and A2E in RPE, therefore reducing oxidative stress and inflammation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). Through these biochemical interactions, rapamycin establishes a cellular environment that is more capable of dealing with metabolic challenges and oxidative damage, both of which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Chang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed hypothesis, the administration of rapamycin in RPE cells is expected to result in a cascade of beneficial cellular events. In our proposed assay, rapamycin is anticipated to inhibit mTORC1 activity, leading to a measurable increase in autophagic flux. This will be evident from the enhanced lipidation of LC3-II, the clearance of p62 (an autophagy adaptor protein that accumulates when autophagy is impaired), and the activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway in response to oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2015).

The specific clearance of damaged mitochondria is particularly critical in the RPE, where mitochondrial dysfunction is a significant contributor to the generation of reactive oxygen species and subsequent cellular damage. By removing these dysfunctional mitochondria, rapamycin is expected to reduce intracellular ROS levels and thereby lower oxidative stress, a driving force in AMD pathology. In parallel, the enhanced autophagic degradation of accumulated lipofuscin and the toxic fluorophore A2E is predicted to further limit the inflammatory and apoptotic cascades triggered by these compounds, thus preserving RPE cell viability and function (Zhang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2025).

Moreover, the expression of PINK1 and Parkin in RPE cells has been well documented, and their activation is indicative of mitophagic turnover. Their proper functioning is a key determinant in mitochondrial quality control, and rapamycin is expected to potentiate this process, ensuring that mitochondria remain healthy and capable of maintaining cellular energy production and reducing the risk of cell death (Pinelli et al., 2025; Hyttinen et al., 2018). Given that impaired mitochondrial function and the resulting energy production deficits are central to the progression of dry AMD, the expected outcomes from rapamycin treatment would include not only a reduction in oxidative stress markers but also improvements in mitochondrial dynamics and overall cellular homeostasis. Such effects would ideally be reflected in functional assays measuring cell viability, mitochondrial respiration, and reductions in inflammatory cytokine production (Zhang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In our comprehensive evaluation of rapamycin as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and potential weaknesses emerge that warrant careful consideration. One of the key strengths of rapamycin lies in its well-characterized mechanism of action and its ability to broadly modulate autophagy through mTORC1 inhibition. Preclinical studies have repeatedly demonstrated that rapamycin can induce autophagic flux, leading to the clearance of cellular debris and damaged mitochondria in RPE cells. This is particularly compelling given the central role of impaired autophagy in the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, which are major pathological features of dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018). The dual-action mechanism—enhancing both autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis via TFEB activation—further supports its potential in addressing multiple aspects of the disease pathology, from oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction to inflammation and cellular senescence (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Another strength is the substantial body of preclinical evidence showing that rapamycin not only stimulates autophagy but also improves mitochondrial function. The activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway is particularly relevant since these proteins are indispensable for mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control. By facilitating the removal of ROS-generating, damaged mitochondria, rapamycin could directly impact the cellular energy balance and reduce damaging oxidative insults in the RPE, which is pivotal for maintaining retinal health (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).

Despite its promising mechanistic profile, several significant challenges remain. Clinical studies investigating the use of rapamycin for AMD have yielded mixed results. While the drug has been shown to be safe and tolerable in ocular applications, several clinical trials, such as those involving subconjunctival or intravitreal administration, did not demonstrate significant efficacy in halting the progression of geographic atrophy or improving visual acuity. In some instances, adverse effects such as decreased visual acuity and retinal thinning have been observed, raising concerns about the balance between therapeutic benefit and potential retinal toxicity (National Eye Institute, 2008; National Eye Institute, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These mixed clinical findings underscore the complexity of modulating mTORC1 in a disease with multifactorial etiology and suggest that the optimal dosage, treatment duration, and patient selection criteria still require refinement.

Furthermore, the variability in response among different donor-derived RPE cells—where only about 50% of AMD donor samples responded positively to rapamycin in certain studies—points to potential issues regarding patient heterogeneity and the need for personalized therapeutic regimens (Ebeling et al., 2020). This heterogeneity may be due to differences in the intrinsic capacity for autophagy, genetic variations affecting mitochondrial quality control, or the extent of existing cellular damage. Such variability complicates the development of standardized treatment protocols and could limit the broad applicability of rapamycin unless predictive biomarkers of response are identified (Zhang et al., 2015).

Another important consideration is the dual nature of autophagy in the context of RPE health. While enhancing autophagy can provide protective benefits by clearing damaged organelles and reducing oxidative stress, excessive autophagic flux under certain stress conditions might paradoxically contribute to cell death. This is especially relevant in advanced stages of dry AMD, where cellular stress is severe and prolonged autophagy induction might tip the balance toward detrimental outcomes rather than recovery (Chang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2019). In addition, the potential for rapamycin to interfere with beneficial mTOR signaling under specific conditions (for example, when mTOR activity supports survival pathways via growth factors such as nerve growth factor) further complicates its use, as evidenced by reports that observed mixed effects on retinal ganglion cell survival in different pathological contexts (Wang et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2021).

The delivery method and pharmacokinetics of rapamycin also represent important variables. While nanotechnology-based delivery systems—such as synthetic high-density lipoprotein nanoparticles—have shown promise in achieving more targeted and sustained delivery of rapamycin to the RPE (Mei et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2021), these strategies require further translational studies to assess their safety, efficacy, and scalability in clinical settings. Moreover, the risk of systemic side effects, including metabolic toxicities and immunosuppression, despite the generally favorable ocular safety profile observed in trials, necessitates caution in developing rapamycin-based therapies for chronic conditions like AMD (Wang et al., 2022).

In summary, rapamycin presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its robust mechanism of action—specifically, its capacity to inhibit mTORC1, thereby stimulating both general autophagy and the selective removal of damaged mitochondria via the PINK1/Parkin pathway. Preclinical evidence strongly supports the idea that such modulation can reduce oxidative stress, clear toxic accumulations like lipofuscin/A2E, and ultimately preserve mitochondrial and RPE cellular function (Zhang et al., 2015; Hyttinen et al., 2018). However, the translation of these benefits into clinical improvements remains uncertain, with several trials indicating that while rapamycin is safe and modulates cellular pathways implicated in AMD, its clinical efficacy in terms of preserving visual function has not been conclusively demonstrated. The heterogeneity in patient responses, the potential for adverse outcomes related to excessive autophagy, and the challenges in optimizing dosing and delivery all represent significant hurdles. These considerations suggest that while rapamycin is a promising candidate worthy of further investigation, its ultimate role in the treatment paradigm for dry AMD will depend on our ability to refine treatment regimens, develop predictive biomarkers for patient selection, and perhaps combine mTOR modulation with complementary therapeutic strategies that reinforce its protective effects while mitigating its risks (Wang et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2019).

Given the cumulative evidence, our overall recommendation is to continue exploring rapamycin as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, but with a strategic focus on further preclinical investigations that address the dose–response relationships in donor-derived RPE models and the development of advanced drug delivery systems. It will also be important to design future clinical trials with stratified patient populations and integrated biomarkers that can help identify responders. This iterative approach could eventually lead to a carefully balanced regimen where rapamycin’s autophagy-enhancing properties are harnessed to maintain retinal integrity while avoiding the pitfalls of over-inhibition or systemic toxicity. In essence, the promise of rapamycin in modulating autophagy to improve mitochondrial health and reduce oxidative stress in RPE cells is clear at the molecular and cellular levels, but translating these benefits into a safe and effective therapy for dry AMD will require overcoming substantial clinical challenges (Mei et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Strengths of rapamycin include its well-established mechanism of action, the significant supportive preclinical data demonstrating improvements in autophagic flux and mitochondrial clearance in RPE models, and its potential to address several key pathological features of dry AMD simultaneously. Weaknesses include the mixed clinical trial outcomes to date, the potential for adverse effects in certain contexts (including decreased visual acuity and retinal thinning), and the observed heterogeneity in therapeutic response among different patient samples. These factors highlight the importance of further mechanistic studies and carefully controlled clinical trials. Overall, rapamycin remains one of the more mechanistically promising candidates for repurposing in dry AMD, yet its future success will depend on how effectively we can tailor its delivery and dosing to maximize protective effects while minimizing risks in the vulnerable RPE of AMD patients (Niu et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022).

In conclusion, rapamycin’s role as an mTORC1 inhibitor with the capacity to induce autophagy and mitophagy presents an exciting therapeutic avenue for addressing the complex pathology of dry AMD. By alleviating the buildup of toxic metabolites and preserving mitochondrial health in RPE cells, rapamycin could potentially slow disease progression and preserve vision. Nonetheless, the balance between benefit and adverse effects remains delicate, and further research is essential to elucidate how best to leverage rapamycin’s molecular actions in a clinically meaningful way. This comprehensive review supports the continued investigation of rapamycin as a candidate for dry AMD therapy, provided that subsequent studies can address the highlighted challenges and refine the therapeutic strategy to achieve consistent, positive clinical outcomes (Mei et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022).
