Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) is a synthetic derivative of fumaric acid that belongs to the class of fumaric acid esters (FAEs) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Chemically, DMF is the dimethyl ester of fumaric acid, with a molecular weight of approximately 144.13 g/mol, and is produced by reacting fumaric acid with methanol in the presence of a strong acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Although fumaric acid occurs naturally as an intermediate in the citric acid cycle, DMF itself is fully synthetically manufactured, conferring the advantages of chemical stability and the ability to precisely modulate its structure to enhance pharmacological properties (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Moreover, DMF is classified as an electrophilic molecule that, due to its α,β-unsaturated ester structure, can covalently modify protein thiols, particularly the cysteine residues within KEAP1, thereby initiating its downstream effects on cellular redox homeostasis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Fumaric acid esters as a class have a long-standing history in pharmacotherapy, originally finding application in dermatology, most notably in the treatment of psoriasis, and have since been repurposed for neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis (MS) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, fumaric acid esters were introduced into clinical practice as antipsoriatic agents in Europe, with formulations such as Fumaderm® entering the market in the 1990s (Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). DMF in particular emerged as a key component in these formulations, and its efficacy in modulating immune responses and suppressing inflammation in skin diseases laid the foundation for its later repurposing in other systemic inflammatory conditions (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Over time, DMF was repurposed and further developed as an oral agent for the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), culminating in its FDA approval in 2013 under the trade name Tecfidera® by Biogen (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163). Clinical trials, including large-scale phase 3 studies, have demonstrated its favorable safety profile and efficacy in reducing relapse rates and slowing disability progression in MS patients (Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 14–16). Although there is no extensive historical record of DMF being used directly for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other primary ocular diseases, recent preclinical findings have indicated that its potent activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway may confer significant protective effects on the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This has sparked considerable interest in repurposing DMF for ocular indications such as geographic atrophy, a late stage of dry AMD, by leveraging its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities observed in nonocular settings (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, DMF functions primarily as a prodrug; upon oral administration it is rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases within the gastrointestinal tract to yield its active metabolite, monomethyl fumarate (MMF) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). The pharmacodynamic actions of DMF principally involve the electrophilic modification of specific cysteine residues—most notably cysteine 151—on Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Under physiological conditions, KEAP1 binds to and retains the transcription factor Nrf2 in the cytoplasm, targeting it for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. However, when DMF covalently modifies KEAP1, it disrupts this complex, allowing Nrf2 to dissociate and translocate into the nucleus (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). In the nucleus, Nrf2 binds to antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoters of numerous genes encoding cytoprotective enzymes, including glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), and various enzymes involved in glutathione (GSH) synthesis and regeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). These molecular interactions lead to enhanced antioxidant defenses, improved detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and overall better maintenance of cellular redox balance (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). In addition to its role in promoting antioxidant gene expression via Nrf2 activation, DMF has been shown to have immunomodulatory properties; it can shift cytokine profiles by increasing interleukin-4 (IL-4)–expressing CD4+ T cells and decreasing the production of proinflammatory cytokines such as interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and interleukin-17 (IL-17) (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Furthermore, DMF has been reported to inhibit nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation in certain cellular contexts, thus contributing to a reduction in inflammatory signaling independently of Nrf2 (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Together, these molecular actions result in lowered cellular oxidative stress and an improved inflammatory milieu, which are critical factors implicated in the pathogenesis of chronic degenerative diseases (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry AMD, particularly the geographic atrophy form, is characterized by the gradual degeneration of RPE cells, which leads to subsequent photoreceptor loss and irreversible vision impairment. Central to the pathophysiology of dry AMD are oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation that progressively compromise RPE viability and function (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). The hypothesis being explored is that DMF, through its robust activation of the Nrf2 pathway, can enhance the expression of ARE-driven genes that encode for antioxidant and cytoprotective proteins, thereby counteracting the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in the RPE (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 13–14). In particular, the upregulation of enzymes involved in glutathione synthesis is expected to increase intracellular levels of GSH, a critical thiol antioxidant that protects mitochondrial membranes and supports cellular bioenergetics (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Preclinical studies in retinal models have demonstrated that DMF can effectively preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and reduce the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β), both of which are hallmarks of RPE distress under oxidative challenge (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Given that the RPE is highly metabolically active and particularly vulnerable to cumulative oxidative damage, the sustained activation of Nrf2 by DMF following oral dosing is anticipated to provide continuous reinforcement of antioxidant defenses and maintain mitochondrial integrity in these cells (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 3–5; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). Moreover, by mitigating inflammatory signaling, DMF may not only protect the RPE but also contribute to a more favorable microenvironment that limits the propagation of cell death signals, thus potentially slowing the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Collectively, these expected cellular effects support the rationale for using DMF as an intervention to preserve retinal structure and function by lowering oxidative damage and supporting bioenergetics in the RPE.

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential of dimethyl fumarate as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD rests on a solid mechanistic rationale combined with an established clinical pedigree in other indications. One of the primary strengths of DMF is its well-characterized pharmacological profile; it is FDA-approved for multiple sclerosis and has been safely administered to thousands of patients over several years, which significantly mitigates the risk and regulatory hurdles typically associated with repurposed drugs (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). The dual actions of DMF—in particular, its ability to both activate the Nrf2 pathway and attenuate proinflammatory signals—directly target the underlying pathological processes in dry AMD, where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central drivers of RPE degeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In vitro studies have provided encouraging evidence that DMF increases intracellular glutathione levels and protects RPE cells from oxidative insults, findings that are directly translatable to the pathobiology of dry AMD (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Nonetheless, several challenges remain. Although DMF is known to be effective in MS and psoriasis, the ocular milieu presents unique pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic challenges that may not be fully addressed by the current oral formulations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18). The rapid hydrolysis of DMF to MMF means that, while the active metabolite does exert therapeutic effects, fine-tuning the dosing regimen to ensure adequate drug levels in the retina while minimizing systemic side effects is necessary (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). In addition, common adverse reactions associated with DMF, such as gastrointestinal discomfort and flushing, though generally mild to moderate, could be more problematic in the typically elderly dry AMD population, necessitating careful monitoring and potentially modified dosing strategies (Camelo, 2025, p. 17; Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13). There is also the question of whether systemic administration of DMF can generate sufficient concentrations in the retina to achieve a meaningful therapeutic effect. While emerging evidence suggests that DMF can cross the blood-retinal barrier and activate Nrf2 in retinal cells (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3), further pharmacokinetic and translational studies are warranted to confirm its retinal bioavailability and the optimal dosing regimen for ocular indications.

Another consideration is the complexity of dry AMD itself, which is a slowly progressive, multifactorial disease with contributions from genetic predispositions, environmental exposures, and systemic metabolic disturbances. It remains to be seen whether the monotherapeutic approach of DMF, targeting primarily oxidative stress via Nrf2 activation, will be sufficient to halt or reverse disease progression, or whether combination therapies will ultimately be required (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Furthermore, while the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms of DMF are well supported by in vitro data and animal studies, there is still limited clinical data on its efficacy in ocular disease settings. Early-phase clinical trials aimed at evaluating DMF in geographic atrophy have to rigorously assess both structural outcomes (e.g., changes in the area of atrophy) and functional endpoints (e.g., visual acuity, retinal sensitivity) to establish its therapeutic benefit in dry AMD (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Despite these limitations, the strengths of DMF are compelling. The drug’s ability to upregulate a broad spectrum of cytoprotective genes via the Nrf2 pathway makes it a versatile candidate for mitigating the oxidative and inflammatory stress that drives RPE degeneration. The fact that DMF has already cleared extensive regulatory and clinical safety evaluations in nonocular indications is a significant advantage, as it greatly accelerates the translational pathway compared to a novel chemical entity (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Additionally, the repurposing of an already approved drug leverages existing manufacturing, formulation, and distribution infrastructure, favorably impacting the cost and timeline associated with drug development (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

In summary, the comprehensive literature review supports the potential of DMF to serve as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its mechanism of action—centered on Nrf2 activation leading to enhanced antioxidant capacity along with anti-inflammatory effects—directly addresses the key pathophysiological mechanisms implicated in dry AMD. The extensive clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis provides a reliable safety and tolerability framework, which is crucial for rapid repositioning into a new clinical area such as geographic atrophy (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). However, it is essential to conduct targeted preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials specifically in ocular disease models to optimize dosing, confirm retinal delivery, and demonstrate clinical efficacy before advancing to larger randomized controlled trials (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Overall, while challenges remain regarding optimal application in the retinal context and potential side effects in an older patient population, DMF—by virtue of its dual antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms and robust clinical background—stands as a viable candidate that merits further investigation for the treatment of dry AMD.

Given the current evidence, the following recommendations are proposed for advancing DMF as a candidate for dry AMD:  

1. Conduct detailed pharmacokinetic studies in animal models to assess the retinal bioavailability of DMF and its active metabolite MMF following systemic administration. This should include studies comparing different dosing schedules and formulations to optimize retinal exposure without exacerbating systemic adverse effects (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2).  

2. Develop and validate preclinical models of dry AMD that recapitulate the key features of human geographic atrophy, with a focus on evaluating the efficacy of DMF in protecting RPE cells against oxidative stress and preserving mitochondrial function (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

3. Investigate the potential benefits of combining DMF with other therapeutic agents that target complementary pathways in dry AMD. For example, agents that modulate complement activation or improve choroidal blood flow may synergize with the Nrf2-mediated antioxidant mechanism of DMF (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).  

4. Initiate early-phase clinical trials in patients with geographic atrophy to establish proof of concept. These studies should include robust biomarker assessments (e.g., measurement of ARE gene expression, retinal imaging for atrophy progression, and functional visual outcomes) to correlate molecular effects with clinical benefit (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

5. Carefully monitor the safety profile of DMF in the elderly population, as the incidence of gastrointestinal side effects and lymphopenia may differ compared to the population with MS. Consider the feasibility of modified-release formulations or alternative routes of administration (e.g., topical ocular delivery) to minimize systemic side effects while maximizing retinal drug concentrations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18).

Overall, the repurposing of dimethyl fumarate for dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a robust mechanistic framework and a significant body of preclinical and clinical data generated in other indications. Its capacity to activate the Nrf2 pathway, enhance mitochondrial glutathione synthesis, and modulate inflammatory responses in RPE cells directly addresses several pivotal aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). While there are challenges regarding optimal retinal delivery and management of systemic adverse effects, the clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis lends considerable support to its translational potential. Consequently, dimethyl fumarate represents a well‐justified and attractive therapeutic candidate for further exploration in the treatment of dry AMD, warranting additional preclinical optimization and clinical investigation to fully define its role in preserving visual function in patients affected by this progressive degenerative disease (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trolox is a synthetic, water-soluble analog of vitamin E widely used as a reference phenolic “chain-breaking” antioxidant in chemical assays and as a biological probe in cells and tissues, including retinal systems (e.g., ARPE-19 RPE, cultured retina) (Zuluaga et al., 2017; Garcia-Medina et al., 2020). In the dry AMD/RPE literature, Trolox is explicitly described as the vitamin E–like antioxidant moiety of troglitazone; in that context it functioned as a stand-alone antioxidant that reproduced troglitazone’s protective effects in ARPE-19 cells exposed to oxidized LDL (oxLDL) (Choi, 2019). Within the chemical class framework, Trolox is a tocopherol analog and a hindered phenolic chain-breaking antioxidant that donates H-atoms to lipid peroxyl radicals and interrupts propagation of lipid autoxidation; this class and related tocopherol analogs are highlighted in the RPE oxLDL literature and in foundational mechanistic work on phenolic antioxidants (Gnanaguru et al., 2022). The vitamin E family is also known to operate in mitochondrial membranes and other lipid-rich compartments; Trolox shares the chromanol phenolic headgroup chemistry responsible for peroxyl radical scavenging, albeit with enhanced aqueous solubility relative to α-tocopherol (Edwards et al., 2022). For RPE experimentation, Trolox is available as a commercial reagent; in the cited ARPE-19 oxLDL studies a concentrated DMSO stock was prepared and working concentrations from ~0.16 to 10.4 μM were tested with final DMSO kept below 0.4% v/v (Choi, 2019). In these same ARPE-19 models, a fluorescein (FITC)–conjugated Trolox derivative localized to intracellular membrane organelles, suggesting that despite higher aqueous solubility, Trolox partitions to (or associates with) organellar membranes such as lysosomes and possibly mitochondria in RPE cells (Choi, 2019).

Therapeutic History  
Multiple independent lines of evidence document Trolox’s antioxidant and cytoprotective actions in retinal models, but there are no animal or human clinical trials of Trolox for dry AMD/geographic atrophy, and human data for vitamin E alone in AMD are mixed or negative outside of multi-antioxidant formulations.

- ARPE-19/oxLDL RPE models (dry AMD–relevant): OxLDL induces ROS, lysosomal destabilization, and NF-κB activation in ARPE-19 cells; Trolox alone mimicked troglitazone’s protective profile by suppressing oxLDL-induced ROS, preserving lysosomal integrity, and inhibiting NF-κB nuclear translocation in a dose-dependent manner, with robust effects at 10.4 μM after 28–36 h of oxLDL exposure (Choi, 2019). Rosiglitazone, a PPARγ agonist lacking a phenolic antioxidant moiety, did not protect, and troglitazone remained protective despite PPARγ knockdown, supporting an antioxidant (phenolic) mechanism of action (Choi, 2019). The authors place these effects in an AMD-relevant cascade: lipid oxidation → ROS → lysosomal destabilization + NF-κB activation → NLRP3 inflammasome → RPE death; they propose Trolox acts upstream by limiting ROS, stabilizing lysosomes, and blunting NF-κB priming, although inflammasome activation was not directly measured (Choi, 2019).  
- Phenolic SAR and potency context in RPE: A more recent screen identified sterically hindered phenols (e.g., BHT, PMC) as more potent than Trolox in protecting RPE from oxLDL-induced death, with evidence for lysosomal localization and stabilization; a PMC analog also increased NPC-1 and reduced cholesterol after oxLDL, indicating effects on lysosomal lipid handling beyond simple antioxidant scavenging (Gnanaguru et al., 2022; Choi, 2019). These data place Trolox within a broader phenolic antioxidant class that is active in RPE lipid-oxidation stress but is not the most potent scaffold against the oxLDL insult (Choi, 2019).  
- Phototoxic lipofuscin/A2E chemistry: In a cell-free A2E photooxidation assay, Trolox reduced A2E loss during 430-nm illumination, consistent with singlet-oxygen/reactive species quenching; however, a comparator (OT-674) quenched singlet oxygen more efficiently than Trolox or α-tocopherol, and under broader 430-nm illumination the differences among Trolox and α-tocopherol were less pronounced, suggesting limited superiority of Trolox in this photochemical context (Zhou et al., 2008).  
- Retinal ganglion cell oxidative injury (non-AMD): Trolox reduced RGC death induced by hydrogen peroxide and superoxide generation in vitro, reinforcing broad neuroprotective antioxidant activity in retinal neurons (Wang et al., 2021).  
- Retinal tissue and diabetic retina contexts: Trolox reduced TBARS (lipid peroxidation) in cultured rat retina and has been reported to support pericyte regeneration in diabetic mice; Trolox-containing antioxidant mixtures reduced NF-κB activation, nitric oxide/nitrotyrosine, TBARS/ROS, and preserved antioxidant enzymes (SOD, catalase, glutathione-related enzymes) in retinal vascular cell models and diabetic retina (Garcia-Medina et al., 2020).  
- Human AMD clinical context for vitamin E: High-quality randomized trials (AREDS/AREDS2) support benefit of multi-agent antioxidant formulations that include vitamin E in slowing AMD progression, but vitamin E alone has not consistently shown benefit; several reviews/meta-analyses conclude little or no effect for vitamin E monotherapy and emphasize inconsistent observational data, limiting attribution of clinical effects to vitamin E or to any analog such as Trolox (Wang et al., 2021; Dziedziak et al., 2021; Edwards et al., 2022; Milbury, 2006).

Mechanism of Action  
Mechanistic evidence in ARPE-19 supports that Trolox acts as a phenolic chain-breaking antioxidant that intercepts oxLDL-driven ROS, preserves lysosomal integrity, and suppresses NF-κB nuclear translocation, thereby potentially blocking both the priming (signal 1) and activation (signal 2) arms of NLRP3 inflammasome signaling upstream of RPE death (Choi, 2019).

- Chain-breaking antioxidant chemistry: As a tocopherol analog with a phenolic chromanol headgroup, Trolox donates a hydrogen atom to lipid peroxyl/alkoxyl radicals, forming a relatively stable phenoxyl radical and interrupting propagation of polyunsaturated lipid autoxidation in membranes; this class behavior is emphasized in the AMD-relevant phenolic antioxidant literature and vitamin E chemistry (Gnanaguru et al., 2022). Vitamin E analogs can protect mitochondrial membranes by reacting with peroxyl radicals in lipid bilayers, an effect relevant to the inner mitochondrial membrane’s high cardiolipin/PUFA content, although Trolox-specific mitochondrial readouts were not reported in ARPE-19 (Edwards et al., 2022).  
- Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory signaling in RPE: In ARPE-19 cells subjected to oxLDL, Trolox dramatically suppressed intracellular ROS at 28 h; the ROS probe used detects H₂O₂, peroxynitrite, and hydroxyl radicals (not superoxide), indicating Trolox’s activity spans these species in this model (Choi, 2019). Trolox dose-dependently inhibited oxLDL-induced NF-κB nuclear translocation; this likely reflects lowered redox-sensitive signaling and/or reduced lysosomal damage-associated molecular patterning that can feed NF-κB activation (Choi, 2019). By suppressing NF-κB priming and preventing lysosomal destabilization (cathepsin release), Trolox is positioned mechanistically to blunt the two classical signals that drive NLRP3 activation in oxLDL-challenged RPE, although caspase-1 activity and IL-1β maturation were not assayed here (Choi, 2019).  
- Lysosomal stabilization and organelle targeting: Trolox significantly increased intact LysoTracker-positive particles after oxLDL, rescuing the 36 h oxLDL-induced loss of lysosomal staining at 10.4 μM; FITC-Trolox localized to membrane organelles (lysosomes/possibly mitochondria), consistent with direct membrane protection against peroxidation or ROS-induced destabilization (Choi, 2019).  
- Distinction from PPARγ agonism: Troglitazone’s protection persisted after PPARγ knockdown and rosiglitazone failed to protect; Trolox reproduced troglitazone’s effects, establishing that the phenolic antioxidant moiety (not PPARγ activation) mediates cytoprotection in this RPE oxLDL model (Choi, 2019).  
- Vitamin E pro-oxidant liabilities relevant to AMD: Tocopherols can, under certain conditions, reduce lipid hydroperoxides or redox-active metals to catalyze fragmentation of hydroperoxy endoperoxides, yielding γ-hydroxyalkenals and protein adducts such as carboxyethylpyrrole (CEP); CEP adducts are elevated in AMD tissue and can be pathogenic (angiogenic/immune activation), indicating that vitamin E chemistry is context-dependent and can potentially exacerbate formation of toxic lipid-derived aldehydes if not paired with appropriate co-antioxidants/metal control (Gu et al., 2011).  
- Transport/delivery context: Retinal vitamin E levels reflect systemic availability and transport via lipoproteins and α-tocopherol transfer proteins; the BRB poses delivery constraints, and α-TTP oligomers facilitate endothelial (not epithelial) transport, complicating systemic delivery to the outer retina/RPE (Edwards et al., 2022). Although Trolox is water-soluble and readily used in vitro, its in vivo distribution to retinal membranes is not characterized in the cited AMD-relevant literature, and targeted delivery (e.g., mitochondria-targeted antioxidants) may be required to reach mitochondrial inner membranes efficiently (Baksheeva et al., 2018).  
- Comparative potency within the class: Hindered phenols (e.g., PMC, BHT) outperformed Trolox in oxLDL-induced ARPE-19 cytotoxicity screens, and PMC additionally modulated lysosomal cholesterol handling (↑NPC-1, ↓cholesterol), suggesting that steric/electronic tuning of phenolic scaffolds can augment both antioxidant and lysosomal pathways more effectively than Trolox (Gnanaguru et al., 2022; Choi, 2019).

Expected Effect  
Under the stated hypothesis—Trolox scavenges mitochondrial lipid peroxyl radicals to preserve inner membrane integrity and electron transport in dry AMD—the expected proximal effects in RPE oxidative-lipid models are: (1) reduced intracellular ROS burden, particularly H₂O₂/peroxynitrite/hydroxyl products detected by standard ROS probes, (2) stabilization of lysosomal membranes against oxLDL-induced destabilization, (3) suppression of NF-κB nuclear translocation (priming), and (4) consequent blunting of downstream inflammasome activation; these effects are documented in ARPE-19/oxLDL at 10.4 μM Trolox (Choi, 2019). In the specific assay context proposed by the team (ARPE-19 under oxidative stress), Trolox is expected to:  

- Lower DCF-type ROS readouts after 28 h oxLDL, consistent with prior ARPE-19 results in which Trolox produced a dramatic reduction of intracellular ROS (Choi, 2019).  
- Restore LysoTracker-positive lysosomal particle counts at 36 h in oxLDL-treated ARPE-19 at the highest micromolar dose tested (10.4 μM), as observed previously; lower Trolox doses are likely insufficient for lysosomal rescue in this system (Choi, 2019).  
- Inhibit NF-κB nuclear translocation at 36 h in oxLDL-exposed ARPE-19 in a dose-dependent manner, with complete suppression at 10.4 μM and partial/absent suppression at 0.16–1.3 μM (Choi, 2019).  
- Notably, the ROS assay kits used in the cited studies do not detect superoxide, so additional measurements (e.g., MitoSOX) will be required to assess superoxide-specific effects in mitochondria, which is relevant for testing the stated mitochondrial hypothesis (Choi, 2019).

Although Trolox’s mitochondrial bioenergetic effects were not reported in the ARPE-19 oxLDL studies, vitamin E analogs are the major chain-breaking antioxidants in mitochondrial membranes and can quench peroxyl radicals propagating in inner membrane lipids; thus, if Trolox reaches mitochondrial membranes in RPE (as suggested by FITC-Trolox organelle localization), it is reasonable to expect partial preservation of Δψm and ATP under lipid-oxidation stress, contingent on subcellular delivery and radical burden (Edwards et al., 2022; Choi, 2019). The A2E/singlet-oxygen literature suggests Trolox will attenuate photooxidative lipofuscin chemistry but may be less efficient than specialized singlet-oxygen quenchers (OT-674), implying limited efficacy in light-dominated injury contexts relative to oxLDL-driven lipid oxidation (Zhou et al., 2008). Finally, expected downstream impact on NLRP3 is inferential (two-signal model) since caspase-1/IL-1β readouts were not measured in Trolox-treated ARPE-19, so inflammasome suppression should be verified explicitly if that is a target endpoint (Choi, 2019).

Overall Evaluation  
Trolox is a mechanistically plausible, well-behaved phenolic antioxidant probe that shows reproducible cytoprotection in an AMD-relevant RPE stress model (oxLDL), with documented suppression of ROS, preservation of lysosomal integrity, and inhibition of NF-κB activation; however, as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, it has notable limitations: absence of mitochondrial bioenergetic evidence in RPE, lack of in vivo efficacy/delivery data, potential vitamin E–class pro-oxidant liabilities, and inferiority to more potent hindered phenol scaffolds and targeted antioxidants in several relevant contexts.

Strengths  
- Clear in vitro activity in AMD-relevant RPE models: Across multiple independent excerpts of the same ARPE-19/oxLDL work, Trolox robustly reduced ROS at 28 h, stabilized lysosomes at 36 h, and suppressed NF-κB at higher micromolar dose, establishing on-pathway effects relevant to lipid oxidation, lysosomal integrity, and inflammatory priming (Choi, 2019). The PPARγ-independence and failure of rosiglitazone confirm that phenolic antioxidant chemistry, not nuclear receptor modulation, mediates these effects (Unknown Reference).  
- Organelle association and lysosomal targeting plausibility: FITC-Trolox localizes to membrane organelles; combined with prior demonstrations that inhibiting lipid peroxidation preserves lysosomes, this supports a direct membrane protective mechanism that is relevant for lysosomal injury in oxLDL-challenged RPE (Choi, 2019).  
- Class coherence and SAR support: Trolox’s efficacy fits within a broader hindered phenol paradigm in RPE, and more potent phenolic analogs (e.g., PMC) outperform Trolox and additionally modulate lysosomal cholesterol handling (↑NPC-1), indicating the pathway is druggable and phenolic scaffolds are tunable (Gnanaguru et al., 2022; Choi, 2019).  
- Cross-model antioxidant precedents: Trolox mitigates A2E photooxidation in a cell-free system, protects RGCs from H₂O₂/superoxide, reduces lipid peroxidation in cultured retina, and benefits diabetic retinal endpoints in antioxidant mixtures—evidence that Trolox engages retinal oxidative pathways across cell types and paradigms (Zhou et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2021; Garcia-Medina et al., 2020).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- No mitochondrial bioenergetic validation in RPE: The ARPE-19 oxLDL studies did not measure Δψm, ATP, oxygen consumption, or mitochondrial lipid peroxidation; thus the central hypothesis (inner membrane peroxyl scavenging preserves electron transport) remains untested in RPE, and the available ROS assay did not detect superoxide, limiting mechanistic resolution in mitochondria (Choi, 2019). By contrast, mitochondria-targeted antioxidants such as SkQ1 demonstrate efficacy and bioavailability in in vivo retinal oxidative stress models, highlighting a potential delivery disadvantage for non-targeted Trolox (Baksheeva et al., 2018).  
- Dosing window and endpoint sensitivity: In ARPE-19, Trolox’s full effects on lysosomal rescue and NF-κB suppression were confined to the highest tested dose (10.4 μM), with lower doses ineffective for these endpoints, suggesting a narrow efficacy window under oxLDL burden (Choi, 2019).  
- Phenolic pro-oxidant potential under metal/peroxide conditions: Vitamin E chemistry can promote fragmentation of lipid hydroperoxides and formation of toxic aldehydes (e.g., CEP) in the presence of redox-active metals; CEP adducts are elevated in AMD and are pathogenic, raising a risk that under certain retinal microenvironments Trolox or its phenoxyl radical could exacerbate deleterious lipid-fragmentation chemistry unless combined with appropriate co-antioxidants/metal control (Gu et al., 2011).  
- Translational uncertainty from vitamin E clinical data: Vitamin E alone has not consistently prevented AMD in human studies; benefits arise in combination formulations (AREDS/AREDS2), making attribution to vitamin E or extrapolation to Trolox as a monotherapy weak, and suggesting that multi-target, multi-antioxidant regimens or more potent/targeted phenolic analogs are more plausible clinical strategies (Wang et al., 2021; Dziedziak et al., 2021; Edwards et al., 2022).  
- Comparative inferiority to optimized scaffolds in key contexts: Hindered phenols such as BHT/PMC outperform Trolox in oxLDL-RPE cytoprotection; OT-674 outperforms Trolox in singlet-oxygen quenching relevant to lipofuscin photooxidation; these head-to-head data argue Trolox is better deployed as a mechanistic probe or reference rather than as the lead therapeutic (Choi, 2019; Gnanaguru et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2008).  
- Delivery/BRB issues: In vivo delivery of vitamin E–like agents to the RPE is constrained by the BRB and lipoprotein/α-TTP–dependent transport; no pharmacokinetic or retinal distribution data exist for Trolox in the cited AMD context, suggesting uncertain target engagement in RPE in vivo (Edwards et al., 2022).

Programmatic Implications  
- As a tool compound, Trolox is well-suited for de-risking the oxLDL→ROS→lysosome→NF-κB→NLRP3 cascade in RPE and establishing that phenolic chain-breaking antioxidants modulate upstream injury steps; its water solubility and reproducible in vitro effects are practical advantages (Choi, 2019).  
- For therapeutic development, Trolox itself is a weak candidate relative to mitochondria-targeted antioxidants and more potent hindered phenols; the near-term focus should be on (a) confirming mitochondrial protection endpoints in RPE (Δψm, ATP, mitochondrial lipid peroxidation) to validate the mitochondrial hypothesis mechanistically and (b) advancing optimized phenolic scaffolds or mitochondria-targeted constructs with superior potency and delivery characteristics (Choi, 2019; Baksheeva et al., 2018).  
- Given vitamin E pro-oxidant risks, incorporate mechanistic controls for hydroperoxide fragmentation and CEP formation in RPE assays, and test combinations with co-antioxidants/metal chelators under conditions that model retinal metal/protein adduct environments (Gu et al., 2011).  
- Do not use TEAC/Trolox-equivalent chemical antioxidant capacity as a surrogate for in-cell efficacy; chemical assays are valuable for initial screening but are poor predictors of subcellular targeting, redox network effects, or clinical performance in the retina (Zuluaga et al., 2017).

Conclusion  
Trolox demonstrates consistent phenolic antioxidant protection in an AMD-relevant ARPE-19 oxLDL model by lowering ROS, preserving lysosomes, and suppressing NF-κB, with plausible but unproven mitochondrial benefits in RPE; however, its therapeutic attractiveness is limited by lack of mitochondrial bioenergetic evidence in RPE, absence of in vivo efficacy/delivery data, potential pro-oxidant liabilities of the vitamin E class, and inferiority to more potent or targeted antioxidants in relevant assays (Choi, 2019; Gu et al., 2011; Baksheeva et al., 2018). As a program decision: use Trolox as a mechanistic positive control and profiling probe for the lipid-oxidation/lysosomal/NF-κB axis in RPE, but prioritize development of mitochondria-targeted antioxidants and optimized hindered phenolic scaffolds (e.g., PMC-like) that have demonstrated higher potency and better alignment with retinal delivery challenges (Gnanaguru et al., 2022; Choi, 2019; Baksheeva et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History (Expanded)  
- AREDS formulations: Benefit in slowing progression to advanced AMD with multi-antioxidant combinations that include vitamin E underscores the plausibility of antioxidant strategies but does not validate vitamin E monotherapy; generalizability and attribution to vitamin E are limited (Wang et al., 2021).  
- Vitamin E alone: Randomized and meta-analytic evidence conclude little or no effect of vitamin E alone for AMD onset/progression; population studies are inconsistent, undermining confidence in translating a single vitamin E analog like Trolox as a standalone therapy (Dziedziak et al., 2021; Milbury, 2006).  
- Phenolic analog discovery: In an AMD-relevant RPE death assay triggered by oxLDL, hindered phenols emerged as superior to Trolox with mechanistic hints of lysosomal membrane stabilization and lipid handling improvements (↑NPC-1), providing a rational medicinal chemistry trajectory away from Trolox (Gnanaguru et al., 2022).  
- RPE in vitro replication and gaps: The ARPE-19 studies explicitly note that all experiments were conducted in a single immortalized line, that the ROS kit did not detect superoxide, and that LysoTracker quantification has size/clumping limitations, arguing for replication in primary hf-RPE and with improved quantitative organelle and ROS probes; no in vivo retinal model data for Trolox are reported (Choi, 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Apocynin (Sigma-Aldrich A1788) is a naturally derived, methoxy-substituted catechol originally isolated from the medicinal herb Picrorhiza kurroa, which has a long history of use in traditional Ayurvedic medicine. It is a small molecule with a molecular weight of approximately 166.17 Da and modest lipophilicity (logP ~ 0.83) that allows it to readily cross cellular membranes and even the blood–brain barrier. As a member of the NADPH oxidase (NOX) inhibitor class, it has been historically used to modulate oxidative stress in a variety of preclinical disease models. The compound’s origin is rooted in natural product chemistry, and its attractive small-molecule structure has encouraged detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic investigations in rodent models, where it has been administered intravenously and orally to assess tissue distribution and rapid clearance kinetics. Its chemical profile and natural derivation position it within a class of therapeutic candidates that have been widely evaluated for their antioxidant properties and their ability to attenuate NOX-mediated reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory diseases (Liu et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Preclinical studies have evaluated apocynin in a range of animal models that address oxidative stress–related pathologies. In cardiovascular and cerebrovascular research, for example, apocynin has been shown to reduce NADPH oxidase activity and resultant oxidative damage in models of isoproterenol-induced cardiac hypertrophy, diabetic cardiac remodeling, and brain oxidative stress associated with high-fat diets (Liu et al., 2020). Its pharmacokinetic profile in mice indicates a rapid plasma peak and an extremely short half-life of around 3–4 minutes after intravenous dosing, with extensive clearance by the kidneys (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2020). In respiratory research, a completed Phase 1 randomized trial in COPD patients demonstrated that nebulized apocynin was well tolerated, produced short-term reductions in exhaled oxidative markers such as hydrogen peroxide and nitrite, and did not affect lung function or systemic safety parameters (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010). Despite these encouraging results, there remains limited data on the longer-term systemic safety or adverse-event profiles of apocynin. Importantly, while apocynin has been extensively studied in cardiovascular and respiratory indications, as well as in models of neurodegeneration and hepatic and renal injury, there is minimal direct evidence of its use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models or in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells such as ARPE-19 (Drummond & Sobey, 2014). Nonetheless, since dry AMD pathogenesis involves oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction within the RPE, the demonstrated efficacy of apocynin in modulating NADPH oxidase–mediated ROS production in other organs builds a rationale for its repurposing for this indication.

Mechanism of Action:  
The central proposed mechanism by which apocynin exerts its therapeutic effects involves the inhibition of NADPH oxidase, particularly by blocking the assembly of the enzyme complex. NADPH oxidases are multi-subunit enzymatic complexes responsible for the regulated generation of superoxide and downstream reactive oxygen species. In cells, the assembly and activation of NOX, especially isoforms such as NOX2, require the translocation of cytosolic regulatory subunits—most notably p47^phox—to the membrane-bound catalytic core. Early studies reported that apocynin can prevent the translocation of p47^phox to the plasma membrane, thereby inhibiting the assembly of the active NOX2 complex and reducing the production of superoxide, which secondarily lowers the formation of hydrogen peroxide and other ROS (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Drummond & Sobey, 2014).  
However, the molecular pharmacology of apocynin is more complex. Its inhibitory activity appears to be dependent on metabolic activation by myeloperoxidase (MPO) in the presence of hydrogen peroxide. This conversion supposedly generates reactive quinone species or even a dimeric form (diapocynin) that can covalently modify cysteine residues in p47^phox, thus interfering with its function (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Ismaeel et al., 2018). Some studies, though, have failed to detect diapocynin in vivo, suggesting that other metabolites, such as apocynin glycoconjugates, might instead be responsible for its activity (Liu et al., 2020). Moreover, apocynin has been reported to possess direct antioxidant properties at higher concentrations by scavenging non-radical oxidants such as hypochlorous acid and hydrogen peroxide, independently of its effects on NOX assembly (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Ismaeel et al., 2018).  
In vitro studies in various cell types have yielded conflicting data regarding whether apocynin primarily functions as a NOX-specific inhibitor or as a broad-spectrum antioxidant. In cell types that are rich in peroxidase activity, such as neutrophils, apocynin’s conversion to an active inhibitor appears robust. In contrast, in cells with lower MPO activity, such as some epithelial or neuronal cells, its efficacy as a NOX inhibitor may be diminished, and observed benefits might be attributable to direct ROS scavenging (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2020). Within the context of RPE cells, the candidate hypothesis posits that apocynin will inhibit the translocation of p47^phox during NOX2 activation, thereby reducing cytosolic ROS production while also limiting the spillover of ROS into mitochondria, which would otherwise trigger mitochondrial membrane potential collapse, fragmentation, and reduced oxygen consumption rate (OCR) (Liu et al., 2020; Liu, 2023). This mechanism, if operative in RPE cells such as ARPE-19, would help preserve mitochondrial integrity by preventing excess ROS accumulation and the ensuing mitochondrial dysfunction—a key pathogenic process in dry AMD (Shu et al., 2023; Liu, 2023).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed mechanism, the use of apocynin in in vitro assays with ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE cultures is expected to yield several beneficial outcomes. First, by blocking p47^phox translocation, apocynin should reduce the assembly of the NOX complex, particularly NOX2, thereby decreasing the production of superoxide and hydrogen peroxide. This reduction in ROS should lead to lower levels of oxidative stress markers, as measured by assays such as lucigenin chemiluminescence, dihydroethidium (DHE) fluorescence, and malondialdehyde (MDA) assays (Liu et al., 2020).  
Second, because ROS are known to damage mitochondrial components, it is expected that apocynin treatment will protect against mitochondrial dysfunction. In ARPE-19 cells challenged with hydrogen peroxide or other oxidative stress inducers, apocynin should help preserve the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), prevent mitochondrial fragmentation, and maintain basal oxygen consumption rates (OCR). This should result in reduced upregulation of proangiogenic factors like VEGF and a decrease in inflammatory cytokine production that can exacerbate retinal degeneration. In effect, apocynin would act not only to maintain mitochondrial function by limiting local oxidative damage but also to modulate the broader redox environment that contributes to RPE cell dysfunction in dry AMD (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Ismaeel et al., 2018).  
As a consequence, in the experimental assay proposed by the team, treatment of ARPE-19 cells with apocynin under conditions of induced oxidative stress should demonstrate a measurable preservation of Δψm by fluorescent imaging or flow cytometry using potentiometric dyes, maintenance of basal OCR as measured via Seahorse extracellular flux analysis, and a reduction in mitochondrial ROS accumulation by specific mitochondria-targeted ROS indicators. Apocynin represents a promising candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its potential to target a core pathogenic mechanism—the dysregulated production of ROS via NADPH oxidase assembly. One of the strengths of apocynin is its extensive preclinical history demonstrating its capacity to lower oxidative stress in various organs, including the heart, liver, brain, and lung, with documented rapid distribution to tissues and a well-characterized pharmacokinetic profile in animal models (Liu et al., 2020; Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014). Its observed safety in a small Phase 1 clinical study in COPD patients further bolsters the case for its safety on at least short-term administration in humans (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010). Moreover, its chemical simplicity as a natural product and its relatively low molecular weight make it attractive for further formulation studies in ocular indications.  
Nevertheless, significant weaknesses and challenges must be addressed. A major issue is the ongoing debate regarding the exact mechanism of action of apocynin. While some studies support its role as a NOX inhibitor via prevention of p47^phox translocation, others have demonstrated that its activity may be largely due to its direct antioxidant properties or require metabolic activation by MPO—a process that may not be robust in retinal pigment epithelial cells (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014). This mechanistic ambiguity raises concerns about its efficacy and specificity in the RPE, where the peroxidase activity necessary for conversion to an active form may be limited.  
Furthermore, the extremely short plasma half-life (approximately 3–4 minutes) observed in rodent models indicates that apocynin is rapidly cleared, which could limit its therapeutic window and necessitate frequent dosing or the development of modified formulations such as a sustained-release ocular implant or a mitochondria-targeted derivative (e.g., mito-apocynin) to achieve prolonged local concentrations in the retina (Liu et al., 2020; Liu, 2023). Another concern is that, despite the general rationale for reducing oxidative stress in the RPE, there is a paucity of direct evidence from ARPE-19 or primary RPE models showing that apocynin effectively prevents mitochondrial fragmentation, preserves the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), or maintains basal oxygen consumption rates. Although some studies have demonstrated that NOX inhibition can reduce ROS levels in retinal cells, apocynin’s specific action in the context of dry AMD has not been rigorously documented (Shu et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2020). Additionally, the variability of its effects across different cell types—dependent on the presence or absence of peroxidase activity—suggests that its efficacy in the RPE may be inconsistent, thereby necessitating further targeted studies.  
There is also the possibility of off-target effects. Because apocynin has been reported to act as a general antioxidant rather than a highly specific NOX inhibitor, it might interfere with normal redox signaling that is essential for cell survival and immune defense, particularly when applied systemically. Caution must be exercised to ensure that suppression of NOX activity does not inadvertently impair protective immune responses or lead to unwanted toxicity, even if short-term clinical data appears reassuring (Drummond & Sobey, 2014; Casas et al., 2015).  
In summary, while the mechanistic rationale behind using apocynin to inhibit NOX assembly in RPE cells is compelling, particularly given the central role of oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD pathogenesis, several critical questions remain. These include the precise mechanism by which apocynin exerts its effects in the RPE, the consistency of its efficacy in protecting mitochondrial function in ARPE-19 cells, its pharmacokinetic limitations, and its potential off-target effects. However, its mechanism remains controversial, and its rapid clearance, potential variability in retinal cells, and limited direct evidence in AMD models represent significant weaknesses that must be overcome through further targeted biochemical, in vitro, and in vivo studies before advancing into clinical trials for dry AMD (Liu et al., 2020; Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010; Shu et al., 2023; Rohowetz et al., 2018; Liu, 2023).

Moreover, efforts to optimize its pharmacokinetic profile—perhaps through formulation modifications or conversion to a mitochondria-targeted analogue—would address one of its key limitations. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin (also known as sirolimus and available as Abcam #ab120224) is a naturally occurring macrolide compound originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus. It belongs to the class of macrocyclic lactones and is known for its potent inhibitory effects on the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). This compound has been extensively used in various contexts such as immunosuppression, cancer therapy, and more recently, as a tool to modulate autophagy in age-related degenerative diseases. In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction and dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), rapamycin is being explored as a repurposed therapeutic candidate with the hypothesis that mTORC1 inhibition will enhance both general autophagy and selective mitophagy. This clearance of reactive oxygen species (ROS)–generating, damaged mitochondria may alleviate oxidative stress, reduce the accumulation of toxic lipofuscin compounds (including A2E), and ultimately slow the progression of dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, rapamycin was first discovered for its potent immunosuppressive properties and later developed for use in preventing transplant rejection and certain cancers. Its ability to inhibit mTORC1 has made it a valuable tool in research related to aging and neurodegeneration. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its effectiveness in modulating autophagy and protecting cellular integrity under stress conditions, particularly in the retinal environment. In animal models of retinal degeneration and even some early clinical trials, rapamycin was shown to reduce the accumulation of autofluorescent granules and inflammatory cytokines in the RPE, which are both hallmarks of dry AMD pathology (Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022). Notably, rapamycin has been administered via diverse routes, including intravitreal and subconjunctival injections, in attempts to treat geographic atrophy or other dry AMD phenotypes, although the clinical outcomes have been mixed. For example, clinical trials such as those referenced in studies with identifiers NCT00766649 and NCT01445548 demonstrated that while rapamycin was generally safe and well-tolerated in ocular applications, its efficacy in slowing down the progression of geographic atrophy and improving visual acuity remained limited (National Eye Institute, 2008; National Eye Institute, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These historical findings highlight both the promise and the challenges associated with translating rapamycin’s mechanistic benefits into robust clinical outcomes for dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary mechanism of rapamycin involves the formation of a complex with the immunophilin FKBP12. This complex binds to mTORC1 and inhibits its kinase activity, leading to a decrease in the phosphorylation of downstream targets such as ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K) and the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 (4EBP1). Under normal circumstances, active mTORC1 suppresses autophagy by phosphorylating these targets, which in turn prevents the formation of autophagosomes. By inhibiting mTORC1, rapamycin effectively removes this blockade, thereby promoting the induction of autophagy as evidenced by increased conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II and clearance of the autophagic substrate p62 (Zhang et al., 2015).

Within retinal pigment epithelial cells, this induction of autophagy is particularly important. RPE cells are responsible for the phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments; a process that generates large amounts of cellular debris and metabolic byproducts such as lipofuscin. In dry AMD, impaired autophagic flux leads to the accumulation of these compounds, which, in turn, contributes to oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Rapamycin’s inhibition of mTORC1 not only enhances general autophagy but also promotes selective mitochondrial clearance (mitophagy). Key players in the mitophagy pathway include the serine/threonine kinase PINK1 and the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin, both of which accumulate on depolarized mitochondria and signal their removal via autophagic mechanisms. By stimulating this PINK1/Parkin pathway, rapamycin enhances the clearance of damaged, ROS-generating mitochondria, thus preserving overall mitochondrial health (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).

Additionally, rapamycin’s downstream effects include activation of transcription factors such as TFEB, which regulates lysosomal biogenesis and further enhances the autophagic process. This dual action—promoting both autophagy and lysosomal function—helps to mitigate the accumulation of toxic aggregates such as lipofuscin and A2E in RPE, therefore reducing oxidative stress and inflammation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). Through these biochemical interactions, rapamycin establishes a cellular environment that is more capable of dealing with metabolic challenges and oxidative damage, both of which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Chang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed hypothesis, the administration of rapamycin in RPE cells is expected to result in a cascade of beneficial cellular events. In our proposed assay, rapamycin is anticipated to inhibit mTORC1 activity, leading to a measurable increase in autophagic flux. This will be evident from the enhanced lipidation of LC3-II, the clearance of p62 (an autophagy adaptor protein that accumulates when autophagy is impaired), and the activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway in response to oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2015).

The specific clearance of damaged mitochondria is particularly critical in the RPE, where mitochondrial dysfunction is a significant contributor to the generation of reactive oxygen species and subsequent cellular damage. By removing these dysfunctional mitochondria, rapamycin is expected to reduce intracellular ROS levels and thereby lower oxidative stress, a driving force in AMD pathology. In parallel, the enhanced autophagic degradation of accumulated lipofuscin and the toxic fluorophore A2E is predicted to further limit the inflammatory and apoptotic cascades triggered by these compounds, thus preserving RPE cell viability and function (Zhang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2025).

Moreover, the expression of PINK1 and Parkin in RPE cells has been well documented, and their activation is indicative of mitophagic turnover. Their proper functioning is a key determinant in mitochondrial quality control, and rapamycin is expected to potentiate this process, ensuring that mitochondria remain healthy and capable of maintaining cellular energy production and reducing the risk of cell death (Pinelli et al., 2025; Hyttinen et al., 2018). Given that impaired mitochondrial function and the resulting energy production deficits are central to the progression of dry AMD, the expected outcomes from rapamycin treatment would include not only a reduction in oxidative stress markers but also improvements in mitochondrial dynamics and overall cellular homeostasis. Such effects would ideally be reflected in functional assays measuring cell viability, mitochondrial respiration, and reductions in inflammatory cytokine production (Zhang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In our comprehensive evaluation of rapamycin as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and potential weaknesses emerge that warrant careful consideration. One of the key strengths of rapamycin lies in its well-characterized mechanism of action and its ability to broadly modulate autophagy through mTORC1 inhibition. Preclinical studies have repeatedly demonstrated that rapamycin can induce autophagic flux, leading to the clearance of cellular debris and damaged mitochondria in RPE cells. This is particularly compelling given the central role of impaired autophagy in the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, which are major pathological features of dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018). The dual-action mechanism—enhancing both autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis via TFEB activation—further supports its potential in addressing multiple aspects of the disease pathology, from oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction to inflammation and cellular senescence (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Another strength is the substantial body of preclinical evidence showing that rapamycin not only stimulates autophagy but also improves mitochondrial function. The activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway is particularly relevant since these proteins are indispensable for mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control. By facilitating the removal of ROS-generating, damaged mitochondria, rapamycin could directly impact the cellular energy balance and reduce damaging oxidative insults in the RPE, which is pivotal for maintaining retinal health (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).

Despite its promising mechanistic profile, several significant challenges remain. Clinical studies investigating the use of rapamycin for AMD have yielded mixed results. It was first identified in microbial systems where it serves as a prosthetic group in enzymes involved in alcohol and sugar oxidation, and it has since been detected at trace levels in human tissues and milk, suggesting dietary exposure through common foods such as fermented soy products, green peppers, spinach, and human milk. PQQ is categorized within the quinone family of compounds and is recognized for its redox‐active properties; in this role, it has been considered a “vitamin‐like accessory factor” by some researchers given its involvement in cellular energy metabolism and antioxidant defense (Petricca et al., 2025; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Commercially, PQQ is available in a water‐soluble disodium salt formulation; for example, the Sigma‐Aldrich PQQ product is typical of these preparations. As a small redox‐active molecule, PQQ is distinct among nutraceuticals and has been explored in several preclinical contexts for its potential to regulate oxidative stress and promote mitochondrial function (Canovai & Williams, 2025). Consequently, this candidate represents a repurposing opportunity where its established dietary exposure, safety profile as assessed by regulatory bodies such as EFSA, and its unique bioactivity as a mitochondrial modulator may be leveraged to address the mitochondrial dysfunction implicated in dry AMD.

Therapeutic History –  
PQQ has been the subject of intensive biochemical and preclinical investigation over the past decades. Early studies concentrated on its role as a microbial cofactor, but subsequent research has documented that dietary supplementation with PQQ produces measurable effects on mitochondrial‐related metabolism and markers of inflammation in animal models and humans (Canovai & Williams, 2025). In various rodent models, oral PQQ has been shown to modulate mitochondrial number and function, thereby improving outcomes in contexts as diverse as cardiac ischemia/reperfusion, neurodegeneration, and metabolic syndrome (Akagawa, Nakano, & Ikemoto, 2016; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Additionally, EFSA conducted a safety assessment of the PQQ disodium salt formulation as a novel food ingredient and concluded that at proposed supplemental doses (up to 20 mg/day) the width of the safety margin is acceptable relative to animal toxicology data (Turck et al., 2017; Hwang & Willoughby, 2018). In human studies, although clinical trials have largely focused on endpoints such as cognition, inflammatory markers, and lipid metabolism, these trials demonstrate that oral PQQ is bioavailable, well‐tolerated, and can meaningfully impact systemic markers of oxidative stress and energy metabolism (Canovai & Williams, 2025). While no study to date has directly employed PQQ in patients with dry AMD, there is indirect evidence suggesting that PQQ’s capacity to improve cellular bioenergetics may be broadly beneficial in clinical states characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction. Some studies even indicate that PQQ upregulates mitochondrial proteins and improves ATP synthesis in cellular models derived from age‐related macular degeneration donor tissues (Canovai & Williams, 2025), although direct evidence in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) remains sparse. In summary, the therapeutic history of PQQ includes diverse preclinical applications ranging from cardioprotection to neuroprotection, with established safety in both animal and limited human studies, making it a plausible candidate for repurposing in dry AMD where mitochondrial dysfunction is a key pathogenic driver.

Mechanism of Action –  
The molecular basis of PQQ’s bioactivity is multifaceted, centering on its redox chemistry and its ability to modulate mitochondrial biogenesis. Chemically, PQQ is a potent redox‐active o‐quinone that undergoes reversible reduction to its hydroquinone form (PQQH₂) via a rapid semiquinone intermediate. This redox cycling allows PQQ to function both as a free radical scavenger and as an electron‐transfer catalyst. In vitro assays have established that the reduced form, PQQH₂, exhibits robust antioxidant capacity, with reports indicating that its aroxyl radical quenching activity can be significantly greater than that of classical antioxidants such as vitamin C and α‐tocopherol (Canovai & Williams, 2025; Charrier et al., 2024). Through its antioxidant activity, PQQ directly neutralizes reactive oxygen species (ROS) and may protect cellular constituents from oxidative damage.

Beyond its direct radical scavenging, PQQ has been implicated as an inducer of mitochondrial biogenesis. Several mechanistic studies indicate that treatment with PQQ leads to the upregulation of key transcriptional regulators involved in mitochondrial proliferation. Specifically, PQQ treatment has been shown to activate the cAMP response element‐binding protein (CREB), which in turn stimulates the expression of peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator‐1 alpha (PGC‐1α) (Charrier et al., 2024; Canovai & Williams, 2025). PGC‐1α is a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and coordinates the transcriptional activation of nuclear respiratory factors (NRF‐1/NRF‐2) and mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM), all of which are critical for the transcription and replication of mitochondrial DNA. Some studies also suggest that PQQ modulates sirtuin activity, particularly SIRT1 and SIRT3, which are NAD⁺‐dependent deacetylases that regulate mitochondrial function and cellular metabolic homeostasis (Canovai & Williams, 2025). In addition, PQQ has been reported to restore mitochondrial membrane potential, reduce proton leak, and enhance ATP production during oxidative challenge in several cellular systems (Petricca et al., 2025; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Thus, the composite mechanism of action posited for PQQ—which includes both robust redox buffering and the activation of mitochondrial biogenesis via CREB/PGC‐1α signaling—provides a molecular rationale for its use in conditions characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative injury.

Mechanistically, it is also suggested that PQQ may improve the NAD⁺/NADH ratio, thereby favoring the activity of sirtuins, which contributes to a more favorable intracellular redox state and efficient energy utilization (Jonscher, Chowanadisai, & Rucker, 2021). Although these effects have been most clearly demonstrated in hepatic, muscular, and neuronal cell models, they are directly relevant to RPE cells that rely heavily on oxidative phosphorylation for their energy demands and, hence, are particularly vulnerable to mitochondrial decay under chronic oxidative stress—a hallmark of dry AMD pathology. It is important to note that PQQ’s actions are context‐dependent; while low concentrations have been associated with protective effects, some studies suggest that higher doses can induce a pro‐oxidant effect and even impair mitochondrial dynamics in sensitive cellular contexts (Petricca et al., 2025; Turck et al., 2017). This biphasic dose response underscores the need to identify an optimal dosing window that maximizes mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defense without tipping cells into oxidative stress.

Expected Effect –  
The central hypothesis guiding the repurposing of PQQ for dry AMD is that it can stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis in the RPE by upregulating PGC‐1α, thereby increasing the antioxidant capacity and restoring optimal mitochondrial respiration in cells under chronic oxidative injury. In the proposed assay, treatment with PQQ is expected to yield multiple beneficial outcomes. First, by activating CREB and augmenting PGC‐1α expression, PQQ should enhance the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial replication and function, leading to an increased mitochondrial mass within RPE cells (Canovai & Williams, 2025; Charrier et al., 2024).

Second, increased mitochondrial mass and improved electron transport chain efficiency are expected to elevate ATP production, thereby restoring cellular energy stores that are typically depleted in dry AMD due to chronic oxidative damage. Experimental data from other cell types, including neuronal and hepatic cells, have shown that PQQ treatment enhances ATP output and normalizes mitochondrial membrane potential under oxidative stress conditions, suggesting that similar responses might be observed in RPE cells (Petricca et al., 2025; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Third, PQQ is anticipated to upregulate antioxidant enzymes, such as manganese superoxide dismutase (SOD2), which plays a critical role in mitigating ROS accumulation in mitochondria. By lowering oxidative stress levels in RPE cells, PQQ can help maintain cellular homeostasis and prevent the degeneration that is characteristic of dry AMD (Canovai & Williams, 2025).

Additionally, there is emerging evidence that certain studies using donor‐derived RPE cells from AMD patients have demonstrated that PQQ treatment can upregulate mitochondrial proteins and improve ATP generation in these cells (Canovai & Williams, 2025). Although the available data in retinal tissues remain limited, these findings align with the overall rationale; because RPE cells are highly metabolically active and heavily reliant on mitochondrial function, the ability to augment their biogenesis and enhance oxidative phosphorylation directly addresses a critical pathogenic mechanism of dry AMD. Complementing these expected biochemical outcomes, one would predict that functional assays (for instance, assessments of oxygen consumption rate and extracellular acidification rate) will reveal improved mitochondrial respiration and overall metabolic resilience in PQQ‐treated RPE cells.

Overall Evaluation –  
In synthesizing the extensive body of literature, we find that PQQ demonstrates considerable promise as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, based on the following strengths and weaknesses:

Strengths:  
1. Robust Mechanistic Rationale: PQQ’s dual role as an antioxidant and an inducer of mitochondrial biogenesis is well documented. The capacity to elevate PGC‐1α expression and thereby drive mitochondrial proliferation and enhanced energy metabolism is highly relevant given that dry AMD is characterized by RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and heightened oxidative stress (Petricca et al., 2025; Charrier et al., 2024; Canovai & Williams, 2025).  
2. Positive Safety and Bioavailability Data: Numerous preclinical studies, alongside regulatory evaluations (e.g., EFSA’s novel food assessment), indicate that PQQ is orally bioavailable and well tolerated in both animal models and limited human studies. The available toxicology data support the safety of typical supplemental doses (up to 20 mg/day), which is encouraging for repurposing efforts (Turck et al., 2017; Hwang & Willoughby, 2018; Canovai & Williams, 2025).  
3. Broad Therapeutic History: Although PQQ has not been directly tested in dry AMD in clinical settings, its prior use as a dietary supplement and its beneficial effects in neuroprotection, cardioprotection, and metabolic regulation suggest therapeutic potential in conditions underpinned by mitochondrial decay and oxidative stress (Canovai & Williams, 2025).  
4. Hypothesis‐Driven Approach: The specific hypothesis—that PQQ will stimulate RPE mitochondrial biogenesis via upregulation of PGC‐1α to improve cellular resilience against chronic oxidative injury—is both plausible and supported by mechanistic data from other cell types. Given that RPE cells are known to express PGC‐1α and that deficits in mitochondrial function have been implicated in AMD pathology, this provides a strong rationale for further investigation (Canovai & Williams, 2025).

Weaknesses:  
1. Limited Direct Evidence in Ocular Tissues: One of the main gaps in the literature is the paucity of direct preclinical studies involving retinal pigment epithelium or in vivo AMD models. Although there is some suggestive data from studies in retinal ganglion cells and donor‐derived RPE cells, definitive evidence that PQQ can counteract the specific aspects of dry AMD pathology in the retina is currently lacking (Ebeling et al., 2020; Petricca et al., 2025).  
2. Context‐Dependent and Biphasic Effects: Several studies indicate that PQQ’s efficacy is highly dose‐dependent. While low concentrations are cytoprotective by enhancing mitochondrial function, higher doses may exert pro‐oxidant effects and even impair mitochondrial membrane potential in sensitive cell types. Establishing the optimal dosing regimen for RPE cells will be critical to avoid potential deleterious effects (Petricca et al., 2025; Turck et al., 2017).  
3. Ocular Pharmacokinetics Uncertain: Although oral absorption in the gastrointestinal tract has been characterized in animal studies with favorable kinetics, it remains unclear whether orally administered PQQ achieves sufficient concentrations—or even penetrates ocular tissues such as the retina—to exert the desired effects. This issue of tissue‐specific bioavailability is a significant barrier that must be addressed in future pharmacokinetic studies (Hwang & Willoughby, 2018).  
4. Quality of Some Supporting Studies: While a substantial body of research supports PQQ’s bioactivity, some of the literature originates from journals or sources with variable quality. This underscores the need for additional high‐quality, rigorously controlled studies—particularly focused on ocular models—to validate the proposed mechanisms and therapeutic outcomes for dry AMD (Akagawa, Nakano, & Ikemoto, 2016; Hwang & Willoughby, 2018).

In conclusion, based on the available biomedical, clinical, and biochemical literature, PQQ emerges as a promising repurposed candidate for dry AMD. Its well‐documented ability to modulate mitochondrial biogenesis—principally through the activation of CREB and upregulation of PGC‐1α—aligns with the mechanistic requirements for restoring mitochondrial function in RPE cells under chronic oxidative stress, a central feature of dry AMD pathogenesis (Petricca et al., 2025; Charrier et al., 2024; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Moreover, the favorable safety profile indicated by both animal toxicology studies and human supplementation trials, combined with its oral bioavailability, adds significant translational appeal.

However, critical gaps remain. Principal among these is the need for direct evidence from retinal models. Specifically, robust, controlled preclinical studies in RPE cells and animal models of dry AMD must be performed to confirm that PQQ can effectively upregulate mitochondrial biogenesis and confer cytoprotection in ocular tissues. Additionally, further investigation into the optimal dosing strategy is required, particularly given the context‐dependent and potentially biphasic nature of PQQ’s activity, as well as the necessity to ascertain whether oral administration can yield therapeutic concentrations in the retina.

Given these considerations, the recommendation is to advance PQQ as a candidate for further investigation in dry AMD. This progression should involve a series of well‐designed in vitro and in vivo experiments targeting RPE‐specific pathways, coupled with ocular pharmacokinetic studies to evaluate tissue penetration and residence times. Should these studies provide supportive evidence, early‐phase human clinical trials focusing on retinal biomarkers and functional outcomes in dry AMD patients would be warranted.

Overall, while the current literature provides a strong mechanistic rationale and preliminary safety data supporting the repurposing of PQQ for dry AMD, it also highlights the need for targeted ocular studies to bridge the gap between systemic mitochondrial enhancements and specific retinal therapeutic benefits. With these additional investigations, PQQ could potentially emerge as a viable therapeutic option in the armamentarium against dry AMD, addressing the unmet need for treatments that restore RPE mitochondrial resilience and retard degeneration (Canovai & Williams, 2025).
