AICAR (5‐Aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide) is a synthetic nucleoside analog originally developed as an AMP mimetic agent that is capable of activating AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) across a range of cell types. It is produced by chemical synthesis and is available commercially (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich A9978), having been studied for several decades in the context of cellular energy metabolism and stress signaling. As a member of a class of compounds that mimic the natural intracellular messenger AMP, AICAR is taken up into cells via adenosine transporters and is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase into its active metabolite, ZMP (5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide monophosphate), which then mimics AMP in its interactions with AMPK (Efstathiou et al., 2020). This compound belongs to a well‐established class of metabolic modulators, and similar agents have been used in experimental settings to modulate glucose uptake, fatty acid oxidation, and overall energy homeostasis in both basic science and translational research contexts (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014). In addition, several preclinical studies have evaluated AICAR’s potential as an “exercise mimetic” due to its ability to enhance energy metabolism in muscle and other tissues, and its synthetic nature allows for reproducible and scalable dosing in research models (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, AICAR was developed primarily as an agent to activate AMPK in metabolic studies and has been investigated in a variety of preclinical models ranging from cancer to cardiovascular disease. In the oncology field, for example, AICAR has been shown to inhibit cancer cell proliferation, induce cell cycle arrest, and promote programmed cell death in several cancer types via AMPK-dependent modulation of pathways such as PI3K-Akt and mTOR (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014; Rattan et al., 2005). Clinical studies, particularly those in the cardiovascular arena, have also evaluated AICAR’s safety profile in the context of ischemia-reperfusion injury, including human trials during cardiac surgery, demonstrating that it can be administered safely in humans (Rattan et al., 2005). In the context of ocular research, AICAR has been studied for its effects on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and other ocular cell types; several studies have demonstrated that AICAR suppresses the production of pro-inflammatory complement components such as complement factor 3 (C3) and complement factor B (CFB) in RPE cells under inflammatory conditions (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017). Although there is no established clinical use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) to date, these preclinical observations, combined with its well-known pharmacological profile, have spurred interest in repurposing AICAR for treating retinal diseases characterized by oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020). Furthermore, studies examining AMPK activators in the eye – including those using AICAR in animal models of uveitis or oxidative stress-induced RPE damage – support the notion that activating this metabolic pathway can protect against retinal degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

Mechanism of Action:  
AICAR exerts its biological activity primarily through the activation of AMPK, a master regulator of cellular energy balance that responds to alterations in the AMP/ATP ratio. Once AICAR is imported into cells through adenosine transporters, it is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase to form ZMP, an analog of AMP. ZMP binds to the regulatory γ subunit of AMPK, causing a conformational change that facilitates AMPK phosphorylation at Thr172 by upstream kinases such as LKB1, thereby fully activating the kinase (Efstathiou et al., 2020). Activated AMPK then phosphorylates a series of downstream targets involved in energy metabolism, including acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) and elements of the mTOR signaling pathway. In RPE cells, this activation is particularly important because AMPK phosphorylates and activates ULK1, a kinase critical for initiating autophagy and mitophagy, thereby promoting the clearance of damaged mitochondria (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Chung et al., 2017).  

A central component of the rationale for using AICAR in dry AMD is its ability to stimulate the transcriptional coactivator PGC-1α. AMPK-mediated phosphorylation of PGC-1α enhances its activity and nuclear translocation, which in turn drives the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant defense, and metabolic adaptation (Hu et al., 2024; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). This mechanism is particularly attractive in dry AMD because mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells is thought to contribute significantly to disease pathogenesis by impairing oxidative phosphorylation, increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and triggering cell senescence or death (Tong et al., 2022; Rego, 2023). In addition to these AMPK-dependent effects, some studies have reported that AICAR exerts certain effects independent of AMPK activation. For instance, AICAR has been shown to suppress TNF-α-induced complement factor expression by mechanisms that do not involve AMPK, suggesting that alternative signaling pathways or direct modulation of transcription factor activity might also contribute to its overall activity profile (Chung et al., 2017; Kirchner et al., 2018). These AMPK-independent actions could either broaden the therapeutic potential of AICAR in modulating inflammatory responses or introduce complexity into its activity profile that will need to be carefully isolated and understood (Kirchner et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
Given its mechanisms of action, the expected effect of AICAR in an assay aimed at treating dry AMD would be multifaceted. In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress—a hallmark of dry AMD—AICAR treatment is expected to lead to robust activation of AMPK, as measured by increased phosphorylation of both AMPK and its downstream substrates such as ACC and ULK1 (Guo et al., 2018; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). As damaged mitochondria are a major source of ROS in stressed RPE cells, the stimulation of autophagy and mitophagy is anticipated to selectively clear these dysfunctional organelles, reducing cellular oxidative stress and preventing the secondary damage that contributes to RPE degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

In addition to these metabolic effects, AICAR is also expected to attenuate inflammatory responses within the RPE and adjacent retinal tissues. These effects are particularly pertinent given that chronic, low-grade inflammation coupled with complement dysregulation is a recognized component of dry AMD pathogenesis.  

At the cellular level, the outcome of AICAR-induced AMPK activation is expected to manifest as enhanced mitochondrial function, improved energy charge (ATP/AMP ratio), reduced ROS accumulation, and, ultimately, a restoration of normal metabolic and autophagic flux in RPE cells (Fisher et al., 2022; Fisher, 2022). This improved bioenergetic profile should translate into protection against RPE cell death, potentially slowing or halting the progression of geographic atrophy associated with dry AMD (Yu et al., 2024; Si et al., 2023). Moreover, since RPE dysfunction in AMD also involves a reduction in the phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, AICAR’s modulatory effects on autophagy may indirectly help to restore the homeostatic functions of RPE cells, reducing the accumulation of damaging lipofuscin and drusen material (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Sung et al., 2015). In summary, the expected effect is a dual-action benefit—mitigation of oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum stresses via improved mitochondrial dynamics and an anti-inflammatory effect stemming from a reduction in complement activation and NF-κB-driven cytokine production (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020).

AICAR represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration owing to its robust and well-characterized mechanism of action via AMPK activation. The strengths of this candidate lie in its dual capacity to modulate critical pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis: on one hand, AICAR enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and promotes the removal of damaged mitochondria through autophagy/mitophagy, and on the other, it attenuates inflammatory cascades that exacerbate RPE cell damage (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hu et al., 2024). The ability of AICAR to upregulate PGC-1α is particularly compelling because mitochondrial dysfunction is now widely recognized as a central element in dry AMD. Preclinical studies have illustrated that dysregulation of mitochondrial function in RPE cells—a decrease in oxidative phosphorylation capacity, increased ROS production, and impaired clearance of damaged organelles—is pivotal in the initiation and progression of AMD (Tong et al., 2022; Rego, 2023). Additionally, the compound’s known clinical safety profile in human studies—albeit in contexts outside ophthalmology—provides an encouraging starting point for repurposing it for dry AMD, where no approved therapeutics currently exist (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017).

For instance, some experimental reports have shown that AICAR can reduce the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments by RPE cells—a process that is essential for retinal health—which may represent a double-edged sword if not carefully titrated (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Yu et al., 2024). Nonetheless, complexities related to AMPK-independent effects, differential responses in healthy versus diseased cells, and potential off-target metabolic changes underscore the need for rigorous preclinical optimization and carefully designed clinical trials before this candidate can be definitively validated for dry AMD treatment (Chung et al., 2017; Fisher et al., 2022; Kirchner et al., 2018).

Moving forward, it will be critical to further elucidate the detailed cellular and molecular responses to AICAR in human RPE cells, determine the optimal dosing and delivery parameters specific to the ocular environment, and perform in vivo studies that mimic the complex pathobiology of dry AMD. With these additional efforts, AICAR could eventually emerge as a valuable addition to the limited therapeutic arsenal available for managing this debilitating condition.

Continued rigorous research and methodical clinical evaluation will determine whether AICAR can be developed into an effective treatment modality for this currently intractable form of macular degeneration.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
BGP-15 is a synthetic, small-molecule nicotinic amidoxime/hydroxylamine derivative whose full chemical name is O-(3-piperidino-2-hydroxy-1-propyl) nicotinic amidoxime, typically used as a dihydrochloride salt; it was developed by N-Gene (US/Hungary) and has been described as water-soluble and mitochondria-targeting in preclinical studies (including ocular applications) (Takács et al., 2024; Horváth et al., 2021). Chemically and pharmacologically, BGP-15 belongs to the hydroximic/hydroxylamine acid derivative family originally advanced as membrane-interacting heat-shock response (HSR) co-inducers that remodel cholesterol-enriched plasma membrane rafts, with pleiotropic, cytoprotective effects in stressed tissues (membrane-lipid therapy) (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011). In parallel, the compound has been positioned as a nicotinamide-related, non-carboxamide “NAM analogue” with in vitro mixed-type (noncompetitive) PARP-1 inhibition, though the authors emphasize that in vivo protective effects likely involve additional mechanisms beyond direct PARP blockade because the in vitro inhibitory concentration exceeds achievable systemic levels (Crul et al., 2013). Independent biophysical and cellular studies show BGP-15 partitions into membranes, increases the fluidity of negatively charged lipid species, preserves heat-challenged raft integrity, and activates stress signaling linked to HSP induction; imaging and molecular dynamics support a direct membrane-interacting mode of action (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

Functionally, BGP-15 is best classified as a multifunctional HSP co-inducer and insulin-sensitizing, mitochondria-targeting cytoprotective agent that remodels membrane rafts, enhances the HSF1–HSP axis, and modulates stress and survival signaling (Akt up, JNK/p38 down), while lowering mitochondrial ROS and stabilizing Δψm; importantly, it preferentially acts in stressed cells, an attribute that underpins its safety rationale (Gombos et al., 2011; Sumegi et al., 2017). The compound concentrates in energized mitochondria driven by its delocalized positive charge, with >85–90% uptake into isolated mitochondria under experimental conditions (Sümegi, 2018). Mitochondrial studies consistently localize the dominant ROS-lowering effect to the respiratory chain at complexes I and III, with minimal direct antioxidant chemistry, and only mild uncoupling at millimolar concentrations that is irrelevant at the micromolar doses used in most cell studies (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018).

Crucial nomenclature caveat: a distinct “BGP-15” reported by a different group denotes a calcipotriene-derived vitamin D3 analog with anticancer activity; this vitamin D3 analog is mechanistically and structurally unrelated to the nicotinic amidoxime HSP co-inducer described above (both were labeled “BGP-15” by their respective originators) (Sintov et al., 2013). For the current program, the candidate of interest is the nicotinic amidoxime/hydroxylamine HSP co-inducer (often supplied by N-Gene or commercial chemical vendors under the amidoxime name), not the vitamin D3 analog (Takács et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
BGP-15 and closely related hydroximic/hydroxylamine acid derivatives have an extensive preclinical history across cardiac, neural, hepatic, renal, skeletal muscle, pulmonary, and metabolic models, with multiple mechanistic readouts converging on membrane remodeling, HSR/HSP co-induction, MAPK and Akt pathway modulation, and mitochondrial protection (Sumegi et al., 2017). Cardiovascular protection has been reported in ischemia–reperfusion, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation, with actions that include reduced ROS, preserved mitochondrial function, and Akt activation with suppression of JNK/p38 (Sumegi et al., 2017). In spontaneously hypertensive rats, BGP-15 increased PGC-1α and mitochondrial mass, decreased interstitial fibrosis, increased MKP-1 and reduced p38/JNK phosphorylation, and activated Akt/GSK-3β signaling (Horváth et al., 2021). BGP-15 prevented imatinib cardiotoxicity, protected against cisplatin nephrotoxicity without impairing antitumor efficacy, and mitigated cisplatin/taxol peripheral neuropathy (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). Hepatoprotection against acetaminophen injury via inhibition of caspase-independent cell death has also been documented (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). In pulmonary arterial hypertension and severe muscular dystrophy models, BGP-15 preserved mitochondrial structure and function and slowed disease progression; mechanistically, mitochondrial fusion via OPA1 activation and Akt signaling were implicated (Szabó et al., 2018).

Neuroprotection and mitochondrial rescue have been demonstrated in vitro and in vivo, including reduced neuronal death and improved mitochondrial potential/ROS at axonal branch points, coupled to HSP72 elevation, reduced phospho-JNK/p38, and enhanced Akt/IGF1R signaling (Ohlen et al., 2017). Consistent with its membrane-raft mechanism, BGP-15 increased HSP expression during heat challenge and remodeled cholesterol-rich platforms that gate stress signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

In ophthalmology, BGP-15 has been applied in multiple retinal disease contexts. It was reported retinoprotective in Goto–Kakizaki rats (type 2 diabetes) with functional preservation on ERG, and later shown to improve survival and retinal function long-term in ZDF rats under uncontrolled diabetes, with increased ocular HSP70 and decreased NFκB (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021). Topical ocular delivery using an SBECD-containing eyedrop improved scotopic/photopic a- and b-waves, restored oscillatory potentials, shortened implicit times, and preserved retinal thickness following global ischemia–reperfusion injury in rats (Takács et al., 2024). These ocular data align with the compound’s mitochondrial and HSP co-inducer mechanisms: accumulation in mitochondria, protection against apoptosis/necrosis in oxidative-stress paradigms, and modulation of stress signaling (Takács et al., 2024).

Clinically, BGP-15 has a proof-of-concept randomized, double-blind trial demonstrating dose-dependent improvement of insulin sensitivity in insulin-resistant patients without apparent short-term toxicity; in parallel, human phase II work in olanzapine-induced metabolic disorder also identified BGP-15 as an insulin sensitizer (Crul et al., 2013; Sümegi, 2018). Safety signals from early human studies and the pharmacology of HSP co-inducers (preferential action in stressed cells) support the translational risk profile; however, systemic serum concentrations reported by the developer are low (≤25 nmol/mL), which has implications for target engagement and favors local ocular delivery for retinal indications (Gombos et al., 2011; Sumegi et al., 2017).

To our knowledge based on the supplied corpus, BGP-15 has not been directly tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) patients or canonical dry AMD animal models; however, its retinoprotective efficacy in diabetic retinopathy models and retinal ischemia–reperfusion suggests relevance to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)/photoreceptor stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammation, which are central to dry AMD biology (Takács et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Membrane-lipid therapy and HSP co-induction. BGP-15 partitions into and remodels membrane lipid domains, particularly cholesterol-rich plasma membrane rafts that organize stress sensing and signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). Under heat stress or analogous perturbations, BGP-15 preserves raft integrity and elevates HSP expression; this is associated with activation of Rac1 and modulation of HSF1 acetylation, leading to prolonged HSF1 DNA binding and robust HSP gene induction without causing protein unfolding, a hallmark of HSP “co-inducers” (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). In HSR-defective melanoma cells, BGP-15 significantly rescued raft domain coverage and shifted the size distribution toward larger platforms, coincident with increased hsp25 expression and Rac1-dependent stress signaling (Gombos et al., 2011). Across cell and tissue contexts, BGP-15 increases HSP70/HSPA1A (HSP72), and this HSP gain is causally linked to improved insulin signaling and cytoprotection in stressed cells (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011).

PARP/NAD+/SIRT1/HSF1 axis. Although BGP-15 demonstrates mixed-type (noncompetitive) inhibition of PARP-1 in vitro, the concentrations required exceed typical in vivo exposures, suggesting that PARP pathway effects in vivo are likely downstream of ROS lowering and reduced DNA single-strand breaks that otherwise drive PARP activation (Crul et al., 2013). In stressed cells, BGP-15 reduces PAR levels, which relieves PARP-mediated suppression of MKP-1/Dusp1, thereby inhibiting JNK/p38 activation; reduced PARP activity also preserves NAD+ and SIRT1 activity, which favors a deacetylated, active HSF1 and a stronger HSR (Crul et al., 2013). This mechanistic loop—less ROS, less PARP activation, more MKP-1, less JNK/p38, and better HSP/SIRT1 tone—aligns with the observed anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective phenotypes (Crul et al., 2013).

Mitochondrial enrichment and respiratory chain modulation. Biophysically, BGP-15 carries a delocalized positive charge, accumulates in energized mitochondria (>85–90% uptake in isolated organelles), and at micromolar doses characteristic of cell studies (1–50 µM) lowers mitochondrial ROS predominantly at complexes I and III without significant baseline depolarization of Δψm (Sümegi, 2018; Sumegi et al., 2017). In oxidative or inflammatory challenges, BGP-15 attenuates H₂O₂- and LPS-induced mitochondrial depolarization and reduces mitochondrial superoxide to near-control levels; MitoTEMPO controls confirm mitochondrial origin of the ROS signal (Sumegi et al., 2017). Importantly, the compound exhibits no meaningful direct antioxidant scavenging in cell-free ROS-generating systems, and only displays mild uncoupling at millimolar concentrations—far above the micromolar exposures used in protective assays—supporting a mechanism of respiratory chain modulation rather than redox scavenging (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). Downstream signaling reflects the lowered mitochondrial ROS burden: JNK/p38 activation is reduced, Akt signaling is enhanced, and caspase-independent death pathways are suppressed (Sumegi et al., 2017).

Mitochondrial dynamics, fusion, and biogenesis. Beyond acute ROS control, BGP-15 promotes mitochondrial fusion and preserves cristae architecture by activating OPA1 GTPase and promoting OPA1 polymerization; genetic suppression of OPA1 or Mfn1/Mfn2 abolishes the fusion phenotype, indicating that BGP-15 acts upstream or within the endogenous fusion machinery (Szabó et al., 2018). In vivo, these effects translate into improved mitochondrial ultrastructure and tissue histology under ROS stress (e.g., monocrotaline-induced PAH) (Szabó et al., 2018). In hypertensive cardiomyopathy, BGP-15 increases PGC-1α and mitochondrial mass, with concurrent shifts in CREB/AMPK phosphorylation consistent with improved energetic signaling, reduced p38/JNK via MKP-1 upregulation, and increased Akt/GSK-3β prosurvival signaling (Horváth et al., 2021).

Insulin-sensitizing stress signaling. In skeletal muscle and human studies, BGP-15 increases HSP72 expression, enhances insulin receptor autophosphorylation (blocking JNK inhibitory phosphorylation), activates RAC1, increases AKT phosphorylation, promotes GLUT4 translocation, increases membrane fluidity, raises AMPK activity, and reduces HSF1 acetylation, altogether improving glucose disposal without overt toxicity in a randomized trial (Crul et al., 2013). These metabolic effects are mechanistically congruent with the membrane–HSR–mitochondrial triad described above (Crul et al., 2013).

Ocular and retinal mechanisms. In rat eyes, BGP-15 increased HSP70 and decreased NFκB, consistent with HSR enhancement and anti-inflammatory signaling in ocular tissues (Wachal et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion and diabetic retinopathy models, functional improvements on ERG, restoration of oscillatory potentials, and preservation of retinal thickness are consistent with mitochondrial protection and stress-response reinforcement in retinal cells (Takács et al., 2024). The topical SBECD formulation demonstrated pharmacologic activity in the retina without systemic pharmacokinetic characterization, indicating local ocular delivery as a viable route for targeting mitochondrial and HSP pathways in the posterior segment (Takács et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
The team’s hypothesis—that BGP-15 stabilizes mitochondrial membrane proteins and co-induces HSF1-driven antioxidant chaperone responses in RPE to mitigate oxidative stress in dry AMD—is aligned with the compound’s demonstrated pharmacology in retinal, cardiac, neural, and pulmonary models: (i) robust mitochondrial enrichment and stabilization of Δψm under oxidative/inflammatory stress, (ii) ROS lowering at complexes I and III without direct radical scavenging, (iii) activation of the HSR via membrane raft remodeling and HSF1 acetylation control, and (iv) suppression of ROS-sensitive injury cascades (JNK/p38) with concurrent activation of pro-survival Akt (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). In retinal disease models, BGP-15 improved ERG measures and retinal thickness and increased ocular HSP70 while decreasing NFκB, providing a direct ocular precedent likely to translate to stressed RPE, where mitochondria and proteostasis are central to survival under chronic oxidative load (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021).

Mechanistically expected in RPE:  
- Membrane-raft remodeling and HSR co-induction. BGP-15 partitions into RPE membranes and remodels cholesterol-rich rafts, preserving raft integrity under stress, activating Rac1, decreasing HSF1 acetylation, and prolonging HSF1 DNA binding, thereby elevating HSP70/HSP25 and enhancing proteostasis capacity in aged/stressed RPE (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).  
- Mitochondrial ROS containment and Δψm preservation. BGP-15 should accumulate in RPE mitochondria, reduce ROS production at complexes I/III, and attenuate oxidative- and inflammation-induced depolarization, thereby maintaining ATP production and limiting mitochondrial permeability transition and AIF translocation, as shown in other cell types (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018).  
- Mitochondrial dynamics and biogenesis. Via OPA1 activation and Akt/GSK-3β signaling, BGP-15 is expected to promote inner-membrane fusion/OPA1 oligomerization and preserve cristae, with possible longer-term increases in mitochondrial biogenesis (PGC-1α), all protective features for RPE faced with chronic oxidative and lipofuscin stress (Szabó et al., 2018; Horváth et al., 2021).  
- Anti-inflammatory signaling rebalancing. By reducing mitochondrial ROS and PARP activation, BGP-15 should relieve PARP-mediated suppression of MKP-1, suppress JNK/p38 activity, decrease NFκB signaling, and bolster SIRT1-HSF1 activity, thereby reducing ROS-amplifying feed-forward loops in RPE (Crul et al., 2013; Wachal et al., 2021).

Assay expectations and endpoints. In standard RPE cell models (primary human RPE, ARPE-19, or iPSC-RPE), BGP-15 at 1–50 µM should (i) reduce H₂O₂- or LPS-induced mitochondrial depolarization (JC-1/TMRM), (ii) lower mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX) and total ROS (DHR123) without acting as a direct antioxidant in cell-free assays, (iii) reduce apoptosis/necrosis after oxidative challenge (annexin V/PI), (iv) increase HSP70/HSF1 pathway activation and decrease HSF1 acetylation, (v) activate Akt and downregulate JNK/p38, and (vi) promote OPA1 oligomerization and mitochondrial fusion (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Szabó et al., 2018). Where possible, complement activation or lipid peroxidation paradigms can be layered to emulate dry AMD stressors; based on the corpus, BGP-15’s effects are strongest under stress, consistent with HSP co-inducer pharmacology (Gombos et al., 2011).

Delivery considerations. Systemic exposures in humans are low (≤25 nmol/mL), suggesting that oral dosing may be insufficient to reach pharmacologic micromolar levels in RPE; conversely, topical ocular delivery with SBECD has demonstrated retinal functional benefits and structural protection, supporting development of a posterior-segment–targeted topical or periocular formulation to enrich the RPE–choroid compartment (Sümegi, 2018; Takács et al., 2024).

Caveats regarding target expression. The corpus documents the relevant targets (HSF1/HSP70, Rac1, OPA1, MKP-1, JNK/p38, Akt) as central to BGP-15’s mechanisms in multiple mammalian tissues and cell types and shows ocular readouts (HSP70 up, NFκB down) in rat eyes; however, it does not provide explicit RPE expression data, which should be confirmed experimentally in our RPE assay systems (Wachal et al., 2021; Gombos et al., 2011; Szabó et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic congruence with dry AMD pathobiology. BGP-15 directly addresses mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic oxidative stress—core drivers of RPE degeneration—by concentrating in mitochondria, lowering ROS at complexes I/III, stabilizing Δψm, and activating survival signaling while suppressing inflammatory stress kinases (Sumegi et al., 2017). Concurrently, it co-induces the HSR by remodeling plasma membrane rafts and modulating HSF1 acetylation, thereby boosting HSP70/HSP25 chaperone capacity and proteostasis—functions that are expected to mitigate protein misfolding and aggregation in aged RPE (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).  
- Demonstrated ocular efficacy in relevant retinal injury contexts. Topical BGP-15 improved ERG a- and b-waves, preserved oscillatory potentials, reduced implicit times, and rescued retinal thickness after ischemia–reperfusion, and it was retinoprotective in diabetic models, with ocular HSP70 increase and NFκB reduction—outcomes consistent with RPE/retinal resilience under oxidative stress (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021).  
- Pleiotropic yet coherent mechanism spanning membrane, nuclear, and mitochondrial nodes. The membrane–HSR–mitochondrial triad, including PARP/MKP-1/JNK–p38 and Akt/GSK-3β axes, provides multiple intervention points likely to translate into robust protection in the multifactorial environment of dry AMD (Crul et al., 2013; Sumegi et al., 2017; Szabó et al., 2018; Horváth et al., 2021).  
- Favorable translational signals. Proof-of-concept human trials in insulin resistance show pharmacodynamic activity without overt safety signals, and HSP co-inducers are known to preferentially act in stressed cells, potentially limiting off-target effects in quiescent tissues; local ocular delivery further improves the therapeutic index (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011; Takács et al., 2024).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Lack of direct dry AMD evidence. No studies in the corpus directly test BGP-15 in dry AMD models or patients; we infer utility from retinal IR/diabetes models and mechanism (Takács et al., 2024).  
- Exposure–response uncertainties for the posterior segment. Systemic serum concentrations are low relative to micromolar efficacious concentrations in vitro, necessitating optimized local delivery to RPE; although eyedrop formulations show retinal effects, posterior-segment delivery by topical route is often limited, and pharmacokinetics were not measured in the cited ocular study (Sümegi, 2018; Takács et al., 2024).  
- Target ambiguity and pleiotropy. While the membrane–HSR–mitochondrial framework is coherent, BGP-15 lacks a single defined receptor/protein target, and its in vitro PARP-1 inhibition likely does not drive in vivo efficacy; this complicates target engagement assays and regulatory narratives (Sümegi, 2018; Crul et al., 2013).  
- Nomenclature confusion. “BGP-15” also denotes a calcipotriene-derived vitamin D3 analog in the oncology literature; chemical identity must be verified to avoid conflation during procurement and CMC (Sintov et al., 2013; Takács et al., 2024).  
- Evidence base heterogeneity. Some ocular and cardiovascular studies are published in lower–quality venues, emphasizing the need for rigorous, blinded replication and GLP toxicology in ocular models (Horváth et al., 2021; Wachal et al., 2021).

Recommended next steps  
- In vitro RPE validation. In human primary or iPSC-derived RPE under oxidative (H₂O₂/tert-butyl hydroperoxide) and inflammatory (LPS/CpG) stress, test BGP-15 at 0.3–30 µM for effects on Δψm (JC-1/TMRM), mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX), total ROS (DHR123), apoptosis/necrosis (annexin V/PI), and mitochondrial respiration; confirm no direct antioxidant scavenging in cell-free systems (Sumegi et al., 2017).  
- Proteostasis and HSR endpoints. Quantify HSP70/HSP25 induction, HSF1 acetylation/binding dynamics, Rac1 activation, and membrane raft integrity using fPEG-cholesterol probes/TOCCSL in RPE; evaluate MKP-1, JNK/p38, and Akt/GSK-3β signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013; Sumegi et al., 2017).  
- Mitochondrial dynamics. Assess OPA1 oligomerization, fusion/fission balance (Mfn1/2 and Drp1 markers), cristae morphology by EM, and PGC-1α/mtDNA copy number to benchmark fusion/biogenesis responses (Szabó et al., 2018; Horváth et al., 2021).  
- Ocular delivery PK/PD. Using the SBECD eyedrop formulation as a starting point, perform ocular pharmacokinetics (vitreous, retina, RPE–choroid) and pharmacodynamics (ocular HSP70, NFκB, mitochondrial markers) to ensure RPE target engagement at tolerated doses (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021).  
- In vivo retinal stress models. Extend to retinal oxidative stress paradigms that capture RPE pathology; leverage ERG, OCT, histology, and mitochondrial ultrastructure endpoints already positive in IR/diabetic models (Takács et al., 2024).  
- Identity control and CMC. Source BGP-15 as O-(3-piperidino-2-hydroxy-1-propyl) nicotinic amidoxime dihydrochloride; confirm identity by NMR/MS to avoid the calcipotriene-derived analog (Takács et al., 2024; Sintov et al., 2013).

Go/no-go considerations for dry AMD  
Given the robust mechanistic alignment—mitochondrial ROS control at complexes I/III, Δψm stabilization, HSR co-induction via membrane raft remodeling and HSF1 acetylation control, OPA1-driven mitochondrial fusion, and suppression of ROS-sensitive inflammatory kinases—plus demonstrable ocular efficacy in retinal injury models, BGP-15 merits advancement to RPE-focused preclinical validation for dry AMD (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Szabó et al., 2018; Takács et al., 2024). The principal risks are translational: ensuring adequate RPE exposures by ocular delivery, confirming RPE target expression/engagement, and generating rigorous GLP pharmacology/toxicology data in ocular species. On balance, the mechanistic breadth that often complicates development is an advantage in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction, proteostasis failure, and chronic inflammation coexist.

Conclusion. BGP-15 is a credible repurposing candidate for dry AMD based on its mitochondria-centered, HSP co-inducing, membrane-lipid–modulating pharmacology and encouraging retinal efficacy in vivo; priority should be given to RPE-targeted PK/PD, mitochondrial and HSR biomarker validation, and controlled efficacy studies in retinal oxidative-stress models to de-risk translation (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Takács et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
L-Carnitine is a naturally occurring quaternary ammonium compound, chemically defined as β-hydroxy-γ-trimethylaminobutyrate, that is both derived from the diet (predominantly found in animal-based foods such as red meat) and biosynthesized endogenously from the essential amino acids lysine and methionine via a vitamin C–dependent pathway primarily in the liver and kidneys (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Mollica et al., 2017). Historically, L-carnitine was first identified as a constituent of muscle tissue in the early 20th century and was later linked to its high content in meat, leading to its designation as “vitamin T” in certain insect models (Mollica et al., 2017). As a member of the carnitine family, it belongs to the class of metabolic cofactors or nutraceutical agents whose primary function is to shuttle activated long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondrial matrix, where they undergo β-oxidation, thereby facilitating aerobic energy production and maintaining the intracellular acyl-CoA/CoA balance (Moos et al., 2017; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). This class of compounds has historically been used as dietary supplements to treat primary and secondary carnitine deficiency, as well as in various metabolic and mitochondrial disorders (Flanagan et al., 2010). L-Carnitine is widely formulated in pharmaceutical products both as a standalone supplement and as an ingredient in combination formulations, which underscores its acceptance as a metabolic supportive agent with a favorable safety profile (Flanagan et al., 2010; Surai, 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, the carnitine family has a long record of use in addressing conditions where fatty acid oxidation is impaired. L-Carnitine has been employed effectively as a life-saving therapy in primary carnitine deficiency—a condition in which mutations of the carnitine transporter (OCTN2) impair cellular uptake—and also in secondary deficiencies associated with conditions like renal failure, liver disease, and certain inborn errors of metabolism (Flanagan et al., 2010). Beyond classical deficiency syndromes, both L-carnitine and its acetylated derivative (acetyl-L-carnitine) have been investigated in a broad range of clinical contexts, including cardiovascular diseases, diabetic complications, and neurodegenerative disorders. For example, acetyl-L-carnitine has been shown to improve parameters of visual function in patients with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and to confer neuroprotective effects in Alzheimer’s disease and mild cognitive impairment (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Calabrese et al., 2009).  
In ophthalmology, while most clinical studies have focused on the use of carnitine derivatives for systemic metabolic or neuroprotective effects, there is preclinical evidence supporting an ocular role. Animal studies have identified high intraocular concentrations of carnitine in the lens and other ocular tissues, hinting at a physiological role in maintaining ocular metabolic balance and osmotic homeostasis (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). Investigations into the protective effects of L-carnitine against oxidative damage, including its potential to safeguard retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and other ocular tissues, provide a rationale for its application in dry AMD, particularly in the context of geographic atrophy where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central features (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c). Moreover, combination therapy regimens incorporating acetyl-L-carnitine with n-3 fatty acids and coenzyme Q10 have also been trialed in experimental settings to address energy metabolism in retinal tissues (Shamsi et al., 2007). Despite these promising findings, direct clinical use of L-carnitine as monotherapy for dry AMD has not been extensively reported, thus making its repurposing an area that merits focused research to bridge the gap between its established metabolic functions and its potential application in retinal degeneration (Flanagan et al., 2010; Mollica et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
The central biochemical role of L-carnitine is to facilitate the transport of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle—a process that is critical for β-oxidation and ATP production. This shuttle is mediated by mitochondrial enzymes such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT-1) on the outer mitochondrial membrane, which converts acyl-CoA to acyl-carnitine, and carnitine acyltransferase (also known as carnitine acetyltransferase or CAT) within the mitochondria that re-forms acyl-CoA for oxidation (Moos et al., 2017; Jones et al., 2010). This process not only fuels ATP generation via the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation but also helps regulate the cellular acyl-CoA/CoA ratio, indirectly influencing multiple metabolic pathways (Surai, 2015).  
Furthermore, L-carnitine exhibits antioxidant properties either directly, through free radical scavenging, or indirectly by preserving mitochondrial integrity and function under oxidative stress conditions (Shamsi et al., 2007; Surai, 2015). It has been shown to reduce lipid peroxidation and prevent the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential—a key step in the cascade leading to cellular apoptosis (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c). In addition to its classical mitochondrial functions, L-carnitine also acts as an osmolyte, protecting cells against hyperosmolarity by stabilizing proteins and cellular membranes, which could further reduce oxidative stress (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b; Mollica et al., 2017).  
At the molecular level in the RPE, the hypothesis is that enhancing mitochondrial fatty acid uptake via L-carnitine supplementation will improve β-oxidation efficiency. This is expected to lead to increased ATP production and a reduction in the accumulation of lipid intermediates that may otherwise result in excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation. The reduction in ROS could mitigate chronic oxidative stress, a well established contributor to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Jones et al., 2010; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). Notably, disrupted mitochondrial metabolism and energy deficits have been implicated in the progression of RPE cell dysfunction, and L-carnitine’s role in restoring metabolic flexibility has been documented in other cell types such as hepatocytes and neuronal cells (Ates et al., 2008; Surai, 2015). Additionally, the modulation of mitochondrial protein acetylation by L-carnitine derivatives, an effect observed in various models of aging and metabolic disease, may further contribute to a neuroprotective milieu in RPE cells (Wang et al., 2024; Virmani & Cirulli, 2022).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its multifaceted mechanisms of action, the anticipated effect of L-carnitine in an assay designed for dry age-related macular degeneration is twofold. First, by enhancing mitochondrial fatty acid uptake and increasing β-oxidation rates, L-carnitine is expected to boost ATP production in RPE cells, thereby ameliorating the energy deficits that contribute to cellular dysfunction in geographic atrophy (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Jones et al., 2010). Second, this improved mitochondrial function should lead to a reduction in the generation of ROS that typically arises from lipid overload and subsequent incomplete oxidation, thereby decreasing oxidative damage to critical cellular structures including mitochondrial membranes and nuclear DNA (Shamsi et al., 2007; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a).  
In in vitro assays using cultured RPE cells, one would expect that L-carnitine treatment leads to enhanced mitochondrial respiration, as measured by oxygen consumption rate (OCR), and an associated elevation in ATP levels. Moreover, reductions in established markers of oxidative stress, such as malondialdehyde (MDA) levels or increased glutathione (GSH) concentrations, would support its antioxidant action (Ates et al., 2008). Expression studies have shown that key mitochondrial enzymes and transporters, including CPT-1 and OCTN2 (the carnitine transporter), are expressed in RPE cells, providing a molecular substrate for L-carnitine’s action in these cells (Ribas et al., 2014; Jones et al., 2010). Furthermore, since mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of dry AMD pathogenesis, the restoration of mitochondrial efficiency by L-carnitine could be measured by improved RPE cell survival and decreased apoptotic markers under conditions of oxidative stress and lipid oversupply.  
Preclinical studies in other tissues such as neuronal cells and hepatocytes have demonstrated that L-carnitine treatment not only restores mitochondrial function but also reduces lipid-induced ROS production and inflammation. Extrapolating from these findings, it is reasonable to expect that in the context of dry AMD, L-carnitine could counteract the metabolic inflexibility of RPE cells, ultimately slowing the progression of geographic atrophy and preserving retinal structure and function (Surai, 2015; Wang et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
L-Carnitine stands out as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to several compelling properties. Its established role in promoting mitochondrial β-oxidation and energy production, combined with demonstrated antioxidant and osmoprotective actions, provides a strong mechanistic rationale for addressing the metabolic and oxidative stress components of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Jones et al., 2010). The compound’s extensive history of use as a dietary supplement and its well-characterized safety profile—in which high oral doses have been administered with minimal toxicity—support its potential for repurposing in an ocular application (Flanagan et al., 2010; Mollica et al., 2017).  
However, there are potential limitations that merit cautious consideration. Direct evidence of L-carnitine’s efficacy in RPE cells specifically within the context of dry AMD is currently limited. While preclinical studies in non-ocular tissues and some ocular models suggest beneficial mitochondrial and antioxidant effects, the precise dosing, ocular bioavailability, and long-term impact on retinal degeneration remain to be rigorously established. Moreover, while L-carnitine can enhance mitochondrial function, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD implies that a monotherapy approach might not be sufficient; a combination therapy strategy—potentially incorporating other mitochondrial or antioxidant agents—may ultimately prove more effective (Shamsi et al., 2007; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a).  
In summary, the strengths of L-carnitine include its well-established role in cellular energy metabolism, its safety profile and widespread clinical use in other metabolic conditions, and its potential to mitigate ROS production and oxidative damage through enhanced fatty acid oxidation. The weaknesses primarily lie in the current paucity of direct evidence in ocular models of dry AMD and the challenges associated with ensuring adequate drug delivery to the RPE in vivo. Nonetheless, given the overall mechanistic promise and the favorable tolerability observed in numerous studies, L-carnitine warrants further investigation – with a focus on in vitro RPE assays under condition of lipid overload and oxidative stress, followed by in vivo preclinical models of geographic atrophy – to validate its efficacy as a repurposed therapy for dry AMD (Jones et al., 2010; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c; Ates et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2024).  
Overall, I recommend proceeding with targeted experiments to assess mitochondrial respiration, ROS levels, and cell survival in RPE cultures treated with L-carnitine. These studies should be complemented with investigations of tissue distribution following ocular delivery to address bioavailability concerns. This comprehensive evaluation supports the potential of L-carnitine as a metabolic and antioxidant therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, while also highlighting areas where additional data are needed before clinical translation.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Mitochonic Acid-5 (MA-5; MedChemExpress HY-104308) is a synthetic, mitochondria‐targeted small molecule originally discovered for its ability to improve mitochondrial function in models of cellular aging. MA-5 belongs to the class of mitochondrial modulators that have been shown to enhance adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production, reduce mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), and extend lifespan in non‐ocular systems such as fibroblasts and Caenorhabditis elegans. The current hypothesis proposes that MA-5 binds directly to mitofilin (also known as Mic60), a key scaffolding protein in the inner mitochondrial membrane that is essential for the proper organization and stability of mitochondrial cristae. This interaction is anticipated to stabilize cristae architecture, thereby preserving optimal assembly of the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and enabling improved mitochondrial bioenergetics—a mechanism particularly appealing in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), where cristae disorganization and mtROS accumulation in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells have been associated with disease pathology (Ji et al., 2021; Ferrington et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
While MA-5 itself has not been previously evaluated in ocular diseases, compounds that modulate mitochondrial function have a long history in preclinical studies for age-related conditions. Several mitochondrial-targeted agents—for example, SkQ1 and elamipretide—have demonstrated promise in ameliorating mitochondrial defects in RPE models and in early clinical trials targeting dry AMD (Ji et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022). In other systems, MA-5 has been reported to improve ATP production, reduce mtROS, and activate the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt) in fibroblast and C. elegans models. Such beneficial effects on mitochondrial function have contributed to the rationale for repurposing MA-5 for dry AMD. Moreover, research in related domains suggests that stabilizing mitochondrial cristae via targeting scaffold proteins such as mitofilin is mechanistically sound given observations of altered mitofilin expression and cristae disruption in AMD RPE (Ferrington et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). However, direct usage of MA-5 in retinal disorders remains unexplored, and its potential has yet to be validated in RPE-specific in vitro or in vivo models.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, MA-5 is proposed to exert its beneficial effects by physically interacting with mitofilin/Mic60, a protein integral to the maintenance of inner mitochondrial membrane architecture and cristae organization. Mitofilin is recognized for its role in stabilizing the cristae junctions and in facilitating the proper assembly and function of the ETC complexes (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Ferrington et al., 2020). In dry AMD, mitochondrial cristae loss has been documented in RPE cells, suggesting that disrupted mitofilin function may underlie some of the bioenergetic deficiencies seen in the disease (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Ferrington et al., 2020). By binding to mitofilin, MA-5 is expected to reinforce cristae integrity; this stabilization can promote the efficient assembly of ETC complexes, thereby leading to improved oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production. Concurrently, enhanced cristae organization is likely to reduce electron leakage from the ETC and lower the production of reactive oxygen species, which in excess contribute to oxidative damage and RPE cell death (Ji et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022).

In addition, emerging evidence suggests that perturbations in mitochondrial structure can trigger the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt), a conserved stress-response pathway that upregulates mitochondrial chaperones such as mtHsp70 and other proteostasis factors to cope with misfolded proteins and oxidative damage. MA-5 is hypothesized not only to stabilize the physical architecture of the mitochondria but also to activate UPRmt pathways, thereby enhancing the endogenous capacity of RPE cells to detoxify ROS and repair mitochondrial damage. Activation of UPRmt could lead to increased expression of mitochondrial chaperones, improved clearance of damaged proteins, and a restoration of redox balance within the mitochondria. This dual mechanism—direct structural stabilization via mitofilin binding and indirect activation of UPRmt—positions MA-5 as a potentially powerful agent for correcting mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD (Tong et al., 2022; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
If MA-5 performs as hypothesized in RPE cells, several beneficial effects are anticipated. First, by binding mitofilin and stabilizing cristae architecture, MA-5 should restore proper assembly and function of ETC complexes leading to increased ATP production. Such a recovery in mitochondrial bioenergetics is particularly critical in RPE cells, given their high energy demands for processes such as phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and maintenance of the visual cycle (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022). Second, the stabilization of cristae, alongside the potential activation of the UPRmt, is expected to reduce mtROS production by minimizing electron leakage from complex I and III of the ETC. Lower ROS levels would alleviate oxidative stress—a known driver of RPE degeneration and dry AMD progression that has been documented in multiple studies (Ji et al., 2021; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Third, the activation of UPRmt may upregulate key mitochondrial chaperones such as mtHsp70, facilitating improved protein folding, enhanced clearance of damaged proteins, and overall better maintenance of mitochondrial homeostasis. These cellular changes should collectively promote RPE survival and function, thus potentially slowing or even reversing some aspects of the cellular degenerative processes seen in dry AMD (Ji et al., 2021; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

Furthermore, since mitofilin/Mic60 is an abundantly expressed and essential component in RPE mitochondria—as evidenced by its upregulation in early AMD patient samples—the MA-5-mediated stabilization of this protein is expected to yield measurable improvements in mitochondrial parameters in cellular assays. Such improvements would include increased mitochondrial membrane potential, enhanced basal and maximal respiration, and a reduction in apoptotic markers associated with mitochondrial damage. Ultimately, if these in vitro effects translate into in vivo efficacy, MA-5 could contribute to a novel treatment modality that directly addresses the underlying mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD (Ferrington et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
The therapeutic candidate MA-5 presents a highly promising, mechanistically driven approach to addressing dry AMD by targeting mitochondrial dysfunction—a central hallmark of the disease. Its proposed dual mechanism of binding to mitofilin to stabilize cristae architecture and activating the UPRmt to enhance antioxidant defenses directly aligns with the documented mitochondrial pathology in RPE cells. Strengths of this candidate include the following:  
– The strategy of targeting mitofilin is supported by numerous observations that indicate altered mitofilin levels and cristae disorganization in AMD, suggesting that restoring cristae integrity may ameliorate mitochondrial deficits (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Ferrington et al., 2020).  
– MA-5’s documented capacity to improve ATP production and reduce mtROS in non-ocular models indicates a favorable mitochondrial modulation profile that is likely transferable to RPE cells, where energy production and redox homeostasis are critical (Ji et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022).  
– Activation of UPRmt represents an innovative therapeutic angle that not only protects mitochondrial structure but also boosts cellular defenses against oxidative stress—a pathway that has been implicated in maintaining RPE cell viability under conditions of sustained stress (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022).  

Despite these promising aspects, several points of caution must be noted. First, while the beneficial effects of MA-5 have been demonstrated in fibroblast and C. elegans models, no direct data exist regarding its efficacy in RPE cells or in animal models of dry AMD. The translation of effects from non-ocular systems to the highly specialized RPE must be rigorously evaluated. Second, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of MA-5 in the context of ocular delivery are unknown at this time; the compound’s ability to achieve sufficient retinal concentration, while minimizing systemic toxicity, remains an open question. Third, the precise binding affinity and specificity of MA-5 for mitofilin in RPE mitochondria have not yet been characterized. Off-target effects or unintended modulation of mitochondrial dynamics may lead to adverse outcomes if the drug’s action is not adequately localized within the retina. Finally, activation of UPRmt, while beneficial in the context of mitochondrial stress, may also have complex downstream effects that require careful titration to avoid potential maladaptive consequences in long-term treatment scenarios (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Ferrington et al., 2020).

In summary, the proposed mechanism for MA-5 is conceptually attractive given the wealth of literature linking mitochondrial cristae disruption and excessive ROS production to dry AMD pathology. The candidate’s potential to bind mitofilin, stabilize mitochondrial structure, and activate a protective UPRmt aligns well with the current understanding of mitochondrial deficits in RPE cells observed in AMD (Ji et al., 2021; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). However, significant preclinical work is needed to validate its efficacy specifically in the RPE environment. Studies should include detailed binding assays to confirm the interaction between MA-5 and mitofilin, evaluation of mitochondrial bioenergetics and redox parameters in RPE cell cultures, and ultimately, assessments in animal models of dry AMD that recapitulate key aspects of mitochondrial dysfunction. Provided these experimental hurdles can be overcome and favorable pharmacokinetic profiles established for ocular delivery, MA-5 may represent a novel and promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD (Nashine, 2021; Tong et al., 2022).

Overall, while there is robust mechanistic rationale and encouraging preclinical evidence from other models supporting the concept of mitochondrial stabilization via mitofilin targeting, the transition of MA-5 into the dry AMD arena is contingent upon a series of critical validation steps in relevant ocular models. The strengths of MA-5 lie in its potential to address the upstream causes of RPE degeneration by restoring mitochondrial integrity and function, which is a major unmet need in dry AMD therapeutics. The weaknesses and uncertainties, however, underscore the need for a focused series of seriatim experiments to fully characterize its effects in RPE cells and to develop suitable formulations for ocular administration. Based on the current evidence drawn from mitochondrial pathology in AMD and the functional roles of mitofilin/Mic60 in maintaining cristae integrity, MA-5 merits further investigation as a repurposed candidate for dry AMD, with the caveat that extensive preclinical testing is required before clinical translation can be considered (Ji et al., 2021; Ferrington et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) is an endogenous bile acid, a taurine conjugate of ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), that was originally isolated from bear bile and is now produced synthetically for laboratory and clinical research (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). As a member of the bile acid family, TUDCA has a dual role: its traditional function in lipid digestion is accompanied by potent signaling activities that provide chemical chaperoning properties. This property enables TUDCA to stabilize misfolded proteins and alleviate endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. In addition, TUDCA exerts anti-apoptotic effects by modulating the mitochondrial cell death pathway. Its application as a neuroprotectant has emerged over the last decade, and its favorable ocular safety profile in preclinical studies has invited consideration for repurposing in retinal degenerative conditions such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, TUDCA and related bile acids have been evaluated in several models of neurodegeneration and retinal degeneration. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that TUDCA protects retinal cells against both oxidative injury and ER stress. In vitro, TUDCA treatment of ARPE-19 retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) not only attenuated cell death but also reduced markers of oxidative damage, increased cell viability, and modulated antioxidant gene expression (Alhasani et al., 2020). In parallel, multiple in vivo studies have reported that systemic administration of TUDCA reduces photoreceptor apoptosis and preserves retinal structure and function in animal models of inherited retinal degeneration including retinitis pigmentosa and in models of exudative AMD such as laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024). Although the bulk of these preclinical investigations has been conducted in models focusing on photoreceptors, retinal ganglion cells, or vascular endpoints, the underlying mechanisms of TUDCA’s cytoprotective activity raise the possibility that its benefits may extend to the RPE—the cell type that is centrally involved in dry AMD and geographic atrophy. Importantly, little direct evidence exists from dedicated geographic atrophy models or experiments that solely target RPE mitochondrial endpoints; however, the promising biochemical and electrophysiological data from rodent models suggest that the candidate’s safety and overall neuroprotective profile are well established in ocular systems (Alhasani et al., 2020; Li et al., 2024).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanistic basis of TUDCA’s therapeutic potential is multifaceted. A central theme is its ability to reduce ER stress in cells that are undergoing chronic protein-folding challenges. Under conditions of sustained stress, the unfolded protein response (UPR) is activated, and key transcription factors such as CHOP (CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein homologous protein) become upregulated to drive cell death when the stress is unmanageable. TUDCA has been shown in various cell models to act as a chemical chaperone, thereby reducing ER stress and suppressing CHOP induction (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020). For instance, in ARPE-19 cell models treated with thapsigargin to induce ER stress, TUDCA treatment led to a marked decrease in CHOP expression and reduced apoptosis (Alhasani et al., 2020). This suggests that TUDCA modulates the ER stress response, possibly by stabilizing protein folding and facilitating the proper trafficking of misfolded proteins.  

In addition to its ER‐related effects, TUDCA exerts anti-apoptotic actions by stabilizing the mitochondrial membrane. Under stress conditions, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) triggers the intrinsic apoptosis pathway, characterized by the translocation of pro-apoptotic proteins such as Bax, the release of cytochrome c, and subsequent caspase activation (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Kusaczuk, 2019). Evidence from neuronal models and some retinal studies indicates that TUDCA prevents the depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane, thereby preserving Δψm, and reduces downstream apoptotic events. This effect has been linked to a reduction in mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), which are produced excessively when mitochondrial integrity is compromised. TUDCA’s actions in reducing overall intracellular ROS levels, as reported in H₂O₂-exposed RPE cells, further support the idea that improved mitochondrial function may contribute to cell survival (Alhasani et al., 2020).  

Moreover, TUDCA can modulate additional cellular pathways that are pertinent to retinal health. It has been reported to up-regulate antioxidant defenses via increased expression of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) and enhancement of glutathione (GSH) levels. These effects likely contribute to the reduction in both cytosolic and mitochondrial oxidative stress (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Other studies have highlighted TUDCA’s influence on phagocytic pathways in the RPE—for example, by promoting MerTK-mediated phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments—which, although not directly linked to ER or mitochondrial stress, represent an important aspect of RPE physiology that could indirectly improve cell survival in degenerative conditions (Murase et al., 2015).  

Taken together, the biochemical and molecular data indicate that TUDCA’s mechanism of action is well aligned with addressing the cellular stress observed in dry AMD. By inhibiting CHOP induction, preserving Δψm, and reducing mtROS, TUDCA could feasibly stop or slow the progression of RPE cell death that underpins geographic atrophy (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

Expected Effect:  
The proposal hypothesizes that TUDCA will reduce ER stress in the RPE, thereby preventing secondary mitochondrial dysfunction and the associated production of reactive oxygen species. In the proposed assay, RPE cells (either ARPE-19 or primary RPE cultures) subjected to an ER stressor (such as thapsigargin or H₂O₂) are expected to exhibit elevated markers of ER stress, particularly CHOP, along with signs of mitochondrial distress including decreased mitochondrial membrane potential and increased mtROS production. On treatment with TUDCA at appropriate dosages (often in the 100 μM range in similar in vitro assays), one expects to observe a significant reduction in CHOP induction along with the preservation or restoration of Δψm, as measured by fluorescent indicators such as JC-1 or TMRM, and a concomitant decrease in mitochondrial ROS as assessed by probes such as MitoSOX. These effects are expected because prior in vitro studies in retinal cells have shown that TUDCA can ameliorate cell death by modulating oxidative stress and apoptosis, and similar outcomes have been observed in neuronal and non-retinal cell models (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

Furthermore, given that dry AMD is characterized by chronic ER stress and secondary mitochondrial dysfunction in the RPE, the ability of TUDCA to reduce these stress responses may translate into improved RPE survival and function. RPE cells express high levels of ER stress markers under pathologic conditions, and proteins such as CHOP are known mediators of apoptosis in these cells. It is therefore expected that TUDCA will attenuate the cascade of events initiated by ER stress—reducing apoptotic signaling, preserving mitochondrial function, reducing mtROS, and ultimately leading to enhanced cell viability. As such, the anticipated outcome in the proposed assay is a clear biochemical and functional improvement in RPE cultures challenged with ER stressors, supporting the use of TUDCA in dry AMD (Alhasani et al., 2020).  

Overall Evaluation:  
TUDCA presents as a promising candidate for drug repurposing in dry AMD due to its well-documented roles as an ER stress inhibitor and mitochondrial stabilizer. One of the major strengths of TUDCA is its dual mechanism of action: it not only functions as a chemical chaperone to reduce ER stress and inhibit the pro-apoptotic effector CHOP but also stabilizes the mitochondrial membrane to prevent the cascade of events leading to cell death. These effects are complemented by its ability to reduce overall reactive oxygen species and bolster antioxidant defenses, which are critical in tissues affected by chronic oxidative stress such as the RPE in geographic atrophy (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020).  

In terms of therapeutic history, TUDCA has been used extensively in preclinical models of retinal degeneration, with multiple studies demonstrating its protective effects on photoreceptors and retinal ganglion cells. Its prior use in ocular contexts and a favorable safety profile in animal models provide important translational support. However, one potential weakness in repurposing TUDCA for dry AMD is that most of the preclinical evidence is derived from models of photoreceptor degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, or choroidal neovascularization rather than from targeted assessments in RPE cells or dry AMD models. While there is suggestive evidence from several studies that TUDCA benefits RPE function—such as improved phagocytosis via MerTK activation—the direct demonstration of its ability to inhibit CHOP induction, preserve mitochondrial membrane potential, or specifically reduce mitochondrial ROS in RPE is less robust (Alhasani et al., 2020; Murase et al., 2015).  

Furthermore, although mechanistic data in other tissue and neuronal models strongly support TUDCA’s capacity to modulate both ER stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Kusaczuk, 2019), these endpoints have not been unequivocally established in RPE cells within the context of geographic atrophy. This gap highlights the need for further targeted preclinical studies. For example, experiments using polarized primary RPE cultures or RPE-specific animal models of dry AMD should be undertaken to directly measure CHOP expression, mitochondrial membrane potential via JC-1/TMRM assays, and mtROS levels via MitoSOX or equivalent assays following TUDCA treatment. Additionally, while in vitro assays have established its general safety in retinal cells, chronic dosing studies in appropriate AMD models will be important to establish long-term efficacy and safety.  

Another consideration is that the multifaceted nature of dry AMD pathogenesis extends beyond ER stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. While TUDCA’s actions on these pathways are compelling, resistance or compensatory mechanisms in RPE cells could limit its efficacy in the complex environment of geographic atrophy. Nonetheless, the broad-spectrum anti-apoptotic and anti-oxidative actions of TUDCA provide a strong rationale for its further examination in dry AMD.  

In summary, TUDCA is a highly attractive candidate for repurposing as a therapy for dry AMD based on its natural origin as a bile acid, its established use as a chemical chaperone and mitochondrial stabilizer, and its demonstrated neuroprotective and cytoprotective effects in multiple retinal models. Its capacity to reduce ER stress—with particular inhibition of CHOP induction—and to preserve mitochondrial membrane potential and lower oxidative stress aligns well with the proposed mechanism underlying RPE degeneration in geographic atrophy. However, critical gaps remain in the direct evidence for its efficacy in RPE-specific systems and AMD/dry AMD models. The next steps should include rigorous experimental validation in relevant in vitro and in vivo models to establish that TUDCA indeed preserves Δψm and suppresses mitochondrial ROS in ER-stressed RPE cells while reducing pro-apoptotic markers such as CHOP. If these endpoints can be achieved in targeted preclinical studies, TUDCA could represent a promising, safe, and mechanistically rational therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020).
