Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Resveratrol is a naturally occurring polyphenolic compound belonging to the stilbene class and is structurally defined as 3,5,4′-trihydroxystilbene. It is biosynthesized by plants such as Vitis vinifera (grapes), Japanese Knotweed, and various berries in response to stress factors like injury or pathogen attack, and it is a well‐recognized phytoalexin with a molecular formula of C14H12O3 (Bel, 2020; Pop et al., 2022). Originally isolated from the White Hellebore in the mid-20th century and later found in red wine due to grape skin fermentation, resveratrol has garnered significant attention not only for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties but also for its potential benefits in cardiovascular and neuroprotective contexts (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pop et al., 2022). As such, resveratrol—and by extension its commercial version (Cayman Chemical #70580) used in our studies—is classified as a nutraceutical and drug candidate with a long track record of investigative research including applications in aging, inflammation, and ocular health (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pop et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
A considerable volume of biochemical, preclinical, and early clinical literature has explored resveratrol’s broad spectrum of activities. Historically, resveratrol has been investigated primarily for its cardioprotective and neuroprotective effects, as well as its anti-aging properties. In the realm of ophthalmology, several in vitro and animal studies have focused on its role in retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD), diabetic retinopathy (DR), and glaucoma. For instance, its use in RPE cell models has shown promising evidence for ameliorating oxidative stress-induced damage, a central factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Clinical investigations have attempted to translate these findings, as exemplified by the terminated clinical trial NCT02625376 that investigated resveratrol for exudative AMD (Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015), highlighting both the potential and the challenges involved in its clinical application (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Beyond ocular applications, resveratrol’s inclusion in various nutraceutical formulations underscores its established safety profile when administered at low-to-moderate doses, although issues pertaining to bioavailability and rapid systemic metabolism have been recurrent themes in the literature (Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, resveratrol exerts its effects primarily by modulating multiple intracellular signaling cascades. The central hypothesis we are testing is that resveratrol activates the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells—a pathway integral to regulating mitochondrial biogenesis and the antioxidant defense system. Activation of SIRT1, a NAD+-dependent deacetylase, by resveratrol increases the deacetylation and activation of its downstream effector, AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Once activated, AMPK facilitates the phosphorylation and activation of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1 alpha (PGC-1α) in the cytoplasm, which subsequently translocates to the nucleus to upregulate the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and antioxidant responses, including the gene encoding superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). This cascade not only improves mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and spare respiratory capacity—critical indicators of cellular health under oxidative stress—but also promotes an overall enhancement of cellular resilience against reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Bel, 2020; Bryl et al., 2022). Further molecular studies indicate that resveratrol can also modulate extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERK1/2) and mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK), contributing additional layers of cytoprotection through anti-apoptotic effects (Pop et al., 2022; Pop et al., 2022). Together, these mechanistic insights provide a comprehensive biochemical framework through which resveratrol is hypothesized to mitigate the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in RPE cells—a primary factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2021; Bryl et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of the proposed assay for dry AMD, our expectation is that resveratrol will exert a multifaceted protective effect on RPE cells under oxidative challenge. Specifically, when RPE cells are exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as a model for oxidative stress, resveratrol is anticipated to counteract the resultant mitochondrial dysfunction by upregulating antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2, thereby reducing intracellular ROS levels (Bel, 2020; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Restoration of the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) is a critical endpoint, as it directly reflects cellular energy status and the ability of mitochondria to sustain ATP synthesis under stress (Buonfiglio et al., 2024). In addition, an improvement in spare respiratory capacity—the measure of a cell’s ability to respond to increased energy demands—should be evident, reflecting enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and a greater capacity for cellular repair mechanisms (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bryl et al., 2022). These cytoprotective effects have been demonstrated in in vitro studies using ARPE-19 and other human retinal pigment epithelial cell lines, and they resonate with the established role of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis in mediating energy metabolism and antioxidative defenses in the retina (Bryl et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021). Moreover, by decreasing the accrual of oxidative damage, resveratrol is expected to limit apoptotic signaling pathways, which are crucial in slowing the progressive degeneration observed in dry AMD (Bel, 2020; Pop et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
The cumulative evidence from preclinical studies strongly supports the potential of resveratrol as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, especially considering its capacity to modulate mitochondrial function and activate intrinsic antioxidant defenses. The activation of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis not only augments mitochondrial biogenesis but also enhances the expression of key antioxidant enzymes required to neutralize ROS, thereby directly addressing one of the primary mechanisms underlying AMD pathology (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bryl et al., 2022). One of the major strengths of resveratrol is its pleiotropic mode of action; beyond its antioxidant properties, its anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic activities further consolidate its candidacy for chronic conditions like dry AMD (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Bel, 2020). Furthermore, extensive safety data in various preclinical models indicate that resveratrol is well tolerated at certain dose ranges, which is a positive indicator for its potential clinical translation (Wang et al., 2021; Bel, 2020).

However, several limitations remain that warrant careful consideration. The primary challenge with resveratrol is its poor bioavailability and rapid metabolism, which may result in subtherapeutic tissue concentrations despite high oral absorption. This has driven research efforts into advanced drug delivery platforms, such as nanoparticle-based systems and liposomal formulations, aimed at enhancing ocular retention and achieving sustained drug levels in the retina (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Additionally, although the in vitro and animal model data are promising, there exists a dearth of robust clinical trial data specifically addressing dry AMD, as evidenced by the terminated trial in exudative AMD (Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015) and the limited clinical evidence in related retinal pathologies (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Another potential weakness is the dose-dependent duality of its mechanism, where low doses predominantly mediate SIRT1-dependent effects, whereas higher doses might trigger SIRT1-independent pathways, possibly leading to off-target effects or toxicity (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Such a narrow therapeutic window necessitates a precise optimization of dosing regimens and formulation strategies. Despite these challenges, the overarching trend in preclinical research underscores that with proper formulation and dosing strategies, resveratrol could excel as an adjuvant or even monotherapy for protecting RPE cells from oxidative injury and, consequently, for the management of dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

In-Depth Analysis of Preclinical and Clinical Evidence:  
Numerous in vitro studies have characterized the effect of resveratrol on retinal pigment epithelial cells, notably ARPE-19 cell lines, under conditions of oxidative stress. Such studies consistently demonstrate that resveratrol treatment leads to a measurable reduction in ROS levels, a decrease in markers of apoptosis, and an overall improvement in mitochondrial parameters including Δψm and spare respiratory capacity (Bel, 2020; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). These findings are reinforced by experiments showing that resveratrol can mitigate blue light-induced retinal damage and preserve cell viability, further supporting its relevance in ocular pathologies where light-induced oxidative stress is a contributing factor (Bel, 2020). Complementary studies in animal models have shown that resveratrol can reduce inflammatory cytokine secretion and inhibit processes such as choroidal neovascularization, which has implications not only for dry AMD but also for its neovascular (wet) counterpart (Bryl et al., 2022; Bel, 2020).

Moreover, mechanistic investigations into the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis reveal that the deacetylation of PGC-1α is a critical step in the upregulation of mitochondrial genes, which directly correlates with increased cellular ATP production and enhanced resistance to oxidative stress (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Experimental data also show that SOD2 expression is significantly increased following resveratrol treatment, corroborating the compound’s role in boosting the cellular antioxidant capacity (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). These molecular events culminate in an environment that is less conducive to oxidative damage, thereby potentially arresting or even reversing some aspects of RPE degeneration that occur in dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021).

From a clinical perspective, the application of resveratrol in ocular disorders has been approached with caution, primarily due to pharmacokinetic challenges. Even though systemic administration of resveratrol has demonstrated efficacy in reducing plasma oxidative markers in diabetic patients and other conditions, the translation to ocular tissue remains hindered by its low aqueous solubility and rapid hepatic metabolism (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Abu-Amero et al., 2016). To overcome these barriers, innovative drug delivery systems such as chitosan-based nanoparticles, polymeric micelles, and liposomal formulations are being actively developed and show promise for achieving therapeutic levels in retinal tissues (Pop et al., 2022; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Such advanced formulations not only improve bioavailability but also allow for controlled release, which is essential for a chronic condition like dry AMD where sustained therapeutic action is desirable.

Additional mechanistic studies also suggest that resveratrol’s efficacy might be enhanced when used in combination with other therapeutic agents. For instance, its synergistic effects with anti-VEGF treatments in mitigating inflammatory cascades and suppressing angiogenesis have been noted in various preclinical models (Rusciano & Bagnoli, 2023; Tong et al., 2022). This combinatorial approach could be particularly valuable in cases where dry AMD transitions toward neovascular complications, thereby broadening the therapeutic window of resveratrol-based interventions.

Challenges in Drug Delivery and Bioavailability:  
While the biochemical rationale for using resveratrol in dry AMD is robust, its clinical development is significantly complicated by pharmacokinetic limitations. The compound is classified as a BCS Class II molecule, meaning that despite having high membrane permeability and lipophilicity, its poor aqueous solubility results in less than 1% bioavailability following oral administration (Kaštelan et al., 2025). As a consequence, only minimal amounts of unchanged resveratrol reach the systemic circulation and, by extension, the ocular tissues. Current research thus prioritizes the optimization of drug delivery vehicles to enhance its stability and target specificity. Nanotechnology-based delivery methods, including polymeric nanoparticles and solid lipid nanoparticles, have demonstrated enhanced tissue penetration and prolonged drug retention in the eye (Pop et al., 2022; Kaštelan et al., 2025). However, these strategies are still in the developmental phase, and their safety, scalability, and reproducibility for routine clinical use remain to be thoroughly validated. The potential for off-target effects and variability in patient-specific pharmacokinetics are additional hurdles that must be addressed in future clinical studies.

Safety and Dosing Considerations:  
Resveratrol has been generally recognized as safe in many preclinical studies, with low-dose regimens showing minimal adverse effects and favorable tolerability profiles (Wang et al., 2021; Bel, 2020). Nonetheless, concerns have been raised regarding gastrointestinal disturbances and other side effects at higher doses, as well as potential interactions with other medications (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Moreover, due to the compound’s rapid metabolism, determining an optimal dosing regimen that achieves effective local concentrations in the retina without inducing systemic toxicity remains challenging. This necessitates further preclinical and early-phase clinical trials to elucidate the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic profiles specific to ocular applications. Tailoring the dosing strategy based on individual metabolic rates and employing controlled-release formulations may help mitigate these issues and maximize therapeutic outcomes (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Kaštelan et al., 2025).

Strategic Direction and Future Perspectives:  
Given the multifaceted biological activities of resveratrol and the encouraging preclinical evidence in models of oxidative stress-induced RPE damage, it holds considerable promise as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to modulate the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis and promote mitochondrial biogenesis presents a novel therapeutic approach that directly targets the cellular dysfunctions underlying RPE degeneration. However, the translation of these findings into clinical practice will require addressing the critical challenges of bioavailability, formulation, and dosing.

Future research should focus on (1) developing and rigorously testing advanced drug delivery systems such as nanoparticle encapsulation methods that can bypass first-pass metabolism and target the retina more effectively, (2) conducting detailed pharmacokinetic studies to determine the optimal dosing regimen for achieving sustained therapeutic concentrations in ocular tissues, and (3) exploring combination therapy approaches that integrate resveratrol with conventional treatments such as anti-VEGF agents or other nutraceuticals to provide a comprehensive strategy against AMD progression (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Pop et al., 2022; Rusciano & Bagnoli, 2023). Furthermore, expanding the investigative efforts into patient-specific and personalized medicine approaches might allow for tailoring treatment protocols based on individual metabolic and genetic profiles, thereby maximizing efficacy and reducing adverse effects (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, resveratrol emerges as a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its extensive preclinical evidence, well-elucidated molecular mechanisms, and potential for modulating critical cellular pathways implicated in retinal degeneration. The strengths of resveratrol are rooted in its natural origin, broad-spectrum antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, and its ability to enhance mitochondrial function through the activation of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α pathway. These attributes are particularly relevant for combating the oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction that are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Nonetheless, its clinical utility is hampered by significant challenges related to bioavailability and metabolism, which necessitate innovative formulation and delivery strategies. Moreover, the variable dose-response observed in preclinical studies highlights the need for precise dose optimization before resveratrol can be reliably integrated into clinical practice for AMD treatment (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Although resveratrol has been investigated in clinical trials for ocular conditions, further large-scale, well-designed studies are essential to validate its efficacy, establish an acceptable safety profile, and determine its long-term benefits in human subjects with dry AMD (Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015; Pop et al., 2022).

Given the current state of evidence, we recommend that the research team continue to explore resveratrol as a candidate for dry AMD with a dual focus: first, to refine and optimize drug delivery systems that enhance its ocular bioavailability, and second, to design and implement comprehensive dose-escalation and safety studies in relevant preclinical models. Collaborative efforts that integrate insights from molecular biology, pharmacology, and clinical research will be critical in overcoming the translational challenges that have traditionally limited the application of resveratrol in ocular therapeutics (Pop et al., 2022; Rusciano & Bagnoli, 2023).

Conclusion:  
Resveratrol represents a promising candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration based on its robust mechanistic rationale and supportive preclinical evidence. Its capacity to activate the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis, promote mitochondrial biogenesis, and enhance antioxidant enzyme expression positions it as a multifaceted agent capable of mitigating oxidative stress in RPE cells—one of the key pathological drivers of AMD (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). While the compound’s safety profile in low-dose regimens is encouraging, its poor bioavailability and rapid metabolism require that future research prioritize advanced drug delivery systems and optimized dosing strategies. With concerted efforts in formulation science, preclinical validation, and clinical evaluation, resveratrol has the potential to become an integral part of a multi-targeted therapeutic approach for dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Kaštelan et al., 2025).

In conclusion, a comprehensive literature review of resveratrol underscores both its therapeutic potential and the challenges that must be overcome before its clinical application in dry AMD can be realized. The strengths of its molecular mechanisms and established safety in various studies are tempered by pharmacokinetic limitations that necessitate further research. The proposed strategy to focus on enhancing bioavailability via innovative drug delivery systems, coupled with rigorous preclinical safety and efficacy evaluations, will determine whether resveratrol can fulfill its promise as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bel, 2020). With continued investigation and collaboration across multidisciplinary research teams, resveratrol could offer a novel and effective means to delay or prevent RPE degeneration and the progression of dry AMD, ultimately improving patient outcomes in this challenging and prevalent ocular disease (Bryl et al., 2022; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Olaparib is a small‐molecule, synthetic inhibitor originally discovered and developed for oncology indications, particularly in cancers harboring BRCA mutations. Olaparib was discovered through high‐throughput screening and subsequently optimized chemically to yield a compound with high potency and selectivity for PARP1 and PARP2. In the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), the hypothesis is that olaparib will inhibit PARP1‐mediated NAD+ consumption in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby preserving both the cellular energy status and, indirectly, the activity of NAD+‐dependent enzymes such as the mitochondrial sirtuin SIRT3. Therapeutic History:  
Olaparib’s primary therapeutic history is rooted in oncology. It has been used clinically to target cancers that are deficient in homologous recombination repair, where its PARP‐inhibitory action leads to synthetic lethality in malignant cells. Over recent years, growing experimental evidence has implicated hyperactivation of PARP1 in a number of non-neoplastic conditions characterized by oxidative DNA damage and subsequent energetic collapse. In animal models that mimic features of dry AMD, such as sodium iodate (SI)-injected mice or rabbits, pharmacologic inhibition of PARP1 with olaparib resulted in preservation of retinal morphology including maintenance of outer nuclear layer thickness and improvements in electrophysiological readouts (Jang et al., 2018). To date, while significant preclinical evaluation has been performed in models of oxidative injury and retinal degeneration, olaparib has not yet been trialed clinically in dry AMD patients. However, the repurposing approach is supported by extensive literature in which PARP inhibitors have been proposed as a therapeutic approach to mitigate oxidative injury in neurodegenerative disorders, with the underlying rationale being the restoration of cellular NAD+ levels as well as improved mitochondrial bioenergetics (Jang et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
The well-established mechanism of action of olaparib is based on the inhibition of the PARP enzyme family, primarily targeting PARP1. Under conditions of oxidative stress, DNA strand breaks activate PARP1, which catalyzes the transfer of ADP-ribose units from NAD+ to several nuclear and mitochondrial proteins. This process, known as poly-ADP-ribosylation, normally plays a role in DNA repair; however, when overactivated—as is observed in conditions of persistent oxidative damage—PARP1 consumes enormous amounts of cellular NAD+, leading to ATP depletion and an ensuing collapse of cellular energy metabolism. Olaparib binds to the catalytic domain of PARP1, thereby preventing the excessive transfer of ADP-ribose moieties and preserving intracellular NAD+ levels. This preservation of NAD+ is critical because NAD+ is a necessary cofactor not only for PARP activity but also for the function of a range of NAD+-dependent deacetylases, including the sirtuin family.

Within the context of dry AMD, RPE cells subjected to oxidative stress exhibit PARP1 hyperactivation, resulting in NAD+ depletion that compromises cellular bioenergetics and contributes to mitochondrial dysfunction. While much of the literature has focused on the interplay between PARP1 and nuclear sirtuin SIRT1 in the context of autophagy, emerging hypotheses posit that similar mechanisms extend to the mitochondria. SIRT3, a key mitochondrial deacetylase, requires NAD+ to catalyze the deacetylation of multiple mitochondrial proteins. One well-characterized substrate is manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), whose deacetylated, active form is responsible for detoxifying reactive oxygen species (ROS) within the mitochondria. The proposed mechanism is that by inhibiting PARP1, olaparib preserves NAD+ pools in RPE cells, which in turn sustains SIRT3 activity. Active SIRT3 would ensure proper deacetylation of mitochondrial proteins, including MnSOD, thus reducing mitochondrial protein hyperacetylation, curtailing mtROS production, and ultimately mitigating oxidative damage (Jang et al., 2018; Lin & Apte, 2018).

Notably, while multiple studies have documented that olaparib effectively reduces NAD+ depletion, preserves ATP levels, and maintains mitochondrial membrane potential in ARPE-19 cells under H2O2 challenge (Jang et al., 2018), direct assessments of SIRT3 activity and the acetylation state of mitochondrial proteins remain to be specifically reported. First, by inhibiting PARP1, olaparib should significantly reduce the accumulation of poly-ADP-ribose (PAR) polymers that are normally generated in response to oxidative DNA damage. Moreover, given the central role of NAD+ as a substrate for mitochondrial sirtuins, it is anticipated that olaparib treatment will indirectly sustain SIRT3 activity within the mitochondria. In animal models designed to mimic the degenerative environment of dry AMD—such as the sodium iodate (SI) induced retinal degeneration model—olaparib has been shown to preserve retinal morphology. The overall evaluation of olaparib as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD proceeds from its well-characterized mechanism of action and a robust body of preclinical evidence, while also acknowledging certain gaps that need to be addressed in future research.

Strengths:  
1. The Mechanism Is Well-Established in Related Contexts: Olaparib’s ability to inhibit PARP1 has been incontrovertibly demonstrated both biochemically and in various disease models. 3. This fundamental mechanism is highly relevant to dry AMD pathogenesis, where oxidative stress-mediated damage to the RPE is a central feature. Moreover, the potential consequences of long-term PARP inhibition—particularly with respect to DNA repair fidelity—and the challenges of delivering adequate concentrations of the drug to the retina without systemic toxicity cannot be overlooked.

In addition, while preclinical studies using SI-induced retinal degeneration models have shown promising results with olaparib in terms of improving retinal morphology and function (as per improvements in ERG wave amplitudes and preservation of outer nuclear layer thickness), these models do not capture the full complexity of dry AMD in humans. Dry AMD is a chronic, multifactorial disorder with contributions from inflammation, drusen formation, and cumulative RPE dysfunction over years; thus, short-term protective effects observed in animal models, while encouraging, might not directly translate to robust clinical efficacy.

Taking into account both the strengths and the weaknesses, the overall potential for olaparib as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is promising but not yet definitive. The strengths lie in its well-documented ability to inhibit PARP1, prevent NAD+ depletion, and improve mitochondrial bioenergetics in models of retinal oxidative injury. Furthermore, the fact that olaparib is already an approved drug for other indications offers a strategic advantage in terms of repurposing and regulatory approval. However, the lack of direct evidence linking olaparib treatment to the restoration of mitochondrial SIRT3 activity and normalization of mitochondrial protein acetylation is a significant gap in the current literature. Addressing this gap would require focused studies that assess SIRT3 enzyme activity, evaluate the acetylation status of mitochondrial proteins such as MnSOD, and determine whether these molecular endpoints correlate with improved RPE survival and function. Additionally, long-term safety studies that investigate the potential risk of impaired DNA repair in retinal cells under chronic PARP inhibition are warranted. Finally, developing an appropriate ocular delivery system that ensures effective local concentrations of olaparib while minimizing systemic exposure will be critical for translating these preclinical findings into a viable clinical candidate.

Its ability to inhibit PARP1 offers a means to preserve NAD+ levels in RPE cells, thereby potentially maintaining mitochondrial function and reducing oxidative injury—a cascade that is highly attractive for a disease characterized by chronic oxidative stress. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) is a synthetic derivative of fumaric acid that belongs to the class of fumaric acid esters (FAEs) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Chemically, DMF is the dimethyl ester of fumaric acid, with a molecular weight of approximately 144.13 g/mol, and is produced by reacting fumaric acid with methanol in the presence of a strong acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Although fumaric acid occurs naturally as an intermediate in the citric acid cycle, DMF itself is fully synthetically manufactured, conferring the advantages of chemical stability and the ability to precisely modulate its structure to enhance pharmacological properties (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Moreover, DMF is classified as an electrophilic molecule that, due to its α,β-unsaturated ester structure, can covalently modify protein thiols, particularly the cysteine residues within KEAP1, thereby initiating its downstream effects on cellular redox homeostasis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Fumaric acid esters as a class have a long-standing history in pharmacotherapy, originally finding application in dermatology, most notably in the treatment of psoriasis, and have since been repurposed for neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis (MS) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, fumaric acid esters were introduced into clinical practice as antipsoriatic agents in Europe, with formulations such as Fumaderm® entering the market in the 1990s (Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). DMF in particular emerged as a key component in these formulations, and its efficacy in modulating immune responses and suppressing inflammation in skin diseases laid the foundation for its later repurposing in other systemic inflammatory conditions (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Over time, DMF was repurposed and further developed as an oral agent for the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), culminating in its FDA approval in 2013 under the trade name Tecfidera® by Biogen (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163). Clinical trials, including large-scale phase 3 studies, have demonstrated its favorable safety profile and efficacy in reducing relapse rates and slowing disability progression in MS patients (Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 14–16). Although there is no extensive historical record of DMF being used directly for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other primary ocular diseases, recent preclinical findings have indicated that its potent activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway may confer significant protective effects on the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This has sparked considerable interest in repurposing DMF for ocular indications such as geographic atrophy, a late stage of dry AMD, by leveraging its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities observed in nonocular settings (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, DMF functions primarily as a prodrug; upon oral administration it is rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases within the gastrointestinal tract to yield its active metabolite, monomethyl fumarate (MMF) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). The pharmacodynamic actions of DMF principally involve the electrophilic modification of specific cysteine residues—most notably cysteine 151—on Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Under physiological conditions, KEAP1 binds to and retains the transcription factor Nrf2 in the cytoplasm, targeting it for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. However, when DMF covalently modifies KEAP1, it disrupts this complex, allowing Nrf2 to dissociate and translocate into the nucleus (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). In the nucleus, Nrf2 binds to antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoters of numerous genes encoding cytoprotective enzymes, including glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), and various enzymes involved in glutathione (GSH) synthesis and regeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). These molecular interactions lead to enhanced antioxidant defenses, improved detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and overall better maintenance of cellular redox balance (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). In addition to its role in promoting antioxidant gene expression via Nrf2 activation, DMF has been shown to have immunomodulatory properties; it can shift cytokine profiles by increasing interleukin-4 (IL-4)–expressing CD4+ T cells and decreasing the production of proinflammatory cytokines such as interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and interleukin-17 (IL-17) (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Furthermore, DMF has been reported to inhibit nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation in certain cellular contexts, thus contributing to a reduction in inflammatory signaling independently of Nrf2 (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Together, these molecular actions result in lowered cellular oxidative stress and an improved inflammatory milieu, which are critical factors implicated in the pathogenesis of chronic degenerative diseases (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry AMD, particularly the geographic atrophy form, is characterized by the gradual degeneration of RPE cells, which leads to subsequent photoreceptor loss and irreversible vision impairment. Central to the pathophysiology of dry AMD are oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation that progressively compromise RPE viability and function (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). The hypothesis being explored is that DMF, through its robust activation of the Nrf2 pathway, can enhance the expression of ARE-driven genes that encode for antioxidant and cytoprotective proteins, thereby counteracting the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in the RPE (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 13–14). In particular, the upregulation of enzymes involved in glutathione synthesis is expected to increase intracellular levels of GSH, a critical thiol antioxidant that protects mitochondrial membranes and supports cellular bioenergetics (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Preclinical studies in retinal models have demonstrated that DMF can effectively preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and reduce the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β), both of which are hallmarks of RPE distress under oxidative challenge (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Given that the RPE is highly metabolically active and particularly vulnerable to cumulative oxidative damage, the sustained activation of Nrf2 by DMF following oral dosing is anticipated to provide continuous reinforcement of antioxidant defenses and maintain mitochondrial integrity in these cells (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 3–5; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). Moreover, by mitigating inflammatory signaling, DMF may not only protect the RPE but also contribute to a more favorable microenvironment that limits the propagation of cell death signals, thus potentially slowing the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Collectively, these expected cellular effects support the rationale for using DMF as an intervention to preserve retinal structure and function by lowering oxidative damage and supporting bioenergetics in the RPE.

The potential of dimethyl fumarate as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD rests on a solid mechanistic rationale combined with an established clinical pedigree in other indications. One of the primary strengths of DMF is its well-characterized pharmacological profile; it is FDA-approved for multiple sclerosis and has been safely administered to thousands of patients over several years, which significantly mitigates the risk and regulatory hurdles typically associated with repurposed drugs (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). The dual actions of DMF—in particular, its ability to both activate the Nrf2 pathway and attenuate proinflammatory signals—directly target the underlying pathological processes in dry AMD, where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central drivers of RPE degeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Although DMF is known to be effective in MS and psoriasis, the ocular milieu presents unique pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic challenges that may not be fully addressed by the current oral formulations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18). The rapid hydrolysis of DMF to MMF means that, while the active metabolite does exert therapeutic effects, fine-tuning the dosing regimen to ensure adequate drug levels in the retina while minimizing systemic side effects is necessary (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). There is also the question of whether systemic administration of DMF can generate sufficient concentrations in the retina to achieve a meaningful therapeutic effect. While emerging evidence suggests that DMF can cross the blood-retinal barrier and activate Nrf2 in retinal cells (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3), further pharmacokinetic and translational studies are warranted to confirm its retinal bioavailability and the optimal dosing regimen for ocular indications.

Another consideration is the complexity of dry AMD itself, which is a slowly progressive, multifactorial disease with contributions from genetic predispositions, environmental exposures, and systemic metabolic disturbances. It remains to be seen whether the monotherapeutic approach of DMF, targeting primarily oxidative stress via Nrf2 activation, will be sufficient to halt or reverse disease progression, or whether combination therapies will ultimately be required (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Furthermore, while the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms of DMF are well supported by in vitro data and animal studies, there is still limited clinical data on its efficacy in ocular disease settings. Early-phase clinical trials aimed at evaluating DMF in geographic atrophy have to rigorously assess both structural outcomes (e.g., changes in the area of atrophy) and functional endpoints (e.g., visual acuity, retinal sensitivity) to establish its therapeutic benefit in dry AMD (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Despite these limitations, the strengths of DMF are compelling. The drug’s ability to upregulate a broad spectrum of cytoprotective genes via the Nrf2 pathway makes it a versatile candidate for mitigating the oxidative and inflammatory stress that drives RPE degeneration. The fact that DMF has already cleared extensive regulatory and clinical safety evaluations in nonocular indications is a significant advantage, as it greatly accelerates the translational pathway compared to a novel chemical entity (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Additionally, the repurposing of an already approved drug leverages existing manufacturing, formulation, and distribution infrastructure, favorably impacting the cost and timeline associated with drug development (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Its mechanism of action—centered on Nrf2 activation leading to enhanced antioxidant capacity along with anti-inflammatory effects—directly addresses the key pathophysiological mechanisms implicated in dry AMD. The extensive clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis provides a reliable safety and tolerability framework, which is crucial for rapid repositioning into a new clinical area such as geographic atrophy (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). However, it is essential to conduct targeted preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials specifically in ocular disease models to optimize dosing, confirm retinal delivery, and demonstrate clinical efficacy before advancing to larger randomized controlled trials (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Overall, while challenges remain regarding optimal application in the retinal context and potential side effects in an older patient population, DMF—by virtue of its dual antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms and robust clinical background—stands as a viable candidate that merits further investigation for the treatment of dry AMD.

Given the current evidence, the following recommendations are proposed for advancing DMF as a candidate for dry AMD:  

1. Conduct detailed pharmacokinetic studies in animal models to assess the retinal bioavailability of DMF and its active metabolite MMF following systemic administration. This should include studies comparing different dosing schedules and formulations to optimize retinal exposure without exacerbating systemic adverse effects (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2).  

2. Develop and validate preclinical models of dry AMD that recapitulate the key features of human geographic atrophy, with a focus on evaluating the efficacy of DMF in protecting RPE cells against oxidative stress and preserving mitochondrial function (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

3. Investigate the potential benefits of combining DMF with other therapeutic agents that target complementary pathways in dry AMD. For example, agents that modulate complement activation or improve choroidal blood flow may synergize with the Nrf2-mediated antioxidant mechanism of DMF (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).  

4. Initiate early-phase clinical trials in patients with geographic atrophy to establish proof of concept. These studies should include robust biomarker assessments (e.g., measurement of ARE gene expression, retinal imaging for atrophy progression, and functional visual outcomes) to correlate molecular effects with clinical benefit (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

5. Carefully monitor the safety profile of DMF in the elderly population, as the incidence of gastrointestinal side effects and lymphopenia may differ compared to the population with MS. Consider the feasibility of modified-release formulations or alternative routes of administration (e.g., topical ocular delivery) to minimize systemic side effects while maximizing retinal drug concentrations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18).

Overall, the repurposing of dimethyl fumarate for dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a robust mechanistic framework and a significant body of preclinical and clinical data generated in other indications. Its capacity to activate the Nrf2 pathway, enhance mitochondrial glutathione synthesis, and modulate inflammatory responses in RPE cells directly addresses several pivotal aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). While there are challenges regarding optimal retinal delivery and management of systemic adverse effects, the clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis lends considerable support to its translational potential. Consequently, dimethyl fumarate represents a well‐justified and attractive therapeutic candidate for further exploration in the treatment of dry AMD, warranting additional preclinical optimization and clinical investigation to fully define its role in preserving visual function in patients affected by this progressive degenerative disease (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin (also known as sirolimus and available as Abcam #ab120224) is a naturally occurring macrolide compound originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus. It belongs to the class of macrocyclic lactones and is known for its potent inhibitory effects on the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). This compound has been extensively used in various contexts such as immunosuppression, cancer therapy, and more recently, as a tool to modulate autophagy in age-related degenerative diseases. In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction and dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), rapamycin is being explored as a repurposed therapeutic candidate with the hypothesis that mTORC1 inhibition will enhance both general autophagy and selective mitophagy. This clearance of reactive oxygen species (ROS)–generating, damaged mitochondria may alleviate oxidative stress, reduce the accumulation of toxic lipofuscin compounds (including A2E), and ultimately slow the progression of dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, rapamycin was first discovered for its potent immunosuppressive properties and later developed for use in preventing transplant rejection and certain cancers. Its ability to inhibit mTORC1 has made it a valuable tool in research related to aging and neurodegeneration. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its effectiveness in modulating autophagy and protecting cellular integrity under stress conditions, particularly in the retinal environment. In animal models of retinal degeneration and even some early clinical trials, rapamycin was shown to reduce the accumulation of autofluorescent granules and inflammatory cytokines in the RPE, which are both hallmarks of dry AMD pathology (Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022). Notably, rapamycin has been administered via diverse routes, including intravitreal and subconjunctival injections, in attempts to treat geographic atrophy or other dry AMD phenotypes, although the clinical outcomes have been mixed. For example, clinical trials such as those referenced in studies with identifiers NCT00766649 and NCT01445548 demonstrated that while rapamycin was generally safe and well-tolerated in ocular applications, its efficacy in slowing down the progression of geographic atrophy and improving visual acuity remained limited (National Eye Institute, 2008; National Eye Institute, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These historical findings highlight both the promise and the challenges associated with translating rapamycin’s mechanistic benefits into robust clinical outcomes for dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary mechanism of rapamycin involves the formation of a complex with the immunophilin FKBP12. This complex binds to mTORC1 and inhibits its kinase activity, leading to a decrease in the phosphorylation of downstream targets such as ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K) and the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 (4EBP1). Under normal circumstances, active mTORC1 suppresses autophagy by phosphorylating these targets, which in turn prevents the formation of autophagosomes. By inhibiting mTORC1, rapamycin effectively removes this blockade, thereby promoting the induction of autophagy as evidenced by increased conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II and clearance of the autophagic substrate p62 (Zhang et al., 2015).

Within retinal pigment epithelial cells, this induction of autophagy is particularly important. RPE cells are responsible for the phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments; a process that generates large amounts of cellular debris and metabolic byproducts such as lipofuscin. In dry AMD, impaired autophagic flux leads to the accumulation of these compounds, which, in turn, contributes to oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Rapamycin’s inhibition of mTORC1 not only enhances general autophagy but also promotes selective mitochondrial clearance (mitophagy). Key players in the mitophagy pathway include the serine/threonine kinase PINK1 and the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin, both of which accumulate on depolarized mitochondria and signal their removal via autophagic mechanisms. By stimulating this PINK1/Parkin pathway, rapamycin enhances the clearance of damaged, ROS-generating mitochondria, thus preserving overall mitochondrial health (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).

Additionally, rapamycin’s downstream effects include activation of transcription factors such as TFEB, which regulates lysosomal biogenesis and further enhances the autophagic process. This dual action—promoting both autophagy and lysosomal function—helps to mitigate the accumulation of toxic aggregates such as lipofuscin and A2E in RPE, therefore reducing oxidative stress and inflammation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). Through these biochemical interactions, rapamycin establishes a cellular environment that is more capable of dealing with metabolic challenges and oxidative damage, both of which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Chang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Based on the proposed hypothesis, the administration of rapamycin in RPE cells is expected to result in a cascade of beneficial cellular events. In our proposed assay, rapamycin is anticipated to inhibit mTORC1 activity, leading to a measurable increase in autophagic flux. This will be evident from the enhanced lipidation of LC3-II, the clearance of p62 (an autophagy adaptor protein that accumulates when autophagy is impaired), and the activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway in response to oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2015).

The specific clearance of damaged mitochondria is particularly critical in the RPE, where mitochondrial dysfunction is a significant contributor to the generation of reactive oxygen species and subsequent cellular damage. By removing these dysfunctional mitochondria, rapamycin is expected to reduce intracellular ROS levels and thereby lower oxidative stress, a driving force in AMD pathology. In parallel, the enhanced autophagic degradation of accumulated lipofuscin and the toxic fluorophore A2E is predicted to further limit the inflammatory and apoptotic cascades triggered by these compounds, thus preserving RPE cell viability and function (Zhang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2025).

Given that impaired mitochondrial function and the resulting energy production deficits are central to the progression of dry AMD, the expected outcomes from rapamycin treatment would include not only a reduction in oxidative stress markers but also improvements in mitochondrial dynamics and overall cellular homeostasis. Such effects would ideally be reflected in functional assays measuring cell viability, mitochondrial respiration, and reductions in inflammatory cytokine production (Zhang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2025).

In our comprehensive evaluation of rapamycin as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and potential weaknesses emerge that warrant careful consideration. One of the key strengths of rapamycin lies in its well-characterized mechanism of action and its ability to broadly modulate autophagy through mTORC1 inhibition. Preclinical studies have repeatedly demonstrated that rapamycin can induce autophagic flux, leading to the clearance of cellular debris and damaged mitochondria in RPE cells. This is particularly compelling given the central role of impaired autophagy in the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, which are major pathological features of dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018). The dual-action mechanism—enhancing both autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis via TFEB activation—further supports its potential in addressing multiple aspects of the disease pathology, from oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction to inflammation and cellular senescence (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Another strength is the substantial body of preclinical evidence showing that rapamycin not only stimulates autophagy but also improves mitochondrial function. The activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway is particularly relevant since these proteins are indispensable for mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control. By facilitating the removal of ROS-generating, damaged mitochondria, rapamycin could directly impact the cellular energy balance and reduce damaging oxidative insults in the RPE, which is pivotal for maintaining retinal health (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).

Despite its promising mechanistic profile, several significant challenges remain. Clinical studies investigating the use of rapamycin for AMD have yielded mixed results. While the drug has been shown to be safe and tolerable in ocular applications, several clinical trials, such as those involving subconjunctival or intravitreal administration, did not demonstrate significant efficacy in halting the progression of geographic atrophy or improving visual acuity. In summary, rapamycin presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its robust mechanism of action—specifically, its capacity to inhibit mTORC1, thereby stimulating both general autophagy and the selective removal of damaged mitochondria via the PINK1/Parkin pathway. Preclinical evidence strongly supports the idea that such modulation can reduce oxidative stress, clear toxic accumulations like lipofuscin/A2E, and ultimately preserve mitochondrial and RPE cellular function (Zhang et al., 2015; Hyttinen et al., 2018). These considerations suggest that while rapamycin is a promising candidate worthy of further investigation, its ultimate role in the treatment paradigm for dry AMD will depend on our ability to refine treatment regimens, develop predictive biomarkers for patient selection, and perhaps combine mTOR modulation with complementary therapeutic strategies that reinforce its protective effects while mitigating its risks (Wang et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2019).

Given the cumulative evidence, our overall recommendation is to continue exploring rapamycin as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, but with a strategic focus on further preclinical investigations that address the dose–response relationships in donor-derived RPE models and the development of advanced drug delivery systems. It will also be important to design future clinical trials with stratified patient populations and integrated biomarkers that can help identify responders. In essence, the promise of rapamycin in modulating autophagy to improve mitochondrial health and reduce oxidative stress in RPE cells is clear at the molecular and cellular levels, but translating these benefits into a safe and effective therapy for dry AMD will require overcoming substantial clinical challenges (Mei et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Strengths of rapamycin include its well-established mechanism of action, the significant supportive preclinical data demonstrating improvements in autophagic flux and mitochondrial clearance in RPE models, and its potential to address several key pathological features of dry AMD simultaneously. By alleviating the buildup of toxic metabolites and preserving mitochondrial health in RPE cells, rapamycin could potentially slow disease progression and preserve vision. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10), also known as ubiquinone, is a naturally occurring lipophilic molecule synthesized endogenously via the mevalonate pathway. It is a quinone class compound that was originally discovered as a crucial component of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) and is essential for adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production. Chemically, CoQ10 contains a benzoquinone ring and a long isoprenoid side chain, which confers its lipid solubility and allows integration into mitochondrial and other cellular membranes. As a therapeutic candidate, it is available commercially (e.g., Cayman Chemical #700105) as a pure formulation that can be used for research purposes and has been repurposed in several settings to address oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Its widespread use as a dietary supplement and as an adjunct therapy in cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and metabolic disorders underlines the extensive clinical experience with this class of compounds. The rationale for its repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is based on the compound’s natural role as a coenzyme, its potent antioxidant properties, and its ability to modulate mitochondrial energy metabolism—all of which are critically compromised in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) of the aging eye (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Maiuolo et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past decades, CoQ10 has been evaluated in multiple experimental and clinical contexts. Biochemical studies have consistently demonstrated its ability to protect mitochondrial structure and function by facilitating electron transport and scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS). In vitro, CoQ10 treatments have been shown to improve mitochondrial respiration and ATP production in various cell types, including ARPE-19 cells, a widely used human RPE model. These studies utilized oxidative stress challenges (e.g., H₂O₂ exposure) to simulate conditions similar to those present in dry AMD, and showed that CoQ10 supplementation lowered levels of apoptotic markers such as caspase-3 and TUNEL staining, effectively reducing cell death (Hernandez et al., 2024). In the clinical arena, several studies have explored the use of CoQ10, sometimes in combination with other nutritional compounds, for early stages of AMD. For instance, combination therapies incorporating CoQ10 with agents such as acetyl-L-carnitine and n-3 fatty acids have resulted in improvements in visual function and fundus appearance among early AMD patients, demonstrating its potential impact in slowing disease progression (Feher et al., 2005). Moreover, its established safety profile in chronic use and its history of use as a metabolic booster and antioxidant in various degenerative conditions further support its potential repurposing for dry AMD, where similar mitochondrial and oxidative stress mechanisms underlie disease pathology (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Kiliç, 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, CoQ10 exhibits a dual mechanism of action that is highly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Firstly, it functions as an obligatory electron carrier within mitochondria. In the ETC, CoQ10 shuttles electrons from complexes I (NADH dehydrogenase) and II (succinate dehydrogenase) to complex III (cytochrome bc₁ complex), thereby driving the proton gradient needed for ATP synthesis by ATP synthase. Its redox-active benzoquinone ring is capable of reversible oxidation and reduction, enabling it to accept and donate electrons during the process of cellular respiration (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Hernandez et al., 2024). This electron-transfer activity is critical in tissues with high metabolic demands such as the retina, where the maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (mt∆ψ) and ATP production are indispensable for cell survival. A second and equally important aspect of CoQ10’s mechanism is its potent antioxidant property. Through its reduced form, ubiquinol, CoQ10 directly scavenges free radicals and prevents lipid peroxidation of cell membranes. This antioxidant activity extends to the regeneration of other lipid-soluble antioxidants such as vitamin E, thereby reinforcing a broader cellular antioxidant defense network (Manzar et al., 2020; Hernandez et al., 2024).

In the context of RPE cells, the protective effects of CoQ10 extend to the stabilization of mitochondrial proteins and prevention of oxidative damage-induced mtDNA release. Notably, CoQ10 has been shown to modulate the expression of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase-2 (SOD2), which further contributes to the reduction of intracellular ROS levels. Additionally, CoQ10 influences mitochondrial dynamics by reducing the activation of pro-fission proteins like DRP-1, thereby inhibiting excessive mitochondrial fragmentation—a phenomenon that has been associated with increased apoptosis in oxidative stress conditions (Hernandez et al., 2024). Its capacity to dampen inflammatory mediators, including the restoration of cytokines such as TNFα and caspase-1 to their baseline levels following oxidative insult, underscores its role in mitigating the inflammatory cascades implicated in AMD pathology (Hernandez et al., 2024). These combined actions—preservation of electron transport efficiency, reduction in ROS-mediated damage, and stabilization of mitochondrial integrity—are central to the hypothesis that exogenous supplementation of CoQ10 can counteract the underlying cellular stress mechanisms in dry AMD (Hernandez et al., 2024; Maiuolo et al., 2022).

Expected Effect in the Assay and Mechanistic Rationale:  
Given the proposed experimental approach—using H₂O₂-challenged ARPE-19 cells as a model to simulate oxidative stress encountered in dry AMD—the expected effect of exogenous CoQ10 supplementation would be multi-fold. Firstly, by increasing the mitochondrial pool of ubiquinone, the supplemented CoQ10 is expected to enhance electron transport efficiency within RPE cells, thereby sustaining ATP production under stress conditions. The repletion of CoQ10 levels would counteract the age-associated decline in endogenous CoQ10 and restore mitochondrial membrane potential, which is critical for normal cell metabolism (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Maiuolo et al., 2022). Secondly, due to its antioxidant properties, CoQ10 is anticipated to directly scavenge ROS generated by H₂O₂ exposure, thereby reducing oxidative lipid peroxidation and preventing damage to mitochondrial membranes and proteins. As a result, key apoptotic markers—such as caspase-3 activity and TUNEL-positive cell counts—should be decreased, reflecting improved cell viability and reduced progression toward cell death (Hernandez et al., 2024).

Moreover, it is expected that CoQ10 may influence the expression of genes related to mitochondrial defense and redox balance, such as those encoding for SOD2 and other antioxidant enzymes, ultimately leading to a more robust cellular response against oxidative insults. Since ARPE-19 cells express the protein machinery integral to both oxidative phosphorylation and antioxidant defense, the modulation of these pathways by CoQ10 would provide a mechanistic basis for its protective effects in vitro (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Hernandez et al., 2024). In addition, the expected synergistic benefits when CoQ10 is combined with a nutritional complex—such as Nutrof—has been documented, where the combination was more effective at reducing oxidative stress markers and apoptosis than CoQ10 alone (Hernandez et al., 2024). This synergistic effect likely arises from the complementary actions of CoQ10 in regenerating other antioxidants and its specific targeting of mitochondrial dysfunction—a key driver of dry AMD pathology (Hernandez et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
The comprehensive review of the literature provides strong mechanistic rationale and preclinical evidence to support the repurposing of CoQ10 for dry AMD. One of the primary strengths of CoQ10 as a candidate is its dual role—facilitating electron transport and exerting antioxidant effects—which addresses two critical pathological features in dry AMD: mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. Its ability to preserve mitochondrial integrity by maintaining the electron transport chain and reducing mitochondrial depolarization directly aligns with the needs of RPE cells, which have high energy demands and are vulnerable to oxidative damage (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Hernandez et al., 2024).

Furthermore, numerous in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have demonstrated that CoQ10 supplementation leads to reduced apoptosis, lower ROS generation, and improved cell viability following oxidative challenges. These studies provide robust biochemical evidence that CoQ10 can counteract cellular stresses that mimic early events in AMD pathogenesis (Hernandez et al., 2024). From a therapeutic history standpoint, the extensive clinical experience with CoQ10 in other degenerative and mitochondrial disorders lends additional credibility to its safety and potential efficacy for ocular applications. Its long history of use as an adjunct supplement in various conditions enhances its attractiveness as a repurposed drug candidate from a regulatory and translational perspective (Feher et al., 2005).

However, several challenges must also be considered. One key weakness is the issue of bioavailability. CoQ10 is a large, lipophilic molecule, and its effective delivery to the retina following systemic or topical administration remains a significant technical hurdle. Although studies have shown that exogenous CoQ10 can elevate retinal levels to some extent, optimizing its formulation for enhanced tissue penetration and sustained release is critical for therapeutic success (Manzar et al., 2020; Qu et al., 2009). Additionally, the variability observed in clinical responses in AMD studies suggests that patient-specific factors or differences in the progression of mitochondrial dysfunction may influence the therapeutic outcomes. Therefore, while the preclinical data are promising, rigorous clinical studies are needed to determine optimal dosing regimens, delivery methods (such as oral versus topical administration), and combination strategies with other antioxidants or mitotropic agents (Feher et al., 2005).

Another important consideration is the multifactorial nature of dry AMD, which involves not only mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress but also chronic inflammation, complement dysregulation, and genetic predispositions. As such, CoQ10 monotherapy may not fully address the complex pathological processes underlying the disease. Combination therapies that target multiple pathways simultaneously, such as those combining CoQ10 with nutritional complexes that include other antioxidants and anti-inflammatory agents, are likely to yield better clinical outcomes. In this regard, CoQ10 appears to be particularly well-suited for inclusion in combination regimens designed to synergistically reduce oxidative stress and support mitochondrial health (Hernandez et al., 2024; Feher et al., 2005).

The mechanistic data support the hypothesis that elevating RPE mitochondrial ubiquinone pools can enhance electron transport efficiency and reduce ROS accumulation. Detailed biochemical analyses have shown that CoQ10 prevents lipid peroxidation and stabilizes the mitochondrial membrane potential, which in turn decreases the release of pro-apoptotic factors such as cytochrome c and prevents the activation of caspases (Hernandez et al., 2024). These effects are particularly relevant to dry AMD, where RPE cell death and the subsequent degeneration of photoreceptors play a central role in disease progression (Hernandez et al., 2024).

Overall, the aggregate evidence from biochemical, in vitro, and early clinical studies strongly supports the continued investigation of CoQ10 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its established role in mitochondrial function and cellular antioxidant defense mechanisms, combined with a favorable safety profile, provides a firm scientific basis for clinical translation. The expected benefits in ARPE-19 assays—namely, enhanced cell viability, reduced ROS levels, and the attenuation of apoptosis—reflect the direct mechanistic impacts of CoQ10 on key aspects of dry AMD pathology. Moreover, the potential to modulate mitochondrial dynamics via regulation of proteins such as DRP-1 and maintain mtDNA integrity further underscores its therapeutic relevance (Hernandez et al., 2024).

In conclusion, while CoQ10 is not without its challenges—primarily related to its delivery and the multifactorial etiology of dry AMD—the strengths of its molecular mechanism and supportive preclinical data render it a highly promising candidate. The potential for topical and systemic administration to elevate retinal levels, combined with its dual action as both a metabolic enhancer and a free radical scavenger, aligns well with the therapeutic needs of dry AMD patients. Nonetheless, further research is warranted to optimize formulations, validate efficacy in larger clinical trials, and explore its integration into multi-targeted therapeutic strategies. Given the existing biochemical and clinical literature, CoQ10 represents a rational and mechanistically sound approach for addressing mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in dry AMD, making it a candidate worthy of further development and investigation (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Hernandez et al., 2024; Feher et al., 2005; Qu et al., 2009).

While human ocular data are pending, the direct mechanistic link to RPE mitochondrial health, measurable biochemical endpoints, and positive results across multiple relevant preclinical systems underpin a strong probability of experimental success and eventual translation.
