Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GC4419 (avasopasem manganese) is a small‐molecule, manganese‐containing superoxide dismutase (SOD) mimetic that was developed by Galera Therapeutics. Its design is based on replicating the catalytic activity of the endogenous mitochondrial enzyme, manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), which naturally detoxifies superoxide radicals by converting them to hydrogen peroxide and oxygen. The compound is formulated as a manganese‐containing macrocyclic ligand complex with a molecular weight of approximately 483, prepared in an aqueous sodium bicarbonate solution (Mapuskar et al., 2024). Originally developed as the enantiomer of M40403, GC4419 belongs to the MnPAM class of SOD mimetics—a subclass of therapeutic agents that have been engineered to overcome the limitations of exogenous SOD proteins, such as immunogenicity and poor pharmacokinetics (Sonis, 2021; Galera Therapeutics, Inc., 2013). SOD mimetics, by virtue of their small molecular weight and catalytic efficiency, have been widely explored clinically as radioprotective agents to mitigate oxidative tissue damage, and they offer an attractive platform for tackling diseases in which oxidative stress is a central pathophysiological driver.

Therapeutic History:  
GC4419 has a well‐documented history in preclinical and clinical settings aimed at ameliorating oxidative tissue injury. Preclinical studies have shown that GC4419 protects against cisplatin‐induced kidney injury in both acute (AKI) and chronic (CKD) murine models by scavenging superoxide radicals and attenuating inflammatory responses (Mapuskar et al., 2024). In the clinical arena, GC4419 has been evaluated in several trials—most notably in Phase 1b/2a and Phase 3 studies—targeting radiation‐induced mucositis in head and neck cancer patients. These trials demonstrated that intravenous infusion of GC4419 not only reduced the incidence and severity of severe oral mucositis but also reduced other therapy‐associated adverse events, such as cisplatin‐induced nephrotoxicity, in a dose‐dependent manner (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Sonis, 2021). Despite this extensive history of use in mitigating radiation‐ and cisplatin‐linked toxicities, there have been no direct reports or preclinical studies that have investigated GC4419 in the context of retinal disorders or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Houldsworth, 2024). This lack of prior application in ocular models underscores the novelty of the repurposing hypothesis—to deploy the compound’s antioxidative properties in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells under chronic oxidative stress conditions such as those elicited by drusen accumulation.

Mechanism of Action:  
GC4419 functions by mimicking the natural enzymatic activity of MnSOD, specifically catalyzing the dismutation reaction of superoxide (O2•–) into hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and molecular oxygen (Mapuskar et al., 2024). Its reported catalytic rate constant of approximately 1×10^7 per mol per second, while lower than that of native mitochondrial SOD (~1.2×10^9 per mol per second), is nonetheless sufficient to achieve a measurable reduction in superoxide levels in stressed tissues (Mapuskar et al., 2024). This selective removal of superoxide is particularly advantageous because GC4419 does not appreciably interact with other reactive oxygen species such as nitric oxide, peroxynitrite, or hydrogen peroxide, thus ensuring a focused mechanism of action (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Galera Therapeutics, Inc., 2013). In preclinical kidney models, treatment with GC4419 has been associated with the restoration of mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) activities, reduced expression of pro-oxidant enzymes like NADPH oxidase 4 (NOX4), and a decrease in markers of inflammation (Mapuskar et al., 2024). Although the detailed chemical structure (e.g., the precise coordination geometry of the manganese ion or whether it resembles a classical Mn-salen derivative) has not been fully disclosed, the compound is understood to be a highly stable, low-molecular-weight agent optimized for biological compatibility and effective redox cycling (Sonis, 2021; Mapuskar et al., 2024). Given its intended mechanism as a mitochondrial SOD mimetic, it is hypothesized that GC4419 can enter cells, localize to mitochondria, and thereby directly attenuate mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production—a rationale that is central to its anticipated repurposing for dry AMD.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
In dry age-related macular degeneration, the retinal pigment epithelium is subject to chronic oxidative stress resulting from cumulative damage due to drusen deposits and impaired cellular clearance mechanisms. RPE cells are rich in mitochondria and depend heavily on efficient oxidative metabolism; however, over time, excessive production of ROS—particularly superoxide generated by dysfunctional mitochondrial electron transport—can lead to cell death and, consequently, to the progression of dry AMD. The underlying hypothesis for repurposing GC4419 in this context is that, by acting as a mitochondrial SOD mimetic, the compound will convert excess superoxide generated within RPE cells into hydrogen peroxide, which can then be further detoxified by endogenous catalase and glutathione peroxidase systems (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Houldsworth, 2024). This conversion is expected to not only alleviate the oxidative burden but also to preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψ_m) and maintain efficient ATP synthesis, which is critical for the survival and function of RPE cells (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Montoro et al., 2023). Furthermore, by reducing superoxide levels, GC4419 may indirectly dampen inflammation mediated by redox-sensitive transcription factors (such as NF-κB), thereby decreasing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines that can exacerbate RPE stress and degeneration (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Houldsworth, 2024). Although direct evidence of GC4419’s efficacy in retinal models has not yet been reported, the known expression of the MnSOD gene (SOD2) in RPE cells and the central role of mitochondrial oxidative damage in dry AMD provide a strong mechanistic rationale for the compound’s potential effectiveness when applied to ocular tissues (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Houldsworth, 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
GC4419 presents several compelling strengths as a candidate for repurposing in the management of dry AMD. Its well-characterized mechanism of action, which involves the selective catalytic removal of superoxide, addresses a key pathogenic factor in dry AMD—oxidative stress within the RPE and its mitochondria (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Sonis, 2021). The compound’s demonstrated ability to restore mitochondrial function and reduce inflammation in preclinical models of cisplatin-induced kidney injury and radiation-induced mucosal damage underscores its potential utility in any tissue where oxidative stress is a driving factor (Mapuskar et al., 2024). Moreover, the pharmacological profile of GC4419—highlighted by its favorable molecular weight, catalytic properties, and prior progression into clinical trials for other indications—supports its viability as a repurposed drug candidate. By leveraging existing clinical data on safety and efficacy in non-ocular settings, the repurposing effort for dry AMD could benefit from relatively expedited translational development.

Nevertheless, there are also notable weaknesses and uncertainties. First, despite the strong theoretical rationale, no direct preclinical or clinical studies have yet evaluated GC4419 in retinal tissues or in animal models of dry AMD; therefore, its ocular pharmacokinetics, penetrance of the blood–retina barrier, and potential for mitochondrial uptake specifically in RPE cells remain unproven (Houldsworth, 2024). Second, the current formulations of GC4419 are designed for intravenous administration as used in radiation mucositis trials; adapting these formulations for local ocular delivery (e.g., via intravitreal injection or targeted sustained-release systems) may present challenges that need to be carefully addressed. Third, while the mechanism of converting superoxide to hydrogen peroxide is beneficial, it is crucial to ensure that the resultant H2O2 is efficiently cleared by endogenous antioxidant defenses in the RPE; accumulation of H2O2 could itself precipitate oxidative damage if the cellular detoxification capacity is overwhelmed (Mapuskar et al., 2024). Moreover, although GC4419 has been referred to in some contexts as part of the “Mn-salen” or MnPAM families of dismutase mimetics, the precise structural classification has not been fully disclosed, which may affect its predicted bio-distribution and interaction with specific intracellular targets (Sonis, 2021; Galera Therapeutics, Inc., 2013). Lastly, differences in the pathological microenvironments between tissues treated for radiation toxicity versus the RPE in dry AMD could influence the overall efficacy of GC4419; thus, careful preclinical studies in ocular disease models will be necessary to confirm that its antioxidative and anti-inflammatory actions translate effectively to an AMD setting (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Sonis, 2021).

Overall, while the strengths of GC4419 are notable—with a robust mechanism, supportive preclinical and clinical history in other indications, and a focused approach to counteracting mitochondrial oxidative stress—the weaknesses highlight the need for further investigation into its ocular pharmacodynamics, formulation for targeted delivery, and comprehensive evaluation in dry AMD-specific models before advancing to clinical trials in this indication (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Sonis, 2021; Galera Therapeutics, Inc., 2013).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Idebenone is a synthetic short‐chain benzoquinone that was designed as an analog of coenzyme Q10. Its chemical derivation from ubiquinone endows it with increased solubility and significantly enhanced antioxidant properties – reportedly up to ten‐fold greater than natural coenzyme Q10 – which in turn improves its capacity to shuttle electrons through the mitochondrial respiratory chain (Arend et al., 2015, pp. 2, 7–8). Originally synthesized as a potential remedy for mitochondrial dysfunction, idebenone belongs to the class of quinone derivatives that have historically been applied to conditions driven by oxidative stress and defective energy metabolism. The compound was discovered through efforts to mimic and improve on the natural electron carrier function of coenzyme Q10, with modifications engineered to optimize cellular uptake and bioavailability, thereby augmenting its use in various neurodegenerative and ophthalmologic applications (Gueven et al., 2015, pp. 4–5; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 7–8).

Therapeutic History:  
Idebenone’s clinical journey commenced with its use in Leber’s Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON), a mitochondrial disorder resulting in acute or subacute vision loss. In LHON, idebenone has been shown to improve visual function, as evidenced by improvements in photopic electroretinography (ERG) and other visual assessments, and has received regulatory approval in certain regions for this indication (Lyseng-Williamson, 2016, pp. 1–2). Preclinical studies have also demonstrated that idebenone exerts cytoprotective effects on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and retinal ganglion cells by preserving mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and reducing apoptosis in the face of oxidative stress (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13). Although idebenone’s original target was LHON, its biochemical properties—particularly its dual role as an electron shuttle and antioxidant—have spurred interest in repurposing the compound for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), a condition likewise characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction and heightened oxidative injury. Several studies have provided evidence from both biochemical assays and animal models that idebenone can modulate pro‐ and anti‐apoptotic protein expression (notably lowering Bax while increasing Bcl-2 levels) and activate the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway in RPE cells, thereby suggesting a potential benefit in retinal diseases beyond LHON (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 7–8).

Mechanism of Action:  
Idebenone operates through a multifaceted mechanism that addresses the dual challenges of mitochondrial energy impairment and oxidative damage. Fundamentally, idebenone is proposed to bypass defects in mitochondrial complex I by serving as an electron carrier that transfers reducing equivalents directly to complex III. This electron shuttling function is critical for maintaining the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and sustaining ATP synthesis when the conventional electron transfer through complex I is compromised due to oxidative damage—a scenario that is hypothesized to occur in the RPE under conditions such as drusen-induced stress (Arend et al., 2015, p. 2; Wang et al., 2025, pp. 5–8). In parallel, idebenone exhibits potent antioxidant activity by scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitigating the lipid peroxidation processes that are thought to contribute to drusen formation in dry AMD (Arend et al., 2015, pp. 7–8).

At the molecular level, idebenone has been shown to influence key cell survival pathways. It modulates the intrinsic mitochondrial apoptotic cascade by upregulating the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2 and concurrently downregulating the pro-apoptotic protein Bax. This shift in the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio helps to curb the initiation of apoptosis and contributes to cell survival in oxidative environments (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 5–6). Furthermore, idebenone stimulates the nuclear translocation of the transcription factor Nrf2, which in turn induces the expression of a suite of antioxidant genes. This activation of the Nrf2 pathway reinforces the cell’s intrinsic defenses against oxidative insult, which is of particular relevance in RPE cells tasked with handling the chronic low-grade oxidative stress present in AMD (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13). However, it is important to note that in certain settings—such as in cells deficient in the enzyme NQO1—idebenone’s efficacy as an electron carrier may be diminished, and higher concentrations may even elicit pro-oxidant or cytotoxic effects (Varricchio et al., 2020, pp. 18–20). These findings underscore the importance of optimizing the dosing strategy and ensuring appropriate cellular context to fully exploit idebenone’s protective actions.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of the proposed application for dry AMD, the hypothesis is that idebenone will act to shuttle electrons to complex III in RPE cells, thereby bypassing complex I defects induced by drusen-associated oxidative stress. This mechanism is expected to preserve the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and sustain ATP production, even under conditions of compromised oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). Preclinical data in RPE cell models have shown that idebenone treatment can mitigate the dissipation of Δψm in the face of hydrogen peroxide-induced stress, suggesting that similar protective effects could be harnessed in AMD where RPE cellular damage is a hallmark (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13).

Beyond its electron shuttling capacity, idebenone’s potent antioxidant action is expected to lower intracellular ROS levels and reduce lipid peroxidation, thereby protecting RPE cell membranes from the oxidative effects linked to drusen formation. This reduction in oxidative stress, coupled with the preservation of mitochondrial function, is anticipated to result in decreased activation of apoptotic pathways. The compound is also predicted to trigger Nrf2-dependent transcription of antioxidant genes within RPE cells—a response that is critical for combating the chronic oxidative stress implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13). 

Functionally, these molecular effects should translate into measurable improvements in cellular assays of mitochondrial function and viability. In vitro, one would expect to observe maintained or restored Δψm and ATP production in idebenone-treated RPE cells versus controls exposed to oxidative stress. In a more integrated system, such as in animal models or clinical assessments, improvements in photopic ERG responses—previously demonstrated in LHON patients under idebenone therapy—may serve as a surrogate marker for the preservation of retinal neuronal function and integrity (Lyseng-Williamson, 2016, pp. 1–2). Nonetheless, although the mechanistic rationale is robust, these expected effects depend critically on fine-tuning dosage to avoid the potential cytotoxicity observed at supra-therapeutic concentrations and to account for inter-patient variability in enzymes such as NQO1 that activate idebenone (Varricchio et al., 2020, pp. 18–20).

Overall Evaluation:  
The evidence reviewed supports idebenone as a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Among its key strengths is its dual action: the capacity to serve as an alternative electron shuttle to bypass complex I defects and the potent antioxidant activity that collectively mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage. These properties are especially relevant to dry AMD, where RPE degeneration and mitochondrial impairment form the basis of disease progression (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 2, 7–8).

Idebenone’s previous clinical approval and widespread use in LHON provide valuable precedent regarding its safety and efficacy in a retinal context. Moreover, preclinical data from in vitro studies in RPE cells offer compelling evidence regarding its ability to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential, sustain ATP synthesis, and modulate apoptotic pathways under oxidative stress conditions—mechanisms that are directly applicable to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 5–6). The activation of Nrf2 and subsequent upregulation of antioxidant defenses further consolidate its therapeutic potential (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13).

Nevertheless, several challenges remain. The efficacy of idebenone in bypassing complex I defects may be restricted by factors such as NQO1 expression, and potential pro-oxidant effects at higher concentrations necessitate careful dose optimization. In addition, while data from LHON and certain RPE cell models are promising, direct evidence from robust preclinical models of dry AMD is still limited. Some studies addressing these mechanisms have appeared in journals with variable impact factors, which calls for cautious interpretation of the data and underscores the need for further high-quality, reproducible research (Varricchio et al., 2020, pp. 15–18; Varricchio et al., 2020, pp. 18–20).

In summary, idebenone’s multifaceted mechanism—comprising electron shuttling to complex III, robust ROS scavenging, modulation of apoptotic signaling, and activation of Nrf2-driven antioxidant responses—aligns well with the therapeutic requirements for mitigating the mitochondrial and oxidative stress pathology present in dry AMD. While the compound’s history in LHON provides a strong foundation, the repurposing of idebenone for dry AMD will require additional rigorous preclinical investigations focusing on AMD-relevant models, followed by carefully designed clinical trials to validate its efficacy, safety, and dosing in this context (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13; Lyseng-Williamson, 2016, pp. 1–2; Gueven & Faldu, 2013, pp. 1–2).

Overall, idebenone represents a compelling candidate for further exploration in the therapeutic landscape of dry AMD. Its dual action addresses key pathophysiological mechanisms in the disease, and its established clinical use in a related ocular disorder provides a promising translational bridge. However, careful attention must be paid to the nuances of its mitochondrial interactions, dose-dependent effects, and the heterogeneous responses in different cellular contexts. Future research focusing on these aspects will be critical to determining whether idebenone can be successfully repurposed to prevent retinal degeneration and preserve vision in patients with dry AMD (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 2, 7–8; Russo et al., 2024, pp. 7–9; Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Alda-1 is a synthetic small molecule discovered through target-directed screening for modulators of mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2), originally identified as “ALDH2 activator 1” with the chemical name N-(1,3-benzodioxol-5-ylmethyl)-2,6-dichlorobenzamide and first demonstrated to reduce myocardial ischemic injury in rodents by directly activating ALDH2 (i.e., increasing its catalytic activity and rescuing function of the common inactive ALDH2*2 variant) (Budas et al., 2009; Kimura et al., 2019). Structurally and mechanistically, Alda-1 binds at the substrate entrance tunnel of ALDH2 and extends toward the active site, where it enhances dehydrogenase activity by favorably altering local dynamics, improving NAD+ engagement, and acting as a chemical chaperone that preserves the functional conformation of critical active-site loops and α-helices, while shielding key catalytic cysteines from irreversible electrophilic adduction by reactive aldehydes such as 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE) (Gao et al., 2022; Wang & He, 2018). In vitro biophysical and enzymology work shows Alda-1 increases wild-type ALDH2 activity approximately twofold and markedly rescues activity of the common East Asian mutant ALDH2*2 (Glu504Lys), restoring heterotetramer activity to near wild-type levels; importantly, Alda-1 is selective against several other ALDHs in original profiling, although later biochemical work suggests some degree of cross-activation of ALDH1A1 under specific assay conditions (Budas et al., 2009; Kotraiah et al., 2013).

Alda-1 belongs to the pharmacologic class of enzyme activators/allosteric agonists targeting mitochondrial ALDH2; the class is characterized by its ability to catalytically enhance clearance of reactive aldehydes generated by oxidative and nitrosative stress (e.g., 4-HNE, malondialdehyde [MDA], acrolein, and catecholamine-derived DOPAL), thereby acting as indirect antioxidants that reduce downstream carbonyl stress, proteotoxicity, and mitochondria-dependent cell death without directly scavenging ROS (Kimura et al., 2019; Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Wang & He, 2018). This mechanism has been applied preclinically across multiple organ systems to mitigate ischemia–reperfusion injury, chronic heart failure, metabolic and neurodegenerative toxicities, and toxin-induced organ damage, providing a consistent translational thread: activation of ALDH2 accelerates detoxification of stable electrophilic products of lipid peroxidation, interrupting aldehyde-driven positive feedback loops that amplify mitochondrial dysfunction, ROS generation, and apoptosis (Budas et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2014; Münzel & Daiber, 2018).

Therapeutic History  
Across cardiovascular models, Alda-1 has repeatedly demonstrated robust cytoprotection in vivo. In rat and mouse myocardial ischemia–reperfusion and infarction models, Alda-1 administration prior to or during ischemia reduced infarct size by approximately 60% and improved long-term survival following myocardial infarction, associating efficacy with increased ALDH2 activity, reduced 4-HNE-protein adducts and protein carbonyls, preserved mitochondrial respiratory control ratio (RCR), reduced mitochondrial H₂O₂ release, protection against Ca²⁺-induced mitochondrial permeability transition (MPT), and decreased cytochrome c release (Budas et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2014). In a chronic post-MI heart-failure model with established aldehydic overload, sustained Alda-1 treatment increased cardiac ALDH2 activity by ~2.7-fold, lowered 4-HNE adducts and protein carbonyls, normalized uncoupler responsiveness, improved RCR by preserving State 3 respiration, lowered mitochondrial ROS emission, and corrected MPT sensitivity; organ-level outcomes included increased contractility, reduced LV dilation, diminished hypertrophy and fibrosis, and anti-remodeling benefits (Gomes et al., 2014). In vitro, Alda-1 shielded isolated cardiac mitochondria from 4-HNE–induced respiratory inhibition, demonstrating direct aldehyde-dependent protection at the mitochondrial level (Gomes et al., 2014).

Hepatic and other organ systems provide convergent evidence. In a mouse acetaminophen hepatotoxicity model, Alda-1 pretreatment substantially reduced liver injury biomarkers (ALT/AST), histologic necrosis, 4-HNE adduct burden, mitochondrial depolarization, and cell death without altering upstream NAPQI bioactivation or JNK phosphorylation, demonstrating that protection is downstream via aldehyde detoxification and preservation of mitochondrial polarization and MPT control (Wimborne et al., 2020). Additional preclinical reports document Alda-1 efficacy in models of lung ischemia/reperfusion, intestinal I/R, kidney injury, neurotoxic injuries, and alcohol-related hepatic injury, again with mechanistic ties to accelerated clearance of reactive aldehydes, restoration of mitochondrial function, and modulation of stress/apoptosis pathways (Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019).

Retina-focused data, while more limited and not in dry AMD models, are directionally supportive. In streptozotocin-induced aged diabetic rats (an early diabetic retinopathy model), systemic Alda-1 improved ERG parameters, preserved outer nuclear layer (ONL) and total retinal thickness on OCT at 7–30 days, increased retinal SOD activity, and decreased retinal TNF-α and IL-6 across multiple timepoints; concurrent upregulation of ALDH2, Nrf2, and Sirt1 was observed by immunofluorescence and Western blot, suggesting that ALDH2 activation engages antioxidant and anti-inflammatory pathways in the retina under hyperglycemic oxidative stress (He et al., 2018). In a separate in vivo retinal degeneration study (MNU-induced photoreceptor damage), systemic Alda-1 preserved ERG amplitudes, mitigated photoreceptor degeneration (OCT, histology), increased retinal ALDH2 and SIRT1 protein, and reduced markers of ER stress (GRP78) and apoptosis (PARP1), supporting the hypothesis that enhancing aldehyde detoxification ameliorates retinal cellular stress downstream of lipid peroxidation (Yan et al., 2020; Carullo et al., 2020). Although neither model recapitulates RPE-centric dry AMD (drusen, complement activation, geographic atrophy), they provide proof-of-principle that ALDH2 activation can protect neural retina under oxidative/aldehydic stress in vivo (Yan et al., 2020; He et al., 2018).

Clinical translation status remains nascent. No human proof-of-concept trials of Alda-1 have been reported, and authoritative reviews note the absence of clinical efficacy data for ALDH2 activators like Alda-1, despite extensive rodent evidence across organs; moreover, no ALDH2 activators are in clinical use at present (Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019). Safety experience is therefore limited to preclinical settings: chronic Alda-1 dosing in naïve rats (10 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks) demonstrated acceptable tolerability (no hemodynamic, biochemical, or organ-weight changes), whereas a separate report described crystalline nephropathy and renal function deterioration after I/R under specific Alda-1 dosing/formulation conditions, suggesting potential tissue-specific or formulation-dependent risks requiring evaluation (Gomes et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2023). With respect to ophthalmology, existing Alda-1 studies are limited to rodent retina in DR and MNU models; there is no published use in dry AMD patients or preclinical AMD-like RPE atrophy models, and there is no reported ocular delivery pharmacokinetics or long-term ocular safety data in the provided literature (Yan et al., 2020; He et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action  
ALDH2 is a mitochondrial, NAD⁺-dependent dehydrogenase that catalyzes the oxidation of reactive aldehydes—most notably acetaldehyde, 4-HNE, MDA, acrolein, and DOPAL—to their corresponding carboxylic acids, thereby detoxifying electrophiles that otherwise form covalent Michael adducts and Schiff bases with cysteine, histidine, and lysine residues on proteins and nucleic acids (Kimura et al., 2019; Budas et al., 2009). The enzyme’s catalytic mechanism involves NAD⁺ binding in the Rossmann fold and activation of the catalytic cysteine (Cys302 in ALDH2), nucleophilic attack on the aldehyde to form a thiohemiacetal, hydride transfer to produce a thioacyl-enzyme intermediate, and Glu268-mediated hydrolysis to release the acid product and NADH; this canonical chemistry underlies ALDH2’s role as an indirect antioxidant via aldehyde clearance rather than direct ROS scavenging (Parajuli, 2013; Wang & He, 2018). Importantly, ALDH2 is highly susceptible to oxidative and electrophilic inactivation—its active-site cysteine cluster (Cys301–Cys303) can be adducted by 4-HNE at micromolar concentrations (>10 µM), establishing a pathogenic feed-forward loop in which lipid peroxidation products both injure proteins and progressively compromise the aldehyde-detoxifying capacity of mitochondria (Karan et al., 2023; Budas et al., 2009).

Alda-1 engages this system at multiple mechanistic levels. Structurally, Alda-1 binds to the substrate entrance tunnel and active site of ALDH2, altering the local environment to increase effective substrate/catalytic-cysteine proximity and improve NAD⁺ binding (lower Kₘ), while simultaneously acting as a molecular chaperone to stabilize conformational elements disrupted in the ALDH2*2 variant (e.g., restoring α-helix and active-site loop structures toward wild-type) (Gao et al., 2022; Wang & He, 2018). Functionally, Alda-1 increases wild-type ALDH2 catalytic activity approximately two-fold, but the effect is more pronounced in ALDH2*2 (10-fold or more in homotetramers), which is clinically relevant in East Asian populations; Alda-1 does not affect ALDH1/ALDH5 in initial selectivity panels, though subsequent biochemical reports indicate potential ALDH1A1 activation under specific conditions (i.e., DOPAL-inactivation assays), a detail that warrants further isozyme-specific profiling in ocular tissues (Budas et al., 2009; Kotraiah et al., 2013). Crucially, Alda-1 also reduces aldehyde access to catalytic cysteines (Cys302/301/303), protecting ALDH2 from 4-HNE–induced inactivation, thereby sustaining endogenous detoxification under aldehyde stress; in direct assays Alda-1 prevents rapid 4-HNE-mediated ALDH2 inactivation and shifts the enzyme to a higher-efficiency state (Gao et al., 2022; Kotraiah et al., 2013). The net biochemical outcome is enhancement of mitochondrial clearance of 4-HNE to the less reactive 4-hydroxynonenoic acid (4-HNA), alongside accelerated metabolism of other toxic aldehydes, which interrupts aldehyde-driven proteotoxic cascades (e.g., proteasomal inhibition, protein carbonyl accumulation) and preserves mitochondrial respiratory function (Budas et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2014).

Systems-level consequences of ALDH2 activation by Alda-1 have been delineated extensively in heart and liver. In failing hearts with elevated aldehydic load, Alda-1 decreased 4-HNE-protein adducts and total carbonyls without altering ALDH2 protein abundance, demonstrating a purely catalytic detoxification effect (i.e., activity increase without expression change) (Gomes et al., 2014). Mitochondrial bioenergetic protection is robust: Alda-1 preserved State 3 respiration, increased RCR, normalized uncoupler responses (CCCP), reduced absolute and relative H₂O₂ release, decreased cytochrome c release, and corrected MPT sensitivity, indicating mitigation of mitochondria-centered death signaling under chronic oxidative/aldehydic stress (Gomes et al., 2014). In isolated mitochondria, pre-incubation with Alda-1 prevented 4-HNE–induced declines in respiratory control and State 3 oxygen consumption, further supporting a direct anti-aldehyde effect on mitochondrial electron transport chain function (Gomes et al., 2014). In the APAP hepatotoxicity model, Alda-1 reduced tissue 4-HNE adduct burden by an order of magnitude, preserved mitochondrial polarization, and reduced cell death, consistent with detoxification of lipid peroxidation products downstream of parent electrophile formation (Wimborne et al., 2020).

Retinal and neuronal contexts provide complementary mechanistic observations. In cultured endothelial cells exposed to amyloid-β₁–₄₀, Alda-1 restored mitochondrial function, reduced 4-HNE adducts and ROS, and rescued angiogenic responses, indicating that ALDH2 activation can directly blunt aldehyde-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction in non-cardiac cells (Chen & Joshi, 2016; Roy, 2022). Within the retina, ALDH2 localizes across layers with predominant co-localization to CRALBP-positive Müller glia, and its expression diminishes with age; transgenic upregulation protects against retinal aging by decreasing oxidative-stress–related apoptosis and enhancing the unfolded protein response (UPR) in the ER, indicating that increased ALDH2 activity has cytoprotective effects in vivo in the aging retina (Karan et al., 2023; Long et al., 2020). In diabetic retinopathy rodent studies, Alda-1 increased retinal ALDH2, SIRT1, and Nrf2 signaling, decreased proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6), and improved electrophysiologic and structural outcomes, suggesting that ALDH2 activation enlists antioxidant and proteostasis pathways beyond direct aldehyde detoxification to preserve retinal function (He et al., 2018). In photoreceptor degeneration, Alda-1 upregulated SIRT1 and decreased ER stress/apoptotic markers, again consistent with mitigation of downstream stress signaling when aldehyde load is reduced (Yan et al., 2020).

Finally, the disease biochemistry underpinning our hypothesis—aldehyde toxicity as a conserved driver downstream of oxidative lipid peroxidation—is well defined in neurodegeneration and retinal biology. 4-HNE forms adducts that impair proteasome activity, promote accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and inflammation, covalently modify and crosslink amyloid peptides, impair ion pumps and transporters, and directly kill neurons at low micromolar concentrations; ALDH2 loss-of-function (including ALDH2*2) exacerbates accumulation of 4-HNE adducts and age-dependent neurodegeneration in rodent models (Chen & Joshi, 2016). In retinal disease, the RPE and photoreceptors operate in a high-oxygen, PUFA-rich environment, with continuous photo-oxidation and phagocytosis of outer segments generating lipid peroxides and aldehydes, and oxidative stress is a central driver of AMD pathogenesis; therapeutic strategies that augment endogenous detoxification (e.g., via Nrf2) have been proposed as rational approaches to bolster RPE resilience (Chen et al., 2023). Collectively, Alda-1’s biochemical action—activation of a mitochondrial enzyme that eliminates 4-HNE/MDA—integrates tightly with the pathophysiology of aldehyde-mediated mitochondrial and proteostatic injury that characterizes oxidatively stressed retinal tissues (Kimura et al., 2019; Budas et al., 2009).

Expected Effect  
In RPE mitochondria subjected to chronic oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, the proposed mechanism predicts that Alda-1 will (i) increase ALDH2 catalytic activity and resilience to aldehyde-induced inactivation, (ii) accelerate metabolic clearance of 4-HNE and related long-lived electrophiles to non-reactive acids, (iii) reduce covalent adduction/carbonylation of mitochondrial and cytosolic proteins, (iv) preserve oxidative phosphorylation (increased State 3 respiration and RCR), (v) lower mitochondrial H₂O₂ production, (vi) increase resistance to Ca²⁺-induced MPT and decrease cytochrome c release, and (vii) therefore reduce apoptotic signaling and downstream inflammation in RPE, which in aggregate should attenuate RPE dysfunction and slow progression of dry AMD (Gomes et al., 2014). The retina’s documented vulnerability to lipid peroxidation (PUFA-rich outer segments, high O₂ consumption, chronic light exposure) and the centrality of oxidative stress to AMD pathogenesis further support that increased mitochondrial aldehyde detoxification should reduce toxic aldehyde burden in RPE and adjacent cells (Chen et al., 2023).

Assay expectations and readouts for validation align closely with prior Alda-1 literature. In isolated RPE mitochondria or permeabilized cells, Alda-1 should preserve ADP-stimulated State 3 oxygen consumption and increase RCR versus vehicle under aldehydic load (e.g., exogenous 4-HNE) or oxidative stress conditions; decreased H₂O₂ release and normalization of uncoupler (CCCP) responses would be predicted based on cardiac mitochondria data (Gomes et al., 2014). Under Ca²⁺ challenge, Alda-1 should increase the threshold for MPT and reduce cytochrome c release; in intact RPE, Alda-1 should maintain Δψm under oxidative stress (e.g., blue light, NaIO₃, HOHA lactone), paralleling hepatocyte in vivo imaging under APAP (Gomes et al., 2014; Wimborne et al., 2020). Downstream stress responses (e.g., ER stress markers such as GRP78, UPR activation; SIRT1 and Nrf2 activity; inflammatory cytokines TNF-α/IL-6) should reflect improved homeostasis, consistent with diabetic retina and MNU data (He et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020). Methodologically, the respiratory chain enzymology and aldehyde reactivity analytics described for RPE systems (e.g., complex I–IV assays in 96-well format, reverse-phase HPLC quantitation of aldehyde scavenging, LC-MS/MS quantitation of aldehyde uptake) are directly applicable to evaluating Alda-1’s effects on mitochondrial function and aldehyde handling in RPE models (Cheng, 2019).

A critical caveat is that ALDH2 distribution within the retina emphasizes Müller cells rather than RPE in available reports, and ALDH2 can be inactivated by high aldehyde levels (>10 µM 4-HNE), implying that the therapeutic window may be constrained under extreme aldehydic stress; Alda-1 is explicitly reported to reduce 4-HNE accessibility to catalytic cysteines and reverse 4-HNE–mediated inhibition, which should mitigate this concern but does not obviate the need to quantify ALDH2 activity and 4-HNE load in RPE during oxidative stress (Karan et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2022). Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic coherence with AMD pathophysiology: Dry AMD is driven in part by oxidative stress in RPE with accumulation of lipid peroxidation products; ALDH2 is a mitochondrial enzyme that detoxifies 4-HNE/MDA and is susceptible to inactivation by aldehydes, establishing a feed-forward injury loop that Alda-1 is designed to interrupt (Chen et al., 2023; Budas et al., 2009; Karan et al., 2023).  
- Direct mitochondrial mechanism with robust preclinical performance: Alda-1 increases ALDH2 activity, reduces 4-HNE adducts and protein carbonyls, preserves State 3 respiration and RCR, reduces mitochondrial H₂O₂ emission, raises MPT thresholds, and decreases cytochrome c release under chronic aldehydic stress; these endpoints directly match the mitochondrial failure features observed in stressed RPE (Gomes et al., 2014).  
- Retinal in vivo signals: In diabetic and photoreceptor degeneration models, Alda-1 improved ERG, preserved retinal structure, increased SIRT1/Nrf2 signaling, reduced inflammatory cytokines, and diminished ER stress/apoptotic markers, collectively supporting retinal tissue benefit under oxidative stress (He et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020).

- Pharmacogenetic upside: Alda-1 rescues ALDH2*2 activity, suggesting potential efficacy in East Asian ALDH2*2 carriers, a large at-risk population for aldehyde-mediated diseases; this also provides a biomarker-based stratification opportunity in trials (Budas et al., 2009; Kimura et al., 2019).  
- Safety signs in chronic rodent dosing: Six-week daily Alda-1 in naïve rats showed no hemodynamic, biochemical, or organ-weight toxicity, supporting tolerability for longer-term therapy (Gomes et al., 2014).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Lack of dry AMD/RPE-specific data: No direct evidence in RPE-focused dry AMD models (e.g., NaIO₃-induced RPE atrophy, complement dysregulation models, aging-driven GA models) is presented in the context, and ALDH2 expression has not been explicitly demonstrated in RPE here; expression across retina with Müller co-localization and protection in aged retina is encouraging but not definitive for RPE (Karan et al., 2023; Long et al., 2020).  
- Clinical translation gap: No human proof-of-concept for Alda-1 or class; no ALDH2 activator currently in clinical use; ocular PK, distribution, and chronic safety are uncharacterized (Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019).  
- Potential safety concerns: A preclinical report of Alda-1–associated crystalline nephropathy after I/R cautions that formulation, dosing, or off-target deposition may cause tissue-specific toxicity; comprehensive toxicology and formulation work are essential, especially for chronic ocular indications (Jin et al., 2023).  
- Biological complexity and compensatory pathways: Chronic acceleration of aldehyde clearance could theoretically blunt electrophile-mediated adaptive antioxidant signaling (Keap1/Nrf2, PPAR), potentially reducing hormetic protection; the balance of detoxification versus adaptation requires careful evaluation in chronic degenerative settings (Münzel & Daiber, 2018).  
- Enzyme inactivation at high aldehyde loads: ALDH2 is inactivated by >10 µM 4-HNE; although Alda-1 protects ALDH2 from 4-HNE and enhances activity, in extreme aldehydic states therapeutic efficacy might be limited, necessitating combination with upstream ROS control or lipid peroxidation inhibitors (Karan et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2022).

Decision-oriented recommendations  
- Mechanistic validation in human/murine RPE: Quantify ALDH2 mRNA/protein/activity and subcellular localization in primary human RPE and iPSC-RPE; test whether Alda-1 increases ALDH2 activity and protects against 4-HNE–induced ALDH2 inactivation in RPE mitochondria; measure 4-HNE/ACR/MDA adduct load ±Alda-1 under blue-light/NaIO₃/HOHA lactone stress (Karan et al., 2023; Cheng, 2019).  
- Mitochondrial function endpoints in RPE: Using established microplate assays and Seahorse OCR, test Alda-1’s effects on State 3 respiration, RCR, Δψm, H₂O₂ release, CCCP response, MPT susceptibility, and cytochrome c release under aldehydic stress (Gomes et al., 2014; Cheng, 2019).

- Formulation and delivery: Develop ocular formulations (e.g., intravitreal, sustained-release) and conduct ocular PK/PD to quantify RPE mitochondrial exposure; evaluate chronic ocular and systemic safety with renal monitoring given crystalline nephropathy risk (Jin et al., 2023).  
- Biomarkers and patient stratification: Consider ALDH2 genotype (ALDH2*2 carriers), circulating/ocular 4-HNE-adduct biomarkers, and retinal imaging endpoints as stratification and PD markers; Alda-1’s rescue of ALDH2*2 suggests a precision-medicine angle (Budas et al., 2009; Münzel & Daiber, 2018).  
- Combinations: Given AMD’s multifactorial pathobiology, test Alda-1 alongside Nrf2 activators or lipid peroxidation suppressors to determine additive/synergistic effects on RPE resilience while monitoring for suppression of adaptive electrophile signaling (Chen et al., 2023; Münzel & Daiber, 2018).

Overall, Alda-1 presents a mechanistically compelling, enzyme-directed strategy to alleviate aldehyde-driven mitochondrial and proteostatic injury in oxidatively stressed retinal tissues, with in vivo retinal efficacy already demonstrated in DR and photoreceptor degeneration contexts, albeit without RPE-centric dry AMD models to date (He et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020). The totality of evidence across organ systems (cardiac, hepatic) underscores that Alda-1 reliably reduces 4-HNE load and preserves mitochondrial function in vivo—precisely the biology we seek to modulate in RPE for dry AMD—making this candidate worthy of structured, stepwise validation in RPE-specific systems and AMD-relevant models (Gomes et al., 2014; Wimborne et al., 2020). Key risks reside in translational gaps (RPE expression, ocular PK/safety), potential toxicity signals (renal crystalline nephropathy under certain conditions), and the possibility that aldehyde detoxification alone will be insufficient to arrest complex AMD progression without adjunctive modulation of complement, lipid trafficking, or lysosomal pathways (Jin et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). With these caveats, Alda-1 merits advancement to focused preclinical validation for dry AMD, with an emphasis on RPE mitochondrial protection endpoints, aldehyde-adduct burden, and rigorous ocular safety assessment before considering first-in-human studies.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Resveratrol is a naturally occurring polyphenolic compound belonging to the stilbene class and is structurally defined as 3,5,4′-trihydroxystilbene. It is biosynthesized by plants such as Vitis vinifera (grapes), Japanese Knotweed, and various berries in response to stress factors like injury or pathogen attack, and it is a well‐recognized phytoalexin with a molecular formula of C14H12O3 (Bel, 2020; Pop et al., 2022). Originally isolated from the White Hellebore in the mid-20th century and later found in red wine due to grape skin fermentation, resveratrol has garnered significant attention not only for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties but also for its potential benefits in cardiovascular and neuroprotective contexts (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pop et al., 2022). As such, resveratrol—and by extension its commercial version (Cayman Chemical #70580) used in our studies—is classified as a nutraceutical and drug candidate with a long track record of investigative research including applications in aging, inflammation, and ocular health (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pop et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
A considerable volume of biochemical, preclinical, and early clinical literature has explored resveratrol’s broad spectrum of activities. Historically, resveratrol has been investigated primarily for its cardioprotective and neuroprotective effects, as well as its anti-aging properties. In the realm of ophthalmology, several in vitro and animal studies have focused on its role in retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD), diabetic retinopathy (DR), and glaucoma. For instance, its use in RPE cell models has shown promising evidence for ameliorating oxidative stress-induced damage, a central factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Clinical investigations have attempted to translate these findings, as exemplified by the terminated clinical trial NCT02625376 that investigated resveratrol for exudative AMD (Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015), highlighting both the potential and the challenges involved in its clinical application (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Beyond ocular applications, resveratrol’s inclusion in various nutraceutical formulations underscores its established safety profile when administered at low-to-moderate doses, although issues pertaining to bioavailability and rapid systemic metabolism have been recurrent themes in the literature (Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, resveratrol exerts its effects primarily by modulating multiple intracellular signaling cascades. The central hypothesis we are testing is that resveratrol activates the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells—a pathway integral to regulating mitochondrial biogenesis and the antioxidant defense system. Activation of SIRT1, a NAD+-dependent deacetylase, by resveratrol increases the deacetylation and activation of its downstream effector, AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Once activated, AMPK facilitates the phosphorylation and activation of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1 alpha (PGC-1α) in the cytoplasm, which subsequently translocates to the nucleus to upregulate the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and antioxidant responses, including the gene encoding superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). This cascade not only improves mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and spare respiratory capacity—critical indicators of cellular health under oxidative stress—but also promotes an overall enhancement of cellular resilience against reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Bel, 2020; Bryl et al., 2022). Further molecular studies indicate that resveratrol can also modulate extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERK1/2) and mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK), contributing additional layers of cytoprotection through anti-apoptotic effects (Pop et al., 2022; Pop et al., 2022). Together, these mechanistic insights provide a comprehensive biochemical framework through which resveratrol is hypothesized to mitigate the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in RPE cells—a primary factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2021; Bryl et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of the proposed assay for dry AMD, our expectation is that resveratrol will exert a multifaceted protective effect on RPE cells under oxidative challenge. Specifically, when RPE cells are exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as a model for oxidative stress, resveratrol is anticipated to counteract the resultant mitochondrial dysfunction by upregulating antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2, thereby reducing intracellular ROS levels (Bel, 2020; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Restoration of the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) is a critical endpoint, as it directly reflects cellular energy status and the ability of mitochondria to sustain ATP synthesis under stress (Buonfiglio et al., 2024). In addition, an improvement in spare respiratory capacity—the measure of a cell’s ability to respond to increased energy demands—should be evident, reflecting enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and a greater capacity for cellular repair mechanisms (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bryl et al., 2022). These cytoprotective effects have been demonstrated in in vitro studies using ARPE-19 and other human retinal pigment epithelial cell lines, and they resonate with the established role of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis in mediating energy metabolism and antioxidative defenses in the retina (Bryl et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021). Moreover, by decreasing the accrual of oxidative damage, resveratrol is expected to limit apoptotic signaling pathways, which are crucial in slowing the progressive degeneration observed in dry AMD (Bel, 2020; Pop et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
The cumulative evidence from preclinical studies strongly supports the potential of resveratrol as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, especially considering its capacity to modulate mitochondrial function and activate intrinsic antioxidant defenses. The activation of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis not only augments mitochondrial biogenesis but also enhances the expression of key antioxidant enzymes required to neutralize ROS, thereby directly addressing one of the primary mechanisms underlying AMD pathology (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bryl et al., 2022). One of the major strengths of resveratrol is its pleiotropic mode of action; beyond its antioxidant properties, its anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic activities further consolidate its candidacy for chronic conditions like dry AMD (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Bel, 2020). Furthermore, extensive safety data in various preclinical models indicate that resveratrol is well tolerated at certain dose ranges, which is a positive indicator for its potential clinical translation (Wang et al., 2021; Bel, 2020).

However, several limitations remain that warrant careful consideration. The primary challenge with resveratrol is its poor bioavailability and rapid metabolism, which may result in subtherapeutic tissue concentrations despite high oral absorption. This has driven research efforts into advanced drug delivery platforms, such as nanoparticle-based systems and liposomal formulations, aimed at enhancing ocular retention and achieving sustained drug levels in the retina (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Additionally, although the in vitro and animal model data are promising, there exists a dearth of robust clinical trial data specifically addressing dry AMD, as evidenced by the terminated trial in exudative AMD (Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015) and the limited clinical evidence in related retinal pathologies (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Another potential weakness is the dose-dependent duality of its mechanism, where low doses predominantly mediate SIRT1-dependent effects, whereas higher doses might trigger SIRT1-independent pathways, possibly leading to off-target effects or toxicity (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Such a narrow therapeutic window necessitates a precise optimization of dosing regimens and formulation strategies. Despite these challenges, the overarching trend in preclinical research underscores that with proper formulation and dosing strategies, resveratrol could excel as an adjuvant or even monotherapy for protecting RPE cells from oxidative injury and, consequently, for the management of dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

In-Depth Analysis of Preclinical and Clinical Evidence:  
Numerous in vitro studies have characterized the effect of resveratrol on retinal pigment epithelial cells, notably ARPE-19 cell lines, under conditions of oxidative stress. Such studies consistently demonstrate that resveratrol treatment leads to a measurable reduction in ROS levels, a decrease in markers of apoptosis, and an overall improvement in mitochondrial parameters including Δψm and spare respiratory capacity (Bel, 2020; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). These findings are reinforced by experiments showing that resveratrol can mitigate blue light-induced retinal damage and preserve cell viability, further supporting its relevance in ocular pathologies where light-induced oxidative stress is a contributing factor (Bel, 2020). Complementary studies in animal models have shown that resveratrol can reduce inflammatory cytokine secretion and inhibit processes such as choroidal neovascularization, which has implications not only for dry AMD but also for its neovascular (wet) counterpart (Bryl et al., 2022; Bel, 2020).

Moreover, mechanistic investigations into the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis reveal that the deacetylation of PGC-1α is a critical step in the upregulation of mitochondrial genes, which directly correlates with increased cellular ATP production and enhanced resistance to oxidative stress (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Experimental data also show that SOD2 expression is significantly increased following resveratrol treatment, corroborating the compound’s role in boosting the cellular antioxidant capacity (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). These molecular events culminate in an environment that is less conducive to oxidative damage, thereby potentially arresting or even reversing some aspects of RPE degeneration that occur in dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021).

From a clinical perspective, the application of resveratrol in ocular disorders has been approached with caution, primarily due to pharmacokinetic challenges. Even though systemic administration of resveratrol has demonstrated efficacy in reducing plasma oxidative markers in diabetic patients and other conditions, the translation to ocular tissue remains hindered by its low aqueous solubility and rapid hepatic metabolism (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Abu-Amero et al., 2016). To overcome these barriers, innovative drug delivery systems such as chitosan-based nanoparticles, polymeric micelles, and liposomal formulations are being actively developed and show promise for achieving therapeutic levels in retinal tissues (Pop et al., 2022; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Such advanced formulations not only improve bioavailability but also allow for controlled release, which is essential for a chronic condition like dry AMD where sustained therapeutic action is desirable.

Additional mechanistic studies also suggest that resveratrol’s efficacy might be enhanced when used in combination with other therapeutic agents. For instance, its synergistic effects with anti-VEGF treatments in mitigating inflammatory cascades and suppressing angiogenesis have been noted in various preclinical models (Rusciano & Bagnoli, 2023; Tong et al., 2022). While the biochemical rationale for using resveratrol in dry AMD is robust, its clinical development is significantly complicated by pharmacokinetic limitations. As a consequence, only minimal amounts of unchanged resveratrol reach the systemic circulation and, by extension, the ocular tissues. Current research thus prioritizes the optimization of drug delivery vehicles to enhance its stability and target specificity. Nanotechnology-based delivery methods, including polymeric nanoparticles and solid lipid nanoparticles, have demonstrated enhanced tissue penetration and prolonged drug retention in the eye (Pop et al., 2022; Kaštelan et al., 2025). However, these strategies are still in the developmental phase, and their safety, scalability, and reproducibility for routine clinical use remain to be thoroughly validated. The potential for off-target effects and variability in patient-specific pharmacokinetics are additional hurdles that must be addressed in future clinical studies.

Safety and Dosing Considerations:  
Resveratrol has been generally recognized as safe in many preclinical studies, with low-dose regimens showing minimal adverse effects and favorable tolerability profiles (Wang et al., 2021; Bel, 2020). Nonetheless, concerns have been raised regarding gastrointestinal disturbances and other side effects at higher doses, as well as potential interactions with other medications (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Moreover, due to the compound’s rapid metabolism, determining an optimal dosing regimen that achieves effective local concentrations in the retina without inducing systemic toxicity remains challenging. This necessitates further preclinical and early-phase clinical trials to elucidate the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic profiles specific to ocular applications. Tailoring the dosing strategy based on individual metabolic rates and employing controlled-release formulations may help mitigate these issues and maximize therapeutic outcomes (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Kaštelan et al., 2025).

Strategic Direction and Future Perspectives:  
Given the multifaceted biological activities of resveratrol and the encouraging preclinical evidence in models of oxidative stress-induced RPE damage, it holds considerable promise as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to modulate the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis and promote mitochondrial biogenesis presents a novel therapeutic approach that directly targets the cellular dysfunctions underlying RPE degeneration. However, the translation of these findings into clinical practice will require addressing the critical challenges of bioavailability, formulation, and dosing.

Future research should focus on (1) developing and rigorously testing advanced drug delivery systems such as nanoparticle encapsulation methods that can bypass first-pass metabolism and target the retina more effectively, (2) conducting detailed pharmacokinetic studies to determine the optimal dosing regimen for achieving sustained therapeutic concentrations in ocular tissues, and (3) exploring combination therapy approaches that integrate resveratrol with conventional treatments such as anti-VEGF agents or other nutraceuticals to provide a comprehensive strategy against AMD progression (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Pop et al., 2022; Rusciano & Bagnoli, 2023). Furthermore, expanding the investigative efforts into patient-specific and personalized medicine approaches might allow for tailoring treatment protocols based on individual metabolic and genetic profiles, thereby maximizing efficacy and reducing adverse effects (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

In summary, resveratrol emerges as a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its extensive preclinical evidence, well-elucidated molecular mechanisms, and potential for modulating critical cellular pathways implicated in retinal degeneration. The strengths of resveratrol are rooted in its natural origin, broad-spectrum antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, and its ability to enhance mitochondrial function through the activation of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α pathway. The integration of this compound as either a monotherapy or as an adjunct to established therapies could provide enhanced protection against oxidative stress, preserve mitochondrial function, and improve retinal cell survival in patients suffering from this debilitating condition. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
EUK-8 is a synthetic catalytic antioxidant that belongs to the manganese‐based salen complexes, a class of low molecular weight enzyme mimetics engineered to replicate key activities of endogenous antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). This compound is synthesized via a condensation reaction between salicylaldehyde derivatives and diamines to form a bis‐Schiff base (salen) ligand, which then coordinates to a manganese ion, thereby producing the characteristic MnN₂O₂ planar core responsible for its redox activity (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rosenthal et al., 2011). The manganese center in EUK-8 undergoes reversible redox cycling between Mn(III) and Mn(II) oxidation states; this reversible cycling is essential for its dual enzyme-mimetic action, as it enables catalytic dismutation of superoxide radicals into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide and further conversion of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, thereby mimicking the combined action of SOD and catalase (Fernandes, 2010; Rouco et al., 2020a). The salen complex scaffold not only confers redox activity but also provides a tunable electronic and steric environment through modification of substituents on the ligand framework, which in turn dictates the redox potential, proton-dissociation properties, and overall catalytic efficacy (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020b). Because of its synthetic origin, EUK-8 is both cost-effective and easily reproducible, making it an appealing candidate for repurposing in therapeutic areas where enhanced antioxidant defenses are required, such as in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rosenthal et al., 2011).

Therapeutic History:  
The EUK series of compounds, which includes EUK-8, have been extensively studied in a plethora of preclinical models addressing a wide range of diseases linked to oxidative stress, including ischemic brain injury, neurodegeneration, cardiac injury, and even lifespan extension models in Caenorhabditis elegans and SOD2 knockout mice (Rouco et al., 2020a). Biochemical studies have demonstrated that EUK-8 exhibits both superoxide dismutase and catalase-like activities at submicromolar concentrations, providing significant protection in vitro and in vivo in models of oxidative injury (Bani & Bencini, 2012). While EUK-8 itself has not been directly evaluated in clinical trials for dry AMD, its protective effects have been documented in several models of neuronal and cardiac injury where mitochondrial dysfunction and excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) production are central to the pathology (Fernandes, 2010; Rouco et al., 2020a). The pharmacological application of salen manganese complexes, including EUK-8, extends to neuroprotective approaches, such as in models of Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and ischemia–reperfusion injury, suggesting that similar mechanisms may be beneficial in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which are notably vulnerable to oxidative stress in dry AMD (Rouco et al., 2020b; Yan et al., 2010). Additionally, the literature reveals that analogous compounds in the EUK series have been examined for their anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, and mitochondrial protective properties in diverse cellular and animal models, lending further credence to their potential for repurposing in ocular degenerative diseases (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rosenthal et al., 2009).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, EUK-8 functions as a catalytic antioxidant by mimicking two key enzymes involved in the detoxification of reactive oxygen species. First, it catalyzes the dismutation of superoxide (O₂•⁻) by virtue of its manganese center undergoing cyclic redox reactions between the Mn(III) and Mn(II) states; in one half-reaction, the Mn(III) state accepts an electron from superoxide to become Mn(II), while in the subsequent half-reaction, Mn(II) is reoxidized to Mn(III) by another molecule of superoxide, resulting in the conversion of superoxide to molecular oxygen and hydrogen peroxide (Fernandes, 2010; Batinić-Haberle et al., 2016). Second, EUK-8 mimics catalase activity by decomposing the generated hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen; it is proposed that hydrogen peroxide reacts with the manganese center to generate a transient high-valent oxo–Mn species, which is then reduced back to the resting state in the presence of a reductant, thus completing the catalytic cycle (Yan et al., 2010; Bani & Bencini, 2012). The structural integrity of the salen ligand is critical in modulating the redox potential of the manganese center, which, when tuned to an optimal range, ensures efficient electron transfer with reactive species while minimizing the risk of metal ion dissociation or inadvertent pro-oxidant activity (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Durand, 2013). In cellular contexts, the dual SOD/catalase activity of EUK-8 is especially relevant to mitochondria, which are the primary source of intracellular ROS; by reducing mitochondrial superoxide and decomposing hydrogen peroxide, EUK-8 helps to preserve mitochondrial respiration and prevent oxidative mitochondrial damage, which is a key contributor to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). Moreover, the reduction of mitochondrial ROS is anticipated to attenuate the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, a multiprotein complex that is known to be triggered by oxidative stress and has been implicated in inflammasome-mediated inflammatory responses in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Rouco et al., 2020a; Bani & Bencini, 2012). The overall biochemical and mechanistic profile of EUK-8, therefore, aligns well with the need to lower mtROS and preserve cellular homeostasis in tissues subjected to chronic oxidative stress.

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by the degeneration of the RPE, a process driven by cumulative oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation leading to cellular senescence and eventual retinal atrophy (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Batinić-Haberle et al., 2016). Given that the RPE expresses high levels of mitochondrial enzymes, including MnSOD, and relies on efficient mitochondrial respiration for normal function, the preservation of mitochondrial integrity is paramount (Fernandes, 2010; Rouco et al., 2020a). EUK-8 is expected to enter RPE cells and preferentially localize to mitochondria where its catalytic dual SOD/catalase activity would reduce the burden of superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, thereby mitigating oxidative damage to mitochondrial proteins, lipids, and DNA (Rosenthal et al., 2011; Rosenthal et al., 2009). By maintaining lower levels of mtROS, EUK-8 would be anticipated to stave off the mitochondrial dysfunction that underlies RPE degeneration and to prevent the activation of pro-inflammatory signaling cascades such as those mediated by the NLRP3 inflammasome, thus potentially preserving cellular viability and function (Batinić-Haberle, 2013; Bigham & Wilson, 2023). In addition, previous studies with related manganosalen complexes have shown that treatment can lead to the reversal of age-related cognitive deficits and the inhibition of pro-apoptotic pathways in neuronal tissues, which are mechanistically analogous to the crises faced by RPE cells in dry AMD (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rouco et al., 2020b). Given that the anticipated mechanism involves modulation of mitochondrial redox balance and prevention of inflammation, the expected molecular targets in RPE cells include key mitochondrial respiratory chain components, antioxidant response elements such as Nrf2, and inflammasome components including caspase-1 and interleukin-1β, all of which have been implicated in the progression of dry AMD (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Durand, 2013). The ability of EUK-8 to act at submicromolar doses further enhances its appeal, as such potency suggests that therapeutic effects may be achieved with minimal exposure, reducing the likelihood of off-target effects and toxicity (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Fernandes, 2010).

From a drug development perspective, EUK-8 emerges as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration, primarily because its dual enzyme-mimetic properties address two central features of RPE pathology—oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). One of the major strengths of EUK-8 lies in its robust catalytic activity; being a regenerative, non-stoichiometric antioxidant means that even at submicromolar concentrations, it can exert sustained protective effects by continuously dismutating ROS, in contrast to traditional antioxidants that are consumed in the process (Rosenthal et al., 2011; Rouco et al., 2020a). Its low molecular weight and non-peptidic nature facilitate cellular uptake and mitochondrial penetration, critical features for targeting the RPE where mitochondrial production of ROS is an important driver of cell injury (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). Furthermore, the extensive preclinical history of manganosalen compounds in models of neuroprotection, cardiac ischemia, and aging provides a solid rationale for their protective capacity in tissues that are equally susceptible to oxidative damage, even if direct studies in dry AMD are limited at present (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rouco et al., 2020b).

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and challenges must be addressed before EUK-8 can be confidently advanced as a therapeutic for dry AMD. First, despite the promising preclinical data in other models, there is a paucity of direct studies evaluating EUK-8 in ocular or RPE-specific models. Dry AMD has its own unique microenvironment, including features such as the Bruch’s membrane, the blood-retinal barrier, and specialized immune processes, which might affect drug delivery and efficacy (Bigham & Wilson, 2023; Yan et al., 2010). Second, the stability of EUK-8 in the complex milieu of the eye must be rigorously tested, especially because the aqueous and proteinaceous environments found in ocular tissues could potentially lead to ligand dissociation or redox inactivation (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). Third, although EUK-8’s catalytic nature means that it is less likely to be consumed during therapy compared to stoichiometric antioxidants, there is always the risk that under certain pathological conditions, such as in the presence of excess hydrogen peroxide or other reactive species, it could exhibit paradoxical pro-oxidant effects if the redox balance is not carefully controlled (Batinić-Haberle et al., 2012; Bani & Bencini, 2012). Fourth, formulation and delivery challenges specific to ocular therapeutics must be overcome; for instance, ensuring adequate penetration across the inner limiting membrane and achieving sufficient concentrations within the RPE are non-trivial hurdles that have derailed otherwise promising compounds in the past (Batinić-Haberle et al., 2016; Rosenthal et al., 2009). Overall, while the preclinical evidence underscores the strong potential of EUK-8 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, its translational success will depend critically on several factors. In conclusion, as a candidate drug for dry age-related macular degeneration, EUK-8 offers a compelling therapeutic strategy that leverages its dual SOD and catalase mimetic activities to target the central biochemical derangements in the RPE associated with oxidative stress and inflammation (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a).
