Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) is a synthetic derivative of fumaric acid that belongs to the class of fumaric acid esters (FAEs) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Chemically, DMF is the dimethyl ester of fumaric acid, with a molecular weight of approximately 144.13 g/mol, and is produced by reacting fumaric acid with methanol in the presence of a strong acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Although fumaric acid occurs naturally as an intermediate in the citric acid cycle, DMF itself is fully synthetically manufactured, conferring the advantages of chemical stability and the ability to precisely modulate its structure to enhance pharmacological properties (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Moreover, DMF is classified as an electrophilic molecule that, due to its α,β-unsaturated ester structure, can covalently modify protein thiols, particularly the cysteine residues within KEAP1, thereby initiating its downstream effects on cellular redox homeostasis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Fumaric acid esters as a class have a long-standing history in pharmacotherapy, originally finding application in dermatology, most notably in the treatment of psoriasis, and have since been repurposed for neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis (MS) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, fumaric acid esters were introduced into clinical practice as antipsoriatic agents in Europe, with formulations such as Fumaderm® entering the market in the 1990s (Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). DMF in particular emerged as a key component in these formulations, and its efficacy in modulating immune responses and suppressing inflammation in skin diseases laid the foundation for its later repurposing in other systemic inflammatory conditions (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Over time, DMF was repurposed and further developed as an oral agent for the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), culminating in its FDA approval in 2013 under the trade name Tecfidera® by Biogen (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163). Clinical trials, including large-scale phase 3 studies, have demonstrated its favorable safety profile and efficacy in reducing relapse rates and slowing disability progression in MS patients (Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 14–16). Although there is no extensive historical record of DMF being used directly for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other primary ocular diseases, recent preclinical findings have indicated that its potent activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway may confer significant protective effects on the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This has sparked considerable interest in repurposing DMF for ocular indications such as geographic atrophy, a late stage of dry AMD, by leveraging its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities observed in nonocular settings (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, DMF functions primarily as a prodrug; upon oral administration it is rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases within the gastrointestinal tract to yield its active metabolite, monomethyl fumarate (MMF) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). The pharmacodynamic actions of DMF principally involve the electrophilic modification of specific cysteine residues—most notably cysteine 151—on Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Under physiological conditions, KEAP1 binds to and retains the transcription factor Nrf2 in the cytoplasm, targeting it for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. However, when DMF covalently modifies KEAP1, it disrupts this complex, allowing Nrf2 to dissociate and translocate into the nucleus (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). In the nucleus, Nrf2 binds to antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoters of numerous genes encoding cytoprotective enzymes, including glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), and various enzymes involved in glutathione (GSH) synthesis and regeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). These molecular interactions lead to enhanced antioxidant defenses, improved detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and overall better maintenance of cellular redox balance (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). In addition to its role in promoting antioxidant gene expression via Nrf2 activation, DMF has been shown to have immunomodulatory properties; it can shift cytokine profiles by increasing interleukin-4 (IL-4)–expressing CD4+ T cells and decreasing the production of proinflammatory cytokines such as interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and interleukin-17 (IL-17) (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Furthermore, DMF has been reported to inhibit nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation in certain cellular contexts, thus contributing to a reduction in inflammatory signaling independently of Nrf2 (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Together, these molecular actions result in lowered cellular oxidative stress and an improved inflammatory milieu, which are critical factors implicated in the pathogenesis of chronic degenerative diseases (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry AMD, particularly the geographic atrophy form, is characterized by the gradual degeneration of RPE cells, which leads to subsequent photoreceptor loss and irreversible vision impairment. Central to the pathophysiology of dry AMD are oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation that progressively compromise RPE viability and function (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). The hypothesis being explored is that DMF, through its robust activation of the Nrf2 pathway, can enhance the expression of ARE-driven genes that encode for antioxidant and cytoprotective proteins, thereby counteracting the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in the RPE (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 13–14). In particular, the upregulation of enzymes involved in glutathione synthesis is expected to increase intracellular levels of GSH, a critical thiol antioxidant that protects mitochondrial membranes and supports cellular bioenergetics (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Preclinical studies in retinal models have demonstrated that DMF can effectively preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and reduce the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β), both of which are hallmarks of RPE distress under oxidative challenge (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Given that the RPE is highly metabolically active and particularly vulnerable to cumulative oxidative damage, the sustained activation of Nrf2 by DMF following oral dosing is anticipated to provide continuous reinforcement of antioxidant defenses and maintain mitochondrial integrity in these cells (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 3–5; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). Moreover, by mitigating inflammatory signaling, DMF may not only protect the RPE but also contribute to a more favorable microenvironment that limits the propagation of cell death signals, thus potentially slowing the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Collectively, these expected cellular effects support the rationale for using DMF as an intervention to preserve retinal structure and function by lowering oxidative damage and supporting bioenergetics in the RPE.

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential of dimethyl fumarate as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD rests on a solid mechanistic rationale combined with an established clinical pedigree in other indications. One of the primary strengths of DMF is its well-characterized pharmacological profile; it is FDA-approved for multiple sclerosis and has been safely administered to thousands of patients over several years, which significantly mitigates the risk and regulatory hurdles typically associated with repurposed drugs (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). The dual actions of DMF—in particular, its ability to both activate the Nrf2 pathway and attenuate proinflammatory signals—directly target the underlying pathological processes in dry AMD, where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central drivers of RPE degeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In vitro studies have provided encouraging evidence that DMF increases intracellular glutathione levels and protects RPE cells from oxidative insults, findings that are directly translatable to the pathobiology of dry AMD (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Nonetheless, several challenges remain. Although DMF is known to be effective in MS and psoriasis, the ocular milieu presents unique pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic challenges that may not be fully addressed by the current oral formulations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18). The rapid hydrolysis of DMF to MMF means that, while the active metabolite does exert therapeutic effects, fine-tuning the dosing regimen to ensure adequate drug levels in the retina while minimizing systemic side effects is necessary (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). In addition, common adverse reactions associated with DMF, such as gastrointestinal discomfort and flushing, though generally mild to moderate, could be more problematic in the typically elderly dry AMD population, necessitating careful monitoring and potentially modified dosing strategies (Camelo, 2025, p. 17; Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13). There is also the question of whether systemic administration of DMF can generate sufficient concentrations in the retina to achieve a meaningful therapeutic effect. While emerging evidence suggests that DMF can cross the blood-retinal barrier and activate Nrf2 in retinal cells (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3), further pharmacokinetic and translational studies are warranted to confirm its retinal bioavailability and the optimal dosing regimen for ocular indications.

Another consideration is the complexity of dry AMD itself, which is a slowly progressive, multifactorial disease with contributions from genetic predispositions, environmental exposures, and systemic metabolic disturbances. It remains to be seen whether the monotherapeutic approach of DMF, targeting primarily oxidative stress via Nrf2 activation, will be sufficient to halt or reverse disease progression, or whether combination therapies will ultimately be required (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Furthermore, while the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms of DMF are well supported by in vitro data and animal studies, there is still limited clinical data on its efficacy in ocular disease settings. Early-phase clinical trials aimed at evaluating DMF in geographic atrophy have to rigorously assess both structural outcomes (e.g., changes in the area of atrophy) and functional endpoints (e.g., visual acuity, retinal sensitivity) to establish its therapeutic benefit in dry AMD (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Despite these limitations, the strengths of DMF are compelling. The drug’s ability to upregulate a broad spectrum of cytoprotective genes via the Nrf2 pathway makes it a versatile candidate for mitigating the oxidative and inflammatory stress that drives RPE degeneration. The fact that DMF has already cleared extensive regulatory and clinical safety evaluations in nonocular indications is a significant advantage, as it greatly accelerates the translational pathway compared to a novel chemical entity (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Additionally, the repurposing of an already approved drug leverages existing manufacturing, formulation, and distribution infrastructure, favorably impacting the cost and timeline associated with drug development (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

In summary, the comprehensive literature review supports the potential of DMF to serve as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its mechanism of action—centered on Nrf2 activation leading to enhanced antioxidant capacity along with anti-inflammatory effects—directly addresses the key pathophysiological mechanisms implicated in dry AMD. The extensive clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis provides a reliable safety and tolerability framework, which is crucial for rapid repositioning into a new clinical area such as geographic atrophy (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). However, it is essential to conduct targeted preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials specifically in ocular disease models to optimize dosing, confirm retinal delivery, and demonstrate clinical efficacy before advancing to larger randomized controlled trials (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Overall, while challenges remain regarding optimal application in the retinal context and potential side effects in an older patient population, DMF—by virtue of its dual antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms and robust clinical background—stands as a viable candidate that merits further investigation for the treatment of dry AMD.

Given the current evidence, the following recommendations are proposed for advancing DMF as a candidate for dry AMD:  

1. Conduct detailed pharmacokinetic studies in animal models to assess the retinal bioavailability of DMF and its active metabolite MMF following systemic administration. This should include studies comparing different dosing schedules and formulations to optimize retinal exposure without exacerbating systemic adverse effects (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2).  

2. Develop and validate preclinical models of dry AMD that recapitulate the key features of human geographic atrophy, with a focus on evaluating the efficacy of DMF in protecting RPE cells against oxidative stress and preserving mitochondrial function (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

3. Investigate the potential benefits of combining DMF with other therapeutic agents that target complementary pathways in dry AMD. For example, agents that modulate complement activation or improve choroidal blood flow may synergize with the Nrf2-mediated antioxidant mechanism of DMF (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).  

4. Initiate early-phase clinical trials in patients with geographic atrophy to establish proof of concept. These studies should include robust biomarker assessments (e.g., measurement of ARE gene expression, retinal imaging for atrophy progression, and functional visual outcomes) to correlate molecular effects with clinical benefit (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

5. Carefully monitor the safety profile of DMF in the elderly population, as the incidence of gastrointestinal side effects and lymphopenia may differ compared to the population with MS. Consider the feasibility of modified-release formulations or alternative routes of administration (e.g., topical ocular delivery) to minimize systemic side effects while maximizing retinal drug concentrations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Metformin is a well‐known therapeutic agent belonging to the biguanide class, originally derived from guanidine compounds found in the plant Galega officinalis. The molecule is a synthetic derivative of naturally occurring galegine and has been refined into a modern oral antihyperglycemic agent (Augustin & Atorf, 2023). This class of compounds has historically been used as a first-line oral treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus, with metformin being one of the most prescribed drugs worldwide for managing hyperglycemia. Its synthesis did not follow the classical target‐driven design path but instead emerged from an adaptation of naturally occurring structures into a chemically optimized, orally bioavailable, and generally well-tolerated drug (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Dang et al., 2021). Given its long clinical history starting from the 1950s and subsequent FDA approval in the 1990s, metformin has accumulated a significant amount of safety data and clinical experience, which collectively make it an attractive candidate for repurposing into other disease areas, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) characterized by geographic atrophy (Amin et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, metformin has been used extensively as an antidiabetic agent to lower hepatic glucose output and improve peripheral insulin sensitivity. Its beneficial pleiotropic effects beyond glycemic control have been recognized over the years; these include anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antiangiogenic properties, which have been observed in both biochemical and clinical investigations. Multiple epidemiologic studies have examined the association between metformin use and ocular outcomes. Retrospective analyses in predominantly diabetic cohorts have indicated that metformin use correlates with reduced odds or hazard for developing age-related macular degeneration and other retinal diseases, although some studies report mixed results depending on cumulative dose, exposure timing, and concomitant diabetes-related complications (Moir et al., 2023; Amin et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2022). Notably, while metformin has not historically been approved for any ocular indication, several preclinical studies using retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cell models have demonstrated that metformin may protect against oxidative damage and improve mitochondrial function. Moreover, a Phase II single-blind randomized trial was initiated to assess the efficacy of metformin in slowing the progression of geographic atrophy among non-diabetic patients with advanced dry AMD (Shen et al., 2024), suggesting that the concept of repurposing metformin for dry AMD is already under active clinical investigation.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, metformin’s primary mechanism of action involves the inhibition of mitochondrial complex I of the electron transport chain, resulting in a decrease in ATP production and a concomitant increase in the intracellular AMP:ATP ratio. This metabolic shift leads to the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a master regulator of cellular energy homeostasis that orchestrates shifts in metabolism under conditions of energy deficit (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). AMPK activation exerts multiple downstream effects that are particularly relevant to RPE cell function and the pathogenesis of geographic atrophy. First, AMPK activation promotes autophagy, including mitophagy, a quality-control mechanism that ensures the removal of dysfunctional mitochondria. Preclinical studies in RPE cell models, such as those using ARPE-19 cells, have provided evidence that metformin increases autophagosome formation, reduces intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS), lowers apoptosis rates, and helps maintain the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) under oxidative stress conditions (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Toppila et al., 2024). Additionally, the activation of AMPK in RPE cells has been associated with upregulation of protective pathways including enhanced nitric oxide (NO) production and increased expression of mitochondrial biogenesis factors such as PGC-1α, which together contribute to improved mitochondrial quality control (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023).  

Furthermore, metformin is known to activate both AMPK-dependent and AMPK-independent signaling pathways. The AMPK-independent effects may include inhibition of NF-κB activation, leading to a reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α, which are implicated in chronic inflammation observed in the aging retina (Jiang et al., 2022; Amin et al., 2022). From a biochemical standpoint, the inhibition of complex I by metformin also directly reduces the leakage of electrons that can form ROS, thereby lowering mitochondrial oxidative stress—a key aspect in the progression of dry AMD pathogenesis (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). It is important to note, however, that several reports have highlighted the concern that activation of AMPK in vivo or in vitro appears to require suprapharmacological doses of metformin, casting uncertainty on whether standard clinical dosing is sufficient to achieve these retinal effects (Moir et al., 2023). Nonetheless, the preclinical evidence supports a model whereby metformin’s inhibition of mitochondrial complex I—thereby reducing ROS and enhancing autophagy—provides a rationale for its potential use in protecting RPE cells from oxidative stress-induced damage (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis driving the repurposing of metformin for dry AMD is predicated on its ability to activate AMPK and inhibit mitochondrial complex I leakage in RPE cells, leading to reduced ROS production and enhanced mitochondrial quality control. In the context of geographic atrophy, RPE dysfunction and death play a central role in the degeneration of photoreceptors and the progression of AMD. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that metformin can protect ARPE-19 cells (an established human RPE cell line) from oxidative insults by lowering intracellular ROS levels, augmenting autophagic processes, and preserving mitochondrial membrane potential (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Toppila et al., 2024). Additionally, through the activation of AMPK, metformin is expected to stimulate the expression of mitochondrial biogenesis factors, leading to improved mitochondrial function, which is critical given the high metabolic demands of the RPE (Moir et al., 2023). 

Epidemiologically, several retrospective cohort and case-control studies have observed associations between metformin use and a reduced risk of developing AMD. Some studies even suggest that these associations are dose- and timing-dependent, with earlier or sustained use of metformin correlating with greater protective effects (Moir et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022). Therefore, in an assay designed to measure the effects of metformin on mitochondrial function and oxidative stress in RPE cells, one would expect to see an enhancement in autophagic flux, decreased markers of oxidative stress, and preservation or restoration of Δψm. These cellular effects would ideally translate into a slower progression of geographic atrophy in vivo, as suggested by the decreased degeneration of the retinal layers that has been observed in certain mouse models of retinal damage (Jiang et al., 2022; Amin et al., 2022). RPE cells are known to express AMPK and other components of the autophagy machinery, which further supports the rationale for targeting these pathways in the treatment of dry AMD (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Moir et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
Metformin shows considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly for geographic atrophy, due to several key strengths. First, its long and well-documented clinical history in the management of type 2 diabetes provides a robust safety profile and widespread clinical familiarity, which is a significant advantage when considering repurposing strategies (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Dang et al., 2021; Amin et al., 2022). Second, the molecular and cellular mechanisms by which metformin acts—namely, the inhibition of mitochondrial complex I, subsequent activation of AMPK, and promotion of autophagy—are highly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. The ability of metformin to reduce ROS and promote mitochondrial quality control addresses one of the core aspects of RPE dysfunction and degeneration seen in geographic atrophy (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Jiang et al., 2022).

Furthermore, the epidemiologic data showing associations between metformin use and a reduced incidence of AMD lend additional support to its potential utility in this setting (Liang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023). The possibility that metformin’s protective effects might be independent of its glycemic control properties is particularly intriguing, as it expands the target population to non-diabetic AMD patients—a group that represents the majority of those affected by geographic atrophy (Moir et al., 2023; Brown et al., 2019; Moir et al., 2024). On a mechanistic level, the detailed understanding of metformin’s interaction with AMPK and mitochondrial pathways not only provides a clear therapeutic target but also offers multiple biomarkers for assessing efficacy in both preclinical and clinical studies.

Despite its strengths, several weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. One significant concern is whether standard clinical doses of metformin are sufficient to activate the AMPK pathway in retinal tissues, given that some in vitro studies indicate suprapharmacological doses are required to see a robust effect (Moir et al., 2023). This raises questions of retinal bioavailability and whether alternative delivery strategies, such as local ocular administration or formulation enhancements, might be required to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE. Additionally, while the epidemiologic studies are promising, they are not uniformly consistent; some retrospective analyses have reported no association or even conflicting results depending on dosing and timing parameters (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Brown et al., 2019; Amin et al., 2022). These discrepancies underscore the inherent limitations of observational data, including potential confounding factors such as the presence and severity of diabetes, concomitant medications, and the challenges of accurately classifying AMD subtypes using administrative coding.

Another consideration is that although metformin’s broad mechanism of action (i.e., modulation of inflammation, oxidative stress, and autophagy) is advantageous in addressing multifactorial diseases like AMD, it may also lead to off-target effects or systemic side effects such as vitamin B12 deficiency or, in rare instances, lactic acidosis (Jiang et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). In elderly populations—who are generally most affected by dry AMD—these risks must be carefully weighed against the potential benefits. Moreover, the heterogeneity in study designs and patient populations in the available epidemiologic literature means that prospective, well-designed clinical trials remain essential to definitively determine whether metformin can meaningfully slow the progression of geographic atrophy in AMD (Shen et al., 2024).

In summary, the overall evaluation of metformin as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. Its well-established safety profile, combined with mechanistic data that align closely with the underlying pathology of geographic atrophy, make it a compelling candidate. The strengths lie in its ability to activate AMPK, thereby reducing mitochondrial ROS, promoting autophagy, and potentially preserving RPE function—molecular actions that directly address key pathological features of dry AMD. However, critical questions regarding dosing, ocular bioavailability, and the variability in epidemiologic outcomes necessitate further rigorous investigation in controlled clinical settings. Moving forward, clinical trials designed to specifically assess metformin’s efficacy in non-diabetic populations with early to intermediate stages of geographic atrophy will be crucial to validate its repurposing potential. Overall, while metformin has significant promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, additional studies are needed to resolve questions about its optimal dosing regimen, delivery method, and long-term efficacy in preserving retinal structure and function (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
S3QEL-2 is a synthetic small‐molecule member of the S3QEL (Suppressors of Superoxide production from mitochondrial Complex III) class, originally discovered through a high‐throughput screen of approximately 635,000 small molecules using isolated mitochondria and an Amplex UltraRed H₂O₂ detection assay (Orr et al., 2015). In this screening paradigm, compounds were rigorously selected for their ability to selectively suppress superoxide generation arising from the Qo site of mitochondrial Complex III without impairing oxidative phosphorylation or altering the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) (Orr et al., 2015). The discovery approach involved counterscreens that monitored Δψm changes, respiration rates, and markers of cellular viability, ensuring that S3QEL-2 exhibits specificity in mitigating reactive oxygen species (ROS) production rather than acting as a nonspecific antioxidant or uncoupler (Orr et al., 2015). S3QEL-2 was sourced from commercial screening collections—for example, vendors such as Chemdiv—and its powder-stock purity was confirmed by HPLC–MS analysis (Orr et al., 2015). As a member of a structurally diverse chemotype group, S3QEL-2 belongs to a new class of mitochondrial ROS-targeted modulators that differ fundamentally from classical Complex III inhibitors such as antimycin A or myxothiazol; unlike these inhibitors, S3QELs do not block the electron transfer chain or impair ATP production, but rather reduce the electron leak from the semiquinone intermediate at the Qo site (Orr et al., 2015). In general, compounds in the S3QEL class have been used experimentally as probes to decouple pathological ROS generation from normal bioenergetic function in diverse cell types, with applications ranging from studies on hypoxia-induced transcription (e.g., HIF-1α signaling) to experiments investigating ROS-mediated cell stress in pancreatic β-cells (Orr et al., 2015). The commercial catalog number Cayman Chemical #26918 identifies S3QEL-2 for research purposes, which suggests that this compound is available for repurposing studies beyond its initial characterization in nonocular systems (Orr et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Although S3QEL-2 was originally developed as a novel chemical probe to selectively suppress Complex III-derived superoxide production, its preclinical evaluation has been extensive within the context of cellular models evaluating ROS-mediated signaling and cell stress responses (Orr et al., 2015). In cellular assays, S3QEL-2 has demonstrated the ability to reduce H₂O₂ production in isolated mitochondria, lower HIF-1α transcription in hypoxia-challenged HEK-293 cells, and protect pancreatic β-cells from oxidative stress-induced apoptosis during islet isolation and culture (Orr et al., 2015). Notably, in studies where cells were exposed to concentrations up to 20× the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC₅₀) determined for site IIIQo superoxide production, S3QEL-2 did not impair basal or uncoupled respiration, nor did it compromise mitochondrial viability (Orr et al., 2015). Additionally, S3QEL-2 has been employed as a pharmacological tool in experiments on human monocyte-derived macrophages, where it contributed to demonstrating that inhibition of mitochondrial ROS can reduce inflammasome activation and subsequent IL-18 secretion upon stimulation by the complement membrane attack complex (MAC) (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). However, despite its utility in these nonocular systems—where mitochondrial ROS inhibition was linked to attenuation of inflammatory cytokine pathways—there is little to no published preclinical or clinical data directly evaluating S3QEL-2 in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models or in other ocular disease contexts (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2015). While the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of dry AMD, particularly those involving chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and associated inflammasome activation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, are well documented (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013), a direct therapeutic history for S3QEL-2 in retinal or AMD models remains absent in the current literature (Korhonen, 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Thus, S3QEL-2 represents a promising repurposing candidate that has been validated in other contexts of ROS-related cellular stress but has not yet been explicitly applied to the treatment of dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of S3QEL-2 is based on its capacity to selectively suppress superoxide generation originating at the Qo site of mitochondrial Complex III. Under normal conditions, the electron transport chain (ETC) can leak electrons during the reduction of oxygen, particularly at the semiquinone intermediate at the Qo site, resulting in the formation of superoxide—a primary reactive oxygen species (Orr et al., 2015). S3QEL-2 does not act as a general ROS scavenger; rather, it modulates the rate constant for the electron transfer from the semiquinone to molecular oxygen without significantly altering the steady-state levels of semiquinone species or the redox poise of the ubiquinone (Q) pool (Orr et al., 2015). This selective inhibition of ROS generation is achieved through an allosteric modulation of protein conformation within Complex III, specifically targeting the Qo site to reduce electron leak while sparing the remainder of the electron transport processes (Orr et al., 2015). By decreasing superoxide production, S3QEL-2 effectively reduces the downstream formation of H₂O₂ as detected by Amplex UltraRed assays, a finding that has been consistently reproduced in isolated mitochondrial studies (Orr et al., 2015). Moreover, because S3QEL-2 does not interfere with the overall electron flux or the maintenance of Δψm, it preserves the bioenergetic capacity of the mitochondria—a critical factor in tissues with high metabolic demands such as the RPE (Orr et al., 2015). On a molecular level, the compound’s activity at nanomolar to low micromolar concentrations (with a reported mean IC₅₀ around 1.7 μM for S3QEL-2) suggests a highly potent modulation of the ROS generation pathway that is independent of the mitochondrial matrix redox state (Orr et al., 2015). This targeted approach is further distinguished from classical Complex III inhibitors like myxothiazol and antimycin A, which disrupt the entire electron transport process and can lead to a collapse in mitochondrial function; in contrast, S3QEL-2 specifically mitigates the pathological component of ROS production while maintaining ATP synthesis and cellular energy homeostasis (Orr et al., 2015). In macrophages and other cell types, the reduction in mitochondrial ROS production by S3QEL-2 has been shown to blunt ROS-dependent signaling pathways, such as the stabilization of the transcription factor HIF-1α under hypoxic conditions, and to decrease the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Toma et al., 2021). Thus, the molecular interactions of S3QEL-2 within Complex III position it as a potential modulator of redox signaling pathways that are implicated in inflammatory and degenerative processes, including those observed in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Based on its established mechanism of action, the use of S3QEL-2 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells is expected to selectively reduce mitochondrial ROS generated at the Complex III Qo site. In dry age-related macular degeneration, one of the prevailing hypotheses attributes disease progression to chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction within the RPE, leading to the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and subsequent secretion of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013). The selective inhibition of ROS by S3QEL-2 should therefore interrupt this pathological signaling cascade. In an in vitro assay using RPE cells—cells that have been shown to express components of the NLRP3 inflammasome and are especially vulnerable to oxidative insults—the drug is anticipated to lower ROS markers, as measured by fluorescent dyes (for example, oxidized carboxy-H₂DCFDA), without compromising the cells' mitochondrial respiration or Δψm (Orr et al., 2015). With less mitochondrial ROS available to act as secondary messengers, the downstream stabilization of HIF-1α under stress conditions is expected to be reduced, and the inflammatory response mediated by inflammasome assembly will likely be attenuated (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Orr et al., 2015). Given that multiple studies have demonstrated the role of mitochondrial ROS in directly or indirectly activating NLRP3 inflammasome signaling in both macrophages and RPE cells (Gao et al., 2015; Campbell & Doyle, 2013; Piippo, 2019), the hypothesis is that S3QEL-2 will break this mtROS–NLRP3 axis. In a therapeutic assay, one would expect that RPE cells treated with S3QEL-2 under conditions of complement dysregulation (a known contributor to dry AMD pathology) would demonstrate not only reduced markers of oxidative stress and inflammasome activation but also improved cellular viability, decreased apoptosis, and maintenance of proper metabolic function (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). Furthermore, if S3QEL-2 can lower the intracellular superoxide burden, it might also reduce the formation of oxidized lipids and other damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that contribute to the progression of AMD (Campbell & Doyle, 2013; Toma et al., 2021). Overall, the strategic downregulation of mitochondrial ROS production should translate into a protective phenotype in RPE cells by interrupting the signaling mechanisms that lead to chronic inflammation and cell death in the context of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
S3QEL-2 emerges as an attractive candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to its unique pharmacological profile and precision in targeting mitochondrial ROS production. One of the key strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its ability to selectively suppress superoxide generation at the Complex III Qo site without impairing the overall electron transport chain function or disrupting mitochondrial membrane potential (Orr et al., 2015). This high degree of specificity is particularly valuable in a disease such as dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central to pathogenesis yet preserving the RPE’s bioenergetic capacity is essential for retinal health (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013). The preclinical data available for S3QEL-2 in nonocular systems—ranging from hypoxia-induced HIF-1α modulation to protection of pancreatic β-cells and dampening of inflammasome activation in macrophages—suggest that its mechanism of action may well translate to the RPE, a cell type that is similarly sensitive to mitochondrial oxidative stress (Orr et al., 2015; Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). Moreover, the ability of S3QEL-2 to reduce mitochondrial ROS levels without interfering with ATP production positions it as a promising agent for interrupting the mtROS–NLRP3 inflammasome axis that is proposed to drive inflammatory responses in the geographic atrophy observed in dry AMD (Orr et al., 2015; Orr et al., 2015).

Delivery of S3QEL-2 to the retina may require formulation strategies that overcome solubility and permeability barriers inherent in drug delivery to the posterior segment of the eye. Another concern is the potential for off-target effects that, while not evident in the isolated systems tested so far, may manifest in the complex in vivo environment or with chronic administration (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Orr et al., 2015).

In addition, the exact molecular site of action on Complex III is not yet fully delineated at the atomic level, meaning that while the compound has been shown to modulate ROS production, the precise binding interactions and potential variability between different cell types or individuals remain uncertain (Orr et al., 2015). This incomplete mechanistic detail could complicate structure-activity relationship (SAR) explorations, as well as efforts to optimize the compound further for better efficacy or reduced toxicity in an ocular setting.

From a therapeutic perspective, the hypothesis that S3QEL-2 can reduce inflammasome activation by lowering mitochondrial ROS is strongly supported by data in other cell types, particularly where a reduction in ROS has been correlated with lower levels of IL-1β and IL-18 secretion (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). Given the well-established involvement of mitochondrial ROS and NLRP3 inflammasome activation in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013), S3QEL-2 holds promise as a tool to dissect and potentially therapeutically modulate this axis. However, concrete evidence in AMD-relevant models, especially primary RPE cells derived from patients or appropriate animal models, is necessary before advancing this compound further in the drug development pipeline (Korhonen, 2024; Macchioni et al., 2020).

In summary, the strengths of S3QEL-2 lie in its high selectivity for Complex III-derived ROS suppression, preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics, and the proven ability to modulate ROS-dependent inflammatory pathways in several preclinical settings (Orr et al., 2015). Its repurposing for dry AMD is biochemically plausible and aligns with the current understanding of the disease, where chronic low-level oxidative stress and inflammasome activation play central roles in RPE dysfunction and geographic atrophy (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013). Conversely, weaknesses include the absence of direct preclinical evidence in ocular models, potential pharmacokinetic and delivery challenges, and an incomplete elucidation of its binding mechanism at the atomic level. Considering these factors, S3QEL-2 represents a highly promising candidate that merits further investigation through targeted preclinical studies in retinal and RPE models, including assessments of its delivery, efficacy in reducing NLRP3-driven cytokine release, and long-term safety in ocular tissues (Gao et al., 2015; Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
MitoTEMPO, marketed as InvivoGen antiox15, is a synthetic mitochondria‐targeted antioxidant that belongs to the class of TPP⁺-linked piperidine nitroxides. Its molecular design is based on the well‐characterized TEMPO (2,2,6,6‐tetramethylpiperidine‐N-oxyl) scaffold, which is a stable nitroxide radical with established antioxidant and redox‐active properties. In MitoTEMPO, a TEMPO derivative is chemically conjugated to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) moiety using an appropriate linker, which ensures selective mitochondrial accumulation by exploiting the large negative mitochondrial membrane potential. The TPP⁺ group, owing to its lipophilicity and delocalized positive charge, facilitates rapid translocation across biological membranes and drives the compound into the mitochondrial matrix by a Nernstian accumulation mechanism. This design confers MitoTEMPO with dual functionality: the piperidine nitroxide core catalytically dismutates superoxide radicals by cycling between nitroxide, hydroxylamine, and oxoammonium states, while the TPP⁺ component achieves a high intramitochondrial concentration necessary for site‐specific antioxidant effects (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Peoples et al., 2019; Sassetti et al., 2021). The synthesis of such compounds generally involves standard organic synthetic methods that couple the nitroxide moiety to a phosphonium salt, yielding molecules that are both redox‐active and selective for mitochondria; these structural modifications represent an evolution from conventional nitroxides such as TEMPOL, improving not only cellular uptake but also intracellular distribution in disease‐relevant contexts (Zinovkin et al., 2023; Forini et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, piperidine nitroxides have been extensively investigated as antioxidants with a range of anti‐inflammatory, radioprotective, and cytoprotective properties. Their applications span preclinical models of cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration, pulmonary injury, and metabolic dysfunction. MitoTEMPO in particular has been applied in several animal studies, where its mitochondrial targeting capability has provided significant protection against oxidative stress‐mediated injury. For example, in cardiovascular models, MitoTEMPO has been shown to reduce mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS), preserve mitochondrial function, and improve cardiac performance by ameliorating the effects of ischemia–reperfusion injury and hypertensive damage (Forini et al., 2020; Grujicic & Allen, 2024). Its efficacy as a superoxide dismutase (SOD) mimetic further underpins its utility in conditions where excess superoxide production drives pathological outcomes. Although direct clinical studies in ocular disorders, including dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), are not available, the preclinical safety profile of MitoTEMPO has been encouraging. Rodent studies report that it is well tolerated at doses up to 5 mg/kg, with no significant hepatic or renal toxicity observed (Forini et al., 2020; Fock & Parnova, 2021). Additionally, TPP⁺‐linked antioxidants as a class, including MitoQ and MitoVitE, have progressed through preclinical evaluation in various diseases, with certain compounds even entering early-phase clinical trials for nonocular indications such as cardiovascular and metabolic disorders. Despite the absence of direct clinical evidence for AMD, there is a growing body of literature supporting the role of mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of geographic atrophy, a late stage form of dry AMD. Thus, the historical application of MitoTEMPO in models that recapitulate oxidative injury provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, where mitochondrial ROS plays a critical role (Peoples et al., 2019; Sassetti et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the core of MitoTEMPO’s pharmacological action is its ability to function as a catalytic SOD mimetic. The piperidine nitroxide moiety of MitoTEMPO undergoes reversible one‐electron redox cycling between three states: the nitroxide radical (R–NO•), the corresponding hydroxylamine (R–NHOH), and the oxoammonium cation (R–NO⁺). In the presence of mitochondrial superoxide (O₂•⁻), MitoTEMPO facilitates the conversion of superoxide to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), thereby mimicking the action of endogenous SOD enzymes. This catalytic cycling is essential for mitigating the deleterious effects of excess superoxide, which include the formation of secondary reactive species such as hydroxyl radicals (•OH) and the initiation of lipid peroxidation cascades that compromise mitochondrial membrane integrity (Forini et al., 2020; Apostolova & Victor, 2015). Furthermore, the compound’s ability to oxidize ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) to its ferric form (Fe³⁺) helps to limit the Fenton reaction, a process responsible for the generation of highly reactive hydroxyl radicals from H₂O₂, further contributing to its antioxidant efficacy (Forini et al., 2020; Peoples et al., 2019).

The triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) group is a critical structural element that differentiates MitoTEMPO from other nitroxides. By virtue of its delocalized positive charge and lipophilic character, the TPP⁺ moiety permits MitoTEMPO to traverse cellular membranes passively and accumulate several hundred‐fold within the mitochondrial matrix relative to the cytosol. This preferential accumulation not only enhances the local concentration of the antioxidant but also positions it in immediate proximity to the major sites of superoxide production, such as the complexes of the electron transport chain. Within the mitochondria, the nitroxide is subjected to a reductive environment wherein it is partially reduced by endogenous reductants such as ubiquinol; this reaction regenerates the active hydroxylamine form, ensuring sustained antioxidant activity despite continuous exposure to ROS (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Sadowska-Bartosz & Bartosz, 2024; Wang et al., 2020).

In biochemical terms, the overall mechanism of action of MitoTEMPO is multifaceted. It acts not only by scavenging superoxide directly but also by interfering with downstream oxidative reactions that lead to lipid peroxidation of mitochondrial membranes. Lipid peroxidation undermines mitochondrial bioenergetics by damaging membrane lipids, impairing the function of membrane-bound enzymes, and ultimately leading to the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm). By preventing such peroxidative damage, MitoTEMPO is postulated to maintain the structural integrity and functional competence of the mitochondria. Additionally, the reduction in intramitochondrial ROS has secondary anti-inflammatory effects, as oxidative stress is known to activate redox-sensitive signaling pathways (such as NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasome pathways) that exacerbate cellular dysfunction and apoptosis. In the context of the RPE, which is particularly vulnerable to oxidative stress due to its high metabolic demands and constant exposure to light and oxygen, the ability of MitoTEMPO to function as a sustained mitochondrial antioxidant is of significant therapeutic interest (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Peoples et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Zielonka et al., 2017).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of MitoTEMPO for dry age‐related macular degeneration is that it will preferentially accumulate in the mitochondria of RPE cells and mitigate oxidative damage by catalytically dismuting superoxide radicals, thereby preventing lipid peroxidation and preserving the bioenergetic function critical for cell survival. In in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells challenged with hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), MitoTEMPO has been observed to reduce the MitoSOX signal, a fluorescent indicator of mitochondrial superoxide, and to restore the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), which is often compromised under oxidative stress conditions. These effects support the notion that MitoTEMPO can protect the RPE from the mitochondrial dysfunction that is thought to contribute to geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Forini et al., 2020; Apostolova & Victor, 2015).

On a molecular level, the expected therapeutic effect in the RPE is mediated by several interrelated processes. First, by lowering the levels of ROS within the mitochondria, MitoTEMPO reduces the oxidative stress burden that leads to peroxidation of phospholipids in the inner mitochondrial membrane. This prevention of lipid peroxidation is crucial because it preserves the functional integrity of the electron transport chain and other membrane-associated processes that generate ATP, the energy currency necessary for RPE cellular functions (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Forini et al., 2020). Second, by dismuting superoxide, MitoTEMPO interrupts the formation of secondary reactive species that would otherwise aggravate cellular injury and trigger apoptotic signaling pathways. As RPE cell loss is a hallmark of geographic atrophy in dry AMD, the preservation of cell viability is a key expected outcome. Third, the antioxidant action at the mitochondrial level is anticipated to modulate redox-sensitive signaling cascades that contribute to chronic inflammation and cellular senescence—both of which are implicated in the progression of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2020; Forini et al., 2020).

The expression of antioxidant enzymes such as MnSOD in the RPE, which is closely linked to mitochondrial oxidative stress, further supports the rationale for a mimetic such as MitoTEMPO. The compound’s SOD-like activity is particularly important because it directly addresses the imbalance between ROS generation and antioxidant defenses that characterizes the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Moreover, in animal models such as the Ccl2⁻/⁻/Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ mouse—a model that recapitulates many features of dry AMD—the administration of MitoTEMPO has been associated with a reduction in mitochondrial ROS and a preservation of Δψm in the RPE. These findings collectively suggest that, when applied to the context of dry AMD, MitoTEMPO is expected to maintain mitochondrial function, reduce oxidative damage, and thereby slow the progression of geographic atrophy (Wang et al., 2020; Forini et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
MitoTEMPO represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration due to its targeted mechanism of action and its ability to counteract mitochondrial oxidative stress—a central pathogenic factor in the progression of geographic atrophy. One of the principal strengths of this candidate is its design as a TPP⁺–linked piperidine nitroxide, which facilitates selective mitochondrial accumulation. This targeting is critical because the mitochondria of RPE cells are a major source of ROS production, and accumulating antioxidant capacity at this subcellular location directly addresses a key contributor to cellular dysfunction in dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Peoples et al., 2019).

Moreover, the catalytic SOD-mimetic activity of MitoTEMPO enables it to continuously cycle between redox states and neutralize multiple superoxide radicals over time, in contrast with stoichiometric antioxidants that are consumed in the reaction. This catalytic mechanism, which involves rapid redox cycling between nitroxide, hydroxylamine, and oxoammonium species, has been well documented in preclinical models and lays a solid biochemical foundation for its use in pathologies where oxidative stress is a driving factor (Forini et al., 2020; Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Wang et al., 2020).

The preclinical tolerability profile is another favorable aspect. Rodent studies have indicated that MitoTEMPO is generally well tolerated, with safe dosing up to 5 mg/kg without overt hepatic or renal toxicity. Given that systemic safety is a crucial consideration for any repurposed therapeutic, these findings provide confidence that the compound may have an acceptable safety margin, although ocular pharmacokinetics remain to be fully characterized (Forini et al., 2020; Fock & Parnova, 2021).

However, there are several weaknesses and challenges that must be carefully considered. First, despite promising in vitro and systemic preclinical data, there is currently insufficient evidence regarding ocular pharmacokinetics and tissue distribution after local (intraocular or topical) administration. The lack of clinical ocular PK data raises concerns about whether effective concentrations can be achieved in the RPE and posterior segment of the eye without systemic side effects. Formulation strategies such as nanoparticle conjugation or controlled‐release systems may be required to overcome these limitations (Bubb et al., 2020; Apostolova & Victor, 2015).

Second, while the SOD-mimetic and lipid peroxidation–preventive mechanisms of MitoTEMPO are well established in other organ systems, the specific microenvironment of the RPE poses unique challenges. The RPE is subject to chronic, cumulative oxidative stress from both endogenous metabolic processes and exogenous light exposure. As such, the long-term stability and sustained activity of the nitroxide may be compromised by rapid bioreduction to its hydroxylamine form, which is EPR silent and potentially less active. This raises the possibility that repeated dosing or modified chemical formulations might be necessary to maintain therapeutic levels over time (Wang et al., 2020; Zielonka et al., 2017).

Third, the potential for off-target redox reactions, particularly under conditions of high local concentration or altered redox state, cannot be ignored. Although MitoTEMPO has been engineered to preferentially scavenge superoxide and prevent lipid peroxidation, there is always a risk that nitroxides could inadvertently interfere with normal cellular signaling pathways that rely on ROS as signaling molecules. In the delicate environment of the retina, where precise redox balance is essential for cell survival and function, such off-target effects could lead to unintended consequences. Detailed studies to map the influence of MitoTEMPO on redox-sensitive signaling cascades in the RPE will be critical in mitigating these risks (Zielonka et al., 2017; Sadowska-Bartosz & Bartosz, 2024).

Additionally, the current body of evidence supporting the use of MitoTEMPO in dry AMD is largely inferential, based on studies conducted in non-ocular systems or in models of general oxidative stress. Although there are promising signs from experiments in ARPE-19 cells and RPE cells derived from dry AMD models (for example, Ccl2⁻/⁻/Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ mice), direct evidence from dedicated ocular studies is still sparse. Bridging this gap will require comprehensive in vivo studies in established models of geographic atrophy to confirm whether the beneficial effects seen in other tissues can be translated to an ocular context (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Bubb et al., 2020).

Finally, while the rationale for targeting mitochondrial dysfunction in the RPE is compelling, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD means that addressing oxidative stress alone might not be sufficient to arrest disease progression. Dry AMD involves a complex interplay of inflammatory, genetic, and environmental factors. Therefore, it is possible that MitoTEMPO, when used as a monotherapy, might need to be combined with additional agents that address other pathogenic pathways, such as complement dysregulation or chronic inflammation, to achieve a clinically meaningful outcome (Gwozdzinski et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2020).

In summary, MitoTEMPO offers a mechanistically elegant approach to mitigating mitochondrial oxidative stress in the RPE by virtue of its unique design as a TPP⁺-linked piperidine nitroxide. Its ability to catalytically dismutate superoxide, prevent lipid peroxidation, and preserve mitochondrial function aligns well with the pathophysiological underpinnings of geographic atrophy in dry AMD. The strengths of this therapeutic candidate lie in its targeted mitochondrial delivery, well-characterized redox cycling, and promising preclinical safety profile. However, the translation of these effects into the ocular environment remains uncertain due to the lack of direct ocular pharmacokinetic and efficacy data, potential issues with nitroxide stability in the face of chronic oxidative stress, and the inherent complexity of dry AMD pathogenesis.

Given these considerations, we recommend that further preclinical studies be undertaken to specifically evaluate the ocular pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and long-term efficacy of MitoTEMPO in relevant models of dry AMD. Additionally, exploration of advanced formulation strategies aimed at enhancing retinal delivery and sustained drug release may be warranted. Overall, while MitoTEMPO represents a promising candidate from a mechanistic standpoint for repurposing in dry AMD, its ultimate clinical utility will hinge on overcoming the challenges associated with ocular delivery and demonstrating durable efficacy in mitigating RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and geographic atrophy (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Forini et al., 2020; Peoples et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Zielonka et al., 2017).

To conclude, MitoTEMPO’s biochemical profile and mechanism of action strongly support its potential as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD by targeting the root cause of oxidative mitochondrial injury in RPE cells. However, its advancement into clinical development for this indication will require a concerted research effort to address key translational hurdles, including formulation optimization for ocular use, comprehensive in vivo validation in disease-specific models, and rigorous safety studies focused on the sensitive retinal environment. If these challenges can be effectively managed, MitoTEMPO may not only complement existing antioxidant strategies but could also emerge as a transformative treatment option for patients suffering from dry AMD.

3. Mechanism of Action  
The molecular mechanisms underpinning the actions of Urolithin A are multifaceted and involve intricate interactions across several cellular pathways. Central to UA’s mechanism is its ability to induce selective autophagy, a process that includes both mitophagy and lysophagy, leading to the clearance of damaged mitochondria and lysosomes, respectively. Under normal physiological conditions, mitochondria that lose membrane potential become marked for degradation through the action of PINK1 (PTEN-induced kinase 1), which accumulates on the outer mitochondrial membrane. This accumulation results in the recruitment and activation of Parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase that ubiquitinates mitochondrial surface proteins, thereby flagging them for autophagic degradation. UA has been shown to upregulate the PINK1/Parkin pathway, thereby enhancing the clearance of dysfunctional mitochondria and ensuring mitochondrial quality control (Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024; Jayatunga et al., 2021).  

In addition to its role in mitophagy, UA has been demonstrated to elicit pronounced effects on lysosomal recycling processes through the promotion of SQSTM1/p62-dependent lysophagy. At the biochemical level, UA influences several upstream signaling pathways. Notably, it activates the AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)/ULK1 axis—a key regulator of autophagy. Activation of AMPK leads to phosphorylation of ULK1, kick-starting the autophagy process, and is associated with improved energy balance and mitochondrial turnover. This activation is complemented by an upregulation of factors such as PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha), which is instrumental in mitochondrial biogenesis. Together, these events not only promote the removal of impaired mitochondria but also support the generation of new, functional mitochondria, thereby restoring mitochondrial homeostasis (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Furthermore, the anti-inflammatory properties of UA are closely tied to its capacity to modulate oxidative stress. These molecular interactions collectively participate in mitigating the inflammatory milieu that is characteristic of neurodegenerative conditions and retinal disorders (Makarov & Korkotian, 2023; Zhang et al., 2025; Jayatunga et al., 2021).

In the context of retinal degeneration, several studies have delineated how UA’s molecular actions translate into cytoprotective outcomes. In SI-induced retinal injury models, the re-establishment of autophagic flux by UA is correlated with reduced RPE cell death and preservation of photoreceptor function. Although some findings suggest that UA’s neuroprotective effects in these models are independent of PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, there is substantial evidence that UA comprehensively enhances cellular quality control mechanisms through both mitophagy and lysophagy. This dichotomy might reflect the compound’s capability to engage multiple parallel pathways to ensure the efficient clearance of damaged organelles (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Fehér et al., 2022). Given that the retina is especially sensitive to oxidative stress and that impaired mitochondrial dynamics are a hallmark of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD, these molecular mechanisms underscore UA’s therapeutic potential.

At a more granular level, it is worth noting that UA appears to influence the expression levels of key mitophagy-related proteins not only at the post-translational level but also transcriptionally. For instance, treatment with UA has been associated with increased expression of Parkin and proteins involved in the formation of autophagosomes, such as BECN1, further reinforcing its role in maintaining mitochondrial and lysosomal integrity. This transcriptional regulation may be mediated by the activation of transcription factors such as FOXO, which have been implicated in cellular stress responses and longevity pathways. As mitochondrial dysfunction contributes significantly to the pathology of dry AMD, the ability of UA to simultaneously promote the degradation of damaged mitochondria and stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis positions it as a strong candidate for addressing the underlying etiologies of RPE degeneration (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

In summary, the detailed biochemistry of UA illustrates that its mechanism of action involves a well-coordinated activation of autophagic processes through both the PINK1/Parkin axis for mitophagy and the SQSTM1/p62 pathway for lysophagy, with auxiliary support from AMPK/ULK1 and SIRT-mediated signaling. This comprehensive modulation of cellular clearance pathways is critical in contexts where mitochondrial dysfunction and lysosomal impairment drive disease progression, such as in dry age-related macular degeneration (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

In these models, UA treatment leads to a restoration of autophagic flux—a critical determinant of cellular health—by enhancing both the degradation of impaired mitochondria and the recycling of damaged lysosomes through the p62-dependent pathway. The net effect is a significant decrease in RPE cell death and, consequently, the preservation of photoreceptor cells and visual function. This outcome is particularly relevant for dry AMD, a condition characterized by geographic atrophy of the RPE and subsequent photoreceptor degeneration (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024).

At the molecular level, the activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway by UA is expected to facilitate the tagging of dysfunctional mitochondria for autophagic removal. In parallel, the activation of AMPK/ULK1 signaling by UA further promotes autophagosome formation, ensuring that the cell’s degradative capacity is optimized to handle the increased load of dysfunctional organelles. The coordinated activation of these pathways not only improves mitochondrial quality control but also indirectly suppresses downstream inflammatory cascades that are typically exacerbated by oxidative stress. For instance, by reducing mtROS levels, UA is anticipated to attenuate the activation of pro-inflammatory transcription factors such as NF-κB, thereby contributing to a more quiescent cellular environment supportive of RPE survival (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

5. Overall Evaluation  
In evaluating Urolithin A as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and potential areas for further investigation emerge. First and foremost, UA offers a robust safety profile supported by both preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials in elderly populations, where it has been administered at relatively high doses without observable toxicity or adverse events (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Liu, 2022). Preclinical data from retinal degeneration models provide compelling evidence that UA can ameliorate pathological features reminiscent of dry AMD. In SI-induced models, UA treatment has resulted in restored autophagic flux, reduced RPE cell death, and preservation of visual function—all of which are promising indicators for its potential to slow or reverse the atrophic processes underlying geographic atrophy in AMD (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). Moreover, its ability to mitigate inflammatory signaling and reduce mtROS production adds another layer of protective activity that is critical in managing chronic retinal degeneration.

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and challenges warrant consideration. One area of potential ambiguity concerns the precise mechanistic contributions of the PINK1/Parkin pathway versus the SQSTM1/p62-mediated lysophagy in mediating UA’s protective effects. While some studies emphasize the role of PINK1/Parkin in clearance of damaged mitochondria, others have reported that UA’s neuroprotective benefits are maintained even with genetic manipulations of these proteins, suggesting that p62-dependent lysophagy may be the predominant mechanism in certain contexts (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Fehér et al., 2022). This duality raises questions regarding which pathway is most critical in RPE cells, particularly given that the proposed hypothesis centers on enhanced PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy. Further mechanistic studies in RPE-specific models will be necessary to delineate the relative contributions of these pathways and to optimize dosing and formulation strategies accordingly.

Another potential weakness is the translational gap between preclinical studies and clinical application in dry AMD. Although UA has shown promise in animal models of retinal degeneration, human disease is complex, and dry AMD is known for its multifactorial etiology. The pharmacokinetic properties of UA, including its relatively short half-life and the challenges associated with ensuring adequate ocular bioavailability, might necessitate novel delivery strategies for effective retinal targeting. Formulation development—potentially involving sustained-release systems or ocular-specific delivery vehicles—may be required to overcome these hurdles (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025). Additionally, while the evidence from non-ocular (e.g., muscle and neural) studies is robust, direct clinical evidence in AMD patients remains sparse, necessitating carefully designed human trials to confirm efficacy and safety in this specific population.

It is also important to contextualize UA’s potential within the current landscape of AMD treatments. While existing therapies for wet AMD (e.g., anti-VEGF agents) have transformed clinical outcomes, there remains no established treatment for dry AMD. The multifaceted mode of action of UA—targeting mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and inflammation—offers a unique therapeutic approach that could complement or, in some cases, provide an alternative to emerging interventions. However, comparative studies against other experimental agents will be critical to fully establish its translational relevance and competitive advantage in the therapeutic space (Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Overall, Urolithin A presents several compelling attributes that support its development as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its origin as a naturally derived, gut-microbiota transformation product provides a favorable starting point from a safety perspective. Preclinical studies consistently demonstrate its ability to enhance autophagic clearance mechanisms, reduce oxidative damage, and improve cell survival in models that recapitulate key features of AMD. The ability of UA to simultaneously stimulate both mitophagy and lysophagy—the former via the PINK1/Parkin pathway and the latter via p62-dependent mechanisms—positions it as a multi-targeted intervention capable of addressing the multifactorial pathology of RPE degeneration (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Nonetheless, for the successful translation of UA into a clinically effective therapy for dry AMD, several challenges need to be addressed. Detailed mechanistic insights specifically in RPE cells are required to understand the relative importance of the PINK1/Parkin versus the lysophagy pathway. Optimizing drug delivery to ensure sustained retinal bioavailability and addressing potential issues related to its pharmacokinetic profile are also key areas that will require further research. Finally, controlled clinical studies in AMD patients will be essential to validate the promising preclinical findings and to ensure that the observed benefits in animal models translate into meaningful clinical outcomes.

In conclusion, based on the comprehensive literature reviewed from biochemical, clinical, and biomedical sources, Urolithin A demonstrates significant potential as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its established ability to enhance mitochondrial quality control through both mitophagy and lysophagy, alongside its additional anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, offers a novel mechanism to counteract the progressive degeneration observed in RPE cells during AMD. Given the encouraging preclinical data and a robust safety profile already evidenced in other indications, further investigations—particularly those focusing on RPE-specific mechanisms and optimized ocular drug delivery—are warranted to fully ascertain UA’s clinical potential in halting or reversing geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024; Jayatunga et al., 2021).
