Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
EUK-8 is a synthetic catalytic antioxidant that belongs to the manganese‐based salen complexes, a class of low molecular weight enzyme mimetics engineered to replicate key activities of endogenous antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). This compound is synthesized via a condensation reaction between salicylaldehyde derivatives and diamines to form a bis‐Schiff base (salen) ligand, which then coordinates to a manganese ion, thereby producing the characteristic MnN₂O₂ planar core responsible for its redox activity (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rosenthal et al., 2011). The manganese center in EUK-8 undergoes reversible redox cycling between Mn(III) and Mn(II) oxidation states; this reversible cycling is essential for its dual enzyme-mimetic action, as it enables catalytic dismutation of superoxide radicals into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide and further conversion of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, thereby mimicking the combined action of SOD and catalase (Fernandes, 2010; Rouco et al., 2020a). The salen complex scaffold not only confers redox activity but also provides a tunable electronic and steric environment through modification of substituents on the ligand framework, which in turn dictates the redox potential, proton-dissociation properties, and overall catalytic efficacy (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020b). Because of its synthetic origin, EUK-8 is both cost-effective and easily reproducible, making it an appealing candidate for repurposing in therapeutic areas where enhanced antioxidant defenses are required, such as in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rosenthal et al., 2011).

Therapeutic History:  
The EUK series of compounds, which includes EUK-8, have been extensively studied in a plethora of preclinical models addressing a wide range of diseases linked to oxidative stress, including ischemic brain injury, neurodegeneration, cardiac injury, and even lifespan extension models in Caenorhabditis elegans and SOD2 knockout mice (Rouco et al., 2020a). Biochemical studies have demonstrated that EUK-8 exhibits both superoxide dismutase and catalase-like activities at submicromolar concentrations, providing significant protection in vitro and in vivo in models of oxidative injury (Bani & Bencini, 2012). While EUK-8 itself has not been directly evaluated in clinical trials for dry AMD, its protective effects have been documented in several models of neuronal and cardiac injury where mitochondrial dysfunction and excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) production are central to the pathology (Fernandes, 2010; Rouco et al., 2020a). The pharmacological application of salen manganese complexes, including EUK-8, extends to neuroprotective approaches, such as in models of Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and ischemia–reperfusion injury, suggesting that similar mechanisms may be beneficial in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which are notably vulnerable to oxidative stress in dry AMD (Rouco et al., 2020b; Yan et al., 2010). Additionally, the literature reveals that analogous compounds in the EUK series have been examined for their anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, and mitochondrial protective properties in diverse cellular and animal models, lending further credence to their potential for repurposing in ocular degenerative diseases (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rosenthal et al., 2009).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, EUK-8 functions as a catalytic antioxidant by mimicking two key enzymes involved in the detoxification of reactive oxygen species. First, it catalyzes the dismutation of superoxide (O₂•⁻) by virtue of its manganese center undergoing cyclic redox reactions between the Mn(III) and Mn(II) states; in one half-reaction, the Mn(III) state accepts an electron from superoxide to become Mn(II), while in the subsequent half-reaction, Mn(II) is reoxidized to Mn(III) by another molecule of superoxide, resulting in the conversion of superoxide to molecular oxygen and hydrogen peroxide (Fernandes, 2010; Batinić-Haberle et al., 2016). Second, EUK-8 mimics catalase activity by decomposing the generated hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen; it is proposed that hydrogen peroxide reacts with the manganese center to generate a transient high-valent oxo–Mn species, which is then reduced back to the resting state in the presence of a reductant, thus completing the catalytic cycle (Yan et al., 2010; Bani & Bencini, 2012). The structural integrity of the salen ligand is critical in modulating the redox potential of the manganese center, which, when tuned to an optimal range, ensures efficient electron transfer with reactive species while minimizing the risk of metal ion dissociation or inadvertent pro-oxidant activity (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Durand, 2013). In cellular contexts, the dual SOD/catalase activity of EUK-8 is especially relevant to mitochondria, which are the primary source of intracellular ROS; by reducing mitochondrial superoxide and decomposing hydrogen peroxide, EUK-8 helps to preserve mitochondrial respiration and prevent oxidative mitochondrial damage, which is a key contributor to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). Moreover, the reduction of mitochondrial ROS is anticipated to attenuate the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, a multiprotein complex that is known to be triggered by oxidative stress and has been implicated in inflammasome-mediated inflammatory responses in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Rouco et al., 2020a; Bani & Bencini, 2012). The overall biochemical and mechanistic profile of EUK-8, therefore, aligns well with the need to lower mtROS and preserve cellular homeostasis in tissues subjected to chronic oxidative stress.

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by the degeneration of the RPE, a process driven by cumulative oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation leading to cellular senescence and eventual retinal atrophy (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Batinić-Haberle et al., 2016). Given that the RPE expresses high levels of mitochondrial enzymes, including MnSOD, and relies on efficient mitochondrial respiration for normal function, the preservation of mitochondrial integrity is paramount (Fernandes, 2010; Rouco et al., 2020a). EUK-8 is expected to enter RPE cells and preferentially localize to mitochondria where its catalytic dual SOD/catalase activity would reduce the burden of superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, thereby mitigating oxidative damage to mitochondrial proteins, lipids, and DNA (Rosenthal et al., 2011; Rosenthal et al., 2009). By maintaining lower levels of mtROS, EUK-8 would be anticipated to stave off the mitochondrial dysfunction that underlies RPE degeneration and to prevent the activation of pro-inflammatory signaling cascades such as those mediated by the NLRP3 inflammasome, thus potentially preserving cellular viability and function (Batinić-Haberle, 2013; Bigham & Wilson, 2023). In addition, previous studies with related manganosalen complexes have shown that treatment can lead to the reversal of age-related cognitive deficits and the inhibition of pro-apoptotic pathways in neuronal tissues, which are mechanistically analogous to the crises faced by RPE cells in dry AMD (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rouco et al., 2020b). Given that the anticipated mechanism involves modulation of mitochondrial redox balance and prevention of inflammation, the expected molecular targets in RPE cells include key mitochondrial respiratory chain components, antioxidant response elements such as Nrf2, and inflammasome components including caspase-1 and interleukin-1β, all of which have been implicated in the progression of dry AMD (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Durand, 2013). The ability of EUK-8 to act at submicromolar doses further enhances its appeal, as such potency suggests that therapeutic effects may be achieved with minimal exposure, reducing the likelihood of off-target effects and toxicity (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Fernandes, 2010).

Overall Evaluation:  
From a drug development perspective, EUK-8 emerges as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration, primarily because its dual enzyme-mimetic properties address two central features of RPE pathology—oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). One of the major strengths of EUK-8 lies in its robust catalytic activity; being a regenerative, non-stoichiometric antioxidant means that even at submicromolar concentrations, it can exert sustained protective effects by continuously dismutating ROS, in contrast to traditional antioxidants that are consumed in the process (Rosenthal et al., 2011; Rouco et al., 2020a). Its low molecular weight and non-peptidic nature facilitate cellular uptake and mitochondrial penetration, critical features for targeting the RPE where mitochondrial production of ROS is an important driver of cell injury (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). Furthermore, the extensive preclinical history of manganosalen compounds in models of neuroprotection, cardiac ischemia, and aging provides a solid rationale for their protective capacity in tissues that are equally susceptible to oxidative damage, even if direct studies in dry AMD are limited at present (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rouco et al., 2020b).

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and challenges must be addressed before EUK-8 can be confidently advanced as a therapeutic for dry AMD. First, despite the promising preclinical data in other models, there is a paucity of direct studies evaluating EUK-8 in ocular or RPE-specific models. Dry AMD has its own unique microenvironment, including features such as the Bruch’s membrane, the blood-retinal barrier, and specialized immune processes, which might affect drug delivery and efficacy (Bigham & Wilson, 2023; Yan et al., 2010). Second, the stability of EUK-8 in the complex milieu of the eye must be rigorously tested, especially because the aqueous and proteinaceous environments found in ocular tissues could potentially lead to ligand dissociation or redox inactivation (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). Third, although EUK-8’s catalytic nature means that it is less likely to be consumed during therapy compared to stoichiometric antioxidants, there is always the risk that under certain pathological conditions, such as in the presence of excess hydrogen peroxide or other reactive species, it could exhibit paradoxical pro-oxidant effects if the redox balance is not carefully controlled (Batinić-Haberle et al., 2012; Bani & Bencini, 2012). Fourth, formulation and delivery challenges specific to ocular therapeutics must be overcome; for instance, ensuring adequate penetration across the inner limiting membrane and achieving sufficient concentrations within the RPE are non-trivial hurdles that have derailed otherwise promising compounds in the past (Batinić-Haberle et al., 2016; Rosenthal et al., 2009). Finally, comprehensive toxicity and pharmacokinetic studies in ocular models are required since systemic dosing data from neurological or cardiovascular models may not transcribe directly to the unique setting of the retina (Batinić-Haberle, 2013; Fernandes, 2010).

In summary, the therapeutic candidate EUK-8 exhibits several key attributes that make it an attractive option for addressing the oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction underlying dry age-related macular degeneration. Its synthetic origin and scalable chemistry, combined with potent dual SOD/catalase enzyme-mimetic activity, have already been validated extensively in diverse preclinical models of oxidative injury (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). The molecular mechanism—involving redox cycling of a manganese center coordinated by a salen ligand—supports the hypothesis that EUK-8 can effectively lower mtROS levels and preserve mitochondrial respiration in cells, such as the retinal pigment epithelium, that are critically dependent on mitochondrial function (Fernandes, 2010; Yan et al., 2010). This mechanistic rationale is further bolstered by studies demonstrating that similar manganosalen complexes can reverse age-related functional deficits and prevent neurodegenerative changes in animal models, suggesting that the beneficial effects observed in cardiac and neuronal tissues might extend to the RPE (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rouco et al., 2020b).

The expected effect of EUK-8 in the context of dry AMD is twofold: first, by acting as both a superoxide dismutase and catalase mimic, it is anticipated to reduce the overall oxidative burden within RPE mitochondria, preserving cellular respiration and preventing damage to key mitochondrial constituents; and second, by mitigating the oxidative activation of the inflammasome (particularly the NLRP3 complex), EUK-8 should help prevent the chronic inflammatory environment that exacerbates RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Rouco et al., 2020a; Bani & Bencini, 2012). This dual mode of action not only targets the root cause of oxidative damage but also addresses a major downstream consequence—persistent inflammation—that has been implicated in the progression of dry AMD (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rosenthal et al., 2009).

Overall, while the preclinical evidence underscores the strong potential of EUK-8 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, its translational success will depend critically on several factors. Strengths of EUK-8 include its well-documented catalytic efficiency, proven efficacy in multiple oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction models, and the capability for extensive structure–activity relationship optimization that allows fine-tuning of its redox properties (Fernandes, 2010; Bani & Bencini, 2012). However, weaknesses such as the lack of ocular-specific preclinical data, potential formulation and delivery challenges specific to the retinal environment, and the need for rigorous ocular toxicity and pharmacokinetic studies remain to be addressed (Bigham & Wilson, 2023; Yan et al., 2010). In the absence of direct evidence in RPE cells or AMD models, it is essential that further studies be conducted to confirm that EUK-8’s in vitro antioxidant effects translate into meaningful protection of RPE mitochondrial function and inhibition of inflammasome activation in vivo (Durand, 2013; Rosenthal et al., 2009). Furthermore, the development of targeted delivery systems—possibly involving nanoparticle encapsulation, intravitreal injections, or sustained-release formulations—may be required to ensure adequate drug concentration at the site of action while minimizing systemic exposure and potential off-target effects (Batinić-Haberle, 2013; Fernandes, 2010).

From a strategic standpoint, the repurposing of EUK-8 for dry AMD appears promising based on its robust mechanistic foundation and extensive preclinical history in related oxidative stress models; however, a focused research program involving detailed studies in ocular tissues, optimization of drug delivery to the retina, and comprehensive toxicity assessments is warranted to overcome the current limitations and uncertainties (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rouco et al., 2020b). If these challenges can be successfully addressed, EUK-8 has the potential to fulfill an unmet clinical need by protecting RPE mitochondria from oxidative damage, thereby slowing the progression of dry AMD and preserving visual function in affected patients (Fernandes, 2010; Rouco et al., 2020a).  

In conclusion, as a candidate drug for dry age-related macular degeneration, EUK-8 offers a compelling therapeutic strategy that leverages its dual SOD and catalase mimetic activities to target the central biochemical derangements in the RPE associated with oxidative stress and inflammation (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). The natural alignment of its mechanism with the pathophysiological features of dry AMD—namely, mitochondrial dysfunction, excessive ROS production, and inflammasome activation—supports the hypothesis that EUK-8 could restore redox balance and inhibit degenerative processes in the retina (Rouco et al., 2020a; Bani & Bencini, 2012). Nonetheless, the ultimate utility of EUK-8 will depend on its ability to overcome delivery and stability challenges in the ocular environment and on the generation of robust preclinical data demonstrating efficacy in relevant AMD models. Given these considerations, it is recommended that targeted in vitro and in vivo studies be prioritized to validate the therapeutic potential of EUK-8 in dry AMD, with particular attention to mitochondrial function, inflammasome activity, and retinal cell survival parameters (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rosenthal et al., 2009).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Honokiol is a naturally occurring polyphenolic neolignan that is primarily isolated from the bark and other tissues of Magnolia species, notably Magnolia officinalis. Traditionally used in Chinese medicine, honokiol has emerged as a promising therapeutic candidate due to its potent antioxidant, anti‐inflammatory, and neuroprotective properties. As a member of the phenylpropanoid class of natural compounds, honokiol has a unique biphenolic structure that enables it to interact with a variety of cellular targets. Its extraction from natural sources and subsequent formulation by vendors such as Sigma-Aldrich (SML0588) provides a well-characterized starting point for drug repurposing strategies. Over the years, synthetic modifications have also been explored to improve its bioavailability, solubility, and therapeutic efficacy, further expanding its potential as a drug candidate in multiple clinical contexts (Faysal et al., 2023). The chemical attributes of honokiol allow it to cross biological barriers effectively, a property that is particularly relevant in diseases involving complex tissue compartments such as the eye’s retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Its classification within the polyphenolic compounds aligns it with other antioxidants known to mitigate cellular damage from reactive oxygen species (ROS) and oxidative stress, making it a promising candidate for repurposing in conditions like dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative injury are predominant pathological features (Faysal et al., 2023; Sasia et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, honokiol has been the subject of extensive biochemical and pharmacological investigations given its wide-ranging protective effects in various tissues. In hepatocyte models, studies have demonstrated that honokiol protects liver cells from oxidative injury induced by compounds such as tert-butyl hydroperoxide (t-BHP) by restoring mitochondrial deacetylase SIRT3 levels, thereby boosting cellular viability and enhancing antioxidant defenses (Liu et al., 2018). These hepatoprotective effects underscore honokiol’s capacity to modulate mitochondrial health, a mechanism that likely underpins its action in other cell types as well. In addition to hepatic models, honokiol has been evaluated in neurological contexts where activation of SIRT3 plays a central role in neuroprotection. For example, in a rat model of ammonia neurotoxicity, honokiol administration led to the recovery of MnSOD activity and the upregulation of transcription factors such as FoxO3a and PGC1α, which are essential for mitochondrial function and cellular antioxidant responses (Trigun & Anamika, 2022; Tyagi & Pugazhenthi, 2023). These findings demonstrate the compound’s ability to counteract oxidative stress via restoration of mitochondrial enzyme activities, an effect that has been linked to improved neurological outcomes including reductions in beta-amyloid accumulation.

More recently, honokiol has shown promising results in ocular models as well. Studies investigating its effects on diabetic retinal microvascular injury have revealed that honokiol can activate SIRT3 in retinal capillary endothelial cells, leading to the deacetylation of mitochondrial proteins—most notably manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD)—and preservation of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) under hyperglycemic conditions (Shi et al., 2024). Although these results have been demonstrated in the context of diabetic retinal injury rather than in models of dry AMD specifically, the mechanistic overlap—centered on mitochondrial protection and the reduction of oxidative stress—strongly supports the potential utility of honokiol in diseases characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction. Despite these advances, there is a notable gap in the literature regarding direct evaluations of honokiol in RPE cells or in models of geographic atrophy, the advanced form of dry AMD. However, the consistency of its protective effects across hepatocytes, neurons, and retinal microvascular cells suggests a broad applicability that merits further exploration for AMD-related indications (Liu et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic potential of honokiol is intimately linked to its capacity to activate mitochondrial SIRT3, a member of the sirtuin family of NAD⁺-dependent deacetylases that serve as key regulators of mitochondrial biology. SIRT3 plays a pivotal role in maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis through the deacetylation and consequent activation of several mitochondrial enzymes implicated in antioxidant defense and metabolic regulation. Among its important targets is manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), an enzyme responsible for the dismutation of superoxide radicals into less reactive molecular species. By deacetylating MnSOD, SIRT3 increases its enzymatic activity, thereby reducing the levels of damaging ROS generated during oxidative phosphorylation (Liu et al., 2018; Trigun & Anamika, 2022). In parallel, SIRT3 is postulated to deacetylate isocitrate dehydrogenase 2 (IDH2), another mitochondrial enzyme critically involved in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and cellular redox balance, although direct evidence for IDH2 deacetylation in the honokiol context is less extensively documented in the current literature. Nevertheless, the hypothesis posits that deacetylation of IDH2 would further contribute to the reduction of mitochondrial ROS, suggesting a dual mechanism through which SIRT3 activation could ameliorate oxidative damage (Tyagi & Pugazhenthi, 2023; Zhang et al., 2020).

In addition to these direct deacetylation events, honokiol-induced SIRT3 activation has been associated with the modulation of several signaling cascades. Notably, SIRT3 activation by honokiol has been correlated with increased levels of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2), a master regulator of the cellular antioxidant response (Liu et al., 2018). The upregulation of Nrf2 can lead to the transcriptional activation of a spectrum of antioxidant enzymes, thereby reinforcing the intracellular capacity to neutralize ROS. Furthermore, SIRT3 activation influences mitochondrial biogenesis via upregulation of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC1α) and the forkhead box O3a (FoxO3a) pathway, which not only supports energy production but also promotes the maintenance of mitochondrial integrity under stress conditions (Trigun & Anamika, 2022). Evidence from neurotoxicity models demonstrates that honokiol can modulate these pathways, leading to improved mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and reduced apoptosis (Trigun & Anamika, 2022; Tyagi & Pugazhenthi, 2023).

Given the well-documented role of SIRT3 in various tissues, the proposed mechanism in RPE cells for dry AMD centers on the hypothesis that honokiol, by enhancing SIRT3 activity, will lead to the deacetylation of MnSOD and IDH2. In RPE cells, which are known to suffer from hyperacetylation-driven mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD, such deacetylation is expected to result in the restoration of enzymatic antioxidant defenses. This, in turn, would mitigate mitochondrial ROS accumulation, thereby stabilizing Δψm and supporting cellular viability under conditions of chronic oxidative stress—a central pathogenic mechanism in geographic atrophy (Liu et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2024). The detailed molecular interactions between honokiol and SIRT3 remain an active area of research, but the cumulative evidence supports a model wherein honokiol binding enhances the enzymatic activity of SIRT3, leading to downstream deacetylation events that ultimately preserve mitochondrial function (Trigun & Anamika, 2022; Tyagi & Pugazhenthi, 2023).

Expected Effect:  
For the proposed application in dry AMD, the expected effect of honokiol in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells is multi-faceted. Primarily, upon exposure to honokiol, one would anticipate activation of SIRT3 within the mitochondria of RPE cells. This activation is expected to promote the deacetylation of critical mitochondrial proteins—including MnSOD and, by extension, IDH2—thereby enhancing their enzymatic activities. The deacetylation of MnSOD is particularly vital, as it increases the dismutation of superoxide radicals, thus reducing the levels of ROS that are known to drive RPE cell dysfunction and death in the context of dry AMD (Liu et al., 2018; Trigun & Anamika, 2022).

In addition to the direct antioxidant effects mediated by MnSOD, the activation of SIRT3 is also expected to trigger a broader mitochondrial protective response. Upregulation of PGC1α and activation of FoxO3a—both of which have been observed in various cellular models after honokiol treatment—would stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis and contribute to the maintenance of the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) (Trigun & Anamika, 2022). A stabilized Δψm is critical in preventing the cascade of events leading to mitochondrial permeability transition and subsequent apoptosis, thereby preserving RPE cell function. Evidence from diabetic retinal microvascular injury models supports the notion that honokiol can indeed preserve Δψm in cells under oxidative stress, suggesting that similar protective mechanisms may be harnessed in RPE cells affected by geographic atrophy (Shi et al., 2024).

Furthermore, the activation of antioxidant transcriptional programs through increased Nrf2 levels may synergize with the direct effects on mitochondrial proteins. Enhanced Nrf2 activity would lead to the upregulation of a suite of antioxidant enzymes and stress response proteins, further bolstering the capacity of RPE cells to handle oxidative insults. This integrative response is expected to reduce the accumulation of mtROS, which is a key mediator of cellular senescence and dysfunction in the aging retina (Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020). Ultimately, the net effect in the assay is predicted to be an improvement in cellular viability and function following oxidative stress, as measured by assays of ROS production, Δψm stability, and overall cell survival. Such outcomes would validate the potential of honokiol to counteract the hyperacetylation-driven mitochondrial defects observed in donor RPE cells from patients with dry AMD (Liu et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of honokiol as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is supported by a convergence of biochemical, cellular, and animal model data that demonstrate its capacity to activate mitochondrial SIRT3 and promote deacetylation of key antioxidant enzymes. On the strength side, honokiol is a well-characterized natural compound with a long history of therapeutic use in traditional medicine and has been shown to exert protective effects across multiple cell types, including hepatocytes, neurons, and retinal microvascular cells. Its ability to enhance SIRT3 activity is particularly compelling given the central role of SIRT3 in preserving mitochondrial function and reducing oxidative stress—a pathogenic hallmark in dry AMD and its advanced form, geographic atrophy (Liu et al., 2018; Trigun & Anamika, 2022; Shi et al., 2024). Moreover, the compound’s lipophilic structure and ability to cross biological barriers further enhance its appeal as a candidate for treating diseases that require delivery to the retinal layers (Faysal et al., 2023).

From a mechanistic standpoint, honokiol’s actions have been well delineated across several experimental models. The documented deacetylation of MnSOD, along with the inferred deacetylation of IDH2, provides a solid biochemical foundation for the proposed mechanism of action in RPE cells. The downstream effects—involving the activation of transcription factors such as Nrf2, FoxO3a, and the upregulation of PGC1α—offer additional layers of protection by promoting mitochondrial biogenesis, energy production, and an enhanced antioxidant response (Trigun & Anamika, 2022; Liu et al., 2018). These multi-dimensional actions are likely to be advantageous in the context of dry AMD, a condition that results from an interplay of oxidative stress, inflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction.

Despite these strengths, several potential challenges must be considered. One significant weakness is the current lack of direct evidence demonstrating honokiol’s efficacy in RPE cells or in models of dry AMD, specifically geographic atrophy. Most of the supporting studies have been conducted in non-ocular systems such as hepatocyte cultures, neurotoxicity models, and diabetic retinal microvascular cells, with only indirect extrapolations made to RPE biology (Liu et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2024). This gap in the literature calls for targeted preclinical studies in RPE cell lines and relevant animal models of geographic atrophy to establish the therapeutic relevance of honokiol in an ocular setting. Additionally, while honokiol has been shown to activate SIRT3 in several systems, the degree to which this activation translates into clinically meaningful improvements in mitochondrial function within the RPE remains to be fully validated. The potential variable expression of SIRT3 in RPE cells under different pathological conditions may also influence the overall efficacy of honokiol (Tyagi & Pugazhenthi, 2023; Zhang et al., 2020).

Another concern involves the pharmacokinetic properties of honokiol when administered for ocular indications. Although its lipophilicity may favor penetration into retinal tissue, detailed studies on its distribution, metabolism, and clearance in the eye are lacking. This raises questions regarding the optimal dosing regimen, route of administration, and potential off-target effects that might arise from systemic exposure. The current body of literature has largely focused on in vitro and animal models in other organ systems; hence, translational research specifically addressing ocular pharmacology is warranted (Shi et al., 2024).

Furthermore, the complexity of dry AMD pathogenesis suggests that a multi-targeted approach might be necessary for effective treatment. While the proposed mechanism—centered on SIRT3 activation and subsequent mitochondrial protection—is attractive, it represents only one facet of the disease process. Inflammation, complement dysregulation, and extracellular matrix alterations also play critical roles in the progression of geographic atrophy. Therefore, honokiol’s utility as a monotherapy may be limited unless it can also modulate these additional pathways or be combined with other therapeutic modalities. Nonetheless, the inherent anti-inflammatory properties of honokiol, as noted in several studies, may provide some degree of pleiotropic benefit (Faysal et al., 2023; Ramesh et al., 2018).

In summary, honokiol exhibits a compelling profile as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD due to its established ability to activate mitochondrial SIRT3 and its consequent effects on antioxidant enzyme deacetylation, mitochondrial membrane potential stabilization, and reduction of oxidative stress. Its documented benefits in diverse models—from hepatocytes to neuronal and retinal microvascular cells—provide a strong rationale for its further investigation in RPE-specific contexts. However, the absence of direct data in RPE cells and AMD models represents a critical gap that must be addressed through targeted preclinical studies. Detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic evaluations will be essential in determining the appropriate dosing strategies and ensuring ocular delivery of honokiol at therapeutically relevant concentrations. Additionally, a broader investigation into its anti-inflammatory and complement-modulating effects may reveal synergistic benefits that are particularly important in the multifactorial etiology of dry AMD (Liu et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2024).

Overall, while current evidence supports the hypothesis that honokiol’s activation of SIRT3 can restore mitochondrial function by facilitating the deacetylation of critical enzymes such as MnSOD and potentially IDH2, thereby reducing mtROS and stabilizing Δψm, the translational relevance to RPE cells in dry AMD requires further empirical substantiation. The strengths of honokiol—in the form of its broad-spectrum antioxidant capacity, favorable pharmacological profile, and well-characterized molecular mechanisms—must be weighed against the limitations of the current evidence base. Based on the comprehensive review of the literature, it is advisable for the research team to pursue further validation studies of honokiol in ocular-specific systems, while also considering its integration into combination therapeutic strategies to address the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathology (Liu et al., 2018; Trigun & Anamika, 2022; Shi et al., 2024).

In conclusion, the repurposing of honokiol for dry age-related macular degeneration holds considerable promise due to its well-documented role in activating SIRT3 and promoting mitochondrial resilience under oxidative stress conditions. The compound’s natural origin, coupled with its established preclinical efficacy in other tissue models, provides a sound scientific foundation for further investigation. Nonetheless, the research team must remain cognizant of the current gaps in data regarding RPE-specific effects and the broader pathogenesis of dry AMD. A judiciously designed series of experiments—ranging from in vitro assays in primary RPE cultures to in vivo studies in geographic atrophy models—will be crucial in validating the therapeutic potential of honokiol and refining its clinical application. The strengths of honokiol’s mechanism of action, particularly its dual capacity to reduce ROS through the activation of MnSOD and possibly IDH2, as well as its ability to stabilize mitochondrial membrane potential, render it an attractive candidate for addressing the mitochondrial dysfunction intrinsic to dry AMD. Simultaneously, challenges related to ocular bioavailability and the need for multi-target intervention strategies underscore the importance of a cautious, stepwise approach in the translational development of honokiol for this indication (Liu et al., 2018; Trigun & Anamika, 2022; Shi et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Kinetin riboside (KR; N6-furfuryladenosine) is an adenine-derived cytokinin riboside originally linked to the discovery of kinetin as a plant hormone from autoclaved herring sperm DNA, and later detected in plant matrices such as coconut water, highlighting its occurrence in natural systems beyond synthetic origins (Yong et al., 2009; Gorincioi, 2010). Evidence from biochemical studies suggests that KR can also form in mammalian systems via oxidative chemistry: hydroxyl radical-induced deoxyribose oxidation generates furfural, which reacts with adenine/adenosine to yield N6-furfuryl adducts including kinetin and its riboside, supporting its characterization as a product of cellular oxidative metabolism and a potential “free radical sink” (Gorincioi, 2010). As a pharmacological entity, KR sits within the cytokinin riboside class, where the riboside and its phosphorylated triphosphate (KTP) function as ATP analogues/substrates for specific protein kinases, most notably PINK1, thereby enabling medicinal chemistry strategies around nucleotide prodrugs (e.g., monophosphate ProTides) to enhance intracellular delivery and activation (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018). Cytokinin ribosides have been explored historically as anti-proliferative agents and differentiation inducers in oncology, and more recently as modulators of mitochondrial quality control and neuroprotective pathways through PINK1 activation (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Lambourne et al., 2023; Voller et al., 2010).

Therapeutic History  
Cytokinins and their ribosides have a long history of investigation in dermatology and oncology, with kinetin demonstrating favorable skin tolerability and anti-photoaging benefits in clinical skin-care contexts, although these data pertain largely to kinetin base rather than KR (Fathy et al., 2022). KR and related ribosides have been extensively profiled as anticancer agents, exhibiting cell cycle modulation and pro-apoptotic activity in diverse tumor lines (e.g., HL-60, HeLa, B16F-10), often with relative sparing of normal fibroblasts at active concentrations, supporting a degree of tumor selectivity (Gorincioi, 2010; Voller et al., 2010). Reported in vivo and in vitro data indicate significant antiproliferative potency at low micromolar concentrations alongside dose-related toxicity (e.g., ~25 mg/kg toxicity in certain models), underscoring a narrow therapeutic index in oncology paradigms (Gorincioi, 2010). Beyond oncology, KR (and related cytokinins) have been investigated for neuroprotective and immunomodulatory effects, including improvement of splicing defects in familial dysautonomia and potential roles in neurodegenerative disease models, although much of the splicing literature historically focuses on kinetin base, and translational clarity for KR per se varies across reports (Fathy et al., 2022; Oshchepkov et al., 2020; Voller et al., 2017).

For PINK1 biology specifically, medicinal chemistry and cell biological studies demonstrate that KR and its phosphorylated metabolites activate PINK1 in mammalian and neuronal cells, positioning this chemotype as a pharmacological tool for augmenting mitophagy in diseases linked to mitochondrial dysfunction such as Parkinson’s disease; more potent KR analogs (e.g., MTK458) further validate this mechanism in cellular and animal models (Hertz et al., 2024; Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Lambourne et al., 2023). Prodrug strategies using kinetin riboside monophosphate (KMP) ProTides improve serum stability and intracellular delivery, yielding robust PINK1 activation in HEK293 cells, which is germane to drug design considerations for KR and derivatives (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018). To our knowledge, there are no published clinical or preclinical studies directly testing KR in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) patients or AMD animal models; however, the target pathway (PINK1/Parkin mitophagy) is mechanistically implicated in RPE degeneration in dry AMD, thus providing a strong rationale for repurposing (Datta et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Skeie et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
- PINK1/Parkin mitophagy axis and AMD relevance in RPE:  
  Upon loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), full-length PINK1 accumulates on the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM), where it phosphorylates both Parkin and ubiquitin to initiate Parkin-dependent mitophagy (Skeie et al., 2021). In RPE, PINK1 and Parkin form the core of a quality-control module that identifies and ubiquitinates dysfunctional mitochondria, recruiting autophagy machinery (p62/LC3) for organelle turnover; cumulative evidence supports that age and stress compromise this system in AMD, resulting in damaged mitochondria, elevated ROS, and RPE degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Skeie et al., 2021). Human and mouse RPE data show that PINK1 loss reduces activated phospho-Parkin (p-PRKN) and blunts mitophagic responses to depolarizing stimuli such as CCCP; conversely, in controls, CCCP elevates MAP1LC3B lipidation, validating PINK1 dependence for mitophagy activation in RPE (Datta et al., 2023). Early AMD human RPE exhibits decreased PINK1 in perifoveal regions, correlating with impaired mitophagy and providing a direct disease-context linkage between PINK1 deficiency and RPE dysfunction (Datta et al., 2023). Studies in AMD-relevant oxidative-stress mouse models (e.g., nfe2l2/pgc-1α−/−) indicate early activation of PINK1/Parkin signaling (e.g., increased Parkin colocalization with pS65 ubiquitin and accumulation of LC3B-positive autophagosomes) but suggest a downstream impairment in autolysosomal clearance, implying that upstream activation alone may not normalize flux under chronic stress (Gurubaran et al., 2020).

- KR → KTP conversion and direct PINK1 activation:  
  KR exerts its PINK1-activating effect primarily through metabolic conversion to kinetin riboside triphosphate (KTP), an ATP neo-substrate that binds PINK1 with higher affinity than ATP, thereby enhancing the kinase’s catalytic activity on relevant substrates (Georgakopoulos et al., 2017; Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018). Cellular enzymology supports that cytosolic nucleotide salvage and phosphoribosylation pathways enable the conversion of adenine derivatives (including kinetin) to triphosphate forms; APRT has been implicated in cytokinin biochemistry in mammalian systems and may contribute to the intracellular generation of KTP from kinetin precursors, though the precise enzymatic steps from KR to KTP in RPE require direct elucidation (Naseem et al., 2020). Pharmacological studies show that KR, KMP, and KTP activate PINK1 in mammalian and neuronal cells; KMP ProTides with various ester masks demonstrate serum stability and intracellular unmasking to yield active nucleotides, suggesting that glycosylation to the riboside and subsequent phosphorylation are key determinants of PINK1 activation (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Lambourne et al., 2023). Stabilized PINK1 then phosphorylates Parkin at serine 656 (as reported in the source text) and ubiquitin at serine 65, which accelerates Parkin recruitment and amplifies ubiquitin chain phosphorylation on OMM substrates, thereby seeding mitophagosome formation and progression (Lambourne et al., 2023). In cell systems, kinetin-derived activation of PINK1 is observed in the context of mitochondrial membrane depolarization and can be potentiated by mild, reversible uncoupling in some chemical series without overt mitochondrial toxicity when carefully tuned, underscoring a feasible pharmacological window (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018). Complementary small molecules (e.g., niclosamide, T0466/T0467, BC1464) act via PINK1 stabilization or degradation-pathway modulation, and USP30 inhibition further biases mitochondrial ubiquitination toward mitophagy, situating KR in a broader druggable landscape for PINK1-pathway enhancement (Masaldan et al., 2022).

- Convergence on RPE pathobiology:  
  Given that PINK1 expression and signaling are reduced in early AMD RPE, an agent that increases PINK1 catalytic activity and stabilizes PINK1 on damaged mitochondria could restore Parkin-dependent tagging and clearance of dysfunctional organelles, thereby lowering ROS loads and downstream RPE stress (Datta et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018). The RPE expresses and utilizes the PINK1/Parkin/LC3 autophagy machinery, as evidenced by immunochemical and functional data linking p-PRKN regulation, LC3B lipidation, and mitophagic flux to PINK1 state in mouse and human RPE systems (Datta et al., 2023). However, AMD models with oxidative stress show that autophagosome accumulation can occur without efficient clearance if lysosomal function is compromised; thus, any PINK1-activating therapy may need to be co-optimized with strategies that maintain autophagosome–lysosome fusion and lysosomal competence to realize net mitochondria turnover (Gurubaran et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
- In RPE assays:  
  KR should increase PINK1 activity upon mitochondrial depolarization or basal damage, resulting in higher levels of phospho-ubiquitin (pS65), increased Parkin recruitment to the OMM, augmented polyubiquitin decoration of OMM proteins (e.g., VDAC), enhanced LC3B-II accumulation, and increased formation of mitophagosomes and subsequent mitolysosomes, assuming lysosomal function is intact (Lambourne et al., 2023; Skeie et al., 2021). In PINK1-proficient RPE, a KR challenge following CCCP or physiological stressors is expected to recapitulate or potentiate the canonical PINK1/Parkin mitophagy cascade; notably, experiments in mouse RPE indicate that CCCP-induced elevation of LC3B lipidation is abrogated in pink1−/−, establishing a dependence of the autophagy readout on PINK1 that KR could rescue only if sufficient PINK1 is present (Datta et al., 2023). Given early AMD’s reduced PINK1 expression in the RPE perifovea, KR’s effect size may scale with residual PINK1 levels; the KTP–PINK1 interaction may partially compensate by enhancing the activity and dwell time of the remaining PINK1 on depolarized mitochondria, but absolute PINK1 scarcity could limit maximal response (Datta et al., 2023; Georgakopoulos et al., 2017). In AMD-like oxidative stress settings where the early mitophagy steps activate but autolysosomal clearance is impaired, KR is predicted to elevate upstream markers (pUb, Parkin localization, LC3B-II) yet may not fully normalize flux without restoring lysosomal function; this risk of autophagosome accumulation has been observed in AMD-model RPE, implying combination approaches (e.g., lysosome enhancers) may be required for optimal benefit (Gurubaran et al., 2020).

- In dry AMD disease biology:  
  By accelerating removal of dysfunctional mitochondria, KR is anticipated to reduce mitochondrial ROS and downstream oxidative damage, restoring bioenergetic homeostasis and decreasing RPE stress signals that contribute to drusen-associated pathology and cell death in dry AMD (Brooks et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018). Mechanistically, successful PINK1 activation should rebalance the population of healthy versus damaged mitochondria, mitigate chronic ROS-driven damage, and potentially stabilize RPE cellular functions (e.g., phagocytic capacity, lysosomal turnover of photoreceptor outer segments) that are compromised in AMD due to accumulation of dysfunctional organelles (Brooks et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018). Because the PINK1/Parkin axis is implicated in RPE degeneration and is downregulated in early AMD, targeted pharmacological enhancement of PINK1 represents a pathway-corrective approach aligned with disease mechanism, though it must be tested under AMD-relevant stressors that include both mitochondrial and lysosomal deficits (Datta et al., 2023; Gurubaran et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History—Safety, Toxicology, and Translational Considerations  
Nonclinical safety evaluations of kinetin (base) indicate a dose-dependent profile: low doses show favorable tolerability in skin applications and animal studies, whereas higher systemic doses (e.g., ≥1 mg/kg in rats) may perturb renal biomarkers, highlighting the need for careful exposure control; while this is not KR, it provides a class-level caution on dosing margins (Fathy et al., 2022; Othman et al., 2021). In mammalian cell systems, kinetin shows a concentration-dependent duality—sub-100 nM levels are cytoprotective against oxidative stress, while ≥500 nM can elicit cytotoxicity and genotoxicity—again reflecting the necessity of tight pharmacological windows in clinical development; KR shares pro-apoptotic properties at higher concentrations in tumor cells, indicating that exposure management will be critical to avoid off-target mitochondrial stress in non-malignant RPE (Gorincioi, 2010; Naseem et al., 2020). Tumor-selective cytotoxicity observed for KR (e.g., activation of caspase-3 following mitochondrial membrane disruption in HeLa and B16F-10) suggests that normal cells may be relatively resistant at appropriate concentrations, but translation to post-mitotic, metabolically active RPE requires dedicated therapeutic index definition (Gorincioi, 2010).

Pharmacokinetics for cytokinin ribosides present challenges, including short plasma half-life and potential limitations in barrier penetration; nevertheless, certain ribosides can achieve tissue exposure, and ProTide engineering of monophosphate forms has demonstrated improved serum stability and intracellular activation, offering a medicinal chemistry route to optimize ocular delivery and target engagement (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Voller et al., 2017). Importantly, the mitochondrial pharmacology dimension requires that PINK1 activation not rely on sustained pathological depolarization; prior work shows that PINK1 activation by certain KR-derived chemotypes can be coupled to reversible membrane effects without lasting mitochondrial injury, implying an achievable safety profile with rational chemistry and dosing (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018). Finally, the target pathway-level success with more potent PINK1 activators (e.g., MTK458) in cellular and animal models of Parkinson’s supports the druggability of this axis and suggests headroom to optimize KR analogs if KR itself proves insufficient in the RPE context (Hertz et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic alignment with AMD pathophysiology in RPE: Dry AMD features impaired mitophagy and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE, and early AMD shows decreased PINK1 expression and diminished mitophagy competence; KR directly activates PINK1, enhances Parkin recruitment via ubiquitin/PRKN phosphorylation, and augments mitophagy flux in mammalian and neuronal cells, providing a targeted correction to a disease-relevant defect (Datta et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Lambourne et al., 2023).  
- Direct enzymatic activation via KTP: KR’s biotransformation to KTP, an ATP neo-substrate with higher affinity for PINK1, offers a plausible biochemical mechanism to boost catalytic throughput even when PINK1 protein is partially reduced, thereby potentially amplifying residual PINK1 signaling in AMD RPE (Georgakopoulos et al., 2017; Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018).  
- Drug development precedent and tool compounds: Demonstrated PINK1 activation by KR, KMP/KTP, and related chemotypes, plus successful implementation of ProTide strategies and in vivo efficacy signals with potent analogs (e.g., MTK458), de-risk the pathway and provide a roadmap for medicinal chemistry and delivery optimization (Hertz et al., 2024; Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018).  
- Disease-biology congruence of pharmacodynamic readouts: RPE models have validated the dependency of CCCP-induced LC3B lipidation and p-PRKN formation on PINK1, while AMD-relevant models show upstream activation markers (pUb, Parkin colocalization) that are rate limited by downstream clearance—clear, quantifiable biomarkers exist to track KR engagement and flux restoration in RPE (Datta et al., 2023; Gurubaran et al., 2020).

Risks and Gaps  
- PINK1 insufficiency in early AMD: The perifoveal reduction of PINK1 in human RPE may limit the magnitude of KR-mediated activation; if PINK1 levels are below a critical threshold, KTP amplification alone might not suffice, necessitating combination with approaches that increase PINK1 expression/stability (e.g., BC1464) or that act downstream (e.g., USP30 inhibition to potentiate ubiquitin signaling) (Datta et al., 2023; Masaldan et al., 2022).  
- Lysosomal/autophagic clearance deficits: Oxidative stress models indicate initiation of PINK1/Parkin mitophagy with impaired autolysosomal clearance; KR may heighten early mitophagy steps without resolving terminal flux, risking autophagosome accumulation unless lysosomal function is co-restored (e.g., via agents that enhance autophagosome–lysosome fusion or lysosomal biogenesis) (Gurubaran et al., 2020).  
- Safety window and mitochondrial stress: KR exhibits pro-apoptotic, mitochondria-targeted cytotoxicity in tumor cells and cytotoxic/genotoxic effects at higher concentrations in non-tumor cells; precise dosing that achieves PINK1 activation without excessive mitochondrial depolarization or non-specific stress in RPE must be empirically determined (Gorincioi, 2010; Naseem et al., 2020).  
- PK and delivery barriers: Cytokinin ribosides generally have short half-lives and potential distribution limitations; ocular delivery (e.g., intravitreal, suprachoroidal, periocular) and ProTide/nanoparticulate strategies may be required to achieve durable RPE exposure while minimizing systemic exposure, an aspect not yet demonstrated for KR in the AMD setting (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Voller et al., 2017).  
- Lack of direct RPE/AMD in vivo efficacy data: While the mechanistic rationale is strong, KR has not been directly tested in RPE AMD models; translational viability will hinge on demonstrating improved mitophagy flux, decreased mitochondrial ROS, and RPE functional rescue in AMD-relevant models (Datta et al., 2023; Gurubaran et al., 2020).

Recommendation and Development Path  
Given the alignment between KR’s mechanism and the pathobiology of dry AMD in RPE, KR is a plausible repurposing candidate, but it should be advanced with a data-driven gating strategy that addresses target sufficiency, lysosomal function, safety window, and ocular delivery:  
- In vitro RPE assays (human primary or hPSC-derived) under AMD-relevant stress (e.g., photo-oxidative stress, lipofuscin/oxLDL exposure): test KR and KMP ProTides for dose–response effects on pUb (S65), p-PRKN, Parkin recruitment, LC3B lipidation, mitolysosome formation, mitochondrial turnover (mtDNA copy loss in mitolysosomes), and mitochondrial ROS/bioenergetics, benchmarking against CCCP controls and PINK1 knockdown/knockout lines (Datta et al., 2023; Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Skeie et al., 2021).  
- Lysosomal competence assays: co-assess autophagic flux with lysosomal pH and cathepsin activity; if KR increases early mitophagy markers without flux completion, evaluate combination with lysosome enhancers or TFEB agonists to restore throughput (Gurubaran et al., 2020).  
- PINK1 sufficiency and sensitization: quantify PINK1 levels in AMD-like conditions and test whether KR effects scale with PINK1 expression; consider combination with agents that stabilize PINK1 (e.g., BC1464) or increase mitochondrial ubiquitination via USP30 inhibition to offset low PINK1 (Datta et al., 2023; Masaldan et al., 2022).  
- Safety and therapeutic window in RPE: map KR exposure–response for PINK1 activation versus cytotoxicity/apoptosis, including concentrations that preserve RPE viability and mitochondrial membrane potential; incorporate off-target stress readouts (e.g., CHOP, ISR activation) (Gorincioi, 2010; Naseem et al., 2020).  
- Medicinal chemistry and delivery: prioritize KMP ProTides with favorable stability and reversible mitochondrial engagement to minimize off-target depolarization; assess ocular pharmacokinetics and RPE distribution in relevant species, given cytokinin riboside PK liabilities (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Voller et al., 2017).  
- In vivo models: test KR/ProTide in AMD-relevant models exhibiting RPE mitochondrial defects (e.g., NFE2L2/PGC-1α pathway disruption, photo-oxidative stress paradigms), with endpoints spanning RPE ultrastructure, mitochondrial turnover, oxidative markers, and functional readouts (ERG, RPE phagocytosis), while monitoring safety (renal/hepatic markers given systemic tox precedent) (Gurubaran et al., 2020; Othman et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Kinetin riboside is a mechanistically credible, pathway-directed candidate for dry AMD that targets a well-established deficit—PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy—in RPE, with robust supportive biology that PINK1 activation can be pharmacologically achieved by KR and its nucleotide metabolites to promote Parkin-dependent mitochondrial clearance (Datta et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Lambourne et al., 2023). The strengths include disease-relevant target engagement, availability of medicinal chemistry tactics (KMP ProTides) to address delivery and stability, and quantifiable pharmacodynamic markers in RPE that predict on-pathway efficacy (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Skeie et al., 2021). The principal risks are biological (insufficient PINK1 in early AMD and lysosomal flux defects that may cap benefit), pharmacological (narrow window between desired PINK1 activation and mitochondrial stress), and translational (PK/ocular delivery), none of which are insurmountable but all of which require rigorous preclinical validation in RPE-centric systems (Datta et al., 2023; Gurubaran et al., 2020; Naseem et al., 2020; Voller et al., 2017).

On balance, KR merits advancement to target-validation studies in human RPE models with concurrent optimization of ProTide prodrugs and combination strategies that secure lysosomal flux, with a clear go/no-go framework based on restoration of mitophagy flux and mitochondrial function without eliciting RPE toxicity (Gurubaran et al., 2020; Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018). If KR proves insufficient alone due to PINK1 insufficiency or PK constraints, more potent or targeted PINK1 activators (e.g., MTK458-class) and/or adjuncts that stabilize PINK1 or enhance downstream ubiquitin signaling may be prioritized, preserving the same mechanistic rationale for treating dry AMD via restoration of mitochondrial quality control in the RPE (Hertz et al., 2024; Masaldan et al., 2022).

Analysis: Candidate 1 (Nicotinamide riboside, ID: 10) and Candidate 2 (Resveratrol, ID: 48) both aim to mitigate oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells, central to dry AMD. NR has robust preclinical evidence showing NAD+ elevation in RPE models, activation of SIRT1/SIRT3 and PARP–mediated DNA repair, and protective effects in light-induced retinal injury models. It benefits from extensive clinical safety data in humans at doses up to 2 g/day, predictable oral bioavailability, and established transport into cells via nucleoside transporters. The key gaps for NR are limited direct studies in geographic atrophy models and ensuring consistent formulation stability, but its well-characterized PK/PD, favorable safety profile, and direct upstream mechanism of replenishing NAD+ make it highly translatable. Resveratrol has convincing in vitro and some animal data demonstrating activation of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis, enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis, and antioxidant enzyme induction, but suffers from poor aqueous solubility, rapid systemic metabolism, and sub-1% oral bioavailability. Its pharmacokinetic challenges necessitate advanced delivery platforms still in development, and clinical trials in AMD have been sparse or terminated. Safety at high doses is less certain, with potential off-target effects and GI toxicity. While resveratrol’s pleiotropic effects and anti-inflammatory properties are attractive, the translational barriers in formulation and dosing precision significantly weaken its near-term viability as a dry AMD therapy.
Reasoning: Between the two, Nicotinamide riboside (NR; ID: 10) presents stronger, more directly relevant preclinical evidence, a clear and upstream mechanism of action in NAD+ metabolism, an excellent safety and tolerability profile in humans, and a feasible oral dosing strategy with predictable tissue uptake. Resveratrol (ID: 48), despite mechanistic plausibility, is hampered by critical bioavailability and formulation challenges, a narrower therapeutic window, and limited clinical advancement in dry AMD. Therefore, NR offers a higher probability of successful experimental outcomes and translation into a viable therapy for dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring vitamin B3–class nucleoside and a leading NAD⁺ precursor that has been isolated from natural sources such as cow milk and other dietary materials, and is now produced by synthetic chemical means for therapeutic applications (Biță et al., 2023). NR belongs to the class of NAD⁺‐precursor nucleosides within the broader family of vitamin B3 compounds, the same family that includes nicotinic acid (NA) and nicotinamide (NAM), which historically have been used to prevent pellagra and improve cellular energy metabolism (Pîrvu et al., 2021; Biță et al., 2023). The synthetic production of NR involves the glycosylation of nicotinamide with appropriately protected ribofuranose donors via methods that require careful control due to the labile and reactive nature of its glycosidic bond, which often results in partial degradation during synthesis and storage (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). In order to overcome these issues, researchers have developed alternative stabilized forms such as NR borate, although the commercially available ChromaDex NR-100 is typically presented as the crystalline chloride salt (NRCl) and has become a benchmark for purity due to its improved manufacturing protocols and rigorous quality control (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Additionally, NR’s classification as an “orally bioavailable” NAD⁺ precursor distinguishes it from other precursors such as NMN by virtue of its ability to directly cross cell membranes without requiring extracellular conversion, with transport mediated by equilibrative nucleoside transporters (Mehmel et al., 2020; Biță et al., 2023). Taken together, these attributes place NR in a unique position as a repurposable compound with potential applications in metabolic, neurodegenerative, and now ocular diseases, including the dry forms of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) characterized by geographic atrophy (Biță et al., 2023; Braidy et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the use of vitamin B3 derivatives such as NA and NAM has been well established in both clinical and biochemical practice for the improvement of energy metabolism and for prevention of niacin deficiency diseases; however, nicotinamide riboside represents a more recently discovered alternative that offers superior pharmacokinetic profiles and fewer side effects such as flushing or liver toxicity (Braidy et al., 2019; Mehmel et al., 2020). Preclinical studies have shown that NR supplementation rapidly increases tissue and circulating NAD⁺ levels across a range of animal models, including mice and rats, where it has been tested for its effects on metabolic dysfunction, neurodegeneration, insulin sensitivity, and mitochondrial biogenesis (Biță et al., 2023). Numerous clinical trials have demonstrated the safety and oral bioavailability of NR in healthy human subjects and in populations with metabolic or neurodegenerative conditions; for example, chronic supplementation at doses up to 2 g/day has been well tolerated and has successfully elevated NAD⁺ in middle-aged and older adults (Mehmel et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023). In addition to these metabolic and neuroprotective applications, NR has been investigated in various models of inflammation, organ injury, and even in oncology-related situations, where its ability to modulate cellular stress responses has proven beneficial (Biță et al., 2023). Notably, while NR has undergone extensive research in contexts such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and peripheral neuropathy, its application in ocular diseases—particularly dry AMD characterized by geographic atrophy—has been less comprehensively studied; however, emerging evidence supports the notion that NAD⁺ decline in the retina and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) may be mitigated by NAD⁺ precursors, providing a rationale for repurposing NR for dry AMD (Braidy et al., 2019). Veterinary studies and animal models have also utilized NR to stimulate mitochondrial function and improve bioenergetics in tissues with high metabolic demands, further solidifying its profile as a potent NAD⁺ booster with broad potential therapeutic applications (Biță et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
NR exerts its biological effects via a well-defined metabolic pathway that begins with its cellular uptake through equilibrative nucleoside transporters (ENT1, ENT2, and ENT4) followed by phosphorylation by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRK1 and NRK2) in the cytosol, which convert NR to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) (Biță et al., 2023; Braidy et al., 2019). NMN is subsequently adenylated by nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferases (NMNATs) to generate NAD⁺, thereby replenishing the intracellular NAD⁺ pool that is essential for numerous metabolic and signaling processes (Mehmel et al., 2020). The elevation of NAD⁺ levels activates a host of NAD⁺-dependent enzymes including sirtuins (SIRT1, SIRT3, among others) and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs), which are critical for deacetylating mitochondrial proteins, enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis, and facilitating DNA repair processes both in the nucleus and mitochondria (Biță et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2016). Activation of SIRT3 in particular within the mitochondria leads to the deacetylation and activation of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2), thereby reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitigating oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020). Moreover, increased NAD⁺ availability supports the activity of PARP enzymes that are required for efficient DNA repair, including the repair of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) damage arising from oxidative stress (Cimaglia et al., 2020). In RPE cells, this mechanism is particularly relevant as the high-energy–demand environment and frequent exposure to light-induced oxidative stress make robust mitochondrial and genomic maintenance critical to cell survival and homeostasis (Zhang et al., 2020). Additionally, NR’s effect on boosting NAD⁺ may facilitate the activation of autophagy and mitophagy pathways, leading to the clearance of damaged cellular components and improved cellular renewal processes (Braidy et al., 2019; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023). Such biochemical actions converge to foster an enhanced cellular defense mechanism against oxidative damage, support mitochondrial function through improved repair and turnover, and ultimately promote cellular longevity (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023; Biță et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underpinning the repurposing of NR for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that supplementation with NR will lead to an elevation of intracellular NAD⁺ pools specifically within retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby enhancing mitochondrial DNA repair and upregulating antioxidant defenses that mitigate the oxidative damage implicated in geographic atrophy (Biță et al., 2023). In vitro studies using iPSC-derived RPE cells from AMD donors have demonstrated that NR supplementation results in rapid increases in intracellular NAD⁺, which is accompanied by the activation of sirtuin-mediated deacetylation of key mitochondrial proteins (Jadeja et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020). This deacetylation is believed to lead to improved mitochondrial function as evidenced by restored maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) measured via Seahorse XF assays, and the lowering of reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels as detected by fluorescent probes such as DCFDA (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016). The expected outcome in RPE is that the elevated NAD⁺ not only promotes the repair of oxidative damage to mitochondrial DNA but also augments the intrinsic antioxidant enzyme systems—including upregulation of enzymes like SOD2 and catalase—which collectively reduce the cellular oxidative burden (Biță et al., 2023). As a result, NR supplementation is anticipated to stabilize the RPE cell phenotype, reduce markers of cellular senescence and apoptosis, and potentially restore a healthier metabolic profile in RPE cells, factors that are critical for halting or even reversing the progression of geographic atrophy (Jadeja et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016). Moreover, by enhancing the NAD⁺-dependent activation of PARP and other DNA repair enzymes, NR may directly improve the repair of mitochondrial and nuclear DNA damage that accumulates under chronic oxidative stress conditions prevalent in the aging retina (Braidy et al., 2019; Mehmel et al., 2020). In preclinical models of retinal degeneration such as light-induced retinal injury, systemic administration of NR has been shown to preserve retinal morphology, reduce photoreceptor apoptosis, and maintain tissue NAD⁺ levels despite strong oxidative challenges, which supports the translational rationale for its application in dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2020; Braidy et al., 2019). Ultimately, the expected therapeutic effect of NR in the treatment of geographic atrophy is to provide cytoprotection to the RPE by mitigating oxidative damage and improving mitochondrial function, thus slowing the progression of RPE degeneration and vision loss (Zhu et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating NR (specifically the ChromaDex NR-100 formulation) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and promising attributes emerge alongside areas that warrant further investigation. One of the primary strengths of NR is its established reputation as a safe and orally bioavailable NAD⁺ precursor with extensive preclinical and clinical data supporting its ability to elevate NAD⁺ levels systemically and within specific target tissues (Mehmel et al., 2020). This property is particularly relevant for RPE cells because the high metabolic demands of the retina make efficient NAD⁺ replenishment crucial for maintaining mitochondrial function and for mediating effective DNA repair mechanisms (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Additionally, the robust mechanistic data showing that NR supplementation activates sirtuin pathways—most notably SIRT1 and SIRT3—and subsequently deacetylates and activates key mitochondrial and antioxidant enzymes provide a compelling molecular rationale for its potential to ameliorate oxidative stress in the RPE (Biță et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). The activation of these pathways not only enhances mitochondrial bioenergetics but also promotes the clearance of damaged cellular components through autophagy, which is expected to contribute to improved cell survival under oxidative challenge (Braidy et al., 2019; Jadeja et al., 2020).  
However, there are some weaknesses and critical gaps in the current data when it comes to translating these beneficial effects specifically to the context of geographic atrophy in dry AMD. Although preclinical models have demonstrated the protective effects of NR in retinal degeneration (particularly in light-induced injury models), direct evidence demonstrating that NR selectively elevates NAD⁺ pools in RPE cells derived from AMD patients, enhances mitochondrial DNA repair specifically in RPE, and reduces ROS levels to a degree that meaningfully impacts the progression of geographic atrophy remains limited (Braidy et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020). Furthermore, the chemical reactivity and inherent instability of NR have historically posed challenges to its synthesis, storage, and consistent formulation, raising concerns about batch-to-batch variability and the possibility of degradation products in commercial formulations; although recent advances and improved production standards appear to have mitigated these issues, further analytical validation is needed to ensure that the NR-100 formulation consistently meets high purity criteria (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Another consideration is that while the mechanisms underlying NR’s beneficial effects are well established in metabolic and neurodegenerative contexts, the unique metabolic and microenvironmental characteristics of the RPE in the aging eye—including the contributions of the local immune system, extracellular matrix alterations, and the interplay with the choroidal circulation—may represent additional variables that could influence NR’s efficacy in dry AMD, and these factors are not yet fully delineated (Biță et al., 2023; Cimaglia et al., 2020).  
From a clinical development perspective, the fact that NR has already been evaluated in multiple Phase I/II clinical trials for other indications, and has demonstrated an excellent safety profile even at high doses, is a significant advantage that could accelerate its repurposing for ocular applications; careful dose-ranging studies focused on ocular bioavailability and pharmacodynamics in the context of AMD will be critical (Mehmel et al., 2020; Biță et al., 2023). Additionally, mechanistic endpoints such as NAD⁺ elevation, sirtuin activation, and improvements in mitochondrial function have been validated in other tissues and could be adapted to RPE-specific assays, including measurements of oxygen consumption rate (OCR), mitochondrial membrane potential, ROS quantification, and biomarkers of DNA repair (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016; Braidy et al., 2019). Resveratrol is a naturally occurring polyphenolic compound belonging to the stilbene class and is structurally defined as 3,5,4′-trihydroxystilbene. A considerable volume of biochemical, preclinical, and early clinical literature has explored resveratrol’s broad spectrum of activities. Historically, resveratrol has been investigated primarily for its cardioprotective and neuroprotective effects, as well as its anti-aging properties. The cumulative evidence from preclinical studies strongly supports the potential of resveratrol as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, especially considering its capacity to modulate mitochondrial function and activate intrinsic antioxidant defenses. Such a narrow therapeutic window necessitates a precise optimization of dosing regimens and formulation strategies. Numerous in vitro studies have characterized the effect of resveratrol on retinal pigment epithelial cells, notably ARPE-19 cell lines, under conditions of oxidative stress. These findings are reinforced by experiments showing that resveratrol can mitigate blue light-induced retinal damage and preserve cell viability, further supporting its relevance in ocular pathologies where light-induced oxidative stress is a contributing factor (Bel, 2020).
