Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring vitamin B3–class nucleoside and a leading NAD⁺ precursor that has been isolated from natural sources such as cow milk and other dietary materials, and is now produced by synthetic chemical means for therapeutic applications (Biță et al., 2023). NR belongs to the class of NAD⁺‐precursor nucleosides within the broader family of vitamin B3 compounds, the same family that includes nicotinic acid (NA) and nicotinamide (NAM), which historically have been used to prevent pellagra and improve cellular energy metabolism (Pîrvu et al., 2021; Biță et al., 2023). The synthetic production of NR involves the glycosylation of nicotinamide with appropriately protected ribofuranose donors via methods that require careful control due to the labile and reactive nature of its glycosidic bond, which often results in partial degradation during synthesis and storage (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). In order to overcome these issues, researchers have developed alternative stabilized forms such as NR borate, although the commercially available ChromaDex NR-100 is typically presented as the crystalline chloride salt (NRCl) and has become a benchmark for purity due to its improved manufacturing protocols and rigorous quality control (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Additionally, NR’s classification as an “orally bioavailable” NAD⁺ precursor distinguishes it from other precursors such as NMN by virtue of its ability to directly cross cell membranes without requiring extracellular conversion, with transport mediated by equilibrative nucleoside transporters (Mehmel et al., 2020; Biță et al., 2023). Taken together, these attributes place NR in a unique position as a repurposable compound with potential applications in metabolic, neurodegenerative, and now ocular diseases, including the dry forms of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) characterized by geographic atrophy (Biță et al., 2023; Braidy et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the use of vitamin B3 derivatives such as NA and NAM has been well established in both clinical and biochemical practice for the improvement of energy metabolism and for prevention of niacin deficiency diseases; however, nicotinamide riboside represents a more recently discovered alternative that offers superior pharmacokinetic profiles and fewer side effects such as flushing or liver toxicity (Braidy et al., 2019; Mehmel et al., 2020). Preclinical studies have shown that NR supplementation rapidly increases tissue and circulating NAD⁺ levels across a range of animal models, including mice and rats, where it has been tested for its effects on metabolic dysfunction, neurodegeneration, insulin sensitivity, and mitochondrial biogenesis (Biță et al., 2023). Numerous clinical trials have demonstrated the safety and oral bioavailability of NR in healthy human subjects and in populations with metabolic or neurodegenerative conditions; for example, chronic supplementation at doses up to 2 g/day has been well tolerated and has successfully elevated NAD⁺ in middle-aged and older adults (Mehmel et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023). In addition to these metabolic and neuroprotective applications, NR has been investigated in various models of inflammation, organ injury, and even in oncology-related situations, where its ability to modulate cellular stress responses has proven beneficial (Biță et al., 2023). Notably, while NR has undergone extensive research in contexts such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and peripheral neuropathy, its application in ocular diseases—particularly dry AMD characterized by geographic atrophy—has been less comprehensively studied; however, emerging evidence supports the notion that NAD⁺ decline in the retina and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) may be mitigated by NAD⁺ precursors, providing a rationale for repurposing NR for dry AMD (Braidy et al., 2019). Veterinary studies and animal models have also utilized NR to stimulate mitochondrial function and improve bioenergetics in tissues with high metabolic demands, further solidifying its profile as a potent NAD⁺ booster with broad potential therapeutic applications (Biță et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
NR exerts its biological effects via a well-defined metabolic pathway that begins with its cellular uptake through equilibrative nucleoside transporters (ENT1, ENT2, and ENT4) followed by phosphorylation by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRK1 and NRK2) in the cytosol, which convert NR to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) (Biță et al., 2023; Braidy et al., 2019). NMN is subsequently adenylated by nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferases (NMNATs) to generate NAD⁺, thereby replenishing the intracellular NAD⁺ pool that is essential for numerous metabolic and signaling processes (Mehmel et al., 2020). The elevation of NAD⁺ levels activates a host of NAD⁺-dependent enzymes including sirtuins (SIRT1, SIRT3, among others) and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs), which are critical for deacetylating mitochondrial proteins, enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis, and facilitating DNA repair processes both in the nucleus and mitochondria (Biță et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2016). Activation of SIRT3 in particular within the mitochondria leads to the deacetylation and activation of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2), thereby reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitigating oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020). Moreover, increased NAD⁺ availability supports the activity of PARP enzymes that are required for efficient DNA repair, including the repair of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) damage arising from oxidative stress (Cimaglia et al., 2020). In RPE cells, this mechanism is particularly relevant as the high-energy–demand environment and frequent exposure to light-induced oxidative stress make robust mitochondrial and genomic maintenance critical to cell survival and homeostasis (Zhang et al., 2020). Additionally, NR’s effect on boosting NAD⁺ may facilitate the activation of autophagy and mitophagy pathways, leading to the clearance of damaged cellular components and improved cellular renewal processes (Braidy et al., 2019; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023). Such biochemical actions converge to foster an enhanced cellular defense mechanism against oxidative damage, support mitochondrial function through improved repair and turnover, and ultimately promote cellular longevity (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023; Biță et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underpinning the repurposing of NR for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that supplementation with NR will lead to an elevation of intracellular NAD⁺ pools specifically within retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby enhancing mitochondrial DNA repair and upregulating antioxidant defenses that mitigate the oxidative damage implicated in geographic atrophy (Biță et al., 2023). In vitro studies using iPSC-derived RPE cells from AMD donors have demonstrated that NR supplementation results in rapid increases in intracellular NAD⁺, which is accompanied by the activation of sirtuin-mediated deacetylation of key mitochondrial proteins (Jadeja et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020). This deacetylation is believed to lead to improved mitochondrial function as evidenced by restored maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) measured via Seahorse XF assays, and the lowering of reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels as detected by fluorescent probes such as DCFDA (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016). The expected outcome in RPE is that the elevated NAD⁺ not only promotes the repair of oxidative damage to mitochondrial DNA but also augments the intrinsic antioxidant enzyme systems—including upregulation of enzymes like SOD2 and catalase—which collectively reduce the cellular oxidative burden (Biță et al., 2023). As a result, NR supplementation is anticipated to stabilize the RPE cell phenotype, reduce markers of cellular senescence and apoptosis, and potentially restore a healthier metabolic profile in RPE cells, factors that are critical for halting or even reversing the progression of geographic atrophy (Jadeja et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016). Moreover, by enhancing the NAD⁺-dependent activation of PARP and other DNA repair enzymes, NR may directly improve the repair of mitochondrial and nuclear DNA damage that accumulates under chronic oxidative stress conditions prevalent in the aging retina (Braidy et al., 2019; Mehmel et al., 2020). In preclinical models of retinal degeneration such as light-induced retinal injury, systemic administration of NR has been shown to preserve retinal morphology, reduce photoreceptor apoptosis, and maintain tissue NAD⁺ levels despite strong oxidative challenges, which supports the translational rationale for its application in dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2020; Braidy et al., 2019). Ultimately, the expected therapeutic effect of NR in the treatment of geographic atrophy is to provide cytoprotection to the RPE by mitigating oxidative damage and improving mitochondrial function, thus slowing the progression of RPE degeneration and vision loss (Zhu et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating NR (specifically the ChromaDex NR-100 formulation) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and promising attributes emerge alongside areas that warrant further investigation. One of the primary strengths of NR is its established reputation as a safe and orally bioavailable NAD⁺ precursor with extensive preclinical and clinical data supporting its ability to elevate NAD⁺ levels systemically and within specific target tissues (Mehmel et al., 2020). This property is particularly relevant for RPE cells because the high metabolic demands of the retina make efficient NAD⁺ replenishment crucial for maintaining mitochondrial function and for mediating effective DNA repair mechanisms (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Additionally, the robust mechanistic data showing that NR supplementation activates sirtuin pathways—most notably SIRT1 and SIRT3—and subsequently deacetylates and activates key mitochondrial and antioxidant enzymes provide a compelling molecular rationale for its potential to ameliorate oxidative stress in the RPE (Biță et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). The activation of these pathways not only enhances mitochondrial bioenergetics but also promotes the clearance of damaged cellular components through autophagy, which is expected to contribute to improved cell survival under oxidative challenge (Braidy et al., 2019; Jadeja et al., 2020).  
However, there are some weaknesses and critical gaps in the current data when it comes to translating these beneficial effects specifically to the context of geographic atrophy in dry AMD. Although preclinical models have demonstrated the protective effects of NR in retinal degeneration (particularly in light-induced injury models), direct evidence demonstrating that NR selectively elevates NAD⁺ pools in RPE cells derived from AMD patients, enhances mitochondrial DNA repair specifically in RPE, and reduces ROS levels to a degree that meaningfully impacts the progression of geographic atrophy remains limited (Braidy et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020). Furthermore, the chemical reactivity and inherent instability of NR have historically posed challenges to its synthesis, storage, and consistent formulation, raising concerns about batch-to-batch variability and the possibility of degradation products in commercial formulations; although recent advances and improved production standards appear to have mitigated these issues, further analytical validation is needed to ensure that the NR-100 formulation consistently meets high purity criteria (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Another consideration is that while the mechanisms underlying NR’s beneficial effects are well established in metabolic and neurodegenerative contexts, the unique metabolic and microenvironmental characteristics of the RPE in the aging eye—including the contributions of the local immune system, extracellular matrix alterations, and the interplay with the choroidal circulation—may represent additional variables that could influence NR’s efficacy in dry AMD, and these factors are not yet fully delineated (Biță et al., 2023; Cimaglia et al., 2020).  
From a clinical development perspective, the fact that NR has already been evaluated in multiple Phase I/II clinical trials for other indications, and has demonstrated an excellent safety profile even at high doses, is a significant advantage that could accelerate its repurposing for ocular applications; careful dose-ranging studies focused on ocular bioavailability and pharmacodynamics in the context of AMD will be critical (Mehmel et al., 2020; Biță et al., 2023). Additionally, mechanistic endpoints such as NAD⁺ elevation, sirtuin activation, and improvements in mitochondrial function have been validated in other tissues and could be adapted to RPE-specific assays, including measurements of oxygen consumption rate (OCR), mitochondrial membrane potential, ROS quantification, and biomarkers of DNA repair (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016; Braidy et al., 2019). Moreover, early translational studies using iPSC-derived RPE from AMD donors have already begun to show that NR can reduce oxidative stress and restore metabolic function in these cells, lending credibility to its potential efficacy in geographic atrophy settings (Biță et al., 2023; Braidy et al., 2019).  
In summary, NR (ChromaDex NR-100) emerges as a highly promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD on the basis of its well-established ability to raise NAD⁺, activate sirtuin-mediated mitochondrial maintenance and DNA repair processes, and mitigate oxidative stress—all of which are central drivers of RPE degeneration in geographic atrophy (Zhang et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016). The strengths of this candidate include a robust mechanistic foundation, a favorable safety and pharmacokinetic profile established in other clinical contexts, and encouraging preclinical data that indirectly support its potential benefit in the retina (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020; Braidy et al., 2019). Nonetheless, significant challenges remain, particularly the need for direct evidence in RPE-specific and geographic atrophy models, confirmation of consistent formulation quality due to NR’s chemical instability, and the potential variability in tissue-specific uptake and metabolism in an aging ocular environment (Mehmel et al., 2020; Biță et al., 2023). Future studies should therefore focus on comprehensive in vitro investigations in primary and iPSC-derived RPE cells, detailed pharmacodynamic assessments in animal models of dry AMD, and ultimately carefully designed early-phase clinical trials targeting RPE function and retinal structure in patient populations with geographic atrophy (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016; Braidy et al., 2019).  
Overall, while there is a compelling mechanistic rationale and a solid foundation of preclinical and clinical data supporting the repurposing of NR for dry AMD, particularly in mitigating oxidative damage, enhancing mitochondrial DNA repair, and improving antioxidant defenses in RPE cells, further targeted research is required to validate these effects specifically in the context of geographic atrophy. The available literature suggests that NR has significant translational promise, and its favorable safety profile alongside extensive clinical experience in other indications positions it as a frontrunner among NAD⁺ precursors for potential therapeutic intervention in dry AMD (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). The next phase of research should therefore include detailed mechanistic studies in ocular models, combined with rigorous clinical endpoint evaluations to determine whether NR supplementation can effectively slow or reverse the degenerative processes underlying geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016; Jadeja et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) is a synthetic derivative of fumaric acid that belongs to the class of fumaric acid esters (FAEs) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Chemically, DMF is the dimethyl ester of fumaric acid, with a molecular weight of approximately 144.13 g/mol, and is produced by reacting fumaric acid with methanol in the presence of a strong acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Although fumaric acid occurs naturally as an intermediate in the citric acid cycle, DMF itself is fully synthetically manufactured, conferring the advantages of chemical stability and the ability to precisely modulate its structure to enhance pharmacological properties (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Moreover, DMF is classified as an electrophilic molecule that, due to its α,β-unsaturated ester structure, can covalently modify protein thiols, particularly the cysteine residues within KEAP1, thereby initiating its downstream effects on cellular redox homeostasis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Fumaric acid esters as a class have a long-standing history in pharmacotherapy, originally finding application in dermatology, most notably in the treatment of psoriasis, and have since been repurposed for neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis (MS) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, fumaric acid esters were introduced into clinical practice as antipsoriatic agents in Europe, with formulations such as Fumaderm® entering the market in the 1990s (Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). DMF in particular emerged as a key component in these formulations, and its efficacy in modulating immune responses and suppressing inflammation in skin diseases laid the foundation for its later repurposing in other systemic inflammatory conditions (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Over time, DMF was repurposed and further developed as an oral agent for the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), culminating in its FDA approval in 2013 under the trade name Tecfidera® by Biogen (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163). Clinical trials, including large-scale phase 3 studies, have demonstrated its favorable safety profile and efficacy in reducing relapse rates and slowing disability progression in MS patients (Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 14–16). Although there is no extensive historical record of DMF being used directly for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other primary ocular diseases, recent preclinical findings have indicated that its potent activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway may confer significant protective effects on the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This has sparked considerable interest in repurposing DMF for ocular indications such as geographic atrophy, a late stage of dry AMD, by leveraging its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities observed in nonocular settings (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, DMF functions primarily as a prodrug; upon oral administration it is rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases within the gastrointestinal tract to yield its active metabolite, monomethyl fumarate (MMF) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). The pharmacodynamic actions of DMF principally involve the electrophilic modification of specific cysteine residues—most notably cysteine 151—on Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Under physiological conditions, KEAP1 binds to and retains the transcription factor Nrf2 in the cytoplasm, targeting it for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. However, when DMF covalently modifies KEAP1, it disrupts this complex, allowing Nrf2 to dissociate and translocate into the nucleus (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). In the nucleus, Nrf2 binds to antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoters of numerous genes encoding cytoprotective enzymes, including glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), and various enzymes involved in glutathione (GSH) synthesis and regeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). These molecular interactions lead to enhanced antioxidant defenses, improved detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and overall better maintenance of cellular redox balance (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). In addition to its role in promoting antioxidant gene expression via Nrf2 activation, DMF has been shown to have immunomodulatory properties; it can shift cytokine profiles by increasing interleukin-4 (IL-4)–expressing CD4+ T cells and decreasing the production of proinflammatory cytokines such as interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and interleukin-17 (IL-17) (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Furthermore, DMF has been reported to inhibit nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation in certain cellular contexts, thus contributing to a reduction in inflammatory signaling independently of Nrf2 (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Together, these molecular actions result in lowered cellular oxidative stress and an improved inflammatory milieu, which are critical factors implicated in the pathogenesis of chronic degenerative diseases (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry AMD, particularly the geographic atrophy form, is characterized by the gradual degeneration of RPE cells, which leads to subsequent photoreceptor loss and irreversible vision impairment. Central to the pathophysiology of dry AMD are oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation that progressively compromise RPE viability and function (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). The hypothesis being explored is that DMF, through its robust activation of the Nrf2 pathway, can enhance the expression of ARE-driven genes that encode for antioxidant and cytoprotective proteins, thereby counteracting the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in the RPE (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 13–14). In particular, the upregulation of enzymes involved in glutathione synthesis is expected to increase intracellular levels of GSH, a critical thiol antioxidant that protects mitochondrial membranes and supports cellular bioenergetics (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Preclinical studies in retinal models have demonstrated that DMF can effectively preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and reduce the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β), both of which are hallmarks of RPE distress under oxidative challenge (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Given that the RPE is highly metabolically active and particularly vulnerable to cumulative oxidative damage, the sustained activation of Nrf2 by DMF following oral dosing is anticipated to provide continuous reinforcement of antioxidant defenses and maintain mitochondrial integrity in these cells (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 3–5; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). Moreover, by mitigating inflammatory signaling, DMF may not only protect the RPE but also contribute to a more favorable microenvironment that limits the propagation of cell death signals, thus potentially slowing the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Collectively, these expected cellular effects support the rationale for using DMF as an intervention to preserve retinal structure and function by lowering oxidative damage and supporting bioenergetics in the RPE.

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential of dimethyl fumarate as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD rests on a solid mechanistic rationale combined with an established clinical pedigree in other indications. One of the primary strengths of DMF is its well-characterized pharmacological profile; it is FDA-approved for multiple sclerosis and has been safely administered to thousands of patients over several years, which significantly mitigates the risk and regulatory hurdles typically associated with repurposed drugs (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). The dual actions of DMF—in particular, its ability to both activate the Nrf2 pathway and attenuate proinflammatory signals—directly target the underlying pathological processes in dry AMD, where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central drivers of RPE degeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In vitro studies have provided encouraging evidence that DMF increases intracellular glutathione levels and protects RPE cells from oxidative insults, findings that are directly translatable to the pathobiology of dry AMD (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Nonetheless, several challenges remain. Although DMF is known to be effective in MS and psoriasis, the ocular milieu presents unique pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic challenges that may not be fully addressed by the current oral formulations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18). The rapid hydrolysis of DMF to MMF means that, while the active metabolite does exert therapeutic effects, fine-tuning the dosing regimen to ensure adequate drug levels in the retina while minimizing systemic side effects is necessary (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). In addition, common adverse reactions associated with DMF, such as gastrointestinal discomfort and flushing, though generally mild to moderate, could be more problematic in the typically elderly dry AMD population, necessitating careful monitoring and potentially modified dosing strategies (Camelo, 2025, p. 17; Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13). There is also the question of whether systemic administration of DMF can generate sufficient concentrations in the retina to achieve a meaningful therapeutic effect. While emerging evidence suggests that DMF can cross the blood-retinal barrier and activate Nrf2 in retinal cells (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3), further pharmacokinetic and translational studies are warranted to confirm its retinal bioavailability and the optimal dosing regimen for ocular indications.

Another consideration is the complexity of dry AMD itself, which is a slowly progressive, multifactorial disease with contributions from genetic predispositions, environmental exposures, and systemic metabolic disturbances. It remains to be seen whether the monotherapeutic approach of DMF, targeting primarily oxidative stress via Nrf2 activation, will be sufficient to halt or reverse disease progression, or whether combination therapies will ultimately be required (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Furthermore, while the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms of DMF are well supported by in vitro data and animal studies, there is still limited clinical data on its efficacy in ocular disease settings. Early-phase clinical trials aimed at evaluating DMF in geographic atrophy have to rigorously assess both structural outcomes (e.g., changes in the area of atrophy) and functional endpoints (e.g., visual acuity, retinal sensitivity) to establish its therapeutic benefit in dry AMD (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Despite these limitations, the strengths of DMF are compelling. The drug’s ability to upregulate a broad spectrum of cytoprotective genes via the Nrf2 pathway makes it a versatile candidate for mitigating the oxidative and inflammatory stress that drives RPE degeneration. The fact that DMF has already cleared extensive regulatory and clinical safety evaluations in nonocular indications is a significant advantage, as it greatly accelerates the translational pathway compared to a novel chemical entity (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Additionally, the repurposing of an already approved drug leverages existing manufacturing, formulation, and distribution infrastructure, favorably impacting the cost and timeline associated with drug development (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

In summary, the comprehensive literature review supports the potential of DMF to serve as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its mechanism of action—centered on Nrf2 activation leading to enhanced antioxidant capacity along with anti-inflammatory effects—directly addresses the key pathophysiological mechanisms implicated in dry AMD. The extensive clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis provides a reliable safety and tolerability framework, which is crucial for rapid repositioning into a new clinical area such as geographic atrophy (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). However, it is essential to conduct targeted preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials specifically in ocular disease models to optimize dosing, confirm retinal delivery, and demonstrate clinical efficacy before advancing to larger randomized controlled trials (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Overall, while challenges remain regarding optimal application in the retinal context and potential side effects in an older patient population, DMF—by virtue of its dual antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms and robust clinical background—stands as a viable candidate that merits further investigation for the treatment of dry AMD.

Given the current evidence, the following recommendations are proposed for advancing DMF as a candidate for dry AMD:  

1. Conduct detailed pharmacokinetic studies in animal models to assess the retinal bioavailability of DMF and its active metabolite MMF following systemic administration. This should include studies comparing different dosing schedules and formulations to optimize retinal exposure without exacerbating systemic adverse effects (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2).  

2. Develop and validate preclinical models of dry AMD that recapitulate the key features of human geographic atrophy, with a focus on evaluating the efficacy of DMF in protecting RPE cells against oxidative stress and preserving mitochondrial function (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

3. Investigate the potential benefits of combining DMF with other therapeutic agents that target complementary pathways in dry AMD. For example, agents that modulate complement activation or improve choroidal blood flow may synergize with the Nrf2-mediated antioxidant mechanism of DMF (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).  

4. Initiate early-phase clinical trials in patients with geographic atrophy to establish proof of concept. These studies should include robust biomarker assessments (e.g., measurement of ARE gene expression, retinal imaging for atrophy progression, and functional visual outcomes) to correlate molecular effects with clinical benefit (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

5. Carefully monitor the safety profile of DMF in the elderly population, as the incidence of gastrointestinal side effects and lymphopenia may differ compared to the population with MS. Consider the feasibility of modified-release formulations or alternative routes of administration (e.g., topical ocular delivery) to minimize systemic side effects while maximizing retinal drug concentrations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18).

Overall, the repurposing of dimethyl fumarate for dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a robust mechanistic framework and a significant body of preclinical and clinical data generated in other indications. Its capacity to activate the Nrf2 pathway, enhance mitochondrial glutathione synthesis, and modulate inflammatory responses in RPE cells directly addresses several pivotal aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). While there are challenges regarding optimal retinal delivery and management of systemic adverse effects, the clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis lends considerable support to its translational potential. Consequently, dimethyl fumarate represents a well‐justified and attractive therapeutic candidate for further exploration in the treatment of dry AMD, warranting additional preclinical optimization and clinical investigation to fully define its role in preserving visual function in patients affected by this progressive degenerative disease (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
BGP-15 is a synthetic, small-molecule nicotinic amidoxime/hydroxylamine derivative whose full chemical name is O-(3-piperidino-2-hydroxy-1-propyl) nicotinic amidoxime, typically used as a dihydrochloride salt; it was developed by N-Gene (US/Hungary) and has been described as water-soluble and mitochondria-targeting in preclinical studies (including ocular applications) (Takács et al., 2024; Horváth et al., 2021). Chemically and pharmacologically, BGP-15 belongs to the hydroximic/hydroxylamine acid derivative family originally advanced as membrane-interacting heat-shock response (HSR) co-inducers that remodel cholesterol-enriched plasma membrane rafts, with pleiotropic, cytoprotective effects in stressed tissues (membrane-lipid therapy) (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011). In parallel, the compound has been positioned as a nicotinamide-related, non-carboxamide “NAM analogue” with in vitro mixed-type (noncompetitive) PARP-1 inhibition, though the authors emphasize that in vivo protective effects likely involve additional mechanisms beyond direct PARP blockade because the in vitro inhibitory concentration exceeds achievable systemic levels (Crul et al., 2013). Independent biophysical and cellular studies show BGP-15 partitions into membranes, increases the fluidity of negatively charged lipid species, preserves heat-challenged raft integrity, and activates stress signaling linked to HSP induction; imaging and molecular dynamics support a direct membrane-interacting mode of action (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

Functionally, BGP-15 is best classified as a multifunctional HSP co-inducer and insulin-sensitizing, mitochondria-targeting cytoprotective agent that remodels membrane rafts, enhances the HSF1–HSP axis, and modulates stress and survival signaling (Akt up, JNK/p38 down), while lowering mitochondrial ROS and stabilizing Δψm; importantly, it preferentially acts in stressed cells, an attribute that underpins its safety rationale (Gombos et al., 2011; Sumegi et al., 2017). The compound concentrates in energized mitochondria driven by its delocalized positive charge, with >85–90% uptake into isolated mitochondria under experimental conditions (Sümegi, 2018). Mitochondrial studies consistently localize the dominant ROS-lowering effect to the respiratory chain at complexes I and III, with minimal direct antioxidant chemistry, and only mild uncoupling at millimolar concentrations that is irrelevant at the micromolar doses used in most cell studies (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018).

Crucial nomenclature caveat: a distinct “BGP-15” reported by a different group denotes a calcipotriene-derived vitamin D3 analog with anticancer activity; this vitamin D3 analog is mechanistically and structurally unrelated to the nicotinic amidoxime HSP co-inducer described above (both were labeled “BGP-15” by their respective originators) (Sintov et al., 2013). For the current program, the candidate of interest is the nicotinic amidoxime/hydroxylamine HSP co-inducer (often supplied by N-Gene or commercial chemical vendors under the amidoxime name), not the vitamin D3 analog (Takács et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
BGP-15 and closely related hydroximic/hydroxylamine acid derivatives have an extensive preclinical history across cardiac, neural, hepatic, renal, skeletal muscle, pulmonary, and metabolic models, with multiple mechanistic readouts converging on membrane remodeling, HSR/HSP co-induction, MAPK and Akt pathway modulation, and mitochondrial protection (Sumegi et al., 2017). Cardiovascular protection has been reported in ischemia–reperfusion, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation, with actions that include reduced ROS, preserved mitochondrial function, and Akt activation with suppression of JNK/p38 (Sumegi et al., 2017). In spontaneously hypertensive rats, BGP-15 increased PGC-1α and mitochondrial mass, decreased interstitial fibrosis, increased MKP-1 and reduced p38/JNK phosphorylation, and activated Akt/GSK-3β signaling (Horváth et al., 2021). BGP-15 prevented imatinib cardiotoxicity, protected against cisplatin nephrotoxicity without impairing antitumor efficacy, and mitigated cisplatin/taxol peripheral neuropathy (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). Hepatoprotection against acetaminophen injury via inhibition of caspase-independent cell death has also been documented (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). In pulmonary arterial hypertension and severe muscular dystrophy models, BGP-15 preserved mitochondrial structure and function and slowed disease progression; mechanistically, mitochondrial fusion via OPA1 activation and Akt signaling were implicated (Szabó et al., 2018).

Neuroprotection and mitochondrial rescue have been demonstrated in vitro and in vivo, including reduced neuronal death and improved mitochondrial potential/ROS at axonal branch points, coupled to HSP72 elevation, reduced phospho-JNK/p38, and enhanced Akt/IGF1R signaling (Ohlen et al., 2017). Consistent with its membrane-raft mechanism, BGP-15 increased HSP expression during heat challenge and remodeled cholesterol-rich platforms that gate stress signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

In ophthalmology, BGP-15 has been applied in multiple retinal disease contexts. It was reported retinoprotective in Goto–Kakizaki rats (type 2 diabetes) with functional preservation on ERG, and later shown to improve survival and retinal function long-term in ZDF rats under uncontrolled diabetes, with increased ocular HSP70 and decreased NFκB (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021). Topical ocular delivery using an SBECD-containing eyedrop improved scotopic/photopic a- and b-waves, restored oscillatory potentials, shortened implicit times, and preserved retinal thickness following global ischemia–reperfusion injury in rats (Takács et al., 2024). These ocular data align with the compound’s mitochondrial and HSP co-inducer mechanisms: accumulation in mitochondria, protection against apoptosis/necrosis in oxidative-stress paradigms, and modulation of stress signaling (Takács et al., 2024).

Clinically, BGP-15 has a proof-of-concept randomized, double-blind trial demonstrating dose-dependent improvement of insulin sensitivity in insulin-resistant patients without apparent short-term toxicity; in parallel, human phase II work in olanzapine-induced metabolic disorder also identified BGP-15 as an insulin sensitizer (Crul et al., 2013; Sümegi, 2018). Safety signals from early human studies and the pharmacology of HSP co-inducers (preferential action in stressed cells) support the translational risk profile; however, systemic serum concentrations reported by the developer are low (≤25 nmol/mL), which has implications for target engagement and favors local ocular delivery for retinal indications (Gombos et al., 2011; Sumegi et al., 2017).

To our knowledge based on the supplied corpus, BGP-15 has not been directly tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) patients or canonical dry AMD animal models; however, its retinoprotective efficacy in diabetic retinopathy models and retinal ischemia–reperfusion suggests relevance to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)/photoreceptor stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammation, which are central to dry AMD biology (Takács et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Membrane-lipid therapy and HSP co-induction. BGP-15 partitions into and remodels membrane lipid domains, particularly cholesterol-rich plasma membrane rafts that organize stress sensing and signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). Under heat stress or analogous perturbations, BGP-15 preserves raft integrity and elevates HSP expression; this is associated with activation of Rac1 and modulation of HSF1 acetylation, leading to prolonged HSF1 DNA binding and robust HSP gene induction without causing protein unfolding, a hallmark of HSP “co-inducers” (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). In HSR-defective melanoma cells, BGP-15 significantly rescued raft domain coverage and shifted the size distribution toward larger platforms, coincident with increased hsp25 expression and Rac1-dependent stress signaling (Gombos et al., 2011). Across cell and tissue contexts, BGP-15 increases HSP70/HSPA1A (HSP72), and this HSP gain is causally linked to improved insulin signaling and cytoprotection in stressed cells (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011).

PARP/NAD+/SIRT1/HSF1 axis. Although BGP-15 demonstrates mixed-type (noncompetitive) inhibition of PARP-1 in vitro, the concentrations required exceed typical in vivo exposures, suggesting that PARP pathway effects in vivo are likely downstream of ROS lowering and reduced DNA single-strand breaks that otherwise drive PARP activation (Crul et al., 2013). In stressed cells, BGP-15 reduces PAR levels, which relieves PARP-mediated suppression of MKP-1/Dusp1, thereby inhibiting JNK/p38 activation; reduced PARP activity also preserves NAD+ and SIRT1 activity, which favors a deacetylated, active HSF1 and a stronger HSR (Crul et al., 2013). This mechanistic loop—less ROS, less PARP activation, more MKP-1, less JNK/p38, and better HSP/SIRT1 tone—aligns with the observed anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective phenotypes (Crul et al., 2013).

Mitochondrial enrichment and respiratory chain modulation. Biophysically, BGP-15 carries a delocalized positive charge, accumulates in energized mitochondria (>85–90% uptake in isolated organelles), and at micromolar doses characteristic of cell studies (1–50 µM) lowers mitochondrial ROS predominantly at complexes I and III without significant baseline depolarization of Δψm (Sümegi, 2018; Sumegi et al., 2017). In oxidative or inflammatory challenges, BGP-15 attenuates H₂O₂- and LPS-induced mitochondrial depolarization and reduces mitochondrial superoxide to near-control levels; MitoTEMPO controls confirm mitochondrial origin of the ROS signal (Sumegi et al., 2017). Importantly, the compound exhibits no meaningful direct antioxidant scavenging in cell-free ROS-generating systems, and only displays mild uncoupling at millimolar concentrations—far above the micromolar exposures used in protective assays—supporting a mechanism of respiratory chain modulation rather than redox scavenging (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). Downstream signaling reflects the lowered mitochondrial ROS burden: JNK/p38 activation is reduced, Akt signaling is enhanced, and caspase-independent death pathways are suppressed (Sumegi et al., 2017).

Mitochondrial dynamics, fusion, and biogenesis. Beyond acute ROS control, BGP-15 promotes mitochondrial fusion and preserves cristae architecture by activating OPA1 GTPase and promoting OPA1 polymerization; genetic suppression of OPA1 or Mfn1/Mfn2 abolishes the fusion phenotype, indicating that BGP-15 acts upstream or within the endogenous fusion machinery (Szabó et al., 2018). In vivo, these effects translate into improved mitochondrial ultrastructure and tissue histology under ROS stress (e.g., monocrotaline-induced PAH) (Szabó et al., 2018). In hypertensive cardiomyopathy, BGP-15 increases PGC-1α and mitochondrial mass, with concurrent shifts in CREB/AMPK phosphorylation consistent with improved energetic signaling, reduced p38/JNK via MKP-1 upregulation, and increased Akt/GSK-3β prosurvival signaling (Horváth et al., 2021).

Insulin-sensitizing stress signaling. In skeletal muscle and human studies, BGP-15 increases HSP72 expression, enhances insulin receptor autophosphorylation (blocking JNK inhibitory phosphorylation), activates RAC1, increases AKT phosphorylation, promotes GLUT4 translocation, increases membrane fluidity, raises AMPK activity, and reduces HSF1 acetylation, altogether improving glucose disposal without overt toxicity in a randomized trial (Crul et al., 2013). These metabolic effects are mechanistically congruent with the membrane–HSR–mitochondrial triad described above (Crul et al., 2013).

Ocular and retinal mechanisms. In rat eyes, BGP-15 increased HSP70 and decreased NFκB, consistent with HSR enhancement and anti-inflammatory signaling in ocular tissues (Wachal et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion and diabetic retinopathy models, functional improvements on ERG, restoration of oscillatory potentials, and preservation of retinal thickness are consistent with mitochondrial protection and stress-response reinforcement in retinal cells (Takács et al., 2024). The topical SBECD formulation demonstrated pharmacologic activity in the retina without systemic pharmacokinetic characterization, indicating local ocular delivery as a viable route for targeting mitochondrial and HSP pathways in the posterior segment (Takács et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
The team’s hypothesis—that BGP-15 stabilizes mitochondrial membrane proteins and co-induces HSF1-driven antioxidant chaperone responses in RPE to mitigate oxidative stress in dry AMD—is aligned with the compound’s demonstrated pharmacology in retinal, cardiac, neural, and pulmonary models: (i) robust mitochondrial enrichment and stabilization of Δψm under oxidative/inflammatory stress, (ii) ROS lowering at complexes I and III without direct radical scavenging, (iii) activation of the HSR via membrane raft remodeling and HSF1 acetylation control, and (iv) suppression of ROS-sensitive injury cascades (JNK/p38) with concurrent activation of pro-survival Akt (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). In retinal disease models, BGP-15 improved ERG measures and retinal thickness and increased ocular HSP70 while decreasing NFκB, providing a direct ocular precedent likely to translate to stressed RPE, where mitochondria and proteostasis are central to survival under chronic oxidative load (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021).

Mechanistically expected in RPE:  
- Membrane-raft remodeling and HSR co-induction. BGP-15 partitions into RPE membranes and remodels cholesterol-rich rafts, preserving raft integrity under stress, activating Rac1, decreasing HSF1 acetylation, and prolonging HSF1 DNA binding, thereby elevating HSP70/HSP25 and enhancing proteostasis capacity in aged/stressed RPE (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).  
- Mitochondrial ROS containment and Δψm preservation. BGP-15 should accumulate in RPE mitochondria, reduce ROS production at complexes I/III, and attenuate oxidative- and inflammation-induced depolarization, thereby maintaining ATP production and limiting mitochondrial permeability transition and AIF translocation, as shown in other cell types (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018).  
- Mitochondrial dynamics and biogenesis. Via OPA1 activation and Akt/GSK-3β signaling, BGP-15 is expected to promote inner-membrane fusion/OPA1 oligomerization and preserve cristae, with possible longer-term increases in mitochondrial biogenesis (PGC-1α), all protective features for RPE faced with chronic oxidative and lipofuscin stress (Szabó et al., 2018; Horváth et al., 2021).  
- Anti-inflammatory signaling rebalancing. By reducing mitochondrial ROS and PARP activation, BGP-15 should relieve PARP-mediated suppression of MKP-1, suppress JNK/p38 activity, decrease NFκB signaling, and bolster SIRT1-HSF1 activity, thereby reducing ROS-amplifying feed-forward loops in RPE (Crul et al., 2013; Wachal et al., 2021).

Assay expectations and endpoints. In standard RPE cell models (primary human RPE, ARPE-19, or iPSC-RPE), BGP-15 at 1–50 µM should (i) reduce H₂O₂- or LPS-induced mitochondrial depolarization (JC-1/TMRM), (ii) lower mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX) and total ROS (DHR123) without acting as a direct antioxidant in cell-free assays, (iii) reduce apoptosis/necrosis after oxidative challenge (annexin V/PI), (iv) increase HSP70/HSF1 pathway activation and decrease HSF1 acetylation, (v) activate Akt and downregulate JNK/p38, and (vi) promote OPA1 oligomerization and mitochondrial fusion (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Szabó et al., 2018). Where possible, complement activation or lipid peroxidation paradigms can be layered to emulate dry AMD stressors; based on the corpus, BGP-15’s effects are strongest under stress, consistent with HSP co-inducer pharmacology (Gombos et al., 2011).

Delivery considerations. Systemic exposures in humans are low (≤25 nmol/mL), suggesting that oral dosing may be insufficient to reach pharmacologic micromolar levels in RPE; conversely, topical ocular delivery with SBECD has demonstrated retinal functional benefits and structural protection, supporting development of a posterior-segment–targeted topical or periocular formulation to enrich the RPE–choroid compartment (Sümegi, 2018; Takács et al., 2024).

Caveats regarding target expression. The corpus documents the relevant targets (HSF1/HSP70, Rac1, OPA1, MKP-1, JNK/p38, Akt) as central to BGP-15’s mechanisms in multiple mammalian tissues and cell types and shows ocular readouts (HSP70 up, NFκB down) in rat eyes; however, it does not provide explicit RPE expression data, which should be confirmed experimentally in our RPE assay systems (Wachal et al., 2021; Gombos et al., 2011; Szabó et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic congruence with dry AMD pathobiology. BGP-15 directly addresses mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic oxidative stress—core drivers of RPE degeneration—by concentrating in mitochondria, lowering ROS at complexes I/III, stabilizing Δψm, and activating survival signaling while suppressing inflammatory stress kinases (Sumegi et al., 2017). Concurrently, it co-induces the HSR by remodeling plasma membrane rafts and modulating HSF1 acetylation, thereby boosting HSP70/HSP25 chaperone capacity and proteostasis—functions that are expected to mitigate protein misfolding and aggregation in aged RPE (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).  
- Demonstrated ocular efficacy in relevant retinal injury contexts. Topical BGP-15 improved ERG a- and b-waves, preserved oscillatory potentials, reduced implicit times, and rescued retinal thickness after ischemia–reperfusion, and it was retinoprotective in diabetic models, with ocular HSP70 increase and NFκB reduction—outcomes consistent with RPE/retinal resilience under oxidative stress (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021).  
- Pleiotropic yet coherent mechanism spanning membrane, nuclear, and mitochondrial nodes. The membrane–HSR–mitochondrial triad, including PARP/MKP-1/JNK–p38 and Akt/GSK-3β axes, provides multiple intervention points likely to translate into robust protection in the multifactorial environment of dry AMD (Crul et al., 2013; Sumegi et al., 2017; Szabó et al., 2018; Horváth et al., 2021).  
- Favorable translational signals. Proof-of-concept human trials in insulin resistance show pharmacodynamic activity without overt safety signals, and HSP co-inducers are known to preferentially act in stressed cells, potentially limiting off-target effects in quiescent tissues; local ocular delivery further improves the therapeutic index (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011; Takács et al., 2024).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Lack of direct dry AMD evidence. No studies in the corpus directly test BGP-15 in dry AMD models or patients; we infer utility from retinal IR/diabetes models and mechanism (Takács et al., 2024).  
- Exposure–response uncertainties for the posterior segment. Systemic serum concentrations are low relative to micromolar efficacious concentrations in vitro, necessitating optimized local delivery to RPE; although eyedrop formulations show retinal effects, posterior-segment delivery by topical route is often limited, and pharmacokinetics were not measured in the cited ocular study (Sümegi, 2018; Takács et al., 2024).  
- Target ambiguity and pleiotropy. While the membrane–HSR–mitochondrial framework is coherent, BGP-15 lacks a single defined receptor/protein target, and its in vitro PARP-1 inhibition likely does not drive in vivo efficacy; this complicates target engagement assays and regulatory narratives (Sümegi, 2018; Crul et al., 2013).  
- Nomenclature confusion. “BGP-15” also denotes a calcipotriene-derived vitamin D3 analog in the oncology literature; chemical identity must be verified to avoid conflation during procurement and CMC (Sintov et al., 2013; Takács et al., 2024).  
- Evidence base heterogeneity. Some ocular and cardiovascular studies are published in lower–quality venues, emphasizing the need for rigorous, blinded replication and GLP toxicology in ocular models (Horváth et al., 2021; Wachal et al., 2021).

Recommended next steps  
- In vitro RPE validation. In human primary or iPSC-derived RPE under oxidative (H₂O₂/tert-butyl hydroperoxide) and inflammatory (LPS/CpG) stress, test BGP-15 at 0.3–30 µM for effects on Δψm (JC-1/TMRM), mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX), total ROS (DHR123), apoptosis/necrosis (annexin V/PI), and mitochondrial respiration; confirm no direct antioxidant scavenging in cell-free systems (Sumegi et al., 2017).  
- Proteostasis and HSR endpoints. Quantify HSP70/HSP25 induction, HSF1 acetylation/binding dynamics, Rac1 activation, and membrane raft integrity using fPEG-cholesterol probes/TOCCSL in RPE; evaluate MKP-1, JNK/p38, and Akt/GSK-3β signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013; Sumegi et al., 2017).  
- Mitochondrial dynamics. Assess OPA1 oligomerization, fusion/fission balance (Mfn1/2 and Drp1 markers), cristae morphology by EM, and PGC-1α/mtDNA copy number to benchmark fusion/biogenesis responses (Szabó et al., 2018; Horváth et al., 2021).  
- Ocular delivery PK/PD. Using the SBECD eyedrop formulation as a starting point, perform ocular pharmacokinetics (vitreous, retina, RPE–choroid) and pharmacodynamics (ocular HSP70, NFκB, mitochondrial markers) to ensure RPE target engagement at tolerated doses (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021).  
- In vivo retinal stress models. Extend to retinal oxidative stress paradigms that capture RPE pathology; leverage ERG, OCT, histology, and mitochondrial ultrastructure endpoints already positive in IR/diabetic models (Takács et al., 2024).  
- Identity control and CMC. Source BGP-15 as O-(3-piperidino-2-hydroxy-1-propyl) nicotinic amidoxime dihydrochloride; confirm identity by NMR/MS to avoid the calcipotriene-derived analog (Takács et al., 2024; Sintov et al., 2013).

Go/no-go considerations for dry AMD  
Given the robust mechanistic alignment—mitochondrial ROS control at complexes I/III, Δψm stabilization, HSR co-induction via membrane raft remodeling and HSF1 acetylation control, OPA1-driven mitochondrial fusion, and suppression of ROS-sensitive inflammatory kinases—plus demonstrable ocular efficacy in retinal injury models, BGP-15 merits advancement to RPE-focused preclinical validation for dry AMD (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Szabó et al., 2018; Takács et al., 2024). The principal risks are translational: ensuring adequate RPE exposures by ocular delivery, confirming RPE target expression/engagement, and generating rigorous GLP pharmacology/toxicology data in ocular species. On balance, the mechanistic breadth that often complicates development is an advantage in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction, proteostasis failure, and chronic inflammation coexist.

Conclusion. BGP-15 is a credible repurposing candidate for dry AMD based on its mitochondria-centered, HSP co-inducing, membrane-lipid–modulating pharmacology and encouraging retinal efficacy in vivo; priority should be given to RPE-targeted PK/PD, mitochondrial and HSR biomarker validation, and controlled efficacy studies in retinal oxidative-stress models to de-risk translation (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Takács et al., 2024).
