Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SRT1720 is a fully synthetic small molecule initially discovered through high‐throughput screening by Sirtris Pharmaceuticals, which sought potent alternatives to the naturally occurring polyphenol resveratrol. Unlike resveratrol—which suffers from low bioavailability, poor metabolic stability, and broad non‐selective target interactions—SRT1720 belongs to the class of synthetic Sirtuin Activating Compounds (STACs) designed to selectively activate the NAD⁺‐dependent deacetylase SIRT1. Chemically, SRT1720 is based on an imidazo[1,2-b]thiazole scaffold and was optimized for its potency; studies have indicated that it is approximately 1000× more potent than resveratrol, with an EC1.5 value of around 0.16 μM and impressive maximal activation percentages in vitro (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Chang et al., 2024). The synthetic origins of SRT1720 represent a deliberate medicinal chemistry effort aimed at overcoming the limitations of natural SIRT1 activators. In the broader context, compounds in this class have been used as investigational drugs targeting pathways involved in metabolism, aging, inflammation, and stress tolerance, thereby establishing a framework for repurposing efforts across various disease areas (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Therapeutic History:  
Preclinical studies of SRT1720 have predominantly focused on its metabolic effects in rodent models characterized by diet-induced obesity, insulin resistance, and other forms of metabolic dysfunction. In these studies, administration of SRT1720 resulted in significant improvements in insulin sensitivity, reduction of plasma glucose levels, and enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis across metabolic tissues such as skeletal muscle, liver, and adipose tissues (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Donmez, 2012). Moreover, in genetically obese and high-fat diet animal models, SRT1720 has been demonstrated to improve mitochondrial function, as indicated by increased ATP production, elevated expression of mitochondrial proteins such as ATP synthase β and NDUFB8, and enhanced oxidative metabolism (Funk et al., 2010). This modulatory effect on mitochondrial biogenesis and function is thought to be mediated via the SIRT1-PGC-1α pathway—a mechanism that has garnered attention in age-related diseases where mitochondrial dysfunction is central. Although SRT1720 has not been directly investigated in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models or explicitly in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, the underlying pathogenic processes in dry AMD—namely, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysregulation—share significant overlap with the tissues previously demonstrated to benefit from SRT1720 treatment (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009). This cross-tissue efficacy provides a compelling rationale to explore SRT1720’s repurposing for dry AMD. Additionally, related compounds in this class (e.g., SRT2104) have advanced into clinical development for other indications, further suggesting that the pharmacological modulation of SIRT1 is a viable therapeutic approach (Hoppner et al., 2014).

Mechanism of Action:  
The underlying mechanism of action of SRT1720 centers on its ability to allosterically activate SIRT1, a key regulator of cellular energy metabolism and stress responses. SIRT1 is an NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase that modulates the activity of various transcription factors and co-regulators, notably PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ coactivator 1-α), which is a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. SRT1720 binds to an allosteric site on the SIRT1 enzyme-peptide substrate complex, situated amino terminal to the enzyme’s catalytic domain. This binding facilitates a conformational change in SIRT1 that lowers the Michaelis constant (K_m) for the acetylated substrates, thereby enhancing the rate of deacetylation (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Wan, 2021). Biochemical assays have demonstrated that SRT1720 increases SIRT1 deacetylase activity in a dose-dependent manner, leading to reduced acetylation of PGC-1α and thus promoting its transcriptional activity in driving mitochondrial gene expression (Funk et al., 2010). In addition to PGC-1α, SRT1720-mediated SIRT1 activation influences the acetylation status of several other proteins involved in stress responses and apoptosis, including FOXO1 and PPARγ, which collectively contribute to improved cellular resilience against oxidative damage (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Hoppner et al., 2014). Of note, many studies have confirmed that the beneficial effects observed with SRT1720 are abrogated in the presence of SIRT1 inhibitors such as nicotinamide and sirtinol, providing strong evidence for a SIRT1-dependent mode of action (Funk et al., 2010; Djouadi & Bastin, 2019). However, it is important to acknowledge that there has been some controversy regarding whether SRT1720 and its structural relatives directly interact with SIRT1 or exert off-target effects; nonetheless, the preponderance of kinetic and biophysical data supports the view that SRT1720 is primarily a SIRT1 activator (Hoppner et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2024).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry AMD is characterized by the degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) accompanied by chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and an overall decline in cellular energy homeostasis. The hypothesis for repurposing SRT1720 in this context is based on its well-documented ability to stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis and enhance oxidative capacity in multiple tissue types. In the RPE, which is a post-mitotic and metabolically demanding cell layer critical for photoreceptor survival, mitochondrial dysfunction is a key pathological feature that contributes to the progression of dry AMD. By activating SIRT1, SRT1720 is expected to promote deacetylation of PGC-1α, thereby upregulating a transcriptional program that enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and repair. This, in turn, would improve oxidative phosphorylation, reduce the production of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), and bolster the cells’ ability to cope with the chronic oxidative stress that underlies dry AMD pathology (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Furthermore, studies in other tissues, such as aged skeletal muscle and hepatocytes, have shown that SRT1720 reduces mtROS and restores cellular ATP levels by increasing mitochondrial number and function (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Funk et al., 2010). It is reasonable to extrapolate that similar benefits could be achieved in RPE cells, where preserved mitochondrial function is essential for maintaining retinal integrity and preventing progression to geographic atrophy, the advanced form of dry AMD. Expression analyses have demonstrated that both SIRT1 and PGC-1α are expressed in RPE cells, and their activities are critical for retinal health; thus, modulation of the SIRT1–PGC-1α axis by SRT1720 offers a mechanistic basis for its expected protective effects in the RPE (Hoppner et al., 2014; Alcaín & Villalba, 2009). It is anticipated that in assays using RPE cell cultures, treatment with SRT1720 will lead to enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis—as evidenced by increased mitochondrial DNA content, elevated levels of mitochondrial proteins, and improved cellular ATP production—while concurrently attenuating markers of oxidative stress. These effects would collectively improve the oxidative resilience of RPE cells, thereby potentially slowing or halting the progression of dry AMD (Funk et al., 2010; Hoppner et al., 2014).

There are several compelling strengths associated with the use of SRT1720 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. First, its synthetic design has led to a compound that is remarkably more potent than resveratrol, addressing one of the key limitations of natural SIRT1 activators. This enhanced potency, coupled with a clearly elucidated mechanism of action involving allosteric activation of SIRT1, provides a robust biochemical rationale for its efficacy. The observed effects in metabolic, hepatic, and renal systems—where SRT1720 has demonstrated significant improvements in mitochondrial biogenesis and reductions in oxidative stress—are highly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells plays a central role (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Another strength is the extensive preclinical data supporting the involvement of the SIRT1-PGC-1α axis in regulating mitochondrial function and cellular energy homeostasis. Since RPE cells share similar reliance on these pathways for maintaining cellular function and resisting oxidative injury, it is plausible that SRT1720 can be effectively translated into a therapeutic for dry AMD. Moreover, the fact that SRT1720’s effects are abrogated by SIRT1 inhibitors reinforces the notion that its beneficial actions are directly linked to SIRT1 activation rather than resulting from non-specific off-target activities, a point underscored by multiple biochemical studies (Wan, 2021; Funk et al., 2010).

However, there are also notable weaknesses and uncertainties that warrant consideration. Although SRT1720 has a well-characterized profile in terms of metabolic and mitochondrial effects in other tissue types, there is a paucity of data directly pertaining to ocular tissues or RPE cells. The retinal environment possesses unique pharmacokinetic and physiological characteristics, and the ability of SRT1720 to reach effective concentrations in the RPE upon systemic or local administration remains to be determined. Moreover, while the SIRT1-PGC-1α axis is a promising target, some studies have raised controversies concerning whether SRT1720 truly acts as a direct SIRT1 activator or if its effects might be partially mediated by off-target pathways, which could complicate both efficacy and safety profiles (Hoppner et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2024). There is also the broader issue of translating findings from systemic models of mitochondrial dysfunction to the highly specialized context of the eye, which may require careful consideration of formulation, dosing regimen, and potential adverse effects that are specific to ocular tissues.

The overall evaluation suggests that SRT1720 has a strong scientific foundation based on its potent SIRT1 activation, its capacity to enhance mitochondrial biogenesis, and its demonstrated ability to mitigate oxidative stress in multiple preclinical models (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Funk et al., 2010). These characteristics are directly relevant to addressing the molecular pathogenesis of dry AMD, where impaired mitochondrial function in the RPE is a key contributor to disease progression. Rigorous in vitro studies in RPE cell cultures and subsequent in vivo models of dry AMD will be essential to validate the therapeutic potential of SRT1720 in the ocular setting. Such studies should also focus on optimizing delivery mechanisms to ensure that effective drug levels are achieved in the retina without systemic toxicity (Hoppner et al., 2014; Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Future investigations should include detailed pharmacokinetic assessments in ocular tissues, evaluation of the specific effects on RPE mitochondrial dynamics, and analyses of potential off-target effects that could compromise safety. Additionally, given the controversies around whether compounds such as SRT1720 function solely via SIRT1 activation, complementary studies using genetic knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of SIRT1 in RPE cells would help to unequivocally determine the mechanism by which SRT1720 exerts its effects. Ultimately, while the translational rationale appears strong, careful attention must be paid to the unique biological milieu of the eye and to the rigorous design of preclinical studies that directly address the therapeutic endpoints relevant to dry AMD (Hoppner et al., 2014; Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

In conclusion, SRT1720 is a promising candidate for repurposing as a treatment for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its potent SIRT1 activation, demonstrated effects on mitochondrial biogenesis, and its ability to reduce oxidative stress, which is central to the pathology observed in RPE cells. The synthetic origin and high potency of SRT1720 distinguish it from natural agents like resveratrol and suggest that it might overcome many of the pharmacokinetic and specificity issues that have historically limited the success of SIRT1 activators in clinical settings. If future studies can confirm that SRT1720 effectively reaches the RPE in therapeutic concentrations and modulates the SIRT1-PGC-1α pathway without deleterious off-target effects, it could represent a significant advancement in our ability to protect the RPE against oxidative stress and slow the progression of dry AMD (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Funk et al., 2010; Hoppner et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation Summary:  
Strengths of SRT1720 include its exceptional potency compared to natural SIRT1 activators, robust preclinical evidence demonstrating mitochondrial biogenesis and reduced oxidative stress in multiple tissues, and a well-elucidated mechanism involving allosteric activation of SIRT1 with consequent deacetylation of PGC-1α. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SkQ1 (10‐(6′‐plastoquinonyl)‐decyltriphenylphosphonium) is a fully synthetic, mitochondria‐targeted antioxidant constructed by conjugating a plastoquinone antioxidant moiety with a decyl linker that is covalently bound to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation. The plastoquinone scaffold is derived from the natural quinone found in chloroplasts, known for its potent reactive oxygen species (ROS)–removing capabilities, while the TPP⁺ moiety acts as a highly lipophilic vector that drives selective accumulation within mitochondria due to the inner mitochondrial membrane’s large negative potential. In essence, by combining these two structural elements, SkQ1 is designed to exploit electrophoretic uptake to achieve extremely high concentrations in the mitochondrial matrix where oxidative damage is a critical pathogenic factor. This compound belongs to the broader class of mitochondria‐targeted quinone antioxidants, often referred to collectively as “SkQ” compounds. Molecules in this class were originally proposed and developed by Skulachev and colleagues, and they have been used experimentally to achieve mitochondrial protection in contexts ranging from ischemia–reperfusion injury and neurodegeneration to aging‐associated dysfunctions (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). The rational design strategy behind SkQ1—linking a redox‐active quinone to a lipophilic cation—has also inspired the development of analogous compounds such as SkQR1, MitoQ, and related derivatives that are being explored for a variety of biomedical applications.

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of SkQ1, as well as that of its parent class of mitochondria‐targeted antioxidants, is extensive and spans multiple preclinical and early clinical studies. In numerous in vitro and in vivo models, SkQ1 has demonstrated robust antioxidant effects. For example, it has been shown to protect mitochondria and cellular membranes against lipid peroxidation—key pathogenic processes underlying aging and degenerative diseases—at nanomolar concentrations. In various rodent models, including studies in OXYS rats (a strain that mimics accelerated senescence), chronic administration of SkQ1 prevented or reversed age‐related abnormalities such as cataract, retinopathy, and even systemic markers of mitochondrial dysfunction (Wanagat et al., 2010; Belenichev et al., 2024; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Moreover, veterinary and preclinical studies have documented SkQ1’s ability to increase lifespan and delay the onset of age‐linked phenotypes, including osteoporosis, immune decline, and neurodegeneration (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Weissig, 2020). Within the ocular field, SkQ1 has been specifically formulated as eye drops—marketed in certain regions under the trade name Visomitin—to treat dry eye syndrome. These formulations have passed early phase safety trials and have now seen clinical use in Russia. Although SkQ1 has not yet been directly trialed in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or geographic atrophy, its documented efficacy in protecting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in animal models and its ability to improve electrophysiological outcomes (such as preserved electroretinography [ERG] responses) support its potential repurposing for AMD (Gueven et al., 2017; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). In several ocular studies in both rodent and primate models, topical administration of SkQ1 has demonstrated the capacity to deliver the drug to the posterior segment with minimal systemic exposure, reducing characteristics like RPE vacuolization and preserving overall retinal function (Weissig, 2020; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). The extensive preclinical and limited clinical history of SkQ1 in ocular applications—most notably in dry-eye syndrome and animal models of retinal degeneration—suggests that the therapeutic candidate has a solid track record of mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction in tissues exposed to chronic oxidative stress, a pathophysiological component also seen in dry AMD (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Wanagat et al., 2010).

Mechanism of Action:  
SkQ1 exerts its biological effects via multiple interrelated molecular mechanisms that center on its ability to accumulate rapidly within mitochondria and scavenge deleterious ROS. The TPP⁺ portion of the molecule, owing to its delocalized positive charge and high lipophilicity, drives the electrophoretic uptake of SkQ1 into the mitochondrial matrix along the steep negative membrane potential (Δψm) that is inherent to healthy mitochondria (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Once localized within these organelles, the plastoquinone group is poised to participate in redox cycling: it is reversibly reduced—often by components of the electron transport chain such as complex III—and subsequently reacts with ROS such as superoxide (O₂•⁻) and lipid peroxyl radicals to convert them into less reactive species (Lukashev et al., 2014; Weissig, 2020). Importantly, the antioxidant effect of SkQ1 is not a one-off reaction; rather, it is “rechargeable,” meaning that following its oxidation by ROS, the quinone moiety can be reduced again, thereby enabling repeated cycles of detoxification. This rechargeable mechanism differentiates SkQ1 from conventional antioxidants that are consumed irreversibly during redox reactions. Additionally, SkQ1 has been shown to form complexes with cardiolipin—a key phospholipid in the inner mitochondrial membrane—and thereby stabilize the membrane structure against peroxidation. Some studies also suggest that the TPP⁺ component might mediate a mild uncoupling effect by facilitating proton translocation (often in conjunction with interacting with fatty acid anions), which can reduce mitochondrial ROS generation by dissipating excessive inner membrane potential under conditions of oxidative overload (Lukashev et al., 2014; Weissig, 2020; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). This dual mechanism of direct ROS scavenging combined with membrane stabilizing and modest uncoupling effects contributes to the preservation of Δψm and the overall integrity of mitochondrial bioenergetics. In RPE cells stressed by chronic photo-oxidative insult, these properties would translate into effective mitigation of oxidative damage, thereby preventing the collapse of mitochondrial membrane potential—a key event that precipitates cell dysfunction and death in dry AMD (Muraleva et al., 2019; Olovnikov et al., n.d.).

Expected Effect:  
The proposed hypothesis for repurposing SkQ1 in dry age-related macular degeneration is predicated on its capacity to target RPE mitochondria and to neutralize both superoxide radicals and lipid peroxyl radicals that accumulate under conditions of chronic light-induced oxidative stress. In vitro assays using ARPE-19 cells have demonstrated that nanomolar concentrations of SkQ1 elicit potent antioxidant responses—as measured by decreases in fluorescence with DCFDA (a marker of ROS) and stabilization of mitochondrial membrane potential via JC-1 assays—indicating that the compound readily scavenges ocular ROS at very low doses (Gueven et al., 2017; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). This antioxidant activity is expected to prevent or delay the loss of Δψm, a critical parameter for cell survival and function, particularly in RPE cells where mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in the pathogenesis of drusen formation and geographic atrophy in dry AMD. In vivo, studies conducted in models such as OXYS rats have shown that chronic administration of SkQ1 not only reduces oxidative markers in mitochondrial membranes (e.g., decreasing levels of malondialdehyde and hydroxynonenal-adducts) but also normalizes cardiolipin content and fatty acid composition—key factors involved in the proper assembly and turnover of respiratory complexes (Wanagat et al., 2010; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Moreover, macaque studies have indicated that topical SkQ1 eye drops achieve significant drug levels in the posterior segment although the dosing remains in the nanomolar range, leading to improvements in ERG function and reduced RPE vacuolization without evidence of systemic toxicity (Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Weissig, 2020). At the molecular level, the expected effect in RPE cells would be a sustained antioxidant environment that preserves mitochondrial function through two primary pathways: first, by directly quenching damaging ROS that would otherwise trigger mitochondrial DNA damage and lipid peroxidation; and second, by maintaining the structural integrity of mitochondrial membranes via stabilization of cardiolipin and prevention of excessive proton leakage. Given that RPE cells express the full complement of mitochondrial electron transport chain proteins, including complex III which is capable of reducing SkQ1 to its active form, these cells are ideal targets for the drug’s mechanism (Muraleva et al., 2019; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Consequently, when used as a therapeutic intervention in dry AMD, SkQ1 is expected to mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction associated with drusen accumulation and, in turn, slow or potentially reverse the progression of geographic atrophy—one of the major sight-threatening complications of the disease.

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, SkQ1 represents a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration based on a robust foundation of molecular design, preclinical efficacy, and established ocular safety. One of the major strengths of SkQ1 lies in its rational design: as a rechargeable, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant, it overcomes limitations faced by conventional antioxidants that lack mitochondrial specificity. The ability of the TPP⁺ moiety to drive precise mitochondrial accumulation ensures that the compound is concentrated at the site of maximal ROS production, while its plastoquinone component provides potent scavenging of both superoxide and lipid peroxyl radicals. This dual functionality not only neutralizes damaging oxidative species but also supports mitochondrial membrane integrity by stabilizing cardiolipin and potentially mitigating excessive proton leakage. Such a mechanism is particularly relevant to RPE cells, where chronic photo-oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Lukashev et al., 2014).

Another significant advantage is the extensive preclinical and early clinical evidence supporting SkQ1’s efficacy in ocular applications. Its use in animal models—spanning species from rodents to macaques—has consistently shown protective effects on retinal structure and function, including preservation of ERG responses and reduced vacuolization of the RPE. Furthermore, the successful clinical trials for dry eye syndrome confirm that topical administration of SkQ1 is not only efficacious but also well-tolerated in humans, thereby reducing the risk related to ocular drug delivery and systemic exposure (Gueven et al., 2017; Weissig, 2020; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

Nevertheless, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be carefully weighed. One concern is the dose-dependent behavior of SkQ1. While nanomolar concentrations are effective and safe, there is evidence that at higher concentrations, the molecule can exhibit prooxidant or detergent-like effects—leading to membrane disruption or uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation. This narrow window between the antioxidant and prooxidant activities necessitates rigorous control of dosing in clinical settings to avoid inadvertent exacerbation of mitochondrial dysfunction (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). Additionally, while many studies have focused on the compound’s ability to protect against acute oxidative insults, the etiology of dry AMD is multifactorial and chronic. Although animal models such as the OXYS rat provide valuable insights into age-related ocular changes, the long-term efficacy and safety of SkQ1 in preventing geographic atrophy in the context of chronic, low-grade oxidative stress remain to be fully established in human subjects (Wanagat et al., 2010; Belenichev et al., 2024).

It is also important to note that while the proposed mechanism of action for SkQ1—namely, quenching of lipid peroxyl radicals and superoxide to preserve mitochondrial membrane potential—has been well-documented in vitro and in animal models (particularly using ARPE-19 assays with JC-1 and DCFDA readouts), extrapolating these findings to the complex human pathology of dry AMD will require careful clinical trial design. Key endpoints such as changes in drusen load, progression of geographic atrophy, and improvements in visual function would need to be monitored over extended periods. Moreover, given that oxidative stress and inflammation are part of an intricate network of pathological events in dry AMD, combination therapies that address multiple targets may ultimately yield more significant benefits than a single-agent approach (Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Gueven et al., 2017).

From a pharmacokinetic perspective, the selective accumulation of SkQ1 in the mitochondria is a highly attractive feature, as it maximizes local drug concentrations while minimizing systemic exposure and potential off-target effects. This is especially critical for ocular applications, where local delivery via eye drops can achieve high retinal levels with minimal systemic absorption. Nonetheless, formulation stability, light sensitivity, and proper storage conditions are factors that must be optimized for successful commercial development (Weissig, 2020; Gueven et al., 2017; Ji et al., 2021).

In aggregate, the overall evaluation of SkQ1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic. The compound’s design as a mitochondria-targeted, rechargeable antioxidant offers compelling advantages in addressing mitochondrial dysfunction—a key element in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its ability to protect RPE cells, preserve mitochondrial membrane potential, and improve retinal function, while early clinical studies in related ocular conditions confirm its safety profile for topical administration. However, due diligence is warranted to establish the optimal dosing regimen that maximizes beneficial antioxidant effects while avoiding potential prooxidant toxicity. Additionally, further rigorous clinical trials specifically targeting dry AMD endpoints are necessary to confirm that the promising outcomes observed in animal studies translate into measurable clinical benefit in patients with geographic atrophy (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Gueven et al., 2017; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Wanagat et al., 2010; Weissig, 2020).

Given the comprehensive body of work underpinning the mechanism of action, the established track record in various preclinical ocular models, and the supporting data from human dry-eye trials, SkQ1 appears to have significant potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its unique targeting of mitochondria—particularly within RPE cells—and its capacity to prevent ROS-induced mitochondrial collapse make it especially well-suited to counteract the chronic photo-oxidative stress that characterizes this disease. The next steps for validating SkQ1 in this indication should include well-designed in vivo studies in AMD-relevant animal models, followed by early phase clinical trials with careful dose-escalation studies and robust assessment of retinal morphology and function. Overall, SkQ1 stands out as a promising therapeutic candidate that merits further investigation within our drug development pipeline (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Weissig, 2020; Gueven et al., 2017; Wanagat et al., 2010).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GKT137831, also known as Setanaxib, is a synthetic small‐molecule drug originally discovered and optimized for its ability to inhibit NADPH oxidase activity, with specificity primarily toward the NOX1 and NOX4 isoforms. It belongs to the dihydropyrazolone chemical class, sharing structural similarity with the free radical scavenger edaravone, and has been further refined from earlier analogues such as GKT136901 through structure–activity relationship studies to improve its potency, selectivity, and oral bioavailability (Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30; Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). The compound was originally developed by Genkyotex as a dual NOX1/NOX4 inhibitor; however, it possesses additional but lower potency activity against NOX2 and even shows some partial inhibition of NOX5 in certain settings (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30). The initial discovery was based on high-throughput screening methods that targeted NADPH oxidase-mediated reactive oxygen species (ROS) production—a process that has been linked to multiple pathological conditions including fibrotic, vascular, and inflammatory diseases. As a representative of its class, GKT137831 exemplifies a modern approach to drug design wherein inhibition of the primary enzymatic source of ROS is favored over conventional antioxidant strategies, which often suffer from non-specificity and poor clinical translation (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26).

Therapeutic History:  
GKT137831 has a distinguished preclinical and clinical history rooted in its application to diseases characterized by oxidative stress and inflammation. In preclinical models, it has been shown to significantly reduce the generation of ROS and the downstream activation of pro-inflammatory signaling. In primary cultured human retinal endothelial cells, for instance, treatment with GKT137831 reduced both ROS generation and VEGFA expression, indicating its potential utility in limiting vascular dysfunction in ocular diseases (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). Beyond ocular applications, the compound has been evaluated in several preclinical models of fibrotic and vascular pathologies including diabetic kidney disease, hypertensive cardiac remodeling, and liver fibrosis, wherein its administration lowered the levels of ROS, inflammatory cytokines, and markers of tissue injury (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Cipriano et al., 2023, pp. 22–23). Clinically, GKT137831 has advanced to Phase II trials in diabetic nephropathy and primary biliary cholangitis, demonstrating both safety and acceptable pharmacokinetic properties in human subjects (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26; Buglak et al., 2018, Art. 2468457). Although it has not been tested directly for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) in clinical trials, several preclinical studies using models of ischemic retinopathy and diabetic retinopathy have provided supportive evidence that NOX inhibition may attenuate oxidative stress and inflammation in retinal tissues (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Gaskin et al., 2021, pp. 15–17). The repurposing rationale for dry AMD hinges on the observation that oxidative stress plays a central role in the degeneration of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and the subsequent progression of AMD—pathophysiological processes that have been effectively modulated by GKT137831 in other experimental disease models (Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 1–7).

Mechanism of Action:  
From a molecular perspective, GKT137831 has been characterized as a dual inhibitor of NOX1 and NOX4, enzymes that catalyze the transfer of electrons from NADPH to molecular oxygen and thereby generate superoxide or hydrogen peroxide, respectively (Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30; Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 4–6). Unlike classical antioxidants that scavenge ROS after they are generated, GKT137831 aims to prevent ROS formation at its source by directly inhibiting NOX enzyme activity. One study demonstrates that it can bind to the extracellular region of the catalytic subunit of NOX enzymes in an allosteric manner, distinct from the NADPH binding site, which leads to a decrease in NADPH-dependent superoxide generation and hydrogen peroxide production (Gorin et al., 2015, pp. 16–20). In addition to its enzyme inhibitory actions, the dihydropyrazolone scaffold confers an inherent ROS scavenging property, enabling the compound to neutralize peroxynitrite and hydrogen peroxide through redox-mediated chemical mechanisms (Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30; Gaskin et al., 2021, pp. 8–9). This dual property—direct enzyme inhibition coupled with ROS scavenging—is theorized to offer a more comprehensive approach to modulating oxidative stress in target tissues. However, there are conflicting reports in the literature regarding the specificity of its NOX inhibition, with some studies suggesting that measured low Ki values may be artifactual due to interference with assay components such as horseradish peroxidase, raising questions about whether the observed effects are entirely attributable to NOX inhibition or, in part, to non-specific redox modulation (Vincent, 2021, pp. 79–80; Demircan et al., 2022, pp. 12–13). Notwithstanding these concerns, the prevailing hypothesis remains that by dampening NOX activity, GKT137831 reduces both cytosolic and mitochondrial ROS. In the context of RPE cells, which are rich in mitochondria and subject to high oxidative loads due to constant light exposure and high metabolic activity, the inhibition of NOX4 is expected to be particularly beneficial for mitigating oxidative damage to the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and preserving the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 24–28).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underpinning the repurposing of GKT137831 for the treatment of dry AMD is that its inhibition of NOX4—and, by extension, NOX1—leads to a substantial reduction in the generation of reactive oxygen species within the retinal pigment epithelium. Oxidative stress in RPE cells is a key driver of mitochondrial dysfunction, particularly impairment of electron transport chain complexes, which in turn leads to decreased cellular energy production and the eventual onset of apoptosis. By pharmacologically reducing the burden of ROS, GKT137831 is expected to prevent the oxidative damage to mitochondrial ETC components, thereby preserving the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and ensuring continued ATP production and cellular viability under conditions of oxidative stress (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 24–28). In vitro assays utilizing RPE cells exposed to high-glucose or other oxidative stress conditions have shown that treatment with GKT137831 can dampen ROS levels, reduce caspase-3 activity (a marker of apoptosis), and decrease the expression of inflammatory molecules (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). Given that the pathogenesis of dry AMD involves chronic, low-grade oxidative damage and inflammation leading to RPE degeneration, the expected therapeutic effect of GKT137831 would be to attenuate these processes at a cellular level, thereby slowing or halting disease progression. Moreover, the expression profile of NOX enzymes—particularly NOX4 in RPE cells—provides a sound molecular basis for this approach, with several studies documenting increased NOX activity under conditions that mimic AMD pathogenesis (Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11; Kulbay et al., 2024, pp. 2–5). Furthermore, the oral formulation of GKT137831, validated in other disease contexts, offers a practical advantage because it facilitates long-term administration, which is essential for a chronic condition like dry AMD where sustained drug exposure is necessary to counteract cumulative oxidative damage (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26).

In evaluating the potential of GKT137831 as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses emerge. Among its major strengths is the robust preclinical evidence that supports the concept of targeting NOX enzymes to mitigate oxidative stress. The dual mode of action—combining direct enzyme inhibition with ROS scavenging—provides a theoretically advantageous approach to protecting RPE cells from both cytosolic and mitochondrial oxidative insults (Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30; Gaskin et al., 2021, pp. 8–9). This is particularly pertinent in dry AMD, a disease where oxidative stress is a driving force behind RPE dysfunction, drusen formation, and subsequent photoreceptor degeneration (Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 1–7). Furthermore, GKT137831’s progression into Phase II clinical trials for other indications such as diabetic nephropathy and primary biliary cholangitis demonstrates that the compound is orally bioavailable and has an acceptable safety profile in human subjects (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26; Buglak et al., 2018, Art. 2468457). This reduces the developmental risk when considering repurposing for dry AMD since chronic administration is feasible and the regulatory pathway may be accelerated based on existing human data.

On the other hand, significant concerns related to the specificity of GKT137831’s mechanism remain. Conflicting evidence suggests that some of the in vitro inhibitory effects attributed to the compound may be partly due to assay artifacts or non-specific redox-modulating activities rather than bona fide NOX inhibition (Vincent, 2021, pp. 79–80; Demircan et al., 2022, pp. 12–13). These findings raise critical questions regarding the extent to which the protective effects observed in retinal and other disease models are directly mediated by diminution of NOX-derived ROS. Additionally, while preclinical studies in diabetic and ischemic retinopathy models have provided promising results, there is a paucity of data directly linking GKT137831 to improved outcomes in dry AMD specifically. GKT137831, with its favorable oral bioavailability and established safety profile from Phase II clinical trials in non-ocular indications, represents a promising candidate for repurposing given the central role of oxidative stress and NOX-mediated ROS production in dry AMD. Nonetheless, weaknesses including unresolved mechanistic ambiguities, potential off-target effects, and limited direct evidence in AMD-relevant models call for rigorous additional research before clinical translation can be confidently pursued (Vincent, 2021, pp. 79–80; Demircan et al., 2022, pp. 2–3, 12–13). Overall, while there is considerable promise in targeting NOX-mediated oxidative stress in the RPE with a compound like GKT137831, the current evidence base necessitates further specific validation within the context of dry AMD. Such an approach would ideally involve a series of well-designed in vitro and in vivo experiments to ascertain pharmacodynamics, tissue distribution within ocular compartments, and ultimately, the functional outcome measures relevant to RPE health and retinal integrity under conditions that closely mimic the human disease state (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Gaskin et al., 2021, pp. 15–17; Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11).  

The next steps for our research team should include initiating experiments using cultured RPE cell lines exposed to oxidative stress paradigms (e.g., high-glucose, light-induced stress) to determine whether GKT137831 effectively preserves mitochondrial function and decreases apoptotic markers. Parallel studies in animal models of dry AMD, particularly those that recapitulate key features such as drusen formation, RPE degeneration, and subsequent photoreceptor loss, will be essential to elucidate the in vivo efficacy of the compound (Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 24–28). Ultimately, while the translational potential is high given its clinical safety record and oral formulation, the mechanistic uncertainties must be thoroughly addressed to confidently advocate for clinical trials in dry AMD patients. In conclusion, GKT137831 remains an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, provided that further targeted research can unequivocally demonstrate its beneficial effects on RPE mitochondrial health and overall retinal preservation (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26; Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring vitamin B3–class nucleoside and a leading NAD⁺ precursor that has been isolated from natural sources such as cow milk and other dietary materials, and is now produced by synthetic chemical means for therapeutic applications (Biță et al., 2023). NR belongs to the class of NAD⁺‐precursor nucleosides within the broader family of vitamin B3 compounds, the same family that includes nicotinic acid (NA) and nicotinamide (NAM), which historically have been used to prevent pellagra and improve cellular energy metabolism (Pîrvu et al., 2021; Biță et al., 2023). The synthetic production of NR involves the glycosylation of nicotinamide with appropriately protected ribofuranose donors via methods that require careful control due to the labile and reactive nature of its glycosidic bond, which often results in partial degradation during synthesis and storage (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). In order to overcome these issues, researchers have developed alternative stabilized forms such as NR borate, although the commercially available ChromaDex NR-100 is typically presented as the crystalline chloride salt (NRCl) and has become a benchmark for purity due to its improved manufacturing protocols and rigorous quality control (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Additionally, NR’s classification as an “orally bioavailable” NAD⁺ precursor distinguishes it from other precursors such as NMN by virtue of its ability to directly cross cell membranes without requiring extracellular conversion, with transport mediated by equilibrative nucleoside transporters (Mehmel et al., 2020; Biță et al., 2023). Taken together, these attributes place NR in a unique position as a repurposable compound with potential applications in metabolic, neurodegenerative, and now ocular diseases, including the dry forms of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) characterized by geographic atrophy (Biță et al., 2023; Braidy et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the use of vitamin B3 derivatives such as NA and NAM has been well established in both clinical and biochemical practice for the improvement of energy metabolism and for prevention of niacin deficiency diseases; however, nicotinamide riboside represents a more recently discovered alternative that offers superior pharmacokinetic profiles and fewer side effects such as flushing or liver toxicity (Braidy et al., 2019; Mehmel et al., 2020). Preclinical studies have shown that NR supplementation rapidly increases tissue and circulating NAD⁺ levels across a range of animal models, including mice and rats, where it has been tested for its effects on metabolic dysfunction, neurodegeneration, insulin sensitivity, and mitochondrial biogenesis (Biță et al., 2023). Numerous clinical trials have demonstrated the safety and oral bioavailability of NR in healthy human subjects and in populations with metabolic or neurodegenerative conditions; for example, chronic supplementation at doses up to 2 g/day has been well tolerated and has successfully elevated NAD⁺ in middle-aged and older adults (Mehmel et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023). In addition to these metabolic and neuroprotective applications, NR has been investigated in various models of inflammation, organ injury, and even in oncology-related situations, where its ability to modulate cellular stress responses has proven beneficial (Biță et al., 2023). Notably, while NR has undergone extensive research in contexts such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and peripheral neuropathy, its application in ocular diseases—particularly dry AMD characterized by geographic atrophy—has been less comprehensively studied; however, emerging evidence supports the notion that NAD⁺ decline in the retina and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) may be mitigated by NAD⁺ precursors, providing a rationale for repurposing NR for dry AMD (Braidy et al., 2019). Veterinary studies and animal models have also utilized NR to stimulate mitochondrial function and improve bioenergetics in tissues with high metabolic demands, further solidifying its profile as a potent NAD⁺ booster with broad potential therapeutic applications (Biță et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
NR exerts its biological effects via a well-defined metabolic pathway that begins with its cellular uptake through equilibrative nucleoside transporters (ENT1, ENT2, and ENT4) followed by phosphorylation by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRK1 and NRK2) in the cytosol, which convert NR to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) (Biță et al., 2023; Braidy et al., 2019). NMN is subsequently adenylated by nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferases (NMNATs) to generate NAD⁺, thereby replenishing the intracellular NAD⁺ pool that is essential for numerous metabolic and signaling processes (Mehmel et al., 2020). The elevation of NAD⁺ levels activates a host of NAD⁺-dependent enzymes including sirtuins (SIRT1, SIRT3, among others) and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs), which are critical for deacetylating mitochondrial proteins, enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis, and facilitating DNA repair processes both in the nucleus and mitochondria (Biță et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2016). Activation of SIRT3 in particular within the mitochondria leads to the deacetylation and activation of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2), thereby reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitigating oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020). Moreover, increased NAD⁺ availability supports the activity of PARP enzymes that are required for efficient DNA repair, including the repair of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) damage arising from oxidative stress (Cimaglia et al., 2020). In RPE cells, this mechanism is particularly relevant as the high-energy–demand environment and frequent exposure to light-induced oxidative stress make robust mitochondrial and genomic maintenance critical to cell survival and homeostasis (Zhang et al., 2020). Additionally, NR’s effect on boosting NAD⁺ may facilitate the activation of autophagy and mitophagy pathways, leading to the clearance of damaged cellular components and improved cellular renewal processes (Braidy et al., 2019; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023). Such biochemical actions converge to foster an enhanced cellular defense mechanism against oxidative damage, support mitochondrial function through improved repair and turnover, and ultimately promote cellular longevity (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023; Biță et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underpinning the repurposing of NR for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that supplementation with NR will lead to an elevation of intracellular NAD⁺ pools specifically within retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby enhancing mitochondrial DNA repair and upregulating antioxidant defenses that mitigate the oxidative damage implicated in geographic atrophy (Biță et al., 2023). In vitro studies using iPSC-derived RPE cells from AMD donors have demonstrated that NR supplementation results in rapid increases in intracellular NAD⁺, which is accompanied by the activation of sirtuin-mediated deacetylation of key mitochondrial proteins (Jadeja et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020). This deacetylation is believed to lead to improved mitochondrial function as evidenced by restored maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) measured via Seahorse XF assays, and the lowering of reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels as detected by fluorescent probes such as DCFDA (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016). The expected outcome in RPE is that the elevated NAD⁺ not only promotes the repair of oxidative damage to mitochondrial DNA but also augments the intrinsic antioxidant enzyme systems—including upregulation of enzymes like SOD2 and catalase—which collectively reduce the cellular oxidative burden (Biță et al., 2023). As a result, NR supplementation is anticipated to stabilize the RPE cell phenotype, reduce markers of cellular senescence and apoptosis, and potentially restore a healthier metabolic profile in RPE cells, factors that are critical for halting or even reversing the progression of geographic atrophy (Jadeja et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016). Moreover, by enhancing the NAD⁺-dependent activation of PARP and other DNA repair enzymes, NR may directly improve the repair of mitochondrial and nuclear DNA damage that accumulates under chronic oxidative stress conditions prevalent in the aging retina (Braidy et al., 2019; Mehmel et al., 2020). In preclinical models of retinal degeneration such as light-induced retinal injury, systemic administration of NR has been shown to preserve retinal morphology, reduce photoreceptor apoptosis, and maintain tissue NAD⁺ levels despite strong oxidative challenges, which supports the translational rationale for its application in dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2020; Braidy et al., 2019). Ultimately, the expected therapeutic effect of NR in the treatment of geographic atrophy is to provide cytoprotection to the RPE by mitigating oxidative damage and improving mitochondrial function, thus slowing the progression of RPE degeneration and vision loss (Zhu et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020).

In evaluating NR (specifically the ChromaDex NR-100 formulation) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and promising attributes emerge alongside areas that warrant further investigation. One of the primary strengths of NR is its established reputation as a safe and orally bioavailable NAD⁺ precursor with extensive preclinical and clinical data supporting its ability to elevate NAD⁺ levels systemically and within specific target tissues (Mehmel et al., 2020). This property is particularly relevant for RPE cells because the high metabolic demands of the retina make efficient NAD⁺ replenishment crucial for maintaining mitochondrial function and for mediating effective DNA repair mechanisms (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Additionally, the robust mechanistic data showing that NR supplementation activates sirtuin pathways—most notably SIRT1 and SIRT3—and subsequently deacetylates and activates key mitochondrial and antioxidant enzymes provide a compelling molecular rationale for its potential to ameliorate oxidative stress in the RPE (Biță et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). The activation of these pathways not only enhances mitochondrial bioenergetics but also promotes the clearance of damaged cellular components through autophagy, which is expected to contribute to improved cell survival under oxidative challenge (Braidy et al., 2019; Jadeja et al., 2020).  
However, there are some weaknesses and critical gaps in the current data when it comes to translating these beneficial effects specifically to the context of geographic atrophy in dry AMD. Although preclinical models have demonstrated the protective effects of NR in retinal degeneration (particularly in light-induced injury models), direct evidence demonstrating that NR selectively elevates NAD⁺ pools in RPE cells derived from AMD patients, enhances mitochondrial DNA repair specifically in RPE, and reduces ROS levels to a degree that meaningfully impacts the progression of geographic atrophy remains limited (Braidy et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020). Furthermore, the chemical reactivity and inherent instability of NR have historically posed challenges to its synthesis, storage, and consistent formulation, raising concerns about batch-to-batch variability and the possibility of degradation products in commercial formulations; although recent advances and improved production standards appear to have mitigated these issues, further analytical validation is needed to ensure that the NR-100 formulation consistently meets high purity criteria (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Another consideration is that while the mechanisms underlying NR’s beneficial effects are well established in metabolic and neurodegenerative contexts, the unique metabolic and microenvironmental characteristics of the RPE in the aging eye—including the contributions of the local immune system, extracellular matrix alterations, and the interplay with the choroidal circulation—may represent additional variables that could influence NR’s efficacy in dry AMD, and these factors are not yet fully delineated (Biță et al., 2023; Cimaglia et al., 2020).

Moreover, early translational studies using iPSC-derived RPE from AMD donors have already begun to show that NR can reduce oxidative stress and restore metabolic function in these cells, lending credibility to its potential efficacy in geographic atrophy settings (Biță et al., 2023; Braidy et al., 2019).  
In summary, NR (ChromaDex NR-100) emerges as a highly promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD on the basis of its well-established ability to raise NAD⁺, activate sirtuin-mediated mitochondrial maintenance and DNA repair processes, and mitigate oxidative stress—all of which are central drivers of RPE degeneration in geographic atrophy (Zhang et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016). The strengths of this candidate include a robust mechanistic foundation, a favorable safety and pharmacokinetic profile established in other clinical contexts, and encouraging preclinical data that indirectly support its potential benefit in the retina (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020; Braidy et al., 2019). Nonetheless, significant challenges remain, particularly the need for direct evidence in RPE-specific and geographic atrophy models, confirmation of consistent formulation quality due to NR’s chemical instability, and the potential variability in tissue-specific uptake and metabolism in an aging ocular environment (Mehmel et al., 2020; Biță et al., 2023). Future studies should therefore focus on comprehensive in vitro investigations in primary and iPSC-derived RPE cells, detailed pharmacodynamic assessments in animal models of dry AMD, and ultimately carefully designed early-phase clinical trials targeting RPE function and retinal structure in patient populations with geographic atrophy (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016; Braidy et al., 2019).  
Overall, while there is a compelling mechanistic rationale and a solid foundation of preclinical and clinical data supporting the repurposing of NR for dry AMD, particularly in mitigating oxidative damage, enhancing mitochondrial DNA repair, and improving antioxidant defenses in RPE cells, further targeted research is required to validate these effects specifically in the context of geographic atrophy. The available literature suggests that NR has significant translational promise, and its favorable safety profile alongside extensive clinical experience in other indications positions it as a frontrunner among NAD⁺ precursors for potential therapeutic intervention in dry AMD (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). The next phase of research should therefore include detailed mechanistic studies in ocular models, combined with rigorous clinical endpoint evaluations to determine whether NR supplementation can effectively slow or reverse the degenerative processes underlying geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016; Jadeja et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin (also known as sirolimus and available as Abcam #ab120224) is a naturally occurring macrolide compound originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus. It belongs to the class of macrocyclic lactones and is known for its potent inhibitory effects on the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). This compound has been extensively used in various contexts such as immunosuppression, cancer therapy, and more recently, as a tool to modulate autophagy in age-related degenerative diseases. In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction and dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), rapamycin is being explored as a repurposed therapeutic candidate with the hypothesis that mTORC1 inhibition will enhance both general autophagy and selective mitophagy. This clearance of reactive oxygen species (ROS)–generating, damaged mitochondria may alleviate oxidative stress, reduce the accumulation of toxic lipofuscin compounds (including A2E), and ultimately slow the progression of dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, rapamycin was first discovered for its potent immunosuppressive properties and later developed for use in preventing transplant rejection and certain cancers. Its ability to inhibit mTORC1 has made it a valuable tool in research related to aging and neurodegeneration. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its effectiveness in modulating autophagy and protecting cellular integrity under stress conditions, particularly in the retinal environment. In animal models of retinal degeneration and even some early clinical trials, rapamycin was shown to reduce the accumulation of autofluorescent granules and inflammatory cytokines in the RPE, which are both hallmarks of dry AMD pathology (Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022). Notably, rapamycin has been administered via diverse routes, including intravitreal and subconjunctival injections, in attempts to treat geographic atrophy or other dry AMD phenotypes, although the clinical outcomes have been mixed. For example, clinical trials such as those referenced in studies with identifiers NCT00766649 and NCT01445548 demonstrated that while rapamycin was generally safe and well-tolerated in ocular applications, its efficacy in slowing down the progression of geographic atrophy and improving visual acuity remained limited (National Eye Institute, 2008; National Eye Institute, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These historical findings highlight both the promise and the challenges associated with translating rapamycin’s mechanistic benefits into robust clinical outcomes for dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary mechanism of rapamycin involves the formation of a complex with the immunophilin FKBP12. This complex binds to mTORC1 and inhibits its kinase activity, leading to a decrease in the phosphorylation of downstream targets such as ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K) and the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 (4EBP1). Under normal circumstances, active mTORC1 suppresses autophagy by phosphorylating these targets, which in turn prevents the formation of autophagosomes. By inhibiting mTORC1, rapamycin effectively removes this blockade, thereby promoting the induction of autophagy as evidenced by increased conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II and clearance of the autophagic substrate p62 (Zhang et al., 2015).

Within retinal pigment epithelial cells, this induction of autophagy is particularly important. RPE cells are responsible for the phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments; a process that generates large amounts of cellular debris and metabolic byproducts such as lipofuscin. In dry AMD, impaired autophagic flux leads to the accumulation of these compounds, which, in turn, contributes to oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Rapamycin’s inhibition of mTORC1 not only enhances general autophagy but also promotes selective mitochondrial clearance (mitophagy). Key players in the mitophagy pathway include the serine/threonine kinase PINK1 and the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin, both of which accumulate on depolarized mitochondria and signal their removal via autophagic mechanisms. By stimulating this PINK1/Parkin pathway, rapamycin enhances the clearance of damaged, ROS-generating mitochondria, thus preserving overall mitochondrial health (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).

Additionally, rapamycin’s downstream effects include activation of transcription factors such as TFEB, which regulates lysosomal biogenesis and further enhances the autophagic process. This dual action—promoting both autophagy and lysosomal function—helps to mitigate the accumulation of toxic aggregates such as lipofuscin and A2E in RPE, therefore reducing oxidative stress and inflammation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). Through these biochemical interactions, rapamycin establishes a cellular environment that is more capable of dealing with metabolic challenges and oxidative damage, both of which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Chang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed hypothesis, the administration of rapamycin in RPE cells is expected to result in a cascade of beneficial cellular events. In our proposed assay, rapamycin is anticipated to inhibit mTORC1 activity, leading to a measurable increase in autophagic flux. This will be evident from the enhanced lipidation of LC3-II, the clearance of p62 (an autophagy adaptor protein that accumulates when autophagy is impaired), and the activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway in response to oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2015).

The specific clearance of damaged mitochondria is particularly critical in the RPE, where mitochondrial dysfunction is a significant contributor to the generation of reactive oxygen species and subsequent cellular damage. By removing these dysfunctional mitochondria, rapamycin is expected to reduce intracellular ROS levels and thereby lower oxidative stress, a driving force in AMD pathology. In parallel, the enhanced autophagic degradation of accumulated lipofuscin and the toxic fluorophore A2E is predicted to further limit the inflammatory and apoptotic cascades triggered by these compounds, thus preserving RPE cell viability and function (Zhang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2025).

Moreover, the expression of PINK1 and Parkin in RPE cells has been well documented, and their activation is indicative of mitophagic turnover. Their proper functioning is a key determinant in mitochondrial quality control, and rapamycin is expected to potentiate this process, ensuring that mitochondria remain healthy and capable of maintaining cellular energy production and reducing the risk of cell death (Pinelli et al., 2025; Hyttinen et al., 2018). Given that impaired mitochondrial function and the resulting energy production deficits are central to the progression of dry AMD, the expected outcomes from rapamycin treatment would include not only a reduction in oxidative stress markers but also improvements in mitochondrial dynamics and overall cellular homeostasis. Such effects would ideally be reflected in functional assays measuring cell viability, mitochondrial respiration, and reductions in inflammatory cytokine production (Zhang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In our comprehensive evaluation of rapamycin as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and potential weaknesses emerge that warrant careful consideration. One of the key strengths of rapamycin lies in its well-characterized mechanism of action and its ability to broadly modulate autophagy through mTORC1 inhibition. Preclinical studies have repeatedly demonstrated that rapamycin can induce autophagic flux, leading to the clearance of cellular debris and damaged mitochondria in RPE cells. This is particularly compelling given the central role of impaired autophagy in the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, which are major pathological features of dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018). The dual-action mechanism—enhancing both autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis via TFEB activation—further supports its potential in addressing multiple aspects of the disease pathology, from oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction to inflammation and cellular senescence (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Another strength is the substantial body of preclinical evidence showing that rapamycin not only stimulates autophagy but also improves mitochondrial function. The activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway is particularly relevant since these proteins are indispensable for mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control. By facilitating the removal of ROS-generating, damaged mitochondria, rapamycin could directly impact the cellular energy balance and reduce damaging oxidative insults in the RPE, which is pivotal for maintaining retinal health (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).

Despite its promising mechanistic profile, several significant challenges remain. Clinical studies investigating the use of rapamycin for AMD have yielded mixed results. While the drug has been shown to be safe and tolerable in ocular applications, several clinical trials, such as those involving subconjunctival or intravitreal administration, did not demonstrate significant efficacy in halting the progression of geographic atrophy or improving visual acuity. In some instances, adverse effects such as decreased visual acuity and retinal thinning have been observed, raising concerns about the balance between therapeutic benefit and potential retinal toxicity (National Eye Institute, 2008; National Eye Institute, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These mixed clinical findings underscore the complexity of modulating mTORC1 in a disease with multifactorial etiology and suggest that the optimal dosage, treatment duration, and patient selection criteria still require refinement.

Furthermore, the variability in response among different donor-derived RPE cells—where only about 50% of AMD donor samples responded positively to rapamycin in certain studies—points to potential issues regarding patient heterogeneity and the need for personalized therapeutic regimens (Ebeling et al., 2020). This heterogeneity may be due to differences in the intrinsic capacity for autophagy, genetic variations affecting mitochondrial quality control, or the extent of existing cellular damage. Such variability complicates the development of standardized treatment protocols and could limit the broad applicability of rapamycin unless predictive biomarkers of response are identified (Zhang et al., 2015).

Another important consideration is the dual nature of autophagy in the context of RPE health. While enhancing autophagy can provide protective benefits by clearing damaged organelles and reducing oxidative stress, excessive autophagic flux under certain stress conditions might paradoxically contribute to cell death. This is especially relevant in advanced stages of dry AMD, where cellular stress is severe and prolonged autophagy induction might tip the balance toward detrimental outcomes rather than recovery (Chang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2019). In addition, the potential for rapamycin to interfere with beneficial mTOR signaling under specific conditions (for example, when mTOR activity supports survival pathways via growth factors such as nerve growth factor) further complicates its use, as evidenced by reports that observed mixed effects on retinal ganglion cell survival in different pathological contexts (Wang et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2021).

The delivery method and pharmacokinetics of rapamycin also represent important variables. While nanotechnology-based delivery systems—such as synthetic high-density lipoprotein nanoparticles—have shown promise in achieving more targeted and sustained delivery of rapamycin to the RPE (Mei et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2021), these strategies require further translational studies to assess their safety, efficacy, and scalability in clinical settings. Moreover, the risk of systemic side effects, including metabolic toxicities and immunosuppression, despite the generally favorable ocular safety profile observed in trials, necessitates caution in developing rapamycin-based therapies for chronic conditions like AMD (Wang et al., 2022).

In summary, rapamycin presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its robust mechanism of action—specifically, its capacity to inhibit mTORC1, thereby stimulating both general autophagy and the selective removal of damaged mitochondria via the PINK1/Parkin pathway. Preclinical evidence strongly supports the idea that such modulation can reduce oxidative stress, clear toxic accumulations like lipofuscin/A2E, and ultimately preserve mitochondrial and RPE cellular function (Zhang et al., 2015; Hyttinen et al., 2018). However, the translation of these benefits into clinical improvements remains uncertain, with several trials indicating that while rapamycin is safe and modulates cellular pathways implicated in AMD, its clinical efficacy in terms of preserving visual function has not been conclusively demonstrated. The heterogeneity in patient responses, the potential for adverse outcomes related to excessive autophagy, and the challenges in optimizing dosing and delivery all represent significant hurdles. These considerations suggest that while rapamycin is a promising candidate worthy of further investigation, its ultimate role in the treatment paradigm for dry AMD will depend on our ability to refine treatment regimens, develop predictive biomarkers for patient selection, and perhaps combine mTOR modulation with complementary therapeutic strategies that reinforce its protective effects while mitigating its risks (Wang et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2019).

Given the cumulative evidence, our overall recommendation is to continue exploring rapamycin as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, but with a strategic focus on further preclinical investigations that address the dose–response relationships in donor-derived RPE models and the development of advanced drug delivery systems. It will also be important to design future clinical trials with stratified patient populations and integrated biomarkers that can help identify responders. This iterative approach could eventually lead to a carefully balanced regimen where rapamycin’s autophagy-enhancing properties are harnessed to maintain retinal integrity while avoiding the pitfalls of over-inhibition or systemic toxicity. In essence, the promise of rapamycin in modulating autophagy to improve mitochondrial health and reduce oxidative stress in RPE cells is clear at the molecular and cellular levels, but translating these benefits into a safe and effective therapy for dry AMD will require overcoming substantial clinical challenges (Mei et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Strengths of rapamycin include its well-established mechanism of action, the significant supportive preclinical data demonstrating improvements in autophagic flux and mitochondrial clearance in RPE models, and its potential to address several key pathological features of dry AMD simultaneously. Weaknesses include the mixed clinical trial outcomes to date, the potential for adverse effects in certain contexts (including decreased visual acuity and retinal thinning), and the observed heterogeneity in therapeutic response among different patient samples. These factors highlight the importance of further mechanistic studies and carefully controlled clinical trials. Overall, rapamycin remains one of the more mechanistically promising candidates for repurposing in dry AMD, yet its future success will depend on how effectively we can tailor its delivery and dosing to maximize protective effects while minimizing risks in the vulnerable RPE of AMD patients (Niu et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022).

In conclusion, rapamycin’s role as an mTORC1 inhibitor with the capacity to induce autophagy and mitophagy presents an exciting therapeutic avenue for addressing the complex pathology of dry AMD. By alleviating the buildup of toxic metabolites and preserving mitochondrial health in RPE cells, rapamycin could potentially slow disease progression and preserve vision. Nonetheless, the balance between benefit and adverse effects remains delicate, and further research is essential to elucidate how best to leverage rapamycin’s molecular actions in a clinically meaningful way. This comprehensive review supports the continued investigation of rapamycin as a candidate for dry AMD therapy, provided that subsequent studies can address the highlighted challenges and refine the therapeutic strategy to achieve consistent, positive clinical outcomes (Mei et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022).
