1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Mdivi-1, known as mitochondrial division inhibitor 1 (catalog number Sigma-Aldrich M0199), is a synthetic small-molecule compound originally developed for research into mitochondrial dynamics. It belongs to a class of therapeutic agents that modulate mitochondrial fission by targeting the dynamin‐related protein 1 (DRP1). DRP1 is an essential GTPase responsible for driving mitochondrial fission, a process that maintains mitochondrial quality control but, when overactivated, can lead to fragmentation associated with cellular stress and apoptosis. Mdivi-1 was discovered via compound screening experiments aimed at identifying inhibitors of DRP1’s GTPase activity and has been characterized extensively in various in vitro and in vivo studies. Its discovery was motivated by the need to therapeutically intervene in pathologies where aberrant mitochondrial fission contributes to cellular dysfunction. As a representative of DRP1 inhibitory agents, Mdivi-1 has been widely used as an investigational tool in studies related to neurodegeneration, ischemia, and ocular diseases, where mitochondrial integrity is a key determinant of cell survival (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2020). Its synthetic origin and well-documented pharmacological profile render it a candidate for drug repurposing, with potential applications extending into the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) by addressing mitochondrial dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells.

2. Therapeutic History  
Mdivi-1 has a robust preclinical research history across a variety of models that involve oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Initial studies demonstrated that in retinal endothelial cells and neuronal tissues, inhibition of DRP1 by Mdivi-1 prevented excessive mitochondrial fragmentation under conditions of acute stress. In models of glaucoma, for instance, DRP1 overactivation associated with ocular hypertension leads to mitochondrial fragmentation and retinal ganglion cell death, and administration of Mdivi-1 was found to rescue these cells by preserving mitochondrial network integrity (Kim et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2021). Similarly, in photoreceptor cells following retinal detachment, Mdivi-1 treatment reduced the activation of apoptotic pathways—through downregulation of cleaved Caspase-3 and Bax—and consequently preserved cell morphology and function, indicating a protective effect mediated through the inhibition of DRP1-dependent fission (She et al., 2018). Furthermore, in ARPE-19 cells, which are commonly used as a model for RPE behavior, Mdivi-1 has been shown to mitigate the cytotoxic effects of oxidative stress induced by hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) by reducing mitochondrial fragmentation and cytochrome c release, thereby improving mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP production (Yako et al., 2021). Although Mdivi-1 has not yet been evaluated in large-scale clinical trials for dry AMD specifically, its use in diverse ocular models—ranging from diabetic retinopathy to retinal ischemia—provides compelling evidence that its mechanism could be beneficial in conditions marked by oxidative stress and RPE dysfunction, two hallmark features of dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). These cumulative findings support the repurposing hypothesis that targeting DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission could restore mitochondrial function and survival in RPE cells, thereby halting or slowing the degenerative cascade observed in dry AMD.

3. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, DRP1 is responsible for mediating mitochondrial fission through the constriction and subsequent division of mitochondrial membranes. Upon receiving various stress signals, DRP1 is recruited from the cytosol to the mitochondrial outer membrane where it oligomerizes and hydrolyzes GTP, driving membrane scission. Mdivi-1 specifically inhibits the GTPase activity of DRP1, thereby preventing its self-assembly and subsequent mitochondrial recruitment. This inhibition effectively blocks the fission process that is typically upregulated under conditions of oxidative stress and other cellular insults (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2020). Detailed biochemical investigations have demonstrated that when DRP1 activity is unopposed, mitochondrial fragmentation ensues, leading to diminished mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, decreased oxygen consumption rate (OCR), reduced ATP synthesis, and an increase in the generation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) (Yako et al., 2021). Mdivi-1 counters these deleterious cellular events by preserving the integrity of the mitochondrial network, enabling enhanced ATP production, and maintaining the mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP). Moreover, by inhibiting DRP1, Mdivi-1 reduces the stress-induced release of cytochrome c from the mitochondria—a central step in the intrinsic apoptotic pathway—thus lowering the activation of downstream caspases (She et al., 2018; Yako et al., 2021). In addition to these primary actions, some studies have noted that Mdivi-1 has reversible inhibitory effects on mitochondrial complex I, suggesting that its impact on mitochondrial bioenergetics may be multifaceted (Yako et al., 2021). Such dual actions may serve to further stabilize mitochondrial function under stress.

4. Expected Effect  
Under conditions relevant to dry age-related macular degeneration, such as chronic oxidative stress incident on RPE cells, Mdivi-1 is anticipated to exert a multi-pronged cytoprotective effect. In the proposed assay using H₂O₂-treated ARPE-19 cells—a well-established in vitro model to mimic the oxidative stress environment of dry AMD—the primary expected effect is the inhibition of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission (Yako et al., 2021). By stabilizing mitochondrial dynamics, Mdivi-1 should also improve cellular bioenergetics through enhanced OCR and increased ATP production, both critical parameters that are typically compromised in stressed RPE cells (Yako et al., 2021). The anticipated outcome of these events is a reduction in cell death and apoptosis, as well as improved phagocytic function—an essential role of RPE cells in the maintenance of retinal homeostasis. Furthermore, by mitigating the accumulation of mtROS, Mdivi-1 is expected to lessen oxidative stress, thereby curbing the degenerative processes that are a central component of dry AMD pathophysiology (Yako et al., 2021; Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025). In essence, the mechanistic intervention afforded by Mdivi-1 aims to interrupt the cycle of mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage that leads to RPE cell apoptosis, which is a critical driver of disease progression in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021).

5. Overall Evaluation  
In evaluating Mdivi-1 as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current body of literature. Among its strengths, Mdivi-1 is underpinned by a strong mechanistic rationale: the inhibition of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission is a well-validated approach to restore mitochondrial function in the face of oxidative stress. Preclinical studies have consistently demonstrated that Mdivi-1 preserves mitochondrial network integrity, reduces the production of harmful reactive oxygen species, and prevents the release of apoptogenic factors, thereby facilitating cell survival in retinal models (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2020; Yako et al., 2021). Its efficacy in multiple ocular contexts—including models of glaucoma, retinal detachment, and diabetic retinopathy—highlights the versatility of its cytoprotective actions, which may be directly relevant to the RPE dysfunction and oxidative injury observed in dry AMD (Kim et al., 2015; She et al., 2018). From a biochemical standpoint, the ability of Mdivi-1 to enhance mitochondrial bioenergetics by improving OCR and ATP production, while simultaneously preserving mitochondrial membrane potential, addresses essential aspects of RPE cell metabolism that are often impaired in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Furthermore, the compound’s capacity to reduce apoptotic signaling, as evidenced by decreased cytochrome c release and lower caspase activity, is particularly promising given the established link between mitochondrial-mediated apoptosis and RPE cell loss in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Despite these promising attributes, several limitations and challenges deserve consideration. First, while the preclinical evidence supporting Mdivi-1’s efficacy is compelling, there remains a notable gap in clinical data, particularly in the context of dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Another potential weakness arises from the dual inhibitory effects of Mdivi-1. Some investigations have reported that Mdivi-1 also exhibits reversible inhibition of mitochondrial complex I, which could complicate its therapeutic profile by inadvertently affecting normal mitochondrial respiration (Yako et al., 2021). Moreover, the chronic inhibition of DRP1 raises important questions about the broader physiological implications of interfering with mitochondrial dynamics (Mohammad & Kowluru, 2022; She et al., 2018). Furthermore, the in vitro models currently used, predominantly involving H₂O₂-treated ARPE-19 cells, may not entirely mimic the in vivo microenvironment of the human retina in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). The overall therapeutic window and safety profile of Mdivi-1 also require further elucidation (Yako et al., 2021). Despite these challenges, the mechanistic insights generated from a diverse array of experimental models suggest that Mdivi-1 holds considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its capacity to restore mitochondrial integrity, mitigate oxidative stress, and inhibit apoptotic cascades directly addresses several of the pathogenic mechanisms implicated in dry AMD. Given that current treatments for dry AMD are limited and mainly supportive, a disease-modifying therapy that targets mitochondrial dysfunction would represent a significant advancement in the management of this debilitating disorder (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2015). In summary, Mdivi-1’s strengths lie in its well-characterized mechanism of action, demonstrated efficacy in preserving mitochondrial dynamics under stress, and its potential to enhance cell survival in models of retinal degeneration (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2015; Yako et al., 2021).

Future studies must address the nuances of chronic DRP1 inhibition, optimize dosing regimens, evaluate long-term safety, and conduct thorough pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiling in ocular tissues to fully realize the potential of Mdivi-1 in the clinical management of dry AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021).

In conclusion, the evidence provided by numerous preclinical studies strongly indicates that Mdivi-1’s inhibition of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission offers a promising therapeutic strategy for dry age-related macular degeneration. The compound’s ability to maintain mitochondrial network integrity, enhance bioenergetics, and suppress apoptotic cascades under conditions of oxidative stress in RPE cells is particularly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Although challenges remain in addressing the potential off-target effects and ensuring long-term safety in the clinical setting, the mechanistic rationale and supporting preclinical data justify further investigation into the utility of Mdivi-1 as a repurposed candidate for this currently untreatable condition. As the drug development process progresses, a focused effort on meticulous in vivo testing, formulation development for ocular delivery, and comprehensive pharmacological evaluations will be critical to harnessing the full therapeutic potential of Mdivi-1 for patients with dry AMD (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2015; She et al., 2018; Yako et al., 2021).

ZLN005 (MedChemExpress HY-100726) is a synthetic small-molecule compound that belongs to the benzimidazole class. Benzimidazole derivatives have a long history in medicinal chemistry for their wide-ranging biological activities, including antihelminthic, anti-inflammatory, and metabolic modulating effects. In the case of ZLN005, it has been identified specifically as a selective transcriptional activator of peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator‐1 alpha (PGC-1α), a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defense. The synthesis and chemical derivation of ZLN005, although not detailed exhaustively in the provided literature, follow typical synthetic protocols for benzimidazole compounds, which often involve the condensation of o-phenylenediamine with carboxylic acid derivatives to yield a benzimidazole core. This structural class is known not only for its high affinity to various protein targets but also for favorable pharmacokinetic properties that have motivated its use in drug development efforts. Several studies have demonstrated that ZLN005 effectively induces PGC-1α expression in various cell types, including skeletal muscle and particularly the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis (Satish et al., 2018). Initially, ZLN005 emerged from screening studies designed to identify small molecules that could stimulate PGC-1α expression. Early research in cellular models demonstrated that ZLN005 enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and upregulates the expression of downstream oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and antioxidant genes, which in turn improves mitochondrial health and overall cellular energy metabolism (Satish et al., 2018). Preclinical studies using ARPE-19 cells—a well-accepted human RPE cell line—demonstrated that ZLN005 markedly upregulates PGC-1α expression and its associated transcription factors and antioxidant enzymes. These investigations have shown that ZLN005 can confer significant protection against oxidative stress-induced cell death when cells are exposed to prooxidative agents such as hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL) and sodium iodate (NaIO₃) (Satish et al., 2018). Although ZLN005 has not yet undergone extensive clinical evaluation specifically for dry AMD, its robust activity in stimulating mitochondrial function and providing cytoprotection in RPE models forms a compelling rationale for its repurposing. Studies in other systems, including cardiomyocytes and skeletal muscle, support its therapeutic use in settings of bioenergetic decline and oxidative damage, which are hallmarks of many age-related degenerative diseases (Ma et al., 2023; Moradi, 2022). Mechanism of Action:  
The pharmacological efficacy of ZLN005 is tightly linked to its mechanism of action as an activator of PGC-1α. PGC-1α is a transcriptional coactivator that regulates a myriad of genes implicated in energy metabolism, mitochondrial biogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, and antioxidant protection. In RPE cells—where the maintenance of a high mitochondrial integrity is crucial for visual function—the expression of PGC-1α is fundamental to mitigating oxidative stress and maintaining metabolic homeostasis (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Iacovelli et al., 2016). ZLN005 increases the expression levels of PGC-1α by enhancing its transcription, culminating in the upregulation of a host of downstream target genes. This includes key mitochondrial genes such as ATP50, COX4, COX5b, and NDUFB5, all of which are involved in oxidative phosphorylation and energy production (Satish et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025).

At the molecular level, ZLN005 promotes the transcriptional program by potentially modulating AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) activity, a well-known regulator of PGC-1α function. The compound’s facilitation of PGC-1α nuclear translocation and its catalytic coactivation leads to the stimulation of mitochondrial replication and repair processes, thereby increasing mitochondrial mass and mtDNA copy number (Satish et al., 2018). In parallel, the upregulation of PGC-1α by ZLN005 induces the expression of several endogenous antioxidant enzymes, including superoxide dismutases (SOD1 and SOD2) and mitochondrial thioredoxin 2 (TXN2). This cascade of events enhances the cellular capacity to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS), thus lowering mitochondrial superoxide production and reducing the levels of oxidative stress markers such as 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), a product of lipid peroxidation frequently associated with degenerative retinal changes (Satish et al., 2018).

Furthermore, ZLN005 appears to improve overall mitochondrial bioenergetics. It has been observed to increase both basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates (OCR) in RPE cells, indicating an enhanced capacity for ATP synthesis under both steady-state and stress conditions (Satish et al., 2018). The compound also augments the spare respiratory capacity, which is critical for cellular survival when faced with acute energy demands during oxidative stress. Such improvements in mitochondrial function are directly relevant to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, where RPE cells experience an energy deficit due to progressive mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic oxidative injury (Felszeghy et al., 2019). Additionally, by upregulating PGC-1α, ZLN005 may indirectly influence other cellular processes, including autophagy and lipid metabolism, both of which are altered in the aging RPE and contribute to the formation of drusen—the hallmark deposits seen in dry AMD (Zhou et al., 2024).

It is important to emphasize that the protective effects of ZLN005 are markedly dependent on the presence of functional PGC-1α. Experiments in which PGC-1α expression was silenced in RPE cells resulted in a significant loss of the cytoprotective benefits conferred by ZLN005, underscoring the compound’s mechanism-specific action (Satish et al., 2018). Parallel studies in non-ocular cell types, such as skeletal muscle myotubes and alveolar epithelial cells, have further supported its role in enhancing mitochondrial function and regulating oxidative stress through similar molecular pathways (Zhang et al., 2013; Bleckwehl et al., 2025). Thus, the molecular interactions initiated by ZLN005—ranging from the activation of PGC-1α to the subsequent stimulation of antioxidant enzymes and mitochondrial biogenesis—form the crux of its therapeutic utility, specifically in countering the bioenergetic decline characteristic of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Given the central involvement of mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the therapeutic hypothesis for ZLN005 is that its activation of PGC-1α in retinal pigment epithelial cells will restore mitochondrial homeostasis and augment cellular antioxidant defenses. In the proposed assays, treatment with ZLN005 is expected to upregulate PGC-1α expression in RPE cells, thereby triggering a cascade of downstream events that lead to enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis. This includes an increase in mtDNA copy number and the expression of mitochondrial genes that are essential for optimal oxidative phosphorylation performance (Satish et al., 2018). As mitochondrial function improves, RPE cells should exhibit higher basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates, indicative of an improved metabolic profile and increased capacity to generate ATP under both normal and stress conditions (Satish et al., 2018).

The antioxidative effects of ZLN005 are also expected to manifest in augmented levels of enzymes such as SOD1, SOD2, and TXN2, which collectively enhance the cell’s capability to scavenge reactive oxygen species. These biochemical events are critical because the accumulation of oxidative stress in RPE cells, driven by chronic exposure to high levels of ROS, is a significant contributor to cell degeneration in dry AMD (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Blasiak et al., 2021). With improved mitochondrial function and reduced oxidative stress, it is anticipated that ZLN005 treatment will lead to a decrease in the accumulation of oxidative damage markers like 4-HNE, thereby mitigating processes that lead to RPE cell apoptosis and the subsequent photoreceptor degeneration observed in dry AMD (Blasiak et al., 2021; Iacovelli et al., 2016).

Therefore, the expected effect of ZLN005 in the proposed assay is a robust cytoprotective response in RPE cells. This would be characterized by improved cell viability, restoration of mitochondrial respiratory function, and a reduction in stress-induced apoptotic markers—a constellation of effects that directly addresses the bioenergetic and oxidative challenges underlying dry AMD (Satish et al., 2018). Additionally, since PGC-1α is known to regulate lipid metabolism and prevent lipid droplet accumulation—a process that may be linked to the formation of drusen in the AMD retina—the activation of PGC-1α by ZLN005 could also have beneficial effects on lipid handling within the RPE (Zhou et al., 2024; Iacovelli et al., 2016). Thus, through these concerted mechanisms, ZLN005 is anticipated to stabilize or even improve RPE function, thereby halting or reversing aspects of the degenerative cascade that leads to vision loss in dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
A comprehensive evaluation of ZLN005 reveals several compelling strengths as well as notable weaknesses that should be weighed in the context of repurposing it for the treatment of dry AMD. One of the principal strengths of ZLN005 lies in its well-defined mechanism of action. By selectively activating PGC-1α, ZLN005 directly targets the mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress that are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. The upregulation of PGC-1α leads to improvements in mitochondrial biogenesis, an increase in the expression of mitochondrial OXPHOS genes, and the enhancement of antioxidant defenses—all factors that are critically compromised in the diseased RPE (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Blasiak et al., 2021). This mechanistic rationale is further supported by in vitro studies showing that ZLN005 can effectively reduce prooxidant-induced cell death and improve mitochondrial respiratory parameters such as basal respiration, maximal respiration, and spare respiratory capacity (Satish et al., 2018).

Another strength is the translational potential implied by the compound’s efficacy in multiple cell types. ZLN005 has not only demonstrated protective effects in RPE cells but has also been shown to modulate mitochondrial activity in skeletal muscle and hepatic cells. This broad-spectrum improvement in energy metabolism indicates that its bioenergetic benefits may be harnessed in the complex metabolic environment of the RPE, where energy deficits contribute to dry AMD pathology (Satish et al., 2018). Achieving a robust activation of PGC-1α is particularly attractive because it addresses both the cellular energy production and ROS management simultaneously, which are two critical determinants of RPE cell survival and function (Iacovelli et al., 2016; Rosales et al., 2019).

Furthermore, the specificity of ZLN005’s action has been validated by studies where the loss of PGC-1α abrogated its cytoprotective effects, underscoring that its efficacy is tightly linked to the activation of this pivotal regulatory pathway (Satish et al., 2018). This is an important consideration because it suggests that the therapeutic effects can be fine-tuned by modulating the expression or activity of PGC-1α. In the context of dry AMD, where PGC-1α levels are often diminished or dysregulated, the targeted upregulation provided by ZLN005 offers a focused therapeutic intervention.

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and challenges remain. Foremost, the majority of the supportive evidence for ZLN005’s efficacy in protecting RPE cells has been generated through in vitro studies using cell lines such as ARPE-19. While these models are indispensable for preliminary evaluation, they do not fully recapitulate the complex in vivo environment of the human retina, and the translatability of these effects into clinical benefit remains to be demonstrated (Satish et al., 2018). Additionally, the current body of literature shows that some reports have emerged from journals of variable quality; this introduces a degree of uncertainty regarding the reproducibility of the findings and necessitates rigorous validation of these results in higher-order in vivo models and, eventually, clinical trials (Satish et al., 2018).

This includes the risk that enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis in non-target cells could lead to dysregulated energy metabolism or contribute to unwanted proliferative responses (Satish et al., 2018; Bleckwehl et al., 2025).

Given the slow progression of dry AMD and the need for long-term treatment, any adverse effects or suboptimal pharmacokinetic properties could significantly limit the compound’s clinical use (Satish et al., 2018; Iacovelli et al., 2016).

Additionally, while the activation of PGC-1α is a promising strategy for mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction, the role of PGC-1α in the retina is complex. Overexpression of PGC-1α has been linked in some studies to increased susceptibility to light-induced retinal damage or other forms of stress, suggesting that a delicate balance must be maintained to achieve therapeutic benefit without tipping the scales towards potential toxicity or dysregulation of cellular homeostasis (Iacovelli et al., 2016; Blasiak et al., 2021). This dual nature of PGC-1α activity means that careful titration of ZLN005 dosing—and possibly the development of combination therapies—may be necessary to harness its protective effects while avoiding exacerbation of retinal stress under certain conditions.

In summary, ZLN005 emerges as a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its well-characterized mechanism of stimulating PGC-1α expression, its ability to enhance mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses, and the encouraging results obtained from in vitro studies in ARPE-19 cells. Its molecular action aligns closely with the pathophysiological profiles observed in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress contribute to RPE degeneration. Key areas that require further investigation include detailed pharmacokinetic studies in ocular models, confirmation of efficacy in animal models of dry AMD, and a full safety profile with chronic dosing regimens (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Blasiak et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2019).

Indeed, the multifactorial nature of AMD means that a monotherapy approach may be insufficient, and ZLN005’s role could be most valuable when combined with other agents that complement its effects on mitochondrial and oxidative stress parameters (Rosales et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2025).

From a strategic drug development perspective, ZLN005 offers several attractive points for further exploration. Its synthetic origin as a benzimidazole derivative means that established methods exist for its production and modification, allowing for potential structure-activity relationship (SAR) studies aimed at enhancing its potency, selectivity, and ocular bioavailability. Such modifications could lead to derivatives with improved pharmacokinetic profiles tailored for retinal delivery. Moreover, leveraging advanced drug delivery systems, such as nanoparticle carriers or sustained-release formulations, could further enhance the therapeutic window of ZLN005 in the eye while minimizing systemic exposure and associated off-target effects (Bleckwehl et al., 2025; Miller et al., 2019).

In conclusion, the repurposing of ZLN005 for the treatment of dry AMD is supported by a compelling mechanistic rationale and a growing body of preclinical evidence that underscores its potential to restore mitochondrial dynamics and counteract oxidative stress in retinal pigment epithelial cells. The strengths of this candidate include its specificity for PGC-1α activation, its demonstrated ability to enhance mitochondrial function and energy metabolism, and its protective effects against oxidative injury in vitro. On the other hand, the limitations primarily stem from the current reliance on in vitro data, the need for more rigorous in vivo validation, and uncertainties regarding its pharmacokinetic behavior in ocular tissues. Therefore, while ZLN005 stands out as a scientifically promising candidate, advancing it through the drug development pipeline will require concerted efforts to address these gaps through detailed preclinical studies, formulation optimization, and eventually, well-designed clinical trials to determine its efficacy and safety in patients with dry AMD (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Rosales et al., 2019).

Overall, the data presented through multiple independent studies provide a strong foundation for considering ZLN005 as a viable therapeutic candidate in the repurposing paradigm for dry age-related macular degeneration. With further validation and refinement, itself or an optimized derivative could potentially offer a new strategy to preserve RPE integrity and maintain visual function in AMD patients, addressing a significant unmet medical need in the realm of retinal degenerative diseases (Rosales et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2025). Continued research efforts should focus on delineating the precise molecular signatures of ZLN005’s effects in RPE cells, assessing its long-term impact on retinal morphology and function in vivo, and investigating its interactions with other signaling cascades implicated in AMD progression (Satish et al., 2018). Only through such thorough and multidisciplinary evaluations can the true therapeutic potential of ZLN005 for dry AMD be accurately determined and translated into clinical benefit.

In summary, while challenges remain in translating the promising in vitro results to clinical outcomes, the accumulated evidence suggests that ZLN005’s activation of PGC-1α represents a credible and innovative strategy to counteract the bioenergetic decline in RPE cells—a central feature in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is a naturally occurring long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (LC-PUFA) that has been isolated from marine sources, such as fish oil, and is commercially available in a highly purified form (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich D2534). DHA is synthesized via metabolic elongation and desaturation of dietary alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) in mammals; however, this endogenous conversion is limited, and direct dietary intake is critical for maintaining adequate retinal DHA levels (Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14). Belonging to the omega-3 class of fatty acids, DHA has long been recognized for its important roles in maintaining membrane structure and function, particularly in neural tissues and the retina where it is highly concentrated in photoreceptor outer segments and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) membranes (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3). Its polyunsaturated nature—with six cis double bonds—confers unique biophysical properties, enabling DHA to increase membrane fluidity and participate in critical signaling cascades. The compound has been used extensively as a nutritional supplement and has been incorporated in various formulations aimed at cardiovascular health, cognitive function, and ocular protection, establishing a robust safety profile over decades of human use (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Skowronska-Krawczyk & Chao, 2019, pp. 3–4).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past two decades, extensive research has explored the role of DHA and related omega-3 fatty acids in maintaining retinal function and potentially preventing age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Epidemiologic studies have consistently demonstrated an inverse association between dietary fish and high omega-3 fatty acid intake and the risk of developing AMD, suggesting that populations with higher DHA consumption tend to exhibit a lower incidence of both early and, to some extent, advanced forms of the disease (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). In clinical settings, large-scale randomized controlled trials, such as AREDS2, incorporated DHA (and EPA) into a multi-nutrient formula designed originally for AMD, though the overall randomized trial outcomes have been mixed, with some studies finding no statistically significant benefit for progression to late AMD (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). Pilot clinical trials and observational cohort studies, including NAT-1 and NAT-2, have assessed DHA supplementation in subjects with drusenoid lesions or early-stage AMD; while some of these studies have shown promising improvements in blood biomarkers (e.g., increased red blood cell DHA levels) and correlations with reduced AMD progression, the clinical efficacy remains under debate (Querques et al., 2016, pp. 2–4; Querques et al., 2011, pp. 7–8). Notably, evidence from animal models suggests that dietary DHA may protect against light-induced retinal degeneration and reduce the accumulation of deleterious lipid peroxidation products, although some preclinical studies also caution that DHA’s susceptibility to oxidation could, under certain conditions, worsen retinal injury (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic hypothesis for using DHA in dry AMD is based on its predicted ability to incorporate into the mitochondrial membranes of RPE cells, thereby enhancing membrane fluidity and protecting against oxidative damage to the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes. Under normal cellular conditions, DHA—owing to its multiple methylene-interrupted cis double bonds—integrates into phospholipid bilayers and modulates biophysical properties such as fluidity, permeability, and thickness (Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33). In mitochondrial membranes, this incorporation is thought to replace more saturated fatty acids such as arachidonic acid, ultimately reducing lipid peroxidation and mitigating oxidative stress that is deleterious to ETC function (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9). In vitro studies have shown that DHA supplementation in retinal cell cultures can decrease markers of apoptosis and preserve mitochondrial membrane integrity, with a concomitant increase in anti-apoptotic proteins (e.g., Bcl-2) (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 2–4).  
In addition, DHA is enzymatically converted under conditions of oxidative stress into neuroprotective docosanoids, such as neuroprotectin D1 (NPD1), which can inhibit pro-inflammatory gene expression and reduce cell death in RPE and photoreceptor cells (Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14; LaFuente et al., 2021, p. 13). This conversion not only contributes to countering local inflammation but also supports cellular health by modulating intracellular signaling pathways, particularly those involving NF-κB and other transcription factors critical for managing oxidative stress (Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14; Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14). The proposition to repurpose DHA for dry AMD is underpinned by compelling mechanistic rationale and epidemiologic associations, yet it is not without its challenges and limitations. One clear strength is DHA’s established role as an essential component of retinal cell membranes. Its ability to modulate membrane fluidity, serve as a precursor to neuroprotective mediators like NPD1, and exert anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions provide multiple mechanistic pathways through which it may mitigate the cellular stressors implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis (Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14; Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14).

A significant weakness in the current body of research is the lack of direct mechanistic studies that quantitatively document DHA incorporation into RPE mitochondrial membranes and its subsequent effects on mitochondrial parameters. In summary, while the epidemiologic literature and preclinical studies provide an encouraging backdrop for the repurposing of DHA as a therapeutic agent in dry AMD—by showing that high DHA intake is associated with a reduced risk of AMD and that DHA can confer mitochondrial and anti-oxidative benefits in retinal models—the critical mechanistic endpoints that support our specific hypothesis are not yet fully substantiated in the published literature. The overall evaluation is that DHA has substantial mechanistic promise, safety, and historical use as a nutritional supplement; however, further robust mechanistic studies and carefully designed clinical trials are necessary to validate its specific effects on mitochondrial function in RPE cells and to determine whether these biochemical improvements translate into a clinically significant slowing of dry AMD progression (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Resveratrol is a naturally occurring polyphenolic compound belonging to the stilbene class and is structurally defined as 3,5,4′-trihydroxystilbene. It is biosynthesized by plants such as Vitis vinifera (grapes), Japanese Knotweed, and various berries in response to stress factors like injury or pathogen attack, and it is a well‐recognized phytoalexin with a molecular formula of C14H12O3 (Bel, 2020; Pop et al., 2022). Originally isolated from the White Hellebore in the mid-20th century and later found in red wine due to grape skin fermentation, resveratrol has garnered significant attention not only for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties but also for its potential benefits in cardiovascular and neuroprotective contexts (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pop et al., 2022). As such, resveratrol—and by extension its commercial version (Cayman Chemical #70580) used in our studies—is classified as a nutraceutical and drug candidate with a long track record of investigative research including applications in aging, inflammation, and ocular health (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pop et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
A considerable volume of biochemical, preclinical, and early clinical literature has explored resveratrol’s broad spectrum of activities. Historically, resveratrol has been investigated primarily for its cardioprotective and neuroprotective effects, as well as its anti-aging properties. In the realm of ophthalmology, several in vitro and animal studies have focused on its role in retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD), diabetic retinopathy (DR), and glaucoma. For instance, its use in RPE cell models has shown promising evidence for ameliorating oxidative stress-induced damage, a central factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Clinical investigations have attempted to translate these findings, as exemplified by the terminated clinical trial NCT02625376 that investigated resveratrol for exudative AMD (Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015), highlighting both the potential and the challenges involved in its clinical application (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Beyond ocular applications, resveratrol’s inclusion in various nutraceutical formulations underscores its established safety profile when administered at low-to-moderate doses, although issues pertaining to bioavailability and rapid systemic metabolism have been recurrent themes in the literature (Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, resveratrol exerts its effects primarily by modulating multiple intracellular signaling cascades. The central hypothesis we are testing is that resveratrol activates the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells—a pathway integral to regulating mitochondrial biogenesis and the antioxidant defense system. Activation of SIRT1, a NAD+-dependent deacetylase, by resveratrol increases the deacetylation and activation of its downstream effector, AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Once activated, AMPK facilitates the phosphorylation and activation of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1 alpha (PGC-1α) in the cytoplasm, which subsequently translocates to the nucleus to upregulate the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and antioxidant responses, including the gene encoding superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). This cascade not only improves mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and spare respiratory capacity—critical indicators of cellular health under oxidative stress—but also promotes an overall enhancement of cellular resilience against reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Bel, 2020; Bryl et al., 2022). Further molecular studies indicate that resveratrol can also modulate extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERK1/2) and mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK), contributing additional layers of cytoprotection through anti-apoptotic effects (Pop et al., 2022; Pop et al., 2022). Together, these mechanistic insights provide a comprehensive biochemical framework through which resveratrol is hypothesized to mitigate the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in RPE cells—a primary factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2021; Bryl et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of the proposed assay for dry AMD, our expectation is that resveratrol will exert a multifaceted protective effect on RPE cells under oxidative challenge. Specifically, when RPE cells are exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as a model for oxidative stress, resveratrol is anticipated to counteract the resultant mitochondrial dysfunction by upregulating antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2, thereby reducing intracellular ROS levels (Bel, 2020; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Restoration of the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) is a critical endpoint, as it directly reflects cellular energy status and the ability of mitochondria to sustain ATP synthesis under stress (Buonfiglio et al., 2024). In addition, an improvement in spare respiratory capacity—the measure of a cell’s ability to respond to increased energy demands—should be evident, reflecting enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and a greater capacity for cellular repair mechanisms (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bryl et al., 2022). These cytoprotective effects have been demonstrated in in vitro studies using ARPE-19 and other human retinal pigment epithelial cell lines, and they resonate with the established role of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis in mediating energy metabolism and antioxidative defenses in the retina (Bryl et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021). Moreover, by decreasing the accrual of oxidative damage, resveratrol is expected to limit apoptotic signaling pathways, which are crucial in slowing the progressive degeneration observed in dry AMD (Bel, 2020; Pop et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
The cumulative evidence from preclinical studies strongly supports the potential of resveratrol as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, especially considering its capacity to modulate mitochondrial function and activate intrinsic antioxidant defenses. The activation of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis not only augments mitochondrial biogenesis but also enhances the expression of key antioxidant enzymes required to neutralize ROS, thereby directly addressing one of the primary mechanisms underlying AMD pathology (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bryl et al., 2022). One of the major strengths of resveratrol is its pleiotropic mode of action; beyond its antioxidant properties, its anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic activities further consolidate its candidacy for chronic conditions like dry AMD (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Bel, 2020). Another potential weakness is the dose-dependent duality of its mechanism, where low doses predominantly mediate SIRT1-dependent effects, whereas higher doses might trigger SIRT1-independent pathways, possibly leading to off-target effects or toxicity (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Such a narrow therapeutic window necessitates a precise optimization of dosing regimens and formulation strategies. Despite these challenges, the overarching trend in preclinical research underscores that with proper formulation and dosing strategies, resveratrol could excel as an adjuvant or even monotherapy for protecting RPE cells from oxidative injury and, consequently, for the management of dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

In-Depth Analysis of Preclinical and Clinical Evidence:  
Numerous in vitro studies have characterized the effect of resveratrol on retinal pigment epithelial cells, notably ARPE-19 cell lines, under conditions of oxidative stress. Such studies consistently demonstrate that resveratrol treatment leads to a measurable reduction in ROS levels, a decrease in markers of apoptosis, and an overall improvement in mitochondrial parameters including Δψm and spare respiratory capacity (Bel, 2020; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). These findings are reinforced by experiments showing that resveratrol can mitigate blue light-induced retinal damage and preserve cell viability, further supporting its relevance in ocular pathologies where light-induced oxidative stress is a contributing factor (Bel, 2020). Complementary studies in animal models have shown that resveratrol can reduce inflammatory cytokine secretion and inhibit processes such as choroidal neovascularization, which has implications not only for dry AMD but also for its neovascular (wet) counterpart (Bryl et al., 2022; Bel, 2020).

Experimental data also show that SOD2 expression is significantly increased following resveratrol treatment, corroborating the compound’s role in boosting the cellular antioxidant capacity (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Given the multifaceted biological activities of resveratrol and the encouraging preclinical evidence in models of oxidative stress-induced RPE damage, it holds considerable promise as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
A-438079 is a synthetic small-molecule antagonist of the purinergic P2X7 receptor (P2X7R) originating from Abbott Laboratories’ disubstituted tetrazole series discovered by high-throughput screening and refined by structure–activity relationship (SAR) optimization within a 1-benzyl-5-aryltetrazole chemotype (tetrazole > triazole > pyrazole/imidazole in potency) (Romagnoli et al., 2008; Carroll et al., 2009). A-438079’s structure has been disclosed as 3-((5-(2,3-dichlorophenyl)-1H-tetrazol-1-yl)methyl)pyridine, capturing the two key medicinal chemistry decisions that produced a selective, drug-like P2X7 antagonist: (i) a conserved 2,3-dichlorophenyl “left-hand” aryl that supports potency and (ii) installation of a 3-pyridyl “right-hand” substituent to overcome the solubility liabilities of the original 1-benzyl-5-aryltetrazoles while maintaining submicromolar activity at human/rat P2X7 (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; Romagnoli et al., 2008; Carroll et al., 2009). Functionally, A-438079 is a reversible, competitive P2X7 antagonist that inhibits BzATP-stimulated calcium flux, P2X7-associated macropore formation, and downstream IL-1β release in macrophage-lineage systems, consistent with canonical P2X7 pharmacology linked to NLRP3 inflammasome activation (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007). Cross-source potency data place A-438079 in the mid-nanomolar to low-submicromolar range at human and rat P2X7: human P2X7 pIC50 values of ~6.3–6.9, rat P2X7 pIC50 ~6.5, and functional IC50 estimates of ~0.1 µM (rat) and ~0.3 µM (human), with high selectivity against other P2 subtypes (e.g., P2X7 IC50 0.06 µM vs >100 µM for other subtypes in one panel) (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; El Idrissi et al., 2024; Nagy, 2013). A-438079 was commercialized by Tocris (circa 2008) as a first widely available, selective P2X7 antagonist probe, enabling consistent interrogation of P2X7 biology in vitro and in vivo beyond earlier nonselective tools (e.g., KN-62, Evans Blue) (Felix et al., 2012). Within the broader class, many P2X7 antagonists have reached advanced preclinical characterization; multi-parameter tables in retinal disease–focused reviews list A-438079 as active at human/rat P2X7 with a reported brain:plasma ratio near 2.0 (suggesting central barrier penetration) and note that progress toward ocular/CNS indications has been limited by species specificity and insufficient barrier penetration for some chemotypes (Fletcher et al., 2019).  

Therapeutic History  
A-438079 and related Abbott “A-series” P2X7 antagonists established robust preclinical efficacy in neuropathic and inflammatory pain models, aligning with the role of P2X7-driven IL-1β/IL-18 signaling in nociception and neuroinflammation (Carroll et al., 2009). A-438079 reduced mechanical allodynia in the Chung and Bennett rat models, showed activity in vincristine neuropathy and the formalin persistent pain test, and inhibited evoked and spontaneous spinal neuronal firing in vivo without motor impairment (rotarod) at high i.p. doses, supporting a favorable preclinical therapeutic index in pain paradigms (Carroll et al., 2009). Beyond pain, class summaries attribute anti-seizure effects to A-438079 in a mouse intra-amygdala kainic acid model, situating P2X7 antagonism within a broader CNS neuroinflammation–linked efficacy landscape (Gelin et al., 2020).  

Human cell assays demonstrate that A-438079 and closely related antagonists abolish ATP-induced P2X7 pore function (ethidium or YO-PRO uptake) yet spare phagocytic uptake in CD14+ human monocytes, indicating that P2X7’s pro-inflammatory macropore function can be selectively blocked while preserving innate scavenger activity; this pharmacological dissociation is a core objective for neurodegenerative/retinal indications where loss of phagocytosis may worsen pathology (Gu & Wiley, 2018).  

Clinically, the P2X7 antagonist class has mixed outcomes in peripheral inflammatory diseases: randomized Phase 2 trials in rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn’s disease failed to meet objective inflammation endpoints (ACR20, CRP), although AZD9056 showed symptom benefit (abdominal pain, mental component score) in Crohn’s disease; no P2X7 antagonist has been trialed in neurodegenerative indications to date, and none has entered clinical testing specifically for ocular/retinal diseases (Gu & Wiley, 2018; Fletcher et al., 2019). Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, P2X7 is a trimeric, low-sensitivity ATP-gated cation channel that mediates Na+, Ca2+, and K+ fluxes and, upon sustained or high agonist exposure, transitions into a large nonselective macropore permeable to molecules up to ~900 Da (e.g., YO-PRO-1), a state tightly coupled to K+ efflux and subsequent NLRP3 inflammasome activation with maturation/release of IL-1β and IL-18 (Fletcher et al., 2019). Two main routes connect P2X7 activity to IL-1β biology: (i) pore-dependent K+ efflux promotes inflammasome assembly and caspase-1 activation to process pro-IL-1β/pro-IL-18; and (ii) P2X7-mediated Ca2+ influx contributes to NF-κB activation and transcriptional priming of inflammasome components and pro-cytokines, forming the two-signal paradigm required for IL-1β/IL-18 maturation and pyroptosis (Calzaferri et al., 2020).  

In the retinal pigment epithelium, extracellular ATP is a canonical danger-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) produced by stressed/dying cells; ARPE-19 cells themselves release ATP and exhibit P2X7- and pannexin-1 (Panx1)-linked mechanisms that drive NLRP3 inflammasome activation, caspase-1 cleavage, gasdermin D pore formation, and secretion of IL-1β/IL-18, pathways that converge on inflammatory and pyroptotic injury of RPE (Youn, 2024). P2X7 functionally recruits Panx1, facilitating ATP and solute release that amplifies local ATP and P2X7 activation; in ARPE-19 cells, 25-hydroxycholesterol triggers P2X7-dependent YO-PRO uptake that is sensitive to Panx1 blockade (probenecid), indicating a Panx1-dependent pore component in RPE injury (Yang, 2017). P2X7 activation is also linked to mitochondrial distress, including cytochrome-c release and activation of executioner caspases (3/8/9), mechanistically tying the receptor to ROS (including mitochondrial ROS) and apoptotic/mixed death cascades relevant to retinal degeneration (Unknown Reference).  

Retinal localization and disease relevance are broad. Multiple P2X7 splice variants are present in the retina (with at least one common knockout deleting only the full-length variant), and P2X7 is reported in neurons (photoreceptors, amacrine, ganglion cells), glia (microglia, Müller cells), and RPE across species; application of BzATP modulates retinal responses that are attenuated in P2X7-null mice, and genetic/clinical associations link P2X7/P2X4 variants to advanced AMD risk (Fletcher et al., 2019). In ARPE-19 and native/cultured human RPE, P2X7 is expressed at mRNA and protein levels, and it is the only P2X subtype that requires high ATP for activation—conditions that occur during retinal injury/inflammation and are observed in ocular fluids in disease (note: P2X4 can be more abundant than P2X7 in ARPE-19 at baseline, which can shape net purinergic responses) (Youn, 2024).  

Within this mechanistic framework, A-438079 engages P2X7 as a reversible, competitive antagonist, blocking ATP/BzATP-evoked channel activation and macropore formation; by doing so, it suppresses P2X7-mediated Ca2+ influx and K+ efflux that are required for NF-κB priming and NLRP3 activation, respectively, leading to reduced caspase-1 cleavage and decreased maturation/secretion of IL-1β/IL-18 (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; Fletcher et al., 2019; Calzaferri et al., 2020). In macrophage-lineage systems and fresh human monocytes, A-438079 or closely related antagonists abolish P2X7 pore function and IL-1β release but preserve phagocytosis, directly supporting a therapeutic goal in neurodegeneration/retinal disease to block pro-inflammatory pore/inflammasome signaling while sparing scavenger functions that may be beneficial for debris clearance (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; Gu & Wiley, 2018).

Given A-438079’s pharmacology and the retinal/RPE biology summarized above, the expected effects under the team’s hypothesis are:

A-438079 is a strong mechanistic fit for the proposed hypothesis in dry AMD: blocking P2X7 on RPE to prevent ATP-induced Ca2+ influx, dampen K+ efflux–dependent NLRP3 activation, reduce caspase-1 cleavage and IL-1β/IL-18 release, mitigate ROS including mtROS, and preserve epithelial barrier integrity (TEER/ZO-1) under ATP-rich or drusen-mimetic stressors (amyloid-β, oxysterols, Alu RNA) (Fletcher et al., 2019; Youn, 2024; Yang, 2017; Calzaferri et al., 2020).
