Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
A-438079 is a synthetic small-molecule antagonist of the purinergic P2X7 receptor (P2X7R) originating from Abbott Laboratories’ disubstituted tetrazole series discovered by high-throughput screening and refined by structure–activity relationship (SAR) optimization within a 1-benzyl-5-aryltetrazole chemotype (tetrazole > triazole > pyrazole/imidazole in potency) (Romagnoli et al., 2008; Carroll et al., 2009). A-438079’s structure has been disclosed as 3-((5-(2,3-dichlorophenyl)-1H-tetrazol-1-yl)methyl)pyridine, capturing the two key medicinal chemistry decisions that produced a selective, drug-like P2X7 antagonist: (i) a conserved 2,3-dichlorophenyl “left-hand” aryl that supports potency and (ii) installation of a 3-pyridyl “right-hand” substituent to overcome the solubility liabilities of the original 1-benzyl-5-aryltetrazoles while maintaining submicromolar activity at human/rat P2X7 (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; Romagnoli et al., 2008; Carroll et al., 2009). Functionally, A-438079 is a reversible, competitive P2X7 antagonist that inhibits BzATP-stimulated calcium flux, P2X7-associated macropore formation, and downstream IL-1β release in macrophage-lineage systems, consistent with canonical P2X7 pharmacology linked to NLRP3 inflammasome activation (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007). Cross-source potency data place A-438079 in the mid-nanomolar to low-submicromolar range at human and rat P2X7: human P2X7 pIC50 values of ~6.3–6.9, rat P2X7 pIC50 ~6.5, and functional IC50 estimates of ~0.1 µM (rat) and ~0.3 µM (human), with high selectivity against other P2 subtypes (e.g., P2X7 IC50 0.06 µM vs >100 µM for other subtypes in one panel) (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; El Idrissi et al., 2024; Nagy, 2013). A-438079 was commercialized by Tocris (circa 2008) as a first widely available, selective P2X7 antagonist probe, enabling consistent interrogation of P2X7 biology in vitro and in vivo beyond earlier nonselective tools (e.g., KN-62, Evans Blue) (Felix et al., 2012). Within the broader class, many P2X7 antagonists have reached advanced preclinical characterization; multi-parameter tables in retinal disease–focused reviews list A-438079 as active at human/rat P2X7 with a reported brain:plasma ratio near 2.0 (suggesting central barrier penetration) and note that progress toward ocular/CNS indications has been limited by species specificity and insufficient barrier penetration for some chemotypes (Fletcher et al., 2019).  

Therapeutic History  
A-438079 and related Abbott “A-series” P2X7 antagonists established robust preclinical efficacy in neuropathic and inflammatory pain models, aligning with the role of P2X7-driven IL-1β/IL-18 signaling in nociception and neuroinflammation (Carroll et al., 2009). A-438079 reduced mechanical allodynia in the Chung and Bennett rat models, showed activity in vincristine neuropathy and the formalin persistent pain test, and inhibited evoked and spontaneous spinal neuronal firing in vivo without motor impairment (rotarod) at high i.p. doses, supporting a favorable preclinical therapeutic index in pain paradigms (Carroll et al., 2009). Beyond pain, class summaries attribute anti-seizure effects to A-438079 in a mouse intra-amygdala kainic acid model, situating P2X7 antagonism within a broader CNS neuroinflammation–linked efficacy landscape (Gelin et al., 2020).  

Human cell assays demonstrate that A-438079 and closely related antagonists abolish ATP-induced P2X7 pore function (ethidium or YO-PRO uptake) yet spare phagocytic uptake in CD14+ human monocytes, indicating that P2X7’s pro-inflammatory macropore function can be selectively blocked while preserving innate scavenger activity; this pharmacological dissociation is a core objective for neurodegenerative/retinal indications where loss of phagocytosis may worsen pathology (Gu & Wiley, 2018).  

Clinically, the P2X7 antagonist class has mixed outcomes in peripheral inflammatory diseases: randomized Phase 2 trials in rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn’s disease failed to meet objective inflammation endpoints (ACR20, CRP), although AZD9056 showed symptom benefit (abdominal pain, mental component score) in Crohn’s disease; no P2X7 antagonist has been trialed in neurodegenerative indications to date, and none has entered clinical testing specifically for ocular/retinal diseases (Gu & Wiley, 2018; Fletcher et al., 2019). Nevertheless, the latest brain-penetrant small molecules (e.g., JNJ55308942, JNJ5417446) demonstrate oral brain exposure and dose-dependent suppression of IL-1β release in stimulated whole blood/PBMCs in humans, suggesting that pharmacodynamic endpoints and barrier penetration necessary for CNS/retinal therapy are tractable within this target class (Fletcher et al., 2019).  

Retinal and AMD-relevant preclinical evidence for P2X7 antagonism is substantial at the class level. P2X7 is expressed across retinal compartments including RPE, photoreceptors, bipolar/horizontal/amacrine neurons, retinal ganglion cells, Müller glia, and microglia in mouse, rat, and human; functional agonism (e.g., BzATP) modulates retinal responses that are attenuated in P2X7-null mice, confirming a functional purinergic ATP/P2X7 axis in vivo (Fletcher et al., 2019). Sustained elevations of extracellular ATP are documented in ocular disease (e.g., human chronic glaucoma aqueous humor), and endogenous ATP mediates acute RGC injury following intraocular pressure spikes in rodents; degrading ATP or blocking P2X7 prevents RGC injury in vivo, demonstrating disease-relevant ATP surges capable of activating P2X7 in the retina (Fletcher et al., 2019). AMD-relevant biology includes high vitreous ATP, P2X7-dependent NLRP3 inflammasome activation by Alu RNA in geographic atrophy (GA) models, and P2X7-driven Ca2+-dependent apoptosis in RPE, together implicating P2X7 as a key upstream activator of inflammasome-mediated retinal degeneration (Calzaferri et al., 2020).  

For A-438079 specifically, a curated review table lists it among P2X7 antagonists evaluated in retinal contexts including ARPE-19 RPE cells, C57BL/6J mouse retinal degeneration models (e.g., MNU), and human pericytes, with endpoints encompassing NLRP3/IL-1β signaling, VEGF, ROS, ZO-1 barrier integrity, NF-κB activation, and apoptosis; outcomes are usually protective though model- and endpoint-specific variability exists (Li & Wang, 2025). In allied class work, selective P2X7 blockade with A-740003 in ARPE-19 cells and C57BL/6 mice exposed to oxidized LDL reduced ROS, suppressed NLRP3 inflammasome and NF-κB activation, decreased IL-1β/IL-18 and proangiogenic factors (VEGF, HIF-1α), alleviated retinal neovascularization, and preserved ERG amplitudes, anchoring mechanistic and functional retinal benefits to P2X7 antagonism (Yang et al., 2021). More broadly, P2X7 antagonists have protected retinal ganglion cells in chronic ocular hypertension by inhibiting microglial activation and reversed hyperpermeability and VEGF/IL-6 increases in diabetic retinal models, indicating barrier and neuroinflammatory benefits that are relevant to AMD pathophysiology (Li & Wang, 2025). Finally, in AMD-relevant disease models, P2X7 antagonists suppressed clinical symptoms of GA and CNV in animals; however, complete genetic ablation yielded mixed results (e.g., P2X7−/− protected from GA but not laser-induced CNV), emphasizing the need to preserve beneficial scavenger functions while blocking pro-inflammatory pore signaling (Gu & Wiley, 2018).  

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, P2X7 is a trimeric, low-sensitivity ATP-gated cation channel that mediates Na+, Ca2+, and K+ fluxes and, upon sustained or high agonist exposure, transitions into a large nonselective macropore permeable to molecules up to ~900 Da (e.g., YO-PRO-1), a state tightly coupled to K+ efflux and subsequent NLRP3 inflammasome activation with maturation/release of IL-1β and IL-18 (Fletcher et al., 2019). Two main routes connect P2X7 activity to IL-1β biology: (i) pore-dependent K+ efflux promotes inflammasome assembly and caspase-1 activation to process pro-IL-1β/pro-IL-18; and (ii) P2X7-mediated Ca2+ influx contributes to NF-κB activation and transcriptional priming of inflammasome components and pro-cytokines, forming the two-signal paradigm required for IL-1β/IL-18 maturation and pyroptosis (Calzaferri et al., 2020).  

In the retinal pigment epithelium, extracellular ATP is a canonical danger-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) produced by stressed/dying cells; ARPE-19 cells themselves release ATP and exhibit P2X7- and pannexin-1 (Panx1)-linked mechanisms that drive NLRP3 inflammasome activation, caspase-1 cleavage, gasdermin D pore formation, and secretion of IL-1β/IL-18, pathways that converge on inflammatory and pyroptotic injury of RPE (Youn, 2024). P2X7 functionally recruits Panx1, facilitating ATP and solute release that amplifies local ATP and P2X7 activation; in ARPE-19 cells, 25-hydroxycholesterol triggers P2X7-dependent YO-PRO uptake that is sensitive to Panx1 blockade (probenecid), indicating a Panx1-dependent pore component in RPE injury (Yang, 2017). P2X7 activation is also linked to mitochondrial distress, including cytochrome-c release and activation of executioner caspases (3/8/9), mechanistically tying the receptor to ROS (including mitochondrial ROS) and apoptotic/mixed death cascades relevant to retinal degeneration (Unknown Reference).  

Retinal localization and disease relevance are broad. Multiple P2X7 splice variants are present in the retina (with at least one common knockout deleting only the full-length variant), and P2X7 is reported in neurons (photoreceptors, amacrine, ganglion cells), glia (microglia, Müller cells), and RPE across species; application of BzATP modulates retinal responses that are attenuated in P2X7-null mice, and genetic/clinical associations link P2X7/P2X4 variants to advanced AMD risk (Fletcher et al., 2019). In ARPE-19 and native/cultured human RPE, P2X7 is expressed at mRNA and protein levels, and it is the only P2X subtype that requires high ATP for activation—conditions that occur during retinal injury/inflammation and are observed in ocular fluids in disease (note: P2X4 can be more abundant than P2X7 in ARPE-19 at baseline, which can shape net purinergic responses) (Youn, 2024).  

Within this mechanistic framework, A-438079 engages P2X7 as a reversible, competitive antagonist, blocking ATP/BzATP-evoked channel activation and macropore formation; by doing so, it suppresses P2X7-mediated Ca2+ influx and K+ efflux that are required for NF-κB priming and NLRP3 activation, respectively, leading to reduced caspase-1 cleavage and decreased maturation/secretion of IL-1β/IL-18 (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; Fletcher et al., 2019; Calzaferri et al., 2020). In macrophage-lineage systems and fresh human monocytes, A-438079 or closely related antagonists abolish P2X7 pore function and IL-1β release but preserve phagocytosis, directly supporting a therapeutic goal in neurodegeneration/retinal disease to block pro-inflammatory pore/inflammasome signaling while sparing scavenger functions that may be beneficial for debris clearance (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; Gu & Wiley, 2018).  

Expected Effect  
Assay context: ATP-challenged ARPE-19 monolayers are expected to exhibit P2X7-mediated Ca2+ influx, macropore formation (with Panx1 participation), and K+ efflux that jointly drive NLRP3 priming and activation, caspase-1 cleavage, gasdermin D pore formation, and secretion of IL-1β/IL-18; these events coincide with increased ROS (including mitochondrial contributions), NF-κB activation (IκBα phosphorylation/degradation), disruption of tight junctions (e.g., ZO-1 discontinuities), reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), and death by apoptosis and pyroptosis (Youn, 2024; Fletcher et al., 2019).  

Given A-438079’s pharmacology and the retinal/RPE biology summarized above, the expected effects under the team’s hypothesis are:  

– Ca2+ influx and priming: A-438079 should inhibit ATP/BzATP-evoked Ca2+ entry through P2X7, reducing NF-κB–dependent transcriptional priming (pro-IL-1β, NLRP3) in ARPE-19; this follows from P2X7’s ion channel function and the class’s consistent suppression of P2X7 FLIPR/Ca2+ responses in immune cells and retinal systems (Fletcher et al., 2019; Calzaferri et al., 2020).  

– Macropore/K+ efflux and inflammasome activation: By preventing P2X7 macropore formation and K+ efflux, A-438079 should blunt the activation signal required for NLRP3 assembly, reduce caspase-1 p20 generation, and attenuate maturation/secretion of IL-1β/IL-18 in ATP-stimulated ARPE-19; these outcomes are standard readouts for selective P2X7 antagonists including A-438079 in macrophage-like cells (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; Fletcher et al., 2019).  

– ROS/mtROS: P2X7 engagement is associated with ROS generation and mitochondrial apoptotic signaling; accordingly, A-438079 is expected to lower ROS and mitochondrial oxidative stress under ATP-rich challenges, analogous to the documented reduction of ROS by the close analogue A-740003 in ARPE-19 and mouse retina under ox-LDL stress (Yang et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021; Unknown Reference).  

– Barrier function (ZO-1/TEER): P2X7 antagonism has reversed increased retinal vascular permeability and reduced VEGF/IL-6 in diabetic models, and ZO-1 integrity appears among P2X7-modulated endpoints in retinal studies; thus, in ATP-challenged ARPE-19 monolayers A-438079 is expected to preserve ZO-1 continuity and TEER, even though direct TEER data with A-438079 in ARPE-19 are not provided in the sources here (Li & Wang, 2025).  

– Cytokines and angiogenic factors: A-438079 should reduce IL-1β/IL-18 release under ATP/NLRP3 activation; although dry AMD is non-neovascular, P2X7 antagonism with A-740003 reduced VEGF/HIF-1α and preserved ERG amplitudes in ox-LDL models, suggesting class-level attenuation of inflammatory/angiogenic signaling that can support retinal function preservation in inflammatory AMD contexts (Yang et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021).  

– Phagocytosis sparing: Given A-438079’s ability to abolish P2X7 pore activity while preserving bead phagocytosis in human monocytes, it is reasonable to expect preservation of RPE–myeloid scavenger function in co-culture, a desired feature in dry AMD where defective debris clearance contributes to pathology (Gu & Wiley, 2018).  

Key contextual notes for assay design and interpretation:  

– P2X7 expression and activation thresholds: ARPE-19 and native/cultured human RPE express P2X7, but P2X4 can be more abundant in ARPE-19; P2X7 requires high extracellular ATP, which is characteristic of tissue injury and documented in ocular disease, but purinergic signaling may involve multiple receptor subtypes under some stimuli (Youn, 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
A-438079 is a mechanistically precise, well-characterized P2X7 antagonist whose potency, selectivity, and competitive reversible mechanism directly address an ATP→P2X7→Ca2+/K+→NLRP3→caspase-1→IL-1β/IL-18 inflammatory axis repeatedly implicated in RPE stress and dry AMD–relevant degeneration.  

Strengths  
– Mechanistic alignment with AMD biology: P2X7 integrates extracellular ATP danger signaling with Ca2+ influx and K+ efflux to gate NLRP3 activation and IL-1β/IL-18 maturation; these cascades are active in RPE and retina, are engaged by drusen-associated stimuli (e.g., oxysterols, amyloid-β, Alu RNA), and have been mitigated by P2X7 antagonists in retinal models (Fletcher et al., 2019; Yang, 2017; Calzaferri et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).  
– Potency/selectivity and pharmacology: A-438079 exhibits mid-nanomolar to low-submicromolar antagonism at human/rat P2X7, is highly selective over other P2 subtypes, and suppresses P2X7 pore formation and IL-1β release in macrophage-like cells; it is a competitive, reversible antagonist suitable for clean target validation in cells and animals (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; El Idrissi et al., 2024; Nagy, 2013).  
– Pore blockade with phagocytosis preservation: In primary human monocytes, A-438079 eliminates P2X7 pore activity without impairing phagocytosis, matching the therapeutic strategy advocated for neurodegenerative/retinal diseases to block pro-inflammatory pore function while preserving P2X7’s scavenger role; this is critical given that complete loss of P2X7 can negate beneficial phagocytic functions and produce mixed outcomes in vivo (Gu & Wiley, 2018).  
– Retinal class-level efficacy: Selective P2X7 antagonists protect retinal neurons in multiple paradigms (light damage, glaucoma), reverse vascular hyperpermeability and inflammatory markers in diabetic models, and suppress RPE inflammasome/NF-κB/angiogenic signaling with functional rescue (ERG) in ox-LDL models, providing strong disease-relevant signals (Li & Wang, 2025; Yang et al., 2021; Fletcher et al., 2019).  
– Evidence of retinal use for A-438079: Review tables list A-438079 among P2X7 antagonists tested in ARPE-19 and mouse retinal degeneration, with endpoints including NLRP3/IL-1β, ROS, ZO-1, VEGF, and apoptosis, and generally protective outcomes, supporting feasibility and relevance of the specific candidate in retinal assays (Li & Wang, 2025).  
– Translational pharmacology: Modern P2X7 antagonists achieve brain penetration and human PD (IL-1β suppression), and a review table lists A-438079 with a brain:plasma ratio around 2.0, suggesting that barrier penetration is potentially achievable for ocular targets, though dedicated ocular PK/PD is still required (Fletcher et al., 2019).  

Weaknesses/Risks  
– Limited A-438079-specific retinal datasets: Most strong retinal evidence is at the class level or with close analogues (e.g., A-740003); A-438079’s quantitative effects on ARPE-19 TEER, mtROS, caspase-1 cleavage, and cytokines under ATP or disease-mimetic stimuli require dedicated experiments to confirm the proposed hypothesis (Yang et al., 2021; Li & Wang, 2025).  
– Dual P2X7 biology: Genetic ablation studies show protection in some contexts (GA) but not others (laser CNV), and can worsen outcomes in select neurodegeneration models, consistent with loss of P2X7’s beneficial scavenger function; pharmacology must be titrated to block pore/inflammasome function while preserving phagocytosis (Gu & Wiley, 2018).  
– Species/polymorphism and translation: Early clinical compounds had unfavorable rodent pharmacology or tissue penetration and P2X7 polymorphisms influence IL-1β secretion, underscoring the need for human-cell validation and careful species model selection during in vivo work (Gelin et al., 2020).  
– Ocular PK/PD unknowns: No direct data are provided on A-438079 retinal exposure, intraocular target engagement, or active efflux across the blood–retinal barrier; formulation and local delivery strategies may be needed to ensure adequate ocular exposure (Fletcher et al., 2019).  
– Purinergic complexity in RPE: Depending on insult, P2Y receptors can dominate RPE injury biology; for example, in an atRAL model suramin and P2Y blockade were protective whereas a pan-P2X antagonist was not, emphasizing the need to confirm P2X7 dependence under the specific ATP/disease-mimetic triggers chosen for ARPE-19 assays (Bao et al., 2024).  
– Clinical precedent: Class-level trials in RA/IBD did not meet objective inflammatory endpoints and no neurodegeneration/retinal trials exist, so the translational path remains unproven for AMD; however, the mechanistic link and preclinical retinal signals support a well-designed translational program (Gu & Wiley, 2018).  

Conclusion and development implications  
A-438079 is a strong mechanistic fit for the proposed hypothesis in dry AMD: blocking P2X7 on RPE to prevent ATP-induced Ca2+ influx, dampen K+ efflux–dependent NLRP3 activation, reduce caspase-1 cleavage and IL-1β/IL-18 release, mitigate ROS including mtROS, and preserve epithelial barrier integrity (TEER/ZO-1) under ATP-rich or drusen-mimetic stressors (amyloid-β, oxysterols, Alu RNA) (Fletcher et al., 2019; Youn, 2024; Yang, 2017; Calzaferri et al., 2020). The compound’s pore-block/phagocytosis-preserve profile in human monocytes maps to the desired retinal strategy to avoid the liabilities of global P2X7 loss while selectively suppressing pro-inflammatory outputs (Gu & Wiley, 2018). Given the breadth of class-level retinal evidence and the explicit inclusion of A-438079 in retinal model tables, the candidate merits systematic validation in AMD-proximal RPE assays and in vivo GA-like models, with early emphasis on human-cell PD (Ca2+ flux, YO-PRO uptake, IL-1β/IL-18), epithelial barrier endpoints (TEER/ZO-1), and ocular PK/PD to quantify target engagement at the retina (Li & Wang, 2025; Yang et al., 2021; Li & Wang, 2025; Fletcher et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SRT1720 is a fully synthetic small molecule initially discovered through high‐throughput screening by Sirtris Pharmaceuticals, which sought potent alternatives to the naturally occurring polyphenol resveratrol. Unlike resveratrol—which suffers from low bioavailability, poor metabolic stability, and broad non‐selective target interactions—SRT1720 belongs to the class of synthetic Sirtuin Activating Compounds (STACs) designed to selectively activate the NAD⁺‐dependent deacetylase SIRT1. Chemically, SRT1720 is based on an imidazo[1,2-b]thiazole scaffold and was optimized for its potency; studies have indicated that it is approximately 1000× more potent than resveratrol, with an EC1.5 value of around 0.16 μM and impressive maximal activation percentages in vitro (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Chang et al., 2024). The synthetic origins of SRT1720 represent a deliberate medicinal chemistry effort aimed at overcoming the limitations of natural SIRT1 activators. In the broader context, compounds in this class have been used as investigational drugs targeting pathways involved in metabolism, aging, inflammation, and stress tolerance, thereby establishing a framework for repurposing efforts across various disease areas (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Therapeutic History:  
Preclinical studies of SRT1720 have predominantly focused on its metabolic effects in rodent models characterized by diet-induced obesity, insulin resistance, and other forms of metabolic dysfunction. In these studies, administration of SRT1720 resulted in significant improvements in insulin sensitivity, reduction of plasma glucose levels, and enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis across metabolic tissues such as skeletal muscle, liver, and adipose tissues (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Donmez, 2012). Moreover, in genetically obese and high-fat diet animal models, SRT1720 has been demonstrated to improve mitochondrial function, as indicated by increased ATP production, elevated expression of mitochondrial proteins such as ATP synthase β and NDUFB8, and enhanced oxidative metabolism (Funk et al., 2010). This modulatory effect on mitochondrial biogenesis and function is thought to be mediated via the SIRT1-PGC-1α pathway—a mechanism that has garnered attention in age-related diseases where mitochondrial dysfunction is central. Although SRT1720 has not been directly investigated in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models or explicitly in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, the underlying pathogenic processes in dry AMD—namely, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysregulation—share significant overlap with the tissues previously demonstrated to benefit from SRT1720 treatment (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009). This cross-tissue efficacy provides a compelling rationale to explore SRT1720’s repurposing for dry AMD. Additionally, related compounds in this class (e.g., SRT2104) have advanced into clinical development for other indications, further suggesting that the pharmacological modulation of SIRT1 is a viable therapeutic approach (Hoppner et al., 2014).

Mechanism of Action:  
The underlying mechanism of action of SRT1720 centers on its ability to allosterically activate SIRT1, a key regulator of cellular energy metabolism and stress responses. SIRT1 is an NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase that modulates the activity of various transcription factors and co-regulators, notably PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ coactivator 1-α), which is a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. SRT1720 binds to an allosteric site on the SIRT1 enzyme-peptide substrate complex, situated amino terminal to the enzyme’s catalytic domain. This binding facilitates a conformational change in SIRT1 that lowers the Michaelis constant (K_m) for the acetylated substrates, thereby enhancing the rate of deacetylation (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Wan, 2021). Biochemical assays have demonstrated that SRT1720 increases SIRT1 deacetylase activity in a dose-dependent manner, leading to reduced acetylation of PGC-1α and thus promoting its transcriptional activity in driving mitochondrial gene expression (Funk et al., 2010). In addition to PGC-1α, SRT1720-mediated SIRT1 activation influences the acetylation status of several other proteins involved in stress responses and apoptosis, including FOXO1 and PPARγ, which collectively contribute to improved cellular resilience against oxidative damage (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Hoppner et al., 2014). Of note, many studies have confirmed that the beneficial effects observed with SRT1720 are abrogated in the presence of SIRT1 inhibitors such as nicotinamide and sirtinol, providing strong evidence for a SIRT1-dependent mode of action (Funk et al., 2010; Djouadi & Bastin, 2019). However, it is important to acknowledge that there has been some controversy regarding whether SRT1720 and its structural relatives directly interact with SIRT1 or exert off-target effects; nonetheless, the preponderance of kinetic and biophysical data supports the view that SRT1720 is primarily a SIRT1 activator (Hoppner et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2024).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry AMD is characterized by the degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) accompanied by chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and an overall decline in cellular energy homeostasis. The hypothesis for repurposing SRT1720 in this context is based on its well-documented ability to stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis and enhance oxidative capacity in multiple tissue types. In the RPE, which is a post-mitotic and metabolically demanding cell layer critical for photoreceptor survival, mitochondrial dysfunction is a key pathological feature that contributes to the progression of dry AMD. By activating SIRT1, SRT1720 is expected to promote deacetylation of PGC-1α, thereby upregulating a transcriptional program that enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and repair. This, in turn, would improve oxidative phosphorylation, reduce the production of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), and bolster the cells’ ability to cope with the chronic oxidative stress that underlies dry AMD pathology (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Furthermore, studies in other tissues, such as aged skeletal muscle and hepatocytes, have shown that SRT1720 reduces mtROS and restores cellular ATP levels by increasing mitochondrial number and function (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Funk et al., 2010). It is reasonable to extrapolate that similar benefits could be achieved in RPE cells, where preserved mitochondrial function is essential for maintaining retinal integrity and preventing progression to geographic atrophy, the advanced form of dry AMD. Expression analyses have demonstrated that both SIRT1 and PGC-1α are expressed in RPE cells, and their activities are critical for retinal health; thus, modulation of the SIRT1–PGC-1α axis by SRT1720 offers a mechanistic basis for its expected protective effects in the RPE (Hoppner et al., 2014; Alcaín & Villalba, 2009). It is anticipated that in assays using RPE cell cultures, treatment with SRT1720 will lead to enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis—as evidenced by increased mitochondrial DNA content, elevated levels of mitochondrial proteins, and improved cellular ATP production—while concurrently attenuating markers of oxidative stress. These effects would collectively improve the oxidative resilience of RPE cells, thereby potentially slowing or halting the progression of dry AMD (Funk et al., 2010; Hoppner et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation:  
There are several compelling strengths associated with the use of SRT1720 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. First, its synthetic design has led to a compound that is remarkably more potent than resveratrol, addressing one of the key limitations of natural SIRT1 activators. This enhanced potency, coupled with a clearly elucidated mechanism of action involving allosteric activation of SIRT1, provides a robust biochemical rationale for its efficacy. The observed effects in metabolic, hepatic, and renal systems—where SRT1720 has demonstrated significant improvements in mitochondrial biogenesis and reductions in oxidative stress—are highly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells plays a central role (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Another strength is the extensive preclinical data supporting the involvement of the SIRT1-PGC-1α axis in regulating mitochondrial function and cellular energy homeostasis. Since RPE cells share similar reliance on these pathways for maintaining cellular function and resisting oxidative injury, it is plausible that SRT1720 can be effectively translated into a therapeutic for dry AMD. Moreover, the fact that SRT1720’s effects are abrogated by SIRT1 inhibitors reinforces the notion that its beneficial actions are directly linked to SIRT1 activation rather than resulting from non-specific off-target activities, a point underscored by multiple biochemical studies (Wan, 2021; Funk et al., 2010).

However, there are also notable weaknesses and uncertainties that warrant consideration. Although SRT1720 has a well-characterized profile in terms of metabolic and mitochondrial effects in other tissue types, there is a paucity of data directly pertaining to ocular tissues or RPE cells. The retinal environment possesses unique pharmacokinetic and physiological characteristics, and the ability of SRT1720 to reach effective concentrations in the RPE upon systemic or local administration remains to be determined. Moreover, while the SIRT1-PGC-1α axis is a promising target, some studies have raised controversies concerning whether SRT1720 truly acts as a direct SIRT1 activator or if its effects might be partially mediated by off-target pathways, which could complicate both efficacy and safety profiles (Hoppner et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2024). There is also the broader issue of translating findings from systemic models of mitochondrial dysfunction to the highly specialized context of the eye, which may require careful consideration of formulation, dosing regimen, and potential adverse effects that are specific to ocular tissues.

The overall evaluation suggests that SRT1720 has a strong scientific foundation based on its potent SIRT1 activation, its capacity to enhance mitochondrial biogenesis, and its demonstrated ability to mitigate oxidative stress in multiple preclinical models (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Funk et al., 2010). These characteristics are directly relevant to addressing the molecular pathogenesis of dry AMD, where impaired mitochondrial function in the RPE is a key contributor to disease progression. Nevertheless, the gaps in the existing literature, particularly the lack of direct ocular studies, necessitate additional targeted preclinical research. Rigorous in vitro studies in RPE cell cultures and subsequent in vivo models of dry AMD will be essential to validate the therapeutic potential of SRT1720 in the ocular setting. Such studies should also focus on optimizing delivery mechanisms to ensure that effective drug levels are achieved in the retina without systemic toxicity (Hoppner et al., 2014; Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Future investigations should include detailed pharmacokinetic assessments in ocular tissues, evaluation of the specific effects on RPE mitochondrial dynamics, and analyses of potential off-target effects that could compromise safety. Additionally, given the controversies around whether compounds such as SRT1720 function solely via SIRT1 activation, complementary studies using genetic knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of SIRT1 in RPE cells would help to unequivocally determine the mechanism by which SRT1720 exerts its effects. Ultimately, while the translational rationale appears strong, careful attention must be paid to the unique biological milieu of the eye and to the rigorous design of preclinical studies that directly address the therapeutic endpoints relevant to dry AMD (Hoppner et al., 2014; Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

In conclusion, SRT1720 is a promising candidate for repurposing as a treatment for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its potent SIRT1 activation, demonstrated effects on mitochondrial biogenesis, and its ability to reduce oxidative stress, which is central to the pathology observed in RPE cells. The synthetic origin and high potency of SRT1720 distinguish it from natural agents like resveratrol and suggest that it might overcome many of the pharmacokinetic and specificity issues that have historically limited the success of SIRT1 activators in clinical settings. However, given that most of the existing evidence arises from non-ocular models, systematic studies focusing on the ocular pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics of SRT1720 are imperative before clinical translation can be considered. If future studies can confirm that SRT1720 effectively reaches the RPE in therapeutic concentrations and modulates the SIRT1-PGC-1α pathway without deleterious off-target effects, it could represent a significant advancement in our ability to protect the RPE against oxidative stress and slow the progression of dry AMD (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Funk et al., 2010; Hoppner et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation Summary:  
Strengths of SRT1720 include its exceptional potency compared to natural SIRT1 activators, robust preclinical evidence demonstrating mitochondrial biogenesis and reduced oxidative stress in multiple tissues, and a well-elucidated mechanism involving allosteric activation of SIRT1 with consequent deacetylation of PGC-1α. These attributes are particularly relevant given the central role of mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD. The SIRT1-PGC-1α pathway is a validated target in several preclinical models of aging and metabolic disease, and its modulation is anticipated to offer significant protection in RPE cells (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Funk et al., 2010).

Weaknesses center on the current lack of direct evidence in retinal cells or animal models of AMD, the need for ocular pharmacokinetic data, and some lingering controversies regarding the specificity of SRT1720’s mechanism of action. The translation of metabolic benefits observed in liver, muscle, and kidney to the RPE requires further study, and potential off-target effects or issues with drug delivery to ocular tissues remain concerns that necessitate additional research (Hoppner et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2024).

Based on the review of the available biochemical, preclinical, and mechanistic literature, SRT1720 shows promise as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. However, its application in this context should proceed with careful preclinical evaluation in relevant ocular models to address the outstanding issues related to tissue-specific pharmacokinetics and potential mechanistic ambiguities. This comprehensive evaluation supports the inclusion of SRT1720 in the research team’s pipeline for further investigation, provided that subsequent studies are designed to directly assess its efficacy and safety in the RPE and in vivo models of dry AMD (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Hoppner et al., 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
EUK-134 is a synthetic antioxidant belonging to the class of manganese salen complexes designed to mimic the endogenous activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase. Its synthesis involves a controlled condensation reaction between salicylaldehyde and ethylenediamine, resulting in a small molecule whose molecular framework is optimized for redox cycling and catalytic detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). As a representative of SOD/catalase mimetics, EUK-134 is engineered to convert the superoxide anion (O2–) into hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and subsequently decompose H2O2 into water and oxygen. Its dual-activity design places it in a promising category for therapeutic intervention in diseases driven by oxidative stress. The compound’s synthetic origin allows for fine-tuning of physicochemical properties such as lipophilicity and catalytic efficiency, making it a candidate for repurposing in disease conditions beyond those for which it was originally developed (Thoma et al., 2020; Grujicic & Allen, 2024). Within the pharmaceutical landscape, this class of compounds has been extensively studied in preclinical models for their ability to mitigate cellular damage by neutralizing ROS; they have been applied experimentally in models of muscle atrophy, ischemia–reperfusion injury, and certain cancer indications, where oxidative stress is known to play a critical role (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). The molecular architecture of EUK-134 notably offers a compact, dual-function approach that, in theory, should counterbalance both superoxide and hydrogen peroxide accumulation—a feature that is especially relevant given that the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is subject to chronic oxidative insult (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of EUK-134 is marked by its application in various preclinical models where oxidative stress and subsequent mitochondrial dysfunction were central to the pathology. In studies involving human skeletal muscle cells, EUK-134 has been shown to attenuate endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress-induced mitochondrial dysfunction induced by tunicamycin, resulting in improved mitochondrial membrane potential and restoration of bioenergetic profiles (Thoma et al., 2020). Moreover, this compound has been evaluated in contexts such as hyperoxic myocardial tissues, where it mitigated oxidative damage and contributed to the preservation of cellular function under stress conditions (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). Its potential benefits in reducing oxidative damage have also been noted in studies involving breast cancer cells and mechanical unloading-induced muscle atrophy, highlighting its versatility as a ROS-scavenging agent (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).  
Despite the significant body of work on EUK-134 in non-ocular tissues, its direct evaluation in dry AMD or similar degenerative retinal conditions has not yet been thoroughly explored. Clinical trials and literature searches focusing on Mn-porphyrin SOD mimetics have yielded extensive data relating to retinal diseases (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.), but EUK-134 itself has not been the primary focus in retinal clinical applications. Nonetheless, its proven mechanism of reducing ROS accumulation positions it as an attractive candidate for extension into the field of ocular therapeutics. In this light, the repurposing of EUK-134 for dry AMD is based on the hypothesis that its antioxidant properties, previously validated in muscle and other tissues, may confer similar protective effects in RPE cells that are chronically exposed to oxidative stress (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, EUK-134 functions by catalytically mimicking the activities of superoxide dismutase and catalase. In its SOD mimetic capacity, EUK-134 accepts electrons from the superoxide anions, facilitating their conversion into hydrogen peroxide—a reaction which is essential to limit direct superoxide-mediated damage (Thoma et al., 2020). Following this, the catalase mimetic activity is intended to decompose the resultant hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, thereby preventing accumulation of H2O2 which can otherwise contribute to oxidative injury through Fenton-type reactions. However, several studies have drawn attention to limitations in this pathway. For example, evidence indicates that EUK-134 may exhibit a lower efficiency in H2O2 scavenging when compared to other antioxidants such as MnTBAP or native catalase, particularly in environments with high oxidative flux (Quan et al., 2017). One key observation is a significant down-regulation of catalase expression – by more than five-fold – upon EUK-134 treatment in some cellular systems, a factor that potentially undermines its capacity to fully counteract H2O2 buildup (Quan et al., 2017).  
On the molecular interaction front, the manganese center within the salen complex undergoes redox cycling, alternating between oxidation states in response to ROS encounters. This cyclic activity contributes to its continuous catalytic turnover and represents the biochemical foundation for its antioxidant action. Furthermore, studies have shown that EUK-134 can modulate various signaling pathways associated with oxidative stress responses, such as the TGF-β1/Smad2 pathway in muscle under atrophy-inducing conditions (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). Despite these promising aspects, challenges such as suboptimal mitochondrial uptake remain a concern since effective neutralization of ROS in RPE cells requires prompt access to the mitochondrial matrix—a compartment frequently characterized by an inherently challenging microenvironment for drug delivery (Quan et al., 2017). In summary, while EUK-134 possesses a dual action mechanism that addresses two key components of the ROS cascade, the efficiency of its H2O2 detoxification and its cellular distribution are critical parameters that must be rigorously characterized in the context of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
In dry AMD and particularly in geographic atrophy, the retinal pigment epithelium is subject to sustained oxidative stress, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and subsequent cell death. The expected therapeutic effect of EUK-134 in this context is to provide robust antioxidant protection within RPE mitochondria, thereby neutralizing excessive superoxide and hydrogen peroxide levels and preserving mitochondrial integrity (Thoma et al., 2020). Restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) is a key indicator of improved mitochondrial function; thus, by mitigating ROS-induced depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane, EUK-134 is anticipated to maintain or restore ATP production and spare respiratory capacity in RPE cells. These effects are crucial given that ATP depletion and bioenergetic failure are prominent features in the pathology of dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012).  
In vitro assays that simulate oxidative stress conditions—such as those employing RPE cell cultures under hypoxic or chemically induced stress—will likely measure parameters including Δψm, ATP levels, ROS quantification, and expression levels of stress-responsive genes. The anticipated outcome is that EUK-134 will lead to a measurable decrease in the levels of ROS as detected by biochemical assays, along with a concomitant stabilization of mitochondrial respiratory function (Thoma et al., 2020; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012). In addition, molecular analyses may reveal a down-regulation of oxidative stress markers and an improvement in the overall redox balance of the cell. It is vital, however, to consider that some studies have noted that EUK-134 does not inhibit all markers of stress uniformly—for example, the continued expression of GADD34 has been observed even where other stress indicators are normalized (Thoma et al., 2020).  
Given that RPE cells naturally express endogenous antioxidant enzymes such as SOD and catalase, supplementation with EUK-134 is expected to either bolster these defenses or compensate for their decline during chronic oxidative challenges. This dual functionality could theoretically translate into a reduced progression of RPE cell death, slower accumulation of drusen, and ultimately a deceleration of geographic atrophy, all of which are hallmarks of dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of EUK-134 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration involves weighing its mechanistic promise against the practical challenges encountered in its preclinical and potential clinical application. On the one hand, EUK-134 embodies several clear strengths. Its dual mimetic activities align well with the fundamental pathophysiology of dry AMD, where both superoxide and hydrogen peroxide are implicated in the oxidative cascade that leads to mitochondrial dysfunction and RPE cell demise (Thoma et al., 2020; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012). The synthetic nature of EUK-134 allows for controlled chemical modifications which could be leveraged to optimize its pharmacokinetic properties, and its relatively small size is an asset for penetrating tissues such as the retina. Additionally, the compound’s history in attenuating ER stress-related mitochondrial dysfunction in muscle cells provides a robust proof-of-concept that similar benefits might be translatable to RPE cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress (Thoma et al., 2020).  
Notwithstanding these advantages, several weaknesses must be scrutinized. A primary concern lies in the evidence that EUK-134 may exhibit limitations in catalase-like activity, particularly with regard to its efficiency in cleaving hydrogen peroxide. Studies have documented a significant down-regulation of catalase expression upon treatment with EUK-134 and noted that its H2O2 scavenging capabilities fall short when benchmarked against other agents such as MnTBAP or even native catalase (Quan et al., 2017). In the context of RPE cells, where the oxidative insult is persistent and multifactorial, such limitations could result in suboptimal clearance of H2O2, thereby potentially compromising the therapeutic efficacy.  
Another critical issue pertains to drug delivery and cellular bioavailability. The lipophilicity of EUK-134 is notably lower compared to some analogues, amounting to roughly 43% less lipophilicity in certain cases, which inherently limits its capacity to traverse cell membranes and accumulate in the mitochondrial matrix, where its activity is most needed (Limoli et al., 2006; Quan et al., 2017). Since efficient mitochondrial delivery is crucial for counteracting localized ROS buildup in RPE cells, a deficiency in this area might significantly restrict the net antioxidant benefit provided by EUK-134.  
Furthermore, the translational history of EUK-134 presents a challenge in directly correlating preclinical observations with anticipated clinical outcomes in dry AMD. While substantial evidence exists linking EUK-134 with improved mitochondrial function in non-ocular tissues—such as the normalization of mitochondrial membrane potential in tunicamycin-induced ER stress models (Thoma et al., 2020)—there remains a paucity of direct data in ocular models. Compared to other antioxidants that have been more rigorously tested in retinal systems, EUK-134’s ocular pharmacodynamics, potential toxicity in the retinal microenvironment, and long-term safety profile are not well established (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Grujicic & Allen, 2024).  
The literature also points to the possibility of a paradoxical pro-oxidant effect. In some cellular environments, the administration of exogenous SOD mimetics can inadvertently shift the oxidative balance toward higher hydrogen peroxide levels if the catalase function is insufficient, thereby exacerbating oxidative stress rather than mitigating it (Limoli et al., 2006; Quan et al., 2017). 1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Mdivi-1, known as mitochondrial division inhibitor 1 (catalog number Sigma-Aldrich M0199), is a synthetic small-molecule compound originally developed for research into mitochondrial dynamics. It belongs to a class of therapeutic agents that modulate mitochondrial fission by targeting the dynamin‐related protein 1 (DRP1). DRP1 is an essential GTPase responsible for driving mitochondrial fission, a process that maintains mitochondrial quality control but, when overactivated, can lead to fragmentation associated with cellular stress and apoptosis. Mdivi-1 was discovered via compound screening experiments aimed at identifying inhibitors of DRP1’s GTPase activity and has been characterized extensively in various in vitro and in vivo studies. Its discovery was motivated by the need to therapeutically intervene in pathologies where aberrant mitochondrial fission contributes to cellular dysfunction. As a representative of DRP1 inhibitory agents, Mdivi-1 has been widely used as an investigational tool in studies related to neurodegeneration, ischemia, and ocular diseases, where mitochondrial integrity is a key determinant of cell survival (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2020). Its synthetic origin and well-documented pharmacological profile render it a candidate for drug repurposing, with potential applications extending into the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) by addressing mitochondrial dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells.

2. Therapeutic History  
Mdivi-1 has a robust preclinical research history across a variety of models that involve oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Initial studies demonstrated that in retinal endothelial cells and neuronal tissues, inhibition of DRP1 by Mdivi-1 prevented excessive mitochondrial fragmentation under conditions of acute stress. In models of glaucoma, for instance, DRP1 overactivation associated with ocular hypertension leads to mitochondrial fragmentation and retinal ganglion cell death, and administration of Mdivi-1 was found to rescue these cells by preserving mitochondrial network integrity (Kim et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2021). Similarly, in photoreceptor cells following retinal detachment, Mdivi-1 treatment reduced the activation of apoptotic pathways—through downregulation of cleaved Caspase-3 and Bax—and consequently preserved cell morphology and function, indicating a protective effect mediated through the inhibition of DRP1-dependent fission (She et al., 2018). Furthermore, in ARPE-19 cells, which are commonly used as a model for RPE behavior, Mdivi-1 has been shown to mitigate the cytotoxic effects of oxidative stress induced by hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) by reducing mitochondrial fragmentation and cytochrome c release, thereby improving mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP production (Yako et al., 2021). Although Mdivi-1 has not yet been evaluated in large-scale clinical trials for dry AMD specifically, its use in diverse ocular models—ranging from diabetic retinopathy to retinal ischemia—provides compelling evidence that its mechanism could be beneficial in conditions marked by oxidative stress and RPE dysfunction, two hallmark features of dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). These cumulative findings support the repurposing hypothesis that targeting DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission could restore mitochondrial function and survival in RPE cells, thereby halting or slowing the degenerative cascade observed in dry AMD.

3. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, DRP1 is responsible for mediating mitochondrial fission through the constriction and subsequent division of mitochondrial membranes. Upon receiving various stress signals, DRP1 is recruited from the cytosol to the mitochondrial outer membrane where it oligomerizes and hydrolyzes GTP, driving membrane scission. Mdivi-1 specifically inhibits the GTPase activity of DRP1, thereby preventing its self-assembly and subsequent mitochondrial recruitment. This inhibition effectively blocks the fission process that is typically upregulated under conditions of oxidative stress and other cellular insults (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2020). Detailed biochemical investigations have demonstrated that when DRP1 activity is unopposed, mitochondrial fragmentation ensues, leading to diminished mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, decreased oxygen consumption rate (OCR), reduced ATP synthesis, and an increase in the generation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) (Yako et al., 2021). Mdivi-1 counters these deleterious cellular events by preserving the integrity of the mitochondrial network, enabling enhanced ATP production, and maintaining the mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP). Moreover, by inhibiting DRP1, Mdivi-1 reduces the stress-induced release of cytochrome c from the mitochondria—a central step in the intrinsic apoptotic pathway—thus lowering the activation of downstream caspases (She et al., 2018; Yako et al., 2021). In addition to these primary actions, some studies have noted that Mdivi-1 has reversible inhibitory effects on mitochondrial complex I, suggesting that its impact on mitochondrial bioenergetics may be multifaceted (Yako et al., 2021). Such dual actions may serve to further stabilize mitochondrial function under stress.

4. Expected Effect  
Under conditions relevant to dry age-related macular degeneration, such as chronic oxidative stress incident on RPE cells, Mdivi-1 is anticipated to exert a multi-pronged cytoprotective effect. In the proposed assay using H₂O₂-treated ARPE-19 cells—a well-established in vitro model to mimic the oxidative stress environment of dry AMD—the primary expected effect is the inhibition of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission (Yako et al., 2021). By stabilizing mitochondrial dynamics, Mdivi-1 should also improve cellular bioenergetics through enhanced OCR and increased ATP production, both critical parameters that are typically compromised in stressed RPE cells (Yako et al., 2021). The anticipated outcome of these events is a reduction in cell death and apoptosis, as well as improved phagocytic function—an essential role of RPE cells in the maintenance of retinal homeostasis. Furthermore, by mitigating the accumulation of mtROS, Mdivi-1 is expected to lessen oxidative stress, thereby curbing the degenerative processes that are a central component of dry AMD pathophysiology (Yako et al., 2021; Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025). In essence, the mechanistic intervention afforded by Mdivi-1 aims to interrupt the cycle of mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage that leads to RPE cell apoptosis, which is a critical driver of disease progression in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021).

5. Overall Evaluation  
In evaluating Mdivi-1 as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current body of literature. Among its strengths, Mdivi-1 is underpinned by a strong mechanistic rationale: the inhibition of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission is a well-validated approach to restore mitochondrial function in the face of oxidative stress. Furthermore, the compound’s capacity to reduce apoptotic signaling, as evidenced by decreased cytochrome c release and lower caspase activity, is particularly promising given the established link between mitochondrial-mediated apoptosis and RPE cell loss in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Despite these promising attributes, several limitations and challenges deserve consideration. First, while the preclinical evidence supporting Mdivi-1’s efficacy is compelling, there remains a notable gap in clinical data, particularly in the context of dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Another potential weakness arises from the dual inhibitory effects of Mdivi-1. Some investigations have reported that Mdivi-1 also exhibits reversible inhibition of mitochondrial complex I, which could complicate its therapeutic profile by inadvertently affecting normal mitochondrial respiration (Yako et al., 2021). Moreover, the chronic inhibition of DRP1 raises important questions about the broader physiological implications of interfering with mitochondrial dynamics (Mohammad & Kowluru, 2022; She et al., 2018). The overall therapeutic window and safety profile of Mdivi-1 also require further elucidation (Yako et al., 2021). Its capacity to restore mitochondrial integrity, mitigate oxidative stress, and inhibit apoptotic cascades directly addresses several of the pathogenic mechanisms implicated in dry AMD. Given that current treatments for dry AMD are limited and mainly supportive, a disease-modifying therapy that targets mitochondrial dysfunction would represent a significant advancement in the management of this debilitating disorder (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2015). In summary, Mdivi-1’s strengths lie in its well-characterized mechanism of action, demonstrated efficacy in preserving mitochondrial dynamics under stress, and its potential to enhance cell survival in models of retinal degeneration (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2015; Yako et al., 2021).

Future studies must address the nuances of chronic DRP1 inhibition, optimize dosing regimens, evaluate long-term safety, and conduct thorough pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiling in ocular tissues to fully realize the potential of Mdivi-1 in the clinical management of dry AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021).

In conclusion, the evidence provided by numerous preclinical studies strongly indicates that Mdivi-1’s inhibition of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission offers a promising therapeutic strategy for dry age-related macular degeneration. The compound’s ability to maintain mitochondrial network integrity, enhance bioenergetics, and suppress apoptotic cascades under conditions of oxidative stress in RPE cells is particularly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Although challenges remain in addressing the potential off-target effects and ensuring long-term safety in the clinical setting, the mechanistic rationale and supporting preclinical data justify further investigation into the utility of Mdivi-1 as a repurposed candidate for this currently untreatable condition. As the drug development process progresses, a focused effort on meticulous in vivo testing, formulation development for ocular delivery, and comprehensive pharmacological evaluations will be critical to harnessing the full therapeutic potential of Mdivi-1 for patients with dry AMD (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2015; She et al., 2018; Yako et al., 2021).

This compound belongs to a distinct chemical class uncovered through high‐throughput screening efforts of over 635,000 compounds, which yielded two primary structural families: the thiazole‐type S1QEL1 series (of which S1QEL-1.1 is a leading representative) and the piperazine‐type S1QEL2 series (Banba et al., 2019). In addition, photoaffinity probe derivatives ([125I]S1QEL1.1_PD1 and PD2) have been prepared to map its binding site in Complex I, underscoring both its synthetic tractability and the sophistication of the medicinal chemistry approach used in its development (Banba et al., 2019). As a class, S1QEL compounds have been primarily engineered to modulate mitochondrial ROS by selectively suppressing superoxide production at the IQ site without broad‐spectrum inhibition of electron transfer, a profile that distinguishes them from canonical Complex I inhibitors such as rotenone and piericidin A (Wong et al., 2019). Historically, S1QEL compounds have been extensively characterized in biochemical assays using isolated mitochondria and submitochondrial particles. In these studies, S1QEL-1.1 and other members of the class were shown to potently suppress superoxide and hydrogen peroxide production specifically from the IQ site during conditions that favor reverse electron transfer, while sparing forward electron transport and thus preserving overall mitochondrial electron flow and ATP production (Wong et al., 2019). Preclinical studies in in vivo models have demonstrated the protective effects of S1QEL compounds in varied contexts; for instance, stress-induced stem cell hyperplasia in the Drosophila gut was ameliorated by S1QEL application, and in perfused mouse heart preparations, S1QELs reduced ischemia–reperfusion injury (Banba et al., 2019). Although these examples involve cardiac and developmental models, the central concept—that selective suppression of mitochondrial ROS can confer tissue protection—has broad implications for diseases where redox imbalance is a critical driver. Importantly, while there are numerous reports underscoring the utility of S1QELs in modulating mitochondrial ROS in neurons, cardiomyocytes, and skeletal muscle mitochondria (Banba et al., 2019), a direct application of S1QEL-1.1 to ocular disorders such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) has not yet been documented. This binding does not fully block electron entry nor does it globally inhibit forward electron transfer, because the inhibitory potency for suppressing ROS generation is approximately 1–2 orders of magnitude lower than that required to inhibit basal respiratory activity (Wong et al., 2019). Furthermore, the mechanism is direction-dependent: S1QEL-1.1 exhibits significantly stronger inhibition of reverse electron transfer-associated ROS production than forward electron transfer, a property that has been linked to structural differences in the ND1 subunit that influence the flux of electrons under various bioenergetic states (Banba et al., 2019). S1QEL-1.1 stands out as a highly promising drug candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration owing to its unique ability to selectively suppress mitochondrial ROS production at the Complex I IQ site without impacting the overall electron transport and ATP production. This raises concerns about the therapeutic window and the optimal route of delivery for chronic conditions like dry AMD. Another limitation is that, despite promising mechanistic data, direct clinical evidence for the use of spermidine in dry AMD is currently lacking. Most of the studies available have been conducted in vitro or in animal models under conditions of oxidative stress, and while these findings are encouraging, they do not fully recapitulate the complex pathophysiology of dry AMD, which involves not only oxidative damage but also chronic inflammation, immune dysregulation, and drusen accumulation (Kim et al., 2021).

Moreover, while the hypothesis emphasizes effects on EP300 inhibition and AMPK activation leading to enhanced LC3-II conversion and Parkin recruitment, the direct evidence linking these specific molecular events to improved outcomes in dry AMD models remains preliminary. There is a need for more comprehensive studies that directly measure these autophagic and mitophagic markers in RPE cells under conditions that mimic the A2E-induced stress typical of dry AMD (Kim et al., 2021). Additionally, the risk that spermidine’s metabolism by amine oxidases may produce toxic aldehyde byproducts such as acrolein must be carefully considered, as these compounds have been implicated in retinal degeneration in some intravitreal models (Ohashi et al., 2017).

In summary, while spermidine has a compelling mechanistic rationale as a modulator of autophagy and mitochondrial quality control, which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the current preclinical evidence is mixed and highlights potential safety challenges related to dosing and administration. Its established role in promoting cellular longevity and mitigating oxidative stress in diverse tissues certainly warrants further investigation, but rigorous studies using dry AMD-specific models are essential to ascertain its efficacy and safety in this context. Regulatory considerations will also require detailed pharmacokinetic and toxicological profiling, particularly given its dual potential for both cytoprotection and cytotoxicity depending on concentration and route of administration (Ohashi et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022).

Overall, our evaluation suggests that spermidine represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD based on its intrinsic properties as an autophagy and mitophagy inducer and its ability to protect RPE cells from oxidative damage; however, its clinical translation will depend on resolving key issues such as dose optimization, route of delivery, and comprehensive validation of its proposed molecular mechanisms in relevant models of AMD. The strengths of spermidine lie in its natural occurrence, multi-targeted action on cellular quality control mechanisms, and established preclinical benefits in other models of aging and oxidative stress. Conversely, the main weaknesses are its narrow therapeutic window, the potential for generation of toxic metabolites, and the current lack of direct clinical or robust in vivo data in dry AMD models. Further research, including detailed investigations in RPE models using A2E and oxidative stress conditions as well as careful titration studies in animal models of dry AMD, is warranted to determine its viability as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for this unmet clinical need (Casero & Marton, 2007; Kim et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022; Ohashi et al., 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Sulforaphane is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate originally identified in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli and Brussels sprouts. It is generated through the hydrolysis of glucoraphanin by the enzyme myrosinase, which is released upon plant tissue damage. As a member of the phytochemical family, sulforaphane belongs to a class of natural compounds known for inducing phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins. Historically, this compound has been extensively investigated for its chemopreventive and cytoprotective properties, particularly through the activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. Being one of the most studied Nrf2 activators, its discovery stemmed from early investigations into dietary antioxidants and their role in reducing carcinogenesis and inflammation. In the context of drug development, sulforaphane is considered a promising candidate for repurposing because it combines a favorable preclinical safety profile with a well-characterized mechanism of action that includes modulation of intracellular redox signaling. Its broad application in preclinical studies to ameliorate oxidative stress and inflammation suggests that targeted delivery to retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells might help alleviate the oxidative injury observed in geographic atrophy, the advanced form of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Bellezza, 2018; Chang et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Sulforaphane has attracted considerable attention for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties over the past two decades. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its protective effects in various models of oxidative stress, including those involving retinal tissues and RPE cells. In in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells—a well-accepted human RPE model—sulforaphane exhibited dose-dependent protection against oxidative insults induced by agents such as tert-butyl hydroperoxide (t-BOOH) and hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂). These experiments demonstrated that sulforaphane pretreatment significantly reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and mitigated mitochondrial membrane potential damage, ultimately leading to reduced apoptotic cell death (Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021). Similarly, other investigations have reported sulforaphane’s ability to induce cytoprotective genes in RPE cells through Nrf2 activation, resulting in improved cell survival under stress conditions (Zhang et al., 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Moreover, several in vivo studies in rodent models have provided evidence of sulforaphane-mediated retinal neuroprotection. Examples include models of photooxidative damage in mice, where sulforaphane delayed photoreceptor degeneration and prevented RPE dysfunction—mechanisms that are highly relevant to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Bellezza, 2018). However, it should be noted that although sulforaphane has been studied in various retinal degeneration models, there is no established clinical history of its use in human dry AMD. Nevertheless, its promising preclinical efficacy in ameliorating oxidative injury in RPE cells, coupled with its demonstrated safety across multiple biological systems including ocular tissues, supports its potential repurposing as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Qin, 2007; del Cano et al., 2008).

Mechanism of Action:  
The principal mechanism underlying sulforaphane’s protective effects is its ability to activate the Nrf2 pathway. Under basal conditions, the transcription factor Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytosol via binding to its inhibitor, Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1), which directs Nrf2 for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Sulforaphane, owing to its electrophilic isothiocyanate moiety, reacts with critical cysteine residues on Keap1. This modification alters the conformation of Keap1 and prevents the degradation of Nrf2, leading to its stabilization and subsequent nuclear translocation (Wherry, 2013). Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to antioxidant response elements (ARE) in the promoter regions of various cytoprotective genes. The result is a robust induction of phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), and superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2). These enzymes play critical roles in neutralizing ROS, repairing oxidative damage, and maintaining cellular redox balance (Qin, 2007; Zhang et al., 2024).

In addition to its classic Nrf2-dependent antioxidant response, sulforaphane has been shown to modulate other cellular pathways that are important for mitochondrial health. In retinal cells, sulforaphane has been reported to attenuate mitochondrial membrane potential collapse and reduce mitochondrial superoxide production, as evidenced by decreased MitoSOX fluorescence in treated ARPE-19 cells (Chang et al., 2020). These mitochondrial protective actions are thought to involve the upregulation of antioxidant enzymes that localize to the mitochondria, as well as enhancement of the spare respiratory capacity—thereby preserving ATP generation under oxidative stress conditions. Furthermore, sulforaphane has been implicated in the regulation of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis, which is critical for mitochondrial biogenesis and metabolic homeostasis. This dual engagement—both through Nrf2-driven transcriptional activation and mitochondrial biogenesis pathways—positions sulforaphane as a multifaceted agent capable of sustaining cellular energy production and reducing oxidative injury in the RPE, a cell type that is particularly vulnerable in geographic atrophy (Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).

Beyond its antioxidant effects, sulforaphane also exerts anti-inflammatory properties by downregulating the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and adhesion molecules (e.g., ICAM-1, MCP-1). This is particularly relevant in the context of AMD, where chronic low-grade inflammation is believed to exacerbate RPE dysfunction and drusen formation (Chang et al., 2020; del Cano et al., 2008). In summary, the molecular interactions of sulforaphane—ranging from direct modification of Keap1 to the induction of mitochondrial antioxidant defenses—provide a robust mechanistic rationale for its potential utility in mitigating the multifactorial oxidative and inflammatory challenges associated with dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Given its well-documented mechanism of action, the hypothesis that sulforaphane induces Nrf2-mediated mitochondrial antioxidant pathways in RPE cells is strongly supported by preclinical evidence. When RPE cells are subjected to oxidative stress, it is expected that sulforaphane treatment will lead to a dose-dependent upregulation of Nrf2 target genes including HO-1, NQO1, and SOD2. The elevation of these transcripts correlates with a reduction in mitochondrial superoxide levels, as measured by decreased MitoSOX fluorescence, and an improvement in the spare respiratory capacity—a surrogate marker for mitochondrial function and ATP generation (Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).

In cellular assays using ARPE-19 cells, administration of sulforaphane prior to oxidative challenge has been shown to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential and decrease cytochrome c release, thereby reducing the activation of downstream apoptotic cascades. The suppression of ROS production and the preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics result in improved cell viability and reduced apoptotic indices. For instance, studies have demonstrated that sulforaphane pretreatment leads to lower levels of cleaved caspase-3 and PARP-1, indicating a direct link between enhanced antioxidant defense and the inhibition of programmed cell death pathways in RPE cells (Yang et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2020).

At the molecular level, the expected outcome of sulforaphane administration in a dry AMD context is multifactorial. The compound would elevate the expression of cytoprotective enzymes that not only detoxify reactive oxygen species but also facilitate the repair of oxidatively damaged macromolecules. This should translate into a measurable decrease in overall oxidative stress markers, preservation of mitochondrial function (evidenced by sustained ATP production and improved spare respiratory capacity), and stabilization of the RPE cell phenotype. Moreover, since mitochondrial dysfunction is a central element of geographic atrophy pathogenesis, sulforaphane’s ability to maintain ATP generation could directly counteract the energy deficit observed in degenerating RPE cells (Zhang et al., 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

These expected effects are supported by a range of preclinical studies. For example, quantitative redox fluorometry results reported in ARPE-19 cells indicate that sulforaphane-treated cells maintain a significantly higher redox ratio during oxidative challenge compared to untreated controls, which is indicative of an enhanced antioxidant state. Additionally, the upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants and improved bioenergetic profiles have been correlated with better cell survival outcomes, reinforcing the concept that sulforaphane can counteract the deleterious cellular changes observed in models of dry AMD (del Cano et al., 2008; Qin, 2007).

Overall Evaluation:  
Sulforaphane, as exemplified by the Sigma-Aldrich S4441 formulation, presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD, particularly targeting the geographic atrophy form characterized by pronounced RPE degeneration. One of the major strengths of sulforaphane lies in its robust preclinical evidence demonstrating its ability to induce the Nrf2 pathway, a master regulator of oxidative stress responses. The compound’s direct modification of Keap1 and subsequent stabilization and nuclear translocation of Nrf2 trigger the upregulation of several antioxidant enzymes, such as HO-1, NQO1, and SOD2—which are critical for detoxifying reactive oxygen species and repairing oxidative damage in RPE cells (Qin, 2007; Zhang et al., 2024).

Furthermore, sulforaphane’s additional capacity to preserve mitochondrial function by maintaining membrane potential and supporting ATP synthesis addresses a major pathological hallmark of geographic atrophy, where mitochondrial dysfunction leads to energy depletion and accelerates cell death. The integration of mitochondrial antioxidant defenses with the broader cytoprotective effects of Nrf2 activation provides a convergent mechanism aimed at both preventing oxidative damage and sustaining cellular energy production under stress conditions (Yang et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2020).

Another notable strength is the extensive safety data available for sulforaphane from preclinical studies. Its natural occurrence, combined with its well-documented bioactivity in a range of cell types, underscores its potential for repurposing in ocular applications. Moreover, sulforaphane’s ability to attenuate inflammatory responses by reducing the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines adds an extra layer of therapeutic benefit, considering the role of chronic inflammation in exacerbating AMD pathology (del Cano et al., 2008; Chang et al., 2020).

Despite these promising attributes, several challenges remain. One potential limitation is the bioavailability of sulforaphane. Like many natural compounds, sulforaphane may face pharmacokinetic hurdles such as poor water solubility and limited tissue penetration, which could complicate systemic delivery or localized administration to the retina. Furthermore, while the preclinical efficacy in ARPE-19 cell models and animal studies is encouraging, the translation of these findings to human patients with dry AMD remains to be validated. Variability in the cellular responses between in vitro models and the complex microenvironment of the human retina, including the influence of the blood–retinal barrier, poses a potential risk for suboptimal therapeutic delivery (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Qin, 2007).

Additionally, some of the supportive data for sulforaphane’s efficacy in ocular systems come from studies published in journals with variable impact, and additional high-quality clinical studies will be necessary to establish its safety and efficacy profile in the context of dry AMD. The dosing regimens, potential off-target effects, and long-term impact of chronic Nrf2 activation in retinal tissues also require careful investigation. There is ongoing debate over the potential for Nrf2 activators to have biphasic dose responses, where excessive activation might inadvertently cause cellular stress or dysregulate normal redox homeostasis (Bellezza, 2018; del Cano et al., 2008).

In conclusion, sulforaphane demonstrates strong mechanistic potential for the treatment of dry AMD by elevating key antioxidant defenses in RPE cells and preserving mitochondrial function under oxidative stress. Its ability to induce HO-1, NQO1, and SOD2 in response to oxidative challenges and thereby reduce superoxide production while maintaining ATP synthesis is directly aligned with the therapeutic needs of geographic atrophy patients. The preclinical evidence suggests that, with appropriate formulation and delivery strategies, sulforaphane could provide a dual benefit by mitigating oxidative injury and reducing inflammation in the retina. However, further studies are required to address bioavailability challenges and to validate its clinical efficacy in well-designed human trials. Overall, sulforaphane merits further investigation as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, and its advancement into early-phase clinical testing is justified by the compelling preclinical data available (Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; del Cano et al., 2008).
