Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
MCC950 is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor that belongs to the diarylsulfonylurea class of compounds originally identified through screening efforts aimed at inhibiting IL-1β processing. Its chemical origins trace back to early studies (circa 2001) that recognized diarylsulfonylurea molecules as cytokine-release inhibitory drugs (CRIDs) before the advent of specific inflammasome inhibitors (Coll et al., 2015). Subsequent medicinal chemistry efforts led to the selection, optimization, and detailed characterization of one member of this series that came to be known as MCC950. Synthetically, MCC950 is produced through a multistep sequence that includes key transformations such as Friedel–Crafts acylation of an indene derivative, acid-promoted cyclization, direct nitration, and subsequent conversion into its final diarylsulfonylurea form, as detailed in the original publication’s Online Methods and Supplementary Materials (Coll et al., 2015; Keuler et al., 2022). Developed initially as an inhibitor of IL-1β post-translational processing, MCC950 was repurposed as a potent and highly selective inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome, exhibiting nanomolar potency (approximately 7.5 nM in murine bone marrow–derived macrophages) with a favorable selectivity profile over other inflammasomes such as AIM2, NLRC4, or NLRP1 (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021; Hill et al., 2017). Marketed under various identifiers – one of which is the Selleckchem product code S8643 – MCC950 represents a well-characterized chemical tool that has continued to serve as both a probe for studying NLRP3 biology and a preclinical candidate in inflammatory disease models (Das et al., 2021; Sharma et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
MCC950 has been extensively evaluated in preclinical studies targeting inflammatory diseases driven by aberrant NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Its discovery followed earlier observations that sulfonylurea agents such as glyburide, traditionally used in type 2 diabetes for their insulin-secretagogue activity via KATP channel inhibition, also inhibited NLRP3-driven processes albeit at micromolar concentrations (Chauhan et al., 2020; Coll et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2017). In contrast, MCC950 exhibits a markedly improved potency at nanomolar levels and a higher degree of specificity. Preclinical evaluations demonstrated that MCC950 effectively blocks both the canonical and noncanonical activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, resulting in suppressed activation of caspase-1 and reduced IL-1β secretion (Das et al., 2021; Hill et al., 2020). Its efficacy has been validated in a wide range of inflammatory disease models including cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS), multiple sclerosis models such as experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), pulmonary and cutaneous inflammation, Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, and even models of kidney and liver fibrosis (Das et al., 2021; Narros-Fernández et al., 2022; Sharma et al., 2023). Although MCC950 has not yet been formally used in clinical applications—and indeed its clinical development was reportedly halted due to safety concerns such as elevated transaminases and organ structural damage in preclinical toxicity studies (Johansson et al., 2025)—its robust preclinical record has established it as the prototype NLRP3 inhibitor. There is emerging interest in exploiting its mechanism for diseases wherein inflammasome-driven pathology is central. While direct data on the use of MCC950 for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) are not available in the literature, the growing evidence implicating the NLRP3 inflammasome in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction suggests that repurposing MCC950 for dry AMD is a scientifically plausible strategy (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021; Keuler et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of MCC950 is one of its most compelling features. At the molecular level, MCC950 selectively inhibits the NLRP3 inflammasome by directly binding to the NACHT domain, specifically targeting the Walker B motif that is essential for ATP hydrolysis and subsequent conformational changes required for inflammasome assembly (Hill et al., 2020; Sharma et al., 2023). In doing so, MCC950 prevents the oligomerization of NLRP3 and the recruitment of the adaptor protein ASC, thereby abrogating the activation of caspase-1 and the maturation and release of proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18 (Coll et al., 2015; Keuler et al., 2022). Structural analyses, including photoaffinity labeling and surface plasmon resonance (SPR) studies, have confirmed the high affinity binding (with SPR-derived K_D values in the low nanomolar range) of MCC950 to its target within NLRP3 (Coll et al., 2019; Hill et al., 2017). Importantly, MCC950 does not interfere with upstream ionic events, such as K^+ efflux or Ca^2+ signaling, which are also involved in NLRP3 activation pathways; rather, its action is confined to the blockade of ATP hydrolysis, offering a direct means to “lock” NLRP3 in an inactive, closed conformation (Das et al., 2021; Keuler et al., 2022; Li, 2020). This precise targeting underpins its exceptional potency and selectivity among inflammasome inhibitors. Moreover, a body of literature has explored the structure–activity relationships (SAR) surrounding the diarylsulfonylurea scaffold of MCC950, confirming that modifications to key structural motifs (for instance, the s-hexahydroindacene group) can have significant impacts on both inhibitory potency and chemical stability; these insights have spurred the design of hybrid molecules that further exploit MCC950’s pharmacophore for dual-target activities (Hill et al., 2017).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
The pathophysiology of dry AMD is characterized by the progressive degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), which results from chronic cellular stress—largely driven by mitochondrial dysfunction and elevated reactive oxygen species (ROS) production—that culminates in an inflammatory cascade. A growing body of evidence implicates the NLRP3 inflammasome as a critical mediator in this process; in the RPE, mitochondrial ROS can instigate NLRP3 activation, leading to the cleavage of caspase-1 and the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, which in turn exacerbate RPE atrophy and compromise the integrity of the retinal barrier (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021). The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of MCC950 for dry AMD is that by selectively inhibiting NLRP3 activation, MCC950 would interrupt this pathogenic cycle. Specifically, its potent inhibition of ATP hydrolysis within the NACHT domain would prevent the inflammasome assembly even in the presence of mitochondrial ROS, thereby blocking caspase-1 activation and subsequent IL-1β secretion. In preclinical models where MCC950 has been tested—such as sodium-iodate-induced damage and laser-induced injury—this compound has been shown to suppress NLRP3-dependent cytokine secretion and preserve barrier function (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021; Narros-Fernández et al., 2022). MCC950 presents several compelling strengths as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its background as a diarylsulfonylurea with well-documented preclinical efficacy in suppressing IL-1β release and blocking caspase-1 activation provides a strong mechanistic foundation. The compound’s history of preclinical success in multiple inflammatory disease models, combined with detailed insights into its mechanism of action, supports its potential repurposing for dry AMD—especially given that inflammasome-mediated inflammation is a key driver of RPE cell degeneration. Ultimately, with rigorous preclinical validation in relevant ocular models and potential formulation optimization to ensure localized protection with minimal systemic exposure, MCC950 could provide an innovative therapeutic approach to halting or slowing the progression of dry AMD (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021; Hill et al., 2020; Johansson et al., 2025; Li, 2020; Sharma et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
BGP-15 is a synthetic, small-molecule nicotinic amidoxime/hydroxylamine derivative whose full chemical name is O-(3-piperidino-2-hydroxy-1-propyl) nicotinic amidoxime, typically used as a dihydrochloride salt; it was developed by N-Gene (US/Hungary) and has been described as water-soluble and mitochondria-targeting in preclinical studies (including ocular applications) (Takács et al., 2024; Horváth et al., 2021). Chemically and pharmacologically, BGP-15 belongs to the hydroximic/hydroxylamine acid derivative family originally advanced as membrane-interacting heat-shock response (HSR) co-inducers that remodel cholesterol-enriched plasma membrane rafts, with pleiotropic, cytoprotective effects in stressed tissues (membrane-lipid therapy) (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011). In parallel, the compound has been positioned as a nicotinamide-related, non-carboxamide “NAM analogue” with in vitro mixed-type (noncompetitive) PARP-1 inhibition, though the authors emphasize that in vivo protective effects likely involve additional mechanisms beyond direct PARP blockade because the in vitro inhibitory concentration exceeds achievable systemic levels (Crul et al., 2013). Independent biophysical and cellular studies show BGP-15 partitions into membranes, increases the fluidity of negatively charged lipid species, preserves heat-challenged raft integrity, and activates stress signaling linked to HSP induction; imaging and molecular dynamics support a direct membrane-interacting mode of action (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

Functionally, BGP-15 is best classified as a multifunctional HSP co-inducer and insulin-sensitizing, mitochondria-targeting cytoprotective agent that remodels membrane rafts, enhances the HSF1–HSP axis, and modulates stress and survival signaling (Akt up, JNK/p38 down), while lowering mitochondrial ROS and stabilizing Δψm; importantly, it preferentially acts in stressed cells, an attribute that underpins its safety rationale (Gombos et al., 2011; Sumegi et al., 2017). The compound concentrates in energized mitochondria driven by its delocalized positive charge, with >85–90% uptake into isolated mitochondria under experimental conditions (Sümegi, 2018). Mitochondrial studies consistently localize the dominant ROS-lowering effect to the respiratory chain at complexes I and III, with minimal direct antioxidant chemistry, and only mild uncoupling at millimolar concentrations that is irrelevant at the micromolar doses used in most cell studies (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018).

Crucial nomenclature caveat: a distinct “BGP-15” reported by a different group denotes a calcipotriene-derived vitamin D3 analog with anticancer activity; this vitamin D3 analog is mechanistically and structurally unrelated to the nicotinic amidoxime HSP co-inducer described above (both were labeled “BGP-15” by their respective originators) (Sintov et al., 2013). For the current program, the candidate of interest is the nicotinic amidoxime/hydroxylamine HSP co-inducer (often supplied by N-Gene or commercial chemical vendors under the amidoxime name), not the vitamin D3 analog (Takács et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
BGP-15 and closely related hydroximic/hydroxylamine acid derivatives have an extensive preclinical history across cardiac, neural, hepatic, renal, skeletal muscle, pulmonary, and metabolic models, with multiple mechanistic readouts converging on membrane remodeling, HSR/HSP co-induction, MAPK and Akt pathway modulation, and mitochondrial protection (Sumegi et al., 2017). Cardiovascular protection has been reported in ischemia–reperfusion, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation, with actions that include reduced ROS, preserved mitochondrial function, and Akt activation with suppression of JNK/p38 (Sumegi et al., 2017). In spontaneously hypertensive rats, BGP-15 increased PGC-1α and mitochondrial mass, decreased interstitial fibrosis, increased MKP-1 and reduced p38/JNK phosphorylation, and activated Akt/GSK-3β signaling (Horváth et al., 2021). BGP-15 prevented imatinib cardiotoxicity, protected against cisplatin nephrotoxicity without impairing antitumor efficacy, and mitigated cisplatin/taxol peripheral neuropathy (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). Hepatoprotection against acetaminophen injury via inhibition of caspase-independent cell death has also been documented (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). In pulmonary arterial hypertension and severe muscular dystrophy models, BGP-15 preserved mitochondrial structure and function and slowed disease progression; mechanistically, mitochondrial fusion via OPA1 activation and Akt signaling were implicated (Szabó et al., 2018).

Neuroprotection and mitochondrial rescue have been demonstrated in vitro and in vivo, including reduced neuronal death and improved mitochondrial potential/ROS at axonal branch points, coupled to HSP72 elevation, reduced phospho-JNK/p38, and enhanced Akt/IGF1R signaling (Ohlen et al., 2017). Consistent with its membrane-raft mechanism, BGP-15 increased HSP expression during heat challenge and remodeled cholesterol-rich platforms that gate stress signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

In ophthalmology, BGP-15 has been applied in multiple retinal disease contexts. It was reported retinoprotective in Goto–Kakizaki rats (type 2 diabetes) with functional preservation on ERG, and later shown to improve survival and retinal function long-term in ZDF rats under uncontrolled diabetes, with increased ocular HSP70 and decreased NFκB (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021). Topical ocular delivery using an SBECD-containing eyedrop improved scotopic/photopic a- and b-waves, restored oscillatory potentials, shortened implicit times, and preserved retinal thickness following global ischemia–reperfusion injury in rats (Takács et al., 2024). These ocular data align with the compound’s mitochondrial and HSP co-inducer mechanisms: accumulation in mitochondria, protection against apoptosis/necrosis in oxidative-stress paradigms, and modulation of stress signaling (Takács et al., 2024).

Clinically, BGP-15 has a proof-of-concept randomized, double-blind trial demonstrating dose-dependent improvement of insulin sensitivity in insulin-resistant patients without apparent short-term toxicity; in parallel, human phase II work in olanzapine-induced metabolic disorder also identified BGP-15 as an insulin sensitizer (Crul et al., 2013; Sümegi, 2018). Safety signals from early human studies and the pharmacology of HSP co-inducers (preferential action in stressed cells) support the translational risk profile; however, systemic serum concentrations reported by the developer are low (≤25 nmol/mL), which has implications for target engagement and favors local ocular delivery for retinal indications (Gombos et al., 2011; Sumegi et al., 2017).

To our knowledge based on the supplied corpus, BGP-15 has not been directly tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) patients or canonical dry AMD animal models; however, its retinoprotective efficacy in diabetic retinopathy models and retinal ischemia–reperfusion suggests relevance to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)/photoreceptor stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammation, which are central to dry AMD biology (Takács et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Membrane-lipid therapy and HSP co-induction. BGP-15 partitions into and remodels membrane lipid domains, particularly cholesterol-rich plasma membrane rafts that organize stress sensing and signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). Under heat stress or analogous perturbations, BGP-15 preserves raft integrity and elevates HSP expression; this is associated with activation of Rac1 and modulation of HSF1 acetylation, leading to prolonged HSF1 DNA binding and robust HSP gene induction without causing protein unfolding, a hallmark of HSP “co-inducers” (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). In HSR-defective melanoma cells, BGP-15 significantly rescued raft domain coverage and shifted the size distribution toward larger platforms, coincident with increased hsp25 expression and Rac1-dependent stress signaling (Gombos et al., 2011). Across cell and tissue contexts, BGP-15 increases HSP70/HSPA1A (HSP72), and this HSP gain is causally linked to improved insulin signaling and cytoprotection in stressed cells (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011).

PARP/NAD+/SIRT1/HSF1 axis. Although BGP-15 demonstrates mixed-type (noncompetitive) inhibition of PARP-1 in vitro, the concentrations required exceed typical in vivo exposures, suggesting that PARP pathway effects in vivo are likely downstream of ROS lowering and reduced DNA single-strand breaks that otherwise drive PARP activation (Crul et al., 2013). In stressed cells, BGP-15 reduces PAR levels, which relieves PARP-mediated suppression of MKP-1/Dusp1, thereby inhibiting JNK/p38 activation; reduced PARP activity also preserves NAD+ and SIRT1 activity, which favors a deacetylated, active HSF1 and a stronger HSR (Crul et al., 2013). This mechanistic loop—less ROS, less PARP activation, more MKP-1, less JNK/p38, and better HSP/SIRT1 tone—aligns with the observed anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective phenotypes (Crul et al., 2013).

Mitochondrial enrichment and respiratory chain modulation. Biophysically, BGP-15 carries a delocalized positive charge, accumulates in energized mitochondria (>85–90% uptake in isolated organelles), and at micromolar doses characteristic of cell studies (1–50 µM) lowers mitochondrial ROS predominantly at complexes I and III without significant baseline depolarization of Δψm (Sümegi, 2018; Sumegi et al., 2017). In oxidative or inflammatory challenges, BGP-15 attenuates H₂O₂- and LPS-induced mitochondrial depolarization and reduces mitochondrial superoxide to near-control levels; MitoTEMPO controls confirm mitochondrial origin of the ROS signal (Sumegi et al., 2017). Importantly, the compound exhibits no meaningful direct antioxidant scavenging in cell-free ROS-generating systems, and only displays mild uncoupling at millimolar concentrations—far above the micromolar exposures used in protective assays—supporting a mechanism of respiratory chain modulation rather than redox scavenging (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). Downstream signaling reflects the lowered mitochondrial ROS burden: JNK/p38 activation is reduced, Akt signaling is enhanced, and caspase-independent death pathways are suppressed (Sumegi et al., 2017).

Mitochondrial dynamics, fusion, and biogenesis. Beyond acute ROS control, BGP-15 promotes mitochondrial fusion and preserves cristae architecture by activating OPA1 GTPase and promoting OPA1 polymerization; genetic suppression of OPA1 or Mfn1/Mfn2 abolishes the fusion phenotype, indicating that BGP-15 acts upstream or within the endogenous fusion machinery (Szabó et al., 2018). In vivo, these effects translate into improved mitochondrial ultrastructure and tissue histology under ROS stress (e.g., monocrotaline-induced PAH) (Szabó et al., 2018). In hypertensive cardiomyopathy, BGP-15 increases PGC-1α and mitochondrial mass, with concurrent shifts in CREB/AMPK phosphorylation consistent with improved energetic signaling, reduced p38/JNK via MKP-1 upregulation, and increased Akt/GSK-3β prosurvival signaling (Horváth et al., 2021).

Insulin-sensitizing stress signaling. In skeletal muscle and human studies, BGP-15 increases HSP72 expression, enhances insulin receptor autophosphorylation (blocking JNK inhibitory phosphorylation), activates RAC1, increases AKT phosphorylation, promotes GLUT4 translocation, increases membrane fluidity, raises AMPK activity, and reduces HSF1 acetylation, altogether improving glucose disposal without overt toxicity in a randomized trial (Crul et al., 2013). These metabolic effects are mechanistically congruent with the membrane–HSR–mitochondrial triad described above (Crul et al., 2013).

Ocular and retinal mechanisms. In rat eyes, BGP-15 increased HSP70 and decreased NFκB, consistent with HSR enhancement and anti-inflammatory signaling in ocular tissues (Wachal et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion and diabetic retinopathy models, functional improvements on ERG, restoration of oscillatory potentials, and preservation of retinal thickness are consistent with mitochondrial protection and stress-response reinforcement in retinal cells (Takács et al., 2024). The topical SBECD formulation demonstrated pharmacologic activity in the retina without systemic pharmacokinetic characterization, indicating local ocular delivery as a viable route for targeting mitochondrial and HSP pathways in the posterior segment (Takács et al., 2024).

The team’s hypothesis—that BGP-15 stabilizes mitochondrial membrane proteins and co-induces HSF1-driven antioxidant chaperone responses in RPE to mitigate oxidative stress in dry AMD—is aligned with the compound’s demonstrated pharmacology in retinal, cardiac, neural, and pulmonary models: (i) robust mitochondrial enrichment and stabilization of Δψm under oxidative/inflammatory stress, (ii) ROS lowering at complexes I and III without direct radical scavenging, (iii) activation of the HSR via membrane raft remodeling and HSF1 acetylation control, and (iv) suppression of ROS-sensitive injury cascades (JNK/p38) with concurrent activation of pro-survival Akt (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) is an endogenous bile acid, a taurine conjugate of ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), that was originally isolated from bear bile and is now produced synthetically for laboratory and clinical research (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). As a member of the bile acid family, TUDCA has a dual role: its traditional function in lipid digestion is accompanied by potent signaling activities that provide chemical chaperoning properties. This property enables TUDCA to stabilize misfolded proteins and alleviate endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. In addition, TUDCA exerts anti-apoptotic effects by modulating the mitochondrial cell death pathway. Its application as a neuroprotectant has emerged over the last decade, and its favorable ocular safety profile in preclinical studies has invited consideration for repurposing in retinal degenerative conditions such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, TUDCA and related bile acids have been evaluated in several models of neurodegeneration and retinal degeneration. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that TUDCA protects retinal cells against both oxidative injury and ER stress. In vitro, TUDCA treatment of ARPE-19 retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) not only attenuated cell death but also reduced markers of oxidative damage, increased cell viability, and modulated antioxidant gene expression (Alhasani et al., 2020). In parallel, multiple in vivo studies have reported that systemic administration of TUDCA reduces photoreceptor apoptosis and preserves retinal structure and function in animal models of inherited retinal degeneration including retinitis pigmentosa and in models of exudative AMD such as laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024). Although the bulk of these preclinical investigations has been conducted in models focusing on photoreceptors, retinal ganglion cells, or vascular endpoints, the underlying mechanisms of TUDCA’s cytoprotective activity raise the possibility that its benefits may extend to the RPE—the cell type that is centrally involved in dry AMD and geographic atrophy. Importantly, little direct evidence exists from dedicated geographic atrophy models or experiments that solely target RPE mitochondrial endpoints; however, the promising biochemical and electrophysiological data from rodent models suggest that the candidate’s safety and overall neuroprotective profile are well established in ocular systems (Alhasani et al., 2020; Li et al., 2024).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanistic basis of TUDCA’s therapeutic potential is multifaceted. A central theme is its ability to reduce ER stress in cells that are undergoing chronic protein-folding challenges. Under conditions of sustained stress, the unfolded protein response (UPR) is activated, and key transcription factors such as CHOP (CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein homologous protein) become upregulated to drive cell death when the stress is unmanageable. TUDCA has been shown in various cell models to act as a chemical chaperone, thereby reducing ER stress and suppressing CHOP induction (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020). For instance, in ARPE-19 cell models treated with thapsigargin to induce ER stress, TUDCA treatment led to a marked decrease in CHOP expression and reduced apoptosis (Alhasani et al., 2020). This suggests that TUDCA modulates the ER stress response, possibly by stabilizing protein folding and facilitating the proper trafficking of misfolded proteins.  

In addition to its ER‐related effects, TUDCA exerts anti-apoptotic actions by stabilizing the mitochondrial membrane. Under stress conditions, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) triggers the intrinsic apoptosis pathway, characterized by the translocation of pro-apoptotic proteins such as Bax, the release of cytochrome c, and subsequent caspase activation (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Kusaczuk, 2019). Evidence from neuronal models and some retinal studies indicates that TUDCA prevents the depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane, thereby preserving Δψm, and reduces downstream apoptotic events. This effect has been linked to a reduction in mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), which are produced excessively when mitochondrial integrity is compromised. TUDCA’s actions in reducing overall intracellular ROS levels, as reported in H₂O₂-exposed RPE cells, further support the idea that improved mitochondrial function may contribute to cell survival (Alhasani et al., 2020).  

Moreover, TUDCA can modulate additional cellular pathways that are pertinent to retinal health. It has been reported to up-regulate antioxidant defenses via increased expression of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) and enhancement of glutathione (GSH) levels. These effects likely contribute to the reduction in both cytosolic and mitochondrial oxidative stress (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Other studies have highlighted TUDCA’s influence on phagocytic pathways in the RPE—for example, by promoting MerTK-mediated phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments—which, although not directly linked to ER or mitochondrial stress, represent an important aspect of RPE physiology that could indirectly improve cell survival in degenerative conditions (Murase et al., 2015).  

Taken together, the biochemical and molecular data indicate that TUDCA’s mechanism of action is well aligned with addressing the cellular stress observed in dry AMD. By inhibiting CHOP induction, preserving Δψm, and reducing mtROS, TUDCA could feasibly stop or slow the progression of RPE cell death that underpins geographic atrophy (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

Expected Effect:  
The proposal hypothesizes that TUDCA will reduce ER stress in the RPE, thereby preventing secondary mitochondrial dysfunction and the associated production of reactive oxygen species. In the proposed assay, RPE cells (either ARPE-19 or primary RPE cultures) subjected to an ER stressor (such as thapsigargin or H₂O₂) are expected to exhibit elevated markers of ER stress, particularly CHOP, along with signs of mitochondrial distress including decreased mitochondrial membrane potential and increased mtROS production. On treatment with TUDCA at appropriate dosages (often in the 100 μM range in similar in vitro assays), one expects to observe a significant reduction in CHOP induction along with the preservation or restoration of Δψm, as measured by fluorescent indicators such as JC-1 or TMRM, and a concomitant decrease in mitochondrial ROS as assessed by probes such as MitoSOX. These effects are expected because prior in vitro studies in retinal cells have shown that TUDCA can ameliorate cell death by modulating oxidative stress and apoptosis, and similar outcomes have been observed in neuronal and non-retinal cell models (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

Furthermore, given that dry AMD is characterized by chronic ER stress and secondary mitochondrial dysfunction in the RPE, the ability of TUDCA to reduce these stress responses may translate into improved RPE survival and function. RPE cells express high levels of ER stress markers under pathologic conditions, and proteins such as CHOP are known mediators of apoptosis in these cells. It is therefore expected that TUDCA will attenuate the cascade of events initiated by ER stress—reducing apoptotic signaling, preserving mitochondrial function, reducing mtROS, and ultimately leading to enhanced cell viability. As such, the anticipated outcome in the proposed assay is a clear biochemical and functional improvement in RPE cultures challenged with ER stressors, supporting the use of TUDCA in dry AMD (Alhasani et al., 2020).  

Overall Evaluation:  
TUDCA presents as a promising candidate for drug repurposing in dry AMD due to its well-documented roles as an ER stress inhibitor and mitochondrial stabilizer. One of the major strengths of TUDCA is its dual mechanism of action: it not only functions as a chemical chaperone to reduce ER stress and inhibit the pro-apoptotic effector CHOP but also stabilizes the mitochondrial membrane to prevent the cascade of events leading to cell death. These effects are complemented by its ability to reduce overall reactive oxygen species and bolster antioxidant defenses, which are critical in tissues affected by chronic oxidative stress such as the RPE in geographic atrophy (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020).  

In terms of therapeutic history, TUDCA has been used extensively in preclinical models of retinal degeneration, with multiple studies demonstrating its protective effects on photoreceptors and retinal ganglion cells. Its prior use in ocular contexts and a favorable safety profile in animal models provide important translational support. However, one potential weakness in repurposing TUDCA for dry AMD is that most of the preclinical evidence is derived from models of photoreceptor degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, or choroidal neovascularization rather than from targeted assessments in RPE cells or dry AMD models. While there is suggestive evidence from several studies that TUDCA benefits RPE function—such as improved phagocytosis via MerTK activation—the direct demonstration of its ability to inhibit CHOP induction, preserve mitochondrial membrane potential, or specifically reduce mitochondrial ROS in RPE is less robust (Alhasani et al., 2020; Murase et al., 2015).  

Furthermore, although mechanistic data in other tissue and neuronal models strongly support TUDCA’s capacity to modulate both ER stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Kusaczuk, 2019), these endpoints have not been unequivocally established in RPE cells within the context of geographic atrophy. This gap highlights the need for further targeted preclinical studies. For example, experiments using polarized primary RPE cultures or RPE-specific animal models of dry AMD should be undertaken to directly measure CHOP expression, mitochondrial membrane potential via JC-1/TMRM assays, and mtROS levels via MitoSOX or equivalent assays following TUDCA treatment. Additionally, while in vitro assays have established its general safety in retinal cells, chronic dosing studies in appropriate AMD models will be important to establish long-term efficacy and safety.  

Another consideration is that the multifaceted nature of dry AMD pathogenesis extends beyond ER stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. While TUDCA’s actions on these pathways are compelling, resistance or compensatory mechanisms in RPE cells could limit its efficacy in the complex environment of geographic atrophy. Nonetheless, the broad-spectrum anti-apoptotic and anti-oxidative actions of TUDCA provide a strong rationale for its further examination in dry AMD.  

In summary, TUDCA is a highly attractive candidate for repurposing as a therapy for dry AMD based on its natural origin as a bile acid, its established use as a chemical chaperone and mitochondrial stabilizer, and its demonstrated neuroprotective and cytoprotective effects in multiple retinal models. Its capacity to reduce ER stress—with particular inhibition of CHOP induction—and to preserve mitochondrial membrane potential and lower oxidative stress aligns well with the proposed mechanism underlying RPE degeneration in geographic atrophy. However, critical gaps remain in the direct evidence for its efficacy in RPE-specific systems and AMD/dry AMD models. The next steps should include rigorous experimental validation in relevant in vitro and in vivo models to establish that TUDCA indeed preserves Δψm and suppresses mitochondrial ROS in ER-stressed RPE cells while reducing pro-apoptotic markers such as CHOP. If these endpoints can be achieved in targeted preclinical studies, TUDCA could represent a promising, safe, and mechanistically rational therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AICAR (5‐Aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide) is a synthetic nucleoside analog originally developed as an AMP mimetic agent that is capable of activating AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) across a range of cell types. It is produced by chemical synthesis and is available commercially (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich A9978), having been studied for several decades in the context of cellular energy metabolism and stress signaling. As a member of a class of compounds that mimic the natural intracellular messenger AMP, AICAR is taken up into cells via adenosine transporters and is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase into its active metabolite, ZMP (5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide monophosphate), which then mimics AMP in its interactions with AMPK (Efstathiou et al., 2020). This compound belongs to a well‐established class of metabolic modulators, and similar agents have been used in experimental settings to modulate glucose uptake, fatty acid oxidation, and overall energy homeostasis in both basic science and translational research contexts (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014). In addition, several preclinical studies have evaluated AICAR’s potential as an “exercise mimetic” due to its ability to enhance energy metabolism in muscle and other tissues, and its synthetic nature allows for reproducible and scalable dosing in research models (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, AICAR was developed primarily as an agent to activate AMPK in metabolic studies and has been investigated in a variety of preclinical models ranging from cancer to cardiovascular disease. In the oncology field, for example, AICAR has been shown to inhibit cancer cell proliferation, induce cell cycle arrest, and promote programmed cell death in several cancer types via AMPK-dependent modulation of pathways such as PI3K-Akt and mTOR (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014; Rattan et al., 2005). Clinical studies, particularly those in the cardiovascular arena, have also evaluated AICAR’s safety profile in the context of ischemia-reperfusion injury, including human trials during cardiac surgery, demonstrating that it can be administered safely in humans (Rattan et al., 2005). In the context of ocular research, AICAR has been studied for its effects on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and other ocular cell types; several studies have demonstrated that AICAR suppresses the production of pro-inflammatory complement components such as complement factor 3 (C3) and complement factor B (CFB) in RPE cells under inflammatory conditions (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017). Although there is no established clinical use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) to date, these preclinical observations, combined with its well-known pharmacological profile, have spurred interest in repurposing AICAR for treating retinal diseases characterized by oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020). Furthermore, studies examining AMPK activators in the eye – including those using AICAR in animal models of uveitis or oxidative stress-induced RPE damage – support the notion that activating this metabolic pathway can protect against retinal degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

Mechanism of Action:  
AICAR exerts its biological activity primarily through the activation of AMPK, a master regulator of cellular energy balance that responds to alterations in the AMP/ATP ratio. Once AICAR is imported into cells through adenosine transporters, it is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase to form ZMP, an analog of AMP. ZMP binds to the regulatory γ subunit of AMPK, causing a conformational change that facilitates AMPK phosphorylation at Thr172 by upstream kinases such as LKB1, thereby fully activating the kinase (Efstathiou et al., 2020). Activated AMPK then phosphorylates a series of downstream targets involved in energy metabolism, including acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) and elements of the mTOR signaling pathway. In RPE cells, this activation is particularly important because AMPK phosphorylates and activates ULK1, a kinase critical for initiating autophagy and mitophagy, thereby promoting the clearance of damaged mitochondria (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Chung et al., 2017).  

A central component of the rationale for using AICAR in dry AMD is its ability to stimulate the transcriptional coactivator PGC-1α. AMPK-mediated phosphorylation of PGC-1α enhances its activity and nuclear translocation, which in turn drives the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant defense, and metabolic adaptation (Hu et al., 2024; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). This mechanism is particularly attractive in dry AMD because mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells is thought to contribute significantly to disease pathogenesis by impairing oxidative phosphorylation, increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and triggering cell senescence or death (Tong et al., 2022; Rego, 2023). In addition to these AMPK-dependent effects, some studies have reported that AICAR exerts certain effects independent of AMPK activation. For instance, AICAR has been shown to suppress TNF-α-induced complement factor expression by mechanisms that do not involve AMPK, suggesting that alternative signaling pathways or direct modulation of transcription factor activity might also contribute to its overall activity profile (Chung et al., 2017; Kirchner et al., 2018). These AMPK-independent actions could either broaden the therapeutic potential of AICAR in modulating inflammatory responses or introduce complexity into its activity profile that will need to be carefully isolated and understood (Kirchner et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2024).  

Furthermore, AICAR has been observed to affect mitochondrial dynamics not only by stimulating biogenesis through PGC-1α activation but also by modifying autophagic flux through mTOR inhibition. In models of RPE oxidative stress, where excessive ROS levels lead to mitochondrial fragmentation and accumulation of dysfunctional organelles, AICAR-induced AMPK activation facilitates the clearance of damaged mitochondria via mitophagy, thus restoring mitochondrial quality and energy production (Fisher et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2024). Moreover, experimental evidence suggests that AICAR can modulate the balance between cellular glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation by shifting metabolism toward a more energy-efficient, oxidative phenotype, thereby increasing the overall oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and potentially improving cellular resilience under oxidative stress (Chan et al., 2020; Fisher, 2022).  

Expected Effect:  
Given its mechanisms of action, the expected effect of AICAR in an assay aimed at treating dry AMD would be multifaceted. In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress—a hallmark of dry AMD—AICAR treatment is expected to lead to robust activation of AMPK, as measured by increased phosphorylation of both AMPK and its downstream substrates such as ACC and ULK1 (Guo et al., 2018; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). This activation should in turn upregulate PGC-1α, resulting in enhanced transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, improved mitochondrial DNA replication, and an increased capacity for ATP production (Hu et al., 2024). As damaged mitochondria are a major source of ROS in stressed RPE cells, the stimulation of autophagy and mitophagy is anticipated to selectively clear these dysfunctional organelles, reducing cellular oxidative stress and preventing the secondary damage that contributes to RPE degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

In addition to these metabolic effects, AICAR is also expected to attenuate inflammatory responses within the RPE and adjacent retinal tissues. For instance, by modulating the activity of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) and reducing the expression of inflammatory mediators such as tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and complement components (e.g., C3 and CFB), AICAR would help to create a less pro-inflammatory microenvironment that could further protect RPE cells from damage (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017; Kirchner et al., 2018). These effects are particularly pertinent given that chronic, low-grade inflammation coupled with complement dysregulation is a recognized component of dry AMD pathogenesis.  

At the cellular level, the outcome of AICAR-induced AMPK activation is expected to manifest as enhanced mitochondrial function, improved energy charge (ATP/AMP ratio), reduced ROS accumulation, and, ultimately, a restoration of normal metabolic and autophagic flux in RPE cells (Fisher et al., 2022; Fisher, 2022). This improved bioenergetic profile should translate into protection against RPE cell death, potentially slowing or halting the progression of geographic atrophy associated with dry AMD (Yu et al., 2024; Si et al., 2023). Moreover, since RPE dysfunction in AMD also involves a reduction in the phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, AICAR’s modulatory effects on autophagy may indirectly help to restore the homeostatic functions of RPE cells, reducing the accumulation of damaging lipofuscin and drusen material (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Sung et al., 2015). In summary, the expected effect is a dual-action benefit—mitigation of oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum stresses via improved mitochondrial dynamics and an anti-inflammatory effect stemming from a reduction in complement activation and NF-κB-driven cytokine production (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020).  

Overall Evaluation:  
AICAR represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration owing to its robust and well-characterized mechanism of action via AMPK activation. The strengths of this candidate lie in its dual capacity to modulate critical pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis: on one hand, AICAR enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and promotes the removal of damaged mitochondria through autophagy/mitophagy, and on the other, it attenuates inflammatory cascades that exacerbate RPE cell damage (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hu et al., 2024). The ability of AICAR to upregulate PGC-1α is particularly compelling because mitochondrial dysfunction is now widely recognized as a central element in dry AMD. Preclinical studies have illustrated that dysregulation of mitochondrial function in RPE cells—a decrease in oxidative phosphorylation capacity, increased ROS production, and impaired clearance of damaged organelles—is pivotal in the initiation and progression of AMD (Tong et al., 2022; Rego, 2023). Thus, a compound like AICAR that can simultaneously restore mitochondrial health and mitigate inflammatory responses offers a multifaceted approach to disease modification.  

From the therapeutic history perspective, AICAR has been extensively studied in various preclinical models, including those of ocular inflammation and oxidative stress in RPE cells. Its ability to safely activate AMPK in vivo has been demonstrated across multiple species and contexts, including settings that mimic some aspects of AMD-related stress, such as endotoxin-induced uveitis and sodium iodate-induced RPE damage (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Chan et al., 2020). Additionally, the compound’s known clinical safety profile in human studies—albeit in contexts outside ophthalmology—provides an encouraging starting point for repurposing it for dry AMD, where no approved therapeutics currently exist (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017).  

However, there are notable weaknesses and challenges that must be addressed. First, while AMPK activation is generally beneficial for energy homeostasis and autophagy, certain studies have indicated that AICAR’s effects on RPE cell biology might be context-dependent. For instance, some experimental reports have shown that AICAR can reduce the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments by RPE cells—a process that is essential for retinal health—which may represent a double-edged sword if not carefully titrated (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Yu et al., 2024). In addition, the existence of AMPK-independent effects—such as the direct inhibition of complement factor expression—introduces complexity into the overall mechanism of action and makes it challenging to predict all downstream outcomes. Differential responses have also been observed between healthy and diseased donor RPE cells, implying that “metabolic memory” or cellular adaptation may influence drug responsiveness (Fisher et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2017). These considerations suggest that while the theoretical underpinnings for using AICAR in dry AMD are solid, the translation of these effects into clinical efficacy may require careful optimization of dosing, delivery, and patient selection.  

Another potential limitation is related to its broad mechanism of action. AICAR activates several metabolic pathways that are intertwined with many aspects of cellular physiology. While this pleiotropy provides the therapeutic benefit of addressing multiple dysregulated pathways in AMD simultaneously, it may also increase the risk of off-target effects or metabolic disturbances in tissues outside the retina (Rattan et al., 2005; Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014). For instance, systemic administration of AICAR has been associated with shifts in glycolytic flux and modifications of lipid metabolism, and it is therefore imperative that strategies for ocular delivery (such as intravitreal injections or topical formulations) be developed to maximize retinal exposure while minimizing systemic exposure (Chan et al., 2020; Kamoshita et al., 2014).  

Moreover, despite the substantial body of preclinical data supporting the role of AICAR in activating AMPK and restoring mitochondrial function, clinical data specific to dry AMD are lacking. Although related studies have shown benefits in models of retinal inflammation and degeneration, the exact therapeutic window, long-term safety, and efficacy in humans with AMD must be thoroughly evaluated in well-designed clinical trials. It is also worth mentioning that other AMPK activators, such as metformin, have independently demonstrated protective effects in AMD models, thereby lending credence to the approach but also raising questions about whether AICAR offers a distinct advantage over these agents (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020).  

In summary, the overall evaluation of AICAR as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. Considering all the available literature, the repurposing of AICAR for dry AMD appears to be a promising strategy that merits further investigation. The compound’s ability to simultaneously address mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and chronic inflammation positions it as a multifaceted agent with the potential to modify disease progression in a condition that currently lacks effective therapeutic options (Chung et al., 2017; Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020). Moving forward, it will be critical to further elucidate the detailed cellular and molecular responses to AICAR in human RPE cells, determine the optimal dosing and delivery parameters specific to the ocular environment, and perform in vivo studies that mimic the complex pathobiology of dry AMD. With these additional efforts, AICAR could eventually emerge as a valuable addition to the limited therapeutic arsenal available for managing this debilitating condition.  

In conclusion, AICAR’s robust preclinical profile as an AMPK activator, its well-understood mechanisms of promoting mitochondrial biogenesis and autophagy, and its capacity to mitigate inflammatory responses provide a solid scientific basis for its potential repurposing in dry AMD (Hu et al., 2024; Hyttinen et al., 2011; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). However, several challenges remain: the dual nature of its effects (both AMPK-dependent and independent), the possibility of adverse effects on key RPE functions such as phagocytosis, and the need for precise ocular drug delivery methods. Therefore, while AICAR is an exciting candidate with considerable mechanistic appeal, its translation from bench to bedside in the treatment of dry AMD will require further detailed studies to fully map its therapeutic window, safety profile, and efficacy in human subjects (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014; Rego, 2023; Kamoshita et al., 2014). Continued rigorous research and methodical clinical evaluation will determine whether AICAR can be developed into an effective treatment modality for this currently intractable form of macular degeneration.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
MitoTEMPO, marketed as InvivoGen antiox15, is a synthetic mitochondria‐targeted antioxidant that belongs to the class of TPP⁺-linked piperidine nitroxides. Its molecular design is based on the well‐characterized TEMPO (2,2,6,6‐tetramethylpiperidine‐N-oxyl) scaffold, which is a stable nitroxide radical with established antioxidant and redox‐active properties. In MitoTEMPO, a TEMPO derivative is chemically conjugated to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) moiety using an appropriate linker, which ensures selective mitochondrial accumulation by exploiting the large negative mitochondrial membrane potential. The TPP⁺ group, owing to its lipophilicity and delocalized positive charge, facilitates rapid translocation across biological membranes and drives the compound into the mitochondrial matrix by a Nernstian accumulation mechanism. This design confers MitoTEMPO with dual functionality: the piperidine nitroxide core catalytically dismutates superoxide radicals by cycling between nitroxide, hydroxylamine, and oxoammonium states, while the TPP⁺ component achieves a high intramitochondrial concentration necessary for site‐specific antioxidant effects (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Peoples et al., 2019; Sassetti et al., 2021). The synthesis of such compounds generally involves standard organic synthetic methods that couple the nitroxide moiety to a phosphonium salt, yielding molecules that are both redox‐active and selective for mitochondria; these structural modifications represent an evolution from conventional nitroxides such as TEMPOL, improving not only cellular uptake but also intracellular distribution in disease‐relevant contexts (Zinovkin et al., 2023; Forini et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, piperidine nitroxides have been extensively investigated as antioxidants with a range of anti‐inflammatory, radioprotective, and cytoprotective properties. Their applications span preclinical models of cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration, pulmonary injury, and metabolic dysfunction. MitoTEMPO in particular has been applied in several animal studies, where its mitochondrial targeting capability has provided significant protection against oxidative stress‐mediated injury. For example, in cardiovascular models, MitoTEMPO has been shown to reduce mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS), preserve mitochondrial function, and improve cardiac performance by ameliorating the effects of ischemia–reperfusion injury and hypertensive damage (Forini et al., 2020; Grujicic & Allen, 2024). Its efficacy as a superoxide dismutase (SOD) mimetic further underpins its utility in conditions where excess superoxide production drives pathological outcomes. Although direct clinical studies in ocular disorders, including dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), are not available, the preclinical safety profile of MitoTEMPO has been encouraging. Rodent studies report that it is well tolerated at doses up to 5 mg/kg, with no significant hepatic or renal toxicity observed (Forini et al., 2020; Fock & Parnova, 2021). Additionally, TPP⁺‐linked antioxidants as a class, including MitoQ and MitoVitE, have progressed through preclinical evaluation in various diseases, with certain compounds even entering early-phase clinical trials for nonocular indications such as cardiovascular and metabolic disorders. Despite the absence of direct clinical evidence for AMD, there is a growing body of literature supporting the role of mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of geographic atrophy, a late stage form of dry AMD. Thus, the historical application of MitoTEMPO in models that recapitulate oxidative injury provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, where mitochondrial ROS plays a critical role (Peoples et al., 2019; Sassetti et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the core of MitoTEMPO’s pharmacological action is its ability to function as a catalytic SOD mimetic. The piperidine nitroxide moiety of MitoTEMPO undergoes reversible one‐electron redox cycling between three states: the nitroxide radical (R–NO•), the corresponding hydroxylamine (R–NHOH), and the oxoammonium cation (R–NO⁺). In the presence of mitochondrial superoxide (O₂•⁻), MitoTEMPO facilitates the conversion of superoxide to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), thereby mimicking the action of endogenous SOD enzymes. This catalytic cycling is essential for mitigating the deleterious effects of excess superoxide, which include the formation of secondary reactive species such as hydroxyl radicals (•OH) and the initiation of lipid peroxidation cascades that compromise mitochondrial membrane integrity (Forini et al., 2020; Apostolova & Victor, 2015). Furthermore, the compound’s ability to oxidize ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) to its ferric form (Fe³⁺) helps to limit the Fenton reaction, a process responsible for the generation of highly reactive hydroxyl radicals from H₂O₂, further contributing to its antioxidant efficacy (Forini et al., 2020; Peoples et al., 2019).

The triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) group is a critical structural element that differentiates MitoTEMPO from other nitroxides. By virtue of its delocalized positive charge and lipophilic character, the TPP⁺ moiety permits MitoTEMPO to traverse cellular membranes passively and accumulate several hundred‐fold within the mitochondrial matrix relative to the cytosol. This preferential accumulation not only enhances the local concentration of the antioxidant but also positions it in immediate proximity to the major sites of superoxide production, such as the complexes of the electron transport chain. Within the mitochondria, the nitroxide is subjected to a reductive environment wherein it is partially reduced by endogenous reductants such as ubiquinol; this reaction regenerates the active hydroxylamine form, ensuring sustained antioxidant activity despite continuous exposure to ROS (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Sadowska-Bartosz & Bartosz, 2024; Wang et al., 2020).

In biochemical terms, the overall mechanism of action of MitoTEMPO is multifaceted. It acts not only by scavenging superoxide directly but also by interfering with downstream oxidative reactions that lead to lipid peroxidation of mitochondrial membranes. Lipid peroxidation undermines mitochondrial bioenergetics by damaging membrane lipids, impairing the function of membrane-bound enzymes, and ultimately leading to the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm). By preventing such peroxidative damage, MitoTEMPO is postulated to maintain the structural integrity and functional competence of the mitochondria. Additionally, the reduction in intramitochondrial ROS has secondary anti-inflammatory effects, as oxidative stress is known to activate redox-sensitive signaling pathways (such as NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasome pathways) that exacerbate cellular dysfunction and apoptosis. In the context of the RPE, which is particularly vulnerable to oxidative stress due to its high metabolic demands and constant exposure to light and oxygen, the ability of MitoTEMPO to function as a sustained mitochondrial antioxidant is of significant therapeutic interest (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Peoples et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Zielonka et al., 2017).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of MitoTEMPO for dry age‐related macular degeneration is that it will preferentially accumulate in the mitochondria of RPE cells and mitigate oxidative damage by catalytically dismuting superoxide radicals, thereby preventing lipid peroxidation and preserving the bioenergetic function critical for cell survival. In in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells challenged with hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), MitoTEMPO has been observed to reduce the MitoSOX signal, a fluorescent indicator of mitochondrial superoxide, and to restore the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), which is often compromised under oxidative stress conditions. These effects support the notion that MitoTEMPO can protect the RPE from the mitochondrial dysfunction that is thought to contribute to geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Forini et al., 2020; Apostolova & Victor, 2015).

On a molecular level, the expected therapeutic effect in the RPE is mediated by several interrelated processes. First, by lowering the levels of ROS within the mitochondria, MitoTEMPO reduces the oxidative stress burden that leads to peroxidation of phospholipids in the inner mitochondrial membrane. This prevention of lipid peroxidation is crucial because it preserves the functional integrity of the electron transport chain and other membrane-associated processes that generate ATP, the energy currency necessary for RPE cellular functions (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Forini et al., 2020). Second, by dismuting superoxide, MitoTEMPO interrupts the formation of secondary reactive species that would otherwise aggravate cellular injury and trigger apoptotic signaling pathways. As RPE cell loss is a hallmark of geographic atrophy in dry AMD, the preservation of cell viability is a key expected outcome. Third, the antioxidant action at the mitochondrial level is anticipated to modulate redox-sensitive signaling cascades that contribute to chronic inflammation and cellular senescence—both of which are implicated in the progression of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2020; Forini et al., 2020).

The expression of antioxidant enzymes such as MnSOD in the RPE, which is closely linked to mitochondrial oxidative stress, further supports the rationale for a mimetic such as MitoTEMPO. The compound’s SOD-like activity is particularly important because it directly addresses the imbalance between ROS generation and antioxidant defenses that characterizes the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Moreover, in animal models such as the Ccl2⁻/⁻/Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ mouse—a model that recapitulates many features of dry AMD—the administration of MitoTEMPO has been associated with a reduction in mitochondrial ROS and a preservation of Δψm in the RPE. These findings collectively suggest that, when applied to the context of dry AMD, MitoTEMPO is expected to maintain mitochondrial function, reduce oxidative damage, and thereby slow the progression of geographic atrophy (Wang et al., 2020; Forini et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
MitoTEMPO represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration due to its targeted mechanism of action and its ability to counteract mitochondrial oxidative stress—a central pathogenic factor in the progression of geographic atrophy. One of the principal strengths of this candidate is its design as a TPP⁺–linked piperidine nitroxide, which facilitates selective mitochondrial accumulation. This targeting is critical because the mitochondria of RPE cells are a major source of ROS production, and accumulating antioxidant capacity at this subcellular location directly addresses a key contributor to cellular dysfunction in dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Peoples et al., 2019).

Moreover, the catalytic SOD-mimetic activity of MitoTEMPO enables it to continuously cycle between redox states and neutralize multiple superoxide radicals over time, in contrast with stoichiometric antioxidants that are consumed in the reaction. This catalytic mechanism, which involves rapid redox cycling between nitroxide, hydroxylamine, and oxoammonium species, has been well documented in preclinical models and lays a solid biochemical foundation for its use in pathologies where oxidative stress is a driving factor (Forini et al., 2020; Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Wang et al., 2020).

The preclinical tolerability profile is another favorable aspect. Rodent studies have indicated that MitoTEMPO is generally well tolerated, with safe dosing up to 5 mg/kg without overt hepatic or renal toxicity. Given that systemic safety is a crucial consideration for any repurposed therapeutic, these findings provide confidence that the compound may have an acceptable safety margin, although ocular pharmacokinetics remain to be fully characterized (Forini et al., 2020; Fock & Parnova, 2021).

However, there are several weaknesses and challenges that must be carefully considered. First, despite promising in vitro and systemic preclinical data, there is currently insufficient evidence regarding ocular pharmacokinetics and tissue distribution after local (intraocular or topical) administration. The lack of clinical ocular PK data raises concerns about whether effective concentrations can be achieved in the RPE and posterior segment of the eye without systemic side effects. Formulation strategies such as nanoparticle conjugation or controlled‐release systems may be required to overcome these limitations (Bubb et al., 2020; Apostolova & Victor, 2015).

Second, while the SOD-mimetic and lipid peroxidation–preventive mechanisms of MitoTEMPO are well established in other organ systems, the specific microenvironment of the RPE poses unique challenges. The RPE is subject to chronic, cumulative oxidative stress from both endogenous metabolic processes and exogenous light exposure. As such, the long-term stability and sustained activity of the nitroxide may be compromised by rapid bioreduction to its hydroxylamine form, which is EPR silent and potentially less active. This raises the possibility that repeated dosing or modified chemical formulations might be necessary to maintain therapeutic levels over time (Wang et al., 2020; Zielonka et al., 2017).

Third, the potential for off-target redox reactions, particularly under conditions of high local concentration or altered redox state, cannot be ignored. Although MitoTEMPO has been engineered to preferentially scavenge superoxide and prevent lipid peroxidation, there is always a risk that nitroxides could inadvertently interfere with normal cellular signaling pathways that rely on ROS as signaling molecules. In the delicate environment of the retina, where precise redox balance is essential for cell survival and function, such off-target effects could lead to unintended consequences. Detailed studies to map the influence of MitoTEMPO on redox-sensitive signaling cascades in the RPE will be critical in mitigating these risks (Zielonka et al., 2017; Sadowska-Bartosz & Bartosz, 2024).

Additionally, the current body of evidence supporting the use of MitoTEMPO in dry AMD is largely inferential, based on studies conducted in non-ocular systems or in models of general oxidative stress. Although there are promising signs from experiments in ARPE-19 cells and RPE cells derived from dry AMD models (for example, Ccl2⁻/⁻/Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ mice), direct evidence from dedicated ocular studies is still sparse. Bridging this gap will require comprehensive in vivo studies in established models of geographic atrophy to confirm whether the beneficial effects seen in other tissues can be translated to an ocular context (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Bubb et al., 2020).

Finally, while the rationale for targeting mitochondrial dysfunction in the RPE is compelling, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD means that addressing oxidative stress alone might not be sufficient to arrest disease progression. Dry AMD involves a complex interplay of inflammatory, genetic, and environmental factors. Therefore, it is possible that MitoTEMPO, when used as a monotherapy, might need to be combined with additional agents that address other pathogenic pathways, such as complement dysregulation or chronic inflammation, to achieve a clinically meaningful outcome (Gwozdzinski et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2020).

In summary, MitoTEMPO offers a mechanistically elegant approach to mitigating mitochondrial oxidative stress in the RPE by virtue of its unique design as a TPP⁺-linked piperidine nitroxide. Its ability to catalytically dismutate superoxide, prevent lipid peroxidation, and preserve mitochondrial function aligns well with the pathophysiological underpinnings of geographic atrophy in dry AMD. The strengths of this therapeutic candidate lie in its targeted mitochondrial delivery, well-characterized redox cycling, and promising preclinical safety profile. However, the translation of these effects into the ocular environment remains uncertain due to the lack of direct ocular pharmacokinetic and efficacy data, potential issues with nitroxide stability in the face of chronic oxidative stress, and the inherent complexity of dry AMD pathogenesis.

Given these considerations, we recommend that further preclinical studies be undertaken to specifically evaluate the ocular pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and long-term efficacy of MitoTEMPO in relevant models of dry AMD. Additionally, exploration of advanced formulation strategies aimed at enhancing retinal delivery and sustained drug release may be warranted. Overall, while MitoTEMPO represents a promising candidate from a mechanistic standpoint for repurposing in dry AMD, its ultimate clinical utility will hinge on overcoming the challenges associated with ocular delivery and demonstrating durable efficacy in mitigating RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and geographic atrophy (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Forini et al., 2020; Peoples et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Zielonka et al., 2017).

To conclude, MitoTEMPO’s biochemical profile and mechanism of action strongly support its potential as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD by targeting the root cause of oxidative mitochondrial injury in RPE cells. However, its advancement into clinical development for this indication will require a concerted research effort to address key translational hurdles, including formulation optimization for ocular use, comprehensive in vivo validation in disease-specific models, and rigorous safety studies focused on the sensitive retinal environment. If these challenges can be effectively managed, MitoTEMPO may not only complement existing antioxidant strategies but could also emerge as a transformative treatment option for patients suffering from dry AMD.

Historically, fumaric acid esters were introduced into clinical practice as antipsoriatic agents in Europe, with formulations such as Fumaderm® entering the market in the 1990s (Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).
