Below is a comprehensive evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO‐Me) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), structured in sections that address its origins, therapeutic history, known mechanisms of action, expected effects in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and an overall assessment of its strengths and challenges.

• Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Bardoxolone methyl is a semisynthetic derivative belonging to the synthetic oleanane triterpenoid class. Its origin stems from oleanolic acid—a naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid abundantly found in various medicinal plants. Early medicinal chemistry programs sought to overcome the modest anti‐inflammatory activity and poor bioavailability of oleanolic acid by introducing targeted modifications. Through chemical derivatization, these programs generated CDDO (2‐cyano‐3,12‐dioxooleana‐1,9‐dien‐28‐oic acid) and subsequently its C‐28 methyl ester, known as Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO‐Me) (Borella et al., 2019). The synthetic process involves the installation of electrophilic Michael acceptor groups at strategic positions on the oleanane scaffold, such as the addition of an α,β‐unsaturated carbonyl in the A‐ring and further incorporation of a cyano group that substantially increases the compound’s potency relative to its natural precursor (Wong et al., 2016; Zhang & Chapman, 2020). These chemical modifications not only enhance the anti‐inflammatory and anticancer properties but also improve chemical stability and oral bioavailability. The structural design, which incorporates a reversible electrophilic reactivity, underpins the compound’s ability to engage diverse cellular targets (Thomas, 2012; Zhou et al., 2014). Bardoxolone methyl thus represents a chemically advanced, highly potent agent from a class of molecules originally designed to trigger cytoprotective responses via direct electrophilic modulation.

• Therapeutic History  
Bardoxolone methyl has undergone extensive preclinical and early clinical evaluation primarily in fields as disparate as oncology and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Initial studies established that synthetic oleanane triterpenoids, including CDDO and its variants, exert dramatic anti‐inflammatory effects by suppressing inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and cyclooxygenase (COX‐2) expression in activated macrophages (Gatbonton‐Schwager, 2014). Preclinical studies in multiple mouse cancer models and inflammatory conditions confirmed its potent anticancer activity and cytoprotective properties, which catalyzed its progression into human clinical trials (Borella et al., 2019; Nakagami, 2016).  
In the clinical arena, Bardoxolone methyl was advanced through Phase I cancer trials, where its once‐daily oral dosing regimen and pharmacokinetic profile—with a terminal half‐life of approximately 39 hours—were characterized (Thomas, 2012; Nakagami, 2016). More notably, its unexpected ability to improve estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in patients with advanced renal disease, particularly in diabetic nephropathy, led to its evaluation in large Phase II and Phase III trials, such as the BEAM and BEACON studies (Yagishita et al., 2020; Tanase et al., 2022). However, the BEACON trial was terminated prematurely due to an increased incidence of cardiovascular events, including heart failure, highlighting concerns about the compound’s systemic safety profile when used at higher doses or in populations with comorbidities (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012).  
Despite its promising preclinical pharmacology and the breadth of clinical data available in non‐ocular indications, to date there is no direct record in the literature of Bardoxolone methyl being used specifically for the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular degenerative conditions (Schiavoni et al., 2025). Nonetheless, the overall safety and pharmacokinetic properties observed in CKD and oncology trials lend valuable insights for considering drug repurposing across therapeutic areas.

• Mechanism of Action  
Bardoxolone methyl is best known for its ability to activate the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway—a master regulator of cellular defense mechanisms against oxidative and electrophilic stress. Under basal conditions, Nrf2 is tightly regulated by Kelch‐like ECH‐associated protein 1 (Keap1), which serves as an adaptor for ubiquitin ligases targeting Nrf2 for proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl functions as a potent electrophile and interacts with sulfhydryl groups on critical cysteine residues within Keap1. This covalent or reversible Michael addition reaction disrupts the Keap1–Nrf2 complex, thereby stabilizing and allowing Nrf2 to translocate into the nucleus (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).  
Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to the antioxidant response element (ARE) in the promoter regions of a host of cytoprotective genes. This transcriptional activation results in the upregulation of a battery of antioxidant and phase II detoxifying enzymes, including but not limited to heme oxygenase‐1 (HO‐1), NAD(P)H dehydrogenase (quinone 1; NQO1), various glutathione transferases, and glutamate–cysteine ligase subunits (Thomas, 2012; Wong et al., 2016). Studies in non‐ocular tissues have shown that at very low (nanomolar) doses, Bardoxolone methyl robustly engages this cytoprotective program while also exerting dose‐dependent biology wherein intermediate and high doses trigger effects such as modulation of cell differentiation and direct anticancer activity, respectively (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).  
It is important to note that while the canonical targets of Nrf2 activation are well characterized, Bardoxolone methyl’s electrophilic character enables it to interact with multiple regulatory proteins. For example, it can inhibit IκB kinase β (IKKβ), leading to suppression of nuclear factor κB (NF‐κB) signaling and subsequent reduction in proinflammatory cytokine production (Zhou et al., 2014; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although the literature does not provide direct experimental evidence that Bardoxolone methyl specifically upregulates mitochondrial antioxidants such as superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) and peroxiredoxin 3 (PRDX3) in RPE cells, the robust, broad‐spectrum transcriptional response induced by Nrf2 activation strongly suggests that mitochondrial and cytoplasmic components of the antioxidant defense system may also be upregulated (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015). Such upregulation would be consistent with previous findings of increased expression of antioxidant genes and improved cellular redox status upon treatment with similar synthetic triterpenoids (Schiavoni et al., 2025; Sporn et al., 2011).

• Expected Effect in Dry AMD  
The pathogenesis of dry age‐related macular degeneration is multifactorial, with chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction playing a central role in the degeneration of the RPE—a critical monolayer that supports photoreceptor health. RPE cells are particularly vulnerable to oxidative damage due to high metabolic activity, exposure to light, and the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). In this context, the proposed mechanism of Bardoxolone methyl, namely activation of the Nrf2/ARE pathway, provides a biologically tenable strategy for neuroprotection and cellular preservation.  
When administered at low doses, Bardoxolone methyl is expected to trigger a cytoprotective transcriptional program in RPE cells. Activation of Nrf2 should lead to the induction of a range of antioxidant enzymes and detoxifying proteins which together help re-establish redox balance in the face of chronic oxidative insult (Borella et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012). One key hypothesis is that, in addition to the already well‐documented induction of cytosolic antioxidants such as HO‐1 and NQO1, Bardoxolone methyl may also promote the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3. SOD2 is the primary defense against superoxide radicals within the mitochondria, and PRDX3 plays a critical role in detoxifying hydrogen peroxide produced by mitochondrial respiration. Although direct data in RPE cells are currently lacking, studies in other cellular contexts have demonstrated that activation of Nrf2 results in the upregulation of a broad spectrum of antioxidant genes, and it is plausible that under the oxidative duress typical of dry AMD, similar effects would be observed in RPE cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
In vitro models simulating oxidative stress—such as exposure of RPE cells to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)—have shown that compounds with similar electrophilic properties, and indeed other members of the CDDO family like CDDO-Im, reduce the intracellular MitoSOX fluorescence signal, indicative of a reduction in mitochondrial ROS (mtROS) (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024). Moreover, improvements in mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) have been correlated with such treatments, suggesting that these molecules can help maintain mitochondrial function under stressful conditions (Nakagami, 2016; Zhou et al., 2014). Such outcomes are highly relevant in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction in the RPE has been implicated in disease progression. The anticipated outcomes, therefore, include a reduction in mtROS, restoration of Δψm, and subsequent preservation of RPE cellular integrity and function.  
Another positive aspect is the compound’s previously established oral bioavailability and pharmacokinetic profile. Clinical studies in CKD patients have demonstrated that therapeutic plasma concentrations can be achieved with once-daily dosing. Although systemic administration in ocular diseases is not ideal, these data provide a strong pharmacological starting point for repurposing. In addition, if systemic toxicity remains a concern—as suggested by the cardiovascular signals in CKD trials—an alternative approach might involve localized ocular delivery (for instance, via intravitreal injection or by developing an ocular formulation) to achieve high retinal bioavailability while minimizing systemic exposure (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).

• Overall Evaluation  
In assessing Bardoxolone methyl for repurposing as a therapeutic for dry AMD, several critical points emerge that underline both its promise and the challenges that must be overcome.

Strengths:  
1. Strong Chemical Rationale and Potency:  
Bardoxolone methyl is a product of sophisticated medicinal chemistry, designed to overcome the limitations of natural triterpenoids like oleanolic acid by installing reactive electrophilic groups that significantly enhance its potency. This design specifically enables the activation of the Nrf2 pathway—a mechanism central to antioxidant defense—at very low concentrations (Borella et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016). The high potency of Bardoxolone methyl as an Nrf2 activator is a significant advantage, particularly when considering that even subtle improvements in cellular antioxidant capacity can have a profound impact on chronic degenerative diseases like dry AMD.

2. Broad Cytoprotective Mechanism:  
The mechanism of Bardoxolone methyl involves the disruption of the Keap1-Nrf2 complex via covalent modification of Keap1 cysteine residues, facilitating the nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and the subsequent transcriptional activation of a broad range of antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes (Zhou et al., 2014; Thomas, 2012). This broad cytoprotective response is particularly relevant to the RPE, where chronic oxidative stress has been implicated in cellular dysfunction and death. The possibility that Bardoxolone methyl may also induce mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3, although not yet directly confirmed in RPE, is an attractive hypothesis; such an effect would directly address the mitochondrial dysfunction that is a hallmark of dry AMD (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).

3. Extensive Clinical Experience and Pharmacokinetic Data:  
Bardoxolone methyl has been evaluated in several clinical trials—most notably in the context of CKD and oncology—yielding a wealth of pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and tolerability data. Its oral bioavailability, with a terminal half-life that supports once-daily dosing, is well documented (Thomas, 2012; Nakagami, 2016). Although the systemic adverse events observed in these trials (such as cardiovascular-related events) present challenges for broad systemic administration, these data nonetheless offer a useful starting point for repurposing. The established clinical profile can inform dose-escalation studies and safety monitoring protocols should Bardoxolone methyl be advanced into ocular trials.

4. Support from Analogous Preclinical Models:  
Several studies in related models have demonstrated that synthetic triterpenoids can protect retinal tissue from oxidative damage. For example, experiments with CDDO-Im, a closely related analogue, have shown protective effects in retinal ischemia–reperfusion injury, including the attenuation of inflammatory responses and preservation of retinal structure (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024). Although these studies are not directly with Bardoxolone methyl, the mechanistic commonalities within this compound class support the notion that the same protective pathways can be harnessed in the context of dry AMD.

Weaknesses and Challenges:  
1. Lack of Direct Evidence in RPE/Dry AMD Models:  
Despite the strong theoretical rationale, direct evidence that Bardoxolone methyl upregulates mitochondrial antioxidants (SOD2, PRDX3) in RPE cells is currently lacking. Most published data are derived from non-ocular cell types or from studies using other analogues such as CDDO-Im (Cai et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2014). It is therefore essential to perform specific in vitro studies in RPE cell lines under oxidative stress conditions to measure the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes and the functional status of mitochondria (e.g., Δψm, mtROS levels) following treatment with Bardoxolone methyl.

2. Safety Concerns from Prior Clinical Experience:  
A significant challenge in repurposing Bardoxolone methyl stems from its safety profile in systemic indications. The Phase III BEACON trial in CKD patients was halted due to an increased incidence of serious cardiovascular events, including heart failure and increased mortality (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although the mechanisms underlying these adverse effects may be related to systemic fluid retention, off‐target reactivity, or other metabolic perturbations, they raise concerns about the safety of systemic administration. For ocular application, it may be necessary to consider alternative dosing strategies or localized delivery methods to avoid systemic exposure while still achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina.

3. Translational and Formulation Challenges:  
The unique anatomy and physiology of the eye introduce additional obstacles in drug repurposing. RPE cells reside in a relatively immune-privileged, isolated microenvironment behind the blood–retinal barrier. The pharmacokinetics and tissue penetration profiles of Bardoxolone methyl observed in systemic circulation may not directly translate to effective intraocular concentrations. Development of specialized ocular formulations—such as sustained-release intravitreal injections or topical applications that can traverse ocular barriers—will be critical for successful translation (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).

4. Multifactorial Nature of AMD Pathogenesis:  
Dry AMD is a complex, multifactorial disease where oxidative stress is only one component of a broader pathogenic network that includes genetic predisposition, inflammation, lipid dysregulation, and complement system activation. While activation of the Nrf2 pathway can counteract oxidative stress and may have secondary anti-inflammatory effects, it is uncertain whether this single mechanism will be sufficient to alter the course of the disease. A combinatorial therapeutic strategy incorporating Nrf2 activation with other modalities might eventually be required to address the full spectrum of dry AMD pathology (Cheng et al., 2021; Thomas, 2012).

5. Dose-Dependent Effects and Narrow Therapeutic Window:  
Bardoxolone methyl exhibits highly dose-dependent pharmacology. At low doses, it predominantly activates Nrf2 and induces cytoprotective genes; however, as the dose increases, additional actions such as pro-apoptotic and cytotoxic effects emerge (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014). Determining the precise dose that is efficacious in RPE cells without triggering deleterious off-target effects will be crucial. This necessitates rigorous dose-ranging studies in preclinical models to define a therapeutic window that maximizes retinal protection while minimizing risks.

• Overall Evaluation and Recommendation  
In summary, Bardoxolone methyl presents a compelling candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD thanks to its well-characterized chemical design, potent induction of the Nrf2 pathway, and a broad cytoprotective mechanism that addresses many aspects of the oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction implicated in RPE degeneration. The extensive clinical data from studies in CKD and oncology provide a valuable foundation for understanding its pharmacokinetics and systemic effects, while the underlying chemistry ensures high potency at low concentrations—features that are highly desirable when targeting a chronic, degenerative condition such as dry AMD (Borella et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012).  
Nonetheless, significant challenges remain. There is a conspicuous gap in the literature regarding the direct evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl in RPE cells and dry AMD models, particularly concerning its ability to upregulate mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes like SOD2 and PRDX3 and thereby mitigate mtROS damage. This gap must be addressed through targeted in vitro assays and in vivo animal studies that simulate the retinal environment and its chronic oxidative stress. Safety concerns, as evidenced by the cardiovascular events observed in CKD trials, underscore the need for caution; these risks may be minimized through localized ocular administration, but careful formulation and dosing studies will be required to establish an acceptable safety profile in the ocular context (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019).  
Given the current state of evidence, it is recommended that Bardoxolone methyl be subjected to further preclinical evaluation in the context of dry AMD. Specifically, studies should focus on:  
 – Conducting detailed in vitro experiments in human RPE cell lines to assess whether exposure to Bardoxolone methyl under oxidative stress conditions leads to the upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants (e.g., SOD2 and PRDX3) and an associated decrease in mtROS (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
 – Evaluating the effects of Bardoxolone methyl on mitochondrial function (including measurements of Δψm, oxygen consumption rate, and mitochondrial integrity) in these cells.  
 – Adapting ocular-specific formulations that allow high local retinal concentrations with minimal systemic exposure, potentially using intravitreal or topical delivery methods, and conducting pharmacokinetic studies that establish retinal tissue exposure (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).  
 – Testing the compound in animal models of dry AMD to determine whether the in vitro antioxidant and mitochondrial protective effects translate into preservation of RPE and photoreceptor structure and function over time (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024).  
If these studies yield positive results that confirm the hypothesized upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants and improved RPE function, Bardoxolone methyl could then be advanced to early-phase clinical trials in patients with dry AMD. Such trials would need to incorporate rigorous safety monitoring protocols to mitigate the known systemic adverse effects. A potential strategy may involve administering the drug in a localized manner or at doses that are effective in the eye but low enough to avoid triggering systemic electrophilic toxicity.

Overall, Bardoxolone methyl holds promise as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD based on its potent Nrf2-activating properties and the central role of oxidative stress in the disease’s pathogenesis. However, its development for an ocular indication will hinge on its ability to selectively and safely modulate the redox status of RPE cells while avoiding systemic side effects. A stepwise, targeted preclinical program that directly addresses these RPE-specific endpoints is therefore critical before consideration of clinical trials in the dry AMD patient population (Nakagami, 2016).

In conclusion, while Bardoxolone methyl offers a strong mechanistic rationale as an Nrf2 activator with the theoretical capacity to upregulate mitochondrial defenses in RPE cells, further targeted studies are essential. The compound’s repurposing for dry AMD is scientifically attractive given the unmet need for effective therapies in this condition; however, the translational path is complex due to safety concerns observed in systemic trials and the lack of direct ocular data. A rigorous preclinical research plan—encompassing in vitro RPE studies, ocular pharmacokinetic assessments, and animal model validation—will be required to determine whether Bardoxolone methyl can be safely and effectively repurposed to preserve RPE function and slow the progression of dry AMD.

• Summary of Key Supporting Points  
– Bardoxolone methyl is a chemically engineered derivative of oleanolic acid that exploits electrophilic modifications to robustly activate the Nrf2 pathway (Borella et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016).  
– Its extensive preclinical and clinical history in oncology and CKD, though not in ocular disease, provides important pharmacokinetic and biological safety data that may be leveraged, with modifications, for ocular use (Nakagami, 2016; Tanase et al., 2022).  
– Its mechanism—covalent modification of Keap1 and subsequent nuclear translocation of Nrf2—leads to the transcriptional upregulation of cytoprotective genes, and it is hypothesized that this would include mitochondrial antioxidants (e.g., SOD2, PRDX3), which are critical for mitigating oxidative damage in RPE cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
– Preclinical data with related triterpenoids in retinal models support the concept that Nrf2 activation can ameliorate oxidative stress and preserve retinal integrity, although direct data for Bardoxolone methyl in dry AMD are presently lacking (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024).  
– Key challenges include the translation of systemic dosing to ocular delivery, the need to specifically validate mitochondrial protective effects in RPE cells, and the resolution of safety issues exemplified by prior cardiovascular signals in systemic trials (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

• Final Recommendation  
Based on the current literature review, Bardoxolone methyl emerges as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its potent Nrf2 activation, broad cytoprotective potential, and a well-documented clinical PK profile. However, its repurposing for ocular application must be preceded by targeted preclinical studies that corroborate its ability to upregulate mitochondrial antioxidants in RPE cells and to reduce mtROS while preserving mitochondrial function. These studies should also explore ocular-specific formulations and dosing regimens that minimize systemic exposure. Only after thorough validation in these preliminary investigations can Bardoxolone methyl be considered a credible candidate for clinical trials in dry AMD patients. Historically, NMN has been investigated in a variety of preclinical settings addressing metabolic dysfunction and age‐associated decline, with numerous studies across biochemical, cellular, and animal models demonstrating that NMN supplementation effectively elevates NAD+ levels and improves mitochondrial function (Chen et al., 2020). In models of retinal degeneration, particularly in contexts simulating photoreceptor loss and retinal detachment, NMN administration has shown neuroprotective effects by restoring NAD+ levels and activating key deacetylases such as SIRT1, which are central to oxidative stress mitigation and cell survival (Chen et al., 2020). Preclinical studies conducted in mouse models of retinal detachment have reported that NMN treatment not only boosts NAD+ concentrations beyond the physiological baseline but also attenuates the inflammatory response and reduces photoreceptor cell death, thereby preserving retinal structure and function (Chen et al., 2020). In addition to these acute models, experimental data from primary retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells derived from donors with age‐related macular degeneration have revealed that NMN can improve mitochondrial respiration and restore the NAD+/NADH balance critical to RPE cell health (Ebeling et al., 2020). Moreover, NMN’s ability to limit cellular senescence has been documented in RPE models challenged with oxidative stressors and pro‐senescent compounds, where supplementation led to a reduction in markers such as p16INK4a and p21Waf/Cip1, along with preservation of SIRT1 expression (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022). Clinical exploration of NMN in the context of aging and metabolic disorders—though not yet fully extended to ophthalmologic diseases—provides an encouraging translational backdrop, indicating that NMN has a robust therapeutic history in conditions characterized by NAD+ depletion and mitochondrial dysfunction (Jadeja et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2024). Collectively, the therapeutic history suggests that NMN has been thoroughly vetted in preclinical settings relevant to neurodegeneration and retinal health, thereby supporting its potential repurposing for dry AMD (Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
NMN exerts its biological effects primarily through its role as a biosynthetic precursor of NAD+, a critical coenzyme involved in numerous cellular processes including energy production, DNA repair, and redox balance (Chen et al., 2020). Once administered, NMN is rapidly taken up by cells and converted via NMNAT enzymes into NAD+, thereby replenishing intracellular NAD+ pools that typically decline with age and stress (Gerdes, 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). This increase in NAD+ levels has a twofold impact. First, elevated NAD+ directly energizes metabolic pathways, namely glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation, by serving as a cofactor for dehydrogenases, which is essential for mitochondrial ATP production (Will-Orrego, 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Second, NAD+ acts as a substrate for a family of NAD+-dependent deacetylases—the sirtuins—most notably SIRT1, SIRT3, and SIRT5, which are involved in regulating mitochondrial integrity and function (Chen et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). In the specific context of dry AMD, the hypothesis posits that NMN-mediated restoration of NAD+ in retinal pigment epithelial cells leads to reactivation of mitochondrial sirtuins SIRT3 and SIRT5. SIRT3, located in the mitochondrial matrix, deacetylates key metabolic enzymes including manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), whose activity is crucial for neutralizing mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) (Gerdes, 2018; Ren et al., 2022). The proper deacetylation of MnSOD enhances its antioxidant capacity, thereby reducing mtROS accumulation and protecting the mitochondria from oxidative damage (Chen et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022). SIRT5, another mitochondrial deacetylase, plays a complementary role by regulating the acylation status of proteins involved in mitochondrial dynamics and energy metabolism; its activation, in turn, contributes to improved mitochondrial respiration and bioenergetics (Ebeling et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). Furthermore, the elevation of NAD+ levels via NMN supplementation is known to indirectly influence other signaling pathways such as those modulated by AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and Akt/mTOR, which are critical for mitochondrial biogenesis and cellular homeostasis (Ren et al., 2022). In dry AMD, where metabolic dysfunction and increased oxidative stress are central to disease progression, the biochemical cascade triggered by NMN restores the balance between energy production and oxidative damage by ensuring that sirtuins are adequately fueled (Jadeja et al., 2018). This cascade not only preserves mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and oxygen consumption rate (OCR) but also limits the proton leak and bioenergetic inefficiency that characterize dysfunctional RPE cells (Ebeling et al., 2020). In summary, at the molecular level, NMN’s mechanism of action in RPE cells aligns with a strategy of metabolic reconditioning, whereby the reactivation of SIRT3 and SIRT5—via increased NAD+ availability—leads to improved deacetylation of mitochondrial enzymes, reduction in mtROS levels, and enhancement of overall mitochondrial function (Lin, 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of a dry AMD model, the anticipated effect of NMN supplementation is the restoration of NAD+ homeostasis within RPE cells and consequent reactivation of mitochondrial sirtuins such as SIRT3 and SIRT5, which will correct mitochondrial deacetylation deficits that are known to contribute to cellular dysfunction (Chen et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). Specifically, NMN is expected to normalize the NAD+/NADH ratio, an essential parameter for efficient electron transport chain function and ATP generation; this normalization is projected to result in enhanced oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and improved mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) in the RPE (Ebeling et al., 2020). As a direct consequence of restored sirtuin activity, particularly SIRT3’s deacetylation of MnSOD, there should be a significant reduction in mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), which in turn decreases the oxidative burden on the RPE cells—a critical factor in the development and progression of dry AMD (Gerdes, 2018; Ren et al., 2022). The expected downstream effects include not only enhanced bioenergetic function but also a reduction in the cellular senescence markers and inflammatory cytokines typically upregulated in the aging and stressed RPE (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022). In vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE cultures have demonstrated that NMN supplementation can rescue cells from FK866-induced NAD+ depletion, thereby restoring ATP levels and maintaining the expression of RPE identity genes, which are fundamental to retinal homeostasis (Will-Orrego, 2020). Moreover, by mitigating oxidative damage and correcting mitochondrial dysfunction, NMN is expected to preserve the structural integrity of the outer retina, which is essential for sustained photoreceptor function and visual acuity in dry AMD (Chen et al., 2020). Ultimately, the mechanistic actions of NMN—spanning from NAD+ replenishment to sirtuin activation—are predicted to yield measurable improvements in both cellular assays (e.g., increased OCR, stabilized Δψm, and decreased ROS levels) and functional endpoints such as electroretinography (ERG) responses in animal models of retinal degeneration (Chen et al., 2020). The robust preclinical data, including evidence of normalized mitochondrial respiration and amelioration of RPE senescence following NMN treatment, provide a strong rationale for expecting similar beneficial effects in a dry AMD assay (Jadeja et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
The cumulative evidence from biochemical, cellular, and in vivo studies positions NMN as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. One of the primary strengths of NMN is its well‐characterized role as a NAD+ precursor, which underpins its ability to restore intracellular NAD+ levels and reactivate essential sirtuin activities—most notably SIRT3 and SIRT5—in metabolically compromised cells (Chen et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). By addressing the root cause of mitochondrial dysfunction observed in dry AMD, namely NAD+ depletion and subsequent impairment of protein deacetylation, NMN targets a fundamental pathogenic mechanism that leads to photoreceptor and RPE degeneration (Chen et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022). The broad spectrum of supportive evidence, ranging from neuroprotective effects in retinal detachment models to the reversal of cellular senescence in AMD-relevant RPE cells, further reinforces the therapeutic rationale behind NMN’s application in dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022). Additionally, the translational feasibility of NMN is bolstered by ongoing clinical developments in aging and metabolic disorders, suggesting that the pharmacokinetic and safety profiles of NMN are sufficiently favorable to warrant its repurposing for retinal diseases (Jadeja et al., 2018).

However, several potential limitations must be considered. Variability in drug response among diseased RPE cells from different AMD donors has been documented, indicating that while NMN can robustly restore mitochondrial function in some cases, a subset of patients may exhibit a less pronounced therapeutic response, necessitating personalized dosing strategies or combinatorial therapies (Ebeling et al., 2020). Furthermore, although NMN’s activation of sirtuins is generally beneficial, there exists a theoretical risk that overactivation of these enzymes could induce off-target effects or exacerbate cellular stress if not properly titrated, as some studies have suggested that SIRT1 overactivation may in certain contexts lead to deleterious outcomes (Chen et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022). Moreover, much of the current evidence derives from preclinical models, and while these data are compelling, the extrapolation of these results to human subjects with dry AMD will require rigorously designed clinical trials to evaluate efficacy and safety in the specific target population (Chen et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024).

In summary, the overall assessment of NMN as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is highly favorable, particularly given its dual capacity to restore NAD+ levels and reengage mitochondrial deacetylation pathways that are crucial for RPE health. Its mechanistic basis, rooted in the reactivation of SIRT3 and SIRT5 leading to improved mitochondrial respiration and reduced oxidative stress, directly addresses the central pathogenic features of dry AMD. The extensive preclinical validation, coupled with encouraging translational data from aging-related indications, positions NMN as a strong candidate for further development and clinical evaluation in dry AMD, albeit with careful consideration of dosing strategies and patient heterogeneity (Cimaglia et al., 2020). Moving forward, prioritizing studies that assess long-term outcomes in appropriate animal models and early-phase clinical trials in AMD patients will be critical to firmly establish NMN’s therapeutic potential and optimize its utility as part of a broader strategy to mitigate vision loss associated with dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2020; Lin, 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Liproxstatin-1 is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor of ferroptosis that was originally discovered using phenotypic high-throughput screening in systems where ferroptosis was induced by either genetic deletion of GPX4 or by glutathione depletion with agents like erastin (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69). Its chemical identity is tied to a unique spiroquinoxalinamine scaffold, which places it in the class of aromatic amine radical-trapping antioxidants (RTAs) – compounds well known in industrial settings to protect hydrocarbon products from autoxidation, as well as in biomedical research to block oxidative lipid chain reactions (Scarpellini, 2023, pp. 41–45; Angeli, Shah, Pratt, & Conrad, 2017, pp. 6–8). In contrast to classical phenolic antioxidants such as α-tocopherol, Liproxstatin-1 is designed to operate in the lipid bilayer, where its aminic (or diarylamine) moieties are less hindered by nonproductive hydrogen-bonding interactions with phospholipid headgroups, thus allowing rapid hydrogen-atom transfer to lipid peroxyl radicals (Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). Although detailed synthetic routes are not provided in the available reports, the discovery process clearly identifies Liproxstatin-1 as a lead candidate that emerged from unbiased cell-based screens aimed at identifying compounds that preserve cell viability in the absence of GPX4 function (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). Its categorization as an RTA is significant because this class of compounds has a long history of being used to inhibit free radical–mediated damage in both industrial and biological contexts (Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6).

Therapeutic History:  
The preclinical history of Liproxstatin-1 is rich with evidence supporting its role as a potent inhibitor of ferroptosis. Early studies demonstrated that Liproxstatin-1 acts at low nanomolar concentrations to prevent ferroptotic cell death in mouse embryonic fibroblasts as well as in specialized cells rendered vulnerable by GPX4 inactivation (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Angeli et al., 2014, p. 10). Beyond in vitro cell survival assays, Liproxstatin-1 has been evaluated in vivo where it has shown remarkable protective effects in models of acute tissue injury including genetic GPX4 deficiency, which induces acute renal failure, and in ischaemia/reperfusion models of liver injury (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10). Although its direct clinical use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) has not been established – with most in vivo data coming from non-ocular models – its success in ameliorating tissue damage by inhibiting lipid peroxidation suggests its potential utility in other degenerative pathologies where oxidative membrane damage drives dysfunction, such as in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) degeneration underlying geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69; Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–21). Moreover, related compounds, notably Ferrostatin-1, have been tested in various retinal cell models and in some in vivo settings pertaining to retinal ischemia–reperfusion injury and oxygen-induced retinopathy, further bolstering the therapeutic concept of using RTA-type ferroptosis inhibitors in ocular settings (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23; Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8). While the bulk of Liproxstatin-1’s therapeutic history centers on its role as an anti-ferroptotic agent in cancer, neurodegeneration, and acute organ failure, its mechanistic overlap with key pathological features observed in dry AMD – such as iron accumulation, glutathione depletion and elevated lipid peroxidation in the RPE – supports evaluating it as a repurposed candidate in this context (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Shen et al., 2025, pp. 1–2).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism by which Liproxstatin-1 exerts its cytoprotective effect is rooted in its function as a radical-trapping antioxidant. Specifically, Liproxstatin-1 reacts rapidly with lipid peroxyl radicals that propagate the autoxidation chain reaction in cellular membranes. Experimental data have established that Liproxstatin-1 exhibits an intrinsic reaction rate constant (k_inh) in the range of approximately 2.4 × 10^5 M^−1 s^−1 in organic solvents such as chlorobenzene at 37 °C, which is comparable to industrial diarylamine antioxidants (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 8–9). Although its intrinsic reactivity in homogeneous organic solutions may appear lower than classical phenolic antioxidants like α-tocopherol, its performance in the lipid bilayer is superior due to reduced hydrogen-bonding interactions with phospholipid headgroups – a feature that enhances its mobility and reactivity in the lipid environment where ferroptosis is executed (Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 8–9; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). The compound functions primarily by donating a hydrogen atom from its arylamine (or diarylamine) N–H group, effectively quenching chain-propagating lipid peroxyl radicals before they can perpetuate lipid hydroperoxide formation (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). Kinetic isotope effect studies and computational analyses have confirmed that the N–H bond dissociation enthalpy is sufficiently low in Liproxstatin-1 to enable rapid hydrogen-atom transfer, which is a critical step in its radical-trapping mechanism (Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 2–3, 5–7). Importantly, Liproxstatin-1 does not exert significant inhibitory effects on enzymes such as human 15-lipoxygenase-1, thereby ruling out an enzymatic inhibition mechanism and reinforcing that its protective effect is solely attributable to non-enzymatic scavenging of peroxyl radicals (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 201–210). In the context of dry AMD, particularly in geographic atrophy where RPE degeneration is a hallmark, the expected effect of Liproxstatin-1 would be to curtail the chain reaction of lipid peroxidation that underpins ferroptotic cell death. In vitro assays using RPE cell lines such as ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cells have demonstrated that targeting lipid peroxidation – as evidenced by reductions in markers like BODIPY-C11 oxidation and ACSL4 expression – can rescue cells from oxidative stress–mediated death (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–23). In essence, when applied to RPE cells under conditions that mimic dry AMD, Liproxstatin-1 should decrease oxidative markers, prevent cell death, and thereby slow or halt the progression of geographic atrophy by restoring the balance between pro-oxidant and antioxidant pathways (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–23).

Liproxstatin-1 stands out as a promising candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic agent against dry AMD, particularly in geographic atrophy, given the mechanistic overlap between ferroptosis and RPE cell death observed in dry AMD. One of its principal strengths lies in its potent radical-trapping antioxidant activity, which is not only effective at low nanomolar concentrations but also uniquely suited to the lipid bilayer environment of the RPE (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). This specificity is critical because retinal cells are subject to a high burden of polyunsaturated lipid content and are therefore particularly sensitive to oxidative damage. The fact that Liproxstatin-1 has demonstrated efficacy in protecting cells under ferroptotic stress in other organ systems – including kidney and liver models – further supports its potential viability in ocular applications (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Peng et al., 2020, pp. 3–5). Its discovery through unbiased screening in ferroptosis-susceptible models and its demonstration of efficacy in multiple organ systems provide a strong foundation for its repurposing in dry AMD. The evidence supports that Liproxstatin-1 could counteract the iron-driven ROS amplification and lipid peroxidation that contribute to RPE cell death in geographic atrophy. Nonetheless, while its mechanistic rationale and preclinical promise are substantial, further research – particularly within retinal models – is necessary to fully evaluate its therapeutic potential and address challenges related to ocular delivery and multi-pathway disease components. Taken together, Liproxstatin-1 represents a compelling candidate for further investigation as a targeted inhibitor of ferroptosis in the treatment of dry AMD (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69, 207–210; Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23).

Olaparib is a small‐molecule, synthetic inhibitor originally discovered and developed for oncology indications, particularly in cancers harboring BRCA mutations. It belongs to the class of PARP (poly[ADP‐ribose] polymerase) inhibitors that function by binding to the catalytic domain of PARP enzymes, competitively inhibiting the binding of NAD+ and thereby blocking poly‐ADP‐ribosylation reactions. Olaparib was discovered through high‐throughput screening and subsequently optimized chemically to yield a compound with high potency and selectivity for PARP1 and PARP2. As a synthetic chemotherapeutic agent, olaparib has been extensively characterized and approved by regulatory agencies for the treatment of various malignancies such as ovarian and breast cancer. Its mechanism involves “trapping” PARP on damaged DNA, although in nononcologic applications the key therapeutic action is related to the inhibition of overactive PARP1 activity in conditions of oxidative DNA damage. In the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), the hypothesis is that olaparib will inhibit PARP1‐mediated NAD+ consumption in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby preserving both the cellular energy status and, indirectly, the activity of NAD+‐dependent enzymes such as the mitochondrial sirtuin SIRT3. This candidate falls within a larger class of repurposed drugs that are being re‐evaluated for neurodegenerative and retinal disorders, where dysregulated PARP activity is thought to be a key driver of cellular dysfunction under chronic oxidative stress (Jang et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Olaparib’s primary therapeutic history is rooted in oncology. It has been used clinically to target cancers that are deficient in homologous recombination repair, where its PARP‐inhibitory action leads to synthetic lethality in malignant cells. Over recent years, growing experimental evidence has implicated hyperactivation of PARP1 in a number of non-neoplastic conditions characterized by oxidative DNA damage and subsequent energetic collapse. Various studies carried out in retinal cell lines such as ARPE-19 under oxidative stress (e.g., H2O2 exposure) have demonstrated that pathological PARP1 activation leads to a depletion of NAD+ and ATP, mitochondrial depolarization, altered mitochondrial morphology, and ultimately, cell death; these studies have employed olaparib to effectively block PARP1 activity and thereby rescue the cells from these metabolic defects (Jang et al., 2018). In animal models that mimic features of dry AMD, such as sodium iodate (SI)-injected mice or rabbits, pharmacologic inhibition of PARP1 with olaparib resulted in preservation of retinal morphology including maintenance of outer nuclear layer thickness and improvements in electrophysiological readouts (Jang et al., 2018). To date, while significant preclinical evaluation has been performed in models of oxidative injury and retinal degeneration, olaparib has not yet been trialed clinically in dry AMD patients. However, the repurposing approach is supported by extensive literature in which PARP inhibitors have been proposed as a therapeutic approach to mitigate oxidative injury in neurodegenerative disorders, with the underlying rationale being the restoration of cellular NAD+ levels as well as improved mitochondrial bioenergetics (Jang et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
The well-established mechanism of action of olaparib is based on the inhibition of the PARP enzyme family, primarily targeting PARP1. Under conditions of oxidative stress, DNA strand breaks activate PARP1, which catalyzes the transfer of ADP-ribose units from NAD+ to several nuclear and mitochondrial proteins. This process, known as poly-ADP-ribosylation, normally plays a role in DNA repair; however, when overactivated—as is observed in conditions of persistent oxidative damage—PARP1 consumes enormous amounts of cellular NAD+, leading to ATP depletion and an ensuing collapse of cellular energy metabolism. Olaparib binds to the catalytic domain of PARP1, thereby preventing the excessive transfer of ADP-ribose moieties and preserving intracellular NAD+ levels. This preservation of NAD+ is critical because NAD+ is a necessary cofactor not only for PARP activity but also for the function of a range of NAD+-dependent deacetylases, including the sirtuin family.

Within the context of dry AMD, RPE cells subjected to oxidative stress exhibit PARP1 hyperactivation, resulting in NAD+ depletion that compromises cellular bioenergetics and contributes to mitochondrial dysfunction. While much of the literature has focused on the interplay between PARP1 and nuclear sirtuin SIRT1 in the context of autophagy, emerging hypotheses posit that similar mechanisms extend to the mitochondria. SIRT3, a key mitochondrial deacetylase, requires NAD+ to catalyze the deacetylation of multiple mitochondrial proteins. One well-characterized substrate is manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), whose deacetylated, active form is responsible for detoxifying reactive oxygen species (ROS) within the mitochondria. The proposed mechanism is that by inhibiting PARP1, olaparib preserves NAD+ pools in RPE cells, which in turn sustains SIRT3 activity. Active SIRT3 would ensure proper deacetylation of mitochondrial proteins, including MnSOD, thus reducing mitochondrial protein hyperacetylation, curtailing mtROS production, and ultimately mitigating oxidative damage (Jang et al., 2018; Lin & Apte, 2018).

Notably, while multiple studies have documented that olaparib effectively reduces NAD+ depletion, preserves ATP levels, and maintains mitochondrial membrane potential in ARPE-19 cells under H2O2 challenge (Jang et al., 2018), direct assessments of SIRT3 activity and the acetylation state of mitochondrial proteins remain to be specifically reported. Several excerpts unequivocally state that although the biochemical cascade from PARP1 hyperactivation to NAD+ loss is well-documented, explicit data connecting PARP inhibition by olaparib to restored SIRT3-mediated mitochondrial deacetylation have not been presented (Jang et al., 2018). Thus, the mechanistic rationale is largely built on the inference that a well-maintained NAD+ pool under olaparib treatment will naturally support the activity of all NAD+-dependent enzymes, including SIRT3 (Jang et al., 2018).

Expected Effect:  
The expected effect of olaparib in experimental models of dry AMD is multifaceted. First, by inhibiting PARP1, olaparib should significantly reduce the accumulation of poly-ADP-ribose (PAR) polymers that are normally generated in response to oxidative DNA damage. This reduction in PARP1 activity would result in preservation of intracellular NAD+ and ATP levels, thereby preventing the energy collapse characteristic of parthanatos—a form of cell death distinct from classical apoptosis that has been implicated in RPE degeneration (Jang et al., 2018).

In in vitro assays using ARPE-19 cells, olaparib is expected to block H2O2-induced mitochondrial dysfunction, as evidenced by improved mitochondrial membrane potential measurements and normalized rates of ATP production. Functionally, such bioenergetic stabilization should correlate with increased cell survival and improved resistance to oxidative stress. Moreover, given the central role of NAD+ as a substrate for mitochondrial sirtuins, it is anticipated that olaparib treatment will indirectly sustain SIRT3 activity within the mitochondria. Although direct measurements of SIRT3 activity and mitochondrial protein acetylation were not explicitly given in the reviewed studies, the biochemical paradigm suggests that when NAD+ concentrations are conserved, SIRT3 maintains the deacetylated and therefore active state of key proteins. For example, the deacetylation of MnSOD by SIRT3 is crucial for controlling mtROS levels. A reduction in mitochondrial protein hyperacetylation would likely result in lower levels of mitochondrial oxidative stress, improved mitochondrial respiration, and an overall protective effect on both the metabolic and structural integrity of RPE cells (Jang et al., 2018; Lin & Apte, 2018).

In animal models designed to mimic the degenerative environment of dry AMD—such as the sodium iodate (SI) induced retinal degeneration model—olaparib has been shown to preserve retinal morphology. For instance, olaparib-treated animals exhibited maintenance of outer nuclear layer thickness and more robust electroretinogram (ERG) wave amplitudes compared to SI-treated controls (Jang et al., 2018). Thus, the expected effect of olaparib extends from the biochemical (preservation of NAD+ and suppression of PAR polymer formation) to the functional (preservation of retinal structure and function) levels. In assays that measure oxidative damage, assays of mitochondrial function, and endpoint assessments of RPE survival, olaparib treatment is therefore predicted to yield significant improvements relative to untreated, oxidatively stressed controls.

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of olaparib as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD proceeds from its well-characterized mechanism of action and a robust body of preclinical evidence, while also acknowledging certain gaps that need to be addressed in future research.

Strengths:  
1. The Mechanism Is Well-Established in Related Contexts: Olaparib’s ability to inhibit PARP1 has been incontrovertibly demonstrated both biochemically and in various disease models. Preclinical studies in ARPE-19 cells have repeatedly shown that olaparib can mitigate PARP1-dependent NAD+ depletion and restore cellular ATP levels under oxidative stress conditions (Jang et al., 2018). This is especially relevant in dry AMD, where RPE loss and mitochondrial dysfunction are driven by oxidative insults and chronic PARP activation.  
2. Preservation of NAD+ Pools: By blocking PARP1 overactivation, olaparib helps preserve the intracellular NAD+ pool, which is critical for maintaining the activity of NAD+-dependent enzymes. Although most studies have focused on the nuclear deacetylase SIRT1, the biochemical logic extends to mitochondrial sirtuins such as SIRT3. Given SIRT3’s essential role in deacetylating enzymes involved in the detoxification of ROS—most notably MnSOD—its preservation is of potential therapeutic importance in the context of dry AMD (Jang et al., 2018).  
3. Preclinical Efficacy in Retinal Models: Several studies have used olaparib in retinal oxidative injury models, demonstrating improvements in mitochondrial potential, cellular bioenergetics, and even in in vivo retinal function as measured by ERG. These data support the notion that PARP inhibition can translate into a meaningful rescue of retinal structure and function (Jang et al., 2018; Akkaya et al., 2025).  
4. Established Clinical Use in Oncology: Olaparib is already approved by major regulatory agencies for several cancer indications, meaning that its pharmacokinetics, safety profile, and manufacturing processes are well characterized. This facilitates the drug repurposing pathway and may allow for a head start in clinical development for dry AMD, provided that formulation and ocular delivery challenges can be overcome (Jang et al., 2018).

Weaknesses and Considerations:  
1. Incomplete Evidence on SIRT3 and Mitochondrial Deacetylation: While the preservation of NAD+ is well documented, direct evidence linking olaparib treatment to sustained SIRT3 activity and the corresponding maintenance of mitochondrial protein deacetylation is sparse in the current literature. Several studies explicitly note that measurements of SIRT3 activity or assessments of mitochondrial protein acetylation status were not performed in the RPE/retinal models reviewed (Jang et al., 2018; Du et al., 2016). Given that the hypothesis specifically posits that olaparib preserves SIRT3 activity—and, by extension, proper mitochondrial deacetylation—this represents a critical gap that must be filled by targeted experimental studies.  
2. DNA Repair and Long-Term Safety: PARP1 plays an important role in normal DNA repair processes. Chronic inhibition in a non‐oncologic setting such as dry AMD raises concerns about potential cumulative genomic instability in retinal cells. Therefore, long-term dosing regimens must be carefully optimized to balance neuroprotection against the risk of impairing physiologic DNA repair mechanisms (Jadeja et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2018).  
3. Delivery and Bioavailability Challenges: Although olaparib is effective systemically in oncology, its bioavailability in ocular tissues following systemic administration may be suboptimal. Successful repurposing for dry AMD may require the development of novel ocular delivery formulations, such as topical eye drops or intravitreal injections, to achieve therapeutic concentrations at the level of the RPE without incurring off-target systemic toxicities (Kovacs et al., 2019; Jang et al., 2018).  
4. Translational Gap: Most of the available evidence for olaparib’s efficacy derives from preclinical models, including in vitro experiments in ARPE-19 cells and in vivo studies in animal models of retinal degeneration. There is currently no clinical trial data for olaparib in dry AMD, which increases the uncertainty associated with its translational potential. Furthermore, the pathophysiology of dry AMD is multifactorial and may involve additional pathways that are not fully addressed by PARP inhibition alone (Jang et al., 2018).  
5. Potential Off-Target Effects: While olaparib is selective for PARP enzymes, the extent to which off-target effects may impact retinal homeostasis is not fully understood. Ocular cells might have unique metabolic or repair requirements that differ from those in oncologic tissues, necessitating careful preclinical toxicology studies.

Overall, the repurposing of olaparib for dry AMD is supported by a robust mechanistic rationale—namely, that excessive PARP1 activation under oxidative stress depletes NAD+ reserves, leading to energy collapse and retinal cell death. By inhibiting PARP1, olaparib rescues NAD+ levels and has been shown to restore mitochondrial integrity and preserve retinal function in preclinical models. This fundamental mechanism is highly relevant to dry AMD pathogenesis, where oxidative stress-mediated damage to the RPE is a central feature. Moreover, given that NAD+ is required for the activity of sirtuins (including nuclear SIRT1 and mitochondrial SIRT3), ultimately ensuring proper deacetylation of key enzymes and maintenance of mitochondrial homeostasis, the overall therapeutic cascade proposed by the hypothesis is well grounded in established biochemistry (Jang et al., 2018).

Nevertheless, while there is convincing evidence regarding the ability of olaparib to inhibit PARP1 and rescue bioenergetic failure in RPE under oxidative stress, a crucial aspect of the proposal—that PARP inhibition preserves SIRT3 activity and thus maintains mitochondrial deacetylation—remains largely inferential. Several studies have noted the absence of direct measurements of SIRT3 activity or mitochondrial protein acetylation status after olaparib treatment in RPE models (Jang et al., 2018; Du et al., 2016). It is conceivable that, if NAD+ pools are restored, SIRT3 function will inherently be maintained; however, without direct experimental validation, this remains an unproven aspect of the therapeutic mechanism. Moreover, the potential consequences of long-term PARP inhibition—particularly with respect to DNA repair fidelity—and the challenges of delivering adequate concentrations of the drug to the retina without systemic toxicity cannot be overlooked.

In addition, while preclinical studies using SI-induced retinal degeneration models have shown promising results with olaparib in terms of improving retinal morphology and function (as per improvements in ERG wave amplitudes and preservation of outer nuclear layer thickness), these models do not capture the full complexity of dry AMD in humans. Dry AMD is a chronic, multifactorial disorder with contributions from inflammation, drusen formation, and cumulative RPE dysfunction over years; thus, short-term protective effects observed in animal models, while encouraging, might not directly translate to robust clinical efficacy.

Taking into account both the strengths and the weaknesses, the overall potential for olaparib as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is promising but not yet definitive. The strengths lie in its well-documented ability to inhibit PARP1, prevent NAD+ depletion, and improve mitochondrial bioenergetics in models of retinal oxidative injury. These effects are directly relevant to the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying dry AMD, where RPE degeneration is driven by chronic oxidative stress. Furthermore, the fact that olaparib is already an approved drug for other indications offers a strategic advantage in terms of repurposing and regulatory approval. However, the lack of direct evidence linking olaparib treatment to the restoration of mitochondrial SIRT3 activity and normalization of mitochondrial protein acetylation is a significant gap in the current literature. Addressing this gap would require focused studies that assess SIRT3 enzyme activity, evaluate the acetylation status of mitochondrial proteins such as MnSOD, and determine whether these molecular endpoints correlate with improved RPE survival and function. Additionally, long-term safety studies that investigate the potential risk of impaired DNA repair in retinal cells under chronic PARP inhibition are warranted. Finally, developing an appropriate ocular delivery system that ensures effective local concentrations of olaparib while minimizing systemic exposure will be critical for translating these preclinical findings into a viable clinical candidate.

In conclusion, olaparib’s repurposing for dry AMD has significant mechanistic and preclinical support. Its ability to inhibit PARP1 offers a means to preserve NAD+ levels in RPE cells, thereby potentially maintaining mitochondrial function and reducing oxidative injury—a cascade that is highly attractive for a disease characterized by chronic oxidative stress. Although the evidence for PARP inhibition in rescuing NAD+ and ATP levels in the RPE is strong (Jang et al., 2018), the specific link between NAD+ preservation and the maintenance of mitochondrial sirtuin SIRT3 activity remains to be directly demonstrated. Addressing this knowledge gap through targeted biochemical assays will be essential before advancing olaparib into clinical trials for dry AMD. Overall, given the compelling preclinical data, existing clinical experience in oncology, and the critical need for novel therapeutics in dry AMD, olaparib represents a promising candidate that merits further investigation. Future studies should focus on elucidating its effects on mitochondrial deacetylation in RPE, optimizing ocular drug delivery, and carefully assessing long-term safety in the context of chronic retinal disease (Jang et al., 2018; Du et al., 2016; Lin & Apte, 2018).

Astaxanthin is a naturally occurring carotenoid belonging to the xanthophyll subclass, first discovered from marine sources such as lobsters and various microalgae, notably Haematococcus pluvialis (Yang & Wang, 2022, pp. 1–2). This red-orange pigment exhibits exceptional antioxidant properties that have been exploited both in natural extraction and through large‐scale synthetic production, with approximately 95% produced synthetically for enhanced economic viability (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 1–3). Astaxanthin is a representative member of a broader class of antioxidants that have historically been used as nutraceuticals and dietary supplements, targeting a range of conditions including cardiovascular, dermatologic, and neurodegenerative diseases. Over the decades, the unique biochemical properties of astaxanthin have motivated extensive research into its therapeutic potential, particularly for conditions associated with oxidative stress. Its regulatory approval as a food supplement in the early 1990s, together with subsequent studies demonstrating its anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic capabilities, have established astaxanthin as a promising candidate for further exploration in the context of ocular diseases (Yang & Wang, 2022, pp. 1–2; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, astaxanthin has been investigated and utilized in various biomedical contexts due to its robust antioxidant function. Clinical research and preclinical models have repeatedly shown that astaxanthin improves retinal function and visual acuity in patients with ocular diseases, including both early and nonadvanced stages of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). In addition to its application in AMD, astaxanthin has been evaluated for therapeutic effects in conditions such as diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and dry eye syndrome, demonstrating broad-spectrum protective activities against the oxidative and inflammatory insults commonly underlying these disorders (Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 2–5; Fong, 2023, pp. 7–10). Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic potential of astaxanthin in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) is thought to stem from its unparalleled antioxidant activity, which is mechanistically linked to its lipophilic and hydrophilic properties. On a molecular level, astaxanthin integrates into cellular membranes—including those of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) mitochondria—where it acts as a chain-breaking antioxidant, quenching reactive oxygen species (ROS) and scavenging free radicals efficiently (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 1–5). Its mechanism involves the neutralization of lipid peroxidation, a process wherein polyunsaturated fatty acids in the cell membrane are damaged by ROS, ultimately leading to the formation of malondialdehyde (MDA) and other toxic aldehyde species that compromise membrane integrity (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–5; Maiuolo et al., 2022, pp. 8–9). By inhibiting lipid peroxidation, astaxanthin stabilizes the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), an essential parameter for maintaining proper mitochondrial function and for preventing the initiation of apoptosis via intrinsic death pathways (Fong, 2023, pp. 7–10; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).  

At the molecular level, studies indicate that astaxanthin modulates key intracellular signaling pathways. This is particularly relevant in the context of dry AMD, where chronic oxidative stress leads to the degeneration of the RPE, a critical cell layer whose dysfunction is central to the pathogenesis of the disease (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 3–5). The collective body of evidence suggests that astaxanthin holds considerable promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. One of its principal strengths lies in its multifaceted action: as a potent antioxidant, it effectively quenches reactive oxygen species and prevents lipid peroxidation, while its ability to integrate into cellular membranes, particularly those of RPE mitochondria, ensures that mitochondrial membrane potential is preserved even under chronic oxidative conditions (Fong, 2023, pp. 7–10; Rodella et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). From the perspective of a drug development team leader focused on repurposing agents for dry AMD, the evidence supports the incorporation of astaxanthin into further preclinical testing and potential early-phase clinical trials. To recapitulate, astaxanthin’s natural origin as a marine-derived carotenoid, its extensive historical use as a nutraceutical, and its documented molecular mechanisms that include inflammation suppression, ROS scavenging, and stabilization of vital mitochondrial functions all contribute to its strong candidacy for repurposing in dry AMD (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 1–3; Yang & Wang, 2022, pp. 1–2; Maiuolo et al., 2022, pp. 8–9).
