Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GKT137831, also known as Setanaxib, is a synthetic small‐molecule drug originally discovered and optimized for its ability to inhibit NADPH oxidase activity, with specificity primarily toward the NOX1 and NOX4 isoforms. It belongs to the dihydropyrazolone chemical class, sharing structural similarity with the free radical scavenger edaravone, and has been further refined from earlier analogues such as GKT136901 through structure–activity relationship studies to improve its potency, selectivity, and oral bioavailability (Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30; Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). The compound was originally developed by Genkyotex as a dual NOX1/NOX4 inhibitor; however, it possesses additional but lower potency activity against NOX2 and even shows some partial inhibition of NOX5 in certain settings (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30). The initial discovery was based on high-throughput screening methods that targeted NADPH oxidase-mediated reactive oxygen species (ROS) production—a process that has been linked to multiple pathological conditions including fibrotic, vascular, and inflammatory diseases. As a representative of its class, GKT137831 exemplifies a modern approach to drug design wherein inhibition of the primary enzymatic source of ROS is favored over conventional antioxidant strategies, which often suffer from non-specificity and poor clinical translation (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26).

Therapeutic History:  
GKT137831 has a distinguished preclinical and clinical history rooted in its application to diseases characterized by oxidative stress and inflammation. In preclinical models, it has been shown to significantly reduce the generation of ROS and the downstream activation of pro-inflammatory signaling. In primary cultured human retinal endothelial cells, for instance, treatment with GKT137831 reduced both ROS generation and VEGFA expression, indicating its potential utility in limiting vascular dysfunction in ocular diseases (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). Beyond ocular applications, the compound has been evaluated in several preclinical models of fibrotic and vascular pathologies including diabetic kidney disease, hypertensive cardiac remodeling, and liver fibrosis, wherein its administration lowered the levels of ROS, inflammatory cytokines, and markers of tissue injury (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Cipriano et al., 2023, pp. 22–23). Clinically, GKT137831 has advanced to Phase II trials in diabetic nephropathy and primary biliary cholangitis, demonstrating both safety and acceptable pharmacokinetic properties in human subjects (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26; Buglak et al., 2018, Art. 2468457). Although it has not been tested directly for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) in clinical trials, several preclinical studies using models of ischemic retinopathy and diabetic retinopathy have provided supportive evidence that NOX inhibition may attenuate oxidative stress and inflammation in retinal tissues (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Gaskin et al., 2021, pp. 15–17). The repurposing rationale for dry AMD hinges on the observation that oxidative stress plays a central role in the degeneration of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and the subsequent progression of AMD—pathophysiological processes that have been effectively modulated by GKT137831 in other experimental disease models (Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 1–7).

Mechanism of Action:  
From a molecular perspective, GKT137831 has been characterized as a dual inhibitor of NOX1 and NOX4, enzymes that catalyze the transfer of electrons from NADPH to molecular oxygen and thereby generate superoxide or hydrogen peroxide, respectively (Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30; Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 4–6). Unlike classical antioxidants that scavenge ROS after they are generated, GKT137831 aims to prevent ROS formation at its source by directly inhibiting NOX enzyme activity. One study demonstrates that it can bind to the extracellular region of the catalytic subunit of NOX enzymes in an allosteric manner, distinct from the NADPH binding site, which leads to a decrease in NADPH-dependent superoxide generation and hydrogen peroxide production (Gorin et al., 2015, pp. 16–20). In addition to its enzyme inhibitory actions, the dihydropyrazolone scaffold confers an inherent ROS scavenging property, enabling the compound to neutralize peroxynitrite and hydrogen peroxide through redox-mediated chemical mechanisms (Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30; Gaskin et al., 2021, pp. 8–9). This dual property—direct enzyme inhibition coupled with ROS scavenging—is theorized to offer a more comprehensive approach to modulating oxidative stress in target tissues. However, there are conflicting reports in the literature regarding the specificity of its NOX inhibition, with some studies suggesting that measured low Ki values may be artifactual due to interference with assay components such as horseradish peroxidase, raising questions about whether the observed effects are entirely attributable to NOX inhibition or, in part, to non-specific redox modulation (Vincent, 2021, pp. 79–80; Demircan et al., 2022, pp. 12–13). Notwithstanding these concerns, the prevailing hypothesis remains that by dampening NOX activity, GKT137831 reduces both cytosolic and mitochondrial ROS. In the context of RPE cells, which are rich in mitochondria and subject to high oxidative loads due to constant light exposure and high metabolic activity, the inhibition of NOX4 is expected to be particularly beneficial for mitigating oxidative damage to the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and preserving the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 24–28).

Expected Effect:

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Resveratrol is a naturally occurring polyphenolic compound belonging to the stilbene class and is structurally defined as 3,5,4′-trihydroxystilbene. It is biosynthesized by plants such as Vitis vinifera (grapes), Japanese Knotweed, and various berries in response to stress factors like injury or pathogen attack, and it is a well‐recognized phytoalexin with a molecular formula of C14H12O3 (Bel, 2020; Pop et al., 2022). Originally isolated from the White Hellebore in the mid-20th century and later found in red wine due to grape skin fermentation, resveratrol has garnered significant attention not only for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties but also for its potential benefits in cardiovascular and neuroprotective contexts (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pop et al., 2022). As such, resveratrol—and by extension its commercial version (Cayman Chemical #70580) used in our studies—is classified as a nutraceutical and drug candidate with a long track record of investigative research including applications in aging, inflammation, and ocular health (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pop et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
A considerable volume of biochemical, preclinical, and early clinical literature has explored resveratrol’s broad spectrum of activities. Historically, resveratrol has been investigated primarily for its cardioprotective and neuroprotective effects, as well as its anti-aging properties. In the realm of ophthalmology, several in vitro and animal studies have focused on its role in retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD), diabetic retinopathy (DR), and glaucoma. For instance, its use in RPE cell models has shown promising evidence for ameliorating oxidative stress-induced damage, a central factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Clinical investigations have attempted to translate these findings, as exemplified by the terminated clinical trial NCT02625376 that investigated resveratrol for exudative AMD (Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015), highlighting both the potential and the challenges involved in its clinical application (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Beyond ocular applications, resveratrol’s inclusion in various nutraceutical formulations underscores its established safety profile when administered at low-to-moderate doses, although issues pertaining to bioavailability and rapid systemic metabolism have been recurrent themes in the literature (Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, resveratrol exerts its effects primarily by modulating multiple intracellular signaling cascades. The central hypothesis we are testing is that resveratrol activates the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells—a pathway integral to regulating mitochondrial biogenesis and the antioxidant defense system. Activation of SIRT1, a NAD+-dependent deacetylase, by resveratrol increases the deacetylation and activation of its downstream effector, AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Once activated, AMPK facilitates the phosphorylation and activation of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1 alpha (PGC-1α) in the cytoplasm, which subsequently translocates to the nucleus to upregulate the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and antioxidant responses, including the gene encoding superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). This cascade not only improves mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and spare respiratory capacity—critical indicators of cellular health under oxidative stress—but also promotes an overall enhancement of cellular resilience against reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Bel, 2020; Bryl et al., 2022). Further molecular studies indicate that resveratrol can also modulate extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERK1/2) and mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK), contributing additional layers of cytoprotection through anti-apoptotic effects (Pop et al., 2022; Pop et al., 2022). Together, these mechanistic insights provide a comprehensive biochemical framework through which resveratrol is hypothesized to mitigate the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in RPE cells—a primary factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2021; Bryl et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of the proposed assay for dry AMD, our expectation is that resveratrol will exert a multifaceted protective effect on RPE cells under oxidative challenge. Specifically, when RPE cells are exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as a model for oxidative stress, resveratrol is anticipated to counteract the resultant mitochondrial dysfunction by upregulating antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2, thereby reducing intracellular ROS levels (Bel, 2020; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Restoration of the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) is a critical endpoint, as it directly reflects cellular energy status and the ability of mitochondria to sustain ATP synthesis under stress (Buonfiglio et al., 2024). In addition, an improvement in spare respiratory capacity—the measure of a cell’s ability to respond to increased energy demands—should be evident, reflecting enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and a greater capacity for cellular repair mechanisms (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bryl et al., 2022). These cytoprotective effects have been demonstrated in in vitro studies using ARPE-19 and other human retinal pigment epithelial cell lines, and they resonate with the established role of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis in mediating energy metabolism and antioxidative defenses in the retina (Bryl et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021). Moreover, by decreasing the accrual of oxidative damage, resveratrol is expected to limit apoptotic signaling pathways, which are crucial in slowing the progressive degeneration observed in dry AMD (Bel, 2020; Pop et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
The cumulative evidence from preclinical studies strongly supports the potential of resveratrol as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, especially considering its capacity to modulate mitochondrial function and activate intrinsic antioxidant defenses. The activation of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis not only augments mitochondrial biogenesis but also enhances the expression of key antioxidant enzymes required to neutralize ROS, thereby directly addressing one of the primary mechanisms underlying AMD pathology (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bryl et al., 2022). One of the major strengths of resveratrol is its pleiotropic mode of action; beyond its antioxidant properties, its anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic activities further consolidate its candidacy for chronic conditions like dry AMD (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Bel, 2020). Furthermore, extensive safety data in various preclinical models indicate that resveratrol is well tolerated at certain dose ranges, which is a positive indicator for its potential clinical translation (Wang et al., 2021; Bel, 2020).

However, several limitations remain that warrant careful consideration. The primary challenge with resveratrol is its poor bioavailability and rapid metabolism, which may result in subtherapeutic tissue concentrations despite high oral absorption. This has driven research efforts into advanced drug delivery platforms, such as nanoparticle-based systems and liposomal formulations, aimed at enhancing ocular retention and achieving sustained drug levels in the retina (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Additionally, although the in vitro and animal model data are promising, there exists a dearth of robust clinical trial data specifically addressing dry AMD, as evidenced by the terminated trial in exudative AMD (Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015) and the limited clinical evidence in related retinal pathologies (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Another potential weakness is the dose-dependent duality of its mechanism, where low doses predominantly mediate SIRT1-dependent effects, whereas higher doses might trigger SIRT1-independent pathways, possibly leading to off-target effects or toxicity (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Such a narrow therapeutic window necessitates a precise optimization of dosing regimens and formulation strategies. Despite these challenges, the overarching trend in preclinical research underscores that with proper formulation and dosing strategies, resveratrol could excel as an adjuvant or even monotherapy for protecting RPE cells from oxidative injury and, consequently, for the management of dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

In-Depth Analysis of Preclinical and Clinical Evidence:  
Numerous in vitro studies have characterized the effect of resveratrol on retinal pigment epithelial cells, notably ARPE-19 cell lines, under conditions of oxidative stress. Such studies consistently demonstrate that resveratrol treatment leads to a measurable reduction in ROS levels, a decrease in markers of apoptosis, and an overall improvement in mitochondrial parameters including Δψm and spare respiratory capacity (Bel, 2020; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). These findings are reinforced by experiments showing that resveratrol can mitigate blue light-induced retinal damage and preserve cell viability, further supporting its relevance in ocular pathologies where light-induced oxidative stress is a contributing factor (Bel, 2020). Complementary studies in animal models have shown that resveratrol can reduce inflammatory cytokine secretion and inhibit processes such as choroidal neovascularization, which has implications not only for dry AMD but also for its neovascular (wet) counterpart (Bryl et al., 2022; Bel, 2020).

Moreover, mechanistic investigations into the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis reveal that the deacetylation of PGC-1α is a critical step in the upregulation of mitochondrial genes, which directly correlates with increased cellular ATP production and enhanced resistance to oxidative stress (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Experimental data also show that SOD2 expression is significantly increased following resveratrol treatment, corroborating the compound’s role in boosting the cellular antioxidant capacity (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). These molecular events culminate in an environment that is less conducive to oxidative damage, thereby potentially arresting or even reversing some aspects of RPE degeneration that occur in dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021).

From a clinical perspective, the application of resveratrol in ocular disorders has been approached with caution, primarily due to pharmacokinetic challenges. Even though systemic administration of resveratrol has demonstrated efficacy in reducing plasma oxidative markers in diabetic patients and other conditions, the translation to ocular tissue remains hindered by its low aqueous solubility and rapid hepatic metabolism (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Abu-Amero et al., 2016). To overcome these barriers, innovative drug delivery systems such as chitosan-based nanoparticles, polymeric micelles, and liposomal formulations are being actively developed and show promise for achieving therapeutic levels in retinal tissues (Pop et al., 2022; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Such advanced formulations not only improve bioavailability but also allow for controlled release, which is essential for a chronic condition like dry AMD where sustained therapeutic action is desirable.

Additional mechanistic studies also suggest that resveratrol’s efficacy might be enhanced when used in combination with other therapeutic agents. For instance, its synergistic effects with anti-VEGF treatments in mitigating inflammatory cascades and suppressing angiogenesis have been noted in various preclinical models (Rusciano & Bagnoli, 2023; Tong et al., 2022). Challenges in Drug Delivery and Bioavailability:  
While the biochemical rationale for using resveratrol in dry AMD is robust, its clinical development is significantly complicated by pharmacokinetic limitations. The compound is classified as a BCS Class II molecule, meaning that despite having high membrane permeability and lipophilicity, its poor aqueous solubility results in less than 1% bioavailability following oral administration (Kaštelan et al., 2025). As a consequence, only minimal amounts of unchanged resveratrol reach the systemic circulation and, by extension, the ocular tissues. Current research thus prioritizes the optimization of drug delivery vehicles to enhance its stability and target specificity. Nanotechnology-based delivery methods, including polymeric nanoparticles and solid lipid nanoparticles, have demonstrated enhanced tissue penetration and prolonged drug retention in the eye (Pop et al., 2022; Kaštelan et al., 2025). However, these strategies are still in the developmental phase, and their safety, scalability, and reproducibility for routine clinical use remain to be thoroughly validated. The potential for off-target effects and variability in patient-specific pharmacokinetics are additional hurdles that must be addressed in future clinical studies.

Safety and Dosing Considerations:  
Resveratrol has been generally recognized as safe in many preclinical studies, with low-dose regimens showing minimal adverse effects and favorable tolerability profiles (Wang et al., 2021; Bel, 2020). Nonetheless, concerns have been raised regarding gastrointestinal disturbances and other side effects at higher doses, as well as potential interactions with other medications (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Moreover, due to the compound’s rapid metabolism, determining an optimal dosing regimen that achieves effective local concentrations in the retina without inducing systemic toxicity remains challenging. This necessitates further preclinical and early-phase clinical trials to elucidate the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic profiles specific to ocular applications. Tailoring the dosing strategy based on individual metabolic rates and employing controlled-release formulations may help mitigate these issues and maximize therapeutic outcomes (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Kaštelan et al., 2025).

Strategic Direction and Future Perspectives:  
Given the multifaceted biological activities of resveratrol and the encouraging preclinical evidence in models of oxidative stress-induced RPE damage, it holds considerable promise as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to modulate the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis and promote mitochondrial biogenesis presents a novel therapeutic approach that directly targets the cellular dysfunctions underlying RPE degeneration. However, the translation of these findings into clinical practice will require addressing the critical challenges of bioavailability, formulation, and dosing.

Future research should focus on (1) developing and rigorously testing advanced drug delivery systems such as nanoparticle encapsulation methods that can bypass first-pass metabolism and target the retina more effectively, (2) conducting detailed pharmacokinetic studies to determine the optimal dosing regimen for achieving sustained therapeutic concentrations in ocular tissues, and (3) exploring combination therapy approaches that integrate resveratrol with conventional treatments such as anti-VEGF agents or other nutraceuticals to provide a comprehensive strategy against AMD progression (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Pop et al., 2022; Rusciano & Bagnoli, 2023). In summary, resveratrol emerges as a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its extensive preclinical evidence, well-elucidated molecular mechanisms, and potential for modulating critical cellular pathways implicated in retinal degeneration. The strengths of resveratrol are rooted in its natural origin, broad-spectrum antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, and its ability to enhance mitochondrial function through the activation of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α pathway. These attributes are particularly relevant for combating the oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction that are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Nonetheless, its clinical utility is hampered by significant challenges related to bioavailability and metabolism, which necessitate innovative formulation and delivery strategies. Moreover, the variable dose-response observed in preclinical studies highlights the need for precise dose optimization before resveratrol can be reliably integrated into clinical practice for AMD treatment (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Although resveratrol has been investigated in clinical trials for ocular conditions, further large-scale, well-designed studies are essential to validate its efficacy, establish an acceptable safety profile, and determine its long-term benefits in human subjects with dry AMD (Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015; Pop et al., 2022).

Given the current state of evidence, we recommend that the research team continue to explore resveratrol as a candidate for dry AMD with a dual focus: first, to refine and optimize drug delivery systems that enhance its ocular bioavailability, and second, to design and implement comprehensive dose-escalation and safety studies in relevant preclinical models. Collaborative efforts that integrate insights from molecular biology, pharmacology, and clinical research will be critical in overcoming the translational challenges that have traditionally limited the application of resveratrol in ocular therapeutics (Pop et al., 2022; Rusciano & Bagnoli, 2023).

Resveratrol represents a promising candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration based on its robust mechanistic rationale and supportive preclinical evidence. Its capacity to activate the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis, promote mitochondrial biogenesis, and enhance antioxidant enzyme expression positions it as a multifaceted agent capable of mitigating oxidative stress in RPE cells—one of the key pathological drivers of AMD (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). With concerted efforts in formulation science, preclinical validation, and clinical evaluation, resveratrol has the potential to become an integral part of a multi-targeted therapeutic approach for dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Kaštelan et al., 2025).

The integration of this compound as either a monotherapy or as an adjunct to established therapies could provide enhanced protection against oxidative stress, preserve mitochondrial function, and improve retinal cell survival in patients suffering from this debilitating condition. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is a naturally occurring long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (LC-PUFA) that has been isolated from marine sources, such as fish oil, and is commercially available in a highly purified form (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich D2534). DHA is synthesized via metabolic elongation and desaturation of dietary alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) in mammals; however, this endogenous conversion is limited, and direct dietary intake is critical for maintaining adequate retinal DHA levels (Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14). Belonging to the omega-3 class of fatty acids, DHA has long been recognized for its important roles in maintaining membrane structure and function, particularly in neural tissues and the retina where it is highly concentrated in photoreceptor outer segments and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) membranes (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3). Its polyunsaturated nature—with six cis double bonds—confers unique biophysical properties, enabling DHA to increase membrane fluidity and participate in critical signaling cascades. The compound has been used extensively as a nutritional supplement and has been incorporated in various formulations aimed at cardiovascular health, cognitive function, and ocular protection, establishing a robust safety profile over decades of human use (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Skowronska-Krawczyk & Chao, 2019, pp. 3–4).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past two decades, extensive research has explored the role of DHA and related omega-3 fatty acids in maintaining retinal function and potentially preventing age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Epidemiologic studies have consistently demonstrated an inverse association between dietary fish and high omega-3 fatty acid intake and the risk of developing AMD, suggesting that populations with higher DHA consumption tend to exhibit a lower incidence of both early and, to some extent, advanced forms of the disease (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). In clinical settings, large-scale randomized controlled trials, such as AREDS2, incorporated DHA (and EPA) into a multi-nutrient formula designed originally for AMD, though the overall randomized trial outcomes have been mixed, with some studies finding no statistically significant benefit for progression to late AMD (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). Pilot clinical trials and observational cohort studies, including NAT-1 and NAT-2, have assessed DHA supplementation in subjects with drusenoid lesions or early-stage AMD; while some of these studies have shown promising improvements in blood biomarkers (e.g., increased red blood cell DHA levels) and correlations with reduced AMD progression, the clinical efficacy remains under debate (Querques et al., 2016, pp. 2–4; Querques et al., 2011, pp. 7–8). Notably, evidence from animal models suggests that dietary DHA may protect against light-induced retinal degeneration and reduce the accumulation of deleterious lipid peroxidation products, although some preclinical studies also caution that DHA’s susceptibility to oxidation could, under certain conditions, worsen retinal injury (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic hypothesis for using DHA in dry AMD is based on its predicted ability to incorporate into the mitochondrial membranes of RPE cells, thereby enhancing membrane fluidity and protecting against oxidative damage to the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes. Under normal cellular conditions, DHA—owing to its multiple methylene-interrupted cis double bonds—integrates into phospholipid bilayers and modulates biophysical properties such as fluidity, permeability, and thickness (Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33). In mitochondrial membranes, this incorporation is thought to replace more saturated fatty acids such as arachidonic acid, ultimately reducing lipid peroxidation and mitigating oxidative stress that is deleterious to ETC function (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9). In vitro studies have shown that DHA supplementation in retinal cell cultures can decrease markers of apoptosis and preserve mitochondrial membrane integrity, with a concomitant increase in anti-apoptotic proteins (e.g., Bcl-2) (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 2–4).  
In addition, DHA is enzymatically converted under conditions of oxidative stress into neuroprotective docosanoids, such as neuroprotectin D1 (NPD1), which can inhibit pro-inflammatory gene expression and reduce cell death in RPE and photoreceptor cells (Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14; LaFuente et al., 2021, p. 13). This conversion not only contributes to countering local inflammation but also supports cellular health by modulating intracellular signaling pathways, particularly those involving NF-κB and other transcription factors critical for managing oxidative stress (Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14; Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14). Despite these promising mechanistic insights, it is important to note that direct, quantitative evidence detailing DHA’s incorporation specifically into RPE mitochondrial membranes and its precise effects on mitochondrial cristae structure, malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, or oxygen consumption rate (OCR) remains limited in the current literature (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, p. 13). Several reviews and preclinical reports acknowledge the theoretical framework while emphasizing the need for more detailed mechanistic studies that directly measure these mitochondrial endpoints (Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the mechanistic hypothesis, DHA supplementation is expected to yield several beneficial effects in retinal cells, particularly within the RPE, which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. In an ideal in vitro or ex vivo assay, DHA would incorporate into RPE cell membranes—including the mitochondrial inner membrane—increasing fluidity and enabling better diffusion of substrates and electron carriers necessary for efficient ATP production. Enhanced mitochondrial membrane fluidity should help reduce the susceptibility of the electron transport chain to oxidative damage, thereby lowering the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the subsequent production of lipid peroxidation byproducts such as MDA (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5). Furthermore, preservation of mitochondrial cristae structure is anticipated to maintain optimal alignment and function of ETC complexes, leading to an improved oxygen consumption rate (OCR) that is directly linked to cellular energy metabolism and overall cell viability (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 2–4; Souied et al., 2016, p. 8).  
At a molecular level, the increased presence of DHA in mitochondrial membranes is expected to initiate a cascade of protective events: reduced oxidative stress and inflammation via inhibition of NF-κB activation, promotion of the antioxidant response through NFE2L2 (NRF2) pathway activation, and enhanced autophagic clearance of damaged proteins and organelles through upregulation of SQSTM1 (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 1–2; Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, p. 3). Additionally, because genes encoding crucial direct mediators of DHA uptake such as Mfsd2a are expressed in RPE cells and photoreceptors, the target tissue is particularly well-positioned to benefit from increased dietary or supplementary DHA (Fathima et al., 2023, p. 8). Overall Evaluation:  
The proposition to repurpose DHA for dry AMD is underpinned by compelling mechanistic rationale and epidemiologic associations, yet it is not without its challenges and limitations. One clear strength is DHA’s established role as an essential component of retinal cell membranes. Its high concentration in photoreceptors and the RPE is functionally integral to maintaining visual function and cellular homeostasis, lending strong biological plausibility to its protective potential in AMD (Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33). Its ability to modulate membrane fluidity, serve as a precursor to neuroprotective mediators like NPD1, and exert anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions provide multiple mechanistic pathways through which it may mitigate the cellular stressors implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis (Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14; Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14).  
From a therapeutic history perspective, DHA is well understood in the context of nutritional supplementation, and numerous epidemiologic studies point toward a lower risk of AMD with higher dietary DHA intake (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). The safety profile of DHA is also well established, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing. However, the clinical trial data to date (including large-scale studies such as AREDS2 and smaller trials like NAT-2) have not consistently demonstrated a clear benefit in altering the progression of advanced AMD, and it remains uncertain whether observed benefits in intermediate AMD or specific cellular endpoints translate into clinically meaningful outcomes in the dry form of the disease (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8).  
A significant weakness in the current body of research is the lack of direct mechanistic studies that quantitatively document DHA incorporation into RPE mitochondrial membranes and its subsequent effects on mitochondrial parameters. In our hypothesis, improved mitochondrial function is key, with expected reductions in MDA levels, preservation of cristae structure, and enhancement of OCR serving as biomarkers of efficacy. Yet, while several in vitro studies and animal experiments have suggested that DHA can reduce markers of oxidative stress and improve mitochondrial integrity in retinal models, the literature provided does not include rigorous, high-resolution measurements of these specific parameters in human RPE cells (Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Jiang et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). This gap in the direct evidence would need to be addressed through targeted preclinical assays employing electron microscopy, lipidomics, and mitochondrial respirometry to validate the proposed mechanism.  
Furthermore, the mode of formulation and bioavailability of DHA is a critical factor that may contribute to the mixed findings in clinical trials; DHA administered as an ethyl ester may have different absorption and incorporation profiles compared to its triglyceride-bound form, and the optimal dosing necessary to achieve sufficient retinal or mitochondrial enrichment remains unclear (Souied et al., 2016, pp. 6–7; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). Potential pro-oxidant effects of DHA in settings where oxidation is excessive must also be carefully monitored, as some animal studies have reported that under specific conditions DHA accumulation may even exacerbate oxidative damage (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5).  
In summary, while the epidemiologic literature and preclinical studies provide an encouraging backdrop for the repurposing of DHA as a therapeutic agent in dry AMD—by showing that high DHA intake is associated with a reduced risk of AMD and that DHA can confer mitochondrial and anti-oxidative benefits in retinal models—the critical mechanistic endpoints that support our specific hypothesis are not yet fully substantiated in the published literature. The overall evaluation is that DHA has substantial mechanistic promise, safety, and historical use as a nutritional supplement; however, further robust mechanistic studies and carefully designed clinical trials are necessary to validate its specific effects on mitochondrial function in RPE cells and to determine whether these biochemical improvements translate into a clinically significant slowing of dry AMD progression (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) is a synthetic derivative of fumaric acid that belongs to the class of fumaric acid esters (FAEs) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Chemically, DMF is the dimethyl ester of fumaric acid, with a molecular weight of approximately 144.13 g/mol, and is produced by reacting fumaric acid with methanol in the presence of a strong acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Although fumaric acid occurs naturally as an intermediate in the citric acid cycle, DMF itself is fully synthetically manufactured, conferring the advantages of chemical stability and the ability to precisely modulate its structure to enhance pharmacological properties (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Moreover, DMF is classified as an electrophilic molecule that, due to its α,β-unsaturated ester structure, can covalently modify protein thiols, particularly the cysteine residues within KEAP1, thereby initiating its downstream effects on cellular redox homeostasis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Fumaric acid esters as a class have a long-standing history in pharmacotherapy, originally finding application in dermatology, most notably in the treatment of psoriasis, and have since been repurposed for neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis (MS) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, fumaric acid esters were introduced into clinical practice as antipsoriatic agents in Europe, with formulations such as Fumaderm® entering the market in the 1990s (Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). DMF in particular emerged as a key component in these formulations, and its efficacy in modulating immune responses and suppressing inflammation in skin diseases laid the foundation for its later repurposing in other systemic inflammatory conditions (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Over time, DMF was repurposed and further developed as an oral agent for the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), culminating in its FDA approval in 2013 under the trade name Tecfidera® by Biogen (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163). Clinical trials, including large-scale phase 3 studies, have demonstrated its favorable safety profile and efficacy in reducing relapse rates and slowing disability progression in MS patients (Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 14–16). Although there is no extensive historical record of DMF being used directly for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other primary ocular diseases, recent preclinical findings have indicated that its potent activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway may confer significant protective effects on the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This has sparked considerable interest in repurposing DMF for ocular indications such as geographic atrophy, a late stage of dry AMD, by leveraging its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities observed in nonocular settings (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, DMF functions primarily as a prodrug; upon oral administration it is rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases within the gastrointestinal tract to yield its active metabolite, monomethyl fumarate (MMF) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). The pharmacodynamic actions of DMF principally involve the electrophilic modification of specific cysteine residues—most notably cysteine 151—on Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Under physiological conditions, KEAP1 binds to and retains the transcription factor Nrf2 in the cytoplasm, targeting it for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. However, when DMF covalently modifies KEAP1, it disrupts this complex, allowing Nrf2 to dissociate and translocate into the nucleus (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). In the nucleus, Nrf2 binds to antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoters of numerous genes encoding cytoprotective enzymes, including glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), and various enzymes involved in glutathione (GSH) synthesis and regeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). These molecular interactions lead to enhanced antioxidant defenses, improved detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and overall better maintenance of cellular redox balance (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). In addition to its role in promoting antioxidant gene expression via Nrf2 activation, DMF has been shown to have immunomodulatory properties; it can shift cytokine profiles by increasing interleukin-4 (IL-4)–expressing CD4+ T cells and decreasing the production of proinflammatory cytokines such as interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and interleukin-17 (IL-17) (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Furthermore, DMF has been reported to inhibit nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation in certain cellular contexts, thus contributing to a reduction in inflammatory signaling independently of Nrf2 (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Together, these molecular actions result in lowered cellular oxidative stress and an improved inflammatory milieu, which are critical factors implicated in the pathogenesis of chronic degenerative diseases (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry AMD, particularly the geographic atrophy form, is characterized by the gradual degeneration of RPE cells, which leads to subsequent photoreceptor loss and irreversible vision impairment. Central to the pathophysiology of dry AMD are oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation that progressively compromise RPE viability and function (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). The hypothesis being explored is that DMF, through its robust activation of the Nrf2 pathway, can enhance the expression of ARE-driven genes that encode for antioxidant and cytoprotective proteins, thereby counteracting the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in the RPE (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 13–14). In particular, the upregulation of enzymes involved in glutathione synthesis is expected to increase intracellular levels of GSH, a critical thiol antioxidant that protects mitochondrial membranes and supports cellular bioenergetics (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Preclinical studies in retinal models have demonstrated that DMF can effectively preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and reduce the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β), both of which are hallmarks of RPE distress under oxidative challenge (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Given that the RPE is highly metabolically active and particularly vulnerable to cumulative oxidative damage, the sustained activation of Nrf2 by DMF following oral dosing is anticipated to provide continuous reinforcement of antioxidant defenses and maintain mitochondrial integrity in these cells (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 3–5; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). Moreover, by mitigating inflammatory signaling, DMF may not only protect the RPE but also contribute to a more favorable microenvironment that limits the propagation of cell death signals, thus potentially slowing the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Collectively, these expected cellular effects support the rationale for using DMF as an intervention to preserve retinal structure and function by lowering oxidative damage and supporting bioenergetics in the RPE.

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential of dimethyl fumarate as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD rests on a solid mechanistic rationale combined with an established clinical pedigree in other indications. One of the primary strengths of DMF is its well-characterized pharmacological profile; it is FDA-approved for multiple sclerosis and has been safely administered to thousands of patients over several years, which significantly mitigates the risk and regulatory hurdles typically associated with repurposed drugs (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). The dual actions of DMF—in particular, its ability to both activate the Nrf2 pathway and attenuate proinflammatory signals—directly target the underlying pathological processes in dry AMD, where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central drivers of RPE degeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Despite these limitations, the strengths of DMF are compelling. The drug’s ability to upregulate a broad spectrum of cytoprotective genes via the Nrf2 pathway makes it a versatile candidate for mitigating the oxidative and inflammatory stress that drives RPE degeneration. Its mechanism of action—centered on Nrf2 activation leading to enhanced antioxidant capacity along with anti-inflammatory effects—directly addresses the key pathophysiological mechanisms implicated in dry AMD. The extensive clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis provides a reliable safety and tolerability framework, which is crucial for rapid repositioning into a new clinical area such as geographic atrophy (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). 1. Conduct detailed pharmacokinetic studies in animal models to assess the retinal bioavailability of DMF and its active metabolite MMF following systemic administration. While there are challenges regarding optimal retinal delivery and management of systemic adverse effects, the clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis lends considerable support to its translational potential. This sustained blockade is especially important in countering the slow, progressive damage associated with dry AMD, where intermittent complement activation can cumulatively lead to RPE dysfunction and eventually photoreceptor loss (Ong et al., 2024; Proctor et al., 2006b; Behnke, 2022). In this context, a reduction in mtROS generation and inflammasome-driven cytokine release would be expected to limit oxidative injury and maintain the homeostatic balance in the delicate retinal environment.

In summary, the expected pharmacodynamic effects of PMX53 in the proposed assays include a measurable reduction in mitochondrial superoxide production, a decrease in caspase-1 activity and IL-1β release, and overall preservation of RPE cell morphology when challenged with complement-active stimuli. These effects, if achieved in vitro and then recapitulated in vivo in an appropriate animal model, would support the notion that PMX53 can effectively disrupt the complement-driven amplification of oxidative and inflammatory damage that contributes to dry AMD progression (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Proctor et al., 2006b).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
5. Overall Evaluation  
────────────────────────────────────────────  
In evaluating PMX53 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several positive factors and potential challenges emerge based on the available literature drawn from preclinical and early clinical studies in systemic inflammatory models.

Strengths:  
•  PMX53 has been extensively characterized as a potent cyclic peptide antagonist of the C5a receptor with a well-rationalized design that exploits the structural features of the endogenous ligand C5a. Its cyclic architecture confers not only high receptor selectivity and metabolic stability but also a mode of action that is classified as “pseudo-irreversible” or insurmountable antagonism. This means that once it binds to the receptor, PMX53 is able to provide sustained receptor blockade even in the presence of high levels of circulating C5a—a feature that is especially appealing for chronic conditions like dry AMD where persistent complement dysregulation is a central pathological driver (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

•  The preclinical body of evidence supporting the anti-inflammatory activity of PMX53 is considerable. In numerous animal models, including those for arthritis, sepsis, and ischemia–reperfusion injury, treatment with PMX53 has been shown to reduce inflammatory cytokine production, limit immune cell degranulation, and preserve tissue integrity (Ramsey, 2018; Hutchison & Krause, 2004; Allegretti et al., 2005). These findings have translated, at least in part, to early-phase clinical studies in which PMX53 was evaluated in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis—diseases that share underlying inflammatory components with dry AMD. The favorable safety profile observed in these studies provides an additional layer of support for considering PMX53 as a repurposed drug candidate (Proctor et al., 2006a; Kumar et al., 2020).

•  A critical advantage of PMX53 for the treatment of dry AMD lies in its mechanistic targeting of the complement system, which is increasingly recognized as a central player in the pathogenesis of retinal degenerations. Studies using human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells have demonstrated that complement activation, particularly via C5a, leads to upregulation of the C5a receptor and primes these cells for inflammasome activation in response to additional stressors such as lipofuscin-mediated photooxidative damage (Brandstetter et al., 2015). By effectively preventing C5a from binding to its receptor, PMX53 is hypothesized to block the initiation of a cascade that culminates in excessive mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) production and subsequent IL-1β release. This would theoretically protect RPE cells from the oxidative insult and inflammation that characterize dry AMD pathology (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Leonar, 2017).

•  Moreover, the pseudo-irreversible nature of PMX53’s receptor binding offers the important potential for prolonged therapeutic effects despite the inherent challenges associated with peptide pharmacokinetics. While it is acknowledged that the peptidic nature of the compound might pose hurdles with respect to systemic clearance and bioavailability—particularly within the ocular environment where drug delivery is complicated by barriers such as the blood–retina barrier—the ability of PMX53 to remain bound to C5aR could mitigate the need for continually high drug concentrations. This quality could be beneficial if innovative delivery strategies, such as intravitreal injections, nanoparticle-based formulations, or sustained-release implants, are employed to achieve localized drug concentrations in the retina (Proctor et al., 2006b; Kumar et al., 2020).

Weaknesses and Concerns:  
•  Despite its many promising aspects, several critical challenges must be considered before PMX53 can be realistically advanced as a treatment for dry AMD. One of the most significant gaps in the current literature is the absence of direct preclinical or clinical data specific to ocular models of AMD. Although the complement system, and in particular the C5a–C5aR axis, is well documented as playing a role in RPE dysfunction and retinal inflammation (Brandstetter et al., 2015), PMX53 itself has not yet been rigorously tested in models that recapitulate the complex microenvironment of the retina. Animal models that faithfully mimic the chronic complement activation and oxidative stress seen in human dry AMD are necessary to determine whether the robust systemic anti-inflammatory activity of PMX53 can be translated to a localized ocular context (Proctor et al., 2006a; Hutchison & Krause, 2004).

•  A second concern relates to species-specific differences in receptor binding affinity. It is well established that PMX53 exhibits high affinity for human and rat C5a receptors (in the range of tens of nanomolar), whereas its affinity for the mouse receptor is markedly lower (approximately 36 µM) (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a). This presents a practical obstacle, as many preclinical studies in ophthalmology rely on murine models to assess disease progression and drug efficacy. To circumvent this pitfall, it may be necessary to utilize alternative animal models with receptor pharmacology that more closely mirrors the human system—such as rat models or non-human primate studies—or to develop further analogues that demonstrate improved cross-species binding (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

•  Another issue is the challenge of delivering a peptide drug to ocular tissues in a sustained and therapeutically effective manner. The ocular barriers, including the corneal epithelium and the blood–retina barrier, limit the penetration and retention of systemically administered drugs. In the case of PMX53, whose peptidic nature predisposes it to rapid clearance and potential degradation, specialized formulation strategies will be essential. Approaches such as encapsulation in biodegradable nanoparticles, development of sustained-release intravitreal implants, or formulation with permeability-enhancing agents could be explored to ensure that therapeutically relevant concentrations of PMX53 reach the RPE and maintain a prolonged therapeutic effect (Kumar et al., 2020).

•  Safety considerations within the ocular environment also warrant close attention. While systemic administration of PMX53 has demonstrated an acceptable side-effect profile in non-ocular applications, the retina is an immunologically privileged and sensitive tissue. Chronic inhibition of complement-mediated signaling in the eye could potentially impair local immune surveillance or interfere with normal cellular homeostasis. Such risks necessitate detailed ocular toxicology studies to assess the potential for adverse effects resulting from long-term C5aR blockade in RPE cells and other retinal tissues (Proctor et al., 2006a; Hutchison & Krause, 2004).

•  Furthermore, the translational relevance of the anti-inflammatory effects observed with PMX53 in systemic diseases may not directly apply to the intricate pathophysiology of dry AMD. Dry AMD is a multifactorial disease influenced by genetic predispositions, environmental stresses (such as oxidative damage from chronic light exposure), and complex interactions between complement proteins, RPE cells, and the extracellular matrix. While the blockade of C5aR is theoretically poised to reduce mtROS production and inflammasome activation, it is possible that additional redundant inflammatory pathways might offset the therapeutic benefit of targeting a single receptor (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Proctor et al., 2006a).

•  Finally, the overall clinical development history of PMX53 indicates that while the compound has progressed to early clinical trials for systemic inflammatory conditions, challenges related to pharmacokinetics and delivery have hindered further clinical advancements. As such, repurposing PMX53 for dry AMD will require a dedicated research program that not only demonstrates efficacy in ocular models but also addresses the unique drug delivery and safety challenges associated with the eye (Proctor et al., 2006a; Proctor et al., 2006b).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
6. Overall Conclusion  
────────────────────────────────────────────  
In summary, PMX53 is a well-characterized cyclic peptidomimetic C5a receptor antagonist that has been evaluated extensively in systemic models of inflammation and has reached early-phase clinical testing for conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis. Its design, which exploits a cyclic structure to achieve pseudo-irreversible antagonism, provides a strong mechanistic rationale for targeting the complement cascade—which is increasingly recognized as a major contributor not only to systemic inflammatory diseases but also to ocular conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

The expected effect of PMX53 in the context of dry AMD is to prevent the binding of C5a to its receptor on retinal pigment epithelial cells, thereby disrupting a key amplification loop that leads to mitochondrial reactive oxygen species overproduction, inflammasome activation, and subsequent IL-1β release. Such a blockade should, in theory, mitigate the chronic inflammatory stress that drives RPE degeneration and, by extension, slow the progression of dry AMD (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Proctor et al., 2006a).

Nonetheless, despite its strong conceptual appeal and preclinical promise in systemic models, significant knowledge gaps remain with respect to its application in the ocular setting. No dedicated studies have yet confirmed the efficacy of PMX53 in reducing complement-driven oxidative stress specifically in the retina, and species-specific differences in receptor binding mean that murine models—a common platform for AMD research—may not accurately reflect the human situation. Additionally, the challenges inherent in delivering a peptide drug effectively to ocular tissues, combined with the potential risks of long-term complement inhibition in the sensitive retinal environment, require careful and systematic investigation through both advanced formulation approaches and dedicated ocular safety studies (Proctor et al., 2006a; Hutchison & Krause, 2004; Kumar et al., 2020).

Overall, while the scientific and mechanistic basis for repurposing PMX53 for dry AMD is compelling—given its ability to disrupt complement-mediated inflammatory cascades and its pseudo-irreversible receptor binding—the translation of these benefits to the ocular milieu remains to be established. A focused research program is needed to conduct in vitro studies in primary human RPE cells exposed to complement activation, followed by in vivo evaluations in non-murine models that more closely mirror human C5aR pharmacology. Further development of ocular delivery systems, including intravitreal implants or nanoparticle-based formulations, will also be essential to overcome the inherent pharmacokinetic challenges posed by a peptide therapeutic.

If these hurdles can be successfully addressed, PMX53 could represent an innovative approach to slow or prevent RPE degeneration by attenuating the complement-driven amplification of mtROS production and inflammasome activation—a cascade that is a key driver of dry AMD pathology. In light of the significant unmet need for effective treatments for dry AMD and the robust preclinical data supporting the anti-inflammatory efficacy of cyclic C5aR antagonists in other contexts, further investigation into PMX53 is both scientifically justified and therapeutically promising (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a; Brandstetter et al., 2015; Ong et al., 2024).

This comprehensive review indicates that while substantial promise exists for PMX53 as a candidate to mitigate the complement-mediated mechanisms underlying dry AMD, its successful repurposing will depend on dedicated ocular pharmacology studies, careful species selection for preclinical investigations, and the development of targeted drug-delivery strategies tailored to the unique anatomical and immunological environment of the eye (Proctor et al., 2006a; Ong et al., 2024; Proctor et al., 2006b).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GC4419 (avasopasem manganese) is a small‐molecule, manganese‐containing superoxide dismutase (SOD) mimetic that was developed by Galera Therapeutics. Its design is based on replicating the catalytic activity of the endogenous mitochondrial enzyme, manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), which naturally detoxifies superoxide radicals by converting them to hydrogen peroxide and oxygen. The compound is formulated as a manganese‐containing macrocyclic ligand complex with a molecular weight of approximately 483, prepared in an aqueous sodium bicarbonate solution (Mapuskar et al., 2024). Originally developed as the enantiomer of M40403, GC4419 belongs to the MnPAM class of SOD mimetics—a subclass of therapeutic agents that have been engineered to overcome the limitations of exogenous SOD proteins, such as immunogenicity and poor pharmacokinetics (Sonis, 2021; Galera Therapeutics, Inc., 2013). SOD mimetics, by virtue of their small molecular weight and catalytic efficiency, have been widely explored clinically as radioprotective agents to mitigate oxidative tissue damage, and they offer an attractive platform for tackling diseases in which oxidative stress is a central pathophysiological driver.

Therapeutic History:  
GC4419 has a well‐documented history in preclinical and clinical settings aimed at ameliorating oxidative tissue injury. Preclinical studies have shown that GC4419 protects against cisplatin‐induced kidney injury in both acute (AKI) and chronic (CKD) murine models by scavenging superoxide radicals and attenuating inflammatory responses (Mapuskar et al., 2024). In the clinical arena, GC4419 has been evaluated in several trials—most notably in Phase 1b/2a and Phase 3 studies—targeting radiation‐induced mucositis in head and neck cancer patients. These trials demonstrated that intravenous infusion of GC4419 not only reduced the incidence and severity of severe oral mucositis but also reduced other therapy‐associated adverse events, such as cisplatin‐induced nephrotoxicity, in a dose‐dependent manner (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Sonis, 2021). Despite this extensive history of use in mitigating radiation‐ and cisplatin‐linked toxicities, there have been no direct reports or preclinical studies that have investigated GC4419 in the context of retinal disorders or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Houldsworth, 2024). This lack of prior application in ocular models underscores the novelty of the repurposing hypothesis—to deploy the compound’s antioxidative properties in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells under chronic oxidative stress conditions such as those elicited by drusen accumulation.

Mechanism of Action:  
GC4419 functions by mimicking the natural enzymatic activity of MnSOD, specifically catalyzing the dismutation reaction of superoxide (O2•–) into hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and molecular oxygen (Mapuskar et al., 2024). Its reported catalytic rate constant of approximately 1×10^7 per mol per second, while lower than that of native mitochondrial SOD (~1.2×10^9 per mol per second), is nonetheless sufficient to achieve a measurable reduction in superoxide levels in stressed tissues (Mapuskar et al., 2024). This selective removal of superoxide is particularly advantageous because GC4419 does not appreciably interact with other reactive oxygen species such as nitric oxide, peroxynitrite, or hydrogen peroxide, thus ensuring a focused mechanism of action (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Galera Therapeutics, Inc., 2013). In preclinical kidney models, treatment with GC4419 has been associated with the restoration of mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) activities, reduced expression of pro-oxidant enzymes like NADPH oxidase 4 (NOX4), and a decrease in markers of inflammation (Mapuskar et al., 2024). Although the detailed chemical structure (e.g., the precise coordination geometry of the manganese ion or whether it resembles a classical Mn-salen derivative) has not been fully disclosed, the compound is understood to be a highly stable, low-molecular-weight agent optimized for biological compatibility and effective redox cycling (Sonis, 2021; Mapuskar et al., 2024). Given its intended mechanism as a mitochondrial SOD mimetic, it is hypothesized that GC4419 can enter cells, localize to mitochondria, and thereby directly attenuate mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production—a rationale that is central to its anticipated repurposing for dry AMD.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
In dry age-related macular degeneration, the retinal pigment epithelium is subject to chronic oxidative stress resulting from cumulative damage due to drusen deposits and impaired cellular clearance mechanisms. RPE cells are rich in mitochondria and depend heavily on efficient oxidative metabolism; however, over time, excessive production of ROS—particularly superoxide generated by dysfunctional mitochondrial electron transport—can lead to cell death and, consequently, to the progression of dry AMD. The underlying hypothesis for repurposing GC4419 in this context is that, by acting as a mitochondrial SOD mimetic, the compound will convert excess superoxide generated within RPE cells into hydrogen peroxide, which can then be further detoxified by endogenous catalase and glutathione peroxidase systems (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Houldsworth, 2024). This conversion is expected to not only alleviate the oxidative burden but also to preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψ_m) and maintain efficient ATP synthesis, which is critical for the survival and function of RPE cells (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Montoro et al., 2023). Furthermore, by reducing superoxide levels, GC4419 may indirectly dampen inflammation mediated by redox-sensitive transcription factors (such as NF-κB), thereby decreasing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines that can exacerbate RPE stress and degeneration (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Houldsworth, 2024). Although direct evidence of GC4419’s efficacy in retinal models has not yet been reported, the known expression of the MnSOD gene (SOD2) in RPE cells and the central role of mitochondrial oxidative damage in dry AMD provide a strong mechanistic rationale for the compound’s potential effectiveness when applied to ocular tissues (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Houldsworth, 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
GC4419 presents several compelling strengths as a candidate for repurposing in the management of dry AMD. Its well-characterized mechanism of action, which involves the selective catalytic removal of superoxide, addresses a key pathogenic factor in dry AMD—oxidative stress within the RPE and its mitochondria (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Sonis, 2021). The compound’s demonstrated ability to restore mitochondrial function and reduce inflammation in preclinical models of cisplatin-induced kidney injury and radiation-induced mucosal damage underscores its potential utility in any tissue where oxidative stress is a driving factor (Mapuskar et al., 2024). Moreover, the pharmacological profile of GC4419—highlighted by its favorable molecular weight, catalytic properties, and prior progression into clinical trials for other indications—supports its viability as a repurposed drug candidate. By leveraging existing clinical data on safety and efficacy in non-ocular settings, the repurposing effort for dry AMD could benefit from relatively expedited translational development.

Nevertheless, there are also notable weaknesses and uncertainties. First, despite the strong theoretical rationale, no direct preclinical or clinical studies have yet evaluated GC4419 in retinal tissues or in animal models of dry AMD; therefore, its ocular pharmacokinetics, penetrance of the blood–retina barrier, and potential for mitochondrial uptake specifically in RPE cells remain unproven (Houldsworth, 2024). Second, the current formulations of GC4419 are designed for intravenous administration as used in radiation mucositis trials; adapting these formulations for local ocular delivery (e.g., via intravitreal injection or targeted sustained-release systems) may present challenges that need to be carefully addressed. Third, while the mechanism of converting superoxide to hydrogen peroxide is beneficial, it is crucial to ensure that the resultant H2O2 is efficiently cleared by endogenous antioxidant defenses in the RPE; accumulation of H2O2 could itself precipitate oxidative damage if the cellular detoxification capacity is overwhelmed (Mapuskar et al., 2024). Moreover, although GC4419 has been referred to in some contexts as part of the “Mn-salen” or MnPAM families of dismutase mimetics, the precise structural classification has not been fully disclosed, which may affect its predicted bio-distribution and interaction with specific intracellular targets (Sonis, 2021; Galera Therapeutics, Inc., 2013). Lastly, differences in the pathological microenvironments between tissues treated for radiation toxicity versus the RPE in dry AMD could influence the overall efficacy of GC4419; thus, careful preclinical studies in ocular disease models will be necessary to confirm that its antioxidative and anti-inflammatory actions translate effectively to an AMD setting (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Sonis, 2021).

In summary, GC4419 (avasopasem manganese) is a well-characterized SOD mimetic that has demonstrated promising protective effects against oxidative stress in non-ocular models, providing a strong biochemical rationale for its potential repurposing as a therapeutic candidate in dry age-related macular degeneration. Its mechanism of selectively dismutating superoxide to hydrogen peroxide could help restore redox balance, preserve mitochondrial integrity, and mitigate inflammatory cascades in the retinal pigment epithelium—a key contributor to dry AMD pathology (Mapuskar et al., 2024). However, the absence of direct evidence in retinal or ocular models and the challenges associated with reformulating a systemically administered drug for local ocular delivery constitute significant hurdles that must be overcome through targeted preclinical research. Overall, while the strengths of GC4419 are notable—with a robust mechanism, supportive preclinical and clinical history in other indications, and a focused approach to counteracting mitochondrial oxidative stress—the weaknesses highlight the need for further investigation into its ocular pharmacodynamics, formulation for targeted delivery, and comprehensive evaluation in dry AMD-specific models before advancing to clinical trials in this indication (Mapuskar et al., 2024; Sonis, 2021; Galera Therapeutics, Inc., 2013).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
MCC950 is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor that belongs to the diarylsulfonylurea class of compounds originally identified through screening efforts aimed at inhibiting IL-1β processing. Its chemical origins trace back to early studies (circa 2001) that recognized diarylsulfonylurea molecules as cytokine-release inhibitory drugs (CRIDs) before the advent of specific inflammasome inhibitors (Coll et al., 2015). Subsequent medicinal chemistry efforts led to the selection, optimization, and detailed characterization of one member of this series that came to be known as MCC950. Synthetically, MCC950 is produced through a multistep sequence that includes key transformations such as Friedel–Crafts acylation of an indene derivative, acid-promoted cyclization, direct nitration, and subsequent conversion into its final diarylsulfonylurea form, as detailed in the original publication’s Online Methods and Supplementary Materials (Coll et al., 2015; Keuler et al., 2022). Developed initially as an inhibitor of IL-1β post-translational processing, MCC950 was repurposed as a potent and highly selective inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome, exhibiting nanomolar potency (approximately 7.5 nM in murine bone marrow–derived macrophages) with a favorable selectivity profile over other inflammasomes such as AIM2, NLRC4, or NLRP1 (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021; Hill et al., 2017). Marketed under various identifiers – one of which is the Selleckchem product code S8643 – MCC950 represents a well-characterized chemical tool that has continued to serve as both a probe for studying NLRP3 biology and a preclinical candidate in inflammatory disease models (Das et al., 2021; Sharma et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
MCC950 has been extensively evaluated in preclinical studies targeting inflammatory diseases driven by aberrant NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Its discovery followed earlier observations that sulfonylurea agents such as glyburide, traditionally used in type 2 diabetes for their insulin-secretagogue activity via KATP channel inhibition, also inhibited NLRP3-driven processes albeit at micromolar concentrations (Chauhan et al., 2020; Coll et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2017). In contrast, MCC950 exhibits a markedly improved potency at nanomolar levels and a higher degree of specificity. Preclinical evaluations demonstrated that MCC950 effectively blocks both the canonical and noncanonical activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, resulting in suppressed activation of caspase-1 and reduced IL-1β secretion (Das et al., 2021; Hill et al., 2020). Its efficacy has been validated in a wide range of inflammatory disease models including cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS), multiple sclerosis models such as experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), pulmonary and cutaneous inflammation, Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, and even models of kidney and liver fibrosis (Das et al., 2021; Narros-Fernández et al., 2022; Sharma et al., 2023). Although MCC950 has not yet been formally used in clinical applications—and indeed its clinical development was reportedly halted due to safety concerns such as elevated transaminases and organ structural damage in preclinical toxicity studies (Johansson et al., 2025)—its robust preclinical record has established it as the prototype NLRP3 inhibitor. There is emerging interest in exploiting its mechanism for diseases wherein inflammasome-driven pathology is central. While direct data on the use of MCC950 for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) are not available in the literature, the growing evidence implicating the NLRP3 inflammasome in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction suggests that repurposing MCC950 for dry AMD is a scientifically plausible strategy (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021; Keuler et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of MCC950 is one of its most compelling features. At the molecular level, MCC950 selectively inhibits the NLRP3 inflammasome by directly binding to the NACHT domain, specifically targeting the Walker B motif that is essential for ATP hydrolysis and subsequent conformational changes required for inflammasome assembly (Hill et al., 2020; Sharma et al., 2023). In doing so, MCC950 prevents the oligomerization of NLRP3 and the recruitment of the adaptor protein ASC, thereby abrogating the activation of caspase-1 and the maturation and release of proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18 (Coll et al., 2015; Keuler et al., 2022). Structural analyses, including photoaffinity labeling and surface plasmon resonance (SPR) studies, have confirmed the high affinity binding (with SPR-derived K_D values in the low nanomolar range) of MCC950 to its target within NLRP3 (Coll et al., 2019; Hill et al., 2017). Importantly, MCC950 does not interfere with upstream ionic events, such as K^+ efflux or Ca^2+ signaling, which are also involved in NLRP3 activation pathways; rather, its action is confined to the blockade of ATP hydrolysis, offering a direct means to “lock” NLRP3 in an inactive, closed conformation (Das et al., 2021; Keuler et al., 2022; Li, 2020). This precise targeting underpins its exceptional potency and selectivity among inflammasome inhibitors. Moreover, a body of literature has explored the structure–activity relationships (SAR) surrounding the diarylsulfonylurea scaffold of MCC950, confirming that modifications to key structural motifs (for instance, the s-hexahydroindacene group) can have significant impacts on both inhibitory potency and chemical stability; these insights have spurred the design of hybrid molecules that further exploit MCC950’s pharmacophore for dual-target activities (Hill et al., 2017).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
The pathophysiology of dry AMD is characterized by the progressive degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), which results from chronic cellular stress—largely driven by mitochondrial dysfunction and elevated reactive oxygen species (ROS) production—that culminates in an inflammatory cascade. A growing body of evidence implicates the NLRP3 inflammasome as a critical mediator in this process; in the RPE, mitochondrial ROS can instigate NLRP3 activation, leading to the cleavage of caspase-1 and the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, which in turn exacerbate RPE atrophy and compromise the integrity of the retinal barrier (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021). The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of MCC950 for dry AMD is that by selectively inhibiting NLRP3 activation, MCC950 would interrupt this pathogenic cycle. Specifically, its potent inhibition of ATP hydrolysis within the NACHT domain would prevent the inflammasome assembly even in the presence of mitochondrial ROS, thereby blocking caspase-1 activation and subsequent IL-1β secretion. In preclinical models where MCC950 has been tested—such as sodium-iodate-induced damage and laser-induced injury—this compound has been shown to suppress NLRP3-dependent cytokine secretion and preserve barrier function (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021; Narros-Fernández et al., 2022).
