Below is our comprehensive evaluation of pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD):

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate –  
Pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) is an aromatic o‐quinone originally discovered as a redox cofactor for bacterial dehydrogenases and is naturally synthesized by various Gram‐negative prokaryotes. It was first identified in microbial systems where it serves as a prosthetic group in enzymes involved in alcohol and sugar oxidation, and it has since been detected at trace levels in human tissues and milk, suggesting dietary exposure through common foods such as fermented soy products, green peppers, spinach, and human milk. PQQ is categorized within the quinone family of compounds and is recognized for its redox‐active properties; in this role, it has been considered a “vitamin‐like accessory factor” by some researchers given its involvement in cellular energy metabolism and antioxidant defense (Petricca et al., 2025; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Commercially, PQQ is available in a water‐soluble disodium salt formulation; for example, the Sigma‐Aldrich PQQ product is typical of these preparations. As a small redox‐active molecule, PQQ is distinct among nutraceuticals and has been explored in several preclinical contexts for its potential to regulate oxidative stress and promote mitochondrial function (Canovai & Williams, 2025). Consequently, this candidate represents a repurposing opportunity where its established dietary exposure, safety profile as assessed by regulatory bodies such as EFSA, and its unique bioactivity as a mitochondrial modulator may be leveraged to address the mitochondrial dysfunction implicated in dry AMD.

Therapeutic History –  
PQQ has been the subject of intensive biochemical and preclinical investigation over the past decades. Early studies concentrated on its role as a microbial cofactor, but subsequent research has documented that dietary supplementation with PQQ produces measurable effects on mitochondrial‐related metabolism and markers of inflammation in animal models and humans (Canovai & Williams, 2025). In various rodent models, oral PQQ has been shown to modulate mitochondrial number and function, thereby improving outcomes in contexts as diverse as cardiac ischemia/reperfusion, neurodegeneration, and metabolic syndrome (Akagawa, Nakano, & Ikemoto, 2016; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Additionally, EFSA conducted a safety assessment of the PQQ disodium salt formulation as a novel food ingredient and concluded that at proposed supplemental doses (up to 20 mg/day) the width of the safety margin is acceptable relative to animal toxicology data (Turck et al., 2017; Hwang & Willoughby, 2018). In human studies, although clinical trials have largely focused on endpoints such as cognition, inflammatory markers, and lipid metabolism, these trials demonstrate that oral PQQ is bioavailable, well‐tolerated, and can meaningfully impact systemic markers of oxidative stress and energy metabolism (Canovai & Williams, 2025). While no study to date has directly employed PQQ in patients with dry AMD, there is indirect evidence suggesting that PQQ’s capacity to improve cellular bioenergetics may be broadly beneficial in clinical states characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction. Some studies even indicate that PQQ upregulates mitochondrial proteins and improves ATP synthesis in cellular models derived from age‐related macular degeneration donor tissues (Canovai & Williams, 2025), although direct evidence in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) remains sparse. In summary, the therapeutic history of PQQ includes diverse preclinical applications ranging from cardioprotection to neuroprotection, with established safety in both animal and limited human studies, making it a plausible candidate for repurposing in dry AMD where mitochondrial dysfunction is a key pathogenic driver.

Mechanism of Action –  
The molecular basis of PQQ’s bioactivity is multifaceted, centering on its redox chemistry and its ability to modulate mitochondrial biogenesis. Chemically, PQQ is a potent redox‐active o‐quinone that undergoes reversible reduction to its hydroquinone form (PQQH₂) via a rapid semiquinone intermediate. This redox cycling allows PQQ to function both as a free radical scavenger and as an electron‐transfer catalyst. In vitro assays have established that the reduced form, PQQH₂, exhibits robust antioxidant capacity, with reports indicating that its aroxyl radical quenching activity can be significantly greater than that of classical antioxidants such as vitamin C and α‐tocopherol (Canovai & Williams, 2025; Charrier et al., 2024). Through its antioxidant activity, PQQ directly neutralizes reactive oxygen species (ROS) and may protect cellular constituents from oxidative damage.

Beyond its direct radical scavenging, PQQ has been implicated as an inducer of mitochondrial biogenesis. Several mechanistic studies indicate that treatment with PQQ leads to the upregulation of key transcriptional regulators involved in mitochondrial proliferation. Specifically, PQQ treatment has been shown to activate the cAMP response element‐binding protein (CREB), which in turn stimulates the expression of peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator‐1 alpha (PGC‐1α) (Charrier et al., 2024; Canovai & Williams, 2025). PGC‐1α is a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and coordinates the transcriptional activation of nuclear respiratory factors (NRF‐1/NRF‐2) and mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM), all of which are critical for the transcription and replication of mitochondrial DNA. Some studies also suggest that PQQ modulates sirtuin activity, particularly SIRT1 and SIRT3, which are NAD⁺‐dependent deacetylases that regulate mitochondrial function and cellular metabolic homeostasis (Canovai & Williams, 2025). In addition, PQQ has been reported to restore mitochondrial membrane potential, reduce proton leak, and enhance ATP production during oxidative challenge in several cellular systems (Petricca et al., 2025; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Thus, the composite mechanism of action posited for PQQ—which includes both robust redox buffering and the activation of mitochondrial biogenesis via CREB/PGC‐1α signaling—provides a molecular rationale for its use in conditions characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative injury.

Mechanistically, it is also suggested that PQQ may improve the NAD⁺/NADH ratio, thereby favoring the activity of sirtuins, which contributes to a more favorable intracellular redox state and efficient energy utilization (Jonscher, Chowanadisai, & Rucker, 2021). Although these effects have been most clearly demonstrated in hepatic, muscular, and neuronal cell models, they are directly relevant to RPE cells that rely heavily on oxidative phosphorylation for their energy demands and, hence, are particularly vulnerable to mitochondrial decay under chronic oxidative stress—a hallmark of dry AMD pathology. It is important to note that PQQ’s actions are context‐dependent; while low concentrations have been associated with protective effects, some studies suggest that higher doses can induce a pro‐oxidant effect and even impair mitochondrial dynamics in sensitive cellular contexts (Petricca et al., 2025; Turck et al., 2017). This biphasic dose response underscores the need to identify an optimal dosing window that maximizes mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defense without tipping cells into oxidative stress.

Expected Effect –  
The central hypothesis guiding the repurposing of PQQ for dry AMD is that it can stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis in the RPE by upregulating PGC‐1α, thereby increasing the antioxidant capacity and restoring optimal mitochondrial respiration in cells under chronic oxidative injury. In the proposed assay, treatment with PQQ is expected to yield multiple beneficial outcomes. First, by activating CREB and augmenting PGC‐1α expression, PQQ should enhance the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial replication and function, leading to an increased mitochondrial mass within RPE cells (Canovai & Williams, 2025; Charrier et al., 2024).

Second, increased mitochondrial mass and improved electron transport chain efficiency are expected to elevate ATP production, thereby restoring cellular energy stores that are typically depleted in dry AMD due to chronic oxidative damage. Experimental data from other cell types, including neuronal and hepatic cells, have shown that PQQ treatment enhances ATP output and normalizes mitochondrial membrane potential under oxidative stress conditions, suggesting that similar responses might be observed in RPE cells (Petricca et al., 2025; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Third, PQQ is anticipated to upregulate antioxidant enzymes, such as manganese superoxide dismutase (SOD2), which plays a critical role in mitigating ROS accumulation in mitochondria. By lowering oxidative stress levels in RPE cells, PQQ can help maintain cellular homeostasis and prevent the degeneration that is characteristic of dry AMD (Canovai & Williams, 2025).

Additionally, there is emerging evidence that certain studies using donor‐derived RPE cells from AMD patients have demonstrated that PQQ treatment can upregulate mitochondrial proteins and improve ATP generation in these cells (Canovai & Williams, 2025). Although the available data in retinal tissues remain limited, these findings align with the overall rationale; because RPE cells are highly metabolically active and heavily reliant on mitochondrial function, the ability to augment their biogenesis and enhance oxidative phosphorylation directly addresses a critical pathogenic mechanism of dry AMD. Complementing these expected biochemical outcomes, one would predict that functional assays (for instance, assessments of oxygen consumption rate and extracellular acidification rate) will reveal improved mitochondrial respiration and overall metabolic resilience in PQQ‐treated RPE cells.

Overall Evaluation –  
In synthesizing the extensive body of literature, we find that PQQ demonstrates considerable promise as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, based on the following strengths and weaknesses:

Strengths:  
1. Robust Mechanistic Rationale: PQQ’s dual role as an antioxidant and an inducer of mitochondrial biogenesis is well documented. The capacity to elevate PGC‐1α expression and thereby drive mitochondrial proliferation and enhanced energy metabolism is highly relevant given that dry AMD is characterized by RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and heightened oxidative stress (Petricca et al., 2025; Charrier et al., 2024; Canovai & Williams, 2025).  
2. Positive Safety and Bioavailability Data: Numerous preclinical studies, alongside regulatory evaluations (e.g., EFSA’s novel food assessment), indicate that PQQ is orally bioavailable and well tolerated in both animal models and limited human studies. The available toxicology data support the safety of typical supplemental doses (up to 20 mg/day), which is encouraging for repurposing efforts (Turck et al., 2017; Hwang & Willoughby, 2018; Canovai & Williams, 2025).  
3. Broad Therapeutic History: Although PQQ has not been directly tested in dry AMD in clinical settings, its prior use as a dietary supplement and its beneficial effects in neuroprotection, cardioprotection, and metabolic regulation suggest therapeutic potential in conditions underpinned by mitochondrial decay and oxidative stress (Canovai & Williams, 2025).  
4. Hypothesis‐Driven Approach: The specific hypothesis—that PQQ will stimulate RPE mitochondrial biogenesis via upregulation of PGC‐1α to improve cellular resilience against chronic oxidative injury—is both plausible and supported by mechanistic data from other cell types. Given that RPE cells are known to express PGC‐1α and that deficits in mitochondrial function have been implicated in AMD pathology, this provides a strong rationale for further investigation (Canovai & Williams, 2025).

Weaknesses:  
1. Limited Direct Evidence in Ocular Tissues: One of the main gaps in the literature is the paucity of direct preclinical studies involving retinal pigment epithelium or in vivo AMD models. Although there is some suggestive data from studies in retinal ganglion cells and donor‐derived RPE cells, definitive evidence that PQQ can counteract the specific aspects of dry AMD pathology in the retina is currently lacking (Ebeling et al., 2020; Petricca et al., 2025).  
2. Context‐Dependent and Biphasic Effects: Several studies indicate that PQQ’s efficacy is highly dose‐dependent. While low concentrations are cytoprotective by enhancing mitochondrial function, higher doses may exert pro‐oxidant effects and even impair mitochondrial membrane potential in sensitive cell types. Establishing the optimal dosing regimen for RPE cells will be critical to avoid potential deleterious effects (Petricca et al., 2025; Turck et al., 2017).  
3. Ocular Pharmacokinetics Uncertain: Although oral absorption in the gastrointestinal tract has been characterized in animal studies with favorable kinetics, it remains unclear whether orally administered PQQ achieves sufficient concentrations—or even penetrates ocular tissues such as the retina—to exert the desired effects. This issue of tissue‐specific bioavailability is a significant barrier that must be addressed in future pharmacokinetic studies (Hwang & Willoughby, 2018).  
4. Quality of Some Supporting Studies: While a substantial body of research supports PQQ’s bioactivity, some of the literature originates from journals or sources with variable quality. This underscores the need for additional high‐quality, rigorously controlled studies—particularly focused on ocular models—to validate the proposed mechanisms and therapeutic outcomes for dry AMD (Akagawa, Nakano, & Ikemoto, 2016; Hwang & Willoughby, 2018).

In conclusion, based on the available biomedical, clinical, and biochemical literature, PQQ emerges as a promising repurposed candidate for dry AMD. Its well‐documented ability to modulate mitochondrial biogenesis—principally through the activation of CREB and upregulation of PGC‐1α—aligns with the mechanistic requirements for restoring mitochondrial function in RPE cells under chronic oxidative stress, a central feature of dry AMD pathogenesis (Petricca et al., 2025; Charrier et al., 2024; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Moreover, the favorable safety profile indicated by both animal toxicology studies and human supplementation trials, combined with its oral bioavailability, adds significant translational appeal.

However, critical gaps remain. Principal among these is the need for direct evidence from retinal models. Specifically, robust, controlled preclinical studies in RPE cells and animal models of dry AMD must be performed to confirm that PQQ can effectively upregulate mitochondrial biogenesis and confer cytoprotection in ocular tissues. Additionally, further investigation into the optimal dosing strategy is required, particularly given the context‐dependent and potentially biphasic nature of PQQ’s activity, as well as the necessity to ascertain whether oral administration can yield therapeutic concentrations in the retina.

Given these considerations, the recommendation is to advance PQQ as a candidate for further investigation in dry AMD. This progression should involve a series of well‐designed in vitro and in vivo experiments targeting RPE‐specific pathways, coupled with ocular pharmacokinetic studies to evaluate tissue penetration and residence times. Should these studies provide supportive evidence, early‐phase human clinical trials focusing on retinal biomarkers and functional outcomes in dry AMD patients would be warranted.

Overall, while the current literature provides a strong mechanistic rationale and preliminary safety data supporting the repurposing of PQQ for dry AMD, it also highlights the need for targeted ocular studies to bridge the gap between systemic mitochondrial enhancements and specific retinal therapeutic benefits. With these additional investigations, PQQ could potentially emerge as a viable therapeutic option in the armamentarium against dry AMD, addressing the unmet need for treatments that restore RPE mitochondrial resilience and retard degeneration (Canovai & Williams, 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Sulforaphane is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate originally identified in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli and Brussels sprouts. It is generated through the hydrolysis of glucoraphanin by the enzyme myrosinase, which is released upon plant tissue damage. As a member of the phytochemical family, sulforaphane belongs to a class of natural compounds known for inducing phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins. Historically, this compound has been extensively investigated for its chemopreventive and cytoprotective properties, particularly through the activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. Being one of the most studied Nrf2 activators, its discovery stemmed from early investigations into dietary antioxidants and their role in reducing carcinogenesis and inflammation. In the context of drug development, sulforaphane is considered a promising candidate for repurposing because it combines a favorable preclinical safety profile with a well-characterized mechanism of action that includes modulation of intracellular redox signaling. Its broad application in preclinical studies to ameliorate oxidative stress and inflammation suggests that targeted delivery to retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells might help alleviate the oxidative injury observed in geographic atrophy, the advanced form of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Bellezza, 2018; Chang et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Sulforaphane has attracted considerable attention for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties over the past two decades. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its protective effects in various models of oxidative stress, including those involving retinal tissues and RPE cells. In in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells—a well-accepted human RPE model—sulforaphane exhibited dose-dependent protection against oxidative insults induced by agents such as tert-butyl hydroperoxide (t-BOOH) and hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂). These experiments demonstrated that sulforaphane pretreatment significantly reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and mitigated mitochondrial membrane potential damage, ultimately leading to reduced apoptotic cell death (Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021). Similarly, other investigations have reported sulforaphane’s ability to induce cytoprotective genes in RPE cells through Nrf2 activation, resulting in improved cell survival under stress conditions (Zhang et al., 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Moreover, several in vivo studies in rodent models have provided evidence of sulforaphane-mediated retinal neuroprotection. Examples include models of photooxidative damage in mice, where sulforaphane delayed photoreceptor degeneration and prevented RPE dysfunction—mechanisms that are highly relevant to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Bellezza, 2018). However, it should be noted that although sulforaphane has been studied in various retinal degeneration models, there is no established clinical history of its use in human dry AMD. Nevertheless, its promising preclinical efficacy in ameliorating oxidative injury in RPE cells, coupled with its demonstrated safety across multiple biological systems including ocular tissues, supports its potential repurposing as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Qin, 2007; del Cano et al., 2008).

Mechanism of Action:  
The principal mechanism underlying sulforaphane’s protective effects is its ability to activate the Nrf2 pathway. Under basal conditions, the transcription factor Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytosol via binding to its inhibitor, Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1), which directs Nrf2 for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Sulforaphane, owing to its electrophilic isothiocyanate moiety, reacts with critical cysteine residues on Keap1. This modification alters the conformation of Keap1 and prevents the degradation of Nrf2, leading to its stabilization and subsequent nuclear translocation (Wherry, 2013). Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to antioxidant response elements (ARE) in the promoter regions of various cytoprotective genes. The result is a robust induction of phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), and superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2). These enzymes play critical roles in neutralizing ROS, repairing oxidative damage, and maintaining cellular redox balance (Qin, 2007; Zhang et al., 2024).

In addition to its classic Nrf2-dependent antioxidant response, sulforaphane has been shown to modulate other cellular pathways that are important for mitochondrial health. In retinal cells, sulforaphane has been reported to attenuate mitochondrial membrane potential collapse and reduce mitochondrial superoxide production, as evidenced by decreased MitoSOX fluorescence in treated ARPE-19 cells (Chang et al., 2020). These mitochondrial protective actions are thought to involve the upregulation of antioxidant enzymes that localize to the mitochondria, as well as enhancement of the spare respiratory capacity—thereby preserving ATP generation under oxidative stress conditions. Furthermore, sulforaphane has been implicated in the regulation of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis, which is critical for mitochondrial biogenesis and metabolic homeostasis. This dual engagement—both through Nrf2-driven transcriptional activation and mitochondrial biogenesis pathways—positions sulforaphane as a multifaceted agent capable of sustaining cellular energy production and reducing oxidative injury in the RPE, a cell type that is particularly vulnerable in geographic atrophy (Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).

Beyond its antioxidant effects, sulforaphane also exerts anti-inflammatory properties by downregulating the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and adhesion molecules (e.g., ICAM-1, MCP-1). This is particularly relevant in the context of AMD, where chronic low-grade inflammation is believed to exacerbate RPE dysfunction and drusen formation (Chang et al., 2020; del Cano et al., 2008). In summary, the molecular interactions of sulforaphane—ranging from direct modification of Keap1 to the induction of mitochondrial antioxidant defenses—provide a robust mechanistic rationale for its potential utility in mitigating the multifactorial oxidative and inflammatory challenges associated with dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Given its well-documented mechanism of action, the hypothesis that sulforaphane induces Nrf2-mediated mitochondrial antioxidant pathways in RPE cells is strongly supported by preclinical evidence. When RPE cells are subjected to oxidative stress, it is expected that sulforaphane treatment will lead to a dose-dependent upregulation of Nrf2 target genes including HO-1, NQO1, and SOD2. The elevation of these transcripts correlates with a reduction in mitochondrial superoxide levels, as measured by decreased MitoSOX fluorescence, and an improvement in the spare respiratory capacity—a surrogate marker for mitochondrial function and ATP generation (Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).

In cellular assays using ARPE-19 cells, administration of sulforaphane prior to oxidative challenge has been shown to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential and decrease cytochrome c release, thereby reducing the activation of downstream apoptotic cascades. The suppression of ROS production and the preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics result in improved cell viability and reduced apoptotic indices. For instance, studies have demonstrated that sulforaphane pretreatment leads to lower levels of cleaved caspase-3 and PARP-1, indicating a direct link between enhanced antioxidant defense and the inhibition of programmed cell death pathways in RPE cells (Yang et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2020).

At the molecular level, the expected outcome of sulforaphane administration in a dry AMD context is multifactorial. The compound would elevate the expression of cytoprotective enzymes that not only detoxify reactive oxygen species but also facilitate the repair of oxidatively damaged macromolecules. This should translate into a measurable decrease in overall oxidative stress markers, preservation of mitochondrial function (evidenced by sustained ATP production and improved spare respiratory capacity), and stabilization of the RPE cell phenotype. Moreover, since mitochondrial dysfunction is a central element of geographic atrophy pathogenesis, sulforaphane’s ability to maintain ATP generation could directly counteract the energy deficit observed in degenerating RPE cells (Zhang et al., 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

These expected effects are supported by a range of preclinical studies. For example, quantitative redox fluorometry results reported in ARPE-19 cells indicate that sulforaphane-treated cells maintain a significantly higher redox ratio during oxidative challenge compared to untreated controls, which is indicative of an enhanced antioxidant state. Additionally, the upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants and improved bioenergetic profiles have been correlated with better cell survival outcomes, reinforcing the concept that sulforaphane can counteract the deleterious cellular changes observed in models of dry AMD (del Cano et al., 2008; Qin, 2007).

Overall Evaluation:  
Sulforaphane, as exemplified by the Sigma-Aldrich S4441 formulation, presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD, particularly targeting the geographic atrophy form characterized by pronounced RPE degeneration. One of the major strengths of sulforaphane lies in its robust preclinical evidence demonstrating its ability to induce the Nrf2 pathway, a master regulator of oxidative stress responses. The compound’s direct modification of Keap1 and subsequent stabilization and nuclear translocation of Nrf2 trigger the upregulation of several antioxidant enzymes, such as HO-1, NQO1, and SOD2—which are critical for detoxifying reactive oxygen species and repairing oxidative damage in RPE cells (Qin, 2007; Zhang et al., 2024).

Furthermore, sulforaphane’s additional capacity to preserve mitochondrial function by maintaining membrane potential and supporting ATP synthesis addresses a major pathological hallmark of geographic atrophy, where mitochondrial dysfunction leads to energy depletion and accelerates cell death. The integration of mitochondrial antioxidant defenses with the broader cytoprotective effects of Nrf2 activation provides a convergent mechanism aimed at both preventing oxidative damage and sustaining cellular energy production under stress conditions (Yang et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2020).

Another notable strength is the extensive safety data available for sulforaphane from preclinical studies. Its natural occurrence, combined with its well-documented bioactivity in a range of cell types, underscores its potential for repurposing in ocular applications. Moreover, sulforaphane’s ability to attenuate inflammatory responses by reducing the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines adds an extra layer of therapeutic benefit, considering the role of chronic inflammation in exacerbating AMD pathology (del Cano et al., 2008; Chang et al., 2020).

Despite these promising attributes, several challenges remain. One potential limitation is the bioavailability of sulforaphane. Like many natural compounds, sulforaphane may face pharmacokinetic hurdles such as poor water solubility and limited tissue penetration, which could complicate systemic delivery or localized administration to the retina. Furthermore, while the preclinical efficacy in ARPE-19 cell models and animal studies is encouraging, the translation of these findings to human patients with dry AMD remains to be validated. Variability in the cellular responses between in vitro models and the complex microenvironment of the human retina, including the influence of the blood–retinal barrier, poses a potential risk for suboptimal therapeutic delivery (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Qin, 2007).

Additionally, some of the supportive data for sulforaphane’s efficacy in ocular systems come from studies published in journals with variable impact, and additional high-quality clinical studies will be necessary to establish its safety and efficacy profile in the context of dry AMD. The dosing regimens, potential off-target effects, and long-term impact of chronic Nrf2 activation in retinal tissues also require careful investigation. There is ongoing debate over the potential for Nrf2 activators to have biphasic dose responses, where excessive activation might inadvertently cause cellular stress or dysregulate normal redox homeostasis (Bellezza, 2018; del Cano et al., 2008).

In conclusion, sulforaphane demonstrates strong mechanistic potential for the treatment of dry AMD by elevating key antioxidant defenses in RPE cells and preserving mitochondrial function under oxidative stress. Its ability to induce HO-1, NQO1, and SOD2 in response to oxidative challenges and thereby reduce superoxide production while maintaining ATP synthesis is directly aligned with the therapeutic needs of geographic atrophy patients. The preclinical evidence suggests that, with appropriate formulation and delivery strategies, sulforaphane could provide a dual benefit by mitigating oxidative injury and reducing inflammation in the retina. However, further studies are required to address bioavailability challenges and to validate its clinical efficacy in well-designed human trials. Overall, sulforaphane merits further investigation as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, and its advancement into early-phase clinical testing is justified by the compelling preclinical data available (Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; del Cano et al., 2008).

1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Urolithin A (UA) is a naturally occurring polyphenolic metabolite that is generated in humans via the microbial transformation of dietary ellagitannins, which are abundant in pomegranates, berries, walnuts, and other fruits and nuts. UA belongs to the class of gut-derived α-benzocoumarin compounds and is produced through the specific metabolic activities of intestinal bacteria on ellagitannins and ellagic acid. The discovery of UA emerged from studies aimed at understanding the beneficial effects of diets rich in polyphenols on aging and cellular health, and its structure was elucidated as a 6H-dibenzopyran-6-one derivative. In general, compounds of this class are known for their anti-oxidative, anti-inflammatory, and pro-mitophagic properties. Over time, UA has been investigated increasingly for its ability to modulate mitochondrial function and cellular homeostasis, garnering interest in its potential applications beyond traditional nutritional supplementation. Its multifaceted biological activities have been documented in several preclinical studies where it enhanced mitochondrial quality control, improved muscle endurance in aging populations, and mitigated neurodegenerative processes by clearing dysfunctional mitochondria, lending support to its candidacy as a repurposed drug for chronic conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Makarov & Korkotian, 2023).  

Historically, naturally derived compounds with similar mechanisms of action have been used to address age-related cellular dysfunction. UA, however, stands out by virtue of its dual ability to invoke both mitophagy and lysophagy, which are critical for the removal of damaged organelles—key processes implicated in aging and neurodegeneration. This compound is not synthesized chemically in the traditional pharmaceutical sense; rather, its production relies on the interplay between dietary intake and the gut microbiota, reinforcing the concept that natural metabolic products can be harnessed as therapeutic agents. Its inclusion in the spectrum of therapeutics aimed at cellular rejuvenation has sparked significant interest, particularly because its widespread availability in the human diet and favorable safety profile, as observed in early clinical trials, set a promising foundation for further drug development (Maksimović et al., 2025; Liu, 2022).

2. Therapeutic History  
Urolithin A has been extensively studied in the context of aging and degenerative diseases, and its therapeutic history spans several biomedical, clinical, and biochemical investigations. Preclinical studies have shown that UA is effective in enhancing mitophagy, thereby promoting the clearance of damaged mitochondria. In animal models, UA supplementation has been correlated with improved mitochondrial function and increased muscle endurance, which has led to its exploration as an “anti-aging” agent. Notably, several clinical trials have confirmed its safety in elderly populations, with doses up to 2,500 mg/day being well tolerated and associated with improvements in mitochondrial biomarkers in skeletal muscle (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Liu, 2022).  

In the realm of neurodegeneration, UA has been recognized for its neuroprotective activities. Studies have demonstrated that UA can ameliorate cognitive impairment and reduce inflammatory markers, suggesting benefits in neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Fehér et al., 2022). Importantly, recent investigations have extended the focus to ocular health. Preclinical models of retinal degeneration—particularly those mimicking dry AMD—have emerged as critical systems in which UA’s multifactorial actions are being tested. In models employing sodium iodate (SI) to induce retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) damage, UA treatment resulted in enhanced RPE cell survival, restoration of autophagic flux, and preservation of visual function (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). These studies underscore UA’s potential in mitigating geographic atrophy, a defining feature of dry AMD.  

Beyond its direct mitochondrial effects, UA has been evaluated for its impact on lysosomal function. Some reports indicate that UA exerts potent neuroprotective benefits by promoting SQSTM1/p62-dependent lysophagy, leading to the clearance of damaged lysosomes and restoration of cellular proteostasis. This lysophagy mechanism appears to be crucial in maintaining retinal cellular homeostasis and preventing RPE atrophy, a process that is marked by an accumulation of dysfunctional organelles and consequent oxidative stress in AMD (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). Although direct clinical use of UA in the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular diseases has not yet been fully realized, the wealth of preclinical evidence—particularly from relevant animal models—provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in this context. In summary, UA’s therapeutic history demonstrates its utility across multiple age-related pathologies, with growing evidence supporting its potential application in dry age-related macular degeneration (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

3. Mechanism of Action  
The molecular mechanisms underpinning the actions of Urolithin A are multifaceted and involve intricate interactions across several cellular pathways. Central to UA’s mechanism is its ability to induce selective autophagy, a process that includes both mitophagy and lysophagy, leading to the clearance of damaged mitochondria and lysosomes, respectively. Under normal physiological conditions, mitochondria that lose membrane potential become marked for degradation through the action of PINK1 (PTEN-induced kinase 1), which accumulates on the outer mitochondrial membrane. This accumulation results in the recruitment and activation of Parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase that ubiquitinates mitochondrial surface proteins, thereby flagging them for autophagic degradation. UA has been shown to upregulate the PINK1/Parkin pathway, thereby enhancing the clearance of dysfunctional mitochondria and ensuring mitochondrial quality control (Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024; Jayatunga et al., 2021).  

In addition to its role in mitophagy, UA has been demonstrated to elicit pronounced effects on lysosomal recycling processes through the promotion of SQSTM1/p62-dependent lysophagy. This pathway is critical because damaged lysosomes, if not effectively removed, can contribute to cellular toxicity and inflammation. The engagement of p62 in the targeting of these vesicles for autophagosome formation has been observed as a necessary step in the restoration of autophagic flux within RPE cells (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). At the biochemical level, UA influences several upstream signaling pathways. Notably, it activates the AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)/ULK1 axis—a key regulator of autophagy. Activation of AMPK leads to phosphorylation of ULK1, kick-starting the autophagy process, and is associated with improved energy balance and mitochondrial turnover. This activation is complemented by an upregulation of factors such as PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha), which is instrumental in mitochondrial biogenesis. Together, these events not only promote the removal of impaired mitochondria but also support the generation of new, functional mitochondria, thereby restoring mitochondrial homeostasis (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Furthermore, the anti-inflammatory properties of UA are closely tied to its capacity to modulate oxidative stress. UA’s activation of SIRT1, SIRT3, and AMPK also play a role in upregulating antioxidant defenses; for instance, the enhanced transcription of Nrf2-dependent genes contributes to a robust antioxidative response. These molecular interactions collectively participate in mitigating the inflammatory milieu that is characteristic of neurodegenerative conditions and retinal disorders (Makarov & Korkotian, 2023; Zhang et al., 2025; Jayatunga et al., 2021).

In the context of retinal degeneration, several studies have delineated how UA’s molecular actions translate into cytoprotective outcomes. This dichotomy might reflect the compound’s capability to engage multiple parallel pathways to ensure the efficient clearance of damaged organelles (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Fehér et al., 2022). In summary, the detailed biochemistry of UA illustrates that its mechanism of action involves a well-coordinated activation of autophagic processes through both the PINK1/Parkin axis for mitophagy and the SQSTM1/p62 pathway for lysophagy, with auxiliary support from AMPK/ULK1 and SIRT-mediated signaling. This comprehensive modulation of cellular clearance pathways is critical in contexts where mitochondrial dysfunction and lysosomal impairment drive disease progression, such as in dry age-related macular degeneration (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

In evaluating Urolithin A as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and potential areas for further investigation emerge. First and foremost, UA offers a robust safety profile supported by both preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials in elderly populations, where it has been administered at relatively high doses without observable toxicity or adverse events (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Liu, 2022). This favorable safety and pharmacokinetic profile is critical given the generally conservative approach required when developing treatments for chronic, age-related conditions like AMD.

The molecular versatility of UA is another significant strength. Its capacity to engage multiple autophagic pathways—specifically, the PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy and the SQSTM1/p62-dependent lysophagy—provides a multifaceted approach to mitigating RPE degeneration. Given that the pathogenesis of dry AMD involves a complex interplay of mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and inflammation, the ability of UA to target these processes simultaneously renders it a particularly attractive candidate (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and challenges warrant consideration. One area of potential ambiguity concerns the precise mechanistic contributions of the PINK1/Parkin pathway versus the SQSTM1/p62-mediated lysophagy in mediating UA’s protective effects. While some studies emphasize the role of PINK1/Parkin in clearance of damaged mitochondria, others have reported that UA’s neuroprotective benefits are maintained even with genetic manipulations of these proteins, suggesting that p62-dependent lysophagy may be the predominant mechanism in certain contexts (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Fehér et al., 2022). This duality raises questions regarding which pathway is most critical in RPE cells, particularly given that the proposed hypothesis centers on enhanced PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy. Further mechanistic studies in RPE-specific models will be necessary to delineate the relative contributions of these pathways and to optimize dosing and formulation strategies accordingly.

Another potential weakness is the translational gap between preclinical studies and clinical application in dry AMD. Although UA has shown promise in animal models of retinal degeneration, human disease is complex, and dry AMD is known for its multifactorial etiology. The pharmacokinetic properties of UA, including its relatively short half-life and the challenges associated with ensuring adequate ocular bioavailability, might necessitate novel delivery strategies for effective retinal targeting. Formulation development—potentially involving sustained-release systems or ocular-specific delivery vehicles—may be required to overcome these hurdles (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025). It is also important to contextualize UA’s potential within the current landscape of AMD treatments. While existing therapies for wet AMD (e.g., anti-VEGF agents) have transformed clinical outcomes, there remains no established treatment for dry AMD. The multifaceted mode of action of UA—targeting mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and inflammation—offers a unique therapeutic approach that could complement or, in some cases, provide an alternative to emerging interventions. However, comparative studies against other experimental agents will be critical to fully establish its translational relevance and competitive advantage in the therapeutic space (Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Overall, Urolithin A presents several compelling attributes that support its development as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its origin as a naturally derived, gut-microbiota transformation product provides a favorable starting point from a safety perspective. Preclinical studies consistently demonstrate its ability to enhance autophagic clearance mechanisms, reduce oxidative damage, and improve cell survival in models that recapitulate key features of AMD. The ability of UA to simultaneously stimulate both mitophagy and lysophagy—the former via the PINK1/Parkin pathway and the latter via p62-dependent mechanisms—positions it as a multi-targeted intervention capable of addressing the multifactorial pathology of RPE degeneration (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Nonetheless, for the successful translation of UA into a clinically effective therapy for dry AMD, several challenges need to be addressed. Detailed mechanistic insights specifically in RPE cells are required to understand the relative importance of the PINK1/Parkin versus the lysophagy pathway. Optimizing drug delivery to ensure sustained retinal bioavailability and addressing potential issues related to its pharmacokinetic profile are also key areas that will require further research. Finally, controlled clinical studies in AMD patients will be essential to validate the promising preclinical findings and to ensure that the observed benefits in animal models translate into meaningful clinical outcomes.

In conclusion, based on the comprehensive literature reviewed from biochemical, clinical, and biomedical sources, Urolithin A demonstrates significant potential as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its established ability to enhance mitochondrial quality control through both mitophagy and lysophagy, alongside its additional anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, offers a novel mechanism to counteract the progressive degeneration observed in RPE cells during AMD. Given the encouraging preclinical data and a robust safety profile already evidenced in other indications, further investigations—particularly those focusing on RPE-specific mechanisms and optimized ocular drug delivery—are warranted to fully ascertain UA’s clinical potential in halting or reversing geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024; Jayatunga et al., 2021).

In these studies, administration of SRT1720 resulted in significant improvements in insulin sensitivity, reduction of plasma glucose levels, and enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis across metabolic tissues such as skeletal muscle, liver, and adipose tissues (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Donmez, 2012). Moreover, in genetically obese and high-fat diet animal models, SRT1720 has been demonstrated to improve mitochondrial function, as indicated by increased ATP production, elevated expression of mitochondrial proteins such as ATP synthase β and NDUFB8, and enhanced oxidative metabolism (Funk et al., 2010). This modulatory effect on mitochondrial biogenesis and function is thought to be mediated via the SIRT1-PGC-1α pathway—a mechanism that has garnered attention in age-related diseases where mitochondrial dysfunction is central. The underlying mechanism of action of SRT1720 centers on its ability to allosterically activate SIRT1, a key regulator of cellular energy metabolism and stress responses. SIRT1 is an NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase that modulates the activity of various transcription factors and co-regulators, notably PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ coactivator 1-α), which is a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. SRT1720 binds to an allosteric site on the SIRT1 enzyme-peptide substrate complex, situated amino terminal to the enzyme’s catalytic domain. This binding facilitates a conformational change in SIRT1 that lowers the Michaelis constant (K_m) for the acetylated substrates, thereby enhancing the rate of deacetylation (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Wan, 2021). However, it is important to acknowledge that there has been some controversy regarding whether SRT1720 and its structural relatives directly interact with SIRT1 or exert off-target effects; nonetheless, the preponderance of kinetic and biophysical data supports the view that SRT1720 is primarily a SIRT1 activator (Hoppner et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2024).

Dry AMD is characterized by the degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) accompanied by chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and an overall decline in cellular energy homeostasis. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

SB 290157 is a synthetic small‐molecule compound that functions as an antagonist of the C3a receptor (C3aR). Chemically, it is defined as N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine, a structure that incorporates an arginine residue with an acyl modification incorporating a 2,2-diphenylethoxy moiety (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Early screening identified a lead compound that underwent extensive chemical optimization – including solid-phase peptide and peptidomimetic synthesis using Fmoc‐based chemistry on Wang resin – to yield SB 290157 (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011). This synthetic approach, employing coupling reagents such as 1-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)-3-ethylcarbodiimide hydrochloride and 4-dimethylaminopyridine, resulted in a non-peptide molecule designed to maximize receptor affinity while minimizing metabolic instability. The compound is commercially available from suppliers such as Cayman Chemical (catalog #10006619) and has served as a prototypic small-molecule C3aR antagonist in numerous preclinical studies (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017).

SB 290157 falls within the broader class of synthetic GPCR modulators that target complement receptors. Historically, such molecules have been exploited as biochemical tools to interrogate the role of anaphylatoxins in inflammatory responses (Ames et al., 2001). C3a, a 77-residue protein fragment produced during complement activation, is recognized by its GPCR, C3aR, and triggers diverse cellular responses (Ames et al., 2001). Multiple research groups have employed small-molecule antagonists like SB 290157 to elucidate the contribution of C3a-mediated signaling in conditions ranging from arthritis to lung inflammation (Ames et al., 2001). The compound’s synthetic origin and chemical tractability have allowed investigators to probe receptor pharmacology in heterologous cell lines (e.g., RBL-C3aR cells, ARPE-19 cells) and primary human cell systems (Ames et al., 2001). In the context of ocular research, SB 290157 has been used experimentally in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) models – particularly in primary human fetal RPE cultures – to block C3a-induced alterations in extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

Beyond its established utility as a research tool, the use of SB 290157 in ocular models speaks to an emerging rationale for targeting complement signaling in degenerative eye diseases. Its inclusion in a commercial catalog further underscores its ready availability to laboratories, enabling reproducibility and fostering further experimentation. In summary, SB 290157 is a synthetic, non-peptide, arginine-based antagonist belonging to a class of compounds that have historically been used to interrogate complement receptor signaling, with a well-defined chemical structure, known synthesis protocols, and broad preclinical application in inflammation research (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

SB 290157 has a storied history in the complement research field. Its initial characterization, as detailed by Ames and colleagues, revealed that SB 290157 competes for C3a binding with an IC₅₀ in the high‐nanomolar range (approximately 200 nM) and potently inhibits C3a-induced intracellular calcium mobilization in sensitive cell lines, such as RBL cells and human neutrophils (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Early studies validated its functional capacity as a selective antagonist in vitro, establishing that it effectively blocked receptor internalization and attenuated downstream signaling events elicited by C3a binding.

Preclinically, SB 290157 has been deployed in a wide range of experimental disease models. For instance, it has been used in animal studies examining anti-inflammatory activity in models such as guinea pig LPS-induced airway neutrophilia and adjuvant-induced arthritis in rats. In the arthritis model, administration of SB 290157 resulted in a significant reduction (approximately 41%) in paw edema, while in airway inflammation models it suppressed neutrophil recruitment, demonstrating its anti-inflammatory efficacy (Ames et al., 2001). These early demonstrations of anti-inflammatory activity provided the impetus to consider SB 290157 for further repurposing in conditions where complement overactivation contributes to pathology.

More recently, attention has turned to the role of complement in ocular diseases, particularly age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Experimental evidence in primary human fetal RPE cultures has shown that exposure to recombinant C3a for periods of 2–4 weeks results in the accumulation of sub-RPE deposits via increased ECM deposition, notably of collagens (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In addition to in vitro data, in vivo models provide further support for the therapeutic potential of modulating C3aR signaling. ────────────────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

SB 290157 exerts its biological effects by competitively binding to the C3a receptor (C3aR), thereby preventing the interaction of endogenous C3a with its receptor. Under normal conditions, the complement cascade, when activated via any of its pathways, leads to the cleavage of complement component C3 and the subsequent release of the anaphylatoxin C3a. This bioactive peptide binds to C3aR, a G protein-coupled receptor present on various cell types including granulocytes, monocytes, and notably retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Once activated, C3aR transduces signals that can lead to intracellular calcium mobilization, triggering a cascade of downstream events such as receptor internalization and activation of inflammatory transcription factors.

In vitro studies using radioligand binding assays have determined that SB 290157 displaces [¹²⁵I]-C3a from its receptor with an IC₅₀ in the high nanomolar range (approximately 200 nM), while functional calcium mobilization assays in cell lines (including RBL cells and human neutrophils) have demonstrated potent inhibition of C3a-stimulated intracellular calcium release at low nanomolar concentrations (approximately 28 nM) (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Mechanistically, by preventing C3a from engaging C3aR, the compound is able to avert subsequent receptor conformational changes that would otherwise lead to G protein coupling and downstream signaling events.

In the context of RPE cells, particularly under conditions of chronic oxidative stress – such as exposure to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) – C3a engagement of its receptor has been implicated in a range of deleterious cellular effects. Studies in ARPE-19 cells have shown that oxidative stress induces a redistribution of C3aR away from its typical plasma membrane localization and promotes its translocation toward the mitochondria (Ishii et al., 2021; Riihilä et al., 2019). At the mitochondrial level, activation of the receptor by C3a leads to an increase in mitochondrial calcium uptake, which in turn results in compromised respiratory function as evidenced by decreased state III (ADP-driven) respiration and reduced maximal respiratory capacity (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). The resultant mitochondrial dysfunction is highly likely to contribute to the generation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS). mtROS are known triggers for the NLRP3 inflammasome, which upon activation facilitates the processing of pro-IL-1β to active IL-1β, a cytokine strongly implicated in chronic inflammatory processes observed in AMD (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024).

Furthermore, in primary human fetal RPE models, prolonged exposure to recombinant C3a has been demonstrated to reduce the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (UPP) without altering mRNA levels for proteasome subunits, indicating a post-transcriptional impairment of proteostasis (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). This impairment in proteasome function is associated with an imbalance in ECM turnover – marked by a reduction in tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases (TIMP-3) abundance and an increase in matrix metalloproteinase (MMP-2) activity – culminating in the pathological deposition of extracellular matrix components (notably collagens IV and VI) beneath the RPE. Such sub-RPE deposit formation, or drusen, is one of the hallmarks of early AMD pathology (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

SB 290157, by blocking C3a from binding to C3aR, therefore interrupts these pathological cascades at two key junctures. First, it prevents the mitochondrial translocation and activation of C3aR in oxidatively stressed ARPE-19 cells, which is predicted to avert the associated mitochondrial calcium overload and respiratory inhibition, thereby reducing the likelihood of mtROS generation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). Second, by inhibiting C3a-induced receptor activation in RPE cells, SB 290157 preserves UPP activity, ensuring proper regulation of ECM component turnover and forestalling the aberrant deposition of sub-RPE material (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

It is important to note, however, that while the majority of evidence supports SB 290157 acting as an effective C3aR antagonist, several reports have cautioned that under certain conditions, the compound may display partial agonist activity. This means that rather than completely blocking receptor activation, SB 290157 might induce a low level of receptor signaling in some cellular contexts, especially when receptor density is high (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001). Such an effect must be carefully considered when interpreting experimental outcomes and when designing therapeutic strategies aimed at persistent modulation of complement activity. In all, the known mechanism of action for SB 290157 can be summarized as competitive inhibition of C3a binding to C3aR, thereby mitigating the downstream signals that lead to mitochondrial calcium dysregulation, proteasome impairment, ECM deposition abnormalities, and ultimately, NLRP3 inflammasome priming and IL-1β secretion (Ames et al., 2001; Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect

The central hypothesis underlying the use of SB 290157 in repurposing for dry AMD is that the blockade of C3aR will attenuate a cascade of deleterious events within the retinal pigment epithelium that contribute to disease progression. In particular, the expected effect is that SB 290157 will reduce complement-driven mitochondrial dysfunction, lower mtROS production, and thereby prevent the priming and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, resulting ultimately in diminished IL-1β secretion and preservation of RPE barrier integrity.

In dry AMD, chronic oxidative stress leads to dysregulated complement activation and subsequent accumulation of complement fragments such as C3a in the subretinal space. RPE cells under oxidative stress have been demonstrated to upregulate C3aR expression, with a portion of the receptor redistributing to the mitochondria—a change that is associated with an increased uptake of calcium into the mitochondria and a pronounced decline in mitochondrial respiratory function (Ishii et al., 2021; Riihilä et al., 2019). The resulting mitochondrial dysfunction is poised to increase the generation of mtROS, which serve as an upstream activator of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Activation of this inflammasome complex culminates in the maturation of IL-1β, a powerful proinflammatory cytokine that has been implicated in propagating RPE injury and the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024).

By competitively inhibiting C3a binding to its receptor, SB 290157 is expected to block these deleterious changes. In cultured ARPE-19 cells—which serve as a well-established model for human RPE—it is anticipated that SB 290157 will prevent the mitochondrial translocation of C3aR, thereby reducing abnormal mitochondrial calcium uptake and preserving normal respiration. This action should limit mtROS generation and consequently reduce the priming threshold for NLRP3 inflammasome activation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). Concurrently, in primary fetal RPE cultures, inhibition of C3aR signaling by SB 290157 has been shown to preserve the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, which in turn maintains the balance of matrix metalloproteinases and their tissue inhibitors. By doing so, the compound prevents the accumulation of sub-RPE deposits—a process that is intimately linked to the early phases of AMD pathology (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

The expression of C3aR in RPE cells, particularly in stressed conditions, is well-documented. This receptor is notably enriched on the basolateral membrane of RPE and even redistributes to mitochondrial compartments under oxidative stress conditions, as confirmed in ARPE-19 cell studies (Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Given that dry AMD is characterized by both heightened complement activation and chronic oxidative stress, the strategic inhibition of C3aR is expected to yield multiple beneficial outcomes: restoration of proteostasis, maintenance of mitochondrial function, reduction in chronic inflammatory cytokine expression, and preservation of the integrity and barrier function of the RPE monolayer. Moreover, in in vivo models such as NaIO₃-induced RPE injury or laser-induced retinal vein occlusion, treatment with a C3aR antagonist (presumably SB 290157) has been associated with reduced photoreceptor loss, attenuated microglial activation, and improved retinal morphology (Wang et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2025).

Furthermore, because mitochondrial reactive oxygen species serve as a trigger for the NLRP3 inflammasome, blocking the upstream signal via C3aR inhibition is hypothesized to break the vicious cycle of complement-mediated inflammation. The decreased activation of NLRP3 would lead to lower levels of IL-1β—a cytokine implicated in the autocrine and paracrine amplification of inflammation within the RPE layer—and thus stabilize the local microenvironment (Ong et al., 2024; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In summary, the expected effect of SB 290157 in the context of dry AMD is multifold: preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics, maintenance of proteasomal activity, prevention of pathological ECM accumulation, and attenuation of inflammasome-mediated inflammatory responses—all of which contribute to the protection of RPE integrity and function.

────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

SB 290157 stands out as one of the best-studied C3a receptor antagonists available today. Its well-documented chemical synthesis, robust in vitro pharmacological profile, and demonstrable efficacy in preclinical models of inflammatory injury provide strong support for its continued evaluation as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. The compound’s origins – as a product of high-throughput screening followed by medicinal chemistry optimization using Fmoc-solid phase techniques – are well established, and its chemical structure (N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine) clearly classifies it as a small-molecule non-peptide antagonist of a key complement receptor (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011).

Strengths of SB 290157 include its proven ability to block C3a-induced signaling cascades across a range of cell types and experimental models. Preclinical studies in RPE cells indicate that it can prevent C3a-induced sub-RPE deposit formation and proteasome impairment—a finding directly relevant to the early pathological events of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Additionally, evidence from ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress suggests that SB 290157 effectively inhibits aberrant mitochondrial Ca²⁺ uptake and consequent respiratory dysfunction—mechanisms known to contribute to mtROS generation and inflammasome activation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). In vivo, its administration in models of retinal injury (such as NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration and laser-induced retinal vein occlusion) has correlated with reduced photoreceptor death, decreased gliosis, and improved retinal architecture (Wang et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2025). These findings collectively underscore the compound’s potential to modulate complement-mediated pathology in the ocular setting.

Nonetheless, SB 290157 is not without its weaknesses. A significant concern noted across several studies is its variable pharmacological behavior. Under some experimental conditions, particularly in cell systems with high receptor density, SB 290157 exhibits partial agonist activity rather than pure antagonism (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001). This paradoxical behavior could lead to unintended receptor activation and potentially undermine its therapeutic benefit, especially in chronic conditions like dry AMD where long-term receptor blockade is desired. Furthermore, while there is compelling preclinical evidence supporting its beneficial impact on mitochondrial function and ECM homeostasis, direct experimental data linking SB 290157 to a reduction in mitochondrial ROS production and consequent suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation in ARPE-19 or primary RPE models remain incomplete or indirect (Wang et al., 2020; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Behnke, 2022). This gap in the literature necessitates further investigation to firmly establish the causal chain from C3aR inhibition to inflammasome modulation.

Another consideration is the translational challenge. SB 290157 has been predominantly utilized as a research tool rather than a clinical candidate. Its pharmacokinetic profile—while adequate for short-term animal experiments—has not been thoroughly characterized for long-term use in ocular applications, where issues such as retinal toxicity, ocular bioavailability, and sustained receptor occupancy become critical. The delicate environment of the retina requires highly specific and safe compounds; thus, the partial agonist activity and potential off-target effects of SB 290157 raise valid concerns regarding its safety profile in humans (Mathieu et al., 2005; Tan et al., 2024).

On the other hand, the dual benefit of SB 290157—in preventing not only aberrant complement signaling but also the downstream mitochondrial dysfunction that leads to inflammasome activation—directly addresses central pathogenic mechanisms in dry AMD. Given that dry AMD is characterized by chronic inflammation, RPE dysfunction, and progressive atrophy correlated with mitochondrial impairment, a drug that can simultaneously modulate these pathways offers a novel therapeutic angle. In this context, the ability of SB 290157 to preserve the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway and maintain ECM turnover may help stabilize the RPE, delay the progression of geographic atrophy, and potentially improve visual outcomes (Ames et al., 2001; Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Wang et al., 2020). Conversely, its partial agonist behavior in certain systems and the current lack of direct evidence linking its action to reduced mtROS and NLRP3 activation in ocular models raise legitimate concerns that must be addressed prior to clinical translation (Mathieu et al., 2005; Behnke, 2022).

Overall, SB 290157 is a compelling candidate for further exploration and mechanistic validation as a repurposed drug for dry AMD, provided that additional research can surmount the challenges associated with its pharmacodynamic variability and confirm its protective effects in retina-specific models.

────────────────────────────────────────  
Conclusion

The comprehensive literature evaluation indicates that SB 290157’s synthetic origins, established use as a C3aR antagonist, and demonstrated efficacy in preclinical models of complement-mediated RPE injury make it a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its mechanism—blocking C3a-induced signaling that otherwise leads to mitochondrial calcium overload, impaired proteostasis, and subsequent inflammasome activation—is highly relevant to the pathophysiology of geographic atrophy. However, the compound’s documented partial agonist effects and potential variability in receptor blockade require careful consideration and further optimization. Additional studies are necessary to firmly establish that SB 290157 can reduce mitochondrial ROS and suppress NLRP3 inflammasome activation in RPE cells under conditions that model dry AMD clinically. Thus, while SB 290157 is an excellent tool for dissecting the complement–mitochondria crosstalk in dry AMD, its suitability as a long-term therapeutic will depend on resolving these outstanding issues through rigorous preclinical and mechanistic evaluation (Ames et al., 2001; Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Mathieu et al., 2005).

Overall, the candidate shows substantial promise as a mechanistic probe and potential therapeutic agent for dry AMD; its ability to block key complement-mediated events that contribute to RPE dysfunction and inflammation positions it as a novel target for drug development. However, given the documented limitations, further studies are strongly recommended to optimize its receptor selectivity, define its pharmacokinetic and safety profile in the ocular context, and conclusively demonstrate its capacity to mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammasome activation in relevant models before advancing it into clinical trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10), also known as ubiquinone, is a naturally occurring lipophilic molecule synthesized endogenously via the mevalonate pathway. Its widespread use as a dietary supplement and as an adjunct therapy in cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and metabolic disorders underlines the extensive clinical experience with this class of compounds. The rationale for its repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is based on the compound’s natural role as a coenzyme, its potent antioxidant properties, and its ability to modulate mitochondrial energy metabolism—all of which are critically compromised in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) of the aging eye (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Maiuolo et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past decades, CoQ10 has been evaluated in multiple experimental and clinical contexts. Biochemical studies have consistently demonstrated its ability to protect mitochondrial structure and function by facilitating electron transport and scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS). In vitro, CoQ10 treatments have been shown to improve mitochondrial respiration and ATP production in various cell types, including ARPE-19 cells, a widely used human RPE model. In the clinical arena, several studies have explored the use of CoQ10, sometimes in combination with other nutritional compounds, for early stages of AMD. At the molecular level, CoQ10 exhibits a dual mechanism of action that is highly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Firstly, it functions as an obligatory electron carrier within mitochondria. In the ETC, CoQ10 shuttles electrons from complexes I (NADH dehydrogenase) and II (succinate dehydrogenase) to complex III (cytochrome bc₁ complex), thereby driving the proton gradient needed for ATP synthesis by ATP synthase. Its redox-active benzoquinone ring is capable of reversible oxidation and reduction, enabling it to accept and donate electrons during the process of cellular respiration (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Hernandez et al., 2024). This electron-transfer activity is critical in tissues with high metabolic demands such as the retina, where the maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (mt∆ψ) and ATP production are indispensable for cell survival. A second and equally important aspect of CoQ10’s mechanism is its potent antioxidant property. Through its reduced form, ubiquinol, CoQ10 directly scavenges free radicals and prevents lipid peroxidation of cell membranes.
