Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SkQ1 (10‐(6′‐plastoquinonyl)‐decyltriphenylphosphonium) is a fully synthetic, mitochondria‐targeted antioxidant constructed by conjugating a plastoquinone antioxidant moiety with a decyl linker that is covalently bound to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation. The plastoquinone scaffold is derived from the natural quinone found in chloroplasts, known for its potent reactive oxygen species (ROS)–removing capabilities, while the TPP⁺ moiety acts as a highly lipophilic vector that drives selective accumulation within mitochondria due to the inner mitochondrial membrane’s large negative potential. In essence, by combining these two structural elements, SkQ1 is designed to exploit electrophoretic uptake to achieve extremely high concentrations in the mitochondrial matrix where oxidative damage is a critical pathogenic factor. This compound belongs to the broader class of mitochondria‐targeted quinone antioxidants, often referred to collectively as “SkQ” compounds. Molecules in this class were originally proposed and developed by Skulachev and colleagues, and they have been used experimentally to achieve mitochondrial protection in contexts ranging from ischemia–reperfusion injury and neurodegeneration to aging‐associated dysfunctions (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). The rational design strategy behind SkQ1—linking a redox‐active quinone to a lipophilic cation—has also inspired the development of analogous compounds such as SkQR1, MitoQ, and related derivatives that are being explored for a variety of biomedical applications.

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of SkQ1, as well as that of its parent class of mitochondria‐targeted antioxidants, is extensive and spans multiple preclinical and early clinical studies. In numerous in vitro and in vivo models, SkQ1 has demonstrated robust antioxidant effects. For example, it has been shown to protect mitochondria and cellular membranes against lipid peroxidation—key pathogenic processes underlying aging and degenerative diseases—at nanomolar concentrations. In various rodent models, including studies in OXYS rats (a strain that mimics accelerated senescence), chronic administration of SkQ1 prevented or reversed age‐related abnormalities such as cataract, retinopathy, and even systemic markers of mitochondrial dysfunction (Wanagat et al., 2010; Belenichev et al., 2024; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Moreover, veterinary and preclinical studies have documented SkQ1’s ability to increase lifespan and delay the onset of age‐linked phenotypes, including osteoporosis, immune decline, and neurodegeneration (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Weissig, 2020). Within the ocular field, SkQ1 has been specifically formulated as eye drops—marketed in certain regions under the trade name Visomitin—to treat dry eye syndrome. These formulations have passed early phase safety trials and have now seen clinical use in Russia. Although SkQ1 has not yet been directly trialed in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or geographic atrophy, its documented efficacy in protecting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in animal models and its ability to improve electrophysiological outcomes (such as preserved electroretinography [ERG] responses) support its potential repurposing for AMD (Gueven et al., 2017; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). In several ocular studies in both rodent and primate models, topical administration of SkQ1 has demonstrated the capacity to deliver the drug to the posterior segment with minimal systemic exposure, reducing characteristics like RPE vacuolization and preserving overall retinal function (Weissig, 2020; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). The extensive preclinical and limited clinical history of SkQ1 in ocular applications—most notably in dry-eye syndrome and animal models of retinal degeneration—suggests that the therapeutic candidate has a solid track record of mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction in tissues exposed to chronic oxidative stress, a pathophysiological component also seen in dry AMD (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Wanagat et al., 2010).

Mechanism of Action:  
SkQ1 exerts its biological effects via multiple interrelated molecular mechanisms that center on its ability to accumulate rapidly within mitochondria and scavenge deleterious ROS. The TPP⁺ portion of the molecule, owing to its delocalized positive charge and high lipophilicity, drives the electrophoretic uptake of SkQ1 into the mitochondrial matrix along the steep negative membrane potential (Δψm) that is inherent to healthy mitochondria (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Once localized within these organelles, the plastoquinone group is poised to participate in redox cycling: it is reversibly reduced—often by components of the electron transport chain such as complex III—and subsequently reacts with ROS such as superoxide (O₂•⁻) and lipid peroxyl radicals to convert them into less reactive species (Lukashev et al., 2014; Weissig, 2020). Importantly, the antioxidant effect of SkQ1 is not a one-off reaction; rather, it is “rechargeable,” meaning that following its oxidation by ROS, the quinone moiety can be reduced again, thereby enabling repeated cycles of detoxification. This rechargeable mechanism differentiates SkQ1 from conventional antioxidants that are consumed irreversibly during redox reactions. Additionally, SkQ1 has been shown to form complexes with cardiolipin—a key phospholipid in the inner mitochondrial membrane—and thereby stabilize the membrane structure against peroxidation. Some studies also suggest that the TPP⁺ component might mediate a mild uncoupling effect by facilitating proton translocation (often in conjunction with interacting with fatty acid anions), which can reduce mitochondrial ROS generation by dissipating excessive inner membrane potential under conditions of oxidative overload (Lukashev et al., 2014; Weissig, 2020; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). This dual mechanism of direct ROS scavenging combined with membrane stabilizing and modest uncoupling effects contributes to the preservation of Δψm and the overall integrity of mitochondrial bioenergetics. In RPE cells stressed by chronic photo-oxidative insult, these properties would translate into effective mitigation of oxidative damage, thereby preventing the collapse of mitochondrial membrane potential—a key event that precipitates cell dysfunction and death in dry AMD (Muraleva et al., 2019; Olovnikov et al., n.d.).

Expected Effect:  
The proposed hypothesis for repurposing SkQ1 in dry age-related macular degeneration is predicated on its capacity to target RPE mitochondria and to neutralize both superoxide radicals and lipid peroxyl radicals that accumulate under conditions of chronic light-induced oxidative stress. In vitro assays using ARPE-19 cells have demonstrated that nanomolar concentrations of SkQ1 elicit potent antioxidant responses—as measured by decreases in fluorescence with DCFDA (a marker of ROS) and stabilization of mitochondrial membrane potential via JC-1 assays—indicating that the compound readily scavenges ocular ROS at very low doses (Gueven et al., 2017; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). This antioxidant activity is expected to prevent or delay the loss of Δψm, a critical parameter for cell survival and function, particularly in RPE cells where mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in the pathogenesis of drusen formation and geographic atrophy in dry AMD. In vivo, studies conducted in models such as OXYS rats have shown that chronic administration of SkQ1 not only reduces oxidative markers in mitochondrial membranes (e.g., decreasing levels of malondialdehyde and hydroxynonenal-adducts) but also normalizes cardiolipin content and fatty acid composition—key factors involved in the proper assembly and turnover of respiratory complexes (Wanagat et al., 2010; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Moreover, macaque studies have indicated that topical SkQ1 eye drops achieve significant drug levels in the posterior segment although the dosing remains in the nanomolar range, leading to improvements in ERG function and reduced RPE vacuolization without evidence of systemic toxicity (Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Weissig, 2020). At the molecular level, the expected effect in RPE cells would be a sustained antioxidant environment that preserves mitochondrial function through two primary pathways: first, by directly quenching damaging ROS that would otherwise trigger mitochondrial DNA damage and lipid peroxidation; and second, by maintaining the structural integrity of mitochondrial membranes via stabilization of cardiolipin and prevention of excessive proton leakage. Given that RPE cells express the full complement of mitochondrial electron transport chain proteins, including complex III which is capable of reducing SkQ1 to its active form, these cells are ideal targets for the drug’s mechanism (Muraleva et al., 2019; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Consequently, when used as a therapeutic intervention in dry AMD, SkQ1 is expected to mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction associated with drusen accumulation and, in turn, slow or potentially reverse the progression of geographic atrophy—one of the major sight-threatening complications of the disease.

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, SkQ1 represents a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration based on a robust foundation of molecular design, preclinical efficacy, and established ocular safety. One of the major strengths of SkQ1 lies in its rational design: as a rechargeable, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant, it overcomes limitations faced by conventional antioxidants that lack mitochondrial specificity. The ability of the TPP⁺ moiety to drive precise mitochondrial accumulation ensures that the compound is concentrated at the site of maximal ROS production, while its plastoquinone component provides potent scavenging of both superoxide and lipid peroxyl radicals. This dual functionality not only neutralizes damaging oxidative species but also supports mitochondrial membrane integrity by stabilizing cardiolipin and potentially mitigating excessive proton leakage. Such a mechanism is particularly relevant to RPE cells, where chronic photo-oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Lukashev et al., 2014).

Another significant advantage is the extensive preclinical and early clinical evidence supporting SkQ1’s efficacy in ocular applications. Its use in animal models—spanning species from rodents to macaques—has consistently shown protective effects on retinal structure and function, including preservation of ERG responses and reduced vacuolization of the RPE. Furthermore, the successful clinical trials for dry eye syndrome confirm that topical administration of SkQ1 is not only efficacious but also well-tolerated in humans, thereby reducing the risk related to ocular drug delivery and systemic exposure (Gueven et al., 2017; Weissig, 2020; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

Nevertheless, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be carefully weighed. One concern is the dose-dependent behavior of SkQ1. While nanomolar concentrations are effective and safe, there is evidence that at higher concentrations, the molecule can exhibit prooxidant or detergent-like effects—leading to membrane disruption or uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation. This narrow window between the antioxidant and prooxidant activities necessitates rigorous control of dosing in clinical settings to avoid inadvertent exacerbation of mitochondrial dysfunction (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). Additionally, while many studies have focused on the compound’s ability to protect against acute oxidative insults, the etiology of dry AMD is multifactorial and chronic. Although animal models such as the OXYS rat provide valuable insights into age-related ocular changes, the long-term efficacy and safety of SkQ1 in preventing geographic atrophy in the context of chronic, low-grade oxidative stress remain to be fully established in human subjects (Wanagat et al., 2010; Belenichev et al., 2024).

It is also important to note that while the proposed mechanism of action for SkQ1—namely, quenching of lipid peroxyl radicals and superoxide to preserve mitochondrial membrane potential—has been well-documented in vitro and in animal models (particularly using ARPE-19 assays with JC-1 and DCFDA readouts), extrapolating these findings to the complex human pathology of dry AMD will require careful clinical trial design. Key endpoints such as changes in drusen load, progression of geographic atrophy, and improvements in visual function would need to be monitored over extended periods. Moreover, given that oxidative stress and inflammation are part of an intricate network of pathological events in dry AMD, combination therapies that address multiple targets may ultimately yield more significant benefits than a single-agent approach (Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Gueven et al., 2017).

From a pharmacokinetic perspective, the selective accumulation of SkQ1 in the mitochondria is a highly attractive feature, as it maximizes local drug concentrations while minimizing systemic exposure and potential off-target effects. This is especially critical for ocular applications, where local delivery via eye drops can achieve high retinal levels with minimal systemic absorption. Nonetheless, formulation stability, light sensitivity, and proper storage conditions are factors that must be optimized for successful commercial development (Weissig, 2020; Gueven et al., 2017; Ji et al., 2021).

In aggregate, the overall evaluation of SkQ1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic. The compound’s design as a mitochondria-targeted, rechargeable antioxidant offers compelling advantages in addressing mitochondrial dysfunction—a key element in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its ability to protect RPE cells, preserve mitochondrial membrane potential, and improve retinal function, while early clinical studies in related ocular conditions confirm its safety profile for topical administration. However, due diligence is warranted to establish the optimal dosing regimen that maximizes beneficial antioxidant effects while avoiding potential prooxidant toxicity. Additionally, further rigorous clinical trials specifically targeting dry AMD endpoints are necessary to confirm that the promising outcomes observed in animal studies translate into measurable clinical benefit in patients with geographic atrophy (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Gueven et al., 2017; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Wanagat et al., 2010; Weissig, 2020).

Given the comprehensive body of work underpinning the mechanism of action, the established track record in various preclinical ocular models, and the supporting data from human dry-eye trials, SkQ1 appears to have significant potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its unique targeting of mitochondria—particularly within RPE cells—and its capacity to prevent ROS-induced mitochondrial collapse make it especially well-suited to counteract the chronic photo-oxidative stress that characterizes this disease. The next steps for validating SkQ1 in this indication should include well-designed in vivo studies in AMD-relevant animal models, followed by early phase clinical trials with careful dose-escalation studies and robust assessment of retinal morphology and function. Overall, SkQ1 stands out as a promising therapeutic candidate that merits further investigation within our drug development pipeline (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Weissig, 2020; Gueven et al., 2017; Wanagat et al., 2010).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Metformin is a well‐known therapeutic agent belonging to the biguanide class, originally derived from guanidine compounds found in the plant Galega officinalis. The molecule is a synthetic derivative of naturally occurring galegine and has been refined into a modern oral antihyperglycemic agent (Augustin & Atorf, 2023). This class of compounds has historically been used as a first-line oral treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus, with metformin being one of the most prescribed drugs worldwide for managing hyperglycemia. Its synthesis did not follow the classical target‐driven design path but instead emerged from an adaptation of naturally occurring structures into a chemically optimized, orally bioavailable, and generally well-tolerated drug (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Dang et al., 2021). Given its long clinical history starting from the 1950s and subsequent FDA approval in the 1990s, metformin has accumulated a significant amount of safety data and clinical experience, which collectively make it an attractive candidate for repurposing into other disease areas, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) characterized by geographic atrophy (Amin et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, metformin has been used extensively as an antidiabetic agent to lower hepatic glucose output and improve peripheral insulin sensitivity. Its beneficial pleiotropic effects beyond glycemic control have been recognized over the years; these include anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antiangiogenic properties, which have been observed in both biochemical and clinical investigations. Multiple epidemiologic studies have examined the association between metformin use and ocular outcomes. Retrospective analyses in predominantly diabetic cohorts have indicated that metformin use correlates with reduced odds or hazard for developing age-related macular degeneration and other retinal diseases, although some studies report mixed results depending on cumulative dose, exposure timing, and concomitant diabetes-related complications (Moir et al., 2023; Amin et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2022). Notably, while metformin has not historically been approved for any ocular indication, several preclinical studies using retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cell models have demonstrated that metformin may protect against oxidative damage and improve mitochondrial function. Moreover, a Phase II single-blind randomized trial was initiated to assess the efficacy of metformin in slowing the progression of geographic atrophy among non-diabetic patients with advanced dry AMD (Shen et al., 2024), suggesting that the concept of repurposing metformin for dry AMD is already under active clinical investigation.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, metformin’s primary mechanism of action involves the inhibition of mitochondrial complex I of the electron transport chain, resulting in a decrease in ATP production and a concomitant increase in the intracellular AMP:ATP ratio. This metabolic shift leads to the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a master regulator of cellular energy homeostasis that orchestrates shifts in metabolism under conditions of energy deficit (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). AMPK activation exerts multiple downstream effects that are particularly relevant to RPE cell function and the pathogenesis of geographic atrophy. First, AMPK activation promotes autophagy, including mitophagy, a quality-control mechanism that ensures the removal of dysfunctional mitochondria. Preclinical studies in RPE cell models, such as those using ARPE-19 cells, have provided evidence that metformin increases autophagosome formation, reduces intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS), lowers apoptosis rates, and helps maintain the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) under oxidative stress conditions (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Toppila et al., 2024). Additionally, the activation of AMPK in RPE cells has been associated with upregulation of protective pathways including enhanced nitric oxide (NO) production and increased expression of mitochondrial biogenesis factors such as PGC-1α, which together contribute to improved mitochondrial quality control (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023).  

Furthermore, metformin is known to activate both AMPK-dependent and AMPK-independent signaling pathways. The AMPK-independent effects may include inhibition of NF-κB activation, leading to a reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α, which are implicated in chronic inflammation observed in the aging retina (Jiang et al., 2022; Amin et al., 2022). From a biochemical standpoint, the inhibition of complex I by metformin also directly reduces the leakage of electrons that can form ROS, thereby lowering mitochondrial oxidative stress—a key aspect in the progression of dry AMD pathogenesis (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). It is important to note, however, that several reports have highlighted the concern that activation of AMPK in vivo or in vitro appears to require suprapharmacological doses of metformin, casting uncertainty on whether standard clinical dosing is sufficient to achieve these retinal effects (Moir et al., 2023). Nonetheless, the preclinical evidence supports a model whereby metformin’s inhibition of mitochondrial complex I—thereby reducing ROS and enhancing autophagy—provides a rationale for its potential use in protecting RPE cells from oxidative stress-induced damage (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis driving the repurposing of metformin for dry AMD is predicated on its ability to activate AMPK and inhibit mitochondrial complex I leakage in RPE cells, leading to reduced ROS production and enhanced mitochondrial quality control. In the context of geographic atrophy, RPE dysfunction and death play a central role in the degeneration of photoreceptors and the progression of AMD. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that metformin can protect ARPE-19 cells (an established human RPE cell line) from oxidative insults by lowering intracellular ROS levels, augmenting autophagic processes, and preserving mitochondrial membrane potential (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Toppila et al., 2024). Additionally, through the activation of AMPK, metformin is expected to stimulate the expression of mitochondrial biogenesis factors, leading to improved mitochondrial function, which is critical given the high metabolic demands of the RPE (Moir et al., 2023). 

Epidemiologically, several retrospective cohort and case-control studies have observed associations between metformin use and a reduced risk of developing AMD. Some studies even suggest that these associations are dose- and timing-dependent, with earlier or sustained use of metformin correlating with greater protective effects (Moir et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022). Therefore, in an assay designed to measure the effects of metformin on mitochondrial function and oxidative stress in RPE cells, one would expect to see an enhancement in autophagic flux, decreased markers of oxidative stress, and preservation or restoration of Δψm. These cellular effects would ideally translate into a slower progression of geographic atrophy in vivo, as suggested by the decreased degeneration of the retinal layers that has been observed in certain mouse models of retinal damage (Jiang et al., 2022; Amin et al., 2022). RPE cells are known to express AMPK and other components of the autophagy machinery, which further supports the rationale for targeting these pathways in the treatment of dry AMD (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Moir et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
Metformin shows considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly for geographic atrophy, due to several key strengths. First, its long and well-documented clinical history in the management of type 2 diabetes provides a robust safety profile and widespread clinical familiarity, which is a significant advantage when considering repurposing strategies (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Dang et al., 2021; Amin et al., 2022). Second, the molecular and cellular mechanisms by which metformin acts—namely, the inhibition of mitochondrial complex I, subsequent activation of AMPK, and promotion of autophagy—are highly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. The ability of metformin to reduce ROS and promote mitochondrial quality control addresses one of the core aspects of RPE dysfunction and degeneration seen in geographic atrophy (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Jiang et al., 2022).

Furthermore, the epidemiologic data showing associations between metformin use and a reduced incidence of AMD lend additional support to its potential utility in this setting (Liang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023). The possibility that metformin’s protective effects might be independent of its glycemic control properties is particularly intriguing, as it expands the target population to non-diabetic AMD patients—a group that represents the majority of those affected by geographic atrophy (Moir et al., 2023; Brown et al., 2019; Moir et al., 2024). On a mechanistic level, the detailed understanding of metformin’s interaction with AMPK and mitochondrial pathways not only provides a clear therapeutic target but also offers multiple biomarkers for assessing efficacy in both preclinical and clinical studies.

Despite its strengths, several weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. One significant concern is whether standard clinical doses of metformin are sufficient to activate the AMPK pathway in retinal tissues, given that some in vitro studies indicate suprapharmacological doses are required to see a robust effect (Moir et al., 2023). This raises questions of retinal bioavailability and whether alternative delivery strategies, such as local ocular administration or formulation enhancements, might be required to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE. Additionally, while the epidemiologic studies are promising, they are not uniformly consistent; some retrospective analyses have reported no association or even conflicting results depending on dosing and timing parameters (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Brown et al., 2019; Amin et al., 2022). These discrepancies underscore the inherent limitations of observational data, including potential confounding factors such as the presence and severity of diabetes, concomitant medications, and the challenges of accurately classifying AMD subtypes using administrative coding.

Another consideration is that although metformin’s broad mechanism of action (i.e., modulation of inflammation, oxidative stress, and autophagy) is advantageous in addressing multifactorial diseases like AMD, it may also lead to off-target effects or systemic side effects such as vitamin B12 deficiency or, in rare instances, lactic acidosis (Jiang et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). In elderly populations—who are generally most affected by dry AMD—these risks must be carefully weighed against the potential benefits. Moreover, the heterogeneity in study designs and patient populations in the available epidemiologic literature means that prospective, well-designed clinical trials remain essential to definitively determine whether metformin can meaningfully slow the progression of geographic atrophy in AMD (Shen et al., 2024).

In summary, the overall evaluation of metformin as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. Its well-established safety profile, combined with mechanistic data that align closely with the underlying pathology of geographic atrophy, make it a compelling candidate. The strengths lie in its ability to activate AMPK, thereby reducing mitochondrial ROS, promoting autophagy, and potentially preserving RPE function—molecular actions that directly address key pathological features of dry AMD. However, critical questions regarding dosing, ocular bioavailability, and the variability in epidemiologic outcomes necessitate further rigorous investigation in controlled clinical settings. Moving forward, clinical trials designed to specifically assess metformin’s efficacy in non-diabetic populations with early to intermediate stages of geographic atrophy will be crucial to validate its repurposing potential. Overall, while metformin has significant promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, additional studies are needed to resolve questions about its optimal dosing regimen, delivery method, and long-term efficacy in preserving retinal structure and function (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin (also known as sirolimus and available as Abcam #ab120224) is a naturally occurring macrolide compound originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus. It belongs to the class of macrocyclic lactones and is known for its potent inhibitory effects on the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). This compound has been extensively used in various contexts such as immunosuppression, cancer therapy, and more recently, as a tool to modulate autophagy in age-related degenerative diseases. In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction and dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), rapamycin is being explored as a repurposed therapeutic candidate with the hypothesis that mTORC1 inhibition will enhance both general autophagy and selective mitophagy. This clearance of reactive oxygen species (ROS)–generating, damaged mitochondria may alleviate oxidative stress, reduce the accumulation of toxic lipofuscin compounds (including A2E), and ultimately slow the progression of dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, rapamycin was first discovered for its potent immunosuppressive properties and later developed for use in preventing transplant rejection and certain cancers. Its ability to inhibit mTORC1 has made it a valuable tool in research related to aging and neurodegeneration. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its effectiveness in modulating autophagy and protecting cellular integrity under stress conditions, particularly in the retinal environment. In animal models of retinal degeneration and even some early clinical trials, rapamycin was shown to reduce the accumulation of autofluorescent granules and inflammatory cytokines in the RPE, which are both hallmarks of dry AMD pathology (Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022). Notably, rapamycin has been administered via diverse routes, including intravitreal and subconjunctival injections, in attempts to treat geographic atrophy or other dry AMD phenotypes, although the clinical outcomes have been mixed. For example, clinical trials such as those referenced in studies with identifiers NCT00766649 and NCT01445548 demonstrated that while rapamycin was generally safe and well-tolerated in ocular applications, its efficacy in slowing down the progression of geographic atrophy and improving visual acuity remained limited (National Eye Institute, 2008; National Eye Institute, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These historical findings highlight both the promise and the challenges associated with translating rapamycin’s mechanistic benefits into robust clinical outcomes for dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary mechanism of rapamycin involves the formation of a complex with the immunophilin FKBP12. This complex binds to mTORC1 and inhibits its kinase activity, leading to a decrease in the phosphorylation of downstream targets such as ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K) and the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 (4EBP1). Under normal circumstances, active mTORC1 suppresses autophagy by phosphorylating these targets, which in turn prevents the formation of autophagosomes. By inhibiting mTORC1, rapamycin effectively removes this blockade, thereby promoting the induction of autophagy as evidenced by increased conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II and clearance of the autophagic substrate p62 (Zhang et al., 2015).

Within retinal pigment epithelial cells, this induction of autophagy is particularly important. RPE cells are responsible for the phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments; a process that generates large amounts of cellular debris and metabolic byproducts such as lipofuscin. In dry AMD, impaired autophagic flux leads to the accumulation of these compounds, which, in turn, contributes to oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Rapamycin’s inhibition of mTORC1 not only enhances general autophagy but also promotes selective mitochondrial clearance (mitophagy). Key players in the mitophagy pathway include the serine/threonine kinase PINK1 and the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin, both of which accumulate on depolarized mitochondria and signal their removal via autophagic mechanisms. By stimulating this PINK1/Parkin pathway, rapamycin enhances the clearance of damaged, ROS-generating mitochondria, thus preserving overall mitochondrial health (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).

Additionally, rapamycin’s downstream effects include activation of transcription factors such as TFEB, which regulates lysosomal biogenesis and further enhances the autophagic process. This dual action—promoting both autophagy and lysosomal function—helps to mitigate the accumulation of toxic aggregates such as lipofuscin and A2E in RPE, therefore reducing oxidative stress and inflammation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). Through these biochemical interactions, rapamycin establishes a cellular environment that is more capable of dealing with metabolic challenges and oxidative damage, both of which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Chang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed hypothesis, the administration of rapamycin in RPE cells is expected to result in a cascade of beneficial cellular events. In our proposed assay, rapamycin is anticipated to inhibit mTORC1 activity, leading to a measurable increase in autophagic flux. This will be evident from the enhanced lipidation of LC3-II, the clearance of p62 (an autophagy adaptor protein that accumulates when autophagy is impaired), and the activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway in response to oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2015).

The specific clearance of damaged mitochondria is particularly critical in the RPE, where mitochondrial dysfunction is a significant contributor to the generation of reactive oxygen species and subsequent cellular damage. By removing these dysfunctional mitochondria, rapamycin is expected to reduce intracellular ROS levels and thereby lower oxidative stress, a driving force in AMD pathology. In parallel, the enhanced autophagic degradation of accumulated lipofuscin and the toxic fluorophore A2E is predicted to further limit the inflammatory and apoptotic cascades triggered by these compounds, thus preserving RPE cell viability and function (Zhang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2025).

Moreover, the expression of PINK1 and Parkin in RPE cells has been well documented, and their activation is indicative of mitophagic turnover. Their proper functioning is a key determinant in mitochondrial quality control, and rapamycin is expected to potentiate this process, ensuring that mitochondria remain healthy and capable of maintaining cellular energy production and reducing the risk of cell death (Pinelli et al., 2025; Hyttinen et al., 2018). Given that impaired mitochondrial function and the resulting energy production deficits are central to the progression of dry AMD, the expected outcomes from rapamycin treatment would include not only a reduction in oxidative stress markers but also improvements in mitochondrial dynamics and overall cellular homeostasis. Such effects would ideally be reflected in functional assays measuring cell viability, mitochondrial respiration, and reductions in inflammatory cytokine production (Zhang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In our comprehensive evaluation of rapamycin as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and potential weaknesses emerge that warrant careful consideration. One of the key strengths of rapamycin lies in its well-characterized mechanism of action and its ability to broadly modulate autophagy through mTORC1 inhibition. Preclinical studies have repeatedly demonstrated that rapamycin can induce autophagic flux, leading to the clearance of cellular debris and damaged mitochondria in RPE cells. This is particularly compelling given the central role of impaired autophagy in the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, which are major pathological features of dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018). The dual-action mechanism—enhancing both autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis via TFEB activation—further supports its potential in addressing multiple aspects of the disease pathology, from oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction to inflammation and cellular senescence (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Another strength is the substantial body of preclinical evidence showing that rapamycin not only stimulates autophagy but also improves mitochondrial function. The activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway is particularly relevant since these proteins are indispensable for mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control. By facilitating the removal of ROS-generating, damaged mitochondria, rapamycin could directly impact the cellular energy balance and reduce damaging oxidative insults in the RPE, which is pivotal for maintaining retinal health (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).

Despite its promising mechanistic profile, several significant challenges remain. Clinical studies investigating the use of rapamycin for AMD have yielded mixed results. While the drug has been shown to be safe and tolerable in ocular applications, several clinical trials, such as those involving subconjunctival or intravitreal administration, did not demonstrate significant efficacy in halting the progression of geographic atrophy or improving visual acuity. In some instances, adverse effects such as decreased visual acuity and retinal thinning have been observed, raising concerns about the balance between therapeutic benefit and potential retinal toxicity (National Eye Institute, 2008; National Eye Institute, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These mixed clinical findings underscore the complexity of modulating mTORC1 in a disease with multifactorial etiology and suggest that the optimal dosage, treatment duration, and patient selection criteria still require refinement.

Furthermore, the variability in response among different donor-derived RPE cells—where only about 50% of AMD donor samples responded positively to rapamycin in certain studies—points to potential issues regarding patient heterogeneity and the need for personalized therapeutic regimens (Ebeling et al., 2020). This heterogeneity may be due to differences in the intrinsic capacity for autophagy, genetic variations affecting mitochondrial quality control, or the extent of existing cellular damage. Such variability complicates the development of standardized treatment protocols and could limit the broad applicability of rapamycin unless predictive biomarkers of response are identified (Zhang et al., 2015).

Another important consideration is the dual nature of autophagy in the context of RPE health. While enhancing autophagy can provide protective benefits by clearing damaged organelles and reducing oxidative stress, excessive autophagic flux under certain stress conditions might paradoxically contribute to cell death. This is especially relevant in advanced stages of dry AMD, where cellular stress is severe and prolonged autophagy induction might tip the balance toward detrimental outcomes rather than recovery (Chang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2019). In addition, the potential for rapamycin to interfere with beneficial mTOR signaling under specific conditions (for example, when mTOR activity supports survival pathways via growth factors such as nerve growth factor) further complicates its use, as evidenced by reports that observed mixed effects on retinal ganglion cell survival in different pathological contexts (Wang et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2021).

The delivery method and pharmacokinetics of rapamycin also represent important variables. While nanotechnology-based delivery systems—such as synthetic high-density lipoprotein nanoparticles—have shown promise in achieving more targeted and sustained delivery of rapamycin to the RPE (Mei et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2021), these strategies require further translational studies to assess their safety, efficacy, and scalability in clinical settings. Moreover, the risk of systemic side effects, including metabolic toxicities and immunosuppression, despite the generally favorable ocular safety profile observed in trials, necessitates caution in developing rapamycin-based therapies for chronic conditions like AMD (Wang et al., 2022).

In summary, rapamycin presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its robust mechanism of action—specifically, its capacity to inhibit mTORC1, thereby stimulating both general autophagy and the selective removal of damaged mitochondria via the PINK1/Parkin pathway. Preclinical evidence strongly supports the idea that such modulation can reduce oxidative stress, clear toxic accumulations like lipofuscin/A2E, and ultimately preserve mitochondrial and RPE cellular function (Zhang et al., 2015; Hyttinen et al., 2018). However, the translation of these benefits into clinical improvements remains uncertain, with several trials indicating that while rapamycin is safe and modulates cellular pathways implicated in AMD, its clinical efficacy in terms of preserving visual function has not been conclusively demonstrated. The heterogeneity in patient responses, the potential for adverse outcomes related to excessive autophagy, and the challenges in optimizing dosing and delivery all represent significant hurdles. These considerations suggest that while rapamycin is a promising candidate worthy of further investigation, its ultimate role in the treatment paradigm for dry AMD will depend on our ability to refine treatment regimens, develop predictive biomarkers for patient selection, and perhaps combine mTOR modulation with complementary therapeutic strategies that reinforce its protective effects while mitigating its risks (Wang et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2019).

Given the cumulative evidence, our overall recommendation is to continue exploring rapamycin as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, but with a strategic focus on further preclinical investigations that address the dose–response relationships in donor-derived RPE models and the development of advanced drug delivery systems. It will also be important to design future clinical trials with stratified patient populations and integrated biomarkers that can help identify responders. This iterative approach could eventually lead to a carefully balanced regimen where rapamycin’s autophagy-enhancing properties are harnessed to maintain retinal integrity while avoiding the pitfalls of over-inhibition or systemic toxicity. In essence, the promise of rapamycin in modulating autophagy to improve mitochondrial health and reduce oxidative stress in RPE cells is clear at the molecular and cellular levels, but translating these benefits into a safe and effective therapy for dry AMD will require overcoming substantial clinical challenges (Mei et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Strengths of rapamycin include its well-established mechanism of action, the significant supportive preclinical data demonstrating improvements in autophagic flux and mitochondrial clearance in RPE models, and its potential to address several key pathological features of dry AMD simultaneously. Weaknesses include the mixed clinical trial outcomes to date, the potential for adverse effects in certain contexts (including decreased visual acuity and retinal thinning), and the observed heterogeneity in therapeutic response among different patient samples. These factors highlight the importance of further mechanistic studies and carefully controlled clinical trials. Overall, rapamycin remains one of the more mechanistically promising candidates for repurposing in dry AMD, yet its future success will depend on how effectively we can tailor its delivery and dosing to maximize protective effects while minimizing risks in the vulnerable RPE of AMD patients (Niu et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022).

In conclusion, rapamycin’s role as an mTORC1 inhibitor with the capacity to induce autophagy and mitophagy presents an exciting therapeutic avenue for addressing the complex pathology of dry AMD. By alleviating the buildup of toxic metabolites and preserving mitochondrial health in RPE cells, rapamycin could potentially slow disease progression and preserve vision. Nonetheless, the balance between benefit and adverse effects remains delicate, and further research is essential to elucidate how best to leverage rapamycin’s molecular actions in a clinically meaningful way. This comprehensive review supports the continued investigation of rapamycin as a candidate for dry AMD therapy, provided that subsequent studies can address the highlighted challenges and refine the therapeutic strategy to achieve consistent, positive clinical outcomes (Mei et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is a naturally occurring nucleotide derivative that functions as a key intermediate in the biosynthesis of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), an essential coenzyme in cellular energy metabolism and redox regulation (Chen et al., 2020). Originally identified as part of the salvage pathway of NAD+ synthesis, NMN is synthesized endogenously from nicotinamide and subsequently converted by NMN adenylyltransferase (NMNAT) into NAD+ (Gerdes, 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). Commercially produced by chemical synthesis and available from suppliers such as Sigma-Aldrich (catalog number N3501), NMN belongs to the class of NAD+ precursors that have attracted considerable attention due to their potential to counteract the age-related decline in NAD+ levels (Chen et al., 2020). Compounds of this class have historically been explored mainly in the context of metabolic and aging interventions, with the rationale that restoring NAD+ pools may reverse or delay cellular senescence and mitochondrial dysfunction (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022). NMN, as a small molecule with a molecular weight of approximately 334 g/mol, has been demonstrated to readily cross cell membranes and enhance cellular bioenergetics, making it a promising candidate for diseases in which energy metabolism is disrupted, such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Chen et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). The compound’s natural occurrence and favorable safety profile observed in preclinical aging models have contributed to its development as a therapeutic candidate across multiple indications, which now includes potential ophthalmological applications (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ebeling et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, NMN has been investigated in a variety of preclinical settings addressing metabolic dysfunction and age‐associated decline, with numerous studies across biochemical, cellular, and animal models demonstrating that NMN supplementation effectively elevates NAD+ levels and improves mitochondrial function (Chen et al., 2020). In models of retinal degeneration, particularly in contexts simulating photoreceptor loss and retinal detachment, NMN administration has shown neuroprotective effects by restoring NAD+ levels and activating key deacetylases such as SIRT1, which are central to oxidative stress mitigation and cell survival (Chen et al., 2020). Preclinical studies conducted in mouse models of retinal detachment have reported that NMN treatment not only boosts NAD+ concentrations beyond the physiological baseline but also attenuates the inflammatory response and reduces photoreceptor cell death, thereby preserving retinal structure and function (Chen et al., 2020). In addition to these acute models, experimental data from primary retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells derived from donors with age‐related macular degeneration have revealed that NMN can improve mitochondrial respiration and restore the NAD+/NADH balance critical to RPE cell health (Ebeling et al., 2020). Moreover, NMN’s ability to limit cellular senescence has been documented in RPE models challenged with oxidative stressors and pro‐senescent compounds, where supplementation led to a reduction in markers such as p16INK4a and p21Waf/Cip1, along with preservation of SIRT1 expression (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022). Clinical exploration of NMN in the context of aging and metabolic disorders—though not yet fully extended to ophthalmologic diseases—provides an encouraging translational backdrop, indicating that NMN has a robust therapeutic history in conditions characterized by NAD+ depletion and mitochondrial dysfunction (Jadeja et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2024). Collectively, the therapeutic history suggests that NMN has been thoroughly vetted in preclinical settings relevant to neurodegeneration and retinal health, thereby supporting its potential repurposing for dry AMD (Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
NMN exerts its biological effects primarily through its role as a biosynthetic precursor of NAD+, a critical coenzyme involved in numerous cellular processes including energy production, DNA repair, and redox balance (Chen et al., 2020). Once administered, NMN is rapidly taken up by cells and converted via NMNAT enzymes into NAD+, thereby replenishing intracellular NAD+ pools that typically decline with age and stress (Gerdes, 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). This increase in NAD+ levels has a twofold impact. First, elevated NAD+ directly energizes metabolic pathways, namely glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation, by serving as a cofactor for dehydrogenases, which is essential for mitochondrial ATP production (Will-Orrego, 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Second, NAD+ acts as a substrate for a family of NAD+-dependent deacetylases—the sirtuins—most notably SIRT1, SIRT3, and SIRT5, which are involved in regulating mitochondrial integrity and function (Chen et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). In the specific context of dry AMD, the hypothesis posits that NMN-mediated restoration of NAD+ in retinal pigment epithelial cells leads to reactivation of mitochondrial sirtuins SIRT3 and SIRT5. SIRT3, located in the mitochondrial matrix, deacetylates key metabolic enzymes including manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), whose activity is crucial for neutralizing mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) (Gerdes, 2018; Ren et al., 2022). The proper deacetylation of MnSOD enhances its antioxidant capacity, thereby reducing mtROS accumulation and protecting the mitochondria from oxidative damage (Chen et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022). SIRT5, another mitochondrial deacetylase, plays a complementary role by regulating the acylation status of proteins involved in mitochondrial dynamics and energy metabolism; its activation, in turn, contributes to improved mitochondrial respiration and bioenergetics (Ebeling et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). Furthermore, the elevation of NAD+ levels via NMN supplementation is known to indirectly influence other signaling pathways such as those modulated by AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and Akt/mTOR, which are critical for mitochondrial biogenesis and cellular homeostasis (Ren et al., 2022). In dry AMD, where metabolic dysfunction and increased oxidative stress are central to disease progression, the biochemical cascade triggered by NMN restores the balance between energy production and oxidative damage by ensuring that sirtuins are adequately fueled (Jadeja et al., 2018). This cascade not only preserves mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and oxygen consumption rate (OCR) but also limits the proton leak and bioenergetic inefficiency that characterize dysfunctional RPE cells (Ebeling et al., 2020). In summary, at the molecular level, NMN’s mechanism of action in RPE cells aligns with a strategy of metabolic reconditioning, whereby the reactivation of SIRT3 and SIRT5—via increased NAD+ availability—leads to improved deacetylation of mitochondrial enzymes, reduction in mtROS levels, and enhancement of overall mitochondrial function (Lin, 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of a dry AMD model, the anticipated effect of NMN supplementation is the restoration of NAD+ homeostasis within RPE cells and consequent reactivation of mitochondrial sirtuins such as SIRT3 and SIRT5, which will correct mitochondrial deacetylation deficits that are known to contribute to cellular dysfunction (Chen et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). Specifically, NMN is expected to normalize the NAD+/NADH ratio, an essential parameter for efficient electron transport chain function and ATP generation; this normalization is projected to result in enhanced oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and improved mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) in the RPE (Ebeling et al., 2020). As a direct consequence of restored sirtuin activity, particularly SIRT3’s deacetylation of MnSOD, there should be a significant reduction in mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), which in turn decreases the oxidative burden on the RPE cells—a critical factor in the development and progression of dry AMD (Gerdes, 2018; Ren et al., 2022). The expected downstream effects include not only enhanced bioenergetic function but also a reduction in the cellular senescence markers and inflammatory cytokines typically upregulated in the aging and stressed RPE (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022). In vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE cultures have demonstrated that NMN supplementation can rescue cells from FK866-induced NAD+ depletion, thereby restoring ATP levels and maintaining the expression of RPE identity genes, which are fundamental to retinal homeostasis (Will-Orrego, 2020). Moreover, by mitigating oxidative damage and correcting mitochondrial dysfunction, NMN is expected to preserve the structural integrity of the outer retina, which is essential for sustained photoreceptor function and visual acuity in dry AMD (Chen et al., 2020). Ultimately, the mechanistic actions of NMN—spanning from NAD+ replenishment to sirtuin activation—are predicted to yield measurable improvements in both cellular assays (e.g., increased OCR, stabilized Δψm, and decreased ROS levels) and functional endpoints such as electroretinography (ERG) responses in animal models of retinal degeneration (Chen et al., 2020). The robust preclinical data, including evidence of normalized mitochondrial respiration and amelioration of RPE senescence following NMN treatment, provide a strong rationale for expecting similar beneficial effects in a dry AMD assay (Jadeja et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
The cumulative evidence from biochemical, cellular, and in vivo studies positions NMN as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. One of the primary strengths of NMN is its well‐characterized role as a NAD+ precursor, which underpins its ability to restore intracellular NAD+ levels and reactivate essential sirtuin activities—most notably SIRT3 and SIRT5—in metabolically compromised cells (Chen et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). AICAR exerts its biological activity primarily through the activation of AMPK, a master regulator of cellular energy balance that responds to alterations in the AMP/ATP ratio. Once AICAR is imported into cells through adenosine transporters, it is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase to form ZMP, an analog of AMP. ZMP binds to the regulatory γ subunit of AMPK, causing a conformational change that facilitates AMPK phosphorylation at Thr172 by upstream kinases such as LKB1, thereby fully activating the kinase (Efstathiou et al., 2020). Activated AMPK then phosphorylates a series of downstream targets involved in energy metabolism, including acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) and elements of the mTOR signaling pathway. In RPE cells, this activation is particularly important because AMPK phosphorylates and activates ULK1, a kinase critical for initiating autophagy and mitophagy, thereby promoting the clearance of damaged mitochondria (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Chung et al., 2017).

These chemical modifications not only enhance the anti‐inflammatory and anticancer properties but also improve chemical stability and oral bioavailability. The structural design, which incorporates a reversible electrophilic reactivity, underpins the compound’s ability to engage diverse cellular targets (Thomas, 2012; Zhou et al., 2014). Bardoxolone methyl thus represents a chemically advanced, highly potent agent from a class of molecules originally designed to trigger cytoprotective responses via direct electrophilic modulation.

• Therapeutic History  
Bardoxolone methyl has undergone extensive preclinical and early clinical evaluation primarily in fields as disparate as oncology and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Initial studies established that synthetic oleanane triterpenoids, including CDDO and its variants, exert dramatic anti‐inflammatory effects by suppressing inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and cyclooxygenase (COX‐2) expression in activated macrophages (Gatbonton‐Schwager, 2014). Preclinical studies in multiple mouse cancer models and inflammatory conditions confirmed its potent anticancer activity and cytoprotective properties, which catalyzed its progression into human clinical trials (Borella et al., 2019; Nakagami, 2016).  
In the clinical arena, Bardoxolone methyl was advanced through Phase I cancer trials, where its once‐daily oral dosing regimen and pharmacokinetic profile—with a terminal half‐life of approximately 39 hours—were characterized (Thomas, 2012; Nakagami, 2016). More notably, its unexpected ability to improve estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in patients with advanced renal disease, particularly in diabetic nephropathy, led to its evaluation in large Phase II and Phase III trials, such as the BEAM and BEACON studies (Yagishita et al., 2020; Tanase et al., 2022). However, the BEACON trial was terminated prematurely due to an increased incidence of cardiovascular events, including heart failure, highlighting concerns about the compound’s systemic safety profile when used at higher doses or in populations with comorbidities (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012).  
Despite its promising preclinical pharmacology and the breadth of clinical data available in non‐ocular indications, to date there is no direct record in the literature of Bardoxolone methyl being used specifically for the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular degenerative conditions (Schiavoni et al., 2025). Nonetheless, the overall safety and pharmacokinetic properties observed in CKD and oncology trials lend valuable insights for considering drug repurposing across therapeutic areas.

• Mechanism of Action  
Bardoxolone methyl is best known for its ability to activate the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway—a master regulator of cellular defense mechanisms against oxidative and electrophilic stress. Under basal conditions, Nrf2 is tightly regulated by Kelch‐like ECH‐associated protein 1 (Keap1), which serves as an adaptor for ubiquitin ligases targeting Nrf2 for proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl functions as a potent electrophile and interacts with sulfhydryl groups on critical cysteine residues within Keap1. This covalent or reversible Michael addition reaction disrupts the Keap1–Nrf2 complex, thereby stabilizing and allowing Nrf2 to translocate into the nucleus (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).  
Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to the antioxidant response element (ARE) in the promoter regions of a host of cytoprotective genes. This transcriptional activation results in the upregulation of a battery of antioxidant and phase II detoxifying enzymes, including but not limited to heme oxygenase‐1 (HO‐1), NAD(P)H dehydrogenase (quinone 1; NQO1), various glutathione transferases, and glutamate–cysteine ligase subunits (Thomas, 2012; Wong et al., 2016). Studies in non‐ocular tissues have shown that at very low (nanomolar) doses, Bardoxolone methyl robustly engages this cytoprotective program while also exerting dose‐dependent biology wherein intermediate and high doses trigger effects such as modulation of cell differentiation and direct anticancer activity, respectively (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).  
It is important to note that while the canonical targets of Nrf2 activation are well characterized, Bardoxolone methyl’s electrophilic character enables it to interact with multiple regulatory proteins. For example, it can inhibit IκB kinase β (IKKβ), leading to suppression of nuclear factor κB (NF‐κB) signaling and subsequent reduction in proinflammatory cytokine production (Zhou et al., 2014; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although the literature does not provide direct experimental evidence that Bardoxolone methyl specifically upregulates mitochondrial antioxidants such as superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) and peroxiredoxin 3 (PRDX3) in RPE cells, the robust, broad‐spectrum transcriptional response induced by Nrf2 activation strongly suggests that mitochondrial and cytoplasmic components of the antioxidant defense system may also be upregulated (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015). Such upregulation would be consistent with previous findings of increased expression of antioxidant genes and improved cellular redox status upon treatment with similar synthetic triterpenoids (Schiavoni et al., 2025; Sporn et al., 2011).

• Expected Effect in Dry AMD  
The pathogenesis of dry age‐related macular degeneration is multifactorial, with chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction playing a central role in the degeneration of the RPE—a critical monolayer that supports photoreceptor health. RPE cells are particularly vulnerable to oxidative damage due to high metabolic activity, exposure to light, and the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). In this context, the proposed mechanism of Bardoxolone methyl, namely activation of the Nrf2/ARE pathway, provides a biologically tenable strategy for neuroprotection and cellular preservation.  
When administered at low doses, Bardoxolone methyl is expected to trigger a cytoprotective transcriptional program in RPE cells. Activation of Nrf2 should lead to the induction of a range of antioxidant enzymes and detoxifying proteins which together help re-establish redox balance in the face of chronic oxidative insult (Borella et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012). One key hypothesis is that, in addition to the already well‐documented induction of cytosolic antioxidants such as HO‐1 and NQO1, Bardoxolone methyl may also promote the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3. SOD2 is the primary defense against superoxide radicals within the mitochondria, and PRDX3 plays a critical role in detoxifying hydrogen peroxide produced by mitochondrial respiration. Although direct data in RPE cells are currently lacking, studies in other cellular contexts have demonstrated that activation of Nrf2 results in the upregulation of a broad spectrum of antioxidant genes, and it is plausible that under the oxidative duress typical of dry AMD, similar effects would be observed in RPE cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
In vitro models simulating oxidative stress—such as exposure of RPE cells to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)—have shown that compounds with similar electrophilic properties, and indeed other members of the CDDO family like CDDO-Im, reduce the intracellular MitoSOX fluorescence signal, indicative of a reduction in mitochondrial ROS (mtROS) (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024). Moreover, improvements in mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) have been correlated with such treatments, suggesting that these molecules can help maintain mitochondrial function under stressful conditions (Nakagami, 2016; Zhou et al., 2014). Such outcomes are highly relevant in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction in the RPE has been implicated in disease progression. The anticipated outcomes, therefore, include a reduction in mtROS, restoration of Δψm, and subsequent preservation of RPE cellular integrity and function.  
Another positive aspect is the compound’s previously established oral bioavailability and pharmacokinetic profile. Clinical studies in CKD patients have demonstrated that therapeutic plasma concentrations can be achieved with once-daily dosing. Although systemic administration in ocular diseases is not ideal, these data provide a strong pharmacological starting point for repurposing. In addition, if systemic toxicity remains a concern—as suggested by the cardiovascular signals in CKD trials—an alternative approach might involve localized ocular delivery (for instance, via intravitreal injection or by developing an ocular formulation) to achieve high retinal bioavailability while minimizing systemic exposure (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).

• Overall Evaluation  
In assessing Bardoxolone methyl for repurposing as a therapeutic for dry AMD, several critical points emerge that underline both its promise and the challenges that must be overcome.

Strengths:  
1. Strong Chemical Rationale and Potency:  
Bardoxolone methyl is a product of sophisticated medicinal chemistry, designed to overcome the limitations of natural triterpenoids like oleanolic acid by installing reactive electrophilic groups that significantly enhance its potency. This design specifically enables the activation of the Nrf2 pathway—a mechanism central to antioxidant defense—at very low concentrations (Borella et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016). The high potency of Bardoxolone methyl as an Nrf2 activator is a significant advantage, particularly when considering that even subtle improvements in cellular antioxidant capacity can have a profound impact on chronic degenerative diseases like dry AMD.

2. Broad Cytoprotective Mechanism:  
The mechanism of Bardoxolone methyl involves the disruption of the Keap1-Nrf2 complex via covalent modification of Keap1 cysteine residues, facilitating the nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and the subsequent transcriptional activation of a broad range of antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes (Zhou et al., 2014; Thomas, 2012). This broad cytoprotective response is particularly relevant to the RPE, where chronic oxidative stress has been implicated in cellular dysfunction and death. The possibility that Bardoxolone methyl may also induce mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3, although not yet directly confirmed in RPE, is an attractive hypothesis; such an effect would directly address the mitochondrial dysfunction that is a hallmark of dry AMD (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).

3. Extensive Clinical Experience and Pharmacokinetic Data:  
Bardoxolone methyl has been evaluated in several clinical trials—most notably in the context of CKD and oncology—yielding a wealth of pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and tolerability data. Its oral bioavailability, with a terminal half-life that supports once-daily dosing, is well documented (Thomas, 2012; Nakagami, 2016). Although the systemic adverse events observed in these trials (such as cardiovascular-related events) present challenges for broad systemic administration, these data nonetheless offer a useful starting point for repurposing. The established clinical profile can inform dose-escalation studies and safety monitoring protocols should Bardoxolone methyl be advanced into ocular trials.

4. Support from Analogous Preclinical Models:  
Several studies in related models have demonstrated that synthetic triterpenoids can protect retinal tissue from oxidative damage. For example, experiments with CDDO-Im, a closely related analogue, have shown protective effects in retinal ischemia–reperfusion injury, including the attenuation of inflammatory responses and preservation of retinal structure (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024). Although these studies are not directly with Bardoxolone methyl, the mechanistic commonalities within this compound class support the notion that the same protective pathways can be harnessed in the context of dry AMD.

Weaknesses and Challenges:  
1. Lack of Direct Evidence in RPE/Dry AMD Models:  
Despite the strong theoretical rationale, direct evidence that Bardoxolone methyl upregulates mitochondrial antioxidants (SOD2, PRDX3) in RPE cells is currently lacking. Most published data are derived from non-ocular cell types or from studies using other analogues such as CDDO-Im (Cai et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2014). It is therefore essential to perform specific in vitro studies in RPE cell lines under oxidative stress conditions to measure the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes and the functional status of mitochondria (e.g., Δψm, mtROS levels) following treatment with Bardoxolone methyl.

2. Safety Concerns from Prior Clinical Experience:  
A significant challenge in repurposing Bardoxolone methyl stems from its safety profile in systemic indications. The Phase III BEACON trial in CKD patients was halted due to an increased incidence of serious cardiovascular events, including heart failure and increased mortality (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although the mechanisms underlying these adverse effects may be related to systemic fluid retention, off‐target reactivity, or other metabolic perturbations, they raise concerns about the safety of systemic administration. For ocular application, it may be necessary to consider alternative dosing strategies or localized delivery methods to avoid systemic exposure while still achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina.

3. Translational and Formulation Challenges:  
The unique anatomy and physiology of the eye introduce additional obstacles in drug repurposing. RPE cells reside in a relatively immune-privileged, isolated microenvironment behind the blood–retinal barrier. The pharmacokinetics and tissue penetration profiles of Bardoxolone methyl observed in systemic circulation may not directly translate to effective intraocular concentrations. Development of specialized ocular formulations—such as sustained-release intravitreal injections or topical applications that can traverse ocular barriers—will be critical for successful translation (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).

4. Multifactorial Nature of AMD Pathogenesis:  
Dry AMD is a complex, multifactorial disease where oxidative stress is only one component of a broader pathogenic network that includes genetic predisposition, inflammation, lipid dysregulation, and complement system activation. While activation of the Nrf2 pathway can counteract oxidative stress and may have secondary anti-inflammatory effects, it is uncertain whether this single mechanism will be sufficient to alter the course of the disease. A combinatorial therapeutic strategy incorporating Nrf2 activation with other modalities might eventually be required to address the full spectrum of dry AMD pathology (Cheng et al., 2021; Thomas, 2012).

5. Dose-Dependent Effects and Narrow Therapeutic Window:  
Bardoxolone methyl exhibits highly dose-dependent pharmacology. At low doses, it predominantly activates Nrf2 and induces cytoprotective genes; however, as the dose increases, additional actions such as pro-apoptotic and cytotoxic effects emerge (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014). Determining the precise dose that is efficacious in RPE cells without triggering deleterious off-target effects will be crucial. This necessitates rigorous dose-ranging studies in preclinical models to define a therapeutic window that maximizes retinal protection while minimizing risks.

• Overall Evaluation and Recommendation  
In summary, Bardoxolone methyl presents a compelling candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD thanks to its well-characterized chemical design, potent induction of the Nrf2 pathway, and a broad cytoprotective mechanism that addresses many aspects of the oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction implicated in RPE degeneration. The extensive clinical data from studies in CKD and oncology provide a valuable foundation for understanding its pharmacokinetics and systemic effects, while the underlying chemistry ensures high potency at low concentrations—features that are highly desirable when targeting a chronic, degenerative condition such as dry AMD (Borella et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012).  
Nonetheless, significant challenges remain. There is a conspicuous gap in the literature regarding the direct evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl in RPE cells and dry AMD models, particularly concerning its ability to upregulate mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes like SOD2 and PRDX3 and thereby mitigate mtROS damage. This gap must be addressed through targeted in vitro assays and in vivo animal studies that simulate the retinal environment and its chronic oxidative stress. Safety concerns, as evidenced by the cardiovascular events observed in CKD trials, underscore the need for caution; these risks may be minimized through localized ocular administration, but careful formulation and dosing studies will be required to establish an acceptable safety profile in the ocular context (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019).  
Given the current state of evidence, it is recommended that Bardoxolone methyl be subjected to further preclinical evaluation in the context of dry AMD. Specifically, studies should focus on:  
 – Conducting detailed in vitro experiments in human RPE cell lines to assess whether exposure to Bardoxolone methyl under oxidative stress conditions leads to the upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants (e.g., SOD2 and PRDX3) and an associated decrease in mtROS (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
 – Evaluating the effects of Bardoxolone methyl on mitochondrial function (including measurements of Δψm, oxygen consumption rate, and mitochondrial integrity) in these cells.  
 – Adapting ocular-specific formulations that allow high local retinal concentrations with minimal systemic exposure, potentially using intravitreal or topical delivery methods, and conducting pharmacokinetic studies that establish retinal tissue exposure (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).  
 – Testing the compound in animal models of dry AMD to determine whether the in vitro antioxidant and mitochondrial protective effects translate into preservation of RPE and photoreceptor structure and function over time (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024).  
If these studies yield positive results that confirm the hypothesized upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants and improved RPE function, Bardoxolone methyl could then be advanced to early-phase clinical trials in patients with dry AMD. Such trials would need to incorporate rigorous safety monitoring protocols to mitigate the known systemic adverse effects. A potential strategy may involve administering the drug in a localized manner or at doses that are effective in the eye but low enough to avoid triggering systemic electrophilic toxicity.

Overall, Bardoxolone methyl holds promise as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD based on its potent Nrf2-activating properties and the central role of oxidative stress in the disease’s pathogenesis. However, its development for an ocular indication will hinge on its ability to selectively and safely modulate the redox status of RPE cells while avoiding systemic side effects. A stepwise, targeted preclinical program that directly addresses these RPE-specific endpoints is therefore critical before consideration of clinical trials in the dry AMD patient population (Nakagami, 2016).

In conclusion, while Bardoxolone methyl offers a strong mechanistic rationale as an Nrf2 activator with the theoretical capacity to upregulate mitochondrial defenses in RPE cells, further targeted studies are essential. The compound’s repurposing for dry AMD is scientifically attractive given the unmet need for effective therapies in this condition; however, the translational path is complex due to safety concerns observed in systemic trials and the lack of direct ocular data. A rigorous preclinical research plan—encompassing in vitro RPE studies, ocular pharmacokinetic assessments, and animal model validation—will be required to determine whether Bardoxolone methyl can be safely and effectively repurposed to preserve RPE function and slow the progression of dry AMD.

• Summary of Key Supporting Points  
– Bardoxolone methyl is a chemically engineered derivative of oleanolic acid that exploits electrophilic modifications to robustly activate the Nrf2 pathway (Borella et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016).  
– Its extensive preclinical and clinical history in oncology and CKD, though not in ocular disease, provides important pharmacokinetic and biological safety data that may be leveraged, with modifications, for ocular use (Nakagami, 2016; Tanase et al., 2022).  
– Its mechanism—covalent modification of Keap1 and subsequent nuclear translocation of Nrf2—leads to the transcriptional upregulation of cytoprotective genes, and it is hypothesized that this would include mitochondrial antioxidants (e.g., SOD2, PRDX3), which are critical for mitigating oxidative damage in RPE cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
– Preclinical data with related triterpenoids in retinal models support the concept that Nrf2 activation can ameliorate oxidative stress and preserve retinal integrity, although direct data for Bardoxolone methyl in dry AMD are presently lacking (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024).  
– Key challenges include the translation of systemic dosing to ocular delivery, the need to specifically validate mitochondrial protective effects in RPE cells, and the resolution of safety issues exemplified by prior cardiovascular signals in systemic trials (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

• Final Recommendation  
Based on the current literature review, Bardoxolone methyl emerges as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its potent Nrf2 activation, broad cytoprotective potential, and a well-documented clinical PK profile. However, its repurposing for ocular application must be preceded by targeted preclinical studies that corroborate its ability to upregulate mitochondrial antioxidants in RPE cells and to reduce mtROS while preserving mitochondrial function. These studies should also explore ocular-specific formulations and dosing regimens that minimize systemic exposure. Only after thorough validation in these preliminary investigations can Bardoxolone methyl be considered a credible candidate for clinical trials in dry AMD patients. Given these considerations, the candidate warrants further investigation despite the existing translational and safety challenges inherent in repurposing a systemically active electrophilic compound for an ocular indication (Borella et al., 2019; Yagishita et al., 2020; Thomas, 2012).
