Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) is an endogenous indoleamine neurohormone first identified as a pineal product and now recognized to be synthesized in many extrapineal tissues, including the human eye (retina, retinal pigment epithelium [RPE], lens, ciliary body) where it is also delivered via the circulation and acts locally through cognate receptors (MT1, MT2) and the MT3 binding site (quinone reductase 2) (Lundmark et al., 2006; Lundmark et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2024). Ocular melatonin is under circadian control and is produced primarily by photoreceptors, with additional production reported in inner retina and potentially the RPE, consistent with a paracrine neuromodulatory role in retinal physiology; importantly, melatonin synthesis has been localized to mitochondria, linking its biosynthesis directly to the organelle most relevant to retinal oxidative metabolism (Blasiak et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024). Biosynthesis proceeds from tryptophan via tryptophan hydroxylase and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase to serotonin, followed by arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase (AANAT) and hydroxyindole-O-methyltransferase (HIOMT) to generate melatonin, which freely diffuses to act in an autocrine/paracrine manner (Ma et al., 2024). As a chemical class, melatonin belongs to amphiphilic indoleamines; it partitions into both aqueous and lipid compartments, crosses biological barriers (including the blood–retinal barrier), and concentrates in mitochondria, properties that underpin its direct antioxidant, membrane-protective, and mitochondrial-modulatory actions described in multiple ocular contexts (Romeo et al., 2024; Rastmanesh, 2011; Ma et al., 2024).

Melatonin’s pharmacology encompasses receptor-dependent signaling via MT1 and MT2 G protein–coupled receptors (G_i and G_q/11 coupling), and receptor-independent actions as a direct free-radical scavenger with active redox metabolites (e.g., AFMK, AMK) capable of sequential radical quenching (“antioxidant cascade”), allowing a single parent molecule to neutralize multiple reactive species; MT3 corresponds to cytosolic quinone reductase 2 (QR2) and represents a distinct enzymatic interaction relevant to ocular physiology (D’Angelo et al., 2024; Lundmark et al., 2007; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Rastmanesh, 2011). This dual pharmacology (receptor-mediated signaling plus direct ROS/RNS scavenging) provides a mechanistic basis for melatonin’s pleiotropic antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, and mitochondrial-protective effects in the retina and RPE, actions widely reported in preclinical models of oxidative retinal injury, diabetic retinopathy, and nonexudative AMD (Crooke et al., 2017; Diéguez et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Within ophthalmology, melatonin and melatonergic agents have been explored across inflammatory, neurodegenerative, and vascular retinal diseases. Topical melatonin (0.1%) reduced intraocular inflammation and blood–ocular barrier permeability in rabbit uveitis while increasing tear and aqueous antioxidant activity (supporting tolerability and local pharmacodynamic engagement), and multiple melatonin analogs lowered intraocular pressure in glaucoma, with nanomicelles extending hypotensive and neuroprotective effects (Rusciano & Russo, 2024). In diabetic retinopathy models, melatonin reduced retinal oxidative and nitrosative stress, decreased hypoxia-inducible factor-1α and VEGF signaling, protected the blood–retinal barrier, and improved neural survival, aligning with its redox, anti-inflammatory, and anti-angiogenic pharmacology (Crooke et al., 2017).

For macular degeneration, mechanistic and efficacy signals span in vitro RPE studies, in vivo retinal protection in mice, and human observational datasets. A protected in vivo AMD-relevant signal includes a subcutaneous melatonin pellet that preserved visual function and outer retinal structure and limited oxidative stress in a nonexudative AMD mouse model (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Independently, rodent studies demonstrate intravitreal melatonin prevents acute photoreceptor loss (MNU model) by lowering oxidative damage markers (retinal MDA, 8-OHdG), increasing mitochondrial MnSOD and total SOD activities, and reducing photoreceptor apoptosis—evidence of both antioxidant and anti-apoptotic benefits from local delivery (Li et al., 2020). In RPE cell models (ARPE-19), melatonin consistently protected against H₂O₂-induced oxidative injury by lowering ROS and lipid peroxidation, restoring mitochondrial membrane potential, reducing Bax/cytochrome c/caspase-7 activation, and promoting autophagy (increased LC3-II and Beclin-1, reduced p62), with low-nanomolar protective effects blocked by the melatonin receptor antagonist luzindole, implicating receptor mediation at physiologic ranges (Chang et al., 2018; Blasiak et al., 2016).

Emerging ferroptosis-focused work further reports that melatonin rescues Aβ₁₋₄₀–induced RPE degeneration by curbing lipid peroxidation, restoring GPX4 and SLC7A11, and normalizing iron handling, with loss-of-function of MDM2 abolishing protection and positioning PI3K/AKT→MDM2→P53→SLC7A11 as a key axis; in vivo, melatonin preserved RPE structure and ERG responses in Aβ₁₋₄₀ models (Wu et al., 2025). These mechanistic and efficacy themes converge with a high-quality in vivo finding that melatonin “protects the retina from experimental nonexudative age-related macular degeneration” in mice (Diéguez et al., 2020).

Clinical observations are suggestive but not definitive. A large real-world EHR cohort analysis (TriNetX) associated chronic melatonin use with lower incidence of AMD and reduced progression from nonexudative to exudative AMD after propensity matching, while acknowledging potential residual confounding and calling for randomized trials (Jeong et al., 2024a). An editorialized report in JAMA Ophthalmology similarly noted protective associations and biological plausibility (RPE protection, VEGF reduction) while emphasizing exploratory design and the need for confirmatory prospective studies (Jeong et al., 2024b). Earlier case-series reported that 3 mg oral melatonin nightly for three months stabilized or improved macular changes in many AMD patients, but these uncontrolled data lack modern trial rigor (Lundmark et al., 2007; Martínez-Águila et al., 2021). Across aging and AMD, reduced nocturnal melatonin and urinary aMT6s have been documented, providing a pathophysiologic rationale for supplementation in older adults; however, oral melatonin exhibits variable and often low bioavailability, and aqueous/topical formulations must address photostability and posterior-segment delivery challenges (Čolak & Žorić, 2019; Blasiak et al., 2016; Jeong et al., 2024b; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Melatonin’s ocular actions relevant to dry AMD encompass receptor-mediated signaling, direct and indirect antioxidant effects, mitochondrial protection, modulation of apoptosis and autophagy/mitophagy, ferroptosis suppression, and immune/vascular regulation.

- Receptor-mediated signaling (MT1/MT2/QR2): MT1 and MT2 are expressed in retina and RPE; MT1 is present in photoreceptor inner segments and inner retinal neurons, MT2 shows high retinal expression and is reported in RPE, while the MT3 binding site corresponds to QR2, an oxidoreductase implicated in ocular physiology (Lundmark et al., 2006; Lundmark et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2024). In RPE, low-dose melatonin protection against oxidants is blocked by luzindole, indicating MT receptor involvement at physiologic concentrations (≤10⁻⁸ M), whereas higher concentrations (>10⁻⁶ M) exert receptor-independent antioxidant effects (Blasiak et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2018). MT1-dependent signaling maintains mitochondrial function under oxidative stress in RPE, underscoring receptor linkage to mitochondrial homeostasis in relevant models (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

- Direct and cascade antioxidant activity: Melatonin directly scavenges ROS/RNS, including hydroxyl radicals, and via successive metabolism (3-hydroxymelatonin → AFMK → AMK) neutralizes multiple radicals (“antioxidant cascade”), affording broad-spectrum redox control across aqueous and lipid compartments due to its amphiphilicity (Rastmanesh, 2011; Čolak & Žorić, 2019). In retinal tissues it reduces lipid peroxidation (MDA) and oxidative DNA damage (8-OHdG), and its metabolites independently contribute to radical quenching in ocular systems (Li et al., 2020; Romeo et al., 2024).

- Indirect antioxidant signaling (Nrf2, Sirtuins, AKT): Melatonin modulates redox-sensitive transcriptional programs; it maintains or enhances Nrf2 nuclear activity in several ocular contexts (though Nrf2 responses can be model-dependent), leading to upregulation of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutases and glutathione peroxidases; it also engages AKT phosphorylation and related DNA damage responses (Blasiak et al., 2016; Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024). Melatonin regulates sirtuins (SIRT1, SIRT3) which link metabolism to antioxidant gene expression, autophagy, and anti-inflammatory effects, with SIRT1/SIRT3 activation reducing apoptosis and VEGF and promoting autophagy gene programs; modulation is context-dependent but provides additional axes by which melatonin can protect RPE mitochondria and restrain inflammatory signaling (Crooke et al., 2017).

- Mitochondrial protection: Melatonin concentrates in mitochondria, stabilizes the electron transport chain, reduces electron leakage, maintains mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), inhibits the mitochondrial permeability transition pore, and can activate uncoupling proteins; it reduces mtDNA damage and restores respiratory control, thereby curbing ROS generation at its source (Blasiak et al., 2016; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Tong et al., 2022). In vivo retina, intravitreal melatonin increased mitochondrial MnSOD (SOD2) activity and total SOD, aligning with enhanced endogenous antioxidant defenses at the organellar level (Li et al., 2020). In RPE cell models, melatonin preserved Δψm (JC-1/TMRM assays) after H₂O₂ challenge (Chang et al., 2018).

- Anti-apoptotic effects: In ARPE-19 cells, melatonin reduced the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, decreased cytochrome c release and caspase-7 activation, and lowered TUNEL positivity, consistent with inhibition of intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptosis; this aligns with higher Bcl-2 mRNA and fewer apoptotic photoreceptors in vivo (Chang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020). Mechanistically, mitochondrial stabilization, reduced ROS, and modulation of NF-κB/JAK-STAT signaling contribute to anti-apoptosis (Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024).

- Autophagy/mitophagy regulation: Melatonin increases LC3-II and Beclin-1 and decreases p62 in RPE oxidative stress models, indicating enhanced autophagic flux; MT2-mediated inhibition of mTOR and SIRT1-linked transcriptional control further connect melatonin to autophagy and mitophagy, processes essential for RPE proteostasis and organellar quality control in aging (Chang et al., 2018; Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024). Given that impaired mitophagy is a feature of early AMD, pharmacologic reinforcement of autophagy/mitophagy by melatonin is mechanistically aligned with disease biology (Crooke et al., 2017).

- Ferroptosis suppression: Aβ₁₋₄₀–induced ferroptosis in RPE is attenuated by melatonin via PI3K/AKT-driven phosphorylation and activation of MDM2, which inhibits p53; this derepresses SLC7A11, restores cystine import and GSH synthesis, and rescues GPX4 activity, thereby reducing lipid peroxidation, Fe²⁺ accumulation, and mitochondrial ultrastructural damage; MDM2 knockdown abrogates these effects, functionally linking melatonin to the PI3K/AKT/MDM2/p53/SLC7A11 axis (Wu et al., 2025). In vivo, melatonin preserved ERG a-/b-waves and outer retinal integrity after Aβ₁₋₄₀ insult (Wu et al., 2025).

- Anti-inflammatory and immune modulation: Melatonin limits NF-κB activation, reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6), and modulates immune cell phenotypes (e.g., promoting macrophage polarization toward tissue-repair M2), contributing to reduced retinal inflammation; it suppresses nitric oxide synthases and decreases NO, relevant to nitro-oxidative stress (Crooke et al., 2017; Diéguez et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024). In models of choroidal neovascularization, melatonin attenuated angiogenesis via HIF-1α–VEGF inhibition and RhoA/ROCK-mediated macrophage/microglia polarization, suggesting an adjunctive anti-neovascular role even though dry AMD lacks CNV (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2024b).

- Telomere/telomerase and DNA repair: Melatonin modulates telomerase and DNA repair pathways in retinal cells, with reports of stimulated telomerase activity and reduced telomere erosion in senescent contexts, and increased efficacy of oxidative DNA damage removal in RPE, potentially mitigating RPE senescence in AMD (Blasiak et al., 2016; Rastmanesh, 2011).

- Electrophysiologic and circadian effects: Melatonin modulates retinal electrophysiology and ERG amplitude in a dose- and time-dependent manner, interacting with PKC, MAPK/ERK, and cAMP/PKA signaling; while protective effects are seen in nocturnal rodent ERGs, a small human study reported reduced b-wave amplitude after a 10 mg oral dose, highlighting the need for careful dosing and chronotherapy alignment (Lundmark et al., 2006; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Collectively, these mechanisms plausibly converge in RPE to reduce mitochondrial ROS, maintain Δψm, prevent cytochrome c release, lower caspase activation, and support autophagy/mitophagy, aligning directly with the pathobiology of dry AMD driven by oxidative/mitochondrial damage and impaired proteostasis (Blasiak et al., 2016; Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
The working hypothesis—melatonin scavenges ROS and upregulates mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes in RPE, preserving Δψm and preventing apoptosis in dry AMD—is consistent with reported assay-level outcomes in RPE and retina and yields clear, testable predictions.

- In RPE oxidative-stress assays (H₂O₂, cigarette-smoke constituents, Aβ₁₋₄₀), melatonin should reduce intracellular ROS (DCF/CellROX), lipid peroxidation (MDA, C11-BODIPY), and Fe²⁺ accumulation (FerroOrange), while increasing reduced glutathione (GSH), restoring mitochondrial membrane potential (JC-1/TMRM), and rescuing viability (MTT/CCK-8/LDH), effects substantiated in ARPE-19 and primary RPE studies (Chang et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2025).

- Mitochondrial antioxidant enzyme readouts are expected to increase: while direct ARPE-19 measures of SOD2/GPx protein can be added to this program, in vivo retinal data show melatonin increases mitochondrial MnSOD (SOD2) activity and total SOD, and multiple reviews report melatonin-induced upregulation of SOD and GPx in ocular tissues via Nrf2 and related signaling, supporting the enzyme-induction arm of the hypothesis (Crooke et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024).

- Intrinsic apoptosis markers should decline: reduced Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, decreased cytochrome c release, and reduced caspase-7/-3 activation, plus fewer TUNEL-positive nuclei, as already demonstrated in ARPE-19 under H₂O₂ and in photoreceptors in vivo (Chang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020).

- Autophagy/mitophagy engagement should be evident: increased LC3-II and Beclin-1 and decreased p62, with flux confirmed by lysosomal inhibitors; mitophagy markers (e.g., PINK1/Parkin) should be assessed given melatonin’s reported influence on mitochondrial quality control (Chang et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022).

- Ferroptosis control should be demonstrable in Aβ₁₋₄₀ and other ferroptotic stressors: upregulation of SLC7A11 and GPX4, normalization of TFR1/ACSL4/FTH1, reduced lipid peroxidation, and dependence on PI3K/AKT→MDM2→p53 signaling tested by pharmacological inhibitors and siRNA, as shown in recent preclinical reports (Wu et al., 2025).

- Anti-inflammatory and transcriptional endpoints should shift: decreased NF-κB nuclear translocation and pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β), increased Nrf2 nuclear retention and target gene expression, and potential SIRT1/SIRT3 upregulation in appropriate contexts (Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024).

- Functional in vivo correlates should include preservation of ERG a-/b-wave amplitudes, photoreceptor/RPE morphology on OCT/H&E, and reduced oxidative tissue biomarkers (MDA, 8-OHdG) under retinal oxidative/AMD-like stressors, consistent with prior animal studies (Diéguez et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2025).

Receptor expression to support target engagement is well documented in retina and RPE, and dependence on MT receptors can be tested with antagonists (luzindole) and MT1/MT2 knockdown, as low-dose protective effects in ARPE-19 are reversibly blocked by luzindole and MT1 knockdown abolishes mitochondrial protective actions under oxidative stress (Blasiak et al., 2016; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Lundmark et al., 2007). Given circadian regulation, repeated dosing aligned with the retinal clock may be necessary to realize full mitochondrial DNA protection and durable antioxidant responses, as suggested by diurnal pretreatment requirements in ARPE-19 (Rastmanesh, 2011).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic convergence on AMD biology: Melatonin’s combined direct scavenging of ROS/RNS, induction of endogenous antioxidant defenses (SODs, GPxs), mitochondrial stabilization (Δψm preservation, mtDNA protection), anti-apoptotic signaling (reduced Bax/cytochrome c/caspases), and autophagy/mitophagy support addresses core pathogenic axes in dry AMD—oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and defective proteostasis in post-mitotic RPE and photoreceptors (Blasiak et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022).

- Demonstrated efficacy in relevant preclinical systems: Protection of RPE from peroxide and Aβ₁₋₄₀ ferroptotic stress in vitro, and preservation of retina/RPE structure and function in AMD-like mouse models, including nonexudative AMD and acute degeneration models, with robust biomarker changes (MDA, 8-OHdG, SOD2 activity) and ERG preservation (Chang et al., 2018; Diéguez et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2025).

- Receptor and nonreceptor pharmacology: Dual mode of action enables efficacy at physiologic concentrations via MT1/MT2 and at higher local concentrations via receptor-independent radical scavenging, offering flexibility across dosing ranges and delivery routes; MT1-linked mitochondrial protection in RPE provides a direct mechanistic link between receptor activation and Δψm preservation (Blasiak et al., 2016; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

- Anti-ferroptotic axis in RPE: PI3K/AKT→MDM2→p53→SLC7A11 mechanism positions melatonin within contemporary cell-death biology relevant to AMD (lipid peroxidation, iron handling, GPX4), offering mechanistic biomarkers and combination opportunities with iron chelators or GPX4-preserving agents (Wu et al., 2025).

- Favorable endogenous safety rationale and clinical signal: As an endogenous molecule with extensive human exposure for sleep disorders, melatonin has a comparatively favorable safety backdrop; observational EHR data provides a clinically relevant association signal for AMD incidence and progression reduction that justifies prospective trials (Jeong et al., 2024a; Jeong et al., 2024b).

- Translational feasibility with targeted delivery: Topical ocular and nanocarrier formulations can improve posterior-segment delivery, and intravitreal administration achieves retinal protection with measurable biochemical and functional benefits; nanotechnologies address melatonin’s aqueous instability and enhance tissue penetration (Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Li et al., 2020).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Evidence base is predominantly preclinical; clinical efficacy in dry AMD is unproven: Apart from exploratory EHR associations and small uncontrolled case-series, there are no randomized controlled trials in dry AMD demonstrating visual function or structural endpoints with melatonin; reliance on animal models and ARPE-19 limits translatability (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2024a; Jeong et al., 2024b).

- Context- and dose-dependent effects: Nrf2 modulation by melatonin can vary by model, and very high exogenous concentrations can worsen photoreceptor light damage; a small human study showed acute ERG b-wave reduction after 10 mg oral melatonin, indicating potential physiological perturbation at certain doses/times and the importance of chronotherapy and dose finding (Blasiak et al., 2016; Tong et al., 2022; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

- Vascular tone considerations: MT1-mediated vasoconstriction in retinal endothelium could theoretically exacerbate early perfusion deficits in AMD; dose, receptor selectivity, and local exposure will be critical to avoid adverse vascular modulation (Ma et al., 2024).

- Delivery and pharmacokinetics: Oral melatonin exhibits highly variable and often low bioavailability due to first-pass metabolism, and aqueous topical formulations face photostability and posterior-segment penetration barriers; while nanocarriers and intravitreal delivery overcome these, each introduces manufacturing and safety considerations (Jeong et al., 2024b; Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

- Aged tissue pharmacodynamics: Age-related declines in retinal melatonin and potential receptor desensitization could diminish responsiveness to exogenous melatonin in elderly AMD populations; some aging-associated retinal rhythms were not rescued by exogenous melatonin in prior studies (Blasiak et al., 2016).

- Safety window for intravitreal dosing: Although protective effects are demonstrated, at least one report cites retinal cell degeneration at high intravitreal doses, underscoring the need for careful dose-range finding and chronic safety assessment (Ma et al., 2024).

- Product-specific gaps: There is insufficient formulation- and impurity-specific information for Sigma-Aldrich M5250 in ocular contexts, and no product-specific ocular PK/PD has been reported in AMD; stability, excipient compatibility, and photostability data must be generated for any clinical candidate (Ma et al., 2024; Romeo et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Assessment against the team’s hypothesis  
Supportive evidence is strong that melatonin reduces ROS, preserves mitochondrial function, and prevents apoptosis in RPE/retina. Multiple ARPE-19 studies demonstrate decreased ROS, increased Δψm, and reduced intrinsic apoptosis markers (Bax, cytochrome c, caspases) under oxidative stress with melatonin, consistent with maintained mitochondrial integrity and suppressed apoptotic cascades (Chang et al., 2018). In vivo, raised mitochondrial MnSOD activity and reduced oxidative biomarkers after intravitreal melatonin substantiate mitochondrial antioxidant engagement in retina (Li et al., 2020). Upregulation of antioxidant enzymes (SOD, GPx) by melatonin in ocular tissues via Nrf2, SIRT1/3, and AKT pathways is reported in leading reviews and experimental models, even though direct SOD2/GPX induction has not been quantified in RPE in all cited primary studies; this constitutes a tractable validation gap for our planned assays (Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024). Ferroptosis suppression via PI3K/AKT/MDM2/p53 further extends the mitochondrial-protective narrative to lipid ROS and iron metabolism, relevant to RPE stress in AMD (Wu et al., 2025).

Programmatic recommendations  
- Formulation and delivery: Given oral PK variability and ocular delivery constraints, prioritize posterior-segment–targeted strategies: (1) intravitreal melatonin for proof-of-mechanism in large animals (define safety window, ocular distribution, and retinal PD biomarkers); (2) develop stabilized topical nanocarriers (e.g., ethylcellulose, PLGA-PEG, nanomicelles) to improve posterior-segment delivery and residence time for chronic use (Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Jeong et al., 2024b).

- Pharmacodynamic biomarkers: In RPE/retina, quantify Δψm, mitochondrial respiration (OCR), ROS (DCF, MitoSOX), lipid peroxidation (C11-BODIPY, MDA), mtDNA integrity (long-amplicon qPCR), SOD2 and GPX4 protein/activity, Bax/Bcl-2, cytochrome c release, caspase-3/-7 activity, LC3-II/Beclin-1/p62 flux, Nrf2 nuclear localization and target genes, and ferroptosis markers (SLC7A11, GPX4, TFR1, ACSL4, FTH1) with pharmacologic/siRNA controls for MT receptors and PI3K/AKT/MDM2/p53 (Chang et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2025).

- Dosing and chronotherapy: Incorporate diurnal dosing regimens to align with retinal circadian biology; evaluate low-dose receptor-mediated windows versus higher-dose antioxidant windows, avoiding concentrations shown to potentiate phototoxicity (Blasiak et al., 2016; Rastmanesh, 2011; Tong et al., 2022).

- Safety and off-target risks: Monitor ERG under different dosing/time-of-day schedules, retinal/choroidal vascular caliber (given MT1-mediated vasoconstriction), photoreceptor light injury susceptibility under high-dose exposure, and long-term ocular histopathology in repeat-dose studies (Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Tong et al., 2022).

- Clinical translation: Design an adaptive, randomized, placebo-controlled Phase 2 in intermediate dry AMD with multimodal endpoints (SD-OCT GA growth, mesopic microperimetry, dark adaptation, low-luminance VA) and fluid biomarkers (plasma/urine aMT6s, systemic oxidative markers), stratified by baseline melatonin levels and sleep parameters; consider an intravitreal proof-of-concept in high-risk early GA to validate local PD and safety prior to chronic topical development (Jeong et al., 2024a; Jeong et al., 2024b; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Conclusion  
Melatonin is a mechanistically well-justified, low-cost, repurposable candidate for dry AMD: it directly and indirectly controls retinal/RPE redox status, stabilizes mitochondrial function (including Δψm), engages endogenous antioxidant enzymes, prevents intrinsic apoptosis, supports autophagy/mitophagy, and suppresses ferroptosis along a defined PI3K/AKT/MDM2/p53 axis, with concordant protection in RPE and retina across preclinical models (Chang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025). Epidemiologic data add a clinically relevant signal for reduced AMD risk and progression with melatonin exposure, and ocular delivery is feasible with modern formulations, though oral PK variability and aqueous instability pose development challenges (Jeong et al., 2024a; Jeong et al., 2024b; Rusciano & Russo, 2024). Key risks—dose-dependent phototoxicity, potential vasoconstrictive effects, variability of Nrf2 responses, and uncertain responsiveness in aged retinas—can be managed through judicious dosing, chronotherapy, receptor-aware design, and robust safety pharmacology (Blasiak et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Net assessment: advance melatonin into a formal translational program for dry AMD centered on posterior-segment–targeted delivery and rigorous mitochondrial/RPE pharmacodynamic validation, while preparing for a randomized clinical evaluation; the mechanistic breadth and preclinical efficacy merit this investment, contingent on resolving dosing, delivery, and safety windows in aged ocular tissue (Diéguez et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of EPI-743 (vatiquinone) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). This report is organized into five sections: an Overview of the Therapeutic Candidate, a review of its Therapeutic History, a detailed discussion of its Mechanism of Action, an outline of the Expected Effects in the dry AMD context, and an Overall Evaluation of its strengths and limitations.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

EPI-743, commonly referred to as vatiquinone, is a synthetic, short-chain quinone derivative that was designed based on biochemical modifications of naturally occurring vitamin E compounds. Its origin can be traced to the oxidation products of tocopherols and tocotrienols—members of the vitamin E family—which, through oxidative metabolism, yield quinone species. Specifically, EPI-743 is produced when these compounds are oxidized (Cores et al., 2023). Chemically, it belongs to the para-benzoquinone class, a subclass of quinones that are characterized by their fully conjugated cyclic unsaturated dione structure and their capacity for reversible redox cycling. Its design intentionally mirrors that of endogenous mitochondrial mediators such as ubiquinone (CoQ10), but significant modifications have been made to enhance aqueous solubility as well as to confer an extraordinary potency; indeed, experimental evidence indicates that on a molar basis, EPI-743 can be 10³ to 10⁴ times more potent than CoQ10 or even idebenone, another short-chain quinone analogue (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Gueven et al., 2017).

The discovery of EPI-743 originated from a small-molecule screening effort in which candidate compounds were evaluated for their ability to rescue cell viability under conditions of oxidative stress and glutathione depletion. This high-throughput screening methodology identified EPI-743 as a promising redox modulator with strong protective activity, leading to its subsequent advancement into preclinical testing and clinical evaluation by companies such as Edison Pharmaceuticals and PTC Therapeutics (Cores et al., 2023). As a representative member of the quinone drug class, EPI-743 is mechanistically designed to act as an electron shuttle, undergoing a reversible two-electron reduction to its corresponding hydroquinone form—a transformation that lies at the heart of its antioxidant activity and distinguishes it from many classical antioxidants. Because quinones in general have been used both as pharmaceutical antioxidants and as electron carriers in mitochondrial function, the chemical heritage of EPI-743 provides a strong rationale for its use in conditions characterized by redox imbalances (Tinker et al., 2021; Hong et al., 2023).

In summary, the chemical origin of EPI-743 is synthetic, being inspired by vitamin E’s tocotrienol derivatives and subsequently optimized to form a para-benzoquinone structure. Its classification among short-chain quinones places it in a well-studied category of compounds that have been used to modulate cellular redox states in various settings, particularly in diseases associated with mitochondrial dysfunction (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Gueven et al., 2017).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

The therapeutic use history of EPI-743 is predominantly rooted in the context of mitochondrial diseases and other disorders associated with oxidative stress. Preclinically, it has been shown to protect various cell types against oxidative insult in vitro, particularly in experimental models where glutathione levels are artificially depleted. Studies have demonstrated that EPI-743 significantly enhances cell viability under conditions that would otherwise trigger cell death mechanisms such as ferroptosis and apoptosis (Gueven et al., 2017; Cores et al., 2023). Furthermore, the compound has been extensively studied in animal models of mitochondrial dysfunction with evidence suggesting that it supports key mitochondrial functions including electron transport and ATP synthesis.

Clinically, EPI-743 has been investigated in several rare inherited mitochondrial disorders. For instance, initial clinical studies in pediatric patients with Leigh syndrome—a severe neurodegenerative disorder characterized by mitochondrial respiratory chain dysfunction—have yielded promising results. In these studies, treatment with EPI-743 correlated with stabilization or even improvement in disease progression markers and had observable beneficial effects on neurological function (Gueven et al., 2017; Ji et al., 2021). In addition, small open-label studies have been conducted in patients with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON), an inherited optic neuropathy known to involve mitochondrial dysfunction in retinal ganglion cells; such studies indicated that early administration of EPI-743 may arrest disease progression and, in some cases, partially reverse visual loss (Gueven et al., 2017; Hong et al., 2023). Further clinical evaluation has expanded EPI-743’s investigation into other mitochondrial and neurodegenerative conditions such as Friedreich’s ataxia and refractory epilepsy, all of which share common mechanistic ties to oxidative stress and impaired bioenergetics (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

Despite its extensive evaluation in mitochondrial diseases and neurodegenerative disorders, there is no direct evidence in the literature indicating that EPI-743 has been used to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar age-related retinal conditions. There are no published studies that have directly tested EPI-743 in preclinical models of AMD, nor are there clinical trial reports of its use in an elderly population suffering from AMD. Although several quinone-based compounds (for example, idebenone) have been evaluated in ocular diseases, and the pathophysiological overlap between mitochondrial dysfunction and retinal degeneration is recognized, the existing body of literature on EPI-743 primarily focuses on inherited mitochondrial encephalomyopathies and optic neuropathies rather than on common, age-related retinal disorders (Gueven et al., 2017).

Overall, while the clinical track record of EPI-743 in conditions characterized by disrupted mitochondrial bioenergetics positions it as a promising candidate from a mechanistic perspective, its therapeutic history does not yet include any studies directly addressing the multifactorial nature of dry AMD. However, the established ability of EPI-743 to modulate cellular redox status suggests that it might have potential in the AMD setting as well (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

At the molecular level, EPI-743 exerts its effects primarily through its redox activity, a function that is intimately linked to its para-benzoquinone core. This structure allows EPI-743 to participate in reversible redox cycling—a process in which the quinone is reduced to its hydroquinone form and oxidized back to the quinone form as needed (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). The reduction is typically mediated by cytosolic oxidoreductases, most notably NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), an enzyme that is ubiquitously expressed, including in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012). NQO1 catalyzes a two-electron transfer reaction that converts the oxidized quinone into its corresponding hydroquinone. This hydroquinone is not only a potent free-radical scavenger but also plays a crucial role in regenerating the cellular pool of reduced glutathione (GSH) (Tinker et al., 2021; Cores et al., 2023).

Reduced glutathione is the primary intracellular antioxidant, essential for neutralizing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and protecting macromolecules from oxidative damage. In scenarios where ROS overwhelm a cell’s antioxidant capacity—such as during mitochondrial dysfunction or in cells under chronic oxidative stress—GSH levels become depleted and oxidized glutathione (GSSG) accumulates. By facilitating the replenishment of GSH, EPI-743 helps re‐establish redox balance and thus serves as an indirect regulator of oxidative stress (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Tinker et al., 2021). This redox cycling is considered “catalytic” because once the hydroquinone form scavenges a radical or reduces another molecule, it is itself reoxidized back to the quinone, whereupon it can undergo another round of reduction. Thus, even at relatively low concentrations, EPI-743 provides a sustained antioxidant effect.

In addition to its role in antioxidant defense, EPI-743 has been shown to modulate specific redox-sensitive enzymes. For example, its activity has been linked to the modulation of 15-lipoxygenase (15-LO), a key enzyme in lipid peroxidation pathways that can trigger ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death associated with lipid peroxidation. By inhibiting 15-LO activity, EPI-743 may reduce the peroxidative damage to polyunsaturated fatty acids within cellular membranes—a damage process that is especially detrimental in cells with a high metabolic rate such as retinal pigment epithelium (Cores et al., 2023; Kayser et al., 2024). This function is particularly relevant since ferroptosis has been implicated in conditions where oxidative stress is central.

Furthermore, the quinone’s ability to modulate intracellular redox signaling involves its interaction with transcription factors such as nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2). By maintaining a favorable GSH/GSSG ratio and reducing the overall burden of ROS, EPI-743 indirectly helps to sustain Nrf2 signaling, which in turn upregulates the expression of a panel of antioxidant genes. This feedback loop reinforces the cell’s capacity to respond to oxidative challenges. Though direct evidence linking EPI-743 to Nrf2 activation in retinal cells is sparse, the dependency of its action on NQO1—which itself is regulated in part by Nrf2—suggests that such interactions are plausible (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

In summary, EPI-743’s mechanism of action is multifaceted. It directly scavenges ROS via its hydroquinone intermediate, it enhances the reduced glutathione pool and thereby improves the cell’s overall antioxidant capacity, and it modulates lipid peroxidation pathways by affecting 15-LO activity. The reliance on NQO1 for its activation further supports its broad potential, given that NQO1 is expressed in many cell types, including those in the retina. These biochemical properties collectively suggest that EPI-743 has the potential to mitigate oxidative damage in environments where mitochondrial dysfunction and redox imbalance predominate (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect in Dry AMD

Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by the progressive degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium and underlying photoreceptors, a process that is driven in part by chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and the accumulation of oxidative DNA lesions. In the RPE, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is particularly vulnerable to oxidative damage because of its proximity to the electron transport chain and its relative lack of protective histones. One of the most common oxidative modifications observed in mtDNA is 8-oxo-2′-deoxyguanosine (8-oxoG), a marker of oxidative base lesions that can lead to mutagenesis and impaired mitochondrial function. The hypothesis underlying the repurposing of EPI-743 for dry AMD is that its potent redox cycling mechanism can reset the oxidative environment in RPE cells by regenerating reduced glutathione and by supporting NQO1-mediated detoxification, thereby reducing the accumulation of damaging oxidative lesions in mtDNA (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

In an in vitro assay designed to analyze oxidative stress in RPE cells, one would expect that treatment with EPI-743 would lead to several measurable outcomes. First, due to its rapid redox cycling and ability to donate electrons, EPI-743 would be anticipated to reduce intracellular levels of ROS, thereby directly lowering the formation of 8-oxoG lesions in mitochondrial DNA. This effect should manifest as a reduction in the cellular markers of oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation. Second, given the established role of NQO1 in catalyzing the conversion of EPI-743 to its hydroquinone form, and the fact that NQO1 is known to be expressed in RPE cells, the compound is expected to increase the intracellular GSH/GSSG ratio in these cells, further reinforcing the antioxidant defense system (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012).

Additionally, improved mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) function is a key expected outcome. In dry AMD, compromised mitochondrial integrity leads to reduced ATP production and increased susceptibility to cell death. By restoring redox balance, EPI-743 should preserve the integrity of mitochondrial membranes and ensure effective electron transport, ultimately resulting in enhanced ATP synthesis. This restoration of mitochondrial function could be assessed via assays that measure mitochondrial membrane potential, ATP synthesis rates, and oxygen consumption rates in RPE cell cultures challenged with oxidants (Kayser et al., 2024; Tinker et al., 2021).

Moreover, an important aspect of EPI-743’s expected effect is its potential to mitigate ferroptotic cell death pathways. Ferroptosis, driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation, has been implicated in the degeneration of RPE cells. By inhibiting 15-lipoxygenase and curbing lipid peroxidation, EPI-743 could help prevent the execution of ferroptotic cell death in RPE cells—a process that may contribute to the progression of dry AMD (Cores et al., 2023).

Taken together, in an experimental model of dry AMD—whether in RPE cell culture or in an appropriate animal model—administration of EPI-743 is expected to lead to: (1) a significant decline in ROS levels, (2) an increased ratio of reduced-to-oxidized glutathione, (3) preservation of mitochondrial DNA integrity as evidenced by reduced 8-oxoG accumulation, (4) improved mitochondrial bioenergetics as indicated by enhanced ATP production and mitochondrial membrane potential, and (5) inhibition of deleterious lipid peroxidation pathways. The successful demonstration of these effects would serve as strong biochemical and cellular evidence supporting the hypothesis that EPI-743 can protect RPE cells from the oxidative insults characteristic of dry AMD (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

Furthermore, since the RPE is known to express NQO1—an enzyme critical for the activation of EPI-743—the molecular basis for its activity is supported by tissue-specific expression data. This provides additional justification for targeting RPE cells with EPI-743 in the context of dry AMD, where bolstering the endogenous antioxidant systems may have a measurable impact on disease progression (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Tinker et al., 2021).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

EPI-743 stands out as a highly promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD owing to several strengths rooted in its potent redox-modulatory properties and well-characterized mitochondrial protective effects. One of its major strengths is its extraordinary antioxidant potency. As a para-benzoquinone analogue that can be reduced via NQO1-catalyzed reactions to its hydroquinone state, EPI-743 is capable of intercepting and neutralizing ROS with an efficiency that surpasses that of conventional antioxidants such as CoQ10 by three to four orders of magnitude (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Gueven et al., 2017). This high level of potency is particularly appealing for conditions like dry AMD, in which the cumulative oxidative stress has a direct impact on mtDNA damage and cellular energetic deficits.

Another significant advantage is the compound’s established clinical track record in diseases marked by mitochondrial dysfunction. Although its clinical applications have thus far been restricted to rare inherited mitochondrial conditions like Leigh syndrome and LHON, the underlying mechanisms—namely, the restoration of mitochondrial bioenergetics and redox balance through effective GSH regeneration—are equally relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Gueven et al., 2017). Its ability to protect retinal ganglion cells in LHON studies suggests that similar beneficial effects might be extrapolated to retinal pigment epithelial cells, which are critically involved in the development of AMD.

Mechanistically, EPI-743’s dual action—both as a direct antioxidant and as a modulator of redox-sensitive pathways involving 15-lipoxygenase—confers a multi-pronged approach to cytoprotection. By reducing ROS and regenerating intracellular glutathione levels, EPI-743 can potentially arrest the oxidative modifications that lead to deleterious mtDNA lesions such as 8-oxoG. Moreover, the inhibition of enzymes that contribute to lipid peroxidation may further protect cellular membranes and reduce downstream inflammatory responses. These attributes provide a compelling scientific rationale for considering EPI-743 as a therapeutic strategy to combat the chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction associated with dry AMD (Tinker et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be acknowledged. First and foremost, the current therapeutic history of EPI-743 shows no direct evidence of efficacy in dry AMD or other age-related retinal conditions. All of the published studies to date have focused on inherited mitochondrial or neurodegenerative disorders. Therefore, there remains a significant gap in our knowledge regarding its pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics in the context of the aging retina, which has a distinct microenvironment compared to the tissues examined in inherited disorders (Gueven et al., 2017).

Another concern is the potential difference in drug metabolism and toxicity between the predominantly pediatric or young adult populations (commonly studied in mitochondrial diseases) and the elderly patient population that is most affected by dry AMD. Age-related alterations in absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) could impact both efficacy and the safety profile of EPI-743 when repurposed for an older demographic (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Hong et al., 2023). Furthermore, while the activation of EPI-743 via NQO1 is a mechanistically attractive feature, the ubiquitous and sometimes unpredictable nature of redox enzyme activity in different tissues raises the possibility of off-target effects. Chronic systemic administration in an elderly population might result in unforeseen modifications in redox homeostasis not only within the retina but also in other vulnerable organs (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

In addition, the multifactorial pathogenesis of dry AMD poses a challenge to any therapeutic approach that primarily targets oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. While these are certainly key components of AMD pathology, the disease also involves chronic inflammation, drusen formation, and alterations in extracellular matrix homeostasis. It is therefore uncertain whether the powerful antioxidant activity of EPI-743 alone would be sufficient to halt or reverse the progression of dry AMD. Successful treatment may require a combination approach that addresses multiple causative factors, and it remains to be seen if EPI-743 can be integrated effectively into such a therapeutic regimen (Gueven et al., 2017; Cores et al., 2023).

Lastly, the translation from preclinical models—where the compound’s efficacy has been demonstrated in controlled settings of inherited mitochondrial dysfunction—to an age-related, multifaceted disease state such as dry AMD is non-trivial. Preclinical RPE-focused studies, including those measuring ROS levels, mitochondrial membrane potential, and direct assessments of mtDNA damage in the context of oxidative challenges, are currently lacking. Such studies are critical to validate whether the mechanisms observed in other cell types or disease models are applicable to the RPE and to the pathophysiology of AMD (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Conclusion

In conclusion, EPI-743 (vatiquinone) exhibits many characteristics that render it an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its synthetic origin from vitamin E–derived tocotrienol derivatives and its classification as a para-benzoquinone confer upon it a robust redox-cycling capacity, enabling it to function as an exceptionally potent mitochondrial antioxidant. Through its ability to be reduced by NQO1 to a hydroquinone state, EPI-743 effectively regenerates intracellular reduced glutathione while simultaneously inhibiting lipid peroxidation via modulation of 15-lipoxygenase activity. These mechanisms collectively support its potential to protect mitochondrial DNA from oxidative damage, preserve electron transport chain function, and maintain ATP production in highly metabolically active cells such as the retinal pigment epithelium (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

The therapeutic history of EPI-743 in inherited mitochondrial disorders and optic neuropathies provides a valuable proof of concept regarding its efficacy in situations where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central to pathogenesis. However, the absence of any direct study in dry AMD represents a significant gap that must be addressed through focused preclinical research. In the context of dry AMD, where chronic oxidative stress leads to the accumulation of damaging mtDNA lesions (including 8-oxoG) and progressive RPE degeneration, a potent redox modulator like EPI-743 theoretically offers a promising means to break the cycle of oxidative damage and mitochondrial decline (Tinker et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

Notwithstanding its potential strengths, several uncertainties must be highlighted. The pharmacokinetics and safety profile of EPI-743 in an elderly population—where changes in drug metabolism are common—remain to be fully elucidated. Moreover, the complex etiology of dry AMD, which involves not only oxidative damage and mitochondrial failure but also inflammatory and extracellular matrix alterations, may necessitate a multifaceted treatment strategy beyond a single antioxidant approach. As such, while the mechanistic rationale for using EPI-743 in dry AMD is well founded by virtue of its antioxidant and mitochondria-protective properties, clinical translation will require rigorous demonstration of efficacy in RPE-based in vitro systems and in animal models that recapitulate the full spectrum of AMD pathology (Gueven et al., 2017; Cores et al., 2023).

Given these considerations, the repurposing of EPI-743 for dry AMD holds promise—but only with additional preclinical studies that specifically assess its ability to ameliorate oxidative damage in the retinal pigment epithelium. Key experiments should focus on measuring changes in redox biomarkers, mtDNA integrity, ATP production, and cellular viability in RPE cells under oxidative stress. Parallel in vivo studies in animal models of AMD will be essential to determine ocular bioavailability, dosing parameters, and potential off-target effects in an aged organism.

Overall, the strengths of EPI-743 lie in its unparalleled antioxidant potency and its established capacity to restore mitochondrial function in disease settings characterized by oxidative damage. Its mechanism—centered on redox cycling via a para-benzoquinone moiety, glutathione regeneration, and modulation of lipid peroxidation—is directly relevant to the pathophysiological challenges found in dry AMD. However, the primary weaknesses include the current absence of direct evidence in retinal disease models, potential pharmacokinetic concerns in the elderly, and the complexity of dry AMD pathology which may require combination therapy for optimal clinical benefit. Thus, while EPI-743 is mechanistically compelling as a candidate drug for dry AMD, its ultimate clinical utility will depend on the outcomes of targeted preclinical evaluations and, subsequently, carefully designed clinical trials that address the specific challenges of age-related retinal degeneration (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024; Tinker et al., 2021).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Final Remarks

EPI-743 (vatiquinone) presents an attractive therapeutic opportunity given its synthetic derivation from vitamin E, its classification as a para-benzoquinone with exceptionally potent antioxidant capabilities, and its ability to support mitochondrial function through NQO1-mediated redox modulation and glutathione regeneration. Although its historical clinical use has been confined to inherited mitochondrial diseases and optic neuropathies rather than age-related conditions, the underlying pathophysiological similarities—namely oxidative stress and mitochondrial compromise—provide a logical foundation for hypothesizing its efficacy in dry AMD. The expected beneficial actions in RPE cells include reduced accumulation of oxidative DNA lesions, improved mitochondrial electron transport and ATP synthesis, and diminished activation of ferroptotic cell death pathways.

Before any clinical repurposing can be considered, it is essential to perform a series of rigorous preclinical studies. These studies should involve well-characterized in vitro models using RPE cell lines that mimic the oxidative challenges seen in dry AMD. Furthermore, in vivo studies employing animal models that recapitulate the complex pathology of AMD will be crucial to assess ocular bioavailability, efficacy, and safety in a context that simulates the aged human retina. Such investigations will inform dosing regimens and help identify any potential off-target effects or toxicities that might arise in the elderly population, which is inherently more vulnerable due to age-related physiological changes (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012).

In summary, while the available data from mitochondrial and neurodegenerative disease studies provide a robust mechanistic rationale for the use of EPI-743 as a potent redox modulator and mitochondria-protective agent, the leap to a therapeutic indication in dry AMD remains largely theoretical at this point. Nonetheless, the convergence of redox dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and oxidative mtDNA damage in AMD creates a promising target for compounds like EPI-743. With appropriate preclinical validation, EPI-743 could emerge as a valuable component of a combination therapy strategy that addresses the multifactorial nature of dry AMD. This repurposing effort would potentially fill a significant therapeutic gap in a disease area where effective treatments are currently lacking (Tinker et al., 2021; Cores et al., 2023; Gueven et al., 2017).

Given the promising mechanistic profile of EPI-743 alongside the identified gaps in its direct application to dry AMD, we recommend that the next phase in drug development should focus on comprehensive preclinical studies specifically targeting RPE dysfunction and oxidative damage in AMD. These studies will be critical in determining whether the redox-modulating properties of EPI-743 can be harnessed to meaningfully slow or reverse the progression of dry AMD in a clinical setting.

To summarize, the compound EPI-743 (vatiquinone) exhibits several important strengths that justify its consideration as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD:

1. Its chemical derivation from vitamin E derivatives places it in the para-benzoquinone class, endowing it with rapid redox-cycling properties and a potency that is orders of magnitude greater than that of more conventional antioxidants such as CoQ10 and idebenone (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Gueven et al., 2017).

2. Its mechanism of action—rooted in the reversible reduction to an active hydroquinone via NQO1, subsequent regeneration of reduced glutathione, and inhibition of oxidative enzymes such as 15-lipoxygenase—offers a multi-modal approach to addressing the oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction that are central to dry AMD pathogenesis (Tinker et al., 2021; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

3. 1. No current preclinical or clinical studies have directly examined the efficacy of EPI-743 in dry AMD models. 2. 3. 4. Finally, while the in vitro evidence in mitochondrial disease models is promising, definitive studies that measure outcomes in RPE cells—such as reductions in 8-oxoG accumulation, restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential, and improved bioenergetic capacity—are necessary to confirm that the mechanistic rationale translates to the AMD context (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Conclusion

EPI-743 (vatiquinone) is a highly potent, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant derived from vitamin E metabolites and classified within the para-benzoquinone family of compounds. Its design is centered on harnessing reversible two-electron redox cycling mediated by NQO1, leading to enhanced intracellular levels of reduced glutathione and effective mitigation of ROS and lipid peroxidation. Clinically, it has shown promise in mitigating the effects of mitochondrial dysfunction in inherited neurodegenerative and optic neuropathic disorders such as Leigh syndrome and LHON. Based on these properties, its proposed repurposing for dry AMD is founded on the hypothesis that by preventing oxidative damage to the mitochondrial DNA of RPE cells, EPI-743 may halt or reverse some of the degenerative processes characteristic of AMD.

Nevertheless, while its mechanistic profile is compelling, the absence of direct evidence in AMD models and uncertainties regarding its systemic pharmacodynamics in the typical AMD patient population represent significant hurdles. Prior to any clinical application in dry AMD, it is imperative to undertake a rigorous series of preclinical studies focused on RPE cells and AMD animal models. These studies must address not only its efficacy in restoring mitochondrial function and reducing oxidative lesions (such as 8-oxoG) but also its safety and appropriate dosing in aged tissues.

In summary, EPI-743 represents an attractive, yet still unproven, candidate for the treatment of dry AMD. Its unmatched antioxidant potency, combined with established benefits in mitochondrial disease models, provides a strong foundation for further exploration. However, significant additional research is required to bridge the translational gap between the current indications for which EPI-743 has been studied and the complex, multifactorial pathology of dry AMD. Given the extensive unmet clinical need in dry AMD and the promising mechanistic rationale, a targeted preclinical evaluation of EPI-743 in ocular systems is both justified and urgent. Should these studies yield positive results, EPI-743 may well emerge as a key component in a future therapeutic strategy aimed at preserving vision in patients with dry AMD (Tinker et al., 2021; Cores et al., 2023; Gueven et al., 2017).

Based on the current literature and mechanistic insights, the following steps are advised before clinical repurposing of EPI-743 for dry AMD is pursued:

1. Develop and validate in vitro RPE cell culture models under conditions of chronic oxidative stress to assess the direct impact of EPI-743 on mitochondrial bioenergetics, redox balance, and mtDNA integrity.  
2. Conduct in vivo studies using animal models of dry AMD or age-related retinal degeneration to evaluate ocular bioavailability, efficacy in reducing oxidative lesions, and overall retinal protection.  
3. Perform pharmacokinetic and toxicological studies specifically in aged animal models to evaluate how the elderly might respond differently to systemic administration of EPI-743.  
4. Explore combination therapies that might pair EPI-743’s potent antioxidant effects with agents targeting other aspects of AMD pathology, such as inflammation and drusen formation.

Overall, while EPI-743 has not yet been evaluated directly in the context of dry AMD, its biochemical properties, proven efficacy in mitochondrial disease models, and mechanistic plausibility render it a candidate worthy of further exploration. With careful and targeted preclinical experimentation, the repurposing of EPI-743 may eventually provide a novel therapeutic option for a patient population in urgent need of effective treatments (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Tinker et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Closing Summary

In conclusion, the evidence from the biochemical, clinical, and therapeutic literature reviewed herein supports the following: EPI-743 (vatiquinone) is a synthetically derived para-benzoquinone that leverages redox cycling and glutathione regeneration via NQO1 to protect mitochondria from oxidative insult. Its clinical history in mitochondrial disorders provides an encouraging precedent, and its detailed mechanism of action is highly relevant to conditions characterized by oxidative mtDNA damage—such as dry AMD. However, the absence of direct preclinical data in AMD models, along with potential pharmacokinetic challenges in an elderly population, necessitates a cautious yet proactive research program. Overall, the candidate shows significant promise as a repurposed drug for dry AMD, meriting additional in vitro and in vivo studies to fully elucidate its potential in this indication before any clinical trials are initiated (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Gueven et al., 2017; Tinker et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Tat‐Beclin 1 has been extensively characterized in preclinical studies as an inducer of autophagy in various cell types including cancer cells, neuronal cells, and immune cells (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). In early studies, it demonstrated potent autophagy‐stimulating effects by enhancing the transformation of LC3‐I to LC3‐II and by decreasing levels of the autophagic substrate p62, thereby leading to augmented autophagic flux (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013). Moreover, experimental applications have shown that Tat‐Beclin 1 can decrease viral titers in infection models such as those involving West Nile virus and chikungunya virus, and it has been explored for promoting autophagic clearance in cancer models, particularly in breast cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma (He et al., 2022; Gao, 2023). Although there is abundant evidence supporting its utility in managing proteotoxic stress and cellular damage in models of neurodegeneration and cancer, direct applications of Tat‐Beclin 1 for treating dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) have not been explicitly reported (Boland et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2016). Nevertheless, separate studies indicate that proper autophagy in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is critical for cellular viability and resistance to oxidative stress, where impaired autophagy contributes to the accumulation of toxic aggregates such as A2E and lipofuscin that are implicated in AMD (Frost et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Hence, while Tat‐Beclin 1 has not been directly applied in AMD models thus far, its mechanism of promoting clearance of damaged organelles and misfolded proteins provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD treatment.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Tat‐Beclin 1 functions by specifically interacting with Beclin 1, a core component of the Class III PI3K complex that regulates autophagosome nucleation (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). In its inactive state, Beclin 1 is sequestered by negative regulatory proteins such as GAPR‐1, which limits its availability for autophagic initiation. Tat‐Beclin 1 is designed to bind to these inhibitory regulators, thereby liberating Beclin 1 and enabling it to participate in the formation of the PI3K complex necessary for phagophore formation (Ha & Kim, 2016; He et al., 2022). This intervention effectively shifts the balance toward autophagy induction by enhancing the generation of autophagosomes and promoting lysosomal degradation of intracellular cargo. Furthermore, research has demonstrated that Tat‐Beclin 1 increases the conversion of LC3‐I to LC3‐II—a hallmark of autophagosome formation—and has been shown to lower p62 levels, which underscores its role in boosting autophagic flux (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013; Si et al., 2023). Additionally, the peptide’s cell‐penetrating Tat domain facilitates its entry into cells and ensures its functional delivery to intracellular compartments, which is critical for engaging the autophagic machinery even in cells with limited uptake capabilities (Saqcena, 2018; He et al., 2022). Through these molecular interactions, Tat‐Beclin 1 not only enhances general autophagy but has also been reported to drive selective autophagic processes such as mitophagy, thereby promoting the turnover of damaged mitochondria (He et al., 2022; Frost et al., 2014). This mechanistic detail is particularly relevant in conditions of oxidative stress where dysfunctional mitochondria accumulate and contribute to cell death, as has been observed in RPE cells during the progression of dry AMD (Frost et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration, the therapeutic hypothesis posits that Tat‐Beclin 1 will promote autophagy initiation in RPE cells to facilitate the turnover of damaged organelles—including mitochondria—that accumulate as a result of chronic oxidative stress (Frost et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). This enhanced autophagic clearance is expected to mitigate the cytotoxic effects associated with the buildup of toxic aggregates such as A2E and lipofuscin, which are known to drive RPE cell dysfunction and death (Zhang et al., 2015; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Experimental evidence from studies on RPE cells has documented that robust autophagic activity is critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis in the face of oxidative and metabolic insults (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Therefore, by increasing autophagic flux, Tat‐Beclin 1 should theoretically lead to a reduction in cellular stress markers and an improvement in mitochondrial quality control mechanisms, thereby preventing the initiation of apoptotic cascades in RPE cells (Saqcena, 2018). In cellular assays, the expected outcome would include an enhanced LC3‐II/LC3‐I ratio, decreased levels of p62, improved lysosomal function, and ultimately enhanced cell viability under oxidative stress conditions (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013; Si et al., 2023). Notably, the efficacy of autophagy induction in rescuing RPE cellular function is supported by literature where pharmacological activation of autophagy—such as through rapamycin or inhibition of mTOR pathways—has been shown to protect RPE cells from degeneration (Frost et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2020). Given the inherent ability of Tat‐Beclin 1 to stimulate autophagy in other cellular models, it is reasonable to expect that similar benefits would be observed upon its application to RPE cells, leading to a deceleration of dry AMD pathology by maintaining mitochondrial turnover and preventing the accumulation of deleterious substrates.

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall potential of Tat‐Beclin 1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD lies in its well‐defined mechanism of action, which directly targets the autophagic machinery through interactions with Beclin 1 (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). One of the primary strengths of this candidate is its demonstrated versatility across different disease models, where enhancement of autophagy has led to reduced apoptosis, improved clearance of toxic protein aggregates, and mitigation of cellular stress in both cancer and neurodegenerative contexts (He et al., 2022; Boland et al., 2018). In the specific arena of RPE cell biology, multiple studies have established that autophagic dysfunction is a hallmark of AMD progression and that stimulating autophagy can improve cellular resilience under oxidative stress (Frost et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Therefore, by repurposing Tat‐Beclin 1 for dry AMD, there exists a compelling translational rationale based on mechanistic insights derived from both in vitro and in vivo studies in other systems.

However, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be considered. Despite extensive preclinical evidence in other domains, there is a lack of direct experimental data demonstrating the efficacy of Tat‐Beclin 1 in ocular models or in RPE-specific assays (He et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2016). This gap in the literature necessitates rigorous validation in relevant RPE cell culture systems and animal models of dry AMD to confirm that the peptide’s autophagy-inducing effects translate to meaningful therapeutic benefits for ocular health. In addition, the potential for overactivation of autophagy poses a safety concern, as excessive autophagic flux can lead to autophagic cell death or unintended degradation of essential cellular components (Pinelli et al., 2025; Peraro et al., 2017). Precise dosing and delivery strategies will therefore be critical to ensure that Tat‐Beclin 1 achieves a balance between sufficient autophagy induction and preservation of RPE cell integrity. 

Pharmacokinetic and biodistribution challenges also remain to be addressed, especially given the unique anatomical barriers of the eye. Although the Tat transduction domain confers robust cell penetration, the stability, half-life, and clearance of the peptide in ocular tissues have yet to be thoroughly investigated (Saqcena, 2018; He et al., 2022). Moreover, the route of administration—potentially through intravitreal injection or topical delivery—must be optimized to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE without eliciting adverse immune responses or off-target effects. It is also important to note that while the autophagy-stimulating effects of Tat‐Beclin 1 have been well documented in various cell types, the specific context of chronic oxidative stress and metabolite accumulation in the aged RPE represents a distinct microenvironment that may influence peptide efficacy (Frost et al., 2014; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Zhang et al., 2015).

Another consideration is the heterogeneity inherent in dry AMD pathology, where oxidative injury, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammatory processes all contribute to disease progression. Although enhancing autophagy could address multiple facets of the disease, the interplay between autophagic flux and other cellular pathways—such as inflammation and lipid metabolism—remains complex and may necessitate combination therapies for optimal outcomes (Zhang et al., 2020; Pinelli et al., 2025). Nonetheless, leveraging the established protective role of autophagy in RPE cells provides a solid foundation for further research on Tat‐Beclin 1, and its repurposing could represent a novel strategy to counteract the multifactorial stressors associated with dry AMD.

In summary, Tat‐Beclin 1 presents a mechanism-driven approach for inducing autophagy that is grounded in sound biochemical principles and supported by extensive preclinical studies in other disease contexts (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). Its ability to prompt autophagosome formation, enhance mitochondrial turnover, and clear toxic protein aggregates aligns well with the cellular deficits observed in dry AMD, particularly in the RPE. The cumulative literature underscores the therapeutic promise of autophagy-inducing peptides in mitigating oxidative stress and improving cellular viability (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Frost et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2020). However, the lack of direct data in AMD-focused models, potential risks associated with overactivation of autophagy, and the need for refined ocular delivery methods represent critical hurdles that must be overcome through further research. 

Given the potential benefits and the mechanistic rationale underpinning its use, Tat‐Beclin 1 merits further investigation in preclinical RPE models, with attention to dose optimization, delivery strategies, and long-term safety assessments in the context of retinal degeneration. Ultimately, if these challenges can be addressed, Tat‐Beclin 1 could emerge as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD by restoring cellular homeostasis and halting the progression of RPE degeneration. This comprehensive evaluation therefore supports the continued exploration of Tat‐Beclin 1’s therapeutic potential while highlighting the necessity for rigorous validation in ocular-specific experimental paradigms (Frost et al., 2014; Saqcena, 2018; Boland et al., 2018; Frost et al., 2014).
