Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) is a synthetic derivative of fumaric acid that belongs to the class of fumaric acid esters (FAEs) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Chemically, DMF is the dimethyl ester of fumaric acid, with a molecular weight of approximately 144.13 g/mol, and is produced by reacting fumaric acid with methanol in the presence of a strong acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Although fumaric acid occurs naturally as an intermediate in the citric acid cycle, DMF itself is fully synthetically manufactured, conferring the advantages of chemical stability and the ability to precisely modulate its structure to enhance pharmacological properties (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Moreover, DMF is classified as an electrophilic molecule that, due to its α,β-unsaturated ester structure, can covalently modify protein thiols, particularly the cysteine residues within KEAP1, thereby initiating its downstream effects on cellular redox homeostasis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Fumaric acid esters as a class have a long-standing history in pharmacotherapy, originally finding application in dermatology, most notably in the treatment of psoriasis, and have since been repurposed for neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis (MS) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, fumaric acid esters were introduced into clinical practice as antipsoriatic agents in Europe, with formulations such as Fumaderm® entering the market in the 1990s (Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). DMF in particular emerged as a key component in these formulations, and its efficacy in modulating immune responses and suppressing inflammation in skin diseases laid the foundation for its later repurposing in other systemic inflammatory conditions (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Over time, DMF was repurposed and further developed as an oral agent for the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), culminating in its FDA approval in 2013 under the trade name Tecfidera® by Biogen (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163). Clinical trials, including large-scale phase 3 studies, have demonstrated its favorable safety profile and efficacy in reducing relapse rates and slowing disability progression in MS patients (Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 14–16). Although there is no extensive historical record of DMF being used directly for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other primary ocular diseases, recent preclinical findings have indicated that its potent activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway may confer significant protective effects on the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This has sparked considerable interest in repurposing DMF for ocular indications such as geographic atrophy, a late stage of dry AMD, by leveraging its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities observed in nonocular settings (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, DMF functions primarily as a prodrug; upon oral administration it is rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases within the gastrointestinal tract to yield its active metabolite, monomethyl fumarate (MMF) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). The pharmacodynamic actions of DMF principally involve the electrophilic modification of specific cysteine residues—most notably cysteine 151—on Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Under physiological conditions, KEAP1 binds to and retains the transcription factor Nrf2 in the cytoplasm, targeting it for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. However, when DMF covalently modifies KEAP1, it disrupts this complex, allowing Nrf2 to dissociate and translocate into the nucleus (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). In the nucleus, Nrf2 binds to antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoters of numerous genes encoding cytoprotective enzymes, including glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), and various enzymes involved in glutathione (GSH) synthesis and regeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). These molecular interactions lead to enhanced antioxidant defenses, improved detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and overall better maintenance of cellular redox balance (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). In addition to its role in promoting antioxidant gene expression via Nrf2 activation, DMF has been shown to have immunomodulatory properties; it can shift cytokine profiles by increasing interleukin-4 (IL-4)–expressing CD4+ T cells and decreasing the production of proinflammatory cytokines such as interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and interleukin-17 (IL-17) (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Furthermore, DMF has been reported to inhibit nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation in certain cellular contexts, thus contributing to a reduction in inflammatory signaling independently of Nrf2 (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Together, these molecular actions result in lowered cellular oxidative stress and an improved inflammatory milieu, which are critical factors implicated in the pathogenesis of chronic degenerative diseases (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry AMD, particularly the geographic atrophy form, is characterized by the gradual degeneration of RPE cells, which leads to subsequent photoreceptor loss and irreversible vision impairment. Central to the pathophysiology of dry AMD are oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation that progressively compromise RPE viability and function (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). The hypothesis being explored is that DMF, through its robust activation of the Nrf2 pathway, can enhance the expression of ARE-driven genes that encode for antioxidant and cytoprotective proteins, thereby counteracting the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in the RPE (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 13–14). In particular, the upregulation of enzymes involved in glutathione synthesis is expected to increase intracellular levels of GSH, a critical thiol antioxidant that protects mitochondrial membranes and supports cellular bioenergetics (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Preclinical studies in retinal models have demonstrated that DMF can effectively preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and reduce the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β), both of which are hallmarks of RPE distress under oxidative challenge (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Given that the RPE is highly metabolically active and particularly vulnerable to cumulative oxidative damage, the sustained activation of Nrf2 by DMF following oral dosing is anticipated to provide continuous reinforcement of antioxidant defenses and maintain mitochondrial integrity in these cells (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 3–5; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). Moreover, by mitigating inflammatory signaling, DMF may not only protect the RPE but also contribute to a more favorable microenvironment that limits the propagation of cell death signals, thus potentially slowing the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Collectively, these expected cellular effects support the rationale for using DMF as an intervention to preserve retinal structure and function by lowering oxidative damage and supporting bioenergetics in the RPE.

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential of dimethyl fumarate as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD rests on a solid mechanistic rationale combined with an established clinical pedigree in other indications. One of the primary strengths of DMF is its well-characterized pharmacological profile; it is FDA-approved for multiple sclerosis and has been safely administered to thousands of patients over several years, which significantly mitigates the risk and regulatory hurdles typically associated with repurposed drugs (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). The dual actions of DMF—in particular, its ability to both activate the Nrf2 pathway and attenuate proinflammatory signals—directly target the underlying pathological processes in dry AMD, where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central drivers of RPE degeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In vitro studies have provided encouraging evidence that DMF increases intracellular glutathione levels and protects RPE cells from oxidative insults, findings that are directly translatable to the pathobiology of dry AMD (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Nonetheless, several challenges remain. Although DMF is known to be effective in MS and psoriasis, the ocular milieu presents unique pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic challenges that may not be fully addressed by the current oral formulations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18). The rapid hydrolysis of DMF to MMF means that, while the active metabolite does exert therapeutic effects, fine-tuning the dosing regimen to ensure adequate drug levels in the retina while minimizing systemic side effects is necessary (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). In addition, common adverse reactions associated with DMF, such as gastrointestinal discomfort and flushing, though generally mild to moderate, could be more problematic in the typically elderly dry AMD population, necessitating careful monitoring and potentially modified dosing strategies (Camelo, 2025, p. 17; Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13). There is also the question of whether systemic administration of DMF can generate sufficient concentrations in the retina to achieve a meaningful therapeutic effect. While emerging evidence suggests that DMF can cross the blood-retinal barrier and activate Nrf2 in retinal cells (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3), further pharmacokinetic and translational studies are warranted to confirm its retinal bioavailability and the optimal dosing regimen for ocular indications.

Another consideration is the complexity of dry AMD itself, which is a slowly progressive, multifactorial disease with contributions from genetic predispositions, environmental exposures, and systemic metabolic disturbances. It remains to be seen whether the monotherapeutic approach of DMF, targeting primarily oxidative stress via Nrf2 activation, will be sufficient to halt or reverse disease progression, or whether combination therapies will ultimately be required (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Furthermore, while the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms of DMF are well supported by in vitro data and animal studies, there is still limited clinical data on its efficacy in ocular disease settings. Early-phase clinical trials aimed at evaluating DMF in geographic atrophy have to rigorously assess both structural outcomes (e.g., changes in the area of atrophy) and functional endpoints (e.g., visual acuity, retinal sensitivity) to establish its therapeutic benefit in dry AMD (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Despite these limitations, the strengths of DMF are compelling. The drug’s ability to upregulate a broad spectrum of cytoprotective genes via the Nrf2 pathway makes it a versatile candidate for mitigating the oxidative and inflammatory stress that drives RPE degeneration. The fact that DMF has already cleared extensive regulatory and clinical safety evaluations in nonocular indications is a significant advantage, as it greatly accelerates the translational pathway compared to a novel chemical entity (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Additionally, the repurposing of an already approved drug leverages existing manufacturing, formulation, and distribution infrastructure, favorably impacting the cost and timeline associated with drug development (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

In summary, the comprehensive literature review supports the potential of DMF to serve as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its mechanism of action—centered on Nrf2 activation leading to enhanced antioxidant capacity along with anti-inflammatory effects—directly addresses the key pathophysiological mechanisms implicated in dry AMD. The extensive clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis provides a reliable safety and tolerability framework, which is crucial for rapid repositioning into a new clinical area such as geographic atrophy (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). However, it is essential to conduct targeted preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials specifically in ocular disease models to optimize dosing, confirm retinal delivery, and demonstrate clinical efficacy before advancing to larger randomized controlled trials (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Overall, while challenges remain regarding optimal application in the retinal context and potential side effects in an older patient population, DMF—by virtue of its dual antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms and robust clinical background—stands as a viable candidate that merits further investigation for the treatment of dry AMD.

Given the current evidence, the following recommendations are proposed for advancing DMF as a candidate for dry AMD:  

1. Conduct detailed pharmacokinetic studies in animal models to assess the retinal bioavailability of DMF and its active metabolite MMF following systemic administration. This should include studies comparing different dosing schedules and formulations to optimize retinal exposure without exacerbating systemic adverse effects (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2).

Develop and validate preclinical models of dry AMD that recapitulate the key features of human geographic atrophy, with a focus on evaluating the efficacy of DMF in protecting RPE cells against oxidative stress and preserving mitochondrial function (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

3. Investigate the potential benefits of combining DMF with other therapeutic agents that target complementary pathways in dry AMD. For example, agents that modulate complement activation or improve choroidal blood flow may synergize with the Nrf2-mediated antioxidant mechanism of DMF (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).  

4. Initiate early-phase clinical trials in patients with geographic atrophy to establish proof of concept. 5. Carefully monitor the safety profile of DMF in the elderly population, as the incidence of gastrointestinal side effects and lymphopenia may differ compared to the population with MS. Consider the feasibility of modified-release formulations or alternative routes of administration (e.g., topical ocular delivery) to minimize systemic side effects while maximizing retinal drug concentrations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18).

Overall, the repurposing of dimethyl fumarate for dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a robust mechanistic framework and a significant body of preclinical and clinical data generated in other indications. Its capacity to activate the Nrf2 pathway, enhance mitochondrial glutathione synthesis, and modulate inflammatory responses in RPE cells directly addresses several pivotal aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). While there are challenges regarding optimal retinal delivery and management of systemic adverse effects, the clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis lends considerable support to its translational potential. Consequently, dimethyl fumarate represents a well‐justified and attractive therapeutic candidate for further exploration in the treatment of dry AMD, warranting additional preclinical optimization and clinical investigation to fully define its role in preserving visual function in patients affected by this progressive degenerative disease (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Deferiprone is a synthetic iron‐chelating agent originally developed for the treatment of transfusional iron overload disorders, particularly in patients with thalassemia major. It belongs to the hydroxypyridinone class of therapeutic compounds and is characterized by its low molecular weight and lipophilic nature, features that allow it to penetrate cell membranes and cross the blood–brain and blood–retinal barriers (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). Chemically, deferiprone is a bidentate ligand that interacts with iron by coordinating via its hydroxypyridinone groups, forming a neutral complex in a 3:1 stoichiometry with ferric iron (Fe3+), although some studies note its affinity for both Fe3+ and Fe2+ under certain conditions (Li et al., 2023). The synthetic origins of deferiprone involve chemical design strategies aimed at generating small, orally active chelators with selective affinity for iron over other metals such as zinc, copper, and aluminium (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). As a member of the iron chelator drug class, deferiprone’s established use in treating systemic iron overload syndromes has provided it with a significant clinical track record over several decades, forming the basis for its repurposing in disorders where iron-induced oxidative damage plays a role.  

Therapeutic History:  
Deferiprone has been used clinically as an orally administered iron chelator in the management of transfusional iron overload, notably in patients with thalassemia major. This usage is supported by multiple clinical studies and reviews that address both its efficacy in reducing systemic iron burden as well as its associated hematologic risks, such as agranulocytosis and neutropenia, which occur in approximately 1% of patients (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). Beyond its systemic application, preclinical models have demonstrated deferiprone’s potential for retinal protection. Several animal studies report that deferiprone, when administered systemically, can reduce retinal and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) iron levels in models of iron overload or light-induced degeneration and produce improvements in oxidative stress markers and retinal functional indices (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). Although deferiprone has not been widely tested or approved specifically for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar ocular conditions in clinical trials, its documented experimental benefits in animal retinal models along with its established clinical safety profile in iron overload therapy have prompted its consideration for repurposing in dry AMD where iron-induced oxidative injury is implicated (Shahandeh et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2021; Ueda et al., 2018).  

Mechanism of Action:  
Deferiprone functions primarily by chelating labile iron, thereby limiting the pool of redox active iron that can participate in the Fenton reaction—a process in which ferrous iron (Fe2+) reacts with hydrogen peroxide to produce highly reactive hydroxyl radicals. The molecular mechanism of deferiprone is based on its bidentate hydroxypyridinone structure that binds Fe3+ to form a stable neutral complex in a 3:1 chelator to iron ratio, a coordination chemistry that has been well documented in several studies (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). This complex formation effectively reduces the availability of free iron in the intracellular labile iron pool, thereby diminishing iron-catalyzed reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. In addition, some data suggest that deferiprone may also interact with ferrous iron under certain conditions, contributing further to its antioxidant effects by interrupting redox cycling associated with both Fe3+ and Fe2+ species (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021).  

From a biochemical standpoint, iron accumulation in the RPE and surrounding retinal tissues is known to promote lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial oxidative stress, leading to cellular dysfunction and death—a pathomechanism observed in dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). Deferiprone’s cell permeability and ability to traverse biological barriers enables it to access the intracellular compartments, including mitochondria. Although direct studies examining deferiprone’s effect specifically on RPE mitochondrial iron pools are still limited, evidence from other systems (such as neuronal and cardiac tissues) demonstrates that reducing mitochondrial iron load can preserve electron transport chain (ETC) integrity by preventing the formation of deleterious hydroxyl radicals that otherwise damage mitochondrial lipids, proteins, and DNA (Li et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023). Furthermore, preclinical models of retinal injury have shown that deferiprone treatment leads to a reduction in oxidative stress markers, including decreased malondialdehyde (MDA) levels and a concomitant increase in antioxidants such as glutathione (GSH), which supports the hypothesis that iron chelation by deferiprone interrupts the cascade of iron-mediated oxidative damage (Shahandeh et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2025). There is also emerging evidence that iron chelators like deferiprone can mitigate cell death pathways such as ferroptosis and parthanatos in retinal tissues, contributing to neuroprotective outcomes (Villarejo-Zori et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025). In summary, the mechanism of action of deferiprone is multifaceted: it directly reduces the labile iron concentration, thereby lowering the potential for Fenton chemistry, indirectly stabilizes mitochondrial function, and may influence downstream iron-dependent cellular pathways that are implicated in retinal degeneration (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2025).  

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of deferiprone for dry AMD is that chelation of labile iron in RPE mitochondria will prevent Fenton reaction–mediated ROS formation and maintain the integrity of the ETC. In the proposed assay and eventual clinical application, treatment with deferiprone is expected to significantly reduce intracellular labile iron, thereby attenuating oxidative stress that leads to lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial dysfunction. This, in turn, should result in a lower rate of RPE cell death and preserve photoreceptor viability, thereby potentially slowing the progression of dry AMD (Liu et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023).  

Experimental studies have shown that oral administration of deferiprone in animal models results in a measurable decrease in retinal iron load without causing retinal toxicity—a finding that is pivotal for any drug intended for chronic ophthalmic use (Zhao et al., 2025; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). In parallel, in vitro studies using retinal cells such as ARPE-19 have demonstrated that deferiprone reduces markers of oxidative stress, including lower MDA levels and preservation of antioxidant enzyme activities (for example, GPX4 upregulation), which are indicative of reduced ROS-mediated damage (Yang et al., 2025; Shahandeh et al., 2020). The proposed mechanism of action implies that by decreasing the availability of iron necessary for Fenton chemistry, deferiprone will decrease the production of hydroxyl radicals, thus protecting mitochondrial membranes and proteins integral to the ETC from oxidative damage (Li et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023). Moreover, since mitochondrial dysfunction is a known contributor to RPE degeneration in dry AMD, its preservation via iron chelation is expected to sustain cellular ATP production and overall cell viability (Zhao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). Given that the RPE expresses iron regulatory proteins and that dysregulated iron metabolism has been observed in AMD retinas (with increased ferritin and altered transferrin receptor expression), the application of deferiprone would ideally restore homeostasis in the labile iron pool and thereby ameliorate the chronic oxidative insult observed in dry AMD (Li et al., 2023; Ashok et al., 2021).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Deferiprone presents several strengths as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD therapy. Firstly, its well-established clinical use in treating systemic iron overload confers a robust foundation regarding its pharmacokinetics, dosing parameters, and safety profile—despite noted hematologic risks such as agranulocytosis that occur in a small percentage of patients (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). Its oral bioavailability and ability to cross the blood–retinal barrier make it uniquely suited for targeting intracellular iron in the retina (Li et al., 2023). Secondly, there is compelling preclinical evidence from various retinal degeneration models that iron chelators, including deferiprone, can reduce retinal iron accumulation, diminish oxidative stress, and improve functional outcomes, which supports the rationale for its repurposing in the context of dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016; Zhao et al., 2025). Thirdly, its mode of action—chelating labile iron to prevent Fenton reaction–mediated ROS production—directly targets a central pathological mechanism implicated in dry AMD. The hypothesis that reducing mitochondrial iron load will preserve ETC integrity is biologically plausible given the importance of iron-catalyzed oxidative stress in mitochondrial dysfunction within the RPE (Li et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023).  

On the other hand, several weaknesses and uncertainties remain. Although deferiprone’s effectiveness in reducing systemic and retinal iron overload has been demonstrated in animal models, direct evidence of its capacity to specifically target RPE mitochondrial iron and preserve ETC function in human RPE cells is currently limited (Zhao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023). The precise molecular details regarding how deferiprone modulates mitochondrial iron trafficking, and how this relates to the functional maintenance of the electron transport chain, require further investigation. Additionally, while preclinical data are supportive, deferiprone has not yet been tested in clinical trials specifically for dry AMD, and its long-term safety and efficacy in the ocular context remain to be established (Zhao et al., 2021; Ueda et al., 2018). Another consideration is the risk of adverse systemic effects, such as neutropenia and agranulocytosis, which, although infrequent, could limit its utility in a population of elderly patients with dry AMD who may have co‐morbidities (Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). Moreover, some reports have suggested that under low concentrations or certain conditions, iron chelators might paradoxically participate in free radical formation, necessitating precise dose titration and careful monitoring (Li et al., 2023; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016).  

In summary, deferiprone appears to be a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its well-documented ability to chelate labile iron, its favorable pharmacologic properties including oral bioavailability and tissue penetration, and preclinical evidence showing retinal protection. Its mechanism of action—reducing the labile iron pool to limit Fenton reaction–induced oxidative stress—addresses a central pathogenic mechanism of dry AMD, namely, iron accumulation leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and lipid peroxidation in the RPE (Zhao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). However, the extrapolation of these preclinical findings to human dry AMD requires additional studies, particularly those that directly measure mitochondrial iron dynamics and ETC activity in RPE cells following deferiprone treatment. Rigorous dose-ranging and safety studies will also be necessary to mitigate the risk of hematologic adverse effects. Therefore, while deferiprone has significant potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD, further preclinical mechanistic studies and early-phase clinical trials are essential to fully validate its efficacy and safety in this new therapeutic context (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Ueda et al., 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
A-438079 is a synthetic small-molecule antagonist of the purinergic P2X7 receptor (P2X7R) originating from Abbott Laboratories’ disubstituted tetrazole series discovered by high-throughput screening and refined by structure–activity relationship (SAR) optimization within a 1-benzyl-5-aryltetrazole chemotype (tetrazole > triazole > pyrazole/imidazole in potency) (Romagnoli et al., 2008; Carroll et al., 2009). A-438079’s structure has been disclosed as 3-((5-(2,3-dichlorophenyl)-1H-tetrazol-1-yl)methyl)pyridine, capturing the two key medicinal chemistry decisions that produced a selective, drug-like P2X7 antagonist: (i) a conserved 2,3-dichlorophenyl “left-hand” aryl that supports potency and (ii) installation of a 3-pyridyl “right-hand” substituent to overcome the solubility liabilities of the original 1-benzyl-5-aryltetrazoles while maintaining submicromolar activity at human/rat P2X7 (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; Romagnoli et al., 2008; Carroll et al., 2009). Functionally, A-438079 is a reversible, competitive P2X7 antagonist that inhibits BzATP-stimulated calcium flux, P2X7-associated macropore formation, and downstream IL-1β release in macrophage-lineage systems, consistent with canonical P2X7 pharmacology linked to NLRP3 inflammasome activation (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007). Cross-source potency data place A-438079 in the mid-nanomolar to low-submicromolar range at human and rat P2X7: human P2X7 pIC50 values of ~6.3–6.9, rat P2X7 pIC50 ~6.5, and functional IC50 estimates of ~0.1 µM (rat) and ~0.3 µM (human), with high selectivity against other P2 subtypes (e.g., P2X7 IC50 0.06 µM vs >100 µM for other subtypes in one panel) (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; El Idrissi et al., 2024; Nagy, 2013). A-438079 was commercialized by Tocris (circa 2008) as a first widely available, selective P2X7 antagonist probe, enabling consistent interrogation of P2X7 biology in vitro and in vivo beyond earlier nonselective tools (e.g., KN-62, Evans Blue) (Felix et al., 2012). Within the broader class, many P2X7 antagonists have reached advanced preclinical characterization; multi-parameter tables in retinal disease–focused reviews list A-438079 as active at human/rat P2X7 with a reported brain:plasma ratio near 2.0 (suggesting central barrier penetration) and note that progress toward ocular/CNS indications has been limited by species specificity and insufficient barrier penetration for some chemotypes (Fletcher et al., 2019).  

Therapeutic History  
A-438079 and related Abbott “A-series” P2X7 antagonists established robust preclinical efficacy in neuropathic and inflammatory pain models, aligning with the role of P2X7-driven IL-1β/IL-18 signaling in nociception and neuroinflammation (Carroll et al., 2009). A-438079 reduced mechanical allodynia in the Chung and Bennett rat models, showed activity in vincristine neuropathy and the formalin persistent pain test, and inhibited evoked and spontaneous spinal neuronal firing in vivo without motor impairment (rotarod) at high i.p. doses, supporting a favorable preclinical therapeutic index in pain paradigms (Carroll et al., 2009). Beyond pain, class summaries attribute anti-seizure effects to A-438079 in a mouse intra-amygdala kainic acid model, situating P2X7 antagonism within a broader CNS neuroinflammation–linked efficacy landscape (Gelin et al., 2020).  

Human cell assays demonstrate that A-438079 and closely related antagonists abolish ATP-induced P2X7 pore function (ethidium or YO-PRO uptake) yet spare phagocytic uptake in CD14+ human monocytes, indicating that P2X7’s pro-inflammatory macropore function can be selectively blocked while preserving innate scavenger activity; this pharmacological dissociation is a core objective for neurodegenerative/retinal indications where loss of phagocytosis may worsen pathology (Gu & Wiley, 2018).  

Clinically, the P2X7 antagonist class has mixed outcomes in peripheral inflammatory diseases: randomized Phase 2 trials in rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn’s disease failed to meet objective inflammation endpoints (ACR20, CRP), although AZD9056 showed symptom benefit (abdominal pain, mental component score) in Crohn’s disease; no P2X7 antagonist has been trialed in neurodegenerative indications to date, and none has entered clinical testing specifically for ocular/retinal diseases (Gu & Wiley, 2018; Fletcher et al., 2019). Nevertheless, the latest brain-penetrant small molecules (e.g., JNJ55308942, JNJ5417446) demonstrate oral brain exposure and dose-dependent suppression of IL-1β release in stimulated whole blood/PBMCs in humans, suggesting that pharmacodynamic endpoints and barrier penetration necessary for CNS/retinal therapy are tractable within this target class (Fletcher et al., 2019).  

Retinal and AMD-relevant preclinical evidence for P2X7 antagonism is substantial at the class level. P2X7 is expressed across retinal compartments including RPE, photoreceptors, bipolar/horizontal/amacrine neurons, retinal ganglion cells, Müller glia, and microglia in mouse, rat, and human; functional agonism (e.g., BzATP) modulates retinal responses that are attenuated in P2X7-null mice, confirming a functional purinergic ATP/P2X7 axis in vivo (Fletcher et al., 2019). Sustained elevations of extracellular ATP are documented in ocular disease (e.g., human chronic glaucoma aqueous humor), and endogenous ATP mediates acute RGC injury following intraocular pressure spikes in rodents; degrading ATP or blocking P2X7 prevents RGC injury in vivo, demonstrating disease-relevant ATP surges capable of activating P2X7 in the retina (Fletcher et al., 2019). AMD-relevant biology includes high vitreous ATP, P2X7-dependent NLRP3 inflammasome activation by Alu RNA in geographic atrophy (GA) models, and P2X7-driven Ca2+-dependent apoptosis in RPE, together implicating P2X7 as a key upstream activator of inflammasome-mediated retinal degeneration (Calzaferri et al., 2020).  

For A-438079 specifically, a curated review table lists it among P2X7 antagonists evaluated in retinal contexts including ARPE-19 RPE cells, C57BL/6J mouse retinal degeneration models (e.g., MNU), and human pericytes, with endpoints encompassing NLRP3/IL-1β signaling, VEGF, ROS, ZO-1 barrier integrity, NF-κB activation, and apoptosis; outcomes are usually protective though model- and endpoint-specific variability exists (Li & Wang, 2025). In allied class work, selective P2X7 blockade with A-740003 in ARPE-19 cells and C57BL/6 mice exposed to oxidized LDL reduced ROS, suppressed NLRP3 inflammasome and NF-κB activation, decreased IL-1β/IL-18 and proangiogenic factors (VEGF, HIF-1α), alleviated retinal neovascularization, and preserved ERG amplitudes, anchoring mechanistic and functional retinal benefits to P2X7 antagonism (Yang et al., 2021). More broadly, P2X7 antagonists have protected retinal ganglion cells in chronic ocular hypertension by inhibiting microglial activation and reversed hyperpermeability and VEGF/IL-6 increases in diabetic retinal models, indicating barrier and neuroinflammatory benefits that are relevant to AMD pathophysiology (Li & Wang, 2025). Finally, in AMD-relevant disease models, P2X7 antagonists suppressed clinical symptoms of GA and CNV in animals; however, complete genetic ablation yielded mixed results (e.g., P2X7−/− protected from GA but not laser-induced CNV), emphasizing the need to preserve beneficial scavenger functions while blocking pro-inflammatory pore signaling (Gu & Wiley, 2018).  

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, P2X7 is a trimeric, low-sensitivity ATP-gated cation channel that mediates Na+, Ca2+, and K+ fluxes and, upon sustained or high agonist exposure, transitions into a large nonselective macropore permeable to molecules up to ~900 Da (e.g., YO-PRO-1), a state tightly coupled to K+ efflux and subsequent NLRP3 inflammasome activation with maturation/release of IL-1β and IL-18 (Fletcher et al., 2019). Two main routes connect P2X7 activity to IL-1β biology: (i) pore-dependent K+ efflux promotes inflammasome assembly and caspase-1 activation to process pro-IL-1β/pro-IL-18; and (ii) P2X7-mediated Ca2+ influx contributes to NF-κB activation and transcriptional priming of inflammasome components and pro-cytokines, forming the two-signal paradigm required for IL-1β/IL-18 maturation and pyroptosis (Calzaferri et al., 2020).  

In the retinal pigment epithelium, extracellular ATP is a canonical danger-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) produced by stressed/dying cells; ARPE-19 cells themselves release ATP and exhibit P2X7- and pannexin-1 (Panx1)-linked mechanisms that drive NLRP3 inflammasome activation, caspase-1 cleavage, gasdermin D pore formation, and secretion of IL-1β/IL-18, pathways that converge on inflammatory and pyroptotic injury of RPE (Youn, 2024). P2X7 functionally recruits Panx1, facilitating ATP and solute release that amplifies local ATP and P2X7 activation; in ARPE-19 cells, 25-hydroxycholesterol triggers P2X7-dependent YO-PRO uptake that is sensitive to Panx1 blockade (probenecid), indicating a Panx1-dependent pore component in RPE injury (Yang, 2017). P2X7 activation is also linked to mitochondrial distress, including cytochrome-c release and activation of executioner caspases (3/8/9), mechanistically tying the receptor to ROS (including mitochondrial ROS) and apoptotic/mixed death cascades relevant to retinal degeneration (Unknown Reference).  

Retinal localization and disease relevance are broad. Multiple P2X7 splice variants are present in the retina (with at least one common knockout deleting only the full-length variant), and P2X7 is reported in neurons (photoreceptors, amacrine, ganglion cells), glia (microglia, Müller cells), and RPE across species; application of BzATP modulates retinal responses that are attenuated in P2X7-null mice, and genetic/clinical associations link P2X7/P2X4 variants to advanced AMD risk (Fletcher et al., 2019). In ARPE-19 and native/cultured human RPE, P2X7 is expressed at mRNA and protein levels, and it is the only P2X subtype that requires high ATP for activation—conditions that occur during retinal injury/inflammation and are observed in ocular fluids in disease (note: P2X4 can be more abundant than P2X7 in ARPE-19 at baseline, which can shape net purinergic responses) (Youn, 2024).  

Within this mechanistic framework, A-438079 engages P2X7 as a reversible, competitive antagonist, blocking ATP/BzATP-evoked channel activation and macropore formation; by doing so, it suppresses P2X7-mediated Ca2+ influx and K+ efflux that are required for NF-κB priming and NLRP3 activation, respectively, leading to reduced caspase-1 cleavage and decreased maturation/secretion of IL-1β/IL-18 (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; Fletcher et al., 2019; Calzaferri et al., 2020). In macrophage-lineage systems and fresh human monocytes, A-438079 or closely related antagonists abolish P2X7 pore function and IL-1β release but preserve phagocytosis, directly supporting a therapeutic goal in neurodegeneration/retinal disease to block pro-inflammatory pore/inflammasome signaling while sparing scavenger functions that may be beneficial for debris clearance (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; Gu & Wiley, 2018).  

Expected Effect  
Assay context: ATP-challenged ARPE-19 monolayers are expected to exhibit P2X7-mediated Ca2+ influx, macropore formation (with Panx1 participation), and K+ efflux that jointly drive NLRP3 priming and activation, caspase-1 cleavage, gasdermin D pore formation, and secretion of IL-1β/IL-18; these events coincide with increased ROS (including mitochondrial contributions), NF-κB activation (IκBα phosphorylation/degradation), disruption of tight junctions (e.g., ZO-1 discontinuities), reduced transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), and death by apoptosis and pyroptosis (Youn, 2024; Fletcher et al., 2019).  

Given A-438079’s pharmacology and the retinal/RPE biology summarized above, the expected effects under the team’s hypothesis are:

– P2X7 expression and activation thresholds: ARPE-19 and native/cultured human RPE express P2X7, but P2X4 can be more abundant in ARPE-19; P2X7 requires high extracellular ATP, which is characteristic of tissue injury and documented in ocular disease, but purinergic signaling may involve multiple receptor subtypes under some stimuli (Youn, 2024).

A-438079 is a mechanistically precise, well-characterized P2X7 antagonist whose potency, selectivity, and competitive reversible mechanism directly address an ATP→P2X7→Ca2+/K+→NLRP3→caspase-1→IL-1β/IL-18 inflammatory axis repeatedly implicated in RPE stress and dry AMD–relevant degeneration.

– Limited A-438079-specific retinal datasets: Most strong retinal evidence is at the class level or with close analogues (e.g., A-740003); A-438079’s quantitative effects on ARPE-19 TEER, mtROS, caspase-1 cleavage, and cytokines under ATP or disease-mimetic stimuli require dedicated experiments to confirm the proposed hypothesis (Yang et al., 2021; Li & Wang, 2025).  
– Dual P2X7 biology: Genetic ablation studies show protection in some contexts (GA) but not others (laser CNV), and can worsen outcomes in select neurodegeneration models, consistent with loss of P2X7’s beneficial scavenger function; pharmacology must be titrated to block pore/inflammasome function while preserving phagocytosis (Gu & Wiley, 2018).

– Ocular PK/PD unknowns: No direct data are provided on A-438079 retinal exposure, intraocular target engagement, or active efflux across the blood–retinal barrier; formulation and local delivery strategies may be needed to ensure adequate ocular exposure (Fletcher et al., 2019).

– Clinical precedent: Class-level trials in RA/IBD did not meet objective inflammatory endpoints and no neurodegeneration/retinal trials exist, so the translational path remains unproven for AMD; however, the mechanistic link and preclinical retinal signals support a well-designed translational program (Gu & Wiley, 2018).  

Conclusion and development implications  
A-438079 is a strong mechanistic fit for the proposed hypothesis in dry AMD: blocking P2X7 on RPE to prevent ATP-induced Ca2+ influx, dampen K+ efflux–dependent NLRP3 activation, reduce caspase-1 cleavage and IL-1β/IL-18 release, mitigate ROS including mtROS, and preserve epithelial barrier integrity (TEER/ZO-1) under ATP-rich or drusen-mimetic stressors (amyloid-β, oxysterols, Alu RNA) (Fletcher et al., 2019; Youn, 2024; Yang, 2017; Calzaferri et al., 2020). The compound’s pore-block/phagocytosis-preserve profile in human monocytes maps to the desired retinal strategy to avoid the liabilities of global P2X7 loss while selectively suppressing pro-inflammatory outputs (Gu & Wiley, 2018). Given the breadth of class-level retinal evidence and the explicit inclusion of A-438079 in retinal model tables, the candidate merits systematic validation in AMD-proximal RPE assays and in vivo GA-like models, with early emphasis on human-cell PD (Ca2+ flux, YO-PRO uptake, IL-1β/IL-18), epithelial barrier endpoints (TEER/ZO-1), and ocular PK/PD to quantify target engagement at the retina (Li & Wang, 2025; Yang et al., 2021; Li & Wang, 2025; Fletcher et al., 2019).

S3QEL-2 (ID 22) is a novel, highly specific small molecule that allosterically suppresses superoxide generation at the Qo site of Complex III without impairing respiratory function. EPI-743 has known safety and PK profiles in humans, including ocular proof-of-concept in neuronal tissues, and plausible oral or systemic delivery to the retina. Although it also lacks direct dry AMD data, the existing clinical history and broader antioxidant and mitochondrial support activities position it as a more advanced repurposing candidate with de-risked safety and feasibility. The multifactorial pathology of dry AMD may benefit from EPI-743’s multi-pronged redox modulation rather than a narrowly targeted ROS suppressor that still requires substantial optimization for ocular delivery and in vivo validation.
Reasoning: EPI-743 is the stronger candidate because it combines a well-characterized mechanism relevant to mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells with an established human safety and pharmacokinetic profile, including ocular indications, thereby accelerating translational potential. In contrast, S3QEL-2, while mechanistically elegant and highly specific, remains at the probe stage with no in vivo or clinical data, unknown ADME/PK, and untested ocular delivery. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
S3QEL-2 is a synthetic small‐molecule member of the S3QEL (Suppressors of Superoxide production from mitochondrial Complex III) class, originally discovered through a high‐throughput screen of approximately 635,000 small molecules using isolated mitochondria and an Amplex UltraRed H₂O₂ detection assay (Orr et al., 2015). In this screening paradigm, compounds were rigorously selected for their ability to selectively suppress superoxide generation arising from the Qo site of mitochondrial Complex III without impairing oxidative phosphorylation or altering the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) (Orr et al., 2015). The discovery approach involved counterscreens that monitored Δψm changes, respiration rates, and markers of cellular viability, ensuring that S3QEL-2 exhibits specificity in mitigating reactive oxygen species (ROS) production rather than acting as a nonspecific antioxidant or uncoupler (Orr et al., 2015). S3QEL-2 was sourced from commercial screening collections—for example, vendors such as Chemdiv—and its powder-stock purity was confirmed by HPLC–MS analysis (Orr et al., 2015). As a member of a structurally diverse chemotype group, S3QEL-2 belongs to a new class of mitochondrial ROS-targeted modulators that differ fundamentally from classical Complex III inhibitors such as antimycin A or myxothiazol; unlike these inhibitors, S3QELs do not block the electron transfer chain or impair ATP production, but rather reduce the electron leak from the semiquinone intermediate at the Qo site (Orr et al., 2015). In general, compounds in the S3QEL class have been used experimentally as probes to decouple pathological ROS generation from normal bioenergetic function in diverse cell types, with applications ranging from studies on hypoxia-induced transcription (e.g., HIF-1α signaling) to experiments investigating ROS-mediated cell stress in pancreatic β-cells (Orr et al., 2015). The commercial catalog number Cayman Chemical #26918 identifies S3QEL-2 for research purposes, which suggests that this compound is available for repurposing studies beyond its initial characterization in nonocular systems (Orr et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Although S3QEL-2 was originally developed as a novel chemical probe to selectively suppress Complex III-derived superoxide production, its preclinical evaluation has been extensive within the context of cellular models evaluating ROS-mediated signaling and cell stress responses (Orr et al., 2015). In cellular assays, S3QEL-2 has demonstrated the ability to reduce H₂O₂ production in isolated mitochondria, lower HIF-1α transcription in hypoxia-challenged HEK-293 cells, and protect pancreatic β-cells from oxidative stress-induced apoptosis during islet isolation and culture (Orr et al., 2015). Notably, in studies where cells were exposed to concentrations up to 20× the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC₅₀) determined for site IIIQo superoxide production, S3QEL-2 did not impair basal or uncoupled respiration, nor did it compromise mitochondrial viability (Orr et al., 2015). Additionally, S3QEL-2 has been employed as a pharmacological tool in experiments on human monocyte-derived macrophages, where it contributed to demonstrating that inhibition of mitochondrial ROS can reduce inflammasome activation and subsequent IL-18 secretion upon stimulation by the complement membrane attack complex (MAC) (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). However, despite its utility in these nonocular systems—where mitochondrial ROS inhibition was linked to attenuation of inflammatory cytokine pathways—there is little to no published preclinical or clinical data directly evaluating S3QEL-2 in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models or in other ocular disease contexts (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2015). While the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of dry AMD, particularly those involving chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and associated inflammasome activation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, are well documented (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013), a direct therapeutic history for S3QEL-2 in retinal or AMD models remains absent in the current literature (Korhonen, 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Thus, S3QEL-2 represents a promising repurposing candidate that has been validated in other contexts of ROS-related cellular stress but has not yet been explicitly applied to the treatment of dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of S3QEL-2 is based on its capacity to selectively suppress superoxide generation originating at the Qo site of mitochondrial Complex III. Under normal conditions, the electron transport chain (ETC) can leak electrons during the reduction of oxygen, particularly at the semiquinone intermediate at the Qo site, resulting in the formation of superoxide—a primary reactive oxygen species (Orr et al., 2015). S3QEL-2 does not act as a general ROS scavenger; rather, it modulates the rate constant for the electron transfer from the semiquinone to molecular oxygen without significantly altering the steady-state levels of semiquinone species or the redox poise of the ubiquinone (Q) pool (Orr et al., 2015). This selective inhibition of ROS generation is achieved through an allosteric modulation of protein conformation within Complex III, specifically targeting the Qo site to reduce electron leak while sparing the remainder of the electron transport processes (Orr et al., 2015). By decreasing superoxide production, S3QEL-2 effectively reduces the downstream formation of H₂O₂ as detected by Amplex UltraRed assays, a finding that has been consistently reproduced in isolated mitochondrial studies (Orr et al., 2015). Moreover, because S3QEL-2 does not interfere with the overall electron flux or the maintenance of Δψm, it preserves the bioenergetic capacity of the mitochondria—a critical factor in tissues with high metabolic demands such as the RPE (Orr et al., 2015). On a molecular level, the compound’s activity at nanomolar to low micromolar concentrations (with a reported mean IC₅₀ around 1.7 μM for S3QEL-2) suggests a highly potent modulation of the ROS generation pathway that is independent of the mitochondrial matrix redox state (Orr et al., 2015). This targeted approach is further distinguished from classical Complex III inhibitors like myxothiazol and antimycin A, which disrupt the entire electron transport process and can lead to a collapse in mitochondrial function; in contrast, S3QEL-2 specifically mitigates the pathological component of ROS production while maintaining ATP synthesis and cellular energy homeostasis (Orr et al., 2015). In macrophages and other cell types, the reduction in mitochondrial ROS production by S3QEL-2 has been shown to blunt ROS-dependent signaling pathways, such as the stabilization of the transcription factor HIF-1α under hypoxic conditions, and to decrease the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Toma et al., 2021). Thus, the molecular interactions of S3QEL-2 within Complex III position it as a potential modulator of redox signaling pathways that are implicated in inflammatory and degenerative processes, including those observed in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Based on its established mechanism of action, the use of S3QEL-2 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells is expected to selectively reduce mitochondrial ROS generated at the Complex III Qo site. In dry age-related macular degeneration, one of the prevailing hypotheses attributes disease progression to chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction within the RPE, leading to the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and subsequent secretion of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013). The selective inhibition of ROS by S3QEL-2 should therefore interrupt this pathological signaling cascade. In an in vitro assay using RPE cells—cells that have been shown to express components of the NLRP3 inflammasome and are especially vulnerable to oxidative insults—the drug is anticipated to lower ROS markers, as measured by fluorescent dyes (for example, oxidized carboxy-H₂DCFDA), without compromising the cells' mitochondrial respiration or Δψm (Orr et al., 2015). With less mitochondrial ROS available to act as secondary messengers, the downstream stabilization of HIF-1α under stress conditions is expected to be reduced, and the inflammatory response mediated by inflammasome assembly will likely be attenuated (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Orr et al., 2015). Given that multiple studies have demonstrated the role of mitochondrial ROS in directly or indirectly activating NLRP3 inflammasome signaling in both macrophages and RPE cells (Gao et al., 2015; Campbell & Doyle, 2013; Piippo, 2019), the hypothesis is that S3QEL-2 will break this mtROS–NLRP3 axis. In a therapeutic assay, one would expect that RPE cells treated with S3QEL-2 under conditions of complement dysregulation (a known contributor to dry AMD pathology) would demonstrate not only reduced markers of oxidative stress and inflammasome activation but also improved cellular viability, decreased apoptosis, and maintenance of proper metabolic function (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). Furthermore, if S3QEL-2 can lower the intracellular superoxide burden, it might also reduce the formation of oxidized lipids and other damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that contribute to the progression of AMD (Campbell & Doyle, 2013; Toma et al., 2021). Overall, the strategic downregulation of mitochondrial ROS production should translate into a protective phenotype in RPE cells by interrupting the signaling mechanisms that lead to chronic inflammation and cell death in the context of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
S3QEL-2 emerges as an attractive candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to its unique pharmacological profile and precision in targeting mitochondrial ROS production. One of the key strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its ability to selectively suppress superoxide generation at the Complex III Qo site without impairing the overall electron transport chain function or disrupting mitochondrial membrane potential (Orr et al., 2015). This high degree of specificity is particularly valuable in a disease such as dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central to pathogenesis yet preserving the RPE’s bioenergetic capacity is essential for retinal health (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013). The preclinical data available for S3QEL-2 in nonocular systems—ranging from hypoxia-induced HIF-1α modulation to protection of pancreatic β-cells and dampening of inflammasome activation in macrophages—suggest that its mechanism of action may well translate to the RPE, a cell type that is similarly sensitive to mitochondrial oxidative stress (Orr et al., 2015; Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). Moreover, the ability of S3QEL-2 to reduce mitochondrial ROS levels without interfering with ATP production positions it as a promising agent for interrupting the mtROS–NLRP3 inflammasome axis that is proposed to drive inflammatory responses in the geographic atrophy observed in dry AMD (Orr et al., 2015; Orr et al., 2015).

However, several weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. Despite the encouraging preclinical data in cell culture and isolated mitochondrial systems, there is currently no direct evidence linking S3QEL-2 to therapeutic benefit in retinal models or in dry AMD specifically (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2015). The candidate has been primarily evaluated in nonocular models, and the complex microenvironment of the retina—including the blood-retinal barrier, immune cell interactions, and local complement dysregulation—may pose significant challenges in translating in vitro efficacy to in vivo benefit (Korhonen, 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Furthermore, while S3QEL-2 has been shown to reduce ROS-mediated signaling in macrophages and pancreatic islets, the pharmacokinetic properties, tissue distribution, and long-term safety profile of this compound in ocular tissues remain to be determined (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Orr et al., 2015). Delivery of S3QEL-2 to the retina may require formulation strategies that overcome solubility and permeability barriers inherent in drug delivery to the posterior segment of the eye. Another concern is the potential for off-target effects that, while not evident in the isolated systems tested so far, may manifest in the complex in vivo environment or with chronic administration (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Orr et al., 2015).

In addition, the exact molecular site of action on Complex III is not yet fully delineated at the atomic level, meaning that while the compound has been shown to modulate ROS production, the precise binding interactions and potential variability between different cell types or individuals remain uncertain (Orr et al., 2015). This incomplete mechanistic detail could complicate structure-activity relationship (SAR) explorations, as well as efforts to optimize the compound further for better efficacy or reduced toxicity in an ocular setting.

From a therapeutic perspective, the hypothesis that S3QEL-2 can reduce inflammasome activation by lowering mitochondrial ROS is strongly supported by data in other cell types, particularly where a reduction in ROS has been correlated with lower levels of IL-1β and IL-18 secretion (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). Given the well-established involvement of mitochondrial ROS and NLRP3 inflammasome activation in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013), S3QEL-2 holds promise as a tool to dissect and potentially therapeutically modulate this axis. However, concrete evidence in AMD-relevant models, especially primary RPE cells derived from patients or appropriate animal models, is necessary before advancing this compound further in the drug development pipeline (Korhonen, 2024; Macchioni et al., 2020).

In summary, the strengths of S3QEL-2 lie in its high selectivity for Complex III-derived ROS suppression, preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics, and the proven ability to modulate ROS-dependent inflammatory pathways in several preclinical settings (Orr et al., 2015). Its repurposing for dry AMD is biochemically plausible and aligns with the current understanding of the disease, where chronic low-level oxidative stress and inflammasome activation play central roles in RPE dysfunction and geographic atrophy (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013). Conversely, weaknesses include the absence of direct preclinical evidence in ocular models, potential pharmacokinetic and delivery challenges, and an incomplete elucidation of its binding mechanism at the atomic level. Considering these factors, S3QEL-2 represents a highly promising candidate that merits further investigation through targeted preclinical studies in retinal and RPE models, including assessments of its delivery, efficacy in reducing NLRP3-driven cytokine release, and long-term safety in ocular tissues (Gao et al., 2015; Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Ultimately, while S3QEL-2 is supported by robust biochemical data in nonocular systems and has a compelling mechanism that could translate into therapeutic benefit for dry AMD, additional focused research in AMD-relevant models is essential to validate its potential as a repurposed drug candidate for this challenging indication.
