Below is a comprehensive evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO‐Me) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), structured in sections that address its origins, therapeutic history, known mechanisms of action, expected effects in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and an overall assessment of its strengths and challenges.

• Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Bardoxolone methyl is a semisynthetic derivative belonging to the synthetic oleanane triterpenoid class. Its origin stems from oleanolic acid—a naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid abundantly found in various medicinal plants. Early medicinal chemistry programs sought to overcome the modest anti‐inflammatory activity and poor bioavailability of oleanolic acid by introducing targeted modifications. Through chemical derivatization, these programs generated CDDO (2‐cyano‐3,12‐dioxooleana‐1,9‐dien‐28‐oic acid) and subsequently its C‐28 methyl ester, known as Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO‐Me) (Borella et al., 2019). The synthetic process involves the installation of electrophilic Michael acceptor groups at strategic positions on the oleanane scaffold, such as the addition of an α,β‐unsaturated carbonyl in the A‐ring and further incorporation of a cyano group that substantially increases the compound’s potency relative to its natural precursor (Wong et al., 2016; Zhang & Chapman, 2020). These chemical modifications not only enhance the anti‐inflammatory and anticancer properties but also improve chemical stability and oral bioavailability. The structural design, which incorporates a reversible electrophilic reactivity, underpins the compound’s ability to engage diverse cellular targets (Thomas, 2012; Zhou et al., 2014). Bardoxolone methyl thus represents a chemically advanced, highly potent agent from a class of molecules originally designed to trigger cytoprotective responses via direct electrophilic modulation.

• Therapeutic History  
Bardoxolone methyl has undergone extensive preclinical and early clinical evaluation primarily in fields as disparate as oncology and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Initial studies established that synthetic oleanane triterpenoids, including CDDO and its variants, exert dramatic anti‐inflammatory effects by suppressing inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and cyclooxygenase (COX‐2) expression in activated macrophages (Gatbonton‐Schwager, 2014). Preclinical studies in multiple mouse cancer models and inflammatory conditions confirmed its potent anticancer activity and cytoprotective properties, which catalyzed its progression into human clinical trials (Borella et al., 2019; Nakagami, 2016).  
In the clinical arena, Bardoxolone methyl was advanced through Phase I cancer trials, where its once‐daily oral dosing regimen and pharmacokinetic profile—with a terminal half‐life of approximately 39 hours—were characterized (Thomas, 2012; Nakagami, 2016). More notably, its unexpected ability to improve estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in patients with advanced renal disease, particularly in diabetic nephropathy, led to its evaluation in large Phase II and Phase III trials, such as the BEAM and BEACON studies (Yagishita et al., 2020; Tanase et al., 2022). However, the BEACON trial was terminated prematurely due to an increased incidence of cardiovascular events, including heart failure, highlighting concerns about the compound’s systemic safety profile when used at higher doses or in populations with comorbidities (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012).  
Despite its promising preclinical pharmacology and the breadth of clinical data available in non‐ocular indications, to date there is no direct record in the literature of Bardoxolone methyl being used specifically for the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular degenerative conditions (Schiavoni et al., 2025). Nonetheless, the overall safety and pharmacokinetic properties observed in CKD and oncology trials lend valuable insights for considering drug repurposing across therapeutic areas.

• Mechanism of Action  
Bardoxolone methyl is best known for its ability to activate the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway—a master regulator of cellular defense mechanisms against oxidative and electrophilic stress. Under basal conditions, Nrf2 is tightly regulated by Kelch‐like ECH‐associated protein 1 (Keap1), which serves as an adaptor for ubiquitin ligases targeting Nrf2 for proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl functions as a potent electrophile and interacts with sulfhydryl groups on critical cysteine residues within Keap1. This covalent or reversible Michael addition reaction disrupts the Keap1–Nrf2 complex, thereby stabilizing and allowing Nrf2 to translocate into the nucleus (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).  
Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to the antioxidant response element (ARE) in the promoter regions of a host of cytoprotective genes. This transcriptional activation results in the upregulation of a battery of antioxidant and phase II detoxifying enzymes, including but not limited to heme oxygenase‐1 (HO‐1), NAD(P)H dehydrogenase (quinone 1; NQO1), various glutathione transferases, and glutamate–cysteine ligase subunits (Thomas, 2012; Wong et al., 2016). Studies in non‐ocular tissues have shown that at very low (nanomolar) doses, Bardoxolone methyl robustly engages this cytoprotective program while also exerting dose‐dependent biology wherein intermediate and high doses trigger effects such as modulation of cell differentiation and direct anticancer activity, respectively (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).  
It is important to note that while the canonical targets of Nrf2 activation are well characterized, Bardoxolone methyl’s electrophilic character enables it to interact with multiple regulatory proteins. For example, it can inhibit IκB kinase β (IKKβ), leading to suppression of nuclear factor κB (NF‐κB) signaling and subsequent reduction in proinflammatory cytokine production (Zhou et al., 2014; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although the literature does not provide direct experimental evidence that Bardoxolone methyl specifically upregulates mitochondrial antioxidants such as superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) and peroxiredoxin 3 (PRDX3) in RPE cells, the robust, broad‐spectrum transcriptional response induced by Nrf2 activation strongly suggests that mitochondrial and cytoplasmic components of the antioxidant defense system may also be upregulated (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015). Such upregulation would be consistent with previous findings of increased expression of antioxidant genes and improved cellular redox status upon treatment with similar synthetic triterpenoids (Schiavoni et al., 2025; Sporn et al., 2011).

• Expected Effect in Dry AMD  
The pathogenesis of dry age‐related macular degeneration is multifactorial, with chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction playing a central role in the degeneration of the RPE—a critical monolayer that supports photoreceptor health. RPE cells are particularly vulnerable to oxidative damage due to high metabolic activity, exposure to light, and the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). In this context, the proposed mechanism of Bardoxolone methyl, namely activation of the Nrf2/ARE pathway, provides a biologically tenable strategy for neuroprotection and cellular preservation.  
When administered at low doses, Bardoxolone methyl is expected to trigger a cytoprotective transcriptional program in RPE cells. Activation of Nrf2 should lead to the induction of a range of antioxidant enzymes and detoxifying proteins which together help re-establish redox balance in the face of chronic oxidative insult (Borella et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012). One key hypothesis is that, in addition to the already well‐documented induction of cytosolic antioxidants such as HO‐1 and NQO1, Bardoxolone methyl may also promote the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3. SOD2 is the primary defense against superoxide radicals within the mitochondria, and PRDX3 plays a critical role in detoxifying hydrogen peroxide produced by mitochondrial respiration. Although direct data in RPE cells are currently lacking, studies in other cellular contexts have demonstrated that activation of Nrf2 results in the upregulation of a broad spectrum of antioxidant genes, and it is plausible that under the oxidative duress typical of dry AMD, similar effects would be observed in RPE cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
In vitro models simulating oxidative stress—such as exposure of RPE cells to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)—have shown that compounds with similar electrophilic properties, and indeed other members of the CDDO family like CDDO-Im, reduce the intracellular MitoSOX fluorescence signal, indicative of a reduction in mitochondrial ROS (mtROS) (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024). Moreover, improvements in mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) have been correlated with such treatments, suggesting that these molecules can help maintain mitochondrial function under stressful conditions (Nakagami, 2016; Zhou et al., 2014). Such outcomes are highly relevant in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction in the RPE has been implicated in disease progression. The anticipated outcomes, therefore, include a reduction in mtROS, restoration of Δψm, and subsequent preservation of RPE cellular integrity and function.  
Another positive aspect is the compound’s previously established oral bioavailability and pharmacokinetic profile. Clinical studies in CKD patients have demonstrated that therapeutic plasma concentrations can be achieved with once-daily dosing. Although systemic administration in ocular diseases is not ideal, these data provide a strong pharmacological starting point for repurposing. In addition, if systemic toxicity remains a concern—as suggested by the cardiovascular signals in CKD trials—an alternative approach might involve localized ocular delivery (for instance, via intravitreal injection or by developing an ocular formulation) to achieve high retinal bioavailability while minimizing systemic exposure (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).

• Overall Evaluation  
In assessing Bardoxolone methyl for repurposing as a therapeutic for dry AMD, several critical points emerge that underline both its promise and the challenges that must be overcome.

Strengths:  
1. Strong Chemical Rationale and Potency:  
Bardoxolone methyl is a product of sophisticated medicinal chemistry, designed to overcome the limitations of natural triterpenoids like oleanolic acid by installing reactive electrophilic groups that significantly enhance its potency. This design specifically enables the activation of the Nrf2 pathway—a mechanism central to antioxidant defense—at very low concentrations (Borella et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016). The high potency of Bardoxolone methyl as an Nrf2 activator is a significant advantage, particularly when considering that even subtle improvements in cellular antioxidant capacity can have a profound impact on chronic degenerative diseases like dry AMD.

2. Broad Cytoprotective Mechanism:  
The mechanism of Bardoxolone methyl involves the disruption of the Keap1-Nrf2 complex via covalent modification of Keap1 cysteine residues, facilitating the nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and the subsequent transcriptional activation of a broad range of antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes (Zhou et al., 2014; Thomas, 2012). This broad cytoprotective response is particularly relevant to the RPE, where chronic oxidative stress has been implicated in cellular dysfunction and death. The possibility that Bardoxolone methyl may also induce mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3, although not yet directly confirmed in RPE, is an attractive hypothesis; such an effect would directly address the mitochondrial dysfunction that is a hallmark of dry AMD (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).

3. Extensive Clinical Experience and Pharmacokinetic Data:  
Bardoxolone methyl has been evaluated in several clinical trials—most notably in the context of CKD and oncology—yielding a wealth of pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and tolerability data. Its oral bioavailability, with a terminal half-life that supports once-daily dosing, is well documented (Thomas, 2012; Nakagami, 2016). Although the systemic adverse events observed in these trials (such as cardiovascular-related events) present challenges for broad systemic administration, these data nonetheless offer a useful starting point for repurposing. The established clinical profile can inform dose-escalation studies and safety monitoring protocols should Bardoxolone methyl be advanced into ocular trials.

4. Support from Analogous Preclinical Models:  
Several studies in related models have demonstrated that synthetic triterpenoids can protect retinal tissue from oxidative damage. For example, experiments with CDDO-Im, a closely related analogue, have shown protective effects in retinal ischemia–reperfusion injury, including the attenuation of inflammatory responses and preservation of retinal structure (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024). Although these studies are not directly with Bardoxolone methyl, the mechanistic commonalities within this compound class support the notion that the same protective pathways can be harnessed in the context of dry AMD.

Weaknesses and Challenges:  
1. Lack of Direct Evidence in RPE/Dry AMD Models:  
Despite the strong theoretical rationale, direct evidence that Bardoxolone methyl upregulates mitochondrial antioxidants (SOD2, PRDX3) in RPE cells is currently lacking. Most published data are derived from non-ocular cell types or from studies using other analogues such as CDDO-Im (Cai et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2014). It is therefore essential to perform specific in vitro studies in RPE cell lines under oxidative stress conditions to measure the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes and the functional status of mitochondria (e.g., Δψm, mtROS levels) following treatment with Bardoxolone methyl.

2. Safety Concerns from Prior Clinical Experience:  
A significant challenge in repurposing Bardoxolone methyl stems from its safety profile in systemic indications. The Phase III BEACON trial in CKD patients was halted due to an increased incidence of serious cardiovascular events, including heart failure and increased mortality (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although the mechanisms underlying these adverse effects may be related to systemic fluid retention, off‐target reactivity, or other metabolic perturbations, they raise concerns about the safety of systemic administration. For ocular application, it may be necessary to consider alternative dosing strategies or localized delivery methods to avoid systemic exposure while still achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina.

3. Translational and Formulation Challenges:  
The unique anatomy and physiology of the eye introduce additional obstacles in drug repurposing. RPE cells reside in a relatively immune-privileged, isolated microenvironment behind the blood–retinal barrier. The pharmacokinetics and tissue penetration profiles of Bardoxolone methyl observed in systemic circulation may not directly translate to effective intraocular concentrations. Development of specialized ocular formulations—such as sustained-release intravitreal injections or topical applications that can traverse ocular barriers—will be critical for successful translation (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).

4. Multifactorial Nature of AMD Pathogenesis:  
Dry AMD is a complex, multifactorial disease where oxidative stress is only one component of a broader pathogenic network that includes genetic predisposition, inflammation, lipid dysregulation, and complement system activation. While activation of the Nrf2 pathway can counteract oxidative stress and may have secondary anti-inflammatory effects, it is uncertain whether this single mechanism will be sufficient to alter the course of the disease. A combinatorial therapeutic strategy incorporating Nrf2 activation with other modalities might eventually be required to address the full spectrum of dry AMD pathology (Cheng et al., 2021; Thomas, 2012).

5. Dose-Dependent Effects and Narrow Therapeutic Window:  
Bardoxolone methyl exhibits highly dose-dependent pharmacology. At low doses, it predominantly activates Nrf2 and induces cytoprotective genes; however, as the dose increases, additional actions such as pro-apoptotic and cytotoxic effects emerge (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014). Determining the precise dose that is efficacious in RPE cells without triggering deleterious off-target effects will be crucial. This necessitates rigorous dose-ranging studies in preclinical models to define a therapeutic window that maximizes retinal protection while minimizing risks.

• Overall Evaluation and Recommendation  
In summary, Bardoxolone methyl presents a compelling candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD thanks to its well-characterized chemical design, potent induction of the Nrf2 pathway, and a broad cytoprotective mechanism that addresses many aspects of the oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction implicated in RPE degeneration. The extensive clinical data from studies in CKD and oncology provide a valuable foundation for understanding its pharmacokinetics and systemic effects, while the underlying chemistry ensures high potency at low concentrations—features that are highly desirable when targeting a chronic, degenerative condition such as dry AMD (Borella et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012).  
Nonetheless, significant challenges remain. There is a conspicuous gap in the literature regarding the direct evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl in RPE cells and dry AMD models, particularly concerning its ability to upregulate mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes like SOD2 and PRDX3 and thereby mitigate mtROS damage. This gap must be addressed through targeted in vitro assays and in vivo animal studies that simulate the retinal environment and its chronic oxidative stress. Safety concerns, as evidenced by the cardiovascular events observed in CKD trials, underscore the need for caution; these risks may be minimized through localized ocular administration, but careful formulation and dosing studies will be required to establish an acceptable safety profile in the ocular context (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019).  
Given the current state of evidence, it is recommended that Bardoxolone methyl be subjected to further preclinical evaluation in the context of dry AMD. Specifically, studies should focus on:  
 – Conducting detailed in vitro experiments in human RPE cell lines to assess whether exposure to Bardoxolone methyl under oxidative stress conditions leads to the upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants (e.g., SOD2 and PRDX3) and an associated decrease in mtROS (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
 – Evaluating the effects of Bardoxolone methyl on mitochondrial function (including measurements of Δψm, oxygen consumption rate, and mitochondrial integrity) in these cells.  
 – Adapting ocular-specific formulations that allow high local retinal concentrations with minimal systemic exposure, potentially using intravitreal or topical delivery methods, and conducting pharmacokinetic studies that establish retinal tissue exposure (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).  
 – Testing the compound in animal models of dry AMD to determine whether the in vitro antioxidant and mitochondrial protective effects translate into preservation of RPE and photoreceptor structure and function over time (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024).  
If these studies yield positive results that confirm the hypothesized upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants and improved RPE function, Bardoxolone methyl could then be advanced to early-phase clinical trials in patients with dry AMD. Such trials would need to incorporate rigorous safety monitoring protocols to mitigate the known systemic adverse effects. A potential strategy may involve administering the drug in a localized manner or at doses that are effective in the eye but low enough to avoid triggering systemic electrophilic toxicity.

Overall, Bardoxolone methyl holds promise as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD based on its potent Nrf2-activating properties and the central role of oxidative stress in the disease’s pathogenesis. However, its development for an ocular indication will hinge on its ability to selectively and safely modulate the redox status of RPE cells while avoiding systemic side effects. A stepwise, targeted preclinical program that directly addresses these RPE-specific endpoints is therefore critical before consideration of clinical trials in the dry AMD patient population (Nakagami, 2016).

In conclusion, while Bardoxolone methyl offers a strong mechanistic rationale as an Nrf2 activator with the theoretical capacity to upregulate mitochondrial defenses in RPE cells, further targeted studies are essential. The compound’s repurposing for dry AMD is scientifically attractive given the unmet need for effective therapies in this condition; however, the translational path is complex due to safety concerns observed in systemic trials and the lack of direct ocular data. A rigorous preclinical research plan—encompassing in vitro RPE studies, ocular pharmacokinetic assessments, and animal model validation—will be required to determine whether Bardoxolone methyl can be safely and effectively repurposed to preserve RPE function and slow the progression of dry AMD.

• Summary of Key Supporting Points  
– Bardoxolone methyl is a chemically engineered derivative of oleanolic acid that exploits electrophilic modifications to robustly activate the Nrf2 pathway (Borella et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016).  
– Its extensive preclinical and clinical history in oncology and CKD, though not in ocular disease, provides important pharmacokinetic and biological safety data that may be leveraged, with modifications, for ocular use (Nakagami, 2016; Tanase et al., 2022).  
– Its mechanism—covalent modification of Keap1 and subsequent nuclear translocation of Nrf2—leads to the transcriptional upregulation of cytoprotective genes, and it is hypothesized that this would include mitochondrial antioxidants (e.g., SOD2, PRDX3), which are critical for mitigating oxidative damage in RPE cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
– Preclinical data with related triterpenoids in retinal models support the concept that Nrf2 activation can ameliorate oxidative stress and preserve retinal integrity, although direct data for Bardoxolone methyl in dry AMD are presently lacking (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024).  
– Key challenges include the translation of systemic dosing to ocular delivery, the need to specifically validate mitochondrial protective effects in RPE cells, and the resolution of safety issues exemplified by prior cardiovascular signals in systemic trials (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

• Final Recommendation  
Based on the current literature review, Bardoxolone methyl emerges as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its potent Nrf2 activation, broad cytoprotective potential, and a well-documented clinical PK profile. However, its repurposing for ocular application must be preceded by targeted preclinical studies that corroborate its ability to upregulate mitochondrial antioxidants in RPE cells and to reduce mtROS while preserving mitochondrial function. These studies should also explore ocular-specific formulations and dosing regimens that minimize systemic exposure. Only after thorough validation in these preliminary investigations can Bardoxolone methyl be considered a credible candidate for clinical trials in dry AMD patients. Given these considerations, the candidate warrants further investigation despite the existing translational and safety challenges inherent in repurposing a systemically active electrophilic compound for an ocular indication (Borella et al., 2019; Yagishita et al., 2020; Thomas, 2012).

This structural class is known not only for its high affinity to various protein targets but also for favorable pharmacokinetic properties that have motivated its use in drug development efforts. Several studies have demonstrated that ZLN005 effectively induces PGC-1α expression in various cell types, including skeletal muscle and particularly the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis (Satish et al., 2018). Its assignment under the benzimidazole class further suggests that ZLN005 may share common metabolic and pharmacological features with other compounds in the same class, which have been employed in different therapeutic areas, supporting its potential for repurposing in ocular disorders such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Sun et al., 2018; Bleckwehl et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Initially, ZLN005 emerged from screening studies designed to identify small molecules that could stimulate PGC-1α expression. Early research in cellular models demonstrated that ZLN005 enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and upregulates the expression of downstream oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and antioxidant genes, which in turn improves mitochondrial health and overall cellular energy metabolism (Satish et al., 2018). In skeletal muscle and hepatic cells, for example, treatment with ZLN005 was associated with increased basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates, an increase in spare respiratory capacity, and a concomitant improvement in glucose uptake and cellular ATP levels (Satish et al., 2018). Such characteristics have spurred interest in its therapeutic application beyond metabolic diseases to conditions where mitochondrial dysfunction is a central pathogenic factor.

Notably, several groups have investigated ZLN005 in the context of retinal diseases. Preclinical studies using ARPE-19 cells—a well-accepted human RPE cell line—demonstrated that ZLN005 markedly upregulates PGC-1α expression and its associated transcription factors and antioxidant enzymes. These investigations have shown that ZLN005 can confer significant protection against oxidative stress-induced cell death when cells are exposed to prooxidative agents such as hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL) and sodium iodate (NaIO₃) (Satish et al., 2018). Although ZLN005 has not yet undergone extensive clinical evaluation specifically for dry AMD, its robust activity in stimulating mitochondrial function and providing cytoprotection in RPE models forms a compelling rationale for its repurposing. Studies in other systems, including cardiomyocytes and skeletal muscle, support its therapeutic use in settings of bioenergetic decline and oxidative damage, which are hallmarks of many age-related degenerative diseases (Ma et al., 2023; Moradi, 2022). However, it should be noted that many of the studies exploring ZLN005 for ocular purposes have been in vitro, and while they present an optimistic scenario, further in vivo animal studies and careful pharmacokinetic analyses in ocular tissues are needed before clinical application in AMD can be considered (Satish et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
The pharmacological efficacy of ZLN005 is tightly linked to its mechanism of action as an activator of PGC-1α. PGC-1α is a transcriptional coactivator that regulates a myriad of genes implicated in energy metabolism, mitochondrial biogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, and antioxidant protection. In RPE cells—where the maintenance of a high mitochondrial integrity is crucial for visual function—the expression of PGC-1α is fundamental to mitigating oxidative stress and maintaining metabolic homeostasis (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Iacovelli et al., 2016). ZLN005 increases the expression levels of PGC-1α by enhancing its transcription, culminating in the upregulation of a host of downstream target genes. This includes key mitochondrial genes such as ATP50, COX4, COX5b, and NDUFB5, all of which are involved in oxidative phosphorylation and energy production (Satish et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025).

At the molecular level, ZLN005 promotes the transcriptional program by potentially modulating AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) activity, a well-known regulator of PGC-1α function. The compound’s facilitation of PGC-1α nuclear translocation and its catalytic coactivation leads to the stimulation of mitochondrial replication and repair processes, thereby increasing mitochondrial mass and mtDNA copy number (Satish et al., 2018). In parallel, the upregulation of PGC-1α by ZLN005 induces the expression of several endogenous antioxidant enzymes, including superoxide dismutases (SOD1 and SOD2) and mitochondrial thioredoxin 2 (TXN2). This cascade of events enhances the cellular capacity to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS), thus lowering mitochondrial superoxide production and reducing the levels of oxidative stress markers such as 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), a product of lipid peroxidation frequently associated with degenerative retinal changes (Satish et al., 2018).

Furthermore, ZLN005 appears to improve overall mitochondrial bioenergetics. It has been observed to increase both basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates (OCR) in RPE cells, indicating an enhanced capacity for ATP synthesis under both steady-state and stress conditions (Satish et al., 2018). The compound also augments the spare respiratory capacity, which is critical for cellular survival when faced with acute energy demands during oxidative stress. Such improvements in mitochondrial function are directly relevant to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, where RPE cells experience an energy deficit due to progressive mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic oxidative injury (Felszeghy et al., 2019). Additionally, by upregulating PGC-1α, ZLN005 may indirectly influence other cellular processes, including autophagy and lipid metabolism, both of which are altered in the aging RPE and contribute to the formation of drusen—the hallmark deposits seen in dry AMD (Zhou et al., 2024).

It is important to emphasize that the protective effects of ZLN005 are markedly dependent on the presence of functional PGC-1α. Experiments in which PGC-1α expression was silenced in RPE cells resulted in a significant loss of the cytoprotective benefits conferred by ZLN005, underscoring the compound’s mechanism-specific action (Satish et al., 2018). Parallel studies in non-ocular cell types, such as skeletal muscle myotubes and alveolar epithelial cells, have further supported its role in enhancing mitochondrial function and regulating oxidative stress through similar molecular pathways (Zhang et al., 2013; Bleckwehl et al., 2025). Thus, the molecular interactions initiated by ZLN005—ranging from the activation of PGC-1α to the subsequent stimulation of antioxidant enzymes and mitochondrial biogenesis—form the crux of its therapeutic utility, specifically in countering the bioenergetic decline characteristic of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Given the central involvement of mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the therapeutic hypothesis for ZLN005 is that its activation of PGC-1α in retinal pigment epithelial cells will restore mitochondrial homeostasis and augment cellular antioxidant defenses. In the proposed assays, treatment with ZLN005 is expected to upregulate PGC-1α expression in RPE cells, thereby triggering a cascade of downstream events that lead to enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis. This includes an increase in mtDNA copy number and the expression of mitochondrial genes that are essential for optimal oxidative phosphorylation performance (Satish et al., 2018). As mitochondrial function improves, RPE cells should exhibit higher basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates, indicative of an improved metabolic profile and increased capacity to generate ATP under both normal and stress conditions (Satish et al., 2018).

The antioxidative effects of ZLN005 are also expected to manifest in augmented levels of enzymes such as SOD1, SOD2, and TXN2, which collectively enhance the cell’s capability to scavenge reactive oxygen species. These biochemical events are critical because the accumulation of oxidative stress in RPE cells, driven by chronic exposure to high levels of ROS, is a significant contributor to cell degeneration in dry AMD (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Blasiak et al., 2021). With improved mitochondrial function and reduced oxidative stress, it is anticipated that ZLN005 treatment will lead to a decrease in the accumulation of oxidative damage markers like 4-HNE, thereby mitigating processes that lead to RPE cell apoptosis and the subsequent photoreceptor degeneration observed in dry AMD (Blasiak et al., 2021; Iacovelli et al., 2016).

Moreover, in vitro studies have demonstrated that under conditions of experimentally induced oxidative stress with agents such as H₂O₂, ox-LDL, or NaIO₃, ZLN005 significantly reduces cell death in ARPE-19 cells (Satish et al., 2018). Therefore, the expected effect of ZLN005 in the proposed assay is a robust cytoprotective response in RPE cells. This would be characterized by improved cell viability, restoration of mitochondrial respiratory function, and a reduction in stress-induced apoptotic markers—a constellation of effects that directly addresses the bioenergetic and oxidative challenges underlying dry AMD (Satish et al., 2018). Additionally, since PGC-1α is known to regulate lipid metabolism and prevent lipid droplet accumulation—a process that may be linked to the formation of drusen in the AMD retina—the activation of PGC-1α by ZLN005 could also have beneficial effects on lipid handling within the RPE (Zhou et al., 2024; Iacovelli et al., 2016). Thus, through these concerted mechanisms, ZLN005 is anticipated to stabilize or even improve RPE function, thereby halting or reversing aspects of the degenerative cascade that leads to vision loss in dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
A comprehensive evaluation of ZLN005 reveals several compelling strengths as well as notable weaknesses that should be weighed in the context of repurposing it for the treatment of dry AMD. One of the principal strengths of ZLN005 lies in its well-defined mechanism of action. By selectively activating PGC-1α, ZLN005 directly targets the mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress that are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. The upregulation of PGC-1α leads to improvements in mitochondrial biogenesis, an increase in the expression of mitochondrial OXPHOS genes, and the enhancement of antioxidant defenses—all factors that are critically compromised in the diseased RPE (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Blasiak et al., 2021). This mechanistic rationale is further supported by in vitro studies showing that ZLN005 can effectively reduce prooxidant-induced cell death and improve mitochondrial respiratory parameters such as basal respiration, maximal respiration, and spare respiratory capacity (Satish et al., 2018).

Another strength is the translational potential implied by the compound’s efficacy in multiple cell types. ZLN005 has not only demonstrated protective effects in RPE cells but has also been shown to modulate mitochondrial activity in skeletal muscle and hepatic cells. This broad-spectrum improvement in energy metabolism indicates that its bioenergetic benefits may be harnessed in the complex metabolic environment of the RPE, where energy deficits contribute to dry AMD pathology (Satish et al., 2018). Achieving a robust activation of PGC-1α is particularly attractive because it addresses both the cellular energy production and ROS management simultaneously, which are two critical determinants of RPE cell survival and function (Iacovelli et al., 2016; Rosales et al., 2019).

Furthermore, the specificity of ZLN005’s action has been validated by studies where the loss of PGC-1α abrogated its cytoprotective effects, underscoring that its efficacy is tightly linked to the activation of this pivotal regulatory pathway (Satish et al., 2018). This is an important consideration because it suggests that the therapeutic effects can be fine-tuned by modulating the expression or activity of PGC-1α. In the context of dry AMD, where PGC-1α levels are often diminished or dysregulated, the targeted upregulation provided by ZLN005 offers a focused therapeutic intervention.

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and challenges remain. Foremost, the majority of the supportive evidence for ZLN005’s efficacy in protecting RPE cells has been generated through in vitro studies using cell lines such as ARPE-19. While these models are indispensable for preliminary evaluation, they do not fully recapitulate the complex in vivo environment of the human retina, and the translatability of these effects into clinical benefit remains to be demonstrated (Satish et al., 2018). Additionally, the current body of literature shows that some reports have emerged from journals of variable quality; this introduces a degree of uncertainty regarding the reproducibility of the findings and necessitates rigorous validation of these results in higher-order in vivo models and, eventually, clinical trials (Satish et al., 2018).

Another pertinent concern is the pharmacokinetic profile of ZLN005 in the ocular environment. While its favorable metabolic effects are evident in cell culture and certain systemic models, its ability to reach and maintain effective concentrations in the RPE following systemic or local administration is not well established in the available reports (Bleckwehl et al., 2025; Miller et al., 2019). In addition, the potential off-target effects of ZLN005, particularly in tissues where mitochondrial modulation may have unintended consequences, have not been fully explored. This includes the risk that enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis in non-target cells could lead to dysregulated energy metabolism or contribute to unwanted proliferative responses (Satish et al., 2018; Bleckwehl et al., 2025).

Moreover, the clinical development pathway for repurposing ZLN005 for ocular indications such as dry AMD will require comprehensive toxicological studies, detailed pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic analyses in ocular tissues, and the establishment of dosing regimens that ensure both efficacy and safety over chronic treatment periods. Given the slow progression of dry AMD and the need for long-term treatment, any adverse effects or suboptimal pharmacokinetic properties could significantly limit the compound’s clinical use (Satish et al., 2018; Iacovelli et al., 2016).

Additionally, while the activation of PGC-1α is a promising strategy for mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction, the role of PGC-1α in the retina is complex. Overexpression of PGC-1α has been linked in some studies to increased susceptibility to light-induced retinal damage or other forms of stress, suggesting that a delicate balance must be maintained to achieve therapeutic benefit without tipping the scales towards potential toxicity or dysregulation of cellular homeostasis (Iacovelli et al., 2016; Blasiak et al., 2021). This dual nature of PGC-1α activity means that careful titration of ZLN005 dosing—and possibly the development of combination therapies—may be necessary to harness its protective effects while avoiding exacerbation of retinal stress under certain conditions.

In summary, ZLN005 emerges as a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its well-characterized mechanism of stimulating PGC-1α expression, its ability to enhance mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses, and the encouraging results obtained from in vitro studies in ARPE-19 cells. Its molecular action aligns closely with the pathophysiological profiles observed in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress contribute to RPE degeneration. However, while the preclinical evidence is robust in terms of establishing a mechanistic framework, significant challenges remain in translating these findings to an in vivo and eventually a clinical setting. Key areas that require further investigation include detailed pharmacokinetic studies in ocular models, confirmation of efficacy in animal models of dry AMD, and a full safety profile with chronic dosing regimens (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Blasiak et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2019).

Moreover, the integration of ZLN005 with current understanding of AMD pathogenesis suggests that the compound could potentially be part of combination therapies that target several pathogenic pathways simultaneously—such as inflammation, lipid dysregulation, and complement activation—in addition to mitochondrial dysfunction. Indeed, the multifactorial nature of AMD means that a monotherapy approach may be insufficient, and ZLN005’s role could be most valuable when combined with other agents that complement its effects on mitochondrial and oxidative stress parameters (Rosales et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2025).

From a strategic drug development perspective, ZLN005 offers several attractive points for further exploration. Its synthetic origin as a benzimidazole derivative means that established methods exist for its production and modification, allowing for potential structure-activity relationship (SAR) studies aimed at enhancing its potency, selectivity, and ocular bioavailability. Such modifications could lead to derivatives with improved pharmacokinetic profiles tailored for retinal delivery. Moreover, leveraging advanced drug delivery systems, such as nanoparticle carriers or sustained-release formulations, could further enhance the therapeutic window of ZLN005 in the eye while minimizing systemic exposure and associated off-target effects (Bleckwehl et al., 2025; Miller et al., 2019).

In conclusion, the repurposing of ZLN005 for the treatment of dry AMD is supported by a compelling mechanistic rationale and a growing body of preclinical evidence that underscores its potential to restore mitochondrial dynamics and counteract oxidative stress in retinal pigment epithelial cells. The strengths of this candidate include its specificity for PGC-1α activation, its demonstrated ability to enhance mitochondrial function and energy metabolism, and its protective effects against oxidative injury in vitro. On the other hand, the limitations primarily stem from the current reliance on in vitro data, the need for more rigorous in vivo validation, and uncertainties regarding its pharmacokinetic behavior in ocular tissues. Therefore, while ZLN005 stands out as a scientifically promising candidate, advancing it through the drug development pipeline will require concerted efforts to address these gaps through detailed preclinical studies, formulation optimization, and eventually, well-designed clinical trials to determine its efficacy and safety in patients with dry AMD (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Rosales et al., 2019).

Overall, the data presented through multiple independent studies provide a strong foundation for considering ZLN005 as a viable therapeutic candidate in the repurposing paradigm for dry age-related macular degeneration. With further validation and refinement, itself or an optimized derivative could potentially offer a new strategy to preserve RPE integrity and maintain visual function in AMD patients, addressing a significant unmet medical need in the realm of retinal degenerative diseases (Rosales et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2025). Continued research efforts should focus on delineating the precise molecular signatures of ZLN005’s effects in RPE cells, assessing its long-term impact on retinal morphology and function in vivo, and investigating its interactions with other signaling cascades implicated in AMD progression (Satish et al., 2018). Only through such thorough and multidisciplinary evaluations can the true therapeutic potential of ZLN005 for dry AMD be accurately determined and translated into clinical benefit.

In summary, while challenges remain in translating the promising in vitro results to clinical outcomes, the accumulated evidence suggests that ZLN005’s activation of PGC-1α represents a credible and innovative strategy to counteract the bioenergetic decline in RPE cells—a central feature in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. For these reasons, further preclinical evaluation and careful optimization of dosing and delivery are warranted to fully ascertain the viability of ZLN005 as a therapeutic option in the ongoing battle against dry age-related macular degeneration (Satish et al., 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
BGP-15 is a synthetic, small-molecule nicotinic amidoxime/hydroxylamine derivative whose full chemical name is O-(3-piperidino-2-hydroxy-1-propyl) nicotinic amidoxime, typically used as a dihydrochloride salt; it was developed by N-Gene (US/Hungary) and has been described as water-soluble and mitochondria-targeting in preclinical studies (including ocular applications) (Takács et al., 2024; Horváth et al., 2021). Chemically and pharmacologically, BGP-15 belongs to the hydroximic/hydroxylamine acid derivative family originally advanced as membrane-interacting heat-shock response (HSR) co-inducers that remodel cholesterol-enriched plasma membrane rafts, with pleiotropic, cytoprotective effects in stressed tissues (membrane-lipid therapy) (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011). In parallel, the compound has been positioned as a nicotinamide-related, non-carboxamide “NAM analogue” with in vitro mixed-type (noncompetitive) PARP-1 inhibition, though the authors emphasize that in vivo protective effects likely involve additional mechanisms beyond direct PARP blockade because the in vitro inhibitory concentration exceeds achievable systemic levels (Crul et al., 2013). Independent biophysical and cellular studies show BGP-15 partitions into membranes, increases the fluidity of negatively charged lipid species, preserves heat-challenged raft integrity, and activates stress signaling linked to HSP induction; imaging and molecular dynamics support a direct membrane-interacting mode of action (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

Functionally, BGP-15 is best classified as a multifunctional HSP co-inducer and insulin-sensitizing, mitochondria-targeting cytoprotective agent that remodels membrane rafts, enhances the HSF1–HSP axis, and modulates stress and survival signaling (Akt up, JNK/p38 down), while lowering mitochondrial ROS and stabilizing Δψm; importantly, it preferentially acts in stressed cells, an attribute that underpins its safety rationale (Gombos et al., 2011; Sumegi et al., 2017). The compound concentrates in energized mitochondria driven by its delocalized positive charge, with >85–90% uptake into isolated mitochondria under experimental conditions (Sümegi, 2018). Mitochondrial studies consistently localize the dominant ROS-lowering effect to the respiratory chain at complexes I and III, with minimal direct antioxidant chemistry, and only mild uncoupling at millimolar concentrations that is irrelevant at the micromolar doses used in most cell studies (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018).

Crucial nomenclature caveat: a distinct “BGP-15” reported by a different group denotes a calcipotriene-derived vitamin D3 analog with anticancer activity; this vitamin D3 analog is mechanistically and structurally unrelated to the nicotinic amidoxime HSP co-inducer described above (both were labeled “BGP-15” by their respective originators) (Sintov et al., 2013). For the current program, the candidate of interest is the nicotinic amidoxime/hydroxylamine HSP co-inducer (often supplied by N-Gene or commercial chemical vendors under the amidoxime name), not the vitamin D3 analog (Takács et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
BGP-15 and closely related hydroximic/hydroxylamine acid derivatives have an extensive preclinical history across cardiac, neural, hepatic, renal, skeletal muscle, pulmonary, and metabolic models, with multiple mechanistic readouts converging on membrane remodeling, HSR/HSP co-induction, MAPK and Akt pathway modulation, and mitochondrial protection (Sumegi et al., 2017). Cardiovascular protection has been reported in ischemia–reperfusion, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation, with actions that include reduced ROS, preserved mitochondrial function, and Akt activation with suppression of JNK/p38 (Sumegi et al., 2017). In spontaneously hypertensive rats, BGP-15 increased PGC-1α and mitochondrial mass, decreased interstitial fibrosis, increased MKP-1 and reduced p38/JNK phosphorylation, and activated Akt/GSK-3β signaling (Horváth et al., 2021). BGP-15 prevented imatinib cardiotoxicity, protected against cisplatin nephrotoxicity without impairing antitumor efficacy, and mitigated cisplatin/taxol peripheral neuropathy (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). Hepatoprotection against acetaminophen injury via inhibition of caspase-independent cell death has also been documented (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). In pulmonary arterial hypertension and severe muscular dystrophy models, BGP-15 preserved mitochondrial structure and function and slowed disease progression; mechanistically, mitochondrial fusion via OPA1 activation and Akt signaling were implicated (Szabó et al., 2018).

Neuroprotection and mitochondrial rescue have been demonstrated in vitro and in vivo, including reduced neuronal death and improved mitochondrial potential/ROS at axonal branch points, coupled to HSP72 elevation, reduced phospho-JNK/p38, and enhanced Akt/IGF1R signaling (Ohlen et al., 2017). Consistent with its membrane-raft mechanism, BGP-15 increased HSP expression during heat challenge and remodeled cholesterol-rich platforms that gate stress signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

In ophthalmology, BGP-15 has been applied in multiple retinal disease contexts. It was reported retinoprotective in Goto–Kakizaki rats (type 2 diabetes) with functional preservation on ERG, and later shown to improve survival and retinal function long-term in ZDF rats under uncontrolled diabetes, with increased ocular HSP70 and decreased NFκB (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021). Topical ocular delivery using an SBECD-containing eyedrop improved scotopic/photopic a- and b-waves, restored oscillatory potentials, shortened implicit times, and preserved retinal thickness following global ischemia–reperfusion injury in rats (Takács et al., 2024). These ocular data align with the compound’s mitochondrial and HSP co-inducer mechanisms: accumulation in mitochondria, protection against apoptosis/necrosis in oxidative-stress paradigms, and modulation of stress signaling (Takács et al., 2024).

Clinically, BGP-15 has a proof-of-concept randomized, double-blind trial demonstrating dose-dependent improvement of insulin sensitivity in insulin-resistant patients without apparent short-term toxicity; in parallel, human phase II work in olanzapine-induced metabolic disorder also identified BGP-15 as an insulin sensitizer (Crul et al., 2013; Sümegi, 2018). Safety signals from early human studies and the pharmacology of HSP co-inducers (preferential action in stressed cells) support the translational risk profile; however, systemic serum concentrations reported by the developer are low (≤25 nmol/mL), which has implications for target engagement and favors local ocular delivery for retinal indications (Gombos et al., 2011; Sumegi et al., 2017).

To our knowledge based on the supplied corpus, BGP-15 has not been directly tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) patients or canonical dry AMD animal models; however, its retinoprotective efficacy in diabetic retinopathy models and retinal ischemia–reperfusion suggests relevance to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)/photoreceptor stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammation, which are central to dry AMD biology (Takács et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Membrane-lipid therapy and HSP co-induction. BGP-15 partitions into and remodels membrane lipid domains, particularly cholesterol-rich plasma membrane rafts that organize stress sensing and signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). Under heat stress or analogous perturbations, BGP-15 preserves raft integrity and elevates HSP expression; this is associated with activation of Rac1 and modulation of HSF1 acetylation, leading to prolonged HSF1 DNA binding and robust HSP gene induction without causing protein unfolding, a hallmark of HSP “co-inducers” (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). In HSR-defective melanoma cells, BGP-15 significantly rescued raft domain coverage and shifted the size distribution toward larger platforms, coincident with increased hsp25 expression and Rac1-dependent stress signaling (Gombos et al., 2011). Across cell and tissue contexts, BGP-15 increases HSP70/HSPA1A (HSP72), and this HSP gain is causally linked to improved insulin signaling and cytoprotection in stressed cells (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011).

PARP/NAD+/SIRT1/HSF1 axis. Although BGP-15 demonstrates mixed-type (noncompetitive) inhibition of PARP-1 in vitro, the concentrations required exceed typical in vivo exposures, suggesting that PARP pathway effects in vivo are likely downstream of ROS lowering and reduced DNA single-strand breaks that otherwise drive PARP activation (Crul et al., 2013). In stressed cells, BGP-15 reduces PAR levels, which relieves PARP-mediated suppression of MKP-1/Dusp1, thereby inhibiting JNK/p38 activation; reduced PARP activity also preserves NAD+ and SIRT1 activity, which favors a deacetylated, active HSF1 and a stronger HSR (Crul et al., 2013). This mechanistic loop—less ROS, less PARP activation, more MKP-1, less JNK/p38, and better HSP/SIRT1 tone—aligns with the observed anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective phenotypes (Crul et al., 2013).

Mitochondrial enrichment and respiratory chain modulation. Biophysically, BGP-15 carries a delocalized positive charge, accumulates in energized mitochondria (>85–90% uptake in isolated organelles), and at micromolar doses characteristic of cell studies (1–50 µM) lowers mitochondrial ROS predominantly at complexes I and III without significant baseline depolarization of Δψm (Sümegi, 2018; Sumegi et al., 2017). In oxidative or inflammatory challenges, BGP-15 attenuates H₂O₂- and LPS-induced mitochondrial depolarization and reduces mitochondrial superoxide to near-control levels; MitoTEMPO controls confirm mitochondrial origin of the ROS signal (Sumegi et al., 2017). Importantly, the compound exhibits no meaningful direct antioxidant scavenging in cell-free ROS-generating systems, and only displays mild uncoupling at millimolar concentrations—far above the micromolar exposures used in protective assays—supporting a mechanism of respiratory chain modulation rather than redox scavenging (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). Downstream signaling reflects the lowered mitochondrial ROS burden: JNK/p38 activation is reduced, Akt signaling is enhanced, and caspase-independent death pathways are suppressed (Sumegi et al., 2017).

Mitochondrial dynamics, fusion, and biogenesis. Beyond acute ROS control, BGP-15 promotes mitochondrial fusion and preserves cristae architecture by activating OPA1 GTPase and promoting OPA1 polymerization; genetic suppression of OPA1 or Mfn1/Mfn2 abolishes the fusion phenotype, indicating that BGP-15 acts upstream or within the endogenous fusion machinery (Szabó et al., 2018). In vivo, these effects translate into improved mitochondrial ultrastructure and tissue histology under ROS stress (e.g., monocrotaline-induced PAH) (Szabó et al., 2018). In hypertensive cardiomyopathy, BGP-15 increases PGC-1α and mitochondrial mass, with concurrent shifts in CREB/AMPK phosphorylation consistent with improved energetic signaling, reduced p38/JNK via MKP-1 upregulation, and increased Akt/GSK-3β prosurvival signaling (Horváth et al., 2021).

Insulin-sensitizing stress signaling. In skeletal muscle and human studies, BGP-15 increases HSP72 expression, enhances insulin receptor autophosphorylation (blocking JNK inhibitory phosphorylation), activates RAC1, increases AKT phosphorylation, promotes GLUT4 translocation, increases membrane fluidity, raises AMPK activity, and reduces HSF1 acetylation, altogether improving glucose disposal without overt toxicity in a randomized trial (Crul et al., 2013). These metabolic effects are mechanistically congruent with the membrane–HSR–mitochondrial triad described above (Crul et al., 2013).

Ocular and retinal mechanisms. In rat eyes, BGP-15 increased HSP70 and decreased NFκB, consistent with HSR enhancement and anti-inflammatory signaling in ocular tissues (Wachal et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion and diabetic retinopathy models, functional improvements on ERG, restoration of oscillatory potentials, and preservation of retinal thickness are consistent with mitochondrial protection and stress-response reinforcement in retinal cells (Takács et al., 2024). The topical SBECD formulation demonstrated pharmacologic activity in the retina without systemic pharmacokinetic characterization, indicating local ocular delivery as a viable route for targeting mitochondrial and HSP pathways in the posterior segment (Takács et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
The team’s hypothesis—that BGP-15 stabilizes mitochondrial membrane proteins and co-induces HSF1-driven antioxidant chaperone responses in RPE to mitigate oxidative stress in dry AMD—is aligned with the compound’s demonstrated pharmacology in retinal, cardiac, neural, and pulmonary models: (i) robust mitochondrial enrichment and stabilization of Δψm under oxidative/inflammatory stress, (ii) ROS lowering at complexes I and III without direct radical scavenging, (iii) activation of the HSR via membrane raft remodeling and HSF1 acetylation control, and (iv) suppression of ROS-sensitive injury cascades (JNK/p38) with concurrent activation of pro-survival Akt (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). In retinal disease models, BGP-15 improved ERG measures and retinal thickness and increased ocular HSP70 while decreasing NFκB, providing a direct ocular precedent likely to translate to stressed RPE, where mitochondria and proteostasis are central to survival under chronic oxidative load (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021).

Mechanistically expected in RPE:  
- Membrane-raft remodeling and HSR co-induction. BGP-15 partitions into RPE membranes and remodels cholesterol-rich rafts, preserving raft integrity under stress, activating Rac1, decreasing HSF1 acetylation, and prolonging HSF1 DNA binding, thereby elevating HSP70/HSP25 and enhancing proteostasis capacity in aged/stressed RPE (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).  
- Mitochondrial ROS containment and Δψm preservation. BGP-15 should accumulate in RPE mitochondria, reduce ROS production at complexes I/III, and attenuate oxidative- and inflammation-induced depolarization, thereby maintaining ATP production and limiting mitochondrial permeability transition and AIF translocation, as shown in other cell types (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018).  
- Mitochondrial dynamics and biogenesis. Via OPA1 activation and Akt/GSK-3β signaling, BGP-15 is expected to promote inner-membrane fusion/OPA1 oligomerization and preserve cristae, with possible longer-term increases in mitochondrial biogenesis (PGC-1α), all protective features for RPE faced with chronic oxidative and lipofuscin stress (Szabó et al., 2018; Horváth et al., 2021).  
- Anti-inflammatory signaling rebalancing. By reducing mitochondrial ROS and PARP activation, BGP-15 should relieve PARP-mediated suppression of MKP-1, suppress JNK/p38 activity, decrease NFκB signaling, and bolster SIRT1-HSF1 activity, thereby reducing ROS-amplifying feed-forward loops in RPE (Crul et al., 2013; Wachal et al., 2021).

Assay expectations and endpoints. In standard RPE cell models (primary human RPE, ARPE-19, or iPSC-RPE), BGP-15 at 1–50 µM should (i) reduce H₂O₂- or LPS-induced mitochondrial depolarization (JC-1/TMRM), (ii) lower mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX) and total ROS (DHR123) without acting as a direct antioxidant in cell-free assays, (iii) reduce apoptosis/necrosis after oxidative challenge (annexin V/PI), (iv) increase HSP70/HSF1 pathway activation and decrease HSF1 acetylation, (v) activate Akt and downregulate JNK/p38, and (vi) promote OPA1 oligomerization and mitochondrial fusion (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Szabó et al., 2018). Where possible, complement activation or lipid peroxidation paradigms can be layered to emulate dry AMD stressors; based on the corpus, BGP-15’s effects are strongest under stress, consistent with HSP co-inducer pharmacology (Gombos et al., 2011).

Delivery considerations. Systemic exposures in humans are low (≤25 nmol/mL), suggesting that oral dosing may be insufficient to reach pharmacologic micromolar levels in RPE; conversely, topical ocular delivery with SBECD has demonstrated retinal functional benefits and structural protection, supporting development of a posterior-segment–targeted topical or periocular formulation to enrich the RPE–choroid compartment (Sümegi, 2018; Takács et al., 2024).

Caveats regarding target expression. The corpus documents the relevant targets (HSF1/HSP70, Rac1, OPA1, MKP-1, JNK/p38, Akt) as central to BGP-15’s mechanisms in multiple mammalian tissues and cell types and shows ocular readouts (HSP70 up, NFκB down) in rat eyes; however, it does not provide explicit RPE expression data, which should be confirmed experimentally in our RPE assay systems (Wachal et al., 2021; Gombos et al., 2011; Szabó et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic congruence with dry AMD pathobiology. BGP-15 directly addresses mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic oxidative stress—core drivers of RPE degeneration—by concentrating in mitochondria, lowering ROS at complexes I/III, stabilizing Δψm, and activating survival signaling while suppressing inflammatory stress kinases (Sumegi et al., 2017). Concurrently, it co-induces the HSR by remodeling plasma membrane rafts and modulating HSF1 acetylation, thereby boosting HSP70/HSP25 chaperone capacity and proteostasis—functions that are expected to mitigate protein misfolding and aggregation in aged RPE (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).  
- Demonstrated ocular efficacy in relevant retinal injury contexts. Topical BGP-15 improved ERG a- and b-waves, preserved oscillatory potentials, reduced implicit times, and rescued retinal thickness after ischemia–reperfusion, and it was retinoprotective in diabetic models, with ocular HSP70 increase and NFκB reduction—outcomes consistent with RPE/retinal resilience under oxidative stress (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021).  
- Pleiotropic yet coherent mechanism spanning membrane, nuclear, and mitochondrial nodes. The membrane–HSR–mitochondrial triad, including PARP/MKP-1/JNK–p38 and Akt/GSK-3β axes, provides multiple intervention points likely to translate into robust protection in the multifactorial environment of dry AMD (Crul et al., 2013; Sumegi et al., 2017; Szabó et al., 2018; Horváth et al., 2021).  
- Favorable translational signals. Proof-of-concept human trials in insulin resistance show pharmacodynamic activity without overt safety signals, and HSP co-inducers are known to preferentially act in stressed cells, potentially limiting off-target effects in quiescent tissues; local ocular delivery further improves the therapeutic index (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011; Takács et al., 2024).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Lack of direct dry AMD evidence. No studies in the corpus directly test BGP-15 in dry AMD models or patients; we infer utility from retinal IR/diabetes models and mechanism (Takács et al., 2024).  
- Exposure–response uncertainties for the posterior segment. Systemic serum concentrations are low relative to micromolar efficacious concentrations in vitro, necessitating optimized local delivery to RPE; although eyedrop formulations show retinal effects, posterior-segment delivery by topical route is often limited, and pharmacokinetics were not measured in the cited ocular study (Sümegi, 2018; Takács et al., 2024).  
- Target ambiguity and pleiotropy. While the membrane–HSR–mitochondrial framework is coherent, BGP-15 lacks a single defined receptor/protein target, and its in vitro PARP-1 inhibition likely does not drive in vivo efficacy; this complicates target engagement assays and regulatory narratives (Sümegi, 2018; Crul et al., 2013).  
- Nomenclature confusion. “BGP-15” also denotes a calcipotriene-derived vitamin D3 analog in the oncology literature; chemical identity must be verified to avoid conflation during procurement and CMC (Sintov et al., 2013; Takács et al., 2024).  
- Evidence base heterogeneity. Some ocular and cardiovascular studies are published in lower–quality venues, emphasizing the need for rigorous, blinded replication and GLP toxicology in ocular models (Horváth et al., 2021; Wachal et al., 2021).

Recommended next steps  
- In vitro RPE validation. In human primary or iPSC-derived RPE under oxidative (H₂O₂/tert-butyl hydroperoxide) and inflammatory (LPS/CpG) stress, test BGP-15 at 0.3–30 µM for effects on Δψm (JC-1/TMRM), mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX), total ROS (DHR123), apoptosis/necrosis (annexin V/PI), and mitochondrial respiration; confirm no direct antioxidant scavenging in cell-free systems (Sumegi et al., 2017).  
- Proteostasis and HSR endpoints. Quantify HSP70/HSP25 induction, HSF1 acetylation/binding dynamics, Rac1 activation, and membrane raft integrity using fPEG-cholesterol probes/TOCCSL in RPE; evaluate MKP-1, JNK/p38, and Akt/GSK-3β signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013; Sumegi et al., 2017).  
- Mitochondrial dynamics. Assess OPA1 oligomerization, fusion/fission balance (Mfn1/2 and Drp1 markers), cristae morphology by EM, and PGC-1α/mtDNA copy number to benchmark fusion/biogenesis responses (Szabó et al., 2018; Horváth et al., 2021).  
- Ocular delivery PK/PD. Using the SBECD eyedrop formulation as a starting point, perform ocular pharmacokinetics (vitreous, retina, RPE–choroid) and pharmacodynamics (ocular HSP70, NFκB, mitochondrial markers) to ensure RPE target engagement at tolerated doses (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021).  
- In vivo retinal stress models. Extend to retinal oxidative stress paradigms that capture RPE pathology; leverage ERG, OCT, histology, and mitochondrial ultrastructure endpoints already positive in IR/diabetic models (Takács et al., 2024).  
- Identity control and CMC. Source BGP-15 as O-(3-piperidino-2-hydroxy-1-propyl) nicotinic amidoxime dihydrochloride; confirm identity by NMR/MS to avoid the calcipotriene-derived analog (Takács et al., 2024; Sintov et al., 2013).

Go/no-go considerations for dry AMD  
Given the robust mechanistic alignment—mitochondrial ROS control at complexes I/III, Δψm stabilization, HSR co-induction via membrane raft remodeling and HSF1 acetylation control, OPA1-driven mitochondrial fusion, and suppression of ROS-sensitive inflammatory kinases—plus demonstrable ocular efficacy in retinal injury models, BGP-15 merits advancement to RPE-focused preclinical validation for dry AMD (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Szabó et al., 2018; Takács et al., 2024). The principal risks are translational: ensuring adequate RPE exposures by ocular delivery, confirming RPE target expression/engagement, and generating rigorous GLP pharmacology/toxicology data in ocular species. On balance, the mechanistic breadth that often complicates development is an advantage in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction, proteostasis failure, and chronic inflammation coexist.

Conclusion. BGP-15 is a credible repurposing candidate for dry AMD based on its mitochondria-centered, HSP co-inducing, membrane-lipid–modulating pharmacology and encouraging retinal efficacy in vivo; priority should be given to RPE-targeted PK/PD, mitochondrial and HSR biomarker validation, and controlled efficacy studies in retinal oxidative-stress models to de-risk translation (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Takács et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Idebenone is a synthetic short‐chain benzoquinone that was designed as an analog of coenzyme Q10. Its chemical derivation from ubiquinone endows it with increased solubility and significantly enhanced antioxidant properties – reportedly up to ten‐fold greater than natural coenzyme Q10 – which in turn improves its capacity to shuttle electrons through the mitochondrial respiratory chain (Arend et al., 2015, pp. 2, 7–8). Originally synthesized as a potential remedy for mitochondrial dysfunction, idebenone belongs to the class of quinone derivatives that have historically been applied to conditions driven by oxidative stress and defective energy metabolism. The compound was discovered through efforts to mimic and improve on the natural electron carrier function of coenzyme Q10, with modifications engineered to optimize cellular uptake and bioavailability, thereby augmenting its use in various neurodegenerative and ophthalmologic applications (Gueven et al., 2015, pp. 4–5; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 7–8).

Therapeutic History:  
Idebenone’s clinical journey commenced with its use in Leber’s Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON), a mitochondrial disorder resulting in acute or subacute vision loss. In LHON, idebenone has been shown to improve visual function, as evidenced by improvements in photopic electroretinography (ERG) and other visual assessments, and has received regulatory approval in certain regions for this indication (Lyseng-Williamson, 2016, pp. 1–2). Preclinical studies have also demonstrated that idebenone exerts cytoprotective effects on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and retinal ganglion cells by preserving mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and reducing apoptosis in the face of oxidative stress (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13). Although idebenone’s original target was LHON, its biochemical properties—particularly its dual role as an electron shuttle and antioxidant—have spurred interest in repurposing the compound for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), a condition likewise characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction and heightened oxidative injury. Several studies have provided evidence from both biochemical assays and animal models that idebenone can modulate pro‐ and anti‐apoptotic protein expression (notably lowering Bax while increasing Bcl-2 levels) and activate the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway in RPE cells, thereby suggesting a potential benefit in retinal diseases beyond LHON (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 7–8).

Mechanism of Action:  
Idebenone operates through a multifaceted mechanism that addresses the dual challenges of mitochondrial energy impairment and oxidative damage. Fundamentally, idebenone is proposed to bypass defects in mitochondrial complex I by serving as an electron carrier that transfers reducing equivalents directly to complex III. This electron shuttling function is critical for maintaining the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and sustaining ATP synthesis when the conventional electron transfer through complex I is compromised due to oxidative damage—a scenario that is hypothesized to occur in the RPE under conditions such as drusen-induced stress (Arend et al., 2015, p. 2; Wang et al., 2025, pp. 5–8). In parallel, idebenone exhibits potent antioxidant activity by scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitigating the lipid peroxidation processes that are thought to contribute to drusen formation in dry AMD (Arend et al., 2015, pp. 7–8).

At the molecular level, idebenone has been shown to influence key cell survival pathways. It modulates the intrinsic mitochondrial apoptotic cascade by upregulating the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2 and concurrently downregulating the pro-apoptotic protein Bax. This shift in the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio helps to curb the initiation of apoptosis and contributes to cell survival in oxidative environments (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 5–6). Furthermore, idebenone stimulates the nuclear translocation of the transcription factor Nrf2, which in turn induces the expression of a suite of antioxidant genes. This activation of the Nrf2 pathway reinforces the cell’s intrinsic defenses against oxidative insult, which is of particular relevance in RPE cells tasked with handling the chronic low-grade oxidative stress present in AMD (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13). However, it is important to note that in certain settings—such as in cells deficient in the enzyme NQO1—idebenone’s efficacy as an electron carrier may be diminished, and higher concentrations may even elicit pro-oxidant or cytotoxic effects (Varricchio et al., 2020, pp. 18–20). These findings underscore the importance of optimizing the dosing strategy and ensuring appropriate cellular context to fully exploit idebenone’s protective actions.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of the proposed application for dry AMD, the hypothesis is that idebenone will act to shuttle electrons to complex III in RPE cells, thereby bypassing complex I defects induced by drusen-associated oxidative stress. This mechanism is expected to preserve the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and sustain ATP production, even under conditions of compromised oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). Preclinical data in RPE cell models have shown that idebenone treatment can mitigate the dissipation of Δψm in the face of hydrogen peroxide-induced stress, suggesting that similar protective effects could be harnessed in AMD where RPE cellular damage is a hallmark (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13).

Beyond its electron shuttling capacity, idebenone’s potent antioxidant action is expected to lower intracellular ROS levels and reduce lipid peroxidation, thereby protecting RPE cell membranes from the oxidative effects linked to drusen formation. This reduction in oxidative stress, coupled with the preservation of mitochondrial function, is anticipated to result in decreased activation of apoptotic pathways. The compound is also predicted to trigger Nrf2-dependent transcription of antioxidant genes within RPE cells—a response that is critical for combating the chronic oxidative stress implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13). 

Functionally, these molecular effects should translate into measurable improvements in cellular assays of mitochondrial function and viability. In vitro, one would expect to observe maintained or restored Δψm and ATP production in idebenone-treated RPE cells versus controls exposed to oxidative stress. In a more integrated system, such as in animal models or clinical assessments, improvements in photopic ERG responses—previously demonstrated in LHON patients under idebenone therapy—may serve as a surrogate marker for the preservation of retinal neuronal function and integrity (Lyseng-Williamson, 2016, pp. 1–2). Nonetheless, although the mechanistic rationale is robust, these expected effects depend critically on fine-tuning dosage to avoid the potential cytotoxicity observed at supra-therapeutic concentrations and to account for inter-patient variability in enzymes such as NQO1 that activate idebenone (Varricchio et al., 2020, pp. 18–20).

Overall Evaluation:  
The evidence reviewed supports idebenone as a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Among its key strengths is its dual action: the capacity to serve as an alternative electron shuttle to bypass complex I defects and the potent antioxidant activity that collectively mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage. These properties are especially relevant to dry AMD, where RPE degeneration and mitochondrial impairment form the basis of disease progression (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 2, 7–8).

Idebenone’s previous clinical approval and widespread use in LHON provide valuable precedent regarding its safety and efficacy in a retinal context. Moreover, preclinical data from in vitro studies in RPE cells offer compelling evidence regarding its ability to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential, sustain ATP synthesis, and modulate apoptotic pathways under oxidative stress conditions—mechanisms that are directly applicable to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 5–6). The activation of Nrf2 and subsequent upregulation of antioxidant defenses further consolidate its therapeutic potential (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13).

Nevertheless, several challenges remain. The efficacy of idebenone in bypassing complex I defects may be restricted by factors such as NQO1 expression, and potential pro-oxidant effects at higher concentrations necessitate careful dose optimization. In addition, while data from LHON and certain RPE cell models are promising, direct evidence from robust preclinical models of dry AMD is still limited. Some studies addressing these mechanisms have appeared in journals with variable impact factors, which calls for cautious interpretation of the data and underscores the need for further high-quality, reproducible research (Varricchio et al., 2020, pp. 15–18; Varricchio et al., 2020, pp. 18–20).

In summary, idebenone’s multifaceted mechanism—comprising electron shuttling to complex III, robust ROS scavenging, modulation of apoptotic signaling, and activation of Nrf2-driven antioxidant responses—aligns well with the therapeutic requirements for mitigating the mitochondrial and oxidative stress pathology present in dry AMD. While the compound’s history in LHON provides a strong foundation, the repurposing of idebenone for dry AMD will require additional rigorous preclinical investigations focusing on AMD-relevant models, followed by carefully designed clinical trials to validate its efficacy, safety, and dosing in this context (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13; Lyseng-Williamson, 2016, pp. 1–2; Gueven & Faldu, 2013, pp. 1–2).

Overall, idebenone represents a compelling candidate for further exploration in the therapeutic landscape of dry AMD. Its dual action addresses key pathophysiological mechanisms in the disease, and its established clinical use in a related ocular disorder provides a promising translational bridge. However, careful attention must be paid to the nuances of its mitochondrial interactions, dose-dependent effects, and the heterogeneous responses in different cellular contexts. Future research focusing on these aspects will be critical to determining whether idebenone can be successfully repurposed to prevent retinal degeneration and preserve vision in patients with dry AMD (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 2, 7–8; Russo et al., 2024, pp. 7–9; Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20).

The mechanism of action of S3QEL-2 is based on its capacity to selectively suppress superoxide generation originating at the Qo site of mitochondrial Complex III. S3QEL-2 emerges as an attractive candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to its unique pharmacological profile and precision in targeting mitochondrial ROS production.
