1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
────────────────────────────────────────────  
PMX53 is a cyclic peptidomimetic antagonist designed to block the complement component C5a receptor (C5aR), which is a critical mediator of pro-inflammatory signaling. The compound is defined by its unique cyclic hexapeptide sequence, AcF[OP(D-Cha)WR], and its design is rooted in systematic modifications of linear peptides derived from the C-terminal region of the endogenous ligand C5a. Early studies revealed that linear C5a fragments possess partial agonist activity; however, by substituting specific residues—most notably replacing phenylalanine with tryptophan at position 5—and then imposing a cyclic conformation through peptide cyclization, researchers were able to generate a molecule that not only negated the agonist properties but also provided potent receptor antagonism (Leonar, 2017).

The cyclic nature of PMX53 is of paramount importance; cyclization confers structural rigidity through a constrained conformation and an inverse γ-turn, which in turn enhances receptor binding selectivity and increases metabolic stability. This rigid structure minimizes entropic penalties upon receptor interaction and enables PMX53 to act in a “pseudo-irreversible” or insurmountable manner, meaning that even transient exposure to the compound can yield a sustained suppression of receptor activity. The cyclic peptide design also imparts resistance to proteolytic degradation—an attribute that is particularly significant for peptide drugs, which are typically prone to rapid enzymatic breakdown (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

Synthesis of PMX53 employs standard peptide synthesis methods. In practice, either solid-phase or solution-phase peptide synthesis techniques are used to assemble the linear precursor via iterative amino acid couplings using Fmoc protocols and appropriate protecting groups. Under dilute conditions, the linear peptide is cyclized using coupling reagents—often in the presence of a base such as DIPEA—to drive intramolecular bond formation, thereby “locking in” the bioactive conformation (Kumar et al., 2020). Although the detailed conditions such as choice of solvent and specific reagents are not provided in the summarized literature excerpts, the robust manufacturing and successful scale-up of PMX53 in preclinical and early clinical settings are evidence of a reliable and reproducible synthetic pathway (Allegretti et al., 2005; Ramsey, 2018).

Belonging to the broader class of cyclic peptide C5aR antagonists, PMX53 represents a well-validated therapeutic modality for modulating complement-mediated inflammatory responses. This class of compounds has been characterized extensively across various models of inflammatory diseases. In addition to systemic inflammatory disorders such as sepsis and arthritis, cyclic C5aR antagonists have been employed in studies assessing tissue injury models including ischemia–reperfusion and immune complex-mediated inflammation (Hutchison & Krause, 2004; Brandstetter et al., 2015). In summary, PMX53’s origins in rational drug design based on structure–activity relationships—its cyclic, constrained architecture, and its demonstrated ability to produce sustained receptor blockade—categorize it as a promising small peptide therapeutic candidate, particularly in indications where complement overactivation is known to play a deleterious role (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
2. Therapeutic History  
────────────────────────────────────────────  
The preclinical history of PMX53 has been marked by extensive evaluation in multiple models of inflammatory disease. Researchers have employed PMX53 in animal studies where its antagonism of the C5a receptor effectively reduced myeloperoxidase (MPO) release from polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs) and inhibited the production of inflammatory cytokines in roles that are essential for mediating tissue damage. For instance, in diverse rodent models of arthritis, sepsis, and inflammatory bowel disease, administration of PMX53—whether via oral, intravenous, or subcutaneous routes—produced significant improvements in disease outcomes. These studies consistently demonstrate that blockade of C5aR by PMX53 can attenuate aspects of the inflammatory cascade that are driven by complement activation (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

Clinical investigations have also been pursued with PMX53. Early-phase clinical trials that targeted diseases characterized by complement dysregulation, such as rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis, indicated that PMX53 exhibits an acceptable safety profile and some limited evidence of efficacy—particularly in psoriasis where a high proportion of patients evidenced lesion improvement (Proctor et al., 2006a; Ramsey, 2018). Although the clinical trajectory for PMX53 was eventually limited by concerns over pharmacokinetic properties and species-specific receptor affinity differences—for example, PMX53 binds human and rat C5aR with submicromolar affinities (approximately 90 nM and 40 nM, respectively) yet exhibits markedly lower affinity for mouse C5aR (~36 µM)—the overall body of evidence from systematic preclinical evaluation supports its robust anti-inflammatory activity (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

Of particular note is that while PMX53 has been primarily investigated in systemic inflammatory models and conditions such as sepsis, arthritis, and immune complex-mediated injuries, there is an emerging conceptual linkage between complement-mediated inflammation and retinal degenerative diseases like dry AMD. Several independent studies have demonstrated that the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) expresses C5a receptors constitutively and that exposure to complement-competent serum or recombinant C5a upregulates receptor expression. These studies further show that C5a primes RPE cells for inflammasome activation—a critical process in the pathogenesis of dry AMD—and that modulation of C5aR signaling can affect pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β) (Brandstetter et al., 2015). Although PMX53 has not been used directly in ocular models or clinical trials for retinal degenerative conditions, its demonstrated efficacy in systemic models and the established role of complement activation in RPE pathology provide a compelling rationale to explore its repurposing for dry AMD (Proctor et al., 2006a; Proctor et al., 2006b).

Additional analogues in this compound class, such as PMX205, have been developed with modifications aimed at improving oral potency and pharmacokinetic properties. PMX205, for example, incorporates a hydrocinnamate moiety that confers increased lipophilicity and enables improved oral bioavailability—a factor that might be advantageous for addressing the challenging delivery needs associated with ocular tissues. While PMX205 itself has been evaluated primarily in models of inflammatory bowel disease and neurodegenerative conditions, the overall historical narrative underscores that the PMX series provides a well-characterized platform with potential for repurposing in retinal diseases (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Proctor et al., 2006b; Proctor et al., 2006a).

Taken together, the therapeutic history of PMX53 confirms that it has undergone extensive biochemical, preclinical, and early clinical scrutiny for diseases driven by complement-mediated inflammation. Despite the lack of direct evidence in ocular or AMD-specific contexts, the extensive data from nonocular models and the mechanistic similarities between systemic complement dysregulation and retinal complement activation lay a strong foundation for further exploration of PMX53 in dry AMD (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
3. Mechanism of Action  
────────────────────────────────────────────  
At the molecular level, PMX53 functions by directly binding to and antagonizing the complement C5a receptor (C5aR), a G-protein–coupled receptor that mediates the downstream pro-inflammatory effects of the anaphylatoxin C5a. The binding of C5a to its receptor on cells, including immune cells and RPE cells, initiates a cascade of inflammatory signaling events characterized by calcium mobilization, activation of kinase pathways (such as PI3K and MAPK), and subsequent transcriptional upregulation of inflammatory mediators including IL-1β. In the context of RPE cells, these events are further linked with the generation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome—a process that underpins cellular stress and eventual degeneration in dry AMD (Brandstetter et al., 2015).

PMX53’s mechanism of action is rooted in its cyclic peptide structure, which endows it with the ability to engage the C5a receptor in a manner that is both highly specific and functionally distinct from simple competitive blockade. Extensive structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies, including receptor mutagenesis and docking experiments, have revealed that PMX53 binds primarily to critical extracellular regions of C5aR—most notably the extracellular loop 2 (ECL2) and portions of the transmembrane domain. For example, mutations in ECL2 residues (such as R175) have been shown to significantly reduce the efficacy of both C5a and PMX53, underscoring the importance of this region in ligand–receptor interactions (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006b).

The binding model for PMX53 suggests that its aromatic and hydrophobic components—such as the tryptophan side chain and the d-cyclohexylalanine residue—fit within a hydrophobic pocket formed by receptor residues including I116 and V286. These interactions, which involve hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, and possibly cation–π interactions, contribute to the stability of the ligand–receptor complex and account for the “pseudo-irreversible” nature of the antagonism. In practical terms, once PMX53 binds to C5aR it exhibits insurmountable antagonism, meaning that even in the presence of high concentrations of the endogenous ligand C5a, the receptor remains blocked and unable to signal. This mode of binding is particularly attractive in chronic inflammatory conditions where sustained receptor occupancy can yield lasting therapeutic benefits despite fluctuations in plasma drug concentrations (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006b; Hutchison & Krause, 2004; Proctor et al., 2006b).

Downstream of receptor blockade, the interruption of C5a signaling by PMX53 results in a reduction in calcium influx and the inhibition of kinase cascades that normally lead to the activation of transcription factors such as NF-κB. The inhibition of NF-κB activity, in turn, leads to decreased transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1β) and chemokines, thereby damping the overall inflammatory response. In RPE cells, it has been demonstrated that complement activation—via either exogenous C5a or complement-competent serum—upregulates C5aR and primes the cells for inflammasome activation, which is dependent on increased mtROS production. Thus, by preventing C5a from binding to its receptor, PMX53 is expected to blunt both the immediate signaling events (calcium mobilization, reactive oxygen species generation) and the subsequent transcriptional upregulation of inflammatory mediators that lead to inflammasome assembly (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020).

Notably, crystallographic and docking studies have reinforced the concept that PMX53 interacts with the receptor in a manner that stabilizes an inactive conformation. These studies show that PMX53’s cyclic structure enables it to engage its target in a stable fashion by “locking” C5aR into a state where conformational changes required for receptor activation are prevented. This effect directly translates into a reduction in downstream signaling events and is consistent with the observed insurmountable antagonism in various functional assays. The pseudo-irreversible binding characteristic ensures that once PMX53 occupies the receptor, it remains bound long enough to counteract episodic or continuous C5a fluctuations, a feature that is particularly beneficial in a disease like dry AMD where chronic complement dysregulation is a hallmark (Liu et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Ramsey, 2018).

In summary, at the molecular level PMX53 functions as a robust inhibitor of C5aR by engaging critical residues on the receptor extracellular region, thereby preventing the pro-inflammatory interactions initiated by C5a binding. This blockade not only halts immediate calcium and kinase signaling events but also disrupts the longer-term transcriptional activation of inflammatory mediators, including those responsible for mtROS overproduction and inflammasome activation in RPE cells (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006b; Brandstetter et al., 2015).

4. Expected Effect

The hypothesis underlying the repurposing of PMX53 for dry AMD is that by antagonizing the C5a receptor on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, the compound can attenuate a critical amplification loop in which complement activation leads to mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) production and NLRP3 inflammasome activation. This persistent activation drives an increase in C5a levels that in turn upregulates C5aR expression on RPE cells, thereby priming these cells for a heightened inflammatory response. Specifically, the engagement of C5aR provokes intracellular signaling cascades that lead to excessive production of mtROS and the subsequent activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, culminating in the maturation and release of interleukin-1β (IL-1β) (Brandstetter et al., 2015).

In an in vitro assay using cultured human RPE cells, treatment with PMX53 is expected to demonstrate a significant reduction in mitochondrial superoxide levels. When RPE cells are challenged with either recombinant C5a or complement-active serum, the normal response is an upregulation of inflammatory mediators and a spike in mtROS production; however, with pre-treatment or co-treatment with PMX53, the binding of C5a to its receptor is blocked and these downstream events are attenuated. One would anticipate the readouts from such an assay to include a decline in the fluorescence signal from mitochondrial superoxide indicators, a reduction in caspase-1 activation (reflecting suppressed inflammasome activity), and lower concentrations of IL-1β in the culture supernatant (Brandstetter et al., 2015).

In animal models that mimic the chronic complement dysregulation observed in dry AMD, the administration of PMX53 may confer protective effects on RPE morphology and retinal architecture. Although PMX53 has not yet been directly deployed in ocular models of AMD, its robust anti-inflammatory effects in systemic models—such as those for arthritis, sepsis, and ischemia–reperfusion injuries—suggest that similar benefits may be observed in the retina when the compound is delivered via an appropriate route (e.g., intravitreal injection, nanoparticle formulations, or sustained-release implants). These models could offer endpoints such as reduced sub-RPE deposit formation, preserved RPE cell integrity, and maintenance of retinal function as measured by electrophysiological assessments (Proctor et al., 2006a; Proctor et al., 2006b).

Furthermore, the pseudo-irreversible binding characteristic of PMX53 represents an important advantage in a chronic condition like dry AMD. Even if the compound is cleared rapidly from the systemic circulation or ocular compartment, its long receptor residence time may ensure continuous inhibition of C5a signaling over extended periods. This sustained blockade is especially important in countering the slow, progressive damage associated with dry AMD, where intermittent complement activation can cumulatively lead to RPE dysfunction and eventually photoreceptor loss (Ong et al., 2024; Proctor et al., 2006b; Behnke, 2022). In this context, a reduction in mtROS generation and inflammasome-driven cytokine release would be expected to limit oxidative injury and maintain the homeostatic balance in the delicate retinal environment.

In summary, the expected pharmacodynamic effects of PMX53 in the proposed assays include a measurable reduction in mitochondrial superoxide production, a decrease in caspase-1 activity and IL-1β release, and overall preservation of RPE cell morphology when challenged with complement-active stimuli. These effects, if achieved in vitro and then recapitulated in vivo in an appropriate animal model, would support the notion that PMX53 can effectively disrupt the complement-driven amplification of oxidative and inflammatory damage that contributes to dry AMD progression (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Proctor et al., 2006b).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
5. Overall Evaluation  
────────────────────────────────────────────  
In evaluating PMX53 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several positive factors and potential challenges emerge based on the available literature drawn from preclinical and early clinical studies in systemic inflammatory models.

Strengths:  
•  PMX53 has been extensively characterized as a potent cyclic peptide antagonist of the C5a receptor with a well-rationalized design that exploits the structural features of the endogenous ligand C5a. Its cyclic architecture confers not only high receptor selectivity and metabolic stability but also a mode of action that is classified as “pseudo-irreversible” or insurmountable antagonism. This means that once it binds to the receptor, PMX53 is able to provide sustained receptor blockade even in the presence of high levels of circulating C5a—a feature that is especially appealing for chronic conditions like dry AMD where persistent complement dysregulation is a central pathological driver (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

•  The preclinical body of evidence supporting the anti-inflammatory activity of PMX53 is considerable. In numerous animal models, including those for arthritis, sepsis, and ischemia–reperfusion injury, treatment with PMX53 has been shown to reduce inflammatory cytokine production, limit immune cell degranulation, and preserve tissue integrity (Ramsey, 2018; Hutchison & Krause, 2004; Allegretti et al., 2005). These findings have translated, at least in part, to early-phase clinical studies in which PMX53 was evaluated in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis—diseases that share underlying inflammatory components with dry AMD. The favorable safety profile observed in these studies provides an additional layer of support for considering PMX53 as a repurposed drug candidate (Proctor et al., 2006a; Kumar et al., 2020).

•  A critical advantage of PMX53 for the treatment of dry AMD lies in its mechanistic targeting of the complement system, which is increasingly recognized as a central player in the pathogenesis of retinal degenerations. Studies using human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells have demonstrated that complement activation, particularly via C5a, leads to upregulation of the C5a receptor and primes these cells for inflammasome activation in response to additional stressors such as lipofuscin-mediated photooxidative damage (Brandstetter et al., 2015). By effectively preventing C5a from binding to its receptor, PMX53 is hypothesized to block the initiation of a cascade that culminates in excessive mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) production and subsequent IL-1β release. This would theoretically protect RPE cells from the oxidative insult and inflammation that characterize dry AMD pathology (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Leonar, 2017).

•  Moreover, the pseudo-irreversible nature of PMX53’s receptor binding offers the important potential for prolonged therapeutic effects despite the inherent challenges associated with peptide pharmacokinetics. While it is acknowledged that the peptidic nature of the compound might pose hurdles with respect to systemic clearance and bioavailability—particularly within the ocular environment where drug delivery is complicated by barriers such as the blood–retina barrier—the ability of PMX53 to remain bound to C5aR could mitigate the need for continually high drug concentrations. This quality could be beneficial if innovative delivery strategies, such as intravitreal injections, nanoparticle-based formulations, or sustained-release implants, are employed to achieve localized drug concentrations in the retina (Proctor et al., 2006b; Kumar et al., 2020).

Weaknesses and Concerns:  
•  Despite its many promising aspects, several critical challenges must be considered before PMX53 can be realistically advanced as a treatment for dry AMD. One of the most significant gaps in the current literature is the absence of direct preclinical or clinical data specific to ocular models of AMD. Although the complement system, and in particular the C5a–C5aR axis, is well documented as playing a role in RPE dysfunction and retinal inflammation (Brandstetter et al., 2015), PMX53 itself has not yet been rigorously tested in models that recapitulate the complex microenvironment of the retina. Animal models that faithfully mimic the chronic complement activation and oxidative stress seen in human dry AMD are necessary to determine whether the robust systemic anti-inflammatory activity of PMX53 can be translated to a localized ocular context (Proctor et al., 2006a; Hutchison & Krause, 2004).

•  A second concern relates to species-specific differences in receptor binding affinity. It is well established that PMX53 exhibits high affinity for human and rat C5a receptors (in the range of tens of nanomolar), whereas its affinity for the mouse receptor is markedly lower (approximately 36 µM) (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a). This presents a practical obstacle, as many preclinical studies in ophthalmology rely on murine models to assess disease progression and drug efficacy. To circumvent this pitfall, it may be necessary to utilize alternative animal models with receptor pharmacology that more closely mirrors the human system—such as rat models or non-human primate studies—or to develop further analogues that demonstrate improved cross-species binding (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

•  Another issue is the challenge of delivering a peptide drug to ocular tissues in a sustained and therapeutically effective manner. The ocular barriers, including the corneal epithelium and the blood–retina barrier, limit the penetration and retention of systemically administered drugs. In the case of PMX53, whose peptidic nature predisposes it to rapid clearance and potential degradation, specialized formulation strategies will be essential. Approaches such as encapsulation in biodegradable nanoparticles, development of sustained-release intravitreal implants, or formulation with permeability-enhancing agents could be explored to ensure that therapeutically relevant concentrations of PMX53 reach the RPE and maintain a prolonged therapeutic effect (Kumar et al., 2020).

•  Safety considerations within the ocular environment also warrant close attention. While systemic administration of PMX53 has demonstrated an acceptable side-effect profile in non-ocular applications, the retina is an immunologically privileged and sensitive tissue. Chronic inhibition of complement-mediated signaling in the eye could potentially impair local immune surveillance or interfere with normal cellular homeostasis. Such risks necessitate detailed ocular toxicology studies to assess the potential for adverse effects resulting from long-term C5aR blockade in RPE cells and other retinal tissues (Proctor et al., 2006a; Hutchison & Krause, 2004).

•  Furthermore, the translational relevance of the anti-inflammatory effects observed with PMX53 in systemic diseases may not directly apply to the intricate pathophysiology of dry AMD. Dry AMD is a multifactorial disease influenced by genetic predispositions, environmental stresses (such as oxidative damage from chronic light exposure), and complex interactions between complement proteins, RPE cells, and the extracellular matrix. While the blockade of C5aR is theoretically poised to reduce mtROS production and inflammasome activation, it is possible that additional redundant inflammatory pathways might offset the therapeutic benefit of targeting a single receptor (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Proctor et al., 2006a).

•  Finally, the overall clinical development history of PMX53 indicates that while the compound has progressed to early clinical trials for systemic inflammatory conditions, challenges related to pharmacokinetics and delivery have hindered further clinical advancements. As such, repurposing PMX53 for dry AMD will require a dedicated research program that not only demonstrates efficacy in ocular models but also addresses the unique drug delivery and safety challenges associated with the eye (Proctor et al., 2006a; Proctor et al., 2006b).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
6. Overall Conclusion  
────────────────────────────────────────────  
In summary, PMX53 is a well-characterized cyclic peptidomimetic C5a receptor antagonist that has been evaluated extensively in systemic models of inflammation and has reached early-phase clinical testing for conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis. Its design, which exploits a cyclic structure to achieve pseudo-irreversible antagonism, provides a strong mechanistic rationale for targeting the complement cascade—which is increasingly recognized as a major contributor not only to systemic inflammatory diseases but also to ocular conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

The expected effect of PMX53 in the context of dry AMD is to prevent the binding of C5a to its receptor on retinal pigment epithelial cells, thereby disrupting a key amplification loop that leads to mitochondrial reactive oxygen species overproduction, inflammasome activation, and subsequent IL-1β release. Such a blockade should, in theory, mitigate the chronic inflammatory stress that drives RPE degeneration and, by extension, slow the progression of dry AMD (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Proctor et al., 2006a).

Nonetheless, despite its strong conceptual appeal and preclinical promise in systemic models, significant knowledge gaps remain with respect to its application in the ocular setting. No dedicated studies have yet confirmed the efficacy of PMX53 in reducing complement-driven oxidative stress specifically in the retina, and species-specific differences in receptor binding mean that murine models—a common platform for AMD research—may not accurately reflect the human situation. Additionally, the challenges inherent in delivering a peptide drug effectively to ocular tissues, combined with the potential risks of long-term complement inhibition in the sensitive retinal environment, require careful and systematic investigation through both advanced formulation approaches and dedicated ocular safety studies (Proctor et al., 2006a; Hutchison & Krause, 2004; Kumar et al., 2020).

Overall, while the scientific and mechanistic basis for repurposing PMX53 for dry AMD is compelling—given its ability to disrupt complement-mediated inflammatory cascades and its pseudo-irreversible receptor binding—the translation of these benefits to the ocular milieu remains to be established. A focused research program is needed to conduct in vitro studies in primary human RPE cells exposed to complement activation, followed by in vivo evaluations in non-murine models that more closely mirror human C5aR pharmacology. Further development of ocular delivery systems, including intravitreal implants or nanoparticle-based formulations, will also be essential to overcome the inherent pharmacokinetic challenges posed by a peptide therapeutic.

If these hurdles can be successfully addressed, PMX53 could represent an innovative approach to slow or prevent RPE degeneration by attenuating the complement-driven amplification of mtROS production and inflammasome activation—a cascade that is a key driver of dry AMD pathology. In light of the significant unmet need for effective treatments for dry AMD and the robust preclinical data supporting the anti-inflammatory efficacy of cyclic C5aR antagonists in other contexts, further investigation into PMX53 is both scientifically justified and therapeutically promising (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a; Brandstetter et al., 2015; Ong et al., 2024).

This comprehensive review indicates that while substantial promise exists for PMX53 as a candidate to mitigate the complement-mediated mechanisms underlying dry AMD, its successful repurposing will depend on dedicated ocular pharmacology studies, careful species selection for preclinical investigations, and the development of targeted drug-delivery strategies tailored to the unique anatomical and immunological environment of the eye (Proctor et al., 2006a; Ong et al., 2024; Proctor et al., 2006b).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is an endogenous ketone body produced by mitochondrial ketogenesis from fatty-acid–derived acetyl-CoA, classically in hepatocytes but also in extrahepatic cell types including the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and several neuronal lineages (enzymatic pathway: ACAT, HMGCS2, HMGCL, and BDH1) (Wang et al., 2021; Gough, 2021). In physiological and nutritional ketosis, circulating BHB rises from baseline (~0.05–0.1 mM) to levels >0.5 mM and up to 5–7 mM with prolonged fasting, providing an alternative oxidative substrate for extrahepatic mitochondria when carbohydrate availability is limited (Wang et al., 2021; Cooper et al., 2023). BHB and acetoacetate are transported into and out of cells via proton-linked monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs) such as MCT1 and MCT2 that are expressed at the blood–retinal barrier and in retinal cells, enabling substrate entry into the retina (Yang, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Gough, 2021). RPEs robustly express mitochondrial HMGCS2 and can ketogenize palmitate to BHB, secreting BHB via MCT1; retinal cells can take up and metabolize BHB into Krebs-cycle intermediates and amino acids, indicating functional capacity to use BHB as mitochondrial fuel in the outer retina (Yang, 2021). More recent mass spectrometry–based reassessment shows that RPE secretion of BHB is substantially lower than previously estimated by enzymatic kits, that RPE exports BHB to both apical and basal compartments, and that RPE both produces and consumes BHB depending on nutrient state—important considerations for experimental design and therapeutic targeting (Gulette et al., 2024).  

BHB belongs to the class of endogenous metabolic intermediates that function dually as oxidative fuels (via oxidation to acetyl-CoA and entry into TCA cycle) and signaling molecules with paracrine/autocrine receptor and epigenetic actions (e.g., agonism at HCAR2/GPR109A and inhibition of class I/IIa histone deacetylases) (Wang et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Kovács et al., 2021). As a therapeutic modality, BHB has been delivered exogenously as salts/esters or induced endogenously through ketogenic diets, fasting, or exercise to support mitochondrial ATP production and alter cellular stress responses in the CNS, heart, and skeletal muscle (Cooper et al., 2023; Kovács et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2022). In retinal disease models, ketogenic interventions or exogenous BHB have reduced oxidative/inflammatory injury and improved functional measures, though direct application to dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) has not yet been clinically tested (Gough, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021).  

Therapeutic History  
Ketone biology has a long history in neurology and cardiometabolic research, where BHB has been shown to preserve mitochondrial function, increase ATP production, and blunt oxidative injury in ischemia, neurodegeneration models, and skeletal muscle stress paradigms (Kovács et al., 2021; Mierziak et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2018). In neural tissues, ketogenic interventions and exogenous ketones prevent synaptic dysfunction induced by respiratory complex inhibitors and increase the brain NAD⁺/NADH ratio, correlating with decreased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation (Morris et al., 2020). In rat skeletal muscle cells, 5 mM BHB for 24–48 h increased respiratory control, ATP-linked respiration, P:O efficiency, lowered H₂O₂ production, and shifted mitochondrial dynamics toward fusion via DRP1 suppression—consistent with enhanced bioenergetics and decreased oxidative stress (Parker et al., 2018). In primary neurons, BHB maintained oxidative phosphorylation under glutamate workload even when cytosolic NADH transfer via the malate–aspartate shuttle was inhibited, demonstrating that BHB can sustain respiration under conditions that impair glycolytic NADH coupling to mitochondria (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

In the retina and optic nerve, multiple preclinical models show that ketogenic exposures or direct ketone administration reduce oxidative stress and inflammation, preserve function, and limit neuronal death. Intraperitoneal BHB and acetoacetate reduced NMDA-induced retinal ganglion cell (RGC) death in rats, and ketogenic diet attenuated NMDA-induced RGC injury in juvenile rats (Gough, 2021). In ocular blast or optic neuropathy paradigms, ketogenic diet prevented increases in superoxide and IL-1α, preserved visual evoked potentials, and reduced astrocytic hypertrophy and optic nerve death (Gough, 2021). In glaucoma models, ketogenic diet improved RGC soma/axon survival, axonal transport, and reduced gliosis, with increases in NAD and NAD:NADH ratio and upregulation of MCT1/MCT2 in optic nerve (Tribble et al., 2021). AAV-mediated MCT2 overexpression (increasing uptake of lactate/pyruvate/ketones) preserved RGCs and optic nerve axons in ocular hypertension and glaucoma models and elevated markers of mitochondrial biogenesis and function (PGC1α, COX, SDH) and antioxidant defense (SOD2) (Gough, 2021). However, in at least one RGC injury model, daily intraperitoneal BHB or acetoacetate did not replicate ketogenic diet neuroprotection, underscoring differences between exogenous ketone dosing and the systemic/multifactorial effects of ketogenic diets (Tribble et al., 2021).  

Within the RPE compartment specifically, two lines of evidence are relevant: (1) BHB protects ARPE-19 cells from high-glucose–induced injury, improving viability, alleviating cell cycle arrest, and modulating inflammatory mediators (IL-8, IL-17α, MCP-1) at millimolar concentrations achievable with nutritional ketosis or exogenous supplementation (Argentino et al., 2025). (2) HCAR2/GPR109A, a BHB receptor, is robustly expressed by the RPE; BHB agonism reduced retinal leukocyte infiltration in LPS-challenged mice in an HCAR2-dependent manner, and loss of HCAR2 in RPE led to barrier dysfunction (ZO-1 defects) and increased immune cell infiltrates, indicating that BHB–HCAR2 signaling can preserve an immunoinhibitory retinal environment (Powell et al., 2021). In diabetic retinopathy models, systemic BHB activation of HCA2 reduced ER stress and NLRP3 inflammasome signaling and ameliorated retinal pathology, establishing anti-inflammatory and ER stress–limiting actions in retina (Trotta et al., 2019).  

In inherited retinal degeneration models, ketogenic interventions delayed photoreceptor degeneration and improved electroretinogram (ERG) amplitudes and outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness in rd10 and Pde6a mice, and a soluble ketogenic formulation partially restored vision and survival in PDH-deficient noir zebrafish—consistent with bypassing PDH to supply acetyl-CoA and support neurotransmitter synthesis (Gough, 2021). Notwithstanding these encouraging signals, the literature consistently notes the absence of clinical trials evaluating ketogenic interventions or BHB in retinitis pigmentosa or AMD patients, and reports potentially adverse effects of ketogenic diets in wild-type mice (decreased ERG amplitudes, altered albumin/weight), highlighting translational uncertainties and the need to distinguish effects of BHB from the broader systemic consequences of diet (Gough, 2021).  

Mechanism of Action  
BHB acts through convergent metabolic, redox, mitochondrial, inflammatory, and epigenetic mechanisms that are mechanistically aligned with the pathophysiology of RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic oxidative/inflammatory stress in dry AMD.  

- Alternative mitochondrial fuel and bioenergetics support. In extrahepatic tissues (including retina), BHB oxidation proceeds via mitochondrial BDH1 (βHB→acetoacetate) followed by SCOT/OXCT1 (AcAc→AcAc-CoA using succinyl-CoA) and acetyl-CoA production for TCA entry and ATP generation, enabling substrate-level maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and oxidative phosphorylation under glucose restriction or impaired glycolytic NADH transfer (Wang et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023). The retina expresses monocarboxylate transport routes (e.g., MCT1 at the inner blood–retinal barrier; MCT2 in neurons), and RPE expresses MCT1 and can both produce and consume BHB, providing a plausible uptake pathway for exogenous BHB into RPE and neighboring retinal cells (Tribble et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Gulette et al., 2024). In neurons, BHB-supported respiration remains robust when the malate–aspartate shuttle is blocked with AOAA—conditions that decrease glucose-fueled ATP synthesis—indicating that BHB can preserve mitochondrial ATP synthesis and respiratory control when cytosolic NADH transfer is compromised, a scenario relevant to glycolysis-impaired RPE (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

- Redox coupling and ROS control. The interconversion of acetoacetate and BHB by βHB dehydrogenase is linked to NADH/NAD⁺ redox; acetoacetate→BHB requires oxidation of NADH to NAD⁺, and nutritional ketosis in human brain increases NAD⁺/NADH ratio, correlating with reductions in mitochondrial ROS generation (Gough, 2021; Morris et al., 2020). Ketones can inhibit mitochondrial ROS production by increasing NADH oxidation, and ketogenic interventions increase NAD⁺/NADH in vivo, though tissue- and context-dependent effects exist (Morris et al., 2020). Complementary cardiac literature reports that β-OHB can reduce the mitochondrial NAD couple while oxidizing coenzyme Q, emphasizing that BHB modulates both NADH/NAD⁺ and Q/QH₂ redox pairs in mitochondria—with directionality that may depend on prevailing substrate status and respiratory state (Chu et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion models and muscle cells, BHB lowers mitochondrial ROS, decreases mitochondrial swelling, maintains Δψm, and increases ATP production, consistent with direct mitochondrial protection (Mierziak et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2018).  

- Antioxidant transcription (Nrf2) and hormesis. Ketogenic exposures can induce a hormetic redox signal that activates Keap1–Nrf2, increasing transcription of detoxification and antioxidant genes; in retina, ketone body exposure mimicked calorie restriction via fumarate–Nrf2 activation (Gough, 2021; Fu et al., 2020). Preclinical optic/retinal models link these antioxidant transcriptional effects to preserved function and reduced oxidative markers (NOS, MDA, superoxide) (Gough, 2021).  

- Anti-inflammatory signaling via HCAR2/ARRB2 and NLRP3/NF-κB suppression. BHB is a ligand for HCAR1/HCAR2 receptors; HCAR2 is robustly expressed in human RPE and retina, and receptor activation by BHB reduces leukocyte infiltration and preserves RPE barrier integrity in inflammation models (Powell et al., 2021). Downstream, BHB–HCAR signaling recruits β-arrestin-2 (ARRB2) that binds NLRP3 to block inflammasome assembly, decreasing ASC and preventing K⁺ efflux to suppress IL-1β maturation; BHB also activates a COX1/PGD2 cascade that inhibits IKK and NF-κB nuclear translocation, reducing TNF-α and microglial/macrophage activation (Gough, 2021). In human iPSC-derived microglia, amyloid-β oligomers increased MCU expression, raised mitochondrial Ca²⁺ ~40%, elevated mtROS, and triggered mPTP opening; BHB normalized MCU, decreased mtCa²⁺/mtROS, and completely reversed mPTP activation, restoring phagocytic function (Jin et al., 2023). Although not conducted in RPE, these mitochondrial-stabilizing effects are mechanistically relevant to post-mitotic cells with high oxidative load.  

- Epigenetic modulation and mitochondrial biogenesis. BHB is an endogenous inhibitor of class I/IIa HDACs at physiological millimolar concentrations, leading to histone hyperacetylation and upregulation of FOXO3a and metallothionein genes that encode antioxidant defenses; BHB also increases intracellular acetyl-CoA and supports protein acetylation, and can β-hydroxybutyrylate histones, adding layers of gene regulatory control tied to mitochondrial status (Yang, 2021; Kovács et al., 2021; Mierziak et al., 2021). In retinal/optic nerve models, ketogenic diet or enhanced monocarboxylate uptake upregulated PGC1α, COX, SDH, and SOD2 while lowering pAMPK/AMPK, linking substrate availability to mitochondrial biogenesis and anti-inflammatory signaling (Gough, 2021).  

- Immunometabolic reprogramming in retina/CNS. Ketogenic interventions increased anti-inflammatory mediators (IL-4, Arginase-1) and M2-like microglia while decreasing IBA-1⁺ macrophage/microglia, consistent with dampened neuroinflammation secondary to improved bioenergetics (reduced AMPK activation) and prevention of NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation (Gough, 2021). BHB also inhibits FFAR3/GPR41, reducing sympathetic activity in mice, indicating broader metabolic signaling roles that could modulate retinal perfusion/metabolism indirectly (Gough, 2021).  

Collectively, these mechanisms—fuel substitution that sustains Δψm and ATP synthesis under glycolytic impairment, improved redox balance with decreased mitochondrial ROS, Nrf2-dependent antioxidant gene induction, NLRP3/NF-κB anti-inflammatory actions via HCAR2/ARRB2, stabilization of mitochondrial Ca²⁺/mPTP, and epigenetic programs that support mitochondrial biogenesis—map directly onto pathologies implicated in RPE degeneration in dry AMD and provide multiple rescue nodes testable in disease-relevant models (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Gough, 2021; Powell et al., 2021).  

Expected Effect

Given the measurement pitfalls documented in RPE ketone assays, BHB should be quantified by LC–MS/MS or after removal of high-MW confounders by size exclusion rather than by standard enzymatic kits (Gulette et al., 2024).  
Protein expression considerations support the mechanism in the target cell type. HCAR2/GPR109A is expressed by RPE and retinal microglia/endothelium and mediates anti-inflammatory effects of BHB in vivo, making receptor-dependent components of BHB action directly testable in RPE (Powell et al., 2021). RPE expresses HMGCS2 and MCT1, and retinal cells metabolize BHB into TCA intermediates, consistent with BDH1/SCOT/OXCT1 pathway activity enabling BHB oxidation in retinal tissues; while direct SCOT expression in RPE is not provided here, the metabolic tracing data indicating conversion of BHB to Krebs intermediates in retinal cells justify testing oxidative utilization in RPE (Yang, 2021; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strength of biological rationale. The core hypothesis—that BHB can act as an alternative mitochondrial fuel to sustain Δψm and lower NADH-driven mitochondrial ROS in glycolysis-impaired RPE—is strongly aligned with BHB’s established roles in extrahepatic tissues and is supported by multiple mechanistic strands in relevant neural and retinal systems (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023). BHB oxidation provides acetyl-CoA and maintains respiration when glycolytic NADH transfer is compromised, as demonstrated in primary neurons; BHB reduces mtROS, preserves Δψm, and increases ATP in ischemic muscle/heart models; and nutrient ketosis increases the NAD⁺/NADH ratio and lowers ROS production in brain—effects that would be expected to decrease reverse-electron transport–driven ROS at complex I and stabilize mitochondrial function in stressed RPE (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023; Mierziak et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020). In retinal tissue, ketogenic interventions and direct ketone administration reduce oxidative injury, preserve function, and enhance mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses in RGC/optic nerve models, while anti-inflammatory benefits via HCAR2—expressed by RPE—reduce leukocyte infiltration and preserve barrier integrity (Gough, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Powell et al., 2021; Trotta et al., 2019). The mitochondrial stabilization effects observed in human microglia—lower MCU/mtCa²⁺, reduced mtROS, prevention of mPTP opening—further support a BHB-mediated mitochondrial resilience phenotype that is likely relevant to RPE (Jin et al., 2023).  

Evidence relevant to the target tissue. RPEs possess ketone-related transport and enzymatic capacity (HMGCS2, MCT1) and can both produce and consume BHB; they are responsive to BHB in vitro under metabolic stress (hyperglycemia) with improved viability and inflammatory marker modulation (Yang, 2021; Argentino et al., 2025). HCAR2-mediated anti-inflammatory and barrier maintenance functions have been demonstrated in RPE/retina, providing a receptor-proximal pathway for BHB to suppress chronic para-inflammation and preserve RPE junctional integrity, both relevant to dry AMD pathobiology (Powell et al., 2021). While direct measurements of BDH1/SCOT activity and NAD⁺/NADH dynamics in human RPE treated with BHB remain to be shown here, the metabolic fate of BHB in retinal cells and robust mitochondrial effects in closely related cell types make the translational experiments technically feasible and mechanistically justified (Yang, 2021; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

Translational gaps and risks. No clinical trials have evaluated ketogenic diets or BHB specifically for RP or AMD, and some ketogenic diet studies reported adverse outcomes in wild-type animals (decreased ERG amplitude, altered serum albumin/weight), emphasizing the need to decouple BHB’s effects from broader dietary/metabolic confounders (Gough, 2021). Direct BHB delivery does not always recapitulate ketogenic diet benefits in RGC injury, suggesting that multi-target effects of diet (e.g., NAD metabolism, mTOR, microbiome) contribute to efficacy; this implies that BHB monotherapy may require combination strategies (e.g., nicotinamide co-therapy) or optimized dosing to achieve comparable benefit (Tribble et al., 2021). Quantification of BHB in RPE experiments is non-trivial due to assay interference; LC–MS/MS or validated size-exclusion protocols must be used to avoid false positives and to measure physiologically relevant, often low-micromolar extracellular BHB in RPE cultures (Gulette et al., 2024). Finally, the directionality of NAD redox effects may be context dependent (reports of both increased NAD⁺/NADH ratio in brain and reduced mitochondrial NAD couple in cardiac models), requiring careful interpretation with compartment-specific assays in RPE (Morris et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2021).  

Development path and decision points. Given the strong mechanistic rationale, retina-focused preclinical evidence, and RPE receptor expression data, BHB is a plausible repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD that merits rigorous, RPE-centric validation. Key go/no-go preclinical criteria should include: (1) demonstration that BHB rescues Δψm and ATP-linked respiration in primary human RPE or iPSC-RPE under glycolytic impairment (e.g., 2-deoxyglucose or low glucose plus workload), (2) reduction of mitochondrial ROS (MitoSOX/H₂O₂ flux) and elevation of cellular NAD⁺/NADH ratio with BHB, (3) suppression of pAMPK and NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation, induction of Nrf2 target genes, and reduction of NLRP3 activation, (4) persistence of benefits under HCAR2 antagonism/knockdown to parse receptor versus fuel contributions, and (5) confirmation that effects are contingent on monocarboxylate transport (MCT inhibition) and SCOT activity (e.g., OXCT1 knockdown), which would mechanistically link outcomes to BHB oxidation rather than unrelated signaling (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023; Gough, 2021; Powell et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021). In vivo, a dry-AMD–relevant RPE degeneration model should test systemic or ocular BHB delivery (dose selection to 0.5–2 mM plasma equivalents) with readouts of RPE mitochondrial structure/function, subretinal inflammation, and lesion progression; blood–retina transport via MCT1 at the inner BRB suggests systemic exposure can reach the retina, though intraocular routes might achieve higher local concentrations (Tribble et al., 2021). Throughout, BHB dosing must be titrated to avoid off-target effects and electrolyte load associated with some salt formulations; direct ketone esters or controlled dietary induction may be considered for translational studies, recognizing model-specific differences seen between exogenous BHB and ketogenic diet (Tribble et al., 2021).  

Strengths  
- Mechanistic breadth and convergence on AMD-relevant pathways: alternative fuel supply to support Δψm/ATP, improved NAD redox and ROS control, Nrf2 antioxidant gene induction, and potent suppression of NLRP3/NF-κB–mediated para-inflammation via HCAR2—each independently linked to retinal/RPE resilience (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Gough, 2021; Powell et al., 2021).  
- Retinal delivery/uptake plausibility: MCT expression at the inner BRB and in RPE, plus RPE’s ability to both produce and consume BHB, establish physiological routes for BHB transit and utilization in target tissues (Tribble et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Gulette et al., 2024).  
- Preclinical efficacy signals in retinal and CNS models: reduced oxidative/inflammatory injury, preserved neuronal function, enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis/antioxidant defenses, and receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory actions in retina (Gough, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Trotta et al., 2019; Powell et al., 2021).  
- Compatibility with RPE stress biology: BHB improved ARPE-19 survival under metabolic stress and modulated cytokines, and microglial mitochondrial data demonstrate BHB reverses mtCa²⁺/mtROS/mPTP derangements that are mechanistically relevant to RPE degeneration (Argentino et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2023).  

Weaknesses and uncertainties  
- Lack of AMD-specific in vivo data and no clinical trials in AMD/RP; extrapolation from RGC/optic nerve/diabetic models requires confirmation in RPE-targeted systems (Gough, 2021).  
- Measurement pitfalls in RPE ketone studies; reliance on inaccurate enzymatic assays historically confounded interpretation, necessitating MS-based quantitation and careful time-course sampling (Gulette et al., 2024).  
- Context-dependent redox effects; reports differ on NAD couple responses to BHB, indicating the need for compartmentalized NAD⁺/NADH readouts in RPE to avoid misattribution (Morris et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2021).  
- Differences between exogenous BHB and ketogenic diet; some benefits in glaucoma were not reproduced with BHB delivery, suggesting that metabolic co-factors (e.g., NAD boosters) or combinatorial strategies may be required (Tribble et al., 2021).  
- Potential systemic/dietary adverse effects; ketogenic diets can reduce ERG amplitudes and alter systemic biomarkers in wild-type mice—although these are not necessarily attributable to BHB per se, they caution against non-specific dietary induction in frail patients (Gough, 2021).  

Overall, BHB (Sigma-Aldrich 389410) is a compelling repurposed candidate for dry AMD based on strong mechanistic plausibility and retina-relevant preclinical evidence, with direct RPE expression of the key anti-inflammatory receptor HCAR2 and demonstrable RPE responses to BHB under metabolic stress (Powell et al., 2021; Argentino et al., 2025). The major risk is the current absence of AMD-specific in vivo evidence and the historical conflation of diet-level ketosis with BHB pharmacology; these can be addressed by an RPE-centric preclinical plan that uses rigorous ketone quantitation, compartmental redox readouts, transporter/enzyme perturbations (MCT/OXCT1), and in vivo validation in RPE degeneration models. If BHB reproducibly maintains Δψm/ATP, reduces mtROS, and suppresses inflammasome/NF-κB signaling in RPE under glycolytic impairment, it would justify advancement to formulation and delivery optimization for ocular exposure and, subsequently, to early clinical safety/pharmacodynamic studies in dry AMD (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023; Gough, 2021; Wang et al., 2021).

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO‐Me) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), structured in sections that address its origins, therapeutic history, known mechanisms of action, expected effects in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and an overall assessment of its strengths and challenges.

• Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Bardoxolone methyl is a semisynthetic derivative belonging to the synthetic oleanane triterpenoid class. Its origin stems from oleanolic acid—a naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid abundantly found in various medicinal plants. Early medicinal chemistry programs sought to overcome the modest anti‐inflammatory activity and poor bioavailability of oleanolic acid by introducing targeted modifications. Through chemical derivatization, these programs generated CDDO (2‐cyano‐3,12‐dioxooleana‐1,9‐dien‐28‐oic acid) and subsequently its C‐28 methyl ester, known as Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO‐Me) (Borella et al., 2019). The synthetic process involves the installation of electrophilic Michael acceptor groups at strategic positions on the oleanane scaffold, such as the addition of an α,β‐unsaturated carbonyl in the A‐ring and further incorporation of a cyano group that substantially increases the compound’s potency relative to its natural precursor (Wong et al., 2016; Zhang & Chapman, 2020). These chemical modifications not only enhance the anti‐inflammatory and anticancer properties but also improve chemical stability and oral bioavailability. The structural design, which incorporates a reversible electrophilic reactivity, underpins the compound’s ability to engage diverse cellular targets (Thomas, 2012; Zhou et al., 2014). Bardoxolone methyl thus represents a chemically advanced, highly potent agent from a class of molecules originally designed to trigger cytoprotective responses via direct electrophilic modulation.

• Therapeutic History  
Bardoxolone methyl has undergone extensive preclinical and early clinical evaluation primarily in fields as disparate as oncology and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Initial studies established that synthetic oleanane triterpenoids, including CDDO and its variants, exert dramatic anti‐inflammatory effects by suppressing inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and cyclooxygenase (COX‐2) expression in activated macrophages (Gatbonton‐Schwager, 2014). Preclinical studies in multiple mouse cancer models and inflammatory conditions confirmed its potent anticancer activity and cytoprotective properties, which catalyzed its progression into human clinical trials (Borella et al., 2019; Nakagami, 2016).  
In the clinical arena, Bardoxolone methyl was advanced through Phase I cancer trials, where its once‐daily oral dosing regimen and pharmacokinetic profile—with a terminal half‐life of approximately 39 hours—were characterized (Thomas, 2012; Nakagami, 2016). More notably, its unexpected ability to improve estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in patients with advanced renal disease, particularly in diabetic nephropathy, led to its evaluation in large Phase II and Phase III trials, such as the BEAM and BEACON studies (Yagishita et al., 2020; Tanase et al., 2022). However, the BEACON trial was terminated prematurely due to an increased incidence of cardiovascular events, including heart failure, highlighting concerns about the compound’s systemic safety profile when used at higher doses or in populations with comorbidities (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012).  
Despite its promising preclinical pharmacology and the breadth of clinical data available in non‐ocular indications, to date there is no direct record in the literature of Bardoxolone methyl being used specifically for the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular degenerative conditions (Schiavoni et al., 2025). Nonetheless, the overall safety and pharmacokinetic properties observed in CKD and oncology trials lend valuable insights for considering drug repurposing across therapeutic areas.

• Mechanism of Action  
Bardoxolone methyl is best known for its ability to activate the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway—a master regulator of cellular defense mechanisms against oxidative and electrophilic stress. Under basal conditions, Nrf2 is tightly regulated by Kelch‐like ECH‐associated protein 1 (Keap1), which serves as an adaptor for ubiquitin ligases targeting Nrf2 for proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl functions as a potent electrophile and interacts with sulfhydryl groups on critical cysteine residues within Keap1. This covalent or reversible Michael addition reaction disrupts the Keap1–Nrf2 complex, thereby stabilizing and allowing Nrf2 to translocate into the nucleus (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).  
Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to the antioxidant response element (ARE) in the promoter regions of a host of cytoprotective genes. This transcriptional activation results in the upregulation of a battery of antioxidant and phase II detoxifying enzymes, including but not limited to heme oxygenase‐1 (HO‐1), NAD(P)H dehydrogenase (quinone 1; NQO1), various glutathione transferases, and glutamate–cysteine ligase subunits (Thomas, 2012; Wong et al., 2016). Studies in non‐ocular tissues have shown that at very low (nanomolar) doses, Bardoxolone methyl robustly engages this cytoprotective program while also exerting dose‐dependent biology wherein intermediate and high doses trigger effects such as modulation of cell differentiation and direct anticancer activity, respectively (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).  
It is important to note that while the canonical targets of Nrf2 activation are well characterized, Bardoxolone methyl’s electrophilic character enables it to interact with multiple regulatory proteins. For example, it can inhibit IκB kinase β (IKKβ), leading to suppression of nuclear factor κB (NF‐κB) signaling and subsequent reduction in proinflammatory cytokine production (Zhou et al., 2014; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although the literature does not provide direct experimental evidence that Bardoxolone methyl specifically upregulates mitochondrial antioxidants such as superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) and peroxiredoxin 3 (PRDX3) in RPE cells, the robust, broad‐spectrum transcriptional response induced by Nrf2 activation strongly suggests that mitochondrial and cytoplasmic components of the antioxidant defense system may also be upregulated (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015). Such upregulation would be consistent with previous findings of increased expression of antioxidant genes and improved cellular redox status upon treatment with similar synthetic triterpenoids (Schiavoni et al., 2025; Sporn et al., 2011).

• Expected Effect in Dry AMD  
The pathogenesis of dry age‐related macular degeneration is multifactorial, with chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction playing a central role in the degeneration of the RPE—a critical monolayer that supports photoreceptor health. RPE cells are particularly vulnerable to oxidative damage due to high metabolic activity, exposure to light, and the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). In this context, the proposed mechanism of Bardoxolone methyl, namely activation of the Nrf2/ARE pathway, provides a biologically tenable strategy for neuroprotection and cellular preservation.  
When administered at low doses, Bardoxolone methyl is expected to trigger a cytoprotective transcriptional program in RPE cells. Activation of Nrf2 should lead to the induction of a range of antioxidant enzymes and detoxifying proteins which together help re-establish redox balance in the face of chronic oxidative insult (Borella et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012). One key hypothesis is that, in addition to the already well‐documented induction of cytosolic antioxidants such as HO‐1 and NQO1, Bardoxolone methyl may also promote the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3. SOD2 is the primary defense against superoxide radicals within the mitochondria, and PRDX3 plays a critical role in detoxifying hydrogen peroxide produced by mitochondrial respiration. Although direct data in RPE cells are currently lacking, studies in other cellular contexts have demonstrated that activation of Nrf2 results in the upregulation of a broad spectrum of antioxidant genes, and it is plausible that under the oxidative duress typical of dry AMD, similar effects would be observed in RPE cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
In vitro models simulating oxidative stress—such as exposure of RPE cells to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)—have shown that compounds with similar electrophilic properties, and indeed other members of the CDDO family like CDDO-Im, reduce the intracellular MitoSOX fluorescence signal, indicative of a reduction in mitochondrial ROS (mtROS) (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024). Moreover, improvements in mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) have been correlated with such treatments, suggesting that these molecules can help maintain mitochondrial function under stressful conditions (Nakagami, 2016; Zhou et al., 2014). Such outcomes are highly relevant in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction in the RPE has been implicated in disease progression. The anticipated outcomes, therefore, include a reduction in mtROS, restoration of Δψm, and subsequent preservation of RPE cellular integrity and function.  
Another positive aspect is the compound’s previously established oral bioavailability and pharmacokinetic profile. Clinical studies in CKD patients have demonstrated that therapeutic plasma concentrations can be achieved with once-daily dosing. Although systemic administration in ocular diseases is not ideal, these data provide a strong pharmacological starting point for repurposing. In addition, if systemic toxicity remains a concern—as suggested by the cardiovascular signals in CKD trials—an alternative approach might involve localized ocular delivery (for instance, via intravitreal injection or by developing an ocular formulation) to achieve high retinal bioavailability while minimizing systemic exposure (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).

• Overall Evaluation  
In assessing Bardoxolone methyl for repurposing as a therapeutic for dry AMD, several critical points emerge that underline both its promise and the challenges that must be overcome.

Strengths:  
1. Strong Chemical Rationale and Potency:  
Bardoxolone methyl is a product of sophisticated medicinal chemistry, designed to overcome the limitations of natural triterpenoids like oleanolic acid by installing reactive electrophilic groups that significantly enhance its potency. This design specifically enables the activation of the Nrf2 pathway—a mechanism central to antioxidant defense—at very low concentrations (Borella et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016). The high potency of Bardoxolone methyl as an Nrf2 activator is a significant advantage, particularly when considering that even subtle improvements in cellular antioxidant capacity can have a profound impact on chronic degenerative diseases like dry AMD.

2. Broad Cytoprotective Mechanism:  
The mechanism of Bardoxolone methyl involves the disruption of the Keap1-Nrf2 complex via covalent modification of Keap1 cysteine residues, facilitating the nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and the subsequent transcriptional activation of a broad range of antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes (Zhou et al., 2014; Thomas, 2012). This broad cytoprotective response is particularly relevant to the RPE, where chronic oxidative stress has been implicated in cellular dysfunction and death. The possibility that Bardoxolone methyl may also induce mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3, although not yet directly confirmed in RPE, is an attractive hypothesis; such an effect would directly address the mitochondrial dysfunction that is a hallmark of dry AMD (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).

3. Extensive Clinical Experience and Pharmacokinetic Data:  
Bardoxolone methyl has been evaluated in several clinical trials—most notably in the context of CKD and oncology—yielding a wealth of pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and tolerability data. Its oral bioavailability, with a terminal half-life that supports once-daily dosing, is well documented (Thomas, 2012; Nakagami, 2016). Although the systemic adverse events observed in these trials (such as cardiovascular-related events) present challenges for broad systemic administration, these data nonetheless offer a useful starting point for repurposing. The established clinical profile can inform dose-escalation studies and safety monitoring protocols should Bardoxolone methyl be advanced into ocular trials.

4. Support from Analogous Preclinical Models:  
Several studies in related models have demonstrated that synthetic triterpenoids can protect retinal tissue from oxidative damage. For example, experiments with CDDO-Im, a closely related analogue, have shown protective effects in retinal ischemia–reperfusion injury, including the attenuation of inflammatory responses and preservation of retinal structure (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024). Although these studies are not directly with Bardoxolone methyl, the mechanistic commonalities within this compound class support the notion that the same protective pathways can be harnessed in the context of dry AMD.

Weaknesses and Challenges:  
1. Lack of Direct Evidence in RPE/Dry AMD Models:  
Despite the strong theoretical rationale, direct evidence that Bardoxolone methyl upregulates mitochondrial antioxidants (SOD2, PRDX3) in RPE cells is currently lacking. Most published data are derived from non-ocular cell types or from studies using other analogues such as CDDO-Im (Cai et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2014). It is therefore essential to perform specific in vitro studies in RPE cell lines under oxidative stress conditions to measure the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes and the functional status of mitochondria (e.g., Δψm, mtROS levels) following treatment with Bardoxolone methyl.

2. Safety Concerns from Prior Clinical Experience:  
A significant challenge in repurposing Bardoxolone methyl stems from its safety profile in systemic indications. The Phase III BEACON trial in CKD patients was halted due to an increased incidence of serious cardiovascular events, including heart failure and increased mortality (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although the mechanisms underlying these adverse effects may be related to systemic fluid retention, off‐target reactivity, or other metabolic perturbations, they raise concerns about the safety of systemic administration. For ocular application, it may be necessary to consider alternative dosing strategies or localized delivery methods to avoid systemic exposure while still achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina.

3. Translational and Formulation Challenges:  
The unique anatomy and physiology of the eye introduce additional obstacles in drug repurposing. RPE cells reside in a relatively immune-privileged, isolated microenvironment behind the blood–retinal barrier. The pharmacokinetics and tissue penetration profiles of Bardoxolone methyl observed in systemic circulation may not directly translate to effective intraocular concentrations. Development of specialized ocular formulations—such as sustained-release intravitreal injections or topical applications that can traverse ocular barriers—will be critical for successful translation (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).

4. Multifactorial Nature of AMD Pathogenesis:  
Dry AMD is a complex, multifactorial disease where oxidative stress is only one component of a broader pathogenic network that includes genetic predisposition, inflammation, lipid dysregulation, and complement system activation. While activation of the Nrf2 pathway can counteract oxidative stress and may have secondary anti-inflammatory effects, it is uncertain whether this single mechanism will be sufficient to alter the course of the disease. A combinatorial therapeutic strategy incorporating Nrf2 activation with other modalities might eventually be required to address the full spectrum of dry AMD pathology (Cheng et al., 2021; Thomas, 2012).

5. Dose-Dependent Effects and Narrow Therapeutic Window:  
Bardoxolone methyl exhibits highly dose-dependent pharmacology. At low doses, it predominantly activates Nrf2 and induces cytoprotective genes; however, as the dose increases, additional actions such as pro-apoptotic and cytotoxic effects emerge (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014). Determining the precise dose that is efficacious in RPE cells without triggering deleterious off-target effects will be crucial. This necessitates rigorous dose-ranging studies in preclinical models to define a therapeutic window that maximizes retinal protection while minimizing risks.

• Overall Evaluation and Recommendation  
In summary, Bardoxolone methyl presents a compelling candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD thanks to its well-characterized chemical design, potent induction of the Nrf2 pathway, and a broad cytoprotective mechanism that addresses many aspects of the oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction implicated in RPE degeneration. The extensive clinical data from studies in CKD and oncology provide a valuable foundation for understanding its pharmacokinetics and systemic effects, while the underlying chemistry ensures high potency at low concentrations—features that are highly desirable when targeting a chronic, degenerative condition such as dry AMD (Borella et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012).  
Nonetheless, significant challenges remain. There is a conspicuous gap in the literature regarding the direct evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl in RPE cells and dry AMD models, particularly concerning its ability to upregulate mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes like SOD2 and PRDX3 and thereby mitigate mtROS damage. This gap must be addressed through targeted in vitro assays and in vivo animal studies that simulate the retinal environment and its chronic oxidative stress. Safety concerns, as evidenced by the cardiovascular events observed in CKD trials, underscore the need for caution; these risks may be minimized through localized ocular administration, but careful formulation and dosing studies will be required to establish an acceptable safety profile in the ocular context (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019).  
Given the current state of evidence, it is recommended that Bardoxolone methyl be subjected to further preclinical evaluation in the context of dry AMD. Specifically, studies should focus on:  
 – Conducting detailed in vitro experiments in human RPE cell lines to assess whether exposure to Bardoxolone methyl under oxidative stress conditions leads to the upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants (e.g., SOD2 and PRDX3) and an associated decrease in mtROS (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
 – Evaluating the effects of Bardoxolone methyl on mitochondrial function (including measurements of Δψm, oxygen consumption rate, and mitochondrial integrity) in these cells.  
 – Adapting ocular-specific formulations that allow high local retinal concentrations with minimal systemic exposure, potentially using intravitreal or topical delivery methods, and conducting pharmacokinetic studies that establish retinal tissue exposure (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).  
 – Testing the compound in animal models of dry AMD to determine whether the in vitro antioxidant and mitochondrial protective effects translate into preservation of RPE and photoreceptor structure and function over time (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024).  
If these studies yield positive results that confirm the hypothesized upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants and improved RPE function, Bardoxolone methyl could then be advanced to early-phase clinical trials in patients with dry AMD. Such trials would need to incorporate rigorous safety monitoring protocols to mitigate the known systemic adverse effects. A potential strategy may involve administering the drug in a localized manner or at doses that are effective in the eye but low enough to avoid triggering systemic electrophilic toxicity.

Overall, Bardoxolone methyl holds promise as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD based on its potent Nrf2-activating properties and the central role of oxidative stress in the disease’s pathogenesis. However, its development for an ocular indication will hinge on its ability to selectively and safely modulate the redox status of RPE cells while avoiding systemic side effects. A stepwise, targeted preclinical program that directly addresses these RPE-specific endpoints is therefore critical before consideration of clinical trials in the dry AMD patient population (Nakagami, 2016).

In conclusion, while Bardoxolone methyl offers a strong mechanistic rationale as an Nrf2 activator with the theoretical capacity to upregulate mitochondrial defenses in RPE cells, further targeted studies are essential. The compound’s repurposing for dry AMD is scientifically attractive given the unmet need for effective therapies in this condition; however, the translational path is complex due to safety concerns observed in systemic trials and the lack of direct ocular data. A rigorous preclinical research plan—encompassing in vitro RPE studies, ocular pharmacokinetic assessments, and animal model validation—will be required to determine whether Bardoxolone methyl can be safely and effectively repurposed to preserve RPE function and slow the progression of dry AMD.

• Summary of Key Supporting Points  
– Bardoxolone methyl is a chemically engineered derivative of oleanolic acid that exploits electrophilic modifications to robustly activate the Nrf2 pathway (Borella et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016).  
– Its extensive preclinical and clinical history in oncology and CKD, though not in ocular disease, provides important pharmacokinetic and biological safety data that may be leveraged, with modifications, for ocular use (Nakagami, 2016; Tanase et al., 2022).  
– Its mechanism—covalent modification of Keap1 and subsequent nuclear translocation of Nrf2—leads to the transcriptional upregulation of cytoprotective genes, and it is hypothesized that this would include mitochondrial antioxidants (e.g., SOD2, PRDX3), which are critical for mitigating oxidative damage in RPE cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
– Preclinical data with related triterpenoids in retinal models support the concept that Nrf2 activation can ameliorate oxidative stress and preserve retinal integrity, although direct data for Bardoxolone methyl in dry AMD are presently lacking (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024).  
– Key challenges include the translation of systemic dosing to ocular delivery, the need to specifically validate mitochondrial protective effects in RPE cells, and the resolution of safety issues exemplified by prior cardiovascular signals in systemic trials (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

• Final Recommendation  
Based on the current literature review, Bardoxolone methyl emerges as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its potent Nrf2 activation, broad cytoprotective potential, and a well-documented clinical PK profile. However, its repurposing for ocular application must be preceded by targeted preclinical studies that corroborate its ability to upregulate mitochondrial antioxidants in RPE cells and to reduce mtROS while preserving mitochondrial function. These studies should also explore ocular-specific formulations and dosing regimens that minimize systemic exposure. Only after thorough validation in these preliminary investigations can Bardoxolone methyl be considered a credible candidate for clinical trials in dry AMD patients. Given these considerations, the candidate warrants further investigation despite the existing translational and safety challenges inherent in repurposing a systemically active electrophilic compound for an ocular indication (Borella et al., 2019; Yagishita et al., 2020; Thomas, 2012).
