As a member of a structurally diverse chemotype group, S3QEL-2 belongs to a new class of mitochondrial ROS-targeted modulators that differ fundamentally from classical Complex III inhibitors such as antimycin A or myxothiazol; unlike these inhibitors, S3QELs do not block the electron transfer chain or impair ATP production, but rather reduce the electron leak from the semiquinone intermediate at the Qo site (Orr et al., 2015). In general, compounds in the S3QEL class have been used experimentally as probes to decouple pathological ROS generation from normal bioenergetic function in diverse cell types, with applications ranging from studies on hypoxia-induced transcription (e.g., HIF-1α signaling) to experiments investigating ROS-mediated cell stress in pancreatic β-cells (Orr et al., 2015). The commercial catalog number Cayman Chemical #26918 identifies S3QEL-2 for research purposes, which suggests that this compound is available for repurposing studies beyond its initial characterization in nonocular systems (Orr et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Although S3QEL-2 was originally developed as a novel chemical probe to selectively suppress Complex III-derived superoxide production, its preclinical evaluation has been extensive within the context of cellular models evaluating ROS-mediated signaling and cell stress responses (Orr et al., 2015). In cellular assays, S3QEL-2 has demonstrated the ability to reduce H₂O₂ production in isolated mitochondria, lower HIF-1α transcription in hypoxia-challenged HEK-293 cells, and protect pancreatic β-cells from oxidative stress-induced apoptosis during islet isolation and culture (Orr et al., 2015). Notably, in studies where cells were exposed to concentrations up to 20× the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC₅₀) determined for site IIIQo superoxide production, S3QEL-2 did not impair basal or uncoupled respiration, nor did it compromise mitochondrial viability (Orr et al., 2015). Additionally, S3QEL-2 has been employed as a pharmacological tool in experiments on human monocyte-derived macrophages, where it contributed to demonstrating that inhibition of mitochondrial ROS can reduce inflammasome activation and subsequent IL-18 secretion upon stimulation by the complement membrane attack complex (MAC) (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). However, despite its utility in these nonocular systems—where mitochondrial ROS inhibition was linked to attenuation of inflammatory cytokine pathways—there is little to no published preclinical or clinical data directly evaluating S3QEL-2 in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models or in other ocular disease contexts (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2015). While the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of dry AMD, particularly those involving chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and associated inflammasome activation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, are well documented (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013), a direct therapeutic history for S3QEL-2 in retinal or AMD models remains absent in the current literature (Korhonen, 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Thus, S3QEL-2 represents a promising repurposing candidate that has been validated in other contexts of ROS-related cellular stress but has not yet been explicitly applied to the treatment of dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of S3QEL-2 is based on its capacity to selectively suppress superoxide generation originating at the Qo site of mitochondrial Complex III. Under normal conditions, the electron transport chain (ETC) can leak electrons during the reduction of oxygen, particularly at the semiquinone intermediate at the Qo site, resulting in the formation of superoxide—a primary reactive oxygen species (Orr et al., 2015). S3QEL-2 does not act as a general ROS scavenger; rather, it modulates the rate constant for the electron transfer from the semiquinone to molecular oxygen without significantly altering the steady-state levels of semiquinone species or the redox poise of the ubiquinone (Q) pool (Orr et al., 2015). This selective inhibition of ROS generation is achieved through an allosteric modulation of protein conformation within Complex III, specifically targeting the Qo site to reduce electron leak while sparing the remainder of the electron transport processes (Orr et al., 2015). By decreasing superoxide production, S3QEL-2 effectively reduces the downstream formation of H₂O₂ as detected by Amplex UltraRed assays, a finding that has been consistently reproduced in isolated mitochondrial studies (Orr et al., 2015). Moreover, because S3QEL-2 does not interfere with the overall electron flux or the maintenance of Δψm, it preserves the bioenergetic capacity of the mitochondria—a critical factor in tissues with high metabolic demands such as the RPE (Orr et al., 2015). On a molecular level, the compound’s activity at nanomolar to low micromolar concentrations (with a reported mean IC₅₀ around 1.7 μM for S3QEL-2) suggests a highly potent modulation of the ROS generation pathway that is independent of the mitochondrial matrix redox state (Orr et al., 2015). This targeted approach is further distinguished from classical Complex III inhibitors like myxothiazol and antimycin A, which disrupt the entire electron transport process and can lead to a collapse in mitochondrial function; in contrast, S3QEL-2 specifically mitigates the pathological component of ROS production while maintaining ATP synthesis and cellular energy homeostasis (Orr et al., 2015). In macrophages and other cell types, the reduction in mitochondrial ROS production by S3QEL-2 has been shown to blunt ROS-dependent signaling pathways, such as the stabilization of the transcription factor HIF-1α under hypoxic conditions, and to decrease the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Toma et al., 2021). Thus, the molecular interactions of S3QEL-2 within Complex III position it as a potential modulator of redox signaling pathways that are implicated in inflammatory and degenerative processes, including those observed in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Based on its established mechanism of action, the use of S3QEL-2 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells is expected to selectively reduce mitochondrial ROS generated at the Complex III Qo site. In dry age-related macular degeneration, one of the prevailing hypotheses attributes disease progression to chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction within the RPE, leading to the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and subsequent secretion of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013). The selective inhibition of ROS by S3QEL-2 should therefore interrupt this pathological signaling cascade. In an in vitro assay using RPE cells—cells that have been shown to express components of the NLRP3 inflammasome and are especially vulnerable to oxidative insults—the drug is anticipated to lower ROS markers, as measured by fluorescent dyes (for example, oxidized carboxy-H₂DCFDA), without compromising the cells' mitochondrial respiration or Δψm (Orr et al., 2015). With less mitochondrial ROS available to act as secondary messengers, the downstream stabilization of HIF-1α under stress conditions is expected to be reduced, and the inflammatory response mediated by inflammasome assembly will likely be attenuated (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Orr et al., 2015). Given that multiple studies have demonstrated the role of mitochondrial ROS in directly or indirectly activating NLRP3 inflammasome signaling in both macrophages and RPE cells (Gao et al., 2015; Campbell & Doyle, 2013; Piippo, 2019), the hypothesis is that S3QEL-2 will break this mtROS–NLRP3 axis. In a therapeutic assay, one would expect that RPE cells treated with S3QEL-2 under conditions of complement dysregulation (a known contributor to dry AMD pathology) would demonstrate not only reduced markers of oxidative stress and inflammasome activation but also improved cellular viability, decreased apoptosis, and maintenance of proper metabolic function (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). Furthermore, if S3QEL-2 can lower the intracellular superoxide burden, it might also reduce the formation of oxidized lipids and other damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that contribute to the progression of AMD (Campbell & Doyle, 2013; Toma et al., 2021). Overall, the strategic downregulation of mitochondrial ROS production should translate into a protective phenotype in RPE cells by interrupting the signaling mechanisms that lead to chronic inflammation and cell death in the context of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
S3QEL-2 emerges as an attractive candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to its unique pharmacological profile and precision in targeting mitochondrial ROS production. One of the key strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its ability to selectively suppress superoxide generation at the Complex III Qo site without impairing the overall electron transport chain function or disrupting mitochondrial membrane potential (Orr et al., 2015). This high degree of specificity is particularly valuable in a disease such as dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central to pathogenesis yet preserving the RPE’s bioenergetic capacity is essential for retinal health (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013). The preclinical data available for S3QEL-2 in nonocular systems—ranging from hypoxia-induced HIF-1α modulation to protection of pancreatic β-cells and dampening of inflammasome activation in macrophages—suggest that its mechanism of action may well translate to the RPE, a cell type that is similarly sensitive to mitochondrial oxidative stress (Orr et al., 2015; Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). Moreover, the ability of S3QEL-2 to reduce mitochondrial ROS levels without interfering with ATP production positions it as a promising agent for interrupting the mtROS–NLRP3 inflammasome axis that is proposed to drive inflammatory responses in the geographic atrophy observed in dry AMD (Orr et al., 2015; Orr et al., 2015).

However, several weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. Despite the encouraging preclinical data in cell culture and isolated mitochondrial systems, there is currently no direct evidence linking S3QEL-2 to therapeutic benefit in retinal models or in dry AMD specifically (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2015). The candidate has been primarily evaluated in nonocular models, and the complex microenvironment of the retina—including the blood-retinal barrier, immune cell interactions, and local complement dysregulation—may pose significant challenges in translating in vitro efficacy to in vivo benefit (Korhonen, 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Furthermore, while S3QEL-2 has been shown to reduce ROS-mediated signaling in macrophages and pancreatic islets, the pharmacokinetic properties, tissue distribution, and long-term safety profile of this compound in ocular tissues remain to be determined (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Orr et al., 2015). Delivery of S3QEL-2 to the retina may require formulation strategies that overcome solubility and permeability barriers inherent in drug delivery to the posterior segment of the eye. Another concern is the potential for off-target effects that, while not evident in the isolated systems tested so far, may manifest in the complex in vivo environment or with chronic administration (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Orr et al., 2015).

In addition, the exact molecular site of action on Complex III is not yet fully delineated at the atomic level, meaning that while the compound has been shown to modulate ROS production, the precise binding interactions and potential variability between different cell types or individuals remain uncertain (Orr et al., 2015). This incomplete mechanistic detail could complicate structure-activity relationship (SAR) explorations, as well as efforts to optimize the compound further for better efficacy or reduced toxicity in an ocular setting.

From a therapeutic perspective, the hypothesis that S3QEL-2 can reduce inflammasome activation by lowering mitochondrial ROS is strongly supported by data in other cell types, particularly where a reduction in ROS has been correlated with lower levels of IL-1β and IL-18 secretion (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). Given the well-established involvement of mitochondrial ROS and NLRP3 inflammasome activation in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013), S3QEL-2 holds promise as a tool to dissect and potentially therapeutically modulate this axis. However, concrete evidence in AMD-relevant models, especially primary RPE cells derived from patients or appropriate animal models, is necessary before advancing this compound further in the drug development pipeline (Korhonen, 2024; Macchioni et al., 2020).

In summary, the strengths of S3QEL-2 lie in its high selectivity for Complex III-derived ROS suppression, preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics, and the proven ability to modulate ROS-dependent inflammatory pathways in several preclinical settings (Orr et al., 2015). Its repurposing for dry AMD is biochemically plausible and aligns with the current understanding of the disease, where chronic low-level oxidative stress and inflammasome activation play central roles in RPE dysfunction and geographic atrophy (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013). Conversely, weaknesses include the absence of direct preclinical evidence in ocular models, potential pharmacokinetic and delivery challenges, and an incomplete elucidation of its binding mechanism at the atomic level. Considering these factors, S3QEL-2 represents a highly promising candidate that merits further investigation through targeted preclinical studies in retinal and RPE models, including assessments of its delivery, efficacy in reducing NLRP3-driven cytokine release, and long-term safety in ocular tissues (Gao et al., 2015; Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Ultimately, while S3QEL-2 is supported by robust biochemical data in nonocular systems and has a compelling mechanism that could translate into therapeutic benefit for dry AMD, additional focused research in AMD-relevant models is essential to validate its potential as a repurposed drug candidate for this challenging indication.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is a naturally occurring long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (LC-PUFA) that has been isolated from marine sources, such as fish oil, and is commercially available in a highly purified form (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich D2534). DHA is synthesized via metabolic elongation and desaturation of dietary alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) in mammals; however, this endogenous conversion is limited, and direct dietary intake is critical for maintaining adequate retinal DHA levels (Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14). Belonging to the omega-3 class of fatty acids, DHA has long been recognized for its important roles in maintaining membrane structure and function, particularly in neural tissues and the retina where it is highly concentrated in photoreceptor outer segments and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) membranes (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3). Its polyunsaturated nature—with six cis double bonds—confers unique biophysical properties, enabling DHA to increase membrane fluidity and participate in critical signaling cascades. The compound has been used extensively as a nutritional supplement and has been incorporated in various formulations aimed at cardiovascular health, cognitive function, and ocular protection, establishing a robust safety profile over decades of human use (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Skowronska-Krawczyk & Chao, 2019, pp. 3–4).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past two decades, extensive research has explored the role of DHA and related omega-3 fatty acids in maintaining retinal function and potentially preventing age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Epidemiologic studies have consistently demonstrated an inverse association between dietary fish and high omega-3 fatty acid intake and the risk of developing AMD, suggesting that populations with higher DHA consumption tend to exhibit a lower incidence of both early and, to some extent, advanced forms of the disease (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). In clinical settings, large-scale randomized controlled trials, such as AREDS2, incorporated DHA (and EPA) into a multi-nutrient formula designed originally for AMD, though the overall randomized trial outcomes have been mixed, with some studies finding no statistically significant benefit for progression to late AMD (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). Pilot clinical trials and observational cohort studies, including NAT-1 and NAT-2, have assessed DHA supplementation in subjects with drusenoid lesions or early-stage AMD; while some of these studies have shown promising improvements in blood biomarkers (e.g., increased red blood cell DHA levels) and correlations with reduced AMD progression, the clinical efficacy remains under debate (Querques et al., 2016, pp. 2–4; Querques et al., 2011, pp. 7–8). Notably, evidence from animal models suggests that dietary DHA may protect against light-induced retinal degeneration and reduce the accumulation of deleterious lipid peroxidation products, although some preclinical studies also caution that DHA’s susceptibility to oxidation could, under certain conditions, worsen retinal injury (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic hypothesis for using DHA in dry AMD is based on its predicted ability to incorporate into the mitochondrial membranes of RPE cells, thereby enhancing membrane fluidity and protecting against oxidative damage to the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes. Under normal cellular conditions, DHA—owing to its multiple methylene-interrupted cis double bonds—integrates into phospholipid bilayers and modulates biophysical properties such as fluidity, permeability, and thickness (Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33). In mitochondrial membranes, this incorporation is thought to replace more saturated fatty acids such as arachidonic acid, ultimately reducing lipid peroxidation and mitigating oxidative stress that is deleterious to ETC function (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9). In vitro studies have shown that DHA supplementation in retinal cell cultures can decrease markers of apoptosis and preserve mitochondrial membrane integrity, with a concomitant increase in anti-apoptotic proteins (e.g., Bcl-2) (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 2–4).  
In addition, DHA is enzymatically converted under conditions of oxidative stress into neuroprotective docosanoids, such as neuroprotectin D1 (NPD1), which can inhibit pro-inflammatory gene expression and reduce cell death in RPE and photoreceptor cells (Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14; LaFuente et al., 2021, p. 13). This conversion not only contributes to countering local inflammation but also supports cellular health by modulating intracellular signaling pathways, particularly those involving NF-κB and other transcription factors critical for managing oxidative stress (Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14; Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14). Despite these promising mechanistic insights, it is important to note that direct, quantitative evidence detailing DHA’s incorporation specifically into RPE mitochondrial membranes and its precise effects on mitochondrial cristae structure, malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, or oxygen consumption rate (OCR) remains limited in the current literature (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, p. 13). Several reviews and preclinical reports acknowledge the theoretical framework while emphasizing the need for more detailed mechanistic studies that directly measure these mitochondrial endpoints (Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the mechanistic hypothesis, DHA supplementation is expected to yield several beneficial effects in retinal cells, particularly within the RPE, which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. In an ideal in vitro or ex vivo assay, DHA would incorporate into RPE cell membranes—including the mitochondrial inner membrane—increasing fluidity and enabling better diffusion of substrates and electron carriers necessary for efficient ATP production. Enhanced mitochondrial membrane fluidity should help reduce the susceptibility of the electron transport chain to oxidative damage, thereby lowering the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the subsequent production of lipid peroxidation byproducts such as MDA (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5). Furthermore, preservation of mitochondrial cristae structure is anticipated to maintain optimal alignment and function of ETC complexes, leading to an improved oxygen consumption rate (OCR) that is directly linked to cellular energy metabolism and overall cell viability (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 2–4; Souied et al., 2016, p. 8).  
At a molecular level, the increased presence of DHA in mitochondrial membranes is expected to initiate a cascade of protective events: reduced oxidative stress and inflammation via inhibition of NF-κB activation, promotion of the antioxidant response through NFE2L2 (NRF2) pathway activation, and enhanced autophagic clearance of damaged proteins and organelles through upregulation of SQSTM1 (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 1–2; Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, p. 3). Additionally, because genes encoding crucial direct mediators of DHA uptake such as Mfsd2a are expressed in RPE cells and photoreceptors, the target tissue is particularly well-positioned to benefit from increased dietary or supplementary DHA (Fathima et al., 2023, p. 8). However, it is also recognized that despite the strong rationale, direct experimental confirmation of these outcomes—specifically measured improvements in MDA levels, cristae ultrastructure integrity, and OCR in human RPE cells—is still pending, and the observed epidemiologic correlations are not yet unequivocally supported by randomized clinical trial data (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).

Overall Evaluation:  
The proposition to repurpose DHA for dry AMD is underpinned by compelling mechanistic rationale and epidemiologic associations, yet it is not without its challenges and limitations. One clear strength is DHA’s established role as an essential component of retinal cell membranes. Its high concentration in photoreceptors and the RPE is functionally integral to maintaining visual function and cellular homeostasis, lending strong biological plausibility to its protective potential in AMD (Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33). Its ability to modulate membrane fluidity, serve as a precursor to neuroprotective mediators like NPD1, and exert anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions provide multiple mechanistic pathways through which it may mitigate the cellular stressors implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis (Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14; Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14).  
From a therapeutic history perspective, DHA is well understood in the context of nutritional supplementation, and numerous epidemiologic studies point toward a lower risk of AMD with higher dietary DHA intake (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). The safety profile of DHA is also well established, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing. However, the clinical trial data to date (including large-scale studies such as AREDS2 and smaller trials like NAT-2) have not consistently demonstrated a clear benefit in altering the progression of advanced AMD, and it remains uncertain whether observed benefits in intermediate AMD or specific cellular endpoints translate into clinically meaningful outcomes in the dry form of the disease (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8).  
A significant weakness in the current body of research is the lack of direct mechanistic studies that quantitatively document DHA incorporation into RPE mitochondrial membranes and its subsequent effects on mitochondrial parameters. In our hypothesis, improved mitochondrial function is key, with expected reductions in MDA levels, preservation of cristae structure, and enhancement of OCR serving as biomarkers of efficacy. Yet, while several in vitro studies and animal experiments have suggested that DHA can reduce markers of oxidative stress and improve mitochondrial integrity in retinal models, the literature provided does not include rigorous, high-resolution measurements of these specific parameters in human RPE cells (Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Jiang et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). This gap in the direct evidence would need to be addressed through targeted preclinical assays employing electron microscopy, lipidomics, and mitochondrial respirometry to validate the proposed mechanism.  
Furthermore, the mode of formulation and bioavailability of DHA is a critical factor that may contribute to the mixed findings in clinical trials; DHA administered as an ethyl ester may have different absorption and incorporation profiles compared to its triglyceride-bound form, and the optimal dosing necessary to achieve sufficient retinal or mitochondrial enrichment remains unclear (Souied et al., 2016, pp. 6–7; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). Potential pro-oxidant effects of DHA in settings where oxidation is excessive must also be carefully monitored, as some animal studies have reported that under specific conditions DHA accumulation may even exacerbate oxidative damage (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5).  
In summary, while the epidemiologic literature and preclinical studies provide an encouraging backdrop for the repurposing of DHA as a therapeutic agent in dry AMD—by showing that high DHA intake is associated with a reduced risk of AMD and that DHA can confer mitochondrial and anti-oxidative benefits in retinal models—the critical mechanistic endpoints that support our specific hypothesis are not yet fully substantiated in the published literature. The overall evaluation is that DHA has substantial mechanistic promise, safety, and historical use as a nutritional supplement; however, further robust mechanistic studies and carefully designed clinical trials are necessary to validate its specific effects on mitochondrial function in RPE cells and to determine whether these biochemical improvements translate into a clinically significant slowing of dry AMD progression (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Mitoquinone mesylate (MitoQ) is a synthetic, mitochondria‐targeted antioxidant originally developed as an analogue of coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) to overcome the bioavailability and uptake limitations of naturally occurring CoQ10. Its chemical design is based on modifying decylubiquinone—a CoQ10 analogue in which the long isoprenoid tail is replaced by a saturated decyl hydrocarbon chain to enhance mitochondrial retention—and covalently linking it to a lipophilic triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation. The inclusion of the TPP⁺ moiety exploits the highly negative membrane potential of the mitochondrial inner membrane, thereby ensuring selective accumulation of MitoQ in the mitochondrial matrix (Cores et al., 2023). This compound belongs to the class of lipophilic cationic antioxidants and is also considered a mitochondria-targeted rechargeable antioxidant (RMA) because, after its active ubiquinone moiety scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS), it is enzymatically reduced to the active hydroquinone form by components of the electron transport chain. The rechargeable property allows MitoQ to be continuously recycled via the respiratory chain, resulting in sustained antioxidant action even at low doses—a property that distinguishes it from conventional antioxidants (Lukashev et al., 2014; Fields et al., 2023). The synthesis strategy for MitoQ involves the chemical conjugation of decylubiquinone with TPP⁺, and it is formulated as a mesylate salt to improve its stability and facilitate pharmaceutical development (Cores et al., 2023; Kim & Han, 2017). Overall, MitoQ is a well‐defined member of a broader class of mitochondria‐targeted redox active compounds that have been widely investigated for their potential to modulate mitochondrial oxidative stress (Zielonka et al., 2017).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past two decades, MitoQ has been extensively characterized in a wide range of preclinical studies spanning neurodegenerative diseases, cardiovascular disorders, metabolic syndrome, sepsis, and other conditions associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and elevated oxidative stress. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that MitoQ confers protection against oxidative injury in cellular models and animal models alike. For example, studies in rodent models of cardiac ischemia–reperfusion injury, hypertension, and pressure‐overload heart failure have shown that MitoQ preserves mitochondrial respiration, decreases ROS production (especially H₂O₂ and superoxide) and reduces lipid peroxidation in the heart (Fairley et al., 2023; Kim & Han, 2017). In addition, significant neuroprotective effects have been reported in multiple models of neurodegeneration—ranging from in vitro experiments using Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease models to in vivo studies in rodent systems—where MitoQ was able to reduce mitochondrial fragmentation, lower markers of apoptosis, and restore mitochondrial membrane potential in neurons (Fields et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). Clinically, MitoQ has advanced into human trials in several indications including studies related to Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and hypertension, with reported safety in over 200 human subjects (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Fairley et al., 2023). Although there is no direct record of its use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), the extensive preclinical history in diseases characterized by oxidative stress and mitochondrial impairment provides a strong precedent for its repurposing. In ocular contexts, early pharmacokinetic studies have demonstrated that MitoQ exhibits measurable retinal uptake (approximately 1% of plasma concentration) after oral or topical administration, suggesting that the compound can reach the retina at therapeutically relevant levels (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). Given that mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative injury in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells are now increasingly recognized as central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the repurposing of MitoQ for this indication is logically supported by its mechanism and prior usage in analogous conditions (Cores et al., 2023; Zielonka et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
MitoQ’s mechanism of action is rooted in its unique chemical architecture that allows selective mitochondrial targeting and continuous ROS scavenging. The TPP⁺ moiety drives the compound’s accumulation into the mitochondrial matrix in a membrane potential–dependent manner. Once inside the mitochondria, MitoQ’s ubiquinone moiety is rapidly reduced by components of the electron transport chain—most notably by electron flow through complex II—and converted to its active form, mitoquinol (ubiquinol) (Cores et al., 2023; Manolis et al., 2021). In its reduced state, mitoquinol acts as a potent antioxidant that intercepts ROS generated primarily at the sites of electron leakage at complexes I and III. The scavenging of ROS, particularly superoxide and peroxyl radicals, prevents oxidative damage to mitochondrial lipids, proteins, and DNA—all of which are crucial for maintaining mitochondrial function (Zielonka et al., 2017; Modi et al., 2024). In effect, the cycle of reduction and oxidation (redox cycling) enables MitoQ to function catalytically, rather than stoichiometrically, thereby amplifying its antioxidant capacity over time (Lukashev et al., 2014; Modi et al., 2024). Moreover, by reducing mitochondrial ROS, MitoQ preserves the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), which is essential for ATP synthesis and overall cellular bioenergetics (Kim & Han, 2017; Gueven et al., 2017). This stabilization of Δψm not only inhibits the initiation of apoptosis but may also dampen downstream inflammatory signaling cascades mediated by ROS-sensitive transcription factors such as NF-κB (Fields et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023). Such detailed molecular interactions—spanning TPP-driven uptake, rapid reduction at the respiratory chain, catalytic ROS neutralization, and subsequent recycling to the active antioxidant form—underscore the multifaceted protection that MitoQ offers against mitochondrial oxidative injury.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the underlying hypothesis is that accumulation of oxidative damage in RPE cells leads to mitochondrial dysfunction, loss of Δψm, increased ROS production, chronic inflammation, and ultimately RPE cell degeneration, which is central to disease progression. Based on in vitro studies performed in ARPE-19 cells, treatment with MitoQ has been shown to reduce mitochondrial ROS levels, as measured by MitoSOX fluorescence, and to preserve Δψm as assessed by TMRM assays when cells are challenged with H₂O₂-induced oxidative stress (Cores et al., 2023; Fields et al., 2023). The expected effect of MitoQ in a dry AMD model is that, upon topical or oral administration, it will accumulate in the mitochondria of RPE cells via TPP-mediated uptake. Once there, its ubiquinone moiety will be reduced to the active antioxidant form by the local respiratory chain, which in turn will neutralize superoxide and other ROS at the sites of electron leakage (primarily complex I and III regions). This ROS scavenging is anticipated to limit oxidative damage to mitochondrial membranes and proteins, maintain efficient electron transport and ATP production, and ultimately restore the mitochondrial membrane potential that is compromised in oxidative stress conditions (Zielonka et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014). Additionally, by lowering oxidative stress, MitoQ is expected to reduce inflammatory signaling within the RPE and adjacent retinal layers—potentially decreasing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and mitigating the chronic low-grade inflammation that contributes to dry AMD pathology (Fairley et al., 2023; Gueven et al., 2017). In an in vitro assay using ARPE-19 cells, one would expect to observe a significant decrease in MitoSOX signal intensity along with increased TMRM fluorescence after treatment with MitoQ, indicating reduced mitochondrial ROS and improved Δψm, respectively (Cores et al., 2023; Fields et al., 2023). Given that ARPE-19 is a well‐accepted model for studying RPE function and oxidative stress, these biochemical endpoints provide compelling mechanistic evidence that MitoQ may slow or even reverse aspects of RPE degeneration—a promising therapeutic outcome for dry AMD (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
MitoQ stands out as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration on the basis of several compelling factors. First, its synthetic origin as a mitochondria-targeted CoQ10 analogue with an appended TPP⁺ group ensures that it concentrates specifically within mitochondria, where oxidative stress is most detrimental (Cores et al., 2023; Zielonka et al., 2017). This targeted delivery is a critical improvement over non-specific antioxidants, which often fail to reach the intracellular compartments where ROS generation is most intense. Second, MitoQ’s well-established mechanism of action—encompassing catalytic ROS scavenging through a continuously rechargeable redox cycle—directly addresses the pathophysiological core of dry AMD, namely the oxidative injury and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells (Lukashev et al., 2014; Fields et al., 2023). Preclinical studies in diverse disease models have robustly demonstrated its capacity to protect mitochondrial structure and function, reduce lipid peroxidation and apoptotic signaling, and ultimately preserve cellular viability (Kim & Han, 2017; Gueven et al., 2017).

On the therapeutic history side, MitoQ has undergone extensive preclinical evaluation in models of neurodegeneration, cardiovascular diseases, and metabolic disorders, and has been tested in several early-phase clinical trials—even if not yet in dry AMD specifically—showing an excellent safety profile in over 200 human subjects (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Fairley et al., 2023). Furthermore, pharmacokinetic studies demonstrating ocular uptake (~1% of plasma levels) provide an encouraging basis for its repurposing in retinal diseases, although the relatively low retinal concentration does suggest that formulation optimization (for instance, via topical delivery systems or enhanced ocular bioavailability formulations) may be required to achieve therapeutic levels in the RPE (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses need to be considered. Clinical trials in other indications such as Parkinson’s disease have reported mixed outcomes with MitoQ, leading to concerns about its translation from well-controlled preclinical settings to the complex environment of human disease (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). Moreover, the potential for pro-oxidant effects at high concentrations—as sometimes observed with redox-active compounds like MitoQ—is a dose optimization challenge that must be carefully managed in any clinical development program (Gueven et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014). The fact that the reported retinal uptake of MitoQ is modest (~1% of plasma levels) may necessitate higher systemic doses or alternative delivery routes to ensure that sufficient drug reaches the RPE, which in turn could raise safety issues if off-target effects occur (Apostolova & Victor, 2015). Additionally, while the biochemical rationale is compelling, there is currently no direct clinical evidence for efficacy in dry AMD; this gap underscores the need for further targeted preclinical investigations using dry AMD-relevant animal models and subsequent early-phase clinical trials.

In summary, the overall evaluation favours exploration of MitoQ as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its strong mechanistic foundation—based on mitochondrial targeting, catalytic ROS scavenging, and preservation of Δψm—aligns well with the known etiopathogenesis of dry AMD, which involves RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. The extensive preclinical and early clinical data supporting MitoQ’s safety and efficacy in other indications further bolster its candidacy. However, attention must be given to optimizing dosing regimens and delivery strategies to overcome the limitation of modest retinal uptake, as well as rigorously establishing its efficacy specifically in models of dry AMD before advancing to large-scale clinical trials. Given its unique properties and the urgent need for effective treatments in dry AMD, MitoQ merits further investigation as part of a comprehensive strategy to combat RPE degeneration and preserve visual function in affected patients (Cores et al., 2023; Zielonka et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014; Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SkQ1 (10‐(6′‐plastoquinonyl)‐decyltriphenylphosphonium) is a fully synthetic, mitochondria‐targeted antioxidant constructed by conjugating a plastoquinone antioxidant moiety with a decyl linker that is covalently bound to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation. The plastoquinone scaffold is derived from the natural quinone found in chloroplasts, known for its potent reactive oxygen species (ROS)–removing capabilities, while the TPP⁺ moiety acts as a highly lipophilic vector that drives selective accumulation within mitochondria due to the inner mitochondrial membrane’s large negative potential. In essence, by combining these two structural elements, SkQ1 is designed to exploit electrophoretic uptake to achieve extremely high concentrations in the mitochondrial matrix where oxidative damage is a critical pathogenic factor. This compound belongs to the broader class of mitochondria‐targeted quinone antioxidants, often referred to collectively as “SkQ” compounds. Molecules in this class were originally proposed and developed by Skulachev and colleagues, and they have been used experimentally to achieve mitochondrial protection in contexts ranging from ischemia–reperfusion injury and neurodegeneration to aging‐associated dysfunctions (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). The rational design strategy behind SkQ1—linking a redox‐active quinone to a lipophilic cation—has also inspired the development of analogous compounds such as SkQR1, MitoQ, and related derivatives that are being explored for a variety of biomedical applications.

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of SkQ1, as well as that of its parent class of mitochondria‐targeted antioxidants, is extensive and spans multiple preclinical and early clinical studies. In numerous in vitro and in vivo models, SkQ1 has demonstrated robust antioxidant effects. For example, it has been shown to protect mitochondria and cellular membranes against lipid peroxidation—key pathogenic processes underlying aging and degenerative diseases—at nanomolar concentrations. In various rodent models, including studies in OXYS rats (a strain that mimics accelerated senescence), chronic administration of SkQ1 prevented or reversed age‐related abnormalities such as cataract, retinopathy, and even systemic markers of mitochondrial dysfunction (Wanagat et al., 2010; Belenichev et al., 2024; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Moreover, veterinary and preclinical studies have documented SkQ1’s ability to increase lifespan and delay the onset of age‐linked phenotypes, including osteoporosis, immune decline, and neurodegeneration (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Weissig, 2020). Within the ocular field, SkQ1 has been specifically formulated as eye drops—marketed in certain regions under the trade name Visomitin—to treat dry eye syndrome. These formulations have passed early phase safety trials and have now seen clinical use in Russia. Although SkQ1 has not yet been directly trialed in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or geographic atrophy, its documented efficacy in protecting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in animal models and its ability to improve electrophysiological outcomes (such as preserved electroretinography [ERG] responses) support its potential repurposing for AMD (Gueven et al., 2017; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). In several ocular studies in both rodent and primate models, topical administration of SkQ1 has demonstrated the capacity to deliver the drug to the posterior segment with minimal systemic exposure, reducing characteristics like RPE vacuolization and preserving overall retinal function (Weissig, 2020; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). The extensive preclinical and limited clinical history of SkQ1 in ocular applications—most notably in dry-eye syndrome and animal models of retinal degeneration—suggests that the therapeutic candidate has a solid track record of mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction in tissues exposed to chronic oxidative stress, a pathophysiological component also seen in dry AMD (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Wanagat et al., 2010).

Mechanism of Action:  
SkQ1 exerts its biological effects via multiple interrelated molecular mechanisms that center on its ability to accumulate rapidly within mitochondria and scavenge deleterious ROS. The TPP⁺ portion of the molecule, owing to its delocalized positive charge and high lipophilicity, drives the electrophoretic uptake of SkQ1 into the mitochondrial matrix along the steep negative membrane potential (Δψm) that is inherent to healthy mitochondria (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Once localized within these organelles, the plastoquinone group is poised to participate in redox cycling: it is reversibly reduced—often by components of the electron transport chain such as complex III—and subsequently reacts with ROS such as superoxide (O₂•⁻) and lipid peroxyl radicals to convert them into less reactive species (Lukashev et al., 2014; Weissig, 2020). Importantly, the antioxidant effect of SkQ1 is not a one-off reaction; rather, it is “rechargeable,” meaning that following its oxidation by ROS, the quinone moiety can be reduced again, thereby enabling repeated cycles of detoxification. This rechargeable mechanism differentiates SkQ1 from conventional antioxidants that are consumed irreversibly during redox reactions. Additionally, SkQ1 has been shown to form complexes with cardiolipin—a key phospholipid in the inner mitochondrial membrane—and thereby stabilize the membrane structure against peroxidation. Some studies also suggest that the TPP⁺ component might mediate a mild uncoupling effect by facilitating proton translocation (often in conjunction with interacting with fatty acid anions), which can reduce mitochondrial ROS generation by dissipating excessive inner membrane potential under conditions of oxidative overload (Lukashev et al., 2014; Weissig, 2020; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). This dual mechanism of direct ROS scavenging combined with membrane stabilizing and modest uncoupling effects contributes to the preservation of Δψm and the overall integrity of mitochondrial bioenergetics. In RPE cells stressed by chronic photo-oxidative insult, these properties would translate into effective mitigation of oxidative damage, thereby preventing the collapse of mitochondrial membrane potential—a key event that precipitates cell dysfunction and death in dry AMD (Muraleva et al., 2019; Olovnikov et al., n.d.).

Expected Effect:  
The proposed hypothesis for repurposing SkQ1 in dry age-related macular degeneration is predicated on its capacity to target RPE mitochondria and to neutralize both superoxide radicals and lipid peroxyl radicals that accumulate under conditions of chronic light-induced oxidative stress. In vitro assays using ARPE-19 cells have demonstrated that nanomolar concentrations of SkQ1 elicit potent antioxidant responses—as measured by decreases in fluorescence with DCFDA (a marker of ROS) and stabilization of mitochondrial membrane potential via JC-1 assays—indicating that the compound readily scavenges ocular ROS at very low doses (Gueven et al., 2017; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). This antioxidant activity is expected to prevent or delay the loss of Δψm, a critical parameter for cell survival and function, particularly in RPE cells where mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in the pathogenesis of drusen formation and geographic atrophy in dry AMD. In vivo, studies conducted in models such as OXYS rats have shown that chronic administration of SkQ1 not only reduces oxidative markers in mitochondrial membranes (e.g., decreasing levels of malondialdehyde and hydroxynonenal-adducts) but also normalizes cardiolipin content and fatty acid composition—key factors involved in the proper assembly and turnover of respiratory complexes (Wanagat et al., 2010; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Moreover, macaque studies have indicated that topical SkQ1 eye drops achieve significant drug levels in the posterior segment although the dosing remains in the nanomolar range, leading to improvements in ERG function and reduced RPE vacuolization without evidence of systemic toxicity (Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Weissig, 2020). At the molecular level, the expected effect in RPE cells would be a sustained antioxidant environment that preserves mitochondrial function through two primary pathways: first, by directly quenching damaging ROS that would otherwise trigger mitochondrial DNA damage and lipid peroxidation; and second, by maintaining the structural integrity of mitochondrial membranes via stabilization of cardiolipin and prevention of excessive proton leakage. Given that RPE cells express the full complement of mitochondrial electron transport chain proteins, including complex III which is capable of reducing SkQ1 to its active form, these cells are ideal targets for the drug’s mechanism (Muraleva et al., 2019; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Consequently, when used as a therapeutic intervention in dry AMD, SkQ1 is expected to mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction associated with drusen accumulation and, in turn, slow or potentially reverse the progression of geographic atrophy—one of the major sight-threatening complications of the disease.

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, SkQ1 represents a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration based on a robust foundation of molecular design, preclinical efficacy, and established ocular safety. One of the major strengths of SkQ1 lies in its rational design: as a rechargeable, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant, it overcomes limitations faced by conventional antioxidants that lack mitochondrial specificity. The ability of the TPP⁺ moiety to drive precise mitochondrial accumulation ensures that the compound is concentrated at the site of maximal ROS production, while its plastoquinone component provides potent scavenging of both superoxide and lipid peroxyl radicals. This dual functionality not only neutralizes damaging oxidative species but also supports mitochondrial membrane integrity by stabilizing cardiolipin and potentially mitigating excessive proton leakage. Such a mechanism is particularly relevant to RPE cells, where chronic photo-oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Lukashev et al., 2014).

Another significant advantage is the extensive preclinical and early clinical evidence supporting SkQ1’s efficacy in ocular applications. Its use in animal models—spanning species from rodents to macaques—has consistently shown protective effects on retinal structure and function, including preservation of ERG responses and reduced vacuolization of the RPE. Furthermore, the successful clinical trials for dry eye syndrome confirm that topical administration of SkQ1 is not only efficacious but also well-tolerated in humans, thereby reducing the risk related to ocular drug delivery and systemic exposure (Gueven et al., 2017; Weissig, 2020; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

Nevertheless, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be carefully weighed. One concern is the dose-dependent behavior of SkQ1. While nanomolar concentrations are effective and safe, there is evidence that at higher concentrations, the molecule can exhibit prooxidant or detergent-like effects—leading to membrane disruption or uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation. This narrow window between the antioxidant and prooxidant activities necessitates rigorous control of dosing in clinical settings to avoid inadvertent exacerbation of mitochondrial dysfunction (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). Additionally, while many studies have focused on the compound’s ability to protect against acute oxidative insults, the etiology of dry AMD is multifactorial and chronic. Although animal models such as the OXYS rat provide valuable insights into age-related ocular changes, the long-term efficacy and safety of SkQ1 in preventing geographic atrophy in the context of chronic, low-grade oxidative stress remain to be fully established in human subjects (Wanagat et al., 2010; Belenichev et al., 2024).

It is also important to note that while the proposed mechanism of action for SkQ1—namely, quenching of lipid peroxyl radicals and superoxide to preserve mitochondrial membrane potential—has been well-documented in vitro and in animal models (particularly using ARPE-19 assays with JC-1 and DCFDA readouts), extrapolating these findings to the complex human pathology of dry AMD will require careful clinical trial design. Key endpoints such as changes in drusen load, progression of geographic atrophy, and improvements in visual function would need to be monitored over extended periods. Moreover, given that oxidative stress and inflammation are part of an intricate network of pathological events in dry AMD, combination therapies that address multiple targets may ultimately yield more significant benefits than a single-agent approach (Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Gueven et al., 2017).

From a pharmacokinetic perspective, the selective accumulation of SkQ1 in the mitochondria is a highly attractive feature, as it maximizes local drug concentrations while minimizing systemic exposure and potential off-target effects. This is especially critical for ocular applications, where local delivery via eye drops can achieve high retinal levels with minimal systemic absorption. Nonetheless, formulation stability, light sensitivity, and proper storage conditions are factors that must be optimized for successful commercial development (Weissig, 2020; Gueven et al., 2017; Ji et al., 2021).

In aggregate, the overall evaluation of SkQ1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic. The compound’s design as a mitochondria-targeted, rechargeable antioxidant offers compelling advantages in addressing mitochondrial dysfunction—a key element in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its ability to protect RPE cells, preserve mitochondrial membrane potential, and improve retinal function, while early clinical studies in related ocular conditions confirm its safety profile for topical administration. However, due diligence is warranted to establish the optimal dosing regimen that maximizes beneficial antioxidant effects while avoiding potential prooxidant toxicity. Additionally, further rigorous clinical trials specifically targeting dry AMD endpoints are necessary to confirm that the promising outcomes observed in animal studies translate into measurable clinical benefit in patients with geographic atrophy (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Gueven et al., 2017; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Wanagat et al., 2010; Weissig, 2020).

Given the comprehensive body of work underpinning the mechanism of action, the established track record in various preclinical ocular models, and the supporting data from human dry-eye trials, SkQ1 appears to have significant potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its unique targeting of mitochondria—particularly within RPE cells—and its capacity to prevent ROS-induced mitochondrial collapse make it especially well-suited to counteract the chronic photo-oxidative stress that characterizes this disease. The next steps for validating SkQ1 in this indication should include well-designed in vivo studies in AMD-relevant animal models, followed by early phase clinical trials with careful dose-escalation studies and robust assessment of retinal morphology and function. Overall, SkQ1 stands out as a promising therapeutic candidate that merits further investigation within our drug development pipeline (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Weissig, 2020; Gueven et al., 2017; Wanagat et al., 2010).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Mitoquinone mesylate (MitoQ) is a synthetic, mitochondria‐targeted antioxidant originally developed as an analogue of coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) to overcome the bioavailability and uptake limitations of naturally occurring CoQ10. Its chemical design is based on modifying decylubiquinone—a CoQ10 analogue in which the long isoprenoid tail is replaced by a saturated decyl hydrocarbon chain to enhance mitochondrial retention—and covalently linking it to a lipophilic triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation. The inclusion of the TPP⁺ moiety exploits the highly negative membrane potential of the mitochondrial inner membrane, thereby ensuring selective accumulation of MitoQ in the mitochondrial matrix (Cores et al., 2023). This compound belongs to the class of lipophilic cationic antioxidants and is also considered a mitochondria-targeted rechargeable antioxidant (RMA) because, after its active ubiquinone moiety scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS), it is enzymatically reduced to the active hydroquinone form by components of the electron transport chain. The rechargeable property allows MitoQ to be continuously recycled via the respiratory chain, resulting in sustained antioxidant action even at low doses—a property that distinguishes it from conventional antioxidants (Lukashev et al., 2014; Fields et al., 2023). The synthesis strategy for MitoQ involves the chemical conjugation of decylubiquinone with TPP⁺, and it is formulated as a mesylate salt to improve its stability and facilitate pharmaceutical development (Cores et al., 2023; Kim & Han, 2017). Overall, MitoQ is a well‐defined member of a broader class of mitochondria‐targeted redox active compounds that have been widely investigated for their potential to modulate mitochondrial oxidative stress (Zielonka et al., 2017).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past two decades, MitoQ has been extensively characterized in a wide range of preclinical studies spanning neurodegenerative diseases, cardiovascular disorders, metabolic syndrome, sepsis, and other conditions associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and elevated oxidative stress. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that MitoQ confers protection against oxidative injury in cellular models and animal models alike. For example, studies in rodent models of cardiac ischemia–reperfusion injury, hypertension, and pressure‐overload heart failure have shown that MitoQ preserves mitochondrial respiration, decreases ROS production (especially H₂O₂ and superoxide) and reduces lipid peroxidation in the heart (Fairley et al., 2023; Kim & Han, 2017). In addition, significant neuroprotective effects have been reported in multiple models of neurodegeneration—ranging from in vitro experiments using Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease models to in vivo studies in rodent systems—where MitoQ was able to reduce mitochondrial fragmentation, lower markers of apoptosis, and restore mitochondrial membrane potential in neurons (Fields et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). Clinically, MitoQ has advanced into human trials in several indications including studies related to Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and hypertension, with reported safety in over 200 human subjects (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Fairley et al., 2023). Although there is no direct record of its use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), the extensive preclinical history in diseases characterized by oxidative stress and mitochondrial impairment provides a strong precedent for its repurposing. In ocular contexts, early pharmacokinetic studies have demonstrated that MitoQ exhibits measurable retinal uptake (approximately 1% of plasma concentration) after oral or topical administration, suggesting that the compound can reach the retina at therapeutically relevant levels (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). Given that mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative injury in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells are now increasingly recognized as central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the repurposing of MitoQ for this indication is logically supported by its mechanism and prior usage in analogous conditions (Cores et al., 2023; Zielonka et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
MitoQ’s mechanism of action is rooted in its unique chemical architecture that allows selective mitochondrial targeting and continuous ROS scavenging. The TPP⁺ moiety drives the compound’s accumulation into the mitochondrial matrix in a membrane potential–dependent manner. Once inside the mitochondria, MitoQ’s ubiquinone moiety is rapidly reduced by components of the electron transport chain—most notably by electron flow through complex II—and converted to its active form, mitoquinol (ubiquinol) (Cores et al., 2023; Manolis et al., 2021). In its reduced state, mitoquinol acts as a potent antioxidant that intercepts ROS generated primarily at the sites of electron leakage at complexes I and III. The scavenging of ROS, particularly superoxide and peroxyl radicals, prevents oxidative damage to mitochondrial lipids, proteins, and DNA—all of which are crucial for maintaining mitochondrial function (Zielonka et al., 2017; Modi et al., 2024). In effect, the cycle of reduction and oxidation (redox cycling) enables MitoQ to function catalytically, rather than stoichiometrically, thereby amplifying its antioxidant capacity over time (Lukashev et al., 2014; Modi et al., 2024). Moreover, by reducing mitochondrial ROS, MitoQ preserves the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), which is essential for ATP synthesis and overall cellular bioenergetics (Kim & Han, 2017; Gueven et al., 2017). This stabilization of Δψm not only inhibits the initiation of apoptosis but may also dampen downstream inflammatory signaling cascades mediated by ROS-sensitive transcription factors such as NF-κB (Fields et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023). Such detailed molecular interactions—spanning TPP-driven uptake, rapid reduction at the respiratory chain, catalytic ROS neutralization, and subsequent recycling to the active antioxidant form—underscore the multifaceted protection that MitoQ offers against mitochondrial oxidative injury.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the underlying hypothesis is that accumulation of oxidative damage in RPE cells leads to mitochondrial dysfunction, loss of Δψm, increased ROS production, chronic inflammation, and ultimately RPE cell degeneration, which is central to disease progression. Based on in vitro studies performed in ARPE-19 cells, treatment with MitoQ has been shown to reduce mitochondrial ROS levels, as measured by MitoSOX fluorescence, and to preserve Δψm as assessed by TMRM assays when cells are challenged with H₂O₂-induced oxidative stress (Cores et al., 2023; Fields et al., 2023). The expected effect of MitoQ in a dry AMD model is that, upon topical or oral administration, it will accumulate in the mitochondria of RPE cells via TPP-mediated uptake. Once there, its ubiquinone moiety will be reduced to the active antioxidant form by the local respiratory chain, which in turn will neutralize superoxide and other ROS at the sites of electron leakage (primarily complex I and III regions). This ROS scavenging is anticipated to limit oxidative damage to mitochondrial membranes and proteins, maintain efficient electron transport and ATP production, and ultimately restore the mitochondrial membrane potential that is compromised in oxidative stress conditions (Zielonka et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014). Additionally, by lowering oxidative stress, MitoQ is expected to reduce inflammatory signaling within the RPE and adjacent retinal layers—potentially decreasing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and mitigating the chronic low-grade inflammation that contributes to dry AMD pathology (Fairley et al., 2023; Gueven et al., 2017). In an in vitro assay using ARPE-19 cells, one would expect to observe a significant decrease in MitoSOX signal intensity along with increased TMRM fluorescence after treatment with MitoQ, indicating reduced mitochondrial ROS and improved Δψm, respectively (Cores et al., 2023; Fields et al., 2023). Given that ARPE-19 is a well‐accepted model for studying RPE function and oxidative stress, these biochemical endpoints provide compelling mechanistic evidence that MitoQ may slow or even reverse aspects of RPE degeneration—a promising therapeutic outcome for dry AMD (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
MitoQ stands out as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration on the basis of several compelling factors. First, its synthetic origin as a mitochondria-targeted CoQ10 analogue with an appended TPP⁺ group ensures that it concentrates specifically within mitochondria, where oxidative stress is most detrimental (Cores et al., 2023; Zielonka et al., 2017). This targeted delivery is a critical improvement over non-specific antioxidants, which often fail to reach the intracellular compartments where ROS generation is most intense. Second, MitoQ’s well-established mechanism of action—encompassing catalytic ROS scavenging through a continuously rechargeable redox cycle—directly addresses the pathophysiological core of dry AMD, namely the oxidative injury and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells (Lukashev et al., 2014; Fields et al., 2023). Preclinical studies in diverse disease models have robustly demonstrated its capacity to protect mitochondrial structure and function, reduce lipid peroxidation and apoptotic signaling, and ultimately preserve cellular viability (Kim & Han, 2017; Gueven et al., 2017).

On the therapeutic history side, MitoQ has undergone extensive preclinical evaluation in models of neurodegeneration, cardiovascular diseases, and metabolic disorders, and has been tested in several early-phase clinical trials—even if not yet in dry AMD specifically—showing an excellent safety profile in over 200 human subjects (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Fairley et al., 2023). Furthermore, pharmacokinetic studies demonstrating ocular uptake (~1% of plasma levels) provide an encouraging basis for its repurposing in retinal diseases, although the relatively low retinal concentration does suggest that formulation optimization (for instance, via topical delivery systems or enhanced ocular bioavailability formulations) may be required to achieve therapeutic levels in the RPE (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses need to be considered. Clinical trials in other indications such as Parkinson’s disease have reported mixed outcomes with MitoQ, leading to concerns about its translation from well-controlled preclinical settings to the complex environment of human disease (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). Moreover, the potential for pro-oxidant effects at high concentrations—as sometimes observed with redox-active compounds like MitoQ—is a dose optimization challenge that must be carefully managed in any clinical development program (Gueven et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014). The fact that the reported retinal uptake of MitoQ is modest (~1% of plasma levels) may necessitate higher systemic doses or alternative delivery routes to ensure that sufficient drug reaches the RPE, which in turn could raise safety issues if off-target effects occur (Apostolova & Victor, 2015). Additionally, while the biochemical rationale is compelling, there is currently no direct clinical evidence for efficacy in dry AMD; this gap underscores the need for further targeted preclinical investigations using dry AMD-relevant animal models and subsequent early-phase clinical trials.

In summary, the overall evaluation favours exploration of MitoQ as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its strong mechanistic foundation—based on mitochondrial targeting, catalytic ROS scavenging, and preservation of Δψm—aligns well with the known etiopathogenesis of dry AMD, which involves RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. The extensive preclinical and early clinical data supporting MitoQ’s safety and efficacy in other indications further bolster its candidacy. However, attention must be given to optimizing dosing regimens and delivery strategies to overcome the limitation of modest retinal uptake, as well as rigorously establishing its efficacy specifically in models of dry AMD before advancing to large-scale clinical trials. Given its unique properties and the urgent need for effective treatments in dry AMD, MitoQ merits further investigation as part of a comprehensive strategy to combat RPE degeneration and preserve visual function in affected patients (Cores et al., 2023; Zielonka et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014; Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Tat‐Beclin 1 is a synthetic peptide designed to induce autophagy by harnessing a key region of the Beclin 1 protein, which is essential for the initiation of autophagosome formation (He et al., 2022). This candidate was originally derived by fusing a peptide fragment from Beclin 1, typically encompassing residues in the range of 267–284, with the HIV‐1 Tat transduction domain (Saqcena, 2018), thereby rendering it cell‐permeable and capable of entering diverse cell types. The synthesis and design of Tat‐Beclin 1 focus on exploiting the naturally occurring autophagy machinery by facilitating the release of inhibitory factors bound to Beclin 1 and enhancing its interactions with class III PI3K complexes (He et al., 2022). As a member of the therapeutic class of autophagy inducers, Tat‐Beclin 1 shares mechanistic commonalities with other peptides such as the stapled derivatives (e.g., Tat‐SP4) that have been developed to improve binding affinity and structural stability (Gao, 2023; Gao, 2023). This class of compounds has been widely investigated for their ability to promote autophagy in cellular models of cancer, neurodegeneration, and infection, and the peptide’s design rests on principles that have proven effective in enhancing cellular clearance mechanisms in several pathological contexts (He et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Tat‐Beclin 1 has been extensively characterized in preclinical studies as an inducer of autophagy in various cell types including cancer cells, neuronal cells, and immune cells (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). In early studies, it demonstrated potent autophagy‐stimulating effects by enhancing the transformation of LC3‐I to LC3‐II and by decreasing levels of the autophagic substrate p62, thereby leading to augmented autophagic flux (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013). Moreover, experimental applications have shown that Tat‐Beclin 1 can decrease viral titers in infection models such as those involving West Nile virus and chikungunya virus, and it has been explored for promoting autophagic clearance in cancer models, particularly in breast cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma (He et al., 2022; Gao, 2023). Although there is abundant evidence supporting its utility in managing proteotoxic stress and cellular damage in models of neurodegeneration and cancer, direct applications of Tat‐Beclin 1 for treating dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) have not been explicitly reported (Boland et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2016). Nevertheless, separate studies indicate that proper autophagy in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is critical for cellular viability and resistance to oxidative stress, where impaired autophagy contributes to the accumulation of toxic aggregates such as A2E and lipofuscin that are implicated in AMD (Frost et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Hence, while Tat‐Beclin 1 has not been directly applied in AMD models thus far, its mechanism of promoting clearance of damaged organelles and misfolded proteins provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD treatment.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Tat‐Beclin 1 functions by specifically interacting with Beclin 1, a core component of the Class III PI3K complex that regulates autophagosome nucleation (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). In its inactive state, Beclin 1 is sequestered by negative regulatory proteins such as GAPR‐1, which limits its availability for autophagic initiation. Tat‐Beclin 1 is designed to bind to these inhibitory regulators, thereby liberating Beclin 1 and enabling it to participate in the formation of the PI3K complex necessary for phagophore formation (Ha & Kim, 2016; He et al., 2022). This intervention effectively shifts the balance toward autophagy induction by enhancing the generation of autophagosomes and promoting lysosomal degradation of intracellular cargo. Furthermore, research has demonstrated that Tat‐Beclin 1 increases the conversion of LC3‐I to LC3‐II—a hallmark of autophagosome formation—and has been shown to lower p62 levels, which underscores its role in boosting autophagic flux (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013; Si et al., 2023). Additionally, the peptide’s cell‐penetrating Tat domain facilitates its entry into cells and ensures its functional delivery to intracellular compartments, which is critical for engaging the autophagic machinery even in cells with limited uptake capabilities (Saqcena, 2018; He et al., 2022). Through these molecular interactions, Tat‐Beclin 1 not only enhances general autophagy but has also been reported to drive selective autophagic processes such as mitophagy, thereby promoting the turnover of damaged mitochondria (He et al., 2022; Frost et al., 2014). This mechanistic detail is particularly relevant in conditions of oxidative stress where dysfunctional mitochondria accumulate and contribute to cell death, as has been observed in RPE cells during the progression of dry AMD (Frost et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration, the therapeutic hypothesis posits that Tat‐Beclin 1 will promote autophagy initiation in RPE cells to facilitate the turnover of damaged organelles—including mitochondria—that accumulate as a result of chronic oxidative stress (Frost et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). This enhanced autophagic clearance is expected to mitigate the cytotoxic effects associated with the buildup of toxic aggregates such as A2E and lipofuscin, which are known to drive RPE cell dysfunction and death (Zhang et al., 2015; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Experimental evidence from studies on RPE cells has documented that robust autophagic activity is critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis in the face of oxidative and metabolic insults (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Therefore, by increasing autophagic flux, Tat‐Beclin 1 should theoretically lead to a reduction in cellular stress markers and an improvement in mitochondrial quality control mechanisms, thereby preventing the initiation of apoptotic cascades in RPE cells (Saqcena, 2018). In cellular assays, the expected outcome would include an enhanced LC3‐II/LC3‐I ratio, decreased levels of p62, improved lysosomal function, and ultimately enhanced cell viability under oxidative stress conditions (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013; Si et al., 2023). Notably, the efficacy of autophagy induction in rescuing RPE cellular function is supported by literature where pharmacological activation of autophagy—such as through rapamycin or inhibition of mTOR pathways—has been shown to protect RPE cells from degeneration (Frost et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2020). Given the inherent ability of Tat‐Beclin 1 to stimulate autophagy in other cellular models, it is reasonable to expect that similar benefits would be observed upon its application to RPE cells, leading to a deceleration of dry AMD pathology by maintaining mitochondrial turnover and preventing the accumulation of deleterious substrates.

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall potential of Tat‐Beclin 1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD lies in its well‐defined mechanism of action, which directly targets the autophagic machinery through interactions with Beclin 1 (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). One of the primary strengths of this candidate is its demonstrated versatility across different disease models, where enhancement of autophagy has led to reduced apoptosis, improved clearance of toxic protein aggregates, and mitigation of cellular stress in both cancer and neurodegenerative contexts (He et al., 2022; Boland et al., 2018). In the specific arena of RPE cell biology, multiple studies have established that autophagic dysfunction is a hallmark of AMD progression and that stimulating autophagy can improve cellular resilience under oxidative stress (Frost et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Therefore, by repurposing Tat‐Beclin 1 for dry AMD, there exists a compelling translational rationale based on mechanistic insights derived from both in vitro and in vivo studies in other systems.

However, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be considered. Despite extensive preclinical evidence in other domains, there is a lack of direct experimental data demonstrating the efficacy of Tat‐Beclin 1 in ocular models or in RPE-specific assays (He et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2016). Pharmacokinetic and biodistribution challenges also remain to be addressed, especially given the unique anatomical barriers of the eye. Although the Tat transduction domain confers robust cell penetration, the stability, half-life, and clearance of the peptide in ocular tissues have yet to be thoroughly investigated (Saqcena, 2018; He et al., 2022). Moreover, the route of administration—potentially through intravitreal injection or topical delivery—must be optimized to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE without eliciting adverse immune responses or off-target effects. It is also important to note that while the autophagy-stimulating effects of Tat‐Beclin 1 have been well documented in various cell types, the specific context of chronic oxidative stress and metabolite accumulation in the aged RPE represents a distinct microenvironment that may influence peptide efficacy (Frost et al., 2014; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Zhang et al., 2015).
