• Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Bardoxolone methyl is a semisynthetic derivative belonging to the synthetic oleanane triterpenoid class. Its origin stems from oleanolic acid—a naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid abundantly found in various medicinal plants. Early medicinal chemistry programs sought to overcome the modest anti‐inflammatory activity and poor bioavailability of oleanolic acid by introducing targeted modifications. Through chemical derivatization, these programs generated CDDO (2‐cyano‐3,12‐dioxooleana‐1,9‐dien‐28‐oic acid) and subsequently its C‐28 methyl ester, known as Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO‐Me) (Borella et al., 2019). The synthetic process involves the installation of electrophilic Michael acceptor groups at strategic positions on the oleanane scaffold, such as the addition of an α,β‐unsaturated carbonyl in the A‐ring and further incorporation of a cyano group that substantially increases the compound’s potency relative to its natural precursor (Wong et al., 2016; Zhang & Chapman, 2020). These chemical modifications not only enhance the anti‐inflammatory and anticancer properties but also improve chemical stability and oral bioavailability. The structural design, which incorporates a reversible electrophilic reactivity, underpins the compound’s ability to engage diverse cellular targets (Thomas, 2012; Zhou et al., 2014). Bardoxolone methyl thus represents a chemically advanced, highly potent agent from a class of molecules originally designed to trigger cytoprotective responses via direct electrophilic modulation.

• Therapeutic History  
Bardoxolone methyl has undergone extensive preclinical and early clinical evaluation primarily in fields as disparate as oncology and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Initial studies established that synthetic oleanane triterpenoids, including CDDO and its variants, exert dramatic anti‐inflammatory effects by suppressing inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and cyclooxygenase (COX‐2) expression in activated macrophages (Gatbonton‐Schwager, 2014). Preclinical studies in multiple mouse cancer models and inflammatory conditions confirmed its potent anticancer activity and cytoprotective properties, which catalyzed its progression into human clinical trials (Borella et al., 2019; Nakagami, 2016).  
In the clinical arena, Bardoxolone methyl was advanced through Phase I cancer trials, where its once‐daily oral dosing regimen and pharmacokinetic profile—with a terminal half‐life of approximately 39 hours—were characterized (Thomas, 2012; Nakagami, 2016). More notably, its unexpected ability to improve estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in patients with advanced renal disease, particularly in diabetic nephropathy, led to its evaluation in large Phase II and Phase III trials, such as the BEAM and BEACON studies (Yagishita et al., 2020; Tanase et al., 2022). However, the BEACON trial was terminated prematurely due to an increased incidence of cardiovascular events, including heart failure, highlighting concerns about the compound’s systemic safety profile when used at higher doses or in populations with comorbidities (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012).  
Despite its promising preclinical pharmacology and the breadth of clinical data available in non‐ocular indications, to date there is no direct record in the literature of Bardoxolone methyl being used specifically for the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular degenerative conditions (Schiavoni et al., 2025). Nonetheless, the overall safety and pharmacokinetic properties observed in CKD and oncology trials lend valuable insights for considering drug repurposing across therapeutic areas.

• Mechanism of Action  
Bardoxolone methyl is best known for its ability to activate the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway—a master regulator of cellular defense mechanisms against oxidative and electrophilic stress. Under basal conditions, Nrf2 is tightly regulated by Kelch‐like ECH‐associated protein 1 (Keap1), which serves as an adaptor for ubiquitin ligases targeting Nrf2 for proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl functions as a potent electrophile and interacts with sulfhydryl groups on critical cysteine residues within Keap1. This covalent or reversible Michael addition reaction disrupts the Keap1–Nrf2 complex, thereby stabilizing and allowing Nrf2 to translocate into the nucleus (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).  
Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to the antioxidant response element (ARE) in the promoter regions of a host of cytoprotective genes. This transcriptional activation results in the upregulation of a battery of antioxidant and phase II detoxifying enzymes, including but not limited to heme oxygenase‐1 (HO‐1), NAD(P)H dehydrogenase (quinone 1; NQO1), various glutathione transferases, and glutamate–cysteine ligase subunits (Thomas, 2012; Wong et al., 2016). Studies in non‐ocular tissues have shown that at very low (nanomolar) doses, Bardoxolone methyl robustly engages this cytoprotective program while also exerting dose‐dependent biology wherein intermediate and high doses trigger effects such as modulation of cell differentiation and direct anticancer activity, respectively (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).  
It is important to note that while the canonical targets of Nrf2 activation are well characterized, Bardoxolone methyl’s electrophilic character enables it to interact with multiple regulatory proteins. For example, it can inhibit IκB kinase β (IKKβ), leading to suppression of nuclear factor κB (NF‐κB) signaling and subsequent reduction in proinflammatory cytokine production (Zhou et al., 2014; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although the literature does not provide direct experimental evidence that Bardoxolone methyl specifically upregulates mitochondrial antioxidants such as superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) and peroxiredoxin 3 (PRDX3) in RPE cells, the robust, broad‐spectrum transcriptional response induced by Nrf2 activation strongly suggests that mitochondrial and cytoplasmic components of the antioxidant defense system may also be upregulated (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015). Such upregulation would be consistent with previous findings of increased expression of antioxidant genes and improved cellular redox status upon treatment with similar synthetic triterpenoids (Schiavoni et al., 2025; Sporn et al., 2011).

• Expected Effect in Dry AMD  
The pathogenesis of dry age‐related macular degeneration is multifactorial, with chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction playing a central role in the degeneration of the RPE—a critical monolayer that supports photoreceptor health. RPE cells are particularly vulnerable to oxidative damage due to high metabolic activity, exposure to light, and the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). In this context, the proposed mechanism of Bardoxolone methyl, namely activation of the Nrf2/ARE pathway, provides a biologically tenable strategy for neuroprotection and cellular preservation.  
When administered at low doses, Bardoxolone methyl is expected to trigger a cytoprotective transcriptional program in RPE cells. Activation of Nrf2 should lead to the induction of a range of antioxidant enzymes and detoxifying proteins which together help re-establish redox balance in the face of chronic oxidative insult (Borella et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012). One key hypothesis is that, in addition to the already well‐documented induction of cytosolic antioxidants such as HO‐1 and NQO1, Bardoxolone methyl may also promote the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3. SOD2 is the primary defense against superoxide radicals within the mitochondria, and PRDX3 plays a critical role in detoxifying hydrogen peroxide produced by mitochondrial respiration. Although direct data in RPE cells are currently lacking, studies in other cellular contexts have demonstrated that activation of Nrf2 results in the upregulation of a broad spectrum of antioxidant genes, and it is plausible that under the oxidative duress typical of dry AMD, similar effects would be observed in RPE cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
In vitro models simulating oxidative stress—such as exposure of RPE cells to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)—have shown that compounds with similar electrophilic properties, and indeed other members of the CDDO family like CDDO-Im, reduce the intracellular MitoSOX fluorescence signal, indicative of a reduction in mitochondrial ROS (mtROS) (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024). Moreover, improvements in mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) have been correlated with such treatments, suggesting that these molecules can help maintain mitochondrial function under stressful conditions (Nakagami, 2016; Zhou et al., 2014). Such outcomes are highly relevant in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction in the RPE has been implicated in disease progression. The anticipated outcomes, therefore, include a reduction in mtROS, restoration of Δψm, and subsequent preservation of RPE cellular integrity and function.  
Another positive aspect is the compound’s previously established oral bioavailability and pharmacokinetic profile. Clinical studies in CKD patients have demonstrated that therapeutic plasma concentrations can be achieved with once-daily dosing. Although systemic administration in ocular diseases is not ideal, these data provide a strong pharmacological starting point for repurposing. In addition, if systemic toxicity remains a concern—as suggested by the cardiovascular signals in CKD trials—an alternative approach might involve localized ocular delivery (for instance, via intravitreal injection or by developing an ocular formulation) to achieve high retinal bioavailability while minimizing systemic exposure (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).

• Overall Evaluation  
In assessing Bardoxolone methyl for repurposing as a therapeutic for dry AMD, several critical points emerge that underline both its promise and the challenges that must be overcome.

Strengths:  
1. Strong Chemical Rationale and Potency:  
Bardoxolone methyl is a product of sophisticated medicinal chemistry, designed to overcome the limitations of natural triterpenoids like oleanolic acid by installing reactive electrophilic groups that significantly enhance its potency. This design specifically enables the activation of the Nrf2 pathway—a mechanism central to antioxidant defense—at very low concentrations (Borella et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016). The high potency of Bardoxolone methyl as an Nrf2 activator is a significant advantage, particularly when considering that even subtle improvements in cellular antioxidant capacity can have a profound impact on chronic degenerative diseases like dry AMD.

2. Broad Cytoprotective Mechanism:  
The mechanism of Bardoxolone methyl involves the disruption of the Keap1-Nrf2 complex via covalent modification of Keap1 cysteine residues, facilitating the nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and the subsequent transcriptional activation of a broad range of antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes (Zhou et al., 2014; Thomas, 2012). This broad cytoprotective response is particularly relevant to the RPE, where chronic oxidative stress has been implicated in cellular dysfunction and death. The possibility that Bardoxolone methyl may also induce mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3, although not yet directly confirmed in RPE, is an attractive hypothesis; such an effect would directly address the mitochondrial dysfunction that is a hallmark of dry AMD (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).

3. Extensive Clinical Experience and Pharmacokinetic Data:  
Bardoxolone methyl has been evaluated in several clinical trials—most notably in the context of CKD and oncology—yielding a wealth of pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and tolerability data. Its oral bioavailability, with a terminal half-life that supports once-daily dosing, is well documented (Thomas, 2012; Nakagami, 2016). Although the systemic adverse events observed in these trials (such as cardiovascular-related events) present challenges for broad systemic administration, these data nonetheless offer a useful starting point for repurposing. The established clinical profile can inform dose-escalation studies and safety monitoring protocols should Bardoxolone methyl be advanced into ocular trials.

4. Support from Analogous Preclinical Models:  
Several studies in related models have demonstrated that synthetic triterpenoids can protect retinal tissue from oxidative damage. For example, experiments with CDDO-Im, a closely related analogue, have shown protective effects in retinal ischemia–reperfusion injury, including the attenuation of inflammatory responses and preservation of retinal structure (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024). Although these studies are not directly with Bardoxolone methyl, the mechanistic commonalities within this compound class support the notion that the same protective pathways can be harnessed in the context of dry AMD.

Weaknesses and Challenges:  
1. Lack of Direct Evidence in RPE/Dry AMD Models:  
Despite the strong theoretical rationale, direct evidence that Bardoxolone methyl upregulates mitochondrial antioxidants (SOD2, PRDX3) in RPE cells is currently lacking. Most published data are derived from non-ocular cell types or from studies using other analogues such as CDDO-Im (Cai et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2014). It is therefore essential to perform specific in vitro studies in RPE cell lines under oxidative stress conditions to measure the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes and the functional status of mitochondria (e.g., Δψm, mtROS levels) following treatment with Bardoxolone methyl.

2. Safety Concerns from Prior Clinical Experience:  
A significant challenge in repurposing Bardoxolone methyl stems from its safety profile in systemic indications. The Phase III BEACON trial in CKD patients was halted due to an increased incidence of serious cardiovascular events, including heart failure and increased mortality (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although the mechanisms underlying these adverse effects may be related to systemic fluid retention, off‐target reactivity, or other metabolic perturbations, they raise concerns about the safety of systemic administration. For ocular application, it may be necessary to consider alternative dosing strategies or localized delivery methods to avoid systemic exposure while still achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina.

3. Translational and Formulation Challenges:  
The unique anatomy and physiology of the eye introduce additional obstacles in drug repurposing. RPE cells reside in a relatively immune-privileged, isolated microenvironment behind the blood–retinal barrier. The pharmacokinetics and tissue penetration profiles of Bardoxolone methyl observed in systemic circulation may not directly translate to effective intraocular concentrations. Development of specialized ocular formulations—such as sustained-release intravitreal injections or topical applications that can traverse ocular barriers—will be critical for successful translation (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).

4. Multifactorial Nature of AMD Pathogenesis:  
Dry AMD is a complex, multifactorial disease where oxidative stress is only one component of a broader pathogenic network that includes genetic predisposition, inflammation, lipid dysregulation, and complement system activation. While activation of the Nrf2 pathway can counteract oxidative stress and may have secondary anti-inflammatory effects, it is uncertain whether this single mechanism will be sufficient to alter the course of the disease. A combinatorial therapeutic strategy incorporating Nrf2 activation with other modalities might eventually be required to address the full spectrum of dry AMD pathology (Cheng et al., 2021; Thomas, 2012).

5. Dose-Dependent Effects and Narrow Therapeutic Window:  
Bardoxolone methyl exhibits highly dose-dependent pharmacology. At low doses, it predominantly activates Nrf2 and induces cytoprotective genes; however, as the dose increases, additional actions such as pro-apoptotic and cytotoxic effects emerge (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014). Determining the precise dose that is efficacious in RPE cells without triggering deleterious off-target effects will be crucial. This necessitates rigorous dose-ranging studies in preclinical models to define a therapeutic window that maximizes retinal protection while minimizing risks.

• Overall Evaluation and Recommendation  
In summary, Bardoxolone methyl presents a compelling candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD thanks to its well-characterized chemical design, potent induction of the Nrf2 pathway, and a broad cytoprotective mechanism that addresses many aspects of the oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction implicated in RPE degeneration. The extensive clinical data from studies in CKD and oncology provide a valuable foundation for understanding its pharmacokinetics and systemic effects, while the underlying chemistry ensures high potency at low concentrations—features that are highly desirable when targeting a chronic, degenerative condition such as dry AMD (Borella et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012).  
Nonetheless, significant challenges remain. There is a conspicuous gap in the literature regarding the direct evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl in RPE cells and dry AMD models, particularly concerning its ability to upregulate mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes like SOD2 and PRDX3 and thereby mitigate mtROS damage. This gap must be addressed through targeted in vitro assays and in vivo animal studies that simulate the retinal environment and its chronic oxidative stress. Safety concerns, as evidenced by the cardiovascular events observed in CKD trials, underscore the need for caution; these risks may be minimized through localized ocular administration, but careful formulation and dosing studies will be required to establish an acceptable safety profile in the ocular context (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019).  
Given the current state of evidence, it is recommended that Bardoxolone methyl be subjected to further preclinical evaluation in the context of dry AMD. Specifically, studies should focus on:  
 – Conducting detailed in vitro experiments in human RPE cell lines to assess whether exposure to Bardoxolone methyl under oxidative stress conditions leads to the upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants (e.g., SOD2 and PRDX3) and an associated decrease in mtROS (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
 – Evaluating the effects of Bardoxolone methyl on mitochondrial function (including measurements of Δψm, oxygen consumption rate, and mitochondrial integrity) in these cells.  
 – Adapting ocular-specific formulations that allow high local retinal concentrations with minimal systemic exposure, potentially using intravitreal or topical delivery methods, and conducting pharmacokinetic studies that establish retinal tissue exposure (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).  
 – Testing the compound in animal models of dry AMD to determine whether the in vitro antioxidant and mitochondrial protective effects translate into preservation of RPE and photoreceptor structure and function over time (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024).  
If these studies yield positive results that confirm the hypothesized upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants and improved RPE function, Bardoxolone methyl could then be advanced to early-phase clinical trials in patients with dry AMD. Such trials would need to incorporate rigorous safety monitoring protocols to mitigate the known systemic adverse effects. A potential strategy may involve administering the drug in a localized manner or at doses that are effective in the eye but low enough to avoid triggering systemic electrophilic toxicity.

Overall, Bardoxolone methyl holds promise as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD based on its potent Nrf2-activating properties and the central role of oxidative stress in the disease’s pathogenesis. However, its development for an ocular indication will hinge on its ability to selectively and safely modulate the redox status of RPE cells while avoiding systemic side effects. A stepwise, targeted preclinical program that directly addresses these RPE-specific endpoints is therefore critical before consideration of clinical trials in the dry AMD patient population (Nakagami, 2016).

In conclusion, while Bardoxolone methyl offers a strong mechanistic rationale as an Nrf2 activator with the theoretical capacity to upregulate mitochondrial defenses in RPE cells, further targeted studies are essential. The compound’s repurposing for dry AMD is scientifically attractive given the unmet need for effective therapies in this condition; however, the translational path is complex due to safety concerns observed in systemic trials and the lack of direct ocular data. A rigorous preclinical research plan—encompassing in vitro RPE studies, ocular pharmacokinetic assessments, and animal model validation—will be required to determine whether Bardoxolone methyl can be safely and effectively repurposed to preserve RPE function and slow the progression of dry AMD.

• Summary of Key Supporting Points  
– Bardoxolone methyl is a chemically engineered derivative of oleanolic acid that exploits electrophilic modifications to robustly activate the Nrf2 pathway (Borella et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016).  
– Its extensive preclinical and clinical history in oncology and CKD, though not in ocular disease, provides important pharmacokinetic and biological safety data that may be leveraged, with modifications, for ocular use (Nakagami, 2016; Tanase et al., 2022).  
– Its mechanism—covalent modification of Keap1 and subsequent nuclear translocation of Nrf2—leads to the transcriptional upregulation of cytoprotective genes, and it is hypothesized that this would include mitochondrial antioxidants (e.g., SOD2, PRDX3), which are critical for mitigating oxidative damage in RPE cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
– Preclinical data with related triterpenoids in retinal models support the concept that Nrf2 activation can ameliorate oxidative stress and preserve retinal integrity, although direct data for Bardoxolone methyl in dry AMD are presently lacking (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024).  
– Key challenges include the translation of systemic dosing to ocular delivery, the need to specifically validate mitochondrial protective effects in RPE cells, and the resolution of safety issues exemplified by prior cardiovascular signals in systemic trials (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

• Final Recommendation  
Based on the current literature review, Bardoxolone methyl emerges as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its potent Nrf2 activation, broad cytoprotective potential, and a well-documented clinical PK profile. However, its repurposing for ocular application must be preceded by targeted preclinical studies that corroborate its ability to upregulate mitochondrial antioxidants in RPE cells and to reduce mtROS while preserving mitochondrial function. These studies should also explore ocular-specific formulations and dosing regimens that minimize systemic exposure. Only after thorough validation in these preliminary investigations can Bardoxolone methyl be considered a credible candidate for clinical trials in dry AMD patients. Given these considerations, the candidate warrants further investigation despite the existing translational and safety challenges inherent in repurposing a systemically active electrophilic compound for an ocular indication (Borella et al., 2019; Yagishita et al., 2020; Thomas, 2012).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Alda-1 is a synthetic small molecule discovered through target-directed screening for modulators of mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2), originally identified as “ALDH2 activator 1” with the chemical name N-(1,3-benzodioxol-5-ylmethyl)-2,6-dichlorobenzamide and first demonstrated to reduce myocardial ischemic injury in rodents by directly activating ALDH2 (i.e., increasing its catalytic activity and rescuing function of the common inactive ALDH2*2 variant) (Budas et al., 2009; Kimura et al., 2019). Structurally and mechanistically, Alda-1 binds at the substrate entrance tunnel of ALDH2 and extends toward the active site, where it enhances dehydrogenase activity by favorably altering local dynamics, improving NAD+ engagement, and acting as a chemical chaperone that preserves the functional conformation of critical active-site loops and α-helices, while shielding key catalytic cysteines from irreversible electrophilic adduction by reactive aldehydes such as 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE) (Gao et al., 2022; Wang & He, 2018). In vitro biophysical and enzymology work shows Alda-1 increases wild-type ALDH2 activity approximately twofold and markedly rescues activity of the common East Asian mutant ALDH2*2 (Glu504Lys), restoring heterotetramer activity to near wild-type levels; importantly, Alda-1 is selective against several other ALDHs in original profiling, although later biochemical work suggests some degree of cross-activation of ALDH1A1 under specific assay conditions (Budas et al., 2009; Kotraiah et al., 2013).

Alda-1 belongs to the pharmacologic class of enzyme activators/allosteric agonists targeting mitochondrial ALDH2; the class is characterized by its ability to catalytically enhance clearance of reactive aldehydes generated by oxidative and nitrosative stress (e.g., 4-HNE, malondialdehyde [MDA], acrolein, and catecholamine-derived DOPAL), thereby acting as indirect antioxidants that reduce downstream carbonyl stress, proteotoxicity, and mitochondria-dependent cell death without directly scavenging ROS (Kimura et al., 2019; Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Wang & He, 2018). This mechanism has been applied preclinically across multiple organ systems to mitigate ischemia–reperfusion injury, chronic heart failure, metabolic and neurodegenerative toxicities, and toxin-induced organ damage, providing a consistent translational thread: activation of ALDH2 accelerates detoxification of stable electrophilic products of lipid peroxidation, interrupting aldehyde-driven positive feedback loops that amplify mitochondrial dysfunction, ROS generation, and apoptosis (Budas et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2014; Münzel & Daiber, 2018).

Therapeutic History  
Across cardiovascular models, Alda-1 has repeatedly demonstrated robust cytoprotection in vivo. In rat and mouse myocardial ischemia–reperfusion and infarction models, Alda-1 administration prior to or during ischemia reduced infarct size by approximately 60% and improved long-term survival following myocardial infarction, associating efficacy with increased ALDH2 activity, reduced 4-HNE-protein adducts and protein carbonyls, preserved mitochondrial respiratory control ratio (RCR), reduced mitochondrial H₂O₂ release, protection against Ca²⁺-induced mitochondrial permeability transition (MPT), and decreased cytochrome c release (Budas et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2014). In a chronic post-MI heart-failure model with established aldehydic overload, sustained Alda-1 treatment increased cardiac ALDH2 activity by ~2.7-fold, lowered 4-HNE adducts and protein carbonyls, normalized uncoupler responsiveness, improved RCR by preserving State 3 respiration, lowered mitochondrial ROS emission, and corrected MPT sensitivity; organ-level outcomes included increased contractility, reduced LV dilation, diminished hypertrophy and fibrosis, and anti-remodeling benefits (Gomes et al., 2014). In vitro, Alda-1 shielded isolated cardiac mitochondria from 4-HNE–induced respiratory inhibition, demonstrating direct aldehyde-dependent protection at the mitochondrial level (Gomes et al., 2014).

Hepatic and other organ systems provide convergent evidence. In a mouse acetaminophen hepatotoxicity model, Alda-1 pretreatment substantially reduced liver injury biomarkers (ALT/AST), histologic necrosis, 4-HNE adduct burden, mitochondrial depolarization, and cell death without altering upstream NAPQI bioactivation or JNK phosphorylation, demonstrating that protection is downstream via aldehyde detoxification and preservation of mitochondrial polarization and MPT control (Wimborne et al., 2020). Additional preclinical reports document Alda-1 efficacy in models of lung ischemia/reperfusion, intestinal I/R, kidney injury, neurotoxic injuries, and alcohol-related hepatic injury, again with mechanistic ties to accelerated clearance of reactive aldehydes, restoration of mitochondrial function, and modulation of stress/apoptosis pathways (Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019).

Retina-focused data, while more limited and not in dry AMD models, are directionally supportive. In streptozotocin-induced aged diabetic rats (an early diabetic retinopathy model), systemic Alda-1 improved ERG parameters, preserved outer nuclear layer (ONL) and total retinal thickness on OCT at 7–30 days, increased retinal SOD activity, and decreased retinal TNF-α and IL-6 across multiple timepoints; concurrent upregulation of ALDH2, Nrf2, and Sirt1 was observed by immunofluorescence and Western blot, suggesting that ALDH2 activation engages antioxidant and anti-inflammatory pathways in the retina under hyperglycemic oxidative stress (He et al., 2018). In a separate in vivo retinal degeneration study (MNU-induced photoreceptor damage), systemic Alda-1 preserved ERG amplitudes, mitigated photoreceptor degeneration (OCT, histology), increased retinal ALDH2 and SIRT1 protein, and reduced markers of ER stress (GRP78) and apoptosis (PARP1), supporting the hypothesis that enhancing aldehyde detoxification ameliorates retinal cellular stress downstream of lipid peroxidation (Yan et al., 2020; Carullo et al., 2020). Although neither model recapitulates RPE-centric dry AMD (drusen, complement activation, geographic atrophy), they provide proof-of-principle that ALDH2 activation can protect neural retina under oxidative/aldehydic stress in vivo (Yan et al., 2020; He et al., 2018).

Clinical translation status remains nascent. No human proof-of-concept trials of Alda-1 have been reported, and authoritative reviews note the absence of clinical efficacy data for ALDH2 activators like Alda-1, despite extensive rodent evidence across organs; moreover, no ALDH2 activators are in clinical use at present (Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019). Safety experience is therefore limited to preclinical settings: chronic Alda-1 dosing in naïve rats (10 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks) demonstrated acceptable tolerability (no hemodynamic, biochemical, or organ-weight changes), whereas a separate report described crystalline nephropathy and renal function deterioration after I/R under specific Alda-1 dosing/formulation conditions, suggesting potential tissue-specific or formulation-dependent risks requiring evaluation (Gomes et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2023). With respect to ophthalmology, existing Alda-1 studies are limited to rodent retina in DR and MNU models; there is no published use in dry AMD patients or preclinical AMD-like RPE atrophy models, and there is no reported ocular delivery pharmacokinetics or long-term ocular safety data in the provided literature (Yan et al., 2020; He et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action  
ALDH2 is a mitochondrial, NAD⁺-dependent dehydrogenase that catalyzes the oxidation of reactive aldehydes—most notably acetaldehyde, 4-HNE, MDA, acrolein, and DOPAL—to their corresponding carboxylic acids, thereby detoxifying electrophiles that otherwise form covalent Michael adducts and Schiff bases with cysteine, histidine, and lysine residues on proteins and nucleic acids (Kimura et al., 2019; Budas et al., 2009). The enzyme’s catalytic mechanism involves NAD⁺ binding in the Rossmann fold and activation of the catalytic cysteine (Cys302 in ALDH2), nucleophilic attack on the aldehyde to form a thiohemiacetal, hydride transfer to produce a thioacyl-enzyme intermediate, and Glu268-mediated hydrolysis to release the acid product and NADH; this canonical chemistry underlies ALDH2’s role as an indirect antioxidant via aldehyde clearance rather than direct ROS scavenging (Parajuli, 2013; Wang & He, 2018). Importantly, ALDH2 is highly susceptible to oxidative and electrophilic inactivation—its active-site cysteine cluster (Cys301–Cys303) can be adducted by 4-HNE at micromolar concentrations (>10 µM), establishing a pathogenic feed-forward loop in which lipid peroxidation products both injure proteins and progressively compromise the aldehyde-detoxifying capacity of mitochondria (Karan et al., 2023; Budas et al., 2009).

Alda-1 engages this system at multiple mechanistic levels. Structurally, Alda-1 binds to the substrate entrance tunnel and active site of ALDH2, altering the local environment to increase effective substrate/catalytic-cysteine proximity and improve NAD⁺ binding (lower Kₘ), while simultaneously acting as a molecular chaperone to stabilize conformational elements disrupted in the ALDH2*2 variant (e.g., restoring α-helix and active-site loop structures toward wild-type) (Gao et al., 2022; Wang & He, 2018). Functionally, Alda-1 increases wild-type ALDH2 catalytic activity approximately two-fold, but the effect is more pronounced in ALDH2*2 (10-fold or more in homotetramers), which is clinically relevant in East Asian populations; Alda-1 does not affect ALDH1/ALDH5 in initial selectivity panels, though subsequent biochemical reports indicate potential ALDH1A1 activation under specific conditions (i.e., DOPAL-inactivation assays), a detail that warrants further isozyme-specific profiling in ocular tissues (Budas et al., 2009; Kotraiah et al., 2013). Crucially, Alda-1 also reduces aldehyde access to catalytic cysteines (Cys302/301/303), protecting ALDH2 from 4-HNE–induced inactivation, thereby sustaining endogenous detoxification under aldehyde stress; in direct assays Alda-1 prevents rapid 4-HNE-mediated ALDH2 inactivation and shifts the enzyme to a higher-efficiency state (Gao et al., 2022; Kotraiah et al., 2013). The net biochemical outcome is enhancement of mitochondrial clearance of 4-HNE to the less reactive 4-hydroxynonenoic acid (4-HNA), alongside accelerated metabolism of other toxic aldehydes, which interrupts aldehyde-driven proteotoxic cascades (e.g., proteasomal inhibition, protein carbonyl accumulation) and preserves mitochondrial respiratory function (Budas et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2014).

Systems-level consequences of ALDH2 activation by Alda-1 have been delineated extensively in heart and liver. In failing hearts with elevated aldehydic load, Alda-1 decreased 4-HNE-protein adducts and total carbonyls without altering ALDH2 protein abundance, demonstrating a purely catalytic detoxification effect (i.e., activity increase without expression change) (Gomes et al., 2014). Mitochondrial bioenergetic protection is robust: Alda-1 preserved State 3 respiration, increased RCR, normalized uncoupler responses (CCCP), reduced absolute and relative H₂O₂ release, decreased cytochrome c release, and corrected MPT sensitivity, indicating mitigation of mitochondria-centered death signaling under chronic oxidative/aldehydic stress (Gomes et al., 2014). In isolated mitochondria, pre-incubation with Alda-1 prevented 4-HNE–induced declines in respiratory control and State 3 oxygen consumption, further supporting a direct anti-aldehyde effect on mitochondrial electron transport chain function (Gomes et al., 2014). In the APAP hepatotoxicity model, Alda-1 reduced tissue 4-HNE adduct burden by an order of magnitude, preserved mitochondrial polarization, and reduced cell death, consistent with detoxification of lipid peroxidation products downstream of parent electrophile formation (Wimborne et al., 2020).

Retinal and neuronal contexts provide complementary mechanistic observations. In cultured endothelial cells exposed to amyloid-β₁–₄₀, Alda-1 restored mitochondrial function, reduced 4-HNE adducts and ROS, and rescued angiogenic responses, indicating that ALDH2 activation can directly blunt aldehyde-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction in non-cardiac cells (Chen & Joshi, 2016; Roy, 2022). Within the retina, ALDH2 localizes across layers with predominant co-localization to CRALBP-positive Müller glia, and its expression diminishes with age; transgenic upregulation protects against retinal aging by decreasing oxidative-stress–related apoptosis and enhancing the unfolded protein response (UPR) in the ER, indicating that increased ALDH2 activity has cytoprotective effects in vivo in the aging retina (Karan et al., 2023; Long et al., 2020). In diabetic retinopathy rodent studies, Alda-1 increased retinal ALDH2, SIRT1, and Nrf2 signaling, decreased proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6), and improved electrophysiologic and structural outcomes, suggesting that ALDH2 activation enlists antioxidant and proteostasis pathways beyond direct aldehyde detoxification to preserve retinal function (He et al., 2018). In photoreceptor degeneration, Alda-1 upregulated SIRT1 and decreased ER stress/apoptotic markers, again consistent with mitigation of downstream stress signaling when aldehyde load is reduced (Yan et al., 2020).

Finally, the disease biochemistry underpinning our hypothesis—aldehyde toxicity as a conserved driver downstream of oxidative lipid peroxidation—is well defined in neurodegeneration and retinal biology. 4-HNE forms adducts that impair proteasome activity, promote accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and inflammation, covalently modify and crosslink amyloid peptides, impair ion pumps and transporters, and directly kill neurons at low micromolar concentrations; ALDH2 loss-of-function (including ALDH2*2) exacerbates accumulation of 4-HNE adducts and age-dependent neurodegeneration in rodent models (Chen & Joshi, 2016). In retinal disease, the RPE and photoreceptors operate in a high-oxygen, PUFA-rich environment, with continuous photo-oxidation and phagocytosis of outer segments generating lipid peroxides and aldehydes, and oxidative stress is a central driver of AMD pathogenesis; therapeutic strategies that augment endogenous detoxification (e.g., via Nrf2) have been proposed as rational approaches to bolster RPE resilience (Chen et al., 2023). Collectively, Alda-1’s biochemical action—activation of a mitochondrial enzyme that eliminates 4-HNE/MDA—integrates tightly with the pathophysiology of aldehyde-mediated mitochondrial and proteostatic injury that characterizes oxidatively stressed retinal tissues (Kimura et al., 2019; Budas et al., 2009).

Expected Effect  
In RPE mitochondria subjected to chronic oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, the proposed mechanism predicts that Alda-1 will (i) increase ALDH2 catalytic activity and resilience to aldehyde-induced inactivation, (ii) accelerate metabolic clearance of 4-HNE and related long-lived electrophiles to non-reactive acids, (iii) reduce covalent adduction/carbonylation of mitochondrial and cytosolic proteins, (iv) preserve oxidative phosphorylation (increased State 3 respiration and RCR), (v) lower mitochondrial H₂O₂ production, (vi) increase resistance to Ca²⁺-induced MPT and decrease cytochrome c release, and (vii) therefore reduce apoptotic signaling and downstream inflammation in RPE, which in aggregate should attenuate RPE dysfunction and slow progression of dry AMD (Gomes et al., 2014). While direct ALDH2 expression in RPE has not been demonstrated in the provided texts, ALDH2 is present across retinal layers (notably Müller glia) and declines with age, and increasing ALDH2 conferred protection in the aged mouse retina in vivo, supporting the rationale that ALDH2 activation in retinal tissue can be beneficial under oxidative stress; confirming ALDH2 expression and activity in human and murine RPE will be a critical enabling experiment (Karan et al., 2023; Long et al., 2020). The retina’s documented vulnerability to lipid peroxidation (PUFA-rich outer segments, high O₂ consumption, chronic light exposure) and the centrality of oxidative stress to AMD pathogenesis further support that increased mitochondrial aldehyde detoxification should reduce toxic aldehyde burden in RPE and adjacent cells (Chen et al., 2023).

Assay expectations and readouts for validation align closely with prior Alda-1 literature. In isolated RPE mitochondria or permeabilized cells, Alda-1 should preserve ADP-stimulated State 3 oxygen consumption and increase RCR versus vehicle under aldehydic load (e.g., exogenous 4-HNE) or oxidative stress conditions; decreased H₂O₂ release and normalization of uncoupler (CCCP) responses would be predicted based on cardiac mitochondria data (Gomes et al., 2014). Under Ca²⁺ challenge, Alda-1 should increase the threshold for MPT and reduce cytochrome c release; in intact RPE, Alda-1 should maintain Δψm under oxidative stress (e.g., blue light, NaIO₃, HOHA lactone), paralleling hepatocyte in vivo imaging under APAP (Gomes et al., 2014; Wimborne et al., 2020). At the biochemical level, 4-HNE-protein adduct quantification (IHC/ELISA/LC-MS) and protein carbonylation assays should show significant reductions with Alda-1 pretreatment; mitochondrial respiratory chain complex activities may be preserved relative to vehicle under electrophile exposure (Gomes et al., 2014; Cheng, 2019). Downstream stress responses (e.g., ER stress markers such as GRP78, UPR activation; SIRT1 and Nrf2 activity; inflammatory cytokines TNF-α/IL-6) should reflect improved homeostasis, consistent with diabetic retina and MNU data (He et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020). Methodologically, the respiratory chain enzymology and aldehyde reactivity analytics described for RPE systems (e.g., complex I–IV assays in 96-well format, reverse-phase HPLC quantitation of aldehyde scavenging, LC-MS/MS quantitation of aldehyde uptake) are directly applicable to evaluating Alda-1’s effects on mitochondrial function and aldehyde handling in RPE models (Cheng, 2019).

A critical caveat is that ALDH2 distribution within the retina emphasizes Müller cells rather than RPE in available reports, and ALDH2 can be inactivated by high aldehyde levels (>10 µM 4-HNE), implying that the therapeutic window may be constrained under extreme aldehydic stress; Alda-1 is explicitly reported to reduce 4-HNE accessibility to catalytic cysteines and reverse 4-HNE–mediated inhibition, which should mitigate this concern but does not obviate the need to quantify ALDH2 activity and 4-HNE load in RPE during oxidative stress (Karan et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2022). Given that dry AMD pathobiology includes chronic oxidative stress, complement-driven inflammation, lysosomal/lipofuscin pathology, and lipid/protein debris accumulation (drusen), the expected benefit of Alda-1 would likely be most pronounced on the oxidative–aldehydic damage axis (mitochondrial and proteostatic integrity) rather than directly addressing complement or lipid trafficking, suggesting it would be a mechanistically complementary therapy potentially combined with agents targeting other AMD pathways (Chen et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic coherence with AMD pathophysiology: Dry AMD is driven in part by oxidative stress in RPE with accumulation of lipid peroxidation products; ALDH2 is a mitochondrial enzyme that detoxifies 4-HNE/MDA and is susceptible to inactivation by aldehydes, establishing a feed-forward injury loop that Alda-1 is designed to interrupt (Chen et al., 2023; Budas et al., 2009; Karan et al., 2023).  
- Direct mitochondrial mechanism with robust preclinical performance: Alda-1 increases ALDH2 activity, reduces 4-HNE adducts and protein carbonyls, preserves State 3 respiration and RCR, reduces mitochondrial H₂O₂ emission, raises MPT thresholds, and decreases cytochrome c release under chronic aldehydic stress; these endpoints directly match the mitochondrial failure features observed in stressed RPE (Gomes et al., 2014).  
- Retinal in vivo signals: In diabetic and photoreceptor degeneration models, Alda-1 improved ERG, preserved retinal structure, increased SIRT1/Nrf2 signaling, reduced inflammatory cytokines, and diminished ER stress/apoptotic markers, collectively supporting retinal tissue benefit under oxidative stress (He et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020).  
- Protective breadth across organs and insults via aldehyde clearance: Repeated demonstration that Alda-1 reduces 4-HNE accumulation and preserves mitochondrial function in heart, liver, lung, intestine, and neuronal contexts increases confidence that the aldehyde-clearance mechanism is conserved and translatable (Wimborne et al., 2020; Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019).  
- Pharmacogenetic upside: Alda-1 rescues ALDH2*2 activity, suggesting potential efficacy in East Asian ALDH2*2 carriers, a large at-risk population for aldehyde-mediated diseases; this also provides a biomarker-based stratification opportunity in trials (Budas et al., 2009; Kimura et al., 2019).  
- Safety signs in chronic rodent dosing: Six-week daily Alda-1 in naïve rats showed no hemodynamic, biochemical, or organ-weight toxicity, supporting tolerability for longer-term therapy (Gomes et al., 2014).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Lack of dry AMD/RPE-specific data: No direct evidence in RPE-focused dry AMD models (e.g., NaIO₃-induced RPE atrophy, complement dysregulation models, aging-driven GA models) is presented in the context, and ALDH2 expression has not been explicitly demonstrated in RPE here; expression across retina with Müller co-localization and protection in aged retina is encouraging but not definitive for RPE (Karan et al., 2023; Long et al., 2020).  
- Clinical translation gap: No human proof-of-concept for Alda-1 or class; no ALDH2 activator currently in clinical use; ocular PK, distribution, and chronic safety are uncharacterized (Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019).  
- Potential safety concerns: A preclinical report of Alda-1–associated crystalline nephropathy after I/R cautions that formulation, dosing, or off-target deposition may cause tissue-specific toxicity; comprehensive toxicology and formulation work are essential, especially for chronic ocular indications (Jin et al., 2023).  
- Biological complexity and compensatory pathways: Chronic acceleration of aldehyde clearance could theoretically blunt electrophile-mediated adaptive antioxidant signaling (Keap1/Nrf2, PPAR), potentially reducing hormetic protection; the balance of detoxification versus adaptation requires careful evaluation in chronic degenerative settings (Münzel & Daiber, 2018).  
- Enzyme inactivation at high aldehyde loads: ALDH2 is inactivated by >10 µM 4-HNE; although Alda-1 protects ALDH2 from 4-HNE and enhances activity, in extreme aldehydic states therapeutic efficacy might be limited, necessitating combination with upstream ROS control or lipid peroxidation inhibitors (Karan et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2022).  
- Isoform selectivity: Some reports suggest Alda-1 can modulate ALDH1A1 activity, while others report inconclusive cross-activation; off-target activation or inhibition in ocular tissues could have unanticipated effects on retinoid metabolism or cellular differentiation, especially given ALDH1A1’s role in retinaldehyde metabolism and Müller cell biology (Kotraiah et al., 2013; Karan et al., 2023).  
- Delivery challenges: Systemic dosing achieves retinal effects in rodent DR/MNU models, but the optimal route for chronic dry AMD (topical, intravitreal, suprachoroidal, systemic) is unknown; achieving therapeutic mitochondrial concentrations in RPE with acceptable safety will be nontrivial and requires PK/PD studies (Yan et al., 2020; He et al., 2018).

Decision-oriented recommendations  
- Mechanistic validation in human/murine RPE: Quantify ALDH2 mRNA/protein/activity and subcellular localization in primary human RPE and iPSC-RPE; test whether Alda-1 increases ALDH2 activity and protects against 4-HNE–induced ALDH2 inactivation in RPE mitochondria; measure 4-HNE/ACR/MDA adduct load ±Alda-1 under blue-light/NaIO₃/HOHA lactone stress (Karan et al., 2023; Cheng, 2019).  
- Mitochondrial function endpoints in RPE: Using established microplate assays and Seahorse OCR, test Alda-1’s effects on State 3 respiration, RCR, Δψm, H₂O₂ release, CCCP response, MPT susceptibility, and cytochrome c release under aldehydic stress (Gomes et al., 2014; Cheng, 2019).  
- Retinal disease models aligned to dry AMD: Progress to NaIO₃-induced RPE injury, photo-oxidative stress, and aging/complement models relevant to geographic atrophy; evaluate RPE survival, autofluorescent lipofuscin, drusen-like deposits, inflammatory markers, and photoreceptor secondary degeneration with functional readouts (ERG/OCT) under Alda-1 (Chen et al., 2023).  
- Formulation and delivery: Develop ocular formulations (e.g., intravitreal, sustained-release) and conduct ocular PK/PD to quantify RPE mitochondrial exposure; evaluate chronic ocular and systemic safety with renal monitoring given crystalline nephropathy risk (Jin et al., 2023).  
- Biomarkers and patient stratification: Consider ALDH2 genotype (ALDH2*2 carriers), circulating/ocular 4-HNE-adduct biomarkers, and retinal imaging endpoints as stratification and PD markers; Alda-1’s rescue of ALDH2*2 suggests a precision-medicine angle (Budas et al., 2009; Münzel & Daiber, 2018).  
- Combinations: Given AMD’s multifactorial pathobiology, test Alda-1 alongside Nrf2 activators or lipid peroxidation suppressors to determine additive/synergistic effects on RPE resilience while monitoring for suppression of adaptive electrophile signaling (Chen et al., 2023; Münzel & Daiber, 2018).

Overall, Alda-1 presents a mechanistically compelling, enzyme-directed strategy to alleviate aldehyde-driven mitochondrial and proteostatic injury in oxidatively stressed retinal tissues, with in vivo retinal efficacy already demonstrated in DR and photoreceptor degeneration contexts, albeit without RPE-centric dry AMD models to date (He et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020). The totality of evidence across organ systems (cardiac, hepatic) underscores that Alda-1 reliably reduces 4-HNE load and preserves mitochondrial function in vivo—precisely the biology we seek to modulate in RPE for dry AMD—making this candidate worthy of structured, stepwise validation in RPE-specific systems and AMD-relevant models (Gomes et al., 2014; Wimborne et al., 2020). Key risks reside in translational gaps (RPE expression, ocular PK/safety), potential toxicity signals (renal crystalline nephropathy under certain conditions), and the possibility that aldehyde detoxification alone will be insufficient to arrest complex AMD progression without adjunctive modulation of complement, lipid trafficking, or lysosomal pathways (Jin et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). With these caveats, Alda-1 merits advancement to focused preclinical validation for dry AMD, with an emphasis on RPE mitochondrial protection endpoints, aldehyde-adduct burden, and rigorous ocular safety assessment before considering first-in-human studies.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
S1QEL-1.1 is a small synthetic molecule identified as a “suppressor of site IQ electron leak” (S1QEL) that has been developed to target mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production selectively at the quinone‐reaction (IQ) site of Complex I. This compound belongs to a distinct chemical class uncovered through high‐throughput screening efforts of over 635,000 compounds, which yielded two primary structural families: the thiazole‐type S1QEL1 series (of which S1QEL-1.1 is a leading representative) and the piperazine‐type S1QEL2 series (Banba et al., 2019). As a thiazole‐type compound, S1QEL-1.1 was chemically synthesized and subsequently optimized using structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies; derivatives such as S1QEL1.1_D1–D3 were generated to probe the essential chemical features required for function (Banba et al., 2019). In addition, photoaffinity probe derivatives ([125I]S1QEL1.1_PD1 and PD2) have been prepared to map its binding site in Complex I, underscoring both its synthetic tractability and the sophistication of the medicinal chemistry approach used in its development (Banba et al., 2019). As a class, S1QEL compounds have been primarily engineered to modulate mitochondrial ROS by selectively suppressing superoxide production at the IQ site without broad‐spectrum inhibition of electron transfer, a profile that distinguishes them from canonical Complex I inhibitors such as rotenone and piericidin A (Wong et al., 2019). S1QEL-1.1 is commercially available (for example, through Cayman Chemical under catalog number #25658), which not only facilitates its procurement for research but also supports its potential repurposing as a therapeutic candidate—particularly in indications where mitochondrial oxidative stress is regarded as a key pathogenic factor.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, S1QEL compounds have been extensively characterized in biochemical assays using isolated mitochondria and submitochondrial particles. In these studies, S1QEL-1.1 and other members of the class were shown to potently suppress superoxide and hydrogen peroxide production specifically from the IQ site during conditions that favor reverse electron transfer, while sparing forward electron transport and thus preserving overall mitochondrial electron flow and ATP production (Wong et al., 2019). Preclinical studies in in vivo models have demonstrated the protective effects of S1QEL compounds in varied contexts; for instance, stress-induced stem cell hyperplasia in the Drosophila gut was ameliorated by S1QEL application, and in perfused mouse heart preparations, S1QELs reduced ischemia–reperfusion injury (Banba et al., 2019). Although these examples involve cardiac and developmental models, the central concept—that selective suppression of mitochondrial ROS can confer tissue protection—has broad implications for diseases where redox imbalance is a critical driver. Importantly, while there are numerous reports underscoring the utility of S1QELs in modulating mitochondrial ROS in neurons, cardiomyocytes, and skeletal muscle mitochondria (Banba et al., 2019), a direct application of S1QEL-1.1 to ocular disorders such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) has not yet been documented. However, given that dry AMD is characterized by heightened oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where Complex I activity plays a central role in cellular metabolism and survival, the extension of S1QEL-1.1 into this field is a compelling and logical repurposing avenue (Banba et al., 2019).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, S1QEL-1.1 acts by selectively suppressing the production of superoxide at the Complex I IQ site—a major source of mitochondrial ROS under conditions of reverse electron transfer. Mechanistic studies using bovine heart submitochondrial particles have revealed that S1QEL-1.1 achieves its effect by modulating the redox chemistry in the quinone-binding region while leaving the NADH oxidation (and hence overall electron flux) largely intact (Banba et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2019). Detailed photoaffinity labeling studies using radiolabeled derivatives ([125I]S1QEL1.1_PD1 and PD2) have mapped its binding to the ND1 subunit of Complex I, particularly near the matrix-side loop connecting transmembrane helices 5 and 6, which is distinct from the canonical quinone-binding pocket typically occupied by classical inhibitors such as rotenone (Banba et al., 2019). This binding does not fully block electron entry nor does it globally inhibit forward electron transfer, because the inhibitory potency for suppressing ROS generation is approximately 1–2 orders of magnitude lower than that required to inhibit basal respiratory activity (Wong et al., 2019). It has been proposed that the binding of S1QEL-1.1 induces subtle conformational changes in Complex I that reduce the probability of electron leakage to oxygen, thereby diminishing superoxide production without altering the essential catalytic cycle of electron transport. Furthermore, the mechanism is direction-dependent: S1QEL-1.1 exhibits significantly stronger inhibition of reverse electron transfer-associated ROS production than forward electron transfer, a property that has been linked to structural differences in the ND1 subunit that influence the flux of electrons under various bioenergetic states (Banba et al., 2019). Notably, competitive studies have demonstrated that the presence of S1QEL-1.1 reduces the inhibitory potency of established quinone-site inhibitors like piericidin A and rotenone, supporting the concept that S1QEL-1.1 interacts directly with, and alters, the conformation of, the quinone-binding region (Wong et al., 2019). Overall, the mechanism of action of S1QEL-1.1 is a fine modulation of the electron leak in Complex I—targeting the very site responsible for superoxide generation—without compromising the bioenergetic integrity of the mitochondrion (Banba et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2019).

Expected Effect:  
Under the hypothesis proposed by the research team, S1QEL-1.1 is expected to yield significant benefits in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) by acting on the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) mitochondria. In dry AMD, chronic light exposure, along with inflammatory and complement-mediated stress, leads to persistent mitochondrial dysfunction and escalated ROS production. Since the IQ site of Complex I has been identified as a major source of mitochondrial superoxide production—particularly under conditions of reverse electron transfer—S1QEL-1.1 is anticipated to selectively lower ROS output from this critical site in RPE mitochondria, thereby reducing oxidative damage (Wong et al., 2019).  
In a proposed RPE model of chronic light-induced stress, application of S1QEL-1.1 would be expected to attenuate mitochondrial superoxide formation significantly while preserving forward electron flux, NADH oxidation, and overall mitochondrial ATP synthesis. This preservation of bioenergetic function is crucial because the RPE relies on high levels of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation to support essential cellular functions, including the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and the recycling of visual pigments. Precedents for such effects have been documented in cardiomyocyte and neuronal models, where S1QEL-1.1 efficiently reduced ROS without impairing mitochondrial respiration, thereby contributing to tissue protection under stress (Banba et al., 2019).  
At the molecular level, by binding near the matrix side of the ND1 subunit and inducing conformational changes within the quinone-binding region, S1QEL-1.1 is projected to decrease electron leak from Complex I. This reduction in superoxide generation will likely translate into a lower burden of hydrogen peroxide and peroxynitrite formation, thus mitigating oxidative damage to mitochondrial and cellular components. The expected outcome is a protective effect in RPE cells under constant oxidative assault from light exposure and inflammation, ultimately contributing to the slowing or potential halting of dry AMD progression (Banba et al., 2019).  
Given that RPE cells express all key Complex I subunits, including the ND1 subunit that has been implicated as the binding site for S1QEL-1.1, it is reasonable to extrapolate that the expression profile in RPE cells is conducive to the compound’s mechanism of action (Banba et al., 2019). Moreover, because dysfunction of Complex I and excess mitochondrial ROS production are established features of age-related degeneration in the retina, selectively targeting the IQ site with S1QEL-1.1 represents an attractive strategy to restore redox balance and improve cell survival in the RPE (Banba et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
S1QEL-1.1 stands out as a highly promising drug candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration owing to its unique ability to selectively suppress mitochondrial ROS production at the Complex I IQ site without impacting the overall electron transport and ATP production. One of the major strengths of S1QEL-1.1 is its mechanism of action, which has been elegantly elucidated: it binds to a region of the ND1 subunit, distinct from the classical quinone-binding pocket, and modulates the rate constants of electron leak specifically associated with superoxide formation. This allosteric mechanism ensures that while pathological ROS production is curtailed, the critical functions of mitochondria—such as NADH oxidation and ATP synthesis—continue without significant perturbation (Banba et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2019). Such properties are particularly advantageous in the context of dry AMD, where maintaining robust cellular bioenergetics in the RPE is essential to counteract chronic stress from light exposure and inflammation.

Another strength lies in its direction-dependent inhibitory profile. S1QEL-1.1 is capable of exerting a more potent suppression of reverse electron transfer-induced ROS generation compared to forward electron transfer, thereby offering a more refined modulation of mitochondrial activity. This selective action is crucial in tissues such as the RPE that must continuously manage oxidative stress while still performing high levels of metabolic activity (Banba et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2019).

Furthermore, the extensive preclinical evaluation of S1QEL-1.1 in non-ocular tissues—including models of ischemia–reperfusion injury and stress-induced stem cell hyperplasia—provides a robust foundation for its potential repurposing. Although these studies were conducted in cardiac and developmental systems, the underlying principle—that targeted suppression of mitochondrial ROS can mitigate tissue damage—translates well to the pathophysiological mechanisms implicated in dry AMD (Banba et al., 2019).  

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered. The therapeutic candidate has not yet been evaluated in any ocular or retinal models; therefore, its pharmacokinetics, tissue penetration, and long-term safety within the unique microenvironment of the eye remain to be established. The blood–retina barrier poses a significant hurdle for systemically administered compounds, and specialized delivery methods (such as intravitreal injection or targeted nanoparticle formulations) may be required to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE (Banba et al., 2019). Additionally, although S1QEL-1.1 exhibits a favorable profile in isolated mitochondria and other cell types, chronic inhibition of mitochondrial ROS could potentially disrupt normal redox signaling mechanisms that are vital for cellular adaptation and homeostasis. Thus, determining the optimal dosing range that provides maximal protective effect without interfering with physiological signaling is critical (Wong et al., 2019).

Another potential limitation is the narrow therapeutic window in which S1QEL-1.1 operates. Preclinical data indicate that while low concentrations effectively suppress pathological superoxide production, higher concentrations may begin to inhibit forward electron transport, which could be deleterious in energy-demanding tissues like the RPE (Banba et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2019). This necessitates precise dose optimization and comprehensive toxicity studies prior to advancing into clinical trials.

Finally, despite a strong mechanistic rationale and promising biochemical data from non-ocular models, there is still an absence of direct evidence for efficacy in models of dry AMD. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
BGP-15 is a synthetic, small-molecule nicotinic amidoxime/hydroxylamine derivative whose full chemical name is O-(3-piperidino-2-hydroxy-1-propyl) nicotinic amidoxime, typically used as a dihydrochloride salt; it was developed by N-Gene (US/Hungary) and has been described as water-soluble and mitochondria-targeting in preclinical studies (including ocular applications) (Takács et al., 2024; Horváth et al., 2021). Chemically and pharmacologically, BGP-15 belongs to the hydroximic/hydroxylamine acid derivative family originally advanced as membrane-interacting heat-shock response (HSR) co-inducers that remodel cholesterol-enriched plasma membrane rafts, with pleiotropic, cytoprotective effects in stressed tissues (membrane-lipid therapy) (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011). In parallel, the compound has been positioned as a nicotinamide-related, non-carboxamide “NAM analogue” with in vitro mixed-type (noncompetitive) PARP-1 inhibition, though the authors emphasize that in vivo protective effects likely involve additional mechanisms beyond direct PARP blockade because the in vitro inhibitory concentration exceeds achievable systemic levels (Crul et al., 2013). Independent biophysical and cellular studies show BGP-15 partitions into membranes, increases the fluidity of negatively charged lipid species, preserves heat-challenged raft integrity, and activates stress signaling linked to HSP induction; imaging and molecular dynamics support a direct membrane-interacting mode of action (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

Functionally, BGP-15 is best classified as a multifunctional HSP co-inducer and insulin-sensitizing, mitochondria-targeting cytoprotective agent that remodels membrane rafts, enhances the HSF1–HSP axis, and modulates stress and survival signaling (Akt up, JNK/p38 down), while lowering mitochondrial ROS and stabilizing Δψm; importantly, it preferentially acts in stressed cells, an attribute that underpins its safety rationale (Gombos et al., 2011; Sumegi et al., 2017). The compound concentrates in energized mitochondria driven by its delocalized positive charge, with >85–90% uptake into isolated mitochondria under experimental conditions (Sümegi, 2018). Mitochondrial studies consistently localize the dominant ROS-lowering effect to the respiratory chain at complexes I and III, with minimal direct antioxidant chemistry, and only mild uncoupling at millimolar concentrations that is irrelevant at the micromolar doses used in most cell studies (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018).

Crucial nomenclature caveat: a distinct “BGP-15” reported by a different group denotes a calcipotriene-derived vitamin D3 analog with anticancer activity; this vitamin D3 analog is mechanistically and structurally unrelated to the nicotinic amidoxime HSP co-inducer described above (both were labeled “BGP-15” by their respective originators) (Sintov et al., 2013). For the current program, the candidate of interest is the nicotinic amidoxime/hydroxylamine HSP co-inducer (often supplied by N-Gene or commercial chemical vendors under the amidoxime name), not the vitamin D3 analog (Takács et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
BGP-15 and closely related hydroximic/hydroxylamine acid derivatives have an extensive preclinical history across cardiac, neural, hepatic, renal, skeletal muscle, pulmonary, and metabolic models, with multiple mechanistic readouts converging on membrane remodeling, HSR/HSP co-induction, MAPK and Akt pathway modulation, and mitochondrial protection (Sumegi et al., 2017). Cardiovascular protection has been reported in ischemia–reperfusion, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation, with actions that include reduced ROS, preserved mitochondrial function, and Akt activation with suppression of JNK/p38 (Sumegi et al., 2017). In spontaneously hypertensive rats, BGP-15 increased PGC-1α and mitochondrial mass, decreased interstitial fibrosis, increased MKP-1 and reduced p38/JNK phosphorylation, and activated Akt/GSK-3β signaling (Horváth et al., 2021). BGP-15 prevented imatinib cardiotoxicity, protected against cisplatin nephrotoxicity without impairing antitumor efficacy, and mitigated cisplatin/taxol peripheral neuropathy (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). Hepatoprotection against acetaminophen injury via inhibition of caspase-independent cell death has also been documented (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). In pulmonary arterial hypertension and severe muscular dystrophy models, BGP-15 preserved mitochondrial structure and function and slowed disease progression; mechanistically, mitochondrial fusion via OPA1 activation and Akt signaling were implicated (Szabó et al., 2018).

Neuroprotection and mitochondrial rescue have been demonstrated in vitro and in vivo, including reduced neuronal death and improved mitochondrial potential/ROS at axonal branch points, coupled to HSP72 elevation, reduced phospho-JNK/p38, and enhanced Akt/IGF1R signaling (Ohlen et al., 2017). Consistent with its membrane-raft mechanism, BGP-15 increased HSP expression during heat challenge and remodeled cholesterol-rich platforms that gate stress signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

In ophthalmology, BGP-15 has been applied in multiple retinal disease contexts. It was reported retinoprotective in Goto–Kakizaki rats (type 2 diabetes) with functional preservation on ERG, and later shown to improve survival and retinal function long-term in ZDF rats under uncontrolled diabetes, with increased ocular HSP70 and decreased NFκB (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021). Topical ocular delivery using an SBECD-containing eyedrop improved scotopic/photopic a- and b-waves, restored oscillatory potentials, shortened implicit times, and preserved retinal thickness following global ischemia–reperfusion injury in rats (Takács et al., 2024). These ocular data align with the compound’s mitochondrial and HSP co-inducer mechanisms: accumulation in mitochondria, protection against apoptosis/necrosis in oxidative-stress paradigms, and modulation of stress signaling (Takács et al., 2024).

Clinically, BGP-15 has a proof-of-concept randomized, double-blind trial demonstrating dose-dependent improvement of insulin sensitivity in insulin-resistant patients without apparent short-term toxicity; in parallel, human phase II work in olanzapine-induced metabolic disorder also identified BGP-15 as an insulin sensitizer (Crul et al., 2013; Sümegi, 2018). Safety signals from early human studies and the pharmacology of HSP co-inducers (preferential action in stressed cells) support the translational risk profile; however, systemic serum concentrations reported by the developer are low (≤25 nmol/mL), which has implications for target engagement and favors local ocular delivery for retinal indications (Gombos et al., 2011; Sumegi et al., 2017).

To our knowledge based on the supplied corpus, BGP-15 has not been directly tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) patients or canonical dry AMD animal models; however, its retinoprotective efficacy in diabetic retinopathy models and retinal ischemia–reperfusion suggests relevance to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)/photoreceptor stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammation, which are central to dry AMD biology (Takács et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Membrane-lipid therapy and HSP co-induction. BGP-15 partitions into and remodels membrane lipid domains, particularly cholesterol-rich plasma membrane rafts that organize stress sensing and signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). Under heat stress or analogous perturbations, BGP-15 preserves raft integrity and elevates HSP expression; this is associated with activation of Rac1 and modulation of HSF1 acetylation, leading to prolonged HSF1 DNA binding and robust HSP gene induction without causing protein unfolding, a hallmark of HSP “co-inducers” (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). In HSR-defective melanoma cells, BGP-15 significantly rescued raft domain coverage and shifted the size distribution toward larger platforms, coincident with increased hsp25 expression and Rac1-dependent stress signaling (Gombos et al., 2011). Across cell and tissue contexts, BGP-15 increases HSP70/HSPA1A (HSP72), and this HSP gain is causally linked to improved insulin signaling and cytoprotection in stressed cells (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011).

PARP/NAD+/SIRT1/HSF1 axis. Although BGP-15 demonstrates mixed-type (noncompetitive) inhibition of PARP-1 in vitro, the concentrations required exceed typical in vivo exposures, suggesting that PARP pathway effects in vivo are likely downstream of ROS lowering and reduced DNA single-strand breaks that otherwise drive PARP activation (Crul et al., 2013). In stressed cells, BGP-15 reduces PAR levels, which relieves PARP-mediated suppression of MKP-1/Dusp1, thereby inhibiting JNK/p38 activation; reduced PARP activity also preserves NAD+ and SIRT1 activity, which favors a deacetylated, active HSF1 and a stronger HSR (Crul et al., 2013). This mechanistic loop—less ROS, less PARP activation, more MKP-1, less JNK/p38, and better HSP/SIRT1 tone—aligns with the observed anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective phenotypes (Crul et al., 2013).

Mitochondrial enrichment and respiratory chain modulation. Biophysically, BGP-15 carries a delocalized positive charge, accumulates in energized mitochondria (>85–90% uptake in isolated organelles), and at micromolar doses characteristic of cell studies (1–50 µM) lowers mitochondrial ROS predominantly at complexes I and III without significant baseline depolarization of Δψm (Sümegi, 2018; Sumegi et al., 2017). In oxidative or inflammatory challenges, BGP-15 attenuates H₂O₂- and LPS-induced mitochondrial depolarization and reduces mitochondrial superoxide to near-control levels; MitoTEMPO controls confirm mitochondrial origin of the ROS signal (Sumegi et al., 2017). Importantly, the compound exhibits no meaningful direct antioxidant scavenging in cell-free ROS-generating systems, and only displays mild uncoupling at millimolar concentrations—far above the micromolar exposures used in protective assays—supporting a mechanism of respiratory chain modulation rather than redox scavenging (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). Downstream signaling reflects the lowered mitochondrial ROS burden: JNK/p38 activation is reduced, Akt signaling is enhanced, and caspase-independent death pathways are suppressed (Sumegi et al., 2017).

Mitochondrial dynamics, fusion, and biogenesis. Beyond acute ROS control, BGP-15 promotes mitochondrial fusion and preserves cristae architecture by activating OPA1 GTPase and promoting OPA1 polymerization; genetic suppression of OPA1 or Mfn1/Mfn2 abolishes the fusion phenotype, indicating that BGP-15 acts upstream or within the endogenous fusion machinery (Szabó et al., 2018). In vivo, these effects translate into improved mitochondrial ultrastructure and tissue histology under ROS stress (e.g., monocrotaline-induced PAH) (Szabó et al., 2018). Insulin-sensitizing stress signaling. In skeletal muscle and human studies, BGP-15 increases HSP72 expression, enhances insulin receptor autophosphorylation (blocking JNK inhibitory phosphorylation), activates RAC1, increases AKT phosphorylation, promotes GLUT4 translocation, increases membrane fluidity, raises AMPK activity, and reduces HSF1 acetylation, altogether improving glucose disposal without overt toxicity in a randomized trial (Crul et al., 2013). On balance, the mechanistic breadth that often complicates development is an advantage in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction, proteostasis failure, and chronic inflammation coexist.
