Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SRT2104 is a second‐generation synthetic small molecule activator of SIRT1 that emerged from a rigorous high‐throughput screening program at Sirtris Pharmaceuticals and was further developed following GlaxoSmithKline’s acquisition of the compound’s intellectual property (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 1–2). The molecule was rationally designed by modifying an imidazo[1,2‐b]thiazole core structure, a strategy intended to overcome the limitations associated with earlier SIRT1 activators such as resveratrol, notably its poor bioavailability and off‐target effects (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; 14–16). As a member of the class of SIRT1 activators, SRT2104 is distinguished by its high specificity and potency, thereby enabling a more targeted modulation of NAD⁺‐dependent deacetylation pathways compared to naturally occurring polyphenols (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16). This class of compounds has been broadly investigated in the context of metabolic, inflammatory, and neurodegenerative disorders due to its capacity to enhance mitochondrial function, reduce oxidative stress, and modulate inflammatory cytokines (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; 10–11). Although its initial therapeutic intent was not directed toward ophthalmological conditions, mechanistic insights into SIRT1’s regulatory functions in cellular metabolism and stress responses have prompted interest in repurposing SRT2104 for conditions such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells play central roles (Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4; Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2).

Therapeutic History:  
Extensive preclinical and early‐phase clinical studies have established a strong safety and tolerability profile for SRT2104, particularly in elderly populations and subjects with type 2 diabetes (Libri et al., 2012, pp. 1–2; Baksi et al., 2014, pp. 7–11). In a pilot randomized, placebo‐controlled trial, SRT2104 was administered to healthy elderly volunteers, demonstrating that the compound was generally well tolerated, with an average peak serum concentration reached within 2 to 4 hours and an elimination half‐life between 15 and 20 hours (Libri et al., 2012, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, studies involving participants on metformin therapy for type 2 diabetes confirmed that SRT2104 exhibits a favorable safety profile, noting stable pharmacokinetics and no serious adverse events over an extended dosing period (Baksi et al., 2014, pp. 7–11). Beyond safety, several clinical studies have reported beneficial effects on metabolic biomarkers: SRT2104 administration was associated with significant reductions in serum cholesterol, low‐density lipoprotein (LDL), and triglyceride levels, suggesting improvements in systemic metabolic health (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 1–2). Additional clinical investigations indicated that adverse reactions—when they occurred—were generally mild and self‐limiting, including transient headaches, dizziness, and mild upper respiratory indications, which further supports its clinical tolerability (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 13–14; 2–4).  
SRT2104 has also been evaluated in the context of neurodegenerative processes; preclinical models demonstrated its ability to cross the blood‐brain barrier and exert neuroprotective effects, for example, in Huntington’s disease models where improvements in survival and motor function were observed along with reduced cerebral atrophy (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 6–7; 7–8). Although none of these studies were primarily focused on dry AMD or similar ocular pathologies, the therapeutic rationale for exploring SRT2104 in AMD is supported by the shared pathophysiological features observed in neurodegenerative disorders and retinal diseases, particularly those aspects involving mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2). It is important to note that while there is substantial clinical evidence for metabolic and neuroprotective effects, no direct clinical trials have yet been conducted in patients with dry AMD, making a translational validation in the specific context of retinal diseases an essential next step (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 14–16).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SRT2104 acts predominantly by binding to and activating SIRT1, a NAD⁺‐dependent histone deacetylase that plays a pivotal role in regulating transcription, cellular metabolism, and stress responses (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16). SIRT1 deacetylates a variety of substrates, including transcription factors such as peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator 1‐alpha (PGC-1α) and factors involved in inflammation such as the NF-κB complex. The deacetylation of PGC-1α is particularly significant because it leads to its activation, thereby enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis and promoting oxidative metabolism (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16). As a consequence, activation of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis results in increased expression of genes involved in antioxidant defense, thus improving cellular resilience to oxidative stress—a key pathological driver in dry AMD (Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4; Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2).  
Moreover, SIRT1 has been shown to deacetylate and modulate the activity of hypoxia‐inducible factor 2α (HIF-2α), which in turn regulates the vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A) promoter (Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4). Given that VEGF-A plays a complex role in retinal homeostasis and neovascular processes, this interaction suggests that SIRT1 activation could fine‐tune vascular responses within the retina. In addition to these effects, SRT2104 has been associated with decreases in pro‐inflammatory cytokine levels including IL-6 and IL-8, thereby potentially mitigating chronic inflammation that contributes to RPE dysfunction and geographic atrophy in AMD (Law et al., 2024, pp. 10–12; Chang et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
It is also noteworthy that SIRT1 is endogenously expressed in human RPE cells and the retina, where it contributes to the maintenance of cellular homeostasis in response to oxidative insults (Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4). In several disease models, suppressed SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling has been linked to mitochondrial disintegration and increased susceptibility to oxidative damage in RPE cells, supporting the therapeutic hypothesis that pharmacologically enhancing SIRT1 activity can restore mitochondrial function and counteract degenerative changes (Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2; 11–13). In summary, the molecular actions of SRT2104 encompass the dual benefits of enhancing mitochondrial respiration via PGC-1α activation and reducing inflammatory mediator production through deacetylation of relevant transcription factors, which together may yield protective effects in the context of dry AMD (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 14–16; 7–8).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underlying the proposed repurposing of SRT2104 for dry AMD is that oral administration of this compound will enhance SIRT1 activity in RPE cells, thereby activating downstream signaling pathways critical to cellular homeostasis (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16). Specifically, increased SIRT1 activity is anticipated to lead to upregulation of PGC-1α, a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis, as well as NRF2, a central transcription factor in the antioxidant defense pathway (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16). As PGC-1α activation drives the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial metabolism and energy production, its upregulation is expected to ameliorate mitochondrial dysfunction—a hallmark feature in the pathogenesis of geographic atrophy within dry AMD (Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4; Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2).  
Furthermore, NRF2 activation is associated with enhanced transcription of a battery of antioxidant enzymes, which can reduce the burden of reactive oxygen species (ROS) that damage RPE cells over time (Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2; 11–13). These biochemical changes are hypothesized to restore the redox balance within RPE cells, thereby slowing or potentially reversing the progression of retinal degeneration observed in dry AMD. In experimental models of metabolic stress, SRT2104 has been shown to improve mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and cellular viability; by extension, similar molecular benefits are anticipated in the RPE, where oxidative damage and mitochondrial dysfunction play crucial roles in disease progression (Libri et al., 2012, pp. 1–2; Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).  
Additionally, given SIRT1’s regulatory role in suppressing pro‐inflammatory gene expression via NF-κB deacetylation, it is expected that SRT2104 will confer anti‐inflammatory effects within the retinal microenvironment, further contributing to the preservation of RPE function (Law et al., 2024, pp. 10–12; Maugeri et al., 2018, pp. 5–7). Although these effects have been robustly documented in systemic tissues such as skeletal muscle and in neuronal models, confirmation in ocular tissues remains a critical area for future preclinical investigation (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 14–16; 6–7). The convergence of improved mitochondrial dynamics, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and reduced inflammatory activity forms the foundational rationale for expecting that SRT2104 can stabilize or restore RPE function, thereby mitigating the development and progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2).

Overall Evaluation:  
SRT2104 presents a compelling candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD given its well‐established safety profile, its potent and selective activation of SIRT1, and the strong mechanistic rationale connecting SIRT1‐mediated pathways to the pathological processes underlying retinal degeneration (Libri et al., 2012, pp. 1–2; Baksi et al., 2014, pp. 7–11; Chang et al., 2024, pp. 13–14). These studies have consistently shown that SRT2104 can be administered with minimal adverse effects, and its pharmacokinetic profile (with rapid absorption and a reasonable half‐life) supports its potential for chronic dosing—an important consideration in the management of a progressive condition like dry AMD (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; 2–4).  
Another significant strength lies in the drug’s mechanism of action: by directly activating SIRT1, SRT2104 engages a fundamental regulator of cellular metabolism that is known to control mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses through the deacetylation of PGC-1α and subsequent NRF2‐mediated gene transcription (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16). Given that mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central drivers of RPE cell degeneration, this targeted mechanism offers a rational therapeutic approach to address the pathophysiological underpinnings of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4; Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2). Preclinical studies in neurodegenerative models further bolster confidence in the neuroprotective aspects of SRT2104, suggesting that similar protective effects might be translated to the retinal environment (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 6–7; 7–8).  
Despite these strengths, several challenges and weaknesses warrant careful consideration. Foremost, there is currently an absence of direct preclinical or clinical data evaluating the efficacy of SRT2104 in ocular models of dry AMD. While the shared molecular pathways between skeletal muscle, neuronal tissue, and RPE cells provide a strong theoretical basis for its repurposing, it remains to be demonstrated experimentally that SRT2104 can adequately penetrate the ocular tissues—in particular, the retina—and reach effective concentrations in the RPE (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 14–16; Hammer et al., 2021, pp. 9–11). The blood‐retina barrier poses unique pharmacokinetic challenges that may not be addressed by data derived solely from systemic administration in non‐ocular tissues.  
Another concern is the translational gap between improvements in biochemical markers and tangible clinical outcomes. For example, while clinical trials in systemic conditions have shown reductions in LDL cholesterol, arterial stiffness, and improvements in mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, similar functional endpoints related to retinal health such as visual acuity or structural preservation of the RPE have not been measured (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; 9–10). This gap underscores the necessity for rigorously designed preclinical models using human RPE cells and animal models of geographic atrophy to ascertain whether the SIRT1 activation by SRT2104 indeed translates into meaningful protection against retinal degeneration (Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2; 2–3).  
There is also the issue of potential off‐target effects or insufficient modulation of the complex interplay between oxidative stress, inflammation, and cellular senescence observed in dry AMD. Although SRT2104’s target specificity is a marked improvement over earlier SIRT1 activators, the multifactorial nature of AMD pathology—including contributions from inflammatory cytokine cascades and abnormal autophagic processes—may require combination therapies or adjunctive strategies beyond SIRT1 activation alone (Maugeri et al., 2018, pp. 5–7).  
Furthermore, some clinical studies have suggested that despite positive modulation of certain biomarkers, SRT2104 may not significantly improve key functional endpoints such as vascular reactivity or insulin sensitivity, suggesting that its efficacy might be context‐dependent or limited to particular physiological systems (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). Although these findings do not directly detract from its potential in AMD, they do highlight the inherent risk in extrapolating systemic benefits to the specialized microenvironment of the retina.  
In summary, while SRT2104 exhibits a strong safety record and a mechanistically robust profile through its activation of SIRT1 and downstream enhancement of mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant capacity, its repurposing as a treatment for dry AMD remains a hypothesis that requires extensive further validation. Key areas for future research include detailed pharmacokinetic studies to ensure adequate ocular tissue penetration, validation of its effects on RPE cell survival and function in both in vitro and in vivo models of geographic atrophy, and ultimately, early‐phase clinical trials designed specifically to evaluate retinal outcomes (Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2; Chang et al., 2024, pp. 14–16). By addressing these gaps, it will be possible to determine whether the encouraging data from metabolic and neurodegenerative indications can indeed be translated into a viable therapeutic strategy for patients with dry AMD.  
In conclusion, SRT2104 is a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate given its ability to activate SIRT1—a key mediator of mitochondrial and antioxidant pathways—in a manner that holds potential to restore RPE function and counteract the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16; Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4). Its clinical safety profile and documented efficacy in modulating systemic metabolic and inflammatory markers provide a favorable foundation for further investigation. However, its application in the ocular arena must overcome several translational barriers, including establishing effective ocular bioavailability and demonstrating specific efficacy in retinal cell models. These challenges underscore the need for targeted preclinical and clinical research to confirm whether SRT2104 can fulfill its therapeutic promise in the context of dry AMD.

────────────────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

SB 290157 is a synthetic small‐molecule compound that functions as an antagonist of the C3a receptor (C3aR). Chemically, it is defined as N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine, a structure that incorporates an arginine residue with an acyl modification incorporating a 2,2-diphenylethoxy moiety (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). SB 290157 was discovered through high-throughput screening efforts aimed at identifying molecules capable of displacing radiolabeled C3a from its receptor. Early screening identified a lead compound that underwent extensive chemical optimization – including solid-phase peptide and peptidomimetic synthesis using Fmoc‐based chemistry on Wang resin – to yield SB 290157 (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011). This synthetic approach, employing coupling reagents such as 1-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)-3-ethylcarbodiimide hydrochloride and 4-dimethylaminopyridine, resulted in a non-peptide molecule designed to maximize receptor affinity while minimizing metabolic instability. The compound is commercially available from suppliers such as Cayman Chemical (catalog #10006619) and has served as a prototypic small-molecule C3aR antagonist in numerous preclinical studies (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017).

SB 290157 falls within the broader class of synthetic GPCR modulators that target complement receptors. Historically, such molecules have been exploited as biochemical tools to interrogate the role of anaphylatoxins in inflammatory responses (Ames et al., 2001). C3a, a 77-residue protein fragment produced during complement activation, is recognized by its GPCR, C3aR, and triggers diverse cellular responses (Ames et al., 2001). Multiple research groups have employed small-molecule antagonists like SB 290157 to elucidate the contribution of C3a-mediated signaling in conditions ranging from arthritis to lung inflammation (Ames et al., 2001). The compound’s synthetic origin and chemical tractability have allowed investigators to probe receptor pharmacology in heterologous cell lines (e.g., RBL-C3aR cells, ARPE-19 cells) and primary human cell systems (Ames et al., 2001). In the context of ocular research, SB 290157 has been used experimentally in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) models – particularly in primary human fetal RPE cultures – to block C3a-induced alterations in extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

Beyond its established utility as a research tool, the use of SB 290157 in ocular models speaks to an emerging rationale for targeting complement signaling in degenerative eye diseases. Its inclusion in a commercial catalog further underscores its ready availability to laboratories, enabling reproducibility and fostering further experimentation. In summary, SB 290157 is a synthetic, non-peptide, arginine-based antagonist belonging to a class of compounds that have historically been used to interrogate complement receptor signaling, with a well-defined chemical structure, known synthesis protocols, and broad preclinical application in inflammation research (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

SB 290157 has a storied history in the complement research field. Its initial characterization, as detailed by Ames and colleagues, revealed that SB 290157 competes for C3a binding with an IC₅₀ in the high‐nanomolar range (approximately 200 nM) and potently inhibits C3a-induced intracellular calcium mobilization in sensitive cell lines, such as RBL cells and human neutrophils (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Early studies validated its functional capacity as a selective antagonist in vitro, establishing that it effectively blocked receptor internalization and attenuated downstream signaling events elicited by C3a binding.

Preclinically, SB 290157 has been deployed in a wide range of experimental disease models. For instance, it has been used in animal studies examining anti-inflammatory activity in models such as guinea pig LPS-induced airway neutrophilia and adjuvant-induced arthritis in rats. In the arthritis model, administration of SB 290157 resulted in a significant reduction (approximately 41%) in paw edema, while in airway inflammation models it suppressed neutrophil recruitment, demonstrating its anti-inflammatory efficacy (Ames et al., 2001). These early demonstrations of anti-inflammatory activity provided the impetus to consider SB 290157 for further repurposing in conditions where complement overactivation contributes to pathology.

More recently, attention has turned to the role of complement in ocular diseases, particularly age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Experimental evidence in primary human fetal RPE cultures has shown that exposure to recombinant C3a for periods of 2–4 weeks results in the accumulation of sub-RPE deposits via increased ECM deposition, notably of collagens (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Importantly, co-treatment with a C3a receptor antagonist – which in many instances has been SB 290157 – successfully prevented the abnormal accumulation of sub-RPE deposits. These studies have helped establish a mechanistic link between C3a/C3aR activation and the proteostasis dysfunction observed in RPE cells, a pathological process believed to contribute to early AMD pathology.

In addition to in vitro data, in vivo models provide further support for the therapeutic potential of modulating C3aR signaling. In a murine model of sodium iodate (NaIO₃)-induced RPE injury – a model that recapitulates aspects of geographic atrophy – systemic administration of SB 290157 reduced photoreceptor death, decreased markers of gliosis and microglial activation, and lowered TNFα and STAT3 signaling levels (Wang et al., 2020). Similarly, in a laser-induced retinal vein occlusion (RVO) model, intravitreal injection of SB 290157 suppressed the up-regulation of both C3 and C3a receptor expression, correlating with partial rescue of retinal morphology and vascular integrity (Zhao et al., 2025). Although these studies were not specifically designed for dry AMD, the similarities in underlying complement-mediated RPE injury and chronic inflammation between these models and the dry AMD phenotype provide a strong rationale for further exploring SB 290157 in this indication.

Despite these promising applications, SB 290157’s therapeutic history is not without controversy. Several studies have reported that, depending on the cell type and receptor density, SB 290157 may exhibit partial agonist activity rather than acting as a pure antagonist (Mathieu et al., 2005). This variable pharmacological profile has raised concerns about its utility as a definitive clinical tool. Nonetheless, as a research probe, SB 290157 has significantly advanced our understanding of complement-mediated cellular responses in inflammatory, vascular, and ocular contexts. Overall, while it has been extensively used in preclinical studies across multiple disease models – including arthritis, lung inflammation, and retinal injury – its use specifically in clinical settings for dry AMD remains investigational (Ames et al., 2001; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Wang et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action

SB 290157 exerts its biological effects by competitively binding to the C3a receptor (C3aR), thereby preventing the interaction of endogenous C3a with its receptor. Under normal conditions, the complement cascade, when activated via any of its pathways, leads to the cleavage of complement component C3 and the subsequent release of the anaphylatoxin C3a. This bioactive peptide binds to C3aR, a G protein-coupled receptor present on various cell types including granulocytes, monocytes, and notably retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Once activated, C3aR transduces signals that can lead to intracellular calcium mobilization, triggering a cascade of downstream events such as receptor internalization and activation of inflammatory transcription factors.

In vitro studies using radioligand binding assays have determined that SB 290157 displaces [¹²⁵I]-C3a from its receptor with an IC₅₀ in the high nanomolar range (approximately 200 nM), while functional calcium mobilization assays in cell lines (including RBL cells and human neutrophils) have demonstrated potent inhibition of C3a-stimulated intracellular calcium release at low nanomolar concentrations (approximately 28 nM) (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Mechanistically, by preventing C3a from engaging C3aR, the compound is able to avert subsequent receptor conformational changes that would otherwise lead to G protein coupling and downstream signaling events.

In the context of RPE cells, particularly under conditions of chronic oxidative stress – such as exposure to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) – C3a engagement of its receptor has been implicated in a range of deleterious cellular effects. Studies in ARPE-19 cells have shown that oxidative stress induces a redistribution of C3aR away from its typical plasma membrane localization and promotes its translocation toward the mitochondria (Ishii et al., 2021; Riihilä et al., 2019). At the mitochondrial level, activation of the receptor by C3a leads to an increase in mitochondrial calcium uptake, which in turn results in compromised respiratory function as evidenced by decreased state III (ADP-driven) respiration and reduced maximal respiratory capacity (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). The resultant mitochondrial dysfunction is highly likely to contribute to the generation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS). mtROS are known triggers for the NLRP3 inflammasome, which upon activation facilitates the processing of pro-IL-1β to active IL-1β, a cytokine strongly implicated in chronic inflammatory processes observed in AMD (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024).

Furthermore, in primary human fetal RPE models, prolonged exposure to recombinant C3a has been demonstrated to reduce the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (UPP) without altering mRNA levels for proteasome subunits, indicating a post-transcriptional impairment of proteostasis (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). First, it prevents the mitochondrial translocation and activation of C3aR in oxidatively stressed ARPE-19 cells, which is predicted to avert the associated mitochondrial calcium overload and respiratory inhibition, thereby reducing the likelihood of mtROS generation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). It is important to note, however, that while the majority of evidence supports SB 290157 acting as an effective C3aR antagonist, several reports have cautioned that under certain conditions, the compound may display partial agonist activity. This means that rather than completely blocking receptor activation, SB 290157 might induce a low level of receptor signaling in some cellular contexts, especially when receptor density is high (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001). Such an effect must be carefully considered when interpreting experimental outcomes and when designing therapeutic strategies aimed at persistent modulation of complement activity. In all, the known mechanism of action for SB 290157 can be summarized as competitive inhibition of C3a binding to C3aR, thereby mitigating the downstream signals that lead to mitochondrial calcium dysregulation, proteasome impairment, ECM deposition abnormalities, and ultimately, NLRP3 inflammasome priming and IL-1β secretion (Ames et al., 2001; Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect

The central hypothesis underlying the use of SB 290157 in repurposing for dry AMD is that the blockade of C3aR will attenuate a cascade of deleterious events within the retinal pigment epithelium that contribute to disease progression. In particular, the expected effect is that SB 290157 will reduce complement-driven mitochondrial dysfunction, lower mtROS production, and thereby prevent the priming and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, resulting ultimately in diminished IL-1β secretion and preservation of RPE barrier integrity.

In dry AMD, chronic oxidative stress leads to dysregulated complement activation and subsequent accumulation of complement fragments such as C3a in the subretinal space. RPE cells under oxidative stress have been demonstrated to upregulate C3aR expression, with a portion of the receptor redistributing to the mitochondria—a change that is associated with an increased uptake of calcium into the mitochondria and a pronounced decline in mitochondrial respiratory function (Ishii et al., 2021; Riihilä et al., 2019). The resulting mitochondrial dysfunction is poised to increase the generation of mtROS, which serve as an upstream activator of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Activation of this inflammasome complex culminates in the maturation of IL-1β, a powerful proinflammatory cytokine that has been implicated in propagating RPE injury and the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024).

By competitively inhibiting C3a binding to its receptor, SB 290157 is expected to block these deleterious changes. In cultured ARPE-19 cells—which serve as a well-established model for human RPE—it is anticipated that SB 290157 will prevent the mitochondrial translocation of C3aR, thereby reducing abnormal mitochondrial calcium uptake and preserving normal respiration. This action should limit mtROS generation and consequently reduce the priming threshold for NLRP3 inflammasome activation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). Concurrently, in primary fetal RPE cultures, inhibition of C3aR signaling by SB 290157 has been shown to preserve the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, which in turn maintains the balance of matrix metalloproteinases and their tissue inhibitors. By doing so, the compound prevents the accumulation of sub-RPE deposits—a process that is intimately linked to the early phases of AMD pathology (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

The expression of C3aR in RPE cells, particularly in stressed conditions, is well-documented. This receptor is notably enriched on the basolateral membrane of RPE and even redistributes to mitochondrial compartments under oxidative stress conditions, as confirmed in ARPE-19 cell studies (Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Given that dry AMD is characterized by both heightened complement activation and chronic oxidative stress, the strategic inhibition of C3aR is expected to yield multiple beneficial outcomes: restoration of proteostasis, maintenance of mitochondrial function, reduction in chronic inflammatory cytokine expression, and preservation of the integrity and barrier function of the RPE monolayer. Moreover, in in vivo models such as NaIO₃-induced RPE injury or laser-induced retinal vein occlusion, treatment with a C3aR antagonist (presumably SB 290157) has been associated with reduced photoreceptor loss, attenuated microglial activation, and improved retinal morphology (Wang et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2025).

Furthermore, because mitochondrial reactive oxygen species serve as a trigger for the NLRP3 inflammasome, blocking the upstream signal via C3aR inhibition is hypothesized to break the vicious cycle of complement-mediated inflammation. The decreased activation of NLRP3 would lead to lower levels of IL-1β—a cytokine implicated in the autocrine and paracrine amplification of inflammation within the RPE layer—and thus stabilize the local microenvironment (Ong et al., 2024; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In summary, the expected effect of SB 290157 in the context of dry AMD is multifold: preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics, maintenance of proteasomal activity, prevention of pathological ECM accumulation, and attenuation of inflammasome-mediated inflammatory responses—all of which contribute to the protection of RPE integrity and function.

────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

SB 290157 stands out as one of the best-studied C3a receptor antagonists available today. Its well-documented chemical synthesis, robust in vitro pharmacological profile, and demonstrable efficacy in preclinical models of inflammatory injury provide strong support for its continued evaluation as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. The compound’s origins – as a product of high-throughput screening followed by medicinal chemistry optimization using Fmoc-solid phase techniques – are well established, and its chemical structure (N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine) clearly classifies it as a small-molecule non-peptide antagonist of a key complement receptor (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011).

Strengths of SB 290157 include its proven ability to block C3a-induced signaling cascades across a range of cell types and experimental models. Preclinical studies in RPE cells indicate that it can prevent C3a-induced sub-RPE deposit formation and proteasome impairment—a finding directly relevant to the early pathological events of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Additionally, evidence from ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress suggests that SB 290157 effectively inhibits aberrant mitochondrial Ca²⁺ uptake and consequent respiratory dysfunction—mechanisms known to contribute to mtROS generation and inflammasome activation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). In vivo, its administration in models of retinal injury (such as NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration and laser-induced retinal vein occlusion) has correlated with reduced photoreceptor death, decreased gliosis, and improved retinal architecture (Wang et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2025). These findings collectively underscore the compound’s potential to modulate complement-mediated pathology in the ocular setting.

Nonetheless, SB 290157 is not without its weaknesses. A significant concern noted across several studies is its variable pharmacological behavior. Under some experimental conditions, particularly in cell systems with high receptor density, SB 290157 exhibits partial agonist activity rather than pure antagonism (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001). This paradoxical behavior could lead to unintended receptor activation and potentially undermine its therapeutic benefit, especially in chronic conditions like dry AMD where long-term receptor blockade is desired. Furthermore, while there is compelling preclinical evidence supporting its beneficial impact on mitochondrial function and ECM homeostasis, direct experimental data linking SB 290157 to a reduction in mitochondrial ROS production and consequent suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation in ARPE-19 or primary RPE models remain incomplete or indirect (Wang et al., 2020; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Behnke, 2022). This gap in the literature necessitates further investigation to firmly establish the causal chain from C3aR inhibition to inflammasome modulation.

Another consideration is the translational challenge. SB 290157 has been predominantly utilized as a research tool rather than a clinical candidate. Its pharmacokinetic profile—while adequate for short-term animal experiments—has not been thoroughly characterized for long-term use in ocular applications, where issues such as retinal toxicity, ocular bioavailability, and sustained receptor occupancy become critical. The delicate environment of the retina requires highly specific and safe compounds; thus, the partial agonist activity and potential off-target effects of SB 290157 raise valid concerns regarding its safety profile in humans (Mathieu et al., 2005; Tan et al., 2024).

Conversely, its partial agonist behavior in certain systems and the current lack of direct evidence linking its action to reduced mtROS and NLRP3 activation in ocular models raise legitimate concerns that must be addressed prior to clinical translation (Mathieu et al., 2005; Behnke, 2022).

Overall, SB 290157 is a compelling candidate for further exploration and mechanistic validation as a repurposed drug for dry AMD, provided that additional research can surmount the challenges associated with its pharmacodynamic variability and confirm its protective effects in retina-specific models.

────────────────────────────────────────  
Conclusion

The comprehensive literature evaluation indicates that SB 290157’s synthetic origins, established use as a C3aR antagonist, and demonstrated efficacy in preclinical models of complement-mediated RPE injury make it a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its mechanism—blocking C3a-induced signaling that otherwise leads to mitochondrial calcium overload, impaired proteostasis, and subsequent inflammasome activation—is highly relevant to the pathophysiology of geographic atrophy. However, the compound’s documented partial agonist effects and potential variability in receptor blockade require careful consideration and further optimization. Additional studies are necessary to firmly establish that SB 290157 can reduce mitochondrial ROS and suppress NLRP3 inflammasome activation in RPE cells under conditions that model dry AMD clinically. Thus, while SB 290157 is an excellent tool for dissecting the complement–mitochondria crosstalk in dry AMD, its suitability as a long-term therapeutic will depend on resolving these outstanding issues through rigorous preclinical and mechanistic evaluation (Ames et al., 2001; Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Mathieu et al., 2005).

Overall, the candidate shows substantial promise as a mechanistic probe and potential therapeutic agent for dry AMD; its ability to block key complement-mediated events that contribute to RPE dysfunction and inflammation positions it as a novel target for drug development. However, given the documented limitations, further studies are strongly recommended to optimize its receptor selectivity, define its pharmacokinetic and safety profile in the ocular context, and conclusively demonstrate its capacity to mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammasome activation in relevant models before advancing it into clinical trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10), also known as ubiquinone, is a naturally occurring lipophilic molecule synthesized endogenously via the mevalonate pathway. It is a quinone class compound that was originally discovered as a crucial component of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) and is essential for adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production. Chemically, CoQ10 contains a benzoquinone ring and a long isoprenoid side chain, which confers its lipid solubility and allows integration into mitochondrial and other cellular membranes. As a therapeutic candidate, it is available commercially (e.g., Cayman Chemical #700105) as a pure formulation that can be used for research purposes and has been repurposed in several settings to address oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Its widespread use as a dietary supplement and as an adjunct therapy in cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and metabolic disorders underlines the extensive clinical experience with this class of compounds. The rationale for its repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is based on the compound’s natural role as a coenzyme, its potent antioxidant properties, and its ability to modulate mitochondrial energy metabolism—all of which are critically compromised in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) of the aging eye (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Maiuolo et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past decades, CoQ10 has been evaluated in multiple experimental and clinical contexts. Biochemical studies have consistently demonstrated its ability to protect mitochondrial structure and function by facilitating electron transport and scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS). In vitro, CoQ10 treatments have been shown to improve mitochondrial respiration and ATP production in various cell types, including ARPE-19 cells, a widely used human RPE model. These studies utilized oxidative stress challenges (e.g., H₂O₂ exposure) to simulate conditions similar to those present in dry AMD, and showed that CoQ10 supplementation lowered levels of apoptotic markers such as caspase-3 and TUNEL staining, effectively reducing cell death (Hernandez et al., 2024). In the clinical arena, several studies have explored the use of CoQ10, sometimes in combination with other nutritional compounds, for early stages of AMD. For instance, combination therapies incorporating CoQ10 with agents such as acetyl-L-carnitine and n-3 fatty acids have resulted in improvements in visual function and fundus appearance among early AMD patients, demonstrating its potential impact in slowing disease progression (Feher et al., 2005). Moreover, its established safety profile in chronic use and its history of use as a metabolic booster and antioxidant in various degenerative conditions further support its potential repurposing for dry AMD, where similar mitochondrial and oxidative stress mechanisms underlie disease pathology (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Kiliç, 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, CoQ10 exhibits a dual mechanism of action that is highly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Firstly, it functions as an obligatory electron carrier within mitochondria. In the ETC, CoQ10 shuttles electrons from complexes I (NADH dehydrogenase) and II (succinate dehydrogenase) to complex III (cytochrome bc₁ complex), thereby driving the proton gradient needed for ATP synthesis by ATP synthase. Its redox-active benzoquinone ring is capable of reversible oxidation and reduction, enabling it to accept and donate electrons during the process of cellular respiration (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Hernandez et al., 2024). This electron-transfer activity is critical in tissues with high metabolic demands such as the retina, where the maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (mt∆ψ) and ATP production are indispensable for cell survival. A second and equally important aspect of CoQ10’s mechanism is its potent antioxidant property. Through its reduced form, ubiquinol, CoQ10 directly scavenges free radicals and prevents lipid peroxidation of cell membranes. This antioxidant activity extends to the regeneration of other lipid-soluble antioxidants such as vitamin E, thereby reinforcing a broader cellular antioxidant defense network (Manzar et al., 2020; Hernandez et al., 2024).

In the context of RPE cells, the protective effects of CoQ10 extend to the stabilization of mitochondrial proteins and prevention of oxidative damage-induced mtDNA release. Notably, CoQ10 has been shown to modulate the expression of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase-2 (SOD2), which further contributes to the reduction of intracellular ROS levels. Additionally, CoQ10 influences mitochondrial dynamics by reducing the activation of pro-fission proteins like DRP-1, thereby inhibiting excessive mitochondrial fragmentation—a phenomenon that has been associated with increased apoptosis in oxidative stress conditions (Hernandez et al., 2024). Its capacity to dampen inflammatory mediators, including the restoration of cytokines such as TNFα and caspase-1 to their baseline levels following oxidative insult, underscores its role in mitigating the inflammatory cascades implicated in AMD pathology (Hernandez et al., 2024). These combined actions—preservation of electron transport efficiency, reduction in ROS-mediated damage, and stabilization of mitochondrial integrity—are central to the hypothesis that exogenous supplementation of CoQ10 can counteract the underlying cellular stress mechanisms in dry AMD (Hernandez et al., 2024; Maiuolo et al., 2022).

Given the proposed experimental approach—using H₂O₂-challenged ARPE-19 cells as a model to simulate oxidative stress encountered in dry AMD—the expected effect of exogenous CoQ10 supplementation would be multi-fold. The repletion of CoQ10 levels would counteract the age-associated decline in endogenous CoQ10 and restore mitochondrial membrane potential, which is critical for normal cell metabolism (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Maiuolo et al., 2022). Secondly, due to its antioxidant properties, CoQ10 is anticipated to directly scavenge ROS generated by H₂O₂ exposure, thereby reducing oxidative lipid peroxidation and preventing damage to mitochondrial membranes and proteins. As a result, key apoptotic markers—such as caspase-3 activity and TUNEL-positive cell counts—should be decreased, reflecting improved cell viability and reduced progression toward cell death (Hernandez et al., 2024).

The comprehensive review of the literature provides strong mechanistic rationale and preclinical evidence to support the repurposing of CoQ10 for dry AMD. One of the primary strengths of CoQ10 as a candidate is its dual role—facilitating electron transport and exerting antioxidant effects—which addresses two critical pathological features in dry AMD: mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. Its ability to preserve mitochondrial integrity by maintaining the electron transport chain and reducing mitochondrial depolarization directly aligns with the needs of RPE cells, which have high energy demands and are vulnerable to oxidative damage (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Hernandez et al., 2024).

CoQ10 is a large, lipophilic molecule, and its effective delivery to the retina following systemic or topical administration remains a significant technical hurdle. Although studies have shown that exogenous CoQ10 can elevate retinal levels to some extent, optimizing its formulation for enhanced tissue penetration and sustained release is critical for therapeutic success (Manzar et al., 2020; Qu et al., 2009). Additionally, the variability observed in clinical responses in AMD studies suggests that patient-specific factors or differences in the progression of mitochondrial dysfunction may influence the therapeutic outcomes. Another important consideration is the multifactorial nature of dry AMD, which involves not only mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress but also chronic inflammation, complement dysregulation, and genetic predispositions. As such, CoQ10 monotherapy may not fully address the complex pathological processes underlying the disease. Combination therapies that target multiple pathways simultaneously, such as those combining CoQ10 with nutritional complexes that include other antioxidants and anti-inflammatory agents, are likely to yield better clinical outcomes. In this regard, CoQ10 appears to be particularly well-suited for inclusion in combination regimens designed to synergistically reduce oxidative stress and support mitochondrial health (Hernandez et al., 2024; Feher et al., 2005).

These effects are particularly relevant to dry AMD, where RPE cell death and the subsequent degeneration of photoreceptors play a central role in disease progression (Hernandez et al., 2024).

Overall, the aggregate evidence from biochemical, in vitro, and early clinical studies strongly supports the continued investigation of CoQ10 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its established role in mitochondrial function and cellular antioxidant defense mechanisms, combined with a favorable safety profile, provides a firm scientific basis for clinical translation. The potential for topical and systemic administration to elevate retinal levels, combined with its dual action as both a metabolic enhancer and a free radical scavenger, aligns well with the therapeutic needs of dry AMD patients. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SRT1720 is a fully synthetic small molecule initially discovered through high‐throughput screening by Sirtris Pharmaceuticals, which sought potent alternatives to the naturally occurring polyphenol resveratrol. Unlike resveratrol—which suffers from low bioavailability, poor metabolic stability, and broad non‐selective target interactions—SRT1720 belongs to the class of synthetic Sirtuin Activating Compounds (STACs) designed to selectively activate the NAD⁺‐dependent deacetylase SIRT1. Chemically, SRT1720 is based on an imidazo[1,2-b]thiazole scaffold and was optimized for its potency; studies have indicated that it is approximately 1000× more potent than resveratrol, with an EC1.5 value of around 0.16 μM and impressive maximal activation percentages in vitro (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Chang et al., 2024). The synthetic origins of SRT1720 represent a deliberate medicinal chemistry effort aimed at overcoming the limitations of natural SIRT1 activators. In the broader context, compounds in this class have been used as investigational drugs targeting pathways involved in metabolism, aging, inflammation, and stress tolerance, thereby establishing a framework for repurposing efforts across various disease areas (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Therapeutic History:  
Preclinical studies of SRT1720 have predominantly focused on its metabolic effects in rodent models characterized by diet-induced obesity, insulin resistance, and other forms of metabolic dysfunction. In these studies, administration of SRT1720 resulted in significant improvements in insulin sensitivity, reduction of plasma glucose levels, and enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis across metabolic tissues such as skeletal muscle, liver, and adipose tissues (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Donmez, 2012). Moreover, in genetically obese and high-fat diet animal models, SRT1720 has been demonstrated to improve mitochondrial function, as indicated by increased ATP production, elevated expression of mitochondrial proteins such as ATP synthase β and NDUFB8, and enhanced oxidative metabolism (Funk et al., 2010). This modulatory effect on mitochondrial biogenesis and function is thought to be mediated via the SIRT1-PGC-1α pathway—a mechanism that has garnered attention in age-related diseases where mitochondrial dysfunction is central. Although SRT1720 has not been directly investigated in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models or explicitly in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, the underlying pathogenic processes in dry AMD—namely, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysregulation—share significant overlap with the tissues previously demonstrated to benefit from SRT1720 treatment (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009). This cross-tissue efficacy provides a compelling rationale to explore SRT1720’s repurposing for dry AMD. Additionally, related compounds in this class (e.g., SRT2104) have advanced into clinical development for other indications, further suggesting that the pharmacological modulation of SIRT1 is a viable therapeutic approach (Hoppner et al., 2014).

Mechanism of Action:  
The underlying mechanism of action of SRT1720 centers on its ability to allosterically activate SIRT1, a key regulator of cellular energy metabolism and stress responses. SIRT1 is an NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase that modulates the activity of various transcription factors and co-regulators, notably PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ coactivator 1-α), which is a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. SRT1720 binds to an allosteric site on the SIRT1 enzyme-peptide substrate complex, situated amino terminal to the enzyme’s catalytic domain. This binding facilitates a conformational change in SIRT1 that lowers the Michaelis constant (K_m) for the acetylated substrates, thereby enhancing the rate of deacetylation (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Wan, 2021). Biochemical assays have demonstrated that SRT1720 increases SIRT1 deacetylase activity in a dose-dependent manner, leading to reduced acetylation of PGC-1α and thus promoting its transcriptional activity in driving mitochondrial gene expression (Funk et al., 2010). In addition to PGC-1α, SRT1720-mediated SIRT1 activation influences the acetylation status of several other proteins involved in stress responses and apoptosis, including FOXO1 and PPARγ, which collectively contribute to improved cellular resilience against oxidative damage (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Hoppner et al., 2014). Of note, many studies have confirmed that the beneficial effects observed with SRT1720 are abrogated in the presence of SIRT1 inhibitors such as nicotinamide and sirtinol, providing strong evidence for a SIRT1-dependent mode of action (Funk et al., 2010; Djouadi & Bastin, 2019). However, it is important to acknowledge that there has been some controversy regarding whether SRT1720 and its structural relatives directly interact with SIRT1 or exert off-target effects; nonetheless, the preponderance of kinetic and biophysical data supports the view that SRT1720 is primarily a SIRT1 activator (Hoppner et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2024).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry AMD is characterized by the degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) accompanied by chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and an overall decline in cellular energy homeostasis. The hypothesis for repurposing SRT1720 in this context is based on its well-documented ability to stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis and enhance oxidative capacity in multiple tissue types. In the RPE, which is a post-mitotic and metabolically demanding cell layer critical for photoreceptor survival, mitochondrial dysfunction is a key pathological feature that contributes to the progression of dry AMD. By activating SIRT1, SRT1720 is expected to promote deacetylation of PGC-1α, thereby upregulating a transcriptional program that enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and repair. This, in turn, would improve oxidative phosphorylation, reduce the production of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), and bolster the cells’ ability to cope with the chronic oxidative stress that underlies dry AMD pathology (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Furthermore, studies in other tissues, such as aged skeletal muscle and hepatocytes, have shown that SRT1720 reduces mtROS and restores cellular ATP levels by increasing mitochondrial number and function (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Funk et al., 2010). It is reasonable to extrapolate that similar benefits could be achieved in RPE cells, where preserved mitochondrial function is essential for maintaining retinal integrity and preventing progression to geographic atrophy, the advanced form of dry AMD. Expression analyses have demonstrated that both SIRT1 and PGC-1α are expressed in RPE cells, and their activities are critical for retinal health; thus, modulation of the SIRT1–PGC-1α axis by SRT1720 offers a mechanistic basis for its expected protective effects in the RPE (Hoppner et al., 2014; Alcaín & Villalba, 2009). It is anticipated that in assays using RPE cell cultures, treatment with SRT1720 will lead to enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis—as evidenced by increased mitochondrial DNA content, elevated levels of mitochondrial proteins, and improved cellular ATP production—while concurrently attenuating markers of oxidative stress. These effects would collectively improve the oxidative resilience of RPE cells, thereby potentially slowing or halting the progression of dry AMD (Funk et al., 2010; Hoppner et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation:  
There are several compelling strengths associated with the use of SRT1720 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. First, its synthetic design has led to a compound that is remarkably more potent than resveratrol, addressing one of the key limitations of natural SIRT1 activators. This enhanced potency, coupled with a clearly elucidated mechanism of action involving allosteric activation of SIRT1, provides a robust biochemical rationale for its efficacy. The observed effects in metabolic, hepatic, and renal systems—where SRT1720 has demonstrated significant improvements in mitochondrial biogenesis and reductions in oxidative stress—are highly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells plays a central role (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Another strength is the extensive preclinical data supporting the involvement of the SIRT1-PGC-1α axis in regulating mitochondrial function and cellular energy homeostasis. Since RPE cells share similar reliance on these pathways for maintaining cellular function and resisting oxidative injury, it is plausible that SRT1720 can be effectively translated into a therapeutic for dry AMD. Moreover, the fact that SRT1720’s effects are abrogated by SIRT1 inhibitors reinforces the notion that its beneficial actions are directly linked to SIRT1 activation rather than resulting from non-specific off-target activities, a point underscored by multiple biochemical studies (Wan, 2021; Funk et al., 2010).

However, there are also notable weaknesses and uncertainties that warrant consideration. Although SRT1720 has a well-characterized profile in terms of metabolic and mitochondrial effects in other tissue types, there is a paucity of data directly pertaining to ocular tissues or RPE cells. The retinal environment possesses unique pharmacokinetic and physiological characteristics, and the ability of SRT1720 to reach effective concentrations in the RPE upon systemic or local administration remains to be determined. Moreover, while the SIRT1-PGC-1α axis is a promising target, some studies have raised controversies concerning whether SRT1720 truly acts as a direct SIRT1 activator or if its effects might be partially mediated by off-target pathways, which could complicate both efficacy and safety profiles (Hoppner et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2024). There is also the broader issue of translating findings from systemic models of mitochondrial dysfunction to the highly specialized context of the eye, which may require careful consideration of formulation, dosing regimen, and potential adverse effects that are specific to ocular tissues.

The overall evaluation suggests that SRT1720 has a strong scientific foundation based on its potent SIRT1 activation, its capacity to enhance mitochondrial biogenesis, and its demonstrated ability to mitigate oxidative stress in multiple preclinical models (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Funk et al., 2010). These characteristics are directly relevant to addressing the molecular pathogenesis of dry AMD, where impaired mitochondrial function in the RPE is a key contributor to disease progression. Nevertheless, the gaps in the existing literature, particularly the lack of direct ocular studies, necessitate additional targeted preclinical research. Rigorous in vitro studies in RPE cell cultures and subsequent in vivo models of dry AMD will be essential to validate the therapeutic potential of SRT1720 in the ocular setting. Such studies should also focus on optimizing delivery mechanisms to ensure that effective drug levels are achieved in the retina without systemic toxicity (Hoppner et al., 2014; Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Future investigations should include detailed pharmacokinetic assessments in ocular tissues, evaluation of the specific effects on RPE mitochondrial dynamics, and analyses of potential off-target effects that could compromise safety. Additionally, given the controversies around whether compounds such as SRT1720 function solely via SIRT1 activation, complementary studies using genetic knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of SIRT1 in RPE cells would help to unequivocally determine the mechanism by which SRT1720 exerts its effects. Ultimately, while the translational rationale appears strong, careful attention must be paid to the unique biological milieu of the eye and to the rigorous design of preclinical studies that directly address the therapeutic endpoints relevant to dry AMD (Hoppner et al., 2014; Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

In conclusion, SRT1720 is a promising candidate for repurposing as a treatment for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its potent SIRT1 activation, demonstrated effects on mitochondrial biogenesis, and its ability to reduce oxidative stress, which is central to the pathology observed in RPE cells. The synthetic origin and high potency of SRT1720 distinguish it from natural agents like resveratrol and suggest that it might overcome many of the pharmacokinetic and specificity issues that have historically limited the success of SIRT1 activators in clinical settings. However, given that most of the existing evidence arises from non-ocular models, systematic studies focusing on the ocular pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics of SRT1720 are imperative before clinical translation can be considered. If future studies can confirm that SRT1720 effectively reaches the RPE in therapeutic concentrations and modulates the SIRT1-PGC-1α pathway without deleterious off-target effects, it could represent a significant advancement in our ability to protect the RPE against oxidative stress and slow the progression of dry AMD (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Funk et al., 2010; Hoppner et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation Summary:  
Strengths of SRT1720 include its exceptional potency compared to natural SIRT1 activators, robust preclinical evidence demonstrating mitochondrial biogenesis and reduced oxidative stress in multiple tissues, and a well-elucidated mechanism involving allosteric activation of SIRT1 with consequent deacetylation of PGC-1α. These attributes are particularly relevant given the central role of mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD. The SIRT1-PGC-1α pathway is a validated target in several preclinical models of aging and metabolic disease, and its modulation is anticipated to offer significant protection in RPE cells (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Funk et al., 2010).

Weaknesses center on the current lack of direct evidence in retinal cells or animal models of AMD, the need for ocular pharmacokinetic data, and some lingering controversies regarding the specificity of SRT1720’s mechanism of action. The translation of metabolic benefits observed in liver, muscle, and kidney to the RPE requires further study, and potential off-target effects or issues with drug delivery to ocular tissues remain concerns that necessitate additional research (Hoppner et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2024).

Based on the review of the available biochemical, preclinical, and mechanistic literature, SRT1720 shows promise as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. However, its application in this context should proceed with careful preclinical evaluation in relevant ocular models to address the outstanding issues related to tissue-specific pharmacokinetics and potential mechanistic ambiguities. This comprehensive evaluation supports the inclusion of SRT1720 in the research team’s pipeline for further investigation, provided that subsequent studies are designed to directly assess its efficacy and safety in the RPE and in vivo models of dry AMD (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Hoppner et al., 2014).

Historically, AICAR was developed primarily as an agent to activate AMPK in metabolic studies and has been investigated in a variety of preclinical models ranging from cancer to cardiovascular disease. AICAR exerts its biological activity primarily through the activation of AMPK, a master regulator of cellular energy balance that responds to alterations in the AMP/ATP ratio. Once AICAR is imported into cells through adenosine transporters, it is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase to form ZMP, an analog of AMP. ZMP binds to the regulatory γ subunit of AMPK, causing a conformational change that facilitates AMPK phosphorylation at Thr172 by upstream kinases such as LKB1, thereby fully activating the kinase (Efstathiou et al., 2020). Activated AMPK then phosphorylates a series of downstream targets involved in energy metabolism, including acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) and elements of the mTOR signaling pathway. In RPE cells, this activation is particularly important because AMPK phosphorylates and activates ULK1, a kinase critical for initiating autophagy and mitophagy, thereby promoting the clearance of damaged mitochondria (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Chung et al., 2017).

Given its mechanisms of action, the expected effect of AICAR in an assay aimed at treating dry AMD would be multifaceted. AICAR represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration owing to its robust and well-characterized mechanism of action via AMPK activation. The strengths of this candidate lie in its dual capacity to modulate critical pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis: on one hand, AICAR enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and promotes the removal of damaged mitochondria through autophagy/mitophagy, and on the other, it attenuates inflammatory cascades that exacerbate RPE cell damage (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hu et al., 2024). Preclinical studies have illustrated that dysregulation of mitochondrial function in RPE cells—a decrease in oxidative phosphorylation capacity, increased ROS production, and impaired clearance of damaged organelles—is pivotal in the initiation and progression of AMD (Tong et al., 2022; Rego, 2023). Below is our comprehensive evaluation of pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD):

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate –  
Pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) is an aromatic o‐quinone originally discovered as a redox cofactor for bacterial dehydrogenases and is naturally synthesized by various Gram‐negative prokaryotes. It was first identified in microbial systems where it serves as a prosthetic group in enzymes involved in alcohol and sugar oxidation, and it has since been detected at trace levels in human tissues and milk, suggesting dietary exposure through common foods such as fermented soy products, green peppers, spinach, and human milk. PQQ is categorized within the quinone family of compounds and is recognized for its redox‐active properties; in this role, it has been considered a “vitamin‐like accessory factor” by some researchers given its involvement in cellular energy metabolism and antioxidant defense (Petricca et al., 2025; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Commercially, PQQ is available in a water‐soluble disodium salt formulation; for example, the Sigma‐Aldrich PQQ product is typical of these preparations. As a small redox‐active molecule, PQQ is distinct among nutraceuticals and has been explored in several preclinical contexts for its potential to regulate oxidative stress and promote mitochondrial function (Canovai & Williams, 2025). Consequently, this candidate represents a repurposing opportunity where its established dietary exposure, safety profile as assessed by regulatory bodies such as EFSA, and its unique bioactivity as a mitochondrial modulator may be leveraged to address the mitochondrial dysfunction implicated in dry AMD.

Therapeutic History –  
PQQ has been the subject of intensive biochemical and preclinical investigation over the past decades. Early studies concentrated on its role as a microbial cofactor, but subsequent research has documented that dietary supplementation with PQQ produces measurable effects on mitochondrial‐related metabolism and markers of inflammation in animal models and humans (Canovai & Williams, 2025). In various rodent models, oral PQQ has been shown to modulate mitochondrial number and function, thereby improving outcomes in contexts as diverse as cardiac ischemia/reperfusion, neurodegeneration, and metabolic syndrome (Akagawa, Nakano, & Ikemoto, 2016; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Additionally, EFSA conducted a safety assessment of the PQQ disodium salt formulation as a novel food ingredient and concluded that at proposed supplemental doses (up to 20 mg/day) the width of the safety margin is acceptable relative to animal toxicology data (Turck et al., 2017; Hwang & Willoughby, 2018). In human studies, although clinical trials have largely focused on endpoints such as cognition, inflammatory markers, and lipid metabolism, these trials demonstrate that oral PQQ is bioavailable, well‐tolerated, and can meaningfully impact systemic markers of oxidative stress and energy metabolism (Canovai & Williams, 2025). While no study to date has directly employed PQQ in patients with dry AMD, there is indirect evidence suggesting that PQQ’s capacity to improve cellular bioenergetics may be broadly beneficial in clinical states characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction. Some studies even indicate that PQQ upregulates mitochondrial proteins and improves ATP synthesis in cellular models derived from age‐related macular degeneration donor tissues (Canovai & Williams, 2025), although direct evidence in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) remains sparse. In summary, the therapeutic history of PQQ includes diverse preclinical applications ranging from cardioprotection to neuroprotection, with established safety in both animal and limited human studies, making it a plausible candidate for repurposing in dry AMD where mitochondrial dysfunction is a key pathogenic driver.

Mechanism of Action –  
The molecular basis of PQQ’s bioactivity is multifaceted, centering on its redox chemistry and its ability to modulate mitochondrial biogenesis. Chemically, PQQ is a potent redox‐active o‐quinone that undergoes reversible reduction to its hydroquinone form (PQQH₂) via a rapid semiquinone intermediate. This redox cycling allows PQQ to function both as a free radical scavenger and as an electron‐transfer catalyst. In vitro assays have established that the reduced form, PQQH₂, exhibits robust antioxidant capacity, with reports indicating that its aroxyl radical quenching activity can be significantly greater than that of classical antioxidants such as vitamin C and α‐tocopherol (Canovai & Williams, 2025; Charrier et al., 2024). Through its antioxidant activity, PQQ directly neutralizes reactive oxygen species (ROS) and may protect cellular constituents from oxidative damage.

Beyond its direct radical scavenging, PQQ has been implicated as an inducer of mitochondrial biogenesis. Several mechanistic studies indicate that treatment with PQQ leads to the upregulation of key transcriptional regulators involved in mitochondrial proliferation. Specifically, PQQ treatment has been shown to activate the cAMP response element‐binding protein (CREB), which in turn stimulates the expression of peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator‐1 alpha (PGC‐1α) (Charrier et al., 2024; Canovai & Williams, 2025). PGC‐1α is a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and coordinates the transcriptional activation of nuclear respiratory factors (NRF‐1/NRF‐2) and mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM), all of which are critical for the transcription and replication of mitochondrial DNA. Some studies also suggest that PQQ modulates sirtuin activity, particularly SIRT1 and SIRT3, which are NAD⁺‐dependent deacetylases that regulate mitochondrial function and cellular metabolic homeostasis (Canovai & Williams, 2025). In addition, PQQ has been reported to restore mitochondrial membrane potential, reduce proton leak, and enhance ATP production during oxidative challenge in several cellular systems (Petricca et al., 2025; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Thus, the composite mechanism of action posited for PQQ—which includes both robust redox buffering and the activation of mitochondrial biogenesis via CREB/PGC‐1α signaling—provides a molecular rationale for its use in conditions characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative injury.

Mechanistically, it is also suggested that PQQ may improve the NAD⁺/NADH ratio, thereby favoring the activity of sirtuins, which contributes to a more favorable intracellular redox state and efficient energy utilization (Jonscher, Chowanadisai, & Rucker, 2021). Although these effects have been most clearly demonstrated in hepatic, muscular, and neuronal cell models, they are directly relevant to RPE cells that rely heavily on oxidative phosphorylation for their energy demands and, hence, are particularly vulnerable to mitochondrial decay under chronic oxidative stress—a hallmark of dry AMD pathology. It is important to note that PQQ’s actions are context‐dependent; while low concentrations have been associated with protective effects, some studies suggest that higher doses can induce a pro‐oxidant effect and even impair mitochondrial dynamics in sensitive cellular contexts (Petricca et al., 2025; Turck et al., 2017). This biphasic dose response underscores the need to identify an optimal dosing window that maximizes mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defense without tipping cells into oxidative stress.

The central hypothesis guiding the repurposing of PQQ for dry AMD is that it can stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis in the RPE by upregulating PGC‐1α, thereby increasing the antioxidant capacity and restoring optimal mitochondrial respiration in cells under chronic oxidative injury. In the proposed assay, treatment with PQQ is expected to yield multiple beneficial outcomes. First, by activating CREB and augmenting PGC‐1α expression, PQQ should enhance the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial replication and function, leading to an increased mitochondrial mass within RPE cells (Canovai & Williams, 2025; Charrier et al., 2024).

Second, increased mitochondrial mass and improved electron transport chain efficiency are expected to elevate ATP production, thereby restoring cellular energy stores that are typically depleted in dry AMD due to chronic oxidative damage. Experimental data from other cell types, including neuronal and hepatic cells, have shown that PQQ treatment enhances ATP output and normalizes mitochondrial membrane potential under oxidative stress conditions, suggesting that similar responses might be observed in RPE cells (Petricca et al., 2025; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Third, PQQ is anticipated to upregulate antioxidant enzymes, such as manganese superoxide dismutase (SOD2), which plays a critical role in mitigating ROS accumulation in mitochondria. By lowering oxidative stress levels in RPE cells, PQQ can help maintain cellular homeostasis and prevent the degeneration that is characteristic of dry AMD (Canovai & Williams, 2025).

Additionally, there is emerging evidence that certain studies using donor‐derived RPE cells from AMD patients have demonstrated that PQQ treatment can upregulate mitochondrial proteins and improve ATP generation in these cells (Canovai & Williams, 2025). Although the available data in retinal tissues remain limited, these findings align with the overall rationale; because RPE cells are highly metabolically active and heavily reliant on mitochondrial function, the ability to augment their biogenesis and enhance oxidative phosphorylation directly addresses a critical pathogenic mechanism of dry AMD. Complementing these expected biochemical outcomes, one would predict that functional assays (for instance, assessments of oxygen consumption rate and extracellular acidification rate) will reveal improved mitochondrial respiration and overall metabolic resilience in PQQ‐treated RPE cells.

In synthesizing the extensive body of literature, we find that PQQ demonstrates considerable promise as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, based on the following strengths and weaknesses:

Strengths:  
1. Robust Mechanistic Rationale: PQQ’s dual role as an antioxidant and an inducer of mitochondrial biogenesis is well documented. The capacity to elevate PGC‐1α expression and thereby drive mitochondrial proliferation and enhanced energy metabolism is highly relevant given that dry AMD is characterized by RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and heightened oxidative stress (Petricca et al., 2025; Charrier et al., 2024; Canovai & Williams, 2025).  
2. Positive Safety and Bioavailability Data: Numerous preclinical studies, alongside regulatory evaluations (e.g., EFSA’s novel food assessment), indicate that PQQ is orally bioavailable and well tolerated in both animal models and limited human studies. 3. Broad Therapeutic History: Although PQQ has not been directly tested in dry AMD in clinical settings, its prior use as a dietary supplement and its beneficial effects in neuroprotection, cardioprotection, and metabolic regulation suggest therapeutic potential in conditions underpinned by mitochondrial decay and oxidative stress (Canovai & Williams, 2025).  
4. Hypothesis‐Driven Approach: The specific hypothesis—that PQQ will stimulate RPE mitochondrial biogenesis via upregulation of PGC‐1α to improve cellular resilience against chronic oxidative injury—is both plausible and supported by mechanistic data from other cell types. Given that RPE cells are known to express PGC‐1α and that deficits in mitochondrial function have been implicated in AMD pathology, this provides a strong rationale for further investigation (Canovai & Williams, 2025).

1. Limited Direct Evidence in Ocular Tissues: One of the main gaps in the literature is the paucity of direct preclinical studies involving retinal pigment epithelium or in vivo AMD models. Although there is some suggestive data from studies in retinal ganglion cells and donor‐derived RPE cells, definitive evidence that PQQ can counteract the specific aspects of dry AMD pathology in the retina is currently lacking (Ebeling et al., 2020; Petricca et al., 2025).
