Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Deferoxamine (also known as desferrioxamine B; DFO) is a natural microbial siderophore originally isolated from Streptomyces pilosus and developed as an iron‐chelating drug in the 1960s, with clinical deployment beginning in 1968 under the trade name Desferal for treatment of iron overload disorders (notably transfusional iron loading in β-thalassemia) (Faa & Crisponi, 1999; Sharpe et al., 2011; Birch et al., 2006). Chemically, DFO is a hexadentate, tris-hydroxamate ligand that coordinates ferric iron (FeIII) at six oxygen donors derived from three bidentate hydroxamate groups to form a very stable 1:1 FeIII–DFO complex with distorted octahedral FeIIIO6 geometry (Sharpe et al., 2011; Richardson & Poňka, 1998). The FeIII affinity is exceptionally high and selective: reported formation constants for FeIII–DFO include log β110 ≈ 30.5 and conditional pM/pFe values around 26–31, while affinity for FeII is ∼20 orders of magnitude lower, consistent with the observation that DFO selectively chelates FeIII in vivo (Sharpe et al., 2011; Kontoghiorghes & Kontoghiorghe, 2020; Birch et al., 2006). The compound is highly hydrophilic, carries a positive charge near physiological pH, and exhibits poor membrane permeability and oral absorption; as a result, DFO is administered parenterally and tends to localize extracellularly or within endosomal/lysosomal compartments after endocytosis (Birch et al., 2006; Kontoghiorghes & Kontoghiorghe, 2020; Zhao et al., 2021). Pharmacokinetically, native DFO has a very short plasma half-life on the order of minutes, with multiple studies reporting ∼10–30 minutes after intravenous dosing, rapid renal clearance, and elimination of chelated iron via urine and bile; the short exposure necessitates prolonged subcutaneous or intravenous infusions for clinical efficacy (Sharpe et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2020; Entezari et al., 2022). DFO is not blood–neural barrier penetrant, limiting access to the central nervous system and retina when given systemically (Li et al., 2023).

As a class, siderophores are low-molecular microbial metabolites evolved for FeIII acquisition and storage; medicinally, DFO is the prototypical siderophore drug and, for decades, has served as the clinical standard for chelation in iron-overload conditions (Hatcher et al., 2009). Within therapeutic iron chelators, DFO’s hexadentate hydroxamate architecture confers high thermodynamic and kinetic stability of FeIII complexes, limiting redox cycling and hydroxyl radical generation relative to weaker or redox-active iron ligands (Hider & Kong, 2013).

Therapeutic History  
DFO has an extensive clinical history as the benchmark iron chelator for transfusional iron overload, especially in β-thalassemia major and other transfusion-dependent anemias; it was approved in the United States in 1968 and used for decades as life-saving therapy, albeit limited by the need for prolonged parenteral infusions and high cost (Sharpe et al., 2011; Birch et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2012). Beyond chronic iron overload, labeled and established uses include acute iron poisoning and treatment of aluminum toxicity, reflecting DFO’s strong FeIII selectivity and capacity to form inert complexes with polyvalent cations in vivo (Jones et al., 2020). The standard practice has involved subcutaneous or intravenous infusions at 20–60 mg/kg daily for 8–24 hours over 5–7 days per week, with urinary and fecal excretion of iron–DFO complexes as pharmacodynamic endpoints; however, adherence and patient acceptance have been major barriers due to the burdensome administration (Tam et al., 2003; Entezari et al., 2022).

The clinical pharmacology and chemistry of DFO have motivated multiple improved-delivery strategies: liposomal encapsulation and multivesicular liposome systems to extend half-life, and macromolecular conjugates (e.g., starch or HES carriers) to prolong exposure and shift biodistribution to iron-storage organs; these approaches have demonstrated prolonged circulation, increased urinary iron excretion, and organ accumulation (Jones et al., 2020; Sharpe et al., 2011; Tam et al., 2003). Nevertheless, DFO remains orally inactive and requires parenteral dosing, in contrast to later oral chelators (deferiprone, deferasirox), which have supplanted it in many indications due to ease of administration while sometimes being deployed in combination regimens with DFO to enhance iron removal and cardiac protection via complementary pharmacokinetics and chelation kinetics (Hider & Kong, 2013; Ma et al., 2012).

In ophthalmology and retinal biology, DFO’s evaluation is mixed. On one hand, iron chelation with DFO has shown protective effects in experimental retinal contexts: it reduced retinal ganglion cell death induced by hydrogen peroxide and paraquat in oxidative-stress paradigms, consistent with inhibition of iron-dependent hydroxyl radical production (Rohowetz et al., 2018). In hemorrhagic retinal injury, DFO protected photoreceptor tissues after subretinal blood in animal models, suggesting iron chelation can blunt heme/Fe-driven toxicity in the subretinal space (Song & Dunaief, 2013). In RPE-relevant cell models, DFO mitigated lipid peroxidation, prevented glutathione depletion, decreased Fe2+ accumulation, and preserved viability of ARPE-19 cells under tert-butyl hydroperoxide and blue-light stress, and it enhanced cell survival by modulating antioxidant defense systems (GSH–GPX4 and FSP1–CoQ10–NADH axes) (Zhao et al., 2025). A zinc–DFO complex (Zn/DFO) designed to improve cellular delivery reduced retinal iron content, lipid peroxidation, and oxidative DNA damage, preserved photoreceptor structure, and improved ERG responses in rd10 mice, demonstrating in vivo neuroprotection when systemic penetration is enhanced (Zhao et al., 2025). Ex vivo, DFO decreased histochemically detectable chelatable iron (Perls–DAB) in macular sections from AMD eyes, supporting the feasibility of removing pathologic labile iron in human AMD tissue (He et al., 2007).

On the other hand, DFO has a documented profile of retinal/ocular toxicity in patients receiving systemic therapy: reports include macular and peripheral pigmentary degeneration, impaired night vision, optic neuritis/neuropathy, cataract, ERG amplitude reductions, and EOG light-peak abnormalities, prompting recommendations for ophthalmic surveillance, and leading some experts to conclude that DFO is a dubious candidate for AMD treatment (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021). In RPE culture, repeated DFO exposure was cytotoxic relative to a prochelator control, and clinical series describe deferoxamine retinopathy across pediatric and adult populations, indicating that while iron chelation can be protective in vitro under specific stress conditions, DFO itself can injure RPE and photoreceptors under sustained or high-exposure regimens (Charkoudian et al., 2008; Błasiak et al., 2011). Importantly, DFO’s poor cell permeability and lack of blood–retinal barrier penetration raise practical concerns about achieving therapeutic intra-retinal exposure without systemic toxicity when administered conventionally (Li et al., 2023; Birch et al., 2006). Finally, although iron chelation is mechanistically compelling for retinal degenerations in which iron accumulation and ferroptotic stress participate, application of systemic chelators like DFO to retinal vascular disease and AMD remains at the basic research stage, with unresolved issues including perturbation of systemic/local iron homeostasis and stability of intracellular chelate complexes (Li et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, DFO is a high-affinity FeIII-selective chelator that forms kinetically inert hexacoordinate FeIIIO6 complexes via three hydroxamate ligands, each providing bidentate O,Oʹ coordination; this renders FeIII chemically sequestered, suppresses redox cycling, and prevents iron from entering the Haber–Weiss/Fenton chemistry that generates hydroxyl radicals from superoxide/hydrogen peroxide (Sharpe et al., 2011; Richardson & Poňka, 1998; Hider & Kong, 2013). The FeIII/FeII couple of ferrioxamine is electrochemically very negative (reported around −468 mV vs. NHE), and the complex is redox-inert under physiological conditions, consistent with its ability to quench iron-mediated ROS production rather than participate in it (Hider & Kong, 2013). In biological systems, DFO preferentially binds non-transferrin-bound iron (NTBI), labile iron pools in hepatocytes/macrophages, and low-molecular-weight iron transiting endosomes/lysosomes after transferrin delivery or ferritin degradation; it can mobilize hepatic stores and iron released by reticuloendothelial cells but cannot effectively strip iron from metalloproteins such as hemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochromes, oxidases, catalase, or peroxidases (Hatcher et al., 2009; Richardson & Poňka, 1998; Faa & Crisponi, 1999). The drug is hydrophilic and generally membrane-impermeant; cellular uptake occurs via fluid-phase endocytosis and pinocytosis, leading to enrichment in endosomal/lysosomal compartments, where it chelates lysosomal labile iron, an activity proposed to block lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis—mechanistically relevant to RPE pathobiology (Zhao et al., 2021; Dayani et al., 2004).

In retina and neural tissues, oxidative damage pathways include iron-dependent conversion of H2O2 to •OH via Fenton chemistry; DFO reduces H2O2-induced damage in retinal ganglion cells and protects against paraquat-generated superoxide by depriving upstream Fenton catalysts of accessible iron (Rohowetz et al., 2018). In RPE and photoreceptors, ferroptosis—a regulated cell death driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation—is closely linked to antioxidant systems centered on glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and, independently, on FSP1-mediated ubiquinol regeneration; DFO’s chelation of FeII/FeIII within lysosomes and cytosolic labile pools acts upstream of these pathways to limit lipid hydroperoxide propagation, preserving GSH–GPX4 and FSP1–CoQ10–NADH defense capacity in ARPE-19 under oxidative stimuli (Zhao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023). In systemic contexts, DFO detoxifies NTBI, reduces heme-derived ferryl species, removes high-oxidation-state heme iron, and directly scavenges some radical species, converging on inhibition of membrane lipid oxidation; these activities potentially translate to retinal cells where heme/iron-driven oxidative stress is implicated (Hatcher et al., 2009).

Notably, DFO’s hexadentate size and hydrophilicity restrict direct ferritin iron extraction and limit chelation in tightly protein-bound pools; smaller chelators can penetrate cells more readily and directly efflux ferritin iron, whereas DFO works primarily by intercepting low-molecular-weight iron pools and forming kinetically inert FeIII complexes that are then cleared, often via hepatobiliary or renal routes (Sharpe et al., 2011; Richardson & Poňka, 1998). In inflamed or ischemic tissues, the depletion of accessible iron by DFO can blunt downstream ROS and inflammatory cascades; however, prolonged systemic chelation perturbs metal homeostasis and can deplete essential iron pools in sensitive tissues, underlying some adverse effects including RPE toxicity, auditory neuropathy, and bone dysplasia (Zhao et al., 2021; He et al., 2007).

Expected Effect  
For dry AMD models centered on RPE iron-dependent oxidative stress, the expected pharmacologic effect of DFO is to reduce the labile Fe pool in lysosomes and cytosol, thereby attenuating hydroxyl-radical production from H2O2 and limiting iron-driven lipid peroxidation; operationally, this should decrease oxidative damage readouts and preserve mitochondrial and cellular function in RPE assays (Rohowetz et al., 2018; Li et al., 2023). Specifically:

- Lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis markers: In ARPE-19 cells, DFO has been shown to mitigate lipid peroxidation under oxidant (tBH) and blue-light stress and to preserve viability, consistent with suppression of ferroptotic death; thus, in RPE assays one should observe reductions in lipid peroxidation assays (e.g., BODIPY-C11) and maintenance of GPX4 activity/content, with complementary preservation of the FSP1–CoQ10–NADH axis (Zhao et al., 2025). The same studies indicate decreased Fe2+ accumulation after DFO, reflecting lower catalytic Fe at sites of peroxidation; similar decreases in labile Fe can be measured via calcein quenching or analogous probes (Zhao et al., 2025).

- Oxidative DNA damage: Systemic Zn/DFO reduced retinal oxidative DNA damage in vivo in rd10 mice; although these are not AMD models, the result predicts that in RPE oxidative stress assays DFO will reduce accumulation of oxidative DNA lesions, including those arising in mitochondrial DNA, where iron-dependent ROS can be particularly damaging (Zhao et al., 2025). Ex vivo human AMD maculas showed decreased Perls–DAB staining after DFO chelation, supporting the feasibility of reducing chelatable iron burden and downstream oxidative chemistry in diseased human retina (He et al., 2007).

- Mitochondrial bioenergetics: Preservation of RPE oxygen consumption rate (OCR) is plausible under DFO exposure insofar as DFO limits lipid peroxidation and maintains the reductive antioxidant systems (GSH–GPX4, FSP1–CoQ10) that protect inner-mitochondrial membranes and electron-transport components from iron-dependent oxidative injury; in ARPE-19, DFO improved survival and redox balance under stress, suggesting OCR preservation would accompany reduced peroxidation (Zhao et al., 2025). In retinal ganglion cells, DFO lessened H2O2-induced cell death, indirectly supporting improved mitochondrial tolerance to oxidant stress; similar protection can be anticipated in RPE where iron-dependent ROS compromise mitochondrial DNA and respiratory complexes (Rohowetz et al., 2018).

- Tissue iron fingerprints: In tissue sections or organoids, DFO exposure is expected to decrease Perls–DAB positive iron signal in regions with elevated chelatable iron, as observed in AMD macular tissue; in vivo, systemic DFO does not cross the BRB well, so demonstration of retinal iron removal may require enhanced uptake strategies (e.g., Zn/DFO) or local delivery (Li et al., 2023; He et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2025).

Caveats critical to experimental design include DFO’s lack of blood–retinal barrier penetration and poor cell permeability, which could limit intracellular RPE exposure and lysosomal targeting in vivo after systemic dosing; thus, in vitro or ex vivo assays will show clearer pharmacodynamic effects than systemic models unless delivery is optimized (e.g., Zn-complexation or nanocarriers) (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025; Jones et al., 2020). Additionally, repeated or high-concentration exposure can be cytotoxic to RPE in vitro and has been associated with clinical retinopathy, so dose–exposure optimization and careful toxicity monitoring are required, especially in chronic paradigms (Charkoudian et al., 2008; He et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Rationale strength and translational plausibility. The mechanistic rationale for iron chelation in dry AMD is strong: AMD retinas accumulate chelatable iron, iron catalyzes hydroxyl-radical generation and lipid peroxidation, and iron-dependent ferroptotic stress has been implicated in RPE dysfunction and photoreceptor degeneration (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023). DFO is a high-affinity FeIII chelator with extensive human experience, and it is proven to suppress iron-mediated ROS by forming kinetically inert FeIII complexes, preventing Fenton chemistry (Sharpe et al., 2011; Hider & Kong, 2013). In retinal and RPE models, DFO reduces oxidative injury, limits lipid peroxidation, and preserves cell viability; improved-delivery variants such as Zn/DFO demonstrate in vivo protection of retinal structure and function with concomitant decreases in retinal iron and oxidative DNA damage (Rohowetz et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2025). Ex vivo AMD maculae show DFO-responsive chelatable iron pools, reinforcing target engagement in human disease tissue (He et al., 2007). Mechanistically, enrichment of DFO in lysosomes—an organelle central to RPE iron handling, ferritinophagy, and lipid peroxidation—supports a proximal mode of action relevant to ferroptosis biology in AMD (Zhao et al., 2021).

Key liabilities and translational risks. Despite its compelling mechanism, DFO’s drug properties and ocular safety profile are unfavorable for repurposing in dry AMD without substantial reformulation or targeting:

- Ocular toxicity. DFO has a recognized spectrum of retinal adverse effects in patients, including pigmentary retinopathy, optic neuropathy, ERG/EOG abnormalities, and visual loss; authoritative reviews judge DFO a dubious candidate for AMD because of these safety concerns, and clinical surveillance is recommended when patients receive systemic DFO (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023). RPE toxicity is documented in vitro and clinically across age groups, indicating a narrow retinal therapeutic window under repeated exposure (Błasiak et al., 2011; Charkoudian et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2021).

- Delivery limitations. DFO is hydrophilic, membrane-impermeant, and not blood–neural/retinal barrier penetrant, which undermines retinal exposure after systemic dosing; achieving therapeutic intra-RPE concentrations without systemic toxicity is unlikely with conventional infusion regimens (Li et al., 2023; Birch et al., 2006). The molecule’s very short plasma half-life further complicates exposure in avascular tissues like the outer retina (Sharpe et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2020).

- Systemic chelation risks. Long-term DFO perturbs systemic iron balance, interacts with microbiological iron acquisition in certain pathogens (e.g., Vibrio, S. aureus) that can exploit ferrioxamine, and carries recognized risks of growth retardation, bone changes, and infection, which are unacceptable for a chronic ocular disease with slow progression (Sharpe et al., 2011; Faa & Crisponi, 1999).

- Clinical maturity in ophthalmology. While iron chelators show promise in preclinical retinal models, clinical translation to retinal vascular disease/AMD remains at the basic research stage; challenges include maintaining retinal iron homeostasis, avoiding off-target metal depletion (e.g., Zn2+), and ensuring intracellular chelate stability and localization (Li et al., 2023).

Risk-mitigation strategies and development path. If DFO were to be advanced, development should avoid systemic DFO infusions for dry AMD. Instead:

- Leverage targeted delivery. The Zn/DFO complex that facilitates cellular uptake has shown robust neuroprotection, retinal iron lowering, and oxidative DNA damage reduction in vivo; such conjugate-based or carrier-based strategies could provide intracellular RPE delivery at lower systemic exposure, meriting further evaluation in AMD-relevant models (e.g., light damage, iron-loading, aged mice) with retinal safety readouts (Zhao et al., 2025). Nanocarriers or depot formulations that increase local ocular exposure while minimizing systemic levels could be explored, given DFO’s history of half-life extension in liposomal and multivesicular formulations systemically (Jones et al., 2020; Sharpe et al., 2011).

- Consider chemical alternatives within class. Other chelators with better cell permeability and ocular safety have shown retinal protection without the retinotoxicity seen with DFO; for example, deferiprone protected against iron-induced and light-induced retinal degeneration in multiple mouse models and was not found to be toxic to mouse retina in the contexts studied, suggesting that a more lipophilic, lower-molecular-weight chelator could be a safer starting point than DFO for dry AMD (Song & Dunaief, 2013; Picard et al., 2020).

- Exploit prochelation. Pro-chelators like BSIH that become active only under oxidative conditions were non-toxic with repeated exposure relative to DFO and may offer a way to achieve context-dependent iron chelation within oxidatively stressed RPE while sparing normal iron pools, lowering the risk of retinopathy (Charkoudian et al., 2008).

Decision framework for go/no-go. On balance, while DFO validates the iron-chelation mechanism in retinal tissues and provides useful tool-compound effects in vitro and in ex vivo AMD maculae, its physicochemical properties, delivery constraints, and retinal toxicity profile argue strongly against repurposing native DFO for chronic treatment of dry AMD (Li et al., 2023; He et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2021). The most credible development path for DFO derivatives would require:

- Demonstrating safe, effective RPE delivery with a DFO-based construct (e.g., Zn/DFO or nanocarrier) that reduces labile iron, lipid peroxidation, and oxidative DNA damage in AMD-relevant in vivo models without ERG/EOG or structural toxicity (Zhao et al., 2025).

- Establishing a therapeutic index in the retina with chronic dosing and appropriate safety pharmacology (ERG, OCT, histopathology), given reported human retinopathies on DFO (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023).

- Benchmarking against alternative chelators (e.g., deferiprone) that already demonstrate retinal protection and better permeability/safety in vivo, to justify a DFO-based approach scientifically and clinically (Song & Dunaief, 2013; Picard et al., 2020).

Strengths  
- Mechanistic fit: chelates FeIII with high selectivity and prevents Fenton chemistry; acts in lysosomes where RPE iron and lipid peroxidation intersect with ferroptosis (Sharpe et al., 2011; Hider & Kong, 2013; Zhao et al., 2021).  
- Demonstrated retinal pharmacology: reduces oxidative injury in retinal neurons and RPE, lowers retinal iron and oxidative DNA damage with improved delivery, and removes chelatable iron from AMD macula ex vivo (Rohowetz et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2025; He et al., 2007).  
- Extensive human experience: well-characterized PK/PD, safety liabilities, and clinical management of chelation therapy (Jones et al., 2020; Tam et al., 2003).

Weaknesses  
- Ocular toxicity liability with systemic DFO, including pigmentary retinopathy and electrophysiologic dysfunction, making native DFO a poor risk–benefit prospect for a chronic retinal indication (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021).  
- Poor retinal exposure after systemic dosing due to hydrophilicity and lack of BRB penetration; very short half-life complicates sustained intraocular levels (Li et al., 2023; Birch et al., 2006; Jones et al., 2020).  
- Systemic risks (growth, bone, infection) incompatible with large, elderly dry-AMD populations unless exposure is tightly localized to the eye (Faa & Crisponi, 1999; Sharpe et al., 2011).  
- Field immaturity: iron chelators for retinal disease remain in basic research with unresolved questions about homeostasis and intracellular stability (Li et al., 2023).

Conclusion  
DFO is a mechanistically validated iron chelator with documented ability to reduce iron-driven oxidative injury in retinal systems; however, as a repurposed systemic drug for dry AMD, its delivery barriers and retinal toxicity outweigh potential benefits (Li et al., 2023; He et al., 2007). If iron chelation is pursued for dry AMD within this program, prioritizing better-penetrant, safer chelators (e.g., deferiprone) or context-activated prochelators over native DFO is the higher-probability path; alternately, DFO-based constructs that demonstrably deliver into RPE (e.g., Zn/DFO) with acceptable chronic retinal safety merit targeted preclinical exploration before considering clinical translation (Song & Dunaief, 2013; Charkoudian et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Mitoquinone mesylate (MitoQ) is a synthetic, mitochondria‐targeted antioxidant originally developed as an analogue of coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) to overcome the bioavailability and uptake limitations of naturally occurring CoQ10. Its chemical design is based on modifying decylubiquinone—a CoQ10 analogue in which the long isoprenoid tail is replaced by a saturated decyl hydrocarbon chain to enhance mitochondrial retention—and covalently linking it to a lipophilic triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation. The inclusion of the TPP⁺ moiety exploits the highly negative membrane potential of the mitochondrial inner membrane, thereby ensuring selective accumulation of MitoQ in the mitochondrial matrix (Cores et al., 2023). This compound belongs to the class of lipophilic cationic antioxidants and is also considered a mitochondria-targeted rechargeable antioxidant (RMA) because, after its active ubiquinone moiety scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS), it is enzymatically reduced to the active hydroquinone form by components of the electron transport chain. The rechargeable property allows MitoQ to be continuously recycled via the respiratory chain, resulting in sustained antioxidant action even at low doses—a property that distinguishes it from conventional antioxidants (Lukashev et al., 2014; Fields et al., 2023). The synthesis strategy for MitoQ involves the chemical conjugation of decylubiquinone with TPP⁺, and it is formulated as a mesylate salt to improve its stability and facilitate pharmaceutical development (Cores et al., 2023; Kim & Han, 2017). Overall, MitoQ is a well‐defined member of a broader class of mitochondria‐targeted redox active compounds that have been widely investigated for their potential to modulate mitochondrial oxidative stress (Zielonka et al., 2017).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past two decades, MitoQ has been extensively characterized in a wide range of preclinical studies spanning neurodegenerative diseases, cardiovascular disorders, metabolic syndrome, sepsis, and other conditions associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and elevated oxidative stress. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that MitoQ confers protection against oxidative injury in cellular models and animal models alike. For example, studies in rodent models of cardiac ischemia–reperfusion injury, hypertension, and pressure‐overload heart failure have shown that MitoQ preserves mitochondrial respiration, decreases ROS production (especially H₂O₂ and superoxide) and reduces lipid peroxidation in the heart (Fairley et al., 2023; Kim & Han, 2017). In addition, significant neuroprotective effects have been reported in multiple models of neurodegeneration—ranging from in vitro experiments using Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease models to in vivo studies in rodent systems—where MitoQ was able to reduce mitochondrial fragmentation, lower markers of apoptosis, and restore mitochondrial membrane potential in neurons (Fields et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). Clinically, MitoQ has advanced into human trials in several indications including studies related to Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and hypertension, with reported safety in over 200 human subjects (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Fairley et al., 2023). Although there is no direct record of its use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), the extensive preclinical history in diseases characterized by oxidative stress and mitochondrial impairment provides a strong precedent for its repurposing. In ocular contexts, early pharmacokinetic studies have demonstrated that MitoQ exhibits measurable retinal uptake (approximately 1% of plasma concentration) after oral or topical administration, suggesting that the compound can reach the retina at therapeutically relevant levels (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). Given that mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative injury in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells are now increasingly recognized as central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the repurposing of MitoQ for this indication is logically supported by its mechanism and prior usage in analogous conditions (Cores et al., 2023; Zielonka et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
MitoQ’s mechanism of action is rooted in its unique chemical architecture that allows selective mitochondrial targeting and continuous ROS scavenging. The TPP⁺ moiety drives the compound’s accumulation into the mitochondrial matrix in a membrane potential–dependent manner. Once inside the mitochondria, MitoQ’s ubiquinone moiety is rapidly reduced by components of the electron transport chain—most notably by electron flow through complex II—and converted to its active form, mitoquinol (ubiquinol) (Cores et al., 2023; Manolis et al., 2021). In its reduced state, mitoquinol acts as a potent antioxidant that intercepts ROS generated primarily at the sites of electron leakage at complexes I and III. The scavenging of ROS, particularly superoxide and peroxyl radicals, prevents oxidative damage to mitochondrial lipids, proteins, and DNA—all of which are crucial for maintaining mitochondrial function (Zielonka et al., 2017; Modi et al., 2024). In effect, the cycle of reduction and oxidation (redox cycling) enables MitoQ to function catalytically, rather than stoichiometrically, thereby amplifying its antioxidant capacity over time (Lukashev et al., 2014; Modi et al., 2024). Moreover, by reducing mitochondrial ROS, MitoQ preserves the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), which is essential for ATP synthesis and overall cellular bioenergetics (Kim & Han, 2017; Gueven et al., 2017). This stabilization of Δψm not only inhibits the initiation of apoptosis but may also dampen downstream inflammatory signaling cascades mediated by ROS-sensitive transcription factors such as NF-κB (Fields et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023). Such detailed molecular interactions—spanning TPP-driven uptake, rapid reduction at the respiratory chain, catalytic ROS neutralization, and subsequent recycling to the active antioxidant form—underscore the multifaceted protection that MitoQ offers against mitochondrial oxidative injury.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the underlying hypothesis is that accumulation of oxidative damage in RPE cells leads to mitochondrial dysfunction, loss of Δψm, increased ROS production, chronic inflammation, and ultimately RPE cell degeneration, which is central to disease progression. Based on in vitro studies performed in ARPE-19 cells, treatment with MitoQ has been shown to reduce mitochondrial ROS levels, as measured by MitoSOX fluorescence, and to preserve Δψm as assessed by TMRM assays when cells are challenged with H₂O₂-induced oxidative stress (Cores et al., 2023; Fields et al., 2023). The expected effect of MitoQ in a dry AMD model is that, upon topical or oral administration, it will accumulate in the mitochondria of RPE cells via TPP-mediated uptake. Once there, its ubiquinone moiety will be reduced to the active antioxidant form by the local respiratory chain, which in turn will neutralize superoxide and other ROS at the sites of electron leakage (primarily complex I and III regions). This ROS scavenging is anticipated to limit oxidative damage to mitochondrial membranes and proteins, maintain efficient electron transport and ATP production, and ultimately restore the mitochondrial membrane potential that is compromised in oxidative stress conditions (Zielonka et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014). Additionally, by lowering oxidative stress, MitoQ is expected to reduce inflammatory signaling within the RPE and adjacent retinal layers—potentially decreasing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and mitigating the chronic low-grade inflammation that contributes to dry AMD pathology (Fairley et al., 2023; Gueven et al., 2017). Overall Evaluation:  
MitoQ stands out as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration on the basis of several compelling factors. First, its synthetic origin as a mitochondria-targeted CoQ10 analogue with an appended TPP⁺ group ensures that it concentrates specifically within mitochondria, where oxidative stress is most detrimental (Cores et al., 2023; Zielonka et al., 2017). This targeted delivery is a critical improvement over non-specific antioxidants, which often fail to reach the intracellular compartments where ROS generation is most intense. Second, MitoQ’s well-established mechanism of action—encompassing catalytic ROS scavenging through a continuously rechargeable redox cycle—directly addresses the pathophysiological core of dry AMD, namely the oxidative injury and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells (Lukashev et al., 2014; Fields et al., 2023). Preclinical studies in diverse disease models have robustly demonstrated its capacity to protect mitochondrial structure and function, reduce lipid peroxidation and apoptotic signaling, and ultimately preserve cellular viability (Kim & Han, 2017; Gueven et al., 2017).

On the therapeutic history side, MitoQ has undergone extensive preclinical evaluation in models of neurodegeneration, cardiovascular diseases, and metabolic disorders, and has been tested in several early-phase clinical trials—even if not yet in dry AMD specifically—showing an excellent safety profile in over 200 human subjects (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Fairley et al., 2023). Furthermore, pharmacokinetic studies demonstrating ocular uptake (~1% of plasma levels) provide an encouraging basis for its repurposing in retinal diseases, although the relatively low retinal concentration does suggest that formulation optimization (for instance, via topical delivery systems or enhanced ocular bioavailability formulations) may be required to achieve therapeutic levels in the RPE (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses need to be considered. Clinical trials in other indications such as Parkinson’s disease have reported mixed outcomes with MitoQ, leading to concerns about its translation from well-controlled preclinical settings to the complex environment of human disease (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). Moreover, the potential for pro-oxidant effects at high concentrations—as sometimes observed with redox-active compounds like MitoQ—is a dose optimization challenge that must be carefully managed in any clinical development program (Gueven et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014). The fact that the reported retinal uptake of MitoQ is modest (~1% of plasma levels) may necessitate higher systemic doses or alternative delivery routes to ensure that sufficient drug reaches the RPE, which in turn could raise safety issues if off-target effects occur (Apostolova & Victor, 2015). Additionally, while the biochemical rationale is compelling, there is currently no direct clinical evidence for efficacy in dry AMD; this gap underscores the need for further targeted preclinical investigations using dry AMD-relevant animal models and subsequent early-phase clinical trials.

In summary, the overall evaluation favours exploration of MitoQ as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its strong mechanistic foundation—based on mitochondrial targeting, catalytic ROS scavenging, and preservation of Δψm—aligns well with the known etiopathogenesis of dry AMD, which involves RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. The extensive preclinical and early clinical data supporting MitoQ’s safety and efficacy in other indications further bolster its candidacy. However, attention must be given to optimizing dosing regimens and delivery strategies to overcome the limitation of modest retinal uptake, as well as rigorously establishing its efficacy specifically in models of dry AMD before advancing to large-scale clinical trials. Given its unique properties and the urgent need for effective treatments in dry AMD, MitoQ merits further investigation as part of a comprehensive strategy to combat RPE degeneration and preserve visual function in affected patients (Cores et al., 2023; Zielonka et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014; Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
S3QEL-2 is a synthetic small‐molecule member of the S3QEL (Suppressors of Superoxide production from mitochondrial Complex III) class, originally discovered through a high‐throughput screen of approximately 635,000 small molecules using isolated mitochondria and an Amplex UltraRed H₂O₂ detection assay (Orr et al., 2015). In this screening paradigm, compounds were rigorously selected for their ability to selectively suppress superoxide generation arising from the Qo site of mitochondrial Complex III without impairing oxidative phosphorylation or altering the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) (Orr et al., 2015). The discovery approach involved counterscreens that monitored Δψm changes, respiration rates, and markers of cellular viability, ensuring that S3QEL-2 exhibits specificity in mitigating reactive oxygen species (ROS) production rather than acting as a nonspecific antioxidant or uncoupler (Orr et al., 2015). S3QEL-2 was sourced from commercial screening collections—for example, vendors such as Chemdiv—and its powder-stock purity was confirmed by HPLC–MS analysis (Orr et al., 2015). As a member of a structurally diverse chemotype group, S3QEL-2 belongs to a new class of mitochondrial ROS-targeted modulators that differ fundamentally from classical Complex III inhibitors such as antimycin A or myxothiazol; unlike these inhibitors, S3QELs do not block the electron transfer chain or impair ATP production, but rather reduce the electron leak from the semiquinone intermediate at the Qo site (Orr et al., 2015). In general, compounds in the S3QEL class have been used experimentally as probes to decouple pathological ROS generation from normal bioenergetic function in diverse cell types, with applications ranging from studies on hypoxia-induced transcription (e.g., HIF-1α signaling) to experiments investigating ROS-mediated cell stress in pancreatic β-cells (Orr et al., 2015). The commercial catalog number Cayman Chemical #26918 identifies S3QEL-2 for research purposes, which suggests that this compound is available for repurposing studies beyond its initial characterization in nonocular systems (Orr et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Although S3QEL-2 was originally developed as a novel chemical probe to selectively suppress Complex III-derived superoxide production, its preclinical evaluation has been extensive within the context of cellular models evaluating ROS-mediated signaling and cell stress responses (Orr et al., 2015). In cellular assays, S3QEL-2 has demonstrated the ability to reduce H₂O₂ production in isolated mitochondria, lower HIF-1α transcription in hypoxia-challenged HEK-293 cells, and protect pancreatic β-cells from oxidative stress-induced apoptosis during islet isolation and culture (Orr et al., 2015). Notably, in studies where cells were exposed to concentrations up to 20× the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC₅₀) determined for site IIIQo superoxide production, S3QEL-2 did not impair basal or uncoupled respiration, nor did it compromise mitochondrial viability (Orr et al., 2015). Additionally, S3QEL-2 has been employed as a pharmacological tool in experiments on human monocyte-derived macrophages, where it contributed to demonstrating that inhibition of mitochondrial ROS can reduce inflammasome activation and subsequent IL-18 secretion upon stimulation by the complement membrane attack complex (MAC) (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). However, despite its utility in these nonocular systems—where mitochondrial ROS inhibition was linked to attenuation of inflammatory cytokine pathways—there is little to no published preclinical or clinical data directly evaluating S3QEL-2 in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models or in other ocular disease contexts (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2015). While the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of dry AMD, particularly those involving chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and associated inflammasome activation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, are well documented (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013), a direct therapeutic history for S3QEL-2 in retinal or AMD models remains absent in the current literature (Korhonen, 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Thus, S3QEL-2 represents a promising repurposing candidate that has been validated in other contexts of ROS-related cellular stress but has not yet been explicitly applied to the treatment of dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of S3QEL-2 is based on its capacity to selectively suppress superoxide generation originating at the Qo site of mitochondrial Complex III. Under normal conditions, the electron transport chain (ETC) can leak electrons during the reduction of oxygen, particularly at the semiquinone intermediate at the Qo site, resulting in the formation of superoxide—a primary reactive oxygen species (Orr et al., 2015). S3QEL-2 does not act as a general ROS scavenger; rather, it modulates the rate constant for the electron transfer from the semiquinone to molecular oxygen without significantly altering the steady-state levels of semiquinone species or the redox poise of the ubiquinone (Q) pool (Orr et al., 2015). This selective inhibition of ROS generation is achieved through an allosteric modulation of protein conformation within Complex III, specifically targeting the Qo site to reduce electron leak while sparing the remainder of the electron transport processes (Orr et al., 2015). By decreasing superoxide production, S3QEL-2 effectively reduces the downstream formation of H₂O₂ as detected by Amplex UltraRed assays, a finding that has been consistently reproduced in isolated mitochondrial studies (Orr et al., 2015). Moreover, because S3QEL-2 does not interfere with the overall electron flux or the maintenance of Δψm, it preserves the bioenergetic capacity of the mitochondria—a critical factor in tissues with high metabolic demands such as the RPE (Orr et al., 2015). On a molecular level, the compound’s activity at nanomolar to low micromolar concentrations (with a reported mean IC₅₀ around 1.7 μM for S3QEL-2) suggests a highly potent modulation of the ROS generation pathway that is independent of the mitochondrial matrix redox state (Orr et al., 2015). This targeted approach is further distinguished from classical Complex III inhibitors like myxothiazol and antimycin A, which disrupt the entire electron transport process and can lead to a collapse in mitochondrial function; in contrast, S3QEL-2 specifically mitigates the pathological component of ROS production while maintaining ATP synthesis and cellular energy homeostasis (Orr et al., 2015). In macrophages and other cell types, the reduction in mitochondrial ROS production by S3QEL-2 has been shown to blunt ROS-dependent signaling pathways, such as the stabilization of the transcription factor HIF-1α under hypoxic conditions, and to decrease the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Toma et al., 2021). Thus, the molecular interactions of S3QEL-2 within Complex III position it as a potential modulator of redox signaling pathways that are implicated in inflammatory and degenerative processes, including those observed in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Based on its established mechanism of action, the use of S3QEL-2 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells is expected to selectively reduce mitochondrial ROS generated at the Complex III Qo site. In dry age-related macular degeneration, one of the prevailing hypotheses attributes disease progression to chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction within the RPE, leading to the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and subsequent secretion of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013). The selective inhibition of ROS by S3QEL-2 should therefore interrupt this pathological signaling cascade. In an in vitro assay using RPE cells—cells that have been shown to express components of the NLRP3 inflammasome and are especially vulnerable to oxidative insults—the drug is anticipated to lower ROS markers, as measured by fluorescent dyes (for example, oxidized carboxy-H₂DCFDA), without compromising the cells' mitochondrial respiration or Δψm (Orr et al., 2015). With less mitochondrial ROS available to act as secondary messengers, the downstream stabilization of HIF-1α under stress conditions is expected to be reduced, and the inflammatory response mediated by inflammasome assembly will likely be attenuated (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Orr et al., 2015). Given that multiple studies have demonstrated the role of mitochondrial ROS in directly or indirectly activating NLRP3 inflammasome signaling in both macrophages and RPE cells (Gao et al., 2015; Campbell & Doyle, 2013; Piippo, 2019), the hypothesis is that S3QEL-2 will break this mtROS–NLRP3 axis. In a therapeutic assay, one would expect that RPE cells treated with S3QEL-2 under conditions of complement dysregulation (a known contributor to dry AMD pathology) would demonstrate not only reduced markers of oxidative stress and inflammasome activation but also improved cellular viability, decreased apoptosis, and maintenance of proper metabolic function (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). Furthermore, if S3QEL-2 can lower the intracellular superoxide burden, it might also reduce the formation of oxidized lipids and other damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that contribute to the progression of AMD (Campbell & Doyle, 2013; Toma et al., 2021). Overall, the strategic downregulation of mitochondrial ROS production should translate into a protective phenotype in RPE cells by interrupting the signaling mechanisms that lead to chronic inflammation and cell death in the context of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
S3QEL-2 emerges as an attractive candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to its unique pharmacological profile and precision in targeting mitochondrial ROS production. One of the key strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its ability to selectively suppress superoxide generation at the Complex III Qo site without impairing the overall electron transport chain function or disrupting mitochondrial membrane potential (Orr et al., 2015). This high degree of specificity is particularly valuable in a disease such as dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central to pathogenesis yet preserving the RPE’s bioenergetic capacity is essential for retinal health (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013). The preclinical data available for S3QEL-2 in nonocular systems—ranging from hypoxia-induced HIF-1α modulation to protection of pancreatic β-cells and dampening of inflammasome activation in macrophages—suggest that its mechanism of action may well translate to the RPE, a cell type that is similarly sensitive to mitochondrial oxidative stress (Orr et al., 2015; Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). Moreover, the ability of S3QEL-2 to reduce mitochondrial ROS levels without interfering with ATP production positions it as a promising agent for interrupting the mtROS–NLRP3 inflammasome axis that is proposed to drive inflammatory responses in the geographic atrophy observed in dry AMD (Orr et al., 2015; Orr et al., 2015).

However, several weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. Despite the encouraging preclinical data in cell culture and isolated mitochondrial systems, there is currently no direct evidence linking S3QEL-2 to therapeutic benefit in retinal models or in dry AMD specifically (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2015). The candidate has been primarily evaluated in nonocular models, and the complex microenvironment of the retina—including the blood-retinal barrier, immune cell interactions, and local complement dysregulation—may pose significant challenges in translating in vitro efficacy to in vivo benefit (Korhonen, 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Furthermore, while S3QEL-2 has been shown to reduce ROS-mediated signaling in macrophages and pancreatic islets, the pharmacokinetic properties, tissue distribution, and long-term safety profile of this compound in ocular tissues remain to be determined (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Orr et al., 2015). Delivery of S3QEL-2 to the retina may require formulation strategies that overcome solubility and permeability barriers inherent in drug delivery to the posterior segment of the eye. Another concern is the potential for off-target effects that, while not evident in the isolated systems tested so far, may manifest in the complex in vivo environment or with chronic administration (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Orr et al., 2015).

In addition, the exact molecular site of action on Complex III is not yet fully delineated at the atomic level, meaning that while the compound has been shown to modulate ROS production, the precise binding interactions and potential variability between different cell types or individuals remain uncertain (Orr et al., 2015). This incomplete mechanistic detail could complicate structure-activity relationship (SAR) explorations, as well as efforts to optimize the compound further for better efficacy or reduced toxicity in an ocular setting.

From a therapeutic perspective, the hypothesis that S3QEL-2 can reduce inflammasome activation by lowering mitochondrial ROS is strongly supported by data in other cell types, particularly where a reduction in ROS has been correlated with lower levels of IL-1β and IL-18 secretion (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). Given the well-established involvement of mitochondrial ROS and NLRP3 inflammasome activation in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013), S3QEL-2 holds promise as a tool to dissect and potentially therapeutically modulate this axis. However, concrete evidence in AMD-relevant models, especially primary RPE cells derived from patients or appropriate animal models, is necessary before advancing this compound further in the drug development pipeline (Korhonen, 2024; Macchioni et al., 2020).

In summary, the strengths of S3QEL-2 lie in its high selectivity for Complex III-derived ROS suppression, preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics, and the proven ability to modulate ROS-dependent inflammatory pathways in several preclinical settings (Orr et al., 2015). Its repurposing for dry AMD is biochemically plausible and aligns with the current understanding of the disease, where chronic low-level oxidative stress and inflammasome activation play central roles in RPE dysfunction and geographic atrophy (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013). Conversely, weaknesses include the absence of direct preclinical evidence in ocular models, potential pharmacokinetic and delivery challenges, and an incomplete elucidation of its binding mechanism at the atomic level. Considering these factors, S3QEL-2 represents a highly promising candidate that merits further investigation through targeted preclinical studies in retinal and RPE models, including assessments of its delivery, efficacy in reducing NLRP3-driven cytokine release, and long-term safety in ocular tissues (Gao et al., 2015; Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Ultimately, while S3QEL-2 is supported by robust biochemical data in nonocular systems and has a compelling mechanism that could translate into therapeutic benefit for dry AMD, additional focused research in AMD-relevant models is essential to validate its potential as a repurposed drug candidate for this challenging indication.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
XJB-5-131 is a synthetic mitochondria‐targeted nitroxide antioxidant that was developed by conjugating a redox‐active nitroxide moiety (derived from TEMPO, 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl) to a mitochondrial‐targeting peptide fragment derived from gramicidin S (often described in the literature as a hemigramicidin or alkene peptide isostere) (Liu et al., 2022; Robinson, 2012). This design harnesses the properties of the nitroxide, which is capable of catalytically scavenging reactive oxygen and lipid radicals through cycling between its nitroxide, hydroxylamine, and oxoammonium states, and the targeting moiety that enhances its lipid membrane permeability while concentrating the compound specifically in mitochondrial membranes (Wipf et al., 2022; Xun et al., 2022). The neutral charge of XJB-5-131 confers an advantage because it permits mitochondrial uptake independent of membrane potential, a feature that distinguishes it from the positively charged mitochondria-targeted antioxidants such as MitoQ (Robinson, 2012; Wipf et al., 2022). Moreover, fluorescent derivatives (e.g., BODIPY-labeled analogs) have been used to confirm its preferential accumulation in mitochondria by co-localization with mitochondrial markers, demonstrating an approximately 600-fold enrichment relative to the cytosol in some animal models (Wipf et al., 2022; Xun et al., 2022). Overall, XJB-5-131 belongs to the class of mitochondria-targeted nitroxides, a class that has been extensively studied for its ability to modulate oxidative stress in cellular and animal models across a variety of tissues (Xun et al., 2022; Robinson, 2012).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, XJB-5-131 has been the subject of preclinical investigation in several models of oxidative stress-related injury. It was originally developed to protect neuronal mitochondria and has been evaluated in models of Huntington’s disease, where it mitigated somatic instability and toxicity by reducing oxidative DNA damage and delaying motor decline (Liu et al., 2022; Xun et al., 2022). In various studies, XJB-5-131 demonstrated robust efficacy in reducing mitochondrial lipid peroxidation and preserving electron transport chain function in brain, neuronal, and even cardiac cell models (Robinson, 2012; Wipf et al., 2022). Additionally, its use in spinal cord injury models has shown that it can attenuate cardiolipin oxidation and reduce the activation of apoptotic cascades, leading to decreased lesion sizes and improved functional recovery (Ji et al., 2015; Robinson, 2012). There is also evidence of its application in models of ischemia–reperfusion injury, where its ability to blunt the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) was associated with neuroprotection (Xun et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022). Outside of central nervous system paradigms, related mitochondria-targeted nitroxides have been applied in experimental settings addressing ferroptosis and other oxidative stress pathologies (Zhang et al., 2024; Xun et al., 2022). However, despite its established role in neurological and other high-oxidative stress tissues, there is no direct published record – within the context of the available literature – demonstrating that XJB-5-131 has been used to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or any retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)-specific diseases (Wipf et al., 2022). Nonetheless, its pharmacological profile suggests potential applicability in settings where chronic oxidative stress drives pathology.

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism by which XJB-5-131 exerts its effects is twofold. First, the nitroxide moiety functions as a redox-active electron scavenger. Under oxidative stress, the nitroxide group readily interconverts with its hydroxylamine and oxoammonium forms; this redox cycling is capable of neutralizing superoxide anions (O2•–) by oxidizing them to molecular oxygen and hydrogen peroxide, effectively mimicking the activity of superoxide dismutase (SOD) (Wipf et al., 2022). Additionally, the hydroxylamine state can donate a hydrogen atom to terminate radical chain reactions, thereby neutralizing lipid peroxyl radicals that propagate lipid peroxidation – a process central to drusen formation and RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Robinson, 2012; Xun et al., 2022). Second, the gramicidin-derived delivery moiety imparts mitochondrial selectivity due to its structural mimicry of naturally occurring cyclic peptides that exhibit high lipid membrane affinity. This results in an efficient and selective accumulation of the antioxidant within the inner mitochondrial membrane, which is particularly important given that mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage have been implicated in aging and various degenerative diseases (Wipf et al., 2022). Experimental studies have shown that XJB-5-131 can act as a mild uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation, leading to a slight increase in oxygen consumption without detrimentally affecting ATP production; this mild uncoupling may serve to lower the mitochondrial membrane potential, thereby reducing the propensity for electron leakage and subsequent ROS generation (Xun et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2024). Furthermore, XJB-5-131’s ability to reduce mitochondrial ROS levels has been documented using both biochemical assays based on Amplex Red for hydrogen peroxide detection and Seahorse assays for oxygen consumption rate (OCR) analysis (Xun et al., 2022). These combined actions—the direct scavenging of radical species and the dampening of ROS-generating processes via mild uncoupling—support a mechanism by which XJB-5-131 could preserve mitochondrial structure (e.g., cristae integrity) and function under chronic oxidative conditions.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD and RPE Context:  
In the context of dry AMD, the pathophysiology is strongly linked to chronic oxidative insult, particularly within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where elevated ROS and lipid peroxidation contribute to mitochondrial dysfunction, accumulation of drusen constituents, and eventual RPE degeneration. The dual mechanism of XJB-5-131 is especially promising for this disease. Given its lipid radical scavenging capabilities, XJB-5-131 is expected to reduce malondialdehyde (MDA) and other markers of lipid peroxidation that are elevated in RPE under chronic UVA or other oxidative stresses (Ji et al., 2015). The compound’s well-documented ability to decrease ROS levels in neuronal and cardiac models, while preserving overall mitochondrial respiration, suggests that similar protective effects can be anticipated in RPE cells, which are highly metabolically active and depend critically on mitochondrial health (Wipf et al., 2022). In preliminary in vitro assays – such as those using pig RPE explants under UVA stress – one would expect XJB-5-131 to reduce MDA-adduct formation and preserve mitochondrial cristae, thereby maintaining cellular homeostasis (the hypothesis provided). At a molecular level, by delivering the nitroxide directly into RPE mitochondria, the compound would catalytically neutralize both superoxide and lipid peroxyl radicals. This dual scavenging effect can interrupt the vicious cycle of chronic oxidative damage that drives RPE dysfunction and drusen accumulation (Liu et al., 2022). Expression studies have demonstrated that genes associated with oxidative stress regulation, such as those encoding SOD and other mitochondrial antioxidants, are active in RPE cells, further supporting the notion that a mitochondria-targeted intervention like XJB-5-131 could restore redox homeostasis in these cells (Wipf et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024). Additionally, by functionally acting as a mild uncoupler, XJB-5-131 may lower mitochondrial membrane potential just enough to reduce electron leakage without compromising adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthesis, a delicate balance that is particularly important given the high energy requirements of the RPE (Zhou et al., 2024; Ji et al., 2015). Altogether, these effects are anticipated to culminate in the preservation of cristae integrity, reduced oxidative damage, and ultimately improved cell survival—key outcomes that align with the therapeutic goals in treating dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, XJB-5-131 emerges as an attractive candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD owing to several intrinsic strengths. Foremost among these is its robust mitochondrial targeting capability. The incorporation of a gramicidin S-derived peptide moiety ensures that the nitroxide antioxidant is selectively delivered to mitochondria, a critical advantage because mitochondrial dysfunction is central to the pathology of dry AMD (Liu et al., 2022; Robinson, 2012). Its redox cycling properties not only mirror those of enzymatic antioxidants like SOD but also extend protection by neutralizing lipid peroxyl radicals, thereby addressing both protein and lipid oxidation pathways that contribute to drusen formation and RPE cell death (Wipf et al., 2022). Moreover, the reported preclinical successes in neurological and cardiac models, where XJB-5-131 has been shown to mitigate oxidative damage, reduce apoptotic signaling, and improve tissue function, suggest potential translatability of these protective effects to the ocular milieu (Robinson, 2012; Xun et al., 2022). The fact that its use as a mild uncoupler does not compromise ATP production provides an additional safety margin when considering tissues with high energy demands such as the RPE (Xun et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2024).

Nevertheless, there are certain limitations and challenges that must be carefully considered before advancing XJB-5-131 into dry AMD studies. Notably, while its efficacy in neuronal, spinal cord, and ischemia-reperfusion models has been well documented, there is a paucity of direct preclinical data demonstrating its benefits specifically in RPE cells or models of retinal degeneration (Wipf et al., 2022; Robinson, 2012). The hypothesis that it can reduce MDA-adduct formation in pig RPE explants under UVA stress is promising; however, this observation must be validated in more comprehensive models of dry AMD that mimic the chronic oxidative environment of the human RPE. Additionally, the complex synthetic route—often reported to involve multiple steps and potentially low water solubility—could pose a challenge for scale-up manufacturing and may necessitate formulation strategies to optimize bioavailability for ocular applications (Wipf et al., 2022; Kaden & Li, 2013). Delivery to the posterior segment of the eye also remains a significant hurdle; while systemic administration has been effective in other animal models, local delivery methods (e.g., intravitreal injection or novel nanocarrier systems) may be required to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE without off-target effects. Furthermore, despite promising indications of safety in long-term animal studies (with chronic dosing in rodent models showing minimal adverse effects), thorough toxicological investigations will be essential given the sensitive nature of the retinal environment (Wipf et al., 2022; Echeverri-Ruiz et al., 2018). Finally, while the dual scavenging of superoxide and lipid radicals is mechanistically compelling, the risk of interfering with physiological redox signaling must be carefully balanced to avoid unintended consequences on cellular homeostasis (Xun et al., 2022).

In summary, XJB-5-131 represents a highly innovative and mechanistically sound candidate with significant potential for repurposing in dry AMD. Its ability to deliver a nitroxide antioxidant directly to mitochondria, neutralize deleterious ROS, and preserve mitochondrial function aligns well with the current understanding of RPE pathology in dry AMD. The extensive preclinical data in other high-oxidative stress models provide a strong rationale for its further evaluation in ocular-specific models. However, the absence of direct RPE or retinal degeneration studies, formulation and delivery challenges, and the inherent complexity of its synthesis necessitate a cautious and well-planned approach moving forward. Future research should focus on rigorous evaluation in RPE cell culture systems and animal models of dry AMD, optimization of ocular delivery strategies, and comprehensive toxicological assessments to ensure both efficacy and safety in the intended indication (Xun et al., 2022; Bowie, 2018; Wipf et al., 2022). Overall, while challenges remain, the unique pharmacological profile of XJB-5-131 provides a strong basis for considering it as a therapeutic candidate in the fight against dry age-related macular degeneration.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Deferiprone is a synthetic iron‐chelating agent originally developed for the treatment of transfusional iron overload disorders, particularly in patients with thalassemia major. It belongs to the hydroxypyridinone class of therapeutic compounds and is characterized by its low molecular weight and lipophilic nature, features that allow it to penetrate cell membranes and cross the blood–brain and blood–retinal barriers (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). Chemically, deferiprone is a bidentate ligand that interacts with iron by coordinating via its hydroxypyridinone groups, forming a neutral complex in a 3:1 stoichiometry with ferric iron (Fe3+), although some studies note its affinity for both Fe3+ and Fe2+ under certain conditions (Li et al., 2023). The synthetic origins of deferiprone involve chemical design strategies aimed at generating small, orally active chelators with selective affinity for iron over other metals such as zinc, copper, and aluminium (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). As a member of the iron chelator drug class, deferiprone’s established use in treating systemic iron overload syndromes has provided it with a significant clinical track record over several decades, forming the basis for its repurposing in disorders where iron-induced oxidative damage plays a role.  

Therapeutic History:  
Deferiprone has been used clinically as an orally administered iron chelator in the management of transfusional iron overload, notably in patients with thalassemia major. This usage is supported by multiple clinical studies and reviews that address both its efficacy in reducing systemic iron burden as well as its associated hematologic risks, such as agranulocytosis and neutropenia, which occur in approximately 1% of patients (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). Beyond its systemic application, preclinical models have demonstrated deferiprone’s potential for retinal protection. Several animal studies report that deferiprone, when administered systemically, can reduce retinal and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) iron levels in models of iron overload or light-induced degeneration and produce improvements in oxidative stress markers and retinal functional indices (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). Although deferiprone has not been widely tested or approved specifically for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar ocular conditions in clinical trials, its documented experimental benefits in animal retinal models along with its established clinical safety profile in iron overload therapy have prompted its consideration for repurposing in dry AMD where iron-induced oxidative injury is implicated (Shahandeh et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2021; Ueda et al., 2018).  

Mechanism of Action:  
Deferiprone functions primarily by chelating labile iron, thereby limiting the pool of redox active iron that can participate in the Fenton reaction—a process in which ferrous iron (Fe2+) reacts with hydrogen peroxide to produce highly reactive hydroxyl radicals. The molecular mechanism of deferiprone is based on its bidentate hydroxypyridinone structure that binds Fe3+ to form a stable neutral complex in a 3:1 chelator to iron ratio, a coordination chemistry that has been well documented in several studies (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). This complex formation effectively reduces the availability of free iron in the intracellular labile iron pool, thereby diminishing iron-catalyzed reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. In addition, some data suggest that deferiprone may also interact with ferrous iron under certain conditions, contributing further to its antioxidant effects by interrupting redox cycling associated with both Fe3+ and Fe2+ species (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021).  

From a biochemical standpoint, iron accumulation in the RPE and surrounding retinal tissues is known to promote lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial oxidative stress, leading to cellular dysfunction and death—a pathomechanism observed in dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). Deferiprone’s cell permeability and ability to traverse biological barriers enables it to access the intracellular compartments, including mitochondria. Although direct studies examining deferiprone’s effect specifically on RPE mitochondrial iron pools are still limited, evidence from other systems (such as neuronal and cardiac tissues) demonstrates that reducing mitochondrial iron load can preserve electron transport chain (ETC) integrity by preventing the formation of deleterious hydroxyl radicals that otherwise damage mitochondrial lipids, proteins, and DNA (Li et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023). Furthermore, preclinical models of retinal injury have shown that deferiprone treatment leads to a reduction in oxidative stress markers, including decreased malondialdehyde (MDA) levels and a concomitant increase in antioxidants such as glutathione (GSH), which supports the hypothesis that iron chelation by deferiprone interrupts the cascade of iron-mediated oxidative damage (Shahandeh et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2025). There is also emerging evidence that iron chelators like deferiprone can mitigate cell death pathways such as ferroptosis and parthanatos in retinal tissues, contributing to neuroprotective outcomes (Villarejo-Zori et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025). In summary, the mechanism of action of deferiprone is multifaceted: it directly reduces the labile iron concentration, thereby lowering the potential for Fenton chemistry, indirectly stabilizes mitochondrial function, and may influence downstream iron-dependent cellular pathways that are implicated in retinal degeneration (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2025).  

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of deferiprone for dry AMD is that chelation of labile iron in RPE mitochondria will prevent Fenton reaction–mediated ROS formation and maintain the integrity of the ETC. In the proposed assay and eventual clinical application, treatment with deferiprone is expected to significantly reduce intracellular labile iron, thereby attenuating oxidative stress that leads to lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial dysfunction. This, in turn, should result in a lower rate of RPE cell death and preserve photoreceptor viability, thereby potentially slowing the progression of dry AMD (Liu et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023).  

Experimental studies have shown that oral administration of deferiprone in animal models results in a measurable decrease in retinal iron load without causing retinal toxicity—a finding that is pivotal for any drug intended for chronic ophthalmic use (Zhao et al., 2025; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). In parallel, in vitro studies using retinal cells such as ARPE-19 have demonstrated that deferiprone reduces markers of oxidative stress, including lower MDA levels and preservation of antioxidant enzyme activities (for example, GPX4 upregulation), which are indicative of reduced ROS-mediated damage (Yang et al., 2025; Shahandeh et al., 2020). The proposed mechanism of action implies that by decreasing the availability of iron necessary for Fenton chemistry, deferiprone will decrease the production of hydroxyl radicals, thus protecting mitochondrial membranes and proteins integral to the ETC from oxidative damage (Li et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023). Moreover, since mitochondrial dysfunction is a known contributor to RPE degeneration in dry AMD, its preservation via iron chelation is expected to sustain cellular ATP production and overall cell viability (Zhao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). Given that the RPE expresses iron regulatory proteins and that dysregulated iron metabolism has been observed in AMD retinas (with increased ferritin and altered transferrin receptor expression), the application of deferiprone would ideally restore homeostasis in the labile iron pool and thereby ameliorate the chronic oxidative insult observed in dry AMD (Li et al., 2023; Ashok et al., 2021).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Deferiprone presents several strengths as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD therapy. Firstly, its well-established clinical use in treating systemic iron overload confers a robust foundation regarding its pharmacokinetics, dosing parameters, and safety profile—despite noted hematologic risks such as agranulocytosis that occur in a small percentage of patients (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). Its oral bioavailability and ability to cross the blood–retinal barrier make it uniquely suited for targeting intracellular iron in the retina (Li et al., 2023). Secondly, there is compelling preclinical evidence from various retinal degeneration models that iron chelators, including deferiprone, can reduce retinal iron accumulation, diminish oxidative stress, and improve functional outcomes, which supports the rationale for its repurposing in the context of dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016; Zhao et al., 2025). Thirdly, its mode of action—chelating labile iron to prevent Fenton reaction–mediated ROS production—directly targets a central pathological mechanism implicated in dry AMD. The hypothesis that reducing mitochondrial iron load will preserve ETC integrity is biologically plausible given the importance of iron-catalyzed oxidative stress in mitochondrial dysfunction within the RPE (Li et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023).  

On the other hand, several weaknesses and uncertainties remain. Although deferiprone’s effectiveness in reducing systemic and retinal iron overload has been demonstrated in animal models, direct evidence of its capacity to specifically target RPE mitochondrial iron and preserve ETC function in human RPE cells is currently limited (Zhao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023). The precise molecular details regarding how deferiprone modulates mitochondrial iron trafficking, and how this relates to the functional maintenance of the electron transport chain, require further investigation. Additionally, while preclinical data are supportive, deferiprone has not yet been tested in clinical trials specifically for dry AMD, and its long-term safety and efficacy in the ocular context remain to be established (Zhao et al., 2021; Ueda et al., 2018). Another consideration is the risk of adverse systemic effects, such as neutropenia and agranulocytosis, which, although infrequent, could limit its utility in a population of elderly patients with dry AMD who may have co‐morbidities (Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). Moreover, some reports have suggested that under low concentrations or certain conditions, iron chelators might paradoxically participate in free radical formation, necessitating precise dose titration and careful monitoring (Li et al., 2023; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016).  

In summary, deferiprone appears to be a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its well-documented ability to chelate labile iron, its favorable pharmacologic properties including oral bioavailability and tissue penetration, and preclinical evidence showing retinal protection. Its mechanism of action—reducing the labile iron pool to limit Fenton reaction–induced oxidative stress—addresses a central pathogenic mechanism of dry AMD, namely, iron accumulation leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and lipid peroxidation in the RPE (Zhao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). However, the extrapolation of these preclinical findings to human dry AMD requires additional studies, particularly those that directly measure mitochondrial iron dynamics and ETC activity in RPE cells following deferiprone treatment. Rigorous dose-ranging and safety studies will also be necessary to mitigate the risk of hematologic adverse effects. Therefore, while deferiprone has significant potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD, further preclinical mechanistic studies and early-phase clinical trials are essential to fully validate its efficacy and safety in this new therapeutic context (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Ueda et al., 2018).
