Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Spermidine is a naturally occurring polyamine that was originally discovered in bovine semen and later shown to be ubiquitous in all forms of life, ranging from bacteria and plants to fungi and mammals. It belongs to the aliphatic polyamine class, characterized by its low molecular weight, linear arrangement, and multiple amino groups that are fully protonated at physiological pH. Its natural origins stem from highly conserved enzymatic biosynthetic pathways—starting either from ornithine via ornithine decarboxylase or from arginine through an agmatine intermediate—resulting in the formation of putrescine, which is subsequently converted to spermidine through the transfer of an aminopropyl group provided by decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine (dcSAM) (Casero & Marton, 2007; Hobley et al., 2017; Khomutov et al., 2019). Although spermidine can be isolated from natural sources such as food and tissues, it is also available in a chemically defined form commercially (for example, Sigma-Aldrich S2626) and has been used in basic research as well as in some experimental therapeutic approaches. This compound is representative of the polyamine family, and these molecules have traditionally been investigated for their roles in cellular proliferation, nucleic acid stabilization, and modulation of various enzymatic activities, which in turn have broad implications for health and disease (Madeo et al., 2020; Nichugovskiy et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, spermidine’s potential therapeutic applications have been explored extensively in the context of its ability to induce autophagy and affect cellular homeostasis. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that spermidine supplementation can extend lifespan and improve the function of various tissues by enhancing autophagy, contributing to cardioprotection, and promoting neuroprotection in animal models (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). In the ocular domain, several studies have examined its effects on retinal cells: in vitro experiments using ARPE-19 retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells have shown that spermidine can protect against oxidative stress induced by hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) by mitigating intracellular calcium overload and maintaining mitochondrial integrity (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021). Additionally, there are preclinical observations in which intravitreal administration of spermidine in animal models produced both protective effects—in terms of reducing RPE apoptosis—and, at higher doses, toxic outcomes such as RPE necrosis and photoreceptor degeneration (Ohashi et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022). Although spermidine has not been clinically trialed specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), its effects on RPE survival and ocular inflammation have been documented in models that mimic some of the pathophysiologic stressors in dry AMD, such as oxidative damage and dysregulated autophagy (Kim et al., 2021; Senekowitsch et al., 2023). In addition, dietary supplementation studies in humans have associated higher spermidine intake with various beneficial health outcomes, including improved endothelial function and cognitive performance; however, the use of spermidine or polyamines more broadly in chronic degenerative ocular conditions remains largely in the preclinical stage (Madeo et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
The hypothesized mechanism for using spermidine in dry AMD is multifaceted and centers on its ability to modulate cellular quality control processes. At the molecular level, spermidine is known to induce autophagy, a process that mediates the degradation and recycling of damaged or dysfunctional cellular constituents. In model systems ranging from yeast to mammalian cells, spermidine has been shown to increase the conversion of the autophagy marker LC3-I to LC3-II, thereby promoting autophagosome formation (Qin et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022). One important molecular target of spermidine appears to be EP300 (p300), a histone acetyltransferase that, when inhibited, leads to reduced acetylation of several autophagy-related proteins. Inhibition of EP300 has been correlated with enhanced autophagic flux, and several studies suggest that spermidine may exert its autophagy-inducing effects partly by downregulating EP300 expression or activity (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020).

In addition to its effects on EP300, spermidine has been implicated in the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), an evolutionarily conserved energy sensor that modulates metabolic homeostasis and mitochondrial quality control. Activation of AMPK can lead to the phosphorylation and activation of downstream effectors that promote both autophagy and mitophagy (the selective autophagic removal of damaged mitochondria). While direct evidence for AMPK activation by spermidine in retinal cells is still emerging, broader studies in other cell types have described an upregulation of pathways associated with mitochondrial biogenesis and quality control, including the deacetylation of proteins by SIRT1, which often acts in concert with AMPK (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). In the specific context of RPE cells under stress from A2E (a component of lipofuscin) or H₂O₂, the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria and high levels of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) play critical roles in cell loss and dysfunction; thus, induction of mitophagy via enhanced AMPK signaling and subsequent Parkin recruitment to depolarized mitochondria could improve mitochondrial homeostasis and reduce oxidative damage (Kim et al., 2021).

Furthermore, spermidine’s role as an intracellular calcium chelator appears pivotal in its protective effect in RPE cells. Studies have demonstrated that pre-treatment of ARPE-19 cells with 10 µM spermidine prior to oxidative stress prevents intracellular Ca²⁺ overload—a phenomenon that can trigger endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and cell death—thereby maintaining cellular integrity independent of direct ROS scavenging (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021). In summary, spermidine is posited to enhance the clearance of damaged organelles—particularly mitochondria—by increasing autophagic flux through EP300 inhibition and AMPK activation, leading to enhanced LC3-II conversion and Parkin-mediated mitophagy. This, in turn, is expected to reduce mtROS and protect RPE cell viability under conditions of oxidative and A2E-induced stress (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its mode of action, the expected effect of spermidine in a dry AMD model would be a pronounced improvement in the quality control mechanisms of RPE cells. The compound is anticipated to induce autophagy, evidenced by a measurable increase in LC3-II levels, alongside enhanced recruitment of the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin to dysfunctional mitochondria. This concerted activation of autophagy and mitophagy should facilitate the clearance of damaged mitochondria, thereby reducing the accumulation of mtROS and attenuating oxidative stress. In the context of A2E accumulation—a key driver of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD—spermidine is predicted to restore mitochondrial function and improve cell viability. Experimental assays are expected to show that spermidine pre-treatment leads to a significant reduction in apoptosis markers (e.g., caspase-3 activation, cytochrome c release), along with improved markers of mitochondrial integrity (e.g., stabilized mitochondrial membrane potential) in ARPE-19 cells exposed to H₂O₂ or A2E (Kim et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating spermidine as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current literature. One major strength is its natural origin and well-documented role as a global inducer of autophagy and mitophagy. This aligns well with the current understanding of dry AMD pathogenesis, in which impaired autophagic clearance and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells play major roles (Nichugovskiy et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2021). The ability of spermidine to inhibit EP300—a factor whose downregulation encourages autophagy—and to potentially activate AMPK signaling suggests that it could enhance several intracellular quality control processes simultaneously (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). The preclinical data showing that spermidine can protect ARPE-19 cells from H₂O₂-induced oxidative injury by blocking Ca²⁺ overload and reducing apoptotic signaling further bolster its potential utility in ocular applications (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021).

However, there are notable challenges and weaknesses associated with this therapeutic candidate. First, the dose response appears to be remarkably narrow; while low micromolar concentrations (e.g., 10 µM) exert cytoprotective effects in vitro, higher doses have been associated with cytotoxicity, including RPE cell death and photoreceptor degeneration in animal models following intravitreal injection (Ohashi et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022). This raises concerns about the therapeutic window and the optimal route of delivery for chronic conditions like dry AMD. Another limitation is that, despite promising mechanistic data, direct clinical evidence for the use of spermidine in dry AMD is currently lacking. Most of the studies available have been conducted in vitro or in animal models under conditions of oxidative stress, and while these findings are encouraging, they do not fully recapitulate the complex pathophysiology of dry AMD, which involves not only oxidative damage but also chronic inflammation, immune dysregulation, and drusen accumulation (Kim et al., 2021).

Moreover, while the hypothesis emphasizes effects on EP300 inhibition and AMPK activation leading to enhanced LC3-II conversion and Parkin recruitment, the direct evidence linking these specific molecular events to improved outcomes in dry AMD models remains preliminary. There is a need for more comprehensive studies that directly measure these autophagic and mitophagic markers in RPE cells under conditions that mimic the A2E-induced stress typical of dry AMD (Kim et al., 2021). Additionally, the risk that spermidine’s metabolism by amine oxidases may produce toxic aldehyde byproducts such as acrolein must be carefully considered, as these compounds have been implicated in retinal degeneration in some intravitreal models (Ohashi et al., 2017).

In summary, while spermidine has a compelling mechanistic rationale as a modulator of autophagy and mitochondrial quality control, which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the current preclinical evidence is mixed and highlights potential safety challenges related to dosing and administration. Its established role in promoting cellular longevity and mitigating oxidative stress in diverse tissues certainly warrants further investigation, but rigorous studies using dry AMD-specific models are essential to ascertain its efficacy and safety in this context. Regulatory considerations will also require detailed pharmacokinetic and toxicological profiling, particularly given its dual potential for both cytoprotection and cytotoxicity depending on concentration and route of administration (Ohashi et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022).

Overall, our evaluation suggests that spermidine represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD based on its intrinsic properties as an autophagy and mitophagy inducer and its ability to protect RPE cells from oxidative damage; however, its clinical translation will depend on resolving key issues such as dose optimization, route of delivery, and comprehensive validation of its proposed molecular mechanisms in relevant models of AMD. The strengths of spermidine lie in its natural occurrence, multi-targeted action on cellular quality control mechanisms, and established preclinical benefits in other models of aging and oxidative stress. Conversely, the main weaknesses are its narrow therapeutic window, the potential for generation of toxic metabolites, and the current lack of direct clinical or robust in vivo data in dry AMD models. Further research, including detailed investigations in RPE models using A2E and oxidative stress conditions as well as careful titration studies in animal models of dry AMD, is warranted to determine its viability as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for this unmet clinical need (Casero & Marton, 2007; Kim et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022; Ohashi et al., 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
L-Carnitine is a naturally occurring quaternary ammonium compound, chemically defined as β-hydroxy-γ-trimethylaminobutyrate, that is both derived from the diet (predominantly found in animal-based foods such as red meat) and biosynthesized endogenously from the essential amino acids lysine and methionine via a vitamin C–dependent pathway primarily in the liver and kidneys (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Mollica et al., 2017). Historically, L-carnitine was first identified as a constituent of muscle tissue in the early 20th century and was later linked to its high content in meat, leading to its designation as “vitamin T” in certain insect models (Mollica et al., 2017). As a member of the carnitine family, it belongs to the class of metabolic cofactors or nutraceutical agents whose primary function is to shuttle activated long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondrial matrix, where they undergo β-oxidation, thereby facilitating aerobic energy production and maintaining the intracellular acyl-CoA/CoA balance (Moos et al., 2017; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). This class of compounds has historically been used as dietary supplements to treat primary and secondary carnitine deficiency, as well as in various metabolic and mitochondrial disorders (Flanagan et al., 2010). L-Carnitine is widely formulated in pharmaceutical products both as a standalone supplement and as an ingredient in combination formulations, which underscores its acceptance as a metabolic supportive agent with a favorable safety profile (Flanagan et al., 2010; Surai, 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, the carnitine family has a long record of use in addressing conditions where fatty acid oxidation is impaired. L-Carnitine has been employed effectively as a life-saving therapy in primary carnitine deficiency—a condition in which mutations of the carnitine transporter (OCTN2) impair cellular uptake—and also in secondary deficiencies associated with conditions like renal failure, liver disease, and certain inborn errors of metabolism (Flanagan et al., 2010). Beyond classical deficiency syndromes, both L-carnitine and its acetylated derivative (acetyl-L-carnitine) have been investigated in a broad range of clinical contexts, including cardiovascular diseases, diabetic complications, and neurodegenerative disorders. For example, acetyl-L-carnitine has been shown to improve parameters of visual function in patients with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and to confer neuroprotective effects in Alzheimer’s disease and mild cognitive impairment (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Calabrese et al., 2009).  
In ophthalmology, while most clinical studies have focused on the use of carnitine derivatives for systemic metabolic or neuroprotective effects, there is preclinical evidence supporting an ocular role. Animal studies have identified high intraocular concentrations of carnitine in the lens and other ocular tissues, hinting at a physiological role in maintaining ocular metabolic balance and osmotic homeostasis (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). Investigations into the protective effects of L-carnitine against oxidative damage, including its potential to safeguard retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and other ocular tissues, provide a rationale for its application in dry AMD, particularly in the context of geographic atrophy where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central features (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c). Moreover, combination therapy regimens incorporating acetyl-L-carnitine with n-3 fatty acids and coenzyme Q10 have also been trialed in experimental settings to address energy metabolism in retinal tissues (Shamsi et al., 2007). Despite these promising findings, direct clinical use of L-carnitine as monotherapy for dry AMD has not been extensively reported, thus making its repurposing an area that merits focused research to bridge the gap between its established metabolic functions and its potential application in retinal degeneration (Flanagan et al., 2010; Mollica et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
The central biochemical role of L-carnitine is to facilitate the transport of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle—a process that is critical for β-oxidation and ATP production. This shuttle is mediated by mitochondrial enzymes such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT-1) on the outer mitochondrial membrane, which converts acyl-CoA to acyl-carnitine, and carnitine acyltransferase (also known as carnitine acetyltransferase or CAT) within the mitochondria that re-forms acyl-CoA for oxidation (Moos et al., 2017; Jones et al., 2010). This process not only fuels ATP generation via the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation but also helps regulate the cellular acyl-CoA/CoA ratio, indirectly influencing multiple metabolic pathways (Surai, 2015).  
Furthermore, L-carnitine exhibits antioxidant properties either directly, through free radical scavenging, or indirectly by preserving mitochondrial integrity and function under oxidative stress conditions (Shamsi et al., 2007; Surai, 2015). It has been shown to reduce lipid peroxidation and prevent the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential—a key step in the cascade leading to cellular apoptosis (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c). In addition to its classical mitochondrial functions, L-carnitine also acts as an osmolyte, protecting cells against hyperosmolarity by stabilizing proteins and cellular membranes, which could further reduce oxidative stress (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b; Mollica et al., 2017).  
At the molecular level in the RPE, the hypothesis is that enhancing mitochondrial fatty acid uptake via L-carnitine supplementation will improve β-oxidation efficiency. This is expected to lead to increased ATP production and a reduction in the accumulation of lipid intermediates that may otherwise result in excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation. The reduction in ROS could mitigate chronic oxidative stress, a well established contributor to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Jones et al., 2010; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). Notably, disrupted mitochondrial metabolism and energy deficits have been implicated in the progression of RPE cell dysfunction, and L-carnitine’s role in restoring metabolic flexibility has been documented in other cell types such as hepatocytes and neuronal cells (Ates et al., 2008; Surai, 2015). Additionally, the modulation of mitochondrial protein acetylation by L-carnitine derivatives, an effect observed in various models of aging and metabolic disease, may further contribute to a neuroprotective milieu in RPE cells (Wang et al., 2024; Virmani & Cirulli, 2022).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its multifaceted mechanisms of action, the anticipated effect of L-carnitine in an assay designed for dry age-related macular degeneration is twofold. First, by enhancing mitochondrial fatty acid uptake and increasing β-oxidation rates, L-carnitine is expected to boost ATP production in RPE cells, thereby ameliorating the energy deficits that contribute to cellular dysfunction in geographic atrophy (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Jones et al., 2010). Second, this improved mitochondrial function should lead to a reduction in the generation of ROS that typically arises from lipid overload and subsequent incomplete oxidation, thereby decreasing oxidative damage to critical cellular structures including mitochondrial membranes and nuclear DNA (Shamsi et al., 2007; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a).  
In in vitro assays using cultured RPE cells, one would expect that L-carnitine treatment leads to enhanced mitochondrial respiration, as measured by oxygen consumption rate (OCR), and an associated elevation in ATP levels. Moreover, reductions in established markers of oxidative stress, such as malondialdehyde (MDA) levels or increased glutathione (GSH) concentrations, would support its antioxidant action (Ates et al., 2008). Expression studies have shown that key mitochondrial enzymes and transporters, including CPT-1 and OCTN2 (the carnitine transporter), are expressed in RPE cells, providing a molecular substrate for L-carnitine’s action in these cells (Ribas et al., 2014; Jones et al., 2010). Furthermore, since mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of dry AMD pathogenesis, the restoration of mitochondrial efficiency by L-carnitine could be measured by improved RPE cell survival and decreased apoptotic markers under conditions of oxidative stress and lipid oversupply.  
Preclinical studies in other tissues such as neuronal cells and hepatocytes have demonstrated that L-carnitine treatment not only restores mitochondrial function but also reduces lipid-induced ROS production and inflammation. Extrapolating from these findings, it is reasonable to expect that in the context of dry AMD, L-carnitine could counteract the metabolic inflexibility of RPE cells, ultimately slowing the progression of geographic atrophy and preserving retinal structure and function (Surai, 2015; Wang et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
L-Carnitine stands out as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to several compelling properties. Its established role in promoting mitochondrial β-oxidation and energy production, combined with demonstrated antioxidant and osmoprotective actions, provides a strong mechanistic rationale for addressing the metabolic and oxidative stress components of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Jones et al., 2010). The compound’s extensive history of use as a dietary supplement and its well-characterized safety profile—in which high oral doses have been administered with minimal toxicity—support its potential for repurposing in an ocular application (Flanagan et al., 2010; Mollica et al., 2017).  
However, there are potential limitations that merit cautious consideration. Direct evidence of L-carnitine’s efficacy in RPE cells specifically within the context of dry AMD is currently limited. While preclinical studies in non-ocular tissues and some ocular models suggest beneficial mitochondrial and antioxidant effects, the precise dosing, ocular bioavailability, and long-term impact on retinal degeneration remain to be rigorously established. Moreover, while L-carnitine can enhance mitochondrial function, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD implies that a monotherapy approach might not be sufficient; a combination therapy strategy—potentially incorporating other mitochondrial or antioxidant agents—may ultimately prove more effective (Shamsi et al., 2007; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a).  
In summary, the strengths of L-carnitine include its well-established role in cellular energy metabolism, its safety profile and widespread clinical use in other metabolic conditions, and its potential to mitigate ROS production and oxidative damage through enhanced fatty acid oxidation. The weaknesses primarily lie in the current paucity of direct evidence in ocular models of dry AMD and the challenges associated with ensuring adequate drug delivery to the RPE in vivo. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
L-Carnitine is a naturally occurring quaternary ammonium compound, chemically defined as β-hydroxy-γ-trimethylaminobutyrate, that is both derived from the diet (predominantly found in animal-based foods such as red meat) and biosynthesized endogenously from the essential amino acids lysine and methionine via a vitamin C–dependent pathway primarily in the liver and kidneys (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Mollica et al., 2017). Historically, L-carnitine was first identified as a constituent of muscle tissue in the early 20th century and was later linked to its high content in meat, leading to its designation as “vitamin T” in certain insect models (Mollica et al., 2017). As a member of the carnitine family, it belongs to the class of metabolic cofactors or nutraceutical agents whose primary function is to shuttle activated long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondrial matrix, where they undergo β-oxidation, thereby facilitating aerobic energy production and maintaining the intracellular acyl-CoA/CoA balance (Moos et al., 2017; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). This class of compounds has historically been used as dietary supplements to treat primary and secondary carnitine deficiency, as well as in various metabolic and mitochondrial disorders (Flanagan et al., 2010). L-Carnitine is widely formulated in pharmaceutical products both as a standalone supplement and as an ingredient in combination formulations, which underscores its acceptance as a metabolic supportive agent with a favorable safety profile (Flanagan et al., 2010; Surai, 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, the carnitine family has a long record of use in addressing conditions where fatty acid oxidation is impaired. L-Carnitine has been employed effectively as a life-saving therapy in primary carnitine deficiency—a condition in which mutations of the carnitine transporter (OCTN2) impair cellular uptake—and also in secondary deficiencies associated with conditions like renal failure, liver disease, and certain inborn errors of metabolism (Flanagan et al., 2010). Beyond classical deficiency syndromes, both L-carnitine and its acetylated derivative (acetyl-L-carnitine) have been investigated in a broad range of clinical contexts, including cardiovascular diseases, diabetic complications, and neurodegenerative disorders. For example, acetyl-L-carnitine has been shown to improve parameters of visual function in patients with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and to confer neuroprotective effects in Alzheimer’s disease and mild cognitive impairment (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Calabrese et al., 2009).  
In ophthalmology, while most clinical studies have focused on the use of carnitine derivatives for systemic metabolic or neuroprotective effects, there is preclinical evidence supporting an ocular role. Animal studies have identified high intraocular concentrations of carnitine in the lens and other ocular tissues, hinting at a physiological role in maintaining ocular metabolic balance and osmotic homeostasis (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). Investigations into the protective effects of L-carnitine against oxidative damage, including its potential to safeguard retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and other ocular tissues, provide a rationale for its application in dry AMD, particularly in the context of geographic atrophy where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central features (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c). Moreover, combination therapy regimens incorporating acetyl-L-carnitine with n-3 fatty acids and coenzyme Q10 have also been trialed in experimental settings to address energy metabolism in retinal tissues (Shamsi et al., 2007). Despite these promising findings, direct clinical use of L-carnitine as monotherapy for dry AMD has not been extensively reported, thus making its repurposing an area that merits focused research to bridge the gap between its established metabolic functions and its potential application in retinal degeneration (Flanagan et al., 2010; Mollica et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
The central biochemical role of L-carnitine is to facilitate the transport of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle—a process that is critical for β-oxidation and ATP production. This shuttle is mediated by mitochondrial enzymes such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT-1) on the outer mitochondrial membrane, which converts acyl-CoA to acyl-carnitine, and carnitine acyltransferase (also known as carnitine acetyltransferase or CAT) within the mitochondria that re-forms acyl-CoA for oxidation (Moos et al., 2017; Jones et al., 2010). This process not only fuels ATP generation via the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation but also helps regulate the cellular acyl-CoA/CoA ratio, indirectly influencing multiple metabolic pathways (Surai, 2015).  
Furthermore, L-carnitine exhibits antioxidant properties either directly, through free radical scavenging, or indirectly by preserving mitochondrial integrity and function under oxidative stress conditions (Shamsi et al., 2007; Surai, 2015). It has been shown to reduce lipid peroxidation and prevent the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential—a key step in the cascade leading to cellular apoptosis (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c). In addition to its classical mitochondrial functions, L-carnitine also acts as an osmolyte, protecting cells against hyperosmolarity by stabilizing proteins and cellular membranes, which could further reduce oxidative stress (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b; Mollica et al., 2017).  
At the molecular level in the RPE, the hypothesis is that enhancing mitochondrial fatty acid uptake via L-carnitine supplementation will improve β-oxidation efficiency. This is expected to lead to increased ATP production and a reduction in the accumulation of lipid intermediates that may otherwise result in excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation. The reduction in ROS could mitigate chronic oxidative stress, a well established contributor to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Jones et al., 2010; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). Notably, disrupted mitochondrial metabolism and energy deficits have been implicated in the progression of RPE cell dysfunction, and L-carnitine’s role in restoring metabolic flexibility has been documented in other cell types such as hepatocytes and neuronal cells (Ates et al., 2008; Surai, 2015). Additionally, the modulation of mitochondrial protein acetylation by L-carnitine derivatives, an effect observed in various models of aging and metabolic disease, may further contribute to a neuroprotective milieu in RPE cells (Wang et al., 2024; Virmani & Cirulli, 2022).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its multifaceted mechanisms of action, the anticipated effect of L-carnitine in an assay designed for dry age-related macular degeneration is twofold. First, by enhancing mitochondrial fatty acid uptake and increasing β-oxidation rates, L-carnitine is expected to boost ATP production in RPE cells, thereby ameliorating the energy deficits that contribute to cellular dysfunction in geographic atrophy (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Jones et al., 2010). Second, this improved mitochondrial function should lead to a reduction in the generation of ROS that typically arises from lipid overload and subsequent incomplete oxidation, thereby decreasing oxidative damage to critical cellular structures including mitochondrial membranes and nuclear DNA (Shamsi et al., 2007; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a).  
In in vitro assays using cultured RPE cells, one would expect that L-carnitine treatment leads to enhanced mitochondrial respiration, as measured by oxygen consumption rate (OCR), and an associated elevation in ATP levels. Moreover, reductions in established markers of oxidative stress, such as malondialdehyde (MDA) levels or increased glutathione (GSH) concentrations, would support its antioxidant action (Ates et al., 2008). Expression studies have shown that key mitochondrial enzymes and transporters, including CPT-1 and OCTN2 (the carnitine transporter), are expressed in RPE cells, providing a molecular substrate for L-carnitine’s action in these cells (Ribas et al., 2014; Jones et al., 2010). Furthermore, since mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of dry AMD pathogenesis, the restoration of mitochondrial efficiency by L-carnitine could be measured by improved RPE cell survival and decreased apoptotic markers under conditions of oxidative stress and lipid oversupply.  
Preclinical studies in other tissues such as neuronal cells and hepatocytes have demonstrated that L-carnitine treatment not only restores mitochondrial function but also reduces lipid-induced ROS production and inflammation. Extrapolating from these findings, it is reasonable to expect that in the context of dry AMD, L-carnitine could counteract the metabolic inflexibility of RPE cells, ultimately slowing the progression of geographic atrophy and preserving retinal structure and function (Surai, 2015; Wang et al., 2024).

L-Carnitine stands out as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to several compelling properties. Its established role in promoting mitochondrial β-oxidation and energy production, combined with demonstrated antioxidant and osmoprotective actions, provides a strong mechanistic rationale for addressing the metabolic and oxidative stress components of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Jones et al., 2010). The compound’s extensive history of use as a dietary supplement and its well-characterized safety profile—in which high oral doses have been administered with minimal toxicity—support its potential for repurposing in an ocular application (Flanagan et al., 2010; Mollica et al., 2017).  
However, there are potential limitations that merit cautious consideration. Direct evidence of L-carnitine’s efficacy in RPE cells specifically within the context of dry AMD is currently limited. While preclinical studies in non-ocular tissues and some ocular models suggest beneficial mitochondrial and antioxidant effects, the precise dosing, ocular bioavailability, and long-term impact on retinal degeneration remain to be rigorously established. Moreover, while L-carnitine can enhance mitochondrial function, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD implies that a monotherapy approach might not be sufficient; a combination therapy strategy—potentially incorporating other mitochondrial or antioxidant agents—may ultimately prove more effective (Shamsi et al., 2007; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a).  
In summary, the strengths of L-carnitine include its well-established role in cellular energy metabolism, its safety profile and widespread clinical use in other metabolic conditions, and its potential to mitigate ROS production and oxidative damage through enhanced fatty acid oxidation. The weaknesses primarily lie in the current paucity of direct evidence in ocular models of dry AMD and the challenges associated with ensuring adequate drug delivery to the RPE in vivo. Nonetheless, given the overall mechanistic promise and the favorable tolerability observed in numerous studies, L-carnitine warrants further investigation – with a focus on in vitro RPE assays under condition of lipid overload and oxidative stress, followed by in vivo preclinical models of geographic atrophy – to validate its efficacy as a repurposed therapy for dry AMD (Jones et al., 2010; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c; Ates et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2024).  
Overall, I recommend proceeding with targeted experiments to assess mitochondrial respiration, ROS levels, and cell survival in RPE cultures treated with L-carnitine. These studies should be complemented with investigations of tissue distribution following ocular delivery to address bioavailability concerns. This comprehensive evaluation supports the potential of L-carnitine as a metabolic and antioxidant therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, while also highlighting areas where additional data are needed before clinical translation.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Honokiol is a naturally occurring polyphenolic neolignan that is primarily isolated from the bark and other tissues of Magnolia species, notably Magnolia officinalis. Traditionally used in Chinese medicine, honokiol has emerged as a promising therapeutic candidate due to its potent antioxidant, anti‐inflammatory, and neuroprotective properties. As a member of the phenylpropanoid class of natural compounds, honokiol has a unique biphenolic structure that enables it to interact with a variety of cellular targets. Its extraction from natural sources and subsequent formulation by vendors such as Sigma-Aldrich (SML0588) provides a well-characterized starting point for drug repurposing strategies. Over the years, synthetic modifications have also been explored to improve its bioavailability, solubility, and therapeutic efficacy, further expanding its potential as a drug candidate in multiple clinical contexts (Faysal et al., 2023). The chemical attributes of honokiol allow it to cross biological barriers effectively, a property that is particularly relevant in diseases involving complex tissue compartments such as the eye’s retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Its classification within the polyphenolic compounds aligns it with other antioxidants known to mitigate cellular damage from reactive oxygen species (ROS) and oxidative stress, making it a promising candidate for repurposing in conditions like dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative injury are predominant pathological features (Faysal et al., 2023; Sasia et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, honokiol has been the subject of extensive biochemical and pharmacological investigations given its wide-ranging protective effects in various tissues. In hepatocyte models, studies have demonstrated that honokiol protects liver cells from oxidative injury induced by compounds such as tert-butyl hydroperoxide (t-BHP) by restoring mitochondrial deacetylase SIRT3 levels, thereby boosting cellular viability and enhancing antioxidant defenses (Liu et al., 2018). These hepatoprotective effects underscore honokiol’s capacity to modulate mitochondrial health, a mechanism that likely underpins its action in other cell types as well. In addition to hepatic models, honokiol has been evaluated in neurological contexts where activation of SIRT3 plays a central role in neuroprotection. For example, in a rat model of ammonia neurotoxicity, honokiol administration led to the recovery of MnSOD activity and the upregulation of transcription factors such as FoxO3a and PGC1α, which are essential for mitochondrial function and cellular antioxidant responses (Trigun & Anamika, 2022; Tyagi & Pugazhenthi, 2023). These findings demonstrate the compound’s ability to counteract oxidative stress via restoration of mitochondrial enzyme activities, an effect that has been linked to improved neurological outcomes including reductions in beta-amyloid accumulation.

More recently, honokiol has shown promising results in ocular models as well. Studies investigating its effects on diabetic retinal microvascular injury have revealed that honokiol can activate SIRT3 in retinal capillary endothelial cells, leading to the deacetylation of mitochondrial proteins—most notably manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD)—and preservation of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) under hyperglycemic conditions (Shi et al., 2024). Although these results have been demonstrated in the context of diabetic retinal injury rather than in models of dry AMD specifically, the mechanistic overlap—centered on mitochondrial protection and the reduction of oxidative stress—strongly supports the potential utility of honokiol in diseases characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction. Despite these advances, there is a notable gap in the literature regarding direct evaluations of honokiol in RPE cells or in models of geographic atrophy, the advanced form of dry AMD. However, the consistency of its protective effects across hepatocytes, neurons, and retinal microvascular cells suggests a broad applicability that merits further exploration for AMD-related indications (Liu et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic potential of honokiol is intimately linked to its capacity to activate mitochondrial SIRT3, a member of the sirtuin family of NAD⁺-dependent deacetylases that serve as key regulators of mitochondrial biology. SIRT3 plays a pivotal role in maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis through the deacetylation and consequent activation of several mitochondrial enzymes implicated in antioxidant defense and metabolic regulation. Among its important targets is manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), an enzyme responsible for the dismutation of superoxide radicals into less reactive molecular species. By deacetylating MnSOD, SIRT3 increases its enzymatic activity, thereby reducing the levels of damaging ROS generated during oxidative phosphorylation (Liu et al., 2018; Trigun & Anamika, 2022). In parallel, SIRT3 is postulated to deacetylate isocitrate dehydrogenase 2 (IDH2), another mitochondrial enzyme critically involved in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and cellular redox balance, although direct evidence for IDH2 deacetylation in the honokiol context is less extensively documented in the current literature. Nevertheless, the hypothesis posits that deacetylation of IDH2 would further contribute to the reduction of mitochondrial ROS, suggesting a dual mechanism through which SIRT3 activation could ameliorate oxidative damage (Tyagi & Pugazhenthi, 2023; Zhang et al., 2020).

In addition to these direct deacetylation events, honokiol-induced SIRT3 activation has been associated with the modulation of several signaling cascades. Notably, SIRT3 activation by honokiol has been correlated with increased levels of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2), a master regulator of the cellular antioxidant response (Liu et al., 2018). The upregulation of Nrf2 can lead to the transcriptional activation of a spectrum of antioxidant enzymes, thereby reinforcing the intracellular capacity to neutralize ROS. Furthermore, SIRT3 activation influences mitochondrial biogenesis via upregulation of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC1α) and the forkhead box O3a (FoxO3a) pathway, which not only supports energy production but also promotes the maintenance of mitochondrial integrity under stress conditions (Trigun & Anamika, 2022). Evidence from neurotoxicity models demonstrates that honokiol can modulate these pathways, leading to improved mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and reduced apoptosis (Trigun & Anamika, 2022; Tyagi & Pugazhenthi, 2023).

Given the well-documented role of SIRT3 in various tissues, the proposed mechanism in RPE cells for dry AMD centers on the hypothesis that honokiol, by enhancing SIRT3 activity, will lead to the deacetylation of MnSOD and IDH2. In RPE cells, which are known to suffer from hyperacetylation-driven mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD, such deacetylation is expected to result in the restoration of enzymatic antioxidant defenses. This, in turn, would mitigate mitochondrial ROS accumulation, thereby stabilizing Δψm and supporting cellular viability under conditions of chronic oxidative stress—a central pathogenic mechanism in geographic atrophy (Liu et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2024). The detailed molecular interactions between honokiol and SIRT3 remain an active area of research, but the cumulative evidence supports a model wherein honokiol binding enhances the enzymatic activity of SIRT3, leading to downstream deacetylation events that ultimately preserve mitochondrial function (Trigun & Anamika, 2022; Tyagi & Pugazhenthi, 2023).

Expected Effect:  
For the proposed application in dry AMD, the expected effect of honokiol in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells is multi-faceted. Primarily, upon exposure to honokiol, one would anticipate activation of SIRT3 within the mitochondria of RPE cells. This activation is expected to promote the deacetylation of critical mitochondrial proteins—including MnSOD and, by extension, IDH2—thereby enhancing their enzymatic activities. The deacetylation of MnSOD is particularly vital, as it increases the dismutation of superoxide radicals, thus reducing the levels of ROS that are known to drive RPE cell dysfunction and death in the context of dry AMD (Liu et al., 2018; Trigun & Anamika, 2022).

In addition to the direct antioxidant effects mediated by MnSOD, the activation of SIRT3 is also expected to trigger a broader mitochondrial protective response. Upregulation of PGC1α and activation of FoxO3a—both of which have been observed in various cellular models after honokiol treatment—would stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis and contribute to the maintenance of the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) (Trigun & Anamika, 2022). A stabilized Δψm is critical in preventing the cascade of events leading to mitochondrial permeability transition and subsequent apoptosis, thereby preserving RPE cell function. Evidence from diabetic retinal microvascular injury models supports the notion that honokiol can indeed preserve Δψm in cells under oxidative stress, suggesting that similar protective mechanisms may be harnessed in RPE cells affected by geographic atrophy (Shi et al., 2024).

Furthermore, the activation of antioxidant transcriptional programs through increased Nrf2 levels may synergize with the direct effects on mitochondrial proteins. Enhanced Nrf2 activity would lead to the upregulation of a suite of antioxidant enzymes and stress response proteins, further bolstering the capacity of RPE cells to handle oxidative insults. This integrative response is expected to reduce the accumulation of mtROS, which is a key mediator of cellular senescence and dysfunction in the aging retina (Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020). Ultimately, the net effect in the assay is predicted to be an improvement in cellular viability and function following oxidative stress, as measured by assays of ROS production, Δψm stability, and overall cell survival. Such outcomes would validate the potential of honokiol to counteract the hyperacetylation-driven mitochondrial defects observed in donor RPE cells from patients with dry AMD (Liu et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of honokiol as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is supported by a convergence of biochemical, cellular, and animal model data that demonstrate its capacity to activate mitochondrial SIRT3 and promote deacetylation of key antioxidant enzymes. On the strength side, honokiol is a well-characterized natural compound with a long history of therapeutic use in traditional medicine and has been shown to exert protective effects across multiple cell types, including hepatocytes, neurons, and retinal microvascular cells. Its ability to enhance SIRT3 activity is particularly compelling given the central role of SIRT3 in preserving mitochondrial function and reducing oxidative stress—a pathogenic hallmark in dry AMD and its advanced form, geographic atrophy (Liu et al., 2018; Trigun & Anamika, 2022; Shi et al., 2024). Moreover, the compound’s lipophilic structure and ability to cross biological barriers further enhance its appeal as a candidate for treating diseases that require delivery to the retinal layers (Faysal et al., 2023).

From a mechanistic standpoint, honokiol’s actions have been well delineated across several experimental models. The documented deacetylation of MnSOD, along with the inferred deacetylation of IDH2, provides a solid biochemical foundation for the proposed mechanism of action in RPE cells. The downstream effects—involving the activation of transcription factors such as Nrf2, FoxO3a, and the upregulation of PGC1α—offer additional layers of protection by promoting mitochondrial biogenesis, energy production, and an enhanced antioxidant response (Trigun & Anamika, 2022; Liu et al., 2018). These multi-dimensional actions are likely to be advantageous in the context of dry AMD, a condition that results from an interplay of oxidative stress, inflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction.

Despite these strengths, several potential challenges must be considered. One significant weakness is the current lack of direct evidence demonstrating honokiol’s efficacy in RPE cells or in models of dry AMD, specifically geographic atrophy. Most of the supporting studies have been conducted in non-ocular systems such as hepatocyte cultures, neurotoxicity models, and diabetic retinal microvascular cells, with only indirect extrapolations made to RPE biology (Liu et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2024). This gap in the literature calls for targeted preclinical studies in RPE cell lines and relevant animal models of geographic atrophy to establish the therapeutic relevance of honokiol in an ocular setting. Additionally, while honokiol has been shown to activate SIRT3 in several systems, the degree to which this activation translates into clinically meaningful improvements in mitochondrial function within the RPE remains to be fully validated. The potential variable expression of SIRT3 in RPE cells under different pathological conditions may also influence the overall efficacy of honokiol (Tyagi & Pugazhenthi, 2023; Zhang et al., 2020).

Another concern involves the pharmacokinetic properties of honokiol when administered for ocular indications. Although its lipophilicity may favor penetration into retinal tissue, detailed studies on its distribution, metabolism, and clearance in the eye are lacking. This raises questions regarding the optimal dosing regimen, route of administration, and potential off-target effects that might arise from systemic exposure. The current body of literature has largely focused on in vitro and animal models in other organ systems; hence, translational research specifically addressing ocular pharmacology is warranted (Shi et al., 2024).

Furthermore, the complexity of dry AMD pathogenesis suggests that a multi-targeted approach might be necessary for effective treatment. While the proposed mechanism—centered on SIRT3 activation and subsequent mitochondrial protection—is attractive, it represents only one facet of the disease process. Inflammation, complement dysregulation, and extracellular matrix alterations also play critical roles in the progression of geographic atrophy. Therefore, honokiol’s utility as a monotherapy may be limited unless it can also modulate these additional pathways or be combined with other therapeutic modalities. Nonetheless, the inherent anti-inflammatory properties of honokiol, as noted in several studies, may provide some degree of pleiotropic benefit (Faysal et al., 2023; Ramesh et al., 2018).

In summary, honokiol exhibits a compelling profile as a candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD due to its established ability to activate mitochondrial SIRT3 and its consequent effects on antioxidant enzyme deacetylation, mitochondrial membrane potential stabilization, and reduction of oxidative stress. Its documented benefits in diverse models—from hepatocytes to neuronal and retinal microvascular cells—provide a strong rationale for its further investigation in RPE-specific contexts. However, the absence of direct data in RPE cells and AMD models represents a critical gap that must be addressed through targeted preclinical studies. Detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic evaluations will be essential in determining the appropriate dosing strategies and ensuring ocular delivery of honokiol at therapeutically relevant concentrations. Additionally, a broader investigation into its anti-inflammatory and complement-modulating effects may reveal synergistic benefits that are particularly important in the multifactorial etiology of dry AMD (Liu et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2024).

Overall, while current evidence supports the hypothesis that honokiol’s activation of SIRT3 can restore mitochondrial function by facilitating the deacetylation of critical enzymes such as MnSOD and potentially IDH2, thereby reducing mtROS and stabilizing Δψm, the translational relevance to RPE cells in dry AMD requires further empirical substantiation. The strengths of honokiol—in the form of its broad-spectrum antioxidant capacity, favorable pharmacological profile, and well-characterized molecular mechanisms—must be weighed against the limitations of the current evidence base. Based on the comprehensive review of the literature, it is advisable for the research team to pursue further validation studies of honokiol in ocular-specific systems, while also considering its integration into combination therapeutic strategies to address the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathology (Liu et al., 2018; Trigun & Anamika, 2022; Shi et al., 2024).

In conclusion, the repurposing of honokiol for dry age-related macular degeneration holds considerable promise due to its well-documented role in activating SIRT3 and promoting mitochondrial resilience under oxidative stress conditions. The compound’s natural origin, coupled with its established preclinical efficacy in other tissue models, provides a sound scientific foundation for further investigation. Nonetheless, the research team must remain cognizant of the current gaps in data regarding RPE-specific effects and the broader pathogenesis of dry AMD. A judiciously designed series of experiments—ranging from in vitro assays in primary RPE cultures to in vivo studies in geographic atrophy models—will be crucial in validating the therapeutic potential of honokiol and refining its clinical application. The strengths of honokiol’s mechanism of action, particularly its dual capacity to reduce ROS through the activation of MnSOD and possibly IDH2, as well as its ability to stabilize mitochondrial membrane potential, render it an attractive candidate for addressing the mitochondrial dysfunction intrinsic to dry AMD. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AICAR (5‐Aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide) is a synthetic nucleoside analog originally developed as an AMP mimetic agent that is capable of activating AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) across a range of cell types. It is produced by chemical synthesis and is available commercially (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich A9978), having been studied for several decades in the context of cellular energy metabolism and stress signaling. As a member of a class of compounds that mimic the natural intracellular messenger AMP, AICAR is taken up into cells via adenosine transporters and is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase into its active metabolite, ZMP (5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide monophosphate), which then mimics AMP in its interactions with AMPK (Efstathiou et al., 2020). This compound belongs to a well‐established class of metabolic modulators, and similar agents have been used in experimental settings to modulate glucose uptake, fatty acid oxidation, and overall energy homeostasis in both basic science and translational research contexts (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014). In addition, several preclinical studies have evaluated AICAR’s potential as an “exercise mimetic” due to its ability to enhance energy metabolism in muscle and other tissues, and its synthetic nature allows for reproducible and scalable dosing in research models (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, AICAR was developed primarily as an agent to activate AMPK in metabolic studies and has been investigated in a variety of preclinical models ranging from cancer to cardiovascular disease. In the oncology field, for example, AICAR has been shown to inhibit cancer cell proliferation, induce cell cycle arrest, and promote programmed cell death in several cancer types via AMPK-dependent modulation of pathways such as PI3K-Akt and mTOR (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014; Rattan et al., 2005). Clinical studies, particularly those in the cardiovascular arena, have also evaluated AICAR’s safety profile in the context of ischemia-reperfusion injury, including human trials during cardiac surgery, demonstrating that it can be administered safely in humans (Rattan et al., 2005). In the context of ocular research, AICAR has been studied for its effects on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and other ocular cell types; several studies have demonstrated that AICAR suppresses the production of pro-inflammatory complement components such as complement factor 3 (C3) and complement factor B (CFB) in RPE cells under inflammatory conditions (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017). Although there is no established clinical use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) to date, these preclinical observations, combined with its well-known pharmacological profile, have spurred interest in repurposing AICAR for treating retinal diseases characterized by oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020). Furthermore, studies examining AMPK activators in the eye – including those using AICAR in animal models of uveitis or oxidative stress-induced RPE damage – support the notion that activating this metabolic pathway can protect against retinal degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

Mechanism of Action:  
AICAR exerts its biological activity primarily through the activation of AMPK, a master regulator of cellular energy balance that responds to alterations in the AMP/ATP ratio. Once AICAR is imported into cells through adenosine transporters, it is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase to form ZMP, an analog of AMP. ZMP binds to the regulatory γ subunit of AMPK, causing a conformational change that facilitates AMPK phosphorylation at Thr172 by upstream kinases such as LKB1, thereby fully activating the kinase (Efstathiou et al., 2020). Activated AMPK then phosphorylates a series of downstream targets involved in energy metabolism, including acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) and elements of the mTOR signaling pathway. In RPE cells, this activation is particularly important because AMPK phosphorylates and activates ULK1, a kinase critical for initiating autophagy and mitophagy, thereby promoting the clearance of damaged mitochondria (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Chung et al., 2017).  

A central component of the rationale for using AICAR in dry AMD is its ability to stimulate the transcriptional coactivator PGC-1α. AMPK-mediated phosphorylation of PGC-1α enhances its activity and nuclear translocation, which in turn drives the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant defense, and metabolic adaptation (Hu et al., 2024; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). This mechanism is particularly attractive in dry AMD because mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells is thought to contribute significantly to disease pathogenesis by impairing oxidative phosphorylation, increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and triggering cell senescence or death (Tong et al., 2022; Rego, 2023). In addition to these AMPK-dependent effects, some studies have reported that AICAR exerts certain effects independent of AMPK activation. For instance, AICAR has been shown to suppress TNF-α-induced complement factor expression by mechanisms that do not involve AMPK, suggesting that alternative signaling pathways or direct modulation of transcription factor activity might also contribute to its overall activity profile (Chung et al., 2017; Kirchner et al., 2018). Furthermore, AICAR has been observed to affect mitochondrial dynamics not only by stimulating biogenesis through PGC-1α activation but also by modifying autophagic flux through mTOR inhibition. In models of RPE oxidative stress, where excessive ROS levels lead to mitochondrial fragmentation and accumulation of dysfunctional organelles, AICAR-induced AMPK activation facilitates the clearance of damaged mitochondria via mitophagy, thus restoring mitochondrial quality and energy production (Fisher et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2024). Moreover, experimental evidence suggests that AICAR can modulate the balance between cellular glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation by shifting metabolism toward a more energy-efficient, oxidative phenotype, thereby increasing the overall oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and potentially improving cellular resilience under oxidative stress (Chan et al., 2020; Fisher, 2022).  

Expected Effect:  
Given its mechanisms of action, the expected effect of AICAR in an assay aimed at treating dry AMD would be multifaceted. In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress—a hallmark of dry AMD—AICAR treatment is expected to lead to robust activation of AMPK, as measured by increased phosphorylation of both AMPK and its downstream substrates such as ACC and ULK1 (Guo et al., 2018; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). This activation should in turn upregulate PGC-1α, resulting in enhanced transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, improved mitochondrial DNA replication, and an increased capacity for ATP production (Hu et al., 2024). As damaged mitochondria are a major source of ROS in stressed RPE cells, the stimulation of autophagy and mitophagy is anticipated to selectively clear these dysfunctional organelles, reducing cellular oxidative stress and preventing the secondary damage that contributes to RPE degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

In addition to these metabolic effects, AICAR is also expected to attenuate inflammatory responses within the RPE and adjacent retinal tissues. For instance, by modulating the activity of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) and reducing the expression of inflammatory mediators such as tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and complement components (e.g., C3 and CFB), AICAR would help to create a less pro-inflammatory microenvironment that could further protect RPE cells from damage (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017; Kirchner et al., 2018). These effects are particularly pertinent given that chronic, low-grade inflammation coupled with complement dysregulation is a recognized component of dry AMD pathogenesis.  

At the cellular level, the outcome of AICAR-induced AMPK activation is expected to manifest as enhanced mitochondrial function, improved energy charge (ATP/AMP ratio), reduced ROS accumulation, and, ultimately, a restoration of normal metabolic and autophagic flux in RPE cells (Fisher et al., 2022; Fisher, 2022). This improved bioenergetic profile should translate into protection against RPE cell death, potentially slowing or halting the progression of geographic atrophy associated with dry AMD (Yu et al., 2024; Si et al., 2023). Moreover, since RPE dysfunction in AMD also involves a reduction in the phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, AICAR’s modulatory effects on autophagy may indirectly help to restore the homeostatic functions of RPE cells, reducing the accumulation of damaging lipofuscin and drusen material (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Sung et al., 2015). In summary, the expected effect is a dual-action benefit—mitigation of oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum stresses via improved mitochondrial dynamics and an anti-inflammatory effect stemming from a reduction in complement activation and NF-κB-driven cytokine production (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020).  

Overall Evaluation:  
AICAR represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration owing to its robust and well-characterized mechanism of action via AMPK activation. The strengths of this candidate lie in its dual capacity to modulate critical pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis: on one hand, AICAR enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and promotes the removal of damaged mitochondria through autophagy/mitophagy, and on the other, it attenuates inflammatory cascades that exacerbate RPE cell damage (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hu et al., 2024). The ability of AICAR to upregulate PGC-1α is particularly compelling because mitochondrial dysfunction is now widely recognized as a central element in dry AMD. Preclinical studies have illustrated that dysregulation of mitochondrial function in RPE cells—a decrease in oxidative phosphorylation capacity, increased ROS production, and impaired clearance of damaged organelles—is pivotal in the initiation and progression of AMD (Tong et al., 2022; Rego, 2023). Thus, a compound like AICAR that can simultaneously restore mitochondrial health and mitigate inflammatory responses offers a multifaceted approach to disease modification.  

From the therapeutic history perspective, AICAR has been extensively studied in various preclinical models, including those of ocular inflammation and oxidative stress in RPE cells. Its ability to safely activate AMPK in vivo has been demonstrated across multiple species and contexts, including settings that mimic some aspects of AMD-related stress, such as endotoxin-induced uveitis and sodium iodate-induced RPE damage (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Chan et al., 2020). Additionally, the compound’s known clinical safety profile in human studies—albeit in contexts outside ophthalmology—provides an encouraging starting point for repurposing it for dry AMD, where no approved therapeutics currently exist (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017).  

However, there are notable weaknesses and challenges that must be addressed. First, while AMPK activation is generally beneficial for energy homeostasis and autophagy, certain studies have indicated that AICAR’s effects on RPE cell biology might be context-dependent. For instance, some experimental reports have shown that AICAR can reduce the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments by RPE cells—a process that is essential for retinal health—which may represent a double-edged sword if not carefully titrated (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Yu et al., 2024). In addition, the existence of AMPK-independent effects—such as the direct inhibition of complement factor expression—introduces complexity into the overall mechanism of action and makes it challenging to predict all downstream outcomes. Differential responses have also been observed between healthy and diseased donor RPE cells, implying that “metabolic memory” or cellular adaptation may influence drug responsiveness (Fisher et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2017). These considerations suggest that while the theoretical underpinnings for using AICAR in dry AMD are solid, the translation of these effects into clinical efficacy may require careful optimization of dosing, delivery, and patient selection.  

Another potential limitation is related to its broad mechanism of action. AICAR activates several metabolic pathways that are intertwined with many aspects of cellular physiology. While this pleiotropy provides the therapeutic benefit of addressing multiple dysregulated pathways in AMD simultaneously, it may also increase the risk of off-target effects or metabolic disturbances in tissues outside the retina (Rattan et al., 2005; Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014). For instance, systemic administration of AICAR has been associated with shifts in glycolytic flux and modifications of lipid metabolism, and it is therefore imperative that strategies for ocular delivery (such as intravitreal injections or topical formulations) be developed to maximize retinal exposure while minimizing systemic exposure (Chan et al., 2020; Kamoshita et al., 2014).  

Moreover, despite the substantial body of preclinical data supporting the role of AICAR in activating AMPK and restoring mitochondrial function, clinical data specific to dry AMD are lacking. Although related studies have shown benefits in models of retinal inflammation and degeneration, the exact therapeutic window, long-term safety, and efficacy in humans with AMD must be thoroughly evaluated in well-designed clinical trials. It is also worth mentioning that other AMPK activators, such as metformin, have independently demonstrated protective effects in AMD models, thereby lending credence to the approach but also raising questions about whether AICAR offers a distinct advantage over these agents (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020).  

In summary, the overall evaluation of AICAR as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. Its well-documented ability to activate AMPK, stimulate PGC-1α-driven mitochondrial biogenesis, and induce autophagy presents a strong mechanistic rationale for protecting RPE cells from the mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress that drive dry AMD pathogenesis (Hu et al., 2024; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2011). The preclinical evidence, gathered from studies in ocular models and other systems, provides encouraging proof-of-concept data that support further investigation (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Hyttinen et al., 2011). Nonetheless, complexities related to AMPK-independent effects, differential responses in healthy versus diseased cells, and potential off-target metabolic changes underscore the need for rigorous preclinical optimization and carefully designed clinical trials before this candidate can be definitively validated for dry AMD treatment (Chung et al., 2017; Fisher et al., 2022; Kirchner et al., 2018).  

Considering all the available literature, the repurposing of AICAR for dry AMD appears to be a promising strategy that merits further investigation. The compound’s ability to simultaneously address mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and chronic inflammation positions it as a multifaceted agent with the potential to modify disease progression in a condition that currently lacks effective therapeutic options (Chung et al., 2017; Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020). Moving forward, it will be critical to further elucidate the detailed cellular and molecular responses to AICAR in human RPE cells, determine the optimal dosing and delivery parameters specific to the ocular environment, and perform in vivo studies that mimic the complex pathobiology of dry AMD. With these additional efforts, AICAR could eventually emerge as a valuable addition to the limited therapeutic arsenal available for managing this debilitating condition.  

In conclusion, AICAR’s robust preclinical profile as an AMPK activator, its well-understood mechanisms of promoting mitochondrial biogenesis and autophagy, and its capacity to mitigate inflammatory responses provide a solid scientific basis for its potential repurposing in dry AMD (Hu et al., 2024; Hyttinen et al., 2011; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). However, several challenges remain: the dual nature of its effects (both AMPK-dependent and independent), the possibility of adverse effects on key RPE functions such as phagocytosis, and the need for precise ocular drug delivery methods. Therefore, while AICAR is an exciting candidate with considerable mechanistic appeal, its translation from bench to bedside in the treatment of dry AMD will require further detailed studies to fully map its therapeutic window, safety profile, and efficacy in human subjects (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014; Rego, 2023; Kamoshita et al., 2014). Continued rigorous research and methodical clinical evaluation will determine whether AICAR can be developed into an effective treatment modality for this currently intractable form of macular degeneration.
