Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SkQ1 (10‐(6′‐plastoquinonyl)‐decyltriphenylphosphonium) is a fully synthetic, mitochondria‐targeted antioxidant constructed by conjugating a plastoquinone antioxidant moiety with a decyl linker that is covalently bound to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation. The plastoquinone scaffold is derived from the natural quinone found in chloroplasts, known for its potent reactive oxygen species (ROS)–removing capabilities, while the TPP⁺ moiety acts as a highly lipophilic vector that drives selective accumulation within mitochondria due to the inner mitochondrial membrane’s large negative potential. In essence, by combining these two structural elements, SkQ1 is designed to exploit electrophoretic uptake to achieve extremely high concentrations in the mitochondrial matrix where oxidative damage is a critical pathogenic factor. This compound belongs to the broader class of mitochondria‐targeted quinone antioxidants, often referred to collectively as “SkQ” compounds. Molecules in this class were originally proposed and developed by Skulachev and colleagues, and they have been used experimentally to achieve mitochondrial protection in contexts ranging from ischemia–reperfusion injury and neurodegeneration to aging‐associated dysfunctions (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). The rational design strategy behind SkQ1—linking a redox‐active quinone to a lipophilic cation—has also inspired the development of analogous compounds such as SkQR1, MitoQ, and related derivatives that are being explored for a variety of biomedical applications.

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of SkQ1, as well as that of its parent class of mitochondria‐targeted antioxidants, is extensive and spans multiple preclinical and early clinical studies. In numerous in vitro and in vivo models, SkQ1 has demonstrated robust antioxidant effects. For example, it has been shown to protect mitochondria and cellular membranes against lipid peroxidation—key pathogenic processes underlying aging and degenerative diseases—at nanomolar concentrations. In various rodent models, including studies in OXYS rats (a strain that mimics accelerated senescence), chronic administration of SkQ1 prevented or reversed age‐related abnormalities such as cataract, retinopathy, and even systemic markers of mitochondrial dysfunction (Wanagat et al., 2010; Belenichev et al., 2024; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Moreover, veterinary and preclinical studies have documented SkQ1’s ability to increase lifespan and delay the onset of age‐linked phenotypes, including osteoporosis, immune decline, and neurodegeneration (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Weissig, 2020). Within the ocular field, SkQ1 has been specifically formulated as eye drops—marketed in certain regions under the trade name Visomitin—to treat dry eye syndrome. These formulations have passed early phase safety trials and have now seen clinical use in Russia. Although SkQ1 has not yet been directly trialed in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or geographic atrophy, its documented efficacy in protecting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in animal models and its ability to improve electrophysiological outcomes (such as preserved electroretinography [ERG] responses) support its potential repurposing for AMD (Gueven et al., 2017; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). In several ocular studies in both rodent and primate models, topical administration of SkQ1 has demonstrated the capacity to deliver the drug to the posterior segment with minimal systemic exposure, reducing characteristics like RPE vacuolization and preserving overall retinal function (Weissig, 2020; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). The extensive preclinical and limited clinical history of SkQ1 in ocular applications—most notably in dry-eye syndrome and animal models of retinal degeneration—suggests that the therapeutic candidate has a solid track record of mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction in tissues exposed to chronic oxidative stress, a pathophysiological component also seen in dry AMD (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Wanagat et al., 2010).

Mechanism of Action:  
SkQ1 exerts its biological effects via multiple interrelated molecular mechanisms that center on its ability to accumulate rapidly within mitochondria and scavenge deleterious ROS. The TPP⁺ portion of the molecule, owing to its delocalized positive charge and high lipophilicity, drives the electrophoretic uptake of SkQ1 into the mitochondrial matrix along the steep negative membrane potential (Δψm) that is inherent to healthy mitochondria (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Once localized within these organelles, the plastoquinone group is poised to participate in redox cycling: it is reversibly reduced—often by components of the electron transport chain such as complex III—and subsequently reacts with ROS such as superoxide (O₂•⁻) and lipid peroxyl radicals to convert them into less reactive species (Lukashev et al., 2014; Weissig, 2020). Importantly, the antioxidant effect of SkQ1 is not a one-off reaction; rather, it is “rechargeable,” meaning that following its oxidation by ROS, the quinone moiety can be reduced again, thereby enabling repeated cycles of detoxification. This rechargeable mechanism differentiates SkQ1 from conventional antioxidants that are consumed irreversibly during redox reactions. Additionally, SkQ1 has been shown to form complexes with cardiolipin—a key phospholipid in the inner mitochondrial membrane—and thereby stabilize the membrane structure against peroxidation. Some studies also suggest that the TPP⁺ component might mediate a mild uncoupling effect by facilitating proton translocation (often in conjunction with interacting with fatty acid anions), which can reduce mitochondrial ROS generation by dissipating excessive inner membrane potential under conditions of oxidative overload (Lukashev et al., 2014; Weissig, 2020; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). This dual mechanism of direct ROS scavenging combined with membrane stabilizing and modest uncoupling effects contributes to the preservation of Δψm and the overall integrity of mitochondrial bioenergetics. In RPE cells stressed by chronic photo-oxidative insult, these properties would translate into effective mitigation of oxidative damage, thereby preventing the collapse of mitochondrial membrane potential—a key event that precipitates cell dysfunction and death in dry AMD (Muraleva et al., 2019; Olovnikov et al., n.d.).

Expected Effect:  
The proposed hypothesis for repurposing SkQ1 in dry age-related macular degeneration is predicated on its capacity to target RPE mitochondria and to neutralize both superoxide radicals and lipid peroxyl radicals that accumulate under conditions of chronic light-induced oxidative stress. In vitro assays using ARPE-19 cells have demonstrated that nanomolar concentrations of SkQ1 elicit potent antioxidant responses—as measured by decreases in fluorescence with DCFDA (a marker of ROS) and stabilization of mitochondrial membrane potential via JC-1 assays—indicating that the compound readily scavenges ocular ROS at very low doses (Gueven et al., 2017; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). This antioxidant activity is expected to prevent or delay the loss of Δψm, a critical parameter for cell survival and function, particularly in RPE cells where mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in the pathogenesis of drusen formation and geographic atrophy in dry AMD. In vivo, studies conducted in models such as OXYS rats have shown that chronic administration of SkQ1 not only reduces oxidative markers in mitochondrial membranes (e.g., decreasing levels of malondialdehyde and hydroxynonenal-adducts) but also normalizes cardiolipin content and fatty acid composition—key factors involved in the proper assembly and turnover of respiratory complexes (Wanagat et al., 2010; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Moreover, macaque studies have indicated that topical SkQ1 eye drops achieve significant drug levels in the posterior segment although the dosing remains in the nanomolar range, leading to improvements in ERG function and reduced RPE vacuolization without evidence of systemic toxicity (Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Weissig, 2020). At the molecular level, the expected effect in RPE cells would be a sustained antioxidant environment that preserves mitochondrial function through two primary pathways: first, by directly quenching damaging ROS that would otherwise trigger mitochondrial DNA damage and lipid peroxidation; and second, by maintaining the structural integrity of mitochondrial membranes via stabilization of cardiolipin and prevention of excessive proton leakage. Given that RPE cells express the full complement of mitochondrial electron transport chain proteins, including complex III which is capable of reducing SkQ1 to its active form, these cells are ideal targets for the drug’s mechanism (Muraleva et al., 2019; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Consequently, when used as a therapeutic intervention in dry AMD, SkQ1 is expected to mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction associated with drusen accumulation and, in turn, slow or potentially reverse the progression of geographic atrophy—one of the major sight-threatening complications of the disease.

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, SkQ1 represents a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration based on a robust foundation of molecular design, preclinical efficacy, and established ocular safety. One of the major strengths of SkQ1 lies in its rational design: as a rechargeable, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant, it overcomes limitations faced by conventional antioxidants that lack mitochondrial specificity. The ability of the TPP⁺ moiety to drive precise mitochondrial accumulation ensures that the compound is concentrated at the site of maximal ROS production, while its plastoquinone component provides potent scavenging of both superoxide and lipid peroxyl radicals. This dual functionality not only neutralizes damaging oxidative species but also supports mitochondrial membrane integrity by stabilizing cardiolipin and potentially mitigating excessive proton leakage. Such a mechanism is particularly relevant to RPE cells, where chronic photo-oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Lukashev et al., 2014).

Another significant advantage is the extensive preclinical and early clinical evidence supporting SkQ1’s efficacy in ocular applications. Its use in animal models—spanning species from rodents to macaques—has consistently shown protective effects on retinal structure and function, including preservation of ERG responses and reduced vacuolization of the RPE. Furthermore, the successful clinical trials for dry eye syndrome confirm that topical administration of SkQ1 is not only efficacious but also well-tolerated in humans, thereby reducing the risk related to ocular drug delivery and systemic exposure (Gueven et al., 2017; Weissig, 2020; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

Nevertheless, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be carefully weighed. One concern is the dose-dependent behavior of SkQ1. While nanomolar concentrations are effective and safe, there is evidence that at higher concentrations, the molecule can exhibit prooxidant or detergent-like effects—leading to membrane disruption or uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation. This narrow window between the antioxidant and prooxidant activities necessitates rigorous control of dosing in clinical settings to avoid inadvertent exacerbation of mitochondrial dysfunction (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). Additionally, while many studies have focused on the compound’s ability to protect against acute oxidative insults, the etiology of dry AMD is multifactorial and chronic. Although animal models such as the OXYS rat provide valuable insights into age-related ocular changes, the long-term efficacy and safety of SkQ1 in preventing geographic atrophy in the context of chronic, low-grade oxidative stress remain to be fully established in human subjects (Wanagat et al., 2010; Belenichev et al., 2024).

It is also important to note that while the proposed mechanism of action for SkQ1—namely, quenching of lipid peroxyl radicals and superoxide to preserve mitochondrial membrane potential—has been well-documented in vitro and in animal models (particularly using ARPE-19 assays with JC-1 and DCFDA readouts), extrapolating these findings to the complex human pathology of dry AMD will require careful clinical trial design. Key endpoints such as changes in drusen load, progression of geographic atrophy, and improvements in visual function would need to be monitored over extended periods. Moreover, given that oxidative stress and inflammation are part of an intricate network of pathological events in dry AMD, combination therapies that address multiple targets may ultimately yield more significant benefits than a single-agent approach (Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Gueven et al., 2017).

From a pharmacokinetic perspective, the selective accumulation of SkQ1 in the mitochondria is a highly attractive feature, as it maximizes local drug concentrations while minimizing systemic exposure and potential off-target effects. This is especially critical for ocular applications, where local delivery via eye drops can achieve high retinal levels with minimal systemic absorption. Nonetheless, formulation stability, light sensitivity, and proper storage conditions are factors that must be optimized for successful commercial development (Weissig, 2020; Gueven et al., 2017; Ji et al., 2021).

In aggregate, the overall evaluation of SkQ1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic. The compound’s design as a mitochondria-targeted, rechargeable antioxidant offers compelling advantages in addressing mitochondrial dysfunction—a key element in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its ability to protect RPE cells, preserve mitochondrial membrane potential, and improve retinal function, while early clinical studies in related ocular conditions confirm its safety profile for topical administration. However, due diligence is warranted to establish the optimal dosing regimen that maximizes beneficial antioxidant effects while avoiding potential prooxidant toxicity. Additionally, further rigorous clinical trials specifically targeting dry AMD endpoints are necessary to confirm that the promising outcomes observed in animal studies translate into measurable clinical benefit in patients with geographic atrophy (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Gueven et al., 2017; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Wanagat et al., 2010; Weissig, 2020).

Given the comprehensive body of work underpinning the mechanism of action, the established track record in various preclinical ocular models, and the supporting data from human dry-eye trials, SkQ1 appears to have significant potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its unique targeting of mitochondria—particularly within RPE cells—and its capacity to prevent ROS-induced mitochondrial collapse make it especially well-suited to counteract the chronic photo-oxidative stress that characterizes this disease. The next steps for validating SkQ1 in this indication should include well-designed in vivo studies in AMD-relevant animal models, followed by early phase clinical trials with careful dose-escalation studies and robust assessment of retinal morphology and function. Overall, SkQ1 stands out as a promising therapeutic candidate that merits further investigation within our drug development pipeline (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Weissig, 2020; Gueven et al., 2017; Wanagat et al., 2010).

1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Mdivi-1, known as mitochondrial division inhibitor 1 (catalog number Sigma-Aldrich M0199), is a synthetic small-molecule compound originally developed for research into mitochondrial dynamics. It belongs to a class of therapeutic agents that modulate mitochondrial fission by targeting the dynamin‐related protein 1 (DRP1). DRP1 is an essential GTPase responsible for driving mitochondrial fission, a process that maintains mitochondrial quality control but, when overactivated, can lead to fragmentation associated with cellular stress and apoptosis. Mdivi-1 was discovered via compound screening experiments aimed at identifying inhibitors of DRP1’s GTPase activity and has been characterized extensively in various in vitro and in vivo studies. Its discovery was motivated by the need to therapeutically intervene in pathologies where aberrant mitochondrial fission contributes to cellular dysfunction. As a representative of DRP1 inhibitory agents, Mdivi-1 has been widely used as an investigational tool in studies related to neurodegeneration, ischemia, and ocular diseases, where mitochondrial integrity is a key determinant of cell survival (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2020). Its synthetic origin and well-documented pharmacological profile render it a candidate for drug repurposing, with potential applications extending into the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) by addressing mitochondrial dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells.

2. Therapeutic History  
Mdivi-1 has a robust preclinical research history across a variety of models that involve oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Initial studies demonstrated that in retinal endothelial cells and neuronal tissues, inhibition of DRP1 by Mdivi-1 prevented excessive mitochondrial fragmentation under conditions of acute stress. In models of glaucoma, for instance, DRP1 overactivation associated with ocular hypertension leads to mitochondrial fragmentation and retinal ganglion cell death, and administration of Mdivi-1 was found to rescue these cells by preserving mitochondrial network integrity (Kim et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2021). Similarly, in photoreceptor cells following retinal detachment, Mdivi-1 treatment reduced the activation of apoptotic pathways—through downregulation of cleaved Caspase-3 and Bax—and consequently preserved cell morphology and function, indicating a protective effect mediated through the inhibition of DRP1-dependent fission (She et al., 2018). Furthermore, in ARPE-19 cells, which are commonly used as a model for RPE behavior, Mdivi-1 has been shown to mitigate the cytotoxic effects of oxidative stress induced by hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) by reducing mitochondrial fragmentation and cytochrome c release, thereby improving mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP production (Yako et al., 2021). Although Mdivi-1 has not yet been evaluated in large-scale clinical trials for dry AMD specifically, its use in diverse ocular models—ranging from diabetic retinopathy to retinal ischemia—provides compelling evidence that its mechanism could be beneficial in conditions marked by oxidative stress and RPE dysfunction, two hallmark features of dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). These cumulative findings support the repurposing hypothesis that targeting DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission could restore mitochondrial function and survival in RPE cells, thereby halting or slowing the degenerative cascade observed in dry AMD.

3. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, DRP1 is responsible for mediating mitochondrial fission through the constriction and subsequent division of mitochondrial membranes. Upon receiving various stress signals, DRP1 is recruited from the cytosol to the mitochondrial outer membrane where it oligomerizes and hydrolyzes GTP, driving membrane scission. Mdivi-1 specifically inhibits the GTPase activity of DRP1, thereby preventing its self-assembly and subsequent mitochondrial recruitment. This inhibition effectively blocks the fission process that is typically upregulated under conditions of oxidative stress and other cellular insults (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2020). Detailed biochemical investigations have demonstrated that when DRP1 activity is unopposed, mitochondrial fragmentation ensues, leading to diminished mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, decreased oxygen consumption rate (OCR), reduced ATP synthesis, and an increase in the generation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) (Yako et al., 2021). Mdivi-1 counters these deleterious cellular events by preserving the integrity of the mitochondrial network, enabling enhanced ATP production, and maintaining the mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP). Moreover, by inhibiting DRP1, Mdivi-1 reduces the stress-induced release of cytochrome c from the mitochondria—a central step in the intrinsic apoptotic pathway—thus lowering the activation of downstream caspases (She et al., 2018; Yako et al., 2021). In addition to these primary actions, some studies have noted that Mdivi-1 has reversible inhibitory effects on mitochondrial complex I, suggesting that its impact on mitochondrial bioenergetics may be multifaceted (Yako et al., 2021). Such dual actions may serve to further stabilize mitochondrial function under stress.

4. Expected Effect  
Under conditions relevant to dry age-related macular degeneration, such as chronic oxidative stress incident on RPE cells, Mdivi-1 is anticipated to exert a multi-pronged cytoprotective effect. In the proposed assay using H₂O₂-treated ARPE-19 cells—a well-established in vitro model to mimic the oxidative stress environment of dry AMD—the primary expected effect is the inhibition of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission (Yako et al., 2021). By stabilizing mitochondrial dynamics, Mdivi-1 should also improve cellular bioenergetics through enhanced OCR and increased ATP production, both critical parameters that are typically compromised in stressed RPE cells (Yako et al., 2021). The anticipated outcome of these events is a reduction in cell death and apoptosis, as well as improved phagocytic function—an essential role of RPE cells in the maintenance of retinal homeostasis. Furthermore, by mitigating the accumulation of mtROS, Mdivi-1 is expected to lessen oxidative stress, thereby curbing the degenerative processes that are a central component of dry AMD pathophysiology (Yako et al., 2021; Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025). In essence, the mechanistic intervention afforded by Mdivi-1 aims to interrupt the cycle of mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage that leads to RPE cell apoptosis, which is a critical driver of disease progression in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021).

5. Overall Evaluation  
In evaluating Mdivi-1 as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current body of literature. Among its strengths, Mdivi-1 is underpinned by a strong mechanistic rationale: the inhibition of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission is a well-validated approach to restore mitochondrial function in the face of oxidative stress. Preclinical studies have consistently demonstrated that Mdivi-1 preserves mitochondrial network integrity, reduces the production of harmful reactive oxygen species, and prevents the release of apoptogenic factors, thereby facilitating cell survival in retinal models (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2020; Yako et al., 2021). Its efficacy in multiple ocular contexts—including models of glaucoma, retinal detachment, and diabetic retinopathy—highlights the versatility of its cytoprotective actions, which may be directly relevant to the RPE dysfunction and oxidative injury observed in dry AMD (Kim et al., 2015; She et al., 2018). From a biochemical standpoint, the ability of Mdivi-1 to enhance mitochondrial bioenergetics by improving OCR and ATP production, while simultaneously preserving mitochondrial membrane potential, addresses essential aspects of RPE cell metabolism that are often impaired in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Furthermore, the compound’s capacity to reduce apoptotic signaling, as evidenced by decreased cytochrome c release and lower caspase activity, is particularly promising given the established link between mitochondrial-mediated apoptosis and RPE cell loss in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Despite these promising attributes, several limitations and challenges deserve consideration. First, while the preclinical evidence supporting Mdivi-1’s efficacy is compelling, there remains a notable gap in clinical data, particularly in the context of dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Another potential weakness arises from the dual inhibitory effects of Mdivi-1. Some investigations have reported that Mdivi-1 also exhibits reversible inhibition of mitochondrial complex I, which could complicate its therapeutic profile by inadvertently affecting normal mitochondrial respiration (Yako et al., 2021). Moreover, the chronic inhibition of DRP1 raises important questions about the broader physiological implications of interfering with mitochondrial dynamics (Mohammad & Kowluru, 2022; She et al., 2018). Furthermore, the in vitro models currently used, predominantly involving H₂O₂-treated ARPE-19 cells, may not entirely mimic the in vivo microenvironment of the human retina in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). The overall therapeutic window and safety profile of Mdivi-1 also require further elucidation (Yako et al., 2021). Despite these challenges, the mechanistic insights generated from a diverse array of experimental models suggest that Mdivi-1 holds considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its capacity to restore mitochondrial integrity, mitigate oxidative stress, and inhibit apoptotic cascades directly addresses several of the pathogenic mechanisms implicated in dry AMD. Given that current treatments for dry AMD are limited and mainly supportive, a disease-modifying therapy that targets mitochondrial dysfunction would represent a significant advancement in the management of this debilitating disorder (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2015). In summary, Mdivi-1’s strengths lie in its well-characterized mechanism of action, demonstrated efficacy in preserving mitochondrial dynamics under stress, and its potential to enhance cell survival in models of retinal degeneration (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2015; Yako et al., 2021).

Future studies must address the nuances of chronic DRP1 inhibition, optimize dosing regimens, evaluate long-term safety, and conduct thorough pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiling in ocular tissues to fully realize the potential of Mdivi-1 in the clinical management of dry AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021).

In conclusion, the evidence provided by numerous preclinical studies strongly indicates that Mdivi-1’s inhibition of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission offers a promising therapeutic strategy for dry age-related macular degeneration. The compound’s ability to maintain mitochondrial network integrity, enhance bioenergetics, and suppress apoptotic cascades under conditions of oxidative stress in RPE cells is particularly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Although challenges remain in addressing the potential off-target effects and ensuring long-term safety in the clinical setting, the mechanistic rationale and supporting preclinical data justify further investigation into the utility of Mdivi-1 as a repurposed candidate for this currently untreatable condition. As the drug development process progresses, a focused effort on meticulous in vivo testing, formulation development for ocular delivery, and comprehensive pharmacological evaluations will be critical to harnessing the full therapeutic potential of Mdivi-1 for patients with dry AMD (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2015; She et al., 2018; Yako et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trolox is a synthetic, water-soluble analog of vitamin E widely used as a reference phenolic “chain-breaking” antioxidant in chemical assays and as a biological probe in cells and tissues, including retinal systems (e.g., ARPE-19 RPE, cultured retina) (Zuluaga et al., 2017; Garcia-Medina et al., 2020). In the dry AMD/RPE literature, Trolox is explicitly described as the vitamin E–like antioxidant moiety of troglitazone; in that context it functioned as a stand-alone antioxidant that reproduced troglitazone’s protective effects in ARPE-19 cells exposed to oxidized LDL (oxLDL) (Choi, 2019). Within the chemical class framework, Trolox is a tocopherol analog and a hindered phenolic chain-breaking antioxidant that donates H-atoms to lipid peroxyl radicals and interrupts propagation of lipid autoxidation; this class and related tocopherol analogs are highlighted in the RPE oxLDL literature and in foundational mechanistic work on phenolic antioxidants (Gnanaguru et al., 2022). The vitamin E family is also known to operate in mitochondrial membranes and other lipid-rich compartments; Trolox shares the chromanol phenolic headgroup chemistry responsible for peroxyl radical scavenging, albeit with enhanced aqueous solubility relative to α-tocopherol (Edwards et al., 2022). For RPE experimentation, Trolox is available as a commercial reagent; in the cited ARPE-19 oxLDL studies a concentrated DMSO stock was prepared and working concentrations from ~0.16 to 10.4 μM were tested with final DMSO kept below 0.4% v/v (Choi, 2019). In these same ARPE-19 models, a fluorescein (FITC)–conjugated Trolox derivative localized to intracellular membrane organelles, suggesting that despite higher aqueous solubility, Trolox partitions to (or associates with) organellar membranes such as lysosomes and possibly mitochondria in RPE cells (Choi, 2019).

Therapeutic History  
Multiple independent lines of evidence document Trolox’s antioxidant and cytoprotective actions in retinal models, but there are no animal or human clinical trials of Trolox for dry AMD/geographic atrophy, and human data for vitamin E alone in AMD are mixed or negative outside of multi-antioxidant formulations.

- ARPE-19/oxLDL RPE models (dry AMD–relevant): OxLDL induces ROS, lysosomal destabilization, and NF-κB activation in ARPE-19 cells; Trolox alone mimicked troglitazone’s protective profile by suppressing oxLDL-induced ROS, preserving lysosomal integrity, and inhibiting NF-κB nuclear translocation in a dose-dependent manner, with robust effects at 10.4 μM after 28–36 h of oxLDL exposure (Choi, 2019). Rosiglitazone, a PPARγ agonist lacking a phenolic antioxidant moiety, did not protect, and troglitazone remained protective despite PPARγ knockdown, supporting an antioxidant (phenolic) mechanism of action (Choi, 2019). The authors place these effects in an AMD-relevant cascade: lipid oxidation → ROS → lysosomal destabilization + NF-κB activation → NLRP3 inflammasome → RPE death; they propose Trolox acts upstream by limiting ROS, stabilizing lysosomes, and blunting NF-κB priming, although inflammasome activation was not directly measured (Choi, 2019).  
- Phenolic SAR and potency context in RPE: A more recent screen identified sterically hindered phenols (e.g., BHT, PMC) as more potent than Trolox in protecting RPE from oxLDL-induced death, with evidence for lysosomal localization and stabilization; a PMC analog also increased NPC-1 and reduced cholesterol after oxLDL, indicating effects on lysosomal lipid handling beyond simple antioxidant scavenging (Gnanaguru et al., 2022; Choi, 2019). These data place Trolox within a broader phenolic antioxidant class that is active in RPE lipid-oxidation stress but is not the most potent scaffold against the oxLDL insult (Choi, 2019).  
- Phototoxic lipofuscin/A2E chemistry: In a cell-free A2E photooxidation assay, Trolox reduced A2E loss during 430-nm illumination, consistent with singlet-oxygen/reactive species quenching; however, a comparator (OT-674) quenched singlet oxygen more efficiently than Trolox or α-tocopherol, and under broader 430-nm illumination the differences among Trolox and α-tocopherol were less pronounced, suggesting limited superiority of Trolox in this photochemical context (Zhou et al., 2008).  
- Retinal ganglion cell oxidative injury (non-AMD): Trolox reduced RGC death induced by hydrogen peroxide and superoxide generation in vitro, reinforcing broad neuroprotective antioxidant activity in retinal neurons (Wang et al., 2021).  
- Retinal tissue and diabetic retina contexts: Trolox reduced TBARS (lipid peroxidation) in cultured rat retina and has been reported to support pericyte regeneration in diabetic mice; Trolox-containing antioxidant mixtures reduced NF-κB activation, nitric oxide/nitrotyrosine, TBARS/ROS, and preserved antioxidant enzymes (SOD, catalase, glutathione-related enzymes) in retinal vascular cell models and diabetic retina (Garcia-Medina et al., 2020).  
- Human AMD clinical context for vitamin E: High-quality randomized trials (AREDS/AREDS2) support benefit of multi-agent antioxidant formulations that include vitamin E in slowing AMD progression, but vitamin E alone has not consistently shown benefit; several reviews/meta-analyses conclude little or no effect for vitamin E monotherapy and emphasize inconsistent observational data, limiting attribution of clinical effects to vitamin E or to any analog such as Trolox (Wang et al., 2021; Dziedziak et al., 2021; Edwards et al., 2022; Milbury, 2006).

Mechanism of Action  
Mechanistic evidence in ARPE-19 supports that Trolox acts as a phenolic chain-breaking antioxidant that intercepts oxLDL-driven ROS, preserves lysosomal integrity, and suppresses NF-κB nuclear translocation, thereby potentially blocking both the priming (signal 1) and activation (signal 2) arms of NLRP3 inflammasome signaling upstream of RPE death (Choi, 2019).

- Chain-breaking antioxidant chemistry: As a tocopherol analog with a phenolic chromanol headgroup, Trolox donates a hydrogen atom to lipid peroxyl/alkoxyl radicals, forming a relatively stable phenoxyl radical and interrupting propagation of polyunsaturated lipid autoxidation in membranes; this class behavior is emphasized in the AMD-relevant phenolic antioxidant literature and vitamin E chemistry (Gnanaguru et al., 2022). Vitamin E analogs can protect mitochondrial membranes by reacting with peroxyl radicals in lipid bilayers, an effect relevant to the inner mitochondrial membrane’s high cardiolipin/PUFA content, although Trolox-specific mitochondrial readouts were not reported in ARPE-19 (Edwards et al., 2022).  
- Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory signaling in RPE: In ARPE-19 cells subjected to oxLDL, Trolox dramatically suppressed intracellular ROS at 28 h; the ROS probe used detects H₂O₂, peroxynitrite, and hydroxyl radicals (not superoxide), indicating Trolox’s activity spans these species in this model (Choi, 2019). Trolox dose-dependently inhibited oxLDL-induced NF-κB nuclear translocation; this likely reflects lowered redox-sensitive signaling and/or reduced lysosomal damage-associated molecular patterning that can feed NF-κB activation (Choi, 2019). By suppressing NF-κB priming and preventing lysosomal destabilization (cathepsin release), Trolox is positioned mechanistically to blunt the two classical signals that drive NLRP3 activation in oxLDL-challenged RPE, although caspase-1 activity and IL-1β maturation were not assayed here (Choi, 2019).  
- Lysosomal stabilization and organelle targeting: Trolox significantly increased intact LysoTracker-positive particles after oxLDL, rescuing the 36 h oxLDL-induced loss of lysosomal staining at 10.4 μM; FITC-Trolox localized to membrane organelles (lysosomes/possibly mitochondria), consistent with direct membrane protection against peroxidation or ROS-induced destabilization (Choi, 2019).  
- Distinction from PPARγ agonism: Troglitazone’s protection persisted after PPARγ knockdown and rosiglitazone failed to protect; Trolox reproduced troglitazone’s effects, establishing that the phenolic antioxidant moiety (not PPARγ activation) mediates cytoprotection in this RPE oxLDL model (Choi, 2019).  
- Vitamin E pro-oxidant liabilities relevant to AMD: Tocopherols can, under certain conditions, reduce lipid hydroperoxides or redox-active metals to catalyze fragmentation of hydroperoxy endoperoxides, yielding γ-hydroxyalkenals and protein adducts such as carboxyethylpyrrole (CEP); CEP adducts are elevated in AMD tissue and can be pathogenic (angiogenic/immune activation), indicating that vitamin E chemistry is context-dependent and can potentially exacerbate formation of toxic lipid-derived aldehydes if not paired with appropriate co-antioxidants/metal control (Gu et al., 2011).  
- Transport/delivery context: Retinal vitamin E levels reflect systemic availability and transport via lipoproteins and α-tocopherol transfer proteins; the BRB poses delivery constraints, and α-TTP oligomers facilitate endothelial (not epithelial) transport, complicating systemic delivery to the outer retina/RPE (Edwards et al., 2022). Although Trolox is water-soluble and readily used in vitro, its in vivo distribution to retinal membranes is not characterized in the cited AMD-relevant literature, and targeted delivery (e.g., mitochondria-targeted antioxidants) may be required to reach mitochondrial inner membranes efficiently (Baksheeva et al., 2018).  
- Comparative potency within the class: Hindered phenols (e.g., PMC, BHT) outperformed Trolox in oxLDL-induced ARPE-19 cytotoxicity screens, and PMC additionally modulated lysosomal cholesterol handling (↑NPC-1, ↓cholesterol), suggesting that steric/electronic tuning of phenolic scaffolds can augment both antioxidant and lysosomal pathways more effectively than Trolox (Gnanaguru et al., 2022; Choi, 2019).

Expected Effect  
Under the stated hypothesis—Trolox scavenges mitochondrial lipid peroxyl radicals to preserve inner membrane integrity and electron transport in dry AMD—the expected proximal effects in RPE oxidative-lipid models are: (1) reduced intracellular ROS burden, particularly H₂O₂/peroxynitrite/hydroxyl products detected by standard ROS probes, (2) stabilization of lysosomal membranes against oxLDL-induced destabilization, (3) suppression of NF-κB nuclear translocation (priming), and (4) consequent blunting of downstream inflammasome activation; these effects are documented in ARPE-19/oxLDL at 10.4 μM Trolox (Choi, 2019). In the specific assay context proposed by the team (ARPE-19 under oxidative stress), Trolox is expected to:  

- Lower DCF-type ROS readouts after 28 h oxLDL, consistent with prior ARPE-19 results in which Trolox produced a dramatic reduction of intracellular ROS (Choi, 2019).  
- Restore LysoTracker-positive lysosomal particle counts at 36 h in oxLDL-treated ARPE-19 at the highest micromolar dose tested (10.4 μM), as observed previously; lower Trolox doses are likely insufficient for lysosomal rescue in this system (Choi, 2019).  
- Inhibit NF-κB nuclear translocation at 36 h in oxLDL-exposed ARPE-19 in a dose-dependent manner, with complete suppression at 10.4 μM and partial/absent suppression at 0.16–1.3 μM (Choi, 2019).  
- Notably, the ROS assay kits used in the cited studies do not detect superoxide, so additional measurements (e.g., MitoSOX) will be required to assess superoxide-specific effects in mitochondria, which is relevant for testing the stated mitochondrial hypothesis (Choi, 2019).

Although Trolox’s mitochondrial bioenergetic effects were not reported in the ARPE-19 oxLDL studies, vitamin E analogs are the major chain-breaking antioxidants in mitochondrial membranes and can quench peroxyl radicals propagating in inner membrane lipids; thus, if Trolox reaches mitochondrial membranes in RPE (as suggested by FITC-Trolox organelle localization), it is reasonable to expect partial preservation of Δψm and ATP under lipid-oxidation stress, contingent on subcellular delivery and radical burden (Edwards et al., 2022; Choi, 2019). The A2E/singlet-oxygen literature suggests Trolox will attenuate photooxidative lipofuscin chemistry but may be less efficient than specialized singlet-oxygen quenchers (OT-674), implying limited efficacy in light-dominated injury contexts relative to oxLDL-driven lipid oxidation (Zhou et al., 2008). Finally, expected downstream impact on NLRP3 is inferential (two-signal model) since caspase-1/IL-1β readouts were not measured in Trolox-treated ARPE-19, so inflammasome suppression should be verified explicitly if that is a target endpoint (Choi, 2019).

Overall Evaluation  
Trolox is a mechanistically plausible, well-behaved phenolic antioxidant probe that shows reproducible cytoprotection in an AMD-relevant RPE stress model (oxLDL), with documented suppression of ROS, preservation of lysosomal integrity, and inhibition of NF-κB activation; however, as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, it has notable limitations: absence of mitochondrial bioenergetic evidence in RPE, lack of in vivo efficacy/delivery data, potential vitamin E–class pro-oxidant liabilities, and inferiority to more potent hindered phenol scaffolds and targeted antioxidants in several relevant contexts.

Strengths  
- Clear in vitro activity in AMD-relevant RPE models: Across multiple independent excerpts of the same ARPE-19/oxLDL work, Trolox robustly reduced ROS at 28 h, stabilized lysosomes at 36 h, and suppressed NF-κB at higher micromolar dose, establishing on-pathway effects relevant to lipid oxidation, lysosomal integrity, and inflammatory priming (Choi, 2019). The PPARγ-independence and failure of rosiglitazone confirm that phenolic antioxidant chemistry, not nuclear receptor modulation, mediates these effects (Unknown Reference).  
- Organelle association and lysosomal targeting plausibility: FITC-Trolox localizes to membrane organelles; combined with prior demonstrations that inhibiting lipid peroxidation preserves lysosomes, this supports a direct membrane protective mechanism that is relevant for lysosomal injury in oxLDL-challenged RPE (Choi, 2019).  
- Class coherence and SAR support: Trolox’s efficacy fits within a broader hindered phenol paradigm in RPE, and more potent phenolic analogs (e.g., PMC) outperform Trolox and additionally modulate lysosomal cholesterol handling (↑NPC-1), indicating the pathway is druggable and phenolic scaffolds are tunable (Gnanaguru et al., 2022; Choi, 2019).  
- Cross-model antioxidant precedents: Trolox mitigates A2E photooxidation in a cell-free system, protects RGCs from H₂O₂/superoxide, reduces lipid peroxidation in cultured retina, and benefits diabetic retinal endpoints in antioxidant mixtures—evidence that Trolox engages retinal oxidative pathways across cell types and paradigms (Zhou et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2021; Garcia-Medina et al., 2020).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- No mitochondrial bioenergetic validation in RPE: The ARPE-19 oxLDL studies did not measure Δψm, ATP, oxygen consumption, or mitochondrial lipid peroxidation; thus the central hypothesis (inner membrane peroxyl scavenging preserves electron transport) remains untested in RPE, and the available ROS assay did not detect superoxide, limiting mechanistic resolution in mitochondria (Choi, 2019). By contrast, mitochondria-targeted antioxidants such as SkQ1 demonstrate efficacy and bioavailability in in vivo retinal oxidative stress models, highlighting a potential delivery disadvantage for non-targeted Trolox (Baksheeva et al., 2018).  
- Dosing window and endpoint sensitivity: In ARPE-19, Trolox’s full effects on lysosomal rescue and NF-κB suppression were confined to the highest tested dose (10.4 μM), with lower doses ineffective for these endpoints, suggesting a narrow efficacy window under oxLDL burden (Choi, 2019).  
- Phenolic pro-oxidant potential under metal/peroxide conditions: Vitamin E chemistry can promote fragmentation of lipid hydroperoxides and formation of toxic aldehydes (e.g., CEP) in the presence of redox-active metals; CEP adducts are elevated in AMD and are pathogenic, raising a risk that under certain retinal microenvironments Trolox or its phenoxyl radical could exacerbate deleterious lipid-fragmentation chemistry unless combined with appropriate co-antioxidants/metal control (Gu et al., 2011).  
- Translational uncertainty from vitamin E clinical data: Vitamin E alone has not consistently prevented AMD in human studies; benefits arise in combination formulations (AREDS/AREDS2), making attribution to vitamin E or extrapolation to Trolox as a monotherapy weak, and suggesting that multi-target, multi-antioxidant regimens or more potent/targeted phenolic analogs are more plausible clinical strategies (Wang et al., 2021; Dziedziak et al., 2021; Edwards et al., 2022).  
- Comparative inferiority to optimized scaffolds in key contexts: Hindered phenols such as BHT/PMC outperform Trolox in oxLDL-RPE cytoprotection; OT-674 outperforms Trolox in singlet-oxygen quenching relevant to lipofuscin photooxidation; these head-to-head data argue Trolox is better deployed as a mechanistic probe or reference rather than as the lead therapeutic (Choi, 2019; Gnanaguru et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2008).  
- Delivery/BRB issues: In vivo delivery of vitamin E–like agents to the RPE is constrained by the BRB and lipoprotein/α-TTP–dependent transport; no pharmacokinetic or retinal distribution data exist for Trolox in the cited AMD context, suggesting uncertain target engagement in RPE in vivo (Edwards et al., 2022).

Programmatic Implications  
- As a tool compound, Trolox is well-suited for de-risking the oxLDL→ROS→lysosome→NF-κB→NLRP3 cascade in RPE and establishing that phenolic chain-breaking antioxidants modulate upstream injury steps; its water solubility and reproducible in vitro effects are practical advantages (Choi, 2019).  
- For therapeutic development, Trolox itself is a weak candidate relative to mitochondria-targeted antioxidants and more potent hindered phenols; the near-term focus should be on (a) confirming mitochondrial protection endpoints in RPE (Δψm, ATP, mitochondrial lipid peroxidation) to validate the mitochondrial hypothesis mechanistically and (b) advancing optimized phenolic scaffolds or mitochondria-targeted constructs with superior potency and delivery characteristics (Choi, 2019; Baksheeva et al., 2018).  
- Given vitamin E pro-oxidant risks, incorporate mechanistic controls for hydroperoxide fragmentation and CEP formation in RPE assays, and test combinations with co-antioxidants/metal chelators under conditions that model retinal metal/protein adduct environments (Gu et al., 2011).  
- Do not use TEAC/Trolox-equivalent chemical antioxidant capacity as a surrogate for in-cell efficacy; chemical assays are valuable for initial screening but are poor predictors of subcellular targeting, redox network effects, or clinical performance in the retina (Zuluaga et al., 2017).

Conclusion  
Trolox demonstrates consistent phenolic antioxidant protection in an AMD-relevant ARPE-19 oxLDL model by lowering ROS, preserving lysosomes, and suppressing NF-κB, with plausible but unproven mitochondrial benefits in RPE; however, its therapeutic attractiveness is limited by lack of mitochondrial bioenergetic evidence in RPE, absence of in vivo efficacy/delivery data, potential pro-oxidant liabilities of the vitamin E class, and inferiority to more potent or targeted antioxidants in relevant assays (Choi, 2019; Gu et al., 2011; Baksheeva et al., 2018). As a program decision: use Trolox as a mechanistic positive control and profiling probe for the lipid-oxidation/lysosomal/NF-κB axis in RPE, but prioritize development of mitochondria-targeted antioxidants and optimized hindered phenolic scaffolds (e.g., PMC-like) that have demonstrated higher potency and better alignment with retinal delivery challenges (Gnanaguru et al., 2022; Choi, 2019; Baksheeva et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History (Expanded)  
- AREDS formulations: Benefit in slowing progression to advanced AMD with multi-antioxidant combinations that include vitamin E underscores the plausibility of antioxidant strategies but does not validate vitamin E monotherapy; generalizability and attribution to vitamin E are limited (Wang et al., 2021).  
- Vitamin E alone: Randomized and meta-analytic evidence conclude little or no effect of vitamin E alone for AMD onset/progression; population studies are inconsistent, undermining confidence in translating a single vitamin E analog like Trolox as a standalone therapy (Dziedziak et al., 2021; Milbury, 2006).  
- Phenolic analog discovery: In an AMD-relevant RPE death assay triggered by oxLDL, hindered phenols emerged as superior to Trolox with mechanistic hints of lysosomal membrane stabilization and lipid handling improvements (↑NPC-1), providing a rational medicinal chemistry trajectory away from Trolox (Gnanaguru et al., 2022).  
- RPE in vitro replication and gaps: The ARPE-19 studies explicitly note that all experiments were conducted in a single immortalized line, that the ROS kit did not detect superoxide, and that LysoTracker quantification has size/clumping limitations, arguing for replication in primary hf-RPE and with improved quantitative organelle and ROS probes; no in vivo retinal model data for Trolox are reported (Choi, 2019).

Mechanistic Considerations (Expanded)  
- NF-κB/NLRP3 axis: The oxLDL RPE literature frames NF-κB nuclear translocation as priming (signal 1) and lysosomal destabilization as signal 2 for NLRP3; Trolox inhibited both upstream inputs, which ought to reduce caspase-1 activation and IL-1β/IL-18 maturation—explicit measurement will be necessary to confirm inflammasome modulation (Choi, 2019).  
- Mitochondrial targeting gap: Vitamin E is abundant in mitochondrial membranes and can protect against peroxyl radical propagation, but Trolox lacks intrinsic mitochondrial targeting; in vivo evidence with SkQ1 underscores that mitochondrial delivery is a key determinant of efficacy in retinal oxidative stress (Edwards et al., 2022; Baksheeva et al., 2018).  
- Photochemical stress: Trolox shows some activity in A2E photooxidation but is outperformed by specialized singlet-oxygen quenchers, suggesting that Trolox will be less effective where singlet oxygen dominates (lipofuscin phototoxicity), whereas it may perform better in lipid autoxidation cascades initiated by oxLDL (Zhou et al., 2008).  
- Pro-oxidant contingencies: The tocopherol radical can participate in metal-mediated hydroperoxide cleavage pathways, potentially increasing toxic aldehyde burden (e.g., CEP) in the retina; careful evaluation of Trolox’s behavior in metal-rich or hydroperoxide-rich conditions pertinent to AMD tissue is mandatory (Gu et al., 2011).

Expected Effect (Expanded Experimental Readouts)  
- Quantify Δψm and ATP preservation under oxLDL ± Trolox using TMRE/TMRM or JC-1 and luciferase ATP assays to test the mitochondrial hypothesis; prior ARPE-19 Trolox studies did not record these endpoints (Choi, 2019).  
- Assess mitochondrial and lysosomal lipid peroxidation directly (e.g., MDA/TBARS, 4-HNE adducts, BODIPY 581/591 C11), as the lysosomal data infer lipid peroxidation blockade, but no direct lipid chemistry readouts were provided; also track CEP adduct formation under redox-active metal supplementation to assess pro-oxidant risk (Gu et al., 2011; Choi, 2019).  
- Profile ROS species more comprehensively, adding MitoSOX for superoxide to complement prior H₂O₂/peroxynitrite/hydroxyl readouts; the earlier ROS kit did not detect superoxide (Choi, 2019).  
- Confirm NLRP3 pathway effects (pro-IL-1β, IκB-α degradation, ASC specking, caspase-1 FLICA activity, IL-1β/IL-18 release) to substantiate the inflammasome hypothesis; earlier work did not directly assay these endpoints (Choi, 2019).

Risk–Benefit and Development Path  
- Risk: Weak clinical translatability signal for vitamin E monotherapy in AMD; potential pro-oxidant liabilities; uncertain retinal bioavailability; narrow in vitro dose window (Dziedziak et al., 2021; Gu et al., 2011; Edwards et al., 2022; Choi, 2019).  
- Benefit: Strong mechanistic alignment in RPE oxLDL injury; tractable in vitro tool for de-risking phenolic antioxidant mechanisms and benchmarking more potent/targeted analogs (Choi, 2019; Gnanaguru et al., 2022).  
- Development recommendation: Deploy Trolox as a mechanistic positive control and assay calibrant in ARPE-19/hf-RPE oxLDL and A2E-photooxidation workflows; prioritize medicinal chemistry on hindered phenols with demonstrated superior potency (PMC/BHT-like) and evaluate mitochondrial targeting strategies to overcome delivery constraints (Gnanaguru et al., 2022; Baksheeva et al., 2018).

In sum, Trolox is valuable for mechanistic validation of the lipid oxidation–lysosome–NF-κB axis in RPE and as a benchmark antioxidant in vitro, but it is not a compelling lead therapeutic for dry AMD given potency, delivery, and class-specific liabilities; efforts should pivot to optimized phenolic scaffolds and mitochondria-targeted antioxidants while using Trolox as a reference compound in RPE assay development and comparative profiling (Choi, 2019; Baksheeva et al., 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AICAR (5‐Aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide) is a synthetic nucleoside analog originally developed as an AMP mimetic agent that is capable of activating AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) across a range of cell types. It is produced by chemical synthesis and is available commercially (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich A9978), having been studied for several decades in the context of cellular energy metabolism and stress signaling. As a member of a class of compounds that mimic the natural intracellular messenger AMP, AICAR is taken up into cells via adenosine transporters and is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase into its active metabolite, ZMP (5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide monophosphate), which then mimics AMP in its interactions with AMPK (Efstathiou et al., 2020). This compound belongs to a well‐established class of metabolic modulators, and similar agents have been used in experimental settings to modulate glucose uptake, fatty acid oxidation, and overall energy homeostasis in both basic science and translational research contexts (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014). In addition, several preclinical studies have evaluated AICAR’s potential as an “exercise mimetic” due to its ability to enhance energy metabolism in muscle and other tissues, and its synthetic nature allows for reproducible and scalable dosing in research models (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, AICAR was developed primarily as an agent to activate AMPK in metabolic studies and has been investigated in a variety of preclinical models ranging from cancer to cardiovascular disease. In the oncology field, for example, AICAR has been shown to inhibit cancer cell proliferation, induce cell cycle arrest, and promote programmed cell death in several cancer types via AMPK-dependent modulation of pathways such as PI3K-Akt and mTOR (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014; Rattan et al., 2005). Clinical studies, particularly those in the cardiovascular arena, have also evaluated AICAR’s safety profile in the context of ischemia-reperfusion injury, including human trials during cardiac surgery, demonstrating that it can be administered safely in humans (Rattan et al., 2005). In the context of ocular research, AICAR has been studied for its effects on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and other ocular cell types; several studies have demonstrated that AICAR suppresses the production of pro-inflammatory complement components such as complement factor 3 (C3) and complement factor B (CFB) in RPE cells under inflammatory conditions (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017). Although there is no established clinical use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) to date, these preclinical observations, combined with its well-known pharmacological profile, have spurred interest in repurposing AICAR for treating retinal diseases characterized by oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020). Furthermore, studies examining AMPK activators in the eye – including those using AICAR in animal models of uveitis or oxidative stress-induced RPE damage – support the notion that activating this metabolic pathway can protect against retinal degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

Mechanism of Action:  
AICAR exerts its biological activity primarily through the activation of AMPK, a master regulator of cellular energy balance that responds to alterations in the AMP/ATP ratio. Once AICAR is imported into cells through adenosine transporters, it is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase to form ZMP, an analog of AMP. ZMP binds to the regulatory γ subunit of AMPK, causing a conformational change that facilitates AMPK phosphorylation at Thr172 by upstream kinases such as LKB1, thereby fully activating the kinase (Efstathiou et al., 2020). Activated AMPK then phosphorylates a series of downstream targets involved in energy metabolism, including acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) and elements of the mTOR signaling pathway. In RPE cells, this activation is particularly important because AMPK phosphorylates and activates ULK1, a kinase critical for initiating autophagy and mitophagy, thereby promoting the clearance of damaged mitochondria (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Chung et al., 2017).  

A central component of the rationale for using AICAR in dry AMD is its ability to stimulate the transcriptional coactivator PGC-1α. AMPK-mediated phosphorylation of PGC-1α enhances its activity and nuclear translocation, which in turn drives the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant defense, and metabolic adaptation (Hu et al., 2024; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). This mechanism is particularly attractive in dry AMD because mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells is thought to contribute significantly to disease pathogenesis by impairing oxidative phosphorylation, increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and triggering cell senescence or death (Tong et al., 2022; Rego, 2023). In addition to these AMPK-dependent effects, some studies have reported that AICAR exerts certain effects independent of AMPK activation. For instance, AICAR has been shown to suppress TNF-α-induced complement factor expression by mechanisms that do not involve AMPK, suggesting that alternative signaling pathways or direct modulation of transcription factor activity might also contribute to its overall activity profile (Chung et al., 2017; Kirchner et al., 2018). These AMPK-independent actions could either broaden the therapeutic potential of AICAR in modulating inflammatory responses or introduce complexity into its activity profile that will need to be carefully isolated and understood (Kirchner et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2024).  

Furthermore, AICAR has been observed to affect mitochondrial dynamics not only by stimulating biogenesis through PGC-1α activation but also by modifying autophagic flux through mTOR inhibition. In models of RPE oxidative stress, where excessive ROS levels lead to mitochondrial fragmentation and accumulation of dysfunctional organelles, AICAR-induced AMPK activation facilitates the clearance of damaged mitochondria via mitophagy, thus restoring mitochondrial quality and energy production (Fisher et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2024). Moreover, experimental evidence suggests that AICAR can modulate the balance between cellular glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation by shifting metabolism toward a more energy-efficient, oxidative phenotype, thereby increasing the overall oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and potentially improving cellular resilience under oxidative stress (Chan et al., 2020; Fisher, 2022).  

Expected Effect:  
Given its mechanisms of action, the expected effect of AICAR in an assay aimed at treating dry AMD would be multifaceted. In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress—a hallmark of dry AMD—AICAR treatment is expected to lead to robust activation of AMPK, as measured by increased phosphorylation of both AMPK and its downstream substrates such as ACC and ULK1 (Guo et al., 2018; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). This activation should in turn upregulate PGC-1α, resulting in enhanced transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, improved mitochondrial DNA replication, and an increased capacity for ATP production (Hu et al., 2024). As damaged mitochondria are a major source of ROS in stressed RPE cells, the stimulation of autophagy and mitophagy is anticipated to selectively clear these dysfunctional organelles, reducing cellular oxidative stress and preventing the secondary damage that contributes to RPE degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

In addition to these metabolic effects, AICAR is also expected to attenuate inflammatory responses within the RPE and adjacent retinal tissues. For instance, by modulating the activity of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) and reducing the expression of inflammatory mediators such as tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and complement components (e.g., C3 and CFB), AICAR would help to create a less pro-inflammatory microenvironment that could further protect RPE cells from damage (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017; Kirchner et al., 2018). These effects are particularly pertinent given that chronic, low-grade inflammation coupled with complement dysregulation is a recognized component of dry AMD pathogenesis.  

At the cellular level, the outcome of AICAR-induced AMPK activation is expected to manifest as enhanced mitochondrial function, improved energy charge (ATP/AMP ratio), reduced ROS accumulation, and, ultimately, a restoration of normal metabolic and autophagic flux in RPE cells (Fisher et al., 2022; Fisher, 2022). This improved bioenergetic profile should translate into protection against RPE cell death, potentially slowing or halting the progression of geographic atrophy associated with dry AMD (Yu et al., 2024; Si et al., 2023). Moreover, since RPE dysfunction in AMD also involves a reduction in the phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, AICAR’s modulatory effects on autophagy may indirectly help to restore the homeostatic functions of RPE cells, reducing the accumulation of damaging lipofuscin and drusen material (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Sung et al., 2015). In summary, the expected effect is a dual-action benefit—mitigation of oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum stresses via improved mitochondrial dynamics and an anti-inflammatory effect stemming from a reduction in complement activation and NF-κB-driven cytokine production (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020).  

Overall Evaluation:  
AICAR represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration owing to its robust and well-characterized mechanism of action via AMPK activation. The strengths of this candidate lie in its dual capacity to modulate critical pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis: on one hand, AICAR enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and promotes the removal of damaged mitochondria through autophagy/mitophagy, and on the other, it attenuates inflammatory cascades that exacerbate RPE cell damage (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hu et al., 2024). The ability of AICAR to upregulate PGC-1α is particularly compelling because mitochondrial dysfunction is now widely recognized as a central element in dry AMD. Preclinical studies have illustrated that dysregulation of mitochondrial function in RPE cells—a decrease in oxidative phosphorylation capacity, increased ROS production, and impaired clearance of damaged organelles—is pivotal in the initiation and progression of AMD (Tong et al., 2022; Rego, 2023). Thus, a compound like AICAR that can simultaneously restore mitochondrial health and mitigate inflammatory responses offers a multifaceted approach to disease modification.  

From the therapeutic history perspective, AICAR has been extensively studied in various preclinical models, including those of ocular inflammation and oxidative stress in RPE cells. Its ability to safely activate AMPK in vivo has been demonstrated across multiple species and contexts, including settings that mimic some aspects of AMD-related stress, such as endotoxin-induced uveitis and sodium iodate-induced RPE damage (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Chan et al., 2020). Additionally, the compound’s known clinical safety profile in human studies—albeit in contexts outside ophthalmology—provides an encouraging starting point for repurposing it for dry AMD, where no approved therapeutics currently exist (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017).  

However, there are notable weaknesses and challenges that must be addressed. First, while AMPK activation is generally beneficial for energy homeostasis and autophagy, certain studies have indicated that AICAR’s effects on RPE cell biology might be context-dependent. For instance, some experimental reports have shown that AICAR can reduce the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments by RPE cells—a process that is essential for retinal health—which may represent a double-edged sword if not carefully titrated (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Yu et al., 2024). In addition, the existence of AMPK-independent effects—such as the direct inhibition of complement factor expression—introduces complexity into the overall mechanism of action and makes it challenging to predict all downstream outcomes. Differential responses have also been observed between healthy and diseased donor RPE cells, implying that “metabolic memory” or cellular adaptation may influence drug responsiveness (Fisher et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2017). These considerations suggest that while the theoretical underpinnings for using AICAR in dry AMD are solid, the translation of these effects into clinical efficacy may require careful optimization of dosing, delivery, and patient selection.  

Another potential limitation is related to its broad mechanism of action. AICAR activates several metabolic pathways that are intertwined with many aspects of cellular physiology. While this pleiotropy provides the therapeutic benefit of addressing multiple dysregulated pathways in AMD simultaneously, it may also increase the risk of off-target effects or metabolic disturbances in tissues outside the retina (Rattan et al., 2005; Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014). For instance, systemic administration of AICAR has been associated with shifts in glycolytic flux and modifications of lipid metabolism, and it is therefore imperative that strategies for ocular delivery (such as intravitreal injections or topical formulations) be developed to maximize retinal exposure while minimizing systemic exposure (Chan et al., 2020; Kamoshita et al., 2014).  

Moreover, despite the substantial body of preclinical data supporting the role of AICAR in activating AMPK and restoring mitochondrial function, clinical data specific to dry AMD are lacking. Although related studies have shown benefits in models of retinal inflammation and degeneration, the exact therapeutic window, long-term safety, and efficacy in humans with AMD must be thoroughly evaluated in well-designed clinical trials. It is also worth mentioning that other AMPK activators, such as metformin, have independently demonstrated protective effects in AMD models, thereby lending credence to the approach but also raising questions about whether AICAR offers a distinct advantage over these agents (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020).  

In summary, the overall evaluation of AICAR as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. Its well-documented ability to activate AMPK, stimulate PGC-1α-driven mitochondrial biogenesis, and induce autophagy presents a strong mechanistic rationale for protecting RPE cells from the mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress that drive dry AMD pathogenesis (Hu et al., 2024; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2011). The preclinical evidence, gathered from studies in ocular models and other systems, provides encouraging proof-of-concept data that support further investigation (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Hyttinen et al., 2011). Nonetheless, complexities related to AMPK-independent effects, differential responses in healthy versus diseased cells, and potential off-target metabolic changes underscore the need for rigorous preclinical optimization and carefully designed clinical trials before this candidate can be definitively validated for dry AMD treatment (Chung et al., 2017; Fisher et al., 2022; Kirchner et al., 2018).  

Considering all the available literature, the repurposing of AICAR for dry AMD appears to be a promising strategy that merits further investigation. The compound’s ability to simultaneously address mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and chronic inflammation positions it as a multifaceted agent with the potential to modify disease progression in a condition that currently lacks effective therapeutic options (Chung et al., 2017; Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020). Moving forward, it will be critical to further elucidate the detailed cellular and molecular responses to AICAR in human RPE cells, determine the optimal dosing and delivery parameters specific to the ocular environment, and perform in vivo studies that mimic the complex pathobiology of dry AMD. With these additional efforts, AICAR could eventually emerge as a valuable addition to the limited therapeutic arsenal available for managing this debilitating condition.  

In conclusion, AICAR’s robust preclinical profile as an AMPK activator, its well-understood mechanisms of promoting mitochondrial biogenesis and autophagy, and its capacity to mitigate inflammatory responses provide a solid scientific basis for its potential repurposing in dry AMD (Hu et al., 2024; Hyttinen et al., 2011; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). However, several challenges remain: the dual nature of its effects (both AMPK-dependent and independent), the possibility of adverse effects on key RPE functions such as phagocytosis, and the need for precise ocular drug delivery methods. Therefore, while AICAR is an exciting candidate with considerable mechanistic appeal, its translation from bench to bedside in the treatment of dry AMD will require further detailed studies to fully map its therapeutic window, safety profile, and efficacy in human subjects (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014; Rego, 2023; Kamoshita et al., 2014). Continued rigorous research and methodical clinical evaluation will determine whether AICAR can be developed into an effective treatment modality for this currently intractable form of macular degeneration.
