Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Metformin is a well‐known therapeutic agent belonging to the biguanide class, originally derived from guanidine compounds found in the plant Galega officinalis. The molecule is a synthetic derivative of naturally occurring galegine and has been refined into a modern oral antihyperglycemic agent (Augustin & Atorf, 2023). This class of compounds has historically been used as a first-line oral treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus, with metformin being one of the most prescribed drugs worldwide for managing hyperglycemia. Its synthesis did not follow the classical target‐driven design path but instead emerged from an adaptation of naturally occurring structures into a chemically optimized, orally bioavailable, and generally well-tolerated drug (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Dang et al., 2021). Given its long clinical history starting from the 1950s and subsequent FDA approval in the 1990s, metformin has accumulated a significant amount of safety data and clinical experience, which collectively make it an attractive candidate for repurposing into other disease areas, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) characterized by geographic atrophy (Amin et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, metformin has been used extensively as an antidiabetic agent to lower hepatic glucose output and improve peripheral insulin sensitivity. Its beneficial pleiotropic effects beyond glycemic control have been recognized over the years; these include anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antiangiogenic properties, which have been observed in both biochemical and clinical investigations. Multiple epidemiologic studies have examined the association between metformin use and ocular outcomes. Retrospective analyses in predominantly diabetic cohorts have indicated that metformin use correlates with reduced odds or hazard for developing age-related macular degeneration and other retinal diseases, although some studies report mixed results depending on cumulative dose, exposure timing, and concomitant diabetes-related complications (Moir et al., 2023; Amin et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2022). Notably, while metformin has not historically been approved for any ocular indication, several preclinical studies using retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cell models have demonstrated that metformin may protect against oxidative damage and improve mitochondrial function. Moreover, a Phase II single-blind randomized trial was initiated to assess the efficacy of metformin in slowing the progression of geographic atrophy among non-diabetic patients with advanced dry AMD (Shen et al., 2024), suggesting that the concept of repurposing metformin for dry AMD is already under active clinical investigation.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, metformin’s primary mechanism of action involves the inhibition of mitochondrial complex I of the electron transport chain, resulting in a decrease in ATP production and a concomitant increase in the intracellular AMP:ATP ratio. This metabolic shift leads to the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a master regulator of cellular energy homeostasis that orchestrates shifts in metabolism under conditions of energy deficit (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). AMPK activation exerts multiple downstream effects that are particularly relevant to RPE cell function and the pathogenesis of geographic atrophy. First, AMPK activation promotes autophagy, including mitophagy, a quality-control mechanism that ensures the removal of dysfunctional mitochondria. Preclinical studies in RPE cell models, such as those using ARPE-19 cells, have provided evidence that metformin increases autophagosome formation, reduces intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS), lowers apoptosis rates, and helps maintain the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) under oxidative stress conditions (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Toppila et al., 2024). Additionally, the activation of AMPK in RPE cells has been associated with upregulation of protective pathways including enhanced nitric oxide (NO) production and increased expression of mitochondrial biogenesis factors such as PGC-1α, which together contribute to improved mitochondrial quality control (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023).  

Furthermore, metformin is known to activate both AMPK-dependent and AMPK-independent signaling pathways. The AMPK-independent effects may include inhibition of NF-κB activation, leading to a reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α, which are implicated in chronic inflammation observed in the aging retina (Jiang et al., 2022; Amin et al., 2022). From a biochemical standpoint, the inhibition of complex I by metformin also directly reduces the leakage of electrons that can form ROS, thereby lowering mitochondrial oxidative stress—a key aspect in the progression of dry AMD pathogenesis (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). It is important to note, however, that several reports have highlighted the concern that activation of AMPK in vivo or in vitro appears to require suprapharmacological doses of metformin, casting uncertainty on whether standard clinical dosing is sufficient to achieve these retinal effects (Moir et al., 2023). Nonetheless, the preclinical evidence supports a model whereby metformin’s inhibition of mitochondrial complex I—thereby reducing ROS and enhancing autophagy—provides a rationale for its potential use in protecting RPE cells from oxidative stress-induced damage (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis driving the repurposing of metformin for dry AMD is predicated on its ability to activate AMPK and inhibit mitochondrial complex I leakage in RPE cells, leading to reduced ROS production and enhanced mitochondrial quality control. In the context of geographic atrophy, RPE dysfunction and death play a central role in the degeneration of photoreceptors and the progression of AMD. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that metformin can protect ARPE-19 cells (an established human RPE cell line) from oxidative insults by lowering intracellular ROS levels, augmenting autophagic processes, and preserving mitochondrial membrane potential (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Toppila et al., 2024). Additionally, through the activation of AMPK, metformin is expected to stimulate the expression of mitochondrial biogenesis factors, leading to improved mitochondrial function, which is critical given the high metabolic demands of the RPE (Moir et al., 2023). 

Epidemiologically, several retrospective cohort and case-control studies have observed associations between metformin use and a reduced risk of developing AMD. Some studies even suggest that these associations are dose- and timing-dependent, with earlier or sustained use of metformin correlating with greater protective effects (Moir et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022). Therefore, in an assay designed to measure the effects of metformin on mitochondrial function and oxidative stress in RPE cells, one would expect to see an enhancement in autophagic flux, decreased markers of oxidative stress, and preservation or restoration of Δψm. These cellular effects would ideally translate into a slower progression of geographic atrophy in vivo, as suggested by the decreased degeneration of the retinal layers that has been observed in certain mouse models of retinal damage (Jiang et al., 2022; Amin et al., 2022). RPE cells are known to express AMPK and other components of the autophagy machinery, which further supports the rationale for targeting these pathways in the treatment of dry AMD (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Moir et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
Metformin shows considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly for geographic atrophy, due to several key strengths. First, its long and well-documented clinical history in the management of type 2 diabetes provides a robust safety profile and widespread clinical familiarity, which is a significant advantage when considering repurposing strategies (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Dang et al., 2021; Amin et al., 2022). Second, the molecular and cellular mechanisms by which metformin acts—namely, the inhibition of mitochondrial complex I, subsequent activation of AMPK, and promotion of autophagy—are highly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. The ability of metformin to reduce ROS and promote mitochondrial quality control addresses one of the core aspects of RPE dysfunction and degeneration seen in geographic atrophy (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Jiang et al., 2022).

Furthermore, the epidemiologic data showing associations between metformin use and a reduced incidence of AMD lend additional support to its potential utility in this setting (Liang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023). The possibility that metformin’s protective effects might be independent of its glycemic control properties is particularly intriguing, as it expands the target population to non-diabetic AMD patients—a group that represents the majority of those affected by geographic atrophy (Moir et al., 2023; Brown et al., 2019; Moir et al., 2024). On a mechanistic level, the detailed understanding of metformin’s interaction with AMPK and mitochondrial pathways not only provides a clear therapeutic target but also offers multiple biomarkers for assessing efficacy in both preclinical and clinical studies.

Despite its strengths, several weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. One significant concern is whether standard clinical doses of metformin are sufficient to activate the AMPK pathway in retinal tissues, given that some in vitro studies indicate suprapharmacological doses are required to see a robust effect (Moir et al., 2023). This raises questions of retinal bioavailability and whether alternative delivery strategies, such as local ocular administration or formulation enhancements, might be required to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE. Additionally, while the epidemiologic studies are promising, they are not uniformly consistent; some retrospective analyses have reported no association or even conflicting results depending on dosing and timing parameters (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Brown et al., 2019; Amin et al., 2022). These discrepancies underscore the inherent limitations of observational data, including potential confounding factors such as the presence and severity of diabetes, concomitant medications, and the challenges of accurately classifying AMD subtypes using administrative coding.

Another consideration is that although metformin’s broad mechanism of action (i.e., modulation of inflammation, oxidative stress, and autophagy) is advantageous in addressing multifactorial diseases like AMD, it may also lead to off-target effects or systemic side effects such as vitamin B12 deficiency or, in rare instances, lactic acidosis (Jiang et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). In elderly populations—who are generally most affected by dry AMD—these risks must be carefully weighed against the potential benefits. Moreover, the heterogeneity in study designs and patient populations in the available epidemiologic literature means that prospective, well-designed clinical trials remain essential to definitively determine whether metformin can meaningfully slow the progression of geographic atrophy in AMD (Shen et al., 2024).

In summary, the overall evaluation of metformin as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. Its well-established safety profile, combined with mechanistic data that align closely with the underlying pathology of geographic atrophy, make it a compelling candidate. The strengths lie in its ability to activate AMPK, thereby reducing mitochondrial ROS, promoting autophagy, and potentially preserving RPE function—molecular actions that directly address key pathological features of dry AMD. However, critical questions regarding dosing, ocular bioavailability, and the variability in epidemiologic outcomes necessitate further rigorous investigation in controlled clinical settings. Moving forward, clinical trials designed to specifically assess metformin’s efficacy in non-diabetic populations with early to intermediate stages of geographic atrophy will be crucial to validate its repurposing potential. Overall, while metformin has significant promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, additional studies are needed to resolve questions about its optimal dosing regimen, delivery method, and long-term efficacy in preserving retinal structure and function (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
EUK-134 is a synthetic antioxidant belonging to the class of manganese salen complexes designed to mimic the endogenous activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase. Its synthesis involves a controlled condensation reaction between salicylaldehyde and ethylenediamine, resulting in a small molecule whose molecular framework is optimized for redox cycling and catalytic detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). As a representative of SOD/catalase mimetics, EUK-134 is engineered to convert the superoxide anion (O2–) into hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and subsequently decompose H2O2 into water and oxygen. Its dual-activity design places it in a promising category for therapeutic intervention in diseases driven by oxidative stress. The compound’s synthetic origin allows for fine-tuning of physicochemical properties such as lipophilicity and catalytic efficiency, making it a candidate for repurposing in disease conditions beyond those for which it was originally developed (Thoma et al., 2020; Grujicic & Allen, 2024). Within the pharmaceutical landscape, this class of compounds has been extensively studied in preclinical models for their ability to mitigate cellular damage by neutralizing ROS; they have been applied experimentally in models of muscle atrophy, ischemia–reperfusion injury, and certain cancer indications, where oxidative stress is known to play a critical role (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). The molecular architecture of EUK-134 notably offers a compact, dual-function approach that, in theory, should counterbalance both superoxide and hydrogen peroxide accumulation—a feature that is especially relevant given that the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is subject to chronic oxidative insult (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of EUK-134 is marked by its application in various preclinical models where oxidative stress and subsequent mitochondrial dysfunction were central to the pathology. In studies involving human skeletal muscle cells, EUK-134 has been shown to attenuate endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress-induced mitochondrial dysfunction induced by tunicamycin, resulting in improved mitochondrial membrane potential and restoration of bioenergetic profiles (Thoma et al., 2020). Moreover, this compound has been evaluated in contexts such as hyperoxic myocardial tissues, where it mitigated oxidative damage and contributed to the preservation of cellular function under stress conditions (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). Its potential benefits in reducing oxidative damage have also been noted in studies involving breast cancer cells and mechanical unloading-induced muscle atrophy, highlighting its versatility as a ROS-scavenging agent (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).  
Despite the significant body of work on EUK-134 in non-ocular tissues, its direct evaluation in dry AMD or similar degenerative retinal conditions has not yet been thoroughly explored. Clinical trials and literature searches focusing on Mn-porphyrin SOD mimetics have yielded extensive data relating to retinal diseases (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.), but EUK-134 itself has not been the primary focus in retinal clinical applications. Nonetheless, its proven mechanism of reducing ROS accumulation positions it as an attractive candidate for extension into the field of ocular therapeutics. In this light, the repurposing of EUK-134 for dry AMD is based on the hypothesis that its antioxidant properties, previously validated in muscle and other tissues, may confer similar protective effects in RPE cells that are chronically exposed to oxidative stress (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, EUK-134 functions by catalytically mimicking the activities of superoxide dismutase and catalase. In its SOD mimetic capacity, EUK-134 accepts electrons from the superoxide anions, facilitating their conversion into hydrogen peroxide—a reaction which is essential to limit direct superoxide-mediated damage (Thoma et al., 2020). Following this, the catalase mimetic activity is intended to decompose the resultant hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, thereby preventing accumulation of H2O2 which can otherwise contribute to oxidative injury through Fenton-type reactions. However, several studies have drawn attention to limitations in this pathway. For example, evidence indicates that EUK-134 may exhibit a lower efficiency in H2O2 scavenging when compared to other antioxidants such as MnTBAP or native catalase, particularly in environments with high oxidative flux (Quan et al., 2017). One key observation is a significant down-regulation of catalase expression – by more than five-fold – upon EUK-134 treatment in some cellular systems, a factor that potentially undermines its capacity to fully counteract H2O2 buildup (Quan et al., 2017).  
On the molecular interaction front, the manganese center within the salen complex undergoes redox cycling, alternating between oxidation states in response to ROS encounters. This cyclic activity contributes to its continuous catalytic turnover and represents the biochemical foundation for its antioxidant action. Furthermore, studies have shown that EUK-134 can modulate various signaling pathways associated with oxidative stress responses, such as the TGF-β1/Smad2 pathway in muscle under atrophy-inducing conditions (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). Despite these promising aspects, challenges such as suboptimal mitochondrial uptake remain a concern since effective neutralization of ROS in RPE cells requires prompt access to the mitochondrial matrix—a compartment frequently characterized by an inherently challenging microenvironment for drug delivery (Quan et al., 2017). In summary, while EUK-134 possesses a dual action mechanism that addresses two key components of the ROS cascade, the efficiency of its H2O2 detoxification and its cellular distribution are critical parameters that must be rigorously characterized in the context of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
In dry AMD and particularly in geographic atrophy, the retinal pigment epithelium is subject to sustained oxidative stress, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and subsequent cell death. The expected therapeutic effect of EUK-134 in this context is to provide robust antioxidant protection within RPE mitochondria, thereby neutralizing excessive superoxide and hydrogen peroxide levels and preserving mitochondrial integrity (Thoma et al., 2020). Restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) is a key indicator of improved mitochondrial function; thus, by mitigating ROS-induced depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane, EUK-134 is anticipated to maintain or restore ATP production and spare respiratory capacity in RPE cells. These effects are crucial given that ATP depletion and bioenergetic failure are prominent features in the pathology of dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012).  
In vitro assays that simulate oxidative stress conditions—such as those employing RPE cell cultures under hypoxic or chemically induced stress—will likely measure parameters including Δψm, ATP levels, ROS quantification, and expression levels of stress-responsive genes. The anticipated outcome is that EUK-134 will lead to a measurable decrease in the levels of ROS as detected by biochemical assays, along with a concomitant stabilization of mitochondrial respiratory function (Thoma et al., 2020; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012). In addition, molecular analyses may reveal a down-regulation of oxidative stress markers and an improvement in the overall redox balance of the cell. It is vital, however, to consider that some studies have noted that EUK-134 does not inhibit all markers of stress uniformly—for example, the continued expression of GADD34 has been observed even where other stress indicators are normalized (Thoma et al., 2020).  
Given that RPE cells naturally express endogenous antioxidant enzymes such as SOD and catalase, supplementation with EUK-134 is expected to either bolster these defenses or compensate for their decline during chronic oxidative challenges. This dual functionality could theoretically translate into a reduced progression of RPE cell death, slower accumulation of drusen, and ultimately a deceleration of geographic atrophy, all of which are hallmarks of dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of EUK-134 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration involves weighing its mechanistic promise against the practical challenges encountered in its preclinical and potential clinical application. On the one hand, EUK-134 embodies several clear strengths. Its dual mimetic activities align well with the fundamental pathophysiology of dry AMD, where both superoxide and hydrogen peroxide are implicated in the oxidative cascade that leads to mitochondrial dysfunction and RPE cell demise (Thoma et al., 2020; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012). The synthetic nature of EUK-134 allows for controlled chemical modifications which could be leveraged to optimize its pharmacokinetic properties, and its relatively small size is an asset for penetrating tissues such as the retina. Additionally, the compound’s history in attenuating ER stress-related mitochondrial dysfunction in muscle cells provides a robust proof-of-concept that similar benefits might be translatable to RPE cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress (Thoma et al., 2020).  
Notwithstanding these advantages, several weaknesses must be scrutinized. A primary concern lies in the evidence that EUK-134 may exhibit limitations in catalase-like activity, particularly with regard to its efficiency in cleaving hydrogen peroxide. Studies have documented a significant down-regulation of catalase expression upon treatment with EUK-134 and noted that its H2O2 scavenging capabilities fall short when benchmarked against other agents such as MnTBAP or even native catalase (Quan et al., 2017). In the context of RPE cells, where the oxidative insult is persistent and multifactorial, such limitations could result in suboptimal clearance of H2O2, thereby potentially compromising the therapeutic efficacy.  
Another critical issue pertains to drug delivery and cellular bioavailability. The strategic pathway forward would involve an in-depth exploration of its pharmacological properties in retinal models, formulation modifications to enhance mitochondrial delivery, and dose-optimization studies to balance antioxidant efficacy with safety. Only after these issues are rigorously addressed can EUK-134 be confidently positioned as a viable repurposed candidate for the treatment of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Quan et al., 2017; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012).

Under normal conditions, the electron transport chain generates a high proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis; however, this gradient is also responsible for the partial leakage of electrons, which react with molecular oxygen to form superoxide radicals. BAM15’s mechanism is predicated on “mild uncoupling,” which entails a limited dissipation of the proton motive force to reduce the probability of electron slippage at complexes I and III without compromising the entirety of ATP generation. At the molecular level, BAM15 inserts into the mitochondrial inner membrane where its lipophilic and protonophoric properties allow it to shuttle protons from the intermembrane space back into the matrix. This process effectively lowers the mitochondrial membrane potential, diminishing the driving force for electron leakage and concomitant ROS formation (Xiong et al., 2023; Jang et al., 2025).  

Furthermore, BAM15’s action is linked with secondary effects on key intracellular signaling pathways. The reduction in ATP production, while carefully moderated, can activate AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a critical sensor of cellular energy status. The overall evaluation of BAM15 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals several strengths but also underscores significant areas requiring further investigation. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10), also known as ubiquinone, is a naturally occurring lipophilic molecule synthesized endogenously via the mevalonate pathway. It is a quinone class compound that was originally discovered as a crucial component of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) and is essential for adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production. Chemically, CoQ10 contains a benzoquinone ring and a long isoprenoid side chain, which confers its lipid solubility and allows integration into mitochondrial and other cellular membranes. As a therapeutic candidate, it is available commercially (e.g., Cayman Chemical #700105) as a pure formulation that can be used for research purposes and has been repurposed in several settings to address oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Its widespread use as a dietary supplement and as an adjunct therapy in cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and metabolic disorders underlines the extensive clinical experience with this class of compounds. The rationale for its repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is based on the compound’s natural role as a coenzyme, its potent antioxidant properties, and its ability to modulate mitochondrial energy metabolism—all of which are critically compromised in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) of the aging eye (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Maiuolo et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past decades, CoQ10 has been evaluated in multiple experimental and clinical contexts. Biochemical studies have consistently demonstrated its ability to protect mitochondrial structure and function by facilitating electron transport and scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS). In vitro, CoQ10 treatments have been shown to improve mitochondrial respiration and ATP production in various cell types, including ARPE-19 cells, a widely used human RPE model. These studies utilized oxidative stress challenges (e.g., H₂O₂ exposure) to simulate conditions similar to those present in dry AMD, and showed that CoQ10 supplementation lowered levels of apoptotic markers such as caspase-3 and TUNEL staining, effectively reducing cell death (Hernandez et al., 2024). In the clinical arena, several studies have explored the use of CoQ10, sometimes in combination with other nutritional compounds, for early stages of AMD. For instance, combination therapies incorporating CoQ10 with agents such as acetyl-L-carnitine and n-3 fatty acids have resulted in improvements in visual function and fundus appearance among early AMD patients, demonstrating its potential impact in slowing disease progression (Feher et al., 2005). Moreover, its established safety profile in chronic use and its history of use as a metabolic booster and antioxidant in various degenerative conditions further support its potential repurposing for dry AMD, where similar mitochondrial and oxidative stress mechanisms underlie disease pathology (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Kiliç, 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, CoQ10 exhibits a dual mechanism of action that is highly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Firstly, it functions as an obligatory electron carrier within mitochondria. In the ETC, CoQ10 shuttles electrons from complexes I (NADH dehydrogenase) and II (succinate dehydrogenase) to complex III (cytochrome bc₁ complex), thereby driving the proton gradient needed for ATP synthesis by ATP synthase. Its redox-active benzoquinone ring is capable of reversible oxidation and reduction, enabling it to accept and donate electrons during the process of cellular respiration (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Hernandez et al., 2024). This electron-transfer activity is critical in tissues with high metabolic demands such as the retina, where the maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (mt∆ψ) and ATP production are indispensable for cell survival. A second and equally important aspect of CoQ10’s mechanism is its potent antioxidant property. Through its reduced form, ubiquinol, CoQ10 directly scavenges free radicals and prevents lipid peroxidation of cell membranes. This antioxidant activity extends to the regeneration of other lipid-soluble antioxidants such as vitamin E, thereby reinforcing a broader cellular antioxidant defense network (Manzar et al., 2020; Hernandez et al., 2024).

In the context of RPE cells, the protective effects of CoQ10 extend to the stabilization of mitochondrial proteins and prevention of oxidative damage-induced mtDNA release. Notably, CoQ10 has been shown to modulate the expression of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase-2 (SOD2), which further contributes to the reduction of intracellular ROS levels. Additionally, CoQ10 influences mitochondrial dynamics by reducing the activation of pro-fission proteins like DRP-1, thereby inhibiting excessive mitochondrial fragmentation—a phenomenon that has been associated with increased apoptosis in oxidative stress conditions (Hernandez et al., 2024). Its capacity to dampen inflammatory mediators, including the restoration of cytokines such as TNFα and caspase-1 to their baseline levels following oxidative insult, underscores its role in mitigating the inflammatory cascades implicated in AMD pathology (Hernandez et al., 2024). These combined actions—preservation of electron transport efficiency, reduction in ROS-mediated damage, and stabilization of mitochondrial integrity—are central to the hypothesis that exogenous supplementation of CoQ10 can counteract the underlying cellular stress mechanisms in dry AMD (Hernandez et al., 2024; Maiuolo et al., 2022).

Expected Effect in the Assay and Mechanistic Rationale:  
Given the proposed experimental approach—using H₂O₂-challenged ARPE-19 cells as a model to simulate oxidative stress encountered in dry AMD—the expected effect of exogenous CoQ10 supplementation would be multi-fold. Firstly, by increasing the mitochondrial pool of ubiquinone, the supplemented CoQ10 is expected to enhance electron transport efficiency within RPE cells, thereby sustaining ATP production under stress conditions. The repletion of CoQ10 levels would counteract the age-associated decline in endogenous CoQ10 and restore mitochondrial membrane potential, which is critical for normal cell metabolism (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Maiuolo et al., 2022). Secondly, due to its antioxidant properties, CoQ10 is anticipated to directly scavenge ROS generated by H₂O₂ exposure, thereby reducing oxidative lipid peroxidation and preventing damage to mitochondrial membranes and proteins. As a result, key apoptotic markers—such as caspase-3 activity and TUNEL-positive cell counts—should be decreased, reflecting improved cell viability and reduced progression toward cell death (Hernandez et al., 2024).

Moreover, it is expected that CoQ10 may influence the expression of genes related to mitochondrial defense and redox balance, such as those encoding for SOD2 and other antioxidant enzymes, ultimately leading to a more robust cellular response against oxidative insults. Since ARPE-19 cells express the protein machinery integral to both oxidative phosphorylation and antioxidant defense, the modulation of these pathways by CoQ10 would provide a mechanistic basis for its protective effects in vitro (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Hernandez et al., 2024). In addition, the expected synergistic benefits when CoQ10 is combined with a nutritional complex—such as Nutrof—has been documented, where the combination was more effective at reducing oxidative stress markers and apoptosis than CoQ10 alone (Hernandez et al., 2024). This synergistic effect likely arises from the complementary actions of CoQ10 in regenerating other antioxidants and its specific targeting of mitochondrial dysfunction—a key driver of dry AMD pathology (Hernandez et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
The comprehensive review of the literature provides strong mechanistic rationale and preclinical evidence to support the repurposing of CoQ10 for dry AMD. One of the primary strengths of CoQ10 as a candidate is its dual role—facilitating electron transport and exerting antioxidant effects—which addresses two critical pathological features in dry AMD: mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. Its ability to preserve mitochondrial integrity by maintaining the electron transport chain and reducing mitochondrial depolarization directly aligns with the needs of RPE cells, which have high energy demands and are vulnerable to oxidative damage (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Hernandez et al., 2024).

Furthermore, numerous in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have demonstrated that CoQ10 supplementation leads to reduced apoptosis, lower ROS generation, and improved cell viability following oxidative challenges. These studies provide robust biochemical evidence that CoQ10 can counteract cellular stresses that mimic early events in AMD pathogenesis (Hernandez et al., 2024). From a therapeutic history standpoint, the extensive clinical experience with CoQ10 in other degenerative and mitochondrial disorders lends additional credibility to its safety and potential efficacy for ocular applications. Its long history of use as an adjunct supplement in various conditions enhances its attractiveness as a repurposed drug candidate from a regulatory and translational perspective (Feher et al., 2005).

However, several challenges must also be considered. One key weakness is the issue of bioavailability. CoQ10 is a large, lipophilic molecule, and its effective delivery to the retina following systemic or topical administration remains a significant technical hurdle. Although studies have shown that exogenous CoQ10 can elevate retinal levels to some extent, optimizing its formulation for enhanced tissue penetration and sustained release is critical for therapeutic success (Manzar et al., 2020; Qu et al., 2009). Additionally, the variability observed in clinical responses in AMD studies suggests that patient-specific factors or differences in the progression of mitochondrial dysfunction may influence the therapeutic outcomes. Therefore, while the preclinical data are promising, rigorous clinical studies are needed to determine optimal dosing regimens, delivery methods (such as oral versus topical administration), and combination strategies with other antioxidants or mitotropic agents (Feher et al., 2005).

Another important consideration is the multifactorial nature of dry AMD, which involves not only mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress but also chronic inflammation, complement dysregulation, and genetic predispositions. As such, CoQ10 monotherapy may not fully address the complex pathological processes underlying the disease. Combination therapies that target multiple pathways simultaneously, such as those combining CoQ10 with nutritional complexes that include other antioxidants and anti-inflammatory agents, are likely to yield better clinical outcomes. In this regard, CoQ10 appears to be particularly well-suited for inclusion in combination regimens designed to synergistically reduce oxidative stress and support mitochondrial health (Hernandez et al., 2024; Feher et al., 2005).

The mechanistic data support the hypothesis that elevating RPE mitochondrial ubiquinone pools can enhance electron transport efficiency and reduce ROS accumulation. Detailed biochemical analyses have shown that CoQ10 prevents lipid peroxidation and stabilizes the mitochondrial membrane potential, which in turn decreases the release of pro-apoptotic factors such as cytochrome c and prevents the activation of caspases (Hernandez et al., 2024). These effects are particularly relevant to dry AMD, where RPE cell death and the subsequent degeneration of photoreceptors play a central role in disease progression (Hernandez et al., 2024).

Overall, the aggregate evidence from biochemical, in vitro, and early clinical studies strongly supports the continued investigation of CoQ10 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its established role in mitochondrial function and cellular antioxidant defense mechanisms, combined with a favorable safety profile, provides a firm scientific basis for clinical translation. The expected benefits in ARPE-19 assays—namely, enhanced cell viability, reduced ROS levels, and the attenuation of apoptosis—reflect the direct mechanistic impacts of CoQ10 on key aspects of dry AMD pathology. Moreover, the potential to modulate mitochondrial dynamics via regulation of proteins such as DRP-1 and maintain mtDNA integrity further underscores its therapeutic relevance (Hernandez et al., 2024).

In conclusion, while CoQ10 is not without its challenges—primarily related to its delivery and the multifactorial etiology of dry AMD—the strengths of its molecular mechanism and supportive preclinical data render it a highly promising candidate. The potential for topical and systemic administration to elevate retinal levels, combined with its dual action as both a metabolic enhancer and a free radical scavenger, aligns well with the therapeutic needs of dry AMD patients. Nonetheless, further research is warranted to optimize formulations, validate efficacy in larger clinical trials, and explore its integration into multi-targeted therapeutic strategies. Given the existing biochemical and clinical literature, CoQ10 represents a rational and mechanistically sound approach for addressing mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in dry AMD, making it a candidate worthy of further development and investigation (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Hernandez et al., 2024; Feher et al., 2005; Qu et al., 2009).

As a member of the phytochemical family, sulforaphane belongs to a class of natural compounds known for inducing phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins. Historically, this compound has been extensively investigated for its chemopreventive and cytoprotective properties, particularly through the activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. Being one of the most studied Nrf2 activators, its discovery stemmed from early investigations into dietary antioxidants and their role in reducing carcinogenesis and inflammation. However, it should be noted that although sulforaphane has been studied in various retinal degeneration models, there is no established clinical history of its use in human dry AMD. The principal mechanism underlying sulforaphane’s protective effects is its ability to activate the Nrf2 pathway. Under basal conditions, the transcription factor Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytosol via binding to its inhibitor, Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1), which directs Nrf2 for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Sulforaphane, as exemplified by the Sigma-Aldrich S4441 formulation, presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD, particularly targeting the geographic atrophy form characterized by pronounced RPE degeneration. Another notable strength is the extensive safety data available for sulforaphane from preclinical studies. Its natural occurrence, combined with its well-documented bioactivity in a range of cell types, underscores its potential for repurposing in ocular applications. Below is a comprehensive evaluation of EPI-743 (vatiquinone) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). This report is organized into five sections: an Overview of the Therapeutic Candidate, a review of its Therapeutic History, a detailed discussion of its Mechanism of Action, an outline of the Expected Effects in the dry AMD context, and an Overall Evaluation of its strengths and limitations.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

EPI-743, commonly referred to as vatiquinone, is a synthetic, short-chain quinone derivative that was designed based on biochemical modifications of naturally occurring vitamin E compounds. Its origin can be traced to the oxidation products of tocopherols and tocotrienols—members of the vitamin E family—which, through oxidative metabolism, yield quinone species. Specifically, EPI-743 is produced when these compounds are oxidized (Cores et al., 2023). Chemically, it belongs to the para-benzoquinone class, a subclass of quinones that are characterized by their fully conjugated cyclic unsaturated dione structure and their capacity for reversible redox cycling. Its design intentionally mirrors that of endogenous mitochondrial mediators such as ubiquinone (CoQ10), but significant modifications have been made to enhance aqueous solubility as well as to confer an extraordinary potency; indeed, experimental evidence indicates that on a molar basis, EPI-743 can be 10³ to 10⁴ times more potent than CoQ10 or even idebenone, another short-chain quinone analogue (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Gueven et al., 2017).

The discovery of EPI-743 originated from a small-molecule screening effort in which candidate compounds were evaluated for their ability to rescue cell viability under conditions of oxidative stress and glutathione depletion. This high-throughput screening methodology identified EPI-743 as a promising redox modulator with strong protective activity, leading to its subsequent advancement into preclinical testing and clinical evaluation by companies such as Edison Pharmaceuticals and PTC Therapeutics (Cores et al., 2023). As a representative member of the quinone drug class, EPI-743 is mechanistically designed to act as an electron shuttle, undergoing a reversible two-electron reduction to its corresponding hydroquinone form—a transformation that lies at the heart of its antioxidant activity and distinguishes it from many classical antioxidants. Because quinones in general have been used both as pharmaceutical antioxidants and as electron carriers in mitochondrial function, the chemical heritage of EPI-743 provides a strong rationale for its use in conditions characterized by redox imbalances (Tinker et al., 2021; Hong et al., 2023).

In summary, the chemical origin of EPI-743 is synthetic, being inspired by vitamin E’s tocotrienol derivatives and subsequently optimized to form a para-benzoquinone structure. Its classification among short-chain quinones places it in a well-studied category of compounds that have been used to modulate cellular redox states in various settings, particularly in diseases associated with mitochondrial dysfunction (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Gueven et al., 2017).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

The therapeutic use history of EPI-743 is predominantly rooted in the context of mitochondrial diseases and other disorders associated with oxidative stress. Preclinically, it has been shown to protect various cell types against oxidative insult in vitro, particularly in experimental models where glutathione levels are artificially depleted. Studies have demonstrated that EPI-743 significantly enhances cell viability under conditions that would otherwise trigger cell death mechanisms such as ferroptosis and apoptosis (Gueven et al., 2017; Cores et al., 2023). Furthermore, the compound has been extensively studied in animal models of mitochondrial dysfunction with evidence suggesting that it supports key mitochondrial functions including electron transport and ATP synthesis.

Clinically, EPI-743 has been investigated in several rare inherited mitochondrial disorders. For instance, initial clinical studies in pediatric patients with Leigh syndrome—a severe neurodegenerative disorder characterized by mitochondrial respiratory chain dysfunction—have yielded promising results. In these studies, treatment with EPI-743 correlated with stabilization or even improvement in disease progression markers and had observable beneficial effects on neurological function (Gueven et al., 2017; Ji et al., 2021). In addition, small open-label studies have been conducted in patients with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON), an inherited optic neuropathy known to involve mitochondrial dysfunction in retinal ganglion cells; such studies indicated that early administration of EPI-743 may arrest disease progression and, in some cases, partially reverse visual loss (Gueven et al., 2017; Hong et al., 2023). Further clinical evaluation has expanded EPI-743’s investigation into other mitochondrial and neurodegenerative conditions such as Friedreich’s ataxia and refractory epilepsy, all of which share common mechanistic ties to oxidative stress and impaired bioenergetics (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

Despite its extensive evaluation in mitochondrial diseases and neurodegenerative disorders, there is no direct evidence in the literature indicating that EPI-743 has been used to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar age-related retinal conditions. There are no published studies that have directly tested EPI-743 in preclinical models of AMD, nor are there clinical trial reports of its use in an elderly population suffering from AMD. Although several quinone-based compounds (for example, idebenone) have been evaluated in ocular diseases, and the pathophysiological overlap between mitochondrial dysfunction and retinal degeneration is recognized, the existing body of literature on EPI-743 primarily focuses on inherited mitochondrial encephalomyopathies and optic neuropathies rather than on common, age-related retinal disorders (Gueven et al., 2017).

Overall, while the clinical track record of EPI-743 in conditions characterized by disrupted mitochondrial bioenergetics positions it as a promising candidate from a mechanistic perspective, its therapeutic history does not yet include any studies directly addressing the multifactorial nature of dry AMD. However, the established ability of EPI-743 to modulate cellular redox status suggests that it might have potential in the AMD setting as well (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

At the molecular level, EPI-743 exerts its effects primarily through its redox activity, a function that is intimately linked to its para-benzoquinone core. This structure allows EPI-743 to participate in reversible redox cycling—a process in which the quinone is reduced to its hydroquinone form and oxidized back to the quinone form as needed (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). The reduction is typically mediated by cytosolic oxidoreductases, most notably NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), an enzyme that is ubiquitously expressed, including in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012). NQO1 catalyzes a two-electron transfer reaction that converts the oxidized quinone into its corresponding hydroquinone. This hydroquinone is not only a potent free-radical scavenger but also plays a crucial role in regenerating the cellular pool of reduced glutathione (GSH) (Tinker et al., 2021; Cores et al., 2023).

Reduced glutathione is the primary intracellular antioxidant, essential for neutralizing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and protecting macromolecules from oxidative damage. In scenarios where ROS overwhelm a cell’s antioxidant capacity—such as during mitochondrial dysfunction or in cells under chronic oxidative stress—GSH levels become depleted and oxidized glutathione (GSSG) accumulates. By facilitating the replenishment of GSH, EPI-743 helps re‐establish redox balance and thus serves as an indirect regulator of oxidative stress (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Tinker et al., 2021). This redox cycling is considered “catalytic” because once the hydroquinone form scavenges a radical or reduces another molecule, it is itself reoxidized back to the quinone, whereupon it can undergo another round of reduction. Thus, even at relatively low concentrations, EPI-743 provides a sustained antioxidant effect.

In addition to its role in antioxidant defense, EPI-743 has been shown to modulate specific redox-sensitive enzymes. For example, its activity has been linked to the modulation of 15-lipoxygenase (15-LO), a key enzyme in lipid peroxidation pathways that can trigger ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death associated with lipid peroxidation. By inhibiting 15-LO activity, EPI-743 may reduce the peroxidative damage to polyunsaturated fatty acids within cellular membranes—a damage process that is especially detrimental in cells with a high metabolic rate such as retinal pigment epithelium (Cores et al., 2023; Kayser et al., 2024). This function is particularly relevant since ferroptosis has been implicated in conditions where oxidative stress is central.

Furthermore, the quinone’s ability to modulate intracellular redox signaling involves its interaction with transcription factors such as nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2). By maintaining a favorable GSH/GSSG ratio and reducing the overall burden of ROS, EPI-743 indirectly helps to sustain Nrf2 signaling, which in turn upregulates the expression of a panel of antioxidant genes. This feedback loop reinforces the cell’s capacity to respond to oxidative challenges. Though direct evidence linking EPI-743 to Nrf2 activation in retinal cells is sparse, the dependency of its action on NQO1—which itself is regulated in part by Nrf2—suggests that such interactions are plausible (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

In summary, EPI-743’s mechanism of action is multifaceted. It directly scavenges ROS via its hydroquinone intermediate, it enhances the reduced glutathione pool and thereby improves the cell’s overall antioxidant capacity, and it modulates lipid peroxidation pathways by affecting 15-LO activity. The reliance on NQO1 for its activation further supports its broad potential, given that NQO1 is expressed in many cell types, including those in the retina. These biochemical properties collectively suggest that EPI-743 has the potential to mitigate oxidative damage in environments where mitochondrial dysfunction and redox imbalance predominate (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect in Dry AMD

Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by the progressive degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium and underlying photoreceptors, a process that is driven in part by chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and the accumulation of oxidative DNA lesions. In the RPE, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is particularly vulnerable to oxidative damage because of its proximity to the electron transport chain and its relative lack of protective histones. One of the most common oxidative modifications observed in mtDNA is 8-oxo-2′-deoxyguanosine (8-oxoG), a marker of oxidative base lesions that can lead to mutagenesis and impaired mitochondrial function. The hypothesis underlying the repurposing of EPI-743 for dry AMD is that its potent redox cycling mechanism can reset the oxidative environment in RPE cells by regenerating reduced glutathione and by supporting NQO1-mediated detoxification, thereby reducing the accumulation of damaging oxidative lesions in mtDNA (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

In an in vitro assay designed to analyze oxidative stress in RPE cells, one would expect that treatment with EPI-743 would lead to several measurable outcomes. First, due to its rapid redox cycling and ability to donate electrons, EPI-743 would be anticipated to reduce intracellular levels of ROS, thereby directly lowering the formation of 8-oxoG lesions in mitochondrial DNA. This effect should manifest as a reduction in the cellular markers of oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation. Second, given the established role of NQO1 in catalyzing the conversion of EPI-743 to its hydroquinone form, and the fact that NQO1 is known to be expressed in RPE cells, the compound is expected to increase the intracellular GSH/GSSG ratio in these cells, further reinforcing the antioxidant defense system (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012).

Additionally, improved mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) function is a key expected outcome. In dry AMD, compromised mitochondrial integrity leads to reduced ATP production and increased susceptibility to cell death. By restoring redox balance, EPI-743 should preserve the integrity of mitochondrial membranes and ensure effective electron transport, ultimately resulting in enhanced ATP synthesis. This restoration of mitochondrial function could be assessed via assays that measure mitochondrial membrane potential, ATP synthesis rates, and oxygen consumption rates in RPE cell cultures challenged with oxidants (Kayser et al., 2024; Tinker et al., 2021).

Moreover, an important aspect of EPI-743’s expected effect is its potential to mitigate ferroptotic cell death pathways. Ferroptosis, driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation, has been implicated in the degeneration of RPE cells. By inhibiting 15-lipoxygenase and curbing lipid peroxidation, EPI-743 could help prevent the execution of ferroptotic cell death in RPE cells—a process that may contribute to the progression of dry AMD (Cores et al., 2023).

Taken together, in an experimental model of dry AMD—whether in RPE cell culture or in an appropriate animal model—administration of EPI-743 is expected to lead to: (1) a significant decline in ROS levels, (2) an increased ratio of reduced-to-oxidized glutathione, (3) preservation of mitochondrial DNA integrity as evidenced by reduced 8-oxoG accumulation, (4) improved mitochondrial bioenergetics as indicated by enhanced ATP production and mitochondrial membrane potential, and (5) inhibition of deleterious lipid peroxidation pathways. The successful demonstration of these effects would serve as strong biochemical and cellular evidence supporting the hypothesis that EPI-743 can protect RPE cells from the oxidative insults characteristic of dry AMD (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

Furthermore, since the RPE is known to express NQO1—an enzyme critical for the activation of EPI-743—the molecular basis for its activity is supported by tissue-specific expression data. This provides additional justification for targeting RPE cells with EPI-743 in the context of dry AMD, where bolstering the endogenous antioxidant systems may have a measurable impact on disease progression (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Tinker et al., 2021).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

EPI-743 stands out as a highly promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD owing to several strengths rooted in its potent redox-modulatory properties and well-characterized mitochondrial protective effects. One of its major strengths is its extraordinary antioxidant potency. As a para-benzoquinone analogue that can be reduced via NQO1-catalyzed reactions to its hydroquinone state, EPI-743 is capable of intercepting and neutralizing ROS with an efficiency that surpasses that of conventional antioxidants such as CoQ10 by three to four orders of magnitude (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Gueven et al., 2017). This high level of potency is particularly appealing for conditions like dry AMD, in which the cumulative oxidative stress has a direct impact on mtDNA damage and cellular energetic deficits.

Another significant advantage is the compound’s established clinical track record in diseases marked by mitochondrial dysfunction. Although its clinical applications have thus far been restricted to rare inherited mitochondrial conditions like Leigh syndrome and LHON, the underlying mechanisms—namely, the restoration of mitochondrial bioenergetics and redox balance through effective GSH regeneration—are equally relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Gueven et al., 2017). Its ability to protect retinal ganglion cells in LHON studies suggests that similar beneficial effects might be extrapolated to retinal pigment epithelial cells, which are critically involved in the development of AMD.

Mechanistically, EPI-743’s dual action—both as a direct antioxidant and as a modulator of redox-sensitive pathways involving 15-lipoxygenase—confers a multi-pronged approach to cytoprotection. By reducing ROS and regenerating intracellular glutathione levels, EPI-743 can potentially arrest the oxidative modifications that lead to deleterious mtDNA lesions such as 8-oxoG. Moreover, the inhibition of enzymes that contribute to lipid peroxidation may further protect cellular membranes and reduce downstream inflammatory responses. These attributes provide a compelling scientific rationale for considering EPI-743 as a therapeutic strategy to combat the chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction associated with dry AMD (Tinker et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be acknowledged. First and foremost, the current therapeutic history of EPI-743 shows no direct evidence of efficacy in dry AMD or other age-related retinal conditions. All of the published studies to date have focused on inherited mitochondrial or neurodegenerative disorders. Therefore, there remains a significant gap in our knowledge regarding its pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics in the context of the aging retina, which has a distinct microenvironment compared to the tissues examined in inherited disorders (Gueven et al., 2017).

Another concern is the potential difference in drug metabolism and toxicity between the predominantly pediatric or young adult populations (commonly studied in mitochondrial diseases) and the elderly patient population that is most affected by dry AMD. Age-related alterations in absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) could impact both efficacy and the safety profile of EPI-743 when repurposed for an older demographic (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Hong et al., 2023). Furthermore, while the activation of EPI-743 via NQO1 is a mechanistically attractive feature, the ubiquitous and sometimes unpredictable nature of redox enzyme activity in different tissues raises the possibility of off-target effects. Chronic systemic administration in an elderly population might result in unforeseen modifications in redox homeostasis not only within the retina but also in other vulnerable organs (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

In addition, the multifactorial pathogenesis of dry AMD poses a challenge to any therapeutic approach that primarily targets oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. While these are certainly key components of AMD pathology, the disease also involves chronic inflammation, drusen formation, and alterations in extracellular matrix homeostasis. It is therefore uncertain whether the powerful antioxidant activity of EPI-743 alone would be sufficient to halt or reverse the progression of dry AMD. Successful treatment may require a combination approach that addresses multiple causative factors, and it remains to be seen if EPI-743 can be integrated effectively into such a therapeutic regimen (Gueven et al., 2017; Cores et al., 2023).

Lastly, the translation from preclinical models—where the compound’s efficacy has been demonstrated in controlled settings of inherited mitochondrial dysfunction—to an age-related, multifaceted disease state such as dry AMD is non-trivial. Preclinical RPE-focused studies, including those measuring ROS levels, mitochondrial membrane potential, and direct assessments of mtDNA damage in the context of oxidative challenges, are currently lacking. Such studies are critical to validate whether the mechanisms observed in other cell types or disease models are applicable to the RPE and to the pathophysiology of AMD (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Conclusion

In conclusion, EPI-743 (vatiquinone) exhibits many characteristics that render it an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its synthetic origin from vitamin E–derived tocotrienol derivatives and its classification as a para-benzoquinone confer upon it a robust redox-cycling capacity, enabling it to function as an exceptionally potent mitochondrial antioxidant. Through its ability to be reduced by NQO1 to a hydroquinone state, EPI-743 effectively regenerates intracellular reduced glutathione while simultaneously inhibiting lipid peroxidation via modulation of 15-lipoxygenase activity. These mechanisms collectively support its potential to protect mitochondrial DNA from oxidative damage, preserve electron transport chain function, and maintain ATP production in highly metabolically active cells such as the retinal pigment epithelium (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

The therapeutic history of EPI-743 in inherited mitochondrial disorders and optic neuropathies provides a valuable proof of concept regarding its efficacy in situations where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central to pathogenesis. However, the absence of any direct study in dry AMD represents a significant gap that must be addressed through focused preclinical research. In the context of dry AMD, where chronic oxidative stress leads to the accumulation of damaging mtDNA lesions (including 8-oxoG) and progressive RPE degeneration, a potent redox modulator like EPI-743 theoretically offers a promising means to break the cycle of oxidative damage and mitochondrial decline (Tinker et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

Notwithstanding its potential strengths, several uncertainties must be highlighted. The pharmacokinetics and safety profile of EPI-743 in an elderly population—where changes in drug metabolism are common—remain to be fully elucidated. Moreover, the complex etiology of dry AMD, which involves not only oxidative damage and mitochondrial failure but also inflammatory and extracellular matrix alterations, may necessitate a multifaceted treatment strategy beyond a single antioxidant approach. As such, while the mechanistic rationale for using EPI-743 in dry AMD is well founded by virtue of its antioxidant and mitochondria-protective properties, clinical translation will require rigorous demonstration of efficacy in RPE-based in vitro systems and in animal models that recapitulate the full spectrum of AMD pathology (Gueven et al., 2017; Cores et al., 2023).

Given these considerations, the repurposing of EPI-743 for dry AMD holds promise—but only with additional preclinical studies that specifically assess its ability to ameliorate oxidative damage in the retinal pigment epithelium. Key experiments should focus on measuring changes in redox biomarkers, mtDNA integrity, ATP production, and cellular viability in RPE cells under oxidative stress. Parallel in vivo studies in animal models of AMD will be essential to determine ocular bioavailability, dosing parameters, and potential off-target effects in an aged organism.

Overall, the strengths of EPI-743 lie in its unparalleled antioxidant potency and its established capacity to restore mitochondrial function in disease settings characterized by oxidative damage. Its mechanism—centered on redox cycling via a para-benzoquinone moiety, glutathione regeneration, and modulation of lipid peroxidation—is directly relevant to the pathophysiological challenges found in dry AMD. However, the primary weaknesses include the current absence of direct evidence in retinal disease models, potential pharmacokinetic concerns in the elderly, and the complexity of dry AMD pathology which may require combination therapy for optimal clinical benefit. Thus, while EPI-743 is mechanistically compelling as a candidate drug for dry AMD, its ultimate clinical utility will depend on the outcomes of targeted preclinical evaluations and, subsequently, carefully designed clinical trials that address the specific challenges of age-related retinal degeneration (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024; Tinker et al., 2021).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Final Remarks

EPI-743 (vatiquinone) presents an attractive therapeutic opportunity given its synthetic derivation from vitamin E, its classification as a para-benzoquinone with exceptionally potent antioxidant capabilities, and its ability to support mitochondrial function through NQO1-mediated redox modulation and glutathione regeneration. Although its historical clinical use has been confined to inherited mitochondrial diseases and optic neuropathies rather than age-related conditions, the underlying pathophysiological similarities—namely oxidative stress and mitochondrial compromise—provide a logical foundation for hypothesizing its efficacy in dry AMD. The expected beneficial actions in RPE cells include reduced accumulation of oxidative DNA lesions, improved mitochondrial electron transport and ATP synthesis, and diminished activation of ferroptotic cell death pathways.

Before any clinical repurposing can be considered, it is essential to perform a series of rigorous preclinical studies. These studies should involve well-characterized in vitro models using RPE cell lines that mimic the oxidative challenges seen in dry AMD. Furthermore, in vivo studies employing animal models that recapitulate the complex pathology of AMD will be crucial to assess ocular bioavailability, efficacy, and safety in a context that simulates the aged human retina. Such investigations will inform dosing regimens and help identify any potential off-target effects or toxicities that might arise in the elderly population, which is inherently more vulnerable due to age-related physiological changes (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012).

In summary, while the available data from mitochondrial and neurodegenerative disease studies provide a robust mechanistic rationale for the use of EPI-743 as a potent redox modulator and mitochondria-protective agent, the leap to a therapeutic indication in dry AMD remains largely theoretical at this point. Nonetheless, the convergence of redox dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and oxidative mtDNA damage in AMD creates a promising target for compounds like EPI-743. With appropriate preclinical validation, EPI-743 could emerge as a valuable component of a combination therapy strategy that addresses the multifactorial nature of dry AMD. This repurposing effort would potentially fill a significant therapeutic gap in a disease area where effective treatments are currently lacking (Tinker et al., 2021; Cores et al., 2023; Gueven et al., 2017).

Given the promising mechanistic profile of EPI-743 alongside the identified gaps in its direct application to dry AMD, we recommend that the next phase in drug development should focus on comprehensive preclinical studies specifically targeting RPE dysfunction and oxidative damage in AMD. These studies will be critical in determining whether the redox-modulating properties of EPI-743 can be harnessed to meaningfully slow or reverse the progression of dry AMD in a clinical setting.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

To summarize, the compound EPI-743 (vatiquinone) exhibits several important strengths that justify its consideration as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD:

1. Its chemical derivation from vitamin E derivatives places it in the para-benzoquinone class, endowing it with rapid redox-cycling properties and a potency that is orders of magnitude greater than that of more conventional antioxidants such as CoQ10 and idebenone (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Gueven et al., 2017).

2. Its mechanism of action—rooted in the reversible reduction to an active hydroquinone via NQO1, subsequent regeneration of reduced glutathione, and inhibition of oxidative enzymes such as 15-lipoxygenase—offers a multi-modal approach to addressing the oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction that are central to dry AMD pathogenesis (Tinker et al., 2021; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

3. The clinical experience with EPI-743 in mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, especially its application in inherited optic neuropathies like LHON, provides important precedent for its potential utility in ocular tissues, even though these studies have not been conducted in the context of age-related retinal degeneration (Gueven et al., 2017; Hong et al., 2023).

However, several challenges temper these strengths:

1. No current preclinical or clinical studies have directly examined the efficacy of EPI-743 in dry AMD models. While the redox mechanisms implicated in inherited mitochondrial diseases overlap with those theorized in AMD, the multifactorial nature of AMD—which involves chronic inflammation, drusen formation, and vascular compromise in addition to oxidative stress—means that a pure antioxidant approach may need to be complemented with additional interventions (Cores et al., 2023).

2. The majority of clinical evaluations of EPI-743 have been performed in younger patient populations with genetic disorders, leaving questions regarding the pharmacokinetics, tolerability, and safety of chronic EPI-743 administration in the elderly, who are most at risk for dry AMD (Hong et al., 2023; Kayser et al., 2024).

3. The potential for off-target effects due to the ubiquitous nature of NQO1 and the broad redox activities of quinones requires careful assessment when considering long-term systemic administration in an older population, where alterations in redox homeostasis can have widespread consequences (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Tinker et al., 2021).

4. Finally, while the in vitro evidence in mitochondrial disease models is promising, definitive studies that measure outcomes in RPE cells—such as reductions in 8-oxoG accumulation, restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential, and improved bioenergetic capacity—are necessary to confirm that the mechanistic rationale translates to the AMD context (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012).

In light of these considerations, EPI-743 is a candidate with strong mechanistic appeal that warrants further, targeted investigation in preclinical AMD models. If subsequent studies in RPE-centric in vitro systems and relevant animal models demonstrate that EPI-743 can reduce oxidative mtDNA damage and preserve mitochondrial function in the aging retina, then its repurposing for dry AMD could represent a critical advance in treatment options for this currently intractable condition.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Conclusion

EPI-743 (vatiquinone) is a highly potent, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant derived from vitamin E metabolites and classified within the para-benzoquinone family of compounds. Its design is centered on harnessing reversible two-electron redox cycling mediated by NQO1, leading to enhanced intracellular levels of reduced glutathione and effective mitigation of ROS and lipid peroxidation. Clinically, it has shown promise in mitigating the effects of mitochondrial dysfunction in inherited neurodegenerative and optic neuropathic disorders such as Leigh syndrome and LHON. Based on these properties, its proposed repurposing for dry AMD is founded on the hypothesis that by preventing oxidative damage to the mitochondrial DNA of RPE cells, EPI-743 may halt or reverse some of the degenerative processes characteristic of AMD.

Nevertheless, while its mechanistic profile is compelling, the absence of direct evidence in AMD models and uncertainties regarding its systemic pharmacodynamics in the typical AMD patient population represent significant hurdles. Prior to any clinical application in dry AMD, it is imperative to undertake a rigorous series of preclinical studies focused on RPE cells and AMD animal models. These studies must address not only its efficacy in restoring mitochondrial function and reducing oxidative lesions (such as 8-oxoG) but also its safety and appropriate dosing in aged tissues.

In summary, EPI-743 represents an attractive, yet still unproven, candidate for the treatment of dry AMD. Its unmatched antioxidant potency, combined with established benefits in mitochondrial disease models, provides a strong foundation for further exploration. However, significant additional research is required to bridge the translational gap between the current indications for which EPI-743 has been studied and the complex, multifactorial pathology of dry AMD. Given the extensive unmet clinical need in dry AMD and the promising mechanistic rationale, a targeted preclinical evaluation of EPI-743 in ocular systems is both justified and urgent. Should these studies yield positive results, EPI-743 may well emerge as a key component in a future therapeutic strategy aimed at preserving vision in patients with dry AMD (Tinker et al., 2021; Cores et al., 2023; Gueven et al., 2017).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Final Recommendations

Based on the current literature and mechanistic insights, the following steps are advised before clinical repurposing of EPI-743 for dry AMD is pursued:

1. Develop and validate in vitro RPE cell culture models under conditions of chronic oxidative stress to assess the direct impact of EPI-743 on mitochondrial bioenergetics, redox balance, and mtDNA integrity.  
2. Conduct in vivo studies using animal models of dry AMD or age-related retinal degeneration to evaluate ocular bioavailability, efficacy in reducing oxidative lesions, and overall retinal protection.  
3. Perform pharmacokinetic and toxicological studies specifically in aged animal models to evaluate how the elderly might respond differently to systemic administration of EPI-743.  
4. Explore combination therapies that might pair EPI-743’s potent antioxidant effects with agents targeting other aspects of AMD pathology, such as inflammation and drusen formation.

Overall, while EPI-743 has not yet been evaluated directly in the context of dry AMD, its biochemical properties, proven efficacy in mitochondrial disease models, and mechanistic plausibility render it a candidate worthy of further exploration. With careful and targeted preclinical experimentation, the repurposing of EPI-743 may eventually provide a novel therapeutic option for a patient population in urgent need of effective treatments (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Tinker et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Closing Summary

In conclusion, the evidence from the biochemical, clinical, and therapeutic literature reviewed herein supports the following: EPI-743 (vatiquinone) is a synthetically derived para-benzoquinone that leverages redox cycling and glutathione regeneration via NQO1 to protect mitochondria from oxidative insult. Its clinical history in mitochondrial disorders provides an encouraging precedent, and its detailed mechanism of action is highly relevant to conditions characterized by oxidative mtDNA damage—such as dry AMD. However, the absence of direct preclinical data in AMD models, along with potential pharmacokinetic challenges in an elderly population, necessitates a cautious yet proactive research program. Overall, the candidate shows significant promise as a repurposed drug for dry AMD, meriting additional in vitro and in vivo studies to fully elucidate its potential in this indication before any clinical trials are initiated (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Gueven et al., 2017; Tinker et al., 2021).
