Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Apocynin (Sigma-Aldrich A1788) is a naturally derived, methoxy-substituted catechol originally isolated from the medicinal herb Picrorhiza kurroa, which has a long history of use in traditional Ayurvedic medicine. It is a small molecule with a molecular weight of approximately 166.17 Da and modest lipophilicity (logP ~ 0.83) that allows it to readily cross cellular membranes and even the blood–brain barrier. As a member of the NADPH oxidase (NOX) inhibitor class, it has been historically used to modulate oxidative stress in a variety of preclinical disease models. The compound’s origin is rooted in natural product chemistry, and its attractive small-molecule structure has encouraged detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic investigations in rodent models, where it has been administered intravenously and orally to assess tissue distribution and rapid clearance kinetics. Its chemical profile and natural derivation position it within a class of therapeutic candidates that have been widely evaluated for their antioxidant properties and their ability to attenuate NOX-mediated reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory diseases (Liu et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Preclinical studies have evaluated apocynin in a range of animal models that address oxidative stress–related pathologies. In cardiovascular and cerebrovascular research, for example, apocynin has been shown to reduce NADPH oxidase activity and resultant oxidative damage in models of isoproterenol-induced cardiac hypertrophy, diabetic cardiac remodeling, and brain oxidative stress associated with high-fat diets (Liu et al., 2020). Its pharmacokinetic profile in mice indicates a rapid plasma peak and an extremely short half-life of around 3–4 minutes after intravenous dosing, with extensive clearance by the kidneys (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2020). In respiratory research, a completed Phase 1 randomized trial in COPD patients demonstrated that nebulized apocynin was well tolerated, produced short-term reductions in exhaled oxidative markers such as hydrogen peroxide and nitrite, and did not affect lung function or systemic safety parameters (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010). Despite these encouraging results, there remains limited data on the longer-term systemic safety or adverse-event profiles of apocynin. Importantly, while apocynin has been extensively studied in cardiovascular and respiratory indications, as well as in models of neurodegeneration and hepatic and renal injury, there is minimal direct evidence of its use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models or in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells such as ARPE-19 (Drummond & Sobey, 2014). Nonetheless, since dry AMD pathogenesis involves oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction within the RPE, the demonstrated efficacy of apocynin in modulating NADPH oxidase–mediated ROS production in other organs builds a rationale for its repurposing for this indication.

Mechanism of Action:  
The central proposed mechanism by which apocynin exerts its therapeutic effects involves the inhibition of NADPH oxidase, particularly by blocking the assembly of the enzyme complex. NADPH oxidases are multi-subunit enzymatic complexes responsible for the regulated generation of superoxide and downstream reactive oxygen species. In cells, the assembly and activation of NOX, especially isoforms such as NOX2, require the translocation of cytosolic regulatory subunits—most notably p47^phox—to the membrane-bound catalytic core. Early studies reported that apocynin can prevent the translocation of p47^phox to the plasma membrane, thereby inhibiting the assembly of the active NOX2 complex and reducing the production of superoxide, which secondarily lowers the formation of hydrogen peroxide and other ROS (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Drummond & Sobey, 2014).  
However, the molecular pharmacology of apocynin is more complex. Its inhibitory activity appears to be dependent on metabolic activation by myeloperoxidase (MPO) in the presence of hydrogen peroxide. This conversion supposedly generates reactive quinone species or even a dimeric form (diapocynin) that can covalently modify cysteine residues in p47^phox, thus interfering with its function (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Ismaeel et al., 2018). Some studies, though, have failed to detect diapocynin in vivo, suggesting that other metabolites, such as apocynin glycoconjugates, might instead be responsible for its activity (Liu et al., 2020). Moreover, apocynin has been reported to possess direct antioxidant properties at higher concentrations by scavenging non-radical oxidants such as hypochlorous acid and hydrogen peroxide, independently of its effects on NOX assembly (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Ismaeel et al., 2018).  
In vitro studies in various cell types have yielded conflicting data regarding whether apocynin primarily functions as a NOX-specific inhibitor or as a broad-spectrum antioxidant. In cell types that are rich in peroxidase activity, such as neutrophils, apocynin’s conversion to an active inhibitor appears robust. In contrast, in cells with lower MPO activity, such as some epithelial or neuronal cells, its efficacy as a NOX inhibitor may be diminished, and observed benefits might be attributable to direct ROS scavenging (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2020). Within the context of RPE cells, the candidate hypothesis posits that apocynin will inhibit the translocation of p47^phox during NOX2 activation, thereby reducing cytosolic ROS production while also limiting the spillover of ROS into mitochondria, which would otherwise trigger mitochondrial membrane potential collapse, fragmentation, and reduced oxygen consumption rate (OCR) (Liu et al., 2020; Liu, 2023). This mechanism, if operative in RPE cells such as ARPE-19, would help preserve mitochondrial integrity by preventing excess ROS accumulation and the ensuing mitochondrial dysfunction—a key pathogenic process in dry AMD (Shu et al., 2023; Liu, 2023).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed mechanism, the use of apocynin in in vitro assays with ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE cultures is expected to yield several beneficial outcomes. First, by blocking p47^phox translocation, apocynin should reduce the assembly of the NOX complex, particularly NOX2, thereby decreasing the production of superoxide and hydrogen peroxide. This reduction in ROS should lead to lower levels of oxidative stress markers, as measured by assays such as lucigenin chemiluminescence, dihydroethidium (DHE) fluorescence, and malondialdehyde (MDA) assays (Liu et al., 2020).  
Second, because ROS are known to damage mitochondrial components, it is expected that apocynin treatment will protect against mitochondrial dysfunction. In ARPE-19 cells challenged with hydrogen peroxide or other oxidative stress inducers, apocynin should help preserve the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), prevent mitochondrial fragmentation, and maintain basal oxygen consumption rates (OCR). These mitochondrial endpoints are critical, as disruption of mitochondrial dynamics and energy production is a hallmark of RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Shu et al., 2023; Drummond & Sobey, 2014).  
Furthermore, given that NOX isoforms such as NOX2 and NOX4 have been implicated in the oxidative stress observed in retinal cells exposed to blue light or metabolic insults (Liu et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020), the inhibition of these enzymes with apocynin is expected to attenuate downstream pro-inflammatory signaling cascades. This should result in reduced upregulation of proangiogenic factors like VEGF and a decrease in inflammatory cytokine production that can exacerbate retinal degeneration. In effect, apocynin would act not only to maintain mitochondrial function by limiting local oxidative damage but also to modulate the broader redox environment that contributes to RPE cell dysfunction in dry AMD (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Ismaeel et al., 2018).  
As a consequence, in the experimental assay proposed by the team, treatment of ARPE-19 cells with apocynin under conditions of induced oxidative stress should demonstrate a measurable preservation of Δψm by fluorescent imaging or flow cytometry using potentiometric dyes, maintenance of basal OCR as measured via Seahorse extracellular flux analysis, and a reduction in mitochondrial ROS accumulation by specific mitochondria-targeted ROS indicators. The reduction in NOX-derived ROS is expected to indirectly prevent mitochondrial fragmentation by mitigating the activation of mitochondrial fission pathways in response to oxidative injury (Liu, 2023; Liu et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
Apocynin represents a promising candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its potential to target a core pathogenic mechanism—the dysregulated production of ROS via NADPH oxidase assembly. One of the strengths of apocynin is its extensive preclinical history demonstrating its capacity to lower oxidative stress in various organs, including the heart, liver, brain, and lung, with documented rapid distribution to tissues and a well-characterized pharmacokinetic profile in animal models (Liu et al., 2020; Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014). Its observed safety in a small Phase 1 clinical study in COPD patients further bolsters the case for its safety on at least short-term administration in humans (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010). Moreover, its chemical simplicity as a natural product and its relatively low molecular weight make it attractive for further formulation studies in ocular indications.  
Nevertheless, significant weaknesses and challenges must be addressed. A major issue is the ongoing debate regarding the exact mechanism of action of apocynin. While some studies support its role as a NOX inhibitor via prevention of p47^phox translocation, others have demonstrated that its activity may be largely due to its direct antioxidant properties or require metabolic activation by MPO—a process that may not be robust in retinal pigment epithelial cells (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014). This mechanistic ambiguity raises concerns about its efficacy and specificity in the RPE, where the peroxidase activity necessary for conversion to an active form may be limited.  
Furthermore, the extremely short plasma half-life (approximately 3–4 minutes) observed in rodent models indicates that apocynin is rapidly cleared, which could limit its therapeutic window and necessitate frequent dosing or the development of modified formulations such as a sustained-release ocular implant or a mitochondria-targeted derivative (e.g., mito-apocynin) to achieve prolonged local concentrations in the retina (Liu et al., 2020; Liu, 2023). This rapid clearance could also complicate the translation of in vivo results to a clinical setting for a chronic disease such as dry AMD.  
Another concern is that, despite the general rationale for reducing oxidative stress in the RPE, there is a paucity of direct evidence from ARPE-19 or primary RPE models showing that apocynin effectively prevents mitochondrial fragmentation, preserves the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), or maintains basal oxygen consumption rates. Although some studies have demonstrated that NOX inhibition can reduce ROS levels in retinal cells, apocynin’s specific action in the context of dry AMD has not been rigorously documented (Shu et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2020). Additionally, the variability of its effects across different cell types—dependent on the presence or absence of peroxidase activity—suggests that its efficacy in the RPE may be inconsistent, thereby necessitating further targeted studies.  
There is also the possibility of off-target effects. Because apocynin has been reported to act as a general antioxidant rather than a highly specific NOX inhibitor, it might interfere with normal redox signaling that is essential for cell survival and immune defense, particularly when applied systemically. Caution must be exercised to ensure that suppression of NOX activity does not inadvertently impair protective immune responses or lead to unwanted toxicity, even if short-term clinical data appears reassuring (Drummond & Sobey, 2014; Casas et al., 2015).  
In summary, while the mechanistic rationale behind using apocynin to inhibit NOX assembly in RPE cells is compelling, particularly given the central role of oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD pathogenesis, several critical questions remain. These include the precise mechanism by which apocynin exerts its effects in the RPE, the consistency of its efficacy in protecting mitochondrial function in ARPE-19 cells, its pharmacokinetic limitations, and its potential off-target effects. Overall, apocynin has strengths as a natural antioxidant with a history of reducing systemic oxidative stress in preclinical models and demonstrating short-term safety in human trials. However, its mechanism remains controversial, and its rapid clearance, potential variability in retinal cells, and limited direct evidence in AMD models represent significant weaknesses that must be overcome through further targeted biochemical, in vitro, and in vivo studies before advancing into clinical trials for dry AMD (Liu et al., 2020; Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010; Shu et al., 2023; Rohowetz et al., 2018; Liu, 2023).  
Given these considerations, further investigation into apocynin’s effects on mitochondrial protection and NOX inhibition in RPE cells is warranted. Such studies should include detailed assessments of p47^phox translocation in ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress, measurement of mitochondrial membrane potential (using dyes such as JC-1 or TMRE), and evaluations of OCR using Seahorse analysis. Moreover, efforts to optimize its pharmacokinetic profile—perhaps through formulation modifications or conversion to a mitochondria-targeted analogue—would address one of its key limitations. Only with these additional data can we determine whether apocynin holds sufficient promise to justify its repurposing for the treatment of dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
BGP-15 is a synthetic, small-molecule nicotinic amidoxime/hydroxylamine derivative whose full chemical name is O-(3-piperidino-2-hydroxy-1-propyl) nicotinic amidoxime, typically used as a dihydrochloride salt; it was developed by N-Gene (US/Hungary) and has been described as water-soluble and mitochondria-targeting in preclinical studies (including ocular applications) (Takács et al., 2024; Horváth et al., 2021). Chemically and pharmacologically, BGP-15 belongs to the hydroximic/hydroxylamine acid derivative family originally advanced as membrane-interacting heat-shock response (HSR) co-inducers that remodel cholesterol-enriched plasma membrane rafts, with pleiotropic, cytoprotective effects in stressed tissues (membrane-lipid therapy) (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011). In parallel, the compound has been positioned as a nicotinamide-related, non-carboxamide “NAM analogue” with in vitro mixed-type (noncompetitive) PARP-1 inhibition, though the authors emphasize that in vivo protective effects likely involve additional mechanisms beyond direct PARP blockade because the in vitro inhibitory concentration exceeds achievable systemic levels (Crul et al., 2013). Independent biophysical and cellular studies show BGP-15 partitions into membranes, increases the fluidity of negatively charged lipid species, preserves heat-challenged raft integrity, and activates stress signaling linked to HSP induction; imaging and molecular dynamics support a direct membrane-interacting mode of action (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

Functionally, BGP-15 is best classified as a multifunctional HSP co-inducer and insulin-sensitizing, mitochondria-targeting cytoprotective agent that remodels membrane rafts, enhances the HSF1–HSP axis, and modulates stress and survival signaling (Akt up, JNK/p38 down), while lowering mitochondrial ROS and stabilizing Δψm; importantly, it preferentially acts in stressed cells, an attribute that underpins its safety rationale (Gombos et al., 2011; Sumegi et al., 2017). The compound concentrates in energized mitochondria driven by its delocalized positive charge, with >85–90% uptake into isolated mitochondria under experimental conditions (Sümegi, 2018). Mitochondrial studies consistently localize the dominant ROS-lowering effect to the respiratory chain at complexes I and III, with minimal direct antioxidant chemistry, and only mild uncoupling at millimolar concentrations that is irrelevant at the micromolar doses used in most cell studies (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018).

Crucial nomenclature caveat: a distinct “BGP-15” reported by a different group denotes a calcipotriene-derived vitamin D3 analog with anticancer activity; this vitamin D3 analog is mechanistically and structurally unrelated to the nicotinic amidoxime HSP co-inducer described above (both were labeled “BGP-15” by their respective originators) (Sintov et al., 2013). For the current program, the candidate of interest is the nicotinic amidoxime/hydroxylamine HSP co-inducer (often supplied by N-Gene or commercial chemical vendors under the amidoxime name), not the vitamin D3 analog (Takács et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
BGP-15 and closely related hydroximic/hydroxylamine acid derivatives have an extensive preclinical history across cardiac, neural, hepatic, renal, skeletal muscle, pulmonary, and metabolic models, with multiple mechanistic readouts converging on membrane remodeling, HSR/HSP co-induction, MAPK and Akt pathway modulation, and mitochondrial protection (Sumegi et al., 2017). Cardiovascular protection has been reported in ischemia–reperfusion, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation, with actions that include reduced ROS, preserved mitochondrial function, and Akt activation with suppression of JNK/p38 (Sumegi et al., 2017). In spontaneously hypertensive rats, BGP-15 increased PGC-1α and mitochondrial mass, decreased interstitial fibrosis, increased MKP-1 and reduced p38/JNK phosphorylation, and activated Akt/GSK-3β signaling (Horváth et al., 2021). BGP-15 prevented imatinib cardiotoxicity, protected against cisplatin nephrotoxicity without impairing antitumor efficacy, and mitigated cisplatin/taxol peripheral neuropathy (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). Hepatoprotection against acetaminophen injury via inhibition of caspase-independent cell death has also been documented (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). In pulmonary arterial hypertension and severe muscular dystrophy models, BGP-15 preserved mitochondrial structure and function and slowed disease progression; mechanistically, mitochondrial fusion via OPA1 activation and Akt signaling were implicated (Szabó et al., 2018).

Neuroprotection and mitochondrial rescue have been demonstrated in vitro and in vivo, including reduced neuronal death and improved mitochondrial potential/ROS at axonal branch points, coupled to HSP72 elevation, reduced phospho-JNK/p38, and enhanced Akt/IGF1R signaling (Ohlen et al., 2017). Consistent with its membrane-raft mechanism, BGP-15 increased HSP expression during heat challenge and remodeled cholesterol-rich platforms that gate stress signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

In ophthalmology, BGP-15 has been applied in multiple retinal disease contexts. It was reported retinoprotective in Goto–Kakizaki rats (type 2 diabetes) with functional preservation on ERG, and later shown to improve survival and retinal function long-term in ZDF rats under uncontrolled diabetes, with increased ocular HSP70 and decreased NFκB (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021). Topical ocular delivery using an SBECD-containing eyedrop improved scotopic/photopic a- and b-waves, restored oscillatory potentials, shortened implicit times, and preserved retinal thickness following global ischemia–reperfusion injury in rats (Takács et al., 2024). These ocular data align with the compound’s mitochondrial and HSP co-inducer mechanisms: accumulation in mitochondria, protection against apoptosis/necrosis in oxidative-stress paradigms, and modulation of stress signaling (Takács et al., 2024).

Clinically, BGP-15 has a proof-of-concept randomized, double-blind trial demonstrating dose-dependent improvement of insulin sensitivity in insulin-resistant patients without apparent short-term toxicity; in parallel, human phase II work in olanzapine-induced metabolic disorder also identified BGP-15 as an insulin sensitizer (Crul et al., 2013; Sümegi, 2018). Safety signals from early human studies and the pharmacology of HSP co-inducers (preferential action in stressed cells) support the translational risk profile; however, systemic serum concentrations reported by the developer are low (≤25 nmol/mL), which has implications for target engagement and favors local ocular delivery for retinal indications (Gombos et al., 2011; Sumegi et al., 2017).

To our knowledge based on the supplied corpus, BGP-15 has not been directly tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) patients or canonical dry AMD animal models; however, its retinoprotective efficacy in diabetic retinopathy models and retinal ischemia–reperfusion suggests relevance to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)/photoreceptor stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammation, which are central to dry AMD biology (Takács et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Membrane-lipid therapy and HSP co-induction. BGP-15 partitions into and remodels membrane lipid domains, particularly cholesterol-rich plasma membrane rafts that organize stress sensing and signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). Under heat stress or analogous perturbations, BGP-15 preserves raft integrity and elevates HSP expression; this is associated with activation of Rac1 and modulation of HSF1 acetylation, leading to prolonged HSF1 DNA binding and robust HSP gene induction without causing protein unfolding, a hallmark of HSP “co-inducers” (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). In HSR-defective melanoma cells, BGP-15 significantly rescued raft domain coverage and shifted the size distribution toward larger platforms, coincident with increased hsp25 expression and Rac1-dependent stress signaling (Gombos et al., 2011). Across cell and tissue contexts, BGP-15 increases HSP70/HSPA1A (HSP72), and this HSP gain is causally linked to improved insulin signaling and cytoprotection in stressed cells (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011).

PARP/NAD+/SIRT1/HSF1 axis. Although BGP-15 demonstrates mixed-type (noncompetitive) inhibition of PARP-1 in vitro, the concentrations required exceed typical in vivo exposures, suggesting that PARP pathway effects in vivo are likely downstream of ROS lowering and reduced DNA single-strand breaks that otherwise drive PARP activation (Crul et al., 2013). In stressed cells, BGP-15 reduces PAR levels, which relieves PARP-mediated suppression of MKP-1/Dusp1, thereby inhibiting JNK/p38 activation; reduced PARP activity also preserves NAD+ and SIRT1 activity, which favors a deacetylated, active HSF1 and a stronger HSR (Crul et al., 2013). This mechanistic loop—less ROS, less PARP activation, more MKP-1, less JNK/p38, and better HSP/SIRT1 tone—aligns with the observed anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective phenotypes (Crul et al., 2013).

Mitochondrial enrichment and respiratory chain modulation. Biophysically, BGP-15 carries a delocalized positive charge, accumulates in energized mitochondria (>85–90% uptake in isolated organelles), and at micromolar doses characteristic of cell studies (1–50 µM) lowers mitochondrial ROS predominantly at complexes I and III without significant baseline depolarization of Δψm (Sümegi, 2018; Sumegi et al., 2017). In oxidative or inflammatory challenges, BGP-15 attenuates H₂O₂- and LPS-induced mitochondrial depolarization and reduces mitochondrial superoxide to near-control levels; MitoTEMPO controls confirm mitochondrial origin of the ROS signal (Sumegi et al., 2017). Importantly, the compound exhibits no meaningful direct antioxidant scavenging in cell-free ROS-generating systems, and only displays mild uncoupling at millimolar concentrations—far above the micromolar exposures used in protective assays—supporting a mechanism of respiratory chain modulation rather than redox scavenging (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). Downstream signaling reflects the lowered mitochondrial ROS burden: JNK/p38 activation is reduced, Akt signaling is enhanced, and caspase-independent death pathways are suppressed (Sumegi et al., 2017).

Mitochondrial dynamics, fusion, and biogenesis. Beyond acute ROS control, BGP-15 promotes mitochondrial fusion and preserves cristae architecture by activating OPA1 GTPase and promoting OPA1 polymerization; genetic suppression of OPA1 or Mfn1/Mfn2 abolishes the fusion phenotype, indicating that BGP-15 acts upstream or within the endogenous fusion machinery (Szabó et al., 2018). In vivo, these effects translate into improved mitochondrial ultrastructure and tissue histology under ROS stress (e.g., monocrotaline-induced PAH) (Szabó et al., 2018). In hypertensive cardiomyopathy, BGP-15 increases PGC-1α and mitochondrial mass, with concurrent shifts in CREB/AMPK phosphorylation consistent with improved energetic signaling, reduced p38/JNK via MKP-1 upregulation, and increased Akt/GSK-3β prosurvival signaling (Horváth et al., 2021).

Insulin-sensitizing stress signaling. In skeletal muscle and human studies, BGP-15 increases HSP72 expression, enhances insulin receptor autophosphorylation (blocking JNK inhibitory phosphorylation), activates RAC1, increases AKT phosphorylation, promotes GLUT4 translocation, increases membrane fluidity, raises AMPK activity, and reduces HSF1 acetylation, altogether improving glucose disposal without overt toxicity in a randomized trial (Crul et al., 2013). These metabolic effects are mechanistically congruent with the membrane–HSR–mitochondrial triad described above (Crul et al., 2013).

Ocular and retinal mechanisms. In rat eyes, BGP-15 increased HSP70 and decreased NFκB, consistent with HSR enhancement and anti-inflammatory signaling in ocular tissues (Wachal et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion and diabetic retinopathy models, functional improvements on ERG, restoration of oscillatory potentials, and preservation of retinal thickness are consistent with mitochondrial protection and stress-response reinforcement in retinal cells (Takács et al., 2024). The topical SBECD formulation demonstrated pharmacologic activity in the retina without systemic pharmacokinetic characterization, indicating local ocular delivery as a viable route for targeting mitochondrial and HSP pathways in the posterior segment (Takács et al., 2024).

The team’s hypothesis—that BGP-15 stabilizes mitochondrial membrane proteins and co-induces HSF1-driven antioxidant chaperone responses in RPE to mitigate oxidative stress in dry AMD—is aligned with the compound’s demonstrated pharmacology in retinal, cardiac, neural, and pulmonary models: (i) robust mitochondrial enrichment and stabilization of Δψm under oxidative/inflammatory stress, (ii) ROS lowering at complexes I and III without direct radical scavenging, (iii) activation of the HSR via membrane raft remodeling and HSF1 acetylation control, and (iv) suppression of ROS-sensitive injury cascades (JNK/p38) with concurrent activation of pro-survival Akt (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). In retinal disease models, BGP-15 improved ERG measures and retinal thickness and increased ocular HSP70 while decreasing NFκB, providing a direct ocular precedent likely to translate to stressed RPE, where mitochondria and proteostasis are central to survival under chronic oxidative load (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021).

- Membrane-raft remodeling and HSR co-induction. BGP-15 partitions into RPE membranes and remodels cholesterol-rich rafts, preserving raft integrity under stress, activating Rac1, decreasing HSF1 acetylation, and prolonging HSF1 DNA binding, thereby elevating HSP70/HSP25 and enhancing proteostasis capacity in aged/stressed RPE (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

BGP-15 should accumulate in RPE mitochondria, reduce ROS production at complexes I/III, and attenuate oxidative- and inflammation-induced depolarization, thereby maintaining ATP production and limiting mitochondrial permeability transition and AIF translocation, as shown in other cell types (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018).

Via OPA1 activation and Akt/GSK-3β signaling, BGP-15 is expected to promote inner-membrane fusion/OPA1 oligomerization and preserve cristae, with possible longer-term increases in mitochondrial biogenesis (PGC-1α), all protective features for RPE faced with chronic oxidative and lipofuscin stress (Szabó et al., 2018; Horváth et al., 2021).

By reducing mitochondrial ROS and PARP activation, BGP-15 should relieve PARP-mediated suppression of MKP-1, suppress JNK/p38 activity, decrease NFκB signaling, and bolster SIRT1-HSF1 activity, thereby reducing ROS-amplifying feed-forward loops in RPE (Crul et al., 2013; Wachal et al., 2021).

Systemic exposures in humans are low (≤25 nmol/mL), suggesting that oral dosing may be insufficient to reach pharmacologic micromolar levels in RPE; conversely, topical ocular delivery with SBECD has demonstrated retinal functional benefits and structural protection, supporting development of a posterior-segment–targeted topical or periocular formulation to enrich the RPE–choroid compartment (Sümegi, 2018; Takács et al., 2024).

The corpus documents the relevant targets (HSF1/HSP70, Rac1, OPA1, MKP-1, JNK/p38, Akt) as central to BGP-15’s mechanisms in multiple mammalian tissues and cell types and shows ocular readouts (HSP70 up, NFκB down) in rat eyes; however, it does not provide explicit RPE expression data, which should be confirmed experimentally in our RPE assay systems (Wachal et al., 2021; Gombos et al., 2011; Szabó et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic congruence with dry AMD pathobiology. BGP-15 directly addresses mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic oxidative stress—core drivers of RPE degeneration—by concentrating in mitochondria, lowering ROS at complexes I/III, stabilizing Δψm, and activating survival signaling while suppressing inflammatory stress kinases (Sumegi et al., 2017). Concurrently, it co-induces the HSR by remodeling plasma membrane rafts and modulating HSF1 acetylation, thereby boosting HSP70/HSP25 chaperone capacity and proteostasis—functions that are expected to mitigate protein misfolding and aggregation in aged RPE (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).  
- Demonstrated ocular efficacy in relevant retinal injury contexts. Topical BGP-15 improved ERG a- and b-waves, preserved oscillatory potentials, reduced implicit times, and rescued retinal thickness after ischemia–reperfusion, and it was retinoprotective in diabetic models, with ocular HSP70 increase and NFκB reduction—outcomes consistent with RPE/retinal resilience under oxidative stress (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021).  
- Pleiotropic yet coherent mechanism spanning membrane, nuclear, and mitochondrial nodes. The membrane–HSR–mitochondrial triad, including PARP/MKP-1/JNK–p38 and Akt/GSK-3β axes, provides multiple intervention points likely to translate into robust protection in the multifactorial environment of dry AMD (Crul et al., 2013; Sumegi et al., 2017; Szabó et al., 2018; Horváth et al., 2021).  
- Favorable translational signals. Proof-of-concept human trials in insulin resistance show pharmacodynamic activity without overt safety signals, and HSP co-inducers are known to preferentially act in stressed cells, potentially limiting off-target effects in quiescent tissues; local ocular delivery further improves the therapeutic index (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011; Takács et al., 2024).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Lack of direct dry AMD evidence. No studies in the corpus directly test BGP-15 in dry AMD models or patients; we infer utility from retinal IR/diabetes models and mechanism (Takács et al., 2024).  
- Exposure–response uncertainties for the posterior segment. Systemic serum concentrations are low relative to micromolar efficacious concentrations in vitro, necessitating optimized local delivery to RPE; although eyedrop formulations show retinal effects, posterior-segment delivery by topical route is often limited, and pharmacokinetics were not measured in the cited ocular study (Sümegi, 2018; Takács et al., 2024).  
- Target ambiguity and pleiotropy. While the membrane–HSR–mitochondrial framework is coherent, BGP-15 lacks a single defined receptor/protein target, and its in vitro PARP-1 inhibition likely does not drive in vivo efficacy; this complicates target engagement assays and regulatory narratives (Sümegi, 2018; Crul et al., 2013).  
- Nomenclature confusion. “BGP-15” also denotes a calcipotriene-derived vitamin D3 analog in the oncology literature; chemical identity must be verified to avoid conflation during procurement and CMC (Sintov et al., 2013; Takács et al., 2024).  
- Evidence base heterogeneity. Some ocular and cardiovascular studies are published in lower–quality venues, emphasizing the need for rigorous, blinded replication and GLP toxicology in ocular models (Horváth et al., 2021; Wachal et al., 2021).

Recommended next steps  
- In vitro RPE validation. In human primary or iPSC-derived RPE under oxidative (H₂O₂/tert-butyl hydroperoxide) and inflammatory (LPS/CpG) stress, test BGP-15 at 0.3–30 µM for effects on Δψm (JC-1/TMRM), mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX), total ROS (DHR123), apoptosis/necrosis (annexin V/PI), and mitochondrial respiration; confirm no direct antioxidant scavenging in cell-free systems (Sumegi et al., 2017).  
- Proteostasis and HSR endpoints. Quantify HSP70/HSP25 induction, HSF1 acetylation/binding dynamics, Rac1 activation, and membrane raft integrity using fPEG-cholesterol probes/TOCCSL in RPE; evaluate MKP-1, JNK/p38, and Akt/GSK-3β signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013; Sumegi et al., 2017).  
- Mitochondrial dynamics. Assess OPA1 oligomerization, fusion/fission balance (Mfn1/2 and Drp1 markers), cristae morphology by EM, and PGC-1α/mtDNA copy number to benchmark fusion/biogenesis responses (Szabó et al., 2018; Horváth et al., 2021).  
- Ocular delivery PK/PD. Using the SBECD eyedrop formulation as a starting point, perform ocular pharmacokinetics (vitreous, retina, RPE–choroid) and pharmacodynamics (ocular HSP70, NFκB, mitochondrial markers) to ensure RPE target engagement at tolerated doses (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021).  
- In vivo retinal stress models. Extend to retinal oxidative stress paradigms that capture RPE pathology; leverage ERG, OCT, histology, and mitochondrial ultrastructure endpoints already positive in IR/diabetic models (Takács et al., 2024).  
- Identity control and CMC. Source BGP-15 as O-(3-piperidino-2-hydroxy-1-propyl) nicotinic amidoxime dihydrochloride; confirm identity by NMR/MS to avoid the calcipotriene-derived analog (Takács et al., 2024; Sintov et al., 2013).

Go/no-go considerations for dry AMD  
Given the robust mechanistic alignment—mitochondrial ROS control at complexes I/III, Δψm stabilization, HSR co-induction via membrane raft remodeling and HSF1 acetylation control, OPA1-driven mitochondrial fusion, and suppression of ROS-sensitive inflammatory kinases—plus demonstrable ocular efficacy in retinal injury models, BGP-15 merits advancement to RPE-focused preclinical validation for dry AMD (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Szabó et al., 2018; Takács et al., 2024). The principal risks are translational: ensuring adequate RPE exposures by ocular delivery, confirming RPE target expression/engagement, and generating rigorous GLP pharmacology/toxicology data in ocular species. On balance, the mechanistic breadth that often complicates development is an advantage in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction, proteostasis failure, and chronic inflammation coexist.

Conclusion. BGP-15 is a credible repurposing candidate for dry AMD based on its mitochondria-centered, HSP co-inducing, membrane-lipid–modulating pharmacology and encouraging retinal efficacy in vivo; priority should be given to RPE-targeted PK/PD, mitochondrial and HSR biomarker validation, and controlled efficacy studies in retinal oxidative-stress models to de-risk translation (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Takács et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is a naturally occurring nucleotide derivative that functions as a key intermediate in the biosynthesis of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), an essential coenzyme in cellular energy metabolism and redox regulation (Chen et al., 2020). Originally identified as part of the salvage pathway of NAD+ synthesis, NMN is synthesized endogenously from nicotinamide and subsequently converted by NMN adenylyltransferase (NMNAT) into NAD+ (Gerdes, 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). Commercially produced by chemical synthesis and available from suppliers such as Sigma-Aldrich (catalog number N3501), NMN belongs to the class of NAD+ precursors that have attracted considerable attention due to their potential to counteract the age-related decline in NAD+ levels (Chen et al., 2020). Compounds of this class have historically been explored mainly in the context of metabolic and aging interventions, with the rationale that restoring NAD+ pools may reverse or delay cellular senescence and mitochondrial dysfunction (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022). NMN, as a small molecule with a molecular weight of approximately 334 g/mol, has been demonstrated to readily cross cell membranes and enhance cellular bioenergetics, making it a promising candidate for diseases in which energy metabolism is disrupted, such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Chen et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). The compound’s natural occurrence and favorable safety profile observed in preclinical aging models have contributed to its development as a therapeutic candidate across multiple indications, which now includes potential ophthalmological applications (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ebeling et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, NMN has been investigated in a variety of preclinical settings addressing metabolic dysfunction and age‐associated decline, with numerous studies across biochemical, cellular, and animal models demonstrating that NMN supplementation effectively elevates NAD+ levels and improves mitochondrial function (Chen et al., 2020). In models of retinal degeneration, particularly in contexts simulating photoreceptor loss and retinal detachment, NMN administration has shown neuroprotective effects by restoring NAD+ levels and activating key deacetylases such as SIRT1, which are central to oxidative stress mitigation and cell survival (Chen et al., 2020). Preclinical studies conducted in mouse models of retinal detachment have reported that NMN treatment not only boosts NAD+ concentrations beyond the physiological baseline but also attenuates the inflammatory response and reduces photoreceptor cell death, thereby preserving retinal structure and function (Chen et al., 2020). In addition to these acute models, experimental data from primary retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells derived from donors with age‐related macular degeneration have revealed that NMN can improve mitochondrial respiration and restore the NAD+/NADH balance critical to RPE cell health (Ebeling et al., 2020). Moreover, NMN’s ability to limit cellular senescence has been documented in RPE models challenged with oxidative stressors and pro‐senescent compounds, where supplementation led to a reduction in markers such as p16INK4a and p21Waf/Cip1, along with preservation of SIRT1 expression (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022). Clinical exploration of NMN in the context of aging and metabolic disorders—though not yet fully extended to ophthalmologic diseases—provides an encouraging translational backdrop, indicating that NMN has a robust therapeutic history in conditions characterized by NAD+ depletion and mitochondrial dysfunction (Jadeja et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2024). Collectively, the therapeutic history suggests that NMN has been thoroughly vetted in preclinical settings relevant to neurodegeneration and retinal health, thereby supporting its potential repurposing for dry AMD (Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
NMN exerts its biological effects primarily through its role as a biosynthetic precursor of NAD+, a critical coenzyme involved in numerous cellular processes including energy production, DNA repair, and redox balance (Chen et al., 2020). Once administered, NMN is rapidly taken up by cells and converted via NMNAT enzymes into NAD+, thereby replenishing intracellular NAD+ pools that typically decline with age and stress (Gerdes, 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). This increase in NAD+ levels has a twofold impact. First, elevated NAD+ directly energizes metabolic pathways, namely glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation, by serving as a cofactor for dehydrogenases, which is essential for mitochondrial ATP production (Will-Orrego, 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Second, NAD+ acts as a substrate for a family of NAD+-dependent deacetylases—the sirtuins—most notably SIRT1, SIRT3, and SIRT5, which are involved in regulating mitochondrial integrity and function (Chen et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). In the specific context of dry AMD, the hypothesis posits that NMN-mediated restoration of NAD+ in retinal pigment epithelial cells leads to reactivation of mitochondrial sirtuins SIRT3 and SIRT5. SIRT3, located in the mitochondrial matrix, deacetylates key metabolic enzymes including manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), whose activity is crucial for neutralizing mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) (Gerdes, 2018; Ren et al., 2022). The proper deacetylation of MnSOD enhances its antioxidant capacity, thereby reducing mtROS accumulation and protecting the mitochondria from oxidative damage (Chen et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022). SIRT5, another mitochondrial deacetylase, plays a complementary role by regulating the acylation status of proteins involved in mitochondrial dynamics and energy metabolism; its activation, in turn, contributes to improved mitochondrial respiration and bioenergetics (Ebeling et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). Furthermore, the elevation of NAD+ levels via NMN supplementation is known to indirectly influence other signaling pathways such as those modulated by AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and Akt/mTOR, which are critical for mitochondrial biogenesis and cellular homeostasis (Ren et al., 2022). In dry AMD, where metabolic dysfunction and increased oxidative stress are central to disease progression, the biochemical cascade triggered by NMN restores the balance between energy production and oxidative damage by ensuring that sirtuins are adequately fueled (Jadeja et al., 2018). This cascade not only preserves mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and oxygen consumption rate (OCR) but also limits the proton leak and bioenergetic inefficiency that characterize dysfunctional RPE cells (Ebeling et al., 2020). In summary, at the molecular level, NMN’s mechanism of action in RPE cells aligns with a strategy of metabolic reconditioning, whereby the reactivation of SIRT3 and SIRT5—via increased NAD+ availability—leads to improved deacetylation of mitochondrial enzymes, reduction in mtROS levels, and enhancement of overall mitochondrial function (Lin, 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of a dry AMD model, the anticipated effect of NMN supplementation is the restoration of NAD+ homeostasis within RPE cells and consequent reactivation of mitochondrial sirtuins such as SIRT3 and SIRT5, which will correct mitochondrial deacetylation deficits that are known to contribute to cellular dysfunction (Chen et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). Specifically, NMN is expected to normalize the NAD+/NADH ratio, an essential parameter for efficient electron transport chain function and ATP generation; this normalization is projected to result in enhanced oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and improved mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) in the RPE (Ebeling et al., 2020). As a direct consequence of restored sirtuin activity, particularly SIRT3’s deacetylation of MnSOD, there should be a significant reduction in mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), which in turn decreases the oxidative burden on the RPE cells—a critical factor in the development and progression of dry AMD (Gerdes, 2018; Ren et al., 2022). The expected downstream effects include not only enhanced bioenergetic function but also a reduction in the cellular senescence markers and inflammatory cytokines typically upregulated in the aging and stressed RPE (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022). In vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE cultures have demonstrated that NMN supplementation can rescue cells from FK866-induced NAD+ depletion, thereby restoring ATP levels and maintaining the expression of RPE identity genes, which are fundamental to retinal homeostasis (Will-Orrego, 2020). Moreover, by mitigating oxidative damage and correcting mitochondrial dysfunction, NMN is expected to preserve the structural integrity of the outer retina, which is essential for sustained photoreceptor function and visual acuity in dry AMD (Chen et al., 2020). Ultimately, the mechanistic actions of NMN—spanning from NAD+ replenishment to sirtuin activation—are predicted to yield measurable improvements in both cellular assays (e.g., increased OCR, stabilized Δψm, and decreased ROS levels) and functional endpoints such as electroretinography (ERG) responses in animal models of retinal degeneration (Chen et al., 2020). The robust preclinical data, including evidence of normalized mitochondrial respiration and amelioration of RPE senescence following NMN treatment, provide a strong rationale for expecting similar beneficial effects in a dry AMD assay (Jadeja et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
The cumulative evidence from biochemical, cellular, and in vivo studies positions NMN as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. One of the primary strengths of NMN is its well‐characterized role as a NAD+ precursor, which underpins its ability to restore intracellular NAD+ levels and reactivate essential sirtuin activities—most notably SIRT3 and SIRT5—in metabolically compromised cells (Chen et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). By addressing the root cause of mitochondrial dysfunction observed in dry AMD, namely NAD+ depletion and subsequent impairment of protein deacetylation, NMN targets a fundamental pathogenic mechanism that leads to photoreceptor and RPE degeneration (Chen et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022). The broad spectrum of supportive evidence, ranging from neuroprotective effects in retinal detachment models to the reversal of cellular senescence in AMD-relevant RPE cells, further reinforces the therapeutic rationale behind NMN’s application in dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022). Additionally, the translational feasibility of NMN is bolstered by ongoing clinical developments in aging and metabolic disorders, suggesting that the pharmacokinetic and safety profiles of NMN are sufficiently favorable to warrant its repurposing for retinal diseases (Jadeja et al., 2018).

However, several potential limitations must be considered. Variability in drug response among diseased RPE cells from different AMD donors has been documented, indicating that while NMN can robustly restore mitochondrial function in some cases, a subset of patients may exhibit a less pronounced therapeutic response, necessitating personalized dosing strategies or combinatorial therapies (Ebeling et al., 2020). Furthermore, although NMN’s activation of sirtuins is generally beneficial, there exists a theoretical risk that overactivation of these enzymes could induce off-target effects or exacerbate cellular stress if not properly titrated, as some studies have suggested that SIRT1 overactivation may in certain contexts lead to deleterious outcomes (Chen et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022). Moreover, much of the current evidence derives from preclinical models, and while these data are compelling, the extrapolation of these results to human subjects with dry AMD will require rigorously designed clinical trials to evaluate efficacy and safety in the specific target population (Chen et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024).

In summary, the overall assessment of NMN as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is highly favorable, particularly given its dual capacity to restore NAD+ levels and reengage mitochondrial deacetylation pathways that are crucial for RPE health. Its mechanistic basis, rooted in the reactivation of SIRT3 and SIRT5 leading to improved mitochondrial respiration and reduced oxidative stress, directly addresses the central pathogenic features of dry AMD. The extensive preclinical validation, coupled with encouraging translational data from aging-related indications, positions NMN as a strong candidate for further development and clinical evaluation in dry AMD, albeit with careful consideration of dosing strategies and patient heterogeneity (Cimaglia et al., 2020). Moving forward, prioritizing studies that assess long-term outcomes in appropriate animal models and early-phase clinical trials in AMD patients will be critical to firmly establish NMN’s therapeutic potential and optimize its utility as part of a broader strategy to mitigate vision loss associated with dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2020; Lin, 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) is a synthetic derivative of fumaric acid that belongs to the class of fumaric acid esters (FAEs) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Chemically, DMF is the dimethyl ester of fumaric acid, with a molecular weight of approximately 144.13 g/mol, and is produced by reacting fumaric acid with methanol in the presence of a strong acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Although fumaric acid occurs naturally as an intermediate in the citric acid cycle, DMF itself is fully synthetically manufactured, conferring the advantages of chemical stability and the ability to precisely modulate its structure to enhance pharmacological properties (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Moreover, DMF is classified as an electrophilic molecule that, due to its α,β-unsaturated ester structure, can covalently modify protein thiols, particularly the cysteine residues within KEAP1, thereby initiating its downstream effects on cellular redox homeostasis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Fumaric acid esters as a class have a long-standing history in pharmacotherapy, originally finding application in dermatology, most notably in the treatment of psoriasis, and have since been repurposed for neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis (MS) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, fumaric acid esters were introduced into clinical practice as antipsoriatic agents in Europe, with formulations such as Fumaderm® entering the market in the 1990s (Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). DMF in particular emerged as a key component in these formulations, and its efficacy in modulating immune responses and suppressing inflammation in skin diseases laid the foundation for its later repurposing in other systemic inflammatory conditions (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Over time, DMF was repurposed and further developed as an oral agent for the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), culminating in its FDA approval in 2013 under the trade name Tecfidera® by Biogen (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163). Clinical trials, including large-scale phase 3 studies, have demonstrated its favorable safety profile and efficacy in reducing relapse rates and slowing disability progression in MS patients (Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 14–16). Although there is no extensive historical record of DMF being used directly for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other primary ocular diseases, recent preclinical findings have indicated that its potent activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway may confer significant protective effects on the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This has sparked considerable interest in repurposing DMF for ocular indications such as geographic atrophy, a late stage of dry AMD, by leveraging its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities observed in nonocular settings (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, DMF functions primarily as a prodrug; upon oral administration it is rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases within the gastrointestinal tract to yield its active metabolite, monomethyl fumarate (MMF) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). The pharmacodynamic actions of DMF principally involve the electrophilic modification of specific cysteine residues—most notably cysteine 151—on Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Under physiological conditions, KEAP1 binds to and retains the transcription factor Nrf2 in the cytoplasm, targeting it for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. However, when DMF covalently modifies KEAP1, it disrupts this complex, allowing Nrf2 to dissociate and translocate into the nucleus (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). In the nucleus, Nrf2 binds to antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoters of numerous genes encoding cytoprotective enzymes, including glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), and various enzymes involved in glutathione (GSH) synthesis and regeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). These molecular interactions lead to enhanced antioxidant defenses, improved detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and overall better maintenance of cellular redox balance (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). In addition to its role in promoting antioxidant gene expression via Nrf2 activation, DMF has been shown to have immunomodulatory properties; it can shift cytokine profiles by increasing interleukin-4 (IL-4)–expressing CD4+ T cells and decreasing the production of proinflammatory cytokines such as interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and interleukin-17 (IL-17) (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Furthermore, DMF has been reported to inhibit nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation in certain cellular contexts, thus contributing to a reduction in inflammatory signaling independently of Nrf2 (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Together, these molecular actions result in lowered cellular oxidative stress and an improved inflammatory milieu, which are critical factors implicated in the pathogenesis of chronic degenerative diseases (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry AMD, particularly the geographic atrophy form, is characterized by the gradual degeneration of RPE cells, which leads to subsequent photoreceptor loss and irreversible vision impairment. Central to the pathophysiology of dry AMD are oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation that progressively compromise RPE viability and function (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). The hypothesis being explored is that DMF, through its robust activation of the Nrf2 pathway, can enhance the expression of ARE-driven genes that encode for antioxidant and cytoprotective proteins, thereby counteracting the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in the RPE (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 13–14). In particular, the upregulation of enzymes involved in glutathione synthesis is expected to increase intracellular levels of GSH, a critical thiol antioxidant that protects mitochondrial membranes and supports cellular bioenergetics (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Preclinical studies in retinal models have demonstrated that DMF can effectively preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and reduce the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β), both of which are hallmarks of RPE distress under oxidative challenge (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Given that the RPE is highly metabolically active and particularly vulnerable to cumulative oxidative damage, the sustained activation of Nrf2 by DMF following oral dosing is anticipated to provide continuous reinforcement of antioxidant defenses and maintain mitochondrial integrity in these cells (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 3–5; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). Moreover, by mitigating inflammatory signaling, DMF may not only protect the RPE but also contribute to a more favorable microenvironment that limits the propagation of cell death signals, thus potentially slowing the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Collectively, these expected cellular effects support the rationale for using DMF as an intervention to preserve retinal structure and function by lowering oxidative damage and supporting bioenergetics in the RPE.

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential of dimethyl fumarate as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD rests on a solid mechanistic rationale combined with an established clinical pedigree in other indications. One of the primary strengths of DMF is its well-characterized pharmacological profile; it is FDA-approved for multiple sclerosis and has been safely administered to thousands of patients over several years, which significantly mitigates the risk and regulatory hurdles typically associated with repurposed drugs (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). The dual actions of DMF—in particular, its ability to both activate the Nrf2 pathway and attenuate proinflammatory signals—directly target the underlying pathological processes in dry AMD, where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central drivers of RPE degeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In vitro studies have provided encouraging evidence that DMF increases intracellular glutathione levels and protects RPE cells from oxidative insults, findings that are directly translatable to the pathobiology of dry AMD (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Nonetheless, several challenges remain. Although DMF is known to be effective in MS and psoriasis, the ocular milieu presents unique pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic challenges that may not be fully addressed by the current oral formulations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18). The rapid hydrolysis of DMF to MMF means that, while the active metabolite does exert therapeutic effects, fine-tuning the dosing regimen to ensure adequate drug levels in the retina while minimizing systemic side effects is necessary (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). In addition, common adverse reactions associated with DMF, such as gastrointestinal discomfort and flushing, though generally mild to moderate, could be more problematic in the typically elderly dry AMD population, necessitating careful monitoring and potentially modified dosing strategies (Camelo, 2025, p. 17; Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13). There is also the question of whether systemic administration of DMF can generate sufficient concentrations in the retina to achieve a meaningful therapeutic effect. While emerging evidence suggests that DMF can cross the blood-retinal barrier and activate Nrf2 in retinal cells (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3), further pharmacokinetic and translational studies are warranted to confirm its retinal bioavailability and the optimal dosing regimen for ocular indications.

Another consideration is the complexity of dry AMD itself, which is a slowly progressive, multifactorial disease with contributions from genetic predispositions, environmental exposures, and systemic metabolic disturbances. It remains to be seen whether the monotherapeutic approach of DMF, targeting primarily oxidative stress via Nrf2 activation, will be sufficient to halt or reverse disease progression, or whether combination therapies will ultimately be required (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Furthermore, while the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms of DMF are well supported by in vitro data and animal studies, there is still limited clinical data on its efficacy in ocular disease settings. Early-phase clinical trials aimed at evaluating DMF in geographic atrophy have to rigorously assess both structural outcomes (e.g., changes in the area of atrophy) and functional endpoints (e.g., visual acuity, retinal sensitivity) to establish its therapeutic benefit in dry AMD (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Despite these limitations, the strengths of DMF are compelling. The drug’s ability to upregulate a broad spectrum of cytoprotective genes via the Nrf2 pathway makes it a versatile candidate for mitigating the oxidative and inflammatory stress that drives RPE degeneration. The fact that DMF has already cleared extensive regulatory and clinical safety evaluations in nonocular indications is a significant advantage, as it greatly accelerates the translational pathway compared to a novel chemical entity (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Additionally, the repurposing of an already approved drug leverages existing manufacturing, formulation, and distribution infrastructure, favorably impacting the cost and timeline associated with drug development (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

In summary, the comprehensive literature review supports the potential of DMF to serve as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its mechanism of action—centered on Nrf2 activation leading to enhanced antioxidant capacity along with anti-inflammatory effects—directly addresses the key pathophysiological mechanisms implicated in dry AMD. The extensive clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis provides a reliable safety and tolerability framework, which is crucial for rapid repositioning into a new clinical area such as geographic atrophy (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). However, it is essential to conduct targeted preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials specifically in ocular disease models to optimize dosing, confirm retinal delivery, and demonstrate clinical efficacy before advancing to larger randomized controlled trials (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Overall, while challenges remain regarding optimal application in the retinal context and potential side effects in an older patient population, DMF—by virtue of its dual antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms and robust clinical background—stands as a viable candidate that merits further investigation for the treatment of dry AMD.

Given the current evidence, the following recommendations are proposed for advancing DMF as a candidate for dry AMD:  

1. Conduct detailed pharmacokinetic studies in animal models to assess the retinal bioavailability of DMF and its active metabolite MMF following systemic administration. This should include studies comparing different dosing schedules and formulations to optimize retinal exposure without exacerbating systemic adverse effects (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2).  

2. Develop and validate preclinical models of dry AMD that recapitulate the key features of human geographic atrophy, with a focus on evaluating the efficacy of DMF in protecting RPE cells against oxidative stress and preserving mitochondrial function (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

3. Investigate the potential benefits of combining DMF with other therapeutic agents that target complementary pathways in dry AMD. For example, agents that modulate complement activation or improve choroidal blood flow may synergize with the Nrf2-mediated antioxidant mechanism of DMF (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).  

4. Initiate early-phase clinical trials in patients with geographic atrophy to establish proof of concept. These studies should include robust biomarker assessments (e.g., measurement of ARE gene expression, retinal imaging for atrophy progression, and functional visual outcomes) to correlate molecular effects with clinical benefit (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

5. Carefully monitor the safety profile of DMF in the elderly population, as the incidence of gastrointestinal side effects and lymphopenia may differ compared to the population with MS. Consider the feasibility of modified-release formulations or alternative routes of administration (e.g., topical ocular delivery) to minimize systemic side effects while maximizing retinal drug concentrations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18).

Overall, the repurposing of dimethyl fumarate for dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a robust mechanistic framework and a significant body of preclinical and clinical data generated in other indications. Its capacity to activate the Nrf2 pathway, enhance mitochondrial glutathione synthesis, and modulate inflammatory responses in RPE cells directly addresses several pivotal aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). While there are challenges regarding optimal retinal delivery and management of systemic adverse effects, the clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis lends considerable support to its translational potential. Consequently, dimethyl fumarate represents a well‐justified and attractive therapeutic candidate for further exploration in the treatment of dry AMD, warranting additional preclinical optimization and clinical investigation to fully define its role in preserving visual function in patients affected by this progressive degenerative disease (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Mitochonic Acid-5 (MA-5; MedChemExpress HY-104308) is a synthetic, mitochondria‐targeted small molecule originally discovered for its ability to improve mitochondrial function in models of cellular aging. The current hypothesis proposes that MA-5 binds directly to mitofilin (also known as Mic60), a key scaffolding protein in the inner mitochondrial membrane that is essential for the proper organization and stability of mitochondrial cristae. This interaction is anticipated to stabilize cristae architecture, thereby preserving optimal assembly of the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and enabling improved mitochondrial bioenergetics—a mechanism particularly appealing in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), where cristae disorganization and mtROS accumulation in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells have been associated with disease pathology (Ji et al., 2021; Ferrington et al., 2020).

While MA-5 itself has not been previously evaluated in ocular diseases, compounds that modulate mitochondrial function have a long history in preclinical studies for age-related conditions. Several mitochondrial-targeted agents—for example, SkQ1 and elamipretide—have demonstrated promise in ameliorating mitochondrial defects in RPE models and in early clinical trials targeting dry AMD (Ji et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022). In other systems, MA-5 has been reported to improve ATP production, reduce mtROS, and activate the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt) in fibroblast and C. elegans models. Such beneficial effects on mitochondrial function have contributed to the rationale for repurposing MA-5 for dry AMD. Moreover, research in related domains suggests that stabilizing mitochondrial cristae via targeting scaffold proteins such as mitofilin is mechanistically sound given observations of altered mitofilin expression and cristae disruption in AMD RPE (Ferrington et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). However, direct usage of MA-5 in retinal disorders remains unexplored, and its potential has yet to be validated in RPE-specific in vitro or in vivo models.

At the molecular level, MA-5 is proposed to exert its beneficial effects by physically interacting with mitofilin/Mic60, a protein integral to the maintenance of inner mitochondrial membrane architecture and cristae organization. Mitofilin is recognized for its role in stabilizing the cristae junctions and in facilitating the proper assembly and function of the ETC complexes (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Ferrington et al., 2020). In dry AMD, mitochondrial cristae loss has been documented in RPE cells, suggesting that disrupted mitofilin function may underlie some of the bioenergetic deficiencies seen in the disease (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Ferrington et al., 2020). By binding to mitofilin, MA-5 is expected to reinforce cristae integrity; this stabilization can promote the efficient assembly of ETC complexes, thereby leading to improved oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production. Concurrently, enhanced cristae organization is likely to reduce electron leakage from the ETC and lower the production of reactive oxygen species, which in excess contribute to oxidative damage and RPE cell death (Ji et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022).

Activation of UPRmt could lead to increased expression of mitochondrial chaperones, improved clearance of damaged proteins, and a restoration of redox balance within the mitochondria. This dual mechanism—direct structural stabilization via mitofilin binding and indirect activation of UPRmt—positions MA-5 as a potentially powerful agent for correcting mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD (Tong et al., 2022; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

If MA-5 performs as hypothesized in RPE cells, several beneficial effects are anticipated. First, by binding mitofilin and stabilizing cristae architecture, MA-5 should restore proper assembly and function of ETC complexes leading to increased ATP production. Such a recovery in mitochondrial bioenergetics is particularly critical in RPE cells, given their high energy demands for processes such as phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and maintenance of the visual cycle (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022). Lower ROS levels would alleviate oxidative stress—a known driver of RPE degeneration and dry AMD progression that has been documented in multiple studies (Ji et al., 2021; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Third, the activation of UPRmt may upregulate key mitochondrial chaperones such as mtHsp70, facilitating improved protein folding, enhanced clearance of damaged proteins, and overall better maintenance of mitochondrial homeostasis. These cellular changes should collectively promote RPE survival and function, thus potentially slowing or even reversing some aspects of the cellular degenerative processes seen in dry AMD (Ji et al., 2021; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

Furthermore, since mitofilin/Mic60 is an abundantly expressed and essential component in RPE mitochondria—as evidenced by its upregulation in early AMD patient samples—the MA-5-mediated stabilization of this protein is expected to yield measurable improvements in mitochondrial parameters in cellular assays. Such improvements would include increased mitochondrial membrane potential, enhanced basal and maximal respiration, and a reduction in apoptotic markers associated with mitochondrial damage. Ultimately, if these in vitro effects translate into in vivo efficacy, MA-5 could contribute to a novel treatment modality that directly addresses the underlying mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD (Ferrington et al., 2020).

The therapeutic candidate MA-5 presents a highly promising, mechanistically driven approach to addressing dry AMD by targeting mitochondrial dysfunction—a central hallmark of the disease. Therapeutic History:  
Deferiprone has been used clinically as an orally administered iron chelator in the management of transfusional iron overload, notably in patients with thalassemia major. This usage is supported by multiple clinical studies and reviews that address both its efficacy in reducing systemic iron burden as well as its associated hematologic risks, such as agranulocytosis and neutropenia, which occur in approximately 1% of patients (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). Several animal studies report that deferiprone, when administered systemically, can reduce retinal and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) iron levels in models of iron overload or light-induced degeneration and produce improvements in oxidative stress markers and retinal functional indices (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). This complex formation effectively reduces the availability of free iron in the intracellular labile iron pool, thereby diminishing iron-catalyzed reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. In addition, some data suggest that deferiprone may also interact with ferrous iron under certain conditions, contributing further to its antioxidant effects by interrupting redox cycling associated with both Fe3+ and Fe2+ species (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021).  

From a biochemical standpoint, iron accumulation in the RPE and surrounding retinal tissues is known to promote lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial oxidative stress, leading to cellular dysfunction and death—a pathomechanism observed in dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). The preclinical history of Liproxstatin-1 is rich with evidence supporting its role as a potent inhibitor of ferroptosis. Early studies demonstrated that Liproxstatin-1 acts at low nanomolar concentrations to prevent ferroptotic cell death in mouse embryonic fibroblasts as well as in specialized cells rendered vulnerable by GPX4 inactivation (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Angeli et al., 2014, p. 10). Moreover, related compounds, notably Ferrostatin-1, have been tested in various retinal cell models and in some in vivo settings pertaining to retinal ischemia–reperfusion injury and oxygen-induced retinopathy, further bolstering the therapeutic concept of using RTA-type ferroptosis inhibitors in ocular settings (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23; Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8). While the bulk of Liproxstatin-1’s therapeutic history centers on its role as an anti-ferroptotic agent in cancer, neurodegeneration, and acute organ failure, its mechanistic overlap with key pathological features observed in dry AMD – such as iron accumulation, glutathione depletion and elevated lipid peroxidation in the RPE – supports evaluating it as a repurposed candidate in this context (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Shen et al., 2025, pp. 1–2).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism by which Liproxstatin-1 exerts its cytoprotective effect is rooted in its function as a radical-trapping antioxidant. Specifically, Liproxstatin-1 reacts rapidly with lipid peroxyl radicals that propagate the autoxidation chain reaction in cellular membranes. Experimental data have established that Liproxstatin-1 exhibits an intrinsic reaction rate constant (k_inh) in the range of approximately 2.4 × 10^5 M^−1 s^−1 in organic solvents such as chlorobenzene at 37 °C, which is comparable to industrial diarylamine antioxidants (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 8–9). The compound functions primarily by donating a hydrogen atom from its arylamine (or diarylamine) N–H group, effectively quenching chain-propagating lipid peroxyl radicals before they can perpetuate lipid hydroperoxide formation (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). Kinetic isotope effect studies and computational analyses have confirmed that the N–H bond dissociation enthalpy is sufficiently low in Liproxstatin-1 to enable rapid hydrogen-atom transfer, which is a critical step in its radical-trapping mechanism (Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 2–3, 5–7).
