These studies have helped establish a mechanistic link between C3a/C3aR activation and the proteostasis dysfunction observed in RPE cells, a pathological process believed to contribute to early AMD pathology.

In addition to in vitro data, in vivo models provide further support for the therapeutic potential of modulating C3aR signaling. In a murine model of sodium iodate (NaIO₃)-induced RPE injury – a model that recapitulates aspects of geographic atrophy – systemic administration of SB 290157 reduced photoreceptor death, decreased markers of gliosis and microglial activation, and lowered TNFα and STAT3 signaling levels (Wang et al., 2020). Similarly, in a laser-induced retinal vein occlusion (RVO) model, intravitreal injection of SB 290157 suppressed the up-regulation of both C3 and C3a receptor expression, correlating with partial rescue of retinal morphology and vascular integrity (Zhao et al., 2025). Although these studies were not specifically designed for dry AMD, the similarities in underlying complement-mediated RPE injury and chronic inflammation between these models and the dry AMD phenotype provide a strong rationale for further exploring SB 290157 in this indication.

Despite these promising applications, SB 290157’s therapeutic history is not without controversy. Several studies have reported that, depending on the cell type and receptor density, SB 290157 may exhibit partial agonist activity rather than acting as a pure antagonist (Mathieu et al., 2005). This variable pharmacological profile has raised concerns about its utility as a definitive clinical tool. Nonetheless, as a research probe, SB 290157 has significantly advanced our understanding of complement-mediated cellular responses in inflammatory, vascular, and ocular contexts. Overall, while it has been extensively used in preclinical studies across multiple disease models – including arthritis, lung inflammation, and retinal injury – its use specifically in clinical settings for dry AMD remains investigational (Ames et al., 2001; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Wang et al., 2020).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

SB 290157 exerts its biological effects by competitively binding to the C3a receptor (C3aR), thereby preventing the interaction of endogenous C3a with its receptor. Under normal conditions, the complement cascade, when activated via any of its pathways, leads to the cleavage of complement component C3 and the subsequent release of the anaphylatoxin C3a. This bioactive peptide binds to C3aR, a G protein-coupled receptor present on various cell types including granulocytes, monocytes, and notably retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Once activated, C3aR transduces signals that can lead to intracellular calcium mobilization, triggering a cascade of downstream events such as receptor internalization and activation of inflammatory transcription factors.

In vitro studies using radioligand binding assays have determined that SB 290157 displaces [¹²⁵I]-C3a from its receptor with an IC₅₀ in the high nanomolar range (approximately 200 nM), while functional calcium mobilization assays in cell lines (including RBL cells and human neutrophils) have demonstrated potent inhibition of C3a-stimulated intracellular calcium release at low nanomolar concentrations (approximately 28 nM) (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Mechanistically, by preventing C3a from engaging C3aR, the compound is able to avert subsequent receptor conformational changes that would otherwise lead to G protein coupling and downstream signaling events.

In the context of RPE cells, particularly under conditions of chronic oxidative stress – such as exposure to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) – C3a engagement of its receptor has been implicated in a range of deleterious cellular effects. Studies in ARPE-19 cells have shown that oxidative stress induces a redistribution of C3aR away from its typical plasma membrane localization and promotes its translocation toward the mitochondria (Ishii et al., 2021; Riihilä et al., 2019). At the mitochondrial level, activation of the receptor by C3a leads to an increase in mitochondrial calcium uptake, which in turn results in compromised respiratory function as evidenced by decreased state III (ADP-driven) respiration and reduced maximal respiratory capacity (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). The resultant mitochondrial dysfunction is highly likely to contribute to the generation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS). mtROS are known triggers for the NLRP3 inflammasome, which upon activation facilitates the processing of pro-IL-1β to active IL-1β, a cytokine strongly implicated in chronic inflammatory processes observed in AMD (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024).

Furthermore, in primary human fetal RPE models, prolonged exposure to recombinant C3a has been demonstrated to reduce the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (UPP) without altering mRNA levels for proteasome subunits, indicating a post-transcriptional impairment of proteostasis (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). This impairment in proteasome function is associated with an imbalance in ECM turnover – marked by a reduction in tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases (TIMP-3) abundance and an increase in matrix metalloproteinase (MMP-2) activity – culminating in the pathological deposition of extracellular matrix components (notably collagens IV and VI) beneath the RPE. Such sub-RPE deposit formation, or drusen, is one of the hallmarks of early AMD pathology (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

SB 290157, by blocking C3a from binding to C3aR, therefore interrupts these pathological cascades at two key junctures. First, it prevents the mitochondrial translocation and activation of C3aR in oxidatively stressed ARPE-19 cells, which is predicted to avert the associated mitochondrial calcium overload and respiratory inhibition, thereby reducing the likelihood of mtROS generation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). Second, by inhibiting C3a-induced receptor activation in RPE cells, SB 290157 preserves UPP activity, ensuring proper regulation of ECM component turnover and forestalling the aberrant deposition of sub-RPE material (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

It is important to note, however, that while the majority of evidence supports SB 290157 acting as an effective C3aR antagonist, several reports have cautioned that under certain conditions, the compound may display partial agonist activity. This means that rather than completely blocking receptor activation, SB 290157 might induce a low level of receptor signaling in some cellular contexts, especially when receptor density is high (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001). Such an effect must be carefully considered when interpreting experimental outcomes and when designing therapeutic strategies aimed at persistent modulation of complement activity. In all, the known mechanism of action for SB 290157 can be summarized as competitive inhibition of C3a binding to C3aR, thereby mitigating the downstream signals that lead to mitochondrial calcium dysregulation, proteasome impairment, ECM deposition abnormalities, and ultimately, NLRP3 inflammasome priming and IL-1β secretion (Ames et al., 2001; Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect

The central hypothesis underlying the use of SB 290157 in repurposing for dry AMD is that the blockade of C3aR will attenuate a cascade of deleterious events within the retinal pigment epithelium that contribute to disease progression. In particular, the expected effect is that SB 290157 will reduce complement-driven mitochondrial dysfunction, lower mtROS production, and thereby prevent the priming and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, resulting ultimately in diminished IL-1β secretion and preservation of RPE barrier integrity.

In dry AMD, chronic oxidative stress leads to dysregulated complement activation and subsequent accumulation of complement fragments such as C3a in the subretinal space. RPE cells under oxidative stress have been demonstrated to upregulate C3aR expression, with a portion of the receptor redistributing to the mitochondria—a change that is associated with an increased uptake of calcium into the mitochondria and a pronounced decline in mitochondrial respiratory function (Ishii et al., 2021; Riihilä et al., 2019). The resulting mitochondrial dysfunction is poised to increase the generation of mtROS, which serve as an upstream activator of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Activation of this inflammasome complex culminates in the maturation of IL-1β, a powerful proinflammatory cytokine that has been implicated in propagating RPE injury and the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024).

By competitively inhibiting C3a binding to its receptor, SB 290157 is expected to block these deleterious changes. In cultured ARPE-19 cells—which serve as a well-established model for human RPE—it is anticipated that SB 290157 will prevent the mitochondrial translocation of C3aR, thereby reducing abnormal mitochondrial calcium uptake and preserving normal respiration. This action should limit mtROS generation and consequently reduce the priming threshold for NLRP3 inflammasome activation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). Concurrently, in primary fetal RPE cultures, inhibition of C3aR signaling by SB 290157 has been shown to preserve the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, which in turn maintains the balance of matrix metalloproteinases and their tissue inhibitors. By doing so, the compound prevents the accumulation of sub-RPE deposits—a process that is intimately linked to the early phases of AMD pathology (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

The expression of C3aR in RPE cells, particularly in stressed conditions, is well-documented. This receptor is notably enriched on the basolateral membrane of RPE and even redistributes to mitochondrial compartments under oxidative stress conditions, as confirmed in ARPE-19 cell studies (Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Given that dry AMD is characterized by both heightened complement activation and chronic oxidative stress, the strategic inhibition of C3aR is expected to yield multiple beneficial outcomes: restoration of proteostasis, maintenance of mitochondrial function, reduction in chronic inflammatory cytokine expression, and preservation of the integrity and barrier function of the RPE monolayer. Moreover, in in vivo models such as NaIO₃-induced RPE injury or laser-induced retinal vein occlusion, treatment with a C3aR antagonist (presumably SB 290157) has been associated with reduced photoreceptor loss, attenuated microglial activation, and improved retinal morphology (Wang et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2025).

Furthermore, because mitochondrial reactive oxygen species serve as a trigger for the NLRP3 inflammasome, blocking the upstream signal via C3aR inhibition is hypothesized to break the vicious cycle of complement-mediated inflammation. The decreased activation of NLRP3 would lead to lower levels of IL-1β—a cytokine implicated in the autocrine and paracrine amplification of inflammation within the RPE layer—and thus stabilize the local microenvironment (Ong et al., 2024; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In summary, the expected effect of SB 290157 in the context of dry AMD is multifold: preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics, maintenance of proteasomal activity, prevention of pathological ECM accumulation, and attenuation of inflammasome-mediated inflammatory responses—all of which contribute to the protection of RPE integrity and function.

────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

SB 290157 stands out as one of the best-studied C3a receptor antagonists available today. Its well-documented chemical synthesis, robust in vitro pharmacological profile, and demonstrable efficacy in preclinical models of inflammatory injury provide strong support for its continued evaluation as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. The compound’s origins – as a product of high-throughput screening followed by medicinal chemistry optimization using Fmoc-solid phase techniques – are well established, and its chemical structure (N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine) clearly classifies it as a small-molecule non-peptide antagonist of a key complement receptor (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011).

Strengths of SB 290157 include its proven ability to block C3a-induced signaling cascades across a range of cell types and experimental models. Preclinical studies in RPE cells indicate that it can prevent C3a-induced sub-RPE deposit formation and proteasome impairment—a finding directly relevant to the early pathological events of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Additionally, evidence from ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress suggests that SB 290157 effectively inhibits aberrant mitochondrial Ca²⁺ uptake and consequent respiratory dysfunction—mechanisms known to contribute to mtROS generation and inflammasome activation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). In vivo, its administration in models of retinal injury (such as NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration and laser-induced retinal vein occlusion) has correlated with reduced photoreceptor death, decreased gliosis, and improved retinal architecture (Wang et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2025). These findings collectively underscore the compound’s potential to modulate complement-mediated pathology in the ocular setting.

Nonetheless, SB 290157 is not without its weaknesses. A significant concern noted across several studies is its variable pharmacological behavior. Under some experimental conditions, particularly in cell systems with high receptor density, SB 290157 exhibits partial agonist activity rather than pure antagonism (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001). This paradoxical behavior could lead to unintended receptor activation and potentially undermine its therapeutic benefit, especially in chronic conditions like dry AMD where long-term receptor blockade is desired. Furthermore, while there is compelling preclinical evidence supporting its beneficial impact on mitochondrial function and ECM homeostasis, direct experimental data linking SB 290157 to a reduction in mitochondrial ROS production and consequent suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation in ARPE-19 or primary RPE models remain incomplete or indirect (Wang et al., 2020; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Behnke, 2022). This gap in the literature necessitates further investigation to firmly establish the causal chain from C3aR inhibition to inflammasome modulation.

Another consideration is the translational challenge. SB 290157 has been predominantly utilized as a research tool rather than a clinical candidate. Its pharmacokinetic profile—while adequate for short-term animal experiments—has not been thoroughly characterized for long-term use in ocular applications, where issues such as retinal toxicity, ocular bioavailability, and sustained receptor occupancy become critical. The delicate environment of the retina requires highly specific and safe compounds; thus, the partial agonist activity and potential off-target effects of SB 290157 raise valid concerns regarding its safety profile in humans (Mathieu et al., 2005; Tan et al., 2024).

On the other hand, the dual benefit of SB 290157—in preventing not only aberrant complement signaling but also the downstream mitochondrial dysfunction that leads to inflammasome activation—directly addresses central pathogenic mechanisms in dry AMD. Given that dry AMD is characterized by chronic inflammation, RPE dysfunction, and progressive atrophy correlated with mitochondrial impairment, a drug that can simultaneously modulate these pathways offers a novel therapeutic angle. In this context, the ability of SB 290157 to preserve the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway and maintain ECM turnover may help stabilize the RPE, delay the progression of geographic atrophy, and potentially improve visual outcomes (Ames et al., 2001; Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Wang et al., 2020). Conversely, its partial agonist behavior in certain systems and the current lack of direct evidence linking its action to reduced mtROS and NLRP3 activation in ocular models raise legitimate concerns that must be addressed prior to clinical translation (Mathieu et al., 2005; Behnke, 2022).

Overall, SB 290157 is a compelling candidate for further exploration and mechanistic validation as a repurposed drug for dry AMD, provided that additional research can surmount the challenges associated with its pharmacodynamic variability and confirm its protective effects in retina-specific models.

────────────────────────────────────────  
Conclusion

The comprehensive literature evaluation indicates that SB 290157’s synthetic origins, established use as a C3aR antagonist, and demonstrated efficacy in preclinical models of complement-mediated RPE injury make it a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its mechanism—blocking C3a-induced signaling that otherwise leads to mitochondrial calcium overload, impaired proteostasis, and subsequent inflammasome activation—is highly relevant to the pathophysiology of geographic atrophy. However, the compound’s documented partial agonist effects and potential variability in receptor blockade require careful consideration and further optimization. Additional studies are necessary to firmly establish that SB 290157 can reduce mitochondrial ROS and suppress NLRP3 inflammasome activation in RPE cells under conditions that model dry AMD clinically. Thus, while SB 290157 is an excellent tool for dissecting the complement–mitochondria crosstalk in dry AMD, its suitability as a long-term therapeutic will depend on resolving these outstanding issues through rigorous preclinical and mechanistic evaluation (Ames et al., 2001; Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Mathieu et al., 2005).

Overall, the candidate shows substantial promise as a mechanistic probe and potential therapeutic agent for dry AMD; its ability to block key complement-mediated events that contribute to RPE dysfunction and inflammation positions it as a novel target for drug development. However, given the documented limitations, further studies are strongly recommended to optimize its receptor selectivity, define its pharmacokinetic and safety profile in the ocular context, and conclusively demonstrate its capacity to mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammasome activation in relevant models before advancing it into clinical trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Honokiol is a naturally occurring polyphenolic neolignan that is primarily isolated from the bark and other tissues of Magnolia species, notably Magnolia officinalis. Traditionally used in Chinese medicine, honokiol has emerged as a promising therapeutic candidate due to its potent antioxidant, anti‐inflammatory, and neuroprotective properties. As a member of the phenylpropanoid class of natural compounds, honokiol has a unique biphenolic structure that enables it to interact with a variety of cellular targets. Its extraction from natural sources and subsequent formulation by vendors such as Sigma-Aldrich (SML0588) provides a well-characterized starting point for drug repurposing strategies. Over the years, synthetic modifications have also been explored to improve its bioavailability, solubility, and therapeutic efficacy, further expanding its potential as a drug candidate in multiple clinical contexts (Faysal et al., 2023). The chemical attributes of honokiol allow it to cross biological barriers effectively, a property that is particularly relevant in diseases involving complex tissue compartments such as the eye’s retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Its classification within the polyphenolic compounds aligns it with other antioxidants known to mitigate cellular damage from reactive oxygen species (ROS) and oxidative stress, making it a promising candidate for repurposing in conditions like dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative injury are predominant pathological features (Faysal et al., 2023; Sasia et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, honokiol has been the subject of extensive biochemical and pharmacological investigations given its wide-ranging protective effects in various tissues. In hepatocyte models, studies have demonstrated that honokiol protects liver cells from oxidative injury induced by compounds such as tert-butyl hydroperoxide (t-BHP) by restoring mitochondrial deacetylase SIRT3 levels, thereby boosting cellular viability and enhancing antioxidant defenses (Liu et al., 2018). These hepatoprotective effects underscore honokiol’s capacity to modulate mitochondrial health, a mechanism that likely underpins its action in other cell types as well. In addition to hepatic models, honokiol has been evaluated in neurological contexts where activation of SIRT3 plays a central role in neuroprotection. For example, in a rat model of ammonia neurotoxicity, honokiol administration led to the recovery of MnSOD activity and the upregulation of transcription factors such as FoxO3a and PGC1α, which are essential for mitochondrial function and cellular antioxidant responses (Trigun & Anamika, 2022; Tyagi & Pugazhenthi, 2023). These findings demonstrate the compound’s ability to counteract oxidative stress via restoration of mitochondrial enzyme activities, an effect that has been linked to improved neurological outcomes including reductions in beta-amyloid accumulation.

More recently, honokiol has shown promising results in ocular models as well. Studies investigating its effects on diabetic retinal microvascular injury have revealed that honokiol can activate SIRT3 in retinal capillary endothelial cells, leading to the deacetylation of mitochondrial proteins—most notably manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD)—and preservation of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) under hyperglycemic conditions (Shi et al., 2024). Although these results have been demonstrated in the context of diabetic retinal injury rather than in models of dry AMD specifically, the mechanistic overlap—centered on mitochondrial protection and the reduction of oxidative stress—strongly supports the potential utility of honokiol in diseases characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction. Despite these advances, there is a notable gap in the literature regarding direct evaluations of honokiol in RPE cells or in models of geographic atrophy, the advanced form of dry AMD. However, the consistency of its protective effects across hepatocytes, neurons, and retinal microvascular cells suggests a broad applicability that merits further exploration for AMD-related indications (Liu et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic potential of honokiol is intimately linked to its capacity to activate mitochondrial SIRT3, a member of the sirtuin family of NAD⁺-dependent deacetylases that serve as key regulators of mitochondrial biology. SIRT3 plays a pivotal role in maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis through the deacetylation and consequent activation of several mitochondrial enzymes implicated in antioxidant defense and metabolic regulation. Among its important targets is manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), an enzyme responsible for the dismutation of superoxide radicals into less reactive molecular species. By deacetylating MnSOD, SIRT3 increases its enzymatic activity, thereby reducing the levels of damaging ROS generated during oxidative phosphorylation (Liu et al., 2018; Trigun & Anamika, 2022). In parallel, SIRT3 is postulated to deacetylate isocitrate dehydrogenase 2 (IDH2), another mitochondrial enzyme critically involved in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and cellular redox balance, although direct evidence for IDH2 deacetylation in the honokiol context is less extensively documented in the current literature. Nevertheless, the hypothesis posits that deacetylation of IDH2 would further contribute to the reduction of mitochondrial ROS, suggesting a dual mechanism through which SIRT3 activation could ameliorate oxidative damage (Tyagi & Pugazhenthi, 2023; Zhang et al., 2020).

In addition to these direct deacetylation events, honokiol-induced SIRT3 activation has been associated with the modulation of several signaling cascades. Notably, SIRT3 activation by honokiol has been correlated with increased levels of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2), a master regulator of the cellular antioxidant response (Liu et al., 2018). The upregulation of Nrf2 can lead to the transcriptional activation of a spectrum of antioxidant enzymes, thereby reinforcing the intracellular capacity to neutralize ROS. Furthermore, SIRT3 activation influences mitochondrial biogenesis via upregulation of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC1α) and the forkhead box O3a (FoxO3a) pathway, which not only supports energy production but also promotes the maintenance of mitochondrial integrity under stress conditions (Trigun & Anamika, 2022). Evidence from neurotoxicity models demonstrates that honokiol can modulate these pathways, leading to improved mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and reduced apoptosis (Trigun & Anamika, 2022; Tyagi & Pugazhenthi, 2023).

Given the well-documented role of SIRT3 in various tissues, the proposed mechanism in RPE cells for dry AMD centers on the hypothesis that honokiol, by enhancing SIRT3 activity, will lead to the deacetylation of MnSOD and IDH2. In RPE cells, which are known to suffer from hyperacetylation-driven mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD, such deacetylation is expected to result in the restoration of enzymatic antioxidant defenses. This, in turn, would mitigate mitochondrial ROS accumulation, thereby stabilizing Δψm and supporting cellular viability under conditions of chronic oxidative stress—a central pathogenic mechanism in geographic atrophy (Liu et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2024). The detailed molecular interactions between honokiol and SIRT3 remain an active area of research, but the cumulative evidence supports a model wherein honokiol binding enhances the enzymatic activity of SIRT3, leading to downstream deacetylation events that ultimately preserve mitochondrial function (Trigun & Anamika, 2022; Tyagi & Pugazhenthi, 2023).

Expected Effect:  
For the proposed application in dry AMD, the expected effect of honokiol in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells is multi-faceted. Primarily, upon exposure to honokiol, one would anticipate activation of SIRT3 within the mitochondria of RPE cells. This activation is expected to promote the deacetylation of critical mitochondrial proteins—including MnSOD and, by extension, IDH2—thereby enhancing their enzymatic activities. The deacetylation of MnSOD is particularly vital, as it increases the dismutation of superoxide radicals, thus reducing the levels of ROS that are known to drive RPE cell dysfunction and death in the context of dry AMD (Liu et al., 2018; Trigun & Anamika, 2022).

In addition to the direct antioxidant effects mediated by MnSOD, the activation of SIRT3 is also expected to trigger a broader mitochondrial protective response. Upregulation of PGC1α and activation of FoxO3a—both of which have been observed in various cellular models after honokiol treatment—would stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis and contribute to the maintenance of the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) (Trigun & Anamika, 2022). A stabilized Δψm is critical in preventing the cascade of events leading to mitochondrial permeability transition and subsequent apoptosis, thereby preserving RPE cell function. Evidence from diabetic retinal microvascular injury models supports the notion that honokiol can indeed preserve Δψm in cells under oxidative stress, suggesting that similar protective mechanisms may be harnessed in RPE cells affected by geographic atrophy (Shi et al., 2024).

Furthermore, the activation of antioxidant transcriptional programs through increased Nrf2 levels may synergize with the direct effects on mitochondrial proteins. Enhanced Nrf2 activity would lead to the upregulation of a suite of antioxidant enzymes and stress response proteins, further bolstering the capacity of RPE cells to handle oxidative insults. This integrative response is expected to reduce the accumulation of mtROS, which is a key mediator of cellular senescence and dysfunction in the aging retina (Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020). Ultimately, the net effect in the assay is predicted to be an improvement in cellular viability and function following oxidative stress, as measured by assays of ROS production, Δψm stability, and overall cell survival. Such outcomes would validate the potential of honokiol to counteract the hyperacetylation-driven mitochondrial defects observed in donor RPE cells from patients with dry AMD (Liu et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of honokiol as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is supported by a convergence of biochemical, cellular, and animal model data that demonstrate its capacity to activate mitochondrial SIRT3 and promote deacetylation of key antioxidant enzymes. On the strength side, honokiol is a well-characterized natural compound with a long history of therapeutic use in traditional medicine and has been shown to exert protective effects across multiple cell types, including hepatocytes, neurons, and retinal microvascular cells. Its ability to enhance SIRT3 activity is particularly compelling given the central role of SIRT3 in preserving mitochondrial function and reducing oxidative stress—a pathogenic hallmark in dry AMD and its advanced form, geographic atrophy (Liu et al., 2018; Trigun & Anamika, 2022; Shi et al., 2024). Moreover, the compound’s lipophilic structure and ability to cross biological barriers further enhance its appeal as a candidate for treating diseases that require delivery to the retinal layers (Faysal et al., 2023).

From a mechanistic standpoint, honokiol’s actions have been well delineated across several experimental models. The documented deacetylation of MnSOD, along with the inferred deacetylation of IDH2, provides a solid biochemical foundation for the proposed mechanism of action in RPE cells. The downstream effects—involving the activation of transcription factors such as Nrf2, FoxO3a, and the upregulation of PGC1α—offer additional layers of protection by promoting mitochondrial biogenesis, energy production, and an enhanced antioxidant response (Trigun & Anamika, 2022; Liu et al., 2018). These multi-dimensional actions are likely to be advantageous in the context of dry AMD, a condition that results from an interplay of oxidative stress, inflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
ZLN005 (MedChemExpress HY-100726) is a synthetic small-molecule compound that belongs to the benzimidazole class. Benzimidazole derivatives have a long history in medicinal chemistry for their wide-ranging biological activities, including antihelminthic, anti-inflammatory, and metabolic modulating effects. In the case of ZLN005, it has been identified specifically as a selective transcriptional activator of peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator‐1 alpha (PGC-1α), a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defense. The synthesis and chemical derivation of ZLN005, although not detailed exhaustively in the provided literature, follow typical synthetic protocols for benzimidazole compounds, which often involve the condensation of o-phenylenediamine with carboxylic acid derivatives to yield a benzimidazole core. This structural class is known not only for its high affinity to various protein targets but also for favorable pharmacokinetic properties that have motivated its use in drug development efforts. Several studies have demonstrated that ZLN005 effectively induces PGC-1α expression in various cell types, including skeletal muscle and particularly the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis (Satish et al., 2018). Its assignment under the benzimidazole class further suggests that ZLN005 may share common metabolic and pharmacological features with other compounds in the same class, which have been employed in different therapeutic areas, supporting its potential for repurposing in ocular disorders such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Sun et al., 2018; Bleckwehl et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Initially, ZLN005 emerged from screening studies designed to identify small molecules that could stimulate PGC-1α expression. Early research in cellular models demonstrated that ZLN005 enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and upregulates the expression of downstream oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and antioxidant genes, which in turn improves mitochondrial health and overall cellular energy metabolism (Satish et al., 2018). In skeletal muscle and hepatic cells, for example, treatment with ZLN005 was associated with increased basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates, an increase in spare respiratory capacity, and a concomitant improvement in glucose uptake and cellular ATP levels (Satish et al., 2018). Such characteristics have spurred interest in its therapeutic application beyond metabolic diseases to conditions where mitochondrial dysfunction is a central pathogenic factor.

Notably, several groups have investigated ZLN005 in the context of retinal diseases. Preclinical studies using ARPE-19 cells—a well-accepted human RPE cell line—demonstrated that ZLN005 markedly upregulates PGC-1α expression and its associated transcription factors and antioxidant enzymes. These investigations have shown that ZLN005 can confer significant protection against oxidative stress-induced cell death when cells are exposed to prooxidative agents such as hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL) and sodium iodate (NaIO₃) (Satish et al., 2018). Although ZLN005 has not yet undergone extensive clinical evaluation specifically for dry AMD, its robust activity in stimulating mitochondrial function and providing cytoprotection in RPE models forms a compelling rationale for its repurposing. Studies in other systems, including cardiomyocytes and skeletal muscle, support its therapeutic use in settings of bioenergetic decline and oxidative damage, which are hallmarks of many age-related degenerative diseases (Ma et al., 2023; Moradi, 2022). However, it should be noted that many of the studies exploring ZLN005 for ocular purposes have been in vitro, and while they present an optimistic scenario, further in vivo animal studies and careful pharmacokinetic analyses in ocular tissues are needed before clinical application in AMD can be considered (Satish et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
The pharmacological efficacy of ZLN005 is tightly linked to its mechanism of action as an activator of PGC-1α. PGC-1α is a transcriptional coactivator that regulates a myriad of genes implicated in energy metabolism, mitochondrial biogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, and antioxidant protection. In RPE cells—where the maintenance of a high mitochondrial integrity is crucial for visual function—the expression of PGC-1α is fundamental to mitigating oxidative stress and maintaining metabolic homeostasis (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Iacovelli et al., 2016). ZLN005 increases the expression levels of PGC-1α by enhancing its transcription, culminating in the upregulation of a host of downstream target genes. This includes key mitochondrial genes such as ATP50, COX4, COX5b, and NDUFB5, all of which are involved in oxidative phosphorylation and energy production (Satish et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025).

At the molecular level, ZLN005 promotes the transcriptional program by potentially modulating AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) activity, a well-known regulator of PGC-1α function. The compound’s facilitation of PGC-1α nuclear translocation and its catalytic coactivation leads to the stimulation of mitochondrial replication and repair processes, thereby increasing mitochondrial mass and mtDNA copy number (Satish et al., 2018). In parallel, the upregulation of PGC-1α by ZLN005 induces the expression of several endogenous antioxidant enzymes, including superoxide dismutases (SOD1 and SOD2) and mitochondrial thioredoxin 2 (TXN2). This cascade of events enhances the cellular capacity to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS), thus lowering mitochondrial superoxide production and reducing the levels of oxidative stress markers such as 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), a product of lipid peroxidation frequently associated with degenerative retinal changes (Satish et al., 2018).

Furthermore, ZLN005 appears to improve overall mitochondrial bioenergetics. It has been observed to increase both basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates (OCR) in RPE cells, indicating an enhanced capacity for ATP synthesis under both steady-state and stress conditions (Satish et al., 2018). The compound also augments the spare respiratory capacity, which is critical for cellular survival when faced with acute energy demands during oxidative stress. Such improvements in mitochondrial function are directly relevant to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, where RPE cells experience an energy deficit due to progressive mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic oxidative injury (Felszeghy et al., 2019). Additionally, by upregulating PGC-1α, ZLN005 may indirectly influence other cellular processes, including autophagy and lipid metabolism, both of which are altered in the aging RPE and contribute to the formation of drusen—the hallmark deposits seen in dry AMD (Zhou et al., 2024).

It is important to emphasize that the protective effects of ZLN005 are markedly dependent on the presence of functional PGC-1α. Experiments in which PGC-1α expression was silenced in RPE cells resulted in a significant loss of the cytoprotective benefits conferred by ZLN005, underscoring the compound’s mechanism-specific action (Satish et al., 2018). Parallel studies in non-ocular cell types, such as skeletal muscle myotubes and alveolar epithelial cells, have further supported its role in enhancing mitochondrial function and regulating oxidative stress through similar molecular pathways (Zhang et al., 2013; Bleckwehl et al., 2025). Thus, the molecular interactions initiated by ZLN005—ranging from the activation of PGC-1α to the subsequent stimulation of antioxidant enzymes and mitochondrial biogenesis—form the crux of its therapeutic utility, specifically in countering the bioenergetic decline characteristic of dry AMD.

Given the central involvement of mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the therapeutic hypothesis for ZLN005 is that its activation of PGC-1α in retinal pigment epithelial cells will restore mitochondrial homeostasis and augment cellular antioxidant defenses. This includes an increase in mtDNA copy number and the expression of mitochondrial genes that are essential for optimal oxidative phosphorylation performance (Satish et al., 2018). As mitochondrial function improves, RPE cells should exhibit higher basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates, indicative of an improved metabolic profile and increased capacity to generate ATP under both normal and stress conditions (Satish et al., 2018).

The antioxidative effects of ZLN005 are also expected to manifest in augmented levels of enzymes such as SOD1, SOD2, and TXN2, which collectively enhance the cell’s capability to scavenge reactive oxygen species. These biochemical events are critical because the accumulation of oxidative stress in RPE cells, driven by chronic exposure to high levels of ROS, is a significant contributor to cell degeneration in dry AMD (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Blasiak et al., 2021). With improved mitochondrial function and reduced oxidative stress, it is anticipated that ZLN005 treatment will lead to a decrease in the accumulation of oxidative damage markers like 4-HNE, thereby mitigating processes that lead to RPE cell apoptosis and the subsequent photoreceptor degeneration observed in dry AMD (Blasiak et al., 2021; Iacovelli et al., 2016).

Moreover, in vitro studies have demonstrated that under conditions of experimentally induced oxidative stress with agents such as H₂O₂, ox-LDL, or NaIO₃, ZLN005 significantly reduces cell death in ARPE-19 cells (Satish et al., 2018). Therefore, the expected effect of ZLN005 in the proposed assay is a robust cytoprotective response in RPE cells. This would be characterized by improved cell viability, restoration of mitochondrial respiratory function, and a reduction in stress-induced apoptotic markers—a constellation of effects that directly addresses the bioenergetic and oxidative challenges underlying dry AMD (Satish et al., 2018). Additionally, since PGC-1α is known to regulate lipid metabolism and prevent lipid droplet accumulation—a process that may be linked to the formation of drusen in the AMD retina—the activation of PGC-1α by ZLN005 could also have beneficial effects on lipid handling within the RPE (Zhou et al., 2024; Iacovelli et al., 2016). A comprehensive evaluation of ZLN005 reveals several compelling strengths as well as notable weaknesses that should be weighed in the context of repurposing it for the treatment of dry AMD. One of the principal strengths of ZLN005 lies in its well-defined mechanism of action. By selectively activating PGC-1α, ZLN005 directly targets the mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress that are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. The upregulation of PGC-1α leads to improvements in mitochondrial biogenesis, an increase in the expression of mitochondrial OXPHOS genes, and the enhancement of antioxidant defenses—all factors that are critically compromised in the diseased RPE (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Blasiak et al., 2021). This mechanistic rationale is further supported by in vitro studies showing that ZLN005 can effectively reduce prooxidant-induced cell death and improve mitochondrial respiratory parameters such as basal respiration, maximal respiration, and spare respiratory capacity (Satish et al., 2018).

Achieving a robust activation of PGC-1α is particularly attractive because it addresses both the cellular energy production and ROS management simultaneously, which are two critical determinants of RPE cell survival and function (Iacovelli et al., 2016; Rosales et al., 2019).

Furthermore, the specificity of ZLN005’s action has been validated by studies where the loss of PGC-1α abrogated its cytoprotective effects, underscoring that its efficacy is tightly linked to the activation of this pivotal regulatory pathway (Satish et al., 2018). This is an important consideration because it suggests that the therapeutic effects can be fine-tuned by modulating the expression or activity of PGC-1α. In the context of dry AMD, where PGC-1α levels are often diminished or dysregulated, the targeted upregulation provided by ZLN005 offers a focused therapeutic intervention.

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and challenges remain. Foremost, the majority of the supportive evidence for ZLN005’s efficacy in protecting RPE cells has been generated through in vitro studies using cell lines such as ARPE-19. While these models are indispensable for preliminary evaluation, they do not fully recapitulate the complex in vivo environment of the human retina, and the translatability of these effects into clinical benefit remains to be demonstrated (Satish et al., 2018). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin (also known as sirolimus and available as Abcam #ab120224) is a naturally occurring macrolide compound originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus. It belongs to the class of macrocyclic lactones and is known for its potent inhibitory effects on the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). This compound has been extensively used in various contexts such as immunosuppression, cancer therapy, and more recently, as a tool to modulate autophagy in age-related degenerative diseases. In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction and dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), rapamycin is being explored as a repurposed therapeutic candidate with the hypothesis that mTORC1 inhibition will enhance both general autophagy and selective mitophagy. This clearance of reactive oxygen species (ROS)–generating, damaged mitochondria may alleviate oxidative stress, reduce the accumulation of toxic lipofuscin compounds (including A2E), and ultimately slow the progression of dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, rapamycin was first discovered for its potent immunosuppressive properties and later developed for use in preventing transplant rejection and certain cancers. Its ability to inhibit mTORC1 has made it a valuable tool in research related to aging and neurodegeneration. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its effectiveness in modulating autophagy and protecting cellular integrity under stress conditions, particularly in the retinal environment. In animal models of retinal degeneration and even some early clinical trials, rapamycin was shown to reduce the accumulation of autofluorescent granules and inflammatory cytokines in the RPE, which are both hallmarks of dry AMD pathology (Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022). Notably, rapamycin has been administered via diverse routes, including intravitreal and subconjunctival injections, in attempts to treat geographic atrophy or other dry AMD phenotypes, although the clinical outcomes have been mixed. For example, clinical trials such as those referenced in studies with identifiers NCT00766649 and NCT01445548 demonstrated that while rapamycin was generally safe and well-tolerated in ocular applications, its efficacy in slowing down the progression of geographic atrophy and improving visual acuity remained limited (National Eye Institute, 2008; National Eye Institute, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These historical findings highlight both the promise and the challenges associated with translating rapamycin’s mechanistic benefits into robust clinical outcomes for dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary mechanism of rapamycin involves the formation of a complex with the immunophilin FKBP12. This complex binds to mTORC1 and inhibits its kinase activity, leading to a decrease in the phosphorylation of downstream targets such as ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K) and the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 (4EBP1). Under normal circumstances, active mTORC1 suppresses autophagy by phosphorylating these targets, which in turn prevents the formation of autophagosomes. By inhibiting mTORC1, rapamycin effectively removes this blockade, thereby promoting the induction of autophagy as evidenced by increased conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II and clearance of the autophagic substrate p62 (Zhang et al., 2015).

Within retinal pigment epithelial cells, this induction of autophagy is particularly important. RPE cells are responsible for the phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments; a process that generates large amounts of cellular debris and metabolic byproducts such as lipofuscin. In dry AMD, impaired autophagic flux leads to the accumulation of these compounds, which, in turn, contributes to oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Rapamycin’s inhibition of mTORC1 not only enhances general autophagy but also promotes selective mitochondrial clearance (mitophagy). Key players in the mitophagy pathway include the serine/threonine kinase PINK1 and the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin, both of which accumulate on depolarized mitochondria and signal their removal via autophagic mechanisms. By stimulating this PINK1/Parkin pathway, rapamycin enhances the clearance of damaged, ROS-generating mitochondria, thus preserving overall mitochondrial health (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).

Additionally, rapamycin’s downstream effects include activation of transcription factors such as TFEB, which regulates lysosomal biogenesis and further enhances the autophagic process. This dual action—promoting both autophagy and lysosomal function—helps to mitigate the accumulation of toxic aggregates such as lipofuscin and A2E in RPE, therefore reducing oxidative stress and inflammation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). Through these biochemical interactions, rapamycin establishes a cellular environment that is more capable of dealing with metabolic challenges and oxidative damage, both of which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Chang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed hypothesis, the administration of rapamycin in RPE cells is expected to result in a cascade of beneficial cellular events. In our proposed assay, rapamycin is anticipated to inhibit mTORC1 activity, leading to a measurable increase in autophagic flux. This will be evident from the enhanced lipidation of LC3-II, the clearance of p62 (an autophagy adaptor protein that accumulates when autophagy is impaired), and the activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway in response to oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2015).

The specific clearance of damaged mitochondria is particularly critical in the RPE, where mitochondrial dysfunction is a significant contributor to the generation of reactive oxygen species and subsequent cellular damage. By removing these dysfunctional mitochondria, rapamycin is expected to reduce intracellular ROS levels and thereby lower oxidative stress, a driving force in AMD pathology. In parallel, the enhanced autophagic degradation of accumulated lipofuscin and the toxic fluorophore A2E is predicted to further limit the inflammatory and apoptotic cascades triggered by these compounds, thus preserving RPE cell viability and function (Zhang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2025).

Moreover, the expression of PINK1 and Parkin in RPE cells has been well documented, and their activation is indicative of mitophagic turnover. Their proper functioning is a key determinant in mitochondrial quality control, and rapamycin is expected to potentiate this process, ensuring that mitochondria remain healthy and capable of maintaining cellular energy production and reducing the risk of cell death (Pinelli et al., 2025; Hyttinen et al., 2018). Given that impaired mitochondrial function and the resulting energy production deficits are central to the progression of dry AMD, the expected outcomes from rapamycin treatment would include not only a reduction in oxidative stress markers but also improvements in mitochondrial dynamics and overall cellular homeostasis. Such effects would ideally be reflected in functional assays measuring cell viability, mitochondrial respiration, and reductions in inflammatory cytokine production (Zhang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In our comprehensive evaluation of rapamycin as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and potential weaknesses emerge that warrant careful consideration. One of the key strengths of rapamycin lies in its well-characterized mechanism of action and its ability to broadly modulate autophagy through mTORC1 inhibition. Preclinical studies have repeatedly demonstrated that rapamycin can induce autophagic flux, leading to the clearance of cellular debris and damaged mitochondria in RPE cells. This is particularly compelling given the central role of impaired autophagy in the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, which are major pathological features of dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018). The dual-action mechanism—enhancing both autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis via TFEB activation—further supports its potential in addressing multiple aspects of the disease pathology, from oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction to inflammation and cellular senescence (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Another strength is the substantial body of preclinical evidence showing that rapamycin not only stimulates autophagy but also improves mitochondrial function. The activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway is particularly relevant since these proteins are indispensable for mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control. By facilitating the removal of ROS-generating, damaged mitochondria, rapamycin could directly impact the cellular energy balance and reduce damaging oxidative insults in the RPE, which is pivotal for maintaining retinal health (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).

Despite its promising mechanistic profile, several significant challenges remain. Clinical studies investigating the use of rapamycin for AMD have yielded mixed results. While the drug has been shown to be safe and tolerable in ocular applications, several clinical trials, such as those involving subconjunctival or intravitreal administration, did not demonstrate significant efficacy in halting the progression of geographic atrophy or improving visual acuity. In some instances, adverse effects such as decreased visual acuity and retinal thinning have been observed, raising concerns about the balance between therapeutic benefit and potential retinal toxicity (National Eye Institute, 2008; National Eye Institute, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These mixed clinical findings underscore the complexity of modulating mTORC1 in a disease with multifactorial etiology and suggest that the optimal dosage, treatment duration, and patient selection criteria still require refinement.

Furthermore, the variability in response among different donor-derived RPE cells—where only about 50% of AMD donor samples responded positively to rapamycin in certain studies—points to potential issues regarding patient heterogeneity and the need for personalized therapeutic regimens (Ebeling et al., 2020). This heterogeneity may be due to differences in the intrinsic capacity for autophagy, genetic variations affecting mitochondrial quality control, or the extent of existing cellular damage. Such variability complicates the development of standardized treatment protocols and could limit the broad applicability of rapamycin unless predictive biomarkers of response are identified (Zhang et al., 2015).

Another important consideration is the dual nature of autophagy in the context of RPE health. While enhancing autophagy can provide protective benefits by clearing damaged organelles and reducing oxidative stress, excessive autophagic flux under certain stress conditions might paradoxically contribute to cell death. This is especially relevant in advanced stages of dry AMD, where cellular stress is severe and prolonged autophagy induction might tip the balance toward detrimental outcomes rather than recovery (Chang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2019). In addition, the potential for rapamycin to interfere with beneficial mTOR signaling under specific conditions (for example, when mTOR activity supports survival pathways via growth factors such as nerve growth factor) further complicates its use, as evidenced by reports that observed mixed effects on retinal ganglion cell survival in different pathological contexts (Wang et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2021).

The delivery method and pharmacokinetics of rapamycin also represent important variables. While nanotechnology-based delivery systems—such as synthetic high-density lipoprotein nanoparticles—have shown promise in achieving more targeted and sustained delivery of rapamycin to the RPE (Mei et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2021), these strategies require further translational studies to assess their safety, efficacy, and scalability in clinical settings. Moreover, the risk of systemic side effects, including metabolic toxicities and immunosuppression, despite the generally favorable ocular safety profile observed in trials, necessitates caution in developing rapamycin-based therapies for chronic conditions like AMD (Wang et al., 2022).

In summary, rapamycin presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its robust mechanism of action—specifically, its capacity to inhibit mTORC1, thereby stimulating both general autophagy and the selective removal of damaged mitochondria via the PINK1/Parkin pathway. Preclinical evidence strongly supports the idea that such modulation can reduce oxidative stress, clear toxic accumulations like lipofuscin/A2E, and ultimately preserve mitochondrial and RPE cellular function (Zhang et al., 2015; Hyttinen et al., 2018). However, the translation of these benefits into clinical improvements remains uncertain, with several trials indicating that while rapamycin is safe and modulates cellular pathways implicated in AMD, its clinical efficacy in terms of preserving visual function has not been conclusively demonstrated. The heterogeneity in patient responses, the potential for adverse outcomes related to excessive autophagy, and the challenges in optimizing dosing and delivery all represent significant hurdles. These considerations suggest that while rapamycin is a promising candidate worthy of further investigation, its ultimate role in the treatment paradigm for dry AMD will depend on our ability to refine treatment regimens, develop predictive biomarkers for patient selection, and perhaps combine mTOR modulation with complementary therapeutic strategies that reinforce its protective effects while mitigating its risks (Wang et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2019).

Given the cumulative evidence, our overall recommendation is to continue exploring rapamycin as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, but with a strategic focus on further preclinical investigations that address the dose–response relationships in donor-derived RPE models and the development of advanced drug delivery systems. It will also be important to design future clinical trials with stratified patient populations and integrated biomarkers that can help identify responders. This iterative approach could eventually lead to a carefully balanced regimen where rapamycin’s autophagy-enhancing properties are harnessed to maintain retinal integrity while avoiding the pitfalls of over-inhibition or systemic toxicity. In essence, the promise of rapamycin in modulating autophagy to improve mitochondrial health and reduce oxidative stress in RPE cells is clear at the molecular and cellular levels, but translating these benefits into a safe and effective therapy for dry AMD will require overcoming substantial clinical challenges (Mei et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Strengths of rapamycin include its well-established mechanism of action, the significant supportive preclinical data demonstrating improvements in autophagic flux and mitochondrial clearance in RPE models, and its potential to address several key pathological features of dry AMD simultaneously. Weaknesses include the mixed clinical trial outcomes to date, the potential for adverse effects in certain contexts (including decreased visual acuity and retinal thinning), and the observed heterogeneity in therapeutic response among different patient samples. These factors highlight the importance of further mechanistic studies and carefully controlled clinical trials. Overall, rapamycin remains one of the more mechanistically promising candidates for repurposing in dry AMD, yet its future success will depend on how effectively we can tailor its delivery and dosing to maximize protective effects while minimizing risks in the vulnerable RPE of AMD patients (Niu et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022).

In conclusion, rapamycin’s role as an mTORC1 inhibitor with the capacity to induce autophagy and mitophagy presents an exciting therapeutic avenue for addressing the complex pathology of dry AMD. By alleviating the buildup of toxic metabolites and preserving mitochondrial health in RPE cells, rapamycin could potentially slow disease progression and preserve vision. Nonetheless, the balance between benefit and adverse effects remains delicate, and further research is essential to elucidate how best to leverage rapamycin’s molecular actions in a clinically meaningful way. This comprehensive review supports the continued investigation of rapamycin as a candidate for dry AMD therapy, provided that subsequent studies can address the highlighted challenges and refine the therapeutic strategy to achieve consistent, positive clinical outcomes (Mei et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BAM15 (Sigma-Aldrich SML1888) is a synthetic, lipophilic mitochondrial uncoupling agent that was discovered and subsequently optimized to achieve a mild protonophoric effect on the inner mitochondrial membrane. As a member of the mitochondrial uncoupler class, BAM15 functions by facilitating proton leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane, thereby dissipating the proton motive force (Δψm) in a controlled manner. The key feature of this compound is its ability to reduce electron leakage from the electron transport chain (ETC) at complexes I and III without completely abolishing ATP synthesis. This is achieved by diminishing the mitochondrial membrane potential enough to lower the rate of superoxide generation while still maintaining sufficient ATP production for cellular energetics. Its synthetic nature and lipophilicity enable BAM15 to permeate the mitochondrial membrane rapidly, a property that distinguishes it from earlier, more toxic uncouplers such as 2,4-dinitrophenol or FCCP. The chemical architecture of BAM15 has been tailored to offer high mitochondrial targeting efficiency and a more favorable safety profile compared to traditional uncouplers. Mitochondrial uncouplers have been historically investigated in various research settings ranging from metabolic studies to neurodegenerative disease models, where their capacity to modulate bioenergetics and reduce oxidative stress has been exploited (Xiong et al., 2023; Jang et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Although BAM15 has not yet been directly tested in clinical settings for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), there exists a robust foundational literature supporting the therapeutic targeting of mitochondrial dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells. Numerous studies have detailed that mitochondrial defects in RPE are a central mediator of AMD pathogenesis, with evidence pointing to disrupted mitochondrial architecture, decreased mitochondrial mass, and increased mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) damage in human donor tissues (Fisher & Ferrington, 2018). In this context, mitochondrial uncouplers have been explored experimentally to compensate for excessive electron leakage and overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS). In vitro and in vivo studies using other uncoupling agents such as FCCP have demonstrated that inducing mild uncoupling can stimulate protective mitochondrial quality control pathways including fission, fusion, and mitophagy; these processes have been shown to restore bioenergetic balance in diseased RPE cells (Fisher, 2022; Fisher et al., 2022). In the broader field of drug development, mitochondrial-targeted compounds such as MTP-131 (Elamipretide) have even advanced into early-phase clinical trials for AMD and related retinal neurodegenerative diseases, establishing a strong precedent for targeting the mitochondrial compartment in ocular pathologies (Cousins, 2015; Butcher, 2022). Meanwhile, BAM15 itself has demonstrated therapeutic potential in other disease models including obesity, sepsis, and neurodegeneration, wherein its mild uncoupling properties reduced mitochondrial oxidative stress and improved metabolic and inflammatory parameters (Xiong et al., 2023). However, despite these encouraging attributes and the compelling rationale derived from the role of mtROS in AMD, BAM15’s usage in the context of ocular diseases, particularly dry AMD, remains largely untested to date (Jang et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
BAM15 exerts its effects by acting as a protonophore that facilitates proton translocation across the mitochondrial inner membrane. Under normal conditions, the electron transport chain generates a high proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis; however, this gradient is also responsible for the partial leakage of electrons, which react with molecular oxygen to form superoxide radicals. BAM15’s mechanism is predicated on “mild uncoupling,” which entails a limited dissipation of the proton motive force to reduce the probability of electron slippage at complexes I and III without compromising the entirety of ATP generation. At the molecular level, BAM15 inserts into the mitochondrial inner membrane where its lipophilic and protonophoric properties allow it to shuttle protons from the intermembrane space back into the matrix. This process effectively lowers the mitochondrial membrane potential, diminishing the driving force for electron leakage and concomitant ROS formation (Xiong et al., 2023; Jang et al., 2025).  

Furthermore, BAM15’s action is linked with secondary effects on key intracellular signaling pathways. The reduction in ATP production, while carefully moderated, can activate AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a critical sensor of cellular energy status. Upon activation, AMPK upregulates peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α), which is instrumental in driving mitochondrial biogenesis and enhancing overall mitochondrial quality control. These processes are particularly relevant in the context of AMD, where impaired mitophagy and mitochondrial turnover have been well documented in RPE cells (Fisher, 2022). BAM15 has also been shown in other tissues to reduce the release of mtDNA into the cytoplasm—a phenomenon that ordinarily triggers NLRP3 inflammasome activation and the subsequent production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Xiong et al., 2023). With reduced mtROS production and lower inflammasome activation, BAM15 could potentially ameliorate chronic inflammatory responses that exacerbate cellular degeneration in the RPE. Importantly, the uncoupling induced by BAM15 is dose-dependent; the compound must be delivered at concentrations that ensure only a modest reduction in Δψm, thus allowing ATP production to remain functionally intact while still mitigating the adverse effects of excessive ROS (Xiong et al., 2023; Jang et al., 2025).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed experimental paradigm focusing on chronic stress conditions typical of dry AMD, BAM15 is anticipated to exert several beneficial effects on RPE cells. Fundamentally, the agent is hypothesized to lower mitochondrial ROS production by reducing the proton motive force sufficiently to minimize electron leakage without precipitating a full collapse of the energy-transducing gradient. In primary RPE cultures, where mitochondrial dysfunction and bioenergetic deficits have already been documented as key contributors to disease progression (Fisher & Ferrington, 2018; Fisher, 2022), BAM15 is expected to normalize several bioenergetic parameters. The effects should include improved basal respiration and maximal respiratory capacity, as well as better spare respiratory capacity, indicative of a healthier mitochondrial network capable of handling metabolic stress.  

Reduction of ROS levels would likely lead to a decrease in oxidative modifications of lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids within the mitochondria. Given that mtDNA damage is a well-established marker of AMD severity and has been implicated in triggering inflammatory cascades via inflammasome activation, a reduction in mtDNA damage—and its consequent release—would be a direct cellular benefit of BAM15 application (Fisher, 2022). As studies in AMD have shown that mtROS and mtDNA release can prime inflammasome development and lead to the secretion of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, BAM15’s action could diminish these pro-inflammatory signals. This anti-inflammatory effect is particularly crucial in the context of dry AMD, where chronic sterile inflammation contributes to retinal pigment epithelium loss and subsequent photoreceptor degeneration (Fisher, 2022).  

Moreover, the activation of AMPK and subsequent engagement of PGC-1α-driven mitochondrial biogenesis may help re-establish cellular homeostasis in RPE cells that have been compromised by prolonged oxidative stress. The fine-tuning of mitochondrial quality control—through enhanced mitophagy and the removal of damaged mitochondria—is expected to contribute to overall cell survival and to slow the progression of AMD pathology. In an in vitro assay, one would anticipate a measurable decrease in ROS levels, reduced markers of inflammasome activation, improved mitochondrial morphology, and increased expression of genes involved in mitochondrial repair and biogenesis. Since the RPE expresses a full complement of metabolic regulators (including AMPK and the NLRP3 inflammasome components) and is highly susceptible to oxidative stress due to its role in photoreceptor support, the expected effect of BAM15 aligns well with the molecular pathology observed in AMD (Fisher & Ferrington, 2018; Fisher, 2022).

The overall evaluation of BAM15 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals several strengths but also underscores significant areas requiring further investigation. One of the chief strengths of BAM15 is its mechanism of mild mitochondrial uncoupling, which is theoretically suited to ameliorating the bioenergetic deficits and oxidative stress characteristic of AMD. The extensive literature on mitochondrial dysfunction in the retinal pigment epithelium supports the idea that reducing mtROS production can have a direct, favorable impact on cell survival and function. Studies have repeatedly demonstrated that RPE cells from AMD donors exhibit compromised mitochondrial architecture, increased mtDNA damage, and heightened levels of ROS, all of which contribute to inflammasome activation and chronic inflammation (Fisher & Ferrington, 2018). Moreover, the activation of AMPK and the ensuing stimulation of mitochondrial biogenesis represent additional advantages because these processes are crucial for cellular recovery and long-term tissue homeostasis (Xiong et al., 2023; Jang et al., 2025).

Another notable strength lies in BAM15’s relatively favorable safety profile when compared to prototypical uncouplers. Early evidence from studies in hepatocytes, neurons, and other models suggests that BAM15 does not cause dramatic drops in ATP levels or induce significant cytotoxicity, provided that dosing is carefully controlled. This is particularly relevant for the RPE, a cell type with a high energy demand where excessive uncoupling could lead to unintended deleterious effects. In addition, the possibility that BAM15 could mitigate inflammasome activation by curtailing the release of mitochondrial DNA into the cytosol offers an attractive method for diminishing pro-inflammatory cascades known to drive AMD progression (Xiong et al., 2023; Jang et al., 2025).

Despite these advantages, several weaknesses must be acknowledged. Currently, there is a conspicuous lack of direct experimental evidence supporting the use of BAM15 in RPE cells or in in vivo models of dry AMD. While there is compelling rationale derived from studies in other tissues and disease models, the translation of these findings to the ocular environment remains unproven (Jang et al., 2025; Xiong et al., 2023). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:

Because of its synthetic origin, EUK-8 is both cost-effective and easily reproducible, making it an appealing candidate for repurposing in therapeutic areas where enhanced antioxidant defenses are required, such as in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rosenthal et al., 2011).
