Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Elamipretide (SS-31; D-Arg-2,6-dimethyl-Tyr-Lys-Phe-NH2) is a synthetic, C-terminally amidated tetrapeptide belonging to the Szeto–Schiller (SS) class of mitochondria-targeted peptides, originally discovered through structure–activity optimization of alternating cationic–aromatic motifs that confer high cell permeability and strong partitioning to the negatively charged inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) enriched in cardiolipin (CL) (Szeto & Schiller, 2011; Tung et al., 2025). Early work demonstrated that an aromatic–cationic design was sufficient to drive potent mitochondrial uptake and that dimethyltyrosine (Dmt) confers radical-scavenging chemistry while improving chemical stability; subnanomolar-to-nanomolar extracellular concentrations concentrate >1 μM at the IMM, yielding robust activity under oxidative stress in diverse cell types (Szeto & Schiller, 2011). SS-31 and related SS peptides were initially identified as potent inhibitors of mitochondrial swelling and oxidative cell death in intact cells and organs, with mechanistic clues pointing to direct interactions with cardiolipin-rich membranes and mitigation of ischemia–reperfusion injury (Szeto & Schiller, 2011; Szeto & Birk, 2014).

Mechanistically, elamipretide selectively binds CL in the IMM via electrostatic anchoring of its cationic residues to anionic phosphate headgroups and hydrophobic partitioning of its aromatic residues into the bilayer interfacial region; biophysical studies (NMR and molecular dynamics simulations) and binding quantitation to model CL-containing bilayers demonstrate CL dependence and saturable effects on bilayer surface electrostatics and lipid packing without destabilizing lamellar phases (Mitchell et al., 2019; Sabbah et al., 2025). Once bound, elamipretide modulates several biophysical and biochemical properties central to mitochondrial function: it down-tunes the negative surface potential of CL-rich membranes, increases CL self-association, reduces lateral lipid diffusivity, and increases lateral packing, changes that preserve cristae architecture and respiratory supercomplex organization under stress while suppressing cytochrome c peroxidase activity and CL oxidation (Sabbah et al., 2025). Collectively, these actions improve electron transfer efficiency, stabilize oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos) protein assemblies, reduce electron leak and reactive oxygen species (ROS), and preserve ATP synthesis capacity in dysfunctional mitochondria (Mitchell et al., 2022; Sabbah et al., 2025; Szeto & Birk, 2014). Importantly for retinal applications, elamipretide uptake is not dependent on mitochondrial membrane potential, supporting entry into depolarized or injured mitochondria—a feature often found in AMD RPE (Ji et al., 2021).

Elamipretide is therefore best classified as a CL-targeting, membrane-active mitochondrial therapeutic that acts primarily by modulating the physicochemical properties of CL-rich IMM domains and CL-dependent protein assemblies, rather than binding a single protein target, with downstream effects on respiratory supercomplex assembly, cytochrome c catalysis, electron-transport efficiency, ROS emission, and ATP production (Mitchell et al., 2019; Sabbah et al., 2025; Mitchell et al., 2022). Members of this class have been deployed across preclinical models of cardiac, skeletal muscle, renal, neurologic, and ocular dysfunction, and a substantial clinical program has tested elamipretide in primary mitochondrial disorders, cardiometabolic diseases, and ophthalmic indications including age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Sabbah et al., 2025; Tung et al., 2025). The drug is water-soluble, with a short elimination half-life on the order of ~2–4 hours in preclinical species and humans, and is administered systemically by daily subcutaneous injection in AMD studies at a nominal 40 mg dose; topical ocular delivery has also been explored preclinically and clinically (Szeto & Birk, 2014; Lenin et al., 2023; Guimaraes et al., 2022; Ji et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
The SS peptide class emerged from efforts to concentrate antioxidant and mitochondrial-protective chemistry directly at the IMM through cationic–aromatic motifs that target anionic phospholipids—principally cardiolipin—enabling inhibition of mitochondrial swelling, reduction of ROS emission, and protection from reperfusion injury in intact cells and organs; SS-31 in particular was estimated to concentrate ~5,000-fold in mitochondria and to inhibit lipid peroxidation, positioning it to prevent CL peroxidation in the IMM (Szeto & Schiller, 2011). These membrane-centric mechanisms rapidly translated into broad preclinical testing across organ systems, demonstrating improvements in OxPhos efficiency, ATP production, ROS control, and preservation of mitochondrial ultrastructure (cristae) in disease and aging models (Szeto & Birk, 2014; Mitchell et al., 2022).

Ocular and retinal applications came into focus as mitochondrial dysfunction in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptors was implicated as a driver of non-neovascular AMD, including reduced OxPhos, increased glycolytic shift, impaired mitophagy, structural cristae disorganization, and accumulation of damaged mitochondria in AMD donor RPE (Ferrington et al., 2020; Fisher, 2022; Fisher et al., 2022). In this context, elamipretide demonstrated several AMD-relevant preclinical effects. In a mouse model of dry AMD-like pathology, subcutaneous elamipretide reversed electroretinographic (ERG) deficits and improved clearance of sub-RPE deposits, corresponding to reversal of vision loss, consistent with activity at both the RPE/sub-RPE interface and photoreceptor function (Kim & Lad, 2021; Ji et al., 2021). In ApoE4 mice with diet-induced sub-RPE deposit formation linked to mitochondrial dysfunction, subcutaneous elamipretide reversed deposit formation, strengthening the mechanistic link to CL-dependent mitochondrial physiology in retinal tissues (Guimaraes et al., 2022). RPE-targeted cytoprotection has also been reported: elamipretide protected primary RPE and improved mitochondrial function in models of AMD and prevented persistent injury phenotypes induced by oxidative stressors such as hydroquinone in cultured RPE cells (Sabbah et al., 2025). Ex vivo and in vivo aging paradigms provide convergent support: in aged mice with visual impairments, elamipretide mitigated visual decline and normalized visual acuity and contrast sensitivity within two months, with delivery via topical eye drops producing effects comparable to subcutaneous injections; in RPE cultures from AMD donors, elamipretide improved RPE cell viability and mitochondrial function (Sabbah et al., 2025; Alam et al., 2020). In an RPE-specific SOD2 knockout model, daily topical elamipretide prevented RPE cell size increase consistent with reduced RPE cell death/senescence, further underscoring RPE-specific benefits (Tong et al., 2022). Additional retinal disease models support cross-indication activity: SS-31 restored visual function in a streptozotocin-induced mouse diabetic retinopathy model (Ferrington et al., 2020). Collectively, preclinical retinal evidence aligns with the hypothesized CL-centric rescue of mitochondrial function at the RPE and photoreceptor inner segments, preventing AMD-relevant cellular dysfunction and functional decline (Ji et al., 2021; Kim & Lad, 2021; Guimaraes et al., 2022).

Clinical development has included both topical and subcutaneous AMD studies. A phase I/II topical study enrolled 21 patients with diabetic macular edema (DME) and non-exudative intermediate AMD, demonstrating feasibility of ocular delivery; subsequent systemic AMD trials have been more extensively reported (Ji et al., 2021). The open-label, 24-week Phase 1 ReCLAIM study administered daily subcutaneous elamipretide (40 mg) to 40 patients with either non-central geographic atrophy (NCGA; n = 19) or high-risk drusen without GA (n = 21), reporting mean functional improvements: in the NCGA subgroup, +4.6 letters in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), +5.4 letters in low-luminance visual acuity (LLVA), and an approximate 25-letter gain in low-luminance reading acuity (LLRA), with a slower GA growth rate than historical natural history; in the high-risk drusen subgroup, mean gains were +3.6 (BCVA), +5.6 (LLVA), and ~15 (LLRA) (Kim & Lad, 2021). Safety was favorable, with no serious adverse events and general tolerability in intermediate AMD (Ji et al., 2021). A subsequent randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled Phase 2 trial (ReCLAIM-2) in ≥55-year-old patients with non-central GA tested daily subcutaneous elamipretide for 48 weeks; it did not meet primary endpoints on LL-BCVA and GA area, but elamipretide was associated with a 43% reduction in mean progression of total ellipsoid zone (EZ) attenuation and a 47% reduction in partial EZ attenuation versus placebo, with a post hoc analysis showing significant reductions and a higher proportion of patients achieving ≥2-line LL-BCVA gains, and a correlation between LL-BCVA change and change in total EZ attenuation (Sabbah et al., 2025). EZ attenuation is a clinically meaningful OCT marker that reflects photoreceptor integrity in mitochondria-rich inner segments and precedes GA and irreversible vision loss; thus, preservation of EZ is mechanistically consistent with the drug’s mitochondrial-protective intent and could represent an early biomarker of benefit (Sabbah et al., 2025). Additional summaries concur: the Phase 2 program reported negative primary endpoints but a structural OCT signal (slowed EZ degradation), warranting confirmatory studies with longer duration and functional correlates (Tung et al., 2025).

Beyond AMD, elamipretide has undergone extensive clinical evaluation in mitochondrial disorders (e.g., Barth syndrome), heart failure, ischemia–reperfusion contexts, and renal microvascular dysfunction, with mixed outcomes: many trials did not meet primary endpoints but reported improvements in mitochondrial bioenergetics, coupling, or patient-reported quality-of-life metrics, consistent with a class effect of improving mitochondrial physiology in vivo (Sabbah et al., 2025; Tung et al., 2025). Pharmacokinetically, elamipretide exhibits rapid distribution/elimination with elimination half-lives of ~2 hours in preclinical species and on the order of ~4 hours in humans, renal excretion of parent/metabolites, and ocular pharmacology indicating that topical dosing in rabbits achieves high anterior-chamber and periocular concentrations with nonzero penetration to the retina; this, together with murine aged-vision data, suggests both topical and systemic routes are viable for retinal targeting, although intraocular/vitreous levels after topical dosing may be low (Szeto & Birk, 2014; Alam et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
Elamipretide’s mechanism centers on high-affinity interaction with cardiolipin in the IMM and consequent modulation of membrane electrostatics, lipid organization, and CL-dependent protein complexes, leading to improved electron transport, reduced ROS production, and preserved ATP synthesis. Several convergent lines of evidence define this mechanism in molecular detail.

1) Cardiolipin-dependent binding and membrane electrostatics. SS-31/ELAM partitions into the interfacial leaflet of CL-containing bilayers with affinity proportional to surface charge, binding via electrostatic interactions of its basic residues with CL phosphates and via hydrophobic interactions of its aromatic residues with lipid acyl chains; no measurable binding occurs to neutral phosphatidylcholine membranes (Mitchell et al., 2019). NMR and molecular dynamics identify two binding modes—“peptide approach” (electrostatic anchoring) and “peptide burial” (aromatic partition)—producing a controlled down-tuning of the negative surface potential, increased CL self-association, and altered lateral packing/diffusivity without disrupting lamellar bilayer integrity (Sabbah et al., 2025). The net effect is to modulate ion distribution at the membrane interface (e.g., divalent cations such as Ca2+), stabilize bilayer structure under electrochemical stress, and resist electroporation-like damage, thereby preserving IMM properties under stress (Mitchell et al., 2019; Tamucci et al., 2025). These membrane-physical changes occur without altering the transmembrane potential per se, consistent with a surface–electrostatics mechanism that adjusts protein–lipid interactions and lipid–lipid organization (Sabbah et al., 2025).

2) Respiratory complexes, supercomplexes, and cytochrome c. Cardiolipin stabilizes respiratory complexes and promotes assembly of supercomplexes to optimize electron transport; elamipretide binding to CL supports supercomplex assembly, increases coupling efficiency, and reduces electron leak and ROS while enhancing ATP synthesis (Mitchell et al., 2022; Sabbah et al., 2025). A central node is the CL–cytochrome c interface: elamipretide is proposed to modulate the hydrophobic/π–π interactions between cytochrome c and CL, promoting efficient electron transfer from complex III to complex IV at the rate-limiting step while inhibiting cytochrome c peroxidase activity that otherwise peroxidizes CL and destabilizes cristae under oxidative stress (Szeto & Birk, 2014). Biochemical studies show that elamipretide reduces cytochrome c peroxidase activity and prevents oxidative modifications of CL acyl chains by forming a complex with CL, thereby protecting membrane integrity (Sabbah et al., 2025). In failing human heart tissue ex vivo, elamipretide improved supercomplex coupling control, respiratory control ratio, and CI/CIV activities, consistent with a supercomplex-stabilizing activity that enhances OXPHOS efficiency (Sabbah et al., 2025).

3) Direct protein interactions and bioenergetic consequences. Proteomics using biotinylated elamipretide (b-ELAM) in cross-linking/MS identified binding to multiple IMM proteins that themselves interact with CL, including complex IV subunit NDUA4 and the adenine nucleotide translocase ANT1; functionally, elamipretide increased maximum uncoupled and CIV respiration and decreased H2O2 production in mitochondria from old mouse hearts, increased ADP sensitivity and uptake via ANT, reduced ANT1-mediated proton leak, stabilized membrane potential, and reduced mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening (Sabbah et al., 2025). Stabilization of larger IMM protein assemblies such as the ATP synthasome (ANT, ATP synthase, creatine kinase, phosphate carrier) has been reported, with improvements in CI–CIII–CIV coupling and oxygen flux in failing human heart tissue (Sabbah et al., 2025). These molecular effects translate to rapid increases in mitochondrial energetic capacity—including a human randomized placebo-controlled trial demonstrating that a single dose of elamipretide increased the maximal rate of ATP production (ATPmax) in skeletal muscle—validating in vivo bioenergetic rescue (Sabbah et al., 2025).

4) ROS control, IMM integrity, and cristae structure. Across cell and organ models, elamipretide reduces ETS-derived ROS without acting as a primary radical scavenger; instead it optimizes respiratory efficiency, reduces electron leak, and protects CL from peroxidation, breaking the cycle of cristae disruption and respiratory dysfunction prevalent in aged or diseased mitochondria (Sabbah et al., 2025; Mitchell et al., 2022). SS-31 lowers intracellular ROS, prevents mitochondrial depolarization, maintains ΔΨm, prevents lipid peroxidation, and curtails oxidative cell death in a dose-dependent manner (Mitchell et al., 2019). In retinal contexts, elamipretide increased mitochondrial cristae density and preserved ultrastructure in aged mouse retinal mitochondria and diabetic mouse retinopathy models, supporting retinal applicability (Sabbah et al., 2025). In multiple disease models, elamipretide increased mitochondrial density and cristae connectivity, normalized proton leak, improved respiratory capacity, and corrected dysregulated fusion/fission and biogenesis regulators after longer treatment, further indicating structural remodeling capacity (Sabbah et al., 2025).

Mechanistic relevance to AMD and RPE is strong. AMD donor RPE exhibits cristae disorganization, accumulation of damaged mitochondria, decreased OxPhos, impaired mitophagy, and significant mtDNA damage in ETC gene regions, all linked to diminished ATP production and a glycolytic shift that disrupts metabolic coupling with photoreceptors and promotes retinal degeneration (Ferrington et al., 2020; Fisher et al., 2022; Fisher, 2022). Because CL is crucial for maintaining OxPhos function and cristae architecture, pharmacologic stabilization of CL and CL-dependent protein assemblies by elamipretide directly addresses these pathologies, offering preservation of ATP production, reduction of ROS, and resistance to mPTP opening and apoptosis in RPE under chronic oxidative stress (Fisher et al., 2022; Sabbah et al., 2025; Szeto & Birk, 2014). Photoreceptors are mitochondria-rich in the inner segments, and OCT-defined EZ attenuation is an early marker of photoreceptor compromise that precedes GA; elamipretide-associated reduction in EZ attenuation progression in AMD patients links its mitochondrial mechanism to clinically observable retinal structure (Sabbah et al., 2025).

Expected Effect  
In RPE cell assays that model AMD-relevant stressors (oxidative and bioenergetic), elamipretide is expected to stabilize IMM biophysics and CL-dependent protein systems, restoring mitochondrial bioenergetics, reducing oxidative injury, and preventing apoptosis. Mechanistically supported expectations include:

- Restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) and coupling: Elamipretide maintains ΔΨm and improves respiratory control, consistent with increased OXPHOS efficiency and reduced proton leak; thus, assays using potentiometric dyes (e.g., JC-1) should show improved ΔΨm relative to oxidant-injured controls (Mitchell et al., 2019; Sabbah et al., 2025).

- Reduction of mitochondrial ROS and lipid peroxidation: By stabilizing CL, optimizing electron transport, and inhibiting cytochrome c peroxidase activity, elamipretide reduces H2O2 emission and lipid peroxidation, leading to lower MitoSOX and lipid oxidation signals under oxidative challenge (Sabbah et al., 2025; Mitchell et al., 2019).

- Preservation of ATP synthesis: In serum-deprivation or oxidant-injury paradigms in RPE cell lines (e.g., ARPE-19), mitochondria-targeted peptides including elamipretide increased cell viability and cellular ATP at nanomolar dosing; this is consistent with expected improvements in ATP content and Seahorse OXPHOS parameters in primary RPE under stress (Mitchell et al., 2021). Human AMD donor RPE exposed ex vivo to elamipretide show improved mitochondrial function and viability, corroborating translatability of these endpoints (Sabbah et al., 2025).

- Cytoprotection against AMD-relevant toxicants: Elamipretide prevents persistent injury phenotypes induced by oxidative stressors (e.g., hydroquinone) in cultured RPE, supporting generalizability to sodium iodate or H2O2 injury; in an RPE SOD2 knockout model, topical elamipretide prevented cell size increase consistent with reduced cell death/senescence (Sabbah et al., 2025; Tong et al., 2022).

- Structural preservation of cristae: Electron microscopy of retinal mitochondria in aged/diabetic mice treated with elamipretide indicates increased cristae density and improved ultrastructure; similar effects are expected in RPE mitochondrial ultrastructure under chronic oxidative stress (Sabbah et al., 2025).

- In vivo retinal/RPE endpoints: In mouse models of AMD-like pathology, elamipretide improved ERG deficits and enhanced clearance of sub-RPE deposits, tracking to improvements in photoreceptor function and RPE health; ERG, OCT (drusen/sub-RPE deposit metrics), and RPE morphometrics are therefore expected to improve (Kim & Lad, 2021; Ji et al., 2021; Guimaraes et al., 2022). In aged-vision paradigms, spatial vision and contrast sensitivity improved with systemic or topical elamipretide, indicating photopic function benefits and supporting cone function endpoints (Alam et al., 2020).

- Clinical correlates: In patients with intermediate AMD or non-central GA, improvements in LLVA/LLRA and slowing of EZ attenuation were observed; therefore, clinical PoC studies should prioritize EZ attenuation as a primary structural endpoint with LL-BCVA/LLVA and reading measures as functionally sensitive secondaries, acknowledging that GA area may not be sensitive over ≤1 year (Kim & Lad, 2021; Sabbah et al., 2025; Tung et al., 2025). Given that photoreceptor inner segments are mitochondria-rich, EZ integrity serves as a proximal clinical biomarker of the drug’s mitochondrial mechanism (Sabbah et al., 2025).

Expression and target rationale in RPE: The target of elamipretide is not a single protein but the CL-rich IMM domain; CL is ubiquitous and crucial for maintaining OxPhos function, cristae architecture, and supercomplex assembly in RPE mitochondria, which are compromised in AMD (Fisher et al., 2022; Ferrington et al., 2020). Deficits in mitophagy (reduced PINK1/Parkin responsiveness), increased fission and delayed fusion, and global OxPhos reduction in AMD donor RPE define a mitochondrial fragility state in which CL stabilization is expected to be beneficial (Fisher et al., 2022). Because elamipretide uptake is not dependent on ΔΨm, it can access depolarized/dysfunctional mitochondria in AMD RPE, positioning it to act upstream of apoptosis (Ji et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Elamipretide presents a coherent, mechanistically grounded, and translationally explored therapeutic candidate for non-neovascular AMD predicated on CL-centric rescue of mitochondrial function in RPE and photoreceptors. The totality of evidence spans molecular biophysics, mitochondrial proteomics, in vivo bioenergetics, preclinical retinal disease models, and controlled clinical imaging and functional outcomes, allowing a sober assessment of strengths and residual risks.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Resveratrol is a naturally occurring polyphenolic compound belonging to the stilbene class and is structurally defined as 3,5,4′-trihydroxystilbene. It is biosynthesized by plants such as Vitis vinifera (grapes), Japanese Knotweed, and various berries in response to stress factors like injury or pathogen attack, and it is a well‐recognized phytoalexin with a molecular formula of C14H12O3 (Bel, 2020; Pop et al., 2022). Originally isolated from the White Hellebore in the mid-20th century and later found in red wine due to grape skin fermentation, resveratrol has garnered significant attention not only for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties but also for its potential benefits in cardiovascular and neuroprotective contexts (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pop et al., 2022). As such, resveratrol—and by extension its commercial version (Cayman Chemical #70580) used in our studies—is classified as a nutraceutical and drug candidate with a long track record of investigative research including applications in aging, inflammation, and ocular health (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pop et al., 2022).

A considerable volume of biochemical, preclinical, and early clinical literature has explored resveratrol’s broad spectrum of activities. Historically, resveratrol has been investigated primarily for its cardioprotective and neuroprotective effects, as well as its anti-aging properties. In the realm of ophthalmology, several in vitro and animal studies have focused on its role in retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD), diabetic retinopathy (DR), and glaucoma. For instance, its use in RPE cell models has shown promising evidence for ameliorating oxidative stress-induced damage, a central factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Clinical investigations have attempted to translate these findings, as exemplified by the terminated clinical trial NCT02625376 that investigated resveratrol for exudative AMD (Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015), highlighting both the potential and the challenges involved in its clinical application (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Beyond ocular applications, resveratrol’s inclusion in various nutraceutical formulations underscores its established safety profile when administered at low-to-moderate doses, although issues pertaining to bioavailability and rapid systemic metabolism have been recurrent themes in the literature (Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, resveratrol exerts its effects primarily by modulating multiple intracellular signaling cascades. The central hypothesis we are testing is that resveratrol activates the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells—a pathway integral to regulating mitochondrial biogenesis and the antioxidant defense system. Activation of SIRT1, a NAD+-dependent deacetylase, by resveratrol increases the deacetylation and activation of its downstream effector, AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). This cascade not only improves mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and spare respiratory capacity—critical indicators of cellular health under oxidative stress—but also promotes an overall enhancement of cellular resilience against reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Bel, 2020; Bryl et al., 2022). Further molecular studies indicate that resveratrol can also modulate extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERK1/2) and mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK), contributing additional layers of cytoprotection through anti-apoptotic effects (Pop et al., 2022; Pop et al., 2022). Together, these mechanistic insights provide a comprehensive biochemical framework through which resveratrol is hypothesized to mitigate the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in RPE cells—a primary factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2021; Bryl et al., 2022).

In the context of the proposed assay for dry AMD, our expectation is that resveratrol will exert a multifaceted protective effect on RPE cells under oxidative challenge. Specifically, when RPE cells are exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as a model for oxidative stress, resveratrol is anticipated to counteract the resultant mitochondrial dysfunction by upregulating antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2, thereby reducing intracellular ROS levels (Bel, 2020; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Restoration of the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) is a critical endpoint, as it directly reflects cellular energy status and the ability of mitochondria to sustain ATP synthesis under stress (Buonfiglio et al., 2024). In addition, an improvement in spare respiratory capacity—the measure of a cell’s ability to respond to increased energy demands—should be evident, reflecting enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and a greater capacity for cellular repair mechanisms (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bryl et al., 2022). These cytoprotective effects have been demonstrated in in vitro studies using ARPE-19 and other human retinal pigment epithelial cell lines, and they resonate with the established role of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis in mediating energy metabolism and antioxidative defenses in the retina (Bryl et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021). Moreover, by decreasing the accrual of oxidative damage, resveratrol is expected to limit apoptotic signaling pathways, which are crucial in slowing the progressive degeneration observed in dry AMD (Bel, 2020; Pop et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
The cumulative evidence from preclinical studies strongly supports the potential of resveratrol as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, especially considering its capacity to modulate mitochondrial function and activate intrinsic antioxidant defenses. The activation of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis not only augments mitochondrial biogenesis but also enhances the expression of key antioxidant enzymes required to neutralize ROS, thereby directly addressing one of the primary mechanisms underlying AMD pathology (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bryl et al., 2022). One of the major strengths of resveratrol is its pleiotropic mode of action; beyond its antioxidant properties, its anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic activities further consolidate its candidacy for chronic conditions like dry AMD (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Bel, 2020). The primary challenge with resveratrol is its poor bioavailability and rapid metabolism, which may result in subtherapeutic tissue concentrations despite high oral absorption. Another potential weakness is the dose-dependent duality of its mechanism, where low doses predominantly mediate SIRT1-dependent effects, whereas higher doses might trigger SIRT1-independent pathways, possibly leading to off-target effects or toxicity (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Such a narrow therapeutic window necessitates a precise optimization of dosing regimens and formulation strategies. Despite these challenges, the overarching trend in preclinical research underscores that with proper formulation and dosing strategies, resveratrol could excel as an adjuvant or even monotherapy for protecting RPE cells from oxidative injury and, consequently, for the management of dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

In-Depth Analysis of Preclinical and Clinical Evidence:  
Numerous in vitro studies have characterized the effect of resveratrol on retinal pigment epithelial cells, notably ARPE-19 cell lines, under conditions of oxidative stress. Such studies consistently demonstrate that resveratrol treatment leads to a measurable reduction in ROS levels, a decrease in markers of apoptosis, and an overall improvement in mitochondrial parameters including Δψm and spare respiratory capacity (Bel, 2020; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). These findings are reinforced by experiments showing that resveratrol can mitigate blue light-induced retinal damage and preserve cell viability, further supporting its relevance in ocular pathologies where light-induced oxidative stress is a contributing factor (Bel, 2020). Complementary studies in animal models have shown that resveratrol can reduce inflammatory cytokine secretion and inhibit processes such as choroidal neovascularization, which has implications not only for dry AMD but also for its neovascular (wet) counterpart (Bryl et al., 2022; Bel, 2020).

Moreover, mechanistic investigations into the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis reveal that the deacetylation of PGC-1α is a critical step in the upregulation of mitochondrial genes, which directly correlates with increased cellular ATP production and enhanced resistance to oxidative stress (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Experimental data also show that SOD2 expression is significantly increased following resveratrol treatment, corroborating the compound’s role in boosting the cellular antioxidant capacity (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). These molecular events culminate in an environment that is less conducive to oxidative damage, thereby potentially arresting or even reversing some aspects of RPE degeneration that occur in dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021).

From a clinical perspective, the application of resveratrol in ocular disorders has been approached with caution, primarily due to pharmacokinetic challenges. Even though systemic administration of resveratrol has demonstrated efficacy in reducing plasma oxidative markers in diabetic patients and other conditions, the translation to ocular tissue remains hindered by its low aqueous solubility and rapid hepatic metabolism (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Abu-Amero et al., 2016). To overcome these barriers, innovative drug delivery systems such as chitosan-based nanoparticles, polymeric micelles, and liposomal formulations are being actively developed and show promise for achieving therapeutic levels in retinal tissues (Pop et al., 2022; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Such advanced formulations not only improve bioavailability but also allow for controlled release, which is essential for a chronic condition like dry AMD where sustained therapeutic action is desirable.

Additional mechanistic studies also suggest that resveratrol’s efficacy might be enhanced when used in combination with other therapeutic agents. For instance, its synergistic effects with anti-VEGF treatments in mitigating inflammatory cascades and suppressing angiogenesis have been noted in various preclinical models (Rusciano & Bagnoli, 2023; Tong et al., 2022). This combinatorial approach could be particularly valuable in cases where dry AMD transitions toward neovascular complications, thereby broadening the therapeutic window of resveratrol-based interventions.

Challenges in Drug Delivery and Bioavailability:  
While the biochemical rationale for using resveratrol in dry AMD is robust, its clinical development is significantly complicated by pharmacokinetic limitations. The compound is classified as a BCS Class II molecule, meaning that despite having high membrane permeability and lipophilicity, its poor aqueous solubility results in less than 1% bioavailability following oral administration (Kaštelan et al., 2025). As a consequence, only minimal amounts of unchanged resveratrol reach the systemic circulation and, by extension, the ocular tissues. Current research thus prioritizes the optimization of drug delivery vehicles to enhance its stability and target specificity. Nanotechnology-based delivery methods, including polymeric nanoparticles and solid lipid nanoparticles, have demonstrated enhanced tissue penetration and prolonged drug retention in the eye (Pop et al., 2022; Kaštelan et al., 2025). However, these strategies are still in the developmental phase, and their safety, scalability, and reproducibility for routine clinical use remain to be thoroughly validated. The potential for off-target effects and variability in patient-specific pharmacokinetics are additional hurdles that must be addressed in future clinical studies.

Safety and Dosing Considerations:  
Resveratrol has been generally recognized as safe in many preclinical studies, with low-dose regimens showing minimal adverse effects and favorable tolerability profiles (Wang et al., 2021; Bel, 2020). Nonetheless, concerns have been raised regarding gastrointestinal disturbances and other side effects at higher doses, as well as potential interactions with other medications (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Moreover, due to the compound’s rapid metabolism, determining an optimal dosing regimen that achieves effective local concentrations in the retina without inducing systemic toxicity remains challenging. This necessitates further preclinical and early-phase clinical trials to elucidate the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic profiles specific to ocular applications. Tailoring the dosing strategy based on individual metabolic rates and employing controlled-release formulations may help mitigate these issues and maximize therapeutic outcomes (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Kaštelan et al., 2025).

Strategic Direction and Future Perspectives:  
Given the multifaceted biological activities of resveratrol and the encouraging preclinical evidence in models of oxidative stress-induced RPE damage, it holds considerable promise as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to modulate the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis and promote mitochondrial biogenesis presents a novel therapeutic approach that directly targets the cellular dysfunctions underlying RPE degeneration. However, the translation of these findings into clinical practice will require addressing the critical challenges of bioavailability, formulation, and dosing.

Future research should focus on (1) developing and rigorously testing advanced drug delivery systems such as nanoparticle encapsulation methods that can bypass first-pass metabolism and target the retina more effectively, (2) conducting detailed pharmacokinetic studies to determine the optimal dosing regimen for achieving sustained therapeutic concentrations in ocular tissues, and (3) exploring combination therapy approaches that integrate resveratrol with conventional treatments such as anti-VEGF agents or other nutraceuticals to provide a comprehensive strategy against AMD progression (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Pop et al., 2022; Rusciano & Bagnoli, 2023). Furthermore, expanding the investigative efforts into patient-specific and personalized medicine approaches might allow for tailoring treatment protocols based on individual metabolic and genetic profiles, thereby maximizing efficacy and reducing adverse effects (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

In summary, resveratrol emerges as a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its extensive preclinical evidence, well-elucidated molecular mechanisms, and potential for modulating critical cellular pathways implicated in retinal degeneration. The strengths of resveratrol are rooted in its natural origin, broad-spectrum antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, and its ability to enhance mitochondrial function through the activation of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α pathway. These attributes are particularly relevant for combating the oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction that are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Nonetheless, its clinical utility is hampered by significant challenges related to bioavailability and metabolism, which necessitate innovative formulation and delivery strategies. Moreover, the variable dose-response observed in preclinical studies highlights the need for precise dose optimization before resveratrol can be reliably integrated into clinical practice for AMD treatment (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Although resveratrol has been investigated in clinical trials for ocular conditions, further large-scale, well-designed studies are essential to validate its efficacy, establish an acceptable safety profile, and determine its long-term benefits in human subjects with dry AMD (Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015; Pop et al., 2022).

Given the current state of evidence, we recommend that the research team continue to explore resveratrol as a candidate for dry AMD with a dual focus: first, to refine and optimize drug delivery systems that enhance its ocular bioavailability, and second, to design and implement comprehensive dose-escalation and safety studies in relevant preclinical models. Collaborative efforts that integrate insights from molecular biology, pharmacology, and clinical research will be critical in overcoming the translational challenges that have traditionally limited the application of resveratrol in ocular therapeutics (Pop et al., 2022; Rusciano & Bagnoli, 2023).

Conclusion:  
Resveratrol represents a promising candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration based on its robust mechanistic rationale and supportive preclinical evidence. Its capacity to activate the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis, promote mitochondrial biogenesis, and enhance antioxidant enzyme expression positions it as a multifaceted agent capable of mitigating oxidative stress in RPE cells—one of the key pathological drivers of AMD (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). While the compound’s safety profile in low-dose regimens is encouraging, its poor bioavailability and rapid metabolism require that future research prioritize advanced drug delivery systems and optimized dosing strategies. With concerted efforts in formulation science, preclinical validation, and clinical evaluation, resveratrol has the potential to become an integral part of a multi-targeted therapeutic approach for dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Kaštelan et al., 2025).

In conclusion, a comprehensive literature review of resveratrol underscores both its therapeutic potential and the challenges that must be overcome before its clinical application in dry AMD can be realized. The strengths of its molecular mechanisms and established safety in various studies are tempered by pharmacokinetic limitations that necessitate further research. The proposed strategy to focus on enhancing bioavailability via innovative drug delivery systems, coupled with rigorous preclinical safety and efficacy evaluations, will determine whether resveratrol can fulfill its promise as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bel, 2020). With continued investigation and collaboration across multidisciplinary research teams, resveratrol could offer a novel and effective means to delay or prevent RPE degeneration and the progression of dry AMD, ultimately improving patient outcomes in this challenging and prevalent ocular disease (Bryl et al., 2022; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Given the existing data and the ongoing improvements in nanoparticle and liposome-based delivery systems, our evaluation supports the further development of resveratrol in the context of dry AMD. The integration of this compound as either a monotherapy or as an adjunct to established therapies could provide enhanced protection against oxidative stress, preserve mitochondrial function, and improve retinal cell survival in patients suffering from this debilitating condition. Future research should aim to bridge the gap between promising in vitro efficacy and clinical applicability, ensuring that the dosing, safety, and delivery challenges are adequately addressed through well-designed preclinical and clinical studies (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015).

The converging lines of evidence from biochemistry, pharmacology, and early clinical investigations provide a strong rationale for continued development, with a focus on overcoming the pharmacokinetic limitations that have hindered its clinical translation thus far (Bryl et al., 2022; Bel, 2020; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). This proposal is therefore highly recommended for further preclinical optimization and subsequent clinical trial evaluation, establishing resveratrol as a potential cornerstone in the management of dry age-related macular degeneration.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Apocynin (Sigma-Aldrich A1788) is a naturally derived, methoxy-substituted catechol originally isolated from the medicinal herb Picrorhiza kurroa, which has a long history of use in traditional Ayurvedic medicine. It is a small molecule with a molecular weight of approximately 166.17 Da and modest lipophilicity (logP ~ 0.83) that allows it to readily cross cellular membranes and even the blood–brain barrier. As a member of the NADPH oxidase (NOX) inhibitor class, it has been historically used to modulate oxidative stress in a variety of preclinical disease models. The compound’s origin is rooted in natural product chemistry, and its attractive small-molecule structure has encouraged detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic investigations in rodent models, where it has been administered intravenously and orally to assess tissue distribution and rapid clearance kinetics. Its chemical profile and natural derivation position it within a class of therapeutic candidates that have been widely evaluated for their antioxidant properties and their ability to attenuate NOX-mediated reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory diseases (Liu et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Preclinical studies have evaluated apocynin in a range of animal models that address oxidative stress–related pathologies. In cardiovascular and cerebrovascular research, for example, apocynin has been shown to reduce NADPH oxidase activity and resultant oxidative damage in models of isoproterenol-induced cardiac hypertrophy, diabetic cardiac remodeling, and brain oxidative stress associated with high-fat diets (Liu et al., 2020). Its pharmacokinetic profile in mice indicates a rapid plasma peak and an extremely short half-life of around 3–4 minutes after intravenous dosing, with extensive clearance by the kidneys (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2020). In respiratory research, a completed Phase 1 randomized trial in COPD patients demonstrated that nebulized apocynin was well tolerated, produced short-term reductions in exhaled oxidative markers such as hydrogen peroxide and nitrite, and did not affect lung function or systemic safety parameters (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010). Despite these encouraging results, there remains limited data on the longer-term systemic safety or adverse-event profiles of apocynin. Importantly, while apocynin has been extensively studied in cardiovascular and respiratory indications, as well as in models of neurodegeneration and hepatic and renal injury, there is minimal direct evidence of its use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models or in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells such as ARPE-19 (Drummond & Sobey, 2014). Nonetheless, since dry AMD pathogenesis involves oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction within the RPE, the demonstrated efficacy of apocynin in modulating NADPH oxidase–mediated ROS production in other organs builds a rationale for its repurposing for this indication.

Mechanism of Action:  
The central proposed mechanism by which apocynin exerts its therapeutic effects involves the inhibition of NADPH oxidase, particularly by blocking the assembly of the enzyme complex. NADPH oxidases are multi-subunit enzymatic complexes responsible for the regulated generation of superoxide and downstream reactive oxygen species. In cells, the assembly and activation of NOX, especially isoforms such as NOX2, require the translocation of cytosolic regulatory subunits—most notably p47^phox—to the membrane-bound catalytic core. Early studies reported that apocynin can prevent the translocation of p47^phox to the plasma membrane, thereby inhibiting the assembly of the active NOX2 complex and reducing the production of superoxide, which secondarily lowers the formation of hydrogen peroxide and other ROS (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Drummond & Sobey, 2014).  
However, the molecular pharmacology of apocynin is more complex. Its inhibitory activity appears to be dependent on metabolic activation by myeloperoxidase (MPO) in the presence of hydrogen peroxide. This conversion supposedly generates reactive quinone species or even a dimeric form (diapocynin) that can covalently modify cysteine residues in p47^phox, thus interfering with its function (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Ismaeel et al., 2018). Some studies, though, have failed to detect diapocynin in vivo, suggesting that other metabolites, such as apocynin glycoconjugates, might instead be responsible for its activity (Liu et al., 2020). Moreover, apocynin has been reported to possess direct antioxidant properties at higher concentrations by scavenging non-radical oxidants such as hypochlorous acid and hydrogen peroxide, independently of its effects on NOX assembly (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Ismaeel et al., 2018).  
In vitro studies in various cell types have yielded conflicting data regarding whether apocynin primarily functions as a NOX-specific inhibitor or as a broad-spectrum antioxidant. In cell types that are rich in peroxidase activity, such as neutrophils, apocynin’s conversion to an active inhibitor appears robust. In contrast, in cells with lower MPO activity, such as some epithelial or neuronal cells, its efficacy as a NOX inhibitor may be diminished, and observed benefits might be attributable to direct ROS scavenging (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2020). Within the context of RPE cells, the candidate hypothesis posits that apocynin will inhibit the translocation of p47^phox during NOX2 activation, thereby reducing cytosolic ROS production while also limiting the spillover of ROS into mitochondria, which would otherwise trigger mitochondrial membrane potential collapse, fragmentation, and reduced oxygen consumption rate (OCR) (Liu et al., 2020; Liu, 2023). This mechanism, if operative in RPE cells such as ARPE-19, would help preserve mitochondrial integrity by preventing excess ROS accumulation and the ensuing mitochondrial dysfunction—a key pathogenic process in dry AMD (Shu et al., 2023; Liu, 2023).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed mechanism, the use of apocynin in in vitro assays with ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE cultures is expected to yield several beneficial outcomes. First, by blocking p47^phox translocation, apocynin should reduce the assembly of the NOX complex, particularly NOX2, thereby decreasing the production of superoxide and hydrogen peroxide. This reduction in ROS should lead to lower levels of oxidative stress markers, as measured by assays such as lucigenin chemiluminescence, dihydroethidium (DHE) fluorescence, and malondialdehyde (MDA) assays (Liu et al., 2020).  
Second, because ROS are known to damage mitochondrial components, it is expected that apocynin treatment will protect against mitochondrial dysfunction. In ARPE-19 cells challenged with hydrogen peroxide or other oxidative stress inducers, apocynin should help preserve the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), prevent mitochondrial fragmentation, and maintain basal oxygen consumption rates (OCR). These mitochondrial endpoints are critical, as disruption of mitochondrial dynamics and energy production is a hallmark of RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Shu et al., 2023; Drummond & Sobey, 2014).  
Furthermore, given that NOX isoforms such as NOX2 and NOX4 have been implicated in the oxidative stress observed in retinal cells exposed to blue light or metabolic insults (Liu et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020), the inhibition of these enzymes with apocynin is expected to attenuate downstream pro-inflammatory signaling cascades. This should result in reduced upregulation of proangiogenic factors like VEGF and a decrease in inflammatory cytokine production that can exacerbate retinal degeneration. In effect, apocynin would act not only to maintain mitochondrial function by limiting local oxidative damage but also to modulate the broader redox environment that contributes to RPE cell dysfunction in dry AMD (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Ismaeel et al., 2018).  
As a consequence, in the experimental assay proposed by the team, treatment of ARPE-19 cells with apocynin under conditions of induced oxidative stress should demonstrate a measurable preservation of Δψm by fluorescent imaging or flow cytometry using potentiometric dyes, maintenance of basal OCR as measured via Seahorse extracellular flux analysis, and a reduction in mitochondrial ROS accumulation by specific mitochondria-targeted ROS indicators. The reduction in NOX-derived ROS is expected to indirectly prevent mitochondrial fragmentation by mitigating the activation of mitochondrial fission pathways in response to oxidative injury (Liu, 2023; Liu et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
Apocynin represents a promising candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its potential to target a core pathogenic mechanism—the dysregulated production of ROS via NADPH oxidase assembly. One of the strengths of apocynin is its extensive preclinical history demonstrating its capacity to lower oxidative stress in various organs, including the heart, liver, brain, and lung, with documented rapid distribution to tissues and a well-characterized pharmacokinetic profile in animal models (Liu et al., 2020; Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014). Its observed safety in a small Phase 1 clinical study in COPD patients further bolsters the case for its safety on at least short-term administration in humans (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010). Moreover, its chemical simplicity as a natural product and its relatively low molecular weight make it attractive for further formulation studies in ocular indications.  
Nevertheless, significant weaknesses and challenges must be addressed. A major issue is the ongoing debate regarding the exact mechanism of action of apocynin. While some studies support its role as a NOX inhibitor via prevention of p47^phox translocation, others have demonstrated that its activity may be largely due to its direct antioxidant properties or require metabolic activation by MPO—a process that may not be robust in retinal pigment epithelial cells (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014). This mechanistic ambiguity raises concerns about its efficacy and specificity in the RPE, where the peroxidase activity necessary for conversion to an active form may be limited.

Another concern is that, despite the general rationale for reducing oxidative stress in the RPE, there is a paucity of direct evidence from ARPE-19 or primary RPE models showing that apocynin effectively prevents mitochondrial fragmentation, preserves the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), or maintains basal oxygen consumption rates. Overall, apocynin has strengths as a natural antioxidant with a history of reducing systemic oxidative stress in preclinical models and demonstrating short-term safety in human trials. However, its mechanism remains controversial, and its rapid clearance, potential variability in retinal cells, and limited direct evidence in AMD models represent significant weaknesses that must be overcome through further targeted biochemical, in vitro, and in vivo studies before advancing into clinical trials for dry AMD (Liu et al., 2020; Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010; Shu et al., 2023; Rohowetz et al., 2018; Liu, 2023).  
Given these considerations, further investigation into apocynin’s effects on mitochondrial protection and NOX inhibition in RPE cells is warranted. Such studies should include detailed assessments of p47^phox translocation in ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress, measurement of mitochondrial membrane potential (using dyes such as JC-1 or TMRE), and evaluations of OCR using Seahorse analysis. Moreover, efforts to optimize its pharmacokinetic profile—perhaps through formulation modifications or conversion to a mitochondria-targeted analogue—would address one of its key limitations. Only with these additional data can we determine whether apocynin holds sufficient promise to justify its repurposing for the treatment of dry AMD.

Liproxstatin-1 is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor of ferroptosis that was originally discovered using phenotypic high-throughput screening in systems where ferroptosis was induced by either genetic deletion of GPX4 or by glutathione depletion with agents like erastin (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69). Although detailed synthetic routes are not provided in the available reports, the discovery process clearly identifies Liproxstatin-1 as a lead candidate that emerged from unbiased cell-based screens aimed at identifying compounds that preserve cell viability in the absence of GPX4 function (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). Its categorization as an RTA is significant because this class of compounds has a long history of being used to inhibit free radical–mediated damage in both industrial and biological contexts (Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6).

Therapeutic History:  
The preclinical history of Liproxstatin-1 is rich with evidence supporting its role as a potent inhibitor of ferroptosis. Early studies demonstrated that Liproxstatin-1 acts at low nanomolar concentrations to prevent ferroptotic cell death in mouse embryonic fibroblasts as well as in specialized cells rendered vulnerable by GPX4 inactivation (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Angeli et al., 2014, p. 10). Beyond in vitro cell survival assays, Liproxstatin-1 has been evaluated in vivo where it has shown remarkable protective effects in models of acute tissue injury including genetic GPX4 deficiency, which induces acute renal failure, and in ischaemia/reperfusion models of liver injury (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10). Although its direct clinical use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) has not been established – with most in vivo data coming from non-ocular models – its success in ameliorating tissue damage by inhibiting lipid peroxidation suggests its potential utility in other degenerative pathologies where oxidative membrane damage drives dysfunction, such as in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) degeneration underlying geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69; Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–21). Moreover, related compounds, notably Ferrostatin-1, have been tested in various retinal cell models and in some in vivo settings pertaining to retinal ischemia–reperfusion injury and oxygen-induced retinopathy, further bolstering the therapeutic concept of using RTA-type ferroptosis inhibitors in ocular settings (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23; Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8). While the bulk of Liproxstatin-1’s therapeutic history centers on its role as an anti-ferroptotic agent in cancer, neurodegeneration, and acute organ failure, its mechanistic overlap with key pathological features observed in dry AMD – such as iron accumulation, glutathione depletion and elevated lipid peroxidation in the RPE – supports evaluating it as a repurposed candidate in this context (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Shen et al., 2025, pp. 1–2).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism by which Liproxstatin-1 exerts its cytoprotective effect is rooted in its function as a radical-trapping antioxidant. Specifically, Liproxstatin-1 reacts rapidly with lipid peroxyl radicals that propagate the autoxidation chain reaction in cellular membranes. Experimental data have established that Liproxstatin-1 exhibits an intrinsic reaction rate constant (k_inh) in the range of approximately 2.4 × 10^5 M^−1 s^−1 in organic solvents such as chlorobenzene at 37 °C, which is comparable to industrial diarylamine antioxidants (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 8–9). Although its intrinsic reactivity in homogeneous organic solutions may appear lower than classical phenolic antioxidants like α-tocopherol, its performance in the lipid bilayer is superior due to reduced hydrogen-bonding interactions with phospholipid headgroups – a feature that enhances its mobility and reactivity in the lipid environment where ferroptosis is executed (Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 8–9; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). The compound functions primarily by donating a hydrogen atom from its arylamine (or diarylamine) N–H group, effectively quenching chain-propagating lipid peroxyl radicals before they can perpetuate lipid hydroperoxide formation (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). Kinetic isotope effect studies and computational analyses have confirmed that the N–H bond dissociation enthalpy is sufficiently low in Liproxstatin-1 to enable rapid hydrogen-atom transfer, which is a critical step in its radical-trapping mechanism (Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 2–3, 5–7). Importantly, Liproxstatin-1 does not exert significant inhibitory effects on enzymes such as human 15-lipoxygenase-1, thereby ruling out an enzymatic inhibition mechanism and reinforcing that its protective effect is solely attributable to non-enzymatic scavenging of peroxyl radicals (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 201–210). Recent studies have even suggested that Liproxstatin-1 may form a complex with iron in certain cellular compartments (e.g., the lysosome), which could further diminish iron-catalysed radical generation under acidic conditions; however, the predominant and well-characterized mechanism remains its role in intercepting lipid peroxyl radicals (Rodriguez et al., 2024, pp. 1–5; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). In the context of dry AMD, particularly in geographic atrophy where RPE degeneration is a hallmark, the expected effect of Liproxstatin-1 would be to curtail the chain reaction of lipid peroxidation that underpins ferroptotic cell death. In vitro assays using RPE cell lines such as ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cells have demonstrated that targeting lipid peroxidation – as evidenced by reductions in markers like BODIPY-C11 oxidation and ACSL4 expression – can rescue cells from oxidative stress–mediated death (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–23). Liproxstatin-1 is anticipated to mitigate the accumulation of lipid hydroperoxides, thus preserving the integrity of cellular membranes and mitochondrial function in the RPE (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Given that geographic atrophy in dry AMD is associated with iron overload and subsequent iron-catalysed lipid peroxidation, the ability of Liproxstatin-1 to trap peroxyl radicals is particularly significant; by reducing lipid ROS, it is expected to prevent the conversion of polyunsaturated fatty acids into cytotoxic lipid hydroperoxides, thereby maintaining cellular viability (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). Liproxstatin-1 stands out as a promising candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic agent against dry AMD, particularly in geographic atrophy, given the mechanistic overlap between ferroptosis and RPE cell death observed in dry AMD. One of its principal strengths lies in its potent radical-trapping antioxidant activity, which is not only effective at low nanomolar concentrations but also uniquely suited to the lipid bilayer environment of the RPE (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). This specificity is critical because retinal cells are subject to a high burden of polyunsaturated lipid content and are therefore particularly sensitive to oxidative damage. Finally, considerations regarding the long-term stability, potential off-target effects, and metabolic fate of Liproxstatin-1 in the eye will be crucial parameters in the drug development process.

In summary, the collective literature indicates that Liproxstatin-1 has a well-defined mechanism as a radical-trapping antioxidant that effectively blocks lipid peroxidation and, by extension, ferroptosis. Its discovery through unbiased screening in ferroptosis-susceptible models and its demonstration of efficacy in multiple organ systems provide a strong foundation for its repurposing in dry AMD. The evidence supports that Liproxstatin-1 could counteract the iron-driven ROS amplification and lipid peroxidation that contribute to RPE cell death in geographic atrophy. Nonetheless, while its mechanistic rationale and preclinical promise are substantial, further research – particularly within retinal models – is necessary to fully evaluate its therapeutic potential and address challenges related to ocular delivery and multi-pathway disease components. Taken together, Liproxstatin-1 represents a compelling candidate for further investigation as a targeted inhibitor of ferroptosis in the treatment of dry AMD (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69, 207–210; Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23).

As a member of the iron chelator drug class, deferiprone’s established use in treating systemic iron overload syndromes has provided it with a significant clinical track record over several decades, forming the basis for its repurposing in disorders where iron-induced oxidative damage plays a role.  

Therapeutic History:  
Deferiprone has been used clinically as an orally administered iron chelator in the management of transfusional iron overload, notably in patients with thalassemia major. This usage is supported by multiple clinical studies and reviews that address both its efficacy in reducing systemic iron burden as well as its associated hematologic risks, such as agranulocytosis and neutropenia, which occur in approximately 1% of patients (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). Beyond its systemic application, preclinical models have demonstrated deferiprone’s potential for retinal protection. Several animal studies report that deferiprone, when administered systemically, can reduce retinal and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) iron levels in models of iron overload or light-induced degeneration and produce improvements in oxidative stress markers and retinal functional indices (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). This complex formation effectively reduces the availability of free iron in the intracellular labile iron pool, thereby diminishing iron-catalyzed reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. In addition, some data suggest that deferiprone may also interact with ferrous iron under certain conditions, contributing further to its antioxidant effects by interrupting redox cycling associated with both Fe3+ and Fe2+ species (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021).  

From a biochemical standpoint, iron accumulation in the RPE and surrounding retinal tissues is known to promote lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial oxidative stress, leading to cellular dysfunction and death—a pathomechanism observed in dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). Deferiprone’s cell permeability and ability to traverse biological barriers enables it to access the intracellular compartments, including mitochondria. Moreover, since mitochondrial dysfunction is a known contributor to RPE degeneration in dry AMD, its preservation via iron chelation is expected to sustain cellular ATP production and overall cell viability (Zhao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). Given that the RPE expresses iron regulatory proteins and that dysregulated iron metabolism has been observed in AMD retinas (with increased ferritin and altered transferrin receptor expression), the application of deferiprone would ideally restore homeostasis in the labile iron pool and thereby ameliorate the chronic oxidative insult observed in dry AMD (Li et al., 2023; Ashok et al., 2021).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Deferiprone presents several strengths as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD therapy. Firstly, its well-established clinical use in treating systemic iron overload confers a robust foundation regarding its pharmacokinetics, dosing parameters, and safety profile—despite noted hematologic risks such as agranulocytosis that occur in a small percentage of patients (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). Its oral bioavailability and ability to cross the blood–retinal barrier make it uniquely suited for targeting intracellular iron in the retina (Li et al., 2023). Secondly, there is compelling preclinical evidence from various retinal degeneration models that iron chelators, including deferiprone, can reduce retinal iron accumulation, diminish oxidative stress, and improve functional outcomes, which supports the rationale for its repurposing in the context of dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016; Zhao et al., 2025). Thirdly, its mode of action—chelating labile iron to prevent Fenton reaction–mediated ROS production—directly targets a central pathological mechanism implicated in dry AMD. The hypothesis that reducing mitochondrial iron load will preserve ETC integrity is biologically plausible given the importance of iron-catalyzed oxidative stress in mitochondrial dysfunction within the RPE (Li et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023).  

On the other hand, several weaknesses and uncertainties remain. Although deferiprone’s effectiveness in reducing systemic and retinal iron overload has been demonstrated in animal models, direct evidence of its capacity to specifically target RPE mitochondrial iron and preserve ETC function in human RPE cells is currently limited (Zhao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023). The precise molecular details regarding how deferiprone modulates mitochondrial iron trafficking, and how this relates to the functional maintenance of the electron transport chain, require further investigation. Additionally, while preclinical data are supportive, deferiprone has not yet been tested in clinical trials specifically for dry AMD, and its long-term safety and efficacy in the ocular context remain to be established (Zhao et al., 2021; Ueda et al., 2018). Another consideration is the risk of adverse systemic effects, such as neutropenia and agranulocytosis, which, although infrequent, could limit its utility in a population of elderly patients with dry AMD who may have co‐morbidities (Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). Moreover, some reports have suggested that under low concentrations or certain conditions, iron chelators might paradoxically participate in free radical formation, necessitating precise dose titration and careful monitoring (Li et al., 2023; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016).  

In summary, deferiprone appears to be a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its well-documented ability to chelate labile iron, its favorable pharmacologic properties including oral bioavailability and tissue penetration, and preclinical evidence showing retinal protection. Its mechanism of action—reducing the labile iron pool to limit Fenton reaction–induced oxidative stress—addresses a central pathogenic mechanism of dry AMD, namely, iron accumulation leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and lipid peroxidation in the RPE (Zhao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). However, the extrapolation of these preclinical findings to human dry AMD requires additional studies, particularly those that directly measure mitochondrial iron dynamics and ETC activity in RPE cells following deferiprone treatment. Rigorous dose-ranging and safety studies will also be necessary to mitigate the risk of hematologic adverse effects. Therefore, while deferiprone has significant potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD, further preclinical mechanistic studies and early-phase clinical trials are essential to fully validate its efficacy and safety in this new therapeutic context (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Ueda et al., 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Mitoquinone mesylate (MitoQ) is a synthetic, mitochondria‐targeted antioxidant originally developed as an analogue of coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) to overcome the bioavailability and uptake limitations of naturally occurring CoQ10. Its chemical design is based on modifying decylubiquinone—a CoQ10 analogue in which the long isoprenoid tail is replaced by a saturated decyl hydrocarbon chain to enhance mitochondrial retention—and covalently linking it to a lipophilic triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation. The inclusion of the TPP⁺ moiety exploits the highly negative membrane potential of the mitochondrial inner membrane, thereby ensuring selective accumulation of MitoQ in the mitochondrial matrix (Cores et al., 2023). This compound belongs to the class of lipophilic cationic antioxidants and is also considered a mitochondria-targeted rechargeable antioxidant (RMA) because, after its active ubiquinone moiety scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS), it is enzymatically reduced to the active hydroquinone form by components of the electron transport chain. The rechargeable property allows MitoQ to be continuously recycled via the respiratory chain, resulting in sustained antioxidant action even at low doses—a property that distinguishes it from conventional antioxidants (Lukashev et al., 2014; Fields et al., 2023). The synthesis strategy for MitoQ involves the chemical conjugation of decylubiquinone with TPP⁺, and it is formulated as a mesylate salt to improve its stability and facilitate pharmaceutical development (Cores et al., 2023; Kim & Han, 2017). Overall, MitoQ is a well‐defined member of a broader class of mitochondria‐targeted redox active compounds that have been widely investigated for their potential to modulate mitochondrial oxidative stress (Zielonka et al., 2017).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past two decades, MitoQ has been extensively characterized in a wide range of preclinical studies spanning neurodegenerative diseases, cardiovascular disorders, metabolic syndrome, sepsis, and other conditions associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and elevated oxidative stress. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that MitoQ confers protection against oxidative injury in cellular models and animal models alike. For example, studies in rodent models of cardiac ischemia–reperfusion injury, hypertension, and pressure‐overload heart failure have shown that MitoQ preserves mitochondrial respiration, decreases ROS production (especially H₂O₂ and superoxide) and reduces lipid peroxidation in the heart (Fairley et al., 2023; Kim & Han, 2017). In addition, significant neuroprotective effects have been reported in multiple models of neurodegeneration—ranging from in vitro experiments using Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease models to in vivo studies in rodent systems—where MitoQ was able to reduce mitochondrial fragmentation, lower markers of apoptosis, and restore mitochondrial membrane potential in neurons (Fields et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). Clinically, MitoQ has advanced into human trials in several indications including studies related to Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and hypertension, with reported safety in over 200 human subjects (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Fairley et al., 2023). Although there is no direct record of its use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), the extensive preclinical history in diseases characterized by oxidative stress and mitochondrial impairment provides a strong precedent for its repurposing. In ocular contexts, early pharmacokinetic studies have demonstrated that MitoQ exhibits measurable retinal uptake (approximately 1% of plasma concentration) after oral or topical administration, suggesting that the compound can reach the retina at therapeutically relevant levels (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). Given that mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative injury in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells are now increasingly recognized as central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the repurposing of MitoQ for this indication is logically supported by its mechanism and prior usage in analogous conditions (Cores et al., 2023; Zielonka et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
MitoQ’s mechanism of action is rooted in its unique chemical architecture that allows selective mitochondrial targeting and continuous ROS scavenging. The TPP⁺ moiety drives the compound’s accumulation into the mitochondrial matrix in a membrane potential–dependent manner. Once inside the mitochondria, MitoQ’s ubiquinone moiety is rapidly reduced by components of the electron transport chain—most notably by electron flow through complex II—and converted to its active form, mitoquinol (ubiquinol) (Cores et al., 2023; Manolis et al., 2021). In its reduced state, mitoquinol acts as a potent antioxidant that intercepts ROS generated primarily at the sites of electron leakage at complexes I and III. The scavenging of ROS, particularly superoxide and peroxyl radicals, prevents oxidative damage to mitochondrial lipids, proteins, and DNA—all of which are crucial for maintaining mitochondrial function (Zielonka et al., 2017; Modi et al., 2024). In effect, the cycle of reduction and oxidation (redox cycling) enables MitoQ to function catalytically, rather than stoichiometrically, thereby amplifying its antioxidant capacity over time (Lukashev et al., 2014; Modi et al., 2024). Moreover, by reducing mitochondrial ROS, MitoQ preserves the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), which is essential for ATP synthesis and overall cellular bioenergetics (Kim & Han, 2017; Gueven et al., 2017). This stabilization of Δψm not only inhibits the initiation of apoptosis but may also dampen downstream inflammatory signaling cascades mediated by ROS-sensitive transcription factors such as NF-κB (Fields et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023). Such detailed molecular interactions—spanning TPP-driven uptake, rapid reduction at the respiratory chain, catalytic ROS neutralization, and subsequent recycling to the active antioxidant form—underscore the multifaceted protection that MitoQ offers against mitochondrial oxidative injury.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the underlying hypothesis is that accumulation of oxidative damage in RPE cells leads to mitochondrial dysfunction, loss of Δψm, increased ROS production, chronic inflammation, and ultimately RPE cell degeneration, which is central to disease progression. Based on in vitro studies performed in ARPE-19 cells, treatment with MitoQ has been shown to reduce mitochondrial ROS levels, as measured by MitoSOX fluorescence, and to preserve Δψm as assessed by TMRM assays when cells are challenged with H₂O₂-induced oxidative stress (Cores et al., 2023; Fields et al., 2023). The expected effect of MitoQ in a dry AMD model is that, upon topical or oral administration, it will accumulate in the mitochondria of RPE cells via TPP-mediated uptake. Once there, its ubiquinone moiety will be reduced to the active antioxidant form by the local respiratory chain, which in turn will neutralize superoxide and other ROS at the sites of electron leakage (primarily complex I and III regions). This ROS scavenging is anticipated to limit oxidative damage to mitochondrial membranes and proteins, maintain efficient electron transport and ATP production, and ultimately restore the mitochondrial membrane potential that is compromised in oxidative stress conditions (Zielonka et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014). Additionally, by lowering oxidative stress, MitoQ is expected to reduce inflammatory signaling within the RPE and adjacent retinal layers—potentially decreasing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and mitigating the chronic low-grade inflammation that contributes to dry AMD pathology (Fairley et al., 2023; Gueven et al., 2017). In an in vitro assay using ARPE-19 cells, one would expect to observe a significant decrease in MitoSOX signal intensity along with increased TMRM fluorescence after treatment with MitoQ, indicating reduced mitochondrial ROS and improved Δψm, respectively (Cores et al., 2023; Fields et al., 2023).
