Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
EUK-8 is a synthetic catalytic antioxidant that belongs to the manganese‐based salen complexes, a class of low molecular weight enzyme mimetics engineered to replicate key activities of endogenous antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). This compound is synthesized via a condensation reaction between salicylaldehyde derivatives and diamines to form a bis‐Schiff base (salen) ligand, which then coordinates to a manganese ion, thereby producing the characteristic MnN₂O₂ planar core responsible for its redox activity (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rosenthal et al., 2011). The manganese center in EUK-8 undergoes reversible redox cycling between Mn(III) and Mn(II) oxidation states; this reversible cycling is essential for its dual enzyme-mimetic action, as it enables catalytic dismutation of superoxide radicals into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide and further conversion of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, thereby mimicking the combined action of SOD and catalase (Fernandes, 2010; Rouco et al., 2020a). The salen complex scaffold not only confers redox activity but also provides a tunable electronic and steric environment through modification of substituents on the ligand framework, which in turn dictates the redox potential, proton-dissociation properties, and overall catalytic efficacy (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020b). Because of its synthetic origin, EUK-8 is both cost-effective and easily reproducible, making it an appealing candidate for repurposing in therapeutic areas where enhanced antioxidant defenses are required, such as in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rosenthal et al., 2011).

Therapeutic History:  
The EUK series of compounds, which includes EUK-8, have been extensively studied in a plethora of preclinical models addressing a wide range of diseases linked to oxidative stress, including ischemic brain injury, neurodegeneration, cardiac injury, and even lifespan extension models in Caenorhabditis elegans and SOD2 knockout mice (Rouco et al., 2020a). Biochemical studies have demonstrated that EUK-8 exhibits both superoxide dismutase and catalase-like activities at submicromolar concentrations, providing significant protection in vitro and in vivo in models of oxidative injury (Bani & Bencini, 2012). While EUK-8 itself has not been directly evaluated in clinical trials for dry AMD, its protective effects have been documented in several models of neuronal and cardiac injury where mitochondrial dysfunction and excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) production are central to the pathology (Fernandes, 2010; Rouco et al., 2020a). The pharmacological application of salen manganese complexes, including EUK-8, extends to neuroprotective approaches, such as in models of Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and ischemia–reperfusion injury, suggesting that similar mechanisms may be beneficial in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which are notably vulnerable to oxidative stress in dry AMD (Rouco et al., 2020b; Yan et al., 2010). Additionally, the literature reveals that analogous compounds in the EUK series have been examined for their anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, and mitochondrial protective properties in diverse cellular and animal models, lending further credence to their potential for repurposing in ocular degenerative diseases (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rosenthal et al., 2009).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, EUK-8 functions as a catalytic antioxidant by mimicking two key enzymes involved in the detoxification of reactive oxygen species. First, it catalyzes the dismutation of superoxide (O₂•⁻) by virtue of its manganese center undergoing cyclic redox reactions between the Mn(III) and Mn(II) states; in one half-reaction, the Mn(III) state accepts an electron from superoxide to become Mn(II), while in the subsequent half-reaction, Mn(II) is reoxidized to Mn(III) by another molecule of superoxide, resulting in the conversion of superoxide to molecular oxygen and hydrogen peroxide (Fernandes, 2010; Batinić-Haberle et al., 2016). Second, EUK-8 mimics catalase activity by decomposing the generated hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen; it is proposed that hydrogen peroxide reacts with the manganese center to generate a transient high-valent oxo–Mn species, which is then reduced back to the resting state in the presence of a reductant, thus completing the catalytic cycle (Yan et al., 2010; Bani & Bencini, 2012). The structural integrity of the salen ligand is critical in modulating the redox potential of the manganese center, which, when tuned to an optimal range, ensures efficient electron transfer with reactive species while minimizing the risk of metal ion dissociation or inadvertent pro-oxidant activity (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Durand, 2013). In cellular contexts, the dual SOD/catalase activity of EUK-8 is especially relevant to mitochondria, which are the primary source of intracellular ROS; by reducing mitochondrial superoxide and decomposing hydrogen peroxide, EUK-8 helps to preserve mitochondrial respiration and prevent oxidative mitochondrial damage, which is a key contributor to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). Moreover, the reduction of mitochondrial ROS is anticipated to attenuate the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, a multiprotein complex that is known to be triggered by oxidative stress and has been implicated in inflammasome-mediated inflammatory responses in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Rouco et al., 2020a; Bani & Bencini, 2012). The overall biochemical and mechanistic profile of EUK-8, therefore, aligns well with the need to lower mtROS and preserve cellular homeostasis in tissues subjected to chronic oxidative stress.

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by the degeneration of the RPE, a process driven by cumulative oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation leading to cellular senescence and eventual retinal atrophy (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Batinić-Haberle et al., 2016). Given that the RPE expresses high levels of mitochondrial enzymes, including MnSOD, and relies on efficient mitochondrial respiration for normal function, the preservation of mitochondrial integrity is paramount (Fernandes, 2010; Rouco et al., 2020a). EUK-8 is expected to enter RPE cells and preferentially localize to mitochondria where its catalytic dual SOD/catalase activity would reduce the burden of superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, thereby mitigating oxidative damage to mitochondrial proteins, lipids, and DNA (Rosenthal et al., 2011; Rosenthal et al., 2009). By maintaining lower levels of mtROS, EUK-8 would be anticipated to stave off the mitochondrial dysfunction that underlies RPE degeneration and to prevent the activation of pro-inflammatory signaling cascades such as those mediated by the NLRP3 inflammasome, thus potentially preserving cellular viability and function (Batinić-Haberle, 2013; Bigham & Wilson, 2023). In addition, previous studies with related manganosalen complexes have shown that treatment can lead to the reversal of age-related cognitive deficits and the inhibition of pro-apoptotic pathways in neuronal tissues, which are mechanistically analogous to the crises faced by RPE cells in dry AMD (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rouco et al., 2020b). Given that the anticipated mechanism involves modulation of mitochondrial redox balance and prevention of inflammation, the expected molecular targets in RPE cells include key mitochondrial respiratory chain components, antioxidant response elements such as Nrf2, and inflammasome components including caspase-1 and interleukin-1β, all of which have been implicated in the progression of dry AMD (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Durand, 2013). The ability of EUK-8 to act at submicromolar doses further enhances its appeal, as such potency suggests that therapeutic effects may be achieved with minimal exposure, reducing the likelihood of off-target effects and toxicity (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Fernandes, 2010).

Overall Evaluation:  
From a drug development perspective, EUK-8 emerges as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration, primarily because its dual enzyme-mimetic properties address two central features of RPE pathology—oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). One of the major strengths of EUK-8 lies in its robust catalytic activity; being a regenerative, non-stoichiometric antioxidant means that even at submicromolar concentrations, it can exert sustained protective effects by continuously dismutating ROS, in contrast to traditional antioxidants that are consumed in the process (Rosenthal et al., 2011; Rouco et al., 2020a). Its low molecular weight and non-peptidic nature facilitate cellular uptake and mitochondrial penetration, critical features for targeting the RPE where mitochondrial production of ROS is an important driver of cell injury (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). Furthermore, the extensive preclinical history of manganosalen compounds in models of neuroprotection, cardiac ischemia, and aging provides a solid rationale for their protective capacity in tissues that are equally susceptible to oxidative damage, even if direct studies in dry AMD are limited at present (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rouco et al., 2020b).

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and challenges must be addressed before EUK-8 can be confidently advanced as a therapeutic for dry AMD. First, despite the promising preclinical data in other models, there is a paucity of direct studies evaluating EUK-8 in ocular or RPE-specific models. Dry AMD has its own unique microenvironment, including features such as the Bruch’s membrane, the blood-retinal barrier, and specialized immune processes, which might affect drug delivery and efficacy (Bigham & Wilson, 2023; Yan et al., 2010). Second, the stability of EUK-8 in the complex milieu of the eye must be rigorously tested, especially because the aqueous and proteinaceous environments found in ocular tissues could potentially lead to ligand dissociation or redox inactivation (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). Third, although EUK-8’s catalytic nature means that it is less likely to be consumed during therapy compared to stoichiometric antioxidants, there is always the risk that under certain pathological conditions, such as in the presence of excess hydrogen peroxide or other reactive species, it could exhibit paradoxical pro-oxidant effects if the redox balance is not carefully controlled (Batinić-Haberle et al., 2012; Bani & Bencini, 2012). Fourth, formulation and delivery challenges specific to ocular therapeutics must be overcome; for instance, ensuring adequate penetration across the inner limiting membrane and achieving sufficient concentrations within the RPE are non-trivial hurdles that have derailed otherwise promising compounds in the past (Batinić-Haberle et al., 2016; Rosenthal et al., 2009). Finally, comprehensive toxicity and pharmacokinetic studies in ocular models are required since systemic dosing data from neurological or cardiovascular models may not transcribe directly to the unique setting of the retina (Batinić-Haberle, 2013; Fernandes, 2010).

In summary, the therapeutic candidate EUK-8 exhibits several key attributes that make it an attractive option for addressing the oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction underlying dry age-related macular degeneration. Its synthetic origin and scalable chemistry, combined with potent dual SOD/catalase enzyme-mimetic activity, have already been validated extensively in diverse preclinical models of oxidative injury (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). The molecular mechanism—involving redox cycling of a manganese center coordinated by a salen ligand—supports the hypothesis that EUK-8 can effectively lower mtROS levels and preserve mitochondrial respiration in cells, such as the retinal pigment epithelium, that are critically dependent on mitochondrial function (Fernandes, 2010; Yan et al., 2010). This mechanistic rationale is further bolstered by studies demonstrating that similar manganosalen complexes can reverse age-related functional deficits and prevent neurodegenerative changes in animal models, suggesting that the beneficial effects observed in cardiac and neuronal tissues might extend to the RPE (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rouco et al., 2020b).

The expected effect of EUK-8 in the context of dry AMD is twofold: first, by acting as both a superoxide dismutase and catalase mimic, it is anticipated to reduce the overall oxidative burden within RPE mitochondria, preserving cellular respiration and preventing damage to key mitochondrial constituents; and second, by mitigating the oxidative activation of the inflammasome (particularly the NLRP3 complex), EUK-8 should help prevent the chronic inflammatory environment that exacerbates RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Rouco et al., 2020a; Bani & Bencini, 2012). This dual mode of action not only targets the root cause of oxidative damage but also addresses a major downstream consequence—persistent inflammation—that has been implicated in the progression of dry AMD (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rosenthal et al., 2009).

Overall, while the preclinical evidence underscores the strong potential of EUK-8 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, its translational success will depend critically on several factors. Strengths of EUK-8 include its well-documented catalytic efficiency, proven efficacy in multiple oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction models, and the capability for extensive structure–activity relationship optimization that allows fine-tuning of its redox properties (Fernandes, 2010; Bani & Bencini, 2012). However, weaknesses such as the lack of ocular-specific preclinical data, potential formulation and delivery challenges specific to the retinal environment, and the need for rigorous ocular toxicity and pharmacokinetic studies remain to be addressed (Bigham & Wilson, 2023; Yan et al., 2010). In the absence of direct evidence in RPE cells or AMD models, it is essential that further studies be conducted to confirm that EUK-8’s in vitro antioxidant effects translate into meaningful protection of RPE mitochondrial function and inhibition of inflammasome activation in vivo (Durand, 2013; Rosenthal et al., 2009). Furthermore, the development of targeted delivery systems—possibly involving nanoparticle encapsulation, intravitreal injections, or sustained-release formulations—may be required to ensure adequate drug concentration at the site of action while minimizing systemic exposure and potential off-target effects (Batinić-Haberle, 2013; Fernandes, 2010).

From a strategic standpoint, the repurposing of EUK-8 for dry AMD appears promising based on its robust mechanistic foundation and extensive preclinical history in related oxidative stress models; however, a focused research program involving detailed studies in ocular tissues, optimization of drug delivery to the retina, and comprehensive toxicity assessments is warranted to overcome the current limitations and uncertainties (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rouco et al., 2020b). If these challenges can be successfully addressed, EUK-8 has the potential to fulfill an unmet clinical need by protecting RPE mitochondria from oxidative damage, thereby slowing the progression of dry AMD and preserving visual function in affected patients (Fernandes, 2010; Rouco et al., 2020a).  

In conclusion, as a candidate drug for dry age-related macular degeneration, EUK-8 offers a compelling therapeutic strategy that leverages its dual SOD and catalase mimetic activities to target the central biochemical derangements in the RPE associated with oxidative stress and inflammation (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). The natural alignment of its mechanism with the pathophysiological features of dry AMD—namely, mitochondrial dysfunction, excessive ROS production, and inflammasome activation—supports the hypothesis that EUK-8 could restore redox balance and inhibit degenerative processes in the retina (Rouco et al., 2020a; Bani & Bencini, 2012). Nonetheless, the ultimate utility of EUK-8 will depend on its ability to overcome delivery and stability challenges in the ocular environment and on the generation of robust preclinical data demonstrating efficacy in relevant AMD models. Given these considerations, it is recommended that targeted in vitro and in vivo studies be prioritized to validate the therapeutic potential of EUK-8 in dry AMD, with particular attention to mitochondrial function, inflammasome activity, and retinal cell survival parameters (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rosenthal et al., 2009).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
L-Carnitine is a naturally occurring quaternary ammonium compound, chemically defined as β-hydroxy-γ-trimethylaminobutyrate, that is both derived from the diet (predominantly found in animal-based foods such as red meat) and biosynthesized endogenously from the essential amino acids lysine and methionine via a vitamin C–dependent pathway primarily in the liver and kidneys (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Mollica et al., 2017). Historically, L-carnitine was first identified as a constituent of muscle tissue in the early 20th century and was later linked to its high content in meat, leading to its designation as “vitamin T” in certain insect models (Mollica et al., 2017). As a member of the carnitine family, it belongs to the class of metabolic cofactors or nutraceutical agents whose primary function is to shuttle activated long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondrial matrix, where they undergo β-oxidation, thereby facilitating aerobic energy production and maintaining the intracellular acyl-CoA/CoA balance (Moos et al., 2017; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). This class of compounds has historically been used as dietary supplements to treat primary and secondary carnitine deficiency, as well as in various metabolic and mitochondrial disorders (Flanagan et al., 2010). L-Carnitine is widely formulated in pharmaceutical products both as a standalone supplement and as an ingredient in combination formulations, which underscores its acceptance as a metabolic supportive agent with a favorable safety profile (Flanagan et al., 2010; Surai, 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, the carnitine family has a long record of use in addressing conditions where fatty acid oxidation is impaired. L-Carnitine has been employed effectively as a life-saving therapy in primary carnitine deficiency—a condition in which mutations of the carnitine transporter (OCTN2) impair cellular uptake—and also in secondary deficiencies associated with conditions like renal failure, liver disease, and certain inborn errors of metabolism (Flanagan et al., 2010). Beyond classical deficiency syndromes, both L-carnitine and its acetylated derivative (acetyl-L-carnitine) have been investigated in a broad range of clinical contexts, including cardiovascular diseases, diabetic complications, and neurodegenerative disorders. For example, acetyl-L-carnitine has been shown to improve parameters of visual function in patients with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and to confer neuroprotective effects in Alzheimer’s disease and mild cognitive impairment (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Calabrese et al., 2009).  
In ophthalmology, while most clinical studies have focused on the use of carnitine derivatives for systemic metabolic or neuroprotective effects, there is preclinical evidence supporting an ocular role. Animal studies have identified high intraocular concentrations of carnitine in the lens and other ocular tissues, hinting at a physiological role in maintaining ocular metabolic balance and osmotic homeostasis (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). Investigations into the protective effects of L-carnitine against oxidative damage, including its potential to safeguard retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and other ocular tissues, provide a rationale for its application in dry AMD, particularly in the context of geographic atrophy where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central features (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c). Moreover, combination therapy regimens incorporating acetyl-L-carnitine with n-3 fatty acids and coenzyme Q10 have also been trialed in experimental settings to address energy metabolism in retinal tissues (Shamsi et al., 2007). Despite these promising findings, direct clinical use of L-carnitine as monotherapy for dry AMD has not been extensively reported, thus making its repurposing an area that merits focused research to bridge the gap between its established metabolic functions and its potential application in retinal degeneration (Flanagan et al., 2010; Mollica et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
The central biochemical role of L-carnitine is to facilitate the transport of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle—a process that is critical for β-oxidation and ATP production. This shuttle is mediated by mitochondrial enzymes such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT-1) on the outer mitochondrial membrane, which converts acyl-CoA to acyl-carnitine, and carnitine acyltransferase (also known as carnitine acetyltransferase or CAT) within the mitochondria that re-forms acyl-CoA for oxidation (Moos et al., 2017; Jones et al., 2010). This process not only fuels ATP generation via the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation but also helps regulate the cellular acyl-CoA/CoA ratio, indirectly influencing multiple metabolic pathways (Surai, 2015).  
Furthermore, L-carnitine exhibits antioxidant properties either directly, through free radical scavenging, or indirectly by preserving mitochondrial integrity and function under oxidative stress conditions (Shamsi et al., 2007; Surai, 2015). It has been shown to reduce lipid peroxidation and prevent the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential—a key step in the cascade leading to cellular apoptosis (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c). In addition to its classical mitochondrial functions, L-carnitine also acts as an osmolyte, protecting cells against hyperosmolarity by stabilizing proteins and cellular membranes, which could further reduce oxidative stress (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b; Mollica et al., 2017).  
At the molecular level in the RPE, the hypothesis is that enhancing mitochondrial fatty acid uptake via L-carnitine supplementation will improve β-oxidation efficiency. This is expected to lead to increased ATP production and a reduction in the accumulation of lipid intermediates that may otherwise result in excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation. The reduction in ROS could mitigate chronic oxidative stress, a well established contributor to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Jones et al., 2010; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). Notably, disrupted mitochondrial metabolism and energy deficits have been implicated in the progression of RPE cell dysfunction, and L-carnitine’s role in restoring metabolic flexibility has been documented in other cell types such as hepatocytes and neuronal cells (Ates et al., 2008; Surai, 2015). Additionally, the modulation of mitochondrial protein acetylation by L-carnitine derivatives, an effect observed in various models of aging and metabolic disease, may further contribute to a neuroprotective milieu in RPE cells (Wang et al., 2024; Virmani & Cirulli, 2022).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its multifaceted mechanisms of action, the anticipated effect of L-carnitine in an assay designed for dry age-related macular degeneration is twofold. First, by enhancing mitochondrial fatty acid uptake and increasing β-oxidation rates, L-carnitine is expected to boost ATP production in RPE cells, thereby ameliorating the energy deficits that contribute to cellular dysfunction in geographic atrophy (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Jones et al., 2010). Second, this improved mitochondrial function should lead to a reduction in the generation of ROS that typically arises from lipid overload and subsequent incomplete oxidation, thereby decreasing oxidative damage to critical cellular structures including mitochondrial membranes and nuclear DNA (Shamsi et al., 2007; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a).  
In in vitro assays using cultured RPE cells, one would expect that L-carnitine treatment leads to enhanced mitochondrial respiration, as measured by oxygen consumption rate (OCR), and an associated elevation in ATP levels. Moreover, reductions in established markers of oxidative stress, such as malondialdehyde (MDA) levels or increased glutathione (GSH) concentrations, would support its antioxidant action (Ates et al., 2008). Expression studies have shown that key mitochondrial enzymes and transporters, including CPT-1 and OCTN2 (the carnitine transporter), are expressed in RPE cells, providing a molecular substrate for L-carnitine’s action in these cells (Ribas et al., 2014; Jones et al., 2010). Furthermore, since mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of dry AMD pathogenesis, the restoration of mitochondrial efficiency by L-carnitine could be measured by improved RPE cell survival and decreased apoptotic markers under conditions of oxidative stress and lipid oversupply.  
Preclinical studies in other tissues such as neuronal cells and hepatocytes have demonstrated that L-carnitine treatment not only restores mitochondrial function but also reduces lipid-induced ROS production and inflammation. Extrapolating from these findings, it is reasonable to expect that in the context of dry AMD, L-carnitine could counteract the metabolic inflexibility of RPE cells, ultimately slowing the progression of geographic atrophy and preserving retinal structure and function (Surai, 2015; Wang et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
L-Carnitine stands out as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to several compelling properties. Its established role in promoting mitochondrial β-oxidation and energy production, combined with demonstrated antioxidant and osmoprotective actions, provides a strong mechanistic rationale for addressing the metabolic and oxidative stress components of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Jones et al., 2010). The compound’s extensive history of use as a dietary supplement and its well-characterized safety profile—in which high oral doses have been administered with minimal toxicity—support its potential for repurposing in an ocular application (Flanagan et al., 2010; Mollica et al., 2017).  
However, there are potential limitations that merit cautious consideration. Direct evidence of L-carnitine’s efficacy in RPE cells specifically within the context of dry AMD is currently limited. While preclinical studies in non-ocular tissues and some ocular models suggest beneficial mitochondrial and antioxidant effects, the precise dosing, ocular bioavailability, and long-term impact on retinal degeneration remain to be rigorously established. Moreover, while L-carnitine can enhance mitochondrial function, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD implies that a monotherapy approach might not be sufficient; a combination therapy strategy—potentially incorporating other mitochondrial or antioxidant agents—may ultimately prove more effective (Shamsi et al., 2007; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a).  
In summary, the strengths of L-carnitine include its well-established role in cellular energy metabolism, its safety profile and widespread clinical use in other metabolic conditions, and its potential to mitigate ROS production and oxidative damage through enhanced fatty acid oxidation. The weaknesses primarily lie in the current paucity of direct evidence in ocular models of dry AMD and the challenges associated with ensuring adequate drug delivery to the RPE in vivo. Nonetheless, given the overall mechanistic promise and the favorable tolerability observed in numerous studies, L-carnitine warrants further investigation – with a focus on in vitro RPE assays under condition of lipid overload and oxidative stress, followed by in vivo preclinical models of geographic atrophy – to validate its efficacy as a repurposed therapy for dry AMD (Jones et al., 2010; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c; Ates et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2024).  
Overall, I recommend proceeding with targeted experiments to assess mitochondrial respiration, ROS levels, and cell survival in RPE cultures treated with L-carnitine. These studies should be complemented with investigations of tissue distribution following ocular delivery to address bioavailability concerns. This comprehensive evaluation supports the potential of L-carnitine as a metabolic and antioxidant therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, while also highlighting areas where additional data are needed before clinical translation.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
A-438079 is a synthetic small-molecule antagonist of the purinergic P2X7 receptor (P2X7R) originating from Abbott Laboratories’ disubstituted tetrazole series discovered by high-throughput screening and refined by structure–activity relationship (SAR) optimization within a 1-benzyl-5-aryltetrazole chemotype (tetrazole > triazole > pyrazole/imidazole in potency) (Romagnoli et al., 2008; Carroll et al., 2009). A-438079’s structure has been disclosed as 3-((5-(2,3-dichlorophenyl)-1H-tetrazol-1-yl)methyl)pyridine, capturing the two key medicinal chemistry decisions that produced a selective, drug-like P2X7 antagonist: (i) a conserved 2,3-dichlorophenyl “left-hand” aryl that supports potency and (ii) installation of a 3-pyridyl “right-hand” substituent to overcome the solubility liabilities of the original 1-benzyl-5-aryltetrazoles while maintaining submicromolar activity at human/rat P2X7 (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; Romagnoli et al., 2008; Carroll et al., 2009). Functionally, A-438079 is a reversible, competitive P2X7 antagonist that inhibits BzATP-stimulated calcium flux, P2X7-associated macropore formation, and downstream IL-1β release in macrophage-lineage systems, consistent with canonical P2X7 pharmacology linked to NLRP3 inflammasome activation (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007). Cross-source potency data place A-438079 in the mid-nanomolar to low-submicromolar range at human and rat P2X7: human P2X7 pIC50 values of ~6.3–6.9, rat P2X7 pIC50 ~6.5, and functional IC50 estimates of ~0.1 µM (rat) and ~0.3 µM (human), with high selectivity against other P2 subtypes (e.g., P2X7 IC50 0.06 µM vs >100 µM for other subtypes in one panel) (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; El Idrissi et al., 2024; Nagy, 2013). A-438079 was commercialized by Tocris (circa 2008) as a first widely available, selective P2X7 antagonist probe, enabling consistent interrogation of P2X7 biology in vitro and in vivo beyond earlier nonselective tools (e.g., KN-62, Evans Blue) (Felix et al., 2012). Within the broader class, many P2X7 antagonists have reached advanced preclinical characterization; multi-parameter tables in retinal disease–focused reviews list A-438079 as active at human/rat P2X7 with a reported brain:plasma ratio near 2.0 (suggesting central barrier penetration) and note that progress toward ocular/CNS indications has been limited by species specificity and insufficient barrier penetration for some chemotypes (Fletcher et al., 2019).  

Therapeutic History  
A-438079 and related Abbott “A-series” P2X7 antagonists established robust preclinical efficacy in neuropathic and inflammatory pain models, aligning with the role of P2X7-driven IL-1β/IL-18 signaling in nociception and neuroinflammation (Carroll et al., 2009). A-438079 reduced mechanical allodynia in the Chung and Bennett rat models, showed activity in vincristine neuropathy and the formalin persistent pain test, and inhibited evoked and spontaneous spinal neuronal firing in vivo without motor impairment (rotarod) at high i.p. doses, supporting a favorable preclinical therapeutic index in pain paradigms (Carroll et al., 2009). Beyond pain, class summaries attribute anti-seizure effects to A-438079 in a mouse intra-amygdala kainic acid model, situating P2X7 antagonism within a broader CNS neuroinflammation–linked efficacy landscape (Gelin et al., 2020).  

Human cell assays demonstrate that A-438079 and closely related antagonists abolish ATP-induced P2X7 pore function (ethidium or YO-PRO uptake) yet spare phagocytic uptake in CD14+ human monocytes, indicating that P2X7’s pro-inflammatory macropore function can be selectively blocked while preserving innate scavenger activity; this pharmacological dissociation is a core objective for neurodegenerative/retinal indications where loss of phagocytosis may worsen pathology (Gu & Wiley, 2018).  

Clinically, the P2X7 antagonist class has mixed outcomes in peripheral inflammatory diseases: randomized Phase 2 trials in rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn’s disease failed to meet objective inflammation endpoints (ACR20, CRP), although AZD9056 showed symptom benefit (abdominal pain, mental component score) in Crohn’s disease; no P2X7 antagonist has been trialed in neurodegenerative indications to date, and none has entered clinical testing specifically for ocular/retinal diseases (Gu & Wiley, 2018; Fletcher et al., 2019). Nevertheless, the latest brain-penetrant small molecules (e.g., JNJ55308942, JNJ5417446) demonstrate oral brain exposure and dose-dependent suppression of IL-1β release in stimulated whole blood/PBMCs in humans, suggesting that pharmacodynamic endpoints and barrier penetration necessary for CNS/retinal therapy are tractable within this target class (Fletcher et al., 2019).  

Retinal and AMD-relevant preclinical evidence for P2X7 antagonism is substantial at the class level. P2X7 is expressed across retinal compartments including RPE, photoreceptors, bipolar/horizontal/amacrine neurons, retinal ganglion cells, Müller glia, and microglia in mouse, rat, and human; functional agonism (e.g., BzATP) modulates retinal responses that are attenuated in P2X7-null mice, confirming a functional purinergic ATP/P2X7 axis in vivo (Fletcher et al., 2019). Sustained elevations of extracellular ATP are documented in ocular disease (e.g., human chronic glaucoma aqueous humor), and endogenous ATP mediates acute RGC injury following intraocular pressure spikes in rodents; degrading ATP or blocking P2X7 prevents RGC injury in vivo, demonstrating disease-relevant ATP surges capable of activating P2X7 in the retina (Fletcher et al., 2019). AMD-relevant biology includes high vitreous ATP, P2X7-dependent NLRP3 inflammasome activation by Alu RNA in geographic atrophy (GA) models, and P2X7-driven Ca2+-dependent apoptosis in RPE, together implicating P2X7 as a key upstream activator of inflammasome-mediated retinal degeneration (Calzaferri et al., 2020).  

For A-438079 specifically, a curated review table lists it among P2X7 antagonists evaluated in retinal contexts including ARPE-19 RPE cells, C57BL/6J mouse retinal degeneration models (e.g., MNU), and human pericytes, with endpoints encompassing NLRP3/IL-1β signaling, VEGF, ROS, ZO-1 barrier integrity, NF-κB activation, and apoptosis; outcomes are usually protective though model- and endpoint-specific variability exists (Li & Wang, 2025). In allied class work, selective P2X7 blockade with A-740003 in ARPE-19 cells and C57BL/6 mice exposed to oxidized LDL reduced ROS, suppressed NLRP3 inflammasome and NF-κB activation, decreased IL-1β/IL-18 and proangiogenic factors (VEGF, HIF-1α), alleviated retinal neovascularization, and preserved ERG amplitudes, anchoring mechanistic and functional retinal benefits to P2X7 antagonism (Yang et al., 2021). More broadly, P2X7 antagonists have protected retinal ganglion cells in chronic ocular hypertension by inhibiting microglial activation and reversed hyperpermeability and VEGF/IL-6 increases in diabetic retinal models, indicating barrier and neuroinflammatory benefits that are relevant to AMD pathophysiology (Li & Wang, 2025). Finally, in AMD-relevant disease models, P2X7 antagonists suppressed clinical symptoms of GA and CNV in animals; however, complete genetic ablation yielded mixed results (e.g., P2X7−/− protected from GA but not laser-induced CNV), emphasizing the need to preserve beneficial scavenger functions while blocking pro-inflammatory pore signaling (Gu & Wiley, 2018).  

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, P2X7 is a trimeric, low-sensitivity ATP-gated cation channel that mediates Na+, Ca2+, and K+ fluxes and, upon sustained or high agonist exposure, transitions into a large nonselective macropore permeable to molecules up to ~900 Da (e.g., YO-PRO-1), a state tightly coupled to K+ efflux and subsequent NLRP3 inflammasome activation with maturation/release of IL-1β and IL-18 (Fletcher et al., 2019). Two main routes connect P2X7 activity to IL-1β biology: (i) pore-dependent K+ efflux promotes inflammasome assembly and caspase-1 activation to process pro-IL-1β/pro-IL-18; and (ii) P2X7-mediated Ca2+ influx contributes to NF-κB activation and transcriptional priming of inflammasome components and pro-cytokines, forming the two-signal paradigm required for IL-1β/IL-18 maturation and pyroptosis (Calzaferri et al., 2020).  

In the retinal pigment epithelium, extracellular ATP is a canonical danger-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) produced by stressed/dying cells; ARPE-19 cells themselves release ATP and exhibit P2X7- and pannexin-1 (Panx1)-linked mechanisms that drive NLRP3 inflammasome activation, caspase-1 cleavage, gasdermin D pore formation, and secretion of IL-1β/IL-18, pathways that converge on inflammatory and pyroptotic injury of RPE (Youn, 2024). P2X7 functionally recruits Panx1, facilitating ATP and solute release that amplifies local ATP and P2X7 activation; in ARPE-19 cells, 25-hydroxycholesterol triggers P2X7-dependent YO-PRO uptake that is sensitive to Panx1 blockade (probenecid), indicating a Panx1-dependent pore component in RPE injury (Yang, 2017). P2X7 activation is also linked to mitochondrial distress, including cytochrome-c release and activation of executioner caspases (3/8/9), mechanistically tying the receptor to ROS (including mitochondrial ROS) and apoptotic/mixed death cascades relevant to retinal degeneration (Unknown Reference).  

Retinal localization and disease relevance are broad. Multiple P2X7 splice variants are present in the retina (with at least one common knockout deleting only the full-length variant), and P2X7 is reported in neurons (photoreceptors, amacrine, ganglion cells), glia (microglia, Müller cells), and RPE across species; application of BzATP modulates retinal responses that are attenuated in P2X7-null mice, and genetic/clinical associations link P2X7/P2X4 variants to advanced AMD risk (Fletcher et al., 2019). In ARPE-19 and native/cultured human RPE, P2X7 is expressed at mRNA and protein levels, and it is the only P2X subtype that requires high ATP for activation—conditions that occur during retinal injury/inflammation and are observed in ocular fluids in disease (note: P2X4 can be more abundant than P2X7 in ARPE-19 at baseline, which can shape net purinergic responses) (Youn, 2024).  

Within this mechanistic framework, A-438079 engages P2X7 as a reversible, competitive antagonist, blocking ATP/BzATP-evoked channel activation and macropore formation; by doing so, it suppresses P2X7-mediated Ca2+ influx and K+ efflux that are required for NF-κB priming and NLRP3 activation, respectively, leading to reduced caspase-1 cleavage and decreased maturation/secretion of IL-1β/IL-18 (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; Fletcher et al., 2019; Calzaferri et al., 2020). In macrophage-lineage systems and fresh human monocytes, A-438079 or closely related antagonists abolish P2X7 pore function and IL-1β release but preserve phagocytosis, directly supporting a therapeutic goal in neurodegeneration/retinal disease to block pro-inflammatory pore/inflammasome signaling while sparing scavenger functions that may be beneficial for debris clearance (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; Gu & Wiley, 2018).

A-438079 is a strong mechanistic fit for the proposed hypothesis in dry AMD: blocking P2X7 on RPE to prevent ATP-induced Ca2+ influx, dampen K+ efflux–dependent NLRP3 activation, reduce caspase-1 cleavage and IL-1β/IL-18 release, mitigate ROS including mtROS, and preserve epithelial barrier integrity (TEER/ZO-1) under ATP-rich or drusen-mimetic stressors (amyloid-β, oxysterols, Alu RNA) (Fletcher et al., 2019; Youn, 2024; Yang, 2017; Calzaferri et al., 2020). The compound’s pore-block/phagocytosis-preserve profile in human monocytes maps to the desired retinal strategy to avoid the liabilities of global P2X7 loss while selectively suppressing pro-inflammatory outputs (Gu & Wiley, 2018). Given the breadth of class-level retinal evidence and the explicit inclusion of A-438079 in retinal model tables, the candidate merits systematic validation in AMD-proximal RPE assays and in vivo GA-like models, with early emphasis on human-cell PD (Ca2+ flux, YO-PRO uptake, IL-1β/IL-18), epithelial barrier endpoints (TEER/ZO-1), and ocular PK/PD to quantify target engagement at the retina (Li & Wang, 2025; Yang et al., 2021; Li & Wang, 2025; Fletcher et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is an endogenous ketone body produced by mitochondrial ketogenesis from fatty-acid–derived acetyl-CoA, classically in hepatocytes but also in extrahepatic cell types including the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and several neuronal lineages (enzymatic pathway: ACAT, HMGCS2, HMGCL, and BDH1) (Wang et al., 2021; Gough, 2021). In physiological and nutritional ketosis, circulating BHB rises from baseline (~0.05–0.1 mM) to levels >0.5 mM and up to 5–7 mM with prolonged fasting, providing an alternative oxidative substrate for extrahepatic mitochondria when carbohydrate availability is limited (Wang et al., 2021; Cooper et al., 2023). BHB and acetoacetate are transported into and out of cells via proton-linked monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs) such as MCT1 and MCT2 that are expressed at the blood–retinal barrier and in retinal cells, enabling substrate entry into the retina (Yang, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Gough, 2021). RPEs robustly express mitochondrial HMGCS2 and can ketogenize palmitate to BHB, secreting BHB via MCT1; retinal cells can take up and metabolize BHB into Krebs-cycle intermediates and amino acids, indicating functional capacity to use BHB as mitochondrial fuel in the outer retina (Yang, 2021). More recent mass spectrometry–based reassessment shows that RPE secretion of BHB is substantially lower than previously estimated by enzymatic kits, that RPE exports BHB to both apical and basal compartments, and that RPE both produces and consumes BHB depending on nutrient state—important considerations for experimental design and therapeutic targeting (Gulette et al., 2024).  

BHB belongs to the class of endogenous metabolic intermediates that function dually as oxidative fuels (via oxidation to acetyl-CoA and entry into TCA cycle) and signaling molecules with paracrine/autocrine receptor and epigenetic actions (e.g., agonism at HCAR2/GPR109A and inhibition of class I/IIa histone deacetylases) (Wang et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Kovács et al., 2021). As a therapeutic modality, BHB has been delivered exogenously as salts/esters or induced endogenously through ketogenic diets, fasting, or exercise to support mitochondrial ATP production and alter cellular stress responses in the CNS, heart, and skeletal muscle (Cooper et al., 2023; Kovács et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2022). In retinal disease models, ketogenic interventions or exogenous BHB have reduced oxidative/inflammatory injury and improved functional measures, though direct application to dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) has not yet been clinically tested (Gough, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021).  

Therapeutic History  
Ketone biology has a long history in neurology and cardiometabolic research, where BHB has been shown to preserve mitochondrial function, increase ATP production, and blunt oxidative injury in ischemia, neurodegeneration models, and skeletal muscle stress paradigms (Kovács et al., 2021; Mierziak et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2018). In neural tissues, ketogenic interventions and exogenous ketones prevent synaptic dysfunction induced by respiratory complex inhibitors and increase the brain NAD⁺/NADH ratio, correlating with decreased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation (Morris et al., 2020). In rat skeletal muscle cells, 5 mM BHB for 24–48 h increased respiratory control, ATP-linked respiration, P:O efficiency, lowered H₂O₂ production, and shifted mitochondrial dynamics toward fusion via DRP1 suppression—consistent with enhanced bioenergetics and decreased oxidative stress (Parker et al., 2018). In primary neurons, BHB maintained oxidative phosphorylation under glutamate workload even when cytosolic NADH transfer via the malate–aspartate shuttle was inhibited, demonstrating that BHB can sustain respiration under conditions that impair glycolytic NADH coupling to mitochondria (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

In the retina and optic nerve, multiple preclinical models show that ketogenic exposures or direct ketone administration reduce oxidative stress and inflammation, preserve function, and limit neuronal death. Intraperitoneal BHB and acetoacetate reduced NMDA-induced retinal ganglion cell (RGC) death in rats, and ketogenic diet attenuated NMDA-induced RGC injury in juvenile rats (Gough, 2021). In ocular blast or optic neuropathy paradigms, ketogenic diet prevented increases in superoxide and IL-1α, preserved visual evoked potentials, and reduced astrocytic hypertrophy and optic nerve death (Gough, 2021). In glaucoma models, ketogenic diet improved RGC soma/axon survival, axonal transport, and reduced gliosis, with increases in NAD and NAD:NADH ratio and upregulation of MCT1/MCT2 in optic nerve (Tribble et al., 2021). AAV-mediated MCT2 overexpression (increasing uptake of lactate/pyruvate/ketones) preserved RGCs and optic nerve axons in ocular hypertension and glaucoma models and elevated markers of mitochondrial biogenesis and function (PGC1α, COX, SDH) and antioxidant defense (SOD2) (Gough, 2021). However, in at least one RGC injury model, daily intraperitoneal BHB or acetoacetate did not replicate ketogenic diet neuroprotection, underscoring differences between exogenous ketone dosing and the systemic/multifactorial effects of ketogenic diets (Tribble et al., 2021).  

Within the RPE compartment specifically, two lines of evidence are relevant: (1) BHB protects ARPE-19 cells from high-glucose–induced injury, improving viability, alleviating cell cycle arrest, and modulating inflammatory mediators (IL-8, IL-17α, MCP-1) at millimolar concentrations achievable with nutritional ketosis or exogenous supplementation (Argentino et al., 2025). (2) HCAR2/GPR109A, a BHB receptor, is robustly expressed by the RPE; BHB agonism reduced retinal leukocyte infiltration in LPS-challenged mice in an HCAR2-dependent manner, and loss of HCAR2 in RPE led to barrier dysfunction (ZO-1 defects) and increased immune cell infiltrates, indicating that BHB–HCAR2 signaling can preserve an immunoinhibitory retinal environment (Powell et al., 2021). In diabetic retinopathy models, systemic BHB activation of HCA2 reduced ER stress and NLRP3 inflammasome signaling and ameliorated retinal pathology, establishing anti-inflammatory and ER stress–limiting actions in retina (Trotta et al., 2019).  

In inherited retinal degeneration models, ketogenic interventions delayed photoreceptor degeneration and improved electroretinogram (ERG) amplitudes and outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness in rd10 and Pde6a mice, and a soluble ketogenic formulation partially restored vision and survival in PDH-deficient noir zebrafish—consistent with bypassing PDH to supply acetyl-CoA and support neurotransmitter synthesis (Gough, 2021). Notwithstanding these encouraging signals, the literature consistently notes the absence of clinical trials evaluating ketogenic interventions or BHB in retinitis pigmentosa or AMD patients, and reports potentially adverse effects of ketogenic diets in wild-type mice (decreased ERG amplitudes, altered albumin/weight), highlighting translational uncertainties and the need to distinguish effects of BHB from the broader systemic consequences of diet (Gough, 2021).  

Mechanism of Action  
BHB acts through convergent metabolic, redox, mitochondrial, inflammatory, and epigenetic mechanisms that are mechanistically aligned with the pathophysiology of RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic oxidative/inflammatory stress in dry AMD.  

- Alternative mitochondrial fuel and bioenergetics support. In extrahepatic tissues (including retina), BHB oxidation proceeds via mitochondrial BDH1 (βHB→acetoacetate) followed by SCOT/OXCT1 (AcAc→AcAc-CoA using succinyl-CoA) and acetyl-CoA production for TCA entry and ATP generation, enabling substrate-level maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and oxidative phosphorylation under glucose restriction or impaired glycolytic NADH transfer (Wang et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023). The retina expresses monocarboxylate transport routes (e.g., MCT1 at the inner blood–retinal barrier; MCT2 in neurons), and RPE expresses MCT1 and can both produce and consume BHB, providing a plausible uptake pathway for exogenous BHB into RPE and neighboring retinal cells (Tribble et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Gulette et al., 2024). In neurons, BHB-supported respiration remains robust when the malate–aspartate shuttle is blocked with AOAA—conditions that decrease glucose-fueled ATP synthesis—indicating that BHB can preserve mitochondrial ATP synthesis and respiratory control when cytosolic NADH transfer is compromised, a scenario relevant to glycolysis-impaired RPE (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

- Redox coupling and ROS control. The interconversion of acetoacetate and BHB by βHB dehydrogenase is linked to NADH/NAD⁺ redox; acetoacetate→BHB requires oxidation of NADH to NAD⁺, and nutritional ketosis in human brain increases NAD⁺/NADH ratio, correlating with reductions in mitochondrial ROS generation (Gough, 2021; Morris et al., 2020). Ketones can inhibit mitochondrial ROS production by increasing NADH oxidation, and ketogenic interventions increase NAD⁺/NADH in vivo, though tissue- and context-dependent effects exist (Morris et al., 2020). Complementary cardiac literature reports that β-OHB can reduce the mitochondrial NAD couple while oxidizing coenzyme Q, emphasizing that BHB modulates both NADH/NAD⁺ and Q/QH₂ redox pairs in mitochondria—with directionality that may depend on prevailing substrate status and respiratory state (Chu et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion models and muscle cells, BHB lowers mitochondrial ROS, decreases mitochondrial swelling, maintains Δψm, and increases ATP production, consistent with direct mitochondrial protection (Mierziak et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2018).  

- Antioxidant transcription (Nrf2) and hormesis. Ketogenic exposures can induce a hormetic redox signal that activates Keap1–Nrf2, increasing transcription of detoxification and antioxidant genes; in retina, ketone body exposure mimicked calorie restriction via fumarate–Nrf2 activation (Gough, 2021; Fu et al., 2020). Preclinical optic/retinal models link these antioxidant transcriptional effects to preserved function and reduced oxidative markers (NOS, MDA, superoxide) (Gough, 2021).  

- Anti-inflammatory signaling via HCAR2/ARRB2 and NLRP3/NF-κB suppression. BHB is a ligand for HCAR1/HCAR2 receptors; HCAR2 is robustly expressed in human RPE and retina, and receptor activation by BHB reduces leukocyte infiltration and preserves RPE barrier integrity in inflammation models (Powell et al., 2021). Downstream, BHB–HCAR signaling recruits β-arrestin-2 (ARRB2) that binds NLRP3 to block inflammasome assembly, decreasing ASC and preventing K⁺ efflux to suppress IL-1β maturation; BHB also activates a COX1/PGD2 cascade that inhibits IKK and NF-κB nuclear translocation, reducing TNF-α and microglial/macrophage activation (Gough, 2021). In diabetic retina, systemic BHB–HCA2 activation suppressed ER stress and NLRP3 inflammasome activity, demonstrating the retinal anti-inflammatory efficacy of this axis (Trotta et al., 2019).  

- Mitochondrial calcium homeostasis and mPTP stabilization. In human iPSC-derived microglia, amyloid-β oligomers increased MCU expression, raised mitochondrial Ca²⁺ ~40%, elevated mtROS, and triggered mPTP opening; BHB normalized MCU, decreased mtCa²⁺/mtROS, and completely reversed mPTP activation, restoring phagocytic function (Jin et al., 2023). Although not conducted in RPE, these mitochondrial-stabilizing effects are mechanistically relevant to post-mitotic cells with high oxidative load.  

- Epigenetic modulation and mitochondrial biogenesis. BHB is an endogenous inhibitor of class I/IIa HDACs at physiological millimolar concentrations, leading to histone hyperacetylation and upregulation of FOXO3a and metallothionein genes that encode antioxidant defenses; BHB also increases intracellular acetyl-CoA and supports protein acetylation, and can β-hydroxybutyrylate histones, adding layers of gene regulatory control tied to mitochondrial status (Yang, 2021; Kovács et al., 2021; Mierziak et al., 2021). Through HDAC inhibition and receptor-mediated signaling, BHB increases BDNF via cAMP/PKA/CREB, activates SIRT1/SIRT3 via AMPK/HCA2/NAD⁺ pathways, and promotes PGC1α-driven mitochondrial biogenesis and UCP2 expression that collectively improve mitochondrial function and antioxidant capacity (Kovács et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022). In retinal/optic nerve models, ketogenic diet or enhanced monocarboxylate uptake upregulated PGC1α, COX, SDH, and SOD2 while lowering pAMPK/AMPK, linking substrate availability to mitochondrial biogenesis and anti-inflammatory signaling (Gough, 2021).  

- Immunometabolic reprogramming in retina/CNS. Ketogenic interventions increased anti-inflammatory mediators (IL-4, Arginase-1) and M2-like microglia while decreasing IBA-1⁺ macrophage/microglia, consistent with dampened neuroinflammation secondary to improved bioenergetics (reduced AMPK activation) and prevention of NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation (Gough, 2021). BHB also inhibits FFAR3/GPR41, reducing sympathetic activity in mice, indicating broader metabolic signaling roles that could modulate retinal perfusion/metabolism indirectly (Gough, 2021).  

Collectively, these mechanisms—fuel substitution that sustains Δψm and ATP synthesis under glycolytic impairment, improved redox balance with decreased mitochondrial ROS, Nrf2-dependent antioxidant gene induction, NLRP3/NF-κB anti-inflammatory actions via HCAR2/ARRB2, stabilization of mitochondrial Ca²⁺/mPTP, and epigenetic programs that support mitochondrial biogenesis—map directly onto pathologies implicated in RPE degeneration in dry AMD and provide multiple rescue nodes testable in disease-relevant models (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Gough, 2021; Powell et al., 2021).  

Expected Effect  
Assay context: The working hypothesis is that exogenous BHB will serve as an alternative mitochondrial substrate in RPE, sustaining Δψm and reducing NADH-driven mitochondrial ROS when glycolysis is impaired—conditions that model bioenergetic stress in geographic atrophy. Mechanistically, this is supported by three converging evidence streams: (1) mitochondrial fuel flexibility to oxidize BHB to acetyl-CoA via BDH1/SCOT, (2) redox modulation that increases NADH oxidation and elevates the NAD⁺/NADH ratio, and (3) multi-layered antioxidant/anti-inflammatory signaling that lowers mitochondrial ROS production and downstream inflammasome/NF-κB activation (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Gough, 2021).  

- Sustained Δψm and ATP under glycolytic impairment. RPE expresses ketogenesis machinery (HMGCS2) and monocarboxylate transport capacity (MCT1) and is capable of both producing and consuming BHB, while inner BRB MCT1 and neuronal MCT2 provide routes for substrate delivery into retinal tissue (Yang, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Gulette et al., 2024). In neurons, BHB preserved oxidative phosphorylation and ATP-linked respiration under MAS inhibition, a condition that effectively reduces mitochondrial access to cytosolic NADH from glycolysis; this predicts that, in RPE exposed to glycolytic blockade or high work demand, BHB could maintain Δψm and respiratory control by supplying acetyl-CoA independent of cytosolic NADH shuttling (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023). In muscle and cardiac models, BHB improved respiratory control ratios, increased ATP production, and maintained Δψm under stress, providing precedent for Δψm preservation in high-energy post-mitotic cells (Parker et al., 2018; Mierziak et al., 2021).  

- Lowered NADH-driven mtROS and improved redox balance. Nutritional ketosis increases the brain NAD⁺/NADH ratio and ketones inhibit mitochondrial ROS production by increasing NADH oxidation, a shift that is expected to suppress reverse electron transport and semiquinone leak at respiratory complexes under high NADH load (Morris et al., 2020). Although some cardiac literature reports context-dependent changes in the mitochondrial NAD couple under BHB with concurrent oxidation of coenzyme Q, the net effect across neural and muscle studies is reduced mitochondrial ROS generation and improved redox handling, a phenotype also observed in optic/retinal models after ketogenic interventions (Chu et al., 2021; Gough, 2021; Mierziak et al., 2021). These redox improvements are reinforced by Nrf2 activation and increased expression of antioxidant defenses (e.g., SOD2), which increase ROS quenching capacity in retinal and optic tissues (Gough, 2021).  

- Anti-inflammatory and barrier-preserving actions in RPE. BHB agonizes HCAR2 expressed by RPE and retinal microglia, reducing leukocyte infiltration, preserving tight junction integrity (ZO-1), and suppressing inflammasome/NF-κB signaling (Powell et al., 2021; Trotta et al., 2019). In hyperglycemic ARPE-19, BHB improved viability and cell cycle progression and modulated inflammatory cytokines, consistent with protection under metabolic stress (Argentino et al., 2025). By preserving ATP and lowering AMPK phosphorylation, BHB/ketone availability is expected to block NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation and downstream expression of IL-6 and TNF-α, reducing the chronic para-inflammatory milieu implicated in RPE degeneration (Gough, 2021).  

- Translational considerations for exposure and transport. Systemically delivered BHB can traverse the blood–retinal barrier via MCT1, and RPE’s own MCT1 provides transmembrane transport capacity; nonetheless, quantitative extracellular BHB at RPE surfaces is likely in the low micromolar range under basal conditions, and RPE produces and consumes BHB dynamically, implying that achieving therapeutic mitochondrial utilization in RPE will require millimolar plasma BHB or local delivery (Tribble et al., 2021; Gulette et al., 2024). Nutritional ketosis and exogenous ketone supplementation readily achieve 0.5–2 mM BHB in plasma in rodent and human studies, which are the concentrations used in many in vitro protection assays (Cooper et al., 2023; Argentino et al., 2025).  

Key readouts and validation metrics for the proposed assay should include Δψm (e.g., TMRM/TMRE), OCR/ECAR profiling and ATP-linked respiration (Seahorse), mitochondrial ROS (MitoSOX and H₂O₂ flux), NAD⁺/NADH ratio (enzymatic cycling and/or fluorescence lifetime imaging), pAMPK/AMPK and NF-κB p65 nuclear localization, Nrf2 translocation and target gene induction (e.g., SOD2), and inflammasome readouts (ASC specks, IL-1β maturation) (Gough, 2021). Given the measurement pitfalls documented in RPE ketone assays, BHB should be quantified by LC–MS/MS or after removal of high-MW confounders by size exclusion rather than by standard enzymatic kits (Gulette et al., 2024).  
Protein expression considerations support the mechanism in the target cell type. HCAR2/GPR109A is expressed by RPE and retinal microglia/endothelium and mediates anti-inflammatory effects of BHB in vivo, making receptor-dependent components of BHB action directly testable in RPE (Powell et al., 2021). RPE expresses HMGCS2 and MCT1, and retinal cells metabolize BHB into TCA intermediates, consistent with BDH1/SCOT/OXCT1 pathway activity enabling BHB oxidation in retinal tissues; while direct SCOT expression in RPE is not provided here, the metabolic tracing data indicating conversion of BHB to Krebs intermediates in retinal cells justify testing oxidative utilization in RPE (Yang, 2021; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strength of biological rationale. The core hypothesis—that BHB can act as an alternative mitochondrial fuel to sustain Δψm and lower NADH-driven mitochondrial ROS in glycolysis-impaired RPE—is strongly aligned with BHB’s established roles in extrahepatic tissues and is supported by multiple mechanistic strands in relevant neural and retinal systems (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023). BHB oxidation provides acetyl-CoA and maintains respiration when glycolytic NADH transfer is compromised, as demonstrated in primary neurons; BHB reduces mtROS, preserves Δψm, and increases ATP in ischemic muscle/heart models; and nutrient ketosis increases the NAD⁺/NADH ratio and lowers ROS production in brain—effects that would be expected to decrease reverse-electron transport–driven ROS at complex I and stabilize mitochondrial function in stressed RPE (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023; Mierziak et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020). In retinal tissue, ketogenic interventions and direct ketone administration reduce oxidative injury, preserve function, and enhance mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses in RGC/optic nerve models, while anti-inflammatory benefits via HCAR2—expressed by RPE—reduce leukocyte infiltration and preserve barrier integrity (Gough, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Powell et al., 2021; Trotta et al., 2019). The mitochondrial stabilization effects observed in human microglia—lower MCU/mtCa²⁺, reduced mtROS, prevention of mPTP opening—further support a BHB-mediated mitochondrial resilience phenotype that is likely relevant to RPE (Jin et al., 2023).  

Evidence relevant to the target tissue. RPEs possess ketone-related transport and enzymatic capacity (HMGCS2, MCT1) and can both produce and consume BHB; they are responsive to BHB in vitro under metabolic stress (hyperglycemia) with improved viability and inflammatory marker modulation (Yang, 2021; Argentino et al., 2025). HCAR2-mediated anti-inflammatory and barrier maintenance functions have been demonstrated in RPE/retina, providing a receptor-proximal pathway for BHB to suppress chronic para-inflammation and preserve RPE junctional integrity, both relevant to dry AMD pathobiology (Powell et al., 2021). While direct measurements of BDH1/SCOT activity and NAD⁺/NADH dynamics in human RPE treated with BHB remain to be shown here, the metabolic fate of BHB in retinal cells and robust mitochondrial effects in closely related cell types make the translational experiments technically feasible and mechanistically justified (Yang, 2021; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

Translational gaps and risks. No clinical trials have evaluated ketogenic diets or BHB specifically for RP or AMD, and some ketogenic diet studies reported adverse outcomes in wild-type animals (decreased ERG amplitude, altered serum albumin/weight), emphasizing the need to decouple BHB’s effects from broader dietary/metabolic confounders (Gough, 2021). Direct BHB delivery does not always recapitulate ketogenic diet benefits in RGC injury, suggesting that multi-target effects of diet (e.g., NAD metabolism, mTOR, microbiome) contribute to efficacy; this implies that BHB monotherapy may require combination strategies (e.g., nicotinamide co-therapy) or optimized dosing to achieve comparable benefit (Tribble et al., 2021). Quantification of BHB in RPE experiments is non-trivial due to assay interference; LC–MS/MS or validated size-exclusion protocols must be used to avoid false positives and to measure physiologically relevant, often low-micromolar extracellular BHB in RPE cultures (Gulette et al., 2024). Finally, the directionality of NAD redox effects may be context dependent (reports of both increased NAD⁺/NADH ratio in brain and reduced mitochondrial NAD couple in cardiac models), requiring careful interpretation with compartment-specific assays in RPE (Morris et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2021).  

Development path and decision points. Given the strong mechanistic rationale, retina-focused preclinical evidence, and RPE receptor expression data, BHB is a plausible repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD that merits rigorous, RPE-centric validation. Key go/no-go preclinical criteria should include: (1) demonstration that BHB rescues Δψm and ATP-linked respiration in primary human RPE or iPSC-RPE under glycolytic impairment (e.g., 2-deoxyglucose or low glucose plus workload), (2) reduction of mitochondrial ROS (MitoSOX/H₂O₂ flux) and elevation of cellular NAD⁺/NADH ratio with BHB, (3) suppression of pAMPK and NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation, induction of Nrf2 target genes, and reduction of NLRP3 activation, (4) persistence of benefits under HCAR2 antagonism/knockdown to parse receptor versus fuel contributions, and (5) confirmation that effects are contingent on monocarboxylate transport (MCT inhibition) and SCOT activity (e.g., OXCT1 knockdown), which would mechanistically link outcomes to BHB oxidation rather than unrelated signaling (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023; Gough, 2021; Powell et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021). In vivo, a dry-AMD–relevant RPE degeneration model should test systemic or ocular BHB delivery (dose selection to 0.5–2 mM plasma equivalents) with readouts of RPE mitochondrial structure/function, subretinal inflammation, and lesion progression; blood–retina transport via MCT1 at the inner BRB suggests systemic exposure can reach the retina, though intraocular routes might achieve higher local concentrations (Tribble et al., 2021). Throughout, BHB dosing must be titrated to avoid off-target effects and electrolyte load associated with some salt formulations; direct ketone esters or controlled dietary induction may be considered for translational studies, recognizing model-specific differences seen between exogenous BHB and ketogenic diet (Tribble et al., 2021).  

Strengths  
- Mechanistic breadth and convergence on AMD-relevant pathways: alternative fuel supply to support Δψm/ATP, improved NAD redox and ROS control, Nrf2 antioxidant gene induction, and potent suppression of NLRP3/NF-κB–mediated para-inflammation via HCAR2—each independently linked to retinal/RPE resilience (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Gough, 2021; Powell et al., 2021).  
- Retinal delivery/uptake plausibility: MCT expression at the inner BRB and in RPE, plus RPE’s ability to both produce and consume BHB, establish physiological routes for BHB transit and utilization in target tissues (Tribble et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Gulette et al., 2024).  
- Preclinical efficacy signals in retinal and CNS models: reduced oxidative/inflammatory injury, preserved neuronal function, enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis/antioxidant defenses, and receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory actions in retina (Gough, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Trotta et al., 2019; Powell et al., 2021).  
- Compatibility with RPE stress biology: BHB improved ARPE-19 survival under metabolic stress and modulated cytokines, and microglial mitochondrial data demonstrate BHB reverses mtCa²⁺/mtROS/mPTP derangements that are mechanistically relevant to RPE degeneration (Argentino et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2023).  

Weaknesses and uncertainties  
- Lack of AMD-specific in vivo data and no clinical trials in AMD/RP; extrapolation from RGC/optic nerve/diabetic models requires confirmation in RPE-targeted systems (Gough, 2021).  
- Measurement pitfalls in RPE ketone studies; reliance on inaccurate enzymatic assays historically confounded interpretation, necessitating MS-based quantitation and careful time-course sampling (Gulette et al., 2024).  
- Context-dependent redox effects; reports differ on NAD couple responses to BHB, indicating the need for compartmentalized NAD⁺/NADH readouts in RPE to avoid misattribution (Morris et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2021).  
- Differences between exogenous BHB and ketogenic diet; some benefits in glaucoma were not reproduced with BHB delivery, suggesting that metabolic co-factors (e.g., NAD boosters) or combinatorial strategies may be required (Tribble et al., 2021).
