Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Deferoxamine (also known as desferrioxamine B; DFO) is a natural microbial siderophore originally isolated from Streptomyces pilosus and developed as an iron‐chelating drug in the 1960s, with clinical deployment beginning in 1968 under the trade name Desferal for treatment of iron overload disorders (notably transfusional iron loading in β-thalassemia) (Faa & Crisponi, 1999; Sharpe et al., 2011; Birch et al., 2006). Chemically, DFO is a hexadentate, tris-hydroxamate ligand that coordinates ferric iron (FeIII) at six oxygen donors derived from three bidentate hydroxamate groups to form a very stable 1:1 FeIII–DFO complex with distorted octahedral FeIIIO6 geometry (Sharpe et al., 2011; Richardson & Poňka, 1998). The FeIII affinity is exceptionally high and selective: reported formation constants for FeIII–DFO include log β110 ≈ 30.5 and conditional pM/pFe values around 26–31, while affinity for FeII is ∼20 orders of magnitude lower, consistent with the observation that DFO selectively chelates FeIII in vivo (Sharpe et al., 2011; Kontoghiorghes & Kontoghiorghe, 2020; Birch et al., 2006). The compound is highly hydrophilic, carries a positive charge near physiological pH, and exhibits poor membrane permeability and oral absorption; as a result, DFO is administered parenterally and tends to localize extracellularly or within endosomal/lysosomal compartments after endocytosis (Birch et al., 2006; Kontoghiorghes & Kontoghiorghe, 2020; Zhao et al., 2021). Pharmacokinetically, native DFO has a very short plasma half-life on the order of minutes, with multiple studies reporting ∼10–30 minutes after intravenous dosing, rapid renal clearance, and elimination of chelated iron via urine and bile; the short exposure necessitates prolonged subcutaneous or intravenous infusions for clinical efficacy (Sharpe et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2020; Entezari et al., 2022). DFO is not blood–neural barrier penetrant, limiting access to the central nervous system and retina when given systemically (Li et al., 2023).

As a class, siderophores are low-molecular microbial metabolites evolved for FeIII acquisition and storage; medicinally, DFO is the prototypical siderophore drug and, for decades, has served as the clinical standard for chelation in iron-overload conditions (Hatcher et al., 2009). Within therapeutic iron chelators, DFO’s hexadentate hydroxamate architecture confers high thermodynamic and kinetic stability of FeIII complexes, limiting redox cycling and hydroxyl radical generation relative to weaker or redox-active iron ligands (Hider & Kong, 2013).

Therapeutic History  
DFO has an extensive clinical history as the benchmark iron chelator for transfusional iron overload, especially in β-thalassemia major and other transfusion-dependent anemias; it was approved in the United States in 1968 and used for decades as life-saving therapy, albeit limited by the need for prolonged parenteral infusions and high cost (Sharpe et al., 2011; Birch et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2012). Beyond chronic iron overload, labeled and established uses include acute iron poisoning and treatment of aluminum toxicity, reflecting DFO’s strong FeIII selectivity and capacity to form inert complexes with polyvalent cations in vivo (Jones et al., 2020). The standard practice has involved subcutaneous or intravenous infusions at 20–60 mg/kg daily for 8–24 hours over 5–7 days per week, with urinary and fecal excretion of iron–DFO complexes as pharmacodynamic endpoints; however, adherence and patient acceptance have been major barriers due to the burdensome administration (Tam et al., 2003; Entezari et al., 2022).

The clinical pharmacology and chemistry of DFO have motivated multiple improved-delivery strategies: liposomal encapsulation and multivesicular liposome systems to extend half-life, and macromolecular conjugates (e.g., starch or HES carriers) to prolong exposure and shift biodistribution to iron-storage organs; these approaches have demonstrated prolonged circulation, increased urinary iron excretion, and organ accumulation (Jones et al., 2020; Sharpe et al., 2011; Tam et al., 2003). Nevertheless, DFO remains orally inactive and requires parenteral dosing, in contrast to later oral chelators (deferiprone, deferasirox), which have supplanted it in many indications due to ease of administration while sometimes being deployed in combination regimens with DFO to enhance iron removal and cardiac protection via complementary pharmacokinetics and chelation kinetics (Hider & Kong, 2013; Ma et al., 2012).

In ophthalmology and retinal biology, DFO’s evaluation is mixed. On one hand, iron chelation with DFO has shown protective effects in experimental retinal contexts: it reduced retinal ganglion cell death induced by hydrogen peroxide and paraquat in oxidative-stress paradigms, consistent with inhibition of iron-dependent hydroxyl radical production (Rohowetz et al., 2018). In hemorrhagic retinal injury, DFO protected photoreceptor tissues after subretinal blood in animal models, suggesting iron chelation can blunt heme/Fe-driven toxicity in the subretinal space (Song & Dunaief, 2013). In RPE-relevant cell models, DFO mitigated lipid peroxidation, prevented glutathione depletion, decreased Fe2+ accumulation, and preserved viability of ARPE-19 cells under tert-butyl hydroperoxide and blue-light stress, and it enhanced cell survival by modulating antioxidant defense systems (GSH–GPX4 and FSP1–CoQ10–NADH axes) (Zhao et al., 2025). A zinc–DFO complex (Zn/DFO) designed to improve cellular delivery reduced retinal iron content, lipid peroxidation, and oxidative DNA damage, preserved photoreceptor structure, and improved ERG responses in rd10 mice, demonstrating in vivo neuroprotection when systemic penetration is enhanced (Zhao et al., 2025). Ex vivo, DFO decreased histochemically detectable chelatable iron (Perls–DAB) in macular sections from AMD eyes, supporting the feasibility of removing pathologic labile iron in human AMD tissue (He et al., 2007).

On the other hand, DFO has a documented profile of retinal/ocular toxicity in patients receiving systemic therapy: reports include macular and peripheral pigmentary degeneration, impaired night vision, optic neuritis/neuropathy, cataract, ERG amplitude reductions, and EOG light-peak abnormalities, prompting recommendations for ophthalmic surveillance, and leading some experts to conclude that DFO is a dubious candidate for AMD treatment (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021). In RPE culture, repeated DFO exposure was cytotoxic relative to a prochelator control, and clinical series describe deferoxamine retinopathy across pediatric and adult populations, indicating that while iron chelation can be protective in vitro under specific stress conditions, DFO itself can injure RPE and photoreceptors under sustained or high-exposure regimens (Charkoudian et al., 2008; Błasiak et al., 2011). Importantly, DFO’s poor cell permeability and lack of blood–retinal barrier penetration raise practical concerns about achieving therapeutic intra-retinal exposure without systemic toxicity when administered conventionally (Li et al., 2023; Birch et al., 2006). Finally, although iron chelation is mechanistically compelling for retinal degenerations in which iron accumulation and ferroptotic stress participate, application of systemic chelators like DFO to retinal vascular disease and AMD remains at the basic research stage, with unresolved issues including perturbation of systemic/local iron homeostasis and stability of intracellular chelate complexes (Li et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, DFO is a high-affinity FeIII-selective chelator that forms kinetically inert hexacoordinate FeIIIO6 complexes via three hydroxamate ligands, each providing bidentate O,Oʹ coordination; this renders FeIII chemically sequestered, suppresses redox cycling, and prevents iron from entering the Haber–Weiss/Fenton chemistry that generates hydroxyl radicals from superoxide/hydrogen peroxide (Sharpe et al., 2011; Richardson & Poňka, 1998; Hider & Kong, 2013). The FeIII/FeII couple of ferrioxamine is electrochemically very negative (reported around −468 mV vs. NHE), and the complex is redox-inert under physiological conditions, consistent with its ability to quench iron-mediated ROS production rather than participate in it (Hider & Kong, 2013). In biological systems, DFO preferentially binds non-transferrin-bound iron (NTBI), labile iron pools in hepatocytes/macrophages, and low-molecular-weight iron transiting endosomes/lysosomes after transferrin delivery or ferritin degradation; it can mobilize hepatic stores and iron released by reticuloendothelial cells but cannot effectively strip iron from metalloproteins such as hemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochromes, oxidases, catalase, or peroxidases (Hatcher et al., 2009; Richardson & Poňka, 1998; Faa & Crisponi, 1999). The drug is hydrophilic and generally membrane-impermeant; cellular uptake occurs via fluid-phase endocytosis and pinocytosis, leading to enrichment in endosomal/lysosomal compartments, where it chelates lysosomal labile iron, an activity proposed to block lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis—mechanistically relevant to RPE pathobiology (Zhao et al., 2021; Dayani et al., 2004).

In retina and neural tissues, oxidative damage pathways include iron-dependent conversion of H2O2 to •OH via Fenton chemistry; DFO reduces H2O2-induced damage in retinal ganglion cells and protects against paraquat-generated superoxide by depriving upstream Fenton catalysts of accessible iron (Rohowetz et al., 2018). In RPE and photoreceptors, ferroptosis—a regulated cell death driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation—is closely linked to antioxidant systems centered on glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and, independently, on FSP1-mediated ubiquinol regeneration; DFO’s chelation of FeII/FeIII within lysosomes and cytosolic labile pools acts upstream of these pathways to limit lipid hydroperoxide propagation, preserving GSH–GPX4 and FSP1–CoQ10–NADH defense capacity in ARPE-19 under oxidative stimuli (Zhao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023). In systemic contexts, DFO detoxifies NTBI, reduces heme-derived ferryl species, removes high-oxidation-state heme iron, and directly scavenges some radical species, converging on inhibition of membrane lipid oxidation; these activities potentially translate to retinal cells where heme/iron-driven oxidative stress is implicated (Hatcher et al., 2009).

Notably, DFO’s hexadentate size and hydrophilicity restrict direct ferritin iron extraction and limit chelation in tightly protein-bound pools; smaller chelators can penetrate cells more readily and directly efflux ferritin iron, whereas DFO works primarily by intercepting low-molecular-weight iron pools and forming kinetically inert FeIII complexes that are then cleared, often via hepatobiliary or renal routes (Sharpe et al., 2011; Richardson & Poňka, 1998). In inflamed or ischemic tissues, the depletion of accessible iron by DFO can blunt downstream ROS and inflammatory cascades; however, prolonged systemic chelation perturbs metal homeostasis and can deplete essential iron pools in sensitive tissues, underlying some adverse effects including RPE toxicity, auditory neuropathy, and bone dysplasia (Zhao et al., 2021; He et al., 2007).

Expected Effect  
For dry AMD models centered on RPE iron-dependent oxidative stress, the expected pharmacologic effect of DFO is to reduce the labile Fe pool in lysosomes and cytosol, thereby attenuating hydroxyl-radical production from H2O2 and limiting iron-driven lipid peroxidation; operationally, this should decrease oxidative damage readouts and preserve mitochondrial and cellular function in RPE assays (Rohowetz et al., 2018; Li et al., 2023). Specifically:

- Lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis markers: In ARPE-19 cells, DFO has been shown to mitigate lipid peroxidation under oxidant (tBH) and blue-light stress and to preserve viability, consistent with suppression of ferroptotic death; thus, in RPE assays one should observe reductions in lipid peroxidation assays (e.g., BODIPY-C11) and maintenance of GPX4 activity/content, with complementary preservation of the FSP1–CoQ10–NADH axis (Zhao et al., 2025). The same studies indicate decreased Fe2+ accumulation after DFO, reflecting lower catalytic Fe at sites of peroxidation; similar decreases in labile Fe can be measured via calcein quenching or analogous probes (Zhao et al., 2025).

- Oxidative DNA damage: Systemic Zn/DFO reduced retinal oxidative DNA damage in vivo in rd10 mice; although these are not AMD models, the result predicts that in RPE oxidative stress assays DFO will reduce accumulation of oxidative DNA lesions, including those arising in mitochondrial DNA, where iron-dependent ROS can be particularly damaging (Zhao et al., 2025). Ex vivo human AMD maculas showed decreased Perls–DAB staining after DFO chelation, supporting the feasibility of reducing chelatable iron burden and downstream oxidative chemistry in diseased human retina (He et al., 2007).

- Mitochondrial bioenergetics: Preservation of RPE oxygen consumption rate (OCR) is plausible under DFO exposure insofar as DFO limits lipid peroxidation and maintains the reductive antioxidant systems (GSH–GPX4, FSP1–CoQ10) that protect inner-mitochondrial membranes and electron-transport components from iron-dependent oxidative injury; in ARPE-19, DFO improved survival and redox balance under stress, suggesting OCR preservation would accompany reduced peroxidation (Zhao et al., 2025). In retinal ganglion cells, DFO lessened H2O2-induced cell death, indirectly supporting improved mitochondrial tolerance to oxidant stress; similar protection can be anticipated in RPE where iron-dependent ROS compromise mitochondrial DNA and respiratory complexes (Rohowetz et al., 2018).

- Tissue iron fingerprints: In tissue sections or organoids, DFO exposure is expected to decrease Perls–DAB positive iron signal in regions with elevated chelatable iron, as observed in AMD macular tissue; in vivo, systemic DFO does not cross the BRB well, so demonstration of retinal iron removal may require enhanced uptake strategies (e.g., Zn/DFO) or local delivery (Li et al., 2023; He et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2025).

Caveats critical to experimental design include DFO’s lack of blood–retinal barrier penetration and poor cell permeability, which could limit intracellular RPE exposure and lysosomal targeting in vivo after systemic dosing; thus, in vitro or ex vivo assays will show clearer pharmacodynamic effects than systemic models unless delivery is optimized (e.g., Zn-complexation or nanocarriers) (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025; Jones et al., 2020). Additionally, repeated or high-concentration exposure can be cytotoxic to RPE in vitro and has been associated with clinical retinopathy, so dose–exposure optimization and careful toxicity monitoring are required, especially in chronic paradigms (Charkoudian et al., 2008; He et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Rationale strength and translational plausibility. The mechanistic rationale for iron chelation in dry AMD is strong: AMD retinas accumulate chelatable iron, iron catalyzes hydroxyl-radical generation and lipid peroxidation, and iron-dependent ferroptotic stress has been implicated in RPE dysfunction and photoreceptor degeneration (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023). DFO is a high-affinity FeIII chelator with extensive human experience, and it is proven to suppress iron-mediated ROS by forming kinetically inert FeIII complexes, preventing Fenton chemistry (Sharpe et al., 2011; Hider & Kong, 2013). In retinal and RPE models, DFO reduces oxidative injury, limits lipid peroxidation, and preserves cell viability; improved-delivery variants such as Zn/DFO demonstrate in vivo protection of retinal structure and function with concomitant decreases in retinal iron and oxidative DNA damage (Rohowetz et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2025). Ex vivo AMD maculae show DFO-responsive chelatable iron pools, reinforcing target engagement in human disease tissue (He et al., 2007). Mechanistically, enrichment of DFO in lysosomes—an organelle central to RPE iron handling, ferritinophagy, and lipid peroxidation—supports a proximal mode of action relevant to ferroptosis biology in AMD (Zhao et al., 2021).

Key liabilities and translational risks. Despite its compelling mechanism, DFO’s drug properties and ocular safety profile are unfavorable for repurposing in dry AMD without substantial reformulation or targeting:

- Ocular toxicity. DFO has a recognized spectrum of retinal adverse effects in patients, including pigmentary retinopathy, optic neuropathy, ERG/EOG abnormalities, and visual loss; authoritative reviews judge DFO a dubious candidate for AMD because of these safety concerns, and clinical surveillance is recommended when patients receive systemic DFO (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023). RPE toxicity is documented in vitro and clinically across age groups, indicating a narrow retinal therapeutic window under repeated exposure (Błasiak et al., 2011; Charkoudian et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2021).

- Delivery limitations. DFO is hydrophilic, membrane-impermeant, and not blood–neural/retinal barrier penetrant, which undermines retinal exposure after systemic dosing; achieving therapeutic intra-RPE concentrations without systemic toxicity is unlikely with conventional infusion regimens (Li et al., 2023; Birch et al., 2006). The molecule’s very short plasma half-life further complicates exposure in avascular tissues like the outer retina (Sharpe et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2020).

- Systemic chelation risks. Long-term DFO perturbs systemic iron balance, interacts with microbiological iron acquisition in certain pathogens (e.g., Vibrio, S. aureus) that can exploit ferrioxamine, and carries recognized risks of growth retardation, bone changes, and infection, which are unacceptable for a chronic ocular disease with slow progression (Sharpe et al., 2011; Faa & Crisponi, 1999).

- Clinical maturity in ophthalmology. While iron chelators show promise in preclinical retinal models, clinical translation to retinal vascular disease/AMD remains at the basic research stage; challenges include maintaining retinal iron homeostasis, avoiding off-target metal depletion (e.g., Zn2+), and ensuring intracellular chelate stability and localization (Li et al., 2023).

Risk-mitigation strategies and development path. If DFO were to be advanced, development should avoid systemic DFO infusions for dry AMD. Instead:

- Leverage targeted delivery. The Zn/DFO complex that facilitates cellular uptake has shown robust neuroprotection, retinal iron lowering, and oxidative DNA damage reduction in vivo; such conjugate-based or carrier-based strategies could provide intracellular RPE delivery at lower systemic exposure, meriting further evaluation in AMD-relevant models (e.g., light damage, iron-loading, aged mice) with retinal safety readouts (Zhao et al., 2025). Nanocarriers or depot formulations that increase local ocular exposure while minimizing systemic levels could be explored, given DFO’s history of half-life extension in liposomal and multivesicular formulations systemically (Jones et al., 2020; Sharpe et al., 2011).

- Consider chemical alternatives within class. Other chelators with better cell permeability and ocular safety have shown retinal protection without the retinotoxicity seen with DFO; for example, deferiprone protected against iron-induced and light-induced retinal degeneration in multiple mouse models and was not found to be toxic to mouse retina in the contexts studied, suggesting that a more lipophilic, lower-molecular-weight chelator could be a safer starting point than DFO for dry AMD (Song & Dunaief, 2013; Picard et al., 2020).

- Exploit prochelation. Pro-chelators like BSIH that become active only under oxidative conditions were non-toxic with repeated exposure relative to DFO and may offer a way to achieve context-dependent iron chelation within oxidatively stressed RPE while sparing normal iron pools, lowering the risk of retinopathy (Charkoudian et al., 2008).

Decision framework for go/no-go. On balance, while DFO validates the iron-chelation mechanism in retinal tissues and provides useful tool-compound effects in vitro and in ex vivo AMD maculae, its physicochemical properties, delivery constraints, and retinal toxicity profile argue strongly against repurposing native DFO for chronic treatment of dry AMD (Li et al., 2023; He et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2021). The most credible development path for DFO derivatives would require:

- Demonstrating safe, effective RPE delivery with a DFO-based construct (e.g., Zn/DFO or nanocarrier) that reduces labile iron, lipid peroxidation, and oxidative DNA damage in AMD-relevant in vivo models without ERG/EOG or structural toxicity (Zhao et al., 2025).

- Establishing a therapeutic index in the retina with chronic dosing and appropriate safety pharmacology (ERG, OCT, histopathology), given reported human retinopathies on DFO (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023).

- Benchmarking against alternative chelators (e.g., deferiprone) that already demonstrate retinal protection and better permeability/safety in vivo, to justify a DFO-based approach scientifically and clinically (Song & Dunaief, 2013; Picard et al., 2020).

Strengths  
- Mechanistic fit: chelates FeIII with high selectivity and prevents Fenton chemistry; acts in lysosomes where RPE iron and lipid peroxidation intersect with ferroptosis (Sharpe et al., 2011; Hider & Kong, 2013; Zhao et al., 2021).  
- Demonstrated retinal pharmacology: reduces oxidative injury in retinal neurons and RPE, lowers retinal iron and oxidative DNA damage with improved delivery, and removes chelatable iron from AMD macula ex vivo (Rohowetz et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2025; He et al., 2007).  
- Extensive human experience: well-characterized PK/PD, safety liabilities, and clinical management of chelation therapy (Jones et al., 2020; Tam et al., 2003).

Weaknesses  
- Ocular toxicity liability with systemic DFO, including pigmentary retinopathy and electrophysiologic dysfunction, making native DFO a poor risk–benefit prospect for a chronic retinal indication (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021).  
- Poor retinal exposure after systemic dosing due to hydrophilicity and lack of BRB penetration; very short half-life complicates sustained intraocular levels (Li et al., 2023; Birch et al., 2006; Jones et al., 2020).  
- Systemic risks (growth, bone, infection) incompatible with large, elderly dry-AMD populations unless exposure is tightly localized to the eye (Faa & Crisponi, 1999; Sharpe et al., 2011).  
- Field immaturity: iron chelators for retinal disease remain in basic research with unresolved questions about homeostasis and intracellular stability (Li et al., 2023).

Conclusion  
DFO is a mechanistically validated iron chelator with documented ability to reduce iron-driven oxidative injury in retinal systems; however, as a repurposed systemic drug for dry AMD, its delivery barriers and retinal toxicity outweigh potential benefits (Li et al., 2023; He et al., 2007). If iron chelation is pursued for dry AMD within this program, prioritizing better-penetrant, safer chelators (e.g., deferiprone) or context-activated prochelators over native DFO is the higher-probability path; alternately, DFO-based constructs that demonstrably deliver into RPE (e.g., Zn/DFO) with acceptable chronic retinal safety merit targeted preclinical exploration before considering clinical translation (Song & Dunaief, 2013; Charkoudian et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) is an endogenous indoleamine neurohormone first identified as a pineal product and now recognized to be synthesized in many extrapineal tissues, including the human eye (retina, retinal pigment epithelium [RPE], lens, ciliary body) where it is also delivered via the circulation and acts locally through cognate receptors (MT1, MT2) and the MT3 binding site (quinone reductase 2) (Lundmark et al., 2006; Lundmark et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2024). Ocular melatonin is under circadian control and is produced primarily by photoreceptors, with additional production reported in inner retina and potentially the RPE, consistent with a paracrine neuromodulatory role in retinal physiology; importantly, melatonin synthesis has been localized to mitochondria, linking its biosynthesis directly to the organelle most relevant to retinal oxidative metabolism (Blasiak et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024). Biosynthesis proceeds from tryptophan via tryptophan hydroxylase and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase to serotonin, followed by arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase (AANAT) and hydroxyindole-O-methyltransferase (HIOMT) to generate melatonin, which freely diffuses to act in an autocrine/paracrine manner (Ma et al., 2024). As a chemical class, melatonin belongs to amphiphilic indoleamines; it partitions into both aqueous and lipid compartments, crosses biological barriers (including the blood–retinal barrier), and concentrates in mitochondria, properties that underpin its direct antioxidant, membrane-protective, and mitochondrial-modulatory actions described in multiple ocular contexts (Romeo et al., 2024; Rastmanesh, 2011; Ma et al., 2024).

Melatonin’s pharmacology encompasses receptor-dependent signaling via MT1 and MT2 G protein–coupled receptors (G_i and G_q/11 coupling), and receptor-independent actions as a direct free-radical scavenger with active redox metabolites (e.g., AFMK, AMK) capable of sequential radical quenching (“antioxidant cascade”), allowing a single parent molecule to neutralize multiple reactive species; MT3 corresponds to cytosolic quinone reductase 2 (QR2) and represents a distinct enzymatic interaction relevant to ocular physiology (D’Angelo et al., 2024; Lundmark et al., 2007; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Rastmanesh, 2011). This dual pharmacology (receptor-mediated signaling plus direct ROS/RNS scavenging) provides a mechanistic basis for melatonin’s pleiotropic antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, and mitochondrial-protective effects in the retina and RPE, actions widely reported in preclinical models of oxidative retinal injury, diabetic retinopathy, and nonexudative AMD (Crooke et al., 2017; Diéguez et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Within ophthalmology, melatonin and melatonergic agents have been explored across inflammatory, neurodegenerative, and vascular retinal diseases. Topical melatonin (0.1%) reduced intraocular inflammation and blood–ocular barrier permeability in rabbit uveitis while increasing tear and aqueous antioxidant activity (supporting tolerability and local pharmacodynamic engagement), and multiple melatonin analogs lowered intraocular pressure in glaucoma, with nanomicelles extending hypotensive and neuroprotective effects (Rusciano & Russo, 2024). In diabetic retinopathy models, melatonin reduced retinal oxidative and nitrosative stress, decreased hypoxia-inducible factor-1α and VEGF signaling, protected the blood–retinal barrier, and improved neural survival, aligning with its redox, anti-inflammatory, and anti-angiogenic pharmacology (Crooke et al., 2017).

For macular degeneration, mechanistic and efficacy signals span in vitro RPE studies, in vivo retinal protection in mice, and human observational datasets. A protected in vivo AMD-relevant signal includes a subcutaneous melatonin pellet that preserved visual function and outer retinal structure and limited oxidative stress in a nonexudative AMD mouse model (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Independently, rodent studies demonstrate intravitreal melatonin prevents acute photoreceptor loss (MNU model) by lowering oxidative damage markers (retinal MDA, 8-OHdG), increasing mitochondrial MnSOD and total SOD activities, and reducing photoreceptor apoptosis—evidence of both antioxidant and anti-apoptotic benefits from local delivery (Li et al., 2020). In RPE cell models (ARPE-19), melatonin consistently protected against H₂O₂-induced oxidative injury by lowering ROS and lipid peroxidation, restoring mitochondrial membrane potential, reducing Bax/cytochrome c/caspase-7 activation, and promoting autophagy (increased LC3-II and Beclin-1, reduced p62), with low-nanomolar protective effects blocked by the melatonin receptor antagonist luzindole, implicating receptor mediation at physiologic ranges (Chang et al., 2018; Blasiak et al., 2016).

Emerging ferroptosis-focused work further reports that melatonin rescues Aβ₁₋₄₀–induced RPE degeneration by curbing lipid peroxidation, restoring GPX4 and SLC7A11, and normalizing iron handling, with loss-of-function of MDM2 abolishing protection and positioning PI3K/AKT→MDM2→P53→SLC7A11 as a key axis; in vivo, melatonin preserved RPE structure and ERG responses in Aβ₁₋₄₀ models (Wu et al., 2025). These mechanistic and efficacy themes converge with a high-quality in vivo finding that melatonin “protects the retina from experimental nonexudative age-related macular degeneration” in mice (Diéguez et al., 2020).

Clinical observations are suggestive but not definitive. A large real-world EHR cohort analysis (TriNetX) associated chronic melatonin use with lower incidence of AMD and reduced progression from nonexudative to exudative AMD after propensity matching, while acknowledging potential residual confounding and calling for randomized trials (Jeong et al., 2024a). An editorialized report in JAMA Ophthalmology similarly noted protective associations and biological plausibility (RPE protection, VEGF reduction) while emphasizing exploratory design and the need for confirmatory prospective studies (Jeong et al., 2024b). Earlier case-series reported that 3 mg oral melatonin nightly for three months stabilized or improved macular changes in many AMD patients, but these uncontrolled data lack modern trial rigor (Lundmark et al., 2007; Martínez-Águila et al., 2021). Across aging and AMD, reduced nocturnal melatonin and urinary aMT6s have been documented, providing a pathophysiologic rationale for supplementation in older adults; however, oral melatonin exhibits variable and often low bioavailability, and aqueous/topical formulations must address photostability and posterior-segment delivery challenges (Čolak & Žorić, 2019; Blasiak et al., 2016; Jeong et al., 2024b; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Melatonin’s ocular actions relevant to dry AMD encompass receptor-mediated signaling, direct and indirect antioxidant effects, mitochondrial protection, modulation of apoptosis and autophagy/mitophagy, ferroptosis suppression, and immune/vascular regulation.

- Receptor-mediated signaling (MT1/MT2/QR2): MT1 and MT2 are expressed in retina and RPE; MT1 is present in photoreceptor inner segments and inner retinal neurons, MT2 shows high retinal expression and is reported in RPE, while the MT3 binding site corresponds to QR2, an oxidoreductase implicated in ocular physiology (Lundmark et al., 2006; Lundmark et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2024). In RPE, low-dose melatonin protection against oxidants is blocked by luzindole, indicating MT receptor involvement at physiologic concentrations (≤10⁻⁸ M), whereas higher concentrations (>10⁻⁶ M) exert receptor-independent antioxidant effects (Blasiak et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2018). MT1-dependent signaling maintains mitochondrial function under oxidative stress in RPE, underscoring receptor linkage to mitochondrial homeostasis in relevant models (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

- Direct and cascade antioxidant activity: Melatonin directly scavenges ROS/RNS, including hydroxyl radicals, and via successive metabolism (3-hydroxymelatonin → AFMK → AMK) neutralizes multiple radicals (“antioxidant cascade”), affording broad-spectrum redox control across aqueous and lipid compartments due to its amphiphilicity (Rastmanesh, 2011; Čolak & Žorić, 2019). In retinal tissues it reduces lipid peroxidation (MDA) and oxidative DNA damage (8-OHdG), and its metabolites independently contribute to radical quenching in ocular systems (Li et al., 2020; Romeo et al., 2024).

- Indirect antioxidant signaling (Nrf2, Sirtuins, AKT): Melatonin modulates redox-sensitive transcriptional programs; it maintains or enhances Nrf2 nuclear activity in several ocular contexts (though Nrf2 responses can be model-dependent), leading to upregulation of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutases and glutathione peroxidases; it also engages AKT phosphorylation and related DNA damage responses (Blasiak et al., 2016; Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024). Melatonin regulates sirtuins (SIRT1, SIRT3) which link metabolism to antioxidant gene expression, autophagy, and anti-inflammatory effects, with SIRT1/SIRT3 activation reducing apoptosis and VEGF and promoting autophagy gene programs; modulation is context-dependent but provides additional axes by which melatonin can protect RPE mitochondria and restrain inflammatory signaling (Crooke et al., 2017).

- Mitochondrial protection: Melatonin concentrates in mitochondria, stabilizes the electron transport chain, reduces electron leakage, maintains mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), inhibits the mitochondrial permeability transition pore, and can activate uncoupling proteins; it reduces mtDNA damage and restores respiratory control, thereby curbing ROS generation at its source (Blasiak et al., 2016; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Tong et al., 2022). In vivo retina, intravitreal melatonin increased mitochondrial MnSOD (SOD2) activity and total SOD, aligning with enhanced endogenous antioxidant defenses at the organellar level (Li et al., 2020). In RPE cell models, melatonin preserved Δψm (JC-1/TMRM assays) after H₂O₂ challenge (Chang et al., 2018).

- Anti-apoptotic effects: In ARPE-19 cells, melatonin reduced the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, decreased cytochrome c release and caspase-7 activation, and lowered TUNEL positivity, consistent with inhibition of intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptosis; this aligns with higher Bcl-2 mRNA and fewer apoptotic photoreceptors in vivo (Chang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020). Mechanistically, mitochondrial stabilization, reduced ROS, and modulation of NF-κB/JAK-STAT signaling contribute to anti-apoptosis (Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024).

- Autophagy/mitophagy regulation: Melatonin increases LC3-II and Beclin-1 and decreases p62 in RPE oxidative stress models, indicating enhanced autophagic flux; MT2-mediated inhibition of mTOR and SIRT1-linked transcriptional control further connect melatonin to autophagy and mitophagy, processes essential for RPE proteostasis and organellar quality control in aging (Chang et al., 2018; Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024). Given that impaired mitophagy is a feature of early AMD, pharmacologic reinforcement of autophagy/mitophagy by melatonin is mechanistically aligned with disease biology (Crooke et al., 2017).

- Ferroptosis suppression: Aβ₁₋₄₀–induced ferroptosis in RPE is attenuated by melatonin via PI3K/AKT-driven phosphorylation and activation of MDM2, which inhibits p53; this derepresses SLC7A11, restores cystine import and GSH synthesis, and rescues GPX4 activity, thereby reducing lipid peroxidation, Fe²⁺ accumulation, and mitochondrial ultrastructural damage; MDM2 knockdown abrogates these effects, functionally linking melatonin to the PI3K/AKT/MDM2/p53/SLC7A11 axis (Wu et al., 2025). In vivo, melatonin preserved ERG a-/b-waves and outer retinal integrity after Aβ₁₋₄₀ insult (Wu et al., 2025).

- Anti-inflammatory and immune modulation: Melatonin limits NF-κB activation, reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6), and modulates immune cell phenotypes (e.g., promoting macrophage polarization toward tissue-repair M2), contributing to reduced retinal inflammation; it suppresses nitric oxide synthases and decreases NO, relevant to nitro-oxidative stress (Crooke et al., 2017; Diéguez et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024). In models of choroidal neovascularization, melatonin attenuated angiogenesis via HIF-1α–VEGF inhibition and RhoA/ROCK-mediated macrophage/microglia polarization, suggesting an adjunctive anti-neovascular role even though dry AMD lacks CNV (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2024b).

- Telomere/telomerase and DNA repair: Melatonin modulates telomerase and DNA repair pathways in retinal cells, with reports of stimulated telomerase activity and reduced telomere erosion in senescent contexts, and increased efficacy of oxidative DNA damage removal in RPE, potentially mitigating RPE senescence in AMD (Blasiak et al., 2016; Rastmanesh, 2011).

- Electrophysiologic and circadian effects: Melatonin modulates retinal electrophysiology and ERG amplitude in a dose- and time-dependent manner, interacting with PKC, MAPK/ERK, and cAMP/PKA signaling; while protective effects are seen in nocturnal rodent ERGs, a small human study reported reduced b-wave amplitude after a 10 mg oral dose, highlighting the need for careful dosing and chronotherapy alignment (Lundmark et al., 2006; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Collectively, these mechanisms plausibly converge in RPE to reduce mitochondrial ROS, maintain Δψm, prevent cytochrome c release, lower caspase activation, and support autophagy/mitophagy, aligning directly with the pathobiology of dry AMD driven by oxidative/mitochondrial damage and impaired proteostasis (Blasiak et al., 2016; Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
The working hypothesis—melatonin scavenges ROS and upregulates mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes in RPE, preserving Δψm and preventing apoptosis in dry AMD—is consistent with reported assay-level outcomes in RPE and retina and yields clear, testable predictions.

- In RPE oxidative-stress assays (H₂O₂, cigarette-smoke constituents, Aβ₁₋₄₀), melatonin should reduce intracellular ROS (DCF/CellROX), lipid peroxidation (MDA, C11-BODIPY), and Fe²⁺ accumulation (FerroOrange), while increasing reduced glutathione (GSH), restoring mitochondrial membrane potential (JC-1/TMRM), and rescuing viability (MTT/CCK-8/LDH), effects substantiated in ARPE-19 and primary RPE studies (Chang et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2025).

- Mitochondrial antioxidant enzyme readouts are expected to increase: while direct ARPE-19 measures of SOD2/GPx protein can be added to this program, in vivo retinal data show melatonin increases mitochondrial MnSOD (SOD2) activity and total SOD, and multiple reviews report melatonin-induced upregulation of SOD and GPx in ocular tissues via Nrf2 and related signaling, supporting the enzyme-induction arm of the hypothesis (Crooke et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024).

- Intrinsic apoptosis markers should decline: reduced Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, decreased cytochrome c release, and reduced caspase-7/-3 activation, plus fewer TUNEL-positive nuclei, as already demonstrated in ARPE-19 under H₂O₂ and in photoreceptors in vivo (Chang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020).

- Autophagy/mitophagy engagement should be evident: increased LC3-II and Beclin-1 and decreased p62, with flux confirmed by lysosomal inhibitors; mitophagy markers (e.g., PINK1/Parkin) should be assessed given melatonin’s reported influence on mitochondrial quality control (Chang et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022).

- Ferroptosis control should be demonstrable in Aβ₁₋₄₀ and other ferroptotic stressors: upregulation of SLC7A11 and GPX4, normalization of TFR1/ACSL4/FTH1, reduced lipid peroxidation, and dependence on PI3K/AKT→MDM2→p53 signaling tested by pharmacological inhibitors and siRNA, as shown in recent preclinical reports (Wu et al., 2025).

- Anti-inflammatory and transcriptional endpoints should shift: decreased NF-κB nuclear translocation and pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β), increased Nrf2 nuclear retention and target gene expression, and potential SIRT1/SIRT3 upregulation in appropriate contexts (Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024).

- Functional in vivo correlates should include preservation of ERG a-/b-wave amplitudes, photoreceptor/RPE morphology on OCT/H&E, and reduced oxidative tissue biomarkers (MDA, 8-OHdG) under retinal oxidative/AMD-like stressors, consistent with prior animal studies (Diéguez et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2025).

Receptor expression to support target engagement is well documented in retina and RPE, and dependence on MT receptors can be tested with antagonists (luzindole) and MT1/MT2 knockdown, as low-dose protective effects in ARPE-19 are reversibly blocked by luzindole and MT1 knockdown abolishes mitochondrial protective actions under oxidative stress (Blasiak et al., 2016; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Lundmark et al., 2007). Given circadian regulation, repeated dosing aligned with the retinal clock may be necessary to realize full mitochondrial DNA protection and durable antioxidant responses, as suggested by diurnal pretreatment requirements in ARPE-19 (Rastmanesh, 2011).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic convergence on AMD biology: Melatonin’s combined direct scavenging of ROS/RNS, induction of endogenous antioxidant defenses (SODs, GPxs), mitochondrial stabilization (Δψm preservation, mtDNA protection), anti-apoptotic signaling (reduced Bax/cytochrome c/caspases), and autophagy/mitophagy support addresses core pathogenic axes in dry AMD—oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and defective proteostasis in post-mitotic RPE and photoreceptors (Blasiak et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022).

- Demonstrated efficacy in relevant preclinical systems: Protection of RPE from peroxide and Aβ₁₋₄₀ ferroptotic stress in vitro, and preservation of retina/RPE structure and function in AMD-like mouse models, including nonexudative AMD and acute degeneration models, with robust biomarker changes (MDA, 8-OHdG, SOD2 activity) and ERG preservation (Chang et al., 2018; Diéguez et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2025).

- Receptor and nonreceptor pharmacology: Dual mode of action enables efficacy at physiologic concentrations via MT1/MT2 and at higher local concentrations via receptor-independent radical scavenging, offering flexibility across dosing ranges and delivery routes; MT1-linked mitochondrial protection in RPE provides a direct mechanistic link between receptor activation and Δψm preservation (Blasiak et al., 2016; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

- Anti-ferroptotic axis in RPE: PI3K/AKT→MDM2→p53→SLC7A11 mechanism positions melatonin within contemporary cell-death biology relevant to AMD (lipid peroxidation, iron handling, GPX4), offering mechanistic biomarkers and combination opportunities with iron chelators or GPX4-preserving agents (Wu et al., 2025).

- Favorable endogenous safety rationale and clinical signal: As an endogenous molecule with extensive human exposure for sleep disorders, melatonin has a comparatively favorable safety backdrop; observational EHR data provides a clinically relevant association signal for AMD incidence and progression reduction that justifies prospective trials (Jeong et al., 2024a; Jeong et al., 2024b).

- Translational feasibility with targeted delivery: Topical ocular and nanocarrier formulations can improve posterior-segment delivery, and intravitreal administration achieves retinal protection with measurable biochemical and functional benefits; nanotechnologies address melatonin’s aqueous instability and enhance tissue penetration (Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Li et al., 2020).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Evidence base is predominantly preclinical; clinical efficacy in dry AMD is unproven: Apart from exploratory EHR associations and small uncontrolled case-series, there are no randomized controlled trials in dry AMD demonstrating visual function or structural endpoints with melatonin; reliance on animal models and ARPE-19 limits translatability (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2024a; Jeong et al., 2024b).

- Context- and dose-dependent effects: Nrf2 modulation by melatonin can vary by model, and very high exogenous concentrations can worsen photoreceptor light damage; a small human study showed acute ERG b-wave reduction after 10 mg oral melatonin, indicating potential physiological perturbation at certain doses/times and the importance of chronotherapy and dose finding (Blasiak et al., 2016; Tong et al., 2022; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

- Vascular tone considerations: MT1-mediated vasoconstriction in retinal endothelium could theoretically exacerbate early perfusion deficits in AMD; dose, receptor selectivity, and local exposure will be critical to avoid adverse vascular modulation (Ma et al., 2024).

- Delivery and pharmacokinetics: Oral melatonin exhibits highly variable and often low bioavailability due to first-pass metabolism, and aqueous topical formulations face photostability and posterior-segment penetration barriers; while nanocarriers and intravitreal delivery overcome these, each introduces manufacturing and safety considerations (Jeong et al., 2024b; Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

- Aged tissue pharmacodynamics: Age-related declines in retinal melatonin and potential receptor desensitization could diminish responsiveness to exogenous melatonin in elderly AMD populations; some aging-associated retinal rhythms were not rescued by exogenous melatonin in prior studies (Blasiak et al., 2016).

- Safety window for intravitreal dosing: Although protective effects are demonstrated, at least one report cites retinal cell degeneration at high intravitreal doses, underscoring the need for careful dose-range finding and chronic safety assessment (Ma et al., 2024).

- Product-specific gaps: There is insufficient formulation- and impurity-specific information for Sigma-Aldrich M5250 in ocular contexts, and no product-specific ocular PK/PD has been reported in AMD; stability, excipient compatibility, and photostability data must be generated for any clinical candidate (Ma et al., 2024; Romeo et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Assessment against the team’s hypothesis  
Supportive evidence is strong that melatonin reduces ROS, preserves mitochondrial function, and prevents apoptosis in RPE/retina. Multiple ARPE-19 studies demonstrate decreased ROS, increased Δψm, and reduced intrinsic apoptosis markers (Bax, cytochrome c, caspases) under oxidative stress with melatonin, consistent with maintained mitochondrial integrity and suppressed apoptotic cascades (Chang et al., 2018). In vivo, raised mitochondrial MnSOD activity and reduced oxidative biomarkers after intravitreal melatonin substantiate mitochondrial antioxidant engagement in retina (Li et al., 2020). Upregulation of antioxidant enzymes (SOD, GPx) by melatonin in ocular tissues via Nrf2, SIRT1/3, and AKT pathways is reported in leading reviews and experimental models, even though direct SOD2/GPX induction has not been quantified in RPE in all cited primary studies; this constitutes a tractable validation gap for our planned assays (Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024). Ferroptosis suppression via PI3K/AKT/MDM2/p53 further extends the mitochondrial-protective narrative to lipid ROS and iron metabolism, relevant to RPE stress in AMD (Wu et al., 2025).

Programmatic recommendations  
- Formulation and delivery: Given oral PK variability and ocular delivery constraints, prioritize posterior-segment–targeted strategies: (1) intravitreal melatonin for proof-of-mechanism in large animals (define safety window, ocular distribution, and retinal PD biomarkers); (2) develop stabilized topical nanocarriers (e.g., ethylcellulose, PLGA-PEG, nanomicelles) to improve posterior-segment delivery and residence time for chronic use (Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Jeong et al., 2024b).

- Pharmacodynamic biomarkers: In RPE/retina, quantify Δψm, mitochondrial respiration (OCR), ROS (DCF, MitoSOX), lipid peroxidation (C11-BODIPY, MDA), mtDNA integrity (long-amplicon qPCR), SOD2 and GPX4 protein/activity, Bax/Bcl-2, cytochrome c release, caspase-3/-7 activity, LC3-II/Beclin-1/p62 flux, Nrf2 nuclear localization and target genes, and ferroptosis markers (SLC7A11, GPX4, TFR1, ACSL4, FTH1) with pharmacologic/siRNA controls for MT receptors and PI3K/AKT/MDM2/p53 (Chang et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2025).

- Dosing and chronotherapy: Incorporate diurnal dosing regimens to align with retinal circadian biology; evaluate low-dose receptor-mediated windows versus higher-dose antioxidant windows, avoiding concentrations shown to potentiate phototoxicity (Blasiak et al., 2016; Rastmanesh, 2011; Tong et al., 2022).

- Safety and off-target risks: Monitor ERG under different dosing/time-of-day schedules, retinal/choroidal vascular caliber (given MT1-mediated vasoconstriction), photoreceptor light injury susceptibility under high-dose exposure, and long-term ocular histopathology in repeat-dose studies (Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Tong et al., 2022).

- Clinical translation: Design an adaptive, randomized, placebo-controlled Phase 2 in intermediate dry AMD with multimodal endpoints (SD-OCT GA growth, mesopic microperimetry, dark adaptation, low-luminance VA) and fluid biomarkers (plasma/urine aMT6s, systemic oxidative markers), stratified by baseline melatonin levels and sleep parameters; consider an intravitreal proof-of-concept in high-risk early GA to validate local PD and safety prior to chronic topical development (Jeong et al., 2024a; Jeong et al., 2024b; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Conclusion  
Melatonin is a mechanistically well-justified, low-cost, repurposable candidate for dry AMD: it directly and indirectly controls retinal/RPE redox status, stabilizes mitochondrial function (including Δψm), engages endogenous antioxidant enzymes, prevents intrinsic apoptosis, supports autophagy/mitophagy, and suppresses ferroptosis along a defined PI3K/AKT/MDM2/p53 axis, with concordant protection in RPE and retina across preclinical models (Chang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025). Epidemiologic data add a clinically relevant signal for reduced AMD risk and progression with melatonin exposure, and ocular delivery is feasible with modern formulations, though oral PK variability and aqueous instability pose development challenges (Jeong et al., 2024a; Jeong et al., 2024b; Rusciano & Russo, 2024). Key risks—dose-dependent phototoxicity, potential vasoconstrictive effects, variability of Nrf2 responses, and uncertain responsiveness in aged retinas—can be managed through judicious dosing, chronotherapy, receptor-aware design, and robust safety pharmacology (Blasiak et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Net assessment: advance melatonin into a formal translational program for dry AMD centered on posterior-segment–targeted delivery and rigorous mitochondrial/RPE pharmacodynamic validation, while preparing for a randomized clinical evaluation; the mechanistic breadth and preclinical efficacy merit this investment, contingent on resolving dosing, delivery, and safety windows in aged ocular tissue (Diéguez et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
EUK-134 is a synthetic antioxidant belonging to the class of manganese salen complexes designed to mimic the endogenous activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase. Its synthesis involves a controlled condensation reaction between salicylaldehyde and ethylenediamine, resulting in a small molecule whose molecular framework is optimized for redox cycling and catalytic detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). As a representative of SOD/catalase mimetics, EUK-134 is engineered to convert the superoxide anion (O2–) into hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and subsequently decompose H2O2 into water and oxygen. Its dual-activity design places it in a promising category for therapeutic intervention in diseases driven by oxidative stress. The compound’s synthetic origin allows for fine-tuning of physicochemical properties such as lipophilicity and catalytic efficiency, making it a candidate for repurposing in disease conditions beyond those for which it was originally developed (Thoma et al., 2020; Grujicic & Allen, 2024). Within the pharmaceutical landscape, this class of compounds has been extensively studied in preclinical models for their ability to mitigate cellular damage by neutralizing ROS; they have been applied experimentally in models of muscle atrophy, ischemia–reperfusion injury, and certain cancer indications, where oxidative stress is known to play a critical role (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). The molecular architecture of EUK-134 notably offers a compact, dual-function approach that, in theory, should counterbalance both superoxide and hydrogen peroxide accumulation—a feature that is especially relevant given that the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is subject to chronic oxidative insult (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of EUK-134 is marked by its application in various preclinical models where oxidative stress and subsequent mitochondrial dysfunction were central to the pathology. In studies involving human skeletal muscle cells, EUK-134 has been shown to attenuate endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress-induced mitochondrial dysfunction induced by tunicamycin, resulting in improved mitochondrial membrane potential and restoration of bioenergetic profiles (Thoma et al., 2020). Moreover, this compound has been evaluated in contexts such as hyperoxic myocardial tissues, where it mitigated oxidative damage and contributed to the preservation of cellular function under stress conditions (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). Its potential benefits in reducing oxidative damage have also been noted in studies involving breast cancer cells and mechanical unloading-induced muscle atrophy, highlighting its versatility as a ROS-scavenging agent (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).  
Despite the significant body of work on EUK-134 in non-ocular tissues, its direct evaluation in dry AMD or similar degenerative retinal conditions has not yet been thoroughly explored. Clinical trials and literature searches focusing on Mn-porphyrin SOD mimetics have yielded extensive data relating to retinal diseases (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.), but EUK-134 itself has not been the primary focus in retinal clinical applications. Nonetheless, its proven mechanism of reducing ROS accumulation positions it as an attractive candidate for extension into the field of ocular therapeutics. In this light, the repurposing of EUK-134 for dry AMD is based on the hypothesis that its antioxidant properties, previously validated in muscle and other tissues, may confer similar protective effects in RPE cells that are chronically exposed to oxidative stress (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, EUK-134 functions by catalytically mimicking the activities of superoxide dismutase and catalase. In its SOD mimetic capacity, EUK-134 accepts electrons from the superoxide anions, facilitating their conversion into hydrogen peroxide—a reaction which is essential to limit direct superoxide-mediated damage (Thoma et al., 2020). Following this, the catalase mimetic activity is intended to decompose the resultant hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, thereby preventing accumulation of H2O2 which can otherwise contribute to oxidative injury through Fenton-type reactions. However, several studies have drawn attention to limitations in this pathway. For example, evidence indicates that EUK-134 may exhibit a lower efficiency in H2O2 scavenging when compared to other antioxidants such as MnTBAP or native catalase, particularly in environments with high oxidative flux (Quan et al., 2017). One key observation is a significant down-regulation of catalase expression – by more than five-fold – upon EUK-134 treatment in some cellular systems, a factor that potentially undermines its capacity to fully counteract H2O2 buildup (Quan et al., 2017).  
On the molecular interaction front, the manganese center within the salen complex undergoes redox cycling, alternating between oxidation states in response to ROS encounters. This cyclic activity contributes to its continuous catalytic turnover and represents the biochemical foundation for its antioxidant action. Furthermore, studies have shown that EUK-134 can modulate various signaling pathways associated with oxidative stress responses, such as the TGF-β1/Smad2 pathway in muscle under atrophy-inducing conditions (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). Despite these promising aspects, challenges such as suboptimal mitochondrial uptake remain a concern since effective neutralization of ROS in RPE cells requires prompt access to the mitochondrial matrix—a compartment frequently characterized by an inherently challenging microenvironment for drug delivery (Quan et al., 2017). In summary, while EUK-134 possesses a dual action mechanism that addresses two key components of the ROS cascade, the efficiency of its H2O2 detoxification and its cellular distribution are critical parameters that must be rigorously characterized in the context of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
In dry AMD and particularly in geographic atrophy, the retinal pigment epithelium is subject to sustained oxidative stress, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and subsequent cell death. The expected therapeutic effect of EUK-134 in this context is to provide robust antioxidant protection within RPE mitochondria, thereby neutralizing excessive superoxide and hydrogen peroxide levels and preserving mitochondrial integrity (Thoma et al., 2020). Restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) is a key indicator of improved mitochondrial function; thus, by mitigating ROS-induced depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane, EUK-134 is anticipated to maintain or restore ATP production and spare respiratory capacity in RPE cells. These effects are crucial given that ATP depletion and bioenergetic failure are prominent features in the pathology of dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012).  
In vitro assays that simulate oxidative stress conditions—such as those employing RPE cell cultures under hypoxic or chemically induced stress—will likely measure parameters including Δψm, ATP levels, ROS quantification, and expression levels of stress-responsive genes. The anticipated outcome is that EUK-134 will lead to a measurable decrease in the levels of ROS as detected by biochemical assays, along with a concomitant stabilization of mitochondrial respiratory function (Thoma et al., 2020; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012). In addition, molecular analyses may reveal a down-regulation of oxidative stress markers and an improvement in the overall redox balance of the cell. It is vital, however, to consider that some studies have noted that EUK-134 does not inhibit all markers of stress uniformly—for example, the continued expression of GADD34 has been observed even where other stress indicators are normalized (Thoma et al., 2020).  
Given that RPE cells naturally express endogenous antioxidant enzymes such as SOD and catalase, supplementation with EUK-134 is expected to either bolster these defenses or compensate for their decline during chronic oxidative challenges. This dual functionality could theoretically translate into a reduced progression of RPE cell death, slower accumulation of drusen, and ultimately a deceleration of geographic atrophy, all of which are hallmarks of dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of EUK-134 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration involves weighing its mechanistic promise against the practical challenges encountered in its preclinical and potential clinical application. On the one hand, EUK-134 embodies several clear strengths. Its dual mimetic activities align well with the fundamental pathophysiology of dry AMD, where both superoxide and hydrogen peroxide are implicated in the oxidative cascade that leads to mitochondrial dysfunction and RPE cell demise (Thoma et al., 2020; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012). The synthetic nature of EUK-134 allows for controlled chemical modifications which could be leveraged to optimize its pharmacokinetic properties, and its relatively small size is an asset for penetrating tissues such as the retina. Additionally, the compound’s history in attenuating ER stress-related mitochondrial dysfunction in muscle cells provides a robust proof-of-concept that similar benefits might be translatable to RPE cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress (Thoma et al., 2020).  
Notwithstanding these advantages, several weaknesses must be scrutinized. A primary concern lies in the evidence that EUK-134 may exhibit limitations in catalase-like activity, particularly with regard to its efficiency in cleaving hydrogen peroxide. Studies have documented a significant down-regulation of catalase expression upon treatment with EUK-134 and noted that its H2O2 scavenging capabilities fall short when benchmarked against other agents such as MnTBAP or even native catalase (Quan et al., 2017). In the context of RPE cells, where the oxidative insult is persistent and multifactorial, such limitations could result in suboptimal clearance of H2O2, thereby potentially compromising the therapeutic efficacy.  
Another critical issue pertains to drug delivery and cellular bioavailability. The lipophilicity of EUK-134 is notably lower compared to some analogues, amounting to roughly 43% less lipophilicity in certain cases, which inherently limits its capacity to traverse cell membranes and accumulate in the mitochondrial matrix, where its activity is most needed (Limoli et al., 2006; Quan et al., 2017). Since efficient mitochondrial delivery is crucial for counteracting localized ROS buildup in RPE cells, a deficiency in this area might significantly restrict the net antioxidant benefit provided by EUK-134.  
Furthermore, the translational history of EUK-134 presents a challenge in directly correlating preclinical observations with anticipated clinical outcomes in dry AMD. While substantial evidence exists linking EUK-134 with improved mitochondrial function in non-ocular tissues—such as the normalization of mitochondrial membrane potential in tunicamycin-induced ER stress models (Thoma et al., 2020)—there remains a paucity of direct data in ocular models. Compared to other antioxidants that have been more rigorously tested in retinal systems, EUK-134’s ocular pharmacodynamics, potential toxicity in the retinal microenvironment, and long-term safety profile are not well established (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Grujicic & Allen, 2024).  
The literature also points to the possibility of a paradoxical pro-oxidant effect. In some cellular environments, the administration of exogenous SOD mimetics can inadvertently shift the oxidative balance toward higher hydrogen peroxide levels if the catalase function is insufficient, thereby exacerbating oxidative stress rather than mitigating it (Limoli et al., 2006; Quan et al., 2017). Given the delicate balance required in the redox regulation of RPE cells, such an imbalance could be particularly detrimental.  
In light of these considerations, EUK-134’s potential for repurposing as a treatment for dry AMD is promising but remains conditional upon further optimization. The strengths of its dual antioxidant mechanism, its capacity to restore mitochondrial function, and its versatility as evidenced by its broad therapeutic history underscore its potential utility. However, the measurable shortcomings regarding efficient H2O2 clearance, the observed down-regulation of catalase expression, and uncertain mitochondrial bioavailability present hurdles that must be addressed in subsequent experimental phases. This will likely involve additional formulation strategies to improve cellular uptake, as well as comprehensive studies in appropriate retinal models to definitively correlate its antioxidant profile with functional improvements in RPE cells (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Quan et al., 2017).  
It is also noteworthy that while a broad range of clinical trials have been initiated for compounds with similar ROS-scavenging profiles in retinal degenerations (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.), there is a lack of direct clinical evidence for EUK-134’s efficacy specifically in the context of dry AMD. This gap further emphasizes the need for targeted preclinical studies focusing on ocular pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Establishing a direct connection between EUK-134’s known in vitro benefits and its performance in animal models of geographic atrophy will be essential prior to any clinical translation.  
In conclusion, the mechanistic rationale behind the use of EUK-134 in dry AMD is strong on theoretical grounds, leveraging its dual capacity to mitigate the damaging effects of both superoxide and hydrogen peroxide. However, the compound’s limitations—namely, its reduced effectiveness in scavenging H2O2 under certain conditions, its potential for down-regulating endogenous catalase, and challenges associated with adequate mitochondrial targeting—necessitate a cautious approach. The strategic pathway forward would involve an in-depth exploration of its pharmacological properties in retinal models, formulation modifications to enhance mitochondrial delivery, and dose-optimization studies to balance antioxidant efficacy with safety. Only after these issues are rigorously addressed can EUK-134 be confidently positioned as a viable repurposed candidate for the treatment of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Quan et al., 2017; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012).
