Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AICAR (5‐Aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide) is a synthetic nucleoside analog originally developed as an AMP mimetic agent that is capable of activating AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) across a range of cell types. It is produced by chemical synthesis and is available commercially (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich A9978), having been studied for several decades in the context of cellular energy metabolism and stress signaling. As a member of a class of compounds that mimic the natural intracellular messenger AMP, AICAR is taken up into cells via adenosine transporters and is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase into its active metabolite, ZMP (5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide monophosphate), which then mimics AMP in its interactions with AMPK (Efstathiou et al., 2020). This compound belongs to a well‐established class of metabolic modulators, and similar agents have been used in experimental settings to modulate glucose uptake, fatty acid oxidation, and overall energy homeostasis in both basic science and translational research contexts (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014). In addition, several preclinical studies have evaluated AICAR’s potential as an “exercise mimetic” due to its ability to enhance energy metabolism in muscle and other tissues, and its synthetic nature allows for reproducible and scalable dosing in research models (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, AICAR was developed primarily as an agent to activate AMPK in metabolic studies and has been investigated in a variety of preclinical models ranging from cancer to cardiovascular disease. In the oncology field, for example, AICAR has been shown to inhibit cancer cell proliferation, induce cell cycle arrest, and promote programmed cell death in several cancer types via AMPK-dependent modulation of pathways such as PI3K-Akt and mTOR (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014; Rattan et al., 2005). Clinical studies, particularly those in the cardiovascular arena, have also evaluated AICAR’s safety profile in the context of ischemia-reperfusion injury, including human trials during cardiac surgery, demonstrating that it can be administered safely in humans (Rattan et al., 2005). In the context of ocular research, AICAR has been studied for its effects on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and other ocular cell types; several studies have demonstrated that AICAR suppresses the production of pro-inflammatory complement components such as complement factor 3 (C3) and complement factor B (CFB) in RPE cells under inflammatory conditions (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017). Although there is no established clinical use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) to date, these preclinical observations, combined with its well-known pharmacological profile, have spurred interest in repurposing AICAR for treating retinal diseases characterized by oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020). Furthermore, studies examining AMPK activators in the eye – including those using AICAR in animal models of uveitis or oxidative stress-induced RPE damage – support the notion that activating this metabolic pathway can protect against retinal degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

Mechanism of Action:  
AICAR exerts its biological activity primarily through the activation of AMPK, a master regulator of cellular energy balance that responds to alterations in the AMP/ATP ratio. Once AICAR is imported into cells through adenosine transporters, it is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase to form ZMP, an analog of AMP. ZMP binds to the regulatory γ subunit of AMPK, causing a conformational change that facilitates AMPK phosphorylation at Thr172 by upstream kinases such as LKB1, thereby fully activating the kinase (Efstathiou et al., 2020). Activated AMPK then phosphorylates a series of downstream targets involved in energy metabolism, including acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) and elements of the mTOR signaling pathway. In RPE cells, this activation is particularly important because AMPK phosphorylates and activates ULK1, a kinase critical for initiating autophagy and mitophagy, thereby promoting the clearance of damaged mitochondria (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Chung et al., 2017).  

A central component of the rationale for using AICAR in dry AMD is its ability to stimulate the transcriptional coactivator PGC-1α. AMPK-mediated phosphorylation of PGC-1α enhances its activity and nuclear translocation, which in turn drives the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant defense, and metabolic adaptation (Hu et al., 2024; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). This mechanism is particularly attractive in dry AMD because mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells is thought to contribute significantly to disease pathogenesis by impairing oxidative phosphorylation, increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and triggering cell senescence or death (Tong et al., 2022; Rego, 2023). In addition to these AMPK-dependent effects, some studies have reported that AICAR exerts certain effects independent of AMPK activation. For instance, AICAR has been shown to suppress TNF-α-induced complement factor expression by mechanisms that do not involve AMPK, suggesting that alternative signaling pathways or direct modulation of transcription factor activity might also contribute to its overall activity profile (Chung et al., 2017; Kirchner et al., 2018). These AMPK-independent actions could either broaden the therapeutic potential of AICAR in modulating inflammatory responses or introduce complexity into its activity profile that will need to be carefully isolated and understood (Kirchner et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2024).  

Furthermore, AICAR has been observed to affect mitochondrial dynamics not only by stimulating biogenesis through PGC-1α activation but also by modifying autophagic flux through mTOR inhibition. In models of RPE oxidative stress, where excessive ROS levels lead to mitochondrial fragmentation and accumulation of dysfunctional organelles, AICAR-induced AMPK activation facilitates the clearance of damaged mitochondria via mitophagy, thus restoring mitochondrial quality and energy production (Fisher et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2024). Moreover, experimental evidence suggests that AICAR can modulate the balance between cellular glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation by shifting metabolism toward a more energy-efficient, oxidative phenotype, thereby increasing the overall oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and potentially improving cellular resilience under oxidative stress (Chan et al., 2020; Fisher, 2022).  

Expected Effect:  
Given its mechanisms of action, the expected effect of AICAR in an assay aimed at treating dry AMD would be multifaceted. In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress—a hallmark of dry AMD—AICAR treatment is expected to lead to robust activation of AMPK, as measured by increased phosphorylation of both AMPK and its downstream substrates such as ACC and ULK1 (Guo et al., 2018; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). This activation should in turn upregulate PGC-1α, resulting in enhanced transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, improved mitochondrial DNA replication, and an increased capacity for ATP production (Hu et al., 2024). As damaged mitochondria are a major source of ROS in stressed RPE cells, the stimulation of autophagy and mitophagy is anticipated to selectively clear these dysfunctional organelles, reducing cellular oxidative stress and preventing the secondary damage that contributes to RPE degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

In addition to these metabolic effects, AICAR is also expected to attenuate inflammatory responses within the RPE and adjacent retinal tissues. For instance, by modulating the activity of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) and reducing the expression of inflammatory mediators such as tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and complement components (e.g., C3 and CFB), AICAR would help to create a less pro-inflammatory microenvironment that could further protect RPE cells from damage (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017; Kirchner et al., 2018). These effects are particularly pertinent given that chronic, low-grade inflammation coupled with complement dysregulation is a recognized component of dry AMD pathogenesis.  

At the cellular level, the outcome of AICAR-induced AMPK activation is expected to manifest as enhanced mitochondrial function, improved energy charge (ATP/AMP ratio), reduced ROS accumulation, and, ultimately, a restoration of normal metabolic and autophagic flux in RPE cells (Fisher et al., 2022; Fisher, 2022). This improved bioenergetic profile should translate into protection against RPE cell death, potentially slowing or halting the progression of geographic atrophy associated with dry AMD (Yu et al., 2024; Si et al., 2023). Moreover, since RPE dysfunction in AMD also involves a reduction in the phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, AICAR’s modulatory effects on autophagy may indirectly help to restore the homeostatic functions of RPE cells, reducing the accumulation of damaging lipofuscin and drusen material (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Sung et al., 2015). In summary, the expected effect is a dual-action benefit—mitigation of oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum stresses via improved mitochondrial dynamics and an anti-inflammatory effect stemming from a reduction in complement activation and NF-κB-driven cytokine production (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020).  

Overall Evaluation:  
AICAR represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration owing to its robust and well-characterized mechanism of action via AMPK activation. The strengths of this candidate lie in its dual capacity to modulate critical pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis: on one hand, AICAR enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and promotes the removal of damaged mitochondria through autophagy/mitophagy, and on the other, it attenuates inflammatory cascades that exacerbate RPE cell damage (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hu et al., 2024). The ability of AICAR to upregulate PGC-1α is particularly compelling because mitochondrial dysfunction is now widely recognized as a central element in dry AMD. Preclinical studies have illustrated that dysregulation of mitochondrial function in RPE cells—a decrease in oxidative phosphorylation capacity, increased ROS production, and impaired clearance of damaged organelles—is pivotal in the initiation and progression of AMD (Tong et al., 2022; Rego, 2023). Thus, a compound like AICAR that can simultaneously restore mitochondrial health and mitigate inflammatory responses offers a multifaceted approach to disease modification.  

From the therapeutic history perspective, AICAR has been extensively studied in various preclinical models, including those of ocular inflammation and oxidative stress in RPE cells. Its ability to safely activate AMPK in vivo has been demonstrated across multiple species and contexts, including settings that mimic some aspects of AMD-related stress, such as endotoxin-induced uveitis and sodium iodate-induced RPE damage (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Chan et al., 2020). Additionally, the compound’s known clinical safety profile in human studies—albeit in contexts outside ophthalmology—provides an encouraging starting point for repurposing it for dry AMD, where no approved therapeutics currently exist (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017).  

However, there are notable weaknesses and challenges that must be addressed. First, while AMPK activation is generally beneficial for energy homeostasis and autophagy, certain studies have indicated that AICAR’s effects on RPE cell biology might be context-dependent. For instance, some experimental reports have shown that AICAR can reduce the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments by RPE cells—a process that is essential for retinal health—which may represent a double-edged sword if not carefully titrated (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Yu et al., 2024). In addition, the existence of AMPK-independent effects—such as the direct inhibition of complement factor expression—introduces complexity into the overall mechanism of action and makes it challenging to predict all downstream outcomes. Differential responses have also been observed between healthy and diseased donor RPE cells, implying that “metabolic memory” or cellular adaptation may influence drug responsiveness (Fisher et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2017). These considerations suggest that while the theoretical underpinnings for using AICAR in dry AMD are solid, the translation of these effects into clinical efficacy may require careful optimization of dosing, delivery, and patient selection.  

Another potential limitation is related to its broad mechanism of action. AICAR activates several metabolic pathways that are intertwined with many aspects of cellular physiology. While this pleiotropy provides the therapeutic benefit of addressing multiple dysregulated pathways in AMD simultaneously, it may also increase the risk of off-target effects or metabolic disturbances in tissues outside the retina (Rattan et al., 2005; Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014). For instance, systemic administration of AICAR has been associated with shifts in glycolytic flux and modifications of lipid metabolism, and it is therefore imperative that strategies for ocular delivery (such as intravitreal injections or topical formulations) be developed to maximize retinal exposure while minimizing systemic exposure (Chan et al., 2020; Kamoshita et al., 2014).  

Moreover, despite the substantial body of preclinical data supporting the role of AICAR in activating AMPK and restoring mitochondrial function, clinical data specific to dry AMD are lacking. Although related studies have shown benefits in models of retinal inflammation and degeneration, the exact therapeutic window, long-term safety, and efficacy in humans with AMD must be thoroughly evaluated in well-designed clinical trials. It is also worth mentioning that other AMPK activators, such as metformin, have independently demonstrated protective effects in AMD models, thereby lending credence to the approach but also raising questions about whether AICAR offers a distinct advantage over these agents (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020).  

In summary, the overall evaluation of AICAR as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. Its well-documented ability to activate AMPK, stimulate PGC-1α-driven mitochondrial biogenesis, and induce autophagy presents a strong mechanistic rationale for protecting RPE cells from the mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress that drive dry AMD pathogenesis (Hu et al., 2024; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2011). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Deferiprone is a synthetic iron‐chelating agent originally developed for the treatment of transfusional iron overload disorders, particularly in patients with thalassemia major. It belongs to the hydroxypyridinone class of therapeutic compounds and is characterized by its low molecular weight and lipophilic nature, features that allow it to penetrate cell membranes and cross the blood–brain and blood–retinal barriers (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). Chemically, deferiprone is a bidentate ligand that interacts with iron by coordinating via its hydroxypyridinone groups, forming a neutral complex in a 3:1 stoichiometry with ferric iron (Fe3+), although some studies note its affinity for both Fe3+ and Fe2+ under certain conditions (Li et al., 2023). The synthetic origins of deferiprone involve chemical design strategies aimed at generating small, orally active chelators with selective affinity for iron over other metals such as zinc, copper, and aluminium (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). As a member of the iron chelator drug class, deferiprone’s established use in treating systemic iron overload syndromes has provided it with a significant clinical track record over several decades, forming the basis for its repurposing in disorders where iron-induced oxidative damage plays a role.  

Therapeutic History:  
Deferiprone has been used clinically as an orally administered iron chelator in the management of transfusional iron overload, notably in patients with thalassemia major. This usage is supported by multiple clinical studies and reviews that address both its efficacy in reducing systemic iron burden as well as its associated hematologic risks, such as agranulocytosis and neutropenia, which occur in approximately 1% of patients (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). Beyond its systemic application, preclinical models have demonstrated deferiprone’s potential for retinal protection. Several animal studies report that deferiprone, when administered systemically, can reduce retinal and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) iron levels in models of iron overload or light-induced degeneration and produce improvements in oxidative stress markers and retinal functional indices (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). Although deferiprone has not been widely tested or approved specifically for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar ocular conditions in clinical trials, its documented experimental benefits in animal retinal models along with its established clinical safety profile in iron overload therapy have prompted its consideration for repurposing in dry AMD where iron-induced oxidative injury is implicated (Shahandeh et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2021; Ueda et al., 2018).  

Mechanism of Action:  
Deferiprone functions primarily by chelating labile iron, thereby limiting the pool of redox active iron that can participate in the Fenton reaction—a process in which ferrous iron (Fe2+) reacts with hydrogen peroxide to produce highly reactive hydroxyl radicals. The molecular mechanism of deferiprone is based on its bidentate hydroxypyridinone structure that binds Fe3+ to form a stable neutral complex in a 3:1 chelator to iron ratio, a coordination chemistry that has been well documented in several studies (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). This complex formation effectively reduces the availability of free iron in the intracellular labile iron pool, thereby diminishing iron-catalyzed reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. In addition, some data suggest that deferiprone may also interact with ferrous iron under certain conditions, contributing further to its antioxidant effects by interrupting redox cycling associated with both Fe3+ and Fe2+ species (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021).  

From a biochemical standpoint, iron accumulation in the RPE and surrounding retinal tissues is known to promote lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial oxidative stress, leading to cellular dysfunction and death—a pathomechanism observed in dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). Deferiprone’s cell permeability and ability to traverse biological barriers enables it to access the intracellular compartments, including mitochondria. Although direct studies examining deferiprone’s effect specifically on RPE mitochondrial iron pools are still limited, evidence from other systems (such as neuronal and cardiac tissues) demonstrates that reducing mitochondrial iron load can preserve electron transport chain (ETC) integrity by preventing the formation of deleterious hydroxyl radicals that otherwise damage mitochondrial lipids, proteins, and DNA (Li et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023). Furthermore, preclinical models of retinal injury have shown that deferiprone treatment leads to a reduction in oxidative stress markers, including decreased malondialdehyde (MDA) levels and a concomitant increase in antioxidants such as glutathione (GSH), which supports the hypothesis that iron chelation by deferiprone interrupts the cascade of iron-mediated oxidative damage (Shahandeh et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2025). There is also emerging evidence that iron chelators like deferiprone can mitigate cell death pathways such as ferroptosis and parthanatos in retinal tissues, contributing to neuroprotective outcomes (Villarejo-Zori et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025). In summary, the mechanism of action of deferiprone is multifaceted: it directly reduces the labile iron concentration, thereby lowering the potential for Fenton chemistry, indirectly stabilizes mitochondrial function, and may influence downstream iron-dependent cellular pathways that are implicated in retinal degeneration (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2025).  

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of deferiprone for dry AMD is that chelation of labile iron in RPE mitochondria will prevent Fenton reaction–mediated ROS formation and maintain the integrity of the ETC. In the proposed assay and eventual clinical application, treatment with deferiprone is expected to significantly reduce intracellular labile iron, thereby attenuating oxidative stress that leads to lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial dysfunction. This, in turn, should result in a lower rate of RPE cell death and preserve photoreceptor viability, thereby potentially slowing the progression of dry AMD (Liu et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023).  

Experimental studies have shown that oral administration of deferiprone in animal models results in a measurable decrease in retinal iron load without causing retinal toxicity—a finding that is pivotal for any drug intended for chronic ophthalmic use (Zhao et al., 2025; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). In parallel, in vitro studies using retinal cells such as ARPE-19 have demonstrated that deferiprone reduces markers of oxidative stress, including lower MDA levels and preservation of antioxidant enzyme activities (for example, GPX4 upregulation), which are indicative of reduced ROS-mediated damage (Yang et al., 2025; Shahandeh et al., 2020). The proposed mechanism of action implies that by decreasing the availability of iron necessary for Fenton chemistry, deferiprone will decrease the production of hydroxyl radicals, thus protecting mitochondrial membranes and proteins integral to the ETC from oxidative damage (Li et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023). Moreover, since mitochondrial dysfunction is a known contributor to RPE degeneration in dry AMD, its preservation via iron chelation is expected to sustain cellular ATP production and overall cell viability (Zhao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). Given that the RPE expresses iron regulatory proteins and that dysregulated iron metabolism has been observed in AMD retinas (with increased ferritin and altered transferrin receptor expression), the application of deferiprone would ideally restore homeostasis in the labile iron pool and thereby ameliorate the chronic oxidative insult observed in dry AMD (Li et al., 2023; Ashok et al., 2021).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Deferiprone presents several strengths as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD therapy. Firstly, its well-established clinical use in treating systemic iron overload confers a robust foundation regarding its pharmacokinetics, dosing parameters, and safety profile—despite noted hematologic risks such as agranulocytosis that occur in a small percentage of patients (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). Its oral bioavailability and ability to cross the blood–retinal barrier make it uniquely suited for targeting intracellular iron in the retina (Li et al., 2023). Secondly, there is compelling preclinical evidence from various retinal degeneration models that iron chelators, including deferiprone, can reduce retinal iron accumulation, diminish oxidative stress, and improve functional outcomes, which supports the rationale for its repurposing in the context of dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016; Zhao et al., 2025). Thirdly, its mode of action—chelating labile iron to prevent Fenton reaction–mediated ROS production—directly targets a central pathological mechanism implicated in dry AMD. The hypothesis that reducing mitochondrial iron load will preserve ETC integrity is biologically plausible given the importance of iron-catalyzed oxidative stress in mitochondrial dysfunction within the RPE (Li et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023).  

On the other hand, several weaknesses and uncertainties remain. Although deferiprone’s effectiveness in reducing systemic and retinal iron overload has been demonstrated in animal models, direct evidence of its capacity to specifically target RPE mitochondrial iron and preserve ETC function in human RPE cells is currently limited (Zhao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023). The precise molecular details regarding how deferiprone modulates mitochondrial iron trafficking, and how this relates to the functional maintenance of the electron transport chain, require further investigation. Additionally, while preclinical data are supportive, deferiprone has not yet been tested in clinical trials specifically for dry AMD, and its long-term safety and efficacy in the ocular context remain to be established (Zhao et al., 2021; Ueda et al., 2018). Another consideration is the risk of adverse systemic effects, such as neutropenia and agranulocytosis, which, although infrequent, could limit its utility in a population of elderly patients with dry AMD who may have co‐morbidities (Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). Moreover, some reports have suggested that under low concentrations or certain conditions, iron chelators might paradoxically participate in free radical formation, necessitating precise dose titration and careful monitoring (Li et al., 2023; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016).  

In summary, deferiprone appears to be a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its well-documented ability to chelate labile iron, its favorable pharmacologic properties including oral bioavailability and tissue penetration, and preclinical evidence showing retinal protection. Its mechanism of action—reducing the labile iron pool to limit Fenton reaction–induced oxidative stress—addresses a central pathogenic mechanism of dry AMD, namely, iron accumulation leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and lipid peroxidation in the RPE (Zhao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). However, the extrapolation of these preclinical findings to human dry AMD requires additional studies, particularly those that directly measure mitochondrial iron dynamics and ETC activity in RPE cells following deferiprone treatment. Rigorous dose-ranging and safety studies will also be necessary to mitigate the risk of hematologic adverse effects. Therefore, while deferiprone has significant potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD, further preclinical mechanistic studies and early-phase clinical trials are essential to fully validate its efficacy and safety in this new therapeutic context (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Ueda et al., 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
L-Carnitine is a naturally occurring quaternary ammonium compound, chemically defined as β-hydroxy-γ-trimethylaminobutyrate, that is both derived from the diet (predominantly found in animal-based foods such as red meat) and biosynthesized endogenously from the essential amino acids lysine and methionine via a vitamin C–dependent pathway primarily in the liver and kidneys (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Mollica et al., 2017). Historically, L-carnitine was first identified as a constituent of muscle tissue in the early 20th century and was later linked to its high content in meat, leading to its designation as “vitamin T” in certain insect models (Mollica et al., 2017). As a member of the carnitine family, it belongs to the class of metabolic cofactors or nutraceutical agents whose primary function is to shuttle activated long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondrial matrix, where they undergo β-oxidation, thereby facilitating aerobic energy production and maintaining the intracellular acyl-CoA/CoA balance (Moos et al., 2017; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). This class of compounds has historically been used as dietary supplements to treat primary and secondary carnitine deficiency, as well as in various metabolic and mitochondrial disorders (Flanagan et al., 2010). L-Carnitine is widely formulated in pharmaceutical products both as a standalone supplement and as an ingredient in combination formulations, which underscores its acceptance as a metabolic supportive agent with a favorable safety profile (Flanagan et al., 2010; Surai, 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, the carnitine family has a long record of use in addressing conditions where fatty acid oxidation is impaired. L-Carnitine has been employed effectively as a life-saving therapy in primary carnitine deficiency—a condition in which mutations of the carnitine transporter (OCTN2) impair cellular uptake—and also in secondary deficiencies associated with conditions like renal failure, liver disease, and certain inborn errors of metabolism (Flanagan et al., 2010). Beyond classical deficiency syndromes, both L-carnitine and its acetylated derivative (acetyl-L-carnitine) have been investigated in a broad range of clinical contexts, including cardiovascular diseases, diabetic complications, and neurodegenerative disorders. For example, acetyl-L-carnitine has been shown to improve parameters of visual function in patients with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and to confer neuroprotective effects in Alzheimer’s disease and mild cognitive impairment (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Calabrese et al., 2009).  
In ophthalmology, while most clinical studies have focused on the use of carnitine derivatives for systemic metabolic or neuroprotective effects, there is preclinical evidence supporting an ocular role. Animal studies have identified high intraocular concentrations of carnitine in the lens and other ocular tissues, hinting at a physiological role in maintaining ocular metabolic balance and osmotic homeostasis (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). Investigations into the protective effects of L-carnitine against oxidative damage, including its potential to safeguard retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and other ocular tissues, provide a rationale for its application in dry AMD, particularly in the context of geographic atrophy where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central features (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c). Moreover, combination therapy regimens incorporating acetyl-L-carnitine with n-3 fatty acids and coenzyme Q10 have also been trialed in experimental settings to address energy metabolism in retinal tissues (Shamsi et al., 2007). Despite these promising findings, direct clinical use of L-carnitine as monotherapy for dry AMD has not been extensively reported, thus making its repurposing an area that merits focused research to bridge the gap between its established metabolic functions and its potential application in retinal degeneration (Flanagan et al., 2010; Mollica et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
The central biochemical role of L-carnitine is to facilitate the transport of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle—a process that is critical for β-oxidation and ATP production. This shuttle is mediated by mitochondrial enzymes such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT-1) on the outer mitochondrial membrane, which converts acyl-CoA to acyl-carnitine, and carnitine acyltransferase (also known as carnitine acetyltransferase or CAT) within the mitochondria that re-forms acyl-CoA for oxidation (Moos et al., 2017; Jones et al., 2010). This process not only fuels ATP generation via the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation but also helps regulate the cellular acyl-CoA/CoA ratio, indirectly influencing multiple metabolic pathways (Surai, 2015).  
Furthermore, L-carnitine exhibits antioxidant properties either directly, through free radical scavenging, or indirectly by preserving mitochondrial integrity and function under oxidative stress conditions (Shamsi et al., 2007; Surai, 2015). It has been shown to reduce lipid peroxidation and prevent the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential—a key step in the cascade leading to cellular apoptosis (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c). In addition to its classical mitochondrial functions, L-carnitine also acts as an osmolyte, protecting cells against hyperosmolarity by stabilizing proteins and cellular membranes, which could further reduce oxidative stress (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b; Mollica et al., 2017).  
At the molecular level in the RPE, the hypothesis is that enhancing mitochondrial fatty acid uptake via L-carnitine supplementation will improve β-oxidation efficiency. This is expected to lead to increased ATP production and a reduction in the accumulation of lipid intermediates that may otherwise result in excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation. Notably, disrupted mitochondrial metabolism and energy deficits have been implicated in the progression of RPE cell dysfunction, and L-carnitine’s role in restoring metabolic flexibility has been documented in other cell types such as hepatocytes and neuronal cells (Ates et al., 2008; Surai, 2015). Based on its multifaceted mechanisms of action, the anticipated effect of L-carnitine in an assay designed for dry age-related macular degeneration is twofold. First, by enhancing mitochondrial fatty acid uptake and increasing β-oxidation rates, L-carnitine is expected to boost ATP production in RPE cells, thereby ameliorating the energy deficits that contribute to cellular dysfunction in geographic atrophy (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Jones et al., 2010). Moreover, reductions in established markers of oxidative stress, such as malondialdehyde (MDA) levels or increased glutathione (GSH) concentrations, would support its antioxidant action (Ates et al., 2008). Preclinical studies in other tissues such as neuronal cells and hepatocytes have demonstrated that L-carnitine treatment not only restores mitochondrial function but also reduces lipid-induced ROS production and inflammation. Overall Evaluation:  
L-Carnitine stands out as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to several compelling properties. Its established role in promoting mitochondrial β-oxidation and energy production, combined with demonstrated antioxidant and osmoprotective actions, provides a strong mechanistic rationale for addressing the metabolic and oxidative stress components of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Jones et al., 2010). However, there are potential limitations that merit cautious consideration. Direct evidence of L-carnitine’s efficacy in RPE cells specifically within the context of dry AMD is currently limited. While preclinical studies in non-ocular tissues and some ocular models suggest beneficial mitochondrial and antioxidant effects, the precise dosing, ocular bioavailability, and long-term impact on retinal degeneration remain to be rigorously established. In summary, the strengths of L-carnitine include its well-established role in cellular energy metabolism, its safety profile and widespread clinical use in other metabolic conditions, and its potential to mitigate ROS production and oxidative damage through enhanced fatty acid oxidation. The weaknesses primarily lie in the current paucity of direct evidence in ocular models of dry AMD and the challenges associated with ensuring adequate drug delivery to the RPE in vivo. Nonetheless, given the overall mechanistic promise and the favorable tolerability observed in numerous studies, L-carnitine warrants further investigation – with a focus on in vitro RPE assays under condition of lipid overload and oxidative stress, followed by in vivo preclinical models of geographic atrophy – to validate its efficacy as a repurposed therapy for dry AMD (Jones et al., 2010; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c; Ates et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2024).  
Overall, I recommend proceeding with targeted experiments to assess mitochondrial respiration, ROS levels, and cell survival in RPE cultures treated with L-carnitine. These studies should be complemented with investigations of tissue distribution following ocular delivery to address bioavailability concerns. This comprehensive evaluation supports the potential of L-carnitine as a metabolic and antioxidant therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, while also highlighting areas where additional data are needed before clinical translation.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Mitochonic Acid-5 (MA-5; MedChemExpress HY-104308) is a synthetic, mitochondria‐targeted small molecule originally discovered for its ability to improve mitochondrial function in models of cellular aging. MA-5 belongs to the class of mitochondrial modulators that have been shown to enhance adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production, reduce mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), and extend lifespan in non‐ocular systems such as fibroblasts and Caenorhabditis elegans. The current hypothesis proposes that MA-5 binds directly to mitofilin (also known as Mic60), a key scaffolding protein in the inner mitochondrial membrane that is essential for the proper organization and stability of mitochondrial cristae. This interaction is anticipated to stabilize cristae architecture, thereby preserving optimal assembly of the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and enabling improved mitochondrial bioenergetics—a mechanism particularly appealing in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), where cristae disorganization and mtROS accumulation in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells have been associated with disease pathology (Ji et al., 2021; Ferrington et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
While MA-5 itself has not been previously evaluated in ocular diseases, compounds that modulate mitochondrial function have a long history in preclinical studies for age-related conditions. Several mitochondrial-targeted agents—for example, SkQ1 and elamipretide—have demonstrated promise in ameliorating mitochondrial defects in RPE models and in early clinical trials targeting dry AMD (Ji et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022). In other systems, MA-5 has been reported to improve ATP production, reduce mtROS, and activate the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt) in fibroblast and C. elegans models. Such beneficial effects on mitochondrial function have contributed to the rationale for repurposing MA-5 for dry AMD. Moreover, research in related domains suggests that stabilizing mitochondrial cristae via targeting scaffold proteins such as mitofilin is mechanistically sound given observations of altered mitofilin expression and cristae disruption in AMD RPE (Ferrington et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). However, direct usage of MA-5 in retinal disorders remains unexplored, and its potential has yet to be validated in RPE-specific in vitro or in vivo models.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, MA-5 is proposed to exert its beneficial effects by physically interacting with mitofilin/Mic60, a protein integral to the maintenance of inner mitochondrial membrane architecture and cristae organization. Mitofilin is recognized for its role in stabilizing the cristae junctions and in facilitating the proper assembly and function of the ETC complexes (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Ferrington et al., 2020). In dry AMD, mitochondrial cristae loss has been documented in RPE cells, suggesting that disrupted mitofilin function may underlie some of the bioenergetic deficiencies seen in the disease (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Ferrington et al., 2020). By binding to mitofilin, MA-5 is expected to reinforce cristae integrity; this stabilization can promote the efficient assembly of ETC complexes, thereby leading to improved oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production. Concurrently, enhanced cristae organization is likely to reduce electron leakage from the ETC and lower the production of reactive oxygen species, which in excess contribute to oxidative damage and RPE cell death (Ji et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022).

In addition, emerging evidence suggests that perturbations in mitochondrial structure can trigger the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt), a conserved stress-response pathway that upregulates mitochondrial chaperones such as mtHsp70 and other proteostasis factors to cope with misfolded proteins and oxidative damage. MA-5 is hypothesized not only to stabilize the physical architecture of the mitochondria but also to activate UPRmt pathways, thereby enhancing the endogenous capacity of RPE cells to detoxify ROS and repair mitochondrial damage. Activation of UPRmt could lead to increased expression of mitochondrial chaperones, improved clearance of damaged proteins, and a restoration of redox balance within the mitochondria. This dual mechanism—direct structural stabilization via mitofilin binding and indirect activation of UPRmt—positions MA-5 as a potentially powerful agent for correcting mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD (Tong et al., 2022; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
If MA-5 performs as hypothesized in RPE cells, several beneficial effects are anticipated. First, by binding mitofilin and stabilizing cristae architecture, MA-5 should restore proper assembly and function of ETC complexes leading to increased ATP production. Such a recovery in mitochondrial bioenergetics is particularly critical in RPE cells, given their high energy demands for processes such as phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and maintenance of the visual cycle (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022). Second, the stabilization of cristae, alongside the potential activation of the UPRmt, is expected to reduce mtROS production by minimizing electron leakage from complex I and III of the ETC. Lower ROS levels would alleviate oxidative stress—a known driver of RPE degeneration and dry AMD progression that has been documented in multiple studies (Ji et al., 2021; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Third, the activation of UPRmt may upregulate key mitochondrial chaperones such as mtHsp70, facilitating improved protein folding, enhanced clearance of damaged proteins, and overall better maintenance of mitochondrial homeostasis. These cellular changes should collectively promote RPE survival and function, thus potentially slowing or even reversing some aspects of the cellular degenerative processes seen in dry AMD (Ji et al., 2021; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

Furthermore, since mitofilin/Mic60 is an abundantly expressed and essential component in RPE mitochondria—as evidenced by its upregulation in early AMD patient samples—the MA-5-mediated stabilization of this protein is expected to yield measurable improvements in mitochondrial parameters in cellular assays. Such improvements would include increased mitochondrial membrane potential, enhanced basal and maximal respiration, and a reduction in apoptotic markers associated with mitochondrial damage. Ultimately, if these in vitro effects translate into in vivo efficacy, MA-5 could contribute to a novel treatment modality that directly addresses the underlying mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD (Ferrington et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
The therapeutic candidate MA-5 presents a highly promising, mechanistically driven approach to addressing dry AMD by targeting mitochondrial dysfunction—a central hallmark of the disease. Its proposed dual mechanism of binding to mitofilin to stabilize cristae architecture and activating the UPRmt to enhance antioxidant defenses directly aligns with the documented mitochondrial pathology in RPE cells. Strengths of this candidate include the following:  
– The strategy of targeting mitofilin is supported by numerous observations that indicate altered mitofilin levels and cristae disorganization in AMD, suggesting that restoring cristae integrity may ameliorate mitochondrial deficits (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Ferrington et al., 2020).  
– MA-5’s documented capacity to improve ATP production and reduce mtROS in non-ocular models indicates a favorable mitochondrial modulation profile that is likely transferable to RPE cells, where energy production and redox homeostasis are critical (Ji et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022).  
– Activation of UPRmt represents an innovative therapeutic angle that not only protects mitochondrial structure but also boosts cellular defenses against oxidative stress—a pathway that has been implicated in maintaining RPE cell viability under conditions of sustained stress (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022).  

Despite these promising aspects, several points of caution must be noted. First, while the beneficial effects of MA-5 have been demonstrated in fibroblast and C. elegans models, no direct data exist regarding its efficacy in RPE cells or in animal models of dry AMD. The translation of effects from non-ocular systems to the highly specialized RPE must be rigorously evaluated. Second, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of MA-5 in the context of ocular delivery are unknown at this time; the compound’s ability to achieve sufficient retinal concentration, while minimizing systemic toxicity, remains an open question. Third, the precise binding affinity and specificity of MA-5 for mitofilin in RPE mitochondria have not yet been characterized. Off-target effects or unintended modulation of mitochondrial dynamics may lead to adverse outcomes if the drug’s action is not adequately localized within the retina. Finally, activation of UPRmt, while beneficial in the context of mitochondrial stress, may also have complex downstream effects that require careful titration to avoid potential maladaptive consequences in long-term treatment scenarios (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Ferrington et al., 2020).

In summary, the proposed mechanism for MA-5 is conceptually attractive given the wealth of literature linking mitochondrial cristae disruption and excessive ROS production to dry AMD pathology. The candidate’s potential to bind mitofilin, stabilize mitochondrial structure, and activate a protective UPRmt aligns well with the current understanding of mitochondrial deficits in RPE cells observed in AMD (Ji et al., 2021; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). However, significant preclinical work is needed to validate its efficacy specifically in the RPE environment. Studies should include detailed binding assays to confirm the interaction between MA-5 and mitofilin, evaluation of mitochondrial bioenergetics and redox parameters in RPE cell cultures, and ultimately, assessments in animal models of dry AMD that recapitulate key aspects of mitochondrial dysfunction. Provided these experimental hurdles can be overcome and favorable pharmacokinetic profiles established for ocular delivery, MA-5 may represent a novel and promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD (Nashine, 2021; Tong et al., 2022).

Overall, while there is robust mechanistic rationale and encouraging preclinical evidence from other models supporting the concept of mitochondrial stabilization via mitofilin targeting, the transition of MA-5 into the dry AMD arena is contingent upon a series of critical validation steps in relevant ocular models. The strengths of MA-5 lie in its potential to address the upstream causes of RPE degeneration by restoring mitochondrial integrity and function, which is a major unmet need in dry AMD therapeutics. The weaknesses and uncertainties, however, underscore the need for a focused series of seriatim experiments to fully characterize its effects in RPE cells and to develop suitable formulations for ocular administration. Based on the current evidence drawn from mitochondrial pathology in AMD and the functional roles of mitofilin/Mic60 in maintaining cristae integrity, MA-5 merits further investigation as a repurposed candidate for dry AMD, with the caveat that extensive preclinical testing is required before clinical translation can be considered (Ji et al., 2021; Ferrington et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin (also known as sirolimus and available as Abcam #ab120224) is a naturally occurring macrolide compound originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus. It belongs to the class of macrocyclic lactones and is known for its potent inhibitory effects on the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). This compound has been extensively used in various contexts such as immunosuppression, cancer therapy, and more recently, as a tool to modulate autophagy in age-related degenerative diseases. In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction and dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), rapamycin is being explored as a repurposed therapeutic candidate with the hypothesis that mTORC1 inhibition will enhance both general autophagy and selective mitophagy. This clearance of reactive oxygen species (ROS)–generating, damaged mitochondria may alleviate oxidative stress, reduce the accumulation of toxic lipofuscin compounds (including A2E), and ultimately slow the progression of dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, rapamycin was first discovered for its potent immunosuppressive properties and later developed for use in preventing transplant rejection and certain cancers. Its ability to inhibit mTORC1 has made it a valuable tool in research related to aging and neurodegeneration. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its effectiveness in modulating autophagy and protecting cellular integrity under stress conditions, particularly in the retinal environment. In animal models of retinal degeneration and even some early clinical trials, rapamycin was shown to reduce the accumulation of autofluorescent granules and inflammatory cytokines in the RPE, which are both hallmarks of dry AMD pathology (Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022). Notably, rapamycin has been administered via diverse routes, including intravitreal and subconjunctival injections, in attempts to treat geographic atrophy or other dry AMD phenotypes, although the clinical outcomes have been mixed. For example, clinical trials such as those referenced in studies with identifiers NCT00766649 and NCT01445548 demonstrated that while rapamycin was generally safe and well-tolerated in ocular applications, its efficacy in slowing down the progression of geographic atrophy and improving visual acuity remained limited (National Eye Institute, 2008; National Eye Institute, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These historical findings highlight both the promise and the challenges associated with translating rapamycin’s mechanistic benefits into robust clinical outcomes for dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary mechanism of rapamycin involves the formation of a complex with the immunophilin FKBP12. This complex binds to mTORC1 and inhibits its kinase activity, leading to a decrease in the phosphorylation of downstream targets such as ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K) and the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 (4EBP1). Under normal circumstances, active mTORC1 suppresses autophagy by phosphorylating these targets, which in turn prevents the formation of autophagosomes. By inhibiting mTORC1, rapamycin effectively removes this blockade, thereby promoting the induction of autophagy as evidenced by increased conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II and clearance of the autophagic substrate p62 (Zhang et al., 2015).

Within retinal pigment epithelial cells, this induction of autophagy is particularly important. RPE cells are responsible for the phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments; a process that generates large amounts of cellular debris and metabolic byproducts such as lipofuscin. In dry AMD, impaired autophagic flux leads to the accumulation of these compounds, which, in turn, contributes to oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Rapamycin’s inhibition of mTORC1 not only enhances general autophagy but also promotes selective mitochondrial clearance (mitophagy). Key players in the mitophagy pathway include the serine/threonine kinase PINK1 and the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin, both of which accumulate on depolarized mitochondria and signal their removal via autophagic mechanisms. By stimulating this PINK1/Parkin pathway, rapamycin enhances the clearance of damaged, ROS-generating mitochondria, thus preserving overall mitochondrial health (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).

Additionally, rapamycin’s downstream effects include activation of transcription factors such as TFEB, which regulates lysosomal biogenesis and further enhances the autophagic process. This dual action—promoting both autophagy and lysosomal function—helps to mitigate the accumulation of toxic aggregates such as lipofuscin and A2E in RPE, therefore reducing oxidative stress and inflammation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). Through these biochemical interactions, rapamycin establishes a cellular environment that is more capable of dealing with metabolic challenges and oxidative damage, both of which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Chang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed hypothesis, the administration of rapamycin in RPE cells is expected to result in a cascade of beneficial cellular events. In our proposed assay, rapamycin is anticipated to inhibit mTORC1 activity, leading to a measurable increase in autophagic flux. This will be evident from the enhanced lipidation of LC3-II, the clearance of p62 (an autophagy adaptor protein that accumulates when autophagy is impaired), and the activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway in response to oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2015).

The specific clearance of damaged mitochondria is particularly critical in the RPE, where mitochondrial dysfunction is a significant contributor to the generation of reactive oxygen species and subsequent cellular damage. By removing these dysfunctional mitochondria, rapamycin is expected to reduce intracellular ROS levels and thereby lower oxidative stress, a driving force in AMD pathology. In parallel, the enhanced autophagic degradation of accumulated lipofuscin and the toxic fluorophore A2E is predicted to further limit the inflammatory and apoptotic cascades triggered by these compounds, thus preserving RPE cell viability and function (Zhang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2025).

Moreover, the expression of PINK1 and Parkin in RPE cells has been well documented, and their activation is indicative of mitophagic turnover. Their proper functioning is a key determinant in mitochondrial quality control, and rapamycin is expected to potentiate this process, ensuring that mitochondria remain healthy and capable of maintaining cellular energy production and reducing the risk of cell death (Pinelli et al., 2025; Hyttinen et al., 2018). Given that impaired mitochondrial function and the resulting energy production deficits are central to the progression of dry AMD, the expected outcomes from rapamycin treatment would include not only a reduction in oxidative stress markers but also improvements in mitochondrial dynamics and overall cellular homeostasis. Such effects would ideally be reflected in functional assays measuring cell viability, mitochondrial respiration, and reductions in inflammatory cytokine production (Zhang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In our comprehensive evaluation of rapamycin as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and potential weaknesses emerge that warrant careful consideration. One of the key strengths of rapamycin lies in its well-characterized mechanism of action and its ability to broadly modulate autophagy through mTORC1 inhibition. Preclinical studies have repeatedly demonstrated that rapamycin can induce autophagic flux, leading to the clearance of cellular debris and damaged mitochondria in RPE cells. This is particularly compelling given the central role of impaired autophagy in the accumulation of lipofuscin and A2E, which are major pathological features of dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018). The dual-action mechanism—enhancing both autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis via TFEB activation—further supports its potential in addressing multiple aspects of the disease pathology, from oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction to inflammation and cellular senescence (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Another strength is the substantial body of preclinical evidence showing that rapamycin not only stimulates autophagy but also improves mitochondrial function. The activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway is particularly relevant since these proteins are indispensable for mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control. By facilitating the removal of ROS-generating, damaged mitochondria, rapamycin could directly impact the cellular energy balance and reduce damaging oxidative insults in the RPE, which is pivotal for maintaining retinal health (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).

Despite its promising mechanistic profile, several significant challenges remain. Clinical studies investigating the use of rapamycin for AMD have yielded mixed results. While the drug has been shown to be safe and tolerable in ocular applications, several clinical trials, such as those involving subconjunctival or intravitreal administration, did not demonstrate significant efficacy in halting the progression of geographic atrophy or improving visual acuity. In some instances, adverse effects such as decreased visual acuity and retinal thinning have been observed, raising concerns about the balance between therapeutic benefit and potential retinal toxicity (National Eye Institute, 2008; National Eye Institute, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These mixed clinical findings underscore the complexity of modulating mTORC1 in a disease with multifactorial etiology and suggest that the optimal dosage, treatment duration, and patient selection criteria still require refinement.

Furthermore, the variability in response among different donor-derived RPE cells—where only about 50% of AMD donor samples responded positively to rapamycin in certain studies—points to potential issues regarding patient heterogeneity and the need for personalized therapeutic regimens (Ebeling et al., 2020). This heterogeneity may be due to differences in the intrinsic capacity for autophagy, genetic variations affecting mitochondrial quality control, or the extent of existing cellular damage. Such variability complicates the development of standardized treatment protocols and could limit the broad applicability of rapamycin unless predictive biomarkers of response are identified (Zhang et al., 2015).

Another important consideration is the dual nature of autophagy in the context of RPE health. The delivery method and pharmacokinetics of rapamycin also represent important variables. While nanotechnology-based delivery systems—such as synthetic high-density lipoprotein nanoparticles—have shown promise in achieving more targeted and sustained delivery of rapamycin to the RPE (Mei et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2021), these strategies require further translational studies to assess their safety, efficacy, and scalability in clinical settings. In summary, rapamycin presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its robust mechanism of action—specifically, its capacity to inhibit mTORC1, thereby stimulating both general autophagy and the selective removal of damaged mitochondria via the PINK1/Parkin pathway. Preclinical evidence strongly supports the idea that such modulation can reduce oxidative stress, clear toxic accumulations like lipofuscin/A2E, and ultimately preserve mitochondrial and RPE cellular function (Zhang et al., 2015; Hyttinen et al., 2018). However, the translation of these benefits into clinical improvements remains uncertain, with several trials indicating that while rapamycin is safe and modulates cellular pathways implicated in AMD, its clinical efficacy in terms of preserving visual function has not been conclusively demonstrated. The heterogeneity in patient responses, the potential for adverse outcomes related to excessive autophagy, and the challenges in optimizing dosing and delivery all represent significant hurdles. These considerations suggest that while rapamycin is a promising candidate worthy of further investigation, its ultimate role in the treatment paradigm for dry AMD will depend on our ability to refine treatment regimens, develop predictive biomarkers for patient selection, and perhaps combine mTOR modulation with complementary therapeutic strategies that reinforce its protective effects while mitigating its risks (Wang et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2019).

Given the cumulative evidence, our overall recommendation is to continue exploring rapamycin as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, but with a strategic focus on further preclinical investigations that address the dose–response relationships in donor-derived RPE models and the development of advanced drug delivery systems. It will also be important to design future clinical trials with stratified patient populations and integrated biomarkers that can help identify responders. This iterative approach could eventually lead to a carefully balanced regimen where rapamycin’s autophagy-enhancing properties are harnessed to maintain retinal integrity while avoiding the pitfalls of over-inhibition or systemic toxicity. In essence, the promise of rapamycin in modulating autophagy to improve mitochondrial health and reduce oxidative stress in RPE cells is clear at the molecular and cellular levels, but translating these benefits into a safe and effective therapy for dry AMD will require overcoming substantial clinical challenges (Mei et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Strengths of rapamycin include its well-established mechanism of action, the significant supportive preclinical data demonstrating improvements in autophagic flux and mitochondrial clearance in RPE models, and its potential to address several key pathological features of dry AMD simultaneously. Weaknesses include the mixed clinical trial outcomes to date, the potential for adverse effects in certain contexts (including decreased visual acuity and retinal thinning), and the observed heterogeneity in therapeutic response among different patient samples. These factors highlight the importance of further mechanistic studies and carefully controlled clinical trials. Overall, rapamycin remains one of the more mechanistically promising candidates for repurposing in dry AMD, yet its future success will depend on how effectively we can tailor its delivery and dosing to maximize protective effects while minimizing risks in the vulnerable RPE of AMD patients (Niu et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022).

In conclusion, rapamycin’s role as an mTORC1 inhibitor with the capacity to induce autophagy and mitophagy presents an exciting therapeutic avenue for addressing the complex pathology of dry AMD. By alleviating the buildup of toxic metabolites and preserving mitochondrial health in RPE cells, rapamycin could potentially slow disease progression and preserve vision. Nonetheless, the balance between benefit and adverse effects remains delicate, and further research is essential to elucidate how best to leverage rapamycin’s molecular actions in a clinically meaningful way. This comprehensive review supports the continued investigation of rapamycin as a candidate for dry AMD therapy, provided that subsequent studies can address the highlighted challenges and refine the therapeutic strategy to achieve consistent, positive clinical outcomes (Mei et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2022).
