Below is a detailed evaluation of SB 290157 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (dry AMD). The review is organized into five sections: (1) Overview of Therapeutic Candidate; (2) Therapeutic History; (3) Mechanism of Action; (4) Expected Effect; and (5) Overall Evaluation. Each section combines biochemical, preclinical, and clinical considerations based solely on the provided context.

────────────────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

SB 290157 is a synthetic small‐molecule compound that functions as an antagonist of the C3a receptor (C3aR). Chemically, it is defined as N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine, a structure that incorporates an arginine residue with an acyl modification incorporating a 2,2-diphenylethoxy moiety (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). SB 290157 was discovered through high-throughput screening efforts aimed at identifying molecules capable of displacing radiolabeled C3a from its receptor. Early screening identified a lead compound that underwent extensive chemical optimization – including solid-phase peptide and peptidomimetic synthesis using Fmoc‐based chemistry on Wang resin – to yield SB 290157 (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011). This synthetic approach, employing coupling reagents such as 1-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)-3-ethylcarbodiimide hydrochloride and 4-dimethylaminopyridine, resulted in a non-peptide molecule designed to maximize receptor affinity while minimizing metabolic instability. The compound is commercially available from suppliers such as Cayman Chemical (catalog #10006619) and has served as a prototypic small-molecule C3aR antagonist in numerous preclinical studies (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017).

SB 290157 falls within the broader class of synthetic GPCR modulators that target complement receptors. Historically, such molecules have been exploited as biochemical tools to interrogate the role of anaphylatoxins in inflammatory responses (Ames et al., 2001). C3a, a 77-residue protein fragment produced during complement activation, is recognized by its GPCR, C3aR, and triggers diverse cellular responses (Ames et al., 2001). Multiple research groups have employed small-molecule antagonists like SB 290157 to elucidate the contribution of C3a-mediated signaling in conditions ranging from arthritis to lung inflammation (Ames et al., 2001). The compound’s synthetic origin and chemical tractability have allowed investigators to probe receptor pharmacology in heterologous cell lines (e.g., RBL-C3aR cells, ARPE-19 cells) and primary human cell systems (Ames et al., 2001). In the context of ocular research, SB 290157 has been used experimentally in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) models – particularly in primary human fetal RPE cultures – to block C3a-induced alterations in extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

Beyond its established utility as a research tool, the use of SB 290157 in ocular models speaks to an emerging rationale for targeting complement signaling in degenerative eye diseases. Its inclusion in a commercial catalog further underscores its ready availability to laboratories, enabling reproducibility and fostering further experimentation. In summary, SB 290157 is a synthetic, non-peptide, arginine-based antagonist belonging to a class of compounds that have historically been used to interrogate complement receptor signaling, with a well-defined chemical structure, known synthesis protocols, and broad preclinical application in inflammation research (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

SB 290157 has a storied history in the complement research field. Its initial characterization, as detailed by Ames and colleagues, revealed that SB 290157 competes for C3a binding with an IC₅₀ in the high‐nanomolar range (approximately 200 nM) and potently inhibits C3a-induced intracellular calcium mobilization in sensitive cell lines, such as RBL cells and human neutrophils (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Early studies validated its functional capacity as a selective antagonist in vitro, establishing that it effectively blocked receptor internalization and attenuated downstream signaling events elicited by C3a binding.

Preclinically, SB 290157 has been deployed in a wide range of experimental disease models. For instance, it has been used in animal studies examining anti-inflammatory activity in models such as guinea pig LPS-induced airway neutrophilia and adjuvant-induced arthritis in rats. In the arthritis model, administration of SB 290157 resulted in a significant reduction (approximately 41%) in paw edema, while in airway inflammation models it suppressed neutrophil recruitment, demonstrating its anti-inflammatory efficacy (Ames et al., 2001). These early demonstrations of anti-inflammatory activity provided the impetus to consider SB 290157 for further repurposing in conditions where complement overactivation contributes to pathology.

More recently, attention has turned to the role of complement in ocular diseases, particularly age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Experimental evidence in primary human fetal RPE cultures has shown that exposure to recombinant C3a for periods of 2–4 weeks results in the accumulation of sub-RPE deposits via increased ECM deposition, notably of collagens (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Importantly, co-treatment with a C3a receptor antagonist – which in many instances has been SB 290157 – successfully prevented the abnormal accumulation of sub-RPE deposits. These studies have helped establish a mechanistic link between C3a/C3aR activation and the proteostasis dysfunction observed in RPE cells, a pathological process believed to contribute to early AMD pathology.

In addition to in vitro data, in vivo models provide further support for the therapeutic potential of modulating C3aR signaling. In a murine model of sodium iodate (NaIO₃)-induced RPE injury – a model that recapitulates aspects of geographic atrophy – systemic administration of SB 290157 reduced photoreceptor death, decreased markers of gliosis and microglial activation, and lowered TNFα and STAT3 signaling levels (Wang et al., 2020). Similarly, in a laser-induced retinal vein occlusion (RVO) model, intravitreal injection of SB 290157 suppressed the up-regulation of both C3 and C3a receptor expression, correlating with partial rescue of retinal morphology and vascular integrity (Zhao et al., 2025). Although these studies were not specifically designed for dry AMD, the similarities in underlying complement-mediated RPE injury and chronic inflammation between these models and the dry AMD phenotype provide a strong rationale for further exploring SB 290157 in this indication.

Despite these promising applications, SB 290157’s therapeutic history is not without controversy. Several studies have reported that, depending on the cell type and receptor density, SB 290157 may exhibit partial agonist activity rather than acting as a pure antagonist (Mathieu et al., 2005). This variable pharmacological profile has raised concerns about its utility as a definitive clinical tool. Nonetheless, as a research probe, SB 290157 has significantly advanced our understanding of complement-mediated cellular responses in inflammatory, vascular, and ocular contexts. Overall, while it has been extensively used in preclinical studies across multiple disease models – including arthritis, lung inflammation, and retinal injury – its use specifically in clinical settings for dry AMD remains investigational (Ames et al., 2001; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Wang et al., 2020).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

SB 290157 exerts its biological effects by competitively binding to the C3a receptor (C3aR), thereby preventing the interaction of endogenous C3a with its receptor. Under normal conditions, the complement cascade, when activated via any of its pathways, leads to the cleavage of complement component C3 and the subsequent release of the anaphylatoxin C3a. This bioactive peptide binds to C3aR, a G protein-coupled receptor present on various cell types including granulocytes, monocytes, and notably retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Once activated, C3aR transduces signals that can lead to intracellular calcium mobilization, triggering a cascade of downstream events such as receptor internalization and activation of inflammatory transcription factors.

In vitro studies using radioligand binding assays have determined that SB 290157 displaces [¹²⁵I]-C3a from its receptor with an IC₅₀ in the high nanomolar range (approximately 200 nM), while functional calcium mobilization assays in cell lines (including RBL cells and human neutrophils) have demonstrated potent inhibition of C3a-stimulated intracellular calcium release at low nanomolar concentrations (approximately 28 nM) (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Mechanistically, by preventing C3a from engaging C3aR, the compound is able to avert subsequent receptor conformational changes that would otherwise lead to G protein coupling and downstream signaling events.

In the context of RPE cells, particularly under conditions of chronic oxidative stress – such as exposure to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) – C3a engagement of its receptor has been implicated in a range of deleterious cellular effects. Studies in ARPE-19 cells have shown that oxidative stress induces a redistribution of C3aR away from its typical plasma membrane localization and promotes its translocation toward the mitochondria (Ishii et al., 2021; Riihilä et al., 2019). At the mitochondrial level, activation of the receptor by C3a leads to an increase in mitochondrial calcium uptake, which in turn results in compromised respiratory function as evidenced by decreased state III (ADP-driven) respiration and reduced maximal respiratory capacity (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). The resultant mitochondrial dysfunction is highly likely to contribute to the generation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS). mtROS are known triggers for the NLRP3 inflammasome, which upon activation facilitates the processing of pro-IL-1β to active IL-1β, a cytokine strongly implicated in chronic inflammatory processes observed in AMD (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024).

Furthermore, in primary human fetal RPE models, prolonged exposure to recombinant C3a has been demonstrated to reduce the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (UPP) without altering mRNA levels for proteasome subunits, indicating a post-transcriptional impairment of proteostasis (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). This impairment in proteasome function is associated with an imbalance in ECM turnover – marked by a reduction in tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases (TIMP-3) abundance and an increase in matrix metalloproteinase (MMP-2) activity – culminating in the pathological deposition of extracellular matrix components (notably collagens IV and VI) beneath the RPE. Such sub-RPE deposit formation, or drusen, is one of the hallmarks of early AMD pathology (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

SB 290157, by blocking C3a from binding to C3aR, therefore interrupts these pathological cascades at two key junctures. First, it prevents the mitochondrial translocation and activation of C3aR in oxidatively stressed ARPE-19 cells, which is predicted to avert the associated mitochondrial calcium overload and respiratory inhibition, thereby reducing the likelihood of mtROS generation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). Second, by inhibiting C3a-induced receptor activation in RPE cells, SB 290157 preserves UPP activity, ensuring proper regulation of ECM component turnover and forestalling the aberrant deposition of sub-RPE material (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

It is important to note, however, that while the majority of evidence supports SB 290157 acting as an effective C3aR antagonist, several reports have cautioned that under certain conditions, the compound may display partial agonist activity. This means that rather than completely blocking receptor activation, SB 290157 might induce a low level of receptor signaling in some cellular contexts, especially when receptor density is high (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001). Such an effect must be carefully considered when interpreting experimental outcomes and when designing therapeutic strategies aimed at persistent modulation of complement activity. In all, the known mechanism of action for SB 290157 can be summarized as competitive inhibition of C3a binding to C3aR, thereby mitigating the downstream signals that lead to mitochondrial calcium dysregulation, proteasome impairment, ECM deposition abnormalities, and ultimately, NLRP3 inflammasome priming and IL-1β secretion (Ames et al., 2001; Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect

The central hypothesis underlying the use of SB 290157 in repurposing for dry AMD is that the blockade of C3aR will attenuate a cascade of deleterious events within the retinal pigment epithelium that contribute to disease progression. In particular, the expected effect is that SB 290157 will reduce complement-driven mitochondrial dysfunction, lower mtROS production, and thereby prevent the priming and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, resulting ultimately in diminished IL-1β secretion and preservation of RPE barrier integrity.

In dry AMD, chronic oxidative stress leads to dysregulated complement activation and subsequent accumulation of complement fragments such as C3a in the subretinal space. RPE cells under oxidative stress have been demonstrated to upregulate C3aR expression, with a portion of the receptor redistributing to the mitochondria—a change that is associated with an increased uptake of calcium into the mitochondria and a pronounced decline in mitochondrial respiratory function (Ishii et al., 2021; Riihilä et al., 2019). The resulting mitochondrial dysfunction is poised to increase the generation of mtROS, which serve as an upstream activator of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Activation of this inflammasome complex culminates in the maturation of IL-1β, a powerful proinflammatory cytokine that has been implicated in propagating RPE injury and the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024).

By competitively inhibiting C3a binding to its receptor, SB 290157 is expected to block these deleterious changes. In cultured ARPE-19 cells—which serve as a well-established model for human RPE—it is anticipated that SB 290157 will prevent the mitochondrial translocation of C3aR, thereby reducing abnormal mitochondrial calcium uptake and preserving normal respiration. This action should limit mtROS generation and consequently reduce the priming threshold for NLRP3 inflammasome activation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). Concurrently, in primary fetal RPE cultures, inhibition of C3aR signaling by SB 290157 has been shown to preserve the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, which in turn maintains the balance of matrix metalloproteinases and their tissue inhibitors. By doing so, the compound prevents the accumulation of sub-RPE deposits—a process that is intimately linked to the early phases of AMD pathology (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

The expression of C3aR in RPE cells, particularly in stressed conditions, is well-documented. This receptor is notably enriched on the basolateral membrane of RPE and even redistributes to mitochondrial compartments under oxidative stress conditions, as confirmed in ARPE-19 cell studies (Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Given that dry AMD is characterized by both heightened complement activation and chronic oxidative stress, the strategic inhibition of C3aR is expected to yield multiple beneficial outcomes: restoration of proteostasis, maintenance of mitochondrial function, reduction in chronic inflammatory cytokine expression, and preservation of the integrity and barrier function of the RPE monolayer. Moreover, in in vivo models such as NaIO₃-induced RPE injury or laser-induced retinal vein occlusion, treatment with a C3aR antagonist (presumably SB 290157) has been associated with reduced photoreceptor loss, attenuated microglial activation, and improved retinal morphology (Wang et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2025).

Furthermore, because mitochondrial reactive oxygen species serve as a trigger for the NLRP3 inflammasome, blocking the upstream signal via C3aR inhibition is hypothesized to break the vicious cycle of complement-mediated inflammation. The decreased activation of NLRP3 would lead to lower levels of IL-1β—a cytokine implicated in the autocrine and paracrine amplification of inflammation within the RPE layer—and thus stabilize the local microenvironment (Ong et al., 2024; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In summary, the expected effect of SB 290157 in the context of dry AMD is multifold: preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics, maintenance of proteasomal activity, prevention of pathological ECM accumulation, and attenuation of inflammasome-mediated inflammatory responses—all of which contribute to the protection of RPE integrity and function.

────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

SB 290157 stands out as one of the best-studied C3a receptor antagonists available today. Its well-documented chemical synthesis, robust in vitro pharmacological profile, and demonstrable efficacy in preclinical models of inflammatory injury provide strong support for its continued evaluation as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. The compound’s origins – as a product of high-throughput screening followed by medicinal chemistry optimization using Fmoc-solid phase techniques – are well established, and its chemical structure (N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine) clearly classifies it as a small-molecule non-peptide antagonist of a key complement receptor (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011).

Strengths of SB 290157 include its proven ability to block C3a-induced signaling cascades across a range of cell types and experimental models. Preclinical studies in RPE cells indicate that it can prevent C3a-induced sub-RPE deposit formation and proteasome impairment—a finding directly relevant to the early pathological events of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Additionally, evidence from ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress suggests that SB 290157 effectively inhibits aberrant mitochondrial Ca²⁺ uptake and consequent respiratory dysfunction—mechanisms known to contribute to mtROS generation and inflammasome activation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). In vivo, its administration in models of retinal injury (such as NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration and laser-induced retinal vein occlusion) has correlated with reduced photoreceptor death, decreased gliosis, and improved retinal architecture (Wang et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2025). These findings collectively underscore the compound’s potential to modulate complement-mediated pathology in the ocular setting.

Nonetheless, SB 290157 is not without its weaknesses. A significant concern noted across several studies is its variable pharmacological behavior. Under some experimental conditions, particularly in cell systems with high receptor density, SB 290157 exhibits partial agonist activity rather than pure antagonism (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001). This paradoxical behavior could lead to unintended receptor activation and potentially undermine its therapeutic benefit, especially in chronic conditions like dry AMD where long-term receptor blockade is desired. Furthermore, while there is compelling preclinical evidence supporting its beneficial impact on mitochondrial function and ECM homeostasis, direct experimental data linking SB 290157 to a reduction in mitochondrial ROS production and consequent suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation in ARPE-19 or primary RPE models remain incomplete or indirect (Wang et al., 2020; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Behnke, 2022). This gap in the literature necessitates further investigation to firmly establish the causal chain from C3aR inhibition to inflammasome modulation.

Another consideration is the translational challenge. SB 290157 has been predominantly utilized as a research tool rather than a clinical candidate. Its pharmacokinetic profile—while adequate for short-term animal experiments—has not been thoroughly characterized for long-term use in ocular applications, where issues such as retinal toxicity, ocular bioavailability, and sustained receptor occupancy become critical. The delicate environment of the retina requires highly specific and safe compounds; thus, the partial agonist activity and potential off-target effects of SB 290157 raise valid concerns regarding its safety profile in humans (Mathieu et al., 2005; Tan et al., 2024).

On the other hand, the dual benefit of SB 290157—in preventing not only aberrant complement signaling but also the downstream mitochondrial dysfunction that leads to inflammasome activation—directly addresses central pathogenic mechanisms in dry AMD. Given that dry AMD is characterized by chronic inflammation, RPE dysfunction, and progressive atrophy correlated with mitochondrial impairment, a drug that can simultaneously modulate these pathways offers a novel therapeutic angle. In this context, the ability of SB 290157 to preserve the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway and maintain ECM turnover may help stabilize the RPE, delay the progression of geographic atrophy, and potentially improve visual outcomes (Ames et al., 2001; Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Wang et al., 2020). Conversely, its partial agonist behavior in certain systems and the current lack of direct evidence linking its action to reduced mtROS and NLRP3 activation in ocular models raise legitimate concerns that must be addressed prior to clinical translation (Mathieu et al., 2005; Behnke, 2022).

Overall, SB 290157 is a compelling candidate for further exploration and mechanistic validation as a repurposed drug for dry AMD, provided that additional research can surmount the challenges associated with its pharmacodynamic variability and confirm its protective effects in retina-specific models.

────────────────────────────────────────  
Conclusion

The comprehensive literature evaluation indicates that SB 290157’s synthetic origins, established use as a C3aR antagonist, and demonstrated efficacy in preclinical models of complement-mediated RPE injury make it a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its mechanism—blocking C3a-induced signaling that otherwise leads to mitochondrial calcium overload, impaired proteostasis, and subsequent inflammasome activation—is highly relevant to the pathophysiology of geographic atrophy. However, the compound’s documented partial agonist effects and potential variability in receptor blockade require careful consideration and further optimization. Additional studies are necessary to firmly establish that SB 290157 can reduce mitochondrial ROS and suppress NLRP3 inflammasome activation in RPE cells under conditions that model dry AMD clinically. Thus, while SB 290157 is an excellent tool for dissecting the complement–mitochondria crosstalk in dry AMD, its suitability as a long-term therapeutic will depend on resolving these outstanding issues through rigorous preclinical and mechanistic evaluation (Ames et al., 2001; Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Mathieu et al., 2005).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
ZLN005 (MedChemExpress HY-100726) is a synthetic small-molecule compound that belongs to the benzimidazole class. Benzimidazole derivatives have a long history in medicinal chemistry for their wide-ranging biological activities, including antihelminthic, anti-inflammatory, and metabolic modulating effects. In the case of ZLN005, it has been identified specifically as a selective transcriptional activator of peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator‐1 alpha (PGC-1α), a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defense. The synthesis and chemical derivation of ZLN005, although not detailed exhaustively in the provided literature, follow typical synthetic protocols for benzimidazole compounds, which often involve the condensation of o-phenylenediamine with carboxylic acid derivatives to yield a benzimidazole core. This structural class is known not only for its high affinity to various protein targets but also for favorable pharmacokinetic properties that have motivated its use in drug development efforts. Several studies have demonstrated that ZLN005 effectively induces PGC-1α expression in various cell types, including skeletal muscle and particularly the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis (Satish et al., 2018). Its assignment under the benzimidazole class further suggests that ZLN005 may share common metabolic and pharmacological features with other compounds in the same class, which have been employed in different therapeutic areas, supporting its potential for repurposing in ocular disorders such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Sun et al., 2018; Bleckwehl et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Initially, ZLN005 emerged from screening studies designed to identify small molecules that could stimulate PGC-1α expression. Early research in cellular models demonstrated that ZLN005 enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and upregulates the expression of downstream oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and antioxidant genes, which in turn improves mitochondrial health and overall cellular energy metabolism (Satish et al., 2018). In skeletal muscle and hepatic cells, for example, treatment with ZLN005 was associated with increased basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates, an increase in spare respiratory capacity, and a concomitant improvement in glucose uptake and cellular ATP levels (Satish et al., 2018). Such characteristics have spurred interest in its therapeutic application beyond metabolic diseases to conditions where mitochondrial dysfunction is a central pathogenic factor.

Notably, several groups have investigated ZLN005 in the context of retinal diseases. Preclinical studies using ARPE-19 cells—a well-accepted human RPE cell line—demonstrated that ZLN005 markedly upregulates PGC-1α expression and its associated transcription factors and antioxidant enzymes. These investigations have shown that ZLN005 can confer significant protection against oxidative stress-induced cell death when cells are exposed to prooxidative agents such as hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL) and sodium iodate (NaIO₃) (Satish et al., 2018). Although ZLN005 has not yet undergone extensive clinical evaluation specifically for dry AMD, its robust activity in stimulating mitochondrial function and providing cytoprotection in RPE models forms a compelling rationale for its repurposing. Studies in other systems, including cardiomyocytes and skeletal muscle, support its therapeutic use in settings of bioenergetic decline and oxidative damage, which are hallmarks of many age-related degenerative diseases (Ma et al., 2023; Moradi, 2022). However, it should be noted that many of the studies exploring ZLN005 for ocular purposes have been in vitro, and while they present an optimistic scenario, further in vivo animal studies and careful pharmacokinetic analyses in ocular tissues are needed before clinical application in AMD can be considered (Satish et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
The pharmacological efficacy of ZLN005 is tightly linked to its mechanism of action as an activator of PGC-1α. PGC-1α is a transcriptional coactivator that regulates a myriad of genes implicated in energy metabolism, mitochondrial biogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, and antioxidant protection. In RPE cells—where the maintenance of a high mitochondrial integrity is crucial for visual function—the expression of PGC-1α is fundamental to mitigating oxidative stress and maintaining metabolic homeostasis (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Iacovelli et al., 2016). ZLN005 increases the expression levels of PGC-1α by enhancing its transcription, culminating in the upregulation of a host of downstream target genes. This includes key mitochondrial genes such as ATP50, COX4, COX5b, and NDUFB5, all of which are involved in oxidative phosphorylation and energy production (Satish et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025).

At the molecular level, ZLN005 promotes the transcriptional program by potentially modulating AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) activity, a well-known regulator of PGC-1α function. The compound’s facilitation of PGC-1α nuclear translocation and its catalytic coactivation leads to the stimulation of mitochondrial replication and repair processes, thereby increasing mitochondrial mass and mtDNA copy number (Satish et al., 2018). In parallel, the upregulation of PGC-1α by ZLN005 induces the expression of several endogenous antioxidant enzymes, including superoxide dismutases (SOD1 and SOD2) and mitochondrial thioredoxin 2 (TXN2). This cascade of events enhances the cellular capacity to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS), thus lowering mitochondrial superoxide production and reducing the levels of oxidative stress markers such as 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), a product of lipid peroxidation frequently associated with degenerative retinal changes (Satish et al., 2018).

Furthermore, ZLN005 appears to improve overall mitochondrial bioenergetics. It has been observed to increase both basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates (OCR) in RPE cells, indicating an enhanced capacity for ATP synthesis under both steady-state and stress conditions (Satish et al., 2018). The compound also augments the spare respiratory capacity, which is critical for cellular survival when faced with acute energy demands during oxidative stress. Such improvements in mitochondrial function are directly relevant to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, where RPE cells experience an energy deficit due to progressive mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic oxidative injury (Felszeghy et al., 2019). Additionally, by upregulating PGC-1α, ZLN005 may indirectly influence other cellular processes, including autophagy and lipid metabolism, both of which are altered in the aging RPE and contribute to the formation of drusen—the hallmark deposits seen in dry AMD (Zhou et al., 2024).

It is important to emphasize that the protective effects of ZLN005 are markedly dependent on the presence of functional PGC-1α. Experiments in which PGC-1α expression was silenced in RPE cells resulted in a significant loss of the cytoprotective benefits conferred by ZLN005, underscoring the compound’s mechanism-specific action (Satish et al., 2018). Parallel studies in non-ocular cell types, such as skeletal muscle myotubes and alveolar epithelial cells, have further supported its role in enhancing mitochondrial function and regulating oxidative stress through similar molecular pathways (Zhang et al., 2013; Bleckwehl et al., 2025). Thus, the molecular interactions initiated by ZLN005—ranging from the activation of PGC-1α to the subsequent stimulation of antioxidant enzymes and mitochondrial biogenesis—form the crux of its therapeutic utility, specifically in countering the bioenergetic decline characteristic of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Given the central involvement of mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the therapeutic hypothesis for ZLN005 is that its activation of PGC-1α in retinal pigment epithelial cells will restore mitochondrial homeostasis and augment cellular antioxidant defenses. In the proposed assays, treatment with ZLN005 is expected to upregulate PGC-1α expression in RPE cells, thereby triggering a cascade of downstream events that lead to enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis. This includes an increase in mtDNA copy number and the expression of mitochondrial genes that are essential for optimal oxidative phosphorylation performance (Satish et al., 2018). As mitochondrial function improves, RPE cells should exhibit higher basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates, indicative of an improved metabolic profile and increased capacity to generate ATP under both normal and stress conditions (Satish et al., 2018).

The antioxidative effects of ZLN005 are also expected to manifest in augmented levels of enzymes such as SOD1, SOD2, and TXN2, which collectively enhance the cell’s capability to scavenge reactive oxygen species. These biochemical events are critical because the accumulation of oxidative stress in RPE cells, driven by chronic exposure to high levels of ROS, is a significant contributor to cell degeneration in dry AMD (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Blasiak et al., 2021). With improved mitochondrial function and reduced oxidative stress, it is anticipated that ZLN005 treatment will lead to a decrease in the accumulation of oxidative damage markers like 4-HNE, thereby mitigating processes that lead to RPE cell apoptosis and the subsequent photoreceptor degeneration observed in dry AMD (Blasiak et al., 2021; Iacovelli et al., 2016).

Moreover, in vitro studies have demonstrated that under conditions of experimentally induced oxidative stress with agents such as H₂O₂, ox-LDL, or NaIO₃, ZLN005 significantly reduces cell death in ARPE-19 cells (Satish et al., 2018). Therefore, the expected effect of ZLN005 in the proposed assay is a robust cytoprotective response in RPE cells. This would be characterized by improved cell viability, restoration of mitochondrial respiratory function, and a reduction in stress-induced apoptotic markers—a constellation of effects that directly addresses the bioenergetic and oxidative challenges underlying dry AMD (Satish et al., 2018). Additionally, since PGC-1α is known to regulate lipid metabolism and prevent lipid droplet accumulation—a process that may be linked to the formation of drusen in the AMD retina—the activation of PGC-1α by ZLN005 could also have beneficial effects on lipid handling within the RPE (Zhou et al., 2024; Iacovelli et al., 2016). Thus, through these concerted mechanisms, ZLN005 is anticipated to stabilize or even improve RPE function, thereby halting or reversing aspects of the degenerative cascade that leads to vision loss in dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
A comprehensive evaluation of ZLN005 reveals several compelling strengths as well as notable weaknesses that should be weighed in the context of repurposing it for the treatment of dry AMD. One of the principal strengths of ZLN005 lies in its well-defined mechanism of action. By selectively activating PGC-1α, ZLN005 directly targets the mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress that are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. The upregulation of PGC-1α leads to improvements in mitochondrial biogenesis, an increase in the expression of mitochondrial OXPHOS genes, and the enhancement of antioxidant defenses—all factors that are critically compromised in the diseased RPE (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Blasiak et al., 2021). This mechanistic rationale is further supported by in vitro studies showing that ZLN005 can effectively reduce prooxidant-induced cell death and improve mitochondrial respiratory parameters such as basal respiration, maximal respiration, and spare respiratory capacity (Satish et al., 2018).

Another strength is the translational potential implied by the compound’s efficacy in multiple cell types. ZLN005 has not only demonstrated protective effects in RPE cells but has also been shown to modulate mitochondrial activity in skeletal muscle and hepatic cells. This broad-spectrum improvement in energy metabolism indicates that its bioenergetic benefits may be harnessed in the complex metabolic environment of the RPE, where energy deficits contribute to dry AMD pathology (Satish et al., 2018). Achieving a robust activation of PGC-1α is particularly attractive because it addresses both the cellular energy production and ROS management simultaneously, which are two critical determinants of RPE cell survival and function (Iacovelli et al., 2016; Rosales et al., 2019).

Furthermore, the specificity of ZLN005’s action has been validated by studies where the loss of PGC-1α abrogated its cytoprotective effects, underscoring that its efficacy is tightly linked to the activation of this pivotal regulatory pathway (Satish et al., 2018). This is an important consideration because it suggests that the therapeutic effects can be fine-tuned by modulating the expression or activity of PGC-1α. In the context of dry AMD, where PGC-1α levels are often diminished or dysregulated, the targeted upregulation provided by ZLN005 offers a focused therapeutic intervention.

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and challenges remain. Foremost, the majority of the supportive evidence for ZLN005’s efficacy in protecting RPE cells has been generated through in vitro studies using cell lines such as ARPE-19. While these models are indispensable for preliminary evaluation, they do not fully recapitulate the complex in vivo environment of the human retina, and the translatability of these effects into clinical benefit remains to be demonstrated (Satish et al., 2018). Additionally, the current body of literature shows that some reports have emerged from journals of variable quality; this introduces a degree of uncertainty regarding the reproducibility of the findings and necessitates rigorous validation of these results in higher-order in vivo models and, eventually, clinical trials (Satish et al., 2018).

Another pertinent concern is the pharmacokinetic profile of ZLN005 in the ocular environment. While its favorable metabolic effects are evident in cell culture and certain systemic models, its ability to reach and maintain effective concentrations in the RPE following systemic or local administration is not well established in the available reports (Bleckwehl et al., 2025; Miller et al., 2019). In addition, the potential off-target effects of ZLN005, particularly in tissues where mitochondrial modulation may have unintended consequences, have not been fully explored. This includes the risk that enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis in non-target cells could lead to dysregulated energy metabolism or contribute to unwanted proliferative responses (Satish et al., 2018; Bleckwehl et al., 2025).

Moreover, the clinical development pathway for repurposing ZLN005 for ocular indications such as dry AMD will require comprehensive toxicological studies, detailed pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic analyses in ocular tissues, and the establishment of dosing regimens that ensure both efficacy and safety over chronic treatment periods. Additionally, while the activation of PGC-1α is a promising strategy for mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction, the role of PGC-1α in the retina is complex. Overexpression of PGC-1α has been linked in some studies to increased susceptibility to light-induced retinal damage or other forms of stress, suggesting that a delicate balance must be maintained to achieve therapeutic benefit without tipping the scales towards potential toxicity or dysregulation of cellular homeostasis (Iacovelli et al., 2016; Blasiak et al., 2021). This dual nature of PGC-1α activity means that careful titration of ZLN005 dosing—and possibly the development of combination therapies—may be necessary to harness its protective effects while avoiding exacerbation of retinal stress under certain conditions.

In summary, ZLN005 emerges as a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its well-characterized mechanism of stimulating PGC-1α expression, its ability to enhance mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses, and the encouraging results obtained from in vitro studies in ARPE-19 cells. Its molecular action aligns closely with the pathophysiological profiles observed in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress contribute to RPE degeneration. However, while the preclinical evidence is robust in terms of establishing a mechanistic framework, significant challenges remain in translating these findings to an in vivo and eventually a clinical setting. Key areas that require further investigation include detailed pharmacokinetic studies in ocular models, confirmation of efficacy in animal models of dry AMD, and a full safety profile with chronic dosing regimens (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Blasiak et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2019).

Moreover, the integration of ZLN005 with current understanding of AMD pathogenesis suggests that the compound could potentially be part of combination therapies that target several pathogenic pathways simultaneously—such as inflammation, lipid dysregulation, and complement activation—in addition to mitochondrial dysfunction. From a strategic drug development perspective, ZLN005 offers several attractive points for further exploration. Its synthetic origin as a benzimidazole derivative means that established methods exist for its production and modification, allowing for potential structure-activity relationship (SAR) studies aimed at enhancing its potency, selectivity, and ocular bioavailability. Such modifications could lead to derivatives with improved pharmacokinetic profiles tailored for retinal delivery. Moreover, leveraging advanced drug delivery systems, such as nanoparticle carriers or sustained-release formulations, could further enhance the therapeutic window of ZLN005 in the eye while minimizing systemic exposure and associated off-target effects (Bleckwehl et al., 2025; Miller et al., 2019).

In conclusion, the repurposing of ZLN005 for the treatment of dry AMD is supported by a compelling mechanistic rationale and a growing body of preclinical evidence that underscores its potential to restore mitochondrial dynamics and counteract oxidative stress in retinal pigment epithelial cells. The strengths of this candidate include its specificity for PGC-1α activation, its demonstrated ability to enhance mitochondrial function and energy metabolism, and its protective effects against oxidative injury in vitro. Overall, the data presented through multiple independent studies provide a strong foundation for considering ZLN005 as a viable therapeutic candidate in the repurposing paradigm for dry age-related macular degeneration. With further validation and refinement, itself or an optimized derivative could potentially offer a new strategy to preserve RPE integrity and maintain visual function in AMD patients, addressing a significant unmet medical need in the realm of retinal degenerative diseases (Rosales et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2025). Continued research efforts should focus on delineating the precise molecular signatures of ZLN005’s effects in RPE cells, assessing its long-term impact on retinal morphology and function in vivo, and investigating its interactions with other signaling cascades implicated in AMD progression (Satish et al., 2018). Only through such thorough and multidisciplinary evaluations can the true therapeutic potential of ZLN005 for dry AMD be accurately determined and translated into clinical benefit.

In summary, while challenges remain in translating the promising in vitro results to clinical outcomes, the accumulated evidence suggests that ZLN005’s activation of PGC-1α represents a credible and innovative strategy to counteract the bioenergetic decline in RPE cells—a central feature in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Analysis: Elamipretide (ID 41) has a rich preclinical and clinical data package directly targeting dry AMD pathobiology. Mechanistically, it specifically binds cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane of RPE and photoreceptors, stabilizing cristae, improving electron transport, reducing ROS, and preserving ATP. This addresses core, upstream mitochondrial dysfunction observed in AMD donor RPE, with robust in vivo mouse AMD‐like models showing ERG improvement, reduced sub-RPE deposits, and preserved visual function. Its MoA is pleiotropic and indirect—up-regulating phase II enzymes via Nrf2—and while safety appears favorable in dietary contexts, ocular bioavailability and delivery across the blood–retinal barrier remain uncertain. The evidence base for sulforaphane in AMD is limited to cell culture and generic oxidative stress paradigms, with unresolved PK/PD and formulation challenges. Sulforaphane, though safe and biologically active, lacks AMD‐specific in vivo efficacy data beyond cell culture, suffers from uncertain ocular delivery, and operates via a broad Nrf2 pathway activation that may not adequately or specifically address the upstream mitochondrial deficits central to dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Elamipretide (SS-31; D-Arg-2,6-dimethyl-Tyr-Lys-Phe-NH2) is a synthetic, C-terminally amidated tetrapeptide belonging to the Szeto–Schiller (SS) class of mitochondria-targeted peptides, originally discovered through structure–activity optimization of alternating cationic–aromatic motifs that confer high cell permeability and strong partitioning to the negatively charged inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) enriched in cardiolipin (CL) (Szeto & Schiller, 2011; Tung et al., 2025). Early work demonstrated that an aromatic–cationic design was sufficient to drive potent mitochondrial uptake and that dimethyltyrosine (Dmt) confers radical-scavenging chemistry while improving chemical stability; subnanomolar-to-nanomolar extracellular concentrations concentrate >1 μM at the IMM, yielding robust activity under oxidative stress in diverse cell types (Szeto & Schiller, 2011). SS-31 and related SS peptides were initially identified as potent inhibitors of mitochondrial swelling and oxidative cell death in intact cells and organs, with mechanistic clues pointing to direct interactions with cardiolipin-rich membranes and mitigation of ischemia–reperfusion injury (Szeto & Schiller, 2011; Szeto & Birk, 2014).

Mechanistically, elamipretide selectively binds CL in the IMM via electrostatic anchoring of its cationic residues to anionic phosphate headgroups and hydrophobic partitioning of its aromatic residues into the bilayer interfacial region; biophysical studies (NMR and molecular dynamics simulations) and binding quantitation to model CL-containing bilayers demonstrate CL dependence and saturable effects on bilayer surface electrostatics and lipid packing without destabilizing lamellar phases (Mitchell et al., 2019; Sabbah et al., 2025). Once bound, elamipretide modulates several biophysical and biochemical properties central to mitochondrial function: it down-tunes the negative surface potential of CL-rich membranes, increases CL self-association, reduces lateral lipid diffusivity, and increases lateral packing, changes that preserve cristae architecture and respiratory supercomplex organization under stress while suppressing cytochrome c peroxidase activity and CL oxidation (Sabbah et al., 2025). Collectively, these actions improve electron transfer efficiency, stabilize oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos) protein assemblies, reduce electron leak and reactive oxygen species (ROS), and preserve ATP synthesis capacity in dysfunctional mitochondria (Mitchell et al., 2022; Sabbah et al., 2025; Szeto & Birk, 2014). Importantly for retinal applications, elamipretide uptake is not dependent on mitochondrial membrane potential, supporting entry into depolarized or injured mitochondria—a feature often found in AMD RPE (Ji et al., 2021).

Elamipretide is therefore best classified as a CL-targeting, membrane-active mitochondrial therapeutic that acts primarily by modulating the physicochemical properties of CL-rich IMM domains and CL-dependent protein assemblies, rather than binding a single protein target, with downstream effects on respiratory supercomplex assembly, cytochrome c catalysis, electron-transport efficiency, ROS emission, and ATP production (Mitchell et al., 2019; Sabbah et al., 2025; Mitchell et al., 2022). Members of this class have been deployed across preclinical models of cardiac, skeletal muscle, renal, neurologic, and ocular dysfunction, and a substantial clinical program has tested elamipretide in primary mitochondrial disorders, cardiometabolic diseases, and ophthalmic indications including age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Sabbah et al., 2025; Tung et al., 2025). The drug is water-soluble, with a short elimination half-life on the order of ~2–4 hours in preclinical species and humans, and is administered systemically by daily subcutaneous injection in AMD studies at a nominal 40 mg dose; topical ocular delivery has also been explored preclinically and clinically (Szeto & Birk, 2014; Lenin et al., 2023; Guimaraes et al., 2022; Ji et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
The SS peptide class emerged from efforts to concentrate antioxidant and mitochondrial-protective chemistry directly at the IMM through cationic–aromatic motifs that target anionic phospholipids—principally cardiolipin—enabling inhibition of mitochondrial swelling, reduction of ROS emission, and protection from reperfusion injury in intact cells and organs; SS-31 in particular was estimated to concentrate ~5,000-fold in mitochondria and to inhibit lipid peroxidation, positioning it to prevent CL peroxidation in the IMM (Szeto & Schiller, 2011). These membrane-centric mechanisms rapidly translated into broad preclinical testing across organ systems, demonstrating improvements in OxPhos efficiency, ATP production, ROS control, and preservation of mitochondrial ultrastructure (cristae) in disease and aging models (Szeto & Birk, 2014; Mitchell et al., 2022).

Ocular and retinal applications came into focus as mitochondrial dysfunction in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptors was implicated as a driver of non-neovascular AMD, including reduced OxPhos, increased glycolytic shift, impaired mitophagy, structural cristae disorganization, and accumulation of damaged mitochondria in AMD donor RPE (Ferrington et al., 2020; Fisher, 2022; Fisher et al., 2022). In this context, elamipretide demonstrated several AMD-relevant preclinical effects. In a mouse model of dry AMD-like pathology, subcutaneous elamipretide reversed electroretinographic (ERG) deficits and improved clearance of sub-RPE deposits, corresponding to reversal of vision loss, consistent with activity at both the RPE/sub-RPE interface and photoreceptor function (Kim & Lad, 2021; Ji et al., 2021). In ApoE4 mice with diet-induced sub-RPE deposit formation linked to mitochondrial dysfunction, subcutaneous elamipretide reversed deposit formation, strengthening the mechanistic link to CL-dependent mitochondrial physiology in retinal tissues (Guimaraes et al., 2022). RPE-targeted cytoprotection has also been reported: elamipretide protected primary RPE and improved mitochondrial function in models of AMD and prevented persistent injury phenotypes induced by oxidative stressors such as hydroquinone in cultured RPE cells (Sabbah et al., 2025). Ex vivo and in vivo aging paradigms provide convergent support: in aged mice with visual impairments, elamipretide mitigated visual decline and normalized visual acuity and contrast sensitivity within two months, with delivery via topical eye drops producing effects comparable to subcutaneous injections; in RPE cultures from AMD donors, elamipretide improved RPE cell viability and mitochondrial function (Sabbah et al., 2025; Alam et al., 2020). In an RPE-specific SOD2 knockout model, daily topical elamipretide prevented RPE cell size increase consistent with reduced RPE cell death/senescence, further underscoring RPE-specific benefits (Tong et al., 2022). Additional retinal disease models support cross-indication activity: SS-31 restored visual function in a streptozotocin-induced mouse diabetic retinopathy model (Ferrington et al., 2020). Collectively, preclinical retinal evidence aligns with the hypothesized CL-centric rescue of mitochondrial function at the RPE and photoreceptor inner segments, preventing AMD-relevant cellular dysfunction and functional decline (Ji et al., 2021; Kim & Lad, 2021; Guimaraes et al., 2022).

Clinical development has included both topical and subcutaneous AMD studies. A phase I/II topical study enrolled 21 patients with diabetic macular edema (DME) and non-exudative intermediate AMD, demonstrating feasibility of ocular delivery; subsequent systemic AMD trials have been more extensively reported (Ji et al., 2021). The open-label, 24-week Phase 1 ReCLAIM study administered daily subcutaneous elamipretide (40 mg) to 40 patients with either non-central geographic atrophy (NCGA; n = 19) or high-risk drusen without GA (n = 21), reporting mean functional improvements: in the NCGA subgroup, +4.6 letters in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), +5.4 letters in low-luminance visual acuity (LLVA), and an approximate 25-letter gain in low-luminance reading acuity (LLRA), with a slower GA growth rate than historical natural history; in the high-risk drusen subgroup, mean gains were +3.6 (BCVA), +5.6 (LLVA), and ~15 (LLRA) (Kim & Lad, 2021). Safety was favorable, with no serious adverse events and general tolerability in intermediate AMD (Ji et al., 2021). A subsequent randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled Phase 2 trial (ReCLAIM-2) in ≥55-year-old patients with non-central GA tested daily subcutaneous elamipretide for 48 weeks; it did not meet primary endpoints on LL-BCVA and GA area, but elamipretide was associated with a 43% reduction in mean progression of total ellipsoid zone (EZ) attenuation and a 47% reduction in partial EZ attenuation versus placebo, with a post hoc analysis showing significant reductions and a higher proportion of patients achieving ≥2-line LL-BCVA gains, and a correlation between LL-BCVA change and change in total EZ attenuation (Sabbah et al., 2025). EZ attenuation is a clinically meaningful OCT marker that reflects photoreceptor integrity in mitochondria-rich inner segments and precedes GA and irreversible vision loss; thus, preservation of EZ is mechanistically consistent with the drug’s mitochondrial-protective intent and could represent an early biomarker of benefit (Sabbah et al., 2025). Additional summaries concur: the Phase 2 program reported negative primary endpoints but a structural OCT signal (slowed EZ degradation), warranting confirmatory studies with longer duration and functional correlates (Tung et al., 2025).

Beyond AMD, elamipretide has undergone extensive clinical evaluation in mitochondrial disorders (e.g., Barth syndrome), heart failure, ischemia–reperfusion contexts, and renal microvascular dysfunction, with mixed outcomes: many trials did not meet primary endpoints but reported improvements in mitochondrial bioenergetics, coupling, or patient-reported quality-of-life metrics, consistent with a class effect of improving mitochondrial physiology in vivo (Sabbah et al., 2025; Tung et al., 2025). Pharmacokinetically, elamipretide exhibits rapid distribution/elimination with elimination half-lives of ~2 hours in preclinical species and on the order of ~4 hours in humans, renal excretion of parent/metabolites, and ocular pharmacology indicating that topical dosing in rabbits achieves high anterior-chamber and periocular concentrations with nonzero penetration to the retina; this, together with murine aged-vision data, suggests both topical and systemic routes are viable for retinal targeting, although intraocular/vitreous levels after topical dosing may be low (Szeto & Birk, 2014; Alam et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
Elamipretide’s mechanism centers on high-affinity interaction with cardiolipin in the IMM and consequent modulation of membrane electrostatics, lipid organization, and CL-dependent protein complexes, leading to improved electron transport, reduced ROS production, and preserved ATP synthesis. Several convergent lines of evidence define this mechanism in molecular detail.

1) Cardiolipin-dependent binding and membrane electrostatics. SS-31/ELAM partitions into the interfacial leaflet of CL-containing bilayers with affinity proportional to surface charge, binding via electrostatic interactions of its basic residues with CL phosphates and via hydrophobic interactions of its aromatic residues with lipid acyl chains; no measurable binding occurs to neutral phosphatidylcholine membranes (Mitchell et al., 2019). NMR and molecular dynamics identify two binding modes—“peptide approach” (electrostatic anchoring) and “peptide burial” (aromatic partition)—producing a controlled down-tuning of the negative surface potential, increased CL self-association, and altered lateral packing/diffusivity without disrupting lamellar bilayer integrity (Sabbah et al., 2025). The net effect is to modulate ion distribution at the membrane interface (e.g., divalent cations such as Ca2+), stabilize bilayer structure under electrochemical stress, and resist electroporation-like damage, thereby preserving IMM properties under stress (Mitchell et al., 2019; Tamucci et al., 2025). These membrane-physical changes occur without altering the transmembrane potential per se, consistent with a surface–electrostatics mechanism that adjusts protein–lipid interactions and lipid–lipid organization (Sabbah et al., 2025).

2) Respiratory complexes, supercomplexes, and cytochrome c. Cardiolipin stabilizes respiratory complexes and promotes assembly of supercomplexes to optimize electron transport; elamipretide binding to CL supports supercomplex assembly, increases coupling efficiency, and reduces electron leak and ROS while enhancing ATP synthesis (Mitchell et al., 2022; Sabbah et al., 2025). A central node is the CL–cytochrome c interface: elamipretide is proposed to modulate the hydrophobic/π–π interactions between cytochrome c and CL, promoting efficient electron transfer from complex III to complex IV at the rate-limiting step while inhibiting cytochrome c peroxidase activity that otherwise peroxidizes CL and destabilizes cristae under oxidative stress (Szeto & Birk, 2014). Biochemical studies show that elamipretide reduces cytochrome c peroxidase activity and prevents oxidative modifications of CL acyl chains by forming a complex with CL, thereby protecting membrane integrity (Sabbah et al., 2025). In failing human heart tissue ex vivo, elamipretide improved supercomplex coupling control, respiratory control ratio, and CI/CIV activities, consistent with a supercomplex-stabilizing activity that enhances OXPHOS efficiency (Sabbah et al., 2025).

3) Direct protein interactions and bioenergetic consequences. Proteomics using biotinylated elamipretide (b-ELAM) in cross-linking/MS identified binding to multiple IMM proteins that themselves interact with CL, including complex IV subunit NDUA4 and the adenine nucleotide translocase ANT1; functionally, elamipretide increased maximum uncoupled and CIV respiration and decreased H2O2 production in mitochondria from old mouse hearts, increased ADP sensitivity and uptake via ANT, reduced ANT1-mediated proton leak, stabilized membrane potential, and reduced mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening (Sabbah et al., 2025). Stabilization of larger IMM protein assemblies such as the ATP synthasome (ANT, ATP synthase, creatine kinase, phosphate carrier) has been reported, with improvements in CI–CIII–CIV coupling and oxygen flux in failing human heart tissue (Sabbah et al., 2025). These molecular effects translate to rapid increases in mitochondrial energetic capacity—including a human randomized placebo-controlled trial demonstrating that a single dose of elamipretide increased the maximal rate of ATP production (ATPmax) in skeletal muscle—validating in vivo bioenergetic rescue (Sabbah et al., 2025).

4) ROS control, IMM integrity, and cristae structure. Across cell and organ models, elamipretide reduces ETS-derived ROS without acting as a primary radical scavenger; instead it optimizes respiratory efficiency, reduces electron leak, and protects CL from peroxidation, breaking the cycle of cristae disruption and respiratory dysfunction prevalent in aged or diseased mitochondria (Sabbah et al., 2025; Mitchell et al., 2022). SS-31 lowers intracellular ROS, prevents mitochondrial depolarization, maintains ΔΨm, prevents lipid peroxidation, and curtails oxidative cell death in a dose-dependent manner (Mitchell et al., 2019). In retinal contexts, elamipretide increased mitochondrial cristae density and preserved ultrastructure in aged mouse retinal mitochondria and diabetic mouse retinopathy models, supporting retinal applicability (Sabbah et al., 2025). In multiple disease models, elamipretide increased mitochondrial density and cristae connectivity, normalized proton leak, improved respiratory capacity, and corrected dysregulated fusion/fission and biogenesis regulators after longer treatment, further indicating structural remodeling capacity (Sabbah et al., 2025).

Mechanistic relevance to AMD and RPE is strong. AMD donor RPE exhibits cristae disorganization, accumulation of damaged mitochondria, decreased OxPhos, impaired mitophagy, and significant mtDNA damage in ETC gene regions, all linked to diminished ATP production and a glycolytic shift that disrupts metabolic coupling with photoreceptors and promotes retinal degeneration (Ferrington et al., 2020; Fisher et al., 2022; Fisher, 2022). Because CL is crucial for maintaining OxPhos function and cristae architecture, pharmacologic stabilization of CL and CL-dependent protein assemblies by elamipretide directly addresses these pathologies, offering preservation of ATP production, reduction of ROS, and resistance to mPTP opening and apoptosis in RPE under chronic oxidative stress (Fisher et al., 2022; Sabbah et al., 2025; Szeto & Birk, 2014). Photoreceptors are mitochondria-rich in the inner segments, and OCT-defined EZ attenuation is an early marker of photoreceptor compromise that precedes GA; elamipretide-associated reduction in EZ attenuation progression in AMD patients links its mitochondrial mechanism to clinically observable retinal structure (Sabbah et al., 2025).

Expected Effect  
In RPE cell assays that model AMD-relevant stressors (oxidative and bioenergetic), elamipretide is expected to stabilize IMM biophysics and CL-dependent protein systems, restoring mitochondrial bioenergetics, reducing oxidative injury, and preventing apoptosis. Mechanistically supported expectations include:

- Restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) and coupling: Elamipretide maintains ΔΨm and improves respiratory control, consistent with increased OXPHOS efficiency and reduced proton leak; thus, assays using potentiometric dyes (e.g., JC-1) should show improved ΔΨm relative to oxidant-injured controls (Mitchell et al., 2019; Sabbah et al., 2025).

- Reduction of mitochondrial ROS and lipid peroxidation: By stabilizing CL, optimizing electron transport, and inhibiting cytochrome c peroxidase activity, elamipretide reduces H2O2 emission and lipid peroxidation, leading to lower MitoSOX and lipid oxidation signals under oxidative challenge (Sabbah et al., 2025; Mitchell et al., 2019).

- Preservation of ATP synthesis: In serum-deprivation or oxidant-injury paradigms in RPE cell lines (e.g., ARPE-19), mitochondria-targeted peptides including elamipretide increased cell viability and cellular ATP at nanomolar dosing; this is consistent with expected improvements in ATP content and Seahorse OXPHOS parameters in primary RPE under stress (Mitchell et al., 2021). Human AMD donor RPE exposed ex vivo to elamipretide show improved mitochondrial function and viability, corroborating translatability of these endpoints (Sabbah et al., 2025).

- Cytoprotection against AMD-relevant toxicants: Elamipretide prevents persistent injury phenotypes induced by oxidative stressors (e.g., hydroquinone) in cultured RPE, supporting generalizability to sodium iodate or H2O2 injury; in an RPE SOD2 knockout model, topical elamipretide prevented cell size increase consistent with reduced cell death/senescence (Sabbah et al., 2025; Tong et al., 2022).

- Structural preservation of cristae: Electron microscopy of retinal mitochondria in aged/diabetic mice treated with elamipretide indicates increased cristae density and improved ultrastructure; similar effects are expected in RPE mitochondrial ultrastructure under chronic oxidative stress (Sabbah et al., 2025).

- In vivo retinal/RPE endpoints: In mouse models of AMD-like pathology, elamipretide improved ERG deficits and enhanced clearance of sub-RPE deposits, tracking to improvements in photoreceptor function and RPE health; ERG, OCT (drusen/sub-RPE deposit metrics), and RPE morphometrics are therefore expected to improve (Kim & Lad, 2021; Ji et al., 2021; Guimaraes et al., 2022). In aged-vision paradigms, spatial vision and contrast sensitivity improved with systemic or topical elamipretide, indicating photopic function benefits and supporting cone function endpoints (Alam et al., 2020).

- Clinical correlates: In patients with intermediate AMD or non-central GA, improvements in LLVA/LLRA and slowing of EZ attenuation were observed; therefore, clinical PoC studies should prioritize EZ attenuation as a primary structural endpoint with LL-BCVA/LLVA and reading measures as functionally sensitive secondaries, acknowledging that GA area may not be sensitive over ≤1 year (Kim & Lad, 2021; Sabbah et al., 2025; Tung et al., 2025). Given that photoreceptor inner segments are mitochondria-rich, EZ integrity serves as a proximal clinical biomarker of the drug’s mitochondrial mechanism (Sabbah et al., 2025).

Expression and target rationale in RPE: The target of elamipretide is not a single protein but the CL-rich IMM domain; CL is ubiquitous and crucial for maintaining OxPhos function, cristae architecture, and supercomplex assembly in RPE mitochondria, which are compromised in AMD (Fisher et al., 2022; Ferrington et al., 2020). Deficits in mitophagy (reduced PINK1/Parkin responsiveness), increased fission and delayed fusion, and global OxPhos reduction in AMD donor RPE define a mitochondrial fragility state in which CL stabilization is expected to be beneficial (Fisher et al., 2022). Because elamipretide uptake is not dependent on ΔΨm, it can access depolarized/dysfunctional mitochondria in AMD RPE, positioning it to act upstream of apoptosis (Ji et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Elamipretide presents a coherent, mechanistically grounded, and translationally explored therapeutic candidate for non-neovascular AMD predicated on CL-centric rescue of mitochondrial function in RPE and photoreceptors. The totality of evidence spans molecular biophysics, mitochondrial proteomics, in vivo bioenergetics, preclinical retinal disease models, and controlled clinical imaging and functional outcomes, allowing a sober assessment of strengths and residual risks.
