Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Sulforaphane is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate originally identified in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli and Brussels sprouts. It is generated through the hydrolysis of glucoraphanin by the enzyme myrosinase, which is released upon plant tissue damage. As a member of the phytochemical family, sulforaphane belongs to a class of natural compounds known for inducing phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins. Historically, this compound has been extensively investigated for its chemopreventive and cytoprotective properties, particularly through the activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. Being one of the most studied Nrf2 activators, its discovery stemmed from early investigations into dietary antioxidants and their role in reducing carcinogenesis and inflammation. In the context of drug development, sulforaphane is considered a promising candidate for repurposing because it combines a favorable preclinical safety profile with a well-characterized mechanism of action that includes modulation of intracellular redox signaling. Its broad application in preclinical studies to ameliorate oxidative stress and inflammation suggests that targeted delivery to retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells might help alleviate the oxidative injury observed in geographic atrophy, the advanced form of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Bellezza, 2018; Chang et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Sulforaphane has attracted considerable attention for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties over the past two decades. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its protective effects in various models of oxidative stress, including those involving retinal tissues and RPE cells. In in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells—a well-accepted human RPE model—sulforaphane exhibited dose-dependent protection against oxidative insults induced by agents such as tert-butyl hydroperoxide (t-BOOH) and hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂). These experiments demonstrated that sulforaphane pretreatment significantly reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and mitigated mitochondrial membrane potential damage, ultimately leading to reduced apoptotic cell death (Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021). Similarly, other investigations have reported sulforaphane’s ability to induce cytoprotective genes in RPE cells through Nrf2 activation, resulting in improved cell survival under stress conditions (Zhang et al., 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Moreover, several in vivo studies in rodent models have provided evidence of sulforaphane-mediated retinal neuroprotection. Examples include models of photooxidative damage in mice, where sulforaphane delayed photoreceptor degeneration and prevented RPE dysfunction—mechanisms that are highly relevant to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Bellezza, 2018). However, it should be noted that although sulforaphane has been studied in various retinal degeneration models, there is no established clinical history of its use in human dry AMD. Nevertheless, its promising preclinical efficacy in ameliorating oxidative injury in RPE cells, coupled with its demonstrated safety across multiple biological systems including ocular tissues, supports its potential repurposing as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Qin, 2007; del Cano et al., 2008).

Mechanism of Action:  
The principal mechanism underlying sulforaphane’s protective effects is its ability to activate the Nrf2 pathway. Under basal conditions, the transcription factor Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytosol via binding to its inhibitor, Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1), which directs Nrf2 for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Sulforaphane, owing to its electrophilic isothiocyanate moiety, reacts with critical cysteine residues on Keap1. This modification alters the conformation of Keap1 and prevents the degradation of Nrf2, leading to its stabilization and subsequent nuclear translocation (Wherry, 2013). Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to antioxidant response elements (ARE) in the promoter regions of various cytoprotective genes. The result is a robust induction of phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), and superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2). These enzymes play critical roles in neutralizing ROS, repairing oxidative damage, and maintaining cellular redox balance (Qin, 2007; Zhang et al., 2024).

In addition to its classic Nrf2-dependent antioxidant response, sulforaphane has been shown to modulate other cellular pathways that are important for mitochondrial health. In retinal cells, sulforaphane has been reported to attenuate mitochondrial membrane potential collapse and reduce mitochondrial superoxide production, as evidenced by decreased MitoSOX fluorescence in treated ARPE-19 cells (Chang et al., 2020). These mitochondrial protective actions are thought to involve the upregulation of antioxidant enzymes that localize to the mitochondria, as well as enhancement of the spare respiratory capacity—thereby preserving ATP generation under oxidative stress conditions. Furthermore, sulforaphane has been implicated in the regulation of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis, which is critical for mitochondrial biogenesis and metabolic homeostasis. This dual engagement—both through Nrf2-driven transcriptional activation and mitochondrial biogenesis pathways—positions sulforaphane as a multifaceted agent capable of sustaining cellular energy production and reducing oxidative injury in the RPE, a cell type that is particularly vulnerable in geographic atrophy (Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).

Beyond its antioxidant effects, sulforaphane also exerts anti-inflammatory properties by downregulating the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and adhesion molecules (e.g., ICAM-1, MCP-1). This is particularly relevant in the context of AMD, where chronic low-grade inflammation is believed to exacerbate RPE dysfunction and drusen formation (Chang et al., 2020; del Cano et al., 2008). In summary, the molecular interactions of sulforaphane—ranging from direct modification of Keap1 to the induction of mitochondrial antioxidant defenses—provide a robust mechanistic rationale for its potential utility in mitigating the multifactorial oxidative and inflammatory challenges associated with dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Given its well-documented mechanism of action, the hypothesis that sulforaphane induces Nrf2-mediated mitochondrial antioxidant pathways in RPE cells is strongly supported by preclinical evidence. When RPE cells are subjected to oxidative stress, it is expected that sulforaphane treatment will lead to a dose-dependent upregulation of Nrf2 target genes including HO-1, NQO1, and SOD2. The elevation of these transcripts correlates with a reduction in mitochondrial superoxide levels, as measured by decreased MitoSOX fluorescence, and an improvement in the spare respiratory capacity—a surrogate marker for mitochondrial function and ATP generation (Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).

In cellular assays using ARPE-19 cells, administration of sulforaphane prior to oxidative challenge has been shown to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential and decrease cytochrome c release, thereby reducing the activation of downstream apoptotic cascades. The suppression of ROS production and the preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics result in improved cell viability and reduced apoptotic indices. For instance, studies have demonstrated that sulforaphane pretreatment leads to lower levels of cleaved caspase-3 and PARP-1, indicating a direct link between enhanced antioxidant defense and the inhibition of programmed cell death pathways in RPE cells (Yang et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2020).

At the molecular level, the expected outcome of sulforaphane administration in a dry AMD context is multifactorial. The compound would elevate the expression of cytoprotective enzymes that not only detoxify reactive oxygen species but also facilitate the repair of oxidatively damaged macromolecules. This should translate into a measurable decrease in overall oxidative stress markers, preservation of mitochondrial function (evidenced by sustained ATP production and improved spare respiratory capacity), and stabilization of the RPE cell phenotype. Moreover, since mitochondrial dysfunction is a central element of geographic atrophy pathogenesis, sulforaphane’s ability to maintain ATP generation could directly counteract the energy deficit observed in degenerating RPE cells (Zhang et al., 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

These expected effects are supported by a range of preclinical studies. For example, quantitative redox fluorometry results reported in ARPE-19 cells indicate that sulforaphane-treated cells maintain a significantly higher redox ratio during oxidative challenge compared to untreated controls, which is indicative of an enhanced antioxidant state. Additionally, the upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants and improved bioenergetic profiles have been correlated with better cell survival outcomes, reinforcing the concept that sulforaphane can counteract the deleterious cellular changes observed in models of dry AMD (del Cano et al., 2008; Qin, 2007).

Overall Evaluation:  
Sulforaphane, as exemplified by the Sigma-Aldrich S4441 formulation, presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD, particularly targeting the geographic atrophy form characterized by pronounced RPE degeneration. One of the major strengths of sulforaphane lies in its robust preclinical evidence demonstrating its ability to induce the Nrf2 pathway, a master regulator of oxidative stress responses. The compound’s direct modification of Keap1 and subsequent stabilization and nuclear translocation of Nrf2 trigger the upregulation of several antioxidant enzymes, such as HO-1, NQO1, and SOD2—which are critical for detoxifying reactive oxygen species and repairing oxidative damage in RPE cells (Qin, 2007; Zhang et al., 2024).

Furthermore, sulforaphane’s additional capacity to preserve mitochondrial function by maintaining membrane potential and supporting ATP synthesis addresses a major pathological hallmark of geographic atrophy, where mitochondrial dysfunction leads to energy depletion and accelerates cell death. The integration of mitochondrial antioxidant defenses with the broader cytoprotective effects of Nrf2 activation provides a convergent mechanism aimed at both preventing oxidative damage and sustaining cellular energy production under stress conditions (Yang et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2020).

Another notable strength is the extensive safety data available for sulforaphane from preclinical studies. Its natural occurrence, combined with its well-documented bioactivity in a range of cell types, underscores its potential for repurposing in ocular applications. Moreover, sulforaphane’s ability to attenuate inflammatory responses by reducing the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines adds an extra layer of therapeutic benefit, considering the role of chronic inflammation in exacerbating AMD pathology (del Cano et al., 2008; Chang et al., 2020).

Despite these promising attributes, several challenges remain. One potential limitation is the bioavailability of sulforaphane. Like many natural compounds, sulforaphane may face pharmacokinetic hurdles such as poor water solubility and limited tissue penetration, which could complicate systemic delivery or localized administration to the retina. Furthermore, while the preclinical efficacy in ARPE-19 cell models and animal studies is encouraging, the translation of these findings to human patients with dry AMD remains to be validated. Variability in the cellular responses between in vitro models and the complex microenvironment of the human retina, including the influence of the blood–retinal barrier, poses a potential risk for suboptimal therapeutic delivery (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Qin, 2007).

Additionally, some of the supportive data for sulforaphane’s efficacy in ocular systems come from studies published in journals with variable impact, and additional high-quality clinical studies will be necessary to establish its safety and efficacy profile in the context of dry AMD. The dosing regimens, potential off-target effects, and long-term impact of chronic Nrf2 activation in retinal tissues also require careful investigation. There is ongoing debate over the potential for Nrf2 activators to have biphasic dose responses, where excessive activation might inadvertently cause cellular stress or dysregulate normal redox homeostasis (Bellezza, 2018; del Cano et al., 2008).

In conclusion, sulforaphane demonstrates strong mechanistic potential for the treatment of dry AMD by elevating key antioxidant defenses in RPE cells and preserving mitochondrial function under oxidative stress. Its ability to induce HO-1, NQO1, and SOD2 in response to oxidative challenges and thereby reduce superoxide production while maintaining ATP synthesis is directly aligned with the therapeutic needs of geographic atrophy patients. The preclinical evidence suggests that, with appropriate formulation and delivery strategies, sulforaphane could provide a dual benefit by mitigating oxidative injury and reducing inflammation in the retina. However, further studies are required to address bioavailability challenges and to validate its clinical efficacy in well-designed human trials. Overall, sulforaphane merits further investigation as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, and its advancement into early-phase clinical testing is justified by the compelling preclinical data available (Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; del Cano et al., 2008).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
EUK-134 is a synthetic antioxidant belonging to the class of manganese salen complexes designed to mimic the endogenous activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase. Its synthesis involves a controlled condensation reaction between salicylaldehyde and ethylenediamine, resulting in a small molecule whose molecular framework is optimized for redox cycling and catalytic detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). As a representative of SOD/catalase mimetics, EUK-134 is engineered to convert the superoxide anion (O2–) into hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and subsequently decompose H2O2 into water and oxygen. Its dual-activity design places it in a promising category for therapeutic intervention in diseases driven by oxidative stress. The compound’s synthetic origin allows for fine-tuning of physicochemical properties such as lipophilicity and catalytic efficiency, making it a candidate for repurposing in disease conditions beyond those for which it was originally developed (Thoma et al., 2020; Grujicic & Allen, 2024). Within the pharmaceutical landscape, this class of compounds has been extensively studied in preclinical models for their ability to mitigate cellular damage by neutralizing ROS; they have been applied experimentally in models of muscle atrophy, ischemia–reperfusion injury, and certain cancer indications, where oxidative stress is known to play a critical role (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). The molecular architecture of EUK-134 notably offers a compact, dual-function approach that, in theory, should counterbalance both superoxide and hydrogen peroxide accumulation—a feature that is especially relevant given that the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is subject to chronic oxidative insult (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of EUK-134 is marked by its application in various preclinical models where oxidative stress and subsequent mitochondrial dysfunction were central to the pathology. In studies involving human skeletal muscle cells, EUK-134 has been shown to attenuate endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress-induced mitochondrial dysfunction induced by tunicamycin, resulting in improved mitochondrial membrane potential and restoration of bioenergetic profiles (Thoma et al., 2020). Moreover, this compound has been evaluated in contexts such as hyperoxic myocardial tissues, where it mitigated oxidative damage and contributed to the preservation of cellular function under stress conditions (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). Its potential benefits in reducing oxidative damage have also been noted in studies involving breast cancer cells and mechanical unloading-induced muscle atrophy, highlighting its versatility as a ROS-scavenging agent (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).  
Despite the significant body of work on EUK-134 in non-ocular tissues, its direct evaluation in dry AMD or similar degenerative retinal conditions has not yet been thoroughly explored. Clinical trials and literature searches focusing on Mn-porphyrin SOD mimetics have yielded extensive data relating to retinal diseases (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.), but EUK-134 itself has not been the primary focus in retinal clinical applications. Nonetheless, its proven mechanism of reducing ROS accumulation positions it as an attractive candidate for extension into the field of ocular therapeutics. In this light, the repurposing of EUK-134 for dry AMD is based on the hypothesis that its antioxidant properties, previously validated in muscle and other tissues, may confer similar protective effects in RPE cells that are chronically exposed to oxidative stress (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, EUK-134 functions by catalytically mimicking the activities of superoxide dismutase and catalase. In its SOD mimetic capacity, EUK-134 accepts electrons from the superoxide anions, facilitating their conversion into hydrogen peroxide—a reaction which is essential to limit direct superoxide-mediated damage (Thoma et al., 2020). Following this, the catalase mimetic activity is intended to decompose the resultant hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, thereby preventing accumulation of H2O2 which can otherwise contribute to oxidative injury through Fenton-type reactions. However, several studies have drawn attention to limitations in this pathway. For example, evidence indicates that EUK-134 may exhibit a lower efficiency in H2O2 scavenging when compared to other antioxidants such as MnTBAP or native catalase, particularly in environments with high oxidative flux (Quan et al., 2017). One key observation is a significant down-regulation of catalase expression – by more than five-fold – upon EUK-134 treatment in some cellular systems, a factor that potentially undermines its capacity to fully counteract H2O2 buildup (Quan et al., 2017).  
On the molecular interaction front, the manganese center within the salen complex undergoes redox cycling, alternating between oxidation states in response to ROS encounters. This cyclic activity contributes to its continuous catalytic turnover and represents the biochemical foundation for its antioxidant action. Furthermore, studies have shown that EUK-134 can modulate various signaling pathways associated with oxidative stress responses, such as the TGF-β1/Smad2 pathway in muscle under atrophy-inducing conditions (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). Despite these promising aspects, challenges such as suboptimal mitochondrial uptake remain a concern since effective neutralization of ROS in RPE cells requires prompt access to the mitochondrial matrix—a compartment frequently characterized by an inherently challenging microenvironment for drug delivery (Quan et al., 2017). In summary, while EUK-134 possesses a dual action mechanism that addresses two key components of the ROS cascade, the efficiency of its H2O2 detoxification and its cellular distribution are critical parameters that must be rigorously characterized in the context of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
In dry AMD and particularly in geographic atrophy, the retinal pigment epithelium is subject to sustained oxidative stress, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and subsequent cell death. The expected therapeutic effect of EUK-134 in this context is to provide robust antioxidant protection within RPE mitochondria, thereby neutralizing excessive superoxide and hydrogen peroxide levels and preserving mitochondrial integrity (Thoma et al., 2020). Restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) is a key indicator of improved mitochondrial function; thus, by mitigating ROS-induced depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane, EUK-134 is anticipated to maintain or restore ATP production and spare respiratory capacity in RPE cells. These effects are crucial given that ATP depletion and bioenergetic failure are prominent features in the pathology of dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012).  
In vitro assays that simulate oxidative stress conditions—such as those employing RPE cell cultures under hypoxic or chemically induced stress—will likely measure parameters including Δψm, ATP levels, ROS quantification, and expression levels of stress-responsive genes. The anticipated outcome is that EUK-134 will lead to a measurable decrease in the levels of ROS as detected by biochemical assays, along with a concomitant stabilization of mitochondrial respiratory function (Thoma et al., 2020; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012). In addition, molecular analyses may reveal a down-regulation of oxidative stress markers and an improvement in the overall redox balance of the cell. It is vital, however, to consider that some studies have noted that EUK-134 does not inhibit all markers of stress uniformly—for example, the continued expression of GADD34 has been observed even where other stress indicators are normalized (Thoma et al., 2020).  
Given that RPE cells naturally express endogenous antioxidant enzymes such as SOD and catalase, supplementation with EUK-134 is expected to either bolster these defenses or compensate for their decline during chronic oxidative challenges. This dual functionality could theoretically translate into a reduced progression of RPE cell death, slower accumulation of drusen, and ultimately a deceleration of geographic atrophy, all of which are hallmarks of dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of EUK-134 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration involves weighing its mechanistic promise against the practical challenges encountered in its preclinical and potential clinical application. On the one hand, EUK-134 embodies several clear strengths. Its dual mimetic activities align well with the fundamental pathophysiology of dry AMD, where both superoxide and hydrogen peroxide are implicated in the oxidative cascade that leads to mitochondrial dysfunction and RPE cell demise (Thoma et al., 2020; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012). The synthetic nature of EUK-134 allows for controlled chemical modifications which could be leveraged to optimize its pharmacokinetic properties, and its relatively small size is an asset for penetrating tissues such as the retina. Additionally, the compound’s history in attenuating ER stress-related mitochondrial dysfunction in muscle cells provides a robust proof-of-concept that similar benefits might be translatable to RPE cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress (Thoma et al., 2020).  
Notwithstanding these advantages, several weaknesses must be scrutinized. A primary concern lies in the evidence that EUK-134 may exhibit limitations in catalase-like activity, particularly with regard to its efficiency in cleaving hydrogen peroxide. Studies have documented a significant down-regulation of catalase expression upon treatment with EUK-134 and noted that its H2O2 scavenging capabilities fall short when benchmarked against other agents such as MnTBAP or even native catalase (Quan et al., 2017). In the context of RPE cells, where the oxidative insult is persistent and multifactorial, such limitations could result in suboptimal clearance of H2O2, thereby potentially compromising the therapeutic efficacy.  
Another critical issue pertains to drug delivery and cellular bioavailability. The lipophilicity of EUK-134 is notably lower compared to some analogues, amounting to roughly 43% less lipophilicity in certain cases, which inherently limits its capacity to traverse cell membranes and accumulate in the mitochondrial matrix, where its activity is most needed (Limoli et al., 2006; Quan et al., 2017). Since efficient mitochondrial delivery is crucial for counteracting localized ROS buildup in RPE cells, a deficiency in this area might significantly restrict the net antioxidant benefit provided by EUK-134.  
Furthermore, the translational history of EUK-134 presents a challenge in directly correlating preclinical observations with anticipated clinical outcomes in dry AMD. While substantial evidence exists linking EUK-134 with improved mitochondrial function in non-ocular tissues—such as the normalization of mitochondrial membrane potential in tunicamycin-induced ER stress models (Thoma et al., 2020)—there remains a paucity of direct data in ocular models. Compared to other antioxidants that have been more rigorously tested in retinal systems, EUK-134’s ocular pharmacodynamics, potential toxicity in the retinal microenvironment, and long-term safety profile are not well established (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Grujicic & Allen, 2024).  
The literature also points to the possibility of a paradoxical pro-oxidant effect. In some cellular environments, the administration of exogenous SOD mimetics can inadvertently shift the oxidative balance toward higher hydrogen peroxide levels if the catalase function is insufficient, thereby exacerbating oxidative stress rather than mitigating it (Limoli et al., 2006; Quan et al., 2017). Given the delicate balance required in the redox regulation of RPE cells, such an imbalance could be particularly detrimental.  
In light of these considerations, EUK-134’s potential for repurposing as a treatment for dry AMD is promising but remains conditional upon further optimization. The strengths of its dual antioxidant mechanism, its capacity to restore mitochondrial function, and its versatility as evidenced by its broad therapeutic history underscore its potential utility. However, the measurable shortcomings regarding efficient H2O2 clearance, the observed down-regulation of catalase expression, and uncertain mitochondrial bioavailability present hurdles that must be addressed in subsequent experimental phases. This will likely involve additional formulation strategies to improve cellular uptake, as well as comprehensive studies in appropriate retinal models to definitively correlate its antioxidant profile with functional improvements in RPE cells (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Quan et al., 2017).  
It is also noteworthy that while a broad range of clinical trials have been initiated for compounds with similar ROS-scavenging profiles in retinal degenerations (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.), there is a lack of direct clinical evidence for EUK-134’s efficacy specifically in the context of dry AMD. This gap further emphasizes the need for targeted preclinical studies focusing on ocular pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Establishing a direct connection between EUK-134’s known in vitro benefits and its performance in animal models of geographic atrophy will be essential prior to any clinical translation.  
In conclusion, the mechanistic rationale behind the use of EUK-134 in dry AMD is strong on theoretical grounds, leveraging its dual capacity to mitigate the damaging effects of both superoxide and hydrogen peroxide. However, the compound’s limitations—namely, its reduced effectiveness in scavenging H2O2 under certain conditions, its potential for down-regulating endogenous catalase, and challenges associated with adequate mitochondrial targeting—necessitate a cautious approach. The strategic pathway forward would involve an in-depth exploration of its pharmacological properties in retinal models, formulation modifications to enhance mitochondrial delivery, and dose-optimization studies to balance antioxidant efficacy with safety. Only after these issues are rigorously addressed can EUK-134 be confidently positioned as a viable repurposed candidate for the treatment of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Quan et al., 2017; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Mitochonic Acid-5 (MA-5; MedChemExpress HY-104308) is a synthetic, mitochondria‐targeted small molecule originally discovered for its ability to improve mitochondrial function in models of cellular aging. MA-5 belongs to the class of mitochondrial modulators that have been shown to enhance adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production, reduce mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), and extend lifespan in non‐ocular systems such as fibroblasts and Caenorhabditis elegans. The current hypothesis proposes that MA-5 binds directly to mitofilin (also known as Mic60), a key scaffolding protein in the inner mitochondrial membrane that is essential for the proper organization and stability of mitochondrial cristae. This interaction is anticipated to stabilize cristae architecture, thereby preserving optimal assembly of the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and enabling improved mitochondrial bioenergetics—a mechanism particularly appealing in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), where cristae disorganization and mtROS accumulation in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells have been associated with disease pathology (Ji et al., 2021; Ferrington et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
While MA-5 itself has not been previously evaluated in ocular diseases, compounds that modulate mitochondrial function have a long history in preclinical studies for age-related conditions. Several mitochondrial-targeted agents—for example, SkQ1 and elamipretide—have demonstrated promise in ameliorating mitochondrial defects in RPE models and in early clinical trials targeting dry AMD (Ji et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022). In other systems, MA-5 has been reported to improve ATP production, reduce mtROS, and activate the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt) in fibroblast and C. elegans models. Such beneficial effects on mitochondrial function have contributed to the rationale for repurposing MA-5 for dry AMD. Moreover, research in related domains suggests that stabilizing mitochondrial cristae via targeting scaffold proteins such as mitofilin is mechanistically sound given observations of altered mitofilin expression and cristae disruption in AMD RPE (Ferrington et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). However, direct usage of MA-5 in retinal disorders remains unexplored, and its potential has yet to be validated in RPE-specific in vitro or in vivo models.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, MA-5 is proposed to exert its beneficial effects by physically interacting with mitofilin/Mic60, a protein integral to the maintenance of inner mitochondrial membrane architecture and cristae organization. Mitofilin is recognized for its role in stabilizing the cristae junctions and in facilitating the proper assembly and function of the ETC complexes (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Ferrington et al., 2020). In dry AMD, mitochondrial cristae loss has been documented in RPE cells, suggesting that disrupted mitofilin function may underlie some of the bioenergetic deficiencies seen in the disease (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Ferrington et al., 2020). By binding to mitofilin, MA-5 is expected to reinforce cristae integrity; this stabilization can promote the efficient assembly of ETC complexes, thereby leading to improved oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production. Concurrently, enhanced cristae organization is likely to reduce electron leakage from the ETC and lower the production of reactive oxygen species, which in excess contribute to oxidative damage and RPE cell death (Ji et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022).

In addition, emerging evidence suggests that perturbations in mitochondrial structure can trigger the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt), a conserved stress-response pathway that upregulates mitochondrial chaperones such as mtHsp70 and other proteostasis factors to cope with misfolded proteins and oxidative damage. MA-5 is hypothesized not only to stabilize the physical architecture of the mitochondria but also to activate UPRmt pathways, thereby enhancing the endogenous capacity of RPE cells to detoxify ROS and repair mitochondrial damage. Activation of UPRmt could lead to increased expression of mitochondrial chaperones, improved clearance of damaged proteins, and a restoration of redox balance within the mitochondria. This dual mechanism—direct structural stabilization via mitofilin binding and indirect activation of UPRmt—positions MA-5 as a potentially powerful agent for correcting mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD (Tong et al., 2022; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
If MA-5 performs as hypothesized in RPE cells, several beneficial effects are anticipated. First, by binding mitofilin and stabilizing cristae architecture, MA-5 should restore proper assembly and function of ETC complexes leading to increased ATP production. Such a recovery in mitochondrial bioenergetics is particularly critical in RPE cells, given their high energy demands for processes such as phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and maintenance of the visual cycle (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022). Second, the stabilization of cristae, alongside the potential activation of the UPRmt, is expected to reduce mtROS production by minimizing electron leakage from complex I and III of the ETC. Lower ROS levels would alleviate oxidative stress—a known driver of RPE degeneration and dry AMD progression that has been documented in multiple studies (Ji et al., 2021; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Third, the activation of UPRmt may upregulate key mitochondrial chaperones such as mtHsp70, facilitating improved protein folding, enhanced clearance of damaged proteins, and overall better maintenance of mitochondrial homeostasis. These cellular changes should collectively promote RPE survival and function, thus potentially slowing or even reversing some aspects of the cellular degenerative processes seen in dry AMD (Ji et al., 2021; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

Furthermore, since mitofilin/Mic60 is an abundantly expressed and essential component in RPE mitochondria—as evidenced by its upregulation in early AMD patient samples—the MA-5-mediated stabilization of this protein is expected to yield measurable improvements in mitochondrial parameters in cellular assays. Such improvements would include increased mitochondrial membrane potential, enhanced basal and maximal respiration, and a reduction in apoptotic markers associated with mitochondrial damage. Ultimately, if these in vitro effects translate into in vivo efficacy, MA-5 could contribute to a novel treatment modality that directly addresses the underlying mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD (Ferrington et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
The therapeutic candidate MA-5 presents a highly promising, mechanistically driven approach to addressing dry AMD by targeting mitochondrial dysfunction—a central hallmark of the disease. Its proposed dual mechanism of binding to mitofilin to stabilize cristae architecture and activating the UPRmt to enhance antioxidant defenses directly aligns with the documented mitochondrial pathology in RPE cells. Strengths of this candidate include the following:  
– The strategy of targeting mitofilin is supported by numerous observations that indicate altered mitofilin levels and cristae disorganization in AMD, suggesting that restoring cristae integrity may ameliorate mitochondrial deficits (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Ferrington et al., 2020).  
– MA-5’s documented capacity to improve ATP production and reduce mtROS in non-ocular models indicates a favorable mitochondrial modulation profile that is likely transferable to RPE cells, where energy production and redox homeostasis are critical (Ji et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022).  
– Activation of UPRmt represents an innovative therapeutic angle that not only protects mitochondrial structure but also boosts cellular defenses against oxidative stress—a pathway that has been implicated in maintaining RPE cell viability under conditions of sustained stress (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022).  

Despite these promising aspects, several points of caution must be noted. First, while the beneficial effects of MA-5 have been demonstrated in fibroblast and C. elegans models, no direct data exist regarding its efficacy in RPE cells or in animal models of dry AMD. The translation of effects from non-ocular systems to the highly specialized RPE must be rigorously evaluated. Second, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of MA-5 in the context of ocular delivery are unknown at this time; the compound’s ability to achieve sufficient retinal concentration, while minimizing systemic toxicity, remains an open question. Third, the precise binding affinity and specificity of MA-5 for mitofilin in RPE mitochondria have not yet been characterized. Off-target effects or unintended modulation of mitochondrial dynamics may lead to adverse outcomes if the drug’s action is not adequately localized within the retina. Finally, activation of UPRmt, while beneficial in the context of mitochondrial stress, may also have complex downstream effects that require careful titration to avoid potential maladaptive consequences in long-term treatment scenarios (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Ferrington et al., 2020).

In summary, the proposed mechanism for MA-5 is conceptually attractive given the wealth of literature linking mitochondrial cristae disruption and excessive ROS production to dry AMD pathology. The candidate’s potential to bind mitofilin, stabilize mitochondrial structure, and activate a protective UPRmt aligns well with the current understanding of mitochondrial deficits in RPE cells observed in AMD (Ji et al., 2021; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). However, significant preclinical work is needed to validate its efficacy specifically in the RPE environment. Studies should include detailed binding assays to confirm the interaction between MA-5 and mitofilin, evaluation of mitochondrial bioenergetics and redox parameters in RPE cell cultures, and ultimately, assessments in animal models of dry AMD that recapitulate key aspects of mitochondrial dysfunction. Historically, astaxanthin has been investigated and utilized in various biomedical contexts due to its robust antioxidant function. Clinical research and preclinical models have repeatedly shown that astaxanthin improves retinal function and visual acuity in patients with ocular diseases, including both early and nonadvanced stages of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic potential of astaxanthin in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) is thought to stem from its unparalleled antioxidant activity, which is mechanistically linked to its lipophilic and hydrophilic properties. On a molecular level, astaxanthin integrates into cellular membranes—including those of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) mitochondria—where it acts as a chain-breaking antioxidant, quenching reactive oxygen species (ROS) and scavenging free radicals efficiently (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 1–5). Its mechanism involves the neutralization of lipid peroxidation, a process wherein polyunsaturated fatty acids in the cell membrane are damaged by ROS, ultimately leading to the formation of malondialdehyde (MDA) and other toxic aldehyde species that compromise membrane integrity (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–5; Maiuolo et al., 2022, pp. 8–9). By inhibiting lipid peroxidation, astaxanthin stabilizes the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), an essential parameter for maintaining proper mitochondrial function and for preventing the initiation of apoptosis via intrinsic death pathways (Fong, 2023, pp. 7–10; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).  

At the molecular level, studies indicate that astaxanthin modulates key intracellular signaling pathways. It downregulates inflammatory mediators by suppressing the NF-κB pathway, thereby reducing the transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–5; Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 3–5). Its role in modulating mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt pathways further contributes to cellular survival by reinforcing anti-apoptotic signaling and inhibiting caspase activation, thereby reducing retinal ganglion cell death (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–5).  

The hypothesis under consideration—that astaxanthin integrates into RPE mitochondrial membranes to quench lipid peroxidation and stabilize Δψm—is supported by its molecular configuration, which allows the compound to embed itself at the interface of membrane lipids without disrupting the bilayer structure (Rodella et al., 2023, pp. 11–13; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 3–4). Once incorporated, astaxanthin acts as a “molecular rivet” that not only prevents oxidative damage but also helps maintain membrane fluidity and structural integrity. This is particularly relevant in the context of dry AMD, where chronic oxidative stress leads to the degeneration of the RPE, a critical cell layer whose dysfunction is central to the pathogenesis of the disease (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 3–5). Additionally, the ability of astaxanthin to traverse cellular and mitochondrial membranes enhances its efficacy in neutralizing ROS, thereby preserving both mitochondrial function and cellular viability within the retina (Manresa et al., 2016, p. 5; Rodella et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).

The collective body of evidence suggests that astaxanthin holds considerable promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) is a synthetic derivative of fumaric acid that belongs to the class of fumaric acid esters (FAEs) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Chemically, DMF is the dimethyl ester of fumaric acid, with a molecular weight of approximately 144.13 g/mol, and is produced by reacting fumaric acid with methanol in the presence of a strong acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Although fumaric acid occurs naturally as an intermediate in the citric acid cycle, DMF itself is fully synthetically manufactured, conferring the advantages of chemical stability and the ability to precisely modulate its structure to enhance pharmacological properties (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Moreover, DMF is classified as an electrophilic molecule that, due to its α,β-unsaturated ester structure, can covalently modify protein thiols, particularly the cysteine residues within KEAP1, thereby initiating its downstream effects on cellular redox homeostasis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Fumaric acid esters as a class have a long-standing history in pharmacotherapy, originally finding application in dermatology, most notably in the treatment of psoriasis, and have since been repurposed for neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis (MS) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, fumaric acid esters were introduced into clinical practice as antipsoriatic agents in Europe, with formulations such as Fumaderm® entering the market in the 1990s (Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). DMF in particular emerged as a key component in these formulations, and its efficacy in modulating immune responses and suppressing inflammation in skin diseases laid the foundation for its later repurposing in other systemic inflammatory conditions (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Over time, DMF was repurposed and further developed as an oral agent for the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), culminating in its FDA approval in 2013 under the trade name Tecfidera® by Biogen (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163). Clinical trials, including large-scale phase 3 studies, have demonstrated its favorable safety profile and efficacy in reducing relapse rates and slowing disability progression in MS patients (Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 14–16). Although there is no extensive historical record of DMF being used directly for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other primary ocular diseases, recent preclinical findings have indicated that its potent activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway may confer significant protective effects on the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This has sparked considerable interest in repurposing DMF for ocular indications such as geographic atrophy, a late stage of dry AMD, by leveraging its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities observed in nonocular settings (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, DMF functions primarily as a prodrug; upon oral administration it is rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases within the gastrointestinal tract to yield its active metabolite, monomethyl fumarate (MMF) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). The pharmacodynamic actions of DMF principally involve the electrophilic modification of specific cysteine residues—most notably cysteine 151—on Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Under physiological conditions, KEAP1 binds to and retains the transcription factor Nrf2 in the cytoplasm, targeting it for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. However, when DMF covalently modifies KEAP1, it disrupts this complex, allowing Nrf2 to dissociate and translocate into the nucleus (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). In the nucleus, Nrf2 binds to antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoters of numerous genes encoding cytoprotective enzymes, including glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), and various enzymes involved in glutathione (GSH) synthesis and regeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). These molecular interactions lead to enhanced antioxidant defenses, improved detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and overall better maintenance of cellular redox balance (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). In addition to its role in promoting antioxidant gene expression via Nrf2 activation, DMF has been shown to have immunomodulatory properties; it can shift cytokine profiles by increasing interleukin-4 (IL-4)–expressing CD4+ T cells and decreasing the production of proinflammatory cytokines such as interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and interleukin-17 (IL-17) (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Furthermore, DMF has been reported to inhibit nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation in certain cellular contexts, thus contributing to a reduction in inflammatory signaling independently of Nrf2 (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Together, these molecular actions result in lowered cellular oxidative stress and an improved inflammatory milieu, which are critical factors implicated in the pathogenesis of chronic degenerative diseases (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry AMD, particularly the geographic atrophy form, is characterized by the gradual degeneration of RPE cells, which leads to subsequent photoreceptor loss and irreversible vision impairment. Central to the pathophysiology of dry AMD are oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation that progressively compromise RPE viability and function (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). The hypothesis being explored is that DMF, through its robust activation of the Nrf2 pathway, can enhance the expression of ARE-driven genes that encode for antioxidant and cytoprotective proteins, thereby counteracting the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in the RPE (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 13–14). In particular, the upregulation of enzymes involved in glutathione synthesis is expected to increase intracellular levels of GSH, a critical thiol antioxidant that protects mitochondrial membranes and supports cellular bioenergetics (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Preclinical studies in retinal models have demonstrated that DMF can effectively preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and reduce the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β), both of which are hallmarks of RPE distress under oxidative challenge (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Given that the RPE is highly metabolically active and particularly vulnerable to cumulative oxidative damage, the sustained activation of Nrf2 by DMF following oral dosing is anticipated to provide continuous reinforcement of antioxidant defenses and maintain mitochondrial integrity in these cells (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 3–5; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). Moreover, by mitigating inflammatory signaling, DMF may not only protect the RPE but also contribute to a more favorable microenvironment that limits the propagation of cell death signals, thus potentially slowing the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Collectively, these expected cellular effects support the rationale for using DMF as an intervention to preserve retinal structure and function by lowering oxidative damage and supporting bioenergetics in the RPE.

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential of dimethyl fumarate as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD rests on a solid mechanistic rationale combined with an established clinical pedigree in other indications. One of the primary strengths of DMF is its well-characterized pharmacological profile; it is FDA-approved for multiple sclerosis and has been safely administered to thousands of patients over several years, which significantly mitigates the risk and regulatory hurdles typically associated with repurposed drugs (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). The dual actions of DMF—in particular, its ability to both activate the Nrf2 pathway and attenuate proinflammatory signals—directly target the underlying pathological processes in dry AMD, where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central drivers of RPE degeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In vitro studies have provided encouraging evidence that DMF increases intracellular glutathione levels and protects RPE cells from oxidative insults, findings that are directly translatable to the pathobiology of dry AMD (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Nonetheless, several challenges remain. Although DMF is known to be effective in MS and psoriasis, the ocular milieu presents unique pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic challenges that may not be fully addressed by the current oral formulations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18). The rapid hydrolysis of DMF to MMF means that, while the active metabolite does exert therapeutic effects, fine-tuning the dosing regimen to ensure adequate drug levels in the retina while minimizing systemic side effects is necessary (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). In addition, common adverse reactions associated with DMF, such as gastrointestinal discomfort and flushing, though generally mild to moderate, could be more problematic in the typically elderly dry AMD population, necessitating careful monitoring and potentially modified dosing strategies (Camelo, 2025, p. 17; Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13). There is also the question of whether systemic administration of DMF can generate sufficient concentrations in the retina to achieve a meaningful therapeutic effect. While emerging evidence suggests that DMF can cross the blood-retinal barrier and activate Nrf2 in retinal cells (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3), further pharmacokinetic and translational studies are warranted to confirm its retinal bioavailability and the optimal dosing regimen for ocular indications.

Another consideration is the complexity of dry AMD itself, which is a slowly progressive, multifactorial disease with contributions from genetic predispositions, environmental exposures, and systemic metabolic disturbances. It remains to be seen whether the monotherapeutic approach of DMF, targeting primarily oxidative stress via Nrf2 activation, will be sufficient to halt or reverse disease progression, or whether combination therapies will ultimately be required (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Furthermore, while the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms of DMF are well supported by in vitro data and animal studies, there is still limited clinical data on its efficacy in ocular disease settings. Early-phase clinical trials aimed at evaluating DMF in geographic atrophy have to rigorously assess both structural outcomes (e.g., changes in the area of atrophy) and functional endpoints (e.g., visual acuity, retinal sensitivity) to establish its therapeutic benefit in dry AMD (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Despite these limitations, the strengths of DMF are compelling. The drug’s ability to upregulate a broad spectrum of cytoprotective genes via the Nrf2 pathway makes it a versatile candidate for mitigating the oxidative and inflammatory stress that drives RPE degeneration. The fact that DMF has already cleared extensive regulatory and clinical safety evaluations in nonocular indications is a significant advantage, as it greatly accelerates the translational pathway compared to a novel chemical entity (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Additionally, the repurposing of an already approved drug leverages existing manufacturing, formulation, and distribution infrastructure, favorably impacting the cost and timeline associated with drug development (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

In summary, the comprehensive literature review supports the potential of DMF to serve as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its mechanism of action—centered on Nrf2 activation leading to enhanced antioxidant capacity along with anti-inflammatory effects—directly addresses the key pathophysiological mechanisms implicated in dry AMD. The extensive clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis provides a reliable safety and tolerability framework, which is crucial for rapid repositioning into a new clinical area such as geographic atrophy (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). However, it is essential to conduct targeted preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials specifically in ocular disease models to optimize dosing, confirm retinal delivery, and demonstrate clinical efficacy before advancing to larger randomized controlled trials (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Overall, while challenges remain regarding optimal application in the retinal context and potential side effects in an older patient population, DMF—by virtue of its dual antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms and robust clinical background—stands as a viable candidate that merits further investigation for the treatment of dry AMD.

Given the current evidence, the following recommendations are proposed for advancing DMF as a candidate for dry AMD:  

1. Conduct detailed pharmacokinetic studies in animal models to assess the retinal bioavailability of DMF and its active metabolite MMF following systemic administration. This should include studies comparing different dosing schedules and formulations to optimize retinal exposure without exacerbating systemic adverse effects (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2).  

2. Develop and validate preclinical models of dry AMD that recapitulate the key features of human geographic atrophy, with a focus on evaluating the efficacy of DMF in protecting RPE cells against oxidative stress and preserving mitochondrial function (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

3. Investigate the potential benefits of combining DMF with other therapeutic agents that target complementary pathways in dry AMD. For example, agents that modulate complement activation or improve choroidal blood flow may synergize with the Nrf2-mediated antioxidant mechanism of DMF (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).  

4. Initiate early-phase clinical trials in patients with geographic atrophy to establish proof of concept. These studies should include robust biomarker assessments (e.g., measurement of ARE gene expression, retinal imaging for atrophy progression, and functional visual outcomes) to correlate molecular effects with clinical benefit (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

5. Carefully monitor the safety profile of DMF in the elderly population, as the incidence of gastrointestinal side effects and lymphopenia may differ compared to the population with MS. Consider the feasibility of modified-release formulations or alternative routes of administration (e.g., topical ocular delivery) to minimize systemic side effects while maximizing retinal drug concentrations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18).

Overall, the repurposing of dimethyl fumarate for dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a robust mechanistic framework and a significant body of preclinical and clinical data generated in other indications. Its capacity to activate the Nrf2 pathway, enhance mitochondrial glutathione synthesis, and modulate inflammatory responses in RPE cells directly addresses several pivotal aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). While there are challenges regarding optimal retinal delivery and management of systemic adverse effects, the clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis lends considerable support to its translational potential. Consequently, dimethyl fumarate represents a well‐justified and attractive therapeutic candidate for further exploration in the treatment of dry AMD, warranting additional preclinical optimization and clinical investigation to fully define its role in preserving visual function in patients affected by this progressive degenerative disease (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12).
