Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Deferoxamine (also known as desferrioxamine B; DFO) is a natural microbial siderophore originally isolated from Streptomyces pilosus and developed as an iron‐chelating drug in the 1960s, with clinical deployment beginning in 1968 under the trade name Desferal for treatment of iron overload disorders (notably transfusional iron loading in β-thalassemia) (Faa & Crisponi, 1999; Sharpe et al., 2011; Birch et al., 2006). Chemically, DFO is a hexadentate, tris-hydroxamate ligand that coordinates ferric iron (FeIII) at six oxygen donors derived from three bidentate hydroxamate groups to form a very stable 1:1 FeIII–DFO complex with distorted octahedral FeIIIO6 geometry (Sharpe et al., 2011; Richardson & Poňka, 1998). The FeIII affinity is exceptionally high and selective: reported formation constants for FeIII–DFO include log β110 ≈ 30.5 and conditional pM/pFe values around 26–31, while affinity for FeII is ∼20 orders of magnitude lower, consistent with the observation that DFO selectively chelates FeIII in vivo (Sharpe et al., 2011; Kontoghiorghes & Kontoghiorghe, 2020; Birch et al., 2006). The compound is highly hydrophilic, carries a positive charge near physiological pH, and exhibits poor membrane permeability and oral absorption; as a result, DFO is administered parenterally and tends to localize extracellularly or within endosomal/lysosomal compartments after endocytosis (Birch et al., 2006; Kontoghiorghes & Kontoghiorghe, 2020; Zhao et al., 2021). Pharmacokinetically, native DFO has a very short plasma half-life on the order of minutes, with multiple studies reporting ∼10–30 minutes after intravenous dosing, rapid renal clearance, and elimination of chelated iron via urine and bile; the short exposure necessitates prolonged subcutaneous or intravenous infusions for clinical efficacy (Sharpe et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2020; Entezari et al., 2022). DFO is not blood–neural barrier penetrant, limiting access to the central nervous system and retina when given systemically (Li et al., 2023).

As a class, siderophores are low-molecular microbial metabolites evolved for FeIII acquisition and storage; medicinally, DFO is the prototypical siderophore drug and, for decades, has served as the clinical standard for chelation in iron-overload conditions (Hatcher et al., 2009). Within therapeutic iron chelators, DFO’s hexadentate hydroxamate architecture confers high thermodynamic and kinetic stability of FeIII complexes, limiting redox cycling and hydroxyl radical generation relative to weaker or redox-active iron ligands (Hider & Kong, 2013).

Therapeutic History  
DFO has an extensive clinical history as the benchmark iron chelator for transfusional iron overload, especially in β-thalassemia major and other transfusion-dependent anemias; it was approved in the United States in 1968 and used for decades as life-saving therapy, albeit limited by the need for prolonged parenteral infusions and high cost (Sharpe et al., 2011; Birch et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2012). Beyond chronic iron overload, labeled and established uses include acute iron poisoning and treatment of aluminum toxicity, reflecting DFO’s strong FeIII selectivity and capacity to form inert complexes with polyvalent cations in vivo (Jones et al., 2020). The standard practice has involved subcutaneous or intravenous infusions at 20–60 mg/kg daily for 8–24 hours over 5–7 days per week, with urinary and fecal excretion of iron–DFO complexes as pharmacodynamic endpoints; however, adherence and patient acceptance have been major barriers due to the burdensome administration (Tam et al., 2003; Entezari et al., 2022).

The clinical pharmacology and chemistry of DFO have motivated multiple improved-delivery strategies: liposomal encapsulation and multivesicular liposome systems to extend half-life, and macromolecular conjugates (e.g., starch or HES carriers) to prolong exposure and shift biodistribution to iron-storage organs; these approaches have demonstrated prolonged circulation, increased urinary iron excretion, and organ accumulation (Jones et al., 2020; Sharpe et al., 2011; Tam et al., 2003). Nevertheless, DFO remains orally inactive and requires parenteral dosing, in contrast to later oral chelators (deferiprone, deferasirox), which have supplanted it in many indications due to ease of administration while sometimes being deployed in combination regimens with DFO to enhance iron removal and cardiac protection via complementary pharmacokinetics and chelation kinetics (Hider & Kong, 2013; Ma et al., 2012).

In ophthalmology and retinal biology, DFO’s evaluation is mixed. On one hand, iron chelation with DFO has shown protective effects in experimental retinal contexts: it reduced retinal ganglion cell death induced by hydrogen peroxide and paraquat in oxidative-stress paradigms, consistent with inhibition of iron-dependent hydroxyl radical production (Rohowetz et al., 2018). In hemorrhagic retinal injury, DFO protected photoreceptor tissues after subretinal blood in animal models, suggesting iron chelation can blunt heme/Fe-driven toxicity in the subretinal space (Song & Dunaief, 2013). In RPE-relevant cell models, DFO mitigated lipid peroxidation, prevented glutathione depletion, decreased Fe2+ accumulation, and preserved viability of ARPE-19 cells under tert-butyl hydroperoxide and blue-light stress, and it enhanced cell survival by modulating antioxidant defense systems (GSH–GPX4 and FSP1–CoQ10–NADH axes) (Zhao et al., 2025). A zinc–DFO complex (Zn/DFO) designed to improve cellular delivery reduced retinal iron content, lipid peroxidation, and oxidative DNA damage, preserved photoreceptor structure, and improved ERG responses in rd10 mice, demonstrating in vivo neuroprotection when systemic penetration is enhanced (Zhao et al., 2025). Ex vivo, DFO decreased histochemically detectable chelatable iron (Perls–DAB) in macular sections from AMD eyes, supporting the feasibility of removing pathologic labile iron in human AMD tissue (He et al., 2007).

On the other hand, DFO has a documented profile of retinal/ocular toxicity in patients receiving systemic therapy: reports include macular and peripheral pigmentary degeneration, impaired night vision, optic neuritis/neuropathy, cataract, ERG amplitude reductions, and EOG light-peak abnormalities, prompting recommendations for ophthalmic surveillance, and leading some experts to conclude that DFO is a dubious candidate for AMD treatment (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021). In RPE culture, repeated DFO exposure was cytotoxic relative to a prochelator control, and clinical series describe deferoxamine retinopathy across pediatric and adult populations, indicating that while iron chelation can be protective in vitro under specific stress conditions, DFO itself can injure RPE and photoreceptors under sustained or high-exposure regimens (Charkoudian et al., 2008; Błasiak et al., 2011). Importantly, DFO’s poor cell permeability and lack of blood–retinal barrier penetration raise practical concerns about achieving therapeutic intra-retinal exposure without systemic toxicity when administered conventionally (Li et al., 2023; Birch et al., 2006). Finally, although iron chelation is mechanistically compelling for retinal degenerations in which iron accumulation and ferroptotic stress participate, application of systemic chelators like DFO to retinal vascular disease and AMD remains at the basic research stage, with unresolved issues including perturbation of systemic/local iron homeostasis and stability of intracellular chelate complexes (Li et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, DFO is a high-affinity FeIII-selective chelator that forms kinetically inert hexacoordinate FeIIIO6 complexes via three hydroxamate ligands, each providing bidentate O,Oʹ coordination; this renders FeIII chemically sequestered, suppresses redox cycling, and prevents iron from entering the Haber–Weiss/Fenton chemistry that generates hydroxyl radicals from superoxide/hydrogen peroxide (Sharpe et al., 2011; Richardson & Poňka, 1998; Hider & Kong, 2013). The FeIII/FeII couple of ferrioxamine is electrochemically very negative (reported around −468 mV vs. NHE), and the complex is redox-inert under physiological conditions, consistent with its ability to quench iron-mediated ROS production rather than participate in it (Hider & Kong, 2013). In biological systems, DFO preferentially binds non-transferrin-bound iron (NTBI), labile iron pools in hepatocytes/macrophages, and low-molecular-weight iron transiting endosomes/lysosomes after transferrin delivery or ferritin degradation; it can mobilize hepatic stores and iron released by reticuloendothelial cells but cannot effectively strip iron from metalloproteins such as hemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochromes, oxidases, catalase, or peroxidases (Hatcher et al., 2009; Richardson & Poňka, 1998; Faa & Crisponi, 1999). The drug is hydrophilic and generally membrane-impermeant; cellular uptake occurs via fluid-phase endocytosis and pinocytosis, leading to enrichment in endosomal/lysosomal compartments, where it chelates lysosomal labile iron, an activity proposed to block lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis—mechanistically relevant to RPE pathobiology (Zhao et al., 2021; Dayani et al., 2004).

In retina and neural tissues, oxidative damage pathways include iron-dependent conversion of H2O2 to •OH via Fenton chemistry; DFO reduces H2O2-induced damage in retinal ganglion cells and protects against paraquat-generated superoxide by depriving upstream Fenton catalysts of accessible iron (Rohowetz et al., 2018). In RPE and photoreceptors, ferroptosis—a regulated cell death driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation—is closely linked to antioxidant systems centered on glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and, independently, on FSP1-mediated ubiquinol regeneration; DFO’s chelation of FeII/FeIII within lysosomes and cytosolic labile pools acts upstream of these pathways to limit lipid hydroperoxide propagation, preserving GSH–GPX4 and FSP1–CoQ10–NADH defense capacity in ARPE-19 under oxidative stimuli (Zhao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023). In systemic contexts, DFO detoxifies NTBI, reduces heme-derived ferryl species, removes high-oxidation-state heme iron, and directly scavenges some radical species, converging on inhibition of membrane lipid oxidation; these activities potentially translate to retinal cells where heme/iron-driven oxidative stress is implicated (Hatcher et al., 2009).

Notably, DFO’s hexadentate size and hydrophilicity restrict direct ferritin iron extraction and limit chelation in tightly protein-bound pools; smaller chelators can penetrate cells more readily and directly efflux ferritin iron, whereas DFO works primarily by intercepting low-molecular-weight iron pools and forming kinetically inert FeIII complexes that are then cleared, often via hepatobiliary or renal routes (Sharpe et al., 2011; Richardson & Poňka, 1998). In inflamed or ischemic tissues, the depletion of accessible iron by DFO can blunt downstream ROS and inflammatory cascades; however, prolonged systemic chelation perturbs metal homeostasis and can deplete essential iron pools in sensitive tissues, underlying some adverse effects including RPE toxicity, auditory neuropathy, and bone dysplasia (Zhao et al., 2021; He et al., 2007).

Expected Effect  
For dry AMD models centered on RPE iron-dependent oxidative stress, the expected pharmacologic effect of DFO is to reduce the labile Fe pool in lysosomes and cytosol, thereby attenuating hydroxyl-radical production from H2O2 and limiting iron-driven lipid peroxidation; operationally, this should decrease oxidative damage readouts and preserve mitochondrial and cellular function in RPE assays (Rohowetz et al., 2018; Li et al., 2023). Specifically:

- Lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis markers: In ARPE-19 cells, DFO has been shown to mitigate lipid peroxidation under oxidant (tBH) and blue-light stress and to preserve viability, consistent with suppression of ferroptotic death; thus, in RPE assays one should observe reductions in lipid peroxidation assays (e.g., BODIPY-C11) and maintenance of GPX4 activity/content, with complementary preservation of the FSP1–CoQ10–NADH axis (Zhao et al., 2025). The same studies indicate decreased Fe2+ accumulation after DFO, reflecting lower catalytic Fe at sites of peroxidation; similar decreases in labile Fe can be measured via calcein quenching or analogous probes (Zhao et al., 2025).

- Oxidative DNA damage: Systemic Zn/DFO reduced retinal oxidative DNA damage in vivo in rd10 mice; although these are not AMD models, the result predicts that in RPE oxidative stress assays DFO will reduce accumulation of oxidative DNA lesions, including those arising in mitochondrial DNA, where iron-dependent ROS can be particularly damaging (Zhao et al., 2025). Ex vivo human AMD maculas showed decreased Perls–DAB staining after DFO chelation, supporting the feasibility of reducing chelatable iron burden and downstream oxidative chemistry in diseased human retina (He et al., 2007).

- Mitochondrial bioenergetics: Preservation of RPE oxygen consumption rate (OCR) is plausible under DFO exposure insofar as DFO limits lipid peroxidation and maintains the reductive antioxidant systems (GSH–GPX4, FSP1–CoQ10) that protect inner-mitochondrial membranes and electron-transport components from iron-dependent oxidative injury; in ARPE-19, DFO improved survival and redox balance under stress, suggesting OCR preservation would accompany reduced peroxidation (Zhao et al., 2025). In retinal ganglion cells, DFO lessened H2O2-induced cell death, indirectly supporting improved mitochondrial tolerance to oxidant stress; similar protection can be anticipated in RPE where iron-dependent ROS compromise mitochondrial DNA and respiratory complexes (Rohowetz et al., 2018).

- Tissue iron fingerprints: In tissue sections or organoids, DFO exposure is expected to decrease Perls–DAB positive iron signal in regions with elevated chelatable iron, as observed in AMD macular tissue; in vivo, systemic DFO does not cross the BRB well, so demonstration of retinal iron removal may require enhanced uptake strategies (e.g., Zn/DFO) or local delivery (Li et al., 2023; He et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2025).

Caveats critical to experimental design include DFO’s lack of blood–retinal barrier penetration and poor cell permeability, which could limit intracellular RPE exposure and lysosomal targeting in vivo after systemic dosing; thus, in vitro or ex vivo assays will show clearer pharmacodynamic effects than systemic models unless delivery is optimized (e.g., Zn-complexation or nanocarriers) (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025; Jones et al., 2020). Additionally, repeated or high-concentration exposure can be cytotoxic to RPE in vitro and has been associated with clinical retinopathy, so dose–exposure optimization and careful toxicity monitoring are required, especially in chronic paradigms (Charkoudian et al., 2008; He et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Rationale strength and translational plausibility. The mechanistic rationale for iron chelation in dry AMD is strong: AMD retinas accumulate chelatable iron, iron catalyzes hydroxyl-radical generation and lipid peroxidation, and iron-dependent ferroptotic stress has been implicated in RPE dysfunction and photoreceptor degeneration (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023). DFO is a high-affinity FeIII chelator with extensive human experience, and it is proven to suppress iron-mediated ROS by forming kinetically inert FeIII complexes, preventing Fenton chemistry (Sharpe et al., 2011; Hider & Kong, 2013). In retinal and RPE models, DFO reduces oxidative injury, limits lipid peroxidation, and preserves cell viability; improved-delivery variants such as Zn/DFO demonstrate in vivo protection of retinal structure and function with concomitant decreases in retinal iron and oxidative DNA damage (Rohowetz et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2025). Ex vivo AMD maculae show DFO-responsive chelatable iron pools, reinforcing target engagement in human disease tissue (He et al., 2007). Mechanistically, enrichment of DFO in lysosomes—an organelle central to RPE iron handling, ferritinophagy, and lipid peroxidation—supports a proximal mode of action relevant to ferroptosis biology in AMD (Zhao et al., 2021).

Key liabilities and translational risks. Despite its compelling mechanism, DFO’s drug properties and ocular safety profile are unfavorable for repurposing in dry AMD without substantial reformulation or targeting:

- Ocular toxicity. DFO has a recognized spectrum of retinal adverse effects in patients, including pigmentary retinopathy, optic neuropathy, ERG/EOG abnormalities, and visual loss; authoritative reviews judge DFO a dubious candidate for AMD because of these safety concerns, and clinical surveillance is recommended when patients receive systemic DFO (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023). RPE toxicity is documented in vitro and clinically across age groups, indicating a narrow retinal therapeutic window under repeated exposure (Błasiak et al., 2011; Charkoudian et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2021).

- Delivery limitations. DFO is hydrophilic, membrane-impermeant, and not blood–neural/retinal barrier penetrant, which undermines retinal exposure after systemic dosing; achieving therapeutic intra-RPE concentrations without systemic toxicity is unlikely with conventional infusion regimens (Li et al., 2023; Birch et al., 2006). The molecule’s very short plasma half-life further complicates exposure in avascular tissues like the outer retina (Sharpe et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2020).

- Systemic chelation risks. Long-term DFO perturbs systemic iron balance, interacts with microbiological iron acquisition in certain pathogens (e.g., Vibrio, S. aureus) that can exploit ferrioxamine, and carries recognized risks of growth retardation, bone changes, and infection, which are unacceptable for a chronic ocular disease with slow progression (Sharpe et al., 2011; Faa & Crisponi, 1999).

- Clinical maturity in ophthalmology. While iron chelators show promise in preclinical retinal models, clinical translation to retinal vascular disease/AMD remains at the basic research stage; challenges include maintaining retinal iron homeostasis, avoiding off-target metal depletion (e.g., Zn2+), and ensuring intracellular chelate stability and localization (Li et al., 2023).

Risk-mitigation strategies and development path. If DFO were to be advanced, development should avoid systemic DFO infusions for dry AMD. Instead:

- Leverage targeted delivery. The Zn/DFO complex that facilitates cellular uptake has shown robust neuroprotection, retinal iron lowering, and oxidative DNA damage reduction in vivo; such conjugate-based or carrier-based strategies could provide intracellular RPE delivery at lower systemic exposure, meriting further evaluation in AMD-relevant models (e.g., light damage, iron-loading, aged mice) with retinal safety readouts (Zhao et al., 2025). Nanocarriers or depot formulations that increase local ocular exposure while minimizing systemic levels could be explored, given DFO’s history of half-life extension in liposomal and multivesicular formulations systemically (Jones et al., 2020; Sharpe et al., 2011).

- Consider chemical alternatives within class. Other chelators with better cell permeability and ocular safety have shown retinal protection without the retinotoxicity seen with DFO; for example, deferiprone protected against iron-induced and light-induced retinal degeneration in multiple mouse models and was not found to be toxic to mouse retina in the contexts studied, suggesting that a more lipophilic, lower-molecular-weight chelator could be a safer starting point than DFO for dry AMD (Song & Dunaief, 2013; Picard et al., 2020).

- Exploit prochelation. Pro-chelators like BSIH that become active only under oxidative conditions were non-toxic with repeated exposure relative to DFO and may offer a way to achieve context-dependent iron chelation within oxidatively stressed RPE while sparing normal iron pools, lowering the risk of retinopathy (Charkoudian et al., 2008).

Decision framework for go/no-go. On balance, while DFO validates the iron-chelation mechanism in retinal tissues and provides useful tool-compound effects in vitro and in ex vivo AMD maculae, its physicochemical properties, delivery constraints, and retinal toxicity profile argue strongly against repurposing native DFO for chronic treatment of dry AMD (Li et al., 2023; He et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2021). The most credible development path for DFO derivatives would require:

- Demonstrating safe, effective RPE delivery with a DFO-based construct (e.g., Zn/DFO or nanocarrier) that reduces labile iron, lipid peroxidation, and oxidative DNA damage in AMD-relevant in vivo models without ERG/EOG or structural toxicity (Zhao et al., 2025).

- Establishing a therapeutic index in the retina with chronic dosing and appropriate safety pharmacology (ERG, OCT, histopathology), given reported human retinopathies on DFO (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023).

- Benchmarking against alternative chelators (e.g., deferiprone) that already demonstrate retinal protection and better permeability/safety in vivo, to justify a DFO-based approach scientifically and clinically (Song & Dunaief, 2013; Picard et al., 2020).

Strengths  
- Mechanistic fit: chelates FeIII with high selectivity and prevents Fenton chemistry; acts in lysosomes where RPE iron and lipid peroxidation intersect with ferroptosis (Sharpe et al., 2011; Hider & Kong, 2013; Zhao et al., 2021).  
- Demonstrated retinal pharmacology: reduces oxidative injury in retinal neurons and RPE, lowers retinal iron and oxidative DNA damage with improved delivery, and removes chelatable iron from AMD macula ex vivo (Rohowetz et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2025; He et al., 2007).  
- Extensive human experience: well-characterized PK/PD, safety liabilities, and clinical management of chelation therapy (Jones et al., 2020; Tam et al., 2003).

Weaknesses  
- Ocular toxicity liability with systemic DFO, including pigmentary retinopathy and electrophysiologic dysfunction, making native DFO a poor risk–benefit prospect for a chronic retinal indication (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021).  
- Poor retinal exposure after systemic dosing due to hydrophilicity and lack of BRB penetration; very short half-life complicates sustained intraocular levels (Li et al., 2023; Birch et al., 2006; Jones et al., 2020).  
- Systemic risks (growth, bone, infection) incompatible with large, elderly dry-AMD populations unless exposure is tightly localized to the eye (Faa & Crisponi, 1999; Sharpe et al., 2011).  
- Field immaturity: iron chelators for retinal disease remain in basic research with unresolved questions about homeostasis and intracellular stability (Li et al., 2023).

Conclusion  
DFO is a mechanistically validated iron chelator with documented ability to reduce iron-driven oxidative injury in retinal systems; however, as a repurposed systemic drug for dry AMD, its delivery barriers and retinal toxicity outweigh potential benefits (Li et al., 2023; He et al., 2007). If iron chelation is pursued for dry AMD within this program, prioritizing better-penetrant, safer chelators (e.g., deferiprone) or context-activated prochelators over native DFO is the higher-probability path; alternately, DFO-based constructs that demonstrably deliver into RPE (e.g., Zn/DFO) with acceptable chronic retinal safety merit targeted preclinical exploration before considering clinical translation (Song & Dunaief, 2013; Charkoudian et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SkQ1 (10‐(6′‐plastoquinonyl)‐decyltriphenylphosphonium) is a fully synthetic, mitochondria‐targeted antioxidant constructed by conjugating a plastoquinone antioxidant moiety with a decyl linker that is covalently bound to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation. The plastoquinone scaffold is derived from the natural quinone found in chloroplasts, known for its potent reactive oxygen species (ROS)–removing capabilities, while the TPP⁺ moiety acts as a highly lipophilic vector that drives selective accumulation within mitochondria due to the inner mitochondrial membrane’s large negative potential. In essence, by combining these two structural elements, SkQ1 is designed to exploit electrophoretic uptake to achieve extremely high concentrations in the mitochondrial matrix where oxidative damage is a critical pathogenic factor. This compound belongs to the broader class of mitochondria‐targeted quinone antioxidants, often referred to collectively as “SkQ” compounds. Molecules in this class were originally proposed and developed by Skulachev and colleagues, and they have been used experimentally to achieve mitochondrial protection in contexts ranging from ischemia–reperfusion injury and neurodegeneration to aging‐associated dysfunctions (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). The rational design strategy behind SkQ1—linking a redox‐active quinone to a lipophilic cation—has also inspired the development of analogous compounds such as SkQR1, MitoQ, and related derivatives that are being explored for a variety of biomedical applications.

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of SkQ1, as well as that of its parent class of mitochondria‐targeted antioxidants, is extensive and spans multiple preclinical and early clinical studies. In numerous in vitro and in vivo models, SkQ1 has demonstrated robust antioxidant effects. For example, it has been shown to protect mitochondria and cellular membranes against lipid peroxidation—key pathogenic processes underlying aging and degenerative diseases—at nanomolar concentrations. In various rodent models, including studies in OXYS rats (a strain that mimics accelerated senescence), chronic administration of SkQ1 prevented or reversed age‐related abnormalities such as cataract, retinopathy, and even systemic markers of mitochondrial dysfunction (Wanagat et al., 2010; Belenichev et al., 2024; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Moreover, veterinary and preclinical studies have documented SkQ1’s ability to increase lifespan and delay the onset of age‐linked phenotypes, including osteoporosis, immune decline, and neurodegeneration (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Weissig, 2020). Within the ocular field, SkQ1 has been specifically formulated as eye drops—marketed in certain regions under the trade name Visomitin—to treat dry eye syndrome. These formulations have passed early phase safety trials and have now seen clinical use in Russia. Although SkQ1 has not yet been directly trialed in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or geographic atrophy, its documented efficacy in protecting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in animal models and its ability to improve electrophysiological outcomes (such as preserved electroretinography [ERG] responses) support its potential repurposing for AMD (Gueven et al., 2017; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). In several ocular studies in both rodent and primate models, topical administration of SkQ1 has demonstrated the capacity to deliver the drug to the posterior segment with minimal systemic exposure, reducing characteristics like RPE vacuolization and preserving overall retinal function (Weissig, 2020; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). The extensive preclinical and limited clinical history of SkQ1 in ocular applications—most notably in dry-eye syndrome and animal models of retinal degeneration—suggests that the therapeutic candidate has a solid track record of mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction in tissues exposed to chronic oxidative stress, a pathophysiological component also seen in dry AMD (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Wanagat et al., 2010).

Mechanism of Action:  
SkQ1 exerts its biological effects via multiple interrelated molecular mechanisms that center on its ability to accumulate rapidly within mitochondria and scavenge deleterious ROS. The TPP⁺ portion of the molecule, owing to its delocalized positive charge and high lipophilicity, drives the electrophoretic uptake of SkQ1 into the mitochondrial matrix along the steep negative membrane potential (Δψm) that is inherent to healthy mitochondria (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Once localized within these organelles, the plastoquinone group is poised to participate in redox cycling: it is reversibly reduced—often by components of the electron transport chain such as complex III—and subsequently reacts with ROS such as superoxide (O₂•⁻) and lipid peroxyl radicals to convert them into less reactive species (Lukashev et al., 2014; Weissig, 2020). Importantly, the antioxidant effect of SkQ1 is not a one-off reaction; rather, it is “rechargeable,” meaning that following its oxidation by ROS, the quinone moiety can be reduced again, thereby enabling repeated cycles of detoxification. This rechargeable mechanism differentiates SkQ1 from conventional antioxidants that are consumed irreversibly during redox reactions. Additionally, SkQ1 has been shown to form complexes with cardiolipin—a key phospholipid in the inner mitochondrial membrane—and thereby stabilize the membrane structure against peroxidation. Some studies also suggest that the TPP⁺ component might mediate a mild uncoupling effect by facilitating proton translocation (often in conjunction with interacting with fatty acid anions), which can reduce mitochondrial ROS generation by dissipating excessive inner membrane potential under conditions of oxidative overload (Lukashev et al., 2014; Weissig, 2020; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). This dual mechanism of direct ROS scavenging combined with membrane stabilizing and modest uncoupling effects contributes to the preservation of Δψm and the overall integrity of mitochondrial bioenergetics. In RPE cells stressed by chronic photo-oxidative insult, these properties would translate into effective mitigation of oxidative damage, thereby preventing the collapse of mitochondrial membrane potential—a key event that precipitates cell dysfunction and death in dry AMD (Muraleva et al., 2019; Olovnikov et al., n.d.).

Expected Effect:  
The proposed hypothesis for repurposing SkQ1 in dry age-related macular degeneration is predicated on its capacity to target RPE mitochondria and to neutralize both superoxide radicals and lipid peroxyl radicals that accumulate under conditions of chronic light-induced oxidative stress. In vitro assays using ARPE-19 cells have demonstrated that nanomolar concentrations of SkQ1 elicit potent antioxidant responses—as measured by decreases in fluorescence with DCFDA (a marker of ROS) and stabilization of mitochondrial membrane potential via JC-1 assays—indicating that the compound readily scavenges ocular ROS at very low doses (Gueven et al., 2017; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). This antioxidant activity is expected to prevent or delay the loss of Δψm, a critical parameter for cell survival and function, particularly in RPE cells where mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in the pathogenesis of drusen formation and geographic atrophy in dry AMD. In vivo, studies conducted in models such as OXYS rats have shown that chronic administration of SkQ1 not only reduces oxidative markers in mitochondrial membranes (e.g., decreasing levels of malondialdehyde and hydroxynonenal-adducts) but also normalizes cardiolipin content and fatty acid composition—key factors involved in the proper assembly and turnover of respiratory complexes (Wanagat et al., 2010; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Moreover, macaque studies have indicated that topical SkQ1 eye drops achieve significant drug levels in the posterior segment although the dosing remains in the nanomolar range, leading to improvements in ERG function and reduced RPE vacuolization without evidence of systemic toxicity (Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Weissig, 2020). At the molecular level, the expected effect in RPE cells would be a sustained antioxidant environment that preserves mitochondrial function through two primary pathways: first, by directly quenching damaging ROS that would otherwise trigger mitochondrial DNA damage and lipid peroxidation; and second, by maintaining the structural integrity of mitochondrial membranes via stabilization of cardiolipin and prevention of excessive proton leakage. Given that RPE cells express the full complement of mitochondrial electron transport chain proteins, including complex III which is capable of reducing SkQ1 to its active form, these cells are ideal targets for the drug’s mechanism (Muraleva et al., 2019; Olovnikov et al., n.d.). Consequently, when used as a therapeutic intervention in dry AMD, SkQ1 is expected to mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction associated with drusen accumulation and, in turn, slow or potentially reverse the progression of geographic atrophy—one of the major sight-threatening complications of the disease.

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, SkQ1 represents a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration based on a robust foundation of molecular design, preclinical efficacy, and established ocular safety. One of the major strengths of SkQ1 lies in its rational design: as a rechargeable, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant, it overcomes limitations faced by conventional antioxidants that lack mitochondrial specificity. The ability of the TPP⁺ moiety to drive precise mitochondrial accumulation ensures that the compound is concentrated at the site of maximal ROS production, while its plastoquinone component provides potent scavenging of both superoxide and lipid peroxyl radicals. This dual functionality not only neutralizes damaging oxidative species but also supports mitochondrial membrane integrity by stabilizing cardiolipin and potentially mitigating excessive proton leakage. Such a mechanism is particularly relevant to RPE cells, where chronic photo-oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Lukashev et al., 2014).

Another significant advantage is the extensive preclinical and early clinical evidence supporting SkQ1’s efficacy in ocular applications. Its use in animal models—spanning species from rodents to macaques—has consistently shown protective effects on retinal structure and function, including preservation of ERG responses and reduced vacuolization of the RPE. Furthermore, the successful clinical trials for dry eye syndrome confirm that topical administration of SkQ1 is not only efficacious but also well-tolerated in humans, thereby reducing the risk related to ocular drug delivery and systemic exposure (Gueven et al., 2017; Weissig, 2020; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

Nevertheless, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be carefully weighed. One concern is the dose-dependent behavior of SkQ1. While nanomolar concentrations are effective and safe, there is evidence that at higher concentrations, the molecule can exhibit prooxidant or detergent-like effects—leading to membrane disruption or uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation. This narrow window between the antioxidant and prooxidant activities necessitates rigorous control of dosing in clinical settings to avoid inadvertent exacerbation of mitochondrial dysfunction (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). Additionally, while many studies have focused on the compound’s ability to protect against acute oxidative insults, the etiology of dry AMD is multifactorial and chronic. Key endpoints such as changes in drusen load, progression of geographic atrophy, and improvements in visual function would need to be monitored over extended periods. Moreover, given that oxidative stress and inflammation are part of an intricate network of pathological events in dry AMD, combination therapies that address multiple targets may ultimately yield more significant benefits than a single-agent approach (Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Gueven et al., 2017).

From a pharmacokinetic perspective, the selective accumulation of SkQ1 in the mitochondria is a highly attractive feature, as it maximizes local drug concentrations while minimizing systemic exposure and potential off-target effects. This is especially critical for ocular applications, where local delivery via eye drops can achieve high retinal levels with minimal systemic absorption. Nonetheless, formulation stability, light sensitivity, and proper storage conditions are factors that must be optimized for successful commercial development (Weissig, 2020; Gueven et al., 2017; Ji et al., 2021).

In aggregate, the overall evaluation of SkQ1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic. The compound’s design as a mitochondria-targeted, rechargeable antioxidant offers compelling advantages in addressing mitochondrial dysfunction—a key element in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its ability to protect RPE cells, preserve mitochondrial membrane potential, and improve retinal function, while early clinical studies in related ocular conditions confirm its safety profile for topical administration. However, due diligence is warranted to establish the optimal dosing regimen that maximizes beneficial antioxidant effects while avoiding potential prooxidant toxicity. Additionally, further rigorous clinical trials specifically targeting dry AMD endpoints are necessary to confirm that the promising outcomes observed in animal studies translate into measurable clinical benefit in patients with geographic atrophy (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Gueven et al., 2017; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Wanagat et al., 2010; Weissig, 2020).

Given the comprehensive body of work underpinning the mechanism of action, the established track record in various preclinical ocular models, and the supporting data from human dry-eye trials, SkQ1 appears to have significant potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its unique targeting of mitochondria—particularly within RPE cells—and its capacity to prevent ROS-induced mitochondrial collapse make it especially well-suited to counteract the chronic photo-oxidative stress that characterizes this disease. The next steps for validating SkQ1 in this indication should include well-designed in vivo studies in AMD-relevant animal models, followed by early phase clinical trials with careful dose-escalation studies and robust assessment of retinal morphology and function. Overall, SkQ1 stands out as a promising therapeutic candidate that merits further investigation within our drug development pipeline (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Olovnikov et al., n.d.; Weissig, 2020; Gueven et al., 2017; Wanagat et al., 2010).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Omaveloxolone (RTA 408) is a semi-synthetic pentacyclic triterpenoid of the cyanoenone (oleanane-derived) chemical class rationally designed to activate the Keap1–Nrf2 pathway by electrophilic modification of redox-sensitive cysteine residues on Keap1, most prominently Cys151 (the key “sensor” cysteine for this chemotype) (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2016). Mechanistically, omaveloxolone forms a covalent adduct with KEAP1 that prevents CUL3–KEAP1–mediated ubiquitination and degradation of Nrf2, thereby allowing Nrf2 stabilization, nuclear translocation, and transcriptional activation via antioxidant response elements (AREs) (Liu et al., 2016; Cai et al., 2021; Bellezza, 2018). In human systems, omaveloxolone induces canonical Nrf2 target genes that collectively bolster mitochondrial and cytosolic antioxidant defenses, including NQO1, HO-1, SOD2, catalase, glutaredoxin-1 (Grx1), and thioredoxin-1 (Trx1) (Liu et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2021).

Discovery and translational development of omaveloxolone followed extensive preclinical work with synthetic triterpenoids showing robust induction of the phase 2 response and protection against oxidant and inflammatory stress in vitro and in vivo, and early first-in-human experience with this class (e.g., bardoxolone methyl) helped establish on-target pharmacology while also highlighting class-specific safety considerations that informed subsequent designs (e.g., exclusion of patients with incipient heart failure risk in kidney indications) (Nakagami, 2016; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic programs in nonhuman primates and humans show that oral omaveloxolone is bioavailable, exhibits dose-proportional increases in Cmax and AUC, and reaches concentrations capable of inducing Nrf2 target genes in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and multiple tissues; tissue distribution studies in cynomolgus monkeys demonstrated exposure slightly above contemporaneous plasma levels in liver, lung, and brain with measurable mRNA induction of canonical Nrf2 targets after repeat dosing (Reisman et al., 2019). In human clinical development, omaveloxolone advanced through a first-in-human oncology study, a dose-ranging Phase 2 program (MOXIe Part 1) in Friedreich ataxia (FA) with clear pharmacodynamic biomarker changes (e.g., ferritin and GGT) and dose/exposure–response relationships, and a registrational, placebo-controlled, 48-week trial (MOXIe Part 2) showing statistically significant improvement in neurological function by mFARS with an acceptable safety profile characterized principally by reversible transaminase elevations, headaches, nausea, and fatigue (Creelan et al., 2017; Lynch et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2021).

This pharmacology is intrinsically aligned with a central pathophysiologic axis in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD): cumulative oxidative stress, sustained mitochondrial dysfunction with increased mtROS, impaired mitophagy, and chronic innate/adaptive inflammation in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and neighboring tissues (Bellezza, 2018; Jarrett & Boulton, 2012). The RPE is enriched in mitochondria and relies on robust antioxidant systems to manage high ROS fluxes from phagocytosis and photo-oxidative challenges; Nrf2 is widely recognized as the “master” antioxidant transcription factor in RPE, transcriptionally controlling the expression of SODs (including mitochondrial SOD2), catalase, NQO1, HO-1, glutathione synthesis enzymes, and thiol-redox enzymes (Trx1/Grx1) (Bellezza, 2018; Lambros & Plafker, 2016; Camelo, 2025). Deficiency of Nrf2 or the mitochondrial SOD2 enzyme in mouse retina/RPE produces AMD-like phenotypes, while exogenous Nrf2 activation in ocular models protects RPE and retinal neurons from oxidative injury, reduces inflammation, and supports mitochondrial homeostasis (Lambros & Plafker, 2016; Jarrett & Boulton, 2012; Chen et al., 2023). Against this mechanistic backdrop, the specific demonstration that omaveloxolone protects primary human RPE from H₂O₂-induced injury via Nrf2—at nanomolar concentrations—by upregulating SOD2, NQO1, HO-1, catalase, Grx1 and Trx1, preserving GSH, lowering ROS, and reducing apoptosis is directly relevant to dry AMD biology (Liu et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History  
Class-wide experience. Cyanoenone triterpenoids have been deployed across multiple preclinical disease models characterized by oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammation, with consistent activation of NRF2 target genes and functional improvements in biochemical and physiologic endpoints. For example, omaveloxolone improved renal function and reduced neutrophil infiltration, apoptosis, ROS production, and oxidative injury in renal ischemia–reperfusion models in an Nrf2-dependent manner, and produced sustained neuroprotection in a rat status epilepticus model with concordant increases in tissue glutathione and ATP (Reisman et al., 2019). These effects map onto the known Nrf2 program (e.g., induction of Nqo1, Gsr, Gclc; increased glutathione) and translate to primates and humans as evidenced by PBMC/tissue gene induction and serum biomarkers (ferritin, GGT) (Reisman et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2019).

First-in-human and oncology safety. In a first-in-human trial in advanced solid tumors, once-daily oral omaveloxolone (2.5–15 mg) was rapidly absorbed (Tmax 2–4 h), exhibited dose-proportional exposure, and had estimated terminal half-lives of ∼9 h on day 1 increasing to ∼20 h by day 28; across a mean exposure of 87 days, no dose-limiting toxicities were observed, adverse events were typically mild/moderate, and increases in select Nrf2 targets were measured in PBMCs (Creelan et al., 2017). The same report and related write-up noted no dose-limiting toxicities attributable to drug, a lack of QTc prolongation, and frequent low-grade laboratory changes (e.g., alkaline phosphatase elevations, anemia) in a small cohort, with PBMC Nrf2 target-gene mRNA serving as a primary pharmacodynamic target-engagement endpoint (Creelan et al., 2017).

Friedreich ataxia (FA) clinical development. Omaveloxolone has been evaluated extensively in FA, a neurodegenerative disease with depressed Nrf2 signaling and mitochondrial dysfunction. In MOXIe Part 1 (12-week, dose-ranging 2.5–300 mg/day), exposure was dose-proportional and PD changes in serum ferritin and GGT were maximal in the 80–160 mg/day range, congruent with improved neurological mFARS scores (placebo-corrected trends) and consistent with an exposure window for maximal biological activity; at 300 mg/day, a nonmonotonic dose–response with reduced Nrf2/mitochondrial effects was observed, suggesting a mid-dose “sweet spot” (Lynch et al., 2019). In MOXIe Part 2, patients treated with 150 mg/day for 48 weeks showed statistically significant improvement in mFARS relative to placebo; safety was acceptable with transient aminotransferase elevations unaccompanied by bilirubin increases, and common adverse events included headache, nausea, and fatigue (Lynch et al., 2021). PK data compiled from FA cohorts show mean terminal half-lives of ∼15–21 h at 80–160 mg/day (supporting once-daily dosing), Cmax in a range predicted by monkey PBMC EC50s to robustly induce Nrf2 targets, and interpatient variability of ∼31–43% for AUC/Cmax (Reisman et al., 2019). Translationally, FA patient biomarkers and platelet isotopologue metabolites indicated dose-dependent modulation of Nrf2-responsive targets (e.g., ferritin, GGT; decreased CK at 80–160 mg) and specific effects on fatty-acid–linked mitochondrial metabolism (reduced ¹³C-palmitate to HMG-CoA conversions with no effect on ¹³C-glucose) (Lynch et al., 2019).

Ophthalmic development context. Within ophthalmology, omaveloxolone has entered topical/ocular clinical testing (e.g., an ophthalmic suspension evaluated for prevention of corneal endothelial cell loss and ocular inflammation post-cataract surgery), and RTA 408 lotions/creams have shown Nrf2 target-gene induction in human skin punch biopsies, demonstrating tissue-level target engagement in humans via local administration (Cheng et al., 2021; Creelan et al., 2017). Although omaveloxolone has not been tested clinically in dry AMD to date, triterpenoid Nrf2 activators (including omaveloxolone) have reproducibly protected human RPE in vitro against oxidative insults (Liu et al., 2016), and related CDDO-derived analogues (e.g., RS9) have improved retinal antioxidant gene expression and function in multiple retinal models (Liu et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2021).

Use in AMD or similar diseases. There are no published clinical studies of omaveloxolone in dry AMD; however, the drug exhibits precisely the mechanistic activities sought for RPE protection in AMD—Nrf2 activation and induction of SOD2/NQO1/HO-1, preservation of glutathione and antioxidant enzyme activities, and suppression of oxidative injury—in primary human RPE models (Liu et al., 2016). Supportive disease-proximal validation comes from a robust literature demonstrating that genetic loss of Nrf2 or SOD2 in retinal tissues produces AMD-like pathology, and that pharmacologic or genetic Nrf2 activation protects RPE and retina in models of oxidative stress, ischemia–reperfusion injury, and diabetic retinopathy (Lambros & Plafker, 2016; Jarrett & Boulton, 2012; Zhang et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
Primary target: Keap1 Cys151 and Nrf2 stabilization. Omaveloxolone engages KEAP1 through covalent modification of Cys151, which is the electro-sensitive sensor residue controlling the high-affinity ETGE “hinge” and low-affinity DLG “latch” interactions that dock NRF2 to KEAP1 for CUL3-mediated ubiquitination under basal redox states (Cai et al., 2021; Reisman et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2016). Electrophilic adduction at KEAP1 cysteines inhibits the E3 ligase function, stabilizes Nrf2, promotes Ser40 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation, and increases binding of Nrf2–Maf heterodimers to AREs, resulting in transcriptional activation of a broad network of cytoprotective genes (estimated in the hundreds) that neutralize ROS, maintain glutathione and thioredoxin pools, and reprogram metabolism toward redox homeostasis (Das & Imanishi, 2022; Cai et al., 2021; Bellezza, 2018). In primates, quantitative PK/PD modeling relating plasma concentration to PBMC mRNA induction of canonical Nrf2 targets yielded EC50s on the order of tens of ng/mL, permitting translational projection of human exposures likely to achieve robust target engagement; observed FA patient Cmax values at 80–160–300 mg overlapped these EC50 ranges, and tissue distribution studies documented meaningful drug levels in liver, lung, and brain with dose-dependent mRNA induction in those tissues (Reisman et al., 2019).

Downstream antioxidant and mitochondrial programs in RPE. In primary human RPE, nanomolar omaveloxolone activated Nrf2 and increased expression and activity of multiple downstream antioxidant enzymes: HO-1 (heme catabolism; biliverdin/bilirubin production), NQO1 (two-electron reductase that supports NADPH-dependent detoxification), SOD2 (mitochondrial matrix superoxide dismutase), catalase (peroxisomal H₂O₂ scavenger), Grx1 and Trx1 (thiol-disulfide oxidoreductases for protein deglutathionylation/disulfide reduction) (Liu et al., 2016). Functionally, omaveloxolone preserved intracellular GSH under oxidative challenge, attenuated GSSG accumulation and protein glutathionylation, and restored enzyme activity of NQO1, Grx1, and Trx1 following H₂O₂ exposure (Liu et al., 2016). By lowering net ROS and preventing depletion/inactivation of thiol-redox systems, omaveloxolone reduced Bax activation and caspase-3 cleavage while increasing Bcl-2, leading to protection against apoptosis and necrosis in RPE; Nrf2 siRNA abrogated these effects, establishing on-target dependence (Liu et al., 2016).

Inflammation and NF-κB/NOS axes. Triterpenoid NRF2 activators can also influence inflammatory signaling. Omaveloxolone suppressed interferon-γ–mediated nitric oxide signaling in macrophages at nanomolar concentrations and reduced nitrotyrosine production in myeloid-derived suppressor cells and tumor xenografts, pointing to a mechanism that diminishes RNS/ROS-coupled inflammatory tone (Creelan et al., 2017). More broadly, Nrf2 activation antagonizes inflammation by mitigating ROS-dependent NLRP3 inflammasome activation and by competing with NF-κB for limiting transcriptional co-activators (e.g., CBP/p300), ultimately blunting IL-6 and IL-1β transcription; in the triterpenoid class, agents have been shown to modulate both NRF2 and NF-κB in cells and models (Camelo, 2025; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although direct inhibition of NF-κB by omaveloxolone in human RPE has not been explicitly demonstrated in the provided sources, multiple reviews and trial descriptions describe omaveloxolone as reducing inflammatory mediators (e.g., TNF-α, IL-6) and blocking KEAP1-mediated NF-κB proinflammatory signaling, consistent with the hypothesized dual-action (Clay et al., 2019; Madsen et al., 2020).

Mitochondrial function and disease-relevant cells. In FA-relevant neuronal and fibroblast systems, omaveloxolone restored mitochondrial OXPHOS complex readouts, reduced mitochondrial ROS, prevented lipid peroxidation, increased cellular glutathione, and elevated Nrf2 transcript/protein with increased NQO1, HO-1, and GCL expression at low nanomolar concentrations, indicating a direct link from KEAP1–NRF2 engagement to improved mitochondrial redox and bioenergetic parameters (Tiberi et al., 2023). Platelet isotopologue analyses in FA patients showed reduced conversion of ¹³C-palmitate to HMG-CoA with increasing omaveloxolone dose and no effect on ¹³C-glucose metabolism, consistent with modulation of fatty-acid–linked mitochondrial metabolism by Nrf2 activation in human tissues (Lynch et al., 2019).

Pharmacokinetics, target engagement, and dose–response. Human oral PK shows rapid absorption (Tmax ≈ 1–3.5 h), dose-proportional exposure, and an apparent terminal half-life of ∼15–21 h at 80–160 mg supporting once-daily administration; in the oncology first-in-human trial Tmax was 2–4 h with terminal half-life ranging from ∼9–20 h between day 1 and day 28, consistent with accumulation to steady state across 28-day cycles (Reisman et al., 2019; Creelan et al., 2017). Monotonicity in Nrf2/mitochondrial biomarker response appears dose-limited at very high exposure; in FA, 300 mg/day fell into a concentration range where reduced Nrf2 induction and mitochondrial function were observed in vitro and clinical PD/functional signals were attenuated relative to 80–160 mg (Lynch et al., 2019). Translational PK/PD alignment from primate PBMC EC50s predicts robust induction of canonical Nrf2 targets at human Cmax achieved with ≥ 80 mg dosing, which is consistent with the observed FA biomarker changes and clinical signals in the mid-dose range (Reisman et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2019).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level expectations in RPE oxidative stress models. The candidate’s cell-autonomous RPE mechanism predicts that, in primary human RPE or iPSC-RPE assays challenged with oxidants (e.g., H₂O₂, t-BHP, photo-oxidative blue light models), omaveloxolone pretreatment at low nanomolar concentrations will:  
- Increase Nrf2 nuclear translocation and upregulate canonical ARE-driven targets including SOD2, NQO1, HO-1, catalase, Grx1, and Trx1, as measured by mRNA, protein, and enzyme activity assays (Liu et al., 2016).  
- Preserve cellular thiol redox status by elevating intracellular GSH, reducing GSSG accumulation, and decreasing protein glutathionylation under oxidative challenge (Liu et al., 2016).  
- Reduce total and mitochondrial ROS burden (by virtue of increased SOD2 and augmented detoxifying capacity), attenuate lipid peroxidation, and maintain activity of antioxidant enzymes otherwise suppressed by oxidant exposure (NQO1, Grx1, Trx1) (Liu et al., 2016).  
- Decrease apoptosis/necrosis readouts (Annexin V/PI, caspase-3 cleavage), with shifts in Bax/Bcl-2 consistent with anti-apoptotic signaling downstream of restored redox homeostasis (Liu et al., 2016).

The RPE expresses all of the above antioxidant effectors (SOD2, NQO1, HO-1, catalase, Grx1, Trx1), and their induction by omaveloxolone has been demonstrated in primary human RPE, making these robust PD endpoints for in vitro validation and mechanistic confirmation of the compound in the exact cell type relevant to dry AMD (Liu et al., 2016). Given compelling preclinical evidence in FA models, we further expect improved mitochondrial bioenergetics (Δψm preservation/OXPHOS complex integrity) and reduced mtROS in RPE with omaveloxolone, although direct Δψm measurements have not been published in RPE for this compound; these endpoints are supported by neuronal/fibroblast data and are mechanistically consistent with Nrf2-driven SOD2/antioxidant induction (Tiberi et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2016).

Inflammation-modulating effects in RPE and retinal milieu. In RPE cultures or co-cultures exposed to pro-inflammatory cytokines or oxidative adducts (e.g., 4-HNE, MDA, CEP), omaveloxolone is expected to reduce ROS-augmented NF-κB–dependent cytokine transcription indirectly via rebalancing redox tone and directly via the triterpenoid class’s interference with NF-κB axes (competition for transcriptional cofactors and proposed KEAP1-linked NF-κB modulation), with measurable decreases in IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α transcription and nitrosative stress markers in settings where these are ROS-coupled (Camelo, 2025; Clay et al., 2019; Madsen et al., 2020; Creelan et al., 2017). In macrophage or microglia co-culture systems, decreased nitrotyrosine and nitric oxide synthase output would be anticipated, consistent with suppression of interferon-γ–driven NO signaling observed at low concentrations (Creelan et al., 2017). These effects target a recognized feed-forward loop in dry AMD in which oxidative damage and inflammatory signaling reciprocally amplify RPE injury (Bellezza, 2018; Camelo, 2025).

In vivo translational expectations and biomarker strategy. For systemic administration, PBMC Nrf2 target mRNA induction has been validated as a sensitive peripheral biomarker for omaveloxolone in primates and humans and should be incorporated as a noninvasive PD readout, with serum ferritin and GGT as additional systemic markers of Nrf2 activation shown to respond in the 80–160 mg range (Reisman et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2019). Tissue-level target engagement in the eye could be assessed in early clinical studies by surrogate accessible tissues (e.g., skin punch biopsy Nrf2 target induction following topical administration as precedent), tears or conjunctival impression cytology for transcript biomarkers, and functional retinal endpoints; preclinical monkey data showing dose-dependent induction of Nrf2 targets in liver/lung/brain establish that tissue-level engagement is achievable, though ocular distribution has not been reported and remains a data gap (Reisman et al., 2019; Creelan et al., 2017). For local ocular delivery, existing clinical experience with RTA 408 ophthalmic preparations and demonstrated Nrf2 target-gene induction in human skin biopsies support feasibility of achieving tissue PD in the eye without systemic exposure (Cheng et al., 2021; Creelan et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic precision for AMD biology. The omaveloxolone mechanism—KEAP1 Cys151 modification → Nrf2 stabilization and ARE-driven transcription—directly addresses core deficits in dry AMD: inadequate antioxidant/mitochondrial defenses and redox-driven inflammation in RPE. Upregulation of SOD2, NQO1, HO-1, catalase, and thiol-redox systems in primary human RPE cells has been demonstrated for omaveloxolone at nanomolar potency with rigorous Nrf2-dependence, and these are precisely the enzymes/activities required to reduce mtROS and protect the high-demand RPE from oxidative apoptosis/necrosis (Liu et al., 2016; Bellezza, 2018; Camelo, 2025).  
- Human translational pharmacology. Oral PK is favorable for chronic dosing (once-daily half-life ∼15–21 h at efficacious exposures), with dose-proportional exposure and well-established PD biomarkers (PBMC Nrf2 transcripts; serum ferritin/GGT) that map to mid-dose ranges yielding clinical signals in FA; primate PK/PD modeling provides concentration–effect relationships for Nrf2 targets that align with human Cmax at 80–160 mg (Reisman et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2019).  
- Tissue distribution and target engagement in vivo. In cynomolgus monkeys, omaveloxolone distributed to major organs, with tissue drug levels at or above plasma and induction of canonical Nrf2 targets in liver and lung; dose-related trends were present in brain, suggesting CNS permeability and supporting the premise of tissue-level engagement beyond blood in primates (Reisman et al., 2019). Topical formulations (RTA 408 lotion/ophthalmic suspension) have induced Nrf2 targets in human skin and advanced into ocular clinical studies, de-risking local ocular delivery modalities for future AMD programs (Creelan et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2021).  
- Clinical proof of mechanism and safety in a mitochondrial disease. In FA, omaveloxolone produced consistent PD biomarker activation (ferritin↑, GGT changes; CK↓ at 80–160 mg), functional improvement (mFARS benefit at 150–160 mg), and tolerability suitable for long-term administration (48 weeks), with reversible transaminase elevations as the principal laboratory signal; importantly, 300 mg exposures showed attenuated biologic responses, informing an exposure window for maximal effect (Lynch et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2021).  
- Anti-inflammatory potential that intersects AMD pathophysiology. Nrf2 activation reduces ROS-dependent inflammasome activation and competes with NF-κB for co-activators; omaveloxolone and its class decrease nitrosative stress signaling and inflammatory mediators in immune cells and models, a mechanistic complement to antioxidant effects in RPE that is germane to dry AMD’s chronic para-inflammation (Camelo, 2025; Creelan et al., 2017; Clay et al., 2019; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

Limitations and risks  
- Absence of ocular pharmacokinetics and retinal tissue PD. No data currently demonstrate omaveloxolone exposure in retina/RPE after systemic dosing or local ophthalmic administration in humans; primate tissue distribution did not include ocular tissues in the reported studies, and brain induction was less robust than peripheral organs, raising questions about effective exposure in ocular compartments with systemic dosing (Reisman et al., 2019). While RTA 408 ophthalmic formulations have entered clinical testing, target engagement in human ocular tissues has not been published (Cheng et al., 2021).  
- Clinical evidence gap in AMD. There are no clinical data in dry AMD populations; pathophysiologic rationale is strong, but translation from FA and preclinical RPE models requires careful dose/exposure selection, PD verification in ocular tissues, and demonstration of structural/functional benefit (e.g., slowing GA growth), none of which are available to date in the provided corpus (Lynch et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2016).  
- Nonmonotonic dose–response at high exposure. FA data indicate that very high exposures (e.g., 300 mg/day) can reduce Nrf2 induction/mitochondrial effects, implying a therapeutic window that must be honored to avoid loss of efficacy or off-target effects; AMD trials will need to target mid-dose ranges (80–160 mg) or use local ocular delivery to minimize systemic exposure while maximizing ocular PD (Lynch et al., 2019).  
- Safety nuances in an elderly population. Although omaveloxolone has an acceptable safety profile in FA and oncology settings (no DLTs up to 15 mg in oncology; reversible ALT/AST elevations in FA), dry AMD patients are older with comorbidities; the triterpenoid class has historical cardiovascular risk signals (bardoxolone methyl in CKD), mandating conservative exclusion criteria and vigilant monitoring, particularly if systemic dosing is pursued (Creelan et al., 2017; Cuadrado et al., 2019).  
- Inflammatory pathway claims in RPE remain inferential. While Nrf2 activation is anti-inflammatory, and omaveloxolone suppresses NO/iNOS/nitrotyrosine signaling in myeloid cells, direct evidence of NF-κB pathway repression by omaveloxolone in human RPE is not established in the cited literature; anti-inflammatory benefits in retinal tissues should be verified in appropriate assays (Creelan et al., 2017; Clay et al., 2019; Madsen et al., 2020).

Programmatic recommendations  
- Preclinical ocular PK/PD. Define ocular exposure and tissue PD after systemic and topical dosing in relevant species. For systemic dosing, quantify omaveloxolone in choroid/RPE/retina and assay canonical Nrf2 targets (Nqo1, Hmox1, Srxn1, Txnrd1, Gsr) to confirm dose-dependent tissue engagement; for topical dosing, leverage the human skin precedent (punch biopsy Nrf2 induction) to design ocular surface/conjunctival PD sampling in early clinical studies (Reisman et al., 2019; Creelan et al., 2017).  
- RPE-centric PD biomarker panel. In vitro and ex vivo human RPE studies should be used to finalize a PD panel including SOD2, NQO1, HO-1, catalase, Grx1, Trx1 mRNA/protein/activity, GSH/GSSG ratios, protein glutathionylation, and apoptosis markers, all of which were responsive to omaveloxolone in primary human RPE (Liu et al., 2016).  
- Dose selection anchored to translational PK/PD. For systemic programs, target exposures corresponding to primate PBMC EC50s and FA mid-dose ranges (80–160 mg) that maximize Nrf2 target induction while avoiding the high-exposure attenuation seen at 300 mg; in early AMD studies, incorporate PBMC Nrf2 gene induction, serum ferritin/GGT, and potentially CK as systemic PD anchors (Reisman et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2019).  
- Anti-inflammatory endpoints. In RPE and myeloid co-cultures, quantify NF-κB–dependent cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and nitrosative stress readouts (iNOS, nitrotyrosine) under oxidative/cytokine challenge with omaveloxolone to confirm expected anti-inflammatory effects; these are relevant given RNS/ROS-driven inflammation in AMD (Creelan et al., 2017; Camelo, 2025).  
- Clinical path. Consider a two-pronged strategy: (i) a topical ocular formulation to deliver drug to RPE/retina with minimal systemic exposure, justified by human skin PD activation and existing ocular formulation experience; (ii) a systemic oral approach with rigorous safety surveillance and mid-dose targeting, using PBMC/serum PD to confirm target engagement while ocular PD is established with surrogate sampling and imaging endpoints. The topical path may be particularly attractive to de-risk systemic safety in an elderly AMD population (Cheng et al., 2021; Creelan et al., 2017; Lynch et al., 2021).

Conclusion  
The totality of mechanistic, cellular, primate, and human clinical pharmacology evidence indicates that omaveloxolone’s core pharmacology—potent Nrf2 activation via KEAP1 Cys151 engagement, coupled with class-associated anti-inflammatory actions—maps directly onto the pathobiology of dry AMD. In primary human RPE, omaveloxolone at nanomolar concentrations induces mitochondrial and cytosolic antioxidant systems (SOD2, NQO1, HO-1, catalase, Grx1, Trx1), preserves GSH and redox enzyme activities, lowers ROS, and prevents apoptosis in an Nrf2-dependent manner, establishing precise on-target activity in the cell type central to AMD (Liu et al., 2016). Clinical development in FA demonstrates that systemic exposures can be achieved safely with pharmacodynamic target engagement (ferritin/GGT; PBMC markers) and functional benefit at mid-range doses (80–160 mg), while primate PK/PD work provides quantitative translational alignment for dose selection (Lynch et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2021; Reisman et al., 2019). The principal gaps for an AMD program are ocular distribution/PD after systemic dosing, absence of clinical AMD data, and the need to validate anti-inflammatory effects in retinal contexts; each is addressable through staged preclinical and early clinical studies, with topical delivery representing an attractive route to maximize ocular exposure and minimize systemic liability (Reisman et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2021; Creelan et al., 2017).

On balance, omaveloxolone is a strong mechanistic candidate for dry AMD: it targets the validated Nrf2 axis in RPE with demonstrated induction of SOD2/NQO1/HO-1 and thiol-redox defenses, supports mitochondrial antioxidant capacity, and carries human translational PK/PD tools to manage dose/exposure windows. Careful attention to dose selection (avoid very high exposures that attenuate desired biology), route of administration, and ocular PD verification will be critical to realizing its potential in AMD (Liu et al., 2016; Reisman et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2021).
