Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Spermidine is a naturally occurring polyamine that was originally discovered in bovine semen and later shown to be ubiquitous in all forms of life, ranging from bacteria and plants to fungi and mammals. It belongs to the aliphatic polyamine class, characterized by its low molecular weight, linear arrangement, and multiple amino groups that are fully protonated at physiological pH. Its natural origins stem from highly conserved enzymatic biosynthetic pathways—starting either from ornithine via ornithine decarboxylase or from arginine through an agmatine intermediate—resulting in the formation of putrescine, which is subsequently converted to spermidine through the transfer of an aminopropyl group provided by decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine (dcSAM) (Casero & Marton, 2007; Hobley et al., 2017; Khomutov et al., 2019). Although spermidine can be isolated from natural sources such as food and tissues, it is also available in a chemically defined form commercially (for example, Sigma-Aldrich S2626) and has been used in basic research as well as in some experimental therapeutic approaches. This compound is representative of the polyamine family, and these molecules have traditionally been investigated for their roles in cellular proliferation, nucleic acid stabilization, and modulation of various enzymatic activities, which in turn have broad implications for health and disease (Madeo et al., 2020; Nichugovskiy et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, spermidine’s potential therapeutic applications have been explored extensively in the context of its ability to induce autophagy and affect cellular homeostasis. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that spermidine supplementation can extend lifespan and improve the function of various tissues by enhancing autophagy, contributing to cardioprotection, and promoting neuroprotection in animal models (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). In the ocular domain, several studies have examined its effects on retinal cells: in vitro experiments using ARPE-19 retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells have shown that spermidine can protect against oxidative stress induced by hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) by mitigating intracellular calcium overload and maintaining mitochondrial integrity (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021). Additionally, there are preclinical observations in which intravitreal administration of spermidine in animal models produced both protective effects—in terms of reducing RPE apoptosis—and, at higher doses, toxic outcomes such as RPE necrosis and photoreceptor degeneration (Ohashi et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022). Although spermidine has not been clinically trialed specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), its effects on RPE survival and ocular inflammation have been documented in models that mimic some of the pathophysiologic stressors in dry AMD, such as oxidative damage and dysregulated autophagy (Kim et al., 2021; Senekowitsch et al., 2023). In addition, dietary supplementation studies in humans have associated higher spermidine intake with various beneficial health outcomes, including improved endothelial function and cognitive performance; however, the use of spermidine or polyamines more broadly in chronic degenerative ocular conditions remains largely in the preclinical stage (Madeo et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
The hypothesized mechanism for using spermidine in dry AMD is multifaceted and centers on its ability to modulate cellular quality control processes. At the molecular level, spermidine is known to induce autophagy, a process that mediates the degradation and recycling of damaged or dysfunctional cellular constituents. In model systems ranging from yeast to mammalian cells, spermidine has been shown to increase the conversion of the autophagy marker LC3-I to LC3-II, thereby promoting autophagosome formation (Qin et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022). One important molecular target of spermidine appears to be EP300 (p300), a histone acetyltransferase that, when inhibited, leads to reduced acetylation of several autophagy-related proteins. Inhibition of EP300 has been correlated with enhanced autophagic flux, and several studies suggest that spermidine may exert its autophagy-inducing effects partly by downregulating EP300 expression or activity (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020).

In addition to its effects on EP300, spermidine has been implicated in the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), an evolutionarily conserved energy sensor that modulates metabolic homeostasis and mitochondrial quality control. Activation of AMPK can lead to the phosphorylation and activation of downstream effectors that promote both autophagy and mitophagy (the selective autophagic removal of damaged mitochondria). While direct evidence for AMPK activation by spermidine in retinal cells is still emerging, broader studies in other cell types have described an upregulation of pathways associated with mitochondrial biogenesis and quality control, including the deacetylation of proteins by SIRT1, which often acts in concert with AMPK (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). In the specific context of RPE cells under stress from A2E (a component of lipofuscin) or H₂O₂, the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria and high levels of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) play critical roles in cell loss and dysfunction; thus, induction of mitophagy via enhanced AMPK signaling and subsequent Parkin recruitment to depolarized mitochondria could improve mitochondrial homeostasis and reduce oxidative damage (Kim et al., 2021).

Furthermore, spermidine’s role as an intracellular calcium chelator appears pivotal in its protective effect in RPE cells. Studies have demonstrated that pre-treatment of ARPE-19 cells with 10 µM spermidine prior to oxidative stress prevents intracellular Ca²⁺ overload—a phenomenon that can trigger endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and cell death—thereby maintaining cellular integrity independent of direct ROS scavenging (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021). In summary, spermidine is posited to enhance the clearance of damaged organelles—particularly mitochondria—by increasing autophagic flux through EP300 inhibition and AMPK activation, leading to enhanced LC3-II conversion and Parkin-mediated mitophagy. This, in turn, is expected to reduce mtROS and protect RPE cell viability under conditions of oxidative and A2E-induced stress (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its mode of action, the expected effect of spermidine in a dry AMD model would be a pronounced improvement in the quality control mechanisms of RPE cells. The compound is anticipated to induce autophagy, evidenced by a measurable increase in LC3-II levels, alongside enhanced recruitment of the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin to dysfunctional mitochondria. This concerted activation of autophagy and mitophagy should facilitate the clearance of damaged mitochondria, thereby reducing the accumulation of mtROS and attenuating oxidative stress. In the context of A2E accumulation—a key driver of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD—spermidine is predicted to restore mitochondrial function and improve cell viability. Experimental assays are expected to show that spermidine pre-treatment leads to a significant reduction in apoptosis markers (e.g., caspase-3 activation, cytochrome c release), along with improved markers of mitochondrial integrity (e.g., stabilized mitochondrial membrane potential) in ARPE-19 cells exposed to H₂O₂ or A2E (Kim et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating spermidine as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current literature. One major strength is its natural origin and well-documented role as a global inducer of autophagy and mitophagy. This aligns well with the current understanding of dry AMD pathogenesis, in which impaired autophagic clearance and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells play major roles (Nichugovskiy et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2021). The ability of spermidine to inhibit EP300—a factor whose downregulation encourages autophagy—and to potentially activate AMPK signaling suggests that it could enhance several intracellular quality control processes simultaneously (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). The preclinical data showing that spermidine can protect ARPE-19 cells from H₂O₂-induced oxidative injury by blocking Ca²⁺ overload and reducing apoptotic signaling further bolster its potential utility in ocular applications (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021).

However, there are notable challenges and weaknesses associated with this therapeutic candidate. First, the dose response appears to be remarkably narrow; while low micromolar concentrations (e.g., 10 µM) exert cytoprotective effects in vitro, higher doses have been associated with cytotoxicity, including RPE cell death and photoreceptor degeneration in animal models following intravitreal injection (Ohashi et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022). This raises concerns about the therapeutic window and the optimal route of delivery for chronic conditions like dry AMD. Another limitation is that, despite promising mechanistic data, direct clinical evidence for the use of spermidine in dry AMD is currently lacking. Most of the studies available have been conducted in vitro or in animal models under conditions of oxidative stress, and while these findings are encouraging, they do not fully recapitulate the complex pathophysiology of dry AMD, which involves not only oxidative damage but also chronic inflammation, immune dysregulation, and drusen accumulation (Kim et al., 2021).

Moreover, while the hypothesis emphasizes effects on EP300 inhibition and AMPK activation leading to enhanced LC3-II conversion and Parkin recruitment, the direct evidence linking these specific molecular events to improved outcomes in dry AMD models remains preliminary. There is a need for more comprehensive studies that directly measure these autophagic and mitophagic markers in RPE cells under conditions that mimic the A2E-induced stress typical of dry AMD (Kim et al., 2021). Additionally, the risk that spermidine’s metabolism by amine oxidases may produce toxic aldehyde byproducts such as acrolein must be carefully considered, as these compounds have been implicated in retinal degeneration in some intravitreal models (Ohashi et al., 2017).

In summary, while spermidine has a compelling mechanistic rationale as a modulator of autophagy and mitochondrial quality control, which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the current preclinical evidence is mixed and highlights potential safety challenges related to dosing and administration. Its established role in promoting cellular longevity and mitigating oxidative stress in diverse tissues certainly warrants further investigation, but rigorous studies using dry AMD-specific models are essential to ascertain its efficacy and safety in this context. Regulatory considerations will also require detailed pharmacokinetic and toxicological profiling, particularly given its dual potential for both cytoprotection and cytotoxicity depending on concentration and route of administration (Ohashi et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022).

Overall, our evaluation suggests that spermidine represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD based on its intrinsic properties as an autophagy and mitophagy inducer and its ability to protect RPE cells from oxidative damage; however, its clinical translation will depend on resolving key issues such as dose optimization, route of delivery, and comprehensive validation of its proposed molecular mechanisms in relevant models of AMD. The strengths of spermidine lie in its natural occurrence, multi-targeted action on cellular quality control mechanisms, and established preclinical benefits in other models of aging and oxidative stress. Conversely, the main weaknesses are its narrow therapeutic window, the potential for generation of toxic metabolites, and the current lack of direct clinical or robust in vivo data in dry AMD models. Further research, including detailed investigations in RPE models using A2E and oxidative stress conditions as well as careful titration studies in animal models of dry AMD, is warranted to determine its viability as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for this unmet clinical need (Casero & Marton, 2007; Kim et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022; Ohashi et al., 2017).

Below is a detailed evaluation of SB 290157 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (dry AMD). The review is organized into five sections: (1) Overview of Therapeutic Candidate; (2) Therapeutic History; (3) Mechanism of Action; (4) Expected Effect; and (5) Overall Evaluation. Each section combines biochemical, preclinical, and clinical considerations based solely on the provided context.

────────────────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

SB 290157 is a synthetic small‐molecule compound that functions as an antagonist of the C3a receptor (C3aR). Chemically, it is defined as N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine, a structure that incorporates an arginine residue with an acyl modification incorporating a 2,2-diphenylethoxy moiety (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). SB 290157 was discovered through high-throughput screening efforts aimed at identifying molecules capable of displacing radiolabeled C3a from its receptor. Early screening identified a lead compound that underwent extensive chemical optimization – including solid-phase peptide and peptidomimetic synthesis using Fmoc‐based chemistry on Wang resin – to yield SB 290157 (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011). This synthetic approach, employing coupling reagents such as 1-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)-3-ethylcarbodiimide hydrochloride and 4-dimethylaminopyridine, resulted in a non-peptide molecule designed to maximize receptor affinity while minimizing metabolic instability. The compound is commercially available from suppliers such as Cayman Chemical (catalog #10006619) and has served as a prototypic small-molecule C3aR antagonist in numerous preclinical studies (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017).

SB 290157 falls within the broader class of synthetic GPCR modulators that target complement receptors. Historically, such molecules have been exploited as biochemical tools to interrogate the role of anaphylatoxins in inflammatory responses (Ames et al., 2001). C3a, a 77-residue protein fragment produced during complement activation, is recognized by its GPCR, C3aR, and triggers diverse cellular responses (Ames et al., 2001). Multiple research groups have employed small-molecule antagonists like SB 290157 to elucidate the contribution of C3a-mediated signaling in conditions ranging from arthritis to lung inflammation (Ames et al., 2001). The compound’s synthetic origin and chemical tractability have allowed investigators to probe receptor pharmacology in heterologous cell lines (e.g., RBL-C3aR cells, ARPE-19 cells) and primary human cell systems (Ames et al., 2001). In the context of ocular research, SB 290157 has been used experimentally in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) models – particularly in primary human fetal RPE cultures – to block C3a-induced alterations in extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

Beyond its established utility as a research tool, the use of SB 290157 in ocular models speaks to an emerging rationale for targeting complement signaling in degenerative eye diseases. Its inclusion in a commercial catalog further underscores its ready availability to laboratories, enabling reproducibility and fostering further experimentation. In summary, SB 290157 is a synthetic, non-peptide, arginine-based antagonist belonging to a class of compounds that have historically been used to interrogate complement receptor signaling, with a well-defined chemical structure, known synthesis protocols, and broad preclinical application in inflammation research (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

SB 290157 has a storied history in the complement research field. Its initial characterization, as detailed by Ames and colleagues, revealed that SB 290157 competes for C3a binding with an IC₅₀ in the high‐nanomolar range (approximately 200 nM) and potently inhibits C3a-induced intracellular calcium mobilization in sensitive cell lines, such as RBL cells and human neutrophils (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Early studies validated its functional capacity as a selective antagonist in vitro, establishing that it effectively blocked receptor internalization and attenuated downstream signaling events elicited by C3a binding.

Preclinically, SB 290157 has been deployed in a wide range of experimental disease models. For instance, it has been used in animal studies examining anti-inflammatory activity in models such as guinea pig LPS-induced airway neutrophilia and adjuvant-induced arthritis in rats. In the arthritis model, administration of SB 290157 resulted in a significant reduction (approximately 41%) in paw edema, while in airway inflammation models it suppressed neutrophil recruitment, demonstrating its anti-inflammatory efficacy (Ames et al., 2001). These early demonstrations of anti-inflammatory activity provided the impetus to consider SB 290157 for further repurposing in conditions where complement overactivation contributes to pathology.

More recently, attention has turned to the role of complement in ocular diseases, particularly age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Experimental evidence in primary human fetal RPE cultures has shown that exposure to recombinant C3a for periods of 2–4 weeks results in the accumulation of sub-RPE deposits via increased ECM deposition, notably of collagens (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Importantly, co-treatment with a C3a receptor antagonist – which in many instances has been SB 290157 – successfully prevented the abnormal accumulation of sub-RPE deposits. These studies have helped establish a mechanistic link between C3a/C3aR activation and the proteostasis dysfunction observed in RPE cells, a pathological process believed to contribute to early AMD pathology.

In addition to in vitro data, in vivo models provide further support for the therapeutic potential of modulating C3aR signaling. In a murine model of sodium iodate (NaIO₃)-induced RPE injury – a model that recapitulates aspects of geographic atrophy – systemic administration of SB 290157 reduced photoreceptor death, decreased markers of gliosis and microglial activation, and lowered TNFα and STAT3 signaling levels (Wang et al., 2020). Similarly, in a laser-induced retinal vein occlusion (RVO) model, intravitreal injection of SB 290157 suppressed the up-regulation of both C3 and C3a receptor expression, correlating with partial rescue of retinal morphology and vascular integrity (Zhao et al., 2025). Although these studies were not specifically designed for dry AMD, the similarities in underlying complement-mediated RPE injury and chronic inflammation between these models and the dry AMD phenotype provide a strong rationale for further exploring SB 290157 in this indication.

Despite these promising applications, SB 290157’s therapeutic history is not without controversy. Several studies have reported that, depending on the cell type and receptor density, SB 290157 may exhibit partial agonist activity rather than acting as a pure antagonist (Mathieu et al., 2005). This variable pharmacological profile has raised concerns about its utility as a definitive clinical tool. Nonetheless, as a research probe, SB 290157 has significantly advanced our understanding of complement-mediated cellular responses in inflammatory, vascular, and ocular contexts. Overall, while it has been extensively used in preclinical studies across multiple disease models – including arthritis, lung inflammation, and retinal injury – its use specifically in clinical settings for dry AMD remains investigational (Ames et al., 2001; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Wang et al., 2020).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

SB 290157 exerts its biological effects by competitively binding to the C3a receptor (C3aR), thereby preventing the interaction of endogenous C3a with its receptor. Under normal conditions, the complement cascade, when activated via any of its pathways, leads to the cleavage of complement component C3 and the subsequent release of the anaphylatoxin C3a. This bioactive peptide binds to C3aR, a G protein-coupled receptor present on various cell types including granulocytes, monocytes, and notably retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Once activated, C3aR transduces signals that can lead to intracellular calcium mobilization, triggering a cascade of downstream events such as receptor internalization and activation of inflammatory transcription factors.

In vitro studies using radioligand binding assays have determined that SB 290157 displaces [¹²⁵I]-C3a from its receptor with an IC₅₀ in the high nanomolar range (approximately 200 nM), while functional calcium mobilization assays in cell lines (including RBL cells and human neutrophils) have demonstrated potent inhibition of C3a-stimulated intracellular calcium release at low nanomolar concentrations (approximately 28 nM) (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Mechanistically, by preventing C3a from engaging C3aR, the compound is able to avert subsequent receptor conformational changes that would otherwise lead to G protein coupling and downstream signaling events.

In the context of RPE cells, particularly under conditions of chronic oxidative stress – such as exposure to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) – C3a engagement of its receptor has been implicated in a range of deleterious cellular effects. Studies in ARPE-19 cells have shown that oxidative stress induces a redistribution of C3aR away from its typical plasma membrane localization and promotes its translocation toward the mitochondria (Ishii et al., 2021; Riihilä et al., 2019). At the mitochondrial level, activation of the receptor by C3a leads to an increase in mitochondrial calcium uptake, which in turn results in compromised respiratory function as evidenced by decreased state III (ADP-driven) respiration and reduced maximal respiratory capacity (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). The resultant mitochondrial dysfunction is highly likely to contribute to the generation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS). mtROS are known triggers for the NLRP3 inflammasome, which upon activation facilitates the processing of pro-IL-1β to active IL-1β, a cytokine strongly implicated in chronic inflammatory processes observed in AMD (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024).

Furthermore, in primary human fetal RPE models, prolonged exposure to recombinant C3a has been demonstrated to reduce the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (UPP) without altering mRNA levels for proteasome subunits, indicating a post-transcriptional impairment of proteostasis (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). This impairment in proteasome function is associated with an imbalance in ECM turnover – marked by a reduction in tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases (TIMP-3) abundance and an increase in matrix metalloproteinase (MMP-2) activity – culminating in the pathological deposition of extracellular matrix components (notably collagens IV and VI) beneath the RPE. Such sub-RPE deposit formation, or drusen, is one of the hallmarks of early AMD pathology (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

SB 290157, by blocking C3a from binding to C3aR, therefore interrupts these pathological cascades at two key junctures. First, it prevents the mitochondrial translocation and activation of C3aR in oxidatively stressed ARPE-19 cells, which is predicted to avert the associated mitochondrial calcium overload and respiratory inhibition, thereby reducing the likelihood of mtROS generation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). Second, by inhibiting C3a-induced receptor activation in RPE cells, SB 290157 preserves UPP activity, ensuring proper regulation of ECM component turnover and forestalling the aberrant deposition of sub-RPE material (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

It is important to note, however, that while the majority of evidence supports SB 290157 acting as an effective C3aR antagonist, several reports have cautioned that under certain conditions, the compound may display partial agonist activity. This means that rather than completely blocking receptor activation, SB 290157 might induce a low level of receptor signaling in some cellular contexts, especially when receptor density is high (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001). Such an effect must be carefully considered when interpreting experimental outcomes and when designing therapeutic strategies aimed at persistent modulation of complement activity. In all, the known mechanism of action for SB 290157 can be summarized as competitive inhibition of C3a binding to C3aR, thereby mitigating the downstream signals that lead to mitochondrial calcium dysregulation, proteasome impairment, ECM deposition abnormalities, and ultimately, NLRP3 inflammasome priming and IL-1β secretion (Ames et al., 2001; Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect

The central hypothesis underlying the use of SB 290157 in repurposing for dry AMD is that the blockade of C3aR will attenuate a cascade of deleterious events within the retinal pigment epithelium that contribute to disease progression. In particular, the expected effect is that SB 290157 will reduce complement-driven mitochondrial dysfunction, lower mtROS production, and thereby prevent the priming and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, resulting ultimately in diminished IL-1β secretion and preservation of RPE barrier integrity.

In dry AMD, chronic oxidative stress leads to dysregulated complement activation and subsequent accumulation of complement fragments such as C3a in the subretinal space. RPE cells under oxidative stress have been demonstrated to upregulate C3aR expression, with a portion of the receptor redistributing to the mitochondria—a change that is associated with an increased uptake of calcium into the mitochondria and a pronounced decline in mitochondrial respiratory function (Ishii et al., 2021; Riihilä et al., 2019). The resulting mitochondrial dysfunction is poised to increase the generation of mtROS, which serve as an upstream activator of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Activation of this inflammasome complex culminates in the maturation of IL-1β, a powerful proinflammatory cytokine that has been implicated in propagating RPE injury and the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024).

By competitively inhibiting C3a binding to its receptor, SB 290157 is expected to block these deleterious changes. Overall Evaluation

SB 290157 stands out as one of the best-studied C3a receptor antagonists available today. Its well-documented chemical synthesis, robust in vitro pharmacological profile, and demonstrable efficacy in preclinical models of inflammatory injury provide strong support for its continued evaluation as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. The compound’s origins – as a product of high-throughput screening followed by medicinal chemistry optimization using Fmoc-solid phase techniques – are well established, and its chemical structure (N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine) clearly classifies it as a small-molecule non-peptide antagonist of a key complement receptor (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Conclusion

The comprehensive literature evaluation indicates that SB 290157’s synthetic origins, established use as a C3aR antagonist, and demonstrated efficacy in preclinical models of complement-mediated RPE injury make it a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its mechanism—blocking C3a-induced signaling that otherwise leads to mitochondrial calcium overload, impaired proteostasis, and subsequent inflammasome activation—is highly relevant to the pathophysiology of geographic atrophy. Additional studies are necessary to firmly establish that SB 290157 can reduce mitochondrial ROS and suppress NLRP3 inflammasome activation in RPE cells under conditions that model dry AMD clinically. Thus, while SB 290157 is an excellent tool for dissecting the complement–mitochondria crosstalk in dry AMD, its suitability as a long-term therapeutic will depend on resolving these outstanding issues through rigorous preclinical and mechanistic evaluation (Ames et al., 2001; Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Mathieu et al., 2005).

Overall, the candidate shows substantial promise as a mechanistic probe and potential therapeutic agent for dry AMD; its ability to block key complement-mediated events that contribute to RPE dysfunction and inflammation positions it as a novel target for drug development. However, given the documented limitations, further studies are strongly recommended to optimize its receptor selectivity, define its pharmacokinetic and safety profile in the ocular context, and conclusively demonstrate its capacity to mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammasome activation in relevant models before advancing it into clinical trials.

The well-established mechanism of action of olaparib is based on the inhibition of the PARP enzyme family, primarily targeting PARP1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Deferoxamine (also known as desferrioxamine B; DFO) is a natural microbial siderophore originally isolated from Streptomyces pilosus and developed as an iron‐chelating drug in the 1960s, with clinical deployment beginning in 1968 under the trade name Desferal for treatment of iron overload disorders (notably transfusional iron loading in β-thalassemia) (Faa & Crisponi, 1999; Sharpe et al., 2011; Birch et al., 2006). Chemically, DFO is a hexadentate, tris-hydroxamate ligand that coordinates ferric iron (FeIII) at six oxygen donors derived from three bidentate hydroxamate groups to form a very stable 1:1 FeIII–DFO complex with distorted octahedral FeIIIO6 geometry (Sharpe et al., 2011; Richardson & Poňka, 1998). The FeIII affinity is exceptionally high and selective: reported formation constants for FeIII–DFO include log β110 ≈ 30.5 and conditional pM/pFe values around 26–31, while affinity for FeII is ∼20 orders of magnitude lower, consistent with the observation that DFO selectively chelates FeIII in vivo (Sharpe et al., 2011; Kontoghiorghes & Kontoghiorghe, 2020; Birch et al., 2006). The compound is highly hydrophilic, carries a positive charge near physiological pH, and exhibits poor membrane permeability and oral absorption; as a result, DFO is administered parenterally and tends to localize extracellularly or within endosomal/lysosomal compartments after endocytosis (Birch et al., 2006; Kontoghiorghes & Kontoghiorghe, 2020; Zhao et al., 2021). Pharmacokinetically, native DFO has a very short plasma half-life on the order of minutes, with multiple studies reporting ∼10–30 minutes after intravenous dosing, rapid renal clearance, and elimination of chelated iron via urine and bile; the short exposure necessitates prolonged subcutaneous or intravenous infusions for clinical efficacy (Sharpe et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2020; Entezari et al., 2022). DFO is not blood–neural barrier penetrant, limiting access to the central nervous system and retina when given systemically (Li et al., 2023).

As a class, siderophores are low-molecular microbial metabolites evolved for FeIII acquisition and storage; medicinally, DFO is the prototypical siderophore drug and, for decades, has served as the clinical standard for chelation in iron-overload conditions (Hatcher et al., 2009). Within therapeutic iron chelators, DFO’s hexadentate hydroxamate architecture confers high thermodynamic and kinetic stability of FeIII complexes, limiting redox cycling and hydroxyl radical generation relative to weaker or redox-active iron ligands (Hider & Kong, 2013).

Therapeutic History  
DFO has an extensive clinical history as the benchmark iron chelator for transfusional iron overload, especially in β-thalassemia major and other transfusion-dependent anemias; it was approved in the United States in 1968 and used for decades as life-saving therapy, albeit limited by the need for prolonged parenteral infusions and high cost (Sharpe et al., 2011; Birch et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2012). Beyond chronic iron overload, labeled and established uses include acute iron poisoning and treatment of aluminum toxicity, reflecting DFO’s strong FeIII selectivity and capacity to form inert complexes with polyvalent cations in vivo (Jones et al., 2020). The standard practice has involved subcutaneous or intravenous infusions at 20–60 mg/kg daily for 8–24 hours over 5–7 days per week, with urinary and fecal excretion of iron–DFO complexes as pharmacodynamic endpoints; however, adherence and patient acceptance have been major barriers due to the burdensome administration (Tam et al., 2003; Entezari et al., 2022).

The clinical pharmacology and chemistry of DFO have motivated multiple improved-delivery strategies: liposomal encapsulation and multivesicular liposome systems to extend half-life, and macromolecular conjugates (e.g., starch or HES carriers) to prolong exposure and shift biodistribution to iron-storage organs; these approaches have demonstrated prolonged circulation, increased urinary iron excretion, and organ accumulation (Jones et al., 2020; Sharpe et al., 2011; Tam et al., 2003). Nevertheless, DFO remains orally inactive and requires parenteral dosing, in contrast to later oral chelators (deferiprone, deferasirox), which have supplanted it in many indications due to ease of administration while sometimes being deployed in combination regimens with DFO to enhance iron removal and cardiac protection via complementary pharmacokinetics and chelation kinetics (Hider & Kong, 2013; Ma et al., 2012).

In ophthalmology and retinal biology, DFO’s evaluation is mixed. On one hand, iron chelation with DFO has shown protective effects in experimental retinal contexts: it reduced retinal ganglion cell death induced by hydrogen peroxide and paraquat in oxidative-stress paradigms, consistent with inhibition of iron-dependent hydroxyl radical production (Rohowetz et al., 2018). In hemorrhagic retinal injury, DFO protected photoreceptor tissues after subretinal blood in animal models, suggesting iron chelation can blunt heme/Fe-driven toxicity in the subretinal space (Song & Dunaief, 2013). In RPE-relevant cell models, DFO mitigated lipid peroxidation, prevented glutathione depletion, decreased Fe2+ accumulation, and preserved viability of ARPE-19 cells under tert-butyl hydroperoxide and blue-light stress, and it enhanced cell survival by modulating antioxidant defense systems (GSH–GPX4 and FSP1–CoQ10–NADH axes) (Zhao et al., 2025). A zinc–DFO complex (Zn/DFO) designed to improve cellular delivery reduced retinal iron content, lipid peroxidation, and oxidative DNA damage, preserved photoreceptor structure, and improved ERG responses in rd10 mice, demonstrating in vivo neuroprotection when systemic penetration is enhanced (Zhao et al., 2025). Ex vivo, DFO decreased histochemically detectable chelatable iron (Perls–DAB) in macular sections from AMD eyes, supporting the feasibility of removing pathologic labile iron in human AMD tissue (He et al., 2007).

On the other hand, DFO has a documented profile of retinal/ocular toxicity in patients receiving systemic therapy: reports include macular and peripheral pigmentary degeneration, impaired night vision, optic neuritis/neuropathy, cataract, ERG amplitude reductions, and EOG light-peak abnormalities, prompting recommendations for ophthalmic surveillance, and leading some experts to conclude that DFO is a dubious candidate for AMD treatment (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021). In RPE culture, repeated DFO exposure was cytotoxic relative to a prochelator control, and clinical series describe deferoxamine retinopathy across pediatric and adult populations, indicating that while iron chelation can be protective in vitro under specific stress conditions, DFO itself can injure RPE and photoreceptors under sustained or high-exposure regimens (Charkoudian et al., 2008; Błasiak et al., 2011). Importantly, DFO’s poor cell permeability and lack of blood–retinal barrier penetration raise practical concerns about achieving therapeutic intra-retinal exposure without systemic toxicity when administered conventionally (Li et al., 2023; Birch et al., 2006). Finally, although iron chelation is mechanistically compelling for retinal degenerations in which iron accumulation and ferroptotic stress participate, application of systemic chelators like DFO to retinal vascular disease and AMD remains at the basic research stage, with unresolved issues including perturbation of systemic/local iron homeostasis and stability of intracellular chelate complexes (Li et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, DFO is a high-affinity FeIII-selective chelator that forms kinetically inert hexacoordinate FeIIIO6 complexes via three hydroxamate ligands, each providing bidentate O,Oʹ coordination; this renders FeIII chemically sequestered, suppresses redox cycling, and prevents iron from entering the Haber–Weiss/Fenton chemistry that generates hydroxyl radicals from superoxide/hydrogen peroxide (Sharpe et al., 2011; Richardson & Poňka, 1998; Hider & Kong, 2013). The FeIII/FeII couple of ferrioxamine is electrochemically very negative (reported around −468 mV vs. NHE), and the complex is redox-inert under physiological conditions, consistent with its ability to quench iron-mediated ROS production rather than participate in it (Hider & Kong, 2013). In biological systems, DFO preferentially binds non-transferrin-bound iron (NTBI), labile iron pools in hepatocytes/macrophages, and low-molecular-weight iron transiting endosomes/lysosomes after transferrin delivery or ferritin degradation; it can mobilize hepatic stores and iron released by reticuloendothelial cells but cannot effectively strip iron from metalloproteins such as hemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochromes, oxidases, catalase, or peroxidases (Hatcher et al., 2009; Richardson & Poňka, 1998; Faa & Crisponi, 1999). The drug is hydrophilic and generally membrane-impermeant; cellular uptake occurs via fluid-phase endocytosis and pinocytosis, leading to enrichment in endosomal/lysosomal compartments, where it chelates lysosomal labile iron, an activity proposed to block lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis—mechanistically relevant to RPE pathobiology (Zhao et al., 2021; Dayani et al., 2004).

In retina and neural tissues, oxidative damage pathways include iron-dependent conversion of H2O2 to •OH via Fenton chemistry; DFO reduces H2O2-induced damage in retinal ganglion cells and protects against paraquat-generated superoxide by depriving upstream Fenton catalysts of accessible iron (Rohowetz et al., 2018). In RPE and photoreceptors, ferroptosis—a regulated cell death driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation—is closely linked to antioxidant systems centered on glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and, independently, on FSP1-mediated ubiquinol regeneration; DFO’s chelation of FeII/FeIII within lysosomes and cytosolic labile pools acts upstream of these pathways to limit lipid hydroperoxide propagation, preserving GSH–GPX4 and FSP1–CoQ10–NADH defense capacity in ARPE-19 under oxidative stimuli (Zhao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023). In systemic contexts, DFO detoxifies NTBI, reduces heme-derived ferryl species, removes high-oxidation-state heme iron, and directly scavenges some radical species, converging on inhibition of membrane lipid oxidation; these activities potentially translate to retinal cells where heme/iron-driven oxidative stress is implicated (Hatcher et al., 2009).

Notably, DFO’s hexadentate size and hydrophilicity restrict direct ferritin iron extraction and limit chelation in tightly protein-bound pools; smaller chelators can penetrate cells more readily and directly efflux ferritin iron, whereas DFO works primarily by intercepting low-molecular-weight iron pools and forming kinetically inert FeIII complexes that are then cleared, often via hepatobiliary or renal routes (Sharpe et al., 2011; Richardson & Poňka, 1998). In inflamed or ischemic tissues, the depletion of accessible iron by DFO can blunt downstream ROS and inflammatory cascades; however, prolonged systemic chelation perturbs metal homeostasis and can deplete essential iron pools in sensitive tissues, underlying some adverse effects including RPE toxicity, auditory neuropathy, and bone dysplasia (Zhao et al., 2021; He et al., 2007).

Expected Effect  
For dry AMD models centered on RPE iron-dependent oxidative stress, the expected pharmacologic effect of DFO is to reduce the labile Fe pool in lysosomes and cytosol, thereby attenuating hydroxyl-radical production from H2O2 and limiting iron-driven lipid peroxidation; operationally, this should decrease oxidative damage readouts and preserve mitochondrial and cellular function in RPE assays (Rohowetz et al., 2018; Li et al., 2023). Specifically:

- Lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis markers: In ARPE-19 cells, DFO has been shown to mitigate lipid peroxidation under oxidant (tBH) and blue-light stress and to preserve viability, consistent with suppression of ferroptotic death; thus, in RPE assays one should observe reductions in lipid peroxidation assays (e.g., BODIPY-C11) and maintenance of GPX4 activity/content, with complementary preservation of the FSP1–CoQ10–NADH axis (Zhao et al., 2025). The same studies indicate decreased Fe2+ accumulation after DFO, reflecting lower catalytic Fe at sites of peroxidation; similar decreases in labile Fe can be measured via calcein quenching or analogous probes (Zhao et al., 2025).

- Oxidative DNA damage: Systemic Zn/DFO reduced retinal oxidative DNA damage in vivo in rd10 mice; although these are not AMD models, the result predicts that in RPE oxidative stress assays DFO will reduce accumulation of oxidative DNA lesions, including those arising in mitochondrial DNA, where iron-dependent ROS can be particularly damaging (Zhao et al., 2025). Ex vivo human AMD maculas showed decreased Perls–DAB staining after DFO chelation, supporting the feasibility of reducing chelatable iron burden and downstream oxidative chemistry in diseased human retina (He et al., 2007).

- Mitochondrial bioenergetics: Preservation of RPE oxygen consumption rate (OCR) is plausible under DFO exposure insofar as DFO limits lipid peroxidation and maintains the reductive antioxidant systems (GSH–GPX4, FSP1–CoQ10) that protect inner-mitochondrial membranes and electron-transport components from iron-dependent oxidative injury; in ARPE-19, DFO improved survival and redox balance under stress, suggesting OCR preservation would accompany reduced peroxidation (Zhao et al., 2025). In retinal ganglion cells, DFO lessened H2O2-induced cell death, indirectly supporting improved mitochondrial tolerance to oxidant stress; similar protection can be anticipated in RPE where iron-dependent ROS compromise mitochondrial DNA and respiratory complexes (Rohowetz et al., 2018).

- Tissue iron fingerprints: In tissue sections or organoids, DFO exposure is expected to decrease Perls–DAB positive iron signal in regions with elevated chelatable iron, as observed in AMD macular tissue; in vivo, systemic DFO does not cross the BRB well, so demonstration of retinal iron removal may require enhanced uptake strategies (e.g., Zn/DFO) or local delivery (Li et al., 2023; He et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2025).

Caveats critical to experimental design include DFO’s lack of blood–retinal barrier penetration and poor cell permeability, which could limit intracellular RPE exposure and lysosomal targeting in vivo after systemic dosing; thus, in vitro or ex vivo assays will show clearer pharmacodynamic effects than systemic models unless delivery is optimized (e.g., Zn-complexation or nanocarriers) (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025; Jones et al., 2020). Additionally, repeated or high-concentration exposure can be cytotoxic to RPE in vitro and has been associated with clinical retinopathy, so dose–exposure optimization and careful toxicity monitoring are required, especially in chronic paradigms (Charkoudian et al., 2008; He et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Rationale strength and translational plausibility. The mechanistic rationale for iron chelation in dry AMD is strong: AMD retinas accumulate chelatable iron, iron catalyzes hydroxyl-radical generation and lipid peroxidation, and iron-dependent ferroptotic stress has been implicated in RPE dysfunction and photoreceptor degeneration (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023). DFO is a high-affinity FeIII chelator with extensive human experience, and it is proven to suppress iron-mediated ROS by forming kinetically inert FeIII complexes, preventing Fenton chemistry (Sharpe et al., 2011; Hider & Kong, 2013). In retinal and RPE models, DFO reduces oxidative injury, limits lipid peroxidation, and preserves cell viability; improved-delivery variants such as Zn/DFO demonstrate in vivo protection of retinal structure and function with concomitant decreases in retinal iron and oxidative DNA damage (Rohowetz et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2025). Ex vivo AMD maculae show DFO-responsive chelatable iron pools, reinforcing target engagement in human disease tissue (He et al., 2007). Mechanistically, enrichment of DFO in lysosomes—an organelle central to RPE iron handling, ferritinophagy, and lipid peroxidation—supports a proximal mode of action relevant to ferroptosis biology in AMD (Zhao et al., 2021).

Key liabilities and translational risks. Despite its compelling mechanism, DFO’s drug properties and ocular safety profile are unfavorable for repurposing in dry AMD without substantial reformulation or targeting:

- Ocular toxicity. DFO has a recognized spectrum of retinal adverse effects in patients, including pigmentary retinopathy, optic neuropathy, ERG/EOG abnormalities, and visual loss; authoritative reviews judge DFO a dubious candidate for AMD because of these safety concerns, and clinical surveillance is recommended when patients receive systemic DFO (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023). RPE toxicity is documented in vitro and clinically across age groups, indicating a narrow retinal therapeutic window under repeated exposure (Błasiak et al., 2011; Charkoudian et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2021).

- Delivery limitations. DFO is hydrophilic, membrane-impermeant, and not blood–neural/retinal barrier penetrant, which undermines retinal exposure after systemic dosing; achieving therapeutic intra-RPE concentrations without systemic toxicity is unlikely with conventional infusion regimens (Li et al., 2023; Birch et al., 2006). The molecule’s very short plasma half-life further complicates exposure in avascular tissues like the outer retina (Sharpe et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2020).

- Systemic chelation risks. Long-term DFO perturbs systemic iron balance, interacts with microbiological iron acquisition in certain pathogens (e.g., Vibrio, S. aureus) that can exploit ferrioxamine, and carries recognized risks of growth retardation, bone changes, and infection, which are unacceptable for a chronic ocular disease with slow progression (Sharpe et al., 2011; Faa & Crisponi, 1999).

- Clinical maturity in ophthalmology. While iron chelators show promise in preclinical retinal models, clinical translation to retinal vascular disease/AMD remains at the basic research stage; challenges include maintaining retinal iron homeostasis, avoiding off-target metal depletion (e.g., Zn2+), and ensuring intracellular chelate stability and localization (Li et al., 2023).

Risk-mitigation strategies and development path. If DFO were to be advanced, development should avoid systemic DFO infusions for dry AMD. Instead:

- Leverage targeted delivery. The Zn/DFO complex that facilitates cellular uptake has shown robust neuroprotection, retinal iron lowering, and oxidative DNA damage reduction in vivo; such conjugate-based or carrier-based strategies could provide intracellular RPE delivery at lower systemic exposure, meriting further evaluation in AMD-relevant models (e.g., light damage, iron-loading, aged mice) with retinal safety readouts (Zhao et al., 2025). Nanocarriers or depot formulations that increase local ocular exposure while minimizing systemic levels could be explored, given DFO’s history of half-life extension in liposomal and multivesicular formulations systemically (Jones et al., 2020; Sharpe et al., 2011).

- Consider chemical alternatives within class. Other chelators with better cell permeability and ocular safety have shown retinal protection without the retinotoxicity seen with DFO; for example, deferiprone protected against iron-induced and light-induced retinal degeneration in multiple mouse models and was not found to be toxic to mouse retina in the contexts studied, suggesting that a more lipophilic, lower-molecular-weight chelator could be a safer starting point than DFO for dry AMD (Song & Dunaief, 2013; Picard et al., 2020).

- Exploit prochelation. Pro-chelators like BSIH that become active only under oxidative conditions were non-toxic with repeated exposure relative to DFO and may offer a way to achieve context-dependent iron chelation within oxidatively stressed RPE while sparing normal iron pools, lowering the risk of retinopathy (Charkoudian et al., 2008).

Decision framework for go/no-go. On balance, while DFO validates the iron-chelation mechanism in retinal tissues and provides useful tool-compound effects in vitro and in ex vivo AMD maculae, its physicochemical properties, delivery constraints, and retinal toxicity profile argue strongly against repurposing native DFO for chronic treatment of dry AMD (Li et al., 2023; He et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2021). The most credible development path for DFO derivatives would require:

- Demonstrating safe, effective RPE delivery with a DFO-based construct (e.g., Zn/DFO or nanocarrier) that reduces labile iron, lipid peroxidation, and oxidative DNA damage in AMD-relevant in vivo models without ERG/EOG or structural toxicity (Zhao et al., 2025).

- Establishing a therapeutic index in the retina with chronic dosing and appropriate safety pharmacology (ERG, OCT, histopathology), given reported human retinopathies on DFO (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023).

- Benchmarking against alternative chelators (e.g., deferiprone) that already demonstrate retinal protection and better permeability/safety in vivo, to justify a DFO-based approach scientifically and clinically (Song & Dunaief, 2013; Picard et al., 2020).

Strengths  
- Mechanistic fit: chelates FeIII with high selectivity and prevents Fenton chemistry; acts in lysosomes where RPE iron and lipid peroxidation intersect with ferroptosis (Sharpe et al., 2011; Hider & Kong, 2013; Zhao et al., 2021).  
- Demonstrated retinal pharmacology: reduces oxidative injury in retinal neurons and RPE, lowers retinal iron and oxidative DNA damage with improved delivery, and removes chelatable iron from AMD macula ex vivo (Rohowetz et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2025; He et al., 2007).  
- Extensive human experience: well-characterized PK/PD, safety liabilities, and clinical management of chelation therapy (Jones et al., 2020; Tam et al., 2003).

Weaknesses  
- Ocular toxicity liability with systemic DFO, including pigmentary retinopathy and electrophysiologic dysfunction, making native DFO a poor risk–benefit prospect for a chronic retinal indication (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021).  
- Poor retinal exposure after systemic dosing due to hydrophilicity and lack of BRB penetration; very short half-life complicates sustained intraocular levels (Li et al., 2023; Birch et al., 2006; Jones et al., 2020).  
- Systemic risks (growth, bone, infection) incompatible with large, elderly dry-AMD populations unless exposure is tightly localized to the eye (Faa & Crisponi, 1999; Sharpe et al., 2011).  
- Field immaturity: iron chelators for retinal disease remain in basic research with unresolved questions about homeostasis and intracellular stability (Li et al., 2023).

Conclusion  
DFO is a mechanistically validated iron chelator with documented ability to reduce iron-driven oxidative injury in retinal systems; however, as a repurposed systemic drug for dry AMD, its delivery barriers and retinal toxicity outweigh potential benefits (Li et al., 2023; He et al., 2007). If iron chelation is pursued for dry AMD within this program, prioritizing better-penetrant, safer chelators (e.g., deferiprone) or context-activated prochelators over native DFO is the higher-probability path; alternately, DFO-based constructs that demonstrably deliver into RPE (e.g., Zn/DFO) with acceptable chronic retinal safety merit targeted preclinical exploration before considering clinical translation (Song & Dunaief, 2013; Charkoudian et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2025).

Liproxstatin-1 is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor of ferroptosis that was originally discovered using phenotypic high-throughput screening in systems where ferroptosis was induced by either genetic deletion of GPX4 or by glutathione depletion with agents like erastin (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69). Its chemical identity is tied to a unique spiroquinoxalinamine scaffold, which places it in the class of aromatic amine radical-trapping antioxidants (RTAs) – compounds well known in industrial settings to protect hydrocarbon products from autoxidation, as well as in biomedical research to block oxidative lipid chain reactions (Scarpellini, 2023, pp. 41–45; Angeli, Shah, Pratt, & Conrad, 2017, pp. 6–8). In contrast to classical phenolic antioxidants such as α-tocopherol, Liproxstatin-1 is designed to operate in the lipid bilayer, where its aminic (or diarylamine) moieties are less hindered by nonproductive hydrogen-bonding interactions with phospholipid headgroups, thus allowing rapid hydrogen-atom transfer to lipid peroxyl radicals (Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). Although detailed synthetic routes are not provided in the available reports, the discovery process clearly identifies Liproxstatin-1 as a lead candidate that emerged from unbiased cell-based screens aimed at identifying compounds that preserve cell viability in the absence of GPX4 function (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). Its categorization as an RTA is significant because this class of compounds has a long history of being used to inhibit free radical–mediated damage in both industrial and biological contexts (Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6).

Therapeutic History:  
The preclinical history of Liproxstatin-1 is rich with evidence supporting its role as a potent inhibitor of ferroptosis. Early studies demonstrated that Liproxstatin-1 acts at low nanomolar concentrations to prevent ferroptotic cell death in mouse embryonic fibroblasts as well as in specialized cells rendered vulnerable by GPX4 inactivation (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Angeli et al., 2014, p. 10). Beyond in vitro cell survival assays, Liproxstatin-1 has been evaluated in vivo where it has shown remarkable protective effects in models of acute tissue injury including genetic GPX4 deficiency, which induces acute renal failure, and in ischaemia/reperfusion models of liver injury (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10). Although its direct clinical use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) has not been established – with most in vivo data coming from non-ocular models – its success in ameliorating tissue damage by inhibiting lipid peroxidation suggests its potential utility in other degenerative pathologies where oxidative membrane damage drives dysfunction, such as in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) degeneration underlying geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69; Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–21). Moreover, related compounds, notably Ferrostatin-1, have been tested in various retinal cell models and in some in vivo settings pertaining to retinal ischemia–reperfusion injury and oxygen-induced retinopathy, further bolstering the therapeutic concept of using RTA-type ferroptosis inhibitors in ocular settings (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23; Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8). While the bulk of Liproxstatin-1’s therapeutic history centers on its role as an anti-ferroptotic agent in cancer, neurodegeneration, and acute organ failure, its mechanistic overlap with key pathological features observed in dry AMD – such as iron accumulation, glutathione depletion and elevated lipid peroxidation in the RPE – supports evaluating it as a repurposed candidate in this context (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Shen et al., 2025, pp. 1–2).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism by which Liproxstatin-1 exerts its cytoprotective effect is rooted in its function as a radical-trapping antioxidant. Specifically, Liproxstatin-1 reacts rapidly with lipid peroxyl radicals that propagate the autoxidation chain reaction in cellular membranes. Experimental data have established that Liproxstatin-1 exhibits an intrinsic reaction rate constant (k_inh) in the range of approximately 2.4 × 10^5 M^−1 s^−1 in organic solvents such as chlorobenzene at 37 °C, which is comparable to industrial diarylamine antioxidants (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 8–9). Although its intrinsic reactivity in homogeneous organic solutions may appear lower than classical phenolic antioxidants like α-tocopherol, its performance in the lipid bilayer is superior due to reduced hydrogen-bonding interactions with phospholipid headgroups – a feature that enhances its mobility and reactivity in the lipid environment where ferroptosis is executed (Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 8–9; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). The compound functions primarily by donating a hydrogen atom from its arylamine (or diarylamine) N–H group, effectively quenching chain-propagating lipid peroxyl radicals before they can perpetuate lipid hydroperoxide formation (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). Kinetic isotope effect studies and computational analyses have confirmed that the N–H bond dissociation enthalpy is sufficiently low in Liproxstatin-1 to enable rapid hydrogen-atom transfer, which is a critical step in its radical-trapping mechanism (Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 2–3, 5–7). Importantly, Liproxstatin-1 does not exert significant inhibitory effects on enzymes such as human 15-lipoxygenase-1, thereby ruling out an enzymatic inhibition mechanism and reinforcing that its protective effect is solely attributable to non-enzymatic scavenging of peroxyl radicals (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 201–210). Recent studies have even suggested that Liproxstatin-1 may form a complex with iron in certain cellular compartments (e.g., the lysosome), which could further diminish iron-catalysed radical generation under acidic conditions; however, the predominant and well-characterized mechanism remains its role in intercepting lipid peroxyl radicals (Rodriguez et al., 2024, pp. 1–5; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). On a molecular level, by halting the autoxidation chain reaction, Liproxstatin-1 preserves mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and prevents the deleterious accumulation of lipid hydroperoxides, events that are central to the execution phase of ferroptosis (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). Thus, by protecting cellular membranes from oxidative deterioration, Liproxstatin-1 interrupts the cascade of events leading to ferroptotic cell death, a process that is implicated in RPE degeneration seen in geographic atrophy (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shen et al., 2025, pp. 1–2).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, particularly in geographic atrophy where RPE degeneration is a hallmark, the expected effect of Liproxstatin-1 would be to curtail the chain reaction of lipid peroxidation that underpins ferroptotic cell death. In vitro assays using RPE cell lines such as ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cells have demonstrated that targeting lipid peroxidation – as evidenced by reductions in markers like BODIPY-C11 oxidation and ACSL4 expression – can rescue cells from oxidative stress–mediated death (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–23). Liproxstatin-1 is anticipated to mitigate the accumulation of lipid hydroperoxides, thus preserving the integrity of cellular membranes and mitochondrial function in the RPE (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Given that geographic atrophy in dry AMD is associated with iron overload and subsequent iron-catalysed lipid peroxidation, the ability of Liproxstatin-1 to trap peroxyl radicals is particularly significant; by reducing lipid ROS, it is expected to prevent the conversion of polyunsaturated fatty acids into cytotoxic lipid hydroperoxides, thereby maintaining cellular viability (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). Moreover, the inhibition of ACSL4-dependent peroxidation pathways – which have been linked to ferroptosis in RPE cells – may also be intercepted by Liproxstatin-1, providing a dual line of defense against ferroptotic signaling (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23; Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8). On a cellular level, the compound is expected to maintain Δψm and reduce indicators of oxidative stress, as previously demonstrated in models addressing GPX4 inhibition (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). In animal models where ferroptosis contributes to tissue degeneration (such as renal or hepatic ischaemia/reperfusion models), treatment with Liproxstatin-1 resulted in reduced TUNEL-positive cell counts and ameliorated tissue injury; these outcomes provide a rationale for its application in preclinical dry AMD models, where similar pathological processes – including mitochondrial dysfunction, iron dysregulation, and excessive lipid peroxidation – are observed (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Peng et al., 2020, pp. 3–5). In essence, when applied to RPE cells under conditions that mimic dry AMD, Liproxstatin-1 should decrease oxidative markers, prevent cell death, and thereby slow or halt the progression of geographic atrophy by restoring the balance between pro-oxidant and antioxidant pathways (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–23).

Overall Evaluation:  
Liproxstatin-1 stands out as a promising candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic agent against dry AMD, particularly in geographic atrophy, given the mechanistic overlap between ferroptosis and RPE cell death observed in dry AMD. One of its principal strengths lies in its potent radical-trapping antioxidant activity, which is not only effective at low nanomolar concentrations but also uniquely suited to the lipid bilayer environment of the RPE (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). This specificity is critical because retinal cells are subject to a high burden of polyunsaturated lipid content and are therefore particularly sensitive to oxidative damage. The fact that Liproxstatin-1 has demonstrated efficacy in protecting cells under ferroptotic stress in other organ systems – including kidney and liver models – further supports its potential viability in ocular applications (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Peng et al., 2020, pp. 3–5). Additionally, the compound’s ability to reduce lipid peroxidation, maintain mitochondrial membrane potential, and possibly engage in secondary iron-inactivating mechanisms (as suggested by lysosomal localization studies) offers multiple avenues through which it may address the multifactorial pathogenesis of dry AMD (Rodriguez et al., 2024, pp. 1–5; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 1–2).

However, several challenges must be considered. Despite the strong preclinical evidence in non-ocular systems, direct evidence of Liproxstatin-1’s efficacy in models of dry AMD or RPE-specific ferroptosis is still limited relative to other compounds such as Ferrostatin-1 or nanoparticle-delivered ferroptosis inhibitors in retinal models (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–23). This gap in ocular preclinical data implies that further dedicated studies using RPE cell models and in vivo dry AMD animal models are necessary to validate its protective effects in the eye. In addition, drug delivery to the retina poses its own set of challenges – the blood-retinal barrier and the unique pharmacokinetic profile required for intravitreal stability must be thoroughly optimized (Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69; Hao, Xu, Zhang, & Xue, 2024, pp. 6–7). Moreover, dry AMD is a multifactorial disease involving not only ferroptosis but also apoptosis, inflammation, and other forms of regulated cell death; therefore, while inhibiting ferroptosis may be beneficial, it is uncertain whether monotherapy with Liproxstatin-1 would be sufficient to arrest disease progression. There is also the matter of safety and tolerability in the context of the ocular environment, as systemic dosing strategies that work in renal or hepatic models may not directly translate to the delicate milieu of retinal tissues (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). Finally, considerations regarding the long-term stability, potential off-target effects, and metabolic fate of Liproxstatin-1 in the eye will be crucial parameters in the drug development process.

In summary, the collective literature indicates that Liproxstatin-1 has a well-defined mechanism as a radical-trapping antioxidant that effectively blocks lipid peroxidation and, by extension, ferroptosis. Its discovery through unbiased screening in ferroptosis-susceptible models and its demonstration of efficacy in multiple organ systems provide a strong foundation for its repurposing in dry AMD. The evidence supports that Liproxstatin-1 could counteract the iron-driven ROS amplification and lipid peroxidation that contribute to RPE cell death in geographic atrophy. Nonetheless, while its mechanistic rationale and preclinical promise are substantial, further research – particularly within retinal models – is necessary to fully evaluate its therapeutic potential and address challenges related to ocular delivery and multi-pathway disease components. Taken together, Liproxstatin-1 represents a compelling candidate for further investigation as a targeted inhibitor of ferroptosis in the treatment of dry AMD (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69, 207–210; Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
A-438079 is a synthetic small-molecule antagonist of the purinergic P2X7 receptor (P2X7R) originating from Abbott Laboratories’ disubstituted tetrazole series discovered by high-throughput screening and refined by structure–activity relationship (SAR) optimization within a 1-benzyl-5-aryltetrazole chemotype (tetrazole > triazole > pyrazole/imidazole in potency) (Romagnoli et al., 2008; Carroll et al., 2009). A-438079’s structure has been disclosed as 3-((5-(2,3-dichlorophenyl)-1H-tetrazol-1-yl)methyl)pyridine, capturing the two key medicinal chemistry decisions that produced a selective, drug-like P2X7 antagonist: (i) a conserved 2,3-dichlorophenyl “left-hand” aryl that supports potency and (ii) installation of a 3-pyridyl “right-hand” substituent to overcome the solubility liabilities of the original 1-benzyl-5-aryltetrazoles while maintaining submicromolar activity at human/rat P2X7 (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; Romagnoli et al., 2008; Carroll et al., 2009). Functionally, A-438079 is a reversible, competitive P2X7 antagonist that inhibits BzATP-stimulated calcium flux, P2X7-associated macropore formation, and downstream IL-1β release in macrophage-lineage systems, consistent with canonical P2X7 pharmacology linked to NLRP3 inflammasome activation (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007). Cross-source potency data place A-438079 in the mid-nanomolar to low-submicromolar range at human and rat P2X7: human P2X7 pIC50 values of ~6.3–6.9, rat P2X7 pIC50 ~6.5, and functional IC50 estimates of ~0.1 µM (rat) and ~0.3 µM (human), with high selectivity against other P2 subtypes (e.g., P2X7 IC50 0.06 µM vs >100 µM for other subtypes in one panel) (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; El Idrissi et al., 2024; Nagy, 2013). A-438079 was commercialized by Tocris (circa 2008) as a first widely available, selective P2X7 antagonist probe, enabling consistent interrogation of P2X7 biology in vitro and in vivo beyond earlier nonselective tools (e.g., KN-62, Evans Blue) (Felix et al., 2012). Within the broader class, many P2X7 antagonists have reached advanced preclinical characterization; multi-parameter tables in retinal disease–focused reviews list A-438079 as active at human/rat P2X7 with a reported brain:plasma ratio near 2.0 (suggesting central barrier penetration) and note that progress toward ocular/CNS indications has been limited by species specificity and insufficient barrier penetration for some chemotypes (Fletcher et al., 2019).  

Therapeutic History  
A-438079 and related Abbott “A-series” P2X7 antagonists established robust preclinical efficacy in neuropathic and inflammatory pain models, aligning with the role of P2X7-driven IL-1β/IL-18 signaling in nociception and neuroinflammation (Carroll et al., 2009). A-438079 reduced mechanical allodynia in the Chung and Bennett rat models, showed activity in vincristine neuropathy and the formalin persistent pain test, and inhibited evoked and spontaneous spinal neuronal firing in vivo without motor impairment (rotarod) at high i.p. doses, supporting a favorable preclinical therapeutic index in pain paradigms (Carroll et al., 2009). Beyond pain, class summaries attribute anti-seizure effects to A-438079 in a mouse intra-amygdala kainic acid model, situating P2X7 antagonism within a broader CNS neuroinflammation–linked efficacy landscape (Gelin et al., 2020).  

Human cell assays demonstrate that A-438079 and closely related antagonists abolish ATP-induced P2X7 pore function (ethidium or YO-PRO uptake) yet spare phagocytic uptake in CD14+ human monocytes, indicating that P2X7’s pro-inflammatory macropore function can be selectively blocked while preserving innate scavenger activity; this pharmacological dissociation is a core objective for neurodegenerative/retinal indications where loss of phagocytosis may worsen pathology (Gu & Wiley, 2018).  

Clinically, the P2X7 antagonist class has mixed outcomes in peripheral inflammatory diseases: randomized Phase 2 trials in rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn’s disease failed to meet objective inflammation endpoints (ACR20, CRP), although AZD9056 showed symptom benefit (abdominal pain, mental component score) in Crohn’s disease; no P2X7 antagonist has been trialed in neurodegenerative indications to date, and none has entered clinical testing specifically for ocular/retinal diseases (Gu & Wiley, 2018; Fletcher et al., 2019). Nevertheless, the latest brain-penetrant small molecules (e.g., JNJ55308942, JNJ5417446) demonstrate oral brain exposure and dose-dependent suppression of IL-1β release in stimulated whole blood/PBMCs in humans, suggesting that pharmacodynamic endpoints and barrier penetration necessary for CNS/retinal therapy are tractable within this target class (Fletcher et al., 2019).  

Retinal and AMD-relevant preclinical evidence for P2X7 antagonism is substantial at the class level. P2X7 is expressed across retinal compartments including RPE, photoreceptors, bipolar/horizontal/amacrine neurons, retinal ganglion cells, Müller glia, and microglia in mouse, rat, and human; functional agonism (e.g., BzATP) modulates retinal responses that are attenuated in P2X7-null mice, confirming a functional purinergic ATP/P2X7 axis in vivo (Fletcher et al., 2019). Sustained elevations of extracellular ATP are documented in ocular disease (e.g., human chronic glaucoma aqueous humor), and endogenous ATP mediates acute RGC injury following intraocular pressure spikes in rodents; degrading ATP or blocking P2X7 prevents RGC injury in vivo, demonstrating disease-relevant ATP surges capable of activating P2X7 in the retina (Fletcher et al., 2019). AMD-relevant biology includes high vitreous ATP, P2X7-dependent NLRP3 inflammasome activation by Alu RNA in geographic atrophy (GA) models, and P2X7-driven Ca2+-dependent apoptosis in RPE, together implicating P2X7 as a key upstream activator of inflammasome-mediated retinal degeneration (Calzaferri et al., 2020).  

For A-438079 specifically, a curated review table lists it among P2X7 antagonists evaluated in retinal contexts including ARPE-19 RPE cells, C57BL/6J mouse retinal degeneration models (e.g., MNU), and human pericytes, with endpoints encompassing NLRP3/IL-1β signaling, VEGF, ROS, ZO-1 barrier integrity, NF-κB activation, and apoptosis; outcomes are usually protective though model- and endpoint-specific variability exists (Li & Wang, 2025). In allied class work, selective P2X7 blockade with A-740003 in ARPE-19 cells and C57BL/6 mice exposed to oxidized LDL reduced ROS, suppressed NLRP3 inflammasome and NF-κB activation, decreased IL-1β/IL-18 and proangiogenic factors (VEGF, HIF-1α), alleviated retinal neovascularization, and preserved ERG amplitudes, anchoring mechanistic and functional retinal benefits to P2X7 antagonism (Yang et al., 2021). More broadly, P2X7 antagonists have protected retinal ganglion cells in chronic ocular hypertension by inhibiting microglial activation and reversed hyperpermeability and VEGF/IL-6 increases in diabetic retinal models, indicating barrier and neuroinflammatory benefits that are relevant to AMD pathophysiology (Li & Wang, 2025). Finally, in AMD-relevant disease models, P2X7 antagonists suppressed clinical symptoms of GA and CNV in animals; however, complete genetic ablation yielded mixed results (e.g., P2X7−/− protected from GA but not laser-induced CNV), emphasizing the need to preserve beneficial scavenger functions while blocking pro-inflammatory pore signaling (Gu & Wiley, 2018).  

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, P2X7 is a trimeric, low-sensitivity ATP-gated cation channel that mediates Na+, Ca2+, and K+ fluxes and, upon sustained or high agonist exposure, transitions into a large nonselective macropore permeable to molecules up to ~900 Da (e.g., YO-PRO-1), a state tightly coupled to K+ efflux and subsequent NLRP3 inflammasome activation with maturation/release of IL-1β and IL-18 (Fletcher et al., 2019). Two main routes connect P2X7 activity to IL-1β biology: (i) pore-dependent K+ efflux promotes inflammasome assembly and caspase-1 activation to process pro-IL-1β/pro-IL-18; and (ii) P2X7-mediated Ca2+ influx contributes to NF-κB activation and transcriptional priming of inflammasome components and pro-cytokines, forming the two-signal paradigm required for IL-1β/IL-18 maturation and pyroptosis (Calzaferri et al., 2020).  

In the retinal pigment epithelium, extracellular ATP is a canonical danger-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) produced by stressed/dying cells; ARPE-19 cells themselves release ATP and exhibit P2X7- and pannexin-1 (Panx1)-linked mechanisms that drive NLRP3 inflammasome activation, caspase-1 cleavage, gasdermin D pore formation, and secretion of IL-1β/IL-18, pathways that converge on inflammatory and pyroptotic injury of RPE (Youn, 2024). P2X7 functionally recruits Panx1, facilitating ATP and solute release that amplifies local ATP and P2X7 activation; in ARPE-19 cells, 25-hydroxycholesterol triggers P2X7-dependent YO-PRO uptake that is sensitive to Panx1 blockade (probenecid), indicating a Panx1-dependent pore component in RPE injury (Yang, 2017). P2X7 activation is also linked to mitochondrial distress, including cytochrome-c release and activation of executioner caspases (3/8/9), mechanistically tying the receptor to ROS (including mitochondrial ROS) and apoptotic/mixed death cascades relevant to retinal degeneration (Unknown Reference).  

Retinal localization and disease relevance are broad. Multiple P2X7 splice variants are present in the retina (with at least one common knockout deleting only the full-length variant), and P2X7 is reported in neurons (photoreceptors, amacrine, ganglion cells), glia (microglia, Müller cells), and RPE across species; application of BzATP modulates retinal responses that are attenuated in P2X7-null mice, and genetic/clinical associations link P2X7/P2X4 variants to advanced AMD risk (Fletcher et al., 2019). In ARPE-19 and native/cultured human RPE, P2X7 is expressed at mRNA and protein levels, and it is the only P2X subtype that requires high ATP for activation—conditions that occur during retinal injury/inflammation and are observed in ocular fluids in disease (note: P2X4 can be more abundant than P2X7 in ARPE-19 at baseline, which can shape net purinergic responses) (Youn, 2024).  

Within this mechanistic framework, A-438079 engages P2X7 as a reversible, competitive antagonist, blocking ATP/BzATP-evoked channel activation and macropore formation; by doing so, it suppresses P2X7-mediated Ca2+ influx and K+ efflux that are required for NF-κB priming and NLRP3 activation, respectively, leading to reduced caspase-1 cleavage and decreased maturation/secretion of IL-1β/IL-18 (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; Fletcher et al., 2019; Calzaferri et al., 2020). In macrophage-lineage systems and fresh human monocytes, A-438079 or closely related antagonists abolish P2X7 pore function and IL-1β release but preserve phagocytosis, directly supporting a therapeutic goal in neurodegeneration/retinal disease to block pro-inflammatory pore/inflammasome signaling while sparing scavenger functions that may be beneficial for debris clearance (Donnelly-Roberts & Jarvis, 2007; Gu & Wiley, 2018).
