Below is our comprehensive evaluation of pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD):

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate –  
Pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) is an aromatic o‐quinone originally discovered as a redox cofactor for bacterial dehydrogenases and is naturally synthesized by various Gram‐negative prokaryotes. It was first identified in microbial systems where it serves as a prosthetic group in enzymes involved in alcohol and sugar oxidation, and it has since been detected at trace levels in human tissues and milk, suggesting dietary exposure through common foods such as fermented soy products, green peppers, spinach, and human milk. PQQ is categorized within the quinone family of compounds and is recognized for its redox‐active properties; in this role, it has been considered a “vitamin‐like accessory factor” by some researchers given its involvement in cellular energy metabolism and antioxidant defense (Petricca et al., 2025; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Commercially, PQQ is available in a water‐soluble disodium salt formulation; for example, the Sigma‐Aldrich PQQ product is typical of these preparations. As a small redox‐active molecule, PQQ is distinct among nutraceuticals and has been explored in several preclinical contexts for its potential to regulate oxidative stress and promote mitochondrial function (Canovai & Williams, 2025). Consequently, this candidate represents a repurposing opportunity where its established dietary exposure, safety profile as assessed by regulatory bodies such as EFSA, and its unique bioactivity as a mitochondrial modulator may be leveraged to address the mitochondrial dysfunction implicated in dry AMD.

Therapeutic History –  
PQQ has been the subject of intensive biochemical and preclinical investigation over the past decades. Early studies concentrated on its role as a microbial cofactor, but subsequent research has documented that dietary supplementation with PQQ produces measurable effects on mitochondrial‐related metabolism and markers of inflammation in animal models and humans (Canovai & Williams, 2025). In various rodent models, oral PQQ has been shown to modulate mitochondrial number and function, thereby improving outcomes in contexts as diverse as cardiac ischemia/reperfusion, neurodegeneration, and metabolic syndrome (Akagawa, Nakano, & Ikemoto, 2016; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Additionally, EFSA conducted a safety assessment of the PQQ disodium salt formulation as a novel food ingredient and concluded that at proposed supplemental doses (up to 20 mg/day) the width of the safety margin is acceptable relative to animal toxicology data (Turck et al., 2017; Hwang & Willoughby, 2018). In human studies, although clinical trials have largely focused on endpoints such as cognition, inflammatory markers, and lipid metabolism, these trials demonstrate that oral PQQ is bioavailable, well‐tolerated, and can meaningfully impact systemic markers of oxidative stress and energy metabolism (Canovai & Williams, 2025). While no study to date has directly employed PQQ in patients with dry AMD, there is indirect evidence suggesting that PQQ’s capacity to improve cellular bioenergetics may be broadly beneficial in clinical states characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction. Some studies even indicate that PQQ upregulates mitochondrial proteins and improves ATP synthesis in cellular models derived from age‐related macular degeneration donor tissues (Canovai & Williams, 2025), although direct evidence in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) remains sparse. In summary, the therapeutic history of PQQ includes diverse preclinical applications ranging from cardioprotection to neuroprotection, with established safety in both animal and limited human studies, making it a plausible candidate for repurposing in dry AMD where mitochondrial dysfunction is a key pathogenic driver.

Mechanism of Action –  
The molecular basis of PQQ’s bioactivity is multifaceted, centering on its redox chemistry and its ability to modulate mitochondrial biogenesis. Chemically, PQQ is a potent redox‐active o‐quinone that undergoes reversible reduction to its hydroquinone form (PQQH₂) via a rapid semiquinone intermediate. This redox cycling allows PQQ to function both as a free radical scavenger and as an electron‐transfer catalyst. In vitro assays have established that the reduced form, PQQH₂, exhibits robust antioxidant capacity, with reports indicating that its aroxyl radical quenching activity can be significantly greater than that of classical antioxidants such as vitamin C and α‐tocopherol (Canovai & Williams, 2025; Charrier et al., 2024). Through its antioxidant activity, PQQ directly neutralizes reactive oxygen species (ROS) and may protect cellular constituents from oxidative damage.

Beyond its direct radical scavenging, PQQ has been implicated as an inducer of mitochondrial biogenesis. Several mechanistic studies indicate that treatment with PQQ leads to the upregulation of key transcriptional regulators involved in mitochondrial proliferation. Specifically, PQQ treatment has been shown to activate the cAMP response element‐binding protein (CREB), which in turn stimulates the expression of peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator‐1 alpha (PGC‐1α) (Charrier et al., 2024; Canovai & Williams, 2025). PGC‐1α is a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and coordinates the transcriptional activation of nuclear respiratory factors (NRF‐1/NRF‐2) and mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM), all of which are critical for the transcription and replication of mitochondrial DNA. Some studies also suggest that PQQ modulates sirtuin activity, particularly SIRT1 and SIRT3, which are NAD⁺‐dependent deacetylases that regulate mitochondrial function and cellular metabolic homeostasis (Canovai & Williams, 2025). In addition, PQQ has been reported to restore mitochondrial membrane potential, reduce proton leak, and enhance ATP production during oxidative challenge in several cellular systems (Petricca et al., 2025; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Thus, the composite mechanism of action posited for PQQ—which includes both robust redox buffering and the activation of mitochondrial biogenesis via CREB/PGC‐1α signaling—provides a molecular rationale for its use in conditions characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative injury.

Mechanistically, it is also suggested that PQQ may improve the NAD⁺/NADH ratio, thereby favoring the activity of sirtuins, which contributes to a more favorable intracellular redox state and efficient energy utilization (Jonscher, Chowanadisai, & Rucker, 2021). Although these effects have been most clearly demonstrated in hepatic, muscular, and neuronal cell models, they are directly relevant to RPE cells that rely heavily on oxidative phosphorylation for their energy demands and, hence, are particularly vulnerable to mitochondrial decay under chronic oxidative stress—a hallmark of dry AMD pathology. It is important to note that PQQ’s actions are context‐dependent; while low concentrations have been associated with protective effects, some studies suggest that higher doses can induce a pro‐oxidant effect and even impair mitochondrial dynamics in sensitive cellular contexts (Petricca et al., 2025; Turck et al., 2017). This biphasic dose response underscores the need to identify an optimal dosing window that maximizes mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defense without tipping cells into oxidative stress.

Expected Effect –  
The central hypothesis guiding the repurposing of PQQ for dry AMD is that it can stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis in the RPE by upregulating PGC‐1α, thereby increasing the antioxidant capacity and restoring optimal mitochondrial respiration in cells under chronic oxidative injury. In the proposed assay, treatment with PQQ is expected to yield multiple beneficial outcomes. First, by activating CREB and augmenting PGC‐1α expression, PQQ should enhance the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial replication and function, leading to an increased mitochondrial mass within RPE cells (Canovai & Williams, 2025; Charrier et al., 2024).

Second, increased mitochondrial mass and improved electron transport chain efficiency are expected to elevate ATP production, thereby restoring cellular energy stores that are typically depleted in dry AMD due to chronic oxidative damage. Experimental data from other cell types, including neuronal and hepatic cells, have shown that PQQ treatment enhances ATP output and normalizes mitochondrial membrane potential under oxidative stress conditions, suggesting that similar responses might be observed in RPE cells (Petricca et al., 2025; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Third, PQQ is anticipated to upregulate antioxidant enzymes, such as manganese superoxide dismutase (SOD2), which plays a critical role in mitigating ROS accumulation in mitochondria. By lowering oxidative stress levels in RPE cells, PQQ can help maintain cellular homeostasis and prevent the degeneration that is characteristic of dry AMD (Canovai & Williams, 2025).

Additionally, there is emerging evidence that certain studies using donor‐derived RPE cells from AMD patients have demonstrated that PQQ treatment can upregulate mitochondrial proteins and improve ATP generation in these cells (Canovai & Williams, 2025). Although the available data in retinal tissues remain limited, these findings align with the overall rationale; because RPE cells are highly metabolically active and heavily reliant on mitochondrial function, the ability to augment their biogenesis and enhance oxidative phosphorylation directly addresses a critical pathogenic mechanism of dry AMD. Complementing these expected biochemical outcomes, one would predict that functional assays (for instance, assessments of oxygen consumption rate and extracellular acidification rate) will reveal improved mitochondrial respiration and overall metabolic resilience in PQQ‐treated RPE cells.

Overall Evaluation –  
In synthesizing the extensive body of literature, we find that PQQ demonstrates considerable promise as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, based on the following strengths and weaknesses:

Strengths:  
1. Robust Mechanistic Rationale: PQQ’s dual role as an antioxidant and an inducer of mitochondrial biogenesis is well documented. The capacity to elevate PGC‐1α expression and thereby drive mitochondrial proliferation and enhanced energy metabolism is highly relevant given that dry AMD is characterized by RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and heightened oxidative stress (Petricca et al., 2025; Charrier et al., 2024; Canovai & Williams, 2025).  
2. Positive Safety and Bioavailability Data: Numerous preclinical studies, alongside regulatory evaluations (e.g., EFSA’s novel food assessment), indicate that PQQ is orally bioavailable and well tolerated in both animal models and limited human studies. The available toxicology data support the safety of typical supplemental doses (up to 20 mg/day), which is encouraging for repurposing efforts (Turck et al., 2017; Hwang & Willoughby, 2018; Canovai & Williams, 2025).  
3. Broad Therapeutic History: Although PQQ has not been directly tested in dry AMD in clinical settings, its prior use as a dietary supplement and its beneficial effects in neuroprotection, cardioprotection, and metabolic regulation suggest therapeutic potential in conditions underpinned by mitochondrial decay and oxidative stress (Canovai & Williams, 2025).  
4. Hypothesis‐Driven Approach: The specific hypothesis—that PQQ will stimulate RPE mitochondrial biogenesis via upregulation of PGC‐1α to improve cellular resilience against chronic oxidative injury—is both plausible and supported by mechanistic data from other cell types. Given that RPE cells are known to express PGC‐1α and that deficits in mitochondrial function have been implicated in AMD pathology, this provides a strong rationale for further investigation (Canovai & Williams, 2025).

Weaknesses:  
1. Limited Direct Evidence in Ocular Tissues: One of the main gaps in the literature is the paucity of direct preclinical studies involving retinal pigment epithelium or in vivo AMD models. Although there is some suggestive data from studies in retinal ganglion cells and donor‐derived RPE cells, definitive evidence that PQQ can counteract the specific aspects of dry AMD pathology in the retina is currently lacking (Ebeling et al., 2020; Petricca et al., 2025).  
2. Context‐Dependent and Biphasic Effects: Several studies indicate that PQQ’s efficacy is highly dose‐dependent. While low concentrations are cytoprotective by enhancing mitochondrial function, higher doses may exert pro‐oxidant effects and even impair mitochondrial membrane potential in sensitive cell types. Establishing the optimal dosing regimen for RPE cells will be critical to avoid potential deleterious effects (Petricca et al., 2025; Turck et al., 2017).  
3. Ocular Pharmacokinetics Uncertain: Although oral absorption in the gastrointestinal tract has been characterized in animal studies with favorable kinetics, it remains unclear whether orally administered PQQ achieves sufficient concentrations—or even penetrates ocular tissues such as the retina—to exert the desired effects. This issue of tissue‐specific bioavailability is a significant barrier that must be addressed in future pharmacokinetic studies (Hwang & Willoughby, 2018).  
4. Quality of Some Supporting Studies: While a substantial body of research supports PQQ’s bioactivity, some of the literature originates from journals or sources with variable quality. This underscores the need for additional high‐quality, rigorously controlled studies—particularly focused on ocular models—to validate the proposed mechanisms and therapeutic outcomes for dry AMD (Akagawa, Nakano, & Ikemoto, 2016; Hwang & Willoughby, 2018).

In conclusion, based on the available biomedical, clinical, and biochemical literature, PQQ emerges as a promising repurposed candidate for dry AMD. Its well‐documented ability to modulate mitochondrial biogenesis—principally through the activation of CREB and upregulation of PGC‐1α—aligns with the mechanistic requirements for restoring mitochondrial function in RPE cells under chronic oxidative stress, a central feature of dry AMD pathogenesis (Petricca et al., 2025; Charrier et al., 2024; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Moreover, the favorable safety profile indicated by both animal toxicology studies and human supplementation trials, combined with its oral bioavailability, adds significant translational appeal.

However, critical gaps remain. Principal among these is the need for direct evidence from retinal models. Specifically, robust, controlled preclinical studies in RPE cells and animal models of dry AMD must be performed to confirm that PQQ can effectively upregulate mitochondrial biogenesis and confer cytoprotection in ocular tissues. Additionally, further investigation into the optimal dosing strategy is required, particularly given the context‐dependent and potentially biphasic nature of PQQ’s activity, as well as the necessity to ascertain whether oral administration can yield therapeutic concentrations in the retina.

Given these considerations, the recommendation is to advance PQQ as a candidate for further investigation in dry AMD. This progression should involve a series of well‐designed in vitro and in vivo experiments targeting RPE‐specific pathways, coupled with ocular pharmacokinetic studies to evaluate tissue penetration and residence times. Should these studies provide supportive evidence, early‐phase human clinical trials focusing on retinal biomarkers and functional outcomes in dry AMD patients would be warranted.

Overall, while the current literature provides a strong mechanistic rationale and preliminary safety data supporting the repurposing of PQQ for dry AMD, it also highlights the need for targeted ocular studies to bridge the gap between systemic mitochondrial enhancements and specific retinal therapeutic benefits. With these additional investigations, PQQ could potentially emerge as a viable therapeutic option in the armamentarium against dry AMD, addressing the unmet need for treatments that restore RPE mitochondrial resilience and retard degeneration (Canovai & Williams, 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AICAR (5‐Aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide) is a synthetic nucleoside analog originally developed as an AMP mimetic agent that is capable of activating AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) across a range of cell types. It is produced by chemical synthesis and is available commercially (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich A9978), having been studied for several decades in the context of cellular energy metabolism and stress signaling. As a member of a class of compounds that mimic the natural intracellular messenger AMP, AICAR is taken up into cells via adenosine transporters and is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase into its active metabolite, ZMP (5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide monophosphate), which then mimics AMP in its interactions with AMPK (Efstathiou et al., 2020). This compound belongs to a well‐established class of metabolic modulators, and similar agents have been used in experimental settings to modulate glucose uptake, fatty acid oxidation, and overall energy homeostasis in both basic science and translational research contexts (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014). In addition, several preclinical studies have evaluated AICAR’s potential as an “exercise mimetic” due to its ability to enhance energy metabolism in muscle and other tissues, and its synthetic nature allows for reproducible and scalable dosing in research models (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, AICAR was developed primarily as an agent to activate AMPK in metabolic studies and has been investigated in a variety of preclinical models ranging from cancer to cardiovascular disease. In the oncology field, for example, AICAR has been shown to inhibit cancer cell proliferation, induce cell cycle arrest, and promote programmed cell death in several cancer types via AMPK-dependent modulation of pathways such as PI3K-Akt and mTOR (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014; Rattan et al., 2005). Clinical studies, particularly those in the cardiovascular arena, have also evaluated AICAR’s safety profile in the context of ischemia-reperfusion injury, including human trials during cardiac surgery, demonstrating that it can be administered safely in humans (Rattan et al., 2005). In the context of ocular research, AICAR has been studied for its effects on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and other ocular cell types; several studies have demonstrated that AICAR suppresses the production of pro-inflammatory complement components such as complement factor 3 (C3) and complement factor B (CFB) in RPE cells under inflammatory conditions (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017). Although there is no established clinical use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) to date, these preclinical observations, combined with its well-known pharmacological profile, have spurred interest in repurposing AICAR for treating retinal diseases characterized by oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020). Furthermore, studies examining AMPK activators in the eye – including those using AICAR in animal models of uveitis or oxidative stress-induced RPE damage – support the notion that activating this metabolic pathway can protect against retinal degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

Mechanism of Action:  
AICAR exerts its biological activity primarily through the activation of AMPK, a master regulator of cellular energy balance that responds to alterations in the AMP/ATP ratio. Once AICAR is imported into cells through adenosine transporters, it is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase to form ZMP, an analog of AMP. ZMP binds to the regulatory γ subunit of AMPK, causing a conformational change that facilitates AMPK phosphorylation at Thr172 by upstream kinases such as LKB1, thereby fully activating the kinase (Efstathiou et al., 2020). Activated AMPK then phosphorylates a series of downstream targets involved in energy metabolism, including acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) and elements of the mTOR signaling pathway. In RPE cells, this activation is particularly important because AMPK phosphorylates and activates ULK1, a kinase critical for initiating autophagy and mitophagy, thereby promoting the clearance of damaged mitochondria (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Chung et al., 2017).  

A central component of the rationale for using AICAR in dry AMD is its ability to stimulate the transcriptional coactivator PGC-1α. AMPK-mediated phosphorylation of PGC-1α enhances its activity and nuclear translocation, which in turn drives the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant defense, and metabolic adaptation (Hu et al., 2024; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). This mechanism is particularly attractive in dry AMD because mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells is thought to contribute significantly to disease pathogenesis by impairing oxidative phosphorylation, increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and triggering cell senescence or death (Tong et al., 2022; Rego, 2023). In addition to these AMPK-dependent effects, some studies have reported that AICAR exerts certain effects independent of AMPK activation. For instance, AICAR has been shown to suppress TNF-α-induced complement factor expression by mechanisms that do not involve AMPK, suggesting that alternative signaling pathways or direct modulation of transcription factor activity might also contribute to its overall activity profile (Chung et al., 2017; Kirchner et al., 2018). These AMPK-independent actions could either broaden the therapeutic potential of AICAR in modulating inflammatory responses or introduce complexity into its activity profile that will need to be carefully isolated and understood (Kirchner et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2024).  

Furthermore, AICAR has been observed to affect mitochondrial dynamics not only by stimulating biogenesis through PGC-1α activation but also by modifying autophagic flux through mTOR inhibition. In models of RPE oxidative stress, where excessive ROS levels lead to mitochondrial fragmentation and accumulation of dysfunctional organelles, AICAR-induced AMPK activation facilitates the clearance of damaged mitochondria via mitophagy, thus restoring mitochondrial quality and energy production (Fisher et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2024). Moreover, experimental evidence suggests that AICAR can modulate the balance between cellular glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation by shifting metabolism toward a more energy-efficient, oxidative phenotype, thereby increasing the overall oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and potentially improving cellular resilience under oxidative stress (Chan et al., 2020; Fisher, 2022).  

Expected Effect:  
Given its mechanisms of action, the expected effect of AICAR in an assay aimed at treating dry AMD would be multifaceted. In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress—a hallmark of dry AMD—AICAR treatment is expected to lead to robust activation of AMPK, as measured by increased phosphorylation of both AMPK and its downstream substrates such as ACC and ULK1 (Guo et al., 2018; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). This activation should in turn upregulate PGC-1α, resulting in enhanced transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, improved mitochondrial DNA replication, and an increased capacity for ATP production (Hu et al., 2024). As damaged mitochondria are a major source of ROS in stressed RPE cells, the stimulation of autophagy and mitophagy is anticipated to selectively clear these dysfunctional organelles, reducing cellular oxidative stress and preventing the secondary damage that contributes to RPE degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

In addition to these metabolic effects, AICAR is also expected to attenuate inflammatory responses within the RPE and adjacent retinal tissues. For instance, by modulating the activity of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) and reducing the expression of inflammatory mediators such as tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and complement components (e.g., C3 and CFB), AICAR would help to create a less pro-inflammatory microenvironment that could further protect RPE cells from damage (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017; Kirchner et al., 2018). These effects are particularly pertinent given that chronic, low-grade inflammation coupled with complement dysregulation is a recognized component of dry AMD pathogenesis.  

At the cellular level, the outcome of AICAR-induced AMPK activation is expected to manifest as enhanced mitochondrial function, improved energy charge (ATP/AMP ratio), reduced ROS accumulation, and, ultimately, a restoration of normal metabolic and autophagic flux in RPE cells (Fisher et al., 2022; Fisher, 2022). This improved bioenergetic profile should translate into protection against RPE cell death, potentially slowing or halting the progression of geographic atrophy associated with dry AMD (Yu et al., 2024; Si et al., 2023). Moreover, since RPE dysfunction in AMD also involves a reduction in the phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, AICAR’s modulatory effects on autophagy may indirectly help to restore the homeostatic functions of RPE cells, reducing the accumulation of damaging lipofuscin and drusen material (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Sung et al., 2015). In summary, the expected effect is a dual-action benefit—mitigation of oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum stresses via improved mitochondrial dynamics and an anti-inflammatory effect stemming from a reduction in complement activation and NF-κB-driven cytokine production (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020).

AICAR represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration owing to its robust and well-characterized mechanism of action via AMPK activation. The strengths of this candidate lie in its dual capacity to modulate critical pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis: on one hand, AICAR enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and promotes the removal of damaged mitochondria through autophagy/mitophagy, and on the other, it attenuates inflammatory cascades that exacerbate RPE cell damage (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hu et al., 2024). The ability of AICAR to upregulate PGC-1α is particularly compelling because mitochondrial dysfunction is now widely recognized as a central element in dry AMD. Preclinical studies have illustrated that dysregulation of mitochondrial function in RPE cells—a decrease in oxidative phosphorylation capacity, increased ROS production, and impaired clearance of damaged organelles—is pivotal in the initiation and progression of AMD (Tong et al., 2022; Rego, 2023). Thus, a compound like AICAR that can simultaneously restore mitochondrial health and mitigate inflammatory responses offers a multifaceted approach to disease modification.  

From the therapeutic history perspective, AICAR has been extensively studied in various preclinical models, including those of ocular inflammation and oxidative stress in RPE cells. Its ability to safely activate AMPK in vivo has been demonstrated across multiple species and contexts, including settings that mimic some aspects of AMD-related stress, such as endotoxin-induced uveitis and sodium iodate-induced RPE damage (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Chan et al., 2020). Additionally, the compound’s known clinical safety profile in human studies—albeit in contexts outside ophthalmology—provides an encouraging starting point for repurposing it for dry AMD, where no approved therapeutics currently exist (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017).

First, while AMPK activation is generally beneficial for energy homeostasis and autophagy, certain studies have indicated that AICAR’s effects on RPE cell biology might be context-dependent. For instance, some experimental reports have shown that AICAR can reduce the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments by RPE cells—a process that is essential for retinal health—which may represent a double-edged sword if not carefully titrated (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Yu et al., 2024). Differential responses have also been observed between healthy and diseased donor RPE cells, implying that “metabolic memory” or cellular adaptation may influence drug responsiveness (Fisher et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2017). These considerations suggest that while the theoretical underpinnings for using AICAR in dry AMD are solid, the translation of these effects into clinical efficacy may require careful optimization of dosing, delivery, and patient selection.  

Another potential limitation is related to its broad mechanism of action. AICAR activates several metabolic pathways that are intertwined with many aspects of cellular physiology. While this pleiotropy provides the therapeutic benefit of addressing multiple dysregulated pathways in AMD simultaneously, it may also increase the risk of off-target effects or metabolic disturbances in tissues outside the retina (Rattan et al., 2005; Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014). In summary, the overall evaluation of AICAR as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. Moving forward, it will be critical to further elucidate the detailed cellular and molecular responses to AICAR in human RPE cells, determine the optimal dosing and delivery parameters specific to the ocular environment, and perform in vivo studies that mimic the complex pathobiology of dry AMD. With these additional efforts, AICAR could eventually emerge as a valuable addition to the limited therapeutic arsenal available for managing this debilitating condition.

However, several challenges remain: the dual nature of its effects (both AMPK-dependent and independent), the possibility of adverse effects on key RPE functions such as phagocytosis, and the need for precise ocular drug delivery methods. Therefore, while AICAR is an exciting candidate with considerable mechanistic appeal, its translation from bench to bedside in the treatment of dry AMD will require further detailed studies to fully map its therapeutic window, safety profile, and efficacy in human subjects (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014; Rego, 2023; Kamoshita et al., 2014). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Deferiprone is a synthetic iron‐chelating agent originally developed for the treatment of transfusional iron overload disorders, particularly in patients with thalassemia major. It belongs to the hydroxypyridinone class of therapeutic compounds and is characterized by its low molecular weight and lipophilic nature, features that allow it to penetrate cell membranes and cross the blood–brain and blood–retinal barriers (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). Chemically, deferiprone is a bidentate ligand that interacts with iron by coordinating via its hydroxypyridinone groups, forming a neutral complex in a 3:1 stoichiometry with ferric iron (Fe3+), although some studies note its affinity for both Fe3+ and Fe2+ under certain conditions (Li et al., 2023). The synthetic origins of deferiprone involve chemical design strategies aimed at generating small, orally active chelators with selective affinity for iron over other metals such as zinc, copper, and aluminium (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). As a member of the iron chelator drug class, deferiprone’s established use in treating systemic iron overload syndromes has provided it with a significant clinical track record over several decades, forming the basis for its repurposing in disorders where iron-induced oxidative damage plays a role.  

Therapeutic History:  
Deferiprone has been used clinically as an orally administered iron chelator in the management of transfusional iron overload, notably in patients with thalassemia major. This usage is supported by multiple clinical studies and reviews that address both its efficacy in reducing systemic iron burden as well as its associated hematologic risks, such as agranulocytosis and neutropenia, which occur in approximately 1% of patients (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). Beyond its systemic application, preclinical models have demonstrated deferiprone’s potential for retinal protection. Several animal studies report that deferiprone, when administered systemically, can reduce retinal and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) iron levels in models of iron overload or light-induced degeneration and produce improvements in oxidative stress markers and retinal functional indices (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Bhoiwala & Dunaief, 2016). Although deferiprone has not been widely tested or approved specifically for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar ocular conditions in clinical trials, its documented experimental benefits in animal retinal models along with its established clinical safety profile in iron overload therapy have prompted its consideration for repurposing in dry AMD where iron-induced oxidative injury is implicated (Shahandeh et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2021; Ueda et al., 2018).  

Mechanism of Action:  
Deferiprone functions primarily by chelating labile iron, thereby limiting the pool of redox active iron that can participate in the Fenton reaction—a process in which ferrous iron (Fe2+) reacts with hydrogen peroxide to produce highly reactive hydroxyl radicals. The molecular mechanism of deferiprone is based on its bidentate hydroxypyridinone structure that binds Fe3+ to form a stable neutral complex in a 3:1 chelator to iron ratio, a coordination chemistry that has been well documented in several studies (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). This complex formation effectively reduces the availability of free iron in the intracellular labile iron pool, thereby diminishing iron-catalyzed reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. In addition, some data suggest that deferiprone may also interact with ferrous iron under certain conditions, contributing further to its antioxidant effects by interrupting redox cycling associated with both Fe3+ and Fe2+ species (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2021).  

From a biochemical standpoint, iron accumulation in the RPE and surrounding retinal tissues is known to promote lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial oxidative stress, leading to cellular dysfunction and death—a pathomechanism observed in dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). EUK-8 is a synthetic catalytic antioxidant that belongs to the manganese‐based salen complexes, a class of low molecular weight enzyme mimetics engineered to replicate key activities of endogenous antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). The manganese center in EUK-8 undergoes reversible redox cycling between Mn(III) and Mn(II) oxidation states; this reversible cycling is essential for its dual enzyme-mimetic action, as it enables catalytic dismutation of superoxide radicals into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide and further conversion of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, thereby mimicking the combined action of SOD and catalase (Fernandes, 2010; Rouco et al., 2020a). The salen complex scaffold not only confers redox activity but also provides a tunable electronic and steric environment through modification of substituents on the ligand framework, which in turn dictates the redox potential, proton-dissociation properties, and overall catalytic efficacy (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020b). Because of its synthetic origin, EUK-8 is both cost-effective and easily reproducible, making it an appealing candidate for repurposing in therapeutic areas where enhanced antioxidant defenses are required, such as in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rosenthal et al., 2011).

The EUK series of compounds, which includes EUK-8, have been extensively studied in a plethora of preclinical models addressing a wide range of diseases linked to oxidative stress, including ischemic brain injury, neurodegeneration, cardiac injury, and even lifespan extension models in Caenorhabditis elegans and SOD2 knockout mice (Rouco et al., 2020a). At the molecular level, EUK-8 functions as a catalytic antioxidant by mimicking two key enzymes involved in the detoxification of reactive oxygen species. First, it catalyzes the dismutation of superoxide (O₂•⁻) by virtue of its manganese center undergoing cyclic redox reactions between the Mn(III) and Mn(II) states; in one half-reaction, the Mn(III) state accepts an electron from superoxide to become Mn(II), while in the subsequent half-reaction, Mn(II) is reoxidized to Mn(III) by another molecule of superoxide, resulting in the conversion of superoxide to molecular oxygen and hydrogen peroxide (Fernandes, 2010; Batinić-Haberle et al., 2016). 3. Mechanism of Action  
The molecular mechanisms underpinning the actions of Urolithin A are multifaceted and involve intricate interactions across several cellular pathways. In summary, the detailed biochemistry of UA illustrates that its mechanism of action involves a well-coordinated activation of autophagic processes through both the PINK1/Parkin axis for mitophagy and the SQSTM1/p62 pathway for lysophagy, with auxiliary support from AMPK/ULK1 and SIRT-mediated signaling. 5. Overall Evaluation  
In evaluating Urolithin A as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and potential areas for further investigation emerge. Its capacity to engage multiple autophagic pathways—specifically, the PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy and the SQSTM1/p62-dependent lysophagy—provides a multifaceted approach to mitigating RPE degeneration. Further mechanistic studies in RPE-specific models will be necessary to delineate the relative contributions of these pathways and to optimize dosing and formulation strategies accordingly.

Another potential weakness is the translational gap between preclinical studies and clinical application in dry AMD. Although UA has shown promise in animal models of retinal degeneration, human disease is complex, and dry AMD is known for its multifactorial etiology. The pharmacokinetic properties of UA, including its relatively short half-life and the challenges associated with ensuring adequate ocular bioavailability, might necessitate novel delivery strategies for effective retinal targeting. Formulation development—potentially involving sustained-release systems or ocular-specific delivery vehicles—may be required to overcome these hurdles (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025). Additionally, while the evidence from non-ocular (e.g., muscle and neural) studies is robust, direct clinical evidence in AMD patients remains sparse, necessitating carefully designed human trials to confirm efficacy and safety in this specific population.

It is also important to contextualize UA’s potential within the current landscape of AMD treatments. While existing therapies for wet AMD (e.g., anti-VEGF agents) have transformed clinical outcomes, there remains no established treatment for dry AMD. The multifaceted mode of action of UA—targeting mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and inflammation—offers a unique therapeutic approach that could complement or, in some cases, provide an alternative to emerging interventions. However, comparative studies against other experimental agents will be critical to fully establish its translational relevance and competitive advantage in the therapeutic space (Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Its origin as a naturally derived, gut-microbiota transformation product provides a favorable starting point from a safety perspective. Nonetheless, for the successful translation of UA into a clinically effective therapy for dry AMD, several challenges need to be addressed. Detailed mechanistic insights specifically in RPE cells are required to understand the relative importance of the PINK1/Parkin versus the lysophagy pathway. Optimizing drug delivery to ensure sustained retinal bioavailability and addressing potential issues related to its pharmacokinetic profile are also key areas that will require further research. Finally, controlled clinical studies in AMD patients will be essential to validate the promising preclinical findings and to ensure that the observed benefits in animal models translate into meaningful clinical outcomes.

In conclusion, based on the comprehensive literature reviewed from biochemical, clinical, and biomedical sources, Urolithin A demonstrates significant potential as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its established ability to enhance mitochondrial quality control through both mitophagy and lysophagy, alongside its additional anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, offers a novel mechanism to counteract the progressive degeneration observed in RPE cells during AMD. Given the encouraging preclinical data and a robust safety profile already evidenced in other indications, further investigations—particularly those focusing on RPE-specific mechanisms and optimized ocular drug delivery—are warranted to fully ascertain UA’s clinical potential in halting or reversing geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024; Jayatunga et al., 2021).

L-Carnitine is a naturally occurring quaternary ammonium compound, chemically defined as β-hydroxy-γ-trimethylaminobutyrate, that is both derived from the diet (predominantly found in animal-based foods such as red meat) and biosynthesized endogenously from the essential amino acids lysine and methionine via a vitamin C–dependent pathway primarily in the liver and kidneys (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Mollica et al., 2017). Historically, L-carnitine was first identified as a constituent of muscle tissue in the early 20th century and was later linked to its high content in meat, leading to its designation as “vitamin T” in certain insect models (Mollica et al., 2017). As a member of the carnitine family, it belongs to the class of metabolic cofactors or nutraceutical agents whose primary function is to shuttle activated long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondrial matrix, where they undergo β-oxidation, thereby facilitating aerobic energy production and maintaining the intracellular acyl-CoA/CoA balance (Moos et al., 2017; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). This class of compounds has historically been used as dietary supplements to treat primary and secondary carnitine deficiency, as well as in various metabolic and mitochondrial disorders (Flanagan et al., 2010). Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, the carnitine family has a long record of use in addressing conditions where fatty acid oxidation is impaired. L-Carnitine has been employed effectively as a life-saving therapy in primary carnitine deficiency—a condition in which mutations of the carnitine transporter (OCTN2) impair cellular uptake—and also in secondary deficiencies associated with conditions like renal failure, liver disease, and certain inborn errors of metabolism (Flanagan et al., 2010). Beyond classical deficiency syndromes, both L-carnitine and its acetylated derivative (acetyl-L-carnitine) have been investigated in a broad range of clinical contexts, including cardiovascular diseases, diabetic complications, and neurodegenerative disorders. For example, acetyl-L-carnitine has been shown to improve parameters of visual function in patients with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and to confer neuroprotective effects in Alzheimer’s disease and mild cognitive impairment (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Calabrese et al., 2009).  
In ophthalmology, while most clinical studies have focused on the use of carnitine derivatives for systemic metabolic or neuroprotective effects, there is preclinical evidence supporting an ocular role. Animal studies have identified high intraocular concentrations of carnitine in the lens and other ocular tissues, hinting at a physiological role in maintaining ocular metabolic balance and osmotic homeostasis (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). Investigations into the protective effects of L-carnitine against oxidative damage, including its potential to safeguard retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and other ocular tissues, provide a rationale for its application in dry AMD, particularly in the context of geographic atrophy where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central features (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c). Moreover, combination therapy regimens incorporating acetyl-L-carnitine with n-3 fatty acids and coenzyme Q10 have also been trialed in experimental settings to address energy metabolism in retinal tissues (Shamsi et al., 2007). Despite these promising findings, direct clinical use of L-carnitine as monotherapy for dry AMD has not been extensively reported, thus making its repurposing an area that merits focused research to bridge the gap between its established metabolic functions and its potential application in retinal degeneration (Flanagan et al., 2010; Mollica et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
The central biochemical role of L-carnitine is to facilitate the transport of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle—a process that is critical for β-oxidation and ATP production. This shuttle is mediated by mitochondrial enzymes such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT-1) on the outer mitochondrial membrane, which converts acyl-CoA to acyl-carnitine, and carnitine acyltransferase (also known as carnitine acetyltransferase or CAT) within the mitochondria that re-forms acyl-CoA for oxidation (Moos et al., 2017; Jones et al., 2010). This process not only fuels ATP generation via the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation but also helps regulate the cellular acyl-CoA/CoA ratio, indirectly influencing multiple metabolic pathways (Surai, 2015).

Its established role in promoting mitochondrial β-oxidation and energy production, combined with demonstrated antioxidant and osmoprotective actions, provides a strong mechanistic rationale for addressing the metabolic and oxidative stress components of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Jones et al., 2010). The compound’s extensive history of use as a dietary supplement and its well-characterized safety profile—in which high oral doses have been administered with minimal toxicity—support its potential for repurposing in an ocular application (Flanagan et al., 2010; Mollica et al., 2017).  
However, there are potential limitations that merit cautious consideration. Direct evidence of L-carnitine’s efficacy in RPE cells specifically within the context of dry AMD is currently limited. While preclinical studies in non-ocular tissues and some ocular models suggest beneficial mitochondrial and antioxidant effects, the precise dosing, ocular bioavailability, and long-term impact on retinal degeneration remain to be rigorously established. Moreover, while L-carnitine can enhance mitochondrial function, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD implies that a monotherapy approach might not be sufficient; a combination therapy strategy—potentially incorporating other mitochondrial or antioxidant agents—may ultimately prove more effective (Shamsi et al., 2007; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a).  
In summary, the strengths of L-carnitine include its well-established role in cellular energy metabolism, its safety profile and widespread clinical use in other metabolic conditions, and its potential to mitigate ROS production and oxidative damage through enhanced fatty acid oxidation. The weaknesses primarily lie in the current paucity of direct evidence in ocular models of dry AMD and the challenges associated with ensuring adequate drug delivery to the RPE in vivo. Nonetheless, given the overall mechanistic promise and the favorable tolerability observed in numerous studies, L-carnitine warrants further investigation – with a focus on in vitro RPE assays under condition of lipid overload and oxidative stress, followed by in vivo preclinical models of geographic atrophy – to validate its efficacy as a repurposed therapy for dry AMD (Jones et al., 2010; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c; Ates et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2024).  
Overall, I recommend proceeding with targeted experiments to assess mitochondrial respiration, ROS levels, and cell survival in RPE cultures treated with L-carnitine. These studies should be complemented with investigations of tissue distribution following ocular delivery to address bioavailability concerns. This comprehensive evaluation supports the potential of L-carnitine as a metabolic and antioxidant therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, while also highlighting areas where additional data are needed before clinical translation.

1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Urolithin A (UA) is a naturally occurring polyphenolic metabolite that is generated in humans via the microbial transformation of dietary ellagitannins, which are abundant in pomegranates, berries, walnuts, and other fruits and nuts. UA belongs to the class of gut-derived α-benzocoumarin compounds and is produced through the specific metabolic activities of intestinal bacteria on ellagitannins and ellagic acid. The discovery of UA emerged from studies aimed at understanding the beneficial effects of diets rich in polyphenols on aging and cellular health, and its structure was elucidated as a 6H-dibenzopyran-6-one derivative. In general, compounds of this class are known for their anti-oxidative, anti-inflammatory, and pro-mitophagic properties. Over time, UA has been investigated increasingly for its ability to modulate mitochondrial function and cellular homeostasis, garnering interest in its potential applications beyond traditional nutritional supplementation. Its multifaceted biological activities have been documented in several preclinical studies where it enhanced mitochondrial quality control, improved muscle endurance in aging populations, and mitigated neurodegenerative processes by clearing dysfunctional mitochondria, lending support to its candidacy as a repurposed drug for chronic conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Makarov & Korkotian, 2023).  

Historically, naturally derived compounds with similar mechanisms of action have been used to address age-related cellular dysfunction. UA, however, stands out by virtue of its dual ability to invoke both mitophagy and lysophagy, which are critical for the removal of damaged organelles—key processes implicated in aging and neurodegeneration. This compound is not synthesized chemically in the traditional pharmaceutical sense; rather, its production relies on the interplay between dietary intake and the gut microbiota, reinforcing the concept that natural metabolic products can be harnessed as therapeutic agents. Its inclusion in the spectrum of therapeutics aimed at cellular rejuvenation has sparked significant interest, particularly because its widespread availability in the human diet and favorable safety profile, as observed in early clinical trials, set a promising foundation for further drug development (Maksimović et al., 2025; Liu, 2022).

2. Therapeutic History  
Urolithin A has been extensively studied in the context of aging and degenerative diseases, and its therapeutic history spans several biomedical, clinical, and biochemical investigations. Preclinical studies have shown that UA is effective in enhancing mitophagy, thereby promoting the clearance of damaged mitochondria. In animal models, UA supplementation has been correlated with improved mitochondrial function and increased muscle endurance, which has led to its exploration as an “anti-aging” agent. Notably, several clinical trials have confirmed its safety in elderly populations, with doses up to 2,500 mg/day being well tolerated and associated with improvements in mitochondrial biomarkers in skeletal muscle (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Liu, 2022).  

In the realm of neurodegeneration, UA has been recognized for its neuroprotective activities. Studies have demonstrated that UA can ameliorate cognitive impairment and reduce inflammatory markers, suggesting benefits in neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Fehér et al., 2022). Importantly, recent investigations have extended the focus to ocular health. Preclinical models of retinal degeneration—particularly those mimicking dry AMD—have emerged as critical systems in which UA’s multifactorial actions are being tested. In models employing sodium iodate (SI) to induce retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) damage, UA treatment resulted in enhanced RPE cell survival, restoration of autophagic flux, and preservation of visual function (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). These studies underscore UA’s potential in mitigating geographic atrophy, a defining feature of dry AMD.  

Beyond its direct mitochondrial effects, UA has been evaluated for its impact on lysosomal function. Some reports indicate that UA exerts potent neuroprotective benefits by promoting SQSTM1/p62-dependent lysophagy, leading to the clearance of damaged lysosomes and restoration of cellular proteostasis. This lysophagy mechanism appears to be crucial in maintaining retinal cellular homeostasis and preventing RPE atrophy, a process that is marked by an accumulation of dysfunctional organelles and consequent oxidative stress in AMD (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). Although direct clinical use of UA in the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular diseases has not yet been fully realized, the wealth of preclinical evidence—particularly from relevant animal models—provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in this context. In summary, UA’s therapeutic history demonstrates its utility across multiple age-related pathologies, with growing evidence supporting its potential application in dry age-related macular degeneration (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

3. Mechanism of Action  
The molecular mechanisms underpinning the actions of Urolithin A are multifaceted and involve intricate interactions across several cellular pathways. Central to UA’s mechanism is its ability to induce selective autophagy, a process that includes both mitophagy and lysophagy, leading to the clearance of damaged mitochondria and lysosomes, respectively. Under normal physiological conditions, mitochondria that lose membrane potential become marked for degradation through the action of PINK1 (PTEN-induced kinase 1), which accumulates on the outer mitochondrial membrane. This accumulation results in the recruitment and activation of Parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase that ubiquitinates mitochondrial surface proteins, thereby flagging them for autophagic degradation. UA has been shown to upregulate the PINK1/Parkin pathway, thereby enhancing the clearance of dysfunctional mitochondria and ensuring mitochondrial quality control (Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024; Jayatunga et al., 2021).  

In addition to its role in mitophagy, UA has been demonstrated to elicit pronounced effects on lysosomal recycling processes through the promotion of SQSTM1/p62-dependent lysophagy. This pathway is critical because damaged lysosomes, if not effectively removed, can contribute to cellular toxicity and inflammation. The engagement of p62 in the targeting of these vesicles for autophagosome formation has been observed as a necessary step in the restoration of autophagic flux within RPE cells (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). The dual activation of mitophagy and lysophagy by UA helps mitigate the accumulation of damaged organelles, thereby reducing the levels of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) and subsequent oxidative stress.

At the biochemical level, UA influences several upstream signaling pathways. Notably, it activates the AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)/ULK1 axis—a key regulator of autophagy. Activation of AMPK leads to phosphorylation of ULK1, kick-starting the autophagy process, and is associated with improved energy balance and mitochondrial turnover. This activation is complemented by an upregulation of factors such as PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha), which is instrumental in mitochondrial biogenesis. Together, these events not only promote the removal of impaired mitochondria but also support the generation of new, functional mitochondria, thereby restoring mitochondrial homeostasis (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Furthermore, the anti-inflammatory properties of UA are closely tied to its capacity to modulate oxidative stress. By clearing mitochondria that are prone to leaking mtROS, UA indirectly diminishes the activation of pro-inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB and AP-1, which have been implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. UA’s activation of SIRT1, SIRT3, and AMPK also play a role in upregulating antioxidant defenses; for instance, the enhanced transcription of Nrf2-dependent genes contributes to a robust antioxidative response. These molecular interactions collectively participate in mitigating the inflammatory milieu that is characteristic of neurodegenerative conditions and retinal disorders (Makarov & Korkotian, 2023; Zhang et al., 2025; Jayatunga et al., 2021).

In the context of retinal degeneration, several studies have delineated how UA’s molecular actions translate into cytoprotective outcomes. In SI-induced retinal injury models, the re-establishment of autophagic flux by UA is correlated with reduced RPE cell death and preservation of photoreceptor function. Although some findings suggest that UA’s neuroprotective effects in these models are independent of PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, there is substantial evidence that UA comprehensively enhances cellular quality control mechanisms through both mitophagy and lysophagy. This dichotomy might reflect the compound’s capability to engage multiple parallel pathways to ensure the efficient clearance of damaged organelles (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Fehér et al., 2022). Given that the retina is especially sensitive to oxidative stress and that impaired mitochondrial dynamics are a hallmark of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD, these molecular mechanisms underscore UA’s therapeutic potential.

At a more granular level, it is worth noting that UA appears to influence the expression levels of key mitophagy-related proteins not only at the post-translational level but also transcriptionally. For instance, treatment with UA has been associated with increased expression of Parkin and proteins involved in the formation of autophagosomes, such as BECN1, further reinforcing its role in maintaining mitochondrial and lysosomal integrity. This transcriptional regulation may be mediated by the activation of transcription factors such as FOXO, which have been implicated in cellular stress responses and longevity pathways. As mitochondrial dysfunction contributes significantly to the pathology of dry AMD, the ability of UA to simultaneously promote the degradation of damaged mitochondria and stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis positions it as a strong candidate for addressing the underlying etiologies of RPE degeneration (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

In summary, the detailed biochemistry of UA illustrates that its mechanism of action involves a well-coordinated activation of autophagic processes through both the PINK1/Parkin axis for mitophagy and the SQSTM1/p62 pathway for lysophagy, with auxiliary support from AMPK/ULK1 and SIRT-mediated signaling. This comprehensive modulation of cellular clearance pathways is critical in contexts where mitochondrial dysfunction and lysosomal impairment drive disease progression, such as in dry age-related macular degeneration (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

4. Expected Effect  
The central hypothesis behind repurposing Urolithin A for dry AMD posits that the compound enhances PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby accelerating the clearance of damaged mitochondria that contribute to excessive mtROS production. In the cellular assays designed to evaluate this therapeutic intervention, the expected effect would be a measurable reduction in mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress within RPE cells, ultimately leading to improved cellular viability and resistance to atrophy.  
 
Experimental models of RPE degeneration, particularly those utilizing sodium iodate (SI) as a toxic insult, have provided a platform for assessing the cytoprotective properties of UA. In these models, UA treatment leads to a restoration of autophagic flux—a critical determinant of cellular health—by enhancing both the degradation of impaired mitochondria and the recycling of damaged lysosomes through the p62-dependent pathway. The net effect is a significant decrease in RPE cell death and, consequently, the preservation of photoreceptor cells and visual function. This outcome is particularly relevant for dry AMD, a condition characterized by geographic atrophy of the RPE and subsequent photoreceptor degeneration (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024).

At the molecular level, the activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway by UA is expected to facilitate the tagging of dysfunctional mitochondria for autophagic removal. Consequently, a reduction in mtROS levels would follow, as damaged mitochondria are a major source of these reactive species. In parallel, the activation of AMPK/ULK1 signaling by UA further promotes autophagosome formation, ensuring that the cell’s degradative capacity is optimized to handle the increased load of dysfunctional organelles. The coordinated activation of these pathways not only improves mitochondrial quality control but also indirectly suppresses downstream inflammatory cascades that are typically exacerbated by oxidative stress. For instance, by reducing mtROS levels, UA is anticipated to attenuate the activation of pro-inflammatory transcription factors such as NF-κB, thereby contributing to a more quiescent cellular environment supportive of RPE survival (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

More specifically, in the assay proposed by the research team, RPE cells would be evaluated for changes in markers of mitophagy and lysophagy as well as for functional readouts of mitochondrial health. Biochemical assays might include quantification of PINK1 and Parkin recruitment to mitochondria, measurement of autophagic flux using LC3 conversion assays, and assessment of p62 levels. Given that studies in animal models have shown that UA treatment not only restores autophagic flux but also leads to increased cone survival and improved visual function, it is reasonable to expect that similar beneficial effects could be recapitulated in RPE cells in vitro (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Another anticipated effect of UA treatment in RPE cells is the upregulation of mitochondrial biogenesis. The activation of AMPK and the consequent stimulation of PGC-1α are critical steps in fostering the production of new mitochondria, which serve to replace those that have been degraded. In evaluating Urolithin A as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and potential areas for further investigation emerge. First and foremost, UA offers a robust safety profile supported by both preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials in elderly populations, where it has been administered at relatively high doses without observable toxicity or adverse events (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Liu, 2022). This favorable safety and pharmacokinetic profile is critical given the generally conservative approach required when developing treatments for chronic, age-related conditions like AMD.

The molecular versatility of UA is another significant strength. Its capacity to engage multiple autophagic pathways—specifically, the PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy and the SQSTM1/p62-dependent lysophagy—provides a multifaceted approach to mitigating RPE degeneration. Given that the pathogenesis of dry AMD involves a complex interplay of mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and inflammation, the ability of UA to target these processes simultaneously renders it a particularly attractive candidate (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). Moreover, its ability to mitigate inflammatory signaling and reduce mtROS production adds another layer of protective activity that is critical in managing chronic retinal degeneration.

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and challenges warrant consideration. One area of potential ambiguity concerns the precise mechanistic contributions of the PINK1/Parkin pathway versus the SQSTM1/p62-mediated lysophagy in mediating UA’s protective effects. Further mechanistic studies in RPE-specific models will be necessary to delineate the relative contributions of these pathways and to optimize dosing and formulation strategies accordingly.

Another potential weakness is the translational gap between preclinical studies and clinical application in dry AMD. Although UA has shown promise in animal models of retinal degeneration, human disease is complex, and dry AMD is known for its multifactorial etiology. The pharmacokinetic properties of UA, including its relatively short half-life and the challenges associated with ensuring adequate ocular bioavailability, might necessitate novel delivery strategies for effective retinal targeting. Formulation development—potentially involving sustained-release systems or ocular-specific delivery vehicles—may be required to overcome these hurdles (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025). Additionally, while the evidence from non-ocular (e.g., muscle and neural) studies is robust, direct clinical evidence in AMD patients remains sparse, necessitating carefully designed human trials to confirm efficacy and safety in this specific population.

It is also important to contextualize UA’s potential within the current landscape of AMD treatments. While existing therapies for wet AMD (e.g., anti-VEGF agents) have transformed clinical outcomes, there remains no established treatment for dry AMD. The multifaceted mode of action of UA—targeting mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and inflammation—offers a unique therapeutic approach that could complement or, in some cases, provide an alternative to emerging interventions. However, comparative studies against other experimental agents will be critical to fully establish its translational relevance and competitive advantage in the therapeutic space (Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Overall, Urolithin A presents several compelling attributes that support its development as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its origin as a naturally derived, gut-microbiota transformation product provides a favorable starting point from a safety perspective. Preclinical studies consistently demonstrate its ability to enhance autophagic clearance mechanisms, reduce oxidative damage, and improve cell survival in models that recapitulate key features of AMD. The ability of UA to simultaneously stimulate both mitophagy and lysophagy—the former via the PINK1/Parkin pathway and the latter via p62-dependent mechanisms—positions it as a multi-targeted intervention capable of addressing the multifactorial pathology of RPE degeneration (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Nonetheless, for the successful translation of UA into a clinically effective therapy for dry AMD, several challenges need to be addressed. Detailed mechanistic insights specifically in RPE cells are required to understand the relative importance of the PINK1/Parkin versus the lysophagy pathway. Optimizing drug delivery to ensure sustained retinal bioavailability and addressing potential issues related to its pharmacokinetic profile are also key areas that will require further research. Finally, controlled clinical studies in AMD patients will be essential to validate the promising preclinical findings and to ensure that the observed benefits in animal models translate into meaningful clinical outcomes.

In conclusion, based on the comprehensive literature reviewed from biochemical, clinical, and biomedical sources, Urolithin A demonstrates significant potential as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its established ability to enhance mitochondrial quality control through both mitophagy and lysophagy, alongside its additional anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, offers a novel mechanism to counteract the progressive degeneration observed in RPE cells during AMD.
