Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Liproxstatin-1 is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor of ferroptosis that was originally discovered using phenotypic high-throughput screening in systems where ferroptosis was induced by either genetic deletion of GPX4 or by glutathione depletion with agents like erastin (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69). Its chemical identity is tied to a unique spiroquinoxalinamine scaffold, which places it in the class of aromatic amine radical-trapping antioxidants (RTAs) – compounds well known in industrial settings to protect hydrocarbon products from autoxidation, as well as in biomedical research to block oxidative lipid chain reactions (Scarpellini, 2023, pp. 41–45; Angeli, Shah, Pratt, & Conrad, 2017, pp. 6–8). In contrast to classical phenolic antioxidants such as α-tocopherol, Liproxstatin-1 is designed to operate in the lipid bilayer, where its aminic (or diarylamine) moieties are less hindered by nonproductive hydrogen-bonding interactions with phospholipid headgroups, thus allowing rapid hydrogen-atom transfer to lipid peroxyl radicals (Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). Although detailed synthetic routes are not provided in the available reports, the discovery process clearly identifies Liproxstatin-1 as a lead candidate that emerged from unbiased cell-based screens aimed at identifying compounds that preserve cell viability in the absence of GPX4 function (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). Its categorization as an RTA is significant because this class of compounds has a long history of being used to inhibit free radical–mediated damage in both industrial and biological contexts (Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6).

Therapeutic History:  
The preclinical history of Liproxstatin-1 is rich with evidence supporting its role as a potent inhibitor of ferroptosis. Early studies demonstrated that Liproxstatin-1 acts at low nanomolar concentrations to prevent ferroptotic cell death in mouse embryonic fibroblasts as well as in specialized cells rendered vulnerable by GPX4 inactivation (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Angeli et al., 2014, p. 10). Beyond in vitro cell survival assays, Liproxstatin-1 has been evaluated in vivo where it has shown remarkable protective effects in models of acute tissue injury including genetic GPX4 deficiency, which induces acute renal failure, and in ischaemia/reperfusion models of liver injury (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10). Although its direct clinical use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) has not been established – with most in vivo data coming from non-ocular models – its success in ameliorating tissue damage by inhibiting lipid peroxidation suggests its potential utility in other degenerative pathologies where oxidative membrane damage drives dysfunction, such as in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) degeneration underlying geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69; Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–21). Moreover, related compounds, notably Ferrostatin-1, have been tested in various retinal cell models and in some in vivo settings pertaining to retinal ischemia–reperfusion injury and oxygen-induced retinopathy, further bolstering the therapeutic concept of using RTA-type ferroptosis inhibitors in ocular settings (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23; Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8). While the bulk of Liproxstatin-1’s therapeutic history centers on its role as an anti-ferroptotic agent in cancer, neurodegeneration, and acute organ failure, its mechanistic overlap with key pathological features observed in dry AMD – such as iron accumulation, glutathione depletion and elevated lipid peroxidation in the RPE – supports evaluating it as a repurposed candidate in this context (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Shen et al., 2025, pp. 1–2).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism by which Liproxstatin-1 exerts its cytoprotective effect is rooted in its function as a radical-trapping antioxidant. Specifically, Liproxstatin-1 reacts rapidly with lipid peroxyl radicals that propagate the autoxidation chain reaction in cellular membranes. Experimental data have established that Liproxstatin-1 exhibits an intrinsic reaction rate constant (k_inh) in the range of approximately 2.4 × 10^5 M^−1 s^−1 in organic solvents such as chlorobenzene at 37 °C, which is comparable to industrial diarylamine antioxidants (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 8–9). Although its intrinsic reactivity in homogeneous organic solutions may appear lower than classical phenolic antioxidants like α-tocopherol, its performance in the lipid bilayer is superior due to reduced hydrogen-bonding interactions with phospholipid headgroups – a feature that enhances its mobility and reactivity in the lipid environment where ferroptosis is executed (Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 8–9; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). The compound functions primarily by donating a hydrogen atom from its arylamine (or diarylamine) N–H group, effectively quenching chain-propagating lipid peroxyl radicals before they can perpetuate lipid hydroperoxide formation (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). Kinetic isotope effect studies and computational analyses have confirmed that the N–H bond dissociation enthalpy is sufficiently low in Liproxstatin-1 to enable rapid hydrogen-atom transfer, which is a critical step in its radical-trapping mechanism (Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 2–3, 5–7). Importantly, Liproxstatin-1 does not exert significant inhibitory effects on enzymes such as human 15-lipoxygenase-1, thereby ruling out an enzymatic inhibition mechanism and reinforcing that its protective effect is solely attributable to non-enzymatic scavenging of peroxyl radicals (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 201–210). Recent studies have even suggested that Liproxstatin-1 may form a complex with iron in certain cellular compartments (e.g., the lysosome), which could further diminish iron-catalysed radical generation under acidic conditions; however, the predominant and well-characterized mechanism remains its role in intercepting lipid peroxyl radicals (Rodriguez et al., 2024, pp. 1–5; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). On a molecular level, by halting the autoxidation chain reaction, Liproxstatin-1 preserves mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and prevents the deleterious accumulation of lipid hydroperoxides, events that are central to the execution phase of ferroptosis (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). Thus, by protecting cellular membranes from oxidative deterioration, Liproxstatin-1 interrupts the cascade of events leading to ferroptotic cell death, a process that is implicated in RPE degeneration seen in geographic atrophy (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shen et al., 2025, pp. 1–2).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, particularly in geographic atrophy where RPE degeneration is a hallmark, the expected effect of Liproxstatin-1 would be to curtail the chain reaction of lipid peroxidation that underpins ferroptotic cell death. In vitro assays using RPE cell lines such as ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cells have demonstrated that targeting lipid peroxidation – as evidenced by reductions in markers like BODIPY-C11 oxidation and ACSL4 expression – can rescue cells from oxidative stress–mediated death (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–23). Liproxstatin-1 is anticipated to mitigate the accumulation of lipid hydroperoxides, thus preserving the integrity of cellular membranes and mitochondrial function in the RPE (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Given that geographic atrophy in dry AMD is associated with iron overload and subsequent iron-catalysed lipid peroxidation, the ability of Liproxstatin-1 to trap peroxyl radicals is particularly significant; by reducing lipid ROS, it is expected to prevent the conversion of polyunsaturated fatty acids into cytotoxic lipid hydroperoxides, thereby maintaining cellular viability (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). Moreover, the inhibition of ACSL4-dependent peroxidation pathways – which have been linked to ferroptosis in RPE cells – may also be intercepted by Liproxstatin-1, providing a dual line of defense against ferroptotic signaling (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23; Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8). On a cellular level, the compound is expected to maintain Δψm and reduce indicators of oxidative stress, as previously demonstrated in models addressing GPX4 inhibition (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). In animal models where ferroptosis contributes to tissue degeneration (such as renal or hepatic ischaemia/reperfusion models), treatment with Liproxstatin-1 resulted in reduced TUNEL-positive cell counts and ameliorated tissue injury; these outcomes provide a rationale for its application in preclinical dry AMD models, where similar pathological processes – including mitochondrial dysfunction, iron dysregulation, and excessive lipid peroxidation – are observed (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Peng et al., 2020, pp. 3–5). In essence, when applied to RPE cells under conditions that mimic dry AMD, Liproxstatin-1 should decrease oxidative markers, prevent cell death, and thereby slow or halt the progression of geographic atrophy by restoring the balance between pro-oxidant and antioxidant pathways (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–23).

Overall Evaluation:  
Liproxstatin-1 stands out as a promising candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic agent against dry AMD, particularly in geographic atrophy, given the mechanistic overlap between ferroptosis and RPE cell death observed in dry AMD. One of its principal strengths lies in its potent radical-trapping antioxidant activity, which is not only effective at low nanomolar concentrations but also uniquely suited to the lipid bilayer environment of the RPE (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). This specificity is critical because retinal cells are subject to a high burden of polyunsaturated lipid content and are therefore particularly sensitive to oxidative damage. The fact that Liproxstatin-1 has demonstrated efficacy in protecting cells under ferroptotic stress in other organ systems – including kidney and liver models – further supports its potential viability in ocular applications (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Peng et al., 2020, pp. 3–5). Additionally, the compound’s ability to reduce lipid peroxidation, maintain mitochondrial membrane potential, and possibly engage in secondary iron-inactivating mechanisms (as suggested by lysosomal localization studies) offers multiple avenues through which it may address the multifactorial pathogenesis of dry AMD (Rodriguez et al., 2024, pp. 1–5; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 1–2).

However, several challenges must be considered. Despite the strong preclinical evidence in non-ocular systems, direct evidence of Liproxstatin-1’s efficacy in models of dry AMD or RPE-specific ferroptosis is still limited relative to other compounds such as Ferrostatin-1 or nanoparticle-delivered ferroptosis inhibitors in retinal models (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–23). This gap in ocular preclinical data implies that further dedicated studies using RPE cell models and in vivo dry AMD animal models are necessary to validate its protective effects in the eye. In addition, drug delivery to the retina poses its own set of challenges – the blood-retinal barrier and the unique pharmacokinetic profile required for intravitreal stability must be thoroughly optimized (Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69; Hao, Xu, Zhang, & Xue, 2024, pp. 6–7). Moreover, dry AMD is a multifactorial disease involving not only ferroptosis but also apoptosis, inflammation, and other forms of regulated cell death; therefore, while inhibiting ferroptosis may be beneficial, it is uncertain whether monotherapy with Liproxstatin-1 would be sufficient to arrest disease progression. There is also the matter of safety and tolerability in the context of the ocular environment, as systemic dosing strategies that work in renal or hepatic models may not directly translate to the delicate milieu of retinal tissues (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). Finally, considerations regarding the long-term stability, potential off-target effects, and metabolic fate of Liproxstatin-1 in the eye will be crucial parameters in the drug development process.

In summary, the collective literature indicates that Liproxstatin-1 has a well-defined mechanism as a radical-trapping antioxidant that effectively blocks lipid peroxidation and, by extension, ferroptosis. Its discovery through unbiased screening in ferroptosis-susceptible models and its demonstration of efficacy in multiple organ systems provide a strong foundation for its repurposing in dry AMD. The evidence supports that Liproxstatin-1 could counteract the iron-driven ROS amplification and lipid peroxidation that contribute to RPE cell death in geographic atrophy. Nonetheless, while its mechanistic rationale and preclinical promise are substantial, further research – particularly within retinal models – is necessary to fully evaluate its therapeutic potential and address challenges related to ocular delivery and multi-pathway disease components. Taken together, Liproxstatin-1 represents a compelling candidate for further investigation as a targeted inhibitor of ferroptosis in the treatment of dry AMD (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69, 207–210; Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) is an endogenous indoleamine neurohormone first identified as a pineal product and now recognized to be synthesized in many extrapineal tissues, including the human eye (retina, retinal pigment epithelium [RPE], lens, ciliary body) where it is also delivered via the circulation and acts locally through cognate receptors (MT1, MT2) and the MT3 binding site (quinone reductase 2) (Lundmark et al., 2006; Lundmark et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2024). Ocular melatonin is under circadian control and is produced primarily by photoreceptors, with additional production reported in inner retina and potentially the RPE, consistent with a paracrine neuromodulatory role in retinal physiology; importantly, melatonin synthesis has been localized to mitochondria, linking its biosynthesis directly to the organelle most relevant to retinal oxidative metabolism (Blasiak et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024). Biosynthesis proceeds from tryptophan via tryptophan hydroxylase and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase to serotonin, followed by arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase (AANAT) and hydroxyindole-O-methyltransferase (HIOMT) to generate melatonin, which freely diffuses to act in an autocrine/paracrine manner (Ma et al., 2024). As a chemical class, melatonin belongs to amphiphilic indoleamines; it partitions into both aqueous and lipid compartments, crosses biological barriers (including the blood–retinal barrier), and concentrates in mitochondria, properties that underpin its direct antioxidant, membrane-protective, and mitochondrial-modulatory actions described in multiple ocular contexts (Romeo et al., 2024; Rastmanesh, 2011; Ma et al., 2024).

Melatonin’s pharmacology encompasses receptor-dependent signaling via MT1 and MT2 G protein–coupled receptors (G_i and G_q/11 coupling), and receptor-independent actions as a direct free-radical scavenger with active redox metabolites (e.g., AFMK, AMK) capable of sequential radical quenching (“antioxidant cascade”), allowing a single parent molecule to neutralize multiple reactive species; MT3 corresponds to cytosolic quinone reductase 2 (QR2) and represents a distinct enzymatic interaction relevant to ocular physiology (D’Angelo et al., 2024; Lundmark et al., 2007; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Rastmanesh, 2011). This dual pharmacology (receptor-mediated signaling plus direct ROS/RNS scavenging) provides a mechanistic basis for melatonin’s pleiotropic antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, and mitochondrial-protective effects in the retina and RPE, actions widely reported in preclinical models of oxidative retinal injury, diabetic retinopathy, and nonexudative AMD (Crooke et al., 2017; Diéguez et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Within ophthalmology, melatonin and melatonergic agents have been explored across inflammatory, neurodegenerative, and vascular retinal diseases. Topical melatonin (0.1%) reduced intraocular inflammation and blood–ocular barrier permeability in rabbit uveitis while increasing tear and aqueous antioxidant activity (supporting tolerability and local pharmacodynamic engagement), and multiple melatonin analogs lowered intraocular pressure in glaucoma, with nanomicelles extending hypotensive and neuroprotective effects (Rusciano & Russo, 2024). In diabetic retinopathy models, melatonin reduced retinal oxidative and nitrosative stress, decreased hypoxia-inducible factor-1α and VEGF signaling, protected the blood–retinal barrier, and improved neural survival, aligning with its redox, anti-inflammatory, and anti-angiogenic pharmacology (Crooke et al., 2017).

For macular degeneration, mechanistic and efficacy signals span in vitro RPE studies, in vivo retinal protection in mice, and human observational datasets. A protected in vivo AMD-relevant signal includes a subcutaneous melatonin pellet that preserved visual function and outer retinal structure and limited oxidative stress in a nonexudative AMD mouse model (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Independently, rodent studies demonstrate intravitreal melatonin prevents acute photoreceptor loss (MNU model) by lowering oxidative damage markers (retinal MDA, 8-OHdG), increasing mitochondrial MnSOD and total SOD activities, and reducing photoreceptor apoptosis—evidence of both antioxidant and anti-apoptotic benefits from local delivery (Li et al., 2020). In RPE cell models (ARPE-19), melatonin consistently protected against H₂O₂-induced oxidative injury by lowering ROS and lipid peroxidation, restoring mitochondrial membrane potential, reducing Bax/cytochrome c/caspase-7 activation, and promoting autophagy (increased LC3-II and Beclin-1, reduced p62), with low-nanomolar protective effects blocked by the melatonin receptor antagonist luzindole, implicating receptor mediation at physiologic ranges (Chang et al., 2018; Blasiak et al., 2016).

Emerging ferroptosis-focused work further reports that melatonin rescues Aβ₁₋₄₀–induced RPE degeneration by curbing lipid peroxidation, restoring GPX4 and SLC7A11, and normalizing iron handling, with loss-of-function of MDM2 abolishing protection and positioning PI3K/AKT→MDM2→P53→SLC7A11 as a key axis; in vivo, melatonin preserved RPE structure and ERG responses in Aβ₁₋₄₀ models (Wu et al., 2025). These mechanistic and efficacy themes converge with a high-quality in vivo finding that melatonin “protects the retina from experimental nonexudative age-related macular degeneration” in mice (Diéguez et al., 2020).

Clinical observations are suggestive but not definitive. A large real-world EHR cohort analysis (TriNetX) associated chronic melatonin use with lower incidence of AMD and reduced progression from nonexudative to exudative AMD after propensity matching, while acknowledging potential residual confounding and calling for randomized trials (Jeong et al., 2024a). An editorialized report in JAMA Ophthalmology similarly noted protective associations and biological plausibility (RPE protection, VEGF reduction) while emphasizing exploratory design and the need for confirmatory prospective studies (Jeong et al., 2024b). Earlier case-series reported that 3 mg oral melatonin nightly for three months stabilized or improved macular changes in many AMD patients, but these uncontrolled data lack modern trial rigor (Lundmark et al., 2007; Martínez-Águila et al., 2021). Across aging and AMD, reduced nocturnal melatonin and urinary aMT6s have been documented, providing a pathophysiologic rationale for supplementation in older adults; however, oral melatonin exhibits variable and often low bioavailability, and aqueous/topical formulations must address photostability and posterior-segment delivery challenges (Čolak & Žorić, 2019; Blasiak et al., 2016; Jeong et al., 2024b; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Melatonin’s ocular actions relevant to dry AMD encompass receptor-mediated signaling, direct and indirect antioxidant effects, mitochondrial protection, modulation of apoptosis and autophagy/mitophagy, ferroptosis suppression, and immune/vascular regulation.

- Receptor-mediated signaling (MT1/MT2/QR2): MT1 and MT2 are expressed in retina and RPE; MT1 is present in photoreceptor inner segments and inner retinal neurons, MT2 shows high retinal expression and is reported in RPE, while the MT3 binding site corresponds to QR2, an oxidoreductase implicated in ocular physiology (Lundmark et al., 2006; Lundmark et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2024). In RPE, low-dose melatonin protection against oxidants is blocked by luzindole, indicating MT receptor involvement at physiologic concentrations (≤10⁻⁸ M), whereas higher concentrations (>10⁻⁶ M) exert receptor-independent antioxidant effects (Blasiak et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2018). MT1-dependent signaling maintains mitochondrial function under oxidative stress in RPE, underscoring receptor linkage to mitochondrial homeostasis in relevant models (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

- Direct and cascade antioxidant activity: Melatonin directly scavenges ROS/RNS, including hydroxyl radicals, and via successive metabolism (3-hydroxymelatonin → AFMK → AMK) neutralizes multiple radicals (“antioxidant cascade”), affording broad-spectrum redox control across aqueous and lipid compartments due to its amphiphilicity (Rastmanesh, 2011; Čolak & Žorić, 2019). In retinal tissues it reduces lipid peroxidation (MDA) and oxidative DNA damage (8-OHdG), and its metabolites independently contribute to radical quenching in ocular systems (Li et al., 2020; Romeo et al., 2024).

- Indirect antioxidant signaling (Nrf2, Sirtuins, AKT): Melatonin modulates redox-sensitive transcriptional programs; it maintains or enhances Nrf2 nuclear activity in several ocular contexts (though Nrf2 responses can be model-dependent), leading to upregulation of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutases and glutathione peroxidases; it also engages AKT phosphorylation and related DNA damage responses (Blasiak et al., 2016; Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024). Melatonin regulates sirtuins (SIRT1, SIRT3) which link metabolism to antioxidant gene expression, autophagy, and anti-inflammatory effects, with SIRT1/SIRT3 activation reducing apoptosis and VEGF and promoting autophagy gene programs; modulation is context-dependent but provides additional axes by which melatonin can protect RPE mitochondria and restrain inflammatory signaling (Crooke et al., 2017).

- Mitochondrial protection: Melatonin concentrates in mitochondria, stabilizes the electron transport chain, reduces electron leakage, maintains mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), inhibits the mitochondrial permeability transition pore, and can activate uncoupling proteins; it reduces mtDNA damage and restores respiratory control, thereby curbing ROS generation at its source (Blasiak et al., 2016; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Tong et al., 2022). In vivo retina, intravitreal melatonin increased mitochondrial MnSOD (SOD2) activity and total SOD, aligning with enhanced endogenous antioxidant defenses at the organellar level (Li et al., 2020). In RPE cell models, melatonin preserved Δψm (JC-1/TMRM assays) after H₂O₂ challenge (Chang et al., 2018).

- Anti-apoptotic effects: In ARPE-19 cells, melatonin reduced the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, decreased cytochrome c release and caspase-7 activation, and lowered TUNEL positivity, consistent with inhibition of intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptosis; this aligns with higher Bcl-2 mRNA and fewer apoptotic photoreceptors in vivo (Chang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020). Mechanistically, mitochondrial stabilization, reduced ROS, and modulation of NF-κB/JAK-STAT signaling contribute to anti-apoptosis (Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024).

- Autophagy/mitophagy regulation: Melatonin increases LC3-II and Beclin-1 and decreases p62 in RPE oxidative stress models, indicating enhanced autophagic flux; MT2-mediated inhibition of mTOR and SIRT1-linked transcriptional control further connect melatonin to autophagy and mitophagy, processes essential for RPE proteostasis and organellar quality control in aging (Chang et al., 2018; Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024). Given that impaired mitophagy is a feature of early AMD, pharmacologic reinforcement of autophagy/mitophagy by melatonin is mechanistically aligned with disease biology (Crooke et al., 2017).

- Ferroptosis suppression: Aβ₁₋₄₀–induced ferroptosis in RPE is attenuated by melatonin via PI3K/AKT-driven phosphorylation and activation of MDM2, which inhibits p53; this derepresses SLC7A11, restores cystine import and GSH synthesis, and rescues GPX4 activity, thereby reducing lipid peroxidation, Fe²⁺ accumulation, and mitochondrial ultrastructural damage; MDM2 knockdown abrogates these effects, functionally linking melatonin to the PI3K/AKT/MDM2/p53/SLC7A11 axis (Wu et al., 2025). In vivo, melatonin preserved ERG a-/b-waves and outer retinal integrity after Aβ₁₋₄₀ insult (Wu et al., 2025).

- Anti-inflammatory and immune modulation: Melatonin limits NF-κB activation, reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6), and modulates immune cell phenotypes (e.g., promoting macrophage polarization toward tissue-repair M2), contributing to reduced retinal inflammation; it suppresses nitric oxide synthases and decreases NO, relevant to nitro-oxidative stress (Crooke et al., 2017; Diéguez et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024). In models of choroidal neovascularization, melatonin attenuated angiogenesis via HIF-1α–VEGF inhibition and RhoA/ROCK-mediated macrophage/microglia polarization, suggesting an adjunctive anti-neovascular role even though dry AMD lacks CNV (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2024b).

- Telomere/telomerase and DNA repair: Melatonin modulates telomerase and DNA repair pathways in retinal cells, with reports of stimulated telomerase activity and reduced telomere erosion in senescent contexts, and increased efficacy of oxidative DNA damage removal in RPE, potentially mitigating RPE senescence in AMD (Blasiak et al., 2016; Rastmanesh, 2011).

Collectively, these mechanisms plausibly converge in RPE to reduce mitochondrial ROS, maintain Δψm, prevent cytochrome c release, lower caspase activation, and support autophagy/mitophagy, aligning directly with the pathobiology of dry AMD driven by oxidative/mitochondrial damage and impaired proteostasis (Blasiak et al., 2016; Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024).

- Ferroptosis control should be demonstrable in Aβ₁₋₄₀ and other ferroptotic stressors: upregulation of SLC7A11 and GPX4, normalization of TFR1/ACSL4/FTH1, reduced lipid peroxidation, and dependence on PI3K/AKT→MDM2→p53 signaling tested by pharmacological inhibitors and siRNA, as shown in recent preclinical reports (Wu et al., 2025).

- Anti-inflammatory and transcriptional endpoints should shift: decreased NF-κB nuclear translocation and pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β), increased Nrf2 nuclear retention and target gene expression, and potential SIRT1/SIRT3 upregulation in appropriate contexts (Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024).

- Functional in vivo correlates should include preservation of ERG a-/b-wave amplitudes, photoreceptor/RPE morphology on OCT/H&E, and reduced oxidative tissue biomarkers (MDA, 8-OHdG) under retinal oxidative/AMD-like stressors, consistent with prior animal studies (Diéguez et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2025).

Receptor expression to support target engagement is well documented in retina and RPE, and dependence on MT receptors can be tested with antagonists (luzindole) and MT1/MT2 knockdown, as low-dose protective effects in ARPE-19 are reversibly blocked by luzindole and MT1 knockdown abolishes mitochondrial protective actions under oxidative stress (Blasiak et al., 2016; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Lundmark et al., 2007). Given circadian regulation, repeated dosing aligned with the retinal clock may be necessary to realize full mitochondrial DNA protection and durable antioxidant responses, as suggested by diurnal pretreatment requirements in ARPE-19 (Rastmanesh, 2011).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic convergence on AMD biology: Melatonin’s combined direct scavenging of ROS/RNS, induction of endogenous antioxidant defenses (SODs, GPxs), mitochondrial stabilization (Δψm preservation, mtDNA protection), anti-apoptotic signaling (reduced Bax/cytochrome c/caspases), and autophagy/mitophagy support addresses core pathogenic axes in dry AMD—oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and defective proteostasis in post-mitotic RPE and photoreceptors (Blasiak et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022).

- Demonstrated efficacy in relevant preclinical systems: Protection of RPE from peroxide and Aβ₁₋₄₀ ferroptotic stress in vitro, and preservation of retina/RPE structure and function in AMD-like mouse models, including nonexudative AMD and acute degeneration models, with robust biomarker changes (MDA, 8-OHdG, SOD2 activity) and ERG preservation (Chang et al., 2018; Diéguez et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2025).

- Receptor and nonreceptor pharmacology: Dual mode of action enables efficacy at physiologic concentrations via MT1/MT2 and at higher local concentrations via receptor-independent radical scavenging, offering flexibility across dosing ranges and delivery routes; MT1-linked mitochondrial protection in RPE provides a direct mechanistic link between receptor activation and Δψm preservation (Blasiak et al., 2016; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

- Anti-ferroptotic axis in RPE: PI3K/AKT→MDM2→p53→SLC7A11 mechanism positions melatonin within contemporary cell-death biology relevant to AMD (lipid peroxidation, iron handling, GPX4), offering mechanistic biomarkers and combination opportunities with iron chelators or GPX4-preserving agents (Wu et al., 2025).

- Favorable endogenous safety rationale and clinical signal: As an endogenous molecule with extensive human exposure for sleep disorders, melatonin has a comparatively favorable safety backdrop; observational EHR data provides a clinically relevant association signal for AMD incidence and progression reduction that justifies prospective trials (Jeong et al., 2024a; Jeong et al., 2024b).

- Translational feasibility with targeted delivery: Topical ocular and nanocarrier formulations can improve posterior-segment delivery, and intravitreal administration achieves retinal protection with measurable biochemical and functional benefits; nanotechnologies address melatonin’s aqueous instability and enhance tissue penetration (Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Li et al., 2020).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Evidence base is predominantly preclinical; clinical efficacy in dry AMD is unproven: Apart from exploratory EHR associations and small uncontrolled case-series, there are no randomized controlled trials in dry AMD demonstrating visual function or structural endpoints with melatonin; reliance on animal models and ARPE-19 limits translatability (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2024a; Jeong et al., 2024b).

- Context- and dose-dependent effects: Nrf2 modulation by melatonin can vary by model, and very high exogenous concentrations can worsen photoreceptor light damage; a small human study showed acute ERG b-wave reduction after 10 mg oral melatonin, indicating potential physiological perturbation at certain doses/times and the importance of chronotherapy and dose finding (Blasiak et al., 2016; Tong et al., 2022; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

- Vascular tone considerations: MT1-mediated vasoconstriction in retinal endothelium could theoretically exacerbate early perfusion deficits in AMD; dose, receptor selectivity, and local exposure will be critical to avoid adverse vascular modulation (Ma et al., 2024).

- Delivery and pharmacokinetics: Oral melatonin exhibits highly variable and often low bioavailability due to first-pass metabolism, and aqueous topical formulations face photostability and posterior-segment penetration barriers; while nanocarriers and intravitreal delivery overcome these, each introduces manufacturing and safety considerations (Jeong et al., 2024b; Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

- Aged tissue pharmacodynamics: Age-related declines in retinal melatonin and potential receptor desensitization could diminish responsiveness to exogenous melatonin in elderly AMD populations; some aging-associated retinal rhythms were not rescued by exogenous melatonin in prior studies (Blasiak et al., 2016).

- Safety window for intravitreal dosing: Although protective effects are demonstrated, at least one report cites retinal cell degeneration at high intravitreal doses, underscoring the need for careful dose-range finding and chronic safety assessment (Ma et al., 2024).

- Product-specific gaps: There is insufficient formulation- and impurity-specific information for Sigma-Aldrich M5250 in ocular contexts, and no product-specific ocular PK/PD has been reported in AMD; stability, excipient compatibility, and photostability data must be generated for any clinical candidate (Ma et al., 2024; Romeo et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Assessment against the team’s hypothesis  
Supportive evidence is strong that melatonin reduces ROS, preserves mitochondrial function, and prevents apoptosis in RPE/retina. Multiple ARPE-19 studies demonstrate decreased ROS, increased Δψm, and reduced intrinsic apoptosis markers (Bax, cytochrome c, caspases) under oxidative stress with melatonin, consistent with maintained mitochondrial integrity and suppressed apoptotic cascades (Chang et al., 2018). In vivo, raised mitochondrial MnSOD activity and reduced oxidative biomarkers after intravitreal melatonin substantiate mitochondrial antioxidant engagement in retina (Li et al., 2020). Upregulation of antioxidant enzymes (SOD, GPx) by melatonin in ocular tissues via Nrf2, SIRT1/3, and AKT pathways is reported in leading reviews and experimental models, even though direct SOD2/GPX induction has not been quantified in RPE in all cited primary studies; this constitutes a tractable validation gap for our planned assays (Crooke et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2024). Ferroptosis suppression via PI3K/AKT/MDM2/p53 further extends the mitochondrial-protective narrative to lipid ROS and iron metabolism, relevant to RPE stress in AMD (Wu et al., 2025).

Programmatic recommendations  
- Formulation and delivery: Given oral PK variability and ocular delivery constraints, prioritize posterior-segment–targeted strategies: (1) intravitreal melatonin for proof-of-mechanism in large animals (define safety window, ocular distribution, and retinal PD biomarkers); (2) develop stabilized topical nanocarriers (e.g., ethylcellulose, PLGA-PEG, nanomicelles) to improve posterior-segment delivery and residence time for chronic use (Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Jeong et al., 2024b).

- Pharmacodynamic biomarkers: In RPE/retina, quantify Δψm, mitochondrial respiration (OCR), ROS (DCF, MitoSOX), lipid peroxidation (C11-BODIPY, MDA), mtDNA integrity (long-amplicon qPCR), SOD2 and GPX4 protein/activity, Bax/Bcl-2, cytochrome c release, caspase-3/-7 activity, LC3-II/Beclin-1/p62 flux, Nrf2 nuclear localization and target genes, and ferroptosis markers (SLC7A11, GPX4, TFR1, ACSL4, FTH1) with pharmacologic/siRNA controls for MT receptors and PI3K/AKT/MDM2/p53 (Chang et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2025).

- Dosing and chronotherapy: Incorporate diurnal dosing regimens to align with retinal circadian biology; evaluate low-dose receptor-mediated windows versus higher-dose antioxidant windows, avoiding concentrations shown to potentiate phototoxicity (Blasiak et al., 2016; Rastmanesh, 2011; Tong et al., 2022).

- Safety and off-target risks: Monitor ERG under different dosing/time-of-day schedules, retinal/choroidal vascular caliber (given MT1-mediated vasoconstriction), photoreceptor light injury susceptibility under high-dose exposure, and long-term ocular histopathology in repeat-dose studies (Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024; Tong et al., 2022).

- Clinical translation: Design an adaptive, randomized, placebo-controlled Phase 2 in intermediate dry AMD with multimodal endpoints (SD-OCT GA growth, mesopic microperimetry, dark adaptation, low-luminance VA) and fluid biomarkers (plasma/urine aMT6s, systemic oxidative markers), stratified by baseline melatonin levels and sleep parameters; consider an intravitreal proof-of-concept in high-risk early GA to validate local PD and safety prior to chronic topical development (Jeong et al., 2024a; Jeong et al., 2024b; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Conclusion  
Melatonin is a mechanistically well-justified, low-cost, repurposable candidate for dry AMD: it directly and indirectly controls retinal/RPE redox status, stabilizes mitochondrial function (including Δψm), engages endogenous antioxidant enzymes, prevents intrinsic apoptosis, supports autophagy/mitophagy, and suppresses ferroptosis along a defined PI3K/AKT/MDM2/p53 axis, with concordant protection in RPE and retina across preclinical models (Chang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025). Epidemiologic data add a clinically relevant signal for reduced AMD risk and progression with melatonin exposure, and ocular delivery is feasible with modern formulations, though oral PK variability and aqueous instability pose development challenges (Jeong et al., 2024a; Jeong et al., 2024b; Rusciano & Russo, 2024). Key risks—dose-dependent phototoxicity, potential vasoconstrictive effects, variability of Nrf2 responses, and uncertain responsiveness in aged retinas—can be managed through judicious dosing, chronotherapy, receptor-aware design, and robust safety pharmacology (Blasiak et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Net assessment: advance melatonin into a formal translational program for dry AMD centered on posterior-segment–targeted delivery and rigorous mitochondrial/RPE pharmacodynamic validation, while preparing for a randomized clinical evaluation; the mechanistic breadth and preclinical efficacy merit this investment, contingent on resolving dosing, delivery, and safety windows in aged ocular tissue (Diéguez et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2024; Rusciano & Russo, 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
MCC950 is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor that belongs to the diarylsulfonylurea class of compounds originally identified through screening efforts aimed at inhibiting IL-1β processing. Its chemical origins trace back to early studies (circa 2001) that recognized diarylsulfonylurea molecules as cytokine-release inhibitory drugs (CRIDs) before the advent of specific inflammasome inhibitors (Coll et al., 2015). Subsequent medicinal chemistry efforts led to the selection, optimization, and detailed characterization of one member of this series that came to be known as MCC950. Synthetically, MCC950 is produced through a multistep sequence that includes key transformations such as Friedel–Crafts acylation of an indene derivative, acid-promoted cyclization, direct nitration, and subsequent conversion into its final diarylsulfonylurea form, as detailed in the original publication’s Online Methods and Supplementary Materials (Coll et al., 2015; Keuler et al., 2022). Developed initially as an inhibitor of IL-1β post-translational processing, MCC950 was repurposed as a potent and highly selective inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome, exhibiting nanomolar potency (approximately 7.5 nM in murine bone marrow–derived macrophages) with a favorable selectivity profile over other inflammasomes such as AIM2, NLRC4, or NLRP1 (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021; Hill et al., 2017). Marketed under various identifiers – one of which is the Selleckchem product code S8643 – MCC950 represents a well-characterized chemical tool that has continued to serve as both a probe for studying NLRP3 biology and a preclinical candidate in inflammatory disease models (Das et al., 2021; Sharma et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
MCC950 has been extensively evaluated in preclinical studies targeting inflammatory diseases driven by aberrant NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Its discovery followed earlier observations that sulfonylurea agents such as glyburide, traditionally used in type 2 diabetes for their insulin-secretagogue activity via KATP channel inhibition, also inhibited NLRP3-driven processes albeit at micromolar concentrations (Chauhan et al., 2020; Coll et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2017). In contrast, MCC950 exhibits a markedly improved potency at nanomolar levels and a higher degree of specificity. Preclinical evaluations demonstrated that MCC950 effectively blocks both the canonical and noncanonical activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, resulting in suppressed activation of caspase-1 and reduced IL-1β secretion (Das et al., 2021; Hill et al., 2020). Its efficacy has been validated in a wide range of inflammatory disease models including cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS), multiple sclerosis models such as experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), pulmonary and cutaneous inflammation, Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, and even models of kidney and liver fibrosis (Das et al., 2021; Narros-Fernández et al., 2022; Sharma et al., 2023). Although MCC950 has not yet been formally used in clinical applications—and indeed its clinical development was reportedly halted due to safety concerns such as elevated transaminases and organ structural damage in preclinical toxicity studies (Johansson et al., 2025)—its robust preclinical record has established it as the prototype NLRP3 inhibitor. There is emerging interest in exploiting its mechanism for diseases wherein inflammasome-driven pathology is central. While direct data on the use of MCC950 for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) are not available in the literature, the growing evidence implicating the NLRP3 inflammasome in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction suggests that repurposing MCC950 for dry AMD is a scientifically plausible strategy (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021; Keuler et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of MCC950 is one of its most compelling features. At the molecular level, MCC950 selectively inhibits the NLRP3 inflammasome by directly binding to the NACHT domain, specifically targeting the Walker B motif that is essential for ATP hydrolysis and subsequent conformational changes required for inflammasome assembly (Hill et al., 2020; Sharma et al., 2023). In doing so, MCC950 prevents the oligomerization of NLRP3 and the recruitment of the adaptor protein ASC, thereby abrogating the activation of caspase-1 and the maturation and release of proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18 (Coll et al., 2015; Keuler et al., 2022). Structural analyses, including photoaffinity labeling and surface plasmon resonance (SPR) studies, have confirmed the high affinity binding (with SPR-derived K_D values in the low nanomolar range) of MCC950 to its target within NLRP3 (Coll et al., 2019; Hill et al., 2017). Importantly, MCC950 does not interfere with upstream ionic events, such as K^+ efflux or Ca^2+ signaling, which are also involved in NLRP3 activation pathways; rather, its action is confined to the blockade of ATP hydrolysis, offering a direct means to “lock” NLRP3 in an inactive, closed conformation (Das et al., 2021; Keuler et al., 2022; Li, 2020). This precise targeting underpins its exceptional potency and selectivity among inflammasome inhibitors. Moreover, a body of literature has explored the structure–activity relationships (SAR) surrounding the diarylsulfonylurea scaffold of MCC950, confirming that modifications to key structural motifs (for instance, the s-hexahydroindacene group) can have significant impacts on both inhibitory potency and chemical stability; these insights have spurred the design of hybrid molecules that further exploit MCC950’s pharmacophore for dual-target activities (Hill et al., 2017).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
The pathophysiology of dry AMD is characterized by the progressive degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), which results from chronic cellular stress—largely driven by mitochondrial dysfunction and elevated reactive oxygen species (ROS) production—that culminates in an inflammatory cascade. A growing body of evidence implicates the NLRP3 inflammasome as a critical mediator in this process; in the RPE, mitochondrial ROS can instigate NLRP3 activation, leading to the cleavage of caspase-1 and the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, which in turn exacerbate RPE atrophy and compromise the integrity of the retinal barrier (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021). The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of MCC950 for dry AMD is that by selectively inhibiting NLRP3 activation, MCC950 would interrupt this pathogenic cycle. Specifically, its potent inhibition of ATP hydrolysis within the NACHT domain would prevent the inflammasome assembly even in the presence of mitochondrial ROS, thereby blocking caspase-1 activation and subsequent IL-1β secretion. In preclinical models where MCC950 has been tested—such as sodium-iodate-induced damage and laser-induced injury—this compound has been shown to suppress NLRP3-dependent cytokine secretion and preserve barrier function (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021; Narros-Fernández et al., 2022). Extrapolating these observations to the context of dry AMD, one would expect that targeted inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome in RPE cells (which are known to express and be affected by proinflammatory cytokines) would confer protection against mitochondrial ROS-induced damage, maintain RPE integrity, and ultimately slow or halt the progression of geographic atrophy that typifies the dry form of AMD. Additionally, since microglial activation and subsequent inflammatory signaling are also contributing factors in dry AMD, the dual inhibitory effect on both RPE and resident microglia further supports the anticipated beneficial impact of MCC950 in this disease setting (Li, 2020; Sharma et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
MCC950 presents several compelling strengths as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. First, its proven high potency (with an IC_50 in the low nanomolar range) and its exquisite selectivity for the NLRP3 inflammasome make it a highly attractive candidate for modulating the pathological inflammation observed in dry AMD (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021). The detailed elucidation of its mechanism of action—specifically, its direct binding to the Walker B motif within the NACHT domain of NLRP3, thereby preventing the critical ATP-driven conformational changes necessary for inflammasome assembly—provides a clear rationale for its use in conditions where aberrant inflammasome activation is pathogenic (Hill et al., 2017; Hill et al., 2020; Sharma et al., 2023). This mechanism directly addresses one of the key molecular events implicated in RPE atrophy: the mitochondrial ROS-induced activation of NLRP3 leading to sustained release of IL-1β and caspase-1-mediated cell death. If MCC950 can similarly suppress these events in RPE and microglia, it is expected to preserve barrier function and cellular viability in the retina, thereby potentially altering the course of dry AMD.

However, several challenges and weaknesses must be considered in the overall evaluation of MCC950 for dry AMD. One major concern is the clinical safety profile of MCC950. Although it has displayed robust anti-inflammatory activity in numerous preclinical models, clinical development efforts involving MCC950 were reportedly halted in part due to safety concerns—including elevations in transaminases and signs of organ structural damage (Johansson et al., 2025). This systemic toxicity is particularly relevant when considering chronic diseases such as AMD, which require long-term treatment. That said, repurposing MCC950 for a localized indication like dry AMD might allow for alternative routes of administration (for instance, intravitreal injection) that could mitigate systemic exposure and reduce the risk of adverse systemic effects. Additionally, the pharmacokinetic challenges noted in certain contexts—such as its poor penetration when adapted as a PET radiotracer for CNS imaging (Hill et al., 2020)—may or may not translate to ocular tissues, where barriers and tissue distribution differ from those of the brain.

Another potential limitation is that, to date, there is limited direct evidence supporting the use of MCC950 in ocular models or specifically in RPE cells. While its efficacy in a variety of inflammatory and neurodegenerative models bodes well for its potential utility in dry AMD, further targeted research is required to confirm that the mechanisms at play in RPE degeneration align sufficiently with those observed in the well-characterized models of CAPS, EAE, and other inflammatory disorders (Das et al., 2021; Narros-Fernández et al., 2022). Moreover, the possibility of unintended off-target effects remains a concern in any repurposing strategy, and the selectivity profile, although excellent in controlled in vitro settings, must be rigorously validated in the complex microenvironment of the retina.

From a formulation and delivery standpoint, achieving the correct drug concentration in the retinal tissues poses an additional challenge. The ocular bioavailability of MCC950, especially given its physicochemical properties as a diarylsulfonylurea, will need to be thoroughly evaluated. The opportunity to leverage existing ophthalmic delivery platforms—such as sustained-release intravitreal implants or nanoparticle-mediated delivery—could provide solutions that maximize the therapeutic effect while minimizing potential toxicity.

In summary, MCC950 stands out as a promising candidate owing to its highly selective inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome, a mechanism intimately linked with the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Its background as a diarylsulfonylurea with well-documented preclinical efficacy in suppressing IL-1β release and blocking caspase-1 activation provides a strong mechanistic foundation. The compound’s history of preclinical success in multiple inflammatory disease models, combined with detailed insights into its mechanism of action, supports its potential repurposing for dry AMD—especially given that inflammasome-mediated inflammation is a key driver of RPE cell degeneration. Nonetheless, caution is warranted due to prior safety concerns encountered in systemic applications, and these must be addressed through careful evaluation of ocular-specific pharmacokinetics, dosing paradigms, and delivery methods. Ultimately, with rigorous preclinical validation in relevant ocular models and potential formulation optimization to ensure localized protection with minimal systemic exposure, MCC950 could provide an innovative therapeutic approach to halting or slowing the progression of dry AMD (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021; Hill et al., 2020; Johansson et al., 2025; Li, 2020; Sharma et al., 2023).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Mitoquinone mesylate (MitoQ) is a synthetic, mitochondria‐targeted antioxidant originally developed as an analogue of coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) to overcome the bioavailability and uptake limitations of naturally occurring CoQ10. Its chemical design is based on modifying decylubiquinone—a CoQ10 analogue in which the long isoprenoid tail is replaced by a saturated decyl hydrocarbon chain to enhance mitochondrial retention—and covalently linking it to a lipophilic triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation. The inclusion of the TPP⁺ moiety exploits the highly negative membrane potential of the mitochondrial inner membrane, thereby ensuring selective accumulation of MitoQ in the mitochondrial matrix (Cores et al., 2023). This compound belongs to the class of lipophilic cationic antioxidants and is also considered a mitochondria-targeted rechargeable antioxidant (RMA) because, after its active ubiquinone moiety scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS), it is enzymatically reduced to the active hydroquinone form by components of the electron transport chain. The rechargeable property allows MitoQ to be continuously recycled via the respiratory chain, resulting in sustained antioxidant action even at low doses—a property that distinguishes it from conventional antioxidants (Lukashev et al., 2014; Fields et al., 2023). The synthesis strategy for MitoQ involves the chemical conjugation of decylubiquinone with TPP⁺, and it is formulated as a mesylate salt to improve its stability and facilitate pharmaceutical development (Cores et al., 2023; Kim & Han, 2017). Overall, MitoQ is a well‐defined member of a broader class of mitochondria‐targeted redox active compounds that have been widely investigated for their potential to modulate mitochondrial oxidative stress (Zielonka et al., 2017).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past two decades, MitoQ has been extensively characterized in a wide range of preclinical studies spanning neurodegenerative diseases, cardiovascular disorders, metabolic syndrome, sepsis, and other conditions associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and elevated oxidative stress. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that MitoQ confers protection against oxidative injury in cellular models and animal models alike. For example, studies in rodent models of cardiac ischemia–reperfusion injury, hypertension, and pressure‐overload heart failure have shown that MitoQ preserves mitochondrial respiration, decreases ROS production (especially H₂O₂ and superoxide) and reduces lipid peroxidation in the heart (Fairley et al., 2023; Kim & Han, 2017). In addition, significant neuroprotective effects have been reported in multiple models of neurodegeneration—ranging from in vitro experiments using Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease models to in vivo studies in rodent systems—where MitoQ was able to reduce mitochondrial fragmentation, lower markers of apoptosis, and restore mitochondrial membrane potential in neurons (Fields et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). Clinically, MitoQ has advanced into human trials in several indications including studies related to Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and hypertension, with reported safety in over 200 human subjects (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Fairley et al., 2023). Although there is no direct record of its use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), the extensive preclinical history in diseases characterized by oxidative stress and mitochondrial impairment provides a strong precedent for its repurposing. In ocular contexts, early pharmacokinetic studies have demonstrated that MitoQ exhibits measurable retinal uptake (approximately 1% of plasma concentration) after oral or topical administration, suggesting that the compound can reach the retina at therapeutically relevant levels (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021). Given that mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative injury in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells are now increasingly recognized as central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the repurposing of MitoQ for this indication is logically supported by its mechanism and prior usage in analogous conditions (Cores et al., 2023; Zielonka et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
MitoQ’s mechanism of action is rooted in its unique chemical architecture that allows selective mitochondrial targeting and continuous ROS scavenging. The TPP⁺ moiety drives the compound’s accumulation into the mitochondrial matrix in a membrane potential–dependent manner. Once inside the mitochondria, MitoQ’s ubiquinone moiety is rapidly reduced by components of the electron transport chain—most notably by electron flow through complex II—and converted to its active form, mitoquinol (ubiquinol) (Cores et al., 2023; Manolis et al., 2021). In its reduced state, mitoquinol acts as a potent antioxidant that intercepts ROS generated primarily at the sites of electron leakage at complexes I and III. The scavenging of ROS, particularly superoxide and peroxyl radicals, prevents oxidative damage to mitochondrial lipids, proteins, and DNA—all of which are crucial for maintaining mitochondrial function (Zielonka et al., 2017; Modi et al., 2024). In effect, the cycle of reduction and oxidation (redox cycling) enables MitoQ to function catalytically, rather than stoichiometrically, thereby amplifying its antioxidant capacity over time (Lukashev et al., 2014; Modi et al., 2024). Moreover, by reducing mitochondrial ROS, MitoQ preserves the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), which is essential for ATP synthesis and overall cellular bioenergetics (Kim & Han, 2017; Gueven et al., 2017). This stabilization of Δψm not only inhibits the initiation of apoptosis but may also dampen downstream inflammatory signaling cascades mediated by ROS-sensitive transcription factors such as NF-κB (Fields et al., 2023; Cores et al., 2023). Such detailed molecular interactions—spanning TPP-driven uptake, rapid reduction at the respiratory chain, catalytic ROS neutralization, and subsequent recycling to the active antioxidant form—underscore the multifaceted protection that MitoQ offers against mitochondrial oxidative injury.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the underlying hypothesis is that accumulation of oxidative damage in RPE cells leads to mitochondrial dysfunction, loss of Δψm, increased ROS production, chronic inflammation, and ultimately RPE cell degeneration, which is central to disease progression. Based on in vitro studies performed in ARPE-19 cells, treatment with MitoQ has been shown to reduce mitochondrial ROS levels, as measured by MitoSOX fluorescence, and to preserve Δψm as assessed by TMRM assays when cells are challenged with H₂O₂-induced oxidative stress (Cores et al., 2023; Fields et al., 2023). The expected effect of MitoQ in a dry AMD model is that, upon topical or oral administration, it will accumulate in the mitochondria of RPE cells via TPP-mediated uptake. Once there, its ubiquinone moiety will be reduced to the active antioxidant form by the local respiratory chain, which in turn will neutralize superoxide and other ROS at the sites of electron leakage (primarily complex I and III regions). This ROS scavenging is anticipated to limit oxidative damage to mitochondrial membranes and proteins, maintain efficient electron transport and ATP production, and ultimately restore the mitochondrial membrane potential that is compromised in oxidative stress conditions (Zielonka et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014). Additionally, by lowering oxidative stress, MitoQ is expected to reduce inflammatory signaling within the RPE and adjacent retinal layers—potentially decreasing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and mitigating the chronic low-grade inflammation that contributes to dry AMD pathology (Fairley et al., 2023; Gueven et al., 2017). In an in vitro assay using ARPE-19 cells, one would expect to observe a significant decrease in MitoSOX signal intensity along with increased TMRM fluorescence after treatment with MitoQ, indicating reduced mitochondrial ROS and improved Δψm, respectively (Cores et al., 2023; Fields et al., 2023). Given that ARPE-19 is a well‐accepted model for studying RPE function and oxidative stress, these biochemical endpoints provide compelling mechanistic evidence that MitoQ may slow or even reverse aspects of RPE degeneration—a promising therapeutic outcome for dry AMD (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
MitoQ stands out as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration on the basis of several compelling factors. First, its synthetic origin as a mitochondria-targeted CoQ10 analogue with an appended TPP⁺ group ensures that it concentrates specifically within mitochondria, where oxidative stress is most detrimental (Cores et al., 2023; Zielonka et al., 2017). This targeted delivery is a critical improvement over non-specific antioxidants, which often fail to reach the intracellular compartments where ROS generation is most intense. Second, MitoQ’s well-established mechanism of action—encompassing catalytic ROS scavenging through a continuously rechargeable redox cycle—directly addresses the pathophysiological core of dry AMD, namely the oxidative injury and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells (Lukashev et al., 2014; Fields et al., 2023). Preclinical studies in diverse disease models have robustly demonstrated its capacity to protect mitochondrial structure and function, reduce lipid peroxidation and apoptotic signaling, and ultimately preserve cellular viability (Kim & Han, 2017; Gueven et al., 2017).

On the therapeutic history side, MitoQ has undergone extensive preclinical evaluation in models of neurodegeneration, cardiovascular diseases, and metabolic disorders, and has been tested in several early-phase clinical trials—even if not yet in dry AMD specifically—showing an excellent safety profile in over 200 human subjects (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Fairley et al., 2023). Furthermore, pharmacokinetic studies demonstrating ocular uptake (~1% of plasma levels) provide an encouraging basis for its repurposing in retinal diseases, although the relatively low retinal concentration does suggest that formulation optimization (for instance, via topical delivery systems or enhanced ocular bioavailability formulations) may be required to achieve therapeutic levels in the RPE (Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses need to be considered. Clinical trials in other indications such as Parkinson’s disease have reported mixed outcomes with MitoQ, leading to concerns about its translation from well-controlled preclinical settings to the complex environment of human disease (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). Moreover, the potential for pro-oxidant effects at high concentrations—as sometimes observed with redox-active compounds like MitoQ—is a dose optimization challenge that must be carefully managed in any clinical development program (Gueven et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014). The fact that the reported retinal uptake of MitoQ is modest (~1% of plasma levels) may necessitate higher systemic doses or alternative delivery routes to ensure that sufficient drug reaches the RPE, which in turn could raise safety issues if off-target effects occur (Apostolova & Victor, 2015). Additionally, while the biochemical rationale is compelling, there is currently no direct clinical evidence for efficacy in dry AMD; this gap underscores the need for further targeted preclinical investigations using dry AMD-relevant animal models and subsequent early-phase clinical trials.

In summary, the overall evaluation favours exploration of MitoQ as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its strong mechanistic foundation—based on mitochondrial targeting, catalytic ROS scavenging, and preservation of Δψm—aligns well with the known etiopathogenesis of dry AMD, which involves RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. The extensive preclinical and early clinical data supporting MitoQ’s safety and efficacy in other indications further bolster its candidacy. However, attention must be given to optimizing dosing regimens and delivery strategies to overcome the limitation of modest retinal uptake, as well as rigorously establishing its efficacy specifically in models of dry AMD before advancing to large-scale clinical trials. Given its unique properties and the urgent need for effective treatments in dry AMD, MitoQ merits further investigation as part of a comprehensive strategy to combat RPE degeneration and preserve visual function in affected patients (Cores et al., 2023; Zielonka et al., 2017; Lukashev et al., 2014; Apostolova & Victor, 2015; Shinn & Lagalwar, 2021).

Spermidine is a naturally occurring polyamine that was originally discovered in bovine semen and later shown to be ubiquitous in all forms of life, ranging from bacteria and plants to fungi and mammals. It belongs to the aliphatic polyamine class, characterized by its low molecular weight, linear arrangement, and multiple amino groups that are fully protonated at physiological pH. Its natural origins stem from highly conserved enzymatic biosynthetic pathways—starting either from ornithine via ornithine decarboxylase or from arginine through an agmatine intermediate—resulting in the formation of putrescine, which is subsequently converted to spermidine through the transfer of an aminopropyl group provided by decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine (dcSAM) (Casero & Marton, 2007; Hobley et al., 2017; Khomutov et al., 2019). Although spermidine can be isolated from natural sources such as food and tissues, it is also available in a chemically defined form commercially (for example, Sigma-Aldrich S2626) and has been used in basic research as well as in some experimental therapeutic approaches. This compound is representative of the polyamine family, and these molecules have traditionally been investigated for their roles in cellular proliferation, nucleic acid stabilization, and modulation of various enzymatic activities, which in turn have broad implications for health and disease (Madeo et al., 2020; Nichugovskiy et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, spermidine’s potential therapeutic applications have been explored extensively in the context of its ability to induce autophagy and affect cellular homeostasis. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that spermidine supplementation can extend lifespan and improve the function of various tissues by enhancing autophagy, contributing to cardioprotection, and promoting neuroprotection in animal models (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). The hypothesized mechanism for using spermidine in dry AMD is multifaceted and centers on its ability to modulate cellular quality control processes. At the molecular level, spermidine is known to induce autophagy, a process that mediates the degradation and recycling of damaged or dysfunctional cellular constituents. In model systems ranging from yeast to mammalian cells, spermidine has been shown to increase the conversion of the autophagy marker LC3-I to LC3-II, thereby promoting autophagosome formation (Qin et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022). Inhibition of EP300 has been correlated with enhanced autophagic flux, and several studies suggest that spermidine may exert its autophagy-inducing effects partly by downregulating EP300 expression or activity (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020).

In addition to its effects on EP300, spermidine has been implicated in the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), an evolutionarily conserved energy sensor that modulates metabolic homeostasis and mitochondrial quality control. Activation of AMPK can lead to the phosphorylation and activation of downstream effectors that promote both autophagy and mitophagy (the selective autophagic removal of damaged mitochondria). While direct evidence for AMPK activation by spermidine in retinal cells is still emerging, broader studies in other cell types have described an upregulation of pathways associated with mitochondrial biogenesis and quality control, including the deacetylation of proteins by SIRT1, which often acts in concert with AMPK (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). This aligns well with the current understanding of dry AMD pathogenesis, in which impaired autophagic clearance and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells play major roles (Nichugovskiy et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2021). There is a need for more comprehensive studies that directly measure these autophagic and mitophagic markers in RPE cells under conditions that mimic the A2E-induced stress typical of dry AMD (Kim et al., 2021). Additionally, the risk that spermidine’s metabolism by amine oxidases may produce toxic aldehyde byproducts such as acrolein must be carefully considered, as these compounds have been implicated in retinal degeneration in some intravitreal models (Ohashi et al., 2017).

Its established role in promoting cellular longevity and mitigating oxidative stress in diverse tissues certainly warrants further investigation, but rigorous studies using dry AMD-specific models are essential to ascertain its efficacy and safety in this context. Regulatory considerations will also require detailed pharmacokinetic and toxicological profiling, particularly given its dual potential for both cytoprotection and cytotoxicity depending on concentration and route of administration (Ohashi et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022).
