Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is a naturally occurring long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (LC-PUFA) that has been isolated from marine sources, such as fish oil, and is commercially available in a highly purified form (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich D2534). DHA is synthesized via metabolic elongation and desaturation of dietary alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) in mammals; however, this endogenous conversion is limited, and direct dietary intake is critical for maintaining adequate retinal DHA levels (Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14). Belonging to the omega-3 class of fatty acids, DHA has long been recognized for its important roles in maintaining membrane structure and function, particularly in neural tissues and the retina where it is highly concentrated in photoreceptor outer segments and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) membranes (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3). Its polyunsaturated nature—with six cis double bonds—confers unique biophysical properties, enabling DHA to increase membrane fluidity and participate in critical signaling cascades. The compound has been used extensively as a nutritional supplement and has been incorporated in various formulations aimed at cardiovascular health, cognitive function, and ocular protection, establishing a robust safety profile over decades of human use (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Skowronska-Krawczyk & Chao, 2019, pp. 3–4).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past two decades, extensive research has explored the role of DHA and related omega-3 fatty acids in maintaining retinal function and potentially preventing age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Epidemiologic studies have consistently demonstrated an inverse association between dietary fish and high omega-3 fatty acid intake and the risk of developing AMD, suggesting that populations with higher DHA consumption tend to exhibit a lower incidence of both early and, to some extent, advanced forms of the disease (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). In clinical settings, large-scale randomized controlled trials, such as AREDS2, incorporated DHA (and EPA) into a multi-nutrient formula designed originally for AMD, though the overall randomized trial outcomes have been mixed, with some studies finding no statistically significant benefit for progression to late AMD (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). Pilot clinical trials and observational cohort studies, including NAT-1 and NAT-2, have assessed DHA supplementation in subjects with drusenoid lesions or early-stage AMD; while some of these studies have shown promising improvements in blood biomarkers (e.g., increased red blood cell DHA levels) and correlations with reduced AMD progression, the clinical efficacy remains under debate (Querques et al., 2016, pp. 2–4; Querques et al., 2011, pp. 7–8). Notably, evidence from animal models suggests that dietary DHA may protect against light-induced retinal degeneration and reduce the accumulation of deleterious lipid peroxidation products, although some preclinical studies also caution that DHA’s susceptibility to oxidation could, under certain conditions, worsen retinal injury (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic hypothesis for using DHA in dry AMD is based on its predicted ability to incorporate into the mitochondrial membranes of RPE cells, thereby enhancing membrane fluidity and protecting against oxidative damage to the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes. Under normal cellular conditions, DHA—owing to its multiple methylene-interrupted cis double bonds—integrates into phospholipid bilayers and modulates biophysical properties such as fluidity, permeability, and thickness (Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33). In mitochondrial membranes, this incorporation is thought to replace more saturated fatty acids such as arachidonic acid, ultimately reducing lipid peroxidation and mitigating oxidative stress that is deleterious to ETC function (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9). In vitro studies have shown that DHA supplementation in retinal cell cultures can decrease markers of apoptosis and preserve mitochondrial membrane integrity, with a concomitant increase in anti-apoptotic proteins (e.g., Bcl-2) (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 2–4).  
In addition, DHA is enzymatically converted under conditions of oxidative stress into neuroprotective docosanoids, such as neuroprotectin D1 (NPD1), which can inhibit pro-inflammatory gene expression and reduce cell death in RPE and photoreceptor cells (Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14; LaFuente et al., 2021, p. 13). This conversion not only contributes to countering local inflammation but also supports cellular health by modulating intracellular signaling pathways, particularly those involving NF-κB and other transcription factors critical for managing oxidative stress (Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14; Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14). Despite these promising mechanistic insights, it is important to note that direct, quantitative evidence detailing DHA’s incorporation specifically into RPE mitochondrial membranes and its precise effects on mitochondrial cristae structure, malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, or oxygen consumption rate (OCR) remains limited in the current literature (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, p. 13). Several reviews and preclinical reports acknowledge the theoretical framework while emphasizing the need for more detailed mechanistic studies that directly measure these mitochondrial endpoints (Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the mechanistic hypothesis, DHA supplementation is expected to yield several beneficial effects in retinal cells, particularly within the RPE, which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. In an ideal in vitro or ex vivo assay, DHA would incorporate into RPE cell membranes—including the mitochondrial inner membrane—increasing fluidity and enabling better diffusion of substrates and electron carriers necessary for efficient ATP production. Enhanced mitochondrial membrane fluidity should help reduce the susceptibility of the electron transport chain to oxidative damage, thereby lowering the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the subsequent production of lipid peroxidation byproducts such as MDA (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5). Furthermore, preservation of mitochondrial cristae structure is anticipated to maintain optimal alignment and function of ETC complexes, leading to an improved oxygen consumption rate (OCR) that is directly linked to cellular energy metabolism and overall cell viability (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 2–4; Souied et al., 2016, p. 8).  
At a molecular level, the increased presence of DHA in mitochondrial membranes is expected to initiate a cascade of protective events: reduced oxidative stress and inflammation via inhibition of NF-κB activation, promotion of the antioxidant response through NFE2L2 (NRF2) pathway activation, and enhanced autophagic clearance of damaged proteins and organelles through upregulation of SQSTM1 (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 1–2; Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, p. 3). Consequently, these effects should translate into preservation of RPE cell function, reduced apoptosis, and maintenance of photoreceptor health—an effect that could help slow the progression of dry AMD by stabilizing the retinal environment and preventing drusen accumulation and other degenerative changes (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5). Additionally, because genes encoding crucial direct mediators of DHA uptake such as Mfsd2a are expressed in RPE cells and photoreceptors, the target tissue is particularly well-positioned to benefit from increased dietary or supplementary DHA (Fathima et al., 2023, p. 8). However, it is also recognized that despite the strong rationale, direct experimental confirmation of these outcomes—specifically measured improvements in MDA levels, cristae ultrastructure integrity, and OCR in human RPE cells—is still pending, and the observed epidemiologic correlations are not yet unequivocally supported by randomized clinical trial data (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).

Overall Evaluation:  
The proposition to repurpose DHA for dry AMD is underpinned by compelling mechanistic rationale and epidemiologic associations, yet it is not without its challenges and limitations. One clear strength is DHA’s established role as an essential component of retinal cell membranes. Its high concentration in photoreceptors and the RPE is functionally integral to maintaining visual function and cellular homeostasis, lending strong biological plausibility to its protective potential in AMD (Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33). Its ability to modulate membrane fluidity, serve as a precursor to neuroprotective mediators like NPD1, and exert anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions provide multiple mechanistic pathways through which it may mitigate the cellular stressors implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis (Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14; Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14).  
From a therapeutic history perspective, DHA is well understood in the context of nutritional supplementation, and numerous epidemiologic studies point toward a lower risk of AMD with higher dietary DHA intake (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). The safety profile of DHA is also well established, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing. However, the clinical trial data to date (including large-scale studies such as AREDS2 and smaller trials like NAT-2) have not consistently demonstrated a clear benefit in altering the progression of advanced AMD, and it remains uncertain whether observed benefits in intermediate AMD or specific cellular endpoints translate into clinically meaningful outcomes in the dry form of the disease (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8).  
A significant weakness in the current body of research is the lack of direct mechanistic studies that quantitatively document DHA incorporation into RPE mitochondrial membranes and its subsequent effects on mitochondrial parameters. In our hypothesis, improved mitochondrial function is key, with expected reductions in MDA levels, preservation of cristae structure, and enhancement of OCR serving as biomarkers of efficacy. Yet, while several in vitro studies and animal experiments have suggested that DHA can reduce markers of oxidative stress and improve mitochondrial integrity in retinal models, the literature provided does not include rigorous, high-resolution measurements of these specific parameters in human RPE cells (Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Jiang et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). This gap in the direct evidence would need to be addressed through targeted preclinical assays employing electron microscopy, lipidomics, and mitochondrial respirometry to validate the proposed mechanism.  
Furthermore, the mode of formulation and bioavailability of DHA is a critical factor that may contribute to the mixed findings in clinical trials; DHA administered as an ethyl ester may have different absorption and incorporation profiles compared to its triglyceride-bound form, and the optimal dosing necessary to achieve sufficient retinal or mitochondrial enrichment remains unclear (Souied et al., 2016, pp. 6–7; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). Potential pro-oxidant effects of DHA in settings where oxidation is excessive must also be carefully monitored, as some animal studies have reported that under specific conditions DHA accumulation may even exacerbate oxidative damage (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5).  
In summary, while the epidemiologic literature and preclinical studies provide an encouraging backdrop for the repurposing of DHA as a therapeutic agent in dry AMD—by showing that high DHA intake is associated with a reduced risk of AMD and that DHA can confer mitochondrial and anti-oxidative benefits in retinal models—the critical mechanistic endpoints that support our specific hypothesis are not yet fully substantiated in the published literature. The overall evaluation is that DHA has substantial mechanistic promise, safety, and historical use as a nutritional supplement; however, further robust mechanistic studies and carefully designed clinical trials are necessary to validate its specific effects on mitochondrial function in RPE cells and to determine whether these biochemical improvements translate into a clinically significant slowing of dry AMD progression (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GKT137831, also known as Setanaxib, is a synthetic small‐molecule drug originally discovered and optimized for its ability to inhibit NADPH oxidase activity, with specificity primarily toward the NOX1 and NOX4 isoforms. It belongs to the dihydropyrazolone chemical class, sharing structural similarity with the free radical scavenger edaravone, and has been further refined from earlier analogues such as GKT136901 through structure–activity relationship studies to improve its potency, selectivity, and oral bioavailability (Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30; Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). The compound was originally developed by Genkyotex as a dual NOX1/NOX4 inhibitor; however, it possesses additional but lower potency activity against NOX2 and even shows some partial inhibition of NOX5 in certain settings (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30). The initial discovery was based on high-throughput screening methods that targeted NADPH oxidase-mediated reactive oxygen species (ROS) production—a process that has been linked to multiple pathological conditions including fibrotic, vascular, and inflammatory diseases. As a representative of its class, GKT137831 exemplifies a modern approach to drug design wherein inhibition of the primary enzymatic source of ROS is favored over conventional antioxidant strategies, which often suffer from non-specificity and poor clinical translation (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26).

Therapeutic History:  
GKT137831 has a distinguished preclinical and clinical history rooted in its application to diseases characterized by oxidative stress and inflammation. In preclinical models, it has been shown to significantly reduce the generation of ROS and the downstream activation of pro-inflammatory signaling. In primary cultured human retinal endothelial cells, for instance, treatment with GKT137831 reduced both ROS generation and VEGFA expression, indicating its potential utility in limiting vascular dysfunction in ocular diseases (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). Beyond ocular applications, the compound has been evaluated in several preclinical models of fibrotic and vascular pathologies including diabetic kidney disease, hypertensive cardiac remodeling, and liver fibrosis, wherein its administration lowered the levels of ROS, inflammatory cytokines, and markers of tissue injury (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Cipriano et al., 2023, pp. 22–23). Clinically, GKT137831 has advanced to Phase II trials in diabetic nephropathy and primary biliary cholangitis, demonstrating both safety and acceptable pharmacokinetic properties in human subjects (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26; Buglak et al., 2018, Art. 2468457). Although it has not been tested directly for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) in clinical trials, several preclinical studies using models of ischemic retinopathy and diabetic retinopathy have provided supportive evidence that NOX inhibition may attenuate oxidative stress and inflammation in retinal tissues (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Gaskin et al., 2021, pp. 15–17). The repurposing rationale for dry AMD hinges on the observation that oxidative stress plays a central role in the degeneration of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and the subsequent progression of AMD—pathophysiological processes that have been effectively modulated by GKT137831 in other experimental disease models (Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 1–7).

Mechanism of Action:  
From a molecular perspective, GKT137831 has been characterized as a dual inhibitor of NOX1 and NOX4, enzymes that catalyze the transfer of electrons from NADPH to molecular oxygen and thereby generate superoxide or hydrogen peroxide, respectively (Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30; Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 4–6). Unlike classical antioxidants that scavenge ROS after they are generated, GKT137831 aims to prevent ROS formation at its source by directly inhibiting NOX enzyme activity. One study demonstrates that it can bind to the extracellular region of the catalytic subunit of NOX enzymes in an allosteric manner, distinct from the NADPH binding site, which leads to a decrease in NADPH-dependent superoxide generation and hydrogen peroxide production (Gorin et al., 2015, pp. 16–20). In addition to its enzyme inhibitory actions, the dihydropyrazolone scaffold confers an inherent ROS scavenging property, enabling the compound to neutralize peroxynitrite and hydrogen peroxide through redox-mediated chemical mechanisms (Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30; Gaskin et al., 2021, pp. 8–9). This dual property—direct enzyme inhibition coupled with ROS scavenging—is theorized to offer a more comprehensive approach to modulating oxidative stress in target tissues. However, there are conflicting reports in the literature regarding the specificity of its NOX inhibition, with some studies suggesting that measured low Ki values may be artifactual due to interference with assay components such as horseradish peroxidase, raising questions about whether the observed effects are entirely attributable to NOX inhibition or, in part, to non-specific redox modulation (Vincent, 2021, pp. 79–80; Demircan et al., 2022, pp. 12–13). Notwithstanding these concerns, the prevailing hypothesis remains that by dampening NOX activity, GKT137831 reduces both cytosolic and mitochondrial ROS. In the context of RPE cells, which are rich in mitochondria and subject to high oxidative loads due to constant light exposure and high metabolic activity, the inhibition of NOX4 is expected to be particularly beneficial for mitigating oxidative damage to the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and preserving the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 24–28).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underpinning the repurposing of GKT137831 for the treatment of dry AMD is that its inhibition of NOX4—and, by extension, NOX1—leads to a substantial reduction in the generation of reactive oxygen species within the retinal pigment epithelium. Oxidative stress in RPE cells is a key driver of mitochondrial dysfunction, particularly impairment of electron transport chain complexes, which in turn leads to decreased cellular energy production and the eventual onset of apoptosis. By pharmacologically reducing the burden of ROS, GKT137831 is expected to prevent the oxidative damage to mitochondrial ETC components, thereby preserving the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and ensuring continued ATP production and cellular viability under conditions of oxidative stress (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 24–28). In vitro assays utilizing RPE cells exposed to high-glucose or other oxidative stress conditions have shown that treatment with GKT137831 can dampen ROS levels, reduce caspase-3 activity (a marker of apoptosis), and decrease the expression of inflammatory molecules (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). Given that the pathogenesis of dry AMD involves chronic, low-grade oxidative damage and inflammation leading to RPE degeneration, the expected therapeutic effect of GKT137831 would be to attenuate these processes at a cellular level, thereby slowing or halting disease progression. Moreover, the expression profile of NOX enzymes—particularly NOX4 in RPE cells—provides a sound molecular basis for this approach, with several studies documenting increased NOX activity under conditions that mimic AMD pathogenesis (Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11; Kulbay et al., 2024, pp. 2–5). Furthermore, the oral formulation of GKT137831, validated in other disease contexts, offers a practical advantage because it facilitates long-term administration, which is essential for a chronic condition like dry AMD where sustained drug exposure is necessary to counteract cumulative oxidative damage (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating the potential of GKT137831 as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses emerge. Among its major strengths is the robust preclinical evidence that supports the concept of targeting NOX enzymes to mitigate oxidative stress. The dual mode of action—combining direct enzyme inhibition with ROS scavenging—provides a theoretically advantageous approach to protecting RPE cells from both cytosolic and mitochondrial oxidative insults (Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 26–30; Gaskin et al., 2021, pp. 8–9). This is particularly pertinent in dry AMD, a disease where oxidative stress is a driving force behind RPE dysfunction, drusen formation, and subsequent photoreceptor degeneration (Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 1–7). Furthermore, GKT137831’s progression into Phase II clinical trials for other indications such as diabetic nephropathy and primary biliary cholangitis demonstrates that the compound is orally bioavailable and has an acceptable safety profile in human subjects (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26; Buglak et al., 2018, Art. 2468457). This reduces the developmental risk when considering repurposing for dry AMD since chronic administration is feasible and the regulatory pathway may be accelerated based on existing human data.

On the other hand, significant concerns related to the specificity of GKT137831’s mechanism remain. Conflicting evidence suggests that some of the in vitro inhibitory effects attributed to the compound may be partly due to assay artifacts or non-specific redox-modulating activities rather than bona fide NOX inhibition (Vincent, 2021, pp. 79–80; Demircan et al., 2022, pp. 12–13). These findings raise critical questions regarding the extent to which the protective effects observed in retinal and other disease models are directly mediated by diminution of NOX-derived ROS. Additionally, while preclinical studies in diabetic and ischemic retinopathy models have provided promising results, there is a paucity of data directly linking GKT137831 to improved outcomes in dry AMD specifically. The absence of studies evaluating blood–retinal barrier permeability, retinal tissue pharmacokinetics, and direct effects on RPE mitochondrial function in the context of AMD remains a notable gap (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Gaskin et al., 2021, pp. 15–17). Moreover, some reports indicate that the antiproliferative or cytoprotective effects observed with GKT137831 are independent of NOX1/4 expression, suggesting that its mechanism of action in certain cell types may be more complex than initially postulated (Demircan et al., 2022, pp. 2–3, 12–13).

Given these considerations, the overall evaluation is cautiously optimistic. GKT137831, with its favorable oral bioavailability and established safety profile from Phase II clinical trials in non-ocular indications, represents a promising candidate for repurposing given the central role of oxidative stress and NOX-mediated ROS production in dry AMD. Its capacity to reduce ROS levels, modulate inflammatory responses, and potentially preserve mitochondrial function in RPE cells offers a compelling therapeutic rationale (Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 1–7; Shi, 2024, pp. 21–24).  

Furthermore, detailed mechanistic studies employing genetic knockdown approaches in RPE cells, coupled with advanced imaging techniques to monitor mitochondrial dynamics, would be critical to discern whether the expected effects are indeed mediated via NOX inhibition or through alternative, non-NOX-related redox pathways (Demircan et al., 2022, pp. 2–3, 12–13). Given that some reports have reported paradoxical increases in ROS in other cell types treated with GKT137831, it is imperative to understand its cell-type-specific and context-dependent effects to mitigate unintended pro-oxidant consequences in the delicate retinal environment (Demircan et al., 2022, p. 13; Vincent, 2021, pp. 13–17).

In summary, the strengths of GKT137831 lie in its dual functional profile as both a NOX inhibitor and an ROS scavenger, its documented efficacy in preclinical models of oxidative stress-induced pathologies, and its demonstrated oral bioavailability with favorable safety outcomes in human trials for other indications (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Buglak et al., 2018, Art. 2468457; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26). These attributes strongly support the rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD, where oxidative stress is a key pathogenic driver. Nonetheless, weaknesses including unresolved mechanistic ambiguities, potential off-target effects, and limited direct evidence in AMD-relevant models call for rigorous additional research before clinical translation can be confidently pursued (Vincent, 2021, pp. 79–80; Demircan et al., 2022, pp. 2–3, 12–13). Overall, while there is considerable promise in targeting NOX-mediated oxidative stress in the RPE with a compound like GKT137831, the current evidence base necessitates further specific validation within the context of dry AMD. Such an approach would ideally involve a series of well-designed in vitro and in vivo experiments to ascertain pharmacodynamics, tissue distribution within ocular compartments, and ultimately, the functional outcome measures relevant to RPE health and retinal integrity under conditions that closely mimic the human disease state (Cai et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Gaskin et al., 2021, pp. 15–17; Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11).  

The next steps for our research team should include initiating experiments using cultured RPE cell lines exposed to oxidative stress paradigms (e.g., high-glucose, light-induced stress) to determine whether GKT137831 effectively preserves mitochondrial function and decreases apoptotic markers. Parallel studies in animal models of dry AMD, particularly those that recapitulate key features such as drusen formation, RPE degeneration, and subsequent photoreceptor loss, will be essential to elucidate the in vivo efficacy of the compound (Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11; Kim et al., 2021, pp. 24–28). Ultimately, while the translational potential is high given its clinical safety record and oral formulation, the mechanistic uncertainties must be thoroughly addressed to confidently advocate for clinical trials in dry AMD patients. In conclusion, GKT137831 remains an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, provided that further targeted research can unequivocally demonstrate its beneficial effects on RPE mitochondrial health and overall retinal preservation (Elbatreek et al., 2020, pp. 12–14; Sassetti et al., 2021, pp. 21–26; Ruan et al., 2021, pp. 10–11).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
MCC950 is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor that belongs to the diarylsulfonylurea class of compounds originally identified through screening efforts aimed at inhibiting IL-1β processing. Its chemical origins trace back to early studies (circa 2001) that recognized diarylsulfonylurea molecules as cytokine-release inhibitory drugs (CRIDs) before the advent of specific inflammasome inhibitors (Coll et al., 2015). Subsequent medicinal chemistry efforts led to the selection, optimization, and detailed characterization of one member of this series that came to be known as MCC950. Synthetically, MCC950 is produced through a multistep sequence that includes key transformations such as Friedel–Crafts acylation of an indene derivative, acid-promoted cyclization, direct nitration, and subsequent conversion into its final diarylsulfonylurea form, as detailed in the original publication’s Online Methods and Supplementary Materials (Coll et al., 2015; Keuler et al., 2022). Developed initially as an inhibitor of IL-1β post-translational processing, MCC950 was repurposed as a potent and highly selective inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome, exhibiting nanomolar potency (approximately 7.5 nM in murine bone marrow–derived macrophages) with a favorable selectivity profile over other inflammasomes such as AIM2, NLRC4, or NLRP1 (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021; Hill et al., 2017). Marketed under various identifiers – one of which is the Selleckchem product code S8643 – MCC950 represents a well-characterized chemical tool that has continued to serve as both a probe for studying NLRP3 biology and a preclinical candidate in inflammatory disease models (Das et al., 2021; Sharma et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
MCC950 has been extensively evaluated in preclinical studies targeting inflammatory diseases driven by aberrant NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Its discovery followed earlier observations that sulfonylurea agents such as glyburide, traditionally used in type 2 diabetes for their insulin-secretagogue activity via KATP channel inhibition, also inhibited NLRP3-driven processes albeit at micromolar concentrations (Chauhan et al., 2020; Coll et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2017). In contrast, MCC950 exhibits a markedly improved potency at nanomolar levels and a higher degree of specificity. Preclinical evaluations demonstrated that MCC950 effectively blocks both the canonical and noncanonical activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, resulting in suppressed activation of caspase-1 and reduced IL-1β secretion (Das et al., 2021; Hill et al., 2020). Its efficacy has been validated in a wide range of inflammatory disease models including cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS), multiple sclerosis models such as experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), pulmonary and cutaneous inflammation, Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, and even models of kidney and liver fibrosis (Das et al., 2021; Narros-Fernández et al., 2022; Sharma et al., 2023). Although MCC950 has not yet been formally used in clinical applications—and indeed its clinical development was reportedly halted due to safety concerns such as elevated transaminases and organ structural damage in preclinical toxicity studies (Johansson et al., 2025)—its robust preclinical record has established it as the prototype NLRP3 inhibitor. There is emerging interest in exploiting its mechanism for diseases wherein inflammasome-driven pathology is central. While direct data on the use of MCC950 for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) are not available in the literature, the growing evidence implicating the NLRP3 inflammasome in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction suggests that repurposing MCC950 for dry AMD is a scientifically plausible strategy (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021; Keuler et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of MCC950 is one of its most compelling features. At the molecular level, MCC950 selectively inhibits the NLRP3 inflammasome by directly binding to the NACHT domain, specifically targeting the Walker B motif that is essential for ATP hydrolysis and subsequent conformational changes required for inflammasome assembly (Hill et al., 2020; Sharma et al., 2023). In doing so, MCC950 prevents the oligomerization of NLRP3 and the recruitment of the adaptor protein ASC, thereby abrogating the activation of caspase-1 and the maturation and release of proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18 (Coll et al., 2015; Keuler et al., 2022). Structural analyses, including photoaffinity labeling and surface plasmon resonance (SPR) studies, have confirmed the high affinity binding (with SPR-derived K_D values in the low nanomolar range) of MCC950 to its target within NLRP3 (Coll et al., 2019; Hill et al., 2017). Importantly, MCC950 does not interfere with upstream ionic events, such as K^+ efflux or Ca^2+ signaling, which are also involved in NLRP3 activation pathways; rather, its action is confined to the blockade of ATP hydrolysis, offering a direct means to “lock” NLRP3 in an inactive, closed conformation (Das et al., 2021; Keuler et al., 2022; Li, 2020). This precise targeting underpins its exceptional potency and selectivity among inflammasome inhibitors. Moreover, a body of literature has explored the structure–activity relationships (SAR) surrounding the diarylsulfonylurea scaffold of MCC950, confirming that modifications to key structural motifs (for instance, the s-hexahydroindacene group) can have significant impacts on both inhibitory potency and chemical stability; these insights have spurred the design of hybrid molecules that further exploit MCC950’s pharmacophore for dual-target activities (Hill et al., 2017).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
The pathophysiology of dry AMD is characterized by the progressive degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), which results from chronic cellular stress—largely driven by mitochondrial dysfunction and elevated reactive oxygen species (ROS) production—that culminates in an inflammatory cascade. A growing body of evidence implicates the NLRP3 inflammasome as a critical mediator in this process; in the RPE, mitochondrial ROS can instigate NLRP3 activation, leading to the cleavage of caspase-1 and the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, which in turn exacerbate RPE atrophy and compromise the integrity of the retinal barrier (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021). The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of MCC950 for dry AMD is that by selectively inhibiting NLRP3 activation, MCC950 would interrupt this pathogenic cycle. Specifically, its potent inhibition of ATP hydrolysis within the NACHT domain would prevent the inflammasome assembly even in the presence of mitochondrial ROS, thereby blocking caspase-1 activation and subsequent IL-1β secretion. In preclinical models where MCC950 has been tested—such as sodium-iodate-induced damage and laser-induced injury—this compound has been shown to suppress NLRP3-dependent cytokine secretion and preserve barrier function (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021; Narros-Fernández et al., 2022). Extrapolating these observations to the context of dry AMD, one would expect that targeted inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome in RPE cells (which are known to express and be affected by proinflammatory cytokines) would confer protection against mitochondrial ROS-induced damage, maintain RPE integrity, and ultimately slow or halt the progression of geographic atrophy that typifies the dry form of AMD. Additionally, since microglial activation and subsequent inflammatory signaling are also contributing factors in dry AMD, the dual inhibitory effect on both RPE and resident microglia further supports the anticipated beneficial impact of MCC950 in this disease setting (Li, 2020; Sharma et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
MCC950 presents several compelling strengths as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. First, its proven high potency (with an IC_50 in the low nanomolar range) and its exquisite selectivity for the NLRP3 inflammasome make it a highly attractive candidate for modulating the pathological inflammation observed in dry AMD (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021). The detailed elucidation of its mechanism of action—specifically, its direct binding to the Walker B motif within the NACHT domain of NLRP3, thereby preventing the critical ATP-driven conformational changes necessary for inflammasome assembly—provides a clear rationale for its use in conditions where aberrant inflammasome activation is pathogenic (Hill et al., 2017; Hill et al., 2020; Sharma et al., 2023). This mechanism directly addresses one of the key molecular events implicated in RPE atrophy: the mitochondrial ROS-induced activation of NLRP3 leading to sustained release of IL-1β and caspase-1-mediated cell death. If MCC950 can similarly suppress these events in RPE and microglia, it is expected to preserve barrier function and cellular viability in the retina, thereby potentially altering the course of dry AMD.

However, several challenges and weaknesses must be considered in the overall evaluation of MCC950 for dry AMD. One major concern is the clinical safety profile of MCC950. Although it has displayed robust anti-inflammatory activity in numerous preclinical models, clinical development efforts involving MCC950 were reportedly halted in part due to safety concerns—including elevations in transaminases and signs of organ structural damage (Johansson et al., 2025). This systemic toxicity is particularly relevant when considering chronic diseases such as AMD, which require long-term treatment. That said, repurposing MCC950 for a localized indication like dry AMD might allow for alternative routes of administration (for instance, intravitreal injection) that could mitigate systemic exposure and reduce the risk of adverse systemic effects. Additionally, the pharmacokinetic challenges noted in certain contexts—such as its poor penetration when adapted as a PET radiotracer for CNS imaging (Hill et al., 2020)—may or may not translate to ocular tissues, where barriers and tissue distribution differ from those of the brain.

Another potential limitation is that, to date, there is limited direct evidence supporting the use of MCC950 in ocular models or specifically in RPE cells. While its efficacy in a variety of inflammatory and neurodegenerative models bodes well for its potential utility in dry AMD, further targeted research is required to confirm that the mechanisms at play in RPE degeneration align sufficiently with those observed in the well-characterized models of CAPS, EAE, and other inflammatory disorders (Das et al., 2021; Narros-Fernández et al., 2022). Moreover, the possibility of unintended off-target effects remains a concern in any repurposing strategy, and the selectivity profile, although excellent in controlled in vitro settings, must be rigorously validated in the complex microenvironment of the retina.

From a formulation and delivery standpoint, achieving the correct drug concentration in the retinal tissues poses an additional challenge. The ocular bioavailability of MCC950, especially given its physicochemical properties as a diarylsulfonylurea, will need to be thoroughly evaluated. The opportunity to leverage existing ophthalmic delivery platforms—such as sustained-release intravitreal implants or nanoparticle-mediated delivery—could provide solutions that maximize the therapeutic effect while minimizing potential toxicity.

In summary, MCC950 stands out as a promising candidate owing to its highly selective inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome, a mechanism intimately linked with the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Its background as a diarylsulfonylurea with well-documented preclinical efficacy in suppressing IL-1β release and blocking caspase-1 activation provides a strong mechanistic foundation. The compound’s history of preclinical success in multiple inflammatory disease models, combined with detailed insights into its mechanism of action, supports its potential repurposing for dry AMD—especially given that inflammasome-mediated inflammation is a key driver of RPE cell degeneration. Nonetheless, caution is warranted due to prior safety concerns encountered in systemic applications, and these must be addressed through careful evaluation of ocular-specific pharmacokinetics, dosing paradigms, and delivery methods. Ultimately, with rigorous preclinical validation in relevant ocular models and potential formulation optimization to ensure localized protection with minimal systemic exposure, MCC950 could provide an innovative therapeutic approach to halting or slowing the progression of dry AMD (Coll et al., 2015; Das et al., 2021; Hill et al., 2020; Johansson et al., 2025; Li, 2020; Sharma et al., 2023).

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO‐Me) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), structured in sections that address its origins, therapeutic history, known mechanisms of action, expected effects in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and an overall assessment of its strengths and challenges.

• Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Bardoxolone methyl is a semisynthetic derivative belonging to the synthetic oleanane triterpenoid class. Its origin stems from oleanolic acid—a naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid abundantly found in various medicinal plants. Early medicinal chemistry programs sought to overcome the modest anti‐inflammatory activity and poor bioavailability of oleanolic acid by introducing targeted modifications. Through chemical derivatization, these programs generated CDDO (2‐cyano‐3,12‐dioxooleana‐1,9‐dien‐28‐oic acid) and subsequently its C‐28 methyl ester, known as Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO‐Me) (Borella et al., 2019). The synthetic process involves the installation of electrophilic Michael acceptor groups at strategic positions on the oleanane scaffold, such as the addition of an α,β‐unsaturated carbonyl in the A‐ring and further incorporation of a cyano group that substantially increases the compound’s potency relative to its natural precursor (Wong et al., 2016; Zhang & Chapman, 2020). These chemical modifications not only enhance the anti‐inflammatory and anticancer properties but also improve chemical stability and oral bioavailability. The structural design, which incorporates a reversible electrophilic reactivity, underpins the compound’s ability to engage diverse cellular targets (Thomas, 2012; Zhou et al., 2014). Bardoxolone methyl thus represents a chemically advanced, highly potent agent from a class of molecules originally designed to trigger cytoprotective responses via direct electrophilic modulation.

• Therapeutic History  
Bardoxolone methyl has undergone extensive preclinical and early clinical evaluation primarily in fields as disparate as oncology and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Initial studies established that synthetic oleanane triterpenoids, including CDDO and its variants, exert dramatic anti‐inflammatory effects by suppressing inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and cyclooxygenase (COX‐2) expression in activated macrophages (Gatbonton‐Schwager, 2014). Preclinical studies in multiple mouse cancer models and inflammatory conditions confirmed its potent anticancer activity and cytoprotective properties, which catalyzed its progression into human clinical trials (Borella et al., 2019; Nakagami, 2016).  
In the clinical arena, Bardoxolone methyl was advanced through Phase I cancer trials, where its once‐daily oral dosing regimen and pharmacokinetic profile—with a terminal half‐life of approximately 39 hours—were characterized (Thomas, 2012; Nakagami, 2016). More notably, its unexpected ability to improve estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in patients with advanced renal disease, particularly in diabetic nephropathy, led to its evaluation in large Phase II and Phase III trials, such as the BEAM and BEACON studies (Yagishita et al., 2020; Tanase et al., 2022). However, the BEACON trial was terminated prematurely due to an increased incidence of cardiovascular events, including heart failure, highlighting concerns about the compound’s systemic safety profile when used at higher doses or in populations with comorbidities (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012).  
Despite its promising preclinical pharmacology and the breadth of clinical data available in non‐ocular indications, to date there is no direct record in the literature of Bardoxolone methyl being used specifically for the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular degenerative conditions (Schiavoni et al., 2025). Nonetheless, the overall safety and pharmacokinetic properties observed in CKD and oncology trials lend valuable insights for considering drug repurposing across therapeutic areas.

• Mechanism of Action  
Bardoxolone methyl is best known for its ability to activate the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway—a master regulator of cellular defense mechanisms against oxidative and electrophilic stress. Under basal conditions, Nrf2 is tightly regulated by Kelch‐like ECH‐associated protein 1 (Keap1), which serves as an adaptor for ubiquitin ligases targeting Nrf2 for proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl functions as a potent electrophile and interacts with sulfhydryl groups on critical cysteine residues within Keap1. This covalent or reversible Michael addition reaction disrupts the Keap1–Nrf2 complex, thereby stabilizing and allowing Nrf2 to translocate into the nucleus (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).  
Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to the antioxidant response element (ARE) in the promoter regions of a host of cytoprotective genes. This transcriptional activation results in the upregulation of a battery of antioxidant and phase II detoxifying enzymes, including but not limited to heme oxygenase‐1 (HO‐1), NAD(P)H dehydrogenase (quinone 1; NQO1), various glutathione transferases, and glutamate–cysteine ligase subunits (Thomas, 2012; Wong et al., 2016). Studies in non‐ocular tissues have shown that at very low (nanomolar) doses, Bardoxolone methyl robustly engages this cytoprotective program while also exerting dose‐dependent biology wherein intermediate and high doses trigger effects such as modulation of cell differentiation and direct anticancer activity, respectively (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).  
It is important to note that while the canonical targets of Nrf2 activation are well characterized, Bardoxolone methyl’s electrophilic character enables it to interact with multiple regulatory proteins. For example, it can inhibit IκB kinase β (IKKβ), leading to suppression of nuclear factor κB (NF‐κB) signaling and subsequent reduction in proinflammatory cytokine production (Zhou et al., 2014; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although the literature does not provide direct experimental evidence that Bardoxolone methyl specifically upregulates mitochondrial antioxidants such as superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) and peroxiredoxin 3 (PRDX3) in RPE cells, the robust, broad‐spectrum transcriptional response induced by Nrf2 activation strongly suggests that mitochondrial and cytoplasmic components of the antioxidant defense system may also be upregulated (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015). Such upregulation would be consistent with previous findings of increased expression of antioxidant genes and improved cellular redox status upon treatment with similar synthetic triterpenoids (Schiavoni et al., 2025; Sporn et al., 2011).

• Expected Effect in Dry AMD  
The pathogenesis of dry age‐related macular degeneration is multifactorial, with chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction playing a central role in the degeneration of the RPE—a critical monolayer that supports photoreceptor health. RPE cells are particularly vulnerable to oxidative damage due to high metabolic activity, exposure to light, and the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). In this context, the proposed mechanism of Bardoxolone methyl, namely activation of the Nrf2/ARE pathway, provides a biologically tenable strategy for neuroprotection and cellular preservation.  
When administered at low doses, Bardoxolone methyl is expected to trigger a cytoprotective transcriptional program in RPE cells. Activation of Nrf2 should lead to the induction of a range of antioxidant enzymes and detoxifying proteins which together help re-establish redox balance in the face of chronic oxidative insult (Borella et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012). One key hypothesis is that, in addition to the already well‐documented induction of cytosolic antioxidants such as HO‐1 and NQO1, Bardoxolone methyl may also promote the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3. SOD2 is the primary defense against superoxide radicals within the mitochondria, and PRDX3 plays a critical role in detoxifying hydrogen peroxide produced by mitochondrial respiration. Although direct data in RPE cells are currently lacking, studies in other cellular contexts have demonstrated that activation of Nrf2 results in the upregulation of a broad spectrum of antioxidant genes, and it is plausible that under the oxidative duress typical of dry AMD, similar effects would be observed in RPE cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
In vitro models simulating oxidative stress—such as exposure of RPE cells to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)—have shown that compounds with similar electrophilic properties, and indeed other members of the CDDO family like CDDO-Im, reduce the intracellular MitoSOX fluorescence signal, indicative of a reduction in mitochondrial ROS (mtROS) (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024). Moreover, improvements in mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) have been correlated with such treatments, suggesting that these molecules can help maintain mitochondrial function under stressful conditions (Nakagami, 2016; Zhou et al., 2014). Such outcomes are highly relevant in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction in the RPE has been implicated in disease progression. The anticipated outcomes, therefore, include a reduction in mtROS, restoration of Δψm, and subsequent preservation of RPE cellular integrity and function.  
Another positive aspect is the compound’s previously established oral bioavailability and pharmacokinetic profile. Clinical studies in CKD patients have demonstrated that therapeutic plasma concentrations can be achieved with once-daily dosing. Although systemic administration in ocular diseases is not ideal, these data provide a strong pharmacological starting point for repurposing. In addition, if systemic toxicity remains a concern—as suggested by the cardiovascular signals in CKD trials—an alternative approach might involve localized ocular delivery (for instance, via intravitreal injection or by developing an ocular formulation) to achieve high retinal bioavailability while minimizing systemic exposure (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).

• Overall Evaluation  
In assessing Bardoxolone methyl for repurposing as a therapeutic for dry AMD, several critical points emerge that underline both its promise and the challenges that must be overcome.

Strengths:  
1. Strong Chemical Rationale and Potency:  
Bardoxolone methyl is a product of sophisticated medicinal chemistry, designed to overcome the limitations of natural triterpenoids like oleanolic acid by installing reactive electrophilic groups that significantly enhance its potency. This design specifically enables the activation of the Nrf2 pathway—a mechanism central to antioxidant defense—at very low concentrations (Borella et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016). The high potency of Bardoxolone methyl as an Nrf2 activator is a significant advantage, particularly when considering that even subtle improvements in cellular antioxidant capacity can have a profound impact on chronic degenerative diseases like dry AMD.

2. Broad Cytoprotective Mechanism:  
The mechanism of Bardoxolone methyl involves the disruption of the Keap1-Nrf2 complex via covalent modification of Keap1 cysteine residues, facilitating the nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and the subsequent transcriptional activation of a broad range of antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes (Zhou et al., 2014; Thomas, 2012). This broad cytoprotective response is particularly relevant to the RPE, where chronic oxidative stress has been implicated in cellular dysfunction and death. The possibility that Bardoxolone methyl may also induce mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3, although not yet directly confirmed in RPE, is an attractive hypothesis; such an effect would directly address the mitochondrial dysfunction that is a hallmark of dry AMD (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).

3. Extensive Clinical Experience and Pharmacokinetic Data:  
Bardoxolone methyl has been evaluated in several clinical trials—most notably in the context of CKD and oncology—yielding a wealth of pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and tolerability data. Its oral bioavailability, with a terminal half-life that supports once-daily dosing, is well documented (Thomas, 2012; Nakagami, 2016). Although the systemic adverse events observed in these trials (such as cardiovascular-related events) present challenges for broad systemic administration, these data nonetheless offer a useful starting point for repurposing. The established clinical profile can inform dose-escalation studies and safety monitoring protocols should Bardoxolone methyl be advanced into ocular trials.

4. Support from Analogous Preclinical Models:  
Several studies in related models have demonstrated that synthetic triterpenoids can protect retinal tissue from oxidative damage. For example, experiments with CDDO-Im, a closely related analogue, have shown protective effects in retinal ischemia–reperfusion injury, including the attenuation of inflammatory responses and preservation of retinal structure (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024). Although these studies are not directly with Bardoxolone methyl, the mechanistic commonalities within this compound class support the notion that the same protective pathways can be harnessed in the context of dry AMD.

Weaknesses and Challenges:  
1. Lack of Direct Evidence in RPE/Dry AMD Models:  
Despite the strong theoretical rationale, direct evidence that Bardoxolone methyl upregulates mitochondrial antioxidants (SOD2, PRDX3) in RPE cells is currently lacking. Most published data are derived from non-ocular cell types or from studies using other analogues such as CDDO-Im (Cai et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2014). It is therefore essential to perform specific in vitro studies in RPE cell lines under oxidative stress conditions to measure the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes and the functional status of mitochondria (e.g., Δψm, mtROS levels) following treatment with Bardoxolone methyl.

2. Safety Concerns from Prior Clinical Experience:  
A significant challenge in repurposing Bardoxolone methyl stems from its safety profile in systemic indications. The Phase III BEACON trial in CKD patients was halted due to an increased incidence of serious cardiovascular events, including heart failure and increased mortality (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although the mechanisms underlying these adverse effects may be related to systemic fluid retention, off‐target reactivity, or other metabolic perturbations, they raise concerns about the safety of systemic administration. For ocular application, it may be necessary to consider alternative dosing strategies or localized delivery methods to avoid systemic exposure while still achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina.

3. Translational and Formulation Challenges:  
The unique anatomy and physiology of the eye introduce additional obstacles in drug repurposing. RPE cells reside in a relatively immune-privileged, isolated microenvironment behind the blood–retinal barrier. The pharmacokinetics and tissue penetration profiles of Bardoxolone methyl observed in systemic circulation may not directly translate to effective intraocular concentrations. Development of specialized ocular formulations—such as sustained-release intravitreal injections or topical applications that can traverse ocular barriers—will be critical for successful translation (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).

4. Multifactorial Nature of AMD Pathogenesis:  
Dry AMD is a complex, multifactorial disease where oxidative stress is only one component of a broader pathogenic network that includes genetic predisposition, inflammation, lipid dysregulation, and complement system activation. While activation of the Nrf2 pathway can counteract oxidative stress and may have secondary anti-inflammatory effects, it is uncertain whether this single mechanism will be sufficient to alter the course of the disease. A combinatorial therapeutic strategy incorporating Nrf2 activation with other modalities might eventually be required to address the full spectrum of dry AMD pathology (Cheng et al., 2021; Thomas, 2012).

5. Dose-Dependent Effects and Narrow Therapeutic Window:  
Bardoxolone methyl exhibits highly dose-dependent pharmacology. At low doses, it predominantly activates Nrf2 and induces cytoprotective genes; however, as the dose increases, additional actions such as pro-apoptotic and cytotoxic effects emerge (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014). Determining the precise dose that is efficacious in RPE cells without triggering deleterious off-target effects will be crucial. This necessitates rigorous dose-ranging studies in preclinical models to define a therapeutic window that maximizes retinal protection while minimizing risks.

• Overall Evaluation and Recommendation  
In summary, Bardoxolone methyl presents a compelling candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD thanks to its well-characterized chemical design, potent induction of the Nrf2 pathway, and a broad cytoprotective mechanism that addresses many aspects of the oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction implicated in RPE degeneration. The extensive clinical data from studies in CKD and oncology provide a valuable foundation for understanding its pharmacokinetics and systemic effects, while the underlying chemistry ensures high potency at low concentrations—features that are highly desirable when targeting a chronic, degenerative condition such as dry AMD (Borella et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012).  
Nonetheless, significant challenges remain. There is a conspicuous gap in the literature regarding the direct evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl in RPE cells and dry AMD models, particularly concerning its ability to upregulate mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes like SOD2 and PRDX3 and thereby mitigate mtROS damage. This gap must be addressed through targeted in vitro assays and in vivo animal studies that simulate the retinal environment and its chronic oxidative stress. Safety concerns, as evidenced by the cardiovascular events observed in CKD trials, underscore the need for caution; these risks may be minimized through localized ocular administration, but careful formulation and dosing studies will be required to establish an acceptable safety profile in the ocular context (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019).  
Given the current state of evidence, it is recommended that Bardoxolone methyl be subjected to further preclinical evaluation in the context of dry AMD. Specifically, studies should focus on:  
 – Conducting detailed in vitro experiments in human RPE cell lines to assess whether exposure to Bardoxolone methyl under oxidative stress conditions leads to the upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants (e.g., SOD2 and PRDX3) and an associated decrease in mtROS (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
 – Evaluating the effects of Bardoxolone methyl on mitochondrial function (including measurements of Δψm, oxygen consumption rate, and mitochondrial integrity) in these cells.  
 – Adapting ocular-specific formulations that allow high local retinal concentrations with minimal systemic exposure, potentially using intravitreal or topical delivery methods, and conducting pharmacokinetic studies that establish retinal tissue exposure (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).  
 – Testing the compound in animal models of dry AMD to determine whether the in vitro antioxidant and mitochondrial protective effects translate into preservation of RPE and photoreceptor structure and function over time (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024).  
If these studies yield positive results that confirm the hypothesized upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants and improved RPE function, Bardoxolone methyl could then be advanced to early-phase clinical trials in patients with dry AMD. Such trials would need to incorporate rigorous safety monitoring protocols to mitigate the known systemic adverse effects. A potential strategy may involve administering the drug in a localized manner or at doses that are effective in the eye but low enough to avoid triggering systemic electrophilic toxicity.

Overall, Bardoxolone methyl holds promise as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD based on its potent Nrf2-activating properties and the central role of oxidative stress in the disease’s pathogenesis. However, its development for an ocular indication will hinge on its ability to selectively and safely modulate the redox status of RPE cells while avoiding systemic side effects. A stepwise, targeted preclinical program that directly addresses these RPE-specific endpoints is therefore critical before consideration of clinical trials in the dry AMD patient population (Nakagami, 2016).

In conclusion, while Bardoxolone methyl offers a strong mechanistic rationale as an Nrf2 activator with the theoretical capacity to upregulate mitochondrial defenses in RPE cells, further targeted studies are essential. The compound’s repurposing for dry AMD is scientifically attractive given the unmet need for effective therapies in this condition; however, the translational path is complex due to safety concerns observed in systemic trials and the lack of direct ocular data. A rigorous preclinical research plan—encompassing in vitro RPE studies, ocular pharmacokinetic assessments, and animal model validation—will be required to determine whether Bardoxolone methyl can be safely and effectively repurposed to preserve RPE function and slow the progression of dry AMD.

• Summary of Key Supporting Points  
– Bardoxolone methyl is a chemically engineered derivative of oleanolic acid that exploits electrophilic modifications to robustly activate the Nrf2 pathway (Borella et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016).  
– Its extensive preclinical and clinical history in oncology and CKD, though not in ocular disease, provides important pharmacokinetic and biological safety data that may be leveraged, with modifications, for ocular use (Nakagami, 2016; Tanase et al., 2022).  
– Its mechanism—covalent modification of Keap1 and subsequent nuclear translocation of Nrf2—leads to the transcriptional upregulation of cytoprotective genes, and it is hypothesized that this would include mitochondrial antioxidants (e.g., SOD2, PRDX3), which are critical for mitigating oxidative damage in RPE cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
– Preclinical data with related triterpenoids in retinal models support the concept that Nrf2 activation can ameliorate oxidative stress and preserve retinal integrity, although direct data for Bardoxolone methyl in dry AMD are presently lacking (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024).  
– Key challenges include the translation of systemic dosing to ocular delivery, the need to specifically validate mitochondrial protective effects in RPE cells, and the resolution of safety issues exemplified by prior cardiovascular signals in systemic trials (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

• Final Recommendation  
Based on the current literature review, Bardoxolone methyl emerges as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its potent Nrf2 activation, broad cytoprotective potential, and a well-documented clinical PK profile. However, its repurposing for ocular application must be preceded by targeted preclinical studies that corroborate its ability to upregulate mitochondrial antioxidants in RPE cells and to reduce mtROS while preserving mitochondrial function. These studies should also explore ocular-specific formulations and dosing regimens that minimize systemic exposure. Only after thorough validation in these preliminary investigations can Bardoxolone methyl be considered a credible candidate for clinical trials in dry AMD patients. Given these considerations, the candidate warrants further investigation despite the existing translational and safety challenges inherent in repurposing a systemically active electrophilic compound for an ocular indication (Borella et al., 2019; Yagishita et al., 2020; Thomas, 2012).
