Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Deferoxamine (also known as desferrioxamine B; DFO) is a natural microbial siderophore originally isolated from Streptomyces pilosus and developed as an iron‐chelating drug in the 1960s, with clinical deployment beginning in 1968 under the trade name Desferal for treatment of iron overload disorders (notably transfusional iron loading in β-thalassemia) (Faa & Crisponi, 1999; Sharpe et al., 2011; Birch et al., 2006). Chemically, DFO is a hexadentate, tris-hydroxamate ligand that coordinates ferric iron (FeIII) at six oxygen donors derived from three bidentate hydroxamate groups to form a very stable 1:1 FeIII–DFO complex with distorted octahedral FeIIIO6 geometry (Sharpe et al., 2011; Richardson & Poňka, 1998). The FeIII affinity is exceptionally high and selective: reported formation constants for FeIII–DFO include log β110 ≈ 30.5 and conditional pM/pFe values around 26–31, while affinity for FeII is ∼20 orders of magnitude lower, consistent with the observation that DFO selectively chelates FeIII in vivo (Sharpe et al., 2011; Kontoghiorghes & Kontoghiorghe, 2020; Birch et al., 2006). The compound is highly hydrophilic, carries a positive charge near physiological pH, and exhibits poor membrane permeability and oral absorption; as a result, DFO is administered parenterally and tends to localize extracellularly or within endosomal/lysosomal compartments after endocytosis (Birch et al., 2006; Kontoghiorghes & Kontoghiorghe, 2020; Zhao et al., 2021). Pharmacokinetically, native DFO has a very short plasma half-life on the order of minutes, with multiple studies reporting ∼10–30 minutes after intravenous dosing, rapid renal clearance, and elimination of chelated iron via urine and bile; the short exposure necessitates prolonged subcutaneous or intravenous infusions for clinical efficacy (Sharpe et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2020; Entezari et al., 2022). DFO is not blood–neural barrier penetrant, limiting access to the central nervous system and retina when given systemically (Li et al., 2023).

As a class, siderophores are low-molecular microbial metabolites evolved for FeIII acquisition and storage; medicinally, DFO is the prototypical siderophore drug and, for decades, has served as the clinical standard for chelation in iron-overload conditions (Hatcher et al., 2009). Within therapeutic iron chelators, DFO’s hexadentate hydroxamate architecture confers high thermodynamic and kinetic stability of FeIII complexes, limiting redox cycling and hydroxyl radical generation relative to weaker or redox-active iron ligands (Hider & Kong, 2013).

Therapeutic History  
DFO has an extensive clinical history as the benchmark iron chelator for transfusional iron overload, especially in β-thalassemia major and other transfusion-dependent anemias; it was approved in the United States in 1968 and used for decades as life-saving therapy, albeit limited by the need for prolonged parenteral infusions and high cost (Sharpe et al., 2011; Birch et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2012). Beyond chronic iron overload, labeled and established uses include acute iron poisoning and treatment of aluminum toxicity, reflecting DFO’s strong FeIII selectivity and capacity to form inert complexes with polyvalent cations in vivo (Jones et al., 2020). The standard practice has involved subcutaneous or intravenous infusions at 20–60 mg/kg daily for 8–24 hours over 5–7 days per week, with urinary and fecal excretion of iron–DFO complexes as pharmacodynamic endpoints; however, adherence and patient acceptance have been major barriers due to the burdensome administration (Tam et al., 2003; Entezari et al., 2022).

The clinical pharmacology and chemistry of DFO have motivated multiple improved-delivery strategies: liposomal encapsulation and multivesicular liposome systems to extend half-life, and macromolecular conjugates (e.g., starch or HES carriers) to prolong exposure and shift biodistribution to iron-storage organs; these approaches have demonstrated prolonged circulation, increased urinary iron excretion, and organ accumulation (Jones et al., 2020; Sharpe et al., 2011; Tam et al., 2003). Nevertheless, DFO remains orally inactive and requires parenteral dosing, in contrast to later oral chelators (deferiprone, deferasirox), which have supplanted it in many indications due to ease of administration while sometimes being deployed in combination regimens with DFO to enhance iron removal and cardiac protection via complementary pharmacokinetics and chelation kinetics (Hider & Kong, 2013; Ma et al., 2012).

In ophthalmology and retinal biology, DFO’s evaluation is mixed. On one hand, iron chelation with DFO has shown protective effects in experimental retinal contexts: it reduced retinal ganglion cell death induced by hydrogen peroxide and paraquat in oxidative-stress paradigms, consistent with inhibition of iron-dependent hydroxyl radical production (Rohowetz et al., 2018). In hemorrhagic retinal injury, DFO protected photoreceptor tissues after subretinal blood in animal models, suggesting iron chelation can blunt heme/Fe-driven toxicity in the subretinal space (Song & Dunaief, 2013). In RPE-relevant cell models, DFO mitigated lipid peroxidation, prevented glutathione depletion, decreased Fe2+ accumulation, and preserved viability of ARPE-19 cells under tert-butyl hydroperoxide and blue-light stress, and it enhanced cell survival by modulating antioxidant defense systems (GSH–GPX4 and FSP1–CoQ10–NADH axes) (Zhao et al., 2025). A zinc–DFO complex (Zn/DFO) designed to improve cellular delivery reduced retinal iron content, lipid peroxidation, and oxidative DNA damage, preserved photoreceptor structure, and improved ERG responses in rd10 mice, demonstrating in vivo neuroprotection when systemic penetration is enhanced (Zhao et al., 2025). Ex vivo, DFO decreased histochemically detectable chelatable iron (Perls–DAB) in macular sections from AMD eyes, supporting the feasibility of removing pathologic labile iron in human AMD tissue (He et al., 2007).

On the other hand, DFO has a documented profile of retinal/ocular toxicity in patients receiving systemic therapy: reports include macular and peripheral pigmentary degeneration, impaired night vision, optic neuritis/neuropathy, cataract, ERG amplitude reductions, and EOG light-peak abnormalities, prompting recommendations for ophthalmic surveillance, and leading some experts to conclude that DFO is a dubious candidate for AMD treatment (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021). In RPE culture, repeated DFO exposure was cytotoxic relative to a prochelator control, and clinical series describe deferoxamine retinopathy across pediatric and adult populations, indicating that while iron chelation can be protective in vitro under specific stress conditions, DFO itself can injure RPE and photoreceptors under sustained or high-exposure regimens (Charkoudian et al., 2008; Błasiak et al., 2011). Importantly, DFO’s poor cell permeability and lack of blood–retinal barrier penetration raise practical concerns about achieving therapeutic intra-retinal exposure without systemic toxicity when administered conventionally (Li et al., 2023; Birch et al., 2006). Finally, although iron chelation is mechanistically compelling for retinal degenerations in which iron accumulation and ferroptotic stress participate, application of systemic chelators like DFO to retinal vascular disease and AMD remains at the basic research stage, with unresolved issues including perturbation of systemic/local iron homeostasis and stability of intracellular chelate complexes (Li et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, DFO is a high-affinity FeIII-selective chelator that forms kinetically inert hexacoordinate FeIIIO6 complexes via three hydroxamate ligands, each providing bidentate O,Oʹ coordination; this renders FeIII chemically sequestered, suppresses redox cycling, and prevents iron from entering the Haber–Weiss/Fenton chemistry that generates hydroxyl radicals from superoxide/hydrogen peroxide (Sharpe et al., 2011; Richardson & Poňka, 1998; Hider & Kong, 2013). The FeIII/FeII couple of ferrioxamine is electrochemically very negative (reported around −468 mV vs. NHE), and the complex is redox-inert under physiological conditions, consistent with its ability to quench iron-mediated ROS production rather than participate in it (Hider & Kong, 2013). In biological systems, DFO preferentially binds non-transferrin-bound iron (NTBI), labile iron pools in hepatocytes/macrophages, and low-molecular-weight iron transiting endosomes/lysosomes after transferrin delivery or ferritin degradation; it can mobilize hepatic stores and iron released by reticuloendothelial cells but cannot effectively strip iron from metalloproteins such as hemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochromes, oxidases, catalase, or peroxidases (Hatcher et al., 2009; Richardson & Poňka, 1998; Faa & Crisponi, 1999). The drug is hydrophilic and generally membrane-impermeant; cellular uptake occurs via fluid-phase endocytosis and pinocytosis, leading to enrichment in endosomal/lysosomal compartments, where it chelates lysosomal labile iron, an activity proposed to block lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis—mechanistically relevant to RPE pathobiology (Zhao et al., 2021; Dayani et al., 2004).

In retina and neural tissues, oxidative damage pathways include iron-dependent conversion of H2O2 to •OH via Fenton chemistry; DFO reduces H2O2-induced damage in retinal ganglion cells and protects against paraquat-generated superoxide by depriving upstream Fenton catalysts of accessible iron (Rohowetz et al., 2018). In RPE and photoreceptors, ferroptosis—a regulated cell death driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation—is closely linked to antioxidant systems centered on glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and, independently, on FSP1-mediated ubiquinol regeneration; DFO’s chelation of FeII/FeIII within lysosomes and cytosolic labile pools acts upstream of these pathways to limit lipid hydroperoxide propagation, preserving GSH–GPX4 and FSP1–CoQ10–NADH defense capacity in ARPE-19 under oxidative stimuli (Zhao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023). In systemic contexts, DFO detoxifies NTBI, reduces heme-derived ferryl species, removes high-oxidation-state heme iron, and directly scavenges some radical species, converging on inhibition of membrane lipid oxidation; these activities potentially translate to retinal cells where heme/iron-driven oxidative stress is implicated (Hatcher et al., 2009).

Notably, DFO’s hexadentate size and hydrophilicity restrict direct ferritin iron extraction and limit chelation in tightly protein-bound pools; smaller chelators can penetrate cells more readily and directly efflux ferritin iron, whereas DFO works primarily by intercepting low-molecular-weight iron pools and forming kinetically inert FeIII complexes that are then cleared, often via hepatobiliary or renal routes (Sharpe et al., 2011; Richardson & Poňka, 1998). In inflamed or ischemic tissues, the depletion of accessible iron by DFO can blunt downstream ROS and inflammatory cascades; however, prolonged systemic chelation perturbs metal homeostasis and can deplete essential iron pools in sensitive tissues, underlying some adverse effects including RPE toxicity, auditory neuropathy, and bone dysplasia (Zhao et al., 2021; He et al., 2007).

Expected Effect  
For dry AMD models centered on RPE iron-dependent oxidative stress, the expected pharmacologic effect of DFO is to reduce the labile Fe pool in lysosomes and cytosol, thereby attenuating hydroxyl-radical production from H2O2 and limiting iron-driven lipid peroxidation; operationally, this should decrease oxidative damage readouts and preserve mitochondrial and cellular function in RPE assays (Rohowetz et al., 2018; Li et al., 2023). Specifically:

- Lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis markers: In ARPE-19 cells, DFO has been shown to mitigate lipid peroxidation under oxidant (tBH) and blue-light stress and to preserve viability, consistent with suppression of ferroptotic death; thus, in RPE assays one should observe reductions in lipid peroxidation assays (e.g., BODIPY-C11) and maintenance of GPX4 activity/content, with complementary preservation of the FSP1–CoQ10–NADH axis (Zhao et al., 2025). The same studies indicate decreased Fe2+ accumulation after DFO, reflecting lower catalytic Fe at sites of peroxidation; similar decreases in labile Fe can be measured via calcein quenching or analogous probes (Zhao et al., 2025).

- Oxidative DNA damage: Systemic Zn/DFO reduced retinal oxidative DNA damage in vivo in rd10 mice; although these are not AMD models, the result predicts that in RPE oxidative stress assays DFO will reduce accumulation of oxidative DNA lesions, including those arising in mitochondrial DNA, where iron-dependent ROS can be particularly damaging (Zhao et al., 2025). Ex vivo human AMD maculas showed decreased Perls–DAB staining after DFO chelation, supporting the feasibility of reducing chelatable iron burden and downstream oxidative chemistry in diseased human retina (He et al., 2007).

- Mitochondrial bioenergetics: Preservation of RPE oxygen consumption rate (OCR) is plausible under DFO exposure insofar as DFO limits lipid peroxidation and maintains the reductive antioxidant systems (GSH–GPX4, FSP1–CoQ10) that protect inner-mitochondrial membranes and electron-transport components from iron-dependent oxidative injury; in ARPE-19, DFO improved survival and redox balance under stress, suggesting OCR preservation would accompany reduced peroxidation (Zhao et al., 2025). In retinal ganglion cells, DFO lessened H2O2-induced cell death, indirectly supporting improved mitochondrial tolerance to oxidant stress; similar protection can be anticipated in RPE where iron-dependent ROS compromise mitochondrial DNA and respiratory complexes (Rohowetz et al., 2018).

- Tissue iron fingerprints: In tissue sections or organoids, DFO exposure is expected to decrease Perls–DAB positive iron signal in regions with elevated chelatable iron, as observed in AMD macular tissue; in vivo, systemic DFO does not cross the BRB well, so demonstration of retinal iron removal may require enhanced uptake strategies (e.g., Zn/DFO) or local delivery (Li et al., 2023; He et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2025).

Caveats critical to experimental design include DFO’s lack of blood–retinal barrier penetration and poor cell permeability, which could limit intracellular RPE exposure and lysosomal targeting in vivo after systemic dosing; thus, in vitro or ex vivo assays will show clearer pharmacodynamic effects than systemic models unless delivery is optimized (e.g., Zn-complexation or nanocarriers) (Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025; Jones et al., 2020). Additionally, repeated or high-concentration exposure can be cytotoxic to RPE in vitro and has been associated with clinical retinopathy, so dose–exposure optimization and careful toxicity monitoring are required, especially in chronic paradigms (Charkoudian et al., 2008; He et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Rationale strength and translational plausibility. The mechanistic rationale for iron chelation in dry AMD is strong: AMD retinas accumulate chelatable iron, iron catalyzes hydroxyl-radical generation and lipid peroxidation, and iron-dependent ferroptotic stress has been implicated in RPE dysfunction and photoreceptor degeneration (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023). DFO is a high-affinity FeIII chelator with extensive human experience, and it is proven to suppress iron-mediated ROS by forming kinetically inert FeIII complexes, preventing Fenton chemistry (Sharpe et al., 2011; Hider & Kong, 2013). In retinal and RPE models, DFO reduces oxidative injury, limits lipid peroxidation, and preserves cell viability; improved-delivery variants such as Zn/DFO demonstrate in vivo protection of retinal structure and function with concomitant decreases in retinal iron and oxidative DNA damage (Rohowetz et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2025). Ex vivo AMD maculae show DFO-responsive chelatable iron pools, reinforcing target engagement in human disease tissue (He et al., 2007). Mechanistically, enrichment of DFO in lysosomes—an organelle central to RPE iron handling, ferritinophagy, and lipid peroxidation—supports a proximal mode of action relevant to ferroptosis biology in AMD (Zhao et al., 2021).

Key liabilities and translational risks. Despite its compelling mechanism, DFO’s drug properties and ocular safety profile are unfavorable for repurposing in dry AMD without substantial reformulation or targeting:

- Ocular toxicity. DFO has a recognized spectrum of retinal adverse effects in patients, including pigmentary retinopathy, optic neuropathy, ERG/EOG abnormalities, and visual loss; authoritative reviews judge DFO a dubious candidate for AMD because of these safety concerns, and clinical surveillance is recommended when patients receive systemic DFO (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023). RPE toxicity is documented in vitro and clinically across age groups, indicating a narrow retinal therapeutic window under repeated exposure (Błasiak et al., 2011; Charkoudian et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2021).

- Delivery limitations. DFO is hydrophilic, membrane-impermeant, and not blood–neural/retinal barrier penetrant, which undermines retinal exposure after systemic dosing; achieving therapeutic intra-RPE concentrations without systemic toxicity is unlikely with conventional infusion regimens (Li et al., 2023; Birch et al., 2006). The molecule’s very short plasma half-life further complicates exposure in avascular tissues like the outer retina (Sharpe et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2020).

- Systemic chelation risks. Long-term DFO perturbs systemic iron balance, interacts with microbiological iron acquisition in certain pathogens (e.g., Vibrio, S. aureus) that can exploit ferrioxamine, and carries recognized risks of growth retardation, bone changes, and infection, which are unacceptable for a chronic ocular disease with slow progression (Sharpe et al., 2011; Faa & Crisponi, 1999).

- Clinical maturity in ophthalmology. While iron chelators show promise in preclinical retinal models, clinical translation to retinal vascular disease/AMD remains at the basic research stage; challenges include maintaining retinal iron homeostasis, avoiding off-target metal depletion (e.g., Zn2+), and ensuring intracellular chelate stability and localization (Li et al., 2023).

Risk-mitigation strategies and development path. If DFO were to be advanced, development should avoid systemic DFO infusions for dry AMD. Instead:

- Leverage targeted delivery. The Zn/DFO complex that facilitates cellular uptake has shown robust neuroprotection, retinal iron lowering, and oxidative DNA damage reduction in vivo; such conjugate-based or carrier-based strategies could provide intracellular RPE delivery at lower systemic exposure, meriting further evaluation in AMD-relevant models (e.g., light damage, iron-loading, aged mice) with retinal safety readouts (Zhao et al., 2025). Nanocarriers or depot formulations that increase local ocular exposure while minimizing systemic levels could be explored, given DFO’s history of half-life extension in liposomal and multivesicular formulations systemically (Jones et al., 2020; Sharpe et al., 2011).

- Consider chemical alternatives within class. Other chelators with better cell permeability and ocular safety have shown retinal protection without the retinotoxicity seen with DFO; for example, deferiprone protected against iron-induced and light-induced retinal degeneration in multiple mouse models and was not found to be toxic to mouse retina in the contexts studied, suggesting that a more lipophilic, lower-molecular-weight chelator could be a safer starting point than DFO for dry AMD (Song & Dunaief, 2013; Picard et al., 2020).

- Exploit prochelation. Pro-chelators like BSIH that become active only under oxidative conditions were non-toxic with repeated exposure relative to DFO and may offer a way to achieve context-dependent iron chelation within oxidatively stressed RPE while sparing normal iron pools, lowering the risk of retinopathy (Charkoudian et al., 2008).

Decision framework for go/no-go. On balance, while DFO validates the iron-chelation mechanism in retinal tissues and provides useful tool-compound effects in vitro and in ex vivo AMD maculae, its physicochemical properties, delivery constraints, and retinal toxicity profile argue strongly against repurposing native DFO for chronic treatment of dry AMD (Li et al., 2023; He et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2021). The most credible development path for DFO derivatives would require:

- Demonstrating safe, effective RPE delivery with a DFO-based construct (e.g., Zn/DFO or nanocarrier) that reduces labile iron, lipid peroxidation, and oxidative DNA damage in AMD-relevant in vivo models without ERG/EOG or structural toxicity (Zhao et al., 2025).

- Establishing a therapeutic index in the retina with chronic dosing and appropriate safety pharmacology (ERG, OCT, histopathology), given reported human retinopathies on DFO (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023).

- Benchmarking against alternative chelators (e.g., deferiprone) that already demonstrate retinal protection and better permeability/safety in vivo, to justify a DFO-based approach scientifically and clinically (Song & Dunaief, 2013; Picard et al., 2020).

Strengths  
- Mechanistic fit: chelates FeIII with high selectivity and prevents Fenton chemistry; acts in lysosomes where RPE iron and lipid peroxidation intersect with ferroptosis (Sharpe et al., 2011; Hider & Kong, 2013; Zhao et al., 2021).  
- Demonstrated retinal pharmacology: reduces oxidative injury in retinal neurons and RPE, lowers retinal iron and oxidative DNA damage with improved delivery, and removes chelatable iron from AMD macula ex vivo (Rohowetz et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2025; He et al., 2007).  
- Extensive human experience: well-characterized PK/PD, safety liabilities, and clinical management of chelation therapy (Jones et al., 2020; Tam et al., 2003).

Weaknesses  
- Ocular toxicity liability with systemic DFO, including pigmentary retinopathy and electrophysiologic dysfunction, making native DFO a poor risk–benefit prospect for a chronic retinal indication (He et al., 2007; Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021).  
- Poor retinal exposure after systemic dosing due to hydrophilicity and lack of BRB penetration; very short half-life complicates sustained intraocular levels (Li et al., 2023; Birch et al., 2006; Jones et al., 2020).  
- Systemic risks (growth, bone, infection) incompatible with large, elderly dry-AMD populations unless exposure is tightly localized to the eye (Faa & Crisponi, 1999; Sharpe et al., 2011).  
- Field immaturity: iron chelators for retinal disease remain in basic research with unresolved questions about homeostasis and intracellular stability (Li et al., 2023).

Conclusion  
DFO is a mechanistically validated iron chelator with documented ability to reduce iron-driven oxidative injury in retinal systems; however, as a repurposed systemic drug for dry AMD, its delivery barriers and retinal toxicity outweigh potential benefits (Li et al., 2023; He et al., 2007). If iron chelation is pursued for dry AMD within this program, prioritizing better-penetrant, safer chelators (e.g., deferiprone) or context-activated prochelators over native DFO is the higher-probability path; alternately, DFO-based constructs that demonstrably deliver into RPE (e.g., Zn/DFO) with acceptable chronic retinal safety merit targeted preclinical exploration before considering clinical translation (Song & Dunaief, 2013; Charkoudian et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2025).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Spermidine is a naturally occurring polyamine that was originally discovered in bovine semen and later shown to be ubiquitous in all forms of life, ranging from bacteria and plants to fungi and mammals. It belongs to the aliphatic polyamine class, characterized by its low molecular weight, linear arrangement, and multiple amino groups that are fully protonated at physiological pH. Its natural origins stem from highly conserved enzymatic biosynthetic pathways—starting either from ornithine via ornithine decarboxylase or from arginine through an agmatine intermediate—resulting in the formation of putrescine, which is subsequently converted to spermidine through the transfer of an aminopropyl group provided by decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine (dcSAM) (Casero & Marton, 2007; Hobley et al., 2017; Khomutov et al., 2019). Although spermidine can be isolated from natural sources such as food and tissues, it is also available in a chemically defined form commercially (for example, Sigma-Aldrich S2626) and has been used in basic research as well as in some experimental therapeutic approaches. This compound is representative of the polyamine family, and these molecules have traditionally been investigated for their roles in cellular proliferation, nucleic acid stabilization, and modulation of various enzymatic activities, which in turn have broad implications for health and disease (Madeo et al., 2020; Nichugovskiy et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, spermidine’s potential therapeutic applications have been explored extensively in the context of its ability to induce autophagy and affect cellular homeostasis. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that spermidine supplementation can extend lifespan and improve the function of various tissues by enhancing autophagy, contributing to cardioprotection, and promoting neuroprotection in animal models (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). In the ocular domain, several studies have examined its effects on retinal cells: in vitro experiments using ARPE-19 retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells have shown that spermidine can protect against oxidative stress induced by hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) by mitigating intracellular calcium overload and maintaining mitochondrial integrity (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021). Additionally, there are preclinical observations in which intravitreal administration of spermidine in animal models produced both protective effects—in terms of reducing RPE apoptosis—and, at higher doses, toxic outcomes such as RPE necrosis and photoreceptor degeneration (Ohashi et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022). Although spermidine has not been clinically trialed specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), its effects on RPE survival and ocular inflammation have been documented in models that mimic some of the pathophysiologic stressors in dry AMD, such as oxidative damage and dysregulated autophagy (Kim et al., 2021; Senekowitsch et al., 2023). In addition, dietary supplementation studies in humans have associated higher spermidine intake with various beneficial health outcomes, including improved endothelial function and cognitive performance; however, the use of spermidine or polyamines more broadly in chronic degenerative ocular conditions remains largely in the preclinical stage (Madeo et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
The hypothesized mechanism for using spermidine in dry AMD is multifaceted and centers on its ability to modulate cellular quality control processes. At the molecular level, spermidine is known to induce autophagy, a process that mediates the degradation and recycling of damaged or dysfunctional cellular constituents. In model systems ranging from yeast to mammalian cells, spermidine has been shown to increase the conversion of the autophagy marker LC3-I to LC3-II, thereby promoting autophagosome formation (Qin et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022). One important molecular target of spermidine appears to be EP300 (p300), a histone acetyltransferase that, when inhibited, leads to reduced acetylation of several autophagy-related proteins. Inhibition of EP300 has been correlated with enhanced autophagic flux, and several studies suggest that spermidine may exert its autophagy-inducing effects partly by downregulating EP300 expression or activity (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020).

In addition to its effects on EP300, spermidine has been implicated in the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), an evolutionarily conserved energy sensor that modulates metabolic homeostasis and mitochondrial quality control. Activation of AMPK can lead to the phosphorylation and activation of downstream effectors that promote both autophagy and mitophagy (the selective autophagic removal of damaged mitochondria). While direct evidence for AMPK activation by spermidine in retinal cells is still emerging, broader studies in other cell types have described an upregulation of pathways associated with mitochondrial biogenesis and quality control, including the deacetylation of proteins by SIRT1, which often acts in concert with AMPK (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). In the specific context of RPE cells under stress from A2E (a component of lipofuscin) or H₂O₂, the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria and high levels of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) play critical roles in cell loss and dysfunction; thus, induction of mitophagy via enhanced AMPK signaling and subsequent Parkin recruitment to depolarized mitochondria could improve mitochondrial homeostasis and reduce oxidative damage (Kim et al., 2021).

Furthermore, spermidine’s role as an intracellular calcium chelator appears pivotal in its protective effect in RPE cells. Studies have demonstrated that pre-treatment of ARPE-19 cells with 10 µM spermidine prior to oxidative stress prevents intracellular Ca²⁺ overload—a phenomenon that can trigger endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and cell death—thereby maintaining cellular integrity independent of direct ROS scavenging (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021). In summary, spermidine is posited to enhance the clearance of damaged organelles—particularly mitochondria—by increasing autophagic flux through EP300 inhibition and AMPK activation, leading to enhanced LC3-II conversion and Parkin-mediated mitophagy. This, in turn, is expected to reduce mtROS and protect RPE cell viability under conditions of oxidative and A2E-induced stress (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its mode of action, the expected effect of spermidine in a dry AMD model would be a pronounced improvement in the quality control mechanisms of RPE cells. The compound is anticipated to induce autophagy, evidenced by a measurable increase in LC3-II levels, alongside enhanced recruitment of the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin to dysfunctional mitochondria. This concerted activation of autophagy and mitophagy should facilitate the clearance of damaged mitochondria, thereby reducing the accumulation of mtROS and attenuating oxidative stress. In the context of A2E accumulation—a key driver of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD—spermidine is predicted to restore mitochondrial function and improve cell viability. The strengths of spermidine lie in its natural occurrence, multi-targeted action on cellular quality control mechanisms, and established preclinical benefits in other models of aging and oxidative stress. Conversely, the main weaknesses are its narrow therapeutic window, the potential for generation of toxic metabolites, and the current lack of direct clinical or robust in vivo data in dry AMD models. 1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
────────────────────────────────────────────  
PMX53 is a cyclic peptidomimetic antagonist designed to block the complement component C5a receptor (C5aR), which is a critical mediator of pro-inflammatory signaling. The compound is defined by its unique cyclic hexapeptide sequence, AcF[OP(D-Cha)WR], and its design is rooted in systematic modifications of linear peptides derived from the C-terminal region of the endogenous ligand C5a. Early studies revealed that linear C5a fragments possess partial agonist activity; however, by substituting specific residues—most notably replacing phenylalanine with tryptophan at position 5—and then imposing a cyclic conformation through peptide cyclization, researchers were able to generate a molecule that not only negated the agonist properties but also provided potent receptor antagonism (Leonar, 2017).

The cyclic nature of PMX53 is of paramount importance; cyclization confers structural rigidity through a constrained conformation and an inverse γ-turn, which in turn enhances receptor binding selectivity and increases metabolic stability. This rigid structure minimizes entropic penalties upon receptor interaction and enables PMX53 to act in a “pseudo-irreversible” or insurmountable manner, meaning that even transient exposure to the compound can yield a sustained suppression of receptor activity. The cyclic peptide design also imparts resistance to proteolytic degradation—an attribute that is particularly significant for peptide drugs, which are typically prone to rapid enzymatic breakdown (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

Synthesis of PMX53 employs standard peptide synthesis methods. In practice, either solid-phase or solution-phase peptide synthesis techniques are used to assemble the linear precursor via iterative amino acid couplings using Fmoc protocols and appropriate protecting groups. Under dilute conditions, the linear peptide is cyclized using coupling reagents—often in the presence of a base such as DIPEA—to drive intramolecular bond formation, thereby “locking in” the bioactive conformation (Kumar et al., 2020). Although the detailed conditions such as choice of solvent and specific reagents are not provided in the summarized literature excerpts, the robust manufacturing and successful scale-up of PMX53 in preclinical and early clinical settings are evidence of a reliable and reproducible synthetic pathway (Allegretti et al., 2005; Ramsey, 2018).

Belonging to the broader class of cyclic peptide C5aR antagonists, PMX53 represents a well-validated therapeutic modality for modulating complement-mediated inflammatory responses. This class of compounds has been characterized extensively across various models of inflammatory diseases. In addition to systemic inflammatory disorders such as sepsis and arthritis, cyclic C5aR antagonists have been employed in studies assessing tissue injury models including ischemia–reperfusion and immune complex-mediated inflammation (Hutchison & Krause, 2004; Brandstetter et al., 2015). In summary, PMX53’s origins in rational drug design based on structure–activity relationships—its cyclic, constrained architecture, and its demonstrated ability to produce sustained receptor blockade—categorize it as a promising small peptide therapeutic candidate, particularly in indications where complement overactivation is known to play a deleterious role (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
2. Therapeutic History  
────────────────────────────────────────────  
The preclinical history of PMX53 has been marked by extensive evaluation in multiple models of inflammatory disease. Researchers have employed PMX53 in animal studies where its antagonism of the C5a receptor effectively reduced myeloperoxidase (MPO) release from polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs) and inhibited the production of inflammatory cytokines in roles that are essential for mediating tissue damage. For instance, in diverse rodent models of arthritis, sepsis, and inflammatory bowel disease, administration of PMX53—whether via oral, intravenous, or subcutaneous routes—produced significant improvements in disease outcomes. These studies consistently demonstrate that blockade of C5aR by PMX53 can attenuate aspects of the inflammatory cascade that are driven by complement activation (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

Clinical investigations have also been pursued with PMX53. Early-phase clinical trials that targeted diseases characterized by complement dysregulation, such as rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis, indicated that PMX53 exhibits an acceptable safety profile and some limited evidence of efficacy—particularly in psoriasis where a high proportion of patients evidenced lesion improvement (Proctor et al., 2006a; Ramsey, 2018). Of particular note is that while PMX53 has been primarily investigated in systemic inflammatory models and conditions such as sepsis, arthritis, and immune complex-mediated injuries, there is an emerging conceptual linkage between complement-mediated inflammation and retinal degenerative diseases like dry AMD. Several independent studies have demonstrated that the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) expresses C5a receptors constitutively and that exposure to complement-competent serum or recombinant C5a upregulates receptor expression. These studies further show that C5a primes RPE cells for inflammasome activation—a critical process in the pathogenesis of dry AMD—and that modulation of C5aR signaling can affect pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β) (Brandstetter et al., 2015). Taken together, the therapeutic history of PMX53 confirms that it has undergone extensive biochemical, preclinical, and early clinical scrutiny for diseases driven by complement-mediated inflammation. Despite the lack of direct evidence in ocular or AMD-specific contexts, the extensive data from nonocular models and the mechanistic similarities between systemic complement dysregulation and retinal complement activation lay a strong foundation for further exploration of PMX53 in dry AMD (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
3. Mechanism of Action  
────────────────────────────────────────────  
At the molecular level, PMX53 functions by directly binding to and antagonizing the complement C5a receptor (C5aR), a G-protein–coupled receptor that mediates the downstream pro-inflammatory effects of the anaphylatoxin C5a. The binding of C5a to its receptor on cells, including immune cells and RPE cells, initiates a cascade of inflammatory signaling events characterized by calcium mobilization, activation of kinase pathways (such as PI3K and MAPK), and subsequent transcriptional upregulation of inflammatory mediators including IL-1β. In the context of RPE cells, these events are further linked with the generation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome—a process that underpins cellular stress and eventual degeneration in dry AMD (Brandstetter et al., 2015).

PMX53’s mechanism of action is rooted in its cyclic peptide structure, which endows it with the ability to engage the C5a receptor in a manner that is both highly specific and functionally distinct from simple competitive blockade. Extensive structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies, including receptor mutagenesis and docking experiments, have revealed that PMX53 binds primarily to critical extracellular regions of C5aR—most notably the extracellular loop 2 (ECL2) and portions of the transmembrane domain. For example, mutations in ECL2 residues (such as R175) have been shown to significantly reduce the efficacy of both C5a and PMX53, underscoring the importance of this region in ligand–receptor interactions (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006b).

The binding model for PMX53 suggests that its aromatic and hydrophobic components—such as the tryptophan side chain and the d-cyclohexylalanine residue—fit within a hydrophobic pocket formed by receptor residues including I116 and V286. These interactions, which involve hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, and possibly cation–π interactions, contribute to the stability of the ligand–receptor complex and account for the “pseudo-irreversible” nature of the antagonism. In practical terms, once PMX53 binds to C5aR it exhibits insurmountable antagonism, meaning that even in the presence of high concentrations of the endogenous ligand C5a, the receptor remains blocked and unable to signal. Downstream of receptor blockade, the interruption of C5a signaling by PMX53 results in a reduction in calcium influx and the inhibition of kinase cascades that normally lead to the activation of transcription factors such as NF-κB. Thus, by preventing C5a from binding to its receptor, PMX53 is expected to blunt both the immediate signaling events (calcium mobilization, reactive oxygen species generation) and the subsequent transcriptional upregulation of inflammatory mediators that lead to inflammasome assembly (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020).

In summary, at the molecular level PMX53 functions as a robust inhibitor of C5aR by engaging critical residues on the receptor extracellular region, thereby preventing the pro-inflammatory interactions initiated by C5a binding. One of the most significant gaps in the current literature is the absence of direct preclinical or clinical data specific to ocular models of AMD. Although the complement system, and in particular the C5a–C5aR axis, is well documented as playing a role in RPE dysfunction and retinal inflammation (Brandstetter et al., 2015), PMX53 itself has not yet been rigorously tested in models that recapitulate the complex microenvironment of the retina. Animal models that faithfully mimic the chronic complement activation and oxidative stress seen in human dry AMD are necessary to determine whether the robust systemic anti-inflammatory activity of PMX53 can be translated to a localized ocular context (Proctor et al., 2006a; Hutchison & Krause, 2004).

•  A second concern relates to species-specific differences in receptor binding affinity. It is well established that PMX53 exhibits high affinity for human and rat C5a receptors (in the range of tens of nanomolar), whereas its affinity for the mouse receptor is markedly lower (approximately 36 µM) (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a). This presents a practical obstacle, as many preclinical studies in ophthalmology rely on murine models to assess disease progression and drug efficacy. To circumvent this pitfall, it may be necessary to utilize alternative animal models with receptor pharmacology that more closely mirrors the human system—such as rat models or non-human primate studies—or to develop further analogues that demonstrate improved cross-species binding (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

•  Another issue is the challenge of delivering a peptide drug to ocular tissues in a sustained and therapeutically effective manner. The ocular barriers, including the corneal epithelium and the blood–retina barrier, limit the penetration and retention of systemically administered drugs. In the case of PMX53, whose peptidic nature predisposes it to rapid clearance and potential degradation, specialized formulation strategies will be essential. Approaches such as encapsulation in biodegradable nanoparticles, development of sustained-release intravitreal implants, or formulation with permeability-enhancing agents could be explored to ensure that therapeutically relevant concentrations of PMX53 reach the RPE and maintain a prolonged therapeutic effect (Kumar et al., 2020).

•  Safety considerations within the ocular environment also warrant close attention. While systemic administration of PMX53 has demonstrated an acceptable side-effect profile in non-ocular applications, the retina is an immunologically privileged and sensitive tissue. Chronic inhibition of complement-mediated signaling in the eye could potentially impair local immune surveillance or interfere with normal cellular homeostasis. Such risks necessitate detailed ocular toxicology studies to assess the potential for adverse effects resulting from long-term C5aR blockade in RPE cells and other retinal tissues (Proctor et al., 2006a; Hutchison & Krause, 2004).

•  Furthermore, the translational relevance of the anti-inflammatory effects observed with PMX53 in systemic diseases may not directly apply to the intricate pathophysiology of dry AMD. Dry AMD is a multifactorial disease influenced by genetic predispositions, environmental stresses (such as oxidative damage from chronic light exposure), and complex interactions between complement proteins, RPE cells, and the extracellular matrix. While the blockade of C5aR is theoretically poised to reduce mtROS production and inflammasome activation, it is possible that additional redundant inflammatory pathways might offset the therapeutic benefit of targeting a single receptor (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Proctor et al., 2006a).

•  Finally, the overall clinical development history of PMX53 indicates that while the compound has progressed to early clinical trials for systemic inflammatory conditions, challenges related to pharmacokinetics and delivery have hindered further clinical advancements. As such, repurposing PMX53 for dry AMD will require a dedicated research program that not only demonstrates efficacy in ocular models but also addresses the unique drug delivery and safety challenges associated with the eye (Proctor et al., 2006a; Proctor et al., 2006b).

────────────────────────────────────────────  
6. Overall Conclusion  
────────────────────────────────────────────  
In summary, PMX53 is a well-characterized cyclic peptidomimetic C5a receptor antagonist that has been evaluated extensively in systemic models of inflammation and has reached early-phase clinical testing for conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis. Its design, which exploits a cyclic structure to achieve pseudo-irreversible antagonism, provides a strong mechanistic rationale for targeting the complement cascade—which is increasingly recognized as a major contributor not only to systemic inflammatory diseases but also to ocular conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a).

The expected effect of PMX53 in the context of dry AMD is to prevent the binding of C5a to its receptor on retinal pigment epithelial cells, thereby disrupting a key amplification loop that leads to mitochondrial reactive oxygen species overproduction, inflammasome activation, and subsequent IL-1β release. Such a blockade should, in theory, mitigate the chronic inflammatory stress that drives RPE degeneration and, by extension, slow the progression of dry AMD (Brandstetter et al., 2015; Proctor et al., 2006a).

Nonetheless, despite its strong conceptual appeal and preclinical promise in systemic models, significant knowledge gaps remain with respect to its application in the ocular setting. No dedicated studies have yet confirmed the efficacy of PMX53 in reducing complement-driven oxidative stress specifically in the retina, and species-specific differences in receptor binding mean that murine models—a common platform for AMD research—may not accurately reflect the human situation. Additionally, the challenges inherent in delivering a peptide drug effectively to ocular tissues, combined with the potential risks of long-term complement inhibition in the sensitive retinal environment, require careful and systematic investigation through both advanced formulation approaches and dedicated ocular safety studies (Proctor et al., 2006a; Hutchison & Krause, 2004; Kumar et al., 2020).

Overall, while the scientific and mechanistic basis for repurposing PMX53 for dry AMD is compelling—given its ability to disrupt complement-mediated inflammatory cascades and its pseudo-irreversible receptor binding—the translation of these benefits to the ocular milieu remains to be established. A focused research program is needed to conduct in vitro studies in primary human RPE cells exposed to complement activation, followed by in vivo evaluations in non-murine models that more closely mirror human C5aR pharmacology. Further development of ocular delivery systems, including intravitreal implants or nanoparticle-based formulations, will also be essential to overcome the inherent pharmacokinetic challenges posed by a peptide therapeutic.

If these hurdles can be successfully addressed, PMX53 could represent an innovative approach to slow or prevent RPE degeneration by attenuating the complement-driven amplification of mtROS production and inflammasome activation—a cascade that is a key driver of dry AMD pathology. In light of the significant unmet need for effective treatments for dry AMD and the robust preclinical data supporting the anti-inflammatory efficacy of cyclic C5aR antagonists in other contexts, further investigation into PMX53 is both scientifically justified and therapeutically promising (Leonar, 2017; Proctor et al., 2006a; Brandstetter et al., 2015; Ong et al., 2024).

This comprehensive review indicates that while substantial promise exists for PMX53 as a candidate to mitigate the complement-mediated mechanisms underlying dry AMD, its successful repurposing will depend on dedicated ocular pharmacology studies, careful species selection for preclinical investigations, and the development of targeted drug-delivery strategies tailored to the unique anatomical and immunological environment of the eye (Proctor et al., 2006a; Ong et al., 2024; Proctor et al., 2006b).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SRT2104 is a second‐generation synthetic small molecule activator of SIRT1 that emerged from a rigorous high‐throughput screening program at Sirtris Pharmaceuticals and was further developed following GlaxoSmithKline’s acquisition of the compound’s intellectual property (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 1–2). The molecule was rationally designed by modifying an imidazo[1,2‐b]thiazole core structure, a strategy intended to overcome the limitations associated with earlier SIRT1 activators such as resveratrol, notably its poor bioavailability and off‐target effects (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; 14–16). As a member of the class of SIRT1 activators, SRT2104 is distinguished by its high specificity and potency, thereby enabling a more targeted modulation of NAD⁺‐dependent deacetylation pathways compared to naturally occurring polyphenols (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16). This class of compounds has been broadly investigated in the context of metabolic, inflammatory, and neurodegenerative disorders due to its capacity to enhance mitochondrial function, reduce oxidative stress, and modulate inflammatory cytokines (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; 10–11). Although its initial therapeutic intent was not directed toward ophthalmological conditions, mechanistic insights into SIRT1’s regulatory functions in cellular metabolism and stress responses have prompted interest in repurposing SRT2104 for conditions such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells play central roles (Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4; Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2).

Therapeutic History:  
Extensive preclinical and early‐phase clinical studies have established a strong safety and tolerability profile for SRT2104, particularly in elderly populations and subjects with type 2 diabetes (Libri et al., 2012, pp. 1–2; Baksi et al., 2014, pp. 7–11). In a pilot randomized, placebo‐controlled trial, SRT2104 was administered to healthy elderly volunteers, demonstrating that the compound was generally well tolerated, with an average peak serum concentration reached within 2 to 4 hours and an elimination half‐life between 15 and 20 hours (Libri et al., 2012, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, studies involving participants on metformin therapy for type 2 diabetes confirmed that SRT2104 exhibits a favorable safety profile, noting stable pharmacokinetics and no serious adverse events over an extended dosing period (Baksi et al., 2014, pp. 7–11). Beyond safety, several clinical studies have reported beneficial effects on metabolic biomarkers: SRT2104 administration was associated with significant reductions in serum cholesterol, low‐density lipoprotein (LDL), and triglyceride levels, suggesting improvements in systemic metabolic health (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 1–2). Additional clinical investigations indicated that adverse reactions—when they occurred—were generally mild and self‐limiting, including transient headaches, dizziness, and mild upper respiratory indications, which further supports its clinical tolerability (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 13–14; 2–4).  
SRT2104 has also been evaluated in the context of neurodegenerative processes; preclinical models demonstrated its ability to cross the blood‐brain barrier and exert neuroprotective effects, for example, in Huntington’s disease models where improvements in survival and motor function were observed along with reduced cerebral atrophy (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 6–7; 7–8). Although none of these studies were primarily focused on dry AMD or similar ocular pathologies, the therapeutic rationale for exploring SRT2104 in AMD is supported by the shared pathophysiological features observed in neurodegenerative disorders and retinal diseases, particularly those aspects involving mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2). It is important to note that while there is substantial clinical evidence for metabolic and neuroprotective effects, no direct clinical trials have yet been conducted in patients with dry AMD, making a translational validation in the specific context of retinal diseases an essential next step (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 14–16).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SRT2104 acts predominantly by binding to and activating SIRT1, a NAD⁺‐dependent histone deacetylase that plays a pivotal role in regulating transcription, cellular metabolism, and stress responses (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16). SIRT1 deacetylates a variety of substrates, including transcription factors such as peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator 1‐alpha (PGC-1α) and factors involved in inflammation such as the NF-κB complex. The deacetylation of PGC-1α is particularly significant because it leads to its activation, thereby enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis and promoting oxidative metabolism (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16). As a consequence, activation of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis results in increased expression of genes involved in antioxidant defense, thus improving cellular resilience to oxidative stress—a key pathological driver in dry AMD (Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4; Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2).  
Moreover, SIRT1 has been shown to deacetylate and modulate the activity of hypoxia‐inducible factor 2α (HIF-2α), which in turn regulates the vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A) promoter (Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4). Given that VEGF-A plays a complex role in retinal homeostasis and neovascular processes, this interaction suggests that SIRT1 activation could fine‐tune vascular responses within the retina. In addition to these effects, SRT2104 has been associated with decreases in pro‐inflammatory cytokine levels including IL-6 and IL-8, thereby potentially mitigating chronic inflammation that contributes to RPE dysfunction and geographic atrophy in AMD (Law et al., 2024, pp. 10–12; Chang et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
It is also noteworthy that SIRT1 is endogenously expressed in human RPE cells and the retina, where it contributes to the maintenance of cellular homeostasis in response to oxidative insults (Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4). In several disease models, suppressed SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling has been linked to mitochondrial disintegration and increased susceptibility to oxidative damage in RPE cells, supporting the therapeutic hypothesis that pharmacologically enhancing SIRT1 activity can restore mitochondrial function and counteract degenerative changes (Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2; 11–13). In summary, the molecular actions of SRT2104 encompass the dual benefits of enhancing mitochondrial respiration via PGC-1α activation and reducing inflammatory mediator production through deacetylation of relevant transcription factors, which together may yield protective effects in the context of dry AMD (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 14–16; 7–8).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underlying the proposed repurposing of SRT2104 for dry AMD is that oral administration of this compound will enhance SIRT1 activity in RPE cells, thereby activating downstream signaling pathways critical to cellular homeostasis (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16). Specifically, increased SIRT1 activity is anticipated to lead to upregulation of PGC-1α, a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis, as well as NRF2, a central transcription factor in the antioxidant defense pathway (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16). As PGC-1α activation drives the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial metabolism and energy production, its upregulation is expected to ameliorate mitochondrial dysfunction—a hallmark feature in the pathogenesis of geographic atrophy within dry AMD (Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4; Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2).  
Furthermore, NRF2 activation is associated with enhanced transcription of a battery of antioxidant enzymes, which can reduce the burden of reactive oxygen species (ROS) that damage RPE cells over time (Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2; 11–13). These biochemical changes are hypothesized to restore the redox balance within RPE cells, thereby slowing or potentially reversing the progression of retinal degeneration observed in dry AMD. In experimental models of metabolic stress, SRT2104 has been shown to improve mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and cellular viability; by extension, similar molecular benefits are anticipated in the RPE, where oxidative damage and mitochondrial dysfunction play crucial roles in disease progression (Libri et al., 2012, pp. 1–2; Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).  
Additionally, given SIRT1’s regulatory role in suppressing pro‐inflammatory gene expression via NF-κB deacetylation, it is expected that SRT2104 will confer anti‐inflammatory effects within the retinal microenvironment, further contributing to the preservation of RPE function (Law et al., 2024, pp. 10–12; Maugeri et al., 2018, pp. 5–7). Although these effects have been robustly documented in systemic tissues such as skeletal muscle and in neuronal models, confirmation in ocular tissues remains a critical area for future preclinical investigation (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 14–16; 6–7). The convergence of improved mitochondrial dynamics, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and reduced inflammatory activity forms the foundational rationale for expecting that SRT2104 can stabilize or restore RPE function, thereby mitigating the development and progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2).

Overall Evaluation:  
SRT2104 presents a compelling candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD given its well‐established safety profile, its potent and selective activation of SIRT1, and the strong mechanistic rationale connecting SIRT1‐mediated pathways to the pathological processes underlying retinal degeneration (Libri et al., 2012, pp. 1–2; Baksi et al., 2014, pp. 7–11; Chang et al., 2024, pp. 13–14). These studies have consistently shown that SRT2104 can be administered with minimal adverse effects, and its pharmacokinetic profile (with rapid absorption and a reasonable half‐life) supports its potential for chronic dosing—an important consideration in the management of a progressive condition like dry AMD (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; 2–4).  
Another significant strength lies in the drug’s mechanism of action: by directly activating SIRT1, SRT2104 engages a fundamental regulator of cellular metabolism that is known to control mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses through the deacetylation of PGC-1α and subsequent NRF2‐mediated gene transcription (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16). Given that mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central drivers of RPE cell degeneration, this targeted mechanism offers a rational therapeutic approach to address the pathophysiological underpinnings of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4; Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2). Preclinical studies in neurodegenerative models further bolster confidence in the neuroprotective aspects of SRT2104, suggesting that similar protective effects might be translated to the retinal environment (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 6–7; 7–8).  
Despite these strengths, several challenges and weaknesses warrant careful consideration. Foremost, there is currently an absence of direct preclinical or clinical data evaluating the efficacy of SRT2104 in ocular models of dry AMD. While the shared molecular pathways between skeletal muscle, neuronal tissue, and RPE cells provide a strong theoretical basis for its repurposing, it remains to be demonstrated experimentally that SRT2104 can adequately penetrate the ocular tissues—in particular, the retina—and reach effective concentrations in the RPE (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 14–16; Hammer et al., 2021, pp. 9–11). The blood‐retina barrier poses unique pharmacokinetic challenges that may not be addressed by data derived solely from systemic administration in non‐ocular tissues.  
Another concern is the translational gap between improvements in biochemical markers and tangible clinical outcomes. For example, while clinical trials in systemic conditions have shown reductions in LDL cholesterol, arterial stiffness, and improvements in mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, similar functional endpoints related to retinal health such as visual acuity or structural preservation of the RPE have not been measured (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; 9–10). This gap underscores the necessity for rigorously designed preclinical models using human RPE cells and animal models of geographic atrophy to ascertain whether the SIRT1 activation by SRT2104 indeed translates into meaningful protection against retinal degeneration (Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2; 2–3).  
There is also the issue of potential off‐target effects or insufficient modulation of the complex interplay between oxidative stress, inflammation, and cellular senescence observed in dry AMD. Although SRT2104’s target specificity is a marked improvement over earlier SIRT1 activators, the multifactorial nature of AMD pathology—including contributions from inflammatory cytokine cascades and abnormal autophagic processes—may require combination therapies or adjunctive strategies beyond SIRT1 activation alone (Maugeri et al., 2018, pp. 5–7).  
Furthermore, some clinical studies have suggested that despite positive modulation of certain biomarkers, SRT2104 may not significantly improve key functional endpoints such as vascular reactivity or insulin sensitivity, suggesting that its efficacy might be context‐dependent or limited to particular physiological systems (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). Although these findings do not directly detract from its potential in AMD, they do highlight the inherent risk in extrapolating systemic benefits to the specialized microenvironment of the retina.  
In summary, while SRT2104 exhibits a strong safety record and a mechanistically robust profile through its activation of SIRT1 and downstream enhancement of mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant capacity, its repurposing as a treatment for dry AMD remains a hypothesis that requires extensive further validation. Key areas for future research include detailed pharmacokinetic studies to ensure adequate ocular tissue penetration, validation of its effects on RPE cell survival and function in both in vitro and in vivo models of geographic atrophy, and ultimately, early‐phase clinical trials designed specifically to evaluate retinal outcomes (Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2; Chang et al., 2024, pp. 14–16). By addressing these gaps, it will be possible to determine whether the encouraging data from metabolic and neurodegenerative indications can indeed be translated into a viable therapeutic strategy for patients with dry AMD.  
In conclusion, SRT2104 is a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate given its ability to activate SIRT1—a key mediator of mitochondrial and antioxidant pathways—in a manner that holds potential to restore RPE function and counteract the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16; Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4). Its clinical safety profile and documented efficacy in modulating systemic metabolic and inflammatory markers provide a favorable foundation for further investigation. However, its application in the ocular arena must overcome several translational barriers, including establishing effective ocular bioavailability and demonstrating specific efficacy in retinal cell models. These challenges underscore the need for targeted preclinical and clinical research to confirm whether SRT2104 can fulfill its therapeutic promise in the context of dry AMD.

1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Mdivi-1, known as mitochondrial division inhibitor 1 (catalog number Sigma-Aldrich M0199), is a synthetic small-molecule compound originally developed for research into mitochondrial dynamics. It belongs to a class of therapeutic agents that modulate mitochondrial fission by targeting the dynamin‐related protein 1 (DRP1). DRP1 is an essential GTPase responsible for driving mitochondrial fission, a process that maintains mitochondrial quality control but, when overactivated, can lead to fragmentation associated with cellular stress and apoptosis. Mdivi-1 was discovered via compound screening experiments aimed at identifying inhibitors of DRP1’s GTPase activity and has been characterized extensively in various in vitro and in vivo studies. Its discovery was motivated by the need to therapeutically intervene in pathologies where aberrant mitochondrial fission contributes to cellular dysfunction. As a representative of DRP1 inhibitory agents, Mdivi-1 has been widely used as an investigational tool in studies related to neurodegeneration, ischemia, and ocular diseases, where mitochondrial integrity is a key determinant of cell survival (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2020). Its synthetic origin and well-documented pharmacological profile render it a candidate for drug repurposing, with potential applications extending into the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) by addressing mitochondrial dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells.

2. Therapeutic History  
Mdivi-1 has a robust preclinical research history across a variety of models that involve oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Initial studies demonstrated that in retinal endothelial cells and neuronal tissues, inhibition of DRP1 by Mdivi-1 prevented excessive mitochondrial fragmentation under conditions of acute stress. These cumulative findings support the repurposing hypothesis that targeting DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission could restore mitochondrial function and survival in RPE cells, thereby halting or slowing the degenerative cascade observed in dry AMD.

3. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, DRP1 is responsible for mediating mitochondrial fission through the constriction and subsequent division of mitochondrial membranes. Upon receiving various stress signals, DRP1 is recruited from the cytosol to the mitochondrial outer membrane where it oligomerizes and hydrolyzes GTP, driving membrane scission. Mdivi-1 specifically inhibits the GTPase activity of DRP1, thereby preventing its self-assembly and subsequent mitochondrial recruitment. This inhibition effectively blocks the fission process that is typically upregulated under conditions of oxidative stress and other cellular insults (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2020). Detailed biochemical investigations have demonstrated that when DRP1 activity is unopposed, mitochondrial fragmentation ensues, leading to diminished mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, decreased oxygen consumption rate (OCR), reduced ATP synthesis, and an increase in the generation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) (Yako et al., 2021). Mdivi-1 counters these deleterious cellular events by preserving the integrity of the mitochondrial network, enabling enhanced ATP production, and maintaining the mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP). Moreover, by inhibiting DRP1, Mdivi-1 reduces the stress-induced release of cytochrome c from the mitochondria—a central step in the intrinsic apoptotic pathway—thus lowering the activation of downstream caspases (She et al., 2018; Yako et al., 2021). In addition to these primary actions, some studies have noted that Mdivi-1 has reversible inhibitory effects on mitochondrial complex I, suggesting that its impact on mitochondrial bioenergetics may be multifaceted (Yako et al., 2021). Such dual actions may serve to further stabilize mitochondrial function under stress.

4. Expected Effect  
Under conditions relevant to dry age-related macular degeneration, such as chronic oxidative stress incident on RPE cells, Mdivi-1 is anticipated to exert a multi-pronged cytoprotective effect. In the proposed assay using H₂O₂-treated ARPE-19 cells—a well-established in vitro model to mimic the oxidative stress environment of dry AMD—the primary expected effect is the inhibition of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission (Yako et al., 2021). By stabilizing mitochondrial dynamics, Mdivi-1 should also improve cellular bioenergetics through enhanced OCR and increased ATP production, both critical parameters that are typically compromised in stressed RPE cells (Yako et al., 2021). The anticipated outcome of these events is a reduction in cell death and apoptosis, as well as improved phagocytic function—an essential role of RPE cells in the maintenance of retinal homeostasis. Furthermore, by mitigating the accumulation of mtROS, Mdivi-1 is expected to lessen oxidative stress, thereby curbing the degenerative processes that are a central component of dry AMD pathophysiology (Yako et al., 2021; Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025). In essence, the mechanistic intervention afforded by Mdivi-1 aims to interrupt the cycle of mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage that leads to RPE cell apoptosis, which is a critical driver of disease progression in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021).

5. Overall Evaluation  
In evaluating Mdivi-1 as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current body of literature. Among its strengths, Mdivi-1 is underpinned by a strong mechanistic rationale: the inhibition of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission is a well-validated approach to restore mitochondrial function in the face of oxidative stress. Preclinical studies have consistently demonstrated that Mdivi-1 preserves mitochondrial network integrity, reduces the production of harmful reactive oxygen species, and prevents the release of apoptogenic factors, thereby facilitating cell survival in retinal models (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2020; Yako et al., 2021). Its efficacy in multiple ocular contexts—including models of glaucoma, retinal detachment, and diabetic retinopathy—highlights the versatility of its cytoprotective actions, which may be directly relevant to the RPE dysfunction and oxidative injury observed in dry AMD (Kim et al., 2015; She et al., 2018). From a biochemical standpoint, the ability of Mdivi-1 to enhance mitochondrial bioenergetics by improving OCR and ATP production, while simultaneously preserving mitochondrial membrane potential, addresses essential aspects of RPE cell metabolism that are often impaired in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Furthermore, the compound’s capacity to reduce apoptotic signaling, as evidenced by decreased cytochrome c release and lower caspase activity, is particularly promising given the established link between mitochondrial-mediated apoptosis and RPE cell loss in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Despite these promising attributes, several limitations and challenges deserve consideration. First, while the preclinical evidence supporting Mdivi-1’s efficacy is compelling, there remains a notable gap in clinical data, particularly in the context of dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Another potential weakness arises from the dual inhibitory effects of Mdivi-1. Some investigations have reported that Mdivi-1 also exhibits reversible inhibition of mitochondrial complex I, which could complicate its therapeutic profile by inadvertently affecting normal mitochondrial respiration (Yako et al., 2021). Moreover, the chronic inhibition of DRP1 raises important questions about the broader physiological implications of interfering with mitochondrial dynamics (Mohammad & Kowluru, 2022; She et al., 2018). Furthermore, the in vitro models currently used, predominantly involving H₂O₂-treated ARPE-19 cells, may not entirely mimic the in vivo microenvironment of the human retina in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). The overall therapeutic window and safety profile of Mdivi-1 also require further elucidation (Yako et al., 2021). Despite these challenges, the mechanistic insights generated from a diverse array of experimental models suggest that Mdivi-1 holds considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its capacity to restore mitochondrial integrity, mitigate oxidative stress, and inhibit apoptotic cascades directly addresses several of the pathogenic mechanisms implicated in dry AMD. Given that current treatments for dry AMD are limited and mainly supportive, a disease-modifying therapy that targets mitochondrial dysfunction would represent a significant advancement in the management of this debilitating disorder (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2015). In summary, Mdivi-1’s strengths lie in its well-characterized mechanism of action, demonstrated efficacy in preserving mitochondrial dynamics under stress, and its potential to enhance cell survival in models of retinal degeneration (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2015; Yako et al., 2021).

Future studies must address the nuances of chronic DRP1 inhibition, optimize dosing regimens, evaluate long-term safety, and conduct thorough pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiling in ocular tissues to fully realize the potential of Mdivi-1 in the clinical management of dry AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021).

In conclusion, the evidence provided by numerous preclinical studies strongly indicates that Mdivi-1’s inhibition of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission offers a promising therapeutic strategy for dry age-related macular degeneration. The compound’s ability to maintain mitochondrial network integrity, enhance bioenergetics, and suppress apoptotic cascades under conditions of oxidative stress in RPE cells is particularly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Although challenges remain in addressing the potential off-target effects and ensuring long-term safety in the clinical setting, the mechanistic rationale and supporting preclinical data justify further investigation into the utility of Mdivi-1 as a repurposed candidate for this currently untreatable condition. As the drug development process progresses, a focused effort on meticulous in vivo testing, formulation development for ocular delivery, and comprehensive pharmacological evaluations will be critical to harnessing the full therapeutic potential of Mdivi-1 for patients with dry AMD (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2015; She et al., 2018; Yako et al., 2021).
