Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
L-Carnitine is a naturally occurring quaternary ammonium compound, chemically defined as β-hydroxy-γ-trimethylaminobutyrate, that is both derived from the diet (predominantly found in animal-based foods such as red meat) and biosynthesized endogenously from the essential amino acids lysine and methionine via a vitamin C–dependent pathway primarily in the liver and kidneys (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Mollica et al., 2017). Historically, L-carnitine was first identified as a constituent of muscle tissue in the early 20th century and was later linked to its high content in meat, leading to its designation as “vitamin T” in certain insect models (Mollica et al., 2017). As a member of the carnitine family, it belongs to the class of metabolic cofactors or nutraceutical agents whose primary function is to shuttle activated long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondrial matrix, where they undergo β-oxidation, thereby facilitating aerobic energy production and maintaining the intracellular acyl-CoA/CoA balance (Moos et al., 2017; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). This class of compounds has historically been used as dietary supplements to treat primary and secondary carnitine deficiency, as well as in various metabolic and mitochondrial disorders (Flanagan et al., 2010). L-Carnitine is widely formulated in pharmaceutical products both as a standalone supplement and as an ingredient in combination formulations, which underscores its acceptance as a metabolic supportive agent with a favorable safety profile (Flanagan et al., 2010; Surai, 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, the carnitine family has a long record of use in addressing conditions where fatty acid oxidation is impaired. L-Carnitine has been employed effectively as a life-saving therapy in primary carnitine deficiency—a condition in which mutations of the carnitine transporter (OCTN2) impair cellular uptake—and also in secondary deficiencies associated with conditions like renal failure, liver disease, and certain inborn errors of metabolism (Flanagan et al., 2010). Beyond classical deficiency syndromes, both L-carnitine and its acetylated derivative (acetyl-L-carnitine) have been investigated in a broad range of clinical contexts, including cardiovascular diseases, diabetic complications, and neurodegenerative disorders. For example, acetyl-L-carnitine has been shown to improve parameters of visual function in patients with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and to confer neuroprotective effects in Alzheimer’s disease and mild cognitive impairment (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Calabrese et al., 2009).  
In ophthalmology, while most clinical studies have focused on the use of carnitine derivatives for systemic metabolic or neuroprotective effects, there is preclinical evidence supporting an ocular role. Animal studies have identified high intraocular concentrations of carnitine in the lens and other ocular tissues, hinting at a physiological role in maintaining ocular metabolic balance and osmotic homeostasis (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). Investigations into the protective effects of L-carnitine against oxidative damage, including its potential to safeguard retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and other ocular tissues, provide a rationale for its application in dry AMD, particularly in the context of geographic atrophy where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central features (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c). Moreover, combination therapy regimens incorporating acetyl-L-carnitine with n-3 fatty acids and coenzyme Q10 have also been trialed in experimental settings to address energy metabolism in retinal tissues (Shamsi et al., 2007). Despite these promising findings, direct clinical use of L-carnitine as monotherapy for dry AMD has not been extensively reported, thus making its repurposing an area that merits focused research to bridge the gap between its established metabolic functions and its potential application in retinal degeneration (Flanagan et al., 2010; Mollica et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
The central biochemical role of L-carnitine is to facilitate the transport of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle—a process that is critical for β-oxidation and ATP production. This shuttle is mediated by mitochondrial enzymes such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT-1) on the outer mitochondrial membrane, which converts acyl-CoA to acyl-carnitine, and carnitine acyltransferase (also known as carnitine acetyltransferase or CAT) within the mitochondria that re-forms acyl-CoA for oxidation (Moos et al., 2017; Jones et al., 2010). This process not only fuels ATP generation via the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation but also helps regulate the cellular acyl-CoA/CoA ratio, indirectly influencing multiple metabolic pathways (Surai, 2015).  
Furthermore, L-carnitine exhibits antioxidant properties either directly, through free radical scavenging, or indirectly by preserving mitochondrial integrity and function under oxidative stress conditions (Shamsi et al., 2007; Surai, 2015). It has been shown to reduce lipid peroxidation and prevent the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential—a key step in the cascade leading to cellular apoptosis (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c). In addition to its classical mitochondrial functions, L-carnitine also acts as an osmolyte, protecting cells against hyperosmolarity by stabilizing proteins and cellular membranes, which could further reduce oxidative stress (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b; Mollica et al., 2017).  
At the molecular level in the RPE, the hypothesis is that enhancing mitochondrial fatty acid uptake via L-carnitine supplementation will improve β-oxidation efficiency. This is expected to lead to increased ATP production and a reduction in the accumulation of lipid intermediates that may otherwise result in excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation. The reduction in ROS could mitigate chronic oxidative stress, a well established contributor to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Jones et al., 2010; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). Notably, disrupted mitochondrial metabolism and energy deficits have been implicated in the progression of RPE cell dysfunction, and L-carnitine’s role in restoring metabolic flexibility has been documented in other cell types such as hepatocytes and neuronal cells (Ates et al., 2008; Surai, 2015). Additionally, the modulation of mitochondrial protein acetylation by L-carnitine derivatives, an effect observed in various models of aging and metabolic disease, may further contribute to a neuroprotective milieu in RPE cells (Wang et al., 2024; Virmani & Cirulli, 2022).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its multifaceted mechanisms of action, the anticipated effect of L-carnitine in an assay designed for dry age-related macular degeneration is twofold. First, by enhancing mitochondrial fatty acid uptake and increasing β-oxidation rates, L-carnitine is expected to boost ATP production in RPE cells, thereby ameliorating the energy deficits that contribute to cellular dysfunction in geographic atrophy (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Jones et al., 2010). Second, this improved mitochondrial function should lead to a reduction in the generation of ROS that typically arises from lipid overload and subsequent incomplete oxidation, thereby decreasing oxidative damage to critical cellular structures including mitochondrial membranes and nuclear DNA (Shamsi et al., 2007; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a).  
In in vitro assays using cultured RPE cells, one would expect that L-carnitine treatment leads to enhanced mitochondrial respiration, as measured by oxygen consumption rate (OCR), and an associated elevation in ATP levels. Moreover, reductions in established markers of oxidative stress, such as malondialdehyde (MDA) levels or increased glutathione (GSH) concentrations, would support its antioxidant action (Ates et al., 2008). Expression studies have shown that key mitochondrial enzymes and transporters, including CPT-1 and OCTN2 (the carnitine transporter), are expressed in RPE cells, providing a molecular substrate for L-carnitine’s action in these cells (Ribas et al., 2014; Jones et al., 2010). Furthermore, since mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of dry AMD pathogenesis, the restoration of mitochondrial efficiency by L-carnitine could be measured by improved RPE cell survival and decreased apoptotic markers under conditions of oxidative stress and lipid oversupply.  
Preclinical studies in other tissues such as neuronal cells and hepatocytes have demonstrated that L-carnitine treatment not only restores mitochondrial function but also reduces lipid-induced ROS production and inflammation. Extrapolating from these findings, it is reasonable to expect that in the context of dry AMD, L-carnitine could counteract the metabolic inflexibility of RPE cells, ultimately slowing the progression of geographic atrophy and preserving retinal structure and function (Surai, 2015; Wang et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
L-Carnitine stands out as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to several compelling properties. Its established role in promoting mitochondrial β-oxidation and energy production, combined with demonstrated antioxidant and osmoprotective actions, provides a strong mechanistic rationale for addressing the metabolic and oxidative stress components of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Jones et al., 2010). The compound’s extensive history of use as a dietary supplement and its well-characterized safety profile—in which high oral doses have been administered with minimal toxicity—support its potential for repurposing in an ocular application (Flanagan et al., 2010; Mollica et al., 2017).  
However, there are potential limitations that merit cautious consideration. Direct evidence of L-carnitine’s efficacy in RPE cells specifically within the context of dry AMD is currently limited. While preclinical studies in non-ocular tissues and some ocular models suggest beneficial mitochondrial and antioxidant effects, the precise dosing, ocular bioavailability, and long-term impact on retinal degeneration remain to be rigorously established. Moreover, while L-carnitine can enhance mitochondrial function, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD implies that a monotherapy approach might not be sufficient; a combination therapy strategy—potentially incorporating other mitochondrial or antioxidant agents—may ultimately prove more effective (Shamsi et al., 2007; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a).  
In summary, the strengths of L-carnitine include its well-established role in cellular energy metabolism, its safety profile and widespread clinical use in other metabolic conditions, and its potential to mitigate ROS production and oxidative damage through enhanced fatty acid oxidation. The weaknesses primarily lie in the current paucity of direct evidence in ocular models of dry AMD and the challenges associated with ensuring adequate drug delivery to the RPE in vivo. Nonetheless, given the overall mechanistic promise and the favorable tolerability observed in numerous studies, L-carnitine warrants further investigation – with a focus on in vitro RPE assays under condition of lipid overload and oxidative stress, followed by in vivo preclinical models of geographic atrophy – to validate its efficacy as a repurposed therapy for dry AMD (Jones et al., 2010; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c; Ates et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2024).  
Overall, I recommend proceeding with targeted experiments to assess mitochondrial respiration, ROS levels, and cell survival in RPE cultures treated with L-carnitine. These studies should be complemented with investigations of tissue distribution following ocular delivery to address bioavailability concerns. This comprehensive evaluation supports the potential of L-carnitine as a metabolic and antioxidant therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, while also highlighting areas where additional data are needed before clinical translation.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, spermidine’s potential therapeutic applications have been explored extensively in the context of its ability to induce autophagy and affect cellular homeostasis. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that spermidine supplementation can extend lifespan and improve the function of various tissues by enhancing autophagy, contributing to cardioprotection, and promoting neuroprotection in animal models (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). In model systems ranging from yeast to mammalian cells, spermidine has been shown to increase the conversion of the autophagy marker LC3-I to LC3-II, thereby promoting autophagosome formation (Qin et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022). Inhibition of EP300 has been correlated with enhanced autophagic flux, and several studies suggest that spermidine may exert its autophagy-inducing effects partly by downregulating EP300 expression or activity (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020).

In addition to its effects on EP300, spermidine has been implicated in the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), an evolutionarily conserved energy sensor that modulates metabolic homeostasis and mitochondrial quality control. Activation of AMPK can lead to the phosphorylation and activation of downstream effectors that promote both autophagy and mitophagy (the selective autophagic removal of damaged mitochondria). While direct evidence for AMPK activation by spermidine in retinal cells is still emerging, broader studies in other cell types have described an upregulation of pathways associated with mitochondrial biogenesis and quality control, including the deacetylation of proteins by SIRT1, which often acts in concert with AMPK (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). In the specific context of RPE cells under stress from A2E (a component of lipofuscin) or H₂O₂, the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria and high levels of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) play critical roles in cell loss and dysfunction; thus, induction of mitophagy via enhanced AMPK signaling and subsequent Parkin recruitment to depolarized mitochondria could improve mitochondrial homeostasis and reduce oxidative damage (Kim et al., 2021).

Furthermore, spermidine’s role as an intracellular calcium chelator appears pivotal in its protective effect in RPE cells. Studies have demonstrated that pre-treatment of ARPE-19 cells with 10 µM spermidine prior to oxidative stress prevents intracellular Ca²⁺ overload—a phenomenon that can trigger endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and cell death—thereby maintaining cellular integrity independent of direct ROS scavenging (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021). In summary, spermidine is posited to enhance the clearance of damaged organelles—particularly mitochondria—by increasing autophagic flux through EP300 inhibition and AMPK activation, leading to enhanced LC3-II conversion and Parkin-mediated mitophagy. This, in turn, is expected to reduce mtROS and protect RPE cell viability under conditions of oxidative and A2E-induced stress (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its mode of action, the expected effect of spermidine in a dry AMD model would be a pronounced improvement in the quality control mechanisms of RPE cells. The compound is anticipated to induce autophagy, evidenced by a measurable increase in LC3-II levels, alongside enhanced recruitment of the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin to dysfunctional mitochondria. This concerted activation of autophagy and mitophagy should facilitate the clearance of damaged mitochondria, thereby reducing the accumulation of mtROS and attenuating oxidative stress. In the context of A2E accumulation—a key driver of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD—spermidine is predicted to restore mitochondrial function and improve cell viability. Experimental assays are expected to show that spermidine pre-treatment leads to a significant reduction in apoptosis markers (e.g., caspase-3 activation, cytochrome c release), along with improved markers of mitochondrial integrity (e.g., stabilized mitochondrial membrane potential) in ARPE-19 cells exposed to H₂O₂ or A2E (Kim et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating spermidine as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current literature. One major strength is its natural origin and well-documented role as a global inducer of autophagy and mitophagy. This aligns well with the current understanding of dry AMD pathogenesis, in which impaired autophagic clearance and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells play major roles (Nichugovskiy et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2021). The ability of spermidine to inhibit EP300—a factor whose downregulation encourages autophagy—and to potentially activate AMPK signaling suggests that it could enhance several intracellular quality control processes simultaneously (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). The preclinical data showing that spermidine can protect ARPE-19 cells from H₂O₂-induced oxidative injury by blocking Ca²⁺ overload and reducing apoptotic signaling further bolster its potential utility in ocular applications (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021).

However, there are notable challenges and weaknesses associated with this therapeutic candidate. First, the dose response appears to be remarkably narrow; while low micromolar concentrations (e.g., 10 µM) exert cytoprotective effects in vitro, higher doses have been associated with cytotoxicity, including RPE cell death and photoreceptor degeneration in animal models following intravitreal injection (Ohashi et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022). This raises concerns about the therapeutic window and the optimal route of delivery for chronic conditions like dry AMD. Another limitation is that, despite promising mechanistic data, direct clinical evidence for the use of spermidine in dry AMD is currently lacking. Most of the studies available have been conducted in vitro or in animal models under conditions of oxidative stress, and while these findings are encouraging, they do not fully recapitulate the complex pathophysiology of dry AMD, which involves not only oxidative damage but also chronic inflammation, immune dysregulation, and drusen accumulation (Kim et al., 2021).

Moreover, while the hypothesis emphasizes effects on EP300 inhibition and AMPK activation leading to enhanced LC3-II conversion and Parkin recruitment, the direct evidence linking these specific molecular events to improved outcomes in dry AMD models remains preliminary. There is a need for more comprehensive studies that directly measure these autophagic and mitophagic markers in RPE cells under conditions that mimic the A2E-induced stress typical of dry AMD (Kim et al., 2021). Additionally, the risk that spermidine’s metabolism by amine oxidases may produce toxic aldehyde byproducts such as acrolein must be carefully considered, as these compounds have been implicated in retinal degeneration in some intravitreal models (Ohashi et al., 2017).

In summary, while spermidine has a compelling mechanistic rationale as a modulator of autophagy and mitochondrial quality control, which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the current preclinical evidence is mixed and highlights potential safety challenges related to dosing and administration. Its established role in promoting cellular longevity and mitigating oxidative stress in diverse tissues certainly warrants further investigation, but rigorous studies using dry AMD-specific models are essential to ascertain its efficacy and safety in this context. Regulatory considerations will also require detailed pharmacokinetic and toxicological profiling, particularly given its dual potential for both cytoprotection and cytotoxicity depending on concentration and route of administration (Ohashi et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022).

Overall, our evaluation suggests that spermidine represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD based on its intrinsic properties as an autophagy and mitophagy inducer and its ability to protect RPE cells from oxidative damage; however, its clinical translation will depend on resolving key issues such as dose optimization, route of delivery, and comprehensive validation of its proposed molecular mechanisms in relevant models of AMD. The strengths of spermidine lie in its natural occurrence, multi-targeted action on cellular quality control mechanisms, and established preclinical benefits in other models of aging and oxidative stress. Conversely, the main weaknesses are its narrow therapeutic window, the potential for generation of toxic metabolites, and the current lack of direct clinical or robust in vivo data in dry AMD models. Further research, including detailed investigations in RPE models using A2E and oxidative stress conditions as well as careful titration studies in animal models of dry AMD, is warranted to determine its viability as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for this unmet clinical need (Casero & Marton, 2007; Kim et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022; Ohashi et al., 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is a naturally occurring nucleotide derivative that functions as a key intermediate in the biosynthesis of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), an essential coenzyme in cellular energy metabolism and redox regulation (Chen et al., 2020). Originally identified as part of the salvage pathway of NAD+ synthesis, NMN is synthesized endogenously from nicotinamide and subsequently converted by NMN adenylyltransferase (NMNAT) into NAD+ (Gerdes, 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). Commercially produced by chemical synthesis and available from suppliers such as Sigma-Aldrich (catalog number N3501), NMN belongs to the class of NAD+ precursors that have attracted considerable attention due to their potential to counteract the age-related decline in NAD+ levels (Chen et al., 2020). Compounds of this class have historically been explored mainly in the context of metabolic and aging interventions, with the rationale that restoring NAD+ pools may reverse or delay cellular senescence and mitochondrial dysfunction (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022). NMN, as a small molecule with a molecular weight of approximately 334 g/mol, has been demonstrated to readily cross cell membranes and enhance cellular bioenergetics, making it a promising candidate for diseases in which energy metabolism is disrupted, such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Chen et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). The compound’s natural occurrence and favorable safety profile observed in preclinical aging models have contributed to its development as a therapeutic candidate across multiple indications, which now includes potential ophthalmological applications (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ebeling et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, NMN has been investigated in a variety of preclinical settings addressing metabolic dysfunction and age‐associated decline, with numerous studies across biochemical, cellular, and animal models demonstrating that NMN supplementation effectively elevates NAD+ levels and improves mitochondrial function (Chen et al., 2020). In models of retinal degeneration, particularly in contexts simulating photoreceptor loss and retinal detachment, NMN administration has shown neuroprotective effects by restoring NAD+ levels and activating key deacetylases such as SIRT1, which are central to oxidative stress mitigation and cell survival (Chen et al., 2020). Preclinical studies conducted in mouse models of retinal detachment have reported that NMN treatment not only boosts NAD+ concentrations beyond the physiological baseline but also attenuates the inflammatory response and reduces photoreceptor cell death, thereby preserving retinal structure and function (Chen et al., 2020). In addition to these acute models, experimental data from primary retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells derived from donors with age‐related macular degeneration have revealed that NMN can improve mitochondrial respiration and restore the NAD+/NADH balance critical to RPE cell health (Ebeling et al., 2020). Moreover, NMN’s ability to limit cellular senescence has been documented in RPE models challenged with oxidative stressors and pro‐senescent compounds, where supplementation led to a reduction in markers such as p16INK4a and p21Waf/Cip1, along with preservation of SIRT1 expression (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022). Clinical exploration of NMN in the context of aging and metabolic disorders—though not yet fully extended to ophthalmologic diseases—provides an encouraging translational backdrop, indicating that NMN has a robust therapeutic history in conditions characterized by NAD+ depletion and mitochondrial dysfunction (Jadeja et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2024). Collectively, the therapeutic history suggests that NMN has been thoroughly vetted in preclinical settings relevant to neurodegeneration and retinal health, thereby supporting its potential repurposing for dry AMD (Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
NMN exerts its biological effects primarily through its role as a biosynthetic precursor of NAD+, a critical coenzyme involved in numerous cellular processes including energy production, DNA repair, and redox balance (Chen et al., 2020). Once administered, NMN is rapidly taken up by cells and converted via NMNAT enzymes into NAD+, thereby replenishing intracellular NAD+ pools that typically decline with age and stress (Gerdes, 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). This increase in NAD+ levels has a twofold impact. First, elevated NAD+ directly energizes metabolic pathways, namely glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation, by serving as a cofactor for dehydrogenases, which is essential for mitochondrial ATP production (Will-Orrego, 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Second, NAD+ acts as a substrate for a family of NAD+-dependent deacetylases—the sirtuins—most notably SIRT1, SIRT3, and SIRT5, which are involved in regulating mitochondrial integrity and function (Chen et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). In the specific context of dry AMD, the hypothesis posits that NMN-mediated restoration of NAD+ in retinal pigment epithelial cells leads to reactivation of mitochondrial sirtuins SIRT3 and SIRT5. SIRT3, located in the mitochondrial matrix, deacetylates key metabolic enzymes including manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), whose activity is crucial for neutralizing mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) (Gerdes, 2018; Ren et al., 2022). The proper deacetylation of MnSOD enhances its antioxidant capacity, thereby reducing mtROS accumulation and protecting the mitochondria from oxidative damage (Chen et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022). SIRT5, another mitochondrial deacetylase, plays a complementary role by regulating the acylation status of proteins involved in mitochondrial dynamics and energy metabolism; its activation, in turn, contributes to improved mitochondrial respiration and bioenergetics (Ebeling et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). Furthermore, the elevation of NAD+ levels via NMN supplementation is known to indirectly influence other signaling pathways such as those modulated by AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and Akt/mTOR, which are critical for mitochondrial biogenesis and cellular homeostasis (Ren et al., 2022). In dry AMD, where metabolic dysfunction and increased oxidative stress are central to disease progression, the biochemical cascade triggered by NMN restores the balance between energy production and oxidative damage by ensuring that sirtuins are adequately fueled (Jadeja et al., 2018). This cascade not only preserves mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and oxygen consumption rate (OCR) but also limits the proton leak and bioenergetic inefficiency that characterize dysfunctional RPE cells (Ebeling et al., 2020). In summary, at the molecular level, NMN’s mechanism of action in RPE cells aligns with a strategy of metabolic reconditioning, whereby the reactivation of SIRT3 and SIRT5—via increased NAD+ availability—leads to improved deacetylation of mitochondrial enzymes, reduction in mtROS levels, and enhancement of overall mitochondrial function (Lin, 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of a dry AMD model, the anticipated effect of NMN supplementation is the restoration of NAD+ homeostasis within RPE cells and consequent reactivation of mitochondrial sirtuins such as SIRT3 and SIRT5, which will correct mitochondrial deacetylation deficits that are known to contribute to cellular dysfunction (Chen et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). Specifically, NMN is expected to normalize the NAD+/NADH ratio, an essential parameter for efficient electron transport chain function and ATP generation; this normalization is projected to result in enhanced oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and improved mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) in the RPE (Ebeling et al., 2020). As a direct consequence of restored sirtuin activity, particularly SIRT3’s deacetylation of MnSOD, there should be a significant reduction in mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), which in turn decreases the oxidative burden on the RPE cells—a critical factor in the development and progression of dry AMD (Gerdes, 2018; Ren et al., 2022). The expected downstream effects include not only enhanced bioenergetic function but also a reduction in the cellular senescence markers and inflammatory cytokines typically upregulated in the aging and stressed RPE (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022). In vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE cultures have demonstrated that NMN supplementation can rescue cells from FK866-induced NAD+ depletion, thereby restoring ATP levels and maintaining the expression of RPE identity genes, which are fundamental to retinal homeostasis (Will-Orrego, 2020). Moreover, by mitigating oxidative damage and correcting mitochondrial dysfunction, NMN is expected to preserve the structural integrity of the outer retina, which is essential for sustained photoreceptor function and visual acuity in dry AMD (Chen et al., 2020). Ultimately, the mechanistic actions of NMN—spanning from NAD+ replenishment to sirtuin activation—are predicted to yield measurable improvements in both cellular assays (e.g., increased OCR, stabilized Δψm, and decreased ROS levels) and functional endpoints such as electroretinography (ERG) responses in animal models of retinal degeneration (Chen et al., 2020). The robust preclinical data, including evidence of normalized mitochondrial respiration and amelioration of RPE senescence following NMN treatment, provide a strong rationale for expecting similar beneficial effects in a dry AMD assay (Jadeja et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
The cumulative evidence from biochemical, cellular, and in vivo studies positions NMN as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. One of the primary strengths of NMN is its well‐characterized role as a NAD+ precursor, which underpins its ability to restore intracellular NAD+ levels and reactivate essential sirtuin activities—most notably SIRT3 and SIRT5—in metabolically compromised cells (Chen et al., 2020; Gerdes, 2018). By addressing the root cause of mitochondrial dysfunction observed in dry AMD, namely NAD+ depletion and subsequent impairment of protein deacetylation, NMN targets a fundamental pathogenic mechanism that leads to photoreceptor and RPE degeneration (Chen et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022). The broad spectrum of supportive evidence, ranging from neuroprotective effects in retinal detachment models to the reversal of cellular senescence in AMD-relevant RPE cells, further reinforces the therapeutic rationale behind NMN’s application in dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022). Additionally, the translational feasibility of NMN is bolstered by ongoing clinical developments in aging and metabolic disorders, suggesting that the pharmacokinetic and safety profiles of NMN are sufficiently favorable to warrant its repurposing for retinal diseases (Jadeja et al., 2018).

However, several potential limitations must be considered. Variability in drug response among diseased RPE cells from different AMD donors has been documented, indicating that while NMN can robustly restore mitochondrial function in some cases, a subset of patients may exhibit a less pronounced therapeutic response, necessitating personalized dosing strategies or combinatorial therapies (Ebeling et al., 2020). Furthermore, although NMN’s activation of sirtuins is generally beneficial, there exists a theoretical risk that overactivation of these enzymes could induce off-target effects or exacerbate cellular stress if not properly titrated, as some studies have suggested that SIRT1 overactivation may in certain contexts lead to deleterious outcomes (Chen et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022). Moreover, much of the current evidence derives from preclinical models, and while these data are compelling, the extrapolation of these results to human subjects with dry AMD will require rigorously designed clinical trials to evaluate efficacy and safety in the specific target population (Chen et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024).

In summary, the overall assessment of NMN as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is highly favorable, particularly given its dual capacity to restore NAD+ levels and reengage mitochondrial deacetylation pathways that are crucial for RPE health. Its mechanistic basis, rooted in the reactivation of SIRT3 and SIRT5 leading to improved mitochondrial respiration and reduced oxidative stress, directly addresses the central pathogenic features of dry AMD. The extensive preclinical validation, coupled with encouraging translational data from aging-related indications, positions NMN as a strong candidate for further development and clinical evaluation in dry AMD, albeit with careful consideration of dosing strategies and patient heterogeneity (Cimaglia et al., 2020). Moving forward, prioritizing studies that assess long-term outcomes in appropriate animal models and early-phase clinical trials in AMD patients will be critical to firmly establish NMN’s therapeutic potential and optimize its utility as part of a broader strategy to mitigate vision loss associated with dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2020; Lin, 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
L-Carnitine is a naturally occurring quaternary ammonium compound, chemically defined as β-hydroxy-γ-trimethylaminobutyrate, that is both derived from the diet (predominantly found in animal-based foods such as red meat) and biosynthesized endogenously from the essential amino acids lysine and methionine via a vitamin C–dependent pathway primarily in the liver and kidneys (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Mollica et al., 2017). Historically, L-carnitine was first identified as a constituent of muscle tissue in the early 20th century and was later linked to its high content in meat, leading to its designation as “vitamin T” in certain insect models (Mollica et al., 2017). As a member of the carnitine family, it belongs to the class of metabolic cofactors or nutraceutical agents whose primary function is to shuttle activated long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondrial matrix, where they undergo β-oxidation, thereby facilitating aerobic energy production and maintaining the intracellular acyl-CoA/CoA balance (Moos et al., 2017; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). This class of compounds has historically been used as dietary supplements to treat primary and secondary carnitine deficiency, as well as in various metabolic and mitochondrial disorders (Flanagan et al., 2010). L-Carnitine is widely formulated in pharmaceutical products both as a standalone supplement and as an ingredient in combination formulations, which underscores its acceptance as a metabolic supportive agent with a favorable safety profile (Flanagan et al., 2010; Surai, 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, the carnitine family has a long record of use in addressing conditions where fatty acid oxidation is impaired. L-Carnitine has been employed effectively as a life-saving therapy in primary carnitine deficiency—a condition in which mutations of the carnitine transporter (OCTN2) impair cellular uptake—and also in secondary deficiencies associated with conditions like renal failure, liver disease, and certain inborn errors of metabolism (Flanagan et al., 2010). Beyond classical deficiency syndromes, both L-carnitine and its acetylated derivative (acetyl-L-carnitine) have been investigated in a broad range of clinical contexts, including cardiovascular diseases, diabetic complications, and neurodegenerative disorders. For example, acetyl-L-carnitine has been shown to improve parameters of visual function in patients with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and to confer neuroprotective effects in Alzheimer’s disease and mild cognitive impairment (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Calabrese et al., 2009).  
In ophthalmology, while most clinical studies have focused on the use of carnitine derivatives for systemic metabolic or neuroprotective effects, there is preclinical evidence supporting an ocular role. Animal studies have identified high intraocular concentrations of carnitine in the lens and other ocular tissues, hinting at a physiological role in maintaining ocular metabolic balance and osmotic homeostasis (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). Investigations into the protective effects of L-carnitine against oxidative damage, including its potential to safeguard retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and other ocular tissues, provide a rationale for its application in dry AMD, particularly in the context of geographic atrophy where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central features (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c). Moreover, combination therapy regimens incorporating acetyl-L-carnitine with n-3 fatty acids and coenzyme Q10 have also been trialed in experimental settings to address energy metabolism in retinal tissues (Shamsi et al., 2007). Despite these promising findings, direct clinical use of L-carnitine as monotherapy for dry AMD has not been extensively reported, thus making its repurposing an area that merits focused research to bridge the gap between its established metabolic functions and its potential application in retinal degeneration (Flanagan et al., 2010; Mollica et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
The central biochemical role of L-carnitine is to facilitate the transport of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle—a process that is critical for β-oxidation and ATP production. This shuttle is mediated by mitochondrial enzymes such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT-1) on the outer mitochondrial membrane, which converts acyl-CoA to acyl-carnitine, and carnitine acyltransferase (also known as carnitine acetyltransferase or CAT) within the mitochondria that re-forms acyl-CoA for oxidation (Moos et al., 2017; Jones et al., 2010). This process not only fuels ATP generation via the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation but also helps regulate the cellular acyl-CoA/CoA ratio, indirectly influencing multiple metabolic pathways (Surai, 2015).  
Furthermore, L-carnitine exhibits antioxidant properties either directly, through free radical scavenging, or indirectly by preserving mitochondrial integrity and function under oxidative stress conditions (Shamsi et al., 2007; Surai, 2015). It has been shown to reduce lipid peroxidation and prevent the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential—a key step in the cascade leading to cellular apoptosis (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c). At the molecular level in the RPE, the hypothesis is that enhancing mitochondrial fatty acid uptake via L-carnitine supplementation will improve β-oxidation efficiency. This is expected to lead to increased ATP production and a reduction in the accumulation of lipid intermediates that may otherwise result in excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation. The reduction in ROS could mitigate chronic oxidative stress, a well established contributor to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Jones et al., 2010; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008b). Notably, disrupted mitochondrial metabolism and energy deficits have been implicated in the progression of RPE cell dysfunction, and L-carnitine’s role in restoring metabolic flexibility has been documented in other cell types such as hepatocytes and neuronal cells (Ates et al., 2008; Surai, 2015). Additionally, the modulation of mitochondrial protein acetylation by L-carnitine derivatives, an effect observed in various models of aging and metabolic disease, may further contribute to a neuroprotective milieu in RPE cells (Wang et al., 2024; Virmani & Cirulli, 2022).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its multifaceted mechanisms of action, the anticipated effect of L-carnitine in an assay designed for dry age-related macular degeneration is twofold. First, by enhancing mitochondrial fatty acid uptake and increasing β-oxidation rates, L-carnitine is expected to boost ATP production in RPE cells, thereby ameliorating the energy deficits that contribute to cellular dysfunction in geographic atrophy (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Jones et al., 2010). Preclinical studies in other tissues such as neuronal cells and hepatocytes have demonstrated that L-carnitine treatment not only restores mitochondrial function but also reduces lipid-induced ROS production and inflammation. Extrapolating from these findings, it is reasonable to expect that in the context of dry AMD, L-carnitine could counteract the metabolic inflexibility of RPE cells, ultimately slowing the progression of geographic atrophy and preserving retinal structure and function (Surai, 2015; Wang et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
L-Carnitine stands out as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to several compelling properties. Its established role in promoting mitochondrial β-oxidation and energy production, combined with demonstrated antioxidant and osmoprotective actions, provides a strong mechanistic rationale for addressing the metabolic and oxidative stress components of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a; Jones et al., 2010). The compound’s extensive history of use as a dietary supplement and its well-characterized safety profile—in which high oral doses have been administered with minimal toxicity—support its potential for repurposing in an ocular application (Flanagan et al., 2010; Mollica et al., 2017).  
However, there are potential limitations that merit cautious consideration. Direct evidence of L-carnitine’s efficacy in RPE cells specifically within the context of dry AMD is currently limited. While preclinical studies in non-ocular tissues and some ocular models suggest beneficial mitochondrial and antioxidant effects, the precise dosing, ocular bioavailability, and long-term impact on retinal degeneration remain to be rigorously established. Moreover, while L-carnitine can enhance mitochondrial function, the multifactorial nature of dry AMD implies that a monotherapy approach might not be sufficient; a combination therapy strategy—potentially incorporating other mitochondrial or antioxidant agents—may ultimately prove more effective (Shamsi et al., 2007; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008a).  
In summary, the strengths of L-carnitine include its well-established role in cellular energy metabolism, its safety profile and widespread clinical use in other metabolic conditions, and its potential to mitigate ROS production and oxidative damage through enhanced fatty acid oxidation. The weaknesses primarily lie in the current paucity of direct evidence in ocular models of dry AMD and the challenges associated with ensuring adequate drug delivery to the RPE in vivo. Nonetheless, given the overall mechanistic promise and the favorable tolerability observed in numerous studies, L-carnitine warrants further investigation – with a focus on in vitro RPE assays under condition of lipid overload and oxidative stress, followed by in vivo preclinical models of geographic atrophy – to validate its efficacy as a repurposed therapy for dry AMD (Jones et al., 2010; Pescosolido, Imperatrice, & Karavitis, 2008c; Ates et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2024).  
Overall, I recommend proceeding with targeted experiments to assess mitochondrial respiration, ROS levels, and cell survival in RPE cultures treated with L-carnitine. These studies should be complemented with investigations of tissue distribution following ocular delivery to address bioavailability concerns. This comprehensive evaluation supports the potential of L-carnitine as a metabolic and antioxidant therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, while also highlighting areas where additional data are needed before clinical translation.

Below is our comprehensive evaluation of pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD):

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate –  
Pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) is an aromatic o‐quinone originally discovered as a redox cofactor for bacterial dehydrogenases and is naturally synthesized by various Gram‐negative prokaryotes. It was first identified in microbial systems where it serves as a prosthetic group in enzymes involved in alcohol and sugar oxidation, and it has since been detected at trace levels in human tissues and milk, suggesting dietary exposure through common foods such as fermented soy products, green peppers, spinach, and human milk. PQQ is categorized within the quinone family of compounds and is recognized for its redox‐active properties; in this role, it has been considered a “vitamin‐like accessory factor” by some researchers given its involvement in cellular energy metabolism and antioxidant defense (Petricca et al., 2025; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Commercially, PQQ is available in a water‐soluble disodium salt formulation; for example, the Sigma‐Aldrich PQQ product is typical of these preparations. As a small redox‐active molecule, PQQ is distinct among nutraceuticals and has been explored in several preclinical contexts for its potential to regulate oxidative stress and promote mitochondrial function (Canovai & Williams, 2025). Consequently, this candidate represents a repurposing opportunity where its established dietary exposure, safety profile as assessed by regulatory bodies such as EFSA, and its unique bioactivity as a mitochondrial modulator may be leveraged to address the mitochondrial dysfunction implicated in dry AMD.

Therapeutic History –  
PQQ has been the subject of intensive biochemical and preclinical investigation over the past decades. Early studies concentrated on its role as a microbial cofactor, but subsequent research has documented that dietary supplementation with PQQ produces measurable effects on mitochondrial‐related metabolism and markers of inflammation in animal models and humans (Canovai & Williams, 2025). In various rodent models, oral PQQ has been shown to modulate mitochondrial number and function, thereby improving outcomes in contexts as diverse as cardiac ischemia/reperfusion, neurodegeneration, and metabolic syndrome (Akagawa, Nakano, & Ikemoto, 2016; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Additionally, EFSA conducted a safety assessment of the PQQ disodium salt formulation as a novel food ingredient and concluded that at proposed supplemental doses (up to 20 mg/day) the width of the safety margin is acceptable relative to animal toxicology data (Turck et al., 2017; Hwang & Willoughby, 2018). In human studies, although clinical trials have largely focused on endpoints such as cognition, inflammatory markers, and lipid metabolism, these trials demonstrate that oral PQQ is bioavailable, well‐tolerated, and can meaningfully impact systemic markers of oxidative stress and energy metabolism (Canovai & Williams, 2025). While no study to date has directly employed PQQ in patients with dry AMD, there is indirect evidence suggesting that PQQ’s capacity to improve cellular bioenergetics may be broadly beneficial in clinical states characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction. Some studies even indicate that PQQ upregulates mitochondrial proteins and improves ATP synthesis in cellular models derived from age‐related macular degeneration donor tissues (Canovai & Williams, 2025), although direct evidence in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) remains sparse. In summary, the therapeutic history of PQQ includes diverse preclinical applications ranging from cardioprotection to neuroprotection, with established safety in both animal and limited human studies, making it a plausible candidate for repurposing in dry AMD where mitochondrial dysfunction is a key pathogenic driver.

Mechanism of Action –  
The molecular basis of PQQ’s bioactivity is multifaceted, centering on its redox chemistry and its ability to modulate mitochondrial biogenesis. Chemically, PQQ is a potent redox‐active o‐quinone that undergoes reversible reduction to its hydroquinone form (PQQH₂) via a rapid semiquinone intermediate. This redox cycling allows PQQ to function both as a free radical scavenger and as an electron‐transfer catalyst. In vitro assays have established that the reduced form, PQQH₂, exhibits robust antioxidant capacity, with reports indicating that its aroxyl radical quenching activity can be significantly greater than that of classical antioxidants such as vitamin C and α‐tocopherol (Canovai & Williams, 2025; Charrier et al., 2024). Through its antioxidant activity, PQQ directly neutralizes reactive oxygen species (ROS) and may protect cellular constituents from oxidative damage.

Beyond its direct radical scavenging, PQQ has been implicated as an inducer of mitochondrial biogenesis. Several mechanistic studies indicate that treatment with PQQ leads to the upregulation of key transcriptional regulators involved in mitochondrial proliferation. Specifically, PQQ treatment has been shown to activate the cAMP response element‐binding protein (CREB), which in turn stimulates the expression of peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator‐1 alpha (PGC‐1α) (Charrier et al., 2024; Canovai & Williams, 2025). PGC‐1α is a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and coordinates the transcriptional activation of nuclear respiratory factors (NRF‐1/NRF‐2) and mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM), all of which are critical for the transcription and replication of mitochondrial DNA. Some studies also suggest that PQQ modulates sirtuin activity, particularly SIRT1 and SIRT3, which are NAD⁺‐dependent deacetylases that regulate mitochondrial function and cellular metabolic homeostasis (Canovai & Williams, 2025). In addition, PQQ has been reported to restore mitochondrial membrane potential, reduce proton leak, and enhance ATP production during oxidative challenge in several cellular systems (Petricca et al., 2025; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Thus, the composite mechanism of action posited for PQQ—which includes both robust redox buffering and the activation of mitochondrial biogenesis via CREB/PGC‐1α signaling—provides a molecular rationale for its use in conditions characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative injury.

Mechanistically, it is also suggested that PQQ may improve the NAD⁺/NADH ratio, thereby favoring the activity of sirtuins, which contributes to a more favorable intracellular redox state and efficient energy utilization (Jonscher, Chowanadisai, & Rucker, 2021). Although these effects have been most clearly demonstrated in hepatic, muscular, and neuronal cell models, they are directly relevant to RPE cells that rely heavily on oxidative phosphorylation for their energy demands and, hence, are particularly vulnerable to mitochondrial decay under chronic oxidative stress—a hallmark of dry AMD pathology. It is important to note that PQQ’s actions are context‐dependent; while low concentrations have been associated with protective effects, some studies suggest that higher doses can induce a pro‐oxidant effect and even impair mitochondrial dynamics in sensitive cellular contexts (Petricca et al., 2025; Turck et al., 2017). This biphasic dose response underscores the need to identify an optimal dosing window that maximizes mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defense without tipping cells into oxidative stress.

Expected Effect –  
The central hypothesis guiding the repurposing of PQQ for dry AMD is that it can stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis in the RPE by upregulating PGC‐1α, thereby increasing the antioxidant capacity and restoring optimal mitochondrial respiration in cells under chronic oxidative injury. In the proposed assay, treatment with PQQ is expected to yield multiple beneficial outcomes. First, by activating CREB and augmenting PGC‐1α expression, PQQ should enhance the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial replication and function, leading to an increased mitochondrial mass within RPE cells (Canovai & Williams, 2025; Charrier et al., 2024).

Second, increased mitochondrial mass and improved electron transport chain efficiency are expected to elevate ATP production, thereby restoring cellular energy stores that are typically depleted in dry AMD due to chronic oxidative damage. Experimental data from other cell types, including neuronal and hepatic cells, have shown that PQQ treatment enhances ATP output and normalizes mitochondrial membrane potential under oxidative stress conditions, suggesting that similar responses might be observed in RPE cells (Petricca et al., 2025; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Third, PQQ is anticipated to upregulate antioxidant enzymes, such as manganese superoxide dismutase (SOD2), which plays a critical role in mitigating ROS accumulation in mitochondria. By lowering oxidative stress levels in RPE cells, PQQ can help maintain cellular homeostasis and prevent the degeneration that is characteristic of dry AMD (Canovai & Williams, 2025).

Additionally, there is emerging evidence that certain studies using donor‐derived RPE cells from AMD patients have demonstrated that PQQ treatment can upregulate mitochondrial proteins and improve ATP generation in these cells (Canovai & Williams, 2025). Although the available data in retinal tissues remain limited, these findings align with the overall rationale; because RPE cells are highly metabolically active and heavily reliant on mitochondrial function, the ability to augment their biogenesis and enhance oxidative phosphorylation directly addresses a critical pathogenic mechanism of dry AMD. Complementing these expected biochemical outcomes, one would predict that functional assays (for instance, assessments of oxygen consumption rate and extracellular acidification rate) will reveal improved mitochondrial respiration and overall metabolic resilience in PQQ‐treated RPE cells.

Overall Evaluation –  
In synthesizing the extensive body of literature, we find that PQQ demonstrates considerable promise as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD, based on the following strengths and weaknesses:

Strengths:  
1. Robust Mechanistic Rationale: PQQ’s dual role as an antioxidant and an inducer of mitochondrial biogenesis is well documented. The capacity to elevate PGC‐1α expression and thereby drive mitochondrial proliferation and enhanced energy metabolism is highly relevant given that dry AMD is characterized by RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and heightened oxidative stress (Petricca et al., 2025; Charrier et al., 2024; Canovai & Williams, 2025).  
2. Positive Safety and Bioavailability Data: Numerous preclinical studies, alongside regulatory evaluations (e.g., EFSA’s novel food assessment), indicate that PQQ is orally bioavailable and well tolerated in both animal models and limited human studies. The available toxicology data support the safety of typical supplemental doses (up to 20 mg/day), which is encouraging for repurposing efforts (Turck et al., 2017; Hwang & Willoughby, 2018; Canovai & Williams, 2025).  
3. Broad Therapeutic History: Although PQQ has not been directly tested in dry AMD in clinical settings, its prior use as a dietary supplement and its beneficial effects in neuroprotection, cardioprotection, and metabolic regulation suggest therapeutic potential in conditions underpinned by mitochondrial decay and oxidative stress (Canovai & Williams, 2025).  
4. Hypothesis‐Driven Approach: The specific hypothesis—that PQQ will stimulate RPE mitochondrial biogenesis via upregulation of PGC‐1α to improve cellular resilience against chronic oxidative injury—is both plausible and supported by mechanistic data from other cell types. Given that RPE cells are known to express PGC‐1α and that deficits in mitochondrial function have been implicated in AMD pathology, this provides a strong rationale for further investigation (Canovai & Williams, 2025).

Weaknesses:  
1. Limited Direct Evidence in Ocular Tissues: One of the main gaps in the literature is the paucity of direct preclinical studies involving retinal pigment epithelium or in vivo AMD models. Although there is some suggestive data from studies in retinal ganglion cells and donor‐derived RPE cells, definitive evidence that PQQ can counteract the specific aspects of dry AMD pathology in the retina is currently lacking (Ebeling et al., 2020; Petricca et al., 2025).  
2. Context‐Dependent and Biphasic Effects: Several studies indicate that PQQ’s efficacy is highly dose‐dependent. While low concentrations are cytoprotective by enhancing mitochondrial function, higher doses may exert pro‐oxidant effects and even impair mitochondrial membrane potential in sensitive cell types. Establishing the optimal dosing regimen for RPE cells will be critical to avoid potential deleterious effects (Petricca et al., 2025; Turck et al., 2017).  
3. Ocular Pharmacokinetics Uncertain: Although oral absorption in the gastrointestinal tract has been characterized in animal studies with favorable kinetics, it remains unclear whether orally administered PQQ achieves sufficient concentrations—or even penetrates ocular tissues such as the retina—to exert the desired effects. This issue of tissue‐specific bioavailability is a significant barrier that must be addressed in future pharmacokinetic studies (Hwang & Willoughby, 2018).  
4. Quality of Some Supporting Studies: While a substantial body of research supports PQQ’s bioactivity, some of the literature originates from journals or sources with variable quality. This underscores the need for additional high‐quality, rigorously controlled studies—particularly focused on ocular models—to validate the proposed mechanisms and therapeutic outcomes for dry AMD (Akagawa, Nakano, & Ikemoto, 2016; Hwang & Willoughby, 2018).

In conclusion, based on the available biomedical, clinical, and biochemical literature, PQQ emerges as a promising repurposed candidate for dry AMD. Its well‐documented ability to modulate mitochondrial biogenesis—principally through the activation of CREB and upregulation of PGC‐1α—aligns with the mechanistic requirements for restoring mitochondrial function in RPE cells under chronic oxidative stress, a central feature of dry AMD pathogenesis (Petricca et al., 2025; Charrier et al., 2024; Canovai & Williams, 2025). Moreover, the favorable safety profile indicated by both animal toxicology studies and human supplementation trials, combined with its oral bioavailability, adds significant translational appeal.

However, critical gaps remain. Principal among these is the need for direct evidence from retinal models. Specifically, robust, controlled preclinical studies in RPE cells and animal models of dry AMD must be performed to confirm that PQQ can effectively upregulate mitochondrial biogenesis and confer cytoprotection in ocular tissues. Additionally, further investigation into the optimal dosing strategy is required, particularly given the context‐dependent and potentially biphasic nature of PQQ’s activity, as well as the necessity to ascertain whether oral administration can yield therapeutic concentrations in the retina.

Given these considerations, the recommendation is to advance PQQ as a candidate for further investigation in dry AMD. This progression should involve a series of well‐designed in vitro and in vivo experiments targeting RPE‐specific pathways, coupled with ocular pharmacokinetic studies to evaluate tissue penetration and residence times. Should these studies provide supportive evidence, early‐phase human clinical trials focusing on retinal biomarkers and functional outcomes in dry AMD patients would be warranted.

Overall, while the current literature provides a strong mechanistic rationale and preliminary safety data supporting the repurposing of PQQ for dry AMD, it also highlights the need for targeted ocular studies to bridge the gap between systemic mitochondrial enhancements and specific retinal therapeutic benefits. With these additional investigations, PQQ could potentially emerge as a viable therapeutic option in the armamentarium against dry AMD, addressing the unmet need for treatments that restore RPE mitochondrial resilience and retard degeneration (Canovai & Williams, 2025).

Several studies have provided evidence from both biochemical assays and animal models that idebenone can modulate pro‐ and anti‐apoptotic protein expression (notably lowering Bax while increasing Bcl-2 levels) and activate the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway in RPE cells, thereby suggesting a potential benefit in retinal diseases beyond LHON (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 7–8).

Mechanism of Action:  
Idebenone operates through a multifaceted mechanism that addresses the dual challenges of mitochondrial energy impairment and oxidative damage. Fundamentally, idebenone is proposed to bypass defects in mitochondrial complex I by serving as an electron carrier that transfers reducing equivalents directly to complex III. This electron shuttling function is critical for maintaining the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and sustaining ATP synthesis when the conventional electron transfer through complex I is compromised due to oxidative damage—a scenario that is hypothesized to occur in the RPE under conditions such as drusen-induced stress (Arend et al., 2015, p. 2; Wang et al., 2025, pp. 5–8). In parallel, idebenone exhibits potent antioxidant activity by scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitigating the lipid peroxidation processes that are thought to contribute to drusen formation in dry AMD (Arend et al., 2015, pp. 7–8).

At the molecular level, idebenone has been shown to influence key cell survival pathways. It modulates the intrinsic mitochondrial apoptotic cascade by upregulating the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2 and concurrently downregulating the pro-apoptotic protein Bax. This shift in the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio helps to curb the initiation of apoptosis and contributes to cell survival in oxidative environments (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 5–6). Furthermore, idebenone stimulates the nuclear translocation of the transcription factor Nrf2, which in turn induces the expression of a suite of antioxidant genes. This activation of the Nrf2 pathway reinforces the cell’s intrinsic defenses against oxidative insult, which is of particular relevance in RPE cells tasked with handling the chronic low-grade oxidative stress present in AMD (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13). However, it is important to note that in certain settings—such as in cells deficient in the enzyme NQO1—idebenone’s efficacy as an electron carrier may be diminished, and higher concentrations may even elicit pro-oxidant or cytotoxic effects (Varricchio et al., 2020, pp. 18–20). These findings underscore the importance of optimizing the dosing strategy and ensuring appropriate cellular context to fully exploit idebenone’s protective actions.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of the proposed application for dry AMD, the hypothesis is that idebenone will act to shuttle electrons to complex III in RPE cells, thereby bypassing complex I defects induced by drusen-associated oxidative stress. This mechanism is expected to preserve the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and sustain ATP production, even under conditions of compromised oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). Preclinical data in RPE cell models have shown that idebenone treatment can mitigate the dissipation of Δψm in the face of hydrogen peroxide-induced stress, suggesting that similar protective effects could be harnessed in AMD where RPE cellular damage is a hallmark (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13).

Beyond its electron shuttling capacity, idebenone’s potent antioxidant action is expected to lower intracellular ROS levels and reduce lipid peroxidation, thereby protecting RPE cell membranes from the oxidative effects linked to drusen formation. This reduction in oxidative stress, coupled with the preservation of mitochondrial function, is anticipated to result in decreased activation of apoptotic pathways. The compound is also predicted to trigger Nrf2-dependent transcription of antioxidant genes within RPE cells—a response that is critical for combating the chronic oxidative stress implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13). 

Functionally, these molecular effects should translate into measurable improvements in cellular assays of mitochondrial function and viability. In vitro, one would expect to observe maintained or restored Δψm and ATP production in idebenone-treated RPE cells versus controls exposed to oxidative stress. In a more integrated system, such as in animal models or clinical assessments, improvements in photopic ERG responses—previously demonstrated in LHON patients under idebenone therapy—may serve as a surrogate marker for the preservation of retinal neuronal function and integrity (Lyseng-Williamson, 2016, pp. 1–2). Nonetheless, although the mechanistic rationale is robust, these expected effects depend critically on fine-tuning dosage to avoid the potential cytotoxicity observed at supra-therapeutic concentrations and to account for inter-patient variability in enzymes such as NQO1 that activate idebenone (Varricchio et al., 2020, pp. 18–20).

Overall Evaluation:  
The evidence reviewed supports idebenone as a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Among its key strengths is its dual action: the capacity to serve as an alternative electron shuttle to bypass complex I defects and the potent antioxidant activity that collectively mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage. These properties are especially relevant to dry AMD, where RPE degeneration and mitochondrial impairment form the basis of disease progression (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 2, 7–8).

Idebenone’s previous clinical approval and widespread use in LHON provide valuable precedent regarding its safety and efficacy in a retinal context. Moreover, preclinical data from in vitro studies in RPE cells offer compelling evidence regarding its ability to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential, sustain ATP synthesis, and modulate apoptotic pathways under oxidative stress conditions—mechanisms that are directly applicable to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 5–6). The activation of Nrf2 and subsequent upregulation of antioxidant defenses further consolidate its therapeutic potential (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13).

Nevertheless, several challenges remain. The efficacy of idebenone in bypassing complex I defects may be restricted by factors such as NQO1 expression, and potential pro-oxidant effects at higher concentrations necessitate careful dose optimization. In addition, while data from LHON and certain RPE cell models are promising, direct evidence from robust preclinical models of dry AMD is still limited. Some studies addressing these mechanisms have appeared in journals with variable impact factors, which calls for cautious interpretation of the data and underscores the need for further high-quality, reproducible research (Varricchio et al., 2020, pp. 15–18; Varricchio et al., 2020, pp. 18–20).

In summary, idebenone’s multifaceted mechanism—comprising electron shuttling to complex III, robust ROS scavenging, modulation of apoptotic signaling, and activation of Nrf2-driven antioxidant responses—aligns well with the therapeutic requirements for mitigating the mitochondrial and oxidative stress pathology present in dry AMD. While the compound’s history in LHON provides a strong foundation, the repurposing of idebenone for dry AMD will require additional rigorous preclinical investigations focusing on AMD-relevant models, followed by carefully designed clinical trials to validate its efficacy, safety, and dosing in this context (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 7–10, 12–13; Lyseng-Williamson, 2016, pp. 1–2; Gueven & Faldu, 2013, pp. 1–2).

Overall, idebenone represents a compelling candidate for further exploration in the therapeutic landscape of dry AMD. Its dual action addresses key pathophysiological mechanisms in the disease, and its established clinical use in a related ocular disorder provides a promising translational bridge. However, careful attention must be paid to the nuances of its mitochondrial interactions, dose-dependent effects, and the heterogeneous responses in different cellular contexts. Future research focusing on these aspects will be critical to determining whether idebenone can be successfully repurposed to prevent retinal degeneration and preserve vision in patients with dry AMD (Clementi et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Arend et al., 2015, pp. 2, 7–8; Russo et al., 2024, pp. 7–9; Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20).
