Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Kinetin riboside (KR; N6-furfuryladenosine) is an adenine-derived cytokinin riboside originally linked to the discovery of kinetin as a plant hormone from autoclaved herring sperm DNA, and later detected in plant matrices such as coconut water, highlighting its occurrence in natural systems beyond synthetic origins (Yong et al., 2009; Gorincioi, 2010). Evidence from biochemical studies suggests that KR can also form in mammalian systems via oxidative chemistry: hydroxyl radical-induced deoxyribose oxidation generates furfural, which reacts with adenine/adenosine to yield N6-furfuryl adducts including kinetin and its riboside, supporting its characterization as a product of cellular oxidative metabolism and a potential “free radical sink” (Gorincioi, 2010). As a pharmacological entity, KR sits within the cytokinin riboside class, where the riboside and its phosphorylated triphosphate (KTP) function as ATP analogues/substrates for specific protein kinases, most notably PINK1, thereby enabling medicinal chemistry strategies around nucleotide prodrugs (e.g., monophosphate ProTides) to enhance intracellular delivery and activation (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018). Cytokinin ribosides have been explored historically as anti-proliferative agents and differentiation inducers in oncology, and more recently as modulators of mitochondrial quality control and neuroprotective pathways through PINK1 activation (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Lambourne et al., 2023; Voller et al., 2010).

Therapeutic History  
Cytokinins and their ribosides have a long history of investigation in dermatology and oncology, with kinetin demonstrating favorable skin tolerability and anti-photoaging benefits in clinical skin-care contexts, although these data pertain largely to kinetin base rather than KR (Fathy et al., 2022). KR and related ribosides have been extensively profiled as anticancer agents, exhibiting cell cycle modulation and pro-apoptotic activity in diverse tumor lines (e.g., HL-60, HeLa, B16F-10), often with relative sparing of normal fibroblasts at active concentrations, supporting a degree of tumor selectivity (Gorincioi, 2010; Voller et al., 2010). Reported in vivo and in vitro data indicate significant antiproliferative potency at low micromolar concentrations alongside dose-related toxicity (e.g., ~25 mg/kg toxicity in certain models), underscoring a narrow therapeutic index in oncology paradigms (Gorincioi, 2010). Beyond oncology, KR (and related cytokinins) have been investigated for neuroprotective and immunomodulatory effects, including improvement of splicing defects in familial dysautonomia and potential roles in neurodegenerative disease models, although much of the splicing literature historically focuses on kinetin base, and translational clarity for KR per se varies across reports (Fathy et al., 2022; Oshchepkov et al., 2020; Voller et al., 2017).

For PINK1 biology specifically, medicinal chemistry and cell biological studies demonstrate that KR and its phosphorylated metabolites activate PINK1 in mammalian and neuronal cells, positioning this chemotype as a pharmacological tool for augmenting mitophagy in diseases linked to mitochondrial dysfunction such as Parkinson’s disease; more potent KR analogs (e.g., MTK458) further validate this mechanism in cellular and animal models (Hertz et al., 2024; Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Lambourne et al., 2023). Prodrug strategies using kinetin riboside monophosphate (KMP) ProTides improve serum stability and intracellular delivery, yielding robust PINK1 activation in HEK293 cells, which is germane to drug design considerations for KR and derivatives (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018). To our knowledge, there are no published clinical or preclinical studies directly testing KR in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) patients or AMD animal models; however, the target pathway (PINK1/Parkin mitophagy) is mechanistically implicated in RPE degeneration in dry AMD, thus providing a strong rationale for repurposing (Datta et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Skeie et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
- PINK1/Parkin mitophagy axis and AMD relevance in RPE:  
  Upon loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), full-length PINK1 accumulates on the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM), where it phosphorylates both Parkin and ubiquitin to initiate Parkin-dependent mitophagy (Skeie et al., 2021). In RPE, PINK1 and Parkin form the core of a quality-control module that identifies and ubiquitinates dysfunctional mitochondria, recruiting autophagy machinery (p62/LC3) for organelle turnover; cumulative evidence supports that age and stress compromise this system in AMD, resulting in damaged mitochondria, elevated ROS, and RPE degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Skeie et al., 2021). Human and mouse RPE data show that PINK1 loss reduces activated phospho-Parkin (p-PRKN) and blunts mitophagic responses to depolarizing stimuli such as CCCP; conversely, in controls, CCCP elevates MAP1LC3B lipidation, validating PINK1 dependence for mitophagy activation in RPE (Datta et al., 2023). Early AMD human RPE exhibits decreased PINK1 in perifoveal regions, correlating with impaired mitophagy and providing a direct disease-context linkage between PINK1 deficiency and RPE dysfunction (Datta et al., 2023). Studies in AMD-relevant oxidative-stress mouse models (e.g., nfe2l2/pgc-1α−/−) indicate early activation of PINK1/Parkin signaling (e.g., increased Parkin colocalization with pS65 ubiquitin and accumulation of LC3B-positive autophagosomes) but suggest a downstream impairment in autolysosomal clearance, implying that upstream activation alone may not normalize flux under chronic stress (Gurubaran et al., 2020).

- KR → KTP conversion and direct PINK1 activation:  
  KR exerts its PINK1-activating effect primarily through metabolic conversion to kinetin riboside triphosphate (KTP), an ATP neo-substrate that binds PINK1 with higher affinity than ATP, thereby enhancing the kinase’s catalytic activity on relevant substrates (Georgakopoulos et al., 2017; Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018). Cellular enzymology supports that cytosolic nucleotide salvage and phosphoribosylation pathways enable the conversion of adenine derivatives (including kinetin) to triphosphate forms; APRT has been implicated in cytokinin biochemistry in mammalian systems and may contribute to the intracellular generation of KTP from kinetin precursors, though the precise enzymatic steps from KR to KTP in RPE require direct elucidation (Naseem et al., 2020). Pharmacological studies show that KR, KMP, and KTP activate PINK1 in mammalian and neuronal cells; KMP ProTides with various ester masks demonstrate serum stability and intracellular unmasking to yield active nucleotides, suggesting that glycosylation to the riboside and subsequent phosphorylation are key determinants of PINK1 activation (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Lambourne et al., 2023). Stabilized PINK1 then phosphorylates Parkin at serine 656 (as reported in the source text) and ubiquitin at serine 65, which accelerates Parkin recruitment and amplifies ubiquitin chain phosphorylation on OMM substrates, thereby seeding mitophagosome formation and progression (Lambourne et al., 2023). In cell systems, kinetin-derived activation of PINK1 is observed in the context of mitochondrial membrane depolarization and can be potentiated by mild, reversible uncoupling in some chemical series without overt mitochondrial toxicity when carefully tuned, underscoring a feasible pharmacological window (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018). Complementary small molecules (e.g., niclosamide, T0466/T0467, BC1464) act via PINK1 stabilization or degradation-pathway modulation, and USP30 inhibition further biases mitochondrial ubiquitination toward mitophagy, situating KR in a broader druggable landscape for PINK1-pathway enhancement (Masaldan et al., 2022).

- Convergence on RPE pathobiology:  
  Given that PINK1 expression and signaling are reduced in early AMD RPE, an agent that increases PINK1 catalytic activity and stabilizes PINK1 on damaged mitochondria could restore Parkin-dependent tagging and clearance of dysfunctional organelles, thereby lowering ROS loads and downstream RPE stress (Datta et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018). The RPE expresses and utilizes the PINK1/Parkin/LC3 autophagy machinery, as evidenced by immunochemical and functional data linking p-PRKN regulation, LC3B lipidation, and mitophagic flux to PINK1 state in mouse and human RPE systems (Datta et al., 2023). However, AMD models with oxidative stress show that autophagosome accumulation can occur without efficient clearance if lysosomal function is compromised; thus, any PINK1-activating therapy may need to be co-optimized with strategies that maintain autophagosome–lysosome fusion and lysosomal competence to realize net mitochondria turnover (Gurubaran et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
- In RPE assays:  
  KR should increase PINK1 activity upon mitochondrial depolarization or basal damage, resulting in higher levels of phospho-ubiquitin (pS65), increased Parkin recruitment to the OMM, augmented polyubiquitin decoration of OMM proteins (e.g., VDAC), enhanced LC3B-II accumulation, and increased formation of mitophagosomes and subsequent mitolysosomes, assuming lysosomal function is intact (Lambourne et al., 2023; Skeie et al., 2021). In PINK1-proficient RPE, a KR challenge following CCCP or physiological stressors is expected to recapitulate or potentiate the canonical PINK1/Parkin mitophagy cascade; notably, experiments in mouse RPE indicate that CCCP-induced elevation of LC3B lipidation is abrogated in pink1−/−, establishing a dependence of the autophagy readout on PINK1 that KR could rescue only if sufficient PINK1 is present (Datta et al., 2023). Given early AMD’s reduced PINK1 expression in the RPE perifovea, KR’s effect size may scale with residual PINK1 levels; the KTP–PINK1 interaction may partially compensate by enhancing the activity and dwell time of the remaining PINK1 on depolarized mitochondria, but absolute PINK1 scarcity could limit maximal response (Datta et al., 2023; Georgakopoulos et al., 2017). In AMD-like oxidative stress settings where the early mitophagy steps activate but autolysosomal clearance is impaired, KR is predicted to elevate upstream markers (pUb, Parkin localization, LC3B-II) yet may not fully normalize flux without restoring lysosomal function; this risk of autophagosome accumulation has been observed in AMD-model RPE, implying combination approaches (e.g., lysosome enhancers) may be required for optimal benefit (Gurubaran et al., 2020).

- In dry AMD disease biology:  
  By accelerating removal of dysfunctional mitochondria, KR is anticipated to reduce mitochondrial ROS and downstream oxidative damage, restoring bioenergetic homeostasis and decreasing RPE stress signals that contribute to drusen-associated pathology and cell death in dry AMD (Brooks et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018). Mechanistically, successful PINK1 activation should rebalance the population of healthy versus damaged mitochondria, mitigate chronic ROS-driven damage, and potentially stabilize RPE cellular functions (e.g., phagocytic capacity, lysosomal turnover of photoreceptor outer segments) that are compromised in AMD due to accumulation of dysfunctional organelles (Brooks et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018). Because the PINK1/Parkin axis is implicated in RPE degeneration and is downregulated in early AMD, targeted pharmacological enhancement of PINK1 represents a pathway-corrective approach aligned with disease mechanism, though it must be tested under AMD-relevant stressors that include both mitochondrial and lysosomal deficits (Datta et al., 2023; Gurubaran et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History—Safety, Toxicology, and Translational Considerations  
Nonclinical safety evaluations of kinetin (base) indicate a dose-dependent profile: low doses show favorable tolerability in skin applications and animal studies, whereas higher systemic doses (e.g., ≥1 mg/kg in rats) may perturb renal biomarkers, highlighting the need for careful exposure control; while this is not KR, it provides a class-level caution on dosing margins (Fathy et al., 2022; Othman et al., 2021). In mammalian cell systems, kinetin shows a concentration-dependent duality—sub-100 nM levels are cytoprotective against oxidative stress, while ≥500 nM can elicit cytotoxicity and genotoxicity—again reflecting the necessity of tight pharmacological windows in clinical development; KR shares pro-apoptotic properties at higher concentrations in tumor cells, indicating that exposure management will be critical to avoid off-target mitochondrial stress in non-malignant RPE (Gorincioi, 2010; Naseem et al., 2020). Tumor-selective cytotoxicity observed for KR (e.g., activation of caspase-3 following mitochondrial membrane disruption in HeLa and B16F-10) suggests that normal cells may be relatively resistant at appropriate concentrations, but translation to post-mitotic, metabolically active RPE requires dedicated therapeutic index definition (Gorincioi, 2010).

Pharmacokinetics for cytokinin ribosides present challenges, including short plasma half-life and potential limitations in barrier penetration; nevertheless, certain ribosides can achieve tissue exposure, and ProTide engineering of monophosphate forms has demonstrated improved serum stability and intracellular activation, offering a medicinal chemistry route to optimize ocular delivery and target engagement (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Voller et al., 2017). Importantly, the mitochondrial pharmacology dimension requires that PINK1 activation not rely on sustained pathological depolarization; prior work shows that PINK1 activation by certain KR-derived chemotypes can be coupled to reversible membrane effects without lasting mitochondrial injury, implying an achievable safety profile with rational chemistry and dosing (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018). Finally, the target pathway-level success with more potent PINK1 activators (e.g., MTK458) in cellular and animal models of Parkinson’s supports the druggability of this axis and suggests headroom to optimize KR analogs if KR itself proves insufficient in the RPE context (Hertz et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic alignment with AMD pathophysiology in RPE: Dry AMD features impaired mitophagy and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE, and early AMD shows decreased PINK1 expression and diminished mitophagy competence; KR directly activates PINK1, enhances Parkin recruitment via ubiquitin/PRKN phosphorylation, and augments mitophagy flux in mammalian and neuronal cells, providing a targeted correction to a disease-relevant defect (Datta et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Lambourne et al., 2023).  
- Direct enzymatic activation via KTP: KR’s biotransformation to KTP, an ATP neo-substrate with higher affinity for PINK1, offers a plausible biochemical mechanism to boost catalytic throughput even when PINK1 protein is partially reduced, thereby potentially amplifying residual PINK1 signaling in AMD RPE (Georgakopoulos et al., 2017; Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018).  
- Drug development precedent and tool compounds: Demonstrated PINK1 activation by KR, KMP/KTP, and related chemotypes, plus successful implementation of ProTide strategies and in vivo efficacy signals with potent analogs (e.g., MTK458), de-risk the pathway and provide a roadmap for medicinal chemistry and delivery optimization (Hertz et al., 2024; Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018).  
- Disease-biology congruence of pharmacodynamic readouts: RPE models have validated the dependency of CCCP-induced LC3B lipidation and p-PRKN formation on PINK1, while AMD-relevant models show upstream activation markers (pUb, Parkin colocalization) that are rate limited by downstream clearance—clear, quantifiable biomarkers exist to track KR engagement and flux restoration in RPE (Datta et al., 2023; Gurubaran et al., 2020).

Risks and Gaps  
- PINK1 insufficiency in early AMD: The perifoveal reduction of PINK1 in human RPE may limit the magnitude of KR-mediated activation; if PINK1 levels are below a critical threshold, KTP amplification alone might not suffice, necessitating combination with approaches that increase PINK1 expression/stability (e.g., BC1464) or that act downstream (e.g., USP30 inhibition to potentiate ubiquitin signaling) (Datta et al., 2023; Masaldan et al., 2022).  
- Lysosomal/autophagic clearance deficits: Oxidative stress models indicate initiation of PINK1/Parkin mitophagy with impaired autolysosomal clearance; KR may heighten early mitophagy steps without resolving terminal flux, risking autophagosome accumulation unless lysosomal function is co-restored (e.g., via agents that enhance autophagosome–lysosome fusion or lysosomal biogenesis) (Gurubaran et al., 2020).  
- Safety window and mitochondrial stress: KR exhibits pro-apoptotic, mitochondria-targeted cytotoxicity in tumor cells and cytotoxic/genotoxic effects at higher concentrations in non-tumor cells; precise dosing that achieves PINK1 activation without excessive mitochondrial depolarization or non-specific stress in RPE must be empirically determined (Gorincioi, 2010; Naseem et al., 2020).  
- PK and delivery barriers: Cytokinin ribosides generally have short half-lives and potential distribution limitations; ocular delivery (e.g., intravitreal, suprachoroidal, periocular) and ProTide/nanoparticulate strategies may be required to achieve durable RPE exposure while minimizing systemic exposure, an aspect not yet demonstrated for KR in the AMD setting (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Voller et al., 2017).  
- Lack of direct RPE/AMD in vivo efficacy data: While the mechanistic rationale is strong, KR has not been directly tested in RPE AMD models; translational viability will hinge on demonstrating improved mitophagy flux, decreased mitochondrial ROS, and RPE functional rescue in AMD-relevant models (Datta et al., 2023; Gurubaran et al., 2020).

Recommendation and Development Path  
Given the alignment between KR’s mechanism and the pathobiology of dry AMD in RPE, KR is a plausible repurposing candidate, but it should be advanced with a data-driven gating strategy that addresses target sufficiency, lysosomal function, safety window, and ocular delivery:  
- In vitro RPE assays (human primary or hPSC-derived) under AMD-relevant stress (e.g., photo-oxidative stress, lipofuscin/oxLDL exposure): test KR and KMP ProTides for dose–response effects on pUb (S65), p-PRKN, Parkin recruitment, LC3B lipidation, mitolysosome formation, mitochondrial turnover (mtDNA copy loss in mitolysosomes), and mitochondrial ROS/bioenergetics, benchmarking against CCCP controls and PINK1 knockdown/knockout lines (Datta et al., 2023; Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Skeie et al., 2021).  
- Lysosomal competence assays: co-assess autophagic flux with lysosomal pH and cathepsin activity; if KR increases early mitophagy markers without flux completion, evaluate combination with lysosome enhancers or TFEB agonists to restore throughput (Gurubaran et al., 2020).  
- PINK1 sufficiency and sensitization: quantify PINK1 levels in AMD-like conditions and test whether KR effects scale with PINK1 expression; consider combination with agents that stabilize PINK1 (e.g., BC1464) or increase mitochondrial ubiquitination via USP30 inhibition to offset low PINK1 (Datta et al., 2023; Masaldan et al., 2022).  
- Safety and therapeutic window in RPE: map KR exposure–response for PINK1 activation versus cytotoxicity/apoptosis, including concentrations that preserve RPE viability and mitochondrial membrane potential; incorporate off-target stress readouts (e.g., CHOP, ISR activation) (Gorincioi, 2010; Naseem et al., 2020).  
- Medicinal chemistry and delivery: prioritize KMP ProTides with favorable stability and reversible mitochondrial engagement to minimize off-target depolarization; assess ocular pharmacokinetics and RPE distribution in relevant species, given cytokinin riboside PK liabilities (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Voller et al., 2017).  
- In vivo models: test KR/ProTide in AMD-relevant models exhibiting RPE mitochondrial defects (e.g., NFE2L2/PGC-1α pathway disruption, photo-oxidative stress paradigms), with endpoints spanning RPE ultrastructure, mitochondrial turnover, oxidative markers, and functional readouts (ERG, RPE phagocytosis), while monitoring safety (renal/hepatic markers given systemic tox precedent) (Gurubaran et al., 2020; Othman et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Kinetin riboside is a mechanistically credible, pathway-directed candidate for dry AMD that targets a well-established deficit—PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy—in RPE, with robust supportive biology that PINK1 activation can be pharmacologically achieved by KR and its nucleotide metabolites to promote Parkin-dependent mitochondrial clearance (Datta et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Lambourne et al., 2023). The strengths include disease-relevant target engagement, availability of medicinal chemistry tactics (KMP ProTides) to address delivery and stability, and quantifiable pharmacodynamic markers in RPE that predict on-pathway efficacy (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Skeie et al., 2021). The principal risks are biological (insufficient PINK1 in early AMD and lysosomal flux defects that may cap benefit), pharmacological (narrow window between desired PINK1 activation and mitochondrial stress), and translational (PK/ocular delivery), none of which are insurmountable but all of which require rigorous preclinical validation in RPE-centric systems (Datta et al., 2023; Gurubaran et al., 2020; Naseem et al., 2020; Voller et al., 2017).

On balance, KR merits advancement to target-validation studies in human RPE models with concurrent optimization of ProTide prodrugs and combination strategies that secure lysosomal flux, with a clear go/no-go framework based on restoration of mitophagy flux and mitochondrial function without eliciting RPE toxicity (Gurubaran et al., 2020; Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018). If KR proves insufficient alone due to PINK1 insufficiency or PK constraints, more potent or targeted PINK1 activators (e.g., MTK458-class) and/or adjuncts that stabilize PINK1 or enhance downstream ubiquitin signaling may be prioritized, preserving the same mechanistic rationale for treating dry AMD via restoration of mitochondrial quality control in the RPE (Hertz et al., 2024; Masaldan et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
3-Mercaptopicolinic acid (3-MPA; also written 3-mercaptopicolinate/3-MP) is a small, thiol-containing picolinic-acid derivative historically identified as a biochemical inhibitor of gluconeogenesis through inhibition of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) and, at higher concentrations, glucose-6-phosphatase (G-6-Pase) in hepatic systems (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001). Early reports in the 1970s established 3-MPA as a preferential inhibitor of the cytosolic PEPCK isoform (PCK1), and the compound has since been used widely as a tool in mechanistic enzymology and physiology of gluconeogenesis across species and contexts (e.g., mammalian liver, pig, and protozoan PEPCKs) (Hidalgo et al., 2016; McLeod et al., 2019; Brearley et al., 2020). While the original discovery route is not detailed in the provided sources, a “convenient synthesis” was reported historically, and numerous structure–mechanism studies have refined the understanding of its binding behavior and chemical liabilities; by contrast, no data in the provided material indicate a natural origin (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001).

Chemically, 3-MPA belongs to the broader class of picolinic-acid–based, anionic, metal-coordinating inhibitors that engage the PEPCK active site by chelating the catalytically essential M1 divalent metal (typically Mn2+) via the ring nitrogen and exocyclic carboxylate; 3-MPA also contains a reactive free sulfhydryl group that drives both potency and time-dependent covalent reactivity with protein cysteines (McLeod et al., 2019). The picolinic-acid scaffold’s anionic, metal-binding character is a recognized design principle for PEPCK inhibitors and has been leveraged to build next-generation derivatives (e.g., 3-((carboxymethyl)thio)-picolinic acid, CMP) that seek to occupy both inner and outer subsites of the OAA/PEP pocket while reducing thiol-mediated liabilities (McLeod et al., 2019).

As a class, such PEPCK-directed small-molecule inhibitors have been applied as biochemical probes of gluconeogenic flux, as antihyperglycemic tools in preclinical metabolic studies, and as chemical probes to dissect PEPCK function in cancer and immunometabolism models; however, the field has wrestled with issues of thiol reactivity, complex multi-site binding kinetics, ADME/PAINS flags, and limited isoform selectivity, all of which complicate translation (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001; McLeod et al., 2019; Baptista et al., 2019; Hidalgo et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History  
3-MPA has a long track record as a research tool in hepatic metabolism. In perfused rat liver and in vivo rat studies, 3-MPA was used to blunt gluconeogenesis and lower blood glucose, with dosing paradigms including intraperitoneal administration (e.g., 100 mg/kg followed by 25 mg/kg three hours later) and 1 mM concentrations in perfusate to suppress fructose- or lactate/pyruvate-stimulated hepatic glucose production (Herling et al., 1998). More recently, 3-MPA has served as a comparator and positive control in modern PEPCK-targeted discovery programs, including enzyme assays against recombinant human cytosolic and mitochondrial PEPCK isoforms (PCK1/PCK2), CETSA target-engagement studies, cell-based functional assays (e.g., insulin secretion), and acute in vivo pharmacodynamic readouts (e.g., fasting glycemia five hours after 50 mg/kg IP administration) (Aragó et al., 2020). In several settings, 3-MPA reduces oncogenic phenotypes: it impairs anchorage-independent growth in MCF7 cells yet shows limited effects on glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in INS-1 cells, suggesting variable target engagement and a modest potency ceiling relative to newer chemotypes (Aragó et al., 2020).

3-MPA has been used to inhibit the mitochondrial isoform PEPCK-M (PCK2) in cancer models. In non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cell lines cultured under glucose deprivation, inhibition of human mitochondrial PEPCK by 3-MPA or genetic knockdown induced apoptosis, consistent with a reliance on PEPCK-mediated anaplerotic/cataplerotic cycling for survival under nutrient stress (Baptista et al., 2019). Computational docking studies against human PEPCK-M have used 3-MPA as a benchmark ligand to set score cutoffs and to elucidate canonical binding interactions (Mn2+ coordination; Arg/Lys salt-bridge network), aligning with structural insights from cytosolic isoforms (Baptista et al., 2019).

In melanoma models, 3-MPA (applied as a PCK1 inhibitor) sensitized vemurafenib-resistant tumors in vitro and in vivo by depressing pentose phosphate pathway–derived NADPH production and elevating ROS through KEAP1/Nrf2 axis modulation, thereby reversing resistance; here, 3-MPA increased oxidative stress rather than alleviating it (Ren et al., 2022). Across immunometabolism, 3-MPA (100 μM) reduced cytotoxic T lymphocyte effector functions and decreased maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) without altering basal glycolysis, indicating impaired mitochondrial respiratory capacity in activated T cells in which PEPCK-M predominates (Brownlie et al., 2025). In skeletal muscle myoblasts (C2C12), 3-MPA (0.25–1 mM) reduced proliferation and induced myogenic differentiation, with Pck2 transcripts predominant over Pck1; however, the compound interfered with enzymatic assays at ≥0.25–0.5 mM, complicating attribution to on-target inhibition (Brearley et al., 2020). Against porcine cytosolic PEPCK isoenzymes, 3-MPA exhibits mid-micromolar IC₅₀ (~65 μM) under saturating substrates and mechanistically mixed/complex kinetics (mixed non-competitive vs PEP; uncompetitive vs GDP/GTP), supporting dual-site binding behavior (Hidalgo et al., 2016).

No study in the provided literature assesses 3-MPA in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), retina, or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD); a comprehensive mechanistic and structural study of related PEPCK inhibitors explicitly contains no mention of eye/RPE/AMD systems, emphasizing that the extant knowledge base for 3-MPA is outside ophthalmology (McLeod et al., 2019). Absent any reported ocular or RPE use, 3-MPA should be regarded as a systemic/metabolic tool compound with evolving applications in cancer and immunometabolism rather than as a precedent therapeutic in retinal degenerations (McLeod et al., 2019).

Mechanism of Action  
Mechanistic biochemistry and structural work converge on a dual-mode model for 3-MPA action on PEPCK:
- Active-site (inner-subsite) binding and Mn²⁺ coordination: The picolinic-acid moiety of 3-MPA coordinates the catalytic M1 Mn²⁺ ion via the ring nitrogen and exocyclic carboxylate oxygen(s), occupying the “inner” OAA/PEP subsite in a manner analogous to oxalate and other carboxylate inhibitors; co-crystal analyses and docking corroborate metal coordination along with salt-bridge/ion-pairing to conserved basic residues (e.g., Arg104/Arg423/Lys261/Lys262 in vertebrate enzymes) (McLeod et al., 2019; Baptista et al., 2019).
- Secondary/allosteric site binding: 3-MPA can occupy a second site near/behind the P-loop, with two molecules bound simultaneously (n≈2 by ITC), producing complex kinetic signatures (mixed non-competitive behavior with respect to PEP/OAA and uncompetitive inhibition versus GDP/GTP), and allowing allosteric influence on substrate/inhibitor binding at the active site (Hidalgo et al., 2016).

Kinetically, these binding modes yield mixed patterns that depend on the variable substrate: mixed non-competitive versus PEP/OAA; uncompetitive versus GDP/GTP, consistent with inhibitor binding to enzyme–nucleotide complexes and allosteric communication to the catalytic pocket (Hidalgo et al., 2016). Across isoforms, micromolar potency is typical: for rat cytosolic PEPCK (rcPEPCK) Kᵢ ~8 μM, for human mitochondrial PEPCK (hmPEPCK) Kᵢ ~3 μM in some determinations, though reported IC₅₀/Kᵢ values vary with assay format and metal/substrate conditions (McLeod et al., 2019). Variability is expected given that picolinic-acid derivatives chelate divalent metal cations; changes in available Mn²⁺ can partially masquerade as noncompetitive inhibition (i.e., by depleting active holoenzyme) in kinetic plots if not tightly controlled (McLeod et al., 2019).

A distinguishing chemical feature of 3-MPA is the free thiol. In vitro, the thiol can form mixed disulfide adducts with reactive cysteines on PEPCK (e.g., C288 on the P-loop in rat cytosolic PEPCK), producing time-dependent, covalent inactivation that contributes to potency but also to off-target reactivity and interpretational complexity; this chemistry is mitigated but not eliminated by inclusion of reducing agents in assays (McLeod et al., 2019). The thiol’s promiscuity likely explains reports of irreversible, time-dependent inhibition of G-6-Pase at millimolar concentrations, a phenomenon exploited historically to dissect gluconeogenic regulation but pharmacologically undesirable for selective PEPCK targeting (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001; McLeod et al., 2019). Because the M1 metal and a basic electrostatic microenvironment (e.g., Arg104/Arg423/Lys261/Lys262) are conserved in PEPCK-M and PEPCK-C, inhibitors that rely on metal chelation and anionic interactions, like 3-MPA, are predicted to show cross-isoform activity; docking against the human mitochondrial isoform reproduces these hallmarks (Baptista et al., 2019).

Several functional studies corroborate that 3-MPA perturbs cellular bioenergetics consistent with PEPCK inhibition but in cell-context-dependent ways. In activated effector T cells (PCK2-predominant), 100 μM 3-MPA reduced maximal OCR without changing basal ECAR, indicating compromised oxidative phosphorylation capacity while leaving basal glycolysis intact (Brownlie et al., 2025). In lung cancer cell lines, PEPCK-M inhibition by 3-MPA induced apoptosis only under glucose deprivation, highlighting the role of PCK2 in enabling biosynthesis from non-glucose substrates under stress (Baptista et al., 2019). Conversely, in BRAFi-resistant melanoma, PCK1 inhibition by 3-MPA depressed PPP-mediated NADPH synthesis, increased ROS by weakening antioxidant buffering (via KEAP1/Nrf2), and sensitized cells to targeted therapy, illustrating that PEPCK inhibition can amplify oxidative stress depending on metabolic wiring (Ren et al., 2022).

Finally, medicinal-chemistry and ADME flags apply. 3-MPA triggers PAINS warnings and violates the Pfizer 3/75 heuristic on polar surface area margins in in silico filtering, and its free thiol confers chemical reactivity that can perturb off-target proteins and auxiliary assay enzymes; analogs that remove the free thiol (e.g., thioethers like CMP) avoid mixed-disulfide inactivation at the cost of reduced potency (order-of-magnitude weaker Kᵢ) (Baptista et al., 2019; McLeod et al., 2019; Hidalgo et al., 2016).

Expected Effect  
The working hypothesis proposes that 3-MPA will inhibit mitochondrial PCK2 in RPE, redirecting flux toward TCA cycle maintenance, enhancing NADH generation, and reducing ROS during bioenergetic stress. Evidence from the supplied literature constrains and complicates each element of this chain:

- Direct engagement of PCK2 by 3-MPA. Biochemical and docking data support that 3-MPA inhibits human PEPCK-M with micromolar potency and establishes the binding physics (Mn²⁺ coordination; cationic pocket interactions), making PCK2 engagement in principle plausible in RPE if the protein is expressed and accessible (McLeod et al., 2019; Baptista et al., 2019). However, the provided sources do not document PCK2 expression in RPE (neither transcript nor protein), so expression in the proposed cell type cannot be confirmed from this corpus (McLeod et al., 2019). The supplied general isoform summary indicates that in humans both isoforms can be approximately equally abundant at the organismal level, underscoring that mitochondrial PEPCK may be physiologically relevant in human tissues, but this does not substitute for RPE-specific evidence (Yun, 2017).

- Direction of flux and impact on TCA maintenance/NADH. In activated T cells (PCK2-predominant), 3-MPA reduced maximal OCR, implying diminished electron transport chain capacity and, by extension, a reduction—not an enhancement—of NADH-supported oxidative phosphorylation reserve; this observation argues that PCK2 inhibition can constrain mitochondrial respiratory capacity in at least some mammalian cell types (Brownlie et al., 2025; Baptista et al., 2019). In NSCLC, PEPCK-M inhibition precipitated apoptosis during glucose deprivation, consistent with failure of metabolic adaptation when cataplerotic/anaplerotic cycling is blocked; this is contrary to the expectation that PCK2 inhibition would “rescue” TCA integrity and support survival under stress (Baptista et al., 2019). Together these data suggest that in cells relying on PEPCK-mediated cycling to support survival or effector function under nutrient/oxidative load, 3-MPA tends to reduce OXPHOS capacity and viability rather than bolster NADH generation and TCA pool maintenance.

- Effect on ROS. In BRAFi-resistant melanoma, 3-MPA decreased NADPH production (via PPP) and increased ROS by attenuating the Nrf2 antioxidant axis (increased KEAP1), thereby sensitizing cells to oxidative injury; this is the opposite sign from the hypothesis that 3-MPA would reduce ROS (Ren et al., 2022). Whether the same redox trajectory would manifest in RPE is uncertain, but the burden of evidence indicates that PEPCK inhibition can aggravate oxidative stress in at least some proliferative/stressed cells.

- Off-target and concentration-dependent effects relevant to RPE. At high exposure (hundreds of micromolar to millimolar), 3-MPA exhibits assay interference and off-target enzyme inhibition (e.g., G-6-P translocase and/or G-6-Pase, time-dependent irreversibility), and has been used at 1 mM in perfused livers, underscoring a risk window where non-PEPCK targets and chemical reactivity dominate (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001; Brearley et al., 2020; Herling et al., 1998). Its free thiol can form mixed-disulfide adducts with reactive cysteines, a liability in redox-sensitive tissues like the RPE where protein thiol chemistry is critical to homeostasis (McLeod et al., 2019). In silico PAINS flags and polarity metrics further caution against promiscuity and suboptimal drug-likeness (Baptista et al., 2019).

In summary, while 3-MPA can inhibit PEPCK-M and therefore could, in principle, modulate RPE mitochondrial metabolism, the best available functional evidence in related mammalian cell systems predicts reduced maximal OXPHOS capacity and, in certain contexts, increased ROS when PEPCK activity is blocked; this contradicts the proposed directionality of benefit for dry AMD. The provided sources do not document PCK2 expression in RPE, so the target linkage in the specified cell type remains unsubstantiated within this corpus (Brownlie et al., 2025; Baptista et al., 2019; Ren et al., 2022; McLeod et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Extensive mechanistic characterization and proven PEPCK engagement. 3-MPA’s dual-site binding, active-site metal coordination, and kinetic behavior are well described, with micromolar potency against both cytosolic and mitochondrial PEPCK isoforms under defined conditions, enabling precise hypothesis testing of PEPCK-dependent biology (McLeod et al., 2019; Hidalgo et al., 2016).  
- Demonstrated modulation of mitochondrial bioenergetics in mammalian cells. The compound reduces maximal OCR in activated T cells (PCK2-predominant), confirming that pharmacologic inhibition of PEPCK-M can reprogram OXPHOS in a predictable direction, albeit one that appears detrimental to respiratory capacity (Brownlie et al., 2025).  
- Tool-compound utility across contexts relevant to stress metabolism. In NSCLC under glucose limitation and in BRAFi-resistant melanoma, 3-MPA perturbs survival pathways and redox control, reinforcing that PEPCK is a nodal metabolic regulator in stress adaptation—an axis of interest in RPE pathobiology in AMD (Baptista et al., 2019; Ren et al., 2022).

- Directionality of effect conflicts with the AMD hypothesis. Available cell-based data indicate 3-MPA reduces maximal mitochondrial respiratory capacity and can increase ROS in specific contexts by depleting PPP-derived NADPH, the opposite of the hypothesized benefit for RPE under bioenergetic/oxidative stress (Brownlie et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2022).  
- Chemical liabilities. The free thiol drives time-dependent covalent reactivity (mixed disulfides) with PEPCK and likely other proteins; at millimolar exposure, 3-MPA causes irreversible, time-dependent inhibition of G-6-Pase, underscoring a broad risk of off-target covalent modification that is unacceptable for ocular therapy without significant medicinal-chemistry mitigation (McLeod et al., 2019; Westergaard & Madsen, 2001). PAINS flags and polarity metrics caution against promiscuity and poor drug-likeness (Baptista et al., 2019).  
- Inconsistent target engagement in cells and modest potency relative to alternatives. Compared with newer PEPCK inhibitors (e.g., iPEPCK-2), 3-MPA shows two orders of magnitude weaker IC₅₀s in some cellular contexts and variable engagement (e.g., limited effect on insulin secretion), suggesting that achieving effective concentrations in relevant compartments may be difficult or that off-target liabilities confound outcomes (Aragó et al., 2020).  
- No precedent in retinal/RPE systems. The provided literature contains no data on 3-MPA in the eye, retina, RPE, or AMD models, and offers no RPE expression evidence for PCK2, making the translational leap speculative from the present corpus (McLeod et al., 2019; Yun, 2017).  
- Concentration-dependent assay interference and off-target effects. In C2C12 cells, 3-MPA interfered with PEPCK assays at ≥0.25–0.5 mM; perfused liver studies used 1 mM; such concentrations raise the likelihood of nonspecific effects in RPE (Brearley et al., 2020; Herling et al., 1998).  

Decision-Critical Gaps for AMD  
- Target validation in RPE. There is no evidence in the supplied material confirming PCK2 expression and activity in RPE, nor any demonstration that PEPCK-M–dependent cycling is maladaptive in dry AMD; this gap precludes mechanistic confidence (McLeod et al., 2019).  
- Directionality of benefit. The compound’s demonstrated tendency to reduce maximal OXPHOS capacity and, in some contexts, to enhance oxidative stress directly contradicts the intended pharmacology (increase NADH/OXPHOS; decrease ROS) in stressed RPE (Brownlie et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2022).  
- Ocular safety. Free-thiol reactivity, metal chelation, and PAINS liabilities make 3-MPA a risky starting point for ocular delivery; no ocular PK/safety data are available in the provided sources (Baptista et al., 2019; McLeod et al., 2019; Westergaard & Madsen, 2001).  

If the project’s strategic objective is to probe whether inhibiting PEPCK-M benefits RPE bioenergetic stability, a safer and more specific chemical tool would be required. Notably, thioether analogs like CMP remove the free thiol and still engage the active site competitively (albeit with ~10× weaker potency), and crystallography confirms occupancy of both inner and outer subsites; such molecules may offer cleaner on-target pharmacology for in vitro RPE studies while avoiding mixed-disulfide covalency (McLeod et al., 2019). However, even for such analogs, the directionality risk remains given that PEPCK-M inhibition has reduced mitochondrial respiratory capacity in mammalian cells that rely on this enzyme under activation stress (Brownlie et al., 2025).

Overall, based on the provided literature, I do not recommend prioritizing 3-MPA as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. The compound’s mechanistic actions and cell-level consequences in related systems predict outcomes counter to the proposed benefit in RPE, and its chemical liabilities are incompatible with ocular drug development without substantial medicinal-chemistry redesign (Brownlie et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2022; McLeod et al., 2019; Baptista et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Metformin is a well‐known therapeutic agent belonging to the biguanide class, originally derived from guanidine compounds found in the plant Galega officinalis. The molecule is a synthetic derivative of naturally occurring galegine and has been refined into a modern oral antihyperglycemic agent (Augustin & Atorf, 2023). This class of compounds has historically been used as a first-line oral treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus, with metformin being one of the most prescribed drugs worldwide for managing hyperglycemia. Its synthesis did not follow the classical target‐driven design path but instead emerged from an adaptation of naturally occurring structures into a chemically optimized, orally bioavailable, and generally well-tolerated drug (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Dang et al., 2021). Given its long clinical history starting from the 1950s and subsequent FDA approval in the 1990s, metformin has accumulated a significant amount of safety data and clinical experience, which collectively make it an attractive candidate for repurposing into other disease areas, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) characterized by geographic atrophy (Amin et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, metformin has been used extensively as an antidiabetic agent to lower hepatic glucose output and improve peripheral insulin sensitivity. Its beneficial pleiotropic effects beyond glycemic control have been recognized over the years; these include anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antiangiogenic properties, which have been observed in both biochemical and clinical investigations. Multiple epidemiologic studies have examined the association between metformin use and ocular outcomes. Retrospective analyses in predominantly diabetic cohorts have indicated that metformin use correlates with reduced odds or hazard for developing age-related macular degeneration and other retinal diseases, although some studies report mixed results depending on cumulative dose, exposure timing, and concomitant diabetes-related complications (Moir et al., 2023; Amin et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2022). Notably, while metformin has not historically been approved for any ocular indication, several preclinical studies using retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cell models have demonstrated that metformin may protect against oxidative damage and improve mitochondrial function. Moreover, a Phase II single-blind randomized trial was initiated to assess the efficacy of metformin in slowing the progression of geographic atrophy among non-diabetic patients with advanced dry AMD (Shen et al., 2024), suggesting that the concept of repurposing metformin for dry AMD is already under active clinical investigation.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, metformin’s primary mechanism of action involves the inhibition of mitochondrial complex I of the electron transport chain, resulting in a decrease in ATP production and a concomitant increase in the intracellular AMP:ATP ratio. This metabolic shift leads to the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a master regulator of cellular energy homeostasis that orchestrates shifts in metabolism under conditions of energy deficit (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). AMPK activation exerts multiple downstream effects that are particularly relevant to RPE cell function and the pathogenesis of geographic atrophy. First, AMPK activation promotes autophagy, including mitophagy, a quality-control mechanism that ensures the removal of dysfunctional mitochondria. Preclinical studies in RPE cell models, such as those using ARPE-19 cells, have provided evidence that metformin increases autophagosome formation, reduces intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS), lowers apoptosis rates, and helps maintain the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) under oxidative stress conditions (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Toppila et al., 2024). Additionally, the activation of AMPK in RPE cells has been associated with upregulation of protective pathways including enhanced nitric oxide (NO) production and increased expression of mitochondrial biogenesis factors such as PGC-1α, which together contribute to improved mitochondrial quality control (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023).  

Furthermore, metformin is known to activate both AMPK-dependent and AMPK-independent signaling pathways. The AMPK-independent effects may include inhibition of NF-κB activation, leading to a reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α, which are implicated in chronic inflammation observed in the aging retina (Jiang et al., 2022; Amin et al., 2022). From a biochemical standpoint, the inhibition of complex I by metformin also directly reduces the leakage of electrons that can form ROS, thereby lowering mitochondrial oxidative stress—a key aspect in the progression of dry AMD pathogenesis (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). It is important to note, however, that several reports have highlighted the concern that activation of AMPK in vivo or in vitro appears to require suprapharmacological doses of metformin, casting uncertainty on whether standard clinical dosing is sufficient to achieve these retinal effects (Moir et al., 2023). Nonetheless, the preclinical evidence supports a model whereby metformin’s inhibition of mitochondrial complex I—thereby reducing ROS and enhancing autophagy—provides a rationale for its potential use in protecting RPE cells from oxidative stress-induced damage (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis driving the repurposing of metformin for dry AMD is predicated on its ability to activate AMPK and inhibit mitochondrial complex I leakage in RPE cells, leading to reduced ROS production and enhanced mitochondrial quality control. In the context of geographic atrophy, RPE dysfunction and death play a central role in the degeneration of photoreceptors and the progression of AMD. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that metformin can protect ARPE-19 cells (an established human RPE cell line) from oxidative insults by lowering intracellular ROS levels, augmenting autophagic processes, and preserving mitochondrial membrane potential (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Toppila et al., 2024). Additionally, through the activation of AMPK, metformin is expected to stimulate the expression of mitochondrial biogenesis factors, leading to improved mitochondrial function, which is critical given the high metabolic demands of the RPE (Moir et al., 2023). 

Epidemiologically, several retrospective cohort and case-control studies have observed associations between metformin use and a reduced risk of developing AMD. Some studies even suggest that these associations are dose- and timing-dependent, with earlier or sustained use of metformin correlating with greater protective effects (Moir et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022). Therefore, in an assay designed to measure the effects of metformin on mitochondrial function and oxidative stress in RPE cells, one would expect to see an enhancement in autophagic flux, decreased markers of oxidative stress, and preservation or restoration of Δψm. These cellular effects would ideally translate into a slower progression of geographic atrophy in vivo, as suggested by the decreased degeneration of the retinal layers that has been observed in certain mouse models of retinal damage (Jiang et al., 2022; Amin et al., 2022). RPE cells are known to express AMPK and other components of the autophagy machinery, which further supports the rationale for targeting these pathways in the treatment of dry AMD (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Moir et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
Metformin shows considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly for geographic atrophy, due to several key strengths. First, its long and well-documented clinical history in the management of type 2 diabetes provides a robust safety profile and widespread clinical familiarity, which is a significant advantage when considering repurposing strategies (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Dang et al., 2021; Amin et al., 2022). Second, the molecular and cellular mechanisms by which metformin acts—namely, the inhibition of mitochondrial complex I, subsequent activation of AMPK, and promotion of autophagy—are highly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. The ability of metformin to reduce ROS and promote mitochondrial quality control addresses one of the core aspects of RPE dysfunction and degeneration seen in geographic atrophy (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Jiang et al., 2022).

Furthermore, the epidemiologic data showing associations between metformin use and a reduced incidence of AMD lend additional support to its potential utility in this setting (Liang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023). The possibility that metformin’s protective effects might be independent of its glycemic control properties is particularly intriguing, as it expands the target population to non-diabetic AMD patients—a group that represents the majority of those affected by geographic atrophy (Moir et al., 2023; Brown et al., 2019; Moir et al., 2024). On a mechanistic level, the detailed understanding of metformin’s interaction with AMPK and mitochondrial pathways not only provides a clear therapeutic target but also offers multiple biomarkers for assessing efficacy in both preclinical and clinical studies.

Despite its strengths, several weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. One significant concern is whether standard clinical doses of metformin are sufficient to activate the AMPK pathway in retinal tissues, given that some in vitro studies indicate suprapharmacological doses are required to see a robust effect (Moir et al., 2023). This raises questions of retinal bioavailability and whether alternative delivery strategies, such as local ocular administration or formulation enhancements, might be required to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE. Additionally, while the epidemiologic studies are promising, they are not uniformly consistent; some retrospective analyses have reported no association or even conflicting results depending on dosing and timing parameters (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Brown et al., 2019; Amin et al., 2022). These discrepancies underscore the inherent limitations of observational data, including potential confounding factors such as the presence and severity of diabetes, concomitant medications, and the challenges of accurately classifying AMD subtypes using administrative coding.

Another consideration is that although metformin’s broad mechanism of action (i.e., modulation of inflammation, oxidative stress, and autophagy) is advantageous in addressing multifactorial diseases like AMD, it may also lead to off-target effects or systemic side effects such as vitamin B12 deficiency or, in rare instances, lactic acidosis (Jiang et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). In elderly populations—who are generally most affected by dry AMD—these risks must be carefully weighed against the potential benefits. Moreover, the heterogeneity in study designs and patient populations in the available epidemiologic literature means that prospective, well-designed clinical trials remain essential to definitively determine whether metformin can meaningfully slow the progression of geographic atrophy in AMD (Shen et al., 2024).

In summary, the overall evaluation of metformin as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. Its well-established safety profile, combined with mechanistic data that align closely with the underlying pathology of geographic atrophy, make it a compelling candidate. The strengths lie in its ability to activate AMPK, thereby reducing mitochondrial ROS, promoting autophagy, and potentially preserving RPE function—molecular actions that directly address key pathological features of dry AMD. However, critical questions regarding dosing, ocular bioavailability, and the variability in epidemiologic outcomes necessitate further rigorous investigation in controlled clinical settings. Moving forward, clinical trials designed to specifically assess metformin’s efficacy in non-diabetic populations with early to intermediate stages of geographic atrophy will be crucial to validate its repurposing potential. Overall, while metformin has significant promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, additional studies are needed to resolve questions about its optimal dosing regimen, delivery method, and long-term efficacy in preserving retinal structure and function (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Shen et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
S3QEL-2 is a synthetic small‐molecule member of the S3QEL (Suppressors of Superoxide production from mitochondrial Complex III) class, originally discovered through a high‐throughput screen of approximately 635,000 small molecules using isolated mitochondria and an Amplex UltraRed H₂O₂ detection assay (Orr et al., 2015). In this screening paradigm, compounds were rigorously selected for their ability to selectively suppress superoxide generation arising from the Qo site of mitochondrial Complex III without impairing oxidative phosphorylation or altering the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) (Orr et al., 2015). The discovery approach involved counterscreens that monitored Δψm changes, respiration rates, and markers of cellular viability, ensuring that S3QEL-2 exhibits specificity in mitigating reactive oxygen species (ROS) production rather than acting as a nonspecific antioxidant or uncoupler (Orr et al., 2015). S3QEL-2 was sourced from commercial screening collections—for example, vendors such as Chemdiv—and its powder-stock purity was confirmed by HPLC–MS analysis (Orr et al., 2015). As a member of a structurally diverse chemotype group, S3QEL-2 belongs to a new class of mitochondrial ROS-targeted modulators that differ fundamentally from classical Complex III inhibitors such as antimycin A or myxothiazol; unlike these inhibitors, S3QELs do not block the electron transfer chain or impair ATP production, but rather reduce the electron leak from the semiquinone intermediate at the Qo site (Orr et al., 2015). In general, compounds in the S3QEL class have been used experimentally as probes to decouple pathological ROS generation from normal bioenergetic function in diverse cell types, with applications ranging from studies on hypoxia-induced transcription (e.g., HIF-1α signaling) to experiments investigating ROS-mediated cell stress in pancreatic β-cells (Orr et al., 2015). The commercial catalog number Cayman Chemical #26918 identifies S3QEL-2 for research purposes, which suggests that this compound is available for repurposing studies beyond its initial characterization in nonocular systems (Orr et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Although S3QEL-2 was originally developed as a novel chemical probe to selectively suppress Complex III-derived superoxide production, its preclinical evaluation has been extensive within the context of cellular models evaluating ROS-mediated signaling and cell stress responses (Orr et al., 2015). In cellular assays, S3QEL-2 has demonstrated the ability to reduce H₂O₂ production in isolated mitochondria, lower HIF-1α transcription in hypoxia-challenged HEK-293 cells, and protect pancreatic β-cells from oxidative stress-induced apoptosis during islet isolation and culture (Orr et al., 2015). Notably, in studies where cells were exposed to concentrations up to 20× the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC₅₀) determined for site IIIQo superoxide production, S3QEL-2 did not impair basal or uncoupled respiration, nor did it compromise mitochondrial viability (Orr et al., 2015). Additionally, S3QEL-2 has been employed as a pharmacological tool in experiments on human monocyte-derived macrophages, where it contributed to demonstrating that inhibition of mitochondrial ROS can reduce inflammasome activation and subsequent IL-18 secretion upon stimulation by the complement membrane attack complex (MAC) (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). However, despite its utility in these nonocular systems—where mitochondrial ROS inhibition was linked to attenuation of inflammatory cytokine pathways—there is little to no published preclinical or clinical data directly evaluating S3QEL-2 in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models or in other ocular disease contexts (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2015). While the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of dry AMD, particularly those involving chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and associated inflammasome activation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, are well documented (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013), a direct therapeutic history for S3QEL-2 in retinal or AMD models remains absent in the current literature (Korhonen, 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Thus, S3QEL-2 represents a promising repurposing candidate that has been validated in other contexts of ROS-related cellular stress but has not yet been explicitly applied to the treatment of dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of S3QEL-2 is based on its capacity to selectively suppress superoxide generation originating at the Qo site of mitochondrial Complex III. Under normal conditions, the electron transport chain (ETC) can leak electrons during the reduction of oxygen, particularly at the semiquinone intermediate at the Qo site, resulting in the formation of superoxide—a primary reactive oxygen species (Orr et al., 2015). S3QEL-2 does not act as a general ROS scavenger; rather, it modulates the rate constant for the electron transfer from the semiquinone to molecular oxygen without significantly altering the steady-state levels of semiquinone species or the redox poise of the ubiquinone (Q) pool (Orr et al., 2015). This selective inhibition of ROS generation is achieved through an allosteric modulation of protein conformation within Complex III, specifically targeting the Qo site to reduce electron leak while sparing the remainder of the electron transport processes (Orr et al., 2015). By decreasing superoxide production, S3QEL-2 effectively reduces the downstream formation of H₂O₂ as detected by Amplex UltraRed assays, a finding that has been consistently reproduced in isolated mitochondrial studies (Orr et al., 2015). Moreover, because S3QEL-2 does not interfere with the overall electron flux or the maintenance of Δψm, it preserves the bioenergetic capacity of the mitochondria—a critical factor in tissues with high metabolic demands such as the RPE (Orr et al., 2015). On a molecular level, the compound’s activity at nanomolar to low micromolar concentrations (with a reported mean IC₅₀ around 1.7 μM for S3QEL-2) suggests a highly potent modulation of the ROS generation pathway that is independent of the mitochondrial matrix redox state (Orr et al., 2015). This targeted approach is further distinguished from classical Complex III inhibitors like myxothiazol and antimycin A, which disrupt the entire electron transport process and can lead to a collapse in mitochondrial function; in contrast, S3QEL-2 specifically mitigates the pathological component of ROS production while maintaining ATP synthesis and cellular energy homeostasis (Orr et al., 2015). In macrophages and other cell types, the reduction in mitochondrial ROS production by S3QEL-2 has been shown to blunt ROS-dependent signaling pathways, such as the stabilization of the transcription factor HIF-1α under hypoxic conditions, and to decrease the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Toma et al., 2021). Thus, the molecular interactions of S3QEL-2 within Complex III position it as a potential modulator of redox signaling pathways that are implicated in inflammatory and degenerative processes, including those observed in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Based on its established mechanism of action, the use of S3QEL-2 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells is expected to selectively reduce mitochondrial ROS generated at the Complex III Qo site. In dry age-related macular degeneration, one of the prevailing hypotheses attributes disease progression to chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction within the RPE, leading to the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and subsequent secretion of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013). The selective inhibition of ROS by S3QEL-2 should therefore interrupt this pathological signaling cascade. In an in vitro assay using RPE cells—cells that have been shown to express components of the NLRP3 inflammasome and are especially vulnerable to oxidative insults—the drug is anticipated to lower ROS markers, as measured by fluorescent dyes (for example, oxidized carboxy-H₂DCFDA), without compromising the cells' mitochondrial respiration or Δψm (Orr et al., 2015). With less mitochondrial ROS available to act as secondary messengers, the downstream stabilization of HIF-1α under stress conditions is expected to be reduced, and the inflammatory response mediated by inflammasome assembly will likely be attenuated (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Orr et al., 2015). Given that multiple studies have demonstrated the role of mitochondrial ROS in directly or indirectly activating NLRP3 inflammasome signaling in both macrophages and RPE cells (Gao et al., 2015; Campbell & Doyle, 2013; Piippo, 2019), the hypothesis is that S3QEL-2 will break this mtROS–NLRP3 axis. In a therapeutic assay, one would expect that RPE cells treated with S3QEL-2 under conditions of complement dysregulation (a known contributor to dry AMD pathology) would demonstrate not only reduced markers of oxidative stress and inflammasome activation but also improved cellular viability, decreased apoptosis, and maintenance of proper metabolic function (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). Furthermore, if S3QEL-2 can lower the intracellular superoxide burden, it might also reduce the formation of oxidized lipids and other damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that contribute to the progression of AMD (Campbell & Doyle, 2013; Toma et al., 2021). Overall, the strategic downregulation of mitochondrial ROS production should translate into a protective phenotype in RPE cells by interrupting the signaling mechanisms that lead to chronic inflammation and cell death in the context of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
S3QEL-2 emerges as an attractive candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to its unique pharmacological profile and precision in targeting mitochondrial ROS production. One of the key strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its ability to selectively suppress superoxide generation at the Complex III Qo site without impairing the overall electron transport chain function or disrupting mitochondrial membrane potential (Orr et al., 2015). This high degree of specificity is particularly valuable in a disease such as dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central to pathogenesis yet preserving the RPE’s bioenergetic capacity is essential for retinal health (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013). The preclinical data available for S3QEL-2 in nonocular systems—ranging from hypoxia-induced HIF-1α modulation to protection of pancreatic β-cells and dampening of inflammasome activation in macrophages—suggest that its mechanism of action may well translate to the RPE, a cell type that is similarly sensitive to mitochondrial oxidative stress (Orr et al., 2015; Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). Moreover, the ability of S3QEL-2 to reduce mitochondrial ROS levels without interfering with ATP production positions it as a promising agent for interrupting the mtROS–NLRP3 inflammasome axis that is proposed to drive inflammatory responses in the geographic atrophy observed in dry AMD (Orr et al., 2015; Orr et al., 2015).

However, several weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. Despite the encouraging preclinical data in cell culture and isolated mitochondrial systems, there is currently no direct evidence linking S3QEL-2 to therapeutic benefit in retinal models or in dry AMD specifically (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2015). The candidate has been primarily evaluated in nonocular models, and the complex microenvironment of the retina—including the blood-retinal barrier, immune cell interactions, and local complement dysregulation—may pose significant challenges in translating in vitro efficacy to in vivo benefit (Korhonen, 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Furthermore, while S3QEL-2 has been shown to reduce ROS-mediated signaling in macrophages and pancreatic islets, the pharmacokinetic properties, tissue distribution, and long-term safety profile of this compound in ocular tissues remain to be determined (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Orr et al., 2015). Delivery of S3QEL-2 to the retina may require formulation strategies that overcome solubility and permeability barriers inherent in drug delivery to the posterior segment of the eye. Another concern is the potential for off-target effects that, while not evident in the isolated systems tested so far, may manifest in the complex in vivo environment or with chronic administration (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Orr et al., 2015).

In addition, the exact molecular site of action on Complex III is not yet fully delineated at the atomic level, meaning that while the compound has been shown to modulate ROS production, the precise binding interactions and potential variability between different cell types or individuals remain uncertain (Orr et al., 2015). This incomplete mechanistic detail could complicate structure-activity relationship (SAR) explorations, as well as efforts to optimize the compound further for better efficacy or reduced toxicity in an ocular setting.

From a therapeutic perspective, the hypothesis that S3QEL-2 can reduce inflammasome activation by lowering mitochondrial ROS is strongly supported by data in other cell types, particularly where a reduction in ROS has been correlated with lower levels of IL-1β and IL-18 secretion (Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022). Given the well-established involvement of mitochondrial ROS and NLRP3 inflammasome activation in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013), S3QEL-2 holds promise as a tool to dissect and potentially therapeutically modulate this axis. However, concrete evidence in AMD-relevant models, especially primary RPE cells derived from patients or appropriate animal models, is necessary before advancing this compound further in the drug development pipeline (Korhonen, 2024; Macchioni et al., 2020).

In summary, the strengths of S3QEL-2 lie in its high selectivity for Complex III-derived ROS suppression, preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics, and the proven ability to modulate ROS-dependent inflammatory pathways in several preclinical settings (Orr et al., 2015). Its repurposing for dry AMD is biochemically plausible and aligns with the current understanding of the disease, where chronic low-level oxidative stress and inflammasome activation play central roles in RPE dysfunction and geographic atrophy (Barnett & Handa, 2013; Campbell & Doyle, 2013). Conversely, weaknesses include the absence of direct preclinical evidence in ocular models, potential pharmacokinetic and delivery challenges, and an incomplete elucidation of its binding mechanism at the atomic level. Considering these factors, S3QEL-2 represents a highly promising candidate that merits further investigation through targeted preclinical studies in retinal and RPE models, including assessments of its delivery, efficacy in reducing NLRP3-driven cytokine release, and long-term safety in ocular tissues (Gao et al., 2015; Jimenez-Duran et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Ultimately, while S3QEL-2 is supported by robust biochemical data in nonocular systems and has a compelling mechanism that could translate into therapeutic benefit for dry AMD, additional focused research in AMD-relevant models is essential to validate its potential as a repurposed drug candidate for this challenging indication.
