Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Elamipretide (SS-31; D-Arg-2,6-dimethyl-Tyr-Lys-Phe-NH2) is a synthetic, C-terminally amidated tetrapeptide belonging to the Szeto–Schiller (SS) class of mitochondria-targeted peptides, originally discovered through structure–activity optimization of alternating cationic–aromatic motifs that confer high cell permeability and strong partitioning to the negatively charged inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) enriched in cardiolipin (CL) (Szeto & Schiller, 2011; Tung et al., 2025). Early work demonstrated that an aromatic–cationic design was sufficient to drive potent mitochondrial uptake and that dimethyltyrosine (Dmt) confers radical-scavenging chemistry while improving chemical stability; subnanomolar-to-nanomolar extracellular concentrations concentrate >1 μM at the IMM, yielding robust activity under oxidative stress in diverse cell types (Szeto & Schiller, 2011). SS-31 and related SS peptides were initially identified as potent inhibitors of mitochondrial swelling and oxidative cell death in intact cells and organs, with mechanistic clues pointing to direct interactions with cardiolipin-rich membranes and mitigation of ischemia–reperfusion injury (Szeto & Schiller, 2011; Szeto & Birk, 2014).

Mechanistically, elamipretide selectively binds CL in the IMM via electrostatic anchoring of its cationic residues to anionic phosphate headgroups and hydrophobic partitioning of its aromatic residues into the bilayer interfacial region; biophysical studies (NMR and molecular dynamics simulations) and binding quantitation to model CL-containing bilayers demonstrate CL dependence and saturable effects on bilayer surface electrostatics and lipid packing without destabilizing lamellar phases (Mitchell et al., 2019; Sabbah et al., 2025). Once bound, elamipretide modulates several biophysical and biochemical properties central to mitochondrial function: it down-tunes the negative surface potential of CL-rich membranes, increases CL self-association, reduces lateral lipid diffusivity, and increases lateral packing, changes that preserve cristae architecture and respiratory supercomplex organization under stress while suppressing cytochrome c peroxidase activity and CL oxidation (Sabbah et al., 2025). Collectively, these actions improve electron transfer efficiency, stabilize oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos) protein assemblies, reduce electron leak and reactive oxygen species (ROS), and preserve ATP synthesis capacity in dysfunctional mitochondria (Mitchell et al., 2022; Sabbah et al., 2025; Szeto & Birk, 2014). Importantly for retinal applications, elamipretide uptake is not dependent on mitochondrial membrane potential, supporting entry into depolarized or injured mitochondria—a feature often found in AMD RPE (Ji et al., 2021).

Elamipretide is therefore best classified as a CL-targeting, membrane-active mitochondrial therapeutic that acts primarily by modulating the physicochemical properties of CL-rich IMM domains and CL-dependent protein assemblies, rather than binding a single protein target, with downstream effects on respiratory supercomplex assembly, cytochrome c catalysis, electron-transport efficiency, ROS emission, and ATP production (Mitchell et al., 2019; Sabbah et al., 2025; Mitchell et al., 2022). Members of this class have been deployed across preclinical models of cardiac, skeletal muscle, renal, neurologic, and ocular dysfunction, and a substantial clinical program has tested elamipretide in primary mitochondrial disorders, cardiometabolic diseases, and ophthalmic indications including age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Sabbah et al., 2025; Tung et al., 2025). The drug is water-soluble, with a short elimination half-life on the order of ~2–4 hours in preclinical species and humans, and is administered systemically by daily subcutaneous injection in AMD studies at a nominal 40 mg dose; topical ocular delivery has also been explored preclinically and clinically (Szeto & Birk, 2014; Lenin et al., 2023; Guimaraes et al., 2022; Ji et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
The SS peptide class emerged from efforts to concentrate antioxidant and mitochondrial-protective chemistry directly at the IMM through cationic–aromatic motifs that target anionic phospholipids—principally cardiolipin—enabling inhibition of mitochondrial swelling, reduction of ROS emission, and protection from reperfusion injury in intact cells and organs; SS-31 in particular was estimated to concentrate ~5,000-fold in mitochondria and to inhibit lipid peroxidation, positioning it to prevent CL peroxidation in the IMM (Szeto & Schiller, 2011). These membrane-centric mechanisms rapidly translated into broad preclinical testing across organ systems, demonstrating improvements in OxPhos efficiency, ATP production, ROS control, and preservation of mitochondrial ultrastructure (cristae) in disease and aging models (Szeto & Birk, 2014; Mitchell et al., 2022).

Ocular and retinal applications came into focus as mitochondrial dysfunction in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptors was implicated as a driver of non-neovascular AMD, including reduced OxPhos, increased glycolytic shift, impaired mitophagy, structural cristae disorganization, and accumulation of damaged mitochondria in AMD donor RPE (Ferrington et al., 2020; Fisher, 2022; Fisher et al., 2022). In this context, elamipretide demonstrated several AMD-relevant preclinical effects. In a mouse model of dry AMD-like pathology, subcutaneous elamipretide reversed electroretinographic (ERG) deficits and improved clearance of sub-RPE deposits, corresponding to reversal of vision loss, consistent with activity at both the RPE/sub-RPE interface and photoreceptor function (Kim & Lad, 2021; Ji et al., 2021). In ApoE4 mice with diet-induced sub-RPE deposit formation linked to mitochondrial dysfunction, subcutaneous elamipretide reversed deposit formation, strengthening the mechanistic link to CL-dependent mitochondrial physiology in retinal tissues (Guimaraes et al., 2022). RPE-targeted cytoprotection has also been reported: elamipretide protected primary RPE and improved mitochondrial function in models of AMD and prevented persistent injury phenotypes induced by oxidative stressors such as hydroquinone in cultured RPE cells (Sabbah et al., 2025). Ex vivo and in vivo aging paradigms provide convergent support: in aged mice with visual impairments, elamipretide mitigated visual decline and normalized visual acuity and contrast sensitivity within two months, with delivery via topical eye drops producing effects comparable to subcutaneous injections; in RPE cultures from AMD donors, elamipretide improved RPE cell viability and mitochondrial function (Sabbah et al., 2025; Alam et al., 2020). In an RPE-specific SOD2 knockout model, daily topical elamipretide prevented RPE cell size increase consistent with reduced RPE cell death/senescence, further underscoring RPE-specific benefits (Tong et al., 2022). Additional retinal disease models support cross-indication activity: SS-31 restored visual function in a streptozotocin-induced mouse diabetic retinopathy model (Ferrington et al., 2020). Collectively, preclinical retinal evidence aligns with the hypothesized CL-centric rescue of mitochondrial function at the RPE and photoreceptor inner segments, preventing AMD-relevant cellular dysfunction and functional decline (Ji et al., 2021; Kim & Lad, 2021; Guimaraes et al., 2022).

Clinical development has included both topical and subcutaneous AMD studies. A phase I/II topical study enrolled 21 patients with diabetic macular edema (DME) and non-exudative intermediate AMD, demonstrating feasibility of ocular delivery; subsequent systemic AMD trials have been more extensively reported (Ji et al., 2021). The open-label, 24-week Phase 1 ReCLAIM study administered daily subcutaneous elamipretide (40 mg) to 40 patients with either non-central geographic atrophy (NCGA; n = 19) or high-risk drusen without GA (n = 21), reporting mean functional improvements: in the NCGA subgroup, +4.6 letters in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), +5.4 letters in low-luminance visual acuity (LLVA), and an approximate 25-letter gain in low-luminance reading acuity (LLRA), with a slower GA growth rate than historical natural history; in the high-risk drusen subgroup, mean gains were +3.6 (BCVA), +5.6 (LLVA), and ~15 (LLRA) (Kim & Lad, 2021). Safety was favorable, with no serious adverse events and general tolerability in intermediate AMD (Ji et al., 2021). A subsequent randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled Phase 2 trial (ReCLAIM-2) in ≥55-year-old patients with non-central GA tested daily subcutaneous elamipretide for 48 weeks; it did not meet primary endpoints on LL-BCVA and GA area, but elamipretide was associated with a 43% reduction in mean progression of total ellipsoid zone (EZ) attenuation and a 47% reduction in partial EZ attenuation versus placebo, with a post hoc analysis showing significant reductions and a higher proportion of patients achieving ≥2-line LL-BCVA gains, and a correlation between LL-BCVA change and change in total EZ attenuation (Sabbah et al., 2025). EZ attenuation is a clinically meaningful OCT marker that reflects photoreceptor integrity in mitochondria-rich inner segments and precedes GA and irreversible vision loss; thus, preservation of EZ is mechanistically consistent with the drug’s mitochondrial-protective intent and could represent an early biomarker of benefit (Sabbah et al., 2025). Additional summaries concur: the Phase 2 program reported negative primary endpoints but a structural OCT signal (slowed EZ degradation), warranting confirmatory studies with longer duration and functional correlates (Tung et al., 2025).

Beyond AMD, elamipretide has undergone extensive clinical evaluation in mitochondrial disorders (e.g., Barth syndrome), heart failure, ischemia–reperfusion contexts, and renal microvascular dysfunction, with mixed outcomes: many trials did not meet primary endpoints but reported improvements in mitochondrial bioenergetics, coupling, or patient-reported quality-of-life metrics, consistent with a class effect of improving mitochondrial physiology in vivo (Sabbah et al., 2025; Tung et al., 2025). Pharmacokinetically, elamipretide exhibits rapid distribution/elimination with elimination half-lives of ~2 hours in preclinical species and on the order of ~4 hours in humans, renal excretion of parent/metabolites, and ocular pharmacology indicating that topical dosing in rabbits achieves high anterior-chamber and periocular concentrations with nonzero penetration to the retina; this, together with murine aged-vision data, suggests both topical and systemic routes are viable for retinal targeting, although intraocular/vitreous levels after topical dosing may be low (Szeto & Birk, 2014; Alam et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
Elamipretide’s mechanism centers on high-affinity interaction with cardiolipin in the IMM and consequent modulation of membrane electrostatics, lipid organization, and CL-dependent protein complexes, leading to improved electron transport, reduced ROS production, and preserved ATP synthesis. Several convergent lines of evidence define this mechanism in molecular detail.

1) Cardiolipin-dependent binding and membrane electrostatics. SS-31/ELAM partitions into the interfacial leaflet of CL-containing bilayers with affinity proportional to surface charge, binding via electrostatic interactions of its basic residues with CL phosphates and via hydrophobic interactions of its aromatic residues with lipid acyl chains; no measurable binding occurs to neutral phosphatidylcholine membranes (Mitchell et al., 2019). NMR and molecular dynamics identify two binding modes—“peptide approach” (electrostatic anchoring) and “peptide burial” (aromatic partition)—producing a controlled down-tuning of the negative surface potential, increased CL self-association, and altered lateral packing/diffusivity without disrupting lamellar bilayer integrity (Sabbah et al., 2025). The net effect is to modulate ion distribution at the membrane interface (e.g., divalent cations such as Ca2+), stabilize bilayer structure under electrochemical stress, and resist electroporation-like damage, thereby preserving IMM properties under stress (Mitchell et al., 2019; Tamucci et al., 2025). These membrane-physical changes occur without altering the transmembrane potential per se, consistent with a surface–electrostatics mechanism that adjusts protein–lipid interactions and lipid–lipid organization (Sabbah et al., 2025).

2) Respiratory complexes, supercomplexes, and cytochrome c. Cardiolipin stabilizes respiratory complexes and promotes assembly of supercomplexes to optimize electron transport; elamipretide binding to CL supports supercomplex assembly, increases coupling efficiency, and reduces electron leak and ROS while enhancing ATP synthesis (Mitchell et al., 2022; Sabbah et al., 2025). A central node is the CL–cytochrome c interface: elamipretide is proposed to modulate the hydrophobic/π–π interactions between cytochrome c and CL, promoting efficient electron transfer from complex III to complex IV at the rate-limiting step while inhibiting cytochrome c peroxidase activity that otherwise peroxidizes CL and destabilizes cristae under oxidative stress (Szeto & Birk, 2014). Biochemical studies show that elamipretide reduces cytochrome c peroxidase activity and prevents oxidative modifications of CL acyl chains by forming a complex with CL, thereby protecting membrane integrity (Sabbah et al., 2025). In failing human heart tissue ex vivo, elamipretide improved supercomplex coupling control, respiratory control ratio, and CI/CIV activities, consistent with a supercomplex-stabilizing activity that enhances OXPHOS efficiency (Sabbah et al., 2025).

3) Direct protein interactions and bioenergetic consequences. Proteomics using biotinylated elamipretide (b-ELAM) in cross-linking/MS identified binding to multiple IMM proteins that themselves interact with CL, including complex IV subunit NDUA4 and the adenine nucleotide translocase ANT1; functionally, elamipretide increased maximum uncoupled and CIV respiration and decreased H2O2 production in mitochondria from old mouse hearts, increased ADP sensitivity and uptake via ANT, reduced ANT1-mediated proton leak, stabilized membrane potential, and reduced mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening (Sabbah et al., 2025). Stabilization of larger IMM protein assemblies such as the ATP synthasome (ANT, ATP synthase, creatine kinase, phosphate carrier) has been reported, with improvements in CI–CIII–CIV coupling and oxygen flux in failing human heart tissue (Sabbah et al., 2025). These molecular effects translate to rapid increases in mitochondrial energetic capacity—including a human randomized placebo-controlled trial demonstrating that a single dose of elamipretide increased the maximal rate of ATP production (ATPmax) in skeletal muscle—validating in vivo bioenergetic rescue (Sabbah et al., 2025).

4) ROS control, IMM integrity, and cristae structure. Across cell and organ models, elamipretide reduces ETS-derived ROS without acting as a primary radical scavenger; instead it optimizes respiratory efficiency, reduces electron leak, and protects CL from peroxidation, breaking the cycle of cristae disruption and respiratory dysfunction prevalent in aged or diseased mitochondria (Sabbah et al., 2025; Mitchell et al., 2022). SS-31 lowers intracellular ROS, prevents mitochondrial depolarization, maintains ΔΨm, prevents lipid peroxidation, and curtails oxidative cell death in a dose-dependent manner (Mitchell et al., 2019). In retinal contexts, elamipretide increased mitochondrial cristae density and preserved ultrastructure in aged mouse retinal mitochondria and diabetic mouse retinopathy models, supporting retinal applicability (Sabbah et al., 2025). In multiple disease models, elamipretide increased mitochondrial density and cristae connectivity, normalized proton leak, improved respiratory capacity, and corrected dysregulated fusion/fission and biogenesis regulators after longer treatment, further indicating structural remodeling capacity (Sabbah et al., 2025).

Mechanistic relevance to AMD and RPE is strong. AMD donor RPE exhibits cristae disorganization, accumulation of damaged mitochondria, decreased OxPhos, impaired mitophagy, and significant mtDNA damage in ETC gene regions, all linked to diminished ATP production and a glycolytic shift that disrupts metabolic coupling with photoreceptors and promotes retinal degeneration (Ferrington et al., 2020; Fisher et al., 2022; Fisher, 2022). Because CL is crucial for maintaining OxPhos function and cristae architecture, pharmacologic stabilization of CL and CL-dependent protein assemblies by elamipretide directly addresses these pathologies, offering preservation of ATP production, reduction of ROS, and resistance to mPTP opening and apoptosis in RPE under chronic oxidative stress (Fisher et al., 2022; Sabbah et al., 2025; Szeto & Birk, 2014). Photoreceptors are mitochondria-rich in the inner segments, and OCT-defined EZ attenuation is an early marker of photoreceptor compromise that precedes GA; elamipretide-associated reduction in EZ attenuation progression in AMD patients links its mitochondrial mechanism to clinically observable retinal structure (Sabbah et al., 2025).

Expected Effect  
In RPE cell assays that model AMD-relevant stressors (oxidative and bioenergetic), elamipretide is expected to stabilize IMM biophysics and CL-dependent protein systems, restoring mitochondrial bioenergetics, reducing oxidative injury, and preventing apoptosis. Mechanistically supported expectations include:

- Restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) and coupling: Elamipretide maintains ΔΨm and improves respiratory control, consistent with increased OXPHOS efficiency and reduced proton leak; thus, assays using potentiometric dyes (e.g., JC-1) should show improved ΔΨm relative to oxidant-injured controls (Mitchell et al., 2019; Sabbah et al., 2025).

- Reduction of mitochondrial ROS and lipid peroxidation: By stabilizing CL, optimizing electron transport, and inhibiting cytochrome c peroxidase activity, elamipretide reduces H2O2 emission and lipid peroxidation, leading to lower MitoSOX and lipid oxidation signals under oxidative challenge (Sabbah et al., 2025; Mitchell et al., 2019).

- Preservation of ATP synthesis: In serum-deprivation or oxidant-injury paradigms in RPE cell lines (e.g., ARPE-19), mitochondria-targeted peptides including elamipretide increased cell viability and cellular ATP at nanomolar dosing; this is consistent with expected improvements in ATP content and Seahorse OXPHOS parameters in primary RPE under stress (Mitchell et al., 2021). Human AMD donor RPE exposed ex vivo to elamipretide show improved mitochondrial function and viability, corroborating translatability of these endpoints (Sabbah et al., 2025).

- Cytoprotection against AMD-relevant toxicants: Elamipretide prevents persistent injury phenotypes induced by oxidative stressors (e.g., hydroquinone) in cultured RPE, supporting generalizability to sodium iodate or H2O2 injury; in an RPE SOD2 knockout model, topical elamipretide prevented cell size increase consistent with reduced cell death/senescence (Sabbah et al., 2025; Tong et al., 2022).

- Structural preservation of cristae: Electron microscopy of retinal mitochondria in aged/diabetic mice treated with elamipretide indicates increased cristae density and improved ultrastructure; similar effects are expected in RPE mitochondrial ultrastructure under chronic oxidative stress (Sabbah et al., 2025).

- In vivo retinal/RPE endpoints: In mouse models of AMD-like pathology, elamipretide improved ERG deficits and enhanced clearance of sub-RPE deposits, tracking to improvements in photoreceptor function and RPE health; ERG, OCT (drusen/sub-RPE deposit metrics), and RPE morphometrics are therefore expected to improve (Kim & Lad, 2021; Ji et al., 2021; Guimaraes et al., 2022). In aged-vision paradigms, spatial vision and contrast sensitivity improved with systemic or topical elamipretide, indicating photopic function benefits and supporting cone function endpoints (Alam et al., 2020).

- Clinical correlates: In patients with intermediate AMD or non-central GA, improvements in LLVA/LLRA and slowing of EZ attenuation were observed; therefore, clinical PoC studies should prioritize EZ attenuation as a primary structural endpoint with LL-BCVA/LLVA and reading measures as functionally sensitive secondaries, acknowledging that GA area may not be sensitive over ≤1 year (Kim & Lad, 2021; Sabbah et al., 2025; Tung et al., 2025). Given that photoreceptor inner segments are mitochondria-rich, EZ integrity serves as a proximal clinical biomarker of the drug’s mitochondrial mechanism (Sabbah et al., 2025).

Expression and target rationale in RPE: The target of elamipretide is not a single protein but the CL-rich IMM domain; CL is ubiquitous and crucial for maintaining OxPhos function, cristae architecture, and supercomplex assembly in RPE mitochondria, which are compromised in AMD (Fisher et al., 2022; Ferrington et al., 2020). Deficits in mitophagy (reduced PINK1/Parkin responsiveness), increased fission and delayed fusion, and global OxPhos reduction in AMD donor RPE define a mitochondrial fragility state in which CL stabilization is expected to be beneficial (Fisher et al., 2022). Because elamipretide uptake is not dependent on ΔΨm, it can access depolarized/dysfunctional mitochondria in AMD RPE, positioning it to act upstream of apoptosis (Ji et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Elamipretide presents a coherent, mechanistically grounded, and translationally explored therapeutic candidate for non-neovascular AMD predicated on CL-centric rescue of mitochondrial function in RPE and photoreceptors. The totality of evidence spans molecular biophysics, mitochondrial proteomics, in vivo bioenergetics, preclinical retinal disease models, and controlled clinical imaging and functional outcomes, allowing a sober assessment of strengths and residual risks.

As a member of a class of compounds that mimic the natural intracellular messenger AMP, AICAR is taken up into cells via adenosine transporters and is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase into its active metabolite, ZMP (5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide monophosphate), which then mimics AMP in its interactions with AMPK (Efstathiou et al., 2020). This compound belongs to a well‐established class of metabolic modulators, and similar agents have been used in experimental settings to modulate glucose uptake, fatty acid oxidation, and overall energy homeostasis in both basic science and translational research contexts (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014). In addition, several preclinical studies have evaluated AICAR’s potential as an “exercise mimetic” due to its ability to enhance energy metabolism in muscle and other tissues, and its synthetic nature allows for reproducible and scalable dosing in research models (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, AICAR was developed primarily as an agent to activate AMPK in metabolic studies and has been investigated in a variety of preclinical models ranging from cancer to cardiovascular disease. In the oncology field, for example, AICAR has been shown to inhibit cancer cell proliferation, induce cell cycle arrest, and promote programmed cell death in several cancer types via AMPK-dependent modulation of pathways such as PI3K-Akt and mTOR (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014; Rattan et al., 2005). Clinical studies, particularly those in the cardiovascular arena, have also evaluated AICAR’s safety profile in the context of ischemia-reperfusion injury, including human trials during cardiac surgery, demonstrating that it can be administered safely in humans (Rattan et al., 2005). In the context of ocular research, AICAR has been studied for its effects on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and other ocular cell types; several studies have demonstrated that AICAR suppresses the production of pro-inflammatory complement components such as complement factor 3 (C3) and complement factor B (CFB) in RPE cells under inflammatory conditions (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017). Although there is no established clinical use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) to date, these preclinical observations, combined with its well-known pharmacological profile, have spurred interest in repurposing AICAR for treating retinal diseases characterized by oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020). Furthermore, studies examining AMPK activators in the eye – including those using AICAR in animal models of uveitis or oxidative stress-induced RPE damage – support the notion that activating this metabolic pathway can protect against retinal degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

Mechanism of Action:  
AICAR exerts its biological activity primarily through the activation of AMPK, a master regulator of cellular energy balance that responds to alterations in the AMP/ATP ratio. Once AICAR is imported into cells through adenosine transporters, it is phosphorylated by adenosine kinase to form ZMP, an analog of AMP. ZMP binds to the regulatory γ subunit of AMPK, causing a conformational change that facilitates AMPK phosphorylation at Thr172 by upstream kinases such as LKB1, thereby fully activating the kinase (Efstathiou et al., 2020). Activated AMPK then phosphorylates a series of downstream targets involved in energy metabolism, including acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) and elements of the mTOR signaling pathway. In RPE cells, this activation is particularly important because AMPK phosphorylates and activates ULK1, a kinase critical for initiating autophagy and mitophagy, thereby promoting the clearance of damaged mitochondria (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Chung et al., 2017).  

A central component of the rationale for using AICAR in dry AMD is its ability to stimulate the transcriptional coactivator PGC-1α. AMPK-mediated phosphorylation of PGC-1α enhances its activity and nuclear translocation, which in turn drives the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant defense, and metabolic adaptation (Hu et al., 2024; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). This mechanism is particularly attractive in dry AMD because mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells is thought to contribute significantly to disease pathogenesis by impairing oxidative phosphorylation, increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and triggering cell senescence or death (Tong et al., 2022; Rego, 2023). In addition to these AMPK-dependent effects, some studies have reported that AICAR exerts certain effects independent of AMPK activation. For instance, AICAR has been shown to suppress TNF-α-induced complement factor expression by mechanisms that do not involve AMPK, suggesting that alternative signaling pathways or direct modulation of transcription factor activity might also contribute to its overall activity profile (Chung et al., 2017; Kirchner et al., 2018). These AMPK-independent actions could either broaden the therapeutic potential of AICAR in modulating inflammatory responses or introduce complexity into its activity profile that will need to be carefully isolated and understood (Kirchner et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2024).  

Furthermore, AICAR has been observed to affect mitochondrial dynamics not only by stimulating biogenesis through PGC-1α activation but also by modifying autophagic flux through mTOR inhibition. In models of RPE oxidative stress, where excessive ROS levels lead to mitochondrial fragmentation and accumulation of dysfunctional organelles, AICAR-induced AMPK activation facilitates the clearance of damaged mitochondria via mitophagy, thus restoring mitochondrial quality and energy production (Fisher et al., 2022; Hyttinen et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2024). Moreover, experimental evidence suggests that AICAR can modulate the balance between cellular glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation by shifting metabolism toward a more energy-efficient, oxidative phenotype, thereby increasing the overall oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and potentially improving cellular resilience under oxidative stress (Chan et al., 2020; Fisher, 2022).  

Expected Effect:  
Given its mechanisms of action, the expected effect of AICAR in an assay aimed at treating dry AMD would be multifaceted. In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress—a hallmark of dry AMD—AICAR treatment is expected to lead to robust activation of AMPK, as measured by increased phosphorylation of both AMPK and its downstream substrates such as ACC and ULK1 (Guo et al., 2018; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). This activation should in turn upregulate PGC-1α, resulting in enhanced transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, improved mitochondrial DNA replication, and an increased capacity for ATP production (Hu et al., 2024). As damaged mitochondria are a major source of ROS in stressed RPE cells, the stimulation of autophagy and mitophagy is anticipated to selectively clear these dysfunctional organelles, reducing cellular oxidative stress and preventing the secondary damage that contributes to RPE degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2011).  

In addition to these metabolic effects, AICAR is also expected to attenuate inflammatory responses within the RPE and adjacent retinal tissues. For instance, by modulating the activity of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) and reducing the expression of inflammatory mediators such as tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and complement components (e.g., C3 and CFB), AICAR would help to create a less pro-inflammatory microenvironment that could further protect RPE cells from damage (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017; Kirchner et al., 2018). These effects are particularly pertinent given that chronic, low-grade inflammation coupled with complement dysregulation is a recognized component of dry AMD pathogenesis.  

At the cellular level, the outcome of AICAR-induced AMPK activation is expected to manifest as enhanced mitochondrial function, improved energy charge (ATP/AMP ratio), reduced ROS accumulation, and, ultimately, a restoration of normal metabolic and autophagic flux in RPE cells (Fisher et al., 2022; Fisher, 2022). This improved bioenergetic profile should translate into protection against RPE cell death, potentially slowing or halting the progression of geographic atrophy associated with dry AMD (Yu et al., 2024; Si et al., 2023). Moreover, since RPE dysfunction in AMD also involves a reduction in the phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, AICAR’s modulatory effects on autophagy may indirectly help to restore the homeostatic functions of RPE cells, reducing the accumulation of damaging lipofuscin and drusen material (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Sung et al., 2015). In summary, the expected effect is a dual-action benefit—mitigation of oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum stresses via improved mitochondrial dynamics and an anti-inflammatory effect stemming from a reduction in complement activation and NF-κB-driven cytokine production (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020).  

Overall Evaluation:  
AICAR represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration owing to its robust and well-characterized mechanism of action via AMPK activation. The strengths of this candidate lie in its dual capacity to modulate critical pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis: on one hand, AICAR enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and promotes the removal of damaged mitochondria through autophagy/mitophagy, and on the other, it attenuates inflammatory cascades that exacerbate RPE cell damage (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hu et al., 2024). The ability of AICAR to upregulate PGC-1α is particularly compelling because mitochondrial dysfunction is now widely recognized as a central element in dry AMD. Preclinical studies have illustrated that dysregulation of mitochondrial function in RPE cells—a decrease in oxidative phosphorylation capacity, increased ROS production, and impaired clearance of damaged organelles—is pivotal in the initiation and progression of AMD (Tong et al., 2022; Rego, 2023). Thus, a compound like AICAR that can simultaneously restore mitochondrial health and mitigate inflammatory responses offers a multifaceted approach to disease modification.  

From the therapeutic history perspective, AICAR has been extensively studied in various preclinical models, including those of ocular inflammation and oxidative stress in RPE cells. Its ability to safely activate AMPK in vivo has been demonstrated across multiple species and contexts, including settings that mimic some aspects of AMD-related stress, such as endotoxin-induced uveitis and sodium iodate-induced RPE damage (Hyttinen et al., 2011; Chan et al., 2020). Additionally, the compound’s known clinical safety profile in human studies—albeit in contexts outside ophthalmology—provides an encouraging starting point for repurposing it for dry AMD, where no approved therapeutics currently exist (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2017).  

However, there are notable weaknesses and challenges that must be addressed. First, while AMPK activation is generally beneficial for energy homeostasis and autophagy, certain studies have indicated that AICAR’s effects on RPE cell biology might be context-dependent. For instance, some experimental reports have shown that AICAR can reduce the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments by RPE cells—a process that is essential for retinal health—which may represent a double-edged sword if not carefully titrated (Qin & De Vries, 2008; Yu et al., 2024). In addition, the existence of AMPK-independent effects—such as the direct inhibition of complement factor expression—introduces complexity into the overall mechanism of action and makes it challenging to predict all downstream outcomes. Differential responses have also been observed between healthy and diseased donor RPE cells, implying that “metabolic memory” or cellular adaptation may influence drug responsiveness (Fisher et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2017). These considerations suggest that while the theoretical underpinnings for using AICAR in dry AMD are solid, the translation of these effects into clinical efficacy may require careful optimization of dosing, delivery, and patient selection.  

Another potential limitation is related to its broad mechanism of action. AICAR activates several metabolic pathways that are intertwined with many aspects of cellular physiology. While this pleiotropy provides the therapeutic benefit of addressing multiple dysregulated pathways in AMD simultaneously, it may also increase the risk of off-target effects or metabolic disturbances in tissues outside the retina (Rattan et al., 2005; Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014). For instance, systemic administration of AICAR has been associated with shifts in glycolytic flux and modifications of lipid metabolism, and it is therefore imperative that strategies for ocular delivery (such as intravitreal injections or topical formulations) be developed to maximize retinal exposure while minimizing systemic exposure (Chan et al., 2020; Kamoshita et al., 2014).  

Moreover, despite the substantial body of preclinical data supporting the role of AICAR in activating AMPK and restoring mitochondrial function, clinical data specific to dry AMD are lacking. Although related studies have shown benefits in models of retinal inflammation and degeneration, the exact therapeutic window, long-term safety, and efficacy in humans with AMD must be thoroughly evaluated in well-designed clinical trials. It is also worth mentioning that other AMPK activators, such as metformin, have independently demonstrated protective effects in AMD models, thereby lending credence to the approach but also raising questions about whether AICAR offers a distinct advantage over these agents (Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020).  

In summary, the overall evaluation of AICAR as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. Its well-documented ability to activate AMPK, stimulate PGC-1α-driven mitochondrial biogenesis, and induce autophagy presents a strong mechanistic rationale for protecting RPE cells from the mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress that drive dry AMD pathogenesis (Hu et al., 2024; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2011). The preclinical evidence, gathered from studies in ocular models and other systems, provides encouraging proof-of-concept data that support further investigation (Efstathiou et al., 2020; Hyttinen et al., 2011). Nonetheless, complexities related to AMPK-independent effects, differential responses in healthy versus diseased cells, and potential off-target metabolic changes underscore the need for rigorous preclinical optimization and carefully designed clinical trials before this candidate can be definitively validated for dry AMD treatment (Chung et al., 2017; Fisher et al., 2022; Kirchner et al., 2018).  

Considering all the available literature, the repurposing of AICAR for dry AMD appears to be a promising strategy that merits further investigation. The compound’s ability to simultaneously address mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and chronic inflammation positions it as a multifaceted agent with the potential to modify disease progression in a condition that currently lacks effective therapeutic options (Chung et al., 2017; Dang et al., 2021; Efstathiou et al., 2020). Moving forward, it will be critical to further elucidate the detailed cellular and molecular responses to AICAR in human RPE cells, determine the optimal dosing and delivery parameters specific to the ocular environment, and perform in vivo studies that mimic the complex pathobiology of dry AMD. With these additional efforts, AICAR could eventually emerge as a valuable addition to the limited therapeutic arsenal available for managing this debilitating condition.  

In conclusion, AICAR’s robust preclinical profile as an AMPK activator, its well-understood mechanisms of promoting mitochondrial biogenesis and autophagy, and its capacity to mitigate inflammatory responses provide a solid scientific basis for its potential repurposing in dry AMD (Hu et al., 2024; Hyttinen et al., 2011; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). However, several challenges remain: the dual nature of its effects (both AMPK-dependent and independent), the possibility of adverse effects on key RPE functions such as phagocytosis, and the need for precise ocular drug delivery methods. Therefore, while AICAR is an exciting candidate with considerable mechanistic appeal, its translation from bench to bedside in the treatment of dry AMD will require further detailed studies to fully map its therapeutic window, safety profile, and efficacy in human subjects (Al‐Moujahed et al., 2014; Rego, 2023; Kamoshita et al., 2014). Continued rigorous research and methodical clinical evaluation will determine whether AICAR can be developed into an effective treatment modality for this currently intractable form of macular degeneration.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) is a synthetic derivative of fumaric acid that belongs to the class of fumaric acid esters (FAEs) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Chemically, DMF is the dimethyl ester of fumaric acid, with a molecular weight of approximately 144.13 g/mol, and is produced by reacting fumaric acid with methanol in the presence of a strong acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Although fumaric acid occurs naturally as an intermediate in the citric acid cycle, DMF itself is fully synthetically manufactured, conferring the advantages of chemical stability and the ability to precisely modulate its structure to enhance pharmacological properties (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Moreover, DMF is classified as an electrophilic molecule that, due to its α,β-unsaturated ester structure, can covalently modify protein thiols, particularly the cysteine residues within KEAP1, thereby initiating its downstream effects on cellular redox homeostasis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106). Fumaric acid esters as a class have a long-standing history in pharmacotherapy, originally finding application in dermatology, most notably in the treatment of psoriasis, and have since been repurposed for neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis (MS) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, fumaric acid esters were introduced into clinical practice as antipsoriatic agents in Europe, with formulations such as Fumaderm® entering the market in the 1990s (Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). DMF in particular emerged as a key component in these formulations, and its efficacy in modulating immune responses and suppressing inflammation in skin diseases laid the foundation for its later repurposing in other systemic inflammatory conditions (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Over time, DMF was repurposed and further developed as an oral agent for the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), culminating in its FDA approval in 2013 under the trade name Tecfidera® by Biogen (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163). Clinical trials, including large-scale phase 3 studies, have demonstrated its favorable safety profile and efficacy in reducing relapse rates and slowing disability progression in MS patients (Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 14–16). Although there is no extensive historical record of DMF being used directly for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other primary ocular diseases, recent preclinical findings have indicated that its potent activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway may confer significant protective effects on the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This has sparked considerable interest in repurposing DMF for ocular indications such as geographic atrophy, a late stage of dry AMD, by leveraging its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities observed in nonocular settings (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, DMF functions primarily as a prodrug; upon oral administration it is rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases within the gastrointestinal tract to yield its active metabolite, monomethyl fumarate (MMF) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). The pharmacodynamic actions of DMF principally involve the electrophilic modification of specific cysteine residues—most notably cysteine 151—on Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Under physiological conditions, KEAP1 binds to and retains the transcription factor Nrf2 in the cytoplasm, targeting it for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. However, when DMF covalently modifies KEAP1, it disrupts this complex, allowing Nrf2 to dissociate and translocate into the nucleus (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). In the nucleus, Nrf2 binds to antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoters of numerous genes encoding cytoprotective enzymes, including glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), and various enzymes involved in glutathione (GSH) synthesis and regeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). These molecular interactions lead to enhanced antioxidant defenses, improved detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and overall better maintenance of cellular redox balance (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). In addition to its role in promoting antioxidant gene expression via Nrf2 activation, DMF has been shown to have immunomodulatory properties; it can shift cytokine profiles by increasing interleukin-4 (IL-4)–expressing CD4+ T cells and decreasing the production of proinflammatory cytokines such as interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and interleukin-17 (IL-17) (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Furthermore, DMF has been reported to inhibit nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation in certain cellular contexts, thus contributing to a reduction in inflammatory signaling independently of Nrf2 (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Together, these molecular actions result in lowered cellular oxidative stress and an improved inflammatory milieu, which are critical factors implicated in the pathogenesis of chronic degenerative diseases (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry AMD, particularly the geographic atrophy form, is characterized by the gradual degeneration of RPE cells, which leads to subsequent photoreceptor loss and irreversible vision impairment. Central to the pathophysiology of dry AMD are oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation that progressively compromise RPE viability and function (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). The hypothesis being explored is that DMF, through its robust activation of the Nrf2 pathway, can enhance the expression of ARE-driven genes that encode for antioxidant and cytoprotective proteins, thereby counteracting the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in the RPE (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 13–14). In particular, the upregulation of enzymes involved in glutathione synthesis is expected to increase intracellular levels of GSH, a critical thiol antioxidant that protects mitochondrial membranes and supports cellular bioenergetics (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Preclinical studies in retinal models have demonstrated that DMF can effectively preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and reduce the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β), both of which are hallmarks of RPE distress under oxidative challenge (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Given that the RPE is highly metabolically active and particularly vulnerable to cumulative oxidative damage, the sustained activation of Nrf2 by DMF following oral dosing is anticipated to provide continuous reinforcement of antioxidant defenses and maintain mitochondrial integrity in these cells (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 3–5; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). Moreover, by mitigating inflammatory signaling, DMF may not only protect the RPE but also contribute to a more favorable microenvironment that limits the propagation of cell death signals, thus potentially slowing the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Collectively, these expected cellular effects support the rationale for using DMF as an intervention to preserve retinal structure and function by lowering oxidative damage and supporting bioenergetics in the RPE.

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential of dimethyl fumarate as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD rests on a solid mechanistic rationale combined with an established clinical pedigree in other indications. One of the primary strengths of DMF is its well-characterized pharmacological profile; it is FDA-approved for multiple sclerosis and has been safely administered to thousands of patients over several years, which significantly mitigates the risk and regulatory hurdles typically associated with repurposed drugs (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). The dual actions of DMF—in particular, its ability to both activate the Nrf2 pathway and attenuate proinflammatory signals—directly target the underlying pathological processes in dry AMD, where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central drivers of RPE degeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In vitro studies have provided encouraging evidence that DMF increases intracellular glutathione levels and protects RPE cells from oxidative insults, findings that are directly translatable to the pathobiology of dry AMD (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Nonetheless, several challenges remain. Although DMF is known to be effective in MS and psoriasis, the ocular milieu presents unique pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic challenges that may not be fully addressed by the current oral formulations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18). The rapid hydrolysis of DMF to MMF means that, while the active metabolite does exert therapeutic effects, fine-tuning the dosing regimen to ensure adequate drug levels in the retina while minimizing systemic side effects is necessary (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). In addition, common adverse reactions associated with DMF, such as gastrointestinal discomfort and flushing, though generally mild to moderate, could be more problematic in the typically elderly dry AMD population, necessitating careful monitoring and potentially modified dosing strategies (Camelo, 2025, p. 17; Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13). There is also the question of whether systemic administration of DMF can generate sufficient concentrations in the retina to achieve a meaningful therapeutic effect. It remains to be seen whether the monotherapeutic approach of DMF, targeting primarily oxidative stress via Nrf2 activation, will be sufficient to halt or reverse disease progression, or whether combination therapies will ultimately be required (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Early-phase clinical trials aimed at evaluating DMF in geographic atrophy have to rigorously assess both structural outcomes (e.g., changes in the area of atrophy) and functional endpoints (e.g., visual acuity, retinal sensitivity) to establish its therapeutic benefit in dry AMD (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Despite these limitations, the strengths of DMF are compelling. The drug’s ability to upregulate a broad spectrum of cytoprotective genes via the Nrf2 pathway makes it a versatile candidate for mitigating the oxidative and inflammatory stress that drives RPE degeneration. The fact that DMF has already cleared extensive regulatory and clinical safety evaluations in nonocular indications is a significant advantage, as it greatly accelerates the translational pathway compared to a novel chemical entity (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Its mechanism of action—centered on Nrf2 activation leading to enhanced antioxidant capacity along with anti-inflammatory effects—directly addresses the key pathophysiological mechanisms implicated in dry AMD. The extensive clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis provides a reliable safety and tolerability framework, which is crucial for rapid repositioning into a new clinical area such as geographic atrophy (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). However, it is essential to conduct targeted preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials specifically in ocular disease models to optimize dosing, confirm retinal delivery, and demonstrate clinical efficacy before advancing to larger randomized controlled trials (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). 1. Conduct detailed pharmacokinetic studies in animal models to assess the retinal bioavailability of DMF and its active metabolite MMF following systemic administration. This should include studies comparing different dosing schedules and formulations to optimize retinal exposure without exacerbating systemic adverse effects (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2).  

2. Develop and validate preclinical models of dry AMD that recapitulate the key features of human geographic atrophy, with a focus on evaluating the efficacy of DMF in protecting RPE cells against oxidative stress and preserving mitochondrial function (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

3. Investigate the potential benefits of combining DMF with other therapeutic agents that target complementary pathways in dry AMD. For example, agents that modulate complement activation or improve choroidal blood flow may synergize with the Nrf2-mediated antioxidant mechanism of DMF (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).  

4. Initiate early-phase clinical trials in patients with geographic atrophy to establish proof of concept. These studies should include robust biomarker assessments (e.g., measurement of ARE gene expression, retinal imaging for atrophy progression, and functional visual outcomes) to correlate molecular effects with clinical benefit (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

5. Carefully monitor the safety profile of DMF in the elderly population, as the incidence of gastrointestinal side effects and lymphopenia may differ compared to the population with MS. Consider the feasibility of modified-release formulations or alternative routes of administration (e.g., topical ocular delivery) to minimize systemic side effects while maximizing retinal drug concentrations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18).

Overall, the repurposing of dimethyl fumarate for dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a robust mechanistic framework and a significant body of preclinical and clinical data generated in other indications. Its capacity to activate the Nrf2 pathway, enhance mitochondrial glutathione synthesis, and modulate inflammatory responses in RPE cells directly addresses several pivotal aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). While there are challenges regarding optimal retinal delivery and management of systemic adverse effects, the clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis lends considerable support to its translational potential. Consequently, dimethyl fumarate represents a well‐justified and attractive therapeutic candidate for further exploration in the treatment of dry AMD, warranting additional preclinical optimization and clinical investigation to fully define its role in preserving visual function in patients affected by this progressive degenerative disease (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12).

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO‐Me) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), structured in sections that address its origins, therapeutic history, known mechanisms of action, expected effects in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and an overall assessment of its strengths and challenges.

• Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Bardoxolone methyl is a semisynthetic derivative belonging to the synthetic oleanane triterpenoid class. Its origin stems from oleanolic acid—a naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid abundantly found in various medicinal plants. Early medicinal chemistry programs sought to overcome the modest anti‐inflammatory activity and poor bioavailability of oleanolic acid by introducing targeted modifications. Through chemical derivatization, these programs generated CDDO (2‐cyano‐3,12‐dioxooleana‐1,9‐dien‐28‐oic acid) and subsequently its C‐28 methyl ester, known as Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO‐Me) (Borella et al., 2019). The synthetic process involves the installation of electrophilic Michael acceptor groups at strategic positions on the oleanane scaffold, such as the addition of an α,β‐unsaturated carbonyl in the A‐ring and further incorporation of a cyano group that substantially increases the compound’s potency relative to its natural precursor (Wong et al., 2016; Zhang & Chapman, 2020). These chemical modifications not only enhance the anti‐inflammatory and anticancer properties but also improve chemical stability and oral bioavailability. The structural design, which incorporates a reversible electrophilic reactivity, underpins the compound’s ability to engage diverse cellular targets (Thomas, 2012; Zhou et al., 2014). Bardoxolone methyl thus represents a chemically advanced, highly potent agent from a class of molecules originally designed to trigger cytoprotective responses via direct electrophilic modulation.

• Therapeutic History  
Bardoxolone methyl has undergone extensive preclinical and early clinical evaluation primarily in fields as disparate as oncology and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Initial studies established that synthetic oleanane triterpenoids, including CDDO and its variants, exert dramatic anti‐inflammatory effects by suppressing inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and cyclooxygenase (COX‐2) expression in activated macrophages (Gatbonton‐Schwager, 2014). Preclinical studies in multiple mouse cancer models and inflammatory conditions confirmed its potent anticancer activity and cytoprotective properties, which catalyzed its progression into human clinical trials (Borella et al., 2019; Nakagami, 2016).  
In the clinical arena, Bardoxolone methyl was advanced through Phase I cancer trials, where its once‐daily oral dosing regimen and pharmacokinetic profile—with a terminal half‐life of approximately 39 hours—were characterized (Thomas, 2012; Nakagami, 2016). More notably, its unexpected ability to improve estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in patients with advanced renal disease, particularly in diabetic nephropathy, led to its evaluation in large Phase II and Phase III trials, such as the BEAM and BEACON studies (Yagishita et al., 2020; Tanase et al., 2022). However, the BEACON trial was terminated prematurely due to an increased incidence of cardiovascular events, including heart failure, highlighting concerns about the compound’s systemic safety profile when used at higher doses or in populations with comorbidities (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012).  
Despite its promising preclinical pharmacology and the breadth of clinical data available in non‐ocular indications, to date there is no direct record in the literature of Bardoxolone methyl being used specifically for the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular degenerative conditions (Schiavoni et al., 2025). Nonetheless, the overall safety and pharmacokinetic properties observed in CKD and oncology trials lend valuable insights for considering drug repurposing across therapeutic areas.

• Mechanism of Action  
Bardoxolone methyl is best known for its ability to activate the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway—a master regulator of cellular defense mechanisms against oxidative and electrophilic stress. Under basal conditions, Nrf2 is tightly regulated by Kelch‐like ECH‐associated protein 1 (Keap1), which serves as an adaptor for ubiquitin ligases targeting Nrf2 for proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl functions as a potent electrophile and interacts with sulfhydryl groups on critical cysteine residues within Keap1. This covalent or reversible Michael addition reaction disrupts the Keap1–Nrf2 complex, thereby stabilizing and allowing Nrf2 to translocate into the nucleus (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).  
Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to the antioxidant response element (ARE) in the promoter regions of a host of cytoprotective genes. This transcriptional activation results in the upregulation of a battery of antioxidant and phase II detoxifying enzymes, including but not limited to heme oxygenase‐1 (HO‐1), NAD(P)H dehydrogenase (quinone 1; NQO1), various glutathione transferases, and glutamate–cysteine ligase subunits (Thomas, 2012; Wong et al., 2016). Studies in non‐ocular tissues have shown that at very low (nanomolar) doses, Bardoxolone methyl robustly engages this cytoprotective program while also exerting dose‐dependent biology wherein intermediate and high doses trigger effects such as modulation of cell differentiation and direct anticancer activity, respectively (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).  
It is important to note that while the canonical targets of Nrf2 activation are well characterized, Bardoxolone methyl’s electrophilic character enables it to interact with multiple regulatory proteins. For example, it can inhibit IκB kinase β (IKKβ), leading to suppression of nuclear factor κB (NF‐κB) signaling and subsequent reduction in proinflammatory cytokine production (Zhou et al., 2014; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although the literature does not provide direct experimental evidence that Bardoxolone methyl specifically upregulates mitochondrial antioxidants such as superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) and peroxiredoxin 3 (PRDX3) in RPE cells, the robust, broad‐spectrum transcriptional response induced by Nrf2 activation strongly suggests that mitochondrial and cytoplasmic components of the antioxidant defense system may also be upregulated (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015). Such upregulation would be consistent with previous findings of increased expression of antioxidant genes and improved cellular redox status upon treatment with similar synthetic triterpenoids (Schiavoni et al., 2025; Sporn et al., 2011).

• Expected Effect in Dry AMD  
The pathogenesis of dry age‐related macular degeneration is multifactorial, with chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction playing a central role in the degeneration of the RPE—a critical monolayer that supports photoreceptor health. RPE cells are particularly vulnerable to oxidative damage due to high metabolic activity, exposure to light, and the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). In this context, the proposed mechanism of Bardoxolone methyl, namely activation of the Nrf2/ARE pathway, provides a biologically tenable strategy for neuroprotection and cellular preservation.  
When administered at low doses, Bardoxolone methyl is expected to trigger a cytoprotective transcriptional program in RPE cells. Activation of Nrf2 should lead to the induction of a range of antioxidant enzymes and detoxifying proteins which together help re-establish redox balance in the face of chronic oxidative insult (Borella et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012). One key hypothesis is that, in addition to the already well‐documented induction of cytosolic antioxidants such as HO‐1 and NQO1, Bardoxolone methyl may also promote the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3. SOD2 is the primary defense against superoxide radicals within the mitochondria, and PRDX3 plays a critical role in detoxifying hydrogen peroxide produced by mitochondrial respiration. Although direct data in RPE cells are currently lacking, studies in other cellular contexts have demonstrated that activation of Nrf2 results in the upregulation of a broad spectrum of antioxidant genes, and it is plausible that under the oxidative duress typical of dry AMD, similar effects would be observed in RPE cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
In vitro models simulating oxidative stress—such as exposure of RPE cells to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)—have shown that compounds with similar electrophilic properties, and indeed other members of the CDDO family like CDDO-Im, reduce the intracellular MitoSOX fluorescence signal, indicative of a reduction in mitochondrial ROS (mtROS) (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024). Moreover, improvements in mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) have been correlated with such treatments, suggesting that these molecules can help maintain mitochondrial function under stressful conditions (Nakagami, 2016; Zhou et al., 2014). Such outcomes are highly relevant in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction in the RPE has been implicated in disease progression. The anticipated outcomes, therefore, include a reduction in mtROS, restoration of Δψm, and subsequent preservation of RPE cellular integrity and function.  
Another positive aspect is the compound’s previously established oral bioavailability and pharmacokinetic profile. Clinical studies in CKD patients have demonstrated that therapeutic plasma concentrations can be achieved with once-daily dosing. Although systemic administration in ocular diseases is not ideal, these data provide a strong pharmacological starting point for repurposing. In addition, if systemic toxicity remains a concern—as suggested by the cardiovascular signals in CKD trials—an alternative approach might involve localized ocular delivery (for instance, via intravitreal injection or by developing an ocular formulation) to achieve high retinal bioavailability while minimizing systemic exposure (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).

• Overall Evaluation  
In assessing Bardoxolone methyl for repurposing as a therapeutic for dry AMD, several critical points emerge that underline both its promise and the challenges that must be overcome.

Strengths:  
1. Strong Chemical Rationale and Potency:  
Bardoxolone methyl is a product of sophisticated medicinal chemistry, designed to overcome the limitations of natural triterpenoids like oleanolic acid by installing reactive electrophilic groups that significantly enhance its potency. This design specifically enables the activation of the Nrf2 pathway—a mechanism central to antioxidant defense—at very low concentrations (Borella et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016). The high potency of Bardoxolone methyl as an Nrf2 activator is a significant advantage, particularly when considering that even subtle improvements in cellular antioxidant capacity can have a profound impact on chronic degenerative diseases like dry AMD.

2. Broad Cytoprotective Mechanism:  
The mechanism of Bardoxolone methyl involves the disruption of the Keap1-Nrf2 complex via covalent modification of Keap1 cysteine residues, facilitating the nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and the subsequent transcriptional activation of a broad range of antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes (Zhou et al., 2014; Thomas, 2012). This broad cytoprotective response is particularly relevant to the RPE, where chronic oxidative stress has been implicated in cellular dysfunction and death. The possibility that Bardoxolone methyl may also induce mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3, although not yet directly confirmed in RPE, is an attractive hypothesis; such an effect would directly address the mitochondrial dysfunction that is a hallmark of dry AMD (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).

3. Extensive Clinical Experience and Pharmacokinetic Data:  
Bardoxolone methyl has been evaluated in several clinical trials—most notably in the context of CKD and oncology—yielding a wealth of pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and tolerability data. Its oral bioavailability, with a terminal half-life that supports once-daily dosing, is well documented (Thomas, 2012; Nakagami, 2016). Although the systemic adverse events observed in these trials (such as cardiovascular-related events) present challenges for broad systemic administration, these data nonetheless offer a useful starting point for repurposing. The established clinical profile can inform dose-escalation studies and safety monitoring protocols should Bardoxolone methyl be advanced into ocular trials.

4. Support from Analogous Preclinical Models:  
Several studies in related models have demonstrated that synthetic triterpenoids can protect retinal tissue from oxidative damage. For example, experiments with CDDO-Im, a closely related analogue, have shown protective effects in retinal ischemia–reperfusion injury, including the attenuation of inflammatory responses and preservation of retinal structure (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024). Although these studies are not directly with Bardoxolone methyl, the mechanistic commonalities within this compound class support the notion that the same protective pathways can be harnessed in the context of dry AMD.

Weaknesses and Challenges:  
1. Lack of Direct Evidence in RPE/Dry AMD Models:  
Despite the strong theoretical rationale, direct evidence that Bardoxolone methyl upregulates mitochondrial antioxidants (SOD2, PRDX3) in RPE cells is currently lacking. Most published data are derived from non-ocular cell types or from studies using other analogues such as CDDO-Im (Cai et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2014). It is therefore essential to perform specific in vitro studies in RPE cell lines under oxidative stress conditions to measure the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes and the functional status of mitochondria (e.g., Δψm, mtROS levels) following treatment with Bardoxolone methyl.

2. Safety Concerns from Prior Clinical Experience:  
A significant challenge in repurposing Bardoxolone methyl stems from its safety profile in systemic indications. The Phase III BEACON trial in CKD patients was halted due to an increased incidence of serious cardiovascular events, including heart failure and increased mortality (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although the mechanisms underlying these adverse effects may be related to systemic fluid retention, off‐target reactivity, or other metabolic perturbations, they raise concerns about the safety of systemic administration. For ocular application, it may be necessary to consider alternative dosing strategies or localized delivery methods to avoid systemic exposure while still achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina.

3. Translational and Formulation Challenges:  
The unique anatomy and physiology of the eye introduce additional obstacles in drug repurposing. RPE cells reside in a relatively immune-privileged, isolated microenvironment behind the blood–retinal barrier. The pharmacokinetics and tissue penetration profiles of Bardoxolone methyl observed in systemic circulation may not directly translate to effective intraocular concentrations. Development of specialized ocular formulations—such as sustained-release intravitreal injections or topical applications that can traverse ocular barriers—will be critical for successful translation (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).

4. Multifactorial Nature of AMD Pathogenesis:  
Dry AMD is a complex, multifactorial disease where oxidative stress is only one component of a broader pathogenic network that includes genetic predisposition, inflammation, lipid dysregulation, and complement system activation. While activation of the Nrf2 pathway can counteract oxidative stress and may have secondary anti-inflammatory effects, it is uncertain whether this single mechanism will be sufficient to alter the course of the disease. A combinatorial therapeutic strategy incorporating Nrf2 activation with other modalities might eventually be required to address the full spectrum of dry AMD pathology (Cheng et al., 2021; Thomas, 2012).

5. Dose-Dependent Effects and Narrow Therapeutic Window:  
Bardoxolone methyl exhibits highly dose-dependent pharmacology. At low doses, it predominantly activates Nrf2 and induces cytoprotective genes; however, as the dose increases, additional actions such as pro-apoptotic and cytotoxic effects emerge (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014). Determining the precise dose that is efficacious in RPE cells without triggering deleterious off-target effects will be crucial. This necessitates rigorous dose-ranging studies in preclinical models to define a therapeutic window that maximizes retinal protection while minimizing risks.

• Overall Evaluation and Recommendation  
In summary, Bardoxolone methyl presents a compelling candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD thanks to its well-characterized chemical design, potent induction of the Nrf2 pathway, and a broad cytoprotective mechanism that addresses many aspects of the oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction implicated in RPE degeneration. The extensive clinical data from studies in CKD and oncology provide a valuable foundation for understanding its pharmacokinetics and systemic effects, while the underlying chemistry ensures high potency at low concentrations—features that are highly desirable when targeting a chronic, degenerative condition such as dry AMD (Borella et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012).  
Nonetheless, significant challenges remain. There is a conspicuous gap in the literature regarding the direct evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl in RPE cells and dry AMD models, particularly concerning its ability to upregulate mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes like SOD2 and PRDX3 and thereby mitigate mtROS damage. This gap must be addressed through targeted in vitro assays and in vivo animal studies that simulate the retinal environment and its chronic oxidative stress. Safety concerns, as evidenced by the cardiovascular events observed in CKD trials, underscore the need for caution; these risks may be minimized through localized ocular administration, but careful formulation and dosing studies will be required to establish an acceptable safety profile in the ocular context (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019).  
Given the current state of evidence, it is recommended that Bardoxolone methyl be subjected to further preclinical evaluation in the context of dry AMD. Specifically, studies should focus on:  
 – Conducting detailed in vitro experiments in human RPE cell lines to assess whether exposure to Bardoxolone methyl under oxidative stress conditions leads to the upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants (e.g., SOD2 and PRDX3) and an associated decrease in mtROS (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
 – Evaluating the effects of Bardoxolone methyl on mitochondrial function (including measurements of Δψm, oxygen consumption rate, and mitochondrial integrity) in these cells.  
 – Adapting ocular-specific formulations that allow high local retinal concentrations with minimal systemic exposure, potentially using intravitreal or topical delivery methods, and conducting pharmacokinetic studies that establish retinal tissue exposure (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).  
 – Testing the compound in animal models of dry AMD to determine whether the in vitro antioxidant and mitochondrial protective effects translate into preservation of RPE and photoreceptor structure and function over time (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024).  
If these studies yield positive results that confirm the hypothesized upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants and improved RPE function, Bardoxolone methyl could then be advanced to early-phase clinical trials in patients with dry AMD. Such trials would need to incorporate rigorous safety monitoring protocols to mitigate the known systemic adverse effects. A potential strategy may involve administering the drug in a localized manner or at doses that are effective in the eye but low enough to avoid triggering systemic electrophilic toxicity.

Overall, Bardoxolone methyl holds promise as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD based on its potent Nrf2-activating properties and the central role of oxidative stress in the disease’s pathogenesis. However, its development for an ocular indication will hinge on its ability to selectively and safely modulate the redox status of RPE cells while avoiding systemic side effects. A stepwise, targeted preclinical program that directly addresses these RPE-specific endpoints is therefore critical before consideration of clinical trials in the dry AMD patient population (Nakagami, 2016).

In conclusion, while Bardoxolone methyl offers a strong mechanistic rationale as an Nrf2 activator with the theoretical capacity to upregulate mitochondrial defenses in RPE cells, further targeted studies are essential. The compound’s repurposing for dry AMD is scientifically attractive given the unmet need for effective therapies in this condition; however, the translational path is complex due to safety concerns observed in systemic trials and the lack of direct ocular data. A rigorous preclinical research plan—encompassing in vitro RPE studies, ocular pharmacokinetic assessments, and animal model validation—will be required to determine whether Bardoxolone methyl can be safely and effectively repurposed to preserve RPE function and slow the progression of dry AMD.

• Summary of Key Supporting Points  
– Bardoxolone methyl is a chemically engineered derivative of oleanolic acid that exploits electrophilic modifications to robustly activate the Nrf2 pathway (Borella et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016).  
– Its extensive preclinical and clinical history in oncology and CKD, though not in ocular disease, provides important pharmacokinetic and biological safety data that may be leveraged, with modifications, for ocular use (Nakagami, 2016; Tanase et al., 2022).  
– Its mechanism—covalent modification of Keap1 and subsequent nuclear translocation of Nrf2—leads to the transcriptional upregulation of cytoprotective genes, and it is hypothesized that this would include mitochondrial antioxidants (e.g., SOD2, PRDX3), which are critical for mitigating oxidative damage in RPE cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
– Preclinical data with related triterpenoids in retinal models support the concept that Nrf2 activation can ameliorate oxidative stress and preserve retinal integrity, although direct data for Bardoxolone methyl in dry AMD are presently lacking (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024).  
– Key challenges include the translation of systemic dosing to ocular delivery, the need to specifically validate mitochondrial protective effects in RPE cells, and the resolution of safety issues exemplified by prior cardiovascular signals in systemic trials (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

• Final Recommendation  
Based on the current literature review, Bardoxolone methyl emerges as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its potent Nrf2 activation, broad cytoprotective potential, and a well-documented clinical PK profile. However, its repurposing for ocular application must be preceded by targeted preclinical studies that corroborate its ability to upregulate mitochondrial antioxidants in RPE cells and to reduce mtROS while preserving mitochondrial function. These studies should also explore ocular-specific formulations and dosing regimens that minimize systemic exposure. Only after thorough validation in these preliminary investigations can Bardoxolone methyl be considered a credible candidate for clinical trials in dry AMD patients. Given these considerations, the candidate warrants further investigation despite the existing translational and safety challenges inherent in repurposing a systemically active electrophilic compound for an ocular indication (Borella et al., 2019; Yagishita et al., 2020; Thomas, 2012).
