Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Resveratrol is a naturally occurring polyphenolic compound belonging to the stilbene class and is structurally defined as 3,5,4′-trihydroxystilbene. It is biosynthesized by plants such as Vitis vinifera (grapes), Japanese Knotweed, and various berries in response to stress factors like injury or pathogen attack, and it is a well‐recognized phytoalexin with a molecular formula of C14H12O3 (Bel, 2020; Pop et al., 2022). Originally isolated from the White Hellebore in the mid-20th century and later found in red wine due to grape skin fermentation, resveratrol has garnered significant attention not only for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties but also for its potential benefits in cardiovascular and neuroprotective contexts (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pop et al., 2022). As such, resveratrol—and by extension its commercial version (Cayman Chemical #70580) used in our studies—is classified as a nutraceutical and drug candidate with a long track record of investigative research including applications in aging, inflammation, and ocular health (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pop et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
A considerable volume of biochemical, preclinical, and early clinical literature has explored resveratrol’s broad spectrum of activities. Historically, resveratrol has been investigated primarily for its cardioprotective and neuroprotective effects, as well as its anti-aging properties. In the realm of ophthalmology, several in vitro and animal studies have focused on its role in retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD), diabetic retinopathy (DR), and glaucoma. For instance, its use in RPE cell models has shown promising evidence for ameliorating oxidative stress-induced damage, a central factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Clinical investigations have attempted to translate these findings, as exemplified by the terminated clinical trial NCT02625376 that investigated resveratrol for exudative AMD (Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015), highlighting both the potential and the challenges involved in its clinical application (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Beyond ocular applications, resveratrol’s inclusion in various nutraceutical formulations underscores its established safety profile when administered at low-to-moderate doses, although issues pertaining to bioavailability and rapid systemic metabolism have been recurrent themes in the literature (Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, resveratrol exerts its effects primarily by modulating multiple intracellular signaling cascades. The central hypothesis we are testing is that resveratrol activates the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells—a pathway integral to regulating mitochondrial biogenesis and the antioxidant defense system. Activation of SIRT1, a NAD+-dependent deacetylase, by resveratrol increases the deacetylation and activation of its downstream effector, AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Once activated, AMPK facilitates the phosphorylation and activation of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1 alpha (PGC-1α) in the cytoplasm, which subsequently translocates to the nucleus to upregulate the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and antioxidant responses, including the gene encoding superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). This cascade not only improves mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and spare respiratory capacity—critical indicators of cellular health under oxidative stress—but also promotes an overall enhancement of cellular resilience against reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Bel, 2020; Bryl et al., 2022). Further molecular studies indicate that resveratrol can also modulate extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERK1/2) and mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK), contributing additional layers of cytoprotection through anti-apoptotic effects (Pop et al., 2022; Pop et al., 2022). Together, these mechanistic insights provide a comprehensive biochemical framework through which resveratrol is hypothesized to mitigate the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in RPE cells—a primary factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2021; Bryl et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of the proposed assay for dry AMD, our expectation is that resveratrol will exert a multifaceted protective effect on RPE cells under oxidative challenge. Specifically, when RPE cells are exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as a model for oxidative stress, resveratrol is anticipated to counteract the resultant mitochondrial dysfunction by upregulating antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2, thereby reducing intracellular ROS levels (Bel, 2020; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Restoration of the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) is a critical endpoint, as it directly reflects cellular energy status and the ability of mitochondria to sustain ATP synthesis under stress (Buonfiglio et al., 2024). In addition, an improvement in spare respiratory capacity—the measure of a cell’s ability to respond to increased energy demands—should be evident, reflecting enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and a greater capacity for cellular repair mechanisms (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bryl et al., 2022). These cytoprotective effects have been demonstrated in in vitro studies using ARPE-19 and other human retinal pigment epithelial cell lines, and they resonate with the established role of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis in mediating energy metabolism and antioxidative defenses in the retina (Bryl et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021). Moreover, by decreasing the accrual of oxidative damage, resveratrol is expected to limit apoptotic signaling pathways, which are crucial in slowing the progressive degeneration observed in dry AMD (Bel, 2020; Pop et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
The cumulative evidence from preclinical studies strongly supports the potential of resveratrol as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, especially considering its capacity to modulate mitochondrial function and activate intrinsic antioxidant defenses. The activation of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis not only augments mitochondrial biogenesis but also enhances the expression of key antioxidant enzymes required to neutralize ROS, thereby directly addressing one of the primary mechanisms underlying AMD pathology (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bryl et al., 2022). One of the major strengths of resveratrol is its pleiotropic mode of action; beyond its antioxidant properties, its anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic activities further consolidate its candidacy for chronic conditions like dry AMD (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Bel, 2020). Furthermore, extensive safety data in various preclinical models indicate that resveratrol is well tolerated at certain dose ranges, which is a positive indicator for its potential clinical translation (Wang et al., 2021; Bel, 2020).

The primary challenge with resveratrol is its poor bioavailability and rapid metabolism, which may result in subtherapeutic tissue concentrations despite high oral absorption. This has driven research efforts into advanced drug delivery platforms, such as nanoparticle-based systems and liposomal formulations, aimed at enhancing ocular retention and achieving sustained drug levels in the retina (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Additionally, although the in vitro and animal model data are promising, there exists a dearth of robust clinical trial data specifically addressing dry AMD, as evidenced by the terminated trial in exudative AMD (Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015) and the limited clinical evidence in related retinal pathologies (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Another potential weakness is the dose-dependent duality of its mechanism, where low doses predominantly mediate SIRT1-dependent effects, whereas higher doses might trigger SIRT1-independent pathways, possibly leading to off-target effects or toxicity (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Such a narrow therapeutic window necessitates a precise optimization of dosing regimens and formulation strategies. Despite these challenges, the overarching trend in preclinical research underscores that with proper formulation and dosing strategies, resveratrol could excel as an adjuvant or even monotherapy for protecting RPE cells from oxidative injury and, consequently, for the management of dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

In-Depth Analysis of Preclinical and Clinical Evidence:  
Numerous in vitro studies have characterized the effect of resveratrol on retinal pigment epithelial cells, notably ARPE-19 cell lines, under conditions of oxidative stress. Such studies consistently demonstrate that resveratrol treatment leads to a measurable reduction in ROS levels, a decrease in markers of apoptosis, and an overall improvement in mitochondrial parameters including Δψm and spare respiratory capacity (Bel, 2020; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). These findings are reinforced by experiments showing that resveratrol can mitigate blue light-induced retinal damage and preserve cell viability, further supporting its relevance in ocular pathologies where light-induced oxidative stress is a contributing factor (Bel, 2020). Complementary studies in animal models have shown that resveratrol can reduce inflammatory cytokine secretion and inhibit processes such as choroidal neovascularization, which has implications not only for dry AMD but also for its neovascular (wet) counterpart (Bryl et al., 2022; Bel, 2020).

Moreover, mechanistic investigations into the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis reveal that the deacetylation of PGC-1α is a critical step in the upregulation of mitochondrial genes, which directly correlates with increased cellular ATP production and enhanced resistance to oxidative stress (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Experimental data also show that SOD2 expression is significantly increased following resveratrol treatment, corroborating the compound’s role in boosting the cellular antioxidant capacity (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). These molecular events culminate in an environment that is less conducive to oxidative damage, thereby potentially arresting or even reversing some aspects of RPE degeneration that occur in dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021).

From a clinical perspective, the application of resveratrol in ocular disorders has been approached with caution, primarily due to pharmacokinetic challenges. Even though systemic administration of resveratrol has demonstrated efficacy in reducing plasma oxidative markers in diabetic patients and other conditions, the translation to ocular tissue remains hindered by its low aqueous solubility and rapid hepatic metabolism (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Abu-Amero et al., 2016). To overcome these barriers, innovative drug delivery systems such as chitosan-based nanoparticles, polymeric micelles, and liposomal formulations are being actively developed and show promise for achieving therapeutic levels in retinal tissues (Pop et al., 2022; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Such advanced formulations not only improve bioavailability but also allow for controlled release, which is essential for a chronic condition like dry AMD where sustained therapeutic action is desirable.

Additional mechanistic studies also suggest that resveratrol’s efficacy might be enhanced when used in combination with other therapeutic agents. For instance, its synergistic effects with anti-VEGF treatments in mitigating inflammatory cascades and suppressing angiogenesis have been noted in various preclinical models (Rusciano & Bagnoli, 2023; Tong et al., 2022). While the biochemical rationale for using resveratrol in dry AMD is robust, its clinical development is significantly complicated by pharmacokinetic limitations. The compound is classified as a BCS Class II molecule, meaning that despite having high membrane permeability and lipophilicity, its poor aqueous solubility results in less than 1% bioavailability following oral administration (Kaštelan et al., 2025). As a consequence, only minimal amounts of unchanged resveratrol reach the systemic circulation and, by extension, the ocular tissues. Current research thus prioritizes the optimization of drug delivery vehicles to enhance its stability and target specificity. Nanotechnology-based delivery methods, including polymeric nanoparticles and solid lipid nanoparticles, have demonstrated enhanced tissue penetration and prolonged drug retention in the eye (Pop et al., 2022; Kaštelan et al., 2025). However, these strategies are still in the developmental phase, and their safety, scalability, and reproducibility for routine clinical use remain to be thoroughly validated. The potential for off-target effects and variability in patient-specific pharmacokinetics are additional hurdles that must be addressed in future clinical studies.

Resveratrol has been generally recognized as safe in many preclinical studies, with low-dose regimens showing minimal adverse effects and favorable tolerability profiles (Wang et al., 2021; Bel, 2020). Nonetheless, concerns have been raised regarding gastrointestinal disturbances and other side effects at higher doses, as well as potential interactions with other medications (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Moreover, due to the compound’s rapid metabolism, determining an optimal dosing regimen that achieves effective local concentrations in the retina without inducing systemic toxicity remains challenging. This necessitates further preclinical and early-phase clinical trials to elucidate the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic profiles specific to ocular applications. Tailoring the dosing strategy based on individual metabolic rates and employing controlled-release formulations may help mitigate these issues and maximize therapeutic outcomes (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Kaštelan et al., 2025).

Strategic Direction and Future Perspectives:  
Given the multifaceted biological activities of resveratrol and the encouraging preclinical evidence in models of oxidative stress-induced RPE damage, it holds considerable promise as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to modulate the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis and promote mitochondrial biogenesis presents a novel therapeutic approach that directly targets the cellular dysfunctions underlying RPE degeneration. Future research should focus on (1) developing and rigorously testing advanced drug delivery systems such as nanoparticle encapsulation methods that can bypass first-pass metabolism and target the retina more effectively, (2) conducting detailed pharmacokinetic studies to determine the optimal dosing regimen for achieving sustained therapeutic concentrations in ocular tissues, and (3) exploring combination therapy approaches that integrate resveratrol with conventional treatments such as anti-VEGF agents or other nutraceuticals to provide a comprehensive strategy against AMD progression (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Pop et al., 2022; Rusciano & Bagnoli, 2023). The strengths of resveratrol are rooted in its natural origin, broad-spectrum antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, and its ability to enhance mitochondrial function through the activation of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α pathway. In this light, the repurposing of EUK-134 for dry AMD is based on the hypothesis that its antioxidant properties, previously validated in muscle and other tissues, may confer similar protective effects in RPE cells that are chronically exposed to oxidative stress (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, EUK-134 functions by catalytically mimicking the activities of superoxide dismutase and catalase. In its SOD mimetic capacity, EUK-134 accepts electrons from the superoxide anions, facilitating their conversion into hydrogen peroxide—a reaction which is essential to limit direct superoxide-mediated damage (Thoma et al., 2020). Following this, the catalase mimetic activity is intended to decompose the resultant hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, thereby preventing accumulation of H2O2 which can otherwise contribute to oxidative injury through Fenton-type reactions. However, several studies have drawn attention to limitations in this pathway. For example, evidence indicates that EUK-134 may exhibit a lower efficiency in H2O2 scavenging when compared to other antioxidants such as MnTBAP or native catalase, particularly in environments with high oxidative flux (Quan et al., 2017). One key observation is a significant down-regulation of catalase expression – by more than five-fold – upon EUK-134 treatment in some cellular systems, a factor that potentially undermines its capacity to fully counteract H2O2 buildup (Quan et al., 2017).  
On the molecular interaction front, the manganese center within the salen complex undergoes redox cycling, alternating between oxidation states in response to ROS encounters. This cyclic activity contributes to its continuous catalytic turnover and represents the biochemical foundation for its antioxidant action. Furthermore, studies have shown that EUK-134 can modulate various signaling pathways associated with oxidative stress responses, such as the TGF-β1/Smad2 pathway in muscle under atrophy-inducing conditions (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). Despite these promising aspects, challenges such as suboptimal mitochondrial uptake remain a concern since effective neutralization of ROS in RPE cells requires prompt access to the mitochondrial matrix—a compartment frequently characterized by an inherently challenging microenvironment for drug delivery (Quan et al., 2017). In summary, while EUK-134 possesses a dual action mechanism that addresses two key components of the ROS cascade, the efficiency of its H2O2 detoxification and its cellular distribution are critical parameters that must be rigorously characterized in the context of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
In dry AMD and particularly in geographic atrophy, the retinal pigment epithelium is subject to sustained oxidative stress, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and subsequent cell death. The expected therapeutic effect of EUK-134 in this context is to provide robust antioxidant protection within RPE mitochondria, thereby neutralizing excessive superoxide and hydrogen peroxide levels and preserving mitochondrial integrity (Thoma et al., 2020). Restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) is a key indicator of improved mitochondrial function; thus, by mitigating ROS-induced depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane, EUK-134 is anticipated to maintain or restore ATP production and spare respiratory capacity in RPE cells. These effects are crucial given that ATP depletion and bioenergetic failure are prominent features in the pathology of dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012).  
In vitro assays that simulate oxidative stress conditions—such as those employing RPE cell cultures under hypoxic or chemically induced stress—will likely measure parameters including Δψm, ATP levels, ROS quantification, and expression levels of stress-responsive genes. The anticipated outcome is that EUK-134 will lead to a measurable decrease in the levels of ROS as detected by biochemical assays, along with a concomitant stabilization of mitochondrial respiratory function (Thoma et al., 2020; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012). In addition, molecular analyses may reveal a down-regulation of oxidative stress markers and an improvement in the overall redox balance of the cell. It is vital, however, to consider that some studies have noted that EUK-134 does not inhibit all markers of stress uniformly—for example, the continued expression of GADD34 has been observed even where other stress indicators are normalized (Thoma et al., 2020).  
Given that RPE cells naturally express endogenous antioxidant enzymes such as SOD and catalase, supplementation with EUK-134 is expected to either bolster these defenses or compensate for their decline during chronic oxidative challenges. This dual functionality could theoretically translate into a reduced progression of RPE cell death, slower accumulation of drusen, and ultimately a deceleration of geographic atrophy, all of which are hallmarks of dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of EUK-134 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration involves weighing its mechanistic promise against the practical challenges encountered in its preclinical and potential clinical application. On the one hand, EUK-134 embodies several clear strengths. Its dual mimetic activities align well with the fundamental pathophysiology of dry AMD, where both superoxide and hydrogen peroxide are implicated in the oxidative cascade that leads to mitochondrial dysfunction and RPE cell demise (Thoma et al., 2020; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012). The synthetic nature of EUK-134 allows for controlled chemical modifications which could be leveraged to optimize its pharmacokinetic properties, and its relatively small size is an asset for penetrating tissues such as the retina. Additionally, the compound’s history in attenuating ER stress-related mitochondrial dysfunction in muscle cells provides a robust proof-of-concept that similar benefits might be translatable to RPE cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress (Thoma et al., 2020).  
Notwithstanding these advantages, several weaknesses must be scrutinized. A primary concern lies in the evidence that EUK-134 may exhibit limitations in catalase-like activity, particularly with regard to its efficiency in cleaving hydrogen peroxide. Studies have documented a significant down-regulation of catalase expression upon treatment with EUK-134 and noted that its H2O2 scavenging capabilities fall short when benchmarked against other agents such as MnTBAP or even native catalase (Quan et al., 2017). In the context of RPE cells, where the oxidative insult is persistent and multifactorial, such limitations could result in suboptimal clearance of H2O2, thereby potentially compromising the therapeutic efficacy.  
Another critical issue pertains to drug delivery and cellular bioavailability. The lipophilicity of EUK-134 is notably lower compared to some analogues, amounting to roughly 43% less lipophilicity in certain cases, which inherently limits its capacity to traverse cell membranes and accumulate in the mitochondrial matrix, where its activity is most needed (Limoli et al., 2006; Quan et al., 2017). Since efficient mitochondrial delivery is crucial for counteracting localized ROS buildup in RPE cells, a deficiency in this area might significantly restrict the net antioxidant benefit provided by EUK-134.  
Furthermore, the translational history of EUK-134 presents a challenge in directly correlating preclinical observations with anticipated clinical outcomes in dry AMD. While substantial evidence exists linking EUK-134 with improved mitochondrial function in non-ocular tissues—such as the normalization of mitochondrial membrane potential in tunicamycin-induced ER stress models (Thoma et al., 2020)—there remains a paucity of direct data in ocular models. Compared to other antioxidants that have been more rigorously tested in retinal systems, EUK-134’s ocular pharmacodynamics, potential toxicity in the retinal microenvironment, and long-term safety profile are not well established (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Grujicic & Allen, 2024).  
The literature also points to the possibility of a paradoxical pro-oxidant effect. In some cellular environments, the administration of exogenous SOD mimetics can inadvertently shift the oxidative balance toward higher hydrogen peroxide levels if the catalase function is insufficient, thereby exacerbating oxidative stress rather than mitigating it (Limoli et al., 2006; Quan et al., 2017). Given the delicate balance required in the redox regulation of RPE cells, such an imbalance could be particularly detrimental.  
In light of these considerations, EUK-134’s potential for repurposing as a treatment for dry AMD is promising but remains conditional upon further optimization. The strengths of its dual antioxidant mechanism, its capacity to restore mitochondrial function, and its versatility as evidenced by its broad therapeutic history underscore its potential utility. However, the measurable shortcomings regarding efficient H2O2 clearance, the observed down-regulation of catalase expression, and uncertain mitochondrial bioavailability present hurdles that must be addressed in subsequent experimental phases. This will likely involve additional formulation strategies to improve cellular uptake, as well as comprehensive studies in appropriate retinal models to definitively correlate its antioxidant profile with functional improvements in RPE cells (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Quan et al., 2017).  
It is also noteworthy that while a broad range of clinical trials have been initiated for compounds with similar ROS-scavenging profiles in retinal degenerations (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.), there is a lack of direct clinical evidence for EUK-134’s efficacy specifically in the context of dry AMD. This gap further emphasizes the need for targeted preclinical studies focusing on ocular pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Establishing a direct connection between EUK-134’s known in vitro benefits and its performance in animal models of geographic atrophy will be essential prior to any clinical translation.  
In conclusion, the mechanistic rationale behind the use of EUK-134 in dry AMD is strong on theoretical grounds, leveraging its dual capacity to mitigate the damaging effects of both superoxide and hydrogen peroxide. However, the compound’s limitations—namely, its reduced effectiveness in scavenging H2O2 under certain conditions, its potential for down-regulating endogenous catalase, and challenges associated with adequate mitochondrial targeting—necessitate a cautious approach. The strategic pathway forward would involve an in-depth exploration of its pharmacological properties in retinal models, formulation modifications to enhance mitochondrial delivery, and dose-optimization studies to balance antioxidant efficacy with safety. Only after these issues are rigorously addressed can EUK-134 be confidently positioned as a viable repurposed candidate for the treatment of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Quan et al., 2017; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Tat‐Beclin 1 is a synthetic peptide designed to induce autophagy by harnessing a key region of the Beclin 1 protein, which is essential for the initiation of autophagosome formation (He et al., 2022). This candidate was originally derived by fusing a peptide fragment from Beclin 1, typically encompassing residues in the range of 267–284, with the HIV‐1 Tat transduction domain (Saqcena, 2018), thereby rendering it cell‐permeable and capable of entering diverse cell types. The synthesis and design of Tat‐Beclin 1 focus on exploiting the naturally occurring autophagy machinery by facilitating the release of inhibitory factors bound to Beclin 1 and enhancing its interactions with class III PI3K complexes (He et al., 2022). As a member of the therapeutic class of autophagy inducers, Tat‐Beclin 1 shares mechanistic commonalities with other peptides such as the stapled derivatives (e.g., Tat‐SP4) that have been developed to improve binding affinity and structural stability (Gao, 2023; Gao, 2023). This class of compounds has been widely investigated for their ability to promote autophagy in cellular models of cancer, neurodegeneration, and infection, and the peptide’s design rests on principles that have proven effective in enhancing cellular clearance mechanisms in several pathological contexts (He et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Tat‐Beclin 1 has been extensively characterized in preclinical studies as an inducer of autophagy in various cell types including cancer cells, neuronal cells, and immune cells (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). In early studies, it demonstrated potent autophagy‐stimulating effects by enhancing the transformation of LC3‐I to LC3‐II and by decreasing levels of the autophagic substrate p62, thereby leading to augmented autophagic flux (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013). Moreover, experimental applications have shown that Tat‐Beclin 1 can decrease viral titers in infection models such as those involving West Nile virus and chikungunya virus, and it has been explored for promoting autophagic clearance in cancer models, particularly in breast cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma (He et al., 2022; Gao, 2023). Although there is abundant evidence supporting its utility in managing proteotoxic stress and cellular damage in models of neurodegeneration and cancer, direct applications of Tat‐Beclin 1 for treating dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) have not been explicitly reported (Boland et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2016). Nevertheless, separate studies indicate that proper autophagy in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is critical for cellular viability and resistance to oxidative stress, where impaired autophagy contributes to the accumulation of toxic aggregates such as A2E and lipofuscin that are implicated in AMD (Frost et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Hence, while Tat‐Beclin 1 has not been directly applied in AMD models thus far, its mechanism of promoting clearance of damaged organelles and misfolded proteins provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD treatment.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Tat‐Beclin 1 functions by specifically interacting with Beclin 1, a core component of the Class III PI3K complex that regulates autophagosome nucleation (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). In its inactive state, Beclin 1 is sequestered by negative regulatory proteins such as GAPR‐1, which limits its availability for autophagic initiation. Tat‐Beclin 1 is designed to bind to these inhibitory regulators, thereby liberating Beclin 1 and enabling it to participate in the formation of the PI3K complex necessary for phagophore formation (Ha & Kim, 2016; He et al., 2022). This intervention effectively shifts the balance toward autophagy induction by enhancing the generation of autophagosomes and promoting lysosomal degradation of intracellular cargo. Furthermore, research has demonstrated that Tat‐Beclin 1 increases the conversion of LC3‐I to LC3‐II—a hallmark of autophagosome formation—and has been shown to lower p62 levels, which underscores its role in boosting autophagic flux (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013; Si et al., 2023). Additionally, the peptide’s cell‐penetrating Tat domain facilitates its entry into cells and ensures its functional delivery to intracellular compartments, which is critical for engaging the autophagic machinery even in cells with limited uptake capabilities (Saqcena, 2018; He et al., 2022). Through these molecular interactions, Tat‐Beclin 1 not only enhances general autophagy but has also been reported to drive selective autophagic processes such as mitophagy, thereby promoting the turnover of damaged mitochondria (He et al., 2022; Frost et al., 2014). This mechanistic detail is particularly relevant in conditions of oxidative stress where dysfunctional mitochondria accumulate and contribute to cell death, as has been observed in RPE cells during the progression of dry AMD (Frost et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration, the therapeutic hypothesis posits that Tat‐Beclin 1 will promote autophagy initiation in RPE cells to facilitate the turnover of damaged organelles—including mitochondria—that accumulate as a result of chronic oxidative stress (Frost et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). This enhanced autophagic clearance is expected to mitigate the cytotoxic effects associated with the buildup of toxic aggregates such as A2E and lipofuscin, which are known to drive RPE cell dysfunction and death (Zhang et al., 2015; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Experimental evidence from studies on RPE cells has documented that robust autophagic activity is critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis in the face of oxidative and metabolic insults (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Therefore, by increasing autophagic flux, Tat‐Beclin 1 should theoretically lead to a reduction in cellular stress markers and an improvement in mitochondrial quality control mechanisms, thereby preventing the initiation of apoptotic cascades in RPE cells (Saqcena, 2018). In cellular assays, the expected outcome would include an enhanced LC3‐II/LC3‐I ratio, decreased levels of p62, improved lysosomal function, and ultimately enhanced cell viability under oxidative stress conditions (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013; Si et al., 2023). Notably, the efficacy of autophagy induction in rescuing RPE cellular function is supported by literature where pharmacological activation of autophagy—such as through rapamycin or inhibition of mTOR pathways—has been shown to protect RPE cells from degeneration (Frost et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2020). Given the inherent ability of Tat‐Beclin 1 to stimulate autophagy in other cellular models, it is reasonable to expect that similar benefits would be observed upon its application to RPE cells, leading to a deceleration of dry AMD pathology by maintaining mitochondrial turnover and preventing the accumulation of deleterious substrates.

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall potential of Tat‐Beclin 1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD lies in its well‐defined mechanism of action, which directly targets the autophagic machinery through interactions with Beclin 1 (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). One of the primary strengths of this candidate is its demonstrated versatility across different disease models, where enhancement of autophagy has led to reduced apoptosis, improved clearance of toxic protein aggregates, and mitigation of cellular stress in both cancer and neurodegenerative contexts (He et al., 2022; Boland et al., 2018). In the specific arena of RPE cell biology, multiple studies have established that autophagic dysfunction is a hallmark of AMD progression and that stimulating autophagy can improve cellular resilience under oxidative stress (Frost et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Therefore, by repurposing Tat‐Beclin 1 for dry AMD, there exists a compelling translational rationale based on mechanistic insights derived from both in vitro and in vivo studies in other systems.

However, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be considered. Despite extensive preclinical evidence in other domains, there is a lack of direct experimental data demonstrating the efficacy of Tat‐Beclin 1 in ocular models or in RPE-specific assays (He et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2016). This gap in the literature necessitates rigorous validation in relevant RPE cell culture systems and animal models of dry AMD to confirm that the peptide’s autophagy-inducing effects translate to meaningful therapeutic benefits for ocular health. In addition, the potential for overactivation of autophagy poses a safety concern, as excessive autophagic flux can lead to autophagic cell death or unintended degradation of essential cellular components (Pinelli et al., 2025; Peraro et al., 2017). Precise dosing and delivery strategies will therefore be critical to ensure that Tat‐Beclin 1 achieves a balance between sufficient autophagy induction and preservation of RPE cell integrity. 

Pharmacokinetic and biodistribution challenges also remain to be addressed, especially given the unique anatomical barriers of the eye. Although the Tat transduction domain confers robust cell penetration, the stability, half-life, and clearance of the peptide in ocular tissues have yet to be thoroughly investigated (Saqcena, 2018; He et al., 2022). Moreover, the route of administration—potentially through intravitreal injection or topical delivery—must be optimized to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE without eliciting adverse immune responses or off-target effects. It is also important to note that while the autophagy-stimulating effects of Tat‐Beclin 1 have been well documented in various cell types, the specific context of chronic oxidative stress and metabolite accumulation in the aged RPE represents a distinct microenvironment that may influence peptide efficacy (Frost et al., 2014; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Zhang et al., 2015).

Another consideration is the heterogeneity inherent in dry AMD pathology, where oxidative injury, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammatory processes all contribute to disease progression. Although enhancing autophagy could address multiple facets of the disease, the interplay between autophagic flux and other cellular pathways—such as inflammation and lipid metabolism—remains complex and may necessitate combination therapies for optimal outcomes (Zhang et al., 2020; Pinelli et al., 2025). Nonetheless, leveraging the established protective role of autophagy in RPE cells provides a solid foundation for further research on Tat‐Beclin 1, and its repurposing could represent a novel strategy to counteract the multifactorial stressors associated with dry AMD.

In summary, Tat‐Beclin 1 presents a mechanism-driven approach for inducing autophagy that is grounded in sound biochemical principles and supported by extensive preclinical studies in other disease contexts (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). Its ability to prompt autophagosome formation, enhance mitochondrial turnover, and clear toxic protein aggregates aligns well with the cellular deficits observed in dry AMD, particularly in the RPE. The cumulative literature underscores the therapeutic promise of autophagy-inducing peptides in mitigating oxidative stress and improving cellular viability (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Frost et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2020). However, the lack of direct data in AMD-focused models, potential risks associated with overactivation of autophagy, and the need for refined ocular delivery methods represent critical hurdles that must be overcome through further research. 

Given the potential benefits and the mechanistic rationale underpinning its use, Tat‐Beclin 1 merits further investigation in preclinical RPE models, with attention to dose optimization, delivery strategies, and long-term safety assessments in the context of retinal degeneration. Ultimately, if these challenges can be addressed, Tat‐Beclin 1 could emerge as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD by restoring cellular homeostasis and halting the progression of RPE degeneration. This comprehensive evaluation therefore supports the continued exploration of Tat‐Beclin 1’s therapeutic potential while highlighting the necessity for rigorous validation in ocular-specific experimental paradigms (Frost et al., 2014; Saqcena, 2018; Boland et al., 2018; Frost et al., 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring vitamin B3–class nucleoside and a leading NAD⁺ precursor that has been isolated from natural sources such as cow milk and other dietary materials, and is now produced by synthetic chemical means for therapeutic applications (Biță et al., 2023). NR belongs to the class of NAD⁺‐precursor nucleosides within the broader family of vitamin B3 compounds, the same family that includes nicotinic acid (NA) and nicotinamide (NAM), which historically have been used to prevent pellagra and improve cellular energy metabolism (Pîrvu et al., 2021; Biță et al., 2023). The synthetic production of NR involves the glycosylation of nicotinamide with appropriately protected ribofuranose donors via methods that require careful control due to the labile and reactive nature of its glycosidic bond, which often results in partial degradation during synthesis and storage (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). In order to overcome these issues, researchers have developed alternative stabilized forms such as NR borate, although the commercially available ChromaDex NR-100 is typically presented as the crystalline chloride salt (NRCl) and has become a benchmark for purity due to its improved manufacturing protocols and rigorous quality control (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Additionally, NR’s classification as an “orally bioavailable” NAD⁺ precursor distinguishes it from other precursors such as NMN by virtue of its ability to directly cross cell membranes without requiring extracellular conversion, with transport mediated by equilibrative nucleoside transporters (Mehmel et al., 2020; Biță et al., 2023). Taken together, these attributes place NR in a unique position as a repurposable compound with potential applications in metabolic, neurodegenerative, and now ocular diseases, including the dry forms of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) characterized by geographic atrophy (Biță et al., 2023; Braidy et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the use of vitamin B3 derivatives such as NA and NAM has been well established in both clinical and biochemical practice for the improvement of energy metabolism and for prevention of niacin deficiency diseases; however, nicotinamide riboside represents a more recently discovered alternative that offers superior pharmacokinetic profiles and fewer side effects such as flushing or liver toxicity (Braidy et al., 2019; Mehmel et al., 2020). Preclinical studies have shown that NR supplementation rapidly increases tissue and circulating NAD⁺ levels across a range of animal models, including mice and rats, where it has been tested for its effects on metabolic dysfunction, neurodegeneration, insulin sensitivity, and mitochondrial biogenesis (Biță et al., 2023). Numerous clinical trials have demonstrated the safety and oral bioavailability of NR in healthy human subjects and in populations with metabolic or neurodegenerative conditions; for example, chronic supplementation at doses up to 2 g/day has been well tolerated and has successfully elevated NAD⁺ in middle-aged and older adults (Mehmel et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023). In addition to these metabolic and neuroprotective applications, NR has been investigated in various models of inflammation, organ injury, and even in oncology-related situations, where its ability to modulate cellular stress responses has proven beneficial (Biță et al., 2023). Notably, while NR has undergone extensive research in contexts such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and peripheral neuropathy, its application in ocular diseases—particularly dry AMD characterized by geographic atrophy—has been less comprehensively studied; however, emerging evidence supports the notion that NAD⁺ decline in the retina and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) may be mitigated by NAD⁺ precursors, providing a rationale for repurposing NR for dry AMD (Braidy et al., 2019). Veterinary studies and animal models have also utilized NR to stimulate mitochondrial function and improve bioenergetics in tissues with high metabolic demands, further solidifying its profile as a potent NAD⁺ booster with broad potential therapeutic applications (Biță et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
NR exerts its biological effects via a well-defined metabolic pathway that begins with its cellular uptake through equilibrative nucleoside transporters (ENT1, ENT2, and ENT4) followed by phosphorylation by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRK1 and NRK2) in the cytosol, which convert NR to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) (Biță et al., 2023; Braidy et al., 2019). NMN is subsequently adenylated by nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferases (NMNATs) to generate NAD⁺, thereby replenishing the intracellular NAD⁺ pool that is essential for numerous metabolic and signaling processes (Mehmel et al., 2020). The elevation of NAD⁺ levels activates a host of NAD⁺-dependent enzymes including sirtuins (SIRT1, SIRT3, among others) and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs), which are critical for deacetylating mitochondrial proteins, enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis, and facilitating DNA repair processes both in the nucleus and mitochondria (Biță et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2016). Activation of SIRT3 in particular within the mitochondria leads to the deacetylation and activation of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2), thereby reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitigating oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020). Moreover, increased NAD⁺ availability supports the activity of PARP enzymes that are required for efficient DNA repair, including the repair of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) damage arising from oxidative stress (Cimaglia et al., 2020). In RPE cells, this mechanism is particularly relevant as the high-energy–demand environment and frequent exposure to light-induced oxidative stress make robust mitochondrial and genomic maintenance critical to cell survival and homeostasis (Zhang et al., 2020). Additionally, NR’s effect on boosting NAD⁺ may facilitate the activation of autophagy and mitophagy pathways, leading to the clearance of damaged cellular components and improved cellular renewal processes (Braidy et al., 2019; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023). Such biochemical actions converge to foster an enhanced cellular defense mechanism against oxidative damage, support mitochondrial function through improved repair and turnover, and ultimately promote cellular longevity (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023; Biță et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underpinning the repurposing of NR for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that supplementation with NR will lead to an elevation of intracellular NAD⁺ pools specifically within retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby enhancing mitochondrial DNA repair and upregulating antioxidant defenses that mitigate the oxidative damage implicated in geographic atrophy (Biță et al., 2023). In vitro studies using iPSC-derived RPE cells from AMD donors have demonstrated that NR supplementation results in rapid increases in intracellular NAD⁺, which is accompanied by the activation of sirtuin-mediated deacetylation of key mitochondrial proteins (Jadeja et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020). This deacetylation is believed to lead to improved mitochondrial function as evidenced by restored maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) measured via Seahorse XF assays, and the lowering of reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels as detected by fluorescent probes such as DCFDA (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016). The expected outcome in RPE is that the elevated NAD⁺ not only promotes the repair of oxidative damage to mitochondrial DNA but also augments the intrinsic antioxidant enzyme systems—including upregulation of enzymes like SOD2 and catalase—which collectively reduce the cellular oxidative burden (Biță et al., 2023). As a result, NR supplementation is anticipated to stabilize the RPE cell phenotype, reduce markers of cellular senescence and apoptosis, and potentially restore a healthier metabolic profile in RPE cells, factors that are critical for halting or even reversing the progression of geographic atrophy (Jadeja et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016). Moreover, by enhancing the NAD⁺-dependent activation of PARP and other DNA repair enzymes, NR may directly improve the repair of mitochondrial and nuclear DNA damage that accumulates under chronic oxidative stress conditions prevalent in the aging retina (Braidy et al., 2019; Mehmel et al., 2020). In preclinical models of retinal degeneration such as light-induced retinal injury, systemic administration of NR has been shown to preserve retinal morphology, reduce photoreceptor apoptosis, and maintain tissue NAD⁺ levels despite strong oxidative challenges, which supports the translational rationale for its application in dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2020; Braidy et al., 2019). Ultimately, the expected therapeutic effect of NR in the treatment of geographic atrophy is to provide cytoprotection to the RPE by mitigating oxidative damage and improving mitochondrial function, thus slowing the progression of RPE degeneration and vision loss (Zhu et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating NR (specifically the ChromaDex NR-100 formulation) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and promising attributes emerge alongside areas that warrant further investigation. One of the primary strengths of NR is its established reputation as a safe and orally bioavailable NAD⁺ precursor with extensive preclinical and clinical data supporting its ability to elevate NAD⁺ levels systemically and within specific target tissues (Mehmel et al., 2020). This property is particularly relevant for RPE cells because the high metabolic demands of the retina make efficient NAD⁺ replenishment crucial for maintaining mitochondrial function and for mediating effective DNA repair mechanisms (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Additionally, the robust mechanistic data showing that NR supplementation activates sirtuin pathways—most notably SIRT1 and SIRT3—and subsequently deacetylates and activates key mitochondrial and antioxidant enzymes provide a compelling molecular rationale for its potential to ameliorate oxidative stress in the RPE (Biță et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). The activation of these pathways not only enhances mitochondrial bioenergetics but also promotes the clearance of damaged cellular components through autophagy, which is expected to contribute to improved cell survival under oxidative challenge (Braidy et al., 2019; Jadeja et al., 2020).  
However, there are some weaknesses and critical gaps in the current data when it comes to translating these beneficial effects specifically to the context of geographic atrophy in dry AMD. Although preclinical models have demonstrated the protective effects of NR in retinal degeneration (particularly in light-induced injury models), direct evidence demonstrating that NR selectively elevates NAD⁺ pools in RPE cells derived from AMD patients, enhances mitochondrial DNA repair specifically in RPE, and reduces ROS levels to a degree that meaningfully impacts the progression of geographic atrophy remains limited (Braidy et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020). Furthermore, the chemical reactivity and inherent instability of NR have historically posed challenges to its synthesis, storage, and consistent formulation, raising concerns about batch-to-batch variability and the possibility of degradation products in commercial formulations; although recent advances and improved production standards appear to have mitigated these issues, further analytical validation is needed to ensure that the NR-100 formulation consistently meets high purity criteria (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Another consideration is that while the mechanisms underlying NR’s beneficial effects are well established in metabolic and neurodegenerative contexts, the unique metabolic and microenvironmental characteristics of the RPE in the aging eye—including the contributions of the local immune system, extracellular matrix alterations, and the interplay with the choroidal circulation—may represent additional variables that could influence NR’s efficacy in dry AMD, and these factors are not yet fully delineated (Biță et al., 2023; Cimaglia et al., 2020).  
From a clinical development perspective, the fact that NR has already been evaluated in multiple Phase I/II clinical trials for other indications, and has demonstrated an excellent safety profile even at high doses, is a significant advantage that could accelerate its repurposing for ocular applications; careful dose-ranging studies focused on ocular bioavailability and pharmacodynamics in the context of AMD will be critical (Mehmel et al., 2020; Biță et al., 2023). Additionally, mechanistic endpoints such as NAD⁺ elevation, sirtuin activation, and improvements in mitochondrial function have been validated in other tissues and could be adapted to RPE-specific assays, including measurements of oxygen consumption rate (OCR), mitochondrial membrane potential, ROS quantification, and biomarkers of DNA repair (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016; Braidy et al., 2019). Moreover, early translational studies using iPSC-derived RPE from AMD donors have already begun to show that NR can reduce oxidative stress and restore metabolic function in these cells, lending credibility to its potential efficacy in geographic atrophy settings (Biță et al., 2023; Braidy et al., 2019).  
In summary, NR (ChromaDex NR-100) emerges as a highly promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD on the basis of its well-established ability to raise NAD⁺, activate sirtuin-mediated mitochondrial maintenance and DNA repair processes, and mitigate oxidative stress—all of which are central drivers of RPE degeneration in geographic atrophy (Zhang et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016). The strengths of this candidate include a robust mechanistic foundation, a favorable safety and pharmacokinetic profile established in other clinical contexts, and encouraging preclinical data that indirectly support its potential benefit in the retina (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020; Braidy et al., 2019). Nonetheless, significant challenges remain, particularly the need for direct evidence in RPE-specific and geographic atrophy models, confirmation of consistent formulation quality due to NR’s chemical instability, and the potential variability in tissue-specific uptake and metabolism in an aging ocular environment (Mehmel et al., 2020; Biță et al., 2023). Future studies should therefore focus on comprehensive in vitro investigations in primary and iPSC-derived RPE cells, detailed pharmacodynamic assessments in animal models of dry AMD, and ultimately carefully designed early-phase clinical trials targeting RPE function and retinal structure in patient populations with geographic atrophy (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016; Braidy et al., 2019).  
Overall, while there is a compelling mechanistic rationale and a solid foundation of preclinical and clinical data supporting the repurposing of NR for dry AMD, particularly in mitigating oxidative damage, enhancing mitochondrial DNA repair, and improving antioxidant defenses in RPE cells, further targeted research is required to validate these effects specifically in the context of geographic atrophy. The available literature suggests that NR has significant translational promise, and its favorable safety profile alongside extensive clinical experience in other indications positions it as a frontrunner among NAD⁺ precursors for potential therapeutic intervention in dry AMD (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). The next phase of research should therefore include detailed mechanistic studies in ocular models, combined with rigorous clinical endpoint evaluations to determine whether NR supplementation can effectively slow or reverse the degenerative processes underlying geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016; Jadeja et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
3-Mercaptopicolinic acid (3-MPA; also written 3-mercaptopicolinate/3-MP) is a small, thiol-containing picolinic-acid derivative historically identified as a biochemical inhibitor of gluconeogenesis through inhibition of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) and, at higher concentrations, glucose-6-phosphatase (G-6-Pase) in hepatic systems (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001). Early reports in the 1970s established 3-MPA as a preferential inhibitor of the cytosolic PEPCK isoform (PCK1), and the compound has since been used widely as a tool in mechanistic enzymology and physiology of gluconeogenesis across species and contexts (e.g., mammalian liver, pig, and protozoan PEPCKs) (Hidalgo et al., 2016; McLeod et al., 2019; Brearley et al., 2020). While the original discovery route is not detailed in the provided sources, a “convenient synthesis” was reported historically, and numerous structure–mechanism studies have refined the understanding of its binding behavior and chemical liabilities; by contrast, no data in the provided material indicate a natural origin (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001).

Chemically, 3-MPA belongs to the broader class of picolinic-acid–based, anionic, metal-coordinating inhibitors that engage the PEPCK active site by chelating the catalytically essential M1 divalent metal (typically Mn2+) via the ring nitrogen and exocyclic carboxylate; 3-MPA also contains a reactive free sulfhydryl group that drives both potency and time-dependent covalent reactivity with protein cysteines (McLeod et al., 2019). The picolinic-acid scaffold’s anionic, metal-binding character is a recognized design principle for PEPCK inhibitors and has been leveraged to build next-generation derivatives (e.g., 3-((carboxymethyl)thio)-picolinic acid, CMP) that seek to occupy both inner and outer subsites of the OAA/PEP pocket while reducing thiol-mediated liabilities (McLeod et al., 2019).

As a class, such PEPCK-directed small-molecule inhibitors have been applied as biochemical probes of gluconeogenic flux, as antihyperglycemic tools in preclinical metabolic studies, and as chemical probes to dissect PEPCK function in cancer and immunometabolism models; however, the field has wrestled with issues of thiol reactivity, complex multi-site binding kinetics, ADME/PAINS flags, and limited isoform selectivity, all of which complicate translation (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001; McLeod et al., 2019; Baptista et al., 2019; Hidalgo et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History  
3-MPA has a long track record as a research tool in hepatic metabolism. In perfused rat liver and in vivo rat studies, 3-MPA was used to blunt gluconeogenesis and lower blood glucose, with dosing paradigms including intraperitoneal administration (e.g., 100 mg/kg followed by 25 mg/kg three hours later) and 1 mM concentrations in perfusate to suppress fructose- or lactate/pyruvate-stimulated hepatic glucose production (Herling et al., 1998). More recently, 3-MPA has served as a comparator and positive control in modern PEPCK-targeted discovery programs, including enzyme assays against recombinant human cytosolic and mitochondrial PEPCK isoforms (PCK1/PCK2), CETSA target-engagement studies, cell-based functional assays (e.g., insulin secretion), and acute in vivo pharmacodynamic readouts (e.g., fasting glycemia five hours after 50 mg/kg IP administration) (Aragó et al., 2020). In several settings, 3-MPA reduces oncogenic phenotypes: it impairs anchorage-independent growth in MCF7 cells yet shows limited effects on glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in INS-1 cells, suggesting variable target engagement and a modest potency ceiling relative to newer chemotypes (Aragó et al., 2020).

3-MPA has been used to inhibit the mitochondrial isoform PEPCK-M (PCK2) in cancer models. In non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cell lines cultured under glucose deprivation, inhibition of human mitochondrial PEPCK by 3-MPA or genetic knockdown induced apoptosis, consistent with a reliance on PEPCK-mediated anaplerotic/cataplerotic cycling for survival under nutrient stress (Baptista et al., 2019). Computational docking studies against human PEPCK-M have used 3-MPA as a benchmark ligand to set score cutoffs and to elucidate canonical binding interactions (Mn2+ coordination; Arg/Lys salt-bridge network), aligning with structural insights from cytosolic isoforms (Baptista et al., 2019).

In melanoma models, 3-MPA (applied as a PCK1 inhibitor) sensitized vemurafenib-resistant tumors in vitro and in vivo by depressing pentose phosphate pathway–derived NADPH production and elevating ROS through KEAP1/Nrf2 axis modulation, thereby reversing resistance; here, 3-MPA increased oxidative stress rather than alleviating it (Ren et al., 2022). Across immunometabolism, 3-MPA (100 μM) reduced cytotoxic T lymphocyte effector functions and decreased maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) without altering basal glycolysis, indicating impaired mitochondrial respiratory capacity in activated T cells in which PEPCK-M predominates (Brownlie et al., 2025). In skeletal muscle myoblasts (C2C12), 3-MPA (0.25–1 mM) reduced proliferation and induced myogenic differentiation, with Pck2 transcripts predominant over Pck1; however, the compound interfered with enzymatic assays at ≥0.25–0.5 mM, complicating attribution to on-target inhibition (Brearley et al., 2020). Against porcine cytosolic PEPCK isoenzymes, 3-MPA exhibits mid-micromolar IC₅₀ (~65 μM) under saturating substrates and mechanistically mixed/complex kinetics (mixed non-competitive vs PEP; uncompetitive vs GDP/GTP), supporting dual-site binding behavior (Hidalgo et al., 2016).

No study in the provided literature assesses 3-MPA in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), retina, or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD); a comprehensive mechanistic and structural study of related PEPCK inhibitors explicitly contains no mention of eye/RPE/AMD systems, emphasizing that the extant knowledge base for 3-MPA is outside ophthalmology (McLeod et al., 2019). Absent any reported ocular or RPE use, 3-MPA should be regarded as a systemic/metabolic tool compound with evolving applications in cancer and immunometabolism rather than as a precedent therapeutic in retinal degenerations (McLeod et al., 2019).

Mechanism of Action  
Mechanistic biochemistry and structural work converge on a dual-mode model for 3-MPA action on PEPCK:
- Active-site (inner-subsite) binding and Mn²⁺ coordination: The picolinic-acid moiety of 3-MPA coordinates the catalytic M1 Mn²⁺ ion via the ring nitrogen and exocyclic carboxylate oxygen(s), occupying the “inner” OAA/PEP subsite in a manner analogous to oxalate and other carboxylate inhibitors; co-crystal analyses and docking corroborate metal coordination along with salt-bridge/ion-pairing to conserved basic residues (e.g., Arg104/Arg423/Lys261/Lys262 in vertebrate enzymes) (McLeod et al., 2019; Baptista et al., 2019).
- Secondary/allosteric site binding: 3-MPA can occupy a second site near/behind the P-loop, with two molecules bound simultaneously (n≈2 by ITC), producing complex kinetic signatures (mixed non-competitive behavior with respect to PEP/OAA and uncompetitive inhibition versus GDP/GTP), and allowing allosteric influence on substrate/inhibitor binding at the active site (Hidalgo et al., 2016).

Kinetically, these binding modes yield mixed patterns that depend on the variable substrate: mixed non-competitive versus PEP/OAA; uncompetitive versus GDP/GTP, consistent with inhibitor binding to enzyme–nucleotide complexes and allosteric communication to the catalytic pocket (Hidalgo et al., 2016). Across isoforms, micromolar potency is typical: for rat cytosolic PEPCK (rcPEPCK) Kᵢ ~8 μM, for human mitochondrial PEPCK (hmPEPCK) Kᵢ ~3 μM in some determinations, though reported IC₅₀/Kᵢ values vary with assay format and metal/substrate conditions (McLeod et al., 2019). Variability is expected given that picolinic-acid derivatives chelate divalent metal cations; changes in available Mn²⁺ can partially masquerade as noncompetitive inhibition (i.e., by depleting active holoenzyme) in kinetic plots if not tightly controlled (McLeod et al., 2019).

A distinguishing chemical feature of 3-MPA is the free thiol. In vitro, the thiol can form mixed disulfide adducts with reactive cysteines on PEPCK (e.g., C288 on the P-loop in rat cytosolic PEPCK), producing time-dependent, covalent inactivation that contributes to potency but also to off-target reactivity and interpretational complexity; this chemistry is mitigated but not eliminated by inclusion of reducing agents in assays (McLeod et al., 2019). The thiol’s promiscuity likely explains reports of irreversible, time-dependent inhibition of G-6-Pase at millimolar concentrations, a phenomenon exploited historically to dissect gluconeogenic regulation but pharmacologically undesirable for selective PEPCK targeting (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001; McLeod et al., 2019). Because the M1 metal and a basic electrostatic microenvironment (e.g., Arg104/Arg423/Lys261/Lys262) are conserved in PEPCK-M and PEPCK-C, inhibitors that rely on metal chelation and anionic interactions, like 3-MPA, are predicted to show cross-isoform activity; docking against the human mitochondrial isoform reproduces these hallmarks (Baptista et al., 2019).

Several functional studies corroborate that 3-MPA perturbs cellular bioenergetics consistent with PEPCK inhibition but in cell-context-dependent ways. In activated effector T cells (PCK2-predominant), 100 μM 3-MPA reduced maximal OCR without changing basal ECAR, indicating compromised oxidative phosphorylation capacity while leaving basal glycolysis intact (Brownlie et al., 2025). In lung cancer cell lines, PEPCK-M inhibition by 3-MPA induced apoptosis only under glucose deprivation, highlighting the role of PCK2 in enabling biosynthesis from non-glucose substrates under stress (Baptista et al., 2019). Conversely, in BRAFi-resistant melanoma, PCK1 inhibition by 3-MPA depressed PPP-mediated NADPH synthesis, increased ROS by weakening antioxidant buffering (via KEAP1/Nrf2), and sensitized cells to targeted therapy, illustrating that PEPCK inhibition can amplify oxidative stress depending on metabolic wiring (Ren et al., 2022).

Finally, medicinal-chemistry and ADME flags apply. 3-MPA triggers PAINS warnings and violates the Pfizer 3/75 heuristic on polar surface area margins in in silico filtering, and its free thiol confers chemical reactivity that can perturb off-target proteins and auxiliary assay enzymes; analogs that remove the free thiol (e.g., thioethers like CMP) avoid mixed-disulfide inactivation at the cost of reduced potency (order-of-magnitude weaker Kᵢ) (Baptista et al., 2019; McLeod et al., 2019; Hidalgo et al., 2016).

The working hypothesis proposes that 3-MPA will inhibit mitochondrial PCK2 in RPE, redirecting flux toward TCA cycle maintenance, enhancing NADH generation, and reducing ROS during bioenergetic stress. Evidence from the supplied literature constrains and complicates each element of this chain:

- Direct engagement of PCK2 by 3-MPA. Biochemical and docking data support that 3-MPA inhibits human PEPCK-M with micromolar potency and establishes the binding physics (Mn²⁺ coordination; cationic pocket interactions), making PCK2 engagement in principle plausible in RPE if the protein is expressed and accessible (McLeod et al., 2019; Baptista et al., 2019). The supplied general isoform summary indicates that in humans both isoforms can be approximately equally abundant at the organismal level, underscoring that mitochondrial PEPCK may be physiologically relevant in human tissues, but this does not substitute for RPE-specific evidence (Yun, 2017).

In NSCLC, PEPCK-M inhibition precipitated apoptosis during glucose deprivation, consistent with failure of metabolic adaptation when cataplerotic/anaplerotic cycling is blocked; this is contrary to the expectation that PCK2 inhibition would “rescue” TCA integrity and support survival under stress (Baptista et al., 2019). At high exposure (hundreds of micromolar to millimolar), 3-MPA exhibits assay interference and off-target enzyme inhibition (e.g., G-6-P translocase and/or G-6-Pase, time-dependent irreversibility), and has been used at 1 mM in perfused livers, underscoring a risk window where non-PEPCK targets and chemical reactivity dominate (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001; Brearley et al., 2020; Herling et al., 1998). Its free thiol can form mixed-disulfide adducts with reactive cysteines, a liability in redox-sensitive tissues like the RPE where protein thiol chemistry is critical to homeostasis (McLeod et al., 2019). In silico PAINS flags and polarity metrics further caution against promiscuity and suboptimal drug-likeness (Baptista et al., 2019).

Strengths  
- Extensive mechanistic characterization and proven PEPCK engagement. 3-MPA’s dual-site binding, active-site metal coordination, and kinetic behavior are well described, with micromolar potency against both cytosolic and mitochondrial PEPCK isoforms under defined conditions, enabling precise hypothesis testing of PEPCK-dependent biology (McLeod et al., 2019; Hidalgo et al., 2016).

- Target validation in RPE. There is no evidence in the supplied material confirming PCK2 expression and activity in RPE, nor any demonstration that PEPCK-M–dependent cycling is maladaptive in dry AMD; this gap precludes mechanistic confidence (McLeod et al., 2019).  
- Directionality of benefit. The compound’s demonstrated tendency to reduce maximal OXPHOS capacity and, in some contexts, to enhance oxidative stress directly contradicts the intended pharmacology (increase NADH/OXPHOS; decrease ROS) in stressed RPE (Brownlie et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2022).

If the project’s strategic objective is to probe whether inhibiting PEPCK-M benefits RPE bioenergetic stability, a safer and more specific chemical tool would be required.
