1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Mdivi-1, known as mitochondrial division inhibitor 1 (catalog number Sigma-Aldrich M0199), is a synthetic small-molecule compound originally developed for research into mitochondrial dynamics. It belongs to a class of therapeutic agents that modulate mitochondrial fission by targeting the dynamin‐related protein 1 (DRP1). DRP1 is an essential GTPase responsible for driving mitochondrial fission, a process that maintains mitochondrial quality control but, when overactivated, can lead to fragmentation associated with cellular stress and apoptosis. Mdivi-1 was discovered via compound screening experiments aimed at identifying inhibitors of DRP1’s GTPase activity and has been characterized extensively in various in vitro and in vivo studies. Its discovery was motivated by the need to therapeutically intervene in pathologies where aberrant mitochondrial fission contributes to cellular dysfunction. As a representative of DRP1 inhibitory agents, Mdivi-1 has been widely used as an investigational tool in studies related to neurodegeneration, ischemia, and ocular diseases, where mitochondrial integrity is a key determinant of cell survival (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2020). Its synthetic origin and well-documented pharmacological profile render it a candidate for drug repurposing, with potential applications extending into the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) by addressing mitochondrial dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells.

2. Therapeutic History  
Mdivi-1 has a robust preclinical research history across a variety of models that involve oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Initial studies demonstrated that in retinal endothelial cells and neuronal tissues, inhibition of DRP1 by Mdivi-1 prevented excessive mitochondrial fragmentation under conditions of acute stress. In models of glaucoma, for instance, DRP1 overactivation associated with ocular hypertension leads to mitochondrial fragmentation and retinal ganglion cell death, and administration of Mdivi-1 was found to rescue these cells by preserving mitochondrial network integrity (Kim et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2021). Similarly, in photoreceptor cells following retinal detachment, Mdivi-1 treatment reduced the activation of apoptotic pathways—through downregulation of cleaved Caspase-3 and Bax—and consequently preserved cell morphology and function, indicating a protective effect mediated through the inhibition of DRP1-dependent fission (She et al., 2018). Furthermore, in ARPE-19 cells, which are commonly used as a model for RPE behavior, Mdivi-1 has been shown to mitigate the cytotoxic effects of oxidative stress induced by hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) by reducing mitochondrial fragmentation and cytochrome c release, thereby improving mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP production (Yako et al., 2021). Although Mdivi-1 has not yet been evaluated in large-scale clinical trials for dry AMD specifically, its use in diverse ocular models—ranging from diabetic retinopathy to retinal ischemia—provides compelling evidence that its mechanism could be beneficial in conditions marked by oxidative stress and RPE dysfunction, two hallmark features of dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). These cumulative findings support the repurposing hypothesis that targeting DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission could restore mitochondrial function and survival in RPE cells, thereby halting or slowing the degenerative cascade observed in dry AMD.

3. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, DRP1 is responsible for mediating mitochondrial fission through the constriction and subsequent division of mitochondrial membranes. Upon receiving various stress signals, DRP1 is recruited from the cytosol to the mitochondrial outer membrane where it oligomerizes and hydrolyzes GTP, driving membrane scission. Mdivi-1 specifically inhibits the GTPase activity of DRP1, thereby preventing its self-assembly and subsequent mitochondrial recruitment. This inhibition effectively blocks the fission process that is typically upregulated under conditions of oxidative stress and other cellular insults (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2020). Detailed biochemical investigations have demonstrated that when DRP1 activity is unopposed, mitochondrial fragmentation ensues, leading to diminished mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, decreased oxygen consumption rate (OCR), reduced ATP synthesis, and an increase in the generation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) (Yako et al., 2021). Mdivi-1 counters these deleterious cellular events by preserving the integrity of the mitochondrial network, enabling enhanced ATP production, and maintaining the mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP). Moreover, by inhibiting DRP1, Mdivi-1 reduces the stress-induced release of cytochrome c from the mitochondria—a central step in the intrinsic apoptotic pathway—thus lowering the activation of downstream caspases (She et al., 2018; Yako et al., 2021). In addition to these primary actions, some studies have noted that Mdivi-1 has reversible inhibitory effects on mitochondrial complex I, suggesting that its impact on mitochondrial bioenergetics may be multifaceted (Yako et al., 2021). Such dual actions may serve to further stabilize mitochondrial function under stress.

4. Expected Effect  
Under conditions relevant to dry age-related macular degeneration, such as chronic oxidative stress incident on RPE cells, Mdivi-1 is anticipated to exert a multi-pronged cytoprotective effect. In the proposed assay using H₂O₂-treated ARPE-19 cells—a well-established in vitro model to mimic the oxidative stress environment of dry AMD—the primary expected effect is the inhibition of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission (Yako et al., 2021). By stabilizing mitochondrial dynamics, Mdivi-1 should also improve cellular bioenergetics through enhanced OCR and increased ATP production, both critical parameters that are typically compromised in stressed RPE cells (Yako et al., 2021). The anticipated outcome of these events is a reduction in cell death and apoptosis, as well as improved phagocytic function—an essential role of RPE cells in the maintenance of retinal homeostasis. Furthermore, by mitigating the accumulation of mtROS, Mdivi-1 is expected to lessen oxidative stress, thereby curbing the degenerative processes that are a central component of dry AMD pathophysiology (Yako et al., 2021; Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025). In essence, the mechanistic intervention afforded by Mdivi-1 aims to interrupt the cycle of mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage that leads to RPE cell apoptosis, which is a critical driver of disease progression in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021).

5. Overall Evaluation  
In evaluating Mdivi-1 as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current body of literature. Among its strengths, Mdivi-1 is underpinned by a strong mechanistic rationale: the inhibition of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission is a well-validated approach to restore mitochondrial function in the face of oxidative stress. Preclinical studies have consistently demonstrated that Mdivi-1 preserves mitochondrial network integrity, reduces the production of harmful reactive oxygen species, and prevents the release of apoptogenic factors, thereby facilitating cell survival in retinal models (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2020; Yako et al., 2021). Its efficacy in multiple ocular contexts—including models of glaucoma, retinal detachment, and diabetic retinopathy—highlights the versatility of its cytoprotective actions, which may be directly relevant to the RPE dysfunction and oxidative injury observed in dry AMD (Kim et al., 2015; She et al., 2018). From a biochemical standpoint, the ability of Mdivi-1 to enhance mitochondrial bioenergetics by improving OCR and ATP production, while simultaneously preserving mitochondrial membrane potential, addresses essential aspects of RPE cell metabolism that are often impaired in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Furthermore, the compound’s capacity to reduce apoptotic signaling, as evidenced by decreased cytochrome c release and lower caspase activity, is particularly promising given the established link between mitochondrial-mediated apoptosis and RPE cell loss in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Despite these promising attributes, several limitations and challenges deserve consideration. First, while the preclinical evidence supporting Mdivi-1’s efficacy is compelling, there remains a notable gap in clinical data, particularly in the context of dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Another potential weakness arises from the dual inhibitory effects of Mdivi-1. Some investigations have reported that Mdivi-1 also exhibits reversible inhibition of mitochondrial complex I, which could complicate its therapeutic profile by inadvertently affecting normal mitochondrial respiration (Yako et al., 2021). Moreover, the chronic inhibition of DRP1 raises important questions about the broader physiological implications of interfering with mitochondrial dynamics (Mohammad & Kowluru, 2022; She et al., 2018). Furthermore, the in vitro models currently used, predominantly involving H₂O₂-treated ARPE-19 cells, may not entirely mimic the in vivo microenvironment of the human retina in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). The overall therapeutic window and safety profile of Mdivi-1 also require further elucidation (Yako et al., 2021). Despite these challenges, the mechanistic insights generated from a diverse array of experimental models suggest that Mdivi-1 holds considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its capacity to restore mitochondrial integrity, mitigate oxidative stress, and inhibit apoptotic cascades directly addresses several of the pathogenic mechanisms implicated in dry AMD. Given that current treatments for dry AMD are limited and mainly supportive, a disease-modifying therapy that targets mitochondrial dysfunction would represent a significant advancement in the management of this debilitating disorder (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2015). In summary, Mdivi-1’s strengths lie in its well-characterized mechanism of action, demonstrated efficacy in preserving mitochondrial dynamics under stress, and its potential to enhance cell survival in models of retinal degeneration (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2015; Yako et al., 2021).

Future studies must address the nuances of chronic DRP1 inhibition, optimize dosing regimens, evaluate long-term safety, and conduct thorough pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiling in ocular tissues to fully realize the potential of Mdivi-1 in the clinical management of dry AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021).

In conclusion, the evidence provided by numerous preclinical studies strongly indicates that Mdivi-1’s inhibition of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission offers a promising therapeutic strategy for dry age-related macular degeneration. The compound’s ability to maintain mitochondrial network integrity, enhance bioenergetics, and suppress apoptotic cascades under conditions of oxidative stress in RPE cells is particularly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Although challenges remain in addressing the potential off-target effects and ensuring long-term safety in the clinical setting, the mechanistic rationale and supporting preclinical data justify further investigation into the utility of Mdivi-1 as a repurposed candidate for this currently untreatable condition. As the drug development process progresses, a focused effort on meticulous in vivo testing, formulation development for ocular delivery, and comprehensive pharmacological evaluations will be critical to harnessing the full therapeutic potential of Mdivi-1 for patients with dry AMD (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2015; She et al., 2018; Yako et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
3-Mercaptopicolinic acid (3-MPA; also written 3-mercaptopicolinate/3-MP) is a small, thiol-containing picolinic-acid derivative historically identified as a biochemical inhibitor of gluconeogenesis through inhibition of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) and, at higher concentrations, glucose-6-phosphatase (G-6-Pase) in hepatic systems (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001). Early reports in the 1970s established 3-MPA as a preferential inhibitor of the cytosolic PEPCK isoform (PCK1), and the compound has since been used widely as a tool in mechanistic enzymology and physiology of gluconeogenesis across species and contexts (e.g., mammalian liver, pig, and protozoan PEPCKs) (Hidalgo et al., 2016; McLeod et al., 2019; Brearley et al., 2020). While the original discovery route is not detailed in the provided sources, a “convenient synthesis” was reported historically, and numerous structure–mechanism studies have refined the understanding of its binding behavior and chemical liabilities; by contrast, no data in the provided material indicate a natural origin (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001).

Chemically, 3-MPA belongs to the broader class of picolinic-acid–based, anionic, metal-coordinating inhibitors that engage the PEPCK active site by chelating the catalytically essential M1 divalent metal (typically Mn2+) via the ring nitrogen and exocyclic carboxylate; 3-MPA also contains a reactive free sulfhydryl group that drives both potency and time-dependent covalent reactivity with protein cysteines (McLeod et al., 2019). The picolinic-acid scaffold’s anionic, metal-binding character is a recognized design principle for PEPCK inhibitors and has been leveraged to build next-generation derivatives (e.g., 3-((carboxymethyl)thio)-picolinic acid, CMP) that seek to occupy both inner and outer subsites of the OAA/PEP pocket while reducing thiol-mediated liabilities (McLeod et al., 2019).

As a class, such PEPCK-directed small-molecule inhibitors have been applied as biochemical probes of gluconeogenic flux, as antihyperglycemic tools in preclinical metabolic studies, and as chemical probes to dissect PEPCK function in cancer and immunometabolism models; however, the field has wrestled with issues of thiol reactivity, complex multi-site binding kinetics, ADME/PAINS flags, and limited isoform selectivity, all of which complicate translation (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001; McLeod et al., 2019; Baptista et al., 2019; Hidalgo et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History  
3-MPA has a long track record as a research tool in hepatic metabolism. In perfused rat liver and in vivo rat studies, 3-MPA was used to blunt gluconeogenesis and lower blood glucose, with dosing paradigms including intraperitoneal administration (e.g., 100 mg/kg followed by 25 mg/kg three hours later) and 1 mM concentrations in perfusate to suppress fructose- or lactate/pyruvate-stimulated hepatic glucose production (Herling et al., 1998). More recently, 3-MPA has served as a comparator and positive control in modern PEPCK-targeted discovery programs, including enzyme assays against recombinant human cytosolic and mitochondrial PEPCK isoforms (PCK1/PCK2), CETSA target-engagement studies, cell-based functional assays (e.g., insulin secretion), and acute in vivo pharmacodynamic readouts (e.g., fasting glycemia five hours after 50 mg/kg IP administration) (Aragó et al., 2020). In several settings, 3-MPA reduces oncogenic phenotypes: it impairs anchorage-independent growth in MCF7 cells yet shows limited effects on glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in INS-1 cells, suggesting variable target engagement and a modest potency ceiling relative to newer chemotypes (Aragó et al., 2020).

3-MPA has been used to inhibit the mitochondrial isoform PEPCK-M (PCK2) in cancer models. In non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cell lines cultured under glucose deprivation, inhibition of human mitochondrial PEPCK by 3-MPA or genetic knockdown induced apoptosis, consistent with a reliance on PEPCK-mediated anaplerotic/cataplerotic cycling for survival under nutrient stress (Baptista et al., 2019). Computational docking studies against human PEPCK-M have used 3-MPA as a benchmark ligand to set score cutoffs and to elucidate canonical binding interactions (Mn2+ coordination; Arg/Lys salt-bridge network), aligning with structural insights from cytosolic isoforms (Baptista et al., 2019).

In melanoma models, 3-MPA (applied as a PCK1 inhibitor) sensitized vemurafenib-resistant tumors in vitro and in vivo by depressing pentose phosphate pathway–derived NADPH production and elevating ROS through KEAP1/Nrf2 axis modulation, thereby reversing resistance; here, 3-MPA increased oxidative stress rather than alleviating it (Ren et al., 2022). Across immunometabolism, 3-MPA (100 μM) reduced cytotoxic T lymphocyte effector functions and decreased maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) without altering basal glycolysis, indicating impaired mitochondrial respiratory capacity in activated T cells in which PEPCK-M predominates (Brownlie et al., 2025). In skeletal muscle myoblasts (C2C12), 3-MPA (0.25–1 mM) reduced proliferation and induced myogenic differentiation, with Pck2 transcripts predominant over Pck1; however, the compound interfered with enzymatic assays at ≥0.25–0.5 mM, complicating attribution to on-target inhibition (Brearley et al., 2020). Against porcine cytosolic PEPCK isoenzymes, 3-MPA exhibits mid-micromolar IC₅₀ (~65 μM) under saturating substrates and mechanistically mixed/complex kinetics (mixed non-competitive vs PEP; uncompetitive vs GDP/GTP), supporting dual-site binding behavior (Hidalgo et al., 2016).

No study in the provided literature assesses 3-MPA in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), retina, or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD); a comprehensive mechanistic and structural study of related PEPCK inhibitors explicitly contains no mention of eye/RPE/AMD systems, emphasizing that the extant knowledge base for 3-MPA is outside ophthalmology (McLeod et al., 2019). Absent any reported ocular or RPE use, 3-MPA should be regarded as a systemic/metabolic tool compound with evolving applications in cancer and immunometabolism rather than as a precedent therapeutic in retinal degenerations (McLeod et al., 2019).

Mechanism of Action  
Mechanistic biochemistry and structural work converge on a dual-mode model for 3-MPA action on PEPCK:
- Active-site (inner-subsite) binding and Mn²⁺ coordination: The picolinic-acid moiety of 3-MPA coordinates the catalytic M1 Mn²⁺ ion via the ring nitrogen and exocyclic carboxylate oxygen(s), occupying the “inner” OAA/PEP subsite in a manner analogous to oxalate and other carboxylate inhibitors; co-crystal analyses and docking corroborate metal coordination along with salt-bridge/ion-pairing to conserved basic residues (e.g., Arg104/Arg423/Lys261/Lys262 in vertebrate enzymes) (McLeod et al., 2019; Baptista et al., 2019).
- Secondary/allosteric site binding: 3-MPA can occupy a second site near/behind the P-loop, with two molecules bound simultaneously (n≈2 by ITC), producing complex kinetic signatures (mixed non-competitive behavior with respect to PEP/OAA and uncompetitive inhibition versus GDP/GTP), and allowing allosteric influence on substrate/inhibitor binding at the active site (Hidalgo et al., 2016).

Kinetically, these binding modes yield mixed patterns that depend on the variable substrate: mixed non-competitive versus PEP/OAA; uncompetitive versus GDP/GTP, consistent with inhibitor binding to enzyme–nucleotide complexes and allosteric communication to the catalytic pocket (Hidalgo et al., 2016). Across isoforms, micromolar potency is typical: for rat cytosolic PEPCK (rcPEPCK) Kᵢ ~8 μM, for human mitochondrial PEPCK (hmPEPCK) Kᵢ ~3 μM in some determinations, though reported IC₅₀/Kᵢ values vary with assay format and metal/substrate conditions (McLeod et al., 2019). Variability is expected given that picolinic-acid derivatives chelate divalent metal cations; changes in available Mn²⁺ can partially masquerade as noncompetitive inhibition (i.e., by depleting active holoenzyme) in kinetic plots if not tightly controlled (McLeod et al., 2019).

A distinguishing chemical feature of 3-MPA is the free thiol. In vitro, the thiol can form mixed disulfide adducts with reactive cysteines on PEPCK (e.g., C288 on the P-loop in rat cytosolic PEPCK), producing time-dependent, covalent inactivation that contributes to potency but also to off-target reactivity and interpretational complexity; this chemistry is mitigated but not eliminated by inclusion of reducing agents in assays (McLeod et al., 2019). The thiol’s promiscuity likely explains reports of irreversible, time-dependent inhibition of G-6-Pase at millimolar concentrations, a phenomenon exploited historically to dissect gluconeogenic regulation but pharmacologically undesirable for selective PEPCK targeting (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001; McLeod et al., 2019). Because the M1 metal and a basic electrostatic microenvironment (e.g., Arg104/Arg423/Lys261/Lys262) are conserved in PEPCK-M and PEPCK-C, inhibitors that rely on metal chelation and anionic interactions, like 3-MPA, are predicted to show cross-isoform activity; docking against the human mitochondrial isoform reproduces these hallmarks (Baptista et al., 2019).

Several functional studies corroborate that 3-MPA perturbs cellular bioenergetics consistent with PEPCK inhibition but in cell-context-dependent ways. In activated effector T cells (PCK2-predominant), 100 μM 3-MPA reduced maximal OCR without changing basal ECAR, indicating compromised oxidative phosphorylation capacity while leaving basal glycolysis intact (Brownlie et al., 2025). In lung cancer cell lines, PEPCK-M inhibition by 3-MPA induced apoptosis only under glucose deprivation, highlighting the role of PCK2 in enabling biosynthesis from non-glucose substrates under stress (Baptista et al., 2019). Conversely, in BRAFi-resistant melanoma, PCK1 inhibition by 3-MPA depressed PPP-mediated NADPH synthesis, increased ROS by weakening antioxidant buffering (via KEAP1/Nrf2), and sensitized cells to targeted therapy, illustrating that PEPCK inhibition can amplify oxidative stress depending on metabolic wiring (Ren et al., 2022).

Finally, medicinal-chemistry and ADME flags apply. 3-MPA triggers PAINS warnings and violates the Pfizer 3/75 heuristic on polar surface area margins in in silico filtering, and its free thiol confers chemical reactivity that can perturb off-target proteins and auxiliary assay enzymes; analogs that remove the free thiol (e.g., thioethers like CMP) avoid mixed-disulfide inactivation at the cost of reduced potency (order-of-magnitude weaker Kᵢ) (Baptista et al., 2019; McLeod et al., 2019; Hidalgo et al., 2016).

Expected Effect  
The working hypothesis proposes that 3-MPA will inhibit mitochondrial PCK2 in RPE, redirecting flux toward TCA cycle maintenance, enhancing NADH generation, and reducing ROS during bioenergetic stress. Evidence from the supplied literature constrains and complicates each element of this chain:

- Direct engagement of PCK2 by 3-MPA. Biochemical and docking data support that 3-MPA inhibits human PEPCK-M with micromolar potency and establishes the binding physics (Mn²⁺ coordination; cationic pocket interactions), making PCK2 engagement in principle plausible in RPE if the protein is expressed and accessible (McLeod et al., 2019; Baptista et al., 2019). However, the provided sources do not document PCK2 expression in RPE (neither transcript nor protein), so expression in the proposed cell type cannot be confirmed from this corpus (McLeod et al., 2019). In NSCLC, PEPCK-M inhibition precipitated apoptosis during glucose deprivation, consistent with failure of metabolic adaptation when cataplerotic/anaplerotic cycling is blocked; this is contrary to the expectation that PCK2 inhibition would “rescue” TCA integrity and support survival under stress (Baptista et al., 2019). At high exposure (hundreds of micromolar to millimolar), 3-MPA exhibits assay interference and off-target enzyme inhibition (e.g., G-6-P translocase and/or G-6-Pase, time-dependent irreversibility), and has been used at 1 mM in perfused livers, underscoring a risk window where non-PEPCK targets and chemical reactivity dominate (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001; Brearley et al., 2020; Herling et al., 1998). The provided sources do not document PCK2 expression in RPE, so the target linkage in the specified cell type remains unsubstantiated within this corpus (Brownlie et al., 2025; Baptista et al., 2019; Ren et al., 2022; McLeod et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Extensive mechanistic characterization and proven PEPCK engagement. 3-MPA’s dual-site binding, active-site metal coordination, and kinetic behavior are well described, with micromolar potency against both cytosolic and mitochondrial PEPCK isoforms under defined conditions, enabling precise hypothesis testing of PEPCK-dependent biology (McLeod et al., 2019; Hidalgo et al., 2016).  
- Demonstrated modulation of mitochondrial bioenergetics in mammalian cells. The compound reduces maximal OCR in activated T cells (PCK2-predominant), confirming that pharmacologic inhibition of PEPCK-M can reprogram OXPHOS in a predictable direction, albeit one that appears detrimental to respiratory capacity (Brownlie et al., 2025).  
- Tool-compound utility across contexts relevant to stress metabolism. In NSCLC under glucose limitation and in BRAFi-resistant melanoma, 3-MPA perturbs survival pathways and redox control, reinforcing that PEPCK is a nodal metabolic regulator in stress adaptation—an axis of interest in RPE pathobiology in AMD (Baptista et al., 2019; Ren et al., 2022).  

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Directionality of effect conflicts with the AMD hypothesis. Available cell-based data indicate 3-MPA reduces maximal mitochondrial respiratory capacity and can increase ROS in specific contexts by depleting PPP-derived NADPH, the opposite of the hypothesized benefit for RPE under bioenergetic/oxidative stress (Brownlie et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2022).  
- Chemical liabilities. The free thiol drives time-dependent covalent reactivity (mixed disulfides) with PEPCK and likely other proteins; at millimolar exposure, 3-MPA causes irreversible, time-dependent inhibition of G-6-Pase, underscoring a broad risk of off-target covalent modification that is unacceptable for ocular therapy without significant medicinal-chemistry mitigation (McLeod et al., 2019; Westergaard & Madsen, 2001). PAINS flags and polarity metrics caution against promiscuity and poor drug-likeness (Baptista et al., 2019).  
- Inconsistent target engagement in cells and modest potency relative to alternatives. Compared with newer PEPCK inhibitors (e.g., iPEPCK-2), 3-MPA shows two orders of magnitude weaker IC₅₀s in some cellular contexts and variable engagement (e.g., limited effect on insulin secretion), suggesting that achieving effective concentrations in relevant compartments may be difficult or that off-target liabilities confound outcomes (Aragó et al., 2020).  
- No precedent in retinal/RPE systems. The provided literature contains no data on 3-MPA in the eye, retina, RPE, or AMD models, and offers no RPE expression evidence for PCK2, making the translational leap speculative from the present corpus (McLeod et al., 2019; Yun, 2017).  
- Concentration-dependent assay interference and off-target effects. In C2C12 cells, 3-MPA interfered with PEPCK assays at ≥0.25–0.5 mM; perfused liver studies used 1 mM; such concentrations raise the likelihood of nonspecific effects in RPE (Brearley et al., 2020; Herling et al., 1998).  

Decision-Critical Gaps for AMD  
- Target validation in RPE. There is no evidence in the supplied material confirming PCK2 expression and activity in RPE, nor any demonstration that PEPCK-M–dependent cycling is maladaptive in dry AMD; this gap precludes mechanistic confidence (McLeod et al., 2019).  
- Directionality of benefit. The compound’s demonstrated tendency to reduce maximal OXPHOS capacity and, in some contexts, to enhance oxidative stress directly contradicts the intended pharmacology (increase NADH/OXPHOS; decrease ROS) in stressed RPE (Brownlie et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2022).  
- Ocular safety. Free-thiol reactivity, metal chelation, and PAINS liabilities make 3-MPA a risky starting point for ocular delivery; no ocular PK/safety data are available in the provided sources (Baptista et al., 2019; McLeod et al., 2019; Westergaard & Madsen, 2001).  

If the project’s strategic objective is to probe whether inhibiting PEPCK-M benefits RPE bioenergetic stability, a safer and more specific chemical tool would be required. Notably, thioether analogs like CMP remove the free thiol and still engage the active site competitively (albeit with ~10× weaker potency), and crystallography confirms occupancy of both inner and outer subsites; such molecules may offer cleaner on-target pharmacology for in vitro RPE studies while avoiding mixed-disulfide covalency (McLeod et al., 2019). However, even for such analogs, the directionality risk remains given that PEPCK-M inhibition has reduced mitochondrial respiratory capacity in mammalian cells that rely on this enzyme under activation stress (Brownlie et al., 2025).

Overall, based on the provided literature, I do not recommend prioritizing 3-MPA as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. The compound’s mechanistic actions and cell-level consequences in related systems predict outcomes counter to the proposed benefit in RPE, and its chemical liabilities are incompatible with ocular drug development without substantial medicinal-chemistry redesign (Brownlie et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2022; McLeod et al., 2019; Baptista et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
BGP-15 is a synthetic, small-molecule nicotinic amidoxime/hydroxylamine derivative whose full chemical name is O-(3-piperidino-2-hydroxy-1-propyl) nicotinic amidoxime, typically used as a dihydrochloride salt; it was developed by N-Gene (US/Hungary) and has been described as water-soluble and mitochondria-targeting in preclinical studies (including ocular applications) (Takács et al., 2024; Horváth et al., 2021). Chemically and pharmacologically, BGP-15 belongs to the hydroximic/hydroxylamine acid derivative family originally advanced as membrane-interacting heat-shock response (HSR) co-inducers that remodel cholesterol-enriched plasma membrane rafts, with pleiotropic, cytoprotective effects in stressed tissues (membrane-lipid therapy) (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011). In parallel, the compound has been positioned as a nicotinamide-related, non-carboxamide “NAM analogue” with in vitro mixed-type (noncompetitive) PARP-1 inhibition, though the authors emphasize that in vivo protective effects likely involve additional mechanisms beyond direct PARP blockade because the in vitro inhibitory concentration exceeds achievable systemic levels (Crul et al., 2013). Independent biophysical and cellular studies show BGP-15 partitions into membranes, increases the fluidity of negatively charged lipid species, preserves heat-challenged raft integrity, and activates stress signaling linked to HSP induction; imaging and molecular dynamics support a direct membrane-interacting mode of action (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

Functionally, BGP-15 is best classified as a multifunctional HSP co-inducer and insulin-sensitizing, mitochondria-targeting cytoprotective agent that remodels membrane rafts, enhances the HSF1–HSP axis, and modulates stress and survival signaling (Akt up, JNK/p38 down), while lowering mitochondrial ROS and stabilizing Δψm; importantly, it preferentially acts in stressed cells, an attribute that underpins its safety rationale (Gombos et al., 2011; Sumegi et al., 2017). The compound concentrates in energized mitochondria driven by its delocalized positive charge, with >85–90% uptake into isolated mitochondria under experimental conditions (Sümegi, 2018). Mitochondrial studies consistently localize the dominant ROS-lowering effect to the respiratory chain at complexes I and III, with minimal direct antioxidant chemistry, and only mild uncoupling at millimolar concentrations that is irrelevant at the micromolar doses used in most cell studies (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018).

Crucial nomenclature caveat: a distinct “BGP-15” reported by a different group denotes a calcipotriene-derived vitamin D3 analog with anticancer activity; this vitamin D3 analog is mechanistically and structurally unrelated to the nicotinic amidoxime HSP co-inducer described above (both were labeled “BGP-15” by their respective originators) (Sintov et al., 2013). For the current program, the candidate of interest is the nicotinic amidoxime/hydroxylamine HSP co-inducer (often supplied by N-Gene or commercial chemical vendors under the amidoxime name), not the vitamin D3 analog (Takács et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
BGP-15 and closely related hydroximic/hydroxylamine acid derivatives have an extensive preclinical history across cardiac, neural, hepatic, renal, skeletal muscle, pulmonary, and metabolic models, with multiple mechanistic readouts converging on membrane remodeling, HSR/HSP co-induction, MAPK and Akt pathway modulation, and mitochondrial protection (Sumegi et al., 2017). Cardiovascular protection has been reported in ischemia–reperfusion, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation, with actions that include reduced ROS, preserved mitochondrial function, and Akt activation with suppression of JNK/p38 (Sumegi et al., 2017). In spontaneously hypertensive rats, BGP-15 increased PGC-1α and mitochondrial mass, decreased interstitial fibrosis, increased MKP-1 and reduced p38/JNK phosphorylation, and activated Akt/GSK-3β signaling (Horváth et al., 2021). BGP-15 prevented imatinib cardiotoxicity, protected against cisplatin nephrotoxicity without impairing antitumor efficacy, and mitigated cisplatin/taxol peripheral neuropathy (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). Hepatoprotection against acetaminophen injury via inhibition of caspase-independent cell death has also been documented (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). In pulmonary arterial hypertension and severe muscular dystrophy models, BGP-15 preserved mitochondrial structure and function and slowed disease progression; mechanistically, mitochondrial fusion via OPA1 activation and Akt signaling were implicated (Szabó et al., 2018).

Neuroprotection and mitochondrial rescue have been demonstrated in vitro and in vivo, including reduced neuronal death and improved mitochondrial potential/ROS at axonal branch points, coupled to HSP72 elevation, reduced phospho-JNK/p38, and enhanced Akt/IGF1R signaling (Ohlen et al., 2017). Consistent with its membrane-raft mechanism, BGP-15 increased HSP expression during heat challenge and remodeled cholesterol-rich platforms that gate stress signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

In ophthalmology, BGP-15 has been applied in multiple retinal disease contexts. It was reported retinoprotective in Goto–Kakizaki rats (type 2 diabetes) with functional preservation on ERG, and later shown to improve survival and retinal function long-term in ZDF rats under uncontrolled diabetes, with increased ocular HSP70 and decreased NFκB (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021). Topical ocular delivery using an SBECD-containing eyedrop improved scotopic/photopic a- and b-waves, restored oscillatory potentials, shortened implicit times, and preserved retinal thickness following global ischemia–reperfusion injury in rats (Takács et al., 2024). These ocular data align with the compound’s mitochondrial and HSP co-inducer mechanisms: accumulation in mitochondria, protection against apoptosis/necrosis in oxidative-stress paradigms, and modulation of stress signaling (Takács et al., 2024).

Clinically, BGP-15 has a proof-of-concept randomized, double-blind trial demonstrating dose-dependent improvement of insulin sensitivity in insulin-resistant patients without apparent short-term toxicity; in parallel, human phase II work in olanzapine-induced metabolic disorder also identified BGP-15 as an insulin sensitizer (Crul et al., 2013; Sümegi, 2018). Safety signals from early human studies and the pharmacology of HSP co-inducers (preferential action in stressed cells) support the translational risk profile; however, systemic serum concentrations reported by the developer are low (≤25 nmol/mL), which has implications for target engagement and favors local ocular delivery for retinal indications (Gombos et al., 2011; Sumegi et al., 2017).

To our knowledge based on the supplied corpus, BGP-15 has not been directly tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) patients or canonical dry AMD animal models; however, its retinoprotective efficacy in diabetic retinopathy models and retinal ischemia–reperfusion suggests relevance to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)/photoreceptor stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammation, which are central to dry AMD biology (Takács et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Membrane-lipid therapy and HSP co-induction. BGP-15 partitions into and remodels membrane lipid domains, particularly cholesterol-rich plasma membrane rafts that organize stress sensing and signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). Under heat stress or analogous perturbations, BGP-15 preserves raft integrity and elevates HSP expression; this is associated with activation of Rac1 and modulation of HSF1 acetylation, leading to prolonged HSF1 DNA binding and robust HSP gene induction without causing protein unfolding, a hallmark of HSP “co-inducers” (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). In HSR-defective melanoma cells, BGP-15 significantly rescued raft domain coverage and shifted the size distribution toward larger platforms, coincident with increased hsp25 expression and Rac1-dependent stress signaling (Gombos et al., 2011). Across cell and tissue contexts, BGP-15 increases HSP70/HSPA1A (HSP72), and this HSP gain is causally linked to improved insulin signaling and cytoprotection in stressed cells (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011).

PARP/NAD+/SIRT1/HSF1 axis. Although BGP-15 demonstrates mixed-type (noncompetitive) inhibition of PARP-1 in vitro, the concentrations required exceed typical in vivo exposures, suggesting that PARP pathway effects in vivo are likely downstream of ROS lowering and reduced DNA single-strand breaks that otherwise drive PARP activation (Crul et al., 2013). In stressed cells, BGP-15 reduces PAR levels, which relieves PARP-mediated suppression of MKP-1/Dusp1, thereby inhibiting JNK/p38 activation; reduced PARP activity also preserves NAD+ and SIRT1 activity, which favors a deacetylated, active HSF1 and a stronger HSR (Crul et al., 2013). This mechanistic loop—less ROS, less PARP activation, more MKP-1, less JNK/p38, and better HSP/SIRT1 tone—aligns with the observed anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective phenotypes (Crul et al., 2013).

Mitochondrial enrichment and respiratory chain modulation. Biophysically, BGP-15 carries a delocalized positive charge, accumulates in energized mitochondria (>85–90% uptake in isolated organelles), and at micromolar doses characteristic of cell studies (1–50 µM) lowers mitochondrial ROS predominantly at complexes I and III without significant baseline depolarization of Δψm (Sümegi, 2018; Sumegi et al., 2017). In oxidative or inflammatory challenges, BGP-15 attenuates H₂O₂- and LPS-induced mitochondrial depolarization and reduces mitochondrial superoxide to near-control levels; MitoTEMPO controls confirm mitochondrial origin of the ROS signal (Sumegi et al., 2017). Importantly, the compound exhibits no meaningful direct antioxidant scavenging in cell-free ROS-generating systems, and only displays mild uncoupling at millimolar concentrations—far above the micromolar exposures used in protective assays—supporting a mechanism of respiratory chain modulation rather than redox scavenging (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). Downstream signaling reflects the lowered mitochondrial ROS burden: JNK/p38 activation is reduced, Akt signaling is enhanced, and caspase-independent death pathways are suppressed (Sumegi et al., 2017).

Mitochondrial dynamics, fusion, and biogenesis. Beyond acute ROS control, BGP-15 promotes mitochondrial fusion and preserves cristae architecture by activating OPA1 GTPase and promoting OPA1 polymerization; genetic suppression of OPA1 or Mfn1/Mfn2 abolishes the fusion phenotype, indicating that BGP-15 acts upstream or within the endogenous fusion machinery (Szabó et al., 2018). In vivo, these effects translate into improved mitochondrial ultrastructure and tissue histology under ROS stress (e.g., monocrotaline-induced PAH) (Szabó et al., 2018). In hypertensive cardiomyopathy, BGP-15 increases PGC-1α and mitochondrial mass, with concurrent shifts in CREB/AMPK phosphorylation consistent with improved energetic signaling, reduced p38/JNK via MKP-1 upregulation, and increased Akt/GSK-3β prosurvival signaling (Horváth et al., 2021).

Insulin-sensitizing stress signaling. In skeletal muscle and human studies, BGP-15 increases HSP72 expression, enhances insulin receptor autophosphorylation (blocking JNK inhibitory phosphorylation), activates RAC1, increases AKT phosphorylation, promotes GLUT4 translocation, increases membrane fluidity, raises AMPK activity, and reduces HSF1 acetylation, altogether improving glucose disposal without overt toxicity in a randomized trial (Crul et al., 2013). These metabolic effects are mechanistically congruent with the membrane–HSR–mitochondrial triad described above (Crul et al., 2013).

Ocular and retinal mechanisms. In rat eyes, BGP-15 increased HSP70 and decreased NFκB, consistent with HSR enhancement and anti-inflammatory signaling in ocular tissues (Wachal et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion and diabetic retinopathy models, functional improvements on ERG, restoration of oscillatory potentials, and preservation of retinal thickness are consistent with mitochondrial protection and stress-response reinforcement in retinal cells (Takács et al., 2024). The topical SBECD formulation demonstrated pharmacologic activity in the retina without systemic pharmacokinetic characterization, indicating local ocular delivery as a viable route for targeting mitochondrial and HSP pathways in the posterior segment (Takács et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
The team’s hypothesis—that BGP-15 stabilizes mitochondrial membrane proteins and co-induces HSF1-driven antioxidant chaperone responses in RPE to mitigate oxidative stress in dry AMD—is aligned with the compound’s demonstrated pharmacology in retinal, cardiac, neural, and pulmonary models: (i) robust mitochondrial enrichment and stabilization of Δψm under oxidative/inflammatory stress, (ii) ROS lowering at complexes I and III without direct radical scavenging, (iii) activation of the HSR via membrane raft remodeling and HSF1 acetylation control, and (iv) suppression of ROS-sensitive injury cascades (JNK/p38) with concurrent activation of pro-survival Akt (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). In retinal disease models, BGP-15 improved ERG measures and retinal thickness and increased ocular HSP70 while decreasing NFκB, providing a direct ocular precedent likely to translate to stressed RPE, where mitochondria and proteostasis are central to survival under chronic oxidative load (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021).

- Membrane-raft remodeling and HSR co-induction. BGP-15 partitions into RPE membranes and remodels cholesterol-rich rafts, preserving raft integrity under stress, activating Rac1, decreasing HSF1 acetylation, and prolonging HSF1 DNA binding, thereby elevating HSP70/HSP25 and enhancing proteostasis capacity in aged/stressed RPE (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

BGP-15 should accumulate in RPE mitochondria, reduce ROS production at complexes I/III, and attenuate oxidative- and inflammation-induced depolarization, thereby maintaining ATP production and limiting mitochondrial permeability transition and AIF translocation, as shown in other cell types (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018).

Via OPA1 activation and Akt/GSK-3β signaling, BGP-15 is expected to promote inner-membrane fusion/OPA1 oligomerization and preserve cristae, with possible longer-term increases in mitochondrial biogenesis (PGC-1α), all protective features for RPE faced with chronic oxidative and lipofuscin stress (Szabó et al., 2018; Horváth et al., 2021).

By reducing mitochondrial ROS and PARP activation, BGP-15 should relieve PARP-mediated suppression of MKP-1, suppress JNK/p38 activity, decrease NFκB signaling, and bolster SIRT1-HSF1 activity, thereby reducing ROS-amplifying feed-forward loops in RPE (Crul et al., 2013; Wachal et al., 2021).

Where possible, complement activation or lipid peroxidation paradigms can be layered to emulate dry AMD stressors; based on the corpus, BGP-15’s effects are strongest under stress, consistent with HSP co-inducer pharmacology (Gombos et al., 2011).

The corpus documents the relevant targets (HSF1/HSP70, Rac1, OPA1, MKP-1, JNK/p38, Akt) as central to BGP-15’s mechanisms in multiple mammalian tissues and cell types and shows ocular readouts (HSP70 up, NFκB down) in rat eyes; however, it does not provide explicit RPE expression data, which should be confirmed experimentally in our RPE assay systems (Wachal et al., 2021; Gombos et al., 2011; Szabó et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic congruence with dry AMD pathobiology. BGP-15 directly addresses mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic oxidative stress—core drivers of RPE degeneration—by concentrating in mitochondria, lowering ROS at complexes I/III, stabilizing Δψm, and activating survival signaling while suppressing inflammatory stress kinases (Sumegi et al., 2017). Concurrently, it co-induces the HSR by remodeling plasma membrane rafts and modulating HSF1 acetylation, thereby boosting HSP70/HSP25 chaperone capacity and proteostasis—functions that are expected to mitigate protein misfolding and aggregation in aged RPE (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

- Pleiotropic yet coherent mechanism spanning membrane, nuclear, and mitochondrial nodes. The membrane–HSR–mitochondrial triad, including PARP/MKP-1/JNK–p38 and Akt/GSK-3β axes, provides multiple intervention points likely to translate into robust protection in the multifactorial environment of dry AMD (Crul et al., 2013; Sumegi et al., 2017; Szabó et al., 2018; Horváth et al., 2021).

Proof-of-concept human trials in insulin resistance show pharmacodynamic activity without overt safety signals, and HSP co-inducers are known to preferentially act in stressed cells, potentially limiting off-target effects in quiescent tissues; local ocular delivery further improves the therapeutic index (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011; Takács et al., 2024).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Lack of direct dry AMD evidence. No studies in the corpus directly test BGP-15 in dry AMD models or patients; we infer utility from retinal IR/diabetes models and mechanism (Takács et al., 2024).  
- Exposure–response uncertainties for the posterior segment. Systemic serum concentrations are low relative to micromolar efficacious concentrations in vitro, necessitating optimized local delivery to RPE; although eyedrop formulations show retinal effects, posterior-segment delivery by topical route is often limited, and pharmacokinetics were not measured in the cited ocular study (Sümegi, 2018; Takács et al., 2024).  
- Target ambiguity and pleiotropy. While the membrane–HSR–mitochondrial framework is coherent, BGP-15 lacks a single defined receptor/protein target, and its in vitro PARP-1 inhibition likely does not drive in vivo efficacy; this complicates target engagement assays and regulatory narratives (Sümegi, 2018; Crul et al., 2013).  
- Nomenclature confusion. “BGP-15” also denotes a calcipotriene-derived vitamin D3 analog in the oncology literature; chemical identity must be verified to avoid conflation during procurement and CMC (Sintov et al., 2013; Takács et al., 2024).  
- Evidence base heterogeneity. Some ocular and cardiovascular studies are published in lower–quality venues, emphasizing the need for rigorous, blinded replication and GLP toxicology in ocular models (Horváth et al., 2021; Wachal et al., 2021).

Recommended next steps  
- In vitro RPE validation. In human primary or iPSC-derived RPE under oxidative (H₂O₂/tert-butyl hydroperoxide) and inflammatory (LPS/CpG) stress, test BGP-15 at 0.3–30 µM for effects on Δψm (JC-1/TMRM), mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX), total ROS (DHR123), apoptosis/necrosis (annexin V/PI), and mitochondrial respiration; confirm no direct antioxidant scavenging in cell-free systems (Sumegi et al., 2017).  
- Proteostasis and HSR endpoints. Quantify HSP70/HSP25 induction, HSF1 acetylation/binding dynamics, Rac1 activation, and membrane raft integrity using fPEG-cholesterol probes/TOCCSL in RPE; evaluate MKP-1, JNK/p38, and Akt/GSK-3β signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013; Sumegi et al., 2017).  
- Mitochondrial dynamics. Assess OPA1 oligomerization, fusion/fission balance (Mfn1/2 and Drp1 markers), cristae morphology by EM, and PGC-1α/mtDNA copy number to benchmark fusion/biogenesis responses (Szabó et al., 2018; Horváth et al., 2021).  
- Ocular delivery PK/PD. Using the SBECD eyedrop formulation as a starting point, perform ocular pharmacokinetics (vitreous, retina, RPE–choroid) and pharmacodynamics (ocular HSP70, NFκB, mitochondrial markers) to ensure RPE target engagement at tolerated doses (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021).  
- In vivo retinal stress models. Extend to retinal oxidative stress paradigms that capture RPE pathology; leverage ERG, OCT, histology, and mitochondrial ultrastructure endpoints already positive in IR/diabetic models (Takács et al., 2024).  
- Identity control and CMC. Source BGP-15 as O-(3-piperidino-2-hydroxy-1-propyl) nicotinic amidoxime dihydrochloride; confirm identity by NMR/MS to avoid the calcipotriene-derived analog (Takács et al., 2024; Sintov et al., 2013).

Go/no-go considerations for dry AMD  
Given the robust mechanistic alignment—mitochondrial ROS control at complexes I/III, Δψm stabilization, HSR co-induction via membrane raft remodeling and HSF1 acetylation control, OPA1-driven mitochondrial fusion, and suppression of ROS-sensitive inflammatory kinases—plus demonstrable ocular efficacy in retinal injury models, BGP-15 merits advancement to RPE-focused preclinical validation for dry AMD (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Szabó et al., 2018; Takács et al., 2024). The principal risks are translational: ensuring adequate RPE exposures by ocular delivery, confirming RPE target expression/engagement, and generating rigorous GLP pharmacology/toxicology data in ocular species. On balance, the mechanistic breadth that often complicates development is an advantage in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction, proteostasis failure, and chronic inflammation coexist.

Conclusion. BGP-15 is a credible repurposing candidate for dry AMD based on its mitochondria-centered, HSP co-inducing, membrane-lipid–modulating pharmacology and encouraging retinal efficacy in vivo; priority should be given to RPE-targeted PK/PD, mitochondrial and HSR biomarker validation, and controlled efficacy studies in retinal oxidative-stress models to de-risk translation (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Takács et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Sulforaphane is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate originally identified in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli and Brussels sprouts. It is generated through the hydrolysis of glucoraphanin by the enzyme myrosinase, which is released upon plant tissue damage. As a member of the phytochemical family, sulforaphane belongs to a class of natural compounds known for inducing phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins. Historically, this compound has been extensively investigated for its chemopreventive and cytoprotective properties, particularly through the activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. Being one of the most studied Nrf2 activators, its discovery stemmed from early investigations into dietary antioxidants and their role in reducing carcinogenesis and inflammation. In the context of drug development, sulforaphane is considered a promising candidate for repurposing because it combines a favorable preclinical safety profile with a well-characterized mechanism of action that includes modulation of intracellular redox signaling. Its broad application in preclinical studies to ameliorate oxidative stress and inflammation suggests that targeted delivery to retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells might help alleviate the oxidative injury observed in geographic atrophy, the advanced form of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Bellezza, 2018; Chang et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Sulforaphane has attracted considerable attention for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties over the past two decades. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its protective effects in various models of oxidative stress, including those involving retinal tissues and RPE cells. In in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells—a well-accepted human RPE model—sulforaphane exhibited dose-dependent protection against oxidative insults induced by agents such as tert-butyl hydroperoxide (t-BOOH) and hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂). These experiments demonstrated that sulforaphane pretreatment significantly reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and mitigated mitochondrial membrane potential damage, ultimately leading to reduced apoptotic cell death (Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021). Similarly, other investigations have reported sulforaphane’s ability to induce cytoprotective genes in RPE cells through Nrf2 activation, resulting in improved cell survival under stress conditions (Zhang et al., 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Moreover, several in vivo studies in rodent models have provided evidence of sulforaphane-mediated retinal neuroprotection. Examples include models of photooxidative damage in mice, where sulforaphane delayed photoreceptor degeneration and prevented RPE dysfunction—mechanisms that are highly relevant to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Bellezza, 2018). However, it should be noted that although sulforaphane has been studied in various retinal degeneration models, there is no established clinical history of its use in human dry AMD. Nevertheless, its promising preclinical efficacy in ameliorating oxidative injury in RPE cells, coupled with its demonstrated safety across multiple biological systems including ocular tissues, supports its potential repurposing as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Qin, 2007; del Cano et al., 2008).

Mechanism of Action:  
The principal mechanism underlying sulforaphane’s protective effects is its ability to activate the Nrf2 pathway. Under basal conditions, the transcription factor Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytosol via binding to its inhibitor, Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1), which directs Nrf2 for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Sulforaphane, owing to its electrophilic isothiocyanate moiety, reacts with critical cysteine residues on Keap1. This modification alters the conformation of Keap1 and prevents the degradation of Nrf2, leading to its stabilization and subsequent nuclear translocation (Wherry, 2013). Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to antioxidant response elements (ARE) in the promoter regions of various cytoprotective genes. The result is a robust induction of phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), and superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2). These enzymes play critical roles in neutralizing ROS, repairing oxidative damage, and maintaining cellular redox balance (Qin, 2007; Zhang et al., 2024).

In addition to its classic Nrf2-dependent antioxidant response, sulforaphane has been shown to modulate other cellular pathways that are important for mitochondrial health. In retinal cells, sulforaphane has been reported to attenuate mitochondrial membrane potential collapse and reduce mitochondrial superoxide production, as evidenced by decreased MitoSOX fluorescence in treated ARPE-19 cells (Chang et al., 2020). These mitochondrial protective actions are thought to involve the upregulation of antioxidant enzymes that localize to the mitochondria, as well as enhancement of the spare respiratory capacity—thereby preserving ATP generation under oxidative stress conditions. Furthermore, sulforaphane has been implicated in the regulation of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis, which is critical for mitochondrial biogenesis and metabolic homeostasis. This dual engagement—both through Nrf2-driven transcriptional activation and mitochondrial biogenesis pathways—positions sulforaphane as a multifaceted agent capable of sustaining cellular energy production and reducing oxidative injury in the RPE, a cell type that is particularly vulnerable in geographic atrophy (Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).

Beyond its antioxidant effects, sulforaphane also exerts anti-inflammatory properties by downregulating the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and adhesion molecules (e.g., ICAM-1, MCP-1). This is particularly relevant in the context of AMD, where chronic low-grade inflammation is believed to exacerbate RPE dysfunction and drusen formation (Chang et al., 2020; del Cano et al., 2008). In summary, the molecular interactions of sulforaphane—ranging from direct modification of Keap1 to the induction of mitochondrial antioxidant defenses—provide a robust mechanistic rationale for its potential utility in mitigating the multifactorial oxidative and inflammatory challenges associated with dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Given its well-documented mechanism of action, the hypothesis that sulforaphane induces Nrf2-mediated mitochondrial antioxidant pathways in RPE cells is strongly supported by preclinical evidence. When RPE cells are subjected to oxidative stress, it is expected that sulforaphane treatment will lead to a dose-dependent upregulation of Nrf2 target genes including HO-1, NQO1, and SOD2. The elevation of these transcripts correlates with a reduction in mitochondrial superoxide levels, as measured by decreased MitoSOX fluorescence, and an improvement in the spare respiratory capacity—a surrogate marker for mitochondrial function and ATP generation (Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).

In cellular assays using ARPE-19 cells, administration of sulforaphane prior to oxidative challenge has been shown to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential and decrease cytochrome c release, thereby reducing the activation of downstream apoptotic cascades. The suppression of ROS production and the preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics result in improved cell viability and reduced apoptotic indices. For instance, studies have demonstrated that sulforaphane pretreatment leads to lower levels of cleaved caspase-3 and PARP-1, indicating a direct link between enhanced antioxidant defense and the inhibition of programmed cell death pathways in RPE cells (Yang et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2020).

At the molecular level, the expected outcome of sulforaphane administration in a dry AMD context is multifactorial. The compound would elevate the expression of cytoprotective enzymes that not only detoxify reactive oxygen species but also facilitate the repair of oxidatively damaged macromolecules. This should translate into a measurable decrease in overall oxidative stress markers, preservation of mitochondrial function (evidenced by sustained ATP production and improved spare respiratory capacity), and stabilization of the RPE cell phenotype. Moreover, since mitochondrial dysfunction is a central element of geographic atrophy pathogenesis, sulforaphane’s ability to maintain ATP generation could directly counteract the energy deficit observed in degenerating RPE cells (Zhang et al., 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

These expected effects are supported by a range of preclinical studies. For example, quantitative redox fluorometry results reported in ARPE-19 cells indicate that sulforaphane-treated cells maintain a significantly higher redox ratio during oxidative challenge compared to untreated controls, which is indicative of an enhanced antioxidant state. Additionally, the upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants and improved bioenergetic profiles have been correlated with better cell survival outcomes, reinforcing the concept that sulforaphane can counteract the deleterious cellular changes observed in models of dry AMD (del Cano et al., 2008; Qin, 2007).

Overall Evaluation:  
Sulforaphane, as exemplified by the Sigma-Aldrich S4441 formulation, presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD, particularly targeting the geographic atrophy form characterized by pronounced RPE degeneration. One of the major strengths of sulforaphane lies in its robust preclinical evidence demonstrating its ability to induce the Nrf2 pathway, a master regulator of oxidative stress responses. The compound’s direct modification of Keap1 and subsequent stabilization and nuclear translocation of Nrf2 trigger the upregulation of several antioxidant enzymes, such as HO-1, NQO1, and SOD2—which are critical for detoxifying reactive oxygen species and repairing oxidative damage in RPE cells (Qin, 2007; Zhang et al., 2024).

Furthermore, sulforaphane’s additional capacity to preserve mitochondrial function by maintaining membrane potential and supporting ATP synthesis addresses a major pathological hallmark of geographic atrophy, where mitochondrial dysfunction leads to energy depletion and accelerates cell death. The integration of mitochondrial antioxidant defenses with the broader cytoprotective effects of Nrf2 activation provides a convergent mechanism aimed at both preventing oxidative damage and sustaining cellular energy production under stress conditions (Yang et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2020).

Another notable strength is the extensive safety data available for sulforaphane from preclinical studies. Its natural occurrence, combined with its well-documented bioactivity in a range of cell types, underscores its potential for repurposing in ocular applications. Moreover, sulforaphane’s ability to attenuate inflammatory responses by reducing the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines adds an extra layer of therapeutic benefit, considering the role of chronic inflammation in exacerbating AMD pathology (del Cano et al., 2008; Chang et al., 2020).

Despite these promising attributes, several challenges remain. One potential limitation is the bioavailability of sulforaphane. Like many natural compounds, sulforaphane may face pharmacokinetic hurdles such as poor water solubility and limited tissue penetration, which could complicate systemic delivery or localized administration to the retina. Furthermore, while the preclinical efficacy in ARPE-19 cell models and animal studies is encouraging, the translation of these findings to human patients with dry AMD remains to be validated. Variability in the cellular responses between in vitro models and the complex microenvironment of the human retina, including the influence of the blood–retinal barrier, poses a potential risk for suboptimal therapeutic delivery (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Qin, 2007).

Additionally, some of the supportive data for sulforaphane’s efficacy in ocular systems come from studies published in journals with variable impact, and additional high-quality clinical studies will be necessary to establish its safety and efficacy profile in the context of dry AMD. The dosing regimens, potential off-target effects, and long-term impact of chronic Nrf2 activation in retinal tissues also require careful investigation. There is ongoing debate over the potential for Nrf2 activators to have biphasic dose responses, where excessive activation might inadvertently cause cellular stress or dysregulate normal redox homeostasis (Bellezza, 2018; del Cano et al., 2008).

In conclusion, sulforaphane demonstrates strong mechanistic potential for the treatment of dry AMD by elevating key antioxidant defenses in RPE cells and preserving mitochondrial function under oxidative stress. Its ability to induce HO-1, NQO1, and SOD2 in response to oxidative challenges and thereby reduce superoxide production while maintaining ATP synthesis is directly aligned with the therapeutic needs of geographic atrophy patients. The preclinical evidence suggests that, with appropriate formulation and delivery strategies, sulforaphane could provide a dual benefit by mitigating oxidative injury and reducing inflammation in the retina. However, further studies are required to address bioavailability challenges and to validate its clinical efficacy in well-designed human trials. Overall, sulforaphane merits further investigation as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, and its advancement into early-phase clinical testing is justified by the compelling preclinical data available (Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; del Cano et al., 2008).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
XJB-5-131 is a synthetic mitochondria‐targeted nitroxide antioxidant that was developed by conjugating a redox‐active nitroxide moiety (derived from TEMPO, 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl) to a mitochondrial‐targeting peptide fragment derived from gramicidin S (often described in the literature as a hemigramicidin or alkene peptide isostere) (Liu et al., 2022; Robinson, 2012). This design harnesses the properties of the nitroxide, which is capable of catalytically scavenging reactive oxygen and lipid radicals through cycling between its nitroxide, hydroxylamine, and oxoammonium states, and the targeting moiety that enhances its lipid membrane permeability while concentrating the compound specifically in mitochondrial membranes (Wipf et al., 2022; Xun et al., 2022). The neutral charge of XJB-5-131 confers an advantage because it permits mitochondrial uptake independent of membrane potential, a feature that distinguishes it from the positively charged mitochondria-targeted antioxidants such as MitoQ (Robinson, 2012; Wipf et al., 2022). Moreover, fluorescent derivatives (e.g., BODIPY-labeled analogs) have been used to confirm its preferential accumulation in mitochondria by co-localization with mitochondrial markers, demonstrating an approximately 600-fold enrichment relative to the cytosol in some animal models (Wipf et al., 2022; Xun et al., 2022). Overall, XJB-5-131 belongs to the class of mitochondria-targeted nitroxides, a class that has been extensively studied for its ability to modulate oxidative stress in cellular and animal models across a variety of tissues (Xun et al., 2022; Robinson, 2012).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, XJB-5-131 has been the subject of preclinical investigation in several models of oxidative stress-related injury. It was originally developed to protect neuronal mitochondria and has been evaluated in models of Huntington’s disease, where it mitigated somatic instability and toxicity by reducing oxidative DNA damage and delaying motor decline (Liu et al., 2022; Xun et al., 2022). In various studies, XJB-5-131 demonstrated robust efficacy in reducing mitochondrial lipid peroxidation and preserving electron transport chain function in brain, neuronal, and even cardiac cell models (Robinson, 2012; Wipf et al., 2022). Additionally, its use in spinal cord injury models has shown that it can attenuate cardiolipin oxidation and reduce the activation of apoptotic cascades, leading to decreased lesion sizes and improved functional recovery (Ji et al., 2015; Robinson, 2012). There is also evidence of its application in models of ischemia–reperfusion injury, where its ability to blunt the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) was associated with neuroprotection (Xun et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022). Outside of central nervous system paradigms, related mitochondria-targeted nitroxides have been applied in experimental settings addressing ferroptosis and other oxidative stress pathologies (Zhang et al., 2024; Xun et al., 2022). However, despite its established role in neurological and other high-oxidative stress tissues, there is no direct published record – within the context of the available literature – demonstrating that XJB-5-131 has been used to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or any retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)-specific diseases (Wipf et al., 2022). Nonetheless, its pharmacological profile suggests potential applicability in settings where chronic oxidative stress drives pathology.

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism by which XJB-5-131 exerts its effects is twofold. First, the nitroxide moiety functions as a redox-active electron scavenger. Under oxidative stress, the nitroxide group readily interconverts with its hydroxylamine and oxoammonium forms; this redox cycling is capable of neutralizing superoxide anions (O2•–) by oxidizing them to molecular oxygen and hydrogen peroxide, effectively mimicking the activity of superoxide dismutase (SOD) (Wipf et al., 2022). Additionally, the hydroxylamine state can donate a hydrogen atom to terminate radical chain reactions, thereby neutralizing lipid peroxyl radicals that propagate lipid peroxidation – a process central to drusen formation and RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Robinson, 2012; Xun et al., 2022). Second, the gramicidin-derived delivery moiety imparts mitochondrial selectivity due to its structural mimicry of naturally occurring cyclic peptides that exhibit high lipid membrane affinity. This results in an efficient and selective accumulation of the antioxidant within the inner mitochondrial membrane, which is particularly important given that mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage have been implicated in aging and various degenerative diseases (Wipf et al., 2022). Experimental studies have shown that XJB-5-131 can act as a mild uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation, leading to a slight increase in oxygen consumption without detrimentally affecting ATP production; this mild uncoupling may serve to lower the mitochondrial membrane potential, thereby reducing the propensity for electron leakage and subsequent ROS generation (Xun et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2024). Furthermore, XJB-5-131’s ability to reduce mitochondrial ROS levels has been documented using both biochemical assays based on Amplex Red for hydrogen peroxide detection and Seahorse assays for oxygen consumption rate (OCR) analysis (Xun et al., 2022). These combined actions—the direct scavenging of radical species and the dampening of ROS-generating processes via mild uncoupling—support a mechanism by which XJB-5-131 could preserve mitochondrial structure (e.g., cristae integrity) and function under chronic oxidative conditions.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD and RPE Context:  
In the context of dry AMD, the pathophysiology is strongly linked to chronic oxidative insult, particularly within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where elevated ROS and lipid peroxidation contribute to mitochondrial dysfunction, accumulation of drusen constituents, and eventual RPE degeneration. The dual mechanism of XJB-5-131 is especially promising for this disease. Given its lipid radical scavenging capabilities, XJB-5-131 is expected to reduce malondialdehyde (MDA) and other markers of lipid peroxidation that are elevated in RPE under chronic UVA or other oxidative stresses (Ji et al., 2015). The compound’s well-documented ability to decrease ROS levels in neuronal and cardiac models, while preserving overall mitochondrial respiration, suggests that similar protective effects can be anticipated in RPE cells, which are highly metabolically active and depend critically on mitochondrial health (Wipf et al., 2022). In preliminary in vitro assays – such as those using pig RPE explants under UVA stress – one would expect XJB-5-131 to reduce MDA-adduct formation and preserve mitochondrial cristae, thereby maintaining cellular homeostasis (the hypothesis provided). At a molecular level, by delivering the nitroxide directly into RPE mitochondria, the compound would catalytically neutralize both superoxide and lipid peroxyl radicals. This dual scavenging effect can interrupt the vicious cycle of chronic oxidative damage that drives RPE dysfunction and drusen accumulation (Liu et al., 2022). Expression studies have demonstrated that genes associated with oxidative stress regulation, such as those encoding SOD and other mitochondrial antioxidants, are active in RPE cells, further supporting the notion that a mitochondria-targeted intervention like XJB-5-131 could restore redox homeostasis in these cells (Wipf et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024). Additionally, by functionally acting as a mild uncoupler, XJB-5-131 may lower mitochondrial membrane potential just enough to reduce electron leakage without compromising adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthesis, a delicate balance that is particularly important given the high energy requirements of the RPE (Zhou et al., 2024; Ji et al., 2015). Altogether, these effects are anticipated to culminate in the preservation of cristae integrity, reduced oxidative damage, and ultimately improved cell survival—key outcomes that align with the therapeutic goals in treating dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, XJB-5-131 emerges as an attractive candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD owing to several intrinsic strengths. Foremost among these is its robust mitochondrial targeting capability. Nevertheless, there are certain limitations and challenges that must be carefully considered before advancing XJB-5-131 into dry AMD studies. Notably, while its efficacy in neuronal, spinal cord, and ischemia-reperfusion models has been well documented, there is a paucity of direct preclinical data demonstrating its benefits specifically in RPE cells or models of retinal degeneration (Wipf et al., 2022; Robinson, 2012). Its ability to deliver a nitroxide antioxidant directly to mitochondria, neutralize deleterious ROS, and preserve mitochondrial function aligns well with the current understanding of RPE pathology in dry AMD. Future research should focus on rigorous evaluation in RPE cell culture systems and animal models of dry AMD, optimization of ocular delivery strategies, and comprehensive toxicological assessments to ensure both efficacy and safety in the intended indication (Xun et al., 2022; Bowie, 2018; Wipf et al., 2022). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Resveratrol is a naturally occurring polyphenolic compound belonging to the stilbene class and is structurally defined as 3,5,4′-trihydroxystilbene. Originally isolated from the White Hellebore in the mid-20th century and later found in red wine due to grape skin fermentation, resveratrol has garnered significant attention not only for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties but also for its potential benefits in cardiovascular and neuroprotective contexts (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pop et al., 2022). As such, resveratrol—and by extension its commercial version (Cayman Chemical #70580) used in our studies—is classified as a nutraceutical and drug candidate with a long track record of investigative research including applications in aging, inflammation, and ocular health (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Pop et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
A considerable volume of biochemical, preclinical, and early clinical literature has explored resveratrol’s broad spectrum of activities. Historically, resveratrol has been investigated primarily for its cardioprotective and neuroprotective effects, as well as its anti-aging properties. In the realm of ophthalmology, several in vitro and animal studies have focused on its role in retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD), diabetic retinopathy (DR), and glaucoma. For instance, its use in RPE cell models has shown promising evidence for ameliorating oxidative stress-induced damage, a central factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Clinical investigations have attempted to translate these findings, as exemplified by the terminated clinical trial NCT02625376 that investigated resveratrol for exudative AMD (Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015), highlighting both the potential and the challenges involved in its clinical application (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Beyond ocular applications, resveratrol’s inclusion in various nutraceutical formulations underscores its established safety profile when administered at low-to-moderate doses, although issues pertaining to bioavailability and rapid systemic metabolism have been recurrent themes in the literature (Abu-Amero et al., 2016).
