At a molecular level, resveratrol exerts its effects primarily by modulating multiple intracellular signaling cascades. The central hypothesis we are testing is that resveratrol activates the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells—a pathway integral to regulating mitochondrial biogenesis and the antioxidant defense system. Activation of SIRT1, a NAD+-dependent deacetylase, by resveratrol increases the deacetylation and activation of its downstream effector, AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Once activated, AMPK facilitates the phosphorylation and activation of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1 alpha (PGC-1α) in the cytoplasm, which subsequently translocates to the nucleus to upregulate the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and antioxidant responses, including the gene encoding superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). This cascade not only improves mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and spare respiratory capacity—critical indicators of cellular health under oxidative stress—but also promotes an overall enhancement of cellular resilience against reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Bel, 2020; Bryl et al., 2022). Further molecular studies indicate that resveratrol can also modulate extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERK1/2) and mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK), contributing additional layers of cytoprotection through anti-apoptotic effects (Pop et al., 2022; Pop et al., 2022). Together, these mechanistic insights provide a comprehensive biochemical framework through which resveratrol is hypothesized to mitigate the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in RPE cells—a primary factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2021; Bryl et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of the proposed assay for dry AMD, our expectation is that resveratrol will exert a multifaceted protective effect on RPE cells under oxidative challenge. Specifically, when RPE cells are exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as a model for oxidative stress, resveratrol is anticipated to counteract the resultant mitochondrial dysfunction by upregulating antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2, thereby reducing intracellular ROS levels (Bel, 2020; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Restoration of the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) is a critical endpoint, as it directly reflects cellular energy status and the ability of mitochondria to sustain ATP synthesis under stress (Buonfiglio et al., 2024). In addition, an improvement in spare respiratory capacity—the measure of a cell’s ability to respond to increased energy demands—should be evident, reflecting enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and a greater capacity for cellular repair mechanisms (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bryl et al., 2022). These cytoprotective effects have been demonstrated in in vitro studies using ARPE-19 and other human retinal pigment epithelial cell lines, and they resonate with the established role of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis in mediating energy metabolism and antioxidative defenses in the retina (Bryl et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021). Moreover, by decreasing the accrual of oxidative damage, resveratrol is expected to limit apoptotic signaling pathways, which are crucial in slowing the progressive degeneration observed in dry AMD (Bel, 2020; Pop et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
The cumulative evidence from preclinical studies strongly supports the potential of resveratrol as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, especially considering its capacity to modulate mitochondrial function and activate intrinsic antioxidant defenses. The activation of the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis not only augments mitochondrial biogenesis but also enhances the expression of key antioxidant enzymes required to neutralize ROS, thereby directly addressing one of the primary mechanisms underlying AMD pathology (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Bryl et al., 2022). One of the major strengths of resveratrol is its pleiotropic mode of action; beyond its antioxidant properties, its anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic activities further consolidate its candidacy for chronic conditions like dry AMD (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Bel, 2020). Furthermore, extensive safety data in various preclinical models indicate that resveratrol is well tolerated at certain dose ranges, which is a positive indicator for its potential clinical translation (Wang et al., 2021; Bel, 2020).

However, several limitations remain that warrant careful consideration. The primary challenge with resveratrol is its poor bioavailability and rapid metabolism, which may result in subtherapeutic tissue concentrations despite high oral absorption. This has driven research efforts into advanced drug delivery platforms, such as nanoparticle-based systems and liposomal formulations, aimed at enhancing ocular retention and achieving sustained drug levels in the retina (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Additionally, although the in vitro and animal model data are promising, there exists a dearth of robust clinical trial data specifically addressing dry AMD, as evidenced by the terminated trial in exudative AMD (Resveratrol for exudative age-related macular degeneration, 2015) and the limited clinical evidence in related retinal pathologies (Abu-Amero et al., 2016). Another potential weakness is the dose-dependent duality of its mechanism, where low doses predominantly mediate SIRT1-dependent effects, whereas higher doses might trigger SIRT1-independent pathways, possibly leading to off-target effects or toxicity (Abu-Amero et al., 2016; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Such a narrow therapeutic window necessitates a precise optimization of dosing regimens and formulation strategies. Despite these challenges, the overarching trend in preclinical research underscores that with proper formulation and dosing strategies, resveratrol could excel as an adjuvant or even monotherapy for protecting RPE cells from oxidative injury and, consequently, for the management of dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Abu-Amero et al., 2016).

In-Depth Analysis of Preclinical and Clinical Evidence:  
Numerous in vitro studies have characterized the effect of resveratrol on retinal pigment epithelial cells, notably ARPE-19 cell lines, under conditions of oxidative stress. Such studies consistently demonstrate that resveratrol treatment leads to a measurable reduction in ROS levels, a decrease in markers of apoptosis, and an overall improvement in mitochondrial parameters including Δψm and spare respiratory capacity (Bel, 2020; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). These findings are reinforced by experiments showing that resveratrol can mitigate blue light-induced retinal damage and preserve cell viability, further supporting its relevance in ocular pathologies where light-induced oxidative stress is a contributing factor (Bel, 2020). Complementary studies in animal models have shown that resveratrol can reduce inflammatory cytokine secretion and inhibit processes such as choroidal neovascularization, which has implications not only for dry AMD but also for its neovascular (wet) counterpart (Bryl et al., 2022; Bel, 2020).

Moreover, mechanistic investigations into the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis reveal that the deacetylation of PGC-1α is a critical step in the upregulation of mitochondrial genes, which directly correlates with increased cellular ATP production and enhanced resistance to oxidative stress (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Experimental data also show that SOD2 expression is significantly increased following resveratrol treatment, corroborating the compound’s role in boosting the cellular antioxidant capacity (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). These molecular events culminate in an environment that is less conducive to oxidative damage, thereby potentially arresting or even reversing some aspects of RPE degeneration that occur in dry AMD (Bryl et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021).

From a clinical perspective, the application of resveratrol in ocular disorders has been approached with caution, primarily due to pharmacokinetic challenges. Even though systemic administration of resveratrol has demonstrated efficacy in reducing plasma oxidative markers in diabetic patients and other conditions, the translation to ocular tissue remains hindered by its low aqueous solubility and rapid hepatic metabolism (Kaštelan et al., 2025; Abu-Amero et al., 2016). To overcome these barriers, innovative drug delivery systems such as chitosan-based nanoparticles, polymeric micelles, and liposomal formulations are being actively developed and show promise for achieving therapeutic levels in retinal tissues (Pop et al., 2022; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Such advanced formulations not only improve bioavailability but also allow for controlled release, which is essential for a chronic condition like dry AMD where sustained therapeutic action is desirable.

Additional mechanistic studies also suggest that resveratrol’s efficacy might be enhanced when used in combination with other therapeutic agents. As a consequence, only minimal amounts of unchanged resveratrol reach the systemic circulation and, by extension, the ocular tissues. Current research thus prioritizes the optimization of drug delivery vehicles to enhance its stability and target specificity. Nanotechnology-based delivery methods, including polymeric nanoparticles and solid lipid nanoparticles, have demonstrated enhanced tissue penetration and prolonged drug retention in the eye (Pop et al., 2022; Kaštelan et al., 2025). Given the multifaceted biological activities of resveratrol and the encouraging preclinical evidence in models of oxidative stress-induced RPE damage, it holds considerable promise as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to modulate the SIRT1/AMPK–PGC-1α axis and promote mitochondrial biogenesis presents a novel therapeutic approach that directly targets the cellular dysfunctions underlying RPE degeneration. In studies involving human skeletal muscle cells, EUK-134 has been shown to attenuate endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress-induced mitochondrial dysfunction induced by tunicamycin, resulting in improved mitochondrial membrane potential and restoration of bioenergetic profiles (Thoma et al., 2020). Moreover, this compound has been evaluated in contexts such as hyperoxic myocardial tissues, where it mitigated oxidative damage and contributed to the preservation of cellular function under stress conditions (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). Its potential benefits in reducing oxidative damage have also been noted in studies involving breast cancer cells and mechanical unloading-induced muscle atrophy, highlighting its versatility as a ROS-scavenging agent (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).  
Despite the significant body of work on EUK-134 in non-ocular tissues, its direct evaluation in dry AMD or similar degenerative retinal conditions has not yet been thoroughly explored. Clinical trials and literature searches focusing on Mn-porphyrin SOD mimetics have yielded extensive data relating to retinal diseases (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.), but EUK-134 itself has not been the primary focus in retinal clinical applications. Nonetheless, its proven mechanism of reducing ROS accumulation positions it as an attractive candidate for extension into the field of ocular therapeutics. In this light, the repurposing of EUK-134 for dry AMD is based on the hypothesis that its antioxidant properties, previously validated in muscle and other tissues, may confer similar protective effects in RPE cells that are chronically exposed to oxidative stress (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, EUK-134 functions by catalytically mimicking the activities of superoxide dismutase and catalase. In its SOD mimetic capacity, EUK-134 accepts electrons from the superoxide anions, facilitating their conversion into hydrogen peroxide—a reaction which is essential to limit direct superoxide-mediated damage (Thoma et al., 2020). Following this, the catalase mimetic activity is intended to decompose the resultant hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, thereby preventing accumulation of H2O2 which can otherwise contribute to oxidative injury through Fenton-type reactions. However, several studies have drawn attention to limitations in this pathway. For example, evidence indicates that EUK-134 may exhibit a lower efficiency in H2O2 scavenging when compared to other antioxidants such as MnTBAP or native catalase, particularly in environments with high oxidative flux (Quan et al., 2017). One key observation is a significant down-regulation of catalase expression – by more than five-fold – upon EUK-134 treatment in some cellular systems, a factor that potentially undermines its capacity to fully counteract H2O2 buildup (Quan et al., 2017).  
On the molecular interaction front, the manganese center within the salen complex undergoes redox cycling, alternating between oxidation states in response to ROS encounters. This cyclic activity contributes to its continuous catalytic turnover and represents the biochemical foundation for its antioxidant action. Furthermore, studies have shown that EUK-134 can modulate various signaling pathways associated with oxidative stress responses, such as the TGF-β1/Smad2 pathway in muscle under atrophy-inducing conditions (Grujicic & Allen, 2024). Despite these promising aspects, challenges such as suboptimal mitochondrial uptake remain a concern since effective neutralization of ROS in RPE cells requires prompt access to the mitochondrial matrix—a compartment frequently characterized by an inherently challenging microenvironment for drug delivery (Quan et al., 2017). In summary, while EUK-134 possesses a dual action mechanism that addresses two key components of the ROS cascade, the efficiency of its H2O2 detoxification and its cellular distribution are critical parameters that must be rigorously characterized in the context of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
In dry AMD and particularly in geographic atrophy, the retinal pigment epithelium is subject to sustained oxidative stress, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and subsequent cell death. The expected therapeutic effect of EUK-134 in this context is to provide robust antioxidant protection within RPE mitochondria, thereby neutralizing excessive superoxide and hydrogen peroxide levels and preserving mitochondrial integrity (Thoma et al., 2020). Restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) is a key indicator of improved mitochondrial function; thus, by mitigating ROS-induced depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane, EUK-134 is anticipated to maintain or restore ATP production and spare respiratory capacity in RPE cells. These effects are crucial given that ATP depletion and bioenergetic failure are prominent features in the pathology of dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012).  
In vitro assays that simulate oxidative stress conditions—such as those employing RPE cell cultures under hypoxic or chemically induced stress—will likely measure parameters including Δψm, ATP levels, ROS quantification, and expression levels of stress-responsive genes. The anticipated outcome is that EUK-134 will lead to a measurable decrease in the levels of ROS as detected by biochemical assays, along with a concomitant stabilization of mitochondrial respiratory function (Thoma et al., 2020; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012). In addition, molecular analyses may reveal a down-regulation of oxidative stress markers and an improvement in the overall redox balance of the cell. It is vital, however, to consider that some studies have noted that EUK-134 does not inhibit all markers of stress uniformly—for example, the continued expression of GADD34 has been observed even where other stress indicators are normalized (Thoma et al., 2020).  
Given that RPE cells naturally express endogenous antioxidant enzymes such as SOD and catalase, supplementation with EUK-134 is expected to either bolster these defenses or compensate for their decline during chronic oxidative challenges. This dual functionality could theoretically translate into a reduced progression of RPE cell death, slower accumulation of drusen, and ultimately a deceleration of geographic atrophy, all of which are hallmarks of dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall evaluation of EUK-134 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration involves weighing its mechanistic promise against the practical challenges encountered in its preclinical and potential clinical application. On the one hand, EUK-134 embodies several clear strengths. Its dual mimetic activities align well with the fundamental pathophysiology of dry AMD, where both superoxide and hydrogen peroxide are implicated in the oxidative cascade that leads to mitochondrial dysfunction and RPE cell demise (Thoma et al., 2020; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012). The synthetic nature of EUK-134 allows for controlled chemical modifications which could be leveraged to optimize its pharmacokinetic properties, and its relatively small size is an asset for penetrating tissues such as the retina. Additionally, the compound’s history in attenuating ER stress-related mitochondrial dysfunction in muscle cells provides a robust proof-of-concept that similar benefits might be translatable to RPE cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress (Thoma et al., 2020).  
Notwithstanding these advantages, several weaknesses must be scrutinized. A primary concern lies in the evidence that EUK-134 may exhibit limitations in catalase-like activity, particularly with regard to its efficiency in cleaving hydrogen peroxide. Studies have documented a significant down-regulation of catalase expression upon treatment with EUK-134 and noted that its H2O2 scavenging capabilities fall short when benchmarked against other agents such as MnTBAP or even native catalase (Quan et al., 2017). In the context of RPE cells, where the oxidative insult is persistent and multifactorial, such limitations could result in suboptimal clearance of H2O2, thereby potentially compromising the therapeutic efficacy.  
Another critical issue pertains to drug delivery and cellular bioavailability. The lipophilicity of EUK-134 is notably lower compared to some analogues, amounting to roughly 43% less lipophilicity in certain cases, which inherently limits its capacity to traverse cell membranes and accumulate in the mitochondrial matrix, where its activity is most needed (Limoli et al., 2006; Quan et al., 2017). Since efficient mitochondrial delivery is crucial for counteracting localized ROS buildup in RPE cells, a deficiency in this area might significantly restrict the net antioxidant benefit provided by EUK-134.  
Furthermore, the translational history of EUK-134 presents a challenge in directly correlating preclinical observations with anticipated clinical outcomes in dry AMD. While substantial evidence exists linking EUK-134 with improved mitochondrial function in non-ocular tissues—such as the normalization of mitochondrial membrane potential in tunicamycin-induced ER stress models (Thoma et al., 2020)—there remains a paucity of direct data in ocular models. Compared to other antioxidants that have been more rigorously tested in retinal systems, EUK-134’s ocular pharmacodynamics, potential toxicity in the retinal microenvironment, and long-term safety profile are not well established (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Grujicic & Allen, 2024).  
The literature also points to the possibility of a paradoxical pro-oxidant effect. In some cellular environments, the administration of exogenous SOD mimetics can inadvertently shift the oxidative balance toward higher hydrogen peroxide levels if the catalase function is insufficient, thereby exacerbating oxidative stress rather than mitigating it (Limoli et al., 2006; Quan et al., 2017). Given the delicate balance required in the redox regulation of RPE cells, such an imbalance could be particularly detrimental.  
In light of these considerations, EUK-134’s potential for repurposing as a treatment for dry AMD is promising but remains conditional upon further optimization. The strengths of its dual antioxidant mechanism, its capacity to restore mitochondrial function, and its versatility as evidenced by its broad therapeutic history underscore its potential utility. However, the measurable shortcomings regarding efficient H2O2 clearance, the observed down-regulation of catalase expression, and uncertain mitochondrial bioavailability present hurdles that must be addressed in subsequent experimental phases. This will likely involve additional formulation strategies to improve cellular uptake, as well as comprehensive studies in appropriate retinal models to definitively correlate its antioxidant profile with functional improvements in RPE cells (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Quan et al., 2017).  
It is also noteworthy that while a broad range of clinical trials have been initiated for compounds with similar ROS-scavenging profiles in retinal degenerations (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.), there is a lack of direct clinical evidence for EUK-134’s efficacy specifically in the context of dry AMD. This gap further emphasizes the need for targeted preclinical studies focusing on ocular pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Establishing a direct connection between EUK-134’s known in vitro benefits and its performance in animal models of geographic atrophy will be essential prior to any clinical translation.  
In conclusion, the mechanistic rationale behind the use of EUK-134 in dry AMD is strong on theoretical grounds, leveraging its dual capacity to mitigate the damaging effects of both superoxide and hydrogen peroxide. However, the compound’s limitations—namely, its reduced effectiveness in scavenging H2O2 under certain conditions, its potential for down-regulating endogenous catalase, and challenges associated with adequate mitochondrial targeting—necessitate a cautious approach. The strategic pathway forward would involve an in-depth exploration of its pharmacological properties in retinal models, formulation modifications to enhance mitochondrial delivery, and dose-optimization studies to balance antioxidant efficacy with safety. Only after these issues are rigorously addressed can EUK-134 be confidently positioned as a viable repurposed candidate for the treatment of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Grujicic & Allen, 2024; Quan et al., 2017; Villamena, Das, & Nash, 2012).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is a naturally occurring long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (LC-PUFA) that has been isolated from marine sources, such as fish oil, and is commercially available in a highly purified form (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich D2534). DHA is synthesized via metabolic elongation and desaturation of dietary alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) in mammals; however, this endogenous conversion is limited, and direct dietary intake is critical for maintaining adequate retinal DHA levels (Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14). Belonging to the omega-3 class of fatty acids, DHA has long been recognized for its important roles in maintaining membrane structure and function, particularly in neural tissues and the retina where it is highly concentrated in photoreceptor outer segments and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) membranes (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3). Its polyunsaturated nature—with six cis double bonds—confers unique biophysical properties, enabling DHA to increase membrane fluidity and participate in critical signaling cascades. The compound has been used extensively as a nutritional supplement and has been incorporated in various formulations aimed at cardiovascular health, cognitive function, and ocular protection, establishing a robust safety profile over decades of human use (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Skowronska-Krawczyk & Chao, 2019, pp. 3–4).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past two decades, extensive research has explored the role of DHA and related omega-3 fatty acids in maintaining retinal function and potentially preventing age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Epidemiologic studies have consistently demonstrated an inverse association between dietary fish and high omega-3 fatty acid intake and the risk of developing AMD, suggesting that populations with higher DHA consumption tend to exhibit a lower incidence of both early and, to some extent, advanced forms of the disease (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). In clinical settings, large-scale randomized controlled trials, such as AREDS2, incorporated DHA (and EPA) into a multi-nutrient formula designed originally for AMD, though the overall randomized trial outcomes have been mixed, with some studies finding no statistically significant benefit for progression to late AMD (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). Pilot clinical trials and observational cohort studies, including NAT-1 and NAT-2, have assessed DHA supplementation in subjects with drusenoid lesions or early-stage AMD; while some of these studies have shown promising improvements in blood biomarkers (e.g., increased red blood cell DHA levels) and correlations with reduced AMD progression, the clinical efficacy remains under debate (Querques et al., 2016, pp. 2–4; Querques et al., 2011, pp. 7–8). Notably, evidence from animal models suggests that dietary DHA may protect against light-induced retinal degeneration and reduce the accumulation of deleterious lipid peroxidation products, although some preclinical studies also caution that DHA’s susceptibility to oxidation could, under certain conditions, worsen retinal injury (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic hypothesis for using DHA in dry AMD is based on its predicted ability to incorporate into the mitochondrial membranes of RPE cells, thereby enhancing membrane fluidity and protecting against oxidative damage to the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes. Under normal cellular conditions, DHA—owing to its multiple methylene-interrupted cis double bonds—integrates into phospholipid bilayers and modulates biophysical properties such as fluidity, permeability, and thickness (Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33). In mitochondrial membranes, this incorporation is thought to replace more saturated fatty acids such as arachidonic acid, ultimately reducing lipid peroxidation and mitigating oxidative stress that is deleterious to ETC function (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9). In vitro studies have shown that DHA supplementation in retinal cell cultures can decrease markers of apoptosis and preserve mitochondrial membrane integrity, with a concomitant increase in anti-apoptotic proteins (e.g., Bcl-2) (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 2–4).  
In addition, DHA is enzymatically converted under conditions of oxidative stress into neuroprotective docosanoids, such as neuroprotectin D1 (NPD1), which can inhibit pro-inflammatory gene expression and reduce cell death in RPE and photoreceptor cells (Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14; LaFuente et al., 2021, p. 13). This conversion not only contributes to countering local inflammation but also supports cellular health by modulating intracellular signaling pathways, particularly those involving NF-κB and other transcription factors critical for managing oxidative stress (Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14; Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14). Despite these promising mechanistic insights, it is important to note that direct, quantitative evidence detailing DHA’s incorporation specifically into RPE mitochondrial membranes and its precise effects on mitochondrial cristae structure, malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, or oxygen consumption rate (OCR) remains limited in the current literature (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, p. 13). Several reviews and preclinical reports acknowledge the theoretical framework while emphasizing the need for more detailed mechanistic studies that directly measure these mitochondrial endpoints (Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the mechanistic hypothesis, DHA supplementation is expected to yield several beneficial effects in retinal cells, particularly within the RPE, which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. In an ideal in vitro or ex vivo assay, DHA would incorporate into RPE cell membranes—including the mitochondrial inner membrane—increasing fluidity and enabling better diffusion of substrates and electron carriers necessary for efficient ATP production. Enhanced mitochondrial membrane fluidity should help reduce the susceptibility of the electron transport chain to oxidative damage, thereby lowering the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the subsequent production of lipid peroxidation byproducts such as MDA (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5). Furthermore, preservation of mitochondrial cristae structure is anticipated to maintain optimal alignment and function of ETC complexes, leading to an improved oxygen consumption rate (OCR) that is directly linked to cellular energy metabolism and overall cell viability (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 2–4; Souied et al., 2016, p. 8).  
At a molecular level, the increased presence of DHA in mitochondrial membranes is expected to initiate a cascade of protective events: reduced oxidative stress and inflammation via inhibition of NF-κB activation, promotion of the antioxidant response through NFE2L2 (NRF2) pathway activation, and enhanced autophagic clearance of damaged proteins and organelles through upregulation of SQSTM1 (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 1–2; Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, p. 3). Consequently, these effects should translate into preservation of RPE cell function, reduced apoptosis, and maintenance of photoreceptor health—an effect that could help slow the progression of dry AMD by stabilizing the retinal environment and preventing drusen accumulation and other degenerative changes (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5). Additionally, because genes encoding crucial direct mediators of DHA uptake such as Mfsd2a are expressed in RPE cells and photoreceptors, the target tissue is particularly well-positioned to benefit from increased dietary or supplementary DHA (Fathima et al., 2023, p. 8). However, it is also recognized that despite the strong rationale, direct experimental confirmation of these outcomes—specifically measured improvements in MDA levels, cristae ultrastructure integrity, and OCR in human RPE cells—is still pending, and the observed epidemiologic correlations are not yet unequivocally supported by randomized clinical trial data (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).

Overall Evaluation:  
The proposition to repurpose DHA for dry AMD is underpinned by compelling mechanistic rationale and epidemiologic associations, yet it is not without its challenges and limitations. One clear strength is DHA’s established role as an essential component of retinal cell membranes. Its high concentration in photoreceptors and the RPE is functionally integral to maintaining visual function and cellular homeostasis, lending strong biological plausibility to its protective potential in AMD (Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33). Its ability to modulate membrane fluidity, serve as a precursor to neuroprotective mediators like NPD1, and exert anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions provide multiple mechanistic pathways through which it may mitigate the cellular stressors implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis (Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14; Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14).  
From a therapeutic history perspective, DHA is well understood in the context of nutritional supplementation, and numerous epidemiologic studies point toward a lower risk of AMD with higher dietary DHA intake (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). The safety profile of DHA is also well established, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing. However, the clinical trial data to date (including large-scale studies such as AREDS2 and smaller trials like NAT-2) have not consistently demonstrated a clear benefit in altering the progression of advanced AMD, and it remains uncertain whether observed benefits in intermediate AMD or specific cellular endpoints translate into clinically meaningful outcomes in the dry form of the disease (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8).  
A significant weakness in the current body of research is the lack of direct mechanistic studies that quantitatively document DHA incorporation into RPE mitochondrial membranes and its subsequent effects on mitochondrial parameters. In our hypothesis, improved mitochondrial function is key, with expected reductions in MDA levels, preservation of cristae structure, and enhancement of OCR serving as biomarkers of efficacy. Yet, while several in vitro studies and animal experiments have suggested that DHA can reduce markers of oxidative stress and improve mitochondrial integrity in retinal models, the literature provided does not include rigorous, high-resolution measurements of these specific parameters in human RPE cells (Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Jiang et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). In summary, while the epidemiologic literature and preclinical studies provide an encouraging backdrop for the repurposing of DHA as a therapeutic agent in dry AMD—by showing that high DHA intake is associated with a reduced risk of AMD and that DHA can confer mitochondrial and anti-oxidative benefits in retinal models—the critical mechanistic endpoints that support our specific hypothesis are not yet fully substantiated in the published literature. The overall evaluation is that DHA has substantial mechanistic promise, safety, and historical use as a nutritional supplement; however, further robust mechanistic studies and carefully designed clinical trials are necessary to validate its specific effects on mitochondrial function in RPE cells and to determine whether these biochemical improvements translate into a clinically significant slowing of dry AMD progression (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is an endogenous ketone body produced by mitochondrial ketogenesis from fatty-acid–derived acetyl-CoA, classically in hepatocytes but also in extrahepatic cell types including the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and several neuronal lineages (enzymatic pathway: ACAT, HMGCS2, HMGCL, and BDH1) (Wang et al., 2021; Gough, 2021). In physiological and nutritional ketosis, circulating BHB rises from baseline (~0.05–0.1 mM) to levels >0.5 mM and up to 5–7 mM with prolonged fasting, providing an alternative oxidative substrate for extrahepatic mitochondria when carbohydrate availability is limited (Wang et al., 2021; Cooper et al., 2023). BHB and acetoacetate are transported into and out of cells via proton-linked monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs) such as MCT1 and MCT2 that are expressed at the blood–retinal barrier and in retinal cells, enabling substrate entry into the retina (Yang, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Gough, 2021). RPEs robustly express mitochondrial HMGCS2 and can ketogenize palmitate to BHB, secreting BHB via MCT1; retinal cells can take up and metabolize BHB into Krebs-cycle intermediates and amino acids, indicating functional capacity to use BHB as mitochondrial fuel in the outer retina (Yang, 2021). More recent mass spectrometry–based reassessment shows that RPE secretion of BHB is substantially lower than previously estimated by enzymatic kits, that RPE exports BHB to both apical and basal compartments, and that RPE both produces and consumes BHB depending on nutrient state—important considerations for experimental design and therapeutic targeting (Gulette et al., 2024).  

BHB belongs to the class of endogenous metabolic intermediates that function dually as oxidative fuels (via oxidation to acetyl-CoA and entry into TCA cycle) and signaling molecules with paracrine/autocrine receptor and epigenetic actions (e.g., agonism at HCAR2/GPR109A and inhibition of class I/IIa histone deacetylases) (Wang et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Kovács et al., 2021). As a therapeutic modality, BHB has been delivered exogenously as salts/esters or induced endogenously through ketogenic diets, fasting, or exercise to support mitochondrial ATP production and alter cellular stress responses in the CNS, heart, and skeletal muscle (Cooper et al., 2023; Kovács et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2022). In retinal disease models, ketogenic interventions or exogenous BHB have reduced oxidative/inflammatory injury and improved functional measures, though direct application to dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) has not yet been clinically tested (Gough, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021).  

Therapeutic History  
Ketone biology has a long history in neurology and cardiometabolic research, where BHB has been shown to preserve mitochondrial function, increase ATP production, and blunt oxidative injury in ischemia, neurodegeneration models, and skeletal muscle stress paradigms (Kovács et al., 2021; Mierziak et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2018). In neural tissues, ketogenic interventions and exogenous ketones prevent synaptic dysfunction induced by respiratory complex inhibitors and increase the brain NAD⁺/NADH ratio, correlating with decreased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation (Morris et al., 2020). In rat skeletal muscle cells, 5 mM BHB for 24–48 h increased respiratory control, ATP-linked respiration, P:O efficiency, lowered H₂O₂ production, and shifted mitochondrial dynamics toward fusion via DRP1 suppression—consistent with enhanced bioenergetics and decreased oxidative stress (Parker et al., 2018). In primary neurons, BHB maintained oxidative phosphorylation under glutamate workload even when cytosolic NADH transfer via the malate–aspartate shuttle was inhibited, demonstrating that BHB can sustain respiration under conditions that impair glycolytic NADH coupling to mitochondria (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

In the retina and optic nerve, multiple preclinical models show that ketogenic exposures or direct ketone administration reduce oxidative stress and inflammation, preserve function, and limit neuronal death. Intraperitoneal BHB and acetoacetate reduced NMDA-induced retinal ganglion cell (RGC) death in rats, and ketogenic diet attenuated NMDA-induced RGC injury in juvenile rats (Gough, 2021). In ocular blast or optic neuropathy paradigms, ketogenic diet prevented increases in superoxide and IL-1α, preserved visual evoked potentials, and reduced astrocytic hypertrophy and optic nerve death (Gough, 2021). In glaucoma models, ketogenic diet improved RGC soma/axon survival, axonal transport, and reduced gliosis, with increases in NAD and NAD:NADH ratio and upregulation of MCT1/MCT2 in optic nerve (Tribble et al., 2021). AAV-mediated MCT2 overexpression (increasing uptake of lactate/pyruvate/ketones) preserved RGCs and optic nerve axons in ocular hypertension and glaucoma models and elevated markers of mitochondrial biogenesis and function (PGC1α, COX, SDH) and antioxidant defense (SOD2) (Gough, 2021). However, in at least one RGC injury model, daily intraperitoneal BHB or acetoacetate did not replicate ketogenic diet neuroprotection, underscoring differences between exogenous ketone dosing and the systemic/multifactorial effects of ketogenic diets (Tribble et al., 2021).  

Within the RPE compartment specifically, two lines of evidence are relevant: (1) BHB protects ARPE-19 cells from high-glucose–induced injury, improving viability, alleviating cell cycle arrest, and modulating inflammatory mediators (IL-8, IL-17α, MCP-1) at millimolar concentrations achievable with nutritional ketosis or exogenous supplementation (Argentino et al., 2025). (2) HCAR2/GPR109A, a BHB receptor, is robustly expressed by the RPE; BHB agonism reduced retinal leukocyte infiltration in LPS-challenged mice in an HCAR2-dependent manner, and loss of HCAR2 in RPE led to barrier dysfunction (ZO-1 defects) and increased immune cell infiltrates, indicating that BHB–HCAR2 signaling can preserve an immunoinhibitory retinal environment (Powell et al., 2021). In diabetic retinopathy models, systemic BHB activation of HCA2 reduced ER stress and NLRP3 inflammasome signaling and ameliorated retinal pathology, establishing anti-inflammatory and ER stress–limiting actions in retina (Trotta et al., 2019).  

In inherited retinal degeneration models, ketogenic interventions delayed photoreceptor degeneration and improved electroretinogram (ERG) amplitudes and outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness in rd10 and Pde6a mice, and a soluble ketogenic formulation partially restored vision and survival in PDH-deficient noir zebrafish—consistent with bypassing PDH to supply acetyl-CoA and support neurotransmitter synthesis (Gough, 2021). Notwithstanding these encouraging signals, the literature consistently notes the absence of clinical trials evaluating ketogenic interventions or BHB in retinitis pigmentosa or AMD patients, and reports potentially adverse effects of ketogenic diets in wild-type mice (decreased ERG amplitudes, altered albumin/weight), highlighting translational uncertainties and the need to distinguish effects of BHB from the broader systemic consequences of diet (Gough, 2021).  

Mechanism of Action  
BHB acts through convergent metabolic, redox, mitochondrial, inflammatory, and epigenetic mechanisms that are mechanistically aligned with the pathophysiology of RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic oxidative/inflammatory stress in dry AMD.  

- Alternative mitochondrial fuel and bioenergetics support. In extrahepatic tissues (including retina), BHB oxidation proceeds via mitochondrial BDH1 (βHB→acetoacetate) followed by SCOT/OXCT1 (AcAc→AcAc-CoA using succinyl-CoA) and acetyl-CoA production for TCA entry and ATP generation, enabling substrate-level maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and oxidative phosphorylation under glucose restriction or impaired glycolytic NADH transfer (Wang et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023). The retina expresses monocarboxylate transport routes (e.g., MCT1 at the inner blood–retinal barrier; MCT2 in neurons), and RPE expresses MCT1 and can both produce and consume BHB, providing a plausible uptake pathway for exogenous BHB into RPE and neighboring retinal cells (Tribble et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Gulette et al., 2024). In neurons, BHB-supported respiration remains robust when the malate–aspartate shuttle is blocked with AOAA—conditions that decrease glucose-fueled ATP synthesis—indicating that BHB can preserve mitochondrial ATP synthesis and respiratory control when cytosolic NADH transfer is compromised, a scenario relevant to glycolysis-impaired RPE (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

- Redox coupling and ROS control. The interconversion of acetoacetate and BHB by βHB dehydrogenase is linked to NADH/NAD⁺ redox; acetoacetate→BHB requires oxidation of NADH to NAD⁺, and nutritional ketosis in human brain increases NAD⁺/NADH ratio, correlating with reductions in mitochondrial ROS generation (Gough, 2021; Morris et al., 2020). Ketones can inhibit mitochondrial ROS production by increasing NADH oxidation, and ketogenic interventions increase NAD⁺/NADH in vivo, though tissue- and context-dependent effects exist (Morris et al., 2020). Complementary cardiac literature reports that β-OHB can reduce the mitochondrial NAD couple while oxidizing coenzyme Q, emphasizing that BHB modulates both NADH/NAD⁺ and Q/QH₂ redox pairs in mitochondria—with directionality that may depend on prevailing substrate status and respiratory state (Chu et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion models and muscle cells, BHB lowers mitochondrial ROS, decreases mitochondrial swelling, maintains Δψm, and increases ATP production, consistent with direct mitochondrial protection (Mierziak et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2018).  

- Antioxidant transcription (Nrf2) and hormesis. Ketogenic exposures can induce a hormetic redox signal that activates Keap1–Nrf2, increasing transcription of detoxification and antioxidant genes; in retina, ketone body exposure mimicked calorie restriction via fumarate–Nrf2 activation (Gough, 2021; Fu et al., 2020). Preclinical optic/retinal models link these antioxidant transcriptional effects to preserved function and reduced oxidative markers (NOS, MDA, superoxide) (Gough, 2021).  

- Anti-inflammatory signaling via HCAR2/ARRB2 and NLRP3/NF-κB suppression. BHB is a ligand for HCAR1/HCAR2 receptors; HCAR2 is robustly expressed in human RPE and retina, and receptor activation by BHB reduces leukocyte infiltration and preserves RPE barrier integrity in inflammation models (Powell et al., 2021). Downstream, BHB–HCAR signaling recruits β-arrestin-2 (ARRB2) that binds NLRP3 to block inflammasome assembly, decreasing ASC and preventing K⁺ efflux to suppress IL-1β maturation; BHB also activates a COX1/PGD2 cascade that inhibits IKK and NF-κB nuclear translocation, reducing TNF-α and microglial/macrophage activation (Gough, 2021). In diabetic retina, systemic BHB–HCA2 activation suppressed ER stress and NLRP3 inflammasome activity, demonstrating the retinal anti-inflammatory efficacy of this axis (Trotta et al., 2019).  

- Mitochondrial calcium homeostasis and mPTP stabilization. In human iPSC-derived microglia, amyloid-β oligomers increased MCU expression, raised mitochondrial Ca²⁺ ~40%, elevated mtROS, and triggered mPTP opening; BHB normalized MCU, decreased mtCa²⁺/mtROS, and completely reversed mPTP activation, restoring phagocytic function (Jin et al., 2023). Although not conducted in RPE, these mitochondrial-stabilizing effects are mechanistically relevant to post-mitotic cells with high oxidative load.  

- Epigenetic modulation and mitochondrial biogenesis. BHB is an endogenous inhibitor of class I/IIa HDACs at physiological millimolar concentrations, leading to histone hyperacetylation and upregulation of FOXO3a and metallothionein genes that encode antioxidant defenses; BHB also increases intracellular acetyl-CoA and supports protein acetylation, and can β-hydroxybutyrylate histones, adding layers of gene regulatory control tied to mitochondrial status (Yang, 2021; Kovács et al., 2021; Mierziak et al., 2021). Through HDAC inhibition and receptor-mediated signaling, BHB increases BDNF via cAMP/PKA/CREB, activates SIRT1/SIRT3 via AMPK/HCA2/NAD⁺ pathways, and promotes PGC1α-driven mitochondrial biogenesis and UCP2 expression that collectively improve mitochondrial function and antioxidant capacity (Kovács et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022). In retinal/optic nerve models, ketogenic diet or enhanced monocarboxylate uptake upregulated PGC1α, COX, SDH, and SOD2 while lowering pAMPK/AMPK, linking substrate availability to mitochondrial biogenesis and anti-inflammatory signaling (Gough, 2021).  

- Immunometabolic reprogramming in retina/CNS. Ketogenic interventions increased anti-inflammatory mediators (IL-4, Arginase-1) and M2-like microglia while decreasing IBA-1⁺ macrophage/microglia, consistent with dampened neuroinflammation secondary to improved bioenergetics (reduced AMPK activation) and prevention of NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation (Gough, 2021). BHB also inhibits FFAR3/GPR41, reducing sympathetic activity in mice, indicating broader metabolic signaling roles that could modulate retinal perfusion/metabolism indirectly (Gough, 2021).  

Collectively, these mechanisms—fuel substitution that sustains Δψm and ATP synthesis under glycolytic impairment, improved redox balance with decreased mitochondrial ROS, Nrf2-dependent antioxidant gene induction, NLRP3/NF-κB anti-inflammatory actions via HCAR2/ARRB2, stabilization of mitochondrial Ca²⁺/mPTP, and epigenetic programs that support mitochondrial biogenesis—map directly onto pathologies implicated in RPE degeneration in dry AMD and provide multiple rescue nodes testable in disease-relevant models (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Gough, 2021; Powell et al., 2021).  

Expected Effect  
Assay context: The working hypothesis is that exogenous BHB will serve as an alternative mitochondrial substrate in RPE, sustaining Δψm and reducing NADH-driven mitochondrial ROS when glycolysis is impaired—conditions that model bioenergetic stress in geographic atrophy. Mechanistically, this is supported by three converging evidence streams: (1) mitochondrial fuel flexibility to oxidize BHB to acetyl-CoA via BDH1/SCOT, (2) redox modulation that increases NADH oxidation and elevates the NAD⁺/NADH ratio, and (3) multi-layered antioxidant/anti-inflammatory signaling that lowers mitochondrial ROS production and downstream inflammasome/NF-κB activation (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Gough, 2021).  

- Sustained Δψm and ATP under glycolytic impairment. RPE expresses ketogenesis machinery (HMGCS2) and monocarboxylate transport capacity (MCT1) and is capable of both producing and consuming BHB, while inner BRB MCT1 and neuronal MCT2 provide routes for substrate delivery into retinal tissue (Yang, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Gulette et al., 2024). In neurons, BHB preserved oxidative phosphorylation and ATP-linked respiration under MAS inhibition, a condition that effectively reduces mitochondrial access to cytosolic NADH from glycolysis; this predicts that, in RPE exposed to glycolytic blockade or high work demand, BHB could maintain Δψm and respiratory control by supplying acetyl-CoA independent of cytosolic NADH shuttling (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023). In muscle and cardiac models, BHB improved respiratory control ratios, increased ATP production, and maintained Δψm under stress, providing precedent for Δψm preservation in high-energy post-mitotic cells (Parker et al., 2018; Mierziak et al., 2021).  

- Lowered NADH-driven mtROS and improved redox balance. Nutritional ketosis increases the brain NAD⁺/NADH ratio and ketones inhibit mitochondrial ROS production by increasing NADH oxidation, a shift that is expected to suppress reverse electron transport and semiquinone leak at respiratory complexes under high NADH load (Morris et al., 2020). Although some cardiac literature reports context-dependent changes in the mitochondrial NAD couple under BHB with concurrent oxidation of coenzyme Q, the net effect across neural and muscle studies is reduced mitochondrial ROS generation and improved redox handling, a phenotype also observed in optic/retinal models after ketogenic interventions (Chu et al., 2021; Gough, 2021; Mierziak et al., 2021). These redox improvements are reinforced by Nrf2 activation and increased expression of antioxidant defenses (e.g., SOD2), which increase ROS quenching capacity in retinal and optic tissues (Gough, 2021).  

- Anti-inflammatory and barrier-preserving actions in RPE. BHB agonizes HCAR2 expressed by RPE and retinal microglia, reducing leukocyte infiltration, preserving tight junction integrity (ZO-1), and suppressing inflammasome/NF-κB signaling (Powell et al., 2021; Trotta et al., 2019). In hyperglycemic ARPE-19, BHB improved viability and cell cycle progression and modulated inflammatory cytokines, consistent with protection under metabolic stress (Argentino et al., 2025). By preserving ATP and lowering AMPK phosphorylation, BHB/ketone availability is expected to block NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation and downstream expression of IL-6 and TNF-α, reducing the chronic para-inflammatory milieu implicated in RPE degeneration (Gough, 2021).  

- Translational considerations for exposure and transport. Systemically delivered BHB can traverse the blood–retinal barrier via MCT1, and RPE’s own MCT1 provides transmembrane transport capacity; nonetheless, quantitative extracellular BHB at RPE surfaces is likely in the low micromolar range under basal conditions, and RPE produces and consumes BHB dynamically, implying that achieving therapeutic mitochondrial utilization in RPE will require millimolar plasma BHB or local delivery (Tribble et al., 2021; Gulette et al., 2024). Nutritional ketosis and exogenous ketone supplementation readily achieve 0.5–2 mM BHB in plasma in rodent and human studies, which are the concentrations used in many in vitro protection assays (Cooper et al., 2023; Argentino et al., 2025).  

Key readouts and validation metrics for the proposed assay should include Δψm (e.g., TMRM/TMRE), OCR/ECAR profiling and ATP-linked respiration (Seahorse), mitochondrial ROS (MitoSOX and H₂O₂ flux), NAD⁺/NADH ratio (enzymatic cycling and/or fluorescence lifetime imaging), pAMPK/AMPK and NF-κB p65 nuclear localization, Nrf2 translocation and target gene induction (e.g., SOD2), and inflammasome readouts (ASC specks, IL-1β maturation) (Gough, 2021). Given the measurement pitfalls documented in RPE ketone assays, BHB should be quantified by LC–MS/MS or after removal of high-MW confounders by size exclusion rather than by standard enzymatic kits (Gulette et al., 2024).  
Protein expression considerations support the mechanism in the target cell type. HCAR2/GPR109A is expressed by RPE and retinal microglia/endothelium and mediates anti-inflammatory effects of BHB in vivo, making receptor-dependent components of BHB action directly testable in RPE (Powell et al., 2021). RPE expresses HMGCS2 and MCT1, and retinal cells metabolize BHB into TCA intermediates, consistent with BDH1/SCOT/OXCT1 pathway activity enabling BHB oxidation in retinal tissues; while direct SCOT expression in RPE is not provided here, the metabolic tracing data indicating conversion of BHB to Krebs intermediates in retinal cells justify testing oxidative utilization in RPE (Yang, 2021; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strength of biological rationale. The core hypothesis—that BHB can act as an alternative mitochondrial fuel to sustain Δψm and lower NADH-driven mitochondrial ROS in glycolysis-impaired RPE—is strongly aligned with BHB’s established roles in extrahepatic tissues and is supported by multiple mechanistic strands in relevant neural and retinal systems (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023). BHB oxidation provides acetyl-CoA and maintains respiration when glycolytic NADH transfer is compromised, as demonstrated in primary neurons; BHB reduces mtROS, preserves Δψm, and increases ATP in ischemic muscle/heart models; and nutrient ketosis increases the NAD⁺/NADH ratio and lowers ROS production in brain—effects that would be expected to decrease reverse-electron transport–driven ROS at complex I and stabilize mitochondrial function in stressed RPE (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023; Mierziak et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020). In retinal tissue, ketogenic interventions and direct ketone administration reduce oxidative injury, preserve function, and enhance mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses in RGC/optic nerve models, while anti-inflammatory benefits via HCAR2—expressed by RPE—reduce leukocyte infiltration and preserve barrier integrity (Gough, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Powell et al., 2021; Trotta et al., 2019). The mitochondrial stabilization effects observed in human microglia—lower MCU/mtCa²⁺, reduced mtROS, prevention of mPTP opening—further support a BHB-mediated mitochondrial resilience phenotype that is likely relevant to RPE (Jin et al., 2023).  

Evidence relevant to the target tissue. RPEs possess ketone-related transport and enzymatic capacity (HMGCS2, MCT1) and can both produce and consume BHB; they are responsive to BHB in vitro under metabolic stress (hyperglycemia) with improved viability and inflammatory marker modulation (Yang, 2021; Argentino et al., 2025). HCAR2-mediated anti-inflammatory and barrier maintenance functions have been demonstrated in RPE/retina, providing a receptor-proximal pathway for BHB to suppress chronic para-inflammation and preserve RPE junctional integrity, both relevant to dry AMD pathobiology (Powell et al., 2021). While direct measurements of BDH1/SCOT activity and NAD⁺/NADH dynamics in human RPE treated with BHB remain to be shown here, the metabolic fate of BHB in retinal cells and robust mitochondrial effects in closely related cell types make the translational experiments technically feasible and mechanistically justified (Yang, 2021; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

Translational gaps and risks. No clinical trials have evaluated ketogenic diets or BHB specifically for RP or AMD, and some ketogenic diet studies reported adverse outcomes in wild-type animals (decreased ERG amplitude, altered serum albumin/weight), emphasizing the need to decouple BHB’s effects from broader dietary/metabolic confounders (Gough, 2021). Direct BHB delivery does not always recapitulate ketogenic diet benefits in RGC injury, suggesting that multi-target effects of diet (e.g., NAD metabolism, mTOR, microbiome) contribute to efficacy; this implies that BHB monotherapy may require combination strategies (e.g., nicotinamide co-therapy) or optimized dosing to achieve comparable benefit (Tribble et al., 2021). Quantification of BHB in RPE experiments is non-trivial due to assay interference; LC–MS/MS or validated size-exclusion protocols must be used to avoid false positives and to measure physiologically relevant, often low-micromolar extracellular BHB in RPE cultures (Gulette et al., 2024). Finally, the directionality of NAD redox effects may be context dependent (reports of both increased NAD⁺/NADH ratio in brain and reduced mitochondrial NAD couple in cardiac models), requiring careful interpretation with compartment-specific assays in RPE (Morris et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2021).  

Development path and decision points. Given the strong mechanistic rationale, retina-focused preclinical evidence, and RPE receptor expression data, BHB is a plausible repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD that merits rigorous, RPE-centric validation. Key go/no-go preclinical criteria should include: (1) demonstration that BHB rescues Δψm and ATP-linked respiration in primary human RPE or iPSC-RPE under glycolytic impairment (e.g., 2-deoxyglucose or low glucose plus workload), (2) reduction of mitochondrial ROS (MitoSOX/H₂O₂ flux) and elevation of cellular NAD⁺/NADH ratio with BHB, (3) suppression of pAMPK and NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation, induction of Nrf2 target genes, and reduction of NLRP3 activation, (4) persistence of benefits under HCAR2 antagonism/knockdown to parse receptor versus fuel contributions, and (5) confirmation that effects are contingent on monocarboxylate transport (MCT inhibition) and SCOT activity (e.g., OXCT1 knockdown), which would mechanistically link outcomes to BHB oxidation rather than unrelated signaling (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023; Gough, 2021; Powell et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021). In vivo, a dry-AMD–relevant RPE degeneration model should test systemic or ocular BHB delivery (dose selection to 0.5–2 mM plasma equivalents) with readouts of RPE mitochondrial structure/function, subretinal inflammation, and lesion progression; blood–retina transport via MCT1 at the inner BRB suggests systemic exposure can reach the retina, though intraocular routes might achieve higher local concentrations (Tribble et al., 2021). Throughout, BHB dosing must be titrated to avoid off-target effects and electrolyte load associated with some salt formulations; direct ketone esters or controlled dietary induction may be considered for translational studies, recognizing model-specific differences seen between exogenous BHB and ketogenic diet (Tribble et al., 2021).  

Strengths  
- Mechanistic breadth and convergence on AMD-relevant pathways: alternative fuel supply to support Δψm/ATP, improved NAD redox and ROS control, Nrf2 antioxidant gene induction, and potent suppression of NLRP3/NF-κB–mediated para-inflammation via HCAR2—each independently linked to retinal/RPE resilience (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Gough, 2021; Powell et al., 2021).  
- Retinal delivery/uptake plausibility: MCT expression at the inner BRB and in RPE, plus RPE’s ability to both produce and consume BHB, establish physiological routes for BHB transit and utilization in target tissues (Tribble et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Gulette et al., 2024).  
- Preclinical efficacy signals in retinal and CNS models: reduced oxidative/inflammatory injury, preserved neuronal function, enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis/antioxidant defenses, and receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory actions in retina (Gough, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Trotta et al., 2019; Powell et al., 2021).  
- Compatibility with RPE stress biology: BHB improved ARPE-19 survival under metabolic stress and modulated cytokines, and microglial mitochondrial data demonstrate BHB reverses mtCa²⁺/mtROS/mPTP derangements that are mechanistically relevant to RPE degeneration (Argentino et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2023).  

Weaknesses and uncertainties  
- Lack of AMD-specific in vivo data and no clinical trials in AMD/RP; extrapolation from RGC/optic nerve/diabetic models requires confirmation in RPE-targeted systems (Gough, 2021).  
- Measurement pitfalls in RPE ketone studies; reliance on inaccurate enzymatic assays historically confounded interpretation, necessitating MS-based quantitation and careful time-course sampling (Gulette et al., 2024).  
- Context-dependent redox effects; reports differ on NAD couple responses to BHB, indicating the need for compartmentalized NAD⁺/NADH readouts in RPE to avoid misattribution (Morris et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2021).  
- Differences between exogenous BHB and ketogenic diet; some benefits in glaucoma were not reproduced with BHB delivery, suggesting that metabolic co-factors (e.g., NAD boosters) or combinatorial strategies may be required (Tribble et al., 2021).  
- Potential systemic/dietary adverse effects; ketogenic diets can reduce ERG amplitudes and alter systemic biomarkers in wild-type mice—although these are not necessarily attributable to BHB per se, they caution against non-specific dietary induction in frail patients (Gough, 2021).  

Overall, BHB (Sigma-Aldrich 389410) is a compelling repurposed candidate for dry AMD based on strong mechanistic plausibility and retina-relevant preclinical evidence, with direct RPE expression of the key anti-inflammatory receptor HCAR2 and demonstrable RPE responses to BHB under metabolic stress (Powell et al., 2021; Argentino et al., 2025). The major risk is the current absence of AMD-specific in vivo evidence and the historical conflation of diet-level ketosis with BHB pharmacology; these can be addressed by an RPE-centric preclinical plan that uses rigorous ketone quantitation, compartmental redox readouts, transporter/enzyme perturbations (MCT/OXCT1), and in vivo validation in RPE degeneration models. If BHB reproducibly maintains Δψm/ATP, reduces mtROS, and suppresses inflammasome/NF-κB signaling in RPE under glycolytic impairment, it would justify advancement to formulation and delivery optimization for ocular exposure and, subsequently, to early clinical safety/pharmacodynamic studies in dry AMD (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023; Gough, 2021; Wang et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Sulforaphane is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate originally identified in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli and Brussels sprouts. It is generated through the hydrolysis of glucoraphanin by the enzyme myrosinase, which is released upon plant tissue damage. As a member of the phytochemical family, sulforaphane belongs to a class of natural compounds known for inducing phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins. Historically, this compound has been extensively investigated for its chemopreventive and cytoprotective properties, particularly through the activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. Being one of the most studied Nrf2 activators, its discovery stemmed from early investigations into dietary antioxidants and their role in reducing carcinogenesis and inflammation. In the context of drug development, sulforaphane is considered a promising candidate for repurposing because it combines a favorable preclinical safety profile with a well-characterized mechanism of action that includes modulation of intracellular redox signaling. Its broad application in preclinical studies to ameliorate oxidative stress and inflammation suggests that targeted delivery to retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells might help alleviate the oxidative injury observed in geographic atrophy, the advanced form of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Bellezza, 2018; Chang et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Sulforaphane has attracted considerable attention for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties over the past two decades. Preclinical studies have demonstrated its protective effects in various models of oxidative stress, including those involving retinal tissues and RPE cells. In in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells—a well-accepted human RPE model—sulforaphane exhibited dose-dependent protection against oxidative insults induced by agents such as tert-butyl hydroperoxide (t-BOOH) and hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂). These experiments demonstrated that sulforaphane pretreatment significantly reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and mitigated mitochondrial membrane potential damage, ultimately leading to reduced apoptotic cell death (Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021). Similarly, other investigations have reported sulforaphane’s ability to induce cytoprotective genes in RPE cells through Nrf2 activation, resulting in improved cell survival under stress conditions (Zhang et al., 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

Moreover, several in vivo studies in rodent models have provided evidence of sulforaphane-mediated retinal neuroprotection. Examples include models of photooxidative damage in mice, where sulforaphane delayed photoreceptor degeneration and prevented RPE dysfunction—mechanisms that are highly relevant to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Bellezza, 2018). However, it should be noted that although sulforaphane has been studied in various retinal degeneration models, there is no established clinical history of its use in human dry AMD. Nevertheless, its promising preclinical efficacy in ameliorating oxidative injury in RPE cells, coupled with its demonstrated safety across multiple biological systems including ocular tissues, supports its potential repurposing as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Qin, 2007; del Cano et al., 2008).

Mechanism of Action:  
The principal mechanism underlying sulforaphane’s protective effects is its ability to activate the Nrf2 pathway. Under basal conditions, the transcription factor Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytosol via binding to its inhibitor, Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1), which directs Nrf2 for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Sulforaphane, owing to its electrophilic isothiocyanate moiety, reacts with critical cysteine residues on Keap1. This modification alters the conformation of Keap1 and prevents the degradation of Nrf2, leading to its stabilization and subsequent nuclear translocation (Wherry, 2013). Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to antioxidant response elements (ARE) in the promoter regions of various cytoprotective genes. The result is a robust induction of phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), and superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2). These enzymes play critical roles in neutralizing ROS, repairing oxidative damage, and maintaining cellular redox balance (Qin, 2007; Zhang et al., 2024).

In addition to its classic Nrf2-dependent antioxidant response, sulforaphane has been shown to modulate other cellular pathways that are important for mitochondrial health. In retinal cells, sulforaphane has been reported to attenuate mitochondrial membrane potential collapse and reduce mitochondrial superoxide production, as evidenced by decreased MitoSOX fluorescence in treated ARPE-19 cells (Chang et al., 2020). These mitochondrial protective actions are thought to involve the upregulation of antioxidant enzymes that localize to the mitochondria, as well as enhancement of the spare respiratory capacity—thereby preserving ATP generation under oxidative stress conditions. Furthermore, sulforaphane has been implicated in the regulation of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis, which is critical for mitochondrial biogenesis and metabolic homeostasis. This dual engagement—both through Nrf2-driven transcriptional activation and mitochondrial biogenesis pathways—positions sulforaphane as a multifaceted agent capable of sustaining cellular energy production and reducing oxidative injury in the RPE, a cell type that is particularly vulnerable in geographic atrophy (Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).

Beyond its antioxidant effects, sulforaphane also exerts anti-inflammatory properties by downregulating the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and adhesion molecules (e.g., ICAM-1, MCP-1). This is particularly relevant in the context of AMD, where chronic low-grade inflammation is believed to exacerbate RPE dysfunction and drusen formation (Chang et al., 2020; del Cano et al., 2008). In summary, the molecular interactions of sulforaphane—ranging from direct modification of Keap1 to the induction of mitochondrial antioxidant defenses—provide a robust mechanistic rationale for its potential utility in mitigating the multifactorial oxidative and inflammatory challenges associated with dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Given its well-documented mechanism of action, the hypothesis that sulforaphane induces Nrf2-mediated mitochondrial antioxidant pathways in RPE cells is strongly supported by preclinical evidence. When RPE cells are subjected to oxidative stress, it is expected that sulforaphane treatment will lead to a dose-dependent upregulation of Nrf2 target genes including HO-1, NQO1, and SOD2. The elevation of these transcripts correlates with a reduction in mitochondrial superoxide levels, as measured by decreased MitoSOX fluorescence, and an improvement in the spare respiratory capacity—a surrogate marker for mitochondrial function and ATP generation (Chang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).

In cellular assays using ARPE-19 cells, administration of sulforaphane prior to oxidative challenge has been shown to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential and decrease cytochrome c release, thereby reducing the activation of downstream apoptotic cascades. The suppression of ROS production and the preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics result in improved cell viability and reduced apoptotic indices. For instance, studies have demonstrated that sulforaphane pretreatment leads to lower levels of cleaved caspase-3 and PARP-1, indicating a direct link between enhanced antioxidant defense and the inhibition of programmed cell death pathways in RPE cells (Yang et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2020).

At the molecular level, the expected outcome of sulforaphane administration in a dry AMD context is multifactorial. The compound would elevate the expression of cytoprotective enzymes that not only detoxify reactive oxygen species but also facilitate the repair of oxidatively damaged macromolecules. This should translate into a measurable decrease in overall oxidative stress markers, preservation of mitochondrial function (evidenced by sustained ATP production and improved spare respiratory capacity), and stabilization of the RPE cell phenotype. Moreover, since mitochondrial dysfunction is a central element of geographic atrophy pathogenesis, sulforaphane’s ability to maintain ATP generation could directly counteract the energy deficit observed in degenerating RPE cells (Zhang et al., 2024; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019).

These expected effects are supported by a range of preclinical studies. For example, quantitative redox fluorometry results reported in ARPE-19 cells indicate that sulforaphane-treated cells maintain a significantly higher redox ratio during oxidative challenge compared to untreated controls, which is indicative of an enhanced antioxidant state. Additionally, the upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants and improved bioenergetic profiles have been correlated with better cell survival outcomes, reinforcing the concept that sulforaphane can counteract the deleterious cellular changes observed in models of dry AMD (del Cano et al., 2008; Qin, 2007).

Overall Evaluation:  
Sulforaphane, as exemplified by the Sigma-Aldrich S4441 formulation, presents a compelling therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD, particularly targeting the geographic atrophy form characterized by pronounced RPE degeneration. One of the major strengths of sulforaphane lies in its robust preclinical evidence demonstrating its ability to induce the Nrf2 pathway, a master regulator of oxidative stress responses. The compound’s direct modification of Keap1 and subsequent stabilization and nuclear translocation of Nrf2 trigger the upregulation of several antioxidant enzymes, such as HO-1, NQO1, and SOD2—which are critical for detoxifying reactive oxygen species and repairing oxidative damage in RPE cells (Qin, 2007; Zhang et al., 2024).

Furthermore, sulforaphane’s additional capacity to preserve mitochondrial function by maintaining membrane potential and supporting ATP synthesis addresses a major pathological hallmark of geographic atrophy, where mitochondrial dysfunction leads to energy depletion and accelerates cell death. The integration of mitochondrial antioxidant defenses with the broader cytoprotective effects of Nrf2 activation provides a convergent mechanism aimed at both preventing oxidative damage and sustaining cellular energy production under stress conditions (Yang et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2020).

Another notable strength is the extensive safety data available for sulforaphane from preclinical studies. Its natural occurrence, combined with its well-documented bioactivity in a range of cell types, underscores its potential for repurposing in ocular applications. Moreover, sulforaphane’s ability to attenuate inflammatory responses by reducing the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines adds an extra layer of therapeutic benefit, considering the role of chronic inflammation in exacerbating AMD pathology (del Cano et al., 2008; Chang et al., 2020).

Despite these promising attributes, several challenges remain. One potential limitation is the bioavailability of sulforaphane. Like many natural compounds, sulforaphane may face pharmacokinetic hurdles such as poor water solubility and limited tissue penetration, which could complicate systemic delivery or localized administration to the retina. Furthermore, while the preclinical efficacy in ARPE-19 cell models and animal studies is encouraging, the translation of these findings to human patients with dry AMD remains to be validated. Variability in the cellular responses between in vitro models and the complex microenvironment of the human retina, including the influence of the blood–retinal barrier, poses a potential risk for suboptimal therapeutic delivery (Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; Qin, 2007).

Additionally, some of the supportive data for sulforaphane’s efficacy in ocular systems come from studies published in journals with variable impact, and additional high-quality clinical studies will be necessary to establish its safety and efficacy profile in the context of dry AMD. The dosing regimens, potential off-target effects, and long-term impact of chronic Nrf2 activation in retinal tissues also require careful investigation. There is ongoing debate over the potential for Nrf2 activators to have biphasic dose responses, where excessive activation might inadvertently cause cellular stress or dysregulate normal redox homeostasis (Bellezza, 2018; del Cano et al., 2008).

In conclusion, sulforaphane demonstrates strong mechanistic potential for the treatment of dry AMD by elevating key antioxidant defenses in RPE cells and preserving mitochondrial function under oxidative stress. Its ability to induce HO-1, NQO1, and SOD2 in response to oxidative challenges and thereby reduce superoxide production while maintaining ATP synthesis is directly aligned with the therapeutic needs of geographic atrophy patients. The preclinical evidence suggests that, with appropriate formulation and delivery strategies, sulforaphane could provide a dual benefit by mitigating oxidative injury and reducing inflammation in the retina. However, further studies are required to address bioavailability challenges and to validate its clinical efficacy in well-designed human trials. Overall, sulforaphane merits further investigation as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, and its advancement into early-phase clinical testing is justified by the compelling preclinical data available (Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2020; Hernández-Rabaza et al., 2019; del Cano et al., 2008).
