Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Alda-1 is a synthetic small molecule discovered through target-directed screening for modulators of mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2), originally identified as “ALDH2 activator 1” with the chemical name N-(1,3-benzodioxol-5-ylmethyl)-2,6-dichlorobenzamide and first demonstrated to reduce myocardial ischemic injury in rodents by directly activating ALDH2 (i.e., increasing its catalytic activity and rescuing function of the common inactive ALDH2*2 variant) (Budas et al., 2009; Kimura et al., 2019). Structurally and mechanistically, Alda-1 binds at the substrate entrance tunnel of ALDH2 and extends toward the active site, where it enhances dehydrogenase activity by favorably altering local dynamics, improving NAD+ engagement, and acting as a chemical chaperone that preserves the functional conformation of critical active-site loops and α-helices, while shielding key catalytic cysteines from irreversible electrophilic adduction by reactive aldehydes such as 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE) (Gao et al., 2022; Wang & He, 2018). In vitro biophysical and enzymology work shows Alda-1 increases wild-type ALDH2 activity approximately twofold and markedly rescues activity of the common East Asian mutant ALDH2*2 (Glu504Lys), restoring heterotetramer activity to near wild-type levels; importantly, Alda-1 is selective against several other ALDHs in original profiling, although later biochemical work suggests some degree of cross-activation of ALDH1A1 under specific assay conditions (Budas et al., 2009; Kotraiah et al., 2013).

Alda-1 belongs to the pharmacologic class of enzyme activators/allosteric agonists targeting mitochondrial ALDH2; the class is characterized by its ability to catalytically enhance clearance of reactive aldehydes generated by oxidative and nitrosative stress (e.g., 4-HNE, malondialdehyde [MDA], acrolein, and catecholamine-derived DOPAL), thereby acting as indirect antioxidants that reduce downstream carbonyl stress, proteotoxicity, and mitochondria-dependent cell death without directly scavenging ROS (Kimura et al., 2019; Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Wang & He, 2018). This mechanism has been applied preclinically across multiple organ systems to mitigate ischemia–reperfusion injury, chronic heart failure, metabolic and neurodegenerative toxicities, and toxin-induced organ damage, providing a consistent translational thread: activation of ALDH2 accelerates detoxification of stable electrophilic products of lipid peroxidation, interrupting aldehyde-driven positive feedback loops that amplify mitochondrial dysfunction, ROS generation, and apoptosis (Budas et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2014; Münzel & Daiber, 2018).

Therapeutic History  
Across cardiovascular models, Alda-1 has repeatedly demonstrated robust cytoprotection in vivo. In rat and mouse myocardial ischemia–reperfusion and infarction models, Alda-1 administration prior to or during ischemia reduced infarct size by approximately 60% and improved long-term survival following myocardial infarction, associating efficacy with increased ALDH2 activity, reduced 4-HNE-protein adducts and protein carbonyls, preserved mitochondrial respiratory control ratio (RCR), reduced mitochondrial H₂O₂ release, protection against Ca²⁺-induced mitochondrial permeability transition (MPT), and decreased cytochrome c release (Budas et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2014). In a chronic post-MI heart-failure model with established aldehydic overload, sustained Alda-1 treatment increased cardiac ALDH2 activity by ~2.7-fold, lowered 4-HNE adducts and protein carbonyls, normalized uncoupler responsiveness, improved RCR by preserving State 3 respiration, lowered mitochondrial ROS emission, and corrected MPT sensitivity; organ-level outcomes included increased contractility, reduced LV dilation, diminished hypertrophy and fibrosis, and anti-remodeling benefits (Gomes et al., 2014). In vitro, Alda-1 shielded isolated cardiac mitochondria from 4-HNE–induced respiratory inhibition, demonstrating direct aldehyde-dependent protection at the mitochondrial level (Gomes et al., 2014).

Hepatic and other organ systems provide convergent evidence. In a mouse acetaminophen hepatotoxicity model, Alda-1 pretreatment substantially reduced liver injury biomarkers (ALT/AST), histologic necrosis, 4-HNE adduct burden, mitochondrial depolarization, and cell death without altering upstream NAPQI bioactivation or JNK phosphorylation, demonstrating that protection is downstream via aldehyde detoxification and preservation of mitochondrial polarization and MPT control (Wimborne et al., 2020). Additional preclinical reports document Alda-1 efficacy in models of lung ischemia/reperfusion, intestinal I/R, kidney injury, neurotoxic injuries, and alcohol-related hepatic injury, again with mechanistic ties to accelerated clearance of reactive aldehydes, restoration of mitochondrial function, and modulation of stress/apoptosis pathways (Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019).

Retina-focused data, while more limited and not in dry AMD models, are directionally supportive. In streptozotocin-induced aged diabetic rats (an early diabetic retinopathy model), systemic Alda-1 improved ERG parameters, preserved outer nuclear layer (ONL) and total retinal thickness on OCT at 7–30 days, increased retinal SOD activity, and decreased retinal TNF-α and IL-6 across multiple timepoints; concurrent upregulation of ALDH2, Nrf2, and Sirt1 was observed by immunofluorescence and Western blot, suggesting that ALDH2 activation engages antioxidant and anti-inflammatory pathways in the retina under hyperglycemic oxidative stress (He et al., 2018). In a separate in vivo retinal degeneration study (MNU-induced photoreceptor damage), systemic Alda-1 preserved ERG amplitudes, mitigated photoreceptor degeneration (OCT, histology), increased retinal ALDH2 and SIRT1 protein, and reduced markers of ER stress (GRP78) and apoptosis (PARP1), supporting the hypothesis that enhancing aldehyde detoxification ameliorates retinal cellular stress downstream of lipid peroxidation (Yan et al., 2020; Carullo et al., 2020). Although neither model recapitulates RPE-centric dry AMD (drusen, complement activation, geographic atrophy), they provide proof-of-principle that ALDH2 activation can protect neural retina under oxidative/aldehydic stress in vivo (Yan et al., 2020; He et al., 2018).

Clinical translation status remains nascent. No human proof-of-concept trials of Alda-1 have been reported, and authoritative reviews note the absence of clinical efficacy data for ALDH2 activators like Alda-1, despite extensive rodent evidence across organs; moreover, no ALDH2 activators are in clinical use at present (Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019). Safety experience is therefore limited to preclinical settings: chronic Alda-1 dosing in naïve rats (10 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks) demonstrated acceptable tolerability (no hemodynamic, biochemical, or organ-weight changes), whereas a separate report described crystalline nephropathy and renal function deterioration after I/R under specific Alda-1 dosing/formulation conditions, suggesting potential tissue-specific or formulation-dependent risks requiring evaluation (Gomes et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2023). With respect to ophthalmology, existing Alda-1 studies are limited to rodent retina in DR and MNU models; there is no published use in dry AMD patients or preclinical AMD-like RPE atrophy models, and there is no reported ocular delivery pharmacokinetics or long-term ocular safety data in the provided literature (Yan et al., 2020; He et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action  
ALDH2 is a mitochondrial, NAD⁺-dependent dehydrogenase that catalyzes the oxidation of reactive aldehydes—most notably acetaldehyde, 4-HNE, MDA, acrolein, and DOPAL—to their corresponding carboxylic acids, thereby detoxifying electrophiles that otherwise form covalent Michael adducts and Schiff bases with cysteine, histidine, and lysine residues on proteins and nucleic acids (Kimura et al., 2019; Budas et al., 2009). The enzyme’s catalytic mechanism involves NAD⁺ binding in the Rossmann fold and activation of the catalytic cysteine (Cys302 in ALDH2), nucleophilic attack on the aldehyde to form a thiohemiacetal, hydride transfer to produce a thioacyl-enzyme intermediate, and Glu268-mediated hydrolysis to release the acid product and NADH; this canonical chemistry underlies ALDH2’s role as an indirect antioxidant via aldehyde clearance rather than direct ROS scavenging (Parajuli, 2013; Wang & He, 2018). Importantly, ALDH2 is highly susceptible to oxidative and electrophilic inactivation—its active-site cysteine cluster (Cys301–Cys303) can be adducted by 4-HNE at micromolar concentrations (>10 µM), establishing a pathogenic feed-forward loop in which lipid peroxidation products both injure proteins and progressively compromise the aldehyde-detoxifying capacity of mitochondria (Karan et al., 2023; Budas et al., 2009).

Alda-1 engages this system at multiple mechanistic levels. Structurally, Alda-1 binds to the substrate entrance tunnel and active site of ALDH2, altering the local environment to increase effective substrate/catalytic-cysteine proximity and improve NAD⁺ binding (lower Kₘ), while simultaneously acting as a molecular chaperone to stabilize conformational elements disrupted in the ALDH2*2 variant (e.g., restoring α-helix and active-site loop structures toward wild-type) (Gao et al., 2022; Wang & He, 2018). Functionally, Alda-1 increases wild-type ALDH2 catalytic activity approximately two-fold, but the effect is more pronounced in ALDH2*2 (10-fold or more in homotetramers), which is clinically relevant in East Asian populations; Alda-1 does not affect ALDH1/ALDH5 in initial selectivity panels, though subsequent biochemical reports indicate potential ALDH1A1 activation under specific conditions (i.e., DOPAL-inactivation assays), a detail that warrants further isozyme-specific profiling in ocular tissues (Budas et al., 2009; Kotraiah et al., 2013). Crucially, Alda-1 also reduces aldehyde access to catalytic cysteines (Cys302/301/303), protecting ALDH2 from 4-HNE–induced inactivation, thereby sustaining endogenous detoxification under aldehyde stress; in direct assays Alda-1 prevents rapid 4-HNE-mediated ALDH2 inactivation and shifts the enzyme to a higher-efficiency state (Gao et al., 2022; Kotraiah et al., 2013). The net biochemical outcome is enhancement of mitochondrial clearance of 4-HNE to the less reactive 4-hydroxynonenoic acid (4-HNA), alongside accelerated metabolism of other toxic aldehydes, which interrupts aldehyde-driven proteotoxic cascades (e.g., proteasomal inhibition, protein carbonyl accumulation) and preserves mitochondrial respiratory function (Budas et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2014).

Systems-level consequences of ALDH2 activation by Alda-1 have been delineated extensively in heart and liver. In failing hearts with elevated aldehydic load, Alda-1 decreased 4-HNE-protein adducts and total carbonyls without altering ALDH2 protein abundance, demonstrating a purely catalytic detoxification effect (i.e., activity increase without expression change) (Gomes et al., 2014). Mitochondrial bioenergetic protection is robust: Alda-1 preserved State 3 respiration, increased RCR, normalized uncoupler responses (CCCP), reduced absolute and relative H₂O₂ release, decreased cytochrome c release, and corrected MPT sensitivity, indicating mitigation of mitochondria-centered death signaling under chronic oxidative/aldehydic stress (Gomes et al., 2014). In isolated mitochondria, pre-incubation with Alda-1 prevented 4-HNE–induced declines in respiratory control and State 3 oxygen consumption, further supporting a direct anti-aldehyde effect on mitochondrial electron transport chain function (Gomes et al., 2014). In the APAP hepatotoxicity model, Alda-1 reduced tissue 4-HNE adduct burden by an order of magnitude, preserved mitochondrial polarization, and reduced cell death, consistent with detoxification of lipid peroxidation products downstream of parent electrophile formation (Wimborne et al., 2020).

Retinal and neuronal contexts provide complementary mechanistic observations. In cultured endothelial cells exposed to amyloid-β₁–₄₀, Alda-1 restored mitochondrial function, reduced 4-HNE adducts and ROS, and rescued angiogenic responses, indicating that ALDH2 activation can directly blunt aldehyde-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction in non-cardiac cells (Chen & Joshi, 2016; Roy, 2022). Within the retina, ALDH2 localizes across layers with predominant co-localization to CRALBP-positive Müller glia, and its expression diminishes with age; transgenic upregulation protects against retinal aging by decreasing oxidative-stress–related apoptosis and enhancing the unfolded protein response (UPR) in the ER, indicating that increased ALDH2 activity has cytoprotective effects in vivo in the aging retina (Karan et al., 2023; Long et al., 2020). In diabetic retinopathy rodent studies, Alda-1 increased retinal ALDH2, SIRT1, and Nrf2 signaling, decreased proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6), and improved electrophysiologic and structural outcomes, suggesting that ALDH2 activation enlists antioxidant and proteostasis pathways beyond direct aldehyde detoxification to preserve retinal function (He et al., 2018). In photoreceptor degeneration, Alda-1 upregulated SIRT1 and decreased ER stress/apoptotic markers, again consistent with mitigation of downstream stress signaling when aldehyde load is reduced (Yan et al., 2020).

Finally, the disease biochemistry underpinning our hypothesis—aldehyde toxicity as a conserved driver downstream of oxidative lipid peroxidation—is well defined in neurodegeneration and retinal biology. 4-HNE forms adducts that impair proteasome activity, promote accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and inflammation, covalently modify and crosslink amyloid peptides, impair ion pumps and transporters, and directly kill neurons at low micromolar concentrations; ALDH2 loss-of-function (including ALDH2*2) exacerbates accumulation of 4-HNE adducts and age-dependent neurodegeneration in rodent models (Chen & Joshi, 2016). In retinal disease, the RPE and photoreceptors operate in a high-oxygen, PUFA-rich environment, with continuous photo-oxidation and phagocytosis of outer segments generating lipid peroxides and aldehydes, and oxidative stress is a central driver of AMD pathogenesis; therapeutic strategies that augment endogenous detoxification (e.g., via Nrf2) have been proposed as rational approaches to bolster RPE resilience (Chen et al., 2023). Collectively, Alda-1’s biochemical action—activation of a mitochondrial enzyme that eliminates 4-HNE/MDA—integrates tightly with the pathophysiology of aldehyde-mediated mitochondrial and proteostatic injury that characterizes oxidatively stressed retinal tissues (Kimura et al., 2019; Budas et al., 2009).

Expected Effect  
In RPE mitochondria subjected to chronic oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, the proposed mechanism predicts that Alda-1 will (i) increase ALDH2 catalytic activity and resilience to aldehyde-induced inactivation, (ii) accelerate metabolic clearance of 4-HNE and related long-lived electrophiles to non-reactive acids, (iii) reduce covalent adduction/carbonylation of mitochondrial and cytosolic proteins, (iv) preserve oxidative phosphorylation (increased State 3 respiration and RCR), (v) lower mitochondrial H₂O₂ production, (vi) increase resistance to Ca²⁺-induced MPT and decrease cytochrome c release, and (vii) therefore reduce apoptotic signaling and downstream inflammation in RPE, which in aggregate should attenuate RPE dysfunction and slow progression of dry AMD (Gomes et al., 2014). While direct ALDH2 expression in RPE has not been demonstrated in the provided texts, ALDH2 is present across retinal layers (notably Müller glia) and declines with age, and increasing ALDH2 conferred protection in the aged mouse retina in vivo, supporting the rationale that ALDH2 activation in retinal tissue can be beneficial under oxidative stress; confirming ALDH2 expression and activity in human and murine RPE will be a critical enabling experiment (Karan et al., 2023; Long et al., 2020). The retina’s documented vulnerability to lipid peroxidation (PUFA-rich outer segments, high O₂ consumption, chronic light exposure) and the centrality of oxidative stress to AMD pathogenesis further support that increased mitochondrial aldehyde detoxification should reduce toxic aldehyde burden in RPE and adjacent cells (Chen et al., 2023).

Assay expectations and readouts for validation align closely with prior Alda-1 literature. In isolated RPE mitochondria or permeabilized cells, Alda-1 should preserve ADP-stimulated State 3 oxygen consumption and increase RCR versus vehicle under aldehydic load (e.g., exogenous 4-HNE) or oxidative stress conditions; decreased H₂O₂ release and normalization of uncoupler (CCCP) responses would be predicted based on cardiac mitochondria data (Gomes et al., 2014). Under Ca²⁺ challenge, Alda-1 should increase the threshold for MPT and reduce cytochrome c release; in intact RPE, Alda-1 should maintain Δψm under oxidative stress (e.g., blue light, NaIO₃, HOHA lactone), paralleling hepatocyte in vivo imaging under APAP (Gomes et al., 2014; Wimborne et al., 2020). At the biochemical level, 4-HNE-protein adduct quantification (IHC/ELISA/LC-MS) and protein carbonylation assays should show significant reductions with Alda-1 pretreatment; mitochondrial respiratory chain complex activities may be preserved relative to vehicle under electrophile exposure (Gomes et al., 2014; Cheng, 2019). Downstream stress responses (e.g., ER stress markers such as GRP78, UPR activation; SIRT1 and Nrf2 activity; inflammatory cytokines TNF-α/IL-6) should reflect improved homeostasis, consistent with diabetic retina and MNU data (He et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020). Methodologically, the respiratory chain enzymology and aldehyde reactivity analytics described for RPE systems (e.g., complex I–IV assays in 96-well format, reverse-phase HPLC quantitation of aldehyde scavenging, LC-MS/MS quantitation of aldehyde uptake) are directly applicable to evaluating Alda-1’s effects on mitochondrial function and aldehyde handling in RPE models (Cheng, 2019).

A critical caveat is that ALDH2 distribution within the retina emphasizes Müller cells rather than RPE in available reports, and ALDH2 can be inactivated by high aldehyde levels (>10 µM 4-HNE), implying that the therapeutic window may be constrained under extreme aldehydic stress; Alda-1 is explicitly reported to reduce 4-HNE accessibility to catalytic cysteines and reverse 4-HNE–mediated inhibition, which should mitigate this concern but does not obviate the need to quantify ALDH2 activity and 4-HNE load in RPE during oxidative stress (Karan et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2022). Given that dry AMD pathobiology includes chronic oxidative stress, complement-driven inflammation, lysosomal/lipofuscin pathology, and lipid/protein debris accumulation (drusen), the expected benefit of Alda-1 would likely be most pronounced on the oxidative–aldehydic damage axis (mitochondrial and proteostatic integrity) rather than directly addressing complement or lipid trafficking, suggesting it would be a mechanistically complementary therapy potentially combined with agents targeting other AMD pathways (Chen et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic coherence with AMD pathophysiology: Dry AMD is driven in part by oxidative stress in RPE with accumulation of lipid peroxidation products; ALDH2 is a mitochondrial enzyme that detoxifies 4-HNE/MDA and is susceptible to inactivation by aldehydes, establishing a feed-forward injury loop that Alda-1 is designed to interrupt (Chen et al., 2023; Budas et al., 2009; Karan et al., 2023).  
- Direct mitochondrial mechanism with robust preclinical performance: Alda-1 increases ALDH2 activity, reduces 4-HNE adducts and protein carbonyls, preserves State 3 respiration and RCR, reduces mitochondrial H₂O₂ emission, raises MPT thresholds, and decreases cytochrome c release under chronic aldehydic stress; these endpoints directly match the mitochondrial failure features observed in stressed RPE (Gomes et al., 2014).  
- Retinal in vivo signals: In diabetic and photoreceptor degeneration models, Alda-1 improved ERG, preserved retinal structure, increased SIRT1/Nrf2 signaling, reduced inflammatory cytokines, and diminished ER stress/apoptotic markers, collectively supporting retinal tissue benefit under oxidative stress (He et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020).  
- Protective breadth across organs and insults via aldehyde clearance: Repeated demonstration that Alda-1 reduces 4-HNE accumulation and preserves mitochondrial function in heart, liver, lung, intestine, and neuronal contexts increases confidence that the aldehyde-clearance mechanism is conserved and translatable (Wimborne et al., 2020; Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019).  
- Pharmacogenetic upside: Alda-1 rescues ALDH2*2 activity, suggesting potential efficacy in East Asian ALDH2*2 carriers, a large at-risk population for aldehyde-mediated diseases; this also provides a biomarker-based stratification opportunity in trials (Budas et al., 2009; Kimura et al., 2019).  
- Safety signs in chronic rodent dosing: Six-week daily Alda-1 in naïve rats showed no hemodynamic, biochemical, or organ-weight toxicity, supporting tolerability for longer-term therapy (Gomes et al., 2014).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Lack of dry AMD/RPE-specific data: No direct evidence in RPE-focused dry AMD models (e.g., NaIO₃-induced RPE atrophy, complement dysregulation models, aging-driven GA models) is presented in the context, and ALDH2 expression has not been explicitly demonstrated in RPE here; expression across retina with Müller co-localization and protection in aged retina is encouraging but not definitive for RPE (Karan et al., 2023; Long et al., 2020).  
- Clinical translation gap: No human proof-of-concept for Alda-1 or class; no ALDH2 activator currently in clinical use; ocular PK, distribution, and chronic safety are uncharacterized (Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019).  
- Potential safety concerns: A preclinical report of Alda-1–associated crystalline nephropathy after I/R cautions that formulation, dosing, or off-target deposition may cause tissue-specific toxicity; comprehensive toxicology and formulation work are essential, especially for chronic ocular indications (Jin et al., 2023).  
- Biological complexity and compensatory pathways: Chronic acceleration of aldehyde clearance could theoretically blunt electrophile-mediated adaptive antioxidant signaling (Keap1/Nrf2, PPAR), potentially reducing hormetic protection; the balance of detoxification versus adaptation requires careful evaluation in chronic degenerative settings (Münzel & Daiber, 2018).  
- Enzyme inactivation at high aldehyde loads: ALDH2 is inactivated by >10 µM 4-HNE; although Alda-1 protects ALDH2 from 4-HNE and enhances activity, in extreme aldehydic states therapeutic efficacy might be limited, necessitating combination with upstream ROS control or lipid peroxidation inhibitors (Karan et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2022).  
- Isoform selectivity: Some reports suggest Alda-1 can modulate ALDH1A1 activity, while others report inconclusive cross-activation; off-target activation or inhibition in ocular tissues could have unanticipated effects on retinoid metabolism or cellular differentiation, especially given ALDH1A1’s role in retinaldehyde metabolism and Müller cell biology (Kotraiah et al., 2013; Karan et al., 2023).  
- Delivery challenges: Systemic dosing achieves retinal effects in rodent DR/MNU models, but the optimal route for chronic dry AMD (topical, intravitreal, suprachoroidal, systemic) is unknown; achieving therapeutic mitochondrial concentrations in RPE with acceptable safety will be nontrivial and requires PK/PD studies (Yan et al., 2020; He et al., 2018).

Decision-oriented recommendations  
- Mechanistic validation in human/murine RPE: Quantify ALDH2 mRNA/protein/activity and subcellular localization in primary human RPE and iPSC-RPE; test whether Alda-1 increases ALDH2 activity and protects against 4-HNE–induced ALDH2 inactivation in RPE mitochondria; measure 4-HNE/ACR/MDA adduct load ±Alda-1 under blue-light/NaIO₃/HOHA lactone stress (Karan et al., 2023; Cheng, 2019).  
- Mitochondrial function endpoints in RPE: Using established microplate assays and Seahorse OCR, test Alda-1’s effects on State 3 respiration, RCR, Δψm, H₂O₂ release, CCCP response, MPT susceptibility, and cytochrome c release under aldehydic stress (Gomes et al., 2014; Cheng, 2019).  
- Retinal disease models aligned to dry AMD: Progress to NaIO₃-induced RPE injury, photo-oxidative stress, and aging/complement models relevant to geographic atrophy; evaluate RPE survival, autofluorescent lipofuscin, drusen-like deposits, inflammatory markers, and photoreceptor secondary degeneration with functional readouts (ERG/OCT) under Alda-1 (Chen et al., 2023).  
- Formulation and delivery: Develop ocular formulations (e.g., intravitreal, sustained-release) and conduct ocular PK/PD to quantify RPE mitochondrial exposure; evaluate chronic ocular and systemic safety with renal monitoring given crystalline nephropathy risk (Jin et al., 2023).  
- Biomarkers and patient stratification: Consider ALDH2 genotype (ALDH2*2 carriers), circulating/ocular 4-HNE-adduct biomarkers, and retinal imaging endpoints as stratification and PD markers; Alda-1’s rescue of ALDH2*2 suggests a precision-medicine angle (Budas et al., 2009; Münzel & Daiber, 2018).  
- Combinations: Given AMD’s multifactorial pathobiology, test Alda-1 alongside Nrf2 activators or lipid peroxidation suppressors to determine additive/synergistic effects on RPE resilience while monitoring for suppression of adaptive electrophile signaling (Chen et al., 2023; Münzel & Daiber, 2018).

Overall, Alda-1 presents a mechanistically compelling, enzyme-directed strategy to alleviate aldehyde-driven mitochondrial and proteostatic injury in oxidatively stressed retinal tissues, with in vivo retinal efficacy already demonstrated in DR and photoreceptor degeneration contexts, albeit without RPE-centric dry AMD models to date (He et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020). The totality of evidence across organ systems (cardiac, hepatic) underscores that Alda-1 reliably reduces 4-HNE load and preserves mitochondrial function in vivo—precisely the biology we seek to modulate in RPE for dry AMD—making this candidate worthy of structured, stepwise validation in RPE-specific systems and AMD-relevant models (Gomes et al., 2014; Wimborne et al., 2020). Key risks reside in translational gaps (RPE expression, ocular PK/safety), potential toxicity signals (renal crystalline nephropathy under certain conditions), and the possibility that aldehyde detoxification alone will be insufficient to arrest complex AMD progression without adjunctive modulation of complement, lipid trafficking, or lysosomal pathways (Jin et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). With these caveats, Alda-1 merits advancement to focused preclinical validation for dry AMD, with an emphasis on RPE mitochondrial protection endpoints, aldehyde-adduct burden, and rigorous ocular safety assessment before considering first-in-human studies.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) is an endogenous bile acid, a taurine conjugate of ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), that was originally isolated from bear bile and is now produced synthetically for laboratory and clinical research (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). As a member of the bile acid family, TUDCA has a dual role: its traditional function in lipid digestion is accompanied by potent signaling activities that provide chemical chaperoning properties. This property enables TUDCA to stabilize misfolded proteins and alleviate endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. In addition, TUDCA exerts anti-apoptotic effects by modulating the mitochondrial cell death pathway. Its application as a neuroprotectant has emerged over the last decade, and its favorable ocular safety profile in preclinical studies has invited consideration for repurposing in retinal degenerative conditions such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, TUDCA and related bile acids have been evaluated in several models of neurodegeneration and retinal degeneration. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that TUDCA protects retinal cells against both oxidative injury and ER stress. In vitro, TUDCA treatment of ARPE-19 retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) not only attenuated cell death but also reduced markers of oxidative damage, increased cell viability, and modulated antioxidant gene expression (Alhasani et al., 2020). In parallel, multiple in vivo studies have reported that systemic administration of TUDCA reduces photoreceptor apoptosis and preserves retinal structure and function in animal models of inherited retinal degeneration including retinitis pigmentosa and in models of exudative AMD such as laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024). Although the bulk of these preclinical investigations has been conducted in models focusing on photoreceptors, retinal ganglion cells, or vascular endpoints, the underlying mechanisms of TUDCA’s cytoprotective activity raise the possibility that its benefits may extend to the RPE—the cell type that is centrally involved in dry AMD and geographic atrophy. Importantly, little direct evidence exists from dedicated geographic atrophy models or experiments that solely target RPE mitochondrial endpoints; however, the promising biochemical and electrophysiological data from rodent models suggest that the candidate’s safety and overall neuroprotective profile are well established in ocular systems (Alhasani et al., 2020; Li et al., 2024).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanistic basis of TUDCA’s therapeutic potential is multifaceted. A central theme is its ability to reduce ER stress in cells that are undergoing chronic protein-folding challenges. Under conditions of sustained stress, the unfolded protein response (UPR) is activated, and key transcription factors such as CHOP (CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein homologous protein) become upregulated to drive cell death when the stress is unmanageable. TUDCA has been shown in various cell models to act as a chemical chaperone, thereby reducing ER stress and suppressing CHOP induction (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020). For instance, in ARPE-19 cell models treated with thapsigargin to induce ER stress, TUDCA treatment led to a marked decrease in CHOP expression and reduced apoptosis (Alhasani et al., 2020). This suggests that TUDCA modulates the ER stress response, possibly by stabilizing protein folding and facilitating the proper trafficking of misfolded proteins.  

In addition to its ER‐related effects, TUDCA exerts anti-apoptotic actions by stabilizing the mitochondrial membrane. Under stress conditions, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) triggers the intrinsic apoptosis pathway, characterized by the translocation of pro-apoptotic proteins such as Bax, the release of cytochrome c, and subsequent caspase activation (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Kusaczuk, 2019). Evidence from neuronal models and some retinal studies indicates that TUDCA prevents the depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane, thereby preserving Δψm, and reduces downstream apoptotic events. This effect has been linked to a reduction in mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), which are produced excessively when mitochondrial integrity is compromised. TUDCA’s actions in reducing overall intracellular ROS levels, as reported in H₂O₂-exposed RPE cells, further support the idea that improved mitochondrial function may contribute to cell survival (Alhasani et al., 2020).  

Moreover, TUDCA can modulate additional cellular pathways that are pertinent to retinal health. It has been reported to up-regulate antioxidant defenses via increased expression of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) and enhancement of glutathione (GSH) levels. These effects likely contribute to the reduction in both cytosolic and mitochondrial oxidative stress (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Other studies have highlighted TUDCA’s influence on phagocytic pathways in the RPE—for example, by promoting MerTK-mediated phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments—which, although not directly linked to ER or mitochondrial stress, represent an important aspect of RPE physiology that could indirectly improve cell survival in degenerative conditions (Murase et al., 2015).  

Taken together, the biochemical and molecular data indicate that TUDCA’s mechanism of action is well aligned with addressing the cellular stress observed in dry AMD. By inhibiting CHOP induction, preserving Δψm, and reducing mtROS, TUDCA could feasibly stop or slow the progression of RPE cell death that underpins geographic atrophy (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

Expected Effect:  
The proposal hypothesizes that TUDCA will reduce ER stress in the RPE, thereby preventing secondary mitochondrial dysfunction and the associated production of reactive oxygen species. In the proposed assay, RPE cells (either ARPE-19 or primary RPE cultures) subjected to an ER stressor (such as thapsigargin or H₂O₂) are expected to exhibit elevated markers of ER stress, particularly CHOP, along with signs of mitochondrial distress including decreased mitochondrial membrane potential and increased mtROS production. On treatment with TUDCA at appropriate dosages (often in the 100 μM range in similar in vitro assays), one expects to observe a significant reduction in CHOP induction along with the preservation or restoration of Δψm, as measured by fluorescent indicators such as JC-1 or TMRM, and a concomitant decrease in mitochondrial ROS as assessed by probes such as MitoSOX. These effects are expected because prior in vitro studies in retinal cells have shown that TUDCA can ameliorate cell death by modulating oxidative stress and apoptosis, and similar outcomes have been observed in neuronal and non-retinal cell models (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

Furthermore, given that dry AMD is characterized by chronic ER stress and secondary mitochondrial dysfunction in the RPE, the ability of TUDCA to reduce these stress responses may translate into improved RPE survival and function. RPE cells express high levels of ER stress markers under pathologic conditions, and proteins such as CHOP are known mediators of apoptosis in these cells. It is therefore expected that TUDCA will attenuate the cascade of events initiated by ER stress—reducing apoptotic signaling, preserving mitochondrial function, reducing mtROS, and ultimately leading to enhanced cell viability. As such, the anticipated outcome in the proposed assay is a clear biochemical and functional improvement in RPE cultures challenged with ER stressors, supporting the use of TUDCA in dry AMD (Alhasani et al., 2020).  

Overall Evaluation:  
TUDCA presents as a promising candidate for drug repurposing in dry AMD due to its well-documented roles as an ER stress inhibitor and mitochondrial stabilizer. One of the major strengths of TUDCA is its dual mechanism of action: it not only functions as a chemical chaperone to reduce ER stress and inhibit the pro-apoptotic effector CHOP but also stabilizes the mitochondrial membrane to prevent the cascade of events leading to cell death. These effects are complemented by its ability to reduce overall reactive oxygen species and bolster antioxidant defenses, which are critical in tissues affected by chronic oxidative stress such as the RPE in geographic atrophy (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020).  

In terms of therapeutic history, TUDCA has been used extensively in preclinical models of retinal degeneration, with multiple studies demonstrating its protective effects on photoreceptors and retinal ganglion cells. Its prior use in ocular contexts and a favorable safety profile in animal models provide important translational support. However, one potential weakness in repurposing TUDCA for dry AMD is that most of the preclinical evidence is derived from models of photoreceptor degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, or choroidal neovascularization rather than from targeted assessments in RPE cells or dry AMD models. While there is suggestive evidence from several studies that TUDCA benefits RPE function—such as improved phagocytosis via MerTK activation—the direct demonstration of its ability to inhibit CHOP induction, preserve mitochondrial membrane potential, or specifically reduce mitochondrial ROS in RPE is less robust (Alhasani et al., 2020; Murase et al., 2015).  

Furthermore, although mechanistic data in other tissue and neuronal models strongly support TUDCA’s capacity to modulate both ER stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Kusaczuk, 2019), these endpoints have not been unequivocally established in RPE cells within the context of geographic atrophy. This gap highlights the need for further targeted preclinical studies. For example, experiments using polarized primary RPE cultures or RPE-specific animal models of dry AMD should be undertaken to directly measure CHOP expression, mitochondrial membrane potential via JC-1/TMRM assays, and mtROS levels via MitoSOX or equivalent assays following TUDCA treatment. Additionally, while in vitro assays have established its general safety in retinal cells, chronic dosing studies in appropriate AMD models will be important to establish long-term efficacy and safety.  

Another consideration is that the multifaceted nature of dry AMD pathogenesis extends beyond ER stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. While TUDCA’s actions on these pathways are compelling, resistance or compensatory mechanisms in RPE cells could limit its efficacy in the complex environment of geographic atrophy. Nonetheless, the broad-spectrum anti-apoptotic and anti-oxidative actions of TUDCA provide a strong rationale for its further examination in dry AMD.  

In summary, TUDCA is a highly attractive candidate for repurposing as a therapy for dry AMD based on its natural origin as a bile acid, its established use as a chemical chaperone and mitochondrial stabilizer, and its demonstrated neuroprotective and cytoprotective effects in multiple retinal models. Its capacity to reduce ER stress—with particular inhibition of CHOP induction—and to preserve mitochondrial membrane potential and lower oxidative stress aligns well with the proposed mechanism underlying RPE degeneration in geographic atrophy. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Spermidine is a naturally occurring polyamine that was originally discovered in bovine semen and later shown to be ubiquitous in all forms of life, ranging from bacteria and plants to fungi and mammals. It belongs to the aliphatic polyamine class, characterized by its low molecular weight, linear arrangement, and multiple amino groups that are fully protonated at physiological pH. Its natural origins stem from highly conserved enzymatic biosynthetic pathways—starting either from ornithine via ornithine decarboxylase or from arginine through an agmatine intermediate—resulting in the formation of putrescine, which is subsequently converted to spermidine through the transfer of an aminopropyl group provided by decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine (dcSAM) (Casero & Marton, 2007; Hobley et al., 2017; Khomutov et al., 2019). Although spermidine can be isolated from natural sources such as food and tissues, it is also available in a chemically defined form commercially (for example, Sigma-Aldrich S2626) and has been used in basic research as well as in some experimental therapeutic approaches. This compound is representative of the polyamine family, and these molecules have traditionally been investigated for their roles in cellular proliferation, nucleic acid stabilization, and modulation of various enzymatic activities, which in turn have broad implications for health and disease (Madeo et al., 2020; Nichugovskiy et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, spermidine’s potential therapeutic applications have been explored extensively in the context of its ability to induce autophagy and affect cellular homeostasis. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that spermidine supplementation can extend lifespan and improve the function of various tissues by enhancing autophagy, contributing to cardioprotection, and promoting neuroprotection in animal models (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). In the ocular domain, several studies have examined its effects on retinal cells: in vitro experiments using ARPE-19 retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells have shown that spermidine can protect against oxidative stress induced by hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) by mitigating intracellular calcium overload and maintaining mitochondrial integrity (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021). Additionally, there are preclinical observations in which intravitreal administration of spermidine in animal models produced both protective effects—in terms of reducing RPE apoptosis—and, at higher doses, toxic outcomes such as RPE necrosis and photoreceptor degeneration (Ohashi et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022). Although spermidine has not been clinically trialed specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), its effects on RPE survival and ocular inflammation have been documented in models that mimic some of the pathophysiologic stressors in dry AMD, such as oxidative damage and dysregulated autophagy (Kim et al., 2021; Senekowitsch et al., 2023). In addition, dietary supplementation studies in humans have associated higher spermidine intake with various beneficial health outcomes, including improved endothelial function and cognitive performance; however, the use of spermidine or polyamines more broadly in chronic degenerative ocular conditions remains largely in the preclinical stage (Madeo et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
The hypothesized mechanism for using spermidine in dry AMD is multifaceted and centers on its ability to modulate cellular quality control processes. At the molecular level, spermidine is known to induce autophagy, a process that mediates the degradation and recycling of damaged or dysfunctional cellular constituents. In model systems ranging from yeast to mammalian cells, spermidine has been shown to increase the conversion of the autophagy marker LC3-I to LC3-II, thereby promoting autophagosome formation (Qin et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022). One important molecular target of spermidine appears to be EP300 (p300), a histone acetyltransferase that, when inhibited, leads to reduced acetylation of several autophagy-related proteins. Inhibition of EP300 has been correlated with enhanced autophagic flux, and several studies suggest that spermidine may exert its autophagy-inducing effects partly by downregulating EP300 expression or activity (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020).

In addition to its effects on EP300, spermidine has been implicated in the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), an evolutionarily conserved energy sensor that modulates metabolic homeostasis and mitochondrial quality control. Activation of AMPK can lead to the phosphorylation and activation of downstream effectors that promote both autophagy and mitophagy (the selective autophagic removal of damaged mitochondria). While direct evidence for AMPK activation by spermidine in retinal cells is still emerging, broader studies in other cell types have described an upregulation of pathways associated with mitochondrial biogenesis and quality control, including the deacetylation of proteins by SIRT1, which often acts in concert with AMPK (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). In the specific context of RPE cells under stress from A2E (a component of lipofuscin) or H₂O₂, the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria and high levels of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) play critical roles in cell loss and dysfunction; thus, induction of mitophagy via enhanced AMPK signaling and subsequent Parkin recruitment to depolarized mitochondria could improve mitochondrial homeostasis and reduce oxidative damage (Kim et al., 2021).

Furthermore, spermidine’s role as an intracellular calcium chelator appears pivotal in its protective effect in RPE cells. Studies have demonstrated that pre-treatment of ARPE-19 cells with 10 µM spermidine prior to oxidative stress prevents intracellular Ca²⁺ overload—a phenomenon that can trigger endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and cell death—thereby maintaining cellular integrity independent of direct ROS scavenging (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021). In summary, spermidine is posited to enhance the clearance of damaged organelles—particularly mitochondria—by increasing autophagic flux through EP300 inhibition and AMPK activation, leading to enhanced LC3-II conversion and Parkin-mediated mitophagy. This, in turn, is expected to reduce mtROS and protect RPE cell viability under conditions of oxidative and A2E-induced stress (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its mode of action, the expected effect of spermidine in a dry AMD model would be a pronounced improvement in the quality control mechanisms of RPE cells. The compound is anticipated to induce autophagy, evidenced by a measurable increase in LC3-II levels, alongside enhanced recruitment of the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin to dysfunctional mitochondria. This concerted activation of autophagy and mitophagy should facilitate the clearance of damaged mitochondria, thereby reducing the accumulation of mtROS and attenuating oxidative stress. In the context of A2E accumulation—a key driver of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD—spermidine is predicted to restore mitochondrial function and improve cell viability. Experimental assays are expected to show that spermidine pre-treatment leads to a significant reduction in apoptosis markers (e.g., caspase-3 activation, cytochrome c release), along with improved markers of mitochondrial integrity (e.g., stabilized mitochondrial membrane potential) in ARPE-19 cells exposed to H₂O₂ or A2E (Kim et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating spermidine as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current literature. One major strength is its natural origin and well-documented role as a global inducer of autophagy and mitophagy. This aligns well with the current understanding of dry AMD pathogenesis, in which impaired autophagic clearance and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells play major roles (Nichugovskiy et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2021). The ability of spermidine to inhibit EP300—a factor whose downregulation encourages autophagy—and to potentially activate AMPK signaling suggests that it could enhance several intracellular quality control processes simultaneously (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). The preclinical data showing that spermidine can protect ARPE-19 cells from H₂O₂-induced oxidative injury by blocking Ca²⁺ overload and reducing apoptotic signaling further bolster its potential utility in ocular applications (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021).

However, there are notable challenges and weaknesses associated with this therapeutic candidate. First, the dose response appears to be remarkably narrow; while low micromolar concentrations (e.g., 10 µM) exert cytoprotective effects in vitro, higher doses have been associated with cytotoxicity, including RPE cell death and photoreceptor degeneration in animal models following intravitreal injection (Ohashi et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022). This raises concerns about the therapeutic window and the optimal route of delivery for chronic conditions like dry AMD. Another limitation is that, despite promising mechanistic data, direct clinical evidence for the use of spermidine in dry AMD is currently lacking. Most of the studies available have been conducted in vitro or in animal models under conditions of oxidative stress, and while these findings are encouraging, they do not fully recapitulate the complex pathophysiology of dry AMD, which involves not only oxidative damage but also chronic inflammation, immune dysregulation, and drusen accumulation (Kim et al., 2021).

Moreover, while the hypothesis emphasizes effects on EP300 inhibition and AMPK activation leading to enhanced LC3-II conversion and Parkin recruitment, the direct evidence linking these specific molecular events to improved outcomes in dry AMD models remains preliminary. There is a need for more comprehensive studies that directly measure these autophagic and mitophagic markers in RPE cells under conditions that mimic the A2E-induced stress typical of dry AMD (Kim et al., 2021). Additionally, the risk that spermidine’s metabolism by amine oxidases may produce toxic aldehyde byproducts such as acrolein must be carefully considered, as these compounds have been implicated in retinal degeneration in some intravitreal models (Ohashi et al., 2017).

In summary, while spermidine has a compelling mechanistic rationale as a modulator of autophagy and mitochondrial quality control, which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the current preclinical evidence is mixed and highlights potential safety challenges related to dosing and administration. Its established role in promoting cellular longevity and mitigating oxidative stress in diverse tissues certainly warrants further investigation, but rigorous studies using dry AMD-specific models are essential to ascertain its efficacy and safety in this context. Regulatory considerations will also require detailed pharmacokinetic and toxicological profiling, particularly given its dual potential for both cytoprotection and cytotoxicity depending on concentration and route of administration (Ohashi et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022).

Overall, our evaluation suggests that spermidine represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD based on its intrinsic properties as an autophagy and mitophagy inducer and its ability to protect RPE cells from oxidative damage; however, its clinical translation will depend on resolving key issues such as dose optimization, route of delivery, and comprehensive validation of its proposed molecular mechanisms in relevant models of AMD. The strengths of spermidine lie in its natural occurrence, multi-targeted action on cellular quality control mechanisms, and established preclinical benefits in other models of aging and oxidative stress. Conversely, the main weaknesses are its narrow therapeutic window, the potential for generation of toxic metabolites, and the current lack of direct clinical or robust in vivo data in dry AMD models. Further research, including detailed investigations in RPE models using A2E and oxidative stress conditions as well as careful titration studies in animal models of dry AMD, is warranted to determine its viability as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for this unmet clinical need (Casero & Marton, 2007; Kim et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022; Ohashi et al., 2017).

1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Mdivi-1, known as mitochondrial division inhibitor 1 (catalog number Sigma-Aldrich M0199), is a synthetic small-molecule compound originally developed for research into mitochondrial dynamics. It belongs to a class of therapeutic agents that modulate mitochondrial fission by targeting the dynamin‐related protein 1 (DRP1). DRP1 is an essential GTPase responsible for driving mitochondrial fission, a process that maintains mitochondrial quality control but, when overactivated, can lead to fragmentation associated with cellular stress and apoptosis. Mdivi-1 was discovered via compound screening experiments aimed at identifying inhibitors of DRP1’s GTPase activity and has been characterized extensively in various in vitro and in vivo studies. Its discovery was motivated by the need to therapeutically intervene in pathologies where aberrant mitochondrial fission contributes to cellular dysfunction. As a representative of DRP1 inhibitory agents, Mdivi-1 has been widely used as an investigational tool in studies related to neurodegeneration, ischemia, and ocular diseases, where mitochondrial integrity is a key determinant of cell survival (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2020). Its synthetic origin and well-documented pharmacological profile render it a candidate for drug repurposing, with potential applications extending into the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) by addressing mitochondrial dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells.

2. Therapeutic History  
Mdivi-1 has a robust preclinical research history across a variety of models that involve oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Initial studies demonstrated that in retinal endothelial cells and neuronal tissues, inhibition of DRP1 by Mdivi-1 prevented excessive mitochondrial fragmentation under conditions of acute stress. In models of glaucoma, for instance, DRP1 overactivation associated with ocular hypertension leads to mitochondrial fragmentation and retinal ganglion cell death, and administration of Mdivi-1 was found to rescue these cells by preserving mitochondrial network integrity (Kim et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2021). Similarly, in photoreceptor cells following retinal detachment, Mdivi-1 treatment reduced the activation of apoptotic pathways—through downregulation of cleaved Caspase-3 and Bax—and consequently preserved cell morphology and function, indicating a protective effect mediated through the inhibition of DRP1-dependent fission (She et al., 2018). Furthermore, in ARPE-19 cells, which are commonly used as a model for RPE behavior, Mdivi-1 has been shown to mitigate the cytotoxic effects of oxidative stress induced by hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) by reducing mitochondrial fragmentation and cytochrome c release, thereby improving mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP production (Yako et al., 2021). Although Mdivi-1 has not yet been evaluated in large-scale clinical trials for dry AMD specifically, its use in diverse ocular models—ranging from diabetic retinopathy to retinal ischemia—provides compelling evidence that its mechanism could be beneficial in conditions marked by oxidative stress and RPE dysfunction, two hallmark features of dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). These cumulative findings support the repurposing hypothesis that targeting DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission could restore mitochondrial function and survival in RPE cells, thereby halting or slowing the degenerative cascade observed in dry AMD.

3. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, DRP1 is responsible for mediating mitochondrial fission through the constriction and subsequent division of mitochondrial membranes. Upon receiving various stress signals, DRP1 is recruited from the cytosol to the mitochondrial outer membrane where it oligomerizes and hydrolyzes GTP, driving membrane scission. Mdivi-1 specifically inhibits the GTPase activity of DRP1, thereby preventing its self-assembly and subsequent mitochondrial recruitment. This inhibition effectively blocks the fission process that is typically upregulated under conditions of oxidative stress and other cellular insults (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2020). Detailed biochemical investigations have demonstrated that when DRP1 activity is unopposed, mitochondrial fragmentation ensues, leading to diminished mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, decreased oxygen consumption rate (OCR), reduced ATP synthesis, and an increase in the generation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) (Yako et al., 2021). Mdivi-1 counters these deleterious cellular events by preserving the integrity of the mitochondrial network, enabling enhanced ATP production, and maintaining the mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP). Moreover, by inhibiting DRP1, Mdivi-1 reduces the stress-induced release of cytochrome c from the mitochondria—a central step in the intrinsic apoptotic pathway—thus lowering the activation of downstream caspases (She et al., 2018; Yako et al., 2021). In addition to these primary actions, some studies have noted that Mdivi-1 has reversible inhibitory effects on mitochondrial complex I, suggesting that its impact on mitochondrial bioenergetics may be multifaceted (Yako et al., 2021). Such dual actions may serve to further stabilize mitochondrial function under stress.

4. Expected Effect  
Under conditions relevant to dry age-related macular degeneration, such as chronic oxidative stress incident on RPE cells, Mdivi-1 is anticipated to exert a multi-pronged cytoprotective effect. In the proposed assay using H₂O₂-treated ARPE-19 cells—a well-established in vitro model to mimic the oxidative stress environment of dry AMD—the primary expected effect is the inhibition of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission (Yako et al., 2021). By stabilizing mitochondrial dynamics, Mdivi-1 should also improve cellular bioenergetics through enhanced OCR and increased ATP production, both critical parameters that are typically compromised in stressed RPE cells (Yako et al., 2021). The anticipated outcome of these events is a reduction in cell death and apoptosis, as well as improved phagocytic function—an essential role of RPE cells in the maintenance of retinal homeostasis. Furthermore, by mitigating the accumulation of mtROS, Mdivi-1 is expected to lessen oxidative stress, thereby curbing the degenerative processes that are a central component of dry AMD pathophysiology (Yako et al., 2021; Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025). In essence, the mechanistic intervention afforded by Mdivi-1 aims to interrupt the cycle of mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage that leads to RPE cell apoptosis, which is a critical driver of disease progression in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021).

5. Overall Evaluation  
In evaluating Mdivi-1 as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current body of literature. Among its strengths, Mdivi-1 is underpinned by a strong mechanistic rationale: the inhibition of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission is a well-validated approach to restore mitochondrial function in the face of oxidative stress. Preclinical studies have consistently demonstrated that Mdivi-1 preserves mitochondrial network integrity, reduces the production of harmful reactive oxygen species, and prevents the release of apoptogenic factors, thereby facilitating cell survival in retinal models (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2020; Yako et al., 2021). Its efficacy in multiple ocular contexts—including models of glaucoma, retinal detachment, and diabetic retinopathy—highlights the versatility of its cytoprotective actions, which may be directly relevant to the RPE dysfunction and oxidative injury observed in dry AMD (Kim et al., 2015; She et al., 2018). From a biochemical standpoint, the ability of Mdivi-1 to enhance mitochondrial bioenergetics by improving OCR and ATP production, while simultaneously preserving mitochondrial membrane potential, addresses essential aspects of RPE cell metabolism that are often impaired in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Furthermore, the compound’s capacity to reduce apoptotic signaling, as evidenced by decreased cytochrome c release and lower caspase activity, is particularly promising given the established link between mitochondrial-mediated apoptosis and RPE cell loss in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Despite these promising attributes, several limitations and challenges deserve consideration. First, while the preclinical evidence supporting Mdivi-1’s efficacy is compelling, there remains a notable gap in clinical data, particularly in the context of dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Another potential weakness arises from the dual inhibitory effects of Mdivi-1. Some investigations have reported that Mdivi-1 also exhibits reversible inhibition of mitochondrial complex I, which could complicate its therapeutic profile by inadvertently affecting normal mitochondrial respiration (Yako et al., 2021). Moreover, the chronic inhibition of DRP1 raises important questions about the broader physiological implications of interfering with mitochondrial dynamics (Mohammad & Kowluru, 2022; She et al., 2018). Furthermore, the in vitro models currently used, predominantly involving H₂O₂-treated ARPE-19 cells, may not entirely mimic the in vivo microenvironment of the human retina in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). The overall therapeutic window and safety profile of Mdivi-1 also require further elucidation (Yako et al., 2021). Despite these challenges, the mechanistic insights generated from a diverse array of experimental models suggest that Mdivi-1 holds considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its capacity to restore mitochondrial integrity, mitigate oxidative stress, and inhibit apoptotic cascades directly addresses several of the pathogenic mechanisms implicated in dry AMD. Given that current treatments for dry AMD are limited and mainly supportive, a disease-modifying therapy that targets mitochondrial dysfunction would represent a significant advancement in the management of this debilitating disorder (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2015). In summary, Mdivi-1’s strengths lie in its well-characterized mechanism of action, demonstrated efficacy in preserving mitochondrial dynamics under stress, and its potential to enhance cell survival in models of retinal degeneration (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2015; Yako et al., 2021).

Future studies must address the nuances of chronic DRP1 inhibition, optimize dosing regimens, evaluate long-term safety, and conduct thorough pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiling in ocular tissues to fully realize the potential of Mdivi-1 in the clinical management of dry AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Rong et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021).

In conclusion, the evidence provided by numerous preclinical studies strongly indicates that Mdivi-1’s inhibition of DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission offers a promising therapeutic strategy for dry age-related macular degeneration. The compound’s ability to maintain mitochondrial network integrity, enhance bioenergetics, and suppress apoptotic cascades under conditions of oxidative stress in RPE cells is particularly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Although challenges remain in addressing the potential off-target effects and ensuring long-term safety in the clinical setting, the mechanistic rationale and supporting preclinical data justify further investigation into the utility of Mdivi-1 as a repurposed candidate for this currently untreatable condition. As the drug development process progresses, a focused effort on meticulous in vivo testing, formulation development for ocular delivery, and comprehensive pharmacological evaluations will be critical to harnessing the full therapeutic potential of Mdivi-1 for patients with dry AMD (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2015; She et al., 2018; Yako et al., 2021).
