Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Omaveloxolone (RTA 408) is a semi-synthetic pentacyclic triterpenoid of the cyanoenone (oleanane-derived) chemical class rationally designed to activate the Keap1–Nrf2 pathway by electrophilic modification of redox-sensitive cysteine residues on Keap1, most prominently Cys151 (the key “sensor” cysteine for this chemotype) (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2016). Within its class, cyanoenone triterpenoids are among the most potent small-molecule NRF2 activators known; they are sensed at KEAP1 C151 and trigger a coordinated induction of antioxidant and cytoprotective programs that normalize cellular metabolism, increase mitochondrial energy production, and reduce ROS (including mtROS), while also exerting anti-inflammatory actions that can include modulation of NF-κB signaling in cells and animal models (Cuadrado et al., 2019). Mechanistically, omaveloxolone forms a covalent adduct with KEAP1 that prevents CUL3–KEAP1–mediated ubiquitination and degradation of Nrf2, thereby allowing Nrf2 stabilization, nuclear translocation, and transcriptional activation via antioxidant response elements (AREs) (Liu et al., 2016; Cai et al., 2021; Bellezza, 2018). In human systems, omaveloxolone induces canonical Nrf2 target genes that collectively bolster mitochondrial and cytosolic antioxidant defenses, including NQO1, HO-1, SOD2, catalase, glutaredoxin-1 (Grx1), and thioredoxin-1 (Trx1) (Liu et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2021).

Discovery and translational development of omaveloxolone followed extensive preclinical work with synthetic triterpenoids showing robust induction of the phase 2 response and protection against oxidant and inflammatory stress in vitro and in vivo, and early first-in-human experience with this class (e.g., bardoxolone methyl) helped establish on-target pharmacology while also highlighting class-specific safety considerations that informed subsequent designs (e.g., exclusion of patients with incipient heart failure risk in kidney indications) (Nakagami, 2016; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic programs in nonhuman primates and humans show that oral omaveloxolone is bioavailable, exhibits dose-proportional increases in Cmax and AUC, and reaches concentrations capable of inducing Nrf2 target genes in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and multiple tissues; tissue distribution studies in cynomolgus monkeys demonstrated exposure slightly above contemporaneous plasma levels in liver, lung, and brain with measurable mRNA induction of canonical Nrf2 targets after repeat dosing (Reisman et al., 2019). In human clinical development, omaveloxolone advanced through a first-in-human oncology study, a dose-ranging Phase 2 program (MOXIe Part 1) in Friedreich ataxia (FA) with clear pharmacodynamic biomarker changes (e.g., ferritin and GGT) and dose/exposure–response relationships, and a registrational, placebo-controlled, 48-week trial (MOXIe Part 2) showing statistically significant improvement in neurological function by mFARS with an acceptable safety profile characterized principally by reversible transaminase elevations, headaches, nausea, and fatigue (Creelan et al., 2017; Lynch et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2021).

This pharmacology is intrinsically aligned with a central pathophysiologic axis in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD): cumulative oxidative stress, sustained mitochondrial dysfunction with increased mtROS, impaired mitophagy, and chronic innate/adaptive inflammation in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and neighboring tissues (Bellezza, 2018; Jarrett & Boulton, 2012). The RPE is enriched in mitochondria and relies on robust antioxidant systems to manage high ROS fluxes from phagocytosis and photo-oxidative challenges; Nrf2 is widely recognized as the “master” antioxidant transcription factor in RPE, transcriptionally controlling the expression of SODs (including mitochondrial SOD2), catalase, NQO1, HO-1, glutathione synthesis enzymes, and thiol-redox enzymes (Trx1/Grx1) (Bellezza, 2018; Lambros & Plafker, 2016; Camelo, 2025). Deficiency of Nrf2 or the mitochondrial SOD2 enzyme in mouse retina/RPE produces AMD-like phenotypes, while exogenous Nrf2 activation in ocular models protects RPE and retinal neurons from oxidative injury, reduces inflammation, and supports mitochondrial homeostasis (Lambros & Plafker, 2016; Jarrett & Boulton, 2012; Chen et al., 2023). Against this mechanistic backdrop, the specific demonstration that omaveloxolone protects primary human RPE from H₂O₂-induced injury via Nrf2—at nanomolar concentrations—by upregulating SOD2, NQO1, HO-1, catalase, Grx1 and Trx1, preserving GSH, lowering ROS, and reducing apoptosis is directly relevant to dry AMD biology (Liu et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History  
Class-wide experience. Cyanoenone triterpenoids have been deployed across multiple preclinical disease models characterized by oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammation, with consistent activation of NRF2 target genes and functional improvements in biochemical and physiologic endpoints. For example, omaveloxolone improved renal function and reduced neutrophil infiltration, apoptosis, ROS production, and oxidative injury in renal ischemia–reperfusion models in an Nrf2-dependent manner, and produced sustained neuroprotection in a rat status epilepticus model with concordant increases in tissue glutathione and ATP (Reisman et al., 2019). These effects map onto the known Nrf2 program (e.g., induction of Nqo1, Gsr, Gclc; increased glutathione) and translate to primates and humans as evidenced by PBMC/tissue gene induction and serum biomarkers (ferritin, GGT) (Reisman et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2019).

First-in-human and oncology safety. In a first-in-human trial in advanced solid tumors, once-daily oral omaveloxolone (2.5–15 mg) was rapidly absorbed (Tmax 2–4 h), exhibited dose-proportional exposure, and had estimated terminal half-lives of ∼9 h on day 1 increasing to ∼20 h by day 28; across a mean exposure of 87 days, no dose-limiting toxicities were observed, adverse events were typically mild/moderate, and increases in select Nrf2 targets were measured in PBMCs (Creelan et al., 2017). The same report and related write-up noted no dose-limiting toxicities attributable to drug, a lack of QTc prolongation, and frequent low-grade laboratory changes (e.g., alkaline phosphatase elevations, anemia) in a small cohort, with PBMC Nrf2 target-gene mRNA serving as a primary pharmacodynamic target-engagement endpoint (Creelan et al., 2017).

Friedreich ataxia (FA) clinical development. Omaveloxolone has been evaluated extensively in FA, a neurodegenerative disease with depressed Nrf2 signaling and mitochondrial dysfunction. In MOXIe Part 1 (12-week, dose-ranging 2.5–300 mg/day), exposure was dose-proportional and PD changes in serum ferritin and GGT were maximal in the 80–160 mg/day range, congruent with improved neurological mFARS scores (placebo-corrected trends) and consistent with an exposure window for maximal biological activity; at 300 mg/day, a nonmonotonic dose–response with reduced Nrf2/mitochondrial effects was observed, suggesting a mid-dose “sweet spot” (Lynch et al., 2019). In MOXIe Part 2, patients treated with 150 mg/day for 48 weeks showed statistically significant improvement in mFARS relative to placebo; safety was acceptable with transient aminotransferase elevations unaccompanied by bilirubin increases, and common adverse events included headache, nausea, and fatigue (Lynch et al., 2021). PK data compiled from FA cohorts show mean terminal half-lives of ∼15–21 h at 80–160 mg/day (supporting once-daily dosing), Cmax in a range predicted by monkey PBMC EC50s to robustly induce Nrf2 targets, and interpatient variability of ∼31–43% for AUC/Cmax (Reisman et al., 2019). Translationally, FA patient biomarkers and platelet isotopologue metabolites indicated dose-dependent modulation of Nrf2-responsive targets (e.g., ferritin, GGT; decreased CK at 80–160 mg) and specific effects on fatty-acid–linked mitochondrial metabolism (reduced ¹³C-palmitate to HMG-CoA conversions with no effect on ¹³C-glucose) (Lynch et al., 2019).

Ophthalmic development context. Within ophthalmology, omaveloxolone has entered topical/ocular clinical testing (e.g., an ophthalmic suspension evaluated for prevention of corneal endothelial cell loss and ocular inflammation post-cataract surgery), and RTA 408 lotions/creams have shown Nrf2 target-gene induction in human skin punch biopsies, demonstrating tissue-level target engagement in humans via local administration (Cheng et al., 2021; Creelan et al., 2017). Although omaveloxolone has not been tested clinically in dry AMD to date, triterpenoid Nrf2 activators (including omaveloxolone) have reproducibly protected human RPE in vitro against oxidative insults (Liu et al., 2016), and related CDDO-derived analogues (e.g., RS9) have improved retinal antioxidant gene expression and function in multiple retinal models (Liu et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2021).

Use in AMD or similar diseases. There are no published clinical studies of omaveloxolone in dry AMD; however, the drug exhibits precisely the mechanistic activities sought for RPE protection in AMD—Nrf2 activation and induction of SOD2/NQO1/HO-1, preservation of glutathione and antioxidant enzyme activities, and suppression of oxidative injury—in primary human RPE models (Liu et al., 2016). Supportive disease-proximal validation comes from a robust literature demonstrating that genetic loss of Nrf2 or SOD2 in retinal tissues produces AMD-like pathology, and that pharmacologic or genetic Nrf2 activation protects RPE and retina in models of oxidative stress, ischemia–reperfusion injury, and diabetic retinopathy (Lambros & Plafker, 2016; Jarrett & Boulton, 2012; Zhang et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
Primary target: Keap1 Cys151 and Nrf2 stabilization. Omaveloxolone engages KEAP1 through covalent modification of Cys151, which is the electro-sensitive sensor residue controlling the high-affinity ETGE “hinge” and low-affinity DLG “latch” interactions that dock NRF2 to KEAP1 for CUL3-mediated ubiquitination under basal redox states (Cai et al., 2021; Reisman et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2016). Electrophilic adduction at KEAP1 cysteines inhibits the E3 ligase function, stabilizes Nrf2, promotes Ser40 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation, and increases binding of Nrf2–Maf heterodimers to AREs, resulting in transcriptional activation of a broad network of cytoprotective genes (estimated in the hundreds) that neutralize ROS, maintain glutathione and thioredoxin pools, and reprogram metabolism toward redox homeostasis (Das & Imanishi, 2022; Cai et al., 2021; Bellezza, 2018). In primates, quantitative PK/PD modeling relating plasma concentration to PBMC mRNA induction of canonical Nrf2 targets yielded EC50s on the order of tens of ng/mL, permitting translational projection of human exposures likely to achieve robust target engagement; observed FA patient Cmax values at 80–160–300 mg overlapped these EC50 ranges, and tissue distribution studies documented meaningful drug levels in liver, lung, and brain with dose-dependent mRNA induction in those tissues (Reisman et al., 2019).

Downstream antioxidant and mitochondrial programs in RPE. In primary human RPE, nanomolar omaveloxolone activated Nrf2 and increased expression and activity of multiple downstream antioxidant enzymes: HO-1 (heme catabolism; biliverdin/bilirubin production), NQO1 (two-electron reductase that supports NADPH-dependent detoxification), SOD2 (mitochondrial matrix superoxide dismutase), catalase (peroxisomal H₂O₂ scavenger), Grx1 and Trx1 (thiol-disulfide oxidoreductases for protein deglutathionylation/disulfide reduction) (Liu et al., 2016). Functionally, omaveloxolone preserved intracellular GSH under oxidative challenge, attenuated GSSG accumulation and protein glutathionylation, and restored enzyme activity of NQO1, Grx1, and Trx1 following H₂O₂ exposure (Liu et al., 2016). By lowering net ROS and preventing depletion/inactivation of thiol-redox systems, omaveloxolone reduced Bax activation and caspase-3 cleavage while increasing Bcl-2, leading to protection against apoptosis and necrosis in RPE; Nrf2 siRNA abrogated these effects, establishing on-target dependence (Liu et al., 2016).

Inflammation and NF-κB/NOS axes. Triterpenoid NRF2 activators can also influence inflammatory signaling. Omaveloxolone suppressed interferon-γ–mediated nitric oxide signaling in macrophages at nanomolar concentrations and reduced nitrotyrosine production in myeloid-derived suppressor cells and tumor xenografts, pointing to a mechanism that diminishes RNS/ROS-coupled inflammatory tone (Creelan et al., 2017). More broadly, Nrf2 activation antagonizes inflammation by mitigating ROS-dependent NLRP3 inflammasome activation and by competing with NF-κB for limiting transcriptional co-activators (e.g., CBP/p300), ultimately blunting IL-6 and IL-1β transcription; in the triterpenoid class, agents have been shown to modulate both NRF2 and NF-κB in cells and models (Camelo, 2025; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although direct inhibition of NF-κB by omaveloxolone in human RPE has not been explicitly demonstrated in the provided sources, multiple reviews and trial descriptions describe omaveloxolone as reducing inflammatory mediators (e.g., TNF-α, IL-6) and blocking KEAP1-mediated NF-κB proinflammatory signaling, consistent with the hypothesized dual-action (Clay et al., 2019; Madsen et al., 2020).

Mitochondrial function and disease-relevant cells. In FA-relevant neuronal and fibroblast systems, omaveloxolone restored mitochondrial OXPHOS complex readouts, reduced mitochondrial ROS, prevented lipid peroxidation, increased cellular glutathione, and elevated Nrf2 transcript/protein with increased NQO1, HO-1, and GCL expression at low nanomolar concentrations, indicating a direct link from KEAP1–NRF2 engagement to improved mitochondrial redox and bioenergetic parameters (Tiberi et al., 2023). Platelet isotopologue analyses in FA patients showed reduced conversion of ¹³C-palmitate to HMG-CoA with increasing omaveloxolone dose and no effect on ¹³C-glucose metabolism, consistent with modulation of fatty-acid–linked mitochondrial metabolism by Nrf2 activation in human tissues (Lynch et al., 2019).

Pharmacokinetics, target engagement, and dose–response. Human oral PK shows rapid absorption (Tmax ≈ 1–3.5 h), dose-proportional exposure, and an apparent terminal half-life of ∼15–21 h at 80–160 mg supporting once-daily administration; in the oncology first-in-human trial Tmax was 2–4 h with terminal half-life ranging from ∼9–20 h between day 1 and day 28, consistent with accumulation to steady state across 28-day cycles (Reisman et al., 2019; Creelan et al., 2017). Monotonicity in Nrf2/mitochondrial biomarker response appears dose-limited at very high exposure; in FA, 300 mg/day fell into a concentration range where reduced Nrf2 induction and mitochondrial function were observed in vitro and clinical PD/functional signals were attenuated relative to 80–160 mg (Lynch et al., 2019). Translational PK/PD alignment from primate PBMC EC50s predicts robust induction of canonical Nrf2 targets at human Cmax achieved with ≥ 80 mg dosing, which is consistent with the observed FA biomarker changes and clinical signals in the mid-dose range (Reisman et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2019).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level expectations in RPE oxidative stress models. The candidate’s cell-autonomous RPE mechanism predicts that, in primary human RPE or iPSC-RPE assays challenged with oxidants (e.g., H₂O₂, t-BHP, photo-oxidative blue light models), omaveloxolone pretreatment at low nanomolar concentrations will:  
- Increase Nrf2 nuclear translocation and upregulate canonical ARE-driven targets including SOD2, NQO1, HO-1, catalase, Grx1, and Trx1, as measured by mRNA, protein, and enzyme activity assays (Liu et al., 2016).  
- Preserve cellular thiol redox status by elevating intracellular GSH, reducing GSSG accumulation, and decreasing protein glutathionylation under oxidative challenge (Liu et al., 2016).  
- Reduce total and mitochondrial ROS burden (by virtue of increased SOD2 and augmented detoxifying capacity), attenuate lipid peroxidation, and maintain activity of antioxidant enzymes otherwise suppressed by oxidant exposure (NQO1, Grx1, Trx1) (Liu et al., 2016).  
- Decrease apoptosis/necrosis readouts (Annexin V/PI, caspase-3 cleavage), with shifts in Bax/Bcl-2 consistent with anti-apoptotic signaling downstream of restored redox homeostasis (Liu et al., 2016).

The RPE expresses all of the above antioxidant effectors (SOD2, NQO1, HO-1, catalase, Grx1, Trx1), and their induction by omaveloxolone has been demonstrated in primary human RPE, making these robust PD endpoints for in vitro validation and mechanistic confirmation of the compound in the exact cell type relevant to dry AMD (Liu et al., 2016). Given compelling preclinical evidence in FA models, we further expect improved mitochondrial bioenergetics (Δψm preservation/OXPHOS complex integrity) and reduced mtROS in RPE with omaveloxolone, although direct Δψm measurements have not been published in RPE for this compound; these endpoints are supported by neuronal/fibroblast data and are mechanistically consistent with Nrf2-driven SOD2/antioxidant induction (Tiberi et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2016).

Inflammation-modulating effects in RPE and retinal milieu. In RPE cultures or co-cultures exposed to pro-inflammatory cytokines or oxidative adducts (e.g., 4-HNE, MDA, CEP), omaveloxolone is expected to reduce ROS-augmented NF-κB–dependent cytokine transcription indirectly via rebalancing redox tone and directly via the triterpenoid class’s interference with NF-κB axes (competition for transcriptional cofactors and proposed KEAP1-linked NF-κB modulation), with measurable decreases in IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α transcription and nitrosative stress markers in settings where these are ROS-coupled (Camelo, 2025; Clay et al., 2019; Madsen et al., 2020; Creelan et al., 2017). In macrophage or microglia co-culture systems, decreased nitrotyrosine and nitric oxide synthase output would be anticipated, consistent with suppression of interferon-γ–driven NO signaling observed at low concentrations (Creelan et al., 2017). These effects target a recognized feed-forward loop in dry AMD in which oxidative damage and inflammatory signaling reciprocally amplify RPE injury (Bellezza, 2018; Camelo, 2025).

In vivo translational expectations and biomarker strategy. For systemic administration, PBMC Nrf2 target mRNA induction has been validated as a sensitive peripheral biomarker for omaveloxolone in primates and humans and should be incorporated as a noninvasive PD readout, with serum ferritin and GGT as additional systemic markers of Nrf2 activation shown to respond in the 80–160 mg range (Reisman et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2019). Tissue-level target engagement in the eye could be assessed in early clinical studies by surrogate accessible tissues (e.g., skin punch biopsy Nrf2 target induction following topical administration as precedent), tears or conjunctival impression cytology for transcript biomarkers, and functional retinal endpoints; preclinical monkey data showing dose-dependent induction of Nrf2 targets in liver/lung/brain establish that tissue-level engagement is achievable, though ocular distribution has not been reported and remains a data gap (Reisman et al., 2019; Creelan et al., 2017). For local ocular delivery, existing clinical experience with RTA 408 ophthalmic preparations and demonstrated Nrf2 target-gene induction in human skin biopsies support feasibility of achieving tissue PD in the eye without systemic exposure (Cheng et al., 2021; Creelan et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic precision for AMD biology. The omaveloxolone mechanism—KEAP1 Cys151 modification → Nrf2 stabilization and ARE-driven transcription—directly addresses core deficits in dry AMD: inadequate antioxidant/mitochondrial defenses and redox-driven inflammation in RPE. Upregulation of SOD2, NQO1, HO-1, catalase, and thiol-redox systems in primary human RPE cells has been demonstrated for omaveloxolone at nanomolar potency with rigorous Nrf2-dependence, and these are precisely the enzymes/activities required to reduce mtROS and protect the high-demand RPE from oxidative apoptosis/necrosis (Liu et al., 2016; Bellezza, 2018; Camelo, 2025).  
- Human translational pharmacology. Oral PK is favorable for chronic dosing (once-daily half-life ∼15–21 h at efficacious exposures), with dose-proportional exposure and well-established PD biomarkers (PBMC Nrf2 transcripts; serum ferritin/GGT) that map to mid-dose ranges yielding clinical signals in FA; primate PK/PD modeling provides concentration–effect relationships for Nrf2 targets that align with human Cmax at 80–160 mg (Reisman et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2019).  
- Tissue distribution and target engagement in vivo. In cynomolgus monkeys, omaveloxolone distributed to major organs, with tissue drug levels at or above plasma and induction of canonical Nrf2 targets in liver and lung; dose-related trends were present in brain, suggesting CNS permeability and supporting the premise of tissue-level engagement beyond blood in primates (Reisman et al., 2019). Topical formulations (RTA 408 lotion/ophthalmic suspension) have induced Nrf2 targets in human skin and advanced into ocular clinical studies, de-risking local ocular delivery modalities for future AMD programs (Creelan et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2021).  
- Clinical proof of mechanism and safety in a mitochondrial disease. In FA, omaveloxolone produced consistent PD biomarker activation (ferritin↑, GGT changes; CK↓ at 80–160 mg), functional improvement (mFARS benefit at 150–160 mg), and tolerability suitable for long-term administration (48 weeks), with reversible transaminase elevations as the principal laboratory signal; importantly, 300 mg exposures showed attenuated biologic responses, informing an exposure window for maximal effect (Lynch et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2021).  
- Anti-inflammatory potential that intersects AMD pathophysiology. Nrf2 activation reduces ROS-dependent inflammasome activation and competes with NF-κB for co-activators; omaveloxolone and its class decrease nitrosative stress signaling and inflammatory mediators in immune cells and models, a mechanistic complement to antioxidant effects in RPE that is germane to dry AMD’s chronic para-inflammation (Camelo, 2025; Creelan et al., 2017; Clay et al., 2019; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

Limitations and risks  
- Absence of ocular pharmacokinetics and retinal tissue PD. No data currently demonstrate omaveloxolone exposure in retina/RPE after systemic dosing or local ophthalmic administration in humans; primate tissue distribution did not include ocular tissues in the reported studies, and brain induction was less robust than peripheral organs, raising questions about effective exposure in ocular compartments with systemic dosing (Reisman et al., 2019). While RTA 408 ophthalmic formulations have entered clinical testing, target engagement in human ocular tissues has not been published (Cheng et al., 2021).  
- Clinical evidence gap in AMD. There are no clinical data in dry AMD populations; pathophysiologic rationale is strong, but translation from FA and preclinical RPE models requires careful dose/exposure selection, PD verification in ocular tissues, and demonstration of structural/functional benefit (e.g., slowing GA growth), none of which are available to date in the provided corpus (Lynch et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2016).  
- Nonmonotonic dose–response at high exposure. FA data indicate that very high exposures (e.g., 300 mg/day) can reduce Nrf2 induction/mitochondrial effects, implying a therapeutic window that must be honored to avoid loss of efficacy or off-target effects; AMD trials will need to target mid-dose ranges (80–160 mg) or use local ocular delivery to minimize systemic exposure while maximizing ocular PD (Lynch et al., 2019).  
- Safety nuances in an elderly population. Although omaveloxolone has an acceptable safety profile in FA and oncology settings (no DLTs up to 15 mg in oncology; reversible ALT/AST elevations in FA), dry AMD patients are older with comorbidities; the triterpenoid class has historical cardiovascular risk signals (bardoxolone methyl in CKD), mandating conservative exclusion criteria and vigilant monitoring, particularly if systemic dosing is pursued (Creelan et al., 2017; Cuadrado et al., 2019).  
- Inflammatory pathway claims in RPE remain inferential. While Nrf2 activation is anti-inflammatory, and omaveloxolone suppresses NO/iNOS/nitrotyrosine signaling in myeloid cells, direct evidence of NF-κB pathway repression by omaveloxolone in human RPE is not established in the cited literature; anti-inflammatory benefits in retinal tissues should be verified in appropriate assays (Creelan et al., 2017; Clay et al., 2019; Madsen et al., 2020).

Programmatic recommendations  
- Preclinical ocular PK/PD. Define ocular exposure and tissue PD after systemic and topical dosing in relevant species. For systemic dosing, quantify omaveloxolone in choroid/RPE/retina and assay canonical Nrf2 targets (Nqo1, Hmox1, Srxn1, Txnrd1, Gsr) to confirm dose-dependent tissue engagement; for topical dosing, leverage the human skin precedent (punch biopsy Nrf2 induction) to design ocular surface/conjunctival PD sampling in early clinical studies (Reisman et al., 2019; Creelan et al., 2017).  
- RPE-centric PD biomarker panel. In vitro and ex vivo human RPE studies should be used to finalize a PD panel including SOD2, NQO1, HO-1, catalase, Grx1, Trx1 mRNA/protein/activity, GSH/GSSG ratios, protein glutathionylation, and apoptosis markers, all of which were responsive to omaveloxolone in primary human RPE (Liu et al., 2016).  
- Dose selection anchored to translational PK/PD. For systemic programs, target exposures corresponding to primate PBMC EC50s and FA mid-dose ranges (80–160 mg) that maximize Nrf2 target induction while avoiding the high-exposure attenuation seen at 300 mg; in early AMD studies, incorporate PBMC Nrf2 gene induction, serum ferritin/GGT, and potentially CK as systemic PD anchors (Reisman et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2019).  
- Anti-inflammatory endpoints. In RPE and myeloid co-cultures, quantify NF-κB–dependent cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and nitrosative stress readouts (iNOS, nitrotyrosine) under oxidative/cytokine challenge with omaveloxolone to confirm expected anti-inflammatory effects; these are relevant given RNS/ROS-driven inflammation in AMD (Creelan et al., 2017; Camelo, 2025).  
- Clinical path. Consider a two-pronged strategy: (i) a topical ocular formulation to deliver drug to RPE/retina with minimal systemic exposure, justified by human skin PD activation and existing ocular formulation experience; (ii) a systemic oral approach with rigorous safety surveillance and mid-dose targeting, using PBMC/serum PD to confirm target engagement while ocular PD is established with surrogate sampling and imaging endpoints. The topical path may be particularly attractive to de-risk systemic safety in an elderly AMD population (Cheng et al., 2021; Creelan et al., 2017; Lynch et al., 2021).

Conclusion  
The totality of mechanistic, cellular, primate, and human clinical pharmacology evidence indicates that omaveloxolone’s core pharmacology—potent Nrf2 activation via KEAP1 Cys151 engagement, coupled with class-associated anti-inflammatory actions—maps directly onto the pathobiology of dry AMD. In primary human RPE, omaveloxolone at nanomolar concentrations induces mitochondrial and cytosolic antioxidant systems (SOD2, NQO1, HO-1, catalase, Grx1, Trx1), preserves GSH and redox enzyme activities, lowers ROS, and prevents apoptosis in an Nrf2-dependent manner, establishing precise on-target activity in the cell type central to AMD (Liu et al., 2016). Clinical development in FA demonstrates that systemic exposures can be achieved safely with pharmacodynamic target engagement (ferritin/GGT; PBMC markers) and functional benefit at mid-range doses (80–160 mg), while primate PK/PD work provides quantitative translational alignment for dose selection (Lynch et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2021; Reisman et al., 2019). The principal gaps for an AMD program are ocular distribution/PD after systemic dosing, absence of clinical AMD data, and the need to validate anti-inflammatory effects in retinal contexts; each is addressable through staged preclinical and early clinical studies, with topical delivery representing an attractive route to maximize ocular exposure and minimize systemic liability (Reisman et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2021; Creelan et al., 2017).

On balance, omaveloxolone is a strong mechanistic candidate for dry AMD: it targets the validated Nrf2 axis in RPE with demonstrated induction of SOD2/NQO1/HO-1 and thiol-redox defenses, supports mitochondrial antioxidant capacity, and carries human translational PK/PD tools to manage dose/exposure windows. Careful attention to dose selection (avoid very high exposures that attenuate desired biology), route of administration, and ocular PD verification will be critical to realizing its potential in AMD (Liu et al., 2016; Reisman et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2021).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is a naturally occurring long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (LC-PUFA) that has been isolated from marine sources, such as fish oil, and is commercially available in a highly purified form (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich D2534). DHA is synthesized via metabolic elongation and desaturation of dietary alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) in mammals; however, this endogenous conversion is limited, and direct dietary intake is critical for maintaining adequate retinal DHA levels (Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14). Belonging to the omega-3 class of fatty acids, DHA has long been recognized for its important roles in maintaining membrane structure and function, particularly in neural tissues and the retina where it is highly concentrated in photoreceptor outer segments and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) membranes (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3). Its polyunsaturated nature—with six cis double bonds—confers unique biophysical properties, enabling DHA to increase membrane fluidity and participate in critical signaling cascades. The compound has been used extensively as a nutritional supplement and has been incorporated in various formulations aimed at cardiovascular health, cognitive function, and ocular protection, establishing a robust safety profile over decades of human use (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Skowronska-Krawczyk & Chao, 2019, pp. 3–4).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past two decades, extensive research has explored the role of DHA and related omega-3 fatty acids in maintaining retinal function and potentially preventing age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Epidemiologic studies have consistently demonstrated an inverse association between dietary fish and high omega-3 fatty acid intake and the risk of developing AMD, suggesting that populations with higher DHA consumption tend to exhibit a lower incidence of both early and, to some extent, advanced forms of the disease (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). In clinical settings, large-scale randomized controlled trials, such as AREDS2, incorporated DHA (and EPA) into a multi-nutrient formula designed originally for AMD, though the overall randomized trial outcomes have been mixed, with some studies finding no statistically significant benefit for progression to late AMD (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). Pilot clinical trials and observational cohort studies, including NAT-1 and NAT-2, have assessed DHA supplementation in subjects with drusenoid lesions or early-stage AMD; while some of these studies have shown promising improvements in blood biomarkers (e.g., increased red blood cell DHA levels) and correlations with reduced AMD progression, the clinical efficacy remains under debate (Querques et al., 2016, pp. 2–4; Querques et al., 2011, pp. 7–8). Notably, evidence from animal models suggests that dietary DHA may protect against light-induced retinal degeneration and reduce the accumulation of deleterious lipid peroxidation products, although some preclinical studies also caution that DHA’s susceptibility to oxidation could, under certain conditions, worsen retinal injury (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic hypothesis for using DHA in dry AMD is based on its predicted ability to incorporate into the mitochondrial membranes of RPE cells, thereby enhancing membrane fluidity and protecting against oxidative damage to the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes. Under normal cellular conditions, DHA—owing to its multiple methylene-interrupted cis double bonds—integrates into phospholipid bilayers and modulates biophysical properties such as fluidity, permeability, and thickness (Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33). In mitochondrial membranes, this incorporation is thought to replace more saturated fatty acids such as arachidonic acid, ultimately reducing lipid peroxidation and mitigating oxidative stress that is deleterious to ETC function (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9). In vitro studies have shown that DHA supplementation in retinal cell cultures can decrease markers of apoptosis and preserve mitochondrial membrane integrity, with a concomitant increase in anti-apoptotic proteins (e.g., Bcl-2) (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 2–4).  
In addition, DHA is enzymatically converted under conditions of oxidative stress into neuroprotective docosanoids, such as neuroprotectin D1 (NPD1), which can inhibit pro-inflammatory gene expression and reduce cell death in RPE and photoreceptor cells (Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14; LaFuente et al., 2021, p. 13). This conversion not only contributes to countering local inflammation but also supports cellular health by modulating intracellular signaling pathways, particularly those involving NF-κB and other transcription factors critical for managing oxidative stress (Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14; Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14). Despite these promising mechanistic insights, it is important to note that direct, quantitative evidence detailing DHA’s incorporation specifically into RPE mitochondrial membranes and its precise effects on mitochondrial cristae structure, malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, or oxygen consumption rate (OCR) remains limited in the current literature (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, p. 13). Several reviews and preclinical reports acknowledge the theoretical framework while emphasizing the need for more detailed mechanistic studies that directly measure these mitochondrial endpoints (Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the mechanistic hypothesis, DHA supplementation is expected to yield several beneficial effects in retinal cells, particularly within the RPE, which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. In an ideal in vitro or ex vivo assay, DHA would incorporate into RPE cell membranes—including the mitochondrial inner membrane—increasing fluidity and enabling better diffusion of substrates and electron carriers necessary for efficient ATP production. Enhanced mitochondrial membrane fluidity should help reduce the susceptibility of the electron transport chain to oxidative damage, thereby lowering the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the subsequent production of lipid peroxidation byproducts such as MDA (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5). Furthermore, preservation of mitochondrial cristae structure is anticipated to maintain optimal alignment and function of ETC complexes, leading to an improved oxygen consumption rate (OCR) that is directly linked to cellular energy metabolism and overall cell viability (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 2–4; Souied et al., 2016, p. 8).  
At a molecular level, the increased presence of DHA in mitochondrial membranes is expected to initiate a cascade of protective events: reduced oxidative stress and inflammation via inhibition of NF-κB activation, promotion of the antioxidant response through NFE2L2 (NRF2) pathway activation, and enhanced autophagic clearance of damaged proteins and organelles through upregulation of SQSTM1 (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 1–2; Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, p. 3). Consequently, these effects should translate into preservation of RPE cell function, reduced apoptosis, and maintenance of photoreceptor health—an effect that could help slow the progression of dry AMD by stabilizing the retinal environment and preventing drusen accumulation and other degenerative changes (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5). Additionally, because genes encoding crucial direct mediators of DHA uptake such as Mfsd2a are expressed in RPE cells and photoreceptors, the target tissue is particularly well-positioned to benefit from increased dietary or supplementary DHA (Fathima et al., 2023, p. 8). However, it is also recognized that despite the strong rationale, direct experimental confirmation of these outcomes—specifically measured improvements in MDA levels, cristae ultrastructure integrity, and OCR in human RPE cells—is still pending, and the observed epidemiologic correlations are not yet unequivocally supported by randomized clinical trial data (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).

Overall Evaluation:  
The proposition to repurpose DHA for dry AMD is underpinned by compelling mechanistic rationale and epidemiologic associations, yet it is not without its challenges and limitations. One clear strength is DHA’s established role as an essential component of retinal cell membranes. Its high concentration in photoreceptors and the RPE is functionally integral to maintaining visual function and cellular homeostasis, lending strong biological plausibility to its protective potential in AMD (Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33). Its ability to modulate membrane fluidity, serve as a precursor to neuroprotective mediators like NPD1, and exert anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions provide multiple mechanistic pathways through which it may mitigate the cellular stressors implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis (Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14; Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14).

In summary, while the epidemiologic literature and preclinical studies provide an encouraging backdrop for the repurposing of DHA as a therapeutic agent in dry AMD—by showing that high DHA intake is associated with a reduced risk of AMD and that DHA can confer mitochondrial and anti-oxidative benefits in retinal models—the critical mechanistic endpoints that support our specific hypothesis are not yet fully substantiated in the published literature. The overall evaluation is that DHA has substantial mechanistic promise, safety, and historical use as a nutritional supplement; however, further robust mechanistic studies and carefully designed clinical trials are necessary to validate its specific effects on mitochondrial function in RPE cells and to determine whether these biochemical improvements translate into a clinically significant slowing of dry AMD progression (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
EUK-8 is a synthetic catalytic antioxidant that belongs to the manganese‐based salen complexes, a class of low molecular weight enzyme mimetics engineered to replicate key activities of endogenous antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). This compound is synthesized via a condensation reaction between salicylaldehyde derivatives and diamines to form a bis‐Schiff base (salen) ligand, which then coordinates to a manganese ion, thereby producing the characteristic MnN₂O₂ planar core responsible for its redox activity (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rosenthal et al., 2011). The manganese center in EUK-8 undergoes reversible redox cycling between Mn(III) and Mn(II) oxidation states; this reversible cycling is essential for its dual enzyme-mimetic action, as it enables catalytic dismutation of superoxide radicals into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide and further conversion of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, thereby mimicking the combined action of SOD and catalase (Fernandes, 2010; Rouco et al., 2020a). The salen complex scaffold not only confers redox activity but also provides a tunable electronic and steric environment through modification of substituents on the ligand framework, which in turn dictates the redox potential, proton-dissociation properties, and overall catalytic efficacy (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020b). Because of its synthetic origin, EUK-8 is both cost-effective and easily reproducible, making it an appealing candidate for repurposing in therapeutic areas where enhanced antioxidant defenses are required, such as in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rosenthal et al., 2011).

Therapeutic History:  
The EUK series of compounds, which includes EUK-8, have been extensively studied in a plethora of preclinical models addressing a wide range of diseases linked to oxidative stress, including ischemic brain injury, neurodegeneration, cardiac injury, and even lifespan extension models in Caenorhabditis elegans and SOD2 knockout mice (Rouco et al., 2020a). Biochemical studies have demonstrated that EUK-8 exhibits both superoxide dismutase and catalase-like activities at submicromolar concentrations, providing significant protection in vitro and in vivo in models of oxidative injury (Bani & Bencini, 2012). While EUK-8 itself has not been directly evaluated in clinical trials for dry AMD, its protective effects have been documented in several models of neuronal and cardiac injury where mitochondrial dysfunction and excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) production are central to the pathology (Fernandes, 2010; Rouco et al., 2020a). The pharmacological application of salen manganese complexes, including EUK-8, extends to neuroprotective approaches, such as in models of Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and ischemia–reperfusion injury, suggesting that similar mechanisms may be beneficial in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which are notably vulnerable to oxidative stress in dry AMD (Rouco et al., 2020b; Yan et al., 2010). Additionally, the literature reveals that analogous compounds in the EUK series have been examined for their anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, and mitochondrial protective properties in diverse cellular and animal models, lending further credence to their potential for repurposing in ocular degenerative diseases (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rosenthal et al., 2009).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, EUK-8 functions as a catalytic antioxidant by mimicking two key enzymes involved in the detoxification of reactive oxygen species. First, it catalyzes the dismutation of superoxide (O₂•⁻) by virtue of its manganese center undergoing cyclic redox reactions between the Mn(III) and Mn(II) states; in one half-reaction, the Mn(III) state accepts an electron from superoxide to become Mn(II), while in the subsequent half-reaction, Mn(II) is reoxidized to Mn(III) by another molecule of superoxide, resulting in the conversion of superoxide to molecular oxygen and hydrogen peroxide (Fernandes, 2010; Batinić-Haberle et al., 2016). Second, EUK-8 mimics catalase activity by decomposing the generated hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen; it is proposed that hydrogen peroxide reacts with the manganese center to generate a transient high-valent oxo–Mn species, which is then reduced back to the resting state in the presence of a reductant, thus completing the catalytic cycle (Yan et al., 2010; Bani & Bencini, 2012). The structural integrity of the salen ligand is critical in modulating the redox potential of the manganese center, which, when tuned to an optimal range, ensures efficient electron transfer with reactive species while minimizing the risk of metal ion dissociation or inadvertent pro-oxidant activity (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Durand, 2013). In cellular contexts, the dual SOD/catalase activity of EUK-8 is especially relevant to mitochondria, which are the primary source of intracellular ROS; by reducing mitochondrial superoxide and decomposing hydrogen peroxide, EUK-8 helps to preserve mitochondrial respiration and prevent oxidative mitochondrial damage, which is a key contributor to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). The overall biochemical and mechanistic profile of EUK-8, therefore, aligns well with the need to lower mtROS and preserve cellular homeostasis in tissues subjected to chronic oxidative stress.

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by the degeneration of the RPE, a process driven by cumulative oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation leading to cellular senescence and eventual retinal atrophy (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Batinić-Haberle et al., 2016). Given that the RPE expresses high levels of mitochondrial enzymes, including MnSOD, and relies on efficient mitochondrial respiration for normal function, the preservation of mitochondrial integrity is paramount (Fernandes, 2010; Rouco et al., 2020a). EUK-8 is expected to enter RPE cells and preferentially localize to mitochondria where its catalytic dual SOD/catalase activity would reduce the burden of superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, thereby mitigating oxidative damage to mitochondrial proteins, lipids, and DNA (Rosenthal et al., 2011; Rosenthal et al., 2009). By maintaining lower levels of mtROS, EUK-8 would be anticipated to stave off the mitochondrial dysfunction that underlies RPE degeneration and to prevent the activation of pro-inflammatory signaling cascades such as those mediated by the NLRP3 inflammasome, thus potentially preserving cellular viability and function (Batinić-Haberle, 2013; Bigham & Wilson, 2023). In addition, previous studies with related manganosalen complexes have shown that treatment can lead to the reversal of age-related cognitive deficits and the inhibition of pro-apoptotic pathways in neuronal tissues, which are mechanistically analogous to the crises faced by RPE cells in dry AMD (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rouco et al., 2020b). The ability of EUK-8 to act at submicromolar doses further enhances its appeal, as such potency suggests that therapeutic effects may be achieved with minimal exposure, reducing the likelihood of off-target effects and toxicity (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Fernandes, 2010).

From a drug development perspective, EUK-8 emerges as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration, primarily because its dual enzyme-mimetic properties address two central features of RPE pathology—oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). Its low molecular weight and non-peptidic nature facilitate cellular uptake and mitochondrial penetration, critical features for targeting the RPE where mitochondrial production of ROS is an important driver of cell injury (Bani & Bencini, 2012; Rouco et al., 2020a). Furthermore, the extensive preclinical history of manganosalen compounds in models of neuroprotection, cardiac ischemia, and aging provides a solid rationale for their protective capacity in tissues that are equally susceptible to oxidative damage, even if direct studies in dry AMD are limited at present (Rouco et al., 2020a; Rouco et al., 2020b).

Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) is a synthetic derivative of fumaric acid that belongs to the class of fumaric acid esters (FAEs) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Fumaric acid esters as a class have a long-standing history in pharmacotherapy, originally finding application in dermatology, most notably in the treatment of psoriasis, and have since been repurposed for neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis (MS) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Historically, fumaric acid esters were introduced into clinical practice as antipsoriatic agents in Europe, with formulations such as Fumaderm® entering the market in the 1990s (Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Over time, DMF was repurposed and further developed as an oral agent for the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), culminating in its FDA approval in 2013 under the trade name Tecfidera® by Biogen (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163). Clinical trials, including large-scale phase 3 studies, have demonstrated its favorable safety profile and efficacy in reducing relapse rates and slowing disability progression in MS patients (Promsote, 2015, pp. 157–163; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 14–16). Although there is no extensive historical record of DMF being used directly for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other primary ocular diseases, recent preclinical findings have indicated that its potent activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway may confer significant protective effects on the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). This has sparked considerable interest in repurposing DMF for ocular indications such as geographic atrophy, a late stage of dry AMD, by leveraging its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities observed in nonocular settings (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, DMF functions primarily as a prodrug; upon oral administration it is rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases within the gastrointestinal tract to yield its active metabolite, monomethyl fumarate (MMF) (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). The pharmacodynamic actions of DMF principally involve the electrophilic modification of specific cysteine residues—most notably cysteine 151—on Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1) (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Under physiological conditions, KEAP1 binds to and retains the transcription factor Nrf2 in the cytoplasm, targeting it for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. However, when DMF covalently modifies KEAP1, it disrupts this complex, allowing Nrf2 to dissociate and translocate into the nucleus (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). In the nucleus, Nrf2 binds to antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the promoters of numerous genes encoding cytoprotective enzymes, including glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), and various enzymes involved in glutathione (GSH) synthesis and regeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). These molecular interactions lead to enhanced antioxidant defenses, improved detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and overall better maintenance of cellular redox balance (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). In addition to its role in promoting antioxidant gene expression via Nrf2 activation, DMF has been shown to have immunomodulatory properties; it can shift cytokine profiles by increasing interleukin-4 (IL-4)–expressing CD4+ T cells and decreasing the production of proinflammatory cytokines such as interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and interleukin-17 (IL-17) (Camelo, 2025, pp. 6–7; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Furthermore, DMF has been reported to inhibit nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation in certain cellular contexts, thus contributing to a reduction in inflammatory signaling independently of Nrf2 (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2). Together, these molecular actions result in lowered cellular oxidative stress and an improved inflammatory milieu, which are critical factors implicated in the pathogenesis of chronic degenerative diseases (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry AMD, particularly the geographic atrophy form, is characterized by the gradual degeneration of RPE cells, which leads to subsequent photoreceptor loss and irreversible vision impairment. Central to the pathophysiology of dry AMD are oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation that progressively compromise RPE viability and function (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). The hypothesis being explored is that DMF, through its robust activation of the Nrf2 pathway, can enhance the expression of ARE-driven genes that encode for antioxidant and cytoprotective proteins, thereby counteracting the deleterious effects of oxidative stress in the RPE (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 13–14). In particular, the upregulation of enzymes involved in glutathione synthesis is expected to increase intracellular levels of GSH, a critical thiol antioxidant that protects mitochondrial membranes and supports cellular bioenergetics (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 20–21). Preclinical studies in retinal models have demonstrated that DMF can effectively preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and reduce the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β), both of which are hallmarks of RPE distress under oxidative challenge (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Given that the RPE is highly metabolically active and particularly vulnerable to cumulative oxidative damage, the sustained activation of Nrf2 by DMF following oral dosing is anticipated to provide continuous reinforcement of antioxidant defenses and maintain mitochondrial integrity in these cells (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 3–5; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). Moreover, by mitigating inflammatory signaling, DMF may not only protect the RPE but also contribute to a more favorable microenvironment that limits the propagation of cell death signals, thus potentially slowing the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Collectively, these expected cellular effects support the rationale for using DMF as an intervention to preserve retinal structure and function by lowering oxidative damage and supporting bioenergetics in the RPE.

Overall Evaluation:  
The potential of dimethyl fumarate as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD rests on a solid mechanistic rationale combined with an established clinical pedigree in other indications. One of the primary strengths of DMF is its well-characterized pharmacological profile; it is FDA-approved for multiple sclerosis and has been safely administered to thousands of patients over several years, which significantly mitigates the risk and regulatory hurdles typically associated with repurposed drugs (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). The dual actions of DMF—in particular, its ability to both activate the Nrf2 pathway and attenuate proinflammatory signals—directly target the underlying pathological processes in dry AMD, where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central drivers of RPE degeneration (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Manai & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). In vitro studies have provided encouraging evidence that DMF increases intracellular glutathione levels and protects RPE cells from oxidative insults, findings that are directly translatable to the pathobiology of dry AMD (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

Nonetheless, several challenges remain. Although DMF is known to be effective in MS and psoriasis, the ocular milieu presents unique pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic challenges that may not be fully addressed by the current oral formulations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18). The rapid hydrolysis of DMF to MMF means that, while the active metabolite does exert therapeutic effects, fine-tuning the dosing regimen to ensure adequate drug levels in the retina while minimizing systemic side effects is necessary (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022). In addition, common adverse reactions associated with DMF, such as gastrointestinal discomfort and flushing, though generally mild to moderate, could be more problematic in the typically elderly dry AMD population, necessitating careful monitoring and potentially modified dosing strategies (Camelo, 2025, p. 17; Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13). There is also the question of whether systemic administration of DMF can generate sufficient concentrations in the retina to achieve a meaningful therapeutic effect. While emerging evidence suggests that DMF can cross the blood-retinal barrier and activate Nrf2 in retinal cells (Shu et al., 2022, pp. 12–13; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3), further pharmacokinetic and translational studies are warranted to confirm its retinal bioavailability and the optimal dosing regimen for ocular indications.

Another consideration is the complexity of dry AMD itself, which is a slowly progressive, multifactorial disease with contributions from genetic predispositions, environmental exposures, and systemic metabolic disturbances. It remains to be seen whether the monotherapeutic approach of DMF, targeting primarily oxidative stress via Nrf2 activation, will be sufficient to halt or reverse disease progression, or whether combination therapies will ultimately be required (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12). Furthermore, while the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms of DMF are well supported by in vitro data and animal studies, there is still limited clinical data on its efficacy in ocular disease settings. Early-phase clinical trials aimed at evaluating DMF in geographic atrophy have to rigorously assess both structural outcomes (e.g., changes in the area of atrophy) and functional endpoints (e.g., visual acuity, retinal sensitivity) to establish its therapeutic benefit in dry AMD (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).

Despite these limitations, the strengths of DMF are compelling. The drug’s ability to upregulate a broad spectrum of cytoprotective genes via the Nrf2 pathway makes it a versatile candidate for mitigating the oxidative and inflammatory stress that drives RPE degeneration. The fact that DMF has already cleared extensive regulatory and clinical safety evaluations in nonocular indications is a significant advantage, as it greatly accelerates the translational pathway compared to a novel chemical entity (Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25). Additionally, the repurposing of an already approved drug leverages existing manufacturing, formulation, and distribution infrastructure, favorably impacting the cost and timeline associated with drug development (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2).

In summary, the comprehensive literature review supports the potential of DMF to serve as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its mechanism of action—centered on Nrf2 activation leading to enhanced antioxidant capacity along with anti-inflammatory effects—directly addresses the key pathophysiological mechanisms implicated in dry AMD. The extensive clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis provides a reliable safety and tolerability framework, which is crucial for rapid repositioning into a new clinical area such as geographic atrophy (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shimizu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). However, it is essential to conduct targeted preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials specifically in ocular disease models to optimize dosing, confirm retinal delivery, and demonstrate clinical efficacy before advancing to larger randomized controlled trials (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3). Overall, while challenges remain regarding optimal application in the retinal context and potential side effects in an older patient population, DMF—by virtue of its dual antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms and robust clinical background—stands as a viable candidate that merits further investigation for the treatment of dry AMD.

Given the current evidence, the following recommendations are proposed for advancing DMF as a candidate for dry AMD:  

1. Conduct detailed pharmacokinetic studies in animal models to assess the retinal bioavailability of DMF and its active metabolite MMF following systemic administration. This should include studies comparing different dosing schedules and formulations to optimize retinal exposure without exacerbating systemic adverse effects (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2022; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 1–2).  

2. Develop and validate preclinical models of dry AMD that recapitulate the key features of human geographic atrophy, with a focus on evaluating the efficacy of DMF in protecting RPE cells against oxidative stress and preserving mitochondrial function (Marchesi et al., 2024, pp. 19–20; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

3. Investigate the potential benefits of combining DMF with other therapeutic agents that target complementary pathways in dry AMD. For example, agents that modulate complement activation or improve choroidal blood flow may synergize with the Nrf2-mediated antioxidant mechanism of DMF (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 2–3).  

4. Initiate early-phase clinical trials in patients with geographic atrophy to establish proof of concept. These studies should include robust biomarker assessments (e.g., measurement of ARE gene expression, retinal imaging for atrophy progression, and functional visual outcomes) to correlate molecular effects with clinical benefit (Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12; Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3).  

5. Carefully monitor the safety profile of DMF in the elderly population, as the incidence of gastrointestinal side effects and lymphopenia may differ compared to the population with MS. Consider the feasibility of modified-release formulations or alternative routes of administration (e.g., topical ocular delivery) to minimize systemic side effects while maximizing retinal drug concentrations (Camelo, 2025, pp. 11–13; Buonfiglio et al., 2024, pp. 17–18).

Overall, the repurposing of dimethyl fumarate for dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a robust mechanistic framework and a significant body of preclinical and clinical data generated in other indications. Its capacity to activate the Nrf2 pathway, enhance mitochondrial glutathione synthesis, and modulate inflammatory responses in RPE cells directly addresses several pivotal aspects of dry AMD pathogenesis (Cuadrado et al., 2019, pp. 21–25; Foresti, 2014, pp. 102–106; Shu et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). While there are challenges regarding optimal retinal delivery and management of systemic adverse effects, the clinical experience with DMF in MS and psoriasis lends considerable support to its translational potential. Consequently, dimethyl fumarate represents a well‐justified and attractive therapeutic candidate for further exploration in the treatment of dry AMD, warranting additional preclinical optimization and clinical investigation to fully define its role in preserving visual function in patients affected by this progressive degenerative disease (Manai, Govoni, & Amadio, 2022, pp. 2–3; Buglak et al., 2018, pp. 11–12).

Spermidine is a naturally occurring polyamine that was originally discovered in bovine semen and later shown to be ubiquitous in all forms of life, ranging from bacteria and plants to fungi and mammals. Its natural origins stem from highly conserved enzymatic biosynthetic pathways—starting either from ornithine via ornithine decarboxylase or from arginine through an agmatine intermediate—resulting in the formation of putrescine, which is subsequently converted to spermidine through the transfer of an aminopropyl group provided by decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine (dcSAM) (Casero & Marton, 2007; Hobley et al., 2017; Khomutov et al., 2019). Although spermidine can be isolated from natural sources such as food and tissues, it is also available in a chemically defined form commercially (for example, Sigma-Aldrich S2626) and has been used in basic research as well as in some experimental therapeutic approaches. This compound is representative of the polyamine family, and these molecules have traditionally been investigated for their roles in cellular proliferation, nucleic acid stabilization, and modulation of various enzymatic activities, which in turn have broad implications for health and disease (Madeo et al., 2020; Nichugovskiy et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, spermidine’s potential therapeutic applications have been explored extensively in the context of its ability to induce autophagy and affect cellular homeostasis.
