Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Alda-1 is a synthetic small molecule discovered through target-directed screening for modulators of mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2), originally identified as “ALDH2 activator 1” with the chemical name N-(1,3-benzodioxol-5-ylmethyl)-2,6-dichlorobenzamide and first demonstrated to reduce myocardial ischemic injury in rodents by directly activating ALDH2 (i.e., increasing its catalytic activity and rescuing function of the common inactive ALDH2*2 variant) (Budas et al., 2009; Kimura et al., 2019). Structurally and mechanistically, Alda-1 binds at the substrate entrance tunnel of ALDH2 and extends toward the active site, where it enhances dehydrogenase activity by favorably altering local dynamics, improving NAD+ engagement, and acting as a chemical chaperone that preserves the functional conformation of critical active-site loops and α-helices, while shielding key catalytic cysteines from irreversible electrophilic adduction by reactive aldehydes such as 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE) (Gao et al., 2022; Wang & He, 2018). In vitro biophysical and enzymology work shows Alda-1 increases wild-type ALDH2 activity approximately twofold and markedly rescues activity of the common East Asian mutant ALDH2*2 (Glu504Lys), restoring heterotetramer activity to near wild-type levels; importantly, Alda-1 is selective against several other ALDHs in original profiling, although later biochemical work suggests some degree of cross-activation of ALDH1A1 under specific assay conditions (Budas et al., 2009; Kotraiah et al., 2013).

Alda-1 belongs to the pharmacologic class of enzyme activators/allosteric agonists targeting mitochondrial ALDH2; the class is characterized by its ability to catalytically enhance clearance of reactive aldehydes generated by oxidative and nitrosative stress (e.g., 4-HNE, malondialdehyde [MDA], acrolein, and catecholamine-derived DOPAL), thereby acting as indirect antioxidants that reduce downstream carbonyl stress, proteotoxicity, and mitochondria-dependent cell death without directly scavenging ROS (Kimura et al., 2019; Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Wang & He, 2018). This mechanism has been applied preclinically across multiple organ systems to mitigate ischemia–reperfusion injury, chronic heart failure, metabolic and neurodegenerative toxicities, and toxin-induced organ damage, providing a consistent translational thread: activation of ALDH2 accelerates detoxification of stable electrophilic products of lipid peroxidation, interrupting aldehyde-driven positive feedback loops that amplify mitochondrial dysfunction, ROS generation, and apoptosis (Budas et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2014; Münzel & Daiber, 2018).

Therapeutic History  
Across cardiovascular models, Alda-1 has repeatedly demonstrated robust cytoprotection in vivo. In rat and mouse myocardial ischemia–reperfusion and infarction models, Alda-1 administration prior to or during ischemia reduced infarct size by approximately 60% and improved long-term survival following myocardial infarction, associating efficacy with increased ALDH2 activity, reduced 4-HNE-protein adducts and protein carbonyls, preserved mitochondrial respiratory control ratio (RCR), reduced mitochondrial H₂O₂ release, protection against Ca²⁺-induced mitochondrial permeability transition (MPT), and decreased cytochrome c release (Budas et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2014). In a chronic post-MI heart-failure model with established aldehydic overload, sustained Alda-1 treatment increased cardiac ALDH2 activity by ~2.7-fold, lowered 4-HNE adducts and protein carbonyls, normalized uncoupler responsiveness, improved RCR by preserving State 3 respiration, lowered mitochondrial ROS emission, and corrected MPT sensitivity; organ-level outcomes included increased contractility, reduced LV dilation, diminished hypertrophy and fibrosis, and anti-remodeling benefits (Gomes et al., 2014). In vitro, Alda-1 shielded isolated cardiac mitochondria from 4-HNE–induced respiratory inhibition, demonstrating direct aldehyde-dependent protection at the mitochondrial level (Gomes et al., 2014).

Hepatic and other organ systems provide convergent evidence. In a mouse acetaminophen hepatotoxicity model, Alda-1 pretreatment substantially reduced liver injury biomarkers (ALT/AST), histologic necrosis, 4-HNE adduct burden, mitochondrial depolarization, and cell death without altering upstream NAPQI bioactivation or JNK phosphorylation, demonstrating that protection is downstream via aldehyde detoxification and preservation of mitochondrial polarization and MPT control (Wimborne et al., 2020). Additional preclinical reports document Alda-1 efficacy in models of lung ischemia/reperfusion, intestinal I/R, kidney injury, neurotoxic injuries, and alcohol-related hepatic injury, again with mechanistic ties to accelerated clearance of reactive aldehydes, restoration of mitochondrial function, and modulation of stress/apoptosis pathways (Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019).

Retina-focused data, while more limited and not in dry AMD models, are directionally supportive. In streptozotocin-induced aged diabetic rats (an early diabetic retinopathy model), systemic Alda-1 improved ERG parameters, preserved outer nuclear layer (ONL) and total retinal thickness on OCT at 7–30 days, increased retinal SOD activity, and decreased retinal TNF-α and IL-6 across multiple timepoints; concurrent upregulation of ALDH2, Nrf2, and Sirt1 was observed by immunofluorescence and Western blot, suggesting that ALDH2 activation engages antioxidant and anti-inflammatory pathways in the retina under hyperglycemic oxidative stress (He et al., 2018). In a separate in vivo retinal degeneration study (MNU-induced photoreceptor damage), systemic Alda-1 preserved ERG amplitudes, mitigated photoreceptor degeneration (OCT, histology), increased retinal ALDH2 and SIRT1 protein, and reduced markers of ER stress (GRP78) and apoptosis (PARP1), supporting the hypothesis that enhancing aldehyde detoxification ameliorates retinal cellular stress downstream of lipid peroxidation (Yan et al., 2020; Carullo et al., 2020). Although neither model recapitulates RPE-centric dry AMD (drusen, complement activation, geographic atrophy), they provide proof-of-principle that ALDH2 activation can protect neural retina under oxidative/aldehydic stress in vivo (Yan et al., 2020; He et al., 2018).

Clinical translation status remains nascent. No human proof-of-concept trials of Alda-1 have been reported, and authoritative reviews note the absence of clinical efficacy data for ALDH2 activators like Alda-1, despite extensive rodent evidence across organs; moreover, no ALDH2 activators are in clinical use at present (Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019). Safety experience is therefore limited to preclinical settings: chronic Alda-1 dosing in naïve rats (10 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks) demonstrated acceptable tolerability (no hemodynamic, biochemical, or organ-weight changes), whereas a separate report described crystalline nephropathy and renal function deterioration after I/R under specific Alda-1 dosing/formulation conditions, suggesting potential tissue-specific or formulation-dependent risks requiring evaluation (Gomes et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2023). With respect to ophthalmology, existing Alda-1 studies are limited to rodent retina in DR and MNU models; there is no published use in dry AMD patients or preclinical AMD-like RPE atrophy models, and there is no reported ocular delivery pharmacokinetics or long-term ocular safety data in the provided literature (Yan et al., 2020; He et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action  
ALDH2 is a mitochondrial, NAD⁺-dependent dehydrogenase that catalyzes the oxidation of reactive aldehydes—most notably acetaldehyde, 4-HNE, MDA, acrolein, and DOPAL—to their corresponding carboxylic acids, thereby detoxifying electrophiles that otherwise form covalent Michael adducts and Schiff bases with cysteine, histidine, and lysine residues on proteins and nucleic acids (Kimura et al., 2019; Budas et al., 2009). The enzyme’s catalytic mechanism involves NAD⁺ binding in the Rossmann fold and activation of the catalytic cysteine (Cys302 in ALDH2), nucleophilic attack on the aldehyde to form a thiohemiacetal, hydride transfer to produce a thioacyl-enzyme intermediate, and Glu268-mediated hydrolysis to release the acid product and NADH; this canonical chemistry underlies ALDH2’s role as an indirect antioxidant via aldehyde clearance rather than direct ROS scavenging (Parajuli, 2013; Wang & He, 2018). Importantly, ALDH2 is highly susceptible to oxidative and electrophilic inactivation—its active-site cysteine cluster (Cys301–Cys303) can be adducted by 4-HNE at micromolar concentrations (>10 µM), establishing a pathogenic feed-forward loop in which lipid peroxidation products both injure proteins and progressively compromise the aldehyde-detoxifying capacity of mitochondria (Karan et al., 2023; Budas et al., 2009).

Alda-1 engages this system at multiple mechanistic levels. Structurally, Alda-1 binds to the substrate entrance tunnel and active site of ALDH2, altering the local environment to increase effective substrate/catalytic-cysteine proximity and improve NAD⁺ binding (lower Kₘ), while simultaneously acting as a molecular chaperone to stabilize conformational elements disrupted in the ALDH2*2 variant (e.g., restoring α-helix and active-site loop structures toward wild-type) (Gao et al., 2022; Wang & He, 2018). Functionally, Alda-1 increases wild-type ALDH2 catalytic activity approximately two-fold, but the effect is more pronounced in ALDH2*2 (10-fold or more in homotetramers), which is clinically relevant in East Asian populations; Alda-1 does not affect ALDH1/ALDH5 in initial selectivity panels, though subsequent biochemical reports indicate potential ALDH1A1 activation under specific conditions (i.e., DOPAL-inactivation assays), a detail that warrants further isozyme-specific profiling in ocular tissues (Budas et al., 2009; Kotraiah et al., 2013). Crucially, Alda-1 also reduces aldehyde access to catalytic cysteines (Cys302/301/303), protecting ALDH2 from 4-HNE–induced inactivation, thereby sustaining endogenous detoxification under aldehyde stress; in direct assays Alda-1 prevents rapid 4-HNE-mediated ALDH2 inactivation and shifts the enzyme to a higher-efficiency state (Gao et al., 2022; Kotraiah et al., 2013). The net biochemical outcome is enhancement of mitochondrial clearance of 4-HNE to the less reactive 4-hydroxynonenoic acid (4-HNA), alongside accelerated metabolism of other toxic aldehydes, which interrupts aldehyde-driven proteotoxic cascades (e.g., proteasomal inhibition, protein carbonyl accumulation) and preserves mitochondrial respiratory function (Budas et al., 2009; Gomes et al., 2014).

Systems-level consequences of ALDH2 activation by Alda-1 have been delineated extensively in heart and liver. In failing hearts with elevated aldehydic load, Alda-1 decreased 4-HNE-protein adducts and total carbonyls without altering ALDH2 protein abundance, demonstrating a purely catalytic detoxification effect (i.e., activity increase without expression change) (Gomes et al., 2014). Mitochondrial bioenergetic protection is robust: Alda-1 preserved State 3 respiration, increased RCR, normalized uncoupler responses (CCCP), reduced absolute and relative H₂O₂ release, decreased cytochrome c release, and corrected MPT sensitivity, indicating mitigation of mitochondria-centered death signaling under chronic oxidative/aldehydic stress (Gomes et al., 2014). In isolated mitochondria, pre-incubation with Alda-1 prevented 4-HNE–induced declines in respiratory control and State 3 oxygen consumption, further supporting a direct anti-aldehyde effect on mitochondrial electron transport chain function (Gomes et al., 2014). In the APAP hepatotoxicity model, Alda-1 reduced tissue 4-HNE adduct burden by an order of magnitude, preserved mitochondrial polarization, and reduced cell death, consistent with detoxification of lipid peroxidation products downstream of parent electrophile formation (Wimborne et al., 2020).

Retinal and neuronal contexts provide complementary mechanistic observations. In cultured endothelial cells exposed to amyloid-β₁–₄₀, Alda-1 restored mitochondrial function, reduced 4-HNE adducts and ROS, and rescued angiogenic responses, indicating that ALDH2 activation can directly blunt aldehyde-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction in non-cardiac cells (Chen & Joshi, 2016; Roy, 2022). Within the retina, ALDH2 localizes across layers with predominant co-localization to CRALBP-positive Müller glia, and its expression diminishes with age; transgenic upregulation protects against retinal aging by decreasing oxidative-stress–related apoptosis and enhancing the unfolded protein response (UPR) in the ER, indicating that increased ALDH2 activity has cytoprotective effects in vivo in the aging retina (Karan et al., 2023; Long et al., 2020). In diabetic retinopathy rodent studies, Alda-1 increased retinal ALDH2, SIRT1, and Nrf2 signaling, decreased proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6), and improved electrophysiologic and structural outcomes, suggesting that ALDH2 activation enlists antioxidant and proteostasis pathways beyond direct aldehyde detoxification to preserve retinal function (He et al., 2018). In photoreceptor degeneration, Alda-1 upregulated SIRT1 and decreased ER stress/apoptotic markers, again consistent with mitigation of downstream stress signaling when aldehyde load is reduced (Yan et al., 2020).

Finally, the disease biochemistry underpinning our hypothesis—aldehyde toxicity as a conserved driver downstream of oxidative lipid peroxidation—is well defined in neurodegeneration and retinal biology. 4-HNE forms adducts that impair proteasome activity, promote accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and inflammation, covalently modify and crosslink amyloid peptides, impair ion pumps and transporters, and directly kill neurons at low micromolar concentrations; ALDH2 loss-of-function (including ALDH2*2) exacerbates accumulation of 4-HNE adducts and age-dependent neurodegeneration in rodent models (Chen & Joshi, 2016). In retinal disease, the RPE and photoreceptors operate in a high-oxygen, PUFA-rich environment, with continuous photo-oxidation and phagocytosis of outer segments generating lipid peroxides and aldehydes, and oxidative stress is a central driver of AMD pathogenesis; therapeutic strategies that augment endogenous detoxification (e.g., via Nrf2) have been proposed as rational approaches to bolster RPE resilience (Chen et al., 2023). Collectively, Alda-1’s biochemical action—activation of a mitochondrial enzyme that eliminates 4-HNE/MDA—integrates tightly with the pathophysiology of aldehyde-mediated mitochondrial and proteostatic injury that characterizes oxidatively stressed retinal tissues (Kimura et al., 2019; Budas et al., 2009).

Expected Effect  
In RPE mitochondria subjected to chronic oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, the proposed mechanism predicts that Alda-1 will (i) increase ALDH2 catalytic activity and resilience to aldehyde-induced inactivation, (ii) accelerate metabolic clearance of 4-HNE and related long-lived electrophiles to non-reactive acids, (iii) reduce covalent adduction/carbonylation of mitochondrial and cytosolic proteins, (iv) preserve oxidative phosphorylation (increased State 3 respiration and RCR), (v) lower mitochondrial H₂O₂ production, (vi) increase resistance to Ca²⁺-induced MPT and decrease cytochrome c release, and (vii) therefore reduce apoptotic signaling and downstream inflammation in RPE, which in aggregate should attenuate RPE dysfunction and slow progression of dry AMD (Gomes et al., 2014). While direct ALDH2 expression in RPE has not been demonstrated in the provided texts, ALDH2 is present across retinal layers (notably Müller glia) and declines with age, and increasing ALDH2 conferred protection in the aged mouse retina in vivo, supporting the rationale that ALDH2 activation in retinal tissue can be beneficial under oxidative stress; confirming ALDH2 expression and activity in human and murine RPE will be a critical enabling experiment (Karan et al., 2023; Long et al., 2020). The retina’s documented vulnerability to lipid peroxidation (PUFA-rich outer segments, high O₂ consumption, chronic light exposure) and the centrality of oxidative stress to AMD pathogenesis further support that increased mitochondrial aldehyde detoxification should reduce toxic aldehyde burden in RPE and adjacent cells (Chen et al., 2023).

Assay expectations and readouts for validation align closely with prior Alda-1 literature. In isolated RPE mitochondria or permeabilized cells, Alda-1 should preserve ADP-stimulated State 3 oxygen consumption and increase RCR versus vehicle under aldehydic load (e.g., exogenous 4-HNE) or oxidative stress conditions; decreased H₂O₂ release and normalization of uncoupler (CCCP) responses would be predicted based on cardiac mitochondria data (Gomes et al., 2014). Under Ca²⁺ challenge, Alda-1 should increase the threshold for MPT and reduce cytochrome c release; in intact RPE, Alda-1 should maintain Δψm under oxidative stress (e.g., blue light, NaIO₃, HOHA lactone), paralleling hepatocyte in vivo imaging under APAP (Gomes et al., 2014; Wimborne et al., 2020). At the biochemical level, 4-HNE-protein adduct quantification (IHC/ELISA/LC-MS) and protein carbonylation assays should show significant reductions with Alda-1 pretreatment; mitochondrial respiratory chain complex activities may be preserved relative to vehicle under electrophile exposure (Gomes et al., 2014; Cheng, 2019). Downstream stress responses (e.g., ER stress markers such as GRP78, UPR activation; SIRT1 and Nrf2 activity; inflammatory cytokines TNF-α/IL-6) should reflect improved homeostasis, consistent with diabetic retina and MNU data (He et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020). Methodologically, the respiratory chain enzymology and aldehyde reactivity analytics described for RPE systems (e.g., complex I–IV assays in 96-well format, reverse-phase HPLC quantitation of aldehyde scavenging, LC-MS/MS quantitation of aldehyde uptake) are directly applicable to evaluating Alda-1’s effects on mitochondrial function and aldehyde handling in RPE models (Cheng, 2019).

A critical caveat is that ALDH2 distribution within the retina emphasizes Müller cells rather than RPE in available reports, and ALDH2 can be inactivated by high aldehyde levels (>10 µM 4-HNE), implying that the therapeutic window may be constrained under extreme aldehydic stress; Alda-1 is explicitly reported to reduce 4-HNE accessibility to catalytic cysteines and reverse 4-HNE–mediated inhibition, which should mitigate this concern but does not obviate the need to quantify ALDH2 activity and 4-HNE load in RPE during oxidative stress (Karan et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2022). Given that dry AMD pathobiology includes chronic oxidative stress, complement-driven inflammation, lysosomal/lipofuscin pathology, and lipid/protein debris accumulation (drusen), the expected benefit of Alda-1 would likely be most pronounced on the oxidative–aldehydic damage axis (mitochondrial and proteostatic integrity) rather than directly addressing complement or lipid trafficking, suggesting it would be a mechanistically complementary therapy potentially combined with agents targeting other AMD pathways (Chen et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic coherence with AMD pathophysiology: Dry AMD is driven in part by oxidative stress in RPE with accumulation of lipid peroxidation products; ALDH2 is a mitochondrial enzyme that detoxifies 4-HNE/MDA and is susceptible to inactivation by aldehydes, establishing a feed-forward injury loop that Alda-1 is designed to interrupt (Chen et al., 2023; Budas et al., 2009; Karan et al., 2023).  
- Direct mitochondrial mechanism with robust preclinical performance: Alda-1 increases ALDH2 activity, reduces 4-HNE adducts and protein carbonyls, preserves State 3 respiration and RCR, reduces mitochondrial H₂O₂ emission, raises MPT thresholds, and decreases cytochrome c release under chronic aldehydic stress; these endpoints directly match the mitochondrial failure features observed in stressed RPE (Gomes et al., 2014).  
- Retinal in vivo signals: In diabetic and photoreceptor degeneration models, Alda-1 improved ERG, preserved retinal structure, increased SIRT1/Nrf2 signaling, reduced inflammatory cytokines, and diminished ER stress/apoptotic markers, collectively supporting retinal tissue benefit under oxidative stress (He et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020).  
- Protective breadth across organs and insults via aldehyde clearance: Repeated demonstration that Alda-1 reduces 4-HNE accumulation and preserves mitochondrial function in heart, liver, lung, intestine, and neuronal contexts increases confidence that the aldehyde-clearance mechanism is conserved and translatable (Wimborne et al., 2020; Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019).  
- Pharmacogenetic upside: Alda-1 rescues ALDH2*2 activity, suggesting potential efficacy in East Asian ALDH2*2 carriers, a large at-risk population for aldehyde-mediated diseases; this also provides a biomarker-based stratification opportunity in trials (Budas et al., 2009; Kimura et al., 2019).  
- Safety signs in chronic rodent dosing: Six-week daily Alda-1 in naïve rats showed no hemodynamic, biochemical, or organ-weight toxicity, supporting tolerability for longer-term therapy (Gomes et al., 2014).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Lack of dry AMD/RPE-specific data: No direct evidence in RPE-focused dry AMD models (e.g., NaIO₃-induced RPE atrophy, complement dysregulation models, aging-driven GA models) is presented in the context, and ALDH2 expression has not been explicitly demonstrated in RPE here; expression across retina with Müller co-localization and protection in aged retina is encouraging but not definitive for RPE (Karan et al., 2023; Long et al., 2020).  
- Clinical translation gap: No human proof-of-concept for Alda-1 or class; no ALDH2 activator currently in clinical use; ocular PK, distribution, and chronic safety are uncharacterized (Münzel & Daiber, 2018; Kimura et al., 2019).  
- Potential safety concerns: A preclinical report of Alda-1–associated crystalline nephropathy after I/R cautions that formulation, dosing, or off-target deposition may cause tissue-specific toxicity; comprehensive toxicology and formulation work are essential, especially for chronic ocular indications (Jin et al., 2023).  
- Biological complexity and compensatory pathways: Chronic acceleration of aldehyde clearance could theoretically blunt electrophile-mediated adaptive antioxidant signaling (Keap1/Nrf2, PPAR), potentially reducing hormetic protection; the balance of detoxification versus adaptation requires careful evaluation in chronic degenerative settings (Münzel & Daiber, 2018).  
- Enzyme inactivation at high aldehyde loads: ALDH2 is inactivated by >10 µM 4-HNE; although Alda-1 protects ALDH2 from 4-HNE and enhances activity, in extreme aldehydic states therapeutic efficacy might be limited, necessitating combination with upstream ROS control or lipid peroxidation inhibitors (Karan et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2022).  
- Isoform selectivity: Some reports suggest Alda-1 can modulate ALDH1A1 activity, while others report inconclusive cross-activation; off-target activation or inhibition in ocular tissues could have unanticipated effects on retinoid metabolism or cellular differentiation, especially given ALDH1A1’s role in retinaldehyde metabolism and Müller cell biology (Kotraiah et al., 2013; Karan et al., 2023).  
- Delivery challenges: Systemic dosing achieves retinal effects in rodent DR/MNU models, but the optimal route for chronic dry AMD (topical, intravitreal, suprachoroidal, systemic) is unknown; achieving therapeutic mitochondrial concentrations in RPE with acceptable safety will be nontrivial and requires PK/PD studies (Yan et al., 2020; He et al., 2018).

Decision-oriented recommendations  
- Mechanistic validation in human/murine RPE: Quantify ALDH2 mRNA/protein/activity and subcellular localization in primary human RPE and iPSC-RPE; test whether Alda-1 increases ALDH2 activity and protects against 4-HNE–induced ALDH2 inactivation in RPE mitochondria; measure 4-HNE/ACR/MDA adduct load ±Alda-1 under blue-light/NaIO₃/HOHA lactone stress (Karan et al., 2023; Cheng, 2019).  
- Mitochondrial function endpoints in RPE: Using established microplate assays and Seahorse OCR, test Alda-1’s effects on State 3 respiration, RCR, Δψm, H₂O₂ release, CCCP response, MPT susceptibility, and cytochrome c release under aldehydic stress (Gomes et al., 2014; Cheng, 2019).  
- Retinal disease models aligned to dry AMD: Progress to NaIO₃-induced RPE injury, photo-oxidative stress, and aging/complement models relevant to geographic atrophy; evaluate RPE survival, autofluorescent lipofuscin, drusen-like deposits, inflammatory markers, and photoreceptor secondary degeneration with functional readouts (ERG/OCT) under Alda-1 (Chen et al., 2023).  
- Formulation and delivery: Develop ocular formulations (e.g., intravitreal, sustained-release) and conduct ocular PK/PD to quantify RPE mitochondrial exposure; evaluate chronic ocular and systemic safety with renal monitoring given crystalline nephropathy risk (Jin et al., 2023).  
- Biomarkers and patient stratification: Consider ALDH2 genotype (ALDH2*2 carriers), circulating/ocular 4-HNE-adduct biomarkers, and retinal imaging endpoints as stratification and PD markers; Alda-1’s rescue of ALDH2*2 suggests a precision-medicine angle (Budas et al., 2009; Münzel & Daiber, 2018).  
- Combinations: Given AMD’s multifactorial pathobiology, test Alda-1 alongside Nrf2 activators or lipid peroxidation suppressors to determine additive/synergistic effects on RPE resilience while monitoring for suppression of adaptive electrophile signaling (Chen et al., 2023; Münzel & Daiber, 2018).

Overall, Alda-1 presents a mechanistically compelling, enzyme-directed strategy to alleviate aldehyde-driven mitochondrial and proteostatic injury in oxidatively stressed retinal tissues, with in vivo retinal efficacy already demonstrated in DR and photoreceptor degeneration contexts, albeit without RPE-centric dry AMD models to date (He et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2020). The totality of evidence across organ systems (cardiac, hepatic) underscores that Alda-1 reliably reduces 4-HNE load and preserves mitochondrial function in vivo—precisely the biology we seek to modulate in RPE for dry AMD—making this candidate worthy of structured, stepwise validation in RPE-specific systems and AMD-relevant models (Gomes et al., 2014; Wimborne et al., 2020). Key risks reside in translational gaps (RPE expression, ocular PK/safety), potential toxicity signals (renal crystalline nephropathy under certain conditions), and the possibility that aldehyde detoxification alone will be insufficient to arrest complex AMD progression without adjunctive modulation of complement, lipid trafficking, or lysosomal pathways (Jin et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). With these caveats, Alda-1 merits advancement to focused preclinical validation for dry AMD, with an emphasis on RPE mitochondrial protection endpoints, aldehyde-adduct burden, and rigorous ocular safety assessment before considering first-in-human studies.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is a naturally occurring long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (LC-PUFA) that has been isolated from marine sources, such as fish oil, and is commercially available in a highly purified form (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich D2534). DHA is synthesized via metabolic elongation and desaturation of dietary alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) in mammals; however, this endogenous conversion is limited, and direct dietary intake is critical for maintaining adequate retinal DHA levels (Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14). Belonging to the omega-3 class of fatty acids, DHA has long been recognized for its important roles in maintaining membrane structure and function, particularly in neural tissues and the retina where it is highly concentrated in photoreceptor outer segments and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) membranes (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3). Its polyunsaturated nature—with six cis double bonds—confers unique biophysical properties, enabling DHA to increase membrane fluidity and participate in critical signaling cascades. The compound has been used extensively as a nutritional supplement and has been incorporated in various formulations aimed at cardiovascular health, cognitive function, and ocular protection, establishing a robust safety profile over decades of human use (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Skowronska-Krawczyk & Chao, 2019, pp. 3–4).

Therapeutic History:  
Over the past two decades, extensive research has explored the role of DHA and related omega-3 fatty acids in maintaining retinal function and potentially preventing age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Epidemiologic studies have consistently demonstrated an inverse association between dietary fish and high omega-3 fatty acid intake and the risk of developing AMD, suggesting that populations with higher DHA consumption tend to exhibit a lower incidence of both early and, to some extent, advanced forms of the disease (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). In clinical settings, large-scale randomized controlled trials, such as AREDS2, incorporated DHA (and EPA) into a multi-nutrient formula designed originally for AMD, though the overall randomized trial outcomes have been mixed, with some studies finding no statistically significant benefit for progression to late AMD (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). Pilot clinical trials and observational cohort studies, including NAT-1 and NAT-2, have assessed DHA supplementation in subjects with drusenoid lesions or early-stage AMD; while some of these studies have shown promising improvements in blood biomarkers (e.g., increased red blood cell DHA levels) and correlations with reduced AMD progression, the clinical efficacy remains under debate (Querques et al., 2016, pp. 2–4; Querques et al., 2011, pp. 7–8). Notably, evidence from animal models suggests that dietary DHA may protect against light-induced retinal degeneration and reduce the accumulation of deleterious lipid peroxidation products, although some preclinical studies also caution that DHA’s susceptibility to oxidation could, under certain conditions, worsen retinal injury (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic hypothesis for using DHA in dry AMD is based on its predicted ability to incorporate into the mitochondrial membranes of RPE cells, thereby enhancing membrane fluidity and protecting against oxidative damage to the electron transport chain (ETC) complexes. Under normal cellular conditions, DHA—owing to its multiple methylene-interrupted cis double bonds—integrates into phospholipid bilayers and modulates biophysical properties such as fluidity, permeability, and thickness (Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33). In mitochondrial membranes, this incorporation is thought to replace more saturated fatty acids such as arachidonic acid, ultimately reducing lipid peroxidation and mitigating oxidative stress that is deleterious to ETC function (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9). In vitro studies have shown that DHA supplementation in retinal cell cultures can decrease markers of apoptosis and preserve mitochondrial membrane integrity, with a concomitant increase in anti-apoptotic proteins (e.g., Bcl-2) (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 2–4).  
In addition, DHA is enzymatically converted under conditions of oxidative stress into neuroprotective docosanoids, such as neuroprotectin D1 (NPD1), which can inhibit pro-inflammatory gene expression and reduce cell death in RPE and photoreceptor cells (Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14; LaFuente et al., 2021, p. 13). This conversion not only contributes to countering local inflammation but also supports cellular health by modulating intracellular signaling pathways, particularly those involving NF-κB and other transcription factors critical for managing oxidative stress (Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14; Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14). Despite these promising mechanistic insights, it is important to note that direct, quantitative evidence detailing DHA’s incorporation specifically into RPE mitochondrial membranes and its precise effects on mitochondrial cristae structure, malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, or oxygen consumption rate (OCR) remains limited in the current literature (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, p. 13). Several reviews and preclinical reports acknowledge the theoretical framework while emphasizing the need for more detailed mechanistic studies that directly measure these mitochondrial endpoints (Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the mechanistic hypothesis, DHA supplementation is expected to yield several beneficial effects in retinal cells, particularly within the RPE, which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. In an ideal in vitro or ex vivo assay, DHA would incorporate into RPE cell membranes—including the mitochondrial inner membrane—increasing fluidity and enabling better diffusion of substrates and electron carriers necessary for efficient ATP production. Enhanced mitochondrial membrane fluidity should help reduce the susceptibility of the electron transport chain to oxidative damage, thereby lowering the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the subsequent production of lipid peroxidation byproducts such as MDA (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5). Furthermore, preservation of mitochondrial cristae structure is anticipated to maintain optimal alignment and function of ETC complexes, leading to an improved oxygen consumption rate (OCR) that is directly linked to cellular energy metabolism and overall cell viability (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 2–4; Souied et al., 2016, p. 8).  
At a molecular level, the increased presence of DHA in mitochondrial membranes is expected to initiate a cascade of protective events: reduced oxidative stress and inflammation via inhibition of NF-κB activation, promotion of the antioxidant response through NFE2L2 (NRF2) pathway activation, and enhanced autophagic clearance of damaged proteins and organelles through upregulation of SQSTM1 (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 1–2; Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, p. 3). Consequently, these effects should translate into preservation of RPE cell function, reduced apoptosis, and maintenance of photoreceptor health—an effect that could help slow the progression of dry AMD by stabilizing the retinal environment and preventing drusen accumulation and other degenerative changes (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5). Additionally, because genes encoding crucial direct mediators of DHA uptake such as Mfsd2a are expressed in RPE cells and photoreceptors, the target tissue is particularly well-positioned to benefit from increased dietary or supplementary DHA (Fathima et al., 2023, p. 8). However, it is also recognized that despite the strong rationale, direct experimental confirmation of these outcomes—specifically measured improvements in MDA levels, cristae ultrastructure integrity, and OCR in human RPE cells—is still pending, and the observed epidemiologic correlations are not yet unequivocally supported by randomized clinical trial data (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).

Overall Evaluation:  
The proposition to repurpose DHA for dry AMD is underpinned by compelling mechanistic rationale and epidemiologic associations, yet it is not without its challenges and limitations. One clear strength is DHA’s established role as an essential component of retinal cell membranes. Its high concentration in photoreceptors and the RPE is functionally integral to maintaining visual function and cellular homeostasis, lending strong biological plausibility to its protective potential in AMD (Johnson & Schaefer, 2006, pp. 2–3; Walchuk & Suh, 2020, pp. 30–33). Its ability to modulate membrane fluidity, serve as a precursor to neuroprotective mediators like NPD1, and exert anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions provide multiple mechanistic pathways through which it may mitigate the cellular stressors implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis (Longoni & Demontis, 2023, pp. 12–14; Figueiredo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14).  
From a therapeutic history perspective, DHA is well understood in the context of nutritional supplementation, and numerous epidemiologic studies point toward a lower risk of AMD with higher dietary DHA intake (Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). The safety profile of DHA is also well established, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing. However, the clinical trial data to date (including large-scale studies such as AREDS2 and smaller trials like NAT-2) have not consistently demonstrated a clear benefit in altering the progression of advanced AMD, and it remains uncertain whether observed benefits in intermediate AMD or specific cellular endpoints translate into clinically meaningful outcomes in the dry form of the disease (Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8).  
A significant weakness in the current body of research is the lack of direct mechanistic studies that quantitatively document DHA incorporation into RPE mitochondrial membranes and its subsequent effects on mitochondrial parameters. In our hypothesis, improved mitochondrial function is key, with expected reductions in MDA levels, preservation of cristae structure, and enhancement of OCR serving as biomarkers of efficacy. Yet, while several in vitro studies and animal experiments have suggested that DHA can reduce markers of oxidative stress and improve mitochondrial integrity in retinal models, the literature provided does not include rigorous, high-resolution measurements of these specific parameters in human RPE cells (Li et al., 2024, pp. 10–11; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Jiang et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). This gap in the direct evidence would need to be addressed through targeted preclinical assays employing electron microscopy, lipidomics, and mitochondrial respirometry to validate the proposed mechanism.  
Furthermore, the mode of formulation and bioavailability of DHA is a critical factor that may contribute to the mixed findings in clinical trials; DHA administered as an ethyl ester may have different absorption and incorporation profiles compared to its triglyceride-bound form, and the optimal dosing necessary to achieve sufficient retinal or mitochondrial enrichment remains unclear (Souied et al., 2016, pp. 6–7; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 7–8). Potential pro-oxidant effects of DHA in settings where oxidation is excessive must also be carefully monitored, as some animal studies have reported that under specific conditions DHA accumulation may even exacerbate oxidative damage (Dziedziak et al., 2021, pp. 7–9; LaFuente et al., 2021, pp. 4–5).  
In summary, while the epidemiologic literature and preclinical studies provide an encouraging backdrop for the repurposing of DHA as a therapeutic agent in dry AMD—by showing that high DHA intake is associated with a reduced risk of AMD and that DHA can confer mitochondrial and anti-oxidative benefits in retinal models—the critical mechanistic endpoints that support our specific hypothesis are not yet fully substantiated in the published literature. The overall evaluation is that DHA has substantial mechanistic promise, safety, and historical use as a nutritional supplement; however, further robust mechanistic studies and carefully designed clinical trials are necessary to validate its specific effects on mitochondrial function in RPE cells and to determine whether these biochemical improvements translate into a clinically significant slowing of dry AMD progression (Huang et al., 2020, pp. 5–7; Querques & Souied, 2014, pp. 3–5; Zeppieri et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is an endogenous ketone body produced by mitochondrial ketogenesis from fatty-acid–derived acetyl-CoA, classically in hepatocytes but also in extrahepatic cell types including the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and several neuronal lineages (enzymatic pathway: ACAT, HMGCS2, HMGCL, and BDH1) (Wang et al., 2021; Gough, 2021). In physiological and nutritional ketosis, circulating BHB rises from baseline (~0.05–0.1 mM) to levels >0.5 mM and up to 5–7 mM with prolonged fasting, providing an alternative oxidative substrate for extrahepatic mitochondria when carbohydrate availability is limited (Wang et al., 2021; Cooper et al., 2023). BHB and acetoacetate are transported into and out of cells via proton-linked monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs) such as MCT1 and MCT2 that are expressed at the blood–retinal barrier and in retinal cells, enabling substrate entry into the retina (Yang, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Gough, 2021). RPEs robustly express mitochondrial HMGCS2 and can ketogenize palmitate to BHB, secreting BHB via MCT1; retinal cells can take up and metabolize BHB into Krebs-cycle intermediates and amino acids, indicating functional capacity to use BHB as mitochondrial fuel in the outer retina (Yang, 2021). More recent mass spectrometry–based reassessment shows that RPE secretion of BHB is substantially lower than previously estimated by enzymatic kits, that RPE exports BHB to both apical and basal compartments, and that RPE both produces and consumes BHB depending on nutrient state—important considerations for experimental design and therapeutic targeting (Gulette et al., 2024).  

BHB belongs to the class of endogenous metabolic intermediates that function dually as oxidative fuels (via oxidation to acetyl-CoA and entry into TCA cycle) and signaling molecules with paracrine/autocrine receptor and epigenetic actions (e.g., agonism at HCAR2/GPR109A and inhibition of class I/IIa histone deacetylases) (Wang et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Kovács et al., 2021). As a therapeutic modality, BHB has been delivered exogenously as salts/esters or induced endogenously through ketogenic diets, fasting, or exercise to support mitochondrial ATP production and alter cellular stress responses in the CNS, heart, and skeletal muscle (Cooper et al., 2023; Kovács et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2022). In retinal disease models, ketogenic interventions or exogenous BHB have reduced oxidative/inflammatory injury and improved functional measures, though direct application to dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) has not yet been clinically tested (Gough, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021).  

Therapeutic History  
Ketone biology has a long history in neurology and cardiometabolic research, where BHB has been shown to preserve mitochondrial function, increase ATP production, and blunt oxidative injury in ischemia, neurodegeneration models, and skeletal muscle stress paradigms (Kovács et al., 2021; Mierziak et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2018). In neural tissues, ketogenic interventions and exogenous ketones prevent synaptic dysfunction induced by respiratory complex inhibitors and increase the brain NAD⁺/NADH ratio, correlating with decreased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation (Morris et al., 2020). In rat skeletal muscle cells, 5 mM BHB for 24–48 h increased respiratory control, ATP-linked respiration, P:O efficiency, lowered H₂O₂ production, and shifted mitochondrial dynamics toward fusion via DRP1 suppression—consistent with enhanced bioenergetics and decreased oxidative stress (Parker et al., 2018). In primary neurons, BHB maintained oxidative phosphorylation under glutamate workload even when cytosolic NADH transfer via the malate–aspartate shuttle was inhibited, demonstrating that BHB can sustain respiration under conditions that impair glycolytic NADH coupling to mitochondria (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

In the retina and optic nerve, multiple preclinical models show that ketogenic exposures or direct ketone administration reduce oxidative stress and inflammation, preserve function, and limit neuronal death. Intraperitoneal BHB and acetoacetate reduced NMDA-induced retinal ganglion cell (RGC) death in rats, and ketogenic diet attenuated NMDA-induced RGC injury in juvenile rats (Gough, 2021). In ocular blast or optic neuropathy paradigms, ketogenic diet prevented increases in superoxide and IL-1α, preserved visual evoked potentials, and reduced astrocytic hypertrophy and optic nerve death (Gough, 2021). In glaucoma models, ketogenic diet improved RGC soma/axon survival, axonal transport, and reduced gliosis, with increases in NAD and NAD:NADH ratio and upregulation of MCT1/MCT2 in optic nerve (Tribble et al., 2021). AAV-mediated MCT2 overexpression (increasing uptake of lactate/pyruvate/ketones) preserved RGCs and optic nerve axons in ocular hypertension and glaucoma models and elevated markers of mitochondrial biogenesis and function (PGC1α, COX, SDH) and antioxidant defense (SOD2) (Gough, 2021). However, in at least one RGC injury model, daily intraperitoneal BHB or acetoacetate did not replicate ketogenic diet neuroprotection, underscoring differences between exogenous ketone dosing and the systemic/multifactorial effects of ketogenic diets (Tribble et al., 2021).  

Within the RPE compartment specifically, two lines of evidence are relevant: (1) BHB protects ARPE-19 cells from high-glucose–induced injury, improving viability, alleviating cell cycle arrest, and modulating inflammatory mediators (IL-8, IL-17α, MCP-1) at millimolar concentrations achievable with nutritional ketosis or exogenous supplementation (Argentino et al., 2025). (2) HCAR2/GPR109A, a BHB receptor, is robustly expressed by the RPE; BHB agonism reduced retinal leukocyte infiltration in LPS-challenged mice in an HCAR2-dependent manner, and loss of HCAR2 in RPE led to barrier dysfunction (ZO-1 defects) and increased immune cell infiltrates, indicating that BHB–HCAR2 signaling can preserve an immunoinhibitory retinal environment (Powell et al., 2021). In diabetic retinopathy models, systemic BHB activation of HCA2 reduced ER stress and NLRP3 inflammasome signaling and ameliorated retinal pathology, establishing anti-inflammatory and ER stress–limiting actions in retina (Trotta et al., 2019).  

In inherited retinal degeneration models, ketogenic interventions delayed photoreceptor degeneration and improved electroretinogram (ERG) amplitudes and outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness in rd10 and Pde6a mice, and a soluble ketogenic formulation partially restored vision and survival in PDH-deficient noir zebrafish—consistent with bypassing PDH to supply acetyl-CoA and support neurotransmitter synthesis (Gough, 2021). Notwithstanding these encouraging signals, the literature consistently notes the absence of clinical trials evaluating ketogenic interventions or BHB in retinitis pigmentosa or AMD patients, and reports potentially adverse effects of ketogenic diets in wild-type mice (decreased ERG amplitudes, altered albumin/weight), highlighting translational uncertainties and the need to distinguish effects of BHB from the broader systemic consequences of diet (Gough, 2021).  

Mechanism of Action  
BHB acts through convergent metabolic, redox, mitochondrial, inflammatory, and epigenetic mechanisms that are mechanistically aligned with the pathophysiology of RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic oxidative/inflammatory stress in dry AMD.  

- Alternative mitochondrial fuel and bioenergetics support. In extrahepatic tissues (including retina), BHB oxidation proceeds via mitochondrial BDH1 (βHB→acetoacetate) followed by SCOT/OXCT1 (AcAc→AcAc-CoA using succinyl-CoA) and acetyl-CoA production for TCA entry and ATP generation, enabling substrate-level maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and oxidative phosphorylation under glucose restriction or impaired glycolytic NADH transfer (Wang et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023). The retina expresses monocarboxylate transport routes (e.g., MCT1 at the inner blood–retinal barrier; MCT2 in neurons), and RPE expresses MCT1 and can both produce and consume BHB, providing a plausible uptake pathway for exogenous BHB into RPE and neighboring retinal cells (Tribble et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Gulette et al., 2024). In neurons, BHB-supported respiration remains robust when the malate–aspartate shuttle is blocked with AOAA—conditions that decrease glucose-fueled ATP synthesis—indicating that BHB can preserve mitochondrial ATP synthesis and respiratory control when cytosolic NADH transfer is compromised, a scenario relevant to glycolysis-impaired RPE (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

- Redox coupling and ROS control. The interconversion of acetoacetate and BHB by βHB dehydrogenase is linked to NADH/NAD⁺ redox; acetoacetate→BHB requires oxidation of NADH to NAD⁺, and nutritional ketosis in human brain increases NAD⁺/NADH ratio, correlating with reductions in mitochondrial ROS generation (Gough, 2021; Morris et al., 2020). Ketones can inhibit mitochondrial ROS production by increasing NADH oxidation, and ketogenic interventions increase NAD⁺/NADH in vivo, though tissue- and context-dependent effects exist (Morris et al., 2020). Complementary cardiac literature reports that β-OHB can reduce the mitochondrial NAD couple while oxidizing coenzyme Q, emphasizing that BHB modulates both NADH/NAD⁺ and Q/QH₂ redox pairs in mitochondria—with directionality that may depend on prevailing substrate status and respiratory state (Chu et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion models and muscle cells, BHB lowers mitochondrial ROS, decreases mitochondrial swelling, maintains Δψm, and increases ATP production, consistent with direct mitochondrial protection (Mierziak et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2018).  

- Antioxidant transcription (Nrf2) and hormesis. Ketogenic exposures can induce a hormetic redox signal that activates Keap1–Nrf2, increasing transcription of detoxification and antioxidant genes; in retina, ketone body exposure mimicked calorie restriction via fumarate–Nrf2 activation (Gough, 2021; Fu et al., 2020). Preclinical optic/retinal models link these antioxidant transcriptional effects to preserved function and reduced oxidative markers (NOS, MDA, superoxide) (Gough, 2021).  

- Anti-inflammatory signaling via HCAR2/ARRB2 and NLRP3/NF-κB suppression. BHB is a ligand for HCAR1/HCAR2 receptors; HCAR2 is robustly expressed in human RPE and retina, and receptor activation by BHB reduces leukocyte infiltration and preserves RPE barrier integrity in inflammation models (Powell et al., 2021). Downstream, BHB–HCAR signaling recruits β-arrestin-2 (ARRB2) that binds NLRP3 to block inflammasome assembly, decreasing ASC and preventing K⁺ efflux to suppress IL-1β maturation; BHB also activates a COX1/PGD2 cascade that inhibits IKK and NF-κB nuclear translocation, reducing TNF-α and microglial/macrophage activation (Gough, 2021). In diabetic retina, systemic BHB–HCA2 activation suppressed ER stress and NLRP3 inflammasome activity, demonstrating the retinal anti-inflammatory efficacy of this axis (Trotta et al., 2019).  

- Mitochondrial calcium homeostasis and mPTP stabilization. In human iPSC-derived microglia, amyloid-β oligomers increased MCU expression, raised mitochondrial Ca²⁺ ~40%, elevated mtROS, and triggered mPTP opening; BHB normalized MCU, decreased mtCa²⁺/mtROS, and completely reversed mPTP activation, restoring phagocytic function (Jin et al., 2023). Although not conducted in RPE, these mitochondrial-stabilizing effects are mechanistically relevant to post-mitotic cells with high oxidative load.  

- Epigenetic modulation and mitochondrial biogenesis. BHB is an endogenous inhibitor of class I/IIa HDACs at physiological millimolar concentrations, leading to histone hyperacetylation and upregulation of FOXO3a and metallothionein genes that encode antioxidant defenses; BHB also increases intracellular acetyl-CoA and supports protein acetylation, and can β-hydroxybutyrylate histones, adding layers of gene regulatory control tied to mitochondrial status (Yang, 2021; Kovács et al., 2021; Mierziak et al., 2021). Through HDAC inhibition and receptor-mediated signaling, BHB increases BDNF via cAMP/PKA/CREB, activates SIRT1/SIRT3 via AMPK/HCA2/NAD⁺ pathways, and promotes PGC1α-driven mitochondrial biogenesis and UCP2 expression that collectively improve mitochondrial function and antioxidant capacity (Kovács et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022). In retinal/optic nerve models, ketogenic diet or enhanced monocarboxylate uptake upregulated PGC1α, COX, SDH, and SOD2 while lowering pAMPK/AMPK, linking substrate availability to mitochondrial biogenesis and anti-inflammatory signaling (Gough, 2021).  

- Immunometabolic reprogramming in retina/CNS. Ketogenic interventions increased anti-inflammatory mediators (IL-4, Arginase-1) and M2-like microglia while decreasing IBA-1⁺ macrophage/microglia, consistent with dampened neuroinflammation secondary to improved bioenergetics (reduced AMPK activation) and prevention of NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation (Gough, 2021). BHB also inhibits FFAR3/GPR41, reducing sympathetic activity in mice, indicating broader metabolic signaling roles that could modulate retinal perfusion/metabolism indirectly (Gough, 2021).  

Collectively, these mechanisms—fuel substitution that sustains Δψm and ATP synthesis under glycolytic impairment, improved redox balance with decreased mitochondrial ROS, Nrf2-dependent antioxidant gene induction, NLRP3/NF-κB anti-inflammatory actions via HCAR2/ARRB2, stabilization of mitochondrial Ca²⁺/mPTP, and epigenetic programs that support mitochondrial biogenesis—map directly onto pathologies implicated in RPE degeneration in dry AMD and provide multiple rescue nodes testable in disease-relevant models (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Gough, 2021; Powell et al., 2021).  

Expected Effect  
Assay context: The working hypothesis is that exogenous BHB will serve as an alternative mitochondrial substrate in RPE, sustaining Δψm and reducing NADH-driven mitochondrial ROS when glycolysis is impaired—conditions that model bioenergetic stress in geographic atrophy. Mechanistically, this is supported by three converging evidence streams: (1) mitochondrial fuel flexibility to oxidize BHB to acetyl-CoA via BDH1/SCOT, (2) redox modulation that increases NADH oxidation and elevates the NAD⁺/NADH ratio, and (3) multi-layered antioxidant/anti-inflammatory signaling that lowers mitochondrial ROS production and downstream inflammasome/NF-κB activation (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Gough, 2021).  

- Sustained Δψm and ATP under glycolytic impairment. RPE expresses ketogenesis machinery (HMGCS2) and monocarboxylate transport capacity (MCT1) and is capable of both producing and consuming BHB, while inner BRB MCT1 and neuronal MCT2 provide routes for substrate delivery into retinal tissue (Yang, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Gulette et al., 2024). In neurons, BHB preserved oxidative phosphorylation and ATP-linked respiration under MAS inhibition, a condition that effectively reduces mitochondrial access to cytosolic NADH from glycolysis; this predicts that, in RPE exposed to glycolytic blockade or high work demand, BHB could maintain Δψm and respiratory control by supplying acetyl-CoA independent of cytosolic NADH shuttling (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023). In muscle and cardiac models, BHB improved respiratory control ratios, increased ATP production, and maintained Δψm under stress, providing precedent for Δψm preservation in high-energy post-mitotic cells (Parker et al., 2018; Mierziak et al., 2021).  

- Lowered NADH-driven mtROS and improved redox balance. Nutritional ketosis increases the brain NAD⁺/NADH ratio and ketones inhibit mitochondrial ROS production by increasing NADH oxidation, a shift that is expected to suppress reverse electron transport and semiquinone leak at respiratory complexes under high NADH load (Morris et al., 2020). Although some cardiac literature reports context-dependent changes in the mitochondrial NAD couple under BHB with concurrent oxidation of coenzyme Q, the net effect across neural and muscle studies is reduced mitochondrial ROS generation and improved redox handling, a phenotype also observed in optic/retinal models after ketogenic interventions (Chu et al., 2021; Gough, 2021; Mierziak et al., 2021). These redox improvements are reinforced by Nrf2 activation and increased expression of antioxidant defenses (e.g., SOD2), which increase ROS quenching capacity in retinal and optic tissues (Gough, 2021).  

- Anti-inflammatory and barrier-preserving actions in RPE. BHB agonizes HCAR2 expressed by RPE and retinal microglia, reducing leukocyte infiltration, preserving tight junction integrity (ZO-1), and suppressing inflammasome/NF-κB signaling (Powell et al., 2021; Trotta et al., 2019). In hyperglycemic ARPE-19, BHB improved viability and cell cycle progression and modulated inflammatory cytokines, consistent with protection under metabolic stress (Argentino et al., 2025). By preserving ATP and lowering AMPK phosphorylation, BHB/ketone availability is expected to block NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation and downstream expression of IL-6 and TNF-α, reducing the chronic para-inflammatory milieu implicated in RPE degeneration (Gough, 2021).  

- Translational considerations for exposure and transport. Systemically delivered BHB can traverse the blood–retinal barrier via MCT1, and RPE’s own MCT1 provides transmembrane transport capacity; nonetheless, quantitative extracellular BHB at RPE surfaces is likely in the low micromolar range under basal conditions, and RPE produces and consumes BHB dynamically, implying that achieving therapeutic mitochondrial utilization in RPE will require millimolar plasma BHB or local delivery (Tribble et al., 2021; Gulette et al., 2024). Nutritional ketosis and exogenous ketone supplementation readily achieve 0.5–2 mM BHB in plasma in rodent and human studies, which are the concentrations used in many in vitro protection assays (Cooper et al., 2023; Argentino et al., 2025).  

Key readouts and validation metrics for the proposed assay should include Δψm (e.g., TMRM/TMRE), OCR/ECAR profiling and ATP-linked respiration (Seahorse), mitochondrial ROS (MitoSOX and H₂O₂ flux), NAD⁺/NADH ratio (enzymatic cycling and/or fluorescence lifetime imaging), pAMPK/AMPK and NF-κB p65 nuclear localization, Nrf2 translocation and target gene induction (e.g., SOD2), and inflammasome readouts (ASC specks, IL-1β maturation) (Gough, 2021). Given the measurement pitfalls documented in RPE ketone assays, BHB should be quantified by LC–MS/MS or after removal of high-MW confounders by size exclusion rather than by standard enzymatic kits (Gulette et al., 2024).  
Protein expression considerations support the mechanism in the target cell type. HCAR2/GPR109A is expressed by RPE and retinal microglia/endothelium and mediates anti-inflammatory effects of BHB in vivo, making receptor-dependent components of BHB action directly testable in RPE (Powell et al., 2021). RPE expresses HMGCS2 and MCT1, and retinal cells metabolize BHB into TCA intermediates, consistent with BDH1/SCOT/OXCT1 pathway activity enabling BHB oxidation in retinal tissues; while direct SCOT expression in RPE is not provided here, the metabolic tracing data indicating conversion of BHB to Krebs intermediates in retinal cells justify testing oxidative utilization in RPE (Yang, 2021; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strength of biological rationale. The core hypothesis—that BHB can act as an alternative mitochondrial fuel to sustain Δψm and lower NADH-driven mitochondrial ROS in glycolysis-impaired RPE—is strongly aligned with BHB’s established roles in extrahepatic tissues and is supported by multiple mechanistic strands in relevant neural and retinal systems (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023). BHB oxidation provides acetyl-CoA and maintains respiration when glycolytic NADH transfer is compromised, as demonstrated in primary neurons; BHB reduces mtROS, preserves Δψm, and increases ATP in ischemic muscle/heart models; and nutrient ketosis increases the NAD⁺/NADH ratio and lowers ROS production in brain—effects that would be expected to decrease reverse-electron transport–driven ROS at complex I and stabilize mitochondrial function in stressed RPE (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023; Mierziak et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020). In retinal tissue, ketogenic interventions and direct ketone administration reduce oxidative injury, preserve function, and enhance mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses in RGC/optic nerve models, while anti-inflammatory benefits via HCAR2—expressed by RPE—reduce leukocyte infiltration and preserve barrier integrity (Gough, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Powell et al., 2021; Trotta et al., 2019). The mitochondrial stabilization effects observed in human microglia—lower MCU/mtCa²⁺, reduced mtROS, prevention of mPTP opening—further support a BHB-mediated mitochondrial resilience phenotype that is likely relevant to RPE (Jin et al., 2023).  

Evidence relevant to the target tissue. RPEs possess ketone-related transport and enzymatic capacity (HMGCS2, MCT1) and can both produce and consume BHB; they are responsive to BHB in vitro under metabolic stress (hyperglycemia) with improved viability and inflammatory marker modulation (Yang, 2021; Argentino et al., 2025). HCAR2-mediated anti-inflammatory and barrier maintenance functions have been demonstrated in RPE/retina, providing a receptor-proximal pathway for BHB to suppress chronic para-inflammation and preserve RPE junctional integrity, both relevant to dry AMD pathobiology (Powell et al., 2021). While direct measurements of BDH1/SCOT activity and NAD⁺/NADH dynamics in human RPE treated with BHB remain to be shown here, the metabolic fate of BHB in retinal cells and robust mitochondrial effects in closely related cell types make the translational experiments technically feasible and mechanistically justified (Yang, 2021; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

Translational gaps and risks. No clinical trials have evaluated ketogenic diets or BHB specifically for RP or AMD, and some ketogenic diet studies reported adverse outcomes in wild-type animals (decreased ERG amplitude, altered serum albumin/weight), emphasizing the need to decouple BHB’s effects from broader dietary/metabolic confounders (Gough, 2021). Direct BHB delivery does not always recapitulate ketogenic diet benefits in RGC injury, suggesting that multi-target effects of diet (e.g., NAD metabolism, mTOR, microbiome) contribute to efficacy; this implies that BHB monotherapy may require combination strategies (e.g., nicotinamide co-therapy) or optimized dosing to achieve comparable benefit (Tribble et al., 2021). Quantification of BHB in RPE experiments is non-trivial due to assay interference; LC–MS/MS or validated size-exclusion protocols must be used to avoid false positives and to measure physiologically relevant, often low-micromolar extracellular BHB in RPE cultures (Gulette et al., 2024). Finally, the directionality of NAD redox effects may be context dependent (reports of both increased NAD⁺/NADH ratio in brain and reduced mitochondrial NAD couple in cardiac models), requiring careful interpretation with compartment-specific assays in RPE (Morris et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2021).  

Development path and decision points. Given the strong mechanistic rationale, retina-focused preclinical evidence, and RPE receptor expression data, BHB is a plausible repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD that merits rigorous, RPE-centric validation. Key go/no-go preclinical criteria should include: (1) demonstration that BHB rescues Δψm and ATP-linked respiration in primary human RPE or iPSC-RPE under glycolytic impairment (e.g., 2-deoxyglucose or low glucose plus workload), (2) reduction of mitochondrial ROS (MitoSOX/H₂O₂ flux) and elevation of cellular NAD⁺/NADH ratio with BHB, (3) suppression of pAMPK and NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation, induction of Nrf2 target genes, and reduction of NLRP3 activation, (4) persistence of benefits under HCAR2 antagonism/knockdown to parse receptor versus fuel contributions, and (5) confirmation that effects are contingent on monocarboxylate transport (MCT inhibition) and SCOT activity (e.g., OXCT1 knockdown), which would mechanistically link outcomes to BHB oxidation rather than unrelated signaling (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023; Gough, 2021; Powell et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021). In vivo, a dry-AMD–relevant RPE degeneration model should test systemic or ocular BHB delivery (dose selection to 0.5–2 mM plasma equivalents) with readouts of RPE mitochondrial structure/function, subretinal inflammation, and lesion progression; blood–retina transport via MCT1 at the inner BRB suggests systemic exposure can reach the retina, though intraocular routes might achieve higher local concentrations (Tribble et al., 2021). Throughout, BHB dosing must be titrated to avoid off-target effects and electrolyte load associated with some salt formulations; direct ketone esters or controlled dietary induction may be considered for translational studies, recognizing model-specific differences seen between exogenous BHB and ketogenic diet (Tribble et al., 2021).  

Strengths  
- Mechanistic breadth and convergence on AMD-relevant pathways: alternative fuel supply to support Δψm/ATP, improved NAD redox and ROS control, Nrf2 antioxidant gene induction, and potent suppression of NLRP3/NF-κB–mediated para-inflammation via HCAR2—each independently linked to retinal/RPE resilience (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Gough, 2021; Powell et al., 2021).  
- Retinal delivery/uptake plausibility: MCT expression at the inner BRB and in RPE, plus RPE’s ability to both produce and consume BHB, establish physiological routes for BHB transit and utilization in target tissues (Tribble et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Gulette et al., 2024).  
- Preclinical efficacy signals in retinal and CNS models: reduced oxidative/inflammatory injury, preserved neuronal function, enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis/antioxidant defenses, and receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory actions in retina (Gough, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Trotta et al., 2019; Powell et al., 2021).  
- Compatibility with RPE stress biology: BHB improved ARPE-19 survival under metabolic stress and modulated cytokines, and microglial mitochondrial data demonstrate BHB reverses mtCa²⁺/mtROS/mPTP derangements that are mechanistically relevant to RPE degeneration (Argentino et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2023).  

Weaknesses and uncertainties  
- Lack of AMD-specific in vivo data and no clinical trials in AMD/RP; extrapolation from RGC/optic nerve/diabetic models requires confirmation in RPE-targeted systems (Gough, 2021).  
- Measurement pitfalls in RPE ketone studies; reliance on inaccurate enzymatic assays historically confounded interpretation, necessitating MS-based quantitation and careful time-course sampling (Gulette et al., 2024).  
- Context-dependent redox effects; reports differ on NAD couple responses to BHB, indicating the need for compartmentalized NAD⁺/NADH readouts in RPE to avoid misattribution (Morris et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2021).  
- Differences between exogenous BHB and ketogenic diet; some benefits in glaucoma were not reproduced with BHB delivery, suggesting that metabolic co-factors (e.g., NAD boosters) or combinatorial strategies may be required (Tribble et al., 2021).  
- Potential systemic/dietary adverse effects; ketogenic diets can reduce ERG amplitudes and alter systemic biomarkers in wild-type mice—although these are not necessarily attributable to BHB per se, they caution against non-specific dietary induction in frail patients (Gough, 2021).  

Overall, BHB (Sigma-Aldrich 389410) is a compelling repurposed candidate for dry AMD based on strong mechanistic plausibility and retina-relevant preclinical evidence, with direct RPE expression of the key anti-inflammatory receptor HCAR2 and demonstrable RPE responses to BHB under metabolic stress (Powell et al., 2021; Argentino et al., 2025). The major risk is the current absence of AMD-specific in vivo evidence and the historical conflation of diet-level ketosis with BHB pharmacology; these can be addressed by an RPE-centric preclinical plan that uses rigorous ketone quantitation, compartmental redox readouts, transporter/enzyme perturbations (MCT/OXCT1), and in vivo validation in RPE degeneration models. If BHB reproducibly maintains Δψm/ATP, reduces mtROS, and suppresses inflammasome/NF-κB signaling in RPE under glycolytic impairment, it would justify advancement to formulation and delivery optimization for ocular exposure and, subsequently, to early clinical safety/pharmacodynamic studies in dry AMD (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023; Gough, 2021; Wang et al., 2021).

By focusing on the upstream source of pathological ROS, S1QEL-1.1 has a stronger rationale for translation into dry AMD therapy compared to EUK-134, which has known efficiency gaps in H2O2 clearance, potential pro-oxidant effects, and no direct retinal validation.
