1. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Urolithin A (UA) is a naturally occurring polyphenolic metabolite that is generated in humans via the microbial transformation of dietary ellagitannins, which are abundant in pomegranates, berries, walnuts, and other fruits and nuts. UA belongs to the class of gut-derived α-benzocoumarin compounds and is produced through the specific metabolic activities of intestinal bacteria on ellagitannins and ellagic acid. The discovery of UA emerged from studies aimed at understanding the beneficial effects of diets rich in polyphenols on aging and cellular health, and its structure was elucidated as a 6H-dibenzopyran-6-one derivative. In general, compounds of this class are known for their anti-oxidative, anti-inflammatory, and pro-mitophagic properties. Over time, UA has been investigated increasingly for its ability to modulate mitochondrial function and cellular homeostasis, garnering interest in its potential applications beyond traditional nutritional supplementation. Its multifaceted biological activities have been documented in several preclinical studies where it enhanced mitochondrial quality control, improved muscle endurance in aging populations, and mitigated neurodegenerative processes by clearing dysfunctional mitochondria, lending support to its candidacy as a repurposed drug for chronic conditions such as dry age-related macular degeneration (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Makarov & Korkotian, 2023).  

Historically, naturally derived compounds with similar mechanisms of action have been used to address age-related cellular dysfunction. UA, however, stands out by virtue of its dual ability to invoke both mitophagy and lysophagy, which are critical for the removal of damaged organelles—key processes implicated in aging and neurodegeneration. This compound is not synthesized chemically in the traditional pharmaceutical sense; rather, its production relies on the interplay between dietary intake and the gut microbiota, reinforcing the concept that natural metabolic products can be harnessed as therapeutic agents. Its inclusion in the spectrum of therapeutics aimed at cellular rejuvenation has sparked significant interest, particularly because its widespread availability in the human diet and favorable safety profile, as observed in early clinical trials, set a promising foundation for further drug development (Maksimović et al., 2025; Liu, 2022).

2. Therapeutic History  
Urolithin A has been extensively studied in the context of aging and degenerative diseases, and its therapeutic history spans several biomedical, clinical, and biochemical investigations. Preclinical studies have shown that UA is effective in enhancing mitophagy, thereby promoting the clearance of damaged mitochondria. In animal models, UA supplementation has been correlated with improved mitochondrial function and increased muscle endurance, which has led to its exploration as an “anti-aging” agent. Notably, several clinical trials have confirmed its safety in elderly populations, with doses up to 2,500 mg/day being well tolerated and associated with improvements in mitochondrial biomarkers in skeletal muscle (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Liu, 2022).  

In the realm of neurodegeneration, UA has been recognized for its neuroprotective activities. Studies have demonstrated that UA can ameliorate cognitive impairment and reduce inflammatory markers, suggesting benefits in neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Fehér et al., 2022). Importantly, recent investigations have extended the focus to ocular health. Preclinical models of retinal degeneration—particularly those mimicking dry AMD—have emerged as critical systems in which UA’s multifactorial actions are being tested. In models employing sodium iodate (SI) to induce retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) damage, UA treatment resulted in enhanced RPE cell survival, restoration of autophagic flux, and preservation of visual function (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). These studies underscore UA’s potential in mitigating geographic atrophy, a defining feature of dry AMD.  

Beyond its direct mitochondrial effects, UA has been evaluated for its impact on lysosomal function. Some reports indicate that UA exerts potent neuroprotective benefits by promoting SQSTM1/p62-dependent lysophagy, leading to the clearance of damaged lysosomes and restoration of cellular proteostasis. This lysophagy mechanism appears to be crucial in maintaining retinal cellular homeostasis and preventing RPE atrophy, a process that is marked by an accumulation of dysfunctional organelles and consequent oxidative stress in AMD (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). Although direct clinical use of UA in the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular diseases has not yet been fully realized, the wealth of preclinical evidence—particularly from relevant animal models—provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in this context. In summary, UA’s therapeutic history demonstrates its utility across multiple age-related pathologies, with growing evidence supporting its potential application in dry age-related macular degeneration (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

3. Mechanism of Action  
The molecular mechanisms underpinning the actions of Urolithin A are multifaceted and involve intricate interactions across several cellular pathways. Central to UA’s mechanism is its ability to induce selective autophagy, a process that includes both mitophagy and lysophagy, leading to the clearance of damaged mitochondria and lysosomes, respectively. Under normal physiological conditions, mitochondria that lose membrane potential become marked for degradation through the action of PINK1 (PTEN-induced kinase 1), which accumulates on the outer mitochondrial membrane. This accumulation results in the recruitment and activation of Parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase that ubiquitinates mitochondrial surface proteins, thereby flagging them for autophagic degradation. UA has been shown to upregulate the PINK1/Parkin pathway, thereby enhancing the clearance of dysfunctional mitochondria and ensuring mitochondrial quality control (Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024; Jayatunga et al., 2021).  

In addition to its role in mitophagy, UA has been demonstrated to elicit pronounced effects on lysosomal recycling processes through the promotion of SQSTM1/p62-dependent lysophagy. This pathway is critical because damaged lysosomes, if not effectively removed, can contribute to cellular toxicity and inflammation. The engagement of p62 in the targeting of these vesicles for autophagosome formation has been observed as a necessary step in the restoration of autophagic flux within RPE cells (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). The dual activation of mitophagy and lysophagy by UA helps mitigate the accumulation of damaged organelles, thereby reducing the levels of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) and subsequent oxidative stress.

At the biochemical level, UA influences several upstream signaling pathways. Notably, it activates the AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)/ULK1 axis—a key regulator of autophagy. Activation of AMPK leads to phosphorylation of ULK1, kick-starting the autophagy process, and is associated with improved energy balance and mitochondrial turnover. This activation is complemented by an upregulation of factors such as PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha), which is instrumental in mitochondrial biogenesis. Together, these events not only promote the removal of impaired mitochondria but also support the generation of new, functional mitochondria, thereby restoring mitochondrial homeostasis (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Furthermore, the anti-inflammatory properties of UA are closely tied to its capacity to modulate oxidative stress. By clearing mitochondria that are prone to leaking mtROS, UA indirectly diminishes the activation of pro-inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB and AP-1, which have been implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. UA’s activation of SIRT1, SIRT3, and AMPK also play a role in upregulating antioxidant defenses; for instance, the enhanced transcription of Nrf2-dependent genes contributes to a robust antioxidative response. These molecular interactions collectively participate in mitigating the inflammatory milieu that is characteristic of neurodegenerative conditions and retinal disorders (Makarov & Korkotian, 2023; Zhang et al., 2025; Jayatunga et al., 2021).

In the context of retinal degeneration, several studies have delineated how UA’s molecular actions translate into cytoprotective outcomes. In SI-induced retinal injury models, the re-establishment of autophagic flux by UA is correlated with reduced RPE cell death and preservation of photoreceptor function. Although some findings suggest that UA’s neuroprotective effects in these models are independent of PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, there is substantial evidence that UA comprehensively enhances cellular quality control mechanisms through both mitophagy and lysophagy. This dichotomy might reflect the compound’s capability to engage multiple parallel pathways to ensure the efficient clearance of damaged organelles (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Fehér et al., 2022). Given that the retina is especially sensitive to oxidative stress and that impaired mitochondrial dynamics are a hallmark of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD, these molecular mechanisms underscore UA’s therapeutic potential.

At a more granular level, it is worth noting that UA appears to influence the expression levels of key mitophagy-related proteins not only at the post-translational level but also transcriptionally. For instance, treatment with UA has been associated with increased expression of Parkin and proteins involved in the formation of autophagosomes, such as BECN1, further reinforcing its role in maintaining mitochondrial and lysosomal integrity. This transcriptional regulation may be mediated by the activation of transcription factors such as FOXO, which have been implicated in cellular stress responses and longevity pathways. As mitochondrial dysfunction contributes significantly to the pathology of dry AMD, the ability of UA to simultaneously promote the degradation of damaged mitochondria and stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis positions it as a strong candidate for addressing the underlying etiologies of RPE degeneration (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

In summary, the detailed biochemistry of UA illustrates that its mechanism of action involves a well-coordinated activation of autophagic processes through both the PINK1/Parkin axis for mitophagy and the SQSTM1/p62 pathway for lysophagy, with auxiliary support from AMPK/ULK1 and SIRT-mediated signaling. This comprehensive modulation of cellular clearance pathways is critical in contexts where mitochondrial dysfunction and lysosomal impairment drive disease progression, such as in dry age-related macular degeneration (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

4. Expected Effect  
The central hypothesis behind repurposing Urolithin A for dry AMD posits that the compound enhances PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby accelerating the clearance of damaged mitochondria that contribute to excessive mtROS production. In the cellular assays designed to evaluate this therapeutic intervention, the expected effect would be a measurable reduction in mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress within RPE cells, ultimately leading to improved cellular viability and resistance to atrophy.  
 
Experimental models of RPE degeneration, particularly those utilizing sodium iodate (SI) as a toxic insult, have provided a platform for assessing the cytoprotective properties of UA. In these models, UA treatment leads to a restoration of autophagic flux—a critical determinant of cellular health—by enhancing both the degradation of impaired mitochondria and the recycling of damaged lysosomes through the p62-dependent pathway. The net effect is a significant decrease in RPE cell death and, consequently, the preservation of photoreceptor cells and visual function. This outcome is particularly relevant for dry AMD, a condition characterized by geographic atrophy of the RPE and subsequent photoreceptor degeneration (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024).

At the molecular level, the activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway by UA is expected to facilitate the tagging of dysfunctional mitochondria for autophagic removal. Consequently, a reduction in mtROS levels would follow, as damaged mitochondria are a major source of these reactive species. In parallel, the activation of AMPK/ULK1 signaling by UA further promotes autophagosome formation, ensuring that the cell’s degradative capacity is optimized to handle the increased load of dysfunctional organelles. The coordinated activation of these pathways not only improves mitochondrial quality control but also indirectly suppresses downstream inflammatory cascades that are typically exacerbated by oxidative stress. For instance, by reducing mtROS levels, UA is anticipated to attenuate the activation of pro-inflammatory transcription factors such as NF-κB, thereby contributing to a more quiescent cellular environment supportive of RPE survival (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

More specifically, in the assay proposed by the research team, RPE cells would be evaluated for changes in markers of mitophagy and lysophagy as well as for functional readouts of mitochondrial health. Biochemical assays might include quantification of PINK1 and Parkin recruitment to mitochondria, measurement of autophagic flux using LC3 conversion assays, and assessment of p62 levels. Furthermore, evaluation of mitochondrial membrane potential and ROS production through fluorometric assays would provide additional functional evidence for UA’s efficacy. Given that studies in animal models have shown that UA treatment not only restores autophagic flux but also leads to increased cone survival and improved visual function, it is reasonable to expect that similar beneficial effects could be recapitulated in RPE cells in vitro (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Another anticipated effect of UA treatment in RPE cells is the upregulation of mitochondrial biogenesis. The activation of AMPK and the consequent stimulation of PGC-1α are critical steps in fostering the production of new mitochondria, which serve to replace those that have been degraded. This replenishment of the mitochondrial pool is essential for maintaining cellular energy homeostasis in an environment that is otherwise challenged by the metabolic demands of ongoing stress. The dual action of UA in both clearing damaged mitochondria and promoting the biogenesis of healthy ones creates a favorable cellular milieu that could slow, or potentially reverse, the progression of RPE atrophy—a key pathological feature of dry AMD (Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Moreover, the expected reduction in mtROS levels upon UA treatment has broader implications for the cellular stress response. High levels of ROS not only cause direct oxidative damage to cellular components but also activate signaling pathways that lead to further inflammation and apoptosis. By mitigating this excessive ROS production, UA is likely to reduce the activation of stress-related kinases and inflammatory mediators that contribute to the degeneration of RPE cells. This protective effect on cellular integrity is anticipated to translate into preserved retinal function, as the health of the RPE is integral to the maintenance of the outer retina and photoreceptor survival (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Fehér et al., 2022).

In summary, the expected effect of UA in the proposed assay is multifactorial:  
– Enhanced clearance of dysfunctional mitochondria via the upregulation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway, as well as p62-dependent lysophagy.  
– A corresponding reduction in mtROS, leading to decreased oxidative stress and lower inflammatory signaling.  
– Improvement in mitochondrial biogenesis and overall cellular energy homeostasis via activation of the AMPK/ULK1 pathway and upregulation of PGC-1α.  
– Ultimately, these molecular changes should culminate in improved RPE cell survival and a delay or reversal of atrophic processes that underpin dry AMD (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

5. Overall Evaluation  
In evaluating Urolithin A as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and potential areas for further investigation emerge. First and foremost, UA offers a robust safety profile supported by both preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials in elderly populations, where it has been administered at relatively high doses without observable toxicity or adverse events (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Liu, 2022). This favorable safety and pharmacokinetic profile is critical given the generally conservative approach required when developing treatments for chronic, age-related conditions like AMD.

The molecular versatility of UA is another significant strength. Its capacity to engage multiple autophagic pathways—specifically, the PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy and the SQSTM1/p62-dependent lysophagy—provides a multifaceted approach to mitigating RPE degeneration. Given that the pathogenesis of dry AMD involves a complex interplay of mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and inflammation, the ability of UA to target these processes simultaneously renders it a particularly attractive candidate (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). Furthermore, the activation of upstream signaling pathways such as AMPK/ULK1 not only enhances autophagic activity but also supports mitochondrial biogenesis, thereby ensuring that the clearance of damaged mitochondria does not result in an energy deficit within RPE cells (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Preclinical data from retinal degeneration models provide compelling evidence that UA can ameliorate pathological features reminiscent of dry AMD. In SI-induced models, UA treatment has resulted in restored autophagic flux, reduced RPE cell death, and preservation of visual function—all of which are promising indicators for its potential to slow or reverse the atrophic processes underlying geographic atrophy in AMD (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). Moreover, its ability to mitigate inflammatory signaling and reduce mtROS production adds another layer of protective activity that is critical in managing chronic retinal degeneration.

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and challenges warrant consideration. One area of potential ambiguity concerns the precise mechanistic contributions of the PINK1/Parkin pathway versus the SQSTM1/p62-mediated lysophagy in mediating UA’s protective effects. While some studies emphasize the role of PINK1/Parkin in clearance of damaged mitochondria, others have reported that UA’s neuroprotective benefits are maintained even with genetic manipulations of these proteins, suggesting that p62-dependent lysophagy may be the predominant mechanism in certain contexts (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Fehér et al., 2022). This duality raises questions regarding which pathway is most critical in RPE cells, particularly given that the proposed hypothesis centers on enhanced PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy. Further mechanistic studies in RPE-specific models will be necessary to delineate the relative contributions of these pathways and to optimize dosing and formulation strategies accordingly.

Another potential weakness is the translational gap between preclinical studies and clinical application in dry AMD. Although UA has shown promise in animal models of retinal degeneration, human disease is complex, and dry AMD is known for its multifactorial etiology. The pharmacokinetic properties of UA, including its relatively short half-life and the challenges associated with ensuring adequate ocular bioavailability, might necessitate novel delivery strategies for effective retinal targeting. Formulation development—potentially involving sustained-release systems or ocular-specific delivery vehicles—may be required to overcome these hurdles (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025). Additionally, while the evidence from non-ocular (e.g., muscle and neural) studies is robust, direct clinical evidence in AMD patients remains sparse, necessitating carefully designed human trials to confirm efficacy and safety in this specific population.

It is also important to contextualize UA’s potential within the current landscape of AMD treatments. While existing therapies for wet AMD (e.g., anti-VEGF agents) have transformed clinical outcomes, there remains no established treatment for dry AMD. The multifaceted mode of action of UA—targeting mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and inflammation—offers a unique therapeutic approach that could complement or, in some cases, provide an alternative to emerging interventions. However, comparative studies against other experimental agents will be critical to fully establish its translational relevance and competitive advantage in the therapeutic space (Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Overall, Urolithin A presents several compelling attributes that support its development as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its origin as a naturally derived, gut-microbiota transformation product provides a favorable starting point from a safety perspective. Preclinical studies consistently demonstrate its ability to enhance autophagic clearance mechanisms, reduce oxidative damage, and improve cell survival in models that recapitulate key features of AMD. The ability of UA to simultaneously stimulate both mitophagy and lysophagy—the former via the PINK1/Parkin pathway and the latter via p62-dependent mechanisms—positions it as a multi-targeted intervention capable of addressing the multifactorial pathology of RPE degeneration (Jiménez-Loygorri & Boya, 2024; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

Nonetheless, for the successful translation of UA into a clinically effective therapy for dry AMD, several challenges need to be addressed. Detailed mechanistic insights specifically in RPE cells are required to understand the relative importance of the PINK1/Parkin versus the lysophagy pathway. Optimizing drug delivery to ensure sustained retinal bioavailability and addressing potential issues related to its pharmacokinetic profile are also key areas that will require further research. Finally, controlled clinical studies in AMD patients will be essential to validate the promising preclinical findings and to ensure that the observed benefits in animal models translate into meaningful clinical outcomes.

In conclusion, based on the comprehensive literature reviewed from biochemical, clinical, and biomedical sources, Urolithin A demonstrates significant potential as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its established ability to enhance mitochondrial quality control through both mitophagy and lysophagy, alongside its additional anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, offers a novel mechanism to counteract the progressive degeneration observed in RPE cells during AMD. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SRT2104 is a second‐generation synthetic small molecule activator of SIRT1 that emerged from a rigorous high‐throughput screening program at Sirtris Pharmaceuticals and was further developed following GlaxoSmithKline’s acquisition of the compound’s intellectual property (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 1–2). The molecule was rationally designed by modifying an imidazo[1,2‐b]thiazole core structure, a strategy intended to overcome the limitations associated with earlier SIRT1 activators such as resveratrol, notably its poor bioavailability and off‐target effects (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; 14–16). As a member of the class of SIRT1 activators, SRT2104 is distinguished by its high specificity and potency, thereby enabling a more targeted modulation of NAD⁺‐dependent deacetylation pathways compared to naturally occurring polyphenols (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16). This class of compounds has been broadly investigated in the context of metabolic, inflammatory, and neurodegenerative disorders due to its capacity to enhance mitochondrial function, reduce oxidative stress, and modulate inflammatory cytokines (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; 10–11). Although its initial therapeutic intent was not directed toward ophthalmological conditions, mechanistic insights into SIRT1’s regulatory functions in cellular metabolism and stress responses have prompted interest in repurposing SRT2104 for conditions such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells play central roles (Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4; Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2).

Therapeutic History:  
Extensive preclinical and early‐phase clinical studies have established a strong safety and tolerability profile for SRT2104, particularly in elderly populations and subjects with type 2 diabetes (Libri et al., 2012, pp. 1–2; Baksi et al., 2014, pp. 7–11). In a pilot randomized, placebo‐controlled trial, SRT2104 was administered to healthy elderly volunteers, demonstrating that the compound was generally well tolerated, with an average peak serum concentration reached within 2 to 4 hours and an elimination half‐life between 15 and 20 hours (Libri et al., 2012, pp. 1–2). Furthermore, studies involving participants on metformin therapy for type 2 diabetes confirmed that SRT2104 exhibits a favorable safety profile, noting stable pharmacokinetics and no serious adverse events over an extended dosing period (Baksi et al., 2014, pp. 7–11). Beyond safety, several clinical studies have reported beneficial effects on metabolic biomarkers: SRT2104 administration was associated with significant reductions in serum cholesterol, low‐density lipoprotein (LDL), and triglyceride levels, suggesting improvements in systemic metabolic health (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 1–2). Additional clinical investigations indicated that adverse reactions—when they occurred—were generally mild and self‐limiting, including transient headaches, dizziness, and mild upper respiratory indications, which further supports its clinical tolerability (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 13–14; 2–4).  
SRT2104 has also been evaluated in the context of neurodegenerative processes; preclinical models demonstrated its ability to cross the blood‐brain barrier and exert neuroprotective effects, for example, in Huntington’s disease models where improvements in survival and motor function were observed along with reduced cerebral atrophy (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 6–7; 7–8). Although none of these studies were primarily focused on dry AMD or similar ocular pathologies, the therapeutic rationale for exploring SRT2104 in AMD is supported by the shared pathophysiological features observed in neurodegenerative disorders and retinal diseases, particularly those aspects involving mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2). It is important to note that while there is substantial clinical evidence for metabolic and neuroprotective effects, no direct clinical trials have yet been conducted in patients with dry AMD, making a translational validation in the specific context of retinal diseases an essential next step (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 14–16).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SRT2104 acts predominantly by binding to and activating SIRT1, a NAD⁺‐dependent histone deacetylase that plays a pivotal role in regulating transcription, cellular metabolism, and stress responses (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16). SIRT1 deacetylates a variety of substrates, including transcription factors such as peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator 1‐alpha (PGC-1α) and factors involved in inflammation such as the NF-κB complex. The deacetylation of PGC-1α is particularly significant because it leads to its activation, thereby enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis and promoting oxidative metabolism (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16). As a consequence, activation of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis results in increased expression of genes involved in antioxidant defense, thus improving cellular resilience to oxidative stress—a key pathological driver in dry AMD (Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4; Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2).  
Moreover, SIRT1 has been shown to deacetylate and modulate the activity of hypoxia‐inducible factor 2α (HIF-2α), which in turn regulates the vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A) promoter (Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4). Given that VEGF-A plays a complex role in retinal homeostasis and neovascular processes, this interaction suggests that SIRT1 activation could fine‐tune vascular responses within the retina. In addition to these effects, SRT2104 has been associated with decreases in pro‐inflammatory cytokine levels including IL-6 and IL-8, thereby potentially mitigating chronic inflammation that contributes to RPE dysfunction and geographic atrophy in AMD (Law et al., 2024, pp. 10–12; Chang et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).  
It is also noteworthy that SIRT1 is endogenously expressed in human RPE cells and the retina, where it contributes to the maintenance of cellular homeostasis in response to oxidative insults (Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4). In several disease models, suppressed SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling has been linked to mitochondrial disintegration and increased susceptibility to oxidative damage in RPE cells, supporting the therapeutic hypothesis that pharmacologically enhancing SIRT1 activity can restore mitochondrial function and counteract degenerative changes (Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2; 11–13). In summary, the molecular actions of SRT2104 encompass the dual benefits of enhancing mitochondrial respiration via PGC-1α activation and reducing inflammatory mediator production through deacetylation of relevant transcription factors, which together may yield protective effects in the context of dry AMD (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 14–16; 7–8).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underlying the proposed repurposing of SRT2104 for dry AMD is that oral administration of this compound will enhance SIRT1 activity in RPE cells, thereby activating downstream signaling pathways critical to cellular homeostasis (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16). Specifically, increased SIRT1 activity is anticipated to lead to upregulation of PGC-1α, a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis, as well as NRF2, a central transcription factor in the antioxidant defense pathway (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16). As PGC-1α activation drives the transcription of genes involved in mitochondrial metabolism and energy production, its upregulation is expected to ameliorate mitochondrial dysfunction—a hallmark feature in the pathogenesis of geographic atrophy within dry AMD (Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4; Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2).  
Furthermore, NRF2 activation is associated with enhanced transcription of a battery of antioxidant enzymes, which can reduce the burden of reactive oxygen species (ROS) that damage RPE cells over time (Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2; 11–13). These biochemical changes are hypothesized to restore the redox balance within RPE cells, thereby slowing or potentially reversing the progression of retinal degeneration observed in dry AMD. In experimental models of metabolic stress, SRT2104 has been shown to improve mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and cellular viability; by extension, similar molecular benefits are anticipated in the RPE, where oxidative damage and mitochondrial dysfunction play crucial roles in disease progression (Libri et al., 2012, pp. 1–2; Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).  
Additionally, given SIRT1’s regulatory role in suppressing pro‐inflammatory gene expression via NF-κB deacetylation, it is expected that SRT2104 will confer anti‐inflammatory effects within the retinal microenvironment, further contributing to the preservation of RPE function (Law et al., 2024, pp. 10–12; Maugeri et al., 2018, pp. 5–7). Although these effects have been robustly documented in systemic tissues such as skeletal muscle and in neuronal models, confirmation in ocular tissues remains a critical area for future preclinical investigation (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 14–16; 6–7). The convergence of improved mitochondrial dynamics, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and reduced inflammatory activity forms the foundational rationale for expecting that SRT2104 can stabilize or restore RPE function, thereby mitigating the development and progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2).

Overall Evaluation:  
SRT2104 presents a compelling candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD given its well‐established safety profile, its potent and selective activation of SIRT1, and the strong mechanistic rationale connecting SIRT1‐mediated pathways to the pathological processes underlying retinal degeneration (Libri et al., 2012, pp. 1–2; Baksi et al., 2014, pp. 7–11; Chang et al., 2024, pp. 13–14). These studies have consistently shown that SRT2104 can be administered with minimal adverse effects, and its pharmacokinetic profile (with rapid absorption and a reasonable half‐life) supports its potential for chronic dosing—an important consideration in the management of a progressive condition like dry AMD (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; 2–4).  
Another significant strength lies in the drug’s mechanism of action: by directly activating SIRT1, SRT2104 engages a fundamental regulator of cellular metabolism that is known to control mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses through the deacetylation of PGC-1α and subsequent NRF2‐mediated gene transcription (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16). Given that mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central drivers of RPE cell degeneration, this targeted mechanism offers a rational therapeutic approach to address the pathophysiological underpinnings of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4; Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2). Preclinical studies in neurodegenerative models further bolster confidence in the neuroprotective aspects of SRT2104, suggesting that similar protective effects might be translated to the retinal environment (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 6–7; 7–8).  
Despite these strengths, several challenges and weaknesses warrant careful consideration. Foremost, there is currently an absence of direct preclinical or clinical data evaluating the efficacy of SRT2104 in ocular models of dry AMD. While the shared molecular pathways between skeletal muscle, neuronal tissue, and RPE cells provide a strong theoretical basis for its repurposing, it remains to be demonstrated experimentally that SRT2104 can adequately penetrate the ocular tissues—in particular, the retina—and reach effective concentrations in the RPE (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 14–16; Hammer et al., 2021, pp. 9–11). The blood‐retina barrier poses unique pharmacokinetic challenges that may not be addressed by data derived solely from systemic administration in non‐ocular tissues.  
Another concern is the translational gap between improvements in biochemical markers and tangible clinical outcomes. For example, while clinical trials in systemic conditions have shown reductions in LDL cholesterol, arterial stiffness, and improvements in mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, similar functional endpoints related to retinal health such as visual acuity or structural preservation of the RPE have not been measured (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 1–2; 9–10). This gap underscores the necessity for rigorously designed preclinical models using human RPE cells and animal models of geographic atrophy to ascertain whether the SIRT1 activation by SRT2104 indeed translates into meaningful protection against retinal degeneration (Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2; 2–3).  
There is also the issue of potential off‐target effects or insufficient modulation of the complex interplay between oxidative stress, inflammation, and cellular senescence observed in dry AMD. Although SRT2104’s target specificity is a marked improvement over earlier SIRT1 activators, the multifactorial nature of AMD pathology—including contributions from inflammatory cytokine cascades and abnormal autophagic processes—may require combination therapies or adjunctive strategies beyond SIRT1 activation alone (Maugeri et al., 2018, pp. 5–7).  
Furthermore, some clinical studies have suggested that despite positive modulation of certain biomarkers, SRT2104 may not significantly improve key functional endpoints such as vascular reactivity or insulin sensitivity, suggesting that its efficacy might be context‐dependent or limited to particular physiological systems (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 1–2). Although these findings do not directly detract from its potential in AMD, they do highlight the inherent risk in extrapolating systemic benefits to the specialized microenvironment of the retina.  
In summary, while SRT2104 exhibits a strong safety record and a mechanistically robust profile through its activation of SIRT1 and downstream enhancement of mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant capacity, its repurposing as a treatment for dry AMD remains a hypothesis that requires extensive further validation. Key areas for future research include detailed pharmacokinetic studies to ensure adequate ocular tissue penetration, validation of its effects on RPE cell survival and function in both in vitro and in vivo models of geographic atrophy, and ultimately, early‐phase clinical trials designed specifically to evaluate retinal outcomes (Golestaneh et al., 2016, pp. 1–2; Chang et al., 2024, pp. 14–16). By addressing these gaps, it will be possible to determine whether the encouraging data from metabolic and neurodegenerative indications can indeed be translated into a viable therapeutic strategy for patients with dry AMD.  
In conclusion, SRT2104 is a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate given its ability to activate SIRT1—a key mediator of mitochondrial and antioxidant pathways—in a manner that holds potential to restore RPE function and counteract the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Chang et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; 14–16; Balaiya et al., 2017, pp. 3–4). Its clinical safety profile and documented efficacy in modulating systemic metabolic and inflammatory markers provide a favorable foundation for further investigation. However, its application in the ocular arena must overcome several translational barriers, including establishing effective ocular bioavailability and demonstrating specific efficacy in retinal cell models. These challenges underscore the need for targeted preclinical and clinical research to confirm whether SRT2104 can fulfill its therapeutic promise in the context of dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Metformin is a well‐known therapeutic agent belonging to the biguanide class, originally derived from guanidine compounds found in the plant Galega officinalis. The molecule is a synthetic derivative of naturally occurring galegine and has been refined into a modern oral antihyperglycemic agent (Augustin & Atorf, 2023). This class of compounds has historically been used as a first-line oral treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus, with metformin being one of the most prescribed drugs worldwide for managing hyperglycemia. Its synthesis did not follow the classical target‐driven design path but instead emerged from an adaptation of naturally occurring structures into a chemically optimized, orally bioavailable, and generally well-tolerated drug (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Dang et al., 2021). Given its long clinical history starting from the 1950s and subsequent FDA approval in the 1990s, metformin has accumulated a significant amount of safety data and clinical experience, which collectively make it an attractive candidate for repurposing into other disease areas, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) characterized by geographic atrophy (Amin et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, metformin has been used extensively as an antidiabetic agent to lower hepatic glucose output and improve peripheral insulin sensitivity. Its beneficial pleiotropic effects beyond glycemic control have been recognized over the years; these include anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antiangiogenic properties, which have been observed in both biochemical and clinical investigations. Multiple epidemiologic studies have examined the association between metformin use and ocular outcomes. Retrospective analyses in predominantly diabetic cohorts have indicated that metformin use correlates with reduced odds or hazard for developing age-related macular degeneration and other retinal diseases, although some studies report mixed results depending on cumulative dose, exposure timing, and concomitant diabetes-related complications (Moir et al., 2023; Amin et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2022). Notably, while metformin has not historically been approved for any ocular indication, several preclinical studies using retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cell models have demonstrated that metformin may protect against oxidative damage and improve mitochondrial function. Moreover, a Phase II single-blind randomized trial was initiated to assess the efficacy of metformin in slowing the progression of geographic atrophy among non-diabetic patients with advanced dry AMD (Shen et al., 2024), suggesting that the concept of repurposing metformin for dry AMD is already under active clinical investigation.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, metformin’s primary mechanism of action involves the inhibition of mitochondrial complex I of the electron transport chain, resulting in a decrease in ATP production and a concomitant increase in the intracellular AMP:ATP ratio. This metabolic shift leads to the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a master regulator of cellular energy homeostasis that orchestrates shifts in metabolism under conditions of energy deficit (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). AMPK activation exerts multiple downstream effects that are particularly relevant to RPE cell function and the pathogenesis of geographic atrophy. First, AMPK activation promotes autophagy, including mitophagy, a quality-control mechanism that ensures the removal of dysfunctional mitochondria. Preclinical studies in RPE cell models, such as those using ARPE-19 cells, have provided evidence that metformin increases autophagosome formation, reduces intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS), lowers apoptosis rates, and helps maintain the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) under oxidative stress conditions (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Toppila et al., 2024). Additionally, the activation of AMPK in RPE cells has been associated with upregulation of protective pathways including enhanced nitric oxide (NO) production and increased expression of mitochondrial biogenesis factors such as PGC-1α, which together contribute to improved mitochondrial quality control (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023).  

Furthermore, metformin is known to activate both AMPK-dependent and AMPK-independent signaling pathways. The AMPK-independent effects may include inhibition of NF-κB activation, leading to a reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α, which are implicated in chronic inflammation observed in the aging retina (Jiang et al., 2022; Amin et al., 2022). From a biochemical standpoint, the inhibition of complex I by metformin also directly reduces the leakage of electrons that can form ROS, thereby lowering mitochondrial oxidative stress—a key aspect in the progression of dry AMD pathogenesis (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). It is important to note, however, that several reports have highlighted the concern that activation of AMPK in vivo or in vitro appears to require suprapharmacological doses of metformin, casting uncertainty on whether standard clinical dosing is sufficient to achieve these retinal effects (Moir et al., 2023). Nonetheless, the preclinical evidence supports a model whereby metformin’s inhibition of mitochondrial complex I—thereby reducing ROS and enhancing autophagy—provides a rationale for its potential use in protecting RPE cells from oxidative stress-induced damage (Amin et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis driving the repurposing of metformin for dry AMD is predicated on its ability to activate AMPK and inhibit mitochondrial complex I leakage in RPE cells, leading to reduced ROS production and enhanced mitochondrial quality control. In the context of geographic atrophy, RPE dysfunction and death play a central role in the degeneration of photoreceptors and the progression of AMD. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that metformin can protect ARPE-19 cells (an established human RPE cell line) from oxidative insults by lowering intracellular ROS levels, augmenting autophagic processes, and preserving mitochondrial membrane potential (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Toppila et al., 2024). Additionally, through the activation of AMPK, metformin is expected to stimulate the expression of mitochondrial biogenesis factors, leading to improved mitochondrial function, which is critical given the high metabolic demands of the RPE (Moir et al., 2023). 

Epidemiologically, several retrospective cohort and case-control studies have observed associations between metformin use and a reduced risk of developing AMD. Some studies even suggest that these associations are dose- and timing-dependent, with earlier or sustained use of metformin correlating with greater protective effects (Moir et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022). Therefore, in an assay designed to measure the effects of metformin on mitochondrial function and oxidative stress in RPE cells, one would expect to see an enhancement in autophagic flux, decreased markers of oxidative stress, and preservation or restoration of Δψm. These cellular effects would ideally translate into a slower progression of geographic atrophy in vivo, as suggested by the decreased degeneration of the retinal layers that has been observed in certain mouse models of retinal damage (Jiang et al., 2022; Amin et al., 2022). RPE cells are known to express AMPK and other components of the autophagy machinery, which further supports the rationale for targeting these pathways in the treatment of dry AMD (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Moir et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
Metformin shows considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly for geographic atrophy, due to several key strengths. First, its long and well-documented clinical history in the management of type 2 diabetes provides a robust safety profile and widespread clinical familiarity, which is a significant advantage when considering repurposing strategies (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Dang et al., 2021; Amin et al., 2022). Second, the molecular and cellular mechanisms by which metformin acts—namely, the inhibition of mitochondrial complex I, subsequent activation of AMPK, and promotion of autophagy—are highly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. The ability of metformin to reduce ROS and promote mitochondrial quality control addresses one of the core aspects of RPE dysfunction and degeneration seen in geographic atrophy (Moir et al., 2023; Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Jiang et al., 2022).

Furthermore, the epidemiologic data showing associations between metformin use and a reduced incidence of AMD lend additional support to its potential utility in this setting (Liang et al., 2022; Moir et al., 2023). The possibility that metformin’s protective effects might be independent of its glycemic control properties is particularly intriguing, as it expands the target population to non-diabetic AMD patients—a group that represents the majority of those affected by geographic atrophy (Moir et al., 2023; Brown et al., 2019; Moir et al., 2024). On a mechanistic level, the detailed understanding of metformin’s interaction with AMPK and mitochondrial pathways not only provides a clear therapeutic target but also offers multiple biomarkers for assessing efficacy in both preclinical and clinical studies.

Despite its strengths, several weaknesses and challenges must be acknowledged. One significant concern is whether standard clinical doses of metformin are sufficient to activate the AMPK pathway in retinal tissues, given that some in vitro studies indicate suprapharmacological doses are required to see a robust effect (Moir et al., 2023). This raises questions of retinal bioavailability and whether alternative delivery strategies, such as local ocular administration or formulation enhancements, might be required to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE. Additionally, while the epidemiologic studies are promising, they are not uniformly consistent; some retrospective analyses have reported no association or even conflicting results depending on dosing and timing parameters (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Brown et al., 2019; Amin et al., 2022). These discrepancies underscore the inherent limitations of observational data, including potential confounding factors such as the presence and severity of diabetes, concomitant medications, and the challenges of accurately classifying AMD subtypes using administrative coding.

Another consideration is that although metformin’s broad mechanism of action (i.e., modulation of inflammation, oxidative stress, and autophagy) is advantageous in addressing multifactorial diseases like AMD, it may also lead to off-target effects or systemic side effects such as vitamin B12 deficiency or, in rare instances, lactic acidosis (Jiang et al., 2022; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). In elderly populations—who are generally most affected by dry AMD—these risks must be carefully weighed against the potential benefits. Moreover, the heterogeneity in study designs and patient populations in the available epidemiologic literature means that prospective, well-designed clinical trials remain essential to definitively determine whether metformin can meaningfully slow the progression of geographic atrophy in AMD (Shen et al., 2024).

In summary, the overall evaluation of metformin as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. Its well-established safety profile, combined with mechanistic data that align closely with the underlying pathology of geographic atrophy, make it a compelling candidate. Below is a comprehensive evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO‐Me) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), structured in sections that address its origins, therapeutic history, known mechanisms of action, expected effects in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and an overall assessment of its strengths and challenges.

• Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Bardoxolone methyl is a semisynthetic derivative belonging to the synthetic oleanane triterpenoid class. Its origin stems from oleanolic acid—a naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid abundantly found in various medicinal plants. Early medicinal chemistry programs sought to overcome the modest anti‐inflammatory activity and poor bioavailability of oleanolic acid by introducing targeted modifications. Through chemical derivatization, these programs generated CDDO (2‐cyano‐3,12‐dioxooleana‐1,9‐dien‐28‐oic acid) and subsequently its C‐28 methyl ester, known as Bardoxolone methyl (CDDO‐Me) (Borella et al., 2019). The synthetic process involves the installation of electrophilic Michael acceptor groups at strategic positions on the oleanane scaffold, such as the addition of an α,β‐unsaturated carbonyl in the A‐ring and further incorporation of a cyano group that substantially increases the compound’s potency relative to its natural precursor (Wong et al., 2016; Zhang & Chapman, 2020). These chemical modifications not only enhance the anti‐inflammatory and anticancer properties but also improve chemical stability and oral bioavailability. The structural design, which incorporates a reversible electrophilic reactivity, underpins the compound’s ability to engage diverse cellular targets (Thomas, 2012; Zhou et al., 2014). Bardoxolone methyl thus represents a chemically advanced, highly potent agent from a class of molecules originally designed to trigger cytoprotective responses via direct electrophilic modulation.

• Therapeutic History  
Bardoxolone methyl has undergone extensive preclinical and early clinical evaluation primarily in fields as disparate as oncology and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Initial studies established that synthetic oleanane triterpenoids, including CDDO and its variants, exert dramatic anti‐inflammatory effects by suppressing inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and cyclooxygenase (COX‐2) expression in activated macrophages (Gatbonton‐Schwager, 2014). Preclinical studies in multiple mouse cancer models and inflammatory conditions confirmed its potent anticancer activity and cytoprotective properties, which catalyzed its progression into human clinical trials (Borella et al., 2019; Nakagami, 2016).  
In the clinical arena, Bardoxolone methyl was advanced through Phase I cancer trials, where its once‐daily oral dosing regimen and pharmacokinetic profile—with a terminal half‐life of approximately 39 hours—were characterized (Thomas, 2012; Nakagami, 2016). More notably, its unexpected ability to improve estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in patients with advanced renal disease, particularly in diabetic nephropathy, led to its evaluation in large Phase II and Phase III trials, such as the BEAM and BEACON studies (Yagishita et al., 2020; Tanase et al., 2022). However, the BEACON trial was terminated prematurely due to an increased incidence of cardiovascular events, including heart failure, highlighting concerns about the compound’s systemic safety profile when used at higher doses or in populations with comorbidities (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012).  
Despite its promising preclinical pharmacology and the breadth of clinical data available in non‐ocular indications, to date there is no direct record in the literature of Bardoxolone methyl being used specifically for the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular degenerative conditions (Schiavoni et al., 2025). Nonetheless, the overall safety and pharmacokinetic properties observed in CKD and oncology trials lend valuable insights for considering drug repurposing across therapeutic areas.

• Mechanism of Action  
Bardoxolone methyl is best known for its ability to activate the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway—a master regulator of cellular defense mechanisms against oxidative and electrophilic stress. Under basal conditions, Nrf2 is tightly regulated by Kelch‐like ECH‐associated protein 1 (Keap1), which serves as an adaptor for ubiquitin ligases targeting Nrf2 for proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl functions as a potent electrophile and interacts with sulfhydryl groups on critical cysteine residues within Keap1. This covalent or reversible Michael addition reaction disrupts the Keap1–Nrf2 complex, thereby stabilizing and allowing Nrf2 to translocate into the nucleus (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).  
Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to the antioxidant response element (ARE) in the promoter regions of a host of cytoprotective genes. This transcriptional activation results in the upregulation of a battery of antioxidant and phase II detoxifying enzymes, including but not limited to heme oxygenase‐1 (HO‐1), NAD(P)H dehydrogenase (quinone 1; NQO1), various glutathione transferases, and glutamate–cysteine ligase subunits (Thomas, 2012; Wong et al., 2016). Studies in non‐ocular tissues have shown that at very low (nanomolar) doses, Bardoxolone methyl robustly engages this cytoprotective program while also exerting dose‐dependent biology wherein intermediate and high doses trigger effects such as modulation of cell differentiation and direct anticancer activity, respectively (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).  
It is important to note that while the canonical targets of Nrf2 activation are well characterized, Bardoxolone methyl’s electrophilic character enables it to interact with multiple regulatory proteins. For example, it can inhibit IκB kinase β (IKKβ), leading to suppression of nuclear factor κB (NF‐κB) signaling and subsequent reduction in proinflammatory cytokine production (Zhou et al., 2014; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although the literature does not provide direct experimental evidence that Bardoxolone methyl specifically upregulates mitochondrial antioxidants such as superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) and peroxiredoxin 3 (PRDX3) in RPE cells, the robust, broad‐spectrum transcriptional response induced by Nrf2 activation strongly suggests that mitochondrial and cytoplasmic components of the antioxidant defense system may also be upregulated (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015). Such upregulation would be consistent with previous findings of increased expression of antioxidant genes and improved cellular redox status upon treatment with similar synthetic triterpenoids (Schiavoni et al., 2025; Sporn et al., 2011).

• Expected Effect in Dry AMD  
The pathogenesis of dry age‐related macular degeneration is multifactorial, with chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction playing a central role in the degeneration of the RPE—a critical monolayer that supports photoreceptor health. RPE cells are particularly vulnerable to oxidative damage due to high metabolic activity, exposure to light, and the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). In this context, the proposed mechanism of Bardoxolone methyl, namely activation of the Nrf2/ARE pathway, provides a biologically tenable strategy for neuroprotection and cellular preservation.  
When administered at low doses, Bardoxolone methyl is expected to trigger a cytoprotective transcriptional program in RPE cells. Activation of Nrf2 should lead to the induction of a range of antioxidant enzymes and detoxifying proteins which together help re-establish redox balance in the face of chronic oxidative insult (Borella et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012). One key hypothesis is that, in addition to the already well‐documented induction of cytosolic antioxidants such as HO‐1 and NQO1, Bardoxolone methyl may also promote the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3. SOD2 is the primary defense against superoxide radicals within the mitochondria, and PRDX3 plays a critical role in detoxifying hydrogen peroxide produced by mitochondrial respiration. Although direct data in RPE cells are currently lacking, studies in other cellular contexts have demonstrated that activation of Nrf2 results in the upregulation of a broad spectrum of antioxidant genes, and it is plausible that under the oxidative duress typical of dry AMD, similar effects would be observed in RPE cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
In vitro models simulating oxidative stress—such as exposure of RPE cells to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)—have shown that compounds with similar electrophilic properties, and indeed other members of the CDDO family like CDDO-Im, reduce the intracellular MitoSOX fluorescence signal, indicative of a reduction in mitochondrial ROS (mtROS) (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024). Moreover, improvements in mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) have been correlated with such treatments, suggesting that these molecules can help maintain mitochondrial function under stressful conditions (Nakagami, 2016; Zhou et al., 2014). Such outcomes are highly relevant in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction in the RPE has been implicated in disease progression. The anticipated outcomes, therefore, include a reduction in mtROS, restoration of Δψm, and subsequent preservation of RPE cellular integrity and function.  
Another positive aspect is the compound’s previously established oral bioavailability and pharmacokinetic profile. Clinical studies in CKD patients have demonstrated that therapeutic plasma concentrations can be achieved with once-daily dosing. Although systemic administration in ocular diseases is not ideal, these data provide a strong pharmacological starting point for repurposing. In addition, if systemic toxicity remains a concern—as suggested by the cardiovascular signals in CKD trials—an alternative approach might involve localized ocular delivery (for instance, via intravitreal injection or by developing an ocular formulation) to achieve high retinal bioavailability while minimizing systemic exposure (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).

• Overall Evaluation  
In assessing Bardoxolone methyl for repurposing as a therapeutic for dry AMD, several critical points emerge that underline both its promise and the challenges that must be overcome.

Strengths:  
1. Strong Chemical Rationale and Potency:  
Bardoxolone methyl is a product of sophisticated medicinal chemistry, designed to overcome the limitations of natural triterpenoids like oleanolic acid by installing reactive electrophilic groups that significantly enhance its potency. This design specifically enables the activation of the Nrf2 pathway—a mechanism central to antioxidant defense—at very low concentrations (Borella et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016). The high potency of Bardoxolone methyl as an Nrf2 activator is a significant advantage, particularly when considering that even subtle improvements in cellular antioxidant capacity can have a profound impact on chronic degenerative diseases like dry AMD.

2. Broad Cytoprotective Mechanism:  
The mechanism of Bardoxolone methyl involves the disruption of the Keap1-Nrf2 complex via covalent modification of Keap1 cysteine residues, facilitating the nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and the subsequent transcriptional activation of a broad range of antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes (Zhou et al., 2014; Thomas, 2012). This broad cytoprotective response is particularly relevant to the RPE, where chronic oxidative stress has been implicated in cellular dysfunction and death. The possibility that Bardoxolone methyl may also induce mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3, although not yet directly confirmed in RPE, is an attractive hypothesis; such an effect would directly address the mitochondrial dysfunction that is a hallmark of dry AMD (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).

3. Extensive Clinical Experience and Pharmacokinetic Data:  
Bardoxolone methyl has been evaluated in several clinical trials—most notably in the context of CKD and oncology—yielding a wealth of pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and tolerability data. Its oral bioavailability, with a terminal half-life that supports once-daily dosing, is well documented (Thomas, 2012; Nakagami, 2016). Although the systemic adverse events observed in these trials (such as cardiovascular-related events) present challenges for broad systemic administration, these data nonetheless offer a useful starting point for repurposing. The established clinical profile can inform dose-escalation studies and safety monitoring protocols should Bardoxolone methyl be advanced into ocular trials.

4. Support from Analogous Preclinical Models:  
Several studies in related models have demonstrated that synthetic triterpenoids can protect retinal tissue from oxidative damage. For example, experiments with CDDO-Im, a closely related analogue, have shown protective effects in retinal ischemia–reperfusion injury, including the attenuation of inflammatory responses and preservation of retinal structure (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024). Although these studies are not directly with Bardoxolone methyl, the mechanistic commonalities within this compound class support the notion that the same protective pathways can be harnessed in the context of dry AMD.

Weaknesses and Challenges:  
1. Lack of Direct Evidence in RPE/Dry AMD Models:  
Despite the strong theoretical rationale, direct evidence that Bardoxolone methyl upregulates mitochondrial antioxidants (SOD2, PRDX3) in RPE cells is currently lacking. Most published data are derived from non-ocular cell types or from studies using other analogues such as CDDO-Im (Cai et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2014). It is therefore essential to perform specific in vitro studies in RPE cell lines under oxidative stress conditions to measure the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes and the functional status of mitochondria (e.g., Δψm, mtROS levels) following treatment with Bardoxolone methyl.

2. Safety Concerns from Prior Clinical Experience:  
A significant challenge in repurposing Bardoxolone methyl stems from its safety profile in systemic indications. The Phase III BEACON trial in CKD patients was halted due to an increased incidence of serious cardiovascular events, including heart failure and increased mortality (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although the mechanisms underlying these adverse effects may be related to systemic fluid retention, off‐target reactivity, or other metabolic perturbations, they raise concerns about the safety of systemic administration. For ocular application, it may be necessary to consider alternative dosing strategies or localized delivery methods to avoid systemic exposure while still achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina.

3. Translational and Formulation Challenges:  
The unique anatomy and physiology of the eye introduce additional obstacles in drug repurposing. RPE cells reside in a relatively immune-privileged, isolated microenvironment behind the blood–retinal barrier. The pharmacokinetics and tissue penetration profiles of Bardoxolone methyl observed in systemic circulation may not directly translate to effective intraocular concentrations. Development of specialized ocular formulations—such as sustained-release intravitreal injections or topical applications that can traverse ocular barriers—will be critical for successful translation (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).

4. Multifactorial Nature of AMD Pathogenesis:  
Dry AMD is a complex, multifactorial disease where oxidative stress is only one component of a broader pathogenic network that includes genetic predisposition, inflammation, lipid dysregulation, and complement system activation. While activation of the Nrf2 pathway can counteract oxidative stress and may have secondary anti-inflammatory effects, it is uncertain whether this single mechanism will be sufficient to alter the course of the disease. A combinatorial therapeutic strategy incorporating Nrf2 activation with other modalities might eventually be required to address the full spectrum of dry AMD pathology (Cheng et al., 2021; Thomas, 2012).

5. Dose-Dependent Effects and Narrow Therapeutic Window:  
Bardoxolone methyl exhibits highly dose-dependent pharmacology. At low doses, it predominantly activates Nrf2 and induces cytoprotective genes; however, as the dose increases, additional actions such as pro-apoptotic and cytotoxic effects emerge (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014). Determining the precise dose that is efficacious in RPE cells without triggering deleterious off-target effects will be crucial. This necessitates rigorous dose-ranging studies in preclinical models to define a therapeutic window that maximizes retinal protection while minimizing risks.

• Overall Evaluation and Recommendation  
In summary, Bardoxolone methyl presents a compelling candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD thanks to its well-characterized chemical design, potent induction of the Nrf2 pathway, and a broad cytoprotective mechanism that addresses many aspects of the oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction implicated in RPE degeneration. The extensive clinical data from studies in CKD and oncology provide a valuable foundation for understanding its pharmacokinetics and systemic effects, while the underlying chemistry ensures high potency at low concentrations—features that are highly desirable when targeting a chronic, degenerative condition such as dry AMD (Borella et al., 2019; Thomas, 2012).  
Nonetheless, significant challenges remain. There is a conspicuous gap in the literature regarding the direct evaluation of Bardoxolone methyl in RPE cells and dry AMD models, particularly concerning its ability to upregulate mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes like SOD2 and PRDX3 and thereby mitigate mtROS damage. This gap must be addressed through targeted in vitro assays and in vivo animal studies that simulate the retinal environment and its chronic oxidative stress. Safety concerns, as evidenced by the cardiovascular events observed in CKD trials, underscore the need for caution; these risks may be minimized through localized ocular administration, but careful formulation and dosing studies will be required to establish an acceptable safety profile in the ocular context (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019).  
Given the current state of evidence, it is recommended that Bardoxolone methyl be subjected to further preclinical evaluation in the context of dry AMD. Specifically, studies should focus on:  
 – Conducting detailed in vitro experiments in human RPE cell lines to assess whether exposure to Bardoxolone methyl under oxidative stress conditions leads to the upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants (e.g., SOD2 and PRDX3) and an associated decrease in mtROS (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
 – Evaluating the effects of Bardoxolone methyl on mitochondrial function (including measurements of Δψm, oxygen consumption rate, and mitochondrial integrity) in these cells.  
 – Adapting ocular-specific formulations that allow high local retinal concentrations with minimal systemic exposure, potentially using intravitreal or topical delivery methods, and conducting pharmacokinetic studies that establish retinal tissue exposure (Nakagami, 2016; Thomas, 2012).  
 – Testing the compound in animal models of dry AMD to determine whether the in vitro antioxidant and mitochondrial protective effects translate into preservation of RPE and photoreceptor structure and function over time (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024).  
If these studies yield positive results that confirm the hypothesized upregulation of mitochondrial antioxidants and improved RPE function, Bardoxolone methyl could then be advanced to early-phase clinical trials in patients with dry AMD. Such trials would need to incorporate rigorous safety monitoring protocols to mitigate the known systemic adverse effects. A potential strategy may involve administering the drug in a localized manner or at doses that are effective in the eye but low enough to avoid triggering systemic electrophilic toxicity.

Overall, Bardoxolone methyl holds promise as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD based on its potent Nrf2-activating properties and the central role of oxidative stress in the disease’s pathogenesis. However, its development for an ocular indication will hinge on its ability to selectively and safely modulate the redox status of RPE cells while avoiding systemic side effects. A stepwise, targeted preclinical program that directly addresses these RPE-specific endpoints is therefore critical before consideration of clinical trials in the dry AMD patient population (Nakagami, 2016).

In conclusion, while Bardoxolone methyl offers a strong mechanistic rationale as an Nrf2 activator with the theoretical capacity to upregulate mitochondrial defenses in RPE cells, further targeted studies are essential. The compound’s repurposing for dry AMD is scientifically attractive given the unmet need for effective therapies in this condition; however, the translational path is complex due to safety concerns observed in systemic trials and the lack of direct ocular data. A rigorous preclinical research plan—encompassing in vitro RPE studies, ocular pharmacokinetic assessments, and animal model validation—will be required to determine whether Bardoxolone methyl can be safely and effectively repurposed to preserve RPE function and slow the progression of dry AMD.

• Summary of Key Supporting Points  
– Bardoxolone methyl is a chemically engineered derivative of oleanolic acid that exploits electrophilic modifications to robustly activate the Nrf2 pathway (Borella et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016).  
– Its extensive preclinical and clinical history in oncology and CKD, though not in ocular disease, provides important pharmacokinetic and biological safety data that may be leveraged, with modifications, for ocular use (Nakagami, 2016; Tanase et al., 2022).  
– Its mechanism—covalent modification of Keap1 and subsequent nuclear translocation of Nrf2—leads to the transcriptional upregulation of cytoprotective genes, and it is hypothesized that this would include mitochondrial antioxidants (e.g., SOD2, PRDX3), which are critical for mitigating oxidative damage in RPE cells (Zhou et al., 2014; Nakagami et al., 2015).  
– Preclinical data with related triterpenoids in retinal models support the concept that Nrf2 activation can ameliorate oxidative stress and preserve retinal integrity, although direct data for Bardoxolone methyl in dry AMD are presently lacking (Cheng et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2024).  
– Key challenges include the translation of systemic dosing to ocular delivery, the need to specifically validate mitochondrial protective effects in RPE cells, and the resolution of safety issues exemplified by prior cardiovascular signals in systemic trials (Tanase et al., 2022; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

• Final Recommendation  
Based on the current literature review, Bardoxolone methyl emerges as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its potent Nrf2 activation, broad cytoprotective potential, and a well-documented clinical PK profile. However, its repurposing for ocular application must be preceded by targeted preclinical studies that corroborate its ability to upregulate mitochondrial antioxidants in RPE cells and to reduce mtROS while preserving mitochondrial function. These studies should also explore ocular-specific formulations and dosing regimens that minimize systemic exposure. Only after thorough validation in these preliminary investigations can Bardoxolone methyl be considered a credible candidate for clinical trials in dry AMD patients. Given these considerations, the candidate warrants further investigation despite the existing translational and safety challenges inherent in repurposing a systemically active electrophilic compound for an ocular indication (Borella et al., 2019; Yagishita et al., 2020; Thomas, 2012).
