Below is a comprehensive evaluation of EPI-743 (vatiquinone) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). This report is organized into five sections: an Overview of the Therapeutic Candidate, a review of its Therapeutic History, a detailed discussion of its Mechanism of Action, an outline of the Expected Effects in the dry AMD context, and an Overall Evaluation of its strengths and limitations.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

EPI-743, commonly referred to as vatiquinone, is a synthetic, short-chain quinone derivative that was designed based on biochemical modifications of naturally occurring vitamin E compounds. Its origin can be traced to the oxidation products of tocopherols and tocotrienols—members of the vitamin E family—which, through oxidative metabolism, yield quinone species. Specifically, EPI-743 is produced when these compounds are oxidized (Cores et al., 2023). Chemically, it belongs to the para-benzoquinone class, a subclass of quinones that are characterized by their fully conjugated cyclic unsaturated dione structure and their capacity for reversible redox cycling. Its design intentionally mirrors that of endogenous mitochondrial mediators such as ubiquinone (CoQ10), but significant modifications have been made to enhance aqueous solubility as well as to confer an extraordinary potency; indeed, experimental evidence indicates that on a molar basis, EPI-743 can be 10³ to 10⁴ times more potent than CoQ10 or even idebenone, another short-chain quinone analogue (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Gueven et al., 2017).

The discovery of EPI-743 originated from a small-molecule screening effort in which candidate compounds were evaluated for their ability to rescue cell viability under conditions of oxidative stress and glutathione depletion. This high-throughput screening methodology identified EPI-743 as a promising redox modulator with strong protective activity, leading to its subsequent advancement into preclinical testing and clinical evaluation by companies such as Edison Pharmaceuticals and PTC Therapeutics (Cores et al., 2023). As a representative member of the quinone drug class, EPI-743 is mechanistically designed to act as an electron shuttle, undergoing a reversible two-electron reduction to its corresponding hydroquinone form—a transformation that lies at the heart of its antioxidant activity and distinguishes it from many classical antioxidants. Because quinones in general have been used both as pharmaceutical antioxidants and as electron carriers in mitochondrial function, the chemical heritage of EPI-743 provides a strong rationale for its use in conditions characterized by redox imbalances (Tinker et al., 2021; Hong et al., 2023).

In summary, the chemical origin of EPI-743 is synthetic, being inspired by vitamin E’s tocotrienol derivatives and subsequently optimized to form a para-benzoquinone structure. Its classification among short-chain quinones places it in a well-studied category of compounds that have been used to modulate cellular redox states in various settings, particularly in diseases associated with mitochondrial dysfunction (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Gueven et al., 2017).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

The therapeutic use history of EPI-743 is predominantly rooted in the context of mitochondrial diseases and other disorders associated with oxidative stress. Preclinically, it has been shown to protect various cell types against oxidative insult in vitro, particularly in experimental models where glutathione levels are artificially depleted. Studies have demonstrated that EPI-743 significantly enhances cell viability under conditions that would otherwise trigger cell death mechanisms such as ferroptosis and apoptosis (Gueven et al., 2017; Cores et al., 2023). Furthermore, the compound has been extensively studied in animal models of mitochondrial dysfunction with evidence suggesting that it supports key mitochondrial functions including electron transport and ATP synthesis.

Clinically, EPI-743 has been investigated in several rare inherited mitochondrial disorders. For instance, initial clinical studies in pediatric patients with Leigh syndrome—a severe neurodegenerative disorder characterized by mitochondrial respiratory chain dysfunction—have yielded promising results. In these studies, treatment with EPI-743 correlated with stabilization or even improvement in disease progression markers and had observable beneficial effects on neurological function (Gueven et al., 2017; Ji et al., 2021). In addition, small open-label studies have been conducted in patients with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON), an inherited optic neuropathy known to involve mitochondrial dysfunction in retinal ganglion cells; such studies indicated that early administration of EPI-743 may arrest disease progression and, in some cases, partially reverse visual loss (Gueven et al., 2017; Hong et al., 2023). Further clinical evaluation has expanded EPI-743’s investigation into other mitochondrial and neurodegenerative conditions such as Friedreich’s ataxia and refractory epilepsy, all of which share common mechanistic ties to oxidative stress and impaired bioenergetics (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

Despite its extensive evaluation in mitochondrial diseases and neurodegenerative disorders, there is no direct evidence in the literature indicating that EPI-743 has been used to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar age-related retinal conditions. There are no published studies that have directly tested EPI-743 in preclinical models of AMD, nor are there clinical trial reports of its use in an elderly population suffering from AMD. Although several quinone-based compounds (for example, idebenone) have been evaluated in ocular diseases, and the pathophysiological overlap between mitochondrial dysfunction and retinal degeneration is recognized, the existing body of literature on EPI-743 primarily focuses on inherited mitochondrial encephalomyopathies and optic neuropathies rather than on common, age-related retinal disorders (Gueven et al., 2017).

Overall, while the clinical track record of EPI-743 in conditions characterized by disrupted mitochondrial bioenergetics positions it as a promising candidate from a mechanistic perspective, its therapeutic history does not yet include any studies directly addressing the multifactorial nature of dry AMD. However, the established ability of EPI-743 to modulate cellular redox status suggests that it might have potential in the AMD setting as well (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

At the molecular level, EPI-743 exerts its effects primarily through its redox activity, a function that is intimately linked to its para-benzoquinone core. This structure allows EPI-743 to participate in reversible redox cycling—a process in which the quinone is reduced to its hydroquinone form and oxidized back to the quinone form as needed (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). The reduction is typically mediated by cytosolic oxidoreductases, most notably NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), an enzyme that is ubiquitously expressed, including in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012). NQO1 catalyzes a two-electron transfer reaction that converts the oxidized quinone into its corresponding hydroquinone. This hydroquinone is not only a potent free-radical scavenger but also plays a crucial role in regenerating the cellular pool of reduced glutathione (GSH) (Tinker et al., 2021; Cores et al., 2023).

Reduced glutathione is the primary intracellular antioxidant, essential for neutralizing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and protecting macromolecules from oxidative damage. In scenarios where ROS overwhelm a cell’s antioxidant capacity—such as during mitochondrial dysfunction or in cells under chronic oxidative stress—GSH levels become depleted and oxidized glutathione (GSSG) accumulates. By facilitating the replenishment of GSH, EPI-743 helps re‐establish redox balance and thus serves as an indirect regulator of oxidative stress (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Tinker et al., 2021). This redox cycling is considered “catalytic” because once the hydroquinone form scavenges a radical or reduces another molecule, it is itself reoxidized back to the quinone, whereupon it can undergo another round of reduction. Thus, even at relatively low concentrations, EPI-743 provides a sustained antioxidant effect.

In addition to its role in antioxidant defense, EPI-743 has been shown to modulate specific redox-sensitive enzymes. For example, its activity has been linked to the modulation of 15-lipoxygenase (15-LO), a key enzyme in lipid peroxidation pathways that can trigger ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death associated with lipid peroxidation. By inhibiting 15-LO activity, EPI-743 may reduce the peroxidative damage to polyunsaturated fatty acids within cellular membranes—a damage process that is especially detrimental in cells with a high metabolic rate such as retinal pigment epithelium (Cores et al., 2023; Kayser et al., 2024). This function is particularly relevant since ferroptosis has been implicated in conditions where oxidative stress is central.

Furthermore, the quinone’s ability to modulate intracellular redox signaling involves its interaction with transcription factors such as nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2). By maintaining a favorable GSH/GSSG ratio and reducing the overall burden of ROS, EPI-743 indirectly helps to sustain Nrf2 signaling, which in turn upregulates the expression of a panel of antioxidant genes. This feedback loop reinforces the cell’s capacity to respond to oxidative challenges. Though direct evidence linking EPI-743 to Nrf2 activation in retinal cells is sparse, the dependency of its action on NQO1—which itself is regulated in part by Nrf2—suggests that such interactions are plausible (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

In summary, EPI-743’s mechanism of action is multifaceted. It directly scavenges ROS via its hydroquinone intermediate, it enhances the reduced glutathione pool and thereby improves the cell’s overall antioxidant capacity, and it modulates lipid peroxidation pathways by affecting 15-LO activity. The reliance on NQO1 for its activation further supports its broad potential, given that NQO1 is expressed in many cell types, including those in the retina. These biochemical properties collectively suggest that EPI-743 has the potential to mitigate oxidative damage in environments where mitochondrial dysfunction and redox imbalance predominate (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect in Dry AMD

Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by the progressive degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium and underlying photoreceptors, a process that is driven in part by chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and the accumulation of oxidative DNA lesions. In the RPE, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is particularly vulnerable to oxidative damage because of its proximity to the electron transport chain and its relative lack of protective histones. One of the most common oxidative modifications observed in mtDNA is 8-oxo-2′-deoxyguanosine (8-oxoG), a marker of oxidative base lesions that can lead to mutagenesis and impaired mitochondrial function. The hypothesis underlying the repurposing of EPI-743 for dry AMD is that its potent redox cycling mechanism can reset the oxidative environment in RPE cells by regenerating reduced glutathione and by supporting NQO1-mediated detoxification, thereby reducing the accumulation of damaging oxidative lesions in mtDNA (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

In an in vitro assay designed to analyze oxidative stress in RPE cells, one would expect that treatment with EPI-743 would lead to several measurable outcomes. First, due to its rapid redox cycling and ability to donate electrons, EPI-743 would be anticipated to reduce intracellular levels of ROS, thereby directly lowering the formation of 8-oxoG lesions in mitochondrial DNA. This effect should manifest as a reduction in the cellular markers of oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation. Second, given the established role of NQO1 in catalyzing the conversion of EPI-743 to its hydroquinone form, and the fact that NQO1 is known to be expressed in RPE cells, the compound is expected to increase the intracellular GSH/GSSG ratio in these cells, further reinforcing the antioxidant defense system (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012).

Additionally, improved mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) function is a key expected outcome. In dry AMD, compromised mitochondrial integrity leads to reduced ATP production and increased susceptibility to cell death. By restoring redox balance, EPI-743 should preserve the integrity of mitochondrial membranes and ensure effective electron transport, ultimately resulting in enhanced ATP synthesis. This restoration of mitochondrial function could be assessed via assays that measure mitochondrial membrane potential, ATP synthesis rates, and oxygen consumption rates in RPE cell cultures challenged with oxidants (Kayser et al., 2024; Tinker et al., 2021).

Moreover, an important aspect of EPI-743’s expected effect is its potential to mitigate ferroptotic cell death pathways. Ferroptosis, driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation, has been implicated in the degeneration of RPE cells. By inhibiting 15-lipoxygenase and curbing lipid peroxidation, EPI-743 could help prevent the execution of ferroptotic cell death in RPE cells—a process that may contribute to the progression of dry AMD (Cores et al., 2023).

Taken together, in an experimental model of dry AMD—whether in RPE cell culture or in an appropriate animal model—administration of EPI-743 is expected to lead to: (1) a significant decline in ROS levels, (2) an increased ratio of reduced-to-oxidized glutathione, (3) preservation of mitochondrial DNA integrity as evidenced by reduced 8-oxoG accumulation, (4) improved mitochondrial bioenergetics as indicated by enhanced ATP production and mitochondrial membrane potential, and (5) inhibition of deleterious lipid peroxidation pathways. The successful demonstration of these effects would serve as strong biochemical and cellular evidence supporting the hypothesis that EPI-743 can protect RPE cells from the oxidative insults characteristic of dry AMD (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

Furthermore, since the RPE is known to express NQO1—an enzyme critical for the activation of EPI-743—the molecular basis for its activity is supported by tissue-specific expression data. This provides additional justification for targeting RPE cells with EPI-743 in the context of dry AMD, where bolstering the endogenous antioxidant systems may have a measurable impact on disease progression (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Tinker et al., 2021).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

EPI-743 stands out as a highly promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD owing to several strengths rooted in its potent redox-modulatory properties and well-characterized mitochondrial protective effects. One of its major strengths is its extraordinary antioxidant potency. As a para-benzoquinone analogue that can be reduced via NQO1-catalyzed reactions to its hydroquinone state, EPI-743 is capable of intercepting and neutralizing ROS with an efficiency that surpasses that of conventional antioxidants such as CoQ10 by three to four orders of magnitude (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Gueven et al., 2017). This high level of potency is particularly appealing for conditions like dry AMD, in which the cumulative oxidative stress has a direct impact on mtDNA damage and cellular energetic deficits.

Another significant advantage is the compound’s established clinical track record in diseases marked by mitochondrial dysfunction. Although its clinical applications have thus far been restricted to rare inherited mitochondrial conditions like Leigh syndrome and LHON, the underlying mechanisms—namely, the restoration of mitochondrial bioenergetics and redox balance through effective GSH regeneration—are equally relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Gueven et al., 2017). Its ability to protect retinal ganglion cells in LHON studies suggests that similar beneficial effects might be extrapolated to retinal pigment epithelial cells, which are critically involved in the development of AMD.

Mechanistically, EPI-743’s dual action—both as a direct antioxidant and as a modulator of redox-sensitive pathways involving 15-lipoxygenase—confers a multi-pronged approach to cytoprotection. By reducing ROS and regenerating intracellular glutathione levels, EPI-743 can potentially arrest the oxidative modifications that lead to deleterious mtDNA lesions such as 8-oxoG. Moreover, the inhibition of enzymes that contribute to lipid peroxidation may further protect cellular membranes and reduce downstream inflammatory responses. These attributes provide a compelling scientific rationale for considering EPI-743 as a therapeutic strategy to combat the chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction associated with dry AMD (Tinker et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be acknowledged. First and foremost, the current therapeutic history of EPI-743 shows no direct evidence of efficacy in dry AMD or other age-related retinal conditions. All of the published studies to date have focused on inherited mitochondrial or neurodegenerative disorders. Therefore, there remains a significant gap in our knowledge regarding its pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics in the context of the aging retina, which has a distinct microenvironment compared to the tissues examined in inherited disorders (Gueven et al., 2017).

Another concern is the potential difference in drug metabolism and toxicity between the predominantly pediatric or young adult populations (commonly studied in mitochondrial diseases) and the elderly patient population that is most affected by dry AMD. Age-related alterations in absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) could impact both efficacy and the safety profile of EPI-743 when repurposed for an older demographic (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Hong et al., 2023). Furthermore, while the activation of EPI-743 via NQO1 is a mechanistically attractive feature, the ubiquitous and sometimes unpredictable nature of redox enzyme activity in different tissues raises the possibility of off-target effects. Chronic systemic administration in an elderly population might result in unforeseen modifications in redox homeostasis not only within the retina but also in other vulnerable organs (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

In addition, the multifactorial pathogenesis of dry AMD poses a challenge to any therapeutic approach that primarily targets oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. While these are certainly key components of AMD pathology, the disease also involves chronic inflammation, drusen formation, and alterations in extracellular matrix homeostasis. It is therefore uncertain whether the powerful antioxidant activity of EPI-743 alone would be sufficient to halt or reverse the progression of dry AMD. Successful treatment may require a combination approach that addresses multiple causative factors, and it remains to be seen if EPI-743 can be integrated effectively into such a therapeutic regimen (Gueven et al., 2017; Cores et al., 2023).

Lastly, the translation from preclinical models—where the compound’s efficacy has been demonstrated in controlled settings of inherited mitochondrial dysfunction—to an age-related, multifaceted disease state such as dry AMD is non-trivial. Preclinical RPE-focused studies, including those measuring ROS levels, mitochondrial membrane potential, and direct assessments of mtDNA damage in the context of oxidative challenges, are currently lacking. Such studies are critical to validate whether the mechanisms observed in other cell types or disease models are applicable to the RPE and to the pathophysiology of AMD (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Conclusion

In conclusion, EPI-743 (vatiquinone) exhibits many characteristics that render it an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its synthetic origin from vitamin E–derived tocotrienol derivatives and its classification as a para-benzoquinone confer upon it a robust redox-cycling capacity, enabling it to function as an exceptionally potent mitochondrial antioxidant. Through its ability to be reduced by NQO1 to a hydroquinone state, EPI-743 effectively regenerates intracellular reduced glutathione while simultaneously inhibiting lipid peroxidation via modulation of 15-lipoxygenase activity. These mechanisms collectively support its potential to protect mitochondrial DNA from oxidative damage, preserve electron transport chain function, and maintain ATP production in highly metabolically active cells such as the retinal pigment epithelium (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

The therapeutic history of EPI-743 in inherited mitochondrial disorders and optic neuropathies provides a valuable proof of concept regarding its efficacy in situations where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central to pathogenesis. However, the absence of any direct study in dry AMD represents a significant gap that must be addressed through focused preclinical research. In the context of dry AMD, where chronic oxidative stress leads to the accumulation of damaging mtDNA lesions (including 8-oxoG) and progressive RPE degeneration, a potent redox modulator like EPI-743 theoretically offers a promising means to break the cycle of oxidative damage and mitochondrial decline (Tinker et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

Notwithstanding its potential strengths, several uncertainties must be highlighted. The pharmacokinetics and safety profile of EPI-743 in an elderly population—where changes in drug metabolism are common—remain to be fully elucidated. Moreover, the complex etiology of dry AMD, which involves not only oxidative damage and mitochondrial failure but also inflammatory and extracellular matrix alterations, may necessitate a multifaceted treatment strategy beyond a single antioxidant approach. As such, while the mechanistic rationale for using EPI-743 in dry AMD is well founded by virtue of its antioxidant and mitochondria-protective properties, clinical translation will require rigorous demonstration of efficacy in RPE-based in vitro systems and in animal models that recapitulate the full spectrum of AMD pathology (Gueven et al., 2017; Cores et al., 2023).

Given these considerations, the repurposing of EPI-743 for dry AMD holds promise—but only with additional preclinical studies that specifically assess its ability to ameliorate oxidative damage in the retinal pigment epithelium. Key experiments should focus on measuring changes in redox biomarkers, mtDNA integrity, ATP production, and cellular viability in RPE cells under oxidative stress. Parallel in vivo studies in animal models of AMD will be essential to determine ocular bioavailability, dosing parameters, and potential off-target effects in an aged organism.

Overall, the strengths of EPI-743 lie in its unparalleled antioxidant potency and its established capacity to restore mitochondrial function in disease settings characterized by oxidative damage. Its mechanism—centered on redox cycling via a para-benzoquinone moiety, glutathione regeneration, and modulation of lipid peroxidation—is directly relevant to the pathophysiological challenges found in dry AMD. However, the primary weaknesses include the current absence of direct evidence in retinal disease models, potential pharmacokinetic concerns in the elderly, and the complexity of dry AMD pathology which may require combination therapy for optimal clinical benefit. Thus, while EPI-743 is mechanistically compelling as a candidate drug for dry AMD, its ultimate clinical utility will depend on the outcomes of targeted preclinical evaluations and, subsequently, carefully designed clinical trials that address the specific challenges of age-related retinal degeneration (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024; Tinker et al., 2021).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Final Remarks

EPI-743 (vatiquinone) presents an attractive therapeutic opportunity given its synthetic derivation from vitamin E, its classification as a para-benzoquinone with exceptionally potent antioxidant capabilities, and its ability to support mitochondrial function through NQO1-mediated redox modulation and glutathione regeneration. Although its historical clinical use has been confined to inherited mitochondrial diseases and optic neuropathies rather than age-related conditions, the underlying pathophysiological similarities—namely oxidative stress and mitochondrial compromise—provide a logical foundation for hypothesizing its efficacy in dry AMD. The expected beneficial actions in RPE cells include reduced accumulation of oxidative DNA lesions, improved mitochondrial electron transport and ATP synthesis, and diminished activation of ferroptotic cell death pathways.

Before any clinical repurposing can be considered, it is essential to perform a series of rigorous preclinical studies. These studies should involve well-characterized in vitro models using RPE cell lines that mimic the oxidative challenges seen in dry AMD. Furthermore, in vivo studies employing animal models that recapitulate the complex pathology of AMD will be crucial to assess ocular bioavailability, efficacy, and safety in a context that simulates the aged human retina. Such investigations will inform dosing regimens and help identify any potential off-target effects or toxicities that might arise in the elderly population, which is inherently more vulnerable due to age-related physiological changes (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012).

In summary, while the available data from mitochondrial and neurodegenerative disease studies provide a robust mechanistic rationale for the use of EPI-743 as a potent redox modulator and mitochondria-protective agent, the leap to a therapeutic indication in dry AMD remains largely theoretical at this point. Nonetheless, the convergence of redox dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and oxidative mtDNA damage in AMD creates a promising target for compounds like EPI-743. With appropriate preclinical validation, EPI-743 could emerge as a valuable component of a combination therapy strategy that addresses the multifactorial nature of dry AMD. This repurposing effort would potentially fill a significant therapeutic gap in a disease area where effective treatments are currently lacking (Tinker et al., 2021; Cores et al., 2023; Gueven et al., 2017).

Given the promising mechanistic profile of EPI-743 alongside the identified gaps in its direct application to dry AMD, we recommend that the next phase in drug development should focus on comprehensive preclinical studies specifically targeting RPE dysfunction and oxidative damage in AMD. These studies will be critical in determining whether the redox-modulating properties of EPI-743 can be harnessed to meaningfully slow or reverse the progression of dry AMD in a clinical setting.

1. Its chemical derivation from vitamin E derivatives places it in the para-benzoquinone class, endowing it with rapid redox-cycling properties and a potency that is orders of magnitude greater than that of more conventional antioxidants such as CoQ10 and idebenone (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Gueven et al., 2017).

2. Its mechanism of action—rooted in the reversible reduction to an active hydroquinone via NQO1, subsequent regeneration of reduced glutathione, and inhibition of oxidative enzymes such as 15-lipoxygenase—offers a multi-modal approach to addressing the oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction that are central to dry AMD pathogenesis (Tinker et al., 2021; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

3. 1. No current preclinical or clinical studies have directly examined the efficacy of EPI-743 in dry AMD models. 2. The majority of clinical evaluations of EPI-743 have been performed in younger patient populations with genetic disorders, leaving questions regarding the pharmacokinetics, tolerability, and safety of chronic EPI-743 administration in the elderly, who are most at risk for dry AMD (Hong et al., 2023; Kayser et al., 2024).

4. Conclusion

EPI-743 (vatiquinone) is a highly potent, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant derived from vitamin E metabolites and classified within the para-benzoquinone family of compounds. Its design is centered on harnessing reversible two-electron redox cycling mediated by NQO1, leading to enhanced intracellular levels of reduced glutathione and effective mitigation of ROS and lipid peroxidation. Clinically, it has shown promise in mitigating the effects of mitochondrial dysfunction in inherited neurodegenerative and optic neuropathic disorders such as Leigh syndrome and LHON. 4. Explore combination therapies that might pair EPI-743’s potent antioxidant effects with agents targeting other aspects of AMD pathology, such as inflammation and drusen formation.

Overall, while EPI-743 has not yet been evaluated directly in the context of dry AMD, its biochemical properties, proven efficacy in mitochondrial disease models, and mechanistic plausibility render it a candidate worthy of further exploration. With careful and targeted preclinical experimentation, the repurposing of EPI-743 may eventually provide a novel therapeutic option for a patient population in urgent need of effective treatments (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Tinker et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Closing Summary

In conclusion, the evidence from the biochemical, clinical, and therapeutic literature reviewed herein supports the following: EPI-743 (vatiquinone) is a synthetically derived para-benzoquinone that leverages redox cycling and glutathione regeneration via NQO1 to protect mitochondria from oxidative insult. Its clinical history in mitochondrial disorders provides an encouraging precedent, and its detailed mechanism of action is highly relevant to conditions characterized by oxidative mtDNA damage—such as dry AMD. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Elamipretide (SS-31; D-Arg-2,6-dimethyl-Tyr-Lys-Phe-NH2) is a synthetic, C-terminally amidated tetrapeptide belonging to the Szeto–Schiller (SS) class of mitochondria-targeted peptides, originally discovered through structure–activity optimization of alternating cationic–aromatic motifs that confer high cell permeability and strong partitioning to the negatively charged inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) enriched in cardiolipin (CL) (Szeto & Schiller, 2011; Tung et al., 2025). Early work demonstrated that an aromatic–cationic design was sufficient to drive potent mitochondrial uptake and that dimethyltyrosine (Dmt) confers radical-scavenging chemistry while improving chemical stability; subnanomolar-to-nanomolar extracellular concentrations concentrate >1 μM at the IMM, yielding robust activity under oxidative stress in diverse cell types (Szeto & Schiller, 2011). SS-31 and related SS peptides were initially identified as potent inhibitors of mitochondrial swelling and oxidative cell death in intact cells and organs, with mechanistic clues pointing to direct interactions with cardiolipin-rich membranes and mitigation of ischemia–reperfusion injury (Szeto & Schiller, 2011; Szeto & Birk, 2014).

Mechanistically, elamipretide selectively binds CL in the IMM via electrostatic anchoring of its cationic residues to anionic phosphate headgroups and hydrophobic partitioning of its aromatic residues into the bilayer interfacial region; biophysical studies (NMR and molecular dynamics simulations) and binding quantitation to model CL-containing bilayers demonstrate CL dependence and saturable effects on bilayer surface electrostatics and lipid packing without destabilizing lamellar phases (Mitchell et al., 2019; Sabbah et al., 2025). Once bound, elamipretide modulates several biophysical and biochemical properties central to mitochondrial function: it down-tunes the negative surface potential of CL-rich membranes, increases CL self-association, reduces lateral lipid diffusivity, and increases lateral packing, changes that preserve cristae architecture and respiratory supercomplex organization under stress while suppressing cytochrome c peroxidase activity and CL oxidation (Sabbah et al., 2025). Collectively, these actions improve electron transfer efficiency, stabilize oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos) protein assemblies, reduce electron leak and reactive oxygen species (ROS), and preserve ATP synthesis capacity in dysfunctional mitochondria (Mitchell et al., 2022; Sabbah et al., 2025; Szeto & Birk, 2014). Importantly for retinal applications, elamipretide uptake is not dependent on mitochondrial membrane potential, supporting entry into depolarized or injured mitochondria—a feature often found in AMD RPE (Ji et al., 2021).

Elamipretide is therefore best classified as a CL-targeting, membrane-active mitochondrial therapeutic that acts primarily by modulating the physicochemical properties of CL-rich IMM domains and CL-dependent protein assemblies, rather than binding a single protein target, with downstream effects on respiratory supercomplex assembly, cytochrome c catalysis, electron-transport efficiency, ROS emission, and ATP production (Mitchell et al., 2019; Sabbah et al., 2025; Mitchell et al., 2022). Members of this class have been deployed across preclinical models of cardiac, skeletal muscle, renal, neurologic, and ocular dysfunction, and a substantial clinical program has tested elamipretide in primary mitochondrial disorders, cardiometabolic diseases, and ophthalmic indications including age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Sabbah et al., 2025; Tung et al., 2025). The drug is water-soluble, with a short elimination half-life on the order of ~2–4 hours in preclinical species and humans, and is administered systemically by daily subcutaneous injection in AMD studies at a nominal 40 mg dose; topical ocular delivery has also been explored preclinically and clinically (Szeto & Birk, 2014; Lenin et al., 2023; Guimaraes et al., 2022; Ji et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
The SS peptide class emerged from efforts to concentrate antioxidant and mitochondrial-protective chemistry directly at the IMM through cationic–aromatic motifs that target anionic phospholipids—principally cardiolipin—enabling inhibition of mitochondrial swelling, reduction of ROS emission, and protection from reperfusion injury in intact cells and organs; SS-31 in particular was estimated to concentrate ~5,000-fold in mitochondria and to inhibit lipid peroxidation, positioning it to prevent CL peroxidation in the IMM (Szeto & Schiller, 2011). These membrane-centric mechanisms rapidly translated into broad preclinical testing across organ systems, demonstrating improvements in OxPhos efficiency, ATP production, ROS control, and preservation of mitochondrial ultrastructure (cristae) in disease and aging models (Szeto & Birk, 2014; Mitchell et al., 2022).

Ocular and retinal applications came into focus as mitochondrial dysfunction in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptors was implicated as a driver of non-neovascular AMD, including reduced OxPhos, increased glycolytic shift, impaired mitophagy, structural cristae disorganization, and accumulation of damaged mitochondria in AMD donor RPE (Ferrington et al., 2020; Fisher, 2022; Fisher et al., 2022). In this context, elamipretide demonstrated several AMD-relevant preclinical effects. In a mouse model of dry AMD-like pathology, subcutaneous elamipretide reversed electroretinographic (ERG) deficits and improved clearance of sub-RPE deposits, corresponding to reversal of vision loss, consistent with activity at both the RPE/sub-RPE interface and photoreceptor function (Kim & Lad, 2021; Ji et al., 2021). In ApoE4 mice with diet-induced sub-RPE deposit formation linked to mitochondrial dysfunction, subcutaneous elamipretide reversed deposit formation, strengthening the mechanistic link to CL-dependent mitochondrial physiology in retinal tissues (Guimaraes et al., 2022). RPE-targeted cytoprotection has also been reported: elamipretide protected primary RPE and improved mitochondrial function in models of AMD and prevented persistent injury phenotypes induced by oxidative stressors such as hydroquinone in cultured RPE cells (Sabbah et al., 2025). Ex vivo and in vivo aging paradigms provide convergent support: in aged mice with visual impairments, elamipretide mitigated visual decline and normalized visual acuity and contrast sensitivity within two months, with delivery via topical eye drops producing effects comparable to subcutaneous injections; in RPE cultures from AMD donors, elamipretide improved RPE cell viability and mitochondrial function (Sabbah et al., 2025; Alam et al., 2020). In an RPE-specific SOD2 knockout model, daily topical elamipretide prevented RPE cell size increase consistent with reduced RPE cell death/senescence, further underscoring RPE-specific benefits (Tong et al., 2022). Additional retinal disease models support cross-indication activity: SS-31 restored visual function in a streptozotocin-induced mouse diabetic retinopathy model (Ferrington et al., 2020). Collectively, preclinical retinal evidence aligns with the hypothesized CL-centric rescue of mitochondrial function at the RPE and photoreceptor inner segments, preventing AMD-relevant cellular dysfunction and functional decline (Ji et al., 2021; Kim & Lad, 2021; Guimaraes et al., 2022).

Clinical development has included both topical and subcutaneous AMD studies. A phase I/II topical study enrolled 21 patients with diabetic macular edema (DME) and non-exudative intermediate AMD, demonstrating feasibility of ocular delivery; subsequent systemic AMD trials have been more extensively reported (Ji et al., 2021). The open-label, 24-week Phase 1 ReCLAIM study administered daily subcutaneous elamipretide (40 mg) to 40 patients with either non-central geographic atrophy (NCGA; n = 19) or high-risk drusen without GA (n = 21), reporting mean functional improvements: in the NCGA subgroup, +4.6 letters in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), +5.4 letters in low-luminance visual acuity (LLVA), and an approximate 25-letter gain in low-luminance reading acuity (LLRA), with a slower GA growth rate than historical natural history; in the high-risk drusen subgroup, mean gains were +3.6 (BCVA), +5.6 (LLVA), and ~15 (LLRA) (Kim & Lad, 2021). Safety was favorable, with no serious adverse events and general tolerability in intermediate AMD (Ji et al., 2021). A subsequent randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled Phase 2 trial (ReCLAIM-2) in ≥55-year-old patients with non-central GA tested daily subcutaneous elamipretide for 48 weeks; it did not meet primary endpoints on LL-BCVA and GA area, but elamipretide was associated with a 43% reduction in mean progression of total ellipsoid zone (EZ) attenuation and a 47% reduction in partial EZ attenuation versus placebo, with a post hoc analysis showing significant reductions and a higher proportion of patients achieving ≥2-line LL-BCVA gains, and a correlation between LL-BCVA change and change in total EZ attenuation (Sabbah et al., 2025). EZ attenuation is a clinically meaningful OCT marker that reflects photoreceptor integrity in mitochondria-rich inner segments and precedes GA and irreversible vision loss; thus, preservation of EZ is mechanistically consistent with the drug’s mitochondrial-protective intent and could represent an early biomarker of benefit (Sabbah et al., 2025). Additional summaries concur: the Phase 2 program reported negative primary endpoints but a structural OCT signal (slowed EZ degradation), warranting confirmatory studies with longer duration and functional correlates (Tung et al., 2025).

Beyond AMD, elamipretide has undergone extensive clinical evaluation in mitochondrial disorders (e.g., Barth syndrome), heart failure, ischemia–reperfusion contexts, and renal microvascular dysfunction, with mixed outcomes: many trials did not meet primary endpoints but reported improvements in mitochondrial bioenergetics, coupling, or patient-reported quality-of-life metrics, consistent with a class effect of improving mitochondrial physiology in vivo (Sabbah et al., 2025; Tung et al., 2025). Pharmacokinetically, elamipretide exhibits rapid distribution/elimination with elimination half-lives of ~2 hours in preclinical species and on the order of ~4 hours in humans, renal excretion of parent/metabolites, and ocular pharmacology indicating that topical dosing in rabbits achieves high anterior-chamber and periocular concentrations with nonzero penetration to the retina; this, together with murine aged-vision data, suggests both topical and systemic routes are viable for retinal targeting, although intraocular/vitreous levels after topical dosing may be low (Szeto & Birk, 2014; Alam et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
Elamipretide’s mechanism centers on high-affinity interaction with cardiolipin in the IMM and consequent modulation of membrane electrostatics, lipid organization, and CL-dependent protein complexes, leading to improved electron transport, reduced ROS production, and preserved ATP synthesis. Several convergent lines of evidence define this mechanism in molecular detail.

1) Cardiolipin-dependent binding and membrane electrostatics. SS-31/ELAM partitions into the interfacial leaflet of CL-containing bilayers with affinity proportional to surface charge, binding via electrostatic interactions of its basic residues with CL phosphates and via hydrophobic interactions of its aromatic residues with lipid acyl chains; no measurable binding occurs to neutral phosphatidylcholine membranes (Mitchell et al., 2019). NMR and molecular dynamics identify two binding modes—“peptide approach” (electrostatic anchoring) and “peptide burial” (aromatic partition)—producing a controlled down-tuning of the negative surface potential, increased CL self-association, and altered lateral packing/diffusivity without disrupting lamellar bilayer integrity (Sabbah et al., 2025). The net effect is to modulate ion distribution at the membrane interface (e.g., divalent cations such as Ca2+), stabilize bilayer structure under electrochemical stress, and resist electroporation-like damage, thereby preserving IMM properties under stress (Mitchell et al., 2019; Tamucci et al., 2025). These membrane-physical changes occur without altering the transmembrane potential per se, consistent with a surface–electrostatics mechanism that adjusts protein–lipid interactions and lipid–lipid organization (Sabbah et al., 2025).

2) Respiratory complexes, supercomplexes, and cytochrome c. Cardiolipin stabilizes respiratory complexes and promotes assembly of supercomplexes to optimize electron transport; elamipretide binding to CL supports supercomplex assembly, increases coupling efficiency, and reduces electron leak and ROS while enhancing ATP synthesis (Mitchell et al., 2022; Sabbah et al., 2025). A central node is the CL–cytochrome c interface: elamipretide is proposed to modulate the hydrophobic/π–π interactions between cytochrome c and CL, promoting efficient electron transfer from complex III to complex IV at the rate-limiting step while inhibiting cytochrome c peroxidase activity that otherwise peroxidizes CL and destabilizes cristae under oxidative stress (Szeto & Birk, 2014). Biochemical studies show that elamipretide reduces cytochrome c peroxidase activity and prevents oxidative modifications of CL acyl chains by forming a complex with CL, thereby protecting membrane integrity (Sabbah et al., 2025). In failing human heart tissue ex vivo, elamipretide improved supercomplex coupling control, respiratory control ratio, and CI/CIV activities, consistent with a supercomplex-stabilizing activity that enhances OXPHOS efficiency (Sabbah et al., 2025).

3) Direct protein interactions and bioenergetic consequences. Proteomics using biotinylated elamipretide (b-ELAM) in cross-linking/MS identified binding to multiple IMM proteins that themselves interact with CL, including complex IV subunit NDUA4 and the adenine nucleotide translocase ANT1; functionally, elamipretide increased maximum uncoupled and CIV respiration and decreased H2O2 production in mitochondria from old mouse hearts, increased ADP sensitivity and uptake via ANT, reduced ANT1-mediated proton leak, stabilized membrane potential, and reduced mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening (Sabbah et al., 2025). Stabilization of larger IMM protein assemblies such as the ATP synthasome (ANT, ATP synthase, creatine kinase, phosphate carrier) has been reported, with improvements in CI–CIII–CIV coupling and oxygen flux in failing human heart tissue (Sabbah et al., 2025). These molecular effects translate to rapid increases in mitochondrial energetic capacity—including a human randomized placebo-controlled trial demonstrating that a single dose of elamipretide increased the maximal rate of ATP production (ATPmax) in skeletal muscle—validating in vivo bioenergetic rescue (Sabbah et al., 2025).

4) ROS control, IMM integrity, and cristae structure. Across cell and organ models, elamipretide reduces ETS-derived ROS without acting as a primary radical scavenger; instead it optimizes respiratory efficiency, reduces electron leak, and protects CL from peroxidation, breaking the cycle of cristae disruption and respiratory dysfunction prevalent in aged or diseased mitochondria (Sabbah et al., 2025; Mitchell et al., 2022). SS-31 lowers intracellular ROS, prevents mitochondrial depolarization, maintains ΔΨm, prevents lipid peroxidation, and curtails oxidative cell death in a dose-dependent manner (Mitchell et al., 2019). In retinal contexts, elamipretide increased mitochondrial cristae density and preserved ultrastructure in aged mouse retinal mitochondria and diabetic mouse retinopathy models, supporting retinal applicability (Sabbah et al., 2025). In multiple disease models, elamipretide increased mitochondrial density and cristae connectivity, normalized proton leak, improved respiratory capacity, and corrected dysregulated fusion/fission and biogenesis regulators after longer treatment, further indicating structural remodeling capacity (Sabbah et al., 2025).

Mechanistic relevance to AMD and RPE is strong. AMD donor RPE exhibits cristae disorganization, accumulation of damaged mitochondria, decreased OxPhos, impaired mitophagy, and significant mtDNA damage in ETC gene regions, all linked to diminished ATP production and a glycolytic shift that disrupts metabolic coupling with photoreceptors and promotes retinal degeneration (Ferrington et al., 2020; Fisher et al., 2022; Fisher, 2022). Because CL is crucial for maintaining OxPhos function and cristae architecture, pharmacologic stabilization of CL and CL-dependent protein assemblies by elamipretide directly addresses these pathologies, offering preservation of ATP production, reduction of ROS, and resistance to mPTP opening and apoptosis in RPE under chronic oxidative stress (Fisher et al., 2022; Sabbah et al., 2025; Szeto & Birk, 2014). Photoreceptors are mitochondria-rich in the inner segments, and OCT-defined EZ attenuation is an early marker of photoreceptor compromise that precedes GA; elamipretide-associated reduction in EZ attenuation progression in AMD patients links its mitochondrial mechanism to clinically observable retinal structure (Sabbah et al., 2025).

Expected Effect  
In RPE cell assays that model AMD-relevant stressors (oxidative and bioenergetic), elamipretide is expected to stabilize IMM biophysics and CL-dependent protein systems, restoring mitochondrial bioenergetics, reducing oxidative injury, and preventing apoptosis. Mechanistically supported expectations include:

- Restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) and coupling: Elamipretide maintains ΔΨm and improves respiratory control, consistent with increased OXPHOS efficiency and reduced proton leak; thus, assays using potentiometric dyes (e.g., JC-1) should show improved ΔΨm relative to oxidant-injured controls (Mitchell et al., 2019; Sabbah et al., 2025).

- Reduction of mitochondrial ROS and lipid peroxidation: By stabilizing CL, optimizing electron transport, and inhibiting cytochrome c peroxidase activity, elamipretide reduces H2O2 emission and lipid peroxidation, leading to lower MitoSOX and lipid oxidation signals under oxidative challenge (Sabbah et al., 2025; Mitchell et al., 2019).

- Preservation of ATP synthesis: In serum-deprivation or oxidant-injury paradigms in RPE cell lines (e.g., ARPE-19), mitochondria-targeted peptides including elamipretide increased cell viability and cellular ATP at nanomolar dosing; this is consistent with expected improvements in ATP content and Seahorse OXPHOS parameters in primary RPE under stress (Mitchell et al., 2021). Human AMD donor RPE exposed ex vivo to elamipretide show improved mitochondrial function and viability, corroborating translatability of these endpoints (Sabbah et al., 2025).

- Cytoprotection against AMD-relevant toxicants: Elamipretide prevents persistent injury phenotypes induced by oxidative stressors (e.g., hydroquinone) in cultured RPE, supporting generalizability to sodium iodate or H2O2 injury; in an RPE SOD2 knockout model, topical elamipretide prevented cell size increase consistent with reduced cell death/senescence (Sabbah et al., 2025; Tong et al., 2022).

- Structural preservation of cristae: Electron microscopy of retinal mitochondria in aged/diabetic mice treated with elamipretide indicates increased cristae density and improved ultrastructure; similar effects are expected in RPE mitochondrial ultrastructure under chronic oxidative stress (Sabbah et al., 2025).

- In vivo retinal/RPE endpoints: In mouse models of AMD-like pathology, elamipretide improved ERG deficits and enhanced clearance of sub-RPE deposits, tracking to improvements in photoreceptor function and RPE health; ERG, OCT (drusen/sub-RPE deposit metrics), and RPE morphometrics are therefore expected to improve (Kim & Lad, 2021; Ji et al., 2021; Guimaraes et al., 2022). In aged-vision paradigms, spatial vision and contrast sensitivity improved with systemic or topical elamipretide, indicating photopic function benefits and supporting cone function endpoints (Alam et al., 2020).

- Clinical correlates: In patients with intermediate AMD or non-central GA, improvements in LLVA/LLRA and slowing of EZ attenuation were observed; therefore, clinical PoC studies should prioritize EZ attenuation as a primary structural endpoint with LL-BCVA/LLVA and reading measures as functionally sensitive secondaries, acknowledging that GA area may not be sensitive over ≤1 year (Kim & Lad, 2021; Sabbah et al., 2025; Tung et al., 2025). Given that photoreceptor inner segments are mitochondria-rich, EZ integrity serves as a proximal clinical biomarker of the drug’s mitochondrial mechanism (Sabbah et al., 2025).

Expression and target rationale in RPE: The target of elamipretide is not a single protein but the CL-rich IMM domain; CL is ubiquitous and crucial for maintaining OxPhos function, cristae architecture, and supercomplex assembly in RPE mitochondria, which are compromised in AMD (Fisher et al., 2022; Ferrington et al., 2020). Deficits in mitophagy (reduced PINK1/Parkin responsiveness), increased fission and delayed fusion, and global OxPhos reduction in AMD donor RPE define a mitochondrial fragility state in which CL stabilization is expected to be beneficial (Fisher et al., 2022). Because elamipretide uptake is not dependent on ΔΨm, it can access depolarized/dysfunctional mitochondria in AMD RPE, positioning it to act upstream of apoptosis (Ji et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Elamipretide presents a coherent, mechanistically grounded, and translationally explored therapeutic candidate for non-neovascular AMD predicated on CL-centric rescue of mitochondrial function in RPE and photoreceptors. The totality of evidence spans molecular biophysics, mitochondrial proteomics, in vivo bioenergetics, preclinical retinal disease models, and controlled clinical imaging and functional outcomes, allowing a sober assessment of strengths and residual risks.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SRT1720 is a fully synthetic small molecule initially discovered through high‐throughput screening by Sirtris Pharmaceuticals, which sought potent alternatives to the naturally occurring polyphenol resveratrol. Unlike resveratrol—which suffers from low bioavailability, poor metabolic stability, and broad non‐selective target interactions—SRT1720 belongs to the class of synthetic Sirtuin Activating Compounds (STACs) designed to selectively activate the NAD⁺‐dependent deacetylase SIRT1. Chemically, SRT1720 is based on an imidazo[1,2-b]thiazole scaffold and was optimized for its potency; studies have indicated that it is approximately 1000× more potent than resveratrol, with an EC1.5 value of around 0.16 μM and impressive maximal activation percentages in vitro (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Chang et al., 2024). The synthetic origins of SRT1720 represent a deliberate medicinal chemistry effort aimed at overcoming the limitations of natural SIRT1 activators. In the broader context, compounds in this class have been used as investigational drugs targeting pathways involved in metabolism, aging, inflammation, and stress tolerance, thereby establishing a framework for repurposing efforts across various disease areas (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Therapeutic History:  
Preclinical studies of SRT1720 have predominantly focused on its metabolic effects in rodent models characterized by diet-induced obesity, insulin resistance, and other forms of metabolic dysfunction. In these studies, administration of SRT1720 resulted in significant improvements in insulin sensitivity, reduction of plasma glucose levels, and enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis across metabolic tissues such as skeletal muscle, liver, and adipose tissues (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Donmez, 2012). Moreover, in genetically obese and high-fat diet animal models, SRT1720 has been demonstrated to improve mitochondrial function, as indicated by increased ATP production, elevated expression of mitochondrial proteins such as ATP synthase β and NDUFB8, and enhanced oxidative metabolism (Funk et al., 2010). This modulatory effect on mitochondrial biogenesis and function is thought to be mediated via the SIRT1-PGC-1α pathway—a mechanism that has garnered attention in age-related diseases where mitochondrial dysfunction is central. Although SRT1720 has not been directly investigated in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models or explicitly in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, the underlying pathogenic processes in dry AMD—namely, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysregulation—share significant overlap with the tissues previously demonstrated to benefit from SRT1720 treatment (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009). This cross-tissue efficacy provides a compelling rationale to explore SRT1720’s repurposing for dry AMD. Additionally, related compounds in this class (e.g., SRT2104) have advanced into clinical development for other indications, further suggesting that the pharmacological modulation of SIRT1 is a viable therapeutic approach (Hoppner et al., 2014).

Mechanism of Action:  
The underlying mechanism of action of SRT1720 centers on its ability to allosterically activate SIRT1, a key regulator of cellular energy metabolism and stress responses. SIRT1 is an NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase that modulates the activity of various transcription factors and co-regulators, notably PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ coactivator 1-α), which is a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. SRT1720 binds to an allosteric site on the SIRT1 enzyme-peptide substrate complex, situated amino terminal to the enzyme’s catalytic domain. This binding facilitates a conformational change in SIRT1 that lowers the Michaelis constant (K_m) for the acetylated substrates, thereby enhancing the rate of deacetylation (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Wan, 2021). Biochemical assays have demonstrated that SRT1720 increases SIRT1 deacetylase activity in a dose-dependent manner, leading to reduced acetylation of PGC-1α and thus promoting its transcriptional activity in driving mitochondrial gene expression (Funk et al., 2010). In addition to PGC-1α, SRT1720-mediated SIRT1 activation influences the acetylation status of several other proteins involved in stress responses and apoptosis, including FOXO1 and PPARγ, which collectively contribute to improved cellular resilience against oxidative damage (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Hoppner et al., 2014). Of note, many studies have confirmed that the beneficial effects observed with SRT1720 are abrogated in the presence of SIRT1 inhibitors such as nicotinamide and sirtinol, providing strong evidence for a SIRT1-dependent mode of action (Funk et al., 2010; Djouadi & Bastin, 2019). However, it is important to acknowledge that there has been some controversy regarding whether SRT1720 and its structural relatives directly interact with SIRT1 or exert off-target effects; nonetheless, the preponderance of kinetic and biophysical data supports the view that SRT1720 is primarily a SIRT1 activator (Hoppner et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2024).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration:  
Dry AMD is characterized by the degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) accompanied by chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and an overall decline in cellular energy homeostasis. The hypothesis for repurposing SRT1720 in this context is based on its well-documented ability to stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis and enhance oxidative capacity in multiple tissue types. In the RPE, which is a post-mitotic and metabolically demanding cell layer critical for photoreceptor survival, mitochondrial dysfunction is a key pathological feature that contributes to the progression of dry AMD. By activating SIRT1, SRT1720 is expected to promote deacetylation of PGC-1α, thereby upregulating a transcriptional program that enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and repair. This, in turn, would improve oxidative phosphorylation, reduce the production of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), and bolster the cells’ ability to cope with the chronic oxidative stress that underlies dry AMD pathology (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Furthermore, studies in other tissues, such as aged skeletal muscle and hepatocytes, have shown that SRT1720 reduces mtROS and restores cellular ATP levels by increasing mitochondrial number and function (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Funk et al., 2010). It is reasonable to extrapolate that similar benefits could be achieved in RPE cells, where preserved mitochondrial function is essential for maintaining retinal integrity and preventing progression to geographic atrophy, the advanced form of dry AMD. Expression analyses have demonstrated that both SIRT1 and PGC-1α are expressed in RPE cells, and their activities are critical for retinal health; thus, modulation of the SIRT1–PGC-1α axis by SRT1720 offers a mechanistic basis for its expected protective effects in the RPE (Hoppner et al., 2014; Alcaín & Villalba, 2009). It is anticipated that in assays using RPE cell cultures, treatment with SRT1720 will lead to enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis—as evidenced by increased mitochondrial DNA content, elevated levels of mitochondrial proteins, and improved cellular ATP production—while concurrently attenuating markers of oxidative stress. These effects would collectively improve the oxidative resilience of RPE cells, thereby potentially slowing or halting the progression of dry AMD (Funk et al., 2010; Hoppner et al., 2014).

Overall Evaluation:  
There are several compelling strengths associated with the use of SRT1720 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. First, its synthetic design has led to a compound that is remarkably more potent than resveratrol, addressing one of the key limitations of natural SIRT1 activators. This enhanced potency, coupled with a clearly elucidated mechanism of action involving allosteric activation of SIRT1, provides a robust biochemical rationale for its efficacy. The observed effects in metabolic, hepatic, and renal systems—where SRT1720 has demonstrated significant improvements in mitochondrial biogenesis and reductions in oxidative stress—are highly relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells plays a central role (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009).

Another strength is the extensive preclinical data supporting the involvement of the SIRT1-PGC-1α axis in regulating mitochondrial function and cellular energy homeostasis. Since RPE cells share similar reliance on these pathways for maintaining cellular function and resisting oxidative injury, it is plausible that SRT1720 can be effectively translated into a therapeutic for dry AMD. Moreover, the fact that SRT1720’s effects are abrogated by SIRT1 inhibitors reinforces the notion that its beneficial actions are directly linked to SIRT1 activation rather than resulting from non-specific off-target activities, a point underscored by multiple biochemical studies (Wan, 2021; Funk et al., 2010).

However, there are also notable weaknesses and uncertainties that warrant consideration. Although SRT1720 has a well-characterized profile in terms of metabolic and mitochondrial effects in other tissue types, there is a paucity of data directly pertaining to ocular tissues or RPE cells. The retinal environment possesses unique pharmacokinetic and physiological characteristics, and the ability of SRT1720 to reach effective concentrations in the RPE upon systemic or local administration remains to be determined. Moreover, while the SIRT1-PGC-1α axis is a promising target, some studies have raised controversies concerning whether SRT1720 truly acts as a direct SIRT1 activator or if its effects might be partially mediated by off-target pathways, which could complicate both efficacy and safety profiles (Hoppner et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2024). There is also the broader issue of translating findings from systemic models of mitochondrial dysfunction to the highly specialized context of the eye, which may require careful consideration of formulation, dosing regimen, and potential adverse effects that are specific to ocular tissues.

The overall evaluation suggests that SRT1720 has a strong scientific foundation based on its potent SIRT1 activation, its capacity to enhance mitochondrial biogenesis, and its demonstrated ability to mitigate oxidative stress in multiple preclinical models (Alcaín & Villalba, 2009; Funk et al., 2010). Liproxstatin-1 is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor of ferroptosis that was originally discovered using phenotypic high-throughput screening in systems where ferroptosis was induced by either genetic deletion of GPX4 or by glutathione depletion with agents like erastin (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69). In contrast to classical phenolic antioxidants such as α-tocopherol, Liproxstatin-1 is designed to operate in the lipid bilayer, where its aminic (or diarylamine) moieties are less hindered by nonproductive hydrogen-bonding interactions with phospholipid headgroups, thus allowing rapid hydrogen-atom transfer to lipid peroxyl radicals (Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). Although detailed synthetic routes are not provided in the available reports, the discovery process clearly identifies Liproxstatin-1 as a lead candidate that emerged from unbiased cell-based screens aimed at identifying compounds that preserve cell viability in the absence of GPX4 function (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). Its categorization as an RTA is significant because this class of compounds has a long history of being used to inhibit free radical–mediated damage in both industrial and biological contexts (Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6).

Therapeutic History:  
The preclinical history of Liproxstatin-1 is rich with evidence supporting its role as a potent inhibitor of ferroptosis. Early studies demonstrated that Liproxstatin-1 acts at low nanomolar concentrations to prevent ferroptotic cell death in mouse embryonic fibroblasts as well as in specialized cells rendered vulnerable by GPX4 inactivation (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Angeli et al., 2014, p. 10). Beyond in vitro cell survival assays, Liproxstatin-1 has been evaluated in vivo where it has shown remarkable protective effects in models of acute tissue injury including genetic GPX4 deficiency, which induces acute renal failure, and in ischaemia/reperfusion models of liver injury (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10). Although its direct clinical use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) has not been established – with most in vivo data coming from non-ocular models – its success in ameliorating tissue damage by inhibiting lipid peroxidation suggests its potential utility in other degenerative pathologies where oxidative membrane damage drives dysfunction, such as in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) degeneration underlying geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69; Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–21). Moreover, related compounds, notably Ferrostatin-1, have been tested in various retinal cell models and in some in vivo settings pertaining to retinal ischemia–reperfusion injury and oxygen-induced retinopathy, further bolstering the therapeutic concept of using RTA-type ferroptosis inhibitors in ocular settings (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23; Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8). While the bulk of Liproxstatin-1’s therapeutic history centers on its role as an anti-ferroptotic agent in cancer, neurodegeneration, and acute organ failure, its mechanistic overlap with key pathological features observed in dry AMD – such as iron accumulation, glutathione depletion and elevated lipid peroxidation in the RPE – supports evaluating it as a repurposed candidate in this context (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Shen et al., 2025, pp. 1–2).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism by which Liproxstatin-1 exerts its cytoprotective effect is rooted in its function as a radical-trapping antioxidant. Specifically, Liproxstatin-1 reacts rapidly with lipid peroxyl radicals that propagate the autoxidation chain reaction in cellular membranes. Experimental data have established that Liproxstatin-1 exhibits an intrinsic reaction rate constant (k_inh) in the range of approximately 2.4 × 10^5 M^−1 s^−1 in organic solvents such as chlorobenzene at 37 °C, which is comparable to industrial diarylamine antioxidants (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 8–9). Although its intrinsic reactivity in homogeneous organic solutions may appear lower than classical phenolic antioxidants like α-tocopherol, its performance in the lipid bilayer is superior due to reduced hydrogen-bonding interactions with phospholipid headgroups – a feature that enhances its mobility and reactivity in the lipid environment where ferroptosis is executed (Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 8–9; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). The compound functions primarily by donating a hydrogen atom from its arylamine (or diarylamine) N–H group, effectively quenching chain-propagating lipid peroxyl radicals before they can perpetuate lipid hydroperoxide formation (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). Kinetic isotope effect studies and computational analyses have confirmed that the N–H bond dissociation enthalpy is sufficiently low in Liproxstatin-1 to enable rapid hydrogen-atom transfer, which is a critical step in its radical-trapping mechanism (Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 2–3, 5–7). Importantly, Liproxstatin-1 does not exert significant inhibitory effects on enzymes such as human 15-lipoxygenase-1, thereby ruling out an enzymatic inhibition mechanism and reinforcing that its protective effect is solely attributable to non-enzymatic scavenging of peroxyl radicals (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 201–210). Recent studies have even suggested that Liproxstatin-1 may form a complex with iron in certain cellular compartments (e.g., the lysosome), which could further diminish iron-catalysed radical generation under acidic conditions; however, the predominant and well-characterized mechanism remains its role in intercepting lipid peroxyl radicals (Rodriguez et al., 2024, pp. 1–5; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). In the context of dry AMD, particularly in geographic atrophy where RPE degeneration is a hallmark, the expected effect of Liproxstatin-1 would be to curtail the chain reaction of lipid peroxidation that underpins ferroptotic cell death. In vitro assays using RPE cell lines such as ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cells have demonstrated that targeting lipid peroxidation – as evidenced by reductions in markers like BODIPY-C11 oxidation and ACSL4 expression – can rescue cells from oxidative stress–mediated death (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–23). Liproxstatin-1 is anticipated to mitigate the accumulation of lipid hydroperoxides, thus preserving the integrity of cellular membranes and mitochondrial function in the RPE (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Given that geographic atrophy in dry AMD is associated with iron overload and subsequent iron-catalysed lipid peroxidation, the ability of Liproxstatin-1 to trap peroxyl radicals is particularly significant; by reducing lipid ROS, it is expected to prevent the conversion of polyunsaturated fatty acids into cytotoxic lipid hydroperoxides, thereby maintaining cellular viability (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). Moreover, the inhibition of ACSL4-dependent peroxidation pathways – which have been linked to ferroptosis in RPE cells – may also be intercepted by Liproxstatin-1, providing a dual line of defense against ferroptotic signaling (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23; Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8). On a cellular level, the compound is expected to maintain Δψm and reduce indicators of oxidative stress, as previously demonstrated in models addressing GPX4 inhibition (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). In animal models where ferroptosis contributes to tissue degeneration (such as renal or hepatic ischaemia/reperfusion models), treatment with Liproxstatin-1 resulted in reduced TUNEL-positive cell counts and ameliorated tissue injury; these outcomes provide a rationale for its application in preclinical dry AMD models, where similar pathological processes – including mitochondrial dysfunction, iron dysregulation, and excessive lipid peroxidation – are observed (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Peng et al., 2020, pp. 3–5). In essence, when applied to RPE cells under conditions that mimic dry AMD, Liproxstatin-1 should decrease oxidative markers, prevent cell death, and thereby slow or halt the progression of geographic atrophy by restoring the balance between pro-oxidant and antioxidant pathways (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–23).

Liproxstatin-1 stands out as a promising candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic agent against dry AMD, particularly in geographic atrophy, given the mechanistic overlap between ferroptosis and RPE cell death observed in dry AMD. One of its principal strengths lies in its potent radical-trapping antioxidant activity, which is not only effective at low nanomolar concentrations but also uniquely suited to the lipid bilayer environment of the RPE (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). Its discovery through unbiased screening in ferroptosis-susceptible models and its demonstration of efficacy in multiple organ systems provide a strong foundation for its repurposing in dry AMD. The evidence supports that Liproxstatin-1 could counteract the iron-driven ROS amplification and lipid peroxidation that contribute to RPE cell death in geographic atrophy. Nonetheless, while its mechanistic rationale and preclinical promise are substantial, further research – particularly within retinal models – is necessary to fully evaluate its therapeutic potential and address challenges related to ocular delivery and multi-pathway disease components. Taken together, Liproxstatin-1 represents a compelling candidate for further investigation as a targeted inhibitor of ferroptosis in the treatment of dry AMD (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69, 207–210; Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23).
