Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) is an endogenous bile acid, a taurine conjugate of ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), that was originally isolated from bear bile and is now produced synthetically for laboratory and clinical research (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). As a member of the bile acid family, TUDCA has a dual role: its traditional function in lipid digestion is accompanied by potent signaling activities that provide chemical chaperoning properties. This property enables TUDCA to stabilize misfolded proteins and alleviate endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. In addition, TUDCA exerts anti-apoptotic effects by modulating the mitochondrial cell death pathway. Its application as a neuroprotectant has emerged over the last decade, and its favorable ocular safety profile in preclinical studies has invited consideration for repurposing in retinal degenerative conditions such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020).  

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, TUDCA and related bile acids have been evaluated in several models of neurodegeneration and retinal degeneration. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that TUDCA protects retinal cells against both oxidative injury and ER stress. In vitro, TUDCA treatment of ARPE-19 retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) not only attenuated cell death but also reduced markers of oxidative damage, increased cell viability, and modulated antioxidant gene expression (Alhasani et al., 2020). In parallel, multiple in vivo studies have reported that systemic administration of TUDCA reduces photoreceptor apoptosis and preserves retinal structure and function in animal models of inherited retinal degeneration including retinitis pigmentosa and in models of exudative AMD such as laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024). Although the bulk of these preclinical investigations has been conducted in models focusing on photoreceptors, retinal ganglion cells, or vascular endpoints, the underlying mechanisms of TUDCA’s cytoprotective activity raise the possibility that its benefits may extend to the RPE—the cell type that is centrally involved in dry AMD and geographic atrophy. Importantly, little direct evidence exists from dedicated geographic atrophy models or experiments that solely target RPE mitochondrial endpoints; however, the promising biochemical and electrophysiological data from rodent models suggest that the candidate’s safety and overall neuroprotective profile are well established in ocular systems (Alhasani et al., 2020; Li et al., 2024).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanistic basis of TUDCA’s therapeutic potential is multifaceted. A central theme is its ability to reduce ER stress in cells that are undergoing chronic protein-folding challenges. Under conditions of sustained stress, the unfolded protein response (UPR) is activated, and key transcription factors such as CHOP (CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein homologous protein) become upregulated to drive cell death when the stress is unmanageable. TUDCA has been shown in various cell models to act as a chemical chaperone, thereby reducing ER stress and suppressing CHOP induction (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020). For instance, in ARPE-19 cell models treated with thapsigargin to induce ER stress, TUDCA treatment led to a marked decrease in CHOP expression and reduced apoptosis (Alhasani et al., 2020). This suggests that TUDCA modulates the ER stress response, possibly by stabilizing protein folding and facilitating the proper trafficking of misfolded proteins.  

In addition to its ER‐related effects, TUDCA exerts anti-apoptotic actions by stabilizing the mitochondrial membrane. Under stress conditions, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) triggers the intrinsic apoptosis pathway, characterized by the translocation of pro-apoptotic proteins such as Bax, the release of cytochrome c, and subsequent caspase activation (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Kusaczuk, 2019). Evidence from neuronal models and some retinal studies indicates that TUDCA prevents the depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane, thereby preserving Δψm, and reduces downstream apoptotic events. This effect has been linked to a reduction in mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), which are produced excessively when mitochondrial integrity is compromised. TUDCA’s actions in reducing overall intracellular ROS levels, as reported in H₂O₂-exposed RPE cells, further support the idea that improved mitochondrial function may contribute to cell survival (Alhasani et al., 2020).  

Moreover, TUDCA can modulate additional cellular pathways that are pertinent to retinal health. It has been reported to up-regulate antioxidant defenses via increased expression of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) and enhancement of glutathione (GSH) levels. These effects likely contribute to the reduction in both cytosolic and mitochondrial oxidative stress (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Other studies have highlighted TUDCA’s influence on phagocytic pathways in the RPE—for example, by promoting MerTK-mediated phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments—which, although not directly linked to ER or mitochondrial stress, represent an important aspect of RPE physiology that could indirectly improve cell survival in degenerative conditions (Murase et al., 2015).  

Taken together, the biochemical and molecular data indicate that TUDCA’s mechanism of action is well aligned with addressing the cellular stress observed in dry AMD. By inhibiting CHOP induction, preserving Δψm, and reducing mtROS, TUDCA could feasibly stop or slow the progression of RPE cell death that underpins geographic atrophy (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

Expected Effect:  
The proposal hypothesizes that TUDCA will reduce ER stress in the RPE, thereby preventing secondary mitochondrial dysfunction and the associated production of reactive oxygen species. In the proposed assay, RPE cells (either ARPE-19 or primary RPE cultures) subjected to an ER stressor (such as thapsigargin or H₂O₂) are expected to exhibit elevated markers of ER stress, particularly CHOP, along with signs of mitochondrial distress including decreased mitochondrial membrane potential and increased mtROS production. On treatment with TUDCA at appropriate dosages (often in the 100 μM range in similar in vitro assays), one expects to observe a significant reduction in CHOP induction along with the preservation or restoration of Δψm, as measured by fluorescent indicators such as JC-1 or TMRM, and a concomitant decrease in mitochondrial ROS as assessed by probes such as MitoSOX. These effects are expected because prior in vitro studies in retinal cells have shown that TUDCA can ameliorate cell death by modulating oxidative stress and apoptosis, and similar outcomes have been observed in neuronal and non-retinal cell models (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

RPE cells express high levels of ER stress markers under pathologic conditions, and proteins such as CHOP are known mediators of apoptosis in these cells. It is therefore expected that TUDCA will attenuate the cascade of events initiated by ER stress—reducing apoptotic signaling, preserving mitochondrial function, reducing mtROS, and ultimately leading to enhanced cell viability. As such, the anticipated outcome in the proposed assay is a clear biochemical and functional improvement in RPE cultures challenged with ER stressors, supporting the use of TUDCA in dry AMD (Alhasani et al., 2020).  

Overall Evaluation:  
TUDCA presents as a promising candidate for drug repurposing in dry AMD due to its well-documented roles as an ER stress inhibitor and mitochondrial stabilizer. Its prior use in ocular contexts and a favorable safety profile in animal models provide important translational support. However, one potential weakness in repurposing TUDCA for dry AMD is that most of the preclinical evidence is derived from models of photoreceptor degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, or choroidal neovascularization rather than from targeted assessments in RPE cells or dry AMD models. Another consideration is that the multifaceted nature of dry AMD pathogenesis extends beyond ER stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Nonetheless, the broad-spectrum anti-apoptotic and anti-oxidative actions of TUDCA provide a strong rationale for its further examination in dry AMD.  

In summary, TUDCA is a highly attractive candidate for repurposing as a therapy for dry AMD based on its natural origin as a bile acid, its established use as a chemical chaperone and mitochondrial stabilizer, and its demonstrated neuroprotective and cytoprotective effects in multiple retinal models. Its capacity to reduce ER stress—with particular inhibition of CHOP induction—and to preserve mitochondrial membrane potential and lower oxidative stress aligns well with the proposed mechanism underlying RPE degeneration in geographic atrophy. However, critical gaps remain in the direct evidence for its efficacy in RPE-specific systems and AMD/dry AMD models. The next steps should include rigorous experimental validation in relevant in vitro and in vivo models to establish that TUDCA indeed preserves Δψm and suppresses mitochondrial ROS in ER-stressed RPE cells while reducing pro-apoptotic markers such as CHOP. If these endpoints can be achieved in targeted preclinical studies, TUDCA could represent a promising, safe, and mechanistically rational therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020).

BAM15 (Sigma-Aldrich SML1888) is a synthetic, lipophilic mitochondrial uncoupling agent that was discovered and subsequently optimized to achieve a mild protonophoric effect on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

SB 290157 is a synthetic small‐molecule compound that functions as an antagonist of the C3a receptor (C3aR). Chemically, it is defined as N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine, a structure that incorporates an arginine residue with an acyl modification incorporating a 2,2-diphenylethoxy moiety (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). SB 290157 was discovered through high-throughput screening efforts aimed at identifying molecules capable of displacing radiolabeled C3a from its receptor. Early screening identified a lead compound that underwent extensive chemical optimization – including solid-phase peptide and peptidomimetic synthesis using Fmoc‐based chemistry on Wang resin – to yield SB 290157 (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011). This synthetic approach, employing coupling reagents such as 1-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)-3-ethylcarbodiimide hydrochloride and 4-dimethylaminopyridine, resulted in a non-peptide molecule designed to maximize receptor affinity while minimizing metabolic instability. The compound is commercially available from suppliers such as Cayman Chemical (catalog #10006619) and has served as a prototypic small-molecule C3aR antagonist in numerous preclinical studies (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017).

SB 290157 falls within the broader class of synthetic GPCR modulators that target complement receptors. Historically, such molecules have been exploited as biochemical tools to interrogate the role of anaphylatoxins in inflammatory responses (Ames et al., 2001). C3a, a 77-residue protein fragment produced during complement activation, is recognized by its GPCR, C3aR, and triggers diverse cellular responses (Ames et al., 2001). Multiple research groups have employed small-molecule antagonists like SB 290157 to elucidate the contribution of C3a-mediated signaling in conditions ranging from arthritis to lung inflammation (Ames et al., 2001). The compound’s synthetic origin and chemical tractability have allowed investigators to probe receptor pharmacology in heterologous cell lines (e.g., RBL-C3aR cells, ARPE-19 cells) and primary human cell systems (Ames et al., 2001). In the context of ocular research, SB 290157 has been used experimentally in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) models – particularly in primary human fetal RPE cultures – to block C3a-induced alterations in extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

Beyond its established utility as a research tool, the use of SB 290157 in ocular models speaks to an emerging rationale for targeting complement signaling in degenerative eye diseases. Its inclusion in a commercial catalog further underscores its ready availability to laboratories, enabling reproducibility and fostering further experimentation. In summary, SB 290157 is a synthetic, non-peptide, arginine-based antagonist belonging to a class of compounds that have historically been used to interrogate complement receptor signaling, with a well-defined chemical structure, known synthesis protocols, and broad preclinical application in inflammation research (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011).

Therapeutic History

SB 290157 has a storied history in the complement research field. Its initial characterization, as detailed by Ames and colleagues, revealed that SB 290157 competes for C3a binding with an IC₅₀ in the high‐nanomolar range (approximately 200 nM) and potently inhibits C3a-induced intracellular calcium mobilization in sensitive cell lines, such as RBL cells and human neutrophils (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Early studies validated its functional capacity as a selective antagonist in vitro, establishing that it effectively blocked receptor internalization and attenuated downstream signaling events elicited by C3a binding.

Preclinically, SB 290157 has been deployed in a wide range of experimental disease models. In the arthritis model, administration of SB 290157 resulted in a significant reduction (approximately 41%) in paw edema, while in airway inflammation models it suppressed neutrophil recruitment, demonstrating its anti-inflammatory efficacy (Ames et al., 2001). SB 290157 exerts its biological effects by competitively binding to the C3a receptor (C3aR), thereby preventing the interaction of endogenous C3a with its receptor. Preclinical studies in RPE cells indicate that it can prevent C3a-induced sub-RPE deposit formation and proteasome impairment—a finding directly relevant to the early pathological events of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In vivo, its administration in models of retinal injury (such as NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration and laser-induced retinal vein occlusion) has correlated with reduced photoreceptor death, decreased gliosis, and improved retinal architecture (Wang et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2025). These findings collectively underscore the compound’s potential to modulate complement-mediated pathology in the ocular setting.

Nonetheless, SB 290157 is not without its weaknesses. A significant concern noted across several studies is its variable pharmacological behavior. Under some experimental conditions, particularly in cell systems with high receptor density, SB 290157 exhibits partial agonist activity rather than pure antagonism (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001). This paradoxical behavior could lead to unintended receptor activation and potentially undermine its therapeutic benefit, especially in chronic conditions like dry AMD where long-term receptor blockade is desired. Furthermore, while there is compelling preclinical evidence supporting its beneficial impact on mitochondrial function and ECM homeostasis, direct experimental data linking SB 290157 to a reduction in mitochondrial ROS production and consequent suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation in ARPE-19 or primary RPE models remain incomplete or indirect (Wang et al., 2020; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Behnke, 2022). This gap in the literature necessitates further investigation to firmly establish the causal chain from C3aR inhibition to inflammasome modulation.

Another consideration is the translational challenge. SB 290157 has been predominantly utilized as a research tool rather than a clinical candidate. Its pharmacokinetic profile—while adequate for short-term animal experiments—has not been thoroughly characterized for long-term use in ocular applications, where issues such as retinal toxicity, ocular bioavailability, and sustained receptor occupancy become critical. The delicate environment of the retina requires highly specific and safe compounds; thus, the partial agonist activity and potential off-target effects of SB 290157 raise valid concerns regarding its safety profile in humans (Mathieu et al., 2005; Tan et al., 2024).

On the other hand, the dual benefit of SB 290157—in preventing not only aberrant complement signaling but also the downstream mitochondrial dysfunction that leads to inflammasome activation—directly addresses central pathogenic mechanisms in dry AMD. Given that dry AMD is characterized by chronic inflammation, RPE dysfunction, and progressive atrophy correlated with mitochondrial impairment, a drug that can simultaneously modulate these pathways offers a novel therapeutic angle. Conversely, its partial agonist behavior in certain systems and the current lack of direct evidence linking its action to reduced mtROS and NLRP3 activation in ocular models raise legitimate concerns that must be addressed prior to clinical translation (Mathieu et al., 2005; Behnke, 2022).

Overall, SB 290157 is a compelling candidate for further exploration and mechanistic validation as a repurposed drug for dry AMD, provided that additional research can surmount the challenges associated with its pharmacodynamic variability and confirm its protective effects in retina-specific models.

────────────────────────────────────────  
Conclusion

The comprehensive literature evaluation indicates that SB 290157’s synthetic origins, established use as a C3aR antagonist, and demonstrated efficacy in preclinical models of complement-mediated RPE injury make it a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its mechanism—blocking C3a-induced signaling that otherwise leads to mitochondrial calcium overload, impaired proteostasis, and subsequent inflammasome activation—is highly relevant to the pathophysiology of geographic atrophy. However, the compound’s documented partial agonist effects and potential variability in receptor blockade require careful consideration and further optimization. Additional studies are necessary to firmly establish that SB 290157 can reduce mitochondrial ROS and suppress NLRP3 inflammasome activation in RPE cells under conditions that model dry AMD clinically. Thus, while SB 290157 is an excellent tool for dissecting the complement–mitochondria crosstalk in dry AMD, its suitability as a long-term therapeutic will depend on resolving these outstanding issues through rigorous preclinical and mechanistic evaluation (Ames et al., 2001; Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Mathieu et al., 2005).

Overall, the candidate shows substantial promise as a mechanistic probe and potential therapeutic agent for dry AMD; its ability to block key complement-mediated events that contribute to RPE dysfunction and inflammation positions it as a novel target for drug development. However, given the documented limitations, further studies are strongly recommended to optimize its receptor selectivity, define its pharmacokinetic and safety profile in the ocular context, and conclusively demonstrate its capacity to mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammasome activation in relevant models before advancing it into clinical trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Spermidine is a naturally occurring polyamine that was originally discovered in bovine semen and later shown to be ubiquitous in all forms of life, ranging from bacteria and plants to fungi and mammals. It belongs to the aliphatic polyamine class, characterized by its low molecular weight, linear arrangement, and multiple amino groups that are fully protonated at physiological pH. Its natural origins stem from highly conserved enzymatic biosynthetic pathways—starting either from ornithine via ornithine decarboxylase or from arginine through an agmatine intermediate—resulting in the formation of putrescine, which is subsequently converted to spermidine through the transfer of an aminopropyl group provided by decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine (dcSAM) (Casero & Marton, 2007; Hobley et al., 2017; Khomutov et al., 2019). Although spermidine can be isolated from natural sources such as food and tissues, it is also available in a chemically defined form commercially (for example, Sigma-Aldrich S2626) and has been used in basic research as well as in some experimental therapeutic approaches. This compound is representative of the polyamine family, and these molecules have traditionally been investigated for their roles in cellular proliferation, nucleic acid stabilization, and modulation of various enzymatic activities, which in turn have broad implications for health and disease (Madeo et al., 2020; Nichugovskiy et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, spermidine’s potential therapeutic applications have been explored extensively in the context of its ability to induce autophagy and affect cellular homeostasis. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that spermidine supplementation can extend lifespan and improve the function of various tissues by enhancing autophagy, contributing to cardioprotection, and promoting neuroprotection in animal models (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). In the ocular domain, several studies have examined its effects on retinal cells: in vitro experiments using ARPE-19 retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells have shown that spermidine can protect against oxidative stress induced by hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) by mitigating intracellular calcium overload and maintaining mitochondrial integrity (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021). Additionally, there are preclinical observations in which intravitreal administration of spermidine in animal models produced both protective effects—in terms of reducing RPE apoptosis—and, at higher doses, toxic outcomes such as RPE necrosis and photoreceptor degeneration (Ohashi et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022). Although spermidine has not been clinically trialed specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), its effects on RPE survival and ocular inflammation have been documented in models that mimic some of the pathophysiologic stressors in dry AMD, such as oxidative damage and dysregulated autophagy (Kim et al., 2021; Senekowitsch et al., 2023). In addition, dietary supplementation studies in humans have associated higher spermidine intake with various beneficial health outcomes, including improved endothelial function and cognitive performance; however, the use of spermidine or polyamines more broadly in chronic degenerative ocular conditions remains largely in the preclinical stage (Madeo et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
The hypothesized mechanism for using spermidine in dry AMD is multifaceted and centers on its ability to modulate cellular quality control processes. At the molecular level, spermidine is known to induce autophagy, a process that mediates the degradation and recycling of damaged or dysfunctional cellular constituents. In model systems ranging from yeast to mammalian cells, spermidine has been shown to increase the conversion of the autophagy marker LC3-I to LC3-II, thereby promoting autophagosome formation (Qin et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022). One important molecular target of spermidine appears to be EP300 (p300), a histone acetyltransferase that, when inhibited, leads to reduced acetylation of several autophagy-related proteins. Inhibition of EP300 has been correlated with enhanced autophagic flux, and several studies suggest that spermidine may exert its autophagy-inducing effects partly by downregulating EP300 expression or activity (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020).

In addition to its effects on EP300, spermidine has been implicated in the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), an evolutionarily conserved energy sensor that modulates metabolic homeostasis and mitochondrial quality control. Activation of AMPK can lead to the phosphorylation and activation of downstream effectors that promote both autophagy and mitophagy (the selective autophagic removal of damaged mitochondria). While direct evidence for AMPK activation by spermidine in retinal cells is still emerging, broader studies in other cell types have described an upregulation of pathways associated with mitochondrial biogenesis and quality control, including the deacetylation of proteins by SIRT1, which often acts in concert with AMPK (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). In the specific context of RPE cells under stress from A2E (a component of lipofuscin) or H₂O₂, the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria and high levels of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) play critical roles in cell loss and dysfunction; thus, induction of mitophagy via enhanced AMPK signaling and subsequent Parkin recruitment to depolarized mitochondria could improve mitochondrial homeostasis and reduce oxidative damage (Kim et al., 2021).

Furthermore, spermidine’s role as an intracellular calcium chelator appears pivotal in its protective effect in RPE cells. Studies have demonstrated that pre-treatment of ARPE-19 cells with 10 µM spermidine prior to oxidative stress prevents intracellular Ca²⁺ overload—a phenomenon that can trigger endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and cell death—thereby maintaining cellular integrity independent of direct ROS scavenging (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021). In summary, spermidine is posited to enhance the clearance of damaged organelles—particularly mitochondria—by increasing autophagic flux through EP300 inhibition and AMPK activation, leading to enhanced LC3-II conversion and Parkin-mediated mitophagy. This, in turn, is expected to reduce mtROS and protect RPE cell viability under conditions of oxidative and A2E-induced stress (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
Based on its mode of action, the expected effect of spermidine in a dry AMD model would be a pronounced improvement in the quality control mechanisms of RPE cells. The compound is anticipated to induce autophagy, evidenced by a measurable increase in LC3-II levels, alongside enhanced recruitment of the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin to dysfunctional mitochondria. This concerted activation of autophagy and mitophagy should facilitate the clearance of damaged mitochondria, thereby reducing the accumulation of mtROS and attenuating oxidative stress. In the context of A2E accumulation—a key driver of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD—spermidine is predicted to restore mitochondrial function and improve cell viability. Experimental assays are expected to show that spermidine pre-treatment leads to a significant reduction in apoptosis markers (e.g., caspase-3 activation, cytochrome c release), along with improved markers of mitochondrial integrity (e.g., stabilized mitochondrial membrane potential) in ARPE-19 cells exposed to H₂O₂ or A2E (Kim et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating spermidine as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses emerge from the current literature. One major strength is its natural origin and well-documented role as a global inducer of autophagy and mitophagy. This aligns well with the current understanding of dry AMD pathogenesis, in which impaired autophagic clearance and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells play major roles (Nichugovskiy et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2021). The ability of spermidine to inhibit EP300—a factor whose downregulation encourages autophagy—and to potentially activate AMPK signaling suggests that it could enhance several intracellular quality control processes simultaneously (Han et al., 2022; Madeo et al., 2020). The preclinical data showing that spermidine can protect ARPE-19 cells from H₂O₂-induced oxidative injury by blocking Ca²⁺ overload and reducing apoptotic signaling further bolster its potential utility in ocular applications (Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021).

However, there are notable challenges and weaknesses associated with this therapeutic candidate. First, the dose response appears to be remarkably narrow; while low micromolar concentrations (e.g., 10 µM) exert cytoprotective effects in vitro, higher doses have been associated with cytotoxicity, including RPE cell death and photoreceptor degeneration in animal models following intravitreal injection (Ohashi et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022). This raises concerns about the therapeutic window and the optimal route of delivery for chronic conditions like dry AMD. Another limitation is that, despite promising mechanistic data, direct clinical evidence for the use of spermidine in dry AMD is currently lacking. Most of the studies available have been conducted in vitro or in animal models under conditions of oxidative stress, and while these findings are encouraging, they do not fully recapitulate the complex pathophysiology of dry AMD, which involves not only oxidative damage but also chronic inflammation, immune dysregulation, and drusen accumulation (Kim et al., 2021).

Moreover, while the hypothesis emphasizes effects on EP300 inhibition and AMPK activation leading to enhanced LC3-II conversion and Parkin recruitment, the direct evidence linking these specific molecular events to improved outcomes in dry AMD models remains preliminary. There is a need for more comprehensive studies that directly measure these autophagic and mitophagic markers in RPE cells under conditions that mimic the A2E-induced stress typical of dry AMD (Kim et al., 2021). Additionally, the risk that spermidine’s metabolism by amine oxidases may produce toxic aldehyde byproducts such as acrolein must be carefully considered, as these compounds have been implicated in retinal degeneration in some intravitreal models (Ohashi et al., 2017).

In summary, while spermidine has a compelling mechanistic rationale as a modulator of autophagy and mitochondrial quality control, which are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the current preclinical evidence is mixed and highlights potential safety challenges related to dosing and administration. Its established role in promoting cellular longevity and mitigating oxidative stress in diverse tissues certainly warrants further investigation, but rigorous studies using dry AMD-specific models are essential to ascertain its efficacy and safety in this context. Regulatory considerations will also require detailed pharmacokinetic and toxicological profiling, particularly given its dual potential for both cytoprotection and cytotoxicity depending on concentration and route of administration (Ohashi et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022).

Overall, our evaluation suggests that spermidine represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD based on its intrinsic properties as an autophagy and mitophagy inducer and its ability to protect RPE cells from oxidative damage; however, its clinical translation will depend on resolving key issues such as dose optimization, route of delivery, and comprehensive validation of its proposed molecular mechanisms in relevant models of AMD. The strengths of spermidine lie in its natural occurrence, multi-targeted action on cellular quality control mechanisms, and established preclinical benefits in other models of aging and oxidative stress. Conversely, the main weaknesses are its narrow therapeutic window, the potential for generation of toxic metabolites, and the current lack of direct clinical or robust in vivo data in dry AMD models. Further research, including detailed investigations in RPE models using A2E and oxidative stress conditions as well as careful titration studies in animal models of dry AMD, is warranted to determine its viability as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for this unmet clinical need (Casero & Marton, 2007; Kim et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022; Ohashi et al., 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
BGP-15 is a synthetic, small-molecule nicotinic amidoxime/hydroxylamine derivative whose full chemical name is O-(3-piperidino-2-hydroxy-1-propyl) nicotinic amidoxime, typically used as a dihydrochloride salt; it was developed by N-Gene (US/Hungary) and has been described as water-soluble and mitochondria-targeting in preclinical studies (including ocular applications) (Takács et al., 2024; Horváth et al., 2021). Chemically and pharmacologically, BGP-15 belongs to the hydroximic/hydroxylamine acid derivative family originally advanced as membrane-interacting heat-shock response (HSR) co-inducers that remodel cholesterol-enriched plasma membrane rafts, with pleiotropic, cytoprotective effects in stressed tissues (membrane-lipid therapy) (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011). In parallel, the compound has been positioned as a nicotinamide-related, non-carboxamide “NAM analogue” with in vitro mixed-type (noncompetitive) PARP-1 inhibition, though the authors emphasize that in vivo protective effects likely involve additional mechanisms beyond direct PARP blockade because the in vitro inhibitory concentration exceeds achievable systemic levels (Crul et al., 2013). Independent biophysical and cellular studies show BGP-15 partitions into membranes, increases the fluidity of negatively charged lipid species, preserves heat-challenged raft integrity, and activates stress signaling linked to HSP induction; imaging and molecular dynamics support a direct membrane-interacting mode of action (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

Functionally, BGP-15 is best classified as a multifunctional HSP co-inducer and insulin-sensitizing, mitochondria-targeting cytoprotective agent that remodels membrane rafts, enhances the HSF1–HSP axis, and modulates stress and survival signaling (Akt up, JNK/p38 down), while lowering mitochondrial ROS and stabilizing Δψm; importantly, it preferentially acts in stressed cells, an attribute that underpins its safety rationale (Gombos et al., 2011; Sumegi et al., 2017). The compound concentrates in energized mitochondria driven by its delocalized positive charge, with >85–90% uptake into isolated mitochondria under experimental conditions (Sümegi, 2018). Mitochondrial studies consistently localize the dominant ROS-lowering effect to the respiratory chain at complexes I and III, with minimal direct antioxidant chemistry, and only mild uncoupling at millimolar concentrations that is irrelevant at the micromolar doses used in most cell studies (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018).

Crucial nomenclature caveat: a distinct “BGP-15” reported by a different group denotes a calcipotriene-derived vitamin D3 analog with anticancer activity; this vitamin D3 analog is mechanistically and structurally unrelated to the nicotinic amidoxime HSP co-inducer described above (both were labeled “BGP-15” by their respective originators) (Sintov et al., 2013). For the current program, the candidate of interest is the nicotinic amidoxime/hydroxylamine HSP co-inducer (often supplied by N-Gene or commercial chemical vendors under the amidoxime name), not the vitamin D3 analog (Takács et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
BGP-15 and closely related hydroximic/hydroxylamine acid derivatives have an extensive preclinical history across cardiac, neural, hepatic, renal, skeletal muscle, pulmonary, and metabolic models, with multiple mechanistic readouts converging on membrane remodeling, HSR/HSP co-induction, MAPK and Akt pathway modulation, and mitochondrial protection (Sumegi et al., 2017). Cardiovascular protection has been reported in ischemia–reperfusion, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation, with actions that include reduced ROS, preserved mitochondrial function, and Akt activation with suppression of JNK/p38 (Sumegi et al., 2017). In spontaneously hypertensive rats, BGP-15 increased PGC-1α and mitochondrial mass, decreased interstitial fibrosis, increased MKP-1 and reduced p38/JNK phosphorylation, and activated Akt/GSK-3β signaling (Horváth et al., 2021). BGP-15 prevented imatinib cardiotoxicity, protected against cisplatin nephrotoxicity without impairing antitumor efficacy, and mitigated cisplatin/taxol peripheral neuropathy (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). Hepatoprotection against acetaminophen injury via inhibition of caspase-independent cell death has also been documented (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). In pulmonary arterial hypertension and severe muscular dystrophy models, BGP-15 preserved mitochondrial structure and function and slowed disease progression; mechanistically, mitochondrial fusion via OPA1 activation and Akt signaling were implicated (Szabó et al., 2018).

Neuroprotection and mitochondrial rescue have been demonstrated in vitro and in vivo, including reduced neuronal death and improved mitochondrial potential/ROS at axonal branch points, coupled to HSP72 elevation, reduced phospho-JNK/p38, and enhanced Akt/IGF1R signaling (Ohlen et al., 2017). Consistent with its membrane-raft mechanism, BGP-15 increased HSP expression during heat challenge and remodeled cholesterol-rich platforms that gate stress signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).

In ophthalmology, BGP-15 has been applied in multiple retinal disease contexts. It was reported retinoprotective in Goto–Kakizaki rats (type 2 diabetes) with functional preservation on ERG, and later shown to improve survival and retinal function long-term in ZDF rats under uncontrolled diabetes, with increased ocular HSP70 and decreased NFκB (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021). Topical ocular delivery using an SBECD-containing eyedrop improved scotopic/photopic a- and b-waves, restored oscillatory potentials, shortened implicit times, and preserved retinal thickness following global ischemia–reperfusion injury in rats (Takács et al., 2024). These ocular data align with the compound’s mitochondrial and HSP co-inducer mechanisms: accumulation in mitochondria, protection against apoptosis/necrosis in oxidative-stress paradigms, and modulation of stress signaling (Takács et al., 2024).

Clinically, BGP-15 has a proof-of-concept randomized, double-blind trial demonstrating dose-dependent improvement of insulin sensitivity in insulin-resistant patients without apparent short-term toxicity; in parallel, human phase II work in olanzapine-induced metabolic disorder also identified BGP-15 as an insulin sensitizer (Crul et al., 2013; Sümegi, 2018). Safety signals from early human studies and the pharmacology of HSP co-inducers (preferential action in stressed cells) support the translational risk profile; however, systemic serum concentrations reported by the developer are low (≤25 nmol/mL), which has implications for target engagement and favors local ocular delivery for retinal indications (Gombos et al., 2011; Sumegi et al., 2017).

To our knowledge based on the supplied corpus, BGP-15 has not been directly tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) patients or canonical dry AMD animal models; however, its retinoprotective efficacy in diabetic retinopathy models and retinal ischemia–reperfusion suggests relevance to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)/photoreceptor stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammation, which are central to dry AMD biology (Takács et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Membrane-lipid therapy and HSP co-induction. BGP-15 partitions into and remodels membrane lipid domains, particularly cholesterol-rich plasma membrane rafts that organize stress sensing and signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). Under heat stress or analogous perturbations, BGP-15 preserves raft integrity and elevates HSP expression; this is associated with activation of Rac1 and modulation of HSF1 acetylation, leading to prolonged HSF1 DNA binding and robust HSP gene induction without causing protein unfolding, a hallmark of HSP “co-inducers” (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). In HSR-defective melanoma cells, BGP-15 significantly rescued raft domain coverage and shifted the size distribution toward larger platforms, coincident with increased hsp25 expression and Rac1-dependent stress signaling (Gombos et al., 2011). Across cell and tissue contexts, BGP-15 increases HSP70/HSPA1A (HSP72), and this HSP gain is causally linked to improved insulin signaling and cytoprotection in stressed cells (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011).

PARP/NAD+/SIRT1/HSF1 axis. Although BGP-15 demonstrates mixed-type (noncompetitive) inhibition of PARP-1 in vitro, the concentrations required exceed typical in vivo exposures, suggesting that PARP pathway effects in vivo are likely downstream of ROS lowering and reduced DNA single-strand breaks that otherwise drive PARP activation (Crul et al., 2013). In stressed cells, BGP-15 reduces PAR levels, which relieves PARP-mediated suppression of MKP-1/Dusp1, thereby inhibiting JNK/p38 activation; reduced PARP activity also preserves NAD+ and SIRT1 activity, which favors a deacetylated, active HSF1 and a stronger HSR (Crul et al., 2013). This mechanistic loop—less ROS, less PARP activation, more MKP-1, less JNK/p38, and better HSP/SIRT1 tone—aligns with the observed anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective phenotypes (Crul et al., 2013).

Mitochondrial enrichment and respiratory chain modulation. Biophysically, BGP-15 carries a delocalized positive charge, accumulates in energized mitochondria (>85–90% uptake in isolated organelles), and at micromolar doses characteristic of cell studies (1–50 µM) lowers mitochondrial ROS predominantly at complexes I and III without significant baseline depolarization of Δψm (Sümegi, 2018; Sumegi et al., 2017). In oxidative or inflammatory challenges, BGP-15 attenuates H₂O₂- and LPS-induced mitochondrial depolarization and reduces mitochondrial superoxide to near-control levels; MitoTEMPO controls confirm mitochondrial origin of the ROS signal (Sumegi et al., 2017). Importantly, the compound exhibits no meaningful direct antioxidant scavenging in cell-free ROS-generating systems, and only displays mild uncoupling at millimolar concentrations—far above the micromolar exposures used in protective assays—supporting a mechanism of respiratory chain modulation rather than redox scavenging (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018). Downstream signaling reflects the lowered mitochondrial ROS burden: JNK/p38 activation is reduced, Akt signaling is enhanced, and caspase-independent death pathways are suppressed (Sumegi et al., 2017).

Mitochondrial dynamics, fusion, and biogenesis. Beyond acute ROS control, BGP-15 promotes mitochondrial fusion and preserves cristae architecture by activating OPA1 GTPase and promoting OPA1 polymerization; genetic suppression of OPA1 or Mfn1/Mfn2 abolishes the fusion phenotype, indicating that BGP-15 acts upstream or within the endogenous fusion machinery (Szabó et al., 2018). In vivo, these effects translate into improved mitochondrial ultrastructure and tissue histology under ROS stress (e.g., monocrotaline-induced PAH) (Szabó et al., 2018). In hypertensive cardiomyopathy, BGP-15 increases PGC-1α and mitochondrial mass, with concurrent shifts in CREB/AMPK phosphorylation consistent with improved energetic signaling, reduced p38/JNK via MKP-1 upregulation, and increased Akt/GSK-3β prosurvival signaling (Horváth et al., 2021).

Insulin-sensitizing stress signaling. In skeletal muscle and human studies, BGP-15 increases HSP72 expression, enhances insulin receptor autophosphorylation (blocking JNK inhibitory phosphorylation), activates RAC1, increases AKT phosphorylation, promotes GLUT4 translocation, increases membrane fluidity, raises AMPK activity, and reduces HSF1 acetylation, altogether improving glucose disposal without overt toxicity in a randomized trial (Crul et al., 2013). These metabolic effects are mechanistically congruent with the membrane–HSR–mitochondrial triad described above (Crul et al., 2013).

Ocular and retinal mechanisms. In rat eyes, BGP-15 increased HSP70 and decreased NFκB, consistent with HSR enhancement and anti-inflammatory signaling in ocular tissues (Wachal et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion and diabetic retinopathy models, functional improvements on ERG, restoration of oscillatory potentials, and preservation of retinal thickness are consistent with mitochondrial protection and stress-response reinforcement in retinal cells (Takács et al., 2024). The topical SBECD formulation demonstrated pharmacologic activity in the retina without systemic pharmacokinetic characterization, indicating local ocular delivery as a viable route for targeting mitochondrial and HSP pathways in the posterior segment (Takács et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
The team’s hypothesis—that BGP-15 stabilizes mitochondrial membrane proteins and co-induces HSF1-driven antioxidant chaperone responses in RPE to mitigate oxidative stress in dry AMD—is aligned with the compound’s demonstrated pharmacology in retinal, cardiac, neural, and pulmonary models: (i) robust mitochondrial enrichment and stabilization of Δψm under oxidative/inflammatory stress, (ii) ROS lowering at complexes I and III without direct radical scavenging, (iii) activation of the HSR via membrane raft remodeling and HSF1 acetylation control, and (iv) suppression of ROS-sensitive injury cascades (JNK/p38) with concurrent activation of pro-survival Akt (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013). In retinal disease models, BGP-15 improved ERG measures and retinal thickness and increased ocular HSP70 while decreasing NFκB, providing a direct ocular precedent likely to translate to stressed RPE, where mitochondria and proteostasis are central to survival under chronic oxidative load (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021).

Mechanistically expected in RPE:  
- Membrane-raft remodeling and HSR co-induction. BGP-15 partitions into RPE membranes and remodels cholesterol-rich rafts, preserving raft integrity under stress, activating Rac1, decreasing HSF1 acetylation, and prolonging HSF1 DNA binding, thereby elevating HSP70/HSP25 and enhancing proteostasis capacity in aged/stressed RPE (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).  
- Mitochondrial ROS containment and Δψm preservation. BGP-15 should accumulate in RPE mitochondria, reduce ROS production at complexes I/III, and attenuate oxidative- and inflammation-induced depolarization, thereby maintaining ATP production and limiting mitochondrial permeability transition and AIF translocation, as shown in other cell types (Sumegi et al., 2017; Sümegi, 2018).  
- Mitochondrial dynamics and biogenesis. Via OPA1 activation and Akt/GSK-3β signaling, BGP-15 is expected to promote inner-membrane fusion/OPA1 oligomerization and preserve cristae, with possible longer-term increases in mitochondrial biogenesis (PGC-1α), all protective features for RPE faced with chronic oxidative and lipofuscin stress (Szabó et al., 2018; Horváth et al., 2021).  
- Anti-inflammatory signaling rebalancing. By reducing mitochondrial ROS and PARP activation, BGP-15 should relieve PARP-mediated suppression of MKP-1, suppress JNK/p38 activity, decrease NFκB signaling, and bolster SIRT1-HSF1 activity, thereby reducing ROS-amplifying feed-forward loops in RPE (Crul et al., 2013; Wachal et al., 2021).

Assay expectations and endpoints. In standard RPE cell models (primary human RPE, ARPE-19, or iPSC-RPE), BGP-15 at 1–50 µM should (i) reduce H₂O₂- or LPS-induced mitochondrial depolarization (JC-1/TMRM), (ii) lower mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX) and total ROS (DHR123) without acting as a direct antioxidant in cell-free assays, (iii) reduce apoptosis/necrosis after oxidative challenge (annexin V/PI), (iv) increase HSP70/HSF1 pathway activation and decrease HSF1 acetylation, (v) activate Akt and downregulate JNK/p38, and (vi) promote OPA1 oligomerization and mitochondrial fusion (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Szabó et al., 2018). Where possible, complement activation or lipid peroxidation paradigms can be layered to emulate dry AMD stressors; based on the corpus, BGP-15’s effects are strongest under stress, consistent with HSP co-inducer pharmacology (Gombos et al., 2011).

Delivery considerations. Systemic exposures in humans are low (≤25 nmol/mL), suggesting that oral dosing may be insufficient to reach pharmacologic micromolar levels in RPE; conversely, topical ocular delivery with SBECD has demonstrated retinal functional benefits and structural protection, supporting development of a posterior-segment–targeted topical or periocular formulation to enrich the RPE–choroid compartment (Sümegi, 2018; Takács et al., 2024).

Caveats regarding target expression. The corpus documents the relevant targets (HSF1/HSP70, Rac1, OPA1, MKP-1, JNK/p38, Akt) as central to BGP-15’s mechanisms in multiple mammalian tissues and cell types and shows ocular readouts (HSP70 up, NFκB down) in rat eyes; however, it does not provide explicit RPE expression data, which should be confirmed experimentally in our RPE assay systems (Wachal et al., 2021; Gombos et al., 2011; Szabó et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic congruence with dry AMD pathobiology. BGP-15 directly addresses mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic oxidative stress—core drivers of RPE degeneration—by concentrating in mitochondria, lowering ROS at complexes I/III, stabilizing Δψm, and activating survival signaling while suppressing inflammatory stress kinases (Sumegi et al., 2017). Concurrently, it co-induces the HSR by remodeling plasma membrane rafts and modulating HSF1 acetylation, thereby boosting HSP70/HSP25 chaperone capacity and proteostasis—functions that are expected to mitigate protein misfolding and aggregation in aged RPE (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013).  
- Demonstrated ocular efficacy in relevant retinal injury contexts. Topical BGP-15 improved ERG a- and b-waves, preserved oscillatory potentials, reduced implicit times, and rescued retinal thickness after ischemia–reperfusion, and it was retinoprotective in diabetic models, with ocular HSP70 increase and NFκB reduction—outcomes consistent with RPE/retinal resilience under oxidative stress (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021).  
- Pleiotropic yet coherent mechanism spanning membrane, nuclear, and mitochondrial nodes. The membrane–HSR–mitochondrial triad, including PARP/MKP-1/JNK–p38 and Akt/GSK-3β axes, provides multiple intervention points likely to translate into robust protection in the multifactorial environment of dry AMD (Crul et al., 2013; Sumegi et al., 2017; Szabó et al., 2018; Horváth et al., 2021).  
- Favorable translational signals. Proof-of-concept human trials in insulin resistance show pharmacodynamic activity without overt safety signals, and HSP co-inducers are known to preferentially act in stressed cells, potentially limiting off-target effects in quiescent tissues; local ocular delivery further improves the therapeutic index (Crul et al., 2013; Gombos et al., 2011; Takács et al., 2024).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Lack of direct dry AMD evidence. No studies in the corpus directly test BGP-15 in dry AMD models or patients; we infer utility from retinal IR/diabetes models and mechanism (Takács et al., 2024).  
- Exposure–response uncertainties for the posterior segment. Systemic serum concentrations are low relative to micromolar efficacious concentrations in vitro, necessitating optimized local delivery to RPE; although eyedrop formulations show retinal effects, posterior-segment delivery by topical route is often limited, and pharmacokinetics were not measured in the cited ocular study (Sümegi, 2018; Takács et al., 2024).  
- Target ambiguity and pleiotropy. While the membrane–HSR–mitochondrial framework is coherent, BGP-15 lacks a single defined receptor/protein target, and its in vitro PARP-1 inhibition likely does not drive in vivo efficacy; this complicates target engagement assays and regulatory narratives (Sümegi, 2018; Crul et al., 2013).  
- Nomenclature confusion. “BGP-15” also denotes a calcipotriene-derived vitamin D3 analog in the oncology literature; chemical identity must be verified to avoid conflation during procurement and CMC (Sintov et al., 2013; Takács et al., 2024).  
- Evidence base heterogeneity. Some ocular and cardiovascular studies are published in lower–quality venues, emphasizing the need for rigorous, blinded replication and GLP toxicology in ocular models (Horváth et al., 2021; Wachal et al., 2021).

Recommended next steps  
- In vitro RPE validation. In human primary or iPSC-derived RPE under oxidative (H₂O₂/tert-butyl hydroperoxide) and inflammatory (LPS/CpG) stress, test BGP-15 at 0.3–30 µM for effects on Δψm (JC-1/TMRM), mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX), total ROS (DHR123), apoptosis/necrosis (annexin V/PI), and mitochondrial respiration; confirm no direct antioxidant scavenging in cell-free systems (Sumegi et al., 2017).  
- Proteostasis and HSR endpoints. Quantify HSP70/HSP25 induction, HSF1 acetylation/binding dynamics, Rac1 activation, and membrane raft integrity using fPEG-cholesterol probes/TOCCSL in RPE; evaluate MKP-1, JNK/p38, and Akt/GSK-3β signaling (Gombos et al., 2011; Crul et al., 2013; Sumegi et al., 2017).  
- Mitochondrial dynamics. Assess OPA1 oligomerization, fusion/fission balance (Mfn1/2 and Drp1 markers), cristae morphology by EM, and PGC-1α/mtDNA copy number to benchmark fusion/biogenesis responses (Szabó et al., 2018; Horváth et al., 2021).  
- Ocular delivery PK/PD. Using the SBECD eyedrop formulation as a starting point, perform ocular pharmacokinetics (vitreous, retina, RPE–choroid) and pharmacodynamics (ocular HSP70, NFκB, mitochondrial markers) to ensure RPE target engagement at tolerated doses (Takács et al., 2024; Wachal et al., 2021).  
- In vivo retinal stress models. Extend to retinal oxidative stress paradigms that capture RPE pathology; leverage ERG, OCT, histology, and mitochondrial ultrastructure endpoints already positive in IR/diabetic models (Takács et al., 2024).  
- Identity control and CMC. Source BGP-15 as O-(3-piperidino-2-hydroxy-1-propyl) nicotinic amidoxime dihydrochloride; confirm identity by NMR/MS to avoid the calcipotriene-derived analog (Takács et al., 2024; Sintov et al., 2013).

Go/no-go considerations for dry AMD  
Given the robust mechanistic alignment—mitochondrial ROS control at complexes I/III, Δψm stabilization, HSR co-induction via membrane raft remodeling and HSF1 acetylation control, OPA1-driven mitochondrial fusion, and suppression of ROS-sensitive inflammatory kinases—plus demonstrable ocular efficacy in retinal injury models, BGP-15 merits advancement to RPE-focused preclinical validation for dry AMD (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Szabó et al., 2018; Takács et al., 2024). The principal risks are translational: ensuring adequate RPE exposures by ocular delivery, confirming RPE target expression/engagement, and generating rigorous GLP pharmacology/toxicology data in ocular species. On balance, the mechanistic breadth that often complicates development is an advantage in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction, proteostasis failure, and chronic inflammation coexist.

Conclusion. BGP-15 is a credible repurposing candidate for dry AMD based on its mitochondria-centered, HSP co-inducing, membrane-lipid–modulating pharmacology and encouraging retinal efficacy in vivo; priority should be given to RPE-targeted PK/PD, mitochondrial and HSR biomarker validation, and controlled efficacy studies in retinal oxidative-stress models to de-risk translation (Sumegi et al., 2017; Gombos et al., 2011; Takács et al., 2024).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
3-Mercaptopicolinic acid (3-MPA; also written 3-mercaptopicolinate/3-MP) is a small, thiol-containing picolinic-acid derivative historically identified as a biochemical inhibitor of gluconeogenesis through inhibition of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) and, at higher concentrations, glucose-6-phosphatase (G-6-Pase) in hepatic systems (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001). Early reports in the 1970s established 3-MPA as a preferential inhibitor of the cytosolic PEPCK isoform (PCK1), and the compound has since been used widely as a tool in mechanistic enzymology and physiology of gluconeogenesis across species and contexts (e.g., mammalian liver, pig, and protozoan PEPCKs) (Hidalgo et al., 2016; McLeod et al., 2019; Brearley et al., 2020). While the original discovery route is not detailed in the provided sources, a “convenient synthesis” was reported historically, and numerous structure–mechanism studies have refined the understanding of its binding behavior and chemical liabilities; by contrast, no data in the provided material indicate a natural origin (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001).

Chemically, 3-MPA belongs to the broader class of picolinic-acid–based, anionic, metal-coordinating inhibitors that engage the PEPCK active site by chelating the catalytically essential M1 divalent metal (typically Mn2+) via the ring nitrogen and exocyclic carboxylate; 3-MPA also contains a reactive free sulfhydryl group that drives both potency and time-dependent covalent reactivity with protein cysteines (McLeod et al., 2019). The picolinic-acid scaffold’s anionic, metal-binding character is a recognized design principle for PEPCK inhibitors and has been leveraged to build next-generation derivatives (e.g., 3-((carboxymethyl)thio)-picolinic acid, CMP) that seek to occupy both inner and outer subsites of the OAA/PEP pocket while reducing thiol-mediated liabilities (McLeod et al., 2019).

As a class, such PEPCK-directed small-molecule inhibitors have been applied as biochemical probes of gluconeogenic flux, as antihyperglycemic tools in preclinical metabolic studies, and as chemical probes to dissect PEPCK function in cancer and immunometabolism models; however, the field has wrestled with issues of thiol reactivity, complex multi-site binding kinetics, ADME/PAINS flags, and limited isoform selectivity, all of which complicate translation (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001; McLeod et al., 2019; Baptista et al., 2019; Hidalgo et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History  
3-MPA has a long track record as a research tool in hepatic metabolism. In perfused rat liver and in vivo rat studies, 3-MPA was used to blunt gluconeogenesis and lower blood glucose, with dosing paradigms including intraperitoneal administration (e.g., 100 mg/kg followed by 25 mg/kg three hours later) and 1 mM concentrations in perfusate to suppress fructose- or lactate/pyruvate-stimulated hepatic glucose production (Herling et al., 1998). More recently, 3-MPA has served as a comparator and positive control in modern PEPCK-targeted discovery programs, including enzyme assays against recombinant human cytosolic and mitochondrial PEPCK isoforms (PCK1/PCK2), CETSA target-engagement studies, cell-based functional assays (e.g., insulin secretion), and acute in vivo pharmacodynamic readouts (e.g., fasting glycemia five hours after 50 mg/kg IP administration) (Aragó et al., 2020). In several settings, 3-MPA reduces oncogenic phenotypes: it impairs anchorage-independent growth in MCF7 cells yet shows limited effects on glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in INS-1 cells, suggesting variable target engagement and a modest potency ceiling relative to newer chemotypes (Aragó et al., 2020).

3-MPA has been used to inhibit the mitochondrial isoform PEPCK-M (PCK2) in cancer models. In non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cell lines cultured under glucose deprivation, inhibition of human mitochondrial PEPCK by 3-MPA or genetic knockdown induced apoptosis, consistent with a reliance on PEPCK-mediated anaplerotic/cataplerotic cycling for survival under nutrient stress (Baptista et al., 2019). Computational docking studies against human PEPCK-M have used 3-MPA as a benchmark ligand to set score cutoffs and to elucidate canonical binding interactions (Mn2+ coordination; Arg/Lys salt-bridge network), aligning with structural insights from cytosolic isoforms (Baptista et al., 2019).

In melanoma models, 3-MPA (applied as a PCK1 inhibitor) sensitized vemurafenib-resistant tumors in vitro and in vivo by depressing pentose phosphate pathway–derived NADPH production and elevating ROS through KEAP1/Nrf2 axis modulation, thereby reversing resistance; here, 3-MPA increased oxidative stress rather than alleviating it (Ren et al., 2022). Across immunometabolism, 3-MPA (100 μM) reduced cytotoxic T lymphocyte effector functions and decreased maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) without altering basal glycolysis, indicating impaired mitochondrial respiratory capacity in activated T cells in which PEPCK-M predominates (Brownlie et al., 2025). In skeletal muscle myoblasts (C2C12), 3-MPA (0.25–1 mM) reduced proliferation and induced myogenic differentiation, with Pck2 transcripts predominant over Pck1; however, the compound interfered with enzymatic assays at ≥0.25–0.5 mM, complicating attribution to on-target inhibition (Brearley et al., 2020). Against porcine cytosolic PEPCK isoenzymes, 3-MPA exhibits mid-micromolar IC₅₀ (~65 μM) under saturating substrates and mechanistically mixed/complex kinetics (mixed non-competitive vs PEP; uncompetitive vs GDP/GTP), supporting dual-site binding behavior (Hidalgo et al., 2016).

No study in the provided literature assesses 3-MPA in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), retina, or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD); a comprehensive mechanistic and structural study of related PEPCK inhibitors explicitly contains no mention of eye/RPE/AMD systems, emphasizing that the extant knowledge base for 3-MPA is outside ophthalmology (McLeod et al., 2019). Absent any reported ocular or RPE use, 3-MPA should be regarded as a systemic/metabolic tool compound with evolving applications in cancer and immunometabolism rather than as a precedent therapeutic in retinal degenerations (McLeod et al., 2019).

Mechanism of Action  
Mechanistic biochemistry and structural work converge on a dual-mode model for 3-MPA action on PEPCK:
- Active-site (inner-subsite) binding and Mn²⁺ coordination: The picolinic-acid moiety of 3-MPA coordinates the catalytic M1 Mn²⁺ ion via the ring nitrogen and exocyclic carboxylate oxygen(s), occupying the “inner” OAA/PEP subsite in a manner analogous to oxalate and other carboxylate inhibitors; co-crystal analyses and docking corroborate metal coordination along with salt-bridge/ion-pairing to conserved basic residues (e.g., Arg104/Arg423/Lys261/Lys262 in vertebrate enzymes) (McLeod et al., 2019; Baptista et al., 2019).
- Secondary/allosteric site binding: 3-MPA can occupy a second site near/behind the P-loop, with two molecules bound simultaneously (n≈2 by ITC), producing complex kinetic signatures (mixed non-competitive behavior with respect to PEP/OAA and uncompetitive inhibition versus GDP/GTP), and allowing allosteric influence on substrate/inhibitor binding at the active site (Hidalgo et al., 2016).

Kinetically, these binding modes yield mixed patterns that depend on the variable substrate: mixed non-competitive versus PEP/OAA; uncompetitive versus GDP/GTP, consistent with inhibitor binding to enzyme–nucleotide complexes and allosteric communication to the catalytic pocket (Hidalgo et al., 2016). Across isoforms, micromolar potency is typical: for rat cytosolic PEPCK (rcPEPCK) Kᵢ ~8 μM, for human mitochondrial PEPCK (hmPEPCK) Kᵢ ~3 μM in some determinations, though reported IC₅₀/Kᵢ values vary with assay format and metal/substrate conditions (McLeod et al., 2019). Variability is expected given that picolinic-acid derivatives chelate divalent metal cations; changes in available Mn²⁺ can partially masquerade as noncompetitive inhibition (i.e., by depleting active holoenzyme) in kinetic plots if not tightly controlled (McLeod et al., 2019).

A distinguishing chemical feature of 3-MPA is the free thiol. In vitro, the thiol can form mixed disulfide adducts with reactive cysteines on PEPCK (e.g., C288 on the P-loop in rat cytosolic PEPCK), producing time-dependent, covalent inactivation that contributes to potency but also to off-target reactivity and interpretational complexity; this chemistry is mitigated but not eliminated by inclusion of reducing agents in assays (McLeod et al., 2019). The thiol’s promiscuity likely explains reports of irreversible, time-dependent inhibition of G-6-Pase at millimolar concentrations, a phenomenon exploited historically to dissect gluconeogenic regulation but pharmacologically undesirable for selective PEPCK targeting (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001; McLeod et al., 2019). Because the M1 metal and a basic electrostatic microenvironment (e.g., Arg104/Arg423/Lys261/Lys262) are conserved in PEPCK-M and PEPCK-C, inhibitors that rely on metal chelation and anionic interactions, like 3-MPA, are predicted to show cross-isoform activity; docking against the human mitochondrial isoform reproduces these hallmarks (Baptista et al., 2019).

Several functional studies corroborate that 3-MPA perturbs cellular bioenergetics consistent with PEPCK inhibition but in cell-context-dependent ways. In activated effector T cells (PCK2-predominant), 100 μM 3-MPA reduced maximal OCR without changing basal ECAR, indicating compromised oxidative phosphorylation capacity while leaving basal glycolysis intact (Brownlie et al., 2025). In lung cancer cell lines, PEPCK-M inhibition by 3-MPA induced apoptosis only under glucose deprivation, highlighting the role of PCK2 in enabling biosynthesis from non-glucose substrates under stress (Baptista et al., 2019). Conversely, in BRAFi-resistant melanoma, PCK1 inhibition by 3-MPA depressed PPP-mediated NADPH synthesis, increased ROS by weakening antioxidant buffering (via KEAP1/Nrf2), and sensitized cells to targeted therapy, illustrating that PEPCK inhibition can amplify oxidative stress depending on metabolic wiring (Ren et al., 2022).

Finally, medicinal-chemistry and ADME flags apply. 3-MPA triggers PAINS warnings and violates the Pfizer 3/75 heuristic on polar surface area margins in in silico filtering, and its free thiol confers chemical reactivity that can perturb off-target proteins and auxiliary assay enzymes; analogs that remove the free thiol (e.g., thioethers like CMP) avoid mixed-disulfide inactivation at the cost of reduced potency (order-of-magnitude weaker Kᵢ) (Baptista et al., 2019; McLeod et al., 2019; Hidalgo et al., 2016).

Expected Effect  
The working hypothesis proposes that 3-MPA will inhibit mitochondrial PCK2 in RPE, redirecting flux toward TCA cycle maintenance, enhancing NADH generation, and reducing ROS during bioenergetic stress. Evidence from the supplied literature constrains and complicates each element of this chain:

- Direct engagement of PCK2 by 3-MPA. Biochemical and docking data support that 3-MPA inhibits human PEPCK-M with micromolar potency and establishes the binding physics (Mn²⁺ coordination; cationic pocket interactions), making PCK2 engagement in principle plausible in RPE if the protein is expressed and accessible (McLeod et al., 2019; Baptista et al., 2019). Strengths  
- Extensive mechanistic characterization and proven PEPCK engagement. 3-MPA’s dual-site binding, active-site metal coordination, and kinetic behavior are well described, with micromolar potency against both cytosolic and mitochondrial PEPCK isoforms under defined conditions, enabling precise hypothesis testing of PEPCK-dependent biology (McLeod et al., 2019; Hidalgo et al., 2016).

The compound reduces maximal OCR in activated T cells (PCK2-predominant), confirming that pharmacologic inhibition of PEPCK-M can reprogram OXPHOS in a predictable direction, albeit one that appears detrimental to respiratory capacity (Brownlie et al., 2025).

- Directionality of effect conflicts with the AMD hypothesis. Available cell-based data indicate 3-MPA reduces maximal mitochondrial respiratory capacity and can increase ROS in specific contexts by depleting PPP-derived NADPH, the opposite of the hypothesized benefit for RPE under bioenergetic/oxidative stress (Brownlie et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2022).  
- Chemical liabilities. The free thiol drives time-dependent covalent reactivity (mixed disulfides) with PEPCK and likely other proteins; at millimolar exposure, 3-MPA causes irreversible, time-dependent inhibition of G-6-Pase, underscoring a broad risk of off-target covalent modification that is unacceptable for ocular therapy without significant medicinal-chemistry mitigation (McLeod et al., 2019; Westergaard & Madsen, 2001). - Inconsistent target engagement in cells and modest potency relative to alternatives. - No precedent in retinal/RPE systems. The provided literature contains no data on 3-MPA in the eye, retina, RPE, or AMD models, and offers no RPE expression evidence for PCK2, making the translational leap speculative from the present corpus (McLeod et al., 2019; Yun, 2017).  
- Concentration-dependent assay interference and off-target effects. In C2C12 cells, 3-MPA interfered with PEPCK assays at ≥0.25–0.5 mM; perfused liver studies used 1 mM; such concentrations raise the likelihood of nonspecific effects in RPE (Brearley et al., 2020; Herling et al., 1998).  

Decision-Critical Gaps for AMD  
- Target validation in RPE. There is no evidence in the supplied material confirming PCK2 expression and activity in RPE, nor any demonstration that PEPCK-M–dependent cycling is maladaptive in dry AMD; this gap precludes mechanistic confidence (McLeod et al., 2019).  
- Directionality of benefit. The compound’s demonstrated tendency to reduce maximal OXPHOS capacity and, in some contexts, to enhance oxidative stress directly contradicts the intended pharmacology (increase NADH/OXPHOS; decrease ROS) in stressed RPE (Brownlie et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2022).

If the project’s strategic objective is to probe whether inhibiting PEPCK-M benefits RPE bioenergetic stability, a safer and more specific chemical tool would be required. Notably, thioether analogs like CMP remove the free thiol and still engage the active site competitively (albeit with ~10× weaker potency), and crystallography confirms occupancy of both inner and outer subsites; such molecules may offer cleaner on-target pharmacology for in vitro RPE studies while avoiding mixed-disulfide covalency (McLeod et al., 2019). However, even for such analogs, the directionality risk remains given that PEPCK-M inhibition has reduced mitochondrial respiratory capacity in mammalian cells that rely on this enzyme under activation stress (Brownlie et al., 2025).

Overall, based on the provided literature, I do not recommend prioritizing 3-MPA as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. The compound’s mechanistic actions and cell-level consequences in related systems predict outcomes counter to the proposed benefit in RPE, and its chemical liabilities are incompatible with ocular drug development without substantial medicinal-chemistry redesign (Brownlie et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2022; McLeod et al., 2019; Baptista et al., 2019).
