Below is a detailed evaluation of SB 290157 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (dry AMD). The review is organized into five sections: (1) Overview of Therapeutic Candidate; (2) Therapeutic History; (3) Mechanism of Action; (4) Expected Effect; and (5) Overall Evaluation. Each section combines biochemical, preclinical, and clinical considerations based solely on the provided context.

────────────────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

SB 290157 is a synthetic small‐molecule compound that functions as an antagonist of the C3a receptor (C3aR). Chemically, it is defined as N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine, a structure that incorporates an arginine residue with an acyl modification incorporating a 2,2-diphenylethoxy moiety (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). SB 290157 was discovered through high-throughput screening efforts aimed at identifying molecules capable of displacing radiolabeled C3a from its receptor. Early screening identified a lead compound that underwent extensive chemical optimization – including solid-phase peptide and peptidomimetic synthesis using Fmoc‐based chemistry on Wang resin – to yield SB 290157 (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011). This synthetic approach, employing coupling reagents such as 1-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)-3-ethylcarbodiimide hydrochloride and 4-dimethylaminopyridine, resulted in a non-peptide molecule designed to maximize receptor affinity while minimizing metabolic instability. The compound is commercially available from suppliers such as Cayman Chemical (catalog #10006619) and has served as a prototypic small-molecule C3aR antagonist in numerous preclinical studies (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017).

SB 290157 falls within the broader class of synthetic GPCR modulators that target complement receptors. Historically, such molecules have been exploited as biochemical tools to interrogate the role of anaphylatoxins in inflammatory responses (Ames et al., 2001). C3a, a 77-residue protein fragment produced during complement activation, is recognized by its GPCR, C3aR, and triggers diverse cellular responses (Ames et al., 2001). Multiple research groups have employed small-molecule antagonists like SB 290157 to elucidate the contribution of C3a-mediated signaling in conditions ranging from arthritis to lung inflammation (Ames et al., 2001). The compound’s synthetic origin and chemical tractability have allowed investigators to probe receptor pharmacology in heterologous cell lines (e.g., RBL-C3aR cells, ARPE-19 cells) and primary human cell systems (Ames et al., 2001). In the context of ocular research, SB 290157 has been used experimentally in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) models – particularly in primary human fetal RPE cultures – to block C3a-induced alterations in extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

Beyond its established utility as a research tool, the use of SB 290157 in ocular models speaks to an emerging rationale for targeting complement signaling in degenerative eye diseases. Its inclusion in a commercial catalog further underscores its ready availability to laboratories, enabling reproducibility and fostering further experimentation. In summary, SB 290157 is a synthetic, non-peptide, arginine-based antagonist belonging to a class of compounds that have historically been used to interrogate complement receptor signaling, with a well-defined chemical structure, known synthesis protocols, and broad preclinical application in inflammation research (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

SB 290157 has a storied history in the complement research field. Its initial characterization, as detailed by Ames and colleagues, revealed that SB 290157 competes for C3a binding with an IC₅₀ in the high‐nanomolar range (approximately 200 nM) and potently inhibits C3a-induced intracellular calcium mobilization in sensitive cell lines, such as RBL cells and human neutrophils (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Early studies validated its functional capacity as a selective antagonist in vitro, establishing that it effectively blocked receptor internalization and attenuated downstream signaling events elicited by C3a binding.

Preclinically, SB 290157 has been deployed in a wide range of experimental disease models. For instance, it has been used in animal studies examining anti-inflammatory activity in models such as guinea pig LPS-induced airway neutrophilia and adjuvant-induced arthritis in rats. In the arthritis model, administration of SB 290157 resulted in a significant reduction (approximately 41%) in paw edema, while in airway inflammation models it suppressed neutrophil recruitment, demonstrating its anti-inflammatory efficacy (Ames et al., 2001). These early demonstrations of anti-inflammatory activity provided the impetus to consider SB 290157 for further repurposing in conditions where complement overactivation contributes to pathology.

More recently, attention has turned to the role of complement in ocular diseases, particularly age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Experimental evidence in primary human fetal RPE cultures has shown that exposure to recombinant C3a for periods of 2–4 weeks results in the accumulation of sub-RPE deposits via increased ECM deposition, notably of collagens (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Importantly, co-treatment with a C3a receptor antagonist – which in many instances has been SB 290157 – successfully prevented the abnormal accumulation of sub-RPE deposits. These studies have helped establish a mechanistic link between C3a/C3aR activation and the proteostasis dysfunction observed in RPE cells, a pathological process believed to contribute to early AMD pathology.

In addition to in vitro data, in vivo models provide further support for the therapeutic potential of modulating C3aR signaling. In a murine model of sodium iodate (NaIO₃)-induced RPE injury – a model that recapitulates aspects of geographic atrophy – systemic administration of SB 290157 reduced photoreceptor death, decreased markers of gliosis and microglial activation, and lowered TNFα and STAT3 signaling levels (Wang et al., 2020). Similarly, in a laser-induced retinal vein occlusion (RVO) model, intravitreal injection of SB 290157 suppressed the up-regulation of both C3 and C3a receptor expression, correlating with partial rescue of retinal morphology and vascular integrity (Zhao et al., 2025). Although these studies were not specifically designed for dry AMD, the similarities in underlying complement-mediated RPE injury and chronic inflammation between these models and the dry AMD phenotype provide a strong rationale for further exploring SB 290157 in this indication.

Despite these promising applications, SB 290157’s therapeutic history is not without controversy. Several studies have reported that, depending on the cell type and receptor density, SB 290157 may exhibit partial agonist activity rather than acting as a pure antagonist (Mathieu et al., 2005). This variable pharmacological profile has raised concerns about its utility as a definitive clinical tool. Nonetheless, as a research probe, SB 290157 has significantly advanced our understanding of complement-mediated cellular responses in inflammatory, vascular, and ocular contexts. Overall, while it has been extensively used in preclinical studies across multiple disease models – including arthritis, lung inflammation, and retinal injury – its use specifically in clinical settings for dry AMD remains investigational (Ames et al., 2001; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Wang et al., 2020).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

SB 290157 exerts its biological effects by competitively binding to the C3a receptor (C3aR), thereby preventing the interaction of endogenous C3a with its receptor. Under normal conditions, the complement cascade, when activated via any of its pathways, leads to the cleavage of complement component C3 and the subsequent release of the anaphylatoxin C3a. This bioactive peptide binds to C3aR, a G protein-coupled receptor present on various cell types including granulocytes, monocytes, and notably retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Once activated, C3aR transduces signals that can lead to intracellular calcium mobilization, triggering a cascade of downstream events such as receptor internalization and activation of inflammatory transcription factors.

In vitro studies using radioligand binding assays have determined that SB 290157 displaces [¹²⁵I]-C3a from its receptor with an IC₅₀ in the high nanomolar range (approximately 200 nM), while functional calcium mobilization assays in cell lines (including RBL cells and human neutrophils) have demonstrated potent inhibition of C3a-stimulated intracellular calcium release at low nanomolar concentrations (approximately 28 nM) (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Mechanistically, by preventing C3a from engaging C3aR, the compound is able to avert subsequent receptor conformational changes that would otherwise lead to G protein coupling and downstream signaling events.

In the context of RPE cells, particularly under conditions of chronic oxidative stress – such as exposure to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) – C3a engagement of its receptor has been implicated in a range of deleterious cellular effects. Studies in ARPE-19 cells have shown that oxidative stress induces a redistribution of C3aR away from its typical plasma membrane localization and promotes its translocation toward the mitochondria (Ishii et al., 2021; Riihilä et al., 2019). At the mitochondrial level, activation of the receptor by C3a leads to an increase in mitochondrial calcium uptake, which in turn results in compromised respiratory function as evidenced by decreased state III (ADP-driven) respiration and reduced maximal respiratory capacity (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). The resultant mitochondrial dysfunction is highly likely to contribute to the generation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS). mtROS are known triggers for the NLRP3 inflammasome, which upon activation facilitates the processing of pro-IL-1β to active IL-1β, a cytokine strongly implicated in chronic inflammatory processes observed in AMD (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024).

Furthermore, in primary human fetal RPE models, prolonged exposure to recombinant C3a has been demonstrated to reduce the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (UPP) without altering mRNA levels for proteasome subunits, indicating a post-transcriptional impairment of proteostasis (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). This impairment in proteasome function is associated with an imbalance in ECM turnover – marked by a reduction in tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases (TIMP-3) abundance and an increase in matrix metalloproteinase (MMP-2) activity – culminating in the pathological deposition of extracellular matrix components (notably collagens IV and VI) beneath the RPE. Such sub-RPE deposit formation, or drusen, is one of the hallmarks of early AMD pathology (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

SB 290157, by blocking C3a from binding to C3aR, therefore interrupts these pathological cascades at two key junctures. First, it prevents the mitochondrial translocation and activation of C3aR in oxidatively stressed ARPE-19 cells, which is predicted to avert the associated mitochondrial calcium overload and respiratory inhibition, thereby reducing the likelihood of mtROS generation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). Second, by inhibiting C3a-induced receptor activation in RPE cells, SB 290157 preserves UPP activity, ensuring proper regulation of ECM component turnover and forestalling the aberrant deposition of sub-RPE material (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

It is important to note, however, that while the majority of evidence supports SB 290157 acting as an effective C3aR antagonist, several reports have cautioned that under certain conditions, the compound may display partial agonist activity. This means that rather than completely blocking receptor activation, SB 290157 might induce a low level of receptor signaling in some cellular contexts, especially when receptor density is high (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001). Such an effect must be carefully considered when interpreting experimental outcomes and when designing therapeutic strategies aimed at persistent modulation of complement activity. In all, the known mechanism of action for SB 290157 can be summarized as competitive inhibition of C3a binding to C3aR, thereby mitigating the downstream signals that lead to mitochondrial calcium dysregulation, proteasome impairment, ECM deposition abnormalities, and ultimately, NLRP3 inflammasome priming and IL-1β secretion (Ames et al., 2001; Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect

The central hypothesis underlying the use of SB 290157 in repurposing for dry AMD is that the blockade of C3aR will attenuate a cascade of deleterious events within the retinal pigment epithelium that contribute to disease progression. In particular, the expected effect is that SB 290157 will reduce complement-driven mitochondrial dysfunction, lower mtROS production, and thereby prevent the priming and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, resulting ultimately in diminished IL-1β secretion and preservation of RPE barrier integrity.

In dry AMD, chronic oxidative stress leads to dysregulated complement activation and subsequent accumulation of complement fragments such as C3a in the subretinal space. RPE cells under oxidative stress have been demonstrated to upregulate C3aR expression, with a portion of the receptor redistributing to the mitochondria—a change that is associated with an increased uptake of calcium into the mitochondria and a pronounced decline in mitochondrial respiratory function (Ishii et al., 2021; Riihilä et al., 2019). The resulting mitochondrial dysfunction is poised to increase the generation of mtROS, which serve as an upstream activator of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Activation of this inflammasome complex culminates in the maturation of IL-1β, a powerful proinflammatory cytokine that has been implicated in propagating RPE injury and the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024).

By competitively inhibiting C3a binding to its receptor, SB 290157 is expected to block these deleterious changes. In cultured ARPE-19 cells—which serve as a well-established model for human RPE—it is anticipated that SB 290157 will prevent the mitochondrial translocation of C3aR, thereby reducing abnormal mitochondrial calcium uptake and preserving normal respiration. This action should limit mtROS generation and consequently reduce the priming threshold for NLRP3 inflammasome activation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). Concurrently, in primary fetal RPE cultures, inhibition of C3aR signaling by SB 290157 has been shown to preserve the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, which in turn maintains the balance of matrix metalloproteinases and their tissue inhibitors. By doing so, the compound prevents the accumulation of sub-RPE deposits—a process that is intimately linked to the early phases of AMD pathology (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

The expression of C3aR in RPE cells, particularly in stressed conditions, is well-documented. This receptor is notably enriched on the basolateral membrane of RPE and even redistributes to mitochondrial compartments under oxidative stress conditions, as confirmed in ARPE-19 cell studies (Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Given that dry AMD is characterized by both heightened complement activation and chronic oxidative stress, the strategic inhibition of C3aR is expected to yield multiple beneficial outcomes: restoration of proteostasis, maintenance of mitochondrial function, reduction in chronic inflammatory cytokine expression, and preservation of the integrity and barrier function of the RPE monolayer. Moreover, in in vivo models such as NaIO₃-induced RPE injury or laser-induced retinal vein occlusion, treatment with a C3aR antagonist (presumably SB 290157) has been associated with reduced photoreceptor loss, attenuated microglial activation, and improved retinal morphology (Wang et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2025).

Furthermore, because mitochondrial reactive oxygen species serve as a trigger for the NLRP3 inflammasome, blocking the upstream signal via C3aR inhibition is hypothesized to break the vicious cycle of complement-mediated inflammation. The decreased activation of NLRP3 would lead to lower levels of IL-1β—a cytokine implicated in the autocrine and paracrine amplification of inflammation within the RPE layer—and thus stabilize the local microenvironment (Ong et al., 2024; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In summary, the expected effect of SB 290157 in the context of dry AMD is multifold: preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics, maintenance of proteasomal activity, prevention of pathological ECM accumulation, and attenuation of inflammasome-mediated inflammatory responses—all of which contribute to the protection of RPE integrity and function.

────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

SB 290157 stands out as one of the best-studied C3a receptor antagonists available today. Its well-documented chemical synthesis, robust in vitro pharmacological profile, and demonstrable efficacy in preclinical models of inflammatory injury provide strong support for its continued evaluation as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. The compound’s origins – as a product of high-throughput screening followed by medicinal chemistry optimization using Fmoc-solid phase techniques – are well established, and its chemical structure (N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine) clearly classifies it as a small-molecule non-peptide antagonist of a key complement receptor (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011).

Strengths of SB 290157 include its proven ability to block C3a-induced signaling cascades across a range of cell types and experimental models. Preclinical studies in RPE cells indicate that it can prevent C3a-induced sub-RPE deposit formation and proteasome impairment—a finding directly relevant to the early pathological events of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Additionally, evidence from ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress suggests that SB 290157 effectively inhibits aberrant mitochondrial Ca²⁺ uptake and consequent respiratory dysfunction—mechanisms known to contribute to mtROS generation and inflammasome activation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). In vivo, its administration in models of retinal injury (such as NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration and laser-induced retinal vein occlusion) has correlated with reduced photoreceptor death, decreased gliosis, and improved retinal architecture (Wang et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2025). These findings collectively underscore the compound’s potential to modulate complement-mediated pathology in the ocular setting.

Nonetheless, SB 290157 is not without its weaknesses. A significant concern noted across several studies is its variable pharmacological behavior. Under some experimental conditions, particularly in cell systems with high receptor density, SB 290157 exhibits partial agonist activity rather than pure antagonism (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001). This paradoxical behavior could lead to unintended receptor activation and potentially undermine its therapeutic benefit, especially in chronic conditions like dry AMD where long-term receptor blockade is desired. Furthermore, while there is compelling preclinical evidence supporting its beneficial impact on mitochondrial function and ECM homeostasis, direct experimental data linking SB 290157 to a reduction in mitochondrial ROS production and consequent suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation in ARPE-19 or primary RPE models remain incomplete or indirect (Wang et al., 2020; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Behnke, 2022). This gap in the literature necessitates further investigation to firmly establish the causal chain from C3aR inhibition to inflammasome modulation.

Another consideration is the translational challenge. SB 290157 has been predominantly utilized as a research tool rather than a clinical candidate. Its pharmacokinetic profile—while adequate for short-term animal experiments—has not been thoroughly characterized for long-term use in ocular applications, where issues such as retinal toxicity, ocular bioavailability, and sustained receptor occupancy become critical. The delicate environment of the retina requires highly specific and safe compounds; thus, the partial agonist activity and potential off-target effects of SB 290157 raise valid concerns regarding its safety profile in humans (Mathieu et al., 2005; Tan et al., 2024).

On the other hand, the dual benefit of SB 290157—in preventing not only aberrant complement signaling but also the downstream mitochondrial dysfunction that leads to inflammasome activation—directly addresses central pathogenic mechanisms in dry AMD. Given that dry AMD is characterized by chronic inflammation, RPE dysfunction, and progressive atrophy correlated with mitochondrial impairment, a drug that can simultaneously modulate these pathways offers a novel therapeutic angle. Conversely, its partial agonist behavior in certain systems and the current lack of direct evidence linking its action to reduced mtROS and NLRP3 activation in ocular models raise legitimate concerns that must be addressed prior to clinical translation (Mathieu et al., 2005; Behnke, 2022).

Overall, SB 290157 is a compelling candidate for further exploration and mechanistic validation as a repurposed drug for dry AMD, provided that additional research can surmount the challenges associated with its pharmacodynamic variability and confirm its protective effects in retina-specific models.

────────────────────────────────────────  
Conclusion

The comprehensive literature evaluation indicates that SB 290157’s synthetic origins, established use as a C3aR antagonist, and demonstrated efficacy in preclinical models of complement-mediated RPE injury make it a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its mechanism—blocking C3a-induced signaling that otherwise leads to mitochondrial calcium overload, impaired proteostasis, and subsequent inflammasome activation—is highly relevant to the pathophysiology of geographic atrophy. However, the compound’s documented partial agonist effects and potential variability in receptor blockade require careful consideration and further optimization. Additional studies are necessary to firmly establish that SB 290157 can reduce mitochondrial ROS and suppress NLRP3 inflammasome activation in RPE cells under conditions that model dry AMD clinically. Thus, while SB 290157 is an excellent tool for dissecting the complement–mitochondria crosstalk in dry AMD, its suitability as a long-term therapeutic will depend on resolving these outstanding issues through rigorous preclinical and mechanistic evaluation (Ames et al., 2001; Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Mathieu et al., 2005).

Overall, the candidate shows substantial promise as a mechanistic probe and potential therapeutic agent for dry AMD; its ability to block key complement-mediated events that contribute to RPE dysfunction and inflammation positions it as a novel target for drug development. However, given the documented limitations, further studies are strongly recommended to optimize its receptor selectivity, define its pharmacokinetic and safety profile in the ocular context, and conclusively demonstrate its capacity to mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammasome activation in relevant models before advancing it into clinical trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Apocynin (Sigma-Aldrich A1788) is a naturally derived, methoxy-substituted catechol originally isolated from the medicinal herb Picrorhiza kurroa, which has a long history of use in traditional Ayurvedic medicine. It is a small molecule with a molecular weight of approximately 166.17 Da and modest lipophilicity (logP ~ 0.83) that allows it to readily cross cellular membranes and even the blood–brain barrier. As a member of the NADPH oxidase (NOX) inhibitor class, it has been historically used to modulate oxidative stress in a variety of preclinical disease models. The compound’s origin is rooted in natural product chemistry, and its attractive small-molecule structure has encouraged detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic investigations in rodent models, where it has been administered intravenously and orally to assess tissue distribution and rapid clearance kinetics. Its chemical profile and natural derivation position it within a class of therapeutic candidates that have been widely evaluated for their antioxidant properties and their ability to attenuate NOX-mediated reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory diseases (Liu et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Preclinical studies have evaluated apocynin in a range of animal models that address oxidative stress–related pathologies. In cardiovascular and cerebrovascular research, for example, apocynin has been shown to reduce NADPH oxidase activity and resultant oxidative damage in models of isoproterenol-induced cardiac hypertrophy, diabetic cardiac remodeling, and brain oxidative stress associated with high-fat diets (Liu et al., 2020). Its pharmacokinetic profile in mice indicates a rapid plasma peak and an extremely short half-life of around 3–4 minutes after intravenous dosing, with extensive clearance by the kidneys (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2020). In respiratory research, a completed Phase 1 randomized trial in COPD patients demonstrated that nebulized apocynin was well tolerated, produced short-term reductions in exhaled oxidative markers such as hydrogen peroxide and nitrite, and did not affect lung function or systemic safety parameters (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010). Despite these encouraging results, there remains limited data on the longer-term systemic safety or adverse-event profiles of apocynin. Importantly, while apocynin has been extensively studied in cardiovascular and respiratory indications, as well as in models of neurodegeneration and hepatic and renal injury, there is minimal direct evidence of its use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models or in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells such as ARPE-19 (Drummond & Sobey, 2014). Nonetheless, since dry AMD pathogenesis involves oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction within the RPE, the demonstrated efficacy of apocynin in modulating NADPH oxidase–mediated ROS production in other organs builds a rationale for its repurposing for this indication.

Mechanism of Action:  
The central proposed mechanism by which apocynin exerts its therapeutic effects involves the inhibition of NADPH oxidase, particularly by blocking the assembly of the enzyme complex. NADPH oxidases are multi-subunit enzymatic complexes responsible for the regulated generation of superoxide and downstream reactive oxygen species. In cells, the assembly and activation of NOX, especially isoforms such as NOX2, require the translocation of cytosolic regulatory subunits—most notably p47^phox—to the membrane-bound catalytic core. Early studies reported that apocynin can prevent the translocation of p47^phox to the plasma membrane, thereby inhibiting the assembly of the active NOX2 complex and reducing the production of superoxide, which secondarily lowers the formation of hydrogen peroxide and other ROS (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Drummond & Sobey, 2014).  
However, the molecular pharmacology of apocynin is more complex. Its inhibitory activity appears to be dependent on metabolic activation by myeloperoxidase (MPO) in the presence of hydrogen peroxide. This conversion supposedly generates reactive quinone species or even a dimeric form (diapocynin) that can covalently modify cysteine residues in p47^phox, thus interfering with its function (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Ismaeel et al., 2018). Some studies, though, have failed to detect diapocynin in vivo, suggesting that other metabolites, such as apocynin glycoconjugates, might instead be responsible for its activity (Liu et al., 2020). Moreover, apocynin has been reported to possess direct antioxidant properties at higher concentrations by scavenging non-radical oxidants such as hypochlorous acid and hydrogen peroxide, independently of its effects on NOX assembly (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Ismaeel et al., 2018).  
In vitro studies in various cell types have yielded conflicting data regarding whether apocynin primarily functions as a NOX-specific inhibitor or as a broad-spectrum antioxidant. In cell types that are rich in peroxidase activity, such as neutrophils, apocynin’s conversion to an active inhibitor appears robust. In contrast, in cells with lower MPO activity, such as some epithelial or neuronal cells, its efficacy as a NOX inhibitor may be diminished, and observed benefits might be attributable to direct ROS scavenging (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2020). Within the context of RPE cells, the candidate hypothesis posits that apocynin will inhibit the translocation of p47^phox during NOX2 activation, thereby reducing cytosolic ROS production while also limiting the spillover of ROS into mitochondria, which would otherwise trigger mitochondrial membrane potential collapse, fragmentation, and reduced oxygen consumption rate (OCR) (Liu et al., 2020; Liu, 2023). This mechanism, if operative in RPE cells such as ARPE-19, would help preserve mitochondrial integrity by preventing excess ROS accumulation and the ensuing mitochondrial dysfunction—a key pathogenic process in dry AMD (Shu et al., 2023; Liu, 2023).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed mechanism, the use of apocynin in in vitro assays with ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE cultures is expected to yield several beneficial outcomes. First, by blocking p47^phox translocation, apocynin should reduce the assembly of the NOX complex, particularly NOX2, thereby decreasing the production of superoxide and hydrogen peroxide. This reduction in ROS should lead to lower levels of oxidative stress markers, as measured by assays such as lucigenin chemiluminescence, dihydroethidium (DHE) fluorescence, and malondialdehyde (MDA) assays (Liu et al., 2020).  
Second, because ROS are known to damage mitochondrial components, it is expected that apocynin treatment will protect against mitochondrial dysfunction. In ARPE-19 cells challenged with hydrogen peroxide or other oxidative stress inducers, apocynin should help preserve the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), prevent mitochondrial fragmentation, and maintain basal oxygen consumption rates (OCR). These mitochondrial endpoints are critical, as disruption of mitochondrial dynamics and energy production is a hallmark of RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Shu et al., 2023; Drummond & Sobey, 2014).  
Furthermore, given that NOX isoforms such as NOX2 and NOX4 have been implicated in the oxidative stress observed in retinal cells exposed to blue light or metabolic insults (Liu et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020), the inhibition of these enzymes with apocynin is expected to attenuate downstream pro-inflammatory signaling cascades. This should result in reduced upregulation of proangiogenic factors like VEGF and a decrease in inflammatory cytokine production that can exacerbate retinal degeneration. In effect, apocynin would act not only to maintain mitochondrial function by limiting local oxidative damage but also to modulate the broader redox environment that contributes to RPE cell dysfunction in dry AMD (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; Ismaeel et al., 2018).  
As a consequence, in the experimental assay proposed by the team, treatment of ARPE-19 cells with apocynin under conditions of induced oxidative stress should demonstrate a measurable preservation of Δψm by fluorescent imaging or flow cytometry using potentiometric dyes, maintenance of basal OCR as measured via Seahorse extracellular flux analysis, and a reduction in mitochondrial ROS accumulation by specific mitochondria-targeted ROS indicators. The reduction in NOX-derived ROS is expected to indirectly prevent mitochondrial fragmentation by mitigating the activation of mitochondrial fission pathways in response to oxidative injury (Liu, 2023; Liu et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
Apocynin represents a promising candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its potential to target a core pathogenic mechanism—the dysregulated production of ROS via NADPH oxidase assembly. One of the strengths of apocynin is its extensive preclinical history demonstrating its capacity to lower oxidative stress in various organs, including the heart, liver, brain, and lung, with documented rapid distribution to tissues and a well-characterized pharmacokinetic profile in animal models (Liu et al., 2020; Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014). Its observed safety in a small Phase 1 clinical study in COPD patients further bolsters the case for its safety on at least short-term administration in humans (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010). Moreover, its chemical simplicity as a natural product and its relatively low molecular weight make it attractive for further formulation studies in ocular indications.  
Nevertheless, significant weaknesses and challenges must be addressed. A major issue is the ongoing debate regarding the exact mechanism of action of apocynin. While some studies support its role as a NOX inhibitor via prevention of p47^phox translocation, others have demonstrated that its activity may be largely due to its direct antioxidant properties or require metabolic activation by MPO—a process that may not be robust in retinal pigment epithelial cells (Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014). This mechanistic ambiguity raises concerns about its efficacy and specificity in the RPE, where the peroxidase activity necessary for conversion to an active form may be limited.  
Furthermore, the extremely short plasma half-life (approximately 3–4 minutes) observed in rodent models indicates that apocynin is rapidly cleared, which could limit its therapeutic window and necessitate frequent dosing or the development of modified formulations such as a sustained-release ocular implant or a mitochondria-targeted derivative (e.g., mito-apocynin) to achieve prolonged local concentrations in the retina (Liu et al., 2020; Liu, 2023). This rapid clearance could also complicate the translation of in vivo results to a clinical setting for a chronic disease such as dry AMD.  
Another concern is that, despite the general rationale for reducing oxidative stress in the RPE, there is a paucity of direct evidence from ARPE-19 or primary RPE models showing that apocynin effectively prevents mitochondrial fragmentation, preserves the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), or maintains basal oxygen consumption rates. Although some studies have demonstrated that NOX inhibition can reduce ROS levels in retinal cells, apocynin’s specific action in the context of dry AMD has not been rigorously documented (Shu et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2020). Additionally, the variability of its effects across different cell types—dependent on the presence or absence of peroxidase activity—suggests that its efficacy in the RPE may be inconsistent, thereby necessitating further targeted studies.  
There is also the possibility of off-target effects. Because apocynin has been reported to act as a general antioxidant rather than a highly specific NOX inhibitor, it might interfere with normal redox signaling that is essential for cell survival and immune defense, particularly when applied systemically. Caution must be exercised to ensure that suppression of NOX activity does not inadvertently impair protective immune responses or lead to unwanted toxicity, even if short-term clinical data appears reassuring (Drummond & Sobey, 2014; Casas et al., 2015).  
In summary, while the mechanistic rationale behind using apocynin to inhibit NOX assembly in RPE cells is compelling, particularly given the central role of oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD pathogenesis, several critical questions remain. These include the precise mechanism by which apocynin exerts its effects in the RPE, the consistency of its efficacy in protecting mitochondrial function in ARPE-19 cells, its pharmacokinetic limitations, and its potential off-target effects. Overall, apocynin has strengths as a natural antioxidant with a history of reducing systemic oxidative stress in preclinical models and demonstrating short-term safety in human trials. However, its mechanism remains controversial, and its rapid clearance, potential variability in retinal cells, and limited direct evidence in AMD models represent significant weaknesses that must be overcome through further targeted biochemical, in vitro, and in vivo studies before advancing into clinical trials for dry AMD (Liu et al., 2020; Cifuentes-Pagano et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2010; Shu et al., 2023; Rohowetz et al., 2018; Liu, 2023).  
Given these considerations, further investigation into apocynin’s effects on mitochondrial protection and NOX inhibition in RPE cells is warranted. Such studies should include detailed assessments of p47^phox translocation in ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress, measurement of mitochondrial membrane potential (using dyes such as JC-1 or TMRE), and evaluations of OCR using Seahorse analysis. Moreover, efforts to optimize its pharmacokinetic profile—perhaps through formulation modifications or conversion to a mitochondria-targeted analogue—would address one of its key limitations. Only with these additional data can we determine whether apocynin holds sufficient promise to justify its repurposing for the treatment of dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring vitamin B3–class nucleoside and a leading NAD⁺ precursor that has been isolated from natural sources such as cow milk and other dietary materials, and is now produced by synthetic chemical means for therapeutic applications (Biță et al., 2023). NR belongs to the class of NAD⁺‐precursor nucleosides within the broader family of vitamin B3 compounds, the same family that includes nicotinic acid (NA) and nicotinamide (NAM), which historically have been used to prevent pellagra and improve cellular energy metabolism (Pîrvu et al., 2021; Biță et al., 2023). The synthetic production of NR involves the glycosylation of nicotinamide with appropriately protected ribofuranose donors via methods that require careful control due to the labile and reactive nature of its glycosidic bond, which often results in partial degradation during synthesis and storage (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). In order to overcome these issues, researchers have developed alternative stabilized forms such as NR borate, although the commercially available ChromaDex NR-100 is typically presented as the crystalline chloride salt (NRCl) and has become a benchmark for purity due to its improved manufacturing protocols and rigorous quality control (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Additionally, NR’s classification as an “orally bioavailable” NAD⁺ precursor distinguishes it from other precursors such as NMN by virtue of its ability to directly cross cell membranes without requiring extracellular conversion, with transport mediated by equilibrative nucleoside transporters (Mehmel et al., 2020; Biță et al., 2023). Taken together, these attributes place NR in a unique position as a repurposable compound with potential applications in metabolic, neurodegenerative, and now ocular diseases, including the dry forms of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) characterized by geographic atrophy (Biță et al., 2023; Braidy et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the use of vitamin B3 derivatives such as NA and NAM has been well established in both clinical and biochemical practice for the improvement of energy metabolism and for prevention of niacin deficiency diseases; however, nicotinamide riboside represents a more recently discovered alternative that offers superior pharmacokinetic profiles and fewer side effects such as flushing or liver toxicity (Braidy et al., 2019; Mehmel et al., 2020). Preclinical studies have shown that NR supplementation rapidly increases tissue and circulating NAD⁺ levels across a range of animal models, including mice and rats, where it has been tested for its effects on metabolic dysfunction, neurodegeneration, insulin sensitivity, and mitochondrial biogenesis (Biță et al., 2023). Numerous clinical trials have demonstrated the safety and oral bioavailability of NR in healthy human subjects and in populations with metabolic or neurodegenerative conditions; for example, chronic supplementation at doses up to 2 g/day has been well tolerated and has successfully elevated NAD⁺ in middle-aged and older adults (Mehmel et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023). In addition to these metabolic and neuroprotective applications, NR has been investigated in various models of inflammation, organ injury, and even in oncology-related situations, where its ability to modulate cellular stress responses has proven beneficial (Biță et al., 2023). Notably, while NR has undergone extensive research in contexts such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and peripheral neuropathy, its application in ocular diseases—particularly dry AMD characterized by geographic atrophy—has been less comprehensively studied; however, emerging evidence supports the notion that NAD⁺ decline in the retina and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) may be mitigated by NAD⁺ precursors, providing a rationale for repurposing NR for dry AMD (Braidy et al., 2019). Veterinary studies and animal models have also utilized NR to stimulate mitochondrial function and improve bioenergetics in tissues with high metabolic demands, further solidifying its profile as a potent NAD⁺ booster with broad potential therapeutic applications (Biță et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action:  
NR exerts its biological effects via a well-defined metabolic pathway that begins with its cellular uptake through equilibrative nucleoside transporters (ENT1, ENT2, and ENT4) followed by phosphorylation by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRK1 and NRK2) in the cytosol, which convert NR to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) (Biță et al., 2023; Braidy et al., 2019). NMN is subsequently adenylated by nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferases (NMNATs) to generate NAD⁺, thereby replenishing the intracellular NAD⁺ pool that is essential for numerous metabolic and signaling processes (Mehmel et al., 2020). The elevation of NAD⁺ levels activates a host of NAD⁺-dependent enzymes including sirtuins (SIRT1, SIRT3, among others) and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs), which are critical for deacetylating mitochondrial proteins, enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis, and facilitating DNA repair processes both in the nucleus and mitochondria (Biță et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2016). Activation of SIRT3 in particular within the mitochondria leads to the deacetylation and activation of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2), thereby reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitigating oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020). Moreover, increased NAD⁺ availability supports the activity of PARP enzymes that are required for efficient DNA repair, including the repair of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) damage arising from oxidative stress (Cimaglia et al., 2020). In RPE cells, this mechanism is particularly relevant as the high-energy–demand environment and frequent exposure to light-induced oxidative stress make robust mitochondrial and genomic maintenance critical to cell survival and homeostasis (Zhang et al., 2020). Additionally, NR’s effect on boosting NAD⁺ may facilitate the activation of autophagy and mitophagy pathways, leading to the clearance of damaged cellular components and improved cellular renewal processes (Braidy et al., 2019; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023). Such biochemical actions converge to foster an enhanced cellular defense mechanism against oxidative damage, support mitochondrial function through improved repair and turnover, and ultimately promote cellular longevity (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023; Biță et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underpinning the repurposing of NR for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that supplementation with NR will lead to an elevation of intracellular NAD⁺ pools specifically within retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby enhancing mitochondrial DNA repair and upregulating antioxidant defenses that mitigate the oxidative damage implicated in geographic atrophy (Biță et al., 2023). In vitro studies using iPSC-derived RPE cells from AMD donors have demonstrated that NR supplementation results in rapid increases in intracellular NAD⁺, which is accompanied by the activation of sirtuin-mediated deacetylation of key mitochondrial proteins (Jadeja et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020). This deacetylation is believed to lead to improved mitochondrial function as evidenced by restored maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) measured via Seahorse XF assays, and the lowering of reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels as detected by fluorescent probes such as DCFDA (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016). The expected outcome in RPE is that the elevated NAD⁺ not only promotes the repair of oxidative damage to mitochondrial DNA but also augments the intrinsic antioxidant enzyme systems—including upregulation of enzymes like SOD2 and catalase—which collectively reduce the cellular oxidative burden (Biță et al., 2023). As a result, NR supplementation is anticipated to stabilize the RPE cell phenotype, reduce markers of cellular senescence and apoptosis, and potentially restore a healthier metabolic profile in RPE cells, factors that are critical for halting or even reversing the progression of geographic atrophy (Jadeja et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016). Moreover, by enhancing the NAD⁺-dependent activation of PARP and other DNA repair enzymes, NR may directly improve the repair of mitochondrial and nuclear DNA damage that accumulates under chronic oxidative stress conditions prevalent in the aging retina (Braidy et al., 2019; Mehmel et al., 2020). In preclinical models of retinal degeneration such as light-induced retinal injury, systemic administration of NR has been shown to preserve retinal morphology, reduce photoreceptor apoptosis, and maintain tissue NAD⁺ levels despite strong oxidative challenges, which supports the translational rationale for its application in dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2020; Braidy et al., 2019). Ultimately, the expected therapeutic effect of NR in the treatment of geographic atrophy is to provide cytoprotection to the RPE by mitigating oxidative damage and improving mitochondrial function, thus slowing the progression of RPE degeneration and vision loss (Zhu et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating NR (specifically the ChromaDex NR-100 formulation) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and promising attributes emerge alongside areas that warrant further investigation. One of the primary strengths of NR is its established reputation as a safe and orally bioavailable NAD⁺ precursor with extensive preclinical and clinical data supporting its ability to elevate NAD⁺ levels systemically and within specific target tissues (Mehmel et al., 2020). This property is particularly relevant for RPE cells because the high metabolic demands of the retina make efficient NAD⁺ replenishment crucial for maintaining mitochondrial function and for mediating effective DNA repair mechanisms (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Additionally, the robust mechanistic data showing that NR supplementation activates sirtuin pathways—most notably SIRT1 and SIRT3—and subsequently deacetylates and activates key mitochondrial and antioxidant enzymes provide a compelling molecular rationale for its potential to ameliorate oxidative stress in the RPE (Biță et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). The activation of these pathways not only enhances mitochondrial bioenergetics but also promotes the clearance of damaged cellular components through autophagy, which is expected to contribute to improved cell survival under oxidative challenge (Braidy et al., 2019; Jadeja et al., 2020).  
However, there are some weaknesses and critical gaps in the current data when it comes to translating these beneficial effects specifically to the context of geographic atrophy in dry AMD. Although preclinical models have demonstrated the protective effects of NR in retinal degeneration (particularly in light-induced injury models), direct evidence demonstrating that NR selectively elevates NAD⁺ pools in RPE cells derived from AMD patients, enhances mitochondrial DNA repair specifically in RPE, and reduces ROS levels to a degree that meaningfully impacts the progression of geographic atrophy remains limited (Braidy et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020). Furthermore, the chemical reactivity and inherent instability of NR have historically posed challenges to its synthesis, storage, and consistent formulation, raising concerns about batch-to-batch variability and the possibility of degradation products in commercial formulations; although recent advances and improved production standards appear to have mitigated these issues, further analytical validation is needed to ensure that the NR-100 formulation consistently meets high purity criteria (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Another consideration is that while the mechanisms underlying NR’s beneficial effects are well established in metabolic and neurodegenerative contexts, the unique metabolic and microenvironmental characteristics of the RPE in the aging eye—including the contributions of the local immune system, extracellular matrix alterations, and the interplay with the choroidal circulation—may represent additional variables that could influence NR’s efficacy in dry AMD, and these factors are not yet fully delineated (Biță et al., 2023; Cimaglia et al., 2020).  
From a clinical development perspective, the fact that NR has already been evaluated in multiple Phase I/II clinical trials for other indications, and has demonstrated an excellent safety profile even at high doses, is a significant advantage that could accelerate its repurposing for ocular applications; careful dose-ranging studies focused on ocular bioavailability and pharmacodynamics in the context of AMD will be critical (Mehmel et al., 2020; Biță et al., 2023). Additionally, mechanistic endpoints such as NAD⁺ elevation, sirtuin activation, and improvements in mitochondrial function have been validated in other tissues and could be adapted to RPE-specific assays, including measurements of oxygen consumption rate (OCR), mitochondrial membrane potential, ROS quantification, and biomarkers of DNA repair (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016; Braidy et al., 2019). Moreover, early translational studies using iPSC-derived RPE from AMD donors have already begun to show that NR can reduce oxidative stress and restore metabolic function in these cells, lending credibility to its potential efficacy in geographic atrophy settings (Biță et al., 2023; Braidy et al., 2019).  
In summary, NR (ChromaDex NR-100) emerges as a highly promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD on the basis of its well-established ability to raise NAD⁺, activate sirtuin-mediated mitochondrial maintenance and DNA repair processes, and mitigate oxidative stress—all of which are central drivers of RPE degeneration in geographic atrophy (Zhang et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016). The strengths of this candidate include a robust mechanistic foundation, a favorable safety and pharmacokinetic profile established in other clinical contexts, and encouraging preclinical data that indirectly support its potential benefit in the retina (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020; Braidy et al., 2019). Nonetheless, significant challenges remain, particularly the need for direct evidence in RPE-specific and geographic atrophy models, confirmation of consistent formulation quality due to NR’s chemical instability, and the potential variability in tissue-specific uptake and metabolism in an aging ocular environment (Mehmel et al., 2020; Biță et al., 2023). Future studies should therefore focus on comprehensive in vitro investigations in primary and iPSC-derived RPE cells, detailed pharmacodynamic assessments in animal models of dry AMD, and ultimately carefully designed early-phase clinical trials targeting RPE function and retinal structure in patient populations with geographic atrophy (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016; Braidy et al., 2019).  
Overall, while there is a compelling mechanistic rationale and a solid foundation of preclinical and clinical data supporting the repurposing of NR for dry AMD, particularly in mitigating oxidative damage, enhancing mitochondrial DNA repair, and improving antioxidant defenses in RPE cells, further targeted research is required to validate these effects specifically in the context of geographic atrophy. The available literature suggests that NR has significant translational promise, and its favorable safety profile alongside extensive clinical experience in other indications positions it as a frontrunner among NAD⁺ precursors for potential therapeutic intervention in dry AMD (Biță et al., 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). The next phase of research should therefore include detailed mechanistic studies in ocular models, combined with rigorous clinical endpoint evaluations to determine whether NR supplementation can effectively slow or reverse the degenerative processes underlying geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2016; Jadeja et al., 2020).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Astaxanthin is a naturally occurring carotenoid belonging to the xanthophyll subclass, first discovered from marine sources such as lobsters and various microalgae, notably Haematococcus pluvialis (Yang & Wang, 2022, pp. 1–2). This red-orange pigment exhibits exceptional antioxidant properties that have been exploited both in natural extraction and through large‐scale synthetic production, with approximately 95% produced synthetically for enhanced economic viability (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 1–3). Its amphipathic structure, characterized by a long polyene chain terminated with polar functional groups, allows it to integrate into both hydrophilic and hydrophobic environments, a property that is fundamental to its ability to span and stabilize cell membranes (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 3–4; Rodella et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). Astaxanthin is a representative member of a broader class of antioxidants that have historically been used as nutraceuticals and dietary supplements, targeting a range of conditions including cardiovascular, dermatologic, and neurodegenerative diseases. Over the decades, the unique biochemical properties of astaxanthin have motivated extensive research into its therapeutic potential, particularly for conditions associated with oxidative stress. Its regulatory approval as a food supplement in the early 1990s, together with subsequent studies demonstrating its anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic capabilities, have established astaxanthin as a promising candidate for further exploration in the context of ocular diseases (Yang & Wang, 2022, pp. 1–2; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, astaxanthin has been investigated and utilized in various biomedical contexts due to its robust antioxidant function. Clinical research and preclinical models have repeatedly shown that astaxanthin improves retinal function and visual acuity in patients with ocular diseases, including both early and nonadvanced stages of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). In addition to its application in AMD, astaxanthin has been evaluated for therapeutic effects in conditions such as diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and dry eye syndrome, demonstrating broad-spectrum protective activities against the oxidative and inflammatory insults commonly underlying these disorders (Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 2–5; Fong, 2023, pp. 7–10). Animal models have provided evidence that dietary supplementation with astaxanthin can mitigate photoreceptor degeneration, reduce choroidal neovascularization (CNV) in models of exudative AMD, and suppress retinal cell apoptosis induced by light or xenobiotic stress (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–7; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5). Despite being explored predominantly for ocular applications, astaxanthin’s history is not limited to ophthalmology alone; its neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory properties have been leveraged in studies addressing broader neurodegenerative and systemic conditions, emphasizing a solid profile for safety and translational potential (Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 2–5). Clinical studies have been encouraging in demonstrating that astaxanthin, when administered as a dietary supplement, exhibits an excellent safety profile with minimal adverse effects, thereby facilitating its clinical translation for chronic, age-related ocular conditions (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5, 13–14). Despite these promising reports, it is important to note that while most available studies indicate significant benefits, the literature also highlights the necessity for further research to determine optimal dosages and to overcome challenges related to bioavailability (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic potential of astaxanthin in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) is thought to stem from its unparalleled antioxidant activity, which is mechanistically linked to its lipophilic and hydrophilic properties. On a molecular level, astaxanthin integrates into cellular membranes—including those of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) mitochondria—where it acts as a chain-breaking antioxidant, quenching reactive oxygen species (ROS) and scavenging free radicals efficiently (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 1–5). Its mechanism involves the neutralization of lipid peroxidation, a process wherein polyunsaturated fatty acids in the cell membrane are damaged by ROS, ultimately leading to the formation of malondialdehyde (MDA) and other toxic aldehyde species that compromise membrane integrity (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–5; Maiuolo et al., 2022, pp. 8–9). By inhibiting lipid peroxidation, astaxanthin stabilizes the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), an essential parameter for maintaining proper mitochondrial function and for preventing the initiation of apoptosis via intrinsic death pathways (Fong, 2023, pp. 7–10; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).  

At the molecular level, studies indicate that astaxanthin modulates key intracellular signaling pathways. It downregulates inflammatory mediators by suppressing the NF-κB pathway, thereby reducing the transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–5; Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 3–5). Additionally, astaxanthin has been shown to enhance the activity of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase (SOD) and glutathione peroxidase (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 1–3; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5), which together help restore cellular redox balance under chronic oxidative stress conditions. Its role in modulating mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt pathways further contributes to cellular survival by reinforcing anti-apoptotic signaling and inhibiting caspase activation, thereby reducing retinal ganglion cell death (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–5).  

The hypothesis under consideration—that astaxanthin integrates into RPE mitochondrial membranes to quench lipid peroxidation and stabilize Δψm—is supported by its molecular configuration, which allows the compound to embed itself at the interface of membrane lipids without disrupting the bilayer structure (Rodella et al., 2023, pp. 11–13; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 3–4). Once incorporated, astaxanthin acts as a “molecular rivet” that not only prevents oxidative damage but also helps maintain membrane fluidity and structural integrity. This is particularly relevant in the context of dry AMD, where chronic oxidative stress leads to the degeneration of the RPE, a critical cell layer whose dysfunction is central to the pathogenesis of the disease (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 3–5). Additionally, the ability of astaxanthin to traverse cellular and mitochondrial membranes enhances its efficacy in neutralizing ROS, thereby preserving both mitochondrial function and cellular viability within the retina (Manresa et al., 2016, p. 5; Rodella et al., 2023, pp. 11–13).  

Expected Effect:  
In the assay proposed for the evaluation of dry AMD treatment, the primary expectation is that astaxanthin supplementation will lead to a marked reduction in oxidative stress markers and preservation of mitochondrial function in RPE cells. Specifically, the anticipated effects include a decrease in MDA formation, indicative of attenuated lipid peroxidation, and stabilization of Δψm, which is critical for preventing loss of mitochondrial integrity and the subsequent cascade of apoptotic signaling (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–5). Based on its molecular actions, astaxanthin is expected to enhance cellular antioxidant defenses by upregulating enzymes such as SOD and glutathione peroxidase, ultimately leading to improved cell survival under conditions of chronic oxidative insult typical of dry AMD (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 1–3; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5).  

RPE cells are known to express high levels of antioxidants and genes responsive to oxidative stress, such as those regulated by the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway (Manresa et al., 2016, p. 5). In vitro assays, therefore, should reveal that astaxanthin treatment results in enhanced Nrf2 activation and subsequent transcription of phase II detoxifying enzymes, which in turn protects against oxidative damage. Furthermore, electrophysiological assessments, such as electroretinograms (ERG), are expected to show functional improvements in retinal activity, corroborating the cytoprotective effects observed at the cellular level (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 5–7).  

In addition to cellular antioxidants, astaxanthin’s anti-inflammatory properties are likely to mitigate the secretion of inflammatory cytokines from RPE cells and reduce the activation of microglial cells in the retina. Such a reduction in the inflammatory milieu is crucial, as chronic inflammation is known to exacerbate retinal degeneration in AMD by promoting pathological angiogenesis and further oxidative damage (Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 2–5). Hence, a combinatorial effect of decreased oxidative stress, improved mitochondrial stability, and reduced inflammation is anticipated to confer significant protection to retinal structures, ultimately delaying or preventing the progression of dry AMD (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 12–14).

Overall Evaluation:  
The collective body of evidence suggests that astaxanthin holds considerable promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. One of its principal strengths lies in its multifaceted action: as a potent antioxidant, it effectively quenches reactive oxygen species and prevents lipid peroxidation, while its ability to integrate into cellular membranes, particularly those of RPE mitochondria, ensures that mitochondrial membrane potential is preserved even under chronic oxidative conditions (Fong, 2023, pp. 7–10; Rodella et al., 2023, pp. 11–13). The convergence of biochemical, cellular, and clinical data highlights its capacity to improve retinal function, as evidenced by improvements in electroretinogram outcomes and visual acuity measurements in clinical trials (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 5–7). Moreover, its favorable safety profile—as demonstrated through extensive use as a dietary supplement—provides an added advantage in terms of translational potential, facilitating the design and execution of clinical studies aimed at validating its efficacy in dry AMD (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 13–14; Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–5).

Another strength is the well-documented anti-inflammatory property of astaxanthin, which complements its antioxidant activity. By downregulating NF-κB and associated pro-inflammatory mediators, this compound mitigates the inflammatory processes that contribute to RPE degeneration and retinal neuronal loss (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–5; Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 3–5). This dual action is particularly significant given the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathogenesis, where both oxidative stress and chronic inflammation play aggravating roles. The integration of these effects suggests that astaxanthin may not only slow disease progression but also restore aspects of retinal function, representing a comprehensive therapeutic approach.

However, several challenges and weaknesses also warrant consideration. Despite the promising mechanistic profile, the translational efficacy of astaxanthin in clinical settings remains to be fully established. Although numerous preclinical models have demonstrated cytoprotective effects in vitro and in animal models, the optimal dosing regimen and formulation for achieving sufficient bioavailability in the human retina are still under investigation (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5; Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 10–11). In summary, astaxanthin stands out as a compelling therapeutic candidate for dry AMD on several fronts. Its remarkable antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, combined with its ability to stabilize mitochondrial membrane potential and prevent lipid peroxidation, directly address key pathogenic mechanisms implicated in dry AMD (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 1–5; D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 4–5). From the perspective of a drug development team leader focused on repurposing agents for dry AMD, the evidence supports the incorporation of astaxanthin into further preclinical testing and potential early-phase clinical trials. A multi-pronged approach that includes detailed pharmacokinetic studies, the exploration of enhanced delivery systems, and the evaluation of combination treatments with complementary agents might maximize its therapeutic potential. In conclusion, while certain hurdles remain to be overcome, the overall strengths of astaxanthin—its potent antioxidant activity, favorable safety profile, and mechanistic relevance to RPE mitochondrial stabilization—render it a highly promising candidate for inclusion in the therapeutic armamentarium against dry age-related macular degeneration (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 3–5; Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 3–7; Fong, 2023, pp. 7–10).

To recapitulate, astaxanthin’s natural origin as a marine-derived carotenoid, its extensive historical use as a nutraceutical, and its documented molecular mechanisms that include inflammation suppression, ROS scavenging, and stabilization of vital mitochondrial functions all contribute to its strong candidacy for repurposing in dry AMD (Giannaccare et al., 2020, pp. 1–3; Yang & Wang, 2022, pp. 1–2; Maiuolo et al., 2022, pp. 8–9). Despite the necessity for further research to optimize formulation and dosing, the body of evidence suggests that astaxanthin merits serious consideration as a component of future therapeutic regimens aimed at mitigating the multifactorial pathology of dry age-related macular degeneration (D’Angelo et al., 2024, pp. 3–5; Lixi et al., 2024, pp. 10–11).

Its natural origin, extensive therapeutic history in ocular and other diseases, detailed molecular mechanisms of action, and expected beneficial effects on mitochondrial stability collectively provide a strong scientific basis for further development.
