────────────────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

SB 290157 is a synthetic small‐molecule compound that functions as an antagonist of the C3a receptor (C3aR). Chemically, it is defined as N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine, a structure that incorporates an arginine residue with an acyl modification incorporating a 2,2-diphenylethoxy moiety (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). SB 290157 was discovered through high-throughput screening efforts aimed at identifying molecules capable of displacing radiolabeled C3a from its receptor. Early screening identified a lead compound that underwent extensive chemical optimization – including solid-phase peptide and peptidomimetic synthesis using Fmoc‐based chemistry on Wang resin – to yield SB 290157 (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011). This synthetic approach, employing coupling reagents such as 1-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)-3-ethylcarbodiimide hydrochloride and 4-dimethylaminopyridine, resulted in a non-peptide molecule designed to maximize receptor affinity while minimizing metabolic instability. The compound is commercially available from suppliers such as Cayman Chemical (catalog #10006619) and has served as a prototypic small-molecule C3aR antagonist in numerous preclinical studies (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017).

SB 290157 falls within the broader class of synthetic GPCR modulators that target complement receptors. Historically, such molecules have been exploited as biochemical tools to interrogate the role of anaphylatoxins in inflammatory responses (Ames et al., 2001). C3a, a 77-residue protein fragment produced during complement activation, is recognized by its GPCR, C3aR, and triggers diverse cellular responses (Ames et al., 2001). Multiple research groups have employed small-molecule antagonists like SB 290157 to elucidate the contribution of C3a-mediated signaling in conditions ranging from arthritis to lung inflammation (Ames et al., 2001). The compound’s synthetic origin and chemical tractability have allowed investigators to probe receptor pharmacology in heterologous cell lines (e.g., RBL-C3aR cells, ARPE-19 cells) and primary human cell systems (Ames et al., 2001). In the context of ocular research, SB 290157 has been used experimentally in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) models – particularly in primary human fetal RPE cultures – to block C3a-induced alterations in extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

Beyond its established utility as a research tool, the use of SB 290157 in ocular models speaks to an emerging rationale for targeting complement signaling in degenerative eye diseases. Its inclusion in a commercial catalog further underscores its ready availability to laboratories, enabling reproducibility and fostering further experimentation. In summary, SB 290157 is a synthetic, non-peptide, arginine-based antagonist belonging to a class of compounds that have historically been used to interrogate complement receptor signaling, with a well-defined chemical structure, known synthesis protocols, and broad preclinical application in inflammation research (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

SB 290157 has a storied history in the complement research field. Its initial characterization, as detailed by Ames and colleagues, revealed that SB 290157 competes for C3a binding with an IC₅₀ in the high‐nanomolar range (approximately 200 nM) and potently inhibits C3a-induced intracellular calcium mobilization in sensitive cell lines, such as RBL cells and human neutrophils (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Early studies validated its functional capacity as a selective antagonist in vitro, establishing that it effectively blocked receptor internalization and attenuated downstream signaling events elicited by C3a binding.

Preclinically, SB 290157 has been deployed in a wide range of experimental disease models. For instance, it has been used in animal studies examining anti-inflammatory activity in models such as guinea pig LPS-induced airway neutrophilia and adjuvant-induced arthritis in rats. In the arthritis model, administration of SB 290157 resulted in a significant reduction (approximately 41%) in paw edema, while in airway inflammation models it suppressed neutrophil recruitment, demonstrating its anti-inflammatory efficacy (Ames et al., 2001). These early demonstrations of anti-inflammatory activity provided the impetus to consider SB 290157 for further repurposing in conditions where complement overactivation contributes to pathology.

More recently, attention has turned to the role of complement in ocular diseases, particularly age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Experimental evidence in primary human fetal RPE cultures has shown that exposure to recombinant C3a for periods of 2–4 weeks results in the accumulation of sub-RPE deposits via increased ECM deposition, notably of collagens (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Importantly, co-treatment with a C3a receptor antagonist – which in many instances has been SB 290157 – successfully prevented the abnormal accumulation of sub-RPE deposits. These studies have helped establish a mechanistic link between C3a/C3aR activation and the proteostasis dysfunction observed in RPE cells, a pathological process believed to contribute to early AMD pathology.

In addition to in vitro data, in vivo models provide further support for the therapeutic potential of modulating C3aR signaling. In a murine model of sodium iodate (NaIO₃)-induced RPE injury – a model that recapitulates aspects of geographic atrophy – systemic administration of SB 290157 reduced photoreceptor death, decreased markers of gliosis and microglial activation, and lowered TNFα and STAT3 signaling levels (Wang et al., 2020). Similarly, in a laser-induced retinal vein occlusion (RVO) model, intravitreal injection of SB 290157 suppressed the up-regulation of both C3 and C3a receptor expression, correlating with partial rescue of retinal morphology and vascular integrity (Zhao et al., 2025). Although these studies were not specifically designed for dry AMD, the similarities in underlying complement-mediated RPE injury and chronic inflammation between these models and the dry AMD phenotype provide a strong rationale for further exploring SB 290157 in this indication.

Despite these promising applications, SB 290157’s therapeutic history is not without controversy. Several studies have reported that, depending on the cell type and receptor density, SB 290157 may exhibit partial agonist activity rather than acting as a pure antagonist (Mathieu et al., 2005). This variable pharmacological profile has raised concerns about its utility as a definitive clinical tool. Nonetheless, as a research probe, SB 290157 has significantly advanced our understanding of complement-mediated cellular responses in inflammatory, vascular, and ocular contexts. Overall, while it has been extensively used in preclinical studies across multiple disease models – including arthritis, lung inflammation, and retinal injury – its use specifically in clinical settings for dry AMD remains investigational (Ames et al., 2001; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Wang et al., 2020).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

SB 290157 exerts its biological effects by competitively binding to the C3a receptor (C3aR), thereby preventing the interaction of endogenous C3a with its receptor. Under normal conditions, the complement cascade, when activated via any of its pathways, leads to the cleavage of complement component C3 and the subsequent release of the anaphylatoxin C3a. This bioactive peptide binds to C3aR, a G protein-coupled receptor present on various cell types including granulocytes, monocytes, and notably retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Once activated, C3aR transduces signals that can lead to intracellular calcium mobilization, triggering a cascade of downstream events such as receptor internalization and activation of inflammatory transcription factors.

In vitro studies using radioligand binding assays have determined that SB 290157 displaces [¹²⁵I]-C3a from its receptor with an IC₅₀ in the high nanomolar range (approximately 200 nM), while functional calcium mobilization assays in cell lines (including RBL cells and human neutrophils) have demonstrated potent inhibition of C3a-stimulated intracellular calcium release at low nanomolar concentrations (approximately 28 nM) (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017). Mechanistically, by preventing C3a from engaging C3aR, the compound is able to avert subsequent receptor conformational changes that would otherwise lead to G protein coupling and downstream signaling events.

In the context of RPE cells, particularly under conditions of chronic oxidative stress – such as exposure to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) – C3a engagement of its receptor has been implicated in a range of deleterious cellular effects. Studies in ARPE-19 cells have shown that oxidative stress induces a redistribution of C3aR away from its typical plasma membrane localization and promotes its translocation toward the mitochondria (Ishii et al., 2021; Riihilä et al., 2019). At the mitochondrial level, activation of the receptor by C3a leads to an increase in mitochondrial calcium uptake, which in turn results in compromised respiratory function as evidenced by decreased state III (ADP-driven) respiration and reduced maximal respiratory capacity (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). The resultant mitochondrial dysfunction is highly likely to contribute to the generation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS). mtROS are known triggers for the NLRP3 inflammasome, which upon activation facilitates the processing of pro-IL-1β to active IL-1β, a cytokine strongly implicated in chronic inflammatory processes observed in AMD (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024).

Furthermore, in primary human fetal RPE models, prolonged exposure to recombinant C3a has been demonstrated to reduce the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (UPP) without altering mRNA levels for proteasome subunits, indicating a post-transcriptional impairment of proteostasis (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). This impairment in proteasome function is associated with an imbalance in ECM turnover – marked by a reduction in tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases (TIMP-3) abundance and an increase in matrix metalloproteinase (MMP-2) activity – culminating in the pathological deposition of extracellular matrix components (notably collagens IV and VI) beneath the RPE. Such sub-RPE deposit formation, or drusen, is one of the hallmarks of early AMD pathology (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

SB 290157, by blocking C3a from binding to C3aR, therefore interrupts these pathological cascades at two key junctures. First, it prevents the mitochondrial translocation and activation of C3aR in oxidatively stressed ARPE-19 cells, which is predicted to avert the associated mitochondrial calcium overload and respiratory inhibition, thereby reducing the likelihood of mtROS generation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). Second, by inhibiting C3a-induced receptor activation in RPE cells, SB 290157 preserves UPP activity, ensuring proper regulation of ECM component turnover and forestalling the aberrant deposition of sub-RPE material (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

It is important to note, however, that while the majority of evidence supports SB 290157 acting as an effective C3aR antagonist, several reports have cautioned that under certain conditions, the compound may display partial agonist activity. This means that rather than completely blocking receptor activation, SB 290157 might induce a low level of receptor signaling in some cellular contexts, especially when receptor density is high (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001). Such an effect must be carefully considered when interpreting experimental outcomes and when designing therapeutic strategies aimed at persistent modulation of complement activity. In all, the known mechanism of action for SB 290157 can be summarized as competitive inhibition of C3a binding to C3aR, thereby mitigating the downstream signals that lead to mitochondrial calcium dysregulation, proteasome impairment, ECM deposition abnormalities, and ultimately, NLRP3 inflammasome priming and IL-1β secretion (Ames et al., 2001; Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

────────────────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect

The central hypothesis underlying the use of SB 290157 in repurposing for dry AMD is that the blockade of C3aR will attenuate a cascade of deleterious events within the retinal pigment epithelium that contribute to disease progression. In particular, the expected effect is that SB 290157 will reduce complement-driven mitochondrial dysfunction, lower mtROS production, and thereby prevent the priming and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, resulting ultimately in diminished IL-1β secretion and preservation of RPE barrier integrity.

In dry AMD, chronic oxidative stress leads to dysregulated complement activation and subsequent accumulation of complement fragments such as C3a in the subretinal space. RPE cells under oxidative stress have been demonstrated to upregulate C3aR expression, with a portion of the receptor redistributing to the mitochondria—a change that is associated with an increased uptake of calcium into the mitochondria and a pronounced decline in mitochondrial respiratory function (Ishii et al., 2021; Riihilä et al., 2019). The resulting mitochondrial dysfunction is poised to increase the generation of mtROS, which serve as an upstream activator of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Activation of this inflammasome complex culminates in the maturation of IL-1β, a powerful proinflammatory cytokine that has been implicated in propagating RPE injury and the progression of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024).

By competitively inhibiting C3a binding to its receptor, SB 290157 is expected to block these deleterious changes. In cultured ARPE-19 cells—which serve as a well-established model for human RPE—it is anticipated that SB 290157 will prevent the mitochondrial translocation of C3aR, thereby reducing abnormal mitochondrial calcium uptake and preserving normal respiration. This action should limit mtROS generation and consequently reduce the priming threshold for NLRP3 inflammasome activation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). Concurrently, in primary fetal RPE cultures, inhibition of C3aR signaling by SB 290157 has been shown to preserve the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, which in turn maintains the balance of matrix metalloproteinases and their tissue inhibitors. By doing so, the compound prevents the accumulation of sub-RPE deposits—a process that is intimately linked to the early phases of AMD pathology (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).

The expression of C3aR in RPE cells, particularly in stressed conditions, is well-documented. This receptor is notably enriched on the basolateral membrane of RPE and even redistributes to mitochondrial compartments under oxidative stress conditions, as confirmed in ARPE-19 cell studies (Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Given that dry AMD is characterized by both heightened complement activation and chronic oxidative stress, the strategic inhibition of C3aR is expected to yield multiple beneficial outcomes: restoration of proteostasis, maintenance of mitochondrial function, reduction in chronic inflammatory cytokine expression, and preservation of the integrity and barrier function of the RPE monolayer. Moreover, in in vivo models such as NaIO₃-induced RPE injury or laser-induced retinal vein occlusion, treatment with a C3aR antagonist (presumably SB 290157) has been associated with reduced photoreceptor loss, attenuated microglial activation, and improved retinal morphology (Wang et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2025).

Furthermore, because mitochondrial reactive oxygen species serve as a trigger for the NLRP3 inflammasome, blocking the upstream signal via C3aR inhibition is hypothesized to break the vicious cycle of complement-mediated inflammation. The decreased activation of NLRP3 would lead to lower levels of IL-1β—a cytokine implicated in the autocrine and paracrine amplification of inflammation within the RPE layer—and thus stabilize the local microenvironment (Ong et al., 2024; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In summary, the expected effect of SB 290157 in the context of dry AMD is multifold: preservation of mitochondrial bioenergetics, maintenance of proteasomal activity, prevention of pathological ECM accumulation, and attenuation of inflammasome-mediated inflammatory responses—all of which contribute to the protection of RPE integrity and function.

────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

SB 290157 stands out as one of the best-studied C3a receptor antagonists available today. Its well-documented chemical synthesis, robust in vitro pharmacological profile, and demonstrable efficacy in preclinical models of inflammatory injury provide strong support for its continued evaluation as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. The compound’s origins – as a product of high-throughput screening followed by medicinal chemistry optimization using Fmoc-solid phase techniques – are well established, and its chemical structure (N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine) clearly classifies it as a small-molecule non-peptide antagonist of a key complement receptor (Ames et al., 2001; Larghi & Kaufman, 2011).

Strengths of SB 290157 include its proven ability to block C3a-induced signaling cascades across a range of cell types and experimental models. Preclinical studies in RPE cells indicate that it can prevent C3a-induced sub-RPE deposit formation and proteasome impairment—a finding directly relevant to the early pathological events of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Additionally, evidence from ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress suggests that SB 290157 effectively inhibits aberrant mitochondrial Ca²⁺ uptake and consequent respiratory dysfunction—mechanisms known to contribute to mtROS generation and inflammasome activation (Ishii et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024). In vivo, its administration in models of retinal injury (such as NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration and laser-induced retinal vein occlusion) has correlated with reduced photoreceptor death, decreased gliosis, and improved retinal architecture (Wang et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2025). These findings collectively underscore the compound’s potential to modulate complement-mediated pathology in the ocular setting.

Nonetheless, SB 290157 is not without its weaknesses. A significant concern noted across several studies is its variable pharmacological behavior. Under some experimental conditions, particularly in cell systems with high receptor density, SB 290157 exhibits partial agonist activity rather than pure antagonism (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001). This paradoxical behavior could lead to unintended receptor activation and potentially undermine its therapeutic benefit, especially in chronic conditions like dry AMD where long-term receptor blockade is desired. Furthermore, while there is compelling preclinical evidence supporting its beneficial impact on mitochondrial function and ECM homeostasis, direct experimental data linking SB 290157 to a reduction in mitochondrial ROS production and consequent suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation in ARPE-19 or primary RPE models remain incomplete or indirect (Wang et al., 2020; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Behnke, 2022). This gap in the literature necessitates further investigation to firmly establish the causal chain from C3aR inhibition to inflammasome modulation.

Another consideration is the translational challenge. SB 290157 has been predominantly utilized as a research tool rather than a clinical candidate. Its pharmacokinetic profile—while adequate for short-term animal experiments—has not been thoroughly characterized for long-term use in ocular applications, where issues such as retinal toxicity, ocular bioavailability, and sustained receptor occupancy become critical. The delicate environment of the retina requires highly specific and safe compounds; thus, the partial agonist activity and potential off-target effects of SB 290157 raise valid concerns regarding its safety profile in humans (Mathieu et al., 2005; Tan et al., 2024).

On the other hand, the dual benefit of SB 290157—in preventing not only aberrant complement signaling but also the downstream mitochondrial dysfunction that leads to inflammasome activation—directly addresses central pathogenic mechanisms in dry AMD. Given that dry AMD is characterized by chronic inflammation, RPE dysfunction, and progressive atrophy correlated with mitochondrial impairment, a drug that can simultaneously modulate these pathways offers a novel therapeutic angle. In this context, the ability of SB 290157 to preserve the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway and maintain ECM turnover may help stabilize the RPE, delay the progression of geographic atrophy, and potentially improve visual outcomes (Ames et al., 2001; Ishii et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Wang et al., 2020). Conversely, its partial agonist behavior in certain systems and the current lack of direct evidence linking its action to reduced mtROS and NLRP3 activation in ocular models raise legitimate concerns that must be addressed prior to clinical translation (Mathieu et al., 2005; Behnke, 2022).

Overall, SB 290157 is a compelling candidate for further exploration and mechanistic validation as a repurposed drug for dry AMD, provided that additional research can surmount the challenges associated with its pharmacodynamic variability and confirm its protective effects in retina-specific models.

────────────────────────────────────────  
Conclusion

The comprehensive literature evaluation indicates that SB 290157’s synthetic origins, established use as a C3aR antagonist, and demonstrated efficacy in preclinical models of complement-mediated RPE injury make it a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its mechanism—blocking C3a-induced signaling that otherwise leads to mitochondrial calcium overload, impaired proteostasis, and subsequent inflammasome activation—is highly relevant to the pathophysiology of geographic atrophy. However, the compound’s documented partial agonist effects and potential variability in receptor blockade require careful consideration and further optimization. Additional studies are necessary to firmly establish that SB 290157 can reduce mitochondrial ROS and suppress NLRP3 inflammasome activation in RPE cells under conditions that model dry AMD clinically. Overall, the candidate shows substantial promise as a mechanistic probe and potential therapeutic agent for dry AMD; its ability to block key complement-mediated events that contribute to RPE dysfunction and inflammation positions it as a novel target for drug development. However, given the documented limitations, further studies are strongly recommended to optimize its receptor selectivity, define its pharmacokinetic and safety profile in the ocular context, and conclusively demonstrate its capacity to mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammasome activation in relevant models before advancing it into clinical trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is an endogenous ketone body produced by mitochondrial ketogenesis from fatty-acid–derived acetyl-CoA, classically in hepatocytes but also in extrahepatic cell types including the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and several neuronal lineages (enzymatic pathway: ACAT, HMGCS2, HMGCL, and BDH1) (Wang et al., 2021; Gough, 2021). In physiological and nutritional ketosis, circulating BHB rises from baseline (~0.05–0.1 mM) to levels >0.5 mM and up to 5–7 mM with prolonged fasting, providing an alternative oxidative substrate for extrahepatic mitochondria when carbohydrate availability is limited (Wang et al., 2021; Cooper et al., 2023). BHB and acetoacetate are transported into and out of cells via proton-linked monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs) such as MCT1 and MCT2 that are expressed at the blood–retinal barrier and in retinal cells, enabling substrate entry into the retina (Yang, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Gough, 2021). RPEs robustly express mitochondrial HMGCS2 and can ketogenize palmitate to BHB, secreting BHB via MCT1; retinal cells can take up and metabolize BHB into Krebs-cycle intermediates and amino acids, indicating functional capacity to use BHB as mitochondrial fuel in the outer retina (Yang, 2021). More recent mass spectrometry–based reassessment shows that RPE secretion of BHB is substantially lower than previously estimated by enzymatic kits, that RPE exports BHB to both apical and basal compartments, and that RPE both produces and consumes BHB depending on nutrient state—important considerations for experimental design and therapeutic targeting (Gulette et al., 2024).  

BHB belongs to the class of endogenous metabolic intermediates that function dually as oxidative fuels (via oxidation to acetyl-CoA and entry into TCA cycle) and signaling molecules with paracrine/autocrine receptor and epigenetic actions (e.g., agonism at HCAR2/GPR109A and inhibition of class I/IIa histone deacetylases) (Wang et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Kovács et al., 2021). As a therapeutic modality, BHB has been delivered exogenously as salts/esters or induced endogenously through ketogenic diets, fasting, or exercise to support mitochondrial ATP production and alter cellular stress responses in the CNS, heart, and skeletal muscle (Cooper et al., 2023; Kovács et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2022). In retinal disease models, ketogenic interventions or exogenous BHB have reduced oxidative/inflammatory injury and improved functional measures, though direct application to dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) has not yet been clinically tested (Gough, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021).  

Therapeutic History  
Ketone biology has a long history in neurology and cardiometabolic research, where BHB has been shown to preserve mitochondrial function, increase ATP production, and blunt oxidative injury in ischemia, neurodegeneration models, and skeletal muscle stress paradigms (Kovács et al., 2021; Mierziak et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2018). In neural tissues, ketogenic interventions and exogenous ketones prevent synaptic dysfunction induced by respiratory complex inhibitors and increase the brain NAD⁺/NADH ratio, correlating with decreased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation (Morris et al., 2020). In rat skeletal muscle cells, 5 mM BHB for 24–48 h increased respiratory control, ATP-linked respiration, P:O efficiency, lowered H₂O₂ production, and shifted mitochondrial dynamics toward fusion via DRP1 suppression—consistent with enhanced bioenergetics and decreased oxidative stress (Parker et al., 2018). In primary neurons, BHB maintained oxidative phosphorylation under glutamate workload even when cytosolic NADH transfer via the malate–aspartate shuttle was inhibited, demonstrating that BHB can sustain respiration under conditions that impair glycolytic NADH coupling to mitochondria (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

In the retina and optic nerve, multiple preclinical models show that ketogenic exposures or direct ketone administration reduce oxidative stress and inflammation, preserve function, and limit neuronal death. Intraperitoneal BHB and acetoacetate reduced NMDA-induced retinal ganglion cell (RGC) death in rats, and ketogenic diet attenuated NMDA-induced RGC injury in juvenile rats (Gough, 2021). In ocular blast or optic neuropathy paradigms, ketogenic diet prevented increases in superoxide and IL-1α, preserved visual evoked potentials, and reduced astrocytic hypertrophy and optic nerve death (Gough, 2021). In glaucoma models, ketogenic diet improved RGC soma/axon survival, axonal transport, and reduced gliosis, with increases in NAD and NAD:NADH ratio and upregulation of MCT1/MCT2 in optic nerve (Tribble et al., 2021). AAV-mediated MCT2 overexpression (increasing uptake of lactate/pyruvate/ketones) preserved RGCs and optic nerve axons in ocular hypertension and glaucoma models and elevated markers of mitochondrial biogenesis and function (PGC1α, COX, SDH) and antioxidant defense (SOD2) (Gough, 2021). However, in at least one RGC injury model, daily intraperitoneal BHB or acetoacetate did not replicate ketogenic diet neuroprotection, underscoring differences between exogenous ketone dosing and the systemic/multifactorial effects of ketogenic diets (Tribble et al., 2021).  

Within the RPE compartment specifically, two lines of evidence are relevant: (1) BHB protects ARPE-19 cells from high-glucose–induced injury, improving viability, alleviating cell cycle arrest, and modulating inflammatory mediators (IL-8, IL-17α, MCP-1) at millimolar concentrations achievable with nutritional ketosis or exogenous supplementation (Argentino et al., 2025). (2) HCAR2/GPR109A, a BHB receptor, is robustly expressed by the RPE; BHB agonism reduced retinal leukocyte infiltration in LPS-challenged mice in an HCAR2-dependent manner, and loss of HCAR2 in RPE led to barrier dysfunction (ZO-1 defects) and increased immune cell infiltrates, indicating that BHB–HCAR2 signaling can preserve an immunoinhibitory retinal environment (Powell et al., 2021). In diabetic retinopathy models, systemic BHB activation of HCA2 reduced ER stress and NLRP3 inflammasome signaling and ameliorated retinal pathology, establishing anti-inflammatory and ER stress–limiting actions in retina (Trotta et al., 2019).  

In inherited retinal degeneration models, ketogenic interventions delayed photoreceptor degeneration and improved electroretinogram (ERG) amplitudes and outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness in rd10 and Pde6a mice, and a soluble ketogenic formulation partially restored vision and survival in PDH-deficient noir zebrafish—consistent with bypassing PDH to supply acetyl-CoA and support neurotransmitter synthesis (Gough, 2021). Notwithstanding these encouraging signals, the literature consistently notes the absence of clinical trials evaluating ketogenic interventions or BHB in retinitis pigmentosa or AMD patients, and reports potentially adverse effects of ketogenic diets in wild-type mice (decreased ERG amplitudes, altered albumin/weight), highlighting translational uncertainties and the need to distinguish effects of BHB from the broader systemic consequences of diet (Gough, 2021).  

Mechanism of Action  
BHB acts through convergent metabolic, redox, mitochondrial, inflammatory, and epigenetic mechanisms that are mechanistically aligned with the pathophysiology of RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic oxidative/inflammatory stress in dry AMD.  

- Alternative mitochondrial fuel and bioenergetics support. In extrahepatic tissues (including retina), BHB oxidation proceeds via mitochondrial BDH1 (βHB→acetoacetate) followed by SCOT/OXCT1 (AcAc→AcAc-CoA using succinyl-CoA) and acetyl-CoA production for TCA entry and ATP generation, enabling substrate-level maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and oxidative phosphorylation under glucose restriction or impaired glycolytic NADH transfer (Wang et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023). The retina expresses monocarboxylate transport routes (e.g., MCT1 at the inner blood–retinal barrier; MCT2 in neurons), and RPE expresses MCT1 and can both produce and consume BHB, providing a plausible uptake pathway for exogenous BHB into RPE and neighboring retinal cells (Tribble et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Gulette et al., 2024). In neurons, BHB-supported respiration remains robust when the malate–aspartate shuttle is blocked with AOAA—conditions that decrease glucose-fueled ATP synthesis—indicating that BHB can preserve mitochondrial ATP synthesis and respiratory control when cytosolic NADH transfer is compromised, a scenario relevant to glycolysis-impaired RPE (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

- Redox coupling and ROS control. The interconversion of acetoacetate and BHB by βHB dehydrogenase is linked to NADH/NAD⁺ redox; acetoacetate→BHB requires oxidation of NADH to NAD⁺, and nutritional ketosis in human brain increases NAD⁺/NADH ratio, correlating with reductions in mitochondrial ROS generation (Gough, 2021; Morris et al., 2020). Ketones can inhibit mitochondrial ROS production by increasing NADH oxidation, and ketogenic interventions increase NAD⁺/NADH in vivo, though tissue- and context-dependent effects exist (Morris et al., 2020). Complementary cardiac literature reports that β-OHB can reduce the mitochondrial NAD couple while oxidizing coenzyme Q, emphasizing that BHB modulates both NADH/NAD⁺ and Q/QH₂ redox pairs in mitochondria—with directionality that may depend on prevailing substrate status and respiratory state (Chu et al., 2021). In ischemia–reperfusion models and muscle cells, BHB lowers mitochondrial ROS, decreases mitochondrial swelling, maintains Δψm, and increases ATP production, consistent with direct mitochondrial protection (Mierziak et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2018).  

- Antioxidant transcription (Nrf2) and hormesis. Ketogenic exposures can induce a hormetic redox signal that activates Keap1–Nrf2, increasing transcription of detoxification and antioxidant genes; in retina, ketone body exposure mimicked calorie restriction via fumarate–Nrf2 activation (Gough, 2021; Fu et al., 2020). Preclinical optic/retinal models link these antioxidant transcriptional effects to preserved function and reduced oxidative markers (NOS, MDA, superoxide) (Gough, 2021).  

- Anti-inflammatory signaling via HCAR2/ARRB2 and NLRP3/NF-κB suppression. BHB is a ligand for HCAR1/HCAR2 receptors; HCAR2 is robustly expressed in human RPE and retina, and receptor activation by BHB reduces leukocyte infiltration and preserves RPE barrier integrity in inflammation models (Powell et al., 2021). Downstream, BHB–HCAR signaling recruits β-arrestin-2 (ARRB2) that binds NLRP3 to block inflammasome assembly, decreasing ASC and preventing K⁺ efflux to suppress IL-1β maturation; BHB also activates a COX1/PGD2 cascade that inhibits IKK and NF-κB nuclear translocation, reducing TNF-α and microglial/macrophage activation (Gough, 2021). In diabetic retina, systemic BHB–HCA2 activation suppressed ER stress and NLRP3 inflammasome activity, demonstrating the retinal anti-inflammatory efficacy of this axis (Trotta et al., 2019).  

- Mitochondrial calcium homeostasis and mPTP stabilization. In human iPSC-derived microglia, amyloid-β oligomers increased MCU expression, raised mitochondrial Ca²⁺ ~40%, elevated mtROS, and triggered mPTP opening; BHB normalized MCU, decreased mtCa²⁺/mtROS, and completely reversed mPTP activation, restoring phagocytic function (Jin et al., 2023). Although not conducted in RPE, these mitochondrial-stabilizing effects are mechanistically relevant to post-mitotic cells with high oxidative load.  

- Epigenetic modulation and mitochondrial biogenesis. BHB is an endogenous inhibitor of class I/IIa HDACs at physiological millimolar concentrations, leading to histone hyperacetylation and upregulation of FOXO3a and metallothionein genes that encode antioxidant defenses; BHB also increases intracellular acetyl-CoA and supports protein acetylation, and can β-hydroxybutyrylate histones, adding layers of gene regulatory control tied to mitochondrial status (Yang, 2021; Kovács et al., 2021; Mierziak et al., 2021). Through HDAC inhibition and receptor-mediated signaling, BHB increases BDNF via cAMP/PKA/CREB, activates SIRT1/SIRT3 via AMPK/HCA2/NAD⁺ pathways, and promotes PGC1α-driven mitochondrial biogenesis and UCP2 expression that collectively improve mitochondrial function and antioxidant capacity (Kovács et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022). In retinal/optic nerve models, ketogenic diet or enhanced monocarboxylate uptake upregulated PGC1α, COX, SDH, and SOD2 while lowering pAMPK/AMPK, linking substrate availability to mitochondrial biogenesis and anti-inflammatory signaling (Gough, 2021).  

- Immunometabolic reprogramming in retina/CNS. Ketogenic interventions increased anti-inflammatory mediators (IL-4, Arginase-1) and M2-like microglia while decreasing IBA-1⁺ macrophage/microglia, consistent with dampened neuroinflammation secondary to improved bioenergetics (reduced AMPK activation) and prevention of NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation (Gough, 2021). BHB also inhibits FFAR3/GPR41, reducing sympathetic activity in mice, indicating broader metabolic signaling roles that could modulate retinal perfusion/metabolism indirectly (Gough, 2021).  

Collectively, these mechanisms—fuel substitution that sustains Δψm and ATP synthesis under glycolytic impairment, improved redox balance with decreased mitochondrial ROS, Nrf2-dependent antioxidant gene induction, NLRP3/NF-κB anti-inflammatory actions via HCAR2/ARRB2, stabilization of mitochondrial Ca²⁺/mPTP, and epigenetic programs that support mitochondrial biogenesis—map directly onto pathologies implicated in RPE degeneration in dry AMD and provide multiple rescue nodes testable in disease-relevant models (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Gough, 2021; Powell et al., 2021).  

Expected Effect  
Assay context: The working hypothesis is that exogenous BHB will serve as an alternative mitochondrial substrate in RPE, sustaining Δψm and reducing NADH-driven mitochondrial ROS when glycolysis is impaired—conditions that model bioenergetic stress in geographic atrophy. Mechanistically, this is supported by three converging evidence streams: (1) mitochondrial fuel flexibility to oxidize BHB to acetyl-CoA via BDH1/SCOT, (2) redox modulation that increases NADH oxidation and elevates the NAD⁺/NADH ratio, and (3) multi-layered antioxidant/anti-inflammatory signaling that lowers mitochondrial ROS production and downstream inflammasome/NF-κB activation (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Gough, 2021).  

- Sustained Δψm and ATP under glycolytic impairment. RPE expresses ketogenesis machinery (HMGCS2) and monocarboxylate transport capacity (MCT1) and is capable of both producing and consuming BHB, while inner BRB MCT1 and neuronal MCT2 provide routes for substrate delivery into retinal tissue (Yang, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Gulette et al., 2024). In neurons, BHB preserved oxidative phosphorylation and ATP-linked respiration under MAS inhibition, a condition that effectively reduces mitochondrial access to cytosolic NADH from glycolysis; this predicts that, in RPE exposed to glycolytic blockade or high work demand, BHB could maintain Δψm and respiratory control by supplying acetyl-CoA independent of cytosolic NADH shuttling (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023). In muscle and cardiac models, BHB improved respiratory control ratios, increased ATP production, and maintained Δψm under stress, providing precedent for Δψm preservation in high-energy post-mitotic cells (Parker et al., 2018; Mierziak et al., 2021).  

- Lowered NADH-driven mtROS and improved redox balance. Nutritional ketosis increases the brain NAD⁺/NADH ratio and ketones inhibit mitochondrial ROS production by increasing NADH oxidation, a shift that is expected to suppress reverse electron transport and semiquinone leak at respiratory complexes under high NADH load (Morris et al., 2020). Although some cardiac literature reports context-dependent changes in the mitochondrial NAD couple under BHB with concurrent oxidation of coenzyme Q, the net effect across neural and muscle studies is reduced mitochondrial ROS generation and improved redox handling, a phenotype also observed in optic/retinal models after ketogenic interventions (Chu et al., 2021; Gough, 2021; Mierziak et al., 2021). These redox improvements are reinforced by Nrf2 activation and increased expression of antioxidant defenses (e.g., SOD2), which increase ROS quenching capacity in retinal and optic tissues (Gough, 2021).  

- Anti-inflammatory and barrier-preserving actions in RPE. BHB agonizes HCAR2 expressed by RPE and retinal microglia, reducing leukocyte infiltration, preserving tight junction integrity (ZO-1), and suppressing inflammasome/NF-κB signaling (Powell et al., 2021; Trotta et al., 2019). In hyperglycemic ARPE-19, BHB improved viability and cell cycle progression and modulated inflammatory cytokines, consistent with protection under metabolic stress (Argentino et al., 2025). By preserving ATP and lowering AMPK phosphorylation, BHB/ketone availability is expected to block NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation and downstream expression of IL-6 and TNF-α, reducing the chronic para-inflammatory milieu implicated in RPE degeneration (Gough, 2021).  

- Translational considerations for exposure and transport. Systemically delivered BHB can traverse the blood–retinal barrier via MCT1, and RPE’s own MCT1 provides transmembrane transport capacity; nonetheless, quantitative extracellular BHB at RPE surfaces is likely in the low micromolar range under basal conditions, and RPE produces and consumes BHB dynamically, implying that achieving therapeutic mitochondrial utilization in RPE will require millimolar plasma BHB or local delivery (Tribble et al., 2021; Gulette et al., 2024). Nutritional ketosis and exogenous ketone supplementation readily achieve 0.5–2 mM BHB in plasma in rodent and human studies, which are the concentrations used in many in vitro protection assays (Cooper et al., 2023; Argentino et al., 2025).  

Key readouts and validation metrics for the proposed assay should include Δψm (e.g., TMRM/TMRE), OCR/ECAR profiling and ATP-linked respiration (Seahorse), mitochondrial ROS (MitoSOX and H₂O₂ flux), NAD⁺/NADH ratio (enzymatic cycling and/or fluorescence lifetime imaging), pAMPK/AMPK and NF-κB p65 nuclear localization, Nrf2 translocation and target gene induction (e.g., SOD2), and inflammasome readouts (ASC specks, IL-1β maturation) (Gough, 2021). Given the measurement pitfalls documented in RPE ketone assays, BHB should be quantified by LC–MS/MS or after removal of high-MW confounders by size exclusion rather than by standard enzymatic kits (Gulette et al., 2024).  
Protein expression considerations support the mechanism in the target cell type. HCAR2/GPR109A is expressed by RPE and retinal microglia/endothelium and mediates anti-inflammatory effects of BHB in vivo, making receptor-dependent components of BHB action directly testable in RPE (Powell et al., 2021). RPE expresses HMGCS2 and MCT1, and retinal cells metabolize BHB into TCA intermediates, consistent with BDH1/SCOT/OXCT1 pathway activity enabling BHB oxidation in retinal tissues; while direct SCOT expression in RPE is not provided here, the metabolic tracing data indicating conversion of BHB to Krebs intermediates in retinal cells justify testing oxidative utilization in RPE (Yang, 2021; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strength of biological rationale. The core hypothesis—that BHB can act as an alternative mitochondrial fuel to sustain Δψm and lower NADH-driven mitochondrial ROS in glycolysis-impaired RPE—is strongly aligned with BHB’s established roles in extrahepatic tissues and is supported by multiple mechanistic strands in relevant neural and retinal systems (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023). BHB oxidation provides acetyl-CoA and maintains respiration when glycolytic NADH transfer is compromised, as demonstrated in primary neurons; BHB reduces mtROS, preserves Δψm, and increases ATP in ischemic muscle/heart models; and nutrient ketosis increases the NAD⁺/NADH ratio and lowers ROS production in brain—effects that would be expected to decrease reverse-electron transport–driven ROS at complex I and stabilize mitochondrial function in stressed RPE (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023; Mierziak et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020). In retinal tissue, ketogenic interventions and direct ketone administration reduce oxidative injury, preserve function, and enhance mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses in RGC/optic nerve models, while anti-inflammatory benefits via HCAR2—expressed by RPE—reduce leukocyte infiltration and preserve barrier integrity (Gough, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Powell et al., 2021; Trotta et al., 2019). The mitochondrial stabilization effects observed in human microglia—lower MCU/mtCa²⁺, reduced mtROS, prevention of mPTP opening—further support a BHB-mediated mitochondrial resilience phenotype that is likely relevant to RPE (Jin et al., 2023).  

Evidence relevant to the target tissue. RPEs possess ketone-related transport and enzymatic capacity (HMGCS2, MCT1) and can both produce and consume BHB; they are responsive to BHB in vitro under metabolic stress (hyperglycemia) with improved viability and inflammatory marker modulation (Yang, 2021; Argentino et al., 2025). HCAR2-mediated anti-inflammatory and barrier maintenance functions have been demonstrated in RPE/retina, providing a receptor-proximal pathway for BHB to suppress chronic para-inflammation and preserve RPE junctional integrity, both relevant to dry AMD pathobiology (Powell et al., 2021). While direct measurements of BDH1/SCOT activity and NAD⁺/NADH dynamics in human RPE treated with BHB remain to be shown here, the metabolic fate of BHB in retinal cells and robust mitochondrial effects in closely related cell types make the translational experiments technically feasible and mechanistically justified (Yang, 2021; Llorente-Folch et al., 2023).  

Translational gaps and risks. No clinical trials have evaluated ketogenic diets or BHB specifically for RP or AMD, and some ketogenic diet studies reported adverse outcomes in wild-type animals (decreased ERG amplitude, altered serum albumin/weight), emphasizing the need to decouple BHB’s effects from broader dietary/metabolic confounders (Gough, 2021). Direct BHB delivery does not always recapitulate ketogenic diet benefits in RGC injury, suggesting that multi-target effects of diet (e.g., NAD metabolism, mTOR, microbiome) contribute to efficacy; this implies that BHB monotherapy may require combination strategies (e.g., nicotinamide co-therapy) or optimized dosing to achieve comparable benefit (Tribble et al., 2021). Quantification of BHB in RPE experiments is non-trivial due to assay interference; LC–MS/MS or validated size-exclusion protocols must be used to avoid false positives and to measure physiologically relevant, often low-micromolar extracellular BHB in RPE cultures (Gulette et al., 2024). Finally, the directionality of NAD redox effects may be context dependent (reports of both increased NAD⁺/NADH ratio in brain and reduced mitochondrial NAD couple in cardiac models), requiring careful interpretation with compartment-specific assays in RPE (Morris et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2021).  

Development path and decision points. Given the strong mechanistic rationale, retina-focused preclinical evidence, and RPE receptor expression data, BHB is a plausible repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD that merits rigorous, RPE-centric validation. Key go/no-go preclinical criteria should include: (1) demonstration that BHB rescues Δψm and ATP-linked respiration in primary human RPE or iPSC-RPE under glycolytic impairment (e.g., 2-deoxyglucose or low glucose plus workload), (2) reduction of mitochondrial ROS (MitoSOX/H₂O₂ flux) and elevation of cellular NAD⁺/NADH ratio with BHB, (3) suppression of pAMPK and NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation, induction of Nrf2 target genes, and reduction of NLRP3 activation, (4) persistence of benefits under HCAR2 antagonism/knockdown to parse receptor versus fuel contributions, and (5) confirmation that effects are contingent on monocarboxylate transport (MCT inhibition) and SCOT activity (e.g., OXCT1 knockdown), which would mechanistically link outcomes to BHB oxidation rather than unrelated signaling (Llorente-Folch et al., 2023; Gough, 2021; Powell et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021). In vivo, a dry-AMD–relevant RPE degeneration model should test systemic or ocular BHB delivery (dose selection to 0.5–2 mM plasma equivalents) with readouts of RPE mitochondrial structure/function, subretinal inflammation, and lesion progression; blood–retina transport via MCT1 at the inner BRB suggests systemic exposure can reach the retina, though intraocular routes might achieve higher local concentrations (Tribble et al., 2021). Throughout, BHB dosing must be titrated to avoid off-target effects and electrolyte load associated with some salt formulations; direct ketone esters or controlled dietary induction may be considered for translational studies, recognizing model-specific differences seen between exogenous BHB and ketogenic diet (Tribble et al., 2021).  

Strengths  
- Mechanistic breadth and convergence on AMD-relevant pathways: alternative fuel supply to support Δψm/ATP, improved NAD redox and ROS control, Nrf2 antioxidant gene induction, and potent suppression of NLRP3/NF-κB–mediated para-inflammation via HCAR2—each independently linked to retinal/RPE resilience (Wang et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2020; Gough, 2021; Powell et al., 2021).  
- Retinal delivery/uptake plausibility: MCT expression at the inner BRB and in RPE, plus RPE’s ability to both produce and consume BHB, establish physiological routes for BHB transit and utilization in target tissues (Tribble et al., 2021; Yang, 2021; Gulette et al., 2024).  
- Preclinical efficacy signals in retinal and CNS models: reduced oxidative/inflammatory injury, preserved neuronal function, enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis/antioxidant defenses, and receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory actions in retina (Gough, 2021; Tribble et al., 2021; Trotta et al., 2019; Powell et al., 2021).  
- Compatibility with RPE stress biology: BHB improved ARPE-19 survival under metabolic stress and modulated cytokines, and microglial mitochondrial data demonstrate BHB reverses mtCa²⁺/mtROS/mPTP derangements that are mechanistically relevant to RPE degeneration (Argentino et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2023).  

Weaknesses and uncertainties  
- Lack of AMD-specific in vivo data and no clinical trials in AMD/RP; extrapolation from RGC/optic nerve/diabetic models requires confirmation in RPE-targeted systems (Gough, 2021).  
- Measurement pitfalls in RPE ketone studies; reliance on inaccurate enzymatic assays historically confounded interpretation, necessitating MS-based quantitation and careful time-course sampling (Gulette et al., 2024).  
- Context-dependent redox effects; reports differ on NAD couple responses to BHB, indicating the need for compartmentalized NAD⁺/NADH readouts in RPE to avoid misattribution (Morris et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2021).

The major risk is the current absence of AMD-specific in vivo evidence and the historical conflation of diet-level ketosis with BHB pharmacology; these can be addressed by an RPE-centric preclinical plan that uses rigorous ketone quantitation, compartmental redox readouts, transporter/enzyme perturbations (MCT/OXCT1), and in vivo validation in RPE degeneration models. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Tat‐Beclin 1 is a synthetic peptide designed to induce autophagy by harnessing a key region of the Beclin 1 protein, which is essential for the initiation of autophagosome formation (He et al., 2022). This candidate was originally derived by fusing a peptide fragment from Beclin 1, typically encompassing residues in the range of 267–284, with the HIV‐1 Tat transduction domain (Saqcena, 2018), thereby rendering it cell‐permeable and capable of entering diverse cell types. The synthesis and design of Tat‐Beclin 1 focus on exploiting the naturally occurring autophagy machinery by facilitating the release of inhibitory factors bound to Beclin 1 and enhancing its interactions with class III PI3K complexes (He et al., 2022). As a member of the therapeutic class of autophagy inducers, Tat‐Beclin 1 shares mechanistic commonalities with other peptides such as the stapled derivatives (e.g., Tat‐SP4) that have been developed to improve binding affinity and structural stability (Gao, 2023; Gao, 2023). This class of compounds has been widely investigated for their ability to promote autophagy in cellular models of cancer, neurodegeneration, and infection, and the peptide’s design rests on principles that have proven effective in enhancing cellular clearance mechanisms in several pathological contexts (He et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Tat‐Beclin 1 has been extensively characterized in preclinical studies as an inducer of autophagy in various cell types including cancer cells, neuronal cells, and immune cells (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). In early studies, it demonstrated potent autophagy‐stimulating effects by enhancing the transformation of LC3‐I to LC3‐II and by decreasing levels of the autophagic substrate p62, thereby leading to augmented autophagic flux (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013). Moreover, experimental applications have shown that Tat‐Beclin 1 can decrease viral titers in infection models such as those involving West Nile virus and chikungunya virus, and it has been explored for promoting autophagic clearance in cancer models, particularly in breast cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma (He et al., 2022; Gao, 2023). Although there is abundant evidence supporting its utility in managing proteotoxic stress and cellular damage in models of neurodegeneration and cancer, direct applications of Tat‐Beclin 1 for treating dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) have not been explicitly reported (Boland et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2016). Nevertheless, separate studies indicate that proper autophagy in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is critical for cellular viability and resistance to oxidative stress, where impaired autophagy contributes to the accumulation of toxic aggregates such as A2E and lipofuscin that are implicated in AMD (Frost et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Hence, while Tat‐Beclin 1 has not been directly applied in AMD models thus far, its mechanism of promoting clearance of damaged organelles and misfolded proteins provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD treatment.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Tat‐Beclin 1 functions by specifically interacting with Beclin 1, a core component of the Class III PI3K complex that regulates autophagosome nucleation (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). In its inactive state, Beclin 1 is sequestered by negative regulatory proteins such as GAPR‐1, which limits its availability for autophagic initiation. Tat‐Beclin 1 is designed to bind to these inhibitory regulators, thereby liberating Beclin 1 and enabling it to participate in the formation of the PI3K complex necessary for phagophore formation (Ha & Kim, 2016; He et al., 2022). This intervention effectively shifts the balance toward autophagy induction by enhancing the generation of autophagosomes and promoting lysosomal degradation of intracellular cargo. Furthermore, research has demonstrated that Tat‐Beclin 1 increases the conversion of LC3‐I to LC3‐II—a hallmark of autophagosome formation—and has been shown to lower p62 levels, which underscores its role in boosting autophagic flux (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013; Si et al., 2023). Additionally, the peptide’s cell‐penetrating Tat domain facilitates its entry into cells and ensures its functional delivery to intracellular compartments, which is critical for engaging the autophagic machinery even in cells with limited uptake capabilities (Saqcena, 2018; He et al., 2022). Through these molecular interactions, Tat‐Beclin 1 not only enhances general autophagy but has also been reported to drive selective autophagic processes such as mitophagy, thereby promoting the turnover of damaged mitochondria (He et al., 2022; Frost et al., 2014). This mechanistic detail is particularly relevant in conditions of oxidative stress where dysfunctional mitochondria accumulate and contribute to cell death, as has been observed in RPE cells during the progression of dry AMD (Frost et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry age‐related macular degeneration, the therapeutic hypothesis posits that Tat‐Beclin 1 will promote autophagy initiation in RPE cells to facilitate the turnover of damaged organelles—including mitochondria—that accumulate as a result of chronic oxidative stress (Frost et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). This enhanced autophagic clearance is expected to mitigate the cytotoxic effects associated with the buildup of toxic aggregates such as A2E and lipofuscin, which are known to drive RPE cell dysfunction and death (Zhang et al., 2015; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Experimental evidence from studies on RPE cells has documented that robust autophagic activity is critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis in the face of oxidative and metabolic insults (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Therefore, by increasing autophagic flux, Tat‐Beclin 1 should theoretically lead to a reduction in cellular stress markers and an improvement in mitochondrial quality control mechanisms, thereby preventing the initiation of apoptotic cascades in RPE cells (Saqcena, 2018). In cellular assays, the expected outcome would include an enhanced LC3‐II/LC3‐I ratio, decreased levels of p62, improved lysosomal function, and ultimately enhanced cell viability under oxidative stress conditions (Shoji-Kawata et al., 2013; Si et al., 2023). Notably, the efficacy of autophagy induction in rescuing RPE cellular function is supported by literature where pharmacological activation of autophagy—such as through rapamycin or inhibition of mTOR pathways—has been shown to protect RPE cells from degeneration (Frost et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2020). Given the inherent ability of Tat‐Beclin 1 to stimulate autophagy in other cellular models, it is reasonable to expect that similar benefits would be observed upon its application to RPE cells, leading to a deceleration of dry AMD pathology by maintaining mitochondrial turnover and preventing the accumulation of deleterious substrates.

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall potential of Tat‐Beclin 1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD lies in its well‐defined mechanism of action, which directly targets the autophagic machinery through interactions with Beclin 1 (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). One of the primary strengths of this candidate is its demonstrated versatility across different disease models, where enhancement of autophagy has led to reduced apoptosis, improved clearance of toxic protein aggregates, and mitigation of cellular stress in both cancer and neurodegenerative contexts (He et al., 2022; Boland et al., 2018). In the specific arena of RPE cell biology, multiple studies have established that autophagic dysfunction is a hallmark of AMD progression and that stimulating autophagy can improve cellular resilience under oxidative stress (Frost et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Therefore, by repurposing Tat‐Beclin 1 for dry AMD, there exists a compelling translational rationale based on mechanistic insights derived from both in vitro and in vivo studies in other systems.

However, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be considered. Despite extensive preclinical evidence in other domains, there is a lack of direct experimental data demonstrating the efficacy of Tat‐Beclin 1 in ocular models or in RPE-specific assays (He et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2016). This gap in the literature necessitates rigorous validation in relevant RPE cell culture systems and animal models of dry AMD to confirm that the peptide’s autophagy-inducing effects translate to meaningful therapeutic benefits for ocular health. In addition, the potential for overactivation of autophagy poses a safety concern, as excessive autophagic flux can lead to autophagic cell death or unintended degradation of essential cellular components (Pinelli et al., 2025; Peraro et al., 2017). Precise dosing and delivery strategies will therefore be critical to ensure that Tat‐Beclin 1 achieves a balance between sufficient autophagy induction and preservation of RPE cell integrity. 

Pharmacokinetic and biodistribution challenges also remain to be addressed, especially given the unique anatomical barriers of the eye. Although the Tat transduction domain confers robust cell penetration, the stability, half-life, and clearance of the peptide in ocular tissues have yet to be thoroughly investigated (Saqcena, 2018; He et al., 2022). Moreover, the route of administration—potentially through intravitreal injection or topical delivery—must be optimized to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE without eliciting adverse immune responses or off-target effects. It is also important to note that while the autophagy-stimulating effects of Tat‐Beclin 1 have been well documented in various cell types, the specific context of chronic oxidative stress and metabolite accumulation in the aged RPE represents a distinct microenvironment that may influence peptide efficacy (Frost et al., 2014; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Zhang et al., 2015).

Another consideration is the heterogeneity inherent in dry AMD pathology, where oxidative injury, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammatory processes all contribute to disease progression. Although enhancing autophagy could address multiple facets of the disease, the interplay between autophagic flux and other cellular pathways—such as inflammation and lipid metabolism—remains complex and may necessitate combination therapies for optimal outcomes (Zhang et al., 2020; Pinelli et al., 2025). Nonetheless, leveraging the established protective role of autophagy in RPE cells provides a solid foundation for further research on Tat‐Beclin 1, and its repurposing could represent a novel strategy to counteract the multifactorial stressors associated with dry AMD.

In summary, Tat‐Beclin 1 presents a mechanism-driven approach for inducing autophagy that is grounded in sound biochemical principles and supported by extensive preclinical studies in other disease contexts (He et al., 2022; Saqcena, 2018). Its ability to prompt autophagosome formation, enhance mitochondrial turnover, and clear toxic protein aggregates aligns well with the cellular deficits observed in dry AMD, particularly in the RPE. The cumulative literature underscores the therapeutic promise of autophagy-inducing peptides in mitigating oxidative stress and improving cellular viability (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Frost et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2020). However, the lack of direct data in AMD-focused models, potential risks associated with overactivation of autophagy, and the need for refined ocular delivery methods represent critical hurdles that must be overcome through further research. 

Given the potential benefits and the mechanistic rationale underpinning its use, Tat‐Beclin 1 merits further investigation in preclinical RPE models, with attention to dose optimization, delivery strategies, and long-term safety assessments in the context of retinal degeneration. Ultimately, if these challenges can be addressed, Tat‐Beclin 1 could emerge as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD by restoring cellular homeostasis and halting the progression of RPE degeneration. This comprehensive evaluation therefore supports the continued exploration of Tat‐Beclin 1’s therapeutic potential while highlighting the necessity for rigorous validation in ocular-specific experimental paradigms (Frost et al., 2014; Saqcena, 2018; Boland et al., 2018; Frost et al., 2014).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Liproxstatin-1 is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor of ferroptosis that was originally discovered using phenotypic high-throughput screening in systems where ferroptosis was induced by either genetic deletion of GPX4 or by glutathione depletion with agents like erastin (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69). Its chemical identity is tied to a unique spiroquinoxalinamine scaffold, which places it in the class of aromatic amine radical-trapping antioxidants (RTAs) – compounds well known in industrial settings to protect hydrocarbon products from autoxidation, as well as in biomedical research to block oxidative lipid chain reactions (Scarpellini, 2023, pp. 41–45; Angeli, Shah, Pratt, & Conrad, 2017, pp. 6–8). In contrast to classical phenolic antioxidants such as α-tocopherol, Liproxstatin-1 is designed to operate in the lipid bilayer, where its aminic (or diarylamine) moieties are less hindered by nonproductive hydrogen-bonding interactions with phospholipid headgroups, thus allowing rapid hydrogen-atom transfer to lipid peroxyl radicals (Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). Although detailed synthetic routes are not provided in the available reports, the discovery process clearly identifies Liproxstatin-1 as a lead candidate that emerged from unbiased cell-based screens aimed at identifying compounds that preserve cell viability in the absence of GPX4 function (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). Its categorization as an RTA is significant because this class of compounds has a long history of being used to inhibit free radical–mediated damage in both industrial and biological contexts (Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6).

Therapeutic History:  
The preclinical history of Liproxstatin-1 is rich with evidence supporting its role as a potent inhibitor of ferroptosis. Early studies demonstrated that Liproxstatin-1 acts at low nanomolar concentrations to prevent ferroptotic cell death in mouse embryonic fibroblasts as well as in specialized cells rendered vulnerable by GPX4 inactivation (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Angeli et al., 2014, p. 10). Beyond in vitro cell survival assays, Liproxstatin-1 has been evaluated in vivo where it has shown remarkable protective effects in models of acute tissue injury including genetic GPX4 deficiency, which induces acute renal failure, and in ischaemia/reperfusion models of liver injury (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10). Although its direct clinical use in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) has not been established – with most in vivo data coming from non-ocular models – its success in ameliorating tissue damage by inhibiting lipid peroxidation suggests its potential utility in other degenerative pathologies where oxidative membrane damage drives dysfunction, such as in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) degeneration underlying geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69; Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–21). Moreover, related compounds, notably Ferrostatin-1, have been tested in various retinal cell models and in some in vivo settings pertaining to retinal ischemia–reperfusion injury and oxygen-induced retinopathy, further bolstering the therapeutic concept of using RTA-type ferroptosis inhibitors in ocular settings (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23; Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8). While the bulk of Liproxstatin-1’s therapeutic history centers on its role as an anti-ferroptotic agent in cancer, neurodegeneration, and acute organ failure, its mechanistic overlap with key pathological features observed in dry AMD – such as iron accumulation, glutathione depletion and elevated lipid peroxidation in the RPE – supports evaluating it as a repurposed candidate in this context (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Shen et al., 2025, pp. 1–2).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism by which Liproxstatin-1 exerts its cytoprotective effect is rooted in its function as a radical-trapping antioxidant. Specifically, Liproxstatin-1 reacts rapidly with lipid peroxyl radicals that propagate the autoxidation chain reaction in cellular membranes. Experimental data have established that Liproxstatin-1 exhibits an intrinsic reaction rate constant (k_inh) in the range of approximately 2.4 × 10^5 M^−1 s^−1 in organic solvents such as chlorobenzene at 37 °C, which is comparable to industrial diarylamine antioxidants (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 8–9). Although its intrinsic reactivity in homogeneous organic solutions may appear lower than classical phenolic antioxidants like α-tocopherol, its performance in the lipid bilayer is superior due to reduced hydrogen-bonding interactions with phospholipid headgroups – a feature that enhances its mobility and reactivity in the lipid environment where ferroptosis is executed (Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 8–9; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). The compound functions primarily by donating a hydrogen atom from its arylamine (or diarylamine) N–H group, effectively quenching chain-propagating lipid peroxyl radicals before they can perpetuate lipid hydroperoxide formation (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). Kinetic isotope effect studies and computational analyses have confirmed that the N–H bond dissociation enthalpy is sufficiently low in Liproxstatin-1 to enable rapid hydrogen-atom transfer, which is a critical step in its radical-trapping mechanism (Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 2–3, 5–7). Importantly, Liproxstatin-1 does not exert significant inhibitory effects on enzymes such as human 15-lipoxygenase-1, thereby ruling out an enzymatic inhibition mechanism and reinforcing that its protective effect is solely attributable to non-enzymatic scavenging of peroxyl radicals (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 201–210). Recent studies have even suggested that Liproxstatin-1 may form a complex with iron in certain cellular compartments (e.g., the lysosome), which could further diminish iron-catalysed radical generation under acidic conditions; however, the predominant and well-characterized mechanism remains its role in intercepting lipid peroxyl radicals (Rodriguez et al., 2024, pp. 1–5; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Thus, by protecting cellular membranes from oxidative deterioration, Liproxstatin-1 interrupts the cascade of events leading to ferroptotic cell death, a process that is implicated in RPE degeneration seen in geographic atrophy (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shen et al., 2025, pp. 1–2).

In the context of dry AMD, particularly in geographic atrophy where RPE degeneration is a hallmark, the expected effect of Liproxstatin-1 would be to curtail the chain reaction of lipid peroxidation that underpins ferroptotic cell death. In vitro assays using RPE cell lines such as ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cells have demonstrated that targeting lipid peroxidation – as evidenced by reductions in markers like BODIPY-C11 oxidation and ACSL4 expression – can rescue cells from oxidative stress–mediated death (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–23). Liproxstatin-1 is anticipated to mitigate the accumulation of lipid hydroperoxides, thus preserving the integrity of cellular membranes and mitochondrial function in the RPE (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 1–2). Given that geographic atrophy in dry AMD is associated with iron overload and subsequent iron-catalysed lipid peroxidation, the ability of Liproxstatin-1 to trap peroxyl radicals is particularly significant; by reducing lipid ROS, it is expected to prevent the conversion of polyunsaturated fatty acids into cytotoxic lipid hydroperoxides, thereby maintaining cellular viability (Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210; Conrad & Pratt, 2019, pp. 5–6). Moreover, the inhibition of ACSL4-dependent peroxidation pathways – which have been linked to ferroptosis in RPE cells – may also be intercepted by Liproxstatin-1, providing a dual line of defense against ferroptotic signaling (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23; Angeli et al., 2017, pp. 6–8). On a cellular level, the compound is expected to maintain Δψm and reduce indicators of oxidative stress, as previously demonstrated in models addressing GPX4 inhibition (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). In essence, when applied to RPE cells under conditions that mimic dry AMD, Liproxstatin-1 should decrease oxidative markers, prevent cell death, and thereby slow or halt the progression of geographic atrophy by restoring the balance between pro-oxidant and antioxidant pathways (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–23).

Liproxstatin-1 stands out as a promising candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic agent against dry AMD, particularly in geographic atrophy, given the mechanistic overlap between ferroptosis and RPE cell death observed in dry AMD. One of its principal strengths lies in its potent radical-trapping antioxidant activity, which is not only effective at low nanomolar concentrations but also uniquely suited to the lipid bilayer environment of the RPE (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). This specificity is critical because retinal cells are subject to a high burden of polyunsaturated lipid content and are therefore particularly sensitive to oxidative damage. The fact that Liproxstatin-1 has demonstrated efficacy in protecting cells under ferroptotic stress in other organ systems – including kidney and liver models – further supports its potential viability in ocular applications (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Peng et al., 2020, pp. 3–5). Additionally, the compound’s ability to reduce lipid peroxidation, maintain mitochondrial membrane potential, and possibly engage in secondary iron-inactivating mechanisms (as suggested by lysosomal localization studies) offers multiple avenues through which it may address the multifactorial pathogenesis of dry AMD (Rodriguez et al., 2024, pp. 1–5; Zilka et al., 2017, pp. 1–2).

However, several challenges must be considered. Despite the strong preclinical evidence in non-ocular systems, direct evidence of Liproxstatin-1’s efficacy in models of dry AMD or RPE-specific ferroptosis is still limited relative to other compounds such as Ferrostatin-1 or nanoparticle-delivered ferroptosis inhibitors in retinal models (Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 20–23). This gap in ocular preclinical data implies that further dedicated studies using RPE cell models and in vivo dry AMD animal models are necessary to validate its protective effects in the eye. In addition, drug delivery to the retina poses its own set of challenges – the blood-retinal barrier and the unique pharmacokinetic profile required for intravitreal stability must be thoroughly optimized (Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69; Hao, Xu, Zhang, & Xue, 2024, pp. 6–7). Moreover, dry AMD is a multifactorial disease involving not only ferroptosis but also apoptosis, inflammation, and other forms of regulated cell death; therefore, while inhibiting ferroptosis may be beneficial, it is uncertain whether monotherapy with Liproxstatin-1 would be sufficient to arrest disease progression. There is also the matter of safety and tolerability in the context of the ocular environment, as systemic dosing strategies that work in renal or hepatic models may not directly translate to the delicate milieu of retinal tissues (Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Shah, 2019, pp. 207–210). Finally, considerations regarding the long-term stability, potential off-target effects, and metabolic fate of Liproxstatin-1 in the eye will be crucial parameters in the drug development process.

In summary, the collective literature indicates that Liproxstatin-1 has a well-defined mechanism as a radical-trapping antioxidant that effectively blocks lipid peroxidation and, by extension, ferroptosis. Its discovery through unbiased screening in ferroptosis-susceptible models and its demonstration of efficacy in multiple organ systems provide a strong foundation for its repurposing in dry AMD. The evidence supports that Liproxstatin-1 could counteract the iron-driven ROS amplification and lipid peroxidation that contribute to RPE cell death in geographic atrophy. Nonetheless, while its mechanistic rationale and preclinical promise are substantial, further research – particularly within retinal models – is necessary to fully evaluate its therapeutic potential and address challenges related to ocular delivery and multi-pathway disease components. Taken together, Liproxstatin-1 represents a compelling candidate for further investigation as a targeted inhibitor of ferroptosis in the treatment of dry AMD (Shah, Margison, & Pratt, 2017, pp. 4–7; Shah, 2019, pp. 66–69, 207–210; Angeli et al., 2014, pp. 9–10; Zhao et al., 2025, pp. 21–23).
