Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
XJB-5-131 is a synthetic mitochondria‐targeted nitroxide antioxidant that was developed by conjugating a redox‐active nitroxide moiety (derived from TEMPO, 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl) to a mitochondrial‐targeting peptide fragment derived from gramicidin S (often described in the literature as a hemigramicidin or alkene peptide isostere) (Liu et al., 2022; Robinson, 2012). This design harnesses the properties of the nitroxide, which is capable of catalytically scavenging reactive oxygen and lipid radicals through cycling between its nitroxide, hydroxylamine, and oxoammonium states, and the targeting moiety that enhances its lipid membrane permeability while concentrating the compound specifically in mitochondrial membranes (Wipf et al., 2022; Xun et al., 2022). The neutral charge of XJB-5-131 confers an advantage because it permits mitochondrial uptake independent of membrane potential, a feature that distinguishes it from the positively charged mitochondria-targeted antioxidants such as MitoQ (Robinson, 2012; Wipf et al., 2022). Moreover, fluorescent derivatives (e.g., BODIPY-labeled analogs) have been used to confirm its preferential accumulation in mitochondria by co-localization with mitochondrial markers, demonstrating an approximately 600-fold enrichment relative to the cytosol in some animal models (Wipf et al., 2022; Xun et al., 2022). Overall, XJB-5-131 belongs to the class of mitochondria-targeted nitroxides, a class that has been extensively studied for its ability to modulate oxidative stress in cellular and animal models across a variety of tissues (Xun et al., 2022; Robinson, 2012).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, XJB-5-131 has been the subject of preclinical investigation in several models of oxidative stress-related injury. It was originally developed to protect neuronal mitochondria and has been evaluated in models of Huntington’s disease, where it mitigated somatic instability and toxicity by reducing oxidative DNA damage and delaying motor decline (Liu et al., 2022; Xun et al., 2022). In various studies, XJB-5-131 demonstrated robust efficacy in reducing mitochondrial lipid peroxidation and preserving electron transport chain function in brain, neuronal, and even cardiac cell models (Robinson, 2012; Wipf et al., 2022). Additionally, its use in spinal cord injury models has shown that it can attenuate cardiolipin oxidation and reduce the activation of apoptotic cascades, leading to decreased lesion sizes and improved functional recovery (Ji et al., 2015; Robinson, 2012). There is also evidence of its application in models of ischemia–reperfusion injury, where its ability to blunt the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) was associated with neuroprotection (Xun et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022). Outside of central nervous system paradigms, related mitochondria-targeted nitroxides have been applied in experimental settings addressing ferroptosis and other oxidative stress pathologies (Zhang et al., 2024; Xun et al., 2022). However, despite its established role in neurological and other high-oxidative stress tissues, there is no direct published record – within the context of the available literature – demonstrating that XJB-5-131 has been used to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or any retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)-specific diseases (Wipf et al., 2022). Nonetheless, its pharmacological profile suggests potential applicability in settings where chronic oxidative stress drives pathology.

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism by which XJB-5-131 exerts its effects is twofold. First, the nitroxide moiety functions as a redox-active electron scavenger. Under oxidative stress, the nitroxide group readily interconverts with its hydroxylamine and oxoammonium forms; this redox cycling is capable of neutralizing superoxide anions (O2•–) by oxidizing them to molecular oxygen and hydrogen peroxide, effectively mimicking the activity of superoxide dismutase (SOD) (Wipf et al., 2022). Additionally, the hydroxylamine state can donate a hydrogen atom to terminate radical chain reactions, thereby neutralizing lipid peroxyl radicals that propagate lipid peroxidation – a process central to drusen formation and RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Robinson, 2012; Xun et al., 2022). Second, the gramicidin-derived delivery moiety imparts mitochondrial selectivity due to its structural mimicry of naturally occurring cyclic peptides that exhibit high lipid membrane affinity. This results in an efficient and selective accumulation of the antioxidant within the inner mitochondrial membrane, which is particularly important given that mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage have been implicated in aging and various degenerative diseases (Wipf et al., 2022). Experimental studies have shown that XJB-5-131 can act as a mild uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation, leading to a slight increase in oxygen consumption without detrimentally affecting ATP production; this mild uncoupling may serve to lower the mitochondrial membrane potential, thereby reducing the propensity for electron leakage and subsequent ROS generation (Xun et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2024). Furthermore, XJB-5-131’s ability to reduce mitochondrial ROS levels has been documented using both biochemical assays based on Amplex Red for hydrogen peroxide detection and Seahorse assays for oxygen consumption rate (OCR) analysis (Xun et al., 2022). These combined actions—the direct scavenging of radical species and the dampening of ROS-generating processes via mild uncoupling—support a mechanism by which XJB-5-131 could preserve mitochondrial structure (e.g., cristae integrity) and function under chronic oxidative conditions.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD and RPE Context:  
In the context of dry AMD, the pathophysiology is strongly linked to chronic oxidative insult, particularly within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where elevated ROS and lipid peroxidation contribute to mitochondrial dysfunction, accumulation of drusen constituents, and eventual RPE degeneration. The dual mechanism of XJB-5-131 is especially promising for this disease. Given its lipid radical scavenging capabilities, XJB-5-131 is expected to reduce malondialdehyde (MDA) and other markers of lipid peroxidation that are elevated in RPE under chronic UVA or other oxidative stresses (Ji et al., 2015). The compound’s well-documented ability to decrease ROS levels in neuronal and cardiac models, while preserving overall mitochondrial respiration, suggests that similar protective effects can be anticipated in RPE cells, which are highly metabolically active and depend critically on mitochondrial health (Wipf et al., 2022). In preliminary in vitro assays – such as those using pig RPE explants under UVA stress – one would expect XJB-5-131 to reduce MDA-adduct formation and preserve mitochondrial cristae, thereby maintaining cellular homeostasis (the hypothesis provided). At a molecular level, by delivering the nitroxide directly into RPE mitochondria, the compound would catalytically neutralize both superoxide and lipid peroxyl radicals. This dual scavenging effect can interrupt the vicious cycle of chronic oxidative damage that drives RPE dysfunction and drusen accumulation (Liu et al., 2022). Expression studies have demonstrated that genes associated with oxidative stress regulation, such as those encoding SOD and other mitochondrial antioxidants, are active in RPE cells, further supporting the notion that a mitochondria-targeted intervention like XJB-5-131 could restore redox homeostasis in these cells (Wipf et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024). Additionally, by functionally acting as a mild uncoupler, XJB-5-131 may lower mitochondrial membrane potential just enough to reduce electron leakage without compromising adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthesis, a delicate balance that is particularly important given the high energy requirements of the RPE (Zhou et al., 2024; Ji et al., 2015). Altogether, these effects are anticipated to culminate in the preservation of cristae integrity, reduced oxidative damage, and ultimately improved cell survival—key outcomes that align with the therapeutic goals in treating dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Overall, XJB-5-131 emerges as an attractive candidate for repurposing as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD owing to several intrinsic strengths. Foremost among these is its robust mitochondrial targeting capability. The incorporation of a gramicidin S-derived peptide moiety ensures that the nitroxide antioxidant is selectively delivered to mitochondria, a critical advantage because mitochondrial dysfunction is central to the pathology of dry AMD (Liu et al., 2022; Robinson, 2012). Its redox cycling properties not only mirror those of enzymatic antioxidants like SOD but also extend protection by neutralizing lipid peroxyl radicals, thereby addressing both protein and lipid oxidation pathways that contribute to drusen formation and RPE cell death (Wipf et al., 2022). Moreover, the reported preclinical successes in neurological and cardiac models, where XJB-5-131 has been shown to mitigate oxidative damage, reduce apoptotic signaling, and improve tissue function, suggest potential translatability of these protective effects to the ocular milieu (Robinson, 2012; Xun et al., 2022). The fact that its use as a mild uncoupler does not compromise ATP production provides an additional safety margin when considering tissues with high energy demands such as the RPE (Xun et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2024).

Nevertheless, there are certain limitations and challenges that must be carefully considered before advancing XJB-5-131 into dry AMD studies. Notably, while its efficacy in neuronal, spinal cord, and ischemia-reperfusion models has been well documented, there is a paucity of direct preclinical data demonstrating its benefits specifically in RPE cells or models of retinal degeneration (Wipf et al., 2022; Robinson, 2012). The hypothesis that it can reduce MDA-adduct formation in pig RPE explants under UVA stress is promising; however, this observation must be validated in more comprehensive models of dry AMD that mimic the chronic oxidative environment of the human RPE. Additionally, the complex synthetic route—often reported to involve multiple steps and potentially low water solubility—could pose a challenge for scale-up manufacturing and may necessitate formulation strategies to optimize bioavailability for ocular applications (Wipf et al., 2022; Kaden & Li, 2013). Delivery to the posterior segment of the eye also remains a significant hurdle; while systemic administration has been effective in other animal models, local delivery methods (e.g., intravitreal injection or novel nanocarrier systems) may be required to achieve therapeutic concentrations in the RPE without off-target effects. Furthermore, despite promising indications of safety in long-term animal studies (with chronic dosing in rodent models showing minimal adverse effects), thorough toxicological investigations will be essential given the sensitive nature of the retinal environment (Wipf et al., 2022; Echeverri-Ruiz et al., 2018). Finally, while the dual scavenging of superoxide and lipid radicals is mechanistically compelling, the risk of interfering with physiological redox signaling must be carefully balanced to avoid unintended consequences on cellular homeostasis (Xun et al., 2022).

In summary, XJB-5-131 represents a highly innovative and mechanistically sound candidate with significant potential for repurposing in dry AMD. Its ability to deliver a nitroxide antioxidant directly to mitochondria, neutralize deleterious ROS, and preserve mitochondrial function aligns well with the current understanding of RPE pathology in dry AMD. The extensive preclinical data in other high-oxidative stress models provide a strong rationale for its further evaluation in ocular-specific models. However, the absence of direct RPE or retinal degeneration studies, formulation and delivery challenges, and the inherent complexity of its synthesis necessitate a cautious and well-planned approach moving forward. Future research should focus on rigorous evaluation in RPE cell culture systems and animal models of dry AMD, optimization of ocular delivery strategies, and comprehensive toxicological assessments to ensure both efficacy and safety in the intended indication (Xun et al., 2022; Bowie, 2018; Wipf et al., 2022). Overall, while challenges remain, the unique pharmacological profile of XJB-5-131 provides a strong basis for considering it as a therapeutic candidate in the fight against dry age-related macular degeneration.

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of EPI-743 (vatiquinone) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). This report is organized into five sections: an Overview of the Therapeutic Candidate, a review of its Therapeutic History, a detailed discussion of its Mechanism of Action, an outline of the Expected Effects in the dry AMD context, and an Overall Evaluation of its strengths and limitations.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate

EPI-743, commonly referred to as vatiquinone, is a synthetic, short-chain quinone derivative that was designed based on biochemical modifications of naturally occurring vitamin E compounds. Its origin can be traced to the oxidation products of tocopherols and tocotrienols—members of the vitamin E family—which, through oxidative metabolism, yield quinone species. Specifically, EPI-743 is produced when these compounds are oxidized (Cores et al., 2023). Chemically, it belongs to the para-benzoquinone class, a subclass of quinones that are characterized by their fully conjugated cyclic unsaturated dione structure and their capacity for reversible redox cycling. Its design intentionally mirrors that of endogenous mitochondrial mediators such as ubiquinone (CoQ10), but significant modifications have been made to enhance aqueous solubility as well as to confer an extraordinary potency; indeed, experimental evidence indicates that on a molar basis, EPI-743 can be 10³ to 10⁴ times more potent than CoQ10 or even idebenone, another short-chain quinone analogue (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Gueven et al., 2017).

The discovery of EPI-743 originated from a small-molecule screening effort in which candidate compounds were evaluated for their ability to rescue cell viability under conditions of oxidative stress and glutathione depletion. This high-throughput screening methodology identified EPI-743 as a promising redox modulator with strong protective activity, leading to its subsequent advancement into preclinical testing and clinical evaluation by companies such as Edison Pharmaceuticals and PTC Therapeutics (Cores et al., 2023). As a representative member of the quinone drug class, EPI-743 is mechanistically designed to act as an electron shuttle, undergoing a reversible two-electron reduction to its corresponding hydroquinone form—a transformation that lies at the heart of its antioxidant activity and distinguishes it from many classical antioxidants. Because quinones in general have been used both as pharmaceutical antioxidants and as electron carriers in mitochondrial function, the chemical heritage of EPI-743 provides a strong rationale for its use in conditions characterized by redox imbalances (Tinker et al., 2021; Hong et al., 2023).

In summary, the chemical origin of EPI-743 is synthetic, being inspired by vitamin E’s tocotrienol derivatives and subsequently optimized to form a para-benzoquinone structure. Its classification among short-chain quinones places it in a well-studied category of compounds that have been used to modulate cellular redox states in various settings, particularly in diseases associated with mitochondrial dysfunction (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Gueven et al., 2017).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History

The therapeutic use history of EPI-743 is predominantly rooted in the context of mitochondrial diseases and other disorders associated with oxidative stress. Preclinically, it has been shown to protect various cell types against oxidative insult in vitro, particularly in experimental models where glutathione levels are artificially depleted. Studies have demonstrated that EPI-743 significantly enhances cell viability under conditions that would otherwise trigger cell death mechanisms such as ferroptosis and apoptosis (Gueven et al., 2017; Cores et al., 2023). Furthermore, the compound has been extensively studied in animal models of mitochondrial dysfunction with evidence suggesting that it supports key mitochondrial functions including electron transport and ATP synthesis.

Clinically, EPI-743 has been investigated in several rare inherited mitochondrial disorders. For instance, initial clinical studies in pediatric patients with Leigh syndrome—a severe neurodegenerative disorder characterized by mitochondrial respiratory chain dysfunction—have yielded promising results. In these studies, treatment with EPI-743 correlated with stabilization or even improvement in disease progression markers and had observable beneficial effects on neurological function (Gueven et al., 2017; Ji et al., 2021). In addition, small open-label studies have been conducted in patients with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON), an inherited optic neuropathy known to involve mitochondrial dysfunction in retinal ganglion cells; such studies indicated that early administration of EPI-743 may arrest disease progression and, in some cases, partially reverse visual loss (Gueven et al., 2017; Hong et al., 2023). Further clinical evaluation has expanded EPI-743’s investigation into other mitochondrial and neurodegenerative conditions such as Friedreich’s ataxia and refractory epilepsy, all of which share common mechanistic ties to oxidative stress and impaired bioenergetics (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

Despite its extensive evaluation in mitochondrial diseases and neurodegenerative disorders, there is no direct evidence in the literature indicating that EPI-743 has been used to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar age-related retinal conditions. There are no published studies that have directly tested EPI-743 in preclinical models of AMD, nor are there clinical trial reports of its use in an elderly population suffering from AMD. Although several quinone-based compounds (for example, idebenone) have been evaluated in ocular diseases, and the pathophysiological overlap between mitochondrial dysfunction and retinal degeneration is recognized, the existing body of literature on EPI-743 primarily focuses on inherited mitochondrial encephalomyopathies and optic neuropathies rather than on common, age-related retinal disorders (Gueven et al., 2017).

Overall, while the clinical track record of EPI-743 in conditions characterized by disrupted mitochondrial bioenergetics positions it as a promising candidate from a mechanistic perspective, its therapeutic history does not yet include any studies directly addressing the multifactorial nature of dry AMD. However, the established ability of EPI-743 to modulate cellular redox status suggests that it might have potential in the AMD setting as well (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action

At the molecular level, EPI-743 exerts its effects primarily through its redox activity, a function that is intimately linked to its para-benzoquinone core. This structure allows EPI-743 to participate in reversible redox cycling—a process in which the quinone is reduced to its hydroquinone form and oxidized back to the quinone form as needed (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021). The reduction is typically mediated by cytosolic oxidoreductases, most notably NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), an enzyme that is ubiquitously expressed, including in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012). NQO1 catalyzes a two-electron transfer reaction that converts the oxidized quinone into its corresponding hydroquinone. This hydroquinone is not only a potent free-radical scavenger but also plays a crucial role in regenerating the cellular pool of reduced glutathione (GSH) (Tinker et al., 2021; Cores et al., 2023).

Reduced glutathione is the primary intracellular antioxidant, essential for neutralizing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and protecting macromolecules from oxidative damage. In scenarios where ROS overwhelm a cell’s antioxidant capacity—such as during mitochondrial dysfunction or in cells under chronic oxidative stress—GSH levels become depleted and oxidized glutathione (GSSG) accumulates. By facilitating the replenishment of GSH, EPI-743 helps re‐establish redox balance and thus serves as an indirect regulator of oxidative stress (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Tinker et al., 2021). This redox cycling is considered “catalytic” because once the hydroquinone form scavenges a radical or reduces another molecule, it is itself reoxidized back to the quinone, whereupon it can undergo another round of reduction. Thus, even at relatively low concentrations, EPI-743 provides a sustained antioxidant effect.

In addition to its role in antioxidant defense, EPI-743 has been shown to modulate specific redox-sensitive enzymes. For example, its activity has been linked to the modulation of 15-lipoxygenase (15-LO), a key enzyme in lipid peroxidation pathways that can trigger ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death associated with lipid peroxidation. By inhibiting 15-LO activity, EPI-743 may reduce the peroxidative damage to polyunsaturated fatty acids within cellular membranes—a damage process that is especially detrimental in cells with a high metabolic rate such as retinal pigment epithelium (Cores et al., 2023; Kayser et al., 2024). This function is particularly relevant since ferroptosis has been implicated in conditions where oxidative stress is central.

Furthermore, the quinone’s ability to modulate intracellular redox signaling involves its interaction with transcription factors such as nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2). By maintaining a favorable GSH/GSSG ratio and reducing the overall burden of ROS, EPI-743 indirectly helps to sustain Nrf2 signaling, which in turn upregulates the expression of a panel of antioxidant genes. This feedback loop reinforces the cell’s capacity to respond to oxidative challenges. Though direct evidence linking EPI-743 to Nrf2 activation in retinal cells is sparse, the dependency of its action on NQO1—which itself is regulated in part by Nrf2—suggests that such interactions are plausible (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

In summary, EPI-743’s mechanism of action is multifaceted. It directly scavenges ROS via its hydroquinone intermediate, it enhances the reduced glutathione pool and thereby improves the cell’s overall antioxidant capacity, and it modulates lipid peroxidation pathways by affecting 15-LO activity. The reliance on NQO1 for its activation further supports its broad potential, given that NQO1 is expressed in many cell types, including those in the retina. These biochemical properties collectively suggest that EPI-743 has the potential to mitigate oxidative damage in environments where mitochondrial dysfunction and redox imbalance predominate (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect in Dry AMD

Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by the progressive degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium and underlying photoreceptors, a process that is driven in part by chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and the accumulation of oxidative DNA lesions. In the RPE, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is particularly vulnerable to oxidative damage because of its proximity to the electron transport chain and its relative lack of protective histones. One of the most common oxidative modifications observed in mtDNA is 8-oxo-2′-deoxyguanosine (8-oxoG), a marker of oxidative base lesions that can lead to mutagenesis and impaired mitochondrial function. The hypothesis underlying the repurposing of EPI-743 for dry AMD is that its potent redox cycling mechanism can reset the oxidative environment in RPE cells by regenerating reduced glutathione and by supporting NQO1-mediated detoxification, thereby reducing the accumulation of damaging oxidative lesions in mtDNA (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

In an in vitro assay designed to analyze oxidative stress in RPE cells, one would expect that treatment with EPI-743 would lead to several measurable outcomes. First, due to its rapid redox cycling and ability to donate electrons, EPI-743 would be anticipated to reduce intracellular levels of ROS, thereby directly lowering the formation of 8-oxoG lesions in mitochondrial DNA. This effect should manifest as a reduction in the cellular markers of oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation. Second, given the established role of NQO1 in catalyzing the conversion of EPI-743 to its hydroquinone form, and the fact that NQO1 is known to be expressed in RPE cells, the compound is expected to increase the intracellular GSH/GSSG ratio in these cells, further reinforcing the antioxidant defense system (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012).

Additionally, improved mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) function is a key expected outcome. In dry AMD, compromised mitochondrial integrity leads to reduced ATP production and increased susceptibility to cell death. By restoring redox balance, EPI-743 should preserve the integrity of mitochondrial membranes and ensure effective electron transport, ultimately resulting in enhanced ATP synthesis. This restoration of mitochondrial function could be assessed via assays that measure mitochondrial membrane potential, ATP synthesis rates, and oxygen consumption rates in RPE cell cultures challenged with oxidants (Kayser et al., 2024; Tinker et al., 2021).

Moreover, an important aspect of EPI-743’s expected effect is its potential to mitigate ferroptotic cell death pathways. Ferroptosis, driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation, has been implicated in the degeneration of RPE cells. By inhibiting 15-lipoxygenase and curbing lipid peroxidation, EPI-743 could help prevent the execution of ferroptotic cell death in RPE cells—a process that may contribute to the progression of dry AMD (Cores et al., 2023).

Taken together, in an experimental model of dry AMD—whether in RPE cell culture or in an appropriate animal model—administration of EPI-743 is expected to lead to: (1) a significant decline in ROS levels, (2) an increased ratio of reduced-to-oxidized glutathione, (3) preservation of mitochondrial DNA integrity as evidenced by reduced 8-oxoG accumulation, (4) improved mitochondrial bioenergetics as indicated by enhanced ATP production and mitochondrial membrane potential, and (5) inhibition of deleterious lipid peroxidation pathways. The successful demonstration of these effects would serve as strong biochemical and cellular evidence supporting the hypothesis that EPI-743 can protect RPE cells from the oxidative insults characteristic of dry AMD (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

Furthermore, since the RPE is known to express NQO1—an enzyme critical for the activation of EPI-743—the molecular basis for its activity is supported by tissue-specific expression data. This provides additional justification for targeting RPE cells with EPI-743 in the context of dry AMD, where bolstering the endogenous antioxidant systems may have a measurable impact on disease progression (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Tinker et al., 2021).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation

EPI-743 stands out as a highly promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD owing to several strengths rooted in its potent redox-modulatory properties and well-characterized mitochondrial protective effects. One of its major strengths is its extraordinary antioxidant potency. As a para-benzoquinone analogue that can be reduced via NQO1-catalyzed reactions to its hydroquinone state, EPI-743 is capable of intercepting and neutralizing ROS with an efficiency that surpasses that of conventional antioxidants such as CoQ10 by three to four orders of magnitude (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Gueven et al., 2017). This high level of potency is particularly appealing for conditions like dry AMD, in which the cumulative oxidative stress has a direct impact on mtDNA damage and cellular energetic deficits.

Another significant advantage is the compound’s established clinical track record in diseases marked by mitochondrial dysfunction. Although its clinical applications have thus far been restricted to rare inherited mitochondrial conditions like Leigh syndrome and LHON, the underlying mechanisms—namely, the restoration of mitochondrial bioenergetics and redox balance through effective GSH regeneration—are equally relevant to the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Gueven et al., 2017). Its ability to protect retinal ganglion cells in LHON studies suggests that similar beneficial effects might be extrapolated to retinal pigment epithelial cells, which are critically involved in the development of AMD.

Mechanistically, EPI-743’s dual action—both as a direct antioxidant and as a modulator of redox-sensitive pathways involving 15-lipoxygenase—confers a multi-pronged approach to cytoprotection. By reducing ROS and regenerating intracellular glutathione levels, EPI-743 can potentially arrest the oxidative modifications that lead to deleterious mtDNA lesions such as 8-oxoG. Moreover, the inhibition of enzymes that contribute to lipid peroxidation may further protect cellular membranes and reduce downstream inflammatory responses. These attributes provide a compelling scientific rationale for considering EPI-743 as a therapeutic strategy to combat the chronic oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction associated with dry AMD (Tinker et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be acknowledged. First and foremost, the current therapeutic history of EPI-743 shows no direct evidence of efficacy in dry AMD or other age-related retinal conditions. All of the published studies to date have focused on inherited mitochondrial or neurodegenerative disorders. Therefore, there remains a significant gap in our knowledge regarding its pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics in the context of the aging retina, which has a distinct microenvironment compared to the tissues examined in inherited disorders (Gueven et al., 2017).

Another concern is the potential difference in drug metabolism and toxicity between the predominantly pediatric or young adult populations (commonly studied in mitochondrial diseases) and the elderly patient population that is most affected by dry AMD. Age-related alterations in absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) could impact both efficacy and the safety profile of EPI-743 when repurposed for an older demographic (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Hong et al., 2023). Furthermore, while the activation of EPI-743 via NQO1 is a mechanistically attractive feature, the ubiquitous and sometimes unpredictable nature of redox enzyme activity in different tissues raises the possibility of off-target effects. Chronic systemic administration in an elderly population might result in unforeseen modifications in redox homeostasis not only within the retina but also in other vulnerable organs (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

In addition, the multifactorial pathogenesis of dry AMD poses a challenge to any therapeutic approach that primarily targets oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. While these are certainly key components of AMD pathology, the disease also involves chronic inflammation, drusen formation, and alterations in extracellular matrix homeostasis. It is therefore uncertain whether the powerful antioxidant activity of EPI-743 alone would be sufficient to halt or reverse the progression of dry AMD. Successful treatment may require a combination approach that addresses multiple causative factors, and it remains to be seen if EPI-743 can be integrated effectively into such a therapeutic regimen (Gueven et al., 2017; Cores et al., 2023).

Lastly, the translation from preclinical models—where the compound’s efficacy has been demonstrated in controlled settings of inherited mitochondrial dysfunction—to an age-related, multifaceted disease state such as dry AMD is non-trivial. Preclinical RPE-focused studies, including those measuring ROS levels, mitochondrial membrane potential, and direct assessments of mtDNA damage in the context of oxidative challenges, are currently lacking. Such studies are critical to validate whether the mechanisms observed in other cell types or disease models are applicable to the RPE and to the pathophysiology of AMD (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Overall Conclusion

In conclusion, EPI-743 (vatiquinone) exhibits many characteristics that render it an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its synthetic origin from vitamin E–derived tocotrienol derivatives and its classification as a para-benzoquinone confer upon it a robust redox-cycling capacity, enabling it to function as an exceptionally potent mitochondrial antioxidant. Through its ability to be reduced by NQO1 to a hydroquinone state, EPI-743 effectively regenerates intracellular reduced glutathione while simultaneously inhibiting lipid peroxidation via modulation of 15-lipoxygenase activity. These mechanisms collectively support its potential to protect mitochondrial DNA from oxidative damage, preserve electron transport chain function, and maintain ATP production in highly metabolically active cells such as the retinal pigment epithelium (Cores et al., 2023; Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021).

The therapeutic history of EPI-743 in inherited mitochondrial disorders and optic neuropathies provides a valuable proof of concept regarding its efficacy in situations where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central to pathogenesis. However, the absence of any direct study in dry AMD represents a significant gap that must be addressed through focused preclinical research. In the context of dry AMD, where chronic oxidative stress leads to the accumulation of damaging mtDNA lesions (including 8-oxoG) and progressive RPE degeneration, a potent redox modulator like EPI-743 theoretically offers a promising means to break the cycle of oxidative damage and mitochondrial decline (Tinker et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

Notwithstanding its potential strengths, several uncertainties must be highlighted. The pharmacokinetics and safety profile of EPI-743 in an elderly population—where changes in drug metabolism are common—remain to be fully elucidated. Moreover, the complex etiology of dry AMD, which involves not only oxidative damage and mitochondrial failure but also inflammatory and extracellular matrix alterations, may necessitate a multifaceted treatment strategy beyond a single antioxidant approach. As such, while the mechanistic rationale for using EPI-743 in dry AMD is well founded by virtue of its antioxidant and mitochondria-protective properties, clinical translation will require rigorous demonstration of efficacy in RPE-based in vitro systems and in animal models that recapitulate the full spectrum of AMD pathology (Gueven et al., 2017; Cores et al., 2023).

Given these considerations, the repurposing of EPI-743 for dry AMD holds promise—but only with additional preclinical studies that specifically assess its ability to ameliorate oxidative damage in the retinal pigment epithelium. Key experiments should focus on measuring changes in redox biomarkers, mtDNA integrity, ATP production, and cellular viability in RPE cells under oxidative stress. Parallel in vivo studies in animal models of AMD will be essential to determine ocular bioavailability, dosing parameters, and potential off-target effects in an aged organism.

Overall, the strengths of EPI-743 lie in its unparalleled antioxidant potency and its established capacity to restore mitochondrial function in disease settings characterized by oxidative damage. Final Remarks

EPI-743 (vatiquinone) presents an attractive therapeutic opportunity given its synthetic derivation from vitamin E, its classification as a para-benzoquinone with exceptionally potent antioxidant capabilities, and its ability to support mitochondrial function through NQO1-mediated redox modulation and glutathione regeneration. Although its historical clinical use has been confined to inherited mitochondrial diseases and optic neuropathies rather than age-related conditions, the underlying pathophysiological similarities—namely oxidative stress and mitochondrial compromise—provide a logical foundation for hypothesizing its efficacy in dry AMD. In summary, while the available data from mitochondrial and neurodegenerative disease studies provide a robust mechanistic rationale for the use of EPI-743 as a potent redox modulator and mitochondria-protective agent, the leap to a therapeutic indication in dry AMD remains largely theoretical at this point. With appropriate preclinical validation, EPI-743 could emerge as a valuable component of a combination therapy strategy that addresses the multifactorial nature of dry AMD. This repurposing effort would potentially fill a significant therapeutic gap in a disease area where effective treatments are currently lacking (Tinker et al., 2021; Cores et al., 2023; Gueven et al., 2017).

1. No current preclinical or clinical studies have directly examined the efficacy of EPI-743 in dry AMD models. While the redox mechanisms implicated in inherited mitochondrial diseases overlap with those theorized in AMD, the multifactorial nature of AMD—which involves chronic inflammation, drusen formation, and vascular compromise in addition to oxidative stress—means that a pure antioxidant approach may need to be complemented with additional interventions (Cores et al., 2023).

2. 4. Conclusion

EPI-743 (vatiquinone) is a highly potent, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant derived from vitamin E metabolites and classified within the para-benzoquinone family of compounds. Its design is centered on harnessing reversible two-electron redox cycling mediated by NQO1, leading to enhanced intracellular levels of reduced glutathione and effective mitigation of ROS and lipid peroxidation. Clinically, it has shown promise in mitigating the effects of mitochondrial dysfunction in inherited neurodegenerative and optic neuropathic disorders such as Leigh syndrome and LHON. Prior to any clinical application in dry AMD, it is imperative to undertake a rigorous series of preclinical studies focused on RPE cells and AMD animal models. However, significant additional research is required to bridge the translational gap between the current indications for which EPI-743 has been studied and the complex, multifactorial pathology of dry AMD. Given the extensive unmet clinical need in dry AMD and the promising mechanistic rationale, a targeted preclinical evaluation of EPI-743 in ocular systems is both justified and urgent. Based on the current literature and mechanistic insights, the following steps are advised before clinical repurposing of EPI-743 for dry AMD is pursued:

1. Develop and validate in vitro RPE cell culture models under conditions of chronic oxidative stress to assess the direct impact of EPI-743 on mitochondrial bioenergetics, redox balance, and mtDNA integrity.

With careful and targeted preclinical experimentation, the repurposing of EPI-743 may eventually provide a novel therapeutic option for a patient population in urgent need of effective treatments (Suárez-Rivero et al., 2021; Tinker et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2024).

Closing Summary

In conclusion, the evidence from the biochemical, clinical, and therapeutic literature reviewed herein supports the following: EPI-743 (vatiquinone) is a synthetically derived para-benzoquinone that leverages redox cycling and glutathione regeneration via NQO1 to protect mitochondria from oxidative insult. Its clinical history in mitochondrial disorders provides an encouraging precedent, and its detailed mechanism of action is highly relevant to conditions characterized by oxidative mtDNA damage—such as dry AMD. S3QEL-2 is a synthetic small‐molecule member of the S3QEL (Suppressors of Superoxide production from mitochondrial Complex III) class, originally discovered through a high‐throughput screen of approximately 635,000 small molecules using isolated mitochondria and an Amplex UltraRed H₂O₂ detection assay (Orr et al., 2015). In this screening paradigm, compounds were rigorously selected for their ability to selectively suppress superoxide generation arising from the Qo site of mitochondrial Complex III without impairing oxidative phosphorylation or altering the mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) (Orr et al., 2015). The discovery approach involved counterscreens that monitored Δψm changes, respiration rates, and markers of cellular viability, ensuring that S3QEL-2 exhibits specificity in mitigating reactive oxygen species (ROS) production rather than acting as a nonspecific antioxidant or uncoupler (Orr et al., 2015). S3QEL-2 was sourced from commercial screening collections—for example, vendors such as Chemdiv—and its powder-stock purity was confirmed by HPLC–MS analysis (Orr et al., 2015). As a member of a structurally diverse chemotype group, S3QEL-2 belongs to a new class of mitochondrial ROS-targeted modulators that differ fundamentally from classical Complex III inhibitors such as antimycin A or myxothiazol; unlike these inhibitors, S3QELs do not block the electron transfer chain or impair ATP production, but rather reduce the electron leak from the semiquinone intermediate at the Qo site (Orr et al., 2015). In general, compounds in the S3QEL class have been used experimentally as probes to decouple pathological ROS generation from normal bioenergetic function in diverse cell types, with applications ranging from studies on hypoxia-induced transcription (e.g., HIF-1α signaling) to experiments investigating ROS-mediated cell stress in pancreatic β-cells (Orr et al., 2015). The commercial catalog number Cayman Chemical #26918 identifies S3QEL-2 for research purposes, which suggests that this compound is available for repurposing studies beyond its initial characterization in nonocular systems (Orr et al., 2015).

Therapeutic History:  
Although S3QEL-2 was originally developed as a novel chemical probe to selectively suppress Complex III-derived superoxide production, its preclinical evaluation has been extensive within the context of cellular models evaluating ROS-mediated signaling and cell stress responses (Orr et al., 2015). In cellular assays, S3QEL-2 has demonstrated the ability to reduce H₂O₂ production in isolated mitochondria, lower HIF-1α transcription in hypoxia-challenged HEK-293 cells, and protect pancreatic β-cells from oxidative stress-induced apoptosis during islet isolation and culture (Orr et al., 2015). Notably, in studies where cells were exposed to concentrations up to 20× the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC₅₀) determined for site IIIQo superoxide production, S3QEL-2 did not impair basal or uncoupled respiration, nor did it compromise mitochondrial viability (Orr et al., 2015). Thus, S3QEL-2 represents a promising repurposing candidate that has been validated in other contexts of ROS-related cellular stress but has not yet been explicitly applied to the treatment of dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of S3QEL-2 is based on its capacity to selectively suppress superoxide generation originating at the Qo site of mitochondrial Complex III. Under normal conditions, the electron transport chain (ETC) can leak electrons during the reduction of oxygen, particularly at the semiquinone intermediate at the Qo site, resulting in the formation of superoxide—a primary reactive oxygen species (Orr et al., 2015). S3QEL-2 does not act as a general ROS scavenger; rather, it modulates the rate constant for the electron transfer from the semiquinone to molecular oxygen without significantly altering the steady-state levels of semiquinone species or the redox poise of the ubiquinone (Q) pool (Orr et al., 2015). This selective inhibition of ROS generation is achieved through an allosteric modulation of protein conformation within Complex III, specifically targeting the Qo site to reduce electron leak while sparing the remainder of the electron transport processes (Orr et al., 2015). S3QEL-2 emerges as an attractive candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to its unique pharmacological profile and precision in targeting mitochondrial ROS production. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Kinetin riboside (KR; N6-furfuryladenosine) is an adenine-derived cytokinin riboside originally linked to the discovery of kinetin as a plant hormone from autoclaved herring sperm DNA, and later detected in plant matrices such as coconut water, highlighting its occurrence in natural systems beyond synthetic origins (Yong et al., 2009; Gorincioi, 2010). Evidence from biochemical studies suggests that KR can also form in mammalian systems via oxidative chemistry: hydroxyl radical-induced deoxyribose oxidation generates furfural, which reacts with adenine/adenosine to yield N6-furfuryl adducts including kinetin and its riboside, supporting its characterization as a product of cellular oxidative metabolism and a potential “free radical sink” (Gorincioi, 2010). As a pharmacological entity, KR sits within the cytokinin riboside class, where the riboside and its phosphorylated triphosphate (KTP) function as ATP analogues/substrates for specific protein kinases, most notably PINK1, thereby enabling medicinal chemistry strategies around nucleotide prodrugs (e.g., monophosphate ProTides) to enhance intracellular delivery and activation (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018). Cytokinin ribosides have been explored historically as anti-proliferative agents and differentiation inducers in oncology, and more recently as modulators of mitochondrial quality control and neuroprotective pathways through PINK1 activation (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Lambourne et al., 2023; Voller et al., 2010).

Therapeutic History  
Cytokinins and their ribosides have a long history of investigation in dermatology and oncology, with kinetin demonstrating favorable skin tolerability and anti-photoaging benefits in clinical skin-care contexts, although these data pertain largely to kinetin base rather than KR (Fathy et al., 2022). KR and related ribosides have been extensively profiled as anticancer agents, exhibiting cell cycle modulation and pro-apoptotic activity in diverse tumor lines (e.g., HL-60, HeLa, B16F-10), often with relative sparing of normal fibroblasts at active concentrations, supporting a degree of tumor selectivity (Gorincioi, 2010; Voller et al., 2010). Reported in vivo and in vitro data indicate significant antiproliferative potency at low micromolar concentrations alongside dose-related toxicity (e.g., ~25 mg/kg toxicity in certain models), underscoring a narrow therapeutic index in oncology paradigms (Gorincioi, 2010). Beyond oncology, KR (and related cytokinins) have been investigated for neuroprotective and immunomodulatory effects, including improvement of splicing defects in familial dysautonomia and potential roles in neurodegenerative disease models, although much of the splicing literature historically focuses on kinetin base, and translational clarity for KR per se varies across reports (Fathy et al., 2022; Oshchepkov et al., 2020; Voller et al., 2017).

For PINK1 biology specifically, medicinal chemistry and cell biological studies demonstrate that KR and its phosphorylated metabolites activate PINK1 in mammalian and neuronal cells, positioning this chemotype as a pharmacological tool for augmenting mitophagy in diseases linked to mitochondrial dysfunction such as Parkinson’s disease; more potent KR analogs (e.g., MTK458) further validate this mechanism in cellular and animal models (Hertz et al., 2024; Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Lambourne et al., 2023). Prodrug strategies using kinetin riboside monophosphate (KMP) ProTides improve serum stability and intracellular delivery, yielding robust PINK1 activation in HEK293 cells, which is germane to drug design considerations for KR and derivatives (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018). To our knowledge, there are no published clinical or preclinical studies directly testing KR in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) patients or AMD animal models; however, the target pathway (PINK1/Parkin mitophagy) is mechanistically implicated in RPE degeneration in dry AMD, thus providing a strong rationale for repurposing (Datta et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Skeie et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
- PINK1/Parkin mitophagy axis and AMD relevance in RPE:  
  Upon loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), full-length PINK1 accumulates on the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM), where it phosphorylates both Parkin and ubiquitin to initiate Parkin-dependent mitophagy (Skeie et al., 2021). In RPE, PINK1 and Parkin form the core of a quality-control module that identifies and ubiquitinates dysfunctional mitochondria, recruiting autophagy machinery (p62/LC3) for organelle turnover; cumulative evidence supports that age and stress compromise this system in AMD, resulting in damaged mitochondria, elevated ROS, and RPE degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Skeie et al., 2021). Human and mouse RPE data show that PINK1 loss reduces activated phospho-Parkin (p-PRKN) and blunts mitophagic responses to depolarizing stimuli such as CCCP; conversely, in controls, CCCP elevates MAP1LC3B lipidation, validating PINK1 dependence for mitophagy activation in RPE (Datta et al., 2023). Early AMD human RPE exhibits decreased PINK1 in perifoveal regions, correlating with impaired mitophagy and providing a direct disease-context linkage between PINK1 deficiency and RPE dysfunction (Datta et al., 2023). Studies in AMD-relevant oxidative-stress mouse models (e.g., nfe2l2/pgc-1α−/−) indicate early activation of PINK1/Parkin signaling (e.g., increased Parkin colocalization with pS65 ubiquitin and accumulation of LC3B-positive autophagosomes) but suggest a downstream impairment in autolysosomal clearance, implying that upstream activation alone may not normalize flux under chronic stress (Gurubaran et al., 2020).

- KR → KTP conversion and direct PINK1 activation:  
  KR exerts its PINK1-activating effect primarily through metabolic conversion to kinetin riboside triphosphate (KTP), an ATP neo-substrate that binds PINK1 with higher affinity than ATP, thereby enhancing the kinase’s catalytic activity on relevant substrates (Georgakopoulos et al., 2017; Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018). Cellular enzymology supports that cytosolic nucleotide salvage and phosphoribosylation pathways enable the conversion of adenine derivatives (including kinetin) to triphosphate forms; APRT has been implicated in cytokinin biochemistry in mammalian systems and may contribute to the intracellular generation of KTP from kinetin precursors, though the precise enzymatic steps from KR to KTP in RPE require direct elucidation (Naseem et al., 2020). Pharmacological studies show that KR, KMP, and KTP activate PINK1 in mammalian and neuronal cells; KMP ProTides with various ester masks demonstrate serum stability and intracellular unmasking to yield active nucleotides, suggesting that glycosylation to the riboside and subsequent phosphorylation are key determinants of PINK1 activation (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Lambourne et al., 2023). Stabilized PINK1 then phosphorylates Parkin at serine 656 (as reported in the source text) and ubiquitin at serine 65, which accelerates Parkin recruitment and amplifies ubiquitin chain phosphorylation on OMM substrates, thereby seeding mitophagosome formation and progression (Lambourne et al., 2023). In cell systems, kinetin-derived activation of PINK1 is observed in the context of mitochondrial membrane depolarization and can be potentiated by mild, reversible uncoupling in some chemical series without overt mitochondrial toxicity when carefully tuned, underscoring a feasible pharmacological window (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018). Complementary small molecules (e.g., niclosamide, T0466/T0467, BC1464) act via PINK1 stabilization or degradation-pathway modulation, and USP30 inhibition further biases mitochondrial ubiquitination toward mitophagy, situating KR in a broader druggable landscape for PINK1-pathway enhancement (Masaldan et al., 2022).

- Convergence on RPE pathobiology:  
  Given that PINK1 expression and signaling are reduced in early AMD RPE, an agent that increases PINK1 catalytic activity and stabilizes PINK1 on damaged mitochondria could restore Parkin-dependent tagging and clearance of dysfunctional organelles, thereby lowering ROS loads and downstream RPE stress (Datta et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018). The RPE expresses and utilizes the PINK1/Parkin/LC3 autophagy machinery, as evidenced by immunochemical and functional data linking p-PRKN regulation, LC3B lipidation, and mitophagic flux to PINK1 state in mouse and human RPE systems (Datta et al., 2023). However, AMD models with oxidative stress show that autophagosome accumulation can occur without efficient clearance if lysosomal function is compromised; thus, any PINK1-activating therapy may need to be co-optimized with strategies that maintain autophagosome–lysosome fusion and lysosomal competence to realize net mitochondria turnover (Gurubaran et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
- In RPE assays:  
  KR should increase PINK1 activity upon mitochondrial depolarization or basal damage, resulting in higher levels of phospho-ubiquitin (pS65), increased Parkin recruitment to the OMM, augmented polyubiquitin decoration of OMM proteins (e.g., VDAC), enhanced LC3B-II accumulation, and increased formation of mitophagosomes and subsequent mitolysosomes, assuming lysosomal function is intact (Lambourne et al., 2023; Skeie et al., 2021). In PINK1-proficient RPE, a KR challenge following CCCP or physiological stressors is expected to recapitulate or potentiate the canonical PINK1/Parkin mitophagy cascade; notably, experiments in mouse RPE indicate that CCCP-induced elevation of LC3B lipidation is abrogated in pink1−/−, establishing a dependence of the autophagy readout on PINK1 that KR could rescue only if sufficient PINK1 is present (Datta et al., 2023). Given early AMD’s reduced PINK1 expression in the RPE perifovea, KR’s effect size may scale with residual PINK1 levels; the KTP–PINK1 interaction may partially compensate by enhancing the activity and dwell time of the remaining PINK1 on depolarized mitochondria, but absolute PINK1 scarcity could limit maximal response (Datta et al., 2023; Georgakopoulos et al., 2017). In AMD-like oxidative stress settings where the early mitophagy steps activate but autolysosomal clearance is impaired, KR is predicted to elevate upstream markers (pUb, Parkin localization, LC3B-II) yet may not fully normalize flux without restoring lysosomal function; this risk of autophagosome accumulation has been observed in AMD-model RPE, implying combination approaches (e.g., lysosome enhancers) may be required for optimal benefit (Gurubaran et al., 2020).

- In dry AMD disease biology:  
  By accelerating removal of dysfunctional mitochondria, KR is anticipated to reduce mitochondrial ROS and downstream oxidative damage, restoring bioenergetic homeostasis and decreasing RPE stress signals that contribute to drusen-associated pathology and cell death in dry AMD (Brooks et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018). Mechanistically, successful PINK1 activation should rebalance the population of healthy versus damaged mitochondria, mitigate chronic ROS-driven damage, and potentially stabilize RPE cellular functions (e.g., phagocytic capacity, lysosomal turnover of photoreceptor outer segments) that are compromised in AMD due to accumulation of dysfunctional organelles (Brooks et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018). Because the PINK1/Parkin axis is implicated in RPE degeneration and is downregulated in early AMD, targeted pharmacological enhancement of PINK1 represents a pathway-corrective approach aligned with disease mechanism, though it must be tested under AMD-relevant stressors that include both mitochondrial and lysosomal deficits (Datta et al., 2023; Gurubaran et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History—Safety, Toxicology, and Translational Considerations  
Nonclinical safety evaluations of kinetin (base) indicate a dose-dependent profile: low doses show favorable tolerability in skin applications and animal studies, whereas higher systemic doses (e.g., ≥1 mg/kg in rats) may perturb renal biomarkers, highlighting the need for careful exposure control; while this is not KR, it provides a class-level caution on dosing margins (Fathy et al., 2022; Othman et al., 2021). In mammalian cell systems, kinetin shows a concentration-dependent duality—sub-100 nM levels are cytoprotective against oxidative stress, while ≥500 nM can elicit cytotoxicity and genotoxicity—again reflecting the necessity of tight pharmacological windows in clinical development; KR shares pro-apoptotic properties at higher concentrations in tumor cells, indicating that exposure management will be critical to avoid off-target mitochondrial stress in non-malignant RPE (Gorincioi, 2010; Naseem et al., 2020). Tumor-selective cytotoxicity observed for KR (e.g., activation of caspase-3 following mitochondrial membrane disruption in HeLa and B16F-10) suggests that normal cells may be relatively resistant at appropriate concentrations, but translation to post-mitotic, metabolically active RPE requires dedicated therapeutic index definition (Gorincioi, 2010).

Pharmacokinetics for cytokinin ribosides present challenges, including short plasma half-life and potential limitations in barrier penetration; nevertheless, certain ribosides can achieve tissue exposure, and ProTide engineering of monophosphate forms has demonstrated improved serum stability and intracellular activation, offering a medicinal chemistry route to optimize ocular delivery and target engagement (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Voller et al., 2017). Importantly, the mitochondrial pharmacology dimension requires that PINK1 activation not rely on sustained pathological depolarization; prior work shows that PINK1 activation by certain KR-derived chemotypes can be coupled to reversible membrane effects without lasting mitochondrial injury, implying an achievable safety profile with rational chemistry and dosing (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018). Finally, the target pathway-level success with more potent PINK1 activators (e.g., MTK458) in cellular and animal models of Parkinson’s supports the druggability of this axis and suggests headroom to optimize KR analogs if KR itself proves insufficient in the RPE context (Hertz et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic alignment with AMD pathophysiology in RPE: Dry AMD features impaired mitophagy and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE, and early AMD shows decreased PINK1 expression and diminished mitophagy competence; KR directly activates PINK1, enhances Parkin recruitment via ubiquitin/PRKN phosphorylation, and augments mitophagy flux in mammalian and neuronal cells, providing a targeted correction to a disease-relevant defect (Datta et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Lambourne et al., 2023).  
- Direct enzymatic activation via KTP: KR’s biotransformation to KTP, an ATP neo-substrate with higher affinity for PINK1, offers a plausible biochemical mechanism to boost catalytic throughput even when PINK1 protein is partially reduced, thereby potentially amplifying residual PINK1 signaling in AMD RPE (Georgakopoulos et al., 2017; Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018).  
- Drug development precedent and tool compounds: Demonstrated PINK1 activation by KR, KMP/KTP, and related chemotypes, plus successful implementation of ProTide strategies and in vivo efficacy signals with potent analogs (e.g., MTK458), de-risk the pathway and provide a roadmap for medicinal chemistry and delivery optimization (Hertz et al., 2024; Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018).  
- Disease-biology congruence of pharmacodynamic readouts: RPE models have validated the dependency of CCCP-induced LC3B lipidation and p-PRKN formation on PINK1, while AMD-relevant models show upstream activation markers (pUb, Parkin colocalization) that are rate limited by downstream clearance—clear, quantifiable biomarkers exist to track KR engagement and flux restoration in RPE (Datta et al., 2023; Gurubaran et al., 2020).

Risks and Gaps  
- PINK1 insufficiency in early AMD: The perifoveal reduction of PINK1 in human RPE may limit the magnitude of KR-mediated activation; if PINK1 levels are below a critical threshold, KTP amplification alone might not suffice, necessitating combination with approaches that increase PINK1 expression/stability (e.g., BC1464) or that act downstream (e.g., USP30 inhibition to potentiate ubiquitin signaling) (Datta et al., 2023; Masaldan et al., 2022).  
- Lysosomal/autophagic clearance deficits: Oxidative stress models indicate initiation of PINK1/Parkin mitophagy with impaired autolysosomal clearance; KR may heighten early mitophagy steps without resolving terminal flux, risking autophagosome accumulation unless lysosomal function is co-restored (e.g., via agents that enhance autophagosome–lysosome fusion or lysosomal biogenesis) (Gurubaran et al., 2020).  
- Safety window and mitochondrial stress: KR exhibits pro-apoptotic, mitochondria-targeted cytotoxicity in tumor cells and cytotoxic/genotoxic effects at higher concentrations in non-tumor cells; precise dosing that achieves PINK1 activation without excessive mitochondrial depolarization or non-specific stress in RPE must be empirically determined (Gorincioi, 2010; Naseem et al., 2020).  
- PK and delivery barriers: Cytokinin ribosides generally have short half-lives and potential distribution limitations; ocular delivery (e.g., intravitreal, suprachoroidal, periocular) and ProTide/nanoparticulate strategies may be required to achieve durable RPE exposure while minimizing systemic exposure, an aspect not yet demonstrated for KR in the AMD setting (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Voller et al., 2017).  
- Lack of direct RPE/AMD in vivo efficacy data: While the mechanistic rationale is strong, KR has not been directly tested in RPE AMD models; translational viability will hinge on demonstrating improved mitophagy flux, decreased mitochondrial ROS, and RPE functional rescue in AMD-relevant models (Datta et al., 2023; Gurubaran et al., 2020).

Recommendation and Development Path  
Given the alignment between KR’s mechanism and the pathobiology of dry AMD in RPE, KR is a plausible repurposing candidate, but it should be advanced with a data-driven gating strategy that addresses target sufficiency, lysosomal function, safety window, and ocular delivery:  
- In vitro RPE assays (human primary or hPSC-derived) under AMD-relevant stress (e.g., photo-oxidative stress, lipofuscin/oxLDL exposure): test KR and KMP ProTides for dose–response effects on pUb (S65), p-PRKN, Parkin recruitment, LC3B lipidation, mitolysosome formation, mitochondrial turnover (mtDNA copy loss in mitolysosomes), and mitochondrial ROS/bioenergetics, benchmarking against CCCP controls and PINK1 knockdown/knockout lines (Datta et al., 2023; Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Skeie et al., 2021).  
- Lysosomal competence assays: co-assess autophagic flux with lysosomal pH and cathepsin activity; if KR increases early mitophagy markers without flux completion, evaluate combination with lysosome enhancers or TFEB agonists to restore throughput (Gurubaran et al., 2020).  
- PINK1 sufficiency and sensitization: quantify PINK1 levels in AMD-like conditions and test whether KR effects scale with PINK1 expression; consider combination with agents that stabilize PINK1 (e.g., BC1464) or increase mitochondrial ubiquitination via USP30 inhibition to offset low PINK1 (Datta et al., 2023; Masaldan et al., 2022).  
- Safety and therapeutic window in RPE: map KR exposure–response for PINK1 activation versus cytotoxicity/apoptosis, including concentrations that preserve RPE viability and mitochondrial membrane potential; incorporate off-target stress readouts (e.g., CHOP, ISR activation) (Gorincioi, 2010; Naseem et al., 2020).  
- Medicinal chemistry and delivery: prioritize KMP ProTides with favorable stability and reversible mitochondrial engagement to minimize off-target depolarization; assess ocular pharmacokinetics and RPE distribution in relevant species, given cytokinin riboside PK liabilities (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Voller et al., 2017).  
- In vivo models: test KR/ProTide in AMD-relevant models exhibiting RPE mitochondrial defects (e.g., NFE2L2/PGC-1α pathway disruption, photo-oxidative stress paradigms), with endpoints spanning RPE ultrastructure, mitochondrial turnover, oxidative markers, and functional readouts (ERG, RPE phagocytosis), while monitoring safety (renal/hepatic markers given systemic tox precedent) (Gurubaran et al., 2020; Othman et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Kinetin riboside is a mechanistically credible, pathway-directed candidate for dry AMD that targets a well-established deficit—PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy—in RPE, with robust supportive biology that PINK1 activation can be pharmacologically achieved by KR and its nucleotide metabolites to promote Parkin-dependent mitochondrial clearance (Datta et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Lambourne et al., 2023). The strengths include disease-relevant target engagement, availability of medicinal chemistry tactics (KMP ProTides) to address delivery and stability, and quantifiable pharmacodynamic markers in RPE that predict on-pathway efficacy (Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018; Skeie et al., 2021). The principal risks are biological (insufficient PINK1 in early AMD and lysosomal flux defects that may cap benefit), pharmacological (narrow window between desired PINK1 activation and mitochondrial stress), and translational (PK/ocular delivery), none of which are insurmountable but all of which require rigorous preclinical validation in RPE-centric systems (Datta et al., 2023; Gurubaran et al., 2020; Naseem et al., 2020; Voller et al., 2017).

On balance, KR merits advancement to target-validation studies in human RPE models with concurrent optimization of ProTide prodrugs and combination strategies that secure lysosomal flux, with a clear go/no-go framework based on restoration of mitophagy flux and mitochondrial function without eliciting RPE toxicity (Gurubaran et al., 2020; Lambourne & Mehellou, 2018). If KR proves insufficient alone due to PINK1 insufficiency or PK constraints, more potent or targeted PINK1 activators (e.g., MTK458-class) and/or adjuncts that stabilize PINK1 or enhance downstream ubiquitin signaling may be prioritized, preserving the same mechanistic rationale for treating dry AMD via restoration of mitochondrial quality control in the RPE (Hertz et al., 2024; Masaldan et al., 2022).
