Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
3-Mercaptopicolinic acid (3-MPA; also written 3-mercaptopicolinate/3-MP) is a small, thiol-containing picolinic-acid derivative historically identified as a biochemical inhibitor of gluconeogenesis through inhibition of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) and, at higher concentrations, glucose-6-phosphatase (G-6-Pase) in hepatic systems (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001). Early reports in the 1970s established 3-MPA as a preferential inhibitor of the cytosolic PEPCK isoform (PCK1), and the compound has since been used widely as a tool in mechanistic enzymology and physiology of gluconeogenesis across species and contexts (e.g., mammalian liver, pig, and protozoan PEPCKs) (Hidalgo et al., 2016; McLeod et al., 2019; Brearley et al., 2020). While the original discovery route is not detailed in the provided sources, a “convenient synthesis” was reported historically, and numerous structure–mechanism studies have refined the understanding of its binding behavior and chemical liabilities; by contrast, no data in the provided material indicate a natural origin (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001).

Chemically, 3-MPA belongs to the broader class of picolinic-acid–based, anionic, metal-coordinating inhibitors that engage the PEPCK active site by chelating the catalytically essential M1 divalent metal (typically Mn2+) via the ring nitrogen and exocyclic carboxylate; 3-MPA also contains a reactive free sulfhydryl group that drives both potency and time-dependent covalent reactivity with protein cysteines (McLeod et al., 2019). The picolinic-acid scaffold’s anionic, metal-binding character is a recognized design principle for PEPCK inhibitors and has been leveraged to build next-generation derivatives (e.g., 3-((carboxymethyl)thio)-picolinic acid, CMP) that seek to occupy both inner and outer subsites of the OAA/PEP pocket while reducing thiol-mediated liabilities (McLeod et al., 2019).

As a class, such PEPCK-directed small-molecule inhibitors have been applied as biochemical probes of gluconeogenic flux, as antihyperglycemic tools in preclinical metabolic studies, and as chemical probes to dissect PEPCK function in cancer and immunometabolism models; however, the field has wrestled with issues of thiol reactivity, complex multi-site binding kinetics, ADME/PAINS flags, and limited isoform selectivity, all of which complicate translation (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001; McLeod et al., 2019; Baptista et al., 2019; Hidalgo et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History  
3-MPA has a long track record as a research tool in hepatic metabolism. In perfused rat liver and in vivo rat studies, 3-MPA was used to blunt gluconeogenesis and lower blood glucose, with dosing paradigms including intraperitoneal administration (e.g., 100 mg/kg followed by 25 mg/kg three hours later) and 1 mM concentrations in perfusate to suppress fructose- or lactate/pyruvate-stimulated hepatic glucose production (Herling et al., 1998). More recently, 3-MPA has served as a comparator and positive control in modern PEPCK-targeted discovery programs, including enzyme assays against recombinant human cytosolic and mitochondrial PEPCK isoforms (PCK1/PCK2), CETSA target-engagement studies, cell-based functional assays (e.g., insulin secretion), and acute in vivo pharmacodynamic readouts (e.g., fasting glycemia five hours after 50 mg/kg IP administration) (Aragó et al., 2020). In several settings, 3-MPA reduces oncogenic phenotypes: it impairs anchorage-independent growth in MCF7 cells yet shows limited effects on glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in INS-1 cells, suggesting variable target engagement and a modest potency ceiling relative to newer chemotypes (Aragó et al., 2020).

3-MPA has been used to inhibit the mitochondrial isoform PEPCK-M (PCK2) in cancer models. In non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cell lines cultured under glucose deprivation, inhibition of human mitochondrial PEPCK by 3-MPA or genetic knockdown induced apoptosis, consistent with a reliance on PEPCK-mediated anaplerotic/cataplerotic cycling for survival under nutrient stress (Baptista et al., 2019). Computational docking studies against human PEPCK-M have used 3-MPA as a benchmark ligand to set score cutoffs and to elucidate canonical binding interactions (Mn2+ coordination; Arg/Lys salt-bridge network), aligning with structural insights from cytosolic isoforms (Baptista et al., 2019).

In melanoma models, 3-MPA (applied as a PCK1 inhibitor) sensitized vemurafenib-resistant tumors in vitro and in vivo by depressing pentose phosphate pathway–derived NADPH production and elevating ROS through KEAP1/Nrf2 axis modulation, thereby reversing resistance; here, 3-MPA increased oxidative stress rather than alleviating it (Ren et al., 2022). Across immunometabolism, 3-MPA (100 μM) reduced cytotoxic T lymphocyte effector functions and decreased maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) without altering basal glycolysis, indicating impaired mitochondrial respiratory capacity in activated T cells in which PEPCK-M predominates (Brownlie et al., 2025). In skeletal muscle myoblasts (C2C12), 3-MPA (0.25–1 mM) reduced proliferation and induced myogenic differentiation, with Pck2 transcripts predominant over Pck1; however, the compound interfered with enzymatic assays at ≥0.25–0.5 mM, complicating attribution to on-target inhibition (Brearley et al., 2020). Against porcine cytosolic PEPCK isoenzymes, 3-MPA exhibits mid-micromolar IC₅₀ (~65 μM) under saturating substrates and mechanistically mixed/complex kinetics (mixed non-competitive vs PEP; uncompetitive vs GDP/GTP), supporting dual-site binding behavior (Hidalgo et al., 2016).

No study in the provided literature assesses 3-MPA in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), retina, or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD); a comprehensive mechanistic and structural study of related PEPCK inhibitors explicitly contains no mention of eye/RPE/AMD systems, emphasizing that the extant knowledge base for 3-MPA is outside ophthalmology (McLeod et al., 2019). Absent any reported ocular or RPE use, 3-MPA should be regarded as a systemic/metabolic tool compound with evolving applications in cancer and immunometabolism rather than as a precedent therapeutic in retinal degenerations (McLeod et al., 2019).

Mechanism of Action  
Mechanistic biochemistry and structural work converge on a dual-mode model for 3-MPA action on PEPCK:
- Active-site (inner-subsite) binding and Mn²⁺ coordination: The picolinic-acid moiety of 3-MPA coordinates the catalytic M1 Mn²⁺ ion via the ring nitrogen and exocyclic carboxylate oxygen(s), occupying the “inner” OAA/PEP subsite in a manner analogous to oxalate and other carboxylate inhibitors; co-crystal analyses and docking corroborate metal coordination along with salt-bridge/ion-pairing to conserved basic residues (e.g., Arg104/Arg423/Lys261/Lys262 in vertebrate enzymes) (McLeod et al., 2019; Baptista et al., 2019).
- Secondary/allosteric site binding: 3-MPA can occupy a second site near/behind the P-loop, with two molecules bound simultaneously (n≈2 by ITC), producing complex kinetic signatures (mixed non-competitive behavior with respect to PEP/OAA and uncompetitive inhibition versus GDP/GTP), and allowing allosteric influence on substrate/inhibitor binding at the active site (Hidalgo et al., 2016).

Kinetically, these binding modes yield mixed patterns that depend on the variable substrate: mixed non-competitive versus PEP/OAA; uncompetitive versus GDP/GTP, consistent with inhibitor binding to enzyme–nucleotide complexes and allosteric communication to the catalytic pocket (Hidalgo et al., 2016). Across isoforms, micromolar potency is typical: for rat cytosolic PEPCK (rcPEPCK) Kᵢ ~8 μM, for human mitochondrial PEPCK (hmPEPCK) Kᵢ ~3 μM in some determinations, though reported IC₅₀/Kᵢ values vary with assay format and metal/substrate conditions (McLeod et al., 2019). Variability is expected given that picolinic-acid derivatives chelate divalent metal cations; changes in available Mn²⁺ can partially masquerade as noncompetitive inhibition (i.e., by depleting active holoenzyme) in kinetic plots if not tightly controlled (McLeod et al., 2019).

A distinguishing chemical feature of 3-MPA is the free thiol. In vitro, the thiol can form mixed disulfide adducts with reactive cysteines on PEPCK (e.g., C288 on the P-loop in rat cytosolic PEPCK), producing time-dependent, covalent inactivation that contributes to potency but also to off-target reactivity and interpretational complexity; this chemistry is mitigated but not eliminated by inclusion of reducing agents in assays (McLeod et al., 2019). The thiol’s promiscuity likely explains reports of irreversible, time-dependent inhibition of G-6-Pase at millimolar concentrations, a phenomenon exploited historically to dissect gluconeogenic regulation but pharmacologically undesirable for selective PEPCK targeting (Westergaard & Madsen, 2001; McLeod et al., 2019). Because the M1 metal and a basic electrostatic microenvironment (e.g., Arg104/Arg423/Lys261/Lys262) are conserved in PEPCK-M and PEPCK-C, inhibitors that rely on metal chelation and anionic interactions, like 3-MPA, are predicted to show cross-isoform activity; docking against the human mitochondrial isoform reproduces these hallmarks (Baptista et al., 2019).

Several functional studies corroborate that 3-MPA perturbs cellular bioenergetics consistent with PEPCK inhibition but in cell-context-dependent ways. In activated effector T cells (PCK2-predominant), 100 μM 3-MPA reduced maximal OCR without changing basal ECAR, indicating compromised oxidative phosphorylation capacity while leaving basal glycolysis intact (Brownlie et al., 2025). In lung cancer cell lines, PEPCK-M inhibition by 3-MPA induced apoptosis only under glucose deprivation, highlighting the role of PCK2 in enabling biosynthesis from non-glucose substrates under stress (Baptista et al., 2019). Conversely, in BRAFi-resistant melanoma, PCK1 inhibition by 3-MPA depressed PPP-mediated NADPH synthesis, increased ROS by weakening antioxidant buffering (via KEAP1/Nrf2), and sensitized cells to targeted therapy, illustrating that PEPCK inhibition can amplify oxidative stress depending on metabolic wiring (Ren et al., 2022).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Directionality of effect conflicts with the AMD hypothesis. Available cell-based data indicate 3-MPA reduces maximal mitochondrial respiratory capacity and can increase ROS in specific contexts by depleting PPP-derived NADPH, the opposite of the hypothesized benefit for RPE under bioenergetic/oxidative stress (Brownlie et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2022).  
- Chemical liabilities. The free thiol drives time-dependent covalent reactivity (mixed disulfides) with PEPCK and likely other proteins; at millimolar exposure, 3-MPA causes irreversible, time-dependent inhibition of G-6-Pase, underscoring a broad risk of off-target covalent modification that is unacceptable for ocular therapy without significant medicinal-chemistry mitigation (McLeod et al., 2019; Westergaard & Madsen, 2001). PAINS flags and polarity metrics caution against promiscuity and poor drug-likeness (Baptista et al., 2019).  
- Inconsistent target engagement in cells and modest potency relative to alternatives. Compared with newer PEPCK inhibitors (e.g., iPEPCK-2), 3-MPA shows two orders of magnitude weaker IC₅₀s in some cellular contexts and variable engagement (e.g., limited effect on insulin secretion), suggesting that achieving effective concentrations in relevant compartments may be difficult or that off-target liabilities confound outcomes (Aragó et al., 2020).  
- No precedent in retinal/RPE systems. The provided literature contains no data on 3-MPA in the eye, retina, RPE, or AMD models, and offers no RPE expression evidence for PCK2, making the translational leap speculative from the present corpus (McLeod et al., 2019; Yun, 2017).  
- Concentration-dependent assay interference and off-target effects. In C2C12 cells, 3-MPA interfered with PEPCK assays at ≥0.25–0.5 mM; perfused liver studies used 1 mM; such concentrations raise the likelihood of nonspecific effects in RPE (Brearley et al., 2020; Herling et al., 1998).  

Decision-Critical Gaps for AMD  
- Target validation in RPE. There is no evidence in the supplied material confirming PCK2 expression and activity in RPE, nor any demonstration that PEPCK-M–dependent cycling is maladaptive in dry AMD; this gap precludes mechanistic confidence (McLeod et al., 2019).  
- Directionality of benefit. The compound’s demonstrated tendency to reduce maximal OXPHOS capacity and, in some contexts, to enhance oxidative stress directly contradicts the intended pharmacology (increase NADH/OXPHOS; decrease ROS) in stressed RPE (Brownlie et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2022).  
- Ocular safety. Free-thiol reactivity, metal chelation, and PAINS liabilities make 3-MPA a risky starting point for ocular delivery; no ocular PK/safety data are available in the provided sources (Baptista et al., 2019; McLeod et al., 2019; Westergaard & Madsen, 2001).  

If the project’s strategic objective is to probe whether inhibiting PEPCK-M benefits RPE bioenergetic stability, a safer and more specific chemical tool would be required. Notably, thioether analogs like CMP remove the free thiol and still engage the active site competitively (albeit with ~10× weaker potency), and crystallography confirms occupancy of both inner and outer subsites; such molecules may offer cleaner on-target pharmacology for in vitro RPE studies while avoiding mixed-disulfide covalency (McLeod et al., 2019). However, even for such analogs, the directionality risk remains given that PEPCK-M inhibition has reduced mitochondrial respiratory capacity in mammalian cells that rely on this enzyme under activation stress (Brownlie et al., 2025).

Overall, based on the provided literature, I do not recommend prioritizing 3-MPA as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. The compound’s mechanistic actions and cell-level consequences in related systems predict outcomes counter to the proposed benefit in RPE, and its chemical liabilities are incompatible with ocular drug development without substantial medicinal-chemistry redesign (Brownlie et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2022; McLeod et al., 2019; Baptista et al., 2019).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
ZLN005 (MedChemExpress HY-100726) is a synthetic small-molecule compound that belongs to the benzimidazole class. Benzimidazole derivatives have a long history in medicinal chemistry for their wide-ranging biological activities, including antihelminthic, anti-inflammatory, and metabolic modulating effects. In the case of ZLN005, it has been identified specifically as a selective transcriptional activator of peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator‐1 alpha (PGC-1α), a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defense. The synthesis and chemical derivation of ZLN005, although not detailed exhaustively in the provided literature, follow typical synthetic protocols for benzimidazole compounds, which often involve the condensation of o-phenylenediamine with carboxylic acid derivatives to yield a benzimidazole core. This structural class is known not only for its high affinity to various protein targets but also for favorable pharmacokinetic properties that have motivated its use in drug development efforts. Several studies have demonstrated that ZLN005 effectively induces PGC-1α expression in various cell types, including skeletal muscle and particularly the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis (Satish et al., 2018). Its assignment under the benzimidazole class further suggests that ZLN005 may share common metabolic and pharmacological features with other compounds in the same class, which have been employed in different therapeutic areas, supporting its potential for repurposing in ocular disorders such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Sun et al., 2018; Bleckwehl et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Initially, ZLN005 emerged from screening studies designed to identify small molecules that could stimulate PGC-1α expression. Early research in cellular models demonstrated that ZLN005 enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and upregulates the expression of downstream oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and antioxidant genes, which in turn improves mitochondrial health and overall cellular energy metabolism (Satish et al., 2018). In skeletal muscle and hepatic cells, for example, treatment with ZLN005 was associated with increased basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates, an increase in spare respiratory capacity, and a concomitant improvement in glucose uptake and cellular ATP levels (Satish et al., 2018). Such characteristics have spurred interest in its therapeutic application beyond metabolic diseases to conditions where mitochondrial dysfunction is a central pathogenic factor.

Notably, several groups have investigated ZLN005 in the context of retinal diseases. Preclinical studies using ARPE-19 cells—a well-accepted human RPE cell line—demonstrated that ZLN005 markedly upregulates PGC-1α expression and its associated transcription factors and antioxidant enzymes. These investigations have shown that ZLN005 can confer significant protection against oxidative stress-induced cell death when cells are exposed to prooxidative agents such as hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL) and sodium iodate (NaIO₃) (Satish et al., 2018). Although ZLN005 has not yet undergone extensive clinical evaluation specifically for dry AMD, its robust activity in stimulating mitochondrial function and providing cytoprotection in RPE models forms a compelling rationale for its repurposing. Studies in other systems, including cardiomyocytes and skeletal muscle, support its therapeutic use in settings of bioenergetic decline and oxidative damage, which are hallmarks of many age-related degenerative diseases (Ma et al., 2023; Moradi, 2022). However, it should be noted that many of the studies exploring ZLN005 for ocular purposes have been in vitro, and while they present an optimistic scenario, further in vivo animal studies and careful pharmacokinetic analyses in ocular tissues are needed before clinical application in AMD can be considered (Satish et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
The pharmacological efficacy of ZLN005 is tightly linked to its mechanism of action as an activator of PGC-1α. PGC-1α is a transcriptional coactivator that regulates a myriad of genes implicated in energy metabolism, mitochondrial biogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, and antioxidant protection. In RPE cells—where the maintenance of a high mitochondrial integrity is crucial for visual function—the expression of PGC-1α is fundamental to mitigating oxidative stress and maintaining metabolic homeostasis (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Iacovelli et al., 2016). ZLN005 increases the expression levels of PGC-1α by enhancing its transcription, culminating in the upregulation of a host of downstream target genes. This includes key mitochondrial genes such as ATP50, COX4, COX5b, and NDUFB5, all of which are involved in oxidative phosphorylation and energy production (Satish et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025).

At the molecular level, ZLN005 promotes the transcriptional program by potentially modulating AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) activity, a well-known regulator of PGC-1α function. The compound’s facilitation of PGC-1α nuclear translocation and its catalytic coactivation leads to the stimulation of mitochondrial replication and repair processes, thereby increasing mitochondrial mass and mtDNA copy number (Satish et al., 2018). In parallel, the upregulation of PGC-1α by ZLN005 induces the expression of several endogenous antioxidant enzymes, including superoxide dismutases (SOD1 and SOD2) and mitochondrial thioredoxin 2 (TXN2). This cascade of events enhances the cellular capacity to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS), thus lowering mitochondrial superoxide production and reducing the levels of oxidative stress markers such as 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), a product of lipid peroxidation frequently associated with degenerative retinal changes (Satish et al., 2018).

Furthermore, ZLN005 appears to improve overall mitochondrial bioenergetics. It has been observed to increase both basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates (OCR) in RPE cells, indicating an enhanced capacity for ATP synthesis under both steady-state and stress conditions (Satish et al., 2018). The compound also augments the spare respiratory capacity, which is critical for cellular survival when faced with acute energy demands during oxidative stress. Such improvements in mitochondrial function are directly relevant to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, where RPE cells experience an energy deficit due to progressive mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic oxidative injury (Felszeghy et al., 2019). Additionally, by upregulating PGC-1α, ZLN005 may indirectly influence other cellular processes, including autophagy and lipid metabolism, both of which are altered in the aging RPE and contribute to the formation of drusen—the hallmark deposits seen in dry AMD (Zhou et al., 2024).

It is important to emphasize that the protective effects of ZLN005 are markedly dependent on the presence of functional PGC-1α. Experiments in which PGC-1α expression was silenced in RPE cells resulted in a significant loss of the cytoprotective benefits conferred by ZLN005, underscoring the compound’s mechanism-specific action (Satish et al., 2018). Parallel studies in non-ocular cell types, such as skeletal muscle myotubes and alveolar epithelial cells, have further supported its role in enhancing mitochondrial function and regulating oxidative stress through similar molecular pathways (Zhang et al., 2013; Bleckwehl et al., 2025). Thus, the molecular interactions initiated by ZLN005—ranging from the activation of PGC-1α to the subsequent stimulation of antioxidant enzymes and mitochondrial biogenesis—form the crux of its therapeutic utility, specifically in countering the bioenergetic decline characteristic of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
Given the central involvement of mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the therapeutic hypothesis for ZLN005 is that its activation of PGC-1α in retinal pigment epithelial cells will restore mitochondrial homeostasis and augment cellular antioxidant defenses. In the proposed assays, treatment with ZLN005 is expected to upregulate PGC-1α expression in RPE cells, thereby triggering a cascade of downstream events that lead to enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis. This includes an increase in mtDNA copy number and the expression of mitochondrial genes that are essential for optimal oxidative phosphorylation performance (Satish et al., 2018). As mitochondrial function improves, RPE cells should exhibit higher basal and maximal oxygen consumption rates, indicative of an improved metabolic profile and increased capacity to generate ATP under both normal and stress conditions (Satish et al., 2018).

The antioxidative effects of ZLN005 are also expected to manifest in augmented levels of enzymes such as SOD1, SOD2, and TXN2, which collectively enhance the cell’s capability to scavenge reactive oxygen species. These biochemical events are critical because the accumulation of oxidative stress in RPE cells, driven by chronic exposure to high levels of ROS, is a significant contributor to cell degeneration in dry AMD (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Blasiak et al., 2021). With improved mitochondrial function and reduced oxidative stress, it is anticipated that ZLN005 treatment will lead to a decrease in the accumulation of oxidative damage markers like 4-HNE, thereby mitigating processes that lead to RPE cell apoptosis and the subsequent photoreceptor degeneration observed in dry AMD (Blasiak et al., 2021; Iacovelli et al., 2016).

Moreover, in vitro studies have demonstrated that under conditions of experimentally induced oxidative stress with agents such as H₂O₂, ox-LDL, or NaIO₃, ZLN005 significantly reduces cell death in ARPE-19 cells (Satish et al., 2018). Therefore, the expected effect of ZLN005 in the proposed assay is a robust cytoprotective response in RPE cells. This would be characterized by improved cell viability, restoration of mitochondrial respiratory function, and a reduction in stress-induced apoptotic markers—a constellation of effects that directly addresses the bioenergetic and oxidative challenges underlying dry AMD (Satish et al., 2018). Additionally, since PGC-1α is known to regulate lipid metabolism and prevent lipid droplet accumulation—a process that may be linked to the formation of drusen in the AMD retina—the activation of PGC-1α by ZLN005 could also have beneficial effects on lipid handling within the RPE (Zhou et al., 2024; Iacovelli et al., 2016). Thus, through these concerted mechanisms, ZLN005 is anticipated to stabilize or even improve RPE function, thereby halting or reversing aspects of the degenerative cascade that leads to vision loss in dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
A comprehensive evaluation of ZLN005 reveals several compelling strengths as well as notable weaknesses that should be weighed in the context of repurposing it for the treatment of dry AMD. One of the principal strengths of ZLN005 lies in its well-defined mechanism of action. By selectively activating PGC-1α, ZLN005 directly targets the mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress that are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. The upregulation of PGC-1α leads to improvements in mitochondrial biogenesis, an increase in the expression of mitochondrial OXPHOS genes, and the enhancement of antioxidant defenses—all factors that are critically compromised in the diseased RPE (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Blasiak et al., 2021). This mechanistic rationale is further supported by in vitro studies showing that ZLN005 can effectively reduce prooxidant-induced cell death and improve mitochondrial respiratory parameters such as basal respiration, maximal respiration, and spare respiratory capacity (Satish et al., 2018).

Another strength is the translational potential implied by the compound’s efficacy in multiple cell types. ZLN005 has not only demonstrated protective effects in RPE cells but has also been shown to modulate mitochondrial activity in skeletal muscle and hepatic cells. This broad-spectrum improvement in energy metabolism indicates that its bioenergetic benefits may be harnessed in the complex metabolic environment of the RPE, where energy deficits contribute to dry AMD pathology (Satish et al., 2018). Achieving a robust activation of PGC-1α is particularly attractive because it addresses both the cellular energy production and ROS management simultaneously, which are two critical determinants of RPE cell survival and function (Iacovelli et al., 2016; Rosales et al., 2019).

Furthermore, the specificity of ZLN005’s action has been validated by studies where the loss of PGC-1α abrogated its cytoprotective effects, underscoring that its efficacy is tightly linked to the activation of this pivotal regulatory pathway (Satish et al., 2018). This is an important consideration because it suggests that the therapeutic effects can be fine-tuned by modulating the expression or activity of PGC-1α. In the context of dry AMD, where PGC-1α levels are often diminished or dysregulated, the targeted upregulation provided by ZLN005 offers a focused therapeutic intervention.

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and challenges remain. Foremost, the majority of the supportive evidence for ZLN005’s efficacy in protecting RPE cells has been generated through in vitro studies using cell lines such as ARPE-19. While these models are indispensable for preliminary evaluation, they do not fully recapitulate the complex in vivo environment of the human retina, and the translatability of these effects into clinical benefit remains to be demonstrated (Satish et al., 2018). Additionally, the current body of literature shows that some reports have emerged from journals of variable quality; this introduces a degree of uncertainty regarding the reproducibility of the findings and necessitates rigorous validation of these results in higher-order in vivo models and, eventually, clinical trials (Satish et al., 2018).

Another pertinent concern is the pharmacokinetic profile of ZLN005 in the ocular environment. While its favorable metabolic effects are evident in cell culture and certain systemic models, its ability to reach and maintain effective concentrations in the RPE following systemic or local administration is not well established in the available reports (Bleckwehl et al., 2025; Miller et al., 2019). In addition, the potential off-target effects of ZLN005, particularly in tissues where mitochondrial modulation may have unintended consequences, have not been fully explored. This includes the risk that enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis in non-target cells could lead to dysregulated energy metabolism or contribute to unwanted proliferative responses (Satish et al., 2018; Bleckwehl et al., 2025).

Moreover, the clinical development pathway for repurposing ZLN005 for ocular indications such as dry AMD will require comprehensive toxicological studies, detailed pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic analyses in ocular tissues, and the establishment of dosing regimens that ensure both efficacy and safety over chronic treatment periods. Given the slow progression of dry AMD and the need for long-term treatment, any adverse effects or suboptimal pharmacokinetic properties could significantly limit the compound’s clinical use (Satish et al., 2018; Iacovelli et al., 2016).

Additionally, while the activation of PGC-1α is a promising strategy for mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction, the role of PGC-1α in the retina is complex. Overexpression of PGC-1α has been linked in some studies to increased susceptibility to light-induced retinal damage or other forms of stress, suggesting that a delicate balance must be maintained to achieve therapeutic benefit without tipping the scales towards potential toxicity or dysregulation of cellular homeostasis (Iacovelli et al., 2016; Blasiak et al., 2021). This dual nature of PGC-1α activity means that careful titration of ZLN005 dosing—and possibly the development of combination therapies—may be necessary to harness its protective effects while avoiding exacerbation of retinal stress under certain conditions.

In summary, ZLN005 emerges as a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its well-characterized mechanism of stimulating PGC-1α expression, its ability to enhance mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses, and the encouraging results obtained from in vitro studies in ARPE-19 cells. Its molecular action aligns closely with the pathophysiological profiles observed in dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress contribute to RPE degeneration. However, while the preclinical evidence is robust in terms of establishing a mechanistic framework, significant challenges remain in translating these findings to an in vivo and eventually a clinical setting. Key areas that require further investigation include detailed pharmacokinetic studies in ocular models, confirmation of efficacy in animal models of dry AMD, and a full safety profile with chronic dosing regimens (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Blasiak et al., 2021; Nashine et al., 2019).

Moreover, the integration of ZLN005 with current understanding of AMD pathogenesis suggests that the compound could potentially be part of combination therapies that target several pathogenic pathways simultaneously—such as inflammation, lipid dysregulation, and complement activation—in addition to mitochondrial dysfunction. Indeed, the multifactorial nature of AMD means that a monotherapy approach may be insufficient, and ZLN005’s role could be most valuable when combined with other agents that complement its effects on mitochondrial and oxidative stress parameters (Rosales et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2025).

From a strategic drug development perspective, ZLN005 offers several attractive points for further exploration. Its synthetic origin as a benzimidazole derivative means that established methods exist for its production and modification, allowing for potential structure-activity relationship (SAR) studies aimed at enhancing its potency, selectivity, and ocular bioavailability. Such modifications could lead to derivatives with improved pharmacokinetic profiles tailored for retinal delivery. Moreover, leveraging advanced drug delivery systems, such as nanoparticle carriers or sustained-release formulations, could further enhance the therapeutic window of ZLN005 in the eye while minimizing systemic exposure and associated off-target effects (Bleckwehl et al., 2025; Miller et al., 2019).

In conclusion, the repurposing of ZLN005 for the treatment of dry AMD is supported by a compelling mechanistic rationale and a growing body of preclinical evidence that underscores its potential to restore mitochondrial dynamics and counteract oxidative stress in retinal pigment epithelial cells. The strengths of this candidate include its specificity for PGC-1α activation, its demonstrated ability to enhance mitochondrial function and energy metabolism, and its protective effects against oxidative injury in vitro. On the other hand, the limitations primarily stem from the current reliance on in vitro data, the need for more rigorous in vivo validation, and uncertainties regarding its pharmacokinetic behavior in ocular tissues. Therefore, while ZLN005 stands out as a scientifically promising candidate, advancing it through the drug development pipeline will require concerted efforts to address these gaps through detailed preclinical studies, formulation optimization, and eventually, well-designed clinical trials to determine its efficacy and safety in patients with dry AMD (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Rosales et al., 2019).

Overall, the data presented through multiple independent studies provide a strong foundation for considering ZLN005 as a viable therapeutic candidate in the repurposing paradigm for dry age-related macular degeneration. With further validation and refinement, itself or an optimized derivative could potentially offer a new strategy to preserve RPE integrity and maintain visual function in AMD patients, addressing a significant unmet medical need in the realm of retinal degenerative diseases (Rosales et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2025). Continued research efforts should focus on delineating the precise molecular signatures of ZLN005’s effects in RPE cells, assessing its long-term impact on retinal morphology and function in vivo, and investigating its interactions with other signaling cascades implicated in AMD progression (Satish et al., 2018). Only through such thorough and multidisciplinary evaluations can the true therapeutic potential of ZLN005 for dry AMD be accurately determined and translated into clinical benefit.

In summary, while challenges remain in translating the promising in vitro results to clinical outcomes, the accumulated evidence suggests that ZLN005’s activation of PGC-1α represents a credible and innovative strategy to counteract the bioenergetic decline in RPE cells—a central feature in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. For these reasons, further preclinical evaluation and careful optimization of dosing and delivery are warranted to fully ascertain the viability of ZLN005 as a therapeutic option in the ongoing battle against dry age-related macular degeneration (Satish et al., 2018).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Omaveloxolone (RTA 408) is a semi-synthetic pentacyclic triterpenoid of the cyanoenone (oleanane-derived) chemical class rationally designed to activate the Keap1–Nrf2 pathway by electrophilic modification of redox-sensitive cysteine residues on Keap1, most prominently Cys151 (the key “sensor” cysteine for this chemotype) (Cuadrado et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2016). Within its class, cyanoenone triterpenoids are among the most potent small-molecule NRF2 activators known; they are sensed at KEAP1 C151 and trigger a coordinated induction of antioxidant and cytoprotective programs that normalize cellular metabolism, increase mitochondrial energy production, and reduce ROS (including mtROS), while also exerting anti-inflammatory actions that can include modulation of NF-κB signaling in cells and animal models (Cuadrado et al., 2019). Mechanistically, omaveloxolone forms a covalent adduct with KEAP1 that prevents CUL3–KEAP1–mediated ubiquitination and degradation of Nrf2, thereby allowing Nrf2 stabilization, nuclear translocation, and transcriptional activation via antioxidant response elements (AREs) (Liu et al., 2016; Cai et al., 2021; Bellezza, 2018). In human systems, omaveloxolone induces canonical Nrf2 target genes that collectively bolster mitochondrial and cytosolic antioxidant defenses, including NQO1, HO-1, SOD2, catalase, glutaredoxin-1 (Grx1), and thioredoxin-1 (Trx1) (Liu et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2021).

Discovery and translational development of omaveloxolone followed extensive preclinical work with synthetic triterpenoids showing robust induction of the phase 2 response and protection against oxidant and inflammatory stress in vitro and in vivo, and early first-in-human experience with this class (e.g., bardoxolone methyl) helped establish on-target pharmacology while also highlighting class-specific safety considerations that informed subsequent designs (e.g., exclusion of patients with incipient heart failure risk in kidney indications) (Nakagami, 2016; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic programs in nonhuman primates and humans show that oral omaveloxolone is bioavailable, exhibits dose-proportional increases in Cmax and AUC, and reaches concentrations capable of inducing Nrf2 target genes in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and multiple tissues; tissue distribution studies in cynomolgus monkeys demonstrated exposure slightly above contemporaneous plasma levels in liver, lung, and brain with measurable mRNA induction of canonical Nrf2 targets after repeat dosing (Reisman et al., 2019). In human clinical development, omaveloxolone advanced through a first-in-human oncology study, a dose-ranging Phase 2 program (MOXIe Part 1) in Friedreich ataxia (FA) with clear pharmacodynamic biomarker changes (e.g., ferritin and GGT) and dose/exposure–response relationships, and a registrational, placebo-controlled, 48-week trial (MOXIe Part 2) showing statistically significant improvement in neurological function by mFARS with an acceptable safety profile characterized principally by reversible transaminase elevations, headaches, nausea, and fatigue (Creelan et al., 2017; Lynch et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2021).

This pharmacology is intrinsically aligned with a central pathophysiologic axis in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD): cumulative oxidative stress, sustained mitochondrial dysfunction with increased mtROS, impaired mitophagy, and chronic innate/adaptive inflammation in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and neighboring tissues (Bellezza, 2018; Jarrett & Boulton, 2012). The RPE is enriched in mitochondria and relies on robust antioxidant systems to manage high ROS fluxes from phagocytosis and photo-oxidative challenges; Nrf2 is widely recognized as the “master” antioxidant transcription factor in RPE, transcriptionally controlling the expression of SODs (including mitochondrial SOD2), catalase, NQO1, HO-1, glutathione synthesis enzymes, and thiol-redox enzymes (Trx1/Grx1) (Bellezza, 2018; Lambros & Plafker, 2016; Camelo, 2025). Deficiency of Nrf2 or the mitochondrial SOD2 enzyme in mouse retina/RPE produces AMD-like phenotypes, while exogenous Nrf2 activation in ocular models protects RPE and retinal neurons from oxidative injury, reduces inflammation, and supports mitochondrial homeostasis (Lambros & Plafker, 2016; Jarrett & Boulton, 2012; Chen et al., 2023). Against this mechanistic backdrop, the specific demonstration that omaveloxolone protects primary human RPE from H₂O₂-induced injury via Nrf2—at nanomolar concentrations—by upregulating SOD2, NQO1, HO-1, catalase, Grx1 and Trx1, preserving GSH, lowering ROS, and reducing apoptosis is directly relevant to dry AMD biology (Liu et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History  
Class-wide experience. Cyanoenone triterpenoids have been deployed across multiple preclinical disease models characterized by oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammation, with consistent activation of NRF2 target genes and functional improvements in biochemical and physiologic endpoints. For example, omaveloxolone improved renal function and reduced neutrophil infiltration, apoptosis, ROS production, and oxidative injury in renal ischemia–reperfusion models in an Nrf2-dependent manner, and produced sustained neuroprotection in a rat status epilepticus model with concordant increases in tissue glutathione and ATP (Reisman et al., 2019). These effects map onto the known Nrf2 program (e.g., induction of Nqo1, Gsr, Gclc; increased glutathione) and translate to primates and humans as evidenced by PBMC/tissue gene induction and serum biomarkers (ferritin, GGT) (Reisman et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2019).

First-in-human and oncology safety. In a first-in-human trial in advanced solid tumors, once-daily oral omaveloxolone (2.5–15 mg) was rapidly absorbed (Tmax 2–4 h), exhibited dose-proportional exposure, and had estimated terminal half-lives of ∼9 h on day 1 increasing to ∼20 h by day 28; across a mean exposure of 87 days, no dose-limiting toxicities were observed, adverse events were typically mild/moderate, and increases in select Nrf2 targets were measured in PBMCs (Creelan et al., 2017). The same report and related write-up noted no dose-limiting toxicities attributable to drug, a lack of QTc prolongation, and frequent low-grade laboratory changes (e.g., alkaline phosphatase elevations, anemia) in a small cohort, with PBMC Nrf2 target-gene mRNA serving as a primary pharmacodynamic target-engagement endpoint (Creelan et al., 2017).

Friedreich ataxia (FA) clinical development. Omaveloxolone has been evaluated extensively in FA, a neurodegenerative disease with depressed Nrf2 signaling and mitochondrial dysfunction. In MOXIe Part 1 (12-week, dose-ranging 2.5–300 mg/day), exposure was dose-proportional and PD changes in serum ferritin and GGT were maximal in the 80–160 mg/day range, congruent with improved neurological mFARS scores (placebo-corrected trends) and consistent with an exposure window for maximal biological activity; at 300 mg/day, a nonmonotonic dose–response with reduced Nrf2/mitochondrial effects was observed, suggesting a mid-dose “sweet spot” (Lynch et al., 2019). In MOXIe Part 2, patients treated with 150 mg/day for 48 weeks showed statistically significant improvement in mFARS relative to placebo; safety was acceptable with transient aminotransferase elevations unaccompanied by bilirubin increases, and common adverse events included headache, nausea, and fatigue (Lynch et al., 2021). PK data compiled from FA cohorts show mean terminal half-lives of ∼15–21 h at 80–160 mg/day (supporting once-daily dosing), Cmax in a range predicted by monkey PBMC EC50s to robustly induce Nrf2 targets, and interpatient variability of ∼31–43% for AUC/Cmax (Reisman et al., 2019). Translationally, FA patient biomarkers and platelet isotopologue metabolites indicated dose-dependent modulation of Nrf2-responsive targets (e.g., ferritin, GGT; decreased CK at 80–160 mg) and specific effects on fatty-acid–linked mitochondrial metabolism (reduced ¹³C-palmitate to HMG-CoA conversions with no effect on ¹³C-glucose) (Lynch et al., 2019).

Ophthalmic development context. Within ophthalmology, omaveloxolone has entered topical/ocular clinical testing (e.g., an ophthalmic suspension evaluated for prevention of corneal endothelial cell loss and ocular inflammation post-cataract surgery), and RTA 408 lotions/creams have shown Nrf2 target-gene induction in human skin punch biopsies, demonstrating tissue-level target engagement in humans via local administration (Cheng et al., 2021; Creelan et al., 2017). Although omaveloxolone has not been tested clinically in dry AMD to date, triterpenoid Nrf2 activators (including omaveloxolone) have reproducibly protected human RPE in vitro against oxidative insults (Liu et al., 2016), and related CDDO-derived analogues (e.g., RS9) have improved retinal antioxidant gene expression and function in multiple retinal models (Liu et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2021).

Use in AMD or similar diseases. There are no published clinical studies of omaveloxolone in dry AMD; however, the drug exhibits precisely the mechanistic activities sought for RPE protection in AMD—Nrf2 activation and induction of SOD2/NQO1/HO-1, preservation of glutathione and antioxidant enzyme activities, and suppression of oxidative injury—in primary human RPE models (Liu et al., 2016). Supportive disease-proximal validation comes from a robust literature demonstrating that genetic loss of Nrf2 or SOD2 in retinal tissues produces AMD-like pathology, and that pharmacologic or genetic Nrf2 activation protects RPE and retina in models of oxidative stress, ischemia–reperfusion injury, and diabetic retinopathy (Lambros & Plafker, 2016; Jarrett & Boulton, 2012; Zhang et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
Primary target: Keap1 Cys151 and Nrf2 stabilization. Omaveloxolone engages KEAP1 through covalent modification of Cys151, which is the electro-sensitive sensor residue controlling the high-affinity ETGE “hinge” and low-affinity DLG “latch” interactions that dock NRF2 to KEAP1 for CUL3-mediated ubiquitination under basal redox states (Cai et al., 2021; Reisman et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2016). Electrophilic adduction at KEAP1 cysteines inhibits the E3 ligase function, stabilizes Nrf2, promotes Ser40 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation, and increases binding of Nrf2–Maf heterodimers to AREs, resulting in transcriptional activation of a broad network of cytoprotective genes (estimated in the hundreds) that neutralize ROS, maintain glutathione and thioredoxin pools, and reprogram metabolism toward redox homeostasis (Das & Imanishi, 2022; Cai et al., 2021; Bellezza, 2018). In primates, quantitative PK/PD modeling relating plasma concentration to PBMC mRNA induction of canonical Nrf2 targets yielded EC50s on the order of tens of ng/mL, permitting translational projection of human exposures likely to achieve robust target engagement; observed FA patient Cmax values at 80–160–300 mg overlapped these EC50 ranges, and tissue distribution studies documented meaningful drug levels in liver, lung, and brain with dose-dependent mRNA induction in those tissues (Reisman et al., 2019).

Downstream antioxidant and mitochondrial programs in RPE. In primary human RPE, nanomolar omaveloxolone activated Nrf2 and increased expression and activity of multiple downstream antioxidant enzymes: HO-1 (heme catabolism; biliverdin/bilirubin production), NQO1 (two-electron reductase that supports NADPH-dependent detoxification), SOD2 (mitochondrial matrix superoxide dismutase), catalase (peroxisomal H₂O₂ scavenger), Grx1 and Trx1 (thiol-disulfide oxidoreductases for protein deglutathionylation/disulfide reduction) (Liu et al., 2016). Functionally, omaveloxolone preserved intracellular GSH under oxidative challenge, attenuated GSSG accumulation and protein glutathionylation, and restored enzyme activity of NQO1, Grx1, and Trx1 following H₂O₂ exposure (Liu et al., 2016). By lowering net ROS and preventing depletion/inactivation of thiol-redox systems, omaveloxolone reduced Bax activation and caspase-3 cleavage while increasing Bcl-2, leading to protection against apoptosis and necrosis in RPE; Nrf2 siRNA abrogated these effects, establishing on-target dependence (Liu et al., 2016).

Inflammation and NF-κB/NOS axes. Triterpenoid NRF2 activators can also influence inflammatory signaling. Omaveloxolone suppressed interferon-γ–mediated nitric oxide signaling in macrophages at nanomolar concentrations and reduced nitrotyrosine production in myeloid-derived suppressor cells and tumor xenografts, pointing to a mechanism that diminishes RNS/ROS-coupled inflammatory tone (Creelan et al., 2017). More broadly, Nrf2 activation antagonizes inflammation by mitigating ROS-dependent NLRP3 inflammasome activation and by competing with NF-κB for limiting transcriptional co-activators (e.g., CBP/p300), ultimately blunting IL-6 and IL-1β transcription; in the triterpenoid class, agents have been shown to modulate both NRF2 and NF-κB in cells and models (Camelo, 2025; Cuadrado et al., 2019). Although direct inhibition of NF-κB by omaveloxolone in human RPE has not been explicitly demonstrated in the provided sources, multiple reviews and trial descriptions describe omaveloxolone as reducing inflammatory mediators (e.g., TNF-α, IL-6) and blocking KEAP1-mediated NF-κB proinflammatory signaling, consistent with the hypothesized dual-action (Clay et al., 2019; Madsen et al., 2020).

Mitochondrial function and disease-relevant cells. In FA-relevant neuronal and fibroblast systems, omaveloxolone restored mitochondrial OXPHOS complex readouts, reduced mitochondrial ROS, prevented lipid peroxidation, increased cellular glutathione, and elevated Nrf2 transcript/protein with increased NQO1, HO-1, and GCL expression at low nanomolar concentrations, indicating a direct link from KEAP1–NRF2 engagement to improved mitochondrial redox and bioenergetic parameters (Tiberi et al., 2023). Platelet isotopologue analyses in FA patients showed reduced conversion of ¹³C-palmitate to HMG-CoA with increasing omaveloxolone dose and no effect on ¹³C-glucose metabolism, consistent with modulation of fatty-acid–linked mitochondrial metabolism by Nrf2 activation in human tissues (Lynch et al., 2019).

Pharmacokinetics, target engagement, and dose–response. Human oral PK shows rapid absorption (Tmax ≈ 1–3.5 h), dose-proportional exposure, and an apparent terminal half-life of ∼15–21 h at 80–160 mg supporting once-daily administration; in the oncology first-in-human trial Tmax was 2–4 h with terminal half-life ranging from ∼9–20 h between day 1 and day 28, consistent with accumulation to steady state across 28-day cycles (Reisman et al., 2019; Creelan et al., 2017). Monotonicity in Nrf2/mitochondrial biomarker response appears dose-limited at very high exposure; in FA, 300 mg/day fell into a concentration range where reduced Nrf2 induction and mitochondrial function were observed in vitro and clinical PD/functional signals were attenuated relative to 80–160 mg (Lynch et al., 2019). Translational PK/PD alignment from primate PBMC EC50s predicts robust induction of canonical Nrf2 targets at human Cmax achieved with ≥ 80 mg dosing, which is consistent with the observed FA biomarker changes and clinical signals in the mid-dose range (Reisman et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2019).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level expectations in RPE oxidative stress models. The candidate’s cell-autonomous RPE mechanism predicts that, in primary human RPE or iPSC-RPE assays challenged with oxidants (e.g., H₂O₂, t-BHP, photo-oxidative blue light models), omaveloxolone pretreatment at low nanomolar concentrations will:  
- Increase Nrf2 nuclear translocation and upregulate canonical ARE-driven targets including SOD2, NQO1, HO-1, catalase, Grx1, and Trx1, as measured by mRNA, protein, and enzyme activity assays (Liu et al., 2016).  
- Preserve cellular thiol redox status by elevating intracellular GSH, reducing GSSG accumulation, and decreasing protein glutathionylation under oxidative challenge (Liu et al., 2016).  
- Reduce total and mitochondrial ROS burden (by virtue of increased SOD2 and augmented detoxifying capacity), attenuate lipid peroxidation, and maintain activity of antioxidant enzymes otherwise suppressed by oxidant exposure (NQO1, Grx1, Trx1) (Liu et al., 2016).  
- Decrease apoptosis/necrosis readouts (Annexin V/PI, caspase-3 cleavage), with shifts in Bax/Bcl-2 consistent with anti-apoptotic signaling downstream of restored redox homeostasis (Liu et al., 2016).

The RPE expresses all of the above antioxidant effectors (SOD2, NQO1, HO-1, catalase, Grx1, Trx1), and their induction by omaveloxolone has been demonstrated in primary human RPE, making these robust PD endpoints for in vitro validation and mechanistic confirmation of the compound in the exact cell type relevant to dry AMD (Liu et al., 2016). Given compelling preclinical evidence in FA models, we further expect improved mitochondrial bioenergetics (Δψm preservation/OXPHOS complex integrity) and reduced mtROS in RPE with omaveloxolone, although direct Δψm measurements have not been published in RPE for this compound; these endpoints are supported by neuronal/fibroblast data and are mechanistically consistent with Nrf2-driven SOD2/antioxidant induction (Tiberi et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2016).

Inflammation-modulating effects in RPE and retinal milieu. In RPE cultures or co-cultures exposed to pro-inflammatory cytokines or oxidative adducts (e.g., 4-HNE, MDA, CEP), omaveloxolone is expected to reduce ROS-augmented NF-κB–dependent cytokine transcription indirectly via rebalancing redox tone and directly via the triterpenoid class’s interference with NF-κB axes (competition for transcriptional cofactors and proposed KEAP1-linked NF-κB modulation), with measurable decreases in IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α transcription and nitrosative stress markers in settings where these are ROS-coupled (Camelo, 2025; Clay et al., 2019; Madsen et al., 2020; Creelan et al., 2017). In macrophage or microglia co-culture systems, decreased nitrotyrosine and nitric oxide synthase output would be anticipated, consistent with suppression of interferon-γ–driven NO signaling observed at low concentrations (Creelan et al., 2017). These effects target a recognized feed-forward loop in dry AMD in which oxidative damage and inflammatory signaling reciprocally amplify RPE injury (Bellezza, 2018; Camelo, 2025).

In vivo translational expectations and biomarker strategy. For systemic administration, PBMC Nrf2 target mRNA induction has been validated as a sensitive peripheral biomarker for omaveloxolone in primates and humans and should be incorporated as a noninvasive PD readout, with serum ferritin and GGT as additional systemic markers of Nrf2 activation shown to respond in the 80–160 mg range (Reisman et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2019). Tissue-level target engagement in the eye could be assessed in early clinical studies by surrogate accessible tissues (e.g., skin punch biopsy Nrf2 target induction following topical administration as precedent), tears or conjunctival impression cytology for transcript biomarkers, and functional retinal endpoints; preclinical monkey data showing dose-dependent induction of Nrf2 targets in liver/lung/brain establish that tissue-level engagement is achievable, though ocular distribution has not been reported and remains a data gap (Reisman et al., 2019; Creelan et al., 2017). For local ocular delivery, existing clinical experience with RTA 408 ophthalmic preparations and demonstrated Nrf2 target-gene induction in human skin biopsies support feasibility of achieving tissue PD in the eye without systemic exposure (Cheng et al., 2021; Creelan et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic precision for AMD biology. The omaveloxolone mechanism—KEAP1 Cys151 modification → Nrf2 stabilization and ARE-driven transcription—directly addresses core deficits in dry AMD: inadequate antioxidant/mitochondrial defenses and redox-driven inflammation in RPE. Upregulation of SOD2, NQO1, HO-1, catalase, and thiol-redox systems in primary human RPE cells has been demonstrated for omaveloxolone at nanomolar potency with rigorous Nrf2-dependence, and these are precisely the enzymes/activities required to reduce mtROS and protect the high-demand RPE from oxidative apoptosis/necrosis (Liu et al., 2016; Bellezza, 2018; Camelo, 2025).  
- Human translational pharmacology. Oral PK is favorable for chronic dosing (once-daily half-life ∼15–21 h at efficacious exposures), with dose-proportional exposure and well-established PD biomarkers (PBMC Nrf2 transcripts; serum ferritin/GGT) that map to mid-dose ranges yielding clinical signals in FA; primate PK/PD modeling provides concentration–effect relationships for Nrf2 targets that align with human Cmax at 80–160 mg (Reisman et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2019).  
- Tissue distribution and target engagement in vivo. In cynomolgus monkeys, omaveloxolone distributed to major organs, with tissue drug levels at or above plasma and induction of canonical Nrf2 targets in liver and lung; dose-related trends were present in brain, suggesting CNS permeability and supporting the premise of tissue-level engagement beyond blood in primates (Reisman et al., 2019). Topical formulations (RTA 408 lotion/ophthalmic suspension) have induced Nrf2 targets in human skin and advanced into ocular clinical studies, de-risking local ocular delivery modalities for future AMD programs (Creelan et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2021).  
- Clinical proof of mechanism and safety in a mitochondrial disease. In FA, omaveloxolone produced consistent PD biomarker activation (ferritin↑, GGT changes; CK↓ at 80–160 mg), functional improvement (mFARS benefit at 150–160 mg), and tolerability suitable for long-term administration (48 weeks), with reversible transaminase elevations as the principal laboratory signal; importantly, 300 mg exposures showed attenuated biologic responses, informing an exposure window for maximal effect (Lynch et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2021).  
- Anti-inflammatory potential that intersects AMD pathophysiology. Nrf2 activation reduces ROS-dependent inflammasome activation and competes with NF-κB for co-activators; omaveloxolone and its class decrease nitrosative stress signaling and inflammatory mediators in immune cells and models, a mechanistic complement to antioxidant effects in RPE that is germane to dry AMD’s chronic para-inflammation (Camelo, 2025; Creelan et al., 2017; Clay et al., 2019; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

Limitations and risks  
- Absence of ocular pharmacokinetics and retinal tissue PD. No data currently demonstrate omaveloxolone exposure in retina/RPE after systemic dosing or local ophthalmic administration in humans; primate tissue distribution did not include ocular tissues in the reported studies, and brain induction was less robust than peripheral organs, raising questions about effective exposure in ocular compartments with systemic dosing (Reisman et al., 2019). While RTA 408 ophthalmic formulations have entered clinical testing, target engagement in human ocular tissues has not been published (Cheng et al., 2021).  
- Clinical evidence gap in AMD. There are no clinical data in dry AMD populations; pathophysiologic rationale is strong, but translation from FA and preclinical RPE models requires careful dose/exposure selection, PD verification in ocular tissues, and demonstration of structural/functional benefit (e.g., slowing GA growth), none of which are available to date in the provided corpus (Lynch et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2016).  
- Nonmonotonic dose–response at high exposure. FA data indicate that very high exposures (e.g., 300 mg/day) can reduce Nrf2 induction/mitochondrial effects, implying a therapeutic window that must be honored to avoid loss of efficacy or off-target effects; AMD trials will need to target mid-dose ranges (80–160 mg) or use local ocular delivery to minimize systemic exposure while maximizing ocular PD (Lynch et al., 2019).  
- Safety nuances in an elderly population. Although omaveloxolone has an acceptable safety profile in FA and oncology settings (no DLTs up to 15 mg in oncology; reversible ALT/AST elevations in FA), dry AMD patients are older with comorbidities; the triterpenoid class has historical cardiovascular risk signals (bardoxolone methyl in CKD), mandating conservative exclusion criteria and vigilant monitoring, particularly if systemic dosing is pursued (Creelan et al., 2017; Cuadrado et al., 2019).  
- Inflammatory pathway claims in RPE remain inferential. While Nrf2 activation is anti-inflammatory, and omaveloxolone suppresses NO/iNOS/nitrotyrosine signaling in myeloid cells, direct evidence of NF-κB pathway repression by omaveloxolone in human RPE is not established in the cited literature; anti-inflammatory benefits in retinal tissues should be verified in appropriate assays (Creelan et al., 2017; Clay et al., 2019; Madsen et al., 2020).

Programmatic recommendations  
- Preclinical ocular PK/PD. Define ocular exposure and tissue PD after systemic and topical dosing in relevant species. For systemic dosing, quantify omaveloxolone in choroid/RPE/retina and assay canonical Nrf2 targets (Nqo1, Hmox1, Srxn1, Txnrd1, Gsr) to confirm dose-dependent tissue engagement; for topical dosing, leverage the human skin precedent (punch biopsy Nrf2 induction) to design ocular surface/conjunctival PD sampling in early clinical studies (Reisman et al., 2019; Creelan et al., 2017).  
- RPE-centric PD biomarker panel. In vitro and ex vivo human RPE studies should be used to finalize a PD panel including SOD2, NQO1, HO-1, catalase, Grx1, Trx1 mRNA/protein/activity, GSH/GSSG ratios, protein glutathionylation, and apoptosis markers, all of which were responsive to omaveloxolone in primary human RPE (Liu et al., 2016).  
- Dose selection anchored to translational PK/PD. For systemic programs, target exposures corresponding to primate PBMC EC50s and FA mid-dose ranges (80–160 mg) that maximize Nrf2 target induction while avoiding the high-exposure attenuation seen at 300 mg; in early AMD studies, incorporate PBMC Nrf2 gene induction, serum ferritin/GGT, and potentially CK as systemic PD anchors (Reisman et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2019).  
- Anti-inflammatory endpoints. In RPE and myeloid co-cultures, quantify NF-κB–dependent cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and nitrosative stress readouts (iNOS, nitrotyrosine) under oxidative/cytokine challenge with omaveloxolone to confirm expected anti-inflammatory effects; these are relevant given RNS/ROS-driven inflammation in AMD (Creelan et al., 2017; Camelo, 2025).  
- Clinical path. Consider a two-pronged strategy: (i) a topical ocular formulation to deliver drug to RPE/retina with minimal systemic exposure, justified by human skin PD activation and existing ocular formulation experience; (ii) a systemic oral approach with rigorous safety surveillance and mid-dose targeting, using PBMC/serum PD to confirm target engagement while ocular PD is established with surrogate sampling and imaging endpoints. The topical path may be particularly attractive to de-risk systemic safety in an elderly AMD population (Cheng et al., 2021; Creelan et al., 2017; Lynch et al., 2021).

Conclusion  
The totality of mechanistic, cellular, primate, and human clinical pharmacology evidence indicates that omaveloxolone’s core pharmacology—potent Nrf2 activation via KEAP1 Cys151 engagement, coupled with class-associated anti-inflammatory actions—maps directly onto the pathobiology of dry AMD. In primary human RPE, omaveloxolone at nanomolar concentrations induces mitochondrial and cytosolic antioxidant systems (SOD2, NQO1, HO-1, catalase, Grx1, Trx1), preserves GSH and redox enzyme activities, lowers ROS, and prevents apoptosis in an Nrf2-dependent manner, establishing precise on-target activity in the cell type central to AMD (Liu et al., 2016). Clinical development in FA demonstrates that systemic exposures can be achieved safely with pharmacodynamic target engagement (ferritin/GGT; PBMC markers) and functional benefit at mid-range doses (80–160 mg), while primate PK/PD work provides quantitative translational alignment for dose selection (Lynch et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2021; Reisman et al., 2019). The principal gaps for an AMD program are ocular distribution/PD after systemic dosing, absence of clinical AMD data, and the need to validate anti-inflammatory effects in retinal contexts; each is addressable through staged preclinical and early clinical studies, with topical delivery representing an attractive route to maximize ocular exposure and minimize systemic liability (Reisman et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2021; Creelan et al., 2017).

On balance, omaveloxolone is a strong mechanistic candidate for dry AMD: it targets the validated Nrf2 axis in RPE with demonstrated induction of SOD2/NQO1/HO-1 and thiol-redox defenses, supports mitochondrial antioxidant capacity, and carries human translational PK/PD tools to manage dose/exposure windows. Careful attention to dose selection (avoid very high exposures that attenuate desired biology), route of administration, and ocular PD verification will be critical to realizing its potential in AMD (Liu et al., 2016; Reisman et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2019; Lynch et al., 2021).

Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a well‐characterized NAD⁺ precursor with extensive preclinical and clinical safety data. NR provides a broader mechanistic approach, more direct retinal evidence, and a robust safety and clinical database, whereas MitoQ needs formulation development and disease-relevant validation.
